Place of Publication: India Title:
Yogavāsiṣṭhaḥ (The Yoga of Vasiṣṭha)
The Yoga-Vāsiṣṭha of Vālmīki
The Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa, together with its commentary titled Tātparyaprakāśa.
Edited by Vāsudeva Śarman, the son of Lakṣmaṇa Śarman Paṇaśīkara.
The second volume,
comprising both the first and second halves of the final chapter on Nirvāṇa,
contains the *Nirvāṇa-pūrvārdha* and the *Nirvāṇa-uttarārdha*.
The Śrī Yogavāsiṣṭha,
accompanied by the commentary titled Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa.
The First Canto, the First Half of the Section on Nirvana. 1.
Śrī Vālmīki said:
Immediately following the section on tranquility, listen to this section on Nirvana, which, when understood, bestows Nirvana. (1)

I praise the reality of the Self, which is auspicious, fearless, without beginning, middle, or end; whose essence is supreme bliss and non-dual consciousness alone; in whom all fluctuations have ceased; who is pure, and who shines by its own innate splendor. (1)

By means of the three chapters known as Origination, Persistence, and Quiescence, [this work] serves to elucidate the reality of the Self through the method of superimposition and negation (*adhyāropa-apavāda*), thereby explaining the Vedānta passages that reveal the birth, persistence, and dissolution of the world— such as "Then, therefore, the instruction: not this, not this"— as well as those that negate the entire phenomenal expansion.

It has been shown that the ultimate aim culminates in the supreme human goal through knowledge extending to the exhaustion of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and the dissolution of the mind (*manonāśa*). Now, [the text proceeds to describe] that which is the "plenum" (*bhūmā*): "where one sees nothing else, hears nothing else, and understands nothing else—that is the plenum; what is the plenum, that is bliss"; and "from whence words turn back, together with the mind, having failed to reach the bliss of Brahman."
The wise man fears nothing whatsoever. This very Brahman is without prior, without posterior, without interior, and without exterior;

this Self is Brahman, the perceiver of all. It is partless, actionless, peaceful, irreproachable, and stainless—the supreme bridge to immortality, like a fire whose fuel has been consumed. Such is the meaning established by the intent of the scriptures, beginning with these words.

In order to explain Nirvāṇa— the fruit which is the direct realization of all that is to be accomplished through the previously mentioned means— and to cause this chapter titled "Nirvāṇa" to be heard, the Blessed Śrī Vālmīki said:
"The daily practice of the listeners arises here from the words of the sage."
The passing of the night is prescribed through the study of sacred texts, reflection on their meaning, and sleep. || 1 ||
Therein, first indicating the logical connection (*hetutā-saṃgati*) between the preceding and following sections, he promises what is to be said:

"O dear one, by means of the illustrations of clay, iron, sparks, and so forth, and according to the principle shown in the Śruti—'Modification is a mere verbal handle, a name; the three forms alone are real'—by means of food..."

"Seek the root of water through its shoot, my dear; seek the root of fire through its shoot, my dear; seek the root of Being through its shoot, my dear. All these creatures, my dear, have Being as their root, Being as their abode, and Being as their support. That which is this subtle essence—this whole world has that as its self; that is the Truth, that is the Self."

Immediately following the three chapters dedicated to establishing that the ultimate purport of the Vedas culminates in the non-dual nature of the Self (*aikātmya*), there follows [the teaching of] "That thou art, O Śvetaketu," which possesses as its fruit the essential definition (*svarūpa-lakṣaṇa*) revealed by such scriptural passages as "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite," "Brahman is Eternal Consciousness and Bliss," and "He understood that Bliss is Brahman."

The meaning is: "Listen to this section called *Nirvāṇa*, because it explains both the meaning of the great sayings (*mahāvākya*) such as 'This Self is Brahman, the experiencer of all,' and the nature of *nirvāṇa* which is the fruit of that realization. (1)
While the leader of sages spoke these unrestrained words,
the prince remained established in silence, his sole delight being the act of listening.

Intending to describe the very subject already promised by relying on the narrative at hand, he speaks of what occurred in the assembly of Daśaratha at the conclusion of the instructions in the Chapter on Quiescence (Upaśama-prakaraṇa)—this is the connection with the sixteenth [chapter]. [The scene was] when the leader of sages, Vasiṣṭha, [was present], and the prince Rāma [was there]. (2)
The assembly of kings stood motionless, as if depicted in a painting, their minds fixed on the meaning of the sage’s words and their ritual observances suspended.

He had abandoned the eight [limbs of yoga], as well as mental austerity, the observation of external objects, ritual action, and bodily movement. He did so by reflecting on the meaning of Vasiṣṭha’s words with reverence,
while his eyebrows quivered and his fingers twitched in a rhythmic motion toward the assembly of sages.
With the gesture of raising and threatening with a finger by snapping the fingers; while her eyebrows were quivering— that is to say, with a knitting of the brows—
the group of matrons, their eyes like bees blossoming with the joy of a gaze of wonder,
attained the state of being like a cluster of flowers on a deep tree.

Wonder, which is of the nature of supreme marvel, is the inner self (pratyagātman); through the radiance of beholding that [self], it has attained a state like that of a tree-cluster whose blossoms are deep with nectar, and which, because of that nectar, is free from clinging bees and devoid of any sound. || 5 ||
When the sun was situated in the fourth part of the day, and the gentle moon had attained a slight tranquility through the dawning of some knowledge; || 6 ||

In that region and place where only the fourth part of the day remained visible, she stood as if to listen; therefore, the connection [of the verse] is drawn from what follows: "as if some dawning of knowledge had occurred," "gentle and pleasing to the sight," and "as if having attained some alleviation of her distress. (6)
While the wind, which bestows the sweet fragrance of the Mandāra flowers, was hushed as if listening and adorned with the gentle swaying of the canopy, there was silence. (7)

The phrase "becoming tranquil upon hearing" (śravaṇāyeva saṃśānte) is connected also with the word "wind" (maruti) by way of the "lamp on the threshold" (dehalī-dīpa) maxim. [The wind] is garlanded by the swaying of a canopy of flowers; therefore, it bestows the sweet fragrance of the Mandāra tree. || 7 ||
The rows of great bees were fast asleep upon the flower-garlands,
as if they were truly possessed of perfect meditation because they had known all that is to be known.
Within the inner chambers enclosed by clusters of pearl lattices,
the water shimmers without movement, as if it has come to a standstill to listen.
Within the interior grounds— the middle regions of the ponds— of the pearl-lattices that serve as enclosures for the ponds,
it shines motionless and free from vibration, as if standing in eager anticipation to hear.
While it was shining with the radiance of pearls and other gems. || 9 ||
When the rays of light had entered deep into the windows of the houses,
the cool air, like travelers in the sky seeking rest, remained for no long time.

When the rays of the sun had entered the interior of the house—which was cool compared to the sunbeams—as if for the sake of rest; and when the travelers in the sky, both by space and by time, had become weary from their long journey through the vast expanse—meaning they were exhausted from wandering over great distances for a long time. (10)
The heat of the day, as the body of the sun-god grew tranquil, seemed to proclaim peace itself, its own self dusted with the ash-like radiance of a lattice of pearls.

As the day, having become the very body [of the sun], was subsiding— its self being sprinkled with the ashes characterized by the mass of light from the clusters of pearls [the clouds], and as the sunlight, possessing the characteristics of an ascetic, entered within it— it seemed to praise, or rather to indicate, the quality of tranquility (śama) in its own self. || 11 ||
They were held in his hands like playful lotuses, and upon the crests of the mountains as if they were their crowns,
while their minds— having heard [the sound]— were drawn away from their natural state by its divine fragrance.
While the lotuses of sport rested upon the hands and crowns— the heads— of the mountain-like kings,

and while their minds, like those [lotuses], were on the verge of closing due to the absence of mental fluctuations (avṛtti) arising from the joy produced by hearing the delightful instruction of Vasiṣṭha, which possessed a beautiful essence; || 12 ||
He was constantly and respectfully urging the womenfolk to provide food for the children, the ignorant people, and the pet birds.
"Among the playful birds," such as parrots and others kept in cages, "who were obstructing [him]," meaning those who were urging him on. || 13 ||
The dust was thoroughly shaken away by the breeze arising from the wings of wandering bees;
the moonlight was fully diffused, and the eyelashes were at rest like whisks.

In the month of Kaumuda, when the dust raised by the breezes from the wings of wandering bees—connected with the white water-lilies (*kumuda*) that were about to slightly blossom—had settled everywhere upon the fly-whisks and the eyelashes; || 14 ||
As if out of fear of the mass of shadows released from the mountain caves, the rays of light flew up through the windows and other openings and entered the interior of the house.

As if out of fear of the mass of shadows released from the caves of Mount Meru and other mountains by the rays of the sun, the darkness has taken flight and fled, entering the interior of houses through windows and other openings to take refuge within them. || 15 ||
A sound from kettledrums, tabors, and conchs, filling the quarters of the sky, arose, intent on making known the existence of the fourth part of the day.
The existence of the fourth part of the day remains; he is intent upon making that known. || 16 ||
Because of that, even his loud voice quickly vanished, just as the cry of a peacock ceases at the roar of a thundercloud. (17)
Resounding even above that, this silence of the Sage—this word of Vasiṣṭha—vanished from sight. || 17 ||
The row of birds staying in their cage, with their wings agitated, was undisturbed [in its place],
like a forest range whose palm fronds were violently shaken during an earthquake.
"Quickly" means with speed [the reading "with strength" is also found], that is to say, she became agitated and trembled;
like a row of forests whose palm leaves are shaken by the wind. || 18 ||
Terrified by fear, the children fled into the space between their nurses' breasts with cries,
like clouds in the rainy season entering the hollows of lofty mountain peaks.
It was "sāravaṃ," meaning accompanied by the sound of weeping, just like the hollow between two horns. || 19 ||
From the crest-ornaments of the kings, garlands of bees flew forth,
like droplets of water from rivers whose currents are slightly turbulent.
"From those whose flow—meaning their current—is slightly fierce or agitated. The simile of water droplets is used to illustrate the whiteness of the pollen of the bees. || 20 ||
Thus, while that house of the son of Daśaratha was agitated at that time,
the day drew toward its end as the sound of the conch shells gradually subsided.
When the day had grown old and the fourth stage of life had been reached. || 21 ||
Withdrawing his discourse on the subject at hand, that tiger among sages spoke in sweet and rhythmic words to the scion of Raghu in the midst of the assembly.
Concluding the subject matter at hand, he summarizes the meaning to be expressed. || 22 ||
O sinless Raghava, this web of words has been spread out by me;
having bound the bird of the mind with it, take it into your embrace and lead it to the state of the Self.
"Having embraced" means having restrained [it] within the heart. || 23 ||
I hope you have grasped the meaning of my words in this way—having abandoned what is difficult to understand, like a swan extracting milk from water. (24)

The meaning of my words is inexhaustible and imperishable. [The phrase] "by the swan from the water" uses the ablative case (*pañcamī*) with the elision of the suffix *lyap*, meaning "having abandoned the water. 24.
Having reflected upon this in its entirety with your own intellect again and again, O virtuous one, you must now proceed by this very path. (25)
By this path of the practice of knowledge, the destruction of latent impressions, the dissolution of the mind, and the restraint of the vital breaths. || 25 ||
O Rāma, by sporting with this very intellect, you will not be bound;
otherwise, you will quickly fall downward, like an elephant into a pit in the Vindhya mountains.
O Rāma, if you do not act upon my words which have been well-grasped by your intellect,
then you will fall like a blind man who has cast away his lamp in the nights.
Just as a blind man or one who has abandoned his lamp falls into a pit or a hole, so it is in that case. || 27 ||

"May his worldly activity proceed without attachment, exactly as it has been attained, for the sake of his success"—taking this very established conclusion of the scriptures to heart, be noble-minded. (28)

The meaning is: for the sake of establishing the truth spoken by the Self, one should act with non-attachment according to the conduct as it has been attained; thus, having taken to heart and reflected upon this conclusion which is the ultimate purport of all scriptures, one should become "udāravān"—that is, possessed of the realization of the unlimited Self. || 28 ||
O members of the assembly, O Great King, and you, Lords of the Earth, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa—
all of you, for now, attend to your daily duties.
For this day is mostly spent in its state of transformation;
we shall deliberate upon what remains once we have returned in the morning to consider it.
Having arrived for the assembly tomorrow morning; the suffix *kta* is used here in the sense of the future, according to the rule "the suffixes [denoting tense] are attached to the verbal root."
Śrī Vālmīki said:
Having been addressed thus by that sage, the entire assembly,
with their lotus-like faces, then rose up like a blooming lotus pond.
Thus she was addressed and commanded; she whose faces were like lotuses, indeed, were truly lotuses. || 31 ||
The kings, having praised the king and performed their salutations to Rāghava,
departed for their own dwellings once Vasiṣṭha had been fully honored.
Those by whom King Daśaratha was praised were "stuta-rājānaḥ"; this occurred when Vasiṣṭha had been praised by all, having been saluted and extolled. || 32 ||
Accompanied by Viśvāmitra, the illustrious Vasiṣṭha, to whom the sky-dwellers had offered salutations, rose from his seat and addressed the sage with these words.
By whom the gods who move through the sky have been paid homage. || 33 ||
Daśaratha and the other kings, as well as the Guṇas,
followed the sage for a long time, addressing him with words appropriate to each.
Having followed for a long time the speaker and instructor to the edge of the hermitage. || 34 ||
Having taken their leave, some went to the sky, some to the interior of the forest,
and some to Rājagṛha— those virtuous ones, like bees rising from a lotus.
Having followed for a long time the speaker and instructor to the edge of the hermitage. || 35 ||
Having offered a pure handful of flowers at the feet of Vasiṣṭha,
the king, followed by his wives, entered the interior of the house.
Untroubled and stainless. || 36 ||
Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, and Śatrughna, having arrived at their preceptor’s hermitage,
reverently worshipped his feet with devotion and then returned to the royal palace.
Untroubled and stainless. || 37 ||
Having reached their respective dwellings, all those listeners approached and worshipped the gods, the Brahmins, and likewise the ancestors, together with the asuras.

They worshipped the gods and the ancestors; they went toward the brahmins and guests—that is, they approached them face-to-face. The meaning is that they made them their own through acts such as visiting them for the sake of honoring them. However, if the reading is *abhyetuḥ*, it should be construed thus: "Among the group of guests who had arrived, they worshipped the brahmins. || 38 ||
In due order, they partook of the food prescribed by the sequence of the duties of their respective castes, together with their own servants and their retinues consisting of Brahmins and others. (39)
He spoke with his attendants and retinues. || 39 ||
When the sun had set along with the activities of the day, and the maker of night had arrived together with the activities of the night. (40)
Having remained upon couches, silken beds, and seats, the kings who were lords of sages and the great seers who move upon the earth [departed]. 41.
With single-minded focus and great reverence, they reflected exactly as it was taught by Vasiṣṭha upon the means for crossing over saṃsāra. (42)
Then, after only a single watch had passed, their faces sealed by sleep,
they approached the beauties of their dreams, like lotuses longing for the day.
Because it indicates future auspiciousness through excellent dreams, [it describes Sundarī as] beautiful and delightful. And thus the Śruti says:
"Now, when one thinks, 'As a god, as a king, indeed I am all this,' that is his supreme world.
This shows that the vision of universal selfhood in a dream indicates the fruit of future liberation for those who desire the day [of awakening].
This means that they are steps leading to the transcendence of sovereignty. || 43 ||
For three watches of the night, Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa,
and Śatrughna contemplated that unimpaired instruction of Vasiṣṭha.
Then, for half a watch, with their eyes closed,
they fell into a sleep that dispelled their fatigue in an instant— a sleep like a pleasant dream.

Thus, for those of pure mind who possessed discernment and whose aspirations were elevated by having attained the essence [of the teaching], the night then reached its end; the moon, like their own faces, assumed a darkened appearance.

For Rāma and the others, whose expansive disposition had arisen through the awakening to the reality of the Self by virtue of having attained its essence, the three-watch night reached its cessation. Consequently, it assumed the state of being one whose face is the moon, which had become dim due to the pervasion of the rays of the dawn. || 46 ||

Thus ends the first canto, titled "Description of Daily Conduct," in the first half of the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa* within the *Mokṣopāya* section of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by the sage Vālmīki, as spoken by the Divine Messenger. || 1 ||
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "Description of Daily Activities," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The Second Canto.
Śrī Vālmīki said:
Then, her moon-like face was drenched with tears, and her steps were utterly unsteady.
As she waned, the dark-complexioned woman shone like the latent impressions (vāsanā) of discernment (viveka).
In this context, the repose in reality through the recollection of the meaning previously stated by Rāma and others to Vasiṣṭha in the morning is described.
Her face was wet and withered like the moon; wasting away, she was on the verge of death. || 1 ||
When the eastern mountain was seen as light because it had been destroyed [by darkness],
the mass of heat assumed the appearance of a crest-jewel upon the western mountain.

Then, as the sun— the dispeller of darkness and the burner with its rays— emerged and was beheld by people facing the east upon the eastern mountain, the serpents, their movement obstructed and suppressed by the mountain’s jagged peaks,
stretched out their hoods toward the light emerging from those various interstices; yet that light was merely false and illusorily imagined.

An *avataṃsa* is an ornament for the head such as a crown; the analysis of the compound is that it "bore a light having that appearance," with the members of the compound being separated and construed accordingly.
Drawing in particles of frost, having touched the orb of the moon,
and appearing as if its very light were swallowing the moonlight, the morning breeze shone forth.

This is a poetic expression based on the superimposition of the status of the sun's eye upon the solar light, which is like the spreading of the eye’s gaze for the purpose of devouring the moonbeams. By this, the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) that he is "as if afflicted by hunger and thirst" is implied. || 3 ||
Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, and Śatrughna, having risen with their attendants and performed their twilight devotions, went to the holy hermitage of Vasiṣṭha.

Since those who have not bathed lack the qualification for hearing [the scripture], they have bathed and performed their twilight devotions (saṃdhyā); the same applies in the following cases as well. || 4 ||
There, even though the sage had already performed his twilight devotions and had departed from the palace, they prostrated at his feet, offering a continuous stream of water for honor.
Of one who has gone out or is about to go out. || 5 ||
In an instant, that palace— previously silent with sages, brahmins, and kings, as well as elephants, horses, chariots, and vehicles— gradually became densely crowded.
The state of being without interstices, the state of being without space. || 6 ||
Then that tiger among sages, followed by Rāma and the others, went at the proper time to the house of Daśaratha together with that very army.
There, the king, having performed his twilight devotions and traveled a long distance, honored him with great respect, mindful of their former connection.
King Daśaratha was one whose zeal for speed was such that he would "bind" or "unite" [his horses] even before entering the house; thus he is described as *pūrvasambandhatvarotsāha*. (8)
Having entered the assembly hall, which was further and exceedingly adorned with clusters of flowers, pearls, and jewels, they all took their seats upon the rows of thrones.

In the phrase *viṣṭarāliṣu*, it refers to rows of seats; the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* occurs according to the rule: "The word *viṣṭara* [is used] for a seat made of grass or a wooden seat. (Pāṇini 8.3.93). || 9 ||
Then, at that moment, all those listeners from the previous day— both those who travel through the sky and those who move upon the earth— arrived together.
Those occurring on the day before yesterday are called *hyastanāḥ*. || 10 ||
Having offered mutual salutations, she entered that gentle assembly;
filled with the presence of kings, it shone like a lotus pond when the wind has subsided. (11)
The meaning is that her posture and physical bearing were identical to those of the king; seeing the king with his speech and bodily movements restrained, everyone else also became so. || 11 ||
When those brahmin-sages, royal sages, and ascetics had quickly settled according to their respective places and at their ease, each in his appropriate location, [the Lord spoke].
When those belonging to the Brahmin and other castes had entered the assembly hall and were seated according to their respective places, following the daily established order of positions. || 12 ||
When the soft sound of "welcome" had gradually subsided, and the bards seated in the corners of the assembly hall had become silent; (13)
In the soft sound of their mutual greetings.
As soon as the sun’s rays had swiftly risen, they seemed to arrive in haste to hear [the news],
having entered through the lattice-windows as if through the openings of the windows.
When the rays of the sun had risen, as if having arrived with speed to hear [the news], they reached from window to window and entered through the lattice openings. || 14 ||
As the pearls fall rapidly into the hands of the listeners who enter quickly,
their clinking sound subsides as if they were falling asleep.

When the tinkling of ornaments such as pearl nets and the like— which arose from the touch of hands and the jostling of limbs of the audience entering the assembly hall— subsided, becoming motionless as if in sleep,
the prince [appeared] like Kaca, the son of Śaṃkara, or like [the sage] Kaca of the preceptor of the gods.
Like Prahlāda to Śukra, or like Suparṇa to the wielder of the Śārṅga bow. || 16 ||
There are many similes used to illustrate the excellence of her vision, such as devotion, reverence, longing, and so forth. (16)
Rāma slowly fixed his gaze upon the face of Vasiṣṭha,
like a female bee hovering near the edge of the sky toward a full-blown lotus.
Just as the time of sunrise and so forth causes a female bee wandering in the sky to settle upon a blooming lotus, so it is in this case. || 17 ||
Then the sage, skilled in speech, spoke in due order to the joy of the Raghus— who was himself an expert in the meaning of words— using those very same words he had previously considered.
By that very sequence previously set forth. || 18 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
"O descendant of Raghu, do you remember the words spoken by me yesterday, which were of exceedingly profound meaning and intended to awaken one to the supreme reality?"
hyas means yesterday; pūrvedyus means on the previous day. || 19 ||
Now, O crusher of enemies, listen further to this which is being spoken by me for the sake of awakening and for the attainment of eternal perfection. (20)
By the power of the practice of dispassion and likewise through the awakening to reality, one crosses over saṃsāra; therefore, apply yourself to that very practice.
He demonstrates by following the very sequence previously stated, beginning with the words "vairāgya" and so forth. || 21 ||

When the realization of the true reality [the reading is *samyakkṛtāvabodhena*] has occurred and ignorance has come to an end, and when the immersion in latent impressions has dissolved, one attains the sorrowless state. || 22 ||
Unconditioned by space, time, and the like, and transcending the two extremes of the seen and the unseen, Brahman alone—though singular—abides as the world, having attained a state of duality. (23)

"Unconditioned by space, time, and so forth" means being devoid of the three kinds of limitation. Its further explanation is "unseen" (*adṛṣṭa*). It is that which has not been seen in terms of place or time; whose two ends—the prior and posterior limits—and whose duality do not exist. In a compound, when the dual ending of the word *ubha* is elided, the suffix *ayac* is applied according to the rule *ubhaya-anyatra*. || 23 ||
That Brahman alone exists which is undivided from all beings, peaceful, and appearing as an equal uniformity; how could there be any otherness therein? (24)

Because it also follows after common universals such as "cowness" (gotva) which are themselves equal, there is the appearance of equality (samasamābhāsatā)—[the reading is *samasamāsattā tatpa*]. This is what manifests through the exclusion of those [other universals]. 24.
Thinking thus, having inwardly uttered "I am," being great with a liberated body,
uniform, and tranquil in soul, become manifest bliss in your own self.

Having thus understood and ascertained the nature of Brahman as described, and having abandoned the conceit of "I," become one whose very self is such that its essence is the beautiful void (kha) or space, or bliss. 25.
There is no mind, nor ignorance, nor manas, nor a living soul;
these, O Rāma, are merely the mental constructs fashioned by Brahman itself.
One's own mental constructs are conceptualizations. || 26 ||
Whatever prosperities, whatever perceptions, whatever consciousnesses, and whatever desires there may be—
all that is Brahman alone, without beginning or end, expanding like the ocean.

Wealth consists of objects of enjoyment; the senses are the instruments for experiencing them; and consciousness (citi) refers either to the reflections of consciousness cast therein or to memories. The "desires" are the longings for those enjoyments. || 27 ||

In the netherworld, on the surface of the earth, in heaven, in a blade of grass, in living beings, and even in the sky—that Supreme Brahman is seen as the very form of consciousness; indeed, there is nothing else.

The meaning is that, whether in different locations such as the netherworld (pātāla) and so forth, or in different objects such as grass and so forth—and by the word "and" (ca), also in different times such as the past and so forth—it is that very [Brahman] alone which is perceived in the form of all that is visible, and nothing else. || 28 ||
Having abandoned relatives— whether those to be rejected or accepted— and having cast off worldly power and the body,
Brahman alone, devoid of beginning and end, expands like the ocean.

The meaning is as follows: in general, things are to be regarded as indifferent, to be abandoned, or to be accepted; even therein, relatives, wealth, and the body are to be understood as progressively more worthy of acceptance in that order. || 29 ||
As long as there is the conceptualization of ignorance, as long as there is the meditation on [the world as] Brahman,
and as long as there is attachment to the web of the world, so long does the construction of the mind and other faculties persist.
Does it always manifest in that way? No; he says "as long as" and so forth [to answer this]. || 30 ||

As long as there is the sense of "I" in the body— and here the word *yāvat* has the sense of limitation or the sense of totality, meaning "in this entire visible world"— and as long as there is the conviction "this is mine" regarding this visible world through the self, for that long there is the delusion of the mind and so forth. (31)
The remainder [of the sentence] is: "by oneself, by one's own self, the conviction 'this is mine' is formed. || 31 ||
As long as you have not risen high through association with the company of the virtuous,
and as long as your folly has not been completely exhausted, so long will there remain a downward inclination of the mind and other faculties.
Elevatedness is fullness; subservience to the mind and other factors is lowness. || 32 ||
As long as this world-creator has not reached a state of relaxation through the power of right vision,
so long will the mind and other faculties remain manifest.

As long as there is ignorance, blindness, and helplessness through longing for sense objects, so long does the conceptualization of the mind and other faculties arise from the heightening of delusion due to folly. // 34 //
Blindness consists in the state of ignorance. || 34 ||
As long as the fragrance of the poison of desire pervades the forest of the heart,
the cakora bird of discernment does not enter within at all.
The foul odor of poison, characterized by longing, does not enter within as long as the chakora bird—characterized by the supreme investigation of the Self—remains outside.
For one whose mind has no longing for enjoyments, who possesses cool and stainless bliss, and whose net of bonds of hope has been severed, the delusion of the mind perishes. (36)
For the man whose consciousness is eternally cool due to the abandonment of craving and delusion,
and whose mind is tranquil, the state of the ordinary mind is awakened and relinquished.
The ground of the mind, when abandoned through non-attachment, becomes awakened and bears the fruit of awakening; it does not bear such fruit when not abandoned—this is the meaning. || 37 ||
For one who perceives the unreal as something unfamiliar, unregarded, and non-existent—seeing his own body as if it were distant—how can there be a "land of the mind" (the mental world)? (38)
With the intention that the non-arising of the mind itself is its abandonment, he says: "unfamiliar" (asaṃstutam).

For one who perceives his own body as something unfamiliar—meaning useless, distant, and insubstantial—and therefore as non-existent, like the form of a man in the clouds, how could there be a "mind-ground" (cittabhūḥ), that is, the dwelling-place of the mind? || 38 ||

For one whose nature consists of the realized reality of infinite consciousness and who perceives the world as withdrawn within his own mind, the delusion regarding the individual soul and other such categories is stilled. (39)
He whose nature is refined and adorned by the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) resulting from cultivation through hearing, reflection, and meditative absorption;
who is the infinite form of pure consciousness alone, possessing a nature entirely different from the forms well-known in worldly existence;
and for whom the entire universe has dissolved within his own heart and mind. || 39 ||
When false vision, which is the cause of erroneous delusion, has been stilled;
and when the supreme sun, the singular vision of ultimate reality, has arisen. (40)
When that ignorance—which consists of incorrect vision, which is opposed to right vision, and which produces false delusions—has perished because its very nature has been destroyed; || 40 ||
Know that the mind has dissolved, like a drop of ghee in fire, or like a parched leaf burnt so as never to be seen again. (41)
The state of mind belonging to those great-souled ones who are liberated while living and who perceive both the higher and the lower is called *sattva*. (42)

To the question, "In the absence of the mind, how can there be worldly discourse? he replies with the words beginning "jīvanmuktāḥ": "The path of the mind is like a line drawn in water or a line drawn in sand once the water has dried; such is the trace of the mind's activity. (42)

In the bodies of those liberated while living, the latent impression that engages in worldly activity no longer exists under the name of "mind," for it has indeed reached the state of pure being (sattva).

For those who know reality are mindless, always established in the state of equanimity; they wander here at their ease, with the effortless playfulness of one whose being is grounded in pure goodness.
They wander about and engage in worldly affairs with a casual indifference and lack of concern toward the established order of sentient beings. 44.

Though engaged in worldly affairs, those who are peaceful, established in being, and have restrained their senses constantly behold that light; for them, there is no latent impression of duality or unity.
In that case, what is the point of their latent impressions (*vāsanā*), given that they perceive both the conventional and the ultimate reality as a unity through non-duality?
To this he says: [it] is possible—this is the meaning. || 45 ||
For the sage who, through inward-turned consciousness, offers the entire three worlds as grass into the fire of pure awareness, the delusions of the mind and other faculties cease within.
He explains that very point clearly with the words: "By way of inward-turnedness" (antarmukhatayā). || 46 ||
A mind made clear by discernment is called *sattva*;
it no longer bears fruit in delusion, just as a burnt seed does not produce a sprout. (47)
For this very reason, with the intention of showing the distinction between the ignorant mind and that of a sentient being, he says: "Through discernment... (verse 47).
As long as there is a being whose inner nature is deluded and subject to rebirth, that which is designated by the term "mind" undergoes inversion through the lack of awakening. (48)

For deluded people, that [sattva] remains characterized by rebirth as long as it is designated by the term "inner mind" (antaścitta). However, through awakening, being sattva, it undergoes a transformation; the meaning is that it performs the contrary effect, which is characterized by the cessation of birth. || 48 ||
You have indeed attained all that is to be attained; the mind, having entered the state of a sentient being, has been consumed by the fire of gnosis and shall not sprout again. (49)
"Your mind"—this is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. || 49 ||
A mind pierced by desires grows back as if struck by an axe or fire; but a mind made clear by awakening is not consumed by the fire of knowledge.

How, then, does it grow again? To this he says: "It grows. It is pierced—that is, interlaced—with *eṣaṇās*, the desires for wealth, progeny, and worlds. Just as grass and the like, though cut by an axe or burnt by fire, sprout again because they are permeated by the internal power of the seed, so it is here. [The text continues: "consumed."
In which the power of the seeds of craving has been utterly consumed. || 50 ||
For the world is indeed the expansion of Brahman, and the expansion of Brahman is the world;
there exists no difference between these two, just as none exists between consciousness and the density of Brahman.

To the question, "How can the power of the seed of the world be burnt away by the fire of knowledge? he says: "Brahman," and so forth. For (hi) because the world is merely an expansion (bṛṃhā)—an increase through superimposed forms—of Brahman alone due to delusion; and because even the world, through knowledge, possesses the expansion of the true nature of Brahman; and because between these two, Brahman and the world, [the distinction] is caused solely by ignorance.
Upon its destruction, no differentiation remains; therefore, it does not sprout again—this is the meaning. || 51 ||

The three worlds exist within consciousness, just as pungency exists within a peppercorn; therefore, consciousness and the world are not distinct, and thus the notions of "existent" and "non-existent" are futile.
The three worlds exist within consciousness as nothing other than the very form of consciousness, just as pungency exists in a peppercorn whose sole essence is pungency.
Therefore, from the perspective of ultimate reality, consciousness and the world are not distinct. Consequently, the arising and dissolution of things—whether existent or non-existent—are in vain;
the meaning is that they are merely an error induced by *māyā*. || 52 ||
In this state, consciousness does not perceive the habitual tendencies of the conventions between words and their referents;
because it is the expanse of consciousness (*cidvyoma*), both appear as unborn, and thus the notions of existence and non-existence are abandoned.

In that case, are the Vedic words "being" and "non-being"—such as in the passage, "In the beginning this was non-being; from that, indeed, being was born"—as well as worldly words like "the jar exists" and "the jar does not exist," devoid of meaning? No, he says: "By words...
Here, in the usage of both Vedic and worldly discourse, mutually exclusive words have been conventionally assigned to mutually exclusive objects.
It is only the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of the speaker and the listener that appears in the form of an exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*). [The reading is *sadasacchabdakṛtā*.

There is no valid cognition (*pramā*) through a consciousness produced by words denoting those parts; for an exclusion, being a non-entity, cannot be the meaning of a word. Thus, when the exclusion is set aside, both are denotable by the words "existent" and "non-existent."

The meaning is that because it is the sky-like consciousness (cidvyoma) which is neither excluded nor followed by anything else, it alone shines forth in the ultimate sense; therefore, that alone is the referent of the term "ultimate reality" (paramārthavastu). || 53 ||
Since you are not composed of consciousness, you are not your own self; why then do you weep?
If the worlds were not composed of consciousness, from where could such a conceptualization arise? (54)

Thus, by abandoning the conceptualization of existence and non-existence and perceiving pure consciousness (cinmātra), even the occurrence of weeping—caused by the attainment of misfortunes such as birth and death, which are prompted by the delusion of identifying the body and so forth with the Self—is no longer possible; thus he says: "Because it is not composed of the insentient" (acinmayatvāt). [This refers to] that which is conventionally designated as "you, you," namely the one named Rāma.

The body, which possesses the nature of both existence and non-existence, is not yourself, because you are not composed of insentient matter (acinmaya). The meaning is: once the insentient nature and the absence [of selfhood] of the entire world are realized, how could the conceptualization of a body and so forth even belong to you? || 54 ||
If everything is always composed of consciousness, then investigate that very nature of consciousness:

it is pure, sentient, and without beginning or end; in that state, my dear, how could there be any conceptual construction? (Or, according to another reading: "how could there be any mental fabrication? 55.

If, however, you think that the world is composed solely of consciousness because you have abandoned mere insentience—which is characterized by the exclusion of consciousness—then investigate the nature of that consciousness. When that is properly investigated, it is found to be pure, devoid of the three kinds of limitation, and of a single essence. In that state, from where could there arise the perception of the body and other such miseries? This is the meaning. || 55 ||
You are the conscious self, you are partless, and you are devoid of near and far shores;
remember your own expansive form, and do not become limited by forgetfulness.
"By non-remembrance," that is, by forgetting the true nature of consciousness, "he is completely deluded," meaning he is limited. || 56 ||
Having attained that state of your own being, you perceive everything as non-everything;
such is your form—you are peaceful, you are consciousness, you are the very nature of Brahman.

Having attained that state of existence which is the abiding in the nature of perfect consciousness, become one who rises—that is, one who possesses the emergence resulting from the attainment of unsurpassed bliss—and contemplate, that is, bring about, the realization that the non-all, the limited world, is the all, the full nature. || 57 ||
You are indeed the interior of the moon's crescent, yet you are not; you are manifold, and yet you are also not so.
You are who you are, yet you are as if not that; you exist and do not exist, for you are self-luminous.

You do not exist as something distinct through a distinct nature; you are not that, yet because you are the ultimate limit of its sublation, you remain as the residue. In that state, since all causes for the activity of speech and mind have vanished, you are "that" and you are "this. If it is asked, "Then are you absolutely imperceptible? he says: "That specific object which is within, you are not; indeed, that does not exist for you. Therefore, you are 'this' (idam)."
O Self, whose nature is the mass of consciousness and who abides in yourself—salutations be unto you! || 59 ||

He explains the portion "in being" (*sadasati*) with the word "that which": that which is the specific exclusion (*viśeṣa*), characterized by differentiation (*vyāvṛtti*), and internal limitation (*antaḥpariccheda*) of all things—that alone, because it is unreal, is the referent of the word "non-existent" (*asat*). "You are not that" is the meaning of the phrase "in being.

That very same thing, when imagined by those engaged in worldly transaction (*vyavahārika*) as having the property of existence through its exclusion from that [unreality], is [designated] as "existence" (*sattā*).

The meaning is that he is designated as "you do not exist at all," which is the sense of the statement "you are non-existent"; thus, with this intention, he was told "you are both existent and non-existent."
You, whose body is a mass of consciousness compressed within the vast space between the stone slabs devoid of beginning and end, you who are as pure as the sky— O Victorious One,
who dwells in the sport of the lines of the sprout-like navel-cavity of Brahmā, may you remain established in your own self; salutations to you!

That which is devoid of beginning and end, vast, like the interior of a crystal stone—dense, compact, and a mass of consciousness—that is your body; its very nature you are, and thus you do not partake in transformations such as suffering. Realizing this, remain established in yourself. Within the belly of your own crystal-stone of consciousness, which is expansive on all sides...

O Rāma, salutations to You who are such—that in whom all the worlds abide through the play of the mind within the various latent impressions (vāsanā) that resemble mere lines of imagined illusion, like a sprout reflected in a mirror. This is the meaning. || 60 ||
Thus ends the second canto, titled "The Strengthening of Rest," in the first half of the Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.

Thus ends the second canto, titled "The Further Consolidation of Rest," in the Nirvāṇa Section of the *Mokṣopāyas* within the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Valmiki, belonging to the *Ārṣa*. 2.
The Third Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Like a mass of water in the ocean containing many future waves, [so it is with this world].
O sinless one, you are he who carries across the infinite worlds.
Through the vision of the identity of Brahman, the individual soul, the mind, the body, and the world,
when the delusion of all duality has subsided, that is called the state of abiding in the one fullness.

Therein, first, he introduces the nature of consciousness as the Self, which is the cause for the appearance of all conceptual constructions, with the word "bhāvi" (the becoming). Just as the mass of water—the commonality of water—is the locus for the manifold conceptualizations of numerous waves arising within the ocean, so too is that consciousness (*cit*) which bears infinite worlds. The particle *u* is used here in the sense of possibility or emphasis.
The meaning is: "Consider that very [nature] to be the Self. || 1 ||
Liberated through the cultivation of being and devoid of both existence and non-existence, O Self of Consciousness, tell me: where indeed could impressions and the like remain? || 2 ||

Following that contemplation, by the mere abandonment of the notion of duality, one experiences its own nature—which is free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*) and devoid of latent impressions (*nirvāsana*)—as expressed in the verse beginning with "Bhava. || 2 ||
This living soul shines forth by itself as "this" through latent impressions;
tell me, my dear, what occasion is there here for any other statement or object? (3)

When the true nature of that [consciousness] is thoroughly known, one is able to experience that the divisions of the individual soul (*jīva*), latent impressions (*vāsanā*), and the world are merely the imagination of a difference in manifestation within consciousness itself, and do not exist separately;

thus he says: "The individual soul" (*jīva*). This refers to the word and its meaning which denote the non-conscious (*acit*), as well as their referent, within this very kind of conscious reality (*cidvastu*). (Verse 3)
The ocean of your own consciousness, vast, deep, and radiant with great waves, is stilled by the wave named Rāma; you are as even and serene as the sky.
In that eternal bliss, the self consisting of consciousness, wherein yogis delight—by the word "Rāma," this Supreme Brahman is designated.
Thus, his name "Rāma" was explained as having a literal etymological meaning. || 4 ||
Just as heat is not distinct from fire, fragrance from the lotus, blackness from soot, whiteness from snow, and sweetness from sugarcane; || 5 ||

In this regard, he establishes the non-difference of the visible from the Seer through examples that demonstrate its being an attribute of the Seer: Light is not distinct from the factor of illumination; likewise, experience is not distinct from consciousness.
Just as a wave is not different from water, so too is the world not different from the nature of consciousness. (6)
From the luminous part of fire comes light. Experience (*anubhūti*) is consciousness reflected in the mental modification (*vṛtti*).
The word "likewise" (*tathā*) serves to collect the preceding examples. The phrase "as non-different" (*yathā abhinna*) is the correct division of the text. || 6 ||
Experience is not different from consciousness, and the "I" is not different from experience;
the individual soul (jīva) is not distinct from me, and the mind is not distinct from the individual soul.

He clarifies the very meaning already stated by revealing the sequence of superimposition (adhyāsa) with the words beginning "of consciousness" (citaḥ): "Of consciousness" (citaḥ) means of the consciousness of Brahman, which is the fundamental substratum (mūlādhiṣṭhāna). "Experience" (anubhavaḥ) is the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa) established through a modification of Māyā. "I" (aham) refers to the individual and collective ego (ahaṃkāra). This should be understood in the same way for the subsequent items up to the body. (7)
The sense organ is not distinct from the mind, nor is the body separate from the sense organ;
the world is not distinct from the body, for indeed there is nothing other than the world.
"Not from the body" means that the world is included within the collective body (samaṣṭi-śarīra); this is the intended meaning. || 8 ||
Thus has this great wheel been set in motion for a long time;
yet nothing has been set in motion, nor is it swift, nor is it slow.

The meaning is this: this present, visible wheel of the world has been set in motion solely by consciousness itself through a succession of superimpositions arising from delusion regarding its own true nature; however, from the perspective of ultimate reality, nothing at all has been set in motion. || 9 ||
Thus, all is one's own infinite consciousness, entirely undivided;
it exists as space within space, in nothing, and is nothing whatsoever.
The void is fully expanded within the void; Brahman is magnified within Brahman;
truth unfolds within truth, abiding like the full within the full. || 11 ||
He describes that very state of unsurpassed fullness through various figurative expressions, beginning with "empty" (śūnyam). || 11 ||
Even while perceiving forms, light, and mental attention, the Knower does nothing at all; for he performs no acts that are to be grasped, since agency belongs only to that which is not the Knower.
For the Knower, there is no agency whatsoever. || 12 ||
That which is perceived as something to be acquired leads to either suffering or happiness for you;
yet, by its very absence, it is not to be acquired, being a non-agent in the production of pleasure and pain. (13)

Whatever collection of objects is grasped with the notion that it is to be accepted, that very thing becomes for you both suffering and happiness. The state of being [an object] is the notion of its acceptability; however, in the absence of that, there is nothing whatsoever that can be called "acceptable. And it is well known that what is not grasped is a non-agent with respect to pleasure and pain; thus, the meaning is that there is no consequence of suffering and so forth. Alternatively, regarding entities...
Because of the non-existence—that is, the absence—of all visible things, there is nothing whatsoever to be acquired; this is the meaning of being a non-agent with respect to pleasure and pain.
Just as the collection of words such as "space," "in space," and "spaces" is neither diverse nor non-diverse,
and though meaningful, is itself utterly empty in nature— such is the sequence of the self and the world.
To the question of how there can be non-existence of entities that are perceived as having diversity, he says: "Just as... (verse 14).
Pure within like the inner sky, he was perfectly adept in external conduct;
amidst the fluctuations of joy and anger, his composure remained as steady as wood or a clod of earth.
"Be like a piece of wood or a clod of earth"—this is the remainder [of the verse]. || 15 ||
He who perceives even that most extreme enemy, intent on killing him with haste, as a genuine friend— he truly sees.

Because even in the body of an enemy, one's own Self is present, the seer of the Self experiences natural affection toward that enemy just as toward his own body; thus he says: "He who... [referring to] a friend, the most beloved. || 16 ||
He who scrapes away both friendship and envy, root and branch, like a tree on a riverbank, is the destroyer of the defects of joy and resentment.

Therefore, he says "samūla... to show that from this very [practice] comes the cessation of the defects of joy and resentment. The meaning is: he who, like a river that scrapes away a tree standing on its own bank—scraping it away root-and-all (*samūlakāṣam*) and uprooting it completely—is alone the destroyer of the defects of joy and resentment. This is derived from the root *kaṣ* with the prefix *samūla-* and the suffix *ṇamul*, according to the rule regarding *kaṣādiṣu*.
The subsequent application [of the verb] follows the manner [of the main verb]. || 17 ||

If the true nature of the transformations of passion and hatred is not contemplated, then even those things that exist will take on the form of non-existence; they will be as if never experienced, even though they have been enjoyed. (18)
If the nature and reality of attachment and aversion, as well as their effects and transformations, are neither contemplated nor investigated,
then even those people renowned among the virtuous for being free from attachment and aversion would be of an unreal nature;
for as long as the reality of attachment and aversion is not fully understood, it is impossible to uproot them, and thus they [will persist].
Because they do not avoid the growth of passion and hatred, therefore, even when cultivated, they are in vain; such is the meaning. || 18 ||
He whose state of being is free from egoism, whose intellect is not tainted—
even by slaying these worlds, he does not kill, nor is he bound.

If it is asked what, then, is the reality of those two, it is simply the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra). Therefore, with the intention that the absolute cessation of attachment and aversion occurs through its abandonment, he cites the verse from the Gītā beginning with "yasya" (of whom). || 19 ||
The realization of the existence of that which does not exist has been described as "illusion" (māyā);
through perfect knowledge alone, it undoubtedly perishes.

However, with the intention that the reality of egoism is indeed ignorance and its cessation comes from the thorough knowledge of one's own Self, he says "That which... (verse 20), demonstrating the well-known meaning of the word *māyā* in that context.
He whose internal burden of latent impressions has been extinguished like an oilless lamp—
by that wise and unchanging man, who is as if painted in a picture, all is conquered.

"By whom the burden of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) has been stilled, by him victory is won. He asks: "Is that victory real? and answers: "No; it is as if by one painted in a picture. Just as a king depicted in a painting might be said to have "won" by cutting off the head of an enemy likewise painted, so too, through the realization that eternally negates the cycle of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*), victory is won by the eternally established, non-dual, and perfect Self. || 21 ||
He for whom this entire collection of objects, whether existent or non-existent, is not to be grasped in any state—
neither for the burning of suffering nor for pleasure— is indeed liberated here while still alive.
For that supreme person, this entire collection of objects of enjoyment— in their states of existence or non-existence,
in their conditions of manifestation or disappearance, in their states of prosperity or poverty, or in their states of superimposition or negation—
is not to be accepted, because they are false in reality, or because they are already eternally attained as his very self.

The meaning is that for one who is joined with the sevenfold union and separation [of the elements], there is neither the burning pain of suffering nor pleasure; rather, even while living here, this living being is indeed liberated. || 22 ||

Thus ends the third canto, titled "The Exposition of the Unity with Brahman," in the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa* of the *Mokṣopāya* section of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*, composed by Vālmīki and belonging to the *Ārṣa* tradition. 3.
Thus ends the third canto, titled "The Exposition of the Unity of Brahman," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa-tātparyaprakāśa*.
The Fourth Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O sinless one, [the constituents are] the mind, the intellect, the ego, the senses, and so forth.
Since everything consists of pure, non-conceptual consciousness, where can things such as living beings reside?
Having cast aside other outward-directed views, Vasiṣṭha established Rāghava here in the inward vision; then, for the sake of quelling his doubts, he was questioned.
Desiring to open Rāma’s inward vision, Vasiṣṭha first addressed him regarding the nature of the mind within spiritual matters:

"This appearance of multiplicity has been bestowed by the Great Soul through a single Self alone, just as the single moon appears manifold through darkness, water, vessels, and mirrors. [Note: *Timira* is a specific eye disease.]
He states the reason for its arising there with the words "by one": it is "given," meaning it is brought about through the superimposition of association with its own existence. (2)
As soon as the possession by the poison of craving for enjoyments has subsided, then likewise ignorance and blindness set, like darkness at the destruction of gloom. (3)

With the intention that, by the very vision of the inner reality (pratyaktattva) which follows after the mind and other faculties, one who has found rest therein experiences the exhaustion of thirst for the enjoyment of external objects; and because even the pure existence (sanmātra) underlying all external things shines forth spontaneously as non-different from the inner self, even the ignorance that causes the superimposition of externality is destroyed— he says "bhāga" etc., with this underlying thought.

The meaning is that when, by seeing the inner reality (pratyaktattva) in the manner described, the possession of the poison of craving for enjoyment has subsided, at that very moment ignorance has set and been dispelled. "Blindness" (āndhya) refers to the incapacity of the eyes to manifest objects. || 3 ||
By the mantra of the inner science (adhyātmaśāstra), when cultivated within, the cholera-like poison of craving is destroyed,
just as mist is dispelled by autumn.
By that which is included within and correctly investigated. || 4 ||
O Rāma, know that when folly is destroyed, the mind along with its kin is likewise destroyed;
just as when the clouds have dissolved in the sky, the dullness subsides without obstacle.
Folly is ignorance; dullness is coldness. || 5 ||
When the mind has reached the state of no-mind, the delusion of latent impressions perishes,
O sinless one, like the scattering of pearls from a necklace when the string is severed.
Those who contemplate the meaning of the scriptures for the purpose of obstructing Raghunātha unite in their minds with those destined for the state of worms and insects.

Having thus correctly unveiled the inward vision (*pratyagdṛṣṭi*), which constitutes the secret essence of all the Vedānta scriptures, [the author] censures those whose contrary view obstructs the meaning of the scriptures, beginning with the words "O Raghunātha. The phrase "having disregarded" implies the disregard of the meaning of the scriptures—that is, the secret of the scriptures—which has been demonstrated. Those who conceive of it otherwise for the sake of obstructing it—
They meet with sinners who are fit for the state of worms and insects, through a mind characterized by evil thoughts caused by passion and the like. || 8 ||
When ignorance has been stilled, the tremulous beauty of her lovely eyes,
which resemble fresh lotuses, remains unimpaired, like the movement of a lotus stalk in a breeze.

By citing by way of a brief illustration that evil intellect which will be elaborated upon in the subsequent creation, he shows that its destruction follows from the destruction of ignorance with the words, "Not so. The ellipsis to be supplied is: "you have become established in stability, free from existence and non-existence, within the physical forms of women and others as imagined by that evil intellect."
He was like a wind in the sky, moving with supreme speed upon his feet.
Now, having observed through signs Rama’s stabilization in the vision of the inner self (pratyagdṛṣṭi) which he had been shown, [the sage] says:
"I believe you have attained awakening through my words, O scion of Raghu; the sleep of ignorance has departed within you, like a king awakened by the beating of drums. (10)
With the drums of the bards and various types of musical instruments for awakening.
The words of a family preceptor indeed take effect upon ordinary people;
O Rāma, how could they fail to take effect upon you, whose intellect is so exceedingly noble? (11)

Now, seeing the fruitfulness of his own instruction, he spoke in praise of Rāma and himself: "Wherein the quality of having speech worthy of acceptance has been cultivated by one's own mind, my words enter deeply, just as water enters a scorched field. (12)
Since you have cultivated and reflected upon my status as one whose words are to be accepted and my state as the most trustworthy person, therefore my speech enters into the depths of your heart.
"O noble one of great power, we are indeed the eternal family preceptors of you, the scions of Raghu's line.
Therefore, O noble one, you must quickly take these auspicious words spoken by me to heart, wearing them like a necklace. (13)

Now, by means of recollection, he prescribes the retention of the very subject matter he has taught—which culminates in its fruit—by proclaiming his own status as a venerable teacher due to his being the object of worship for his lineage; thus he says: "We... Because we are the family preceptors (*kulaguru*) of all you Ikṣvākus, and especially of the descendants of Raghu, therefore by you...
"This auspicious speech uttered by me should be held fast; that is to say, it should be made firm through repeated reflection.
Thus ends the fourth canto, titled "The Exposition of the Absence of Mind," in the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa* of the *Mokṣopāya* within the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki. 4.
Thus ends the fourth canto, titled "The Exposition on the Absence of the Mind," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The Fifth Chapter.
Śrī Rāma said:
"Oh! Through the contemplation of the meaning of your words, I have attained the state of consciousness."
O Lord, this web of the world, though standing before me, is peaceful.
Here, the awakened Śrī Rāma, resting in supreme bliss,
described his own experience in detail before his guru.
O Consciousness, you are the state of the Self, filled with the single essence of pure consciousness. || 1 ||
Reflecting thus, I have set out toward the bliss found in the Supreme Self, just as the surface of the earth, scorched by a long drought, is refreshed by rain. || 2 ||
It was scorched by a long-lasting drought, that is, by a prolonged obstruction of rain. || 2 ||
I am stilled, having a cool nature; I abide in bliss alone. Having attained serenity, I am like a lake free from all agitation. (3)
"Nirvāraṇa" means one from whom the elephant has departed; that is to say, one for whom the cause of agitation has ceased. || 3 ||
O Sage, I now perceive this entire circle of the quarters as perfectly serene and free from mist, seeing it exactly as it truly is.
It is as it truly is, having the nature of mere existence that is real and in accordance with reality. || 4 ||
I am born, my doubts dispelled, the mirage of hope extinguished;
liberated from both passion and its opposite—[the reading *rāganīhāra* is also found]—and cooled like a savory wild meat.

"Liberated from *rāgas* (passions), which are the coloring of sense objects, and from *nīrāgas* (their opposites), such as the mental states of dispassion (*vairāgya*) and so forth. "Savory" (*mṛṣṭa*).
Like an autumnal forest from which the mist and dust have been wiped away, he was cool. || 5 ||
By myself alone have I attained that inner bliss which is devoid of end;
wherein, O Lord, even the taste of the elixir of immortality counts as no more than a blade of grass.
Even the taste of that elixir, which is nectar itself, becomes like a blade of grass—insipid or even negligible—in comparison to that bliss. || 6 ||
Today I am established in my true nature; I am self-abiding and I am joyful.
I am the delight of the world, I am Rāma; salutations to me, and salutations be to you!

*Prakṛti* is the ultimate nature; I abide in that. That bliss (*sukha*) in which the worlds (*loka*) delight and find rest—that I am. For the Śruti says: "Other beings subsist on a mere fraction of this very bliss. Therefore, according to the etymology previously shown—namely, "that wherein yogis delight" (*ramante*)—I am *Rāma*. Thus, the true significance of my own name is realized by me today.
The meaning is that it is accomplished. Salutations to you, who reveal that [truth], and to me, who am such [a recipient]. || 7 ||
Those doubts and those mental constructions— all have set for me,
like the world of nocturnal ghosts at dawn when the sun has risen.
All conceptualizations are delusions. In the night, the world, its wanderings, or its family—imagined by the childlike confusion of a ghost—is like a pond that has become vast, pure, and cool as ice;
in such a state, my mind has attained peace, just as a lake does in autumn.
In autumn, the mind attains peace—a state of rest free from distraction—just as a great lake reaches tranquility. || 9 ||
Doubts such as "Why" and "How" did this blemish come upon the Self have surely been uprooted, just as darkness vanishes before the moon. 10.

From what cause has the stain of ignorance and the like come to the Self, which is of the nature of pure consciousness and a single essence? How does that [stain] abide within that which is self-luminous? How can it veil that which is unattached and indivisible? And how can there be the experience of worldly transformations for one who is immutable? Such are the doubts.
Through the departure of ignorance, which is the root of all doubt, it has reached a state of being rootless. || 10 ||
Everything everywhere and at all times is the Self alone, whose form is ever-manifest;
how then can there be the false conceptualization that "this is one thing" and "that is another"?
One whose form is cultivated and whose appearance is radiant. || 11 ||
"Who was I previously that I bound my very inner self with such chains of craving? Thus I laugh, full of blossoming joy.
Now that I have blossomed forth as the Self, experienced as transcending hunger and other such needs, I laugh within myself at who I was when I was bound by the shackles of former cravings. 12.
Now I have clearly remembered how I am this very person who stands here,
bathed by the flood of the nectar of your speech.
The particle *ā* is a nipāta (indeclinable) indicating remembrance. Because it is a *pragṛhya* by the rule *nipāta ekājanāṅ*, there is no sandhi [with the following vowel].

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "By me, who have bathed in the flood of the nectar of Your speech, this entire self—whatever it is and how it exists in ultimate reality—is now remembered. (13)
"Oh, how wonderful! I have ascended to this vast, purifying expanse, standing right here where the sun remains as if situated in the netherworld! (14)

Remaining right here, I have ascended to a certain vast and limitless realm of Brahman, in which realm the sun does not shine, even though it remains as if situated in the netherworld (pātāla), being located in an exceedingly low position.
For it is from the *kārya-brahmaloka* (the effected world of Brahman) that he is situated below, not from the *parabrahmaloka* (the supreme world of Brahman). There, the sun does not shine...
The intention is that this is based on such scriptural passages as "the moon and the stars" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.7.4). || 14 ||

Salutations eternally to the one worthy of worship; I, having attained my true being from the ocean of existence consisting of being and non-being, bow down to the Self by means of the self within the self. 15.

"From the ocean of existence characterized by being and non-being"—this is the ablative case used with the elision of a word ending in the suffix *lyap*. The meaning is: "having crossed the ocean of existence characterized by being and non-being, and having attained that state of pure Being which is its shore and its substratum. Since I, by my own self, triumph—that is, I abide in supreme excellence—within the Self, within my own glory, I am therefore to be eternally saluted by all at all times.
The meaning is: "to one who is worthy of being saluted. || 15 ||

O Lord, by the power of experience, having clearly attained the state of being free from sorrow and long filled with joy through your excellent word here, I have reached a condition within the calyx of my heart-lotus that has become like a blooming lotus.

O Lord, the meaning is this: by your excellent words, which have clearly attained stability like a bee within the calyx of my heart-lotus, I have—through the power of my own experience—attained in this very place and at this very time the state of liberation while living (*jīvanmukta*), a state free from sorrow, ever-arisen, and full of joy. || 16 ||

Thus ends the fifth canto, titled "The Description of Rāghava’s Resting," in the Nirvāṇa section of the *Deva-mokṣopāya* within the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki according to the tradition of the Ṛṣis.
Thus ends the fifth canto, titled "The Description of Rāghava’s Resting," in the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa-tātparya-prakāśa*.
The Sixth Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
O mighty-armed one, listen once more to my supreme word.
That which I shall speak to you, who are well-disposed toward me, out of a desire for your welfare.

In this context, the distinction between the body and the self is described; for the deluded, suffering arises from the view that the body is the self, and through attachment to women, the increase of delusion is depicted.

In this manner, although Śrī Rāma was already perfectly awakened, the venerable Vasiṣṭha, proceeding to generate awakening in other listeners as well, spoke the words beginning with "bhūya eva" (once more indeed) to encourage Rāma toward listening to the forthcoming discrimination between the body and the Self,
addressing him who was full of joy.

The meaning is: "Listen to that which I shall speak out of a desire for the welfare of all people, for you who are the recipient of the joy characterized by the experience of the Self as unsurpassed bliss, which is the intended subject of this instruction. || 1 ||
Even if you accept their difference, listen for the sake of increasing your understanding, so that even those of little awakening may not suffer. (2)

[Objection: But since the distinctions between the listener, the teacher, the object to be heard, and so forth, are sublated, how can there be your engagement in hearing, or what could its fruit be? To this, he says: "Distinction" (bhedam). Your engagement in hearing is established by the acceptance of distinction through the persistence of what has been sublated.
The meaning is that the result of this is the increase of awakening and the deliverance of those who have awakened only slightly. || 2 ||
The ignorant man whose very body is the object of his self-conception due to his lack of knowledge is overwhelmed by the enemies of the senses, as if they were provoked to anger.

In this regard, first observing through signs the desire of the listeners—arising from their inability to conquer the senses—to know how the mind, being drawn away by them, might find firm establishment in the Supreme Self, [the Lord says]: "But he who is devoid of discernment and whose mind is always uncontrolled, his senses remain unsubdued, like the vicious horses of a charioteer; whereas he who possesses discernment..."

"Always with a disciplined mind; his senses are under control like the well-trained horses of a charioteer"—following this very direction indicated by these two Vedic verses, he gradually overcomes that [state] with the two verses beginning with "yasya" (of whom).
Precisely because of this offense consisting in identifying with the unreal self, the senses, becoming enemies and adversaries, act out of extreme anger.
They overcome—that is, they defeat—that ignorant person. || 3 ||
For that blameless one in whom the knower— the self consisting of knowledge— abides in its own true nature, the senses, acting as friends out of contentment alone, do not strike him down.

The meaning is that, through contentment—acting like dear friends by generating a sense of satisfaction born from the realization of the true Self—the senses do not strike [the practitioner], but rather protect him by acting in accordance with the increase of knowledge. || 4 ||
Why does he, for whom there is no praise for an object that appears before him except through censure,
take up a body for the sake of bodily suffering? (The reading "duḥkhārta" occurs in both places.)

That man who, while acting and engaging in worldly affairs, never perceives any fault in objects of enjoyment and—apart from censure and reproach—never forms a notion of praise or excellence toward them, that man [takes up] the body for the sake of the suffering associated with the body. (Note: Both *duḥkhārthaṃ* and *duḥkhārtaṃ* are found as readings. The body.
For what reason does one grasp [it] as a self? The meaning is that there is no cause for it therein. || 5 ||
The self is not connected to the body, nor is the body in the self;
these two are mutually distinct, just like light and darkness. (6)
Now, in order to dispel the delusion of the identity between the body and the self, he introduces logical arguments beginning with the words "not the self" (nātma).

The intention is that since the body and the self are contradictory by virtue of being insentient and sentient respectively, even a relationship such as that of container and contained is difficult to establish; identity, however, is dismissed out of hand. || 6 ||
Permanently liberated from all modifications of existence and untainted, the Blessed Lord, the Self, neither sets nor rises; He is eternally risen.

Thus, he says "by all" (sarvaiḥ) [in verse 7], meaning that even due to the contradiction arising from such factors as being changeless versus being subject to change, there is no possibility of that [objection] applying.
"Let whatever happens to this dull-witted, ignorant, contemptible, ungrateful, and perishable body—this mere lump of flesh—be so. (8)
Having obtained the assistance of self-manifestation which is dependent upon itself, it is ungrateful because it causes suffering to that very self. (8)
How then can that which is always perceived as eternally consisting of consciousness [be so], when the comprehension of one of these two results in the very dullness of the other? (9)

Anticipating the objection that "let consciousness also be a property of the body alone, and thus there would be no contradiction," he says: "If that [consciousness] were possible [as a property of the body], then since another body remains as purely insentient (jaḍa), how could it assume consciousness, which is contrary to its own nature? This is the meaning. || 9 ||
Of what nature is the shared state of pleasure and pain between those two, who are always equal and possess identical dharmas? How could it ever be otherwise?

Now, one might argue: since the body is seen to become emaciated through the soul’s experience of mental suffering, and the soul is seen to experience suffering through the body’s being struck and so forth, their identity must exist because they are observed to share the same pleasure and pain. To this, he replies with the words "of those two": the soul and the body are like fire and an iron ball—identical and undifferentiated.
The meaning is as follows: because of the mutual exchange of their respective qualities, the two appear as if they possess identical qualities; yet, when separated, they never appear in that way.
Therefore, it is impossible to state what kind of shared experience of pleasure and pain they actually have, or how such a state could exist as ultimate truth. || 10 ||
Even if they were unattached and mutually joined together, how could the gross take on the form of the subtle, and how could the subtle become gross? (11)
Furthermore, since even the conjunction of the extremely subtle, unattached Self with the gross body is difficult to achieve, let alone their identity, he says: "Even as long as... (verse 11).
When one arises, there is no existence of a second during day and night;
knowledge does not become ignorance, nor does shadow turn into heat.
He states that there is no possibility of identity even because they are by nature mutually destructive: "eka... (verse 12).
The true Brahman does not become non-existent even amidst diverse views; nor is there even the slightest attachment for the embodied soul, though it is omnipresent. (13)

The true Brahman does not possess the nature of the unreal body and so forth; nor is there even the slightest connection between the existent embodied self—the inner witness who presides over the body—and the body superimposed upon it. || 13 ||
Just as there is no contact whatsoever between a lotus and the water, so too there is not even the slightest contact between the embodied one—who dwells within the body—and the body;

for Brahman has no connection with the existence of the body. [Regarding this, it is said: "What relation can there be between the Self of the world and that which possesses a body? Therefore, this succession of pleasure and pain is entirely in vain; from where could it arise?"
An interpolated verse is found in the printed edition. || 14 ||
Having already stated this, he speaks again—"by the body"—in order to provide an illustration. To the question "Why is there no connection [between the Self and the body]?

he replies with the words of the venerable teacher (Bhagavatpāda): "For where there is superimposition of one thing upon another, that [substratum] is not connected even in the slightest degree with the quality or defect produced by that [superimposed thing]. || 14 ||
Even though it has entered [the body], it does not participate in those [states], just as the sky is unaffected by the wind;
thus, old age, death, calamity, pleasure and pain, and existence and non-existence [do not affect it]. (15)
