The meaning is that because it does not function as such [i.e., like the body] and because it is untainted, the Self— which possesses a nature distinct from that [body], like the sky— does not possess even the slightest defects such as decay and so forth arising from the body and other factors, just as the sky is free from defects such as drying up, trembling, or being stained by dust due to the wind. || 15 ||
Not even the slightest [defilement] exists here; therefore, be at peace.

Even while remaining in the form of a body, there is only this great delusion consisting of the rising and falling of the cycle of existence. (Note: The reading "pātotpātamayo mahābhramaḥ" is also found.)

The meaning is that although one remains in the state of identifying the body as the self through the view of the body as the self (*dehātma-dṛṣṭi*), the delusion of birth, death, and so forth—when viewed from the perspective of Brahman as the Self—is seen as being nothing but Brahman within Brahman, like a mass of waves in water. || 16 ||
Only Brahman is seen, just as a collection of waves is seen in water;
for here, because it subsists upon the existence of the Self, it indeed experiences the Self.
This bodily machine exists like a wave arising from the mere presence of water; O dear one, depending on the movement of its support, it may either be agitated or remain still. (18)

Just as water, by its very nature, remains while appearing to undergo the state of being waves, so it is here. Just as when a reflection is disturbed by the movement of its substrate, there is not even the slightest disturbance in the sun or other source of light, so too, even when the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa) is disturbed by the body, there is no disturbance for the embodied one—the witness of the body; this is the meaning. || 18 ||

Just as the reflection of the sun and so forth [is seen] by means of a body, so too, when the reality of things is correctly perceived as it truly is, [knowledge] arises precisely with respect to that reality. (19)
When there is right vision, stability arises in the reality itself; the delusion of ignorance consisting of the body comes to an end.
(19) Stability consists of the delusion of knowledge regarding the body, and that too comes to an end;
through the knowledge of the body and the embodied one as they truly are, there is stability in the thing as it really is. (20)

Through the investigation into the two things as they truly are—the body and its witness, whose essential natures have been extracted as the ultimate reality—there arises, through knowledge, the state of the body being characterized by non-existence and the state of its witness being characterized by existence; that is, it becomes manifest. || 20 ||
The arising characterized by both existence and non-existence is like that between a lamp and the object illuminated by it;
for one who lacks right vision [the reading is *asamyagjñāninaḥ*], it occurs through the revolutions and counter-revolutions of the body.

"Because darkness is consumed and dispelled by a lamp, [the verse speaks of] 'from a lamp' (*dīpāt*) and 'a lamp' (*pradīpa*); the meaning is that these two possess a nature of mutual arising. Now, he elaborates with the words beginning "of one who does not see correctly" (*asamyagdarśinaḥ*) in order to censure the manner in which the ignorant perceive the world. (21)
Empty within, these trees of delusion—Arjuna and Pāda—thrive here;
they have not reflected upon their own true purpose, nor have they touched the essence of consciousness.
Those of dull intellect, being devoid of consciousness, quiver like blades of grass; because they have not tasted the true nature of the mind, all are as inert as earth, water, fire, and air.

"Impelled" means released by that volition (*cetanā*). [The suffix] *ini* is added to the noun *citi-* ending in the *ghañ* suffix to express the sense of possession (*matvartha*), from which *tal* is then applied. The underlying meaning is that it is not appropriate to say that volitions are non-conscious, being identical in nature to the body. If they were non-conscious, then how could they speak or engage in activities such as gathering grass and wood? To this, he replies with the words beginning "anāsvādita... (not tasted...).

The connection with the subsequent verse is as follows: although all those [reeds] are insentient, wherever they are overcome by the impulse arising from the hollows of their mouths, noses, and other apertures— by means of the winds moving through them like the sound of *kīcaka* reeds— they shriek, quiver, and move about.
Rising and falling here and there, they shriek and quiver;
they seize and cast away everything, including grass, wood, and the like.
Rich with sound, touch, and form, their limbs tremulous like waves;
though inert, they possess a radiant appearance and are filled with the abundant nectar of rasa. || 25 ||

They consider themselves wealthy and fulfilled merely by obtaining objects such as forms accompanied by sounds and touches; for them, the expansive "flavor" is their very attachment to sensual enjoyment, which intoxicates them like liquor. (25)
For all these [beings], who possess dwellings, births, and deaths like a great flood, this [nature] remains constant and imperishable, even for those of dull intellect.
Just as great rivers and the like, though insentient, are endowed with activities such as moving, coming, and going, so too are those of dull intellect.
Is it that they have no consciousness of the Self at all? No; rather, although it exists, it has become useless and ineffective due to lack of realization. Thus he says:
"But by the power of non-realization, she has fallen into a state of extreme wretchedness."
For the continuities of breath are like the bellows of an ignorant blacksmith.
"From the ignorant fool"—the phrase "issuing forth" is to be understood as the ellipsis. || 27 ||

They are seen to act only for the sake of mere agitation and not as performers of purposeful deeds, like the threatening gestures and roaring of a fool, or like the bow, the staff, and the string. (28)

It is for the sole purpose of stimulating the digestive fire (*jaṭharāgni*). Thus, he says that the threatening and roaring produced by a fool is not a sign of consciousness, because it is merely a cause for misfortune such as death, like the twanging of a bowstring:
"That which is devoid of conscious awareness is heard [only] for the sake of death."
Even the enjoyment of the fruit obtained from a fool is like that from a tree in the forest. || 29 ||
The enjoyment of the fruit is the attainment of the fruit. || 29 ||
Resting upon him is like resting upon a stone slab; association with him would be like being with a tree stump in a wilderness.
On a stone slab, on a heated stone slab—just so—and by a pillar from which the base of the tree has been cut away.
Whatever has been done for that purpose is like striking the sky with clubs;
what is given to such a base person—is it not as if it were thrown away into the mud?
That which was done was a favor rendered by himself. "With clubs" means with sticks; "struck" means beaten. || 31 ||
The conversation he had with him regarding the summoning of the dog from the sky was [the result of] ignorance;
for what calamity indeed does not befall one who lacks knowledge? (32)
*Kauleya* means a dog. The elision of the *ḍhak* suffix (which is prescribed by the rule *kulakukṣi-* etc. is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*).
This censure of ignorance is intended to demonstrate that ignorance is to be abandoned out of compassion, not out of hatred for the ignorant; with this intention, he says: "Ignorance... (verse 32).
This stream of saṃsāra flows for the ignorant due to negligence; for the ignorant, there are fierce sufferings as well as seemingly firm pleasures. (33)
They return again and again like mountains at the end of an eon, as they continue to maintain their attachment to the body, wealth, wife, and so forth. (34)
Like mountains, they were firm and difficult to overcome, [standing] against the plow or the chariot marked by the yoke. || 34 ||
This suffering of the ignorant is never stilled,
for he has conceived the notion of a self within this deceitful body which is not the self. (35)
How indeed can this illusion, consisting of the perception of the non-existent, ever perish for one of evil intent, whose mind is self-deceived, who is blind to reality, and of wicked intellect? (36)
One whose intellect is well-slain, bent down, and pervaded by wicked dispositions. || 36 ||
For one who possesses eyes and stumbles at every step upon a non-existent object,
poison arises from the moon, just as fragrance arises from a flower.
That is to say, for one with eyes who perceives that which is not a real thing—that which is a non-existent thing. || 37 ||

And as thorns emerge from the earth like sprouts of durva grass from the soil, so do these bodies arise from the milk of worldly existence; they are the silk-cotton trees for the female serpents of the body and the chains for the elephant of the mind. (38)

From milk (*payasaḥ*), which is *kṣīra*, the thorn (*kaṇṭaka*) comes forth—that is, it arises. Dwellers within the hollow of the *śālmali* tree characterized by the body—those who have become female serpents (*bhoginyaḥ sarpiṇībhūtāḥ*)—give birth to hopes (*āśāḥ*) that are serpents such as passion, greed, and dejection.
Alternatively, hopes, which serve as chains for the afflictions of the mind, give birth to sufferings.
Having conceived a distinction between the quarters based on the division of internal and external objects, two metaphors are to be applied. || 38 ||
The hopes of the ignorant spring forth like rice from well-tilled soil; here, ignorance is the splendor of hell, entwined by the serpents of evil deeds. (39)
From a well-tilled field; he who possesses no knowledge is "ignorant," and the splendor of hell protects—that is, awaits—him. || 39 ||
She protects him with joy, like a peahen guarding a rain-cloud;
her eyes are as restless as hovering bees, and her sprout-like lower lip quivers.
A woman blooms only for the sake of a fool, like a poisonous creeper; her tender shoots grow only in the heart of the ignorant, as if upon fertile ground. (41)
In the heart, which is the true ground characterized by the mind. || 41 ||
There exists the evil tree of passion, which provides shade for birds;
it has the leaves of trees that are like rising smoke, and its clusters of weapons are like firebrands.
He whose throbbing lips take the place of tree leaves from which flash the smoke of his sighs;

whose teeth, like a mass of weapons, crackle like firebrands; for whom hatred itself is a forest fire; and who, as it were, blazes and turns to ashes in the desert of the heart—that is, the waterless wilderness characterized by the mind. (42)
The forest fire of hatred blazes in the desert of the heart, causing calamity to the body;
it resides in the mind of the ignorant and envious, with slander of others as its foliage. (43)
In the mind that is filled with the water of stinginess, in the mental faculty of the ignorant person who possesses a stingy mind—this reading is correct. (43)
The lotus-pond of envy, with anxiety as its bees, blooms profusely;
it is agitated by the swirling waves of intense suffering that have been rubbed away in birth after birth. (44)

Wherein the delusions of the surging waves of intense suffering have been wiped away and cleansed by the gradual approach of various remedial means—that ocean consisting of water, which is inert and ignorant, and wherein the submarine fire (vāḍava) characterized by death [rages]—[that ocean he has crossed]. || 44 ||
The submarine fire of death repeatedly approaches that which is inert;
birth passes into childhood, childhood into youth, and youth into old age.
He states that birth and the subsequent stages result only in the attainment of further misfortune: "Birth... (45).
The fool alone undergoes old age and death again and again, plunging into this world—which is like a dilapidated water-wheel—by means of the cycle of rebirth. (46)
In an *āraghaṭṭa*, that is, in a machine, a water-wheel. || 46 ||

Through repeated submerging and emerging, the ignorant man becomes like a water-jar within the machine; yet to the intellect of the wise, this world is as fragile as the water filling a cow’s hoofprint.
"Goṣpadāpūra" means that which fills a cow's footprint; the meaning is that it consists mostly of very little water. || 47 ||
That very [intellect] of the Great-Souled One, which is shoreless, boundless, and unfathomable, appeared like the unseen [depths] of the ignorant man's long cavernous belly. (48)

For one who is not a great soul— whose vision of the self is limited to the body— the [ocean] becomes shoreless, boundless, and unfathomable. Therefore, like a blind man, the intellects of the ignorant do not reach the further, long shore of the ocean of saṃsāra, due to the bondage of attachment to filling the hollow of the belly and nourishing the stomach.
The syntactical connection is that they go forth. || 48 ||
They do not reach the further shore, like birds from a cage,
for they are the naves of the wheel of the burden of latent impressions whose transformation depends solely upon their own state of being.

To the question "Why do they not proceed there?", he says "bhāva... and so forth. According to the Vedic scripture: "The Self-existent One pierced the openings [of the senses] outward; therefore one looks outward, not at the inner self," those whose hearts and navels are overwhelmed by the burden of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) turned toward external objects alone, remain stuck in the mire of sense-objects.
The great rims of the wheel of birth—the groups of sense-faculties that serve as the very circumference—cannot be extracted, clarified, or purified. || 49 ||
The spokes of the wheel of birth cannot be made clear by the ignorant man, who, for the sake of the vultures that are the senses, has used his body as a quarry out of passion. (50)
By means of the vulture’s footprint, hawks useful for hunting are to be caught. "Tanu" refers to the succession of one's own bodies.
"From afar" means at all times and in all places, even across distant regions and times. "Rāgāt" means from the addiction to hunting. || 50 ||
In the forest of saṃsāra, the vision consisting of the mountain of the elements—which is merely a fragment of clay and flesh—is spread out like a lump of bait from afar. (51)

Regarding the use of the suffix *-vat* in the phrase "like a lump of meat," he says "consisting of elements" (*bhūta*) with the intention that, from the perspective of deluded vision, there is no similarity because there is no difference [between the perception and its object]. In reality, the vision— which consists of the elements (*bhūtamayī*), which abounds in living beings such as humans, cattle, and so forth, and which abounds in mountains such as the Himavat, Vindhya, and Malaya— is merely a fragment of flesh.

The phrase "consisting of mere particles of clay" is to be construed by dividing it and connecting it out of its sequential order. The meaning is that, solely due to delusion—which is the failure to investigate reality—one perceives [the world] through such conceptual constructions as "cow," "horse," "man," "mother," "brother," "Himalaya," "Malaya," and so forth.
Through delusion, it appears as a variegated coloring of infinite objects;
victorious is this wish-fulfilling tree of conceptual construction with its manifold volitions. (52)

Therefore, victorious is the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpapādapa), characterized by the formation of manifold mental constructs (analpa-saṃkalpa-kalanā), which possesses infinite delights through its various words and meanings. The meaning is that it exists in a state of supreme excellence because it is capable of fulfilling all desires, even by means of objects that are utterly non-existent. || 52 ||
Since the succession of leaves that is the world has issued forth from ignorance, it rests upon Him, shines within Him, enters into Him, and sports within Him. (53)

Now he describes that forest region of saṃsāra, pervaded by tens of millions of such wish-fulfilling trees (kalpavṛkṣa): Wherein the various births are the leaves and the web of karma is the bud; it is filled with diverse arrangements and abounds with serpents as its birds. (54)
*Parṇāni* means sprouts; *korakam* means a bud. The neuter gender is Vedic (*chāndasī*). || 54 ||
Merits and demerits are the fruits, and worldly power and splendor are the blossoms; clearly, these women are medicinal herbs that sprout when the moon of ignorance rises. 55.
In this forest tract of saṃsāra, whose characteristics have been thus described, the women, the medicinal herbs, and the creepers have attained supreme beauty. || 55 ||
In this forest grove of saṃsāra, they have attained supreme splendor;
yet it is filled with the multitude of the web of births, where darkness rises at the time of death.
He establishes the reason for ignorance being called "the moon" with the verse beginning *janma*: "At the time of darkness," meaning at the time of the setting of the sun of discrimination;

"in the void," meaning in Brahman which is devoid of phenomenal expansion (*niṣprapañca*), as well as in the physical sky; "one whose self has arisen," meaning shining forth; "the lord of the night," that is, of the night of defects (*doṣā*). || 56 ||
Victorious is the moon of ignorance, the lord of defects, whose nature arises from emptiness;
through the grace of this lunar ignorance, which abounds in the nectar of latent impressions (vāsanā). 57.
The playful female royal swans, their limbs cooled by frost, were gratified by that cakora bird who sought the nectar of the jewel of his mind. (58)

By him the cakora birds, characterized by their longing, were gratified and nourished. The jewel characterized by the mind is the sun; its essence is the nectar of tasting sense-objects. The meaning is that, just as the moon is filled during the bright fortnight by the nectar situated within the solar orb, so too [is the mind fulfilled]. || 58 ||
The lovely night-lilies of women shine, with their flickering eyes as bees, their dark tresses as the play of shadows, and their gleaming pale breasts. 59.
That women shine like jewels is a manifestation of his stupidity. (60)
That the nights—consisting of women who lack the marks of beauty (rāmā-lakṣaṇā-rajanī)—shine forth is merely the manifestation of the foolishness of those who behold them;
the sense is that they have transformed into the form of splendor, yet in reality, there is nothing beautiful therein whatsoever. || 60 ||

O Rāma, these are the various and abundant fruits that have spread forth from the tree of ignorance: they possess sweetness only at first sight, their essence is misfortune, they have both a beginning and an end, and they are fragile throughout their entire existence. (51)

Demonstrating that ignorance alone is the cause of all misfortune, he concludes with the verse beginning "āpāta": O Rāma, regarding sense objects, that which is well known— their sweetness only at first sight, their culminating in misfortune, their possession of a beginning and an end, their limitation by space, and their fragility and perishability in all states of existence.
All that consists of the various kinds of fruits of the tree characterized by ignorance;
these have spread out in the form of the world through the succession of seeds and sprouts. Therefore, the sense is that ignorance alone is its root and must be eradicated. || 61 ||

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Greatness of Delusion," in the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa* of the *Mokṣopāyas*, spoken by the Divine Messenger, within the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki. || 6 ||
Thus ends the sixth canto, titled "The Greatness of Delusion," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The Seventh Canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Those women shine, adorned with strings of pearls and decorated with jewels.
When the moon of intoxication has risen, the waves of the milk-ocean of Love are stirred. || 1 ||

The manifestations of ignorance are described here in detail: how desire and the like bring about the perception of worthiness, purposefulness, and beauty in things that are actually worthless and harmful.

In this regard, with the intention that women— who strip away all discernment and cause one to fall immediately into the pit of misfortune— are indeed the great manifestations of ignorance and desire, he first describes them alone, beginning with the words "That which...
This relative pronoun *yat* (that which) is connected to every single verse in each individual sentence.
The connection [of the phrase] "that is the manifestation of ignorance" (*tadajñānavijṛmbhitam*) occurs in the second half-verse near the end of the sixty-seventh canto.

When the moon characterized by intoxication has risen, that which appears like the waves of the agitated ocean of the milk of desire in women—that is the manifestation, the power, of ignorance; this should be applied to each sentence. || 1 ||
The eyes of the women, swaying upon the surface of their cheeks, possess the beauty of a swarm of bees hovering over the interior of a golden lotus.
That they maintain such a view is likewise a manifestation of ignorance. || 2 ||
In the garden groves during the springtime, when the earth is moistened by rut,
the lovely flowers shine like servants of the god of love.

In the springtime of Madhu, within the forest groves, upon the trees, and on the ground, the servants of the Mind-born God—having become intoxicated with honey and having generated madness in lovers—seem as if they have been commanded to act. || 3 ||
Women who are like flesh-eating vultures, jackals, and dogs with mangled limbs are compared to the moon, sandalwood, and lotuses. (4)

Carnivores are those such as tigers and others that feed exclusively on raw flesh; however, vultures, jackals, and the like eat food such as cooked grain when it is available, which is why they are mentioned again. || 4 ||
The row of a woman’s breasts appears like golden jars, lotus buds, or citrons, yet it is red, putrid, and foul-smelling. (5)
The row of breasts of women, which possesses a fragrance that is actually the stench of blood and pus, appears like golden jars and the like; this is merely a manifestation of ignorance. || 5 ||
A fleshy fragment called a lip, moistened with saliva, is compared to the liquid of honey-filled bimba-fruit wine, which flows from the moon of elixir.
The flow from the moon is nectar. || 6 ||
With their small, knobby protrusions resembling the shape of a camel's hump, and their arms like cruel bone-stakes,
they are described by auspicious poets using the metaphor of great, vine-like arms.
When analyzed individually according to their appearance, there are very small bones at the joints; those having that shape and designated by the term "arms" are the cruel bone-pikes. || 7 ||
Filled with thighs as beautiful as the massed trunks of plantain trees,
the row of arches shines, providing the joy appropriate for the beauty of her breasts.

Likewise, that a girdle— which serves as a festoon for the gateway of the temple of Love— shines forth from her, who possesses such beautiful women whose abundant equipment consists of nothing but plantain trunks, and from whom the joy of the eyes of beholders is appropriate for the beauty of their jar-like breasts; this too is a manifestation of ignorance.
As before. || 8 ||
Even prosperity, which is slow and sweet at its onset, fraught with the succession of dualities in its middle,
and fleeting and sparse at its end, is nonetheless desired.

At the outset—that is, at the beginning—it is sweet for the dull-witted, or perhaps only slightly sweet at first. In the middle—that is, at the time of its expenditure—it follows after the dualities of passion, hatred, and so forth. Its end is swift, meaning its destruction is rapid. Since it is seen only among a few people, such fortune is rare; that even this [fortune] is desired, as before. (9)
The mind encounters both suffering and happiness, which branch out into a hundred directions;
yet it is the branches of suffering that arise as the various fruits of karma, while prosperity is their fruit. (10)

Whatever suffering one encounters, whatever happiness spreads into a hundred branches, and whatever glories—which are the fruits of various karmas—arise with sufferings as their very branches; all that is also [transient], as previously stated. (10)
The words situated within the dense thicket of their expansion resemble ropes for the purpose of binding, appearing like thick nets. (11)

With the intention that if ignorance is the manifestation of the Śruti, then the words of the *Karmakāṇḍa* which incite one toward those optional rites (*kāmyakarman*) that are its fruit must all the more be so, he says: "bound" (*baddhā*). Like creepers situated in a dense forest characterized by the expansion (*pratāna*) of optional rites.

Dense and thick in form due to being bound by various nets of fruits and desires, they thus stand like ropes for guarding the prison of those bound by karma—the gods and others who are debtors. They resemble the lips, which are the coverings (*chada*) of the teeth (*data*); that is to say, they are characterized primarily by passion and fickleness. Such are they.

The meaning is that even the words of the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa) are but the manifestation of ignorance. In the compound, the non-elision of the case-ending and the visarga after the word *chandaḥ* are Vedic (archaic). This has been made clear by the Blessed One in the Gītā, beginning with the verse: "This flowery speech which... (Gītā 2.42). || 11 ||
Like the Yamunā river in the monsoon season— dark as the gloom of night, spreading a torrent of water, and emitting a thick mist of delusion— it remains for a long time, scorching all.

With the intention that it would be as improper— as forcing a blind man or a madman who is already falling into a well by himself to fall even more forcefully— to urge with scripture those who have already engaged in desirable objects out of their own delusion,
he shows their self-initiated activity arising from delusion with the verse beginning "saṃtata... [referring to] actions.

The river of worldly activity (pravṛtti), spreading wide with its characteristic downpours, is a vast mist characterized by delusion; naturally dark, it becomes turbid with passion (rajas) during the rainy season, and even more intensely darkened by the gloom of night. Just as the Yamunā flows, so too does this [delusion] flow of its own accord. The meaning is that, having blinded the person, it causes them to engage with sense objects. || 12 ||
With his inner heart made bitter by various pleasures,
he grows while devoid of affection, like the taste of the poison of rebirth.
And as one becomes engaged in enjoyments, attachment increases toward sense objects, children, grandchildren, and so forth; thus he says: "Bitterly," etc.

Because they are skilled in various pleasures only at first sight, yet result in suffering in the end and generate hatred, envy, anxiety, and the like, [he describes them] as being such that their affection has departed.
With the inner heart made bitter, passion—which, like the sap of a poisonous creeper characterized by rebirth, provides the growth of its shoots—increases. || 13 ||
Driven by the winds of their own karma, the rows of leaves scattered throughout the world— shaken, withered, and strewn about— blow away as various kinds of dust from the refuse heaps.
And then, with the intention that a succession of sorrows from separation follows the death of sons and others in due order, he says:

[the trees] are such that their rows of leaves are the very groups of attendants consisting of sons and so forth; likewise, they possess various kinds of fragments of dust like refuse, which—like the varieties of mental distraction (*vikṣepa*) that steal away the vision of discernment (*viveka*)—are characterized by the ripening of one's own evil karma.
The winds blow. || 14 ||
This Time, whose belly has the habit of devouring all, is not satiated even by kalpas, though it has swallowed the infinite worlds like ripe fruits. 15.
Then, thinking "death will come even to me," one is thus always entering the mouth of death through the succession of births;
so he says: "Time" (verse 15).
Having drunk the wind of delusion through their skin,
the various serpents here, moving restlessly, quiver with a cool mountain-like radiance.
Thus, he perceives these ignorant living beings as serpents through the lens of their lack of benefit—[expressed by the verse beginning] "moha" (delusion).

The luminous manifestations of the cool, immovable Brahman—which is devoid of the threefold heat—are like the various serpents in this worldly existence. Why is that? Because these [beings], having drunk in and filled themselves with the wind characterized by delusion (*moha*), [wander about].

Furthermore, they remain characterized by a skin marked by various bodily features that are being separated [from them]; moving unevenly and following crooked paths, they quiver—the meaning being that they move about. || 16 ||
Afflicted by the demoness of anxiety and lacking the rising moon of solitude, the night of youth passes away as if in total darkness, devoid of light. (17)

With the intention that youth, though attained in every birth, passes away in vain because it is not employed for the means of liberation—such as discernment (*viveka*), dispassion (*vairāgya*), and hearing the scriptures (*śravaṇa*)—he says "Cintā" (Thought). The words "of them" (*teṣām*) are to be supplied to complete the sense. || 17 ||
My tongue has become worn out by the fevers of vulgar entreaties,
like a thread situated within the hollow of a lotus bud that is frozen by the cold.

Thus, he demonstrates the futility and harmfulness of his tongue and other organs with the verse beginning "jihvā" (the tongue). The "conciliation" (*anunaya*) of common, vulgar people—such as wives, sons, and others—refers to the removal of their anger; the "stitches" (*sūtrapada*) caused by the fevers and torments resulting from that [conciliation] serve to justify the comparison to a tongue. By the word "stitch," the inner petal firmly held by it is indicated. This has been stated.
This same principle should be understood to apply to the limbs as well, such as the eyes and so forth. || 18 ||
The sturdy śālmali tree of poverty, with suffering and grief as its great roots and hardships and thorns as its dense undergrowth, spreads out a thousand branches.
The stones are the knots. || 19 ||
Having made his dwelling in the temple of the mind— which is empty within and whose loftiness has been destroyed—
the owl of greed prowls about during the night thick with illusion.

Because it does not rely upon any real entity, the tree of the mind— characterized by a hollow interior and a cavity, bent down by the weight of its own loftiness, and serving as a dwelling place— is situated there during the thick night of illusion, the darkness of the waning fortnight. (20)
Having first seized it with her ears and trembling, she who is certain [of her intent]— old age, like a decrepit female cat, devours the mouse of youth. (21)
Previously, at the time of beginning [the rite], having grasped the two cheeks adjacent to the ears with both ears... || 21 ||
This creation, devoid of essence and having gradually surpassed the height of the mountains, attains fullness like a mass of foam. (22)

Furthermore, he demonstrates the expansion of creation arising solely from ignorance with the verse beginning "niḥsārā" and so forth. It is that which has gradually transcended—that is, begun to be fashioned—possessing an elevation like that of the mountain among mountains (the Himalayas).
Such is the well-known creation, the perception of the world, which is like a mass of foam or froth. || 22 ||
The creeper of existence, white with the flowers of radiance, adorned with the sprouts of the world, has blossomed, bearing the fruits of dharma and artha. || 23 ||

The "appearance" (ābhāsa) is the illumination of the reflection of consciousness; the creeper is existence, characterized by being white and radiant with the flowers that possess those characteristics, and defined by empirical reality. || 23 ||
The house of the three worlds is upheld—beautiful, with Mount Sumeru as its great pillar, the moon and sun as its windows, and the sky as its roof. (24)
That [palace] which has the great mountains, characterized by Mount Sumeru, as its pillars (stambhas), and whose roof (chadi) is nothing other than movement. 24.
In the vast lake of saṃsāra, the bees that are living beings move about within the lotuses that are bodies, drinking the nectar of the nature of consciousness.

The meaning is as follows: in the vast and expansive lake of saṃsāra, the bee-like vital breaths (prāṇa) move about within the lotuses of bodies, habitually drinking the nectar of the consciousness-form situated therein; for the Śruti declares, "Other beings subsist on a mere portion of this very bliss," and "Born of bliss, they live by bliss," and so forth. (25)
The lamp of the sun shines within the interior of the belly of the world, resting exclusively upon the great sapphire pavement of the path of the sky.

On a vast artificial ground fashioned from sapphire, characterized by the path of the sky, the sun-lamp—exquisite within the belly of the world, most beautiful, and shining with singular grace—is radiant; yet even that is a manifestation of ignorance, as it is everywhere [declared]. 26.
The world is like a decrepit bird, its limbs bound by the thread of hope,
confined within the cage of the senses fastened inside the pegs of its own latent impressions (vāsanā).

The Jāgatī, characterized by the multitude of living beings within the world, is like an aged bird; that it is bound to the cage of the senses—the body—by the pegs of its own latent impressions (vāsanās), is also [the case]. (27)
Touched by the wind, the creeper of worldly existence— consisting of a succession of leaves that have become like an unceasingly falling net— has trembled for a long time.
She was touched and shaken by the vital breath (prāṇa) of the Maruts. || 28 ||
For a short time after creation, those of noble lineage were filled with joy; they had cast down the mire of the fierce hells and were for a moment freed from all doubt. (29)

Furthermore, it is as if the Creator, in order to clearly demonstrate [the consequences] in the netherworld (pātāla), fashioned the fierce hells and their mud; yet, even while existing there, they are free from the fear of falling into them, and thus they are joyful—this too is as explained previously. Alternatively, through the superimposition of identity with one's own self, they are as if made low or disregarded, yet they remain fierce (ugra).

The meaning is this: those who, despite having bodies that are a mire of hellish filth consisting of blood, flesh, excrement, urine, and so forth, are nonetheless delighted by such conceits as "we are of noble lineage," "we are great-souled," and so on, being free from any fear of that [mire]. || 29 ||
Within the lake of the path to heaven, where moss-like clouds float upon the surface and fragments of the moon’s orb serve as pebbles, the divine nectars shimmer with exquisite flavor.
Furthermore, that which flashes forth as the gods—the deities who are like cranes—dwelling in the lake situated upon the cloudless path that characterizes heaven; that too.
Stained by various fruits and mangoes, garlanded with a web of latent impressions (vāsanā), filled with the fragrance of vibration, expansive, and possessing bees that blossom through action— (31)
And even that lotus-pond, characterized by ritual actions, which was once soiled by bees in the form of various desired fruits, has now blossomed. || 31 ||
The wretched fish of worldly existence, quivering in the pond of saṃsāra, is seized by the deceitful, aged vulture of Death. 32.
The *śapharī* is a species of small fish known by the name *proṣṭhī*. || 32 ||
Like a garland of waves and foam, that very same thing appears as something else, fragile and transient;
day by day, a variety of forms arises like the crescent of another moon.
Day after day, it is different in measure every single day, like the crescent of the moon. || 33 ||
This wheel is being turned around by the potter Time, who fashions the many beings as its clay shards, all subject to momentary destruction.
They are subject to momentary destruction and perish before long. || 34 ||
Incalculable eons have passed in the immovable state; the dense thickets of the world-forest have been consumed by the fire of the cosmic age. (35)
For kalpas capable of all worldly transactions, in the immovable state of Brahman, by the fire of the age, the fire at the end of the age. || 35 ||
Through endless states of existence and non-existence, and through hundreds of conditions of pleasure and pain, the worldly condition thus undergoes perpetual transformation. (36)
The opposite is transformation. || 36 ||
The fortitude of one who has not awakened to the Buddha was not broken by the tossing of world-ages, nor by the chains of latent tendencies, nor by the falls of great thunderbolts. (37)

To the question, "Even when such a succession of misfortunes is witnessed, why do the ignorant not feel world-weariness? he says: "Because their fortitude, characterized by the firmness of ignorance, has not been shattered by anyone"—this is the meaning. (37)

The latent impression (vāsanā) bears the body of Indra, which was praised by the sons of Danu who had fled by the hundreds, and whose speed was broken due to the destruction [of his power] by Śiva. (38) *Note: "bhavabhagnatayā" is a form derived from the root *gam* (to go), meaning "due to being broken by Bhava. An alternative reading is "bhagnarayām," meaning "whose speed was broken."*

With the intention of showing by what other means there could possibly be the destruction of that latent impression (*vāsanā*) which— despite the sublation of ignorance through knowledge— maintains a body such as that of Indra for the duration of a *manvantara* due to the force of the *prārabdha* karma of its office, he provides this illustration:
"They maintain and protect [it] again out of a desire for battle."

The meaning is this: even that very body of Indra—which was praised by the sons of Danu who had likewise fled from their enemies, and whose momentum regarding rebirth and such matters had been broken—was still carried by his latent impressions (vāsanā), which means it continued to be maintained as long as his office lasted. || 38 ||
This whirlwind of destiny constantly enters the throat of the serpent of Time, where a continuous succession of dust-like created beings falls incessantly. (39)

In this world, where the creation of beings is like a succession of dust particles, there is a whirlwind characterized by destiny that enters the throat of the serpent characterized by Time; this is a poetic fancy (utprekṣā), based on the well-known fact that serpents feed upon air.
All things are like fruits and foam in the waters of worldly objects, floating everywhere.
They fall incessantly into the mouth of the submarine fire of non-existence.
Non-existence is destruction; even that which falls into its characteristic mark, the mouth of the submarine fire (vaḍavāgni), [is likewise destroyed]. || 40 ||
The powers of various substances, suddenly aroused and throbbing,
arise as if they were merely the inherent nature of things, like the beauty of the movement of water.
The very nature of one's own being—the existence of the substratum—is established and has attained its own form merely by that much;
yet, that which flashes forth and expands, having been stirred up and set in motion by the accidental and inconceivable variety of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), that too [is the same]. 41.
The lion of Death, with his mane bristling, devours even the vast and numerous young elephants of the world, which are filled with the pearls of living beings.
He also gave away young elephants and rutting tuskers. || 42 ||

The birds of the world are born, die, and live; they have the great mountain ranges for their perches, masses of clouds for their wings, and the fruits [of existence] for their straight paths. || 43 ||

The principal mountain ranges, such as the Himavat and others, are the "fruits" because they are objects of enjoyment and because of their great size; those [clouds] have "wing-flocks" which are actually clouds, due to the similarity between them and the form of moving through the sky. They are called *phalāmṛjaḥ* because they "wipe," that is, they completely cleanse and gather the fruits. The suffix *ka* is applied to the root *mṛj* by virtue of its frequent occurrence (*bāhulaka*). They go.

The meaning is that the constant wandering of the worlds along the paths of the northern and southern solstices and so forth, and the fact that living beings— those "birds" characterized by such [wandering]— are born in it, die in it, are sustained in it, and live therein until death, is all a manifestation of ignorance. In this regard, [the text refers to] the base, middle, and summit portions of the principal mountain ranges (kulācala).

One should understand that because they are to be enjoyed by *nāgas*, mortals, and gods, there is a poetic conceit (*utprekṣā*) of the clouds being "fruits"; and because they facilitate upward and downward movement through their nature as smoke, mist, clouds, and so forth during the stages of the southern solstice path, there is a poetic conceit of them being "wings.
Upon the wall of consciousness, which is bright with vibration, by means of the five colors of the sense organs—
The painter of destiny unfolds the variegated pictures of saṃsāra.
Relying on the doctrine of *dṛṣṭisṛṣṭi* (creation as perception), he says: "Cid" [consciousness].

Because its obscuration has been removed by the "spandais"—that is, by the pervasions of the functions of the eyes and other senses—it is "śubhrāyām" (in that which is pure). With the "raṅgaiḥ"—meaning with the five external senses, which stand in the place of coloring substances—he "vidadhāti," meaning he creates by mere perception.
He alone is the ordainer, the witness, and the painter.
Constantly moving, effecting all transformations,
possessing parts that constitute a hundredth part of a moment, and whose sprouts are difficult to accomplish through falsehood.

Regarding that creation through vision (*dṛṣṭisṛṣṭi*), he first demonstrates the distinction in the experience of the stationary and the moving beings by means of two verses beginning with "ajasra" (uninterrupted). The species of stationary beings [perceive] their own emergence— the illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) in the form of the world— as a subtle [power] characterized by attributes such as being uninterrupted, fleeting, and so forth.
The meaning of the two [verses] is that they remain having observed the measurement of time through meditation alone—an internal experience incapable of manifest external conventional usage. || 45 ||
Having perceived through meditation alone this subtle calculation of time that brings about their own arising, these stationary species remain established [in their state]. (46)
All classes of moving beings are worn out by the disease of old age and death, which arises from passion and hatred and consists of existence and non-existence. (47)
Next, he demonstrates the distinction among mobile beings with the verse beginning "rāga" (passion), etc. || 47 ||
On the surface of the earth, those who practiced the highest meditation with great wickedness are inevitably bound for a fixed period of time and tormented as rows of worms. (48)
Among those as well, he shows the intensity of the experience of suffering of worms, insects, and so forth, along with its cause: "those whose nature it is to move about" (tathāvidhāḥ). || 48 ||
In an instant, this serpent of Time— whose hole is difficult to perceive, who possesses vast coils, and who is full of ease— swallows this entire world while remaining invisible.

Based on the Vedic scripture stating, "Whatever he created, he resolved to devour," [the author] says "in an instant" (kṣaṇena) to show that the state of being swallowed by Time is common to both the stationary and the moving. || 49 ||
At times, appearing somewhat agitated by their own bodies,
they were intensely affected by cold, wind, and heat, yet possessed the brilliance of blossoming flowers.

Thus, he shows that among stationary beings (*sthāvara*), the specific characteristics are the possession of a transformation of fruits, flowers, and so forth at a fixed time, and the capacity to endure unavoidable cold, wind, heat, and the like—expressed by the verse beginning with "by time" (*kālena*) for one and a half verses. A "cavity" (*śvabhra*) is a hole in the earth; [the body] has entered therein.

Those immobile beings whose very roots constitute their bodies, having perceived some consumer—whether human, bird, snake, or other—and taking that as a cause, dwell in their own bodies being agitated and afflicted; yet, according to the distinctions of seasons such as spring, they possess the splendor of blossoming flowers and yield fruits. For this very reason:

Those possessed of virtue—endowed with austerity, tranquility, self-control, forbearance, magnanimity, and other such qualities—conduct themselves as if they were virtuous men and pass their time accordingly. || 50 ||
Those endowed with virtuous conduct move about here bestowing fruits, their bodies like those of serpents within the hollow of the lotus that is the three worlds, where the masses of water rest.

Now, having conceptualized the three worlds as a triad of lotuses, he imagines the multitude of living beings therein as a swarm of bees with the following half-verses beginning with *payaḥ*. Although it is well known from the Purāṇas and other sources that the earth alone is established upon the water like a lotus leaf, while the intermediate space and the celestial realm are not, nevertheless—
The word *paṭala* is used to indicate that, because it is an effect of water composed of the three elements (*trivṛtkṛta*), it indeed exists as established upon a portion of water. 51.
The venerable Goddess Kālī, whose very nature is action, is a basket for the bees that are living beings; she makes a great humming sound with this vessel of alms, which is the cosmic egg.

*Ghuṅghumam* means the humming sound of *guñjā* seeds. *Bhramarapeṭikā* means a swarm of bees. Now, he imagines that the activity of living beings—which is certain to bear fruit—is Kālī herself, the universe is her begging bowl, and the fourfold collection of elemental beings is her alms-food—expressed in the verse beginning with "brahmāṇḍa. Kālī is the female form of Time (*kāla*), who has previously accepted [the universe].
The meaning is that she repeatedly gave the alms of the spirits to her own husband, Kāla, and having given them again and again, desired to take other and further alms of the spirits. || 52 ||
Having herself given and indeed given away the alms of all beings, she desires to seize them back;
she whose tresses are the false darkness and whose restless eyes are the sun and moon. (53)
Now, he describes the three worlds—which are the fruit of his creative action—as being like an aged woman, beginning with the verse starting "timira...
The word *alīka* is used in the sense of a pretext. (53)
She who contains Brahmā, Upendra, Mahendra, and others, as well as the earth and the best of mountains;
she who is the sole repository of the reality of Brahman; she whose breasts hang down. (54)

Brahmā, Upendra, Mahendra, and the rest [are Her manifestations] by virtue of their internal conscious nature; while the earth, the great mountains, and so forth, are [Her manifestations] by virtue of their external, gross, and insentient nature. She is that whose single Brahma-reality, like a swelling within the heart, is always concealed and protected from being revealed by the bonds [of worldly existence]. (54)
The power of consciousness (cicchakti) is the mother-essence (mātṛkā), gross yet flickering, as fickle as a dense cloud;
she has the multitude of stars for her teeth, and the earth is more ruddy than the twilight. 55.
The power of consciousness (cicchakti) is the manifestation of consciousness (cidābhāsa); she alone is its nourisher, like a mother. For this very reason, she is "gross" (sthūlā). 55.
Holding all the lotus-ponds in her hands, with the city of Indra as her face,
she has the seven oceans as her pearl necklace and is enveloped in dark blue garments.

She whose hands are all the lotus-creepers; she is enveloped by the blue sky, which is her very garment and upper robe (*uttarīya*). [The form *parīvṛtā* is derived from the root *vṛñ* with the suffix *kvip*, where the lengthening of the vowel occurs according to the rule *nahivṛtivṛdhītyādinā pare dīrghaḥ*. According to the opinion of Bhāguri, the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is applied by the rule *āpaṃ caiva halantānām*. 56.
The great navel of Jambudvīpa, with the beauty of its forest as its line of body hair,
having come into being again and again, perishes like an aged woman of the three worlds.
Having repeatedly perished and been born again, causing great delusion,
she is now submerged by others in the terrifying great ocean of time, only to emerge once more.
Now he describes time by way of its being like a great ocean—with the verse beginning "immersed" (magnam). The two suffixes [niṣṭhā] are used in the sense of the action itself (bhāve). || 58 ||
At every moment, as each kalpa passes, the bubble-like universes perish; thus, in time, within the flow of the unfathomable ocean, they remain for a while and then again and again [reappear]. (59)

The *kalpas* themselves are the *kṣaṇas*. This is an *avyayībhāva* compound used in the sense of repetition (*vīpsā*). It refers to that [ocean] in which there flows an unfathomable stream of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), which is a stream of the water of thirst for thousands of delusions. || 59 ||
The cranes that are the causes [of creation] have flown away in the blink of an eon;
the lightnings of creation, having arisen again and again, are destroyed and scorched.
The essence of Hiraṇyagarbha is the cause. From the connection with the *sārasa* (crane), the imagination of Time as a "crying" (*nadat*) entity is understood.
He imagines it as a cloud: "arising again and again," etc. (60).
In the dark cloud of time, these efforts of the light of consciousness flash forth;
like birds of living beings falling from it, they descend in incessant wandering.
"Vana" is the act of choosing or resorting to; "vananā" is the effort toward that [resorting] by means of which there is the power of illumination.
This is according to the Vedic scripture: "By its light all this shines. (61)
From the exceedingly violent drumbeat of Time, the lords of the gods— the guardians of the fruit that is the cosmic egg— brought forth the creations of Brahmā through their opening of the eyes.

From the lofty *tāla* tree, characterized by its height and dark color, living beings—meaning creatures—and birds characterized as such, namely crows, are falling; likewise, rows (*pālayaḥ*) of fruits characterized as the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) are falling. Because it indicates that the cause is unexpected, the maxim of "the crow and the palm fruit" (*kākatālīya-nyāya*) is here employed as a poetic fancy (*utprekṣita*).
The leaders of the gods are those known as Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva. || 62 ||
Somewhere there are certain beings who effect destruction in the blink of an eye; by the mere opening and closing of their eyes, they cause thousands of networks of kalpas to perish.
Furthermore, some Rudras exist within that supreme consciousness;
yet even they come into being and cease to be in the twinkling of his eye.
Even those Rudras [are absorbed] in the supreme, ultimate cause, which is of the nature of consciousness. 64.
Even such a Lord of Gods exists, for this state of activity is infinite within the void of Brahmā’s station, which consists of infinite volitions.
This state of ritual action, ending with Rudra, is the state of the existence of the fruits of karma and upāsanā; it is infinite and innumerable.
If one asks, "How is this possible?", [the author] says "infinite" (anantā) with the intention that since everything is possible within Māyā, no lack of possibility is appropriate here. || 65 ||

What powers indeed do not exist that fill the world with variety? Thus, this worldly conceptualization, which shines with the weight of objects obtained through unexhausted volitions, is the manifestation of ignorance. (66)
They are the fulfillers of a thousand wonders. He concludes the expansion of the manifestations of ignorance:
"Those prosperities which are, in fact, continuous calamities; those afflictions of childhood, youth, old age, and death;
and that immersion in successions of pleasure and pain—these are the manifestations of the intense darkness of ignorance."

Thus ends the seventh canto, titled "The Greatness of Ignorance," in the Nirvāṇa Section of the Means to Liberation, spoken by the Divine Messenger, in the glorious Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa of Valmīki, composed in the style of the Ṛṣis. || 7 ||
Thus ends the seventh canto, titled "The Greatness of Ignorance," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The Eighth Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
In this forest tract of worldly existence, situated on the slope of the mountain of consciousness, [the mind] dwells.
Of what nature is this creeper called the ignorance of creation, and when did it blossom? (1)
The causal ignorance, whose manifestations are the worlds, has been described;
here, the effect-ignorance is described as being like a creeping vine in the forest of worldly existence.

Therein, having first indicated the subject matter, he introduces the manner of description with the verse beginning "saṃsāra... (The world...). Consciousness itself, being immutable (*kūṭastha*), is the mountain; the ignorance of manifestation, situated on its slope, is called "creation-ignorance" (*sṛṣṭyavidyā*) in order to distinguish it from causal ignorance (*kāraṇāvidyā*). The phrase "at what time and of what nature?
is intended to illuminate the variety of its expansion through the divisions of time. "We shall describe that; let it be heard"—this is the ellipsis to be supplied. || 1 ||
This slender body of hers, which illuminates the three worlds, is rich with joints as large as great mountains and is enveloped by the skin of the cosmic egg.

The great mountains, such as Meru and others, are themselves the "joints" (parvaṇi), meaning the articulations of the sections; she is enriched by them. By the term "egg of Brahmā" (brahmāṇḍa), its coverings are understood; she is completely enveloped by their characteristic "skins. She is "verdant" (kāsinī) with worlds—that is, with people—like the blossoming of leaves, sprouts, and so forth. This triple world is her slender body, her physical form. || 2 ||
Pleasure, pain, existence, non-existence, knowledge, and ignorance—these are the extensive branches and the roots and fruits within this [tree]. (3)
Existence is birth; state is persistence. Here, within this creeper of ignorance, there are extensive functions whose nature is to increase day by day. (3)
From pleasure, ignorance arises intensely, and it yields that very same thing at the end; from pain, ignorance arises intensely, and it fully bears that very fruit.

He establishes the nature of being a root and a fruit with respect to pleasure and so forth by means of the passage beginning with "sukhāt" (from pleasure). From the pleasure of prosperity and the like that is currently being experienced, there arises an ignorance characterized by passion in the form of the thought, "May I have even greater prosperity than this in the future. And that [ignorance], through the medium of dharma such as sacrifice and charity, bears the fruit of pleasure. And from the suffering of poverty and the like...

Ignorance, characterized by thirst for wealth and so forth, arises. And that [ignorance], through the door of engaging in unrighteous acts such as improper acceptance of gifts and theft due to sinful latent impressions (*vāsanā*), results in even greater suffering than before;
this should be understood in all cases. The particle *eva* (only/just) is to be construed out of its position in every instance, to be joined as "it certainly bears fruit" (*phalaty eva*). || 4 ||
This ignorance arises from existence and clearly bears fruit for that very existence;
it attains being through existence and bears fruit for that very existence in an instant. (5)
Through ignorance it increases, and that indeed becomes its manifest fruit;
through knowledge it brings about true realization, and that alone it bestows in the end.

Through knowledge— that is, through the inquiry into the reality of the inner self— there arises an expansion of knowledge characterized by ascending to ever-higher stages, culminating finally in the seventh stage.
Her body, possessing various kinds of delight and abounding in joy, expands, shimmering with dense sprouts.
Having established the incidental point, he describes the creeper under discussion itself with the verse beginning "of various kinds" (nānāvidha). || 7 ||
This [world-tree] has the days for its blossoming flowers, the nights for its restless bees,
and it is constantly quivering as the sprouts of living beings fall away.

He elaborates on this [description] as "full of various delights" and so forth: she is one whose sprouts are the living beings—the creatures themselves—who fall and rush about due to passion and other afflictions. (8)
Coming again and again, it falls upon the discerning faculty at times;
though shaken off and its dust removed, it returns once more to its attachment.
Having arrived again and again, having been whirled about repeatedly by the wind of karma,

it eventually falls upon the female elephant characterized by discernment (viveka) at some particular part of the sprout-like faculty of authority. And by that [female elephant], through the tip of her trunk of inquiry, it is shaken and tossed about by the uprooting of the tree of objects that serve as its support.

Though she has shaken off the dust of worldly existence and cast away the pollen of evil latent impressions, by fate she has fallen from his hand and once again becomes attached to the young trees of sensory objects.
Abounding with sprouting coral shoots, bristling with newly formed buds, endowed with the flowers of every season, and possessing the fullness of all essences. (10)
Rich with the spreading branches of friends, cattle, and the like being born, and bristling with the sprouts of sons, grandsons, and others already born, her face is radiant with the smile of bliss.
It flows incessantly with the streams of birth, it is eager for the openings of destruction,
it is filled with the essence of the expansion of enjoyments, and it is gnawed by the woodworm of solitary reflection.

At the joints characterized by birth, it is densely packed and without space due to the snakes of suffering, disease, and the like; at the joints of the branches characterized by destruction—namely deaths—it is as if forcibly torn asunder, being restless and agitated; and it is filled with the nectar of passion for the experience (*ābhoga*) of enjoyments (*bhoga*), that is, sense objects. (11)
The circles of the moon and sun blooming daily on all sides are, it is said, her flowers, tossed by the wind in the sky; these are indeed the planets. 12.
He explains what was stated—that it is "endowed with flowers of all seasons"—with the words "blooming. The planets (*graha*) take the form of the nine planets;
together with the moon and the sun, they are "rows" (*āvalayaḥ*), meaning lines of luminaries. || 12 ||
O descendant of Raghu, the stars are the blossoms that have reached the state of buds upon this [night], which has filled the hollow of the sky with their shimmering forms.
The light of the moon, sun, and fire is but the floral pollen of this [Goddess];
for by this, she—whose limbs are as radiant as the Ruru deer—draws away the hearts of men like a woman. 14.

That [city] is renowned for having the light and radiance of the moon, the sun, and fire; it draws the hearts [of people] by means of this well-known *kausuma* pollen—that is, the dust associated with flowers. The meaning is that it appears captivatingly beautiful. 14.
Shaken by the elephant of the mind, with the warbling cuckoo of conceptualization, crowded with the serpents of the senses, and stained by the bark of craving. (15)

Having attained height by resting upon the body of the Tamāla tree against the blue sky, she stands as a firm pillar supporting the two worlds (Heaven and Earth), adorning the garden of the universe. [The reading "bhūsthitā" is also found. || 16 ||
It has attained height and expansion by taking refuge upon the limbs of the *tamāla* tree, which is characterized by its dark-blue hue like the sky;
it is that [city] whose sturdy pillars, shaped like bent knees, are the very heaven and earth (the two worlds), supported on all sides by their roots. 16.
In the lower sections of the cosmic egg (or, according to the reading in the commentary, "in the lower sections of the worlds"), she was entwined by her own root-basin;
she was sustained by the watering of all the waters of the oceans, such as milk and the rest. 17.

Supported by a beautiful basin characterized by the number of seven oceans (47), she receives the pouring of the waters of all the oceans, such as milk and the rest; thus, through the spreading of her root-branches, she is woven like a net throughout the regions of the netherworlds. || 17 ||
The three Vedas are the restless bees upon this cluster of flowers that is woman;
she is stirred by the wind of the movement of consciousness and filled with the vast swarms of ritual actions.

The "trayī" refers to the three Vedas characterized by the section on optional rites (*kāmyakarmakāṇ�ḍa*); she is "tremulous" (*vilolā*) because those very people who are full of passion (*rāgijanāḥ*) are her bees.

For this reason, the women who are to be enjoyed by them are her clusters of flowers. By the word "action" (*kriyā*), people intent on natural worldly activity are indicated; they alone constitute her abundant roots, leaves, stalks, and so forth.
In which there are wandering gnats, that is, species of minute insects. || 18 ||
Enveloped by the python of evil deeds, it is a bower of flowers that is the splendor of heaven;
it is densely packed with the very life of living beings, bestowing various forms of joy and intoxication. (19)
"Kukarma" refers to actions prohibited by the scriptures. It is "nīrandhra," meaning full or dense, with the "jīvana" of living beings—that is, the means of their livelihood.
By means of the words beginning with "nānā," [the author] demonstrates its various diversities, which are distinct from those of a common creeper:
it bestows intoxication upon the deluded through "nānāvidha āmoda," that is, the fragrances of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) for sense objects. (19)
It shines with the variety of various tranquilities, it is adorned with various flowers, it is filled with rows of various fruits, and it blossoms with various seasons. || 20 ||
But for the discerning, it shines with the variety of many flowers characterized by manifold forms of tranquility;
it blossoms through their outward appearance, which rains down the pollen, nectar, fruits, and flowers of spiritual realization.
It possesses circles of various flower-beds, it harbors various kinds of birds;
it is rough with various pollens, and it contains various networks of mountains.
It was filled with the buds of various arts, arisen from various groups of forests,
grown upon the slopes of various mountains, and dense with various leaves.
She is born and being born, dying and likewise dead;
she is half-severed and likewise unsevered, and she is eternally incapable of being severed.
It is eternal, flowing in a continuous stream without interruption. || 23 ||
The past and the present are always as if non-existent even while existing; she is eternally perpetually youthful, yet eternally undergoing withering.
"Constantly" means repeatedly. "Taruṇī" means sprouted. || 24 ||
For this is indeed a great poisonous creeper; when embraced with impetuosity, it causes the fainting spell of the poison of saṃsāra, but when touched [with discernment], it perishes. (25)
When it is grasped and examined, it perishes. || 25 ||
Within that vast [expanse], she is dissolved; within the ignorant, she is established and endowed [with all].
Here is water, here are mountains, here are serpents, and here are gods. (26)

For that investigator, [the notion of duality] has dissolved within the expansive, full Self and is sublated; however, for the ignorant person, it persists internally, remaining as something entirely pervasive. He elaborates upon that very persistence with the words beginning "from here" (itaḥ) and so forth. || 26 ||
From here she attained the state of the earth, and likewise from here she exists as radiance;
from here she reached the state of the moon and sun, and likewise from here she took the form of the stars.
From here is darkness, from there is light; from here is the sky, from there is the fertile earth;
from here is the treatise, from there is the Veda; from here is that which is devoid of duality.
The earth is fertile, rich with crops; from this [state], it is devoid of both dissolution and deep sleep. (28)
In one place she flew aloft as a bird; in another she rose up as a goddess; in another she was rooted as a pillar; and in another she attained the state of the wind.
In one place she is merged in hell; in another, she sports in heaven;
in one place she has attained the state of a god; and in another, she exists as a worm. (30)
In the form of hell-beings, they are hidden within the hollows of the netherworld (pātāla). || 30 ||
In one place Viṣṇu, in another Brahmā, in another Rudra, in another Ravi; in one place Agni, in another Vāyu, in another Candra, and in another Yama. || 31 ||
O dear one, whatever is visible in the worlds— whether pervaded by great majesty or reduced to the state of withered straw—
even if it flashes forth as Śiva and the like, know that to be ignorance; know this for the sake of its destruction.
Its acquisition of selfhood occurs through its state of having passed away. || 32 ||

Know that whatever manifest object exists— whether it be unencompassed by the excellence of power through its great majesty, such as Hara and others, or whether it has reached the state of being like a blade of withered grass due to its meager power,

extending even to the end of all that is dissolved— know all that to be ignorance (*avidyā*), for the sake of its destruction or sublation through the awakening to reality (*tattva-bodha*). By means of that sublation, [one realizes] the Self as transcending it.
The meaning is that "gain" refers to liberation. || 32 ||

Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Play of the Creeper of Ignorance," in the Nirvāṇa Section of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, within the *Deva-mokṣopāya*.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Play of the Creeper of Ignorance," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The Ninth Chapter.
Śrī Rāma said:
Even the entire range of manifested forms, including Viṣṇu, Śiva, and others, is pure.
"O Brahmin, having heard that it is indeed ignorance alone, I have fallen into a state of confusion. (1)

In this [chapter], the division of the three qualities (guṇas) is described, as well as the state of pure sattva belonging to Hara and others, the nature of knowledge and ignorance, and that which transcends them.
Regarding what was stated—that one should know even Hara and others who appear as the manifest world to be that very ignorance—therein [it is said]:
"The Supreme Brahman, the Truth, the Reality, the Puruṣa, dark and tawny, with upward-turned semen, the three-eyed one;
salutations again and again to the one of universal form, whose body is the essence of Being-Consciousness-Bliss, condensed from the stream of nectar."

Because the Vāsudeva-form is well-known in the Purāṇas as being the Supreme Brahman, whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānanda*), as established in such Śruti and Smṛti texts; and because this does not contradict its sovereignty over all knowledge, which is established in such Śruti passages as "The Lord of all sciences, the Sovereign of all beings."

The remainder [of the meaning] is this: since its status as the Fourth (turīya) and as the Supreme Brahman is well-established, one who considers it impossible for it to be ignorance (avidyā) has, by way of this incidental discussion, fallen into a false delusion as if it were an error; therefore, remove that [delusion]. || 1 ||

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: That which is untouched by any object of perception, which is peaceful, the self of all, and composed of the manifestation of Being-Consciousness— such exists here, devoid of all mental construction.

In that regard, since it is impossible for the immutable, pure consciousness—which is like clarified butter—to undergo condensation or assume a formal shape by itself, and since its being subject to transformations dependent on *māyā* is thus established, one must postulate a specific aspect of *māyā* as the cause of those transformations; this very aspect, which does not obscure the nature of the consciousness as clear, subtle, and most luminous, is what constitutes the *parabrahman* mentioned in scripture, so as to avoid contradiction. It is precisely this [aspect].

He is called the Pure Being (*śuddhasattva*). Because he is the most translucent, because he receives the reflection of consciousness, because he illuminates all knowledge, and because he does not obscure his own nature, there is no contradiction in his sovereignty over all knowledge. But where everything has become the Self alone for him—by what means could one see whom? Furthermore, in the end, there is the cessation of the entire illusion (*viśvamāyānivṛttiḥ*).

With the intention that there is no room for doubt here—since it is ignorance (*avidyā*) because it is sublated by our knowledge of reality as established by such scriptural passages as these—Vasiṣṭha, wishing to state the answer and intending to describe the sequence of its conceptualization, first shows the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) with the words: "by the object of cognition" (*saṃvedyena*). [The Self is] untouched by the object of cognition in the form of the world.

Because it is variegated by the illusion consisting of the accumulated formative impressions (saṃskāra) of the entire world, it is of the nature of all things; therefore, even prior to creation, there exists only pure Being (sanmātra), which is abundant with the light of consciousness—this is the meaning. || 2 ||
Therefore, from itself arises the *kalā*, whose nature is that of a mental construct (*kalana*), appearing as a shimmering fluidity, like a line of whirlpools arising from water. (3)

*Kalā* is the differentiation [of consciousness], characterized by the awakening of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the world; it is the manifestation of the reflection of Consciousness (*cidābhāsa*). At the time of creation and so forth, it arises as if slightly distinct from Consciousness through its own existence, becoming fit for the conventional usage of the distinction between the possessor of qualities (*guṇin*) and the quality (*guṇa*), though it remains established by its very nature.
Therefore, a corresponding illustration is given: "like a line of a whirlpool. || 3 ||
It is conceived as threefold— subtle, intermediate, and gross— and subsequently, by means of that mind, it is known again through its own form.

The meaning is that this *kalā*, distinct from the sun, is conceived as threefold—subtle, intermediate, and gross—just as there is a diminution of light in the various distinctions of intense heat, mild heat, and shade. After the subtle conception, that conceiving agent perceives it as the mind (*manas*) and as Hiraṇyagarbha in its intermediate state; thereafter, it perceives it again as a body (*vapus*).
The connection with the subsequent [phrase] is: "Known in the form of the gross Virāj, it remains exactly as such. || 4 ||
It persists through these states, and is conceptually differentiated as threefold:
sattva, rajas, and tamas; this indeed is remembered as Prakṛti.

Since this very nature of the indeterminate adjunct (avyākṛtopādhi) exists in three ways, for that very reason it is conceived as threefold even in these subtle and other states; such is the logical connection. || 5 ||
Know ignorance to be primordial nature (prakṛti), whose characteristic is the three qualities (guṇas).
This very [ignorance] is the cycle of worldly existence for a living being; its further shore is the supreme state.
In order to accord with the answer to the question, he states that primordial nature (prakṛti) is ignorance (avidyā): "Ignorance," etc. (verse 6).
In this regard, those three qualities which have been mentioned are also traditionally held to be of three kinds;
each quality—sattva, rajas, and tamas—is divided individually.
He states the threefold sub-division of each individual quality based on their commonality with respect to effect, cause, and ignorance, [beginning] with the words "In this regard" (atra). || 7 ||
Thus, this ignorance is divided into nine types according to the distinction of its qualities;
whatever is seen here is entirely dependent upon it.
The seers, the sages, the perfected ones, the nāgas, the vidyādharas,
and the gods— know these, O Rāghava, to be the sattvic portion of ignorance.
In that regard, in the first section, he illustrates the aspect of sentient beings with the words: "The sages," etc. (9).
Of this sattvic portion, the Nāgas and Vidyādharas are Tamas;
the Munis and Siddhas are Rajas; and the gods, Hara and the others, are Sattva. (10)
He provides examples for all three within their respective subdivisions, beginning with "of the sāttvika" (sāttvikasya). || 10 ||
Among the class of beings born from the divine womb, those such as Hari, Hara, and others have attained the stainless state through the primordial qualities of pure *sattva*. (11)
He states the justification for Śiva and the others having bodies of pure *sattva* included within the quality of *sattva*: "In the class of *sattva*" (*sattvajātāv iti*).

The meaning is that their own state (*svātmapada*), which is stainless—meaning ever devoid of the veil of ignorance—is always attained through innate knowledge (*vidyā*); therefore, they are of pure *sattva*. By this, [it is shown that] Brahmā and Śiva do not possess bodies of *rajas* and *tamas*, respectively.

The popular notion among the ignorant has been refuted. "Sattva, rajas, and tamas are the qualities of *prakṛti*; the Supreme Person, though one, being joined with these, assumes here in this world the names Hari, Viriñci, and Hara for the sake of its maintenance and other functions. Among those, indeed, the highest blessings for men shall belong to Him whose nature is *sattva*. Such are the statements from the *Bhāgavata Purāṇa* and other texts. Likewise: "He whose body is *tamas* directly..."

The quality [of Sattva] is [the domain] of Viṣṇu; he alone, and no other, is the protector of the three forms (trimūrti). Furthermore, the statement from the Skanda Purāṇa—that [Brahmā and Śiva] are bodies by way of metaphorical designation for the sake of the instruments of creation and so forth—is intended as praise for one [Viṣṇu] through the two others, according to the maxim of a "circle of suitors," and does not aim to establish the inferiority of the other two.

This is because omniscience, the truthfulness of one’s resolve, the capacity to awaken devotees, and being the cause of ultimate liberation are most renowned in the Śruti, Smṛti, and Purāṇas as belonging to all three forms [of the Divine]. Furthermore, regarding those who are obsessed with the contentious insistence that "this one is supreme" and "that one is not," it is said:
"They are born as Yātudhānas and Piśācas; of this there is no doubt. Thus, there is the observation of such degradation.

The sense is that, because the three deities are censured [in comparison], and because [the Lord] is of one essence as belonging to the category of Īśvara, it is not possible for him to be inferior; therefore, it is appropriate that his body consists of pure *sattva*, which is the cause of supreme excellence. || 11 ||
O Rāma, he who becomes a knower of that which is the constituent part of primordial nature (prakṛti) characterized by sattva, does not arise again; therefore, he is called liberated.
Therefore, it is well known that even for those who worship Him, there is the cessation of rebirth through the attainment of knowledge; thus he says [in the verse beginning with] *ata eva*.

Because the three forms (Trimūrtis) are free from obscuration (*āvaraṇa*), they possess innate liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*); thus he says *tena*. This refers to Hari, Hara, and the others. || 12 ||
Therefore, O Mahāmati, these beings such as Rudra and others remain liberated as long as the world endures, remaining in their bodies for the duration of the world's existence.
As long as they possess a body, these great-souled ones remain established as liberated while living;
at the end of the body, they shall abide in the Supreme Lord as those liberated beyond the body.
In the Supreme Lord, whose essential nature is pure Brahman. || 14 ||
This portion belongs to ignorance alone, yet it has thus attained the state of knowledge;
the seed attains the state of the fruit, and the fruit attains the state of the seed. (15)

Having concluded the resolution of the question, he introduces the subject at hand once more with the words "the portion": "The fruit of the effect-avidyā, upon its dissolution, attains the state of being a seed, which is the nature of the cause-avidyā. (15)
Ignorance arises from knowledge like a bubble from water;
indeed, ignorance dissolves into knowledge like a bubble into water. (16)

Furthermore, because they serve as the substratum for the emergence and dissolution of the ignorance pertaining to effects, those bodies of knowledge are indeed of the nature of ignorance; thus he says:
"From that [source], the creation characterized by the ignorance of effects arises, and in that very place it is dissolved at the time of dissolution. (16)
Just as the distinction between milk and its waves arises solely from the perception of duality,
so too the distinction between knowledge and ignorance arises solely from the perception of difference.
And thus it is established that even the distinction between knowledge and ignorance is merely imagined; so he says: "The water... (verse 17).
