Just as, from the perspective of ultimate reality, there is an identity between the milk and its waves, so here nothing whatsoever exists that can be called either ignorance or knowledge. (18)

Furthermore, with the intention that when both knowledge and ignorance are sublated by the vision of knowledge, there is all the more no possibility of their distinction, he says: "Not even the state of being ignorance. (18)
O scion of Raghu, having abandoned the views of knowledge and ignorance, that which truly exists here indeed exists;
this is so by virtue of the exclusion of its opposite. 19.

The views of knowledge (*vidyā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*) are perspectives that perceive their respective distinctions and oppositions. Now, since the view of ignorance is sublated, let its abandonment be granted; but by what means is the view of knowledge—which is the sublater—abandoned? To this he says: "the counter-positive" (*pratiyogī*). When ignorance is rendered non-existent through sublation, the status of being a sublater (*bādhakatā*) defined in relation to it [ceases].

The meaning is that because the establishment of a negation depends upon the establishment of its exclusion, which in turn depends upon the establishment of the counter-correlative that is to be excluded. || 19 ||
The two views of knowledge and ignorance do not exist; remain firmly established in what remains.
Neither ignorance exists nor does knowledge exist; enough with this conceptualization.
In the remainder, there is only the residual pure consciousness. || 20 ||
There is something which is nothing, yet it exists as consciousness and awareness;
that very thing, when its manifestation is not recognized, is designated as ignorance (avidyā). || 21 ||
To demonstrate what that "remainder" (śeṣa) is, he says "something" (kiñcit), implying that it is conceptualized as ignorance prior to awakening in that state. He explains:
"There is nothing whatsoever apart from itself; that [state] is 'nothing' (nakiñcit). (21)
This very reality is known as the destruction of ignorance;
due to the absence of true knowledge, the false conceptualization called "ignorance" arises.
When ignorance has dissolved, like shade and sunlight within their own hearts, those two very conceptual constructions are exhausted. (23)

Within the heart, in the mind, between those two—knowledge and ignorance—which are mutually opposed like shadow and sunlight, when ignorance has dissolved within consciousness through sublation, [then... || 23 ||
These two, O Raghava, dissolve; only that which is unattainable remains.
Through the destruction of ignorance, even the side of knowledge is exhausted, O Raghava. (24)

The fruit of knowledge, which is the manifestation of the nature of full bliss, is what is to be attained. [An objection: But since knowledge itself is free from all affliction, why does it not remain? To this he says: "due to the destruction of ignorance. The sense is that it is like fire when its fuel is exhausted.
That which remains is either nothing at all, or else this very world is spread out as such.
In that very state, everything is seen, yet nothing at all is seen. || 25 ||

Because it consists entirely of sublation, nothing [exists] as having the nature of ultimate reality; because it is not anything at all, the vision of that very [reality] is, in truth, the vision of everything and the vision of the sublation of everything. Thus he says: "In that regard, in this manner.
In this way, by the aforementioned real form (*tāttvika-rūpa*); however, by the illusory form (*māyika-rūpa*), not even the slightest thing is seen. || 25 ||
Just as a banyan tree exists within its seed, possessing flowers, fruits, and so forth, so too are you a possessor of all powers; you are the "somethingness" that is the casket containing all power.

Even in the state of being veiled by ignorance, although that [Brahman] itself is "nothingness," it is well known to possess a degree of "somethingness" characterized by being the essence of all things in both their gross and subtle states, like the seed of a banyan tree; thus he says, beginning with "And the banyan tree... (verse 26).
It is emptier even than the sky, yet it is not empty, for its nature is consciousness;
just as fire exists within a sun-crystal, or ghee within milk. (27)
In this regard, all this is established within the sequential emergence of space and time, just as sparks arise from fire and as rays from the sun. (28)
In this context, the connection with what follows is that they "emerge from that" because it exists as a reality (*sattva*) alone, even as it arises in the sequence of space and time.

For this very reason, with the intention of showing that the emergence of individual souls (*jīvas*) from that [source] along with their limiting adjuncts (*upādhis*) is well-known in the scriptures according to the analogy of sparks from a fire and so forth, he says "just as," and so on. (28)
Therefore, these flickering cognitions emerge from consciousness just as waves arise from the ocean, or as rays of light from a pure gem. (29)

Therefore, precisely because they abide therein, these well-known individual consciousnesses (*jīvacit*) emerge from the presence of the consciousness of Brahman. For this very reason, he says "just as" to show that Brahman is the sheath (*kośa*) of all individual consciousnesses. || 29 ||
The treasury is eternally the source of infinite cognitions and their splendors;
indeed, within and without, everything exists as a real entity within the reality itself.

[The word] *tviṣām* refers to those things that serve as the locus for delusion. By stating that [the world] is the limit of emergence and by citing the example of the luster of a gem, [the author], while warding off the possibility that the individual soul (*jīva*) and the world exist outside of Brahman, says: "both external and internal. The connection is: "it exists only in the Reality (*vastu*). For since it is real as the Reality, its existence is dependent upon the Reality. || 30 ||
Just as the sky is by all means of an indestructible nature for jars, so too is there agency on the part of the magnet when iron moves toward it. (31)

The reality (*vastu*), because it is never subject to destruction, is characterized by being devoid of the three kinds of limitations; that is to say, it is infinite. And thus, the departure of the living soul from within the interior of the jar is metaphorically equivalent to the departure of the jar itself, just as the departure of the space within the jar follows upon the departure of the jar. With this intention, he says: [Note: The phrase *kumbhākāśodare* appears to be an additional locative case ending.]
For in that same way, agency is attributed to that [Self] which is actually non-agent;
just as inert iron vibrates by the mere proximity of a magnet, so too this body, though insentient in nature, perceives through the existence of that [Self]. (32)
This entire world is situated there, within that single seed of the universe called Consciousness (citi), through the conceptualization of imagined constructs by awareness;
it possesses various forms like a mass of restless waves upon water, yet it is formless even more than space, wherein nothing at all exists.

He summarizes the point already stated with the word "therein" (*tatra*). Therein, while Brahman remains unknown, this world exists through successive conceptualizations impelled by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the world previously imagined;

[this occurs] therein—meaning in that which, when known, is formless even like the ether (*ākāśa*), devoid of the nature of both the formed (*mūrta*) and the formless (*amūrta*), and wherein nothing else whatsoever exists.

Thus ends the ninth canto, titled "The Refutation of False Knowledge," in the Nirvāṇa Section of the Means to Liberation, as spoken by the Divine Messenger in the glorious Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa of Valmīki, a work of the Seers. || 9 ||
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Refutation of Knowledge," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The Tenth Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Therefore, this entire world, consisting of the stationary and the moving, is nothing at all.
Know, O friend, that whatever has attained the state of being nothing at all is indeed "something."
The delusion of the bond of ignorance and the persistence of the mind in immobile beings are explained; through investigation preceded by intelligence, liberation from bondage is elaborated.

Therefore, since the distinction between the world and the individual soul consists merely of the unknown Brahman, the meaning is that once that [Brahman] is known, this [distinction] is nothing at all.
O Rāma, where there is no conceptualization whatsoever consisting of existence and non-existence, this entire world of living beings and so forth is vain; why do you strive for it?

This entire world, beginning with the individual soul (jīva), is none other than that very Brahman wherein there exists no conceptualization whatsoever consisting of existence or non-existence; and such being the case, why do you strive or desire anything in vain? || 2 ||
This very connection which is designated within the inner heart—we do not find it, just as one does not find the snake in the delusion of a rope-snake. (3)
The connection characterized by "I-ness" and "mine-ness" regarding the body and external objects of enjoyment—we do not find that [connection] through investigation;
this is the remainder [of the sentence]. (3)
The very self, when not fully known, becomes the source of delusion for wandering beings; once known, it attains the state of the Self—the ultimate limit of all consciousness.
The delusion of the world for those who wander [in saṃsāra].
In the world, it is called ignorance when consciousness rests upon the impurity of the object of thought;
but when freed from all limiting adjuncts, it attains the state of a self that transcends the object of thought. || 5 ||
The impurity, which has become the seed of the object of consciousness, is supported by the imposition of its own existence; it "comes" by means of *vidyā*—this is the ellipsis. || 5 ||
For the person is indeed mind-only; when that [mind] perishes, he perishes.
When it remains, this self remains, just as the space within a jar remains when the jar exists.
Having thus described the nature of ignorance, he shows the delusion of the Self’s bondage through the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of its effects:

"It perishes as it were"—according to such scriptural passages as, "Arising from these elements, it perishes after them; having gone to destruction, it becomes [non-existent]," and so forth. The phrase "just like the space within a jar" is to be supplied as the remainder of the comparison. || 6 ||
Just as a child, while walking, sees one who is walking, and while standing, sees one who is standing,
so too this deluded mind perceives itself as agitated.
Thus, he says "going" (gacchan) to show that [the self] likewise superimposes mental states such as movement onto its own nature:
this very self perceives this deluded mind—the agitated mind itself—as the self. (7)
Like a silkworm, it encloses itself within the mind with the fine threads of latent impressions; yet, due to its childishness, it does not realize this within.
Therefore, he says "the cocoon-maker" (kośa) to show that one binds oneself by means of the latent impressions (vāsanā) residing therein: the "cocoon-maker" is a specific kind of insect;
[it does so] because of its childhood and lack of discrimination. || 8 ||
Śrī Rāma said: O Lord, what becomes of that ignorance which has reached a state of extreme density and remains fixed, having attained the bodies of immobile beings and the like?

In the context of the lack of discrimination mentioned in the verse concerning the "fool" (*bāla*), Śrī Rāma, desiring to know the state of consciousness in immobile beings who represent the ultimate limit of non-discrimination, asks: "Maurkhya... [etc.]. It is "evenly situated," meaning supported [by that state]. || 9 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having attained neither the state of non-mind nor having fallen from the state of mind,
this consciousness remains in immobile beings by resorting to a neutral form.
The state of being "without mind" (*amanastva*) is the dissolution of the mind that renders one incapable of experiencing pleasure or pain, as in deep sleep (*suṣupti*).
It has fallen away even from that state of "mind-ness" characterized by the capacity for reflection capable of discerning the preceding and succeeding [moments].
Relying upon a neutral form characterized by stupefaction (*mugdhatā*), consciousness (*cit*)—that is, living-consciousness (*jīvacit*)—[remains]. 10.

In that state, O best among those who know the objects of knowledge, I consider liberation to be situated at a distance, where consciousness remains as the eightfold city of dreams (puryaṣṭaka), bestowing suffering;
there it abides merely by its existence, like one who is mute, blind, and inert. (11)
"Sleeping" means being incapable of discrimination (*viveka*). By the term "the city of eight" (*puryaṣṭaka*), the entire collection of external and internal organs contained therein is indicated.

For this very reason, because it is incapable of remedying suffering, it bestows much suffering. By the term "mute," the absence of the organs of action (*karmendriya*) is meant. By the term "blind," the absence of the functioning of the organs of knowledge (*jñānendriya*) is meant. By the term "insentient" (*jaḍa*)...
The emptiness of the expansion of the mind is characterized. || 11 ||

Śrī Rāma said: O best among those who know what is to be known, I consider that liberation is not far off for those in whom consciousness is established among immobile beings through the non-duality of existence.

Rāma asks with the following intention: "If consciousness (cit) remains as mere existence (sattāmātra), devoid of the activity of the organs of knowledge and action, then since the destruction of latent impressions (vāsanākṣaya) and the dissolution of the mind (manonāśa)—as occurs for yogins—would arise very quickly in such a state, liberation would be attained without delay. Therefore, what is your intention in asserting that 'liberation is far off'? Thus he asks: "Sattā... (verse 12).

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: If that which is the realization of the universal existence (sattāsāmānya), arising from investigating this with full awareness and perceiving it as it truly is, were liberation, then it would be eternal.

Liberation is indeed the abiding in pure Being (*sattāsāmānya*), brought about by the destruction of the mind along with its root latent impressions (*vāsanā*) through the direct realization of reality (*tattvasākṣātkāra*). This realization arises from the processes of hearing, reflection, and meditative absorption (*śravaṇa-manana-nididhyāsana*), which are supported by the fourfold means of purification (*sādhanacatuṣṭaya*) achieved through the performance of actions prescribed by the scriptures. Furthermore, this state is attained through the dissolution of the mind and the eradication of its root impressions, which otherwise arise from the seeds of endless evil deeds and corrupt tendencies.

The venerable Vasiṣṭha describes the intention behind his own statement—that for those who are mostly hell-beings and immobile beings, it is even more difficult to obtain a birth eligible for the study of the scriptures—beginning with the words "buddhipūrvam" (with conscious intent) and so forth. || 13 ||

The supreme abandonment of latent impressions (vāsanās) through thorough comprehension—that which consists of the nature of universal existence (sattāsāmānyarūpatva)—the wise know as the state of absolute liberation (kaivalya). || 14 ||
"Having fully understood the reality of the self"—this is the ellipsis. || 14 ||

Having reflected and investigated the scriptures together with the noble ones through the cultivation of inner self-knowledge (adhyātma-bhāvanā), they know that which is established in the universal existence (sattā-sāmānya) as the Supreme Brahman. || 15 ||

Having deliberated upon the scriptures together with noble teachers, fellow students, and others, and having perceived the reality through the practice of internal meditation preceded by reflection and contemplation (nididhyāsana). || 15 ||
Know that state to be deep sleep (suṣuptatva) wherein the latent impression (vāsanā) remains dormant and slow within, like a sprout in a seed, which again bestows birth. (16)

He establishes that [this state] is even further removed among stationary beings by means of the verse beginning with "antaḥ" and so forth: "Like deep sleep is 'suṣuptatva' (the state of being like deep sleep).
With the mind dissolved within and latent impressions (vāsanās) asleep on all sides, this state of deep sleep—though characterized by insentience—is a birth that bestows hundreds of miseries. (16–17)
Even though it possesses the nature of insentience, like the state of stones and such, it is devoid of activity. || 17 ||
For all these beings, beginning with the immobile, possess the nature of insentience;
they have ascended to the state of deep sleep and are fit for birth again and again. (18)
Just as flowers and the like reside within seeds, and as a jar resides within a heap of clay, so too, O holy one, does one's own latent impression (vāsanā) reside within immobile beings.

He dispels the dull-witted doubt that there is no latent impression (*vāsanā*) at all in stationary beings with the words "Just as" (*yathā*). The expression "flower and so forth" (*puṣpādi*) is stated out of sequence; it means [the series] beginning with the sprout and ending with the flower. || 19 ||
That state where the seed of latent impressions (vāsanā) still exists is not the true deep sleep (suṣupta) for the sake of spiritual perfection;
that state where latent impressions are seedless is known as the Fourth State (turya), which bestows perfection.
It is seedless, its power of the seed having been scorched by the fire of knowledge. || 20 ||
In the same way, even a tiny remnant of latent impressions (vāsanā), fire, debt, disease, enemies, affection, enmity, or poison causes affliction. (21)

For this very reason, even a small residual impression (*vāsanā*), like the remnants of a fire and so forth, becomes a cause of great misfortune through gradual increase; therefore, with the intention that its destruction must be carried out without remainder, he says: "Of the impression" (verse 21).
[The one] who possesses the nature of the universal existence of the seed of impressions once burnt away...
Whether with body or without body, one shall no longer be a partaker of suffering.

The power of consciousness, whose form consists of the seeds of latent impressions, exists eternally as the essence within all things, from stationary objects to those possessing the nature of dreams.

The power of consciousness (cicchakti), whose nature is veiled consciousness, is the latent impression (vāsanā) or the seed-power; it is like the sap in a seed characterized by the potential for sprouting, which is destroyed by roasting. || 23 ||
In seeds, it exists as radiance; in insentient forms, as inertia;
in substances, as the nature of substance; and in others, as hardness.
He states that this very [power] exists in all causes, such as seeds and so forth, in various forms, beginning with the words "In seeds" (*bījeṣu*).
"Ullāsa" (expansion) is the state of blossoming resulting from the union of earth and water; it is defined by that sign and experienced as such.
Thus, the power to produce a sprout has the form of *ullāsa*. In its essence, it exists within substances—such as wealth, jewels, and the like—in the form of a substance (*dravyabhāvena*).

This is because of the state of being "capable" (bhavyatva), which is the cause for being desirable, according to the grammatical rule that "the word *dravya* [is used] in the sense of *bhavya*. In the case of others, such as stones and so forth, there is a relation of identity (*abhedānvaya*), just as in the expression "a child's family" (where "child" is read as "evil" in some versions). || 24 ||
Then she took an impermanent form in the ashes, and a subtle form in the dust; she remained dark among the dark things by her stationing in darkness, and she was a white edge among the swords.

In ashes and even in dust, she exists in an impermanent form, consisting of the destruction of former wood, clods of earth, and so forth; and though her form is subtle, she exists in dark and impure things through a state of blackness and impurity and softness, and in swords such as scimitars through the state of having a bright edge—that is, a sharp edge. || 25 ||
The Self is the power within all things, such as jars, cloths, and the like;
it abides everywhere by relying upon the form of the universal existence (sattāsāmānya).

The meaning is that in all things, such as jars and cloths, it is the Self alone that exists everywhere, assuming the form of the universal existence (sattāsāmānya) and persisting through various powers such as carrying water and warding off cold. || 26 ||
Thus, this entire visible state remains filling [all space],
just as a mass of clouds during the rainy season rests upon the expanse of the sky.
The rainy season (prāvṛṭ) is such that its covering cloth (paṭa) is indeed the mass of clouds (meghajāla), with the jars (ghaṭa) [serving as its ornaments]. || 27 ||
And thus its own nature has been described and investigated:
it is non-universal yet all-pervading, existent, and consisting of the nature of latent impressions (vāsanā). (28)
This view of a self is a non-view that causes the wandering of saṃsāra;
when seen, it brings about the destruction of all sufferings. (29)
Of this power of consciousness (cicchakti) veiled by ignorance; that which consists of non-being, being unreal, and having attained identity with the transformations of māyā.
The non-perception of this [Self] is called ignorance (avidyā) by the wise;
for ignorance is indeed the cause of the world, and from it everything proceeds. (30)
The non-perception of this view of self is of the nature of an obscuration that is opposed to vision. || 30 ||
As soon as ignorance is perceived to be devoid of form,
it dissolves instantly, like a particle of frost in the sunlight.
Devoid of form, she is empty of intrinsic nature. || 31 ||
Just as when a man whose sleep is fading reflects upon his inner state for even a brief moment through the faculty of discernment, his sleep dissolves away.
He states other examples as well with the words "Just as," etc.; "intention" (āśaya) refers to the state of one's own mind. || 32 ||
To whatever extent one conceptualizes what this state is like, to that same extent ignorance is destroyed, just as darkness is dispelled by light. (33)
With the intention that the cessation of delusions such as [the perception of] a snake upon the thorough investigation of reality is also an illustration here, he says "Just as" (yathā).

What is the nature of the unreal snake and so forth? Is it real, or is it imagined through my own delusion? As long as this is being conceptualized—that is, investigated—blindness (*andhatā*) is the obstruction of the power of vision caused by darkness. || 33 ||
Just as one approaches with a lamp in hand out of a desire to see forms obscured by darkness,
so too does all darkness dissolve through these heats, just like clarified butter.
The word "if it approaches" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. Just as darkness dissolves, so too does the entire world together with ignorance [dissolve]. 34.
And in a lamp, no determination of the form of darkness is perceived;
rather, there arises only the destruction of gloom, which possesses a stainless form. (35)

He explains the illustration regarding the non-perception and perception of the form of darkness with the words "And not... (na ca). The ellipsis to be supplied is: "when the lamp is being brought in. (35)
Thus, when being observed, she flees and goes away somewhere;
for she is of unreal form because she is a non-entity, yet she is seen due to a lack of investigation.
When looked at mildly, she moves slowly; when looked at intently, she flees.
Just as darkness is perceived when light has arrived, so too is the unreality of ignorance perceived once its lack of substantiality is realized. (37)

If it is asked, "How can that [ignorance] possess the status of being 'praised' (āstuti)? he replies, "In light," meaning: when light has arrived, just as that darkness is seen to be of an unreal nature, so too is that ignorance seen to be unreal. Now, one might object: there is no sublation (*bādha*) of darkness by light, because its existence across the three periods of time is not perceived. Rather, it is merely a disappearance (*tirobhāva*), like the coldness of water by heat.

"Furthermore, because that [darkness] is seen again when the light has departed. The meaning is: while it may be granted that darkness is a non-entity (avastu) in that sense, the non-reality of ignorance (avidyā) is indeed perceived through the experience of its sublation throughout the three periods of time. || 37 ||
As long as it is not illuminated, nothing at all is seen;
once it is illuminated, ignorance is realized for what it truly is. (38)

The meaning is this: whether it be mother-of-pearl, a rope, or the like, or even silver, a snake, and so forth, as long as one does not look after having investigated them, they are not seen in their true nature;
but once they are looked upon, ignorance is understood exactly as it is in its own nature, and the reality of the object is realized exactly as it exists. || 38 ||
As soon as one reflects for oneself, "Who am I in this machine of blood, flesh, and bone?", everything immediately dissolves away.
He explains how one should perform investigation and observation: "Red," etc. (Verse 39).
When that which is unreal in form at the beginning and the end has certainly been discarded by the heart,
they know that which remains as the destruction of ignorance.

Thus, when all that is visible—which is unreal in its beginning and end—is discarded by the heart and mind possessed of such inquiry, that which remains is the residual conscious self (cidātman). The sense is that the substratum is non-different from the sublated superimposition. || 40 ||
That is neither nothing nor something; it is the eternal Brahman itself.
That reality is to be accepted as the goal when ignorance is dispelled. (41)
Form is known to be devoid of intrinsic nature by its very name alone;
for the taste of what is being tasted on the tongue is not perceived through anything else. (42)
If that which is sublated lacks its own nature, or if its sublation is nothing but the Self itself, no other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) need be sought;
for terms such as "illusion" (*māyā*) or "ignorance" (*avidyā*) are conventionally established only with respect to such objects as those experienced in dreams. Thus he says: "The form... (Verse 42):
"Ignorance does not exist anywhere; this is only the undivided Brahman."
By whom the entire expansion of the manifestation of existence and non-existence has been adorned. || 43 ||
Ignorance consists solely in the certainty that "this is not Brahman";
its destruction consists solely in the certainty that "this is Brahman. (44)
This being the case, he states the extracted essential nature of ignorance and its destruction: "etāvat" (this much).
The words "the nature of ignorance" are to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. || 44 ||
If it is asserted here that "the pervasive Lord is not the web of appearances consisting of pots, cloths, and carts," then that is indeed ignorance;
but if it is held that "the pervasive Lord is the web of appearances consisting of pots, cloths, and carts," then that ignorance has surely dissolved away. (45)

Explaining this very point, he concludes with the word "jar" (*ghaṭa*): The entire web of the world appearing as jars, cloths, carts, and so forth, is not something other than the all-pervading, unlimited Self consisting of Being-Consciousness (*saccidātman*); rather, the superimposition (*āropa*) of such views is itself ignorance (*avidyā*), and its negation (*apavāda*) is the vision of the unlimited Pure Being alone.
The meaning is "the destruction of that. || 45 ||

Thus ends the tenth canto, titled "The Treatment of Ignorance," in the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa* of the *Mokṣopāya* section of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Valmiki, according to the tradition of the Rishis. 10.
Thus ends the tenth canto, titled "The Treatment of Ignorance," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The Eleventh Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
O Rāma, this is being stated by me again and again for the sake of awakening.
O virtuous one, without practice, the cultivation of the self does not arise.
That vision by which Hari, Hara, and the other gods abide as liberated while living—
the vision that "all is Brahman"— is what is taught here to Rāma.

The repeated instruction of the very same matter through different modes is for the purpose of strengthening the disciple's comprehension of the subject. Indeed, hearing and other such practices, which have visible results like the threshing of grain, must be repeated until the fruit arises. For it has been said by the Blessed One:

"Bādarāyaṇa’s Sūtra states: 'There is repetition [of meditation], because of the instruction given more than once. Thus, revealing this to generate enthusiasm by removing the fault of monotony (*jāmitā*), he turns Rāma toward listening to the remaining vision concerning the destruction of ignorance, beginning with the words 'Again and again'. || 1 ||
This ignorance, powerful and known by names other than "avidyā," has arisen from thousands of previous births and has reached a state of dense solidity.
To the question "Why does it not arise [in him]?", he says: "Ignorance" (*ajñānam*). The word *sahasra* signifies infinity.

Thus, the meaning is that because it has been stabilized by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of duality practiced throughout infinite millions of births, it is not utterly destroyed by a single instruction. || 2 ||
It is experienced by all the senses, both externally and internally;
because of this, the body has attained extreme density amidst existence and non-existence.

And because it takes the form of non-duality, which is grasped by many stronger internal and external means of knowledge such as the eyes and so forth, he states its preeminence with the words "with the external and the internal. When the body exists—in states such as living and waking—it is perceived through the senses; when the body is absent—in states such as death and dissolution—it is always perceived by the Witness.
Excessive density and excessive intensity. || 3 ||
Self-knowledge, however, is beyond the range of all the senses;
it attains its mere existence when the six senses, with the mind as the sixth, have ceased.
And he shows the difficulty of obtaining the totality of conditions for knowledge with two verses beginning with "The self" (ātma). || 4 ||
How indeed can that which remains transcending the functioning of the senses,
and whose nature lies beyond direct perception, ever come within the range of a living being's direct experience?
"Having leaped over," that is, having transcended. || 5 ||
For your own spiritual perfection, sever with the strokes of the sword of the playful practice of knowledge this creeper of ignorance that has taken root in the tree of your heart.

Therefore, with the intention that the repeated instruction and the practice of reflection (*manana*) and so forth possess purposefulness by cutting through the manifold spreading of the creeper of ignorance (*avidyā*), he concludes with the verse beginning "Thou" (tvam). || 6 ||
O Rāghava, dwell in the same manner as King Janaka, who had realized that which is to be known and was devoted to the practice of self-knowledge.
This was the firm conviction of him who dwells in what is to be done and what is not to be done;
whether waking or even standing still, because of that [realization], there is truth for those who know it.

This certainty, following my own experience, belonged to that dweller [of the Self] through both outward activity (*kārya*) and non-activity (*akārya*), namely meditative absorption (*samādhi*). That very knowledge is the fruit of practice; by that knowledge alone the reality of one's true nature (*svarūpa*) is manifested, not by superficial cognition (*apātajñāna*)—this is the meaning. || 8 ||
It is certain that by whatever means Hari, performing various modes of conduct, descends into the wombs upon the earth, that is declared to be his "knowledge of those specific circumstances. (9)

He enters into wombs and other such difficult states of dwelling in the womb; yet even while entering, he is not touched by the sufferings associated with them—this is the meaning. The same should be inferred for the subsequent cases as well. || 9 ||
O Rāghava, may you possess the same certainty as the three-eyed Lord Śiva while dwelling with his beloved, or that of Brahmā, who is free from passion.
Whatever certainty belongs to the Preceptor of the Gods (Bṛhaspati), to Bhārgava (Śukra), to the Sun, to the Moon, to the Wind, and to Fire; 11.
Of Nārada, Pulastya, and likewise of myself, Aṅgiras;
of Pracetas, Bhṛgu, Kratu, Atri, and Śuka.
O best of Brahmins, O Raghava, let that very resolve which belongs to other royal sages who are liberated while still living be yours as well.
The word "eva" (only) is connected with the phrase "of those who are living. || 13 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
O Blessed One, O Brahmin, tell me in truth how these wise and high-minded ones, through their firm resolve, remain established free from sorrow.
The question is clear. || 14 ||
The venerable Vasiṣṭha said:
O prince of mighty arms, you who have understood everything that is to be known, listen clearly to how this matter was asked; for this indeed is their settled conclusion.
This is of the manner that will be described hereafter. || 15 ||
Whatever web of the world appears here as an object of experience, all that is established as the stainless Brahman; this is the settled conclusion.
He states that very point with the words "That which is this," and so forth. "Established" means remaining in its ultimate nature by abandoning both its illusory and non-illusory forms. || 16 ||
Brahman is consciousness, Brahman is the world, and Brahman is the succession of all beings.
I am Brahman; my enemy is Brahman; and my good friends and kinsmen are Brahman. (17)
He demonstrates in detail what was stated in brief: "Brahman," etc. (verse 17).
Brahman is the threefold time, and that is established in Brahman alone;
just as the ocean increases within itself by means of its waves and surges. (18)
It increases and expands. || 18 ||
Thus, by means of the splendor of the categories of existence, this Brahman increases in this manner;
Brahman is grasped by Brahman, and Brahman is enjoyed by Brahman.
With the intention that Brahman alone is the essence of all actions, agents, and fruits, he says: "It is grasped" (verse 19).
Brahman expands within Brahman by means of its own expansive powers, as if through the power of Brahman itself;
yet if my enemy, who is of the nature of Brahman, acts to the detriment of Brahman, he [is destroyed]. || 20 ||

By the power of Brahman, that is, by Māyā; by means of expansions (bṛṃhābhiḥ), which are illusory transformations (vivartaiḥ). It expands, as it were, increases—as if. With this perspective, he says "Brahman" with the intention that there is no attachment whatsoever to hatred, passion, or the like. An "unpleasant-doer" is one who performs what is undesirable. || 20 ||
That which is established in Brahman within Brahman—what else has been done by anyone?
The persistence of imagined passions and the like is like a tree in the sky.
Then that [is the case]. || 21 ||
For those who have perished through the absence of conceptualization, what further attachment could arise here?
Indeed, all movement, vibration, and so forth, exist only within Brahman. (22)
In this Brahman, which is all-pervading and complete, there is the movement of the feet, that is, walking and so forth. || 22 ||
The entire Brahman vibrates; how can there be happiness or sorrow?
Brahman is fully satisfied in Brahman; Brahman is established in Brahman.
Since the entire Brahman manifests as having the singular essence of bliss, whence can there be suffering and the like? (23)
Brahman vibrates within Brahman; "I am not another self.
The pot is Brahman, the cloth is Brahman, and I am this all-pervading Brahman. (24)
Therefore, when the Brahman of the body has merged into the Brahman of death, what false construction can there be here regarding passion and dispassion? (25)
With this perspective, he speaks of the attainment of absolute fearlessness, beginning with the word "death" (maraṇa). || 25 ||
For those who are suffering, what else could there be [but sorrow], comparable to the delusion of a rope-snake?
When the Brahman of the body is established in the Brahman that is blissful in its enjoyment and so forth, [what sorrow remains]? (26)
Thus, he says "saṃbhoga... [verse 26], showing that the absolute cessation of attachment to enjoyments is also established.
"How could this notion, 'this has been accomplished by me,' be anything but vain?
For it is not other than the water itself, just as the waves and the water are both characterized by motion. (27)
*Kalanā* means desire. The meaning is that just as there is nothing whatsoever other than water when it is in a state of vibration, so it is here. || 27 ||
In Brahman, whose nature is vibration, "thou-ness" and "I-ness" do not exist in such a way that anything could ever perish,
just as nothing ever dies when there is no water to whirl.

"Vibration" (spanda) is movement caused by passion, hatred, and so forth; it is of that nature. [The term "of those"] means "of those which cause that. "Upon the destruction of the whirlpool" means upon its death.

When the Brahman-body has thus attained the state of death, it remains neither in the notion of "you" nor in the notion of "I," just as [the notions of] movement and stillness do not persist in water.
Likewise, even when the Brahman of the body has attained the state of the Brahman of death, the meaning is that nothing whatsoever dies.
He negates the notion that Brahman-hood might be grasped in all its successive states while not abandoning its insentient form, by saying "as" (yathā).
"Moving and unmoving" means either the flickering and the non-flickering, or the moving and the unmoving. || 29 ||
Likewise, the forms of the insentient and the sentient do not truly exist within the Supreme Self, just as the state of being a bracelet does not exist in gold, nor as a whirlpool in water. (30)

The sense is that, in the absence of the nature of insentience (jaḍa), since the counter-correlate (pratiyogin) is not established, there is likewise no establishment of its exclusion, namely the nature of non-insentience (ajaḍa). || 30 ||
In this same way, the nature of the Self consists of both being that and not being that;
for this [nature] may be of the form of the individual soul (jīva) or it may be of the form of the insentient (jaḍa). || 31 ||

He states that "this" [is as follows] (verse 31): by which [power] there occurs the manifestation of that very [Reality] as if it were not that—such a nature is illusory (*māyika*) by its own essence;
and it is solely through its influence that the conceptualization of distinctions between the forms of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the insentient (*jaḍa*) arises. Thus he says: "This... (31).
Thus, delusion belongs to one whose nature is ignorance, and never to one whose nature is knowledge;
for the ignorant person, the world consists of a flood of suffering, while for the wise, it consists of bliss.
Therefore, the knower of reality says that the entire world has only the single flavor of bliss: "Of the ignorant," etc. (32).
To the blind man, the world is darkness; but to the one with sight, it is light.
To the wise man, the world is of a single nature; to the fool, it is exceedingly painful.
Like a night in which Yakṣas flicker for a child, it is merely empty space for a man;
yet this single Brahma-pot is eternally present everywhere. (34)

Just as the night appears to a child as being filled with a yakṣa conjured by his own delusion, yet to a man—whether young or old—it is merely devoid of any yakṣa; so it is with the jar of full nectar characterized by Brahman. || 34 ||
Nothing indeed dies, nor does anything live;
just as in the play of manifestations, nothing is destroyed and nothing is born. (35)
Just as waves and the like exist within the great ocean, so does the multitude of beings exist within the Self;
the notion that "this does not exist" or "this exists" is merely a delusion of the Self regarding itself.
Power alone, being causeless, vibrates within like the rays of a crystal;
the Self itself, as the essence of the power of the universe, is Brahman abiding within its own self. (37)

The power (*śakti*) of the crystal of *māyā* is its transparency, which renders it capable of receiving multiple reflections; just as that [transparency] vibrates internally in the form of a variety of various reflections, such as qualities and actions, so too does it vibrate and manifest in the form of the universe and in the form of the powers of those respective objects. And that manifestation is the Self itself, and that [Self] is...
Brahman is established solely within its own non-dual self. || 37 ||
Just as dense water does not cease to be water because of a web of ripples and droplets, how could there be the notion of death regarding Brahman through the destruction of the body? (38)
Therefore, he establishes by means of four examples that there is no destruction of the self through the destruction of the body. || 38 ||
For indeed, nothing such as the body exists apart from Brahman, just as waves and the like do not exist apart from the water in the great ocean. (39)
Whatever drop or droplet, whatever ripple or wavelet,
whatever foam or surge there may be, it is just as water is within water.
Whatever body, whatever mental construction, whatever visible object, whatever decay and non-decay, whatever arrangement of phenomena, and whatever purpose— by all that, it is Brahman within Brahman.

Kalanā is the activity of the senses; the visible is the object of enjoyment; decay and non-decay are misfortune and prosperity; states (bhāvas) are the arrangement of joy, sorrow, and so forth; and the purpose (artha) is the experience of the goals of human life. || 41 ||
The diverse arrangement of forms belongs to Brahman, like [ornaments] made from gold; it is not of a different nature. The perception of duality is merely false for those who are deluded.
The mind, the intellect, the ego, the subtle elements, and the senses—all this is Brahman alone; there is no manifold self, and neither pleasure nor pain exists. 43.
Through speech arising from such meanings as "this is that," "I am this," and "this is the mind," the self expands within itself, like an echo of sound in a mountain cave.

Just as a single sound, in the presence of a mountain or rock, expands as if doubled by means of an echo in the form of a resonance (*pratidhvani*), so too the Self alone expands through the distinctions of names such as body, mind, external objects, and so forth; this is the meaning. || 44 ||
Brahman itself, when unknown, remains as if it has arrived at a state of ignorance;
for indeed, in a dream, the self is perceived by the mind as the self of the self. (45)

Ignorance constitutes the state of being a living soul and the world. Regarding that, he cites the example of a dream as stated by Bādarāyaṇa in the passage beginning with "And indeed, within that very Self, there are various [creations]," saying: "For it is thus. (45)
If Brahman is not cultivated as such, it becomes the impurity of ignorance regarding Brahman;
just as gold that is not refined as gold becomes mere clay. || 46 ||
It is well known in the world that ignorance possesses the power to produce effects that are utterly contradictory and impossible; thus he says: "unconsidered" (abhāvitam).
The knowers of Brahman know that the Self, the Lord, the Great Soul, is indeed Brahman itself.
That which is not fully understood is called "ignorance" for those who are ignorant. (47)

Therefore, he says "the self-sovereign Lord" (svayaṃprabhuḥ) to show that this [world] is of the nature of ignorance only from the perspective of the ignorant, and not from the perspective of those who know reality.
When known as Brahman, Brahman becomes Brahman itself in an instant;
when known as gold, gold becomes gold itself in an instant. (48)

For Brahman is the Self, possessing all powers; therefore, whatever it intensely contemplates, that very thing it immediately perceives by its own power, spontaneously and without external cause. (49)
The Self itself manifests as the living being and the world, or as the ultimate form of Brahman, according to how one contemplates it. || 49 ||
Those who know Brahman know Brahman to be without action, without agent, without instrument, without cause, and free from affliction— the self-sovereign Great Soul.

Therefore, he says "akarma" (free from action) to show that those who know reality do not perceive [the world] as the state of a living being or the world. Because he manifests by himself within his own nature through his own awakening, he is the Self-Master (Svayambhū). 50.
That which is not fully known is called ignorance because of its lack of knowledge;
when it is fully known, it becomes knowledge, which brings about the complete destruction of ignorance. 51.
Indeed, a kinsman who is not fully understood is called a non-kinsman; once fully understood, he becomes a kinsman through the destruction of the delusion of being a non-kinsman. 52.
When one internally recognizes, "This is improper," that cultivation arises;
for it is by means of this [cultivation] that one becomes dispassionate through distaste for what is improper. (53)

If it is asked, "Why then does the contemplation (*bhāvanā*) of the living being and the world as being nothing but Brahman not arise all at once for everyone?"—the answer is that it is due to the absence of dispassion (*vairāgya*).
If so, let the causes of that [absence] be stated; to this he says, beginning with "This, however" (*idaṃ tu*):
When it is known that this form of the living being and the world is improper and cannot withstand inquiry, that contemplation of Brahman arises.

The meaning is that because of the well-known distaste for things such as silver in a mother-of-pearl shell—which are logically untenable—one becomes dispassionate toward the entire category of objects of enjoyment, just as one is toward the world, by means of this very inquiry. || 53 ||
Once duality is internally realized as unreal, this realization arises;
through it, one indeed becomes dispassionate toward that duality due to a sense of distaste. (54)

With the intention that the aforementioned investigation regarding the world culminates in the purification of the referent of the term "That" (tatpadārtha), he clearly restates what was already said concerning the aspect of the world: "Duality... (verse 54).
When it is clearly known that "this is not I," the cultivation [of this truth] arises;
through this, one certainly becomes detached from false egoism. (55)

With the intention that even in the portion concerning the individual soul (jīvāṃśa), [the inquiry] culminates in the purification of the meaning of the term "thou" (tvaṃpadārtha), he clarifies what was stated regarding that portion as well: "This... When it is known that this aggregate of causes and effects, beginning with the body, is not the "I," [then the inquiry into the self proceeds]. || 55 ||
When the knowledge "I am indeed Brahman" is true, that realization arises;
it becomes fully absorbed within that true, innate form.

With the intention that this [realization] culminates in the knowledge of the indivisible meaning of the sentence (vākyārtha), which is the fruit of the purification of the meanings of words (padārtha), he clarifies the dissolution characterized by the sublation of the states of the individual soul and the world within that [Brahman], stating: "Brahman alone... (56).
When that [Brahman], which arises from expansion, exists, I know this world as "Brahman";
when the notions of "you" and "I" and so forth are sublated, that which resides in the world is "Sat" (Being) and so on. || 57 ||

With the intention that when there is the realization of the undivided form (*akhaṇḍākāra-bodha*), even though the world remains, it is nothing other than Brahman, whose single essence is Being (*sat-ekarasa*), and is no longer of the nature of suffering as before, he says in two verses beginning with "When [that] exists" (*sati*). When that meaning of the indivisible sentence (*akhaṇḍa-vākyārtha*), born of expansion and manifesting as an unlimited nature, has come forth, then [notions such as] "you," "I," and so forth, as well as "this-ness" (*idantvam*)— [The rest of the verse: ...all these vanish like the waves of the ocean. Just as the waves of the ocean, which are of the nature of water, do not exist apart from the water, so too, O wise one, this entire world does not exist apart from Brahman. When those [attributes] are sublated, that which was previously established as "Being" (sat) and so forth—appearing as the beloved (priya) and the form of cognition (māna)—is understood to be Brahman alone;
this is the meaning of the statement that this entire collection of objects existing in the world, consisting of these five forms, is indeed Brahman. || 57 ||
I know this Brahman to be the truth, enriched with every excellence;
for me there is no suffering, no karmas, no delusion, and no desire. (58)
I am equanimous, established in my own nature, and free from sorrow; "I am Brahman"—this is the truth.
I am liberated from the stain of temporal parts; I am everything, free from all ailment.
He describes that very state, which abides in its own nature, as the supreme human goal, beginning with the words "sama" (equal) and so forth. || 59 ||
I neither renounce nor do I desire; "I am Brahman"—this is the truth.
I am the blood, I am the flesh, I am the bones, and I am the body. (60)
Even the purification of the meaning of that term [the "I"] is intended solely for the purpose of removing the limitations and the state of being an object;

for when those are removed and one attains the state of being the Self of all (*sārvātmya*), even the body and so forth, consisting of blood, flesh, and the like, are the Self itself and thus not fit for rejection—with this intention, he says: "I am the blood," and so forth. (60)
"I am consciousness and I am the sentient; I am Brahman—this is the truth.
I am the sky, I am space, I am with the sun, I am the quarters, and I am the earth as well. (61)
"I am the form of the pot and the cloth; 'I am Brahman' is the truth.
I am the grass, I am the earth, I am the shrub, and I am the forest and so forth. (62)
I am the caravan leader through mountains and oceans; indeed, the unity of Brahman is established.
The powers of the elements are preceded by taking, giving, and contraction.
I am the mountains, the oceans, the caravan, and the multitude of living beings; I am the elemental powers and the attributes of sentient beings. 63.
I am indeed the conscious Self, the Brahman that assumes the form of all-pervading existence;
I am the source of the arising of creepers, shrubs, sprouts, and all other things that seek birth.
"Origination" (saṃbhavana) refers to the manifestation of sprouts, stalks, spreading branches, and so forth, for those who desire such things. (64)
The Supreme Brahman, whose essence is bliss, is peaceful and resides within the conscious self;
that in which all is contained, from which all proceeds, which is all, and which exists everywhere.
The certainty is that He who is considered as the one Self of all is the Supreme Brahman;
He is known by the names Cit-ātman (the conscious self), Brahman, Sat (Being), Satya (Truth), Ṛta (Cosmic Order), and Jña (the Knower). 66.
The all-pervading reality is declared to be pure consciousness alone, devoid of any object of thought; it is stainless, a mere manifestation, and the awakener of the self within all beings. (67)
The conscious Brahman, which is peaceful and omnipresent, is experienced as being endowed with the entire array of mental constructs belonging to the group of mind, intellect, and senses.

"It is experienced"—the remainder of the sentence being "by the knowers of Brahman. Now, one might object: since consciousness (citi) is experienced as differentiated according to the distinct functions of the mind, intellect, and senses for each individual, how can it be Brahman? To this, he says, beginning with "the mind" and so forth: "pervading," meaning following along with or inherent in all mental constructions (kalanā), that is, in all functions (vṛtti). || 68 ||
Having abandoned all differentiation, I am the stainless Brahman-consciousness, my own manifestation, the cause of all things such as sound and the rest, and the sustainer of the world. (69)

One's own nature, which is the very form of direct perception, is self-luminous valid cognition; it is the manifestation of existence whose nature is the expansion of being, providing space for the reality of words and other causes such as ether, as well as for the maintenance of the world produced by them. (69)
I am the pure Brahman-consciousness that provides space for reality; there is no decay for me, for my nature is a dense mass of streams of pure consciousness flowing without interruption.
Establishing the state of being endowed with all temporal divisions (*kalā*), he clearly states what was already mentioned: "Unceasingly," etc.

The form of the inner self (*pratyagātman*) is like a deep mine—the source—of those streams of consciousness which flow and issue forth incessantly through the streams of limiting adjuncts (*vṛttyupādhi*), similar to a continuous stream of sparks from a fire. || 70 ||
Light is the silence of the wise mind; I am the supreme, immortal Brahman-consciousness, whose form flows incessantly, and who eternally experiences the nectar of realization.

The silence experienced by the *sumanas* yogins is such that it cannot be described even while being experienced; it is the supreme nectar (*amṛta*), consisting of an objectless bliss. Establishing this as before, he says "anārata" and so forth, with reference to all the circles of enjoyers (*bhoktṛ-cakra*) without exception, which are characterized by the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*).

The grammatical connection is as follows: "I am the Consciousness-Brahman, whose singular essence is the bliss of immutable, eternal experience, and whose form flows incessantly like a stream of honey through the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of the various functions of worldly enjoyment. || 71 ||
I am all the wheels without exception; I am the stainless Brahman-consciousness, tranquil like deep sleep, and essentially pure light.
Establishing through the experience of being established in samādhi that one constantly experiences the nectar [of the Self], he says: "In deep sleep... and so forth.
I am the supreme consciousness-Brahman, the manifestation of the highest enjoyment, free from all latent impressions;
only a slight trace remains of the perception of tastes such as the sweetness of sugar-candy and the like.
"Enjoyments" (*saṃbhoga*) refer to the pleasures of sense objects beginning with human bliss and ending with that of Hiraṇyagarbha; [the bliss of the Self] is superior even to those.
"The manifestation" (*ābhāsa*) is that which shines forth from all sides. Having thus established what was called "the highest enjoyment," he causes it to be experienced:
"The perception of the sweetness of pieces of sugar and the like is but a slight portion of the undivided essence [of the Self] from the perspective of the tongue."

That very [consciousness], which remains delimited by a very small space and time extending only as far as the throat, becomes the Self devoid of cessation even when the limiting adjuncts of delimitation have fallen away—provided that the mind, the object of thought, and the thinker, which are the causes of its own delimitation, are realized as being of the single flavor of self-luminous bliss; such is the connection [of the realization]: "I am that Brahman, the unsurpassed bliss."
When the mind and other faculties have been fully realized, one truly becomes that Brahman, the Imperishable;
just as when the moon has risen for one whose mind is fixed upon his beloved. (74)

Now, one might object that the state of consciousness (citi) as liberated from the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of an object is simply unestablished; anticipating this, [the author] demonstrates its establishment with the verse beginning "kāntā" (the beloved). When the moon rises at night for one whose mind is attached to his beloved, and he perceives both the moon and the moonstone (candrakānta) in the space between them—[this refers to the state of the consciousness].

Because its continuity is not perceived even up to the cognition of the form of the moon, the consciousness-Brahman—which consists of an uninterrupted existence and is devoid of objects—is well-known; the meaning is that "I am that very thing. || 74 ||
I am the stainless Consciousness-Brahman, existing by virtue of the moon as a condition,
just as the moon appears in the sky to the eyes of men standing on the ground who are fixed upon it.
The term "situated on the ground" (bhūmiṣṭhā) is a clarification of that very same point. || 75 ||
Indeed, that power of consciousness which abides in the void is the stainless Brahman-consciousness;
likewise, it is pure and devoid of any conceptualization of pleasure, pain, and the like.
"Abiding in the sky" means situated in the intermediate space of the atmosphere.

With the intention that the manifestation of one's own self as being devoid of objects is well-known during the state of those who are indifferent (*udāsīna*), when they are empty of other mental modifications (*vṛtti*) such as pleasure or pain, he says "pleasure," etc. (verse 76).
I am the eternal Self, whose nature is the experience of truth—the Consciousness-Brahman—while the traveler of the world remains unacquainted [with me] as the mind is fixed elsewhere. 77.

Thus, when the mind of a person staying here is situated in such a way that it has not cultivated— that is, has not produced— the perception of objects located on the intervening path for travelers toward another distant object, then in that intermediate space, those [perceptions] which are "guiltless"— meaning free from the fault of contact with the object— [arise].
The meaning is that cognition is pure consciousness alone. || 77 ||
That consciousness which is free from offense—that all-pervading Brahman am I—just as it exists in the causal activities of the sprout when there is a conjunction of earth, water, air, and seed. (78)

When there is a connection—that is, a union—in the actions characterized by sprouts, which are the effects to be produced, that power of consciousness (cicchakti) which is directed toward emerging or moving outward is Brahman; this is the meaning. || 78 ||
I am that pervasive Consciousness-Brahman, whose power resides within the *udgamanīya* [vessel];
I abide of my own accord within myself, just as the dates, nimba fruits, and bimba fruits abide within themselves.

The meaning is that the very existence of taste— which, in the case of fruits such as the date palm and others, remains within their own insentient nature and consists of a manifestation in the form of a conceptualization (prathā) internalized by itself through the activity of gustatory perception— that alone is Brahman. || 79 ||
That which is the existence of one's own essence, dissolved within, is that Brahman; I am the Consciousness, equal [to all].
My inner consciousness is free from weariness and joy, arising from pure reflection.

Furthermore, that very consciousness which is well known to be characterized by sorrow or joy upon the gain or loss of what is desired, when purified by the arising of reflection in accordance with the scriptures, becomes free from sorrow and joy; that indeed is Brahman—thus he says:
"In the event of gain or loss, my consciousness is equal; I am the stainless Brahman."
When the line of vision is extended as far as the earth and the sun, [it is called the *dṛṣṭisūtra*]. (81)

For a person standing on the ground looking at the sun, there is a stretched-out and extended line characterized by the vision— the eye— extending from the earth to the sun, encompassing the space between them; the midpoint of that line,
which is the portion not touching either the eye or the sun, is similar [to the soul], and though it is capable of illuminating objects, [it does not do so].
The meaning is that it is liberated from that. || 81 ||
Pervading that [universe], I am the pervasive Consciousness—tranquil, stainless, and resembling the midst of that [space];
it has arisen likewise in the waking state, in deep sleep, and in the dream state as well.
Thus, he says "jāgrati" etc. (verse 82) to show that when those three states are abandoned, that which is the witness of the three states indeed becomes the Fourth (turya), which is Brahman.
I am the fourth state, the formless, without beginning or end, the pure consciousness-Brahman, free from all ailment;
I abide like the sweetness inherent in hundreds of sugarcane fields of embodied beings.
Within all men, it exists in a single form.
That consciousness, which is of one form in all, is Brahman; I am that, abiding in equanimity.
It is all-pervading, inherent, and of a clear nature, like the radiance of the sun.
I am this pervasive Consciousness-Brahman, the beloved who creates light, possessing the power of the taste of nectar like a fragment of the bliss of divine enjoyment. 85.
I am that imperishable Brahman-consciousness which is known solely through one's own direct experience;
it is woven through every limb of the body, yet its face remains hidden, like a fiber within a lotus stalk.
Regarding its pervasion of all limbs down to the tips of the nails and its indestructibility even when the body is being cut, he says:
"In cutting or in breaking, I am the stainless Brahman-consciousness, whose form flashes forth;
like a mass of clouds pervading the world, I am possessed of vibration. (87)
The worlds, the elements, and the waters [are contained] within that which possesses vibration and non-vibration due to the limiting adjuncts of the functional winds.

The pervasive power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) is I; it consists of subtle forms that are difficult to perceive, is inwardly established in the nature of experience, and is characterized solely by affection. (88)
Subtle atoms and minute living beings, as well as drops of water, are difficult to perceive; she whose imagined form consists of these.
She whose essence resides within and is composed of experience, accessible through experience alone. She who is characterized solely by moisture, smoothness, and supreme love. (88)
Just as the existence of ghee is inherent in milk, so am I consciousness, devoid of decay;
yet the fashioning of bracelets, armlets, and upper-arm ornaments is not composed of that [gold].
The ellipsis is to be supplied as follows: "that [consciousness] is non-material, like the essence of gold in gold. (89)
Like gold situated within a vessel, I am the all-pervading Self, consciousness and Brahman,
always existing both inside and outside the multitude of objects, such as mountains and the rest, throughout my entire body.
That which, in the form of the universal essence of existence, is the stainless "I-consciousness" (citso'ham), the uncreated mirror of all experiences; || 91 ||
Of experiences, that is, of the various modifications consisting of the act of experiencing. || 91 ||
That great reality of consciousness, which bestows the fruits of all intentions and illuminates all splendors, is inaccessible to those whose minds are stained by impurity. || 92 ||
We worship the conscious self (cidātman), which is the ultimate limit of all that is to be accepted, resting within all its parts yet transcending all parts. 93.
Since the appropriation of all things to be appropriated is for the sake of the self, that [self] constitutes the limit.
We worship the Self of Consciousness, whose form is eternally uncontracted,
which vibrates perpetually within the pot, the cloth, the bank, the well, and within the body.

It exists as the nature of being (*sadrūpa*) in objects such as jars and cloths; within the body, it is the fourfold physical form, vibrating, manifesting, and serving as the cause of all activity. Even in the waking state, it remains, in ultimate reality, as if in deep sleep, due to its absolute non-differentiation. || 94 ||
We worship the conscious Self, which remains in the state of deep sleep even while one is awake—just as heat exists in fire, coldness in ice, sweetness in food, and sharpness in a razor. (95)
With the intention that even the existence of fire, heat, and so forth is merely the radiance of consciousness (cit), and thus in the ultimate sense they are nothing but that itself, he says:
We worship the Self of Consciousness—black in darkness, white in the moon, and the light residing both outside and within, abiding in all things. (96)
We worship the conscious Self (cidātman), which, though not distant, remains as if far away—just as sweetness exists within sweet things and sharpness within sharp things. 97.
Although it is not distant because it is one's own inner self, it appears distant due to ignorance. || 97 ||
We worship the conscious Self that has entered into all categories of objects,
throughout the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, and in the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta).
The word "gone" (gatam) connects with what precedes it. || 98 ||
We worship the conscious Self, which is always equal everywhere, in whom all volitions have been stilled and from whom all curiosity has departed. 99.
Kautuka is desire. || 99 ||
We worship the conscious self (cidātman), from which all agitation has departed, which is free from curiosity, devoid of undertaking, effortless, and indeed everything. 100.
*Saṃrambha* is anger; *kautuka* is the longing for enjoyment; *ārambha* is exertion; *īhā* is effort. *Sarvam* means without remainder. || 100 ||
We worship the conscious self (cidātman), which is partless and free from ego, abiding within all things, yet itself being everything and of an infinite, singular form. 101.
Having attained the conscious self, which begins with infinite consciousness,
he reached the high, extended thread of those whose bodies are the three worlds.
Because its undertakings consist of reflections of infinite things, it is the thread for the liberated ones who reside in the three worlds and possess the characteristics of bodies. 102.
Having attained the conscious self that restricts all activity,
it embraces within its fold the birds of the world— those that were dormant within and those that were active without.
Regarding *pracārācārau*: here, only *pracārau* is required.

By means of a *dvandva* compound with the word *pracāra*—which has been formed as a dual ending through the application of *ekaśeṣa*—the two states of waking and dreaming are obtained from the word *pracāra*. Here, the inclusion of the term *ācāra* (conduct) is to be considered. Waking and dreaming.

Contraction is deep sleep; that which effects it [is the cause]. Having embraced—that is, having internalized and pervaded with itself—the birds characterized as the world both within and without, he remains dissolved, existing in a state of concealment.
Having approached the conscious Self, which is like a vast and variegated net,
one realizes that all this exists there, yet does not exist there even in the slightest degree.
Having attained that single Self of consciousness, whose nature is both being and non-being, one reaches the supreme realization—the full abode of all prosperity. (105)

The sense is that it is of the nature of existence (*sad-rūpa*) because it brings about the manifestation of all beings during creation, and it is of the nature of non-existence (*asad-rūpa*) because it brings about the dissolution of all beings during the cosmic withdrawal (*pralaya*).

Alternatively, it is the supreme object of cognition, worthy of absolute trust, and whose sole essence is consciousness (*cidekarasa*). It is the abode and foundation of all prosperities and fragments of happiness. || 105 ||

Having approached the conscious self (cidātman) abiding in all modes of existence, one then [perceives] that which is the substratum of affection, yet unpeaceful, due to the delusions caused by the blows of the dull winds; [this is the view of the Chāndasikas, who maintain that the nature of things is characterized by both existence and non-existence]. 106.

Oil is affection (*sneha*), and love free from conditions is its substratum. The "striking" (*āhati*) of inert things such as the body, the internal winds (*vāta*), and the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), as well as the external winds of rain—namely, superimposition (*adhyāsa*) and impact (*abhighāta*)—is unappeased and undestroyed by the delusions produced thereby. It is joined with these by one of deluded vision, but not by one of true vision.
And it is liberated. || 106 ||

We worship the lamp of consciousness, which is both joined and liberated, the root-stalk of the lotus in the lake of the heart, the thread that is beautiful in every limb, existing both within and without. 107.
Like the root-stalk hidden within the lake of the heart, it is the beautiful, firm support for all limbs such as the hands and feet— a foundation like a rope.
Having attained the conscious Self, which is the means of livelihood for all people, he reached that which is born from the milk-ocean and is devoid of the moon. 108.
He states the distinction from the well-known nectar [of immortality] with the verse beginning "akṣīrārṇava" (108).
We worship the Self of Consciousness, which is unassailable, immortal, and true, appearing through sound, form, taste, touch, and smell. 109.
"Unassailable" (ahārya) means incapable of being taken away by Garuḍa and others; "manifestation" (ābhāsa) means becoming clearly evident. || 109 ||
Having attained the peaceful self of consciousness, which is devoid of those very [states], he is as pure as the expanse of space and is the delight of the entire world. || 110 ||
Coloration is that which manifests [the object] through its own pervasion. || 110 ||
He has realized the conscious self (cidātman), which is neither passion nor space;
which is endowed with great majesty yet devoid of all manifestations;
and which, though the agent, is a non-agent within the state of agency. || 111 ||
"All this is mine, everything belongs to me alone; yet I am not even I, nor is anything other than I.
For one who has realized this regarding the world created by me, let it remain as it is or let it perish—I become free from the fever of anxiety.

Through the vision of superimposition as identity (*tādātmyādhyāropa*), "I am everything"; through the vision of superimposition as conjunction (*saṃsargādhyāropa*), however, "everything is mine. But through the vision of negation (*apavāda*), even the ego (*ahaṃkāra*)—which is the cause for the superimposition of "I-ness"—is not "I," and anything else is certainly not "I. For me, who has thus known the reality through these two methods of superimposition and negation, the world created [by ignorance] is artificial.
Whether it be composed of illusion (māyāmaya), or whether it be stable and uncreated, or even the Self itself—in either case, I shall be free from fever; this is the meaning. || 112 ||

Thus ends the eleventh canto, titled "The Instruction on the Yoga of Certainty regarding Liberation while Living," in the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa* of the *Mokṣopāya* section of the *Śrī Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa*, the work of the Sage. 11.

Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Yoga of Certainty regarding Liberation while Living," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa-tātparyaprakāśa*.
The Twelfth Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Thus, those great ones, possessing such certainty and free from sin, [proceeded].
Established in truth upon the true and peaceful state, they abide in bliss. || 1 ||
Rāma here received from his Guru the state of Janaka and others, which is free from passion and attachment externally, while internally it is pure and self-luminous.
Janaka and the others were liberated while living (jīvanmukta), established within the state of truth, which is the purified meaning of the term "That" (tatpadārtha). || 1 ||
Thus, the wise ones of perfected intellect, whose minds are free from passion, neither despise nor rejoice in life, nor likewise in death. (2)

Those whose intellects are full externally and who have purified the meaning of the term *tvaṃpada* (the "you" aspect); for this very reason, their minds are equal in passion both internally and externally.
Thus, like the arms of Nārāyaṇa, they possess an inconceivable wonder;
yet, being straight and appearing to stumble, they are like other Meru mountains.

Those whose skill in piercing exists even in that which is most subtle and imperceptible; for this very reason, they stand like the arms of Nārāyaṇa—possessing a form that falters [only toward the target] yet being humble by nature, while remaining as firm as other Meru mountains. (3)
They gazed upon forest tracts, islands, and cities,
as well as rows of celestial groves and heavens, like gods.
He elaborates on their dwelling with an equal vision by means of the passage beginning with "they rejoiced" (remire) and so forth. || 4 ||
They wandered among the flower-filled swings swaying back and forth,
and upon the peaks of Mount Meru adorned with various forest groves.
In those [women] who were moving due to the swaying of swings.
They established kingdoms that had conquered their enemies, possessed fly-whisks and royal umbrellas, contained manifold wealth, and were characterized by diverse customs.
Those [works] in which there are various subjects pertaining to the three aims of life (trivarga). || 6 ||
They followed all these people, whose conduct and activities were diverse,
regarding their duties as those prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti.
They followed the dharmas practiced and performed by those of various conducts and diverse refined customs;

that is to say, they themselves also performed them. Thus, they followed the procedure (itikartavyatā) characterized by such undertakings and efforts as are prescribed in the Śruti and Smṛti—namely, the sacrifices and other rites together with their constituent parts (sāṅga). || 7 ||
Adorned with such enjoyments— delightful, captivating with the smiles of beautiful women, and charming with pastimes and food— they were immersed in the fullness of sensory pleasures.
In such delightful expanses and collections of enjoyments, which are endowed with the perfection of both visible and invisible means. || 8 ||
And they entered the grounds of the Nandana grove, filled with the songs of Apsarases, adorned with lovely mango trees, and entwined with Mandāra flowers.
They entered; they withdrew. || 9 ||

Among all beings, both moving and unmoving, in which every creature finds its rest, and within the various stages of domestic life consisting of the series of sacrificial rites performed in due order— (10)

In all the worlds, together with the moving and unmoving beings, all creatures find rest and happiness through such collections of sacrificial rites and domestic lives. Indeed, this Self is the world of all beings;
just as hungry children wait upon their mother, so do all [beings wait upon it].
The intention is that this is based on such scriptural passages as, "The elements worship the agnihotra. || 10 ||
In the pathways of the ocean of battle, where lordly elephants had been slaughtered, where numerous jackals wandered about, and which were terrifying with the booming sounds of kettledrums.
They returned to their own abodes. || 11 ||
They remained steadfast amidst all dualistic conditions— whether those characterized by harsh thoughts, or by arrogance born of plundered wealth, or by the ferocity of violent agitation.

In those harsh, cruel, and affliction-devouring mental states—namely, in adversities consisting of dualistic conflicts where one is overwhelmed and humiliated by enemies who have stolen one's wealth. || 12 ||
But their minds have become free from passion, unconditioned, devoid of delusion, unattached, liberated, profoundly tranquil, and have reached the supreme state of pure being. || 13 ||
They did not sink at all, even in great perils,
just as the great mountain ranges do not submerge when vast bodies of water come upon them.
"Even great sovereignty"—this is the ellipsis. "Kulaśailas" refers to the Himavat and other principal mountain ranges. || 14 ||
O descendant of Raghu, he shone with the most beautiful Śrī, who sported like a playful maiden, just as the mass of waters shines with the splendor of the full moon.
"A mass of water" is an example by way of contrast; the lengthening of the vowel occurs according to the rule "when *ḍha* is elided. || 15 ||
She did not wither from the sorrow of grief, as a forest glade does not from the summer heat; nor did she rejoice in floods of enjoyments, as medicinal herbs do not in the dews.
For they, O Rāma, being entirely undistracted while performing the Kāmamañjarī rite, neither clung to nor abandoned the fruits of their actions, whether desired or undesired.

"Unperturbed" means free from the insistence on being an agent. "Desires" (kāmāḥ) are so called because they are desired; they are enjoyments, and "forming clusters" (mañjarīḥ kurvantah) refers to experiencing those characterized as such. || 17 ||

They did not rejoice when their undertakings were successful, nor did they sink into despair when overcome by them; they did not exult upon attaining happiness, nor did they wither away even in times of distress.
When the task of Śatruñjaya and other works was successfully accomplished, they did not attain an upward increase; yet, when assailed by enemies, they did not undergo a downward decline. || 18 ||
They did not become bewildered by delusions, nor did they sink under the weight of calamities; they did not rejoice at auspicious events, nor did they weep at sorrows like you do.
In delusions and the causes of delusion, in hardships, and by the successive onsets of calamities. || 19 ||
Performing only their duties as required by their natural conduct,
they remained free from agitation, like other Meru mountains.
"Prakṛta" means natural; "prākṛta" refers to conduct appropriate to one's own caste (varṇa), [which is followed] when the proper occasion has arrived. || 20 ||
O Raghava, having firmly grasped that vision which destroys all evil,
roam about in due order, free from egoism, though possessing a body.
