In that state of non-egoism—wherein there is pure consciousness alone, stripped of egoism—one who possesses the notion of "I" (the self) regarding that [state] is of such a kind. || 21 ||
Beholding this very succession of creations as it truly is,
remain seated with equanimity, free from delusion, like Mount Meru standing firm and as deep as the ocean.
As it truly is, as it stands; firm and stable like Mount Meru. || 22 ||
All this is indeed pure consciousness alone that has come to appear in this manner;
here there is nothing whatsoever that exists as either real or unreal anywhere.
He explains what that vision of reality as it truly is (yathābhūtadarśana) is like: "It is pure consciousness alone" (cinmātra). || 23 ||

Relying on the stainless greatness [of the Self], abandon this world with indifference; O noble one, become one whose intellect is unattached everywhere, and thus bring about the destruction of worldly existence. 24.
Greatness, the state of Brahman. || 24 ||
"Why do you weep with such intense agitation, and why do you grieve like a fool? You wander with a bewildered mind, O gentle one, like a blade of grass caught in a whirlpool. (25)
Śrī Rāma said:
Oh, Blessed One! Truly, that which was not [previously] born has now been born perfectly;
through your grace I have awakened, like a lotus at the touch of the sun. (26)
The words of Rāma are clear. || 26 ||
My delusion has surely vanished like mist in autumn;
with all my doubts completely stilled, I shall carry out your word.

O virtuous one, if you speak here with a mind that has long been free from intoxication and delusion, released from pride and envy, whose soul has long been joyful and whose grief is stilled— a mind that is pure and single-pointed and does not again fall into suffering— then I shall do it without hesitation.

Since there is no happiness in that, it is "unhappiness," which is the delusion of being a bound self. Whatever means for strengthening [the mind] you speak of regarding this subject of the taught meaning—whether by means of one-pointed or decisive intellect, or otherwise through duties such as the protection of the kingdom—I shall perform that without hesitation. 28.

Thus ends the twelfth canto, titled "The Description of Doubts Regarding the Living Liberated," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa, within the Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa of Valmīki, concerning the means to liberation. Canto 12.
Thus ends the twelfth canto, titled "The Description of the Doubts of the Jivanmukta," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa-tātparyaprakāśa*.
The Thirteenth Chapter.
Śrī Rāma said:
When the dissolution of latent impressions arises through the play of perfect knowledge, [the state of liberation is attained].
O Brahmin, I have indeed found rest in the state of liberation while living. || 1 ||

The process of the dissolution of latent impressions through the awakening of reality has been described; now, a preliminary foundation is being laid here to explain that same process by means of the restraint of the vital breath (prāṇa).

Between the two methods for the destruction of latent impressions (*vāsanākṣaya*)— namely, the sequence of knowledge (*jñāna*) and yoga— which were shown in the section on tranquility (*upaśama*), Rāma, having attained the fruit of the dissolution of latent impressions through the play of knowledge (*jñānavilāsa*) intended for those of the highest capacity and thus having achieved his purpose, nevertheless describes the manner of destroying latent impressions by means of the sequence of yoga as well, for the benefit of those of dull and middling capacities.
Desiring to know, he asks with two verses beginning with "properly" (samyak). || 1 ||
O Brahmin, when the dissolution of latent impressions arises through the cessation of the vibration of the vital breath, tell me: how does one rest in the state of liberation while living?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
The method for crossing over the cycle of worldly existence is expressed by the word "yoga.
Know that it is of two kinds, characterized by the pacification of the mind.

In order to provide an answer to what was asked, Vasiṣṭha, reminding [Rāma] of the two methods of Rājayoga and Haṭhayoga as already described in the *Upaśama-prakaraṇa*, makes his formal declaration with the two verses beginning with "saṃsāra... (verse 3).
Self-knowledge is one method of this [practice] manifested on earth;
hear now of the second, the restraint of breath (prāṇasaṃrodha), which is being described by me. (4)
Śrī Rāma said: Of these two, which is the better—one that is easy to attain and free from suffering—by the mere understanding of which further agitation does not afflict one? (5)
In this regard, he first asks which of the two is easier to accomplish, [inquiring about] the distinction with the words "because of its ease of attainment.
*Kṣobha* means agitation or distraction. || 5 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Although both methods are indeed denoted by the word "yoga," nevertheless, this term has become firmly established primarily in the sense of being joined with the vital breath (prāṇa).
The word "yoga" refers to the conjunction with the vital breath (prāṇa) and the restraint of the vital breath. 6.
In the process of crossing over saṃsāra, yoga and likewise jñāna are the two equal means; they alone are said to bestow a single fruit. (7)
For some, yoga is unattainable; for others, the certainty of knowledge.
But for me, O virtuous one, the certainty of knowledge is considered easily attainable.
For someone of a delicate mind who cannot endure the suffering of restraining the vital breaths, haṭhayoga is unattainable;

for one of a hard-hearted mind who is unskilled in inquiry, the certainty of knowledge is unattainable. The meaning is that for me, whose mind is pure and who am skilled in inquiry, the certainty of knowledge is considered easily attainable. || 8 ||
Furthermore, ignorance that remains unknown would not exist even in dreams;
knowledge, however, operates eternally in all states.

For unskillfulness in discernment would indeed consist in the incapacity to distinguish between the essential natures of knowledge and ignorance; however, since that is impossible even in a dream for one who is skilled in the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), he says with this intention: "Ignorance. It proceeds and manifests by itself.
Thus, because ignorance is always established through the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*) and because knowledge is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*), [the distinction is clear].

The sense is that knowledge is easy because the dissimilarity [between the Self and the non-Self] is established by itself and through experience alone, and thus their distinction is possible; however, yoga is not so, and is therefore difficult to achieve. || 9 ||

Or else, it is not at all fitting to say that yoga is difficult to accomplish because it must be achieved through the practice of concentration (dhāraṇā), the proper posture (āsana), the specific location (deśa), and so forth; for such a conceptualization is not beautiful.
Yoga is difficult to accomplish even because of its dependence on external factors such as an auspicious place, time, and object; thus he says, "dhāraṇā" (retention).

The place for retention (*dhāraṇā-deśa*) is external, such as a mountain peak, the moon, or the stars, as well as internal locations such as the heart, throat, root of the palate, and the center of the brows.
The place for the posture (*āsana-deśa*), however, is one that is level, clean, free from pebbles, fire, and sand, and devoid of noise, bodies of water, and similar disturbances.

"One should employ [the practice] in a place agreeable to the mind, not one that afflicts the eyes, and which provides shelter secluded from caves. Thus, yoga—which is well-known through the Śruti, Smṛti, and Śāstras as being achievable through those means—does not become easy to accomplish for those who lack enthusiasm, the dull-witted, the foolish, or the lowest of men; it is not so for the steadfast and capable person.

He says "Or rather" (athavā) to show that it is appropriate for an aspirant who is striving in the scriptural means to consider whether [the goal] is easily accomplished or accomplished with difficulty. || 10 ||
"O descendant of Raghu, it is said that there are indeed only two types of yoga taught in the scriptures: knowledge and action.
Of these, knowledge has been described to you as being inwardly situated and pure in its object. (11)
Having thus set aside this intermediate question, he begins to state the answer to the previous question with the words "Two," and so forth.
Established through the movement of prāṇa and apāna, dwelling within the cave of the firm body, this yoga bestows infinite perfections and grants wisdom; listen, O virtuous one! (12)
It is established and renowned as the attainment of the equilibrium of the *prāṇa* and *apāna* through their state as *prāṇa* and *apāna*;

it bestows infinite accomplishments such as *khecarī-vidyā* upon those desiring supernatural powers (*siddhi*), and for those desiring knowledge, it bestows wisdom as the cause of direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*). Therefore, the meaning is: "Listen to that. || 12 ||

O Prince, having attained stability through the cessation of the movement of the breath from the mouth, and remaining with a mind fixed on the imperishable, you shall dwell here in the supreme state, absorbed in meditative concentration and with all speech stilled, by means of the practice of yoga.

Encouraging him further by proclaiming the fruit of resting in the bliss of that very samādhi, he says: "With the mouth... O Prince, you—having attained such a state and established yourself therein—will achieve [this] through the cessation of the vibration, that is, the movement, of the breath (mukhānila) by means of a mind that is intensely applied (udyuktacitta); thus, you shall abide here in the supreme, imperishable syllable (akṣara) which is the nature of consciousness.

When there is yoga in the state [of the Self], which is the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind, through the practice of that [yoga] and by means of its application, you—being established in meditative absorption (samādhi)—will dwell, that is, you will remain, having become one whose form is unsurpassed bliss beyond the reach of speech and the gods. || 13 ||

Thus ends the thirteenth canto, titled "Instruction on the Yoga of Discerning Knowledge," in the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa* of the *Mokṣopāya* section of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*, composed by Vālmīki and belonging to the *Ārṣa* tradition. 13.
Thus ends the thirteenth canto, titled "Instruction on the Yoga of Discerning Knowledge," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The Fourteenth Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Indeed, this [universe] exists somewhere within that infinite one.
The vibration that takes the form of the world is like a mirage in the desert. || 1 ||

In this section, the journey of Bhuśuṇḍi to Vasiṣṭha’s hermitage on Mount Meru, out of a desire to behold him, and the description of that mountain peak, are described as heard from the mouth of Surasaṃsat.

Intending to describe in detail the sequence of yoga beginning with breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) and so forth—which has been introduced—by means of an elaborate exposition through the words of Bhuśuṇḍa, he begins the narrative of Bhuśuṇḍa with the words "There exists... and so on. [He refers to] that supreme state (*paramapada*), described as the place of rest for the yogi, which, in a certain region veiled by ignorance, has its "foot" in all beings according to the Vedic text: "Of this [Self], all beings are one foot."
According to scripture, the world-form is a vibration in the shape of the cosmic egg, which is a phenomenal manifestation (vivarta). || 1 ||
There, Brahmā, born from the lotus, became the cause;
he remained as the Grandfather, his mind reeling under the weight of the created beings.
In that cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), he has become the cause of Manu, Prajāpati, and the others. || 2 ||
I am his mind-born son, Vasiṣṭha, of excellent conduct;
I dwell in every age within the circle of the stars held fast by Dhruva.
In the circle of bears, in the circle of constellations, in the world of the Seven Sages; by the word "yuga," a collection of yugas—the Vaivasvata Manvantara—is indicated. || 3 ||
Once, while I was staying in the assembly hall of Śatakratu in heaven,
I heard from Nārada and others a discourse concerning those who possess very long lives.
In the assembly hall, the seat of Śatakratu Indra. || 4 ||
Then, during the course of a certain conversation,
a sage named Śātātapa— who was silent, dignified, and high-minded— spoke there.
He was silent and spoke little; he was honorable and worthy of respect, and skilled in the means of valid cognition. || 5 ||
In the northeastern corner of Meru, in the sky composed of rubies,
there stands the glorious Kalpavṛkṣa tree, known as the Mango (Cūta) on its peak.

He states what he said with the words beginning "of Meru" and so forth: on a peak made of ruby, in the sky—that is, in a region of the heavens—there exists a famous and renowned *kalpavṛkṣa* known as Cūta.
At the summit of that wish-fulfilling tree, within the hollow of its southern branch,
there exists a bird's nest entwined with silver creepers.
It was made of refined gold and silver, and inlaid with wish-fulfilling creepers fashioned from those same materials.
In that vast hollow dwelt a glorious crow named Bhuśuṇḍa,
free from passion, like Brahmā in his own lotus.
Just as he lives here for a long time within the treasury of the worlds, so shall Cirañjīvī live in heaven; no one has ever lived, nor will anyone ever live, like him.
He is long-lived, free from passion, glorious, and possessed of great intelligence;
he is one whose mind is at rest, tranquil, beloved, and skilled in the knowledge of time.
Because his mind is at rest, he is therefore peaceful. || 10 ||
If one lives here just as that bird lives, then that life would be meritorious, long-lasting, and truly purposeful. || 11 ||

Such a long life would be meritorious during the stage of its accomplishment and would result in prosperity during the stage of its fruition, being endowed with the attainment of the supreme human goal; the optative suffix (*liṅ*) is used here in the sense of possibility. 11.
Thus, being questioned further by him, Bhuśuṇḍa described it exactly as it was, speaking the truth in the assembly of the gods. || 12 ||

When questioned once again by me, that Śātātapa described Bhuśuṇḍa in the very manner already stated. He says, "He spoke the truth," to ward off any suspicion that his account might be mere praise. || 12 ||
Then, when the assembly of gods had departed and the occasion for conversation had subsided,
I went out of curiosity to see the bird Bhuśuṇḍa.
Where Bhuśuṇḍa was stationed, there I reached in an instant that great northern peak of Meru, which is composed of rubies.
With a splendor as lovely as red chalk and possessing the brilliance of fire,
it colored the quarters of the sky as if with the essence of honey and wine.

He describes that very peak with the verse beginning "ratnaiḥ" and so forth: by means of lovely gems and red chalk (gairika), and by its essence—like an intoxication induced by honey-wine—it colors the host of the quarters, the directions, turning them red;
for it is well known that those who are drunk become flushed red. || 15 ||
It was like a mass of mountains ablaze with the fire at the end of an eon,
with the smoke from the crests of sapphires reddening the sky with its light.
The mountain has become as if a solid mass of flames rising from the conflagration at the end of an aeon—this is the poetic fancy (utprekṣā).
It is "accumulated," meaning augmented by its splendor. The justification for the poetic fancy is that its upward-spreading luster, like the crests of sapphires, is itself the smoke. || 16 ||
It stood like a heap of all passions gathered together on Mount Meru,
like a single dense mine for the entire web of twilight clouds.
Of all rednesses—that is, of all crimson hues—or of the passions of all living beings, or of their desires for sight. || 17 ||
As Meru was departing,
the lovely submarine fire— the digestive heat of the stomach— emerged through the Brahma-nāḍī alone and reached his head.

For one who desires to effect departure by means of the yoga of *utkrānti* (ascension) through the *brahmanāḍī* or *suṣumṇā*, piercing the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), there is a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*): [the breath] stands like the submarine fire (*vāḍava*)—resembling the fire of the mare (*vaḍavāgni*)—having emerged from the belly of Meru and reached the head, the region of the crown. || 18 ||
Like a goddess of the Sumeru forest, she playfully extended the tip of her finger into the sky, as if to grasp the moon dyed with fresh lac-dye.

Out of the playful curiosity of sport, the goddess of the Sumeru forest extended her hand— stained with the juice of red lac— as if it were a mass of fingers gathered together like flames, and carried it into the sky to seize and grasp the moon.
With its red garlands like flames, the sky, with its face of water,
seemed to throb as if to go toward the mountain, appearing like the submarine fire (Vāḍava) situated upon a peak.
With its flames as if strung together like garlands, it seemed to move with a flickering motion as if to ascend to the sky; therefore,

it stood like the sacrificial fire (*adhvarāgni*) belonging to a Brahmin (*vāḍava*), which, by virtue of being a carrier of oblations, has the milk of the *agnihotra* and other offerings in its mouth— this being the case for the fire, while in the case of the mountain peak, "milk" refers to water.
One whose mouth, at its upper part, has water from a mountain torrent. || 20 ||
With three fingers, as it were, whose tips are the shimmering rays of its nails, it seems to touch the sky and to kiss its heights.

With its three peaks as fingers, whose nail-tips are the rays of glittering gems, it seems to kiss the sky, reaching out and pervading it as if to touch, stroke, and count the stars beginning with Aśvinī; thus it stands lofty. 21.
The pavilion of the mountains, with its thundering mṛdaṅga drums,
was rich with clusters of blossoming flowers and filled with the humming of swarms of bees.

The *murajas* are varieties of percussion instruments. It stands like a dance pavilion for the forest glories nourished—that is, made to flourish—by the earth (*bhuvā*), meaning the forest ground; it is that in which there is a swarm (*peṭaka*) of humming bees. || 22 ||
With rows of teeth like palm leaves quivering as if in jest,
it possessed a noble and intoxicated passion, with throngs of celestial nymphs swaying like those on a swing.
By means of the row of palm leaves, which was like a row of teeth as it blossomed open; in which [tree] there were the noble pride and passion of all living beings.
His mountain caves were inhabited by pairs of deities resting upon the rocks;
he wore choice garments and skins, and the bright Gaṅgā served as his sacred thread.
He imagines her to be an ascetic, saying: "O excellent one... (verse 24).
He saw a hermit standing like Piṅgala, holding a bamboo staff,
amidst a bower of creepers resounding with the roar of the Ganges' cascades, like an immortal.

The peak of Mount Meru, tawny-hued and adorned with stars like jewels, reached the very limit of the sky; it was sweetened by a breeze fragrant with the lovely songs of Gandharvas and graced by crowns of blooming golden lotuses. (26)
The limit is the upper boundary. || 26 ||
With heaps of forest flowers in fresh hues— white, green, yellow, pale red, and white—
the pure paintings upon the sky were fashioned there for the pleasure-mountain of the host of celestial maidens.

I reached the peak of Mount Meru, the pleasure-mountain of the host of celestial maidens, which is like a play-hill fashioned as if painted in the sky by daily fresh colors— white, green, and other hues— characterized by heaps of forest flowers and coloring substances, and thus rendered spotless and variegated.
The connection with all [the preceding verses] is through the fourteenth verse mentioned previously. || 27 ||

Thus ends the fourteenth canto, titled "The Description of the Summit of Mount Meru," in the *Bhuśuṇḍa-ākhyāna*, within the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa* of the *Mokṣopāya*, in the *Divyopākhyāna* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki. 14.
Thus ends the fourteenth canto, titled "Description of the Summit of Mount Meru," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
Fifteenth Canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Upon his head, whose locks of hair were like clouds filled with flowers—
I beheld the constituent part of the eon standing there like a wheel of branches.
On the peak is a wish-fulfilling tree and a mango tree, with the abundance of flowers, birds, and so forth;
on its trunk is a flock of crows, and herein is described the story of Bhuśuṇḍa.
On the summit— the head-region— of that peak, which has locks of hair like clouds of the Kalpa age filled with flowers,
there stands [the tree] whose limbs, branches, and other parts are "kalpa-like," meaning they are capable of fulfilling the desired objects of living beings, situated all around.

Because its rows of branches were spread out evenly, it stood like a wheel of branches; having attained a supreme variety of forms—thus characterized by the attributes mentioned in the final twelve verses—it follows that, by implication, I beheld that mango tree described by Śātātapa. This is the connection [of the verse]. || 1 ||
Enveloped by clouds of flower-pollen and bristling with clusters of jewels,
its height surpassing the sky, it was like one peak placed upon another.
Enveloped and pervaded by clouds characterized by the pollen of flowers; "height" refers to loftiness;
"on the peak" means on the peak of Meru described previously. || 2 ||
With a flood of flowers twice as abundant as stars, with sprouts twice as numerous as clouds,
with dust twice as dense as rays of light, and with clusters of blossoms twice as brilliant as lightning.
It is not only by its height that it has surpassed the sky, but also by its mass of flowers and so forth, which are double those of the stars and such; thus he says [the following verse]:
the prohibition of the short vowel is Vedic, and there is the elision of the *kap* suffix. (3)
In its branches resounded the song of the kinnarīs, doubled by the humming of bees; its foliage was made to seem doubly lush by the world of apsarases swaying upon their swings.
Its foliage was doubled by the bud-like lips, hands, and feet of the celestial nymphs who sway like cradles in the world above.
The birds there were twice as numerous as the throngs of Siddhas and Gandharvas;
its bark-garments were doubled by a clear frost that possessed the luster of jewels.

Because it can assume any form at will, it is as if the hosts of *siddhas* and *gandharvas*, having assumed the guise of birds for the sake of wandering at their own pleasure, have arisen and become twice as numerous as birds within it;
it is like a garment donned by a fine cloth that is doubled by clear frost, characterized by the luster of jewels.
It is established. || 5 ||
Its large fruit was doubled by its embrace of the lunar orb;
its joints were doubled by clouds resembling those dissolved at the root of the world-period.

Because its fruits were doubled in size— due to their extreme height, their contact with the lunar orb, and as if filled with the essence of nectar— they were consequently large; furthermore, its joints at the base of the trunk appeared to be doubled in bulk by the clouds of the kalpa-age clinging to them.
Its trunk was entwined with lovely creepers, and kinnaras rested upon its branches; it was like a cloud amidst the forest thickets, while gods and other beings slept by its marshy banks.

Having driven away the bees with the tinkling sounds of their bracelets, [the women]— who were like female bees among the Apsarases— held flowers within their hands, which were naturally beautiful and expansive.
He was one from whose midst the bees— the Apsarases characterized by their bee-like qualities— were driven away by the sounds of bracelets and the tinkling of armlets,
while they took for themselves the nectar from the flowers; the word "ca" (and) serves to connect him with the previously mentioned attributes,
and he was accompanied by the best of the Suras, Kinnaras, Gandharvas, and Vidyādharas.
Like the web of the universe, it fills the infinite quarters and spaces of the sky. || 9 ||
The web of the world stands like the cosmic egg, filling the infinite and boundless ten directions.
It possessed a dense network of buds, dense and tender shoots,
dense blossoming flowers, and was garlanded with dense forests.
It was a dense mass of flower-clusters, a thick cluster of jewels, enriched with garments and gems that were without gaps, and agitated by the playful movement of creepers. || 11 ||
The playful dance of the creepers, rich with divine garments and jewels as if fulfilling the desires of supplicants. || 11 ||
Everywhere it attained a supreme variety through floods of flowers, everywhere with fruits and sprouts, and everywhere with masses of fragrant pollen.
In its armpits, in its groves, in the leaves of its creepers, at its joints,
and among its flowers, I saw birds nestled within their dwellings.
In the armpits, at the joints of the shoulder-branches, in the bowers, and at the tips of branches covered by creepers. || 13 ||
They were nourished by pieces of lotus stalks as delicate as a fragment of the moon’s digit,
and they fed upon morsels of the roots of the *arjuna* lotus, like Brahmin cranes.

He describes a specific distinction among the birds with the words "niśānātha" and so forth: [he saw] the *sārasa* cranes, who serve as the vehicles of Brahmā; they were nourished and increased by the digits of the moon (*niśākara-kalā*) which were like pieces of lotus stalks (*khaṇḍāmṛṇāla-śakala*), and likewise, they had for their food tender white lotus roots (*arjuna-ambhojinī-kanda*). || 14 ||
He saw the young ones of the swans belonging to Viriñci, who were chanting the Sāman,
friends of the Veda through the syllable Om, and instructors of the knowledge of Brahman.
Because they assist in contemplating the secret meaning of the syllable *oṃ* and the Vedas, they are "friends" (*suhṛdaḥ*), meaning they have become like friends;
they are those for whom there is instruction in the knowledge of the higher and lower Brahman from the mouth of a guru according to the prescribed rule. || 15 ||
They vomited forth a multitude of mantras with sounds resembling the utterance of "svāhā," appearing like dark clouds filled with lightning flashes amidst their bones.

The parrots that serve as Agnivāhana’s mounts describe [the scene] there with the words beginning "udgīrṇa" and so forth: their bones are like conch shells; they possess many, numerous, comparisons in color to masses of lightning and dark blue clouds. || 16 ||
He saw parrots, dark as the fire-god, young with crests like the tips of peacock plumes, constantly perched upon the leafy shoots of the sacrificial altar-creeper, being gazed upon by the gods.
The phrase "I saw the parrots that serve as his mounts, dark green like the leaves of the green kuśa grass spread upon the sacrificial altars," applies throughout [the verse].
He describes the young peacocks with the words beginning "śiśūn" (the young ones): their crests are radiant like the crests of the fire-god Śikhin.
Of those. || 17 ||
[He saw] the excellent peacocks of Kumāra, whose plumage was protected by Gaurī,
and who were experts in the entirety of Śiva’s knowledge imparted by Skanda.
He saw his kinsmen, who were like autumn clouds in appearance, dwelling in the sky— great beings born and perished within the very heavens, like birds of the air.

[He saw] those birds of various species who were born from the sky itself and perished in that very place; who, until their death, descended upon the earth—and for that very reason, being great due to their superior strength, were renowned by the name "Sky-Birds";
and who, because they were constant companions in play, were his kinsmen, having built their dwellings and constructed their nests [there]. || 19 ||
Others were born from the swan of Brahmā (Virañci), others from Agniśuka,
others from the peacock of Kumāra, and others from the bird of the sky (Ambara).
He also saw Bharadvāja birds with two beaks, golden-crested birds,
sparrows, cranes, vultures, cuckoos, krauñcas, and wild cocks.
O Raghava, I saw there many other birds as well— parrots, blue jays, cranes, and so forth— a multitude of creatures like the earth itself.
The "multitude of beings" refers to the collection of living creatures; "therein" means upon that tree. || 22 ||
Then, while standing in the sky, I beheld her situated on a distant branch of the southern shoulder, where the leaves were lush and full.
She whose leaves are lush and thick. || 23 ||
In time, there appeared upon the Lokāloka mountain a circle of crows garlanded with clusters of blossoms, standing like a mass of clouds at the end of an eon in the forest.

At that time, immediately after the appearance of the southern branch, there was a circle—a swarm—of *kākolās*, a specific species of crows known as *droṇakākas*; it stood like a flood of the clouds of cosmic dissolution (*kalpābhra*). || 24 ||
There, I saw that in a hollow of a tree at the edge of the grove, which was strewn with various flowers and filled with manifold fragrances, [there lay the body]. (25)
In the assembly hall of the meritorious women in heaven, which is perfumed by clusters of beloved flowers, the crows remain with their forms undisturbed.

The connection with the preceding verse is as follows: in the hollow of the trunk [of the tree], which is like a dwelling for women who have performed meritorious deeds—namely, the Apsarases—who are fit for the enjoyment of the pleasures of delight in heaven; they possess unagitated forms because they are endowed with qualities such as tranquility. || 26 ||
The clouds, scattered by the wind as if by an equal force, were dispersed;
in their midst stood the illustrious Bhuśuṇḍa, of towering form. (27)
Like clouds dispersed by a wind that is equal and even in its force—shattered, cut apart, and driven away as if they were forced into hollows. || 27 ||
And in the midst of the fragments of glass, he was as prominent as a sapphire;
his mind was fully contented, he was dignified, equanimous, and beautiful in every limb. (28)
The proud one is worthy of honor. || 28 ||
Through constant attention to the movement of the vital breath, he was inwardly turned and happy;
he became renowned as "Cirañjīvī" (the Long-lived One) because of that long life.
By means of the restraint [attained] through the focused attention on the vibration of the vital breath; by that which is most well-known. || 29 ||
Renowned throughout the world as Bhuśuṇḍa, he was celebrated for his long life;
his mind was matured by witnessing the conditions of the arrival and departure of the ages (yugas).
And at every kalpa, weary from counting the succession of world-protectors— Śarvas, Śakras, and Marutvats— through their cycles of births, he grew exhausted.

From the recitation which consists mostly of the names of the world-protectors—such as Śarvas, Īśānas, Śakras, Indras, Marutvants, and Marutsakhās—he became weary and despondent, counting the succession of their births. || 31 ||
He was a rememberer of the past kings of gods, asuras, and mortals;
his mind was serene and profound, and his speech was elegant, affectionate, and charming.
He is gentle and clever. || 32 ||
He is the speaker of the unmanifest, the knower, free from possessiveness and free from egoism;
he is the well-wisher, the kinsman, as well as the friend, the son of Death, the teacher, and the lord;
he is always and in every way truth, and everything in the praise of all.

He is a speaker who makes clear those things that are unmanifest, indistinct, and of the subtlest meaning; for he is their knower, as dear as a son to Death. He is capable and powerful enough to rival even the preceptor Bṛhaspati through his intellect. To the question "Why is he a friend to all? the author replies with the word "always" (*sarvadā*); for he is [the friend] of everyone.
Because it is the substratum underlying all superimpositions for the entire class of living beings, it is "truth" (satyam) in every way, in every manner, and at all times;
that is to say, it is so according to all opinions in the context of praising or describing anything whatsoever. || 33 ||
Gentle, serene, sweet, and full of flavor, that great-souled one was heart-pleasing like a lake whose inner depths are cool;
he who knew the ways of the world dwelt within the hollow of the lotus of the heart.
Having abandoned impurity through profundity, he possesses the glory of a manifest intention.

The qualifiers are clear in both interpretations. "The cavity of the heart-lotus" means having the form of the *dahara* (small) space. To exclude the possibility that this refers to the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*), he says: "the knower of worldly affairs. In the case of the lake interpretation, it refers to one in whose heart there is a hollow dug out as a receptacle for lotuses. Birds...
The "birds" are their "withdrawal," which is their rest; he who knows that has the glory of a manifest intention because of his state of supreme purity. 34.

Thus ends the fifteenth canto, titled "The Vision of Bhuśuṇḍa," within the *Bhuśuṇḍopākhyāna* (The Narrative of Bhuśuṇḍa) of the *Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa* (Section on Liberation), in the *Mokṣopāya* (Means to Liberation) of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa*, a work of the Sage (*ārṣa*). Canto 15.
Thus ends the fifteenth canto, titled "The Vision of Bhuśuṇḍa," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The sixteenth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Then, with my body blazing, I fell before him.
He slightly agitated the assembly, like a star falling from the sky onto a mountain.

Having been honored with a seat and other offerings by Vasiṣṭha, who had arrived before him, the question concerning the birth, deeds, and so forth of Bhuśuṇḍa was asked; that [account] is now described here.
Then I descended before that Bhuśuṇḍa, like a star falling from the immovable sky. || 1 ||
The crow-haunted place, resembling a lake of blue lotuses, was agitated by the gentle breeze of my descent, as if by an earthquake at the coming of the ocean. || 2 ||
He explains the phrase "having slightly agitated the assembly" with the word "cukṣobha. The assembly (*sabhā*) is the gathering place (*āsthāna*) of the crows. (2)
Although he arrived unexpectedly immediately after my appearance,
Bhuśuṇḍa recognized him, thinking, "This is Vasiṣṭha who has arrived."

The meaning is that he has understood that even I, whose arrival was unanticipated, unthought of, and unexpected, have reached him, precisely because he possesses the vision of the three periods of time. || 3 ||
From the heap of leaves, he rose up like a young cloud from a lightning-flash;
"O Sage, welcome," he said in sweet-sounding syllables.
A "cloud-child" means subtle, that is to say, like a cloud. || 4 ||
With his two hands born from mere volition, he immediately offered me a handful of flowers, just as a cloud pours down a heap of gold.
At that very moment, at the time of his welcoming words, [he was like] snow itself—*haima*—like a mass of cold autumnal rain. || 5 ||
When the leader of the crows had dismissed his attendants and brought forward a fresh leaf from the Kalpavṛkṣa tree, saying, "Here is a seat," [the Lord sat down].
"Having abandoned [all concern for] death": the meaning is that, instead of having a seat brought by means of a servant, she herself respectfully brought the seat forward. || 6 ||
When Bhuśuṇḍa had risen and his own flock of birds had also risen,
they saw the sage seated there with his gaze directed toward his own seat.

The phrase "ending with *utthita*" connects back to what precedes it. It refers to birds whose wings spread like their own digits (or rays of light), and who are of that same nature as iron [in the context of the previous simile]. || 7 ||
Then, surrounded on all sides by a multitude of birds along with Bhuśuṇḍa,
I sat down upon a seat in that cluster of wish-fulfilling creepers.
Then, immediately after that, I sat down together with Bhuśuṇḍa. || 8 ||
Having prepared the water for honor (arghya), the water for the feet (pādya), and other offerings, Bhuśuṇḍa, with a delighted mind and great splendor, spoke to me in sweet words out of friendship.
Bhuśuṇḍa said: "Oh, for a long time the Blessed One has shown us his grace, since we,
who are like noble trees, have been sprinkled by the nectar of your vision!"

*Prasādaḥ* means grace or favor. *Saddrumāḥ* refers to those acting like virtuous trees, or perhaps including the wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpavṛkṣa*). The plural number in *vayam* (we) is used to denote a genus, as prescribed by the rule *jātyākhyāyām*, in order to indicate our low birth and so forth. || 10 ||
O Sage, most worthy of honor, by whom you are honored, impelled now by the long-accumulated store of my merit, from where have you come?
From where? From which place? || 11 ||
I hope that, as you dwell for a long time in this great delusion,
your unbroken equanimity remains established in your pure mind.
In the world, which is the effect of primordial ignorance (mūlājñāna) and is characterized by my own non-delusion. || 12 ||
Why have you troubled yourself with the hardship of coming here today?
You ought to grant us an order, for we are eager to hear your words. (13)

For us, who were longing and yearning upon hearing your command, [you have fulfilled] the command—that which was to be commanded. (13) O Sage, by the mere sight of your feet, everything has been understood by me;
by the merit of your arrival, we have been graced by you. (14)
We have come to your memory through our long-standing discussions on longevity;
therefore, you have now sanctified this abode with your feet.

He clarifies the statement "everything is known" with the word *ciram* (for a long time): [it refers to those] whose long lives have been spent in discussions and deliberations concerning them, which took place in the assembly of Indra. || 15 ||
O Sage, since this is already known, I nevertheless ask you here;
for my desire to taste the nectar of your words is now fully awakened.
If it is already known, then for what purpose do you ask? To this he replies: "By your word... (verse 16).
Having spoken thus, that bird Bhuśuṇḍa, who has lived for a long time and possesses stainless knowledge of the three periods of time, said this to me there.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
O great king of birds, what you have said is true;
I have come today specifically to see you, who are long-lived.
With a heart cooled within, by good fortune you are well;
you have not fallen, O soul of the Buddha, into the terrifying snare of worldly existence.
Having fallen, he entered. || 19 ||
Therefore, O Blessed One, cut through this doubt of mine according to the truth:
in what family were you born, and how did you become one who has known that which is to be known? (20)

"O Blessed One, he who knows the birth and destruction, the coming and going of beings, as well as knowledge and ignorance—he is to be called 'Bhagavān'. Thus, he is endowed with the aforementioned knowledge. 20.
O holy one, how long is your lifespan, and what conduct do you remember? By whom was this dwelling-place pointed out to you, O far-sighted one? (21)
"Vṛtta" refers to conduct that transcends the end of a kalpa; "nivāsa" means he who dwells here in this form of a tree. || 21 ||
Bhuśuṇḍa said:
"O sage, I shall describe all that you ask;
this narrative should be heard with effort by a high-souled person who is free from agitation. (22)
It is to be proclaimed; it is to be heard. || 22 ||

That which persons like you—whose forms are worthy of worship by the Lord of the Three Worlds, who are great and noble-minded—listen to, brings about the destruction of evil through its proclamation, just as the heat of the sun is dispelled by the presence of clouds. (23)

When those like you hear a certain account, by the recounting of that very account, misfortune and destruction come upon the speakers and other listeners as well; just as the heat of the sun is destroyed by the power of rain, shade, and forests provided by the clouds. || 23 ||
Thus ends the sixteenth canto, titled "The Union of Vasiṣṭha and Bhuśuṇḍa," in the Nirvāṇa Section of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Valmiki, within the *Deva-mokṣopāya*.
Thus ends the sixteenth canto, titled "The Union of Vasiṣṭha and Bhuśuṇḍa," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The seventeenth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Now, O Rāma, that Bhuśuṇḍa was neither delighted nor was his mind crooked.
Beautiful in every limb and dark-complexioned, like a rain cloud in the monsoon season. || 1 ||
Having thus described Bhuśuṇḍa here as possessing the qualities appropriate for one liberated while living (jīvanmukta),
it is now told that he proceeded to explain the matter asked about in detail.

Then Bhuśuṇḍa spoke this, which is connected to the final verse of the chapter: "Delighted" means possessed of joy arising from the attainment of what is desired; "crooked-minded" means one whose intellect is not upright. || 1 ||
His speech was smooth and profound, and he always addressed others with a smile;
he weighed the three worlds as easily as a bilva fruit held in his hand.
By whom the three worlds were weighed, as it were, upon a scale and determined in their exact measure. || 2 ||

Having viewed all things as mere straw, he has rendered the cycle of worldly existence an object of his knowledge; having seen the world’s state of constant flux, he has realized the higher and lower levels of wisdom.

By whom the entire multitude of enjoyments was viewed as mere straw; by whom, having thoroughly investigated the world’s state of constant coming and going in the pursuit of desires, the cycle of birth, death, and so forth was made an object of knowledge and determined to be its fruit; and by whom the supreme and lower Brahman was seen through wisdom. || 3 ||
Steadfast, of great form, and with a voice deep in repose,
he arrived like the pure Ocean of Milk, his mind perfectly fulfilled.
Immediately after the production of the nectar, Mount Mandara went there, for it had come to rest like the Ocean of Milk. || 4 ||
With his intellect fully rested and tranquil, reeling with supreme bliss,
he was a knower of the manifestation and disappearance of worldly births.

With his intellect resting externally and reeling with supreme bliss within, he knows both the principle of *māyā* and the principle of the Self (*ātmatattva*) as the respective causes for the manifestation and disappearance of all things—those very manifestations and disappearances that constitute birth in *saṃsāra* for such beings; thus, he is "one who knows manifestation and disappearance. (5)
His form was delightful with a face full of impetuous joy; his speech was charming and pleasant, suited to his sweet singing;
as if he himself had newly assumed a body that dispels all fear, he was filled with great rapture.
Bhusuṇḍa— whose speech was pleasant, sweet, worthy of being heard, and as heart-pleasing as the sound of a lute,

which by its mere direct perception removes all fear, for he himself was Brahman alone who had assumed a new body for the sake of uplifting the world— being filled with the joy of innate bliss, spoke the answer to the question.
The connection with the subsequent clause is: "being of delightful form, he spoke this with a face full of impetuosity and effort. (6)
With pure speech and a flawless sequence of words, he spoke this stainless nectar;
like a charming cloud revealing its entire nature through thunder, he proclaimed his own true form.

That Bhuśuṇḍa, with pure speech and without any lapse in his natural composure, yet not abandoning the refinements of modesty, formal courtesy, and enthusiasm, spoke this narrative about to be told in due order to me, who was entirely pure and immortal: "Just like a charming and beautiful cloud..."
By means of his "stanita"—the sound of his own thundering—he says the very same thing to the "madhupa," the bee who is a connoisseur of drinking nectar;

it is just like that. Thus, the sense is: since I have already long ago awakened as one who relishes the essence of the bliss of Brahman (*brahmānanda*), his statement is not an instruction (*upadeśa*), but merely a restatement (*anuvāda*). || 7 ||

Thus ends the seventeenth canto, titled "The Description of Bhuśuṇḍa’s True Nature," in the *Bhuśuṇḍa-ākhyāna* of the *Pūrva-bhāga* within the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*, composed by the Sage Vasiṣṭha. 17.
Thus ends the seventeenth canto, titled "The Description of Bhuśuṇḍa’s True Nature," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The eighteenth canto.
Bhuśuṇḍa said:
"In this world, there is one who is the most excellent among all the inhabitants of heaven."
The god of gods named Hara is saluted by the gods of gods. || 1 ||
Hara [Śiva] spoke of his own birth to Atrī and the others, as well as their attendant Mothers;
the intoxication resulting from their festival of drinking is described here by Bhuśuṇḍa.
Therein, he prepares the introductory context to provide the answer to the first question—"In what family were you born?"—as follows:
[He is] the most excellent among even the gods by virtue of qualities such as knowledge, sovereignty, and power; he is the one to be sacrificed to and worshipped by the gods;
and he is always saluted, prostrated to, and praised from all sides by the gods, beginning with Brahmā.
By means of these three qualifications, it is shown that this very [knowledge] possesses the state of being the ultimate limit of excellence in every respect.

Through this, it should be understood that, by implication, an auspicious invocation (*maṅgala*) has also been performed at the commencement of the Brahma-vidyā which is about to be expounded. || 1 ||
She whose eyes were like rows of bees,
whose breasts were like lofty flower-clusters, was like a graceful creeper clinging to half the body of a mango tree.
Her eyes were like a row of six-legged bees. || 2 ||
Whose mass of matted hair is encircled by the Gaṅgā, who is white as snow and a necklace of pearls, and who is entwined with clusters of waves like garlands of flowers.
Like snow and like a pearl necklace, she is filled—meaning, strung together—with clusters characterized by white waves. || 3 ||
Born from the ocean of milk, with its outpouring streams of nectar,
the glorious moon— acting as a mirror— is his crest-jewel.
He is the maker of reflections, the mirror-like crest-jewel. || 4 ||
He who has rendered the Kālakūṭa poison nectar-like through the incessant flow from the moon upon his head, for whom that poison is an ornament upon his neck like a sapphire; (5)
By the continuous flow of nectar from the moon upon his head, its power of poison was dispelled and its power of restoration was bestowed; thus, he was rendered immortal. (5)
The great whirlpool of dust-lines arises from the pure fire;
his ash consists of atoms, and his white water is knowledge.
Likewise, from that whose clear eye-fire brings about the dissolution of the world, there arises such a streak of dust—

a great whirlwind of the dissolution consisting of rows of particles— from which, through the process of gross elements entering into increasingly subtle states until only the supreme subtle unmanifest remains, [the world] becomes composed of atoms.

It is white and pure because it is flooded by the waters characterized by pure consciousness alone; thus, the water of knowledge is the ash for that Brahman variegated by *māyā*, whose ornamentation [by ash] is implied. "Hara, becoming agitated, resorts to this through the rite of smearing himself with ash," so says the venerable Śaṅkarācārya. (6)
His very bones are stainless jewels, surpassing the moon, polished and well-fashioned, composed of the splendor of his body.
Polished by the rubbing of whetstones and purified like gems, they were therefore fashioned into the form of garlands and so forth.

"Radiant upon the bodies" means they were beautiful and pleasing to the mind; "consisting of those" means they were modifications (vikāra) of those [bodies], namely the bodies of Brahmā and others. || 7 ||
His garment is like the sky, washed with the nectar of the moon, possessing the hue of dark rainclouds, and variegated by the specks of stars.
The blue clouds—the rain-clouds—are themselves the sprouts that form its fringe; "āmbara" refers to the sky, meaning the directions, while "ambara" means a garment. (8)
The house of which has become a cremation ground outside, white as snow, filled with the cooked great flesh and rice of female jackals wandering about.

It was crowded with wandering female jackals (*śivāṅganā*) and female dholes (*kroṣṭrī*), as well as offerings of cooked human flesh (*mahāmāṃsa*), human meat (*narāmiṣa*), and rice-balls for ritual oblations (*baliodana*). It lay outside the villages and cities.
[It was also filled] with wandering female jackals and women dressed in auspicious attire (*kalyāṇaveṣā*).

It is also metaphorically superimposed [on the city] that it is "filled" (ākula) with cooked, large, most refined, and praiseworthy foods such as meat and rice, and that it is "situated outside all defects" (sarvadoṣebhyo bahirbhūta). || 9 ||
Adorned with garlands of skulls, wearing yellow and red garments and smeared with fat and wine, their bodies entwined with wreaths of entrails— these are his kinsmen and mothers.
The mothers are those who will be described hereafter; they are called "relatives" (bandhavaḥ) because they bind [one] with affection, being constant companions in play. || 10 ||
Whose bracelets were serpents with smooth bodies and the luster of shining gold, moving about with the jewels on their heads sparkling.
Moving about in turn, they glide forward to adorn their respective limbs; their bodies are smooth, all their members are glossy, and they possess the radiant luster of gold.

The playful sport of his conduct as Bhairava—by the mere glance of whose eye the king of mountains was consumed, who is eager to swallow the world, and by whom the Asuras were terrified—is [described]. 12.
He whose conduct was terrifying and formidable—of him he speaks by way of illustration:

"The movement of his hand, occurring by chance, brought about the destruction of the cities of the Asuras, while his mind remained fixed upon its own activity for the sake of establishing the world in well-being. (13)

Because his resolve is true, he has restored the world to health through auspicious thought alone; such is he. Furthermore, for one whose mind is established in that very state of self-activity known as *samādhi*, even the movement of a hand that occurs by chance when the *samādhi* is momentarily broken destroys the cities of the Asuras along with the Asuras themselves.
The distinction is that it destroys [the enemy], whereby there occurs such a destruction of the cities of the Asuras. || 13 ||
Those mountains, whose forms were one-pointed and who were free from affection, passion, and hatred, were his own food; though full of sap, they were yet devoid of moisture.

With the intention of showing that their one-pointedness is well-established during the time of meditative absorption (samādhi) and is visibly perceived even in objects such as the earth, mountains, and their physical forms, he says: "ekāgra" (one-pointed). Though they are "sarasāḥ"—meaning endowed with *rasa*, which refers to both the earth and water, and thus possessed of moisture—they are "nīrasāḥ," like those who are satiated by excellent food, being entirely free from all defects such as affection, passion, and hatred.

The meaning is that those mountains, such as Meru and Himavat, which are well known to be devoid of hunger, thirst, and other cravings, are renowned as the single-pointed meditative forms of Hara. || 14 ||
Whose attendants— the Pramathas— playfully sport with those who have heads for hooves, hooves for hands, hands for teeth, and mouths for bellies,
and who possess the faces of bears, camels, goats, and snakes.

Now he describes all the hosts of that [Lord] who possesses all powers in every limb, beginning with "the heads": those whose heads are hooves, possessing the power of hooves for running, trampling, and so forth; likewise, those whose hooves are hands, possessing the power of hands for various crafts and the like; and likewise, those whose hands are tusks, mouths, and bellies.

Those who possess the power of chewing, eating, sowing, and so forth—those whose mouths are like those of bears (*ṛkṣa*), brown bears (*bhallūka*), camels (*uṣṭra*), goats (*aja*), and snakes (*ahi*)—such are the *pramathas* who are his attendants; that is to say, they are his playmates and companions in sport. || 15 ||
With a face radiant with three eyes, his retinue consists of other Mothers whose pure splendors are like those of his Gaṇas.
Just like the Gaṇas, the Mothers—possessing all powers in all their limbs and having various forms and faces—are his retinue. || 16 ||
Before him, the Mothers dance, bowed down by hosts of spirits;
they are the sole consumers of the infinite multitudes of beings belonging to the fourteen classes. (17)

Those whose primary food is the one principal sustenance—namely, the infinite classes of beings, numbering fourteen according to the count of the worlds and according to their own individual counts. || 17 ||
With faces shaped like those of donkeys and camels, drinking blood, fat, and marrow, wandering through the quarters of the sky, they wore garlands made of the limbs of bodies. (18)
Whose limbs—the hands, feet, and other parts of the corpse—are like garlands, and whose blood, fat, and marrow are always to be drunk like an intoxicating liquor; (18)
Upon the peaks of the Vindhya mountains, in the sky, and in the intermediate worlds;
in chasms, in cremation grounds, and within the bodies of embodied beings. (19)
Jayā, Vijayā, Jayantī, Aparājitā, Siddhā, Raktālambusā, and Utpalā—these are the deities. (20)
He states the names of those [goddesses] who abide during that kalpa, beginning with "Jayā" and so forth. The deities are the Mother-Goddesses (mātṛdevyaḥ). || 20 ||
Of all the Mothers, these eight are indeed the principal leaders; others follow them, and yet others follow those. (21)

Now, one might object: since it is well known that there are many such numbers as "hundreds of millions of Cāmuṇḍās" and so forth, why is it said that there are eight? To this he replies: "Of all of them indeed... (verse 21).
O Leader of Sages, O Bestower of Honor, among those highly esteemed mothers there exists one renowned as Mātā Alambuṣā.
Among them, the seventh which exists—her vehicle is a crow named Caṇḍa; this is how it connects with what follows. || 22 ||
And Vajrāsthituṇḍa, known as Caṇḍa, resembles a mountain of sapphire;
his vehicle is a crow, just as Garuḍa is the vehicle of Vaiṣṇavī. (23)
Thus endowed with the eightfold sovereign powers, those Mothers of fierce deeds once gathered together in the sky for some reason or other. (24)
Thus, O Mother, she whose characteristics have been described [stayed] for some reason of wandering. || 24 ||
These women, who follow the Vāma stream and have taken refuge in Rudra-Tumburu, performed a supreme festival that reveals the ultimate truth.
Through the door of one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgrya*), there is the festival of drinking that reveals the reality of one's own self, which is the ultimate truth within *samādhi*.

The left current (*vāmasrotas*) is the method of propitiating the Supreme Power (*paraśakti*) by way of the left path; those belonging to it have taken refuge in the specific form of Rudra named Tumburu as their object of worship. [The verse states: "Tumburu, Rudra, the Left Current..."
Or rather, those situated on the left side are called *satyas* because they are dependent upon it. || 25 ||
Having worshipped the two gods Tumburu and Bhairava, who are worthy of worship by the entire world,
they— delighted by the intoxication of wine— related stories of diverse meaning.
Then, during the course of their conversation, this talk arose:
"Does the divine Lord of Umā regard us with indifference? (27)

By way of the occasion of the discourse, through the context of mutual conversation and the incidental slighting of Rudra performed by Mātra, the speech arrived. He demonstrates that very speech [with the words] "us," etc. (verse 27).
"Let us display our prowess to him, so that he, whose great power has been seen by us only just now, will not treat us with contempt. (28)
Then, the construction of the sentence is as follows: "As soon as he saw that great power of Umāpati, he became such that his influence was [diminished];
therefore, we shall demonstrate his power in such a way that he will not again direct toward us any disregard or contempt. || 28 ||
Having thus resolved, those goddesses, having brought Umā herself under their control, respectfully sprinkled her whose face and limbs were pale.

Having brought Umā, the power (śakti) of Rudra, under their control— making her subject to them by means of her being an internal aspect of their own forms— they sprinkled her with water accompanied by mantras in the sacrifice, like a sacrificial animal. By the phrase "with her face and limbs turned pale," it is indicated that Umā was suddenly sprinkled by her husband through the imposition of a different color upon her face and other limbs.
It is indicated that this results in making [the object] impossible to fully comprehend. || 29 ||
The goddesses gazed upon her, whose hair was disheveled, who had been snatched from her husband's body by illusion and brought to the arena, and who had fallen into a state of weeping.

The *raṅga* is the center of the circle of Mothers (*mātṛmaṇḍala*). They [the Mothers] acted as if to reduce it to the state of being rice (*odanatāṃ gatāṃ kartuṃ*)—that is, to turn it into all kinds of food, such as boiled rice, solid foods, soft foods, things to be licked, and drinks. Since Umā is one of the forms of the Mothers, there can be no primary curse upon her own self; furthermore, because this is a playful jest, there is not even the fault of disparaging her own form. "The state of being rice" means having become the nature of all edible items, including boiled rice and so forth.
The word "to do" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. || 30 ||
On that day of Pārvatī’s consecration, a great festival took place there,
enchanting with the dancing and singing of all those women.
The sky shone with excessive joy and unrestrained clamor,
while their hips and bellies expanded with the tossing of their long limbs.
Others laughed with unrestrained, loud shouts and deep roars,
their limbs quivering with excitement, making the mountains and forests resound.
They laughed with a deep, thunderous sound produced by clapping their hands (tāla), snapping their fingers (karatāla), shouting (kṣveḍā), and roaring like lions (siṃhanāda). || 33 ||
Others, delighted by the drinking bout, sang within the mountain-cave as if it were a water-vessel,
filling the hollow of the world-orb with their resonant sound.
In such a manner that the mountains and houses resounded during that action,
they roared like the waters of the ocean, being colored by the hue of the rising moon and making a thunderous sound.
Others drank their fill, their limbs, heads, and hooves smeared with nourishment,
as they made playful *ghur-ghur* sounds that echoed through the hollow of the sky.
With their limbs smeared and anointed with sandalwood paste, blood, fat, wine, and the like, their heads adorned with flowers, the goddesses went about swiftly, spoke loudly, laughed, shouted,
fell down, leaped high, danced incessantly, and ate delicious meat; thus the three worlds were overturned.
They acted like those who have gone mad. || 36 ||
Describing some of their intoxicated behaviors, he concludes with the verse beginning "papuḥ": they drank drinks;

they protected one another; they offered [their lips] as oblations into the fire of each other's mouths; and they abandoned their proper conduct (*sad-vṛtta*), whether by turning away from it or by being deprived of it through the instruction of good behavior. || 36 ||

Thus ends the eighteenth sarga, titled "Description of the Mother’s Conduct," in the *Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa* of the *Mokṣopāya* section of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, according to the tradition of the Ṛṣis. 18.
Thus ends the eighteenth canto, titled "Description of the Mother's Conduct," in the first half of the Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The nineteenth canto.
Bhuśuṇḍa said:
While this festival was thus proceeding, their excellent mounts [arrived].
In that very same way, intoxicated, they laughed, danced, and even drank blood.
Through the fierce yoga with Haṃsī, Brāhmī attained her own birth together with her brothers;
it is said that by the grace of Brāhmī, she obtained knowledge and reached the station of her father.
Of those Mothers; and the *vāhas* are those who serve as their mounts, such as Caṇḍa and others. || 1 ||
There, in one place, certain celestial swans (rathahaṃsyas) belonging to Brahmā, intoxicated by the flow [of nectar], danced in the sky; and Kāka was the charioteer of Alambuṣā.

There, at that festival, the Brāhmya [goddesses] belonging to Brahmā’s retinue, along with the chariot-swan of Alambuṣā and the crow named Caṇḍa who served as her vehicle, all stood together and danced. || 2 ||
And as the female swans danced and drank the wine,
they experienced perfect delight upon the surface of the ocean shores.
"On the level ground at the base of the ocean shores and the coasts" is the statement of the excitant (uddīpana-vibhāva). "Rati" means passionate attachment (anurāga). || 3 ||
Then, having become intoxicated with passion, all those female swans in turn took their pleasure even with the crow, for they were indeed then in a state of intoxication.

The word "even" (api) is used to indicate that because of intoxication, even for female swans of superior species, an amorous union with a crow of inferior species—which is otherwise improper—has nonetheless come to pass. || 4 ||
That crow was the beloved of seven noble female swans;
he took his pleasure with them one by one, as long as it was mutually desired.

The word "ekatra" (in one) is used distributively. The meaning is that in each individual female swan, there was a lack of flavor [in their union] until their mutual desire was fully satisfied. || 5 ||
Then those queens became pregnant and were exceedingly delighted; having performed their dances, they returned to a state of perfect tranquility.

Then those goddesses and the Mothers, having performed their festive rites, approached Rudra— who was perfectly tranquil and free from anger— due to their failure to reflect upon the workings of their own *māyā*.
Those goddesses turned the great illusion, Umā, who is dear to the Lord, into the state of being frog-food for the sake of a meal for the wielder of the trident.
Therefore, they gave Umā, who had become rice, to that Lord as food. || 7 ||
When the moon-crested Lord learned that [the goddesses] had said, "He gave us our beloved food," he became enraged toward the group of Mothers.
When the moon-crested Lord, perceiving that his beloved had been given away as food, became enraged toward the group of Mothers,
then those Mothers offered Pārvatī their own bodies by giving their respective limbs— head, hands, feet, and so forth— in order to pacify him;
such is the connection between these two [verses].
Then, having brought her forth once more by the gift of their own limbs,
they gave Pārvatī again in marriage to the Moon-crested Lord.
Then the goddesses, Hara, and their retinue—
all with contented minds— departed each to their own respective quarters.

Regarding these two, the Goddess and Hari: because they are unified through the Mothers being portions of the Goddess, the dual number is used by means of a single-remainder compound (ekaśeṣa). || 10 ||
Having become pregnant, those Brāhmī swans related the news to the lord of sages exactly as it had occurred regarding the goddess Brāhmī.
Those who are pregnant are called *antarvatnyaḥ*. || 11 ||
Brāhmī said: "O calves, at present you are not capable of the work of drawing my chariot; therefore, roam about freely for now."
The cows have calves and are pregnant. || 12 ||
Having spoken thus to the swans languid with pregnancy, the goddess Brāhmī, devoted to compassion, remained at her ease in a state of unwavering meditative absorption.
Having been addressed thus, for the sake of favoring her, she abandoned all movement and entered into the meditative absorption known as *nirvikalpa*. || 13 ||

O Lord of Sages, those royal swans, languid from pregnancy, wandered within the lotus-pond of the Creator— the source of the lotuses that are the faces of the gods— located at the navel of the Unborn.
They moved about within the lotus-stalk of the unborn Viṣṇu, at the base of the lotus of Brahmā, the source and place of origin.
(14) Thus, with their embryos fully developed, they gave birth upon the sprout of the navel-lotus to soft eggs, just as creepers produce shoots. (15)
Upon the sprout of the navel-lotus, in the region of its tender leaf. || 15 ||
When the time arrived, those twenty-one eggs split in two through the entry of the embryo, like the substantial cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas).
By the descent of the embryo and the kicking of the feet of the fully developed fetus, they split in two;

they were shattered, just as the golden and silver shells of the cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas) are split apart. [The word] "sāravat" is used in the singular by way of grammatical transposition (vyatyaya) for "sāravanti. || 16 ||
"O Sage, it is from those very eggs that we twenty-one crows, the sons of Caṇḍa, were thus born as brothers. (17)
They were born and grew to maturity upon that lotus petal;
having developed their wings, they became capable of soaring through the sky.
Then the Blessed Lady Brāhmī, together with her mothers who were like female swans,
having been properly propitiated for a long time and being fully detached from worldly existence through meditative concentration (samādhi), remained there.
To provide an answer to the question, "How have you come to know that which is to be known?", he begins as follows:
"Then, at the proper time, by the Blessed Lady herself, who was intent on showing grace, we were thus favored with her very limbs, whereby we remain liberated. (20)
Thus, we have been graced by such a state of direct realization of reality. || 20 ||
"With our minds thoroughly stilled and at peace, we shall remain established in meditation in solitude"—having resolved thus, we went to the side of our father. (21)
Having resolved, "We shall stay; we shall remain," they stayed by their father's side in the valley of the Vindhya mountains.
Then we were embraced by our father, and after Alambusā had honored us,
she looked upon us with favor as we remained there, self-restrained.
Those by whom Alambusā was worshipped were self-controlled, restrained by virtues such as discipline. || 22 ||
Caṇḍa said:
My sons, have you indeed emerged from this snare of saṃsāra, which is surely enveloped by the threads of the cords of limitless latent impressions? (23)
"Have you perhaps emerged from the net characterized by saṃsāra, which binds the wings and brings exhaustion?"—this is the inquiry regarding what is desired. (23)
If we do not entreat this Blessed One, who is so kind to her servants, [to grant that] you may become those who have reached the further shore of knowledge. (24)
For that respective purpose; you shall become, you will exist. || 24 ||
The crows said:
"O Father, by the grace of the Goddess Brāhmī, that which is to be known has been fully known; however, we desire an excellent place for dwelling in solitude. (25)
We desire a dwelling place, a site suitable for staying and remaining in solitude. || 25 ||
Caṇḍa said:
"There indeed exists a mountain named Meru, the support of all collections of jewels and the refuge of all the gods, which possesses a truly great height. (26)
He is the golden pillar within the pavilion of the universe, for whom the moon and sun are the lamps and the multitude of living beings are the wives. (27)

He describes him alone with the words beginning with "lasat" and so forth: He is the central pillar within the pavilion-like house characterized by the universe, which possesses a family (kuṭumbin) consisting of hosts of living beings (bhūtavṛnda); he is enriched by a golden moon-throne and has fingers in the form of peaks adorned with jewels.
With its sounding islands and oceanic girdle, it was like the upraised arm of the Earth. || 28 ||

His arm was raised aloft by the earth—[an arm] possessing a golden throne in the shape of the moon that resembled his *mūlabandha* (the base-knot) and was enriched by the multitude of regions such as Kimpuruṣa; [an arm] whose fingers were the peaks themselves, enriched with jewel-encrusted rings;
and whose bracelets were the resounding islands and oceans. Such was the arm he held high.
He stood as if [immovable]. || 28 ||
Surrounded by the neighboring mountain ranges, seated upon the throne of Jambudvīpa,
the king, whose eyes were like the sun and moon, caused his splendor to shine forth among the mountains.
He describes that very [Lord] as a king with the words beginning with "vṛta" (surrounded). On the throne characterized by Jambūdvīpa—that is, on the lion-throne—the king [is seated];

the word "of mountains" (śailānām) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. For this very reason, he is "whirling his eyes," which are the moon and sun, upon the mountain-like assembly. || 29 ||
He is a garland of jasmine flowers for the multitude of stars, the sole garment for the ten directions,
his self abiding in the two species of serpents, and the ornament of the lord of heaven.
One whose garlands of *mālatī* flowers are merely the multitude of stars; one whose ten directions are his garments;

one whose single garment is the sky itself, which is the very expanse of space; and one whose self is such that it is the locus for the two classes of beings—the serpents and the elephants—which constitute the meaning of the word "nāga."

The meaning resulting from the compound *svarūpaṃ yasya* is as follows: [in the word *sthā*, the suffix *kvip* is used in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*]; He whose ornaments are the leaders of heaven (*nākanāyakāḥ*), namely Indra and the others. || 30 ||
He is being fanned on all sides by beautiful women from every direction, who adorn the city,
with cool, flowing yak-tail whisks.
The dense clouds are characterized by blue, white, and other colored chowries.
Sixteen thousand yojanas of his feet remain below in the earth, where they are worshipped by the nāgas, asuras, and mahoragas.
His body, eighty thousand yojanas in extent, has the sun and moon for eyes;
he is worshipped in the celestial abode by gods, gandharvas, and kinnaras.
He is worshipped and served. || 33 ||
Just as kinsmen depend upon a householder, so do beings of fourteen kinds subsist upon him, having previously seen his dwelling place.
The Brahman-sages, celestial sages, royal sages, gods, ancestors, Gandharvas, Kinnaras, Apsarases,

Vidyādharas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Pramathas, Guhyakas, and Nāgas— these fourteen classes of beings, because of their extreme vastness, did not see one another in those cities, abodes, and places, as follows:
In that way, they subsist upon it. || 34 ||
In its northeastern direction, however, there exists a great peak composed of ruby, like another sun risen in the sky. (35)
Upon his back stands a great wish-fulfilling tree (kalpataru), surrounded by hosts of beings, appearing like a reflection in the mirror of the world’s summit. (36)
Upon the mirror of coral that is the peak’s characteristic, the wish-fulfilling tree stands as if it were the reflection of the world. || 36 ||
On its southern shoulder there is a branch with golden shoots, densely covered with clusters of jewels, and bearing fruits that shine like the orb of the moon. (37)
In which the fruits shine like the orbs of the moon. || 37 ||
There, O sons, a nest was formerly built by me—shining with jewels—wherein I indeed took delight while the Goddess sat absorbed in meditation. (38)
A nest of such a kind, in which jewels were sparkling. || 38 ||
It was covered with petals of jewel-flowers, endowed with fruits that were elixirs,
and its verandas were fashioned with rods of wish-fulfilling gems.
In which [palace] the arrangement of the outer vestibule and the construction of the outer gateway-chambers were fashioned with wish-fulfilling gem-sticks. || 39 ||
The lake was filled with young crows whose every movement was preceded by intelligence;
its interior was cool and it was brimming with heaps of flowers.
By those whose conduct is preceded by intelligence and whose manner of dealing is characterized by prior deliberation. || 40 ||
Therefore, go, O sons, to that nest which is difficult even for the inhabitants of heaven to reach;
staying there, you shall surely attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation without obstacle.
It is difficult to reach even for the gods who possess celestial chariots.
Having spoken thus, our father there kissed us and embraced us, and he gave us that meat which the goddess had brought for us. (42)
Āmiṣa means meat. || 42 ||
Having eaten that, and having prostrated at the feet of the goddess and their father,
we leaped from that place, from the marshy region of the Vindhya, away from Ālambusa.
Because of their dwelling in the Ālambusā and Dalambusā [trees]. || 43 ||
Gradually having ascended into the sky and emerged through the hollows of the clouds,
they reached the mass of wind and paid homage to those who travel through the firmament.
By whom the gods who travel through the sky have been saluted. || 44 ||
"O Lord of Sages, having avoided the Lord of Day who has gone to the city of the other world, we have bypassed heaven and arrived at the world of Brahmā."
From this world to another world—namely heaven—and its city, Amarāvatī. || 45 ||
There, preceded by a prostration, he immediately reported those words of his father exactly as they were to his mother, to the Blessed One, and to Brāhmī.
There, in that Brahma-world. || 46 ||
Having been embraced affectionately by them and encouraged by their command,
"Go," we offered our salutations and departed from the world of Brahmā.
They were encouraged and strengthened by the command "Go!", by the granting of that command, and by his blessing. || 47 ||
Having leaped over the cities of the world-protectors, they move through the sky, radiant as the sun, restless, and traveling upon the mass of wind.
Resplendent like the sun. || 48 ||
"O Sage, having obtained this wish-fulfilling tree and entered our own nest, we remain established in silence, with all afflictions cast far away. (49)
They remained established in such a way that they were silent; that is to say, they were always devoted to meditative absorption (samādhi). || 49 ||

Just as we were born and have reached this state, having attained awakening with minds thoroughly pacified in accordance with reality—this very thing has been fully and flawlessly declared by me to you. O high-souled one, instruct me further regarding what remains.

He concludes what has been said with the words "We are born. O Mahānubhāva, we have indeed been born. And how we have attained this state—having reached realization exactly as it is—and how we have come to dwell in this very place: all of this, which is the answer to your three questions, has been told to you in its entirety without omission. Hereafter, by way of the remainder that is left over...

"O holy one, what is your lifespan, and do you remember anything of your past conduct?"—by answering these two questions or by some other matter that must be spoken, please instruct and command me properly; I shall tell you even that, is the meaning.

Thus ends the nineteenth sarga, titled "The Attainment of the Abode," in the *Bhuśuṇḍa* section of the *Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa*, within the *Mokṣopāya* division of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, according to the tradition of the Ṛṣis. 19.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Attainment of the Abode," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The Twentieth Chapter.
Bhuśuṇḍa said:
"In a former kalpa, there was once a world that had existed for a long time."
And because of its configuration, this [world] even today has not gone far away. (1)
In this account, Bhuśuṇḍa spoke of the uniformity of the world in every kalpa, as well as the death of his brothers,
and maintained the stability of his own mind even during the dissolution of the universe.
In this regard, wishing to provide a detailed answer to the question, "Do you remember what happened there?",

and fearing that a contradiction between earlier and later statements might arise— given the mention of his own life spanning many kalpas in the passage beginning with "Having reached this wish-fulfilling tree and entered my own nest"— [the author] [speaks of] the Kalpa-tree, Meru, and so forth.
He shows the view that there is a doctrine of identity due to the similarity of configuration in every *kalpa* with the words beginning "It existed" (*āsīt*).

In the previous *kalpa*, which was the cause of this [present] birth, whatever multitude of worldly objects had long endured, that existed with the same arrangement—that is, with the same configuration of parts, form, and so forth—as these [objects] belonging to the present *kalpa*. Therefore, even today, it is not [different].

The meaning is that because of the superimposition of non-difference upon that which is distant, there is the designation "this is the wish-fulfilling tree" and so forth, through the cognition that it is indeed present.
O Lord of Sages, this account has been described by me through practice while living in the present, in order to bring about awakening, as I perceive the similarity with my previous births. (2)
Therefore, although the world has passed away, it is described as being one with the present world due to the habitual practice of delusion.
(2) "O Sage, today my merits accumulated over a long time have borne fruit, since I behold you here without any obstacle. (3)

In this context, lest there be a delay in the worship during the course of a long discourse, he first turns [the Lord] toward him by means of praise, in order to request the acceptance of the worship, with the two verses beginning "Today" (adya). || 3 ||
This nest, this branch, myself, and this tree—
today all these have attained purification through the sight of you.
