"This nest follows this branch. [In the compound] "etāni," there is a singular remainder (ekaśeṣa) in the neuter gender according to the rule "napuṃsakamanapuṃsakenaikavaccāsyānyatarasyām" (Pāṇini 1.2.69). || 4 ||
"O sir, having accepted this water for the hands and this water for the feet offered by the bird, and having surely rendered them pure, quickly give us your command with what remains. (5)
The meaning is: "By means of the remainder"—that is, by way of the subject matter concerning the remaining service—command me to speak the questions. || 5 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāma, when that bird Bhuśuṇḍa had himself offered this water for honor and water for the feet once more, I spoke these words to him.
"Again" means for a second time; "spoke" means he asked. || 6 ||
O Lord of Birds, why are those brothers of yours—possessing such courage and great intelligence—not seen here? For you alone are seen. (7)
Bhuśuṇḍa said:
"O Sage, O Sinless One, a vast amount of time has passed while we have remained here; the successions of ages have been exhausted like the passing of days."
After this much time, all my younger brothers,
having cast off their bodies like blades of grass, were perfected in the auspicious state.
*tanūḥ* means bodies. || 9 ||
Even those who are long-lived, great, virtuous, and powerful—
all are swallowed up by Time, whose nature is beyond measure.
By one whose self is unmeasured, by one whose true nature is unperceived.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: "O dear one, as the winds of the atmospheric layers, carrying the sun and moon upon their shoulders, blow incessantly with great speed, are you not distressed by them?"

In those [clouds] which were like garlands strung upon the aggregates, and which surpassed the winds such as the Vātaskandha-pravāha by means of their twelve suns and moons, and which were varieties of the winds of universal dissolution; || 11 ||
O Father, I hope you are not weary from the rays of the sun, which have long been so close to you that they burn the forest groves upon the great mountains of sunrise and sunset? (12)
O dear one, I hope you are not distressed by the cool rays of the moon, which turn the water into ice, and by the falling of nearby hailstones? (13)
The waters were turned into solid stone by the rays of such a moon,
as well as by the falling of hailstones from the clouds at the time of the dissolution.
O Father, I hope you are not weary from these circles of world-destroying clouds that rest here incessantly, their frost-like mist cut away by the axe of time.
Here on the peak of Meru, those who have found rest cut even axes; they cause the mists to become solidified as soon as their edges are blunted.
Established in such a high station amidst the turbulent upheavals of the world, how is it that this lofty Kalpavṛkṣa tree does not succumb to agitation? (15)
Bhuśuṇḍa said: "O Brahmin, the life of a bird is without support or fixed abode, despised by all the worlds, and held in contempt by all living beings."
In times of hardship, even for the great, weariness is considered possible; how much more so for one born from the lowest of bird-species?

Nevertheless, because of the power of discernment (*viveka*), there is no attachment to weariness for me. To express this, he states the insignificance of his own species' livelihood in comparison to other livelihoods with the words "without support" (*nirālamba*). [The sky] is without support, and she has that as her abode. (16)
And in such beings, in lonely forests, or in the empty path of the sky, the Creator has established their fixed abode. (17)

The meaning is this: it is truly marvelous that the Creator has ordained a stable livelihood through reliance and affection even for such insignificant beings and origins. The word "vā" is used here in the sense of "iva" (as if). || 17 ||
O Lord, how can there be freedom from sorrow for this long-lived bird born in this world, who remains bound by the snares of hope? (18)
But we, O Blessed One, are always established in self-contentment;
we are never deluded by those whose confusions have arisen regarding that which is formless.
In that which is formless and devoid of intrinsic nature. || 19 ||
Satisfied with our own nature alone, freed from hardships and from strenuous efforts,
O Brahman, we simply pass the time here in our own abode.
They are freed from hardships, the fruits of afflictions, and from activities such as causing pain to others. || 20 ||
There is no obstruction to the body of karma through either life or death;
we remain just as we were established, even when our desires have come to an end.

"From life" means from living. "The activity of the body" refers to actions performed for the sake of results pertaining to this world or the next. Nor does one desire the "obstruction or destruction of the body through death"—the word "desire" (vāñchām) is to be supplied in both cases. Just as we remain now by our established nature as the Self, which is eternally accomplished and unsurpassed bliss, so too shall we remain hereafter by that very same nature, with all worldly desires extinguished.
The meaning is: "We shall remain with our desires fulfilled. || 21 ||
The state of the world has been observed, and various illustrative examples have been seen; surely our flickering body has been abandoned by the mind. (22)
The ten states of the worlds—such as birth, death, and other calamities—are seen through the illustrations of dreams and so forth, which lead to the determination of falsity. || 22 ||
In the self-luminous light that is free from passion, which is eternally without distress,
I always perceive the movement of the smallest units of time above the end of the aeon.

In that regard, he says "anārata... and so forth, [meaning]: "Until the end of the kalpa, due to the power of the *kalpavṛkṣa* (wish-fulfilling tree) itself, there is no possibility of exhaustion for us. [This refers to] the *kalpāga*, which is the *kalpavṛkṣa*. 23.
O Brahmin, in this house of the Kalpalatā creeper, richly illuminated by clusters of jewels,
I perceive an unbroken aeon through the flow of the prāṇa and apāna breaths.
To the question, "Since there is no discernible division between day and night here due to the abundance of light, how do you know the passage of time and its divisions? he replies:
"For on this lofty mountain peak, where day and night are unknown, I understand the progression of the world's time through my own intelligence. (25)
O Sage, my mind has attained rest through awakening; it discriminates between the essential and the non-essential, is free from fickleness, tranquil, and well-stabilized. (26)
With the intention that "even by the power of mental steadiness, there is no possibility of distress for me," he says: "The essence... (verse 26).
By the unreal snares of hope arising from the worldly affairs of saṃsāra, I fall into helplessness like a frog at the outpourings of a crow. (27)
With little sound, consisting mostly of the noise of belching, I am like a common earth-crow; I do not fall into helplessness or fear. || 27 ||
Beholding the world’s illusion with an intellect that is cooled by light and possesses the nature of supreme tranquility, we have attained steadfastness. (28)
He says "pare" [in verse 28] to show that even because of their steadfastness, no attachment to weariness arises in us.
O one of great intelligence, even when terrible conditions arrive in their proper sequence, those whose minds are unshakable remain like pure crystals. (29)
Following the sequence of the ten stages, even when those terrible stages are reached, a stainless stone such as crystal and the like becomes of that form—that is, similar to it. (29)
This worldly condition, though charming in its undertakings and fickle, does not fail to cause affliction whenever it is repeatedly scrutinized. (30)
He says "this" [in verse 30] to show that even through the power of further reflection on the reality of the world, there is no occasion for weariness.
O Blessed One, do all these nets of beings necessarily go forth and return, or not? What cause for fear is there for us in this matter? (31)

For, according to the perspective shown by the Blessed One—that "death is certain for one who is born, and birth is certain for one who has died"—there may be no occasion for fear due to the certainty that suffering is unavoidable for all beings alike; thus he says, "all," etc.
Or rather (*vā*), they do not go forth nor do they come back; this is the meaning from the standpoint of ultimate reality (*paramārthadṛṣṭi*). || 31 ||
As the river of worldly existence, with its waves of the net of living beings, enters the ocean of time, we remain disregarded even though we stand upon its bank. 32.

He states—beginning with the word "bhūta"—that for one who knows reality, there is no possibility of fear because, by virtue of being an onlooker, he perceives the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) of all beings, and thus lacks attachment to it. || 32 ||
We do not cast off [leaves], nor do we grasp them; we neither stand here, nor are we situated here.
With soft feet yet cruel eyes, we abide upon this tree. (33)

Because they tread upon the world of saṃsāra with caution—as if on thorny ground—for the sake of establishing mere conventional reality, their feet are soft; yet, because they have uprooted saṃsāra through the vision of ultimate truth, they are harsh. (33)
We have been favored by you, the best of men, who are free from sorrow, fear, and fatigue; being satisfied, you have bestowed your grace upon us, and we remain here, freed from all affliction.
He says "vīta... [verse 34], meaning that even through the favor of the great ones, there is no possibility of distress for us.
Furthermore, O Blessed One, our mind has been overturned and rolled about, yet it has found no stability in worldly activities, nor has it grasped the true meaning of reality.
For the sake of establishing mere conventional usage, although it has been overturned from this and that [position], it has not rolled about within the functions of passion and the like. || 35 ||
When the self has become tranquil— changeless and free from agitation—
we have awakened as waves of consciousness, like great oceans on a full-moon day.

We have become awakened like great oceans on a full-moon day—those whose waves consist of consciousness overflowing with the rising moon of mental fluctuations in the form of Brahman, surging from every side. || 36 ||
O Brahmin, because of your arrival, our hearts are now filled with joy; for by you, the Ocean of Milk—with all its limbs stirred up by Mount Mandara—is being expanded.

We have now become such as we are because of your arrival; that is to say, our hearts have become gladdened by that very nectar for the sake of which the Ocean of Milk was churned—its entire body agitated by Mount Mandara—and from which it was drawn forth. Even with the reading *khanyate*, the meaning is the same: it is dug out, that is, churned. || 37 ||
I consider nothing to be more beneficial for myself than this: that the virtuous, who have renounced all desires, are followed by me. (38)
What is obtained from enjoyments that are pleasant only at first sight?
From the wish-fulfilling gem of association with the virtuous, the essence of all things is obtained. (39)
Knowledge is the essence of all. || 39 ||
With speech that is smooth, profound, gentle, sweet, noble, and steady,
you alone act as a bee within this lotus-bud of the three worlds.

O holy one, I believe that even for one who has realized the Supreme Self, this birth today has become fruitful through beholding you, whose evil deeds have been stilled; for the company of the virtuous removes all fear.

By the sight of you, my evil deeds and wicked undertakings have been pacified; thus, for one such as I, this birth has today become fruitful, endowed with the fruit of unsurpassed bliss—this is the meaning. || 41 ||

Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Description of Bhuśuṇḍa’s True Nature," in the *Bhuśuṇḍa-Opākhyāna* (The Narrative of Bhuśuṇḍa), within the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa* (Section on Liberation) of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*, according to the *Ārṣa* (Sage) tradition. 20.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Liberation of Bhuśuṇḍa’s True Nature," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The twenty-first canto.
Bhuśuṇḍa said:
"During the terrible upheavals of the ages and amidst harsh words..."
This firm wish-fulfilling tree never trembles at any time. || 1 ||
The majesty of the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa), its persistence through the dissolution of the universe,
destiny, and the memory of manifold diverse objects are described herein.
This place is inaccessible to all beings dwelling in other worlds;
therefore, O virtuous one, we remain here in true happiness.

In order to provide an answer to the question, "Do you remember what happened, and do you know anything else?", while describing the majesty of the Kalpa-tree that is his own abode, he begins by elaborating on how no weariness attaches to him even during the calamities at the end of an eon and so forth, starting with the verse beginning *yugakṣobheṣu* (1–2).
When Hiraṇyākṣa swiftly seized the surface of the earth, encircled by the seven continents, even then the tree did not tremble.
Although the removal of even the Kalpa tree along with the earth is indeed possible, the intention is that [the mountain] did not tremble due to the power of its divine majesty. || 3 ||
When the divine mountain became unsteady in its form,
not even a single tree shook, for it had been rendered equal [in stability] on all sides by the mountain.

The mountain Amaraparvata, which was given on all sides for the sake of stability like supporting stones for a pillar—this is understood to mean, by implication, that it was [given] by Varāha at the time of re-establishing the earth. || 4 ||
When Nārāyaṇa, who had bent Mount Meru by the pressure of his arms,
lifted up Mount Mandara, even then the tree did not tremble.
Regarding the word "bhujā" (with arms): here too, it is understood that he, being four-armed, supported Meru with two arms and lifted up Mandara with the other two. || 5 ||
When the world was violently agitated, with the orbs of the sun and moon falling due to the turmoil of the gods and asuras, even then the tree did not shake.
Due to the agitation between the gods and the asuras and their fierce battle, the orbs of the moon and the sun fell down.
When the winds of calamity blew, uprooting the rocks of the great mountains and shaking the trees of Mount Meru, even then that tree did not tremble.
When the rows of clouds at the end of the eon moved, shaking the mountain caves with winds from the surging Milk Ocean, even then that tree did not tremble.
They were shaken, as if by the winds from the caves of Mount Mandara tossing in the Ocean of Milk. || 8 ||
When Mount Meru stood on all sides within the arms of Kālanemi,
having been slightly uprooted, even then the tree did not tremble.
He was renowned for having been shaken by the arm of Kālanemi in the battle known as Tārakāmaya.
When the winds from the wings of the Lord of Birds blew during the battle for the seizure of the nectar,
and the Siddhas were falling [from the sky], this tree did not fall.
The "assault on the nectar" (amṛtākrānti) is the seizing of the nectar; for that purpose, the Siddhas fell upon them in battle. || 10 ||
When Rudra, whose single effort was not yet complete, went toward the cosmic egg in the form of Śeṣa,
then even the tree Garuḍa did not tremble.

"As soon as Garuḍa was born, all the worlds trembled; the entire earth trembled, and the seven continents shook. Because of that portent, Hari, in the form of Saṃkarṣaṇa, supported with his thousands of heads the earth which was sinking like a boat in the water. Following this narrative, he says "yadā" (when). Rudra here refers to Saṃkarṣaṇa-Rudra.

Even now, the single feat characterized by the supporting of the earth—the conduct of her who possesses such a form as Śeṣa—is not yet finished; the meaning is that even when Garuḍa, having leaped up, went toward the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), she did not tremble. || 11 ||
When the flames of the fire at the end of the eon, along with the mountains, oceans, and all else, were consumed by the rays of the sun,
even then that tree did not tremble.

With his hoods and mouths, he emitted and swallowed the fierce and unbearable flames of the fire of cosmic dissolution that consume all mountains, oceans, and living beings; for it is well known in the Purāṇas that at the end of the dissolution, [the world] is consumed by the fire from the mouth of Saṃkarṣaṇa.
O tiger among sages, how could there be calamity for those who dwell upon such an excellent tree? For us, indeed, calamities arise from our own state of wretchedness. (13)
By way of "dauḥsthitya," that is, by dwelling in a corrupt place. || 13 ||

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O one of great intelligence, when the winds of calamity blow at the ends of kalpas, and when the moon, the stars, and the sun are falling away, how do you remain free from distress?

The sense is that when the moon, the planets, the lunar mansions, and the suns are falling down, and likewise at that time of dissolution (pralaya) there is a burning of the very end of the earthly world, there can be no hope for protection from Mount Meru, the Kalpa-trees, or other such things. || 14 ||
Bhuśuṇḍa said:
When worldly activity fell away at the end of the kalpa, leaving no trace of the world's existence, I then abandoned my nest like an ungrateful man abandons a true friend.
"At the end of the eon" means at the conclusion of a thousand great yugas. || 15 ||
I abide in space itself, free from all conceptual construction,
with all my limbs fixed in their natural state, like a mind devoid of latent impressions.
He whose all limbs were rigid by nature and immovable in their very essence.
When the suns blaze forth, shattering the mountains to pieces, then, having fixed the Vāruṇī concentration, I remain with a steady mind. (17)
Having stated the state of abiding in space in general, he elaborates upon it in detail through the various types of *dhāraṇās*, beginning with "pratapanti" (they shine).

The continuous concentration (*dhāraṇā*) in the mind that "I am indeed Varuṇa himself, whose nature is water, pervading and defining the entire circle of the quarters which are exceedingly cool"—this is called the *vāruṇī-dhāraṇā*. For by means of this, one always regards oneself as Varuṇa.

The meditations (dhāraṇās) on Pārvatī and the others should also be inferred in this very same way. Vasiṣṭha himself will explain in detail the method for the meditations on the five elements, beginning with earth, in the latter half [of the verse]. || 17 ||
When the winds of dissolution blow, shattering the great mountains, I remain unmoved in the sky, having bound myself with the mountain-like meditative concentration (dhāraṇā). || 18 ||
"Immovable" (acalam) is an adverbial modifier of the action. || 18 ||
When the world, including Mount Meru and all else, dissolves and becomes a single ocean,
he of unshakable intellect then binds the concentration on air during that deluge.
When the wind has moved and he is one whose self-awareness is thus [dissolved], he merges into the ether.
Having reached the far shore of the cosmic egg at the end of the principles (tattvas) in that stainless state,
I remain for that long in the state of deep sleep, with an immovable form.
Regarding how long one thus floats there, he says:

"Having reached the unmanifest (avyākṛta), which is the ultimate limit and boundary of the cosmic egg— the aggregate of the gross and subtle [universe]— at the end of the twenty-four, twenty-six, or thirty-six principles, or at the end of those beginning with Name and ending with Prāṇa."
In the state called Bhūmā, by means of the condition of non-conceptual samādhi which is of a single flavor like deep sleep. || 20 ||
Furthermore, as long as the Lotus-born remains engaged in the work of creation,
I shall enter that cosmic egg and remain there in the abode of birds.

If it is asked how long one remains in such a state of meditative absorption, he says: "As long as... There, once again, for the sake of the work of creation, I remain in our abode, the dwelling place of us birds, which serves as the equivalent of the Kalpa-tree. || 21 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Lord of Birds, why is it that other yogins do not remain unbroken by their meditative concentrations (dhāraṇās) at the end of the kalpas, as you do?

Why do other yogis likewise not remain [in their bodies]? For what purpose do they go to another body for the sake of office or to liberation? The meaning is: why do they not remain with that very same body, just as you do? || 22 ||
Bhuśuṇḍa said:
"O Brahmin, this destiny of the Supreme Lord is indeed difficult to transcend. I must become such as I am; others likewise must become what they are destined to be. (23)

In this regard, he states—beginning with "O Brahman"—that the cause of the established order is none other than the sovereign decree of the Lord, which consists of His true resolve (satya-saṃkalpa) and conforms to each individual's powerful *prārabdha* karma. || 23 ||
It is impossible to weigh destiny; for whatever is to happen will happen exactly so, for this is the certainty of intrinsic nature itself. (24)

To weigh means to determine through the intellect that "this is exactly thus. Whatever has been brought forth by the *prārabdha* (commenced karma) is exactly as it is; such is the nature of necessity (*niyati*). || 24 ||
"By the power of my own resolve alone, in kalpa after kalpa, again and again, this very tree comes into being upon this mountain peak. (25)

He says "mad" (by me) [in verse 25], meaning that even in the creation of this world anew at every kalpa, the very cause is my own volition, which is rooted in the unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) of the enjoyers.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: You are one whose long life is for the sake of ultimate liberation; you are a leader who provides instruction, possessed of both theoretical knowledge and realized wisdom, steadfast, and one whose mental faculty is fit for yoga.

He whose long and indefinable life is like liberation; or rather, he whose long life is characterized by liberation—that is, by *jīvanmukti*. For this very reason, he is the foremost leader (*nāyaka*) in the matter of describing ancient subjects. (26)
O auspicious one, having witnessed many various minor creations and their cycles of coming and going, what wonders do you remember in this sequence of the world? (27)
The meaning is: "By whom various kinds of births have been seen individually—tell me, what wonderful and marvelous things do you remember here in this sequence of the world witnessed by you? (27)
Bhuśuṇḍa said:
"I remember this earth below, which was once devoid of mountains, forests, and multitudes of trees, and where there were no grasses or creepers, yet which possessed vast rocks and trees. (28)
He is even vaster; [he dwells] below Meru. || 28 ||
For ten thousand years and ten hundred years,
I remember the earth below as being filled with a mass of ashes.
I remember the earth below, where the lord of the day had not yet arisen, where the orb of the moon was unknown, and where the light of day was undivided. (30) [The reading "ajāta" is also found.]
The Lord of Day is the Sun; he is not divided by the splendors of Mount Meru—that is to say, he is not separate, nor does he exist as something distinct.
Daylight is the illumination that is the cause of the day. || 30 ||
With its hollows half-revealed by the radiance of the jewels that are the Meru mountains,
I recall this world as being like the Lokāloka mountain range.

It was a world in which half was manifest and luminous, like a hollow (koṭara), and for that very reason it stood like the Lokāloka mountain; moreover, it was a realm where certain mountains were richly endowed with light. 31.
I remember this earth fleeing in every direction, her inner strength wasting away here during the great battle with the Asuras.
By the indication of the word "fleeing," it means crowded with people who were fleeing. || 32 ||
I remember this earth, which was overrun for four yugas by the intoxicated Asuras, and which fell into the state of being the inner apartments of the Daityas.
The word "caturyugāni" (four yugas) takes the accusative case because it denotes time and expresses an uninterrupted duration.
I meditate upon the hut of the universe, whose interior is completely filled with the furthest reaches of the infinite, and which remains as the residue of the three unborn goddesses.

In which [city] all other regions—every area except for Mount Meru—are completely set aside and covered by the ocean, disappearing in successive stages; and on Mount Meru, the triad of deities known as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra remains as the "remainder" (śeṣa). 34.
I remember this earth for another half of the four ages, dense with forest trees, where no other creation was to be seen.
For half of the four ages—that is, for the duration of two ages—not even the creation of anything other than trees was seen in that [age].
Thus I remember this earth, covered by dense and immovable mountains for more than four yugas, and devoid of the conduct of human beings.

It is well known in the Purāṇas that for a period exceeding four yugas by a quarter, the earth was covered with dense, solid mountains; however, the great Cakravartin [Bhagīratha], having pushed aside the mountains with the tip of his bow, subsequently leveled the ground. 36.
I remember this earth as being strewn all around and completely filled for ten thousand years with mountains of bones from deceased Daityas. (37)
I remember the sky, where all the Vaimānika gods had vanished out of fear, and the earth, stripped of all its trees and shrouded in darkness.

He made the sky—the worlds beginning with the intermediate space—and by the word "and" (ca), the earth entirely devoid of trees. In the reading *nirṛkṣā*, this is an adjective qualifying the sky alone; *ṛkṣas* means stars. Furthermore, the phrase *tamomayīm*—meaning "abounding in darkness"—is an adjective qualifying both [the sky and the earth].
When the great Vindhya mountain was intoxicated and had reached the state of being the sole mountain for the unextinguishable and unextinguished quarters of the sky,
I remember the world as a mere hut.

When the mountain, having attained the status of a single peak due to the absence of any boundary between the Malaya, Dardura, and Sahya mountains, grew vast in its intoxication with the desire to rival Mount Meru; 39.
I remember these and many other such events;
what is the use of speaking at length? Hear the essential point in brief. (40)
O Brahmin, I remember hundreds of countless Manus who have passed away,
as well as all the hundreds of cycles of four yugas, which were full of intense activity.
With many outbursts of passion and extraordinary powers. || 41 ||
I remember a certain creation that was entirely alone, self-pure, devoid of men and asuras, and consisting of a single mass of light. (42)

He states another marvel: "Only one," etc. When the Virāj, whose body is the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), having just arisen, remained for some time with a concentrated mind in order to contemplate the reality of his own self—that state is described here. It was devoid of Puruṣas, such as the Suras and Asuras. It was the one [element] of the *ālokas*, which are luminous by nature and composed of fire (*taijasa*).
The aggregate and the totality—that is the cosmic egg, which is of the nature of that [Brahman]. || 42 ||
I remember a certain creation in which there was a Brāhmaṇa who drank liquor while intoxicated, a Śūdra who had forbidden himself from liquor, and a virtuous wife who had many husbands. (43)
Recalling the creation and maintenance of the Kali age, he said: "Surāpa... [verse 43]. In that age, there will be Brāhmaṇas who drink liquor;

likewise, there will be wicked Śūdras who have abandoned the gods (surāḥ = devāḥ) and are thus censured and forbidden from them. There will be virtuous women who have many masters (bahunāthāḥ = anekabhartṛkāḥ).
I remember a certain creation in which the surface of the earth was densely covered with trees, where there was no created great ocean, and where a Puruṣa had arisen of his own accord.

He speaks of another wonder with the words "vṛkṣa" (trees) and so forth. This was well known prior to the birth of Priyavrata, the creator of the ocean: that in which the male progenitors such as Bhṛgu and others were born spontaneously through a mental creation, without the union of male and female. || 44 ||
I remember a certain creation situated in the sky, devoid of mountains and the earth, containing neither gods nor humans, and enriched by a radiance that surpassed both the moon and the sun. (45)

Recalling that state when the earth was submerged in water and only the activities of the worlds beginning with Janaloka—characterized by abundant light—were discernible, he says: "Without mountains" (Aparvatam). In that [state], the immortals (amarāḥ) dwelling in the sky were the gods and humans who had attained perfection through yoga. || 45 ||

I remember a certain creation in which there was no Indra, no great king, and no distinction between the neutral, the base, and the excellent; in that world-cycle, the circle of the quarters was equal to the region of Andhaka.

In which there exist neither those who are middling, nor inferior, nor superior; for this very reason, it is "equal," wherein the circles of the quarters of space are blind. This is a statement regarding the stability of the world, characterized by the end of the previous kalpa and the end of the manvantara. 46. The calculation of the commencement of creation is the division within the three worlds.
Jambūdvīpa stands distinct, having the configuration of a principal mountain range. || 47 ||
Explaining that many beings with a lifespan equal to this kalpa possess the memory of the events of this kalpa, he says:

"O dear one, even by children those [events] are remembered"—this is the grammatical connection (*anvaya*). First, at the beginning, there is the *kalanā* (calculation or formation) of the Creator for the purpose of initiating creation (*sarga*);
from that comes the *vibhāga* (division), which is the differentiation of the various sub-regions such as the continents and so forth within the three worlds; and after that...

The sequence should be understood as follows: first, the configuration of the principal mountain ranges and the arrangement of their appropriate locations; then, having entered Jambūdvīpa situated separately from those, the creation of the castes such as Brāhmaṇas, their respective duties, their intellects, and the various branches of knowledge suited to each—according to what is appropriate. || 47 ||
The division of the creation of the castes, duties, and intellects; the arrangement of the terrestrial mandala;
the configuration of the circle of stars; and the very construction of the Pole Star (Dhruva). || 48 ||
[He described] the establishment of Indra and Upendra by Janman, Indu, Bhāskara, and others;
the abduction of Hiraṇyākṣa, and the lifting of the earth by the Boar.
The lifting of the earth by the Boar.
The imagining of kings, the bringing of the Vedas, the uprooting of Mount Mandara, and the churning of the ocean for the sake of nectar; || 50 ||
The conceptualization of kings among the gods, dānavas, humans, and others individually; and the retrieval of the Vedas during the Fish Incarnation.

"The Garuḍa with unformed wings," "the origin of the oceans," and other such traditional recollections (smṛtis) concerning the sequence of the world that occurred long ago—even children remember these, my dear; what cause for concern is there in them? (51)

They are called *smṛtis* because they are things that must necessarily be remembered. Compared to the many kalpas witnessed by me, the sequences of the past worlds accomplished in this single kalpa alone are very few. The meaning is that even those such as you, who are like children in comparison to me—being of extremely young age even by the standards of those born in this kalpa—do indeed remember them. || 51 ||

I, whose life is sustained, have envisioned him who has Garuda as his vehicle, who has a bird as his vehicle, who has a bird as his vehicle, and who has a bull as his vehicle; I have envisioned him who has a bull as his vehicle and who has Garuda as his vehicle.

Even while mentioning other things seen by himself in other kalpas, he concludes with the words "having Garuḍa as his vehicle. Being one who has attained (kalita) long life, I, having become four-faced, [mounted] that bird, the best of birds, the swan, which is renowned in this kalpa as having Garuḍa as its vehicle.

He perceived [the Lord] fulfilling His office of creation regarding the gods, Daityas, and others; likewise, having become Rudra, He perceived Him as Brahmā, whose vehicle is a bird, performing His office of dissolution while mounted upon a bull.
In this manner, having assumed the body of Viṣṇu with Garuḍa as his vehicle, He likewise perceived Rudra with the bull as his vehicle.
The meaning is that it is a great wonder and a profound mystery that he perceived [the Lord] as exercising the authority of protection. || 52 ||

Thus ends the twenty-first canto, titled "The Narration of the Account of Longevity," in the *Bhuśuṇḍopākhyāna* of the *Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa*, within the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, according to the tradition of the Ṛṣis. || 21 ||
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Narration of the Account of Cirajīvin," in the first half of the Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The Twenty-second Chapter.
Bhuśuṇḍa said:
"Then, O Blessed One, when you and others had been born in the world..."
[He was born] among Bharadvāja, Pulastya, Atri, Nārada, Indra, and Marīci. || 1 ||
The eight births of Vasiṣṭha and others, as well as the creation of equal and half-equal [beings],
and the churning of the ocean of milk and so forth, have been seen again and are here described.

Then, immediately thereafter, when some time had passed and the present creations had arisen—including those beginning with you and ending with Bhagīratha, Śuka, and others—what account could there be of them in memory? Thus, in the seventh [verse], all the words ending in the locative case are to be connected. || 1 ||
Among Pulaha, Oḍālaka, and the others; among Ṛtu, Bhṛgu, and Aṅgiras; and among Sanatkumāra, Bhṛṅgīśa, Skanda, Gajānana, and the rest; || 2 ||
Among the Brahman-sages ending with Sanatkumāra; among the Siddha-sages beginning with Bhṛgu and Aṅgiras; and among the attendants of Śiva, such as Skanda and the mouth-born [Gaṇeśa], etc. || 2 ||
In Gaurī, Sarasvatī, Lakṣmī, Gāyatrī, and many others;
on Meru, Mandara, Kailāsa, Himavat, Dardura, and so forth. (3)
In Gaurī and the other [goddesses], who are her powers (śaktis); in Meru and the other mountains. || 3 ||
Among Hayagrīva, Hiraṇyākṣa, Kālanemi, Bala, and others; among Hiraṇyakaśipu, Krātha, Bali, Prahlāda, and others.
Among the Dānavas such as Hayagrīva and others; among the Daityas such as Hiraṇyākṣa and others. || 4 ||
In Śibi, Aṅku, Pṛthu, Lāṅkā, Vainya, Nābhāga, Keli, Nala, Māndhātṛ, Sagara, Dilīpa, Nahuṣa, and others; (5)
Among kings beginning with Śibi. || 5 ||
Among Ātreya, Vyāsa, Vālmīki, Śuka, Vātsyāyana, and others; among Upamanyu, Maṇi, Maṅkī, Bhagīratha, Śuka, and others.
Among the sages beginning with Ātreya. || 6 ||
When [events] occurred only a short time ago, or were somewhat distant, or even within the creations of this very day—what need is there for calculation when they are remembered? (7)
The meaning is that since it is indeed a matter of counting, there is not even the possibility of forgetfulness in that regard. || 7 ||
O Sage, this is indeed the account of the eight births of you, the son of Brahmā;
I remember that in the eighth creation, you were united with me.
In the eighth birth or aeon, you became united with me, having met together with me. || 8 ||
Sometimes you are born from the sky, sometimes you are born from water;
sometimes from the wind or the mountains, and sometimes you are born from fire.
He says "kadācit" (at some time) to show that it was not the case that he was born as the son of Brahmā in all eight births. || 9 ||
Whatever its nature, whatever its conduct, and whatever its configuration and directions—
such three creations as this one, I remember.

Although the presiding persons (adhikāripuruṣas) in all kalpas possess identical names and forms, there is no rule that all objects, structures, and customs must be the same; rather, their similarity occurs only occasionally by way of the "crow-and-palm-fruit" maxim (kākatālīya). With this intention, he says: "Of whatever kind... (verse 10).
I remember ten creations that were simultaneous, possessing stable endurance, and consisting of gods who maintained an entirely uniform conduct and appearance. (11)
"Simultaneous" means having equal lifespans. "Firm" means not shaken by the Asuras; "stabilities" refers to those fixed positions of the gods at specific times and places. || 1 ||
O Sage, the Earth disappeared for five days; she was then lifted from the ocean by Kūrma himself during five creations.

Having stated the similarity of conduct, he speaks of its difference: "Antardhānam" (disappearance). Antardhāna means concealment by submerging in water. Dhātrī means the earth. [This was done] by Kūrma alone, not by Varāha. || 12 ||
I remember this twelfth [manifestation]: the churning of the ocean of nectar, which threw the gods and asuras into utter confusion by the force of Mandara being pulled [as the churning-stick]. 13.
Then, at the time of the offering, Vāratrayahiraṇyākṣa, the seizer of the oblation, brought down from heaven to the earth all the juices of every medicinal herb.
"Baligrāha" means one who receives tribute (bali) or tax from heaven (divaḥ), that is to say, from the celestial realm; it refers to one who has made the entire host of gods pay tribute.
"Adhaḥ" refers to the netherworld (pātāla). || 14 ||
Having assumed the state of being the son of Reṇukā for the sixth time, this Hari brought about the destruction of the Kṣatriyas, even across many cycles of creation.
Even by means of many intervening creations that were devoid of the incarnation of Paraśurāma. || 15 ||
O leader of sages, I remember that a hundred Kali Yugas and a thousand states of Buddhahood were attained by Hari solely through his birth as a boar. 16.
Śauka refers to a specific region of the Kīkaṭa country; by virtue of being its king, he is [called] Śauka, which is to say, by virtue of being the son of that king named Śuddhodana. || 16 ||
I remember thirty disturbances of the three cities, two destructions of Dakṣa’s sacrifice, and ten slayings of Śakra, all performed by the one who wears the moon upon his crest.

During thirty kalpas, he performed thirty destructions by burning the three cities (Tripura). In each kalpa, two well-known instances of the destruction of Dakṣa’s sacrifice occurred, namely in the Svāyambhuva and Cākṣuṣa intermediate periods. Furthermore, ten Indras who had committed offenses against the Moon-crested Lord were cast down from their positions and confined within mountain caves.
The staffs that have the characteristic of cessation, or those with the characteristic of adamantine arm-pillars, are the ordainers. || 17 ||
I remember the eight battles fought by Hari and Śarva for the sake of the arrow— battles involving the mantras of Jvara and Pramatha, which threw the armies of the gods into turmoil.

He [addressed] the incantators of the Pramathas—those known as the Jvaras, specifically the varieties of fever called Māheśvara and Vaiṣṇava—who, by generating valor and enthusiasm, act as instigators; that is to say, those who incite them. In the reading "kṣurapramathamantrakān," however, it means those who crush (mathnanti), i.e., cut through, the kṣurapras—a specific type of arrow—and are thus "kṣurapra-mathas" of that kind.
The meaning is: those in which there are mantras and mantra-weapons. || 18 ||
O Sage, due to the deficiency or excellence of the intellects of men in each age,
I remember the Vedas as being endowed with various differences in their ritual applications and recitations.
"In every age, in each successive age. The distributive sense (*vīpsā*) is indicated by the prepositional particle *prati*.

Due to the deficiency or excellence of the intellects (*dhiyām*, i.e., understandings) of men—that is, of the persons who study—[there is variation] regarding such practices as celibacy, service to the teacher, sleeping on the ground, and so forth, as well as the auxiliary sciences such as phonetics (*śikṣā*).

And [he heard] recitations characterized by the pronunciation of vowels, consonants, and so forth with careful attention, which were endowed with a variety of effects produced by deficiencies or excesses [in their execution]. || 19 ||
O sinless one, the Purāṇas— which possess a single meaning, are complete, and exist in many recensions— circulate and spread forth in each successive age.
There are many recensions due to the differences among the authors of the subsequent Dvāpara ages. || 20 ||
Furthermore, I remember those very same ones, as well as others, composed by experts in the Vedas and other sciences, throughout age after age. (21)

Furthermore, [he studied] those very same historical epics, such as the *Mahābhārata* and the *Rāmāyaṇa*, composed again and again by Vyāsa, Vālmīki, and others who were learned in the Vedas and other scriptures.
I remember another history of great wonder called the Rāmāyaṇa,
measuring one hundred thousand verses, which is a scripture of knowledge.
The scripture of knowledge known as the Mahārāmāyaṇa was taught by Brahmā to Vasiṣṭha, Viśvāmitra, and others. || 22 ||
"One should behave like Rāma, not like the licentious Rāvaṇa"—wherein such wisdom is placed in the hands of the intellect as if it were a fruit. (23)
"This has been done by Vālmīki, and now you shall know whatever he will do; furthermore, you shall know from time what else remains manifest in the world. (24)

Furthermore, that *Mahārāmāyaṇa* consisting of thirty-two thousand verses, which takes the form of a dialogue between Vasiṣṭha and Rāma, I remember as having been experienced through the power of divine knowledge; you too shall know it in due course of time. (24)
Whether composed by that very soul named Vālmīki or by another, this work—which had been forgotten—is now being performed for the twelfth time. (25)

This work, in the form of a dialogue between Vasiṣṭha and Rāma, was indeed composed previously by a living being named Vālmīki— whether that be the same person from a former kalpa or another— and has now, upon the cessation of the state of an active agent through the loss of memory,
been brought forth for the twelfth time, completing the number twelve. || 25 ||
I remember a second work of his, equal to it, known by the name Bhārata, composed by Vyāsa in a former age, which has now been forgotten in the world. (26)
Whether composed by that very soul named Vyāsa or by another, this [work], having been forgotten, is now being performed for the seventh time. (27)
O Lord of Sages, I remember the narrative scriptures that appeared in each successive age, possessing diverse structures. (28)
O virtuous one, again and again, in age after age, I behold and indeed remember those very same objects, as well as others.
For the destruction of the Rākṣasas, Viṣṇu will now undergo his eleventh incarnation on earth under the name of Rāma. || 30 ||
Now, in the present Tretā Yuga.
With his man-lion body, Hari struck Hiraṇyakaśipu three times, like a lion strikes an elephant.
O Lord of Sages, for the sake of relieving the earth's burden, this will now be the sixteenth birth of Viṣṇu in the house of Vasudeva.
Now, at the end of the Dvāpara age within this cycle of four yugas. || 32 ||
This delusion, which consists of the world, never truly exists;
yet it appears at times, persisting like a bubble upon water. (33)
With the intention that the notion "this is born externally" is merely an illusion, he says: "consisting of the world. (33)
This impermanent delusion of the visible world, residing within the conscious self, arises and dissolves instantly, as flickering as a wave upon the water. (34)
I remember the three worlds as having many equal arrangements and many unequal ones, as well as those with the form of being half-equal.

He states that even the rule regarding the similarity of the arrangement and so forth of the worlds and other entities at every secondary creation (*pratisarga*) is general (*autsargika*), with the words "samā" [etc. (verse 35).
I remember those very same deeds and such other conducts of theirs, as well as those other beings and their various actions here in this world.
He states that there is also a general similarity regarding the arrangement, conduct, and other attributes of the authoritative persons, such as Manu and others:

"O Brahmin, at the end of every Manvantara, when the order of the world has been overturned, when the arrangement [of society] has become otherwise, and when the people have passed away and are heard of no more... (37)
In what is heard and renowned. || 37 ||
My friends are indeed different, and my kinsmen are also different;
my new servants are indeed different, and those who provide me shelter are likewise different. (38)
The bases and dwellings are indeed different. || 38 ||
At times I made my dwelling in a secluded spot in the Vindhya marshlands; at times my abode was on the Sahya mountains, and at times in Dardura.
He elaborates on the very distinction of the substratum with the words beginning "at times," etc. (verse 39).
Sometimes he was a dweller of the Himalayas, sometimes the Malaya mountain,
and sometimes a mountain according to his former configuration.
On Mount Malaya, the mountain is firm and steady. || 40 ||
And having reached a branch of a mango tree, O leader of sages, I build my nest; thus it has been through ages that have passed away without beginning or end.
The word "prāpya" (having reached) is connected with the preceding word "bhūdharam" (the mountain). [This occurs] in those beginningless and endless, innumerable [kalpas]. || 41 ||
"O virtuous one, this tree was born with its very same configuration as before;
having cast off its body, it has attained happiness and has not undergone any change from that state. (42)

Therefore, he has not undergone a transformation into another configuration from his previous configuration. If so, why is the tree not long-lived like you? To this he says: "having abandoned the body" (dehaṃ tyaktvā). || 42 ||
This tree has grown with the very same configuration as it possessed when its father was alive; the splendor of this excellent tree remains exactly as it was then.

And thus, although there is an identity between the tree and that which lives upon it, he says "by that [tree's] own" (*tadīyena*) to indicate that the metaphorical identification is based merely on the similarity of their beautiful arrangement;
and "when the father was fierce" (*caṇḍe tāte*). || 43 ||
Having previously established my residence, I have come to stay here;
formerly, neither this northern quarter nor this mountain existed here.
Thus, he says "not so" (neha) [in verse 44], meaning that even the recognition of identity between the directions and the mountains occurs solely due to the similarity of their arrangement.
Previously, there was another mountain, Diguttarābhu,
where the arrival of the night of Brahmā had ceased for each individual embodied being.
"In the past, the northern direction was one thing and this [present one] is another; likewise, even the mountain was quite different.

Thus, there is a logical connection (*anvaya*) through both recurrence (*āvṛtti*) and transformation (*vipariṇāma*). To the objection—"In that case, why should you not also be different in every *kalpa*, while maintaining the same configuration?"—he says: "I am one... and so on. I am that very same one, by means of that very same...
One whose arrival at the dawn of Brahman has passed away by means of the bodily constitution is of such a kind. || 45 ||

At the conclusion of my meditation, having beheld this very creation as it truly is, I trembled; [I perceived] the directions such as Meru and others, established by the movement of the sun and the stars. (46)

To explain why that is so, he says: "at the end of meditation" (*dhyānānte*). For, at the conclusion (*avasāne*) of the non-conceptual samādhi—which is meditation firmly established through the previously mentioned *dhāraṇā*s at the end of the kalpa—one perceives this newly arisen creation and recognizes it as such:
"This is that very Meru; this is that very tree. It is within that very reality thus being recognized that one knows this creation.
The point is this: if I were someone else, then there would be no recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) at all that penetrates [the identity] of that very person.

Thus, by perceiving a different configuration than the previous one, he establishes the statement "this direction is other" as containing the intention that "there is no destruction of me, the observer of that [direction]," and thereby explains the verse beginning with "of the sun and so forth. [This refers to] the directions.

The directions such as the East and so forth are established through the fixed movements—such as the rising and setting—of the sun, the moon, and the lunar mansions (nakṣatras), which have their locations determined by Meru and other points situated in the fixed northern direction. || 46 ||
When that [consciousness] exists, the spatial configurations appear otherwise, and the directions likewise shift;
I consider the world to be neither existent nor non-existent, merely causing the intellect to wander in delusion. (47)

But in another creation, when that Meru itself exists in a different manner—by way of another arrangement—the directions, being dependent on the Meru and so forth as depicted in a painted cloth, undergo a change of configuration and reach a reversed state, as if following its transformation; this is the meaning. Thus, the falsity of the directions follows from their lack of fixed location.

He states, beginning with "na sat," that for the entire world, which is composed of parts arranged in a fixed configuration according to that [avidyā], falsity—characterized by being indefinable (anirvacanīya)—is thus revealed. || 47 ||
This manifestation of the wonder of the Self’s own vibration unfolds:
the son becomes the father, and likewise, a friend turns into an enemy. (48)

The self’s wonder of vibration (*spandacamatkāra*) is the power of illusory projection (*māyikavikṣepaśakti*), and its manifestation is as follows: just as a reversal of spatial order is observed among worldly objects, a reversal of temporal order is also seen; explaining this in detail, he shows it with the verse beginning "son," etc. (48).

I remember hundreds of women who have become men, and likewise men who have become women; I remember those practicing the conduct of the Kṛta Yuga during the Kali Yuga, and those abiding by the ways of the Kali Yuga during the Kṛta Yuga.
O Lord of Sages, I remember that in both the Tretā and Dvāpara ages,
those who had not seen the Vedas nor understood their meaning wandered about according to their own private conventions.
The connection [of the verse] is made by drawing together the conduct of the Kṛta age, as well as the condition of the Kali age, in relation to the Tretā and Dvāpara ages.
He explains the condition of the Kali age itself in brief: "adṛṣṭa... (verse 50).
O Brahmā, as I meditate upon you, the Brahman, I remember certain beings here and there from the beginning of creation— those whose conduct was unrestrained, including gods, asuras, and humans.

In some cases, this even occurred at the beginning of the Kṛta Yuga. For instance, it is well known that even in the Kṛta Yuga, Puṣkara defeated Bala at dice through trickery, and despite the latter's innocence, he was banished along with his wife while wearing only a single garment. || 51 ||
At the end of a thousand cycles of the four yugas, I remember the world as empty;
I remember ten creations consisting of mental fabrications devoid of earthly forms, pervaded by beings composed of air.

O Brahmin, at the end, at the conclusion of a thousand cycles of four yugas, when the Creator has lain upon the waters in the process of withdrawing the form of the universe, while the Supreme Self—the Brahman—is the meditator under the guise of yogic sleep, I remember that the world, including gods, asuras, and humans, has become empty, as if it had attained non-existence; such is the meaning. Thus, even though [the world] has dissolved in this way...
In this world, the aforementioned creations of the mind of Aindava are pervaded by beings consisting mostly of wind, that is, by creatures composed of air. || 52 ||

I remember all those [worlds] throughout the days of Brahmā— possessing regions of diverse and particular configurations, filled with the storehouses of beings engaged in various activities, and adorned with the playful dress of diverse arrangements.

He summarizes everything that has been said in brief with the word "vicitra" (variegated): the meaning is that I remember all creations without exception—those which are like treasuries for beings who are occupied with various activities—occurring in such variegated regions characterized by specific diverse locations throughout the Brahma-days, that is, the Kalpas. || 53 ||
Thus ends the twenty-second canto, titled "The Description of the Long Life of Bhuśuṇḍa," in the Nirvāṇa Section of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Valmiki, within the *Deva-mokṣopāya*.
Thus ends the twenty-second canto, titled "The Description of Longevity," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa-tātparya-prakāśa*.
The Twenty-third Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Then that best of crows [spoke] this for the sake of inquiry by me:
O mighty-armed one, he was questioned once more regarding the tip of the creeper on the wish-fulfilling tree.
When those defects have been abandoned, death no longer afflicts a man;
therefore, everything that must be done regarding the supreme mind is here proclaimed.
This refers to what is about to be stated: the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the secondary object (*gauṇa-karman*) of the verb *pracch* (to ask). || 1 ||
O King of Birds, how is it that death does not afflict the body of even those who move about within the treasury of the world and engage in worldly affairs? (2)
In what manner? That is, by what method of abandoning faults and acquiring virtues. || 2 ||
Bhuśuṇḍa said:
O omniscient Brahman, although you already know [the answer], you question me as if out of a desire to learn; for masters always incite their servants to speak.
They cause one to speak fluently and make one eloquent; that is to say, they manifest skill in speech through the medium of questions. || 3 ||
Nevertheless, I shall explain to you that which you ask me:
they say that the primary way of propitiating the virtuous is simply the carrying out of their commands.
Death does not seek to slay him in whose heart the continuous thread of latent impressions (vāsanā)— spoken of as pearls strung upon a string— is no longer knotted.

In this regard, he states that the destruction of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) which are the substratum of all defects is indeed the primary means for crossing over death—beginning with the word "doṣa.
The meaning is understood by implication to be: just as thieves do not wish to kill one who has discarded ornaments such as necklaces, so it is in this case. || 5 ||
Mental anguish does not shatter him whom the saws of sighing and the woodworms of all the body’s creepers do not pierce; death does not seek to slay such a one.

Sighs are the saws that cut down the tree of the body; mental afflictions (*ādhayaḥ*), which are like wood-worms, are the insects that consume all the creepers of the body—namely, the hands, feet, and other limbs that constitute the branches of the bodily tree. (6)

The multitudes of serpents that are the bodies of worldly existence, with their hoods—their heads—raised up by the poison of anxiety, do not burn within him whose hopes have perished; nor does death seek to slay him.
They are like swarms of serpents dwelling within the hollows of the tree of the body; for this very reason, they have placed hoods upon their heads characterized by anxiety.
Yet, they do not burn [the body] with the fire of their own venom—this is the implied meaning.
Death does not seek to slay him whom the serpent of greed— filled with the poison of passion and hatred, dwelling in the cave-dwelling of one's own mind— does not consume.
It does not eat, nor does it bite. || 8 ||
Death does not seek to slay him whom anger— like the submarine fire (vāḍava) in the ocean of the body, which has drunk up all the water of discernment— does not utterly consume.
He is like the Vāḍava fire within the ocean of the body; for this very reason, he has drunk up the entire water of discernment.
Death does not seek to slay him whom the bodiless god of love cannot crush—that firm mass of sesame seeds, as if a formidable and agitated heap. (10)
"Ākulam" means agitated; "tilānāṃ rāśim" (a heap of sesame seeds); "karmayantram" (a mechanical device for processing); and "ugram" (fierce)—these are adverbs modifying the action. || 10 ||
Death does not seek to slay him by whom the rest of the mind has been taken refuge in that single, stainless, and supremely purifying state.
With the intention that rest in Brahman as the Self alone is the means for the ultimate conquest of death, he says: "In the one... (verse 11).
Death does not seek to slay him whose mind is not fickle, like a monkey that has fallen upon a fragment of its own body.
Having fallen upon that forest grove in full bloom—which was like the bodily characteristics [of the sage]—he cried out with intense force, like a monkey;
the neuter gender here is Vedic (chāndasa). 12.
O Brahmin, these great defects, which are the causes of the disease of saṃsāra,
do not disturb even in the slightest degree a single, concentrated mind.

Without enumerating the defects, with the intention of stating the qualities that are the cause for their conquest—namely, that concentration (*samādhi*) itself is the primary quality—he praises it with the verse beginning "These," etc. (13).
Sufferings arising from mental and physical ailments, stirred up by great delusions, do not overwhelm a single mind that is concentrated in meditative absorption. (14)
For one whose mind is composed, there is neither setting nor rising, neither recollection nor forgetfulness, and it is neither asleep nor awake. 15.
Thoughts born of the transformations of desire and anger do not afflict the mind of one whose heart-space has been blinded and whose consciousness is composed.
He neither gives nor takes, he neither abandons nor begs;
indeed, he performs all his duties whose mind is thus composed.
Even while performing actions and conducting affairs according to the scriptures, || 17 ||
Those things which are of evil meaning, of evil undertaking, of evil quality, of evil expression, and of evil sequence—these do not cut the mind of one whose heart is composed. (18)
"Evil undertakings" (*ārambhāḥ*) are those things such as agriculture, houses, and wealth, which are commenced for the sake of acquiring ill-gotten riches and the like.

"Qualities" (*guṇāḥ*) are passion, hatred, and so forth. "Utterances" (*udāhṛtāḥ*) are statements that reveal one's vital secrets. "Courses" (*kramāḥ*) are methods of policy. These do not "cut," meaning they do not cause suffering through their evil consequences. || 18 ||
For one whose mind is concentrated, all things—vast in meaning, great, and endowed with excellence—shine forth and follow after it. (19)
All these shine forth, manifesting vast meanings and yielding abundant gains; the remainder [of the sense] is that they are all indeed sources of happiness.
They "run after" means they pursue [them]. || 19 ||
One should direct the mind toward that supreme truth which is beneficial in its ultimate result, which is undecaying, free from delusion, and liberated from the vision of evil intentions. (20)

*Udarka* refers to future happiness; that which is beneficial for it is [the goal]. With a vision of *durīhita*—that is, with a perspective characterized by the desire for worldly enjoyments—one becomes liberated from that [desire], which is directed toward the supreme state characterized by the attainment of one's own true Self. (20)
That which is unseen by the impure mind— which brings about mental agitation and is like a demon of manifoldness— one should cause the mind to direct toward that Supreme.

The desolation of the mind is its alienation from the goals of human endeavor; multiplicity is the perception of duality. That supreme happiness which is not seen by the demon characterized by these [faults] is the highest. (21)

That which is most appropriate for the long term—at the beginning, in the middle, and likewise at the end—and which is beautiful, sweet, and wholesome—that one should direct the mind toward above all else. (22)
That supreme knowledge is pleasant to begin with, sweet even during its middle stage of partial maturation, and beneficial at the end, bringing about the cessation of all suffering. 22.
One should direct the mind toward that which is infinite, beneficial to the mind, true, devoid of beginning, middle, and end, and cherished by all the virtuous; that is the supreme [object]. (23)
The bliss of the Self, which exists at the beginning, end, and middle, and which persists through all states.
One should direct the mind toward that which is the supreme light of the intellect, the primordial, the ultimate nectar, and the unsurpassed good fortune.
Because there exists no such supreme fortune as this—meaning, one characterized by eternal and unsurpassed bliss. || 24 ||
In heaven, along with its gods, asuras, and gandharvas, together with the vidyādharas, kinnaras, and hosts of celestial women, there is nothing whatsoever that is stable or auspicious.
He establishes this very state of unsurpassed good fortune by elaborating upon the impermanence of other pleasures, beginning with the words "sāmara":
"O dear one, on this earth—along with its gods, its lords of men, its mountains, cities, and villages, and including the oceans—there is nothing whatsoever that is beautiful and stable. (26)
In Pātāla, including the entire assembly of Nāgas and Asuras, as well as the hosts of Asura women, there is nothing whatsoever that is beautiful or stable.
In this entire world—including heaven, the realm of the gods, the netherworld, and the quarters of the sky—there is nothing whatsoever that is beautiful and stable. (28)
Having thus described the impurity of the three worlds, he speaks of the world composed of them as follows: "sasvarga" (along with heaven), etc. || 28 ||
In activities that are agitated by mental and physical ailments and enveloped by floods of suffering, which are eternally trivial, there is nothing whatsoever that is stable or auspicious. (29)
By the word "action" (kriyā), its fruits are indicated. || 29 ||
In thoughts that cause the mind to tremble, that delight the heart,
and that are fluctuations of the intellect, nothing whatsoever is stable or auspicious.
The term "cintā" (reflection) also refers merely to mental activity and indicates its result. || 30 ||
Even amidst the Mandara mountains of the surging milk-ocean of the heart, though they are in motion,
there is nothing whatsoever that is stable or auspicious within one's own volitions and conceptual constructions.

When the Mandara-like churning of the milk-ocean characterized by the heart and mind proceeds—that is, when it acts as the agitator—this [verse] serves as an illustration for the mere activity of the mind. (31)
Even amidst various activities that are as unstable as the tips of swords, characterized by incessant coming and going, nothing whatsoever is stable or auspicious.

In the activities of the senses and so forth, which possess extremely variegated forms and are exceedingly wonderful, and for that very reason are like the edge of a sword—possessing the nature of a sword-blade. || 32 ||

Neither is sovereignty over the entire earth a boon, nor is the form of an immortal among the gods a boon, nor even the status of a Naga beneath the surface of the earth; for the mind of the virtuous finds its true stability only where [the Lord] resides. 33.

Thus, because it is impermanent and trivial, no worldly pleasure is to be desired by those possessed of discernment; this he states with the words beginning "not better" (*na varam*). Sovereignty over the entire earth, being unique and unrivaled, is not better.
Likewise, the nature of those gods who are most highly learned, such as Indra, Bṛhaspati, and others—that state is not better.

The meaning is that there is nothing whatsoever— whether it be the kingdom of heaven and so forth, or even the surface of the earth, or the netherworld (pātāla) where Śeṣanāga, capable of supporting the entire earth, dwells as the king of the subterranean realm— in which the mind of the wise, being discerning, attains stability and rest through the fulfillment of all desires. || 33 ||

Neither is the investigation of confused treatises excellent, nor is the deliberation on the affairs of others excellent, nor is the description of the sequence of foremost stories excellent—that wherein the minds of the virtuous find their rest. (34)

Thus, because of their difficulty and vastness, and due to the cause of confusion among the various treatises of the fourteen branches of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*), even scholarship characterized by the capacity for extraction through investigation is not superior. Likewise, having investigated other matters through the excellence of one's intellect, [that which is characterized by] the capacity for discernment—

The capacity to please the world is not excellent; likewise, the capacity to describe the sequence of the foremost narratives such as the *Bhārata* and others is also not excellent, as previously stated. (34)
Neither is long life consisting of mere worldly attachment better than death, nor is firm delusion better;
neither is hell better nor is heaven, for the mind finds no stability anywhere at all.

If life is not preferable because of the abundance of suffering, then death might be preferable because it brings about the cessation of all suffering; to this he replies: "Because of the firmness of delusion. The meaning is that even death is not preferable, because of the persistence of delusion, which is the root cause of all suffering.
If it is argued that enjoyment is preferable because it brings about the destruction of all suffering, he says "no"—*na hi*—meaning it is not so.
Bhāvaḥ means sovereignty over all the worlds (viṣṭapa). || 35 ||
Thus, all these various sequences of the world appear delightful to a man only because of his mental delusion;
how could the great ones find lasting stability in objects that consist of such extremely unstable processes? (36)

When all the various sequences of the world are investigated in this manner by a discerning person— that is, a man— they are not at all delightful. For, because those sequences of the world are perceived through a most unstable mode of perception and the realization of their impermanence, how could the great ones find pleasure in objects so grasped?
The meaning is that they attain long-lasting stability and ultimate rest. || 36 ||

Thus ends the twenty-third canto, titled "The Refutation of the Conceptualization of Samādhi," in the *Bhuśuṇḍopākhyāna* of the *Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa*, within the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki. 23.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Refutation of the Resolve for Attainment," in the First Part of the Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The twenty-fourth canto.
Bhuśuṇḍa said:
There is but one vision alone—free from peril and devoid of delusion.
Among all forms of knowledge, she exists as the most excellent and exalted.
Accompanied by the sequence of the body's channels, endowed with the heart of the six chakras,
and rich in the divisions of the vibration of the vital breath (prāṇa), the contemplation of prāṇa is described here.

If there is nothing beautiful or stable in the world, then what is that which is both beautiful and stable wherein the minds of the wise find rest? To this he says, beginning with "The one alone," and so forth: Among all forms of wealth—that is, among all types of knowledge—she is the most excellent and elevated; she is difficult to ascend to suddenly. (1)
Contemplation of the self brings an end to all sufferings;
it removes the wandering in saṃsāra, which is like a long-accumulated nightmare. (2)

Contemplation of the self (*ātmacintā*) is the investigation of the self culminating in direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*). It has the nature of removing the delusion of saṃsāra—which, like a bad dream, has arisen from the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of desire and action since the beginningless past. (2)
Moving through the vast courtyard of the stainless path of the mind, she likewise destroys all sufferings, anxieties, and misfortunes. (3)

In that courtyard of the inner self (*pratyagātman*), which is characterized by unsurpassed, infinite bliss (*niratiśaya-bhūmānanda*)— wherein the mind itself is the path, being turned inward and free from the stains of *māyā* and other defects, and which is thus a pathless state inaccessible even to the mind—
one who is habituated to wandering; likewise, one for whom all present sufferings [have been removed].
And it is the destroyer of all calamities, such as anxiety, which are pursued by the anticipation of future suffering. || 3 ||
O Blessed One, that contemplation of one's own self, which is entirely free from all mental constructs, arises within as a sufficient antidote to darkness, just as moonlight is to darkness. (4)

The plural number is used because it includes the enumerations of darknesses along with their effects, which are delusions. "Alam" means "excessively"; "anta" means "end," that is, destruction—this is the ellipsis. || 4 ||
It is easily attained by those such as you, yet it is indeed difficult to attain for those such as we;
it transcends all mental constructs and has reached the supreme pinnacle.
He states the reason for the restriction "it is indeed difficult to attain" with the verse beginning "samasta... (verse 5).
O great sage, how can those of ordinary intellect attain this state, which is the friend of that woman who delights in the contemplation of the Self?

"Those of common intellect" means those whose minds are impure and natural. If it is asked, "In that case, how did she become so easily accessible to you?", he sets forth the introductory framework to describe her concern for his life, with the intention of saying, "By resorting to her friends":
"Having attained a slight similarity [to them], they are cooled by the moon of discernment."
O Lord of Munis, [this concerns] the various [beings] who are equal to those who contemplate the self.
From among my companions who contemplate the Self, I have chosen one that brings about the destruction of all suffering and increases all prosperity. (8)
"The cause for life here is based on the concern for the vital breath.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
To the bird Bhuśuṇḍa who had spoken thus, I again—
Although he already knew this, he questioned the sage calmly as if in jest.
Out of contempt and curiosity. || 9 ||
O you who sever all doubts, O one of exceedingly long life!
Tell me truly, O holy one, what is meant by "reflection on the vital breath" (prāṇacintā)? || 10 ||
What is it like? || 10 ||
Bhuśuṇḍa said:
"O sage, you are a knower of all the Vedāntas and the destroyer of all doubts;
yet you ask me about a crow for the sake of jest."
Or rather, O Blessed One, let it be for you alone to train yourself;
what harm has come upon me by my replying thus? (12)

In the presence of you venerable ones, headed by yourself, I shall speak this vision of the vital breath (*prāṇadarśana*) in order to train [in it], to understand it specifically, and to provide further answers. I shall give the answer to your question. (The imperative mood, first person singular. 12.
Listen to this "Prāṇa-samādhi" which I shall now describe; it restores life to Bhuśuṇḍa and grants Bhuśuṇḍa his own true self. (13)
This will be explained in the sequence of describing the body as a house. ||13||
"Behold, O Blessed One, this entire body-house, so enchanting, with its three kinds of great pillars and enclosed by nine doors. (14)
It is that which has three kinds of great supporting pillars made of wood, characterized by wind, bile, and phlegm.
It was protected on all sides by the householder ego, together with his wife, the subtle body (puryaṣṭaka), and his kinsmen, the subtle elements (tanmātra).
The "eightfold city" (puryaṣṭaka) has been explained previously; he whose [only] kinsmen and relatives are that very eightfold city. 15.
Within, you see [the body] with the excellent ear-cavities as its attic rooms, the hair as its covering, and the large eyes as its windows. (16)
As the inner witness, you behold and directly experience this body-house as it is being described by me;
that house which possesses two moon-chambers in the form of the two ear-pits, and which is covered with hair like locks of matted locks. 16.
With the mouth as its principal gateway, the sides of the arms as its side-chambers, and the hollows of the doorways adorned with the garlands of the rows of teeth; (17)
Its arms and sides are the side-chambers (*upamandira*), and its temple-wings are the wings of the structure;
its main entrance-opening is adorned with rows of teeth—the rows of tusks—which serve as its decorative filaments (*kesara*).
Constantly, like gatekeepers, it guards the doors of form, taste, and touch. 17.
It was filled with a tumultuous light and established its presence within the courtyard of the stars.

The mention of the apprehension of form and taste is an illustration for all external objects. Those sense organs which touch them—that is, bring them inward—are like gatekeepers characterized by that function. In this regard, because the skin pervades all limbs, it acts as the gatekeeper for all doors; thus, one should understand that the same applies to the two lower apertures as well. In every case, this is to be understood collectively.

It is enveloped—that is, pervaded—by the light of the Self which has spread through the pervasion of the subtle body (*liṅgadeha*). Specifically, during the waking state, the Lord’s presence is established in the two *alinda*s (porches) characterized by the pupils of the eyes, which are the "stars" (*tāra*), namely the uppermost door-chambers. This person who is in the right eye is indeed named "Indha," the one who is awake within the eye.
The intention is that this is because of the Vedic revelation stating, "one should know. || 18 ||
Smeared with blood, flesh, and fat, entwined with a network of sinews, bound together by the timber of thick bones, it was like a well-constructed wall, perfectly assembled. (19)
Smeared with blood, flesh, and fat, as if with water, clay, and cow dung, it is built up by plastering;
it is encircled and confined by a network of sinews and veins, and for this very reason, it possesses excellent walls. 19.
O leader of sages, the Iḍā and Piṅgalā [nāḍīs] of this body are well-situated,
soft, in the middle, and closed within the side cavities.

Within this body, there are two delicate and subtle channels called Iḍā and Piṅgalā, situated on the left and right sides respectively; they are closed and unmanifest, yet they become manifest through the sign of the movement of the vital breath (prāṇa) and remain well-established within the two nostrils. || 20 ||
The yantra consists of three pairs of lotuses made of bone and flesh, soft, with stalks extending upward and downward, and possessing delicate, well-formed petals that meet one another.

In that regard, [the text] demonstrates the three heart-lotus mechanisms (*hṛtpadmayantra*), which serve as the substratum for all vital energies (*prāṇaśakti*), consist of a root-network branching into seventy-two thousand channels (*nāḍī*), are named *purītat*, and have the form of three joined lotus-pairs with stalks. 1.35–36.
By way of being joined together, the soft petals meet; therefore, each [petal] is a machine in the form of a machine. || 21 ||
With its petals opening by means of sprinkling from one who moves through the entire sky, its leaves, pervaded by the wind, move gently. (22)

Its petals and leaves bloom through the sprinkling of the nectar of the downward-moving wind (apāna-vāyu), known as the moon, which moves through the entire space of the body from the tip of the nose to the feet. By implication, it is understood that the petals slightly contract through the movement of the upward-moving wind (prāṇa).
Therefore, the petals of that machine, being pervaded by the prāṇa and apāna winds, move gently.
The meaning is that with every inhalation and exhalation, they slightly contract and expand. || 22 ||
As those leaves moved, that wind increased,
like the wind blowing from all sides through a mass of vine-leaves shaken by the breeze.

To explain what happens there when [the breaths] move, he says: "calatsv iti" (when they move). "It expands" (parivardhate) means that by spreading everywhere, having entered the openings of all the channels connected to the *purītat*, it becomes manifold; the meaning is that it is just like when wind strikes a network of creepers and leaves in a forest outside, the air spreads in all directions. || 23 ||
Having been increased and having established itself in many ways within the channels,
it then spreads throughout this body, moving both upwards and downwards.
Having been thus brought to growth, it—
having established and fashioned many locations characterized by the heart, anus, navel, throat, and all the limbs,
and being designated by the five names beginning with *prāṇa*— resides within the seventy-two thousand branching channels that extend upward and downward.
The meaning is that, having entered the one hundred and one channels, it spreads throughout the body. || 24 ||
Then, that wind of the heart is designated by those who know it through technical terms such as prāṇa, apāna, samāna, and so forth, according to its various modes of conduct and activity.
He states that very point: "prāṇa... (verse 25).
All the vital energies (prāṇa-śaktis) within the three lotus-machines of the heart extend upward and downward through the body, like rays from the orb of the moon.
He demonstrates the expansion of the vital powers (*prāṇa-śakti*) throughout all the limbs along with those vital breaths (*prāṇa*) in the verse beginning with "hṛtpadma" (the heart-lotus).
They go and come, they pull and they carry away, and they sport; they fly up and fall down swiftly—these are the powers of the vital breath (prāṇa-śakti). || 27 ||
