He describes the activity of those [channels] within the channels for the purpose of distributing the essence of food throughout the body, beginning with the words "yānti" (they go). || 27 ||
This very breath, residing in the heart-lotus, is called "prāṇa" by the wise;
O Sage, a certain power of this [breath] causes the eyes to blink. (28)
The heart alone is the primary seat of the vital breath (*prāṇa*); its preeminence is such that the others are merely modifications of its functions.

Through these [modifications], the *prāṇa* itself performs all the activities of the body, senses, and so forth by means of its various powers; this he explains with the words beginning "sa eṣa" (That is this...). 28.
One [power] perceives touch, while another carries [the breath] through the nose.
One digests food, while another speaks words. || 29 ||
What need is there for much speaking here? The Blessed Wind performs everything within the body, just as a mechanic operates a machine.
The mechanical device here refers to the dancing and other movements of a statue or similar contrivance; the "mechanical operator" is the master craftsman of the machine. || 30 ||
Therein, O Sage, the two winds that have issued forth according to the dual convention of upward and downward are renowned as Prāṇa and Apāna; these two are the manifest and excellent winds.
These two possess the dual conventions of "ascending" and "descending. || 31 ||
O Sage, I remain constantly following the course of those two, whose bodies are cold and hot, and who are ever travelers in the sky. (32)
Having thus described all the introductory matter, he now shows the contemplation of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) being performed by himself:
"By abandoning the internal limitation through the maintenance of the state of identity with that [breath] in the form of the thread-self (*sūtrātman*) belonging to the divine sphere,
there occurs the practice of the vow of the subtle elements (*tanmātra-vrata*), following the renunciation of all sensory vows corrupted by attachment and impurity."

For the vow of the organs of speech and the rest consists in their addiction to their respective objects such as speaking; and since that is defiled by attachment and sin, it is broken by death characterized by exhaustion. But for the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the vow is simply its movement through the locations of the mouth, nose, and so forth; and since that is not defiled by attachment to sense-objects, it is not overcome by the nature of exhaustion. Thus, the *prāṇa* alone—

One who is free from the violation of his vow is not swallowed by death; therefore, the intention is that through the contemplation of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), characterized by the mere performance of its vows and the maintenance of its identity, one has conquered death. And this contemplation of the vital breath, accompanied by the observance of the *prāṇa*-vow, is described in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka*.

The detailed exposition of this is to be understood from the very passage beginning with "Now, therefore, the investigation of the vow" (*athāto vratamīmāṃsā*) and ending with "Therefore, one should observe only one vow: one should breathe in and breathe out, lest the evil death should seize him; if he should observe it, he would desire to complete it; thereby he wins union with and residence in the same world as this deity."
He also states their other qualities worthy of veneration with the verse beginning "śītoṣṇavapuṣoḥ" (32).
Of the body and the great machine, which are free from fatigue;
and of the sun and moon in the sky of the heart, whose nature is fire and soma. || 33 ||

Regarding the phrase "of the two, exertion and the inferior": the meaning is based on the Vedic scripture which states, "Death, having become exhaustion, approached them; but it did not reach this very one, which is the middle vital breath. || 33 ||
Of this mind, which is the guardian of the city of the body; of these two chariot wheels, which are the praised and beloved horses of King Egoism. (34)
As I followed those two winds known as prāṇa and apāna, which move through the body until the dissolution of the body, I observed their course.
This applies as long as one lives, provided that the two meditations on the breath (prāṇa) and the wind (vāyu) are performed without interruption. Thus, the Śruti was cited earlier:
"If he should speak [out], he should desire to complete it. For its meaning is: "He should not interrupt it. || 35 ||
O Brahmin, for those who are always equal in the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, the days pass like those of one established in deep sleep.
"Of equal form" means that, through the excellence of practice, they move through a distance measured by only twelve or sixteen finger-breadths (aṅgulas), both externally and internally. || 36 ||
Even though their movement exists, it is more subtle and difficult to perceive in these two than in one whose limbs have been cut a thousand times, or even in a fragment of a lotus fiber. (37)

With the intention that, due to the practice of *prāṇāyāma* and because of bringing those two [the breaths] to a state of extreme subtlety, there is no possibility of their exiting [the body], he says: "Suddenly" (*sahasā*). Alternatively, why is the internal movement within the channels (*nāḍī*) of these two not perceived, as is the case with their movement through the mouth and nose? To this, he says: "Suddenly."

The intention is that, according to the Vedic scripture stating, "It remains as subtle as a hair split a thousandfold," because the channels themselves are extremely subtle and difficult to perceive, the movement of these two [the breaths] within them is all the more difficult to observe. || 37 ||

Having understood the movement of the two winds that flow without ceasing, and having followed that movement impelled within the heart, O Great-souled One, the man whose mind is gladdened and whose bonds are destroyed is never born again in this world. (38)
Having described the contemplation of the vital breaths (*prāṇacintā*), he concludes by indicating the occasion for the inquiry into the methods that are about to be described,

with the words "uninterrupted" (*avirata*). This refers to the [contemplation] enjoined in various Vedic scriptures within the respective sections on the worship of the vital breaths, concerning those two winds— *prāṇa* and *apāna*— whose movement has proceeded uninterruptedly in the heart and other locations such as the *hṛdaya*.

The meaning is that by following the path— which is manifoldly established and distinguished by numerous qualities such as faultlessness, freedom from fatigue, unbrokenness of vows, and the attainment of [divine] companionship— and by worshipping it in the manner to be described hereafter, a person, having destroyed the bonds of death and become liberated while living through the knowledge of reality, is not born again in this cycle of existence. The word "hi" (indeed) [indicates certainty].

This is intended to show that it is well-known in the Śrutis that even meditations on the vital breath (prāṇa) and so forth, when performed without desire, serve as causes for liberation by way of leading to knowledge. || 38 ||

Thus ends the twenty-fourth canto, titled "The Examination of the Vital Breath," in the *Bhuśuṇḍa-ākhyāna*, within the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa* of the *Mokṣopāya* section of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*, a work of the Sage. 24.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Investigation of Vital Breath," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The Twenty-fifth Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
While the bird was speaking in this manner, he was questioned by me there once again.
"O Raghava, what indeed is the movement of the vital breath? || 1 ||
In this context, the arrangement of exhalation (recaka) and so forth within the movements of the prāṇa and apāna breaths is described;
furthermore, Brahman is portrayed as the locus where the arising and dissolution of the prāṇa and apāna occur.
He says that he asked about the various ways in which the life-force moves through the body— a subject for reflection indicated by the granting of an opportunity for inquiry:
Bhuśuṇḍa said,
"O Sage, although you know everything, why do you ask me this as if in play?"
I shall speak according to what was asked; listen also to my words on that matter.
O Brahmin, this vital breath (prāṇa) is the power of vibration, ever-moving;
this prāṇa is situated above within the body, both externally and internally.

One occurrence of the word *prāṇa* is used in its conventional sense (*rūḍha*), while the other, as in "the movement of the vital breath" (*prāṇagati*), is etymological (*yaugika*) and refers to its defining characteristic.
In accordance with this definition, he demonstrates the upward position by gesturing: "This one is situated above. || 3 ||
O Brahman, the apāna too is a power of vibration that is always in motion;
within the body, both externally and internally, this apāna is situated downwards.
In this way, the term *apāna* is also a single derivative [term], and everything [regarding it] is as previously [explained]. (4)
O Knower of Reality, listen now for the sake of your highest good regarding that from which this supreme prāṇāyāma proceeds, both while one is awake and while one is sleeping. || 5 ||

Having thus demonstrated the distinction according to their characteristics, he shows the contemplation of the constant establishment of the nature of *prāṇāyāma* within those states without effort, beginning with the words "of one who is awake" (*jāgrataḥ*) and so forth. || 5 ||
The wise know that outward movement of the vital breaths from the hollow of the heart-lotus, occurring by its own natural impulse and without effort, to be *recaka*.

In that regard, from the heart up to the crown of the head, the half [of the breath] moving during exhalation should be contemplated as internal *recaka* (exhalation). However, the other half, from the crown of the head outwards to a distance of twelve finger-breadths, should be contemplated as external *pūraka* (inhalation); thus he says with two verses beginning with "bāhya" (external).
When the breaths extend downward, reaching as far as twelve finger-breadths outside,
that contact of the breaths with the body is called *pūraka*.
When one, free from effort, causes the external breath to enter within,
this filling touch is known by the wise as *pūraka* (inhalation).

Thus, the meaning is that the internal inhaler (pūraka) knows both kinds of touch of the wind: that which falls inward and enters from an external location, extending from the tip of the nose up to the head, and that which extends from the head down to the heart.
When the apāna has set and the prāṇa has not yet arisen in the heart, that state of kumbhaka is experienced by yogis. (9)

Now, he defines internal kumbhaka by way of its commonality to both the conceptualized and non-conceptualized [states], beginning with the words "in apāna": when it has set, that is, when it has become quiescent. || 9 ||
Exhalation (recaka), retention (kumbhaka), and inhalation (pūraka) exist in three ways;
they are located at the site of the arising of the apāna, twelve finger-breadths below and outside [the navel].

And he begins to demonstrate the exhalation (*recaka*) and other [breath-controls] even externally with the words "exhalation" (*recaka*), etc. [Verse 10]: at the place of the arising of the *apāna*, twelve finger-breadths outside from the tip of the nose.
O Mahāmati, listen to those natures which have been described by those of expansive intellect as existing at all times and devoid of any effort toward perfection.
Those which are called *recaka* and so forth are *svabhāvas*, because they arise from themselves alone. || 11 ||
O Lord, from the outside limit of twelve finger-breadths,
whatever wind arises, its [states of] inhalation and so forth occur right there by its very nature.

"Abhyuditaḥ" means standing facing [the breath]. "Of that wind" refers to that very external region; the remainder of the sense is that the external inhalations (*bāhyapūraka*) and so forth are to be contemplated. || 12 ||
The state [of the breath] outside, at a distance of twelve finger-breadths, level with the tip of the nose and facing it, is like that of an unformed pot situated within clay. (13)

Therein, by means of the unification of the external wind and the internal breath, he conceives of a state that is almost motionless as *kumbhaka* (retention), with the verse beginning "mṛdantarastha" (situated within the earth), consisting of one and a half verses. || 13 ||
The wise know that to be the *kumbhaka* of the *apāna* which is constant in the ether;
it is the movement of the outward-tending breath reaching as far as the tip of the nose. (14)

One should also conceive that movement which, by virtue of its previous state as the vital breath, proceeds from the heart up to the tip of the nose, as being the external inhalation; thus he says: "of that which is directed outward. (14)
Those who know yoga understand that first [breath] to be the external inhalation;
its movement extends even beyond the tip of the nose, reaching as far as the *dvādaśānta*.
Then, one conceives of the external movement as being internal by means of the outer filling [of the breath], starting from the tip of the nose. || 15 ||
The wise know that state of the breath to be the "external filling" (bāhyapūraka), which occurs when the prāṇa has set outside and the apāna has not yet arisen. || 16 ||
The passage beginning with "outside" (bahiḥ) is a restatement of what was previously mentioned. || 16 ||
They know that to be the full, balanced, external kumbhaka wherein there is an inward-turning of the breath without the rising of the apāna.
He describes the method for conceiving the two external exhalations (recaka) with the words "yattat" (that which...). "Without arising" means without vibration (praspanda).
Thus, the meaning is: that inward-turned state which exists in the moment preceding the vibration, being oriented toward vibration. || 17 ||
One should know that external exhalation (bāhyarecaka), when contemplated, bestows liberation;
it is that supreme fullness of form which arises from the "end of the twelve" (dvādaśānta).

From the "end of the twelve"—the outermost part at twelve finger-breadths beyond—the fullness [of the breath] arises through the movement of the apāna until it reaches the tip of the nose, by means of the manifestation of its own nature. 18.
They know that which is external to the apāna breath as the subsequent pūraka;
these, such as kumbhaka and others, both external and internal, should be practiced incessantly.
Having understood them as being of the nature of prāṇa and apāna, one is not born again;
these eight, O one of great intelligence, are to be recollected day and night. (20)
"Having understood and worshipped [it], one is not born again"—this is a praise by means of the fruit of knowledge which is necessarily inherent. Regarding the phrase "eight":

although there are ten [breaths] because exhalation (*recaka*) and inhalation (*pūraka*) each have two types both externally and internally, nevertheless, this statement is made with reference to the eight limbs, based on the predominance of the two retentions (*kumbhaka*). || 20 ||
I have described the natures of the bodily winds as bestowing liberation,
whether one is walking or standing, waking or even sleeping.
He says "gacchataḥ" (as one goes) to indicate that through this practice, the restraint of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) also occurs at the [proper] time. || 21 ||
These [senses], which by their very nature are like excessively fickle winds, come to cessation;
for one who acts or eats while fully mindful through the intellect alone [attains this].
With the intention that even the conceit of being an agent and an enjoyer is destroyed by this, he says: "Whatever one does," etc. (22).
In that state, a person is not at all an agent within himself regarding breath-retentions (kumbhaka) and the like;
for in this practice, the mind remains undistracted while completely abandoning external activity.

He states that by abandoning external views, the attainment of the supreme state is also accomplished through the arising of the vision of the inner self—thus he says, "unperturbed" (*avyagram*). Being fully absorbed in this activity of contemplating the vital breath (*prāṇa*), one therefore completely abandons—that is, renounces—external objects. (23)
For a person practicing this, even within a few days, the state of absolute oneness (kevala) is attained, while external tendencies toward sense objects [cease]. 24.
Their minds do not form an attachment, just as a Brahmin does not feel desire for a dog's skin;
those of perfected intellect who remain firm, having grasped this view. (25)
"In a dog's season" means in a dog-skin bellows, that is to say, in the milk and so forth contained therein. || 25 ||
Indeed, they alone have attained everything that is to be attained, for they remain unwearied—
whether standing, walking, sleeping, or likewise waking.
If this view is observed, then that bondage is not attained;
[it is sufficient] for those who possess the awakening gained through following the prāṇa and apāna. 27.

"Following" (anusāra) means the tracking and contemplation of the prāṇa and apāna breaths; by that [means], in the inner self (pratyagātman) situated here within the heart, [there arises] for those men who have attained awakening through a mind whose impurities and delusions are completely stilled. || 27 ||
With his impurities and delusion completely stilled, being established in himself, the wise man—remaining ever pure—will here within burn away all undertakings, O people. (28)
Having attained the movement of the prāṇa and apāna, one who is well-established prospers in happiness;
O Brahmin, the rising of the prāṇa occurs from the lotus-petal situated within the heart.
"The prosperity of the vital breath," and so forth, is a restatement of what was previously mentioned. || 29 ||
O great sage, this prāṇa sets outside at a distance of twelve finger-breadths; the apāna rises from the external "end of twelve" (dvādaśānta).
Then, the setting [of the breath] occurs within the lotus situated in the heart;
there, the vital breath (prāṇa) arrives at the twelve-finger space in the station of the ether.

"Situated in the heart, in the middle of the lotus"—the remainder of the sense is "the setting of the apāna. Wherein, in which station of space (abhaḥpade), the prāṇa comes together and reaches its completion. || 31 ||
Immediately after that, this apāna moves downward from the feet;
then the prāṇa, directed toward the external space, flows upward like a flame of fire.

Therefore, from that cavity, the apāna moves upward and emerges. He establishes—by means of the passage beginning with "external"—the previously stated fact that prāṇa and apāna consist of Agni and Soma, by demonstrating their qualities of heat and cold, and their upward and downward orientations. || 32 ||
The apāna, directed toward the space of the heart, flows downward like water;
the apāna, which is the moon, nourishes the body from the outside.
The vital breath (prāṇa), whether as the sun or as fire, digests this body within;
for the prāṇa, heating the space of the heart at every moment, [performs this function]. (34)
With the intention that their nature as the sun and the moon might also be considered, he establishes that as well, beginning with the words "prāṇa" and so forth.
The supreme sun, having reached the sky at the tip of the mouth, causes [the world] to feel remorse; but the moon of the apāna, having flooded the sky of the heart, reaches the tip of the mouth. 35.
Immediately after the closing of the eyes, this [prāṇa] causes nourishment;
the digit residing within the moon of apāna is made to swell by the sun of prāṇa.
A *kalā* is the final part; having remained in that *hārda* Brahman, [the rays] are swallowed, having reached that Brahman. || 36 ||
Having reached that state where [the breath] is swallowed, one no longer grieves;
likewise, when the sun of the prāṇa is situated within by means of the moon of the apāna. (37)

The meaning is: having reached that state of Brahman characterized by the external space extending twelve finger-breadths, which is swallowed by the downward-moving breath (apāna) existing therein. || 37 ||
Having attained that state, the person who has been swallowed [by it] does not undergo birth again;
the vital breath itself attains the nature of the sun within the space both outside and inside.
One should consider that two powers arise sequentially from the very same wind; thus he says, beginning with "prāṇa eva":
"Subsequently, the vital breath itself assumes the state of the moon, which bestows nourishment upon the body, having abandoned its lunar nature. (39)
Āpyāyana means nourishment; āpyāya means refreshment. || 39 ||
In an instant he attains the state of the sun, the position that causes total desiccation;
yet, having completely abandoned the nature of the sun, he does not reach the state of the moon.

In that state, when the *prāṇa* has extended to the limit of twelve finger-breadths (*dvādaśāṅgula*) outwardly, as long as it has not abandoned its solar nature and heat to assume the lunar nature and coolness, that is the transitional state (*saṃdhyavasthā*) between *prāṇa* and *apāna*. In that state, due to the dissolution of the *prāṇa* outside the body, the true natures of the Self— such as bodilessness, actionlessness, and mindlessness— are manifested.

Because they can be realized, they are now investigated. Among them, regarding external *kumbhaka*, since there is no spatial limitation such as the body and so forth, it is related to the lifespan governed by the activities of *prāṇa* and *apāna*, which consist of the moon and the sun.
First, *prāṇa* is investigated: "One does not grieve when [the breath] is neither in space nor in time."
Having known the constant setting and rising of the moon and the sun within the heart, [one attains liberation]. || 41 ||

Thus, even in internal *kumbhaka*, because the mind established in the junction of *prāṇa* and *apāna* at the heart necessarily attains the awakening to the Supreme Self, which is its own true substratum, there is no further involvement with birth and so forth; thus he says:
"The mind is not born again once it has reached the Self's own support."
Along with its rising and setting, with the moon, with its rays, and with its coming and going.

The support or substratum of one's own mind is the Supreme Self; or rather, it is one's very own self residing in the heart that is the sun of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which manifests as the moon of the downward breath (*apāna*) and through its various functions such as the diffused breath (*vyāna*)— acting as its rising and setting rays— as a phenomenal transformation (*vivarta*), yet it is not distinct from that [Self].
He states that the contemplation that "something exists" is the cause for the realization of one's own Self: "With its rising and setting," etc. (Verse 42).
He who beholds the divine Sun within his heart truly sees;
for external darkness, whether diminished or undiminished, does not lead to spiritual perfection.

Now, one might ask: "What is the use of the internal direct realization of the Self? Since the external darkness merely veils the Self—which is actually unlimited even externally—why not seek external light itself for its destruction? To this, he says: "No" (verse 43).
One should destroy the darkness within the heart; when that is destroyed, supreme perfection arises.
When external darkness is completely exhausted, the Lokāloka mountain comes into being.

Regarding the phrase "but [it is] of the heart": the idea is that even the conceptualization of external darkness occurs solely by virtue of the darkness of the heart; therefore, when that [internal darkness] is destroyed, its destruction follows as a matter of course.

With the intention that the dispelling of external darkness by means of external light serves only as a cause for perceiving forms and so forth, and not as a cause for the perception of the Self within, he says: "In the external," and "is perceived."
The world is of the nature of the moving universe. || 44 ||
O Sage, when the darkness within the heart has been destroyed, one's own light arises;
that which brings about the destruction of the heart’s darkness, when fully known, bestows liberation.
With effort, one should observe the sun of the vital breath (prāṇa) until its setting with the moon;
for the moon of the downward breath (apāna) sets there within the hollow of the heart-lotus.
Having spoken of the external and internal [breaths], and wishing to elaborate for the sake of encouragement upon the establishment of *kumbhaka*, he prepares the introductory stage:
From that state, the sun of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) rises within, directed outward;
when the downward breath (*apāna*) has set, the *prāṇa* rises from the lotus of the heart. (47)
When the shadow has dissolved its limbs, just as the heat [vanishes] right there instantly, when the prāṇa has set, apāna immediately arises from the exterior. (48)
O noble-minded one, know that when the heat has vanished from all sides, the apāna breath likewise perishes immediately upon the ground where the prāṇa was born, just like a shadow.
Know indeed that the prāṇa has perished in the birthplace of the apāna;
when the prāṇa has set, the apāna is intent upon its own rising. (50)
The intention is that it is precisely the state of being oriented toward arising that must be restrained. || 50 ||
By relying upon external retention (bāhya-kumbhaka) for a long time, one no longer grieves;
when the apāna has set and the prāṇa is slightly inclined toward rising. (51)
By relying upon internal retention (*antaḥ-kumbhaka*), one does not grieve again for a long time;
by relying upon the exhalation of the vital breath (*prāṇa-recaka*), it goes to a distance far beyond the downward breath (*apāna*).
From the downward breath (apāna), from its point of emergence, located twelve finger-breadths away, it extends to the distant tip, reaching out sixteen finger-breadths; this is the meaning. || 52 ||
By practicing the pure kumbhaka, one no longer suffers;
[one should practice] the support for exhalation in the apāna, situated between the filling of the prāṇa and the internal [kumbhaka].

[The breath] becomes clear through the complete expulsion of the air. It enters within through the nostrils into the *apāna* [channel], which serves as the support for the external exhalation (*bāhyarecaka*).

Having perceived—that is, having meditated upon—the *pūraka* (the filling) of the *prāṇa*, which is established within for that purpose, has entered, is situated in itself, and is located inside the body; || 53 ||
Having perceived the internal retention (pūraka) established within oneself, a person is not born again,
wherein both prāṇa and apāna have dissolved within.
Wherein, in the Brahman within the heart. || 54 ||

Taking hold of that peaceful state, one does not regret oneself, even when the *apāna* is intent on consuming the vital breath (*prāṇa*), having realized the partless nature of both place and time. (55)

Now, explaining what was said— that one is lamented for being at an improper place and time until, having completely abandoned the state of the sun (arka), one has reached the state of the moon (candra)— he demonstrates that the sublation of place and time mentioned regarding external *kumbhaka* is also extended to internal *kumbhaka*: "facing the consumption of the vital breath" (*prāṇabhakṣonmukha*).

By such means as these, having investigated—through the sublation [of all else]—that within the consciousness which is the locus of the external dissolution of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), or within the consciousness which is the source of the internal withdrawal of the vital breath, space, time, and the entire multitude of objects existing therein are nothing but the partless pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) alone; this is the meaning.
Having thus investigated, whether externally or internally, one no longer grieves.
When the vital breath (prāṇa) is intent upon consuming the downward breath (apāna), both within the heart and externally; || 56 ||
Having thoroughly observed the place and the time, the mind is no longer born;
for there, the prāṇa is indeed merged with the apāna, and the apāna with the prāṇa.
Having swallowed both external and internal space and time, and beholding for a moment that which has set its vital breath (prāṇa) and is devoid of the rising of the downward breath (apāna); || 58 ||
The meaning is: "Behold that space and time have been swallowed up along with the prāṇa and apāna.

At the moment of the junction of prāṇa and apāna in such a state, this occurs for all living beings; however, the yogi alone knows it, not others—thus he says, beginning with "the moment" (kṣaṇam). || 58 ||
They know that external kumbhaka, accomplished without effort, to be that state;
for internal kumbhaka, accomplished without effort, is indeed the supreme state. (59)
The wise know [this]; "the yogins" is the ellipsis to be supplied. || 59 ||
This is that very form of the Self; this is pure, supreme consciousness itself. This is that which is eternally manifest; having attained this, one does not grieve.
Like fragrance within a flower, it resides within the vital breath;
we worship that conscious Self which is neither the prāṇa nor the apāna.

Having thus described the method of contemplating the vital breath (*prāṇa*) as divided by its various functions, and intending to state that after its mastery one must practice the meditation on the conscious Self (*cidātman*) which presides over the internal [breaths] such as *prāṇa* and *apāna*, he says:
"Is it the nature of *apāna* characterized by the dissolution of *prāṇa*? He replies, "No, nor is it *apāna*. And so it is said:
The intention is that it was stated to be "situated within the vital breath" for the sake of familiarization with it, but not as a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) for meditation (*upāsana*). || 61 ||

We worship the conscious Self (cidātman), which, like the taste within water, resides within the downward breath (apāna); it is neither endowed with vital breath (prāṇa) nor devoid of vital breath. [The reading "na vā'pānaḥ" is to be considered. 62.
It is called *āsvāda* because it is tasted, like sweetness. "With breath" means possessing life; "without breath" means devoid of life. || 62 ||
We worship the conscious Self, situated at the boundary of the exhaustion of prāṇa, reaching the limit of the exhaustion of apāna, and existing in the middle between prāṇa and apāna. 63.

We worship the conscious Self (cidātman), the foremost bearer of the burden, who is the supreme vitalizing force of the vital breath (prāṇa), the highest life-force of the living being (jīva), and the sustainer of the body. 64.

Regarding the phrase "of breath": this is because of such scriptural passages as "He is indeed the breath of breath. The meaning of all the successive sections (paryāyas) is that [the Self] is the instrumental cause for the functions of breathing and so forth. || 64 ||
We worship the conscious Self, which is the truth that consists of the thinking of the mind, the singular awakening of the intellect, and the egoity of the ego-maker. 65.
We worship that reality of consciousness (cittattva), in which all exists, from which all proceeds, which is all, and which is all-pervading; it is eternal and consists of all things.
The light that illuminates is merit, the purifier of all purifiers;
we worship that state of mind which is not merely a mental cultivation.

The light of lights, the radiance of radiance; bow down—that is, become humble—through various states such as the fluctuations of the mind and intellect, yet do not fall away from your original nature. "Nūnam" (surely) is used here for certainty. || 67 ||

We worship that reality of consciousness (cittattva), free from the stains of temporal parts (kalā), wherein the apāna has set and the prāṇa has not yet arisen for even a moment. (Note: This verse is sometimes read as "apāno'staṃ gataḥ" [the apāna has gone to its setting].)
We worship that reality of consciousness (cittattva), where the apāna breath has not arisen and the prāṇa breath has come to its end— the whirlpool in the space at the tip of the nose.

The space of the sky at a distance of twelve finger-breadths marked by the tip of the nose is the "whirlpool" (*āvarta*), which is the junction of the flow of the *prāṇa* and *apāna* breaths; for whirlpools indeed occur at the junction of two opposing flows. (68)
We worship that reality of consciousness (cittattva) wherein the prāṇa sets, wherein the apāna also sets, and wherein both have not yet arisen. 69.

Now, setting aside the distinctions of external and internal spatial limitations, having taken to heart the meaning of the Śruti passage—"The gods established that as Dharma, from which the sun rises and where it sets; that indeed is today, and that is tomorrow; this is truly That"—he says:
"In the place of origin and abode of Prāṇa and Apāna, situated both externally and internally."
We worship that reality of consciousness (cittattva), which is the support for the two feet of the Yogins. || 70 ||
The two places where the arising of the prāṇa and apāna is perceived—that is, reached—by yogins are called "places" (pada).
The meaning is that the reality of consciousness (cittattva), which is their support and their substratum, is that [which is to be known]. || 70 ||
We worship that essence of consciousness (cittattva), which is the form of power among all powers, mounted upon the chariot of prāṇa and apāna, yet neither prāṇa nor apāna itself.

The meaning is this: that which, having mounted upon the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of prāṇa and apāna, being unextended yet appearing limited, becomes the aggregate of prāṇa and apāna—the power of inhalation and exhalation; likewise, it is that which constitutes the essential form of the powers of the other organs as well. || 71 ||

We worship that essence of consciousness (cittattva), which is the Lord of the heart and the kumbhaka of prāṇa, as well as the kumbhaka of apāna outside, that which is released from the portion of the inhalation (pūraka). 72.

He states that this very [reality] manifests through the state of the breath-retentions (kumbhaka) of prāṇa and apāna, and through the various states of emission (visarga), exhalation (recaka), and so forth; therefore, that alone is to be worshipped—thus he says: "In the heart" (hṛdi). || 72 ||

We worship that reality of consciousness (cittattva), which is the realization of existence, which is formless, and which is to be attained by the contemplation of the vital breath (prāṇa), through the reflective awareness of the prāṇa and apāna.

The "perception" (*parāmarśa*) of the *prāṇa* and *apāna* is their movement; the meaning is that it consists of the awareness of their existence, which serves as the cause for that [movement]. Thus, he states that the very same thing is the fruit of the worship of *prāṇa*, and therefore it is the object of worship: "that which is to be attained. (73)
We worship that essence of consciousness (cittattva), which is the vibration of the vital breath, which produces the bliss of vibration, and which is the cause of all causes.
The movement of the senses toward the region of their objects is vibration (spanda), and the enjoyment thereof is bliss (ānanda); [the latter] is the cause of both.

I take refuge in that supreme, ultimate state, which is free from the stain of all worldly activity, yet is eternally surrounded by a multitude of arts; it is the glory of self-realization, the foremost station, and is bowed to by all the gods. (75)

I take refuge in that state of the Supreme Self, which is in the ultimate sense free from the stain of all mental constructions (*kalana*), yet which— when viewed by the eye of superficial perception—

is perpetually enveloped and encircled by the group of sixteen digits (*kalā*) beginning with *prāṇa*, which constitute the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the individual soul; it is such a state, whose majesty consists in perfect self-realization and unsurpassed sovereignty, that I thus attain.
The meaning is "I worship. || 75 ||

Thus ends the twenty-fifth canto, titled "Description of Samādhi," in the *Bhuśuṇḍopākhyāna*, within the *Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa* concerning the means to liberation, in the *Śrī Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa*, the *Uttarakāṇḍa*. || 25 ||
Thus ends the twenty-fifth canto, titled "Description of Samādhi," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The twenty-sixth canto.
Bhuśuṇḍa said:
"This indeed is the repose of the mind attained by me through the samādhi of the vital breath."
By this sequence, it has been attained by itself within its own stainless self.
Having thus described his own self-knowledge, Bhuśuṇḍa now explains here the causes of long life through the contemplation of the vital breath (prāṇa).
By this manner described above. || 1 ||
"O Great Sage, holding fast to this view, I remain established;
I do not waver even for the fraction of a moment, as Mount Meru does not shake. (2)
The movement of Meru is even more unstable than that. || 2 ||
Whether walking or standing, waking or even sleeping,
this perfect meditative absorption of mine does not waver from my self, even in a dream.
Firmly established amidst the ever-changing and unstable conditions of the world,
I remain inward-turned, abiding by myself within the Self through my own will.
Firmly established and undisturbed amidst the conditions of the world characterized by the desirable and the undesirable, [he acts] according to his own desire and his own will. || 4 ||
Even the wind might be obstructed, or even water from its course;
yet I do not recall anything contrary to this state of perfect composure.

The wind called Pravaha is the support of the wheel of luminaries; water [is the support] of the great rivers. Because it carries [them] along, it obstructs the movement—meaning it might even block it. "Opposing" means that which causes one to deviate toward the multitude of sense objects.
Through following the inhalation and exhalation and by beholding the Supreme Self,
I have attained the sorrowless, primordial state of great austerity.
He was one of great asceticism. || 6 ||
O Brahmin, even now, with a steady mind, I live observing the emergence and submergence of beings until the great dissolution.
I never think of what has been nor what will be;
relying solely on direct perception, I abide here by means of my own self in the present. (8)
The present [consciousness], which has the nature of being eternally present, is the witness-vision; [perceive it] by means of the self through the mind. || 8 ||
Just as when duties have been accomplished, having abandoned all longing for their fruits,
I abide solely in pure consciousness, like one in the state of deep sleep.
By virtue of being free from conceit, it is like the state of deep sleep.
Having reflected upon the thought consisting of existence and non-existence, accompanied by the desired and the undesired, I abide within the Self; free from affliction, I live for a long time.
Having reflected upon it and determined it to be something to be abandoned, by that [means] I live for a long time. || 10 ||
Constantly recollecting the time of the union of the prāṇa and apāna breaths, I myself am content within my own self; I live for a long time, free from ailment.
The union is the junction; that moment is what is meant by "Brahman shines forth there. || 11 ||
"I have obtained this today; I shall obtain that which is beautiful"—such thoughts I do not harbor, and therefore I live long and free from affliction.
O virtuous one, I neither praise nor blame anything whatsoever, whether concerning myself or another, at any time; by that means, I have attained auspiciousness.
Of oneself, of another, or of someone else; the word "action" (ceṣṭita) is to be understood as the ellipsis. || 13 ||
I am not gratified by attaining the auspicious, nor do I feel distress even regarding the inauspicious; my mind is always equanimous, and for that reason, I have attained the auspicious.
From the context, life is auspicious. 14.
Relying upon supreme renunciation, I have indeed always relinquished everything, including my very life; by that means, I have attained auspiciousness.
But renunciation is characterized by the sublation of all duality; life begins with the absence of attachment to living. 15.
O Sage, my mind is stilled of its restlessness, free from sorrow, established in itself, and composed; it is peaceful, and by that I live free from affliction. (16)
I see wood, a graceful woman, a mountain, grass, fire, snow, and the sky as equal everywhere; therefore, I live free from affliction.
"What has been accomplished by me today, or what will happen again tomorrow morning?"—such a fever of anxiety does not exist for me; therefore, I live free from ailment. (18)
It is accomplished; it has been attained. || 18 ||
I neither fear the sufferings of old age and death, nor do I rejoice in the pleasures of attaining a kingdom; therefore, I live free from affliction.
"O Brahmin, I do not know, 'This one is my kinsman and this one is a stranger; this one is mine and that one is from elsewhere. Because of that, I live free from affliction. (20)
Of one [thing] from another. || 20 ||
I know that everything—which appears as all things—is without beginning or end and free from affliction;
by knowing "I am consciousness," I live free from affliction.
Everything is indeed consciousness alone. Because everything appears as various distinct entities, it is called the "appearance of everything" (*sarvapadābhāsa*). 21.
Whether eating, moving about, standing, rising, breathing, or sleeping, I do not perceive "I am the body"; by that, I have become long-lived.
Taking up; seizing. || 22 ||
Abiding like the state of deep sleep regarding this undertaking of saṃsāra, I perceive it as if it were non-existent; therefore, I live free from affliction.
That which occurs in saṃsāra is "saṃsāric"; it refers to an undertaking or an action. || 23 ||
"Since gain and loss, occurring at their proper time through skillful means, are equal to me—like my two hands situated upon my own body—I live free from affliction. (24)
"At the proper time" means having arrived according to the timing of the enjoyment presented by the *prārabdha* (commenced karma). || 24 ||
With my steady power of vision, gentle and charming, I look straight ahead everywhere; by that, I live free from ailment. (25)

By means of an unwavering power of mental steadiness that does not deviate from its own true nature; by a clear vision consisting of the perception of oneself in all beings; and by being straightforward—that is, free from crookedness. Thus it is said in the *Bhārata*: "Everything crooked is the domain of death; straightforwardness is the domain of Brahman. Such is the scope of knowledge; what more is there to say?"
He will act. Thus [ends the twenty-fifth].
In this body, from the feet to the top of the head, my sense of "mine-ness" has been abandoned;
thus, with the series of egoisms cast off, I live free from affliction.
Whatever I do and whatever I eat, having renounced that—even while possessing those things—my mind adopts a state of actionlessness; by that means I live free from affliction.

Having abandoned that respective conceit, even though I possess a body, my mind assumes—that is, takes on—the state of being neither an agent nor an enjoyer, which is the nature of *naiṣkarmya*. || 27 ||
O Sage, whenever I understand even a little, at that very moment my mind does not become arrogant; by that means I live free from affliction. (28)
It does not fall into restlessness or lack of discipline. || 28 ||
Though I am a lord, I do not commit aggression; though I suffer, I am not dejected.
Though I am poor, I have no longing; therefore, I live free from affliction.
Though capable of attacking others, I do not inflict attack or humiliation; likewise, because of my disposition toward endurance, I am not distressed by the suffering caused by others. (29)
Behold: within this body composed of form, the Self—the abode of consciousness—resides as the locus of the elements;
through its identity with the aggregate of elements, I live, free from affliction.

Even while this body, which consists primarily of volition, is manifesting its form, I am the locus of consciousness, perceiving only consciousness [the reading "not perceiving the body as the self" is found hereafter]. And thus, because the conscious Self is equal in all beings, being the Self abiding in all beings, one regards the multitude of beings as one's own body.
The word "I see" should be supplied and connected [to the sentence]. || 30 ||
Being composed, I do not allow the contact of my inner mental state with that which is driven by the snares of hope; therefore, I live free from affliction.
Remaining always in a state of meditative absorption, I do not allow the mental fluctuations, which are driven by the snares of hope, to enter into contact within the inner heart. || 31 ||
I perceive the non-existence of the world and the existence of the Self, like a bilva fruit in the palm of my hand;
having awakened from sleep, I see this, and therefore I am long-lived. (32)

The syntactical connection is as follows: being asleep with regard to the objects of external vision, I perceive the non-existence of the world; yet, being awakened within, I perceive the existence of the Self like a wood-apple fruit held in the palm of my hand. || 32 ||
I see everything as worn out, broken, loose, decayed, agitated, crushed, and gone to destruction; yet, because of that, I live free from affliction like one who is ever-new.

I see everything— whether slack with relaxed limbs, wasted with emaciated bodies, agitated with active members, or crushed with shattered parts— as if it were new, through the vision that perceives all things of the past, future, and present as being nothing but the eternal, changeless Self. 33
I am happy when people are happy, and I am sorrowful when they are sorrowful;
as a beloved friend to everyone, I live free from affliction because of that. (34)
In adversity I am immovable and steadfast, and in prosperity I am a friend to the world; I am not affected by the presence or absence of things, and therefore I live free from affliction.
Existences are like the increases of wealth and other such things, while non-existences are their decreases; I am not attached to these three.
"I do not exist, nor does anything else belong to me, nor do I belong to anyone else"—thus has my mind been cultivated, and by that I live free from affliction. (36)
I am the world, I am the ether, and I bring about the succession of space and time; I am action, such is my intellect, and therefore I live free from affliction.
The pot is consciousness, the cloth is consciousness, space is consciousness, the forest is consciousness, and the cart is consciousness;
"all is consciousness"—this is my conviction, and by it I live free from affliction. (38)
Is the notion of "I" present everywhere without discarding dullness? He says "no," [illustrating it with] "the jar. || 38 ||
Thus, O tiger among sages, I am known as Bhuśuṇḍa, the crow, a long-lived one who is like a bee to the lotus of the three worlds. (39)
He concludes with the word "iti" (thus). Because he dwells upon the pericarp of Mount Meru and because he is dark blue, he is like a bee for the lotus of the three worlds.

Beholding and contemplating for a long time the waves of the triple world tossed about in the ocean of Brahma—waves whose forms are altered by the process of creation and subsequent dissolution; waves that are submerged, uplifted, and seen in a state of agitation—I have remained here.

"Productions" refers to creations (*sarga*). From the first term [of the compound], "growth," "transformation," and "decay" are understood; it is that whose forms have reached a state of diversity (*vaicitrya*), being differentiated by their respective characteristics—namely, by mutual overcoming and mutual obstruction. In this manner, it is repeatedly raised up and dissolved, agitated and wandering—the witness-perceived aggregate of intellect, mind, and senses.

The meaning is: I have remained for a long time, observing the visible world at the time of its emergence, conceptualizing it during the state of meditative absorption (samādhi), and dissolving it away. || 40 ||

Thus ends the twenty-sixth canto, titled "The Narration of the Cause of Longevity by Bhuśuṇḍa," in the Nirvāṇa Section of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, within the *Deva-mokṣopāya*.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth canto, titled "The Narration of the Cause of Longevity," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa-tātparya-prakāśa*.
The twenty-seventh canto.
Bhuśuṇḍa said:
"O Brahman, I have thus told you who I am and how I exist here."
O you who have reached the further shore of knowledge, it was out of audacity that I acted solely for the sake of accomplishing your command.
In this section, the praise of Bhuśuṇḍa is described, his worship by [the King] as he was about to depart,
and Vasiṣṭha’s attainment of his own world through the power of traveling through the sky.

"In whatever manner" means by which mode I have lived for a long time; the meaning is that what I am, in this ultimate sense within this aggregate of causes and effects (the body), has been told. "By audacity" means by boldness. || 1 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Oh, how wonderful! O Blessed One, this account of your own self that you have narrated is an ornament to the Vedas and a cause of supreme amazement.
"Ātmodantaḥ" means one's own account or history. || 2 ||
Blessed are those who behold you, a great soul of exceedingly long life,
as if seeing a second Brahmā.
How fortunate are our eyes today, since you have related in its entirety, exactly as it is, your own purifying life-story that cleanses the intellect. (4)
"Blessed are the eyes of those who behold you," [he said], intending that his own eyes might find their purpose by remaining steady for as long as today. (4)
Dawn has broken in all directions, and the splendors of the gods have been seen;
yet in this world, no one as great as you has ever been beheld.
The prosperities—the wealth consisting of knowledge and sovereignty—of the *vibudhas*, meaning both the gods and the learned, have been observed. || 5 ||
Someone may perhaps be found after much wandering, as happens with the great multitude;
but a noble-souled person like you is not easily found anywhere in this world.
Even after wandering with effort and searching for a long time, a person who knows the truth is only found with great difficulty; and even among such, one like your honor is not easily encountered.
Just as a pearl is produced within a certain section of a bamboo stalk,
so too is one such as you seen within a certain fragment of the world.
In the bamboo grove (vaṃśakhaṇḍa) at Veṇuvana; for even bamboos are reckoned among the eight sources of pearls. || 7 ||
Indeed, a very great and auspicious task has been accomplished by me today,
in that you, whose self is liberated from the body of merit, have been beheld by me.
May there be prosperity for you; enter your auspicious inner chamber, for it is now midday and I must depart for the abode of the gods.
By the term "midday," the midday ritual is indicated. A temple of the gods is a seven-storied building, while one's own home is [a single-story] residence.
Having heard this, Bhuśuṇḍa rose from his seat and took with both hands, which he had previously resolved upon, the golden sprout that had been offered.

The one of perfected intellect filled that vessel with the pollen of the flowers of the wish-fulfilling tree and creepers, with moonlight as the cold water, and with pearls as the respectful offering (arghya).
With the water for the *arghya* offering, which possesses the characteristics of a pearl and serves as the water for the *arghya* rite. || 11 ||
With that water for honor, water for the feet, and flowers, my elder brother devoutly worshipped me from head to foot, as if I were the Three-eyed Lord Śiva.
From the simile "as if three-eyed," it is understood that he was also constantly devoted to the worship of Śiva; "pūrvaja" means ancient. || 12 ||
Saying, "Enough, O Lord of Birds, with this hardship of following me," I rose from my seat and then leaped up like a bird.
Saying, "Enough of this exhaustion and fatigue caused by the trouble of following you, O lord of birds," I leaped up and flew into the sky;
yet that bird, having followed me for the distance of a yojana,
seized my hand with his own and forcibly restrained me.
Restrained; turned back. || 14 ||
In an instant, having departed upon the path of the sky, that lord of birds became invisible; he had turned back, for the company of the virtuous is difficult to abandon.
Like waves in the ocean, we too have become invisible to one another in this sky; yet, through the memory of our former selves as birds, I recognize the sages.

We both became invisible to one another. Then, by means of uninterrupted mindfulness, I was recognized through my recollection of the bird Bhuśuṇḍa; having reached the sphere of the Seven Sages (Saptarṣimaṇḍala), I beheld the great sages—this is the ellipsis.
Having reached the sphere of the Seven Sages, I was honored by my wife.
Formerly, at the beginning of the Kṛtayuga, when two hundred years had passed.
He states the time of the meeting with Bhuśuṇḍa for her, who had been addressed by her wife Arundhatī, with the words "When [the year] had passed," etc. (verse 17).
I met with Bhuśuṇḍa on a tree atop a peak of Mount Meru;
O Rāma, now that the Kṛta age has waned, the Tretā age is currently prevailing.
O crusher of enemies, you were born in the middle of this Tretā Yuga;
and again today, in your eighth year, you met my Bhuśuṇḍa on that very same mountain peak, who likewise possesses an ageless form.
Of the mountain Meru. || 19 ||
Having heard this wonderful and excellent account of Bhuśuṇḍa’s experience as it was thus related, and having reflected upon it within yourself, perform that which is appropriate.
He summarizes with the word "iti" (thus). || 20 ||
Śrī Vālmīki said:

The one of pure intellect who shall here contemplate this excellent discourse between Sumati and Bhuśuṇḍa will forcibly cross the river of unreality, which is agitated by the many fears of worldly existence. (21)

Regarding the word "iti": he who shall thoroughly investigate this excellent discourse of Sumati-Bhuśuṇḍa will cross over this well-known river of unreality—the stream of Māyā—which is inhabited by those living beings who are crowded and agitated by the fears of existence, birth, and so forth, right here in this very body. The word "prasabham" (forcefully) is used for the purpose of highlighting the primacy of human effort (*pauruṣa*).
Thus ends the twenty-seventh canto, titled "The Conclusion of Bhuśuṇḍa," in the Nirvāṇa Section of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, within the *Deva-mokṣopāya*.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh canto, titled "The Conclusion," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The twenty-eighth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
"O sinless one, thus have I related to you the account of Bhuśuṇḍa."
By means of this wisdom, Bhuśuṇḍa has crossed over the peril of delusion. || 1 ||
The connection with the narrative, the description of the non-fixity of the body,
and the fact that the body and so forth are merely objects of initial delusion are described here.
He shows the connection of the narrated story of Bhuśuṇḍa to the instruction at hand:
"O mighty-armed one, having firmly grasped this vision preceded by the practice of [controlling] your own vital breaths, become like Bhuśuṇḍa—one who has crossed the great ocean. (2)

In this context, "practice of breath" (prāṇābhyāsa) refers either to the restraint of the vital breath or to its meditative worship; by means of that [restraint], the "great ocean"—that is, the vast cycle of worldly existence (saṃsāra)—is swallowed and comprehended. || 2 ||
Just as Bhuśuṇḍa attained that state which is to be attained through knowledge and yoga born of continuous practice, so too may you reach that same state.
All those whose intellects are unattached, observing the vital breaths (prāṇa and apāna), attain a state like that of Bhuśuṇḍa within the supreme reality.
Those who observe the prāṇa and apāna breaths are those whose conduct consists of the aforementioned forms of worship. || 4 ||
These various perspectives on consciousness have been heard by you;
now, relying upon your own intellect, do as you wish.
Do as you wish—whether it be the establishment of yourself in your own Self preceded by yoga or preceded by upāsanā. || 5 ||
Śrī Rāma said: O Blessed One, by you— the sun of the earth— with the rays of your knowledge,
all the darkness of unruly wickedness within my heart has been wiped away.

Setting aside the practice of yoga, Rāma—indicating that the realization of his own true nature was accomplished merely by hearing your instruction—and desiring to know the very nature of the body and the house as introduced in the course of the narrative, asks with the words "O Blessed One," and so forth.
[He refers to you] as the Sun descended upon the earth, shining like the sun itself; [he refers to his own] unrestrained wickednesses.
Because the perceptions of selfhood in what is not-self and the wicked deeds motivated by them arise from such darkness within the heart. (6)
We are awakened; we are delighted; we have entered our own abode.
We stand with all that is to be known now known, for you are indeed like the Supreme Self.
Another second [type] is like you, sirs. || 7 ||
Oh, the life-story of Bhuśuṇḍa is most wondrous!
O Blessed One, it has been narrated by you, providing an awakening to the supreme goal.

O Brahmin, regarding this account of Bhuśuṇḍa told by you, that which was described as the house of the body, constructed of flesh, skin, and bone— 9. O Brahmin, regarding this account of Bhuśuṇḍa told by you, that which was described as the house of the body, constructed of flesh, skin, and bone—
By whom indeed was it created, or from where did it arise?
How has it attained its existence, or who dwells therein? (10)
The questions concern the agent, the cause, the mode of existence, that which is situated within it, and the Lord. 10.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāghava, for the sake of realizing the supreme truth and for the removal of defects, listen to this which is being told by me according to its true nature.
O Rāma, this dwelling of the body— with bones for its pillars, nine gates, and plastered with blood and flesh— was not created by anyone at all.
Regarding that, he states the answer to the first [objection]: "It is not," [verse 12].
This is merely an appearance that manifests in this very way;
it has the form of the delusion of two moons, established as both existent and non-existent. (13)

[Objection: Surely the Lord (Īśvara) is the creator of this body, as is well known from the Śrutis, Purāṇas, and traditional narratives; and the individual soul (jīva), for its part, is the one who causes it to be created for the sake of experiencing its own karma. How then can these two be denied? To this, he says: "It is a mere reflection" (ābhāsamātram). It is exactly thus; that is to say, even without a creator. For indeed, the reflection of the moon in water does not require a creator, nor does it...

The meaning is that it is like the delusion of a second moon imagined by one suffering from ophthalmia (*taimirika*). Furthermore, the Lord’s status as a creator is based on scripture (*śrauta*) and is not primary, because of the observation of the analogy of a person’s effortless exhalation (*puruṣa-niḥśvasita*). The same applies to the individual soul’s (*jīva*) capacity to create; the point is that such creation cannot be preceded by conscious deliberation (*abuddhipūrvatva*), nor can it involve the creation of what is undesirable (*aniṣṭa-nirmāpaṇa*). || 13 ||
In the process of seeing two moons, there is indeed always a duality of moons;
yet in reality, there is only one moon, and the body is exactly like that.
He states that the falsity of the body is established just like the duality of the moon, because it exists only for the duration of its perception:
"For indeed, in that very way. The grammatical connection is: "But in reality, the moon is always indeed one. (14)
For at the time when the body is perceived, this body remains present;
yet it is non-existent, and therefore it is said to be of the nature of both being and non-being. || 15 ||
He states clearly what has already been said: "The body," etc. It is called "existent" figuratively, because it has as its substratum that which is ultimately real. || 15 ||
When one recognizes a dream as a dream, it is indeed otherwise; for at other times, it is truly in vain.
A bubble is real when it is in the state of being a bubble, and false at other times. (16)

Where has the delusion of existence in what is non-existent ever been seen? To this he replies: "In a dream. It is "vain," that is, purely false; it is like the perception of a bubble when there is actually the presence of a bubble-like phenomenon. 16.

The body is real in the context of being a body, but unreal in the context of anything else; likewise, water exists as real during the appearance of its manifestation, but otherwise it is non-existent. (17)
In the case of the other two types, when there is the existence of the vision of the pure self, [the former] is like water and [the latter] like the water of a mirage. || 17 ||
In the process of manifestation, the body is considered both existent and non-existent at other times;
thus, this appears now as mere appearance alone. (18)
Regarding the phrase "in the process of manifestation," there is no tautology, as it serves as a conclusion to the points already established. || 18 ||
The thought "I am named so-and-so" remains as an internal mental grasping;
the delusion that "I am this body composed of flesh and bone" [is likewise established]. (19)
Establishing that [the body] is a mere appearance, he causes one to abandon the conceit regarding it with the words "This":

"Abandon this very mental construction (manana) which previously assumed the form of a body; because of the firmness of its latent impressions (saṃskāra), it persists again and again in the form of a body. There are thousands of bodies created by imagination."
By means of that dream-body, he [reached] the horizons while lying upon a comfortable bed.
"Abandon them"—this connects with what precedes. Having cited the very bodies constructed by imagination as examples, he demonstrates their unreality:
"O Rāma, you wander about; where is that body of yours situated, by which [you travel] from one heavenly city to another during the kingdom of the mind in the waking state? (21)
In the state of wakefulness, one is awake. The feminine gender is a Vedic (chāndasa) usage. 21.
You wander about Mount Meru; where, then, is that body of yours situated, by which you traverse the slopes of the earth even within dreams?
O Rāma, you wander about; where is that body of yours situated?
It is a kingdom of the mind within a kingdom of the mind, amidst lands of great opulence.

In another kingdom imagined within a kingdom of one's desires, amidst vast realms of splendor— where, when the substitution of *āt* for *mahat* (as required by the rule *ānmahataḥ samānādhikaraṇajātīyayoḥ*) ought to have occurred, its absence is a Vedic anomaly— or rather, in the realms of the great ones such as Indra, Candra, and others. (23)
Where does that body abide by which you wander here?
As for those various worldly activities in the kingdom of the mind, they are performed by bodies that have already passed away.
By those who have dissolved along with the dissolution of conceptual construction. || 24 ||
O mighty-armed one, you perform [these deeds]; where do those bodies of yours reside, by which you exist as a beloved created by the will of that playful and affectionate woman? (25)
"You are attaining liberation through the body; where, then, does that body abide?
O Rāma, these bodies are likewise composed of the existence and non-existence of the mind. (26)

The statement "you shall attain liberation and the bliss of enjoyment" is expressed in the present tense by way of fitness [for the future]. In this same manner, future bodies—whether they be those of dreams or of mental constructions (manorājya)—may also be cited as examples.

Since the falsity and the nature of being purely conceptualized in those [bodies] are certain, [the author] establishes that the same applies to the body under discussion with the words "these... (verse 26).
In the same way, this body, characterized by such conduct, is known to be [merely] of the mind;
the notions "this is wealth," "this is the body," and "this is the country" are delusions.

With the intention that the principle demonstrated regarding the body as the object of the superimposition of "I-ness" (ahaṃtādhyāsa) applies equally to wealth and other objects which are the domain of the superimposition of "mine-ness" (mamatādhyāsa), he says: "This is wealth. (27)
All that is the manifestation of the mental energy of volition;
know this to be either a long dream or a prolonged delusion of the mind. (28)

However, the notion that the body and so forth differ from dreams and the like is due merely to their long duration, and not because they are real or non-illusory; with this intention, he says: "dīrgha... (verse 28).
Or even this long kingdom of the mind, O descendant of Raghu, you shall attain awakening to the cycle of existence when, by your own will, through the Supreme Self.
For this very reason, with the intention of showing that its sublation by the knowledge of reality is logically established, he says: "Upon awakening" (prabodham). || 29 ||
Then you will see this correctly, just as at sunrise [one sees clearly], that the state of the world is indeed something else, like a web of dreams and mental constructs. (30)
You will see [reality] correctly as nothing but the self alone remaining, just as one who has awakened at sunrise sees the objects of a dream. || 30 ||
For in this very same way, this particular construction of conceptual thought is indeed just like that which I previously described as the birth of the Lotus-born One.

The meaning is that it is something indefinable and merely false. Regarding this stated point, he causes one to remember what was explained at length previously in the section on origination, beginning with the words "Just as... (31).
Arising from the very mind itself through the activity of internal volition, the mind— endowed with manifold constructions— therein experiences its own delusion.
This manifestation is merely the movement of conceptual construction,
just as the imagined appearance of the mind attained the state of being born from a lotus.
He says that even what was stated in the Aindavopākhyāna should be remembered: "Just as it was imagined," etc. (33).
Just as one body is conceived from the body, so indeed does another remain;
that which has been long practiced through the prior flow [of thoughts] by means of an abundance of latent impressions (vāsanā). // 34 //
The body that was contemplated at the time of departing from the previous body. || 34 ||
In that very same way, the body is seen through the manifestation of its form; for consciousness itself is indeed volition, brought forth by human effort.

Likewise, by the emergence of form—that is, by the perfection of such a configuration—and through human effort, having turned the mind inward toward the vision of one's own Self, there is the following connection: this conceptualization in the form of the body and the world is indeed Consciousness alone;
otherwise it is conceived, O Rāma, and thus it becomes otherwise here.
When one contemplates: "This is he, this is he, and this is my own saṃsāra. || 36 ||
"If it is cultivated otherwise"—this is the ellipsis. "Then it becomes otherwise"—that is, when it has been cultivated, it is experienced exactly in that way; this is the ellipsis. || 36 ||
O Rāma, that which is cultivated becomes real through the firmness of its cultivation;
for whatever is cultivated with intense force, that alone quickly comes to pass.
For that very thing is seen; thus is the connection with what follows. || 37 ||
O Rāma, it is seen everywhere like a beloved daughter, exceedingly dear;
just as the recurring of the day is perceived within dreams through habitual practice. (38)
The withdrawal from activity during the day is according to what has been practiced. || 38 ||
Thus, when cultivated through meditation, even this cycle of existence is perceived in such a way that it appears as fleeting as the vision of a dream. (39)
Perishing rapidly and swiftly, it appears as a manifestation lasting from a moment up to thirty ghaṭikās. || 39 ||
In the same way, this [world], though existing for only a short time, appears to be stable;
just as a river is seen in the sky when it is heated by the sun's glare.
Stable and eternal; in the sky, in the desert land, in the atmosphere; a river, a mirage-river. 40.
Even though the earth does not exist, it is seen due to mental construction;
likewise, it is seen as a peacock-feather fan in the sky due to a defect in vision.
*Dharā* means the earth; by the word *api* (also), the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*) and the three worlds (*trilokī*) are included. *Picchikā* is a peacock-feather broom (*narhamuṣṭi*). || 41 ||
In the same way, this fortune of the world appears due to ignorance;
it is seen by an equal vision, just as a peacock-feather fan is not seen in the sky.
Due to faulty knowledge and delusion. || 42 ||
Through right view, this worldly splendor no longer appears [as it once did], so that a timid person does not fall into agitation amidst their own mental constructions. (43)
Even a timid person experiences agitation—that is, fear—regarding their own mental constructs, such as elephants, tigers, and so forth, imagined within the kingdom of their own desires. || 43 ||
For in this world created by one's own volition, O wise one, these things do not cause fear in such a way;
for it is simply one's own nature that now appears in this manner. (44)
The essential nature is the Self; this refers to the present state of outward orientation. 44.
In this state of wandering through the stream of saṃsāra, why should anyone here be afraid, and of what?
That very [mind] alone must be somewhat purified; when it has attained purity through cleansing, it reaches stainlessness. (45)
That from which one fears—what is that fear? The meaning is that there exists nothing whatsoever apart from one's own Self. He who fears must himself be somewhat purified and investigated. || 45 ||
O Rāma, this delusion of the world is not seen therein; by the mere sight of it correctly, one's own nature attains purity. (46)
This delusion, characterized by fear and so forth, is not seen in the non-dual, pure Self. And thus says the Śruti:
"From duality, indeed, fear arises. By what means, then, is the Self purified? To this he replies: "Properly," etc.
The Self is one's own nature. (46)
It does not take on further impurity, just as gold does not lose its nature despite the appearance of copper;
this triple world is a mere appearance, neither existent nor non-existent.

Furthermore, he dispels the doubt regarding the attainment of impurity by saying "no. The meaning is that it is like gold, which by its very nature is perceived as copper due to delusion, yet when its true form is manifested through heating and other means, its state of being copper no longer remains. If one asks, "Why is there purity for this [Self] merely through seeing? he replies: "Because the impurity of the visible is a mere appearance."
Thus, the wise know that the abandonment of all other mental constructions is perfect vision;
it is death and life, heaven, knowledge, and even ignorance itself. (48)

For this reason, the connection with the preceding verse is as follows: "The wise know that right vision itself is the abandonment and cessation of all other mental constructions. He then describes what that right vision is like, beginning with the words "death," and so forth. (48)
"There is nothing apart from the reflection of consciousness"—this is right vision, which perceives oneness.
To me, the world of "you" and "I" and so forth does not exist as the ten directions.

Apart from the manifestation of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*), which is the light of consciousness (*citprakāśa*), nothing exists separately; thus, oneness is the result—the remaining of pure consciousness alone—and this is the meaning of "right vision. "Thou-ness" (*tvantā*) is the state of being a consciousness distinct from oneself.

"I-ness" (*ahantā*) is the state of being a consciousness limited solely to one's own body. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the internal objects of the conceits of "thou-ness" and "I-ness" are included.
The collection of causes and effects is called *saṃsāra* because it causes the self to wander through other worlds and among sense-objects;

thus, the entire range of perceptible things—including the ten directions which serve as the support for that collection of objects—do not exist separately from me or as belonging to me. Rather, the logical connection (*anvaya*) is that there exists only my own manifestation, the very nature of the self which is self-luminous. || 49 ||

The wise know that the correct vision is the realization that everything is merely one's own appearance, through seeing things as they truly are within this saṃsāra composed of both the existent and the non-existent. (50)

He states the fruit of right vision [in the verse beginning] with "consisting of the real and the unreal": from the Real (sat) comes Brahman, and the Unreal (asat) is Māyā; [the world] has both of these as its material cause (upādāna).
Through correct insight, the mind neither sets nor rises, having determined that all phenomena are neither non-existent nor existent. (51)
Non-existence is sublated; existence remains as the mere reality of the substratum. || 51 ||
Through right insight, the mind free from desire attains peace;
it neither censures nor praises, neither rejoices nor grieves.
It is free from desire because its desires have been fulfilled; it is without longing. || 52 ||
Through right perception, the mind attains the coolness of truth;
for it is certain that all kinsmen must indeed die. (53)

Regarding the cool state in which the three-fold affliction has been stilled: even though one is liberated oneself, because the bondage of kinsmen has not ceased, the heat born from seeing their death and so forth is difficult to ward off; concerning this, he says "inevitably," etc.—so why do you lament in vain over the separations from kinsmen?
And it is certain that I must inevitably die; this is my resolve. || 54 ||
With the intention that even the distress caused by the fear of one's own death during the state of ignorance can be avoided by this means, he says: "Necessarily indeed" (avaśyameva). || 54 ||
Thus, when your own death has arrived, why do you grieve in vain?
For one who is born, some degree of prosperity and the like is inevitable. (55)
"What is to be attained by a man"—what occasion indeed is there for joy in this, for every man engaged in worldly affairs within the cycle of existence? (56)
Since you have come for the sake of a purpose, what occasion indeed is there for grief?
For sorrow swells, rises, and surges like a mass of bubbles in the ocean. (57)
Calamity, such as the miserable state of poverty and the like, inevitably arises from wealth itself; it swells and increases. || 57 ||
For this is but a web of worlds; what lamentation can there be in this?
That which is real is always real, and that which is unreal is always unreal.

The meaning is: since even that which is non-existent is always only non-existent and has never attained existence, what else is there in this phenomenal world—which consists merely of the diverse transformations of illusion—to lament over? "I" am not the self of egoism (ahaṃkāra). || 58 ||
But regarding the mere diversity of actions, what else is there to lament?
"I am not, nor did I exist, nor shall I be; he [the agent] does not exist now. (59)
This body arises from manifold defects; what else is there to lament?
O friend, if I am indeed distinct from the body as the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa), then [why grieve]? 60.

The "reflection of consciousness" (cidābhāsa) is the manifestation of consciousness arising from the defects of ignorance (avidyā), desire (kāma), action (karman), and latent impressions (vāsanā). The word "aṅga" is used as a gentle form of address. 60.
"The two states of existence and non-existence in which one suffers—such is the mind of the sage whose nature is perfect knowledge, possessed of certainty. (61)

"Those two which have the final result as their fruit" refers to the two [ends] that serve as the cause for the suffering in which [the action occurs]; "in which" is an adverbial phrase modifying the action. || 61 ||
It neither sets nor rises; it does not end, for it is peaceful. Established in the unsurpassed state, one who has attained transcendence does not suffer. (62)

Established in the unsurpassed state, the knower of Brahman, amidst all existing things, accepts and appropriates only that supreme nature which is Brahman— nature which is devoid of destruction and remains even after sublation— and not the hardness that exists only at the time of perception. Just as a female partridge, for the purpose of building a nest, discards the hard parts from the roots of the grasses and accepts only the soft tips of the grass.
The meaning is "in that same way. || 62 ||
The partridge seizes even a soft, stainless tip of grass;
for this reason, not even the slightest reliance should be placed upon this unreality.
For this purpose, namely, for the sake of avoiding the harsh portion of saṃsāra. || 63 ||
Just as an ox is bound by a rope, a living being is bound by its attachment;
therefore, you must firmly resolve this through your intellect. (64)
Having determined, by the reasoning already stated, that "this is the supreme Brahman," [he says: 64.
O sinless one, you should conduct yourself here with a mind free from attachment;
that which is to be done must indeed be done, while that which is not to be done is simply disregarded.
In that case, one might ask: "Should one abandon all reliance [on dharma] and act according to one's own whims? He says, "No;
it must indeed be done," meaning that only what is prescribed [by scripture] should be performed. || 65 ||
Having abandoned both the existent and the non-existent with great ease through his vast intellect,
for him this entire world appears as a mere reflection.
With ease, without exertion. || 66 ||
Just as the world attains inner coolness at the end of the day,
so he attains it by abandoning the appearance of the multitude of objects.
