At the end of the day, when the heat of the sun has subsided and when only the pure essence (sanmātra) pervading all things is perceived, he states the means [of realization]: "a manifestation" (pratibhāsa).

This means a specific form (viśeṣākāra). It refers to the multitude of objects such as jars and cloths, which consist of the collection (paṭala) or aggregate of the five elements (pañcabhūta). || 67 ||
O sinless one, behold this as a mere commonality of appearance;
O Rāma, it is a mere appearance, stained by the mental grasping of the mind. 68.
The ellipsis implies that it became defiled by the mind's grasping, that is, by the conceptualization of distinctions. || 68 ||
Then, having abandoned even that, O Supreme One, become free from appearances—eternally consisting of the space of consciousness, all-pervading, and devoid of everything. (69)

Having completely abandoned even that appearance which consists of mere existence, and having relinquished it through the realization that it is distinct from one's own Self, one becomes free from appearances (nirābhāsa), devoid of the triad [of knower, known, and knowing], all-pervading, and full. || 69 ||
When appearances are abandoned, existence becomes entirely stainless;
when it is realized, "I am not, nor are my enjoyments real. (70)

He states two types of reflection that serve as the means for establishing the state of non-appearance (nirābhāsatā), beginning with "I am not," etc. When [this] has been cultivated and contemplated on all sides, [the result follows]. (70)
This empty ostentation does not appear to lead to any harm, for when it is thus contemplated that "I alone am indeed all consciousness," [it becomes clear]. (71)
There are two types of contemplation: contemplating the sublation of everything within consciousness, or contemplating everything as having the nature of the conscious self. || 71 ||
This display is not in vain; it appears for the sake of [attaining] the goal.
Both of these systems of philosophy are true and grant ultimate perfection.
O Rāma, O sinless one, resort to whichever one of these two you know to be more delightful; or else, O blameless one, resort to both of these visions here.
There is no contradiction between these two even when taken as a cumulative option (*aicchika-samuccaya*), because in effect they result in the same state; with this intention, he says:
"O virtuous one, while dwelling [in this world], bring about the complete destruction of passion and hatred—whatever has arisen in the world, whether in the sky or in heaven. (74)
He states with the words beginning "Perform" that the two types of reflection are fruitful only when accompanied by the destruction of defects such as passion, and not otherwise;
he praises the very destruction of passion and so forth through its principal fruits with the words "Whatever... (verse 74).

All that is attained, O Rāma, through the complete destruction of passion and hatred; for whatever action is performed, O Rāma, with a mind struck by passion and the like, [that result alone is obtained]. (75)
That very same thing quickly turns into its opposite for the deluded; for when the fluctuations of the mind are obstructed by the waves of the fault of hatred, virtues do not take root. 76.
Like deer treading upon scorched ground, they set foot [upon worldly objects];
yet the two serpents of passion and hatred have not dissolved within the mind. (77)
The station is stability. || 77 ||
From that wish-fulfilling tree (kalpataru), what indeed is not obtained?
For those who are wise—[the reading "prājñā viniyatāḥ" is found in some versions]—who are self-disciplined, clever, and possessed of learning in the scriptures. || 78 ||
"What indeed is the fruit of suffering?"—this is the remainder [of the question]. || 78 ||
Those who are filled with passion and hatred are indeed jackals; fie upon them!
My wealth has been consumed by another, and my wealth has been given away by me to another. (79)

"Even though they were learned in the scriptures"—this is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. "Those people" refers to those well-known jackals in the forest; the word *vai* is used in the sense of *eva* (indeed).
He describes the process of passion and hatred along with its root: "My wealth," etc.
Wealth that must necessarily be seized from another was abandoned through negligence. || 79 ||
Thus, what are these worldly pursuits in the face of passion and hatred? Wealth, kinsmen, and friends come and go again and again. (80)

Thus, in this manner, regarding matters such as wealth gained and lost, the sequences of attachment and aversion—characterized by the pursuit of activities such as killing and imprisonment for the sake of seizing them—are trivial; this is the meaning.
To explain why they are trivial, he says: "Wealth," and so forth. (80)
Why would a wise man feel attachment or aversion toward these?
This manifestation of existence and non-existence is the sovereign illusion of the Supreme Lord.
In which [state] there is an expansion of existence through the state of objects being dear and the absence of objects being unloved. || 81 ||
The entire construction of saṃsāra is sufficient to cause one who is attached to it to fall;
in reality, O Rāghava, neither wealth, nor people, nor even the self is true.
Attached and lecherous. || 82 ||
It is clearly observed that this [world] is falsely determined as false;
everything is non-existent at the beginning and the end, and even in the middle, it is unstable for one possessed by mental anguish. (83)
Thus, by the reasoning to be stated, that which is determined to be false is perceived as nothing but false. He states that reasoning:
"Where indeed would a wise man fix his affection upon a celestial tree imagined by another?
One person imagines a woman in the sky, while another, far away, enjoys her. (84)
Regarding the worthlessness of *saṃsāra*—that is, its fitness for bondage—he provides an illustration with the words beginning "anyā" (verse 84).
Thus, my dear friend, this is the structure of saṃsāra; do not be deluded by this vast and agitated state of constant coming and going of beings. 85.
The wise know this world to be as unreal as a city of Gandharvas or a magical creation; it has arisen as something entirely non-existent, like a city seen in a dream or produced by mere volition.
The wise know [this]. || 86 ||
Everywhere this world exists as if it were fallen into deep sleep;
you behold the city-trees of this long dream of saṃsāra.

Because conceptualization is possible everywhere and because the consciousness that serves as the substratum exists everywhere, [the world] is situated in all places; yet it is fallen away [from its true nature], having entered into states such as dreams, like one in deep sleep. || 87 ||
"O Acyuta, you who are by nature prone to rolling about in the sleep of ignorance, you remain here deluded by the dream of saṃsāra. (88)

"Imperishable" (acyuta) connects with "eternally continuous" (ajasrānusyūta); "preceded by" (pūrvānvayi) connects with "you"; "possessing auspiciousness" (śubhavān) connects with "you" (tvam); and "abandon this sleep" (enāṃ nidrāṃ tyaja) connects with the subsequent part (uttarānvayi). || 88 ||
Therefore, abandon this widespread sleep, which consists of dense ignorance,
just as the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama) abandons the goddess Lakṣmī once he has obtained his treasure.
Awaken and behold your own Self, ever-risen, free from conceptual construction, the manifestation of consciousness—just as the morning lotus beholds the sun. (90)
The reflection of consciousness, the illumination of consciousness. || 90 ||
Awake, awake! Again and again you are being awakened by me, O mighty-armed one; behold the sun of the Self, which is free from all affliction.
O Rāma, you have indeed been awakened by this very cool water of knowledge that I have showered upon you, which is endowed with beautiful sound. 92.
By me, who am like a cloud; through wordplay (*śleṣa*), the term "suśabda" also refers to thundering. || 92 ||
Attain the supreme awakening; O Rāghava, let there be enlightenment this very day!
Behold the truth, having abandoned this false delusion of the world.
Being one who possesses such preeminent awakening even this very day, behold the truth of your own essential nature.
For you there is no birth, no suffering, no defects, and no delusions.
Abandoning all mental constructs, remain well-established in the Self. 94.
You have cast off the net of defects born from conceptual construction; you possess the gentle vision of the essence of deep sleep.
For the sake of supreme purity, remain, O Great Soul, established in the self of total tranquility within this vast expanse. 95.

He concludes: "Parigalita" means: you, whose vision is serene, free from distraction, and like a deep sleep of excellent essence—you are indeed this very Brahman, which is eternally immediate and all-pervading; therefore, for the sake of perfect purity, remain absorbed in that very Self which is the nature of total tranquility. This is the meaning. || 95 ||

Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "Instruction on the Yoga of Ultimate Reality," in the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa* of the *Mokṣopāya* section of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, according to the tradition of the Ṛṣis.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "Instruction on the Yoga of Ultimate Reality," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The twenty-ninth canto.
Śrī Vālmīki said:
While Rāghava was thus listening, composed and even-minded, [Vasiṣṭha spoke].
When one has come to rest freely in one's own self, having attained supreme bliss. || 1 ||
Through Rāma’s awakening comes rest; this is a detailed expansion of a meaning already stated.
Furthermore, Śiva’s own instruction on Mount Kailāsa is thus proclaimed. (1)

Śrī Vālmīki spoke of the unwavering state of Śrī Rāma— having been awakened by the wondrous instructions of the compassionate Śrī Vasiṣṭha— and of the other listeners, through the dawning of the direct realization of reality (tattva-sākṣātkāra) and their absorption in the samādhi of resting in their own true nature for half a muhūrta.
And while all those present there were abiding in tranquility,
[Vasiṣṭha spoke] this nectar-like speech for the sake of establishing Rāghava’s repose in the Self.

The phrase "tatrastheṣu" (among those situated therein) should be construed by changing the case ending as "tatrasthaiḥ" (by those situated therein), meaning "having come to rest within their own selves. The connection with the following clause is: "the nectar of the sage’s speech ceased. || 2 ||
The sage’s speech ceased, like rain from a cloud ceasing upon the crops;
then, when half a muhūrta had passed, Rāghava was awakened.

Just as the water from a cloud ceases once the crops have been satiated by rain, so too does [the flow of speech] cease when he has been awakened—that is, raised up from his meditative absorption—by Vasiṣṭha himself; this is understood from the context. || 3 ||
Vasiṣṭha, the best among speakers, spoke again on that very same matter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
"O Rāma, you are perfectly awakened; you have attained your own Self."
The meaning is that he speaks again in order to strengthen that very same point. || 4 ||
In this very way, rely upon the ultimate reality and remain; do not set foot here in this world.
For this wheel of saṃsāra has its hub in mere conceptual construction alone.
"Artha" means the ultimate reality, the true nature of the Self. "Do not make a station"—that is, do not establish a dwelling—here in this saṃsāra.
He states the means for that [liberation] as follows: "This... (verse 5).
O descendant of Raghu, when the mind is restrained, this wheel of worldly existence is held back from revolving; yet when it is agitated within the navel of the mind, it continues to turn.
When it has been agitated—that is, when it has been brought to distraction by passion, hatred, and so forth. || 6 ||
Even though it was restrained with great effort, it flowed forth with force;
therefore, one should exert supreme human endeavor, relying upon strength and wisdom through proper means.
Human effort is characterized by the firmness of practice and dispassion. || 7 ||
One should extinguish the mind itself at the hub of the wheel of saṃsāra, by means of that which is endowed with wisdom and gentleness, and fortified by the scriptures. (8)
That which cannot be attained through human effort is not to be found anywhere;
therefore, abandon reliance on fate alone, which is devised by the understanding of the ignorant.
Relying on one's own effort, one should first restrain the mind from the delusion consisting of ignorance that has been active since the time of Viriñca.
O sinless one, this which appears as existent is indeed non-existent;
O sinless one, its forms are merely the expansion of the delusion of ignorance.
The forms are the shapes of the visible world. || 11 ||
These bodies wander here, having arisen from all dharmas;
yet, at times, there may still be volition for the sake of the body. (12)

Since all phenomena (*dharma*) are conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*), therefore all phenomena are volitional intentions (*saṃkalpa*). Regarding the expression "from the absolute absence of phenomena" (*dharmādanickevalāt*), the absence of the suffix *-aniC* in this context is a Vedic archaism (*chāndasa*). For this very reason, the desired goal is not accomplished merely by the destruction of this body, because the volitional intention that produces a succession of future bodies still exists. If so, what is the means for abandoning volitional intention?
He says "for the sake of the body," and so forth. || 12 ||
O Rāma, a wise person should not concern themselves with pleasure and pain;
for one whose face is withered by sorrow becomes moist with distress, whereas one who is serene is free from such moisture.
He censures as inferior even to a man depicted in a painting the man who is intent on the thoughts of bodily pleasure and pain:
"A man of flesh is considered far more insignificant than even a man in a painting, for he withers under mental and physical ailments, is subject to decay, and perishes of his own accord. (14)
The stability of the body of a person in a painting is not as firm as that of the living one;
for indeed, the body depicted in a painting perishes when destroyed, and not otherwise. (15)
It is indeed well known (*kila prasiddham*). He states that its causeless perishability is a defect even greater than its variegated body, saying: "destroyed" (*vināśita*). || 15 ||
The body, whose nature is flesh and which is destined for inevitable destruction, perishes by itself;
yet, when nurtured, it assumes a remarkably stable beauty—how wondrous is man! (16)
The meaning is: by itself, without any cause. || 16 ||
But even if this physical body is highly nourished, it surely perishes and does not flourish;
therefore, the excellent body is the "painted" body (citra-deha), and not this body of mere conceptualization (saṃkalpa-deha). || 17 ||
The body is created by conceptualization. || 17 ||
Indeed, those qualities which exist in a painted body do not exist in a body made of mere imagination;
for this [imaginary body] is surely more insignificant than even a painted body, being as it is insentient.
O sinless one, what reliance can you have on this body composed of flesh?
O high-minded one, this body is merely a product of long-standing mental constructs; why then do you place such reliance upon it?
The remainder [of the sentence] is that "it is not logical that there be no basis. || 19 ||
For this [body] is even more insignificant than one born of a dream or a mental construction;
being produced from a slight volition, it is not seized by long-lasting pleasures and pains.
Now, with the verse beginning with "svapna" (dream), he describes how this [body] is even more contemptible than bodies that exist merely in one's own mental fantasies.
Born of long-standing volitions, this body is afflicted by long-lasting suffering;
for the body consists of volition, and it neither exists nor does it not exist for us.
This [self] does not exist by itself; or rather, it does not exist as "ours" (asmin), because the Self is unattached and non-dual—this is the intended meaning. || 21 ||
Why is this effort in vain? For this fool is merely a vessel for suffering;
just as when a man made of a painting is wounded or destroyed, there is no injury to the [real] person. (22)

Therefore, he says "as... [in the verse], meaning that just as there is no injury to a painting or the like, there is likewise no injury to this [Self] to be lamented; for that Self, there is no injury.
Likewise, when the person of one's own conceptualization is wounded or diminished, there is no real injury;
just as when a kingdom of the mind is wounded or diminished, there is no real injury.
Just as when the second moon is wounded or diminished, there is no injury to that [true] moon;
and just as when something begun in a dream is wounded or diminished, there is no injury to that [waking reality]. || 24 ||

Just as when the water of a river is damaged or diminished by the heat of the sun, there is no lasting harm, for it was fashioned merely by conceptualization and is by its very nature subject to destruction. (25)
Likewise, when this bodily machine is wounded or worn out, there is no injury to that [Self],
for it consists of a long dream fashioned by the volitions of the mind.
Whether the body is adorned or defiled, there is no injury whatsoever to the consciousness;
the consciousness does not reach its end, nor does the Self move, O Rāghava.
To the question "Why is it not injured there?", he says: "Not consciousness," etc. (27).
Brahman does not undergo transformation, nor is it harmed by the destruction of the body;
for it is like one standing above a revolving wheel, remaining unmoved by the successive revolutions of the spokes below.

The "subsidiary wheel" (upacakra) is a great wheel situated around or near the previously mentioned self-established wheel, serving as its counterpart; the meaning is that he perceives the circle of the directions as revolving in a manner contrary to his own wheel. || 28 ||
Just as one who is utterly deluded sees the circle of the quarters spinning, due to a false cognition that has suddenly arisen and is leaping up. (29)
Remaining there, one perceives this wheel of the body in that very same way:
as being spun, as having the nature of spinning, as falling, and as having been made to fall. (30)
By the individual soul (jīva) situated there, residing within the wheel of false knowledge (mithyājñānacakra). || 30 ||
The wheel of the body is seen both destroyed and being destroyed;
relying on pure fortitude, one should abandon this dense delusion. (31)
The wheel of the body is the wheel of the succession of bodies. || 31 ||
The body, whether existent or non-existent, is created by false knowledge through mental construction;
since it is produced by that which is unreal, it can never be real.

Although it exists from the perspective of conventional cognition, it does not exist from the perspective of ultimate reality; for this reason, it is produced by that which is unreal, such as ignorance and so forth. || 32 ||
The body, having arisen from the unreal like the perception of a snake in a rope,
performs the activities of the world as if it were real, even though it is truly unreal.
O Rāma, that which is performed by the insentient is not said to be "done" [by the self];
for even while acting, the body is never at any time the agent.
The phrase "it is not said to be caused by that" is the ellipsis; the meaning is that no attribution of fault is observed in an insentient object, which is devoid of consciousness. || 34 ||
For the body is indeed inert and devoid of effort; it has no desire of its own.
There is no agent whatsoever; therefore, the Self is merely its witness. (35)
For agency would arise from desire, yet that is not possible in the inert body or in the changeless Self; thus he says:
"Just as a lamp in a windless place remains fixed within itself, so should one abide amidst the existence of the world like a witness. (36)
He states the result of the ascertainment of the non-agent self with the words "Just as" (yathā). || 36 ||
Just as the sun performs its daily tasks while remaining healthy and clear— [the variants "svastha" and "svaccha" both being possible readings]—
so too, O Rāma, perform this royal duty.
To the question, "In that case, how is the establishment of the kingdom's stability achieved? he says: "Just as... (verse 37).
In this empty house of the body, which has arisen from what is non-existent and attained a semblance of being, it is like a yakṣa imagined falsely by a child.

But since the egoism characterized by the conceit of "I" cannot be avoided when the reality of the body is perceived, one will inevitably remain its servant; thus he says, beginning with the words "In this," etc. (verse 38).
Having arrived from somewhere, this essenceless and wicked vampire of egoism, named "mind," which is shunned by all virtuous people, has entered [me]. (39)
The word "should have entered" is the ellipsis to be supplied. || 39 ||
Do not enter into the service of this one who is evil-minded with egoism;
O Rāma, by serving him, hell is obtained as the fruit.
Within the house of the body, by the play of its own volitions,
the hideous Vetāla of the intoxicated mind leaps about with ease.
Regarding the true ego, he states that there is no difference from the object itself by means of the words beginning with "svasaṃkalpa" (one's own volition), etc. || 41 ||
Having entered the empty house of the body, that which was created by the yakṣa of the mind causes even the great ones, though established in meditative absorption, to tremble with fear. (42)
Having expelled the vetāla of the mind from the temple of his own body,
he never again fears anything in the empty city of saṃsāra.
In this house of the body, which is overcome by the element of consciousness, why do those who delight in it still remain today as if possessed of a self? How strange! (44)

Attached and clinging to the house of the body, they remain even now—despite the destruction of infinite millions of bodies—joined to the body through the identification of "selfhood. The meaning is that it is truly strange that they do not make an effort to disjoin themselves from it, even though the suffering of being so joined is experienced at all times. || 44 ||
O Rāghava, those who have died while their body-dwelling was seized by the demon of the mind possess a consciousness like that of a demon, not unlike that of one who is no longer possessed.
"Of those who have died"—this is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. || 45 ||
O virtuous one, you dwell with attachment in this body, which is like a house inhabited by the great yakṣa of egoism; yet, indeed, it is not at all stable.
A person who dwells with attachment toward this body, which is constantly consumed by the fire of the threefold suffering, is indeed a *piśāca* (demon);
this is to be supplied by changing the case-ending (*vibhaktivipariṇāmena*). To the question "Why is attachment not appropriate there?", he replies: "But not... (verse 46).
Having abandoned the state of following after egoism with an expansive intellect, and having attained the non-recollection of egoism, let one's own Self alone be firmly grasped. 47.

Having first abandoned the state of being a follower and a servant to the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), and then, through the practice of the stages of yoga (yogabhūmikā), having attained its non-recollection—that is, its absolute forgetfulness—[he remains]. || 47 ||
For those who, seized by the demon of egoism, seek only hell,
and who are blinded by the intoxication of delusion, there are neither friends nor kinsmen.

"Not friends" means that because those possessed of egoism find it difficult to be disciplined and because arrogance is inevitable for them, no one feels affection toward them; this is the sense. || 48 ||
Whatever action is performed with an intellect impaired by egoism, its fruit will be like that of a poisonous creeper—consisting of death. (49)
Know that the fool by whom the great festival of his own ego is maintained, being devoid of discernment and fortitude, has indeed quickly perished. (50)
The fruit consists of strife, enmity with people, and so forth; for this very reason, it is essentially death. || 49 || 50 ||
Those wretched ones who have been brought under the sway of the demon of egoism,
O Raghava, have become fuel for the fires of hell.
He states that for such a person there is only suffering even in the next world: "Egoism... (verse 51).
The tree of one's own body, in whose hollow the serpent of egoism flickers, is quickly felled by the undisciplined. (52)
In the hollow of whose heart-tree of his own body—that tree of his own body [resides]—there is the singular number used for the plural due to the unity of the genus (*jātyaikya*).
The word *adhīraiḥ* (by the undisciplined) is the correct division [of the compound]. || 52 ||
Whether this demon of egoism remains in this body or departs from it,
O best among the great, do not regard it with your mind.
Do not look! 53.
For once you have become an avadhūta, disregarded and mentally set aside,
the demon of egoism will do nothing to you here.
To the question of what would happen by merely not looking [at it], he says: "The *avadhūta*. (54)
O Rāma, while this demon of the mind manifests within the abode of the body, what indeed has happened to the Self, which possesses infinite play? (55)

Misfortune arises for the self precisely from following after that [mind]. But if it is disregarded, it is of no consequence even while it remains; thus he says: "In the abode of the body" (verse 55).
The extensive calamities that befall men who are overcome by the yakṣas of the mind cannot be fully enumerated even in hundreds of years. (56)
The term "citta" is a designation for the very same ego-sense under discussion, used here to explain its capacity to produce harm even through other mental modifications. || 56 ||
"Alas, alas! I am dead! I am burned!"—these indeed are the modes of suffering;
they are the powers of the demon of egoism, O sinless one, and not of anything else. (57)
Just as space, though all-pervading, has no connection with anything here,
so too the Self, though all-pervading, is not joined with the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra).
He dispels the misconception of the Naiyāyikas and others—that the self is experienced as "I" alone—by stating "all-pervading" (sarvaga).
"Connection" (saṃbandha) means that which is connected; the sense is that it is intimately joined. || 58 ||
O Rāma, whatever this moving machine of a body performs or acquires is the activity of egoism, joined to the rope of the vital breath.
The wind-rope is the vital breath whose essence is the thread. || 59 ||
Just as space, though itself a non-agent, is said to be the cause for the growth of a tree,
so too the Self, abiding within itself, is the cause for the activities of the mind.

If the ego alone is the cause of all activity and not the Self, then by whom is the mind impelled and sent forth? By whom is the first vital breath joined? The first vital breath goes upward when joined; it draws the prāṇa upward and casts the apāna downward. And the All-Gods worship the Self seated in the midst.

Regarding the contradiction with such scriptural passages [as those cited], he says: "In the case of the tree's production. The meaning is that the Self, established in its own glory, is figuratively designated as the cause by the scriptures. || 60 ||
By the mere proximity of the Self, the mind, assuming a form, manifests clearly, just as a pure reflection on a wall appears by the mere presence of a lamp. 61.
He states that the reason for the metaphorical application [of the term "self"] to the mind and so forth is precisely their bestowing existence and manifestation; thus he says: "The Self.
This refers to the imagined gross body which has acquired its existence by having assumed a form. (61)
O Rāma, what connection can there ever be between one's own body and mind when they are separated, like heaven and earth, or like light and darkness? (62)
Of the manifest and the unmanifest, and of consciousness and insentience. || 62 ||
O descendant of Raghu, due to ignorance, the mind— which is enveloped by these restless flickerings of its own powers— is perceived as the Self.

Anticipating the objection that "if there is no connection, the existence and manifestation of the mind and so forth would be unestablished, whereas if there is a connection, the soul's state of non-attachment (asaṅgatva) would be unestablished," he says: "capala... [and so on]. That which causes the impelling of restless movements are the "capalaspandanerāḥ"; by such powers of the soul's vital breath (prāṇa), [the mind] is enveloped and brought under control.

The mind is enveloped and brought under control by the powers of the vital breath (prāṇa) through the characteristic of superimposition of identity; it is perceived through the ignorance of delusion characterized by such superimposition of identity, and not according to the actual state of reality—this is the meaning.
In the reading "nābhiḥ," it serves as an adjective for the mind. || 63 ||
The Self is indeed of the nature of light, eternal, all-pervading, and omnipresent;
know the mind to be deceitful egoism, while the Great One resides within the heart.
In order to establish non-attachment, he elaborates upon its very opposite—[the nature of] the self—with the word "ātma" (self). "Śaṭham" means deceitful or fraudulent.
For you are indeed the Self, the omniscient one; the mind is certainly not so. Cast the delusion of the mind far away; why are you attached to this? 65.
O Rāma, even a Piśāca dwelling in the empty house of the body,
this evil-minded one, contemplates while touching upon supreme silence.

The construction of the sentence is as follows: that supreme demon of the mind, even without touching the self, conceives itself to be touched by silence—that is, by being in a state of utter stillness. 66.
Having cast off the demon of the mind— which brings about existence, is utterly inauspicious, and robs one of the very essence of fortitude— be who you truly are, and remain steadfast.
When a person is firmly seized by the yakṣa of the mind, neither treatises, nor kinsmen, nor even teachers are able to protect that human being. (68)
The teacher, the meaning of the scriptures, and kinsmen are able to rescue one whose mind-demon has been completely stilled,
just as they can lift a deer from a small puddle.
"Completely pacified" means, that is to say, pure mind. "The deer" refers to the fawn, which resembles a deer. || 69 ||
In this empty city of the world, everything has been utterly corrupted by the intoxicated yakṣa of the mind, which leaps about within the house of the body.
This entire forest of the world, born from fragments of the body and haunted by the vetāla of the mind, is empty; for whom does it not cause fear? (71)
Born in a section characterized by the body, that is, in a delimited portion. || 71 ||
In this city of the world, however, the body-house— whose demon of the mind has been stilled— is inhabited by only a few virtuous ones.
The general rule is that [all directions] are equal; however, since it is observed that in some cases there is otherwise, he says: "The world," etc. "Yat" means "because. 72–73.

"O descendant of Raghu, whatever direction is heard of here, that very same direction is filled with the corpses of the cremation grounds—namely, bodies possessed by the Vetālas of intoxicated delusion."
For this very reason, he censures those whose bodies are ignorant, saying they are like cremation grounds: "In this world... (verse 73).
In this vast wilderness of the world, one who is deluded like a bewildered child should, by his own effort, cultivate a portion of fortitude and thereby uplift himself. (74)
Having propitiated the portion of fortitude and firmly relying upon it. || 74 ||
O Rāma, do not seek stability through the juices of grass in this forest of worldly decay, where herds of living beings roam like young deer.
One should maintain steadfastness and the sense of having fulfilled one's purpose regarding the tastes of sensory objects, which are as worthless as blades of grass.
In this forest upon the surface of the earth, young deer roam;
having devoured the elephant of ignorance, you should adopt the conduct of a lion.
Others, like fawns, are deluded; if they continue to graze upon the grasses of sense-objects, let them indeed do so. (76)
Other deluded human-beasts roam in their own jungles within Jambudvīpa; O Rāma, O sinless one, roam in that same manner.
One should not plunge into a puddle that is like a friend— though it appears pleasant but is actually a source of mire— even as a buffalo might do, for its coldness lasts but a very short time.

[Objection: "Is it not observed that constant dwelling together with kinsmen, due to their shared character, is happiness? What fault is there in that? To this he replies: "Exceedingly slight," etc. The qualifying adjectives are to be applied to both [cases]. || 78 ||
One should cast out enjoyments and non-enjoyments; one should follow the path of the Noble One.
Having investigated the great purpose, one should take refuge in oneself alone. (79)
For the sake of this impure, worthless, unfortunate, and ill-formed body, one should not plunge into the most dreadful river of anxiety. (80)

"One must not plunge into the mire of attachment"—this is the implied sense. For the fierce, wrathful, and most terrible ogress characterized by anxiety devours those who are submerged therein; such is the meaning. || 80 ||
The body is fashioned by one [agent], it is inhabited by another yakṣa, and yet another is the experiencer of suffering; wonderful is this cycle of folly! (81)

By another action; by the yakṣa that is egoism (ahaṃkāra); of another mind; another is the individual soul (jīva). The succession of the revolving wheel of folly is manifold; the meaning is that it is of a wondrous nature. || 81 ||
Just as a stone possesses a single, solid form within itself, so too does the Self,
because there exists no other possibility than that which is the universal commonality of pure existence alone.

With the intention that there is no room for other forms—such as suffering, the experience of that suffering, or the body of the experiencer—within the Self because it is a single, undivided mass of existence, he says "just as" and so forth in three verses. The sense is that the term "other" (itara), meaning a form other than the nature of existence (sadrūpa), is well-known through words such as "non-existent" (asat) and "unreal" (alīka) precisely because it is the opposite of existence. || 82 ||
Just as solidity belongs to a stone, so do the mind and other faculties belong to the self;
for they are non-different from mere existence, and since this [self] does not exist as a distinct entity, it cannot have a specific configuration. || 83 ||

Just as the density or hardness of a stone does not exist separately from the stone itself, so too the "mental" (mānasa)—meaning the aggregate of individual and collective minds—and, by the word "etcetera," the gross phenomenal world consisting of their respective effects, [do not exist apart]. Why?
Because it is non-different from that whose nature is pure existence (sattāmātra); the meaning is that there is no separate establishment of this mental realm and so forth.
Just as the nature of a stone is not distinct from the stone itself, and the nature of a jar is not distinct from the jar,
so too the mind and other faculties are non-different from the Self by virtue of their mere existence.

And this principle should be applied to each instance, such as the jar, the subtle elements (tanmātra), and mental modifications; thus he says "just as" [yathā] to show that only the reality of non-duality (sadadvaita) is established. || 84 ||
In this regard, hear now this other vision which destroys great delusion, which was previously told to me in a cave on Kailāsa. (85)
In this regard, concerning this matter, hear this view which is about to be described, characterized by the mental worship of Śiva. || 85 ||

For the sake of pacifying the suffering of saṃsāra, there exists one who has reached the further shore of heaven, resplendent with a mass of moonbeams, whose crest is adorned by the crescent moon, and who is the Lord himself. (86)

Therein, he introduces the narrative at the outset by means of a description of Kailāsa, beginning with the words "There exists" (*asti*) and so forth: "Resplendent like a mass, a collection, of moonbeams. (86)
There stands Kailāsa, the king of mountains, the abode of Gaurī’s lover;
there dwells the blessed Lord Hara, who bears the digit of the moon.
In former times, while worshipping that Great God on that very mountain,
I once dwelt upon the bank of the Gaṅgā, having constructed a hermitage there.
For the sake of austerity, he had long established himself in the conduct of an ascetic;
surrounded by hosts of perfected beings (siddhas), he had mastered the essential meaning of the scriptures.

"Tāpasācāra" refers to the conduct practiced by ascetics, such as the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa* penances; being one whose stability is fixed (*niyata-sthiti*) in that [conduct], he is of such a nature. || 89 ||
Carrying a woven pouch for flowers and a collection of many books—such was he, distinguished by these qualities, in a grove of the Kailāsa forest. (90)
O Rāma, as I was engaged in my ascetic penance, time passed by;
then once, on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, [it happened].

On the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa, at the beginning of the night, during the twilight (pradoṣa), when [the obstacles] have been brought to an end through worship, recitation, meditation, and so forth; || 91 ||
When the first part of the night in the dark fortnight of Śrāvaṇa had passed and was drawing to a close,
the quarters of the sky appeared perfectly tranquil, as if they were standing in the silence of a wooden log.

When the movement of living beings and other such activity has ceased, and the quarters of space have become perfectly still, the vow of wooden silence (*kāṣṭha-mauna*) consists in not communicating one's purpose even by gestures of the hands, as if remaining fixed like a piece of wood.
In the darkness that could be cut by a sword, amidst thickets and dense forests,
during this interval when the first half-watch had passed.
In the dense forests. || 93 ||
Having extended my concentration and remaining with my gaze fixed on the external,
I suddenly beheld a radiance arisen in the forest.
"Tanutām" means a slight inclination toward the outside; that is to say, [the state of being slightly directed outward]. || 94 ||
Having then beheld that [light], which resembled a hundred white clouds and was like a multitude of moon-disks,
illuminating the quarters and groves, I was filled with wonder.
From pride or from wonder. || 95 ||

Beheld with an outward gaze that was inwardly radiant—[the reading "with the gaze of the intellect" (buddhidṛṣṭyā) is also found]—"I saw as far as that mountain peak where the bearer of the crescent moon had arrived. (96)

The meaning is that he looked outward and reflected inwardly. And having reflected, the meaning is that as soon as I saw that ridge—the level ground—standing before me, he had already arrived there. || 96 ||
With his hand placed in the hand of Gaurī, his forepart cleared away by Nandin,
he, being well-restrained, instructed the disciples standing there and took the water of honor (arghya).
Well-restrained and attentive. || 97 ||
With a joyful mind, I approached him who was purified by his vision; there, having offered a handful of flowers from afar, the three-eyed Lord [Śiva] appeared before me.
Sumanāḥ means with a contented mind. Puraḥ means the space in front. || 98 ||
Having offered the guest-water (arghya), I bowed down and paid homage to the Lord;
then, with that [gaze] of hers which was named Candraprabhā—straight and cooling—99.

Having prostrated with the eight limbs of perfect devotion, he was saluted and praised; he then describes the falling of her glance of grace upon himself as the great arising of his own fortune, beginning with the word "tataḥ" (then).
By her—that [glance] which causes the wonder of the manifestation of an extraordinary, unsurpassed bliss experienced by him. || 99 ||
For a long time, I have been made the abode of his glance, which removes all suffering—to him, the witness of the three worlds, who sits upon the mountain of flowers. 100.
Having approached, I offered water for honor, flowers, and water for the feet;
many handfuls of mandāra flowers were scattered before me. (101)
Having approached, that is, having gone near while facing [him]. || 101 ||
Śiva was worshipped with various kinds of prostrations and hymns;
thereafter, the blessed Gaurī was likewise honored with such same worship.
By such worship, that is, by a service resembling the worship of Śiva. || 102 ||
Thus honored, together with her companions and the circle of attendants,
she spoke at the conclusion of the worship in a voice as cooling as the rays of the full moon.
By his command, she sat down there upon the mountain peak with her husband.
As I sat there, he who bears the crescent of the moon spoke to me:
"O Brahmin, you who are endowed with tranquility and have attained rest in the supreme state. (104)

In that context, when it was time to inquire about his welfare, the Blessed One, desiring first of all to show favor, asked—"O Brahmin"—referring specifically to the repose of the mind in the Supreme Self, which is the ultimate pinnacle of all skill. 104.
I trust that your virtuous companions remain steadfast in the higher realms; I trust that your auspicious austerity proceeds without obstacle.
The fluctuations of the mind are [merely] consciousness with respect to the supreme reality, the Supreme Self. || 105 ||
"Has that which was to be attained been attained? Are all fears now stilled?"—thus spoke the Lord of Gods, the sole creator of all the worlds.
"O descendant of Raghu, O Maheśvara, I spoke with words full of conciliation: 'For those here who possess the auspiciousness of the remembrance of the Three-Eyed One (Śiva)..."
Conciliation and humility are expressed by that [meter] (śālinī). || 107 ||
For those whose minds are reeling with the bliss of recollecting you, nothing at all is difficult to attain, nor are there any fears whatsoever. (108)
Those countries, those provinces, those directions, and those mountains do not exist within the treasury of the world which do not bow down again and again. 109.

In the treasury of the world, there are no living beings who do not bow down to you; the meaning is that everyone indeed bows down. The meaning is that those lands are most excellent. The excellence is understood through a figure of speech similar to the Vedic expression: "Cattle other than cows and horses are indeed not cattle; cows and horses are the [true] cattle. || 109 ||
Where people abide with minds solely intent on recollecting you, that is the fruit of past merit and the nourishment of present merit. (110)

It extends—that is, it causes to expand by way of infinite millions of qualities—the fruit of past accumulated merit, which stands in the place of a tree; and it extends—that is, it causes to increase as if by sprinkling with nectar—the nourishment of present merit, beginning from this current body.
O Lord, the remembrance of you sows the seed for the future;
you are the unique jar of the nectar of knowledge and the moon of the moonlight of fortitude. (111)
He sows the seed for the sake of the increase of that which is yet to come and is about to be performed. || 111 ||
O Lord, mindfulness of you is the gateway to the city of liberation; by me, who possesses the noble wish-fulfilling gem of mindfulness of you, [all desires are fulfilled]. (112)
"O Lord of Beings, you have placed your foot upon the head of all calamities.
Having spoken thus to the blessed Maheśvara, who was exceedingly gracious, [he bowed]. (113)
Of all those that are present and those yet to come. || 113 ||
Having bowed down, I said: "O Rāma, listen to this!
O Blessed One, by your grace, all directions are filled for me. (114)
"Filled with desired objects"—this is the ellipsis. || 114 ||
But I ask you, O Lord of Gods, for a resolution regarding that doubt;
speak with a gracious intellect, free from agitation and free from affliction. (115)

The syntactical connection with the subsequent clause is as follows: "Tell me that procedure for the worship of the deity in which anxieties—the causes of mental agitation—have been abandoned. || 115 ||
O Lord, what is the procedure for the worship of the gods that brings about the destruction of all sins and the increase of all that is auspicious? (116)
The Lord said: Listen, O best among the knowers of Brahman, to the unsurpassed worship of the Deity;
I shall describe that by which, if performed even once, one is indeed liberated. (117)

By the statement, "All directions are full for me," the absence of any longing for the enjoyment of sense objects on the part of Vasiṣṭha is indicated; furthermore, this is confirmed by the two qualifying phrases, "which destroys all sins" and "which increases all auspiciousness."

Having determined that this question concerns precisely the means for attaining liberation— which is characterized by the cessation of all misfortune and consists of unsurpassed bliss— the omniscient and supremely compassionate Lord imparted the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) alone as the means for achieving the supreme human goal to Vasiṣṭha, who had surrendered with his whole being.
Desiring to teach that which constitutes the supreme secret of the worship of all the gods, he makes this promise: "Listen," [verse 117].
"Do you know, O mighty-armed twice-born one, who might be the true God?
Neither the lotus-eyed one is the God, nor is the three-eyed one the God. (118)

In this context, in order to instruct the disciple on the extraordinary nature of the deity—which accords with the worship of the deity to be described hereafter—the Teacher asks "Kaccit" (Is it so?), thereby generating the disciple's desire to know that [nature]. He addresses him as "O Mahābāho" (O mighty-armed one), meaning one who has made his arms fruitful through constant worship of the deity; this is intended to highlight the mere heroism associated with external worship that depends upon the arms.
This is an address. Vasiṣṭha, thinking, "Are not the gods such as Puṇḍarīkākṣa and Trilocana already well-known? Why does the Blessed One consider me ignorant even regarding this much?
first removes his dullness of faith concerning those [gods] who are limited, by saying "Not a god," and so forth. 118.
Neither is he the god born from the lotus, nor the god who is the lord of the thirty-three;
neither is he the god Wind, nor the Sun, nor Fire, nor the Maker of Night (the Moon). || 119 ||

Brahmā was born from the lotus; Indra is the lord of the thirty-three gods. The eclipse of the moon is an indicative mark for the bodies of the thirty-three million deities, whose physical forms are dependent upon its digits. 119.
There is no Brahmin, no king, no "I," and no "you," O best of the twice-born;
for there is no god in the form of the body, nor is there a god who assumes the form of the mind.
Furthermore, the negation "neither I nor you" refers to Rudra and Vasiṣṭha; they are called *rudras* because they cause others to weep (*rodayanti*).

This is because in such scriptural passages as "I am Vasiṣṭha, therefore you are Vasiṣṭha," the state of being the primary collective vital breath (*mukhya-samaṣṭi-prāṇatā*) is well-established. Moreover, since the scripture states, "Which one is the single deity? The vital breath (*prāṇa*)," it is evident that through the nature of the vital breath (*prāṇabhāvena*), the vital breath itself is the self of all the deities.

This is for the purpose of precluding the status of being a deity [for all things]. For in such scriptural passages as "The gods did not attain this first" (*nainad devā āpnuvan pūrvam arśat*), the word "deity" (*deva*) is seen to apply to internal organs such as the eyes; and because of the indicative marks of mantras such as "Svāhā to the skin," "Svāhā to the body hairs," and so forth, there is the possibility that even internal entities like the body and its parts might possess the status of a deity.
"He wards it off as having the form of the body. || 120 ||
The god is not the form of Kamalā, nor is the god the intellect (mati);
that which is uncreated, without beginning or end, and divine in nature is called "God" (deva).

Since the context concerns the internal (ādhyātmika), "lotus" (*kamala*) here refers to the beauty of the body and so forth. The mention of "intellect" (*mati*) is intended as an illustration for all internal states. By the same logic, it should be understood that the absence of divinity (*adevatva*) has been stated regarding all external (*ādhibhautika*) entities as well. Who, then, is a deity? To this he says: "the uncreated" (*akṛtrima*).

From the root *ḍukṛñ* (to do/make), by the rule *ḍvitaḥ ktriḥ*, the suffix *ktri* is applied; then, by the rule *krermamrityam*, the suffix *map* is added. Thus, *kṛtrimaṃ* means that which is produced by action (*kriyāsādhya*).
That which is distinct from this is the Supreme Divine (*paramārthadevatā*), meaning the Divine is the Light of Consciousness (*citprakāśa*) characterized by unsurpassed bliss.

Indeed, everything from Puṇḍarīkākṣa (Viṣṇu) down to a blade of grass has its existence and manifestation dependent upon the Light of Consciousness; therefore, they are superimposed (*adhyasta*) upon It. Their...

If one were to separate them from the light of consciousness (*citprakāśa*), even their own essential nature would be difficult to establish, let alone their divinity; therefore, even among them, it is the very existence and light (*sattāprakāśa*) that shines everywhere as the one unobscured God.

It is precisely due to the excellence of the manifestation of this [light] that Puṇḍarīkākṣa and others are called "Gods" (*deva*), because their dullness has been overcome, just as glowing embers are called "fire" (*vahni*).
Thus, the sense is that there is no contradiction even with the doctrines of the Śruti, Smṛti, and so forth. || 121 ||
How can that which is uncreated, without beginning or end—the divine Consciousness-Śiva—be known within an object that is measured and delimited by forms and the like? || 122 ||
When [an object] is delimited by space through its form and so forth, and when it is measured and delimited by time, how can there be that "diving" (devanam)?

This is the point: since the word *deva* is derived from the root *div*, which is well-known in ten meanings—namely, play (*krīḍā*), desire for victory (*vijigīṣā*), worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), brilliance (*dyuti*), praise (*stuti*), joy (*moda*), intoxication (*mada*), sleep (*svapna*), beauty (*kānti*), and motion (*gati*)—by adding the suffix *ac* according to the rule *pacādyac*, the application of the term is restricted to a specific sense.

Due to the absence of any [external] means of knowledge, the two primary objects of [the Lord's] activity are His own splendor and joy, which arise from His unimpeded illusory sovereignty and His play at will, His desire for victory, and His worldly dealings;

these two are possible only in Brahman, which is self-luminous and consists of eternal, unsurpassed bliss, and not in limited, insentient things. Therefore, one should [worship] in reality the very God who is the innate, conscious Śiva.
The meaning is that they know. || 122 ||
That very [reality] is expressed by the word "God"; one should worship that, because it alone exists as everything, assuming the nature of both being and non-being. (123)

Since the entire world, consisting of living beings and their cycle of existence (saṃsāra), possesses its nature of being solely through the existence of That [Brahman] and not by itself, the meaning is that only That exists and nothing else. || 123 ||
For those who do not know the true principle of Śiva, worship through forms and other such means is performed;
for one incapable of traveling the path of a *yojana*, a path of a *krośa* is devised.
If so, is the ritual of worshiping in the form of Puṇḍarīkākṣa and others entirely useless? No; he says: "performed" means carried out when [the true nature] is unknown. || 124 ||
The fruit obtained from Rudra and others is limited by such measures as "this much" and so forth;
however, the fruit of the Self is innate bliss, without beginning or end.
The meaning is: from [the Lord] who is pleased by worship culminating in the direct realization of the self's true nature. || 125 ||
He who abandons the unartificial fruit and pursues an artificial one is like one who leaves the grove of Mandāra trees and goes to a forest of Kārañja trees.
Since success is achieved through artificial enjoyments of desire and self-worship, one should perform only artificial worship for that purpose;
regarding this, he says: "Artificial... (verse 126).

Awakening, equanimity, and tranquility are the flowers and the foremost [offerings] therein; those who know the object of worship recognize the worshipful as the stainless, pure consciousness that is Śiva. (127)
If that is so, what is the requisite collection for uncontrived worship? He states it: "Awakening" (bodha). It is equanimity, seeing everywhere through the analogy of oneself. (127)
Know that when the divine Self is worshipped with the flowers of tranquility, awakening, and so forth, that indeed is the worship of the Divine; the worship of forms is not true worship.
But those people who, having abandoned the worship of the Divine which consists of self-realization, are attached to artificial images, undergo long-lasting suffering. 129.
O Brahmin, those virtuous ones who have known what is to be known regard the worship of gods as being like the play of children, except for the meditation on the Self. (130)

The meaning is that those who have known what is to be known, having at times arisen from self-meditation, if they are seen performing the worship of deities with form, they do so like children’s play; it is not out of a desire for artificial enjoyments.
The self alone is the divine Lord Śiva, the supreme cause;
he is to be worshipped at all times with the incessant offering of the light of knowledge. 131.

Know that you yourself are this space of consciousness, the self, the imperishable living soul, and your own true nature; there is no other worthy of worship, for worship is the worship of the Self. 132.

Know yourself to be the living soul, which is uncreated by nature, imperishable, the space of consciousness, the space of pure awareness, and Brahman; no other non-self is to be worshipped. The meaning is that worship characterized by knowledge—that is, the worship of the Self alone—is the primary worship, and nothing else. As they say: "The body is declared to be the temple, and the living soul is the deity, Sadāśiva."
"One should discard the floral remains of ignorance and worship with the sense of 'I am He' (so'ham-bhāva). Thus [ends verse 132].
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Lord, just as this world consists of the nature of the space of consciousness alone,
so too let that state of the conscious self as the individual soul (jīva) and so forth be explained.

"That alone exists, from which everything assumes the form of existence and non-existence"—thus it has been stated that the world, the individual soul, and its transmigratory existence abide as the very essence of Brahman. Desiring to know the proof for this, Vasiṣṭha asks: "The conscious... (verse 133).
Īśvara said:

Indeed, there exists here only the space of consciousness (cidvyoma), devoid of near and far; it is that which remains at the end of the kalpa, wherein no object of thought (cetya) can possibly exist anywhere. || 134 ||

In this regard, it is well-established that the existence of consciousness (*citsattā*) does not depend upon the objects of cognition (*cetya*), because it does not perish even during the dissolution of all objects of cognition.

Therefore, since an object of cognition whose manifestation depends [on consciousness] lacks any other mode of being—just as it lacks another manifestation—it is illogical for it to have a separate existence.
Thus, he states the logical proof: "Even at the time of creation, the object of cognition is impossible [without consciousness]."

The logical proof indicated here by the definition of inference is to be understood as follows: "Because it is devoid of any delimitation such as 'beyond' or 'this side,' like the time of universal dissolution.
Furthermore, that which shines forth by itself—of that self-shining [reality], its own vibration is what is called this world; enough said! (135)

How, then, does the appearance of the world-form arise therein? To this he says: "Whatever... Because that [Reality] is indeed undivided, and because there is no possibility of the veil of *māyā* within it—[the reading being "due to the non-existence of the veil of *māyā*"]—there is no differentiation;
nevertheless, by way of illusory latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and so forth, there is a vibration (*spanditam*) well known as if it were a movement (*spandanam*). By means of that, this...

The world shines sufficiently. For instance, whatever—such as the sun, the moon, a lamp, the senses, the mind, and so forth—shines by itself and becomes a mass of light, because that self-shining [object] does not perceive its own reflection, it vibrates by itself from that reflection outward in the form of radiance; this very [vibration] is what is known as "spandana" (vibration).
The meaning is that it is extremely well known—indeed, too well known—that the world consists of forms such as blue, yellow, and so forth, along with their corresponding objects. || 135 ||
Thus, the world, which is of the nature of consciousness, appears like a city in a dream;
likewise, the world is purely of the nature of the space of consciousness, transparent and without foundation.

Thus, in the manner described, this world of diverse forms, being essentially of the nature of consciousness (*cidātman*), appears through delusion as if it were consciousness itself, like a city in a dream. However, when examined according to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) in the way I have explained, the world has no foundation; it is formless, transparent, and consists of nothing but the void of consciousness (*cidvyoma*). This is the meaning. || 136 ||
Because it is absolutely impossible for anything else to exist, the object of cognition—the visible world—is merely the space of consciousness (cidvyoma).
Due to its nature as consciousness, that which shines forth at the beginning of creation is known as the "world" (jagat).
If so, does it perceive itself as having transformed into some specific object of cognition? No; he says "absolutely" (atyanta).

Because it is unchanging and non-dual, an object of cognition is absolutely impossible. Therefore, that which appears or manifests otherwise—due to its nature being veiled consciousness—that alone is the visible world (dṛśya-jagat); this is the meaning. || 137 ||
Therefore, as for this world that appears in the form of a city in a dream, what kind of otherness could there possibly be therein, since its essence is nothing but the space of consciousness? (138)
The mountains are pure consciousness alone; the sky of the world is pure consciousness alone.
The Self and the individual soul are pure consciousness alone; the succession of all beings is pure consciousness alone.
For this very reason, he says that one should perceive the nature of pure consciousness by subverting superimposed forms:
"Other than the mere space of consciousness (cidvyoma), tell me, what could possibly exist at the beginning of creation—whether in all-knowingness, or in a separate heaven, or even in a city? (140)

In heaven, in the higher worlds, in one’s own city, or even by the word "api" (also) in the netherworlds—tell me, O experts in investigation, can anything exist that is distinct from consciousness (*cit*)? For if the non-conscious (*acit*) were to possess existence and manifestation (*sphūrti*) by itself, its status as non-conscious would be contradicted; and in the absence of such [existence and manifestation], it would be unreal (*alīka*). Furthermore, if the unreal were to possess existence and manifestation through consciousness, its status as non-conscious would again be contradicted; and in the absence of such [consciousness], it could not exist.

The meaning is that because the unreal is unreal, it is not seen to be revived even by consciousness; furthermore, since consciousness is unattached, its connection with the non-conscious is impossible, and no other means of proof is established. || 140 ||
"Space, supreme space, the space of Brahman, and the consciousness of the world"—these are synonymous names for that [reality], just as the terms 'pāda' and 'vṛkṣa' refer to the same tree. (141)

If it is argued that, just as there is a distinction of actions based on different words such as "he sacrifices," "he gives," and "he offers oblations," there might likewise be a distinction [of Brahman] based on different names such as "consciousness" (cit), "space" (ākāśa), and "the world" (jagat), the author replies to this with the word "space" (ākāśa).
This is intended to show that [the term "space"] refers to three possible meanings: the elemental space (bhūtākāśa), the unevolved space (avyākṛtākāśa), and so forth.

Since all three instances of the word *ākāśa* can possibly denote pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) by following the meaning of the verbal root *kāśṛ* (to shine), and because of the grammatical rule that "those roots which have the sense of motion also have the sense of knowledge," and furthermore,

because even though the suffix *kvip* is applied after the root *gam* (to go)— resulting in the forms *pṛṣat*, *mahat*, *bṛhat*, and *jagat* through reduplication and other operations while [the sense of] present time is maintained— [the term *ākāśa* likewise denotes consciousness].
The meaning is that because the state of having knowledge as its object never departs, it is logically established that "consciousness" (cit) is a synonym [for that state]. || 141 ||
In this way, both [the dreamer and the dream] are experienced through dreams, mental constructs, and illusions;
at that time, indeed, it is the space of consciousness alone that shines as the world.

The word "tadā" (then) implies that "yadā" (when) should be supplied [from the preceding verse]. Thus, when duality is experienced as being equal to dreams and so forth by one who perceives reality—that is the meaning of "tadā. || 142 ||
Just as this space of consciousness appears in the form of the world within a dream,
so too does that very same thing appear to us in what is called the waking state.
Just as in a dream-city nothing whatsoever can exist apart from the space of consciousness, so it is in the waking state for the Great Consciousness.
The second word "even" (api) has the sense of "also.

Since no other object of cognition whatsoever exists, therefore this entire world remains as the non-object of cognition, even though it consists of both the cognizing mind and the objects of cognition. 144–145.
The entire mind, as well as the world that is its object of thought, remains as the non-objective Pure Being alone. || 145 ||
Know that the three worlds, which have arisen of their own accord as a manifestation within the supreme space, are like a dream within the sky of consciousness; they do not exist as a duality.

The "calculation" (kalana) of the supreme space that is Brahman— meaning the very first volition shown in the Śruti, "May I be many, may I procreate"— having become the three worlds, arose of its own accord as if possessing duality, that is to say, like a real entity as conceived by the proponents of duality. Just as in a dream, objects such as pots and cloths appear from the mere self of the space of consciousness...
Even at the very beginning of creation, this creation is likewise nothing but the void of consciousness.

He demonstrates that the principle stated regarding the world in general also applies to specific objects such as jars and cloths, beginning with the words "Just as" (yathā). "Sarga" refers to the creation of jars, cloths, and so forth. || 147 ||
Just as nothing exists other than pure consciousness alone within a city of dreams, so it is within these three worlds.
Whatever perceptions there may be, and whatever entities or non-entities exist throughout the three periods of time—
all that, together with space, time, and the mind, is nothing but the void of consciousness (cidvyoma).
This very deity has been described as that which is supreme from the perspective of ultimate reality;
he who is you, he who is I, and he who is the entire world in its totality. (150)
That God, who is to be worshipped through knowledge, has been described as the answer to the first question. || 150 ||
For the body of every class of entity, of the world, of you, and of me, is indeed the space of consciousness—the Supreme Self alone and nothing else. (151)
The body is the ultimate essential nature. || 151 ||
Just as in a city of dreams within a mental construction, there exists no body whatsoever other than the space of consciousness,
so too in this creation, O Sage, from the very first and sole creation onwards, there has been no other form.

Having restated what was said, he concludes with the words "saṃkalpana" (in imagination): "In this creation, which has proceeded from the first creation of Hiraṇyagarbha, there is no other form [of the world] than that which consists of imagination, like a dream-city or a body. (152)

Thus ends the twenty-ninth sarga, titled "The Description of the World as Consisting of the Supreme Self," in the first part of the Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki.

Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the World as Consisting of the Supreme Self," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The Thirtieth Chapter. 30.
The Lord said:
"In this way, this entire universe is nothing but the Supreme Self alone."
Brahman alone is the supreme ether; this is remembered as the highest deity.

The state of the *citta* as the self of all is its abiding through the nature of being the enjoyer of all; how it attains the condition of the individual soul (*jīva*), and how it exists therein, is also described here.

"O Lord, that which you asked—'How is all this, whose nature is consciousness and space alone?'—its answer has been described," he said: "Thus [it is]. O mighty-armed one, do you know who the deity might be? O twice-born one," [he continued], referring to the fundamental secret regarding the procedure for the worship of the deity that was asked of you by me.
He says that this too is precisely this very thing: "This is the God. || 1 ||
This very worship is the highest good; from it, everything is obtained.
It alone is the source of creation, and all this is established within it. || 2 ||

He says "This very [state]" to show that the worship of limited deities yields limited fruit, whereas this worship has as its fruit the attainment of the bliss of the Infinite (bhūman), which is the ground for the fulfillment of all desires, and is therefore the most excellent;
it is the ground of creation (sargabhūḥ), the substratum for the superimposition of the creation of the entire universe. || 2 ||
Therefore, that bliss which is uncreated, without beginning or end, non-dual, indivisible, and not to be accomplished by external means, is attained. (3)

In this regard, he dispels the doubt that it might require the expenditure of much wealth and effort by stating "not external" (abahiḥ). The analysis of the compound is: "that which has no external means of accomplishment and is not impossible to accomplish. || 3 ||
O best of sages, you are awakened; therefore, this is being told to you:
a great abundance of flowers and incense is not suitable for the worship of the supreme deity.
One who is awakened and discerning is, in other words, the primary qualified candidate; he is an "atideva," one who has surpassed the gods, in his worship of Him. || 4 ||
For those whose intellects are undeveloped and whose minds are as fragile as children's, worship of the deity is said to consist of artificial images. (5)

Regarding the worship of deities in the form of icons and so forth, he states who the qualified practitioners (*adhikārin*) are: "the unlearned" (*avyutpanna*), etc. For this very reason, he says "artificial" (*kṛtrima*), meaning an artificial image and so on, as well as the materials required for it; *arcā* means an image, and [the compound] refers to that which abounds in such images. || 5 ||
For in the absence of tranquility, awakening, and so forth, they indeed worship with flowers and other offerings;
thus, they worship a mere imagined form within an imagined nature, all of which is entirely false.
And he says that this [practice] is like eating *krodrava* grain when *śāli* rice is available: "It is tranquility," etc. (6).
Having performed worship through the sequences created by their own imagination,
the children, being diligent, attain satisfaction through offerings of flowers, incense, and even fragments of leaves.
Having performed worship, they attain and experience satisfaction. || 7 ||
Having performed the worship of the gods in vain with objects created by their own imagination,
they lead themselves to nothing but false results from whatever source.

Since they attain fruits such as heaven—which are inherently illusory—by means of instruments like celestial chariots and apsarases that are themselves like dreams, the argument that [their efforts] are in vain is established. || 8 ||
O Brahman, the worship with flowers and incense is intended for those of childish intellect;
I shall now describe that form of worship which is suitable for those such as you.
O best among the wise, he is some deity such as ourselves;
that deity is indeed the Supreme Self, the support of the three worlds, and nothing else. (10)

The meaning is this: he whose beginning or cause is we—such a one, "originating from us"—is included within the phenomenal world (prapañca) imagined by us; that deity, possessing a visible form consisting of the eyes and other organs, is some indefinable being composed solely of Māyā. Who, then, is the ultimate (pāramārthika) deity? To that, he says: "The Deity" (deva). || 10 ||
Śiva transcends all states and surpasses all conceptual constructions;
though encompassed by all conceptualizations, he is neither the "all" nor the "possessor of all."

His mental fluctuations have transcended all volitions even of the gods such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra; he has gone beyond them, for the Śruti declares: "From whom words turn back, along with the mind, not having attained Him. But he who is enveloped and surrounded by all volitions for the enjoyment of sense-objects, whose nature consists of the stations of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others—he is not "all" in terms of his means (*sādhana*), nor is he "all" in terms of his fruit (*phala*). Who [is he]? Kaṃ.

The meaning is that such [a state] possesses the happiness of enjoyment; for there, one obtains the materials of enjoyment and a portion of the resulting happiness precisely according to the gradations of one's own respective karma and spiritual practice (upāsanā). || 11 ||
O Sage, he who is unconditioned by space, time, and the like; who is the illuminator of all undertakings; whose form is pure consciousness alone; and who is stainless—he is called God.

But the Self-deity (Ātmadeva), both in the state of worship and in the state of the fruit [of that worship], possesses as its sole essential nature eternal, unsurpassed, ultimate reality, and perfect bliss; therefore, He alone is worthy of being called "the Deity.
Thus he says: "Dikkāla... (Verse 12).
Consciousness transcends all parts (kalās), abides within all beings, is the goddess who bestows existence upon all, and is the one who takes away the existence of all. 13.
Brahman is that which is said to be between existence and non-existence; it is called the Supreme Self (Paramātman), and it is designated as "Sat" and "Om. || 14 ||

It is "middle" because it is of the nature of pure consciousness as the witness, or because it is the substratum, existing between the existent and non-existent, being and non-being, the present time and other times, the formed and the formless, cause and effect, or the empirical and the apparent.

That which is superior to the lights of the sun, moon, fire, and other luminaries— namely, the Self itself— is that whose supreme splendor (*abhikhyā*) is capable of illuminating everything; such being the case, the Śruti declares through the word *Oṃ* that, by dissolving the entire phenomenal world consisting of the three quarters beginning with Virāj, it is considered the auspicious non-dual Fourth (*turīya*).
The meaning is that it has been declared: "That is the Self; that is to be known. || 14 ||
By its nature as the Great Being, it has attained equality everywhere;
it is proclaimed as "Great Consciousness" (mahācit) and is heard of as the "Ultimate Reality" (paramārtha). || 15 ||
Everything indeed exists everywhere, just as sap exists within all creepers;
it exists both in the form of the universal essence of being (sattāsāmānya) and as the nature of the Great Being (mahāsattā).

In all empirical usage, it exists by way of the form of the universal "existence" (sattāsāmānya); but when all [particular] negations are made, it exists as the nature of the "Great Existence" (mahāsattā).
O sinless one, that reality of mind which belongs to Arundhatī, that reality of mind which belongs to you,
that reality of mind which belongs to Pārvatī, and that reality of mind which resides in the Gaṇas— [all these are one].
He states with the words beginning "That which... that its divinity is primary because it is the self of all [entities], including the deities and so forth.
Those of supreme intellect who know reality understand that this principle of consciousness which is mine, and that principle of consciousness which exists in the three worlds, is the God. (18)
He states with the words "That which... and so forth that its divinity is primary because it is the very self (ātman) of all [entities] such as the deities.
O Brahmin, tell me truly: what essence can there be in any other deity conceived as possessing feet, hands, and so forth, if it is apart from pure consciousness? (19)
He states that because it is the essence of all deities, that very [consciousness] is the deity itself—beginning with the word "pāda" (foot). The ellipsis is: "What is its essence?

Pure consciousness alone is the essence of transmigratory existence; having attained the state of being the essence of everything, that deity is "I am all. Therefore, everything is obtained from that. (20)
The meaning is that he is entirely full, being the very God himself, and not limited. || 20 ||
O Brahmin, he does not stand at a distance, nor is he difficult for anyone to attain;
he is ever established within the body, as well as everywhere in space.
He acts and he eats; he sustains and he moves forward. He breathes, he is the knower, and he knows each and every limb.
He states that this very [Self] is the doer of all and the enjoyer of all by means of the passage beginning with "He acts," and so forth. || 22 ||
O Lord of Sages, he dwells in this city which manifests various activities through his power and is bound to his own essential nature.
"He dwells in the city"; the meaning is that this is according to the Vedic scripture: "He has entered here even unto the tips of the nails. || 23 ||
And by His grace,
He is the Lord of the Cave (Guheśvara) within this cave of the heart, which has a deep inner treasury, even though the abode of the body is transient.

In that [body] which is a dwelling, a great mansion; in that which is dense and difficult to discern, having outer sheaths consisting of food and so forth; in that which is a cave, because the heart-intellect (hṛd-buddhi) itself conceals [the Self] within it—the Lord of the cave of the sheath of bliss (ānandamaya-kośa). 24.

For that stainless Self, which transcends the existence of the activity of the six organs including the mind, the designation "Consciousness" (cit) is conceptually fashioned for the sake of conventional discourse. (25)
For the purpose of conventional usage in instruction. || 25 ||
This very one, consisting of consciousness, subtle, all-pervading, and stainless,
produces this radiant manifestation, and yet does not produce it.

It acts as if it performs superimposition (*adhyāropa*), yet it does not perform its negation (*apavāda*); the meaning is that because [the Self] is eternally manifest, there is no act of "making" it so. || 26 ||
That consciousness, which is utterly pure, colors this worldly activity for the sake of the world,
just as a wise man colors a sweet creeper with juice.
It delights and beautifies; "madhu" refers to spring. || 27 ||
Those beautiful wonders which, as they truly exist, cause astonishment within consciousness—by that very fact, some indeed are designated as "space" (nabhas). (28)

The "marvels" (*camatkārāḥ*) consist in bestowing the manifestation of existence; they are situated within consciousness as variegated by *māyā*, and according to the influence of prior desires, actions, and latent impressions (*vāsanā*), they bring about a fixed wonder, manifesting [their effects].
He designates those very wonders of consciousness through the conceptualization of names, beginning with the words "some," and so forth, according to the distinctions of creation.
The statement regarding the multiplicity of space. || 28 ||
Some are designated as "living beings" (jīva), some are designated as "mind" (citta);
some are designated as "creative power" (kalā), and some are designated as "space" (deśa). || 29 ||
Some denote actions, some denote substances;
some denote states, transformations, and so forth, as well as generic categories and propriety. (30)

The modifications of being (bhāvavikāra) mentioned by Yāska—namely, "is born," "exists," "grows," "transforms," "declines," and "perishes"—as well as the various qualities implied by the word "and so forth" (ādi), possess diverse designations according to their genus, variety, and propriety. || 30 ||
Some are designated as "Light," some as "Mountain" or "Darkness";
some are designated as "Sun," "Moon," and so forth, while others are designated as "Yakṣas. (31)
He elaborates upon those very points—i.e., he elucidates them. || 31 ||
Just as a sprout is extended by the spring season through its own nature of desirelessness,
even so is this splendor of the world extended by the conscious Self.
