One might ask: does the Consciousness (Cid) create the world out of a desire for its own enjoyment? No; he says "without desire" (niriccha). Thus it has been stated by the venerable Gauḍapādācārya: "Some say creation is for the sake of enjoyment, others say it is for the sake of sport;

this is the very nature of the Divine, who has all desires fulfilled—what longing could He have? Nor is it the case that [the Upanishad] says, "He desired: 'May I become many,'" [implying a lack of fulfillment].

There would be a contradiction with such scriptural passages as "May I be born," etc.; for in another scriptural passage—"The Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, and so forth, are the breath of this great Being"—it is stated that [the Vedas] are like a breath, independent of will, effort, and the like. This is in order to accord with other scriptural passages of identical purport, such as "It thought: May I be many, may I procreate."
Because the statement "He desired" has the sole purpose of precluding the suspicion that [the world] was created by an insentient principle such as Pradhāna;
and thus there is the sūtra of the venerable Bādarāyaṇa: "And because of desire, there is no dependence on inference. (32)
Indeed, even when all these [bodies] are present together, the network of bodies—which resides within the ocean of the three worlds—is always but a single entity. (33)

When the configurations—the actual states—of the oceans characterized by the three worlds are investigated, consciousness alone is the body, the real essence; the "web of water-born" (lotuses), which stands in place of the mass of water, is of that very nature and nothing else. This is the meaning. || 33 ||
The Sovereign Consciousness tastes the essence of the honey of volition, which is gathered by the bee of the mind wandering within the lotus of the body. (34)

With the intention that it is precisely her capacity to manifest the triad of subject, object, and means of knowledge—constructed by the mental volitions of the mind—that is conceived as "subject-hood" due to the non-discrimination of the subject, he says: "The body... [and so on]. She is the Sovereign (Īśvarī), capable of manifesting everything superposed upon herself. 34.
The world, including the gods, asuras, and gandharvas, along with its mountains and oceans,
remains upon consciousness and flows like water in a whirlpool.

With the intention that agency (*kartṛtva*) likewise belongs to her only insofar as it is the cause for the manifestation of the revolving cycle of causal factors superimposed upon her, he says: "Together with gods and demons" (*sasurāsura*).
It flows, that is, it revolves. || 35 ||
The wheel of saṃsāra, consisting of the conduct of a bound mind and characterized by a clever circle of delusion, revolves within the wheel of consciousness as a vessel of wandering.
It is called "bond" (*bandha*) because it binds; such is that mental disposition consisting of agency and enjoyership.

By means of that, the individual souls (*vyaṣṭijīva*), being clever, skillful, and restless, revolve within the wheel of transmigration—the wheel of the collective soul (*jīvasamaṣṭi-saṃsāracakra*)—which revolves upon the wheel of consciousness variegated by *māyā*. || 36 ||
In the form of a four-armed being, he struck down the host of asuras,
just as the sun destroys the heat with a mass of rain-clouds equipped with its weapons.
Having described the characteristics of consciousness alone, he specifically elaborates upon its status as the agent and enjoyer of all things, beginning with the words "Consciousness...
[verse 37]. Time—the rainy season—[destroys] the heat, like a mass of clouds disguised by a weapon-bearing form, namely the rainbow and the thunderbolt.
O Brahmin, by virtue of having the eye of Citriṇī and bearing the emblems of the bull and the moon, he became like a bee upon the lotus-face of Gaurī-Kamalinī. 38.

Having attained the state of being adorned by the lotus of Viṣṇu, with her mind dependent on the meditation of consciousness, the Triple Veda maintains its position within the lake of the lotus of Brahmā.
Having attained, as it were, the state of a bee within the lotus of Viṣṇu’s navel, the three Vedas reached the form of a great lake—the very essence of that lotus-pond. || 39 ||

O Brahman, here in this world, diverse bodies are fashioned from the conscious principle in great abundance, just as leaves are produced from a tree or as bracelets and other ornaments are wrought from gold. (40)
It is like the creation of actions for armlets and other ornaments. || 40 ||
With her feet worshipped by the entire host of gods,
she bears the status of the crest-jewel of the three worlds through her effortless sovereignty.
"Being the crest-jewel" means being worthy of veneration. || 41 ||
Having attained the state of pure luminosity within the vast expanse of the three worlds,
it falls, rises, and moves within its own self alone, like the water of the ocean.
The state of being brilliantly radiant, having the nature of the splendor of the sun and other luminaries. || 42 ||
The moonlight, spreading its radiance in the four directions,
causes all the night-lotuses of living beings to blossom.
He also states directly that she is the cause for the manifestation of joy: "the moonlight of consciousness" (ciccandrikā). || 43 ||
The Great Lakṣmī, who is the mirror of consciousness, receives the triple world reflected within her by means of her grace, just as a pregnant woman carries her own embryo within her womb. 44.
Great is the Fortune (Lakṣmī), characterized by pure luster and radiance; she is the splendor of Viṣṇu, or rather, his Māyā.
The glorious waters, like the ocean containing its own treasures, bring forth the great mandalas of the fourteen elements.

It brings about the existence—that is, it accomplishes the being—of all beings residing within the fourteen worlds. Just as the glory of water, the power of essence, being in the form of a mass of water (an ambudhi), accomplishes the nature of the ocean—the very existence of the ocean's own form—in that same way. || 45 ||

With manifold lights as its flowers and dense volitions as its sprouts, it has ascended the field-plot of the sky and abounds in the fruit of the flood of existence. (In this verse, the reading "phaladāyinī" [fruit-bestowing] would be more consistent with the commentary. || 46 ||
Now, he describes that very consciousness as being like a creeper, beginning with the words "The sky" (vyoma) and so forth:

"The sky here is the space of *māyā*; in the field-plot characterized by that [space], it has taken root and sprouted in the form of Hiraṇyagarbha. It yields fruit characterized by the flood of existence—the reality of all things. (46)
Colored by the essence of the latent impressions of the mass of dust from the net of living beings, enveloped in the skin of sensation, and agitated by the buds of mental activity— (47)
Perceptions are conceptual cognitions; mental impulses are the fluctuations of the mind. || 47 ||
She whose radiant form is the filaments of the three worlds beyond counting in the past;
she who smiles with the exuberant play of incessant vibration.
Roughened by all seasons and by the joints of its knots, it is like a dull mountain or a shrub;
entwined with the knots of its physical form, it is turned upside down from root to tip.

Inert things such as mountains and the like are its shrubs and root-sprouts; it is entwined by knots which are the fourfold bodies (vigrahas); and it is encircled from root to tip by the spreading creepers of worldly activity (pravṛtti). || 49 ||
This mind is blossomed, delicate, and composed of both existence and non-existence;
it is a manifold flower of the visible world, variegated and unable to endure scrutiny. (50)
The connection with the subsequent clause is as follows: "the visible flower, characterized by such qualifiers as 'delicate' and so forth, is produced by this [illusion].
The justification for the phrase "having a form that is both existent and non-existent" is that it is incapable of being referred to [as a real object]. || 50 ||
For here, by means of this [imagination], everything everywhere arises like a cool shade;
the object is conceived, expanded, sung of, and even brought into being. (51)
One considers the clearly visible flower to be as pure as the luster of the moon and so forth;
it is taken as an object of conceit and expanded, that is, elaborated upon. || 51 ||
By means of this Great Consciousness, the sun and other luminaries shine eternally;
and bodies take pleasure in one another through the delusions of existence, consciousness, and insentience.
Of that [pair], the conscious is the existent reality (sat) and the sentient; the insentient is the object of consciousness.

Due to the delusions of being enjoyer and enjoyed, which are prompted by the failure to distinguish between consciousness and its objects, the bodies of the couple—though in reality of an inauspicious nature—mutually please one another and become objects of affection. || 52 ||
Whirled within the vortex of consciousness, the very reality of that [consciousness] dances as the perfected one;
it is the web of the world, a streak of dust, appearing in embodied form. 53.

The whirlpool, or rather the whirlwind’s vortex, is established by consciousness alone as it revolves therein; by its very existence, the dust-streak of the world-web—embodied in the visible, possessing forms fit for perception—appears as if distinct from consciousness and dances forth.
Consciousness fully manifests this entire undertaking of the world, just as a lamp with a flame capable of illuminating the three worlds reveals the objects resting upon its colors.

Consciousness is the crest of the lamp that illuminates the three worlds; just as a well-known lamp reveals a material object possessing form by depending on its constituent elements, so too does consciousness reveal all things. 54.
Just as the moon obtains union with the stainless lunar orb,
so too does the beauty of all objects existing in the world attain visibility everywhere.

He elaborates upon the fact that the manifestation of the world is dependent solely on the light of consciousness (cit) with the verse beginning "In the lunar orb of consciousness" (ciccandrabimbe), etc. || 55 ||
By the sprinkling of the elixir of consciousness, the series of clusters of objects attains both form and fruit, like a beautiful creeper nourished by the rains.
And by its very shadow, the insentience of this entire body arises perfectly, just as darkness arises here within a house. (57)
Now, if consciousness, like an elixir (*rasāyana*), pervades and vibrates throughout the entire multitude of objects, then there would be no insentience therein;
for indeed, when something is moist with juice on all sides, there is no possibility of dryness. To this, he replies: "By the shadow of consciousness alone.
Just as, through the process of quintuplication (*pañcīkaraṇa*), even a house is pervaded by light on all sides, so that although darkness cannot possibly exist within it, [it still appears].
Just as the luminosity of fire, due to its being overwhelmed by the portions of other elements,

gives rise to internal darkness through the shadow cast by the solar light manifested externally when it pervades it, so too, the luminosity of the consciousness that underlies objects such as a jar— though overwhelmed by the superimposed [ignorance]— shines forth when it is pervaded by the consciousness manifested externally through visual functions and the like.
The meaning is that through its shadow, inner dullness arises. || 57 ||
If these wonders of consciousness did not exist within the body, then, having abandoned the body of the three worlds, they would indeed not touch any form at all. (58)

And so, just as the variety of forms such as houses and palaces is established solely by virtue of the light of the sun and other sources, likewise the variety of forms such as cows, horses, cloth, and pots is established solely by virtue of the wonder of the consciousness of the subject manifested within the body, and not otherwise; thus he says: "the wonders of consciousness."

The embodied beings of the three worlds—those material objects contained within the three worlds—would, having abandoned their shadow-like dullness, not even touch upon form or configuration, because of the absence of any other practitioner; this is the meaning. || 58 ||
Within this luminous expanse of consciousness, which sustains the infant of volition, the restless bride of action flashes forth in the house of the body. (59)
Action consists of engaging in what is prescribed and avoiding what is forbidden; that indeed is the conduct of a noble wife. || 59 ||
Without the light of consciousness, how and when could aesthetic flavor (rasa)—even if vibrating at the tip of the tongue—become manifest, or where could it ever be perceived? (60)
In order to demonstrate the stated point, he establishes it through examples well-known by way of negative concomitance (vyatireka):
"By means of the three interrogative pronouns (kiṃvṛtta), there is the exclusion of [specification regarding] manner, time, and place. (60)

Listen, my dear: even if it possesses beautiful branches in the form of one's own limbs and is fully adorned with the creepers of tresses, how can the tree of the body shine without immersion in consciousness? 61.
He whose branches are his own limbs; in whom the creeper is the mass of hair (kuntalāli); [the term] "cinmajjaja" means without the pervasion of consciousness (cidvyāptim vinā). 61.
Consciousness alone expands, rolls about, and devours, acting as both the moving and the unmoving; consciousness alone exists, nothing else exists—this entire world has arisen as mere consciousness.

And thus, because all states—such as birth, growth, and so forth—are dependent upon consciousness (cit), it is established that from the perspective of ultimate reality (paramārtha), consciousness alone is real, just as waves and other phenomena, which depend on water for all their states, are nothing but water; he concludes this with the verse: "It grows... (62).
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāma,
when the Three-eyed Lord had spoken thus with a voice as clear as the moon,
he was questioned by me once again with a voice as clear as the moon.

O Lord, if consciousness were one and all-pervading, and this world were of the same nature as it, then why does this [consciousness] not perceive the vast expanse of the earth, as if it were blind? (64)

If there exists only one consciousness (cit), then this body—composed of that [consciousness] during sleep, fainting, and death, and by the force of the word "and" (ca), during other perceived states—is like a wall made of clay, consisting of the expansion of the earth and being a transformation of abundant material elements; it is blind, lacking eyes and other senses, and does not perceive. This is the meaning of how [this could be]. || 64 ||
"How can this conceptualization—that 'this [person], having previously possessed consciousness, now exists devoid of consciousness'—be based on direct experience in the world? (65)

He states that very point more clearly again with the words "this": "This," referring to the body and so forth, "was previously conscious"—that is, possessed of consciousness—during the prior state of life due to the absence of death. [Note: The form *cit* is used here because the suffix *t* in *tasau matvarthe* functions as a *bha*-stem, thus preventing the change of *j* to *g*]. Having been so, it now remains "devoid of consciousness" in the visible state of death and so on; how can such a conceptualization be possible?
The meaning of the question is: since consciousness has an indestructible nature and is unchanging, how could insentience possibly be associated with it? || 65 ||
Īśvara said:
Listen to all this, O Brahman, which you have asked; I shall speak it to you.
This question you have posed is great, O best among the knowers of Brahman. (66)
Without having heard the answer to his previous question—namely, that the state of being a living soul (*jīva*) and so forth belongs to consciousness alone—Vasiṣṭha posed another question.
Desiring to provide the answer to both questions simultaneously, the Lord said:
"Indeed, Consciousness exists here within the body, whose nature consists of all beings."
But that which is of the nature of being about to arise, non-conceptual, and supreme, is remembered as the one [consciousness]. || 67 ||

By way of an introduction to what is about to be explained, he first demonstrates the twofold nature of consciousness (*cit*) within the body as the original image (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*):

The one denoted by the term "consisting of consciousness" (*vijñānamaya*) has the nature of being an agent and an enjoyer; this is the meaning. But the supreme, immutable consciousness (*kūṭastha-cit*), which is free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpā*) and awakened through volition (*saṃkalpa-buddhā*), remains as if it were something else, though it is itself situated within.
Just as a woman who had requested one boon ended up with the opposite, so too did she fall into immoral conduct.
With the intention that its state of being manifold is likewise caused solely by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), just like its nature of movement, he says: "By [the act of] volition," etc.

By the volition shown in the Śruti—"Well, let me enter these three deities with this living self (*jīva-ātman*) and manifest names and forms"—the Intellect (*buddhi*) perceives itself as the living self; the suffix *kta* is used here in the sense of an initial action.

In the phrase "kartari ca," the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). Just as a woman of excellent character (*suśīlā*) who, in a dream, has conceived of a tree as her husband, becomes one who has fallen into immorality (*dauḥśīlya*) and thus becomes like a second [woman], so it is in this case. 68.
For that very same person, through anger and so forth, becomes as if another in an instant;
in this way, consciousness, marked by conceptual construction, attains a state of otherness from its own true nature. (69)
A man becomes like another person who is cruel, just as a *rākṣasa* is; it is just like that. || 69 ||
O Brahman, that which is imagined through conceptual construction, having fallen away from the nature of consciousness,
gradually brings about insentience and reaches the state of being an object of mental fabrication.

In this manner, consciousness (cit), having fallen away from its own true nature, gradually contemplates insentience and identity with the insentient; thus, by its own imagination alone, it becomes the locus—that is, the object—of conceptualization, which is the discursive intellect (savikalpabuddhi). This is the meaning. || 70 ||
Consciousness itself attains the state of being an object of cognition, taking on the nature of a subtle atom of space;
subsequently, consisting of the seed of sound, it moves toward the subtle element of air.

The atoms, together with space, constitute the subtle elements; they reach the state of being the objects of consciousness characterized by *māyā*, which is the nature of their existence and the seed-nature of the objects of enjoyment— sound, touch, form, taste, and smell— and subsequently, the air-tanmātra becomes the state of the collective vital breath (*samaṣṭiprāṇa*) directed toward that [state].
It comes to be. || 71 ||

Having sequentially become the individual soul (jīva), enveloped by the subtle elements (tanmātra) up to the divisions of space and time, it then quickly becomes the intellect (buddhi), and thereafter the ego (ahaṃkāra) and the mind (manas).

Thus, he shows that for her who has become so, there arises the state of the gross body— consisting of the aggregate and individual gross elements produced through quintuplication (pañcīkaraṇa)— the state of the individual soul (jīva) within that subtle body (liṅgadeha), and the state of the intellect (buddhi) and so forth therein, [in the verse beginning with] "deśa".
When combined and intermingled with the subtle elements (tanmātras), she sequentially becomes the division of space— extending from the five islands up to the fourteen worlds—
and the division of time— extending from a moment (nimeṣa) up to the limit of two parārdhas. Then, therein...

The meaning is that by sustaining the vital breaths it becomes the *jīva*, and from that [state], it becomes the intellect (*buddhi*), the ego (*ahaṃkāra*), the mind (*manas*), and, by implication, the consciousness (*citta*). || 72 ||
When the state of "mind" (manastva) arises, it clings to saṃsāra;
just as a twice-born man [attains] the status of a caṇḍāla by thinking, "I am a caṇḍāla. || 73 ||
Unawakened by her own volition, she is the one who awakens the entire world from its dullness; having assumed a variegated form, she incessantly proceeds through volitions and the like.

Indeed, the Brahman-consciousness itself, through lack of awakening—that is, through ignorance—having assumed a variegated form and being conceptualized in the shape of the body and the individual soul (jīva), becomes non-omniscient due to the dullness induced by that [ignorance]; thus, through repeated volitions for experience, it goes on incessantly, transmigrating. || 74 ||
Consisting of infinite volitions and thickened by the volition of inertia,
consciousness attains the state of dull matter through that inertia, just as water attains the state of stone.
Just as water attains the state of stone through the form of hail, so does delusion lead to the illusion of living existence. 75.
Thereafter, O Sage, that which is designated as the mind (citta), the delusion of the intellect (manas), and illusion (māyā),
arises in saṃsāra by resorting to a profound dullness.
She has fallen into the dullness of delusion, is tormented by the fetters of craving, is possessed by desire, anger, and fear, and is prone to swinging between existence and non-existence. (77)
Existence is prosperity; non-existence is poverty, which follows upon that [existence]. (77)
Having abandoned her own infinite enjoyments, she is subject to the transformations of limitation;
scorched by the forest fire of suffering, her heart is emaciated by the inauspiciousness of grief. (78)
In times of separation from wife, children, and others, she undergoes transformations such as grief; emaciated by misfortunes and sorrows, she is wretched and ill-reputed. (78)
By the thought "I am this," she was rendered destitute by emptiness;
having placed her reliance on the body alone, she has fallen into supreme wretchedness. (79)
This is due to the delusion consisting of the notion "I am indeed this very self whose nature is direct suffering, delusion, and so forth. (79)
Sunk in the great mire of delusion like an aged forest elephant, her body trembles violently upon the swing of the creeper of existence and non-existence. (80)
Dealing with the transformations of this essence-less and shoreless saṃsāra, her heart was scorched by suffering and colored by the radiance of passion. || 81 ||
She is colored by passion, splendor, and anger. || 81 ||
Like a doe strayed from her herd, she has fallen into a state of helplessness;
her form appeared when she was manifest, and it has set when she has vanished.
Upon the manifestation of prosperities or the mere elements, she is one whose form has arisen, being joyful or manifest; or [upon their loss], wretchedness or disappearance [occurs]. 82.
Like a young girl fleeing from Vetālas, she flees from others who have arrived through her own imagination, their eyes wide with agitation and fear. (83)
Like a camel seeking a sweet drop of conditioned pleasure,
one falls from one fault into another and sinks downward.

Just as a female camel, while chewing on thorns, neem leaves, and the like, longs for a very small drop of sweet juice conditioned by its own habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), so too does one long for happiness amidst sense objects that abound in suffering; this is the meaning.
Or alternatively, just as a female camel...

The meaning is that, like one who— desiring to climb a tree in order to lick drops of honey oozing from a swarm of bees clinging to the tops of trees growing on uneven and high embankments— falls down simultaneously with those very bees, so it is here. || 84 ||
She has indeed fallen into extreme adversity, passing from one crisis to another;
she has descended from sorrow to sorrow, remaining in calamity after calamity.
Endowed with a multitude of various misfortunes, her disposition rendered helpless by her own actions,
she has fallen from misery to even greater misery, tormented by intense anguish.
In the realms such as the hells, they have encountered misery upon misery. || 86 ||
Gradually, having acquired proficiency through constant practice, she reached the stage of mastery;
she then attained the pinnacle of skill in the composition of diverse poetic meters.

Even upon obtaining human birth in due course, having mastered the practice of poetic composition, drama, logic, and so forth— through the skill acquired from practicing worldly conventions since childhood, and through cleverness and proficiency— she [composed] her own diverse work.

The meaning is that the prowess exerted in the creation of wealth, houses, fields, attendants, and so forth, has reached only that state [of worldly activity], and not the state of discernment (viveka) conducive to liberation. || 87 ||
Terrified and having reached the brink of death, she was suspicious of everything,
like a small fish in dwindling water, intent only on writhing about.

Thus, having reached the end of her life in due course and having arrived at the point of death, she became terrified on all sides and grew apprehensive; she was solely intent upon rolling about and wallowing on the ground. (88)
In childhood, all her faculties were powerless; in youth, she was shrouded by anxiety;
even in old age, she was afflicted by extreme suffering; and when dead, she was made subject to the power of karma. 89.

He elaborates upon what was stated in brief with the verse beginning "In childhood" (*bālye*). "Whose"—meaning whose—all objects and enjoyments (*artha-bhoga*) are "helpless," that is, dependent on others.
"By anxiety"—meaning by anxiety regarding wealth, sense-objects, and so forth—"obstructed," meaning her discrimination (*viveka*) is covered. || 89 ||
She is born as a Nāgī in the city of heaven, as a Daitya woman in the hollows of Pātāla, as an Asurī in the caverns of the Daityas, and as a human woman on the surface of the earth. (90)
He elaborates upon the very course of karma with the words beginning "is born," and so forth. || 90 ||
A Rākṣasī resides on the support of the Rākṣasas, a Vānarī in the hollow of a forest tree, a Siṃhī on the peak of the lord of mountains, and a Kinnarī on the Kulaparvata mountain. || 91 ||
On the Kulaparvatas, such as Himavat and others. || 91 ||
A Vidyādharī on Mount Devagiri, a serpent in a forest pit; a creeper upon a tree, a bird in its nest; a shrub on a mountain peak, and a doe in the forest. (92)
Devagiri is Mera; vīrut is a shrub. || 92 ||
Nārāyaṇa reclines in the ocean; the lotus-born Brahmā is absorbed in meditation in the city of Brahman; Hara has gone to his beloved on the mountain; and Hari, the best of gods, is in heaven.

This is because of the *Śiva Purāṇa*, which states: "Even for Nārāyaṇa and others, there is indeed a manifestation within the states of individual souls (*jīva-gati*); for they are remembered as being eternal, yet subject to the states of impermanence," and so forth. Alternatively, this may be applied to the context of liberated souls who are similar to Nārāyaṇa and others.
Or else, from this point onward, the various states of the individual soul are no longer elaborated; rather, it is the nature of consciousness (*cit*) that is described.
There is no fault, for it is indeed the state of being the agent of all activities. "Gone with his beloved" means joined with her as half of his body. || 93 ||
The sun of sharp rays creates the day; the cloud rains water; and consciousness creates the wind, along with the mountains and the great oceans. 94.
By words such as "breathing" (śvasana) and so forth, the functions of air and the other elements are indicated. || 94 ||
The wheel of the seasons swiftly turns the circle of time; day and night arrive in succession, bringing light and darkness in turn. (95)
The wheel of the year is composed of the seasons; it is the circle of time, consisting of the yugas, manvantaras, and so forth. 95.
In one place, there is the swelling sap of seeds; in another, the silence of stones;
in one place, a river full of water; and in another, the expanse of night-lotuses.
In some trees and such, she exists as the essence of the seed, which is the cause of its sprouting; and as the essence of sap, she is the vitalizing growth.
She is silent and motionless among stones. 96.
In some places by the ripening of rows of fruits, in some by wood fires and the like, in some by the cold of snow and water, and in some by the sky—there is nothing at all [to provide relief]. 97.

After the two words ending in the third case, the word "upalakṣitā" (characterized by) is to be supplied. She whose water is like frost—acting as frost or being frost-like—in its coolness; [she who is characterized by] the sky (space), and from the first word [of the compound], wind, and elsewhere, something else. 97.
In some places it has a blazing form, in some places it is a formidable rock,
in some places it is blue, in some green, in some places fire, and in some places earth.
It is difficult and impassable, filled with kusha grass, thorns, and the like. || 98 ||
Because she is the self of all, because she is omnipresent, because she is endowed with all powers,
and because she is indeed everything— such is that Supreme One, even clearer than the sky.

Māyā is the state of possessing all powers; by virtue of its connection with that [Śiva], it takes on this form because of its universality, appearing as the very form of the world. The masculine form (*sarvatvam*) has not been applied in place of the feminine *sarvā* in the simple sense of the word due to Vedic usage (*chāndasatvāt*). In the ultimate sense, however, the meaning is that she is even clearer than the sky, and she is Consciousness (*cit*). || 99 ||
Just as water, by its own movement, constructs itself as waves and so forth—according to what, where, and when—it experiences itself in that very same way. (100)

The meaning is that by whatever state of being, in whatever place, and in whatever manner the conscious self accumulates—that is, brings about an increase through transformation—it experiences that very state of being accordingly. || 100 ||

A female swan, a female curlew, a female crane, a female crow, a female sarasa bird, a female horse, a female wolf, a female heron, a female egret, a female deer, a female monkey, a female kinnara, and a female dog. (101)
He further elaborates on those entities with the verse beginning "The female swan" (haṃsī) and so forth.

The mention of the "female heron" (bakī) again is for the purpose of including other species characterized by very long legs and beaks. Similarly, the mention of the "balākā" crane is for the purpose of including the species characterized by an extremely white downy throat. || 101 ||
Vaṭīkā, Piṅgalī, Śālī, Makṣikā, Bhramarī, Śukī;
Dhīḥ, Śrīḥ, Hrīḥ, Prītī, Ratī, Śambarī, Śarvarī, and Śaśī. || 102 ||

*Vaṭīkā* and others are specific varieties of birds. *Śālī* is a *śārikā* (maina bird). In the word *prītī*, the vowel is lengthened according to the rule *ḍhralope* (Pāṇini 6.3.111). *Śambarī* is illusion (*māyā*). || 102 ||
He wanders through these and other various wombs, revolving in saṃsāra like a blade of grass in a whirlpool of water. (103)
In various wombs, that is, in different types of bodies. || 103 ||
Then she fears her own mental construction, just as a female donkey fears its own braying;
there is no other woman so deluded, so fickle, and so weak as she.
A woman is weak and frail. || 104 ||
O great sage, this power of life (jīva-śakti) has been described to you;
it is wretched, subject to the sway of natural impulses, and characterized by the nature of a bound soul (paśu). 105.

Having attained the designation "the self of karma," she is called the "miserable" one; though belonging to the Supreme Self, she has herself resorted to delusion—an infinite state abounding in suffering. (106)
The self is of the nature of action, following the course of its deeds. And thus says the Śruti: "As one acts, as one behaves, so does one become;
a doer of good becomes good, a doer of evil becomes evil; one becomes virtuous by virtuous action, and sinful by sinful action. (106)
The innate impurity, which is non-existent yet pervaded by this [power], is perishable;
it is situated as something inseparable, like the husk upon a grain of rice. [Note: The lengthening of the vowel in "kañcūkam" is an archaic Vedic usage for the sake of meter. || 107 ||
By means of non-dual ignorance—which is devoid of any appearance of existence separate from itself—the [world] is undetermined and unstable. || 107 ||
Deprived of infinite prosperity and tormented by misfortune, she grieved for her life, like a heroine who has lost her husband. 108.
The ellipsis implies that she remained like a mistress deprived of her husband, left without a protector. || 108 ||
Behold the power of the movement of the dull-witted mind here: without the remembrance of its own state, it goes toward the misery of falling downward, like the heavy base of a water-wheel's bucket.

O Rāma, behold the power and capacity of ignorance (*avidyā*), which moves inertly; for by reason of this, the consciousness (*cit*), though its very nature is the full Brahman, becomes like the dense mass of space that has entered into the buckets of a water-wheel (*araghaṭṭa*). [Thus it obscures] its own state of unsurpassed bliss and fullness.
And considering that the capacity to contemplate the entire world, characterized by oceans of clouds and all else, cannot exist without Smara—

while she herself was limited to her body alone, and he was limited to a mere jar— and that with the exhaustion of the merit that causes enjoyment, she would become empty like a small vessel leaking away its little water, she thought again and again of falling back [into the ocean].
It goes lower and lower; that is the meaning of "it is miserable. || 109 ||

Thus ends the thirtieth sarga, titled "The Contemplation of Consciousness Directed Toward the Inner Self," within the section on Nirvāṇa, in the episode of the Worship of Śiva, in the glorious Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa composed by the Sage. 30.

Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Investigation into Consciousness Directed Toward Objects of Thought," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa-tātparyaprakāśa*.
The Thirty-first Chapter. 31.
The Lord said:
In this way, through the contemplation that "I am truly suffering," one accumulates nothing but falsehood.
Just as one who has fallen into the delusion of being intoxicated by a dream of consciousness might act in agitation. || 1 ||
By negating the living self and so forth, that pure consciousness is revealed,
through which there arises the manifestation of the external and internal via the mind, vital breath, and senses.
In this manner described, one accumulates—that is, constructs through superimposition—the unreal and non-existent state of the living world due to ignorance;
one has fallen into a delusion caused by the intoxication of sleep, like the intoxication of wine. || 1 ||
Just as a woman whose mind is deluded weeps, thinking "I am dead" when she is actually immortal, so too does the consciousness weep, thinking "I am destroyed" even though it is not destroyed.
The bride is innocent. || 2 ||
Just as this world, though causeless, delusive, and unstable, is perceived by a perverted mind as if it were stable, so too does consciousness perceive through the delusion of "I-ness. (3)
Just as one perceives a rotating potter’s wheel and the like as steady and motionless, so too one perceives the world as steady.
(3) For the mind is indeed the cause of this experience of saṃsāra; yet that [world] is not the cause of the mind, because it is impossible for anything other than consciousness to exist. (4)

That mind is not any entity whatsoever. Why? Because both its being "mind" and its being "other than that" are absolutely impossible. The meaning is that if it were non-mind, it would fall within the category of the world, and thus it could not serve as the cause for the conceptualization of that [world]. || 4 ||
For in this way, due to the absence of a cause, that which is to be perceived is impossible;
therefore, that mind by which it is perceived with effort does not exist.
Since consciousness itself is non-existent, the non-existence of that world of objects of consciousness is also established; thus he says, "In this way.

By whatever consciousness (*cit*) the mind (*citta*) is perceived with effort, that consciousness is not dependent on the mind nor is it the object of perception; rather, its meaning is that it is purely pure. || 5 ||
It does not possess the nature of the seen, the seeing, or the seer, like oil in a stone;
nor does it possess the nature of agent, action, or instrument, like darkness in the moon of perception.

Since the negation of consciousness (*citi*) itself entails the negation of the triad consisting of the seen, the act of seeing, and the seer—which are produced by the eye and other faculties—he states this with the words beginning "not" (*na*). [In the phrase] "in the seeing-consciousness" (*dṛśi citi*), [it refers to] consciousness (*citi*). || 6 ||
The knower, the object of knowledge, and the means of knowledge do not exist [in it], just as a new sprout does not exist in the sky;
nor do consciousness, the conscious subject, and the objects of consciousness, just as a khadira tree does not exist in the Nandana grove.

The fluctuations of consciousness (citta-vṛtti), the conscious agent (cetana), and its substratum (tad-āśraya) are the [subjective] categories; their objects (tad-viṣaya) are indicated by the word "and so forth" (ādi-pada), which includes the knower (mantṛ), the thinking (mati), the object of thought (mantavya), the intellect (buddhi), the cognition (bodha), and the object of cognition (boddhavya), as well as the ego-agent (ahaṃ-kartṛ), the ego-sense (ahaṃ-kāra), and the objects of the ego (ahaṃ-kārya). || 7 ||
The states of "I-ness" and "you-ness," as well as "thatness" and so forth, do not exist in the sky as they do in a mountain;
nor do the states of having one's own body or another's body exist [in the Self] as "whiteness" exists in a conch shell or "blackness" in lampblack.
Reality (*tattva*) is the state of being another entity that is imperceptible. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), its substratum, its pervasion, and its relation are included.
It is neither manifold nor non-manifold, nor are they distinct like Mount Sumerus;
nor is it a mere verbal designation of meaning and sound, like a great creeper in a barren wasteland.

There are various distinctions among living beings, yet there is no non-distinction, for the superimposition of identity with the Self occurs within every body. Like Sumerus contained within a single atom, there is not even a mention of the splendor of words—their names and their forms as objects—for those [distinctions]. || 9 ||
"Not so, not so"—it is not like night in the orb of the sun, nor is it like heat in frost, whether in regard to reality or unreality. (10)

Now, therefore, regarding the scriptural negations of all perceived objects, such as "not this, not this" (neti neti) and so forth: these too exist only until the true nature of reality is revealed. Once the essence of consciousness (cittattva) is seen, since no counter-correlate (pratiyogin) is established, even those negations do not occur; thus he says, "not this. There are no properties called "reality" or "unreality" that exist apart from the real entity itself. || 10 ||
Neither emptiness nor non-emptiness exist, like a tree within a stone casket;
that which is called the "emptiness of emptiness" is as vast and uncarved as space. 11.

Just as within the interior or womb of a stone, there exists the well-known great voidness and non-voidness—which is characterized solely by the state of absolute oneness (kevalībhāva) and is merely the transparency of its own nature—so too, upon reflection, not even an atom of difference remains; such is the connection with the subsequent [verse]. || 11 ||
Only the purity of the state of the Absolute remains;
this is not attained by anyone through any defect of the mind. 12.

[Objection: "In that case, is it not rather the collective mind (*samaṣṭicitta*) consisting of Hiraṇyagarbha itself that is the defect—the cause of all misfortune—for this individual consciousness (*citi*)? For it is due to that very cause that this [individual consciousness], having been born within the four types of bodies, undergoes the suffering of this saṃsāra. And we are unable to eradicate that [collective mind]. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Not from the mind," meaning "not from a defect of the consciousness. From the consciousness...
The meaning is this: this suffering is not obtained merely from the causal mind of Hiraṇyagarbha, who is of the nature of a defect;

rather, this aforementioned misfortune characterized by worldly existence (saṃsāra) persists solely through the mental conception (*bhāvanā*) that "I" and "mine" are real with respect to all those bodies, senses, and objects created by Him. || 12 ||
That misfortune which has arisen and persists merely through the non-contemplation of all things is pacified merely through the contemplation of them by one who knows that [truth]. || 13 ||
For this very reason, he says "even toward one who knows that" (tajjñe 'pi) to show that [anger] subsides through mere non-contemplation even in the case of a knower of reality. || 13 ||
Even for one who knows that [truth], it serves no other purpose than the mere absence of mental cultivation;
for there is neither a blade of grass nor the three worlds here, since everything is dependent upon oneself. 14.

For this very reason, he says "not even a blade of grass," meaning that although the objects of the three worlds could be disparaged as being like a blade of grass, they remain difficult to overcome for those who do not know reality solely through the power of mental cultivation (bhāvanā). || 14 ||
This goal is indeed within one's own power, yet it is difficult to accomplish when one remains merely at the level of mental cultivation.
Whatever is not accomplished by a person—how and where could that ever be obtained? (15)

[Objection: Surely the abandonment of cultivation is extremely easy; why then does it not succeed by itself? To this he says: "Whatever... The sense is that even a mere blade of grass is never seen to be obtained without the effort of stretching out one's hand. || 15 ||
That consciousness which is non-conceptual and non-dual, which pervades all things, is the supreme, unique, and ultimate reality; it is the direct illuminator even of lights.

With the intention that the ultimate consciousness (*paramārthacit*), which constitutes the supreme human goal, is easily accessible everywhere once mere mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is abandoned, he describes it with the verse beginning "nirvikalpa" (verse 16).
This very [consciousness] is the illuminator, all-pervading, eternally pure,
perpetually risen, devoid of the mind, changeless, and stainless.
She is established in the jar, the cloth, the banyan tree, the wall, the cart, the monkey, the donkey, the asura, the ocean, the spirit, the man, and the serpent.
Existing as a witness, she does not move anywhere;
like a lamp for the purpose of illuminating, she performs no further action. (19)
The meaning is that just as a lamp, for the purpose of illuminating objects, is capable through its own abiding nature alone and does not perform any action, so too is consciousness. || 19 ||
Though impure, this [intellect] is rich in non-conceptuality yet possesses conceptualization;
though inert, it appears as if conscious; and while not all-pervasive, it appears as if all-pervading. (20)
Although this consciousness possesses such power, by means of this very perception of a body and so forth, it has become defiled even though it was previously undefiled.
Thus, the application should be made everywhere: although it is rich in non-conceptuality, it has become conceptualizing. (20)
Non-conceptual, supreme, and subtle, consciousness perceives its own self-awareness,
just as the movement of wind affects the limbs, vital points, and so forth when a mechanical device is wound.

Now, he provides the reasoning for the intensification of consciousness— which is all-pervading and most subtle— characterized by its specific pervasion within each individual body from the tips of the nails, in the verse beginning with "nirvikalpā" (free from conceptual construction).

The supreme, all-pervading, and subtle consciousness (*cit*), which is free from conceptual construction— that is, untouched by conceptualizations such as specific ego-identification— is [present] in the wind, primarily the vital breath (*prāṇa*).

Having entered the subtle body (*liṅgadeha*) by way of reflection, it pervades the limbs such as the hands and feet, the vital points (*marman*) such as the heart and other locations, and—by the force of the word "etcetera"—the seventy-two thousand channels (*nāḍī*).
Having thus drawn its own all-pervasive consciousness into that very [subtle body], it accumulates it, that is, brings it to increase. Just as:

The meaning is as follows: just as a thread made of long, fine silk and so forth, when wound upon the needle of a shuttle or loom, withdraws its own length—which though very great—into that small space and brings about an accumulation in the form of a jujube fruit or similar object. || 21 ||
Consciousness, when enveloped by form, light, and mental attention, becomes non-awakening;
yet through awakening itself, it becomes both existent and non-existent sleep. (22)

Therefore, for a person who is awake, consciousness—being enveloped by the perception of external forms and so forth and by internal mental activities—exists on the side of cognition (*bodha*). However, for one who is going toward sleep, whether in the waking state or in a dream, consciousness—being enveloped by the perception of forms consisting of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and by mental activities—exists in both states: on the side of internal cognition and on the side of external non-cognition (*abodha*). This is also the case in deep sleep (*suṣupti*).

Because it is the witness of mere ignorance, and because of the reflection of one who has awakened—"I did not know anything"—even that which exists is as if non-existent; the meaning is that it belongs solely to the side of non-awakening. || 22 ||
That supreme consciousness itself, through its own awareness, becomes exceedingly clear thought;
just as a virtuous person becomes like a non-virtuous one when the desires of the wicked are cultivated.

That consciousness, though exceedingly pure and consisting of Brahman alone, comes to entertain thoughts regarding the attainment of what is favorable and the avoidance of what is unfavorable toward the body and so forth. The meaning is that it becomes like an honest man who, through long association with the wicked and the cultivation of such impressions in his mind, becomes dishonest upon encountering the desires of the wicked. || 23 ||
Just as gold, through the removal of impurity, loses its copperiness due to that stain and returns once more to its state of pure gold— so too is the supreme consciousness.

For this very reason, with the intention that "when the mind has been cultivated as having Brahman as its self, it becomes Brahman itself," he provides an illustration: "Just as one's own mirror, through the cessation of its own [reflected] superimpositions, attains the state of being a mere image-receptacle, so too, having entered as if into creation, the mind returns to its own state [the state of the Self] through awakening. [The reading "citpadam" is also found.]

Just as a beautiful mirror or looking-glass, through the removal of the impurities superimposed upon it, attains a state of clarity—a state of peace—rendered fit for the repeated manifestation of reflections by means of the stability of its own image;

so too does Consciousness (cit), having seemingly entered into the creation of the inert state of the individual soul (jīva) and so forth due to ignorance (ajñāna). [The suffix *lyap* is used here, allowing for the optional elision of the nasal sound.]
The meaning is that, having arrived and remained [there], one attains that state of absolute liberation (kaivalya) through the awakening to reality (tattva). || 25 ||
From the perception of non-existence, this saṃsāra proceeds;
however, from the perception of intrinsic nature (svabhāva), it ceases as something that was never real. || 26 ||
Non-existence is false cognition; [it is so called] because of the awareness of that. || 26 ||
When, by virtue of its consciousness, it gathers within itself another unreal state, then,
as if having attained a sense of "I-ness," that imperishable [consciousness] seems to perish.
The meaning is that this is based on the Vedic scripture: "He who perceives any difference or division [between them], then fear comes upon him.
(27) Just as a fruit falls from the edge of a cliff when it has slightly wobbled, so too is this great downfall from consciousness. (28)

From a slight vibration, there occurs a mere falling away from the stalk; from the edge of that, Bhṛgu [fell] to the mountain slope. This state of being a living soul (jīvabhāva) is merely the existence of form and so forth; yet this is nothing but the stainless consciousness itself.
Duality and unity, which arise from ignorance, dissolve through awakening. (29)

"It is consciousness alone" means that the superimposed has no existence apart from its substratum; this is the intended sense. Duality and unity are the superimpositions of difference and non-difference. || 29 ||
The awakening of the mind toward the mental faculties and so forth occurs by its mere existence, just as worldly activity proceeds by the mere existence of light. (30)
Of the mind, which has the mind as its witness. || 30 ||
The throbbing of the pupil due to wind is called the "illumination" (dīpti) of sight;
the cognition of the form of an external object existing outside that [pupil] is the supreme consciousness (citparā). 31.

Having stated it in general terms, he now demonstrates that consciousness alone is the result in all cases by analyzing it specifically with respect to the eyes and so forth, beginning with the words "from the wind" (vātāt) and so on. Due to the wind—the vyāna breath—impelled by the proximity of consciousness, movement occurs in the pupils of the eyes. Residing therein...

The luminous faculty (*taijasa-indriya*) is called *dīpti* (radiance) and *cakṣus* (the eye). Through it—as water [flows] through the opening of a canal—that internal organ (*antahkarana*) which is to be brought outside reaches the external object; in that [organ] which possesses [the object], namely in the jar or other such thing pervaded by it, there arises the cognition, the manifestation of existence, of its form—that is, of a form identical in shape to it, such as blue, yellow, and so forth, as well as the form of the jar itself. That is the supreme [cognition].
The meaning is "nothing but consciousness" (cideva). || 31 ||
Skin and wind are inert and insubstantial; their conjunction is called touch.
The awareness of touch is the act of thinking, while the awareness of that [thinking] is the supreme Consciousness.

Likewise, in the case of the triad of touch, both the skin and the air are insentient and trivial by their own nature, being devoid of existence and manifestation (*sphūrti*) independently. Therefore, it is solely through the power of existence and manifestation dependent upon Consciousness that their conjunction occurs; because this serves as the basis for the conceptualization of the tactile organ, it is called "touch.
Through that [conjunction], the mental engagement with objects such as cold or heat joined with it—the mental modification (*manovṛtti*) taking on their form—is what constitutes perception.

The awareness of contact is thus described. However, the manifestation of the "threefold circle" (tripuṭī) consisting of that contact, its object, and the subject—which is delimited by it—is the supreme consciousness alone; this is the meaning. || 32 ||
The connection between the subtle element of smell and the wind is the consciousness of smell; however, the perception of these [objects] devoid of the mind is supreme consciousness itself.

Thus, when the subtle element of odor (*gandha-tanmātra*)—which is differentiated by way of the nature of the olfactory faculty and the nature of odor—is brought into contact with the air entering the nostrils, it becomes the cause of the cognitions of odor; that is, it is the cause of the internal mental modifications (*antaḥkaraṇa-vṛtti*) that take on the form of odor. Of these [cognitions], which consist of the threefold division (*tripuṭī*),...
That which is devoid of the mind, solitary, and characterized by manifestation—that feeling is the supreme consciousness itself; such is the meaning. || 33 ||

When there is contact with the wind of hearing the subtle element of sound (śabdatanmātra) even without the mind, consciousness that resembles deep sleep is declared to be the supreme consciousness (cit). || 34 ||
Thus, from the conjunction of the subtle element of sound (śabda-tanmātra), the sense of hearing, and the Vyāna-vāyu, mental modifications arise in the form of the perception of sound.
Among these, that which is changeless and resembles deep sleep—occurring when the mind has abandoned what is agreeable—is the witness-consciousness (sākṣi-saṃvit);

that is the supreme consciousness (cit). The intended meaning is that, in this manner, the triad of the gustatory faculty, its object, and the witness-consciousness must also be discerned by the observer.
The tendency toward action arises from volition; volition is the process of mental reflection;
reflection is the turbidity of the mind; and the Self is consciousness, which remains stainless. (35)

Thus, he states that the Self-consciousness must be discriminated by means of its witnesshood over the impurity of the mental modification consisting of volition, which is the cause for the activity of the organs of action: "The state of being oriented toward action" (kriyonmukhatvam). || 35 ||
Consisting of the light of consciousness, eternal, and abiding solely within her own self, she bears this internal universe as its arrangement, just as a stone [bears its internal structure]. (36)

Thus, since all manifestation of duality—both internal and external—is of the nature of the witness-consciousness alone (*sākṣicinmātra*), it follows that all duality is superimposed upon that [consciousness] itself; this he states with the word "cit" (consciousness). Just as a crystal slab bears within itself the arrangement of reflections such as forests, mountains, and rivers, so it is here. || 36 ||
Holding this world as non-dual and devoid of modifications and the like, it neither sets nor rises; it does not vibrate, nor does it increase.
"Free from modification and so forth" is an adverbial modifier; or alternatively, it means "free from modification and so forth by virtue of being the reality that is the substratum."
Having attained the state of being a living soul through volition, she— by means of her own self which is devoid of volition—
contemplates the nature of the conscious-inert, yet remains established in herself as neither inert nor conscious.

The meaning is that the Consciousness, contemplating the world—which is insentient, yet not [merely] insentient nor [merely] sentient—as having a real nature, remains established in its own essential form. || 38 ||
The vital breath (jīva) is the chariot of this consciousness (cit); the ego (ahaṃkṛti) is the chariot of the vital breath;
the intellect (buddhi) is the chariot of the ego; and from that, the mind (manas) is the chariot of the intellect. || 39 ||
Now, imagining a succession of chariots for the consciousness's wandering outside [the body], he says in two verses beginning with "The chariot": || 39 ||

The chariot of the mind is the vital breath; the chariot of the vital breath is the collection of sense-faculties; the chariot of the multitude of faculties is the body; and the chariot of the body is its movement.
The group of organs of action is characterized by vibration. || 40 ||
Vibration is action within saṃsāra, the cage of old age and death;
thus has this wheel been set in motion, born from primordial manifestation.

The movement and wandering of all chariots in saṃsāra is their very function; this is the meaning of "to be accomplished. The cage-like bodies characterized by old age and death constitute the swing-wheel for the bird of the individual soul (jīva), which has arisen through the power of Māyā—the sovereign majesty—of Īśvara, the primordial root cause. || 41 ||
It appears as if real within itself, like a pervasive dream that is non-existent; yet it does not possess even the slightest degree of reality, remaining like the water of a mirage. (42)
He establishes its very nature as illusory (māyika) with the words: "it appears" (pratibhāsate). || 42 ||

O Lord of Sages, in this conceptualization, the vital breath (prāṇa) is traditionally regarded as the chariot; wherever there is the movement of the vital breath, there the faculty of thought (manana) is firmly established. (43)

Regarding what was stated—that the mind is the chariot and the vital breath (prāṇa) is [the horse]—he states the logical justification to express a specific detail relevant to the meaning that will be explained hereafter, beginning with the word "chariot. The ellipsis to be supplied is: "because it is the cause for the mental construction" (kalpanā).
He demonstrates this very point with the words beginning "where," etc. (verse 43).
Wherever the glory of light is established, there form alone shines;
wherever the vital breath is powerfully situated, that very thing trembles.
Being in the form of a thread, Bālī is capable of supporting and moving everything. || 44 ||
Just as a gust of wind that blows into a forest causes it to tremble, so too does the vital breath (prāṇa) shake when the mind is not merged in the space [of the Self].
But when the mind is dissolved in the space [of the Self], the vital breath does not tremble. 45.

Thus, he states by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) that the mind also possesses the quality of being the cause of the activity of the vital breaths, saying "when the mind... [and so forth]. When the mind has dissolved into the space—that is, the space within the heart (*hārdākāśa*)—[the vital breaths cease their activity]. || 45 ||
When the fire has ceased to exist, it no longer shines, just as its form does not appear;
when the vital breath has subsided, there is not even the slightest mind within the wind.

The meaning is that form does not shine, just as [the dust does not stir]. Thus, he states that the mind is also restrained through the restraint of the vital breath (prāṇa): "When the wind has subsided, the dust does not tremble;
wherever the vital breath (marut) goes, there the mind remains. (47)
For this very reason, he states [in the verse beginning with] "yatra" that its status as a chariot has been declared. || 47 ||
Wherever the chariot follows, there the charioteer is present;
impelled by the vital breath, the mind travels to another land in an instant. (48)
Otherwise, it would perish there like a stone released from a sling;
where there is a flower, there is fragrance, and where there is fire, there is heat. (49)
*Kṣepaṇa* is a specific type of mechanical device (*yantra*). Otherwise, when the vital breaths are obstructed, the mind perishes; that is to say, it is destroyed. || 49 ||
Where the vital breath (prāṇa) goes as the wind (marut), there the moon (indu) possesses its luster;
that consciousness arises from the vibration of the wind, and it is the very touch of the channels (nāḍīs). 50.
Prāṇa is both the collective and the individual form; *indu* is the moon and the mind (*manas*) which is a portion thereof; *chavi* is the moonlight and the fluctuations of the mind (*manovṛtti*).

For this very reason, with the intention of showing that air (*vāyu*) is also a causal factor in each of the perceptions such as sight, he says: "perception" (*saṃvitti*). [This is] for the purpose of the entry of the essence of food into all the limbs.
And that wind is the one that touches all the channels. || 50 ||
The expansion of consciousness is the mind; that [mind] resides within the cavity of the vital breath.
Everywhere—in both the insentient and the sentient—consciousness exists, as clear as the sky.

Since that [body] consists of the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*) formed by the fusion of consciousness and mind, the expansion of consciousness within the cavity of the vital breath (*prāṇakoṭara*)—resulting from its doubling through the relationship of the original image and its reflection—is established precisely from that; thus he says: "In consciousness... (verse 51).
It is experienced as if it were trembling due to the vibration of the vital breath (prāṇa),
yet it remains established in insentient things in the form of pure existence alone.

He states the reason for arising therein: "as if they were agitated. The meaning is that because consciousness is experienced within the subtle body (liṅga), it appears to vibrate due to its clear manifestation. || 52 ||
"Awakened by the vital breath, even the insentient body perceives through its nature as sensation"—this is the reading in the root text;
elsewhere, there is an explanatory reading beginning with "even the insentient body, being awakened by the vital breath... and so forth.
In the insentient, it perceives by virtue of having sensation as its essence.
He who formerly used to leap about with the various outbursts of expansion,
once the vital breath has passed away, he becomes thoughtless and does not tremble even quickly.

Although the body is insentient, being awakened by the vital breath (prāṇa), it perceives through the nature of experiencing creation and so forth, by virtue of its identification with the superimposed mind (ādhyāsika-citta). That very same body which previously moved about and acted during the state of life does not tremble or shake [now].
O Sage, the Supreme Self alone is reflected within the city of eight constituents;
it is seen like a reflection in a mirror, but not in stones or similar objects.

The wise know the *liṅga* as the "city of eight" (*puryaṣṭaka*), which is joined with the elements, the internal organ, the vital breaths, and the organs of knowledge and action, and is filled with ignorance, desire, and karma. Within that city of eight... (54)
Know the mind to be the city of eight constituents (puryaṣṭaka), the sole cause of all effects; it is described by others through various distinctions conceived according to their own inclinations.

Now, an objection may be raised: "Was it not stated that the reflection of consciousness in the mind is caused by the vital breath (*prāṇa*), yet now in the *Pūrvāṣṭaka* it is said to be otherwise? How then is there no contradiction? To this he replies with the verse beginning with "the mind" (*mana*). [It is] by means of other methods devised by other teachers according to their own inclinations for the purpose of instructing disciples.
(55) "For from which [source] arises the entire web of the perceivable world, agitated by mental constructions, and which is intensely experienced as if residing therein..."

Since the mind revolves through the perception of the body, know that all of this is indeed the Supreme Reality, the Lord of the Universe. Now, because the universe— characterized by the individual soul, its limiting adjuncts, and its objects of enjoyment— is dependent upon Brahman, which is pure Being whose sole essence is consciousness, during its creation, maintenance, and dissolution, it is in the ultimate sense Brahman alone.
Experiencing this as "That," he concludes with the words "because": because for that reason, consciousness alone arises there;

and because it remains in that very place (the word *ca* implies that it also dissolves therein); and because for that reason the mind itself revolves and wanders through the perception of the body (the use of the *parasmaipada* ending is Vedic). Therefore, the universe is the Supreme Reality.
The meaning is: "Know that it is Brahman alone and nothing else. || 56 ||

Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Unity of Mind and Vital Breath," in the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa* of the *Mokṣopāya* section of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Valmiki, according to the tradition of the Sages.
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Unity of Mind and Vital Breath," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The thirty-second canto. Īśvara said:
O Sage, listen to how she, who is characterized by vibration, brings about all effects.
And moving through the bodies of men, she attains the supreme designation. || 1 ||
Just as the *puryaṣṭaka* (the subtle body), having entered [the state], causes the body and so forth to move,
and just as it goes to another body— all that is described here.

How does the supreme consciousness (cit), having entered the body— the *puryaṣṭaka*— of persons moving according to the manner previously described, perform actions pertaining to this world and the next? And how,

being characterized by that [activity] and possessing the movement of the body and other organs favorable to it, does it engage in verbal expression, move, bathe, eat, and sacrifice, such that one says, "The Brāhmaṇa is sacrificing"?
The meaning is: "I shall tell you all that [the body] attains the fitness for being designated by such verbal expressions as 'a Kṣatriya' or 'Devadatta'; listen. || 1 ||
By means of those various winds of karma that have grown exceedingly thick— arising from the mental constructions and desires of their own minds in previous lives— they are indeed struck down.

The movement of the living being (jīva), which is the reflection of consciousness (cit) in the vibration of the body, is caused by that [movement]; and in its movement, the cause is the power of Māyā—which, having transformed into the mind in the form of the "city-staff" (puryaṣṭaka) as its limiting adjunct, conceals the true nature of consciousness. When that [Māyā] transforms into the form of the mind, the cause is precisely the mass of karma accumulated through the transformations at the end of each successive body. As stated in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad:

[The citation mentioned in the second footnote of the fifth chapter of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka is actually found at the end of the second Brāhmaṇa of the third chapter of the Nirṇayasāgara edition of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka;
we consider it an error on the part of previous editors to have stated that it belongs to the fifth chapter.]

And in the third commentary, the word "hetuṣu" (among causes) was inserted based on the manuscript copy; in the second Brāhmaṇa: "They both spoke of action alone"—that is, in that state of deliberation, having retired to a secluded place, they both spoke of action alone as the basis, the cause for the repeated undertaking of effects and instruments. Not only did they speak of it...
"But regarding the causes accepted by Kāla, Īśvara, and others, they praised only action;

indeed, they praised only action. Thus, it was only action that they praised, as it is the cause of bondage in the form of the "seizers" (graha) and "over-seizers" (atigraha)—the seizers being the vital breath, the tongue, speech, and the eye.
The ears, mind, hands, and skin are the "seizers" (atigrahas), while the excretory organs, tongue, form, name, sound, desire, action, touch, and consciousness are the objects seized.
With the intention of establishing them within their respective functions, he says "by the former ones," and so forth.
Power (*śakti*) is the power of Brahman, whose nature is beginningless *māyā*. By its own concealing power (*āvaraṇa-śakti*), it indeed obstructs Brahman, its own substratum.

Having rendered it incapable of being perceived— such that one thinks "it does not exist" or "it does not appear"— through those mental efforts and various imaginings, which have been accumulated since beginningless time and have become exceedingly swollen and highly nourished by diverse latent impressions of desire.
Through the various signs consisting of the multitude of performed and prohibited actions in the form of bodily and vocal movements,

the mind— which is essentially the *puryaṣṭaka*— having become transformed by its own nature, attains a state of mixture with consciousness (*cit*) due to the power of its own inherent character; thus, while being like consciousness because of the existence of the consciousness that is its own substrate, it nevertheless becomes as if inert, becoming fit for the worldly transactions of knowledge and action.

The meaning of these two verses is this: through this power of her own, acting as the conduit for the organs of knowledge and action and so forth, that very power of *māyā* manifests and dances in the form of the ninefold cycle of worldly existence—consisting of the seer, the seeing, the seen, and the rest—and nothing else whatsoever exists. || 2 ||
O Brahman, the power of consciousness has become as if insentient by having attained the state of the mind; it vibrates through this [mind], which has become its appropriate power.
O Sage, by her grace, that consciousness here, though possessed of a slight blemish,
creates and yet does not create this world, which is like a city of Gandharvas.

The connection is that this power of illusion (māyā-śakti), through its characteristic of non-investigation and through its characteristic of investigation respectively, "acts" and "does not act. || 4 ||
Due to the non-existence of the mind and other faculties, the body remains mute like a wall;
indeed, through their existence, it vibrates like a stone propelled by the wind in the sky.
In that case, since the body alone acts as everything due to the proximity of the knower of Brahman (*brahmacit*), what is the use of postulating the mind and so forth? To this, he says:
"Just as this [iron] consisting of extreme dullness vibrates in the presence of a magnet, so does this individual soul (*jīva*) vibrate when the all-pervading Supreme Being is present. (6)

He states that Brahman is the common cause for the activities of the vital breaths and the organs of action in the living being (jīva) merely by its proximity, using the words "just as" (yathā). || 6 ||
This individual soul (jīva) shines forth abundantly by its own inherent power alone,
just as a mirror receives the reflection even from an object situated outside its own substance.

With the intention that [the mind] is the uncommon cause for the manifestation of the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth, as well as for the functions of the organs of knowledge (*jñānendriya*), by means of casting a reflection, he says: "residing in all" (*sarvasthayā*). It manifests through the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) which is the very nature of the Self, and thus becomes capable of manifesting both itself and others. Now, one might object: since it is material and established in the nature of a substance, it serves as the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the individual soul (*jīva*).

If it is asked, "How can the *liṅga* (the subtle body) take on a reflection from Brahman, which is not of the nature of a substance (*adravyasvabhāva*), given that we observe the rule that a reflection occurs only of a substance within a substance?"—to this he replies: "In a mirror.

For it is observed that even though qualities, actions, universals (*jāti*), and so forth do not reside in a mirror—which is of the nature of a substance—they nonetheless appear as reflections; therefore, [reflection does not arise] from a substance alone.
The meaning is that there is a rule [to the effect] that the reflection is the object of apprehension. || 7 ||
Due to the forgetting of its own true nature, this living being has fallen into a state of insentience,
like a noble twice-born man who, through delusion and the loss of his essential character, sinks to the status of a śūdra.

If the individual soul (*jīva*) is a reflection of Brahman, then how can it experience the dullness (*jāḍya*) consisting of ignorance, sleep, lethargy, and so forth? For it is impossible for a reflection of the sun to possess a lack of luminosity. Anticipating this objection, he says: "Having forgotten... (verse 8).
For consciousness, having forgotten its own true nature, has fallen into the state of the mind;
due to its intellect being struck by delusion, it experiences a profound sense of wretchedness.
The nature of consciousness consists of mental qualities such as dullness, impurity, and so forth, which are very great, like those of Gādhi, Lavaṇa, Hariścandra, and others.
The body, being inert and powerless, is moved by this [mind] which possesses the force of the wind,
just as water is moved by a succession of waves.

Because of the superimposition of identity with the mind (*citta*), its mental attributes such as dejection and so forth are attained by it, just as [the self attains] the state of being the prāṇa. Likewise, because of the superimposition of identity with the prāṇa, it is established that this [self] is also the cause of the movement of the body, which is an attribute of that [prāṇa]. Thus he says: "By the inert one" (*jaḍayā*). The power of wind (*vāta-śakti*) is the *prāṇa*; through the attainment of identity with it, [the self becomes] equal to it. (10)
By this wretched living being, whose nature is karma and who possesses this mind,
the machines of the bodies are set in motion, like stones by the wind.

By the mind—which, as previously stated, has attained the nature of activity through its karmic essence and possesses the power of reflection; which is wretched and utterly miserable due to its subjection to limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*); just as stones situated on a boat are moved by the wind under the influence of limiting adjuncts such as long cloths tied to the boat's mast.
In the same way, they are moved toward their desired destination. || 11 ||
O Brahmin, for the purpose of drawing the chariots of the body, the Supreme Self has created the mind and the vital breaths, which are firm and engaged in action.
The arising of the mind and the vital breath are like two servants or two oxen whose actions are performed by the powers of the mind and the vital breath. || 12 ||
Having made the insentient body its chariot and having attained the state of a living soul, it mounts the chariot of the mind and drives the horses of the vital breaths. (13)

In order to establish the commonality with the activities of a dream, it is conceived that the mind alone is the chariot, while the primary and secondary vital breaths (prāṇas) are the horses; with this intention, he says: "Cid... (verse 13).
In some places there is the state of things having arisen; in some, the state of things having perished;
in some, the state of many things; and in some, the state of a single thing.
In some cases, during waking and dreaming, there is the state of objects having arisen, the state of objects having become manifest, and the state of many objects;

in other cases, in deep sleep, one reaches the state where objects have perished, the state where all objects have become concealed, and the state where ignorance alone remains as the single object—thus is the connection with the subsequent [text]. || 14 ||

Just as water remains even when waves have arisen or ceased, so too she does not abandon her own state; though appearing as both existent and non-existent, she is like water manifesting as the state of waves. (15) [Note: Regarding the word *padam* in the phrase "not abandoning her own *pada*," the reading *vapuḥ* ("body" or "form") would be more appropriate for the commentary.]
Has she perished through transformation into the state of the living world, just as milk perishes by becoming curds? He says "She exists" to show that she has not.

Although transformed in this way, she does not abandon her own ultimate body—her true nature—and thus, from the perspective of reality (tattvadṛśā), she is like an unreal waking state, yet from the perspective of worldly convention (vyavahāradṛśā), she is like an unreal dream; "ā uditā" means slightly blossomed. || 15 ||
The supreme form of the Self shines forth within its own modifications (vṛttis),
just as the beauty of forms existing in the visible world depends upon this light.

He says "upajīvya" (depending upon) because, precisely due to being superimposed upon the Self, the mental form—the individual soul and the world—manifests solely through the power of the Self-consciousness reflected in a mental modification (*manovṛtti*), depending entirely upon the very existence of the Self. || 16 ||
When the stainless supreme Self, which is the essence of consciousness, remains present, the individual soul lives with light, just as a house does when a lamp is present. || 17 ||
In that which has consciousness alone as its ultimate reality and essential nature.
His mental anxieties and physical ailments indeed swell to great intensity,
just as water becomes waves and waves become foam.

Thus, the fact that consciousness is the cause of the body's activity has been established. Now, in order to explain the manner in which it attains another body and to cultivate detachment, [the author] elaborates upon the miseries caused by the body, beginning with the verse starting "Mental agonies" (ādhayaḥ). || 18 ||
The living being, whose lotus-body is swarmed by mental and physical afflictions, undergoes instability just as water turns into the state of waves. 19.
Inequality consists of wretchedness, suffering, and so forth. || 19 ||

Because the power of consciousness possesses all powers, through the contemplation "I am not consciousness," that very [power] falls into helplessness here, just as the sun is obscured by radiant clouds.

In this body, just as the sun undergoes a state of helplessness— such as being obscured, withered, or fragmented— by means of clouds (ambuda) that are themselves ignited and self-luminous, so it appears to the vision of the observer. || 20 ||
Due to helplessness it falls away, and due to delusion it does not find self-awareness,
like one overcome by dense numbness who feels the crushing of his own limbs.
"Descending" (*cyavatī*) means entering into wombs that are not fit for [the exercise of] knowledge. The absence of the *num* augment in the form *śapśyanoh* is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*).
