Just as a person overcome by the stupor of intoxication from wine and the like does not perceive—that is, does not take cognizance of—the severing of his own limbs by a sword or similar weapon, so it is in this case. || 21 ||
And having attained this contemplation, delusion perishes,
just as a person who is intent on dense delusion loses the memory of his own purpose.

When, then, does the delusion of consciousness perish? To this he says: "Having attained... Just as a living being who is devoted to dense delusion such as intoxication becomes free from delusion after some time through the recollection of his own past actions, so it is here. || 22 ||
When the power of the wind’s movement within the consciousness of the limbs is lost through impairment, one does not perform synthesis, just as a leper does not seek out movement. (23)

Now he begins to describe the manner of casting off the body, starting with the words "When": when the vibratory power of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) no longer effects the coordination of the limbs— the perceptions of the limbs extending from the tips of the nails to the heart— due to the withdrawal of the subtle body (*liṅga*) into the heart, and because of its disappearance caused by this circumstance, it no longer maintains the awareness of the hands, feet, and so forth.

Just as a leper does not seek to move his withered fingers and other limbs, so too, the lotus-leaf situated in the heart—which was described in the *Bhuśuṇḍopākhyāna*—does not throb or tremble due to its conformity with the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇa*). This is how it connects with the subsequent verse. || 23 ||

Due to the vibration of non-awareness, the lotus situated in the heart within the body does not manifest when it is not touched, just like a wooden vessel outside that does not move when untouched. (24)
Just as a wooden vessel that has not been handled by the officiating priests at a sacrifice does not tremble, so it is in this case. || 24 ||
When the lotus petal is motionless, these vital breaths within attain peace,
just as the powers of the wind outside cease when the palm-leaf fan is still.
Peace dissolves into radiance; for the Veda declares: "The mind [dissolves] into breath, and breath into radiance. (25)

When the vital breath has ceased and all other sensations have subsided— [there is also a reading: "when internal sensations have subsided"]— the living being enters a state of complete silence, just as dust is no longer visible when the wind in the sky has calmed.

Through the dissolution of the limiting adjunct of form, he becomes unimpeded and full; and through the dissolution of the limiting adjunct of name, he who is the causal self becomes silent and attains that state.
O Sage, when the mind is free from passion and devoid of support, it remains established, having attained its own state, like the seed of a tree [remains] within the water. (27)

Due to the very cessation of the vital breath (prāṇa), which is the support characterized by the predominance of the quality of rajas, the mind—becoming stainless and devoid of support—attains, along with that breath, the state of the causal self (kāraṇātmapada) and remains as that very essence. If one asks, "Has it then departed entirely?
he says: "It remains."
The meaning is that it remains intent upon the manifestation of a body again, like a seed of an earthly tree supported by the elements such as water. || 27 ||
Thus, when the multitude of causal factors have reached their exhaustion from all sides and the "eightfold city" has come to rest, the body falls motionless.
He says that this very thing constitutes her abandonment of the body: "Thus," [he says]. || 28 ||
Due to the delusion of thinking "I am the thinker," latent impressions (vāsanās) undergo vibration;
impelled by that, the mind internally remembers one thing and forgets another of its own accord.

If it is asked by what cause the emergence of the *puryaṣṭaka* (the subtle body) occurs, it is due to the vibration of the heart-lotus; and that vibration arises from the recollection of one's prior states as an enjoyer and so forth. That recollection, in turn, arises from the vibration of latent impressions (*vāsanā*); and in the vibration of latent impressions, the cause is the consciousness of the Intellect (*cit*) taking on the form of an object due to the ignorance of its own true nature. Thus, [the process] is directed toward the reality.

The mind’s state of being directed toward objects of cognition—characterized by the process of apprehension and consisting essentially in extroversion—is the very first thing that must be restrained through human effort;
with this intention, he says: "Because the mind ceases from cognizing objects. (29)
Through the throbbing of the petals of the heart-lotus, the subtle body (puryaṣṭaka) becomes manifest;
when the flow within the machine of the heart-lotus is obstructed, the subtle body perishes.
"Because of being obstructed by movement from the vehicle," that is to say, while it is stationary. || 30 ||
As long as the *puryaṣṭaka* exists within the body, so long does that [individual] live;
when the *puryaṣṭaka* has ceased, O twice-born one, the body is said to be dead. (31)
When, due to the awakening of conflicting impurities and by virtue of the states of cutting and piercing,
the mechanism of the heart-lotus does not vibrate within, [then the supreme state arises].

This is due to the awakening and provocation of the mutually contradictory impurities known as wind, bile, and phlegm, as well as the impurities of the latent tendencies of passion, hatred, and so forth;
and because of the cutting, piercing, and other such injuries to the body caused by weapons and the like. "Internally" means within the body. (32)
Then the city of eight (puryaṣṭaka) gradually attains peace in the sky,
just as a succession of winds ceases when the mechanism of the wind is obstructed.
In a wind-machine, such as a fan and the like. || 33 ||
By the power of self-awareness, the individual soul falls into a state of helplessness;
the lotus-machine situated within the body flows perpetually.

One's own consciousness is volition; through its power comes helplessness, the thousands of sufferings such as death, and so forth. Whether it be all or one, that which exists at that time—[the form] "dā" is used here because of the rule for the suffix *dā*, and thus "nityadā" is a Vedic usage. || 34 ||
Those from whose hearts pure latent impressions (*vāsanā*) do not depart, who possess a stable and uniform life-force—they are liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*) and long-lived. (35)

For this very reason, he says "vāsanā" [in verse 35], stating that for those who are devoid of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of enjoyment, there is no subjection to death due to the absence of the corresponding volitions (*saṃkalpa*); "vimalā" means free from impurities such as passion (*rāga*).
When the lotus-machine is restrained and the vital breath has attained peace, this body, losing its fortitude, falls upon the earth like a piece of wood or a clod of earth. (36)
Just as the subtle body (puryaṣṭaka) becomes merged in the wind within the ether,
even so, O Sage, the mind then attains dissolution right there.
In the space-wind, that is, in the vital breath (prāṇa) which is the wind within the space of the heart. || 37 ||
But the mind, long practiced in such states and inscribed with latent impressions (vāsanā), wanders here and there and perceives the manifold world of heaven, hell, and so forth. (38)

Thus, for one whose mind has become sluggish and who, awakened by unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) that brings about experiences in heaven, hell, and so forth, the departure from the space of the heart (*hārdākāśa*) through the eyes, the crown of the head, or other parts of the body,
as well as the journey to the world of Yama and the enjoyment of heaven and hell, is merely one's own mental construction; heaven and the like do not exist externally.
With the intention that there are other names [for it], he says "sucira" (for a very long time).

This means: by which [name] there has been, from a very long time—that is, from beginningless time—the state of possessing various bodies and so forth suitable for those respective enjoyments. The phrase "wherever that may be" is intended to refute the notion that heaven and the like exist in a fixed location. || 38 ||
Deprived of mind and vital breath, the body becomes a corpse, just as a house falls into utter desolation when its inhabitants have gone far away. (39)
The all-pervading consciousness, through its power of intellection, having become a living soul, resides in the mind;
assuming the body of the "eightfold city," it becomes the subtle, transportable embodied being.

He describes the sequence of her assumption of another body with the verse beginning "sarvagā" (all-pervading). She is the all-pervading consciousness of Brahman itself, [acting] from the state of consciousness that has entered into the forms of name and form, as stated in the Śruti: "Having entered by means of this living self, let me manifest names and forms. || 40 ||
Having embraced the five subtle elements (tanmātra) within the mind, she remains established there;
through the power of mental construction, she perceives a gross form like the delusion of a dream. (41)

The subtle elements are the *tanmātras*; the aggregate of these five is the mind, known as the *puryaṣṭaka* or subtle body (*ativāhika-deha*). [This arises] from *bhāva*, which means from volitional intention (*saṃkalpa*). || 41 ||
Through firm cultivation, one who is thereafter filled with aesthetic relish (rasa) forgets, in an instant, the entire state of the subtle body (ātivāhika-deha).
Possessing aesthetic flavor, she is endowed with the power of the ego-sense. || 42 ||
While this body is indeed unreal, the cultivation of artificial conceptions leads the unreal to the state of reality and even leads the real to the state of unreality. (43)

In this gross body of the aforementioned characteristics, [the mind] brings about the unreality of the world—that is, it causes it to appear real through superimposition—and [it brings about] its own reality, which is its state of being Brahman; [it also brings about] its unreality, meaning its status of not existing or not appearing, which is its fitness for its own non-perception. || 43 ||
For, having become individual souls through its conscious aspect, it becomes the mind; the mind then mounts the chariot of the subtle body (puryaṣṭaka), and from that, the world arises.
He states the sequence of the mind's wandering with the words "sarvaga" (all-pervading): by means of a portion—that is, by means of the portion reflected in the intellect (buddhi). || 44 ||
It fully raises up the body consisting of the eightfold city and composed of wind;
then, like a Vetāla animated by the beating of the heart, it is said that "it lives. (45)

It consists of wind and is abundant with the vital breath that has become like a thread. When he causes it to rise, then, having entered the heart, he becomes like a Vetāla—meaning, one who is throbbing and characterized by movement—and thus he is said by people to be "living," as if he were Śiva. || 45 ||
When the eightfold city [of the subtle body] has perished and the mind dissolves into the ether, then this body throbs and is called "dead. (46)
In the sky—that is, in the heart-space (hārdākāśa) which is Brahman—he, though insentient like wood or a clod of earth, shines forth and becomes manifest. || 46 ||
By the power of its own nature, the living being falls into forgetfulness and reaches a state of impotence, like a leaf that becomes withered through helplessness under the sway of time. (47)
Having forgotten his own nature as the ageless and deathless Brahman, he himself encounters and attains the incapacity residing in the aged body. || 47 ||
O Sage, when the lotus-mechanism is seized and obstructed by the power of the individual soul (jīva-śakti), and when the vital breath (prāṇa) has come to a complete stop,
the human being dies.

Then he says that one dies as before: "by the power of the individual soul" (jīvaśaktyā). This means when [the mind] is untouched by the power of memory related to the individual soul as previously described, and for that very reason, being obstructed from its movement. || 48 ||
Just as leaves, one after another, fall from a tree over time, so too do the bodies of men perish. (49)

With the intention that "transmigration" (saṃsaraṇa) therein should be understood as the repeated assumption of various bodies ending in old age and death, he says "yathā" (as). [This refers to] "of men," that is, of living beings. || 49 ||
The bodies of embodied beings are born and they die, as are the leaves of trees; what cause for lamentation is there in that? (50)
In the ocean of consciousness, these rows of body-bubbles surge forth—some here, others there; the wise man places no reliance upon them. 51.
Although consciousness is all-pervading, it is reflected in this mind; for no other thing can receive an object except through a mirror. 52.
He restates what has already been said in order to conclude it: "sarvagā" (all-pervading), etc. || 52 ||
In the vast, pure sky of consciousness, efforts take form and manifest as things not identical with it;
clamorous with noise and clearly beautiful, they serve only to cause the torment of delusion regarding various bodies. (53)

Spread all around in the pure sky of consciousness (*cit*), they consist of efforts—the maturation of one's own previous virtuous and non-virtuous endeavors. For this very reason, they are resonant with the clamor of laughter, weeping, and other sounds during the experience of the fruits of pleasure and pain. Yet, being not identical to that [consciousness], they take the form of the world of living beings, which abounds in both consciousness and the unconscious.

Conceptual constructions, vivid and delightful, appearing charming at first glance, manifest for the sake of tormenting the self-delusion through the error of birth, death, and so forth by means of various bodies; that is to say, they appear. || 53 ||
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "Reflection on the Fall of the Body," in the Nirvāṇa Section of the Means to Liberation, within the glorious Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa composed by the Sage.
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "Reflection on the Fall of the Body," in the first half of the Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The Thirty-third Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
O you who bear the crescent moon as your crest-ornament, [listen to this] of the great-souled essence of consciousness (cittattva).
How has duality come to that which is infinite and of a single form? || 1 ||

Just as the distinctions between the individual soul and the world are constructed by the conceptualizations of delusion, so too are they to be understood through inquiry alone; this is explained here by means of reasoning.

Regarding what was stated—that although consciousness is all-pervading, it is reflected in this mind—and what was further stated—that through firm contemplation, it subsequently becomes imbued with aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) therein—Vasiṣṭha raises an objection concerning the inconsistency of both these points:

"O you who bear the crescent moon as your crest! [For] the word 'half' (*ardha*) refers to the sixteenth part... (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the full argument would likely continue by pointing out that since the moon has sixteen digits, the term "half" implies eight, whereas the reflection of the entire consciousness in a single mind is logically problematic.)

Since the word *ardha* does not denote an equal part, it is not neuter; consequently, the rule *ardhaṃ napuṃsakam* does not apply, and thus [the compound] is a genitive *tatpuruṣa*. Of that reality (*tattva*) characterized by consciousness—which is infinite (devoid of limitations imposed by space, time, or substance), uniform, and free from internal, external, or other-internal distinctions—that which has the nature of a living being (*jīva*) is its "homogeneous" aspect.

And how has this duality—the form of the insentient world consisting of a different genus—come to be? Is it from itself or from another? Not the first, because [the Self] is changeless and partless. Nor the second, because a second entity is simply unestablished; such is the meaning. || 1 ||
And how, O Mahādeva, does that which is rooted and crowded with synonyms lead to the affliction of suffering when it is warded off by wisdom? (2)

But if you say that it has simply vanished because it was without a cause, then— since there is no evidence for such a contraction— that [samsara], which is crowded and pervaded by bonds consisting of infinite millions of its own permutations, and which has become firmly established through long-standing continuity,

how could it be overcome by wisdom? For through the realization of reality, [the bondage] is extremely weak when compared to [the samsaric state] in terms of both its unity and its adventitious nature.
Even if it were prevented, it would lead to the infliction of ultimate suffering;
for the annihilation of even a single signless [bond] is not established, and even if one were somehow annihilated, because other infinite such bonds remain,
the repeated arising of various other signless bonds would be unavoidable.
It is not tenable to argue that there is no fault because that [world] is merely false, having as its cause the *māyā*—the power of Brahman—described previously;
for is that [power] adventitious or innate? In the first case, upon reflection, is it produced from itself or is it something to be imposed through connection with another?

Since this leads to faults such as the impossibility of liberation (*anirmokṣa*) or infinite regress (*anavasthā*), [it cannot be the former]. As for the innate [power], like the heat of fire, while [it exists],...

Because it would be impossible to remove [the world] from Brahman, liberation would remain an impossibility, and there would be the undesirable consequence of rendering the scriptural teachings on non-duality (aikarasya) tasteless.

Furthermore, if the power of Māyā were false, then because it would be absolutely non-existent, it could not produce effects from what is non-existent; thus, that very doctrine of causeless dualistic production would arise. If, however, it were real, [it would be removed] by knowledge...

Because cessation is impossible, there is the fault of non-liberation; thus, "non-liberation" is a rope with two ends. Furthermore, in the final analysis, no one can establish a third category distinct from existence and non-existence. For by that very same category, duality would remain unavoidable even after the attainment of knowledge. Indeed, that third category is neither the first nor the second, as understood by the knower.
It is possible [to say this], because knowledge is not an agent and because it is impossible for one thing to possess the nature of another.
The Lord said: "For when that Brahman exists as the one Reality, it is indeed all-powerful."
Then this arising of the conceptualization of duality and unity is indeed rootless. || 3 ||

We have not set out to establish the duality of the living world and so forth by means of valid means of knowledge; rather, we rely on the method of superimposition and negation (*adhyāropāpavāda*) in order to negate that which has been clung to through delusion since beginningless time. In that regard, concerning superimposition at the beginning of creation:

The conceptualization of all things—the instrumental causes such as desire, action, and latent impressions; the material cause such as Brahman-ignorance (avidyā) and so forth; the sequence beginning with space; and the various distinctions of the individual and collective, gross and subtle, and the sheaths (kośas)—all of this, though itself unreal, has been devised by the Śruti as a means for becoming acquainted with the Real Entity.

Because it is non-deceptive regarding its purpose—the ultimate truth—it is superior in comparison to the conceptualizations of other proponents; thus, for the sake of generating confidence in listeners, it is established in the scriptures through arguments based on the worldly perspective alone. However, once that which is the self of all and the witness of all has been familiarized, then, in order to bring about the realization of its non-duality, one relies solely on the vision of ultimate reality and [the worldly perspective] is set aside.

Thus, having accepted oneness in that [Brahman], the Lord Śrī Bhagavān provides a resolution with the words beginning "possessing all powers," intending to show: "How do you not perceive that by pointing out the impossibility of duality—which is contradictory to that oneness—you are contradicting what you yourself have accepted and contradicting your own established doctrine? This is when Brahman, from the perspective of conventional discourse...

But from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha-dṛśā*), it is established that only the One, which possesses all powers (*sarvaśakti*), exists; thus, when these two views are accepted, then the arising of that [duality]— which is characterized by duality and unity and originates from a single portion of the one possessing all powers— is entirely baseless in relation to that [ultimate reality].

Since superimposition occurs from the perspective of empirical convention (*vyavahāra-dṛṣṭi*) and negation (*apavāda*) occurs from the perspective of the Supreme Self (*paramātma-dṛṣṭi*), it is not the case that—

according to the empirical view— the arrival of the duality of the individual soul and the world is untenable in light of the Omniscient and Omnipotent One who is established by the Śruti as "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving, whose austerity consists of knowledge."

Because its very nature is determined by the means of knowledge that apprehends the subject (the substratum), this very Brahman is without prior, without posterior, without interior, and without exterior; it is that which is to be reached through the vision of ultimate reality as shown in the scripture: "Where one sees nothing else, hears nothing else, and understands nothing else—that is the Infinite (bhūmā). But in that [Brahman], there is never at any time...
The meaning is that since either duality or its opposite, unity, would necessarily follow, the objection raised regarding the impossibility of those [states] therein is entirely baseless. || 3 ||
If duality exists, then indeed oneness would not exist; if oneness exists, then there would be a dual nature.
Since both parts are of the nature of consciousness, that [duality] is also unreal because of its being of the nature of consciousness.

[Objection: Surely, by such scriptural passages as "In this, there is no diversity whatsoever; for there is not a second thing existing other than that, which is all-pervading, consisting of consciousness and bliss, formless, and wonderful," duality alone is negated and not unity; thus, since unity is not contradictory [to scripture], how can it be negated on an equal footing with duality? To this, he says: "satī" (being).

When duality is established, unity is postulated in order to exclude it; and when unity is established, that very same unity is postulated as being accompanied by another unity to constitute duality. Since these are postulations that are mutually dependent, they are of equal status.
In that case, if one were to postulate a property characterized as unity that is distinct from those [two unities], [the same logic would apply].
The meaning is that this too is non-existent, because it would entail the contradiction of the absolute uniformity of consciousness. || 4 ||
Due to the absence of one, there is an absence here of both oneness and duality;
without one, there is no second, and without a second, there is no oneness.
Because cause and effect possess the same essence, they are of one form;
thus, here, even for seeds and the like that end in a fruit, there is the conceptualization of transformation.

Now, he says "kārya... [in the verse], stating that even when there is a mixing of the two views—the conventional and the ultimate—for the sake of practical discourse such as instruction, there is no contradiction between the ultimate reality and the duality of the living beings and the world through conventional existence, because a twofold nature of existence is postulated. This is illustrated by the case of a seed and so forth, ending with its fruit, where one perceives, "This is that very same thing."

The meaning is that, just as in the case of a substance that persists and is recognized as having a single nature, the conceptualization of multiplicity due to modification is likewise tenable. || 6 ||
The state of consciousness, being identical with that [object], manifests by itself through the non-duality of subject and object;
it does not differ from modifications and the like, because they are internal to it and because it is their essence.

If, however, a conventional reality (*vyāvahārikasattā*) distinct from ultimate reality (*paramārthasattā*) is not admitted for all transformations (*vikāra*), then duality is all the more clearly established as being merely a mental construction (*cittvikalpa*); thus, with the intention that your objection is equivalent to pointing out a contradiction regarding the duality of Rāhu’s head (which is non-existent), he says: "The state of being mind" (*cittvam*). This is because its very essence (*sāra*) and ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) is that [mind] alone within. And so:

Whether it be the position that illusion and its effects possess a separate existence, the position that they do not possess a separate existence, the third alternative position of non-existence, or any other position imagined by various disputants— such as the positions of primordial matter (pradhāna), atoms (paramāṇu), momentariness, non-momentariness, consciousness (vijñāna), or emptiness (śūnyatā)— whatever [it may be].

Let some [position] be accepted by you; nevertheless, since everything that touches the non-attached, non-dual pure consciousness is established in dependence upon that consciousness and is merely a mental construct (cittavikalpa), bondage is impossible for consciousness at any time. Therefore, the suggestion that there could be no liberation is utterly cast aside—this is the intended meaning. || 7 ||
This conceptualization of modifications and so forth, arising from that [reality] with respect to objects, attains meaningfulness through various relations of cause and effect and the like. (8)
He establishes that very fact of its being the essence [of all things] with the words "vikārādi" (modification,

etc.). Since this conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), characterized by the six modifications of existence (*ṣaḍbhāvavikāra*) and characterized by its substrata such as jars and the like, arises and manifests from the existent reality (*sadvastu*) itself, it attains purposefulness through its capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*)— such as the fetching of water— and other such functions.
It culminates in enjoyment; and since enjoyment consists in nothing other than resting within consciousness, the meaning is that its essence is solely that [consciousness]. || 8 ||
The waves that exist in water are equal to those on a mountain;
even he for whom a sprout from the moon is real is like the horn of a hare.

Thus, since the world consists of nothing but conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), some things—such as waves in water—are conventional (*vyāvahārika*); the waves in the water of a mirage in the desert are apparent (*prātibhāsika*);
and things such as the son of a barren woman or the horn of a hare are absolutely non-existent (*atyantāsant*).

Thus, he says "waves" to show that even the conceptualization of internal differences belongs only to the ignorant. For that knower of reality for whom even a sprout of rice or barley emerging from a hare is nothing but Brahman,
those waves well-known in water are equal to the waves imagined upon the water atop a mountain— even that mountain itself.

It is equal to a hare’s horn; the meaning is that there is equality among all three cases regarding both the inherent non-existence [of the hare’s horn] and the conceptualization of existence through the reality of Brahman. || 9 ||
The realization of the reality here brings about integration; therefore, enough with verbal conceptualizations!
For exclusion and the like, O twice-born one, are indeed difficult to sever from that which is expressed by words. (10)

However, in this world, that exclusion (*vyavaccheda*)—characterized by the mutual differentiation of all things—which arises from ignorance, is unified by the cognition of reality, which is the very direct realization of truth (*tattvasākṣātkāra*). It brings these shattered fragments to a state of oneness, as if by means of a repair. In such a matter, enough with verbal conceptualizations and the presentation of logical arguments!

There is no goal to be accomplished. For as long as ignorance has not departed, even through thousands of arguments concerning words, their referents, and so forth, duality—such as exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) and the like—which is established by immediate error, is difficult to eradicate; this is the meaning. || 10 ||
The omnipotence of Brahman is not truly divided [into parts], just as the collection of waves, droplets, and billows is not distinct from the mass of water. || 11 ||

But when viewed through the vision of reality, Brahman’s possession of all powers—its illusory form as the entire universe—is not distinct from it in essence; it merely remains latent within that very [Brahman]. This is the meaning. || 11 ||
Just as flowers, shoots, leaves, and so forth belong to the creeper and nothing else,
so too duality, unity, the world, "thou-ness," and "I-ness" belong to Consciousness alone.

And thus, according to the principle shown in the Śruti—“The nature of fire has departed; the modification is a mere handle of speech, a name; the truth is simply the three forms”—just as the distinctions between its flowers, shoots, and so forth vanish upon seeing the unity of the creeper, so too the distinctions of the world are unreal upon seeing the Reality. Therefore, he says that your question is utterly groundless.
Any differentiation of consciousness that is produced by factors such as place, time, and modification—that is declared to be unreal; therefore, this question of yours is not appropriate here.
That division which was made—that is consciousness; it is indeed consciousness alone, for duality does not exist there at all.
Thus, your statement that "how has duality come to be there? is an assertion of what is unreal. The meaning is that your question regarding this unreal subject matter is not appropriate. || 13 ||
Furthermore, the powers such as those of space, time, action, existence, and necessity are indeed of the nature of consciousness;
they have descended spontaneously from the very being of consciousness itself.
Since they have fallen from consciousness itself and possess the reality of existence, they are therefore of the very nature of consciousness. 14.
In this world, the reality of consciousness (cittattva) is known by such designations as "mind" (citta), "object of thought" (cetya), "consciousness" (cit), "Brahmā," and so forth;
just as a wave of water remains the same water while being fit for the designation of "wave" and the like.

The mind, the object of thought, and their activities—their aggregate is the proliferation of form (rūpa-prapañca), which is indeed the reality of consciousness (cittattva). Thus, even the proliferation of names (nāma-prapañca) consisting of all things from Brahmā down to a blade of grass is known to be nothing but consciousness. Just as the common essence of water, which follows along with the waves, remains capable of being designated by terms such as "wave" and so forth, so it is in this case. || 15 ||
To the extent that there is a state of being wavy in the great ocean of the play of consciousness—which itself never possesses waves—that indeed is attachment to the objects of thought. 16.
The meaning is that this very transformation, which is like being rippled, is itself the connection with the object of cognition. || 16 ||
This very supreme Brahman is celebrated by such names as Satya, Īśvara, Śiva, Śūnya, Eka, Paramātman, and so forth. || 17 ||
By the word "void" (śūnya), the term "non-existent" (asat) found in the Śruti passage, "In the beginning this was non-existent," is indicated. || 17 ||
Thus, that form of the Supreme Self which transcends the category of form, and that which is my stainless name, is not an object of words. (18)

He says "thus" (evam) to show that, in the ultimate sense, that alone is the true self (mattattva). "That which transcends forms, words, and names is 'I'. The word "but" (tu) serves to exclude the forms with specific shapes currently being perceived. That [Self] is not an object of speech (girām), of words (vācām), nor of the mind (manasām). || 18 ||
Whatever is seen there belongs to that great consciousness, which is like a creeper; for it is not distinct from it, since it consists of that very essence. 19.

The syntactical connection is as follows: that which is seen as this world is the fruit, sprout, flower, and so forth, of that creeper characterized by consciousness (cilliṅga), which is consciousness itself (acit). || 19 ||
When consciousness, being called "existence," undergoes the initiation of great ignorance,
it perceives itself as a living soul and externality, just as one sees two moons.

But if you ask for the sake of discernment about the very unreal nature of the living world, then listen: that Great Ignorance (avidyā) is like a spectacles-plate colored with various hues; when she becomes such as this, she is designated as the "living being" (jīva). Being thus designated, she perceives her own externality as if there were two moons.
The meaning is that one perceives the state of the external world of living beings. || 20 ||
Having contemplated by its own nature that "I am indeed thus," it spontaneously undergoes, as it were, a state of otherness consisting of its own conceptual construction.
I am other than that—un-Brahman and of the nature of non-consciousness. || 21 ||
That form which possesses a stain, though its nature is stainless,
perceives by means of consciousness alone once it has entered the river of saṃsāra.

The meaning is this: although it abides in a form that is entirely stainless, because it has assumed the form of the "eightfold city" (puryaṣṭaka) as if it were stained, it reaches the river of saṃsāra and perceives only through its conditioned consciousness (aupādhika-cetana), not through its stainless consciousness. || 22 ||
By this very [consciousness], the embodied consciousness attains oneness with the state of being a living soul;
through the manifestation of the principle of consciousness (cittattva), the living soul lives, being composed of that.

By means of this "city of eight" (puryaṣṭaka), it attains oneness with it, characterized by the superimposition of identity; being composed of that and abounding in consciousness, it lives—that is, it undergoes the activities of breathing and so forth. || 23 ||
Even the subtle body (ātivāhika-deha), having reached the state of living beings, becomes the fivefold mental conception and fully perceives, "I am a material substance. (24)

Having thus resolved the objection that "although consciousness is omnipresent, it is reflected in this mind," he now describes the sequence of its acquisition of the gross body in order to resolve the subsequent objection that "it becomes possessed of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) therein through firm contemplation" (*dṛḍhabhāvanā*). He begins with the phrase "the subtle body" (*ātivāhika*), referring to the fivefold process of contemplation (*bhāvanāpañcaka*).

Having become of the nature of the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the gross body composed of the five elements, it knows: "I have become the substance consisting of rice, barley, sesame, beans, and so forth, for the sake of obtaining a body. This is the meaning of the Vedic text: "These are born here as rice, barley, sesame, and beans. In this Śruti, the word "iti" is intended to indicate merely those substances suitable for a future body.

Therefore, the general statement "he knows 'I am substance'" is made to indicate that even in places where he attains bodies such as those of immobile beings or those born from sweat, there exists for him the presence of substances such as water that are conducive to the respective seeds [of those bodies]. || 24 ||
That substance, once consumed by a living being, quickly attains the state of *vīrya* (vital potency);
from that, I am born as one possessed of life, knowing—that is, consisting of—experiential awareness. (25)

The meaning is that [the soul] knows itself as virility in the form of semen, then as the state of a seed in trees and other plants, and thereafter, through the process of conception in a woman, it perceives: "I have become a vital, gross body. || 25 ||
Through the sequence beginning with egoity (ahaṃtā), due to the delusion of experiencing the five [elements], one perceives everything as stationary or moving; thus it truly becomes that very thing.
Brahman itself, whose nature is pure experience, through the aforementioned sequence of "I-ness" (ahaṃtā) and so forth, becomes the aggregate of the five—the pentad—which is the gross body.
Through the doors of the eyes and other senses, it perceives the external world, both the stationary and the moving, as a delusion of that experience;
furthermore, by means of the latent impressions (vāsanā) thereof, it itself becomes those very things—this is the meaning. || 26 ||
Through a chance occurrence like the "crow and the palm fruit," and by the exhaustion of firm habitual practice,
it abandons its subtle form due to its connection with other latent impressions (vāsanā).

Now, one might ask: when the body of a mosquito or similar creature was previously abandoned, how did the cessation of the subtle state of the *puryaṣṭaka*—which remained in the form of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) shaped by that body and possessed a firmly practiced form as a mosquito—occur; and how was the acquisition of the gross state in the form of an elephant, which had not been so practiced, attained? To this, he says: "By chance" (*kākatālīya*).
Just as in the accidental encounter between a crow and a palm fruit, the very karma that causes the death of the crow is the cause and nothing else, so too,

when deeply ingrained latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are overcome and the latent impression of being an "I" as an elephant— which has long been suppressed— arises, karma alone is the cause. However, due to its conjunction with another manifest latent impression of an elephant, even that which has been practiced for a long time [is displaced].
The meaning is that it abandons the subtle form of a mosquito. || 27 ||
Through its own consciousness of duality, duality arises even for a single person, just as a radiant vampire appears through a man's mental construction of a vampire. (28)

He states the illustrations for the suppression of prior latent impressions (*vāsanā*) by the arising of opposing latent impressions, and for the strengthening of the subsequent impression through repeated practice, beginning with the words "dvitva" (duality), etc. (Verse 28).
From the realization of non-duality, duality ceases even for the Self;
just as the agency of a person ceases through the resolve, "I do not act. (29)
From the conceptualization of duality, duality arises even for that which is one;
through the cognition of non-duality, duality perishes even for that which is manifold. (30)
[This applies] even to a manifold world. || 30 ||
Indeed, duality does not exist in the Self by virtue of its being the supreme Self, because it is eternally changeless and so forth, and because it is omnipresent. (31)
For that which is fashioned by one's own volition indeed ceases with the cessation of volition;
O Sage, it is like a kingdom of the mind or a city of the Gandharvas.
That which is destroyed through the absence of volitional construction (*asaṃkalpa*)—such is [the nature of] that which is well-known. || 32 ||
Likewise, there is suffering in the forming of a mental construction, not in the destruction of that construction;
the yakṣa of mental construction exists in the creation of a city of Gandharvas, but not in its dissolution.

The word *tathā* is used in the sense of "moreover. There is hardship—that is, fatigue—in the act of *saṃkalpana*, which is the mental effort of construction; however, there is no such hardship in the destruction of that *saṃkalpa*. This is because its accomplishment occurs spontaneously through mere indifference (*audāsīnya*). And since this meaning is well-known, he says: "The Yakṣa of *saṃkalpa*. Here, *gandharva* refers to the mind, and its city is the city constructed by the desires of the mind.

The meaning is that in the act of creation, *saṃkalpa* (volition) alone is renowned as the divine artisan (*yakṣa*) because of its capacity for constructing even the most inconceivable designs; however, this is not the case regarding their destruction. || 33 ||
Since this suffering has arrived merely through the intensification of one's own volition, it can be destroyed merely by the absence of such volition; what cause for distress is there in this? (34)
Affliction is suffering. || 34 ||
Whatever one conceives in thought, a person sinks into suffering;
by not conceiving anything at all, one enjoys imperishable happiness. (35)
When your consciousness was not liberated from the serpent of volitional construction,
you did not shine brilliantly in the Nandana grove.
Even though you are situated in the Nandana garden, which is preeminent in all virtues, you do not shine as one whose afflictions have been completely exhausted. 36.
Having brought about the destruction of the clouds of conceptualization with the winds of your own discernment, attain supreme purity, like the expanse of the sky in autumn. (37)
If so, what is the means for the destruction of conceptual construction? He states it: "By one's own discrimination," and so forth. (37)
Dry up the intoxicated river of conceptualization with the jewel-mantra;
there, having comforted yourself while being carried along, remain free from mental activity.
Shaken by the wind of volition and wandering like bits of leaves and straw, behold the conscious self by taking refuge in the elemental ether. 39.
It is deluded like fragments or pieces of leaves and grass; [it exists] in the elemental space and in the space of the hearts of all beings.
Having warded off the impurity of your own mental constructs by means of the Self, and having attained supreme serenity, become possessed of the highest bliss. (40)
For the Self consists of all powers; in whatever manner it intensely contemplates, it then perceives that very thing as a manifestation of its own volition.
Whatever object [is perceived]. || 41 ||
This world has arisen as mere conceptualization and is false;
O Brahman, it dissolves somewhere by mere non-conceptualization.
The entire cluster of the web of births, stirred by the wind of volitional thought,
comes to rest in the supreme state through contact with the wind of non-volition.
The mass of clouds, characterized by births and manifested as networks, is stirred and brought forth by the east wind characterized by volitional thought (*saṃkalpa*);
yet, through contact with the west wind characterized by non-volitional thought (*asaṃkalpa*), it comes to rest in the supreme state, the space of Brahman—that is to say, it dissolves. || 43 ||
Make this thorny creeper of craving, which has reached such growth, withered away by uprooting its foundation: conceptual construction. 44.
The arising of appearances and the cessation of appearances—just as a city of the Gandharvas, so too is the delusion of cyclic existence. 45.

With the intention that even when ignorance, desire, and volition have perished, if the world should still appear, then the doctrine of "creation upon perception" (dṛṣṭasṛṣṭivāda)—established by the experience of those liberated while living—is what remains; thus he says:
"Forgetting for a time that 'I am the Lord,' the king grieves."
As long as the thought "I am the lord of the earth" has not arisen in his heart, [he remains a fool]. (46)

With the intention that the appearance of the world is a cause of sorrow only as long as there is ignorance, and not thereafter, he says: "O Brahmin, for him, the memory of that [past state] does not exist through the present [knowledge], just as the rainy season is dispelled by the arrival of autumn, which carries away its dullness. (47)

Now, one might object: "Even for a knower of reality (*tattvavid*), the current memory 'I am Brahman' might be obscured by a continuous succession of memories of worldly existence long practiced in the past; and thus, there would again be the possibility of the sorrow of *saṃsāra*. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Not for him" (*nāsya*). For this sovereign of the stages (*bhūmipa*)—that is, the knower of reality—the memory "I am a king" [does not arise] because of the present memory born from that authoritative instruction (*āptopadeśa*).

The memory of former suffering, sublated by the recollection "I am Brahman," is not capable of obscuring—that is, of concealing—the [Self] through its own dullness; just as the rainy season, once dispelled by the arrived autumn, is no longer capable of obscuring through the dullness of its clouds—this is the meaning. || 47 ||
By means of a continuous flow, that very desire suddenly increases within the mind;
just as the high-pitched sound of a lute string itself pervades the auditory sense. (48)

If one asks what the cause of its predominance is, [the answer is: produced by human effort characterized by the practice of reflection (*manana*) and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*), that very mental modification (*cittavṛtti*)—which flows with a dense current—increases spontaneously and becomes capable of suppressing the others. Just as, between the sounds of a high-pitched and a low-pitched string, whichever sound is louder suppresses the other and prevails in the auditory perception (*śruti*).
It pervades the ear; the meaning is that it is heard. || 48 ||
Cultivate this single contemplation: "I am alone; I am the Self. Endowed with that contemplation, you shall indeed become that very [Self] sufficiently. 49.

With the intention that "this continuous, uninterrupted remembrance 'I am indeed Brahman' alone is my primary mental worship, not external," he says: "I am. I alone, without a second, am Śiva, the Lord;

and He, characterized by the notion of "I" (ahaṃtva) and ego (ahaṃkāra), is the Self, whose sole essence is eternal, immediate consciousness. Thus, [he offers] this single, uninterrupted [remembrance].

Cultivate the flow of mindfulness through meditation. Endowed with such a form of meditative worship of the Divine, you yourself become Śiva; you are fully and utterly so, and not by any other kind of worship—this is the meaning. || 49 ||

For thus, this reality—which is impossible [to conceive as separate], radiant with passionlessness, the supreme state, and the one supreme God—is, in acts of worship, the form of the worshiper, the act of worship, and the object of worship; being both something and yet nothing, it is the single embodiment of the state of consciousness.

In the manner thus described, this external worship is simply impossible for those such as you. For it shines forth brilliantly only among those who lack dispassion and are attached to trivial fruits. That which is worthy of you, however, is the supreme state, that ultimate reality, the one God who is the Supreme Brahman itself—the very one who, in acts of worship, is both the worshiper and the owner of the materials of worship.

The worship performed with the sixteen services, as well as the object of worship such as an image or a liṅga, becomes something insignificant, as if nothing at all; for that entire collection is merely the steps of the mind, its volitions, and thus has the meaning of being nothing more than a mental construction. || 50 ||

Thus ends the thirty-third canto, titled "The Exposition of Duality and Unity," in the first part of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa, within the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, concerning the means to liberation.
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "The Exposition of Duality and Unity," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The thirty-fourth canto.
Īśvara said:
Thus does this universe exist, consisting of both the existent and the non-existent, and having the form of the gods.
Therefore, it is free from the state of both duality and unity, yet it is also joined with duality and unity. || 1 ||
The state of deep sleep, the fourth (turya), and likewise the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta) are taught here;
finally, it is described that the Lord rests therein.

Thus, by this worship of the deity, the universe—which is unreal from the perspective of the obstructing vision (*bādhadṛśā*) and real from the perspective of the foundational vision (*adhiṣṭhānadṛśā*)—is appropriately endowed with the form of a deity. In reality, it is free from the states of duality and unity, yet in conventional practice (*vyavahāre*), it is appropriately characterized by both duality and unity; such is the meaning of the resolution of all contradictions. || 1 ||
The state of being stained and deformed belongs to the realm of saṃsāra;
that which is stainless and beyond saṃsāra is of the nature of non-dual identity.

From where could there be that which consists of duality and unity, or from where could there be that which is free from them? To this he says: "of consciousness" (citer). The meaning is: because of the conceptualization that "blemish" is delusion, and the resulting deformity is the state of insentience. The phrase "not subject to transmigratory existence" (asaṃsāri) is used because it is so perceived; this is the ellipsis to be supplied. || 2 ||
The mind, having incurred the stain of the thought "I am this," becomes bound;
by realizing that this very power (kalā) is non-different from itself, one is liberated. (3)

He explains that very point clearly with the words "this" (iyam): "This" refers to that which takes the form of the visible body and so forth; [it is] this digit of consciousness (citkalā) which is capable of manifesting the visible world. || 3 ||
Due to the absence of the form of an object of consciousness, it abandons the non-existence of duality;
yet, because it does not maintain a state merged with pleasure and so forth as being real, it ceases in an instant.

Having attained duality through the existence of the form of objects—that is, due to the cause of mental cultivation—the star that is the nature of consciousness abandons its own undivided being and forgets it. United with the body, pleasure, pain, and so forth, it maintains its own state as "existent," whether that state be real or unreal; this is the stained condition. || 4 ||
Whether it be pure or partless, real or unreal—
thus freed from all names, words, and meanings, it is like space, though the soul of all.

He states the state of being free from blemish with the word "pure" (śuddhā): the meaning is that she is liberated from all conceptual constructions, such as "real" or "unreal," which are words whose referents are mere names; although she consists of all names and forms in conventional usage, her nature is like the sky—void (śūnya). || 5 ||
All this is incomparable and peaceful, traversing the three paths by means of the mind;
this is Brahman, the expanded, which has been expanded by the power that is the manifestation of space.
Having stated the meaning of the stainless state of *pratiṣṭhā*, he begins to demonstrate the distinctions between the stages (*bhūmikā*) such as deep sleep (*suṣupti*) and so forth:

"It expands"—that is, through the expansion of space (*ākāśavikāsā*), by means of its own power of *māyā* in such a manner, it proceeds via three paths characterized by waking, dreaming, and deep sleep; or characterized by creation, maintenance, and withdrawal; or characterized by the internal (*adhyātma*), the elemental (*adhibhūta*), and the celestial (*adhidaiva*).
The world has proceeded forth, manifested by the mind alone.
When the mind has been severed within the mind, which consists of one's own senses and limbs, and when the web of the world has vanished, concealed by the light of truth; || 7 ||
Therefore, he says "by the mind" to show that its cutting occurs precisely through the severing of the mind; [this is achieved] from the light of truth, that is, from direct realization.
The conceptual nature of the world-process, which consists of the fabrication of saṃsāra, is severed;
the existence of the one called the "living soul" (jīva) is like a parched seed. 8.

Thus, when conceptual constructions have been severed from the mind through the awakening to reality, he shows by means of characteristics and names that stage upon which the state of one liberated while living (jīvanmukta) first occurs, citing the *Śvetāśvatara*, *Kaṭhaka*, and *Chāndogya* Upaniṣads: "His greatness... and "...free from sorrow."

Regarding the etymological derivation (*nirvacana*) of the name "Svapiti" (He sleeps), in the analysis *svam api iti*, because of its usage with the word *iti*, the meaning is that it is a name derived from a particle (*itipadika*).

Although the name "Svapiti" exists even in the deep sleep (*suṣupti*) of the ignorant, nevertheless, through the awakening to reality (*tattvabodha*), there is the sublation (*bādha*) of ignorance, its marks (*liṅga*), and so forth; thus, in whichever limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) or in whichever ignorance (*avidyā*) [this occurs]...

The sense is that, because the two states of "laya" (dissolution) and "apya-ya" (merging) are absent, the word "api" which conveys merging also ceases; thus, only the word "iti," which signifies the attainment of one's own essential nature (svarūpa), remains, and it thereby becomes his name. || 8 ||
Known as Paśyantī, she casts off the chewing of objects of thought that have been grasped;
freed from the clouds of mental delusion, she is like the expanse of the autumnal sky.

Thus, because all objects of perception are sublated and only direct perception alone remains, she is also called "Paśyantī" (the Seer); this he states with the word "paśyantī. She is "utsṛjantī," meaning she abandons—that is, she relinquishes—the "carvaṇā" (chewing) of the "cetya" (the object of thought), which is the repeated recollection of it with pleasure. || 9 ||
Pure, abiding in the state of pure consciousness alone, yet having attained the agitation of the object of thought and consciousness,
she becomes possessed of all common characteristics while having crossed the ocean of worldly existence.

Although she previously experienced the restlessness of the knowable and the non-conscious, she now abides solely in the nature of consciousness; she is the universal existence (sattā) common to all, and it means that she remains as that alone. In this state, even while in the condition of being alive, one has crossed the ocean of worldly existence. || 10 ||

Having attained the supreme state, she who is matured by the expertise in the state of dreamless sleep from which there is no rebirth, has come to rest; having come to rest, she is expanded within that vast state.

Regarding the term *sauṣuptam*: according to the etymology provided by the author of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, "suṣuptam" means that which is "well" (*suṣṭhu*)—that is, consisting of unsurpassed bliss—and "slept" (*suptam*), meaning its own attainment. *Pāṇḍityam* is the state of being a *paṇḍita*; a *paṇḍita* is one who has attained (*itaḥ*) *paṇḍā*, which is knowledge born of the scriptures. Furthermore, [the text mentions] "one who is learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), free from evil (*avṛjin*), and unassailed by desire (*akāmahata*)."

This [bliss] is established by the experience of the wise, whose characteristics are shown in the Śruti, as in the passage beginning "He who among men is successful," which describes the progressively superior objective blisses— each hundredfold greater than the last— starting from human bliss and ending with the bliss of Hiraṇyagarbha; or else, it is the wisdom belonging to the state of deep sleep (*sauṣupta-pada*), that is, the station of deep sleep.

Her essential nature is self-luminous, consisting of the single mass of consciousness and full bliss, from which the dullness of one's own ignorance has been cast away; she is therefore "plump" (*pīvarī*) because of that.

Consequently, by the method of *bhāgatyāga-lakṣaṇā* (indication through the exclusion of a part), she is also designated as the state of "great sleep" (*mahāsuptapada*); this is the intended meaning. || 11 ||
This first step has been explained to you when the mind is stilled;
now hear, O best of Brahmins, the second, which is most purifying, regarding this Śakti.
Desiring to describe the subsequent state, he concludes the description of the first state with the word "etad" (this).
[This is] because of the strengthening of the power of consciousness (cicchakti). || 12 ||
This very power of consciousness (cicchakti), liberated from the mind and abounding in peace,
is free from all light and darkness, as beautiful as the vast expanse of space.
She is liberated from the lights—consisting of the sun, moon, fire, speech, and the organs of action—as well as from the darknesses, which are the obscurations of ignorance and their effects.
Like a dense line of deep sleep within a stone, like the flavor within salt, and like the power of vibration within the wind. || 14 ||

He states those specific qualities of it relative to the previous state in the verse beginning with "dense" (*ghana*). The connection is that "the supreme transformation" (*parāṃ pariṇatim*)—referring to all [the words], as the word *padānām* is understood as the remainder—is to be related as the object of comparison in what follows. || 14 ||
When, in due course, it reaches its ultimate transformation right there,
it then goes to the supreme space like the power of emptiness within the ether.
When that which belongs to the prior stage, through the power of practice, reaches a supreme transformation like the dense state of deep sleep and so forth,

then the void-potency (śūnya-śakti) existing in space becomes as if it has attained the state of the supreme space— the space of Brahman which is a single mass of consciousness— and thus abandons its orientation toward the objective aspect (cetyāṃśa).
The sequence follows from what precedes it. The meaning is that the emptiness of emergence by itself constitutes a distinction in terms of the result as well, compared to the previous state. || 15 ||
It surely abandons its orientation toward the objective sphere, just as water abandons its turbulence, as a gust of wind abandons its movement, and as a flower abandons its fragrance. (16)
Having abandoned both temporality and spatiality, she is entirely both with parts and without parts;
neither inert nor non-inert, vast, she bears an unnamed existence.

For action (*kriyā*) is a fraction (*kalā*) of time (*kāla*). A delimited object that requires space is a fraction of space (*ākāśa*). Because of these two, [the Self] possesses both temporality and spatiality; yet, by abandoning them—that is, by casting off everything merely visible—it does not "count" (conceptualize) anything, and thus it is the "partless-with-parts" (*sakalākalā*). It is not non-inert (*anajaḍā*) because there is no insentient thing to be excluded from it. It is "nameless" (*anāmikā*), meaning it is unfit for verbal designation.
It sustains existence characterized by the qualifiers to be mentioned hereafter. || 17 ||
She has attained the state of Great Being (Mahāsattā), which is unconditioned by space, time, and the like;
she is endowed with the fourth part of the fourth state (turyaturya), stainless, and free from disease. || 18 ||
She who is manifested by that fourth part which is beyond waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, and which is the fourth aspect beyond Virāj, Hiraṇyagarbha, and the Unmanifest.

O large-eyed one, [one should contemplate] that very [consciousness] which stands like a witness, which is everywhere and at all times, and which is intent upon the sweetness of universal illumination. (19)

Therefore, [she is] superior to all manifestations, all cognitions, and all sweet pleasures that have as their objects all things at all times and are based on all causal signs; she possesses such excellence and is more desirable [than they]. || 19 ||
This second state of the word has been explained to you, O observer of noble vows;
now listen as I shall declare the third, O best among those who know the words. (20)
Having concluded the second stage, called the Fourth (turyā), he introduces the third with the words "This" (eṣā):
"pada" means stage (bhūmikā). || 20 ||
This vision, by ceasing the vibration of the cognizable, reaches the state of the objectless reality;
transcending the meanings of words such as "Brahman" and "Self," it arises as the absolute alone.

Regarding that [state], he states the distinctions compared to the previous one with the words beginning "This" (*eṣā*) and so forth. "Vision" (*dṛk*) is the undivided mental modification (*akhaṇḍavṛtti*) having the form of Brahman; "the object" (*artha*) is Brahman pervaded by that [vision]. Because of the "turning" (*valana*) of these two—their becoming one like milk and water—they "cause to incline" (*namayati*), meaning they make it their sphere of experience; thus, it is the aspect that grasps the name. That which is sought (*arthyate*) or reached (*gamyate*) is the "object" (*artha*).

The aspect of the object of apprehension has reached the state of emptiness regarding both [subject and object]; for this very reason, it transcends the meaning of words and sentences such as "Brahman is the Self. Thus, the sense is that while the preceding stage is accessible only through *samprajñāta-samādhi* (cognitive absorption), this [present] stage is accessible through the establishment of *asamprajñāta-samādhi* (non-cognitive absorption); this is the distinction. || 21 ||
Through stability over time, she becomes established in her own state, stainless by virtue of the Supreme Self;
and because she possesses names such as "Beyond the Fourth" (turyātīta), she attains the supreme state.

By its steadfastness—that is, by being devoid of the six modifications of existence—it is self-abiding and stable even throughout time. By its own self, which is beyond even darkness (ignorance), it is free from all stain. That which is the supreme state, meaning the ultimate goal of human endeavor (paramapuruṣārtha). || 22 ||
That is the supreme, the ultimate limit, the primary state by virtue of its nature as Śiva;
it is the one, undivided consciousness, the third, purifying state. (23)
The supreme among all supremes, the ultimate pinnacle, the limit, by virtue of being the state of Śiva;

because it is the highest auspiciousness, it is the foremost among all auspicious things. It is the one, the primary, the undivided—that is, the state of consciousness free from interruption; this is the meaning of "the third. || 23 ||
O dear one, that [reality], which has long been established in this state and has gone far beyond all paths and travelers,
does not even come within the range of my words.
Abiding on this foundation, this stage,

[the practitioner] performs worship through all the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan) renowned in the Śaiva scriptures, through the paths such as Dhūmārcis and others renowned in the Vedas, and through those who traverse those paths.
The meaning is that it does not come within the range of the sense objects, but rather is experienced by itself alone. || 24 ||
"O Sage, you have described that which transcends the reckoning of the three paths;
remain eternally in that state," so said the eternal Lord. (25)

The meaning is that the eternal (sanātana) and constant (nitya) God is one who has transcended the three paths beginning with waking—namely, the mental construction (kalanā) and the number four (turīyatva) which depends upon it—and He is not anything else; for the Śruti says, "Other than this is the afflicted" (ato 'nyad ārtam). || 25 ||
O Sage, this entire universe consists of that [Brahman], because it is known as being composed of that;
through the realization of the Truth, O Lord of Sages, there is neither "this" nor "not this."
Because one perceives that [the world] consists of that [consciousness] through the experience of sensations composed of it, it is "composed of this.

However, because of the realization of the non-dual truth which transcends such material causes (upādāna), there is neither "this" nor "that. The meaning is that it transcends the two kinds of conceptual construction (vikalpa). || 26 ||
Nothing here proceeds, and nothing here ceases;
peaceful and appearing as an absolute equality, it manifests like its own sheath.
He states that very point clearly: "Not this," etc. It is like his own sheath, namely his belly. || 27 ||
Because of its non-dual unity, its lack of agitation, that dense consciousness,
and because it possesses qualities such as being changeless, it is eternally both permanent and impermanent.

From where does it arise that there is an appearance of equality even toward those who are equal? He states the reason for this in two verses beginning with "advaitaikyāt" (due to non-duality and unity).
He says that even in the absence of duality and unity, as in the case of the ocean at the time of dissolution (*pralaya*), there would be no agitation within one's own Self.

[He explains: Just as in a lump of salt (*saindhavakhaṇḍa*), modifications such as liquidity are seen to be nothing other than its own taste; likewise, he says that whatever might appear therein is of the same nature.
Because it is of such a nature. || 28 ||
Because they consist of the density of consciousness, there is not even the slightest difference between infants, stones, and the sheaths of worlds, whether they be existent or non-existent. (29)

The meaning is that it is well said that there is "an appearance of absolute equality," for there is not even the slightest difference between the worlds of the wise and the ignorant—those which are like stone boxes imagined in the sky by children—because they are all, in essence, the density of consciousness (ciddhana). || 29 ||

The all-encompassing, auspicious, peaceful, and transcendent state that lies beyond the play of speech—by means of the mere utterance of "Om," that is the supreme goal, which is the fourth state (turyā). || 30 ||

Establishing the state of being beyond the fourth (*turyātītatva*) which has already been mentioned, he concludes with the verse beginning "samastam": Of this syllable *oṃ*, which is divided into four quarters (*pāda*)—Virāṭ and the others—imagined as the distinctions of the *mātrās* beginning with *a*, there is that which is called Nāda, Bindu, Śakti, and Śānta; among those *mātrās*, the half-*mātrā* is the one called Śānta, and that is the Fourth (*turyā*).

It is the supreme goal. For it is the state called "non-conceptual" (avikalpā), which is the fourth-of-the-fourth (turīyaturīyā) among the states known as "the Pervaded," "the Permitted," and "the Non-permitted," that is expounded as the supreme goal in the Tāpanīya Śruti; this is the intended meaning. || 30 ||
Śrī Vālmīki said:

Having spoken thus, he of stainless vision remained silent there with that sage, his mental activities stilled, at that shore of the state known as "Utter Peace" (samupaśānta-rava), which arises from spiritual maturation.
The Lord [remained] for a moment. || 31 ||
Having spoken and taught in the manner described— that "Īśa" is Śiva— then, together with this sage Vasiṣṭha and others such as Skanda, Nandin, and so forth, [he entered] this place named Śāntarava,
according to the etymology: "that in which the sound (rava) has become perfectly stilled (upaśānta), specifically the final portion consisting of half a mātrā of the Praṇava."

He, whose mental activity had come to rest through its transformation into a state of oneness with that stainless vision— the consciousness of the bliss of the Infinite— which resides at the shore of all saṃsāra in the station of the fourth-of-the-fourth (turīyaturīya), remained for a moment in that hermitage of Vasiṣṭha,
silent and motionless, as his mind rested in the supreme state.
The meaning is that this is because the activity of all the sense organs, which is dependent upon it, becomes blunted. || 31 ||

Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Instruction of the Supreme Lord," in the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa* of the *Mokṣopāya* section of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, according to the tradition of the Ṛṣis. 34.
Thus ends the thirty-fourth canto, titled "The Instruction of the Supreme Lord," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The Thirty-fifth Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Then, in a moment, Hara [reached] Gaurī’s lotus-pond.
Intent upon my blossoming, it freely assumed its outward expansion. || 1 ||
Among Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Hara, and the others, he who is the supreme father— Mahādeva, the Supreme Self— is proclaimed as the ultimate limit of worship.

Due to his extraordinary affection for his devotees, being impelled by the rise of my good fortune, he became intent upon my blossoming and awakening; thus, he undertook external expansion—the opening of his eyes. || 1 ||
The mass of vision, arisen from the expanse of the sky of the face,
illuminated consciousness, like a mass of rays rising from the sun within a casket.
On the face of Hara, because of its stainlessness and because it was marked with the three lines of the *tripuṇḍra* like autumn clouds,

the moon rose in the expanse of the sky; and for those whose eyes are characterized by the moon, sun, and fire, that collection [of rays] illuminated the awakening— the state of being fully enlightened— of their meditative absorption (*samādhi*), as if emerging from a casket, a cloud-enclosure, or the enclosure of heaven and earth.

The meaning is that the sun, as a mass of rays, illumines the day; likewise [is the case here]. Regarding the expression "arka" for "aṃśurāśi," the substitution of *ya* for *ra* is a Vedic (chāndasa) anomaly. || 2 ||
Īśvara said:

O sage, summoning your faculty of reflection (manana), let your own being be quickly measured; do not seize upon the object of thought as a substantial entity, just as the wind does not grasp the movement it causes.
In this regard, the Blessed One first speaks of the essence of the means and the end, as they are conducive to the awakening to reality, beginning with the word "O Sage.

O Sage, having first summoned—that is, brought near—reflection and inquiry (*manana-vicāra*), let the existence of your own inner self (*pratīc*), which is its ultimate nature, be quickly measured and determined by the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). In that inner self, [one should recognize] the absence of evil...

By causing [the mind] to turn outward, do not bring forth the "thou-aspect" (tvamartha)—the insentient portion fit for the notion of "you" (*yuṣmat-pratyaya*), which is the root of all misfortune. This is an analogy for the "thou-aspect": just as the wind, while moving the immovable sky, makes it appear to possess heat, dust, dullness, and so forth. || 3 ||
Whatever is to be seen here has been seen; what use is it with delusions? For I see nothing here to be rejected or accepted by one who knows that.

[Objection: But surely, even among the objects of the "thou" (tvam-artha), there is much that must be seen as either to be abandoned or to be accepted; why then should that not be attended to? [Reply: To this he says:

"By the vision of the Self alone," etc. According to such scriptural passages as "He becomes all" (*bhavati*), since all things that are to be seen are seen in their true nature through the vision of the Self alone, what purpose is served by delusions—whether perceived or unperceived—in conjunction with [that vision]?
Those who know that [reality] are the knowers of reality; "here" means in this sphere of delusion. || 4 ||

The sword [of wisdom], shattering these conceptual constructions consisting of both the peaceful and the non-peaceful, is your own steadfast intellect; it is not otherwise. Abiding thus, become yourself the seer of the Self.

Those objects of desire that have been grasped are abandoned, and those undesirable ones are likewise relinquished; because they are causes for the mind’s consolation, they consist of tranquility (*śāntimaya*). Their opposites, being causes for distraction, consist of non-tranquility (*aśāntimaya*). You alone, O steadfast one, shatter these very conceptual constructions; thus you are a sword. Otherwise, however, you would not be steadfast. Therefore, having established yourself and cultivated firm resolve, become both a seer of the self and steadfast. And so it is said:

The intended meaning is that the primary conceptualization is precisely the state of abiding in the essential nature of consciousness itself, which is not overwhelmed by the forms of the visible. || 5 ||
Either quickly resorting to this state of perception for the sake of external understanding, or else listen to what I have said; for what is the use of remaining silent? (6)

If you are incapable in that regard, then for the sake of attaining it, rely for a time upon only a few external perspectives conducive to hearing [the teachings] and so forth; strive continuously for the attainment of reality and never desist through negligence. Thus he says: "To this extent... Just as the sun is the eye for the entire world for the sake of external perception, [so too is this teaching].

"The eye is stained by external defects; likewise, the one Inner Self of all beings, being external, is not stained by the suffering of the world. To establish this state of being unstained (*alepakatva*), for the sake of realizing the Self shown as being outside the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*), what is the point of remaining silent—remaining without effort to attain the Self? What is the human goal (*puruṣārtha*) [in such a state]?
This is the meaning. || 6 ||
Having said this, the wielder of the trident [said], "Do not become one whose consciousness is directed outward";
for by means of the vital breath (prāṇa), this house of the body vibrates like a machine.

Vasiṣṭha says: "Among all perceptions of external forms, the perception of the body as the self is indeed the greatest misfortune and the seed of all calamities; therefore, the Blessed One has set out to make me abandon that very [notion].
With the intention that such a state may not arise for him, he states the means for dispelling the delusion regarding the body as the self which is about to be described.

This should be explained by completing [the sentence], or the text should be sought elsewhere as it is fragmentary (*triṭita*). In that regard, with the intention that just as the body’s power of action is dependent on another, so too its power of consciousness is dependent, and thus there is no connection to a self (*ātman*), he says: "Deprived of breath, it remains motionless like a mute."
The power of purification is the winnowing-basket; the power is consciousness, which is the faculty of perception. || 8 ||

The power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) is that which moves the body and is conducive to motion; the purifying power (*pāvanī*) is that which is impelled by the vital wind (*pavana*); and the power of perception (*saṃvedanī-śakti*) is, in fact, the consciousness of the Self (*ātma-citi*) itself—this is the meaning. || 8 ||
She is more transparent than even the ether, and her very existence as pure Being is the cause here;
for when one perishes, the vital breath and the body vanish like the wind upon separation.
In that regard, he says that while the root and the substratum of the power of action perish, the power of consciousness does not perish:
"The conscious self is clearer than even the sky and does not perish; what is the use of delusions?
The principle of consciousness arises within the body composed of mind and vital breath. (10)

To provide the reason why it does not perish there, he says: "In the one consisting of mind and vital breath" (*manaḥprāṇamaye*). This means: "in that which is conjoined with the subtle body" (*liṅgadeha*). It is "fully born," meaning it is manifested without obscuration. || 10 ||
For in a mirror of stainless luster, a reflection arises even though the object standing before it is present without performing the act of reflecting. (11)

But the gross body alone lacks the capacity to manifest consciousness because of its impurity; this he establishes by means of an illustration: "O Leader of Sages, just as there is no reflection in a mirror covered with grime, so too there is no manifestation [of consciousness] when the vital breath has departed, even though the body remains. (12)

Although consciousness is all-pervading, through the swelling of awareness it undergoes vibration and so forth; yet, through that very awareness, consciousness—purified of all blemish—is itself the supreme Śiva.

For this very reason, although consciousness is all-pervading, because it is veiled by the stain of *māyā*, it is incapable of external actions and of the awakening to its own true nature outside of the subtle body (*liṅgadeha*); yet, because it is not disregarded within the subtle body, it is capable of both through the medium of that body's functions. Thus he says: "all-pervading."

Due to the cause of the mental modification (*buddhi-vṛtti*) which is swollen with external forms and consists of cognition, it is capable of [producing] bodily movements, the perception of jars, and so forth. However, through the cognition of the form of Brahman, being purified of the stain of *māyā*— [meaning, having abandoned the stain and become pure]— it itself becomes the supreme Śiva, the ultimate auspiciousness known as liberation (*kaivalya*).
The meaning is that it remains established. || 13 ||
Then he perceived that God, the manifestation of all, the bestower of the welfare of all beings;
He is Hari, He is Śiva, He is the Unborn, He is Brahmā, and He is the Lord of the Gods.

For this very reason, he states "they know" (*viduḥ*) regarding the position of the wise: that consciousness itself, when manifested, is called *deva* (the Divine) based on the etymology "it plays" (*divyati*) or "it shines" (*dyotate*), because it is the cause of the existence and manifestation of all things. With the intention that the preeminence of even deities such as Hari and Hara arises solely from the excellence of its manifestation—that is, the manifestation of its reflected form—he says: "He... (*sa*).
"Haris" refers to the unborn Hiraṇyagarbha; "Brahmā" refers to the four-faced one. || 14 ||
