That Supreme Lord has the wind, fire, moon, and sun as His body;
He is this very Self, omnipresent, known as the mine of consciousness and pure awareness. (15)
The "mine of consciousness" (citkhani) has the form of all consciousness. || 15 ||

The Lord of gods, the sustainer of gods, the creator, the God of gods, the Lord of heaven—the great consciousness, whose radiant splendor causes even those who are not deluded to appear as if they were bewildered. (16)

The meaning is that those who, having attained the unsurpassed manifestation of the great consciousness as its full blossoming, do not— as it were— become deluded or fall under the sway of false ignorance, they are these well-known supreme deities in the world, such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Hara, and others. || 16 ||
Those who are indeed known in this world as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Hara, and the others—
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Hara, and the others have all emerged from the Supreme One.
But he who [views] the Supreme Brahman as God says with the intention that these [deities], who identify with only a portion of the qualities (guṇa),
appear for the sake of tasks such as creation like sparks— just as sparks from heated iron or drops from the ocean:
"Like sparks from heated iron, or like droplets from the ocean..."
As if they had arisen from the supreme state, though they are merely illusory delusions.
The two examples are given respectively according to the predominance of the substratum (*upādhi*) and the superimposed object (*upahita*).

This has been stated from the perspective of non-scriptural worldly usage; however, from the perspective of discernment (*vimarśa*), even for Brahmā and the others, there is [the manifestation of] activities such as creation, grace, instruction, and sovereignty over the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*).
While the seeds of delusion, which produce the web of conceptual construction, remain present, this thick ignorance arises with its hundreds and thousands of branches. (19)
The mass of tangled roots of the multitude of living beings consists of the Vedas, the meaning of the Vedas, the Vedāngas, and so forth;
from that infinite [root], it has spread out again and again. (20)

Ignorance (*avidyā*) consists of a series or succession comprising: the Vedas; the meanings of the Vedas; the sequence of creation and so forth; the entire range of ritual acts along with their primary and secondary limbs (*aṅga-upāṅga*); the various forms of meditative worship (*upāsanā*); the various means for ascertaining the reality of Brahman; the individual souls who are the qualified practitioners thereof; and the tangles of misfortune such as desire, action, latent impressions (*vāsanā*), birth, death, and the rest. This is ignorance.
The connection is with what precedes. He says "from that" (tataḥ) because the varieties of the play of ignorance are impossible to describe due to their infinity. || 20 ||
What sequence could there be in descriptions of one whose place and time are perfect?
Therefore, he is the supreme father of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Hara, and the others. (21)

In descriptions [of the sequence], what person could proceed? Thus, "sequence" (*krama*) would be ineffective; the meaning is that no one [could do so]. Alternatively, "sequence" (*krama*) means "that which is proceeded through," i.e., a purpose. What would be the purpose? None at all; this is the meaning.
Since even Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others assume bodies and limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) dependent upon Him, therefore this is the conscious Self (*cidātman*).

The meaning is that Mahādeva is the father even of them. Thus says the Atharvaśiras Śruti: "One should meditate upon Īśāna, who is to be meditated upon. All this—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Indra, and all the sense organs along with the elements—is produced from Him. He is not a cause; He is the Ordainer and Meditator of causes. But He, as the Cause, is to be meditated upon."
"Śambhu, endowed with all sovereignty and the Lord of All, [resides] in the midst of space.

It is also stated in the Purāṇas: "Those three, whose nature is causal, were born directly from Maheśvara; having gratified that Father, the Supreme Lord, through austerity, they are born from one another, each desiring victory over the other. (21)
Mahādeva is the root-seed, like a tree to its sprouts;
he is everything designated as all sentient beings, the universal one who alone effects all perception.

He is called Mahādeva because he is magnified—meaning he is honored and exists with supreme excellence—in the great, unlimited sovereignty of the yoga of self-knowledge. And thus says the Śruti: "He who, having renounced all states of being, is magnified in the great sovereignty of the yoga of self-knowledge;
therefore he is called Mahādeva. He whose powers and names are [the powers and names] of all living beings. 22
It bestows all existence, is radiant, venerable, and worthy of worship by those who know it;
its object is a perceptible reality, and it is ever-arisen everywhere.

For a person who knows that [reality] and has become familiar with it, that very [reality]—and nothing else—is the object, because it manifests as the direct perception of every sense-faculty and in relation to every individual thing. || 23 ||
Since she has entered into the range of all things by virtue of her nature as pure consciousness,
no invocation, mantras, or other such means are of any use for her.

Invocations are employed for the purpose of bringing [the deity] near, and mantras for the purpose of manifestation; the sense is that there is a need for both invocation and mantras regarding that which is omnipresent and eternally manifest. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the inclusion of rites such as installation (*pratiṣṭhāpana*), veiling (*avaguṇṭhana*), and confinement (*avarodhana*) is intended. || 24 ||
Constantly invoked, he who dwells in all things is obtained everywhere by one’s own consciousness; O Sage, whatever state of an object one encounters, from that very state one attains Śiva.
It is obtained from that very [source]. || 25 ||
He attains his own true nature, which is the object of sight for the mind through forms and light—
the primordial Lord of the gods, who is worthy of worship, salutation, praise, and the offering of water (arghya).

The meaning is that one’s own essential nature (svarūpa) alone—consisting of forms, the perceptions thereof, the mental faculties characterized by the reflection upon them, and the witness-consciousness of those—attains and sustains itself, and nothing else.
Therefore, know Him alone to be the primordial deity who first manifests before you, the one worthy of worship through all rituals such as formal adoration. || 26 ||
Know this to be the ultimate limit of all that is to be known, even among the great.
Having beheld this Self, which removes old age, sorrow, and fear, a living being does not sprout again, just like a scorched seed. (27)
He says "enam" [in the verse] to show that this indeed is the limit even for those things to be known. || 27 ||

That which bestows fearlessness upon all living beings, known as the primordial and effortless object of worship—you are that unborn, supreme state residing within the self; why then do you remain deluded regarding [external] perceptions? 28.

That which is known as the Reality among all living beings, which bestows fearlessness, which is the primordial source of all, and which is to be worshipped without effort—that unborn state (*aja-pada*) is you alone; therefore, the meaning is: why do you become deluded by external perceptions? || 28 ||

Thus ends the thirty-fifth canto, titled "The Description of the Supreme Limit of Worship by Mahādeva," in the *Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa* of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, belonging to the *Ārṣa* tradition. 35.

Thus ends the thirty-fifth canto, titled "The Description of Mahādeva as the Ultimate Limit of the Worshipful," in the first half of the Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The thirty-sixth canto.
The Lord said:
Thereupon, there is only the single form of consciousness (cid-rūpa), which abides within the essence of all beings.
They know the pure Lord Rudreśvara to consist of his own direct experience. || 1 ||
Because He is the source of the emergence of the entire universe, because He exists in every form,
because He is untouched by anything, and because of His absolute purity, His universal sovereignty is proclaimed.

Because, having beheld this Self, one does not grow old again, for that reason He is *Rudra*—so called because He alone, upon being seen, dissolves the affliction of *saṃsāra*. Furthermore, He is the *Īśvara*, the Lord and Master, because He rules over the entire universe; thus do the knowers of Brahman understand Him.
And so says the Śruti: "When He is seen, may He be gracious to us; under this Protector may we remain secure. (1)
Know that the stainless element of consciousness (ciddhātu) is the seed of all seeds, the essence of the wandering in saṃsāra, and the supreme action among all actions.
The element of consciousness, the essence of consciousness. || 2 ||
It is the cause of the floods of causes, yet itself causeless and untroubled;
it is the cultivation of the floods of cultivations, yet itself uncultivable and devoid of the nature of becoming.

It is the cause of the power of action; by its own existence, it brings about the manifestation of all things and bestows being upon them. However, in the ultimate sense, it is without cause, not an object of manifestation, and devoid of the nature of becoming.
He is consciousness among the floods of consciousness, the conscious one within the self of consciousness;
he is both the object of thought and the non-conscious, the supreme object of thought, and the manifold creative contemplation.

Consciousness (*cetana*) is the illuminator of the floods of volition (*cetanaugha*), that is, of all modifications of the intellect (*buddhivṛtti*). Within the living self (*jīva*), which is of the nature of consciousness, it is the internal essence, being consciousness itself in the form of pure intelligence (*cidrūpa*). It is the consciousness directed toward itself as the innermost reality (*pratyagbhūta*), and it is the manifester of even those objects of thought (*cetya*)—the external objects of knowledge—by means of the manifestation produced through the pervasion of the intellect's modifications. Of these objects of thought...
He is the supreme reality that constitutes the very foundation; he is the one who, through manifold meditation, has manifested his own self as a multiplicity by means of *māyā*. || 4 ||
The wise know that pure mass of consciousness (cidghana) to be light upon light, stainless, beyond the range of sight, born of light, the seed of the multitude of seeds, and immaculate.

It is the light of lights—the illuminator of the eyes and other senses, as well as of the sun and other luminaries—according to the Vedic revelation: "That which is white, the light of lights. It is "not to be seen" (anālokya), meaning it cannot be illuminated by the eyes, the sun, or other such means. It is "super-illuminating" (ālokaja), meaning it is beyond ordinary illumination; it is the light itself. It is the one and only seed, existing in the form of a multitude of seeds. || 5 ||
Know that which is unreal yet composed of reality, peaceful, and devoid of both truth and untruth;
from the existence of Mahāsattā down to the existence of Sattā, know it to be pure consciousness alone and nothing else.

That wherein neither earth, water, fire, air, nor space exists; that which is devoid of the three states—the empirical reality (vyāvahārika), the illusory appearance (prātibhāsika), and the unreal (asatya); that which is Great Being (mahāsattā), World-being (jagatsattā), Primordial Being (ādisattā), and the unmanifest causal being (kāraṇāvyākṛtasattā)—know that to be the Pure Consciousness (cinmātra) which remains as the witness when those two [the world and its causes] are sublated. This is the meaning. || 6 ||
One becomes passionate oneself, the impassioned one, and the passion that causes coloring;
even empty space itself quickly becomes a decorated wall.

In the state of the seed of attachment (*rañjana-bīja*), the essence of passion (*rāgātman*) is called *rajaka* (the dyer) because it agitates the mind during the recollection of objects. Attachment (*rañjana*) occurs upon contact with an object; it is called *rajas* (the dye) because it is the cause of mental turbidity when that object is absent. Just as even the formless sky becomes colored by paintings and the like on a material wall, so too does the mind become affected. || 7 ||
Within this vast consciousness, millions of world-illusory mirages have flashed, will flash, and are flashing forth. (8)
In this [state], within its own radiance, there exists only that state which is perfected by its own mere existence;
nothing else whatsoever is perfected therein, just as heat and so forth are not distinct from fire.

The meaning is this: although the state of the world has come into being within this Self—whose nature is its own light and which is established merely by its own existence—it has not become anything at all distinct [from it], because there is no other entity.
Just as in fire, although there is a variety of flames, embers, sparks, and radiance, these are not other than the fire itself because its sole nature is heat; so it is here. || 9 ||
They know that which contains Mount Meru within itself to be equal to an atom;
they know that which covers Mount Meru to be equal to an atom. || 10 ||

For this very reason, with the intention of showing that the Śruti passage, "smaller than the small, greater than the great," demonstrates the coexistence of all seemingly contradictory attributes therein, he says: "garbhīkṛta" (contained within). To ward off the doubt that this "containing" is merely figurative, the second half of the verse explains it as "concealed" (ācchādita). || 10 ||
This blink of an eye is said to contain within it a great kalpa;
yet, even while occupied by such a kalpa, its nature as a blink of an eye is not abandoned.

He states that even in terms of time, its length and subtlety are not contradictory by saying "garbhīkṛta-": "That by which the *kalpa*—the period ending with two *parārdhas*—is pervaded, being encompassed on all sides. Here too, as before, there is no tautology. || 11 ||
Even though this entire earth, clothed by the seven oceans, is pervaded by him who is subtler than the tip of a hair, it does not reach his end.
He elaborates on what was stated with the verse beginning "vālāgra" (the tip of a hair), etc. 12.
Without even acting, he has attained the state of being an agent of the construction of saṃsāra;
yet while performing great deeds, he does nothing at all.
Though possessing substance, he is without substance; though without substance, he indeed possesses substance.
Though bodiless, he has a great body; though having a great body, he is bodiless.
Mahākāya means having the cosmic egg as his body. || 14 ||
Even now this [state] is always "morning," yet it has reached the state of being "today";
it is neither "today" nor "morning," for today is morning and morning is always [today]. (15)

Even that which consists of sixty *ghaṭikās* denoted by the word "today" (*adya*)—such as the morning consisting of merely the first three *muhūrtas*—is in the ultimate sense neither the first *muhūrta*, nor today, nor even the morning. If the words "today," "morning," and so forth, possess a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) directed toward the Consciousness that is their respective substrate, then the meaning is that Consciousness is always fit to be designated by those respective words. || 15 ||
Bhiṇḍin, bhiṇḍin, khila, matta, puru, picchili, sāladha;
viviccala, itsadāloka, lāsa, gulugulu, and śilī. 16.
In this way, he shows that even the web of meaningless, corrupt words uttered by the insane, children, and others is that very same [language], by imitating some of them; thus: *bhiṇḍim* || 16 ||
Such meaningless statements as these are likewise true, and he himself is that;
there is nothing that is not true, and there is nothing that is not he [the reading "na yanmṛṣā" is also found].

Likewise, that very same [Self] is the meaningful web of words such as the Vedas and the Shastras; having summarized everything thus stated, he also expresses it by way of negation: "There is nothing else" (verse 17).
Salutation to that Self of All, in whom is everything, from whom is everything, who is everything, who is everywhere, and who is eternally composed of all things.
Recalling that this very same [Lord] was previously seen and bowed to by Prahlāda as well, he concludes with the verse beginning "yasmin" (in whom).

There, by the dense thicket of the intermediate space, which was darkened by the playful tossing of thick clouds by Vilāsavatī, the creeper of Fortune—adorned with garlands of pure sprouts and petals—was as if grasped in a clenched fist. 19.

Regarding the statement that "through the imposition of a journey, even what is non-existent attains existence," which was said for the sake of conceiving the possible; with the intention of providing an illustration—just as verses that are meaningless may become meaningful—the author cites a meaningless verse, beginning with "yatra.
The word-meaning (*śabdārtha*) of words such as "yatra" and so forth is of the nature of reality (*satyarūpiṇī*).
Where there is a syntactical connection with the beginning of a subsequent section, we shall explain that there. || 19 ||

Thus ends the thirty-sixth canto, titled "The Description of the Supreme Lord," in the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa* of the *Mokṣopāya* section of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, according to the tradition of the Seers.
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Supreme Lord," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The Thirty-Seventh Chapter.
Īśvara said:
O you whose form is truth, such is the glorious meaning of these and other words.
In that Lord of All, the casket containing the jewel of all existence; || 1 ||
Through immediate conjunction, the non-existent becomes existent; here, the infinite powers of Śiva, the regulation of the primary power (pradhāna-śakti), and the cosmic dance are described.
In that Lord— in whom the splendor of the meaning of words such as "in whom" and so forth, beginning with the verse cited at the end of the section on creation,

becomes of the nature of truth or predominantly true— within that All-pervading Lord who is like a casket for the jewel characterized by the existence of the entire universe and who is variegated by *māyā*, what stainless radiances of power do not shine?
The connection with what follows [is as stated]. The way in which that verse possesses true meaning both from a worldly perspective and from the perspective of ultimate reality is now described.

Regarding that, first from a worldly perspective, a certain tree is described by this [verse] as being garlanded on all sides by beautiful creepers—creepers adorned with fresh sprouts, tender shoots, and unblemished green leaves—and by lovely jasmine vines.

"By being embraced by creepers" means [that]. For this very reason, in the intervals—the hollows of the trunks and the spaces between the branches—which were formidable (*karāleṣu*) and dense (*gahanena*), meaning difficult to enter (*duṣpraveśena*), or rather, difficult to climb (*durāroheṇa*); and by this tree itself, which was stainless (*amaleṇa*), unfading (*amlāneṇa*), and youthful (*taruṇā*), through its abundance of flowers, fruits, sprouts, bees, birds, and so forth, which was full of charm (*vilāsavatyā*), [the wind acted] with ease (*helayā*), that is, with disregard (*avahelanena*), [toward] the flickering things (*vilolāni*).
By whom the clouds were made to tremble—that is, by whom they were caused to manifest the playful beauty of an excellence of dark, cool, and glossy splendor through the flashing of lightning;
or, if the reading is *garjitaiḥ*, it should be construed as "by whom they were made to roar out of pride in that excellence of beauty. Now, by this [unconventional] method...

By its own characteristic, the creeper of Fortune—famous among other trees, in various forests, or throughout the entire world—is here coiled within itself, withdrawn as if into a fist, meaning it is made dense and compact. Alternatively, the Lord Viṣṇu is described here: he is adorned with fresh sprouts and leaves by means of his pure forest garland.

Among men, he was preeminent as a wrestler, stainless in the ultimate sense, and pure in his garments, ornaments, and so forth; within his belly, which was profound because it contained the fourteen worlds, dwelt Viṣṇu;
and with the splendor of his own body—which, as before, possessed the playful beauty that deludes the world and was like the effortless, rolling thunder of a rain cloud—he shone.
Even Lakṣmī, the woman endowed with auspicious marks, while embracing her own [Lord], was turned away as if by a clenched fist—meaning she was not separated from Him.
Even in ultimate reality, she is obstructed by the neck characterized by ignorance, which is dense with the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of various worldly desires;
and by the sprout-like subtle elements, the leaf-like gross elements that are their effects, and the world-intoxicating [objects].

[There is also a reading: *bhuvanāmodaiḥ*. By means of the elephantine Brahma-vidyā—which possesses the grace (*vilāsa*) of sporting with the hearing of great sayings that are like the thundering of clouds tossing playfully in the sky, and which, through its effortless sport, is the creeper of Fortune for the worlds that have been garlanded—acting as a wrestler...
It is like a fist clenched and turned back for the purpose of striking an opponent, made dense with consciousness and without interval.

In this manner, other meanings of this verse should also be inferred by the wise. Regarding the phrase "of such [sentences] and so forth," the word "and so forth" (ādipada) includes sentences such as "the old cow," "ten pomegranates," and others, which are well-known to be devoid of meaning.

"An old bull, standing at the door with his woolen sandals, sings *madraka* songs; his Brahmin wife, desiring a son, asks, 'O King, what is the price of garlic in Ruma? Whether this has a worldly or a transcendental meaning can be determined only through the power of Brahman. To illustrate, first, its worldly meaning: [The verse continues: "An old bull, standing at the door with his woolen sandals, sings *madraka* songs; his Brahmin wife, desiring a son, asks, 'O King, what is the price of garlic in Ruma? In this context, "old bull" (*jaradgava*) refers to the sun, which is "old" because it has reached the end of its day. "Woolen sandals" (*kambalapādukābhyām*) refers to the two solstices (*ayana*). "Standing at the door" (*dvāri sthitaḥ*) means situated at the gateway of the zodiac signs. "Sings *madraka* songs" means that he shines intensely upon the regions of Madra and other lands. "His Brahmin wife" (*taṃ brāhmaṇī*) refers to the Earth, who is called "Brahmin" because she is the source of all sacred knowledge. "Desiring a son" (*putrakāmā*) means she desires the offspring of the gods and sages. "O King" (*rājan*) is an address to the sovereign. "What is the price of garlic in Ruma?"—here, "garlic" (*laśuna*) refers to the moon, so called because it is the source of nectar (*rasa*). "Ruma" refers to the city of the gods, Amarāvatī. Thus, the meaning is: "O King, what is the value of the moon in the city of the gods? This is the worldly interpretation. Alternatively, the transcendental meaning is as follows: "Old bull" refers to the Supreme Lord (*Parameśvara*), who is "old" because He is eternal. "Woolen sandals" refers to the two powers of grace and concealment (*anugraha* and *tirodhāna*). "Standing at the door" means abiding at the entrance to the path of liberation. "Sings *madraka* songs" means He proclaims the supreme bliss of the Self. "His Brahmin wife" refers to the individual soul (*jīva*), who is called "Brahmin" because she is essentially Brahman. "Desiring a son" means she desires the realization of her own true nature. "O King" is an address to the seeker. "What is the price of garlic in Ruma?"—here, "garlic" refers to the ignorance (*avidyā*) that conceals the Self, and "Ruma" refers to the city of the heart (*hṛdayapura*). Thus, the meaning is: "O King, what is the value of the ignorance that veils the Self within the city of the heart? This is the transcendental interpretation. Thus, both the worldly and the ultimate meanings of this verse can be conceived solely through the creative power of Brahman. Therefore, it is established that all things, whether worldly or transcendental, are manifestations of Brahman.

A Vāhīka man, standing at the door of his own house, was singing *madraka* songs— songs famous in the Madra country. A certain Brāhmaṇī woman, who was about to go to a salt-mine on some necessary business accompanied by her son, who suffered from a disease treatable by garlic, and who was there longing for her son's life, heard from the people that this [man] had come from the salt-mine.
Having heard this, the meaning is that he addresses him with great respect, saying "O King," and asks: "In Ruma, in the salt-mine, what is the price of garlic?
Is garlic cheap or is it expensive? Even for one who stands for the sake of enjoying sense objects—like an old ox—the soul (jīva) indeed regards only sensual pleasures as its "drinks" (madrakāni).

The extroverted person sings auspicious songs concerning women, sons, and the like, and does not desire to behold even slightly his own true nature. Perceiving such a person, [the Lord] protects him from the hell of transmigratory existence called "man" (puṃnāma); thus, "son" (putra) refers to the awakening to the identity of Brahman and the Self. Those who desire that [awakening] are like a Brāhmaṇī woman. (Note: There is also a reading: *bhuvanāmodaiḥ*.)
The Brahmin lady Śruti asks: "O King, you who shine by your own luminosity, O Self, who delight the entire universe with your own consciousness— within your own nature,
which is supremely pure and like a salt-mine or saline soil because it destroys all seeds of ignorance, desire, and action in the 'Rumā' [desert] of the heart."
Since that which is enjoyed is utterly impure—equal to garlic, which is unfit for a Brāhmaṇa to consume—what value or consideration of price can you have for it?
Therefore, with the intention that you should abandon the external view and become one who delights in your own Self, we inquire: "What is this Self?
"Which of these is the Self? "What is the cause, Brahman? "From where were we born? and so forth.

The meaning is "he asks. In this way, the existence of meaning should also be inferred for sentences such as "ten pomegranates" (*daśadāḍima*). As for the verse beginning with *bhiṃḍi bhiṃḍi*, which is an imitation of the indistinct chatter of children, the intoxicated, and so forth, its meaningfulness consists solely in the objects being imitated. [This applies] to the object being imitated...
Precisely because it is unmanifest, it is not a sentence. || 1 ||
What indeed are those stainless luminosities that do not shine within that supreme jewel of consciousness, they which discern the manifold worlds? (2)
Those powers of the seed which pervade the worlds and project them—what indeed are those pure manifestations that, having become manifest, do not shine forth, do not appear? || 2 ||
This consciousness, existing as pure being within the seed and grain, having obtained its own body consisting of earth,
time, water, and so forth, brings about the sprout and the ear of grain.

He illustrates those very powers through reasoning, beginning with the words "This [power]," and so forth: This divine consciousness-existence (*citsattā*), residing within the seed-grains of rice and other crops, having obtained the field and the auxiliary causes such as prepared soil, time, and water, first produces a sprout; then, gradually becoming rice, it manifests as cooked rice (*odana*) which is directly fit for human consumption.
The meaning is "he performs. || 3 ||
Existing within the whirlpools and eddies of foam, taking the form of fluidity,
she causes the movement of waters when in contact with the solid sense organs.

The divine power (*aiśvarī śakti*), which exists within or follows along with the foam, whirlpools, and eddies of that [river], takes the form of a common essence (*rasasāmānyarūpinī*). Through contact with hard surfaces such as stone slabs—characterized by flowing toward lower ground—or through contact with the sense of taste (*jihvendriya-saṃyoga*), it produces a vibration (*spanda*) characterized by flowing toward the interior of the belly. 4.
This [scent] resides in the clusters of flowers in the form of essence;
it shines forth through the nostrils and brings about full blossoming.
In the form of sap—that is, in the form of fragrance blended with nectar—may it blossom within the two nostrils. || 5 ||

The Lord of Mountains, through his play of sustaining existence, maintains the state that serves as the foundation for creation—the reality of the non-existent, which appears as the limbs of stone, yet is the very essence of consciousness (cit-sattā). (Note: Regarding the reading *śilāṅgasthā*, the text reads *śilāṅgābhām*; however, it should be understood that in the root text, "consciousness" (*cit*) is the subject established from the opening of the verse.)

An image made of stone possesses the luster of that [stone]; it does not exist as something separate from the stone. It is the locus of conventional reality. That which is "created" is the *sarga* (the effect), and its substratum is the stone;
thus, the unmodified [stone] maintains the state of conceptual differentiation (*bhedavikalpa*). Just as the unmodified...
The meaning is that it is just as the Lord of Mountains supports the effects such as grass, trees, and creepers. || 6 ||
On pages 860 and 861, it repeats:
"Like the skin-sense organ, which has the nature of the sheath of the vibration of the wind, [the intellect] accomplishes its own son through this [sheath], as a father does through his own self. (7)

In this way, that which is characterized by wind—the sheath of all movements and actions—is the skin-sense organ (*tvagindriya*); it accomplishes and facilitates the perception of touch, being identical in nature to that [wind]. Just as a father impels his own son toward his own duty, so it is here.
By this method, it should be understood that the powers of activity exist in the other sense organs as well; such is the meaning. || 7 ||

Having meditated upon the Self as the condensed essence of all things without exception for the sake of its own realization, it thoroughly renders even the nature of space into a state of non-existence.

Just as one transmigrates through the power of phenomenal activity (*pravṛtti-śakti*), so too, by means of the power of cessation (*nivṛtti-śakti*), one should contemplate— through the methods of hearing, reflection, and so forth— for the sake of one's own realization and liberation, the Self (*ātman*) as a single, solid mass that is the condensed essence of all beings in the entire world; and then, by the negation of everything through "not this, not this" (*neti neti*), [one realizes] a state of being nothing at all, like emptiness (*śūnyatva*).
It performs [this] for everyone. || 8 ||
Within the interior of the mirror of space, which reflects the image of its own existence,
it bears a stainless body called Time, marked by the moments of conceptualization.
These [modifications] consist of transformation up to the Great One (Mahat) and the five elements;
the necessity that "this is thus" and "this is not so" arises spontaneously.

Having unified all the various powers, he determines the extent of their effects with the words "beginning from Āma": Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva—encompassing up to the fifth, Īśāna-Sadāśiva, in this hierarchy of excellence, Niyati is the root power that ordains all effects. || 10 ||

In that Witness, the expansive manifestation, all activities shine forth like objects in a house illuminated by a lamp; within that Reality, the successive variegated displays of the universe are revealed. (11)

If it is asked how that [consciousness] itself becomes the regulator (niyati), he says "the witness" (sākṣiṇī), because it is the cause of its manifestation through necessity. In the "expansive" (sphāre), which is undivided; in the "luminous appearance" (ābhāse), which is light. || 11 ||
In the grounds of the dance-hall of the city of the supreme ether,
she remains like a witness, observing the cycle of worldly existence as the unfolding of her own power.
It is like a city in the sky, a city of the Gandharvas, or the ground of a theatrical pavilion within it, appearing as if waking in dreams and so forth. || 12 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
O Lord of the World, what are the powers (śaktis) of this Śiva, and how do they abide?
What is his witness-nature (sākṣitā), and what is their activity; how much indeed is it?
"What" is a question concerning the portion that is the general object; "how" is a question concerning the specific distinctions of individual modes. || 13 || 14 ||
Īśvara said: Of the immeasurable, peaceful Śiva, the Supreme Self, who is gentle, whose nature is pure consciousness alone, and who is entirely formless; || 14 ||
O observer of noble vows, there is the existence of desire, the existence of space, and likewise the existence of time; similarly, there is the existence of destiny and the great existence.

"He desired, 'May I be many,'" according to the Śruti; thus, first the existence of desire is manifested. Then, upon the manifestation of space (*vyoman*), the existence of that [space] is manifested. Therein, upon the manifestation of the thread of time (*sūtra*) which is the nature of time, the existence of time is manifested.

Then, upon the appearance of the elements and elemental bodies with fixed configurations, the existence of necessity (*niyati*) is manifested. [The existence of consciousness] is the one that persists through all of these.
The meaning is "Great Being" (mahāsattva). || 15 ||
The power of knowledge, the power of action, agency, and even non-agency—there is no end to such powers belonging to the one whose self is Śiva. (16)
Having described the uncommon varieties of powers belonging to the Lord, he now states those that are common to the individual soul (*jīva*): "The power of knowledge," and so forth.
Agency is the power of engagement (*pravṛtti-śakti*), and non-agency is the power of withdrawal (*nivṛtti-śakti*); these are sub-varieties of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*).
Although the power of will (*icchā-śakti*) also exists in the individual soul, nevertheless—unlike the Lord—it accomplishes its own object only through [the mediation of] knowledge and action.

The meaning is that [the power of action] is included within that very [power of will], being subject to the power of action (*kriyāśakti*). Although they have been enumerated in this general way, he states "of these and so forth" (*ityādikānām*) because they cannot be enumerated in their individual forms.
By this, the answer to the fourth question has also been stated. || 16 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
From where do these powers arise, and how is there multiplicity among them?
O Lord, how does their emergence occur, and what is the nature of their difference and non-difference? (17)

Considering that even in the case of a non-dual [entity], the cause for the distinction between power (*śakti*) and the possessor of power (*śaktimat*) is difficult to state—let alone the diversity of the internal distinctions among powers—Vasiṣṭha raises an objection with the words "the powers.
The meaning is: how can the difference and non-difference of power and its possessor be anything other than contradictory? What kind of logical justification could there be for this? || 17 ||
Īśvara said:
This very power is said to belong to Śiva, whose form is infinite and whose nature is pure consciousness; therefore, it is not different from him even in the slightest degree.

The Lord provides the resolution with the intention that there is no contradiction whatsoever, on the grounds that the very divisions of consciousness (cit-bheda) induced by the conceptualization of illusory constructs (māyika-vikalpaka-kalpanā) are called "powers" (śakti), and that these are in reality non-different from Śiva. He says: "Of Śiva," and "of the one of infinite forms. For Māyā [reveals] Śiva, who is infinite by his very nature, as infinite in terms of qualities, powers, and effects.

The sense is that while performing [the action], she seems to increase its infinity rather than diminish it; the meaning is that even through the slightest conceptualization, they are not different in reality. || 18 ||
Through the manifestation of knowerhood, agency, enjoyership, witnesshood, and so forth, the powers assume various forms, like water in many vessels. (19)
Because of its manifestation and conceptualization, it is like water that appears as "much water" through various conceptual distinctions such as waves and so forth. || 19 ||
Thus they dance in the world, within the cosmic egg as a theater for dancing,
having been gradually trained by Time, as if by a dancer.
Like actors well-trained in the sequence of time, such as seasons and months. || 20 ||
This very manifestation as another is called Niyati (Destiny);
it is given such names as Action, Deed, Will, Time, and so forth.

The higher [time] is designated as consisting of two *parārdhas*; the lower is designated as consisting of intermediate *kalpas* and their subdivisions. Whether proponents conceive of this as the "action" (*kṛti*) or "effort" (*yatna*) of Īśvara, or alternatively as his "will" (*icchā*) or "desire" (*kāma*), the meaning is that time is merely a mental construction (*kalpanāmātra*). Thus, it is designated by synonyms of "conceptualization" (*vikalpa*), such as "kalpa," which is derived from the root *kḷp* (to construct). This is the intended sense.

Because this world, from the great Rudra down to a blade of grass, exists in such a fixed manner, and because it proceeds from the lotus-born Brahmā according to a restrictive rule, it is known as Niyati (the principle of necessity).
In that power of Time (kāla-śakti), he explains the term "niyati" (restriction): "from Āma to Hara. For restriction is indeed twofold:

the restriction of form (*ākāra-niyama*), such as "this has such-and-such a configuration," and the restriction of modification (*vikāra-niyama*). Among these, the former extends from the blade of grass up to Mahārudra, while the latter extends from the blade of grass up to the vibration of the Lotus-born Brahmā; thus it is twofold.
The meaning is that she is denoted by the word *niyati* because of her function of restriction (*niyamana*). || 22 ||
Necessity (niyati), which is eternal, devoid of agitation, and unpolished, indeed performs this dance—the drama of the web of the world. 23.
The meaning is that it continues to dance as long as it has not been cleansed by the awakening to reality. || 23 ||
Rich with the playful display of various flavors, accompanied by the dramatic gestures of transformations,
it resounded with the gurgling roar of many Puṣkarāvarta clouds struck down in an instant by the fire at the end of the aeon.
He demonstrates the characteristics of drama (*nāṭaka*) within that dance by means of the verse beginning with "nānā" and so forth. *Kalpa* refers to the dissolution (*pralaya*);

at the moment of its conclusion, which is the moment of the cessation of the dramatic performance, many clouds known as Puṣkarāvarta—which are like thundering cymbals (*gharghara*) struck by the impact of lightning—are present there. || 24 ||
It was strewn with flowers of every season, a temple of swirling rain-showers,
where masses of sweat-water fell repeatedly like pouring rain.
The streams are the showers of rain; that very cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍagolaka), which possesses these, is his great theater for the drama. || 25 ||
It creates the illusion of a dark blue sky stirred by clouds like swaying sprouts;
it is filled and crowded with the circular mass of jewels from the seven pure oceans.

Where the blue sky—restless with clouds that are like sprouts at the edges of its ten directions—is, through poetic pun (*śleṣa*), a blue garment; and where there is the confusion of various costumes such as day and night created by that [garment];
and which is crowded with bracelets encrusted with masses of jewels, characterized by the seven oceans and thoroughly purified and polished. 26.
The sky was illuminated by the side-glances of those watching for the watches, fortnights, and days;
the crests of the ranges of principal mountains were busily engaged in repeatedly sinking and emerging.

Wherein the mountain ranges themselves serve as the crest-ornaments on the heads [of the ocean], being occupied by those two: submergence, which is concealment by bracelets, and emergence, which is their uncovering.
It possesses three pearls of the Gaṅgā strung upon the revolving moon-stone,
and its sprout-like hands are seen flickering amidst the clouds of twilight.
By the phrase "three pearls," the three necklaces are indicated. || 28 ||
Gentle as an ornament for the world, which is restless with its incessant wandering;
he whose footsteps traverse the vast surface of the earth, the netherworld, and the expanse of the sky. (29)

"Loka" means people or worlds; "padakrama" refers to the various positions for the placement of a dancer's feet, so called because they are traversed by words that are soft and beautiful due to ornaments characterized by those [worlds]. || 29 ||
With a multitude of great, rising and falling drops of sweat like stars,
his face— the very sky— was made manifest by the smile quivering from his moon and sun earrings.

Where the great, radiant stars—submerged, emerged, sinking, and rising—are like clusters of drops of perspiration; where the face of the celestial actress, characterized by the sky, is clearly manifested through the movements and smiles of the moon and sun earrings. 30.
It has for its canopy the door-panels of the many imagined Brahmāṇḍas;
it possesses the internal flavors of the presence and absence of the states of pleasure and pain, and of defects.
By the term "Brahmāṇḍa" (the cosmic egg), its walls are indicated; these very walls serve as curtains and canopies like door-panels where [the scene is set].
Therein, the masses of worlds from the upper and lower regions, tossed about by the Asuras and rolling along, act as the tinkling strings of pearls on the fringes of the upper and lower garments.

In this state, there is the manifestation of pleasure and pain; the conditions and defects that cause them are the *sthāyibhāvas* (permanent emotions), while those distinct from them are the *vibhāvas* (determinants), the *saṃcāribhāvas* (transitory emotions), the other *rasas* (aesthetic sentiments), and the various subdivisions of *rasas* such as the *śṛṅgāra* (erotic). It is precisely these *sthāyibhāvas*, when manifested through the *vibhāvas* and so forth, [that constitute the aesthetic experience].
The meaning is that this is because of the established doctrine of the Alaṃkārikas (theorists of poetics) regarding the nature of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*). || 31 ||

In this essence of the long drama called saṃsāra—the play of destiny veiled by transformations—this one Supreme Lord stands as the witness with his ever-risen form; he is neither distinct from that [saṃsāra] nor distinct from him [the individual soul]. || 32 ||

Having thus described the drama, he shows the Supreme Self—the observer of that drama—to remain as pure consciousness alone during the contemplation (vimarśa), by means of the words "in this" (*asmin*).

This refers to the stage where the actress of Necessity (*niyati*) is adorned with well-known transformations (*vikāra*), such as those famous in the science of dramaturgy: perspiration, paralysis, horripilation, and so forth.

In this play, which is the essence of the long-standing drama called saṃsāra, this Supreme Lord alone exists in His own essential form as the witness—the direct observer who stands in the place of the master—and He is not ultimately different from that actress or that drama; such is the meaning. || 32 ||
Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Dance of Destiny," in the first part of the Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa of the glorious Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa composed by Vālmīki.
Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Dance of Destiny," in the first half of the Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The Thirty-Eighth Chapter.
Īśvara said:
This is that supreme deity; he is always to be worshipped by the virtuous.
Pure consciousness, whose nature is experience, is all-pervading and the refuge of all. || 1 ||
The worship of Śiva, whose form is infinite consciousness, through external meditation and through knowledge, is said to yield great merit and the fruit of liberation.
This very one, the witness of the drama of destiny, is the supreme deity, the conscious self alone. || 1 ||
Abiding in the jar, the cloth, the banyan tree, the wall, the cart, and the monkey, he is Śiva, Hara, Hari, Brahmā, Śakra, Vaiśravaṇa, and Yama. || 2 ||

With the intention that the worship of all deities is included within the worship of this [deity] in the manner about to be described, he states its nature as the self of all: "In the jar," etc. (Verse 2).
This Blessed One, the Self of all, who is both outside and within, is always worshipped by those of excellent intellect through various successive rites.
In various ways, according to the sequence of the distinctions between the external and internal that will be described hereafter. || 3 ||
O Great Sage, first listen to how [the deity] is worshipped externally in sequence, O Knower of Reality; thereafter you shall hear the internal procedure.
In all sequences of worship, the body-house is the object to be purified;
however, that which consists of the realization of the Self within the body is the supreme object to be purified with great effort.
Even this body-house, though purified by the purificatory rites (saṃskāra) prescribed in the scriptures such as bathing and sipping water (ācamana), must be diligently abandoned.

The understanding of the body is the light of the witness-consciousness (sākṣicaitanya); that supreme purity, which is its very form, should be diligently cleansed and grasped—this is the implied meaning. || 5 ||
Worship is indeed meditation itself; there is no other worship for it.
Therefore, one should always worship the support of the three worlds through meditation.
The means of worship, the ritual action, and meditation itself. || 6 ||

One should take refuge in one's own essence of "I-ness," which is the nature of consciousness, possessing the luster of a million suns, illuminating all manifestations, and containing within itself the light of consciousness.

The illumination of all appearances—of the splendors of the sun and other luminaries as well as the fluctuations of the intellect—is the essence of the ego; it is the purified light of consciousness residing within.
His neck has the vast expanse of the boundless supreme ether;
his lotus-feet are the vessel for the infinite space below.
His neck—the upper portion above the throat—possesses an expansive reach even greater than space; and the infinite expanse of space below belongs to the growth of his lotus-like feet.
Adorned by a circle of arms that span the expanse of the infinite quarters of space,
he holds supreme weapons of various kinds belonging to the great worlds.
He whose supreme weapons are the worlds— such as Satyaloka and others— which are situated throughout the various cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas) and are held by the serpents of the directions.
Within the corner of the cavity of whose heart rests the infinite succession of cosmic eggs,
and whose boundless form reaches beyond the supreme space of light.

In that case, are they outside the universe? No; he says: "hṛtkośa... etc. His form (vigraha) is his very nature (svarūpa), which is of the essence of light, beyond the darkness of the supreme ether (paramākāśa), and itself boundless (apāra). || 10 ||
Below, above, in the four cardinal directions, and in the intermediate directions,
it was filled without interval by a circle of gods headed by Brahmā, Indra, Hari, Rudra, and Īśa.
This too is to be explained through the distinctions among the lower cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas) and the distinctions among Brahmā, Indra, and the other deities. || 11 ||
One should contemplate this line of hair on his body as the true glory;
it is the ropes of the machine of the three worlds that set various undertakings in motion. (12)

One should contemplate Bhūtaśrī as the splendor of the fourfold elements; and the powers such as Will (icchā) and the rest, which are directed toward the movement of all objects throughout the three worlds like the strings of a machine, should be considered as the channels (nāḍīs) residing within his body. || 12 ||
His powers, beginning with Will (icchā), residing within his body, are to be meditated upon;
he is this supreme God, who is always to be worshipped by the virtuous.
Pure consciousness, whose nature is experience, all-pervading and the refuge of all, resides in the pot, the cloth, the banyan tree, the wall, the cart, or the monkey. (14)
Śiva, Hara, Hari, Brahmā, Śakra, Vaiśravaṇa, and Yama—he whose singular form is pure existence alone, supported by the One without a second, Ananta. || 15 ||

The substratum of infinite words, through their various forms, is the expressed meaning; when those distinctions are set aside, the substratum of a single word is that which is indicated—the essence consisting solely of pure Being (sattā). || 15 ||
Time, which has caused the web of the universe to revolve, is its gatekeeper;
this entire sphere of the cosmic egg, with its vast extent of worlds and mountains, [is his domain]. 16.
The gatekeeper is one who obstructs the entry of the mind within during the state of impurity, but during purification, he is favorable to its entry. || 16 ||
One should contemplate Mahādeva, who possesses a thousand ears and eyes, as having become a certain corner of the body and a part of one's own limb. (17)

Upon his own body, which is variegated by *māyā*, [one should contemplate] the state of being limbs—that is, the state of being constituent parts. Alternatively, he states that the universal form (*viśvarūpa*) is to be meditated upon as having the ears, eyes, head, hands, and other limbs of all living beings belonging to him alone:
"Having a thousand heads, peaceful, and adorned with a thousand arms."
Rich with the power of vision everywhere, and possessing the power of smell in every direction.
It consists of touch everywhere, is endowed with the sense of taste on all sides,
is filled with hearing in every place, and is possessed of the faculty of thought everywhere.
He who is entirely beyond all conceit, who is everywhere the supreme auspiciousness,
who is at all times the creator of all, and who bestows every object conceived by the mind.
He says "from all" (sarvataḥ) to show that even while reflecting in such a manner, its non-attachment and non-duality must not be forgotten from the perspective of reality. || 20 ||
Having thus reflected that the Lord of Gods dwells within all beings, is everything, and is the sole means for accomplishing all things, one should then worship him according to the prescribed rule.
"The single means for everything is the state of being and manifestation"—thus, in the manner described. || 21 ||
O best among the knowers of Brahman, hear this procedure for worship:
this God, whose self is one's own consciousness, is not worshipped with material offerings.
That which is offered is called an *upahāra*; by means of that offering, consisting of perfumes, flowers, and so forth, he is worshipped. || 22 ||
Not by means of lamps, nor incense, nor the offering of an abundance of flowers;
not by the giving of food and other gifts, nor by the anointing with sandalwood paste. (23)
He elaborates on that very point with the words: "Not so" (neti). || 23 ||
Nor by various applications of saffron, camphor, and unguents, nor by others;
[but] by that which is eternally obtainable without effort, cool, and imperishable.
By others, through the offering of parasols, chowries, mirrors, and so forth. || 24 ||
He is worshipped by means of that very single nectar, which is his own awakening;
this alone is known as the supreme meditation, and this alone is considered the highest worship. (25)
By means of one's own self-natured awakening, which has ascended the stream of uninterrupted direct realization;
with the intention that even the aforementioned reflection is a limb of this [practice], and thus this alone is the most principal of all forms of worship, he says:
"That which is the incessant perception of pure consciousness alone abiding within."
Seeing, hearing, touching, smelling, eating, moving, sleeping, and breathing; || 26 ||
He says that it should be performed at all times because there is no fixed rule regarding its timing: "Beholding," etc. (verse 26).
While speaking, releasing, or grasping, one should remain composed of pure consciousness;
having worshipped oneself as the Lord with the nectar of meditation. (27)
By means of the nectar of meditation, with the self as the support for the aforementioned knowledge. || 27 ||
With flowers offered by one who is liberated and possessed of supreme relish, the self itself is the offering of meditation; for meditation is indeed his desired goal. (28)

The meaning of the phrase "endowed with supreme relish" is as follows: the offering of objects such as flowers to the Lord does not constitute a direct bestowal of uninterrupted bliss; rather, it is an indirect manifestation of His very slight pleasure, much like offering a handful of rice to one who is hungry—it does not result in such satisfaction. This [offering], however, is for the sake of the Inner Self (Pratyagātman) Himself.
By means of purification, one manifests the nature of unsurpassed bliss; then, through absolute oneness with that eternal and unsurpassed state, worship consists of offering it to Śiva.
This worship, characterized by supreme aesthetic relish (*paramāsvādana*), is the desired worship appropriate for such a deity, and not flowers and the like—this is the meaning. || 28 ||
Meditation is the water for honoring and the water for the feet, consisting of pure consciousness;
the awareness of meditation is the flower—those who know the supreme state of meditation recognize all of this as such. (29)
Therefore, he says "meditation" (dhyāna) to show that the accomplishment of all ritual offerings (upacāra) occurs through meditation alone, as defined above.

Consciousness (caitanya), which is the awareness manifested by meditation, is the "flower" because it constitutes the very purpose of the flower. Thus, the wise know that every ritual offering is indeed consciousness itself, for the enjoyment of an offering is not established if it is not consciously perceived. || 29 ||
Without that other [means], this self is certainly not attained;
through meditation, one attains serenity from all enjoyments, pleasures, and splendors. (30)
"Clarity" (*prasāda*) means the manifestation of one's own true nature (*svarūpa*). To explain what follows from that, he says "all," etc.

The connection with the subsequent clause is as follows: "This serene Self enjoys the splendor of the bliss of enjoyment belonging to all beings, from humans up to Hiraṇyagarbha. As it is said: "He who knows [the Self] hidden in the cave of the heart, in the highest heaven—he attains all desires together."
"Because of scripture"—that is, because of the scriptural statement. || 30 ||
O Sage, this Self, in the form of the body, enjoys [objects] within the house as it were;
by means of this meditation, O wise one, for thirteen moments (nimeṣas). || 31 ||

Just as one who identifies with the body experiences enjoyments in his own home while embodied, so too does he experience the bliss of the Self alone, which is manifested through the mental modification (*vṛtti*) produced by contact with sense objects. The point is that all forms of happiness are included within the bliss of the Brahman-Self. Now, even in the absence of the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of reality—

He states that even by means of mere meditation as previously described, there is a corresponding excellence in the fruit according to the excellence of that meditation, beginning with the words "by meditation" (dhyānena) and so forth. || 31 ||
Even a fool, having worshipped the Lord, shall obtain the fruit of giving a cow;
likewise, by worshipping the Lord for even a single hundred moments (nimeṣas). || 32 ||
A person obtains the fruit of the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha) by worshipping his own self as the Lord for even half a ghaṭikā.
A person obtains the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices by offering himself as a sacrifice to the Self through the power of meditation.
He who worships for even one ghaṭikā shall obtain the merit of a Rājasūya sacrifice;
by worshipping thus at midday, one obtains the fruit of one hundred thousand Rājasūyas.

Now, if meditating for half a *ghaṭikā* yields the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices (*aśvamedha*), then it must be said that meditating for a full *ghaṭikā* yields even greater fruit than that. So how can it be proclaimed that the fruit is merely that of a single *rājasūya* sacrifice? For the fruit of the *rājasūya* is certainly not superior to that of the horse-sacrifice. This is stated in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad*, in the question of Bhujyu: "Where do those who have performed the horse-sacrifice go?"

Having stated the dimensions of the earth, the oceans, and so forth— beginning with "This world extends for thirty-two days' journey of a divine chariot"— and then having described the gap between the two shell-halves of the cosmic egg as being "as much as the edge of a razor or the wing of a fly," [the text continues].
Indra, having become a *suparṇa* (eagle), delivered them to Vāyu; Vāyu, remaining within himself,

brought them to that place where the performers of the Aśvamedha sacrifice were— thus, by means of Vāyu, they were led out through the aperture at the joint of the shell of the cosmic egg for those who have performed the Aśvamedha.

Because this contradicts the scriptural teaching that [the path of knowledge] leads to the attainment of a station superior to the fruits of all actions; because of the well-known saying, "There is nothing superior to the killing of a Brahmin or the Aśvamedha among merits and sins"; and because it contradicts the words of Śrī Rāma in the *Ilā-upākhyāna* of the earlier *Rāmāyaṇa*: "There is no sacrifice superior to the Aśvamedha, and it is dear to the Great-Souled One. [This applies] to those engaged in other ritual acts in the *Śārīraka*.

If it is argued that this is not a fault because the established conclusion (*siddhāntādhikaraṇa*)—that the attainment of the lunar orb by way of the path beginning with smoke belongs specifically to one who has performed the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*), whereas the attainment of the world of Brahmā by way of the path beginning with light belongs to others—proves that the fruit of the horse sacrifice is superior to that of the royal consecration (*rājasūya*); [we reply: this is not a fault, for [the case] of the other...
This is because it is logically consistent, as it does not contradict what has preceded and thus does not invalidate it.

Where the worship for half a *ghaṭikā* yields the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices (*aśvamedha*), it follows by necessity that worship for a full *ghaṭikā* would yield double that amount; in that case, the fruit is that of the *rājasūya*, characterized by sovereign rule (*svārājya*).

Since that which is heard [as a result] culminates in sovereign power (*svārājya*) for the others who have performed the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*), a great excellence of enjoyment is established for the worshipper of Ghaṭikā, just as it is for a king toward his subjects. Nor is it appropriate here to resort to the logic of the "curd for Kauṇḍinya" (*takrakauṇḍinyanyāya*), because that would result in the redundancy of the statement. And thus, in such a case...

It is stated in the *Mahābhāṣya*: "Indeed, sublation occurs only when coexistence is impossible; however, there is the possibility that both may exist. Furthermore, there is no occasion here for the application of the principle of the section on the "Successive Disjunction" (*apacchedādhikaraṇa*), because there is no contradiction between the two fruits—the world of Brahman and self-sovereignty—just as there is none between the state of being without sacrificial fees and the state of having fees in the *Sāmaveda*.
The word "tu" (but/however) is used for the purpose of indicating a distinction. || 35 ||
Having thus worshipped during the day, a person shall dwell in the supreme abode.
This is that supreme yoga; this is that supreme ritual. This is declared to be the highest external worship of the Self. (36)
"During the day," he says; the sense is that when there is a long-standing longing, the arising of knowledge is inevitable. || 36 ||
That man who, unwearied, shall practice even for a moment this purifying [teaching], which is the cause of the destruction of all sins,
will be saluted by the multitudes of the worlds of gods and asuras— having attained a station in the world like me, liberated in the Self.

Praising the external worship thus described, he concludes with the words "etad" (this). The address "O Ātman" is Vasiṣṭha’s invocation out of an excess of affection. He who, being unwearied—meaning free from the exhaustion of mental distraction—shall practice this aforementioned worship even for a moment, him [the Lord] will gradually liberate from all bonds; therefore...
Having gained a firm footing, the multitude of the worlds of gods and asuras will pay homage to me in this world; that is to say, they will honor me with salutations, praises, and so forth. || 37 ||

Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "External Worship," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa, within the *Mokṣopāya* section of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Valmīki, according to the tradition of the Ṛṣis. || 38 ||
Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "External Worship," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The thirty-ninth canto.
Īśvara said:
That which is the purifier of purifiers, and that which is the destruction of all darkness—
Now, therefore, I shall explain the internal worship of the Self.
Here, the internal worship of the auspicious inner self (pratyagātma-śiva), which shines through the limbs and minor members [of the body] when objects such as sound are attained, is described.
It is called "destruction" (kṣaya) because it is the cause for the destruction of all darknesses, that is, all forms of ignorance. || 1 ||
Whether walking or standing, waking or even sleeping—this worship, consisting of constant meditation, pervades all modes of conduct. (2)
She has followed and conformed to all modes of conduct and worldly transactions.
One should constantly meditate upon this supreme Śiva, who dwells within the body,
the agent of all cognitions, as one's very own self by means of the self.
[He is] the agent of all conditions, the producer by mere proximity, and the awakener. || 3 ||
Whether lying down or risen, walking or standing, touching that which is to be touched or abandoning it on all sides; || 4 ||
The tangible object is the sense-field of touch and so forth; [the Lord perceives it] as being touched, or being enjoyed, or else being abandoned out of aversion. || 4 ||
He enjoys and renounces enjoyments that are abundant even without effort;
he is the fashioner of external objects and the bestower of the essential nature of all undertakings.

He explains that very point clearly with the words "bhuñjānam" (enjoying): [he is] the fashioner—that is, the creator—of external objects, such as the objects of the waking state and so forth, by means of superimposing his own nature upon them; and the giver of the essential form—that is, the giver of existence—to all effects. || 5 ||

One should worship the *bodhaliṅga*— which is established in peace within the *dehaliṅgas*, having abandoned other [external] liṅgas and so forth— through the realization of whatever objects are encountered as they arise.

In the signs characterized by one's own body; for it is well known that when one is seated in the lotus posture (*padmāsana*) or other such postures, with hands extended forward and joined in *añjali*, the body takes on the form of the Śiva-linga. Therefore, other lingas made of clay, wood, stone, and so forth—where "and so forth" includes other images—are abandoned once [the mind] has become tranquil.
The mark of awakening resides in a nature free from distraction. || 6 ||
Abiding in the reality that has entered the stream, purified by the bath of one's own awakening,
one should worship the *bodhaliṅga* with the daily offering of awakened consciousness.
Remaining amidst objects and enjoyments that have fallen into the stream of *prārabdha* karma, even though impurity may persist,
he is ever pure through the constant bath characterized by the awakening of the Self as non-attachment.
It shines like the sun, having cultivated the expanse of the solar nature;
it has arisen as the moon, having cultivated the expanse of the lunar nature.

If, during such worship, the mind sinks into darkness, then one should contemplate oneself as the solar disc—unbroken, non-dual, and completely filling all space both internally and externally; but if it sinks into distress, then one should contemplate oneself as having arisen in the form of such a lunar disc. Thus he says: "The solar... and so forth.

In the full external space of the heart, which has been meditated upon through the expansion of an imagined manifestation as the nature of the sun— with its own expansive form— there appears a radiant light.
[He is] the consciousness that eternally perceives the flood of manifested objects,
flowing through the bodily gateways, having the nature of the vital breath (prāṇa) at its mouth.

That which is the nature of consciousness—eternally cognized and pervading the appearances of the internal and external functions of the intellect, as well as the multitude of objects illuminated by them—is that very form. Having made the vital breath, the mind, and the noble steed of the senses into a state of aesthetic relish (*rasīkṛtya*), [it carries] that which bears its own manifestations, bringing them to the location of external objects. || 9 ||
Mounted upon the chariot of the prāṇa and apāna breaths, it is hidden, dwelling within the inner cave.

*Rasa* means that which is tasted, namely the objects such as sound and so forth; having thus made those objects flavorful by means of the flavor of one's own bliss—that is, having sweetened them—the remainder of the sense is "as if tasting them. He is one whose two horses, characterized by breath and mind, are *udātta*, meaning excellent.
The knower of all objects of knowledge, the doer of all actions, the enjoyer of all things to be enjoyed, and the rememberer of all cognitions. (11)

One should contemplate Śiva, who is the flood of limbs fully and correctly perceived, cultivated through the cultivation of both existence and non-existence, vast, luminous with radiance, and all-pervading. 12.

Just as the single sun illuminates this entire world, so too does the Knower of the Field (kṣetrī) illuminate the entire field (kṣetra)—according to the manner stated by the Blessed One. Thus, it is that in which the entire mass of limbs is perfectly known through consciousness;
it is characterized (*bhāvita*) by states (*bhāvaiḥ*), meaning by the contemplations of objects and by non-contemplations; [it is] from the breaths (*āsāsebhyah*).

It is more radiant than all other luminous things; since the object to be qualified (viśeṣya) is dependent [on its qualifier], the compound is valid because there is no obstruction to its semantic capacity (sāmarthya). || 12 ||
It is both partless and with parts, residing within the body and moving through space;
it is unstained and yet stained, eternally conscious of its own limbs.

In its essential extraction it is partless; otherwise, it is with parts. It has the nature of moving within the void, the space of the heart. It is the consciousness of limb and limb, pervading every member, and is of the nature of pure awareness. 13.
Abiding in the power of mental reflection, arisen between the prāṇa and apāna breaths,
situated in the heart, throat, and palate, it rests upon the seats of the brows and the nostrils.
He explains that very point: "The mental cogitation... (verse 14).
He abides within thirty-six crores of planes, transcending the state of Unmanī;
he causes the internal sounds and other phenomena to arise, impelling the bird-like mind.
The thirty-six *padās* are the thirty-six *tattvas* well-known in the Śaiva scriptures; [He is] situated in the final station of these.
In the division of the powers (*śaktis*) such as Kālī, Raudrī, and Kalavikaraṇī, He has transcended even the internal state of Unmanī and Manonmanī.
Or, the state of Unmanī well-known in the Yoga of Śiva, which consists of seeded meditative absorption (*sabīja-samādhi*), has been transcended by Him. He is impelling [the soul].
Impelling [them]. || 15 ||
It abides in two kinds of verbal paths: the conceptual and the non-conceptual;
it dwells within all limbs like oil within sesame seeds. (16)

In conventional discourse characterized by conceptualization, as well as in the seedless samādhi and liberation which are non-conceptual, [these exist] in the form of the signified and the signifier within the path of speech.
Free from the stain of parts (kalā-kalaṅka) yet firm with its multitude of parts (kalā-gaṇa),
it is situated in one place within the lotus of the heart and throughout the entire body.
Through the groups of time and the elemental measures, having transformed into the nature of the gross body, it becomes solid and material. || 17 ||
Pure consciousness alone, appearing as stainless light, is the conceptualization of parts and their arrangements;
it is everywhere directly perceptible and consists of the nature of one's own experience.

The "kalpana" (conceptualization) of the superimpositions and conceptual constructions of various arts and crafts is the "adhiṣṭhāna" (substratum). The suffix *lyuṭ* is used here in the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇe*). || 18 ||
The individual conscious self, remaining in a state of longing,
quickly approached all objects and, in an instant, became as if it had attained duality.

Furthermore, due to forgetting its own true nature, it remains in a state of seeking enjoyment; having itself assumed the guise of objects external to itself, it quickly—in a mere moment—comes to exist as if it had attained duality solely through its own convention.
One should contemplate: "This is the Lord (deva), appearing as the manifestation of the consciousness of one's own body, complete with hands, feet, and limbs, along with hair, nails, and teeth. (20)
He whose manifestations are the perceptions of his own body serve as his indicators.
Many diverse powers, whose behaviors are manifold, constantly attend upon me in my mental state, as wives attend upon an excellent husband. (21)
This mind of mine is the gatekeeper who announces the three worlds;
this thought of mine is the female usher, pure in form, stationed at the door. (22)
Because its object of perception is pure existence alone, it is of a pure nature. || 22 ||
My own self is my power, my intellect is my action, and O beautiful woman, my various forms of knowledge are the ornaments upon my limbs. (23)

The intellect (*buddhi*), which is characterized by the self and made an object of affection for others like the self, is the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*). The vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*).
And various forms of knowledge, both scriptural and worldly, are the ornaments. (23)
The organs of action, together with the groups of sense organs, are merely gateways;
I am that very Self, infinite, whose form is devoid of all limitation. (24)
"I abide as the single, filled self, full and filling all things," thus one relies upon the divine, pure, and wondrous manifestation of the Self. (25)
The divine, supramundane self-wonder, which is the acquaintance with the reality of the innermost Self. || 25 ||
Fulfilled within by his divinity, he remains with an inner spirit free from dejection; he neither sets nor rises, and he neither rejoices nor is provoked to anger.
He states the fruits of the maturation resulting from such worship with the words beginning "it does not set," and so forth. || 26 ||
He experiences neither satiety nor hunger; he desires nothing and abandons nothing.
He is equanimous, with equal conduct, equal appearance, and equal form.
One whose conduct is equal internally and equal externally, like those liberated while living. || 27 ||
Having attained pure gentleness and possessing a beautiful disposition on all sides,
he alone— his great intelligence unbroken [or, according to another reading, "unconfused"]—
performs the worship of the gods continuously, day and night, for as long as he lives.
The body, which does not deviate from the essence of consciousness, is declared to be his deity. || 29 ||

Regarding the question, "Who is its deity? How does one worship it as long as the body lasts?", he says [the following] beginning with the words "cittatva" (the state of being consciousness), etc. || 29 ||
With every object as it is obtained, he honors him with an entirely equanimous intellect; for the supreme consciousness of the deity is pure consciousness alone.
By means of the object in the form of a triad; it is beyond the cognitions of the senses, which are reflections of mental modifications, being rather their original prototype. || 30 ||
One should worship with all things arising in the sequence as they are obtained;
no effort whatsoever should be made here regarding anything not previously available.
In every respect, with all internal and external objects, and with unprecedented objects such as the offerings of incense, flowers, and so forth. || 31 ||
One should worship the auspicious Lord— who has eternally attained a body and likewise performs this purposeful activity— by means of indulging one's desires.

By means of purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*) and worldly conduct (*vyavahāra*) appropriate to one's own body—such as that of a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya—as it has been obtained and in accordance with the scriptures; and by the cultivation of those things called "desires" (*kāma*), namely food, drink, and so forth, which have the mere maintenance of the body as their cause. || 32 ||
One should worship Śiva with various kinds of food, both solid and soft, as well as drinks, all endowed with manifold excellence, and with beds, seats, and vehicles as they may be obtained.
He states that very point clearly: "Having consumed," etc. (33).
One should worship the Self with perfect awakening through every form of happiness, such as the enjoyment of beloved food, drink, and various luxuries.

"Having fully awakened" means having known [it] according to reality. And thus, the sense is that as long as that ignorance persists, one should continue to indulge in the enjoyment of sensual pleasures. || 34 ||
One who is overcome by mental and physical ailments, possessed by delusion and agitation, and afflicted by every kind of calamity and suffering, should worship the Self. 35.
Thus, even when experiencing suffering as it arises, one should maintain only the perception of it as worship and not feel agitation; this is what he says with the verse beginning "ādhi" (verse 35).
One should worship the Self through all the activities of all beings in the world—through death, life, dreaming, and so forth—as they occur. (36)
[The phrase "by the fruits" (phalaiḥ) is to be supplied] with respect to all the activities related to the stability of the world. || 36 ||
Whether in poverty or in sovereignty, with a self surrendered to the current of worldly flow,
one should worship the pure Self with the flowers of diverse activities.
One should worship the serene Self with the playful display of passion and hatred, which is graced by the splendor of women who are like waves of various quarrels.
One should worship the Self residing within the heart with a friendliness that reaches the hearts of the virtuous, which is firmly rooted, cool as the moon, and characterized by sweetness. (39)
If so, should one also engage in quarrels and the like? No; he says "of the virtuous" (satām) [to answer this]. || 39 ||
One should worship the Self with equanimity, compassion, and constant joy within the heart, through the pure path of power and through awakening. 40.

He states the means for avoiding the onset of quarrels and the like: "by indifference. Power (*śakti*) is the capacity to restrain anger and so forth; it is by way of that [power] [that one acts]. (40)

One should worship oneself with whatever has been obtained—whether it comes unexpectedly, remains for a time, or is unstable; whether it is a single enjoyment, a multitude of enjoyments, or the mere act of enjoying. || 41 ||
With the intention that one should not likewise be obsessed with enjoyments, he says: "Accidental," etc. This means:
[the attainment] of some particular enjoyment at some time among the various enjoyments—that is, within the totality of enjoyments. (41)
One should worship one's own pure self by either renouncing all enjoyments—both those not prohibited and those prohibited—or by means of excessive attachment to them. 42.

The primary rule is the constant renunciation of both prohibited and unprohibited things; alternatively, the secondary rule is [the renunciation] of unprohibited things when they are pursued with passion. || 42 ||

One should worship the Lord of all objects by means of wealth— whether acquired through a flood of desired or undesired actions, or whether it be appropriate or inappropriate, and whether it has been relinquished or retained.
The construction follows the reverse order: "by the unrighteous self that has been abandoned" and "by the righteous self that has been taken up.
[He is] the lord and enjoyer of objects. 43.
One should remain indifferent toward what is lost and gather what is obtained;
for this state of changelessness is indeed the supreme worship of the Self.
Now he states the essence of the primary mode of worship with the verse beginning "naṣṭam" and so forth: one should disregard it and not grieve. || 44 ||
Always, amidst all perceptions— whether desirable or undesirable—
having established supreme equanimity, one should observe the vow of the constant worship of the Self.
One should perceive everything as most auspicious; one should know all that is auspicious and inauspicious.
