One should make everything consist of the Self and constantly observe the vow of worshiping the Self.
Through the vision that "it is Brahman alone," one should perceive and grasp everything as being exclusively auspicious;
however, through the vision that it consists of Māyā permeated by Brahman, one should know everything as a mixture of the auspicious and the inauspicious.
In both cases, because there is an absence of any cause for perceiving inequality due to equanimity, [one realizes] "the Self alone is composed of the Self."
One should either conceive of or perceive [the world] as abounding in the Self or consisting of the Self. || 46 ||

Having understood that whatever is pleasant at first sight and whatever is extremely difficult to bear at first sight are all entirely equal, one should observe the vow of worshiping the eternal Self.
Having understood it to be perfectly even according to the method described above. || 47 ||
One should completely abandon the distinction between "this is I" and "this is not I";
having resolved that "all is Brahman," one should practice the vow of constant self-worship.
Thus, "vibhāgam" means differentiation or distinction. || 48 ||
At all times, in every form, and through all modes of transformation, one should worship the Self with everything, in every possible way, as it has been attained. (49)

One should worship the Self, which is everything and whose essence is all things, at all times—with whatever is obtained, with every modification, in every manner, in every form, and by every name. || 49 ||
Having repeatedly abandoned both the undesired and likewise the desired, one should always worship the Self by relying upon neither.
Having abandoned [the former] through the notion of falsity, and having accepted both by resorting to them with the notion that they are merely one's own self.
Neither by desiring nor by rejecting, but as they arrive through destiny and according to one's nature, the fields of enjoyment should be experienced, just as rivers are received by the ocean. 51.
The objects of the senses are the grounds for enjoyment and the causes of pleasure and pain. || 51 ||
One should not experience agitation regarding views, whether they be trivial or profound, for it is like the sky falling upon extended and variegated objects. 52.

One should not follow after the agitation that has fallen upon—that is, descended into and become attached to—views such as emptiness and contempt, which are "not empty" [in their consequences], namely views involving execution, imprisonment, and the loss of all one's possessions. Regarding the reading *patiteṣu*, it means: even when things have fallen—that is, when they have long persisted and continued, such as various objects that are straight, crooked, cold, or burning—the mind remains like the sky. This is the illustration.
It should be applied. || 52 ||
Whatever auspicious or inauspicious result arises from the conjunction of place, time, and action—one should worship the Self with that very thing, even if it has undergone transformation. 53.
Whatever substances and riches have been prescribed in this ritual for self-worship,
these are all to be infused with a single equal amount of liquid.

If it is asked, "How can the splendors of objects of enjoyment—which possess uneven tastes such as pure, impure, pungent, and bitter, and which are the causes of various transformations like suffering, attachment, and aversion—be grasped without undergoing transformation? the intention is that they can be so grasped because all their inequalities are eliminated and rendered sweet by a single uniform taste (*samarasa*). With this in mind, he says: "By the worship of the Self" (*ātmārcanā*). [They are] thoroughly permeated (*paribhāvitā*).
The connection with the subsequent clause is as follows: "Being flooded [with nectar], they do not become sour or bitter, but rather possess a single sweet flavor. || 54 ||
They were neither sour nor pungent, nor bitter, nor astringent;
though smeared with various flavors, they were indeed sweet. 55.

The sweetness of equanimity, whose power of aesthetic flavor (*rasa-śakti*) is beyond the reach of the senses—by that, whatever object of consciousness is permeated becomes nectar in that very instant. (56)

Alternatively, because they are perceived as equal by virtue of being transformations of the single flavor of bliss (*ānandaikarasavivarta*), their apprehension is established without modification; with this intention, he says "samatā" (equality). The power of flavor (*rasaśakti*) is the Self (*ātman*) as shown in the Vedic scripture: "He is indeed flavor" (*raso vai saḥ*).
Whatever indeed is contemplated in the form of the nectar of equanimity, that attains a supreme sweetness, like [the nectar] flowing from the moon. (57)
Like nectar flowing from the moon. || 57 ||
When the mind has become like the sky of equanimity, and remains dissolved, changeless, and effortless—that alone is called true worship. (58)

The meaning is that the primary form of worship is that state of abiding in which the mind is dissolved by means of equanimity characterized by the vision of one's identity with Brahman, having oneself become like space. || 58 ||
One should become like the full moon—perfect, with an even radiance, transparent, consisting solely of the mass of consciousness, and wise even while appearing in the form of a stone. (59)
With a form like stone, yet as pure and firm as a crystal slab. || 59 ||
Clear as the intermediate space, performing external natural functions, free from the mist of passion, the wise worshipper is complete. (60)
Such a knower, who indeed knows reality, is the primary devotee; the meaning is that he is my true worshiper. || 60 ||
When the clouds of ignorance have vanished, the knower shines like the autumnal sky— free from the mental impressions seen even in dreams and with the mist of egoism and other such traits stilled.
In that [state], there is no "hṛllekha"—that is, no desire, lightning, or the like—which is seen to "scratch" (disturb) the heart; rather, the wise one who knows reality is like the autumnal sky.

Beholding the mind as the setting sun and moon, where subject and object have vanished; seeing the seed of consciousness and the intellect as perfectly tranquil, like the pain of a newborn infant; remain established in the unsurpassed state even while living. 62.
Being completely filled with the nectar of bliss, it is indeed the Moon;

yet, due to its excellence of stainless self-luminosity, it is likewise the Sun. It is that state wherein the mind, its mental fluctuations, the knower, and the known have all set. [It belongs to] one who has just been born.

Seeing that which is the seed and the fundamental root of the conscious mind and the luminosity of consciousness—a state where the expansion of dualistic thought has ceased and which is like the pain-free state of an infant—be one whose intellect is utterly tranquil; thus beholding your own Self as Śiva, you abide in the unsurpassed state of liberation while living (jīvanmukti).
Remain established in that very state; for that alone is the supreme worship. This is the meaning. 62.

Constantly worship the Lord of the body with all the delusions of pleasure and pain arising from objects through the sequence of place, time, and action; remain with a mind whose every desire has become stilled.

He summarizes what has been explained at length: "Dwell" (deśa). The meaning is: remain within your own self with such an intellect (*dhī*) in which all activities and desires (*īhā*) have become stilled; that alone is the primary worship of Śiva. || 63 ||

Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Ritual for Worshipping the Devas," in the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa* of the *Mokṣopāya* section of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Valmiki, according to the tradition of the Rishis.
Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Ritual of Worshiping the Deities," in the first half of the Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The Fortieth Chapter. 40.
The Lord said:
"Whatever you do, you do not do it at the proper time or with the proper undertaking."
That very [state] within Śiva, who is pure consciousness, is the worship of the Self. || 1 ||
Śiva, who is free from conceptual constructions such as the worshiper, the object of worship, and the act of worship,
is the very essence of the deity, proclaimed to be the perfectly pure conscious self.

He states that for the knower of the Self, every action—whether performed or not—is indeed the worship of Śiva, using the words "yathākālam" (at the proper time). This means according to the commencement [of the rite] and according to one's capacity. || 1 ||
By that very [means], He attains delight and likewise manifests Himself;
for the Lord exists by His own nature through His very self.

To the question "Why is that so?", he says: "By that very [means]. By that very worship of such a kind, while remaining as it is in its ultimate essential nature (*svarūpa*), it attains joy—the manifestation of the nature of unsurpassed bliss—and reaches a state of clarity through the removal of veils. || 2 ||
In the stainless Self, the objects denoted by terms such as "attachment" and "aversion" do not exist as something other [than the Self], appearing as distinct forms like sparks within a fire. (3)
If it is objected: "Surely every natural activity, being rooted in attachment and aversion, is a cause of misfortune; how then could it be worship? [The author] replies:
"Because apart from one's own self, no conceptualization of attachment or aversion is perceived"—thus he says, "Attachment... (verse 3).
Whatever experience there may be— whether of royalty or wretchedness, or of pleasure, pain, and so forth—
whether belonging to oneself or to another, each and every one of those is the worship of the Self.
Royalty is prosperity; wretchedness is poverty. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), hunger, thirst, and the like are included.

Their "perception" (*vedana*) is their superimposition (*adhyāropaṇa*). The sense is that this is because it is well known that the very act of superimposing flowers, leaves, and so on upon a deity constitutes worship.
The perception of the universe itself is the ritual worship (*arcā*), and [the perception] of the eternal Self alone [is the worship of the Self].
Brahman is itself the Self, and likewise, it is the very nature of the pot and other such objects.

Thus, the worship of the eternal Śiva, the Self, and the inner witness (pratyagātman), as well as of the universe characterized by ether and so forth, and characterized by the waking state and so forth, is indeed the superimposition of consciousness (saṃvitti). Just as Brahman is itself adorned by the sequence of ether and so forth through its identity with pots and other objects, and likewise the inner witness (pratyagātman) itself [is adorned], so too [is it adorned] by the sequence of the waking state and so forth.
The meaning is that it is adorned precisely by having the nature of a jar and so forth. || 5 ||
Auspicious, peaceful, non-manifest, one, and luminous—this has come to be;
this entire world, appearing as a mental construct, stands as the very form of the Self. (6)
And thus, this entire world has come forth as one form—either the form of Śiva or the form of the inner self (pratyagātman)—appearing through its cognition;
it is radiant by its illumination and persists by its persistence. This is the meaning. || 6 ||
Oh, how wondrous! It is indeed the Self alone that exists as other things such as jars;
it is certainly the inner nature of the individual soul and so forth, appearing as if possessed of forgetfulness.

Thus, upon reflection, it is the innermost Self alone that, as if possessing forgetfulness within itself, exists as the individual soul (jīva) and its own nature, as well as the other world-forms such as pots; the meaning is that nothing else exists at all. || 7 ||
Within Śiva himself—the infinite Self who is the essence of all—how indeed could the delusion known as the worshipper, the worshipped, and the act of worship arise? (8)

Thus, when one sees according to reality, the entire triad consisting of the worshiper, the object of worship, and so forth, is sublated; as it is said: "O Brahmin, a fixed form is not possible in the peaceful Lord, wherein the sequence consisting of the worshiper and the act of worship is conceptualized. (9)

In that [state] where a sequence consisting of the worshiper, the object of worship, and so forth is conceptualized within a fixed form, such a fixed form—that is, a delimited configuration—is not possible. || 9 ||
The deity, as delimited by worship, offerings, and so forth, is not the locus of the lordship of the eternal, stainless Self,
who is omnipotent and infinite.
"Of the eternally pure self" is a qualification of "Lordship" (īśvaratva) that contains a reason. || 10 ||

O Brahman, it is indeed not appropriate to apply the designation "Lord" to the Self, whose nature is pure consciousness pervading the three worlds—[according to another reading: "pervading and exceedingly pure"]—and who is formless. || 11 ||

The two genitive cases in "of the form of the Lord" (īśvarasya ākṛteḥ) are in different grammatical relations (vyadhikaraṇa). Even verbal designation—that is, expression by speech—is not tenable. || 11 ||
Those for whom the Supreme Lord is limited by space and time are to be instructed by us; they are not wise among the wise.
"O Vipaścit" is an address; or [it may mean] "to those who are more wise than even the wise. || 12 ||
Having abandoned his former view and likewise having taken hold of this one,
he becomes equanimous, pure-minded, peaceful, free from passion, and free from affliction.
"Relying upon this unbounded vision spoken by me, remain while honoring [me] with the enjoyment of desires"—this is the connection with what follows. (13)
Worship yourself with offerings of sensual pleasures as they arise from all sides, remaining undaunted in mind; abide thus amidst happiness and suffering, the auspicious and the inauspicious.
Since you have attained mastery over the virtuous and are alone, your life-force being stirred by such [a state], not even the slightest suffering of birth or the like can cling to you.
It is as if a blemish cannot adhere to a spotless lap made entirely of crystal, like a new mansion. (15)
In such a perfected being (*sādhau*)— one who has purified and thereby separated the individual soul (*jīva*) from the body, who possesses qualities such as humility (*amānitva*),
and who has consequently attained his own true nature (*svatattva*) through the contemplation of reality that transcends the roles of worshiper and worshipped—
in you, who are thus free from the stain of *māyā* and entirely devoid of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) which is its effect, there is not even the slightest suffering of birth and so forth.

It does not adhere. The meaning is as follows: just as a crystal slab in a new house—where every part of its surface is free from other objects such as blue or red things nearby—does not acquire the stain of coloring such as blueness, whether through smearing or by reflection, so it is in this case. || 15 ||
Thus ends the fortieth sarga, titled "The Investigation into the True Nature of the Deity," in the first part of the Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa of the glorious Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa composed by Vālmīki.
The forty-first canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
"O Lord, what is called Śiva? What is called the Supreme Brahman?"
O Lord, what is called the "self," and what is called the "supreme self"? || 1 ||
The fruitfulness of the scriptures, teachers, and so forth; the conceptualization of different names; and the method of superimposition followed by negation are subsequently demonstrated.
Regarding what was stated previously— "O Brahman, a designation for the formless Lord is indeed not logical"— and so forth,

he asks "Śiva" with the intention of questioning how that reality which is worshipful, formless, and indescribable can be designated even by words such as "Śiva," should there be any [basis] whatsoever for the application of words like "Śiva."

If it does not then touch that *dharma*, for what reason is it called "Auspicious" (*śiva*)? The meaning is: for what reason are such terms as "Supreme Brahman" (*paraṃbrahma*) and so forth also used? || 1 ||
O Blessed One, Lord of the Three Worlds, why are such distinctions as "that is real," "it is something," "it is nothing," "it is empty," and "it is consciousness alone" spoken of? (2)

In such designations as "Oṃ tat sat—this threefold designation of Brahman is remembered," the word *bheda* (difference) means a specific name that functions as a differentiator, serving as the ground for mutual exclusion; the question is: on what basis is this stated? || 2 ||
Īśvara said:
There exists here a certain Reality that is without beginning or end and without appearance;
because it is inaccessible to the senses, it remains as if it were nothing at all.

Regarding the names [of Brahman] such as "sat" (being) and so forth when they are questioned: first of all, no other ground for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of the name "sat" need be stated. This is because, with respect to its referent, there is no requirement for exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), precisely because that which is to be excluded is not established. Furthermore, since it is by its very nature excluded from non-existence (*asat*), it lacks the quality of having its application-ground constituted by an exclusion produced by something else. Otherwise, [it would follow that...]

Furthermore, since it is impossible for that which is non-existent to serve as the ground for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of a word by excluding what is existent, one must necessarily assert its existence; yet, by the same logic, another ground for the application of the word "existent" would have to be stated for that too, and so on ad infinitum, resulting in the fallacy of infinite regress (*anavasthā*). The same applies to the words "something" (*kiñcit*) and "nothing" (*na kiñcit*), because they are not cognizable by the senses.

Because it is impossible to designate that [reality] through properties that are themselves cognizable, the application of words toward it is possible only by way of independence from exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*). For it cannot be said that words do not at all cause the cognition of that which is non-excluded or devoid of differentiating properties; for words such as "non-excluded" (*avyāvṛtta*) and "propertyless" (*nirdharmaka*) possess the capacity to produce cognition.

Because this is established by all experience; for it is impossible to say that "being devoid of attributes" (nirdharmakatva) is itself an attribute, or that "the non-excluded" is excluded from the excluded, as such a statement would be contradictory, like saying "one's own mother is barren.
And thus, even in the case of words such as "Śiva," [the application of the term] to the mere nature of faultless, unsurpassed bliss is entirely independent of any etymological cause (nimitta).
The occurrence [of the term "Śiva"] is established by the same logic; or rather, the exclusion of suffering and so forth in Śiva is indeed caused by His very nature.
Thus, with the intention that there is no inconsistency regarding the difference in names, he provides the answer: "without beginning or end" (*anādyantam*).
This means it is inherently distinguished from both beginning and end through the absence of such limitations.

Non-manifestation (*anābhāsa*), independent of other manifestations, self-luminous—such is the Real Entity (*sad-vastu*) that exists here in its own majesty by itself alone; the meaning is that it does not exist through a being dependent on others, such as space, time, attributes, or light, nor through an exclusion dependent on others. The word "as if" (*iva*) is intended to indicate the falsity (*mithyātva*) of even the slightest degree of [phenomenal] existence therein. || 3 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
O Lord, how can that which has become invisible even to the senses when joined with the intellect and other faculties be approached without hesitation?

Since the mental constructs (*saṃkalpa*) of the mind (*manas*), intellect (*buddhi*), ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), and consciousness (*citta*) have as their domain only the objects grasped by the senses, it follows by implication that [the Self] is inaccessible even to the intellect and the other faculties. Furthermore, since no means for the cognition of that which is inaccessible even to the intellect is possible, there is no possibility of a means for cognizing it, even though it exists; thus, one should remain free from doubt.
By what qualified person, free from the doubt that distress might arise, is that Brahman approached—that is, attained?
The meaning is: it is directly realized. || 4 ||
Īśvara said: He who desires liberation, being a portion of ignorance yet purely sattvic by name, [is characterized] by those very portions of ignorance known as the scriptures and so forth.

The veil of ignorance (*avidyā-āvaraṇa*) is removed by a mental modification (*vṛtti*) in the form of Brahman, which is produced by the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and consists of the transformation of the pure *sāttvika* portion [of the mind]. Upon the removal of the veil, however, Brahman shines forth in its true nature precisely because it is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*).
This alone constitutes its direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*), and not a mere pervasion by consciousness manifested through a mental modification.

The seeker of liberation (mumukṣu), characterized by the desire for release, is a purely sattvic portion of ignorance (avidyā) due to being purified by the means of practice such as tranquility (śama) and self-control (dama); he is endowed with that excellence produced by purely sattvic portions of ignorance known as the true scripture, the true guru, and the company of the virtuous.
Through a succession of its own internal states culminating in hearing, reflection, meditation, and direct realization—

and because it is nourished by the store of merits such as sacrifices and gifts accumulated over many births— it remains for a long time, washing away its own primary effect, which is ignorance. || 5 ||
Washing away ignorance with the most excellent [knowledge], he remains here;
just as a skilled washerman removes dirt by means of dirt.
When the destruction of ignorance subsequently occurs by chance, like the "crow-and-palm" coincidence, the self perceives itself by means of itself; this is the certainty regarding its own nature.

What follows from that? He says: "By the crow... and so on. Then, due to long-term practice, by the maxim of the "crow and the palm fruit" (kākatālīya), through the ripening of fortune, when the destruction of ignorance—its complete eradication—has occurred via a mental modification (*vṛtti*) arising in the form of the full Brahman, the unobscured Self perceives the Self by means of the Self alone.

The meaning is that one remains established in the very nature of the manifestation of reality (*vastava-svapratyaya-svabhāva*). This "certainty" (*niścaya*) regarding the nature of the Self is precisely the aforementioned residue of the self-luminous essence; it is a direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) that is free from doubt and error, and not of any other kind. Alternatively, it is the certainty of the destruction of the very nature of ignorance (*avidyā*) in the manner described.
The meaning is that it is not otherwise. || 7 ||
Just as a child, by somehow rubbing against charcoal and washing it,
attains purity of hand when the blackness of the charcoal has been removed, so too does one attain purity.

He provides an illustration for the purification of the self by the self itself upon the destruction of ignorance through the very portion of ignorance [itself]: "Just as when charcoal is exhausted, even though the hand has been washed, it attains cleanliness of the palm through repeated rubbing;
but when the charcoal is exhausted, the blackness characterized by the succession of dust particles produced by that rubbing [also vanishes]."
Just as one who washes away soot from his hand attains its inherent purity and beauty by itself through that very act,

so too, if both the *sāttvika* and *tāmasa* portions of ignorance were to investigate themselves in any way whatsoever— aided by other internal factors such as the scriptures— the destruction of both those portions would follow.
And the manifestation of the stainless Self is accomplished; this is the meaning. || 8 ||
In whatever manner one may analyze the parts through the divisions of the scriptures and so forth, there are the *sāttvika* and *tāmasa* portions; likewise, the arising of the Self pertains to both.
The Self alone perceives itself and investigates by means of itself;
that "only the Self exists here, there is no ignorance"—this they know as the destruction of ignorance.

If it is objected: "The Self is determined by being investigated through the intellect; why then is the Self not an object of perception for the intellect? We say no. For the insentient intellect possesses no independence in investigation and the like; rather, it is the Self alone who, having sublated ignorance through means such as the intellect via investigation and so forth, manifests Himself. Thus he says: "He sees. (10)
Whatever various objects exist here, let it be understood that they are not the Self;
furthermore, the sequence beginning with the teacher’s instruction is not the cause of self-knowledge. (11)

For this very reason, the various distinctions such as gurus and scriptures are neither the Self nor the causes for the knowledge of the Self, because the nature of the Self and its knowledge do not depend upon any means of accomplishment; with this intention, he says "yāvat" (as long as). || 11 ||
The Guru is the self whose nature consists of the functioning of the senses; Brahman is attained through the cessation of all the senses.
Whatever object is to be reached upon the cessation of something else, that object is not attained while that thing still exists.
Regarding that, he states another reason for rebirth: "The guru" refers to the self, which is the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*) composed of the functioning senses.

O twice-born one, even those things which are not causes have become powerful causes for the attainment of self-knowledge, such as the instructions of the guru and so forth, through successive stages. 13.
If so, are the Guru and others useless? He says "no": "They are not causes," meaning they are for the sake of attainment, like the recovery of a golden necklace forgotten around one's neck. || 13 ||
When the instructions of the guru proceed in due order through the awakening of the disciple,
the Self— though inexpressible and invisible— becomes gracious of its own accord.
It becomes serene; it becomes manifest. || 14 ||
The Self is not understood through the meanings of the scriptures, nor is it understood from the words of a teacher;
rather, it is understood by itself alone, through the power of its own awakening. || 15 ||
To the question, "If it is thus necessary, how can it be said to be without a cause? he replies: "By the meanings of the scriptures" (verse 15).
Without the meaning of the scriptures and the instructions of the guru, the Self is not realized;
it is only through the existence of this conjunction that the knowledge of one's own Self is illumined. 16.
Illuminating means manifesting. || 16 ||
Through the long-standing association of the teacher, the meaning of the scriptures, and the disciples,
self-knowledge proceeds just as the conduct of people proceeds through the course of days.
When karma, the organs of sense and action, and the extremes of pleasure, pain, and so forth are destroyed, the Self is called Śiva by such names as "Tat" and "Sat. (18)

Therefore, it has been stated that the Self, which is supreme bliss and from which all inauspiciousness has been dispelled by awakening, is inherently worthy of the designation "Śiva" (the Auspicious One) and does not depend upon any external ground for its application; thus he says: "Karma... (verse 18).
That wherein this entire [universe] does not exist, yet exists precisely in that form—indeed, it exists as if real, infinite, and clearer than space. (19)
The world does not exist [ultimately], yet it exists [as a superimposition]. That reality which is its substratum certainly exists;
indeed, it exists as if real, because of its distinction from the empirical. || 19 ||
In which [state], due to a lack of rest, seekers of liberation possessing limited knowledge have their selves stained by the blemish of various impure mental conceptions. || 20 ||

He states that even the conceptualization of names such as Śiva, Brahmā, and Sadāśiva is solely for the purpose of awakening those qualified [disciples] who are liberated while living (jīvanmukta): "And the reflection upon reality"—those whose minds are possessed by a stain characterized by that [reality] within the pure Self.

Standing not far away within the range of vision of the one liberated while living (jīvanmukta), they exist for the sake of awakening those who aspire to liberation and for the composition of the meaning of the scriptures. || 21 ||

For the sake of the liberation of those devotees who are his own worshippers— standing within the range of vision of one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*) and situated near the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*)— and for the purpose of awakening them through the composition and thorough exposition of the meaning of the scriptures, namely the principles, the knowledge thereof, and the means thereto. || 21 ||
By the world-protectors headed by Brahmā, Indra, and Rudra, who were highly learned and whose souls were purified for the sake of establishing the doctrines of the Purāṇas and the Vedas. || 22 ||
For the establishment—that is, for the purposeful realization—of the Purāṇas, the Vedas, and the philosophical systems such as the Sūtras of Bādarāyaṇa.
"Consciousness, Brahman, Śiva, Ātman, Īśa, Paramātman, Īśvara, and so forth—these are conceptual designations imagined within this Lord who is beyond all designation and distinct [from them]. (23)
Distinct designations have been conceptually constructed. || 23 ||
Thus is this reality of the world, your own reality named Śiva;
in every way, at all times, and as the totality of all things—O, enjoy that bliss! 24.

O Vasiṣṭha, having ascertained that—because it is the substratum for the superimposition of the world beginning with space, it is the reality of the world; and because it is the substratum for the superimposition of the three states [of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep], it is one's own true nature; and that which always, in every way, brings about the existence of all things and all states—that is nothing other than the singular bliss of Brahman, and there is not even an atom’s worth of anything else.
May you remain. || 24 ||
Terms such as "Śiva," "Ātman," and "Supreme Brahman" were established by the ancients as distinct designations; yet, in reality, there is no difference in him. (25)
O leader of sages, the wise man who thus performs the daily worship of the gods goes to that supreme state where we and others serve as attendants. (26)

Thus has been described the nature of the worship of the Deity. In that state of Supreme Śiva, we and others—each possessing pride in a single attribute—are like servants, constrained by the duties of creation and so forth. || 26 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: "O Blessed One, you ought to explain to me in brief how this [universe], though non-existent, remains as if it were existent. (27)
Now, Vasiṣṭha, desiring to know how the state of being a living soul and its transmigration are superimposed upon pure consciousness, asks: The Lord said:
Know that which is the referent of words such as "Brahmā" and so forth to be nothing but consciousness alone.
Even the clear sky appears gross to him, like Mount Meru to an atom. (28)
In order to describe the progressive increase in grossness through successive superimpositions (*uttarottarāropa*), he shows the root which is of the most subtle form—this is the meaning. || 28 ||
Moving here toward the state of the knowable, she attains fitness for the name "Citta"; yet, truly, when established in the stage at the end of Unmanā, she is indeed devoid of the knowable.

The meaning is that when that consciousness (*cit*), due to the awakening of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) within the sphere of the knowable, becomes oriented toward the conceptualization of the knowable, it then becomes fit for the designation "consciousness" (*cid*) and for the activity [of cognition]. Even though it remains in the state culminating in *unmanī*, which is the nature of the single flavor of the bliss of consciousness established in non-conceptual samādhi (*nirvikalpa-samādhi*). || 29 ||
Because its state of being perceivable arises in an instant, it follows after the sense of "I-ness," just as a man, by virtue of his humanity, assumes the form of a wild elephant in a dream.
Having attained spatiality and temporality within this [consciousness] whose nature consists of "I-ness" and so forth, those [mental constructs] then become merely friends whose form is void. (31)
Because they penetrate such limits and sequences, these mental constructs (kalpanās) attain the nature of space and time;
and since they are the companions of the ego-sense (ahaṃtā), this is a poetic conceit (utprekṣā). || 31 ||
That very existence, when conjoined with those [qualities], becomes designated as the "living soul" (jīva),
characterized by vibration and consciousness, like the scribbled trace of the wind.

Interwoven with those conceptualizations of space and time, that [consciousness], becoming a vibration-cognition through the awakening of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) within the sphere of the locus of "I-ness," becomes what is termed the "living being" (*jīva*), existing as the internal vibration of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), like a streak of wind. [The root] *jīv* means "to sustain the vital breath."
The meaning is: because of the conformity with the root-meaning. || 32 ||
The power of the individual soul (jīva-śakti), being of such a nature and delighting solely in certainty,
follows the state of intellect (buddhi) and remains situated in the condition of ignorance.
Thus, because the latent impression of certainty is awakened, it also becomes denotable by words such as "intellect" (buddhi) and so forth; he states this with the verse beginning "jīva. || 33 ||
It is followed by the power of sound, the power of action, and the power of knowledge;
each of these vibrates within, its form revealed.

Then, through the awakening of the latent impressions (saṃskāra) of physical, vocal, and mental activity, the ego-sense (ahaṃtā) follows along by the power of sound and other objects; it does not reveal the true nature of the Self, which remains utterly concealed by it.
When this group [of senses] quickly unites and brings about mindfulness,
the mind becomes the seed of the self of beings for the tree of volitional construction (saṃkalpa).
The wise know that to be the vehicle of the subtle body (ātivāhika-deha),
which, through the power of Brahman residing within, perceives the Self by itself as the form of the Knower.

Because he knows that [the world] is pervaded by the power of Brahman (brahmaśakti)—which resides within and consists of the unobscured Witness—he becomes a "knower" (jña), attaining the state of a subject (pramātṛ). And this occurs solely through the power of the Self's self-luminosity; thus it is said:
"For these powers, while indeed being manifested within this mind..."
Afterwards, those rays situated outside here rise up, even though they have not yet risen.

Thus, he states that internal conceptualization is the cause for the conceptualization of the existence of external objects by saying, "becoming manifest" (*saṃpadyamānāḥ*). These [conceptualizations] are those which are about to be described. || 37 ||
The existence of wind, the existence of vibration, the existence of touch, as well as the existence of the skin and the existence of light, are likewise the illuminators of existence. (38)
The existence of the eye is that which manifests the existence of light. || 38 ||
The existence of form, the existence of water, and likewise the existence of taste;
likewise the existence of flavor, and likewise the existence of fragrance. || 39 ||
That which tastes is taste; it is the sense organ of taste, the existence of which [is established]. || 39 ||

She is the essence of the earth, the essence of gold, and the essence of the gathered mass; she is the plump one, the essence of space, the essence of time, and devoid of all forms of worldly wealth. (40)

By the word "hema" (gold), the two hemispherical shells of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) composed of silver and gold are to be understood. "Pīvarī" refers to the exceedingly vast, solid existence of the cosmic egg. 40.
Embracing this entire multitude of beings as its own nature, it vibrates while resting upon the petals and other parts; having become the seed itself, it manifests from the seed.

"Having embraced," that is, having grasped [the effects] through identity with its own nature (*svarūpa*). Just as a seed, having reached the state of being a seed and so forth through successive transformations, manifests by embracing the sprout, the stalk, the branch, the leaf, and so on; likewise [it is here].
In the reading *bījādbījāditām*, it means "seeds and so forth" (*bījanti*) referring to the subsequent seeds.
From which [seeds] such successions of sprouts, stalks, and so forth have attained their beginning and their primary cause. || 41 ||

Know this to be the "city of eight" (puryaṣṭaka), and this body is the subtle transport-body (ativāhika). O dear one, though it is boundless consciousness, it manifests as if possessing distinct divisions.

This means that the *puryaṣṭaka*—which encompasses the nature of all existing beings and consists of the three bodies beginning with the gross (*sthūla*)—is itself the subtle body (*ātivāhika-deha*) in the form of latent impressions (*vāsanā*). That which is Brahman alone, whose nature is consciousness (*cit*) and which is boundless and undivided, shines forth in this manner as the aforementioned divisions; nothing else exists. || 42 ||
Thus, it is endowed with the primary factors, yet it is not endowed with anything at all;
it is neither knowledge, nor that form, nor consciousness, nor even the sentient mind. (43)
Having thus elaborated upon the process of superimposition (*āropa*), he demonstrates negation (*apavāda*) with the words "evamādi" (and so forth).

From the perspective of the ignorant, it appears as something fully accomplished; however, from the perspective of the vision of reality (*tattvadṛśā*), nothing at all is accomplished. That [body] consists of the *puryaṣṭaka* (the eightfold city);
even though it is conscious, it is not truly conscious, being merely accumulated there and there by the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*).
The Supreme alone shines forth in the Supreme; it is the absolute reality, the very self of the Absolute, like the play of liquid water within the interior of a basin of water.
Of the "water-seat" (jalapīṭha), that is, the reservoir of water; [this refers to] the ocean. || 44 ||
This insentient world, which is essentially one with consciousness and its perception, becomes something entirely separate when fully understood as being like a city of imagination. (45)
How is this known? To that he says: "But that which is separated from consciousness is insentient and devoid of an illuminator; thus, in either case, it does not live"—this is the meaning. || 45 ||
Through perception and thorough knowledge, one attains nothing other than the state of Śiva;
for how could that which is unknown attain the status of a real entity? (46)
Furthermore, is this [object] real as something known or as something unknown? It is neither; thus he says, "Because of cognition" (*saṃvedanāt*).
The explanation of "because of cognition" is "because of thorough knowledge" (*parijñānāt*). || 46 ||
Then, by its own internal volition, it attains a state of being a part;
the existence of that atom [of consciousness] perceives this within the body.

Now, if someone should say that even this entity, though its own nature is pure consciousness, attains the state of being an object of perception within itself through the volition "May I become many; may I procreate," then— since that which is fashioned by volition is false— the existence of that atom-like, most subtle Self would consist only of that [volition] during the first moment of its conceptualization.
Through long practice, one perceives grossness even within the subtle body of the physical form. || 47 ||
He quickly perceives that very [subtle element] as having attained grossness;
he perceives its apertures of the subtle elements according to their respective locations. || 48 ||

And due to its connection with the gross body, that very Brahman perceives—through its own conceptualization—all four internal sheaths as well as the entire collection of external objects as having attained grossness. Furthermore, in the perception of external forms and so forth, it beholds the eyes and other organs of that body as established according to their respective objects, serving as gateways for the subtle elements (*tanmātra*). || 48 ||

Then, by virtue of the singular contemplation on the form of the Person, having seen [the deity] with a human form—just like the coincidence of the crow and the palm fruit—one becomes exceedingly satisfied and nourished. (49)

Then, by cultivating the notion of oneness in the form of a person within the collection of limbs such as hands and feet, and within the internal cavities, one perceives the figure of a person. Seeing that this [form] has suddenly become fit for worldly transaction, one becomes satisfied and nourished. || 49 ||
He perceives this body remaining in such a state as if it were living,
though it is utterly non-existent, like a city of Gandharvas or a man in a dream.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Even though the world has the appearance of a city of Gandharvas and is comparable to a man in a dream, it leads to suffering; what logic is there for its destruction? (51)

Thinking that even though the world is known to be illusory (*mithyā*), it still produces suffering, and therefore the treatment for suffering must be stated as something other than the knowledge of its illusoriness, Vasiṣṭha asks: "Gandharva... (51). The Lord said:
Suffering arises through the power of latent impressions (vāsanā), and that [suffering] would exist only while [the world] exists;
yet the world is non-existent, like the shimmering water of a mirage.

With the intention that the means for the cessation of suffering is not merely an initial conviction, but rather a firm certainty of its falsity persisting until the exhaustion of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), he gives the following reply: "Latent impressions... (Verse 52).
Therefore, what is perfumed, by what, whose is the perfuming, or from where?
How, my dear, can the water of a mirage be drunk by a man in a dream? (53)

He states that when there is a firm conviction in the absolute non-existence [of the world], the non-arising of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) is established precisely because of the absence of a substratum, an object, and so forth: "But for one who sees reality, when that [world]—along with its beginningless [causes] such as mind and mental activity—is no longer present, whatever exists is seen as the [ultimate] reality. (54)
When the world, including the seer and so forth, no longer exists, that which remains is either pure consciousness alone, or that very [Self] remains. || 54 ||

Where there is neither latent impression (*vāsanā*), nor an impressioner, nor the state of being impressed—there is only the state of absolute oneness (*kevalībhāva*), in which the delusion of mental construction has completely subsided. (55)
For one for whom even the Yakṣa—whether real or unreal—is indeed empty, he has dissolved through absolute liberation; what else remains for him? (56)
Whether real in the empirical sense or unreal as a mere appearance, the Yakṣaka is eternally dissolved through the vision of that mature [yogin], due to its emptiness. || 56 ||
For this mental impression called "the world" has arisen in this way like a void, just like a ghost; therefore, when it is stilled, peace remains unimpaired.
"Fie on that wretched man who places his trust in egoism, in the world, and in the water of a mirage; such a person is not fit to be instructed. (58)
Those who know reality (tajjñāḥ) teach that the living self (jīva) here is the discerning one; they do not [teach] the child, the deluded, the unreal, or that which is abandoned by the noble ones.

Indeed, he who instructs the ignorant is like one who gives his daughter to a man seen in a dream—[the question arises] why would he not be instructed? To this he says: "The living self," etc. Those who know reality are the knowers of the Self (ātmajñāḥ); [they teach] the discerning one...

They instruct one who possesses the qualifications for authority, but not a fool who lacks such qualification, who is deluded, full of many errors, abandoned and disregarded by the noble ones, and who— due to the false conceit of identifying with the body and so forth— is composed of unreality;
he who instructs or teaches such an ignorant person [is like one who would give] his own daughter, who is as radiant as gold and beautiful, [to him].
He gives [a gift] to a man seen in a dream; the point is that he too is simply a fool. || 59 ||
Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Falsity of the World," in the first part of the Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa of the glorious Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa composed by Vālmīki.
Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "The Demonstration of the Falsity of the World," in the first half of the Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The forty-second canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Then, O Blessed One, that living being beheld the delusion of the body.
Indeed, at the beginning of creation, while situated in the sky, he attains whatever state he desires.
Having taught that the construction of the collective and individual cycles of existence is preceded by Īśvara and is nothing but Māyā, Śambhu departed for his own abode.

At the conclusion of the superimposition (adhyāropa) described as "he sees this body remaining in such a state while alive," Vasiṣṭha, desiring to know the remainder of that matter, asks with the words "Then" (*tataḥ*). The phrase "in the primary creation" (*ādisarge*) refers to the sequence of superimpositions at the beginning of a kalpa; the restatement of what was previously said is for the purpose of reconnecting with the preceding context. || 1 ||
Īśvara said: In the supreme void beyond the supreme, the individual soul perceives a body produced according to the sequence previously described, just like a man in a dream. || 2 ||
And that living being (jīva) sees the most expansive universe within the most subtle channels, just as a man in a dream does;
likewise, he sees it even within the supremely subtle space of consciousness (cidākāśa)—this is the meaning. || 2 ||
For because the mass of consciousness is all-pervading, even as a person in a dream acts swiftly toward an effect, so too does the individual soul (jīva) even now while assuming a body.

He explains the underlying intention of the illustration already mentioned with the words "because of its omnipresence" (*sarvagatvāt*). The sense is that even upon entering the interior of the channels (*nāḍī*), it exists as the possessor of all powers. The meaning is that it is well known to everyone even today how it creates the effect, namely the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*). || 3 ||
Then, he quickly bestows upon himself the designation "I am the eternal, unmanifest Person"; by that, he is proclaimed as the first Person.

He is that very one who, at the initial creation, possessing the aggregate as his limiting adjunct (upādhi) and known by the name Hiraṇyagarbha, declares the distinction of names both within himself and in external objects; thus he says: "The Eternal" (sanātana). || 4 ||
Thus, in one creation he was the first Sadāśiva,
in another he was called Viṣṇu, and in another the Grandfather (Brahmā) born from his navel.

He states with the words "In this way" (evam) that, among the Sāttvika, Rājasa, and Tāmasa Kalpas, it is fixed that the other Kalpas have Sadāśiva and the other forms as their primary [deities]. || 5 ||
He was the Grandfather (Brahmā) in one instance, and in another he was someone else;
he was that Puruṣa of volition who assumed a physical form through his own resolve.

With the intention that there is no fixed rule regarding the origin of the Grandfather (Brahmā), based on the statement in the *Pūrva-Rāmāyaṇa* that "Brahmā is born from space," he says: "the Grandfather. "The other" refers to Durgā, Bhairava, Vināyaka, and so forth;
for even they are well-known in the portions of the Purāṇas and other texts that establish their respective greatness as being the cause of the origin of Brahmā and the others. He...

The Puruṣa, beginning with Sadāśiva, has been described as consisting of volition (saṃkalpamaya). He is of the nature of the Māyic volition mentioned in the Śruti: "He desired, 'May I be many, may I procreate. (6)
The first resolve, having become nourished and established in that mental form,
experiences whatever it conceives exactly as it does so, immediately and fully.

The meaning is that the very first volition, having become nourished by means of the creation of subtle elements, assumes the form of the collective and individual mentalities (manas) of that time; then, existing in the form of Hiraṇyagarbha and others, it conceives the creation of the worlds and living beings as they are, and experiences them accordingly in a manner fit for worldly transaction. || 7 ||

The entire world is of the nature of reality, yet it appears as a void-ghost through the vision of delusion; thus, the movement of the world is the ego-sense (ahaṃtā) which perceives it as having the nature of existence.
From the perspective of ultimate reality, it is of the nature of non-existence; yet from the perspective of delusion, it appears as if real, having the nature of existence. || 8 ||
Indeed, the person who is the seer and so forth thus becomes himself;
at every moment, he emerges into the void and is then led away.

In the manner thus described, that Primordial Being who becomes the observer of his own creation, even during a *nimeṣa*—that is, in a moment of time discernible by a blink—by the mere contemplation of his own nature, the void (*vyoma*), which is nothing but the space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*), arises. Then, upon forgetting his own nature, in just a *nimeṣa*, he is led toward the infinite and boundless cycle of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*). || 9 ||
A single moment is indeed an eon, for it fully experiences a succession of great eons through the mere reversal of appearances. (10)
*Kalpa* means capable of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). The error (*viparyāsa*) of appearance is its orientation toward the external, by virtue of that [appearance] alone. (10)
In every atom, in every void, and in every moment,
there arise for you the existence and non-existence of creations, kalpas, and great kalpas.
Even in the sky, that is, in space such as the hole of a needle and so forth. || 11 ||
Some are seen by one another due to the similarity of their latent impressions (*vāsanā*);
others are not seen by each other because of the constant nature of what is perceived. (12)

And those various creations, for as many individual souls as there are whose latent impressions (vāsanā) arise simultaneously with respect to the same objects, are mutually consistent in their worldly transactions such as seeing and so forth; for others, however, they are empty of that [creation].
Relying on the principle of the *Aindava-upākhyāna*, he says: "They are seen. And as for non-perception:
Regarding the imagined aspect, [it is not directly perceived]; however, regarding the substratum aspect, all have direct and immediate perception (nityāparokṣatā). Thus he says: "By what is seen."
Creations arise everywhere through the process of creation, yet they do not exist within you, O Auspicious One;
for in the supreme ether, they are themselves of the nature of ether. 13.

Regarding this, he states the reasoning: "creations" (*sargāḥ*). Since creations come into being only as they are conceived by the *jīva* who exists in the form of creation, they do not exist in Śiva, the supreme ether whose nature is ultimate reality; for in that [reality], they resolve solely into the nature of ether—this is the meaning. || 13 ||
And being themselves of the nature of both existence and non-existence, they dissolve like mountains in a dream;
by these creations, neither space, nor time, nor agency is ever transgressed.

Now, one might object: "Let the creations exist independently of the reality of Brahman, either by their own existence or by an existence obtained through the power of their relation to space and time.

To this he says: "And by themselves," etc. They are of the nature of both being and non-being, meaning their essential nature is not restricted to one or the other. Thus, space and time were not pervaded by the creations prior [to their emergence]; for since those two are also included within the creations, they possess a form that is dependent upon the creations.

The meaning is that [the Self] is dependent on conceptualization (kalpanā) regarding creation. If it is argued that "then let creation itself effect its own existence—whether in the form of a connection with time and so forth, or otherwise," he replies: "not by agency" (na kartṛtā).
The word "of creations" (sargāṇām) is to be supplied by ellipsis, with a change in grammatical number. || 14 ||
These are neither of the nature of existence nor are they to be conceptualized as such, nor are they momentary;
nothing whatsoever is born here, and nothing whatsoever perishes. (15)

"In that case, let the creations themselves remain of the nature of existence until dissolution"; to this he replies: "And these [are not so]. For if the terms "creation" (*sarga*) and "existence" (*sat*) were synonymous, it would follow that destruction could not occur. The sense is that this accords with the Lord's established doctrine: "Non-existence does not exist for that which is real. If it is then argued that existence must be merely superimposed upon the creation, to this he replies: "No."

"Imaginable" (*kalpyam*): the sense is that it is impossible for that which is non-existent to serve as the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) for the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of existence. If one were to say, "In that case, let existence be something that persists through a series (*anugata*), just like the momentary form in the doctrine of the Nihilists (*vaināśika*)," he replies: "Nor even... Because existence in the form of a moment does not persist until the time of cognition, its existence would belong even to that which is utterly uncognized and false (*alīka*).

The sense is that this would entail that very [absurd] consequence. With the intention of showing that by this [argument] the birth and destruction of the creation—defined as the connection with the initial and final moments—are also refuted, he says: "And this is not so. || 15 ||
Everything manifests as a wonder within consciousness through the form of volition;
the world is like the creation, descent, and ascent of a city in a dream.
With the intention that our own established doctrine alone is the refuge, he recalls what was stated previously with the words: "All... (verse 16).
And it does not undergo even the slightest succession of space and time,
just as [the mind] perceives the infinite— space, time, and so forth— through the mountain of its own conceptualization.
How, then, is there the cognition of being pervaded by space and time? To this he says, beginning with "yathā" (just as), etc. (verse 17).
Though it was indeed overwhelmed by the world of the living, it remained as if unoverwhelmed;
or rather, according to another reading, "though not overwhelmed," it was as if overwhelmed by the Meru-mountain of his own volition.

Just as Mount Meru, though situated high above, is not actually traversed by one standing there, yet at the time of the mental resolve it appears as if it were traversed—such is the connection with what follows. || 18 ||
Just as the place, time, and other factors are high, so too does the world exist; for that Puruṣa is the agent of all things.

For this very reason, he states that the diversity of births—such as those of humans, insects, and stationary beings—occurs solely in accordance with one's *saṃkalpa* (volitional resolve), saying: "He becomes... [and so forth].
"The agent of all" (*sarvakāraka*) means one who is capable of performing all actions pertaining to both this world and the next. || 19 ||
By this very process, a worm is produced here in an instant;
indeed, the four classes of beings that remain stationary here are likewise produced in this manner. (20)

He also becomes the source of stationary beings that remain fixed; the meaning is that in this very way, the fourfold classes of birth, such as those born from eggs and so forth, come into being. || 20 ||
From Rudra down to a blade of grass, beings come into existence at every moment;
some are like atoms, while others are even smaller than atoms.

At every moment, for the one presiding over the illusion, at the very instant of his volition, there exist creations that—due to the subtlety of latent impressions—are like atoms when slightly expanded, and like motes of dust in the current state of manifestation. (21)
This is indeed the sequence for them, whether creation exists or not,
because of the cultivation of such objects within this illusion of saṃsāra.

He states "this very [process]" to show that the sequence of past and future creations should be understood as being exactly like the present creation—referring to those [beings] from Rudra down to a blade of grass. To the question, "How then does the cessation of creation occur?", he replies with "of this":
through the contemplation, that is, the direct realization, of such a supreme reality (paramārthatattva). || 22 ||
Through the cessation of differentiation by means of practice, one attains Śiva;
the supreme consciousness lasts for no more than half of a hundredth part of a moment. (23)
He says that even for a mere fraction of a moment, when the conscious self (cidātman) turns its face outward, there arises a proliferation of misfortunes extending over tens of millions of kalpas:
"If this very [consciousness] should fall from its own nature, this instability arises;
yet, being of the nature of the Knower, it remains within the self of consciousness like the space within a stone. (24)

"Ruṭhitā" means fallen away. He says "sā" (she) to indicate that the state of being Brahman is precisely the establishment in one's own true nature (*svarūpa*). She is "jñarūpā," meaning she is experienced or manifested by the "knower" (*jña*), who is the knower of reality (*tattvavid*). || 24 ||
That which is of the nature of beginningless manifestation is denoted by the word "Brahman.
When this creation has reached maturity, there is no further illumination of the Great Consciousness.

He says that as the creation attains maturity through the increase of ego-inflation (*abhimāna*), so too does the effulgence of the conscious self (*cidātman*) diminish, and the self’s pettiness, occasioned by an excess of limitation, increases:
"The state of being composed of parts such as direction, space, time, and atoms, which are associated with the unreal..."
It has come to the living beings through the sequence of the evolution of the elements and the subtle constituents (tanmātras). || 26 ||

The extreme minuteness and subtlety of the self—ranging from the ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*) down to mosquitoes and gnats—is due to its limitations and divisions created by space, direction, and time, which are unreal when considered in their aggregate. This is the ellipsis for "of the self. However, according to the reading *paramāṇunā*, it means that having attained the state of being Brahman, consciousness, and the individual soul (*jīva*) through the supreme subtle adjunct (*liṅgopādhi*).

O friend, through the sequence of the development of the body, senses, and so forth—designated as the gross elements (bhūta) and subtle elements (tanmātra)—one becomes a doe, a creeper, a tree, or a worm, god, or demon; this is the connection with what follows. || 26 ||
O dear one, the deer, creepers, insects, gods, asuras, and so forth exist within that which is eternal, pervasive, infinite, and firm, like a garland upon it. (27)

For this very reason, he says "in which" (yasmin) [in verse 27], meaning that the universe, consisting of both the existent and the non-existent, remains strung together like a garland upon a firm thread.
The universe, woven from both the existent and the non-existent, resides within the omnipresent Viśvakarman;
it is neither far nor near, neither above nor below, nor is it distinct from Him.
It was not in the past, nor is it today, nor in the morning; it is neither being, nor non-being, nor something intermediate.

But in the state of discernment (*viveka*), that [Self] is indeed entirely free from delimitation by directions, time, and so forth; thus he says, "Not that" (*na tat*). It is not yours (*te*); it is not mine (*me*); nor is it intermediate (*mādhyamaṃ*), that is, indescribable (*anirvacanīya*) as lying between the positions of existence and non-existence. || 28 ||
When the nectar of the time of experience has been attained, the mother [of cognition] no longer exists amidst all conceptual constructions;
the garland of means of knowledge, though possessing the vast power of its fruit, finds no standing, just as fire does not exist in water. // 29 //

For this very reason, he says "anubhava" (experience), meaning that in that state, self-experience alone is the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and the worldly subject, means of knowledge, and so forth do not operate there. Thus, when all conceptual constructions (*vikalpana*) are absent, there is no other subject or experiencer for his own experience-forming activity (*kalanā*)—which is self-luminous consciousness—apart from that [consciousness] itself. As for that which is worldly...

The extensive splendor of worldly transactions bears fruit from her presence; yet such a garland of means of valid cognition (pramāṇamālā) finds no footing there, like fire in water. The meaning is that in that state, only the triad [of subject, object, and cognition] is sublated. || 29 ||
O Sage, that which was asked has been told; may it be well with you.
We shall now depart for our desired direction; arise, O Pārvatī! (30)

Showing that there was no remainder of any other instruction to be given, the Lord, having favored Vasiṣṭha with a benediction for the sake of the subject he had taught, concluded his teaching and rose; thus he says: "Just as... (verse 30).
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Having spoken thus, that Nīlakaṇṭha, while I was still holding the handful of flowers,
crossed into the expanse of the sky together with his retinue.
He crossed over; he leaped. || 31 ||

When that Lord of Umā, the sovereign of the three worlds, had departed, I remained for a moment; then, with a mind newly purified by faith, I accepted the worship of my own inner deity, which had previously been abandoned by me as one possessed of tranquility.
Indeed, even before this, while I was tranquil, I had already accepted that [worship] taught by that venerable Guru, the Lord himself, preceded by his constant remembrance.

The meaning is this: I have resolved to perform the worship of the eternally perceptible God with a mind purified by faith and other virtues and refined by the nine-fold path; at the same time, I desire to abandon that previous worship of inert deities.
Thus ends the [thirty-second] chapter in the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa*, the work of Valmiki, concerning the means to liberation. Pūrvārdha.
The forty-second canto, titled "The Designation of the Supreme Self."
Thus ends the forty-second chapter, titled "The Designation of the Supreme Self," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The forty-third canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: This supreme truth was spoken by him, and I myself know it as well.
O Rāma, you too know how this matter stands.
Having heard here [this teaching] along with the doctrine of detachment, Rāma,
awakened and having accomplished his purpose, described his own worship of Śiva as established therein.

Praising the worship of one’s own self as Śiva—which was taught by Īśvara and culminates in the vision of reality—for the sake of perfecting Śrī Rāma’s extraordinary faith, he himself instructs him once more in that very practice with the words beginning "This... and so forth.
"Supreme" means most excellent. "This" refers to the reality of the universe. || 1 ||
In this illusory world of saṃsāra, where the unreal is perceived by means of the unreal within the unreal, what is real and what is composed of unreality?
In that illusion—which is false, an error, and constituted by false limiting adjuncts—the world, which is itself non-existent and false, is perceived by the false individual soul (jīva). || 2 ||
Just as something is described by whatever conceptualization or by whichever conceptualization, so too is it experienced even when not present, by means of that very same mental construction. (3)

In this regard, he states "just as" (*yathā*) to show that when a king or similar figure is described through the Mount Meru imagined by a poet, such an experience is the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*).

One who imagines in various ways is the "imagination" (*vikalpa*); by whatever poet, in whatever king or subject, there is the imagination of various states such as Mount Meru—that is his "imagination.
Just as it is narrated through the composition of poetry by that imagination, so too, having heard it, one perceives oneself—

The phrase "imagines" (kalpayati) refers to the "self-imagining" (ātmakalpa), such as a king and so forth; by means of this, even though Mount Meru or the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa) have not actually entered into his own [perception], they are experienced [as such].

Otherwise, how could there be for him the aesthetic wonder (camatkāra) of tasting the meaning of poetry, and how could the poet obtain great wealth, honor, and the like? This is the intended meaning. || 3 ||
Just as liquidity exists in water, as movement exists in the wind,
and as emptiness exists in space, so does the nature of creation exist within the Self.

With the intention that various conceptual constructions are indeed the very nature of the unknown Self, he states further examples: "From that time onwards, following that very same sequence, I have remained until today performing the worship of the Self, free from distraction. (5)

Thus, he says "Then" (tataḥ) [in verse 5], meaning that from that time until the present day, he has remained performing the very contemplation of worship as being nothing other than the superimposition of conceptual construction upon the essential nature itself.
O Rāma, by means of this ritual of worship, these days are passed by me without weariness,
even though I am occupied with worldly affairs.
The worship of oneself with the flowers of ritual conduct as they are obtained was never interrupted, even for a single day or night, though it had been severed.

The meaning is that although [consciousness] was interrupted during the time of deep sleep, it was never actually severed; for even then, there exists the worship of the three flowers consisting of the mental modification (*vṛtti*) of ignorance, which serves as the cause for the subsequent recollection upon waking: "I slept happily, I was not conscious of anything. || 7 ||
When there is a connection between the grasped and the grasper, which is common to all embodied beings, that state of attentiveness on the part of the yogi is the worship of the Self. (8)
If that is so, since even the ignorant always perform such worship of Śiva, what is your distinction over them? To this he says:
"O Lord of the Raghus, with a mind liberated from attachment through this vision, wander in this sparse forest of worldly existence; you shall not suffer. (9)
Showing that such attentiveness is indeed the abandonment of attachment, he urges Rāma toward worship by proclaiming the abundance of visible fruits: "Having seen," etc. (9).
When great suffering has arrived, born from the loss of wealth and kin, hold fast to this view and reflect upon it, O observer of noble vows. (10)
He states that for one who has renounced and is free from attachment, the firmness of discernment regarding non-arising is the cause; thus he says: "In suffering... (verse 10).
One should not feel joy or sorrow at the rise or fall of wealth and kinsmen;
indeed, all such perceptions regarding worldly existence are constantly of this nature. (11)
Pleasure and pain, joy and despair—such things as these are merely transitory. || 11 ||
You surely know the manifold course of the sense-objects, which are so destructive—that how they come, how they go, and how they overwhelm us. (12)
They come first and then they go; through attachment to their own calamities, they treat a man with contempt. 12.
In this very way do affections and riches arise;
in this very way they are lost through unexamined causes. (13)
Without being examined and without being reflected upon. || 13 ||
Those world-activities are not yours, nor are you theirs; they are pure within.
Why do you fruitlessly suffer over this world being such as it is? 14.
He is stainless; worldly activities are within you, yet you are not within them; there is nothing at all that is void.
You here are the form of the universe, O you whose nature is the expansion of pure consciousness; when your own limbs are withdrawn, what room is there for joy or sorrow? (15)

But if you do not accept the insubstantiality of the world, then perceive the world as being none other than the Self. Even when perceiving it thus, there is no occasion for joy or sorrow upon liberation from bondage and so forth, just as there is none when one's own limbs are rearranged; thus he says: "Thou... (verse 15).
O dear one, you are of the nature of pure consciousness; this world is not distinct from you.
Therefore, how and where could there be for you any conceptualization of what is to be rejected or accepted? (16)
Thus, in the ocean of the world which consists of consciousness, where the wheel of consciousness is ever-fickle, what room is there for joy or sorrow within the mass of waves in that very ocean? 17.
Thus, according to the manner described, [this occurs] regarding the flickering movement of the wheel of the world within the nature of consciousness. || 17 ||
Having attained one-pointedness of consciousness and reached the state of deep sleep, from this day forward, O Rāma, may you become the very essence of the fourth state (turya). 18.
He establishes Rāma at the ultimate limit of the aforementioned worship with the words: "the state of being solely intent upon consciousness" (cidekatānatām). || 18 ||
Equanimous, appearing with equal composure, possessing a radiant body and noble intellect, remain always devoted to the worship of the Self, like the perfectly full ocean. || 19 ||
He is himself equal, liberated from all inequality; he is one for whom the appearances of the world have attained equality and uniformity with Brahman.
Having heard all this, you stand here with a perfected intellect;
O delight of the Raghus, ask whatever else you wish to inquire.
"Whatever was asked in the first kalpa, that you should now put to me again.
Śrī Rāma said:
"O Brahman, my doubt has now been especially dispelled. (21)

Regarding those questions you asked me today during the first chapter on the commencement of inquiry, in the section on dispassion—if there remains anything among them that is yet unresolved, then challenge it and ask. || 21 ||
Everything that was to be known has been known; natural satisfaction has arisen.
O Sage, there is no impurity, no duality, no object of thought, and no conceptual construction.
Impurity is ignorance; duality is the distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman; that by which this is imagined is the mind (manas), which is the imagination itself. || 22 ||
At that time my ignorance was present, but now it has been stilled; yet the notion that "there is a stain upon the Self" arose through the force of that very ignorance. (23)
That delusion which existed has now ceased through your grace;
the Self is neither born nor does it die, nor is it ever defiled. (24)
Indeed, I have been sufficiently awakened to the fact that all this is composed of Brahman,
in response to all questions, doubts, and desires from every side.
It is Brahman itself, consisting of Brahman, or an evolution of Brahman; and it is "withdrawn from all desires"—this is the ellipsis. || 25 ||
My mind has become pure and stainless, as if by the turning of a lathe by the divine artisan Tvaṣṭṛ, regarding all instructions on conduct received from and proclaimed by the virtuous. (26)

Having placed it upon a lathe by Tvaṣṭṛ, its whirling was performed; that which is characterized by such whirling is "turning" (*takṣaṇa*)—[the word *takṣaṇa* is not read in some versions]. Therefore, like the solar orb, it is pure and radiant. For the sake of disciples who have arrived and approached from those who have attained perfection, all the prescribed conducts [are taught].
He is free from all desire regarding the instructions for spiritual practices. || 26 ||
I remain within myself, free from longing, like Mount Sumeru amidst gold;
there is nothing where hope exists, and there is nothing that is desired.
The distinction is that "hope" pertains to what is obtainable after a long time, whereas "desire" pertains to what is obtainable at every step. || 27 ||
There is nothing to be taken up, nothing to be abandoned, and nothing intermediate among the moving and the unmoving;
this is to be abandoned, this is to be accepted, this is existent, and this too is non-existent. (28)
The middle [type] is to be disregarded. || 28 ||
Thus, O supreme sage, my whirlpool of anxious thought has been stilled;
I do not long for heaven, nor do I loathe the Raurava hell. (29)
Nor do I hate even Raurava, that particular hell. || 29 ||
For I abide in myself alone, like the cloudless Mount Mandara,
amidst the flow of the milk-ocean of the three worlds scattered in fragments.
[She] by whom the three worlds have been scattered, dispersed, and—so to speak—destroyed by dividing them into grains and atoms;
such is the milk-ocean whose pervasion is like a universal diffusion. This is a poetic conceit (autprekṣika).
Alternatively, [she is she] by whom the three worlds have been strewn and sprinkled with drops of the milk of fame spreading out grain by grain.

The connection with the subsequent verse is as follows: he whose worldly existence (*saṃsṛti*)—the ocean of milk for his lineage—is of such a nature, who has long been wandering like Mount Mandara characterized by Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, has now become fulfilled through the production of the nectar of awakening; he has now come to rest, his delusion having ceased. || 30 ||
O Rāma, Mandara, having rested after long wandering, is now free from delusion;
the conceptualization that "this is non-substance" and "this is substance" has utterly ceased.

O Lord of Sages, behold this meaning of my words so that you may verify it through your own experience: for that fool who perceives this world as it is seen—nothing other than its apparent form—and believes that no other reality exists, his heart is set ablaze by a web of false doubts. For him, the mental fabrication of "this is real" and "that is unreal" is a source of excessive torment; therefore, look [into this matter].
The positive concomitance [is established] by means of another. || 31 ||
O Lord of Sages, his heart was intensely inflamed by a web of false doubts regarding that which he had known as "this world is thus. (32)
Whatever state of wretchedness he encounters, that is not found in the world, for the world is insentient, devoid of activity, and characterized by diverse, turbulent waves. (33)

That such a deluded person falls into miserliness regarding objects such as wealth—which belong to the world—is because, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*tattvadṛśā*), those things are not obtained by us; this is the implied sense. For we are diverse, agitated waves characterized by hunger and other such states—the six waves (*ṣaḍūrmayaḥ*).

The connection with the following verse is as follows: "By your grace, we have crossed over that ocean of worldly existence (bhavasāgara), which is insentient and devoid of the activity of such pure consciousness-forms. || 33 ||
"O Blessed One, by your grace we have crossed over the ocean of existence;
the limit of prosperity has been known, and the boundary of calamities has been seen. (34)

O Supreme Lord, we are undaunted even in the face of all essential hardships; we are full. Our mind has attained perfect heroism in the ocean of worldly existence, having crushed the elephant of desire that cannot be pierced by others. (35)

We are not dejected, for we have eternally attained even that which is the essence of all—the realm of the bliss of the Infinite (Bhūmānanda). Our mind has reached a perfect heroism, impenetrable by others, such that it has shattered the elephant of hope within the battle characterized by the cycle of worldly existence (saṃsāra). || 35 ||

My mind has attained a state where conceptual constructions have dissolved; its longing has ebbed away, and its essential strength is undaunted. In the three worlds, it possesses a form of supreme clarity, and within, it is most joyfully exalted.

Describing the state of mind that is truly full, he concludes with the verse beginning "parigalita-": "He whose essence is undepressed— that is, whose fortitude (*sattva*) is firm and free from meanness— and whose forms are as serene as those renowned throughout the three worlds,
such as the full moon, the ocean of milk, and the autumnal sky."

These [states] have been transcended; its form is exceedingly serene. The compound is a *sāpekṣasamāsa* (a dependent compound) used in the Vedic style (*chāndasa*). The meaning is: "Therefore, my mind, being inwardly delighted, remains established in that which is unsurpassed. || 36 ||
Thus ends the forty-third canto, titled "The Description of Rest," in the section on Nirvāṇa within the Means to Liberation, in the glorious Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa, a work of the Ṛṣis.
Thus ends the forty-third canto, titled "The Description of Rest," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The forty-fourth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
