[That which exists] together with the senses alone, abiding in present objects...
Whatever you do with a mind free from attachment, that is not considered "done" [in the worldly sense]. || 1 ||

Furthermore, the means for the destruction of attachment— beginning with the renunciation of desire and ending with the dissolution of the mind— were taught by the Guru for the sake of strengthening one's knowledge.

Even though Rāma has described his own rest in the realization of reality (*tattvabodha*), the venerable Vasiṣṭha—wishing to establish the very sequence of previously mentioned means, which constitutes the characteristics of one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*) like a succession of wedges for the firmness of a pillar driven into stone, so that there might be no falling away prior to its full maturation—proceeds with what was stated before: [The text continues from the previous section: ...in the aforementioned [state], [he says: "O King, this is the supreme state; this is the supreme peace; this is the supreme liberation; this is the supreme goal. Having said this, the venerable Vasiṣṭha remained silent. Then, having heard these words of the venerable Vasiṣṭha, Rāma, his mind filled with joy, spoke again to the venerable Vasiṣṭha: "O venerable one, by what signs is one known to be liberated while living? And how does one remain in that state? To him, the venerable Vasiṣṭha replied: "O King, one who remains in the state of the Self, free from all mental constructs, whose mind is tranquil, and who perceives the world as if it were a dream or a city of the Gandharvas—he is known as liberated while living. [The text continues: ...and so forth. Having heard this, Rāma asked again: "O venerable one, by what further signs is one known to be liberated while living? To him, the venerable Vasiṣṭha replied: "O King, he whose mind is not agitated by the arrival of gain or loss, whose mind is not affected by praise or blame, whose mind is not moved by pleasure or pain, and whose mind remains equanimous toward friends and enemies—he is known as liberated while living. [The text continues: ...and so forth. Having heard this, Rāma asked again: "O venerable one, by what further signs is one known to be liberated while living? To him, the venerable Vasiṣṭha replied: "O King, he who acts without attachment, without expectation of fruit, and without egoism, performing actions merely as a movement of the body, like a wheel turning on its axle—he is known as liberated while living. [The text continues: ...and so forth. Having heard this, Rāma asked again: "O venerable one, by what further signs is one known to be liberated while living? To him, the venerable Vasiṣṭha replied: "O King, he who dwells in the Self, remaining as a witness to the activities of the mind and senses, like a spectator watching a play, without being involved in the drama—he is known as liberated while living. [The text continues: ...and so forth. Having heard this, Rāma asked again: "O venerable one, by what further signs is one known to be liberated while living? To him, the venerable Vasiṣṭha replied: "O King, he whose mind is not bound by the objects of the senses, who has transcended all dualities, who is free from desire and aversion, and who has attained the state of pure consciousness—he is known as liberated while living. [The text continues: ...and so forth. Having heard this, Rāma asked again: "O venerable one, by what further signs is one known to be liberated while living? To him, the venerable Vasiṣṭha replied: "O King, he who, even while engaged in worldly affairs, remains inwardly established in the Self, like a lotus leaf untouched by water, and whose mind is never disturbed—he is known as liberated while living. [The text continues: ...and so forth. Having heard this, Rāma asked again: "O venerable one, by what further signs is one known to be liberated while living? To him, the venerable Vasiṣṭha replied: "O King, he who, having realized the truth, remains in the state of non-duality, seeing the entire universe as the Self alone, and who has no sense of 'I' or 'mine'—he is known as liberated while living. [The text continues: ...and so forth. Having heard this, Rāma asked again: "O venerable one, by what further signs is one known to be liberated while living? To him, the venerable Vasiṣṭha replied: "O King, he who, having cast off all mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), remains in the state of pure being, like the sky free from clouds, and who is beyond all change—he is known as liberated while living. [The text continues: ...and so forth. Having heard this, Rāma asked again: "O venerable one, by what further signs is one known to be liberated while living? To him, the venerable Vasiṣṭha replied: "O King, he who, having attained the state of supreme peace, remains indifferent to the body, the senses, and the mind, and who perceives the world as a mere illusion—he is known as liberated while living. [The text continues: ...and so forth. Having heard this, Rāma asked again: "O venerable one, by what further signs is one known to be liberated while living? To him, the venerable Vasiṣṭha replied: "O King, he who, having reached the end of all inquiry, remains in the state of absolute stillness, where there is neither subject nor object, and who is established in the unchanging Reality—he is known as liberated while living. [The text continues: ...and so forth. Having heard this, Rāma asked again: "O venerable one, by what further signs is one known to be liberated while living? To him, the venerable Vasiṣṭha replied: "O King, he who, having transcended the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, remains in the fourth state (*turya*), which is pure consciousness, and who is free from all limitations—he is known as liberated while living. [The text continues: ...and so forth. Having heard this, Rāma asked again: "O venerable one, by what further signs is one known to be liberated while living? To him, the venerable Vasiṣṭha replied: "O King, he who, having realized that the world is but a projection of the mind, remains in the state of the Self, free from all mental fluctuations, and who is established in the eternal and immutable Truth—he is known as liberated while living. [The text continues: ...and so forth. Having heard this, Rāma asked again: "O venerable one, by what further signs is one known to be liberated while living? To him, the venerable Vasiṣṭha replied: "O King, he who, having attained the state of supreme bliss, remains in the state of the Self, free from all desires, and who perceives the universe as the Self alone—he is known as liberated while living. [The text continues: ...and so forth. Having heard this, Rāma asked again: "O venerable one, by what further signs is one known to be liberated while living? To him, the venerable Vasiṣṭha replied: "O King, he who, having cast off all attachments, remains in the state of the Self, free from all mental constructs, and who is established in the state of pure awareness—he is known as liberated while living. [The text continues: ...and so forth. Having heard this, Rāma asked again: "O venerable one, by what further signs is one known to be liberated while living? To him, the venerable Vasiṣṭha replied: "O King, he who, having reached the state of non-attachment, remains in the state of the Self, free from all dualities, and who is established in the state of absolute peace—he is known as liberated while living. [The text continues: ...and so forth. Having heard this, Rāma asked again: "O venerable one, by what further signs is one known to be liberated while living? To him, the venerable Vasiṣṭha replied: "O King, he who, having realized the truth of the Self, remains in the state of the Self, free from all mental activity, and who is established in the state of pure being—he is known as liberated while living. [The text continues: ...and so forth. Having heard this, Rāma asked again: "O venerable one, by what further signs is one known to be liberated while living? To him, the venerable Vasiṣṭha replied: "O King, he who, having transcended the body and the senses, remains in the state of the Self, free from all limitations, and who is established in the state of the infinite and eternal Truth—he is known as liberated while living. [The text continues: ...and so forth. Having heard this, Rāma asked

Even in the worship of Śiva, which is characterized by the enjoyment of worldly activities as they are obtained, there would indeed be [the occurrence of faults], according to the maxim that "all undertakings are enveloped by defect,
just as fire is by smoke," because of the unavoidable possibility of injury, hostility, and other undesirable results through negligence, and because enjoyment itself is a cause of misfortune.
Warding off the apprehension that there might be the misfortune of rebirth and so forth, he says: "by the solitary one. By the solitary one, meaning by one devoid of passion and the like;
and for that very reason, by the unattached one, meaning by one free from association with action characterized by the conceit of agency. || 1 ||
Just as an object at the very moment of attainment brings satisfaction, so it does not do so even for a single moment thereafter; who has not experienced this? (2)
An objection is raised: "Since there is a rule that objects invariably produce satisfaction, how can attachment to them be abandoned?

Anticipating this, he says: "Just as... The meaning is that this is not an invariable rule, because their status as causes of satisfaction is seen to deviate in the time preceding and following the moment of acquisition. || 2 ||
Just as an object brings satisfaction at the time it is desired, but not otherwise,
therefore the fool, and no one else, fixes his attachment upon momentary pleasure.
Therefore, he says "vāñchā" (desire) to show that even attachment to momentary pleasure for the sake of long-term harm is not appropriate;
by the word "vāñchā," "attainment" (lābha) is indicated. || 3 ||
At the time of desire, that which leads to satisfaction is desire itself;
yet satisfaction ends in dissatisfaction—therefore, abandon desire.

When even a momentary cessation of desire, brought about by the acquisition of an object, is a cause of happiness, then it follows by implication that the absolute eradication of desire is the cause of unsurpassed bliss; and with the intention that desire itself is a misfortune, he says: "At the time of desiring. Here, *tuṣṭi* means bliss (*ānanda*).
Discontent is precisely that desire which is the opposite of contentment; it is such that its limit is [its own] cessation. || 4 ||
If, through the passage of time, you should ever attain that state,
then you must never again be immersed in the form of the notion of "I."

"Surely I have attained the state of full bliss; for what purpose, then, do you give me this instruction on the renunciation of desire for sense objects? To this he replies with the words "yadi" (if).
This is for the sake of strengthening one's stability in that state, so that there may be no further sinking into the mire of egoism even at a later time.
The meaning is that it is a further instruction. || 5 ||
O Rāma, you have found rest upon the peak of the mountain of self-knowledge;
you ought not to fall again into the great abyss of egoism.
For one who has attained the summit of the Meru of knowledge through the recollection of the infinite, true vision—
how could there again be a fall into the underworld that resembles the womb?

Even though there is firmness [of realization], why is further immersion not feared? To this he says: "Since" (yat). Because of which reason the embryo situated within the mother's womb follows that physical mass (piṇḍa) and brings about the misfortunes of birth and so forth—thus, the ego-sense (ahaṃbhāva) that conforms to the embryo is like a subterranean cave characterized by that [womb]. In that [cave], [there is]...
The meaning is that for one whose knowledge has become firm, the seed of the evil of ignorance is necessarily destroyed. || 7 ||
This nature of yours is seen to consist of the truth of equanimity;
I believe you have exhausted all conceptual constructions and have become one for whom time has been destroyed.

With the intention that "this was spoken by me for the benefit of others, but as for you, your ignorance has been destroyed," as it was indeed perceived by me through signs such as equanimity (*samatā*) and so forth, he says: "It is seen. *Kālikā* refers to ignorance (*avidyā*). || 8 ||
"O gentle Rāma, your stainless equanimity, resembling a full ocean, seems to inform me that you are firmly established in your own true nature. (9)
May hope turn into hopelessness, and may the sense of existence turn into non-existence; may the mind turn into mindlessness for you who live in non-attachment. 10.
There is no arising of attachment for one who lives by that [means]; the *loṭ* suffix is used in the sense of approval or benediction. (10)
Whatever perception of an object you may have, in each and every one of them resides Brahman, the mass of expanded consciousness, in the form of the universal existence (sattāsāmānya). || 11 ||

It is not out of despair from the frustration of my desires, nor from hopelessness, that I pray; rather, it is with the intention that I may attain the Brahman, which is unsurpassed bliss in every respect, that he says: "Whichever [state]... (verse 11).
One who does not know the Self is bound; one who knows the Self is not bound.
Therefore, O Rāma, you must by all means awaken yourself through your own self. 12.
By force, that is, through the firmness resulting from reflection and so forth. || 12 ||
Know that state to be freedom from latent impressions (avāsanatva)—a serenity as soft as the sky—in which an object does not taste sweet to oneself, yet tastes sweet as it comes. 13.

Now, he states the definition of the state of being free from latent impressions (*nirvāsanatva*), which is to be realized through one's own experience, in the verse beginning with *yatra*: "The object" refers to the pleasure of enjoyment;
"as it comes" refers even to the suffering brought about by the force of past karma (*prārabdha*). || 13 ||
Perform your activities with the internal senses free from latent impressions (vāsanā);
you shall not undergo transformation even by hundreds of disturbances, remaining like the sky.
Like the sky, like space. || 14 ||
The knower, knowledge, and the object of knowledge—these three are unified within the Self;
having become incapable of experiencing anything other than the peaceful Self, you shall no longer partake in worldly existence.

It is impossible to experience even suffering and the like as being the self through the unification of the three factors [knower, known, and knowing]; therefore, its disagreeableness is pacified—this is the intended meaning. || 15 ||
The emergence and dissolution of saṃsāra occur through the opening and closing of the eyes of the mind;
by restraining the latent impressions and the vital breath, make the mind unblinking.

With the intention that the conceptualization of aversion toward suffering and so forth is a mental construction, and that this very [construction] must be restrained according to the reasoning stated by Bhusuṇḍa, he says: "The mind... (verse 16).
Through the opening and closing of the vital breath (prāṇa), there occur the dissolution and emergence of worldly existence;
by means of practice and application, render that [breath] devoid of its opening.
The dissolution and emergence of karmas occur through the opening and closing of the eyes of ignorance;
dissolve that [ignorance] by force through the restraint of the meaning of the Guru’s teachings and the scriptures. 18.

Or rather, ignorance itself, by way of leading to worldly activity, is the root cause of misfortune; therefore, that very ignorance must be dispelled through the firmness of knowledge. Thus he says: "By folly... (verse 18).

Just as the sky appears as the perception of existence due to the vibration caused by contact with wind-dust, so too does this [world] arise from the vibration of consciousness through its state of being an object of cognition.
Regarding what was stated— "by the opening and closing of the mind"— he clarifies this through an illustration, beginning with "just as" (yathā):

just as the sky (kha), which is space (ākāśa), comes to possess the perception of being stained and moving due to its contact with wind and dust and due to its own vibration, so too does consciousness (cit) come to possess the state of being an object (cetyatā) due to the vibration characterized by the mind (citta).
The meaning is that this collection of misfortunes has presented itself. || 19 ||
This course of the world vibrates through the movement of the relationship between the seen and the seeing,
just as the perception of color flashes forth from the contact of light with a wall or other objects.
He demonstrates the positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) regarding the stated point with two verses beginning with "dṛśya":
"Like the cognition of variegated color produced by the contact of sunlight entering through various apertures with a wall. (20)
In the absence of the vibration of the relationship between the seen and the seeing, no sensation arises that appears as existence within the heart of the variegated person. 21.
The world exists as the appearance of becoming; just as no mental cultivation arises in the heart or the mind of men depicted in a painting, so it is with this. || 21 ||
Illusion arises from the vibration of the mind; in its absence, it dissolves. A wave arises from the vibration of water; in its absence, it perishes.

When the mind has attained a state of motionlessness through the abandonment of the portion of latent impressions, through awakening, or through the restraint of the vital breaths, how can there be the possibility of movement? (23)
Of vibration, which consists in the departure from immutability. || 23 ||
By the mere cessation of the vibration of consciousness, the mind attains the state of non-mind; or else, by the restraint of the vital breaths, that very same supreme state is reached. (24)
And the word "ca" (and) has the sense of "hi" (for/indeed). || 24 ||

In the relationship between the seen and the seeing, that which is the ultimate happiness is attained through the realization of the final limit; by means of the vision of Brahman, there is the dissolution of the mind.

He explains the statement "or from awakening," which refers to the middle means (*madhyamopāya*), with the word "perceiving" (*dṛśya*). That pleasure which is well-known to arise from the contact between the sense objects and the senses is, in the ultimate sense, nothing other than the bliss of Brahman; for the Śruti declares: "Of this very bliss, other beings live on only a small portion. Therefore, its end—
The ultimate limit is shown by the Śruti as an increase of a hundredfold at each successive stage, beginning from human bliss:
"From which words turn back, together with the mind, not having attained it—he who knows the bliss of Brahman never fears.
The dissolution of the mind occurs through the vision of Brahman, which consists of the realization of that [bliss] as its own nature, filled with that alone, and characterized by absolute oneness.
The meaning is that it is accomplished. || 25 ||
Wherever the mind has not arisen, there that bliss is unconditioned;
it does not exist in heaven and the like, just as a house of ice cannot exist in a desert.

That respective happiness is the bliss of Brahman, and that does not exist on the planes of enjoyment such as heaven; the meaning is that there, the mind is defiled by desire, envy, and so forth. "Hima" means cold water, and its "house" (gṛha) is a lake. || 26 ||
The bliss born from the tranquility of the mind is expansive and inexpressible by words;
free from decay and excess, it neither arises nor ceases. (27)
"It cannot be spoken" means it is impossible to express; the sense is that it is to be known solely through one's own direct experience. || 27 ||
From awakening comes the end of the mind; from lack of awakening comes the perception of a mind.
Through that [latter], like a child’s ghost, the splendor of delusion has attained density.

The "end" of the mind is its destruction. Since the perception of the mind's existence arises solely through the power of delusion—which is difficult to comprehend—delusion is destroyed by true comprehension; thus, the destruction of the mind is logical. This is the intended meaning. It is like a ghost imagined by a child. [This occurs] because of that difficult-to-comprehend [delusion]. (28)
For even though this mind exists, it dissolves through awakening;
though real, it appears as if unreal, just like copper when it has been turned into gold.
[Objection: Since even the wise are seen to engage in worldly activity, they must still possess a mind; how then can it be said that the mind is destroyed by knowledge? [Response:
Because existence and non-existence are contradictory in one and the same place at the same time, he says in reply: "Even though it exists," etc. (Verse 29).
The mind of the Knower is not what is called "mind"; the mind of the Knower is called *sattva*.
Through awakening, the mind undergoes a change in its name and essence, just as copper becomes gold.
It is called "possessing otherness" because it partakes in otherness both by name and by meaning.
The nature of mind cannot exist [as a separate entity]; therefore, it dissolves away.
Delusion is stilled by awakening; there is no non-existence of that which is real. (31)

The meaning is that the very nature of the mind (*cittatā*) consists in being the seed of delusion, and that [nature] is dissolved through awakening (*bodha*). Since even upon the destruction of a jar or similar object, one observes a remainder in the form of shards and so forth, the destruction of an existent thing in its own essential form is nowhere established; thus he says:
"Mind and the like, being of the nature of conceptual construction, are indeed non-existent, like the horn of a hare."
All that belongs to the self; therefore, indeed, it dissolves through awakening.

He says, "It is indeed non-existent," because it is well known that the realization of the reality [of the Self] sublates only the imagined portion consisting of non-entities, and thus there is no possibility of it sublatting the existent portion. The remainder of the sentence is: "All that, beginning with the mind, is a transformation (vivarta) of the ultimate Self. || 32 ||

The mind, having attained the state of being a sentient being for some time during the persistence of the world, dwells in the fourth state (turya) and thereafter becomes that which transcends the fourth (turyātīta). || 33 ||
If one asks, "In that case, is the state of the mind of one liberated while living (jīvanmukta) capable of worldly activity merely real? he says: "The mind...

That state, which extends up to the direct realization of the samādhi of sporting (vihāra-samādhi), is not real; rather, it is a persistence of what has been sublated, produced by a trace of ignorance obstructed by prārabdha-karma.
The intended meaning is that for him, only the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta), which has manifested as disembodied liberation (videhakaivalya), is the reality. || 33 ||
Brahman alone, through the flood of delusions arising from manifold existences, remains thus as the one and only reality in its manifoldness.

It is the Self of all that comes into being; nothing else exists, my dear, not even the mind and so forth, for they have no existence apart from it, just as a mental impression has no location other than the heart.
As long as that Brahman which transcends the fourth state (turyātīta) is not known, so long do the mind, the world, and so forth remain in the guise of falsehood, appearing as the self of all;

yet there is no other distinct entity whatsoever called "mind" or the like. With the intention that it is logical for the mind and its associates to be reduced to nothing but that [Brahman] through mere knowledge, he says: "Brahman alone. As in the heart...

Just as the arrangement of palaces, groves, ponds, and so forth imagined by the mind does not exist because it cannot enter into that [reality], so too the world does not exist because it cannot enter into Brahman—which is supremely subtle, a dense mass of the single essence of flawless consciousness; this is the meaning. || 34 ||
Thus ends the forty-fourth canto, titled "The Indication of the Existence of the Mind," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the glorious Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa composed by Vālmīki. 44.
Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Indication of the Existence of the Mind," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The forty-fifth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Now, for the sake of this awakening, [I shall relate] this story which brings forth the joy of wonder.
O Rāma, listen to this unprecedented, beautiful story in brief. || 1 ||
The Supreme Brahman, which is filled with the essence of its own bliss and is the locus for the conceptualization of the three worlds, is here described by way of the bilva fruit.
The narrative known as the Bilva-ākhyāna. || 1 ||
There exists a great bilva fruit, thousands of yojanas in extent, vast, stainless, and radiant, whose form remains undecaying even through the ages.
That whose nature is such that it does not decay is "of undecaying form" (ajara-rūpa). || 2 ||
It possesses the essence of imperishable flavor, like the sweet essence of nectar;
though ancient, it is as beautiful and soft as the crescent of the new moon.
Or rather, like nectar in comparison to the earth, it is possessed of an exceedingly sweet essence;
like the petals of the young moon’s sprout, which increase day by day, those digits (kalās) are beautiful through their softness, being pleasant to the touch for the eyes. (3)
He was like Mount Meru in the midst of the array, as immovable as Mount Mandara,
and unshaken even by the force of the winds at the end of a great kalpa.
It was like Mount Meru situated in the midst of the array of worlds, serving as a central pillar; it was as immovable and firm as Mount Mandara.
Even by hundreds of lakhs of millions of ten-thousand yojanas, the extent of the primordial root of the world's existence is immeasurable. (5)
He explains that the previously mentioned "thousandfold" refers to the "innumerable," stating: "The root of the world's maintenance, support, and regulation. (Verse 5)
The universe, which once seemed so vast, now merely mimics the playfulness of a line of mustard seeds at the foot of the mountain compared to the great bilva fruit.
They carry away and bear off; *rājikā* refers to small mustard seeds, and "of that" refers to the line or row of those [seeds] that have been pierced. || 6 ||
O Rāghava, there is no one who surpasses him in that sweet wonder of aesthetic flavor, which is filled with a surging essence and consists of the six tastes.
Or it is well known as the six flavors, a mere fragment of the happiness ending in the world of Brahmā that is enjoyed by the six sense faculties. || 7 ||
That which never meets with destruction through cooking, and which, my dear, is eternally cooked yet is not afflicted by old age; (2)

Even though it is cooked with such flavorful ingredients, it does not attain the state of falling—that is, it does not fall [into the mouth]. Then, does it simply decay in its own place? No; he says: "always" (sadaiva). || 8 ||
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, Rudra, and others— only some among them are ancient— who do not know his origin, nor his root, nor even his stalk.
They are aged and long-lived. || 9 ||
Of this fruit of great magnitude, whose sprouts and tree have not been seen, whose form of flowers has not been seen, and which possesses neither stem, root, nor branches. || 10 ||
It possesses a vast grossness in the form of a single, solid mass, and no transformation such as birth or alteration is observed in it. (11)
That which is "vitata" means extremely extensive; those possessing such "sthaulya," or largeness, [are so described]. || 11 ||
Of this great work, which is the fruit containing the essence of all fruits, there is neither pith nor seed; it is expansive, changeless, and stainless.
Among all fruits and among all human goals (puruṣārtha), there is no core, no seed, that is more essential or supreme. 12.
Like a solid rock without interstices, yet like the shimmering orb of the moon;
it is as if the nectar of its own self-awareness, to be tasted within, is vibrating as immortality.

It is dense and compact like the interior of a stone, for the Śruti declares it to be "purely of the nature of consciousness. It flows forth with the essence of unsurpassed bliss, like the nectar of one's own self-awareness, resembling the flowing orb of the moon. || 13 ||
The marrow is like a treasury of all happiness, creating a cooling light;
it resembles a mountain and a mass of nectar, for it is established as the fruit of the self.
Regarding the term "treasury" (kośa): according to the Śruti, "Other beings subsist on a mere fraction of this very bliss.
It is the marrow, the essence, consisting of the soul's abiding in the fruits of karma, beginning from human bliss and ending with the bliss of Hiraṇyagarbha. 14.
Therefore, that which is the supreme marrow—the wondrous manifestation of one's own self—is eternally protected by Anantarakṣita; being non-dual, it has attained the fruit of glory.

Therefore, he is the marrow of even that supreme unmanifest which is the fruit of the bliss of Hiraṇyagarbha; he is protected by the Infinite alone, whose very nature is devoid of the three kinds of limitations. He has gone to the *śrīphala*—the auspicious *bilva* fruit—which is his own self;
and he is non-different from it. The meaning is that he is indeed non-dual. || 15 ||
By that slender girl, though she was very young and physically stout, her own bodily configuration reached a state of diversity that resulted in a sense of otherness, yet she did not abandon it. 16.

In order to establish non-difference itself, he reveals the inherent power of the term "wonder" (*camatkṛti*): having attained the state of being the fruit and the supreme purpose of the entire range of duality, this [world]— consisting of difference and so forth— has been produced and brought into being by [Consciousness] itself, while not abandoning its ultimate nature as the unique character of its own internal arrangement, which consists in immersion in the single essence of Consciousness.

The connection [of the verse] is with what follows. The contradictory qualifiers such as "slender" (*tanvyā*) and so forth are employed to establish her nature as a source of aesthetic wonder (*camatkṛti*) even through other modes. She is "slender" because she is subtler than the subtle; "stout" because she is greater than the great;
and "exceedingly young" because, despite being ancient, she is devoid of modifications such as growth. || 16 ||
Through the conceptualization "I am this," that which is unreal— the impurity of otherness—
has been produced and cultivated by itself, even though such distinctions and so forth are impossible.

He states the cause for the production of even this non-existent difference: "This [is it]. The meaning is that the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of "this-ness" upon that which is not "this"—namely, the thought "I am this"—is itself the cause of that [difference]. Otherwise, separateness would be the cause; thus, ignorance (*avidyā*) produces such distinctions among the worlds and so forth.

By the word "impossible" (asaṃbhavat), it is illuminated that since impurity itself has no possibility of existence within that which consists of the single essence of self-luminous consciousness, its effects—namely, differentiation—certainly have none either. || 17 ||
Immediately upon the emergence of the power of the ego (ahaṃkalā), she [the primordial nature] was enveloped by the atoms of the three worlds, whose bodies consist of the sounds of space. || 18 ||

She attains a state of identification through the production of the ego-sense (*ahaṃtā*) by means of the various categories such as the elements and the worlds produced by herself; thus he says: "I" (*aham*). The *ahaṃkalā* is the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*);

its emergence (*samudaya*) occurs in the form of both the individual (*vyaṣṭi*) and the collective (*samaṣṭi*), immediately following which space (*ākāśa*) and its quality, sound (*śabda*), arise as its limbs.
By those atoms of the individual and collective bodies characterized by the three worlds, which possess substances, qualities, and constituent parts; || 18 ||
Thus, proceeding in this sequence, consciousness reaches the state of its own essential power;
the marrow, having first attained its own prior configuration, then completely abandons it.

He concludes with "iti" (thus), signifying that he has described in this manner the great self-wonder (*ātmacamatkṛti*) consisting precisely in the attainment of such a form without abandoning one's own essential nature (*svasvarūpa*). Power (*śakti*) is the capacity for worldly transaction (*vyavahāra-samarthatā*); [he describes] its very nature. 19.
By that power of consciousness, which there assumes various shifting forms, the vision is thus extended toward its own very nature, which is equanimity.
In this way, the vision in the form of the world has been projected within its own innate, changeless nature. || 20 ||
This is the infinitely vast ether; this is the digit consisting of time;
this is called destiny; and this is action, whose form is vibration.
And thus, one should see that everything beginning with space is this very [consciousness] and nothing else; so he says:

"This expansion of conceptualization, this wandering among various desires, this state of attachment and aversion, and this notion of what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted—[all this is but consciousness]. (22)
He says "this" [in the verse] to show that internal objects are also of this very same nature. || 22 ||
This is you, this is I, and this very one is established as "this" by itself;
this flood of cosmic eggs stands above, yet it is itself both above and below, O dear one. (23)
"This is in front, this is at the side, this is behind, and this is far away; this is a past thing, this is present, and this is also future. (24)
The difference in gender is to be construed by supplying the words denoting the subjects, such as "the Self" (ātman) or "Brahman" (brahma). "Davīyasī" means more distant.
This is the circle of the pleasure-pavilion for the crest-jewel of the pavilion of the universe, an abode of many lotuses of internal conceptualization.
It is that wherein dwell infinite living beings, who are abodes for the lotuses of conceptual constructions; such is it. (25)
This pericarp of the heart-lotus of Hari, which has blossomed through the reality of infinite time, is the rosary of lotus-seeds of the worlds.
It is completely overspread with infinite principles of manifestation and the secrets of their arrangement. || 26 ||
This long path of clouds, its hollows filled with throngs of scattered great Rudras, is powerful enough to destroy those who wander astray.
The path of the clouds—the track of the sky—has its hollows filled by the hosts of Mahārudra scattered and pervading everywhere.
[This occurs] in this great ocean, the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*); for the meaning is according to the Śruti: "O Bhavas, O blue-necked ones, O white-throated Śarvas.
From the destructions—that is, the downward falls—of those who are deluded, being greedy for sense-objects, and fallen from their own state.

She is "radiant" (prabhāvinī), "majestic" (pratāpavatī), or "luminous" (prakāśavatī) because of her manifestation from the signs [of the zodiac]; that is to say, because the persistence of light is observed in the sky-path, which is the vessel of the stars. || 27 ||
This is Mount Meru, the pericarp of the lotus of the world situated here in the cardinal direction,
where the gods act as bees, greedy for the joy of the honey from the shimmering moon.
In this northern quarter, there is that [place] in which the gods, who are like bees, are greedy for the nectar-essence—the overflowing honey characterized by the moon. || 28 ||
This is a cluster of flowers from the celestial glory of unrestrained fragrance, belonging to the ancient tree of the world whose roots are in the dust of hell. (29)

The meaning is this: for the world-tree, which has its roots in passion and other afflictions that are the effects of the quality of *rajas* and is subject to the sufferings of hell, this very thing—characterized by the splendor of heaven—is like a cluster of blossoms possessing unrestrained fragrance. || 29 ||
And this lotus-pond of the play of the infinite sky, situated on the shore of the ocean of Brahman, has the stars as its filaments and extends to the very limits of the boundless beyond.

Extending upwards, without end, and on all sides, limitless and boundless; this very one is the play of the sky, having the form of the sky—the lotus-lake, the lotus-pond—such is the meaning. || 30 ||
This is the succession of waves, flickering with activity; it is the multitude of beings situated within the formation of the whirlpools of creation.

In her, ritual actions and deeds are grasped on all sides; in her, the succession of months and seasons is as flickering as waves; and in her, the multitude of beings remains fixed within the performance of the whirlpools—that is, the activity characterized by the procreation of offspring. 31.
Spreading forth with such magnitude, with moments and kalpas as its tender shoots,
having brilliance for its lion, she is the lotus-plant of time, with the sky as her lotus.

This very one is the lotus of Time (kālanalinī), which has spread out by means of its extent—the measure of the lifespan of living beings—and which possesses manes of splendors such as fire, the sun, and the moon; it is that whose lotus is the sky itself. 32.

These views on the meaning of the scriptures are rich with the transformations of existence, abounding in the fevers of old age, death, and disease, and filled with the playful manifestations of knowledge and ignorance. (33)
Thus, that very essence of the wood-apple tree, possessing the wonder of its own marrow,
took up its residence within the interior of his mental resolve.
Thus, all the types described are merely her own wonder of marrow;
she whose internal abiding consists of the arrangement of individual and collective volitions in such a manner. (34)
Peaceful, self-abiding, free from affliction, gentle, and liberated from mental cultivation;
having rendered both agency and non-agency as if they were neither performed nor unperformed, it remains established. (35)
This very one, though appearing as manifold and diverse, is indeed neither of a single nature nor manifold; it is that very same one, that very same one.

Abiding in truth, possessing the uniform form of universal peace, being the soul of all and exceedingly great, she is the power whose form is consciousness (the reading *mahatīti nirūpaśaktiḥ* is found in the printed edition). || 36 ||
Having concluded the narrative of Bilva, he concludes by describing consciousness (citi) in its own essential nature with the words "This [is it]":

because even the number one implies duality, it is neither of a single nature nor manifold; rather, that very [consciousness] is oneness, and that alone is the one. Alternatively, through repetition (vīpsā), there is the exclusion of all that is similar and dissimilar. This is due to the cessation of the entire proliferation of dualistic conceptualization.

"Of uniform form. By this, even internal differentiation is excluded. The meaning is that the power which is the very nature of consciousness—the ultimate reality indicated by the word "Brahman"—is thus explained as being exceedingly vast. || 36 ||

Thus ends the forty-fifth canto, titled "The Story of Bilva," in the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa* of the *Mokṣopāya* section of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, according to the tradition of the Ṛṣis.
Thus ends the forty-fifth canto, titled "The Story of Bilva," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The forty-sixth canto.
Śrī Rāma said:
"O Blessed One, knower of the essence of all things, by you this [tree] in the form of a bilva..."
It is my conviction that the being here described is the mass of great consciousness. || 1 ||
In this world, Brahman— adorned with clusters of lotuses perceived by the mind of an artisan— is said to appear as a manifold expansion, like the interior of a stone.
Śrī Rāma demonstrates his understanding of the purport of the narrative concerning the Bilva tree with the two verses beginning with "O Blessed One. (1)
This entire expanse, beginning with the ego-sense, is of the nature of pure consciousness;
there is not even the slightest difference consisting of the conceptualization of duality or unity.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Just as the existence of Mount Meru and other things resides within the marrow of the cosmic gourd,
so too does this existence of the world, beginning with the cosmic egg, reside within the marrow of the bael fruit of consciousness.

With the intention that it should be understood without reservation that the core of the consciousness-fruit (cidbilva) is not merely the absence of egoism (nāhaṃtā) and so forth, but rather everything including the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) and beyond, Vasiṣṭha said, beginning with "Just as... (yathā). || 3 ||
The consciousness-embryo (cidbilva) of creation would be the marrow [of that tree] if there were the possibility of its support being something other than itself;
however, for this omnipresent [consciousness], destruction is not at all possible.

When it is said that the "marrow of the *cid-bilva* (the wood-apple of consciousness)" refers to a specific transformation consisting of the condensed essence (*rasaghana*) of the constituent parts located within the interior region, the author preempts a certain misconception by stating: "creation" (*sṛṣṭi*). Just as the shell of a wood-apple is the support for its marrow, so too, while it is possible for there to be a difference between the support of the marrow characterized as creation and its own contained marrow—which occupies the place of the shell—[the two are not distinct].

The marrow would be that which is the form of its internal transformation. In that case, if this all-pervading conscious self were to undergo transformation either in its entirety or in part, its destruction would be unavoidable. Furthermore, since this [self] is partless, neither an "internal region" nor "transformation" is possible in a primary sense; thus, the word "marrow" does not refer to a transformation—this is the meaning. || 4 ||
The marvelous manifestation called the world resides within the seed of the *citermarīca* (the light of consciousness),
like an engraving within a stone, remaining within the serenity of deep sleep.

If it is asked, "Then what is its purpose?", the author says "of consciousness" (citer) with the intention that it is for the sake of the wonder characterized by manifestation (vivarta). The meaning is: like the arrangement of a forest of lotuses imagined by an artisan's mind within a stone. || 5 ||
O moon-faced one, listen now to another delightful and wonderful narrative, full of amazement, which I am about to relate. (6)
In order to explain the illustration, he introduces the narrative of the Brahma-stone with the words "herein" (atra). || 6 ||
There exists somewhere a great stone, glossy, clear, soft to the touch, possessed of vast extent, dense, and eternally unshakable.
Within it, there are indeed many beautiful lotuses in full bloom, as numerous as those in a lake; they are truly infinite.
They are infinite because of the infinity of mental constructions. || 8 ||
Their petals were interlaced with one another, yet they were also mutually separated;
they were both hidden from one another and concealed, as well as manifest.
"Upanigūḍhāni" means closely joined. || 9 ||
Some were facing downward, some upward, and others sideways;
their bases were joined together, and their openings were likewise interlaced.
The bases of the network of pericarp-filaments have their pericarps at the end of the roots;
some have their roots above, others have their roots below, and others are rootless.

Since mental construction can also arise from what is contrary to what is seen, he says "karṇikā" (the pericarp). Those whose roots are in the networks of pericarps; others, however, are some that are rootless. || 11 ||
And near them there are conchs by the hundreds of thousands,
and great masses of discs arranged like lotuses.
The conch shells are arranged like lotus buds; by implication, it is understood that the multitudes of wheels are arranged like full-blown lotuses. 12.
Śrī Rāma said:
This is true; I have seen that great stone of such a kind, which exists as an attendant in Śālagrāma, the abode of Hari. (13)

Rama himself, remembering from the words of his guru a stone he had seen at the sacred site of Śālagrāma during his pilgrimage, and considering that very stone to have been cited here by the Lord as an illustration of Brahman accompanied by the world-creation, said:
"This is true. It is surrounded [by Lakṣmī], who is encircled by a forest of lotuses marked with the lotus-sign. || 13 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
You understand it thus; you have seen that stone, and whatever life-force was there, it was entirely of the same nature as yourself.

Vasiṣṭha, expressing his approval by saying, "The connection between the illustration and the thing illustrated has been correctly understood by you," spoke as follows: "The Conscious Self (cidātman), which is the subject of the illustration, is of such a nature: it is immediate, without intervening space, a mass of consciousness, equal even to the life-force (prāṇa), and its very form is unsurpassed bliss—even in that [state]."
"You have seen it in the object; thus you know. || 14 ||
But this unprecedented Śilā has been described by me here to you;
within its vast interior, everything both exists and does not exist.

However, I did not intend the rock seen by you to serve as the illustrative example; rather, having imagined Brahman itself—which was previously unknown—to be a rock, I presented it as being like a wood-apple fruit. With the intention that "even if there is a discrepancy regarding the means (*upāya*), there is no discrepancy regarding the goal (*upeya*)," he says:
"But by me... (verse 15).
This "cicchilā" (consciousness-rock) has been described by me to you, within which the worlds indeed exist; by virtue of its nature as a single, solid unity, this consciousness is itself a rock.
He shows the qualities that serve as the grounds for applying the word "stone" figuratively to the conscious self (cidātman) in the verse beginning with "solidity" (ghanatva).
By the word "etc. (ādi), qualities such as indivisibility, homogeneity, and immutability are included. || 16 ||
Even within one whose body is exceedingly dense and whose form is without any interstices, the multitude of worlds exists within, just as the vast wind exists within the sky. (17)
The contradiction indicated by the two words "api" (even/also) is to be resolved through *māyā* (illusory power). || 17 ||
The sky, the earth, the wind, the ether, the mountains, the rivers, and the directions—
all these exist within that stone, yet there is not even the slightest cavity in it.
Within this very dense-bodied self, the lotus of the world unfolds;
in reality, there is nothing other than this, nor anything else that is of a pure nature.

He says, "In this very [world]," to show that the world itself was envisioned by me there as a lotus-forest. And although that world appears as if it were something else, in reality it is not other; nor is it merely pure consciousness, but rather it is *māyā* alone—this is the meaning. || 19 ||
Just as the world with its conchs, lotuses, and so forth is engraved upon stone,
so too are the past, the present, and the future like carved figures upon a rock.

Regarding the statement, "And near them there are conch shells by the hundreds of thousands," he states the intended meaning [of the verse]: "The entire world is a creation; therein, a carved figure exists as if it were real"—this is the connection with what follows.
Likewise, all those various forms exist there in reality, just as the internal arrangement within a stone, though consisting of many distinct parts, attains the state of a single mass. (21)
Just as it was grasped, so this [consciousness] is a single, dense mass in the form of a lump of intellect;
like a lotus not yet separated from its sheath of stone, its body consists of that very [intellect].
It takes up, that is, it appropriates; likewise, this consciousness also appropriates a dense, singular, unified mass—this is the meaning. || 22 ||
Likewise, although the creation is non-different from the form of consciousness, it consists of the body;
just as the lines of wheels and lotuses exist within a stone by way of the state of deep sleep.

The meaning is that although it is non-different from its own essential nature, it appears as if possessing a limited form consisting of a physical body; "by means of the state of deep sleep" means by way of being unmanifest prior to the cutting [of the stone] with a chisel. || 23 ||
Just as it exists within consciousness, so does this series of worlds exist—
like a row of lotus designs within a stone, or a pungent flavor within black pepper.
Just as creation neither rises nor sets, so it is within consciousness;
just as a mortal is within a pregnant woman, or as marrow is within a wood-apple fruit.
The meaning is that just as for a stone and black pepper, which exist, there is neither rising nor setting; likewise, within the mind of a virtuous woman, her mortal husband always exists. 25.
Likewise, the multitude of cosmic eggs within consciousness, though rich with infinite transformations, is that very same [consciousness];
thus, the statement that "there are transformations and so forth" is merely empty and purposeless talk. (26)

When the cosmic eggs (*brahmāṇḍa*), which are subject to transformation, are [realized to be] pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), then it follows as a matter of course that the distinctions of their transformations—the worlds, bodies, and so forth—are also pure consciousness;
therefore, the statement [to that effect] is merely empty and fruitless. || 26 ||
It quickly attains that very state, like a drop of water in water;
because consciousness is infinite, this world of modifications and so forth is indeed consciousness. (27)

To the question "How is it devoid of objects? he says: "That state" (tattām). Because this [universe], consisting of modifications and so forth, at the very moment of perceiving the pure consciousness of the cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas), attains that state of pure consciousness; for this reason, not even a single atom remains separate. || 27 ||
That which is attained through speech dissolves by merging into that;
this very Brahman is free from modifications and the like, being devoid of the objects of modification and so forth. (28)

He states that because it is established by mere verbal expression—like the variety of a city of Gandharvas described by poets—it consists of nothing but the consciousness of the perceiver: "By expression," etc. This is based on such scriptural passages as: "He, uttering 'bhūḥ', created the earth;
'eta' (these), indeed, Prajāpati created the gods; 'asṛgram' (they were emitted), [he created] humans; 'indavaḥ' (drops), [he created] the ancestors," and so forth.
Since it has been stated that the creation of the world and so forth is preceded by names, the dissolution [of the world] should likewise be inferred as occurring within the names. || 28 ||
The rejection or acceptance of an object occurs solely through the power of Brahman's infinity;
Brahman alone exists as the modifications and so forth, and Brahman alone is produced in succession.
He states that even the avoidance of objects such as modifications is not a separate entity: "avoidance," etc. (verse 29).
Know this to be for another purpose here: it is like the water of a mirage;
the seed contains the flower and fruit within, yet there is no other self-nature within the seed.

He states that everything is indeed consciousness (*cit*) alone—because, like a seed, the persistence of the existence of consciousness (*citsattā*) is observed everywhere throughout its own effects, ending with flowers and fruits—by means of the verse beginning with "bīja" (the seed), etc. (30).
In whatever manner the existence of the seed develops, it proceeds further and further;
that which is the density of consciousness within the mass of consciousness is itself the sequence of the three worlds. (31)
Existing indeed throughout the successive transformations beginning with the sprout, it then proceeds toward the stalk, branches, shoots, and so forth at a later time. || 31 ||
The oneness of these two is their duality; in the absence of one, both are lost.
The arising of the world from anything else never occurs; such is its nature.
He states that the reality is unimagined pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) because even the imagination of duality as one is dependent upon another imagination; thus he says, "oneness.
The existence of these two—the seed and its effect—depends on the imagination of insentience (*jaḍya*) distinct from consciousness, and their manifestation is dependent upon that.
However, that nature of consciousness can never possibly possess such a character of insentience; this is the meaning. || 32 ||
The two—consciousness and the unconscious—never exist as a duality within one another; they are non-dual.

Just as there exists within a massive rock a division consisting of its surface lines, so too the three worlds, which are both different from and non-different from it, exist within the mass of consciousness, like marrow within a bone. (33) [Note: The reading "yato bahu" is found in some versions.]

Clarifying that very point, he applies it to the present context with the word "consciousness" (cit); the phrase "in the bilva-fruit of the marrow and so forth" is to be supplied as the remainder. || 33 ||
Just as a single massive stone is encircled by lines and sub-lines,
so too is the one Brahman seen as encompassing the three worlds.
The one Brahman is perceived in the form of the well-known world. || 34 ||
Just as these lotuses and other things within the stone are eternally in a state of deep sleep,
neither setting nor rising, so too is the ego and the course of the world.
Deep sleep is merely the latent impression (vāsanā) of the artisan.

Just as an inscription within a stone is not distinct from the interior of the stone because it is of its very essence, so too the world-creator and the qualities of being a creator are not distinct from the consciousness of the world, for they are its very essence.
Just as the arising and ceasing, or the movement and stillness, of lotuses within a rock do not become objects of perception,
so too the creators of the world do not become objects of perception.

The creator of the world, in the form of both the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara), as well as his agency and the world itself, is consciousness alone; existence and non-existence are merely manifestation and disappearance.
This is never created, nor does it ever perish;
like a mountain, its nature consists of the manifestation and playful display of creative power.
Just as stones do not become objects when the truth is perceived, so too agents do not become objects when the reality of the Self is perceived;
this is the meaning. || 38 ||
Just as it is, wherever it is, and whatever its form may be, so indeed is it there;
for everything consists of the essence of Brahman's existence, remaining as if situated in deep sleep. (39)

The meaning is that it is like a stone or a mountain peak because of its immutability. For this very reason, just as a stone remains the same despite the various conflicting mental constructions of different artisans, so too Brahman remains in its very own nature even amidst the diverse and conflicting conceptualizations of the various individual souls (jīvas); thus he says "yathā" (as). The ellipsis is to be supplied as "yadākāraṃ kalpyate" (in whatever form it is conceptualized). || 39 ||
Know that this great delusion of the world, which is rich with manifold transformations of states,
is indeed like deep sleep, just as a lotus and the like exist within a stone.

The meaning is that, just as the state of deep sleep (suṣupta) residing within each individual soul tolerates the various distinctions of imagined dream-objects without contradiction, so it is here. Deep sleep consists merely of unmanifested latent impressions (vāsanā). 40.

The play of the world is eternally nothing but the state of deep sleep, because its true nature is that of the Self—the void of Brahman, which is perfectly tranquil, uniform, and a mass of consciousness.

These states of creation are as insubstantial as lotuses within a stone; they are seen [to be unreal] and never truly enter into the body. (41) He concludes by summarizing the purport of the narrative: "Eternally," etc. That which is the void of Brahman is a mass of consciousness (*ciddhana*).

Because they are of that nature: the states beginning with creation are insubstantial and hollow, like lotuses within a stone; even though they are perceived within the Self, they never at any time attain the state of being the body or the true nature of the Self—this is the meaning. || 41 ||

Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Rock-Casket," in the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa* of the *Mokṣopāya* section of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, according to the tradition of the Sages.
Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Casket of Stone," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The forty-seventh canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Just as the fruit of the essence of consciousness arises from the successive stages of the mind's own sleep, [so too does this world appear].
That which exists as the manifestation of its own being is established as creation.
Here, the purport of the narrative known as the *Bilvaśilā* is described;
it is like the various colors and shapes found within the fluid of a peacock's egg.

Lest there be a misconception regarding the intended meaning— that by virtue of the example of the wood-apple (*bilva*), the seed within it is indeed insentient in nature (just like the marrow and so forth), and that the emergence of the creation possessing the same level of reality as that [seed] occurs therein through internal differentiation— he explains that intended meaning with the words "of the principle of consciousness" (*cittattvasya*).
The principle whose nature is consciousness remains devoid of the recognition of its own true nature for as long as...

The illustration of the insentient fruit is given precisely to illuminate the point that [the world] contains within it the process of creation (*sargagarbha*). Furthermore, this "creation" is a state of sleep distinct from the well-known sleep of consciousness (*cita*); it is indeed a dream that proceeds according to the sequence of ages (*yuga*), years, and so forth, with a structural arrangement imagined by its own existence, and not one possessing the same ontological status as consciousness itself.
The meaning is: "a difference inherent within itself. || 1 ||
Since even space, time, action, and so forth consist of that very nature,
the distinction "this is one thing" and "that is another" is not tenable here.
If so, is creation something entirely different from the nature of consciousness? To show that this too is difficult to maintain, he says: "Space," etc. (verse 2).
For one who knows how to grasp the impressions of all words and their meanings,
how could it be said that "this is non-existent," since [all things] are of a single nature?
If it is asked, "In that case, is this beginning of creation merely non-existent?"—that too is difficult to maintain; thus he says: "samasta... (all).

The meaning is that since all words, their objects, their latent impressions (*vāsanā*), and the conceptual constructions (*saṃkalpa-vikalpa*) induced by them are of one essence with the knower even throughout the three states [of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep], they must be real; for otherwise, it would be impossible for that which is absolutely non-existent to be known or perceived by him. || 3 ||
Just as the internal arrangement of a fruit exists according to the sequence of its names,
so too does the density of the consciousness's own being exist as both non-different and yet differentiated.

Therefore, he says that they are conceived as results precisely with the intention of their variegated sequence being phenomenal and dependent upon consciousness: "Though not manifold, it appears as manifold; though agitated, it is as if unagitated.
Just as its own non-existence exists within the fruit, so do the accomplishments exist within consciousness. (5)

In that regard, he says "anānaiva" (only non-differentiation), meaning that the aspect of non-differentiation alone is real because it is primary. "Kṣubdhā" means as if agitated or transformed. "Siddhayaḥ" refers to the accomplishments of structural formations. || 5 ||
In the mirror of the city of the world, one's own reflection is gathered; it appears as if shimmering, yet it does not shimmer, like the internal arrangement within a stone.

He shows the purport of the narrative concerning the stone with the words "The world," etc. The meaning is that the purport is this: just as it was stated that the world is like the internal arrangement within a stone, so too, like a city reflected in a mirror, it is the very form of consciousness itself that shines forth—though perhaps dimly—as its own respective form. || 6 ||
Within the supreme jewel of consciousness, even hundreds of millions of worlds exist,
just as infinite fruits are fully contained within a wish-fulfilling gem.

Alternatively, because it possesses infinite illusory powers (*māyika-ananta-śaktimat*), one should describe the intended meaning of the scripture as being that the entire world exists within Consciousness (*cit*), just as the fruits of the desires of a thinker exist within a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*). Thus he says: "In the Supreme" (*parame*). The sense is that they are "rested upon" (*arpitāni*) according to the Śrutis, based on the presentation of the analogy of the hub and spokes of a wheel. || 7 ||
This entire world appears as a single casket of consciousness, carved out from its limbs and spread wide; it shines like a pearl, composed of its own rays, yet appearing as something else.

He states that the intended meaning regarding the existence of the world within consciousness is like that of pearls within the hollow of a pearl-oyster shell, by way of an imagined relationship between the parts and the whole (*aṃśāṃśibhāva*); thus he says: "The casket of consciousness" (*citsamudgaka*). "Engraved upon its part" (*tadaṅgotkīrṇam*) means as if engraved within its interior.
He explains this very point by saying: "Consisting of its own parts" (*tadaṃśamayam*). || 8 ||
Constantly transforming perceptions and non-perceptions throughout day and night,
the radiant sun of consciousness stands manifesting the substances of the world.

The sun creates the division of day and night, consisting of the manifestation and concealment of its own form; likewise, the gem-stone of consciousness (cinmaṇiśilā) performs within itself the illumination and non-illumination of the substance of the world, which consists of the cognition and non-cognition of its own awareness. With this meaning, he states the purport [of the verse] as "day and night" (ahorātram). "Vikarayan" means making diverse, that is to say, transforming. || 9 ||
Like the playful movement of water in the whirlpools and hollows of the ocean,
and like the various internal formations within a single stone, consciousness itself is both non-dual and manifold.

He states that the intended meaning is that, just as the various distinctions of movement— such as whirlpools and waves— are nothing but the ocean within the hollow of its womb, so too all the distinctions of the world are of the nature of pure consciousness alone:
"Whatever exists is a statue carved upon the stone body of Consciousness."
That which does not exist is like a carved figure on a stone body. || 11 ||

Alternatively, its purport is to demonstrate that the present creation, as well as past and future creations, are identical in their nature as pure consciousness (cinmātra). He states this with the words "yadasti" (that which exists): a *śālabhañjikā* is a statue, whether carved or uncarved. || 11 ||
That which is the truth amidst existence and non-existence is like the very marrow of consciousness;
for the splendor of all objects has the essence of that marrow, and it is indeed composed of that alone.

With the intention that even for the world known as the *bilva* fruit, consciousness (*cit*) is its essential core (*sāra*), he says "bhāva" etc. That which is real is indeed the Truth (*tattva*), and that is of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*), like the marrow (*majjā*). The meaning is that the splendor of objects—the splendor of objects such as the *bilva* fruit—is well-known to have marrow alone as its essence. || 12 ||

Just as the various meanings of words such as "lotus" and so forth are abandoned within the interior of a stone, so too is this world of diversity; that very reality is non-dual and consists of this [diversity]. 13.

He states that the purport [of the scripture] is either the non-existence of the referents of words such as "lotus" when they are separated from their substratum (the stone), or the non-existence of the world when it is separated from Consciousness—just like the non-existence of the lotus and so forth: "Padma... (verse 13).
Just as the reflection of a lotus is neither manifold nor one within the interior of a stone, being of an undivided nature, so too is this [universe] within the mass of consciousness.

He clarifies this portion—that "this is composed of that" and is non-dual—by saying "not manifold" (nānā). If the world is not made separate from consciousness, then even though it appears manifold, it becomes non-manifold due to its identity with the self of consciousness, just like the interior of a stone; such is the meaning. || 14 ||
Just as the rays of the sun appear to those with a dull intellect to be either present or absent within a vessel of pure water,
so too you, O Consciousness, whose nature is both being and non-being, appear as if you were not, though you truly exist.

Just as a mirage in the desert appears to the sight of deer as a pure reservoir of water, a mass of liquid; to those with the notion of "land," it appears simply as land; yet to the vision of the wise, it is merely the radiance of the sun, the heat of the sun itself—wherein the heat and so forth exist, while the water and such do not—it shines as a form both existent and non-existent; in this same way, You, whose nature is consciousness, also shine.
In reality, however, the meaning is that you do not possess a nature that is either existent or non-existent. || 15 ||

Just as the mass of water within the hollow of a cloud, being about to manifest as rain, vibrates due to its fluidity even while remaining motionless, so too does this interior of the dense mass of consciousness.

Just as a mass of water within a hollow vibrates due to its fluidity, so too, although it is motionless, that which is internal to the mass of consciousness vibrates as it were; this is the meaning. || 16 ||

Know that consciousness is like a stone within which the world—including objects such as the earth, water, conchs, and lotuses—exists; though it appears as those things, it is not composed of them, for it is distinct from the stone-like matter of the world. 17.

If that is so, why is the world-conch, the world-lotus, and so forth—not being composed of stone—no more clearly perceived as being composed of consciousness (*cinmaya*), just as the lotuses and other objects there [in the dream] are clearly perceived as being composed of stone?

To this he replies with the words "cicchile" (on the stone of consciousness). The ellipsis is to be supplied as: "because one who is not composed of that [consciousness] lacks the realization of it. For this very reason, he says "jagat" (the world), meaning: "you should perceive it in that way. || 17 ||

This mass of consciousness, like a great solid stone, possesses a stone-like interior; it is without apertures, non-dual, transparent, unborn, perfectly tranquil, yet possessed of a structural arrangement.

He says "mahāśilā" (the great rock) with the intention that even though a solid rock was used as the illustrative example, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha-dṛṣṭi*), it has itself become the interior of the rock of consciousness (*cic-chilodara*). Therefore, with the underlying thought that even by thousands of efforts on the part of a craftsman,
there is not even the possibility of a cavity or the like therein, he qualifies it as "without cavities" (*arandhra*).
The meaning is that it appears as if possessing a real arrangement, due to a false arrangement. || 18 ||
This world-Brahman shines like the stainless autumn season;
this world-Brahman flashes forth like the gentle, flowing moon. (19)

Just as during the autumn season the sun blazes and the moon, dripping with nectar, shines— whereby the sun and the moon, though identical in their nature as Time, are designated through the relationship of action and agent by imagining internal distinctions— so too is there the designation that Brahman illumines the world and shines forth as the world itself; thus he says, "it blazes," and "the lunar."
The delight of the eyes. || 19 ||
This world is like deep sleep within Brahman; it does not exist, yet it is indestructible, like a lotus in a stone.
Just as the nature of Brahman exists in Brahman, so too does this world abide.

With the intention that it can thus be conceived that the world exists as eternally undestroyed by virtue of its nature as Brahman, he says: "In Brahman" (brahmaṇi). Because it consists of nothing but latent impressions (*vāsanā*), it resembles deep sleep. The meaning is: just as a stone-lotus is eternally non-existent as a lotus yet eternally existent as a stone, so too is this [world]. || 20 ||
No difference exists between these two, just as there is none between the words "taru" and "pādapa";
whatever worlds exist here, they are nothing other than the form of consciousness.
He states that there is no difference between the meanings of the words "world" (jagat) and "Brahman" when they exist as the conscious self (cidātman): "Not of these two," etc. (21).
For these [phenomena], there is never at any time existence, non-existence, and so forth, just as in that [mirage];
the world-appearance is Brahman alone, like water in a mirage caused by the wind.
Of these worlds; as if of that form of consciousness. 22.
Just as water becomes pure by the sight of the sun, so too does Brahman become pure through vision—whether it be Mount Meru or a blade of grass, a shrub, the mind, or even the entire universe. (23)

Even the most massive object, such as Mount Meru and the like, becomes nothing but Brahman—pure and characterized by the absence of grossness and other qualities—when viewed through the vision of reality. Just as ice and the like become nothing but water, so it is here. Therefore, this applies to the entire universe, from the external grass and shrubs up to the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), and internally, from the mind up to Hiraṇyagarbha.

That which is supreme, progressively subtler than water and so forth, ending with the subtle elements (*bhūtasūkṣma*), the unmanifest (*avyākṛta*), and the imperishable (*akṣara*)—the form that remains at the end through such differentiation is known as the Supreme by the knowers of Brahman; this is the connection with the subsequent [verse].
They know that form which exists through the supreme differentiation of water to be the Supreme;
its collection is likewise the mind, whether it be as high as Mount Meru or as small as a blade of grass.
He provides the reasoning for the fact that upon the investigation of the gross, it is reduced to the subtle alone, stating: "its aggregate" (tatsamūha).

For the fivefold-composed (pañcīkṛta) world is indeed an aggregate of the non-fivefold-composed (apañcīkṛta) elements; and the non-fivefold-composed elements, in turn, are nothing but the mind—this is the meaning to be understood through this sequence. || 24 ||
For that which is essential even in its subtlety is indeed more essential in its grossness;
just as the power whose nature is rasa exists, O sinless one, in the form of the atom.

He says, "Even in its subtlety," because even while remaining subtle, due to its very essence consisting of existence (*sat*), the state of being more essential—characterized by being more real—is experienced by common people within the phenomenal world (*prapañca*). For this very reason, he says, "Just as," illustrating how the power of taste residing in an atom becomes an object of the senses in gross water, so too the existence of Brahman (*brahmasattā*) becomes an object of the senses in objects such as jars. Thus, [the world] is full of milk (*pāyasī*).
"Being established in gross water, she is fit"—this is the ellipsis. || 25 ||
Likewise, the state of Brahman exists within all objects of the world as the essence of milk;
it is like the power of sap [present] in various grasses, shrubs, creepers, and waters.

With the intention that such examples should be conceived—namely, that the diversity of existence arises from the nature of intermediate universals (sāmānya) within existence itself, just as there is a diversity of gross forms—he says "the power of taste," and so forth. || 26 ||
In that same way, that very Brahman-hood arises as manifoldness, appearing as this or that,
just as the atoms of light constitute the various displays of forms.

Just as the extreme subtlety—the most subtle form and commonality—of the various manifestations of color, such as blue, yellow, and so forth, consists in the atoms of light (*āloka-paramāṇu*), so it is here; this is to be understood as the logical connection (*yathā tathā*). || 27 ||

The supreme nature of these [powers], which consist of the essence of qualities, the qualified, objects, and existence itself, resides in consciousness within the mind, because Mount Meru and other such things exist as its manifesting medium. (28)
Just as there is hardness in the fluid of a peacock’s egg due to the mass of its feathers and wings,
so too does multiplicity exist within the principle of consciousness (citi-tattva), which is the self that manifests that [multiplicity].

The implication is that even the supreme selfhood (*parātmatā*) and the existence of Brahman (*brahmasattā*) constitute the nature of the essence (*sattātmarūpiṇī*) of these individual manifestations such as jars, for the sake of establishing the subordinate specificities (*avāntaravaijātya*) in the form of qualities and the possessor of qualities (*guṇaguṇirūpa*). Just as it is said that during the state of manifestation the cause alone exists in the form of the effect, so too during the state of concealment the effect certainly exists in the form of the cause. This is also [the case].

He establishes this through an illustration with the verse beginning "citī" (consciousness). In consciousness variegated by *māyā* (*māyā-śabala-citi*), when [the world] is entirely concealed, and in the mind (*citta*), when it is half-concealed, the entire collection of gross effects such as Mount Meru exists. The meaning is that it is just as the feathers, the mass of wings, and hardness exist within the fluid of the peacock's egg, which is the material cause (*upādāna*) of the peacock. || 28 || 29 ||
Just as a cluster of variegated tail-feathers [appears] in the fluid of a peacock's egg,
so too does the manifold self indeed arise when nourished by the fluid of the peacock's egg.
By means of the vision of discernment, that is, by means of the vision of differentiation. || 30 ||
When seen through the vision of discernment, both that Brahman and the world exist in such a way:
though appearing manifold, they are not manifold, just as the egg, its fluid, and the peacock [are one].

And just as in that case a conceptual distinction does not contradict actual non-difference, so it is here as well; thus he says: "as manifold. Within the egg, the peacock (barhin) exists in the form of its essence (rasa). || 31 ||
The delusion of Brahman and the world has the nature of both non-duality and duality;
it is like the existence of both the real and the unreal abiding in a state of equality. || 32 ||
In that case, let Brahman itself consist of both duality and non-duality, just as there is the delusion that the world is real and that it is Brahman;

likewise, [let it be] of the nature of both duality and non-duality. By this much, no inconsistency arises. The meaning is that just as there is an abiding in the equality of existence between the existent and the non-existent, so too is there [an abiding] from the determination of that [Brahman]. || 32 ||
Therefore, know that supreme reality to be the form of both the existent and the non-existent abiding within all beings;
this world, consisting of both diversity and non-diversity, is experienced as having no true origin.
[Objection: But surely, for the sake of avoiding inequality, why should there not be a state of remaining in the very equality of existence? [Response:
Anticipating the objection that inequality is avoided even in emptiness characterized by the attainment of mere non-existence, he says "yataḥ" (because).
Form (*rūpa*) is reality (*tattva*); it culminates in an existent thing (*sad-vastu*) residing in being, and does not terminate in emptiness. This is because even non-existence...
Because its definition is dependent upon that [Brahman], know that very entity to be the Supreme Brahman itself.

And because it is non-dual, this world-form—which consists of both the manifold and the non-manifold, and possesses a nature that is both different and non-different—is "not-possible" (*na-sambhavam*);
that is, it is impossible [to exist independently]. This is a *bahuvrīhi* compound where the negative particle *na*, having the sense of negation, functions as the first member. || 33 ||
Behold the movement of the entire world within the peacock's egg,

like a peacock in its essence; just as the principle of consciousness (cittattva) is in the world, so is the world in the principle of consciousness— both manifold and non-manifold, yet one, just like the fluid within a peacock's egg.
