With the intention that even for one who has not yet attained realization, this state of oneness should be understood through the very same analogy of the peacock in the egg-essence, he says:
"See the world dissolved within the essence of consciousness, just as the peacock is in the essence"—this is the meaning. (34)
The primordial consciousness (cit-ādi), filled with the plumage of the delusion of various objects, is the essence within the egg of the world-peacock;
know that its form as a peacock is not a peacock, for it is the state of pure existence within—how then can there be any duality? (35)

Unifying the meaning to be illustrated with the metaphorical image, he eliminates the notion of difference by stating "not manifold" (nānā). The primordial consciousness of Brahman itself is the essence (*rasa*) of the cosmic egg of the world, which is filled with feathers characterized by the delusions of various kinds of objects. As for the form of the peacock that is the world appearing therein—

Know that the supreme reality, the ultimate entity, is the state characterized by pure existence, which is not of the nature of a peacock; for in that state, how could there be any differentiation? Such is the meaning. || 35 ||

Thus ends the forty-seventh canto, titled "The Instruction on the Mass of Consciousness," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, belonging to the *Ārṣa*.
Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Mass of Consciousness," in the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The Forty-Eighth Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
In that [state] where all this is spread out, its nature being unarisen, everything exists.
Like a peacock within its seed, so too does that [Self] exist within egoity and the rest.
That which reflects existence, manifestation, and bliss within the imagined world is described by extracting it as Brahman— the forest of Being-Consciousness-Bliss (saccidānanda).

Lest there arise the delusion that— based on the analogy of the peacock's egg— the reality is merely the undifferentiated (*avyākṛta*) seed-potency consisting of a mixture of consciousness (*cit*) and unconsciousness (*acit*), containing within it the hidden diversity of the world, and that there exists nothing further beyond it as a pure reality, Śrī Vasiṣṭha [proceeds] to extract and demonstrate its substratum, which is the state of non-dual plenitude (*bhūman*) in the form of bliss (*ānanda*).

He said: "Where... etc. The meaning is this: within the seed (the causal state) and the egg (the cosmic manifestation), just as a peacock is described within [an egg], there exists everything—the internal ego and so forth, as well as the external directions and the elements like ether—within that pure [reality] whose nature has not arisen even in the three periods of time. That very reality, whose own form is unoriginated, is the intended object of the aforementioned illustration; it is not the variegated [phenomenal world]. || 1 ||
Where nothing has arisen, there everything exists;
in that very place, O Aṅgiras, it reflects the essence of the bliss of heaven.
Where, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), nothing at all has arisen, there alone does the entire world exist through ignorance (*avidyā*).

That very same [reality], O Aṅgiras, exists here in this body as the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which is the essence of the limbs; it takes on the form of diverse enjoyments through various modifications of the mind (*cittavṛtti*) consisting of the essence of worldly pleasures such as heaven and the like.

Just as the moon is reflected in a crystal mirror and the like, so too, by the power of the experience of sensory pleasure, the existence of that unexcelled bliss which constitutes its reflection is to be inferred; such is the meaning. || 2 ||
And likewise, the sages, gods, hosts, perfected beings, and great seers,
relishing their own true nature, always abide in the state of the Fourth (turya).

Having stated the means of valid cognition through inference regarding its existence as common to all, he also states the means of valid cognition through the experience of the wise, beginning with "And thus": "Its own form" refers to the bliss of the Infinite (bhūmānanda) which is one's own self-nature. || 3 ||
These are they whose gaze is fixed with unblinking eyes;
they are established in the relinquishing of the vibration of attachment to the seen and the seer. || 4 ||

If it is asked why this is not experienced by everyone, understand that it is due to attachment to the seen and the seer, and due to the distraction caused by the vibration of the vital breath (*prāṇa*). For this very reason, yogis— having restrained their gaze upon the tip of the nose— are intent on the cessation of the vital breath in order to avoid both of these.
He says "these" [are seen]—meaning those whose eyes, that is, the eyeballs, are fixed, and whose senses are likewise fixed upon them. (4)

Those for whom there is no cultivation [of thought] regarding things that have not yet arisen, and who remain established even in their actions, and who abide in the relinquishing of the vibration of the relationship between consciousness and the object of consciousness; || 5 ||

This, however, refers to those who have not yet ascended to the sixth stage and beyond. But those who have ascended to the sixth and seventh stages, even while engaged in worldly activities (*vyavahāra*), always taste the bliss of their own self (*ātmasukha*) as if they were in meditative absorption (*samāhita*) belonging to the preceding stages; thus he says, "not remaining" (*na-sthitāḥ*). For those who, even while remaining amidst actions and worldly dealings, [possess this...]

For those who have reached the sixth stage and beyond, the cultivation of the reality of external objects does not persist even slightly. And as for those who have reached the preceding stages and abide in the samādhi characterized by the abandonment of the connection between consciousness and the object of consciousness—
those whose vital breath and mind do not vibrate— in such a state, there is the abandonment of both the attachment to the mind and the objects of thought.
The meaning of these two and a half verses is: "They abide in a state of equality in the plane of the bliss of plenitude.
"The breath of those does not vibrate, like bodies depicted in a painting;
the mind of those does not vibrate, like bodies depicted in a painting. (6)
Having abandoned attachment to the mind and its objects, they abide in their own true state;
through subtle vibration, they accomplish their purpose just as a lord does by a fraction of his power.

Those who have reached the sixth stage and beyond, by means of the vibration of the stream of consciousness that functions as an uninterrupted mass within the form of Brahman, accomplish in that very part the supreme human goal characterized by the savoring of unsurpassed bliss; and in exactly the same way, through the vibration of the mind and its objects externally, they also maintain the established order of worldly transaction. Just as the Lord of the World always [remains] internally...
The meaning is that, although established in the bliss of his own essential nature (*svarūpānanda*), he likewise maintains the cosmic order of the world through external *māyā*. || 7 ||
In the very same way, through the vibration of mind, objects of thought, and so forth, they maintain their existence,
just as the clear lunar ray gladdens the sprout [the reading "svastha" is also found].

In their worldly activity, when there is a conjunction of the various perceptions—the functions of the intellect—with visible external objects, the unsurpassed blissful Self, manifest even within that "triplicity," gladdens the inner being; thus, every worldly transaction is indeed of the nature of happiness.
The meaning is that it is just as the moonbeam, having entered within the sprout of a tree, gladdens it from the inside.

In the same way, the Self brings delight within upon the union of the seer and the seen, even though it has moved far from the original object and has not fallen upon the wall [of the senses]. || 9 ||
Regarding the fact that the internal bliss of their own true nature is even more free from distraction, he provides an illustration here as well:
"That very form [of the sun] is experienced by them as the undistracted joy of the Supreme Self. This is the meaning. || 9 ||
That which is the form of the splendor of the sun is the form of pure consciousness;
it is not an object of sight, it is not fit for instruction, it is neither too near nor far away.
The pure nature of the Self is of the form of consciousness, attainable through solitary experience;
it is neither the body, nor the senses and vital breaths, nor the mind, nor even latent impressions.
He states that the very reality of the Self is that which is liberated from all adjuncts such as the body and so forth, by means of the verse beginning with "not the body" (na deha). || 11 ||
There is no living soul, nor even vibration; there is neither consciousness nor indeed the world.
It is neither existent nor non-existent, nor is it the middle; it is neither empty nor non-empty.
Neither that [object] nor anything else exists as space, time, substance, and so forth;
it is entirely free from all these, as well as from the hundredfold sheaths within the heart.

Having examined place, time, and substance through the threefold determination and so forth, Brahman alone exists. [It exists] by means of these bodies and so forth. The word "hundred" (śata) refers to infinity, because of the infinity of the sheaths of past and future bodies which reside in the heart in the form of latent impressions (vāsanā). || 13 ||
Wherever this visible world vibrates, that very thing becomes the state of the Self;
for it neither has a beginning nor an end at the dissolution of the aeon, nor is it a substance subject to the elements such as air and the rest.

Thus, by means of a hundred sheaths within the heart-mind—wherever that [sheath] exists, it vibrates through the manifestation and disappearance of this visible world—that which is merely Being (*sanmātra*) would be the realized state of the Self; this is the meaning.
He says "And that which... to show that it is to be conceived as distinct from cause and effect: that Brahman which is primordial.

At the time of the great eon (*mahākalpa*) and so forth, that which exists is the cause known as the unmanifest (*avyākṛta*). Likewise, at the end of the eon, it does not become something else in the form of the dissolution of primordial matter (*prākṛtapralaya*) and so on. Even at the time of creation, in this world or in the next world beyond, there is nothing other than the nature of existence (*sadrūpa*) anywhere, due to transformations such as drying, burning, moistening, or splitting by wind and other elements.
The meaning is that it is not an object possessing modification, nor, by virtue of the first word [of the compound], does it possess its modifications. || 14 ||
In this world and the next, due to its true nature, it sometimes becomes otherwise;
thousands of body-jars are born and die. (15)
Now, one might ask: "Could there not be a modification of the nature of Being (sadrūpa) which persists through those modifications such as the body? To this, he says: "And they are born," etc.

O best among the knowers of the Self, there is no fragmentation of this space of the Self, which is both internal and external; for that entire aggregate, beginning with the body, is indeed the Self alone.
In that case, does the body and so forth exist separately? He says "no," stating: "And that... (verse 16).
Merely due to a lack of perfect awakening, the universe—which is in every respect identical with the Self—stands as if slightly separate; yet it is known by a well-perfected intellect.
Everywhere, by means of that which is well-perfected and refined through the methods of hearing and so forth. || 17 ||
Even while blazing amidst worldly affairs, remain extinguished and free from the sense of "mine.
Whatever is seen here, this entire world of moving and unmoving beings— || 18 ||
Therefore, it is said that even while engaged in worldly activity, one should remain established in the nature of the eternally liberated self through the vision of the changeless Self:
"All that is Brahman—devoid of attributes, devoid of qualities, pure in essence, changeless, without beginning or end, eternal, peaceful, and equanimous. (19)

For you who have seen that everything—the performance of death, the agent, the cause, the effect, birth, existence, dissolution, and recollection—is Brahman, O dear one, what further wandering remains for you when you possess the vision of the Self? You are indeed perfectly well. (20)

O dear one, for you who have perceived the entire world, beginning with time (*kāla*), as Brahman through the vision of the Self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), how could further instruction (*bramaṇa*) possibly be possible? The meaning is that it is not at all possible. This is because you have always already attained your own nature, which is in reality equal and non-unequal; thus, you are indeed "equal" (*sama*). (The reading *gacchasi* is also found. You have gone to—that is, you have eternally reached—your true self. Therefore, you are truly equal.
The meaning is that this is according to the Vedic scripture: "Being Brahman, he merges into Brahman. || 20 ||

Thus ends the forty-eighth sarga, titled "The Exposition of the Unity of Brahman and the Self," in the former portion of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa*, composed by Vālmīki, belonging to the *Ārṣa* tradition.
Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Unity of Brahman and the Self," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The forty-ninth canto.
Śrī Rāma said:
"O Brahman, if there is no modification or the like within the expanded Brahman,"
How does this world, consisting of existence and non-existence, appear? || 1 ||
Here, the distinction between the transformation and the emergent manifestation is stated:
through lack of awakening, ignorance exists; upon awakening, it does not exist.

Desiring to know the distinction between illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) and transformation (*vikāra*) or origination (*ārambha*) by way of their defining characteristics, Rāma asks: "In that which is devoid of the threefold limitation," meaning, in that which is free from the distinctions of subject, object, and means of knowledge. || 1 ||

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O dear one, that which is a reversal of its own nature— a state from which there is no returning— is what constitutes modification and so forth, as is found in milk and other such substances.

In that regard, the emergence of the effect from the cause is fivefold: (1) with its prior state unobscured, (2) with its prior state obstructed, (3) with its prior state concealed, (4) with its prior state unconcealed, and (5) with its prior state destroyed. The first is the state of a jar and so forth arising from clay and so forth. The second is the state of ice or hail arising from water. The third is [the state of] a rope...

The state of being a serpent; the fourth is the state of water becoming a wave; the fifth is the state of milk becoming curd. Among these, only the last constitutes a transformation (*vikāra*) such as birth and so forth, as well as a modification (*pariṇāma*); the others, however, are merely varieties of illusory manifestation (*vivarta*). With this intention, Vasiṣṭha first states the definition of transformation, beginning with the words "apunar... (not again), referring to things such as milk, rice, and so on.

The effect, characterized by curd, whiteness, and so forth, exists as being devoid of its previous state of existence as milk and the like, and consists of the reversal of the essential nature of the milk;
this very thing is what is denoted by such terms as "modification" (vikāra), "conditioning" (saṃskāra), and "transformation" (pariṇāma). This is the meaning. || 2 ||
Having become curd, it returns again to the state of milk, yet it is no longer milk;
likewise, the stainless Brahman remains Brahman alone in the beginning, middle, and end, once it has been realized.
He states that the effect characterized as the world does not exist in Brahman in that same way, because of its difference from it, with the words "unperceived" (abuddham) || 3 ||
Therefore, Brahman possesses no quality of being subject to transformation, unlike milk and other such substances;
nor does it undergo the process of becoming a composite whole, for it is devoid of beginning, end, and division.

"Let it be then that there is a sequence of the production of composite wholes from atoms, as in the case of dyads and so forth. To this he replies: "without beginning or end" (*anādyanta*). The meaning is that the sequence of the production of composite wholes would apply to parts characterized by spatial limitation—defined by a beginning and an end—and possessing actions, conjunctions, disjunctions, and so on; but such a sequence does not apply to Brahman, which is distinct from those characteristics. By this [it is shown...]

The definition of "initiation" (*ārambhakatva*)—as intended by the Vaiśeṣikas and others—is the capacity to produce a single effect through inherence (*samavāya*), whether the entities are conjoined (*saṃyukta*) or combined (*samaveta*), either in themselves or in that which inheres in their own substratum. For example, as threads [produce] a cloth;
or as the qualities of the cause [produce] a quality of the effect. And thus:
Kaṇāda’s Sūtra: Substances originate another substance, and qualities originate another quality. (4)
Know that this transformation which is seen at the beginning and end of a problem is merely the agitation of consciousness; for there is no modification in that which is changeless.
Since Brahman alone remains as the substratum of the world, its nature as a *vivarta* (illusory manifestation) is established; he demonstrates this by means of its definition:
"The appearance of a disparity that does not touch [the underlying reality] is *vivarta*; such is its definition"—this is the intended meaning. || 5 ||
Neither the object of cognition nor the act of cognition exists there in that Brahman;
it is designated by the word "Brahman" and consists of consciousness devoid of all relations.
He shows that it is beyond contact with this: "it is not an object of cognition. || 6 ||
Whatever the nature of a thing is at its beginning and end, that is exactly how it is said to be;
whatever difference appears in the middle is a manifestation arising from ignorance.

If it is asked how the non-contact with modifications in the middle is known, he says—“of such a nature” (yādṛk)—on the ground that this is established by the very mark of determining the absence of contact with those [modifications] at the beginning and the end. || 7 ||
The Self, however, is equal everywhere and at all times—in the beginning, the end, and the middle;
it never attains even its own otherness, nor does the reality of the Self ever change.

The identity of the self-entity as being of the nature of luminosity is established by universal experience; furthermore, its lack of self-nature (*anātmatva*) is utterly impossible for it. Thus he says: "But the self... (verse 8).
Because he is formless, because he is one, and because he is eternal,
this Lord never falls under the sway of the modifications of existence.
Śrī Rāma said: While Brahman alone exists, eternally one and absolutely pure,
what is the origin of ignorance, which is essentially a delusion of consciousness?

Rāma raises an objection from the perspective of one who has awakened to the truth: "While [Brahman] exists... (verse 10). He asks how ignorance, whose nature is diametrically opposed to Brahman—which consists solely of the essence of the light of consciousness—could possibly have any connection with it, such that the world could be a phenomenal transformation (*vivarta*) therein.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
This entire reality is the essence of Brahman; it has been, it is, and it will be.
It is changeless, without beginning or end, and it is certain that ignorance does not exist.

We do not assert the existence of ignorance from the perspective of one who has awakened; rather, with the intention that it is for the sake of instructing the unawakened through conceptualization, he gives the answer: "The reality of Brahman. Everything is complete. 11.
As for the sequence of the signified and the signifier expressed by the word "Brahman," even there,
that sequence is intended only to teach the absence of difference.
We do not say that there is an existence or a real being in otherness; rather, the meaning is that this sequence is merely imagined for the purpose of instruction.
You, I, the world, the quarters, the sky, the earth, and fire and the rest—all are nothing but Brahman, without beginning or end; there is not even the slightest trace of ignorance.
The wise know that this so-called "ignorance" is merely an error and is unreal;
for how indeed could that which does not exist be real? (14)
Śrī Rāma said: "O Lord, in yesterday’s discourse on the topic of tranquility, it was stated by you that this ignorance is to be investigated in such and such a manner. (15)

Rāma raises an objection: "If ignorance does not exist at all, then why was it stated by you yourself in the section on tranquility that 'this ignorance is an error, and it is investigated in such and such a manner,' thereby acknowledging the existence of ignorance?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha replied:
O scion of Raghu, you remained unenlightened for all this time;
it is said that you were awakened by these very stratagems devised by me. (16)

He says—“etāvantam” (for this long)—to show that while you were in a state of ignorance, that was spoken according to a conceptualization following your own intellect; but now you are awakened, so there is no occasion for such conceptualization, and thus there is no contradiction.

This sequence of conceptualizations, such as "this individual soul (jīva) consists of ignorance," was devised by the best among those skilled in speech for the purpose of awakening the unawakened. (17)
As long as the mind remains unawakened,
it does not attain awakening even through hundreds of reproaches, provided there is no delusion.
That mind is the conceptualization of delusion, ignorance, and other such technical conventions of the scriptures. 18.
Only by means of reasoning is this individual soul awakened and united with the Self;
if a task is accomplished through reasoning, it cannot be achieved even by hundreds of efforts.
The meaning is that this is because arguments serve to eliminate personal defects such as incredulity and the like. || 19 ||
If one were to say "everything is Brahman" to an unawakened person of dull intellect, he acts like a friend by merely reporting pain to a log. (20)
But since the instruction on reality would be useless if these defects exist, he says "all" with this intention. || 20 ||
The fool is awakened by means of reasoning; the wise man is awakened by means of reality.
The fool attains wisdom not without being awakened by reasoning. (21)
For so long a time you were unawakened; now you have been awakened by me through reasoning, as you are being enlightened by me.
By whatever instruction and of whatever kind he was awakened, [he said], "Listen to that"—this is the ellipsis. || 22 ||
I am Brahman; the three worlds are Brahman; you are Brahman—indeed, the ground of the visible world is Brahman. There is no second conceptualization; do as you wish. (23)
He says that very thing: "Brahman" and "as you wish. The sense is that there is no loss of its actual nature as Brahman due to usage based on one's own preference. || 23 ||
The three worlds are nothing but the pinnacle of great consciousness that is beyond perception; though you perceive them as a single internal cognition, you remain untainted. 24.

The "limit" (koṭi) is that alone which is the boundary for the sublation of all delusions. Regarding the word "one" (ekā): the sense is that it is based on such scriptural passages as, "What delusion, what sorrow can there be for one who perceives oneness? (Īśa Upaniṣad 7). || 24 ||
"I am the Supreme Self— luminous in form, conscious, and all-pervading"—
remaining within this realization of Rāghava, stay, move, breathe, and sleep.
O Raghava, whether standing, walking, breathing, or sleeping, experience within yourself that which is the nature of the ego-sense as the Self.
If you are wise and virtuous, free from the sense of "mine" and free from the ego,
then become that which is the realization of Brahman— tranquil and abiding in all beings. (26)
Become Brahman, whose single essence is consciousness and feeling. 26.

That very reality, which is without beginning or end and is pure luminosity, is the supreme state; you abide as that, consisting of the nature of pure consciousness, the one self that pervades all. (27)
You alone are that very Self, consisting of all-pervading, unitary, pure consciousness; you abide as the supreme state, which is established by the Vedas and is without beginning or end.

That which is Brahman, the Self, and the Fourth (turya), that which is ignorance (avidyā) and primordial nature (prakṛti)—the single, eternal Self is non-different from all these, just as clay is [the common substance] in hundreds of jars. (28)

That which is known as Brahman, as Ātman, and also as the Fourth (Turya), and that which is known as ignorance (avidyā), as primordial nature (prakṛti)—and by the word "ca" [also] as the world (jagat)—all that has the single essence of non-dual Pure Being (sanmātra); this is the meaning. || 28 ||
The material nature is not different from the Self, just as the earthenness is not different from a jar;
and just as pure clay alone exists within, so does material nature abide as the very Self. (29)
Just as the earthen nature of a jar is its true reality, which is merely clay, so too is the meaning of "prakṛti. || 29 ||
This very vibration of the Self, which is like the swirling of water,
is designated here by the word "prakṛti" (nature), for it is indeed that [vibration] itself.

"Spanda" means transformation. Therefore, the meaning is that within its own transformation, by virtue of having pure Being as its essential nature, only that Self exists here, and not even an atom of anything else. || 30 ||
Just as the single vibration and wind are distinct in name but not in reality,
so too the one Self and primordial nature are distinct in name but not in reality.
By way of existence, according to the actual state of things. || 31 ||
The distinction between these two exists due to ignorance; it dissolves through awakening alone.
Through ignorance, that which is pure being appears as [something else], just as the delusion of a snake occurs in a rope.
Consisting of existence, being pure existence; it goes—“to another form,” is the ellipsis. || 32 ||
When this seed of mental construction, vibrating, falls upon the field of consciousness,
from it arises the sprout of the mind, which is a fragment of the future cycle of existence.
The meaning is that from that very sprout of the mind, there arises a shimmering future forest-thicket of cyclic existence (saṃsāra).
This very [seed], once burnt by the realization of the Self, is not capable of sprouting again even if it is diligently sprinkled with the waters of latent impressions (vāsanā). // 34 //
This is indeed the seed-syllable of time. || 34 ||
If the seed of conceptualization does not fall into the field of consciousness, then the sprouts of the mind—the trees of the waves of pleasure and pain—will not arise. (35)

If the tree-like bodies that bear the fruits of pleasure and pain do not fall, then such sprouts of the mind will not arise; abandon the duality grasped in the world, born of ignorance, for you have attained awakening which destroys ignorance. Through the power of the singular nature of the Self, you are one whose being is fearless; "there is no suffering at all"—this is the essence of our ultimate truth.

He concludes the secret of the instruction begun with the words "duality": "O Rāma, abandon—cast off—the duality that is unreal and acquired through delusion in this world. [The change from *jahāhi* to *jahihi* occurs because of the rule] *ā ca hau*.
Since you have attained awakening, become one with the Self (*abhyātmā*), characterized by the state of oneness with the Self and the splendor of unsurpassed bliss."
The meaning is that our instruction in the *Paramārthasāra* is that suffering does not exist even in the three periods of time. || 36 ||

Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Yoga of Reflecting on Saṃsāra," in the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa* of the *Mokṣopāya* section of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*, composed by Vālmīki, according to the tradition of the Ṛṣis. || 49 ||
Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Yoga of Contemplating Saṃsāra," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
Fifty-fifth Sarga.
Śrī Rāma said:
"Everything that is to be known has been known; everything that is to be seen has been seen without flaw."
We have been completely filled by you with the nectar of the knowledge of Brahman. || 1 ||
In this system, the emergence of the subtle body (liṅga-puryaṣṭaka) within the individual soul (jīva) has been described through conceptualization;
likewise, the process by which that [body] perceives external objects through the senses has been explained.

"the knot of the heart is broken and all doubts are severed"—according to this Vedic scripture, although Rāma has himself severed all doubts through the direct realization of reality (*tattvasākṣātkāra*), he desires to inquire into the locus of those doubts for the sake of benefiting others.
Thus, first expressing his own experience, he demonstrates it with the words beginning "It is known," etc. We are yours.
We have been completely filled by the nectar of the knowledge of Brahman belonging to you. || 1 ||
From the Full, this Full arises; from the Full, the Full is produced.
The Full is filled by the Full, and the state of fullness abides within the Full.

He corroborates this with the Śruti: "That is full, this is full; from the full, the full arises. Having taken the fullness of the full, the full alone remains. He explains [the verse] beginning with "from the full":
from the full Brahman, having entered into the limiting adjunct (upādhi), this form of the individual soul (jīva) is full up to the tips of its nails.

In the ultimate sense, it is Brahman alone that is full. Since from that which is full, space and the rest are produced in succession, even that which takes the form of the individual and collective limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) is produced as nothing but fullness itself. Therefore, when, through the knowledge "I am Brahman" arising from the Great Sayings (*mahāvākya*), the delimitation caused by the limiting adjuncts is removed at its very root, [the individual] becomes full by means of the full Brahman.

When the reality of the living self (jīva-tattva) is filled by way of undivided unity, then that "imagined fullness" vanishes; the meaning is that for that which is already full, its fullness remains exactly as it was before. || 2 ||
O Brahman, I ask this merely as a play for the further increase of my understanding; you should not be angry, like a father with his child. (3)
For the sake of increasing the awakening of many people, you ought not to feel anger toward this child’s playful questioning, O Brahmin,
even though the ear, eye, sense of touch, tongue,
and nose are clearly present and visible.

Because the manifestation of the experience of objects is seen within the heart of all living beings, because the pleasure and pain produced by the sight of the pleasant and unpleasant are experienced within the heart,
and because the recollection of even long-past external objects is seen to occur within the heart alone, [it exists] in the heart alone.

The experience of external objects must also be explained. In that regard, since the sense organs such as the ear and the eye lack the power to bring external objects into the heart, and because they are insentient and thus incapable of going out themselves, experiencing [the object], and returning to report it, the postulation of sense organs distinct from the physical seats (golaka) of the ear and so forth is useless. Nor can it be [maintained] that [the experience occurs] within the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa).

The hypothesis that the living consciousness itself, having emerged through the channel of the senses, pervades external objects such as a jar and thereby experiences them, is also untenable. For if that were the case, it would follow that the experience is recorded as occurring entirely outside [the self];
furthermore, it would follow that pleasures and pains resulting from the sight of the pleasant and the unpleasant would also arise externally.

Furthermore, there would be the consequence that internal memory could not occur at a later time. This is because internal experience is impossible without the entry [of the object] into the internal [organ]. Nor can it be said that an external modification of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇavṛtti), having taken up the so-called impression (*saṃskāra*)—which is marked by the form of the object through its embrace of that object—and having entered within, experiences and causes one to remember that [object] by mimicking its form like an actor.

The conceptual construction that "it is said [to be known]" is also logical. For if one were to construct the view that experiences of forms such as jars have as their object the "marking" (*lāñchana*) of those [external objects], there would result no distinction between error and valid cognition, which would lead to a lack of confidence in all cases whatsoever. Furthermore, there would be the consequence that the externality of jars and so forth could not be experienced. Thus, experience is internal, while jars and so forth are external.

Thus, because there is no connection between these two, it is in no way possible to establish that an external object enters into experience. For this very reason, the Naiyāyikas and others maintain that the relation between experience and its objects is a relation of the nature of "object and subject" (*viṣaya-viṣayibhāva*), and not a relation characterized by physical contact (*saṃśleṣa*) or the like; yet even that [position] is not tenable.

Because that which lacks a specific nature cannot be restricted to particular objects due to its being non-distinct with respect to all objects, there can be no such restriction. Nor can there be a restriction based on a sequence— such as the self conjoining with the mind, the mind with the sense organ, and the sense organ with the object—
through a succession of relations like "conjunction with what is conjoined with what is conjoined with one's own substrate."

Because a non-sequential (ananugata) indirect relation (*paramparā-sambandha*) cannot serve as the determinant for the respective objects of memory, inference, and so forth; and because, since an indirect relation cannot account for the immediacy (*aparokṣya*) of external objects, it would have to be that very [immediacy] which serves as the determinant.

Furthermore, it is because the postulation of an essential relation (*svarūpasaṃbandha*) is redundant. By this, the established rule—that an object is the "object" (*viṣaya*) of a particular cognition if it generates that specific cognition by means of contact—is also refuted; for it would follow that the sense organs and so forth would also be objects of that cognition.
Therefore, the experience of internal and external objects must be said to arise solely through the power of the illusory capacity (*māyā-śakti*), which is capable of bringing about the impossible.

This being the case, what is the purpose of postulating sense organs distinct from the physical spheres such as the ears? It would be more appropriate to hold that the conscious self (*cidātmā*) experiences external objects through those very [spheres] according to actual experience. If that were so, then even in a dead body, the ears and other organs—[would still function].

Rāma raises an objection with the verse beginning "the ear" (*śrotra*), wondering: since the Self is all-pervading and eternal, why does it not experience external objects even there? In this context, words such as "ear" refer to the physical cavities (the sense organs). For this very reason, the qualification "even though clearly visible" (*sphuṭaṃ dṛśyamānam api*) is employed. || 4 ||
How is it that a deceased being does not perceive its own realm, and how is it that while living, one perceives everything as one's own realm? (5)
How is it that the sense organs, though insentient, experience the externality of jars and other objects within the body, yet do not likewise experience [their own] internality? (6)

If someone were to say that the sense organs, such as the eye, go out themselves, experience the externality of objects like jars, and then enter back inside and speak [of them], to that he says: "They are insentient" (*jaḍāni*). The meaning is that they possess neither individual consciousness nor the capacity for speech. If someone were to say regarding the sense organs...

Regarding the claim that one brings external objects into the heart and establishes them there, he says "again" (punaḥ) in response. The sense is that if an object were established in the heart, there would have to be repeated experience of it within the heart; for we never observe a jar or the like being drawn out from the heart. || 6 ||

Regarding the two—namely, the pot and the sense organ—which are like iron rods that do not touch one another, how indeed could this [consciousness] be produced between them by their mutual interaction? (7)
An objection might be raised: "Surely the collection of objects such as a jar first draws toward itself the collection of sense organs such as the eyes;

and that drawn-in organ, having enveloped the object, leads it inward by some part of itself to the enjoyer situated within the heart, just as the nose carries fragrance"—anticipating this conception, he says: "This [is not so]."

Objects would attract the sense organs only by coming into contact with them, not without such contact; for we do not observe that unattached ropes and the like can attract jars or similar objects. Nor is contact possible between jars and the like and the sense organs when they do not reach the region of the physical organ (golaka). Furthermore, there is neither contact of the sense organs with the jar—like that of a rope—or the power to attract it.
This is well known. He says that because they occupy different locations, it is like two iron rods driven into the ground at separate points;

therefore, how can the fact that [the eyes] possess a mutual attractive power and yet allow large objects such as jars to enter through the small apertures of the pupils not contradict the experience of everyone? This is the meaning. || 7 ||
Although you already know these distinctions in their hundreds of variations, I ask them again; therefore, please explain them in their entirety out of compassion.

[Objection: But for you, whose every doubt has been severed by the awakening to reality (tattva), how can such a doubt exist regarding this worldly transaction (vyavahāra), which is composed of illusion (māyā) and the locus of all logical impossibilities? To this, he replies: "Even though I know," and so forth. "I ask again in a hundred ways, in many ways"—the meaning is that it is for the purpose of grasping [the truth] through the removal of ignorance. || 8 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
O dear one, neither the senses and so forth, nor the mind and so forth, nor even objects such as a jar,
exist separately here apart from the stainless consciousness.

This which is said—that there are no sense organs apart from the physical globes—is far too little. For, upon thorough investigation, no disputant whatsoever is able to define any divisions of subject, means of knowledge, or object of knowledge as distinct from consciousness. With this intention, Vasiṣṭha first provides the resolution: "The senses, etc. (Verse 9).

Even more transparent than the sky, that consciousness, by its own nature, having conceived its own form through the very activity of its own being as the *puryaṣṭaka* due to its conscious nature, has brought it into existence.

If, however, you consider the existence of the seer and the seen to be established through conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), then—since such construction is possible even by way of the "eightfold city" (*puryaṣṭaka*) composed of the senses and so forth, according to preceding latent impressions (*vāsanā*)—nothing at all is untenable. With this intention, he says: "Even from the sky," and likewise, "by consciousness, that is, by the Self."

The meaning is that its own form, by way of its nature being variegated by *māyā* and by way of the *puryaṣṭaka*, is "cultivated"—that is, imagined—through the function of objective existence (*bhāvavṛtti*) in accordance with preceding and preceding latent impressions (*vāsanā*). || 10 ||
And that very [principle] has become the primordial nature (prakṛti) for the persistence of the world;
from its constituent parts are born the sense organs and so forth, as well as jars and so forth. (11)

To provide scriptural authority for the meaning already stated, he cites the Śruti: "One should know Māyā as Prakṛti, but the Great Lord (Maheśvara) as the wielder of Māyā; by His constituent parts, this entire universe is pervaded"—this is expressed by the words "And that very [Śruti]," etc. (verse 11).
The mind, which by its own nature has attained the state of the "city of eight" (puryaṣṭaka),
reflects objects such as jars within its own constituent parts.

Thus, when the mind— which constitutes the *puryaṣṭaka*— emerges outwardly through the doors of the senses and pervades an object such as a jar, it brings that jar back into the heart in the very form of its external appearance as reflected in its own mental modification (*vṛtti*), and subsequently manifests it; likewise, at a later time, there is memory, and in a dream, there is the experience of that which was internal precisely as if it were external.

With the intention that everything is thus established, he says: "the state of being the *puryaṣṭaka*. In this manner, the very principle whose nature is consciousness (*cidrūpa-tattva*) arrives at the state of being the *puryaṣṭaka*; for, because the *puryaṣṭaka* has as its essential nature the mind (*citta*) and other factors, it itself becomes its own part, namely the mental modification called "mind" (*cittavṛtti*). Within that part, external objects such as jars [are perceived].

It reflects only in an external form. However, in the case of a dead body, because the individual soul (*jīva*), which consists of the subtle body (*liṅga* or *puryaṣṭaka*), departs by its own volition according to the manner shown in the story of Līlā, it lacks the capacity for seeing and other such functions; this is the sense in which all objections are avoided. || 12 ||
Śrī Rāma said: O Blessed One, tell me what is the nature of the mirror that possesses the majesty of creating thousands of worlds, and what is the form of the city of eight (puryaṣṭaka)?

"If this is so, then tell me, O Rāma: what is the nature of that very *puryaṣṭaka* (the subtle body), which—by means of its portion consisting of the fivefold elements transformed into the form of the universe, and by means of its portion consisting of the subtle body as the effect of the non-fivefold elements—serves as a mirror for the apprehension of that reflection? Thus Rāma asks: "The universe... (verse 13).
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:

That Brahman which exists as the seed of the universe, without beginning or end, free from affliction, whose nature is light, consisting of pure consciousness alone, and devoid of all parts or mental constructs; || 14 ||

To explain its true nature, Vasiṣṭha points to the root of that—the unknown reality of Brahman: "When it becomes oriented toward conceptualization (kalanā), it is known internally as the 'living being' (jīva). That very jīva indeed clearly accumulates [karma] and vibrates within this body. (15)

The meaning is as follows: that Brahman, having created the subtle elements beginning with space (*viyat*), and having created by means of those unquintuplicated elements the subtle body (*liṅga*) and by means of the quintuplicated elements the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), became intent upon the process of assuming the characteristic of being a reflection within it; thus, because it sustains itself through the identification with the thread-like vital breaths (*prāṇas*), it is known as the "individual soul" (*jīva*). It accumulates (*cinoti*).

It becomes augmented by the accumulation of latent impressions (vāsanā) and by the growth of its constituent parts; and having become thus augmented, it vibrates through the nature of internal and external activity—this is the meaning. || 15 ||
From the sense of "I" it is called the ego (ahaṃkāra); from the act of thinking it is called the mind (manas);
from the determination of cognition it is called the intellect (buddhi); and likewise, from the perception of Indra, it is called the sense organ (indriya).

He states the different names for that very [ego] according to the distinctions in its functions, such as conceit (abhimāna) and so forth, beginning with the words "from the sense of 'I'" (ahaṃbhāvāt) and so on. || 16 ||
Through the contemplation of a body, it becomes a body; through the contemplation of a jar, a jar.
This very self-nature is remembered by people as the "city of eight" (puryaṣṭaka). || 17 ||
The self whose nature is common to all activities is remembered by the name "puryaṣṭaka" (the eightfold city). || 17 ||
That consciousness which descends into the states of knowerhood, agency, enjoyership, and witnesshood is called the *jīva*; indeed, the wise know that to be the *puryaṣṭaka*.

Through the operation of the organs of knowledge (*jñānendriya*), it possesses the nature of a knower (*jñatva*); through the operation of the organs of action (*karmendriya*), it possesses the nature of an agent (*kartṛtva*);

through being the locus of the pleasure and pain that are the fruits thereof, it possesses the nature of an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*); and through its universal indifference and luminosity, it possesses the nature of a witness (*sākṣitva*).

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the inclusion of being the instrument of experience, the abode, and so forth is intended. That [superimposition] which, falling upon this [Self], has these as its attributes through superimposition (*adhyāsa*)—[is what is meant].

That very consciousness, when the aspect of consciousness (cit) predominates, is called the individual soul (jīva); when the inert aspect (jaḍāṃśa) predominates, that same [consciousness] is known as the "eightfold city" (puryaṣṭaka)—this is the meaning. || 18 ||

Then, from time to time, the living being itself becomes something else by its own nature, through the arising of minute particles of infinite latent impressions (*vāsanā*) that have been cultivated into specific forms. (19)

Therefore, because the forms of the intellect (buddhyākāra), which are conditioned by identity with the self, undergo differentiation according to the difference in time, the individual soul (jīva) also appears as if manifold when colored by desire, anger, joy, dejection, and so forth; thus he says, "At every moment.
The connection with the following verse is: "it assumes a form consisting of the arising of infinitesimal particles of latent impressions (vāsanā). || 19 ||

By means of the nature of the city-of-eight (puryaṣṭaka), it assumes a form through time, just as a seed reaches the state of a sprout through watering according to its latent impressions (vāsanā). // 20 //

With the intention that the entire world takes on the form of this very seed—the individual soul (jīva) as both the aggregate (samaṣṭi) and the individual (vyaṣṭi)—just as a sprout, stalk, leaf, and so forth [arise from a seed], he says "Just as" (yathā). || 20 ||
"I am the body and so forth, the immobile and the mobile"—thus one perceives through false knowledge that "I am not the primordial conscious Self. (21)

Therefore, the primordial conscious self does not perceive or see itself as "I am," but rather perceives and sees through false knowledge (mithyājñāna) that "I am merely the form of the body and so forth. || 21 ||
The living being of the world, enveloped by latent impressions (vāsanā), wanders for a long time indeed, moving up and down like a piece of wood struck by waves in the ocean. (22)
Someone, due to the purity of their birth, immediately after being released from the bondage of existence, realizes the Self and attains the state that is devoid of beginning and end. ||23||

"Someone equal to Sanaka and others" means that at the very beginning of a kalpa, immediately after the bondage of existence from the previous kalpa, in that very first birth; and this entire classification has been explained in the section on origination (*utpatti-prakaraṇa*) during the description of the distinctions between *jīvas* such as the *sāttvika* and *rājasa*. || 23 ||
Someone who, after a long time, has become weary of the multitude of births he has experienced,
attains the supreme state of the Self through the power of self-knowledge.
O wise one, listen now to how this soul, having assumed such a form as a body, perceives objects like jars through the eyes and other senses, just as one perceives what is inside a jar. (25)

Regarding the question asked—how it is that jars and other external objects exist while the sense organs are insentient—that has been resolved in general terms; now he resolves it specifically with the words beginning "of such a form" (evaṃrūpa). || 25 ||
When the consciousness, which is the limit of all calculation, has departed from its state of life, this body remains as a collection of the six sense organs with the mind as the sixth.

The consciousness (*caitanya*) of the individual soul (*cit*), which terminates at the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*), exists as the measurer by pervading everything from the tips of the nails through its reflection therein; it is thus delimited as an object of cognition. Consequently, the living consciousness is always limited by the body and, being situated within the body, experiences only that which is connected with pleasure, pain, and so forth, and not what is external. || 26 ||
When another [element] falls from all bodies into the sky in the form of the eye, then, through contact with that life-force, it attains oneness with the living self (jīvātman). || 27 ||

But when another external object, such as a jar, is to be perceived, then—just as water overflowing from a pond flows out through the mouth of a canal—the eye and other senses, having overflowed from all the bodies, fall—that is, they go forth—into the external space (kha) ending with the jar, by way of the door consisting of the subtle forms (akṣarūpiṇā) of the eyes and so on. To the question "What happens then?", he says: "tadā" (then).

Then, through contact—that is, through pervasion—by means of the soul (jīva) emerging via the door of the eyes and so forth toward that jar or other object, and by way of the pervasion of a mental modification (vṛtti) in its own form, it attains oneness with the consciousness of the living being; it reaches the state of being an object, characterized by a superimposed identity with the mind (adhyāsika-cittādātmya). || 27 ||
In the perception of external objects, the constant connection of the sense organ with the mind is the causal factor;
never that of one who is liberated from the mind. (28)

And that connection of the sense organ with the mind occurs only for one who is alive and possessed of consciousness, acting as the cause for the cognition of external objects, and not for one who is dead or liberated; such is the meaning. || 28 ||
Whatever is clearer than that reflects within it like the sky;
joined with the individual soul (jīva), even the external soul lives.
Let it be so externally; nevertheless, how is there an internal experience of that? To this he replies with the words beginning "yadyat" (whatever).

Whatever object—whether in the form of a modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa-vṛtti*) or in the form of a ray of light from the eye—is more transparent, in that [object] external things such as a jar are reflected; and that reflection is [perceived] by the individual soul (*jīva*) situated within that modification.

[The ego] becomes conjoined [with the vital breath]. If that is so, why is it not experienced as "I am experiencing the jar" while remaining strictly outside? To this he says: [the *nalopa*—the elision of the *n*—is Vedic (*chāndasa*). Or, it may be a compound with a verbal form as its final member, like the word *anuvyacalat*. The meaning is: wherever there is the pervasion of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), there alone is the awareness of "I," and not outside. || 29 ||
When the pupils of the eyes possess the luster of freshly polished jewels, then external objects are reflected within them. (30)

Let it be so; however, even if the production of the fruit of manifestation occurs in the jar, how does the form of the jar enter within the heart? To this he says: "polished," etc. When the pupils of the eyes, due to the absence of defects such as cataracts, possess the luster of a freshly polished sapphire, then—
The mental modification (cittavṛtti) of those two eyes, accompanied by the reflection of the jar, enters [the mind]; thus it is said that the external object, such as the jar, is reflected. || 30 ||
Thereupon, O Rāghava, an external object becomes joined with the individual soul (jīva) by way of being its reflection, and thus it comes to be known by that soul. 31.

The meaning is that this object, having thus entered the pupil of the eye, becomes joined with the heart by way of being reflected there in the *jīva*, which possesses the ego-sense (*ahaṃ-abhimāna*). Thus, in this manner, an external object such as a jar, while appearing externally, comes to be known within the heart by the *jīva* conjoined with the ego-sense. || 31 ||
For even a child perceives that which comes into contact [with the senses];
why then would a living being—not even a beast or an immobile thing—not perceive it? (32)
The author states "that which... because the rule regarding sensation upon contact with an object for a sentient being is well-established even among children, cattle, and so forth.

The underlying point is that since one observes the closing of leaf-buds in certain shrubs even through mere touch, such sensation is inferred to exist everywhere, including in stationary beings. || 32 ||
Furthermore, the rays of the clear eye are enveloped by the living soul (jīva);
they fully embrace the visible object, and the soul perceives it through its true nature.
Dispelling the suspicion of the common folk as to how an object situated at a distance can come into contact with the physical orb [of the eye], he says:
"Being enveloped by the *jīva*, they embrace—that is, they take hold of—the object standing before them. (33)

This very same sequence applies to touch; the arising of cognition is the connection [between sense and object]. It is likewise declared for taste and smell, arising from the contact of the living being. (34)
He extends the sequence stated regarding the eye to touch and the other [objects] as well: "This very same... (verse 34).
But sound, because it resides in space, enters the space of the ear and in an instant enters the internal space of the living being; in this way, the perceptions of the senses [occur]. (35)

He states the distinction regarding sound: "But sound... The point is that sound can enter within directly through the ear even without the reflection of its function (*vṛtti*). With the intention that, in this manner, let it be granted that smell also has the possibility of entering within by way of the wind (*pavana*), [he says...]
He concludes the principle stated according to the circumstances with the word "ittham" (thus). || 35 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
O Brahman, tell me, what is the nature of this which is seen reflected in the mirror of the mind, as well as within machines, wood, and bellies? (36)
Now, Rāma, desiring to know the true nature of all reflections in this context, asks:

"Tell me, what is the essence of that reflection of the light of a jar's mouth and so forth which appears within glass, bronze, gems, water, and the like, as well as within machines and wood, and which emerges from their interiors onto fresh sprouts and other objects? This is the meaning. || 36 ||

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O best among those who know what is to be known, understand that this mutual reflection between these two, which are as utterly insentient as two living beings, is merely an illusion of the eye.

In this context, even though the original object (*bimba*) is real, the individual and collective living beings (*jīva*), which are reflections of consciousness, possess forms over and above that of the original object which are established merely through illusion and cannot be definitively described;
in such a case, between two things that are utterly insentient— such as a face and a mirror, or a jar and a mental modification (*cittavṛtti*)— there exists a mutual dependence.
With the intention of stating that the nature of a reflection is difficult to describe, he provides the answer: "Atyanteti" (It is beyond...).
Know that this is an illusion of the Seer, whose nature is consciousness. || 37 ||
Let there be no conviction in you here that this world is merely that much;
the wave of "I" and so forth is always present within the water. (38)
He says "tāvat" (only so much) to show that the error is not merely a reflection, but the entire world as well.
The word "tu" (but/also) is used in the sense of "even. "Tāvanmātram" means merely an error. Therefore, let there be no confidence in you regarding this world;
the meaning is that the phenomenal expansion beginning with "I" is like a wave, non-existent apart from the water of consciousness. As for what is currently existing...
The meaning is that it is always nothing but consciousness and water. || 38 ||
In the supreme ocean, however, there is no such thing as space, time, action, and so forth;
because of its eternal identity with that [ocean], the Self is omnipresent and all-pervading everywhere. (39)

Always with an unattached mind and a joyful soul, having known within yourself that peace which is free from false pleasure and pain, remain with your intellect established in equanimity, having cast off all the diseases of worldly existence and all deceit. 40.

O Rāma, you, being always one whose mind is unattached, and having become one whose intellect knows that pleasure and pain are false— thus possessing the "knowledge of the falsity of pleasure and pain"— and being one from whom all the delusion (māyā) characterized by worldly existence and consisting of the form of disease has been cast away, [abide] in equanimity, which is the very nature of Brahman.
The meaning is: "stay," [that is,] with a settled mind. || 40 ||

Thus ends the fiftieth chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Yoga of Contemplating the Perception of the Senses," in the *Pūrvārdha* of the *Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa*, within the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa* composed by the sage Vālmīki. 50.
Thus ends the fiftieth chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Yoga of Contemplating the Perception of the Senses," in the *Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa* of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The fifty-first canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
"The eyes and other senses were not produced for you previously."
Just as all of this concerning the Lotus-born One has been heard by you. || 1 ||
The notions of "living being," "senses," "mind," "body," and "the city of eight" are merely delusions arising from ignorance;
however, upon awakening, it is declared that Brahman alone is the one reality.

With the words "having become oriented toward the fruit" (*phalanonmukhatām yātam*), etc., he first restates [the point] for the sake of the introduction to what is to be said next: that the conceptualization (*kalpana*) of the ego, body, senses, and so forth—which were previously non-existent—is equal for you as well as for the lotus-born Brahmā, who represents the collective totality (*jīva-samaṣṭi*) just as [the individual soul] represents the individual manifestation (*vyaṣṭi*). This intent is already known to you. The word *punaḥ* is used in the sense of *api* (even/also).

The word [is]: "Just as for the Lotus-born [Brahmā], so too for you, who abide in the nature of Brahman described as being without beginning or end prior to creation, the eyes and other senses have not come into being"—all this very point of the purport of my speech has been heard by you; that is to say, it has been understood. || 1 ||
Just as the consciousness of objects arises first within the eightfold city of Brahmā,
so too does it arise at all times within every eightfold city.

Thus, following the conceptualization of the *puryaṣṭaka*, he states that the conceptualization of objects for practical usage (*vyavahāryārtha*) occurs for individuals (*vyaṣṭi*) just as it does for the collective (*samaṣṭi*), beginning with the words "Brahmā": Brahmā is Hiraṇyagarbha; just as at the beginning of creation, the consciousness of objects to be used arose for his collective *puryaṣṭaka*, so too does it arise for every individual *puryaṣṭaka*. (2)
Know that the "vital principle" (jīva) is the city-of-eight (puryaṣṭaka), which is the emergence of the senses within the womb;
whatever it conceives of in whatever manner, it immediately perceives exactly as such.

He demonstrates that very state, beginning from the period of remaining in the womb, with the words "Know" (viddhi). The meaning is this: the individual soul (*vyaṣṭijīva*), while still in the womb, becomes endowed with the emergence of the senses such as sight and so forth, consisting of the *puryaṣṭaka* (the eightfold subtle body), in the sixth month; from that time onward, whatever object it conceives as something to be experienced, it perceives that very thing through its own latent impressions (*vāsanā*). || 3 ||
Know that the senses and what is called the objects of the senses constitute one's own perception;
and how this is fully accomplished, that has been explained to you regarding the state of the primordial mind.

And thus, just as one's own self-awareness arises along with the senses and what is called the objects of the senses during the primordial state of the mind—the mental activity of Hiraṇyagarbha—so too has that arisen for you, O individual soul (vyaṣṭi); this is the meaning of my statement that it bears fruit. || 4 ||
Pure consciousness, arising as irreproachable self-awareness,
then becomes endowed with the awareness of "I" and the infinite subtle bodies (puryaṣṭaka) of living beings.

Prior to creation, pure consciousness exists as one and the same in both the individual (vyaṣṭi) and the collective (samaṣṭi); thereafter, although it becomes endowed with the subtle bodies (puryaṣṭaka) of infinite individual souls characterized by the sense of "I," its nature as pure awareness remains irreproachable—this is the meaning. || 5 ||
But she does not abide as something other [than the self], because she is non-dual, infinite, unknowable, free from affliction, non-existent [as a separate entity], manifold, and non-empty.

If it is asked, "Since that cognition [of the object] arises from a defect in the object of knowledge (*vedya*), why is it not censured?", he says: "[Because] the object of knowledge does not exist in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*).

The logical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: and regarding its non-existence, there are three reasons: because it is a non-entity (*abhāvatva*), because it possesses delimitation by space and time, and because it possesses delimitation by substance (*vastu*).
Because it is a non-entity, because it possesses delimitation by space and time, and because it possesses delimitation by substance, [it does not exist].
Through the cognition of "I am" and so forth, that [Self] does not become the mind,
nor does it attain the state of the individual soul (jīva), nor does it consist of the subtle body (puryaṣṭaka).

Now, it might be argued: "If it is said that consciousness itself undergoes the state of being the mind and so forth, then if the mind and the rest are unreal, why would consciousness itself not also be unreal? To this, he says: "cetyādi" (the object of thought, etc.).

That [state] is merely a superimposition (*adhyāropa*) of the mental modification (*buddhi-vṛtti*) whose objects are the thinkable (*cetya*), the conceivable (*mantavya*), and so on; it is not a real attainment of the state of being the mind.
This is the meaning of the verse. || 7 ||
There is no manifestation of ignorance and the like; He who always exists as if non-existent is called the Supreme Self, transcending the mind and the six senses.

In that case, since its true nature is manifested through the play of knowledge (*vidyā*), why was it not non-existent even before? To this he says: "No. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the inclusion of the final means of knowledge, reflection, and so forth is intended. That Supreme Self, who is imagined by the deluded as if He did not exist, always exists. (8)
Therefore, the individual soul (jīva), whose form is consciousness and whose nature is thought, is produced from that;
[the notion that it is otherwise] is merely an illusion—this and other such points are proclaimed for the sake of instruction. || 9 ||

If it is argued: "Since He is indeed without a second, how is the manifestation of individual souls (jīvas) described in the Śruti through the analogy of sparks from a fire as 'all these selves emerge from Him'? [The author] replies that this is for the sake of instruction by means of a conceptualization:
"Because, when some affliction consisting of ignorance has arisen from any cause whatsoever..."
Through the instruction of the teacher, [the mind] dissolves as a result of inquiry. || 10 ||

For this very reason, one should not contemplate the root of the disease of ignorance; rather, only its treatment should be contemplated. Thus, he says "yataḥ" (since), meaning that the postulation of a root and so forth is merely a means of treatment and is not real. The connection with the subsequent clause is: "When [ignorance] has dissolved, only the knowledge of one's own true nature remains. || 10 ||
There remains only that knowledge in which all forms have been stilled, wherein even space appears as gross as a great mountain within an atom. 11.
Abandoning the objects of the world—which, though appearing as active conduct, exist as if non-existent even while being real—you should remain within your own stainless body. 12.

In that state where even the "truth of empirical reality"— which is characterized by rising conduct and the performance of actions for the sake of accomplishing worldly affairs— is situated as if it were unreal and empty, you, having abandoned the objects of the world, remain as one liberated while living in a stainless body. 12.
That very form of ignorance is indeed composed of non-existence;
for once it is truly perceived, it surely perishes and is no longer seen. (13)
Now he states the essential nature of ignorance: "consisting of non-existence" (asanmaya). || 13 ||
How indeed can that which is called "the seen" be obtained as a non-entity, even when attained with great effort, like the waters of a mirage? (14)
The meaning is that even the illustrative example is unestablished, like water in a mirage. || 14 ||
That which is non-existent appears as existent; its reality arises from the cognition of it as such. Through knowledge, the object is seen as it truly is, and delusion perishes. (15)
The logical connection is this: since that which is unreal appears as real, its reality arises solely from ignorance (ajñāna). || 15 ||

This investigation into ignorance—consisting of the individual soul, the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*), and so forth—is a conceptual construction belonging to one who has constructed a self, even though that ignorance is absolutely unreal. (16)
The meaning is that, due to the proximity of the True Self, even the utterly unreal ignorance is imagined; it is a mental construction. || 16 ||

For the sake of instructing him, this conceptualization of the individual soul (jīva) and so forth was fashioned by the scriptures for the purpose of awakening; listen to it with a one-pointed mind. || 17 ||
For the sake of instructing that individual soul (jīva), the conceptualization of the soul and so forth was made on account of that ignorance (avidyā). || 17 ||

Residing in the state of the "eightfold city" (puryaṣṭaka), consciousness has attained, as it were, the condition of a living being; it is a digit (kalā) marred by blemish, yet oriented toward awakening.
The connection with what follows is: "being intent on awakening and eager to perceive external objects, she meditates in whatever manner.
Being eager to perceive external objects, she meditates in whatever manner—this is the connection with what follows. || 18 ||
Whatever one meditates upon in such a manner, that very thing one experiences fully and swiftly—whether it be real or unreal, like a young child’s perception of a yakṣa at night. (19)

Like a Yakṣa imagined by a child, let it be real or unreal; however, this [intellect] imagines the bodily formation—which consists of the quintuplication (*pañcīkaraṇa*) of the five subtle elements—as being existent and real. This is the connection with what follows. (19) It imagines the formation of the five subtle elements as being existent.
There, he perceives the apertures within himself as they have arisen in that manner.
In that context, "in the self" refers to the self consisting of the body; "apertures" refers to the doors of the senses. The masculine gender is used according to Vedic usage (chāndasam). 20.
From these very [elements] arises the fivefold external gross elements;
one perceives them as non-different [from consciousness], yet appearing as different, just as a sprout [gives rise to] a hundred branches.
From these five subtle elements, one perceives through the doors of the senses that which is in reality entirely other than them and appears as something else. || 21 ||
Then, one who possesses the conviction that "this is internal" and "this is external," the individual soul (jīva) assumes a state of being, and subsequently solidifies it accordingly.

In this context, that which consists of the senses, mind, vital breath, and so forth is internal; that which consists of jars and the like is external. "Bhāva" refers to latent impressions (vāsanā). || 22 ||
When the manifestation of the self is like the web of rays from the moon, it is by that very [manifestation] that it is accepted as having external tangibility. (23)

In this regard, he says "the web of rays" (verse 23), meaning that one perceives nothing other than the bliss of one's own self— which is manifested through the contact of the sense objects and the senses— as being the pleasure derived from objects.
Just as the heat of a mirage, just as the emptiness of the sky, and just as the perception of a self—each of these exists as if it were something else. (24)

Thus, he states—beginning with the words "of the pepper"—that one conceives of this very self-awareness, which is innate and produced from the contact with an object, as a quality of the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra). || 24 ||
Having formed a firm resolve right here, the restraint was made very firm; "it must be thus by this means, and thus by that means"—thus it was established without fragmentation. (25)

In this regard, having firmly resolved that the ultimate human goal lies solely in the enjoyment of worldly objects, the rule for performing actions pertaining to both this world and the next has been made very firm. This means it was done with a view toward fragmentary and perishable happiness attained through these worldly actions or these Vedic rituals. || 25 ||
This [world], consisting of its own volitions, exists at some time as something called "nature" or something else; it comes to be through nature alone, and not otherwise. (26)
In this regard, one type of restriction on activity is produced by natural passion and the like, while the other is produced by scripture.

Both of these consist essentially of volition; among them, at times only one prevails over the other through the effort of a person acting according to nature, and not otherwise—this is the meaning. || 26 ||
All this duality has arisen from the non-dual Self alone,
just as a piece [of sugar] arises from sweet juice, or a great jar from clay.

In both cases, he says "by the Self alone" (ātmanaiva) to show that it is the very Self, though ignorant, which undergoes transformation (vivartate) as the means and results of those respective activities, in accordance with either its own nature or the scriptures. *Khaṇḍa* is a specific kind of honey-sugar. || 27 ||
Because of the occurrence of spatial arrangement, transformation, and so forth, as well as place, time, and other factors,
these are possible here [in the world], but not in the Lord (Īśa), because place, time, and other such factors are impossible in Him.

Although the broken pieces and the pot are modifications resulting from the destruction of their previous states as liquid and a mass [of clay], nevertheless, because the essential natures of sweetness and clay are not destroyed, they serve as examples of *vivarta* (apparent transformation) in that respect. However, such modification is not possible in the case of Brahman due to its dissimilarity to those cases; thus he says: "saṃniveśa... and so on. Here, "in this" refers to honey, clay, and the like. "Īśe" means "the Lord."
In Brahman. || 28 ||
Just as one who has arisen with the thought, "The flower is here,
the leaf is there," perceives duality within his own undivided self, so too does the essence of existence carry duality within non-duality.

Alternatively, regarding the sentence "as sugar by sweet juice," *khaṇḍa* means a forest thicket (*vanakhaṇḍa*), and *madhurasena* means by the spring-fluid (*vasantadrava*). Thus, with the intention that the portion of water which is the cause of the tree's modification is itself unmodified, he says "from this": just as the sap that has entered the tree [thinks], "I am from this [water] the leaf, from this the flower."

Having arisen in manifold variety, even while being non-dual, it is seen as bearing duality; in the same way, know that Brahman—which is established in our own self as the nature of existence—also brings about duality within itself through such distinctions as "fall from here," "the wall," and "I," assuming the form of the entire universe. This is how it connects with the subsequent verse. || 29 ||
"From this [arises] the cloth, from this the wall, and so forth; likewise, know that Brahman is the Self within the self as the universal soul—do not entertain duality. (30)
"Just as a cloud remains as it is—today a sprout, today the radiance of the sun, and today a rain-cloud—so too does the Self abide, possessing both existent and non-existent forms. (31)
Or, for example, just as a cloud (*ambhoda*) exists today in the heat of summer with the thought "I am like the sun," and then at the onset of the first rains,
at the time of giving water, it exists with the thought "I am the rain-giver" (*vārida*); and then,
upon entering the earth through the entry of sprouts and the internal essence of water, it exists with the thought "Today I am the sprout"— so too is the Self (*ātman*).
The meaning is that it remains, having become the form of existence and non-existence through the distinction of time. || 31 ||
Thus, as this entire universe is pervaded by the Lord of All through such contemplation, who indeed in this world possesses the power to disrupt the [divine] sequence? (32)
And he says "iti" (thus), meaning that this sequence of the world's evolution, though conceptualized, cannot be made otherwise by anyone;
[this occurs] in Brahman, the Lord of all, which is "tataṃ," i.e., well-known. || 32 ||
In a space as clear as a mirror, one's own self does not reflect at all;
for since no distinction [between subject and object] is possible, it merely shines forth in its absolute unity.

With the intention that even the determination of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of an entity, being differentiated by the distinctions among entities, cannot be made otherwise, he states the distinction between the nature of space and so forth and the nature of Brahman when it is unknown, [beginning with the verse]:
"It reflects... Why? Because a difference (*vyatireka*) is impossible, whether in space itself or in another element which is an effect of space.

Because there is no division in space; rather, it is space alone that shines by its own clarity, like the interior of a mirror that does not reflect images. The meaning is that it simply glows. || 33 ||
But in Brahman, the Self alone, abiding by means of the Self, shines and reflects;
though bodiless, it appears as duality due to its inherent nature of being composed of consciousness.

But Brahman is not like that when associated with ignorance; thus he says, "In the two Brahmans. It shines—that is, it blazes—by way of the powers and other attributes of all things. It reflects as the individual soul (jīva). And through the conceptualization of difference, it becomes dualistic. || 34 ||
In whatever manner one knows that manifestation of the self, let it be so for oneself;
even though it is unreal, it never deviates from its nature in this world. (35)

"Let it be so; what follows from that? To this he replies with the words "yad... (that which...). In that regard, at the beginning of creation, whatever entity occurred as a self-manifestation by its own nature—that nature, even if unreal, you perceive as existing through your own real Self; and since that rule never deviates, the entirety of *niyati* (destiny/fate) is established—this is the meaning. || 35 ||

The two states of being gold and being a bracelet possess the natures of reality and unreality, just as consciousness and unconsciousness exist in the Self when it has assumed the form of a golden vessel. (Regarding the reading *hamebhāṇḍagate*: he provides an illustration based on the principle shown in the scriptural passage concerning "the origin of speech" (*vācārambhaṇa*) regarding the union of the real and the unreal. *Note: The provided text contains a citation marker (##) and a parenthetical remark regarding a variant reading.*

Because consciousness is all-pervasive, the nature of consciousness is eternally present in the mind; it is perceived [this is the reading "vedyate"], just as the nature of gold remains in a bracelet even when it is in another state, namely, its insentient condition.
