Therefore, at the first moment of action, a dual nature consisting of both consciousness and insentience is observed in the mind; regarding that which is eternal therein as being real, he says: "Because of its omnipresence" (*sarvagatvāt*). The meaning of "at another time" (*anyadā*) is "at some other time. || 37 ||

The mind, which is by nature both conscious and insentient, itself firmly cultivates whatever state it intends; in whatever manner and at whatever time it contemplates a particular state, it becomes exactly that at that very moment. (38)

Regarding the reading *cittajāḍya*: the dullness (*jāḍya*) of the mind consists in its taking on the form of an insentient body or sense-objects; when the mind, through firm contemplation, becomes whatever state it may be—be it that of a god, a human, a stationary being, or in whatever manner and at whatever time—it then becomes that very state. The meaning is that it experiences it as such. || 38 ||
From time to time, the soul itself becomes variously manifested, assuming different forms within due to the emergence of the buds of latent impressions (*vāsanā*). (39)

Therefore, he says "Time" to explain that the experience of different forms of the "I" (ahaṃkāra) for the individual soul occurs due to the difference in time: because of the arising—that is, the blossoming—of the buds of internal latent impressions (*vāsanā*) within consciousness, the soul, possessing a form conditioned by their diversity, becomes variously different from one moment to another.
Just as a village seen in a dream moves away upon the perception of another state of being,
so too does this body, which is of the nature of a mental projection, pass from one body to another.

Just as a village seen in a dream attains the state of being a forest and so forth through the perception of the existence of forests and such, so too this living being (*jīva*), having become embodied, attains the state of another body after leaving one; for the meaning is that, like a dream, its nature is merely appearance. || 40 ||
Just as in a dream a person may perceive a wall or a cloth, so too this other body exists by its own nature, though it is entirely unreal. 41.

Just as in a dream, that which appears as a manifestation—such as a man seen being suddenly transformed into a wall and then becoming a cloth—likewise, even during death and fainting, this other body comes into being as a manifestation; such is the meaning.
That which is unreal indeed dies, and the unreal is born again;
the living being, through its own manifestation, appears like a dream or like another's form.
"Now, this body is visibly seen to die and to be burned; how then can it become another body? To this he says:
"The perception of burning and so forth belongs only to that which is imagined by one's own ignorance (avidyā), not to that which consists of its latent impressions (vāsanā).
The meaning is: "as one's own [form] is different [from what it was], so is another body. (42)
In the course of time, this very form does not indeed undergo any change;
established in its inherent nature and fixed in certainty, these beings wander through existence by their own power.
In that case, is this other body also a temporal transformation of this present body, like youth and old age? No; he says:

"This present body is established by the certainty of recognition as being 'this very same one,' even amidst the differences of states such as childhood and so forth. These bodies of the past and future, however, are not."

Because they lack recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), they fall into such delusions as "others exist" or "others do not exist"; therefore, for them, existence occurs spontaneously while still living, meaning it arises through latent impressions (*vāsanā*). || 43 ||
An object, whether seen or unseen, is experienced in a dream;
O best among those who know what is to be known, know that the form of the world is likewise in the dream of the living soul. (44)

[Objection: Surely, since the state of possessing bodies such as those of gods was never previously seen, how could there be any latent impression (*vāsanā*) for it? To this, he says: "The object," etc.

One should know that this world-form is contained within the dream of the individual soul (*jīva*). The meaning is that according to the Śruti, "For him, there are three abodes, which are dreams. This, however, is the perception here even of that which has not been experienced in a [prior] dream.

This is stated with the intention that [the soul] has not experienced [everything] in this particular birth; it is said by relying on the scriptural statement: "One sees all—that which was seen and that which was unseen, that which was heard and that which was unheard, that which was experienced and that which was unexperienced. In reality, however, within this beginningless saṃsāra, there is nothing whatsoever that has not been experienced at the time of death.
It should be understood that the arising of another body occurs precisely in accordance with the latent impressions (vāsanā) awakened by the karma that initiates that future body. || 44 ||

That which is seen by one who does not perceive while awake, and which is impelled by its own designations and so forth—that dream does not exist; therefore, the pure self is mere consciousness alone.

In that case, one might ask: why should the state of Brahman, attainable through the direct realization of Brahman produced by the Great Sentence (*mahāvākya*), not likewise be a mere dream consisting of latent impressions (*vāsanāmaya*) like any other subsequent body? To this, he says: "not waking" (*ajāgrad*). The Supreme Self, who is designated as the non-dual Śiva, the Fourth (*turīya*), and perceived through the vision of the Fourth—that is, the vision of non-waking—belongs to Him.

The threefold dream, as previously defined, does not exist even in the waking state; because there is no experience of it during waking, its latent impression (vāsanā) is unestablished, and thus it is impossible for that [waking state] to consist of such impressions. Therefore, the meaning is that this [waking state] is the pure Self, which is mere consciousness (caitanyamātra). || 45 ||
Just as one sees something called "unprecedented" in a dream and not otherwise, so too does consciousness perceive an object never before seen. (46)

That very conscious self, having become the sentient individual soul (jīva), perceives today an unprecedented, novel, and present object exactly as it is from its own nature as consciousness and not otherwise; likewise, it perceives even an object seen previously in that same way—this is the meaning. || 46 ||
Even long-standing past impressions are overcome by human effort; indeed, through exertion today, yesterday’s evil action becomes a virtuous deed. (47)

For this very reason, it is shown that the intensity of human effort triumphs over even an object not previously perceived, because the latent impression (vāsanā) strengthened by the accumulation of mental cultivation (bhāvanā) overcomes the latent impression of objects previously seen; thus he says: "The former... (verse 47).
Except through liberation, the eyes and other senses of living beings do not find peace;
they merely rise and sink according to place and time.

Thus, the bondage of the individual soul (jīva) consisting of the body and so forth, characterized by the transformation of latent impressions (vāsanā), has been described. Now, in response to the desire to know when its cessation occurs, he says: "From liberation" (mokṣāt). || 48 ||
Due to its own mental construction, the body of that consciousness remains as if fierce;
though unreal, it is imagined as having fivefold nature, like a great yakṣa to a child.

To the question, "Why should there not be the cessation of the body and so forth even without liberation? he says: "Of consciousness" (citaḥ). Because until liberation, the latent impression (*vāsanā*) that fashions the form of the body persists within consciousness. This very fashioning of its own results in the fivefold body of this living being appearing as if it stands before it. The meaning is that, just as a great yakṣa imagined by a child appears standing before him, so too is this [body] difficult to dispel. || 49 ||
The mind, the intellect, the ego, and likewise the five subtle elements—this is declared to be the "city of eight" (puryaṣṭaka); this is the subtle body (ātivāhika-deha). || 50 ||

Now, with the intention that even if the gross body is somehow warded off, the *puryaṣṭaka*—characterized as the subtle body (*liṅgadeha*)—is difficult to ward off without liberation, he demonstrates this by saying "the mind," etc. (50).
The mind-soul is indeed formless; its extreme density is like the nature of space.
Its state as wind is a great tumor, and its state as a body is like Mount Sumeru.

Now, it may be objected that in the scriptures the senses of knowledge, the organs of action, the vital breaths, the elements, the internal organ, ignorance, desire, and karma are called the "city of eight" (puryaṣṭaka); yet that [city] is also a formal, corporeal form composed of the gross elements such as ether and air, which are themselves products of quintuplication (pañcīkaraṇa).

One might ask: how is it that this group of eight—consisting of the formless mind (*manas*), intellect (*buddhi*), and so forth—is called the "puryaṣṭaka"? To this he says: "It is indeed formless. Your stated "puryaṣṭaka of form" would only be possible if there were a grossification of the formless subtle elements (*tanmātras*) through the process of quintuplication (*pañcīkaraṇa*). However, this subtle body (*liṅga-ātman*), which consists of the subtle elements, is indeed formless. Of this...

The sky is fivefold; its extreme fatness is an infinite bulk, yet that is not possible. For even when millions of formless latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are combined, no bulk is observed. Since even its "sky-ness" is thus difficult to find, then its being a thick wind—a great tumor like a tree—is utterly inconceivable. Thus...

[It would involve] gross fire, water, and earth as well. Thus, since even gross elements are impossible [in this context], the state of being a body for this extremely subtle atom is as utterly inconceivable as Mount Sumeru; the meaning is that the *puryaṣṭaka* is not described as ending with a material (bhautika) body. || 51 ||
One who is free from passion (virajas) becomes established in the state beyond all conditions (niravastha) and partakes in liberation;
by this [state], even the dull-witted are embraced within the single condition of deep sleep (suṣuptataikāvasthā). 52.

With the intention that even because it is useless for liberation, the postulation of the existence of gross objects is not appropriate in this treatise on liberation, he says: "When [the self] is free from passion (virajastva), or when there is the perfection of the means such as tranquility (śama) and so forth, through the sequence of the arising of knowledge from the [great] statement (vākya), there occurs the sublation of the phenomenal world— which is like a dream imagined by the mind— and of the ignorance which is its root."
Liberation is possible for one who is devoid of the two-fold bondage consisting of the states of being an agent and an object;

however, if one accepts the existence of a gross world-complex composed of elements and elemental bodies, liberation is not possible because such a world is never seen to be sublated by knowledge—this is the meaning. And thus, in this summary, there are two states: dream and deep sleep.

With the intention that no other state characterized by gross objects can be established as distinct from these two states known as waking and deep sleep, he shows them divided by means of one and a half verses beginning with "suṣuptatā": [In this state] all inert things, such as the entire manifold of the body and so forth, are withdrawn and embraced within the form of latent impressions (vāsanā). (52)
Likewise, this state called "dream," characterized by the perception of a body, wanders here until liberation through all things mobile and immobile. (53)
Thus, in this manner, by means of the forms of both the stationary and the moving, it is the subtle body (*ātivāhika-deha*) alone that wanders until liberation; such is the meaning. || 53 ||
For sometimes remaining in deep sleep and sometimes situated as if in a dream,
this subtle body (ātivāhika-deha) persists for everyone.
When one abides in the state of deep sleep, pierced by the portents of future suffering dreams, then one remains with an unmanifest form, like the fire of cosmic destruction.

Pierced—as if transfixed—by impending bad dreams that have entered within in the form of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), he stands there with his memory lost; for this very reason, because he is inlaid with the reflection of consciousness and because he has withdrawn the world, he remains blazing like the fire of cosmic destruction (*kālānala*). By this, the deep sleep (*suṣupti*) of the Naiyāyikas and others, who are inwardly devoid of knowledge, is indicated. || 55 ||
In states such as those of stationary objects and in the conditions of the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa),
he remains indeed in deep sleep, dense as a solid stone of thick delusion.
Regarding this, he says that in inferior states such as those of stationary beings (sthāvara), there is an abundance of deep sleep (*suṣupti*) due to the excess of insentience (*jāḍya*).

Although there is an abundance of bliss (*ānanda*) because of the lack of suffering such as hunger and thirst—due to the excellence of merit (*puṇya*)—there is no awakening as there is for humans and others; thus, the meaning is that they remain characterized by darkness (*tamasvin*). || 56 ||
Its state of deep sleep is insentience, for this transmigratory existence arises from dreaming;
that which is its awakening is liberation, while its waking state is the fourth (turya).

And thus, it is concluded that deep sleep (*suṣupti*) is simply the intensification of the mind's dullness, transmigratory existence (*saṃsṛti*) is merely the exhaustion of the mind, liberation from bondage is the mind’s awakening to reality, and its waking state is its very fourth state (*turyatā*); this he expresses with the verse beginning "suṣuptatā" (verse 57).

For liberation indeed arises from the awakening of the individual soul; through that awakening, it attains the state of the Supreme Self, just as copper, when its impurities are washed away, attains the state of gold.
The liberation that arises from the awakening of the individual soul (jīva) is said here to be of two kinds:
the first is liberation while living (jīvanmukti), and the second is liberation from the body (dehamukti). || 59 ||
For liberation while living is indeed the state of the Fourth (turya), and beyond that is the state transcending the Fourth (turyātīta).
The individual soul (jīva) is consciousness (bodha), and this awakening (prabodha) arises through the effort of the intellect.
Awakening consists of the nature of Brahman, which is the supreme pure consciousness; and that awakening arises from the effort of the person through the intellect.
The living being, whose measure is consciousness, who knows as the inner controller and is composed of that [consciousness], perceives here this very fear as the delusion of a very long dream. (61)

The meaning is this: the witness who knows and illumines the soul (*jīva*)—in its true nature, however much it may be, and whatever its extent—is itself composed of that [pure consciousness]. As for the one whose measure is unknown, even he is in reality established in his own self;
yet, due to ignorance, within his heart—which has become as solid as a stone—he experiences the intense fear of the long-lasting delusion of a dream.
The connection with the subsequent word is "he sees. || 61 ||
When one's own heart is firmly established in its natural state, that which was previously falsely uttered ceases;
for within living beings, there exists nothing else whatsoever apart from the digit of consciousness (citkalā).
In that case, is there any real fear in the hearts of living beings? He says "no," beginning with the words "of living beings" (jīvānām) and so forth. || 62 ||
Seeing that very [Self] as something else, one grieves in vain;
for within the living atom (jīvāṇu), there is nothing other than the Supreme. 63.
Wherever the world is perceived, alas, it is the manifestation of illusion (māyā), just as various delusions arise within water boiling in a pot. 64.
In the same way, there arises within living beings (jīvas) an internal false transmigration;
their bondage is the bondage of latent impressions (vāsanā), while liberation is the dissolution of those latent impressions.

The state of deep sleep (sauṣuptī) ends with latent impressions (vāsanā), while in the dream state, existence manifests as a vibration; this living being (jīva), deluded by dense latent impressions, partakes in the condition of stationary objects and so forth.

For this living being (*jīva*), the state of deep sleep (*sauṣuptī sthiti*) is the limit and boundary of latent impressions (*vāsanā*). This is because the states of the Fourth (*turya*) and that which transcends the Fourth (*turyātīta*) are devoid of latent impressions.
And it is in the dream state that this [state] manifests, meaning it becomes clearly evident through its manifold variety. To explain how it becomes clearly evident, he says:
"The animal and human beings who possess dense [latent impressions], those with moderate latent impressions, and those with thin latent impressions..."
When, internally, there is an end to life, then externally, jars and other such things are born.

He states that through the progressive intensification of the exhaustion of those latent impressions (*vāsanā*), there is the attainment of increasingly auspicious births—this is expressed by the words "the indifferent one" (*madhyastha*). A "person" (*puruṣa*) refers to humans, celestial musicians (*gandharva*), divine musicians, and so forth.

Having described the manifestation of diversity through the varying degrees of the exhaustion of latent impressions, he further describes it through the diversity of the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasping (*grahaṇa*), etc., with the words beginning "when... (*yadā*).

When, at the time of emerging from deep sleep, there arises within an internal limitation such as "I am only this much, limited by the body," characterized by the life-force (jīvita) consisting of the sense of "I" (ahaṃbhāva) and the vital breath (prāṇa) pervading the interior of the body down to the tips of the nails; then objects such as jars and the like come to exist externally. || 67 ||
Then, due to the identity of the individual soul (jīva), there is the existence of both the grasped and the grasper;
when consciousness (cit) externally and internally encompasses both self and non-self. (68)
"Let there be [consciousness] outside; what of it? To this he replies: "Because of the identity of the individual soul (jīva).

At that time, when jars and other objects are pervaded by the individual soul delimited by the mental modification (vṛtti) which has emerged through the internal organ via the doors of the eyes and so forth, the existence of the grasped and the grasper—consisting of latent impressions (vāsanā)—manifests with their respective diversities in the form, "I know the jar."

The meaning is that it becomes manifest. He states this very point clearly with the words "the Self" (ātma). When the Self—the individual soul (jīva) situated within—becomes externally enveloped by the non-Self, then consciousness (cit) arises along with its increase, through the superimposed distinction of the grasped and the grasper, like a mirage; such is the meaning. || 68 ||
Then the cognition of the grasped and the grasper, along with its latent tendencies, is like a mirage;
nothing at all is abandoned here, and nothing at all is grasped here. (69)
Thus, he says "not here" (neha) to show that even the diversity of what is to be abandoned and what is to be accepted is merely superimposed upon latent impressions (vāsanā) and is not real.
The single conscious Self shines forth as the form of both external and internal aspects;
the three worlds are but the wonder of consciousness, so enough with conceptualizations of duality!
For a long time we have been adorned within consciousness, including both the external and internal. (Note: the reading "sabāhyādyaṃ na" is preferred.)
It exists. || 70 ||

They are adorned by the awakening to reality and shine resplendently; the meaning is that the entire world, both internal and external, is not found to be separate from consciousness even throughout the three periods of time. || 70 ||
Just as water cast into the ocean is devoid of all distinctions, and as the entire sky is but one pure,
clear, and singular fluid,
so too this primordial, supreme state is realized as being entirely free from disease and devoid of the entire collection of differentiated categories.

Just as the ocean, when examined in its true nature, is seen to be nothing but a single, pure, and all-pervading water— clearer even than the sky (ākāśa)— with all distinctions such as waves and bubbles cast aside; so too, when this entire world is understood in its true nature,
the multitude of distinctions arising from the diversity of latent impressions and states is discarded and eliminated by that [realization].
The meaning is that such a state is indeed the supreme, disease-free station. || 71 ||

Thus ends the fifty-first chapter, titled "The Examination of the Perception of Objects by the Senses," in the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa* of the *Mokṣopāya* section of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, according to the tradition of the Seers (*ārṣa*).

Thus ends the fifty-first chapter, titled "The Examination of the Perception of Objects by the Senses," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*. || 51 ||
The Fifty-second Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
That dream of the living soul which, from the very beginning, is tender with various mental constructions—
Know this very cycle of existence (saṃsāra) to be neither real nor composed of unreality.
The world is a dream of the living soul; its dissolution occurs through non-attachment to it.
For that purpose, the narrative of Arjuna is brought down by Vasiṣṭha.

Now, one might object: "Surely a dream is distinct for each individual soul, whereas the waking world is common to all and is experienced by everyone as being different from a dream; how then can it be a dream? To this he replies:
"Know that this very world, which we conceive of as 'waking,' is a dream. (1)
A dream is never possible for the individual soul (jīva) as it is for a man;
therefore, these states here are produced by waking and dreaming while one is awake.
If it is asked why this is so conceived, [the author] says: "Because, like the individual states (vyaṣṭi), no separate dream-state within a dream is established for the collective state (samaṣṭi).
The meaning is that those [dreams] which arise from both the waking and dreaming stages do not differ from the dream itself. || 2 ||
O best among those who know what is to be known, understand this long dream of worldly existence to be unreal because it lacks substantiality, even though it appears so swiftly.

Establishing its dream-like nature through both its unreality and its lack of substantiality, he shows the cause for the experience of dissimilarity by stating "the dream of the individual soul" (*jīvasvapnam*). Because it is not perceived as being quickly sublated—unlike our own dreams—it is "long. Thus, the point is that this very length is the cause of the delusion regarding its dissimilarity. || 3 ||
Moving from one dream to another,
O sinless one, living beings perceive what is utterly unreal with the density of reality.
O dear one, insentience has arisen in the sentient, and sentience in the insentient;
and unreality has appeared as reality due to the delusion regarding the experience of the individual soul.

He states that this [world] is a dream because it is seen as the opposite of the true nature of things, saying "in the non-inert" (*ajaḍe*). In the non-inert Brahman, there arises the inertness of the elements and the worlds; likewise, in the inert [body], from the ego-sense up to the physical body, there arises non-inertness through the conceit of being the Self. This occurs due to the delusion characterized by the experience of individual souls (*vyaṣṭijīva*), which are but partial manifestations of the universal soul (*samaṣṭi*). || 5 ||
Perceiving the entire threefold world as existing within even the sun,
living beings wander like those deluded by a dream, led astray by the bees of dualistic distinctions.
Living beings wander about through a succession of conceptualizations of difference created by the various schools of thought.
Because it is all-pervading and infinite, whatever the living soul (jīva) contemplates while living, that very thing it attains immediately, as if it were real.

He states the reason for superimposing reality upon imagined distinctions: "because of being all-pervading" (*sarvagatvāt*). Precisely because it is the individual self (*jīva*), which is itself the ultimate living principle, and because it is, in the highest sense, all-pervading, infinite, and real by virtue of its non-limitation, whatever they meditate upon, that very thing they quickly perceive as if it were real through attachment to it and the superimposition of their own existence.

And thus, by abandoning attachment to that [world], once the delusion regarding its reality has ceased, liberation while living (jīvanmukti) in the true nature of the Buddha is accomplished; this is the intended meaning. || 7 ||
O mighty-armed one, [I shall describe] that auspicious state of non-attachment taught by Puṇḍarīkākṣa, embracing which the great sage becomes liberated while living.

The author states that this very same meaning was also taught by the Blessed One to Arjuna in the Bhagavadgītā, beginning with the words "O lotus-eyed one. The phrase "listen to the auspicious" is to be understood as the ellipsis. || 8 ||
Pāṇḍu’s son, named Arjuna, will spend his own life happily and free from suffering; therefore, spend your life in the same way.
To that end, he introduces the narrative of Arjuna with the words "Of Pāṇḍu" (*pāṇdoḥ*). "Sukham" means distinguished by the bliss of *jīvanmukti* (liberation while living).

He will "quickly spend his life" (*jīvitam āśu kṣipayiṣyati*), meaning he will cast it away. The absence of *guṇa* substitution in the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasaḥ*). || 9 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
O Brāhmaṇa, when will that Arjuna, the son of Pāṇḍu, appear?
And what kind of detachment will Hari describe to him?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: There exists that which is pure existence alone, designated by the name "Ātman," abiding within itself without beginning or end, like the great sky within the sky.

In order to state the cause for the descent of Arjuna, he introduces the root of all things with the words beginning "There exists" (asti) and so forth. Regarding the phrase "is established": it is because of the Vedic scripture which says, "He is established in His own glory. || 11 ||
In that stainless [reality], this delusion of saṃsāra is seen, just as bracelets and the like are seen in gold, or waves and the like in water. (12)
Fourteen kinds of living beings flutter intensely within this web of saṃsāra, like birds caught in a net. (13)
While that web of saṃsāra is being seen, the birds are the winged creatures. || 13 ||

In this regard, these—Yama, Candra, Arka, Śakra, and the others—who follow the praised sequence, have attained the status of guardians of the world within the cycle of existence consisting of the five elements. (14)
Among those classes of beings (bhūtajāti), their "course" (krama)—meaning their conduct—is "praised" (śaṃsita), described in the Śrutis, Smṛtis, and other scriptures.

Their "lordship over the worlds" (lokapālatva) refers to sovereignty over various worlds within that cycle of transmigration characterized by the five elements (bhūtapañcaka), which are the fivefold (pañcīkṛta) subtle elements (tanmātra). || 14 ||
"This is merit and should be adopted; this, however, is evil and should be abandoned"—such is the established order maintained by them through a cognition constructed by their own volition. (15)

The established order (maryādā) has been fixed through the knowledge formed by a resolve corresponding to one's own qualification, namely: "This merit, enjoined by the Śruti, Smṛti, and traditional practice, is to be adopted; this sin, prohibited by them, is to be abandoned. || 15 ||
O sinless one, until this very day, his mind has remained as steady as a mountain, fixed upon his own karma that has fallen into the stream of existence.

Let it be so; what follows from that? To this he says: "Of him" (tasya). Of him—of Yama who is about to be described—until today, for all this time, his mind (citta), that is, his internal organ (manas), has remained as steady as a mountain in his own office and duty. || 16 ||
After some time has passed in each cycle of four ages, that Lord Yama performs penance out of fear of sin resulting from the destruction of living beings.

*Praticaturyugam*: this is an *avyayībhāva* compound used in the sense of repetition (*vīpsā*). He performs some slight austerity at certain times; or rather, "at the end of each Dvāpara age, when a certain portion of each four-age cycle has passed. || 17 ||
Sometimes for eight years, or even ten or twelve;
sometimes five, seven, and so forth, and sometimes even sixteen.
Regarding this, he says "at some time" to indicate that there is no fixed rule concerning the time. || 18 ||
While he remains seated like one indifferent, established in self-restraint,
death does not harm any living beings within the web of the world.
While he remained established in self-restraint and discipline, seated in austerity, Mṛtyu did not harm even a few living beings.
Because of that, the surface of the earth became so crowded with throngs of creatures that there was no passage through it,
like an elephant sweating in the rainy season due to swarms of mosquitoes.
By that cause of non-violence, the surface of the earth becomes impassable—meaning unfit for movement—due to the dense masses of many living beings. "Svedī" means one who possesses sweat. || 20 ||
Then, O Rāma, these gods, by means of many stratagems, cast away these various beings from the earth for the sake of relieving its burden.

The gods, Viṣṇu and others, indeed cause [the world] to waste away—meaning they thin it out through destruction—by means of logical stratagems such as partial incarnations (aṃśāvatāra) and the Bharata war. || 21 ||
In this way, thousands of yugas and hundreds of worldly transactions have passed away,
as well as infinite beings and worlds.
And since this conventional usage, such as "the removal of the burden" and so forth, has been employed many times, he says: "In this way," [verse 22].
O virtuous one, this Yama, the son of Vivasvat and leader of the ancestors,
has now [arrived] when some [of the fruits of their deeds] have been exhausted.
In order to destroy the sins of the ages, one must here perform the practice of vows for twelve years in one's own person, keeping those who cause agitation at a distance.

"For the destruction of sins and evils"—the word "shall be performed" is understood as the ellipsis. "In which the dragging and tormenting of people has gone far away"—from this qualification, it is understood that the practice of the vow consists of non-violence and so forth, in the form of nirvikalpa-samādhi (non-conceptual meditative absorption). || 24 ||
Therefore, this earth will become densely crowded with mortal beings who are like unto immortals; oppressed by those who have become a burden, it will fall into distress like a thicket.
"Prapannagulmā" means that which is crowded with forest thickets. || 25 ||
With her body overwhelmed by the burden of the earth, she will seek refuge in Hari,
just as a beloved wife, distressed and overcome by bandits, seeks refuge with her husband.
Then Hari shall descend to the earth with two bodies,
together with all the portions of the gods who have entered into Nara and Nārāyaṇa.
By Nara and Nārāyaṇa, who had followed after him and descended for the sake of providing assistance—so it means. || 27 ||
The son of Vasudeva alone shall be known as Vāsudeva;
he will be the body of Hari, while the second shall be Arjuna, the Pāṇḍava.
He shall be known as Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma;
that knower of righteousness, the son of Pāṇḍu, will be the sovereign of the earth girt by the oceans. (29)

A king is a ruler of the earth, which has the ocean as its girdle; or, he is one who protects the earth that has the ocean as its girdle. [The suffix] *ka* is applied after a verbal root ending in *ā* when no preposition (*upasarga*) precedes it. (Pāṇini 3.2.3)
He will have a brother born of his paternal uncle, known as Duryodhana;
between them there will be a firm enmity, like that of Bhima toward the tawny snake.
His paternal uncle’s son will be his brother; it should be understood that Bhīma will be his opponent in single combat. Babhru is Nakula. [He will be like] a snake, as it were. || 30 ||
As those two, eager for battle, seize the earth from one another,
eighteen terrifying akṣauhiṇīs will be arrayed here.
Because it protects from all sides (*āsamantāt trāyati*), it is called *ātra*; these are the armies, namely the *akṣauhiṇīs*. They will engage here, either in this war or on Kurukṣetra. || 31 ||
Upon their destruction, Viṣṇu will bring about the division of the earth through the bodies of Rāghava and Arjuna, the wielder of the great Gāṇḍīva bow.

O Rāghava, he whose bow is the great Gāṇḍīva—by means of such a body as Arjuna’s, which [is formed] with the suffix *anaṅ* after the word *dhanus*, he will perform the "bearing of the burden" (*vibhāratvam*), that is, the removal of the world's weight; this is the connection with what precedes. || 32 ||
At the beginning, when Viṣṇu assumes the name Arjuna, his body will abide in a natural state, possessed of joy and indignation, and subject to human characteristics.
That is to say, human nature is for the most part characterized by ignorance. || 33 ||
Seeing his own kinsmen stationed in both armies and facing death,
he will fall into despondency and will not exert himself for battle.
One's own people and kinsmen. || 34 ||
O Rāghava, Hari will awaken that body named Arjuna by means of a body as Buddha, for the sole purpose of accomplishing the task at hand.
By the Buddha, who possesses a dark body and whose self-realization is established by itself. || 35 ||
It is never born, nor does it ever die; having come into being, it will not cease to be.
Unborn, eternal, everlasting, and ancient, it is not slain when the body is slain. (36)

He describes the manner of awakening in detail with the words beginning "it is not born" (*na jāyate*). Having negated the first and last modifications (*vikāra*), he precludes the four intermediate modifications that might otherwise be implied with the words "this [Self] is not" (*nāyam*). This is the negation of future birth and the other states.
He who perceives this as a slayer, and he who thinks of it as slain—both of them do not understand; this does not slay, nor is it slain. (37)

He who perceives this Self—which has been described as having such a nature—as a slayer, and he who deems himself slain, both of them do not know the Self according to reality; that is to say, it is ignorance alone that is the cause of the delusion regarding the state of being a slayer and a victim.
(37) [Of that which is] infinite, uniform, existent, and subtler even than space...
What, how, and by what means can the Supreme Lord, who is one's own self, ever perish? (38)
By means of three interrogative particles (*kiṃvṛtta*), there is a rejection of the destruction, the object to be destroyed, the manner of destruction, and the cause of destruction. || 38 ||
O Self of pure consciousness, behold the Self—endless, unmanifest, and without beginning or middle.
You are the expansive body of consciousness, free from defect; you are unborn, eternal, and beyond all affliction.
You are indeed the very nature of consciousness (caitanya), whose form is awareness (saṃvid); therefore, you are vast and unlimited, and for that very reason, you have not acquired any defect.
For this same reason, you are unborn; you are eternal, and you are free from the stain of ignorance and its effects.
Thus, the sense is that suffering caused by the possibility of attachment to kinsmen, death, and so forth, is not appropriate for you. || 39 ||
Thus ends the fifty-second chapter, titled "The Narration of the Incarnation of Nara and Nārāyaṇa," in the *Arjuna-episode* of the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa* within the *Vālmīki-vāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa*.
Thus ends [the section] in the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa*, *Pūrvārdha*, of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa-tātparya-prakāśa*.
The fifty-second canto, titled "The Narration of the Incarnation of Nara and Nārāyaṇa."
The Fifty-third Chapter.
The Blessed One said:
"O Arjuna, you are not the slayer; abandon this impurity of egoism."
You yourself are the eternal Self, liberated from old age and death. || 1 ||
The renunciation of egoism, characterized by the abandonment of attachment and so forth, is described;
and [the nature of] that which is to be worshipped and that which is to be known are established as distinct states.

In this regard, [the Lord] says "O Arjuna" to indicate that the ego-conceit (*ahaṃkāra*) in the form of "I am the slayer of my own kinsmen," and the possessive conceit (*mamatā*) in the form of "these are my relatives," are the primary causes of all your suffering; therefore, these alone must be abandoned.
O Arjuna, you are free from the six waves of old age, death, and so forth, and for that very reason, you are eternal with respect to your kinsmen and others.
You are yourself the manifest Self of all beings; therefore, you are not the slayer of anyone. The meaning is: utterly abandon the conceit that "I am the slayer. || 1 ||
He whose state of being is free from egoism, whose intellect is not tainted—
even by slaying these worlds, he does not kill, nor is he bound.
He states the fruit of abandoning pride with the words "of whom" (yasya). At the time of engaging in an act such as killing,

he who has no sense of egoism— no thought such as "I am killing this person"— and whose intellect is not tainted in subsequent time by joy, dejection, or other emotions regarding the results of that act, that person [is one who sees] all these worlds, for they are seen (lokyante) by him.

The meaning is this: even by killing the worlds—the four classes of living beings—and depriving them of their lives, one does not kill anything at all. This is because the eternal, singular reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*) is everywhere untouched by modifications such as being killed, since it remains exactly as it is; and because bodies and the like, being mere illusion (*māyāmātra*), are eternally non-existent, just like the son of a barren woman, such that the act of killing them is impossible.
Therefore, the meaning is that he is not bound even by the fruit of the sin committed through that [agency], just like the Lord. || 2 ||
Whatever consciousness arises within, that alone is experienced;
abandon the internal consciousness of "this is he," "I am this," and "that is mine. (3)

The appearance of qualities such as being a "killer" within the self occurs solely through the power of the perception of the delusion of identity with the body and so forth—which possess those qualities—and not inherently. Therefore, he says that one should first abandon that very [delusion]:
"Consciousness is the mental modification consisting of the identification with the body and so forth, or otherwise... "I..."

The meaning is: abandon such a consciousness, which is a function of delusion, namely, "I am the agent who destroys this aggregate of causes and effects," and "this body and so forth belong to me, and those relatives and so forth are mine. || 3 ||
O Bhārata, joined by this very [thought], you suffer helplessly from both pleasure and pain on all sides, thinking, "I am possessed" and "I am ruined."

Through this aforementioned consciousness, you suffer from pleasure and pain due to the delusion that "I am possessed of agency and so forth; I am ruined by the sins resulting therefrom; and I am joined with worldly misfortunes such as the loss of kinsmen, as well as with otherworldly misfortunes such as falling into hell. || 4 ||
Actions performed by the qualities through their own constituent parts are [perceived] in their respective portions;
yet one whose self is deluded by egoism thinks, "I am the doer. (5)

Actions are those performed by means of the body, senses, and so forth, which are modifications of the qualities such as *sattva* and the rest, acting as partial limitations of one's own self as if they were its parts. || 5 ||
Let the eye see, let the ear hear, let the skin touch this, and let the tongue taste flavor; what is the status of "Who am I" in this regard? (6)

However, upon reflection, it is only the eyes and other sense organs that engage with objects such as form, and not the Self; thus, there is no possibility of the Self being an agent through those [organs]. With this intention, he says: "The eye... and so forth. Here, in this aggregate of causes and effects consisting of the eyes and other instruments, who am I? I am nothing at all. What is the status of the "I"? It is none.
The meaning is "it is logical. || 6 ||
Even when the mind of the Great-Souled One is intent on the work of fashioning [the world], there is no sense of "I" therein; what portion of affliction, then, could there be for you?

The meaning is this: although the mind is occupied and attached to its own activity characterized by imagination and the like, that object for which you grieve has not entered into it at all; therefore, it does not exist. || 7 ||
O Bhārata, that which is accomplished by many through their collective effort is seized by a single person out of pride and sorrow, only for the sake of ridicule.

When even each individual within a collective suffers grief due to the pain of identifying with that collective in a matter created by the group, what need is there to mention the ridicule one faces when grieving for someone outside of that group? With this intention, he says: "Only a single person ought to grieve. (8)
With body, mind, intellect, and even with the senses alone,
yogis perform action, having abandoned attachment, for the sake of self-purification.

Furthermore, for one who is free from egoism, the threefold scriptural action—bodily and so forth—performed without attachment to its fruits leads solely to the supreme goal of man, because it kindles knowledge by means of purifying the mind; thus, there is no possibility of suffering arising from the abandonment of one's own duty (svadharma). To this effect, he says: "By the body... [In this context, those who are seekers of yoga...]
The reading is "mumukṣavaḥ" (those desiring liberation). || 9 ||
Those whose bodies have not been slain by the powder of the poison of "I-ness"—
even while they are taking or giving— do not become free from the cholera of worldly existence.

"Not killed" means not intentionally slain; rather, the meaning is that they were repeatedly impelled toward death by their craving for the objects of experience that cause rebirth. "Free from cholera" means those from whom the diseases of passion and so forth have been cast out. Even while performing worldly or scriptural actions, they take away—that is, enjoy—the incidental fruits thereof, yet they are not the ones who perform [those actions].
The meaning is "taking away. || 10 ||
Nowhere does this body shine, being defiled by the impurity of possessiveness;
it is like a man who, though wise and even very learned, is ruined by immoral conduct.
In some cases, it does not shine in either worldly or scriptural practice; that is to say, it is not fit for the human goal when it is overwhelmed by misfortunes.
Free from possessiveness and free from ego, equal in pain and pleasure, and patient— he who acts, whether in what ought to be done or what ought not to be done, is not defiled.

*Kārya* refers to that which must necessarily be done, namely action prescribed by the scriptures (*śāstrīya-karma*). *Akārya* refers to that which is not necessary, namely worldly action (*laukika*). It does not, however, refer to what is prohibited (*niṣiddha*), because such an action is not even applicable [in this context]. || 12 ||
And this, O son of Pāṇḍu, is your own excellent kṣatriya duty;
even if it is cruel, it is most beneficial for happiness and for prosperity.
The duty prescribed for Kṣatriyas—never fleeing from battles—is indeed cruel because it involves the slaughter of kinsmen;

nevertheless, by means of the purification of the mind, it leads only to the bliss of the knowledge of Brahman and so forth, as well as to prosperity such as dharma, fame, sovereignty, and heaven. Thus, the meaning is that it is truly the highest good. || 13 ||
Even if it be contemptible, or even something else consisting of unrighteousness— be as you are in this world, like your own excellent karma, and become one who speaks the immortal truth.

Then, in order to dispel Arjuna’s doubt regarding the unrighteousness of that act— namely, his concern as to how he could perform such a despicable deed as the killing of his elders, Drona, Bhishma, Kripa, and others, which is distinct from the slaughter of his kinsmen—
the Lord spoke the words beginning with "api" (even), while bestowing a blessing through a truthful oath upon those who are worthy of honor.

By that same truth—by which your own martial deed, though consisting of a sequence abounding in unrighteousness such as the raising of weapons contrary to those [rules], is nevertheless excellent according to the authority of the scriptures—by that truth, may you be victorious in this battle, being immortal, characterized by non-death. This is the meaning. || 14 ||
Even for a fool, one's own action alone leads to the highest good; how much more so for one of noble mind?
When the intellect has its egoism dissolved, it is not tainted even when fallen.

Since even for an ignorant person one's own duty leads to the highest good, for one who knows the truth it is even further removed from the possibility of falling into hell and other such states. With the intention that there is no taint for one whose mind is free of egoism, even by millions of great sins (mahāpātaka) that cause a fall from one's status, he says: "Even for the fool... (verse 15).
Established in yoga, perform your actions, O Dhanañjaya, having abandoned attachment;
being free from attachment and performing whatever action comes to you, you shall not be bound. 16.

Furthermore, in a war motivated by greed for the acquisition of a kingdom and the like, there might occasionally be an attachment to unrighteousness (*adharma*), according to the maxim: "Sins have greed as their root, and diseases likewise have taste as their root. However, for one who stands in yoga—characterized by equanimity toward success and failure through the abandonment of attachment to results—there is not even the possibility of such an attachment; therefore, [the Lord speaks of] that...
He teaches the state of being established in yoga: "Established in yoga" (yogasthaḥ). || 16 ||
Having become one whose body is the peaceful Brahman, perform action consisting of Brahman;
through the practice of offering everything to Brahman, you shall become Brahman itself in an instant.

Alternatively, he says "peaceful" (śānta) to show that this scriptural action, performed with the understanding of offering it to Brahman as defined by the characteristics to be described later, does not lead to bondage for you. || 17 ||
With all your purposes surrendered to the Lord, with the Lord as your very self, free from affliction, you—being the self of all beings—become one who adorns the surface of the earth. 18.

If one lacks the capacity for that [liberation] due to the absence of knowledge of the non-differentiated reality of Brahman, he says—starting with "In the Lord"—that one should perform action with the intention of dedicating it to the Lord endowed with attributes; even from that, there is no bondage of action. || 18 ||
Having renounced all volitional thoughts, equanimous, with a peaceful mind, and being a sage whose self is joined to the yoga of renunciation, remain liberated in intellect while acting. (19)

Alternatively, he says "saṃnyasta" (having renounced) to show that even through the application of the yoga of renunciation characterized by the abandonment of all mental constructs, there is no attachment to the bondage of action for you. || 19 ||
Arjuna said:

O Blessed One, [I wish to understand] the renunciation of attachment, as well as that which consists of offering to Brahman—that is, the form of surrendering to the Lord—and the renunciation of all actions in every respect. (20)
Thus instructed, Arjuna, desiring to know the distinction between renunciation of attachment and the others through their respective characteristics, asks:
"O Lord, what is the nature of the distinction between knowledge and yoga?
Tell me this in due order for the sake of dispelling my great delusion. (21)
The Blessed Lord said:
When all volitional constructions have subsided and dense latent impressions are stilled, that which possesses no form of conceptualization—know that to be the supreme Brahman. (22)

Since the abandonment of attachment in its absolute sense is impossible without the thorough knowledge of reality, the Blessed One first points out the very reality of the self as Brahman by means of its defining characteristics, beginning with the word "all. Thus,
it is the non-differentiated (niṣprapañca) reality, established through the direct experience of the maturation of non-conceptual samādhi.
The meaning is that Brahman is indeed the nature of the inner self (pratyagātman). || 22 ||
Those of perfected intellect know that exertion to be knowledge and yoga;
they know the offering to Brahman to be the realization: "All the world and I am Brahman. (23)

The meaning is this: they call "knowledge" (*jñāna*) that mental state which is characterized by effort toward that [knowledge], whose mental activity is focused on its form, and which is endowed with the fruit of the cessation of ignorance; whereas they call "yoga" that which consists merely in a continuous flow favorable to that [knowledge]. He states that the sublation of the world—which is the object of identification within Brahman—and of the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*)—the subject of that identification—is the primary "offering unto Brahman" (*brahmārpaṇa*), in the verse beginning with "Brahman."
Empty within and empty without, like a heart of stone;
it is tranquil, as clear as the expanse of space, neither an object of sight nor beyond the power of vision.

In order to establish the sublation of both the world and the ego within Brahman, he states the nature of Brahman—beginning with "empty within," and so forth—in order to describe its being superimposed thereon. Regarding the phrase "not the visible": one might raise the objection that if all visible objects are negated, then since the seer (*dṛk*) is also an object of sight (*dṛśyatva*), why should it not also be negated? Anticipating this, he says: "there is nothing beyond the seer."
The negation of the visibility of seeing would only occur if there were another seeing distinct from that seeing; however, the meaning is that such [another seeing] does not exist. || 24 ||
Then, that slight emergence which arises as something slightly other than that [emptiness]—this manifestation of the world—is like space, [itself] emptiness. (25)
Therefore, that arising which emerges as slightly different from such a nature is this very appearance of the world;
it is like a city of Gandharvas in the sky. The meaning is that it is nothing but emptiness. || 25 ||
This notion that "I am an entity" arises in each individual consciousness as a mere infinitesimal fraction of its infinite millions of parts; why, then, is there such attachment toward it? 26.

In order to justify the description of renunciation (saṃnyāsa), he says [in two verses beginning with] "bhāva" (verse 26): just as the world is superimposed upon Brahman, so too is there an individual superimposition of the sense of "I" (ahaṃbhāva) upon each of its parts—the individual souls (jīvas); therefore, it is not proper to be attached to that [superimposed state].
This [Self], though indeed non-different, remains as if it were different;
for one who does not realize "I am not" has no end to this sense of separateness. || 27 ||

The notion "I am this" is indeed not distinct from its own substratum; for the reason that "separateness"—meaning limitation or delimitation—does not exist in Brahman, and no one perceives "I am non-existent.
Thus, the establishment of separateness occurs through the very fact of being a perceiver, and not by means of actual separateness.

Since the status of being a cognizer is thus untenable, the sense is that one must necessarily abandon either [of the two]; and between these, it is the very notion of separateness (*pṛthaktva*) that is devoid of logical justification and must therefore be abandoned. || 27 ||
Just as there is "I" here, so too is there a jar and so forth here; likewise, there is this "monkey" and this "ocean. Why then is there such a grasping at egoity? 28.

Showing that the reasoning stated regarding the "I-impulse" (*ahaṃtā*) should also be applied here to the "monkey-like impulse" characterized by the conceit of objects such as pots, he confirms the abandonment of the grasp of that root "I-ness" with the words: "Just as...
Just as the "I-impulse"—the state of being "I"—does not exist separately, so too here, the monkey characterized by the impulse of conceiving objects such as pots does not exist separately.

The word "not" (na) should be supplied by way of connection [to the preceding]. Thus, the meaning is that since both [the self and the world] here are like the ocean—being one's own Self alone in its fullness—it is not proper to maintain the grasping at egoism (ahaṃtā). || 28 ||

When the differentiation of conceptual constructions flashes forth within the self whose essence is pure consciousness—even though it is variegated by that diversity—why is there no apprehension of its underlying unity? (29)

Furthermore, even while the manifold variety of all conceptual distinctions—such as "I" and "mine"—shines forth in its diverse objects, there also shines forth the unity within the inner self (pratyagātman). This inner self is the cause of the manifestation and existence of those very distinctions; it persists through the three states of consciousness, has pure awareness as its sole essence, and is the witness to the coming and going of all conceptual constructions. Such being the case:
In that case as well, attachment is appropriate; the meaning is: why is it not practiced by us? || 29 ||
Thus, for one who has understood this distinction, there is the complete destruction of that [ignorance] within the intellect;
the wise know that renunciation (saṃnyāsa) to be the relinquishing of the fruits of actions.

Thus, having reflected in the manner described, for the person who has discerned the distinction between the essential and the non-essential, there occurs in his intellect a complete exhaustion of that grasping characterized by "I" and "mine"; and by means of that, renunciation—characterized by a lack of longing for the fruits of all actions—is established as a matter of course. || 30 ||
Renunciation is said to be the non-attachment to the web of mental constructs;
it is the contemplation of the oneness of the Lord within the entire web of conceptualizations.

And by that, non-attachment, characterized by the abandonment of all conceptual constructions (*saṃkalpa*), is accomplished; thus he says "abandonment" (*tyāga*) to indicate that the first question has also been answered. He provides the answer to the fourth question with the words "of the whole" (*samasta*): the meaning is the contemplation of the entire web of duality as being nothing but the Lord (*Īśvara*), its sole material cause, according to the logic stated in the scriptural passage beginning with "the beginning of speech" (*vācārambhaṇa*). || 31 ||
This very offering to the Lord, in which the appearance of duality has dissolved, is [the true state];
yet, due to the power of ignorance, there is a distinction among these [offerings] within the conscious Self merely by name.
Regarding that, he states the reason for rebirth there: "by virtue of non-awakening" (abodhavaśataḥ). || 32 ||
The meaning of the word is indeed the self of awakening; the world is one, there is no doubt.
I am the quarters, I am the world, I am myself, and I am also action. (33)

To strengthen that [realization], the Blessed One describes His own manifestation characterized by universal selfhood, beginning with "I am hope" (aham āśā) and so forth. That which moves is the *jagat* (the world); it is the locus of its own action (*sva-karma*). || 33 ||
I am Time; I am non-duality, and I am duality; I am the universe.
Fix your mind on me, be my devotee, sacrifice to me, and bow down to me.
Thus, with your self disciplined and taking me as your supreme goal, you shall come to me. 34.

The meaning is this: non-duality is my supreme form, while duality is my inferior form; and I alone am that world which is governed by those two. Thus, become one whose mind is fixed on Me (man-manāḥ) in Me who possess these two forms, according to the gradations of qualification.

Toward such a Me, likewise become a devotee (bhakta), possessing the ninefold devotion consisting of hearing, chanting, and so forth. [Worship] Me, who am such, with the sacrifice of knowledge (jñāna-yajña).

The meaning is: "Or, become one whose nature is to sacrifice through the sacrifice of action. Thus, by being disciplined in either of these two ways mentioned, having fixed the mind on Me, you will attain Me alone as your very Self—meaning you will reach Me both directly and through a succession of stages. || 34 ||
Arjuna said:
O Lord of Gods, you have two forms—the supreme and the non-supreme.
Of what nature is that [supreme] form, and at what time shall I abide by resorting to it for the sake of perfection? (35)
Thus addressed, Arjuna, desiring to know those two forms, the corresponding qualification for each, and the division of time, asks: "Two... (verse 35).
The Blessed Lord said:
"O sinless one, know that my two forms are the common and the supreme.
The common form is endowed with hands and other limbs, and bears the conch, the discus, and the mace. (36)
"Common" means shared by all people; that is to say, it is easily understood. || 36 ||
That supreme form of mine, which is without beginning or end, unique and free from affliction, is expressed by such terms as Brahman, Ātman, and Paramātman. (37)
But it is difficult to attain for those with impure minds. || 37 ||
As long as you remain unawakened, dwelling in ignorance of the self, so long remain devoted to the worship of the deity in the form of the four-armed one. 38.
Through that sequence you shall become fully awakened, and from that you will know my supreme form, which is without beginning or end, by means of which one is not born again. (39)
Then, by means of the sequence for the purification of the mind. || 39 ||
Or if that being is indeed known through direct perception, O crusher of enemies, then quickly take refuge in my very self by means of your own self. (40)

The word *vā* has the sense of *tu*. Furthermore, I have described this worship of the qualified [Brahman] (*saguṇabhajana*) to you, anticipating the absence of purity of mind (*cittaśuddhyabhāva*) on your part.
However, if your state of being—that is, your mind—is "vijñāta," meaning it is fit for knowledge (*vedanārha*), then [it is as follows]. The suffix *kta* is used here in the sense of *bhāva*.
If you consider yourself thus purified—meaning one whose nature is solely consciousness (*vijñānaikasvabhāva*) with respect to Brahman—then that is mine.

Having made one with the same essence the Lord’s Self—which is the purified meaning of the word *tat* and constitutes His ultimate nature—and your own Self—which is the purified meaning of the word *tvam*, take refuge in the indivisible, perfect Self; the meaning is that, having realized this, become established in That. || 40 ||
"That which I declare as 'this am I' and 'that am I'—this indeed is the reality of the Self (ātmatattva) that I teach to you. (41)

He states that even the instruction regarding such manifestations as "I am the quarters" and "I am the world" has its ultimate purport solely in the purification of the true nature of their respective substrates: "And this is I. (41)
I believe you have awakened rightly; you have found rest in the supreme state.
You are now liberated from all mental constructs; become one whose very essence is truth alone.

Thinking, "By understanding my instruction, your rest in your own true nature (*svarūpa*) will be accomplished immediately," he says "I consider" (*manye*) as if it were already established, in order to generate enthusiasm. || 42 ||
Behold the Self abiding in all beings, and all beings in the Self; with your mind disciplined by yoga, perceive the same everywhere. 43.
The self is followed as the substratum; [the objects] are superimposed upon the self. 43.
One who perceives the Self abiding in all beings, through the unity of the Self,
is not born again, regardless of how one may conduct oneself.
In every way and by every means, whether functioning through the operation of meditative absorption (samādhi) or through worldly activity (vyavahāra). || 44 ||
Oneness is the meaning of all words; it is the meaning of the word "one" regarding the Self.
And for one who realizes that the Self is neither existent nor non-existent, that oneness is swiftly attained.

He himself explains the purport of the verse beginning with "the Self abiding in all beings" as follows: "Unity. When one perceives the Self abiding as the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) within all beings, then, because nothing apart from that substratum is found, the referent of the word "all" attains unity; and that [Self] is the referent of the word "one."

That Self, which culminates in the nature of the inward Self, is neither existent—having the nature of the three gross elements—nor non-existent—having the nature of the two subtle elements; rather, it has the singular nature of plenitude, bliss, and consciousness.
For one who has attained the experience of that, at the very moment of such realization, there is freedom from all modifications, beginning with birth.
The meaning is that the intended purport [of the scripture] is that liberation culminates in the nature of the bliss of plenitude (bhūmānanda). || 45 ||
That illuminating inner light within the minds of the three worlds, which has ascended to the level of direct experience—that is the certainty that "I am the Self. (46)
To ward off the consequence that this [Self] is absolutely beyond perception because it is not experienced by anyone, he says "trailokya" and so forth:
"O Bhārata, that experience of taste which exists within the waters of the three worlds—both those produced from cows and those born of the ocean—that is this very Self. (47)

The meaning is as follows: the experience of taste—whether it be of the waters existing in the three worlds, of products of the cow such as milk and the like, of sea-born substances such as salt and the like, or of sugarcane, honey, and so forth, brought close to the tip of the tongue—is this very Self; thus, there is no possibility of its being an object of indirect knowledge (pārokṣya). || 47 ||
That subtle experience which resides within all bodies, being liberated from anything to be experienced, is this all-pervading Self. (48)
It is free from and devoid of the various kinds of objects to be experienced; therefore, because it is difficult to perceive, it is subtle. || 48 ||
Just as ghee exists within milk that has been fully processed, so too does the Supreme abide within all objects and bodies. 49.
He abides as the inner substratum of all objects and as the illuminator within bodies.
Just as light exists within and without all the jewels of the oceans,
so do I exist within bodies, though appearing as if not established therein.

He clarifies the abiding within the body by means of an illustration with the words "sarva... etc. The meaning is: just as the luster inherent within all gems illuminates even the exterior, so it is in this case. || 50 ||
Just as there is space both inside and outside thousands of jars,
so do I, the Self, abide within the bodies of the three worlds.

He clarifies the state of being "unstained"—the intended meaning of the expression "as if not situated"—by means of another illustration: "Just as a thread, though its body is strung through hundreds of pearls, remains unperceived; so too does this Self abide within hundreds of thousands of bodies, yet remains unperceived. (52)
To provide an illustration for its being unperceivable even while acting as the sustainer by abiding within all bodies as the inner controller (antaryāmin), he says:
"That which is the universal existence (sattāsāmānya) in the entire collection of objects, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass—that they know to be the unborn Self. (53)

In this regard, the state of Brahman is the abiding as changeless through its nature as the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*); that alone is the reality. However, that which exists as the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) like a thread within liberated souls, and that which exists as the manifest individual soul (*jīva*) like a luster within gems—both of these depend upon superimposition (*adhyasta*) and are imagined for the sake of worldly transaction; therefore, the "slayer" is not a real entity to be slain.
With the intention that the one who bestows the fruit of the sin committed by him might be someone other than his own self, he says in three verses beginning with "In Brahman, etc.":
"Brahman alone remains as Brahman, its form only slightly manifest;
[yet] through the deluding process, it sequentially appears as 'I-ness' and so forth, and as the world and so forth. (54)
This entire world is but the Self; what is it here that is slain or that slays?
O Arjuna, how can this [Self] be tainted by the auspicious or inauspicious sufferings of the world? (55)
He who sees that which remains like a witness, like a mirror amidst reflections—unperishing even when things perish—he truly sees. 56.
He provides another illustration regarding the fact that [the Self] is untainted by superimposed defects such as killing: "In reflections," etc. (verse 56).
"This is mine and this is not mine"—thus is it spoken by me.
"In this way I am the Self, the Self of all; know me thus, O Pāṇḍava. (57)

The expression of the distinction—"I am indeed the conscious element manifesting as 'I, I' in all bodies, while the portion consisting of the inert body, senses, and objects is not I"—is just like the statement regarding the distinction between the mirror and what is not the mirror; it is intended solely for the purpose of identifying the distinct nature of the mirror among various jars and other objects reflected in many different mirrors. Thus he says: "This..."
"And I [am that]. The first occurrence of the word *iti* refers to the manner of dividing the meaning, while the second refers to the manner of dividing the statement;
thus, there is no tautology. In this way, like a mirror, the Self alone is untainted and non-dual;
being that very Self, I am the Self of all. || 57 ||
All these transformations of creation and dissolution proceed within the Self, residing in the mind as the sense of "I," like the ripples of water in the ocean.
Egoity is the function of self-conceit; they are "situated therein" because they abide in the mind which possesses that [egoity]. || 58 ||
Just as there is the nature of stone in mountains, the nature of wood in trees,
and the nature of water in waves, so too is the Self the essential nature of all things.
The meaning is that selfhood is ultimate. || 59 ||
He who sees the Self abiding in all beings and all beings in the Self,
and likewise sees the Self as the non-agent— he truly sees.
The meaning is that it is a non-agent, inactive like a mirror amidst the movements of its reflections. || 60 ||

Just as water remains the same amidst waves of various forms and transformations, or as gold remains the same in bracelets and other ornaments, so too, O Arjuna, does the Self remain amidst the elements.
Just as various groups of waves are restless in water,
or as bracelets and other ornaments [are present] in gold, so too are the elements within the Supreme Self.
O Bhārata, know that the entire collection of categories, the elements, and the Great Brahman are all one and the same; there is not even the slightest degree of difference between them.
It is one and the same, like a mirror and its reflection. || 63 ||
Is there anything in the three worlds that can be perceived as a modification of those states? Where are they, or where is this world? Why do you delude yourself in vain? (64)

When there is only the one, changeless Brahman, then what else exists that could serve as the substratum for the perceived modifications of existence such as birth and so forth? Where do those modifications of existence, such as the killing of kinsmen, reside?
Or does the world exist as something else? The meaning is: nothing at all. || 64 ||
Having heard this and having internalized fearlessness with firm certainty,
the virtuous ones, whose inner dispositions are equal in flavor, wander here as those liberated while living.
Having meditated upon Brahman as fearlessness within and having experienced it perfectly. || 65 ||
Free from pride and delusion, having conquered the fault of attachment, ever established in the inner self, with desires turned away,
and liberated from the dualities known as pleasure and pain— the undeluded go to that imperishable state.
With the intention of stating that even the attainment of disembodied liberation (*videhakaivalya*) belongs to those very ones characterized by the aforementioned qualities, he says:

Thus ends the fifty-third canto, titled "The Instruction to Arjuna," within the "Story of Arjuna" in the first part of the *Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa* of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa*, composed by the sage Vālmīki. 53.
Thus ends the fifty-third chapter, titled "The Instruction to Arjuna," in the first half of the Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The Fifty-Fourth Chapter.
The Blessed Lord said: O mighty-armed one, listen once more to my supreme word.
That which I shall speak to you, who are well-disposed toward me, out of a desire for your welfare.
The cause for the connection with pleasure, pain, and so forth, as well as the sequence of their abandonment,
and that which is the object of focus for such abandonment— all of this is proclaimed here.
It has been stated that those who are liberated from the pairs of opposites characterized by pleasure and pain go to that state.

Regarding this, the Blessed One—desiring to teach the reality of the Self by way of resolving the doubt as to what the cause of connection with these pairs is, what the means of liberation from them is, and upon what support they depend—said: "Furthermore... (Bhūya eva).
To one who is pleased and desires to hear, he is satisfied by the grasping of the meaning as it is being taught out of affection. || 1 ||
For the contacts of the senses with their objects, O son of Kuntī, which give rise to cold and heat, pleasure and pain, are fleeting and transitory; endure them, O Bhārata. (2)

In this regard, first of all, in order to dispel the delusion that objects themselves are of the nature of pleasure and pain, he says: "The contacts of the senses" (*mātrāsparśāḥ*). They are called *mātrā* because objects are measured by them; they are the senses. Their "contacts" with objects are the causes of pleasure and pain resulting from the experience of cold, heat, and so forth. Alternatively, they are called *sparśāḥ* because they are touched.

Sound and the other [objects of the senses]. The mention of cold and heat is for the sake of illustration. Just as cold is pleasant in summer while heat is painful, yet those same two are the reverse in winter, the meaning is that objects of the senses do not inherently consist of pleasure or pain. Having thus demonstrated the causes of suffering, he states the means for their removal: "Endure them."
The mention of endurance (titikṣā) is also an indicator of detachment (vairāgya). Thus, the meaning is: "Be dispassionate toward pleasant things, and endure unpleasant things. || 2 ||
But they are not distinct from the one Self; therefore, where is there suffering and where is there happiness?
In that which is without beginning or end and without parts, how can there be filling or depletion?

He explains that intellect by which detachment from those [objects] and endurance [of opposites] are accomplished: "But those... Those are the objects of the senses (*mātrāḥ*) and the contacts (*sparśāḥ*), or rather, pleasure and pain; the word "and" (*ca*) implies other things as well. They are not different from the one Self—the Self whose nature is non-dual, full bliss—therefore they do not exist apart from it. The meaning is: "from such an awakening. Furthermore:
Through the delusion that "I am filled with the abundance of beloved wealth, sons, and so forth," there arises the pleasure of self-conceit;

and through the loss of those or the occurrence of what is unpleasant, there arises the suffering of thinking "I am broken. He says, "without beginning or end," meaning that both of these cease when one perceives that filling and breaking are impossible in that which is partless. || 3 ||
Established in that which is called the mere touch of the senses, consisting of the delusion regarding the contact of the senses,
the steadfast one who remains equanimous in pleasure and pain is fit for immortality.

The meaning is this: for one whose description—i.e., the designation, truth, and perception—of touches, objects, elements, and senses has become established and pacified, that living being, which consists of the delusion regarding the touches of the elements, is "steadfast" (dhīra); thus, being steadfast as a seer of reality and becoming equal in pain and pleasure, he is fit for immortality. || 4 ||
Because the Self is all-pervasive, these [distinctions] exist as if they were distinct divisions;
yet, being unreal in nature, how can that which is unreal be unable to endure? (5)

[Objection: But how could unpleasant things such as suffering abandon their own nature of being felt as disagreeable, by which they might become endurable? To this he replies: "Because of its universality" (*sarvatvāt*). Since the Self alone—which has the singular flavor of unsurpassed bliss—is universal, these various distinctions such as suffering and so forth exist as beautiful distinctions, excellent distinctions, just like the distinctions of most beloved wealth, sons, and the like.
They do not partake of the state of being experienced as disagreeable; rather, the meaning is that by virtue of their prior nature of disagreeableness, they are of the form of non-existence.
Pleasure and pain do not exist at all, even in the slightest degree;
since the reality of the Self is omnipresent, how could there be the existence of a non-self?
He clarifies and supports that very point with the words "even in the slightest" (manāg api). || 6 ||
The non-existent has no being, and the existent has no non-being;
pleasure, pain, and the like do not exist at all, for the omnipresent Supreme Self alone exists. (7)

One might object: "Even that which is non-existent arises within the self, for the very definition of the arising of a non-existent thing—such as suffering—is its inherence in its own cause, its connection with its own existence, or its relation to the first moment. To refute this argument of Kaṇāda (the Eater of Grains) and Akṣapāda (Gautama), the author says: "Not of the non-existent.
For a non-existent thing such as suffering, existence (*sattā*) does not occur; nor does non-existence (*asattā*), which is the absence of existence, occur for that which is already existent.

Because it is impossible for the intrinsic nature [of a thing] to be otherwise; for, according to scriptural passages such as "a mere beginning in speech," it is certain that all modifications are non-existent. Now, if all modifications were non-existent, one would not perceive clay or other materials—their primordial nature—unassociated with any particular modification such as a lump or the like; therefore, that [primordial nature] too must be non-existent.

If it is asked, "Why should there not be a remainder of emptiness (*śūnyatā*)?", we say no. Because the cognition of existence that persists through modifications cannot be without an object, even if the modifications themselves are non-existent, a remainder of emptiness does not result. If even that [existence] were non-existent, then the cognition would have followed along as "the pot is non-existent, the cloth is non-existent. However, what persists is "existent, existent"; therefore, that alone remains as the remainder. As for that which...

The conceit that "this [world] exists" amidst modifications arises solely from the penetration of the reality of the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) and not from itself; thus, the meaning is that pleasure, pain, and so forth do not exist at all. || 7 ||
Having abandoned the notions of existence and non-existence regarding these two— the world and the self—
and having abandoned everything in between, remain established in that which remains.

Having abandoned the notion of the reality of the world and the notion of the unreality of the Self—which is unsurpassed bliss—and having abandoned the extremely insignificant mental darkness that serves as the cause for the conjunction of both the world and the Self in the interval between them, remain with your feet firmly planted in that which remains: the Consciousness-Self (cidātmā). 8.

The Self does not rejoice in pleasures nor does it languish in sorrows, O Arjuna—even though it is the conscious perceiver of what is seen and resides within the body. (Note: The sandhi here follows the archaic usage.)

The "seer of the seen" (dṛśyadṛk) is so called because it perceives as a witness the objects of sight, such as joy, dejection, and so forth; the meaning is that those objects of sight cannot possibly be attributes of the Seer. || 9 ||
Inert matter such as the mind and so forth, having attained the state of a body, is the vessel of suffering;
yet, when this is wounded or destroyed, there is no injury whatsoever to the Self.
