What then? To explain that it is the vessel for suffering, joy, and so forth, he says: "insentient" (jaḍam). In this [vessel], namely the mind and so on. || 10 ||
O dear one, know that this insentient body and so forth, which exists as the experiencer of suffering and the like,
is merely an illusion of māyā arising from the power of ignorance.
This is the form of the individual soul (jīva), composed of mind and the other [elements]. || 11 ||
Nothing at all—neither the body and so forth, nor suffering and so forth—exists as something separate from the Self; therefore, what could be experienced by whom? (12)
O Bhārata, that which I speak of here perishes by that very [realization]; for delusion, which arises from ignorance, is destroyed by perfect awakening.

That which is suffering arises from the delusion born of non-awakening; therefore, it is destroyed by that very right awakening. "In this regard, I shall tell an illustration"—this is the syntactical connection. || 13 ||

Just as the fear of a snake in a rope perishes through awakening, having arisen from non-awakening, so too do suffering and the like regarding the body and so forth perish through awakening, having arisen from non-awakening. 14.
The unborn Brahman, all-pervading and encompassing the universe, neither perishes nor is born;
know this to be the supreme truth—this indeed is the highest awakening. (15)
"What is that awakening like? He replied: "All-pervadingly. The universe is all-pervading; it is Brahman alone, complete. || 15 ||
Having become a mere wave in the ocean of Brahman, you dissolve;
now you manifest within the whirlpool of Brahman—you are indeed Brahman itself, free from all affliction.
Today, at the time of the arising of enlightenment. || 16 ||
Just as the commands for the time of death are like those for soldiers, so too are the movements in Brahman; herein, the delusions of existence and non-existence do not exist.

The word *yāvat* signifies "entirety. There is a *dvandva* compound of "time" (*kāla*) and the others. "Error regarding existence and non-existence" refers to the conceptual constructions of being and non-being (*bhāvābhāvavikalpa*). || 17 ||
Abandon pride, intoxication, grief, fear, desire, and pleasure and pain;
this duality is of an unreal nature—be one, possessing the nature of reality.
Through the destruction of the akṣauhiṇīs of men, which consists of experience,
make the pure Brahman— expanded by Brahmā— consist of Brahman.

The meaning is: even by means of the Brahman—which consists of the destruction of the *akṣauhiṇīs* of men that you are about to bring about—it is expanded (*bṛṃhitam*); therefore, make it consist of Brahman (*brahmamayam*), for it is pure Brahman itself by virtue of being the nature of experience. || 19 ||

Without perceiving pleasure or pain, gain or loss, victory or defeat, engage in pure meditation and attain oneness with Brahman; for you, O Bhārata, are indeed the ocean of Brahman. (Note: An alternative reading is "engage in battle, O Bhārata, and go to oneness with Brahman; for you, O Bhārata, are the ocean of Brahman.")
Becoming equal toward gain and loss, and indeed possessing nothing at all, remain motionless like a breeze in a hollow; perform your natural duty.
Surely, by the certainty of reality, nothing of the world— having taken the form of the body and so forth—
remains, like a gust of wind confined within a cave.
Whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer in sacrifice, whatever you give, and whatever you shall do, O son of Kuntī—regard all that as the Self; remain steadfast in this conviction.
With the intention that "the firmness of the certainty that Brahman alone is the reality behind all actions" is itself "offering unto Me," he says: "That which..."
Whatever one is inwardly inclined toward, that one undoubtedly attains;
therefore, in order to attain the truth of Brahman, become one whose inner being is absorbed in Brahman.
Whatever it is composed of, with whatever form the mind possesses. || 23 ||
Having become Brahman, whose fruit is independent, and having realized "I am Brahman," the knower of Brahman performs action merely as it comes, without attachment.

The absence of dependence is *anapekṣam*. When there is an absence of an object, an *avyayībhāva* compound is formed. Having himself become that fruit—the cessation of all desires, which is the supreme goal of man—he performs action that is sublated by the contemplation (*bhāvanā*) that "Brahman is merely a futile exertion," even though it takes the form of mere activity. || 24 ||
He who sees inaction in action, and action in inaction, he is wise among men; he is called a performer of all actions. (25)

That person who, according to the manner described, perceives *akarma*— the actionless Brahman— within *karman*, and perceives that *karman*, which consists of unwavering steadfastness in the actionless Brahman, is necessarily to be performed; he is wise and discerning,
and he alone is said to be a "performer of complete action" (*kṛtsnakarmakṛt*), because he performs action in its entirety, both in terms of its essential nature and its fruit.
The meaning is "by the learned. || 25 ||
Do not become motivated by the fruit of action; let there be no attachment to inaction.
Established in yoga, perform your actions, O Dhanañjaya, having abandoned attachment. (26)

May you not be one for whom the fruits of action—such as gain and so forth—are the cause, that is, the motive for engagement. May there be no attachment or clinging on your part even toward *akarmaṇi*, the non-performance of required duties. Be established in yoga, firmly grounded in the previously mentioned equanimity of vision regarding success and failure.
Without relying on attachment to action, nor likewise relying on delusion,
and even without relying on inaction, remain established as you are.
Folly regarding the vision of reality; negligence. || 27 ||
Having abandoned attachment to the fruits of action, ever-contented and independent, even though fully engaged in action, he does nothing at all. (28)
They say that attachment constitutes agency; even for one who does not act, that [agency] may arise.
For when foolishness resides in the mind, one should therefore abandon foolishness. (29)
The meaning is that when foolishness and the aforementioned negligence persist, attachment will inevitably arise, and from that follows a succession of calamities.
By relying on a supreme knower of reality, the great-souled one who has abandoned all attachment does not experience the sense of agency anywhere, even while engaged in all activities.
But when there is no negligence due to the vision of reality, non-agency is established by itself through detachment; thus he says "the supreme" (param). || 30 ||

Due to the absence of agency, there is the absence of being an enjoyer; due to the absence of being an enjoyer, there is equanimity and oneness; due to equanimity and oneness, there is infinity; from that, the state of Brahman is attained [the reading *brahmatvam āgatam* is also found, by which it is said that through the sequence of stages, one attains everything up to videha-kaivalya]. Thus he says: "Due to the absence of agency... (31).
Having cast off the impurity of diversity and attained oneness with the Supreme Self,
you are not truly an agent, O Arjuna, whether performing what is to be done or what is not to be done.
Doing what should not be done and what is forbidden through negligence. || 32 ||
The wise call him a sage whose every undertaking is free from desire and volition, and whose actions have been consumed by the fire of knowledge. 33.
He who remains equanimous, gentle, steady, self-abiding, tranquil, and free from desire for all objects,
has attained a state of complete composure even while appearing distracted.
Though he was attentive and active, he attained a state of non-distraction and non-action.

Free from dualities, eternally established in purity, devoid of the concern for acquisition and preservation, and possessed of the Self—you, who have adorned the surface of the earth, remain content with whatever comes to you. (35)
Yoga is the acquisition of what has not been acquired; security (kṣema) is the preservation of what has been acquired; one who is free from concern for both of these is [a yogin]. || 35 ||
He who restrains his organs of action but sits dwelling upon the objects of the senses with his mind is a deluded soul; he is called a hypocrite.
He says that for one who has renounced all actions, if there remains attachment to mental objects, that renunciation is merely hypocritical:
"But he who, O Arjuna, restraining the senses with the mind, undertakes the yoga of action through the organs of action while remaining unattached—he is superior. (37)

With the intention that even for one who possesses restraint over the senses and the mind and engages in worldly activity according to the scriptures, the fruit of renunciation (saṃnyāsa) indeed exists because of the abandonment of attachment to results, the Lord praises him by saying, "But he who... (yastu).
Just as the waters enter the ocean, which is being filled yet remains established in stillness, so do all desires enter him; he attains peace, but not the one who hankers after desires. 38.
Therefore, he concludes that the supreme goal of human life belongs only to the renunciant who has restrained all the senses through the cessation of all desires,

and not to anyone else— by the words "being filled" (*āpūryamāṇam*). Just as rivers enter the ocean which is being filled and dissolve, having attained its very nature, even so is he whose foundation is in the immovable Brahman.

For the renunciant (saṃnyāsī), all desires—having their objects sublated by the realization of their falsity—enter into the Self alone and, dissolving therein, attain the state of being nothing but the Self. He alone attains liberation, characterized by the cessation of all misfortunes; however, "desires" (kāmāḥ) do not mean that objects are desired, but rather that one whose nature is the longing for them [is meant]. || 38 ||
Thus ends the fifty-fourth canto, titled "The Instruction on Self-Knowledge," within the Story of Arjuna, in the First Part of the Nirvāṇa Section of the glorious Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa of Valmīki.
Thus ends the fifty-fourth chapter, titled "Instruction on Self-Knowledge," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
Fifty-fifth canto. The Blessed One said:
One should not practice the renunciation of enjoyments, nor should one cultivate a preoccupation with enjoyments.
One should remain perfectly equanimous, following exactly what has been attained.
Even upon the destruction of the body, the Self is indestructible; it is the same for both the ignorant and the knower of reality.
The ignorant person undergoes birth and so forth due to delusion, whereas the knower does not—this is now described.

"Bhogas" are those things—such as food and drink—that are enjoyed and serve as the means for maintaining the body; one should not renounce them. The meaning is that one should instead adopt wholesome, moderate, and pure food and so forth. One should not engage in the "contemplation of enjoyments," which refers to anxiety or a compulsive addiction to acquiring their excellence. One should remain perfectly equanimous toward their gain or loss and other such circumstances.
The meaning is that one should remain [in that state]. || 1 ||
Do not conceive the notion of self in the body, which is non-self, nor in worldly existence, which is characterized by becoming;
rather, conceive the notion of self only in the true Self, whose nature is the cessation of becoming.

Thus, he says "in the non-self" (anātmani) to show that the notion of the body being the self should not be entertained either; [this refers to] the self that exists as the nature of transformations such as birth and so forth.
O mighty-armed one, upon the destruction of the body, nothing at all is destroyed;
for the destruction of the self would indeed be destruction, yet the self is eternal and does not perish. (3)
For one whose self is without mind and who has renounced all possessions does not perish;
even though engaged in action, he truly does nothing at all.
Regarding the point stated, he cites the scripture, "For it is indestructible, indeed it is not destroyed," as proof;

he says that it is precisely the identification with the body that leads to the attribution of bodily attributes such as destruction to the Self, whereas when that identification is abandoned, there is no possibility of such destruction occurring—[as in the case of] battle and so forth. || 4 ||
They say that attachment constitutes agency; even for one who does not act, that [agency] may arise.
For when the mind is established in ignorance, therefore one should abandon ignorance. (5)
When situated in folly, one has fallen into ignorance. || 5 ||
By relying on the Great-Souled One who knows the supreme reality and is free from desire,
the sense of being an agent never arises in one, even though they may be engaged in all types of action.
Regarding that, he states the means: "The supreme," etc. (6).
They know the Self to be indestructible, without beginning or end, and ageless.

Let there not be for you the misconception that "the Self perishes," for such a view is difficult to understand and brings suffering in this world. (Note: An alternative reading is *mā tavāstvatiduḥkhadaḥ*, meaning "let it not be for you a source of extreme suffering.")
The supreme ones who have realized the Self do not perceive [the world] in that way;
those who imagine themselves as the Self see the Self within their own self by means of the non-Self.
Likewise, they do not perceive that "the self perishes" in such a manner. Why do they not see it?
Because, regarding the self as the very self, they do not perceive their own self as being of the nature of the non-self, such as the body and so forth; this is the meaning. || 8 ||
Arjuna said:
"If this is so, O Lord of the three worlds, O bestower of honor even upon the foolish,
then when the destruction of the body occurs, nothing desired has been lost at all."

"Now, if this is so, let the deluded indeed perceive [the self] through the notion that the body and so forth are the self; nevertheless, since for them there is no destruction of the self upon the destruction of those [bodies], death and the like would not be a calamity. Thus Arjuna raises an objection with the words "If it be so" (*evaṃ cet*).
[He argues: "Nothing beloved—that is, most dear—has been lost. (In the reading *dṛṣṭam*: "Nothing seen... [has been lost].
It is to be understood through a vision that accords with reality. || 9 ||
The Blessed Lord said:
"It is even so, O mighty-armed one; nothing whatsoever perishes anywhere.
The Self alone exists as the imperishable essence; what of it could perish, and where?"
The Blessed One refutes this by accepting the point as it stands, with the words "It is so," and so forth. || 10 ||
"This is lost, this is joined"—from such delusive confusion one grasps;
yet I do not see anything else in that way, just as one does not see the son of a barren woman.

How then is it that the destruction of the body, the birth of a son, and so forth, are considered either non-beneficial or beneficial? To this he says: "This... [and so on]. The meaning is that it is logical [to say they are obtained], because even in a dream, due to the delusion of a son's death or birth, one observes the practical functioning of what is non-beneficial and so forth. || 11 ||
The unreal has no being, nor does the real have non-being;
the truth regarding both of these has been perceived by the seers of reality. 12.

Therefore, it was stated previously that the body and so forth do not possess existence, because existence is incompatible with non-existence. This is expressed in the words "not of the non-existent" (nāsataḥ).

Regarding both the existent and the non-existent: the conclusion (anta) reached by the seers of reality—that the existent is indeed existent and the non-existent is indeed non-existent, and there is no reversal of their intrinsic natures—is what has been seen, not by the deluded. This is the meaning. || 12 ||
But know that to be indestructible by which all this is pervaded;
no one is able to effect the destruction of this immutable.

Thus, with the intention that "whatever exists is indestructible, and whatever is destructible is merely non-existent," there is no real harm whatsoever in the destruction of non-existent things such as kinsmen or the body in battle; he says this in two verses beginning with "indestructible" (avināśī). || 13 ||
These bodies are said to have an end, belonging to the eternal, indestructible, and immeasurable embodied self; therefore, fight, O Bharata! (14)
The Self is one; there is no duality. How could that which is non-existent come into being? It is indestructible and infinite; for that which exists, destruction does not occur.
He says "the self" (ātma) [in verse 15] to show that because non-duality exists, and because destruction is not established, there is no possibility of the destruction of the self.
When duality and unity are abandoned, that which remains as the residue—tranquil, the middle between existence and non-existence—that is the supreme state here. (16)
Unity is the cause, denoted by the word "Being" (sat); duality is the effect, which is non-existent and unreal;
that which lies between them is the intermediate state, the pure substratum of Being alone.
Arjuna said:
"O Blessed One, why is it that men have the conviction, 'I am dead'?
And how, O Lord, do heaven and hell exist for people within the state of worldly existence?"

Thus, Arjuna asks—"What then?"—regarding the cause of the delusion concerning the suffering of death and so forth for the Self, which is in fact unlimited: "What is the cause (*kiṃkṛtā*) by which [this] has been obtained? What is the fixed state (*sthitir niyatiḥ*)? And within that state, what is the cause of heaven as happiness and hell as suffering? (17)
The Blessed Lord said:
Earth, water, fire, air, ether, mind, and intellect—this jīva, whose nature consists of the web of these subtle elements, dwells within bodies. (18)
The Blessed One provides the resolution in accordance with the purport of the Śruti text, "Having arisen from these elements, it perishes after them," by stating "Earth" and so forth:

[the gross body] is composed of the individual and collective (vyāṣṭi-samaṣṭi) gross forms, constructed from the mind, intellect, and other faculties fashioned from the subtle constituents (mātrā) of the five elements.
The meaning is that it is the cause of the necessity of delusion regarding birth, death, pleasure, pain, and so forth. || 18 ||
He is dragged about by latent impressions as if by a rope, like a young animal;
he remains within the body like a bird in a cage. (19)
He states the cause for his assumption of various bodies and the diversity of corresponding activities in the verse beginning with "sa" (verse 19).
Due to the body having reached a state of decay from the effects of time and place,
it passes away under the influence of latent impressions (vāsanā), just as sap flows from a fig leaf.
He states that even when moving from one body to another body, the latent impression (*vāsanā*) alone is the cause, beginning with the word "sa" (he). || 20 ||
Having taken these— the ear, the eye, the sense of touch, the tongue, and the nose—
it departs just as the wind carries fragrances from their source.
"Āśaya" means that in which something lies; it refers to the previous body, flowers, and so forth, from which [the soul] departs. || 21 ||
This body belongs to him solely because of his latent impressions (vāsanā), and not due to any other logical cause;
it perishes when the latent impressions are abandoned, and once they are exhausted, that supreme state is attained.

For this very reason, even its gross body is essentially composed of latent impressions (vāsanā); the notion of its solidity is merely an illusion due to long-standing persistence. With this intention, he says:

"Endowed with latent impressions and nourished by others, the individual soul (jīva), burdened by the weight of delusion, wanders through various wombs, just like a puppet-man (māyāpuruṣaka) [controlled by a magician]. (23)

It is nourished by another who has become its very self through food, drink, and so forth; or else, the subtle body (*liṅgadeha*), which is permeated by latent impressions (*vāsanā*), is nourished by the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) through a twofold entry by way of both limitation (*avaccheda*) and reflection (*pratibimba*).
The meaning is that it becomes manifest, just as a man created by magic wanders in the sky through the power of illusion (*māyā*).
The suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of the object (karma) according to the rule "he bears a great weight of delusion" (*bhramabharam āvibharti*). || 23 ||

Under the influence of latent impressions (vāsanā), the individual soul (jīva) departs from the body, taking with it all the sense-faculties in their essential nature, just as the wind carries fragrance from a flower. || 24 ||
He explains what was stated—that [the senses] are hearing, sight, and touch—by saying "the natures of the faculties" (*akṣasvabhāvān*).
This refers to the inherent capacities for grasping sound and the other objects. (24)
O son of Kuntī, when the life-force has departed, the body becomes motionless, its limbs and form devoid of movement like a tree when the wind has ceased. (25)
He says "the body" (deha) to show that this very thing is what is commonly known in the world as death. || 25 ||
Devoid of activity and having reached invisibility through defects such as cutting and piercing, the body with its life departed is therefore called "dead. (26)
Wherever that living soul, whose form is breath, resides in space,
it perceives each respective extended form due to the habitual practice of its own latent impressions (vāsanā).

In whatever form—whether in the space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*) or the elemental space (*bhūtākāśa*)—and in whatever place, body, time, or object of experience it may abide, that which is impelled by the unseen merit and demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) of the enjoyer perceives that very form. || 27 ||
For this body is perceived by the living soul as if it were non-existent;
upon its destruction, you too should likewise perceive it as such, or else remain like one in deep sleep.

Even upon the destruction of this body, see its non-existence in this very way; or rather, do not perceive the body, its destruction, or that non-existence, as if in deep sleep. The meaning is: just as one who is in deep sleep perceives nothing, so it is here. || 28 ||
Just as he perceives their forms, so too does he perceive their destruction;
for at the time of the initial creation, through meditative cultivation, he indeed discerns them in this manner. (29)
Since the counter-objects (*pratiyogin*) are constructed by latent impressions (*vāsanā*), it is established that their destructions are likewise so from the beginning of creation;

thus he says, "Just as... For at the beginning of creation, by the Creator (Caturmukha), within these creations having the forms of cows, horses, and so forth, such a form [arises] solely through *vibhāvana*—that is, by the power of *vibhāvanā*, which is the latent impression (*vāsanā*) resulting from the experience of a previous creation through imaginative contemplation (*bhāvanā*).
It is "imagined" (kalpita), but not something fashioned by taking clay, a staff, and so forth, like a potter;
the word "kila" indicates what is well-known from the Śruti and Purāṇas.
For at the moment of its sudden emergence, whatever appears before it,
that very thing remains inseparably connected to this consciousness until its final fall.

Now, one might object: "Granted that at the time of its arising the world, consisting of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), may be false; however, at the time of its persistence, because it is capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā-samartha*) and because it is experienced as real by all people, it must indeed be real. Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Whether it is real or not, that which is perceived before one remains exactly so until its destruction; it does not become something else, for its nature is precisely that."

It assumes another nature; for this [nature], which serves as the substratum for that [consciousness], is the cause for the persistence of consciousness in its arisen form, since their existence is never observed apart from consciousness—this is the intended meaning.
The root of past latent impressions is overcome by human effort; indeed, through present exertion, it is quickly subdued just as yesterday's foundation is by today's.
Let it be granted that the forms of the body and so forth consist of latent impressions (*vāsanā*); what follows from that? To this he says: "The former...

The sense is that the complete destruction, along with its root, of the forms of the body and so forth imagined by impure impressions is the fruit of the practice of pure impressions, which produce a mental modification (*vṛtti*) in the form of Brahman; this is achieved through human effort (*puruṣārtha*).
It is overcome— that is, sublated— by the knowledge of the undivided whole (*akhaṇḍākāra-jñāna*) produced by human effort such as hearing (*śravaṇa*), reflection (*manana*), and so forth.
Just as the unrighteous conduct (*adharma-anuṣṭhāna*) of yesterday and the day before is overcome by the present effort of penance (*prāyaścitta*) and the like,
or just as a thatched hut from yesterday and the day before is destroyed by the present effort of burning it.
Or, it is "like that. || 31 ||
That very portion of the preceding and succeeding distinctions which is perceived by a powerful human effort in an instant—that alone clearly triumphs. (32)

If it is objected that the effort of many striving for knowledge is seen to be destroyed by powerful latent impressions (*vāsanās*) of past desire, anger, and so forth, and therefore being "subsequent" is not the cause of its superiority, he says in response: "Whichever [is] mine..."— meaning, among dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, whichever one is mine.

That very specific element of effort, perceived through the obsession that human exertion is indispensable, is the factor that causes victory in both the preceding and subsequent attempts. Thus, the sense is that their defeat results from the weakness of their obsession for liberation and the firmness of their obsession for worldly enjoyment. || 32 ||
Even if the Vindhya mountain should split asunder or the wind of universal destruction should blow, a wise man must never abandon human effort in accordance with the scriptures. (33)
Therefore, he says "even" (api) to indicate that one should maintain a firm resolve toward scriptural effort. || 33 ||

Under the influence of latent impressions (vāsanā) regarding the creation of hells, heavens, and so forth, the individual soul (jīva), whose intellect is clouded by long-standing delusion, perceives these things on all sides as if they were long-practiced realities.

When that [intellect] is dull, a succession of pleasure, pain, and misfortune becomes utterly irresistible from all sides due to the diversity of past impressions (*pūrvavāsanā*); with this intention, he says "In hell," etc. "One whose intellect is steeped in delusion" means one whose mind is stupefied by beginningless ignorance (*anādyajñāna*).
Arjuna said:
O Lord of the World, tell me what is the cause of this world’s existence—the agitation of the creation of hells, heavens, and so forth—for the individual soul? (35)

Arjuna, desiring to know clearly by dispelling doubts regarding other causes well-known from such statements as the words of Vyāsa— “This ignorant creature is not master of its own pleasure or pain; impelled by the Lord, it may go either to heaven or to hell”— [speaks as follows].
He asks: "Regarding hell... [and so forth]. This refers to this living being (*jīva*), who is the cause of the persistence of the world's existence. (35)

The Blessed Lord said: In this world, the destruction of latent impressions (vāsanā) leads to the highest good; however, when these impressions have become mature through long-standing habituation, they cause the delusion of saṃsāra. (36)

No other cause is to be imagined, because even God, desire, karma, and so forth, bring about pleasure and pain only in accordance with latent impressions (*vāsanā*). Therefore, latent impression alone—being the unique cause of transmigratory existence, firmly established through long-term habituation—is what must be eliminated by every effort by one who seeks the supreme human goal; this is the intended meaning.

Clarifying this, the Blessed One said: "In a dream," and so forth. The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: by that very cause—namely, that the latent impression (*vāsanā*), which is like a dream and has become mature through long-term habituation even without scriptural effort, is the giver of the delusion of saṃsāra—therefore, through the practice of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), there is the destruction of the latent impressions along with their roots for the sake of the highest good (*śreyaḥ*). || 36 ||
Arjuna said:
"O Lord of the God of Gods, what is the means for rising [above], and how is latent impression (vāsanā) destroyed?
The Blessed One replied:
The latent impression, which arises from the delusion of ignorance as the conception of a self in that which is not-self,
dissolves through the great awakening of self-knowledge.

Desiring to know the root of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), Arjuna asks: "What gives rise to it? The Blessed One replies: "Ignorance alone is its root; by knowledge alone is it destroyed along with its root"—thus [he says] in verse 37: "By folly... etc.
O son of Kuntī, you have cultivated the self and have realized the truth;
abandon the latent impression that "this is he," "I am this," or "these people are mine. (38)

In that state, through inquiry, there has arisen an acquaintance with the true nature of the Self; by the firmness of that realization, the notions of "I" and "mine" regarding the body, its relations, kinsmen, and so forth [are dissolved]. He says—[in the verse beginning with] "bhāvita"—that only the exhaustion of latent impressions (vāsanākṣaya) remains to be accomplished. || 38 ||
Arjuna said:
Upon the dissolution of latent impressions (vāsanā), the individual soul (jīva) dissolves of its own accord;
for whatever has swollen through the existence of something else, it dissolves upon the destruction of that thing. (39)

But surely, the subtle body (*liṅga*) consists of nothing but latent impressions (*vāsanā*); the individual soul (*jīva*) is its reflection, arising from it, and upon the destruction of those impressions, the soul itself must perish.
With the intention that knowledge of reality and the destruction of impressions would thus lead only to misfortune, Arjuna raises this doubt:
"When the soul has undergone dissolution, with its spatial and temporal conditions transformed..."
Who is it that becomes a fit vessel for birth and death? (40)

This should be explained through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) as follows: "Who becomes the recipient of birth—that is, the supreme human goal characterized by the manifestation of supreme bliss—and of death—that is, the absolute destruction of misfortune? No one at all.

However, the commonly known [physical] birth and death are not to be understood here. For when the knower of reality destroys the root along with the latent impressions (*vāsanā*), [the cycle ceases].
Because there is no possibility of such an implication, and because it would be inconsistent with the preceding and following passages. || 40 ||
The Blessed One said:

O high-minded one, know that very thing which is the unobstructed form of the Self, consisting of its own imagined volitions, to be the individual soul (jīva) characterized by latent impressions (vāsanā). || 41 ||

This fault would arise if the transmigrating individual soul (*jīva*) were accepted as being merely a reflection, distinct from the original source (*bimba*), and produced by the elements (*bhūtamātra*), differentiated by distinctions of place and time; but this is not the case. Rather, it is Brahman itself which, though ultimately pure, is concealed by its own unreal ignorance (*avidyā*) and, failing to know its own true nature, [appears as the *jīva*].

The scriptural conclusion is this: that very Self, through the conceptualization of the distinction between the individual soul and the world within its own self, appears as if it transmigrates; yet, by means of the effort of hearing and so forth according to the scriptures, having awakened to its own true nature and shaken off ignorance along with its latent impressions (*vāsanā*), it abides in its own essential being—this indeed is its liberation. With the intention that no fault has been raised against this position, [the author says]:
The Blessed One provides the resolution himself with the words beginning "svayam" (himself), etc. || 41 ||
O Bhārata, know that liberation is that immutable nature of the Self which is independent, free from volition, and released from latent impressions through awakening. 42.
Independent, not dependent on another. || 42 ||
O mighty-armed one, while still living, perceive reality as it truly exists;
one who is liberated from the weight of latent impressions (vāsanā) is called "liberated. (43)

And that liberation from latent impressions along with their roots, which is known here as *jīvanmukti* (liberation while living) as long as the body is maintained, can be experienced by you even in this very life; therefore, one should not entertain doubt regarding the attainment of the fruit of liberation—with this intention, he says:
"He who is not free from latent impressions is surely [unsuccessful], even if he is devoted to all dharmas."
Even the Omniscient One is bound on all sides, like a bird confined within a cage. || 44 ||

And that liberation is not to be attained through ritual actions nor through scholarship concerning the sphere of external objects, but rather solely through the knowledge of the Self; with this intention, he says: "He who... (verse 44).

He within whose subtle latent impression (vāsanā) flickers like a peacock feather in the sky of the difficult-to-perceive [mind], becomes liberated in this very world; for indeed, latent impression alone is bondage, and its destruction is surely liberation. (45)
He summarizes the previously stated resolution briefly with the words "of the one difficult to perceive":

because it is concealed by its own *māyā*, that Supreme Self— which is difficult to perceive, which is without logic (*anaya*), and for whom the authority of the Vedānta has not been attained— possesses a subtle latent impression (*sūkṣmavāsanā*) that produces manifold delusions in the sky, like a peacock feather created by a magician.

That very [Self], which vibrates within in the form of the living world, manifests itself; however, when it attains the system of Vedānta within the body of a qualified seeker (adhikārin) and realizes the knowledge of reality, it becomes liberated from the bondage of latent impressions (vāsanā) along with their roots. "Here" means in this Supreme Self.
[Now, the word "here" (iha) has the sense of a reason: because the bondage is indeed the latent impression together with its root, therefore its destruction alone [is liberation].
And "liberation" is the meaning. || 45 ||

Thus ends the fifty-fifth canto, titled "The Determination of the Nature of the Living Being," in the *Arjunopākhyāna* (The Narrative of Arjuna) within the *Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa* (Section on Liberation) of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa*, the Great Epic of Vasiṣṭha, composed by the Sage. 55.
Thus ends the fifty-fifth canto, titled "The Determination of the Nature of the Living Being," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The Fifty-sixth Chapter.
The Blessed One said:
"Thus, O Arjuna, by means of being free from latent desires, you have attained liberation while living."
Having attained inner coolness, abandon completely the impurity of grief for kinsmen.
In this work, the establishment of liberation while living (jīvanmukti) is taught to Arjuna,
along with a detailed exposition on the nature of consciousness as the reality of the world and the mind as a variegated painting.
The suffering caused by the loss of kinsmen, and the suffering caused by the killing of kinsmen. || 1 ||

O sinless one, you are free from fear regarding old age and death; your disposition is as clear as space; having abandoned all thoughts of the desirable and the undesirable, you are devoid of passion.
This task has fallen into the stream of events just as it came;
perform your duties and actions, for nothing here is ever lost.

The meaning is this: perform this battle, which has entered the stream of worldly existence and come down through the tradition of the conduct of the learned, as well as other necessary duties such as sacrifices and acts of charity; by doing so, there shall be no impairment whatsoever to the realization of the ultimate truth. || 3 ||
Whatever action is performed that has simply fallen into the natural flow, this is the very nature of one liberated while living; such is liberation while living.

One's own nature is indeed the very form of one's inherent duty (*svadharma*). That well-known state of liberation while living (*jīvanmuktatā*) is of that same kind; the meaning is that it does not consist merely in the abandonment of bodily activity. || 4 ||
The resolve, "I shall abandon this action" or "I shall resort to this," is the nature of the deluded mind; for the wise, however, there is equanimity.
Performing actions that have fallen into the natural flow, with peaceful minds,
those liberated while living shine here like those in deep sleep, remaining as if in deep sleep.
Remaining in their own self as if in deep sleep, free from all volitional thought, they are "those whose state is deep sleep";
like the nature of deep sleep, they manifest as nothing but the self-luminous Self, devoid of distinctions and with only the self remaining. || 6 ||
The senses of one whose [mind] naturally abide in the heart, withdrawn from the objects of the senses on all sides, attain a steady state like the limbs of a tortoise.
He says that there is yet another characteristic of the one liberated while living (jīvanmukta) which is similar to deep sleep, beginning with the word "sthirām":

his senses, because they have been sublated by knowledge, are naturally—without any effort—withdrawn from the objects of the senses, which are trivial; and together with the mind, they are fixed and motionless within the heart, in the Supreme Self residing in the heart.

They attain stability through a state of uniformity (*ekarasya*). Just as the head, feet, and other limbs of a tortoise enter within instantly even with a slight movement [of the shell], so too is such a person one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*); this is the meaning. || 7 ||
In the same way, the painter of the mind creates within the Universal Self the picture of the three worlds— arisen throughout the three periods of time— without any supporting wall.

If it is asked, "How then do those liberated while living perceive the world during the time of worldly activity?", [the author] begins to describe the entire world until the end of creation as being like a picture fashioned by the mind, in order to demonstrate that it is indeed like the variety of a painting produced without a real object through the imagination of the mind: "In the Self of the Universe," and so forth.

The construction of the sentence is as follows: the painter whose characteristic is consciousness, acting as an artisan within the Self—the substratum of the universe—creates the entire universe, a painting of the three worlds without a wall (abhitti), that is, without a physical support, through those various infinite diversities well-known to all people. || 8 ||
In the sky, although it is of the nature of space, a manifold painting has been spread out by the painter of the mind, clearly displayed through the application of its various modes of activity.

In the sky— that is, in the space of ignorance (ajñānākāśa)— which, being of the nature of mere ignorance, is unfit for manifestation, a wonderful and marvelous painting has been clearly manifested and spread out, made visible by means of the wicks characterized as the functions of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) accompanied by the semblance of consciousness (sābhāsa). || 9 ||
"A wall was made behind it, yet it has the nature of space—oh, what a delusion! This auspicious wall, made of straw, is truly unprecedented and a great illusion. (10)

He demonstrates its very nature as a marvel by contrasting it with the well-known characteristics of ordinary painting—starting with the word "afterwards" (*paścāt*). Because the collective mind possesses the power of true resolve (*satya-saṃkalpatva*), the world-picture was created at the very same moment as the resolve;
only after that was the wall, which serves as its support, created in the form of space—that is, in the form of the formless ether—for the purpose of holding the painting.

"It is truly marvelous that she is so unfit; therefore, this is merely an illusion"—this is the meaning. He elaborates on the meaning of the words "aho" (oh! and "bhrama" (illusion) in sequence, beginning with "apūrvā" (unprecedented), and so forth: "This composition is unprecedented—exceedingly wondrous illusion (*atimāyā*)—which, though utterly insubstantial like grass or a wall, appears beautiful to the deluded eye. (10)
There is not even the slightest difference between these clearly perceived walls produced by the painting of the mind; they are perceived as being identical. (11)

He shows another marvel with the words, "not even in the slightest. In well-known paintings, the walls are distinct from the paintings; however, in these walls of space and so forth which are perceived as born from the painting of the mind, there is not even the slightest difference between the support and the supported, because they are both equally of the nature of the mind.
The meaning is that it is a marvel that [it] does not exist. || 11 ||
O lotus-eyed one, know that those [worlds] are more empty than the sky,
just as the arising and passing away of worlds appear in an instant within the mind during delusion.

Having elaborated on the portion "aho" (oh! in the phrase "aho bhramaḥ" (Oh, what an illusion!), he now elaborates on the portion "bhramaḥ" (illusion) with the words beginning "vyomnaḥ" (of the sky). Those mental paintings are more void than the sky; that is to say, they are utterly unreal. O lotus-eyed one! Regarding this, he provides the illustration of the three worlds of a momentary dream with the word "kṣaṇena" (in a moment).
A sixth part of a ghaṭikā is a kṣaṇa. || 12 ||
The self and this world, including all that is external and internal, are like the sky;
they are merely the long-standing kingdom of the mind, and it is from that alone that their reality arises.
The meaning is that the self, the mind, its effects, and the world are like a dream—empty and non-existent, like the sky.

To the question, "Whence then does people's perception of reality arise?", he says: "Because it has persisted for a long time" (*ciraṃtana*). This means because it has continued for a long duration. The particle *kila* is used to indicate that this is not the ultimate truth. || 13 ||
But even when not yet perceived, truth exists within error;
through gradual perception, that truth is dissolved by the light of knowledge. (14)

What, then, is that reality? To this he says: "But what... Regarding the collection of objects imagined through delusion (*bhrānti*) within error (*vibhrama*), that which is the state of having true resolve—which does not exist at all even throughout the three periods of time—what could it possibly be if it has not been perceived in its true nature (*tattvataḥ*), i.e., if it has not been seen prior to the knowledge of reality? The meaning is: it could not be anything at all. However, as for [the sequence] of spring and other seasons, or the sequence of stages such as childhood and so forth...

Alternatively, conventional reality— characterized by the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*) or established through the sequence of the six transformations of existence (*ṣaḍbhāvavikāra*), or otherwise— is dissolved by the light characterized by the vision of that reality (*tattvadarśana*). Just as a visible mass of autumnal mist, when seen by the light of the sun, is dissolved while being dried up by that very same light.
The connection with the subsequent [verse] is "in the same way. || 14 ||
Though visible, it is as insubstantial as a circle of clouds in autumn;
like painted figures situated within a painting created by the artist that is the mind. (15)
Thus, since the mind is merely an illusion, it is logical that it should be stained by the afflictions of killing kinsmen and so forth; to this he says:
"Since there is no wall, the three worlds and so forth outside are formless.
They do not exist, nor do you exist; why then are you obstructed by anything? (16)
It is obstructed and destroyed. || 16 ||
Abandoning the delusion regarding the obstructed and the obstructor, become stainless in the void;
for there is no activity in the sky, and activity itself is of the nature of the void.
This refers, in short, to the delusion regarding the obstructed and the obstructor, the confusion between the victim and the slayer, and the resulting sorrow and impurity.

In the "kha," that is, in the space of Brahman (brahmākāśa), because in the void of the consciousness-space (cidākāśa) there is no activity such as killing at all. As for that which appears to be an illusory activity, it is of the nature of the void itself, being essentially the form of the space of Brahman. || 17 ||
Therefore, the sky—which is stainless of time, action, walls, and parts—is situated within the mind like a painting; it possesses form and consists of everything.

*Kalā* is the skill in the composition of painting; from the word "ādi" (and so forth), it includes its various distinct varieties. It is the stainless sky, which is Brahman itself. Just as a mental painting existing within the mind—though consisting of the entire phenomenal world—is of the nature of the sky because of its emptiness, so too the visible world, though perceived, is the most empty of the sky; this is the connection with the following verse. || 18 ||
Know this entire world to be even more empty than the sky; it is a painting drawn upon the wall of the mind by the painter that is consciousness. (19)
Now, even if one imagines that consciousness itself, being unknown, is the painter and the mind is its wall, it ultimately results in nothing but emptiness; thus he says: "The mind... (verse 19).
Through universal emptiness, it does not differ from space even in the slightest;
just as the manifestation and dissolution of the world-creation appear within the mind. (20)
In that regard as well, he states "just as" (yathā) [in verse 20], indicating that the world, which is momentary like a kingdom of the mind, serves as the illustrative example.
Know, O friend, that in an instant these two remain exactly as they were on the earth;
today, within the kingdom of the mind which consists of various experiences, they have perished.

The conceptualization of the relationship between victim and executioner and so forth, imagined through momentary delusion within the kingdom of your mind—which consists of various experiences—has today been exhausted by my instruction. (21)
Conceptual construction is imagined through a delusion that arises in an instant;
just as the mind is capable of creating a mental kingdom that is utterly non-existent. (22)

Now, one might ask: how can a mental kingdom characterized by a saṃsāra vast and beginningless and endless in its duration be created by a delusion that lasts but a moment? To this he says: "Asadeva" (even though it is non-existent). The meaning is that just as the mind is capable of producing birth and so forth even from what is non-existent, so too it is powerfully capable of transforming a single moment into an aeon. || 22 ||
In the same way, the powerful mind can turn a moment into an eon;
it transforms a moment into an eon and makes that which is small into something vast.

To regard a moment as an eon is a minor marvel, and to produce that which is non-existent is likewise a minor marvel; however, even greater than these is the marvel that the mind renders the non-existent world as existent—it is through such power of the mind that this delusion of the world arises. This is the logical connection. || 23 ||
"This delusion has arisen that quickly treats the non-existent as existent;
in an instant, a kingdom of the mind appears by its very nature. (24)
He says that very thing: "In an instant alone," etc. (24).
That which is of manifold nature is established as this web of the world;
because it culminates in liberation at the time of creation, it has arisen as consisting of moments.

Thus, because it is superposed upon the Self—which is eternally liberated in Nirvāṇa—and because it arises merely as a manifestation, the world is insubstantial, consisting of mere moments, and momentary; yet, by those who do not know this, such a creation is imagined by the deluded to possess the hardness of a diamond and to be difficult to sever. (25)
The quality of being as solid as a diamond is merely imagined here based on appearance alone;
for it is merely a perversion of appearance regarding that whose true form is unknown. (26)

And that [position] is not tenable; thus he says: "The appearance... etc. For one whose form is unknown—that is, for the Self whose true nature is uncomprehended—this world is merely a reversal of appearance, an appearance otherwise.
What adamantine hardness can there be in such a thing regarding its engagement through superimposition, or its cessation through sublation? The meaning is: none at all. || 26 ||
Whether in engagement or in withdrawal, what indeed is this adamantine essence?
When has the world-picture, painted by the mind, ever existed within the consciousness? (27)
For that which already exists requires effort for its removal; however, this [universe] has never existed anywhere at any time.

Thus he says: "Alas, what a marvel! Though without walls and devoid of colors, this vast [universe] appears right before us as if richly colored. Truly, a brilliant painting has arisen without any canvas! (28)
"It is a marvel that even though it does not exist by itself or through its own causal totality, it flashes forth before us," he says:
"The world is a clear enchantment for the eyes, a painting with the ink of manifold darkness, yet anointed with the rays of manifold light. (29)

He explains how it stands before one with the words beginning "surañjana" and so forth. It is called *surañjana* because it thoroughly colors (*suṣṭhu rañjayati*) or attaches itself. The mention of "the sight" is an elliptical expression intended to include the senses, the mind, and so on. (29)
It possesses limbs and members consisting of various ritual procedures, is colored by various passions,
is rich with the play of various views, and has eyes that perceive various experiences.
He whose limbs and parts consist of kalpas, yugas, ages, and so forth.
The sky is a blue lake, shimmering with the fierce rays of various planets, with its diverse forms as the foremost and the last, and with the blooming lotuses of the stars, moon, and sun.

In that [place] where the east and west are distinguished as front and back through various forms at times such as sunrise and sunset, he describes the variegated lotus groves and so forth with the verse beginning "The sky" (vyoma) and so on. // 31 //

The leaf-patterns were formed by rows of clouds engaged in various arrangements; the walls of the sky were like young women adorned with the supreme light, upon which the forms of gods, asuras, and human princesses were inscribed within the niches.

In which [palace] there are leaves and flower-clusters characterized by rows of clouds, joined upwards with various arrangements according to the divisions of time such as autumn; in which there are figurines representing gods, demons, and humans, depicted all around within the cubicles—that is, the various painted compartments—characterized by the three worlds; and which is supremely excellent.

In which [palace] there is a wall characterized by the sky, which shines like a young woman due to a coating of plaster possessing the characteristics of the light of the moon, sun, and other celestial bodies. || 32 ||
This charming little daughter, who captivates the three worlds, is fashioned from space alone as a single stage for her manifestation;
she colors all the worlds with the wheel of pure consciousness, and is made restless by the playful artist of the flickering mind.

Now, having conceptualized the three worlds themselves as a painted doll in the form of a divine dancer, he describes her with five verses beginning with "In the sky itself. By the fickle painter characterized by the mind—
that is, the passionate lover— this enchanting dancer, characterized by the three worlds, is being depicted right here in the Brahma-sky of one's own seat (svādhiṣṭhāna).

The daughter has been fashioned. She is one whose primary stage—the main hall of dance—is the intellect (*pratibhā*) itself, characterized by ever-new manifestations. By her, the worlds have been colored and illuminated on all sides with the ornaments of the fluctuations of the intellect (*buddhi-vṛtti*), which, like wheels, flash forth as they capture reflections, serving as the lamps for the witness-consciousness (*sākṣi-caitanya*) that stands in the place of the dance hall.
She was agitated by playful gestures such as dancing, amorous expressions, emotional states, and graceful charms.
Her creeper-like body is of gold, her mass of hair is thick, and she gazes upon the world with the movement of the eyes of the sun and moon;
she is clothed in the scriptures that regulate virtue, wealth, and pleasure, and her high hips are the earth while her feet move through the network of the underworld.
He further qualifies that very [goddess] with the word "golden" (*hema*): "That egg became golden, possessing a splendor equal to a thousand suns," according to the statement in the *Purāṇa*.
Thus, she is one whose firm, immovable creeper-like limbs are the golden cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) itself;
she is one whose masses of hair are the thick clouds; and her turns of movement are the regulated pursuits of virtue (*dharma*), wealth (*artha*), and pleasure (*kāma*).

She whose two garments are the two treatises on worldly engagement (*pravṛtti*) and withdrawal (*nivṛtti*) of such a kind; she whose two feet consist of seven parts—thighs, knees, calves, ankles, soles, and toes—which are the seven netherworlds (*pātāla*) consisting of the network of subterranean realms; she whose hips are the elevated earth. || 34 ||

Her four arms are as formidable as those of Brahmā, Indra, Rudra, and Hari; her slender body shimmers with breasts that rise high, covered by living beings; she sits upon a lotus-throne whose base is the earth encircled by great serpents; and the interior of the vast world, including its mountains, has become the leaves for her garment.
She is formidable and capable by virtue of her four arms beginning with Brahmā;

she is radiant with a slender body whose breasts are the elevated virtues of discernment and dispassion, which are themselves veiled by the garment characterized by the quality of *sattva*; and she rests upon the surface of the earth, shaped like a lotus and encircled by excellent serpents such as Śeṣa.

She whose seat (*pīṭha*) is her throne; she whose belly is the great world-system (*mahābhuvana*)—that is, the middle world (*madhyaloka*) itself—which contains various mountains of many colors, such as Meru, Añjana, and Himavat, serving as the site for the arrangement of multi-colored leaf-designs made from *gorocanā*, musk, and other substances. 35.

Her eye-movement dispels the flickering darkness of night; her hair stands on end like the formidable stars; her row of teeth is like a diamond; she causes horripilation to arise through the fourteen kinds of tremulous supernatural powers; she is like the *kadamba* flower at the time of universal dissolution.

She possesses eyes characterized by the sun and moon which seize, emulate, and remove the fickleness of Meru’s circumambulation caused by the darkness of night; her row of teeth is indeed lightning; and she [is the source of] the fourteenfold, incomparable, and mutually dissimilar divisions of the world.
She whose horripilation manifests as the very elements born of existence;

she whose foot-encircling garlands of *kadamba* flowers are those very winds of dissolution that destroy the mountains of the world of beings— well-known among those elements— because they spread the filaments of true wisdom in all directions to listeners, and because they impart the fragrance of the pure latent impressions (*suvāsanā*) of dispassion (*vairāgya*).

The three worlds, endowed with living beings, fashioned out of space itself and diverse in nature, were created by the mind— which is like the sky— by that long-practiced master painter who knows the art of painting, as if they were a magnificent puppet filled with manifold delights.
Endowed with the individual and collective soul (jīva), it experiences—that is, attains—the various artistic works which serve as its instruments:

namely, the diverse latent impressions (vāsanās), desires, and karmas. Thus, by means of such a mind—capable of creating and therefore distinct from itself—it [experiences] the three worlds characterized in the manner described.
The concluding summary is that the excellent little daughter has been fashioned within the very sky of consciousness of one's own self-consecration (svādhiṣṭhāna). || 37 ||
Thus ends the fifty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Mind," in the Story of Arjuna, within the Nirvāṇa Section of the Holy Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa of Valmīki.
Thus ends the fifty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Mind," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The Fifty-Seventh Chapter.
The Blessed Lord said:
Know this, O Arjuna, as a great marvel indeed, that which is occurring here.
First the variegated painting arises, and only afterwards does the wall appear.
That vision by which the mind immediately becomes free from latent desires,
and which results in the remainder of the self as non-dual bliss, is here taught.

Therein, he first describes the very vision of the world’s wonder shown previously, as it is useful for loosening latent impressions (*vāsanā*), beginning with the words "This...": First, the painting of the world arises in the mind without a wall—that is, without any support—due to the mental construction of the world's form; subsequently, the wall of the Virāj, consisting of the elements and the worlds, appears as its substratum within that [painting].

When it is being conceptualized, it arises. Alternatively, because the Virāj—the collective totality (samaṣṭi)—of the individual entities (vyaṣṭi) depends upon the conceptualization of those individuals, its arising occurs later. || 1 ||
When a painting has been produced without a wall, a vast wall is seen;
oh, how wonderful is this illusion! A gourd sinks, while a stone floats.

With the intention of showing that this *māyā* is of an absolutely impossible nature, and that its impossibility arises from its contradictory character, he cites a well-known example of such *māyā*: "The gourd [is] sunk," and so forth. The word *tumba* refers to the fruit of the *tumbī* plant; the suffix *luk* is applied to the word for "fruit.
It is indeed said that while the gourd is submerged in water, the stone floats; such a thing is possible only in dreams, magical illusions (*indrajāla*), and the like.
The meaning is "in that same way. || 2 ||
In the three worlds, which are like a painting situated within the mind and whose very self is space,
why does this "I-ness" arise in you, whose self is space, from that which is space?

Let the wonder of the variegated world remain; even more wondrous than that is the arising of the sense of "I" (*ahaṃtā*) within you, whose nature is emptiness and whose essence is the space of consciousness (*cidvyoman*). Thus he says: "Of the mind... (verse 3).
Everything is made of space; by space, in space, space dissolves.
Space is enjoyed within space; space is spread throughout space.

But if you perceive even this world as being nothing but the expanse of consciousness (*cidvyoma*), then that very vision culminates in this [realization]; thus he says "all" (verse 4), expressing that it is indeed a marvel.
Bound by the rope of latent impressions (vāsanā) like a long tethering-cord,
O Arjuna, this [mind] is unloosed here precisely by the untying of those latent impressions.

The meaning is this: the long wandering in saṃsāra is such a variegated world-picture; though the space of consciousness (cidvyoma) is here in this world entwined by the rope of latent impressions (vāsanā) that extends like a cord, it is nevertheless untied simply by the untying of those latent impressions.
Just as a reflection appears in a mirror, so does this [universe] appear within Brahman itself;
it is inaccessible to cutting, piercing, and the like, by virtue of its non-difference from its substratum.
He states that even the difficulty of severing this [superimposition] by means other than knowledge is due solely to the strength of the firmness of the substrate, and not by itself:

"Since there is no cutting or splitting distinct from [itself] in Brahman, which is like the sky for the knowers of Brahman—what is cut, how, whose, by what, or where is it cut, or where is it split? (7)

Therefore, with the intention that all latent impressions (*vāsanās*) must be uprooted by perceiving the world’s unfitness for any conventional usage such as cutting or piercing—based solely on the power of the vision of the non-difference of the world from Brahman—it is said:
"non-different" (*ananyat*). When the entire collection of conventional usages such as cutting and piercing appears within Brahman...

And since the universe that has become the object of that [consciousness] is non-different from Brahman—being indeed the ether of Being-Consciousness (*saccidambara*)—then by what agent, by what instrument, in what manner, for the sake of what fruit, in what place or at what time, could anything be cut or split?
The meaning is that discursive practices such as "cutting" and so forth are observed to have objects other than Brahman. || 7 ||
Therefore, through this awakening, the absence of latent impressions has indeed been accomplished for you;
for one who is not free from latent impressions is surely not truly devoted to all dharmas, even if they are so intent.
Therefore, by this means, through awakening, the non-existence of even those latent impressions (*vāsanās*) apart from Brahman is indeed accomplished.
He recalls what was stated previously—that in the absence of such knowledge, the bondage of latent impressions is truly difficult to sever—with the words "He who":
"Even though he is omniscient, his self remains bound, like a peacock confined within a cage. (8)
He who possesses even a very small seed of latent impression (vāsanā) residing in the ground of consciousness (citibhūmi).

Hari is a lion, or a parrot of green color; not even an atom of latent impression (vāsanā) should be maintained, because it is the seed of thousands of misfortunes—with this intention he says: "Of whom... (verse 9).
For him, the forest of saṃsāra grows vast once more;
however, when the seed of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) has been utterly consumed by the fire of the awakening to truth— which has taken root in the heart through practice— it does not sprout again.
It has been completely consumed by fire. || 10 ||
But when the seed of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) is burnt—[according to the commentary, the reading *nirdagdha-vāsanā-bījam* is required here]—it no longer sinks into objects;
it remains as pure amidst pleasure, pain, and the like, like a lotus leaf in water. (11)
The mind of one whose seeds of latent impressions have been completely burnt away is of such a nature. || 11 ||

With a tranquil self, free from fear, having abandoned all immeasurable desires, extinguished, and with the great delusion of the mind dissolved—having understood that purifying truth which has been heard—abide in the Self as one whose form is singular peace, devoid of injury to others.
(12) Concluding the sequence of the aforementioned instruction, [the Lord] establishes Arjuna in the state of abiding free from latent tendencies (*nirvāsana*): "With a tranquil self," and so forth.

O Arjuna, you, having abandoned immeasurable hopes, being such as you are, have heard that purifying and renowned teaching in the form of the Bhagavad Gītā; having fully understood my instruction, with the great delusion of your mind dissolved,

and having become free from the affliction of the slaughter of kinsmen and other sufferings, you shall be one whose mind is tranquil and whose consciousness has dissolved within the self that is devoid of latent desires.
The meaning is: "Abide as the single, peaceful form of Brahman; therefore, being free from fear, you are liberated (nirvāṇa), supremely at peace. || 12 ||

Thus ends the fifty-seventh canto, titled "The Description of Arjuna’s Rest," in the *Arjunopākhyāna* (Episode of Arjuna) within the *Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa* (Section on Liberation) of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*, the Great Epic of Vasiṣṭha, composed by the Sage. 57.
Thus ends the fifty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of Arjuna’s Resting," in the first half of the Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
Fifty-eighth canto.
Arjuna said:
"O Acyuta, through your grace, my delusion has been destroyed and memory has been regained by me."
I stand here with my doubts dispelled; I shall carry out your word.
Through the awakening to reality, the destruction of the latent impressions of ignorance occurs;
this is established here, and by that means, Arjuna’s purpose is fulfilled.
O Acyuta, through your grace, by means of the instruction bestowed as a favor, my delusion—consisting of ignorance along with its latent impressions (vāsanās)—has been destroyed.
Like the recovery of the memory of a golden necklace previously forgotten around one's own neck, I have attained the realization of the self-nature that is inherently established;
and by that realization, because the seed of all doubt has been destroyed, the doubt regarding my agency in the killing of kinsmen and other such acts has vanished.

I stand firm; therefore, I shall carry out—that is, I shall observe—your word concerning the state of reality as it truly is, and concerning the performance of worldly duties as they ought to be performed. || 1 ||
The Blessed One said:
"If the mental modifications have clearly subsided within the heart through awakening, know that the mind is indeed internally stilled and has attained the state of pure being (sattva). (2)

Although Arjuna has thus demonstrated that his purpose is fulfilled, the Blessed Lord spoke— beginning with the words "The modifications" (*vṛttayaḥ*)— in order to strengthen, through reasoned arguments, the destruction of all latent impressions (*vāsanā*) along with their roots by means of the realization of reality (*tattva-bodha*) which He Himself has taught.
If, through the realization of reality, the mental modifications such as attachment and the like are entirely stilled within the heart, then...

Know that the mind, which consists of latent impressions (*savāsanātmaka*), when stilled, becomes that reality (*sattva*) which has attained the state of being free from impressions (*nirvāsanatva*). And so says the Śruti: "When all the desires that dwell within his heart are cast away, then the mortal becomes immortal;
here he attains Brahman. (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 2.3.14) || 2 ||

In this context, that which is devoid of "that" and "this," which is named direct consciousness (*pratyak-cetana*), which is entirely free from all [limitations], which is everything, and which is everywhere—[that is the Self]. (3)

In this state of being, that which consists of inward consciousness—which in worldly transaction appears as everything, yet in reality is entirely free from all [attributes]—becomes Brahman, devoid of thought-constructs (cetya); this is the remainder of the sense. || 3 ||
None of those belonging to the world and so forth know that state, just as [people on the ground] do not perceive a bird flying high in the sky above the earth. || 4 ||

The eyes and other senses of worldly people, as well as certain ignorant folk—this is the meaning of the word "etcetera"—do not know that state, which is exalted and situated in the upper region. || 4 ||
Know this Self to be inwardly conscious, appearing as a reflection, pure, devoid of volition, and inaccessible— just as it is remote from the senses of sight.
It is a manifestation that illuminates thirteen kinds of fields, beginning with the great elements; it is inaccessible and beyond the range of the senses, as if far removed from sight. || 5 ||
That which is utterly transcendent and exceedingly clear cannot be seen by one whose own latent impressions are impure; just as the vision of ordinary people cannot perceive atoms.

And regarding that vision, he states—beginning with "beyond all"—that meditation known as *nididhyāsana*, which is practiced through the repeated cultivation of that [reality] determined by hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth, is indispensable. It is exceedingly clear due to its nature as consciousness; it is pure because of its non-attachment. (6)
Upon the attainment of which all these things, such as pots and cloths, are utterly exhausted—
what can that wretched latent impression (vāsanā) do there in the supreme state?
He states—“When that is attained”—that where even gross things such as jars are sublated, the persistence of the most subtle latent impressions (vāsanās) is simply impossible. || 7 ||
Just as even a trace of snow dissolves upon reaching a mountain of fire,
so too does ignorance dissolve upon attaining the pure reality of the mind (cittattva).
Where is this wretched, trivial latent impression of passion that binds one to enjoyment, and where is the vast wind of the true nature of consciousness that fills the entire web of the universe? (9)
Like dust and pollen, they are worthless and trivial. || 9 ||
This ignorance, which undergoes various transformations of form, flickers only so long as this pure self has not been fully realized by the self. (10)
All perceptions of the visible have ceased, and thus pure transparency alone has arisen;
it is like the sky in that state, within one's own self which fulfills all things.
In such a being, who fills and devours everything within his own self and his own belly; || 11 ||
That supreme reality, which possesses all forms yet is devoid of all forms, and which transcends speech—by what indeed can it be compared? (12)
Its nature is completeness, being the totality of all forms; yet it is devoid of all worldly forms. || 12 ||

Therefore, having skillfully cast off the latent impressions of existence that cause the cholera-like plague of the poison of sense-objects, become a sovereign through the application of the mantra of abandoning what is desired; O Blessed One, be one who is no longer a ground for fears.

Therefore, O Arjuna, by means of the mantra-technique characterized by the cessation of desired objects— which is nothing other than the perception of the Full Self— you shall become powerful once you have skillfully cast away that latent impression (*vāsanā*) residing in the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which is the cause of constant worldly activity and which, like cholera induced by the poison of sense-objects, maintains the state of egoism.
"Free from the bonds of saṃsāra, the ground of all fears and misfortunes, and whose very nature is fearlessness—may I become that very Blessed One.
This is the summary instruction at the conclusion of the entire meaning of the Bhagavad Gītā. || 13 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
When the Lord of the Three Worlds had spoken thus and remained silent before him for a moment,
then the son of Pāṇḍu addressed these words there, like a bee at a cluster of blue lotuses.
When he had approached silence and stood before him. || 14 ||

Arjuna said: O Blessed One, by your word, this mind of mine has reached the highest exaltation, its entire burden of sorrow having dissolved, like a lotus-plant awakened by the sun, the lord of the world.
Having spoken thus, Arjuna, the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow who has Hari as his charioteer, will rise up and perform the sport of battle, free from all doubt.

Arjuna is he whose bow is the Gāṇḍīva. The suffix *vaḥ* is applied in the sense of possession according to the rule "gāṇḍyajagātsaṃjñāyām," and the substitution of *anaṅ* occurs by the rule "dhanuṣaśca. || 16 ||
He will make the earth a place where great rivers of blood flow swiftly from wounded elephants, horses, and charioteers;
and he will make the sky such that the sun, its eyes, is hidden by the vast dust-storm rising from the spreading flight of his arrows.
That Arjuna will make the earth such that it possesses great rivers flowing with blood, in which wounded elephants, horses, and charioteers have been swiftly driven along;
and he will make the sky such that the sun is obscured by the spreading masses of his arrows and by the plains created from the great dust.
The meaning is that he will make her one whose eyes are of such a kind. || 17 ||

Thus ends the fifty-eighth sarga, titled "The Attainment of Purpose by Arjuna," in the *Arjunopākhyāna* of the *Pūrva-khaṇḍa*, within the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki.
Thus ends the fifty-eighth sarga, titled "The Attainment of Arjuna’s Purpose," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The Arjunopākhyāna is completed.
The fifty-ninth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
O Raghava, firmly grasping this vision which destroys all evil, remain established in the nature of self-surrender to Brahman through detached renunciation. 1.
The state of consciousness that is free from vibration and liberated from the perceived object is the condition of one liberated while living;
that vision by which this state becomes perfectly stable is described here.

[She is] the destroyer of sin, the one who effects the destruction of all evils. Renunciation, characterized by non-attachment, is the abandonment of everything; it is the purification of the meaning of the term *tvaṃ* (Thou). The offering to Brahman—which consists in sublation (*bādha*) of the entire universe within Brahman—is the purification of the meaning of the term *tat* (That). From that which remains as the result of both [purifications], there arises the ground of the single essence of Being-Consciousness-Bliss, which is the indivisible meaning of the Great Sentence (*mahāvākya*).
"Do not stay"—this is the meaning. || 1 ||
Know that Supreme Self in whom all is contained, from whom all proceeds, who is all, who is everywhere, and who eternally consists of all. (2)

In whom all things abide; from whom all things proceed in creation; who is all things in dissolution; and who is everywhere throughout the three periods of time—even so, know that very Self to be eternal and supreme, though He consists of the entire manifold of impermanent phenomena; the meaning is that He is not of a limited nature. || 2 ||
Though situated at a distance, it is not distant; it is all-pervading and yet remains right where it is.
Abiding in that, you attain its very existence; that indeed is it, free from doubt.
Because it exists outside of all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), it is distant; yet because it is within everything, it is not distant from anything.

Thus, although it is all-pervading like space, it remains situated [within each thing], and like a universal (*jāti*), it is fully present in each respective object. Since it is established that in every respect there is only this one reality and nothing else, you [should realize] it even in its seemingly limited form.

"You abide in that"—meaning you attain existence solely through the existence of that [Being] and not by your own independence. This being so, what is the use of your conceit regarding limitation? You are that very same undivided Pure Being. Therefore, the meaning is: let there be for you the cessation of doubt concerning limitation. || 3 ||
Know that to be the supreme state which is consciousness free from the object of cognition, uncreated, liberated from the thinkable, and the manifestation of pure awareness.
For the nature of the conscious self (cidātman) is experienced by those possessed of discrimination as being twofold:

one is the form consisting of the manifestation of objects of cognition, reflected in the mind and its modifications, and produced by the mind; the other is the form of witness-consciousness (sākṣisaṃvit), which is uncreated and consists of the witnessing of all states—such as the arrival and departure—of the mind, its modifications, and their objects.

It is eternally established. The meaning is: know that when both of these are perceivable by consciousness yet free from the triad [of subject, object, and means], they have become the supreme state, which is Brahman itself. || 4 ||
She is the supreme, the ultimate pinnacle; she is the unsurpassed vision among all visions;
she is the greatness of all greatnesses, and likewise, she is the greatest of the great.

And she is the state of consciousness liberated from the object of cognition; she is the supreme pinnacle of the succession of the excellence of bliss, as declared by such scriptural passages as "from which words turn back. She is the greatest among the great, the most venerable among the venerable; the meaning is that there is nothing higher than her. || 5 ||
That is the Self and that is consciousness; that is the void, that is the supreme Brahman;
that is the highest good, that is Śiva, the peaceful; that is knowledge, that is the ultimate state.
This very Self within consciousness, whose nature is universal experience,
is that wherein all objective entities relish their own existence through the power of its being.
He is the essence of the sesame oil of the world; He is the lamp for the house of the world;
He is the sap of the tree of the world; He is the protector of the cattle of the world.
He states that this very [reality] is the essence of the entire world with the words beginning with "sa" (he), etc. || 8 ||
He is the thread upon which the pearls of liberated beings are strung, filling the expanse of the heart;
he is likewise the supreme pungency of the mass of black pepper that is all beings.
