He is the object-ness in an object; He is that reality which is unsurpassed; He is the existence of an existent thing, or the non-existence of an existent thing by its own nature.
He states that this very [nature] is the unique, specific essence (*asādhāraṇa-svarūpa*) of all categories of entities by saying "sa" (that). *Sattva* means reality (*samyaktva*).
He who is himself attained as the very Self through the diversity of his own consciousness—indeed, all the states of the world are beautiful when not subjected to analytical inquiry. 11.

Who is he? He is that by whom everything is realized as being none other than the Self itself—through his own consciousness in its ultimate form, which is awakening—and by means of various extraordinary, non-worldly methods; this is the meaning. || 11 ||
Existing entities are non-existent, crumbling under scrutiny;
they exist within the web of the world—whose nature is a mass of false delusion—beginning with the notion of "I."

It has been stated that the states of the existent Supreme Self are conceptual constructions that perish upon investigation; therein, he demonstrates by means of the verse beginning with "I" (*aham*) what kind of investigation causes the states of the world to dissolve. || 12 ||
Having become what, do I persist? How has the intellect attained its state?
I am the beginning, middle, and end; I am the measures and the mental constructions of volition.

"Adopt a mode of conduct. [The opponent objects: "Surely even for you, who are pure, the intellect (*dhī*) itself will be the cause for establishing a bond of dependence. To this he replies: "How? Even the intellect (*buddhi*), being non-attached and non-dual, how could it have reached me? The meaning is that there is no cause for its attainment. Or, even if it were to reach me, nevertheless, the delimitations such as beginning, middle, and end would still be produced by it.

With the intention that "I alone am the fabrications of conceptualization (saṃkalpa), and they do not exist apart from me; thus, in this inquiry, there is no possibility of my [as Brahman] being limited," he says: "ādyā... (verse 13).
"The space of Brahman is without beginning or end; what limit can there be to my own Self?"—thus being inwardly certain, he conducts himself perfectly in outward affairs. (14)

With the intention that for one who reflects in this way, that state does not depart even during the time of worldly activity that is not contrary to the scriptures, he says: "Always internally free from rising and setting, that mind, established in perfect equanimity, neither sets nor rises. (15)

He whose mind is established in Brahman, which is equal even to equals—that great-souled one is always free from the rising and setting [of mental fluctuations] within; such is the connection with the following verse. || 15 ||
He whose emptiness is like that of space is a great soul here, possessing that very body;
he has ascended to the state of non-dual existence with a mind as profound as deep sleep.

He states the justification for not deviating from such a state during the time of worldly activity (*vyavahāra*) with the word "bhāva" (in thought). The meaning is that this [realization] is ascended to the state of non-duality through contemplation (*bhāvanā*) alone, and not through worldly activity. Thus they have said: "One should always maintain the non-duality of being (*bhāva-advaita*), but never the non-duality of action (*kriyā-advaita*). There may be non-duality throughout the three worlds, but there must be no non-duality with one's teacher. (16)

Even while engaged in worldly activity, he does not undergo agitation, just like a man who sees his reflection; for even though he possesses worldly activity, he is like the person reflected in the mirror.
He whose heart experiences not even the slightest agitation partakes of liberation; he is reflected within the jewel of consciousness as if indivisibly, like [an image] in a mirror. 18.

The "scratching of the heart" refers to the suffering of honor, dishonor, and so forth. To the question of how worldly activity can proceed toward such a liberated person (jīvanmukta) who is like a jewel of consciousness, he states that "the mirror" is the very illustration for this—namely, "without division. The particle *iva* is displaced [in the compound]. Just as the worldly activity of people seen in a mirror does not affect the non-differentiation of the mirror...
The meaning is that, in the same way, it is reflected in the jewel of consciousness (*cinmaṇi*) without undergoing any transformation consisting of a differentiation of variety. || 18 ||
Due to the supreme purity of consciousness, worldly transaction proceeds as it has always done; this world appears as nothing other than the wonder of consciousness itself. (19)
Herein there is neither unity nor duality; even my instruction is composed of that [reality].
Through the words of the teacher, the student, the expressed and the expresser, and through these wondrous experiences, [this is realized]. (20)

Through the wonders of the conceptualization of the signified and the signifier, the disciple and his inquiry, the teacher and his words, and so forth, even my instruction and your teaching are composed of that [Reality], which is indeed consciousness alone. 20.
Within consciousness itself, the tranquil consciousness alone manifests as a wondrous play within consciousness;
for the vibration of consciousness is saṃsāra, while its non-vibration is the supreme state.
It wonders and undergoes transformation; vibration is indeed transformation itself. || 21 ||

This cycle of existence is stilled by the calming of the vibration of consciousness; when the Great Consciousness has been bowed to, there is no object, for that is the exhaustion of mental cultivation.

When your mind has become inclined toward and transformed into the vast, undivided form of Brahman, that which is the departure of the state of being a partial portion—that is, the state of being a single part characterized as the individual soul (jīva) and the world—is the goal, the supreme human aim;
this very thing is the exhaustion of mental cultivation (bhāvanā), meaning the exhaustion of latent impressions (vāsanā). || 22 ||
Even though it is non-existent, its own nature is described as the vibration of that consciousness;
that which is emptiness yet not insentient, they call the supreme body of consciousness. (23)
For this reason— that even though it is non-existent, the vibration of consciousness (saṃvitspanda) brings about a state of insentient nature—
it is therefore said by those established in experience that the very absence of such vibration is the non-insentient, supreme body or essential nature of consciousness. || 23 ||
In reality, this cycle of existence is experienced as dependent upon mental cultivation;
through the mere dissolution of such cultivation, it becomes essentially insubstantial.

The meaning is as follows: that cycle of worldly existence (*saṃsṛti*), which consists in the vision of non-self, is dependent upon the cultivation of the reality and the true nature of the world-as-non-self; it is experienced exactly in that way. Merely by the absence of such cultivation, that cycle of existence for one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*)—due to the dissolution of its latent impressions (*bhāvanālaya*)—becomes essence-less like a burnt cloth and is no longer capable of causing bondage. || 24 ||
Through the state of absolute isolation (*kevalībhāva*), that very [consciousness] remains in its pure form;
the wise know that the vibration of consciousness alone is what sets the wheel of saṃsāra in motion. (25)
How, then, is that [world] said to remain in the state of liberation while living? To this he says: "Only" (kevalam).
Due to the state of being absolute (kevalībhāvāt)—that is, due to becoming pure consciousness devoid of vibration—that world remains as that very form, namely, the form of consciousness itself.
Therefore, the meaning is that they say the world-process, consisting of the knower, the means of knowledge, and so forth, is nothing but the vibration of consciousness. || 25 ||

Just as bracelets and other ornaments do not exist separately from gold, so too the knower, the means of knowledge, the object of knowledge, and so forth, do not exist apart from consciousness; and what movement of consciousness could there be that would constitute transmigratory existence? (26)
And since that [unreal] does not exist apart from consciousness, it follows that transmigratory existence is nothing but ignorance. || 26 ||
The mind alone is the vibration of consciousness; indeed, the lack of awareness of that [consciousness] is transmigratory existence.
In the mere absence of awareness, the vibration of consciousness arises like the state of being a bracelet.
O Rāma, when this [mind] has dissolved through mere awakening, pure consciousness remains;
by mere awakening to one's own nature, the latent impression of enjoyment is destroyed. (28)
Intrinsic nature is the reality of one's own self; [liberation occurs] by the mere awakening to that. || 28 ||
In this world, the non-cultivation of enjoyments alone is the supreme characteristic of one who possesses knowledge; for by its very nature, no enjoyments whatsoever are desired by the knower. (29)

The non-contemplation of even those enjoyments that are spontaneously accomplished due to the exhaustion of the latent impressions of enjoyment is indeed the characteristic of wisdom and of liberation while living. To the question "Why does he not contemplate these enjoyments?", he says: "From this" (verse 29).
For who, being truly satisfied, would ever desire bad food?
Know this alone to be another characteristic of true wisdom. (30)

The phrase "they come to be" (bhavanti) connects with what precedes. This is another characteristic, distinct from those characterized by discernment and so forth described in the passage beginning with "who, having not been... (ko na bhūtvā). || 30 ||
It is certain that the mere desire for enjoyments, which is like a wish-fulfilling gem, exists by its very nature as the vibration of the mind, whose form is the self of all. (31)

Now he states another definition: "Consciousness" (cid). The meaning is that the firm internal conviction—that one's own conscious self alone vibrates in the form of the enjoyer, the enjoyed, and the act of enjoyment, and thus, having become those vibrations, exists as the form of all selves—and that this well-practiced [conviction] being fully established, is itself the definition of the state of being a knower. || 31 ||
That internalized and well-practiced habit is designated by the term "knowledge" (jñatva).
He who does not enjoy even the objects of enjoyment being presented to him is truly wise;
for the sake of conforming to worldly conventions, he strikes at the sky with sticks.
But as for his engagement in enjoyments for the sake of maintaining a body like that of an ordinary person, that is merely a futile exertion; thus he says:

"The wise one who knows reality, like a person intent on striking at the sky out of delusion, strikes at the sky himself with clubs for the sake of fulfilling the expectations of the world—such is the meaning: his exertion is likewise merely futile. (32)
Without an artificial intellect, success is not attained. || 33 ||

Now, if that [notion] were a futile effort, then since the consciousness of the Self—which has transformed into the form of the enjoyer, the enjoyed, and the enjoyment for all people—is itself the nature of all selves, the previously mentioned cognition would also be merely artificial, like the deluded thought "the beating of the mallet by the public is mine alone. To this, he says: *na*... [etc.]

The meaning is that the definition of the vision of the entire self-nature has been stated because it is conducive to the realization of reality by means of the elimination of the view of a limited self. || 33 ||

Even when perceiving itself through the wounding of its own limbs, consciousness— remaining at the limit of the objects of thought— perceives delusion for as long as it exists within the sphere of the thinkable.

In that case, since it serves as a means for perceiving reality by way of dispelling the notion that the body is the self, why would even a rash act such as crushing one's own limbs—the hands, mace, and so forth—not also be a defining characteristic? To this he replies: [only] if its utility in the perception of one's own Self were as well-known as its utility in the perception of the Self of all, then that too would be a defining characteristic.

The meaning is that it may not exist [in that way]. Alternatively, there is a word-break as *akṛtrimayā* (by the unartificial). In the vision of the Self (*ātmāvaloka*), which is the manifestation of one's own nature, without an unartificial—that is, devoid of limited forms—intellect whose form is the undivided Brahman, there can be no yoga consisting of perfection, even through the "tearing of one's own limbs," that is, even by millions of such rash acts resembling the tearing of one's own limbs.

The meaning is that [it] is not understood. To explain why that is so, he says "Consciousness" (cit) in three verses: As long as this consciousness remains unawakened—that is, veiled by ignorance—it stands within the sphere of the objectified (cetya), having entered into the sphere of the self-luminous intellect and so forth;
becoming, as it were, itself of the nature of vibration, it vibrates toward the external object of cognition (cetya), and thereby [produces] delusion.
He sees. || 34 ||
This [universe], whose nature is until-enlightenment, vibrates as the form of vibration;
yet when perfect enlightenment arises within, there occurs the sequence of states of both vibration and non-vibration.

When the arising of perfect awakening occurs within, then the sequence of states involving vibration and non-vibration, along with its designations, goes somewhere—that is, it is sublated—along with its own name. || 35 ||
And that which is designated as "he" goes somewhere, like a lamp whose flame has been extinguished; this occurs by the very nature of the lamp of consciousness, which is of a peaceful form. (36)
Here, there is not even the slightest talk of vibration or non-vibration; for that which is non-vibrating wind is neither existent, nor non-existent, nor something intermediate.
He states that the absolute cessation of vital movement is also that very same [state] with the words "yad" (that which): "That form which is neither describable as going nor as not going. (37)
That very form is the subsiding of the vibration of non-awareness within consciousness;
the vibration of consciousness, assuming the nature of the expansion of pure consciousness, becomes non-different from consciousness itself.

The meaning is that they know that first [state] called liberation, which is that consciousness (*cit*) wherein there exists neither non-perception, nor ignorance, nor vibration. When the mind-self—the vibration of consciousness—is the vision of that pure consciousness, whose form is the expansion of Brahman, then it leads neither to bondage nor to liberation. 38.
Established solely within the Self, neither for bondage nor for liberation,
if consciousness perceives only useless cognitions, it does not find nirvāṇa.

If one does not perceive either the consciousness in the meaningless or the useless—that which is the form of the mind (cittākāra) and its cessation as being Nirvāṇa—then even the names of the sides of bondage and liberation do not exist here.
The internal thought "let there be liberation" is itself an end; it is the cause of exhaustion. (40)
Then that [is the case]. || 40 ||
Even the thought "may they be equal" is a bond; the highest good is the supreme non-perception [of duality]. Know that which is without appearance and is not inert to be the supreme state. (41)

Even the desire, "May that liberation not exist; rather, let there be consciousness (cit) that is equanimous and undistracted," is bondage. What, then, is the highest good? He states it with one and a quarter verses beginning with "The highest good" (śreya). || 41 ||
The nature and configuration of the individual consciousness (citta) consists in its orientation toward that which is not an object of cognition;
it is the vibration of the Great Consciousness (mahācit) whose form is the conceptualization of words and their meanings. (42)
What, then, is the entity fit for the conventional usage of bondage, liberation, and so forth? He states it with the word "ya" (which...). || 42 ||
This [self], which is subject to bondage, liberation, and so forth, perishes when it is scrutinized;
for by that very scrutiny, the ego-sense (ahaṃbhāva) becomes pacified and remains without a substrate.
We do not know by what, what, or for whom one is bound or liberated;
for the wise man who is free from the sense of duality, it is merely a mental construction.

What, then, is the means for abandoning the movement of volition (*saṃkalpa*)? He states it: "In volition itself. When the wise discerning person abandons the distinction within his own created volition—by reflecting on the preceding and succeeding moments as to whether "this was willed by me" or "this was not"—then that volition, even if it has arisen, is rendered useless, being incapable of producing external movement.
The meaning is that, by the very fact of its destruction, everything has already become unobstructed, free from volition, and motionless. || 44 ||
Therefore, everything that has arisen is without volition and without vibration, remaining unobstructed;
for within the wind consisting of vibration, it is always [perceived] by consciousness due to its identity with that [consciousness].

Thus, when vibration (*spanda*) has been dissolved by consciousness awakened through such reflection, and the wind consisting of vibration has also been dissolved, the cycle of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*), which is rooted in that, is likewise dissolved; thus he says: "In vibration... (verse 45).
When [the mind] has been utterly exhausted, there is no longer saṃsāra, as one remains in the motionless mass of consciousness;
for when it is continuously realized that the vibration of consciousness is nothing other than the radiance of consciousness itself.

Alternatively, since it is observed that there is no vibration other than the light of consciousness (cit), its cessation [is achieved] through that very insight; thus he says: "Consciousness..."—apart from consciousness, no vibration remains whatsoever.
The Knower does not undergo delusion, because his own awareness is all-pervasive. (47)
Delusion is the error consisting of the movement of one's own [mind] and so forth. || 47 ||

Understand that [Reality] by means of meditation alone, wherein the existence of the consciousness of creation rises forth incessantly and forcefully, wherein all these stains of the forms of manifold mental constructs dissolve,
and wherein all perceptions arise as delightful to relish.
The inner self within. 48.

In which [consciousness], even though they are forcibly restrained incessantly, the perceptions of the forms of the entire world arise—arise in such a way as to be auspicious by means of the tasting of the bliss produced by that [perception] and its own relishing; likewise, the very existence and stability of all those aforementioned cognitions also emerges therein. These are of the nature of the aforementioned cognitions.

The meaning is: through meditation and inquiry in the manner described, realize—that is, behold—the inner self (pratyagātman) in whom all the mud of the forms of the creative powers (kalā) dissolves and merges. || 48 ||

Thus ends the fifty-ninth canto, titled "The Realization of the Inner Self," in the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa* of the *Mokṣopāya* section of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Valmiki, according to the tradition of the Rishis.
Thus ends the fifty-ninth chapter, titled "The Realization of the Inner Self," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The Sixtieth Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Thus is the primordial, supreme reality, the mass of consciousness, the highest state.
Established therein are these great forms, beginning with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara. || 1 ||
The manifestation (*vibhūti*) of that which is non-dual, pure, and supreme, abiding here in all forms through its own inherent power (*nijamāyā*), is thus taught.

Desiring to elaborate upon the manifestations (*vibhūtayaḥ*) of the Brahman described above, he first points out the principal ones therein—the sense being that they range from humans up to the destroyers of the world (*harānta*). || 1 ||
People, like kings, rejoice with great splendor, shining intensely through their powers;
they sport for a long time in diversions such as traveling through the sky.

"Kings are as if filled with the abundance of human bliss"—this indicates the first stage in the progressive sequence of excellence in bliss shown by the *Taittirīya* Śruti. Regarding the excellence of happiness in those aforementioned stages, he says: "In the space," etc. The connection with the subsequent [verse] is: "One plays there with the very people residing therein. (2)

Just as those dwelling in heaven [are honored] by the people residing there, so too [is he honored]. Having attained that, my dear, one does not die; having attained that, my dear, one does not grieve. (3)

In that Brahman, there exists a gradation of the destruction of impurity which obstructs the manifestation of bliss; one who abides therein is "one who stands in that" (*tatsthaḥ*), such as a human, a celestial musician (*gandharva*), and so forth. The phrase "as [the dwellers of heaven]" (*yathā*)—where both *svargaukasaḥ* and *svargaukasām* are read—is intended to provide examples from the higher levels, beginning with the *gandharvas* and those above them.
Having attained through the awakening to reality that Brahman which constitutes the ultimate limit of the excellence of all bliss—[the word] "Aṅga" is used as a form of address. || 3 ||
Having attained that, my dear, one lives; having attained that, my dear, one is no longer obstructed—[the state] of the Supreme Self, whose nature is the boundless, supreme ether.
It does not live—that is, it is not afflicted by hunger and other such causes for the maintenance of life; nor is it obstructed by walls and the like. || 4 ||
If even for a moment the universal form of existence is clearly perceived,
then in an instant that person becomes a sage whose mind is liberated;
performing the activities of worldly life, you shall no longer suffer.

The connection with the subsequent verse is as follows: "If even a living being who possesses the body of an ordinary creature were to possess that very reality (tattva), you would not be distressed; how much less so, then, one who possesses a superior body? (5)
Śrī Rāma said:

Where the mind (manas), intellect (buddhi), ego (ahaṃkāra), and consciousness (citta) have come to an end, and where only the universal existence (sattāsāmānya) shines forth—who is that called a wise man? (6)

With the intention that—since a living being is no longer tormented by the contemplation (*vibhāvanā*) of that which is the nature of the universal essence of existence (*sattāsāmānyarūpa*), is that [essence] without distinction or with distinction?

In the first case, the description of its manifestation (*vibhūti*) would be inconsistent; in the second case, the description of the absolute cessation of torment, stating that "having attained that, the living being is no longer tormented," would be untenable. With this in mind, Rāma asks: "The mind... (*manaḥ*).

"O Mind-Buddhi, is that which you call 'existence-in-general' (sattāsāmānya)—the non-differentiated, full pure consciousness (pūrṇacinmātra) where all duality has come to an end—merely what is expressed by the word 'Mind'? Or is it the possessor of mind, the one who possesses the intellect?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
That Brahman which resides within all bodies, which eats, drinks, moves about, takes up, and destroys from within— consciousness itself, devoid of anything to be known by consciousness.

In this context, the universal existence (*sattāsāmānya*) is not described by dividing it into that which remains as "without attributes" (*nirviśeṣa*) after the sublation of phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*), or that which is "with attributes" (*saviśeṣa*) prior to that; rather, it is that very pure being (*sanmātra*) which is woven through all states of living beings, the state of the Lord, and liberation—a single, uninterrupted whole. That alone is the reality (*tattva*) of the world. In that regard:

With the intention that there is no contradiction whatsoever with what you have proposed, Vasiṣṭha provides the resolution: "That which... (verse 7). It takes [the world] within during the time of the creation of waking and dreaming; it casts it out during deep sleep and cosmic dissolution; and it remains devoid of both consciousness and the objects of consciousness in the state of the Fourth (turiya).
That which is all-pervading, devoid of beginning and end, established, and unacquired—the universal existence (sattāsāmānya) as a whole—is here called the reality of things (vastutattva). || 8 ||
It remains just as it is, acquired through awakening like a golden necklace around one's neck. || 8 ||
It exists as space within the sky, as sound within sound;
it exists as touch within touch, and as the skin-sense within the skin.

He says, beginning with "That," [in order to demonstrate its universal nature]: that very [Brahman], which is interwoven through the effects such as space and so forth, is described as their manifestation (vibhūti). || 9 ||
It is perceived as taste through its nature as taste and absorbed in the tongue through its nature as that;
it is seen as form through its nature as form and absorbed in the eye through its nature as sight.
By that state, as the sense-organ of taste; the two eyes are the sense-organs of sight. || 10 ||
The nose is seen as the nature of smelling; fragrance is declared to be the nature of scent; the body is nourished by the nature of the body; and even the earth is seen as the nature of the element.
It exists as liquidity in water, as the nature of air in air,
as the nature of fire in fire, and it has entered into the intellect as the nature of intellect.
Through the state of mind, it is rooted in the internal ego within the mind;
through consciousness, it is established in pure awareness; and through the intellect, it arises as the nature of the mind.

By means of "I-making" (ahaṃkṛti), that is, by way of the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra); in consciousness (saṃvit), that is, in the intellect (buddhi); by means of perception (saṃvitti), that is, by way of the intellect (buddhi). || 13 ||
It is attached to the tree as the tree-ness, manifested on the cloth as the cloth-ness,
established in the jar as the jar-ness, and arisen in the banyan tree as the banyan-ness.
In the stationary as stationariness, in the moving as movability, in the stone as stoneness, and in the conscious as consciousness. (15)
And consciousness exists in the four kinds of beings. || 15 ||
Among the immortals by way of immortality, among men by way of humanity, among animals by way of animality, and among worms by way of being a worm. (16)
In that regard, he says "among the immortals" [verse 16] to show that even the existence of specific forms is that very same thing.

In the sequence of time, the all-pervading Lord exists as time itself; likewise, in each season, he exists as that very season; and in moments such as the *truṭi*, the *kṣaṇa*, and the *nimeṣa*, he is established as those very units.
In the sequence of time, there are distinctions such as the *yuga* and the year; "in the season" (*ṛtau*) and so forth are its detailed expansions. || 17 ||
It exists as whiteness in the white, and as blackness in the black;
it exists as vibration in actions, and as restraint in the rules of discipline.
By rule, that is, by necessity. || 18 ||
The Supreme Lord abides as stability in that which is stable, as destruction in destruction, and as the form of origination in origination. || 19 ||
He rests in childhood by means of childhood, in youth by means of youth,
in the form of old age by means of old age, and in death by means of death.
The expressions beginning with "by childhood" (*bālyena*) are indications where the abstract state (*bhāva*) is the primary referent. || 20 ||
Thus, the Supreme Lord is non-different from all categories of objects, just as the mass of water in the ocean is non-different from its waves, spray, and ripples. (21)
The weight of her breasts is like the commonality of water. || 21 ||
This diversity of theirs is indeed unreal; for by means of this very reality, it is imagined through the nature of consciousness, just as a ghost is imagined by a child.

If it is asked how this very [Self], which is one, exists as manifold, he says "nānātā" (manifoldness) [in verse 22]: it is only through the conceptualization of the delusion of one's own ignorance, not in reality.

"O Great-souled One, remain at ease with a tranquil mind, realizing: 'This entire universe is pervaded everywhere by Me, who am established in all things and free from affliction, through various playful manifestations; it is by My own conscious nature that this world has been fashioned as its very self. (23)
Śrī Vālmīki said:
When the sage had thus spoken, the day departed; the sun went to its setting for the sake of the evening rites.
Having offered salutations, the assembly departed to bathe; and at the end of the night, they returned along with the rays of the sun.

O Great-Souled One, this manifestation of the world has been fashioned and conceived by me alone—by my own Self, which is of the nature of consciousness and established everywhere. This entire universe is pervaded by me through various playful manifestations; it is my own glory, and there is nothing whatsoever apart from me. Thinking thus, remain with a mind that is perfectly tranquil in your own majesty.
The meaning is "stay. || 23 || 24 ||
Thus ends the sixtieth chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Yoga of Vibhūtis," in the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa* of the *Mokṣopāya* section of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Valmiki.
Thus ends the sixtieth sarga, titled "Instruction on the Yoga of Manifestation," in the first half of the Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The sixteenth day. || 16 ||
The sixty-first canto.
Śrī Rāma said:
O Sage, just as for us there is this circle of dream-cities and towns, [so it is for others].
In the same way, if there were the assumption of a body for Padmajā and the others, [then... || 1 ||
Here it is established through reasoning that the world is like a dream or an illusion;
and because there is no contradiction anywhere, everything arises through delusion.

If the entire world is an illusion fashioned by delusion, resembling a dream, belonging to the Supreme Self, then from the perspective of Brahmā and others, it appears precisely as a dream-like illusion; yet from our own perspective, it does not appear like a dream, but rather as something more solid and real—what is the cause of this discrepancy? Nor can it be argued that for us it is so because of its persistence over a long period of time.

The resolution that "it appears" is logical; for even for Brahmā and others whose lifespan is two *parārdhas*, because they continue in *saṃsāra* for a period even longer than that, there arises an excess of firmness regarding its reality. With this intention, Rāma asks:
"If all this has arisen in that very way, and everything consists of unreality (*asat*)," [he continues].
How has such a firm conviction arisen within us? || 2 ||
The meaning is: why has such an extremely firm conviction in the reality of phenomenal proliferation (prapañca) arisen for us alone, and not for those born from the lotus and others? || 2 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
The previous creation of Prajāpati appears like our own creation;
it exists as a manifestation of consciousness throughout its life, but it is not real.

With the intention that it is precisely an uncontradicted long-standing persistence that is the cause for the firmness of the delusion of reality— and not a contradicted long-standing persistence— Vasiṣṭha replies with the verse beginning "Asmad-": "When this lotus-born one was previously in the state of a practitioner,
then, due to the absence of knowledge of reality, the creation of that time belonging to this Prajāpati..."

Now, although this world— which consists of the manifestation of living beings characterized by the fourfold collection of elements— appears as truly real on all sides, just like the creation currently being experienced by us, nevertheless,
because it has been sublated by the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), it does not exist in an ultimate sense.
Because consciousness is all-pervading, the individual soul is everything and transmigrates everywhere;
and that [transmigration] arises from incorrect vision and is destroyed by correct vision.

As long as there is ignorance, so long—because consciousness (citi) is all-pervading—everything becomes the individual soul (jīva). And transmigratory existence (saṃsṛti) occurs only when that [ignorance] exists.
That [transmigratory existence] arises from ignorance, which is the opposite of right vision; the meaning is that it is of such a nature that it is liable to be destroyed by right vision. || 4 ||
This appearance that has arisen, which consists solely of the notion of "I," is like a dream; yet it remains exceedingly firm. (5)

Therefore, that appearance of the world which arose for this Prajāpati— illusory like a dream and fragile, though sublated by his knowledge of reality— became fused into a single identity with the sense of "I" (ahaṃtā) held by ignorant people such as ourselves, and thus remained exceedingly firm. || 5 ||
Just as a man does not perceive the rapid destruction occurring within a dream,
so too is this [transience] perceived here by the Brahmins in every dream.

If it is asked, "In that case, why is the rapid perishability of the phenomenal world (prapañca) imagined by the Prajāpatis not experienced through their realization of its true nature?"—the answer is given with the intention that it is due to obstruction by the unseen merit/demerit (adṛṣṭa) of the enjoyer: "In a dream," etc. Just as for a sleeping person, because it is obstructed by karma that produces dream-enjoyment, the rapid perishability—though present in the dream—is not perceived.
The meaning is that just as it is seen in a collective dream, so too in this world, an obstruction to the realization of the perishability of the lotus-born Brahmas is observed. || 6 ||
This dream belongs to this person who experiences the manifestation;
likewise, Rāma, who is the self of all including ourselves, is exactly like that.

O Rāma, just as this well-known dream of this sleeping man—consisting of the perception of appearances—is such that its nature as the self of the entire world of all living beings like ourselves is a beginningless and endless flow, so too must it be for Prajāpati; such is the meaning. || 7 ||
That which is born from a dream-person has that dream-person as its essence;
for this is indeed experienced, just as a fruit has whatever was the seed as its nature. (8)

Let it be so; what follows from that? To this he says: "yad" (that which). The meaning is: just as the seed of that mango tree or the like is itself transformed into the form of the tree and fruit produced from it, and is not a different entity, so too is this case. || 8 ||
Know that to be unreal which is accomplished by means of the unreal;
even when an object is capable, it is not proper to engage in intense contemplation upon what is unreal. (9)

"Let it be so; even from that, what follows? To this he says: "It is indeed unreal. It is established that whatever is accomplished by the mind-person (*manaḥ-puruṣa*), which is itself unreal, is likewise unreal. Therefore, the meaning is that even though [the mind] is capable of causal efficacy regarding matters such as future births, heaven, and hell, it is not proper to cultivate a dense conviction in its reality. || 9 ||
Whatever arises from a person in a dream or similar state, which is firmly believed [to be real] though it is an unreal mental construction—that must be relinquished by whatever means possible. (10)
If by a certain reason something is not logical, then by that same reason even that which is firmly trusted should be abandoned. || 10 ||
That very [creation] appears to the self as a firm conviction, such as the beginning of creation;
this dream of creation standing before one lasts for no more than a moment. (11)
Furthermore, even for people like us, whatever appears as a dream-creation and so forth at that time is indeed characterized by firm conviction;

it is not perceived at that moment as a false cognition. However, the meaning is that its reality does not follow merely from this. All of this has been stated assuming that the creation of Prajāpati endures for a long period; in reality, however, even its duration...
He says that this occurs even in a short time, like the long duration of Hariścandra’s dream: "In a mere moment. This creation-dream of Prajāpati has increased like the annual flood of a city. 11.
In that very instant, the state of an eon (kalpa) is imagined,
just as this long fragment of a dream arises for Prajāpati.

He says that, just as in the case of Prajāpati, at that time there is indeed the perception of vast expansion for all beings within their respective dreams: "In the same way, what is called 'creation' has arisen for every single living being;
the succession of the multitude of creations exists solely through the nature of the principle of consciousness (cittattva). (13)

With the intention that "being perceivable"—meaning having its establishment dependent upon consciousness—is the determinant for falsity, and that this is common to both [the self and the world], he says: "of the principle of consciousness" (cittattvasya). || 13 ||
Just as water quivers through its fluidity by means of the swirling of eddies,
so too this splendor of creation is merely of the nature of a dream and is not real.
Then indeed this world arises; that state has reached dissolution.
Just as, in whatever manner, and of whatever nature it was seen, so does it exist in that same way. || 15 ||

That state belonging to Prajāpati, together with creation and so forth, having gone to dissolution, is indeed absolutely non-existent; thus, there is neither cessation nor origination, neither the bound nor the seeker, neither the one desiring liberation nor liberation—this is the ultimate reality (*paramārthatā*). The meaning is that this well-known scriptural statement is possible. [Objection: But if this is absolutely non-existent, how is it fit for worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*)?
Since it is observed to be so, there is nothing here to be questioned; thus he says: "In whatever manner... (yadyathā). || 15 ||
For the ways of dream-delusions are not to be questioned;
there is nothing in this world that cannot occur within a delusion.
He states that ignorance is not to be questioned even because of its power to bring about the impossible—“not that,” [verse 16].

Diverse perceptions of reality (or, according to another reading, diverse creations of objects) are seen throughout the three worlds, such as fire burning in the midst of water, like the submarine fire in the ocean. (17)
He illustrates the appearance of many improbable things in the world with the verse beginning "vicitrā" (various), etc. (17).
Cities exist in the sky like the abodes of the celestial beings; lotuses grow upon stones, and trees flourish upon the Golden Mountain. (18)
In the Hemādri [section], it is stated: "without earth. (18)
In that solitary place, all merits reside like those on a wish-fulfilling tree;
the rocks bear fruit as if they were fruit-bearing trees, and the clusters of gems are like blossoms. (19)

In a certain secluded spot, all merits—meaning all desired objects that constitute the fruits of merit; if the reading is *paṇyāni*, it refers to commodities, that is, things suitable for trade; but if the reading is *puṣpāṇi*, it is clear [that they are flowers]. The words "just as" (*yathā*) are used everywhere for the purpose of illustration. "Like a fruit-bearing tree" means like a tree laden with fruit. "Jeweled clusters" (*ratnagulucchaka*) are clusters of wish-fulfilling gems (*cintāmaṇi*). || 19 ||
Living beings exist within stones, like frogs inside a rock;
or water issues forth from stones, as from a moonstone.
In a mere moment, a jar becomes a cloth within the consciousness of sleep;
just as in a dream, one may perceive even that which is unreal, such as one's own death.
In the consciousness of sleep, [that is] in a dream. || 21 ||
Just as water belonging to the elements is held spontaneously in the sky,
so does the water remain in the firmament like a canopy, like the celestial river.
The Svarṇadī is the Mandākinī. || 22 ||
Large stones fly up like winged mountains;
indeed, everything is obtained within the stone, just as from a wish-fulfilling gem.
O Raghava, thoughts bear fruit quickly, just as they do within the gardens of the gods; yet those very same thoughts do not bear fruit quickly for liberation and the like.

They do not bear fruit; they do not arise. The meaning is that even the thoughts of those whose resolutions are true do not bear fruit regarding such matters as: "Let liberation arise," "Let Brahmā perish," "Let the phenomenal world be real," "Let enjoyments be eternal," "Let destiny be broken," or "Let the Vedas become non-authoritative. || 24 ||
Even though devoid of consciousness, it performs action like a mechanical man;
such are these and other various manifestations of diverse undertakings. (25)

The grammatical connection is as follows: "Impossible things, improbable things, and other various bewildering undertakings were seen through the playful illusions of Śambara, Gandharva, and others. (25)
Even through the playful illusions of Śambara and the Gandharvas, things have never been seen that could be produced by the movement of space, time, action, substances, or jewels. (26)

The meaning is that various diverse manifestations and delusions have been observed: such as [the moon appearing] the size of a thumb due to distance and so forth in terms of *deśa* (place); the appearance of a headless trunk (*kabandha*) in the sky during portents and so forth in terms of *kāla* (time); and those produced through the performance of mantra-practices and the like, by means of medicinal substances, gems, jewels, vehicles for traveling, and the entry of *piśācas*, intoxication, and so forth. || 26 ||
Objects produced by Gandharvas are infinite and arise from truth;
yet this impossibility itself becomes possible when it is to be so. (27)
The connection with the preceding clause is as follows: "Those from which the occurrence of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) has been observed to be like that of real things.
Now, even this impossibility—the future destruction of the universe and so forth—is possible; thus, its occurrence is logically established.
Manifestation and non-manifestation are both rightly for the sake of accomplishment; it is a delusion like a dream.
There is nothing that is not true, and there is nothing that is not false.

Thus, even this manifestation in the form of creation is a delusion like a dream; its non-existence during dissolution and upon the awakening to reality serves for the sake of accomplishment—that is, for resting in one's own true nature. And so, it is established that when viewed as Brahman, nothing is unreal, whereas when viewed as the world, nothing is real; thus he says: "Not that... (28).
Everything, by everything, everywhere—in that which is called a creation, within a dream—a living being whose intellect is immersed in the dream perceives it as if it were stable. (29)
With his intellect immersed in the dream of creation, he perceives stability in that same way;
moving from one delusion to another, passing from one dream to another,
the living being here becomes utterly bewildered by the experience of an exceedingly firm conviction.

Just as a bewildered deer, falling into the fault of plunging into a chasm, enters another abyss, so too does the living being, deluded by the fall into cyclic existence, enter a state of confusion whose sole nature is that of a downfall.
Just as a deluded deer causes itself to fall into pits—

being "pit-fallers" (*śvabhranipāta*) because of such a defect of its own delusion— and thus goes from one pit to another, so too do passion and the like cause one to fall into the cycle of existence; they are "existence-fallers" (*saṃsṛtipātāḥ*), and the deluded soul, by virtue of being subject to falling, [enters them].

There is no exit from the midst of the forest of worldly existence that is uniform; the meaning is that therein one falls into such delusion—the error of entering the pit of the body and so forth. || 31 ||

Thus ends the sixty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the World as a Dream," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the Mokṣopāya section of the Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa composed by Vālmīki.
Thus ends the sixty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the World as a Dream," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The sixty-second canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: "In this regard, O Rāghava, I shall relate this ancient history; listen."
This is the account of a certain monk who was possessed of some degree of reflective discernment.
In the narrative of Jīvaṭa, the mental activity of the mendicant is described as the delusion of attaining various bodies due to the connection with diverse latent impressions (vāsanās).
In this regard, concerning the matter described as "moving from one delusion to another," there is an ancient history (itihāsa) which serves as an illustration;
that is, the account of what actually occurred. || 1 ||
There was a certain great monk who was devoted to the practice of meditative absorption; he spent his entire day constantly engaged in his own religious observances. (2)

A great mendicant (bhikṣu) is one endowed with tranquility, self-control, dispassion, and so forth; by his own conduct—that is, by the conduct appropriate to his stage of life, such as hearing, reflecting, and so on. || 2 ||
That mind of his, purified by the practice of meditative concentration, instantly contemplates whatever it thinks of and quickly attains that state, just as water becomes waves.

Samādhi is the bringing about of the mind’s voidness of its prior nature through the firmness of the form of the object of meditation; for it is said by Patañjali: "That very state, in which only the object appears and [the mind] is as if void of its own nature, is samādhi. Through the practice of that, [the mind] becomes pure and capable of abandoning former latent impressions (vāsanā), just as water [is free from] waves. || 3 ||
Once, having ceased from his meditative absorption and remaining one-pointed in mind,
he sat upon his seat and reflected for a moment on the sequence of ritual actions.
Single-minded, with a one-pointed mind. || 4 ||
As he was reflecting, this thought arose spontaneously within him:
"I shall quickly manifest the conduct of an ordinary person for the sake of my divine play."
Ordinary people, devoid of refinement through the scriptures, [perceive] that state as being merely a conformity with the movements of the mind. || 5 ||
Having reflected thus, his mind remained for a moment in an intermediate state,
like water returning to its source simply by abandoning its vibration and configuration.

The "other person" (*narāntaram*) refers to another common man who is not restrained by the duties of an ascetic. Just as when water is made to whirl, it remains in the form of a vortex called an *āvarta*—which has the shape of a navel—merely by abandoning its previous state of flow and its uniform distribution, so too is it here. || 6 ||
Then, by that man of consciousness, a name was assumed out of self-desire;
suddenly, "I am Jīvaṭa" became established, as if by the coincidence of the crow and the palm fruit.
In that regard, he states the necessary conceptual construction of the name with the words "by that" (tena). || 7 ||
Then Jīvaṭa, that man created by a dream, wandered for a long time through the streets of a certain city constructed within a dream.
There he drank the drink, intoxicated like a bee drinking the nectar of a lotus;
being firmly delighted, he fell asleep with a deep slumber as if in sport.
Joyful and intoxicated. || 9 ||
In a dream, he beheld his own state as a Brahmin, content with study and ritual practice,
endowed with mere intuitive insight, as if having reached another land within his own mind.

That best of the twice-born was ever content with his recitations, studies, and the performance of virtuous deeds; he was never satisfied by the conduct of ordinary people. Through his dedication to his daily duties, he slept with his internal faculties withdrawn, like a tree whose activity has returned to its state as a seed.

The word "exhausted" (śrāntaḥ) is to be understood as the ellipsis [of the phrase], meaning "exhausted by his devotion to daily activities. One whose worldly activity has dissolved into the nature of internal latent impressions (saṃskāra);
just as a tree exists within the state of a seed with its latent impressions of branches and so forth remaining inside, so it is here. || 11 ||
Then, in a dream, the twice-born man himself saw the status of a feudal lord within himself;
that lord, having finished his meal, once fell into a deep sleep.
The state of being a vassal, that is, the kingship of a local ruler. || 12 ||
In a dream, he saw her possessing royal splendor as she protected the circle of the quarters,
cherished by a multitude of enjoyments like a creeper nurtured by a profusion of flowers.
Having taken his meal and eaten, he fell into a deep sleep; [he then beheld] her who was such that her nature was to protect the circles of the quarters, the sovereignty of the world. 13.
Once, that king, his desires stilled, slept peacefully;
his own future conduct was present before him, as if the effect were manifest within its cause.

One whose own inherent nature (*ācāra*), consisting of the flow of blood from women, is present and ready to yield its fruit; [this refers to] one's own effect, such as a tree, [arising] from its cause, the seed. || 14 ||
In a dream, she beheld within herself the irreproachable state of a celestial woman,
appearing like a blossoming cluster of flowers arising from the exuberance of the sap within a tree’s core.

Even though she enjoys the company of many men, her state as a celestial woman—that is, as an *apsaras*—is irreproachable; this description is either a figurative expression based on the attribution of sentience during the height of passion, or it is a statement regarding the "life" (*jīva*) of a tree.
Exhausted by passion, that celestial woman fell into a deep sleep;
she naturally transformed herself into a female deer, just as water turns into ice.
It is implied that she perceived herself as a doe due to the latent desire for the beauty of a doe’s eyes; *ambutā* refers to the state of being equal to water. || 16 ||
Once, that doe with tremulous eyes was overcome by sleep;
in a dream, she beheld within herself, through her own habitual practice, the state of being a creeper.
Even animals perceive dreams due to the nature of the mind;
for those things seen and heard, the memory in the consciousness remains unimpaired.

To those who doubt whether animals possess the experience of dreams or not, he says: "Animals [also have it]. The intention is that because the mind grasps the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of what has been seen and heard, when such an impression exists, the dream-experience—just like memory—is unavoidable. || 18 ||
She became like a forest goddess sporting in a bower of creepers within the woodland garden, graced with flowers, fruits, and tender shoots. (19)
Due to her attachment to the sprouts of the creeper, she became like a forest goddess who delights in a famous bower of creepers in the woods. (19)
By means of an internal consciousness that had ascended to the form of a sprout situated within a seed,
she clearly perceived her own cutting.

That creeper, having for some time experienced the dullness of sleep— the state of deep slumber— through internal awareness, that is, through the witnessing consciousness, [then] by means of a mind intent on dreaming, whose nature was like that of the intellect (dhi) abiding within a seed and possessing the form of a future sprout, and which had awakened the latent impressions (saṃskāra) in the form of a bee, [she perceived] herself.
The grammatical construction is: "He saw the bee. || 20 ||
Having remained in deep sleep for some time and experienced a dense state of insentience through his subtle power (kalā),
he then beheld himself as a steady bee.
Then that six-footed one roamed in the forest among the forest creepers and in the blooming lotus ponds, like a lover among young women.
The floral honey, possessing a taste like that of the sweet nectar from the lips of beloved women,
abounded among the swarms of bees hovering over clusters of blossoms and amidst the graceful play of pearl-like creepers.
"He drank the flower-honey, the nectar"—this is the ellipsis. || 23 ||
He became addicted to the lotus stalks within the lotus pond;
for even the mind of one with dull intellect finds delight in something or other. (24)
Being addicted and excessively attached, he became like a lotus stalk that has become entangled within another lotus stalk. || 24 ||
An elephant came to that lotus pond to agitate it;
for the foot of the deluded is raised only for the destruction of beautiful things. (25)
The state is determined; it yawns, that is, it expands. || 25 ||
That very lotus pond was crushed along with him, and he, like a six-legged bee,
having entered between the tusks, was reduced to powder like a grain of rice.

That lotus pond, frequented by bees, was crushed by that elephant; along with its stalk, the bee entered between the elephant's tusks and, being chewed like a black grain of rice stuck to a stalk of corn, was reduced to powder.
From the sight of the elephant and through the mental cultivation of that sight of the elephant, the bee perceived itself as having arisen in the form of a scent-intoxicated elephant.

Because the elephant is seen by means of light, that which is seen is "light" (āloka), meaning its form; through the cultivation of that [form], he saw himself arisen and transformed into the state of a rutting elephant. || 27 ||
The elephant fell into a pit as deep as a dried-up ocean, like a living being in this empty world, dense with thick darkness. (28)

That elephant, in the pit dug by the mahouts, experienced the sufferings of helplessness like a living being in this dense and harsh cycle of existence (saṃsāra), even more so than from thick chains and other bonds. || 28 ||
He became the king’s favorite, a destroyer of great enemy forces; always intoxicated by the power of his rut, that night-stalker seemed as if he were reeling. (29)
"Niśācara" (night-walker) is to be construed with what follows. || 29 ||
Once, severed by a sword, it went to its destruction,
like the individual soul (jīva) within the self when its form has been blown away by the wind of discernment (viveka).

Once, while moving about as a "night-walker" (niśācara) during the onset of a nocturnal battle, he was cut down by "thirty-fingers" (nistriṃśa)— that is, by thirty long swords— and having been severed by those small blades, he met his death. His life-force...
The limiting adjunct of the individual soul (jīvopādhi) is like the conceit of being the body and so forth. || 30 ||
Seeing the bees rising from the frontal globes of the temples of the herd of elephants, the elephant—due to his habit of seeing bees on his own temples—once again became a bee. (31)

[He saw] those [bees] that had flown up from the tops of the frontal globes (*kumbha*) of the herds of elephants (*gajaghaṭā*, i.e., multitudes of elephants). The intention is as follows: due to the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) resulting from long-term practice and constant cultivation, the latent impression for the perception of flying up was awakened.
While enjoying the forest creeper, he returned once more to the lotus pond; for the habitual tendencies of one who lacks awakening are difficult to abandon and hard to overcome. (32)

The meaning is "again by means of former impressions. [The word] *abodhinaḥ* means "of the ignorant one. The genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used in the sense of the remaining relation (*śeṣe*), and not in the sense of the agent (*kartari*), because of the prohibition [contained in the rule] *na lokāvyayaniṣṭhākhalarthatṛnām*. || 32 ||
There, being trampled by the elephant's hoof, he was once again crushed to pieces;
yet, through the perception of a swan standing nearby, he became a *kalahaṃsaka* (a type of small crane).
"By perception" means by direct vision; that is to say, by the latent impression (vāsanā) awakened thereby. || 33 ||
After wallowing for a very long time in other wombs,
Kalahaṃsa eventually came together with many swans and sported with them.

By the statement "rolling about in other wombs," it is understood that eighty-five births occurred in the interim, according to the direction that will be stated later: "Having become a swan in a lotus grove, an elephant in the Vindhya marshes, a deer in the body-machine, and so forth. Thus, after the two births as a swan mentioned here, he attained the state of Rudra.

"At the end of a hundred cycles of saṃsāra, I am established as that Rudra"—thus he will say. The meaning is that once, having attained birth again as a swan, he sported in the company of other swans. || 34 ||
Consciousness, consisting of the Brahman-goose, possesses the word and its meaning to a slight degree;
therein, it becomes nourished within, like a peacock in the midst of the juice of a mango fruit.

In that assembly of swans, because of hearing the descriptions of the qualities, form, and so forth of the Brahma-swans, his consciousness—consisting of the nature of a Brahma-swans—became twofold: both accompanied by sound (the utterance of their names) and endowed with meaning (the mental image of their forms). Consequently, in that very birth, for him who had become a swan, there arose the latent impression (*vāsanā*): "May I too become such a Brahma-swans."
The mind of the monk is nourished, as previously described, like a peacock situated in the essence of an egg; the meaning is that it has become solidified. || 35 ||
While dwelling upon that thought, he died, severely afflicted by disease and woodworms;
through the continued connection with that consciousness, he was born as a crane in the lake of the Lotus-born One.

Constantly practicing and revolving that very thought of the Brahman-goose, he—struck by disease like a wood-worm—became the "Borne One" (*bhṛta*) of the Lotus-born; that is to say, by figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), he became the goose who is the vehicle (*vāhana*). || 36 ||

In that state—both in that birth and in the world of Brahmā—for one who possesses exceedingly constant discernment and has been awakened by aesthetic delights, whose vision of worldly objects has vanished, and who stands liberated; indeed, what is there to be contemplated regarding what might happen to him at the dissolution of the age, since he is already liberated while in the body? (37) In that [birth] and in the world of Brahmā, for one who possesses discernment that is pre-eminently continuous...

Having been perfectly enlightened by Prajāpati through the playful instructions on discernment (*viveka*), dispassion (*vairāgya*), and knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), he—being one for whom the perception of substantiality in worldly objects and the category of enjoyments has thus vanished—remained liberated, that is, as one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*). Thus, while still alive, having attained the bliss of liberation consisting of unsurpassed bliss, [the text continues: "with Brahmā, they..."

"When the dissolution has arrived at the end of the supreme [cycle], those of perfected self enter the supreme state"—according to this Vedic scripture, at the conclusion of the two *parārdhas* during the ritual of the end of the age (*yugānta*), what further goal remains to be accomplished for that Swan, who is liberated from the body along with Brahmā? This should be discerned and reflected upon by the wise. The particle *u* is used here in the sense of deliberation (*vitarka*). By means of knowledge, even in this very life...

The meaning is that he has accomplished all that was to be done, because the cessation of misfortune along with its root has been achieved, the attainment of unsurpassed bliss has been secured, and there exists no further human goal (puruṣārtha) beyond that. || 37 ||
Thus ends the sixty-second chapter, titled "The Example of the Monk’s Saṃsāra," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.

Thus ends the sixty-second canto, titled "The Example of the Monk’s Saṃsāra," within the *Śata-rudrīya-svapna* section of the *Jīvaṭa-upākhyāna*, in the *Mokṣopāya* of the *Vāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa*. This concludes the portion concerning the ancient sage (*ārṣa*).
The sixty-third canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Once, that bird then beheld Rudra in the city of Rudra.
By means of the effortless acquisition of the playful stalk of the lotus of Brahmā. || 1 ||
By him, having become Rudra, there occurs here the awakening of his former body;
and their state as the hundred Rudras and their identity with him are described in this [chapter].
That swan, by means of his effortless play—

namely, through the attainment of sport (*līlā*) upon the stalk of the lotus-throne of Brahmā (which signifies the power of attaining liberation in the proximity of the Lotus-born)— once went to the city of Rudra with the Lotus-born and beheld Rudra. || 1 ||
There, the thought "I am Rudra" arose in him with certainty, reflected instantly like an image in a mirror. (2)

In that state, because he perceived the preeminence of all qualities—such as knowledge, yoga, and sovereignty—in Rudra, the Haṃsa developed a resolute intellect, thinking through the contemplation of "I am Rudra": "May I also become Rudra. Now, one might ask: how can there be such a longing for the state of Rudra in a Haṃsa who is liberated while living (jīvanmukta) and free from latent impressions (nirvāsana)? [The answer is: Through the practice of that contemplation and the subsequent casting off of the body...

And there is the assumption of Rudra’s body. However, if—according to the principle that Bharata [attains liberation] through three births—he assumes another body due to the remainder of his *prārabdha* karma to be experienced in various forms, then the description of his maintaining the identity of Rudra would result in being irrelevant; for since Rudra is the Lord (*Īśvara*), that state [of identity] is [eternal].
If it is argued that this is because [such a state] is incompatible with being the fruit of karma, he replies: "Like a reflection. This state of Rudra is not primary;

rather, it is liberation through similarity (sārūpya-mukti), which is indeed the fruit of ritual action and meditation, according to the Vedic scripture: "Having become a god, one goes to the gods" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.1.2). This is the intended meaning. || 2 ||
There, that being whose body was composed of Rudra abandoned his physical form,
just as a fragrance released from a cluster of flowers attains the state of the wind.

Nor was this another birth; rather, it was merely the abandonment of his former body through the mental construction of another body, like a yogi, by means of a desire brought about by the remnants of his *prārabdha* karma.
With this intention, he says: "That Rudra sported at will in the abode of Rudra."
By those various practices of the Śiva-purāṇa, [she was honored] by that which is most eminent among ten million Gaṇas.
By means of that which is most weighty and most excellent among millions of groups—that is to say, by the rank of the lordship over the Gaṇas. || 4 ||
Rudra, however, by means of that singular manifestation of unsurpassed knowledge,
perceived with his intellect his own entire previous history.

With the intention that even though there is an absence of authority over activities such as the dissolution of the world in the state of liberation characterized by similarity (sārūpya-mukti), there still exists equality with the well-known Rudra by virtue of his knowledge, sovereignty, and so forth, he says: "But Rudra...
[meaning] through identity and equality with the well-known Rudra by means of unsurpassed knowledges and the play of sovereignties. || 5 ||
Then that Blessed One, whose body is consciousness free from obscuration,
spoke of his own accord in private, amazed by the hundreds of his own dreams.
He spoke thus to himself in solitude, as if within his own mind.
Oh, how wondrous is this illusion, which spreads and deludes the entire world;
though unreal, it appears as real, like water in the desert sands.
Thus, first it was realized: "I, who am consciousness, have attained the state of the mind, through the contemplation of the sky-like nature of the All-perfect and All-knowing One. (8)
The particle *ā* is a nipāta (indeclinable) used to indicate recollection (*smaraṇa*). The meaning is that I first existed as pure consciousness (*cit*) alone through my prior ultimate state;

then, through *māyā*, I attained the state of being the mind (*cittatā*)—the activity of the volition of creation, thinking "May I become many, may I be born"—and thus this was known and remembered. It is from such a volition alone that I have become possessed of everything.
The meaning is that he has become omniscient in his conscious aspect, while in his insentient aspect he possesses divisions such as space and so forth. || 8 ||
Abiding by chance, the individual soul, colored by the subtle elements of the beings, became in a certain creation a mendicant, entirely unperturbed.

Then, by chance, through the entry of the self as the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) into the individual and collective gross bodies (*sthūladeha*) consisting of the subtle and gross elements, and by means of the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of identity with those bodies, the self—
being colored like a canvas by the variety of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) residing therein— becomes the *jīva* and remains as "I. And that...

The individual soul (jīva), experiencing a succession of births since beginningless time, became in a certain creation a mendicant wandering ascetic (bhikṣu-parivrāj), undisturbed by sense objects due to his proficiency in dispassion and meditative absorption.
Thus, through the union of the parts, when she sports freely outside with a playful and undisturbed form, she is "Rati" by virtue of her essential nature.

He demonstrates the arising of the power to completely forget his former body and so forth— through the proficiency gained by practicing the restraint of the mind via the grasping of "this" or the grasping of "I" toward beautiful external objects, while being devoid of self-knowledge—
by means of the passage beginning with "By him," etc.: "By that mendicant, through the stability of the bound lotus posture..."

When, through the binding and restraint of the limbs of the gross body— such as the hands and feet— and the limbs of the subtle body— such as the vital breaths and the senses— the play of mental worship and so forth toward external objects like deities is commenced with the feeling that it alone is delightful, then, by the power of that practice, he [the practitioner] engages in that very play.
The connection with the subsequent [verse] is: "He experienced [this] by means of the crushing of all those various opposing states. || 10 ||

At that time, through the power of that practice and by the total dissolution of all objective existents, that monk experienced that very [state], having abandoned any other arising of mental construction. (11)
Whatever wonder has taken root in the mind, that alone unfolds;
a creeper scorched by the summer heat does not yield even when water sweet as honey is drunk.

He provides an illustration for the sublation of even a previously established wonder by a subsequent, firmly rooted wonder: "The creeper" (vallī). A creeper pervaded by the wonder of the summer heat (*naidāghī*) abandons—even though it has drunk water during the spring season (*mādhavam*)—the wonder of its verdant state; that is to say, it withers away. || 12 ||
Having become that monk Jīvaṭa, a living being with deeply ingrained latent impressions,
he wandered through those bodies like an ant through holes.

He states with the words "sa" and so forth that even for one who has attained perfection (*siddha*), if he engages in mental play that is contrary to the scriptures, there arises a succession of misfortunes. In those bodies, that is, in those wombs; by the phrase "one whose latent impressions have become worn out" (*jaraṭhavāsana*), [it is meant] when the latent impressions based on the scriptures have become lax.
It is indicated that the arising from the beginningless latent impressions of what is harmful is inevitable. || 13 ||
Then, due to his devotion to the twice-born within himself, he perceived his own state as that of a twice-born;
for in the reversal of existence and non-existence, that which is powerful alone increases.
He elaborates on those very points with their respective causes, beginning with the words "in the self" and so forth.

When the reversal—that is, the inversion—of both manifest existence (*bhāva*) and unmanifest non-existence (*abhāva*) is to be established, it is the accumulation of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) alone that increases and emerges through the power of proficiency in practice, while the other becomes concealed; this is the meaning. || 14 ||
That brahmin attained the state of being constantly meditated upon;
for a sap, when drunk continuously, reaches fruition in a tree.
Because he performed acts of righteousness for the sake of his kingdom, he became a king;
yet, due to his lustfulness, that king attained the state of a celestial nymph.
By means of lustfulness accompanied by an accumulation of merit. || 16 ||
Out of a longing for her eyes, that fawn, full of passion, became deluded by latent impressions; alas, such infatuation leads to suffering for living beings! (17)
By the word *locanā*, the beauty of the deer-eyed one is indicated; out of longing for that, she is restless, full of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), and enamored. (17)
Alas, that doe remained fixed in her mind upon the creeper in the forest;
she, the little creeper, inevitably experienced being cut down.
Salt is the cutting [agent]. || 18 ||
Then, through that crushing pressure, she— being permeated by that state of being— beheld within herself the condition of a bee, long practiced through internal consciousness.
"With crushing" means with creepers and other things accompanied by cutting and crushing. || 19 ||
Then, having experienced the crushing of elephants and donkeys,
he wandered again and again through the agitations of the great cycle of existence.
By the phrase "again and again," the ninety-nine intermediate births— such as those as an elephant, a snake, a swan, and so forth— are said to be remembered.
At the end of hundreds of such transmigrations, I remain as that very Rudra,
amidst this frantic activity of saṃsāra which is a delusion consisting solely of one's own mind.
That monk remained thinking, "I am indeed Rudra. || 21 ||
Thus, in these many and exceedingly variegated forest-lands of saṃsāra, I have wandered excessively and repeatedly, as if they were not empty. (22)
While they appear as if real and non-empty. || 22 ||
In one creation I was named Jīvaṭa;
in another, I was an excellent Brāhmaṇa; and in another, a lord of the earth.
Having been a swan in a lotus grove and an elephant in the Vindhya marshlands, I have now reached this state as a deer within the machinery of a body. (24)

In the Vindhya valley, I was an elephant and a deer; thus, from my first birth, within this machine of a body—and likewise within the machine of the mind—I have reached this state described above. (24)
Here, infinite thousands of years and hundreds of four-age cycles (caturyugas) have passed, along with the movements of days and seasons.

From the time of my first creation, ever since I moved away from and fell from the supreme state whose nature is the single essence of consciousness, infinite thousands of years and hundreds of four-age cycles have passed in this world, as well as endless days, seasons, and courses of time.
For me, as soon as I first moved away from the supreme state, the sequence of fitness for mendicancy was established through my realization of reality. (26)

The sequence of practice (*abhyāsakrama*) is as follows: even though the capacity for becoming a knower of reality through the state of being a monk—consisting of the repeated cultivation of hearing, reflection, and so forth—has been firmly established, one may, due to negligence, overstep it and repeatedly attain the status of a "Brahma-swans" (liberated souls) through a succession of births; that very same prior practice is what is then cultivated again.

The connection between the two is that [the state] has become Rudra through the arising of union with Rudra, and it has borne fruit by means of the fruit of the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna). || 26 ||
Having transcended even further again and again, he attained the state of a Brahman-swan;
that very same former practice had borne fruit through the arising of this auspicious association.
Whatever firm habit arises for this living being without obstruction,
that very habit it quickly pursues, even if it be utterly devoid of flavor.

For this very reason, the practice of scriptural means is superior, for even when interrupted by many contradictory births, it arises again and certainly accomplishes the goal of human life; thus he says: "Firm practice.
The ellipsis is: "even though it has been interrupted for a thousand births by one who is utterly devoid of taste [for spiritual matters]. (28)
Sometimes, through a chance encounter like that of the crow and the palm fruit, the soul's habitual practice of impure contemplation ceases due to association with the virtuous. (29)

In that case, by the same logic, even the cultivation of the impure might arise again, even if it has been interrupted by the practice of the pure; to this he replies: "by chance" (kākatālīya). || 29 ||
Furthermore, this prior habituation to latent impressions (vāsanā), acquired through association, depends solely upon its own arising; it awaits the effort of the seeker.

In that case, one might object: "Since the practice of virtuous impressions (*śubhavāsanā*) will arise spontaneously from previous latent tendencies (*saṃskāra*), and by their power alone this person will abandon unvirtuous impressions (*aśubhavāsanā*), the prescription of human effort is useless. Anticipating this, he says: "By association," etc. [referring to the one] who abandons the web of evil impressions.

For a person desiring to abandon [the world], this prior practice of virtuous latent impressions (*sadvāsanā*) awaits and expects its own manifestation at a later time through the effort of a holy person; the meaning is that it does not arise without that [effort]. || 30 ||
Whatever is practiced here incessantly, and whatever is practiced even in another body, though it be unreal in waking and dreaming states, it is experienced as real. (31)

And that effort becomes capable of destroying evil tendencies (*durvāsanā*) only through the firmness of virtuous tendencies (*sadvāsanā*) cultivated over many lifetimes, not all at once; with this intention, he says "and whatever" (*yacca*). By the phrase "even though unreal" (*asadapi*), it is meant that even an effort directed toward the worship of a deity or similar objects—which have an unreal nature—is [included] therein.

If one becomes capable of attaining results such as the state of a deity through the experience of the reality of the waking and dreaming states, then what need is there to mention that the effort of hearing [the scriptures] and so forth, which has the ultimate reality as its object, leads to the attainment of the nature of the ultimate truth accessible through valid means of knowledge? This is what is indicated. || 31 ||
That which performs various purposeful actions for the sake of both suffering and happiness arises from mental cultivation; therefore, victory consists in the cultivation of non-cultivation.
For this very reason, even the scriptural practice of contemplation (*bhāvanā*) directed toward the non-self leads only to pleasure mixed with suffering;

thus, the absolute conquest of misfortune consists solely in the eradication of all such contemplations, rather than in the intermediate attainment of divinity and so forth. With this intention, he says: "tattad" (that and that). That and that...

The practice of contemplating the selflessness [of all things] consists in cultivating the thought that [all phenomena] perform purposeful functions, such as the bodies and enjoyments of deities. (32)
Meditation itself perceives its own self as "this body," which is merely an expansion of non-existence, just as a sprout develops into a thicket.

Furthermore, with the intention that "this misfortune is caused solely by the lack of cultivation [of the self]; how then can it be pursued by one who fears it?", he says: "Cultivation alone... (verse 33).
When this cultivation is scrutinized, nothing at all remains here;
nor does it even exist. Therefore, let us have enough of that delusion. (34)

He says that it is destroyed merely by the vision of reality—namely, "by cultivation" (bhāvanā). Alternatively, he says "nor" (na ca) [is its destruction to be accomplished], because there is no destruction to be achieved for that which is non-existent, as it is eternally destroyed. || 34 ||
May this mere non-perception alone suffice for our cleansing of this worldly delusion, which has arisen like the color of the sky. 35.
This supreme Being, whose very nature is not composed of material elements, is to be cherished;
if she remains for the sake of diversion, she will do nothing else.

Alternatively, let there be no non-perception [of it]; for even if it is perceived, since it has been sublated by the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), it lacks the capacity to produce fear—just like a snake that has been [magically] dispelled—and thus it is not a source of harm. On the contrary, it serves as a cause for sport. Thus he says: "Consisting of the unreal" (*asanmayī*)... "merely a cause for curiosity. If it exists by way of apparent reality (*prātibhāsika-sattā*), then it is only for the sake of diversion.
