The meaning is that she will not cause even the slightest bit of harm, not even so much as an atom. || 36 ||
Having arisen, I behold all those individual cycles of transmigration;
by bestowing perfect vision upon them, I unify them.
Therefore, out of curiosity alone, having risen and gone there, I shall, by bestowing perfect vision—that is, awakening—unify my own self, which is distinct from those limiting adjuncts. || 37 ||
Having reflected thus, Rudra went to that creation where the mendicant was staying in his monastery, lying asleep like a corpse. (38)
Then, having awakened that monk through his own mind and intention, he joined him [to the truth]; and the monk also remembered his own delusion. (39)

Having awakened him and made him vigilant through his own mental portion— the mind, consciousness, and volition characterized as the reflection of his own essential consciousness— he united him with the *jīva* that knows reality. For this very reason, by means of the mendicant’s awakening, there is no longer the proliferation of sleep as seen in those such as ourselves, nor the bodies of living beings from Jīvaṭa up to Rudra, nor their respective worlds.

The consequence of the impossibility of continued persistence has been refuted; for, by the hypothesis that a portion of Rudra enters as the individual soul (jīva) everywhere, it is possible for all things—even those subject to sublation—to persist until the end of the kalpa, through the power of his true resolve (satyasaṃkalpa) and the force of the remainder of the diverse meritorious and demeritorious karma (adṛṣṭa) that brings about experience. || 39 ||
Beholding Rudra as his own self, and likewise as consisting of Jīvaṭa and others,
that mendicant, though not worthy of astonishment due to his awakening, nevertheless experienced amazement.

"From awakening," that is, from the vision of reality; "he was struck with wonder" because he beheld a marvel characterized by the experience of many births over a long period within a short time, as well as the persistence of his dream-body as Rudra and so forth. || 40 ||
Then Rudra and the mendicant both rose up and went together to some place within a single corner of the space of consciousness— the world of Jīvaṭa.
The cycle of existence for living beings is within the interior of the cosmic egg. || 41 ||
Having gone there to that world, to that continent,
to that region, to that country, and to that city, he took him by the hand with a sword grasped [in his other].

There, having entered the world by the manner described in the narrative of Līlā—that is, having gone to the earthly realm (bhūloka)—they saw Jīvaṭa there in that very place: on the island which was his dwelling, in the region within the district, and specifically in that house; and they saw him holding a sword in his hand. || 42 ||
They saw Jīvaṭaka sleeping, unconscious, like a corpse;
having established his physical state as radiant amidst the realms of existence. (43)

Like a corpse asleep; because the people there were unfit to behold him, he concealed his true nature as the mendicant Rudra and his intention to awaken Jīvaṭa. Having established all that splendor of Rudra—which possesses the brilliance of ten million suns—and having hidden it through the power of disappearance, [he remained] within the realms of worldly existence.
In the regions of the transmigratory existence of living beings. || 43 ||
Having quickly awakened him and directed him through both mind and consciousness, those who were of one form became threefold: Rudra, Jīva, and the mendicant.
"By the mind," and so forth, as before. Internally they have one form; externally they have three forms. || 44 ||
Though they were enlightened, they appeared as if unenlightened; though filled with wonder, they remained without wonder.
For a moment, they stood in silence like figures in a painting.
They possess forms fashioned by a painter, as if they were painted in a picture. || 45 ||
Then they all went to a certain place situated in the sky,
where a multitude of brahmins had begun a discourse, filled with a great clamor.

Established in the sky of consciousness (*cidākāśa*), it is situated in the midst [of all]; it is the "projected" (*ārabdha*) world, consisting of the transformations of the individual soul’s mind (*jīvaṭacitta*); it is filled with a humming sound, a clamor, from living beings on all sides. (46)
Having gone there to that world, they reached that island, that region, that district, that village, and that abode of the Brāhmaṇa. || 47 ||
"Those there," and so forth, as before. || 47 ||
They saw the Brahmin sleeping in his house, surrounded by his wife;
he was held by the neck by the Brahmin woman, appearing as if he were still alive.
His wife and the group of dependents were like his most beloved life-force that had gone outside.
Having quickly awakened him and directed him with both mind and consciousness, many others who were situated there likewise became filled with wonder and free from wonder. (49)
Then they went to the royal realm, which was filled with consciousness and perceived by the intellect, a sovereign domain beautiful in its expansive expanse of wandering.
The object of consciousness is the form of transformation belonging to the intellect (citi), which has evolved into the form of the mind (citta). || 50 ||
Then they reached the world, that island, and that region;
there they beheld the intoxicated Sāmanta sleeping upon a lotus-shaped couch.
In the lotus characterized by the paryaṅka posture. || 51 ||
Like a female bee following her mate sleeping within the calyx of a lotus, she— golden-limbed— placed him, white as gold, within the hollow of her breast.
He was surrounded by beloved women like a tree entwined with blossoming clusters,
standing amidst a network of lamps like a mass of gold set with a multitude of jewels.
Having quickly awakened him and directed him with both mind and consciousness,
those many who were situated there became as one— both filled with wonder and free from wonder.
"Abiding in that" means being situated there. || 54 ||
Then they went to the royal world; having awakened him there, they wandered thus by means of their minds through other realms of worldly existence.

By means of the mind alone, that is, by means of the subtle body (*ātivāhika-śarīra*) itself. In this interval, it should be understood that for those who are asleep there is merely awakening, whereas for those who are dead there is even restoration to life (*saṃjīvana*). || 55 ||
Having attained that state of Rudra through their desire for the Brahman-swan,
they all became the hundred supreme Rudras and shone forth.

The activity (*īhā*) in the form of a Brahma-swans is a transformation of the mind; it is supreme because it possesses both mental volition and consciousness, and because it is endowed with knowledge and sovereignty, being composed of portions of Rudra’s mental consciousness. All those bodies of the Rudras number one hundred.
That form of the Supreme Lord is of a single nature yet possesses manifold appearances; its body is differentiated within a single consciousness and is encompassed by diverse activities. (57)
He states that very point: "One," etc. (verse 57).
Then, that hundredfold [state] of the Rudras is composed of unobscured consciousness;
it abides as the connection to all saṃsāra and is situated throughout the entire world. || 58 ||
It is the foundational substratum related to the entire phenomenal world of appearance, and it abides within the whole universe itself as the inner controller (antaryāmin). || 58 ||
O Rāma, there are indeed hundreds of great Śatarudras here— [the reading "hundreds of ten Rudras" (daśarudraśatāni) is in accordance with the commentary].
Know this to be the eleventh, established throughout the cycle of worldly existence.
With the intention of explaining the state of those Rudras well-known from such Vedic passages as "Thousands upon thousands of such Rudras who are upon the earth," he says:
"A hundred..."— meaning that among the hundreds of worlds imagined by the mendicant Rudra,
this world which exists as being experienced by you and me is the eleventh.
Know the cycle of worldly existence to be like that of bees and Rudras. || 59 ||
Whatever arises on all sides for the individual soul is indeed its worldly existence (saṃsāra).
In that state, the multitudes of unawakened souls do not perceive one another.
[Objection: But why are all the dreams, monks, and transmigrations not experienced by everyone? To this he says: "Whichever...
That transmigratory existence of the individual soul (jīva), characterized as previously described, which arises on all sides—in those [transmigrations]... [60]
For those awakened in mind meet together like waves in the ocean;
but those who are unawakened, being limited to the mere objects [of perception], remain like clods of earth.
The intention is that those who know reality perceive everything through the mind, merging with those living beings. || 61 ||
Just as water in waves thoroughly mingles with one another due to its fluidity,
so too do the multitudes of awakened living beings thoroughly mingle with one another because of their consciousness.
And with the intention that the cause for their merging is the removal of grossness, he says "just as" (yathā). || 62 ||
When these two arise individually within saṃsāra, the multitudes of living beings exist as if real,
though they are unreal, due to the all-pervasive nature of the element of consciousness.

With the intention that the very attainment of oneness with Brahman—the reality of all living beings—is the merging with all those individual souls whose nature is merely imagined by Him, he says: "Each one... [referring to] the element of consciousness, the essence of consciousness, which is Brahman. (63)
Whatever is excavated from the earth, that very thing is called "space";
likewise, whatever is projected by the all-pervading consciousness, that is precisely consciousness itself.
It is carried away and removed—that is, it is eliminated by the vision of reality because of its lack of true existence—and thus, like the sky, only consciousness remains.
(64) Just as you perceive all the elements of phenomenal expansion here in this world, so too does the nature of consciousness, which is the self of all beings, exist everywhere. (65)
"Just as [the ether] manifests its existence everywhere like the sky, it makes its being experienced everywhere"—this is the meaning of "all" (*sarva*).

Just as you experience all the manifold particulars (*prapañca*) and their specific divisions, as well as the five elements associated with them, so too does your own consciousness (*cit*), which is the very nature of existence (*sattā*) that constitutes the self of all beings, exist everywhere; therefore, experience that. This is the sense of verse 65.

Just as a carved figure (śālabhañjikā) is seen in a tree, on a mountain, or in a chasm, having reached its end [therein], so too the single Self is perceived as the world situated within consciousness.
Regarding its omnipresence and the conceptualization of all things therein, he provides an illustration with the words "yad" (as for that which). Just as when, in a tree,
a piece of wood, a mountain, or a stone pillar, a cavity is carved by artisans using a chisel in accordance with the form of various images, [the space within] becomes the end (antakam).

The meaning is as follows: just as when the discernment of forms such as a man, an elephant, or a horse occurs, one perceives that very same [single] statue (*śālabhañjikā*) in various forms like a man and so forth;

in the same way, the single Self, which is of the nature of existence and possesses all forms, is perceived, and within that consciousness-nature (*cidrūpa*), the world is likewise perceived as situated. || 66 ||
In the supreme, pure state beyond sensation, that which exists as sensation in the world is without cause and lacks consciousness, being like the sky in its emptiness.
In the case of trees and the like, the delimitation is produced by axes or chasms; but here, what produces it? To this he replies: "In non-perception" (*avedane*).

The meaning is that when there is perception—that is, the bringing of the supreme, pure, and non-objective reality into the state of being an object—which is otherwise a form of ignorance, that alone constitutes the world and stands as the cause of delimitation within Brahman, whose sole essence is consciousness.
That insentience and dullness which takes the form of the world is without cause and entirely without basis; thus it exists as a void, like the sky. || 67 ||
Sensation exists as the bondage of the visible, while the absence of sensation is liberation. Whatever may be pleasing to you, that very thing you should quickly make firm.

And thus, it follows that such an experience itself is his bondage to the visible world, and its cessation alone is liberation; this is what he states in the verse beginning with "vidyate" (verse 68).
Creation and non-creation, bondage and liberation, consisting of sensation and the absence of sensation—both are non-different due to awakening; therefore, act as you wish.
Because of the awakening [of that], it is the witness of both. || 69 ||
But for one who lacks attachment, what distress can there be when that which did not exist is lost?
Know that whatever is to be attained through silence has already been swiftly attained. (70)
Since that which does not exist—due to a lack of perception arising from non-cognition—is a non-entity, what distress or exertion can there be for its destruction?

Furthermore, that happiness which is to be attained through silence has already been attained immediately; the meaning is that even in that case, there is no dependence on exertion. Indeed, that whose nature is mere cognition is such that its cessation occurs through the absence of cognition.
One should practice that which is desired by the feeling of that very feeling. || 71 ||
That which is the form of the world is essentially nothing but cognition; its destruction is precisely that which is non-cognition and non-perception.
It follows that the cognition of that world-cognition—which is the witnessing consciousness—is indeed attained.
Just as a wave is a vibration of water, so too is the world [a vibration] in Consciousness.
O descendant of Raghu, the difference here is merely this much: || 72 ||
He shows the dissimilarity between the example and the subject of the example with the words "only this much. Dissimilarity (vailakṣaṇya) means difference (bheda). || 72 ||

While place, time, and intrinsic nature exist in the case of water with its waves and so forth, at the beginning of the world, however, place and the rest do not exist, even though they are perceived in the world. (73)

He states that very point with the words "deśa" (space) and so forth: in Brahman, which is the primary material cause of the world's manifestation, space and the other categories—which were previously non-existent—are subsequently superimposed; they are perceived only within the sphere of the world, which constitutes the effect. || 73 ||

The triple world shines as the radiant Ābhāsvara; one's own consciousness, which is pure awareness itself, is the very nature of the intellect (*citi*). This [nature] remains present in speech, yet it becomes afflicted by differentiation through conceptualization; however, the supreme self, Śiva, is one whose speech is utterly tranquil.

That very consciousness (*caitanya*), which is its own nature, luminous and self-revealing, becomes as if non-luminous—possessing only a slight radiance—due to the veil of ignorance (*avidyā*). Having transcended the three worlds, it appears as something other than its true nature. The ultimate reality (*pāramārthika*) of that consciousness, which is of the nature of intelligence (*cit*), is pure knowing.

Knowledge alone is not inert; this triple world is afflicted by the differentiation [of that knowledge]. Gather and consolidate [this understanding] through the means shown in such scriptural passages as, "O gentle one, seek the root of water through its shoot, which is food," and so forth.

Once thus consolidated, [realize that] it is merely a modification—a mere name originating from speech—according to the direction shown in the scripture: "A modification is a mere name, a handle arising from speech."
It remains as mere speech; where even peaceful speech is merely speech, such is the Supreme Śiva—the meaning is that he is the Supreme Self (Paramātman). || 74 ||
In this world, all things are consciousness; thus, these two—word and meaning—are never distinct from one another.
To say that "the wave and the water are two" is not a fitting statement; indeed, such a claim would only be appropriate for one who is ignorant.

Thus, consciousness, which is the self's own sentience, and the entire world have become distinct from both word and object; these two never exist [as such]. The meaning is that this [distinction] is appropriate only when there is ignorance of the Self of the aforementioned nature, but not when there is knowledge. || 75 ||

Thus ends the sixty-third canto, titled "The Narration of the Hundred Rudras in a Dream," in the *Jīvaṭopākhyāna* of the *Pūrva-nirvāṇaprakaraṇa*, within the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by the sage Vālmīki.
Thus ends the sixty-third chapter, titled "The Narration of the Dream and the Śatarudrīya," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The sixty-fourth canto.
Śrī Rāma said:
O Lord of Sages, [tell me] about Jīvaṭa, the Brāhmaṇa, and the others, such as the swans.
What could be more perfect than this for the bodies of monks in their dreams? || 1 ||
Through those various bodies, their remaining experience (śeṣabhoga) is described here;
thereafter follows the attainment of the status of a Rudra-gaṇa and the process of stabilizing one's resolve (saṃkalpa).

Rāma asks about the state of Jīvaṭa—whether the remnants of the *prārabdha* karma of the enjoyer still exist within the eighty-nine intermediate bodies from the body of the monk up to the body of Rudra—or whether they do not, by asking "Jīvaṭa": the meaning is, did he meet with sublation like a dream-body, or has his worldly activity continued further? || 1 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Having come together with Rudra, they all became awakened; having mutually perceived the nature of saṃsāra, those who were portions of Rudra remained in happiness.
Those portions of Rudra, having previously witnessed each other's successive transmigrations, remained happy because they had accomplished all that was to be done. || 2 ||
Having observed that illusion as it had been described, Rudra sent his own partial incarnations back once more to maintain the state of worldly existence.
By that Rudra, who first set out to see the spectacle, [he perceived] that very state of worldly existence belonging to Jīvaṭa and the others.
Śrī Rudra said:
"Go quickly to your own abode; having enjoyed pleasures there together with your wives for some time, you shall return to my presence."
"You shall become my portions, you who are the hosts adorning my city;
thereafter, from the great dissolution, we shall go to that supreme state."

[This occurs] from the great dissolution up to the end of two parārdhas, upon the exhaustion of prārabdha [karma], along with a trace of avidyā that impels [the soul], or through the cessation of the manifestation of the world. || 5 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Having spoken thus, the blessed Lord Rudra vanished from their sight;
he entered into the midst of the Rudras who were engaged in the enumeration of the final cycle of worldly existence.

The witness-consciousness (sākṣicaitanya) that existed at that time as the perception and enumeration of the entire cycle of existence (saṃsāra) of all those Rudras—including the final Rudra—entered into each individual cycle of existence, such as that of Jīvaṭa and others, which lies in the intermediate state;
the meaning is that it was like a dream-witness entering into the waking state. || 6 ||
Jīvaṭa, the Brāhmaṇa, and the others also returned to their own abodes;
then, having spent their lives together with their wives, they eventually cast off their bodies in due time.
Having reached the world of Rudra, they will become the foremost of the Gaṇas;
at times they are seen in the sky, appearing in the form of stars.
From the statement "they will come to be," it is understood that at the time of the dialogue between Vasiṣṭha and Rāma, they were situated within their respective worlds of transmigration. || 8 ||
Śrī Rāma said:

Those beings, such as Jīvaṭa, the Brāhmaṇa, and others, were merely of the nature of the mendicant’s mental resolve (saṃkalpa). How did they attain reality? Wherein lies the reality of an object of a mental resolve?
The question is explicit, being a further inquiry regarding the very same matter already asked many times before, out of a desire for specific detail. || 9 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Abandon the notion of the reality of mental constructs within that part [of yourself] which consists of mental constructs;
for that which does not exist there does not exist at all, since that state is the self of all.

In the part that is the substratum-consciousness (*adhiṣṭhāna-cid-aṃśa*) alone; but as for the superimposed part, abandon through discrimination the notion of reality regarding that which is a product of volition (*saṃkalpa*). In that regard, within an object of volition composed of both the real and the unreal, that which—being distinct from the real—is absent in both prior and subsequent times, that alone does not exist. However, the substratum (*tatpada-adhiṣṭhāna*) exists indeed, because it is the self of all; therefore, by its very existence...
The meaning is that the capacity for causal efficacy belongs to an object of volition (saṃkalpika) awakened by the unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) of the enjoyer (bhojaka). || 10 ||
Whatever is seen in a dream and whatever is beheld through mental constructs exists in that very way there; at all times, it is of that same nature.
Having become identical with that which is the constant substratum at all times, it exists there eternally by virtue of being the very nature of that place and time. || 11 ||
Just as one goes to another place by means of having that [other] place and time as one's own nature,
so too there is no going from one place to another without the self and other such factors whose nature is movement.
He explains the phrase "having gone to another country" with the words "from a country," and so forth.

Just as from a country such as Mathurā one goes to another country such as Pāṭaliputra, there [in that new place], although [these things] exist, the movement—the going—is the self; the mind is composed; by the word "etcetera" [is meant] the proficiency of the eyes and other senses; time such as day and night; and the person who instructs in the discrimination [of reality].

Without such a collection of causes as these, [a dream] is not obtained; likewise, a dream is not obtained there—meaning in the states of waking or deep sleep, nor within another dream—this is the connection with the subsequent clause. || 12 ||
Just as a dream is not found apart from that [waking state], so too nothing is found apart from it;
everything exists within the treasury of consciousness, exactly as it perceives it.

In the treasury of consciousness— which resembles a storehouse and is the locus of all latent impressions (vāsanās) within ignorance— the more one observes and reflects through latent impressions awakened by the unseen force (adṛṣṭa) of the experiencer, the more that undivided, complete consciousness assumes the form of those objects as something visible. || 13 ||
He attains that very state of mind unimpaired, because he is the self of all; for, my dear, it is by means of that same condition that volition and dreaming are reached.
If there is a simultaneous perception of everything, such as dreams and mental constructs, then what is the means [to attain that state]? He says: "By resolve" (saṃkalpa).
The ellipsis is "hear how that state is attained. || 14 ||
But this is not obtained without supreme practice and yoga;
however, for those whose insights into the knowledge of yoga have borne fruit and remain steadfast, [it is attained]. (15)

Regarding the word "supreme" (param): the meaning is that it refers specifically to the stage of the ripening of the yoga of practice. In this regard, he states the distinction—namely, that for certain lords (*īśvara*), the fruit of yogic perfection exists by itself even without practice—with the words "But for those... (verse 15).
Since Śaṅkara and the others see everything everywhere, this object standing before me has been thus conceived by me. (16)
Practice (*abhyāsa*) and yoga are useful only insofar as they bring about one-pointedness (*aikāgrya*) regarding the object intended;
however, in the absence of one-pointedness, the mind, being distracted by many objects, does not obtain even that single object intended by its own volition.
With the intention that his power of true resolve (*satya-saṃkalpatā*) has thus failed, [the author] says "this," and so forth, [referring to the thought] "by me."

Because that which is devoid of one-pointedness cannot be attained, since the mind—by relying on both the intended object and its opposite—undergoes a fall from both and does not become steady in either; this is the connection with what follows. || 16 ||
Nor does he suffer the loss of both, because he relies upon both;
for every desired task is accomplished by one who is devoted to a single purpose. (17)

In the word *yataḥ*, the sandhi is archaic (*ārṣa*) because the elision of the *y* (yalopa) is treated as non-existent (*asiddha*). He supports the very point already stated with general statements, beginning with "all" (*sarvam*), etc. || 17 ||
Who, while going toward the southern quarter, reaches the northern direction?
Only by those intent on the object of their resolve is that intended object realized. (18)
The quarter of Kakubha. || 18 ||

Those intent on the object situated at the tip perceive the object established at the tip; he who desires to attain the mental resolve situated at the tip perceives that which is established in the intellect. (19)
Then, because of the absence of being fixed upon a single goal, he would destroy that pair;
therefore, by being fixed upon a single purpose, the life of a mendicant attains the state of Rudra.
He applies this to the subject at hand: "Therefore," etc. (20).
Having attained everything through their entire being, and having likewise obtained all things as they exist,
those who live by the resolve of mendicants each perceive that world as distinct.
In that same way, everything was obtained through omniscience, just as it is with the well-known Rudra, because his state is likewise established.

As for those intermediate living beings such as Jīvaṭa and others—the ninety-eight monks born of volitional resolve—since each of them abides in their own respective world-system, they do not see one another. || 21 ||
And they do not perceive one another except through the knowledge of Rudra;
therefore, these unawakened souls are born as living beings whose consciousness ends with the individual soul.

To the question of how they could have seen one another in the presence of Rudra, he says: "unawakened" (aprabuddhāḥ). The internal distinctions of transmigratory existence belonging to individual souls arise through the will of that Rudra, who awakens them. || 22 ||
By His will, they quickly assume those forms here, and they become many-formed;
"May I be a Vidyādhara here, may I be a scholar here. (23)

The meaning is that they are born in that form or in many forms solely by His will. However, regarding the perception of individual transmigratory existence, He states that their own will is the cause: "In this world... (verse 23).
Thus, the fruitfulness of single-minded concentration is the illustration for this state of action;
whether it be unity or multiplicity, or even folly or wisdom. (24)

For other living beings as well, within this well-known established order of activity— that is, within the system of their respective worldly conventions— this very creation resulting from the monk’s resolve serves as the illustrative example. This living being, in accordance with his efforts in concentration (*dhāraṇā*), meditation (*dhyāna*), and exertion (*yatna*), can achieve whatever he desires, whether sequentially or simultaneously, according to his will.
He states that [the Lord] is capable of doing so with the words beginning "oneness," etc. (verse 24).

Through the effort of concentration (*dhāraṇā*) and meditation (*dhyāna*), one is fully capable of simultaneously assuming both divinity and humanity by means of the sequences of place, time, and action. (25)
He is capable and able to perform [these actions] simultaneously through the sequences of place, time, and action. || 25 ||

The individual soul (*jīva*) possesses a single power by virtue of its essential nature, as stated by Kaiyaṭa in the Bhāṣya on the rule *śaktiyaṣṭyor īkak* (Pāṇini 5.2.103)— which notes that the suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied because it belongs to the *bahu-ādi* group— where he says "it has all powers.
Furthermore, its nature is inherently infinite and yet connected with limits (or endowed with them).

Regarding this, he states the reason: "sarva... (all). Since this individual soul (*jīva*) is, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), infinite, it therefore possesses all powers; yet, since it is conjoined with a limitation (*pariccheda*) characterized by the conceit (*abhimāna*) of each individual body, it consequently possesses power only for a single function at a time. And in accordance with the nature of its power, its own nature is determined by the specific nature of each respective function.
The meaning is "established. || 26 ||
O dear one, whether expanding or contracting, the living being who is non-violent toward that Self of Consciousness attains by itself whatever it desires.

For this very reason, the Lord of the World— though expanding through the creation of thousands of misfortunes such as heaven and hell according to the karma of living beings, and contracting through the dissolution of all living beings— is indeed non-violent (*ahiṃsra*),
being free from the defects of partiality and cruelty inherent in the act of violence; for this host of living beings is itself [the cause].

Whatever this Lord, whose nature is consciousness, desires, that very thing is accomplished according to His own will through His volition; the meaning is that nothing undesirable is done by Him to anyone. And thus is the aphorism of the venerable Bādarāyaṇa:
"Partiality and cruelty [are not attributed to the Lord] because He has regard for [other factors]. || 27 ||
By means of these very sequences of place, time, and action, which they themselves have accomplished,
yoginīs and yogins abide here, and wherever else they may be.

Now, he elaborates by way of an illustration the state of existing as one or many at will, which is the fruit of the effort of *dhāraṇā*, *dhyāna*, and *yoga*—beginning with the words "by those [powers] accomplished by himself.
Here, [it refers to] the sequences of actions pertaining to his office, such as the play of favoring or restraining living beings according to their respective places and times. In this world...
In their own home or elsewhere, wherever they desire, they remain by means of the mental construction of various bodies and so forth. || 28 ||
This has been seen many times through experience both here and in the hereafter:
while staying in his own home, Kārtavīrya caused fear to all. (29)

The connection with the preceding [verse] is as follows: in this world or in the next, such as the heavenly realms, the yogins remain through the simultaneous enjoyment of their *prārabdha* (commenced karma).

Such is the conduct of the yogins. And he became a ruler who struck fear into all, including thieves and others, by his presence in various places; and that was the power of yoga obtained through the grace of the Blessed One Dattātreya.
This is well known from the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa and other sources. || 29 ||
Viṣṇu, remaining in the ocean of milk, becomes manifest as Puruṣa on earth;
for the sake of the sacrificial animal, the Yoginīs remain within the host of Yoginīs.

She is born and engages in worldly activities such as taking birth; while remaining in the heavenly world amidst the host of Yoginīs, she goes to the earthly realm for the purpose of accepting offerings such as animal sacrifices. || 30 ||
While Śakra remains seated on his heavenly throne, he descends to the earth for the sake of sacrifice;
likewise, Janārdana becomes one thousandfold in this world.
In this incarnation as Rāma, Janārdana manifested as a thousand [Rāmas] in Janasthāna for the sake of slaying fourteen thousand rākṣasas, and then becomes one again. || 31 ||
Hundreds of devoted men attain human birth by bowing to him;
likewise, this Janārdana alone becomes a thousandfold.

Through the prostrations, salutations, and prayers of those devotees, he returns to human form once more in the Yadu clan in order to bestow grace upon hundreds of devoted men; and therein, for the purpose of deluding Duryodhana and others in the assembly of the Kurus, he becomes one thousandfold. || 32 ||
Through the playful acts of partial incarnations, he alone maintains the stability of the world;
like one who blinks his eyes, he simultaneously enjoys thousands of beloveds with equal passion.
The remainder [of the verse] implies that he enjoys sixteen thousand beloved women simultaneously.

Therein lies the illustration: "like a blink. Just as the royal sage Nimi, having attained a bodiless state (videhatva), dwells within the eyes of all living beings and performs their blinks at once, so too [does he]. || 33 ||
In this way, those monks, Saṅkalpa, Jīvaṭa, the Brāhmaṇa, and the others,
by the power of Rudra’s consciousness, went to the city of their own volition.

He states "in this manner" (*evam*) to show that what has been described should be understood to apply to the present case as well. The meaning is: Rudra’s permission (*abhyanujñā*) is under the control of that [will]; Rudra’s permission follows precisely his resolve (*saṃkalpa*), by virtue of its power. || 34 ||
Having enjoyed pleasures there for a long time and thereafter reaching the city of Rudra,
they shall dwell as attendants (gaṇas), remaining together with their retinues.

Then, in the various worlds and in the cities of Śiva, the Vidyādharīs— wearing the crowns of the immortals— shone together with Rudra within the dwellings of ever-blooming new Kalpa-creeper groves and amidst clusters of great jewels.

He says "constantly" (*nityam*) to indicate that at that time, a simultaneous, voluntary manifestation of many bodies occurred for them as well, both in their own abodes and in all worlds. Those hosts [of attendants] were together with Rudra in houses made of blossoming new *kalpa*-creepers, which were clusters of vast jewels and bunches of many gems; likewise, they were in various kinds of worlds and universes.

Wandering through the auspicious cities and towns such as Kailāsa, Vaikuṇṭha, and the world of Brahmā, they are borne upon the crests of the immortals and are bowed to everywhere among the Vidyādharīs who are skilled in song, instrumental music, dance, and the like; thus they are "those who wear the crests of the immortals. [The term] *amara* refers to the moon, which prevents death and is filled with nectar.
Or, because they wear [the crowns] upon their heads, being "wearers of the crowns of the immortals," they shone and gleamed. || 36 ||
Thus ends the sixty-fourth chapter, titled "The Attainment of the State of a Gaṇa," in the Nirvāṇa Section of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa*, composed by Vālmīki, within the *Divya-mokṣopāya*.
Thus ends the sixty-fourth sarga, titled "The Attainment of the State of a Gaṇa," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The *Svapnaśatarudrīya* is completed.
The sixty-fifth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Just as a delusion in the mind was only slightly perceived by that monk, so too does he see reality clearly once he has distinguished it from effort itself. (1)
The rule regarding nuns is said here to apply equally to all living beings;
furthermore, the searching for a monk at night and his rising from the communal meal are described.
For every living being who appears as a soul, the state consisting of birth and death occurs;
it is indeed the very form of the space of consciousness that has assumed a physical shape.
That delusion which was slightly perceived and momentarily conceived in his own mind by that monk in the manner described—
this monk [perceives] that very delusion, which is real and characterized by his own prior wholesome and unwholesome karma,
as if it were an effort itself existing in the state of its fruit, distinct and separate from his own self, and he sees it very clearly.
He perceives; the meaning is that he does not see even an atom's worth of anything else. || 1 || 2 ||
Having separated itself, one's own self, that fragment of saṃsāra, attains unity;
every living being who has died is like a distinct dream.

In the same way, it should be understood that for all living beings as well, their own karma, awakened at the time of death, appears in the form of the world like a dream until liberation; thus he says: "All indeed... (3).
Thus, although the embodied soul possesses such a nature, it remains distressed until liberation;
this host of living beings has been described by me to you through this narrative.

Thus, the meaning is that although the embodied soul (dehī) possesses a nature that is as pervasive and undivided as a mendicant (bhikṣu), it nevertheless remains agitated until liberation, as if limited by a body; this is illustrated by the story of the mendicant. || 4 ||
"O Rāma, it is not only monks who think 'the self is moved by another';
day after day, our very life-force (jīva) passes from one delusion to another. (5)

The meaning is that every living being (*jīva*), having its self vibrated from the Supreme which is the perfect nature, is of this very same character—not only the mendicant. "Day after day" means every single day; "in dream" means it is established by our own experience. || 5 ||
Just as a stone fallen from a mountain peak descends lower and lower,
so too the individual soul (jīva), having strayed from the Supreme Self, perceives this firm dream.
For this reason as well, one sees that from one dream one goes again to another dream;
falling from dream to dream, this world is indeed certainly nothing but a falsehood.
The connection with the subsequent [verse] is as follows: "One perceives this suffering, beginning with birth, through some cause or another at some time. (7)
The individual soul, worn out by internal illusion, perceives [the world] here sometimes,
through some means, or even at times by itself.
One who ends with the notion "I am the body" is liberated and attains his own true nature.
Śrī Rāma said:
Alas! How terrible is this delusion that arises for this living being! (9)

Now, he states the essence of bondage and liberation in brief: "deha" and so forth. The meaning is that the conclusion is this: the very identification with the body known as "I" is bondage, and the attainment of one's own true Self is liberation. Desiring to ask something, Rāma expresses his awakening to the described matter through a gesture of wonder, beginning with "Aho! (Oh! and so on. || 9 ||
Just as for one who is asleep, by means of a slight illusion—consisting of various forms and transformations—that fierce night of false knowledge, he falls utterly [into delusion]. (10)

Even by a slight cause, such as intoxication or fatigue, when one has fallen asleep, the mind—through the illusion of a dream—falls into an extreme and most terrifying state of imbalance and the peril of suffering; and that [state] is spoken of as if it were one's own child, or one's own son, or one's own [possession]. "Aho! (Oh, what a wonder!)—this is the connection with the following verse. || 10 ||
"Alas! Indeed, what a terrible disparity is spoken of as if it were natural—O Blessed One, regarding everything at all times and in every way for the maintenance of the world! (11)
And as for what you said—that everything arises everywhere and at all times—that too has become established in my own experience; thus he says: "O Blessed One," [verse 11].
"It was said by you that it arises [from you], and so it is experienced;
thus, that mendicant is a self characterized by such qualities, yet his nature is deluded. (12)

Having pleased the Guru by rejoicing in the meaning thus taught, you ask out of curiosity and with the doubt as to whether such a person exists— asking, "Has this monk been described by you for my awakening as being distinguished by such qualities?"—
because your nature is deluded, that is, because your nature is deluded regarding such living beings and so forth. 12.
"Look within and tell me quickly: does it exist anywhere, or does it not?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
"Last night, while established in samādhi, [I beheld] this very hut of the three worlds."

"Although I spoke to the monk after having envisioned him through internal yoga for the sake of awakening you, nevertheless, because it is impossible for his words to be false, he must certainly exist somewhere. And with the thought that there might be a delay in seeing him now through yoga or in his rising [from meditation], Vasiṣṭha spoke what was appropriate for that occasion, beginning with 'Today'. || 13 ||
"Having observed whether a certain monk exists or not, I shall speak of him tomorrow morning.
Vālmīki said:
While the sage was speaking thus, the midday drum resounded outside.
The *ḍiṇḍima* is a specific type of musical instrument that signals the midday hour suitable for rising; it refers, in other words, to its sound. || 14 ||
There arose a sound as deep as the thundering of clouds agitated at the time of universal dissolution;
successions of handfuls of flowers fell at his feet. (15)
"Like the thundering of a rain-cloud," meaning deep and full; "of him," that is, of Vasiṣṭha. || 15 ||
Like flowers on trees shaken by the wind, the citizens fell at the feet of the best of sages; having paid their respects, they rose from their seats.
Like trees shaken and made to tremble by the wind. || 16 ||
Thereupon, the assembly rose with a succession of salutations;
then, in the same manner as the previous day, the sky-dwellers and earth-dwellers departed.
By that which existed yesterday, [namely] by what existed on the previous day. || 17 ||
In their respective abodes, all of them, diligently engaged in daily activities according to the scriptures, performed their own duties as was appropriate for each stage of life.
They performed their daily duties and fulfilled their own religious obligations. || 18 ||

Reflecting upon that which was spoken by the Sage, those who move upon the earth and those who move in the sky spent their nights as if they were mere moments, and even their kalpas as if they were a single night.

Reflecting upon and practicing the knowledge and scriptures proclaimed by the Sage, they spent what was like a moment in the joy of contemplating the instructed meanings; yet, due to their intense longing to hear further teachings that would nourish Rāma’s welfare, and because of their lack of sleep, it seemed like a kalpa. || 19 ||

In the morning, when the people had again become intent on a succession of activities, the assembly of beings moving through the air and upon the earth remained just as before, honoring those worthy of worship by conversing with one another and fashioning stories for the world.

The assembly of beings moving through the air and those dwelling upon the earth, having passed the night, gathered at the court of Daśaratha when the populace had arisen in the morning and was intent on their respective duties; they remained there just as they had done the previous day, arranging the seating order of the assembly suited for hearing the exposition by means of the composition of the narrative for the people.
Thus ends the sixty-fifth canto, titled "The Description of Vidyottara’s Amazement," in the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa* of the *Mokṣopāya* section of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*, composed by Vālmīki. 65.
Thus ends the sixty-fifth canto, titled "The Description of Vidyottara’s Amazement," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The sixty-sixth canto.
Vālmīki said:
Accompanied by the sage Vasiṣṭha and joined by Viśvāmitra and the others, [they departed].
The hosts of sky-faring Siddhas remained stationed there, as did the weary leaders of men.
It is said that here, after diligent searching, the vision of the mendicant is attained;
likewise, the vision of other such sages who have existed or will exist.
They remained standing; then the kings, the leaders, the vassals, and the others sat down once they had rested. || 1 ||
Then that very same assembly hall shone forth, together with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa;
it was gentle and possessed a perfectly even expanse, like a lotus pond when the wind has subsided.
Padminī, Padmavatī, and Sarasī. || 2 ||
Then the lord of sages, disregarding her words and her question, spoke;
for the virtuous, being compassionate, indeed instruct others by force.
Without considering the question and without waiting for a reply, he spoke these words; the sense is that this was because he had himself promised, "I shall speak tomorrow morning. || 3 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O King, moon of the sky of Raghu’s lineage, delight of the Raghus,
yesterday that mendicant was observed by me for a long time with the eye of knowledge.
He was gazed upon and sought for a long time; or, having sought him for a long time, he was gazed upon. || 4 ||
Through meditation, I wandered for a long time in search of such a monk,
across the seven vast continents and the great earth with its principal mountain ranges and peaks.
Indeed, nowhere has such a monk ever been found;
for how, indeed, could a kingdom of the mind be perceived even externally? (6)
The connection with the preceding verse is: "As long as [it] was not obtained, for that long I wandered for a long time. (6)
Then, when one-third of the night remained, I again set out toward the northern region by means of my intellect, like a coastal wind moving across the ocean.
"He went to a region within the northern direction" means that he mentally reflected upon it. || 7 ||
There exists that great and glorious region named Jinanāma;
there, upon an anthill, stands a monastery that serves as a refuge for people.

Beyond and further on from the district named Valmīka, there is this famous district called Jina; in that district, there is a place of resort for people known as Vihāra, a region inhabited by many folk. || 8 ||
In that monastery, within his own small cell, a monk named Dīrghadṛś, who had tawny hair, remained standing for the sake of meditative concentration.

According to the opinion of Bhāguri, the word *dṛś* is derived from the root *dṛś* with the suffix *ṭāp* added after the consonant-final stem, followed by lengthening; thus it is etymologically explained as "one whose [eyes] are like those of a deer" (*yasya dṛśau*).
And for twenty-one nights, as he remained thus established,
they did not enter his house— which was secured with firm bolts— fearing that their meditative absorption might be interrupted.
Fearing the interruption of his meditation, even his dear servants reportedly do not enter his hut-like dwelling.
Indeed, his servants were dear to him; yet that mendicant remains there, for such is the condition of destiny, which he must experience this very day.

Of that monk—to realize, that is, to attain the final direct realization for the sake of disembodied liberation (*videhakaivalya*). Why is that? Because it is determined by *niyati* (the principle of necessity), which is the controller and ordainer of his lifespan. || 11 ||
Twenty-one nights passed for him as he remained fixed in meditation;
yet, in his mind, it seemed as though a thousand years had gone by.
"In that manner" means in the way previously described. || 12 ||
In a certain former kalpa, there was once a monk;
today, however, I am the second in this [kalpa], and a third is not to be found. (13)
"Thus, thus it was. "In this present aeon. "This is the second [time]. The meaning is that "at that time, a third [instance] was not perceived by me. || 13 ||
But I, moreover, having searched with my fourfold mind like a bee within the lotus of the world, found no other such third monk. (14)
In this lotus of the world, as I wander like a bee, no third [creation] is perceived within this creation; thus the connection is either with what precedes or with what follows. || 14 ||
From that creation, a third one was obtained with a similar disposition;
thereafter, other creations were envisioned by me as a mere play.
Then, by me, through play, other creations were observed beyond this creation; therein, a third [creation] of such an intention was found—this is the grammatical connection. || 15 ||
As long as that creation remains resting within the hollow of space,
there exists a third monk who is equal in conduct to a brahmin.

He states that very point with the words "as far as" (yāvat). The Brahma-world (*brāhma*) is that which is fashioned by the Brahmā residing there; a world-order exactly like this one exists there as well. || 16 ||
In this very manner, with that very same arrangement, all things have come to be and will continue to be in abundance throughout the succession of creations. (17)

With the intention that, in this sequence of entities which is similar across the divisions of the universe (*brahmāṇḍa*), there likewise exist infinite such mendicants, he says "evam" (thus). || 17 ||
Even those sages and brahmins who are in this assembly must likewise conduct themselves with such behavior, as must many others as well. (18)
In this context, elaborating further on the very matter already stated regarding the conduct of those seeking liberation (mumukṣu), he says "in this [state]" and so forth.

The meaning is that even by them—those whose conduct is like that of a mendicant (bhikṣu) and those whose conduct is like their own—it must be maintained; and by others as well, it must be maintained according to these practices of the sage and the practices of the mendicant. || 18 ||
"This one must be Nārada, and that other one must be this [other person];
thus, by means of their forms and actions, he was joined with many others in abundance. (19)
Knowledge, action, and conduct—by one endowed with these two [knowledge and action]. || 19 ||
Thus Janma and the others were to be born, as were Vyāsa and Śuka;
furthermore, Śaunaka was to be born, along with Kratu and Pulaha.
By Agastya, Pulastya, Bhṛgu, and also by Aṅgiras—these and others likewise were the locus for such ritual actions. (21)
The meaning is that they will become the locus for such a form, configuration, and activities. || 21 ||
After a long, long time, this illusion will expand again;
for there will arise many others, both those born with conduct similar to his and others besides them. (22)
Again and again they revolve through creations like waves in water;
some are entirely identical, while others follow a sequence that is only half-similar.
Some are slightly equal [to others], while some are never again so;
thus is this vast delusion that infatuates even the great. (24)
In this world, O sinless one, our karma ceases in an instant, for our realization blossoms; whereas twenty-one days and nights are but a mere fraction of infinite forms.

In a *kṣaṇa*, which is by nature partless time, even *īhā*—mental effort—is absent; and since action characterized by physical movements such as those of the body is even more remote, it is certainly non-existent. What then? Only the delusion of perception (*pratipatti-bhrānti*) unfolds. This very point is made clear here in the conduct of a mendicant (*bhikṣu-caritra*), as he says: "Where... [referring to] the infinite forms of creation, such as living beings and so forth; of these, enough!
And where is there any correct apprehension? // 25 //
Where indeed is their perception? Oh, how formidable is the course of the mind!
This which has thus blossomed and persists is merely a mental representation (pratibhā). 26.
Just as a lotus in the water at dawn [emerges] from amidst the waves of various conflicts, this [world],
though originally pure, has become impure solely through the arising of consciousness;
thus the entire web of saṃsāra has arisen like sparks of fire from a flame.
It is like a lotus blossomed at dawn; in that context, one should understand that various quarrels of bees and the like, as well as waves of water, are to be observed.
Accompanied by rays of light, the great fire with its flames—just as this impure world arises from pure consciousness alone, like sparks from a fire—so too has this world been born. 27.
Thus, each manifested fragment is likewise present within other fragments;
indeed, all these diverse fragments are not mutually false, for they flash forth within this causal cause which is the Self of all.
Thus, just as in the mind of a single monk, so too within the minds of all living beings, a fragment of the world-appearance arises;

and within each of those internal fragments of living beings, a diverse fragment of creation arises. The meaning is that this is simply an infinite regress, like the nature of illusion (*māyā*). Those initial fragments themselves, and the world-fragments contained within them, are likewise [illusory].
From the perspective of their respective individual transactions, things are not false but are indeed real. To the question, "Are they so by their own nature? he says: "In the Self of All.

This means that when this Supreme Self—the single essence of the existence of consciousness—shines forth through identity, and when, by that awakening to one's own true nature, the state of being [those objects] is abandoned, then nothing at all is real. || 28 ||

Thus ends the sixty-sixth canto, titled "The Narration of the Monk’s Transmigration," in the *Jīvaṭopākhyāna* of the *Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa*, within the *Mokṣopāya* of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa* composed by the sage Vālmīki.
Thus ends the sixty-sixth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Monk’s Transmigration," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The sixty-seventh canto.
Daśaratha said:
"O leader of sages, go and awaken that mendicant."
"Let men dispatched by me quickly bring him here from his hut. || 1 ||
The destruction of the body of a monk who is liberated in meditative absorption is described here;
for others, bondage and liberation are like the delusion of a monk, arising from their own lack of awakening.
Let them awaken [him] and cause him to rise from his meditative absorption. Let these men, my envoys sent by me, bring [him here] at your command. (1)
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
O King, that body of the great mendicant, deprived of life, became moist and discolored; it was no longer a vessel for life.

"Today itself this is the determination of destiny to experience that," saying thus, Vasiṣṭha spoke—"O King!"—indicating that you have asked this while forgetting what I had said. "Moisture" (kleda) refers to the portion of the essence of food that supports the vital breath; through desiccation, it has reached a state of discoloration. || 2 ||
Having become the life-force of that monk, this soul of his became a swan born from a lotus;
remaining liberated while living, he was no longer a vessel for the cycle of worldly existence.

"In that case, let him live by your own power of true resolve (satya-saṃkalpa)"; to this he replies: "Of him" (tasya). The sense is: my resolve operates only as long as there remains a residue of prārabdha-karma to be experienced through that body, and not otherwise. || 3 ||
At the end of the month, their bolts were forcibly removed from that house;
yet the servants remain in the intermediate space, desiring to see the alms.

He said that because the house was guarded by the attendants of the resident monks— who had been commanded that the door-bolt must not be removed for a month— it was impossible even for his own ministers to awaken him;
for the servants, desiring to see the body of the monk, were stationed outside the doorway by the force of the monk’s command.
Then, having reassembled their shattered limbs, they will emerge from the water;
they will abandon one [monk] and take up another monk of unbroken mind.
Then, at the end of the month, having extracted and removed the body—the corpse of the monk—they will cast it into the water and submerge it.

In that cell, they will fashion another form, a stone statue in the shape of that body, as a monk, in order to carry out activities such as worship and devotion. Because of its solidity, the mind remains unimpaired.
The form of the deity imagined by the mind of the devotee; this is a *karmadhāraya* compound. || 5 ||
By this very means, the monk remains liberated even while possessing a body; how could that perished little body in the monastery be awakened?

Thus, according to the manner described, he is liberated; in the state of abiding (vihāra), regarding the sphere of activities such as the movements of the vital breath, he is "destroyed," meaning dead. || 6 ||

This very illusion, composed of the qualities (guṇas), is difficult to understand and hard to transcend for one who lacks comprehension; yet it is easily crossed by one who constantly possesses the realization of truth. (7)

Having stated an incidental question, he returns to the subject at hand with the words "This" and so forth. By means of the power of distraction—the cause of a succession of delusions that is difficult to comprehend—it is carried away, that is, cast aside. || 7 ||
Just as the state of being a bracelet is produced from gold while [the gold] itself remains unchanged,
its arising has as its cause nothing but the error of appearance.

Though non-existent and indeed unmanifest, she has brought about the commencement of the world; she is that from which arises the emergence of delusion, whose sole cause is the error—that is, the appearance in another form—of the manifestation, just as gold appears in the form of a bracelet. (8)
Thus, this Māyā is inferred within the Supreme Self, vanishing upon mere observation, like a series of waves in water. (9)

By means of the scriptural statements of examples, such as "Modification is a mere verbal handle, a name; 'clay' alone is the truth," it is likewise inferred that Māyā, the subject of the example, is of a false nature. || 9 ||
For the Knower, by virtue of being an object of perception, passes from one long dream to another;
thus, through the lack of discrimination, the all-seeing Self assumes the state of a living soul.

The Knower, who is indeed the Supreme Self, thus attains the state of being a living soul (jīva) due to lack of discrimination; yet, through self-discrimination, he perceives "the Self is everything," and as one who sees the Self, pure consciousness alone remains—this is the meaning. || 10 ||
Whatever appears as a manifestation is indeed the Self itself from the perspective of its own awareness;
that very same thing arises as saṃsāra, like the sight of a thorny *karañja* bush (or, according to another reading, "bearing a thicket").
(11) From the perspective of its own awareness, it is the Self alone; however, from the perspective of non-awareness, that very same thing arises in the form of saṃsāra. (11)
To the monk, the entire circle of cyclic existence, though arisen from each individual element, appeared like a dream or like the supreme ripples upon the water. (12)
With respect to each being among the multitude of living creatures, an individual cycle of saṃsāra has arisen and been produced through delusion.

The meaning intended is that, just as for a monk in a dream there is a manifestation of water with its various divisions such as whirlpools and waves, so too has this dream of the world arisen from the Lotus-born Lord himself.
In the very same way, that which arises from an impure mind becomes firmly established toward all people.

Since this creation is merely a mental construction of Hiraṇyagarbha, the collective totality, it is indeed like a dream; therefore, the individual manifestation (*vyaṣṭi*) must likewise be so. He says "it is presented" (*prastuta*) to explain that because it arises from an impure mind, the other [the collective] appears as if stable.
The creation appears like the sport of the Grandfather (Brahmā), like the play of a dream;
by him, it arises as if as individual cosmic eggs numbering in the millions.
But when the mind is purified, [the world] appears as unreal, like the grandfather of one's grandfather or like the play of a dream;
by such an appearance, it is known that it is determined to have arisen individually in the millions, like these cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas).
This is the meaning. || 14 ||
Whether throbbing or otherwise, the living soul perceives delusion within this heart; it is capable of experiencing a long, internal dream-like state.

Let this individual soul (jīva) manifest in whatever manner it may— whether as the individual phenomenal world (vyaṣṭi-prapañca), the collective phenomenal world (samaṣṭi-prapañca), the common phenomenal world, or the unique phenomenal world for each—
it nevertheless perceives within its heart a long-lasting delusion capable of appearing there; such is he.
The meaning is that it is indeed false, like a dream. || 15 ||
Having attained mere existence as consciousness, and by the mere fact of being subject to perception, it has become, in some instances, a vessel for the sufferings of old age and death. (16)
He states the cause for the perception of a long dream: "merely the existence of consciousness" (*citsattāmātra*).

Having fallen away from the realization of reality and having returned, one reaches and relies upon that alone—the mere existence of consciousness—within some particular body, such as that of a god, a human, or an animal. (16)

Adorned with her own meritorious deeds, she remained as if she had repeatedly reached both the netherworld (pātāla) and the world of Brahmā (brahmaloka) by the mere vibration of a fraction of her mind.

The meaning is that there, in that dream, the living consciousness (jīvacit), endowed with various merits, remains experiencing [objects] by repeatedly creating—through the mere vibration of a portion of its own mind—either the netherworld (pātāla) below or the world of Brahmā (brahmaloka) above. || 17 ||
Taking the form of the vibration of consciousness, she enters the self that has assumed the name and form of the individual soul;
then, captivating all with her agitation, she wanders elsewhere and rolls about.

The consciousness of the Supreme Self itself, by means of the conceptualization of the vital breath (prāṇa), becomes a vibration dependent upon it; having assumed through that medium the form known as the individual soul (jīva), it rolls about, first assuming within the self the delusion of the body’s form, and then going elsewhere outwardly, assuming the delusion of the forms of sense-objects. || 18 ||

Is the mind the Supreme Self? It is neither the Supreme Self, nor is it not [the Supreme Self], nor anything else; for this [mind], which bears names such as "living being" (jīva) and "body," possesses the status of being like a reflection or the like. // 19 //

"Let it be so that through delusion there is this distinction of names and forms such as 'jīva' and so forth; nevertheless, this [jīva] is indeed the Supreme Self, because even through a thousand superimpositions, it is impossible for the substratum to become something else. Thus, he strengthens the identity of the jīva and Brahman, which is the fruit of the supreme human goal, with the words "citteti" (the mind). [This refers to] the inner self (*pratyagātman*).
Is it because of the fault of the mere delusion regarding the forms of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) that the Supreme Self is not Brahman, or that Brahman is not the Supreme?

Is it not the case that the Self is the inner self (*pratyagātman*), just as the name "living being" (*jīva*)— which is merely adventitious due to limiting adjuncts like the reflection of this face of Brahman in a mirror— is applied to the names of bodies such as Devadatta and Yajñadatta?

From the word "and so forth" (*ādipadāt*), it is not that one brings in names such as "breath," "speech," and "eye"; rather, even though there is non-difference [between the Self and these functions], everything is indeed possible through the influence of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). And thus says the Śruti: "This very [Self] has entered here unto the tips of the nails; breathing, it is called 'breath'; speaking, it is 'speech'; seeing, it is 'the eye'; hearing, it is 'the ear'; thinking, it is 'the mind'."
"These are indeed merely names for his actions. || 19 ||
In Brahman alone the Supreme Brahman exists as the perception of the world, like pure space within space, or like pure water within water. 20.
Thus, in the vision of unity, it is through the perspective of worldly convention—that is, the perception of the world—that the Supreme Brahman is established within Brahman itself;

what need is there to mention that this is so from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha-dṛṣṭi*), when all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) have been eradicated at their very root? This is the intended meaning.
This world exists in the forms of the universe solely within Brahman.
One fears awakening as something other [than oneself], just as a child fears a reflection. || 21 ||

Furthermore, in the case of a mirror and the like, since the face exists as something entirely distinct from it, there might even be the possibility of an error [that the face is elsewhere]. However, this world of living beings abides within the very forms of the universe—both manifest and unmanifest—as Brahman itself, which is one's own self and free from fear; thus, even the possibility of such an error does not exist. Nevertheless, due to the sense of "otherness," one perceives another as distinct from the Self, thinking, "This is other than me."
The meaning is that it is a marvel that one fears because of the realization that a cause for fear exists. || 21 ||
When vibration has been rendered non-vibrating here, consciousness itself dissolves;
that too, through complete transformation, dissolves like ghee in fire.

And since the vibration of the intellect (*buddhi-spanda*) is the cause for the cognition of otherness, when that vibration is rendered motionless through the practice of meditative absorption (*samādhi*),
the notion characterized by the perception of duality dissolves of its own accord within the intellect. That intellect, too,
is fully dissolved into the form of the perfect Brahman through the final transformation characterized by direct realization, like clarified butter offered into a fire.
The meaning is that it dissolves into Brahman, which is kindled by that. || 22 ||
The vibration of consciousness alone unfolds within the vibration of consciousness, which is the self of all;
thus, vibration and non-vibration, as well as unfolding and so forth, are merely conceptual constructs and not real here. (23)

If it is asked how the world—which is as difficult to pierce as the tip of a spade—dissolves through mere awareness, the answer is that it is because it is nothing but an unreal vibration of consciousness; thus he says: "It is indeed a vibration of consciousness. (23)
Here there is neither vibration nor non-vibration, neither unity nor duality;
it is the pure essence of consciousness alone, and it remains exactly as it is.
If it is asked how it is known that [the world] is imagined (kalpita), he says "No" (na), meaning that it is because it is not seen by one who perceives reality (tattvadṛś). || 24 ||
But through essential inquiry, when both all words and their referents are known to be identical with pure consciousness alone, even this [notion] that "this does not exist" is no longer found. (25)

When the nature of all words and their referents is known to be uniform and of a single flavor, pure consciousness alone is the ultimate reality. The meaning is that this phenomenal world (*prapañca*), which is even non-existent as a negation (*abhāva*), does not exist; far less does its positive existence (*bhāva*) exist.
Duality arises from the cognition of difference; such difference is the characteristic mark of *prakṛti*.
When everything has dissolved through the realization of non-duality, only the Supreme remains.
Its very multiplicity is due to its being perceived; that perception, however, arises from non-contemplation.
And thus, the questioner indeed exists; therefore, there is supreme freedom from doubt.

Vasiṣṭha asserts that the actual state of things is exactly as described and cannot be altered by anyone: "There is no multiplicity. The two particles *eva* (only/exactly) are displaced in their order. O Rāma, you are indeed a multiplicity only through lack of awakening (*abodha*). But because you do not perceive that multiplicity which consists of non-awakening, you are simply awakening, the very form of the full consciousness (*pūrṇacidrūpa*). Regarding this matter, ask whatever you wish.
In this very way, the ultimate reality exists; therefore, it is meant that supreme freedom from doubt is established for you, for me, and for others. || 27 ||
Therefore, there is neither dream, nor waking, nor deep sleep, nor the fourth state (turya);
there is neither bondage nor liberation, nor anything consisting of conceptual construction.
Then, he says "tataḥ" (therefore) [in verse 28], meaning that from the very power of such fearlessness, the denial of duality across all states, beginning with the waking state, has proceeded.
Peace alone is called the world; peace remains established in this very way.
Since ignorance is therefore unreal, where is there any seer, seen, or seeing? (29)

The world, consisting of the triad of the seer, the seen, and so forth, exists solely by the power of ignorance (*abodha*). However, when that ignorance is itself unreal, then the cessation of that [ignorance] alone—being the nature of the pure Self—is what is called "the world. For, by the etymological derivation that "it goes" (*gacchati*) or "pervades everywhere" (*vyāpnoti*), it is established as being fit for the name "world" precisely because it is that very cessation which proceeds and pervades all things.
The triad consisting of the seer, the seen, and the act of seeing, however, is absolutely unestablished; therefore, the meaning is that it does not then exist under the name of the "world. || 29 ||
Even vibration would be non-vibration for you due to the absence of volition;
consciousness devoid of volition is not distinct from either vibration or non-vibration. (30)

If it is asked, "How can the vibration of the mind, the vital breath, and so forth cease through mere awareness?", he says, "Vibration," [in verse 30], implying that it occurs precisely through the destruction of the volitions that are its cause.

Devoid of the conceptualization of duality and unity, the mental construction of forms arises from the non-contemplation of consciousness; yet, through mere contemplation, that [construction] vanishes and Brahman alone remains. (31)

The conceptualization (saṃkalpa) consisting of forms such as duality or unity arises from the non-contemplation and non-perception of Consciousness (cit); and that [conceptualization] has vanished through mere contemplation and mere perception. Thus, the logical connection is that only Consciousness—Brahman itself—remains, devoid of both duality and unity. || 31 ||
That which appears like a shimmering stain of conceptualization upon the disc of consciousness is not a stain at all; know that it is the very dense body of the mass of pure consciousness.
He describes the manner of perceiving that [reality] with the words: "In the lunar orb of consciousness" (ciccandrabimbe). || 32 ||

"Since you strive for that state which is neither existent nor non-existent for the one who is a mass of consciousness (cidghana), this compendium of the essence of great awakening, free from defects, has been composed. (Or, if the reading "kuru" is preferred, it would be: "...this compendium... should be made. || 33 ||

He provides the reasoning for the statement "this is not a stain" with the words *cidghanasya* ("of the mass of consciousness"): "You should abide in the expansive state of the mass of consciousness (*cidghana*). For this reason—that because of abiding in the state of fullness, volition and the like attain a state of identity with you, such that they do not exist separately but exist as your very self—it is by this very reasoning [that it is not a stain].
Perform the perfect grasping—that is, the correct taking hold—of the essence of faultless awakening, which brings about the singular unity of the self in all things. 33.
The immortal form of the moon’s orb, free from the stain of conceptual construction,
has been touched by you— a fortunate one— through the realization of the destruction of both existence and non-existence.

O Disc of the Moon, O you who are free from the stain of conceptual thought! Every single object, when touched by you—who are auspicious and whose nature is the destruction of both existence and non-existence—becomes an embodiment of nectar. Oh, how great is your majesty! This is the meaning. || 34 ||
Having brought all conceptualizations of existence, non-existence, and so forth to the state of pure consciousness,
rest at ease within the inner radiance and playfulness of the Intellect.
O mind, which possesses the playful charm of intense radiance, breathe deeply within and attain perfect rest.
Know that vibration and non-vibration, or conceptualization and non-conceptualization, are the tradition of the mind, O you named after the ocean;
for cessation in all its forms is the reality of peace, and both the full and the incomplete abide as one alone. || 36 ||

O Rāma, you exist as the one whose essential nature is called the ocean of bliss (*ānandasamudra*). Whatever extent of the tradition of the mind (*cittāmnāya*)—the distinction of mental delusion consisting of vibration and non-vibration, imagination and volition, or non-imagination and conceptualization—all that is simply the peace of every form, the very existence of tranquility whose sole flavor is happiness, abiding in such and such a manner. And these:
Know that my own true nature is one and the same, whether in the state of fullness or in the state of non-fullness. || 36 ||

Thus ends the sixty-seventh chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Unity of Brahman," in the *Pūrva-mokṣopāya* section of the *Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*, composed by Vālmīki.
Thus ends the sixty-seventh chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Unity with Brahman," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The sixty-eighth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Having become one who maintains the silence of deep sleep and having abandoned the playfulness of the mind, [one attains liberation].
Freed from the impurity of temporal succession, remain firmly established in that state. || 1 ||
In this context, fourfold silence is described according to its characteristics;
among these, there is the silence of deep sleep, which is established in that which transcends the fourth state (turyātīta).
The playfulness of the mind, its following along with its own natural tendencies. || 1 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
O Lord of Mauna, O Brahmin, I wish to understand the fourfold mauna—vāṅmauna, akṣamauna, kāṣṭhamauna, and suṣuptamauna. Please tell me what each of these is called.

The restraint of speech and the other senses is *mauna* (silence). Being like a piece of wood (*kāṣṭha*) is *kāṣṭhamauna*. You are the Lord of silence (*mauneśa*), meaning you are capable and masterful among all forms of silence. || 2 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
O Rāma, here the sages among the best of sages declare that there are two kinds of sages:
one is a practitioner of asceticism like a piece of wood, and the other is liberated while living.

"Of two kinds" means that the three types of ascetics known to you, despite their differences in degree, belong to only one category because they lack self-knowledge; this is the intended meaning. || 3 ||
When spiritual practice has not been cultivated and remains withered, one who is firmly resolved yet forcibly subdues the collection of senses becomes a wooden ascetic—a mere sage in name. || 4 ||

He clarifies that very point with the words "in that which is uncultivated" (abhāvitāyām). "Cultivated" refers to the contemplation of the reality of the Self; [the practice] devoid of that is "dry," meaning it is devoid of the essence of the experience of that [Self].
This refers to ritual acts such as the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa* penances. || 4 ||

Having understood this as it truly is, one whose self is cultivated and who abides within the self—even if appearing like an ordinary person—is inwardly satisfied; such a one is remembered as a liberated sage. || 5 ||
In worldly affairs, though appearing like any other ascetic, he is inwardly satiated by the taste of unsurpassed bliss. || 5 ||
That state which belongs to these two lords of sages when they are at peace—
a nature consisting of the certainty of the mind— is designated by the word "mauna" (silence).
Having explained the meaning of the base, he explains the meaning of the suffix with the words "of these two" (etayoḥ). || 6 ||
Those who know silence say that it is of four kinds:
silence of speech, silence of the senses, the wooden [silence], and the deep-sleep [silence].
The meaning is that the sages have declared the fourfold silence by dividing the first [of these] into three parts. || 7 ||
Vāṅmauna is the restraint of speech; balāt-indriya-nigraha is the forcible control of the senses;
akṣamauna is the renunciation of all activities; and that which is designated as kāṣṭha is [the state of] being like a log.
He states their respective characteristics with the words "vāṅmauna" and so forth: restraint of the senses is "akṣamauna."

The fifth is mental silence (manomauna), which exists in the state of a wooden ascetic (kāṣṭhatāpasa) when he has died; the sixth, called the silence of deep sleep (suṣuptamauna), the one liberated while living (jīvanmukta) lives in.

Thus, when examining the various classifications, although mental silence (*manomauna*) as a fifth type is indeed possible, it occurs only in the case of a "wooden ascetic" (*kāṣṭhatāpasa*), or during death, fainting, and deep sleep, and not otherwise; therefore, it was not included among them—this is the meaning. The particle *ca* is used in the sense of "but. *Bhāve* refers to the experience of the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*). || 9 ||
Among the three specific types of silence, the subject is the wooden ascetic (kāṣṭhatāpasa).
