That very state which is the silence of deep sleep is the fourth (turyā); that alone is the liberated intellect.

The subject matter has been introduced. "Turyā" means the fourth. It is called "muktadhīḥ" because it is fixed (dhīyate) upon those who are liberated, that is, those liberated while living (jīvanmukteṣu). || 10 ||
It is established that silence is indeed verbal silence; however, it is said that the mind, when defiled, leads to bondage for the living being, and thus the wooden ascetic remained fixed therein.

Although the state of being "mauna" (silence/meditative restraint) is established in the three types of *mauna*, nevertheless, since they consist merely of a firm resolve of the impure mind, they lead only to the bondage of the individual soul (*jīva*); thus he says: "Speech... (verse 11).
Neither recollecting us, nor touching our visible forms or our speech,
indeed seeing while not seeing, he remains in the silence of wood.
In that case, he explains how the wooden ascetic who possesses such qualities remains in meditative absorption (*samādhi*) with the words "our...

and so forth: by forcibly restraining the mind, he does not touch upon the recollection or continuous mental engagement (*anusandhāna*) of the internal movement of the ego-sense (*ahaṃbhāva*), nor even the external manifold of forms (*rūpaprapañca*) or the manifold of names consisting of speech (*vāṅmaya*).

The meaning is that, although not touching [objects] and not seeing the Self because it is veiled by ignorance— as in deep sleep— he remains seeing by means of the light of the witness alone, since there is no loss of the eternal vision of the Self, like a fire covered by ashes. || 12 ||
This threefold silence is known as the vibration of the flickering mind;
those who dwell there through the play of that state become silent sages, not because they are knowers of that [reality].
At the time of emergence (vyutthāna), however, these three forms of silence are merely the flickering movement of the mind. In that regard, the three types of sages mentioned previously are silent;

but those who know [the truth] do not exist there [in that state] because of the obstruction of the mind, for they abide in the play of the cessation and emergence of that [mind]. This is the meaning.
In this triad of silences, it is said that there is no cognition of anything to be adopted; this has been spoken by him as a mere play. Therefore, let those who know it be angry or not.

Alternatively, regarding the phrase "by the play of that state" (*tatsthalīlayā*), it means "by the play of abiding in the state of the perfect Self. Those who know that [Self] may be angry—thinking that these three previous forms of silence, being essentially bondage, must be cast aside—or they may not be angry, considering them to be merely the manifestation of the bliss of Consciousness (*cidānanda*).
Nevertheless, the intended meaning is that they lack any knowledge of what is to be accepted here; thus he says: "Not here" (*nātra*) || 14 ||
This is indeed the silence of deep sleep, established as the state of one liberated while living;
listen to this ornament for the ears concerning the person who is not subject to rebirth. (15)
The measure of those liberated while living (jīvanmukta) is experience; it is the remainder [of the sentence] that for such a person this state arises. Therefore, you too should listen.
Here the vital breath is neither restrained nor joined in the threefold manner;
the perceptions of all the senses neither exult nor languish.
Since the vision of reality (tattvadarśana) is established, that [liberation] is accomplished without effort; thus, it does not depend on the previous hardship of silence (mauna). He says:
"They do not weary from the hardship of restraint (nirodha). (16)
This perception of multiplicity neither stirs nor subsides;
it is neither mind, nor non-mind, nor not mind, neither existent, nor non-existent, nor anything else.
Regarding how his mind, sublated by knowledge, abides at that time, he says: "The mind... (verse 17).

That which is without division, without practice, and established as being without beginning or end—whether one is meditating or not meditating, this is called the silence of deep sleep (sauṣupta-mauna). || 18 ||
It is undivided because of the destruction of the discriminating conceptualization and because of the absence of any distinction of degrees;
for this very reason, it is non-repeated, being independent of repetition; and because its nature is an unlimited self, it is without beginning or end. || 18 ||
Having understood this delusion of the world's diversity as it truly is—
exactly as it exists and without doubt— that alone is the silence of deep sleep.
Having understood this reality of the Self as it truly exists—that in which the delusion of manifoldness called "the world" occurs—[one is liberated]. || 19 ||
"This entire expanse is indeed Śiva, whose nature consists of manifold consciousness"—this state established as infinite is called the silence of deep sleep (sauṣupta-mauna). || 20 ||
The meaning is: that which is the abode of worldly existence is pervaded and filled by that very Śiva, who is the self of all things consisting of consciousness in their manifold forms. || 20 ||
Space is neither space nor is it everything; it both exists and does not exist.
That mind which is thus even and tranquil is silence, like deep sleep. (21)
And because of the absence of the nature of emptiness, it is certainly not in space either. || 21 ||
All is empty, without support, peaceful, and mere representation-only;
that in which one abides as neither existent nor non-existent is the supreme silence.
In which state of liberation while living (jīvanmukta-dashā) one has remained or abided. || 22 ||
They know that supreme silence to be the non-appearance of consciousness through the distinctions of existence and non-existence, states, places, and so forth, which arise from falsehood.
(23) The non-appearance of consciousness through the distinctions of existence, non-existence, and so on, is its non-illusory state. (23)
That which is the non-recurrence of the movement of consciousness— due to its absolute non-existence within the mind whose nature is non-functioning— that is imperishable silence.
Because it is sublated, it is absolutely non-existent. || 24 ||
"I am not, nor does another exist; there is no mind, nor anything mental"—this awareness of non-awareness is uninterrupted supreme silence.
Mental conceptualization is thus the non-perception and non-appearance of that which has been sublated by consciousness. || 25 ||
"I am in this world merely the referent of the word 'well-being,' being simply the universal of existence (sattāsāmānya)"; this is called the silence of deep sleep.
Hail! All that consists of mere word and meaning is free from affliction; it is simply the universal of existence. 26.
Since there is only pure consciousness, how could there be any conceptualization of "self" or "other"?
Therefore, the infinite state of deep sleep is all-pervasive silence.
Because of which reason it is *amā*—devoid of the final cognitive state (*caramavṛtti*) that possesses its own form and sublates all obstructors—it is as if it swallows even that;
therefore, [it is the dissolution] of itself, of another, and of difference, etc., as indicated by the word "and so forth" (*ādipadāt*). || 27 ||
Know this very state of deep sleep and silence to be like awakening due to its infinity;
know it as the Fourth (turya), the stainless, and even that which transcends the Fourth (turyātīta).
The fourth state arises from the sublation of ignorance; the state beyond the fourth arises from the sublation even of those mental modifications that sublate ignorance. || 28 ||
Indeed, the state of being established solely in deep sleep, as well as the samādhi of the fourth (turya), or the samādhi beyond the fourth (turyātīta), can occur even while one is awake. || 29 ||
Among the seven stages of knowledge previously mentioned, these three stages beginning with the fifth are of the nature of specific states of meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
He says that they occur alternately even for one who knows reality while awake—the word "also" (*api*) implying while dreaming—as well as while remaining in the fourth state (*turya*):
"Remaining in the fourth state alone, characterized by entirely pure and peaceful activity, he conducts himself skillfully and completely even while awake."
O Brahmin, O virtuous one, it is said that [the self] exists eternally, whether embodied or even disembodied, as being indeed of the nature of space.

O Brahmin, O you who have become Brahman, O holy one! Whether you are active, skillfully engaged in worldly affairs on all sides, or whether you have abandoned such activity and remain established in *samādhi*—as long as you are liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*), constantly abiding in the state of total, stainless peace, you are indeed ever situated in the Fourth State (*turya*), and likewise in the disembodied state (*videha*).
And this state consists in the non-appearance of the obstruction of both gross and subtle forms.

The meaning is that this state belongs only to him who has become like the sky (*nabhas*), and not to anyone else. Alternatively, *nabhaḥ* is itself an address; the meaning is that this condition exists for you alone, O Sky-like One, and not for another. Or else, "it belongs to you, Bhavān," is a statement made to Rāma as if it were an established fact. || 30 ||

"Oṃ! Remain as the One, with the latent impressions of worldly existence cast aside; neither you, nor I, nor anything else here exists as reality. Yet, it is said that everything is perceived here as a mere internal appearance; therefore, O Knower, remain established solely in the single digit of the treasury of the sky of consciousness. (31) O Rāma, you—according to the method taught in the Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad regarding the syllable "Oṃ"— [The remainder of the verse continues: "...should remain as the One, with the latent impressions of worldly existence cast aside. Neither you, nor I, nor anything else here exists as reality. Yet, it is said that everything is perceived here as a mere internal appearance; therefore, O Knower, remain established solely in the single digit of the treasury of the sky of consciousness. (31) O Rāma, you—according to the method taught in the Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad regarding the syllable "Oṃ"—

By dissolving even the very measure of the quarters beginning with Virāj, remain as the one form of the Fourth (turya), from which the latent impressions of worldly existence have been cast out. Regarding that which is indeed well-known here as "everything exists," understand it to be like a dream experienced within the internal channels;
thus, being a wise one liberated while living, remain established solely in a single portion of the expanse of the sky of consciousness—this is the meaning. || 31 ||

Thus ends the sixty-eighth chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Effort of Great Silence," in the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa* of the *Mokṣopāya* section of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Valmiki, according to the tradition of the Rishis.
Thus ends the sixty-eighth chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Effort of Great Silence," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The sixty-ninth canto.
Śrī Rāma said:
"O leader of sages, from where did the hundredfold nature of the Rudras arise?"
Tell me quickly: who are those Gaṇas, and who are those Rudras? || 1 ||
Even among the Gaṇas there is the state of Rudra-hood, while for the liberated there is a state of voluntary existence;
through yoga, the dissolution of the vital breath occurs, whereas after death, its emergence is said to take place.

"Having attained that state of Rudra—the desire for Brahma and the Swan—they all came together and shone as the hundred supreme Rudras. Thus, the status of being the supreme among hundreds of Rudras was mentioned previously; and in the subsequent creation, by the command of Rudra, they experienced the remainder of their *prārabdha* karma within those various bodies. Having enjoyed [the fruits] there for a long time...

"Having obtained enjoyments, they shall dwell as Gaṇas in Rudrapura along with their retinues. Having been told this there, Rāma, being in doubt as to whether the hundred forms of Rudra constitute a single Gaṇa or whether each form of Rudra is a separate one, asks: "From where?"—that is, from where did the hundredfold nature of the Rudras arise? Is it together with the Gaṇas?

Or rather, because of the enumeration of those very Rudras distinct from [the Gaṇas]. The word "uta" (or) has the sense of "eva" (indeed). The meaning is: "Are those very groups mentioned by you the same as those Rudras who were mentioned, or are they indeed different Rudras? || 1 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
A hundred dreams, each involving a hundred bodies, were seen by the mendicant;
they were all understood in their general outline, and therefore they were not described by me in detail.

Regarding this, Vasiṣṭha offers the following reply based on the very first eon: "Of dreams... Since you already know them from the previous accounts concerning those various births and so forth described by way of brief indication (*uddeśataḥ*), I have not mentioned them by name in detail through the enumeration of the hundreds of Rudras. || 2 ||
Those forms which were seen in the dream are remembered as those hundreds of various Gaṇas;
this is the hundred Rudras, for even the Rudras are Gaṇas in the ritual ordinance.
In the *Bhikṣu-svapna*, those forms such as Jīvaṭa and others are traditionally recorded as being approximately one hundred in number, corresponding to that very form.
This same group is also called the "One Hundred Rudras" because of their equality in enjoyment and sovereignty, and because they are portions of Rudra. Now, one might object:
"The 'Gaṇas' are said to be the servants and attendants (*pārṣadas*) of Rudra; how then could they be the primary Rudras themselves?"

If it is argued that because the states of master and servant are contradictory, they cannot coexist in one place; and furthermore, since the hundredth [Rudra] is the primary Rudra himself and thus lacks the status of a subordinate attendant (*gaṇa*), the expression "a hundred attendants" is logically untenable—to this he replies: "The Rudras too. These hundred are themselves Rudras who, in the performance of service and other duties, [act for] the previously established Rudra who constitutes the very pinnacle of the Lord (*īśvara*).
They indeed become hosts (gaṇas). The meaning is that this is because the attainment of their sovereignty over the enjoyment of the fruits of karma is dependent upon them. || 3 ||
Śrī Rāma said: O Blessed One, how was a hundredfold mind produced from a single mind?
That was done by Rudra while dreaming, just as a hundred lamps are lit from a single lamp.

Having awakened that monk through his own mind and consciousness, and so forth—Rāma, not believing what was previously stated regarding the awakening of the monk and others by means of the hundredth Rudra (Śiva) appearing in the form of a monk through the granting of the sentience of his own mind, asks: "From one... (verse 4).
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Indeed, those whose true being is unobstructed experience exactly that which they conceive, for their consciousness is permeated by the essence of aesthetic flavor (rasa).

He offers a rebuttal—stating "unobscured" (*nirāvaraṇa*)—to the objection that while such [qualities] might not be seen in non-lords (*anīśvara*) who are ignorant, their impossibility cannot be maintained in the case of lords (*īśvara*), namely the liberated ones (*mukta*). By means of the sovereignty of knowledge they are "unobscured," and by means of the sovereignty of yoga they possess "true being" (*sadbhāva*), meaning they have true resolve (*satyasaṃkalpa*). This is according to the Vedic scripture: "He is indeed *rasa*; for having obtained *rasa*, this [individual] becomes blissful. *Rasa*...
The bliss of plenitude (*bhūmānanda*) encompasses—that is, accepts and takes as its own—for the sake of attaining the existence of all objects of volition on every side;
the meaning is that this occurs by the power of that *māyā* which is the consciousness of reflection, known as omniscience and omnipotence. || 5 ||
Since the Self is all-pervading and omnipresent, whatever is conceived in whatever manner and wherever,
that very thing is experienced there in that same way by the intellect through its faculty of knowing.
He says "of the universal self" (sarvātmanaḥ) to show that by the power of being the universal self, there is the accomplishment of all intended objects for them. || 6 ||

Śrī Rāma said: O Brahman, can the Lord truly be one who wears a garland of skulls as an ornament, is smeared with ashes, is clothed only by the directions, dwells in cremation grounds, and is a lustful man?

With this sovereignty in mind, Rāma asks with the intention of wondering: "For what purpose do Hari, Hara, and the others subject themselves to the afflictions of taking birth in human wombs and so forth, or dwelling in cremation grounds; why do they not instead create only that which is auspicious? [He asks: "Kapāla... [One who] is characterized by the habit of shining or being beautiful with ashes.
The meaning is: although the Lord is endowed with all powers, for what purpose does He remain as He is? || 7 ||

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: For the great lords, the perfected ones, who possess bodies while already liberated in life, there is no rule regarding ritual action here; for such a rule is devised only for the ignorant.

There is no rule that ritual actions must be exclusively scriptural, exclusively of the nature of auspiciousness (*maṅgala*), or exclusively resulting in the enjoyment of pleasure, because they lack the status of being subservient to injunctions (*vidhi*). This is because, from the perspective of one who sees reality (*tattvadṛśā*), there is no difference in the fact that all things—including those considered auspicious by the perception of the ignorant—are equally the most inauspicious. Furthermore, due to the absence of unwholesome karma (*aśubhakarma*), even for them, the causal complex of suffering does not arise.
The meaning is that this is because the experience of suffering does not arise for anyone, and because there is no distinction in the fact that everything is of the nature of happiness. || 8 ||

But the ignorant one— [the analysis "because his mind is afflicted" (tuditacittatvāt) is also accepted by some, yet we have not adopted it because it is not accepted by the author of the commentary, is not found in other manuscripts, and is illogical.]— [acts] without the restraint of action due to having an afflicted mind.
Indeed, by following the law of the fish, one surely undergoes supreme suffering.

Being well-versed in wisdom, they do not sink into objects that are either desirable or undesirable, because their senses are restrained, because they have attained Buddhahood, and likewise because they are free from latent predispositions (vāsanā). 10.

Because their minds are directed toward this world, and because their minds are shattered by thousands of defects such as passion, hatred, and greed, they proceed—like fish among fish according to the well-known maxim of the weak preying upon their own and other species—toward further births and the sufferings of the successive hells and so forth, without any restraint on their actions. For "hi" indicates what is well-established in the scriptures. 9–10.
They always perform actions that have become as natural as the "crow-and-palm" coincidence;
yet they do not actually perform anything at all, for they have no attachment whatsoever to anything.
"Rūḍhām" means arisen suddenly; "grahaḥ" means attachment. || 11 ||
By a stroke of chance, Viṣṇu was impelled to such action in the past;
likewise was the Three-eyed One, and likewise was the Lotus-born One, engaged in such deeds.
"Having such karma" refers to the karma pertaining to birth as a human being and so forth. 12.

For the one who possesses knowledge, there is never anything blameworthy nor anything blameless, nothing to be accepted nor anything to be rejected, and no action that is either one's own or another's. (13)

The ellipsis is "there is nothing for anyone to abandon. One's own [duty] (*ātmīyam*) is that which is appropriate for one's own caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama*); the other (*param*) is different from that. It is called an "object" (*viṣaya*) because it "binds" (*viṣiṇoti*) the wise (*jñāḥ*), meaning those who have attained perfection; the sense is that such a thing does not exist anywhere. || 13 ||
Just as heat and other qualities became established in fire and the rest at the beginning of creation,
so too did the activities of Hara and others, as well as the castes of the twice-born, become established.

If that is so, how is it that there is a fixed rule regarding the conduct, dress, and actions of Hara, or a fixed rule regarding the conduct, dress, and so forth of Hari, or a fixed rule regarding the conduct of the highest Brahmins for those such as yourself? Since these would not be possible according to the maxim of the "crow and the palm fruit" (i.e., by mere chance), he says: "Of fire and the others. This refers to the *jātis*—the fixed rules of action appropriate to each respective caste.
The meaning is that it is precisely the beginningless necessity (niyati), which consists of the will of the Supreme Lord, that establishes that [distinction]. || 14 ||
Once creation has reached full development, through the power of convention, various wonders resulting from experience are imagined; they are imagined by themselves. 15.
However, the conduct of the ignorant is not fixed like ritual acts such as the fire-oblation (*agnihotra*); rather, it becomes manifest at the beginning of creation.

But once the creation has become established, their actions—both scriptural and natural—result in the experience of worldly and otherworldly pleasure and pain, according to the power of conventions regarding the distinctions of caste (*varṇa*) and so forth.
The meaning is that there is an inequality because [the world] is imagined by itself under the influence of passion and other afflictions. || 15 ||

Therefore, O scion of Raghu’s line, I have not described to you that supreme silence of the fourth state (turyamauna), which pertains to one liberated while in the body (videhamukta); rather, it concerns the disembodied state.
Having thus resolved the question, he shows what remains to be said regarding the silences (*mauna*) introduced [previously] by saying "videha" (the disembodied).
The connection with the following verse is: "Listen to that which was not told to you, which is beyond the four well-known types of silence belonging to one who possesses a body.
The space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*), whose nature is pure awareness, is far more transparent than even the ether (*kha*).
The attainment of thatness is the supreme good; hear how it is attained. (17)
The attainment of that state of being "that-ness" is the supreme good, which is liberation. || 17 ||
Those who have awakened through the realization of perfect knowledge by means of constant one-pointed concentration,
and who have understood through enumeration itself, are remembered as Sāṃkhya-yogins.

Intending to describe that Sāṃkhya and Yoga are the means for attaining that [liberation], he defines the Sāṃkhya-yogins with the word "samyak" (correctly). [They are those who] by means of *saṃkhyā*—that is, by means of Rājayoga employed through discriminative inquiry. || 18 ||
Those who have, through skillful means, attained the state where the vital breaths such as prāṇa and the rest are completely stilled,
are remembered as yogins of yoga, free from affliction and without beginning or end.
He defines the practitioner of karma-yoga with the words "prāṇa" and so forth. By means of *yukti*—that is, by the haṭha-yoga previously described. || 19 ||
But that which is to be accepted by all is the peaceful, unconditioned state;
some have attained it through enumeration (saṃkhyā), and others from the body through yoga.
That which is to be accepted is to be attained through the direct realization of reality as its fruit; for all yogis of both kinds, by means of this very body. 20.
He who sees Sāṃkhya and Yoga as one truly sees;
for the supreme state that is attained by the followers of Sāṃkhya is indeed the very same as that attained by the followers of Yoga. 21.
Consequently, he clarifies this very point with the words "that which" (yad iti). || 21 ||
Where the activity of the vital breath and the mind is not perceived at all,
and where one has escaped the snare of latent impressions— know that to be the supreme state.
[Objection: But how can there be a single fruit for those two, which have distinct forms? To this he says: "Where...

The meaning is that because both the functions of prāṇa and manas are characterized by absolute dissolution, the state in which one has escaped the snare of the latent impressions (vāsanā) of both is itself that supreme state; therefore [it is so called]. || 22 ||
They say that the mind itself is the latent impression (vāsanā), for it is the cause of transmigratory existence;
when it dissolves within both types of karma, it ceases to be a cause.

If it is argued that, since they have a single fruit— just as fire and water are combined when rice is being cooked— the combination (*samuccaya*) of Sāṃkhya and Yoga is appropriate rather than an option (*vikalpa*), he replies to that with the words "the latent impression" (*vāsanām*).

For transmigratory existence (*saṃsṛti*), which consists of the activities of the external and internal organs, the vital breaths, and so forth, the mind alone is its essence, being composed of a mass of those latent impressions.

That cause, whether by means of Sāṃkhya or Yoga alone, dissolves and transforms into the nature of the knowledge of reality; thus, for both the instrument (the body) and the vital breath, it becomes a non-cause regarding their respective functions and activities.
Therefore, since the fruit of both is accomplished by each one individually, there is no need for their combination—this is the meaning. || 23 ||
The mind indeed perceives the body as a child perceives a ghost;
having led its own self to dissolution, it no longer perceives it.

He says "the mind" (verse 24) to show that the entire cycle of worldly existence is preceded by the perception of the body as the self; the mind is its root, and thus it is logical that when the mind is stilled, the entire cycle of worldly existence is stilled.
The mind has arisen in vain and as something non-existent due to a lack of discernment;
like one observing the form of one's own death in a dream, it is not found to exist.
If it is asked, "In that case, how does the destruction of the mind occur through the vision of the Self? he says: because it is produced by the non-vision of that [Self].
"The world of transmigration (*saṃsāra*) arises from the mind; where is 'mine' and 'I', and where is the lineage (*saṃtati*) or the cycle of existence (*saṃsṛti*)?
Where, then, are the teacher and the taught, or bondage and liberation? (26)

He states that when the mind is sublated by knowledge, all conceptual constructions—from its effects, such as the bonds of "I-ness" and "mine-ness," up to liberation itself—are sublated; this is expressed in the verse beginning with *mano'bhava*. The words "where" (*kva*) and "from whence" (*kutaḥ*) are to be construed with each respective word in the following line. || 26 ||
The intensive practice of a single principle, the dissolution of the vital breaths,
and the restraint of the mind— this is the summary of the meaning of the word "liberation."

Now, according to the sequence of the superior, inferior, and middling authorities, he demonstrates the three means to liberation by summarizing the essential purport of all the scriptures—beginning with the verse "Eka... (verse 27).
Śrī Rāma said:
O Sage, if indeed the dissolution of the vital breaths is the cause of liberation, then I consider all living beings to be liberated simply by dying. (28)
Among those, Rāma refutes the middle position with the words "yadi" (if). The sense is that, upon death, it is well known that the vital breaths of all beings dissolve. || 28 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Among these three practices, know that the pacification of the mind is the best; understand that it alone is to be accomplished quickly, so that it may become auspicious.

All three means are causes for liberation only through the dissolution of the mind (*manonāśa*). Furthermore, at the time of death, there is neither the dissolution of the mind nor the destruction of the vital breath (*prāṇa*);

rather, during the state of fainting, [the mind] exists within ignorance (*avidyā*) in the form of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), like salt dissolved in water, and it manifests again at the time of departure. He becomes possessed of consciousness (*savijñāna*).

This is because of the scriptural statement, "He descends with consciousness itself," because of the well-known illustration of the caterpillar, and because it is impossible for the dissolved vital breaths (*prāṇas*) to depart through the gates of the eyes and other senses.
Furthermore, there can be no dissolution of those [breaths] that have gone outside due to the absence of a support in the form of the gross body; rather, they dissolve in the external space.

Know that the pacification of the mind alone is the best, the most excellent, and the goal to be achieved—namely, the conceptualization of a body suitable for immediate worldly activity by means of the subtle elements (bhūtamātrās) that have emerged together [with the soul]. || 29 ||
When the vital breaths depart from this body for the sake of Nirvana,
they experience union with the subtle elements (tanmātras) and proceed into the ether.
When the vital breaths (*prāṇas*)— which are like a wound that emits sound— leave this little body, becoming completely still and free from the gurgling noise, then,

having experienced the form of the future body brought forth by latent impressions (*vāsanā*), desire (*kāma*), and karma, they enter into union with the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) and gross elements (*bhūtamātra*) in the external ether, which are conducive to the commencement of such a body. And thus:

The scripture says: "He becomes endowed with consciousness; he passes on indeed endowed with consciousness. Just as a goldsmith, taking a portion of gold, fashions another form that is newer and more beautiful, even so this Self, having cast off this body and dispelled ignorance, fashions for itself another form that is newer and more beautiful—whether it be the form of a father, or...
"Whether it be the Gāndharva, the Daiva, the Prājāpatya, the Brāhma, or that of other beings," so it is said.
In the Śruti, *peśaskārī* means a goldsmith; "having taken up portions (*mātrām*) of *peśas*, that is, fragments of gold," is the meaning.
Know that the subtle elements (tanmātras) are indeed characterized by latent impressions (vāsanā).
They unite with those vital breaths (prāṇas) which possess the nature of the mind, and not with others.

In that case, why do those elemental bodies not coalesce even with the external life-forces (*prāṇas*) along with the internal living souls? To this he replies: "By latent impressions" (*vāsanā*). The meaning is that it is established that these bodies—which consist solely of the latent impressions of their respective living souls—coalesce only with the life-forces associated with a mind possessing such latent impressions, and not with others.
Arising along with their latent impressions (vāsanās), the vital breaths (prāṇas) abandon the body;
they then enter into union with the space and wind for the sake of suffering, like a scent.

The vital breaths and so forth arise within another body accompanied precisely by the latent impressions (vāsanā) of that [previous] body; for they abandon even the previous body only while accompanied by the latent impressions of the future body. And in the other body, they enter into union with its internal space (hārdavyoman) and with the winds contained therein, just as the fragrance of a flower [enters] into sesame seeds.
Just as [the body] reaches a state of adhesion with the oil contained therein at every joint, so too does it become subject to the suffering of being crushed by machines and the like. || 32 ||
The mind, along with its latent impressions (*vāsanā*), does not become stilled, just as the ocean does not cease to be water;
nor can the vital breaths exist without the mind, just as rays cannot exist without the sun. (33)

For this very reason, he states that the mind is not destroyed merely by death, nor even by the destruction of the vital breaths, saying: "The mind... Just as a water-filled jar, when submerged in the ocean, does not cease to exist or perish even though it is no longer seen by outsiders; [the author] demonstrates the coexistence of the mind and the vital breaths both through the method of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) and the method of positive concomitance (*anvaya*). Thus: [he says: "The mind... etc. Just as a jar full of water, having been cast into the great ocean, does not become extinguished—that is, does not perish—merely because it is no longer perceived by people on the outside; so too, the mind, though it may not be perceived by others, does not cease to exist simply because it is not seen. Therefore, the mind is not destroyed by death alone. Nor is the vital breath destroyed, for they are invariably concomitant. He shows this through both negative and positive concomitance: "The mind... etc. Just as a jar full of water, having been thrown into the great ocean, does not become extinguished—that is, does not perish—merely because it is not perceived by people on the outside; so too, the mind, though it may not be perceived by others, does not cease to exist simply because it is not seen. The mind never abandons the vital breaths without knowledge, just as a partridge does not leave a blade of grass without another blade of grass. 34.
Through knowledge, the mind attains a state free from latent impressions (vāsanā) and reaches its own dissolution;
it no longer takes up movement from the vital breath (prāṇa), and thus only peace remains.
For this very reason, he says "from knowledge" (jñānāt) [in verse 35], meaning that when the latent impressions (vāsanā) are destroyed by knowledge, there is the destruction of both.
From knowledge, the non-existence of all objects arises fully;
thence, my dear, from the destruction of latent impressions, comes the dissociation of the vital breath and the mind. (36)
Then the mind, being utterly tranquil, no longer perceives the state of embodiment;
having attained the state through its own dissolution, the wise know that the mind is nothing but latent impression (vāsanā).

If it is asked how the destruction of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) occurs through knowledge, he says: "Through knowledge," because of the sublation of duality, which is the cause of those impressions.
(36–37) For the mind consists of nothing but latent impressions; in their absence, there is the supreme state.
Knowledge becomes that very reality; they say that knowledge is inquiry. (38)
O Rāma, the end of this cycle of existence proceeds by means of discernment alone, just as the delusion of a snake in a rope comes to an end. (39)

That knowledge as well, having sublated everything along with its latent impressions (vāsanās), becomes the very reality of the Self; and that reality—because of the non-difference between the letters *ra* and *la*, being "free from movement" (*vicāraṇa*)—is the immovable knowledge alone that remains; thus say those established in direct experience. || 38 || 39 ||
The practice of a single object, the restraint of the vital breath, and the dissolution of the mind—
when even one of these is fully perfected, they all become perfected through one another.

He introduces the subject at hand with the word "eka": "One object" means the non-dual reality; its "practice" is the repetition of hearing [the teachings] and so forth. "Just as the wind is stilled when the movement of the palm-leaf fan has ceased, so too the mind is stilled when the vibration of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) has ceased. (41)
Upon the dissolution of the body, the vital breath (prāṇa) attains the state of the wind in space;
or rather, it perceives everything there exactly as it has been perfumed.

While this sequence may apply when the vital breath (*prāṇa*) departs from an existing body, what is the sequence where the body itself is destroyed by a curse, a cut, or other means? He states that [sequence]: "The vital breath... [Verse 42]. It attains the state of space-wind (*vyomavāyutām*), that is, the state of merging with the wind residing in the external ether; there, in that external ether.
Just as the Videhas perceive their bodies in the ether, so too do they,
together with their minds, experience all conduct and everything else.

Just as they perceive a body—whether that of a god, a human, a beast, or the like—which consists of latent impressions manifested by their respective karma, so too do they experience conduct and behavior corresponding exactly to that. || 43 ||
Just as fragrance subsides when the movement of the wind has ceased, so too do the vital breaths subside when the movement of the mind has ceased. (44)
The vital breath and the mind are eternally inseparable in living beings; they exist as a mixture, like the fragrance of a flower or like sesame oil and its seeds. (45)
In sesame oil, which was mixed with the fragrance transferred from flowers. || 45 ||
The vibration of the mind is the vital breath; the vibration of the vital breath is the mind.
These two always move together like a chariot and its driver.
Like a chariot and its driver, they move about and coordinate their mutual movements. || 46 ||
Like the container and the contained, these two perish in the absence of one another;
and by their own destruction, they bring about the supreme effect known as liberation.
Like the container and the contained, or like fire and its heat. || 47 ||
Through the intense practice of a single reality, the mind becomes thoroughly stilled;
because its very nature is absorbed therein, the vital breath (prāṇa) is also stilled by that means. 48.
It is peaceful, with the latent impressions of duality suppressed; for the nature of the vital breath has dissolved into that mind, having become one with it.
Having reflected upon that reality of the infinite Self, lead the mind to identification with it; then, through absorption in that, the mind itself becomes stable as that very reality. (49)
Through absorption into that reality of the Self, that very reality of the Self becomes firm. || 49 ||
Whatever is the supreme good regarding both non-perception and perception—
since both are non-existent, remain established in that, or even in what remains.
Non-perception is ignorance; perception is the mental modification (vṛtti) in the form of Brahman which sublates that [ignorance].

When both of these—being non-existent—have ceased, that which remains is the "residue" (śeṣa). The meaning is: remain steady in that pure consciousness (cinmātra) through the sustenance of life-force (prāṇadhāraṇā). || 50 ||
One should contemplate the existence within a single, firmly established reality until, through thorough practice, that existence attains the state of non-existence. (51)

Regarding how long the meditation on a single principle (*ekatattva-bhāvanā*) should be maintained, he says: "In one... The word *bhāva* refers to the stream of mental modifications (*vṛtti-dhārā*) bearing that form. The meaning is: for as long as that stream of modifications—being consumed by the final direct realization—reaches the state of non-existence (*abhāvatva*), so long [should the meditation be maintained]. || 51 ||
For those who possess the power of withdrawal (pratyāhāra), the mind dissolves of its own accord, as if due to the exhaustion of objects of enjoyment;
together with the vital breaths, it vanishes, and only the Supreme remains.
Due to the exhaustion of what is to be experienced and the exhaustion of nourishment, it dissolves by itself, like the body. || 52 ||
When the mind becomes one-pointed, it instantly becomes that in which the entire flood of particularities has been stilled, due to its nature as long-cultivated practice. (53)

When the external forms of the mind have been dissolved by the five limbs ending with *dhāraṇā*, the state of being Brahman is accomplished through the perfection of non-conceptual *samādhi*—attained by means of the three limbs beginning with *dhāraṇā*—which results in the attainment of one-pointedness upon Brahman; thus he says: "That which is one-pointed" (verse 53).
Having understood through reasoned intellect that this ignorance does not exist, the supreme state is attained through knowledge alone; thereafter, its cultivation [is required]. (54)

Since there is no hearing or reflection, and because the practice of meditation and concentration is impossible, that which arises as duality through hearing and reflection is merely ignorance; and since that [ignorance] does not exist at all, the supreme state is attained solely through the knowledge of reality— having thus understood this, up to the point of dispelling the defects of doubt regarding the means of knowledge and their objects, one should thereafter proceed.
The meaning is that one should practice knowledge through meditation, concentration, and so forth. || 54 ||
When the mind is stilled, this mirage of saṃsāra subsides,
just as the mist composed of it vanishes when the cloud has reached its dissolution.

When autumn has arrived, there is the fading away of old age in the clouds; therefore, she has come from that [state], being composed of that. Regarding the sense "come from that," the suffix *mayaṭ* is applied according to the rule *hetumanuṣyebhyo 'nyatarasyāṃ mayaṭ ca*. 55.
Know that ignorance is mind-only; therefore, bring about its destruction by that very means.
O Rāma, that which is of the nature of the mind is the Self; for the supreme state is not non-existence.

By that very mind transformed into the form of Brahman, bring about the destruction of that [ordinary] mind. As for the nature of that destruction of the mind, it is the Self itself as the substratum of consciousness, not emptiness (śūnyatā). For the meaning is that its mere non-existence is not the supreme state, nor the supreme human goal. || 56 ||
If the mind attains nirvāṇa for even a moment in the supreme state,
know that it has been transformed into that very state and has experienced its flavor therein.
The particle *eva* is used in the sense of "also. Nirvāṇa has come to rest. Therefore, know that it is indeed that Brahman itself which has undergone transformation;
for there is no essential nature of the superimposed [object] apart from its substratum.
Thus, having attained the taste of unsurpassed, self-luminous bliss within that very [Brahman], it does not desire to emerge again—this is the meaning.

And so it has been said in the *Śivadharmottara*: "He by whom the nectar-like essence of knowledge has been tasted even once—having abandoned all other activities, his mind runs toward that alone. (57)
If your mind has found rest through Sāṃkhya or even through Yoga,
having attained the state of pure being for a moment, it will not be born here again.
He states that this very thing is the single fruit of the two systems under discussion, Sāṃkhya and Yoga, with the words "yat" (that which). || 58 ||
The mind from which ignorance has dissolved is designated by the term "sentient being" (sattva);
having burnt the seed of saṃsāra, it does not provide an interval for rebirth again. || 59 ||
He himself states the meaning of the word *sattva*: "the mind" (*cetaḥ*). "Internal" (*antaraṃ*) refers to the interruption of the state of Brahman. || 59 ||
A certain person whose ignorance has dissolved, who is established in being and whose latent impressions are stilled,
immediately beholds the supreme light, which is like emptiness, and becomes tranquil.

He says "someone" (kaścit) to indicate that those people who are oriented toward seeing That are indeed rare: from the perspective of the ignorant, it is like a void due to a lack of conviction; but from the perspective of the wise, it is the supreme light. || 60 ||
O fortunate one, that state in which the sense of self has dissolved and the mind has melted away is indeed called "pure being" (sattva) here;
it does not return again to the state stained by the parts [of worldly existence], just as copper that has attained the state of gold does not revert [to its former condition]. 61.

Reiterating the very meaning already stated, he concludes with the verse beginning "vigalita": O fortunate one, you whose states characterized by the delusion of the waking, dreaming, and deep sleep stages— along with their seeds and the perception thereof— have dissolved through the practice of the three aforementioned means, and who yourself have likewise dissolved and been rendered sublated through the destruction of ignorance.
In this state of liberation while living (jīvanmukti), the mind—of which nothing remains but its mere appearance, like a burnt cloth—is called *sattva*.

Because the power of the seeds of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) has been incinerated, it does not again enter the realm of transmigratory existence, stained by the subtle constituents of passion, hatred, and egoism. Just as copper that has attained the state of gold through contact with the touchstone (*sparśamaṇi*) [does not revert].
The meaning is that, in the same way, it does not attain a copper-colored state defiled by the presence of a stain. || 61 ||

Thus ends the sixty-ninth canto, titled "An Investigation into the Union of Vital Breath and Mind," in the Holy Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa, belonging to the Ṛṣis, within the section on Liberation (Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa), in the portion concerning the Great Delusion (Mokṣopāya).
Thus ends the sixty-ninth chapter, titled "An Investigation into the Union of Vital Breath and Mind," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The Seventieth Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
The living soul quickly becomes non-living; the mind attains the state of being no-mind.
Liberation is said to be the end of the ignorance of the sun of discernment. || 1 ||
In order to purify the conscious self from the instability of illusion and delusion, this auspicious narrative of the dialogue between the Vetāla king is here set forth. (1)

It has been said that when the mind is stilled, this mirage of saṃsāra subsides; and for the stilling of the mind, inquiry alone—carried on until the dawning of knowledge—is the means. Thus he says: "The living soul. By this means, that which is the end—the destruction—of both the effect and the cause of ignorance is designated as liberation (mokṣa). || 1 ||
The mind, ego, and so forth are perceived like the water of a mirage; though they are entirely non-existent, they appear slightly so, yet they dissolve through inquiry. || 2 ||
He dispels the misconception of firmness regarding the phenomenal world—the cause for doubting the meaning already stated—by saying "like a mirage."
Listen to these auspicious questions, uttered by a Vetāla during the delusion of the dream of saṃsāra, which have come to my memory through this present occasion. (3)
He introduces a narrative (ākhyāyikā) to support the meaning already stated—that [the world] is indeed non-existent, yet appearing as if real—beginning with the words "saṃsṛti... (verse 3).
In the great Vindhya forest, there was a Vetāla of massive form;
out of pride, he came to a certain region with the intent to kill.
Out of pride, they show contempt for ignorant people who deserve to be punished. || 4 ||
Formerly, that Vetāla dwelt in a certain abode of virtuous people,
happy because he was constantly satisfied by the offering of many sacrifices.

To expand upon what was stated in brief, he begins again from the beginning with the word "sa" (he). In the land of King Sajjana, namely the kingdom of the Kirātas, he—like a *karkaṭī* (crab)—was constantly satisfied by the great offerings of human sacrifices made by the king, and thus remained happy in his undisturbed meditative concentration (*samādhi*). || 5 ||
Even though he was hungry, he did not kill a man who had arrived before him without cause or fault; for the virtuous are indeed observers of justice.
In due time, that forest-dweller went to another city,
driven by hunger, to consume people through fraudulent means.
At that time, at the time when no person to be executed could be found there; for whom the forest was his home.
There he encountered the king, who had gone out on a night patrol;
that fierce night-stalker addressed him with a deep and terrible voice.

Nightly conduct refers to wandering about at night within the city for the purpose of identifying wicked persons and for the sake of executing thieves and others; it is that which has gone out for such purposes. (8)
The Vetāla said:
"O King, you have now been caught by me, the Bhīma Vetāla!
Where are you going? You are ruined; become my food this very day!"
The king said:
"O night-stalker, if you devour me here by force despite it being unjust, your head shall split into a thousand pieces; of this there is no doubt. (10)
One should sprinkle [it] with what is unjust, by means of a sequence devoid of logic. || 10 ||
The Vetāla said:
"I shall not devour you, for this is an injustice; indeed, I am speaking what is just.
You are a king, and all the hopes of those who seek your favor must be fulfilled by you. (11)

"All hopes" (āśāḥ) refers to all desired objects that are wished for. The word "kila" [in the root text; note: the reading "kila" in the commentary is not seen in the manuscripts near me] indicates what is well-known in the *Dharmaśāstra*. 11.
O King, fulfill this request of mine which seeks a meaningful outcome;
you ought to correctly explain these questions that I have posed.
If he is ignorant, a thousand offenses are easily committed; if he is wise, he does not offend at all.

And since he is to be protected even when a thousand offenses exist, he requests only the completion of the questions for the sake of examination—thereby demonstrating that he has no inclination toward the killing of others. (12)
To which sun do the worlds appear as mere minute atoms?
In what wind do the great particles of the vast sky manifest? (13)
The superficial meaning of all these questions is clear; however, their intended significance will be clarified in the following chapter.
(13) Just as one moving from one dream to another dream by the hundreds and thousands neither abandons nor does not abandon one's own pure and luminous nature, who [could do so]? (14)
Even though one abandons the reality of each preceding stage in a dream as each subsequent dream arises, one does not abandon that clear, true nature of the self which illuminates them all. || 14 ||
Just as the core of a plantain trunk consists of nothing but layers of leaves, one after another, so too does that very same subtle atom exist within, within, and within again. 15.

Just as the trunk of a plantain tree (rambhā) is hollow within and within it there is only leaf and bark; the point of the illustration is that while in the example there is an interior of bark similar to that [of the trunk], in the case being illustrated, it is that very [trunk] itself—this is the distinction. || 15 ||
For whom, not abandoning their atomic nature, would the Brahma-egg, the ether, the flood of elements, the solar orb, and Mount Meru be mere atoms? (16)

By the term "multitude of beings" (bhūtaugha), the worlds that serve as their substrates are indicated. Those things renowned for their extreme vastness, such as the ether of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) and so forth, are yet the most minute atoms (paramāṇavaḥ)—that is, exceedingly small—when compared with that atom [of the Lord]. || 16 ||
Within the stone of a single, partless atom—
a great mountain— the marrow of the three worlds exists as a dense, singular form.
Of that which is the subtle atom itself, yet [appears as] the great mountain—whose very marrow and essence is that existence which is dense, most solid, and of an exclusively singular nature. (17)
If you speak thus to me, O evil-souled one, then having swallowed you here, O self-destroyer,
I shall forcibly seize your orb like a fruit, just as the God of Death seizes the world.

"If you do not answer these six questions of mine, then [I shall treat] you as one who has killed himself—meaning that the body and so forth, which are actually non-self, are considered by you to be the self;

and for that very reason, you have destroyed the unlimited Self through the limitation [of identifying it with the body]. Therefore, O self-killer, because of this offense of not answering, I shall forcibly and violently swallow you like a fruit."
"I shall devour the maṇḍala and the people situated within the maṇḍala. In the reading "grase 'ham," the substitution of the verbal suffix (vikaraṇa) is a Vedic anomaly (chāndasa). || 18 ||
Thus ends the seventieth chapter, titled "The Question of the Vetāla," in the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa* of the *Mokṣopāya* section of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki. 70.
Thus ends the seventieth chapter, titled "The Question of the Vetāla," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The seventy-first canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
When the Vetāla had spoken thus, he laughed and proceeded to answer the questions.
The king, whose garments were white with the luster of his teeth, spoke these words.
The resolution of the first question is described here in detail through conceptualizations such as the fruit-trees and other features of infinite millions of cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas).

Smiling with the rays of his teeth, [he spoke] with the intention that what you said— that well-known universes constitute a *trasareṇu*— was based on a narrow perspective, for according to the conception to be described, even universes containing millions upon millions of embryos could possibly be considered *trasareṇus* therein.
Being one whose garments, clothes, and the sky itself were made white by his radiances. || 1 ||
The King said:
"If this cosmic egg indeed exists as an imperishable fruit,
it is surrounded by successive layers of elemental skins, each ten times greater than the preceding one."

Therein, first, in order to state the answer to the initial question—"How many atoms of the universe are there in the rays of the sun?"—the King, displaying a certain marvel of his own imagination while setting aside the Vetāla’s pride in his supreme expertise, says: "It exists," and so forth. This [universe] has been conceived by both you and me through the vision of the universe as a sacrifice.
It is ageless, progressively increasing tenfold at each stage, and enveloped by coverings of earth, water, and so forth, which consist of the elements. || 2 ||
Indeed, there were thousands of such fruits upon it;
its branches were exceedingly high, vast, and possessed trembling foliage. (3)

1. This Brahmāṇḍa; 2. the fivefold-composed (pañcīkṛta) gross elements containing within them thousands of such Brahmāṇḍas; 3. the subtle element of smell (gandhatanmātra) contained within those; 4–7. the subsequent subtle elements of taste and so forth, each containing the preceding within it;
8. the mind of Hiraṇyagarbha contained within those; 9. the infinite masses of the mere elements (bhūtamātrārāśi), past and future, contained within that; [10. those contained within that.
The periods of the Kalpas (10) are the internal contents of those [Kalpas], serving as the days for each subsequent one;

these are the life-spans of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, and they are of the same nature as those [Kalpas]. That which initiates the existence, manifestation, and worldly activity of those infinite millions is Brahman variegated by Māyā (māyā-śabala). 14.

He demonstrates these fourteen categories here in their proper sequence through the fourteen conceptualizations beginning with "fruit" and "branch," starting with the words "tādṛśānām" (of such [categories]) and so forth.
In that [Nature], the worlds are as unstable as tender leaves. (3)
Furthermore, there is a great tree of vast form, difficult to perceive, upon which there exist thousands of such branches. || 4 ||
Where there are thousands of such trees,
that forest is exceedingly lofty, filled with infinite trees and shrubs.
Where there are thousands of such forests,
there stands the great Bṛhacchṛṅga, exceedingly high and of massive form.
By the word "peak" (śṛṅga), it is the mountain itself that is primarily intended here, because of its extreme vastness and its form which is filled on all sides.
Furthermore, there is a vast region with extensive hollows where there exist thousands of such peaks.
Furthermore, where there are thousands of such regions,
there exists a great island (Bṛhaddvīpa) endowed with vast lakes and rivers.
It was endowed with the activities of the vital breaths (*prāṇa* and others), which flow whether manifest or unmanifest, like the currents of great lakes and rivers. || 8 ||
Furthermore, where there exist thousands of such islands,
there is likewise a surface of the earth endowed with various wonderful arrangements.
It is endowed with various compositions of names and so forth. || 9 ||
Furthermore, where there exist thousands of such worlds,
there exists that vast and expansive grand display of the great universe.
Furthermore, there exists a vast cosmic egg (aṇḍa) like a fierce seat of the sky, wherein there are thousands of such worlds.
There is a vast ocean, a sea devoid of movement, wherein thousands of such eggs are like small caskets.
There exists a great ocean, pure and consisting of its own playful manifestation, wherein even hundreds of thousands of such oceans would be but a faint ripple. (13)
Furthermore, suppose there were some man of such exceedingly tall stature and massive form that the waters within his belly could hold thousands of such oceans. (14)
The Person is Viṣṇu. || 14 ||
There exists a Supreme Person, the foremost among all beings, upon whose chest a garland made of hundreds of thousands of such men rests. (15)
Rudra is the Supreme Person. || 15 ||
Thousands of such great-souled men flash forth within his mandala like the network of hairs on his own body.

"Tanūruhāḥ" refers to the hair of the body and head, like a net produced from that [body]. And thus says the Śruti: "Just as the hair of the body and head arises from an existing person, so does this universe arise here from the Imperishable (akṣara). || 16 ||
There exists such a Great Sun within hundreds of perceptions;
all these various mental constructs are but His radiance.

Those hundreds and countless manifestations and appearances— beginning with Rudra and ending with the cosmic egg— which appear through outward perceptions other than the inward vision, are all directly perceived by every living being as the splendors and rays of that Sun.
The atoms of the cosmic egg are but sparks from the radiance of this sun;
I have been called the Sun of Consciousness, and he alone illumines all this.

I have stated that the conscious self (cidātman) possesses such power as this sun; in response to your question, I have said that it is this [self] which heats and illuminates this entire world. || 18 ||
The supreme sun, whose intention is purified, is indeed the very self of consciousness;
these expansive worlds are but the motes of dust within its light. (19)
The expanses of the worlds are the cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas). || 19 ||
By the radiance of the supreme sun of consciousness, these fortunes of the day of the world shine and come into being, just as the splendors of the sun appear at times.
They shine, that is, they attain manifestation; they come into being, that is, they attain existence. || 20 ||

O living beings, within this self which is consciousness alone, the jewel of the pavilion of the three worlds remains unmanifest; yet here, you scribble the frantic delusions of worldly existence upon the birth of consciousness—alas, there is not even the slightest trace of peace, so remain at rest!

O Vetāla, regarding the Sun— the jewel of the pavilion of the three worlds, whose variegated characteristics as Brahman have been described— there arises, among the primary qualified aspirants who constitute his ultimate reality,
a realization consisting of the unbroken-form direct intuition produced by the scriptures; and by that alone, [the Sun] shines forth within the individual self as one's own self.

But in this inner self (pratyagātman), which is merely a non-qualified being, devoid of expansion and unmanifest, there exist the delineations and impressions of the birth of consciousness and the world— like sparks from a fire— as well as the separate existence of the individual soul (jīva) and the universe, along with the infinite delusions of agency, enjoyership, and so forth.

But from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), they do not exist even in the slightest; therefore, the meaning is: "Remain quiet, putting an end to this ostentatious display of questioning."

Thus ends the seventy-first chapter, titled "The Description of the First Question and Answer of the Vetāla," in the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa* of the *Mokṣopāya* section of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, according to the tradition of the Ṛṣis.

Thus ends the seventy-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Response to the First Question of the Vetāla," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The seventy-second canto.
The King said:
"The existence of time, the existence of space, and the existence of vibration are composed of consciousness."
And the existence of pure consciousness—everything such as this is purifying. || 1 ||
Here, the king correctly proclaims the answers to the five remaining questions, in due order, to the vigilant Vetāla.

Having thus resolved the first question, the King answers the second question—"In which wind do the great particles of the sky manifest?"—with the words beginning with "kālasattā" (the existence of time). In this context, by the term "gagana" (sky), it is intended that the well-known sky itself is being grasped; however, because it is qualified by the word "mahat" (great), it is understood through secondary (gauṇī) indication.

Whether it be the space of *māyā* conjoined with consciousness in the form of Mahākāla, or the space of the *sūtrātman* characterized primarily by the power of vibration (*spanda-śakti*), or the space of the individual soul (*jīvākāśa*) defined as the manifestation of pure consciousness extracted from that [space], or whatever else it may be—in all these conceptualizations, it is their very existence (*sattā*) that is the subtlest of all; therefore, those have been called "particles" (*reṇu*) by you. Thus he says: "the existence of time" (*kālasattā*). Vibration (*spanda*).

The *sūtrātmā* (the thread-self), whose primary attribute is the power of action (*kriyāśakti*), is its existence; from that, the pure consciousness is extracted as the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*), and its existence, and so forth—all this, because of its subtlety, is purifying and faultless. It flashes forth within the great wind of the Supreme Self (*paramātman-mahāvāyu*), flickering with the many transformations imagined therein; such is the connection with the subsequent [verse]. || 1 ||
In the great wind of the Supreme Self, the restless dust vibrates; like fragrance in a flower-body, it is by its very nature both identical with and distinct from that form.

Now, since it is the Supreme Self alone that exists as the nature of existence (*sattā*) pervading all things, how can there be a designation of a relationship between substratum and superstratum (*ādhārādheya-bhāva*) such that the existence of time and so forth manifests therein? To this he says: "In the flower" (*kusumāṅge*).
Just as the flower itself, having by its own nature imagined a distinction called fragrance within its own parts, [manifests] in the flower...

The meaning is that, just as a fragrance exists by being inherent in its substrate, so too ultimate existence itself remains after having conceptually projected within itself the nature of various distinctions such as the existence of time and so forth. || 2 ||
In the great dream called the world, as one passes from one dream to another dream,
the tranquil form of Brahman— which is the expansion of peace— does not abandon its state of peace.

He provides the answer to the third question, beginning with "Moving from one dream to another," in the verse starting with *jagadākhye*: "The world-renowned [Brahman] is peaceful, its various defects of dreaming being thoroughly stilled, and it is of the nature of unattached light. Therefore, because it is pure consciousness, Brahman is both peace and expansion. (3)
Just as a plantain trunk consists of nothing but layers within layer,
so too this entire universe, though it is Brahman, is a mere appearance within appearance.
With the words "the plantain trunk," he answers the fourth question, "Is it merely a leaf?"—namely, "the plantain trunk.

It "revolves within" (vivarti) Brahman; by the word "also" (api), it is implied that it is also subject to transformation (pariṇāma) in intermediate causes. Therefore, it is subtle (aṇu); the meaning is that it is subtler even than that [Brahman]. || 4 ||
That which is praised by these words such as "Being," "Brahman," and "Self" is,
according to you, a void, indefinable, and nothing at all.

He states in verse 5 that it is only by virtue of being the cause for the expansion of the world through illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) and so forth that [the Self] becomes the referent of various terms such as "Brahman" and "Ātman," but not in reality, because it is devoid of all attributes (*sarvadharmaśūnyatva*). Thus he says: "Brahman... (verse 5).
Whatever existence is conceptualized, each is fashioned by experience;
like the trunk of a plantain tree, it is merely this pure, pervasive consciousness alone.
For this very reason, the existence of the cloth culminates in the existence of the threads; the existence of the threads in the existence of the cotton;
that [existence] in the existence of its fruit; that in the existence of the shrub; and that in the existence of the seed, the earth, water, and so forth.
In this sequence, whatever existence is discerned, each of them—having abandoned the various forms constructed by their respective experiences—is like a plantain trunk.

Since it culminates in pure consciousness (cinmātra), which consists of those various experiences, the meaning is that this very stainless [consciousness] is spread out—that is, expanded—in the form of the world. || 6 ||
Because of its subtlety and its unattainability, the Supreme Self is the supreme atom;
yet because of its infinity, it alone has attained the state of being the foundation for Mount Meru and all else.

Regarding that, he states the reason for proceeding word by word: "because of its subtlety" (*sūkṣmatvāt*). Thus, even in such subtlety, there is no loss of fullness; therefore, even the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) and other such things, when viewed from that perspective, are like atoms due to their extreme limitation.
Consequently, the fifth question—concerning the ether of the cosmic egg, the elements, and so forth—is also answered.

With this intention, he says: "Because of its infinity. By the phrase "Meru and so forth," the five [elements] mentioned in the question, ending with Meru, are taken in reverse order; their "root-ness" means their status as the substratum. || 7 ||
Even for this person who is subtler than the subtle and infinitely vast, the world and so forth appear like an atom, because they are perceived as being devoid of form.

The fivefold group beginning with the world and the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) is non-eternal because it is perceived; because it is delimited by infinitesimal particles of consciousness (citkaṇa) as defined by mental modifications (vṛtti) in the form of those respective objects; and because it possesses form, just like an atom (paramāṇu). || 8 ||
This person (puruṣa) is subtler than an atom because he cannot be grasped, yet he is like a great mountain because he fills [all space];
though he consists of all limbs, he is devoid of limbs.
He answers the sixth question—"Of what partless [entity] is the atom and the great mountain?"—with the words "The supreme atom" (*paro’ṇu*).

Because it is unobtainable, that is, because it cannot be grasped by the sense organs such as the eyes; this supreme atom is the great mountain because it fills [all space], being pervaded everywhere. From the perspective of superimposition (*adhyāropa*), it is that of which everything, both the formed (*mūrta*) and the formless (*amūrta*), is a constituent part (*avayava*).
With the negation "not this, not this," its constituent parts are cast away. || 9 ||
O virtuous one, know that this triple world is indeed the mere marrow of this pure consciousness;
for the triple world has pure awareness alone as its very core.

In this regard, he reveals the portion consisting of the three worlds as the marrow, which is of a single, dense form within the stone (the heart), with the words "of this" (*asya*). For the meaning is:

know that the interior of the middle [space], like marrow, is well-known in such Vedic passages as "The three worlds—heaven and earth—are indeed contained within [it]," as being the mere consciousness whose nature is the space within the heart (*hārdākāśa*).
The worlds, perceived as mere mental constructs of consciousness, are by nature peaceful, delicate, and infinite in form;
O child Vetāla, that state is truly unassailable—realize this for yourself and remain in peace.

By dispelling all questions, as if outdoing the Vetāla with his own maturity, he concludes the stated subject matter in brief with the verse beginning "vijñāna": "O young Vetāla, the worlds are the manifestation— the display— of the various manifestations of pure consciousness, which are its own skills."

And that nature of the self-consciousness is indeed unassailable and unassailable by such as you— those who are like goblin-attendants; therefore, according to my words, realize the self as being of this very nature and ascend to that direct experience.
The meaning is: "Remain with your pride stilled. || 11 ||
Thus ends the seventy-second chapter, titled "The Resolution of the Vetāla’s Questions," in the Nirvāṇa Section of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, within the *Deva-mokṣopāya*.
Thus ends the seventy-second chapter, titled "The Dispelling of the Vetāla’s Questions," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The seventy-third canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Having heard this from the mouth of the king, the Vetāla attained peace.
By means of an intellect cultivated therein and suited for investigation, [one should proceed]. || 1 ||
Having taught here the conclusion of the Vetāla’s questions,
another account concerning Bhagīratha is also described therein.

In that case, with respect to that king, [the word "therefore" (*tatra*)] is used as a cause characterized by an intellect suited for deliberation, by an inferred state of being cultivated within oneself, and by the knowledge of reality;
or, in the case of the *vetāla*, all [these factors] are to be applied accordingly. || 1 ||
Having become tranquil in mind and considering solitude to be blameless,
he became absorbed in unwavering meditation, forgetting his agonizing hunger.
"One whose meditation is unshakable" means, in other words, one who is established in samādhi. || 2 ||
O Rāma, this web of questions from the Vetāla has been told to you by me;
in this manner, this entire world is established within that atom of consciousness.
In this manner, according to the sequence described by the king. || 3 ||
The entire universe, which resides within the sheath of the body, dissolves through inquiry;
that state which remains is like the body of a corpse-demon (vetāla). || 4 ||
It dissolves like the body of a vetāla imagined through the delusion of a child. || 4 ||
Withdrawing the mind from all directions with a tranquil inner self,
remaining desireless and abiding in its own true nature, stay with a peaceful intellect.
Having withdrawn the mind from everything, one should cause that which has fallen upon one's own nature as the Supreme Self to become firmly established there.
O Sage, having made the mind itself as clear as space by means of the mind alone,
remain with a self that is uniquely stilled and tranquil, perceiving equality everywhere.
O sage Rāma, one who is reflective by nature possesses tranquility (śama) regarding a single object, which is the dissolution of all mental functions;
by that, his self is peaceful and his mind is stilled. For this very reason, he is one of equal vision (samadarśana), seeing Brahman as the same everywhere.
For a king who is firm-minded, undeluded, and follows what has been attained, even that which is difficult to accomplish succeeds, just as it did for King Bhagīratha.

The phrase ending with "unconfused" (asaṃmūḍha) follows from what precedes. Now, one might ask: "If I am established in this way, how can the maintenance of my bodily existence (dehayātrā) be accomplished? To this he says:
"For one whose mind is completely tranquil, whose activity is fully satisfied, and who always abides within the Self which is equanimous and composed of bliss..."
Even desired objects that are most difficult to attain are accomplished, just as the excavation of the ocean was achieved at the descent of the Gaṅgā.

Just as the descent of the Gaṅgā— which was more difficult to obtain for Sagara, Aṃśumat, Dilīpa, and others than even the substance of the oceans dug by the sons of Sagara, namely the ocean itself and the life-restoring jewel— was achieved without effort by Bhagīratha, who was endowed with qualities such as tranquility, contentment, and equanimity; so too [is this].
The meaning is that it is established in the same manner. || 8 ||
Thus ends the seventy-third chapter, titled "The Narrative of the Vetāla," in the Nirvāṇa Section of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa* of Valmīki, within the *Dehādhikāra* on the means to liberation.
Thus ends the seventy-third chapter, titled "The Narrative of the Vetāla," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The seventy-fourth canto.
Śrī Rāma said:
Just as the descent of Gaṅgā was brought about for the king through the wondrous power of his mind...
O Lord, tell me how that was accomplished for Bhagīratha.
In this [chapter], the virtues of Bhagīratha and the reflection born of inquiry are described,
as well as his dialogue with Trita arising from a desire to renounce.
By means of the wonder characterized by the fullness of the mind, etc. || 1 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
There was a most righteous king named Bhagīratha,
who was like a tilaka ornament upon the circle of the earth bounded by the oceans.
He was the king of the earth bounded by the oceans, and was like the preeminent ornament of his own kingdom of Kosala. || 2 ||
Immediately upon their resolve, those who seek [his favor] obtain whatever they desire from him,
whose face is as serene as the moon, as if from a wish-fulfilling gem.

He describes his generosity with the words "immediately after the resolve" (*saṃkalpānantaram*). As soon as Bhagīratha had formed the resolve to give, those who were petitioners—suppliants—obtained the object of their desire exactly as they wished, without even the exertion of approaching him or speaking; that is, they attained it without such effort. The suffix *kta* is used here in the sense of the agent, according to the rule *gatyarthākarmaka-* (Pāṇini 3.4.72).

By the phrase "with a face as bright as the moon," it is illuminated that due to his enthusiasm for giving, there is an extraordinary clarity on his face, and not a withering caused by the pain of expending wealth. || 3 ||
He who gave away wealth incessantly for the sake of establishing the righteous takes up only a blade of grass at times, like a wish-fulfilling gem.

He restrains giving to unworthy recipients by saying "to the virtuous. To the question, "How can one who is disposed toward such expenditure obtain wealth? he replies with the words "even as much as a blade of grass. This means that at some source of income, he accepts even a mere blade of grass obtained through his own duty (*svadharma*). Because of the risk of tautology and because the term "blade of grass" is not well-known in the context of the Cintāmaṇi jewel, [the author] uses the word "Cintāmaṇi."
The wish-fulfilling cow is perceived. || 4 ||
He who shattered the iron machine with its gem at the bottom— like a blazing-rimmed wheel set upon a core of diamond— is the conduct of all wicked men.

Just as a *vajravedhana* gem— which is fastened or bound below by an iron mechanism (*ayoyantra*)— shines and radiates its own brilliance as it revolves within a diamond-hard, exceedingly firm, and inner diamond casing; having thus pierced [the object] in such a manner, it [reaches] that which is strung upon it and fit for its qualities.

He who is like Bhagīratha acts in such a way that he subdues even the most powerful wicked person and all their activities by means of his own majesty; and while doing so, he seizes them— pierced by weapons and missiles— and casts them down beneath his feet, such that the circles of the earth marked by the rims of his chariot wheels shine brightly as he performs this deed.

The meaning is that he made an iron instrument (ayoyantra) by which [the enemy] was constrained by shackles and the like, and having broken it—as if having shattered it—he rendered him full of virtues. Even in the reading "vajrasāram api," this same intended meaning is conveyed through the metaphorical expression (rūpaka). || 5 ||
Though his body was weary from the lack of smoke and fire, and though he was utterly destitute,
he dispelled the darkness of men, just as the sun dispels the nocturnal gloom of houses.

Though he himself was not fatigued by wandering everywhere day and night for the protection of his subjects, he removed the darkness of the house of *tamas*—the cause of men’s engagement in unrighteousness—as well as their wretchedness and poverty;
just as the sun removes the nocturnal darkness of houses and the distress of worldly affairs. The adjectives apply to both cases.
It should be applied. || 6 ||
Scattering a shower of sparks born from his own prowess on all sides,
he blazes among his enemies like the fire produced by a midday sun-gem.
