Scattering a shower—a stream—of sparks born from his own majesty, prowess, and intense heat, he blazes like a fire from sun-crystal stones ignited at midday among his enemies; in the case of fire, "ariṇa" refers to grass and the like, so called because they possess "arīṇi," meaning tips or points. || 7 ||
That which has a soft and cool touch, gladdening the mind of the wise, causes them to melt with affection, just as a moonstone melts at the sight of the moon.
Those who know the reality of Brahman are well-acquainted with them; in their presence, the moonstone—the *candrakānta*—[melts]. || 8 ||
By him, the third strand of this Ganges-stream— whose sacred thread is the universe and which flows through heaven and the netherworld— has been replenished in this world.

By him, the third strand of the thread of the world’s sacred thread—characterized by the flow of the Gaṅgā and resembling the current of the Gaṅgā—was fulfilled on this earth through the descent of the Gaṅgā. || 9 ||

The ocean, which had been dried up by Agastya, was filled once more by the flood of the Gaṅgā— just as a great caravan of supplicants, though difficult to satisfy, is replenished by one who fulfills their needs.
It was like a great caravan or assembly of supplicants from every quarter of the horizon, [provided] with wealth.
By him, the friend of the world, those dwelling in the netherworld were joined with the realm of Brahmā by means of a flight of stairs leading up the Gaṅgā.

Because they were hostile to living beings and consumed by the Brahma-staff (brahmadaṇḍa), the kinsmen—the sons of Sagara—had attained an inferior state and dwelt in the netherworld; yet, by means of that flight of stairs characterized as Gaṅgā, they were joined with, that is, elevated to, the world of Brahman. || 11 ||
He who propitiated Brahmā, Śaṅkara, and Jahnu through austerity repeatedly experienced exhaustion, yet his resolve never wavered.
From one's own mind, which is characterized by a non-empty resolve and possesses an uninterrupted, firm conviction. || 12 ||
Even for that lord of the earth, while he was in the prime of youth and reflecting upon this worldly course which is so full of turmoil, [the following occurred].
By the force of the word "api," it is understood that [the result] belongs to you alone. || 13 ||
A tiny spark of the wonder of dispassion arose within her;
yet, even though she was in the bloom of youth, by fate it was as if a creeper had grown in a desert.
The phrase "in youth" (*marāviva*) is used to illustrate that the arising of discernment and dispassion during youth is extremely rare. || 14 ||
In private, this lord of the earth reflected thus:
"This course of the world is eternally inconsistent and agitated. (15)

Thus, in the manner about to be described, he reflected upon this course of worldly existence. He states the very manner of that reflection: "Again the day, again the night, and again hundreds of acts of giving and taking;
yet for those performing such actions, it all appears as nothing but the insipid taste of what has already been enjoyed. (16)

The night is dark. The meaning is that for all those who act, only such fruit as has been eaten many times and is tasteless is perceived, and not a new fruit consisting of the supreme goal of human life (paramapuruṣārtha). || 16 ||
I consider that deed to be truly well-done by which, once accomplished, nothing remains in this world yet to be attained; all other action is but a painful indigestion.
The meaning is that whatever action has been performed as a means to attain various [worldly goals] results only in impurity and suffering, like a piercing colic (viṣūcikā). || 17 ||
Repeatedly performing his habitual deeds without shame, who indeed would act like a fool with such deluded and senseless intellect? (18)
Then once, his mind agitated and fearing worldly existence, Bhagīratha questioned his guru Tritala in private.
Then, immediately after that thought was expressed, being utterly and completely terrified of worldly existence (saṃsṛti), [he spoke]. || 19 ||
Bhagīratha said: "O Lord, having wandered for a very long time within these forest-like worldly conditions that are empty at their core, we are utterly exhausted."
Of wandering living beings, amidst these wildernesses of heaven, hell, and the human state—which are the results of worldly conditions such as passion and hatred—[there is no end]. || 20 ||
O Blessed One, how does the end come about for all sufferings—such as old age, death, and delusion—which cause worldly existence? (21)
Tritala said: O King, for one whose self is long since equanimous, who delights in the undivided, and whose soul is filled with the full realization of that which is to be known— ‖ 22 ‖
Through the means of hearing and reflecting upon the fourfold qualifications (*sādhanacatuṣṭaya*), that which has been long practiced—

a samādhi devoid of the imbalance between equanimity and distraction— arises as the very nature of the Self. By means of the awakening to the object of knowledge, the innermost reality (*pratyaktattva*), which manifests through the form of the eternally established Brahman, all sufferings are destroyed.
The subsequent [inference] is by means of positive concomitance. || 22 ||
All sufferings are exhausted, the knots are severed on all sides, doubts reach a state of equanimity, and all actions are brought to rest, O sinless one. (23)
They know the Self to be the object of knowledge, perfectly pure and consisting of consciousness;
it is omnipresent and eternal, neither setting nor rising.
And it does not undergo arising. || 24 ||
Bhagīratha said:

"O Lord of Sages, I know that there exists only pure consciousness—devoid of qualities, peaceful, stainless, and infallible—and that nothing else, such as the body and so forth, exists apart from it. (25)

Thus instructed, Bhagīratha, having reflected within himself upon the reality of the Self through discernment and having reached an initial certainty, found no firm footing for his mind there due to its great restlessness. Reporting the portion he had understood to the Guru, he asks for the means to clarify that [reality] and to pacify the distractions, saying: "Pure Consciousness alone... and so forth.
By the word "it exists," it is indicated that the portion of ignorance in me which establishes non-existence has been destroyed.
Furthermore, through faith in Your words and by my own reasoning, I know that everything else—down to the body, senses, vital breath, mind, intellect, and ignorance—is not the Self. (25)
"Is it that my practice of that [truth] becomes clear, and not the other? O Blessed One, how may I possess this much realization alone? (26)

In this context, he shows that the portion of ignorance which causes non-appearance and the portion of distraction which is the cause for the appearance of the other have not perished in himself—by asking "Why? Here, between these two—the knowledge that discriminates between the existent and the non-existent—the former realization, which consists of the knowledge of the Self as the Existent, does not attain clarity, that is, distinctness like a myrobalan fruit in the palm of one's hand; what then [is the reason]?
The reason is this: by what means and how might I attain the cessation of all distractions and this state of pure awareness alone? Such is the meaning. || 26 ||
Tritala said:
Through knowledge, the mind attains a state of absorption in the object of knowledge within the sky of the heart;
thereafter, having become the universal body, the living soul is not born again.

In this regard, having determined that Bhagīratha’s distraction arises precisely from his identification with sovereignty and other such things—due to which his mind runs after various objects—and that because of the intensity of this distraction he does not have a clear realization of the Self, Tritala first instructs him on the means such as humility (*amānitva*) mentioned in the *Gītā* in order to cause him to abandon them, saying: "By knowledge... (*jñānena*).

"Knowledge" (jñāna) is that by which something is known, namely humility and so forth; "that which is to be known" (jñeya), which I shall declare, and so on—this means that one does not fall away from the nature of the Absolute (pūrṇasvabhāva). || 27 ||
Non-attachment and absence of possessiveness toward children, wife, home, and so forth; and constant equanimity of mind amidst the occurrence of the pleasant and the unpleasant. (28)

He elaborates upon some of the qualities beginning with "non-conceit" (amānitva) through detailed explanation, including partial citations and restatements, starting with the verse beginning "Non-attachment" (asakti).
Constant meditation upon that through yoga inseparable from the Self, resorting to solitary places, and a lack of delight in the assembly of people. (29)
He shows the intended meaning of the statement, "and unswerving devotion to Me through the yoga of exclusive concentration," by means of the word *ātmanaḥ*:

the meaning is that here, devotion to the Blessed One consists solely in the contemplation of the isolated Self (*niṣkṛṣṭātman*), and not the hearing or chanting of His qualities and deeds, as intended by the Blessed One. || 29 ||
Constancy in the knowledge of the inner self and the vision of the goal of the knowledge of reality—this is declared to be knowledge; that which is contrary to this is ignorance. (30)

Constancy in the knowledge of the inner self is the practice of hearing, reflection, and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*). The vision of the reality of the object—the supreme self-reality—through the knowledge of truth, which you have asked about, is that which constitutes the fruit of all spiritual means. || 30 ||
O King, knowledge is attained when the sense of "I" is stilled; it has the form of the destruction of passion and hatred, and is the medicine for the disease of saṃsāra.

The practice characterized by non-egoism (anahaṃkāra) is the root of all spiritual practices; for when egoism exists, qualities such as humility (amānitva) and the like are difficult to achieve—with this intention, he says: "In the state of 'I-ness'... (verse 31).
Bhagīratha said: O illustrious one, this sense of "I" has long been rooted in this body like a tree upon its own mountain; tell me, how is it to be abandoned?
Then he asks, "Tell me the very means for its abandonment," [referring to] the body: || 32 ||
Tritala said:
By means of human effort, having abandoned the inclination toward the flood of enjoyments and having attained the blossomed state of pure being, the ego dissolves.

The ellipsis is to be supplied as: "of one who, having become the pure form of the Self, remains [in that state] after the existence—which had been obscured by being struck by desire—has blossomed and become manifest. || 33 ||
As long as the cage of constraints, such as shame and the like, remains entirely unbroken,
so long does the ego-sense manifest clearly, leaving nothing but the state of absolute poverty.
"Having renounced the kingdom, people will not hold me in high regard, and my enemies will mock me;

since I am capable of fulfilling all desires, how shall I wander for alms? How shall I live on poor food and drink?"—driven by such anxieties, shame, pride, and the like, he remained at home just as before.

The meaning is that as long as the cage characterized by restraint has not been broken through the total renunciation of everything until nothing remains, so long does the ego-sense dance, clearly and in full bloom. || 34 ||
If you remain motionless, having abandoned all this through the intellect, then, upon the dissolution of egoism, you yourself are the supreme state. (35)
Then, in that case: || 35 ||
With all distinctions stilled, free from fear, and having utterly abandoned all desires, he surely attained a state of total poverty after relinquishing his entire fortune among his enemies;
with his egoism pacified and his sense of bodily identity vanished, if he were now wandering for alms among those very same people, he has indeed forsaken me as well.
You are the loftiness of existence; you are the supreme height. || 36 ||

He elaborates on the necessity of renouncing everything by saying "śānta" and so forth: being one who possesses peaceful and infinite royal insignia such as the parasol and the fly-whisk, yet truly being utterly destitute,
having abandoned all royal splendor among his enemies and being free from the conceit of a body, he wanders for alms among those very enemies— [he seeks] me.

Even though you were fully satisfied with your Guru, you left him because there was no further matter remaining to be asked, and not because of a lack of desire to serve; for if you were to do otherwise, it would contradict the authority of such scriptures as, "As long as one lives, three are to be revered: the Vedānta, the Guru, and the Lord. Therefore, if you are endowed with such characteristics as these, then—

The meaning is: you have risen high through all the qualities of those seeking liberation; you are indeed the supremely exalted Brahman itself, and for you there is not even the possibility of worldly existence. || 36 ||
Thus ends the seventy-fourth sarga, titled "The Instruction of Bhagīratha," in the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa* of the *Mokṣopāya* section of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki.
Thus ends the seventy-fourth chapter, titled "The Instruction of Bhagīratha," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa-tātparya-prakāśa*.
The seventy-fifth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Then, having heard this from the mouth of his guru, Bhagīratha—
Having resolved this in his mind, he became intent upon his own duty. || 1 ||
In this work, the king’s renunciation of all his possessions under the pretext of a sacrifice is described;
as well as his wandering for alms on a certain mountain and his dwelling together with Tritala.
Being one by whom that which is to be done—described below—is placed and resolved within the mind; such being the case. || 1 ||
Then, after only a few days had passed,
he performed the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice for the sole purpose of attaining complete renunciation.
The mention of the Agniṣṭoma is an elliptical indication (upalakṣaṇa) of all the Soma-sacrifices ending with the Viśvajit.
Discerning between the virtuous and the non-virtuous, he gave away his entire wealth— cows, land, horses, gold, and so forth— to the twice-born and his own kinsmen.
Without examining whether [the person] lacks qualities such as learning and study, for fear of delay in investigating those qualities. || 3 ||
Within merely three days, having renounced everything entirely,
that King Bhagīratha remained with nothing but his life-breath remaining.
The vital breaths (asavaḥ) are the life-forces; [the state] where only these remain is "having only the subtle elements remaining" (tanmātrāvaśeṣaḥ). || 4 ||
Then, his kingdom being devoid of all purpose and its subjects and citizens exhausted, he gave it to his enemy, the ruler of the bordering territory, like a blade of grass.
To Sīmāntin, who is present at the boundary. || 5 ||
When his kingdom, palace, and circle of vassals were seized by the enemy, the sage,
possessing nothing but his lower garment, departed from his own realm.
The lower garment is that which covers the private parts; anything remaining beyond that is superfluous. || 6 ||
Where he was not known by name, and where he was not recognized by his face—
in such villages, forests, and distant places, the steadfast man dwelt.

In such places as these, where even though he was seen by people himself, he was not recognized by the name Bhagīratha, and where even his own name was neither known nor heard from the mouths of people— there, in such places as those.
Thus, in a very short time, having all his desires stilled,
he attained rest within himself through supreme tranquility.
Thus, proceeding in this manner... || 8 ||
Wandering over the islands on the surface of the earth, he once, by the turn of fate and against his will,
reached that very city which had been seized by his enemy.
The continents are circles separated by rivers; being powerless, his mind is dependent upon seeing them. || 9 ||
There, the peaceful sage begged for alms from various houses, from those who had fallen into calamity, and from the citizens and ministers alike.

Having reached various dwellings that had come down by tradition and were attained in due course—[the masculine gender is Vedic]; the word "having reached" (prāpya) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. || 10 ||
The citizens and ministers beheld King Bhagīratha;
then, filled with despondency, they honored him with respectful service.
They understood; they discerned. || 11 ||
Although entreated by his enemy with the words, "O Lord, accept the kingdom," the sage did not accept it,
having disregarded everything except for food, not even a blade of grass.
By whom the entire kingdom was disregarded. || 12 ||
Having spent a few days there, he departed for another place;
this Bhagīratha was lamented by the people, crying out, "Alas! What a tragedy! (13)
"Śocitaḥ" means made an object of grief. || 13 ||
Then, elsewhere, with his self pacified and his intellect fully at rest,
that happy man once reached the teacher Tritala, who delights in the Self.
Having offered him his own welcome, Bhagīratha dwelt for some time with him on the mountain, in the forest, in the village, in the city, and among the people.
"One's own teacher" connects with what precedes; "receiving him with a welcome" is an elliptical expression for salutation and so forth. || 15 ||
Having attained equanimity, those two—the teacher and the disciple—stood as equals; established in their own nature, they regarded the maintenance of the body as a mere pastime.
The maintenance of the body is merely for amusement and curiosity.
"Why is this body being maintained? Or rather, what is the use of it being abandoned by us? Let it remain as it is, according to its natural state, following its proper sequence and conduct. (17)

"Let us remain according to the sequence—that is, following the order prescribed in the scriptures—and according to custom—that is, in accordance with the conduct of the elders. Having thus resolved, the two forest-dwellers departed from that forest.
[They experienced] neither lack of bliss nor supreme bliss, neither unhappiness nor that which is intermediate. (18)

The ellipsis is to be supplied: "They attained such supreme bliss (*parānanda*) wherein sensual pleasures (*viṣayānanda*) do not exist. He further qualifies that very state with the words "not non-bliss" (*nāsukham*). "Non-bliss" (*asukha*) means suffering; it is devoid of that. "Intermediate" (*madhyama*) refers to the intermediate state between the two, which is empty of both pleasure and pain; it is distinct from that. (18)
Wealth, the eightfold sovereignty consisting of horses, riches, and so forth—even when offered by the Siddhas out of satisfaction—they both regarded it as withered grass. (19)
He demonstrates the firmness of their dispassion toward divine enjoyments as well, just as toward human ones, with the words "Wealths... and so on.

They regarded even that sovereignty—offered and bestowed by the Siddhas, Brahmā, and others who were satisfied by their conduct, renowned as being eightfold through the distinctions of the *aṇiman* powers and the like—as utterly worn out and decayed, like a blade of grass. (19)
Thinking, "This body must be sustained by one's own karma alone for as long as there is life,
even against one's will," they both remained there by their own karma.

Having resolved that they must maintain themselves for as long as their existence lasts—that is, for the duration of their life—by means of the very karma initiated at their own commencement, they remained there. || 20 ||

The two supreme sages, who were by nature perfectly equanimous and self-restrained, welcomed his arrival; though they were free from desire for pleasure or pain, they rejoiced in the joy arising from their own customary conduct, remaining ever equal and impartial.

Those two sages, according to their own former mode of conduct, welcomed both the pleasure that arose and the discomfort as well as the pain; for they were equally even-minded toward all things within the Brahman, having become perfectly equanimous and of one flavor, and by their very nature, being self-restrained, they possessed supreme tranquility. 21.

Thus ends the seventy-fifth canto, titled "The Liberation of Bhagīratha," in the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa* of the *Mokṣopāya* section of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*, composed by Vālmīki according to the tradition of the Ṛṣis.
Thus ends the seventy-fifth canto, titled "The Liberation of Bhagīratha," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa-tātparya-prakāśa*.
The seventy-sixth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Now, once upon a time, in a certain excellent city within a particular district—
Death seizes a childless king, as a fish seizes its prey. || 1 ||
Furthermore, the attainment of the kingdom by Bhagīratha here is proclaimed,
as well as his propitiation of Brahmā, Rudra, and others, and the descent of the Gaṅgā.
From the region of Kosala and from the region of Bhagīrathāspada, I struck [and thus killed] [the fish] in another region;
"prey" refers to small fish and the like. || 1 ||
There, the subjects, weary and having lost their sense of order, sought a king endowed with vast excellence and glory.

The traditional order of the country and its protective boundaries had perished; being in such a state, they sought a king endowed with the excellence of qualities capable of providing protection. || 2 ||
Having approached that steadfast sage Bhagīratha who was wandering for alms,
and having recognized him, they brought him back and installed him as the lord of the army.
Recognizing that he was endowed with all the splendors of virtue and identifying him as such, they consecrated him as the lord of the earth once their army had arrived there.
In an instant, Bhagīratha, surrounded by his heavy army like a lake filled with water during the rainy season, quickly mounted his elephant.
Instantly he resorted to the elephant; that is, he mounted it. || 4 ||
The great caves of the lords of mountains became completely filled with the clamor of the people crying out, "Victory to Bhagīratha, the Lord of the World! (5)
The state of being without gaps; fullness. || 5 ||
While he was protecting that kingdom there, the original subjects, showing him great respect, approached the king and spoke thus to the lord of men: (6)

At that very time, by a stroke of fate, even though the king of Kosala had perished, the subjects residing in Ayodhyā approached Bhagīratha and made their request; this is stated in the verse beginning with "tatra. These were the former ministers, priests, and other officials belonging specifically to Bhagīratha.
The subjects said:
"O King, that lord of ours who was placed at the forefront by you has been swallowed up by death, like soft meat by a fish."
By you, who were renouncing the kingdom, that enemy living on the border was honored with the gift of the kingdom. || 7 ||
It behoves you to show favor so that each of these may protect the kingdom;
moreover, it is not proper to abandon wealth that has come unasked. (8)
Therefore, for that reason, that former kingdom [is restored]. || 8 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Thus entreated, the king accepted those words and became the lord of the earth marked by the seven oceans.
Equanimous, with a tranquil mind, observant of silence, free from passion and devoid of envy,
he performed only what was required for the task at hand, having cast aside all wonder.

He is silent, speaking measured, beneficial, and truthful words; he is concealed by the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna), and his sense of wonder has been sublated even amidst great curiosity—that is, his perception of things as marvelous has ceased. || 10 ||
He heard that the water of the Gaṅgā was capable of delivering his ancestors, who had perished in the depths of Pātāla and had become like the ocean itself.
Those whose nature it was to dig into the earth in search of horses, thereby creating a pit as vast as the ocean;

for whom ordinary water would not suffice to rescue their grandfathers— who had been reduced to ashes and perished at the bottom of Pātāla by the fire of Kapila’s wrath— by bathing them in the waters of the Gaṅgā and offering them the funeral libation (jalāñjali).
The meaning is that he heard Tārkṣya’s words through a succession of people. || 11 ||
At that time, it is said, the celestial river did not flow upon the earth;
therefore, the handful of Gaṅgā water was known as "Bhūta" (earthly) for the ancestors.
At that time, one might wonder why an offering of water (jalāñjali) was not made right there on the surface of the earth where the Gaṅgā was present; anticipating this doubt, he says:
"He became one whose fame was renowned"—that is to say, his renown was well-known. || 12 ||
And from that time forward, King Bhagīratha maintained a vow in order to bring the Gaṅgā down from heaven to the earth.
From that day of hearing it onwards.
Then, having renounced the kingdom, the peaceful king, whose desire was directed toward what ought to be done, went to a solitary forest for the sake of asceticism.
He whose effort and exertion were directed toward that task which consists of asceticism and other such acts for the purpose of bringing down the Gaṅgā. || 14 ||
There, having propitiated Brahmā, Śaṅkara, and Jahnu again and again for thousands of years, he established the Gaṅgā upon the earth.
He joined them together, having brought them down [from their respective positions]. || 15 ||

From that time forth, the triple-pathed river (Gaṅgā), possessing waves of pure ripples and clinging to the body of the Lord of the World who bears the moon, falls from the vault of heaven to the earth like the vast succession of merits of great souls.
Clinging to the body of Śiva, the Lord of the World who bears the moon, she is joined upon his head;

although the compound would be ungrammatical due to its dependency, it is Vedic (chāndasa). The ellipsis is "by the command of Brahmā, the Lord of the World. She falls from the vault of the sky to the earth (gām). [This descent] is for the sake of the many [souls] of the great-souled ones dwelling in heaven.
The phrase "as if a continuous stream of merit" is a poetic conceit (utprekṣā). || 16 ||
With its quivering waves and breaking surges, smiling with its masses of foam, and appearing as if joined by a cluster of blossoms of serene merit,
that triple-pathed river became, during the reign of King Bhagīratha, a thoroughfare for the circulation of his fame upon the surface of the earth.
This is a poetic metaphor (*rūpakotprekṣā*) suggesting that the [Ganges] is like a path for the eternal fame born of King Bhagīratha to spread as far as the ocean. || 17 ||

Thus ends the seventy-sixth chapter, titled "The Descent of the Gaṅgā," in the Nirvāṇa Section of the *Mokṣopāya* within the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, according to the tradition of the Sages.
Thus ends the seventy-sixth sarga, titled "The Descent of the Gaṅgā," in the first half of the Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The seventy-seventh canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Having taken hold of this vision, maintained with the same resolve as Bhagīratha’s, [one attains liberation].
Equanimous, established in yourself, and tranquil in intellect, perform the task as it has arisen.
The narrative of Cūḍālā is introduced here to strengthen the meaning already expressed;
it contains the majesty of Śikhidhvaja and the sequence of his marriage and amorous sports.
Later, during his reign, it was upheld by Bhagīratha through his wisdom.
Having first renounced this world and having brought the bird of the mind under control,
remain peaceful within yourself, immovable like Śikhidhvaja.
Having renounced this collection of worldly existences, and having embraced the bird of the mind, one should restrain it within the heart. || 2 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
Who was this one named Śikhidhvaja, and how did he attain that state?
O Brahman, tell me this again for the further increase of my understanding. (3)
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
In the previous Dvāpara age, and likewise now in the one yet to come,
that very same couple attained a state of mutual affection through that very same disposition.
In a previous Dvāpara age, there were a husband and wife; now, in the first Dvāpara of the twenty-eighth cycle of four ages, they shall exist again in that very same form.
Śrī Rāma said: O Blessed One, that which existed previously is indeed exactly the same now;
why will it be so in the future? Tell me this, O best among speakers.
The meaning of Rāma's question is: "What is the cause for the similarity between what has been and what will be? (5)
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: This state of the consciousness of Brahmā and others, which constitutes the fixed order of the world’s creation, is eternally established as arising from an irresistible nature.
The meaning is that in the creation of the world, the very nature of the consciousness of Brahmā and others— which consists of the realization of true resolve— is itself an irresistible cause.

That which, having been manifold, becomes abundant once again; and that which, having not existed at all, comes into being as something else, and then ceases to exist entirely—[this is the nature of the world]. (7)

Having stated "it is such," he elaborates with the words "yad" (that which). Just as on a single mango tree various fruits appear many times, and having appeared, they repeatedly become that very same kind in great numbers; whereas a banyan tree from a trunk (*skandha*) comes into being without having previously existed, and once cut down, it does not arise again in that same place. || 7 ||
Anything other than that [which is] rich in prior arrangement appears to quiver due to similarity,
just as similar and dissimilar waves appear alike upon a lake.
Just so, other various conditions are seen within saṃsāra;
therefore, like a king, the Lord will once again [act] as in the story to be told hereafter.

"In transmigratory existence" (saṃsṛtau) means even in the cycle of birth and death of Śikhidhvaja and others; "the king" refers to the sovereign lord who, like the past Śikhidhvaja, is the protagonist to be described in the narrative that follows. || 9 ||
He will be of great splendor; hear this account of him. Formerly, in the Dvāpara age, when the seventh Manu had passed away, [it occurred].
In this fourth creation of the four-yuga cycle, in the lineage of the Kurus,
situated not far from the famous Vindhya mountain in Jambūdvīpa.

In the family and lineage of the Kurus—the lords of the Kuru country—and their descendants; [the suffix] expressing "their king" is elided when applied to many [descendants]. The absence of lengthening in the case of the *nām* ending is a Vedic (archaic) feature. || 11 ||
In the city of the Mālavas, there was a glorious lord named Śikhidhvaja,
endowed with the qualities of fortitude and magnanimity, and possessed of patience, tranquility, and self-restraint.
In the city of the Mālavas, that is to say, in Ujjayinī. || 12 ||
He was a hero of auspicious conduct, a silent sage, a mine of multitudes of virtues, a performer of all sacrifices, and a conqueror of all archers. (13)
The creator of all works, the sustainer of the earth in his former body,
he was graceful, affectionate, sweet, clever, and an ocean of love.
He is skilled in all undertakings such as ponds, wells, tanks, and gardens, and is proficient in both worldly affairs and the scriptures. || 14 ||
He will be handsome, peaceful, auspicious, majestic, and devoted to righteousness;
he will be a speaker of the principles of discipline and a bestower of all forms of prosperity. (15)

He is peaceful and fortunate, endowed with the marks of good fortune, and is a speaker—one who utters—words that are for the sake of discipline, serving as causes for the training in discipline even for others. || 15 ||
He was an enjoyer who associated with the virtuous and was a fine listener of all sacred scriptures;
he was one who honored the Vedas without fail and treated women as lightly as a blade of grass, remaining untouched by their influence.
He knows and understands everything; nevertheless, he is devoid of honor—the pride of being an expert—and of *straiṇa*, such as addiction to women and the like. || 16 ||
When his father had ascended to heaven, he, though still a boy, being self-controlled and possessed of supreme vigor,
personally undertook the conquest of the quarters for sixteen years.

"By supreme power, by the heroism of his own arm"—by this it is understood that although his father was merely a local ruler (*māṇḍalika*), he became a universal monarch (*samrāj*) solely through the heroism of his own arm. || 17 ||
Surely, through the perfection of his imperial sovereignty, he united the circle of the earth;
he remained free from all apprehension, protecting his subjects in accordance with righteousness. || 18 ||

By means of the prosperity employed for universal sovereignty; for at that time, because there is an absence of bandits anywhere, the wealth of the subjects increases, being free from the apprehension of the existence of enemies who must be conquered. 18.
Then, as the years passed and spring blossomed forth in full splendor, that wise king, together with his ministers, whitened the quarters with his glory.
As the years passed—meaning, when he had reached his youth—the connection with the fifth [verse] is that then his mind became intensely longing for his beloved. || 19 ||
While the flowers were blooming and the moonbeams were shimmering,
within the inner apartments of the tree-branches, there were swings formed by clusters of blossoms.

"Viṭapa" means a branch; the connection with the distant word "gāyat" (singing) is as follows: while pairs of bees were singing upon the swings formed by clusters of blossoms within the interior of the harem, which was characterized by such branches. || 20 ||
In that place, where the door-panels were formed of curling petals white as camphor and saffron,
and where a canopy was fashioned from clusters of blossoms shimmering with fragrance.
He describes that very inner apartment by imagining it as a collection of such things, beginning with the verse "rajaḥ" (dust). || 21 ||
While pairs of bees hummed loudly together in the dense thickets, and as a sweet breeze, cool with the spray of moonbeams, blew through the air; (22)
It was cooled by the moon and by sprays of water.
His heart, dwelling upon his beloved, became filled with longing for her who delights in the groves of plantain trees and the young shoots of the *talapallava* plant. (23)

The *kadalī* is well known. *Kandalīs* are a species of shrubs; [the wind] is "dancing" (*lāsini*)—that is, characterized by the grace of dance—among their thickets and foliage, which serves to establish its coolness and gentleness. By the expression "dwelling" (*vasat*), it is understood that he was already enamored of Cūḍālā due to having previously heard of her virtues, beauty, and so forth. (23)
Intoxicated by the sweet liquors fragrant with the abundance of flowers, his mind found no other resting place, as if it were the rising of spring itself.

Like a forest in springtime, intoxicated by the sweet liquors characterized by the fragrance of gathered blossoms, his mind— arisen and sprouted with passion— did not take up residence elsewhere, nor did it rely upon objects other than his beloved.
When, upon the swings in the garden groves and amidst the playful lotus ponds, shall I [behold] my charming beloved, whose breasts are like golden lotus buds? (25)
He elaborates on the manner of that longing with the verse beginning "In the garden," and so forth. || 25 ||
"When shall I place her, marked with saffron, upon my lap on a couch, like a female bee upon the swings of lotus creepers? (26)
I shall gaze upon that unsteady young woman, whose creeper-like arms reach out toward me,
as she longs for a garland of lotus stalks and a cluster of kunda flowers like the moon.

"I shall settle her; I shall marry her. With the intention that "when will she too experience the same anguish driven by her own longing as mine, so that our union may soon take place? he says: "Mṛṇālā... The *vṛndavallyaḥ* are the creepers gathered together in the form of flowering vine-cottages; she is one who longs for them [or, she is longing for him]. || 27 ||
"Will Indusundarī ever become tormented by love on my account?"—becoming absorbed in this thought, he turned his attention toward gathering flowers. (28)
He dwelt in the forest edges and in flower gardens,
upon the rows of groves and in his pleasure lotus-pools.
In houses encircled by creepers, in various garden grounds, and in places adorned with descriptions of the arrangements of forests and groves; (30)
The connection with the locative case (saptamī) is as follows: she took delight in the descriptions of the qualities of forests and groves, and in the narratives that had been recounted. || 30 ||
With his mind distracted by stories filled with the sentiment of erotic love,
he [beheld] in her heart the swaying creeper-like curls of hair and a body shimmering with necklaces.
He worshipped the maidens, whose breasts were like golden jars;
I believe that wise ministers understood this to be the king's resolve.

She worshipped the young maidens in her heart, held them in high esteem, and adorned them with ornaments created by her own resolve. The indeclinable *manye* is used here in the sense of deliberation (*vitarka*). This statement of deliberation serves as an embellishment for Vasiṣṭha’s speech. || 32 ||
The supreme position of a minister consists precisely in discerning others through gestures and facial expressions;
then, the circle of ministers deliberated for his marriage.
The characteristic of ministers is their station; one should examine their mutual affection and the excellence of their qualities, character, lineage, and so forth. || 33 ||
He requested the daughter of the lord of Surāṣṭra,
who was endowed with youth and possessed of fresh bloom, as his excellent wife according to the prescribed rites.

A group of young women is called *yauvata*; the masculine form is applied here because of the rule "bhasyāḍhe taddhite" (the base form is used for a feminine word ending in long ā when followed by a Taddhita suffix beginning with a vowel or a semi-vowel). She was endowed with that [beauty], and possessed of fresh youth and vitality. || 34 ||
He married her, who was like his own image;
she was a beauty fit for a king, renowned on earth by the name Cūḍālā.
Like a statue or a reflection, it was similar and corresponding [to her]. || 35 ||
Having obtained that husband, she shone like a lotus-pond in full bloom;
Śikhidhvaja [gazed upon] that Cūḍālā, whose eyes were like blue lotuses.
Out of affection, he caused [her] to blossom, just as the divine sun causes the lotus-pond to bloom;
the love between those two, whose hearts were offered to one another, increased.
He caused it to blossom and he gladdened it. || 37 ||
With her limbs rich in gestures, emotions, and charms, she was like a moving vine; he, having entrusted all affairs to his excellent minister, was happy with his subjects well-established. (38)
The ellipsis is to be supplied as follows: "She shone, as if she were dancing, with limbs enriched by the various gestures of love (śṛṅgāraceṣṭā), such as *hāva* and *bhāva*.

Alternatively, it means: "To whom all objects of enjoyment were offered by beautiful, loyal ministers who followed the king's mind"; or else, "all [objects] were offered to every supplicant by beautiful, righteous ministers."
He whose desired objects were attained; for this very reason, with his subjects well-established and being free from the distraction of protecting them, he took delight. || 38 ||
Like a royal swan with a lotus-pond, he took delight with that beloved wife within the inner apartments, upon swings, and amidst artificial lotus-pools.
In gardens and monasteries, in the gathering of creepers and flowers, in the rows of Kadamba forests, and along the paths of sandalwood and agallochum; || 40 ||
In streets fragrant with sandalwood and aloe-wood, and in rows of sandalwood and aloe-wood trees. || 40 ||
Upon the clusters of mandāra flowers and the tender shoots of plantains, at the edges of cities and the borders of forests, at the ends of the quarters and upon the lakes; (41)
In the forests and at the edges of human settlements, among rose-apple and citron trees,
everything they did for one another was full of delight.

Because of their constant non-separation, like the two beloved ones—the sky and the earth—acting as the foremost bearers of the burden for six years, and because of the affection for their conduct; (43) (Note: The reading "nityamevāviyuktatvāt" is found in the manuscript.)
In fields ploughed by excellent, powerful oxen, there was a truly delightful rain; they were like heaven and earth, beautiful with the abundance of clouds and crops respectively. || 43 ||
Those two became experts in each other’s entire range of arts; having attained friendship, they maintained as one and the same form.
Because they taught one another and because they desired mutual equality, the two became highly skilled and exceptionally wise;
for this very reason, due to the equality of all their qualities and their coloring by that likeness through affection, it is said that they attained a state as if their lives were one:
"As if residing in each other's hearts, [their knowledge] was transmitted unimpaired."
Mastery over the meaning of all scriptures, as well as painting and other arts, [issued] from the mouth of the Lord. (45)
Because they reside within each other's hearts, the nature of the individual soul (*jīva*) is indeed one and the same, even as it is transferred between two bodies.
Furthermore, skill in arts such as painting is acquired by learning from the mouths of those proficient in those respective crafts and then practicing it. (45)

Though she was but a child, she became an expert in all subjects, just as one might grasp the seasons; and from the mouth of Cūḍālā, she learned everything including dance, instrumental music, and the rest.

Just as a young boy of twelve years receives the knowledge of the Vedas according to the time prescribed by the scriptures for Vedic celibacy (*brahmacarya*), so it was with her; she is Cūḍālā, and he is Śikhidhvaja. || 46 ||
Then he studied and became exceedingly proficient in the arts,
like the moon and the sun shining together on the new moon day.
The word "having reached the new moon" (amāvāsyām prāpya) is to be understood as the ellipsis. Being situated within each other's hearts like the moon and the sun, they attained oneness. || 47 ||
Those two, dwelling within each other's hearts, attained oneness;
both beloveds remained established in a single essence with one another. 48.
They possess a single flavor, like milk and water that have been mixed together. || 48 ||
Like the fragrance inseparable from the flower, like Śiva and Pārvatī dwelling upon the earth, they possessed minds beautiful with wit and were learned in the meaning of all the scriptures. (49)
Standing upon the ground, they descended to earth like Śiva and Gaurīśaṅkara. || 49 ||
And for the sake of their mission, Lakṣmī and the Consort of Lakṣmī arrived upon the earth;
out of affection, they were gracious and sweet, speaking with words of perfect wisdom.

Those two who possess the habit of speaking together, or individually, on a matured point of doubt—the secret of worldly treatises—which is understood equally, at the same time, and concerning the same subject. || 50 ||

They were devoted to following the ways of the world and were experts in its affairs; endowed with a full range of artistic skills, they were like two moons risen together, possessing the elixir of radiant aesthetic flavor, their limbs cool, smooth, and charming. (51)
They were devoted to the service of one another, their gurus, the twice-born, and those worthy of honor, as well as to conduct such as affection, benevolence, and humility;

they were experts in the ways of the world and in the secrets of dharma accessible only through the scriptures; and they shone with the elixirs characterized by the nine sentiments, beginning with the erotic (śṛṅgāra). 51.
He abandoned that peerless couple, who were radiant with the splendor of wealth, pleasures, and amorous delights within the inner apartments—
like a pair of royal swans moving slowly with blooming pride and passion within the hollows of the cosmic egg.
Like a pair of royal swans in the hollows of deep lakes within Satyaloka, which is a portion of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) and a part of the universe. || 52 ||

Thus ends the seventy-seventh canto, titled "The Narration of Śikhidhvaja’s Pastimes," in the *Pūrva-cūḍālā-upākhyāna* of the *Mokṣopāya*, within the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*. Canto 77.
Thus ends the seventy-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of Śikhidhvaja’s Pastimes," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The seventy-eighth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
In this manner, for many years, the couple remained filled with intense longing.
Day by day, she delighted in the ever-increasing sports of her youth.
In this [chapter], the gradual detachment of the two, their devotion to the study of the true scriptures,
Cūḍālā’s discernment, and her attainment of knowledge are described.
"Intense longing" means firm love; "the couple" refers to that pair consisting of a woman and a man. || 1 ||
Then, after many years had passed in their cycle of recurrence,
his youth gradually ebbed away like water from a broken jar.

Then, as their youth gradually faded away, that couple, having reached this conclusion, began to investigate the scripture esteemed by those devoted to the inner self; such is the connection between the tenth and eleventh chapters. || 2 ||
In this world of worldly affairs, as fragile as a mass of surging waves, death is as unavoidable as the falling of a ripe fruit. (3)
He elaborates upon the reason for the definitive conclusion and the investigation performed therein, beginning with the words "taraṅga... and so forth:
"O embodied being, whose nature is worldly activity through a body that is fragile like a mass of waves; death is the separation from the body. (3)
Like a frost-bolt upon a lotus, old age is poised to fall;
life flows away incessantly, like water from the palm of the hand. (4)
From where does this difficulty arise? To that he says: "The thunderbolt of snow" (himāśani). || 4 ||
Like a gourd-vine in the rainy season, the single thirst has grown long;
like the current of a mountain river, youth indeed flows away. (5)

In the rainy season of craving—that which consists of the pursuit of objects and the means to attain them—it grows to great length, like the vine of the bitter gourd; "it increases" is the meaning. Here, "impetuosity" (raya) refers to the monsoon flood. || 5 ||
Life is as unreal as a magician's trick, its established order decayed;
pleasures flee away like arrows loosed from a bow. (6)
That in which one lives is "jīvana," namely the body and so forth.
Mental sufferings fall upon the mind like a vulture upon meat;
the body is as momentary as a bubble in the waters during the rainy season. (7)
Sufferings, such as those internal and so forth, and craving fall upon the mind; "falling," it means they strike it. || 7 ||
Worldly activity, when examined, is as insubstantial as the core of a plantain tree; youth passes away quickly, like a lover who fails to please his beloved.
[Regarding "apriyām": here, the explanation that "she desires the seduction of a co-wife" is appropriate;

for if one were to follow the literal explanation, the grammatical transformation into the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) would be untenable. For him who desires a co-wife, his beloved is indeed as dear as his own wife. (8)
By force, a lack of passion has come upon me, like saplessness upon a tree;
therefore, what here could be auspicious in form, stable, and exceedingly beautiful? (9)

Discontent (*arati*) is dejection caused by the failure to obtain desired objects; it is a loss of relish, a drying up of the essence. In this very world (*iha*), having determined that which, once attained, no longer causes the mind to suffer amidst the various conditions of existence—that pair is the medicine for the disease of *saṃsāra*. (9–10)

The grammatical connection is as follows: having reflected upon that pair—the "ten" (daśā) being the miserable conditions such as birth and death, and the "pair" (yugma) being the couple—and having determined therein that the very science of the inner self (adhyātma-śāstra) is the medicine for the disease of worldly existence, he deliberated upon that alone.
He reflected for a long time upon the scripture esteemed as the inner self;
[he realized that] by the knowledge of the Self alone, the cholera known as worldly existence [is cured].

Having resolved that he would be pacified, the two remained devoted to him; their minds were fixed on him, their lives were centered in him, they were established in him, and they took refuge in those who knew him.
Those two for whom the knowers of that—that is, the knowers of the inner science (adhyātmaśāstra)—are the refuge and the shelter. || 12 ||
Then, intent on his worship and engaged in his activities, the two of them shone there,
having practiced intensely, as they enlightened one another.
Through mutual affection for that [recitation], the two of them became engaged in its performance together.
Then, O Rāma, she [began] incessantly [to recite] those verses whose phrasing was most beautiful.

She was Cūḍālā, whose undertaking consisted of the thorough contemplation of that very same spiritual science (adhyātma-śāstra), its mutual hearing from one another, and its mutual awakening, and so forth. || 14 ||

Having heard from the mouths of those who know the inner self the meanings of the scriptures that are capable of delivering one [from suffering], he reflected in this manner upon his own self day and night. (15)
"In this way" means by the manner that is about to be described. || 15 ||
Whether inactive or active, one should purify the mind with a pure intellect;
one should personally examine one's own self, thinking, "What might I become? (16)
Inactive, having abandoned bodily activity, I shall observe—that is, I shall see clearly—whether I might be the conscious principle within this aggregate of causes and effects. (16)
Whose is this delusion that has come, how has it arisen, or where?
First of all, the body is inert and deluded; the certainty is simply this: "I am not [the body]. (17)

From whom has this delusion—the characteristic of saṃsāra—come? For he whose error has arisen would be at ease in removing it; the meaning is: who indeed is that person? "How" (*katham*) refers to the inquiry regarding the cause (*nimitta*). "Where" (*kva*) refers to the inquiry regarding its root. For when the root is fully understood, one can uproot it by means of its eradication.
It is possible. || 17 ||
This is well-established even among children and is experienced within the mind itself;
furthermore, the group of organs of action consists of parts that are non-different from it. (18)

The meaning is that its insentience (*jaḍatva*) consists in the fact that it is experienced only when there are mental modifications (*buddhi-vṛtti*) such as "I am fat" or "I am fair," and not by itself; [it is] composed of limbs such as hands and feet which are non-different from this body. || 18 ||
There is no difference between the part and the whole, and it is indeed insentient;
likewise, the aggregate of the intellect and the senses is seen to be nothing but insentient. (19)

The group of cognitive faculties (*buddhīndriya*) is likewise composed of limbs of the body. Although Bādarāyaṇa established as his final conclusion in the Sūtra "And [the elements] are atoms" that the senses, vital breaths, and so forth are subtle limbs of the *liṅga-deha* (subtle body) and not limbs of the gross body (*sthūla-deha*), nevertheless, their...

The intention is that, because it is experienced by the unlearned and the common folk as being merely a limb of the body, and because it is conjoined with the body like a limb, it must necessarily be insentient, just like those limbs. || 19 ||

Since the mind is impelled by [the Self] like a clod of earth on the ground by a staff, I consider the mind itself to be inert, given that it possesses the power of volition [according to the reading *saṃkalpātmakaśakti*]. How could it [act] without a cause? (20)

Since even the mind and so forth are the movers of the insentient body and other such things, their insentience is established by their being substances capable of conjunction with [an agent], like a staff or similar objects; thus he says, beginning with "is impelled" (preryate), etc. (20).

Just as a stone is propelled by throws, so is the intellect impelled by determinations; thus, the intellect consists of determination itself, for it is the insentient existence that is the determination. (21)
It is certain that insentient existence has the very nature of insentience, just as [objects are moved] by throws or by rope-machines. || 21 ||
Just as a river is surely carried away by its own channel, so too am I carried away by egoism;
for egoism itself is substanceless, inert, and essentially like a corpse. (22)
By the "ditch"—that is, by the low-lying ground situated between two embankments—that intelligence is carried away, meaning it is impelled [toward the object]. || 22 ||
The Yakṣa is generated by the individual soul (jīva), like a delusive phantom created by a child;
and the jīva is the space of consciousness, consisting of vital air, situated within the heart. (23)

It is produced—that is, superimposed—by the *jīva*, which is the reflection of consciousness delimited by the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Thus, the meaning is that, like the body of a Yakṣa, it is insentient precisely because it is superimposed. The "wind-self" (*vātātmā*) is that which has the vital breath as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). || 23 ||
The delicate one lives on by some internal means;
oh, how this has been understood by him who is stained by the conceptualization of "I" and "mine"! 24.

He lives filled with his own internal presiding reflected-consciousness (*bimba-caitanya*); by that consciousness, which is almost defiled by the stain of the mental impression of objects—the manifestation of objects as a witness-state—he [perceives]. || 24 ||
The individual soul lives by means of that which has become aged—the form of the Self, whose nature is consciousness;
the individual soul lives by means of the very form of consciousness, even while possessed of the delusion of objects of thought.
By that which is decayed and ancient. || 25 ||

Just as fragrance [is carried] by the wind, or the current of a river by a channel, the body of consciousness becomes inert through the accumulation of the unreal, insentient, and objective portions. 26.
He provides the logical justification for [the Self] being "stained by the impression of the object of thought" with the word "asatyā" (unreal).

The meaning is that because of the accumulation [of impressions] and through the superimposition of identity and relation, the body of consciousness—though its very nature is consciousness—becomes, as it were, insentient. || 26 ||
For, like fire submerged in a great flood, it abandons its own form;
when samādhi of consciousness is present, whatever appears by itself—whether real or unreal—is [thus relinquished]. (27)

Just as fire situated within great water, heated water, or the ocean abandons— that is, relinquishes— its own luminous form, so too, having attained a semblance of difference from consciousness (cit) in the aspect of existence (sattā), existence is experienced as being of one flavor with the non-conscious forms of jars, cloths, and so forth, such that one says, "the jar exists," "the cloth exists. When the form of the jar and so forth dissolves back into the clay and other materials, the jar [is no longer perceived].

The meaning is that by saying "the cloth does not exist," it abandons even the form of existence and thus falls into non-existence. In the meditative absorption of consciousness (*citsamādhi*), whether it be of the nature of being or non-being, whatever is presented by latent impressions (*vāsanā*) appears spontaneously; that very thing, in an instant, completely relinquishes its own limited form and becomes that [very object] itself in that very moment—this is the connection with the following verse. || 27 ||
Having cast off the impurity of its own nature, that very [consciousness] becomes [the object] in an instant;
in this same way, this very form of consciousness, by its own inclination toward the object of thought (cetya), [becomes such]. 28.

In the manner thus described, although the ultimate reality is of the nature of consciousness (*cid-rūpa*), it becomes, due to the veil of ignorance (*avidyā-āvaraṇa*) and through a succession of superimpositions (*adhyāsa-paramparā*), inert, void, and as if non-existent, taking the form of the world; yet, by means of the very consciousness whose nature is unobscured, which pervades the various mental modifications (*vṛtti*) assuming those respective forms, it is awakened through the destruction of the veil of root-ignorance.
The subsequent [connection] is by means of another. || 28 ||
"Inert, empty, and like something non-existent, it is awakened by consciousness"—having reflected thus, Cūḍālā wondered, "By whom has this been made conscious by the Intellect? (29)

Then, she reflected: "By what means might this consciousness of Brahman, through the destruction of the veil of root-ignorance, abandon the dream of the visible world and become awakened? To this, he says: "Thus... (verse 29).
Thus he reflected, and after a long time he awakened in this way:
"Aha! After a long time, that which is to be known—the state free from affliction—has finally been realized. (30)
In this manner, by the method being described, he awakened; that is to say, [he realized] the reality of the Self. || 30 ||
Indeed, once that which is to be known has been realized, no one falls away again;
for these—the mind, intellect, senses, and so forth—end in the play of consciousness.

The meaning is that no person whatsoever is lost—that is, they do not fall away from the supreme goal of human life (*puruṣārtha*). Alternatively, no desired object whatsoever is lost—that is, it does not suffer diminution—because by attaining that [supreme goal], all desires are fulfilled. Or else, nothing whatsoever is lost through the cognition that it is a means to suffering.
It is abandoned; the meaning is that this occurs because everything possesses the nature of having bliss as its sole essence (*ānandaikarasatva*).

The statement regarding the impossibility of relinquishment is also indicative of the impossibility of acquisition. Alas, all those things which serve as causes for limitation—the boundaries of the play of consciousness—are non-existent, like the position of a second moon.
In this world, there exists only one Great Consciousness, which is called the "Great Being."
They abide in the place, the position, of the second moon imagined by the vision of one suffering from ophthalmia—that is to say, imagined through delusion.
It is stainless, even, pure, and of the nature of non-egoism;
it has the form of pure consciousness, and is Śiva, who is pure existence alone and immutable. (33)
She whose very nature is pure consciousness alone;
who is Śiva because she is the supreme auspiciousness consisting of the bliss of plenitude (bhūmānanda), and who is infallible (acyuta) because she never deviates from such a nature;
who shines forth once and for all, is stainless, and is eternally risen.
She is celebrated by such names as Brahman, Paramātman, and so forth. || 34 ||
Because it shines forth once and for all through the destruction of the veil of root-ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*) and is never again covered by anything, it is "shining once" (*sakṛdvibhātā*).
For this very reason, it is figuratively celebrated in the Vedāntic and other spiritual treatises as "possessing eternal rising" (*nityodayavatī*). 34.
The objects of cognition, the unconscious, the mind, and so forth, are not different from her in terms of their measure;
by her this glorious Consciousness is cognized, and she is remembered as the primordial Consciousness.

The web of the threefold division (tripuṭī), consisting of the object and so forth, is not a reality distinct from her; for this triad is perceived by her as the witness-consciousness, and is not established through any means of knowledge (māna). This very witness-consciousness is primordial, because she is self-established even prior to the operation of the triad. || 35 ||
That which is this consciousness, being unchanging, is its undiminished form;
it alone unfolds through the forms of mind, intellect, the senses, and their objects. (36)
It yawns and it revolves. || 36 ||
This manifestation of the existence of objects in the form of the world, like the movement of waves, droplets, and billows, flashes forth within the Cognizer, who is the Self of Consciousness. (37)

When the conscious Self, the knower, assumes the state of a subject through the transformations of the mind, intellect, and so forth, the existence—the reality—of the objects of the world, consisting of the elements and their derivatives, manifests there like the appearance of waves and the like. || 37 ||
This is that supreme form of that very Great Consciousness;
for she is like a pure jewel of consciousness, arisen in perfect equanimity.

That which is known as the form of the existence of the world is, in fact, merely another form of that very Great Consciousness (mahāciti) which serves as its substrate. The word "khalu" is used to indicate the well-known scriptural authority, such as in the passage: "There are indeed two forms of Brahman—the formed and the formless. For she [the Great Consciousness] is indeed...

Like a crystal gem of consciousness, it holds the reflection of the world entirely without attachment; this very existence of the world is equally the same in both the empirical and the illusory realms, arising in accordance with its respective substratum. (38)
Indeed, that existence which persists through the unfolding of the world by means of its own non-dual power cannot possibly exist here as anything other than Māyā. (39)
For this very reason, since it is impossible to define the existence of the world as being anything other than the existence of its substratum, he declares that it is mere illusion (*māyāmātra*):
"Just as the various forms of vessels are indeed [nothing but] gold, so too does that [consciousness] arise;
it perceives itself as having that very form. (40)
Therefore, at the dissolution of the specific manifestations of name and form, the existence of the world remains only as the essence of Brahman variegated by *māyā*.
But when *māyā* is sublated, one personally experiences the Self, which consists solely of the single flavor of bliss and pure existence; thus he says:
"In that same way, it arises with the essence of golden existence"—meaning that it emerges in that manner. (40)

Just as the state of being waves and so forth arises in waters through the fluidity of one's own mind, so too does the world appear to arise from the Great Consciousness through the individual mind, though it does not actually arise.

With the intention that, by the very same logic demonstrated regarding existence (*sattā*), even the various distinctions of consciousness (*cidbheda*)— which consist in the manifestation of the world's diversity— when analyzed as being false due to their difference in objective forms, ultimately resolve into nothing but the undivided consciousness of the Supreme Brahman, he says: "Just as waves and the like, though not actually arising, seem to arise within the waters of the ocean and so forth which are already established, so too [do they appear] within the Great Consciousness, Brahman."

The meaning is that the world arises from the collective mind (*samaṣṭicitta*), even though it does not [previously] arise. The compound *anudeti* is formed either by the rule of *yogavibhāga* (splitting the rule) which allows the negative particle *nañ* to be compounded with a verbal form ending in a *tiṅ* suffix, or it is a Vedic usage. 41.
Just as that very self, though possessing form, becomes fluid and enters into the ocean,
so too am I pure consciousness alone, expanded as the state of non-egoity.

Let it be so; what follows from that? To this he says: "That" (tat). In that dream, the Self, whose nature is consciousness (*cidrūpa*), appears as if possessing form by way of being imagined by the mind in the form of water, and thus undergoes various transformations such as waves and other substances. Yet, therein there is not even an atom's worth of anything distinct from the Self.
Thus, I am pure consciousness alone, appearing through the various distinctions of the manifestation of the world, and not [anything else].

From the perspective of ultimate reality (paramārthataḥ), there is not even an atom’s worth of anything distinct from me, who am the fullness of consciousness; thus, because even the sense of "I" (ahambhāva) has been entirely eliminated, the meaning is that non-"I"-ness (anahambhāva) is nothing but consciousness alone, spread out and expansive. || 42 ||
For that sky of pure consciousness, there is neither birth nor death, neither the states of existence nor non-existence; for it, no destruction ever occurs anywhere.
Death is the separation from the body; "destruction" (nāśa) and "ruin" (dhvaṃsa) are its synonyms. The two courses of existence, good and evil, are heaven and hell. 43.
This sun of consciousness is indestructible, unburnable, and exceedingly pure; oh, after such a long time, am I now at peace and fully liberated? 44.
In this regard, he shows the resting point for the investigation currently underway with the words: "indestructible" (acchedya). || 44 ||
I am extinguished, free from delusion, like the ocean when Mount Mandara has been removed; I am the appearance of the non-existent, utterly pure, infinite, unborn, and immutable. 45.

By the rule *āse tāsastyoḥ*, there is the elision of the *s* [of *asti*]. That in which there is the appearance of non-existence (*asan*) is [the state] where there is no appearance of what is seen. || 45 ||
This space is the Self—unobstructed, stainless, supreme, eternal, and infinite;
it is this very space that constitutes the multitude of fruits, beginning with those that are fruitless.
"Enduring" means devoid of limitation by time. "Infinite" means devoid of limitation by space or substance.

From Brahmā down to a blade of grass, the floods of karmic fruits of living beings, and—by the force of the word "and"—the activities that serve as their means, as well as fruitless undertakings and vain efforts, all this is indeed this very space (ākāśa) and nothing else. 46.
This entire universe, including the gods and demons, is composed of me and is uncreated;
the army consisting of men and their karma is entirely like a mere lump of clay.

Masculinity (*puṃstva*) is the genus of persons such as potters and others; it consists of their actions and is fashioned by them. Alternatively, masculinity is the person-genus attributed to the image; its action consists of movements corresponding to that [genus], and it is "made of" that—that is, abundant in it—just like an army of clay soldiers fashioned by children.
Existence consisting of the seer and the seen is likewise composed of the unity of pure consciousness;
it is this unity, this duality, "I," and "not-I. (48)
What delusion or confusion could there be? How, for whom, from where, or where [could it exist]?
I am established in my own infinite, effortless, and perfectly tranquil state.
The four interrogative particles (*kiṃvṛtta*) are for the purpose of [respectively] expressing manner, the experiencer, cause, locus, possibility, and negation.
The phrase "having attained its own ultimate nature" is to be understood as the ellipsis. || 49 ||
He who shines forth as the one who perceives— whether he be insentient or sentient— is one who has attained Nirvana and final liberation, having transcended all feverish distress.

In the bliss of liberation within Nirvana, I am completely extinguished and at peace; having transcended the fever of worldly existence, I have attained my own true nature, like a golden ornament found upon one's neck. Whatever appears, whether insentient or sentient, and whoever is the experiencer who perceives both—whatever that Brahman is, whose nature is non-different from the self that shines forth, that is the Void (Kha).
The connection with what follows is: "It is indeed the space of consciousness. (50)
That form, whose nature is luminous, is the void established within the Great Consciousness.
This is not "this," nor "I," nor anything else; there is no arising of existence or non-existence.
All is peaceful, without support, and the Supreme alone remains. 51.
He says "not this" (neti) to show that Brahman does not abandon its own nature even while [appearing as] the world characterized by "this-ness," "I-ness," "other-ness," and so forth. || 51 ||
Thus devoted to inquiry, having realized through supreme awakening this reality of the Supreme Self as it truly exists,
she became peaceful— her play of passion, fear, and delusion entirely stilled— like a streak of cloud in an autumn sky.

He summarizes what has already been stated in brief with the word "ittham" (thus): she is one in whom passion and the other manifestations of darkness (*tamas*), which are like dreams within the three states of existence, have been completely stilled through supreme awakening—that is, through the departure of the sleep of absolute delusion. || 52 ||
Thus ends the seventy-eighth canto, titled "The Awakening of Cūḍālā," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the glorious Vāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa, the work of the Sage.
Thus ends the seventy-eighth chapter, titled "The Awakening of Cūḍālā," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The seventy-ninth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Day after day, by means of that very state of delighting in one’s own Self, [she remained thus].
She remained established in her natural state, constantly turned inward.
Having seen her unprecedented splendor, when questioned by the King,
Cūḍālā described here the cause of her own beauty, which is awakening.
Thus, he describes the progressive stabilization in successive stages through the practice of the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna) that has arisen from such inquiry:
"Form is established, being situated therein. || 1 ||
Free from passion, free from attachment, free from the pairs of opposites, and free from desire,
she neither abandons nor acquires anything, moving according to her natural conduct.
He states the characteristics of its establishment with the verse beginning "free from passion" (nīrāga) and so forth. || 2 ||
Having crossed the ocean of existence and stilled the web of doubts,
his inner self was completely filled with the supreme attainment of the Great Self.
She whose innermost self, more internal even than the mind within the body, is completely full. || 3 ||
Having rested for a very long time, weary though she was, she found a firm footing within the dense [reality] and,
by transcending all analogies, entered into a state beyond description.
Having long been weary of the prior cycle of saṃsāra, they then found rest in that other state, the supreme goal, which is a mass of unsurpassed bliss once knowledge has been attained. || 4 ||
Thus, in a very short time, that passionate woman Cūḍālā of excellent complexion attained the state of one who has known all that is to be known.
Just as this certain worldly delusion of movement has come into being,
so too does it all dissolve of its own accord within one who possesses the knowledge of reality.

To the question, "How can there be the cessation of an error that is beginningless and vast through an awakening that takes only a short time? he says, "Just as" (yathā). The meaning is that just as some inexplicable delusion of movement arises all at once in an ignorant person, so too everything without exception dissolves all at once in one who possesses the knowledge of reality. In the long reading, it is "just as."
It should be explained somehow that she dissolved [into Brahman] in such a way that she became possessed of the knowledge of reality. || 6 ||
Having attained rest in that peaceful state where all is unseen,
she shone like a streak of cloudless autumnal clouds, free from all agitation.
In that state where all duality is no longer seen.
Unperturbed, she remained gazing at herself within herself through her own lack of connection,
like an old cow that has found a grassy mountain peak and stays there.

Just as an old cow, having by chance reached a grassy spot with water— meaning a place where grass and water are present— and a mountain peak with a pleasant view where one may enjoy equal sunshine and moonlight, remains there undisturbed, so too did she.

The meaning is that she has attained the inner self (pratyagātman)— the uniform light present in all states such as waking and so forth— by means of her own nature which is unrelated to waking and the rest, and thus she remains established, undisturbed, in that very self. || 8 ||
By virtue of her intense practice of self-discrimination,
she shone with the dawning of the Self, like a beautiful flowering creeper that has newly sprouted.
By the arising brought about by the vision of the reality of the Self, through the manifestation of the nature of full bliss. || 9 ||

Then, on one occasion, having beheld that woman of faultless limbs and unprecedented beauty, Śikhidhvaja spoke with a smile: 10. Then, on one occasion, having beheld that woman of faultless limbs and unprecedented beauty, Śikhidhvaja spoke with a smile.
Smiling, with a face radiant with wonder. || 10 ||
O slender one, you shine forth even more intensely, as if endowed with renewed youth and adorned again and again, just as the world shines when possessed of a king. 11.

*Jagat* is *jagatī*. Because of the extended application of the *śatṛ*-suffix—according to the rule "In the present tense, [the words] *pṛṣat*, *mahat*, *bṛhat*, and *jagat* behave like the *śatṛ*-participle"—the suffix *ṅīp* (which would normally apply to stems ending in long vowels by the rule *ugitaśca*) is not applied here due to its Vedic character (*chāndasatva*). [The name] *Rājavatī* or *Rājavantī* means "possessing a king," or "possessing the full moon"; thus, you shine just as a king shines. || 11 ||
O beloved, you shine intensely as if filled with the essence of nectar, as if having attained the state that is to be reached, and as if overflowing with a flood of bliss. 12.
Bearing a beautiful body that is both tranquil and lovely,
O passionate woman, you surpass the moon and possess an indescribable splendor.
O beloved, I behold your mind as free from worldly attachment yet compassionate, tranquil yet vigorous, attained to equanimity, profound, and perfectly serene.
"Powerful" means powerful through discernment (*viveka*). "Tranquil" means possessing qualities such as calmness (*śama*). "Composed" means having stilled all restlessness. (14)
O beloved, I behold your mind—tranquil yet infinitely exuberant—which treats the three worlds as a mere blade of grass and has tasted the essence of the entire universe. 15.
O illustrious lady, no object of worldly prosperity or pleasure can equal your mind, which is as beautiful as the ocean of milk in a desert.
It was beautiful like a desert due to its lack of water and dullness, yet like the Ocean of Milk due to its fullness. || 16 ||
With those very limbs, tender as young plantain trees, lotus stalks, and new sprouts, you appear as though you have attained stability and reached full growth. (17)
She seemed to have attained stability and steadiness through those very same limbs and members from before, as if she had grown by means of an exceeding brilliance.
Thus, remaining in that very same configuration,
you have attained a different state, like a creeper at the change of season.
At the end of the season, when the cold has passed away. || 18 ||
Have you drunk the nectar of immortality, or have you attained universal sovereignty? Or have you reached deathlessness itself through the application of the yoga of practice? (19)

"Prayoga" refers to the application of elixirs (*rasāyana*) and the like; "āyoga" refers to the accomplishment of mantras and so forth; and "yuktis" refers to the methods of Rājayoga, Haṭhayoga, and other means—from these [it arises], hence "tataḥ" (from that). || 19 ||
O lady with eyes like blue lotuses, what have you not already attained that remains unattained—whether it be a kingdom, the wish-fulfilling gem, or even the three worlds? (20)
Cūḍālā said:

"I have come having abandoned this form which is neither 'nothing' nor 'something'; therefore, by means of that which is neither 'nothing' nor 'something,' I remain as the Illustrious One (Śrīmatī). (21)

Thus questioned by the king, Cūḍālā first gave her answer in an enigmatic manner, explaining that the cause of her extraordinary splendor was the abandonment of the limited identity of the body and the attainment of the nature of Brahman, which is full and non-dual— beginning with the words "na kiṃcit.
Having abandoned this identification with the body, which is well-known among ignorant people as "I am this [body]," there exists nothing whatsoever (*akiṃcit*).

That state of being Brahman-Atman, in which all things whatsoever—without exception—in their forms of name and form have arrived through the awakening to reality (*tattvabodha*), and not merely by means of practices such as mantras or elixirs (*rasāyana*). "Something" (*kiṃcit*) means a little, something trifling, in the form of various supernatural powers (*siddhi*); that is the meaning. Alternatively, [it may mean] "I am something" in some particular form.
The meaning is: she has not entered the two states of waking and dreaming, nor has she reached the state of deep sleep which is "not anything" (*akiñcit-kiñcit*) in form;

rather, having abandoned even these three states, she has attained the nature of the Fourth (*turya*). Alternatively, [the meaning is]: by means of ritual action, meditation, and so forth, I have attained some particular form—the station beginning with Indra and Candra and ending with Hiraṇyagarbha.

It has not come about through the establishment of identity produced by meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*). Nor is it something that is "not anything at all" (*akiṃcitkiṃcit*)—that is, having an unmanifest form;

rather, the meaning is that, having abandoned all this, it remains established in its own essential nature (*svarūpa*), for that reason.
