Alternatively, having abandoned this "I," which is delimited by the subtle body (*liṅgadeha*) and takes the form of the individual soul (*jīva*), it is that whose form consists of everything—that which is "not anything at all."

In that manner, she has attained—that is, reached—that Brahman which, from the perspective of ultimate reality (paramārthataḥ), is nothing at all, yet possesses some form; such is the meaning of "by that reason" (tena hetunā). || 21 ||
Having renounced all this and having taken refuge in that which is other than all else—
whether it be truth or untruth— it is by that alone that I remain possessed of glory.

He states the same meaning once more in a different manner with the words "This" (*idam*). Having abandoned all this limited (*paricchinna*) universe, I have taken refuge in that which is entirely unlimited (*aparicchinna*) and other than this. What is it? That which is the Truth (*satya*), uncontradicted;

that which is not found as a limited form (*san-mūrta*); that which is formless (*amūrta*), and [according to another reading] that which is other than the formless, being of the nature of the phenomenal world (*prapañca-rūpa*).
"Wherein" refers to that which is unreal, and "by that" is as explained previously. || 22 ||
Whatever exists and whatever does not exist, I know that as it truly is—how it arises and how it perishes; by this, I abide as the Illustrious One (Śrīmatī).

He describes his own statement—that it is "neither something nor nothing"—in another manner with the words "yad" (that which): that reality which, by not transcending its arising (udaya), is seen through the perspective of creation as some limited "something," and which, likewise, by not transcending its destruction (anāśa), becomes "nothing" when seen through the perspective of dissolution; that [reality] is such [as he has described].
The meaning is that I know [the Self] as abiding by its own nature of immutable, abundant bliss. || 23 ||
I am satisfied by enjoyments as if they were already consumed and long departed;
I neither rejoice nor do I become angry, and for that reason I remain possessed of prosperity.
I delight in the solitary heart, which is like the infinite sky;
I do not delight in royal pastimes, and for that reason I remain possessed of glory (Śrīmatī).
By the word "heart" (hṛdaya), the Brahman within the heart (hārda) is indicated. || 25 ||
For I abide in the Self alone, whether in my seats, gardens, or palaces;
I dwell neither in enjoyments nor in modesty, and thus I remain possessed of glory.

Whether seated on a throne or in a garden, even while the body remains present, I abide only in the Perfect Self and not in bodily or mental enjoyments such as ornaments or honors, nor in the shame caused by their absence. || 26 ||
"I am indeed the sovereign of the worlds, not one whose form consists of even the slightest thing";
thus I am satisfied with myself alone, and by that I abide as the Illustrious One (Śrīmatī).
"I am this, and I am not that; I am truth, yet I am not even that.
I am everything, and yet I am nothing; therefore, I abide as the Illustrious One."
This body and so forth, along with their objects of enjoyment, belong to the perspective of the substrate; however, from the perspective of superimposition, they are not "I. (28)
I do not long for pleasure, nor wealth, nor misfortune, nor any other state;
I rejoice in whatever comes to me, and by that I remain in prosperity. (29)
The ellipsis is "I do not desire to abandon what is harmful. || 29 ||
Through wisdoms that are like slender, hostile queens and through visions of the scriptures, I delight with these companions; therefore, I remain possessed of glory. (30)
I delight with my companions— those who have become friends— with my own insights and scriptural perspectives, by which both hatred and passion have been thinned and diminished. Alternatively,
[I delight] with those whose instruments are scriptural perspectives, and by whom hatred and passion have become thin and small.
I take delight together with such companions and friends.

"O Lord, whatever I perceive here with the rays of my eyes, with the sense-faculties, or with the mind—indeed, O dear one, I see nothing at all; yet, when devoid of those, I see nothing within. Thus, seeing correctly, I have long since arisen [from delusion]. (31)

"O Lord, whatever I perceive here in this world through the rays of my eyes, or by other senses, or by the mind, that is entirely unreal. But devoid of that which is seen by the senses and the mind, I perceive within me nothing at all—a reality free from conceptual proliferation (niṣprapañca). For this reason, as described, it exists in a perfectly uncontradicted form both internally and externally."
I see it; for that reason, I have long been continuously joyful, possessing the supreme glory of prosperity—this is the meaning. || 31 ||

Thus ends the seventy-ninth canto, titled "Cūḍālā’s Attainment of Her True Self," in the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the Mokṣopāya section of the glorious Vāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa of Valmīki, composed by the Sage. 79.
Thus ends the seventy-ninth sarga, titled "The Attainment of Self by Cūḍālā," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The Eightieth Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: To that fair-faced woman who was speaking thus, resting within her own self, [he replied].
Not understanding the meaning of their words, the king laughed and said: || 1 ||
The description by the ignorant king of that speech as being incoherent,
as well as the seed of the supernatural powers such as moving through the air (*khecaratva*), is explained here.
Thus, she spoke of the signs indicating her own extraordinary beauty in the manner described. || 1 ||
Śikhidhvaja said:
"O lady of excellent complexion, you are but a child engaged in incoherent prattle;
you take delight in royal pastimes, so enjoy them, O daughter of a king!"
"You are a child of immature intellect," that is to say, you are unskilled in uttering words conducive to the awakening of others. || 2 ||
How indeed can he shine, who, having abandoned something, has gone to that which is nothing yet established as direct perception, and who has thus abandoned the true nature of direct perception? (3)
He demonstrates that [the state of] incoherent prattle is indeed "nothing at all" through such statements as "not anything whatsoever"—namely, the word "something" (*kiṃcit*).

It is well known that beauty belongs only to that which possesses form. The meaning is: how could that which has abandoned the generality of form and attained formlessness—being almost like a void—be beautiful? || 3 ||

How indeed can he appear dignified who abandons enjoyments out of anger, thinking, "I am content even without having enjoyed these pleasures," while still keeping his seats, beds, and other such things? (4)
Regarding what you said—that "I am satisfied even by enjoyments that have not been experienced"—that too is incoherent; thus he says, "By enjoyments," etc., as if with anger (ruṣā). || 4 ||
But how indeed can he shine, who, having abandoned both enjoyment and non-enjoyment, delights in the empty sky alone, having renounced everything? (5)
Regarding what you said—that "I delight in the solitary heart which resembles space"—that too is inconsistent; for he says:

"Only one who, having abandoned the combination of 'enjoyment' (ābhoga) and 'eating' (ābhojana) by friends, servants, and others, and having renounced all the means thereto such as wealth, wanders alone like a ghost in the empty sky—he indeed shines."
The meaning is: how can these two be reconciled? || 5 ||
How indeed can he who, having abandoned all things such as clothing, food, and bedding, remains alone by himself, appear beautiful? (6)

The meaning is that one of steady intellect, through the power of fortitude alone as if against excessive anger and so forth, endures the sufferings of cold, heat, hunger, thirst, and the like. || 6 ||
"I am not the body," "otherwise I am," "I am nothing," and "I am everything"—how indeed can he who possesses such chatter be considered handsome? (7)
Regarding what was said—that "this is I" and "this is not I"—he states that this too is incoherent: "Not I. (7)
"What I see, I do not see; what I see is something else entirely"—how indeed can such idle chatter be fitting for one who has not renounced? (8)

He concludes that "these are not grounds for beauty" with the verse beginning "yad" (8), summarizing: "That which is said to be perceived by the rays of the eyes or known by the sense organs is utterly inconsistent."
Therefore, you are a child, you are bewildered, and you are fickle, O playful one;
I sport with various conversations and dalliances—sport, O beautiful one! (9)
Laughing loudly with a boisterous laugh at his beloved, saying "Śikhidhvaja," he rose to bathe at midday and departed from the women's quarters.
"Alas! He did not find rest within himself, nor did he understand my words;
'He is but a king,' thought Cūḍālā, distressed by the failure of her own efforts. (11)
"It is a pity," [he says], for the meaning is that according to such Vedic texts as, "If one has not realized this here, there is great ruin," and so forth. || 11 ||
Then, my dear, as those two remained there with such dispositions,
a great deal of time passed in those royal pastimes.
"O dear one" (aṅga) is an address to Rāma. || 12 ||
Once, although she was eternally satisfied and free from desire,
Cūḍālā herself felt a longing for the playful journey to her own heaven.
The desire arose within him to travel through the sky, moving like a god, in that region;
the meaning is that this was due to the remaining force of such *prārabdha* (the karma already in operation). || 13 ||
Then, for the sake of attaining the power to travel through the sky, that princess disregarded all enjoyments and went to a secluded place.
Alone, devoted to solitude, with her body seated in its own posture, she practiced for a long time the upward movement of the vital breath (prāṇa). || 15 ||

"Only one" means that, by implication, it is understood that for the king’s victory over his enemies, she should be two or three years old at the time of departure; otherwise, since she would be dependent on others, her devotion to her lover would be impossible. "Of the upward-moving vital breath," [he says] the practice of restraint in the region between the eyebrows and so forth for a long time, which is conducive to the accomplishment of moving through the sky (khecaratva). 15.
Śrī Rāma said:
How is it that this entire world, whether stationary or moving, which is perceived here, is experienced as being devoid of vibration, even though it is designated by the name "action"? (16)

In the context of the practice that brings about the power of moving through the air (*khecarīsiddhi*), Rāma, desiring to know the cause of action in general, raises an objection with the words "this which... This world, both stationary and moving, is seen to be entirely devoid of vibration and produced by action; [yet it appears so] even without the vibration of the causal factors such as the agent (*kartṛ*).

Since the arising of anything whatsoever is not observed, such being the case, how can there be the production of that which is called "action" (*spanda*)? Is it from something possessing action, or from something immutable (*kūṭastha*)? In the first case, there would be either self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*) or an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). In the second case, there is a contradiction, as well as the absence of cessation and the non-termination of results. How, then, can the production of a thing called "action" be experienced or even enter the path of experience?
The meaning is "in that same way. || 16 ||
O Brahmin, tell me, what playful vibration and what intense practice of mine—possessing such singular effort—is it that has this as its fruit: the ability to travel through the sky and so forth? (17)

Having thus raised an objection, he asks about the subject at hand: "Of whom? The meaning is: tell me also, of which play of vibration (*spandavilāsa*) is this collection of supernatural powers, such as traveling through the sky and so forth, the fruit? || 17 ||
Whether one knows the Self or does not know the Self, or even for the sake of spiritual perfection or as a mere pastime—O Lord, tell me how this is accomplished. (18)

The meaning is: "Tell me also how and by what sequence one who does not know the Self accomplishes this collection of supernatural powers for the sake of attainment, and how one who knows the Self accomplishes it as if in play. || 18 ||

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O dear one, O Rāghava, every object to be accomplished here in this world arises in three ways: as something to be accepted, as something to be rejected, and likewise as something to be disregarded.

This defect, such as infinite regress based on self-dependence, would arise if there were a requirement for causal factors (*kāraka*) merely to establish the essential nature of the action itself. But that is not the case; rather, it is for the sake of the fruit to be accomplished by the action. For the causal factors, having been set in motion for the production of the fruit, depend upon the action as an inseparable concomitant. By means of that action, the status of the fruit as the "to-be-accomplished" (*sādhya*) and the status of the causal factors as the "means of accomplishment" (*sādhana*) are established.

It can be so designated. Thus, since an action—which is distinct from both the goal (*sādhya*) and the means (*sādhana*)—does not require any further means beyond those required for the goal, the dilemma as to whether its cause is active (*sakriya*) or immutable (*kūṭastha*) has no place at all; with this intention, Vasiṣṭha [proceeds] to provide an answer favorable to the subsequent question.
He shows, by dividing it, that which is common to both the secondary and the primary, and is to be accomplished through action—namely, "it is threefold.

An object that has become the focus of the cognition of acquisition (*upādāna*) is "to be acquired" (*upādeya*), the domain of engagement (*pravṛtti*). An object known through the cognition of avoidance (*hāna*) is "to be avoided" (*heya*), the domain of withdrawal (*nivṛtti*). An object accessible to the cognition of indifference (*upekṣā*) is "to be disregarded" (*upekṣya*), and that pertains even to neutrality (*audāsīnya*).
Because of the metaphorical application of action—seeing worldly usage such as "this person has caused this harm through indifference"—the object to be accomplished (sādhya) is figurative. || 19 ||
That which is beneficial to oneself is to be acquired with effort;
that which is to be abandoned is discarded once known; and that which is neutral between these two is to be disregarded. (20)
He demonstrates the distinction between their results with the words "become one's own self" (*ātmabhūtam*). This means favorable to oneself.
It is that which lies in the interval between these two: the rejectable and the acceptable. (20)
Whatever causes delight is to be accepted according to the sound view; that which is contrary to it is not to be accepted. They know that which is indifferent to be neutral. (21)

That which causes delight is directly or indirectly conducive to happiness. The point is that even a means for warding off suffering is adopted precisely because it is conducive to happiness. That which is opposed to this [happiness] is an obstacle to happiness;
the point is that suffering is also detested precisely because it obstructs the happiness of well-being. || 21 ||
When everything has become identical with the Self for the wise man of right perception who knows,
then these three positions do not arise at all.
He states that these three varieties of the goal belong only to those who lack knowledge, with the words "of the non-discerning" (sanmateḥ) || 22 ||
At times, she may simply regard all this with indifference, having cast it aside as a mere sport, or perhaps she does not look upon it at all.
With the intention that there is no fault whatsoever even if the learned accept the third alternative, he says: "Only... (23).
That which is characterized by equanimity for the wise becomes something to be rejected by the ignorant;
it is to be abandoned by one of expansive dispassion—listen now to how the sequence of attainment proceeds.

With the intention that a single object becomes threefold for a single person through the different states of cognition, passion, and dispassion—[the reading being "the state of delusion and dispassion"]—he says: "of the knower.
Having thus stated the justification for the two parts of the question—"for the sake of attainment" or "as a sport"—how [is it so]?
He causes [the disciple] to hear the resolution of this part, stating "Listen," and so forth, by declaring: "He accomplishes this in this manner. || 24 ||
All accomplishments, achieved through the means of place, time, action, and material substances, delight living beings here just as spring delights the surface of the earth. (25)
Regarding that, he states the causes for the gradations of attainment and the dependence on effort that is either long or short-term, beginning with the word "deśa" (place). || 25 ||

O virtuous one, among these four alone, the predominance of action is conceived in the accomplishment of success (siddhi) and so forth, because those stages (krama) consist of that very [action] in their respective order.

Among these four—place and so forth—the conception of the primacy and excellence of practices such as the recitation of mantras and yoga arises from the swift attainment of success when there is a conjunction of the four superior factors, such as the Śrīśaila region; for the excellence of the fruit is likewise dependent upon that [excellence of the means]. Thus he says:
The meaning is that they consist of that [nature] and follow the excellence of such actions. || 26 ||
The description of the sequence of practices involving pills, collyrium, the sword, and so forth,
as well as the faults of those who are unrighteous therein, would result in excessive prolixity here and would detract from the subject at hand.

"Let it be so; what follows from that? To this he replies: "The pill," and so forth. In that regard, there exist means for achieving flight through the air and other such feats—such as the perfected pill (*siddhaguṭikā*), the perfected collyrium (*siddhāñjana*), the perfected sword (*siddhakhaḍga*), and the perfected sandals (*siddhapādukā*)—which are well-known from many extensive texts, including the *Uḍḍāmaratantra*, the *Yoginīkalpa*, and others. How [is this so]?

"O Lord, tell me how they accomplish this correctly"— if this is your intention regarding your question, that the sequence of their practice must be described, then it should be explained in detail, since it cannot be accomplished through a brief statement. Therefore, in that regard, concerning those accomplishments (*siddhis*),
for those listeners other than yourself who are non-existent [in merit], who lack the desire to know, and who do not know reality:

If, by chance, a desire were to arise for that [object], engaging in it would result in great harm; furthermore, since such an expansion would constitute an obstacle to the present purpose of hearing the truth of the Self (*ātmatattva*), it would be a hindrance. Therefore, the meaning is that its detailed description is not appropriate here. || 27 ||
The detailed description of gems, medicinal herbs, austerities, mantras, and ritual procedures—let this elaboration indeed cease, for it detracts from the subject at hand. (28)

He states with two verses beginning with "ratna" that this same principle is to be applied both in determining the sequence of accomplishing success through gems, mantras, and so forth, and in determining the sequence of accomplishing success by residing in places where perfected beings (siddhas) dwell, such as Śrīśaila. || 28 ||
Whether by dwelling on Śrīśaila, in a land of the Siddhas, or on Mount Meru and the like,
even the expansion known as "attainment" (siddhi) destroys the primary purpose for one who has already achieved his goal.
The address "O one who has accomplished his purpose" (kṛtārtha) is intended to show that those supernatural powers (siddhis) are trivial from the perspective of someone like you. || 29 ||

Therefore, listen to this practice of the cultivation of the vital breaths and other winds, which yields the fruit of supernatural powers, as it arises in the course of the narrative concerning Śikhidhvaja.
Lest Rāma feel despondent, thinking that his question has thus become futile,

[the author] teaches the sequence of breath-control (prāṇāyāma)— which is not overly prolix, is connected to the narrative being told, and serves as an incidental means for attaining powers such as moving through the air, which are useful for strengthening the knowledge under discussion— beginning with the words "Therefore" (tasmāt).

For, having abandoned all latent impressions other than those concerning the goal to be accomplished, one should indeed remain within, contracting the openings such as the anus by means of the sequential actions of the places of articulation and so forth. (31)

Therein, first, he states briefly by showing their seeds that one must be established in the restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*): "Having abandoned the internal *sthānas*, which are the objects to be accomplished, and the other *sthānas*, which are the means of accomplishment, as well as the latent impressions (*vāsanās*), one should occupy the seats such as *siddha* and so forth—
the word 'and so forth' including the alignment of the body, head, and neck, immobility, gazing at the tip of the nose, and so on."

Through purity of food and seat, through contemplation on the meaning of the scriptures of the virtuous, through one's own proper conduct, through association with good people, through total renunciation, and through a comfortable posture; || 32 ||
He elaborates upon that very sequence of practice by breaking it down [into its parts], beginning with "eating" (bhojana).
[This is achieved] through the thorough cultivation and repeated study of the meaning of the Yogaśāstra. || 32 ||

O Rāma, O observer of noble vows, through the intense practice of breath control over some period of time, and by abandoning anger, greed, and the like, as well as the renunciation of worldly enjoyments— || 33 ||

In the acts of relinquishing, grasping, and restraining, all the vital breaths come completely under the control of the man who knows that [reality], just as servants are subject to their master’s authority. (34)

The meaning is that when the practices of exhaling (*recana*), inhaling (*pūraka*), and retention (*kumbhaka*) have been thoroughly mastered, all the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) come under the control and subjection of the yogi who knows them— just as servants submit to a worldly master— due to his sovereignty, which is the attainment of mastery over the vital breaths. || 34 ||
O Rāghava, all prosperities, from sovereignty up to liberation, are attainable by everyone because they depend upon the control of the body and the vital breaths. (35)

He says "rājya" (sovereignty) because, when the vital breaths are under one's own control, the mastery over the accomplishments connected with them is also established for every qualified practitioner. || 35 ||
Circular in shape and resting upon the vital points (marmasthāna),
the channel named Āntraveṣṭanikā is supported by hundreds of channels.

Now, in order to establish that all supernatural powers (*siddhis*) are subject to the control of the bodily winds (*dehānila*), [the author] describes the primary channels (*nāḍī*)— numbering seventy-two thousand branches— that extend throughout the entire body, which originate from the *mūlādhāra*, enter into the seven wheels (*cakras*) starting from the *mūlādhāra* up to the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*), and emerge back into the *mūlādhāra*.
He describes the *suṣumnā* channel as having within it the power of *kuṇḍalinī* sleeping amidst three and a half coils;

because it is encircled, it has a circular shape, and for this very reason, since the intestines (*antra*) are also enveloped by its channels, it is called the "Intestine-Enveloper" (*āntraveṣṭanikā*). 36.
It resembles the whorl at the tip of a lute, is like a whirlpool in water,
has the form of the half-syllable *oṃ* of the script, and is situated in the shape of a spiral earring.
He describes that [power] at the *mūlādhāra* in accordance with the configuration of the *kuṇḍalinī* residing within it: "Like a lute...

It is similar to the whorl found at the base—the root portion—of the neck of a lute (*vīṇādaṇḍa*), which consists of lines formed by the winding of the strings or by the swirling of water. However, when demonstrated through writing in script (*lipi*), [it appears as follows]:

The term *ardhāṃkāra* means half of the syllable *oṃ*; she whose form (*saṃsthāna*) is like that [half]. The meaning is that her form should be written as the first half in the Dravidian script, or as the second half in the Nāgara script. The compound *ardha-napuṃsakam* is a partitive compound (*ekadeśin*), and the substitution of the single substitute form (*pararūpa*) is according to the rule *omāṅośca*. || 37 ||
It is declared to exist among gods, asuras, and humans; among deer, crocodiles, birds, and the like;
and among all living beings, from insects up to those born from lotuses. (38)
And this [power] exists not only among humans, but in the bodies of all living beings; thus he says: "O God," etc. (verse 38).
Her body is coiled in a circle like the coils of the lord of serpents sleeping from the cold;
she is white like the moon melting away in the fire of cosmic dissolution, with her hair bound in a topknot.

Afflicted by cold, she has formed a firm circle (maṇḍala) to ward off the suffering of the cold; that is to say, she has formed a circle like the body (bhoga) of the lord of serpents (bhogīndra) when he is asleep in such a manner. She is white and radiant. Her form is bound in the shape of a coiled bracelet (kuṇḍalī-valaya), resembling the moon—white and bright—which is being dissolved by the fire at the end of the aeon (kalpāgni) and is clearly marked with lines in the form of an inner circle.

Alternatively, "kalpa" means that which is capable of digesting; thus, it refers to the digestive fire (*jāṭharāgni*). By that [fire], the moon—which is well-known in the Yoga scriptures as being located at the head—melts.
Having melted, it flows down to the *mūlādhāra*, where it becomes solidified and remains there in the form of a bound coil (*baddhakuṇḍalākṛti*); such is the poetic conceit (*utprekṣā*). || 39 ||
Touching the thighs, the space between the eyebrows, and the apertures, she remains restless in her movement, constantly vibrating with the vital breath (pavamāna). || 40 ||

By the word "thigh" (ūru), the anal region (guda)—the joint at the root of the thighs—is indicated through figurative usage (lakṣaṇā). Starting from there up to the midpoint between the eyebrows, she touches those apertures and is woven through them; she is restless within through the fluctuations of the mind, and she vibrates externally through the vital breath (prāṇa) and so forth. || 40 ||
Within that [lotus], which is as delicate as the sheath of a plantain tree,
there vibrates the Supreme Power (parā śakti), whose movement is as graceful as the motion of a lute.
At its root, he shows the power of consciousness (cicchakti) known as Kuṇḍalinī, which has the form of three and a half coils within.

That very [power] is called Parā; it is the movement that is the root of all sound, consisting of the Word-Brahman (śabdabrahman), and its manifestation is such that, through contact with the vital breath (prāṇa), it becomes progressively more manifest in the regions of the navel, heart, and throat, becoming respectively Paśyantī and Madhyamā.

"It assumes the distinctions such as *vaikharī* and so forth. Thus it has been said in the *Mantraśāstra*: "That which they know as the Consciousness of all beings, the *Śabdabrahman*, having reached the form of *Kuṇḍalinī* situated in the middle of the bodies of living creatures, manifests itself in the form of phonemes (*varṇa*) through the distinctions of prose, verse, and so on. It has also been stated by Sāmba: "That which..."

"Rising from the seat of Mitra and Varuṇa, she brings forth sixty-three phonemes here through the organs of articulation by union with the vital breath (prāṇa). I take refuge in that speech which is first arisen as Paśyantī, then as Madhyamā abiding in the intellect, and finally as Vaikharī made clear by the organs in the mouth. Thus [ends verse 41].
And she is called by the name Kuṇḍalinī, flowing in the form of a coil;
she is the supreme power of living beings, bestowing the vitality of all powers. (42)
She is the bestower of vitality, for she sustains the existence, manifestation, and activity of all powers, including those of the vital breath, the senses, and the intellect.
Constantly sighing like an angry female serpent,
she remained with her face upturned, having become motionless.

In that regard, as to how the vital energy (*prāṇa-śakti*) bestows speed, he says: "unceasingly" (*aniśam*). The meaning is that it is in the form of constant exhalation, for it itself constantly ejects the *prāṇa* upward from its own mouth and draws the *apāna* downward. || 43 ||
When the vital breath enters the seat of Kuṇḍalinī in the heart,
then consciousness arises within, which is the source of the seeds of the subtle elements (tanmātras).

He explains how it bestows the power and momentum of the intellect: "When... When the *prāṇa* situated in the heart, having been drawn up by the *kuṇḍalinī*, reaches the station of the *kuṇḍalinī* through the function of the *apāna*, then—in such an internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) whose seed or material cause consists of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) of the gross elements, that is, the unquintuplicated (*apañcīkṛta*) elements—[the intellect arises].

The meaning is that "it becomes" (bhavati) refers to the consciousness of the individual soul (jīvasaṃvit), which arises internally through various modifications such as memory, volition, determination, egoism, passion, and so forth. || 44 ||
Just as the Kuṇḍalinī vibrates within the body like a female bee in a lotus,
so too does consciousness arise within through the awakening brought about by the power of subtle touch.
And how does she bestow the power, speed, and vitality of the senses? To this he says: "Just as...

Thus, when Kuṇḍalinī—having deposited her own powers of knowledge and action within the vital breath (prāṇa) and the intellect (buddhi)—is present through the awakening of the senses such as the eyes, which possess soft touch and contact with their objects, then, in the body, in whatever manner...

The meaning is that consciousness arises in such and such a manner—characterized by the manifestation of specific objects through the respective sense organs and the subsequent experience of their results—in accordance with the diversity of the causal complex consisting of the unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) of the enjoyer. || 45 ||
There, through the soft mutual embrace of the two instruments,
the *kuṇḍalinī* quickly ascends with such force that consciousness arises intensely.

How does she follow the influence of the soft touch? To this he says: "Touching. Kuṇḍalinī vibrates with such speed that first there arises the touching of objects by the eyes and other senses through a soft [contact]. And thus, the "possessor of the machine" (yantrayuk)—the subject who joins the "machine," which is the aggregate of the body and the organs—[perceives] as it has gone outward through the door of the mental modification (vṛtti).
*Mutual embrace* (*anyonyāliṅgikā*) refers to the mutual embracing with an external object; the suffix *ṇvul* is used here in the sense of a state (*bhāve*).

An all-pervasiveness (*vyāpti*) arises, brought about by the activity of pervasion. And by that [pervasion], just as when the covering of the object is shattered, consciousness (*saṃvit*) emerges as something exceedingly clear—the manifestation (*prathā*) of the jar and so forth—so too does it arise in each respective manner; such is the meaning. || 46 ||
In that [space], all the channels connected to the cavity of the heart arise and dissolve, like rivers in the great ocean. (47)

In this regard, with the intention that the channels (*nāḍīs*) serve as the gateway for the activation of the eyes and other senses by Kuṇḍalinī residing in the *mūlādhāra*, he says: "In that [channel]... They arise, meaning they expand (or according to another reading, "they are perceived");
they dissolve, meaning they contract. || 47 ||
Constantly eager to fall and oriented toward entry, she alone is declared to be the common seed of all consciousnesses. (48)

He explains how they arise and dissolve with the word "constantly" (*nityam*). [They arise] by means of that [power] which, in the form of *prāṇa*, is eager to move upward, and in the form of *apāna*, is intent on entering downward. He concludes what has been said with the word "she" (*sā*): "She" (*sā*) means common (*sāmānī*), i.e., universal (*sādhāraṇī*). From the word *samāna*, the suffix *ṣyañ* is added in the sense of the abstract state or as a pleonasm; then, by the rule *halas taddhitasya*, there is the elision of the *y*. 48.

Śrī Rāma said: Since consciousness (cit-saṃvit), uninterrupted until the end of the kalpa, indeed exists as everything, for what reason does its manifestation clearly arise from the sheath of Kuṇḍalinī? (49)

Rāma asks: "How and for what purpose does the emergence of the limited Kuṇḍalinī—known as a portion of one's own self—occur from the unlimited consciousness at the root of the channels in the Mūlādhāra?
[The author] replies with the verse beginning "ākalpāt": in terms of time, it is everything; and in terms of substance, it is unlimited.
The inclusion of both [terms] is intended to show that the absence of spatial delimitation is also subsumed within the absence of substantial delimitation. || 49 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
O sinless one, consciousness (*cit-saṃvit*) exists everywhere, at all times, and as everything;
however, its manifestation occurs in certain places due to the influence of the elements and their subtle constituents (*tanmātra*).
Vasiṣṭha, however, [argues that] since the absence of limitation by time is already included therein,
its separate mention is redundant; if it is mentioned separately for the sake of clarification,
then the same applies to the absence of limitation by space— thus, under the guise of restating the triad, he shows [the point] regarding the formless [Brahman].

And for the sake of manifesting consciousness (*cit*), which is devoid of objects, either in the form of a living being (*jīva*) or as having jars and other things as its domain, at that time consciousness arises—containing within it the seeds of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*).

Intending to explain this stated meaning in detail, [the author] says that the specific manifestation of consciousness is dependent upon the elements transformed into the two forms of the gross and subtle bodies: *...tadā saṃvidudetyantarbhūtatanmātrabījabhūri...* [He explains: The specific manifestation of consciousness occurs only in dependence upon the elements that have evolved into the forms of both the gross and the subtle bodies. Thus he says: [text continues].
Although present everywhere within bodies, it appears to flicker; for although the solar heat pervades all things, it indeed manifests specifically upon walls and such.

Now, one might object: "If there is no spatial limitation, would consciousness not manifest everywhere? Anticipating this, he explains—using an illustration—that its manifestation occurs solely by virtue of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), stating: "Everywhere. It appears tremulous in the intellect because it enters as if doubled through both limitation and reflection, thereby becoming dense.

The meaning is that it becomes restless due to the restlessness of the intellect, like the reflection of the sun in water. Regarding its manifestation through the expansion produced by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), he states the illustration: "all-pervading" (verse 51).
In one place it is lost, in another it is manifest, and in another it has reached a state of disappearance;
thus is an object perceived within an object, unfolding through the various modes of existence.

In that regard, he says "in some places" (*kvacid*) to show that there is a gradation in the manifestation of consciousness (*cid-abhivyakti*) according to the degree of impurity of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*).

In objects such as clay or stone, that reality of consciousness (*cid-vastu*), being overwhelmed by the dullness of ignorance (*avidyā-jāḍya*), has perished—like the coldness in heated water—and has gone out of sight; however, in the forms (*liṅga*) of gods, humans, and so forth, it is clearly manifested.

In signs such as trees and the like, one observes a state of extreme concealment, characterized by an incapacity for external perception and discernment. He states—using the word "tat"—that there is no gradation in the aspect of existence (*sattā*), just as there is none in the aspect of consciousness (*cit*). This is because, through the very marks of the existence of those three kinds of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) established by universal experience, that [existence] is present everywhere.
"Manifested" means "unconquered. || 52 ||
O sinless one, listen further as I shall explain to you in due order how the process consisting of pure consciousness arises intensely within one's own body. (53)
He promises to describe, in due order until the end of creation, the very gradation of manifestation already mentioned, with the words "etad" (this). [He explains:
"In one's own [bodies], such as those of humans and so forth, and in the bodies of lower animals, plants, and so forth, according to whatever kind of gradation. (53)

All that is born of the elements, whether conscious or unconscious, as well as the entire expanse of space—all this is nothing but pure consciousness, nothing but pure existence, and nothing but emptiness, just like the sky. || 54 ||

By way of this introduction, in order to elaborate upon the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of the subtle and gross elements, [the author] first points out the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*), which is the single essence of existence and consciousness (*saccidekarasa*) as the substrate of all, and which is devoid of the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*) and its attributes—beginning with the words "Consciousness" (*cetana*). It is like the sky, unattached, all-pervading, and subtle. (54)
For that [reality] is indeed pure consciousness, pure existence, immutable, and self-named;
situated somewhere, it is consciousness itself as the five subtle elements (tanmātra) of the gross elements.

While that [universe] remains exactly as it was in that single portion fashioned by Māyā, through the successive superimposition (adhyāsa) of the subtle elements beginning with space, that very same thing remains in the form of the essence of the mere elements; thus he says: "For that... (55).
You perceive that duality as having become fivefold within your own self-consciousness,
with all modifications and the like contained therein, just as a hundred lamps arise from a single lamp.

Having entered as a reflection that subtle body (liṅgaśarīra)— which consists of those five subtle elements (tanmātras), along with prāṇa, mind, intellect, the organs of knowledge, and the organs of action, thus comprising fivefold divisions— you have become like one lamp from which a hundred lamps are produced; within you,
your own consciousness contains the modifications such as birth and so forth, and by the word "and so forth" (ādipadāt), the various distinctions of states such as waking and the rest.
In that [Self] wherein such duality—meaning the state of being a living soul—is perceived; you perceive it. The change in voice (upagraha) is Vedic. || 56 ||
By their mere existence alone, in the form of a fragment of volition, certain groups of five here attain the state of being a body. (57)

Certain residual portions of the subtle elements (liṅgārambhapariśiṣṭāni), consisting of quintuplets (pañcakāni), attain the state of a gross body through the process of quintuplication (pañcīkaraṇa) by means of their own mere existence, which takes the form of a trace of volition (saṃkalpalavarupeṇa) following the latent impressions (vāsanā) for the forms of gods, humans, and so forth, of the living being (jīvasya). || 57 ||
Some [words] denote the state of being an animal and so forth, some the state of being gold and so forth;
some denote the state of being a region and so forth, and some the state of being a substance and so forth. (58)

Due to the variety of bodies, there is the state of being gold and so forth, as well as the state of having the bodies of stationary beings such as the *dhattūra* plant; or else, by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the inclusion of stationary bodies is understood, such as the state of being animals and so on.

By the phrase "the state of being gold and so forth," the meaning is the nature of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) characterized by gold, silver, and earthenware bowls, as well as the state of being the objects of enjoyment for the worlds contained within it.

For thus it is established that the world consists of nothing more than the vibration of the five elements; O descendant of Raghu, the consciousness of pure awareness (citsaṃvit) is present everywhere here. 59.

"Let it be so; what follows from that? To this he says: "For thus... [The word] *sthitam* means established or proven. Then, since the consciousness that serves as the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna-caitanya*) exists everywhere, why would even a jar or similar object not be conscious? To this he says: "Consciousness... (verse 59).
It is solely by virtue of the five [elements] that there is the designation "consciousness" in relation to the body and so forth;
in some cases, such as in stationary beings, there is the designation "insentient vibration," and in others, the designation "insentient."

Due to the predominance of the subtle body (liṅgadeha), which is composed of the five vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth that manifest consciousness by virtue of the group of five [elements], the term "consciousness" (*cetanā*) is used in its primary sense in human bodies and the like. In some cases among animals, because of the equal predominance of both the subtle body and the gross body (*sthūladeha*), there is the designation "insentient vibration" (*jaḍaspanda*) or "insentient-consciousness" (*jaḍacetanā*). However, in the case of stationary beings (*sthāvara*) and so forth...

The meaning is that because the *liṅga* consists of mere internal sensation, it is not perceived as conscious by people outside; therefore, it is well known by the designation "insentient" (*jaḍa*). || 60 ||
Just as a wave stands motionless like dry land, so too this consciousness, though possessing a flickering form, becomes joined with insentience within the five [elements]. (61)

Regarding how consciousness (*cit*) exists with varying degrees of intensity across these three states, he provides an illustration with the word "yathā" (just as): Just as the ocean of water, melted during the day, remains solid and motionless at the edge of the shore in the evening due to contact with the cool breeze and its gradual thickening; yet it is mobile like a wave in the liquid portion, and slightly mobile in the slightly thickened portion.

The meaning is that, just as a mountain remains like solid ground in an extremely dense region, so too this consciousness (citi), in the form of the five classes of beings— humans, animals, birds, reptiles, and stationary objects— remains in the form of the world, slightly wavering and endowed with extreme inertia. || 61 ||

Just as we do not think, "O gentle one, why is the ocean restless here and calm there?", so too this pentad of the insentient and the sentient is [not to be analyzed] through conceptual construction and the like. (62)

Just as in some cases, even when there is a state of solidification and an absence of mobility, its nature as the ocean is not contradicted, so too, even in the state of being stationary objects and the like, there is no impairment of its conscious nature (cidrūpatā). Thus he says: "iti" (thus). The word "no" is interrogative (kāku). Is it not the case that the designation "ocean" does not apply? On the contrary, it certainly does; and just as that is so, so it is with this [consciousness] in the various conceptualizations of gods, humans, animals, and so forth.

The meaning is that consciousness is unimpaired. Alternatively, with the intention that the distinction between the insentient and the sentient belongs only to the superimposed fivefold group (pañcaka) and is not a property of consciousness—since consciousness is devoid of properties—the author says: "For the fivefold group... (verse 62).
The fivefold group beginning with the body is the living soul; vibration, mountains, and so forth are inert;
and that which vibrates as wind in stationary objects and the like exists by the power of its own nature, O sinless one. (63)
He says "the body, etc. because such numerous conceptualizations are seen in the *pañcaka* (pentad) by virtue of its own nature.

The pentad, which has transformed into the form of the body and so forth, is the individual soul (*jīva*) through its consciousness and vibration dependent upon the maintenance of vital breath (*prāṇa*). That which impels it is consciousness; whereas mountains and the like are merely insentient (*jaḍa*). However, the bodies of immobile beings and the like—

The meaning is that fixed conceptual distinctions, such as "the external [body] vibrates dependent on the wind" and "the internal [mind] is conscious," are observed by the force of their own inherent nature. || 63 ||
O descendant of Raghu, words must be questioned regarding their inherent nature;
for speech is observed to be like cold and heat, or like snow and fire. (64)

Now, surely an entity (*bhāva*) that is its own nature (*svabhāva*)—being self-constituted—how could it consist of contradictory conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*)? For contradiction (*virodha*) is dependent upon another, whereas one's own nature (*svo bhāvaḥ*) is independent of anything else. Even if one’s own nature were defined as "one's own state" (*svīyo bhāvaḥ*), it would still depend solely on itself and not on another; so how could it be the essential form or cause of a conceptual construction that is dependent on another?
If it is asked, "Or could it be so?", then you must question the words themselves, setting aside their inherent nature;

for those very words, consisting of terms such as "conscious" (*cit*) and "insentient" (*jaḍa*), exclude their own meanings through repetition and thus convey the contradictory states of consciousness and insentience. In this same way, every word—whether referring to attributes such as coldness and heat, or to substrates such as snow and fire—functions in the same manner.

The meaning is that it is observed everywhere in exactly this manner. The ablative case in "svabhāvāt" (from its own nature) is used with the elision of a suffix ending in -lyap, governing the object. 64.

Indeed, when subjected to critical inquiry, the persistence of the five groups [of elements], which have acquired portions of latent impressions and undergo transformation through the absence of nourishment, must be accounted for.

Alternatively, even speech itself is not to be questioned, because it is dependent on that [reality], merely echoing the fivefold objects as they appear through conceptual constructions fashioned by latent impressions (*vāsanā*). Rather, it is the very persistence of the fivefold groups of *liṅga*-selves—which are subject to modification due to the presence of various conflicting conceptualizations regarding the portions of latent impressions already grasped—that should be the object of inquiry. Thus he says: [the verse beginning with] *pañcaka-sthitiḥ*.
However, these perverted latent impressions can be easily directed from here to there by a wise man through proper inquiry. (66)
Alternatively, even they are not at fault, for they follow the tendencies (*vāsanā*) of thousands of conflicting conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) from preceding moments. Therefore,

by a wise person seeking the root of these conflicting conceptual constructions, it can be concluded that it is the distorted or distracted tendencies themselves that are capable of leading the mind here and there among thousands of conflicting conceptual constructions.
He says "it is not intrinsic nature and so forth," namely: "it is the latent predisposition" (vāsanā). || 66 ||

Whether it be regarding the impure or the pure, he is questioned by that [opponent] concerning another pentad: that which possesses awakened latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and that which possesses dormant latent impressions. (67)

In men, whether in an inauspicious state such as that of animals or stationary beings, or in an auspicious state such as that of gods and so forth, the pentad [of elements] remains with either awakened or dormant latent impressions (*vāsanā*). Therefore, the logical conclusion is that the latent impression alone is to be questioned as the cause of that [state].
One should apply that [method] where the fruit of inquiry is experienced; one should not strike at empty space with one's fists. (68)
Furthermore, the inquiry into latent impressions (*vāsanā*) is fruitful because it leads to the application of the means for their destruction;
however, the inquiry into intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and so forth yields no result at all. Thus he says: "Where... (verse 68).
Indeed, the aggregates of the five elements range from Mount Meru and others down to the tip of a blade of grass;
likewise, among these stationary and moving beings, they range from insects and others down to those established in discernment. (69)

For this very reason, upon the destruction of latent impressions (vāsanā) and the attainment of the full Self, even mountains such as Meru and heaps of gold become "grass-tip-niṣṭhas"— that is, they reach a state of utter insignificance like that of a blade of grass. He says "tṛṇāgra" (like the tip of a blade of grass) to show that those established in discernment (viveka), even if their bodies enjoy the pleasures of gods and others, become far more insignificant than insects and the like.
Some have dormant latent impressions (vāsanās), such as the species of stationary beings;
others have awakened latent impressions, such as humans, gods, and so forth.

For this very reason, having cited the diversity among the five classes of beings— such as the stationary and so forth— as resulting precisely from the varying degrees of the sleep and awakening of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), he demonstrates this through the two verses beginning with "prasupta" (70).
Some are turbid with latent impressions (*vāsanā*), such as these animals and others;
some have their latent impressions cast off, such as these who are destined for liberation. (71)
"Accompanied by impure minds turbid with latent impressions (vāsanā), they are 'possessed of turbid latent impressions' (savāsanāvilāḥ).
Those who have cast off latent impressions are 'those whose latent impressions have been abandoned' (prakṣiptavāsanāstyaktavāsanāḥ). || 71 ||
Then, within their own respective cognitions, mind, intellect, and so forth were established by means of the fivefold aggregates (skandhas) associated with hands, feet, and other limbs. (72)

Precisely due to the variety of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), there arises the fivefold aggregate of gods, humans, and so forth, as well as various worldly transactions such as traveling through the sky or on the earth;

within one's own cognitions alone, there exist the internal and external instruments (*karaṇa*)— namely mind (*manas*), intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṃkāra*), thought (*citta*), eye, ear, breath, tongue, skin, and so on— which are suitable for the worldly transactions of humans and others.
The meaning is that designations and conventions have been established; for this very reason, they are seen to possess diverse natures according to each individual living being. || 72 ||
Other designations have been devised by others, such as the animals and so forth; other and yet other perceptions have been established by others, such as the stationary beings and so forth. (73)
For animals such as cattle and the like, there are four legs, a horn, and a tail; for birds, a beak, two wings, a tail, and feet; for snakes, a hood, a body, and a tail;
and for worms, insects, gadflies, mosquitoes, and the like, they possess whatever is suitable for their respective activities according to their own latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
The meaning is that conventions such as "parts" (avayava) and so forth are merely conceptual constructs. || 73 ||
Thus, O virtuous one, these various pentads of dispositions manifest themselves through forms that are moving or unmoving, sentient or insentient, in their beginning, middle, and end. (74)

O Lord of the Earth, among these, the single volition (abhisaṃkalpa) is the atom; it is the seed of these creations, which are like trees growing in the sky— unstable, subject to change, and insentient at their beginning, end, and middle, yet supported by that which is immovable and sentient in its true nature.

Having thus described the infinite varieties of the *liṅga* known as the "five-crested" (*pañcaka*), [the author] states "of these" (*eṣām*) to show that for one who has attained the collective ego-sense (*ahaṃbhāva*) as the fruit of performing the combination of ritual action (*karman*) and meditation (*upāsana*), a certain single atom of volition (*saṃkalpa-paramāṇu*) is the seed of this tree of the world-space (*saṃsāra-nabhas*).

Because it is the object of the collective totality (*samaṣṭi*), the pervasive volition (*saṃkalpa*) is the "intention" (*abhisaṃkalpa*); that which is characterized by this is the atom (*paramāṇu*), the seed of the "space-trees" (*ākāśavṛkṣa*) that constitute creation.
And within those space-trees of creation, [one finds] these fivefold groups—oh, what a wonder is Māyā! This is the meaning. || 75 ||
The sense organs are indeed like flowers, possessing the fragrance of their objects; the flickering activities of desire are like shimmering bees and radiant clusters of blossoms. (76)

He explains the statement that the worlds (sargas) are like trees in the sky by means of the metaphor of flowers and their fragrance: "That which is characterized by the objects [of the senses] is the Pradhāna—that is to say, it is that which has the nature of abiding in the fragrances [represented by the objects]. The activities of the flickering organs of action... (verse 76).
The clear intermediate spaces between the worlds are its thickets; Mount Meru is its root;
the dark clouds are its sprouts; and the ten flickering directions are its creeping vines. (77)
The pure intermediate worlds such as Svarga and others are the shrubs and branches; all the mountains, together with Meru, are the root. || 77 ||
O descendant of Raghu, those innumerable fruits—both those existing now and those yet to come—are yours. 78.
The elements are the fourfold bodies; that belongs to that tree. 78.
O Rāma, these five seeds are indeed the five trees;
they arise by themselves from their own nature and perish by themselves in the course of time. (79)
From the self, which by its very nature is empty of its own differentiation. || 79 ||
They themselves undergo diversity and, due to long-standing inertia, they manifest;
yet, being distinct from themselves, they come to rest like waves in the ocean. (80)
They are seen as distinct from oneself by means of the vision of discernment. || 80 ||
From here they go toward exaltation, and from here they go toward tranquility of their own accord;
like waves in the ocean, these [states] arise through dullness and discernment. (81)

Summarizing exactly what was stated in the two preceding verses, he says: "From this... "O Rāma, those who, by virtue of discrimination, have entered the abode from this outward vision—that is, from the perspective of the external—and have likewise entered the abode from this inward vision, they do not return here to further existence; others, however, wander repeatedly throughout the world. (82)

O Rāma, those who have come under the sway of discrimination—those multitudes of the fivefold play who have reached the abode [of the Self] extending as far as the cessation of latent impressions (nirvāsana) and its destruction—do not undergo again in this saṃsāra the state of assuming a body, birth, death, and so forth. But others, however, continue to wander in the world just as before; such is the meaning. || 82 ||

Thus ends the eightieth chapter, titled "The Play of the Five," in the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa* of the *Mokṣopāya* section of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, according to the tradition of the Ṛṣis. 80.
Thus ends the eightieth chapter, titled "The Play of the Five," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa-tātparya-prakāśa*.
The eighty-first canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
This seed-syllable of the five elements resides within that very interior of Kuṇḍalinī.
In that [state], the vital breath always vibrates in the form of the wind.

In this work, everything is described in detail: the sequence for the arising and pacification of diseases through the context of Kuṇḍalinī, as well as the means for perceiving the attainment of supernatural powers (siddhi) and so forth.

"When the vital breath (prāṇānila) enters the seat of Kuṇḍalinī in the heart, then consciousness arises within, which is the source of the seeds of the subtle elements (tanmātra) of the [gross] elements. This was stated in order to clarify the portion "source of the seeds of the subtle elements of the [gross] elements" within the demonstration of how it bestows the momentum of the power of the intellect (buddhi-śakti).

Synthesizing the investigation of the fivefold [categories] in their gross and subtle aspects, which is useful for the practice of breath (*prāṇa*)—the seed of the *khecarī* and other supernatural powers—he demonstrates the manner in which the vital breaths and so forth arise within the present Kuṇḍalinī, stating:
"This... Within that fivefold set consisting of the gross body, at its center in the *mūlādhāra*, in that [place] previously described...

The meaning is that within this Kuṇḍalinī, the first subtle element (*bhūtasūkṣma*), which is the material cause (*upādāna*) of these five [entities] whose nature is the *liṅga*, flashes forth in the form of the five vital breaths (*prāṇapañcaka*). || 1 ||
The stainless digit of consciousness is the touch of the internal vibration of Kuṇḍalinī;
it is called "kalā" because of its quickening (kalanena), and it is called "cit" because of its awareness (cetanena).

That Kuṇḍalinī, throbbing within in the form of the vital breath (prāṇa), having become the threefold conceptualization of vibration (spanda), touch (sparśa), and consciousness (saṃvit) through its own nature and the nature of the wind, acquires such names as "power" (kalā), "conscious individual soul" (cij-jīva), "mind" (manas), "volition" (saṃkalpa), "intellect" (buddhi), "ego" (ahaṃkāra), "the city of eight" (puryaṣṭaka), and "subtle body" (liṅga) by means of the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of its various functions such as conceptualization; thus he says: "She who is within... (sāntar).
By three. || 2 ||
From life she has become the living soul; from thinking she is established as the mind (manas);
from volition she is indeed volition (saṃkalpa), and from awareness she is known as the intellect (buddhi). || 3 ||
Having attained the nature of the ego, this very one, known as the "eightfold city" (puryaṣṭaka),
abides in the body as the unsurpassed power of the individual soul (jīvaśakti), namely Kuṇḍalinī.
Having reached the lower region, the *apāna* flows constantly downward;
the *samāna*, situated in the middle of the navel, and the one called *udāna*, located above, [flow respectively]. (5)
In this regard, he demonstrates the threefold nature of the primary functions and locations of the power of vibration (*spanda-śakti*) with the words "by means of the apāna," etc. (verse 5).
Below, it exists solely in the form of apāna; in the middle, it is always purely saumya;
and even when nourished, it remains in the form of udāna alone, abiding as the very self of the person.

He states the purposes for the different functions [of the breaths] with the word "below" (*adha*). The meaning is that the movement of the *apāna* and so forth is indeed the purpose. Although it is drawn upward by both the *apāna* and the *udāna*, it is itself gentle and perfectly still. Precisely because it is held fast by that [lower breath], even though it is nourished and powerful, it remains established in its own state as the upward-functioning *udāna* itself; it does not [disturb] the *liṅga*.
The meaning is that he causes [the breath] to go out externally. || 6 ||
If it moves downward despite every effort and is not held back by exertion,
then the person meets death because of that [fluid] having been forcibly expelled.

He states that even when it functions downwards, that [consciousness] is obstructive: "with all effort" (*sarvaprayatnam*). If it is not sustained by means of the general function, then that consciousness of the individual soul (*jīvasaṃvit*), being drawn upward by the downward-moving function (*apānavṛtti*) with every possible exertion, goes out through the lower path. He asks what happens then and says: "that" (*tad*). || 7 ||
If the entire [vital force] rises upward and is not restrained by means of yoga,
then the person meets death because it has forcefully departed.
He states clearly what was previously mentioned: "All together," etc. (verse 8).
If one should abide entirely within the self, having abandoned upward and downward movement,
then that person’s disease is destroyed by the obstruction of the internal wind.

For this very reason, it is said—namely, "in every way"—that by the practice of restraining the movement of the prāṇa and apāna breaths, and thereby conquering both the equalized function and the other functions throughout all the limbs, there is the accomplishment of the destruction of all diseases and the conquest of death; [this occurs] in the self, that is, in the body. || 9 ||
From the impairment of the general channels, general diseases arise;
from the impairment of the principal channels, principal diseases arise. (10)
There are one hundred principal channels, while their branches are the common channels; among these, the channel of the samāna-vṛtti, which conveys the essence of food, is that very place where,

due to the accumulation of phlegm, bile, and so forth, there occurs a state of impairment and non-functioning, and precisely there, through an imbalance with the other vital airs (vāyu), the drawing in of the essence of food takes place.
He states that there is the occurrence of both minor diseases and major diseases by saying "sāmānya" (general), etc. || 10 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
O Lord of Sages, what are the causes of destruction and what are the causes of origin for mental afflictions and physical diseases in this body? Tell me this quickly and exactly as it is.
Why [is it asked]: "Of what are those things whose destruction they possess the destruction"? Likewise, "of what are they the production"? (11)
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Mental anxieties and physical ailments—these two are the causes of suffering.
One should know that their cessation is happiness; their destruction is called liberation.

Their cessation through medicines and conciliatory measures is a temporary pacification. Because the Self, whose nature is bliss, remains as a residue, there is happiness. Their destruction at the root by means of knowledge is liberation; this is the meaning. || 12 ||
In the physical body, mental anguish and physical disease sometimes arise separately, sometimes simultaneously, and sometimes in alternation.

Because they are mutually caused by one another, they occur in a continuous sequence; sometimes they arise simultaneously due to external causes, occurring together at once; and sometimes they occur alternately, being intervened by pleasure. || 13 ||

They know physical suffering to be disease, which is called mental distress and consists of latent impressions; for they should understand that its root is ignorance, and it is destroyed through the knowledge of reality. (14)
Folly is ignorance; it is rooted in that [ignorance]. || 14 ||

Due to the power of ignorance regarding reality, without the subduing of one's own senses, and having abandoned the attenuation [of the mind] within the heart, [one remains] incessantly in passion and hatred. (15)

In that regard, he states the causes for the arising of [these] afflictions: "through the lack of knowledge of reality" (atattvajñāna), etc. "Assault" (ākramaṇa) means restraint; the meaning is "in its absence.

"In the heart" (hṛdi)—that is, in the mind—one abandons "tenuity" (tānava), which is a state of subtlety that serves as the cause of well-being and consists primarily of still air; this is because of attachment to passion and hatred. This is the ellipsis to be supplied. || 15 ||
"‘This has been obtained’ or ‘this has not’—from such dullness or dense delusion, mental agonies arise like mist in the rainy season. (16)

The phrase "of the thought" (*cintāyāḥ*) is to be supplied as the object of the sentence, meaning "of the thought that 'this has been attained' or 'this has not been attained'. They are called "givers of dense delusion" (*ghanamohadāḥ*) because, upon the occurrence of causes for fear and grief, they bestow a thick delusion characterized by the lack of knowledge regarding the means to counteract them. || 16 ||
When desires throb violently and the mind has not been conquered by folly, it is through the consumption of improper food and by wandering into improper regions. (17)

Now he states the causes for the arising of physical diseases with the verse beginning "excessively" (*bhṛśam*), and so forth. Desire and ignorance are internal causes; however, bad food and the like are external. Bad locations refer to places such as cremation grounds. (17)
Through the conduct of an evil age, through the manifestation of wicked deeds, through the fault of association with the base, and through the provocation of evil thoughts; || 18 ||
[One should avoid] wicked people by engaging in activities such as eating and sexual intercourse during times such as midnight or the onset of evening;
and [one should avoid] evil intentions by not giving rise to suspicions of poison, snakes, tigers, thieves, and so forth in their minds. (18)

Due to the depletion or the fullness of the channels and their network of apertures, when the vital breath (prāṇa) has fallen into disorder and the body has been rendered impaired, [the soul departs]. || 19 ||

When [the body] has become impaired—either due to depletion from the non-entry of food and fluids into the channels, or due to being overfilled by the entry of double the amount of fluids, wind, and so forth;
or when it has been rendered disordered and agitated by the provocation of phlegm, bile, and other humors, or by injury and the like. || 19 ||
Due to faults, disease arises in the body as the cause of a miserable state,
just as the alteration of a river's form occurs due to the rainy season and the summer heat.
Dauḥsthitya is ill-being, its cause is disease, which is the alteration of the body's form. || 20 ||
Whether it be from a previous life or this one, whether auspicious or inauspicious, whichever cognition is predominant, that very one engages [the person] in that manner within the sequence.
And he says—“prāktanī” (arising from the past)—to show that this collection of mental and physical afflictions comes together in accordance with previous and present karma. || 21 ||
In this way, mental afflictions and physical diseases arise within the five elements;
hear now, O upholder of the Raghu lineage, how they are destroyed.
In this world, there are two kinds of disease: the common and the essential.
The common is that which pertains to worldly affairs, while the essential is said to consist of birth. (23)

It is common, fragile, yet substantial and more firm. It is called "vyavahāra" because it is that which is transacted; it consists of hunger, thirst, longing for women and children, and so forth, as well as their arising. It is composed of birth, being the root of transformations such as birth and the rest. || 23 ||
Worldly concerns perish simply by obtaining what is desired;
mental afflictions are destroyed by the exhaustion of those very afflictions, and even physical diseases are likewise thoroughly subdued.
By means of desired food, drink, women, sons, and so forth. || 24 ||
O Raghava, without the knowledge of the Self, the essence does not perish;
for indeed, by the realization that it is a rope, the snake in the rope vanishes. (25)

Mental anguish and physical disease arise repeatedly from the constant habituation of the world, until there is an awakening that culminates in the realization of the true nature of the rope [behind the illusion of the snake].
O Rāma, the destruction of the essence of mental anguish and physical disease is the eradicator of the root of them all, just as a river in the rainy season destroys the shrubs on its banks. (25–26)

Just as a river in the rainy season [destroys] all the creepers on its banks, so too the destruction of the core disease is the destroyer of the root, the uprooter of all the manifestations of mental anguish and physical illness; such is the connection [of the verse]. || 26 ||

However, diseases not born of mental afflictions are destroyed here either by means of substances, mantras, and auspicious rituals as prescribed in medical treatises and other sciences, or by other methods.
With the intention that non-mental diseases among common ailments are easily curable, he says: "non-mental" (anādhijā).
[They are cured] by treatments taught through the tradition of other elders. || 27 ||
The bathing rites, mantras, medicinal remedies, and the methods of the teacher—all these medical treatises have been mastered by you; what else remains to be taught? (28)

"Bathing at holy sites such as Lolārka; mantras, medicinal herbs, and other such means—[it is understood that] you already know these medicinal herbs and medical treatises acquired from your elders. Śrī Rāma said:
How does disease arise from a latent affliction, and how is it destroyed by means other than physical substances—namely, through methods such as mantras and medicinal herbs? (29)
Rāma asks about the manner in which afflictions (ādhi) give rise to diseases (vyādhi) and the means for their medical treatment, beginning with the word "ādheḥ.
The phrase "by means other than substances such as medicines" refers to methods such as mantras and merit, stated according to his own estimation. || 29 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
When the mind is agitated, the body undergoes extreme turmoil;
for instance, a person who is enraged does not even see what is right before him.

Therein, he first describes the manner of its arising with the words beginning "In the mind" (*citte*). "Afflicted" (*vidhurite*) means agitated by mental disturbances (*ādhibhiḥ*). He establishes the stated point through an illustration with the verse beginning "For instance" (*tathā hi*), consisting of one and a half verses. "The front" (*agram*) refers to the path ahead. || 30 ||
Without looking at the path ahead,
he runs off-course like a deer afflicted by an arrow that has left the natural track.
Due to agitation, the vital breaths abandon their equilibrium and flow [unsteadily] within the body,
like waters on a riverbank when an elephant has entered it.

In the case of the illustration as well, it is exactly the same: due to the agitation caused by the subject under discussion, the vital breaths (prāṇavāyu) abandon their equilibrium and flow through an improper path.
Just as the waters of a river on its bank, agitated by the entry of an elephant, flow out of their course, so it is here. || 32 ||
When the vital breath flows unevenly, the channels fall into disorder, just as the stages of the social orders and disciplines collapse when the body is improperly constituted. (33)
"Uneven" means irregular; "distortion" refers to an irregular configuration caused by being filled with phlegm, bile, and so forth. || 33 ||
Some channels reach fullness while others become empty,
throughout the body when it is deprived of vital breath, like rivers in every direction.

He says that very thing with the words "kāścit" (some): when the body is deprived of its vital breaths and rendered utterly overwhelmed on all sides, the channels (*saritaḥ*)—meaning the nerves (*nāḍyaḥ*)—are like streams (*srotāṃsi*). || 34 ||
Whether it be under-digestion, indigestion, or even over-digestion,
food leads only to harm due to the improper movement of the vital breaths.
Just as the current of a river carries logs toward the eastern region,
so the internal vital air (prāṇavāta) carries food to its own seat.
The vital air called *samāna* carries all the food that has been consumed throughout its entire abode, the whole body, having transformed it into nutrient essence (*rasa*).
The meaning is that this *samāna* is indeed in the middle, for according to the Vedic scripture, "it carries the offered food equally. (36)
Those foods which remain within the body through the process of digestion, they indeed become diseased by the very nature of their transformation. || 37 ||
By virtue of the nature of the transformation resulting from the disharmony of the elements. || 37 ||
In this way, disease arises from mental affliction (ādhi), and in its absence, it perishes.
Listen now to that method by which diseases are destroyed through mantras. || 38 ||
He summarizes with the word "thus": because of non-existence, that is, destruction. || 38 ||
Just as myrobalan fruits cause purgation by their very nature, so too do the letters ya, ra, la, va, and others perform their function through the power of mental cultivation (bhāvanā). // 39 //

The fruits of the *harītakī* are called *harītakyaḥ*. Due to the rule that "in the case of the elision of the suffix *phal*, there is no application of the masculine form for number in the case of *harītakī* and similar words," the masculine gender does not apply to the plural. Likewise, the mantra-syllables such as *ya-ra-la-va*, which consist of the seeds of air, fire, earth, and water, [reside] within the channels (*nāḍī*) by virtue of the practitioner's meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
The meaning is that they perform functions such as extracting and digesting the essences of food that have been transformed into the form of diseases. || 39 ||
O virtuous one, through pure and meritorious action and service to the holy, the mind attains clarity, just as gold does upon a touchstone. (40)
He states the means for the pacification of the afflictions with the verse beginning "By purity," etc. (40).
O Rāghava, when the mind is pure, bliss increases within the body, just as clarity prevails in the world when the full moon has risen. (41)
Through the purification of the *sattva*, these vital breaths (*prāṇavāyu*) flow in their proper sequence; likewise, they digest the foods, and by that means, disease is destroyed. (42)
The sequences of the destruction of mental and physical ailments and their subsequent arising have been declared to you;
now, through the discourse on Kuṇḍalinī, hear that which is relevant to the present subject. (43)
Having concluded the incidental discussion of questions and answers, he introduces the examination of the cause for establishing the subject at hand:
"Know that Kuṇḍalinī, who is called 'Prāṇa' (the vital breath), belongs to the individual soul (jīva) known as the 'puryaṣṭaka'; she is like a flower-cluster within the fragrance. (44)
[She is] the support for the individual soul (jīva), which is the subtle body (liṅga) known as the "eightfold city" (puryaṣṭaka). || 44 ||
When one remains in equilibrium after filling [the body] through the practice of inhalation (pūraka),
then the stability of Meru is attained, as well as the swelling of the body.
The meaning is that one should fill [the body] and arrest the vital breath (*prāṇa*) within the tortoise-channel (*kūrmanāḍī*). Accordingly, there is the *sūtra* of Patañjali:

"Stability [is attained] through the tortoise-channel" (*kūrmanāḍyāṃ sthairyam*). Regarding this, his *bhāṣya* states: "Below the pit of the throat, in the chest, there is a channel shaped like a tortoise;
by practicing restraint (*saṃyama*) upon it, one attains stability, just like a snake or a lizard. [The result is] the swelling of the body.
The meaning is that the siddhi known as Garimā likewise succeeds in such a manner, becoming Bhairavī. || 45 ||
When the vital breath (prāṇa), drawn inward and filled by inhalation (pūraka), is led upward by consciousness itself to endure the exhaustion and fatigue of heat; || 46 ||

By what means, then, is the accomplishment of ascending through the sky achieved? He explains this with the words beginning with "yadā" (when). When, by means of inhalation (*pūraka*), the vital air (*prāṇamāruta*)—having been drawn upward, lengthened from the *mūlādhāra* at the base of the body up to the *brahmarandhra*, and having been extended along the path within the body—is [held] in such a manner that consciousness (*saṃvit*) [is likewise directed], then [the result follows].

The Kuṇḍalinī is led upward so that, through proficiency in practice and by means of the immersion in nectar, it may render bearable the heat arising from the restraint of the vital breath (prāṇa), as well as the resulting physical exhaustion and mental fatigue.
Like a serpent, it moves swiftly upward, having assumed the likeness of a staff;
taking up all the channels that bind the body like creepers, it ascends. (47)

And as she is being led upward, having attained a length comparable to a staff due to that drawing up, she moves swiftly upward like a snake because of her proficiency in practice. To explain how she moves, he says: "the channels" (nāḍīḥ). || 47 ||
Then this entire body is completely filled with water, like a leather bellows filled tightly with air and its interior expanded. (48)
Then, this entire body— from the feet to the head— having attained lightness and being filled with air through the channels so as to be without gaps or empty space,
its interior is stretched and pervaded, like a leather bellows being drawn upward from a well.
Just as one might cause water to float upwards, it causes [the body] to fly up; that is the meaning of his "traveling through space. || 48 ||
Thus, through yoga that moves through the sky by the grace of practice,
yogins attain the highest state, just as the wretched [gods] attained the status of Indra.
