Thus, by means of such a playful practice of yoga characterized by *saṃyama* on the connection between the body and space; and accordingly, there is the aphorism of the venerable Patañjali: "From *saṃyama* on the connection between the body and space, and from mastery (*samāpatti*) over lightness like that of cotton, there is movement through space," as well as its commentary where—

The body is space; the connection of the body with that [space] is its acquisition. Having practiced *saṃyama* upon that, the yogi, having conquered that connection, attains meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) in light things such as cotton down, starting from gross objects down to the subtle atoms. Having conquered the connection and become light, he moves through water on his feet due to that lightness; then, having moved upon a mere spider’s thread, he moves upon the rays of light.
From that, he dwells as he desires, and his movement becomes like that of space. || 49 ||
When the Kuṇḍalinī energy, through the flow of the Brahma-nāḍī, moves outward above the skull-door at a distance of twelve finger-breadths; || 50 ||

Now he describes the means for the vision of the Siddhas, beginning with the words "the Brahma-nāḍī": when the Kuṇḍalinī power is drawn upward by the practice of exhalation (recaka), it enters the Brahma-nāḍī— that is, the Suṣumnā—
along with the flow of the vital breath (prāṇa) into its interior, [reaching] the door characterized by the junction of the two skull-halves.

When one attains stability for even a moment in the place called the "sixteen-finger limit" (ṣoḍaśānta), located twelve finger-breadths outside the crown of the head, then there occurs the vision of the sky-going Siddhas; this is how it connects with what follows. And likewise is the sūtra of the venerable Patañjali: "In the light at the crown of the head, there is the vision of the Siddhas. And its commentary [states] regarding the skull of the head:
The aperture within is luminous; by practicing *saṃyama* upon that light, there arises the vision of perfected beings (*siddhas*) who move in the space between heaven and earth. || 50 ||
By means of the practice of exhalation (recaka), which restrains the other channels, one attains stability for a moment; then, there is the vision of the sky-dweller.
Śrī Rāma said:
O Brahman, what kind of vision can there be without the multitude of rays from the eyes?
How could the true nature of non-divine sense organs be such as you have described?
The two genitive cases in "of the divine senses" (*ādivyānām indriyāṇām*) are used respectively in the sense of a characteristic (*bhāvalakṣaṇe*) and in the sense of disregard (*anādare*).

When, for those like us whose senses are non-divine, the reality— that is, the state of being within the range— of perfected beings (*siddhas*) is difficult to attain even when there is contact with them, then [how much more so] without the mass of rays from the eyes, that is, without the contact of visual light?
The meaning is: how does the vision of the Siddhas occur merely by holding the breath at the end of the sixteen [fingers], and what is that like? || 52 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
O mighty-armed one, no beings moving upon the earth are perceived by the senses of men through their worldly knowledge, unless they are celestial beings. (53)

Regarding the question of how that could be so, Vasiṣṭha answers by conceding the point with the words "not at all. The meaning is: it is indeed true, as you have said, that those who have become like the wind (nabhasvantaḥ), having attained perfection through impure knowledge, human faculties, or other non-divine means, are not seen. Thus, he refutes the objection by accepting its premise. 53.
O Rāghava, by means of the eye of the intellect situated far beyond ordinary consciousness,
the perfected beings (siddhas) moving through the sky are seen, bestowing their own purposes just like dreams.
By what means, then, are they seen? To this he says: "From consciousness"—that is, from one whose mind has been refined by the practice of yoga through consciousness. (54)
The vision of the perfected ones (siddhas) is just like the observation of a dream;
however, this is the sole distinction: that upon attaining the perfected state, there is stability of purpose.

He provides the answer to the portion of the question "of what kind? with the words: "the vision of dreams. The meaning is that the distinction [of this state] from a dream consists in its stability—the quality of having a reality capable of supporting worldly transactions such as corroboration, the attainment of boons, and the acquisition of fruits.
[This occurs] through the practice of exhalation (*recaka*) from the mouth out to the *dvādaśānta*.
When the vital breath has been made to remain for a long time, it enters the next city.

Now he explains the means by which entry into another's body is accomplished, beginning with the words "from the mouth": "at the *dvādaśānta*, at the limit measuring twelve finger-breadths [above the head]. (56)
Śrī Rāma said:
"O Brahmin, tell me how the nature of things possesses such immovable stability;
for compassionate speakers do not feel weary even when asked a difficult question. (57)

Regarding what was stated—that this "stability of the object" (*sthirārthatā*) constitutes the excellence (*viśeṣa*) in attaining perfection—therein the very nature (*svabhāva*) must be cited as the cause.

Since the entire world consists of illusion (*māyāmaya*), its lack of fixed stability has been demonstrated by you yourself many times previously through such examples as "the state of a cloth being seen in a jar. In that case, Rāma, how can there be a fixed stability for a single nature?
He asks: "Speak! || 57 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
It is certain that the power known as inherent nature (svabhāva), which manifests from the Self during creation and so forth, likewise attains the state of maintenance. 58.

With the intention that even the determination of the nature of things, which is impelled by the will of the Lord whose volitions are true, exists only for as long as the period of creation and does not exist during dissolution—and thus there is no contradiction with the doctrine that all determinations cease—Vasiṣṭha, reminding us of what was stated previously, gives the following reply: "Power," etc. (verse 58).
Because ignorance is not a real entity, its power over objects may sometimes be differentiated; for indeed, my dear, autumnal fruit is seen [to appear] in the springtime.
Since it is observed that the power of an entity is not restricted even by difference of place, just as by difference of time, he says: "Because of its non-substantiality" (avastutvāt).
In certain places, such as the land of Kāmarūpa, the fruit of rice and other crops is autumnal. || 59 ||
All this is indeed Brahman, existing through both diversity and non-diversity;
it unfolds for the sake of worldly transaction, its state being merely described as such.

All this is indeed Brahman, existing through a state of both diversity and non-diversity, and by virtue of having an indeterminate nature. The meaning is that Brahman is fixed in a single form solely by its own nature, and not by anything else. To the question, "How then is there the fixed rule regarding fire rising upward and so forth? he says: "It unfolds" (jṛmbhate).

The meaning is that Brahman itself, while remaining unknown, expands in various ways for a certain period of time, having become established in such a state, for the sake of the worldly transaction consisting of living beings, their karma, and the experience of its fruits. || 60 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
How is this body brought to either minuteness or bulkiness, for the purpose of passing through subtle apertures and the like, or for the purpose of filling up space? (61)
Now Rāma asks by what means the supernatural powers known as *aṇiman* (minuteness) and *mahiman* (magnitude) are accomplished—
[to which] Śrī Vasiṣṭha replied: "Just as a cut proceeds from the joining of wood and a saw..."
In the same way, fire is produced from its own nature through the friction of two [sticks]. || 62 ||

Intending to explain the answer to this question in detail in the subsequent chapter, and wishing first to establish the pervasion of Agni and Soma within the body as an introductory premise, he provides an illustration regarding the production of the digestive fire (*jāṭharāgni*) in the interval resulting from the friction between *prāṇa* and *apāna*:
"Like wood... (*kāṣṭha-iti*). "Cutting" (*cheda*) means being split into two parts; [this occurs] between the two, namely *prāṇa* and *apāna*.
The digestive fire is the gastric fire. || 62 ||
The flesh situated within the interior of the small machine (the body) has its ends joined together,
like reeds in deep water whose thick trunks meet from above and below.
He states the cause for their mutual attraction, which results in the friction of the *prāṇa* and *apāna*:

"A thick muscle [is located] above and below the navel, meeting there; for that very reason, its two openings are joined together, having the form of a pair of bellows consisting of the stomach (*āmāśaya*) and the large intestine (*pakvāśaya*)."

The meaning is that it remains trembling like a thicket of reeds being pulled in opposite directions— downward by water and upward by wind— characterized by parts situated in the sky above, resting in the atmosphere, and submerged in the water below, all of which are mutually joined together. 63.
His Kuṇḍalinī Lakṣmī was hidden within her own abode,
like a string of pearls inside a casket of rubies.

Let that be so; what follows from it? To this he says: "of that" (tasya). Of that flesh, in its own abode—the root-base (*mūlādhāra*) which is the lower part of the bellows—resides the previously mentioned Kuṇḍalinī.
She is *Lakṣmī* because she bestows life upon the entire aggregate of causes and effects. || 64 ||
Like a garland of whirlpool-fruit, it is constantly shimmering;
like a female serpent struck by a staff, it coils upward with rising undulations.

At the time of recitation (*japa*), like a rosary of rudrākṣa beads and other fruits being turned, it constantly and repeatedly vibrates with a soft rustling sound through the exhalation and inhalation of the *prāṇa* and *apāna* breaths, producing an indistinct noise due to its trembling.

The suffix *kyaṅ* is applied in the sense of "acting as" (karoti) after an indeclinable expressing imitation, by virtue of the rule allowing for the frequent use of such forms. Its "elevation" (*samunnati*) consists in its upward-facing orientation.
By that [nature], it is "vivartinī," meaning characterized by transformation. || 65 ||
Abiding between heaven and earth like the very act of vibration,
she is the sun that awakens the honey of consciousness, the bee within the hollow of the heart-lotus.

Like the performance of prescribed and prohibited actions, which is the cause of the upward and downward movement of living beings between heaven and earth, she possesses the nature of vibration because she is the cause of the upward and downward movement of the prāṇa and apāna breaths; she stands like the sun for the awakening of the honey-like objects of perception, such as form and so forth, which are characterized by visual and other sensory experiences. 66.
All that— the power, the lotus, and so forth—
is shaken on all sides by her internal winds within the heart, like a cluster of leaves.

The "powers" (śaktayaḥ) refer to the powers of the organs of cognition and action, and so forth. The previously mentioned heart-lotus and, by the word "and so forth," the network of channels within the heart are shaken—that is, made to tremble—by the internal winds. The meaning is that it is just as a cluster of tree leaves is shaken by the external wind. || 67 ||
Just as, my dear, winds arise from the very nature of the sky and violently devour whatever there is— whether strong or weak, or anything at all— so it is here.

Just as the vast external sky naturally causes the winds to swallow, as it were, and over time to wear away strong wood, stones, earth, leaves, grass, and so forth, in the same way, the vital breaths (*prāṇavāyu*) within the internal sky digest the food and other things that have been eaten; this is the meaning. || 68 ||
Struck by the winds, that lotus and the rest tremble; through their own activity, they move here and there, just like the sprouts and other parts of a tree.

He describes the very process of digestion with the words "by the winds" (*vātaiḥ*). That previously mentioned heart-lotus, the channels, the bellows, and so forth, being struck and blown by the vital winds (*prāṇavātaiḥ*) like a blacksmith’s bellows, becomes agitated.
Of that [bellows] which is thus agitated, the first essence of the food that has entered within the heart arises; from that essence comes blood, and from blood, flesh.
From flesh comes skin, from skin fat, from fat marrow, from marrow bones, and from bones semen;

thus, through various effects, the transformation of one thing proceeds into another. The meaning is that it is just as when, in spring, the earthy sap absorbed within a tree results in sprouts, clusters, flowers, fruits, and so forth. || 69 ||
Every day within the bodies, the vital air (pavana) generates the digestive fire (agni) from all the fluids through mutual friction, like that between bamboo sticks in a forest.

In this regard, with the intention that the manifestation of the digestive fire (*jāṭharāgni*) occurs through mutual friction for the sake of achieving the successive transformation of all seven constituent elements (*dhātu*), he says: "In the bodies... The term *ājaraṇam* means until the final transformation of the last constituent element, by way of a continuous series of digestions (*jaraṇa*). || 70 ||
Then, by that [fire], whose nature is cool wind, his body attained heat;
it arose throughout all his limbs, just as the world is warmed by the risen sun.
That body attains heat through that digestive fire which has arisen and blazed up within all its limbs. || 71 ||
That splendor, shaped like a star, should be meditated upon by yogis as having entered the golden bee within the heart-lotus, moving everywhere therein. 72.

He says "from all sides" to explain that the digestive fire (jāṭharāgni), which pervades the entire body, is worshipped by yogis in the form of a star within the heart-lotus; [this occurs] in this body. || 72 ||
When that knowledge, consisting of light, is contemplated, it bestows [the power] by which an object situated even a hundred thousand yojanas away is indeed seen constantly. (73)

He says "That" (verse 73) to show that when that very [object] is contemplated as being of the nature of consciousness (cidrūpa), it produces the accomplishment of seeing all objects, even those that are obstructed or remote.
For that fire dwelling within the sheath of the heart-lake— rich with the lotus-clumps of flesh— the water has dried up like fuel for the submarine fire.

He states the fuel for that fire with the word "tasya" (of that). Just as the ocean water is the fuel for the submarine fire (*vāḍava*), so too for that digestive fire (*jāṭharāgni*) lying within the sheath of the heart-lake—which is rich with clusters of lotuses characterized by their fleshy parts—the bodily water in the form of the essence of food (*annarasa*) is the fuel, meaning it is dried up and thus fit for combustion. || 74 ||
That which is clear and cool is called its "self-moon";
thus, that fire has arisen from the moon, for the body consists of both Agni and Soma.
Having distinguished the portion of the moon that serves as fuel within the body by means of its characteristics, he explains the body's nature as consisting of fire and moon:
"They know all that is of the nature of heat to be designated as the sun and fire, while that which is of the nature of cold is called the moon; by these two alone is the world created. (76)
He states that even externally, the world should be known as consisting of Agni and Soma by means of light and heat, as well as cold and inertia—thus: "All," etc. (verse 76).
By means of that very [consciousness] by which the entire world— consisting of both the existent and the non-existent— is produced in the form of knowledge and ignorance, it is thus divided.
Alternatively, it is Brahman itself—composed of both consciousness and inertia, consisting of both being and non-being, and variegated by ignorance—that has manifested in the form of the world;
thus, it is that very same [Brahman] which is divided into the forms of Agni and Soma as the nature of luminosity and inertia. He says:
"The wise know the light of consciousness, beginning with knowledge (*vidyā*), to be the Sun and the Fire."
The wise say that darkness consists of ignorance and the like, while the moon consists of non-attachment and clarity.
He explains that very division clearly with the words "consciousness" (saṃvit) and so forth. "Vidyā" refers to the manifestation of the reality of the Self;
by the word "and so forth" (ādipada), the manifestation of external objects is also included. || 78 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
O Lord of Sages, O best among speakers, you have stated that fire arises from the self of wind and from the moon;
now tell me, O foremost of those who speak, about the origin of the moon.

"Day after day, the wind within bodies causes the fire to arise from the mutual friction of all the bodily fluids, like that of bamboo in a forest. According to your statement, and because we observe both externally and within the body that the emergence and manifestation of fire, the sun, and so forth are dependent upon the wind, fire is of the nature of wind.
The phrase "I have realized that [the Self] rises from the *soma*" is the intended meaning; the remainder is clear. || 79 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Agni and Soma are established as mutual cause and effect;
in turn, these two sustain one another equally.
They live and seek victory by turns against one another. The absence of reduplication and the *kutva* change [of *jy* to *ji*] in the desiderative (*san*) is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*).
The lengthening [of the vowel] follows the rule *aj-jhan-gamām sani*. However, if the reading is *prajīvete*, the meaning is that they subsist upon one another. || 80 ||
Just as birth is to the body and the seed is to the sprout, and likewise as day is to night, their existence is like that of shadow and sunlight; it is merely the coexistence of these two. (81)

Of these two, like the seed and sprout of a plant, they are mutually constitutive; and like day and night, they are mutually instrumental. Their persistence, however, is like that of shadow and sunlight: it means they are mutually destructive. || 81 ||
The coexistence of shadow and sunlight occurs in this way because they are perceived at the same time;
their existence is characterized by the perception of only one [of them] at a time, like day and night.

He states another intended meaning for the presentation of the different examples: "tulya" (equal), etc. The meaning is that when there is simultaneous perception, the state of shadow and sunlight is the example; when there is successive perception, the state of day and night is the example. || 82 ||
And the causal relationship between these two is said to be of two kinds:
that which arises from transformation into an existent form, and that which arises from transformation into destruction. (83)

He states—“And the relation of cause and effect”—that even in the view that the two examples refer to the two types of causal relations, there is also an intention regarding the two further internal subdivisions. || 83 ||

That which arises from one as a second, like a sprout from a seed, is the relation of cause and effect; it is born from the transformation of that which has the nature of existence (sadrūpa). || 84 ||
He establishes the first of these two [positions] with the words: "From one," [verse 84].
When one perishes, the existence of the second occurs like day and night;
this is the relation of cause and effect, born from destruction and transformation. (85)
He establishes the second [point] with the words "eka" etc. "Bhāva" means origination. || 85 ||
Since the transformation into the form of an existent object— such as the sequence of clay and jar—
is perceived by the senses, no other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is required.

Regarding the first [point], that the cause exists during the state of the effect, he states that perception—such as "this jar is of the nature of clay"—is the proof. Although inference and other means of knowledge are also possible, they are not sought after when an object is already established by perception; thus, there is a statement regarding their lack of utility. As it is said in the *Nyāyavācaspatya*: "For indeed..."

When an elephant is seen, those who measure it infer its existence by means of its trumpeting; the intention [of the author] is that, due to the presence of the established entity (siddhi), the cause consisting of the state of being a subject (pakṣatā) is absent. || 86 ||

Even the non-existence of the sequence of day and night, which constitutes the transformation of destruction, has attained the status of a primary means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) when residing in a single entity. (87)

Thus, even in the second case, regarding the state of the effect while the cause is absent, he states that non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), saying "vināśa... (destruction). [This] resides in a single object and is not contradicted by perception (*pratyakṣa*) which grasps only that single object.
Those who argue through fallacious reasoning that there is no attachment and no agency, and who deny their own direct experience, should be cast out with contempt. 88.

Now, is it not the case that a cause is so called because it performs an effect? And that agency of the cause is observed only when there is an underlying persistence (*āsthā*) characterized by attachment to that [effect]. However, for the day, which is exhausted merely by its manifestation, there is no persistence toward the production of the night; thus, it possesses no agency. The same applies to the night regarding the production of the day.

The causal relationship is stainless through the transformation of non-existence, in the sense that "it does not exist. Thus, it is impossible for an insentient entity such as clay to have an inclination toward the production of a jar and so forth, because such an inclination is a property of consciousness. Furthermore, a jar is not produced from a lump of clay without its destruction; rather, when the lump of clay is destroyed, [the jar arises].

Since it surely perishes, how could it transform into the form of an existent entity? Furthermore, there exists no third thing called "clay" there that is distinct from both the lump and the jar and yet common to both. Moreover, would the seed and so forth—whether existing, about to perish, currently perishing, or already perished—produce the sprout? Not the first, because that would entail the consequence [of production] even in cases such as a granary. Nor the second or third, because at those times...

What logic can there be in saying that something which is incapable of protecting itself is capable of producing another? As for the fourth alternative, it is contradicted by everyone’s experience; therefore, nothing arises from anything, nor does anything perish [from anything], but rather everything arises and perishes solely by its own nature (*svabhāvataḥ*). In this regard, due to the observation of temporal sequence (*paurvāparya*), those lacking discrimination— [The text continues: ...regard the preceding as the cause and the subsequent as the effect. However, since the distinction between the two is not perceived, the relationship of cause and effect is merely a mental construction (*kalpanāmātra*). Furthermore, because the prior entity is not perceived at the time of the subsequent one, and because the subsequent entity is not perceived at the time of the prior one, there is no causal relation whatsoever. Thus, all things arise and perish spontaneously, like the flame of a lamp or the ripples on water. Therefore, the world is devoid of a creator; it is beginningless and endless, and its nature is that of momentary existence (*kṣaṇikatva*). This is established by both direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*). For instance, the cognition of a jar is momentary because it is a cognition, just like the cognition of a lamp-flame. Moreover, if a thing were eternal, it would either have to exist always or never exist at all, because a permanent entity cannot undergo change. Since we observe change, it follows that all things are impermanent. Thus, the doctrine of momentariness is proven. Furthermore, since the self (*ātman*) is not perceived by any means of valid cognition, it does not exist. Consequently, there is no transmigrating agent; rather, the stream of consciousness (*vijñānasaṃtāna*) alone proceeds, driven by the force of karma and afflictions (*kleśa*). Through the cultivation of the path, when these are exhausted, the stream is severed, and one attains liberation (*mokṣa*), which is the cessation of all suffering. This is the ultimate truth. Those who propound such fallacious arguments as "the alternatives regarding the nature of cause and effect" are to be refuted simply by pointing out their contradiction with their own experience;

thus he says, "without hope. Such and other [arguments] are "fallacious arguments" (*duryukti*); those who propound them are "proponents of fallacious arguments. With contempt—that is, with disdain—one should describe their denial of their own experience in this manner:

If the cognition characterized by detachment and so forth produces the cognition of non-agency and so forth, then the causal relationship between those two is established for you through experience; how then can you deny that general principle? If it does not produce it, then your presentation of reasonings with the desire to instruct others—while you yourself possess such an experience—is in contradiction with your own experience.

Regarding the term "pralāpa" (nonsense): in this way, night also is established by one's own experience as the cause of the day through a transformation into non-existence (*abhāvapariṇāma*), which consists of the final modification of existence (*bhāvavikāra*). Nor is destruction not a modification of existence; for it is experienced as a property of existence (*bhāvadharma*), just like origination and the rest. Thus, [it is] that which persists through states such as the seed and the sprout...

Substance (*dravya*), too, established by the experience of uncontradicted recognition, is not fit to be denied. That very [substance], remaining as it is, experiences within its own self the various states—such as "about to perish," "perishing," and "perished"—and thus is the cause of the sprout and so forth, and not [the cause] of the differences among those states; therefore, there is no difference in substance among them.

The meaning is that fools who prattle on about [theories] such as causelessness and the like—which are devoid of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and seized by excessive arrogance—should be excluded with utter contempt. || 88 ||
O descendant of Raghu, even non-existence is indeed valid knowledge, just like direct perception;
for all living beings, the absence of fire is a means of valid cognition regarding cold. (89)

He removes the doubt regarding the validity of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) by stating "just like perception" (*pratyakṣavat*). It is indeed a valid cognition (*pramā*), and indeed a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). One should not be deluded into thinking that the status of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*) is never observed in the case of absence (*abhāva*) elsewhere; for it is well known that the absence of light (*tejo'bhāva*) functions as an instrument by way of being a logical mark (*liṅga*) in the inference of cold. Thus he says: "the absence of fire" (*agnyabhāva*). || 89 ||
Fire, through its state as smoke, goes toward the sky and attains the nature of clouds;
by means of this transformation of its true form, that fire becomes the cause of the moon.
He illustrates how fire serves as the cause of the moon through a transformation into the form of existence (sadrūpapariṇāma) outside of fire itself—namely, "fire" and so forth. That [is] there. 90.

"By its state of disappearance, or by its coldness, that very fire indeed goes to the state of wind"—this is the reading; however, in the root text where it reads "by its state of disappearance" (*agnirnaṣṭatayā*), it should be understood that the phrase "to the state of wind" (*vāyubhāvam*) is supplied by ellipsis.
By its coldness, that very [fire] proceeds to that [state].
Through the transformation of destruction, that fire becomes the cause of the moon.
He illustrates that [transformation] even through the transformation into non-existence with the word "fire": this fire, when it attains the state of wind;
for according to the Vedic scripture, "When fire goes out, it enters into the wind alone. (91)
Having drunk the waters of the seven oceans, the submarine fire (Vāḍava) produces that very same water in abundance through its emission of smoke, which has assumed the form of clouds.
He illustrates the mutual causality of Agni and Soma through their transformation into similar forms with the verse beginning "Seven," and so forth.
The submarine fire (Vāḍava), having itself assumed the state of clouds, produces the waters of those seven oceans by its very own nature.
Since milk, curd, clarified butter, and the like are also of the nature of Soma as essence (rasa), the term "water" (payas) applies to them all. || 92 ||
Having drunk the lord of the night again and again on the new moon day,
the sun vomits it forth during the bright fortnight, just as a crane spits out a lotus stalk.

"Āmāvāsya" means "until the new moon. In the compound *āmāvāsyam*, the term is an avyayībhāva according to the rule *āṅ maryādābhividhyoḥ*, and the neuter short vowel is applied. The meaning is "up to the new moon in the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*). "Amale" refers to the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*). || 93 ||
Having drunk the cool nectar-like soma at the onset of the breath, the vital force (prāṇa),
having become full, fills the body upon the arrival of the clouds.

When the spring and summer seasons arrive—which are like the moon shining as the very face [of the year]—the vital breath (*prāṇa*), possessing heat, drinks the terrestrial water; then, upon the arrival of the clouds in the rainy season, having attained fullness through that [water], it fills the body of the world once again with rain. Alternatively, the *prāṇa* is purely internal, belonging to the *soma*, which is the *apāna*.

When food, drink, and so forth enter the stomach from the mouth, one drinks that essence which is like nectar and, having become full, fills and nourishes the body by its passage through the network of all the channels, pervading them like a cloud. This indeed is his further transformation as soma; thus [it is said]: "He desired to grasp that with the out-breath (apāna); he grasped it; this is the grasping of food."

This is the sense of the scriptural statement (*śruti*). However, according to the reading "somaṃ sukhāgame," the vital breath (*prāṇa*), having become fire, drinks the cool, nectar-like Soma juice at the sacrifice; then, at the arrival of happiness—namely heaven—it reaches the moon upon arriving at the lunar orb via the path characterized by the stages beginning with smoke (*dhūma*) and ending with the "cloud" (*abhra*), which is the intermediate stage of the sky situated near the moon.

Having attained that state, he fills his own body with its constituent parts (*kalā*); this very process constitutes his fullness on the day of the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*), which means it is once again the transformation of the Soma. The path beginning with smoke and the attainment of the lunar state have been shown by the Śruti itself: "Now, those here who worship sacrifice, merit, and charity as 'this' [the world], they pass into the smoke."

From smoke they go to the night; from the night to the waning half of the month; from the waning half of the month to those six months when the sun moves southward. These reach the year. From the months they go to the world of the fathers;
from the world of the fathers to space; from space to the moon. That is King Soma, the food of the gods.
And in the knowledge of the five fires (*pañcāgnividyā*), it is said: "In this very fire, the gods offer faith; from that oblation, King Soma arises. (94)
Even water, through its experience of becoming the waters of the clouds, attains the state of the sun’s rays;
by that transformation of its true form, that water becomes the cause of fire.
If you think that it is not the wind that dries up the moisture of the earth, but rather the sun’s rays themselves drink it up—

because they exist even at night in the form of heat— then, with the intention that those very rays are the example, he says: [the water] goes to the state of being rays through a transformation of its own nature, because the persistence of water is observed there in the form of whiteness.
The meaning is that this is based on the Vedic scripture which states: "That which is the red form of the sun is the form of fire; that which is white is [the form] of water. (95)
For water attains the state of fire through its nature of destruction, due to its heat;
by means of the transformation of destruction, that water becomes the cause of fire. (96)

However, since in that case there is the destruction of coldness and fluidity and the emergence of heat and dryness, there is also transformation through destruction in that respect; thus he says, "by way of having the nature of destruction," [presenting] this as a mixed example. || 96 ||
Upon the destruction of fire, the moon is the transformation of its true nature;
upon the destruction of the moon, fire is the transformation of its true nature. (97)

With the intention that, in every transformation consisting of the nature of Agni and Soma, even the intermingling of both forms can be perceived by one with subtle vision, he says [the following] in two verses beginning with "Of fire" (97).
Just as fire, having met its destruction, becomes the moon, and just as the day, having met its destruction, becomes the night; || 98 ||
Between darkness and light, shadow and sunshine, and day and night, a distinct form in the middle cannot be found even by the wise.

If it is asked: "In that case, what is the underlying form common to darkness and light, or to shadow and sunlight, by virtue of which they could be transformations of the nature of Being (*sadrūpa*)?"—the answer is: That is Brahman itself. And yet, even by those who possess supreme knowledge, it cannot be grasped by pointing directly (like seizing a horn). Thus he says: "Darkness... [and so on]. It is the underlying [reality] in the midst [of these], distinct from and different in character from both the excluded darkness and light.

It has the form of pure existence (*sanmātra*). Alternatively, it is distinct from both at the junction in the middle. The suffix at the end of the compound *dinarātrayoḥ* is Vedic (*chāndasa*). || 99 ||
The junction (saṃdhi) as well would be non-contradictory, for its very nature consists of these two alone;
indeed, just as existence and non-existence are both established in a single locus, so too are these two.

Now, one might object that the junction (*saṃdhi*) between darkness and light consists in the disappearance of both, being of the nature of a void (*śūnya*); thus, there would be no form there at all that is distinct from both. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The junction. Even the junction of these two must be non-disappearance (*avalopa*), that is, not of the nature of a void; for the nature of their junction is the very form of these two themselves, joined together with one another.

For there is no such thing as a "junction" (saṃdhi) between two things that are empty, nor is emptiness something that exists for those who are signless (nirnimitta). If it is asked, "How then do those two exist at the junction? [the answer is: it is like existence and non-existence in the prior and subsequent moments. The plural number is used because of the abundance of examples. [They exist] by way of their nature as entities when analyzed independently of one another.
Through its definition as being relative and its nature as an absence, this darkness is a single entity consisting solely of the absence of light;
and this light, too, is a single entity consisting solely of the absence of darkness. Because this is the experience of everyone, these two remain established in a state of mutual dependence;
for they exist in that very way even during the transition [between day and night]. The meaning is that they do not differ by even an atom's worth. || 100 ||
Indeed, all beings manifest through the two qualities of consciousness and inertia, just as day and night appear upon the earth through darkness and light. (101)
This existence of the world is commenced from both the nature of consciousness and the nature of insentience, like the cool body of a river formed by the mixture of water and nectar. 102.

Just as days and nights are composed of the mutually opposed light and darkness, so too all worldly transactions are composed of both consciousness and the insentient; thus he says, "of the nature of consciousness" (*cidrūpa*). Like the lunar body, which is produced from both [the sun and the moon] through the gradual filling of the watery reflection by the nectar-like digits residing in the solar orb via the rays of the sun.
O Rāghava, know that the luminous fire and the sun are of the nature of consciousness;
know that which is insentient by nature and of the form of darkness is the body of Soma.

He states that the world consists of the nature of Agni and Soma because it has manifested as both light and non-light through these two very aspects of consciousness and inertia—namely, "light" and so forth. || 103 ||
When the stainless sun of consciousness is seen, the arising of worldly existence perishes,
just as the darkness of a black night vanishes when the sun is seen in the sky outside.

Just as external darkness ceases with the rising of the sun, so too does the fundamental darkness of the world cease through the rising of the sun of consciousness (cid-āditya) by means of the final mental modification (carama-vṛtti); thus he says: "In the sun of consciousness" (citsūrye). That darkness from which the arising of existence (bhava-udaya) occurs is the darkness [that is dispelled]. // 104 //
When the inert body is perceived, one's own consciousness appears as if real, just as the mass of the sun's radiance appears in a lotus blooming at midnight. || 105 ||

When one's own inner self—the inert lunar body—is perceived, even though the [intellect] shines forth through identity with that [body], it appears as if it has acquired the quality of being a mental attribute (*cittadguṇatva*).
Having become existent only by the existence of that [body], as if possessing other qualities, it becomes as if non-existent by its own existence.
Just as at midnight, when the moon shines upon a lotus, [a reflection] shines by entering into it.

The meaning is this: when the mass of solar radiance, having become the moonlight of the moon's nature, appears as if existent through the existence of the moon, yet becomes as if non-existent through its own [independent] existence—since it is experienced by all people that at that time "the mass of solar radiance does not exist"—then [the former is sublated]. || 105 ||
Fire reveals the Soma, which is the long-lasting radiance of the body of consciousness;
the Moon consists of one's own self-awareness, while the form born of the Sun resides within that body of consciousness.
He states the logical justification and the result for both the illustration and the illustrated case with the words "the moon" (*somam*).

Having entered the lunar orb, the fire in the form of the sun's radiance makes the moon—the watery lunar disc—manifest, rendering it radiant. But within the body, having entered as the nature of the individual soul (*jīva*), consciousness [makes] the body... for a long time.

"As long as he makes his renown through the greatness of his life-span, radiance, and so forth— just as the one sun illuminates this entire world, so too, O Bhārata, does the Knower of the Field illuminate the entire field"—
according to these words of the Blessed One. Thus, through mutual conjunction and the superimposition of identity, the solar form [arises].

The orb of light becomes the moon; and consciousness, consisting of its own self-awareness, becomes the form residing in the body according to one's own experience—such as "I am a man" or "I am sentient"—this is the logical connection. || 106 ||
But that consciousness, which is actionless and nameless, is not perceived in its absolute state;
it is apprehended only through the body, just as light is made known by a lamp.

For this reason as well, he says "cit" etc., to show that there is a delusion regarding her being subject to the nature of the body; "nāma" means an adjunct (upādhi) because it bends or contracts [the consciousness], and she is "devoid of that" (tacchūnyā). 107.
The mind’s acquisition [of objects] through its orientation toward the objectifiable is itself the cycle of existence (saṃsṛti);
the splendor of the mind when free from the objectifiable is indeed that very acquisition which is nirvāṇa. 108.

It is precisely because of the necessity of the manifestation of the intellect (citi), which is veiled by ignorance, being oriented toward the limiting adjuncts of the objects of thought (cetya) that the attainment of misfortune occurs; thus he says:
"Thus, these two—Fire and Moon—should be known as the body and the embodied soul, joined together like a wall and its light, having obtained their true status through mutual acquisition. (109)

In the manner thus described, these two—the body and the embodied soul—should also be understood as being of the nature of fire and moon, existing in a state of mutual interpenetration like the light of a wall and the sun, and thereby becoming the object of verbal designation. 109.
O limb, when there is an excess of nirvāṇa and an excess of inertia,
the state of Agni and Soma exists in its entirety.
Where is the unmixed, individual state of these two established? To this he says: "Excelling.

When liberation—defined as the manifestation of bliss through the cessation of limiting adjuncts—is established as something excelling, that is, absolute, there exists the exclusive state of fire. But when dullness is excelling, as in the case of water, stone, and so forth, there exists the exclusive state of soma.
The meaning is that stability comes about. || 110 ||
Prāṇa is fire, having heat as its nature, while apāna is the moon, being cool;
these two are situated like shade and sunlight, moving along the path of the mouth.
To remind us of what was previously stated—that the *prāṇa* and *apāna* breaths consist of the nature of Agni and Soma—for the sake of the present context, he says:
"The hot fire of *prāṇa* attains existence within the cool *apāna*, just as a reflection appears in a mirror; and it is exactly the same way that [the former] exists in the latter. (112)
He demonstrates the state of mutual identity between those two, like that of a wall and its light, in the verse beginning with "apāne" (112).

The fire of consciousness, by means of its radiance and through experience, generates here the moon consisting of speech situated upon the lotus-leaf, just as light outside produces the appearance of a wall.

The fire of consciousness (cidagni), whose form is the root-prāṇa-kuṇḍalinī, resides upon the petals of the lotuses located from the base (ādhāra) up to the throat, beginning with the four-petaled [lotus].

It consists of speech ranging from Parā down to Vaikharī. By its radiance—that is, by its power to illuminate objects—and by its experience—that is, by its manifestation in the form of the presentation of meaning when there is a desire to speak—it is like the sun externally; this is the implied sense. || 113 ||
Just as at the beginning of cyclic existence, a certain consciousness, consisting of the nature of cold and heat,
attained the designation of Agni and Soma, so too does that very same [consciousness] exist here in the creation of men.
The meaning is that just as at the beginning of creation, Brahman— variegated by *māyā* and consisting of consciousness in the form of cold and heat—
attained the designation of *agni* (fire) and *soma* (moon) in the form of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), so too does it occur at the creation of the individual bodies of men. || 114 ||
Wherein the sixteenth digit of the moon is swallowed by the sun for a moment,
and [the shadow] extends from the mouth a distance of one span (vitasti), there you should stand with feet firmly planted.
Let it be so that the body, like the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), consists of the nature of fire and moon (*agnīṣoma*); what is to be done with that? To this he says:

On the lunar days beginning with the first (*pratipad*), [the sun] gradually swallows [the digits] one by one, leaving behind only the digit called *dhruvā*, which is of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*).
Then, during the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*), it gradually emits heat; being filled by those [digits] in succession, the *dhruvā* digit becomes the full moon.

Thus, the solar *prāṇa* situated in the heart swallows the fifteen cool digits (*kalā*) of the lunar *apāna* that have entered through the mouth and nostrils; leaving behind only one digit called *dhruvā* outside the mouth, it then emits those [digits] as heat. Being filled by them, the lunar *apāna* is produced externally.

In that regard, the time of the junction between the external *prāṇa* and *apāna* is the full moon (*pūrṇamāsī*), while the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) is in the heart. Within the intermediate region, in the six subsidiary branch-nāḍīs of each of the *iḍā* and *piṅgalā*, due to the flow of the *prāṇa*-sun, there are two solstices (*ayana*), twelve months beginning with Aries, and the transits (*saṃkrānti*) in between. [Likewise] for the *apāna*-moon...

It is the direct perception of yogis that from this flow the months such as Caitra, the lunar days (yogas) such as Viṣkambha, and other festival days (parvan) are produced; by others, however, they are to be known from treatises such as the *Svarodaya*. This being the case, first, through three [verses], the various types of concentration (*dhāraṇā*) useful for the subtlety and grossness of the body to be described hereafter are presented.

These matters are taught in verses: where, in the external region outside the mouth, the sixteenth digit of the moon—the *apāna* known as *dhruvā*—which has been swallowed by the sun, is being replenished by the digits emitted by the *prāṇa*, and for a moment becomes the size of a span like the full-moon in the east; there [is that state].
The meaning is: become firm, having established your footing through mental concentration by means of the external *kumbhaka* (breath-retention) described in the *Bhuśuṇḍopākhyāna*. || 115 ||
Surely you have reached the state of the Sun, wherein the Moon resides within the sky of the heart;
surely, remain there with steadfast composure, having fixed your footing.

Likewise, in that expanse of the heart (*hṛdambara*), where the moon known as *apāna*— being gradually swallowed by the consumption of its digits (*kalā*)— remains on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) in a state consisting solely of the pure consciousness-natured digit called *dhruvā*, there you should fix your footing through internal retention (*antaḥ-kumbhaka*). 116.
Fire and the sun are said to be heat, while the moon is declared to be coldness;
wherever these two exist as reflections, there establish your firm footing.

Now, by means of either half-exhalation or half-inhalation, having brought about a state of identical form—like an object and its reflection—through the simultaneous restraint of the vital breath (prāṇa) at the interval, he describes the concentration (dhāraṇā) with the verse beginning "hot" (uṣṇam). || 117 ||
O sinless one, you are a knower of the transits of the Moon, Sun, and Fire within the body;
for in that regard, the external times of transit are considered as insignificant as blades of grass.

Just as during the seasons of spring, summer, the rains, and autumn, there is a transition of the moon into fire through the gradual swallowing of cold by heat; and during autumn, winter, and the dewy season, there is a transition of fire into the moon through the gradual swallowing of heat by cold— at their junctions, which are the equinoxes, there is likewise a transition of the sun into Aries and the other signs— so too within the body is there the [transition] of the coolness of the *apāna*.

Through the digestion of the lunar nectar (*soma*) by the digestive fire (*jaṭharāgni*), there is the transference of *agni* into *soma*. Through the external cooling of the heat of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) by its consumption, there is the transference of *soma* into *agni*. One who knows those transferences of the sun (*sūrya*) as previously described becomes a "knower of that" (*tajjña*).
This is the rule concerning the limb of concentration (*dhāraṇāṅga*) mentioned earlier; the knowledge of that [transference] is incidental.

This is either a praise by means of the primary fruit, consisting in the proclamation of a most excellent fruit superior to the well-known fruits of bathing at the transition of the sun (saṃkrānti), giving gifts, and so forth; || 118 ||

"O dear one, if you perceive the transit (*saṃkrānti*), the northern course (*uttarāyaṇa*), the correct time (*samyakkāla*), and likewise the two equinoxes (*viṣuvat*) through the bodily winds—both internally and externally, just as they are experienced—then you shine here; but not if you have merely accepted [the teachings] without further realization. Having restated the knowledge of the limbs (*aṅga*) thus mentioned, he encourages the qualified practitioner to engage in it by saying "the transit," etc. [The word] *kālam* refers to...
The year, consisting of the two solstices, is [experienced] through the bodily winds (*dehavāta*).

The plural number is used because of the various movements following the branches of the twelve channels (*nāḍī*) of the *prāṇa* and *apāna*. Just as it is well-known externally, so too is the internal [year] experienced through the practice of yoga as a direct perception according to how it is perceived.

If you understand this as clearly as a jar or other such objects, then indeed you shine amidst these discourses on yoga. However, if you have accepted something other than what I have taught and are engaged in another distraction, then you do not shine; therefore, this is the rule for single-minded devotion to that alone.
Thus ends the eighty-first sarga, titled "The Investigation of Agni and Soma," in the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa* of the *Mokṣopāya* within the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*, composed by the sage Vālmīki. 81.
Thus ends the eighty-first chapter, titled "The Investigation of Agni and Soma," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa-tātparya-prakāśa*.
The eighty-second canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Just as yogins attain either minuteness or even grossness, so it is.
Now listen to this which is correctly described as that which is called the body. || 1 ||

The methods for attaining minuteness and magnitude, as well as the yogi’s accomplishments through knowledge— such as entering another's body and experiencing various enjoyments— are described here with logical arguments.

Having thus understood that the body and so forth consist of the nature of Agni and Soma, the author promises to describe the methods by which a yogi—who has refined his vital breath, mind, and body through the practice of the three types of concentration (dhāraṇā) and who perceives the transition into the Moon, Sun, and Fire—attains the supernatural powers (siddhis) such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest: "Atomization," etc. (Verse 1).
Above the sheath of the lotus-wheel in the heart, a spark of fire flashes forth,
like a golden bee or like a fragment of twilight lightning in a cloud.

Therein, first, for the sake of attaining minuteness and for the dissolution of the body, one enters the space of the heart through the subtle aperture of the stalk of the heart-lotus from the blazing digestive fire located in the region above the navel; then, within the pericarp of the heart-lotus, one beholds the crest-lock (*śikhā*) which serves as the seat of the Supreme Self—thus it says, "In the heart. This is upon the upper pericarp of the lotus-stalk.

And likewise, in the Upaniṣad of the Taittirīyas, concerning the digestive fire (*jāṭharānala*), it is heard: "In its center stands a flame of fire, minute and upward-pointing; brilliant like a streak of lightning in the midst of dark clouds, slender as the awn of a grain of *nīvāra* rice, and yellow. "In its center is a great fire, with universal radiance and faces on all sides. Thus, having introduced the digestive fire, it is stated that there exists within it a flame of fire, exceedingly small and directed upwards, shining like a flash of lightning amidst dark rain-clouds, as thin as the stalk of a wild grain, and golden-yellow.

It is like a radiant atom. "The Supreme Self is situated in the center of that crest"—the qualification "like a flash of lightning at twilight" is for the purpose of making known the excellence of its yellow color. || 2 ||
Through the consciousness of its own growth, it increases rapidly like a whirlwind;
by virtue of its nature as pure consciousness, it surely rises like the sun.

Just as that spark of fire, having pervaded the entire body through its expansion, blazes forth, so too does it do so through the knowledge of the means of expansion. And once it has been fully expanded, it does not burn the body like fire; rather, by virtue of its nature as consciousness, it attains a preeminent radiance like the rising sun. || 3 ||
Resembling the first rays of the sun amidst the twilight clouds, it attains growth in an instant and melts away the entire body along with its limbs, just as fire melts gold.

At twilight and at dawn, it has the luster of the sun first risen in the cloudless sky. It causes [the body] to dissolve—that is, it causes it to melt away—the physical body along with its limbs such as hands and feet. The meaning is that it withdraws the earth-element portion, namely the quality of odor and solidity, into the water-element portion which constitutes its material cause. || 4 ||
One who is unable to endure the touch of water may dissolve it even from the tips of the toes through reasoning;
for fire exists externally through touch, but within the mind through the particularity of objects.
In this way, one should cause [the fire] to dissolve— that is, to liquefy— everything from the insteps up to the tips of the feet. Then, by means of the method of drying,
due to the specific nature of the object and the particular nature of the fire, that fire— which cannot endure the touch or coldness of water—
[overcomes] even the water through the power of its own heat and the method of withdrawing its liquidity upon contact.

One should dissolve and dry it; in this manner, having become external to the body, one remains within one's own heart, in the form of the mind, as the mere subtle body (ātivāhika-deha)—this is the remainder of the sense. || 5 ||
Having subsequently shaken off the two bodies, he dissolves somewhere,
just as mist is dispersed by a whirlwind when the vital breath is agitated.

Thus, having shaken off the two bodies—the earthly and the watery—that fire, withdrawn by the agitated *prāṇa*, dissolves somewhere; or else, as the scripture states, "When the fire goes out, it enters into the wind alone"—this is the meaning. || 6 ||
Deprived of the foundational channels, the Kuṇḍalinī power remains situated in the void,
having emerged like a streak of smoke from a fire.

At that time, the Kuṇḍalinī power, though deprived of the Suṣumnā channel located in the Mūlādhāra, remains in the space of the subtle body (ātivāhika-deha) which retains its impressions; thus he says: "From the Ādhāra," like a streak of smoke emerging from fire. (7)
Having embraced the egoity consisting of mind, intellect, and the individual soul (jīva),
she possesses an inner, throbbing wonder, like a streak of smoke from a firebrand.
And remaining there, she was embraced and integrated into the subtle body (*liṅga-śarīra*) composed of mind and intellect and constructed from the vital breaths (*jīva*) and so forth,

such that she possessed the ego-function (*ahaṃkṛti*); being one in whom the wonder of the inner flashing light of consciousness and the wonder of the power of wandering at will reside, [she entered] through the extremely subtle aperture of a lotus fiber.
Regarding mountains and other such places, he says that one enters at the very point from which it is appropriate to exit; thus, having entered, one emerges:
"In water, on a mountain, in grass, in a wall, on a stone, in the sky, or on the ground—just as she (the breath) is applied wherever it is suitable, in that same way one may sufficiently emerge. (9)
O dear one, that very consciousness proceeds through the sequence beginning with *rasa* and ending with *anta*;
it attains fullness through *rasa*, like the resonance of a lute string through water.
Having thus described the manner of becoming subtle,
he explains the manner of conceiving various bodies at will through the process of grossification, beginning with the words "by means of rasa" (rasena).
When that Kuṇḍalinī— the vital power of the yogin— releases the watery portion previously withdrawn into the fire, then by means of that *rasa*...

It becomes completely filled from all sides. Just as a leather bag, which is a specific type of leather vessel that carries a string and a leather thong—referred to here as "tantrībhāra"—when thrown into a well becomes filled with water, so it is in this case. || 10 ||
Filled with aesthetic flavor (rasa), that which one contemplates in whatever form quickly assumes that very nature,
just as a painter’s lines on the mind, O Rāma, take on the appearance of a finished work.
Thus, being filled with rasa, she assumes through the power of yoga that very form which she had previously intended to create by withdrawing the earthly portion; this is the meaning. || 11 ||
Then, by the power of its firm disposition, it reaches the internal bones,
like the extremely subtle state of a sprout within those situated in the mother’s womb.

Regarding that, he describes the manner of conceptualizing the bones and so forth with the word "firm" (*dṛḍha*). Within the *kalala* stages situated in the mother’s womb, the extremely subtle seed-potency exists like the state of the sprouts that are the bones, hands, feet, and other limbs. || 12 ||
O Rāghava, the power of the individual soul (jīva-śakti) attains whatever form it desires as its measure of reality, whether it be Mount Sumeru or a blade of grass.

Just as it desires, it assumes a form according to its own will—be it great, like Mount Sumeru, or small, like a blade of grass. You have heard of the attainment of powers such as *aṇimā* (minuteness) through the practice of yoga;
now listen to that which is accomplished through knowledge, an ornament for the ears.

Having concluded the description of the sequence for attaining the states of gross and subtle [realization] according to the perfection of yoga (yogasiddhi), he causes the audience to hear the primary subject matter in order to explain that which is distinct from it by means of the perfection of knowledge (jñānasiddhi): "It has been heard," and so forth.
There exists here only one pure, gentle, and unperceived Consciousness alone;
subtler than the subtlest, peaceful, neither the world nor the activity of the world.

When that [consciousness], having turned toward volitional construction (saṃkalpa), gathers itself by means of itself and thus falls into a state of turbidity, it is then called the "living being" (jīva). 16.
It accumulates; it increases through superimposition. || 16 ||
Through the delusion of mental construction, this body— which is indeed unreal—
is perceived by the foolish-souled living being, just as a child perceives a towering phantom.
The meaning is that the individual soul (jīva) perceives that very thing as its gross state. || 17 ||
But when the perfect illumination has arrived by means of the lamp of knowledge,
the delusion of conceptualization in the living being perishes like an autumn cloud.
He states the sequence for attaining subtlety with the words beginning "But when," etc. (verse 18).
This body attains peace through the total destruction of all volitional thoughts;
then, O Raghava, it is completely extinguished, just as a lamp is when its oil is exhausted. (19)
Peace, indeed! || 19 ||
Just as a living being does not see a dream once sleep has departed,
so too the individual soul, when the Truth has been cultivated, no longer perceives the body.
When it has been cultivated and realized. || 20 ||
The living being, enveloped by the body, remains established in the perception of reality within that which is unreal;
yet, through the singular contemplation of reality, he becomes bodiless, illustrious, and happy. (21)
O dear one, that conception of a self in what is not-self, such as the body and so forth,
is a terrible darkness within the heart, difficult to pierce even by the light of the sun and other luminaries.
It is difficult to pierce and impossible to destroy by means of worldly lights such as those of the sun. || 22 ||
By the sun of knowledge— "I am the stainless, pure consciousness, all-pervading and untainted within my very self through the nature of the Self"— it perishes.
By what, then, does that destruction [of the world] occur through Āditya? He states this: "In the Self alone," etc. (23).
And others who have realized the Self, whatever they meditate upon in whatever manner, they quickly perceive that very thing exactly so, by means of that firm meditation.

Even when this perfection of knowledge (*jñānasiddhi*) is firmly established, for those liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*), the conceptualization of gross, subtle, and apparent bodies occurs by their own will for the sake of diversion; thus he says: "And others... (24).
O Raghava, even those who are utterly deluded, by maintaining a firm conviction,
transform poison into nectar and nectar even into poison.

The deluded, such as those who mistake poison for insects, perceive it as nectar—that is, as food like nectar; yet through a firm delusion, they perceive this nectar, such as milk and rice mixed with poison, as being poison itself. || 25 ||
Thus, whatever is cultivated here through firm meditation, that very thing is quickly attained; for it has been observed repeatedly that "as one thinks, so one becomes. (26)
Thus, such an example has been observed repeatedly and many times in the world; this is the meaning. || 26 ||
When this body is viewed through the contemplation of reality, it truly becomes the body;
yet when viewed through the contemplation of unreality, this physical form attains the state of space.
The state of being the sky, that is, the state of the Brahman-space. || 27 ||
O virtuous Rāma, you have heard from the scriptures that the application of knowledge leads to the attainment of powers such as *aṇimā*; now hear this other method from me.

With the intention that this very [power] constitutes for him all the unsurpassed supernatural attainments (siddhis), such as *aṇimā* and so forth, he concludes: "The state of *aṇimā* and so forth," [referring to] others, characterized by the attainment of enjoyments through entering the bodies of others. || 28 ||
By means of the practice of exhaling (recaka), the individual soul is drawn up from the abode of Kuṇḍalinī and joined [to the supreme], just as fragrance is drawn from the wind. 29.

Therein, first he states the means for abandoning the previous body with the words "recaka" and so forth. The connection with the subsequent clause is as follows: "As long as [the consciousness] is drawn up and expelled outside, and joined to another body, so long is this body abandoned. This is just as the fragrance of a flower, having transferred to the external air, is drawn from the air and joined to the sense of smell. (29)
This body, whose vibration has ceased, is abandoned like a piece of wood or a clod of earth;
yet there is regard for both the body and the living soul, as if they were a vessel for the Self.

With his vibration ceased and his activity stilled, he becomes like a piece of wood or a clod of earth. His own life-force is directed into the body, life, and even the mind of others in order to experience their prosperity; just as a man with a watering-pot pours water from the vessel in his hand upon whichever tree or creeper he wishes to water, so it is here as well.
The grammatical connection is that "respect" [is shown] according to one's own preferred desire. || 30 ||
Whether in a stationary object or a moving one, according to his own desire and will,
the individual soul (jīva) is properly inserted within it to enjoy its prosperity.
Thus, having enjoyed the glory of supernatural powers (siddhi), if that body remains, one may enter it again,
or one's own [previous] body, or whatever else pleases you, my dear.

The meaning is as follows: having thus enjoyed the glory of supernatural powers (siddhiśrī) within another body while remaining there, if the yogin’s own former body still exists, he may re-enter it; if not, he may enter whatever else appears desirable at that time, for however long he wishes. || 32 ||
Or else, having likewise pervaded all bodies and so forth with consciousness, as well as the entire universe, one remains completely full. || 33 ||
Alternatively, after experiencing the enjoyments of another's body, the yogi fills the world by expanding his own internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*);
[then] bodies and so forth— where the nominative case is used in the sense of the accusative—
are the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) consisting of the reflections of all bodies, both stationary and moving, as well as the individual souls (*jīva*) which are their reflections.

The meaning is that one should remain in such a way that one is completely filled by the self-awareness (svātma-saṃvit) which pervades everything—including the qualities of sattva and so forth belonging to those reflected images (bimba) as limiting adjuncts (upādhi), as well as the reflected objects (bimba) characterized by consciousness (cit) as delimited by them. || 33 ||

O Rāma, having known that which is ever-arisen and free from defects, whatever the Lord— the light of consciousness— desires in whatever manner, he attains that very thing in no time; the wise know the state of perfection to be nothing other than this state of being unobstructed.

He provides a summary with the words "having known": The Lord, endowed with the sovereignty of yoga, whose nature is the light of the living consciousness, having known his own true essence—which is eternally risen, perpetually self-luminous, and free from all defects—obtains whatever he desires exactly as he wishes, and that very soon. This being so, those who know reality do not hold lesser accomplishments in high regard.
Rather, the meaning is that they know the state of being free from obscuration alone to be the unsurpassed bliss and the perfect state. || 34 ||

Thus ends the eighty-second chapter, titled "Instruction on the Yoga for Attaining the Powers such as Aṇimā," in the first part of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the glorious Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa, composed by the sage Vālmīki.

Thus ends the eighty-second chapter, titled "Instruction on the Yoga for Attaining the Powers such as Aṇimā," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The eighty-third canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Endowed with the sovereign powers of the qualities such as *aṇimā* and the rest, that beautiful queen—
Thus did Cūḍālā become, possessing intense and steady practice.

Thus, Cūḍālā, having practiced the intense cultivation of breath-retention and other techniques according to the manner previously described, became endowed with the sovereign powers of the *aṇimā* and other qualities. || 1 ||
She traveled by way of the sky, entered the hollow of the ocean,
and moved across the surface of the earth like the Gaṅgā, pure and cool.

He elaborates upon that very sovereignty by way of a detailed exposition beginning with "She went," and so forth: [the river] is pure and cool because of the subsiding of the turbidity of delusion and the threefold suffering. || 2 ||
Not having departed from her husband’s chest for even a moment, nor likewise from his heart,
she dwelt in all kingdoms and throughout the worlds like the goddess Lakṣmī.

He describes her mastery over the conceptualization of bodily arrays and so forth with the words "even for a moment. She dwelt in kingdoms, in nations, and in worlds, never departing and never separated [from him]. || 3 ||
Moving through the sky, dark-hued and adorned with flashes of lightning,
she wandered over the surface of the earth like a garland of clouds upon a range of mountains.
Whose ornaments shine like the flashes, or the very manifestations, of lightning. || 4 ||
Wood, grass, stone, earth, ether, wind, fire, and water—
all these entered him without obstruction, just as a thread passes through a pearl.
Upon the peaks of Meru and in the cities of the world-protectors,
he roamed at his pleasure through the cardinal directions, the sky, and the hollows of space.
The meaning is: "all those world-cavities that are well-known within the interior of the quarters and of the sky."
She carried out her worldly affairs with animals, bhūtas, piśācas, and others, as well as with nāgas, gods, asuras, vidyādharas, apsarases, and siddhas.
Through knowledge of the cries of all beings, [he engages in] social interaction such as conversation and so forth. || 7 ||
With great effort, Cūḍālā repeatedly instructed her husband regarding the nectar of self-knowledge, yet he did not understand it.
"He repeatedly awakened him"—the connection with this distant [verb] is a Vedic usage (chāndasa). || 8 ||
"She is skilled in the arts, yet innocent; she is my young wife"—in this way alone did the king perceive Cūḍālā.
Even after such a length of time, that king did not recognize Cūḍālā, who was endowed with such virtues, just as a child does not recognize a branch of knowledge.

Just as a child, at the time of studying the Vedas, does not know the Vedic knowledge which possesses qualities such as illuminating all objects conducive to human goals, so it is in this case. || 10 ||
But she, having not yet attained repose within her own self,
did not reveal that glory of her spiritual perfection to the king, just as a sacrifice is not revealed to a Śūdra.
Śrī Rāma said:
"O Lord, even Śikhidhvaja did not attain awakening despite his efforts toward that great Siddhayoginī; how then can another understand it?"

Rāma raises a doubt: "If she, who possesses all perfections (*sarvasiddhiśālinī*), is incapable of awakening her husband, then the capacity of other gurus, who are devoid of such perfections, to awaken their disciples is cast far aside. He says this with the words "mahatyā" (by the great one) and so forth; "of her too" means by means of effort, that is, through the exertion of instruction. || 12 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
O Rāma, the sequence of instruction is merely the maintenance of order;
the cause of realization, however, O Raghava, is solely the pure intelligence of the disciple.

The meaning is as follows: the established limit prescribed by the scriptures, beginning with "for the sake of knowing that, one should approach a guru alone," consists merely in observing that [limit] and following the sequence of instruction imparted by the guru; however, this [instruction] cannot forcibly produce knowledge even in one who lacks qualification. The mention of "wisdom" (prajñā) refers to wisdom accompanied by the fourfold means (sādhanacatuṣṭaya).
The object of knowledge of the self is not known through learning nor through merit;
the self alone knows the self, just as a snake [knows] its own tracks.

By "learning" (*śruta*), one means proficiency in treatises other than those concerning the Self (*anātma-śāstra*). By "merit" (*puṇya*), one means the category of optional rites (*kāmya-karma*) which are not a factor for the purification of the mind. Alternatively, by "learning," one means verbal, indirect knowledge (*parokṣa-jñāna*). Brahman, which is the reality of the Self and that which is to be known, is not known [in this way];
unlike other objects, it is not made into an objective domain. Nor is it attained through merit alone, such as the enjoyment of heaven, without inquiry (*vicāra*).

Knowledge is produced; however, when inquiry has been generated by those two [means], the meaning is that the Self, having ascended through the final direct-perception modification (*sākṣātkāra-vṛtti*), knows itself by itself alone. The word "like" (*iva*) is used in the sense of "just as," as in "like a snake. Śrī Rāma said:
This being so, O Sage, how is it that in the maintenance of this world, the sequence known as the teacher’s instruction is the cause of self-knowledge? (15)
In that case, how and by what means does the sequence known as the "instruction of the Guru" [occur]? || 15 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
There was a certain extremely miserly Kirāta, possessed of wealth and grain,
who lived with his family in a thicket of the Vindhya forest like a Brāhmaṇa householder.

In order to explain that the instruction of a guru and other such means serve as causes for knowledge by way of inducing a student’s mind toward an inclination toward the inward (the Self)— according to the maxim of the "thick Arundhatī"— Vasiṣṭha relates the story of the Kirāta:
"Once, as he was walking through the Vindhya jungle, [a deer] fell before him..."
O Rāma, there was a single cowrie shell in a place covered by a thicket of grass. || 17 ||
Out of miserliness, he diligently threshed everything— grass, husks, and so forth—
for three days on all sides for the sake of a single cowrie shell.
Out of *kārpaṇya*—that is, from his own nature of wretchedness—he purified [it]. || 18 ||
"O Bhavata, there shall be four and then eight cowries in due time;
thereafter, a hundred, a thousand, and then by the mind, another thousand. (19)

He states his intention, which was the cause for his exertion in searching for him: "kapardakāḥ" (cowries). "Upon obtaining [the cowrie], you should buy something with this cowrie in my hand; from its sale, there would be four cowries, then eight, then a hundred, then a thousand, and then two thousand"—thinking thus, he reflected in his mind. || 19 ||
Wandering through the wilderness, miserable and unwearied day and night, he did not perceive even a thousand laughs from the people; indeed, he perceived nothing else.
To indicate that even an undertaking for a small purpose becomes highly fruitful if one’s firm exertion remains unbroken by obstacles such as the laughter of foolish people, he says:
"Then, at the end of three days, from that forest..."
He is like the orb of the full moon; the great wish-fulfilling gem has been obtained.
Having attained that, with a contented heart, he returned home in happiness;
having acquired all the prosperity of the world, he remained established in universal peace.
He by whom all the worldly enjoyments for the prosperity of the world have been attained, and by whom all calamities such as poverty have been pacified—
he remains in such a state.
Thus, just as that jewel, which is worth the entire world, was obtained by the Kirāta through his search for cowrie shells, without weariness day or night. (23)
That jewel is such that its value is the entire world.
In this way, through the instruction of the scriptures, knowledge of one's own self is attained; for by following the lineage of the Guru, one seeks one thing and indeed obtains another.
Likewise, through the sequence of the guru’s instruction, one seeks another form of verbal knowledge that is mostly indirect; yet another, which is eternally direct, is attained. || 24 ||
Brahman transcends all the senses; it is not through the cognitions of the senses, such as hearing and the rest, that the reality of the Self is attained, O sinless one, by means of instruction.

He explains what that other [means] is by saying "Brahman. The cognitions produced by the senses—such as the hearing of words from the Vedas and so forth, and the resulting verbal comprehension—are mental modifications (*cittavṛtti*). Furthermore, through the instruction of a teacher, only verbal mental modifications are generated.
Among these, within the final modification which is the most extremely clear, there occurs the manifestation of the eternally immediate Brahman.
The meaning is that [the realization] is caused solely by both the purity of the disciple’s intellect and the nature of Brahman; instruction is not its cause.
Furthermore, without the teacher’s instruction, there can be no attainment of the reality of the Self.
By whom has the wish-fulfilling gem been obtained without searching for cowrie shells? (26)
Nevertheless, because of scriptural passages such as "A person who has a teacher knows," he states that instruction from a guru is necessary:

"The exposition by a guru regarding this reality of great significance has reached [the state of being] the cause for that which was previously causeless, just as a cowrie shell [becomes the cause] for a gem. (27)

The meaning is that, just as a cowrie shell [is found] through searching, the teacher's instruction—though lacking an apparent cause—becomes a cause because its fruit is seen to be inevitable through the process of reflection. || 27 ||
Behold, O Rāghava, this delusive illusion which confounds even the great:
one thing is sought with effort, yet another fruit is obtained.
A person performs one action, yet obtains a result quite different from it, as is observed throughout the three worlds.
Therefore, for this worldly delusion that follows immediately upon existence, the best course is to pass beyond it through non-attachment and desirelessness alone.

Thus, the instruction of the Guru and so forth is the cause for the attainment of the Self precisely without any other cause; yet once the Self has been attained, the destruction of the delusion of the world—brought about by the remnants of *prārabdha* karma—is accomplished through mere indifference, and thus requires no further effort. To this he says: "Anything else," because it is observed and heard in this way throughout the three worlds.
