Therefore, immediately after attaining the Self, the best course is simply to pass through the delusion of the world—which has been brought about by the remainder of one's commenced karma—by means of indifference, without desire, so that there may be non-attachment; this is the meaning. || 29 ||
Thus ends the eighty-third canto, titled "The Narrative of the Kirāta," in the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa* of the *Mokṣopāya* section of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*, composed by the sage Vālmīki. 83.
Thus ends the eighty-third chapter, titled "The Narrative of the Kirāta," in the first half of the Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The eighty-fourth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Then King Śikhidhvaja, being without the state of knowledge of reality, [continued...]
He fell into a supreme delusion, like a childless man entering the blinding darkness.
The detachment of Śikhidhvaja, Cūḍālā’s consolation in the forest,
his departure alone at night, and his dwelling on Mount Mandara are recounted.

Without that state which consists of the knowledge of reality—the place of ultimate rest—a man who is childless, his lineage destroyed, is as if blinded by the darkness of grief and other afflictions. || 1 ||
With his mind set ablaze by the fire of suffering, he did not take even the slightest delight in those riches brought before him, as if they were flames of fire.
Regarding the splendors such as jewels brought forward by beloved vassals and others. || 2 ||
In solitary places, at the ends of the horizon, by waterfalls, and in caves,
that living being found delight like a hunter whose arrow has been released.
Just as a creature such as a deer, released by an arrow and thus spared by fate, being terrified of the hunter, finds delight in solitary places and the like; so it is with him. || 3 ||
O Raghava, like you, all kings, when entreated by their servants with conciliation, persuasion, and instruction,
are made to perform their daily duties.

The entire day's activities are performed; since the root *kṛ* (to do) is used with *ha* (to abandon), by the rule *hakror anyatarasyām*, the agent of the *aṇi*-form becomes the object of the *ṇi*-form, and thus the suffix *la* is applied in the sense of the object.
Constantly possessing unrestrained dispassion and a tranquil mind like a wandering mendicant,
he was distressed even while remaining in the midst of great enjoyments and royal splendor.
Like a wandering mendicant, he remains distressed while seeking to enjoy great wealth and prosperity; the particle *ca* has the sense of conjunction with the meaning of the preceding clause. (5)
O giver of honor, he bestowed exceedingly great gifts— cows, land, gold,
and so forth— upon the gods, the brahmins, and his own kinsmen.
And he practiced austerities, performing such penances as the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa*;
he wandered through sacred fords, forests, and hermitages.
In order to purify his body and mind, he performed austerities such as the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa penances.
Nevertheless, he did not obtain even the slightest freedom from sorrow,
just as one seeking treasure who digs the earth finds no treasure when there is none.
Day and night, this great [body] was indeed wasting away like a fire;
he reflected again and again upon the medicine for the disease of saṃsāra.
By means of thought—that fire characterized by anxiety—(he was consumed). || 9 ||
Overwhelmed by anxiety and dejected, he did not perceive his own kingdom— even with its great splendor— as anything but poison before him, for his mind was distressed.
Then once, when Cūḍālā had come into his lap while they were in a secluded place, Śikhidhvaja spoke these words to her in a sweet voice: || 11 ||
Śikhidhvaja said:
"I have enjoyed the kingdom for a long time and experienced the grounds of worldly prosperity;
now, filled with dispassion, I am going to the forest."
The stages of non-existence are the states of non-existence. || 12 ||
Neither pleasures nor pains, neither calamities nor prosperities, embrace the one who dwells in the mind alone, O slender-limbed one. (13)
They embrace; they cling. || 13 ||
There is no delusion caused by the ruin of one's country, nor is there the destruction of people in battle;
I consider the happiness of those dwelling in the forest to be even greater than that of a kingdom.
He shows the causes for the abundance of happiness: "Not [limited] by place," etc. (14).
They bear clusters [of flowers] as breasts, have red sprouts for hands, wear garlands of blossoms, and possess shimmering white clouds for garments. (15)
Now, having accepted the rows of women as being like the *cūḍālā* plants, he describes them with five verses beginning with "stabaka-".
For the most part, there are metaphors (*rūpaka*) throughout. (15)
They are colored by the pollen of their own and others' [trees], adorned with floral ornaments, and beautified by the slopes of their hips which are golden rocks worthy of being enjoyed. || 16 ||
Those women for whom flower-like ornaments were made solely of flowers, and whose hips, adorned by those [ornaments], were fit to be served as golden slabs. 16.
Enveloped by pearl necklaces in the form of rivers threaded with pearls that are the waves,
they are embraced by their companions in the form of creepers— the very innocent young fawns.
They were surrounded by river-pearl necklaces strung with pearls in the form of waves; their young children were nothing other than most charming fawns.
Possessing a natural fragrance that is unrestrained, they offer food in the form of ripened fruits;
their eyes are the rows of bees, and their bodies are creepers filled with blossoms. (18)
Those by whom fruits and foods were bestowed upon the hungry; those whose very limbs, such as their arms, were like creepers filled with flowers (puṣpāpūra). 18.
O fair-faced one, these forest paths— cool and pure of limb, having attained a state of throbbing sweetness when tasted— delight me just as you do.
The forest avenues—rows of forests—have attained that state [of being] whose flow is the trickling down of waves, which is like the taste of your lower lip. 19.
As the mind becomes solitary, secluded, and tranquil in a remote place,
it does not become so even amidst the orbs of the moon, nor in the abodes of Brahmā and Indra.
O slender one, you ought not to create an obstacle to this consultation;
for noble women do not thwart the desire of their husband even in a dream. (21)
Regarding this matter of going to the forest, in this wise counsel and excellent deliberation. || 21 ||
Cūḍālā said:
"O Lord, an action performed when the time has arrived shines, and nothing else;
a flower shines in spring, and fruit shines in autumn. (22)

Desiring to test the firmness of his dispassion, and as if assenting to his former attachment to love by describing how it was appropriate for his age, Cūḍālā attempted to shake him— following the maxim of "shaking a pillar"— saying, beginning with the words "She has arrived," etc. (22).
Resorting to the forest is appropriate for those whose bodies are worn out by old age, but not for the young, such as yourself; therefore, this does not please me.
O Great King, as long as we have not been abandoned by youth, we shine in our home like trees with a profusion of flowers. (24)
"We adorn the house," meaning "we shall dwell" therein; the plural number is used according to the rule *asmado dvayośca* (Pāṇini 1.2.59). || 24 ||
Accompanied by Puṣpamitra, who has grown old along with me, we shall go together from our home to the forest, like swans departing from a lake. (25)

The meaning is that friendship with the flower-white creepers—upon which flowers are placed and worn—is appropriate only during a state of equality with them, as their old age is measured by the flowers resting upon his head. || 25 ||
For a Kṣatriya who abandons the protection of his subjects when it is the improper time, there will be a great sin due to that very lapse. (26)
"For the sake of a vulnerability" means for the sake of a flaw in the kingdom; "enaḥ" means sin. || 26 ||
The subjects indeed restrain a king who acts prematurely;
likewise, servants restrain their master from improper deeds, each restraining the other.
They obstruct and restrain. || 27 ||
Śikhidhvaja said:
"Enough, O lotus-petal-eyed one, with this obstacle to my desired goal;
know that I have already departed from here for a distant, solitary forest. (28)
Thus, although he was thus provoked, Śikhidhvaja—whose dispassion remained unshaken—consoled her with the words beginning "Enough," and so forth. || 28 ||
"O girl of faultless limbs, you must not come to the forest;
for even for men, O soft-limbed one, this forest retreat is difficult to penetrate. (29)
A forest refuge, a region of the woods, is difficult to penetrate; it can only be entered with great hardship. || 29 ||
Even women who are otherwise hardy are not capable of dwelling in the forest;
for clusters of flowers in the woods are unable to withstand the edge of a blade. (30)

"Though they have hard and firm limbs"—the meaning is that just as flower-clusters grown in a forest, though hard, are unable to endure the swarm of bees (*śaktālim*) compared to those grown in a garden, so it is here. In the reading *śaktālim*, it should be explained as "a row (*āli*) of powerful birds (*śakta*). || 30 ||
"You must remain here protecting this excellent kingdom;
for when the husband has departed, it is the vow of women to bear the burden of the family. (31)
Regarding what you said—that it is "untimely for the king"—with the intention that the remedy for that fault must likewise be performed by her, he says: "by you" (bhavatyā). || 31 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Having spoken thus to his beloved, whose face was like the moon, the self-controlled king arose to bathe and performed all his daily duties.
Then, having abandoned his activity for the sake of his subjects, Ravi went to the western mountain,
as Śikhidhvaja had gone to the forest, which is inaccessible to all people.
The qualifiers of the two subjects of comparison (upameya) should also be applied to the two objects of comparison (upamāna). || 33 ||
Having withdrawn her expanded form, the radiance followed that very Lord as he departed from his palace, like a devoted female crest-ornament following its master.
The dark night arrived, making the world grey with ash;
like the Yamunā, it embraced Śiva, who bore the celestial river Gaṅgā upon his head.

The Yamunā is imagined (utprekṣā) as being like the Gaṅgā herself, who—having embraced Śarva in such a manner that he holds his own friend, the celestial river (vyomāpagā), likewise embraces her out of desire; thus she is "Saṃśleṣā" (the Embracer). The suffix *ṇa* is used here in the active sense (*kartari*) according to the rule *śliṣ-ād-vya-dhāḥ*. || 35 ||
The quarters of the sky, marked by the young Tamāla trees, stood like women with teeth of clouds at twilight, while he sat within his consecrated circle, marked by the rising smile of moonlight. (36)

In those directions where there were women with children marked by *tamāla* leaves held in their laps, [the stars] stood as if forming a circle all around, marked by the rising of a smile of moonlight, as if from witnessing the deeds of Yamunā.
From this point onward, all the words ending in the locative case are connected to the phrase "the host of stars was seen. (36)
As the couple proceeded toward the further shore, the abode of Meru—
a celestial garden for the sake of sporting— became the splendor of the day and the lord of the day.
And while Dinaśrī and Dinanātha, a couple possessing such forms, were going to sport on the other shore—the northern half—of Mount Meru, which abounds in celestial gardens; || 37 ||
This shore was indeed abandoned by the two fierce-rayed ones as they approached;
yet for the couple consisting of Night and the Lord of Night, it was once again Mount Merau.

Likewise, this formidable shore was abandoned by the fierce rays of the sun— those terrible heats that cause torment and consume through sins— and while the couple, characterized as the moon and the night, were arriving there to sport.
Then the host of stars was seen scattered upon the pavement of the sky,
like a handful of auspicious parched grain released by the bridegrooms of the quarters.

The multitude of stars was seen upon the surface of the sky, which appeared like a mosaic floor on the terrace of a palace, as if it were a handful of auspicious fried grains released and scattered by the brides of the quarters.
The night, moon-faced, dark as the gloom, weary yet smiling with flowers, attained her youth, with the buds of the lotuses for her breasts. (40)

Exhausted by the search for her own lord and by waiting for his appearance, she is radiant with smiles in the form of white water-lilies and other flowers; this refers to youth as the very fruit of one's own youth. (40)
Having performed his evening rituals together with Cūḍālā,
he slept again upon his bed like Mount Maināka in the ocean.
Then, at the time of midnight, when the region had become silent and all people were hidden within the stone-wombs of deep sleep; (42)
While she was fast asleep upon that bed of soft silk, utterly overcome by slumber like a female bee within a lotus, he— || 43 ||
While that Cūḍālā was fast asleep, being utterly stupefied by deep slumber. || 43 ||
King Śikhidhvaja gently, very gently, released his sleeping beloved from his lap,
just as Rāhu releases the moonlit quarter of the sky.
Just as the mouth of Rāhu, at the time of releasing the moon, very slowly and gradually releases the lunar light toward the eastern direction, so it was. 44.
He rose from his bed, from which the hem of the garment was half-hidden by his clinging bride,
like Hari rising from the Ocean of Milk whose surging waves are restless with the splendor of Lakṣmī.
From that couch (paryaṅka) which possessed a covering cloth (aṃśuka) such that its half-portion (ardha-bhāga) had its edge (añcala) tucked away like a bashful bride (līna-vadhūka);
and whose restless waves were accompanied by splendors (lakṣmī) like the beloveds of Lakṣmī herself.
In whom [resided] such [qualities], as if from an ocean that had been exhausted. || 45 ||
Thinking, "I am going for the sake of the Vīrakrama," that one of perfected intellect departed from the city, having stationed his host of followers right there.

The "heroic stride" (*vīrakrama*) is the practice at night for the purpose of suppressing thieves and the wicked; therein, having assigned and appointed the host of followers to that very heroic stride, he is one of full intelligence and free from desire. (46)
Having said, "Obeisance to you, O Goddess of Royal Fortune," he departed from the circle and entered the formidable forest alone, like a river entering the ocean.
"Ugrām" means fierce; "araṇyānīm" means a great forest, [the suffix] "ānuk" being applied according to the rule "himāraṇyayormahattve" (Pāṇini 5.4.103). 47.
That vast forest-like night, thick with dense darkness, filled with swarms of cruel spirits, and harsh with its multitude of small beings, was passed by him together with her.
That vast forest and the night were both spent—passed over—by him, which was filled with thickets characterized by darkness and resembling dense gloom. || 48 ||
Having led her through the empty forest for the long day,
he rested with the sun upon a certain woodland clearing.
By the statement "he rested together with Arka," it is understood that he indeed departed until evening. || 49 ||
When the sun had become invisible, she performed her bath and other rites there,
ate some fruit and such, and passed that night.
The dark night. || 50 ||
Again at dawn, the king swiftly crossed over cities, high mountain ranges, and rivers for twelve nights.
Then he reached a forest situated on the slope of Mount Mandara, inaccessible to people,
where the cities of men lay at an extreme distance.
Because [it is] from which the people—meaning the multitudes of people, that is to say, the districts—and the cities are situated extremely far away. || 52 ||
The trees were encircled by the water from the ponds flowing through the gurgling conduits;
it was a hermitage of twice-born sages known from former times by its ruined altars and dwellings. (53)

In which [place] the trees were made exceedingly strong by being encircled by such ponds from which waters flowed noisily through bamboo conduits; and in which there were hermitages of the twice-born that had existed in former times. 53.
It was a dwelling of creepers frequented by perfected beings (siddhas) and free from small creatures;
it was filled with trees and creepers, and with fruits that provide sustenance for living beings.
There, on a single level, pure, and water-girdled spot— cool, dark with young grass, moist, and filled with fruit-bearing trees— (55)
[The word] *śyāma* [means] dark due to *śādvalas*, which are regions covered with green grass; [the suffix] *valac* is applied after *naḍa* and *śāda*. (Pāṇini 4.2.88)
With creepers bearing clusters of blossoms, he constructed a hut-dwelling,
just as the rainy season builds a cage of dark clouds accompanied by lightning.
A *uṭaja* is a leaf-hut; it is a dwelling in the form of that [hut]. || 56 ||
A smooth bamboo staff, a vessel for eating fruit, a water-offering bowl, a flower-basket, a rosary, and a water-pot. || 57 ||
Having brought a patched garment to ward off the cold, as well as a grass mat and a deer-skin, the king prepared them within that small hermitage cell.
Whatever other object was suitable for the practice of asceticism,
he established it there, just as the Creator established the order of the world.
Fate (Vidhi), the Ordainer (Dhātṛ), in this world within its own created universe, [establishes] a sequence, just as one establishes the collection of means for worldly activity. || 59 ||
He performed his morning recitation during the first watch, preceded by the twilight prayers;
in the second watch, however, he gathered flowers, followed by bathing and the worship of the deity.
"An accumulation of flowers" means a collection; this is also indicative of fruits, roots, kuśa grass, wood, and so forth. "Then" means on the third [day]. || 60 ||
Afterwards, having eaten some forest fruit, wild tubers, lotus stalks,
and the like, that self-controlled man, intent on his recitations, passed the night alone.
Thus, within a hut constructed on the shore of Mount Mandara, the lord of Mālava spent the day without weariness;
he did not even remember the splendor of his former kingship—for what indeed does not vanish when discernment flashes in the heart? || 62 ||

Having restated what was said, he concludes with the word "iti": Śikhidhvaja, whose entry into impurity had been described in the manner mentioned, spent his days—indeed many days—without weariness while staying inside a hut constructed on the shore near Mount Mandara. He did not remember that new royal splendor previously experienced. To the question "Why was that? he says:
They are able to bring [others] under control by generating desire; the meaning is that they cannot do so for anyone at all. || 62 ||

Thus ends the eighty-fourth canto, titled "The Renunciation of Śikhidhvaja," in the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa* of the *Mokṣopāya* section of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*, composed by the sage Vālmīki. 84.
Thus ends the eighty-fourth chapter, titled "The Renunciation of Śikhidhvaja," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The eighty-fifth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Thus Śikhidhvaja remained in the forest at Pūrṇamaṭhikā.
Now listen: what did Cūḍālā do while at home? || 1 ||
The queen’s awakening, her search for the king, the sight of him on the road,
the vision of the destined future at that time, and her subsequent awakening are all described in detail.
Having restated what was said, he connects it with the narrative about to be told: "Thus," etc. (1).
There, at the hour of midnight, when Śikhidhvaja had gone far away,
Cūḍālā woke up in fear like a doe sleeping in a village.

The phrase "as if asleep in a village" is intended to illustrate that, although she was always awake due to her fear of separation from the King, she was nevertheless overcome by sleep through the power of destiny. || 2 ||
Deprived of her husband, she beheld the bed that had become empty,
like the sky when it is devoid of the sun, the moon is not full, and its splendor has been stilled.
Deprived of her husband, she was abandoned. || 3 ||
She rose up with her face somewhat withered and full of dejection,
like a great creeper poorly watered, its sprouts— the limbs of her body— devoid of vitality.
Sprinkled with contemptible water such as alkaline mud and the like; the qualifying term [“sprinkled”] is to be applied commonly [to all]. || 4 ||
Neither clear nor pure, she became agitated;
like the beauty of day turned grey by mist, she remained thus.
For a moment, while still seated upon her bed, she reflected with deep anxiety:
"Alas! Having abandoned his sovereignty and his home, the Lord has gone to the forest."
The meaning is that, with this thought, he meditated upon what is about to be described. || 6 ||
"What task is there for me today that involves him? I shall go into his presence;
for destiny has ordained that the husband alone is the refuge of women. (7)

He says that very thing with the word "that" (tat). According to the rule—that is, according to the scripture—the husband alone is designated and ordained as the primary course or refuge. The underlying meaning is that when the husband is absent, sons and others become the refuge. || 7 ||
Having thus reflected, Cūḍālā rose up to follow her husband; emerging through a crevice in the wind, she ascended into the sky.
A *vātarandhra* is a window; by means of that. || 8 ||
The yoginī wandered through the path of the sky by means of a gust of wind, creating the illusion of another moon with her face as she moved before the caravan of the siddhas.
The delusion of another moon is the error of perceiving a second moon. || 9 ||
Then, at night, she saw her husband returning as he had come, wandering alone in a secluded spot, bearing a sword, appearing like one possessed by a vetāla.
At a time suitable for a vetāla, it appeared shining forth in the night. || 10 ||
Beholding such a husband and remaining within the hollow of the sky,
she reflected upon everything concerning her husband’s future in its entirety.
The future collection of objects pertaining to her husband. || 11 ||
O Rāghava, one must proceed by that [path] in such a manner, at such a time, in such a place, for as long as the task requires, according to its arising, and until vast liberation is attained. 12.

He says "yathā" (just as) to explain that she reflected by analyzing [the matter] through future types of gods, signs, time, place, action, quantity, worldly prosperity, and the ultimate limit of liberation (*niḥśreyasa*). "Sphārā nirvṛtiḥ" means repose in the abundance of bliss. || 12 ||
Seeing that it was inevitable and that her husband stood before her,
she turned back from her departure in order to confirm that very thing.

Having seen [the Lord] as if standing before him through the power of yoga, as if directly perceived, in order to confirm it—that is to say, to act in accordance with that realization—[he spoke]. || 13 ||
Let my departure today wait; for it shall not be long before I must go to his side—this is the decree of destiny.
Having reflected thus, Cūḍālā entered the inner apartments once more and slept upon the bed of Śambhu, like the digit of the moon upon his head.
"For some reason, that lord of the earth has departed at this moment"; having thus consoled all the citizens, the woman remained there. (16)
With an even gaze, she protected her husband’s kingdom in due order,
just as a woman guarding rice fields protects the ripening grain over time.
Kālāmagopikā and Śālipālikā. || 17 ||
As that couple remained there,
each guarding the kingdom and the forest respectively, time passed while they did not see one another’s faces.
He brought; he went. || 18 ||
Then a day passed, and then a fortnight, a month, a season, and a year,
in the forest of Śikhidhvaja and in the palace of Cūḍālā.
He states how he went there: "He went," etc. A year consists of [six] seasons. || 19 ||
What need is there for much speaking here? For eighteen years, Śikhidhvaja dwelt in the house of Cūḍālā, while the woman lived in a forest thicket.
Then, after many years had passed and he was enveloped by old age,
Śikhidhvaja dwelt in a cave on the slope of a great mountain.

Having observed that the ripening of his husband's ascetic discipline had been long protected, and when those years had passed, he was then overtaken by old age in the forest—[in the reading *jarasā vane*, it means "in the forest";
in the reading *jarasopalakṣitasya*, it means "of him characterized by old age"; and in the reading *vṛte*, the construction is "when Śikhidhvaja was enveloped by old age"].

"Having observed the ripening of the *kaṣāyas*, that is, the latent impressions (*vāsanās*) such as passion and so forth—for that duration, [the body] was protected and awaited by her; this is the meaning. The phrase beginning with "Then" (*tadā*) and so forth is a restatement of what has been said for the purpose of introducing the matter about to be explained. || 22 ||
Then, because the fulfillment of her own purpose was destined to occur in that way, she thought: "Now is the time for me to go into the presence of my husband. (23)
Because one's own duty, which is the awakening of one's master, must necessarily be accomplished through one's own instruction in the manner that will be described hereafter. || 23 ||
Having reflected, she made up her mind to go to the vicinity of Mount Mandara;
she departed from the inner apartments at night and traversed the path of the sky.
He crossed over; he leaped. || 24 ||
Traveling through the sky by means of a gust of wind,
she beheld celestial trees covered with garments, adorned with clusters of jewels, and draped in the silken raiment of the kalpavṛkṣa trees.
Residing in the Nandana grove, these red-hued women, like *siddha* maidens going to meet their lovers,
grasp fragments of the moon that rain down droplets of frost.
Reddish, they were deeply attached to their beloveds; by them, the fragments of the moon's digits had been grasped. (26)
He caused the winds, which possessed the supreme fragrance of the Siddhas,
to touch him like a succession of great waves from the ocean of nectar in the lunar orb.

She touched— that is, she came into contact with— the breezes that had acquired and taken up the fragrances of Mandāra garlands, yellow sandalwood, musk, and so forth from the Siddhas who were supreme;
and [she touched] the stainless moonlight, which was like a succession of great waves from the ocean of nectar characterized by the lunar orb.
Having reached the interiority, that is, the state of being situated within the sky, she beheld it. || 27 ||
He beheld the stainless moonlight reaching into the midst of the sky,
as well as the lightning moving within the clouds and clinging to them.
Not separated from her husband, she gazed at him again and again, and said to herself: "Alas! For all embodied beings, [this state lasts] as long as life. (29)

He beheld the lightning flashes, which were not separated from their own husband, the cloud; he spoke to them with his very mind. What he said then is expressed by the words beginning with "Aho" (Oh!). 29.
My mind, too, finds no peace; it is filled with longing. When shall I again see that lion-shouldered one, so devoted to affection? (30)
"When it is said, 'I see my beloved,' even my mind becomes filled with longing; so too do the creepers, entwined with clusters of blossoms, long for their own husband, the tree. (31)
"Even though my mind is being awakened by discernments, it still yearns," so he spoke. || 31 ||
My mind also yearns, thinking that they do not leave for even a moment,
as this elder sister goes to her beloved like a woman successful in her secret tryst.
Born at the beginning, in the most excellent light of the gods, she is the first-born (Agrajā).
"Likewise, my mind was fixed on the thought, 'When shall I also come?
These breezes are gentle, and these are the rays of the moon. (33)
Alas, these very things that delight the king of the forest cause me, too, great longing!
O mind, you remain within like one senseless and deluded, performing a frantic dance for naught. (34)
O ignorant fool! You have danced in vain and for no purpose; what is the meaning of your remaining thus? || 34 ||
O virtuous one, where has that discernment of yours gone, which was as pure as the sky?
Or rather, O friend, is it that your mind longs for its own master? (35)
Alternatively, the ellipsis "this is not a fault" is to be supplied. To the question "Why?", he says: "The husband," etc. (35).
"Stay! Why do you distress me with such longing?
Why do you long in vain, O perverse woman? Your husband has reached old age. (36)

Now, with regard to the body, he asks: "What? The meaning is: O woman, that husband of yours for whose sake you long to embrace him and so forth—he must have grown old and can be expected to be entirely indifferent to you.
Furthermore, he would be an ascetic, emaciated in limb, and likewise devoid of worldly desires.
I believe that the mind’s attachment to the enjoyment of sovereignty and other such pleasures has reached its very root in this [state].

I consider, or rather believe, that his mind has reached a state of rootlessness and total eradication because of his non-enjoyment of kingship and other such things, for the sake of non-enjoyment itself. || 37 ||
Like a river in the rainy season that has reached the ocean, the creeper of latent impressions (vāsanā) is extinguished;
he is devoted solely to solitude, unified in self, devoid of worldly flavor, and his impressions are stilled.

The remainder of the verse is that his creeper-like latent impression (*vāsanā*) has become so integrated that it no longer remains distinct, just as a small river during the rainy season, having entered a great river, does not remain separate. He delights in solitude and is attached to it; for this very reason, he is a single-souled one (*ekātman*). He is devoid of worldly flavor (*nīrasa*), meaning free from desire. || 38 ||
I think my husband has become like a withered tree;
nevertheless, O mind, you are filled with longing because of his longing. (39)

Thus, as if reviving her despondent mind by demonstrating this state of hopelessness, she says: "Even so. Let him be such as you describe; nevertheless, O mind, what is your anxiety? By means of yoga—by awakening my husband's intellect through the method to be described and making him a knower of reality—I shall [unite] my husband with his longing for the enjoyment of the remainder of his *prārabdha* karma.
The syntactic connection with the subsequent verse is: "I shall unite with you; you should not feel longing. (39)
Having awakened my intellect through yoga, I shall unite myself with my husband,
having purified the mental impurities of my lord and brought the mind of the sage into harmony.
He states that very point clearly: "pramṛṣṭa... (verse 40).
"I shall appoint you to the very kingdom; we two shall dwell happily for a long time.
Oh, after such a long duration, this auspicious desire has been fulfilled! (41)
I shall attain that which is intended for my husband;
this alone stands above all multitudes of bliss. (42)

For this reason—that is, because her husband will become one whose internal and external thoughts are equal in form to mine through the awakening to reality—the remainder of the sentence is "he will become such. Praising him for that very reason, she says: "Samagra... (verse 42).
Thinking, "What happiness lies in tasting the attachment to uniform mental states," Cūḍālā traversed the mountains through the sky.
She traversed countries, oceans, and the ends of the quarters until she reached a cave of Mount Mandara;
remaining invisible while stationed in the sky, she entered the interior of the forest.
The clouds of the year; "vanāntaram" means the interior of the forest. || 44 ||
Like a whirlwind, with its coming and going made known by the swaying of trees and creepers, she entered a leaf-hut built in a certain part of the forest and approached her husband. (45)
Her coming and going are to be inferred from the swaying of the trees and the creepers. || 45 ||
Having seen him through yoga, he recognized that he was as if situated in another body, adorned with necklaces, armlets, bracelets, earrings, and other ornaments. (46)

"By means of yoga, with a concentrated mind"—this is the sense. The connection with what follows is as follows: he who, while adorned with necklaces, armlets, and other ornaments, possessed the splendor of Mount Meru, was seen right here in the hut on Mount Mandara with such characteristics as a lean body and so forth. || 46 ||
She beheld there that very same one who once possessed the splendor of Mount Meru, now with emaciated limbs and darkened complexion, standing like a withered leaf. (47)
Bathed in a flood of collyrium-water, like Bhṛṅgīśa himself, he was free from desire,
wearing garments of bark, peaceful, and standing all alone.
Like the famous Bhṛṅgīśa, the gatekeeper of Rudra. || 48 ||
Seeing him seated on the ground, weaving flowers and marked by matted locks, Cūḍālā, of faultless limbs and full breasts, [approached]. (49)
He was weaving garlands of flowers for the worship of the gods and guests, marked and distinguished by his matted locks. || 49 ||
With a slight sense of despondency having arisen, she spoke thus to herself in her mind:
"Alas! How terrible is this folly, which consists in the lack of knowledge of the Self! (50)
Ignorance is the state of not knowing the self; it consists of that [non-self]. || 50 ||
Such conditions as these arise through the favor of ignorance;
for this is that same prosperous king, my husband, who is so very dear to me. (51)

Since, for this reason—that my husband, who is so dear to me, has fallen into this state of being crushed and struck in his heart by a mass of delusion—therefore, in this very hermitage, this very day, I shall certainly lead my lord, my husband, to the state of one who knows what is to be known, and likewise to the glory of worldly enjoyment and liberation; such is the connection with the following verse. || 51 ||
Having reached this state, crushed by a dense cloud of delusion within my heart,
I must certainly approach the Lord, who knows all that is to be known, this very day.
I shall lead you here, of this there is no doubt, to the glory of worldly enjoyment and liberation;
having cast off this form, by means of some other form.
"I shall go into his presence to grant him unsurpassed awakening;
for this young woman, though I have told her 'she is my beloved,' does not at all act accordingly. (54)
To the question "For what purpose is this form to be abandoned?", he says: "The child," etc. (verse 54).
Therefore, in the form of an ascetic, I shall awaken my husband in an instant;
for my husband stands with a mind fully ripened through the maturation of his austerities.
How much less, then, could he have been awakened by one in the guise of an ascetic? To this, he says: "By her husband," etc. (55).
Thinking, "Today, my own true nature is reflected in this stainless mind," Cūḍālā became a young brahmin boy.
A "dvijadāraka" is the son of a brahmin. || 56 ||
Having slightly changed her form through meditation, like a wave of water in an instant,
she fell in that forest in the form of the son of a brahmin.
He explains how that came to be with the word "īṣat" (slightly): from a slight meditation accompanied by the previously mentioned dhāraṇā of Agni and Soma.
"Anyatva" means the state of being male. || 57 ||
With her face radiant with a gentle smile, she approached her husband;
then Śikhidhvaja saw that son of a brahmin walking ahead of him.
The "front" (agra) refers to the space in front. || 58 ||
He had come from within the forest, appearing as if asceticism itself had taken form;
his body was fair like molten gold, and he was adorned with a necklace of pearls.
His limbs were fair and clear yellow, like asceticism embodied or like molten gold. || 59 ||
Śikhidhvaja saw before him a lovely man walking ahead, his body adorned with a white sacred thread and clothed in a pair of white garments, carrying a water-pot.
He stood with a beautiful rosary of twice the length of his forearm encircling it,
its cord not touching the ground and measuring exactly one cubit.

He was characterized by a rosary of beads (akṣamālā) that extended from the forearm to the wrist, doubled in length on the outside; thus, being only a *kiṣku* (the span of a cubit) long—or, due to its doubling, only a *vitasti* (the span of a span)—and because it was not excessively long, its body did not touch the ground. || 61 ||
His head was covered with locks of hair like a lotus adorned with a garland of *sālī* flowers,
and he illuminated that region with circles of radiance emanating from his body.
His face was adorned with earrings like the newly risen sun;
with a mandāra flower fixed in his topknot, he resembled a mountain with the moon resting upon its peak.
He stood like a mountain, upon whose peak the moon was situated as if almost clinging to the summit. || 63 ||
He possessed a body that was both lovely and tranquil, yet powerful and with senses fully conquered;
adorned with a tilaka of ash as white as snow, he was beautiful to behold.
Beholding that son of the twice-born, who was as flickering as the full moon resting upon the golden slopes of Mount Meru, Śikhidhvaja rose up.
By the phrase "the golden slope of Meru," the flow of the Gaṅgā situated there is indicated; [he beheld] the full moon reflected therein, as if it were flickering.
Thinking that he was a son of the gods, he completely set aside his sandals and said:
"O son of the gods, salutations to you; please be seated on this seat. (66)
Thus he showed him a seat of leaves with his hand,
and placed a handful of flowers into the palm of the brahmin’s son.
A seat or mat made of leaves; in the hollow of the hand or upon the palm. || 67 ||
"Like moonlight upon a cluster of night-lotuses, or frost upon a sprout—O royal sage, salutations to you! thus spoke the son of the twice-born. (68)
Upon the sprout of a cluster of white water-lilies, it was like a mass of frost consisting of a multitude of ice particles.
Having taken flowers from it, he entered upon a seat of leaves.
Śikhidhvaja said:
"O son of a god, O highly fortunate one, from where have you come?"
I consider this day fruitful, since I have seen you today. (69)
Since I have seen you today on this very day. || 69 ||
This is the water for honor, this is the water for the feet, and these are the flowers, O giver of respect;
let these woven garlands be accepted—may it be well with you. (70)
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having spoken thus, O sinless one, Śikhidhvaja gave all of that— the water for the feet, the respectful offering, the garland, and the flowers— to the Goddess he desired.

"Without transgressing anything stated in the scriptures"—this is "yathākhilam. This is an *avyayībhāva* compound in the sense of "according to the object," used here to mean not exceeding the literal meaning of the words. (71)
Cūḍālā said:
I have wandered through very many abodes upon the earth,
yet this honor that I have received from you has not been obtained by me from anyone else.
It is understood that it was not obtained in such a manner from any other source. || 72 ||
O sinless one, by this charming, fitting, and humble demeanor of yours, I truly believe that you will surely live for an exceedingly long time.
The meaning is that by means of humility and discipline—indeed, by these characteristics, human beings become long-lived. || 73 ||
O holy one, have you perhaps accumulated the austerity for the sake of Nirvana with a peaceful mind, noble, and free from conceptual construction? (74)

In which [state] conceptual constructions and intentions regarding results have been cast far away and at a distance; for that very reason, you have gathered and accumulated noble austerity for the sake of Nirvana. "Kaccit" is a particle used in an inquiry regarding a desired matter. || 74 ||
O gentle one, this vow of yours is like the edge of a sword;
for you have abandoned a flourishing kingdom to dwell in the great forest. (75)

The meaning is that for those who are peaceful, free from anger, ascetics dwelling in the forest, this practice of frequenting the great forest—which has become their very vow—is as cruel as the edge of a sword and must be accomplished through extreme vigilance. || 75 ||
Śikhidhvaja said:
"O Blessed One, you know everything; you are a god, so what wonder is there in this? You are recognized by your world-transcending splendor itself, which serves as your identifying mark. (76)
Since it would be inappropriate to praise his abandonment of the kingdom and his practice of asceticism for the sake of attaining nirvana while they remain unknown,
the king— anticipating that he might achieve omniscience through those austerities— praises the son of the twice-born for his excellence in beauty and other qualities:
"It is my conviction that these limbs of yours were fashioned from the moon."
Or rather, why do you sprinkle me with what seems like nectar by your very glance? (77)
Or rather, what need is there for much? By your perfect gaze and by the luster of your body, you seem to sprinkle me with nectar. || 77 ||
"I have a beloved wife; she rules my kingdom today.
O handsome one, her limbs are seen here just like yours. (78)
And with this flower, he covered her body— from head to foot— which was tranquil and lovely, like a white cloud covering a mountain peak.
The "peak" (śṛṅga) is the summit of Mount Meru. By this [offering] in the form of a garland given by me. || 79 ||
I believe your body, which resembles the stainless moon and is as delicate as a flower petal, is suffering exhaustion from the splendor of the sun.
Your body is as delicate and tender as a petal or leaf of the *sumana* flower.
"O dear one, this white garment has been prepared by me in this manner for the worship of the gods; let it attain its purposeful fulfillment through contact with your body. (81)
This collection of flowers has been strung together white in this manner of visible variety; [the suffix] *kta* is used in the passive sense (*karman*) after the root *ṣiñ*, meaning "to bind.
"Aṅga" is a vocative particle. Therefore, the meaning is: "from the worship of you, the God. || 81 ||
One's life attains fulfillment by honoring a guest who has arrived;
to the virtuous, a guest is more worthy of honor than even a god. (82)

Since the honoring of guests is superior even to the worship of the gods, that alone is a cause for the success of one's birth; however, in your worship, both have been accomplished simultaneously for me, and thus my life is exceedingly successful—with this intention, he says: "My life... [and so forth].
Who are you, whose son are you, and by what grace have you come here?
O you with a face like the stainless moon, sever this doubt of mine.
Therefore, immediately after accepting the worship offered by me—this is the ellipsis. || 83 ||
The Brāhmaṇa said:
O King, listen to me; I shall speak without omission that which you have asked.
For what man would deceive one who inquires with such humility? (84)
Without overstepping what has been nourished, according to what was asked.
In this world-egg there exists the sage Nārada, whose soul is pure;
he is like a camphor tilaka upon the lovely face of auspicious Fortune. 85.
That which resembles the most fragrant camphor tilaka upon the lovely face of the beloved of the Goddess of Fortune—by this it is understood that Nārada has a fair-complexioned body. (85)
Once, that divine sage was established in meditation within a cave;
there, on the golden bank, the Ganges flows with its vast waves.
"In the cave of Meru"—this is the ellipsis to be supplied. || 86 ||
They shone like shimmering pearl necklaces upon the beauty of Mount Meru.
Once, on the bank of a river at the conclusion of his meditation, the sage Nārada—
Hearing the sound of tinkling bracelets and the playful chatter, he became somewhat curious, wondering, "What is this? (88)

In which [place] such a playful clamor—that sound of the tumult of water-sports—is resounded by tinkling bracelets; for the word *prāya* exists with a short final vowel (*a*) due to the abundance of its usage, as seen in the applications of Pāṇini, Jaimini, and others: "that food is in *prāya*," "a name in *prāya*," "born in *prāya*," and "from the form *prāya*. (88)
Looking casually at the river today, he saw a multitude of women,
mostly Rambhā and Tilottamā, who had come out for water-sports.
"Niryātam" means emerged from the water; "jalalīlayā" means by way of sporting in the water, such as splashing water and so forth. || 89 ||
She was playing, divested of her garments, in a place devoid of men,
with her rounded breasts resembling golden lotus buds.
Like trees with beautiful fruits entwined with one another,
they shone with expansive forms filled to overflowing with the essence of molten gold.

"Mutually entwined" means wrapped around; that is to say, "interlocked. With thighs that are radiant with a fullness and a configuration of luster—like the overflowing, excessive flow of molten liquid gold—he was creating a collection of pillars for his own temple of desire.
The subsequent [connection] is by means of another. || 91 ||
He was creating, with his thighs, a multitude of pillars for the temple of desire;
she, the celestial maiden, was pervaded by him who had purified the moon.

With the reflection of the moon rendered spotless by the purity of his own waters, he seemed to threaten and even humble the celestial river Mandākinī—the beauty of whose form plays throughout the sky—as she is entirely pervaded by that reflection; this is a poetic conceit (utprekṣā). || 92 ||
With its flood of the essence of loveliness, it seemed to threaten the river at its very edge;
with its ramparts, it was like the chariot wheels of the God of Love in the celestial gardens.

By him, the waters of the Gaṅgā were diverted from their course while playing in the Nandana grove— the celestial garden of the gods— due to obstructions formed by the ridges of his hips, which served as the rims of a chariot wheel for the Mind-born One, Kāma.
With the waters of the Gaṅgā diverted from their course by the embankments on the slopes of his hips,
he stood like the Universal Form (Viśvarūpa), with every limb visible everywhere.
Because it has attained a state of mutual reflection due to its extreme transparency, it possesses all its limbs reflected everywhere and has all its limbs seen everywhere;

thus, like the Universal Form (viśvarūpa) arisen from the presence of the Lord— the Kalpataru who is the Self of Time— it is known as "having hands and feet everywhere, and having eyes, heads, and faces everywhere."
The meaning is that it is established. || 94 ||
With all its limbs reflected and having become a mirror for one another,
it was like a leafy sprout from the branch of the rain-cloud upon the Kalpa-tree of Time.

The Lord’s nature as Time was demonstrated by His own words when He, having shown His universal form, was asked by Arjuna—who was terrified by that universal form—“Who are you, O one of such fierce form? and replied, “I am Time, the destroyer of worlds, grown mature; I have set out here to gather the worlds. Therefore, [Arjuna] [sought refuge] in Him alone, whose essence is Time.
He describes [the Lord] as being like a wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpataru*) because He bestows the fruits of all conceptualizations, using the words "rainy-season branches," and so forth.

The "branches" (*viṭapa*) are the trunks (*skandha*), which are the sixty years beginning with *prabhava*. By this, it is implicitly stated that the two solstices (*ayana*) and the months are His twigs. || 95 ||
From the forest of the sky, born from the pollen of the flowers of light, which is crowded with the buds of the splendor of day and possesses a network of various circular creepers; (96)

Born in the Nandana grove, which is characterized by a forest whose features are the unmanifest sky and various clusters of creepers with distinct characteristics consisting of groups of intermediate branches. 96.
From the single horse of the seven oceans, pierced by the birds of the shimmering waters, it was filled with intense passion as it vied with the clusters of her bud-like breasts. (97)

The connection with the preceding [verse] is as follows: it stands like the universal form (viśvarūpa) arisen from Viṣṇu—the Kalpa-tree of Time—from which seven oceans constitute a single basin (*ālavāḍaka*), for *ā* and *la* are interchangeable; and which is overspread by water-birds, that is, the gods, because their bodies are transformations of the moon consisting of water, and thus they are shimmering.

Furthermore, he further distinguishes that very group of young women with the words "breasts," etc.: by their repeatedly lifting [the lotuses] from the stalks and striking them against one another’s clusters of bud-like breasts— due to a rivalry prompted by the perception of a similarity in beauty— the lotus buds and petals were completely crushed.
The subsequent [sequence] follows from another. || 97 ||

Repeatedly lifting up her face, which was like a fully blossomed lotus with its petals slightly parted, and upon which the trembling curls of her hair and the pupils of her eyes appeared like hovering bees; (98)

By implication, it is that in which the tremulous curls—the *cūrṇakuntala* locks—upon the lotus-faces, the long tresses, the pupils of the eyes, and, by extension, the emerald and sapphire gems set in the forehead ornaments, act as honey-bees (*madhuvrata*). || 98 ||
By those who accumulated a treasury for the sake of warding off the calamities of death, [the lotus was made] difficult for the hosts of beings to attain—a blooming golden lotus. (99)
Furthermore, he describes what kind of group of women it was with the words beginning "amṛta":

by the gods (suraiḥ), who act as the repositories for the collection of the digits of nectar (amṛtakalākośasaṃgrahakāribhiḥ), [the place] was guarded (gupte) in a secluded spot for the sake of warding off the calamities (vighātāya) of the nectar brought about by those who would steal it, such as Rāhu and Garuḍa.

It was gathered together in one place within the interior of Meru’s cave, remaining like the full orb of the moon. To justify what was said there—that it was "hidden" (gupte)—he qualifies it as "difficult to reach" (duṣprāpe). The other qualifiers are intended to demonstrate that it is a location worthy of being a treasury of nectar (amṛtanidhāna). || 99 ||
In a secret cave within Mount Meru, concealed by the sprouts of lotus plants, on the cool bank of the celestial river whose impurities were washed away by the waters of the gods; (100)
Beholding that lovely woman, whose form was like the fullness of the lunar orb gathered together in one place, the mind of the sage was suddenly captivated. (101)

Having beheld such a lovely company of women, the mind of the sage thereafter became gladdened and intoxicated; the connection with the subsequent verse is that it became such that the portion of discernment was no longer relied upon. || 101 ||
When the mind was enveloped in bliss and agitated, and the vital breath (prāṇānila) remained steady, it became radiant and joyful, having transcended the portion consisting of discernment. 102.
Then, as he was filled with joy, there occurred a discharge of semen,
like a fruit full of juice, or like a raincloud at the end of summer.
Due to the agitation of the mind, there occurred a disturbance of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) throughout all the limbs; by that, the emission of semen—the essence of all the limbs—took place.
Thus he says, "it happened" (*babhūva*). Regarding this, he provides examples with the words beginning "the fruit" (*phalam*). || 103 ||
Like the finest stalk of a creeper severed from a fresh tree, or like the moon trembling with droplets of dew, so was the sage. (104)
Like a fresh, young tree—such as a banyan or similar species—whose root-stalk and base of the branches have been cut or wounded; "O Supreme One" (*uttama*) is an address to the King. 104.
The poison became like a double-falling [liquid], its essential juice trickling away.
Śikhidhvaja said:
"Even though that sage was such a man—possessed of great knowledge and liberated while living (jīvanmukta)—" (105).
"Like a lotus stalk (*bisam*) that has been suddenly split in two, or whose essence—the sap—has drained away;
[such is] the king's question, which is clear. (105)
Though free from desire, though free from attachment, and beyond all comparison, he is eternally as pure as space within and without. (106)
"Nārada too, O Brahmin, how did he become waylaid by passion?
Cūḍāla said: "O royal sage, for every species of living being in all the three worlds... (107)

He provides the answer with the words beginning "sarvasyā eva" (of everyone indeed), stating that even for those who possess knowledge of reality, there is still sometimes a persistence in the characteristics of the body due to the obstruction of the portion of discernment by extremely powerful *prārabdha* karma. 107.
This body of even the gods and others is by its very nature dualistic in essence;
whether one is ignorant or a knower of reality, as long as there is a physical frame, it remains so. (108)
"Until the end of one's own heart" means until the point of one's own destruction. || 108 ||
O dear one, it is remembered that the entire world consists of nothing but pleasure and pain;
pleasure increases through some object such as satisfaction and the like. (109)
He demonstrates that [the world] consists precisely of pleasure and pain by means of examples, beginning with "satisfaction" (tṛpti) and so forth. || 109 ||
For suffering is indeed [removed] by some object such as light by means of a lamp, or the great ocean by means of the moon, or hunger and so forth by some substance. (110)
" suffering increases"—this is what is being referred to. || 110 ||
For here, the cause is indeed one's own nature, like a veil of dark clouds, when the pure, true essential form has been forgotten for even a moment. (111)

Just as darkness increases at night when a cloth with the characteristics of a cloud is spread out, so it is here; for if such calamities occur even for those who possess the knowledge of reality when they momentarily forget their true nature, what need is there to mention those who lack such knowledge? With this intention, he says:
"The visible world attains expansion, like a rain-cloud in the monsoon."
Even from uninterrupted continuity, there is no opening [of the eyes] as long as it is not forgotten.

For this very reason, with the intention that one must always remain in a state of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) characterized by the non-forgetfulness of one's true nature (*svarūpa*) so as not to give rise to the visible world, he says: "Without ceasing" (*anārata*). Even for the duration of the interval between an opening and a closing of the eyes, this demon of the visible world does not cease to manifest within the mind in its true nature.
Just as day and night exist through the presence of darkness and light. || 113 ||
In the same way, the body has come to its state of existence through pleasure and pain;
for thus, these two—pleasure and pain—are seen to be the cause of birth. 114.

Thus, even though there is equality between the knower and the ignorant regarding the experience of the fruits of *prārabdha* karma, there is indeed a distinction caused by attachment and non-attachment;

this he establishes through two examples with the words beginning "evam" (thus): "Because of the perception of the cause of birth, which is the identification of the body and so forth as the Self. (114)
Just as saffron adheres firmly to a cloth that has become thick with ignorance,
it does not cling even slightly to the body of one who knows that reality, nor is he under its influence.
But for one who knows that, by virtue of that—that is, by virtue of the knowledge of reality—it does not adhere even in the slightest degree. || 115 ||
Just as the pure and impure [objects], being more intensely overcome by passion and so forth, cause a crystal to undergo coloring through the nature of the objects situated before it. (116)
Just as, within a crystal gem, due to the coloring through identification with a dye—
by the inclusion of the word "etcetera," including the superimposition of sapphire, ruby, and so forth— the two colors,
auspicious and inauspicious, such as saffron or indigo, become excessively transferred even though they are merely [superficially] covered by the dye, just like the coloring of a cloth.

The meaning is that, just as [the reflection] does not adhere to a gem due to its purity or impurity and other such qualities—implied by the word "ādi"—it is the same in this case. Now, he states the distinction [of the knower] from even a crystal, because the knower is clearer than the crystal: "puraḥsthe" (standing before one). A crystal may undergo a temporary coloring through the presence of objects such as a hibiscus flower standing before it; however, the knower [does not undergo even that].
The meaning is "it does not go. || 116 ||
The sage whose mind is liberated while living does not go [to rebirth] in that way due to his awakening;
rather, his intellect attains a state intensely colored by the mere superimposition of the objective world.

He explains what was stated—that [the error] reaches a state of firmness in the ignorant—by means of the verse beginning with "of the object" (vastunaḥ) and so forth. "Dense coloring" (ghana-rañjana) refers to the act of coloring. The word "intellect" (dhīḥ) is to be understood as "of the ignorant" (ajñasya), which is the ellipsis. || 117 ||
Even when the object has departed, the mind remains intensely tormented;
even when the saffron has vanished, the garment retains its coloring.
He asks "whence" regarding that, saying "even when gone": the meaning is that she becomes tormented for this reason. || 118 ||
Just as the deluded man does not abandon his attachment to sense objects, so too, by this very sequence, bondage and liberation are established. 119.

One does not abandon the coloring by objects. Thus, it follows that in the intellect (buddhi), the very accumulation of the latent impressions (vāsanā) of the coloring by objects is bondage, and their destruction alone is liberation; this is what he states with the words "by this. || 119 ||
Liberation is the attenuation of mental cultivation, for bondage is indeed firm cultivation.
Śikhidhvaja said:
Upon the attainment of the cause of one's own birth, how can there be either suffering or happiness? (120)

[The king asks] how pleasure and pain arise for one who identifies with sons, kingdom, and so forth—which are distant—or even for those things that are proximate, such as the gain or loss of wealth, when their causes of production are encountered; he asks this by saying, "svotpattī" (at their own production). || 120 ||
"Tell me, O Lord, how it arises even for those who are far away;
your speech is exceedingly noble, exceedingly pure, and full of profound meaning. (121)
"I do not reach satiety in hearing it, like a peacock at the sounds of clouds.
Cūḍālā said:
"Having obtained the delightful cause of its own origin through body, eyes, and hands... (122)
Therein, he first describes the manner in which happiness arises, beginning with the word "sa" (she).
Having obtained—that is, having perceived—a nearby object through the body, the senses, and the hands, and a distant object through sound, inference, and so forth;
this consciousness of happiness certainly arises spontaneously in the young girl. || 122 ||
Having reached the heart, she becomes agitated and enters the living soul situated within the Kuṇḍalinī.
Because they are ignorant of their own undivided true nature, this power residing in the heart— that is, situated within the intellect—
having become agitated by the agitation of the consciousness of one's own bliss, proceeds, according to the manner previously described,
toward the individual soul (*jīva*), the enjoyer, who is located in the *kuṇḍalinī*, since it brings about the vital breath originating from the mouth of the *kuṇḍalinī*.
It flashes forth and manifests from its own nature as the inner self (pratyagātmatattva), like sparks from a fire;
for the meaning is that according to the Śruti, "Other beings subsist on a mere fraction of this very bliss. || 123 ||
The channels of the living being are fixed, having established their positions separately within the body;
the living being, vibrating, enters those channels filled with vital breath.

Regarding the soul residing in the heart, he explains the distinction of the paths it takes when proceeding to the specific locations of experience, such as the eyes, tongue, ears, and so forth, for the sake of the experiencer: "of the jīva," etc. (verse 124).
With its essence awakened solely by contact—[the reading "of the nature of a stream" is consistent with the commentary]—it is like the sap of a tree or a creeper;
likewise during the movement of pleasant awakening and the arrival of painful awakening. (125)

The connection with what precedes is: "being of the nature of a continuous flow focused solely on each respective object through contact with that [object]. He provides an illustration for the soul's entry into the entire body by way of the channels (*nāḍī*): "As sap," etc. The meaning is: just as sap, when poured at the root, enters all parts of trees and creepers by way of their channels, so it is in this case. || 125 ||
The channels of the living being are fixed, yet they assume distinct positions within the body;
this [state] manifests quickly as fortitude for the happy one, but not for the suffering one.
The meaning is that they are fixed separately and not of a single form. From where is this known? To this he says: "of those who are happy.

For one who is happy—that is, for a living being engaged in the experience of pleasure—steadfastness, which is composure, shines forth; but not for one who is miserable, engaged in the experience of pain. For the latter is unsteady and wavering.
The meaning is that because he experiences himself as if being scorched, one infers that his channel-pathways are filled with the heat of bile and other such factors, and are agitated. || 126 ||
For those paths of one who is well-dressed and those of one who is poorly dressed are not auspicious;
rather, it is only as long as this life remains unquivering that it attains complete peace.

For this very reason, even in the world, it is well known that for those such as kings who are well-dressed and engaged in enjoyment, the paths are swept clean, sprinkled with camphor, sandalwood water, and flowers, and made fragrant with incense, musk, and the like; whereas for those who are ill-dressed and base, they are the opposite. Thus he says: "Those indeed... And so, as long as this individual soul [remains in this state]...

As long as [the mind], by not entering the pathways of the most flickering channels (*nāḍī*), does not vibrate and is itself devoid of flickering, there is no attachment to suffering for it. Then, through the mental modification (*vṛtti*) having the form of garlands, sandalwood, and so forth, its own innate bliss (*svātmasukha*) is manifested; however, through the modification having the form of Brahman, it is [manifested as] full. Thus, although there is a difference in degree, [the nature remains the same].

Because there is an absence of distraction, it indeed becomes completely tranquil; therefore, understand that for that duration, this [mind] remains in its own primordial state and is truly liberated.
The meaning is that liberation is simply the manifestation of one's own inherent bliss, since that is the very definition of liberation. || 127 ||
Know that he is indeed liberated for as long as this [state] remains; however, for as long as a greater measure of agitated wind continues to manifest, he is not yet fully released.
Know from me that this bound soul remains bound for exactly that duration; the vibration of even a fraction of pleasure or pain is the bondage of the living being, and nothing else.

In that case, why is it that the experience of liberation is not realized by the *jīva* at the time of experiencing sensory pleasure? [The answer is: "Because there is no pleasure" (*asukha*) therein.

The mention of "suffering" (*duḥkha*) is for the sake of providing an illustration. The "apprehension of a portion" (*kalānubhava*) refers to the perception of even sensory pleasure as being nothing but suffering; for that purpose, there is the outward movement of the mind toward passion and so forth, as well as the interruption of pleasure.

The state of instability, which is the vibration toward the acquisition of the means for that [instability] amidst thousands of misfortunes—that alone is the bondage of the living soul, and not even a fraction of repose in happiness;

thus, since liberation would indeed occur through even a moment’s repose in happiness when that [bondage] is absent, it follows that I have stated the twofold establishment of bondage and liberation by way of wandering in saṃsāra and not wandering. This is the connection with what follows.
For in the absence of that [duality], liberation would occur; thus there is a twofold establishment [of the path].
As long as the states of pleasure and pain are brought about by the deceitful senses, [liberation remains unattained]. (130)
He elaborates on the very point already stated with the verse beginning "pleasure and pain" (sukhaduḥkha) and so forth. || 130 ||
For that long, the gentle Jīva remains peaceful, as if in a state of equanimity with happiness;
yet, upon perceiving pleasure or pain, his body begins to tremble, having transcended the senses.
That which transcends the senses, is inaccessible to the faculties, and is, in short, self-luminous. || 131 ||
The individual soul rejoices within upon seeing [the Self], like the ocean at the sight of the moon;
yet, O dear one, the soul is agitated by the perception of pleasure and other such experiences. (132)
One is agitated by perceived pleasure and so forth—by pleasure, its means, the objects thereof, and the wealth that serves as its instrument—as well as by the consciousness of attachment toward them.
The word "aṅga" is used for the purpose of addressing [the listener]. || 132 ||
Just as a cat [is driven] by meat, here the cause is nothing but ignorance;
for one whose nature consists of the knowledge of one's own self through pure awakening of that which is to be known. 133.

In this context of agitation (*kṣobha*), the cause is ignorance of one's own true nature (*svatattva*), which is nothing other than delusion (*maurkhya*). By what, then, does its cessation lead to rest? To this he says: "By the pure," and so forth. One's own self (*svātman*) is that which must necessarily be known;
[rest is attained] through the awakening to that. 133.
Thinking that pleasure, pain, and so forth do not exist, he thereby attains a state of serenity:
"That pleasure and so forth do not belong to me, nor does this 'I' of mine exist in vain. (134)
Gentleness and rest. || 134 ||

Thus, when awakened, the living soul indeed attains nirvāṇa and becomes tranquil; for through the internal consciousness of awakening, it realizes that pleasure and the like are non-entities, lacking its true nature. (135)
The individual soul does not turn toward that [external world], but merely becomes stilled when there is a firm conviction that the entire expanse of consciousness is Brahman. (136)
When it has reached stability, the individual soul attains tranquility like a lamp without oil;
it reaches peace like a lamp when the fuel of pleasure and other attachments is exhausted. (137)
Attachment to pleasure and the like is passion; when that is extinguished, [passion ceases]. || 137 ||

Through the knowledge that "all is thus" and by contemplating the non-duality of the living soul, one realizes that everything is indeed only space; having understood this, one does not undergo agitation.

From the knowledge that the entire world is thus nothing but pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), there arises non-duality (*advaita*) and unity through the contemplation thereof; [the world] is like the empty sky. || 138 ||
What indeed can be the agitation or delusion of a soul that is empty of such [qualities], just as it was from the very beginning of creation by means of such a soul? (139)

By this reason—namely, the contemplation of oneness with Brahman—one who is devoid of separateness or devoid of bondage [is liberated]. If so, how then did this delusion of agitation come to him? To that he says: "by the individual soul" (*jīvena*).

By such an imagined primordial individual soul, Hiraṇyagarbha himself, who is the self of all individual souls, [thinking] "I shall indeed transmigrate," [he conceives this] from the lack of awakening to his own true nature.

The meaning is that, having imagined the paths of bondage and liberation through one's own conceptualization alone—thinking "I shall gradually become liberated"—one simply follows that very [conceptual construction]. || 139 ||
"The path is known by oneself; one travels along it even today by that very same way.
Śikhidhvaja said:
"While the vital breath moves through the channels suitable for easy passage,"
The question is clear. || 140 ||
"O Devaputra, how does that loss of vigor occur?
Cūḍālā replied:
"The individual soul (jīva), when agitated, disturbs the series of vital breaths beginning with prāṇa. (141)
Being agitated by the awakening of the latent impression of passion upon seeing the body of a woman. || 141 ||
By means of consciousness, through its mere cognitive aspect, it stands like a king over an army;
within it, differentiation and the very essence of the marrow are established by the movement of the vital breath.
He explains how it causes agitation there: "by consciousness, by the mere portion of knowledge.

The meaning is this: the "command" (ājñā) is of the nature of permission, which conforms to the arising of mental states such as passion in the individual soul's consciousness (jīva-saṃvit)—the presiding power over the vital breaths (prāṇa) and so forth, which are active by nature—by means of that mere portion [of consciousness]. There is a distinction [between this] and that which moves within from beginning to end.
By the vibration— that is, the impulsion— of the vyāna-vāyu, the internal essence situated in all the limbs, including the marrow-essence,
quickly sheds its own subtle portion of *rajas*, which is followed by a state of exquisite fragrance;
just as a leaf, fruit, or the like, when its stalk is severed, sheds the portion of water within it through the vibration of the internal air.
The meaning is "just like that. || 142 ||
Just as dust, petals, fruits, and the like quickly lose their fragrance and,
once displaced by a thunderclap or similar force, fall downward from the sky, so too does it [the mind] fall away.
That *rajas*, having been abandoned, moves from all the limbs and, through the channels (*nāḍīs*), goes downward to the location of the *mūlādhāra*.

Just as water spread everywhere in the sky becomes a thundering mass due to the "thunder"—the *purovāta* wind—and by that cause becomes unified into a dense cloud, reaching states such as a rain-cloud and becoming intent on raining; so too [does the *rajas*].
The meaning is that it goes to a place where it was not present, just like that [sound]. || 143 ||
"Through the channel of the body's veins, the semen naturally flows outward.
Śikhidhvaja said:
"O son of a god, you are one of great knowledge; you know both the past and its present state. (144)
"By itself," that is, by its own nature (*svabhāvataḥ*). Regarding what you have said—that even for gods and others, this body is inherently composed of two parts—the King asks:
"O son of a god, what is the meaning of the word 'nature' (*svabhāva*)? [The Bodhisattva replies:
"I am one who is both great and wise (*mahājña*), a knower of the reality of the self (*ātmatattvavid*); yet prior to the knowledge of the self, I was also aware of the existence of worldly objects."
You understand through skill in reasoning and so forth. || 144 ||
"You are known by your speech alone; for what is called 'intrinsic nature'?
Cūḍālā said: "Just as in the primal creation, Brahman immediately manifested within Brahman. (145)

To the question, "How am I known by her to be such?", he says: "You are known. At the time of creation and so forth, when Brahman is oriented toward emanation, whatever object manifests within its own self with whatever specific attributes in accordance with the prior karma of living beings, there is for that object a fixed necessity (*niyati*) to possess those same attributes until the dissolution (*pralaya*).
He states that the word "nature" (svabhāva) refers to the meaning [of the term]—namely, "in the first creation"—in verse 145.
The nature of jars, pits, cloths, and so forth is likewise established from the very beginning;

like a chance occurrence (*kākatālīya*), like the arising and perishing of water bubbles, or like letters carved by a woodworm (*ghuṇākṣara*), the wise know that [world] to be a mere swelling [of appearance]. (146)
The diversity of the natures of present objects such as jars could be accounted for even by the diversity of perceived causal conditions (*sāmagrī*).

However, at the beginning of creation, since such an investigation is impossible, it is like a palm fruit falling by chance onto a crow’s head at the very moment the crow arrives; thus, the destruction [of the world] is brought about solely by the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*).

He reveals his intention—that the pursuit of the first creation is for the sake of awakening—by means of the verse beginning with "kāka. The suffix *cha* (forming *cchapa*) is used here in the sense of the third type of comparison (*iva*), according to the rule "from a compound [ending in *iva*] when it refers to that object," meaning from a compound whose objects are the two senses of *iva*. Even regarding the diversity of natures restricted by place and time in contemporary individual entities, it is impossible to determine the full extent of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*).

With the intention that it is possible, he states another illustration: "like a water bubble. With the intention that because it is merely an illusion (māyāmātra), its occurrence may be accidental, he states another illustration: "like the letters [carved] by a wood-boring insect. || 146 ||
In this world grown forth by the power of its own nature, various bodies wander about with diverse transformations;
some, through the exhaustion of their latent impressions (*vāsanā*), do not come into being again, while others, possessing dense attachments, arise once more.

In this world, which has grown forth by virtue of the nature of the characteristics already described, bodies of four kinds—such as those born from eggs and so forth—which consist of various transformations, wander about. Among them, some are bodies of knowledge; because their latent impressions (*vāsanā*) have been exhausted, they do not come into existence again. Others, however, are bodies of ignorance; they do indeed come into existence again, because they remain attached solely to enjoyments.
The meaning is that there is intense attachment. || 147 ||

Thus ends the eighty-fifth chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Yoga of Contemplating Happiness," in the *Pūrva-cūḍā* of the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*, composed by Vālmīki. 85.
Thus ends the eighty-fifth chapter, titled "Instruction on the Yoga of Contemplating Happiness," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa-tātparyaprakāśa*.
The eighty-sixth canto.
Cūḍālā said:
This great world has arisen through the power of the inherent nature of the Self.
Having attained its state through latent impressions (vāsanā), it remains under the influence of merit and demerit (dharma-adharma). || 1 ||
In this [chapter], it is described how the birth of Kumbha occurred from Kumbha, his growth, his meeting with Brahmā,
and how, at that time, the disciple attained omniscience, and so forth.

Just as the nature characterized as previously described is established in all things until the final dissolution, so too the nature of the Self, variegated by *māyā*, consisting of creation and so forth, is established by the *Śruti* and other authorities; the meaning is that [the world] proceeds under its control.
Some say creation is for the sake of enjoyment, others say it is for the sake of sport; this is the inherent nature of the Divine, who has attained all desires.
"What longing could there be?"—thus says the venerable Gauḍapāda. (1)
"O Sage, our view is that once the latent impressions have been attenuated, one is no longer grasped by merit and demerit; consequently, a living being is not born again. (2)
The reduction of latent impressions through the practice of knowledge and their subsequent exhaustion—this is our view; this is our experience. (2)
Śikhidhvaja said:

"O best among speakers, you speak that which is exceedingly noble and of great significance; it has ascended to the level of direct experience, yet it is profound and possesses the nature of the supreme reality."

When this aesthetic wonder of experience had been thus described, the King, desiring to hear its specific mode and praising her, said "It is most noble," and so forth, in order to conclude the remaining part of the narrative currently underway in brief. (3)
O handsome one, by hearing this power of your speech today, I have attained an inner coolness as if I had drunk nectar. (4)
Therefore, tell me briefly and quickly that very account of your own birth;
thereafter, I shall listen with diligence to your speech which is pregnant with knowledge.
Tell me today exactly how that heroic deed was performed by that noble sage Nārada, the son of Padmaja.
Where and by whom was it made and established? || 6 ||

Cūḍālā said: Then, by him [the King], who was binding the intoxicated elephant of the mind to the vast tethering post of discernment with the pure rope of wisdom, [the state of liberation was attained].
At the *ālāna*, the pillar for tying an elephant; by means of the excellent triple-stranded leather rope, characterized as such. || 7 ||
That potency is like the liquid of the moon melted by the fire at the end of an aeon;
it is the coloring agent for divine substances such as mercury and the rest. (8)
That which has the appearance of the liquid of the moon melted by the fire associated with the end of the eon (kalpa);
that is to say, it resembles—meaning it imitates—the coloring of the essences of mercury, gold, silver, and so forth, which are the vital energies (vīrya) of Śambhu. || 8 ||
By the Sage, his form was placed, as if the moon were set within the moon, into a wondrous crystal pitcher standing at his side, which shone with radiant luster. || 9 ||
There, on that mountain which was vast and beautiful, [the cave] was thick on all its sides,
