with a deep interior, very firm, and capable of withstanding the striking of stones.

There, on Mount Meru—on its sides and all around—it was thick and vast, and for that very reason it had a deep interior. It was capable of withstanding being struck or pounded against stones; the proof of its extreme solidity was that it did not crack even while being beaten. Such was that jar, which was filled with milk produced by the mental resolve of Nārada.
The subsequent [inference] is by means of positive concomitance (anvaya). || 10 ||
That jar was filled by him with the milk he had intended,
just as the ocean of nectar was filled by Brahmā with the overflowing flood of nectar.

The meaning is as follows: by the Creator—who is of the nature of a flood of nectar created by His own volition—through a distinct and divided method, the ocean of nectar well-known in the Vedas within the world of Brahmā was filled, just as [this] ocean has been filled.
Therein, the sage’s sequence of slow oblations increased for a month.
In the ocean of nectar, he was a beautiful embryo, like a second moon born after the moon.

There, because he was slow in the sequence of offerings for the fire-rituals as the sage was intent on the milk for the oblation, he is called "Munimandāhutikrama"; thus, like the moon's younger brother [the planet Mercury] reflected in the ocean of nectar, he grew. 12.
In due time, Ghaṭa gave birth to a lotus-petal-eyed embryo, just as the month gives birth to the full moon, or as the spring brings forth a flower.
Like the full moon at the end of the month. || 13 ||
With all his limbs fully complete, the fetus emerged from the jar like another moon, free from waning, arising from the subtle depths of the ocean.
Like another moon that is free from waning, [arising] from the ocean of milk, which is subtle and limited by a jar. || 14 ||
In just a few days, he attained full growth, his bodily beauty becoming immeasurable like the moon in the bright fortnight. || 15 ||
In that sage Nārada, who was endowed with all accomplishments,
he won the entire wealth of knowledge, as if transferring it from one vessel to another.
When that son was endowed with all the purificatory rites (saṃskāra), beginning with the birth-ceremony (jātakarman) and ending with the initiation (upanayana). || 16 ||
In just a few days, having mastered the entirety of all branches of knowledge,
the best of sages made him his very own reflection.
One by whom all branches of learning and the fields of knowledge have been understood without exception—such a person [is he]. (17)
With that son who was a sage,
the Leader of Sages shone like the moon risen at twilight upon a mountain of jewels, reflected therein.
On the jewel-mountain, the crystal peak; that is to say, the full moon has risen at twilight. || 18 ||
Then, taking his son with him, Nārada went to the world of Brahmā and paid homage to his father, Brahmā.
Then Brahmā, having received the salutation from his grandson who had first offered salutations to the Vedas and other sciences, took him onto his own lap.

Having had him play before him after he had been tested by playing the lute with proficiency in grasping and retaining the music, he should affectionately place such a person—who has examined all branches of knowledge beginning with the Vedas—upon his lap. || 20 ||
Then, by means of a mere benediction, the Lotus-born [Brahmā] made that grandson named Kumbha omniscient and one who had reached the further shore of knowledge.
In Jñānā, he brought his realization of reality to rest, having reached the further shore, which is the ultimate limit. || 21 ||
"O virtuous one, I am he; I am this jar. I am the grandson of the Lotus-born Brahmā, the son of the sage Nārada; I am named Kumbha, born from a jar."

"O virtuous one, that jar is this very one standing before you; it is I. "But how can such a falsehood be spoken by the daughter of Vidarbha, Cūḍālā, who knows the dharma, in the presence of her own husband, who is the supreme deity for women?
A man kills a hundred horses by lying regarding a horse, but he kills a thousand cows by lying regarding a cow; by lying regarding himself, he kills his own kin."

"Regarding falsehood concerning a person"—thus was the statement of Śrī Rāma in the *Pūrva-Rāmāyaṇa*. And in the *Mahābhārata*, Śakuntalā’s words to Bharata are: "He who represents himself as one thing when he is another—what sin has not been committed by that thief who steals his own self? If it is argued that [the opponent] would be thus provoked, this is not a fault.

Since there is no falsehood in the statement "Babara Pravāhaṇi desired," "The mind is a thief, speech is a liar," and "The pressing-stones float"— insofar as it serves to inspire interest in the Brahma-vidyā about to be taught and does not contradict the meaning that constitutes its intended purport.

This is because its validity is established just like Vedic explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) such as those cited above. Furthermore, through the power of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), one attains universal identity; thus, statements such as "I was Manu and Sūrya," spoken by Vāmadeva, or "I am this jar," are not false. Nor is there the fault of deceiving one's husband, for [the wife] always [acts] through action, mind, and speech...

Because of the injunction that "one should act for the benefit of one's husband," this statement—which produces the husband's confidence in learning—is his supreme benefit; therefore, it cannot be considered a deception. || 22 ||
I dwell at ease with my father in the city of the Lotus-born;
the four Vedas are my friends, sporting in playful delight. (23)
Gāyatrī is my maternal aunt and Sarasvatī is my mother;
my home is in the world of Brahmā, and there I, as a grandson, am well-established.
With the intention that, in the absence of his own mother, the mother and others of his father are indeed his own mother and others, he says:
"I wander through the worlds in their entirety according to my will, out of playful sport because of my perfection, and not for any purpose whatsoever. (25)
Though my feet move, they do not fall upon the earth; dust does not touch my limbs, and my body feels no fatigue. || 26 ||
To inspire confidence in what has been said, he displays his own divine marks: "The earth," etc.
While I am falling toward the earth and moving through the world of mortals, my feet do not touch the surface of the ground. (26)
"Today, traveling through the path of the sky, I saw you before me; therefore, my dear, I have come here and have told you everything. (27)
"O you who know that forest life, I have indeed described everything exactly as it was experienced by me, thinking 'this is I.
For the virtuous, being skilled in auspicious conduct, find great delight in conversation with the best of noble people."

He concludes the discourse with the words "eṣa" (this one). O knower of forest-dwelling—meaning you who know the virtues of forest life and its fruit, which is the purification of the mind—I am this very person possessing the aforementioned birth and so forth; thus, everything you asked has been described by me exactly as it was experienced. The substitution of "te" for "tvayi" at the beginning of the verse is a Vedic usage (*chandasaḥ*). [This applies] among the best of noble persons.

When people ask questions, the virtuous indeed engage in discourse; for they are skilled in the practice of dialogue consisting of questions and answers with noble and fortunate persons. Therefore, ask whatever you desire;
the sense is that I am capable of explaining it. || 28 ||
Śrī Vālmīki said:
When the sage had thus spoken, the day passed away; the sun went to its setting for the performance of the evening rites.
Having offered salutations, the assembly departed to bathe; and at the end of the night, they returned along with the rays of the sun.
Thus ends the eighty-sixth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Birth of the Jar-born," in the *Pūrva-cūḍālā-upākhyāna* within the *Mokṣa-nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*.
Thus ends the eighty-sixth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Birth of the Jar-born," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa-tātparya-prakāśa*.
The eighteenth day;
the eighty-seventh canto.
Śikhidhvaja said:
I believe you have been sent here by my merits, which are manifesting in this creation,
like a cloud driven by great winds on a mountain that are gathered but remain invisible.
In this [chapter], the praise of Kumbha, the king’s disclosure of his own suffering,
his discipleship for the sake of instruction, and his trust are described.

I believe—that is, I imagine—that you have been sent here to this Mount Mandara by my merits, which were accumulated and stored throughout the cycle of existence (saṃsāra) characterized by a succession of births; which, through the simultaneous ripening of destiny and other factors, are now manifesting to bestow their fruit. [This is due to] the great winds from the east. || 1 ||
O virtuous one, by virtue of my meeting with you today through your speech that distills nectar, I stand at the forefront of the blessed. (2)
To indicate that my fulfillment of purpose is certain to occur through your instruction, he speaks as if it were already accomplished:
"No worldly conditions whatsoever cool my heart in the same way that the company of the virtuous does—not even these things such as the acquisition of a kingdom. (3)
Where the unobstructed aesthetic flavor unfolds in its universality, that state—free from thoughts of passion and the like—brings the bliss of creative imagination. (4)
He demonstrates the excellence found in the assembly of the virtuous by contrast with the pursuit of royal power and the like, stating: "Nirargala...

In that assembly of the virtuous, where there is unrestrained rasa—the undivided bliss of Brahman—it unfolds in such a way that all mental constructions such as passion and the like are liberated, and this occurs in a general manner common to all people, including the poor and the rest.
The meaning is that the attainment of such things as that kingdom brings only trivial pleasure through mere imagination; it does not bring unimpeded happiness, nor is it common [to all]. || 4 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: While the king was speaking thus, Cūḍālā, who had assumed the form of a young sage, interrupted his words and spoke once more.
"Having projected and suppressed" means: before the intended meaning has even been completed. || 5 ||
Cūḍālā said: Let this story rest for now; I have described everything to you.
O virtuous one, tell me: who are you, and what are you doing on this mountain?
Let this discourse in praise of me be; "all that you asked" is the understood remainder. || 6 ||
To what extent will this forest-dwelling of yours continue?
Ascetics know how to speak both truth and untruth regarding our affairs. (7)
"How long will it last? means "what is its duration until its end?"—that is, "how much time does it extend to?

Tell the truth regarding the purpose and the task to be accomplished through dwelling in the forest; do not conceal it. For ascetics such as you do not know how to speak untruth; indeed, they do not know [how to do so]. || 7 ||
Śikhidhvaja said:
"You are a son of the gods; you know everything exactly as it is.
You are an expert in the affairs of the world; what else shall I say?"
"O Noble One, because I am terrified by the fear of saṃsāra, I dwell within the forest; though you already know me, I shall nevertheless tell you something of myself."
*Manāk* means slightly; that is to say, in brief. || 9 ||
"I am King Śikhidhvaja; having renounced my kingdom, I have stayed here.
O knower of reality, I am deeply afraid of rebirth within this cycle of worldly existence. (10)
"He is established in austerity"—this is the ellipsis. O knower of reality, he is afraid of rebirth. || 10 ||
"O knower of reality, because happiness repeatedly turns into suffering and birth and death recur, I am distressed while wandering through the forest paths. (11)
They are born from you; I am performing austerity, I am consumed by heat, and I practice penance. || 11 ||
Though wandering to the ends of the earth and though roaming about, O scorcher of foes,
I find no rest, like a poor man who has not found a single treasure.
O holy one, though I am effortless, fruitless, solitary, incomplete, and devoid of companionship, I wither here in this forest like a tree gnawed by woodworms. (13)

"Exertionless" means one whose effort has been blunted; "fruitless" means one who has not attained the fruit; "alone" means without assistance; "by whom the association with the virtuous—well-known during the time of his reign—and the association with creepers and the like, have been cast away"; and "gnawed by woodworms" means pierced or damaged by insects that eat wood. || 13 ||
Even while perfectly performing this unimpaired practice, I pass from sorrow to a flood of sorrows; for me, nectar has become poison. (14)

This [practice], consisting of fasting, worship of the deity, honoring guests, and so forth, is "unbroken," meaning it is observed for a fixed duration. Furthermore, although it has been adopted for the sake of final repose—based on such scriptural passages as, "He who knows both knowledge and ignorance together; having crossed over death by means of ignorance, he enjoys immortality through knowledge"—wherein "immortality" is understood as the cause of liberation (amṛtatva), [the text continues]:
My meditation, accumulated through ritual action, stands like poison because it produces no rest; the sense is: for what reason is that so? || 14 ||
Cūḍālā said: "O Grandfather, once in the past I asked this of you:
'O Lord, tell me which is superior—the path of action or the path of knowledge? (15)

Thinking that liberation results from the combined practice of ritual action and meditation, the king’s delusion must first be dispelled; otherwise, he will not comprehend the reality of the Self even when it has been taught. To dispel that delusion, [the teacher] causes him to hear the sequence taught by his own grandfather, beginning with the words "the grandfather. Between ritual action and knowledge, whichever one...
The meaning is: "Tell me that which is the cause of liberation. || 15 ||
Brahmā said:
"Knowledge is indeed the supreme good; through it, one fully realizes absolute liberation (kaivalya).
Ritual action has been prescribed merely for the passing of time and for diversion."

He knows and directly experiences [the Self]. As for ritual action (*kriyā*), although it is undertaken for the sake of the diversion of enjoying heaven and so forth, because its fruit is trivial and lacks the status of a true human goal (*puruṣārtha*), it is merely taught by the Śruti as a means to pass the duration of one's life by not accumulating misfortune; this is the meaning. And thus says the Śruti: "Performing actions here indeed, one should desire to live a hundred years; even so in you..."
"There is no other way than this; action does not cling to the man. || 16 ||
For those who have not attained the vision of knowledge, ritual action is centered on their offspring;
how can one who possesses neither a garment, nor a cloth, nor a blanket give anything away? (17)

For this very reason, this Śruti passage—"knowledge and ignorance"—and the other Śruti passage concerning those not qualified for knowledge, intend that the "crossing over death" therein refers to the cessation of natural evil conduct, and that "immortality" is intended in a relative sense; with this intention, he says: "not having obtained... Since a grandson is also an offspring, he uses the term "son."
For the ignorant person, all actions are fruitful because they have the latent impressions (vāsanā) alone as their essence;
for the knower, however, they are entirely fruitless due to the total destruction of those very latent impressions.
But surely, even those possessing knowledge are seen performing actions appropriate to their own caste and stage of life;
how then can it be said that ritual action is a refuge only for those who have not yet attained the vision of knowledge? To this, he says: "Vāsanā.
One who possesses faith or one who is attached experiences the fruit of prescribed and prohibited actions. And yet—
The sense is that faith can arise only when the latent impressions (vāsanās) of being an agent and an enjoyer have been destroyed;
the word "mātra" signifies totality. || 18 ||
For in the absence of latent impressions (vāsanā), all actions become fruitless, just as even productive creepers wither in the absence of watering. (19)
"Are impure actions likewise [destroyed]? He says, "Yes"—that is, "indeed all. Regarding the phrase "even those that bear fruit":

where even actions whose fruits have already begun (ārabdhaphala) become like mere dry twigs, fruitful only through a persistence of what has been obstructed, then what need is there to mention that those whose fruits have not yet begun perish? Where trees are burned, what [remains] of the grasses there?
The meaning is that it is according to the principle of "kathā" (the story/discourse). || 19 ||
Just as the seasonal product of a previous season dissolves when another season arrives, even so the fruit of action perishes upon the destruction of its latent impressions (vāsanā). || 20 ||
"In another season," such as summer, autumn, and so forth; "the previous seasonal sign," such as frost, clouds, and the like. (20)
Just as the fruit of the *śarala* reed does not ripen by its own nature, so too,
O son, an action devoid of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) does not bear fruit.

If it is asked, "Why does even an action devoid of latent impressions (vāsanā) not bear fruit?", he says "No," [meaning it does not], because its very nature is like that of a blade of grass. || 21 ||
A fool whose latent impressions are those of a yakṣa sees a yakṣa, and not otherwise;
a deluded person whose latent impressions are those of suffering sees suffering, and not otherwise. (22)

With the intention that it is precisely the latent impression (*vāsanā*)—namely, "I am fit to experience pleasure and pain"—that serves as the seed for the emergence of this or that [experience], just as the impression of a child's ghost (*yakṣa*) is the cause for the fruit of the delusion of a ghost, he says: "sayakṣa... (verse 22).
Even an action that is highly brilliant in its form does not yield fruit—
whether auspicious or inauspicious— for one who knows that [reality], just like a blossoming *śaralata* creeper.
In this state, there is no latent impression (vāsanā) whatsoever consisting of egoism and the like;
it has arisen as something unreal through ignorance, like a mirage-ocean in a desert. (24)

Now, one might ask: since a latent impression (*vāsanā*) is capable of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) during the state of ignorance, how can it be sublated by knowledge? To this, he says: "The latent impression... [and so on]. Here, even in the state of ignorance... (24)
For one whose ignorance has reached its end through the contemplation that "all is Brahman," no latent impression arises,
just as the ocean does not exist in a desert for a wise man.
Even if past latent impressions (*vāsanā*) have been destroyed, one might argue that action performed after the arising of knowledge should still bear fruit; to this he says:
"By the complete abandonment of all latent impressions, the living being attains within itself that state which is free from old age and death, and further devoid of rebirth. (26)
The "foot" (pada) is the reality that is the supreme human goal. || 26 ||
The mind accompanied by latent impressions (vāsanā) is the object of knowledge; the mind free from latent impressions is knowledge itself.
Having reached the object of knowledge through knowledge, the living being is not born again.
He concludes the statement of the Grandfather with the words: "By knowledge" (jñānena). || 27 ||
Cūḍālā said:
"O royal sage, even Brahmā and the other great ones have declared that knowledge alone is the supreme good; why then do you remain in ignorance? (28)
The meaning is: having abandoned knowledge and being ignorant, what did he do after resolving that austerity alone is the cause of liberation? || 28 ||
The water-pot is here, the wooden staff is there, and the grass mat is over there;
O Lord of the Earth, why do you take delight in this display of useless things? (29)

With the intention that for one devoid of discrimination and turned toward the external world, even a small thing such as a staff or a water-pot is sufficient for misfortune when it becomes an object of possessiveness and the like, he says: "From this... (29).
"Who am I? How was this world born? And how is it pacified?
O King, why do you not investigate these things; why do you remain like one who is ignorant? (30)
If even austerity is useless and should be abandoned, then what is to be adopted? To this he says: "Who am I?"—you do not look upon it, you do not investigate it.
"O King, why do you not serve the feet of those who know the near and the far shores, while posing such questions as 'What is bondage? and 'What is liberation? (31)
He shows that just like *vicāra* (investigation), approaching, serving, and questioning the Guru are also to be adopted—answering the question "How?"—by stating:

"The further shore (*pāra*) of the ocean of *saṃsāra* is the purified referent of the word *tat*, whose nature is pure Being (*sanmātra*). The near shore (*avāra*) is the referent of the word *tvaṃ*, whose nature is pure Consciousness (*cinmātra*)."

The meaning is: "of those who know the meaning of the sentence characterized by the indivisible unity [of Brahman], whose *tat* and *tvam* components have been purified. Alternatively, it means: "of those who know the ocean of supreme bliss (*pārāvāra*). || 31 ||
Why do you remain like a stone-worm in a mountain cave, passing your life with this activity of barely perceptible consciousness? (32)

By means of this practice of austerity—which consists of a self-awareness inclined toward activities that yield suffering such as vows, fasting, cold, and heat, and which is difficult to endure—he was wasting away his life, which is like iron. || 32 ||
That yoga, by which one is liberated, is obtained through inquiry, service, and association with the virtuous who possess equal vision. (33)
That method of knowledge bestows the bliss of rest desired by you. || 33 ||
Eating your morsel of food only with the virtuous, remain in the hollow of a forest tree, suppressing your wicked impulses like a worm in a crevice of the earth. (34)

If so, how should I conduct myself now? To this he says: "By the virtuous one alone" (*sādhunaiva*). Being one by whom outward-directed evil activities—such as the hardships of asceticism (*tapas*) and the like—are suppressed or restrained, he should, together with a virtuous Guru, eat his morsel of food while being intent on serving him and devoted to the meaning taught by him.
The meaning is: remain motionless like an insect in a hole in the earth. || 34 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Thus enlightened by that wife of divine form,
Śikhidhvaja, his face filled with tears, spoke these words.
Śikhidhvaja said:
"O son of a god, today at long last I have been awakened by you!
Out of folly, I abandoned the company of noble men and dwelt in the forest."
"Aha! I believe my sin has been entirely destroyed, since you yourself have come here and awakened me. (37)
"You are my guru, you are my father, and you are my friend, O fair-faced one;
as a disciple, I now bow at your feet—please show me your compassion. (38)
Teach me quickly that Brahman which you know to be the most sublime, by knowing which one no longer grieves, and through which I may become liberated.
He is extinguished and rests in bliss. || 39 ||
Within consciousness there are numerous divisions, such as the cognition of a jar and so forth;
among these cognitions, which one would be the supreme cognition that acts as a savior? (40)

Regarding what you have called the supreme, liberating knowledge—that "knowledge alone is the highest good"—among these various forms of knowledge, which one would it be? The sense is: is that knowledge merely concerned with an external object, or is it of a different nature? || 40 ||
Cūḍālā said: "O royal sage, if my words are worthy of being accepted by you, then I shall speak to you;
otherwise, I will not speak this knowledge at all, like the woodpecker and the pillar. (41)

"Have faith, O gentle one"—according to this Vedic injunction, instruction given even to those lacking faith is as useless and contemptible as the cawing of a crow before a pillar; therefore, He says "If [you have faith]" so that you may first become faithful.
Then, in that case, I shall speak—that is, declare—this knowledge which you have asked about, exactly as it is. || 41 ||
The words of a speaker whose speech is not to be accepted, when questioned in jest, go to fruitlessness—just as visual perceptions do in the darkness. (42)
The words of a speaker who is questioned playfully or without serious intent are like the cognitions of the senses arising from the contact of the eyes with objects. 42.
Śikhidhvaja said:
"Whatever you say is to be accepted by me, like the injunction of the Veda;
this word of mine is true and must be carried out immediately without hesitation. (43)

The meaning is that, just as the injunctions of the Veda such as "one desiring heaven should sacrifice" are adopted by the learned without doubt—being ascertained through their flawless authority—so too [the Vedānta] is to be accepted. [The opposite view is] unexamined, being fabricated due to doubt regarding its authority and so forth. (43)
Cūḍālā said:
"Just as a child accepts his father’s word even when it is devoid of reasons and supporting arguments, so too should you accept these words of mine. (44)
Even that which is devoid of logical justification, he accepts with the conviction that it is a valid means of knowledge. || 44 ||
Immediately after hearing it, contemplating with your intellect that it is indeed auspicious,
listen to my words as if they were a song, having abandoned the desire for reasons.

Cultivating the thought that this is auspicious and for your own benefit, listen with pleasure to this song, which brings delight to the ears, just as one listens to music. I shall relate a sequence of stories that is pleasing to the mind—a narrative suited to your own conduct, a long-delayed awakening for her who is now rising, and one that makes the fear of worldly existence easy to cross for those of great intelligence. Listen!

Therein, at the outset, he introduces the narrative of Maṇikāca and the narrative of Hastika in order to cause the abandonment of the conceit of being the body and so forth, and to demonstrate the root cause of suffering; he does so by saying "svacarita" (by your own conduct): [the teaching] which is similar to your own conduct, and likewise for those of dull intellect, through the arising of reflection over a long period of time, it arises within their understanding.

Because such an awakening of the intellect for those of great intelligence brings about the immediate and easy crossing over the fear of worldly existence—the reversal of the order of the qualifiers [in the compound] being a Vedic (chāndasa) usage—I shall tell this sequence of discourse; the meaning is, "Listen."

Thus ends the eighty-seventh canto, titled "The Awakening of Śikhidhvaja," in the first part of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa, within the *Mokṣopāya* section of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Valmiki, according to the tradition of the Rishis.
Thus ends the eighty-seventh chapter, titled "The Awakening of Śikhidhvaja," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The eighty-eighth canto.
Cūḍālā said:
"Is there some illustrious man who is the abode of two eternally opposed things?"
Just as the ocean is the complete repository of both its qualities and its splendor, as well as of the submarine fire and its waters. || 1 ||
It is told that someone, out of folly, having obtained a wish-fulfilling gem, neglected it and after a long time of asceticism took up a piece of glass, mistaking it for a jewel.

He is the eternal abode and dwelling place of both mutually contradictory qualities: the excellence of magnanimity, dispassion, and the renunciation of all possessions, as well as the prosperity of worldly fortune; just as the ocean is the abode of both the submarine fire and water, which are likewise opposites. (1)
Possessing the arts, skilled in weapons, and expert in worldly affairs,
he has reached the limit of all conceptual thought, yet he does not know that supreme state.
But he does not know that state of the Supreme Self. || 2 ||
He set out to accomplish that which is achieved only through infinite effort— the attainment of the wish-fulfilling gem— just as the submarine fire strives to dry up the ocean.
What did she do then? He says: "Anantair... etc.

She engaged in asceticism and other such practices for the attainment of the *cintāmaṇi*, which is to be accomplished through endless efforts within the scope of austerity (*tapas*), recitation (*japa*), prayer to the deity, searching, and so forth. || 3 ||
Through great effort and persistent resolve over time, he attained the wish-fulfilling gem; for what indeed cannot be accomplished by those who exert themselves with a disciplined mind?

For that resolute man of firm conviction, through great and intense effort and exertion, the wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi) was accomplished in a very short time and stood before him. This demonstrates the rule that there is a necessary certainty of fruit in firm endeavor:
"If one applies oneself to activity, exertion, and wisdom without weariness..."
Even one who possesses nothing attains power without obstacle.
"By means of wisdom"—the word "relying upon" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. || 5 ||
He saw him standing almost at the tip of the jewel, within reach of his hand,
like a sage situated on the eastern peak of Mount Meru beholding the risen moon.

Just as a sage standing on the peak of the Sunrise Mountain (Udayācala) might, due to delusion, perceive the moon that has risen right there as if it had risen on Mount Meru—distant, difficult to reach, and seemingly out of grasp—so too did he see; such is the meaning. || 6 ||
Although he was among the sovereigns of the lords of jewels, he did not possess any certainty,
like a wretched commoner who has suddenly attained a kingdom.
For this very reason, he had no certainty regarding that wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi), the sovereign lord of all jewels;
he was utterly dejected and most impoverished. || 7 ||
He reflected thus with a mind full of wonder,
characterized by long-standing distress and agitation, yet possessed of equanimity.
"With pride" means filled with wonder; "with a mind characterized by agitation" means with a bewildered mind; "this" refers to the manner that is about to be described. || 8 ||
"This is a jewel; if it were not a jewel, it would not be such.
I touch it, yet I do not touch it; at times, it passes away through the sense of touch. (9)

"This is a jewel" is initial cognition (*āpātajñāna*). "This is not a jewel" is error (*bhrama*). "If it were a jewel, then it would not be within my direct perception; therefore, I shall touch it, I might touch it"—this is desire and longing (*icchābhilāṣa*). "I do not touch it, nor shall I touch it," because perhaps, for me who am unfortunate, it might not be a jewel.
By touch, one shall attain invisibility.
The supreme jewel is certainly not accomplished in merely this much time;
according to the tradition of the scriptures, it is accomplished through effort that may extend to the end of one's life.
To address this doubt, he states the seed [of the answer]: "Not merely by these two. Here, *āgama* refers to tradition (*aitihya*) and its sequence. (10)
Miserable, with one eye squinted, I behold the light of the jewels like the flickering of a fly-whisk, as if seeing two moons through delusion. (11)
Regarding how that perception of the light of the jewel is direct, he says: "I am a wretch.

Due to the impairment of my vision, I—being a miserable person—perceive the light of the jewel through eyes that are squinted and contracted by delusion, seeing it erroneously as being like a whirling firebrand. 11.
Whence has such abundant prosperity and fortune come to me, that even now I obtain this sovereign jewel which grants all perfections? (12)
Fortune (bhāgya) is merit (puṇya); its perfection is prosperity. || 12 ||
Indeed, only some great souls become truly fortunate, for whom the goddesses of prosperity become manifest in a short period of time. (13)
"I am indeed a mere human, a wretched man of little austerity; how can the supernatural powers come to me, who am the sole vessel of misfortune? (14)
Thus, for a long time, the ignorant man, reflecting with conceptualizations and mental constructions, made no effort to grasp the jewel, being deluded by his own folly. (15)
When something is not to be obtained by someone at a certain time, he does not obtain it then;
even though the wish-fulfilling gem was found, it was cast away with indifference by one of dull intellect.
To the question "Why did he not do so?", he replies: "Not that which... (na yadā). The word "that which was to be obtained" (labdhavyam) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. || 16 ||
While he remained thus, the jewels and supernatural powers departed; for they abandon one who treats them with contempt, just as an arrow leaves the bowstring once it has been released.

To explain why he departed by flying up, he says: "For the supernatural powers (siddhis) abandon him. Just as an arrow released from a bowstring abandons its string but does not abandon the earth, so it is here. || 17 ||
It is said that spiritual accomplishments (siddhis) come to a man only after he has slain the state of wisdom;
once arrived, they bestow everything, yet they depart without taking anything away.
Now, you previously stated at the beginning of the discussion that the man was skilled in worldly affairs;

where did that skill go at the time of attaining the jewels? To this he replies with the word "having killed" (*hatvā*). When the *siddhis* have arrived, they bestow upon the man the status of a wise one—that is, discernment (*vicakṣaṇatā*). But when [the man] is unable to endure them—that is, when he is indifferent—then enough! [of them].

They depart and they go away; the meaning is that they all depart indeed, having struck down and destroyed even his former state of wisdom and discernment. As it has been said: "The gods do not take up a staff to punish the offender; they withdraw his intellect, by which he is punished of his own accord. (18)
The man again exerted effort toward the acquisition of the supreme jewel;
for resolute people do not falter in their own undertakings. (19)
Then he saw an unbroken piece of glass, shimmering in form,
placed before him by invisible, laughing, and deceptive Siddhas.
It was placed before him, set in front by the Siddhas, who were laughing and intent on jesting, and for that very reason, acting as deceivers. || 20 ||
Thinking "this is a wish-fulfilling gem," the fool perceives reality in that [clod];
for the ignorant man, deluded, regards clay as gold.
The reality of being worthy of acceptance. || 21 ||
The delusion residing in the mind makes eight things—namely, the sixth [note], the enemy, the friend, the rope, the serpent, land, water, the two moons, nectar, and poison—appear as such. (22)
He illustrates the well-known nature of delusion (*moha*) as acting otherwise: "Eight," etc.
Due to confusion regarding numbers, one sometimes turns the eight categories into six; likewise, one turns an enemy into a friend, and so forth—this is to be applied accordingly. (22)
Taking that burnt jewel and abandoning his former fortune, he reflected:
"Everything is obtained from this wish-fulfilling gem; what is the use of other riches here? (23)
The word *dagdha* (burnt) is intended as a term of reproach. *Śrī* refers to prosperity consisting of wealth, grain, and so forth. || 23 ||
"This land is unpleasant and harsh, filled with sinful people; what use have I for that home which is as good as lost? What indeed are my kinsmen? (24)

Thus, he says "the country" and so forth, to show that he abandoned even his country, home, kinsmen, and others due to delusion: "The country" means it was arid and devoid of affectionate people; "almost gone" means, in other words, decayed. || 24 ||
"Having gone far away, I shall dwell happily according to my desire through this prosperity. Thinking thus, the fool took the jewel and went into the empty forest. (25)
A jewel [is compared to] a piece of glass. || 25 ||
There, by means of that fragment of glass, he went to her;
it was like the luster of the mountain of collyrium, O dear one, which is equal to the very essence of ignorance.
That calamity which is as intensely dark as the luster of a mountain of collyrium, which is equal to and corresponds with ignorance itself—that is to say, it is the very form of death. || 26 ||
Those sufferings which arise through the power of folly are neither calamities nor even old age and death;
for folly alone stands at the head of all misfortunes, like the mass of black hair upon the bodies of people, O Kṛṣṇa. (27)
Therefore, he concludes that folly alone is the ultimate limit among the causes of suffering, stating: "Sufferings.
Those sufferings which are well known through the power of folly do not arise from the loss of all one's possessions, nor from calamities, nor even from old age or death, once folly has departed.

Because those who know reality perceive no suffering even amidst thousands of calamities and the like, whereas one who lies upon a golden couch may still experience thousands of sufferings if he possesses ignorance; therefore, ignorance alone stands at the head of all calamities. The meaning is that it is just as the mass of black hair stands upon the head of every person. || 27 ||

Thus ends the eighty-eighth canto, titled "The Narrative of Maṇikāca," in the *Pūrva-cūḍā* section of the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa* within the *Vāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa*, a work of the Sage (*ārṣa*). Volume 1, Part 2, Section on Liberation (*mokṣopadeśa*). Canto 88.
Thus ends the eighty-eighth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Maṇikāca," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa-tātparyaprakāśa*.
The eighty-ninth canto.
Cūḍālā said:
Now, O lord of the earth, hear this other delightful account.
O virtuous one, this supreme awakening of the intellect is truly worthy of yourself. || 1 ||

Even after exerting effort to sever the bonds of the great elephant of the Vindhya mountains that had been captured, the failure to slay the enemy resulted in his own fall into a pit; this is not described as anything other than a downfall.
In this regard, there is also the illustration of the story of the elephant; therefore, he says "Now," [instructing you] to listen to that as well.
"Vṛttānta" means a narrative. "Similar to yourself" means like you. || 1 ||
In the Vindhya forest there was an elephant, the leader of a great herd;
by virtue of his pure intellect born of the lineage of Agastya, he rose up of his own accord as if by the Vindhya mountain itself.

This belongs to Agastya; thus it is *Āgastī*. By that [river], according to the rule "sūryatiṣya-", there is the elision of the *y*. Because of the long-standing observance of his command, by her who was pure and gracious with a mind intent on favoring him, he was raised up—meaning manifested—in his own former elevated form [by the Vindhya, i.e., in the form of his own previous high state]. He appeared, having become manifest in his own former elevated form.
The word "iva" indicates a poetic fancy (utprekṣā). || 2 ||
Her two fangs were sharp, long, and white like vajra-flames; they were equal to the crests of the fire at the end of an aeon and capable of uprooting Mount Sumeru.
The two rays of the vajra are like flames—uneven and sharp. || 3 ||
Bound by an iron net and tormented by the elephant-keeper,
he was like Mount Vindhya subdued by the Lord of Sages, or like Bali subdued by Upendra.
By means of a net made of iron; by Agastya, the Lord of Sages. || 4 ||
Bound and afflicted by weapons and jars,
the elephant endured that agony which a steadfast man undergoes when entering a new fire.

"Restraint" means confinement. That pain which the three cities (*tripura*) experience while being consumed by the fire of Hara’s arrow—fire that is both unprecedented (*nava*) because it was never before imagined and extraordinary (*alaukika*)—that very pain [is what she feels]. || 5 ||
When his enemy, the elephant-driver, was seen from afar,
that elephant entered the iron casket in which he had been confined for three days.
In a small box, within a net-like casket.
Then, out of weariness, that elephant made an effort to break his fetters; at another time, he produced the tinkling sound of small bells by flapping his trunk.
A sound like the tinkling of small bells.
With those two teeth, he exerted himself for two moments and broke the network of chains, just as an Asura breaks the bolt of heaven.
Like the Asura Bali, he was the bolt—the crossbar for the door-panel—of Amarāvatī, the celestial city of heaven.
From afar, his enemy beheld that severing of his fetters,
just as Hari saw the shattering of Bali’s heaven from the summit of Mount Meru.
As his bonds were severed, the enemy fell upon his head like a palmyra fruit;
then, step by step, Hari ascended to heaven, as Bali did from Mount Meru.

The enemy was the elephant-driver. Having climbed from one palmyra tree to another, he then fell upon the head of that elephant. It was just as when, at the sacrifice of Bali, having accepted the earth measured by three steps—taking the earth with the first step and heaven with the second—Bali fell upon the head of Bheru from the presence of Viṣṇu in order to complete the third step.
The meaning is "in that same way. || 10 ||
Falling from his two lotus-feet, yet failing to reach the elephant’s head,
he fell agitated to the ground like a ripe fruit struck down by the wind.
Seeing him fallen before him, the great elephant felt compassion;
for the virtuous, whose qualities are vast and radiant, exist even among those of the animal realm.
Compassion and so forth [arise] in the womb. || 12 ||
"What manliness is there in my merely crushing one who has fallen?
Even though he was an elephant," so reflecting, he did not slay that enemy.
Thus perceiving and reflecting, he [remained].
Having shattered the array of fetters, he advanced alone,
like a vast torrent of water sweeping away a wide-spreading dam.
The array of fetters is a network of chains. 14.
Relying on compassion, Mātaṅga broke through the net and departed, like the sun in the sky piercing through a mass of clouds. || 15 ||
When the elephant had gone, the mahout stood up with his body and mind restored to health;
his pain vanished completely along with the elephant itself. (16)
Being one whose body and intellect are thus established in their own natural state. || 16 ||
Even though he fell from the peak of that lofty palm tree in such a manner, he did not suffer any injury; I consider the bodies of the wicked to be truly indestructible.
"Division" means the breaking apart of the head, feet, and so forth. || 17 ||
The strength of the wicked increases in evil deeds like a cloud in the rainy season;
at that time, he was exceedingly energetic in his wandering.
In the sense of walking, it refers to moving with the feet. || 18 ||
The enemy of elephants (the lion), his limbs unfulfilled, departed; the elephant went away in sorrow. Having arrived, Vardhana vanished once more, like a hidden treasure.
For one whose limbs [of the syllogism] are not established and whose means are not properly employed, [there is no success]; for this very reason, it is said "by those who have gone. 19.
He diligently searched for the elephant hidden within the thickets of the forest,
just as Rāhu seeks to devour the moon in the sky when it is massed with clouds.
It was covered and concealed by masses of clouds.
After a long time, he found the lord of elephants staying in a certain forest, resting at the foot of a tree as if he had just emerged from battle. (21)
Then, at the place where the elephant was stationed, [he prepared] a trap capable of binding it,
using the highest quality of royal materials suited for those who lust after elephants.

In that vicinity, by means of a collection of excavations employed by the king, which was characterized by an abundance—that is, a great multitude—of those who were greedy for elephants, [the task was accomplished]. || 22 ||
The elephant trainer had a circular trench dug all around him in the forest,
just as the Creator fashioned the ring of the ocean upon the earth in every direction.
The Creator is the Ordainer. || 23 ||
That rogue covered it from above with a mass of young creepers,
just as the autumn season covers the sky with a web of thin clouds.

The deceitful deceiver covered that pit from above with a network of young creepers, just as the autumn season covers the sky with a mass of white clouds resembling a web of threads that conceals the void. || 24 ||
Within just a few days, while roaming in that forest, the elephant fell into a pit like a mountain falling into a dried-up ocean. || 25 ||
As he was walking, he fell into a circular well as terrifying as the depths of Pātāla,
located beneath a dry, excavated ocean-bed, which served as a casket for the jewel among elephants.

The connection with the following verse is as follows: "Even though that elephant was moving within that circular pit—which had the shape of a bracelet and was situated at the bottom of the dried-up ocean—it remains even today firmly bound within the casket of the jewel-elephant in this manner. || 26 ||
Thus, having been bound even more firmly by that elephant-keeper,
he remains even today in suffering within the subterranean abode, like Bali.
If he had struck down the enemy who stood before him earlier,
he would not have suffered that grief which comes from an elephant digging up its own tethering post.
If he had not struck [it], then that suffering caused by the wound would not have been perceived. || 28 ||
Out of folly, a man who does not purify his future time through the sequence of present actions goes to suffering, just like an elephant in the Vindhya mountains.
For this very reason, it is said— "out of folly"— that a wise person should, even now, purify the seeds of suffering through scriptural human efforts for the sake of future time.
Indeed, an elephant is satisfied thinking, "I am released from the iron shackles."
Moreover, even when situated far away, where does folly not cause affliction? (30)

With the intention that as long as ignorance—the source of all suffering—is not severed, the cessation of suffering remains utterly futile even if attempted through thousands of efforts, he says: "I am liberated. The word *ca* (and) is used here in the sense of *kila* (indeed/it is said). || 30 ||
O Great-Souled One, know that ignorance is indeed the supreme bondage; yet one who is bound thinks "I am not bound," and thus strives for liberation in his mind.
For one who remains in ignorance, the entire arising of the self within the three worlds—which is in truth identical with the Self—is suddenly [lost].
It is all stages. || 31 ||

Therefore, demonstrating that ignorance alone is the fundamental bondage and that its cessation occurs only through the knowledge of the non-dual reality of the Self, he concludes with the verse beginning "Maurkhyam" (Folly). O Great-souled One, the folly in one's mind that thinks, "I am not bound, I am eternally free from bondage," yet "I am myself bound"—that very folly is the supreme affliction; therefore, for the sake of liberation from it, [you should seek the knowledge of the Self].

Know that the entire universe consists of the Self; it arises from the Self alone as the three worlds whose nature is the threefold limitation—internal, celestial, and elemental—and which constitutes the bondage of the Self.
Through such knowledge, because nothing remains apart from the Self, the Self becomes eternally liberated. In the absence of such knowledge...
The meaning is that for a man established in ignorance, his very self suddenly becomes the ground and the field of growth for the seeds of all sufferings, such as bondage and the like. || 31 ||
Thus ends the eighty-ninth sarga, titled "The Narrative of Hastikopa," in the Pūrva-cūlikā of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa, within the Vālmīki-deśīya Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa composed by the Sage.
Thus ends the eighty-ninth chapter, titled "The Narrative of the Elephant’s Wrath," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The Ninetieth Chapter.
Śikhidhvaja said:
"O son of the gods, [you have performed] the acquisition of jewels, the binding of the Vindhya elephant, and other such deeds."
Reveal once more to me that web of stories which has been briefly indicated.
There, Cūḍālā, in the form of Kumbha, explained before the king the underlying meaning of the narrative concerning Maṇikā and Acaśubhā.

O son of the Immortals, O divine prince, reveal that web of stories concerning the attainment of jewels which you mentioned as being equal to your own life’s history, indicating it to be the means for my awakening. || 1 ||
Cūḍālā said:
Through the perfection of perceiving the meaning of words within the house of the heart upon the walls of the mind, listen as I myself tell this wondrous tale; I shall open up a vision for you. (2)

The word *hṛd* means "heart," and by extension, it refers to the house characterized by that heart. Within the walls characterized as a "picture" (*citra*), I shall "unveil"—that is, I shall manifest through the variety of descriptive colors—a picture that has already been "unveiled" merely by its outlines; this is the meaning. || 2 ||
O Lord of the Earth, you alone are he who is described as one skilled in the meaning of the scriptures, yet unlearned in the knowledge of reality— a seeker of jewels.
Regarding that, he says that you yourself are indeed that practitioner of the jewel (maṇisādhaka) who was described at the beginning with the words "there is a certain glorious man," and so forth:
"You are a knower of those scriptures, like the sun upon the slopes of Mount Meru;
yet you are not one who has found rest in the knowledge of reality, like a stone in water. (4)
He says "tajjñaḥ" (knower of that) to show that you possess the characteristics previously mentioned, such as being possessed of the arts and skilled in the scriptures. || 4 ||
Know, O holy one, that the genuine renunciation of everything is the wish-fulfilling gem;
you, pure in intellect, shall accomplish that which is the end of all sufferings.
He explains what that wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi) is, for the sake of which I have engaged in its accomplishment, saying: "Know... (verse 5).
O sinless one, through pure renunciation of everything, everything is attained;
for the renunciation of all is indeed sovereignty—what could possibly be greater than the wish-fulfilling gem?
He establishes its nature as a wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi) with the words "by the renunciation of everything": sovereignty is the state of absolute fulfillment of all desires.
O virtuous one, the renunciation of everything has been accomplished by you;
likewise, the rise of the Self through knowledge, which diminishes the prosperity of the world, has been fully realized.

That by which the world-renowned succession of prosperity and sovereignty—extending even to the station of Hiraṇyagarbha—is rendered dwarfish and trivial; such is the awakening of one's own self characterized by knowledge (*vidyā*).
And that from which there arises an unsurpassed joy and exaltation (*abhyudaya*); such is total renunciation (*sarvaparityāga*). The word *tathā* is used here in the sense of "and. (7)
You have renounced the kingdom, along with your wife, wealth, and kinsmen,
just as Brahmā abandons the activity of creating the world at the onset of his own night.
How it was accomplished, he states: "It was completely abandoned" by Brahmā, the creator. (8)
"You have come to my hermitage from a place very far from your own country,
like Garuda carrying the Tortoise came to the edge of the earth for rest."

The mention of the capture of the tortoise is also an illustration for the elephant and the branch of the *nyagrodha* tree; this story of Vainateya is well known from the *Mahābhārata* and other sources. (9)
In the renunciation of everything, only the notion of "I" was left by you,
like the pure essence of its own existence remaining in the sky after all impurities have been wiped away by the wind.
Ignorance consists of the conceit of "I" and self-importance; it is that autumnal breeze by which all stains, such as clouds and mist, have been wiped away.
When the mind alone is abandoned within the heart, the world attains fullness;
yet you are obscured by the conceptual fluctuations of renunciation and non-renunciation, like the sky covered by clouds.

When the notion of "I" (ahaṃmati) is abandoned, the Supreme Goal—the Self of perfect bliss—manifests directly within the heart by its own nature; thus, renunciation of everything culminates in liberation. With the intention that this supreme bliss is like a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*) and that once it is attained, one need not seek anything else, he says: "In the mind alone. But you—

He says, "by the conceptual constructions of renunciation and non-renunciation," because [the mind] is still enveloped by the residual conceit of being a renouncer, and thus has not attained fullness. || 11 ||
"This is not that supreme bliss, the great success of total renunciation;
it is something else entirely, loftier, difficult to achieve over a long time, and vast. (12)
He says, "This is not so," [verse 12], meaning that even though you have attained the renunciation of everything through the power of conceptual thought alone, you still lacked confidence.
When thought, having gradually gained growth through the grasping of volition,
moved like a gust of wind in the trembling of a forest tree, your renunciation flew up and departed.
Thus, when your intention grew over a long time through such reflection and the grasping of mental constructs, that "renunciation of everything" of yours flew away and departed.
How can there be renunciation for one who even allows anxiety to envelop him? How can there be stillness in a tree that is possessed by the movement of the wind?
And he who entertains even the slightest thought—that is, accepts it even slightly—[is affected by it]. || 14 ||
They say that thought itself is the mind, which has "volition" as its other name;
while that very [thought] is vibrating, how could the mind be abandoned? (15)

The renunciation of the mind alone is the primary renunciation of all; for when there is thought, the mind is difficult to abandon. Since the entire world is grasped by the mind through the door of volition (*saṃkalpa*), no one’s renunciation can be established [if the mind remains]. With this intention, he says:
"But when the mind is seized by thought, the web of the three worlds [is grasped] in an instant."
O virtuous one, how is that stainless renunciation of everything attained? (16)
By grasping at mental constructs, O dear one, your internal renunciation has flown away like a village bird upon hearing a sound. (17)
The village bird refers to pigeons and the like. || 17 ||
Having attained supreme freedom from anxiety through the renunciation of everything, that person has departed;
having been honored and bid farewell, does such a being cause any suffering? (18)
He imagines that the state of being free from anxiety—the fruit of total renunciation—has been brought about as if by the departure of renunciation itself.
With the intention of asking, "How much more so, then, in failing to honor one who has arrived with a thousand prayers? he says: "Having addressed... (verse 18).
O lotus-eyed one, since all renunciation has thus vanished, have you seen the glass gem of asceticism with the eye of your own mental resolve? (19)
Then he said, "What is this piece of glass that was taken by me with the notion that it was a gem?"—[the answer being] "It is penance" (verse 19).
By you, in that very asceticism which arose from an optical illusion,
a single-pointed cultivation was fixed upon what is to be grasped, just as one might fix it upon the moon’s reflection in water.

The meaning is that because it is the cause of suffering, the firm conviction (*dṛḍhaniścaya*) that "it is suffering" and "it must be grasped as such" is like the fixed perception of a real moon within the reflection of the moon in water. || 20 ||

Austerity performed without latent impressions (vāsanā) and without attachment may be endless; yet, when accompanied by latent impressions and uneven in its beginning, middle, and end, such practice of austerity leads only to suffering. (21)

Having first undertaken the renunciation of everything without attachment so that it would be free from latent impressions (*vāsanā*), he later performed endless ascetic practices accompanied by such impressions; yet those were in vain. The meaning is that this [practice] leads only to suffering: it was difficult at the beginning due to the abandonment of home, wealth, and wife; difficult at the end due to attachment to the fruits [of action]; and difficult in the middle due to enduring cold, wind, and other hardships while dwelling in the forest.
He who abandons immeasurable bliss that is easily attained and exerts himself toward a limited object that is difficult to achieve is considered a rogue and a destroyer of his own self. (22)

He who abandons the immeasurable bliss of the Self, which is easily accomplished, and instead engages in limited and difficult-to-accomplish matters such as asceticism and the like, is a rogue; the meaning is that he is his own enemy because he destroys the true nature of the immeasurable Self. || 22 ||
Having undertaken the renunciation of everything, you have not accomplished this [goal] while bound by the knowledge of the oneness of suffering in the abode of the forest. (23)

Thus, while dwelling in the forest hermitage, bound by the suffering of austerities described in such a manner and by the ignorance that causes attachment to that very state, you did not accomplish this total renunciation which you had previously begun. || 23 ||
O virtuous one, having escaped from the bondage of kingship which was filled with spreading suffering, you have now been bound by the visible fetters known as dwelling in the forest.
Those concerns regarding cold, wind, heat, and so forth are indeed doubled;
I consider forest life to be more than mere imprisonment for those who do not understand it. (25)
For those who are delicate, unacquainted with dwelling in the forest, and have never experienced it before, I consider dwelling in the forest to be a suffering greater than bondage. || 25 ||
"You have thought enough that you have obtained a wish-fulfilling gem;
O virtuous one, you have not even obtained a fragment of crystal. (26)
Even a fragment or a small piece. || 26 ||
Thus, my dear lotus-eyed one, I have fully related to you this account which is similar to the story of the seeker of the jewel.
Having understood this stainless truth for yourself, you should realize it and bring its fruition to maturity within the treasury of your mind.
(27) He concludes the comparison with the conduct of the seeker of the jewel by saying "ittham" (thus): "aṅga, O lotus-eyed one, by me..."
Thus, your conduct has been perfectly revealed and made manifest through this narrative of the effort regarding the jewel.

Having yourself reflected upon this analogy of the jewel and its counterpart according to the method I have stated, and having understood it in its true essence, you should place within the treasury of your own mind that which you recognize— whether it be total renunciation or asceticism— as being stainless and faultless like the *cintāmaṇi*.
The meaning is: "Having set it down, lead it to its transformation until the attainment of the fruit. || 27 ||

Thus ends the ninetieth canto, titled "The Narrative of the Accomplishment of the Wish-Fulfilling Gem," in the first part of the Nirvāṇa section of the Liberation chapter of the glorious Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa, the work of the Sage. 90.
Thus ends the ninetieth chapter, titled "The Narrative of the Seeker of the Wish-Fulfilling Gem," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The ninety-first canto.
Cūḍālā said:
"Now, O tiger among kings, for the sake of attaining the true state of things—"
Listen to the account of the events at Vindhya, which causes wonder.
Herein, the story of the elephant of the Vindhya mountains is related as an illustrative example,
along with the life of King Kumbha, for the sake of achieving the renunciation that culminates in awakening.
For the sake of the correct realization—that is, for the awakening—to the reality of things; "smaya" means wonder; [the verse describes] that which produces it. || 1 ||
That elephant which was in the Vindhya forest is you upon this earth;
that detachment and discernment are its two white tusks.
The grammatical connection is that those two teeth of his are known as detachment (vairāgya) and discernment (viveka). || 2 ||
And that elephant-driver who stood intent on mounting the elephant—that ignorance of yours, likewise intent on mounting [the world], brings you suffering. (3)
O King, though you are exceedingly powerful, you are led by your own folly from sorrow to sorrow and from fear to fear, like an elephant by a powerless mahout.
Though you are exceedingly powerful and strong, you are led from sorrow to greater sorrow and from fear to greater fear by ignorance, which is powerless and weak.
Just as an elephant is bound by a tether made of the essence of iron and adamant,
so you are encompassed by the calamity of worldly existence through the snare-net of desire.

He reveals the statement "he was bound with an iron net" by saying "yat" (that). That he was "bound," meaning restrained on all sides; that you were "enveloped in calamity," meaning from head to foot, during the time of governing the kingdom—this is the sense. || 5 ||
For hope is more treacherous, vast, and firm than iron ropes;
iron may decay with time, but craving only increases.
That ignorance which an enemy, unobserved from afar, watches as a pair—a single elephant bound for sport—watches you. 7.

By the phrase "not seeing the enemy elephant-driver from afar," his sight is indicated; he illustrates that sight with the words "yad" (that which). "In a pair" means in secret. This is a figurative expression (vāda) based on attributing sentience to ignorance. || 7 ||
Just as an elephant breaks the binding of a network of chains belonging to its enemy,
so you have abandoned this kingdom, free from all thorns, which is like a land of sensual enjoyment.
He states the intended meaning of the statement "with those two teeth with effort" as follows: "That which... (verse 8).
O virtuous one, while it may sometimes be easy to break the bonds of weapons or iron chains, it is not so easy to restrain this mind from its longing for worldly enjoyments.
Just as the elephant driver fell when he violently tore apart the bonds,
so too did ignorance fall away when you renounced that kingdom.

Regarding the statement that "falling from his two lotus-feet, he reached the elephant's head and then fell upon the earth," this also demonstrates ignorance; for it is said: *yadibhe* (if on the elephant). The meaning is that you have caused [the elephant] to fall, as it were, having shattered it so that it fell just as it did. || 10 ||
When a dispassionate person desires to abandon the hope for enjoyment, then ignorance trembles like a demon in a tree that is about to be cut down. (11)
He clarifies that very point with the words: "When... (verse 11).
When the discerning person remains having completely renounced enjoyments,
then ignorance flees like a ghost from a felled tree.
When the flood of enjoyments has surely been cast off, the state of ignorance falls away, just as a nest situated in a tree falls when the tree is cut by a saw. (13)
When you departed for the forest, ignorance was wounded by you;
though it fell down, it was not slain by the great sword of the renunciation of the mind.

The meaning is this: although the mind had become wounded and weakened, it was not yet slain by the great sword characterized by "mindlessness" (*nirmanaskatā*) through the knowledge of the reality of renunciation; for it was only upon hearing the words of Cūḍāla that the opportunity for the awakening to reality arose at that very moment. || 14 ||
Rising up once more and remembering the humiliation he had suffered, he has cast you into this dense pit dug by the elaborate display of his asceticism.
By that ignorance which was disregarded by you. || 15 ||
If you had known the Tathāgata in that way at that very moment,
then when he was about to renounce his kingdom, he would not have struck you down as you were already approaching your end.

The meaning is that at the very moment of the act of renouncing the kingdom, ignorance would have fallen [like a tree]; had you not destroyed it, it would have perished right then and there, and you would not have slain beings by the falling of the heat of your ascetic penance. || 16 ||
That the enemy caused you to be placed within a circular pit was because all that suffering from penance was offered to you by ignorance. (17)
He states the intended meaning of the statement "he made the circle of the ocean" with the words beginning "yat" (verse 17).
O best of kings, that royal splendor which belonged to him, the enemy of elephants (the king of serpents), now dwells within the mind of you, the king who disregards it. 18.

He clarifies the collection of qualities pertaining to passion (*rājasāmagrī*) mentioned in the verse "with a supreme collection of passion, the grounds for one greedy for elephants" with the words "that which belongs to him.

That royal fortune (*śrī*), the excellence of the equipment for the elephant-digging, belonging to that elephant-killer (*gajāri*)— the mahout— employed by the king, which was previously described, became internal to the king who was characterized by contempt (*avajñāna*), meaning a lack of consideration or disregard for reflection.
She is the internal sovereign power; for thought alone is the entire essence of non-discrimination—this is the intended meaning. || 18 ||
"O virtuous one, you are a lordly elephant, while he, though not an elephant, has been swiftly cast down by that enemy of ignorance into this vast forest. (19)

"O holy man, although this lordly elephant is not a physical elephant, it is endowed with the discernment described; yet, by this enemy characterized as ignorance, it has been swiftly cast into a pit dug all around. (19)
The circular moat, which was once concealed by young creepers,
is now covered by the slight hardships of the ascetic life, resembling the conduct of virtuous people.
That rogue [the mind] covered it from above with a mass of tender creepers; he clarifies the meaning of this with the word "yad" (which).
It was slightly veiled by the conduct of the virtuous—that is, by qualities such as tranquility and forbearance—and by associations with holy people. || 20 ||
Thus, even now, O King, you remain in this most dreadful pit of penance and suffering at the bottom of the netherworld, bound like Bali.

"Thus he was bound even more firmly by that elephant-driver; even today he remains in pain in his subterranean abode, like Bali. Explaining the purport of this conclusion, the author concludes: "Thus even today," etc. (21).
You are the elephant, the directions are the fetters, delusion is the enemy, and the fierce bond is the stake;
the earth is the Vindhya mountain—such is the report concerning you; now do whatever you must do.

Having summarized what has been said and what remains unsaid, he says: "O Elephant! You are the elephant; hope is your chain; delusion is your enemy, the mahout; persistence in fierce asceticism is the stake driven into the ground; and the Vindhya mountains are the earth. Thus, this account of your situation has been told by me through the allegory of the elephant. Having understood this, emerge from the trench of asceticism.
The meaning is: do whatever you must do for the destruction of that enemy; do not delay. || 22 ||

Thus ends the ninety-first chapter, titled "The Explanation of the Essential Meaning of the Narrative of the Elephant," in the *Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa* of the *Mokṣopāya*, within the *Dehastha-mokṣa* section of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa* composed by the sage Vālmīki. 91.

Thus ends the ninety-first chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Meaning of the Narrative of the Elephant and the Crow," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The ninety-second canto.
Cūḍālā said:
"That which was spoken by her, who is endowed with statesmanship and has realized all that is to be known—"
Why, then, was that knowledge not accepted by Cūḍālā? || 1 ||
Having heard these words of Kumbha here, the king, intent on total renunciation,
abandoned everything in the forest and burned all his own belongings in the fire.
When you set out for the forest, you said that ignorance had fallen but was not yet destroyed;

at that time, Cūḍālā, reflecting on the king’s apprehension—wondering by whom the means of renunciation had been taught to her mind which she had previously neglected—said: "As for what was said... (1).
For she is the foremost among those who know reality; whatever she speaks and whatever she does, all that is indeed true, my dear, and should be practiced with reverence.

He dispels the suspicion that she might be ignorant of reality or a speaker of falsehood with the words "For she... (sā hi). The phrase "it became something to be performed" (anuṣṭheyam abhūt) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. || 2 ||
O King, if her words were not carried out by you,
why was the renunciation of everything not skillfully accomplished?

"If you might have lived long by means of the thought of self (*ātmabuddhi*), especially by means of the thought of the Guru, [but] because of the saying that 'the thought of another leads to destruction' and 'the thought of women brings about ruin,' you disregarded the thought of women and firmly held to the thought of self, considering the renunciation of everything to be most excellent—then why was that very thing not made stable by you? Thus he says: "But if... (verse 3).
Śikhidhvaja said:
"The kingdom has been abandoned, the home abandoned, and likewise the country; even the wife has been abandoned. Yet, my dear friend, why has total renunciation not been performed?"

"O virtuous one, by the mere renunciation of the kingdom and such, the renunciation of everything has been accomplished for you; thus it has been stated by you yourself that 'the power of knowledge which diminishes the prosperity of the world, as well as the dawning of one's own Self, is thereby achieved. Furthermore, I have not taken back the kingdom and other things once abandoned. So how is it that I have not perfected the renunciation of all?"—thus spoke Śikhidhvaja.
He asks: "The kingdom. || 4 ||
Cūḍālā said:
"Wealth, wife, home, kingdom, land, the royal parasol, and kinsmen—all these are yours, O King; for what is your renunciation? (5)

"Only in the renunciation of everything was the notion of 'I' left remaining by you"— this was the answer I gave previously, yet he did not understand it due to a lack of discernment (*viveka*). Therefore, even though he has been made to relinquish everything— including his remaining attachments to the forest hermitage, his hut, his water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*), and so forth— how might he now somehow attain discernment, cast off the knot of egoism (*ahaṅkāra*), and become complete?

Thinking that this might come to pass, and gradually leading his mind toward the realization of that [truth], Cūḍālā, with a hidden intention, said: "Wealth. For when everything that belongs to one's own self is renounced, the renunciation of all is accomplished. Yet, the kingdom and such things do not belong to one's own self, nor is everything [one's own]. For it is the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) that thinks, "The kingdom and so forth are mine."

The sense is that, by imagining [the self] to possess ownership over those [objects], one considers them "mine" rather than the self; thus, because there is no such attainment [of the self as owner], your renunciation of everything is not established. || 5 ||
There remains for you one supreme portion, not yet relinquished;
by renouncing that entirely, you shall attain a state free from sorrow.

If it were argued that the self has attained lordship over the kingdom and so forth through the superimposition of identity upon the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), then the renunciation of the kingdom and such would be accomplished simply by its [the ego-sense’s] abandonment, and not otherwise. With the intention that you have not abandoned that [ego-sense], he said:
Śikhidvaja spoke:
If my entire kingdom were not mine, then this entire forest would be mine;
yet even this place, rich with mountains, trees, and shrubs, I shall abandon.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
O Rāma, even as he was speaking thus, impelled by the words of Kumbha,
the self-controlled hero Śikhidhvaja, in the mere twinkling of an eye—

Not understanding the intended meaning [of the previous statement], Śikhidhvaja thought: "Since you previously renounced the kingdom and so forth, you have no connection to the kingdom now; therefore, there is no need for further renunciation. However, because you currently possess mountains, trees, and the like, your perfection of universal renunciation cannot be achieved without abandoning those. Thinking thus, Śikhidhvaja—
He said, "The kingdom. In this way, even hereafter, the confusion regarding a difference in the king's intention is to be inferred. || 7 || 8 ||
Having made a very firm resolve, he completely wiped away that attachment to the forest,
just as the flood of the rainy season washes away the streaks of dust on a riverbank by its own force.
The rainy season is like a torrential downpour for you; [he saw] a streak of dust as if it were a trail of pollen.
Śikhidhvaja said:
"I have indeed abandoned all attachment even to this forest with its trees, mountains, groves, and caves; my renunciation is now firmly established."
Having abandoned the latent impressions and the sense of "mine," my renunciation has become established and perfected. || 10 ||
Kumbha said:
"The mountain slope, the forest, the chasm, the water, the trees, the ground—none of these belong to you; how then can there be 'renunciation of everything' for you? (11)
The pitcher-abode is as before. || 11 ||
There remains for you one supreme portion that has not yet been relinquished;
by renouncing it entirely, you shall attain supreme freedom from sorrow.
Śikhidhvaja said: "If all this does not belong to me, then my entire hermitage—including the pond, the ground, and the hut—is mine; I shall abandon that very place immediately. (13)

The meaning is: having yourself reflected upon renunciation of the forest and so forth according to your own method, and having understood the truth in its essence, you should place within the treasury of your own mind that which you know to be stainless and faultless—whether it be total renunciation or austerity—just like a wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi), and lead it to its final fruition until the attainment of the result. || 27 ||

Thus ends the ninetieth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Account of the Seeker of the Wish-Fulfilling Gem," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The ninety-first canto.
Cūḍālā said:
"Now, O tiger among kings, for the sake of attaining the true state of affairs—"
Listen to the account of the Vindhya mountain, which causes wonder.
Here, the story of the elephant of the Vindhya mountains is told as an illustration for the conduct of King Kumbha, in order to achieve the perfection of renunciation at the end of his awakening.
For the sake of the correct realization—that is, for the awakening—to the reality of things; "smaya" means wonder, [referring to] that which produces it. || 1 ||
That elephant which was in the Vindhya forest is you here upon this earth;
that detachment and discernment are its two white tusks.
The grammatical connection is that those two teeth of his are known as detachment (vairāgya) and discernment (viveka). || 2 ||
And that elephant-driver who stood intent on mounting the elephant—that ignorance of yours, intent on mounting [the world], brings you suffering. (3)
O King, though you are exceedingly powerful, you are led by your own folly from sorrow to sorrow and from fear to fear by that which is powerless, just as an elephant is led by its keeper.
Though you are exceedingly powerful and strong, you are led from sorrow to sorrow and from fear to fear by ignorance, which is powerless and weak. || 4 ||
Just as an elephant is bound by a chain made of adamantine iron,
so you are encompassed by calamity through the snare of the noose of desire.

He clarifies the statement "he was bound with a net of iron" with the word *yat*: that he was "bound," meaning restrained on all sides; that you were "enveloped by calamity," reaching down to your feet—that is to say, at the time of governing the kingdom. || 5 ||
For hope is more treacherous, vast, and firm than iron ropes;
iron may decay with time, but craving only increases.
That ignorance which an enemy, unobserved from afar, watches as a pair—namely, the elephant and the hunter—watches you, who are bound alone for the sake of sport. (7)

By the phrase "not seeing the enemy, the elephant-driver, from afar," he illustrates that very act of seeing with the words "yad" (that which). "In a pair" means in secret. This is a figurative statement (vāda) based on superimposing sentience upon ignorance. || 7 ||
Just as an elephant breaks the binding of a network of chains belonging to its enemy,
so have you abandoned this kingdom, free from all thorns, which is like a land of sensual enjoyment.
He states the intended meaning of the statement "with those two teeth, with effort" as follows: "That which... (verse 8).
O virtuous one, at times it may be easy to break free from the bonds of weapons or chains, but it is not so easy to restrain this mind from its longing for worldly enjoyments.
Just as the elephant driver fell when he forcefully tore apart their bonds,
so too did ignorance fall away when you renounced that kingdom.

Regarding the statement that "falling from his two lotus-feet, he reached the elephant's head and then fell upon the earth," this also demonstrates ignorance; for it says, "yadibhe" (if on the elephant). The meaning is: it was made by you to fall, as if it were already fallen, that is, it was shattered. || 10 ||
