When a dispassionate person desires to abandon the hope for enjoyment, then ignorance trembles like a demon in a tree about to be cut down. (11)
He clarifies that very point with the words "When... (yadā). || 11 ||
When the discerning person remains having completely renounced enjoyments,
then ignorance flees like a ghost from a tree that has been cut down.
When the flood of enjoyments has surely been cast off, the state of ignorance falls away, just as a nest situated in a tree falls when the tree is cut by a saw. (13)
When you departed for the forest, ignorance was wounded by you;
though it fell down, it was not slain by the great sword of the renunciation of the mind. || 14 ||

The meaning is this: although the mind was wounded and rendered lax, it was not yet slain by the great sword characterized by "mindlessness" (nirmanaskatā) through the knowledge of the reality of renunciation; rather, the opportunity for the awakening to that reality occurred at that very moment upon hearing the words of Cūḍāla. || 14 ||
Rising up once more and remembering the insult he had suffered,
he has cast you into this dense pit of his elaborate display of asceticism.
By that ignorance which was disregarded by you. || 15 ||
If you had known the Tathāgata in that way at that very moment,
then when he was about to renounce his kingdom, he would not have struck you down as you were already approaching your end.

The meaning is that at the very moment of the renunciation of the kingdom, ignorance likewise fell [before you]; had you not destroyed it then and there, it would have brought about the destruction of all beings by the onset of the heat of its ascetic penance. || 16 ||
That the enemy caused you to be placed within a circular pit was because all that suffering from penance was offered to you by ignorance. (17)
He states the intended meaning of the statement "he made a circle with his armlet" in the verse beginning with "yad" (17).
O best of kings, that royal splendor which belonged to the enemy of the elephant-king (Śiva) now dwells within the thoughts of you, the king who disregards him. 18.

He clarifies the collection of qualities pertaining to passion (*rājasāmagrī*) mentioned in the verse "by a supreme collection of passion, the grounds of elephant-obsession" with the words "that which belongs to him.

That royal fortune (*śrī*), the excellence of the equipment for the excavation [of the earth], employed by the king for that elephant-killer— the mahout— is indeed present within that monarch who is characterized by contempt, meaning a lack of regard for reflection.
She is the internal sovereign power; for thought alone is the entire essence of non-discrimination—this is the intended meaning. || 18 ||
O virtuous one, you are a lordly elephant, yet this other, though not an elephant, has been swiftly cast down by that enemy of ignorance into the vast forest. (19)

"O holy man, although this lordly elephant is not a physical elephant, it is endowed with the discernment described; yet it has been swiftly cast into a pit dug all around by this enemy characterized by ignorance. (19)
That which was encircled by bracelets of scars and veiled by young creepers was covered with the slight hardships of asceticism, like the conduct of the virtuous.
That rogue covered it from above with a mass of young creepers; he clarifies the meaning of this with the word "yat" (which).
It was slightly veiled by the conduct of the virtuous—that is, by qualities such as tranquility and forbearance—as well as by associations with holy men. || 20 ||
Thus, even now, O King, you remain bound in this most dreadful pit of penance, situated at the bottom of the underworld like Bali.

"Thus, having been bound even more firmly by that elephant-driver, he remains even today in pain within the abode of the earth, like Bali. Explaining the purport of this conclusion, he concludes: "Thus even today," etc. (21).
You are the elephant, the directions are the fetters, delusion is the enemy, and the intense bondage is the stake;
the earth is the Vindhya mountain—such is the report concerning you. Now, do whatever you must do.
Having summarized what has been said and what has not been said, he says: "O elephant! You are the elephant; hope is your chain; delusion is the mahout;

persistence in fierce asceticism is the stake driven into the ground; and the surface of the earth is the Vindhya mountain. Thus, this report concerning you has been told by me through the allegory of the elephant. Having understood this, emerge from the pit of asceticism.
The meaning is: "Do whatever you must do for the destruction of that enemy; do not delay. || 22 ||

Thus ends the ninety-first chapter, titled "The Explanation of the Essential Meaning of the Narrative of the Elephant," in the *Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa* of the *Mokṣopāya*, within the *Dehali-mokṣa* section of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by the sage Vālmīki. 91.

Thus ends the ninety-first chapter, titled "The Explanation of the Essential Meaning of the Narrative of the Elephant and the Crow," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The ninety-second canto.
Cūḍālā said:
"That which was spoken by her, who is possessed of political wisdom and knows all that is to be known—"
Why, then, was that knowledge not accepted by Cūḍālā? || 1 ||
Having heard these words of Kumbha here, the king, intent on total renunciation,
abandoned everything from the forest onwards and burnt all his own belongings in the fire.

Cūḍālā said—referring to what was spoken [by the King]: "When you set out for the forest, you said that ignorance had fallen but was not destroyed; in that regard, by whom was this means of renouncing my mind now taught, which I previously overlooked? Thus she spoke, reflecting on the King's apprehension. || 1 ||
For she is the foremost among those who know reality; whatever she speaks and whatever she does, all that is indeed true, my dear, and should be practiced with reverence. (2)

He dispels the suspicion that she might be ignorant of reality or a speaker of falsehood with the words "For she... (sā hi). The phrase "became something to be performed" (anuṣṭheyam abhūt) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. || 2 ||
O King, if her words were not carried out by you,
why was the renunciation of everything not skillfully accomplished?

"If one might live long by means of the thought of self, and especially by the thought of the Guru, whereas the thought of 'another' leads to destruction and the thought of 'woman' brings about utter ruin"—given this saying, you have disregarded the thought of woman and firmly resolved upon the thought of self, considering the renunciation of everything to be most excellent; why then have you not made that very [renunciation] firm? To this he says: "But if... (verse 3).
Śikhidhvaja said:
"The kingdom has been abandoned, the home abandoned, and likewise the country; even the wife has been abandoned. Yet, my dear friend, why has total renunciation not been performed?"

"O virtuous one, by the mere renunciation of the kingdom and so forth, the renunciation of everything has been accomplished for you; thus it was said by you yourself that 'the power of knowledge which diminishes the prosperity of the world, as well as the dawning of one's own Self, is thereby achieved. Furthermore, I have not taken back the kingdom and other things once they were abandoned. So how is it that I have not perfected the renunciation of all?"—thus spoke Śikhidhvaja.
He asks: "The kingdom"? || 4 ||
Cūḍālā said:
"Wealth, wife, home, kingdom, land, the royal parasol, and kinsmen—all these are yours, O King; what, then, is this 'renunciation of everything' of yours? (5)

"My previous answer—that 'only the notion of "I" (ahaṃmati) remained in you after the renunciation of everything else'—is precisely the response to this. However, due to a lack of discrimination (viveka), he did not accept it. Therefore, even though he has been made to renounce entirely all remaining possessions such as his forest hermitage, cottage, water-pot (kamaṇḍalu), and so forth, he has somehow attained discrimination, cast off the knot of egoism (ahaṃkāra), and become complete."

Thinking that this might come to pass, and gradually leading his mind toward the realization of that [truth], Cūḍālā, with a hidden intention, said: "Wealth. For when everything that belongs to oneself is renounced, total renunciation is accomplished. Yet the kingdom and such things do not belong to oneself, nor is everything [one's own]. For it is the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) that thinks, "The kingdom and so forth are mine."

The sense is that by imagining [the self] as possessing ownership over those [objects], one considers them "mine" rather than being the self; thus, because such a state of attainment does not exist, your renunciation of everything is not established. || 5 ||
There remains for you an unsurpassed portion that has not yet been relinquished;
by renouncing it entirely, you shall attain a state free from sorrow.

If it were said that the self has attained lordship over the kingdom and so forth due to the superimposition of identity upon the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), then the abandonment of the kingdom and such would be accomplished only through the abandonment of that [ego-sense], and not otherwise. With the intention that you have not abandoned that [ego-sense], he says:
Śikhidvaja said:
If my entire kingdom were not mine, then all this forest would be mine;
yet even this forest, rich with mountains, trees, and shrubs, I shall abandon.

Śikhidhvaja, failing to understand the intended meaning [of his teacher], thought: "Since you previously renounced the kingdom and so forth, you have no connection to the kingdom now; therefore, there is no need for further renunciation. However, because you currently possess mountains, trees, and other things, your perfection of 'renouncing everything' cannot be achieved without abandoning those. Thinking thus, Śikhidhvaja...
He said, "The kingdom. In the same way, even hereafter, one should infer the King's confusion regarding the difference in his underlying intention (*tātparya*). || 7 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
O Rāma, even as he was speaking thus, impelled by the words of Kumbha,
the self-controlled hero Śikhidhvaja, in a mere twinkling of an eye—
Having made a firm resolve, he completely wiped away that attachment to the forest,
just as the flood of the rainy season washes away a streak of dust upon its bank.
The rainy season was like a flood from the lap of the clouds; it was like a streak of dust, a line of rising soil.
Śikhidhvaja said:
"Indeed, my latent desire (vāsanā) for the forest—with its trees, mountains, groves, and caves—has been abandoned by me; my renunciation is now firmly established."
Having abandoned latent impressions and the sense of "mine," my renunciation has become established and perfected. || 10 ||
Kumbha said:
"The mountain slope, the forest, the chasm, the water, the ground with its trees—none of these belong to you; how then can you claim total renunciation?"
The "residing in a jar" [posture] is as described before. || 11 ||
There remains for you indeed one supreme portion that has not yet been relinquished;
by renouncing it entirely, you shall attain supreme freedom from sorrow.
Śikhidhvaja said: "If all this does not belong to me, then my entire hermitage—including the pond, the ground, and the hut—is mine; I shall abandon it immediately. (13)

Thinking, "Let it be granted that 'everything [belongs] to you' because of your renunciation of the forest and so forth; nevertheless, since the existence of your hermitage remains, how is total renunciation established? Śikhidhvaja said: "If this...
The particle *eva* has the sense of "even" (*api*). || 13 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāma, while speaking thus, the self-controlled hero Śikhidhvaja, awakened by the words of Kumbha, [attained his goal] in a mere moment of meditation.
He thoroughly wiped away that state of mental fatigue within his heart by means of pure consciousness,
just as the wind removes a streak of dust by its very movement.
In the hermitage, he wiped away his attachment and sense of "mine-ness."
Śikhidhvaja said:
"That tree, the hut, the creepers, and even the very seat of my hermitage have surely been abandoned by me; total renunciation has now become established within me."
Kumbha said:

"A tree, a pond, dry land, a shrub, a hut, or a fence of creepers—none of these belong to you; since you possess nothing at all, how can there be such a thing as 'renunciation of everything' for you? (17)
The disposition of the pitcher and the disposition of the king are as before. || 17 ||
You possess another supreme portion that has not yet been relinquished;
having renounced it entirely, you shall attain the highest state.
Śikhidhvaja said: "If all this does not belong to me, then I shall abandon all of it— my vessels and the like, as well as my leather bags, walls, and huts."
Walls are *kuḍya*s; a small hut is a *kuṭīra*. || 19 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Having spoken thus, that tranquil sage of pure soul rose from his seat with an undisturbed mind,
like an autumnal cloud from a mountain peak.

From the word *viṣṭara*, meaning a seat; the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* occurs according to the rule: "The word *viṣṭara* is used for both a tree and a seat. *Avadātātmā* means one whose mind is pure. || 20 ||
But Kumbha, observing those actions himself with a smile,
remained seated in his worldly duties like the sun in its own movement.
The sun, Aṃśumān, remained as if gazing while seated upon his own seat, which was like a chariot in its movement; this is the implied sense. || 21 ||
"Whatever one does, let him do this; for this is his supreme purification.
Having said this, Kumbha stood silent and gazed at Śikhidhvaja.
Śikhidhvaja, however, brought all that household equipment from the hermitage to one single spot,
just as the ocean brings the waters of the earth to one place.

Just as the earth, which has the ocean for its belly, brings together the waters of rain, rivers, and so forth from both low-lying ground and elevated terrain into one place, so too does it [the yogi]. || 23 ||
Having established it, he kindled the fire with dry fuel,
just as the sun, moving across the sky with its rays, ignites the surface of a sun-crystal.

Just as the sun, having moved and entered [the sunstone], ignites the fire residing within the sun-crystal (sūryakānta) by means of its rays—its beams—so too [is it here]. Since the root *jval* is intransitive (*akarmaka*), when it is conjugated with the causative suffix *ṇic*, the fire (*pāvaka*), which was the agent in the basic sense, becomes the object (*karman*).
Furthermore, the cooking utensils and implements are also intended to be the object, because they serve as the substratum for the result, namely their being reduced to ashes.
Due to the optionality of the substitution of *m* for *jval*, there is an absence of shortening of the penultimate vowel.
Having cast that collection of vessels and utensils into the fire, he entered [the fire] himself,
like the sun upon the peak of Mount Meru after having consumed the world as its sacrificial offering.
"He entered upon a seat of grass"—this is the ellipsis. *Dhvaṃsikā* refers to the dissolution at the junction of Manvantaras;
just as the Sun, having offered the world as an oblation into the fire he himself has kindled, sits upon the peak of Mount Meru, so too [did he]. || 25 ||
"O beloved of your husband, since you have lived for all this time with an undivided intellect, let it be so for you because of that very fact. (26)

Now, desiring to abandon Akṣamālā and avoiding the fault of revealing the favors he had done for her, he said to her: "By me—who am such that my mind has abandoned the distinction [between self and others] and the impulse to achieve my own ends—you have been made to undergo the fatigue of wandering for all this time; by that alone, let your service to me be considered sufficient. (26)
But now that delusion has been turned back, you no longer benefit me;
for long have I wandered in the forest of mantras and roamed along the paths of ritual action.
The meaning is: "Now that the delusion regarding the necessity of performing austerities, recitations, and so forth has been removed, you no longer benefit me;

therefore, I shall let you rest, so as not to involve you in further toil. He says this because he too, through the delusion of recitation, has wandered through various forests of mantras along with you, and now intends to rest.
"I have seen the sacred sites; now I shall rest, my friend," Śikhidhvaja said, and having spoken thus, he cast his rosary into the fire.
The seats of Dharma are the penance groves, the fields of spiritual accomplishment, and so forth. || 28 ||
Just as the wind [sweeps] the pure row of stars from the sky at the fire of the end of an eon,
so have you been long ago snatched by me, the man-deer, from the forest deer.
Just as the wind at the end of an aeon scatters the host of stars—the garland of constellations—from the sky, so it is here;
by this, it is understood that the rosary is made of crystal. He speaks regarding the deer-skin with the words "by me. (29)
Out of ignorance, you held this very deer-skin upon your grass mat;
now go, and may your paths to that which is worthless be auspicious. (30)

On a seat of *vṛsī* or a cushion of *kuśa* grass; the ellipsis is "may this very thing be a service to you. To the base one, whose nature is the *māyā* that is the root cause; "paths" refers to the ways characterized by the dissolution of intermediate causes.
"Go to the state of fire; the sky with its stars is equal to you.
Having grasped it by its corners with both hands, he cast away that hide.
By the statement "the sky with its stars is equal to yours," it is understood that the hide of Pṛṣata was variegated with white spots;
for its attainment of the state of being a starry sky is indeed appropriate. || 31 ||
"O you of great conduct, by you my water has been withheld, just as fire from the ocean, wind from the sea, or forest fire from a mountain. (32)
Having said "O King," he drew the hide from the seat of grass with both hands and cast it into the fire; this is the connection with the preceding passage.

Just as the wind of universal dissolution (pralayavāta) draws the mountains from the ocean and casts them into the forest fire, so did he act. Now, desiring to discard his water-pot (kamaṇḍalu), he praises it in order to demonstrate his gratitude:
This word "bhavat" ends with the suffix śatṛ. || 32 ||
O virtuous water-pot, you have not been properly requited for your charming friendship, your benevolence, and your steadfastness. (33)
A return favor has not been rendered; the words such as "friendship" (*sauhṛda*) and so forth should also be applied through double entendre (*śleṣa*) according to the context. || 33 ||
And you alone are the supreme abode of all excellence,
by means of that very fire with which you purified your body before coming to me.

Regarding the phrase "by whom indeed": it is understood from this that he himself had previously taken possession of that water-pot after purifying it by burning with fire for the sake of purification from some Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*); and having purified it again by burning, he gave it to another Vedic scholar. || 34 ||
"Go by that very path, O friend; may your ways be auspicious.
Having spoken thus, he then gave the water-pot to the Vedic scholar.
Whatever is good should be given even to the great Agni;
for like the mind of a fool kept in secret, one always falls downward.

The meaning is that, according to the rule that whatever implement is excellent and worthy of being used should be given to Agni or even to Mahādeva and presented as a gift; [the author] states the fault appropriate to that [rule] regarding the grass mat (*bṛsī*) he intends to burn: "You too always fall into the hidden lower region. (36)
"That very destination is fitting for you; O Bṛsikā, turn to ashes!
Having said this, he took the Bṛsikā and Mṛdvikā and cast them directly into the fire.

"Therefore, O *bṛsikā*, like one of foolish intellect, that very state of burning and torment is fitting for you; thus, go to the state of ashes"—this is the meaning. Having said this, he cast the extremely soft *mṛdvikā* grass-mat into the blazing fire itself; this is to be connected with the following verse. || 37 ||
For the sake of purification and for the sake of a seat, she indeed cast it upon the radiant funeral pyre;
for that which is to be abandoned should indeed always be abandoned without delay.

For what purpose did he renounce everything? He says: "for the sake of purification. This means for the sake of purifying the mind within the consciousness of Brahman-caitanya. It also means for the sake of a seat—that is, for the sake of rest. Regarding the *kumbha* (the pot), he says:
"one must linger"—this is the meaning. || 38 ||
It is the established rule that the virtuous provide detailed explanations regarding what is to be adopted;
however, I shall quickly abandon this entire collection of vessels into the fire. (39)

To explain why this is so, he says: "In detail. For it is a well-known fact in the world that when those existing vessels are present, an expansion is made even toward other implements suitable for collection;
therefore, I shall quickly cast all these collections of vessels into the fire. (39)
Fire burns its fuel only once, yet it serves for one's satisfaction;
O virtuous one, I renounce these instruments of action for you who are beyond action.
You should not feel any distress in this matter; for who indeed would carry what is unfit for them? (40)

The meaning is this: since a vessel that is always combustible burns everything at once and simultaneously, it leads to my satisfaction and contentment through total renunciation. Now, O jar, you should not feel distress regarding this total renunciation performed by me; for even in the world, who would carry or support what is unfit? And likewise, for one who is inactive...
The sense is that my implements for ritual action are indeed unsuitable; thus, they are not fit to be worn. || 40 ||
Having spoken thus, the king instantly offered into the fire his entire collection of vessels and utensils suitable for the pleasures of forest life;
he cast that multitude of implements into the flames all at once, like the Time of Destruction when the world blazes with its final radiance. (41)

King Śikhidhvaja, having spoken thus, immediately offered into the fire all that collection of vessels—primarily consisting of the finest eating utensils and everything else suitable for the pleasures of forest life—all at once and simultaneously. The meaning is that it was just as when Time, blazing with the splendor of the end of an aeon, offers the entire universe into the fire all at once. || 41 ||

Thus ends the ninety-second sarga, titled "The Practice of Total Renunciation," in the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa* of the *Mokṣopāya* section of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*, composed by Vālmīki, according to the tradition of the Ṛṣis. 92.
Thus ends the ninety-second chapter, titled "The Act of Renouncing Everything," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The ninety-third canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Then, having risen, he set fire to that dry grass hut.
It was falsely constructed through the conceptualizations of one's own ignorant mind. || 1 ||
Having burned his implements and desiring to cast off his body, Śikhidhvaja was restrained there by Kumbha and instructed on the relinquishment of the mind.
That hut-like grass-cottage was imagined and established by one's own mind through the vain conceptualization of "mine-ness. || 1 ||
Whatever remained, all of that Śikhidhvaja,
with an unperturbed mind and observing silence, gradually [consumed] with a composed intellect.
Whatever there was—pots, bowls, heaps of grass and wood, and so forth—all that he burned; this is the syntactical connection with what follows. || 2 ||
He burnt, threw away, abandoned,
or broke various kinds of vessels, his own clothing, food, and so forth, as if he were satisfied.
One's own garment is a bark-cloth; that in which one eats, such as a leaf-cup and the like, is the food. (3)
That hermitage of his became a place where people were seen and then vanished,
resembling the hermitage of Dakṣa’s sacrifice after it had been destroyed by the army of Vīrabhadra.
The compound *pūrvakāla* means "a time previously seen," where the state of people has vanished from sight and disappeared.
The herds of deer fled from the hermitage, abandoning their chewing of the cud,
like terrified people fleeing from a great city engulfed in flames.
He establishes that very point with the words: "From the stage of life," etc. (5).
The king said: "That collection of goods, along with its dry fuel, is consumed by fire; yet he who possesses only his physical form and lacks oil is content. (6)
He was a mere physical form, with nothing remaining but his body.
Śikhidhvaja said:
"Having completely abandoned all latent impressions (*vāsanā*) therein, I indeed stand as one who has renounced everything.
Oh! After a long time, O son of a god, I have finally been awakened."
"Vāsanām" means attachment (mamatā). "In that regard" refers to all the requisites; the words "you have awakened [me]" are to be supplied as the ellipsis. || 7 ||
I am perfected, absolute, pure, and awakened through bliss;
what indeed could this entity be, other than a sequence born of my own volition?

The meaning is: for one whose method of accumulation is driven by the mental construction of "mine-ness," this entire collection of requisites is of such a nature that it is nothing at all substantial or worthy of being grasped. || 8 ||
To the extent that various causes of bondage are abandoned,
to that same extent the mind attains supreme bliss.
Acting out the bliss of that renunciation, he says: "As much as... as much as" (yāvad yāvad). || 9 ||
I am stilled, I have attained final nirvana, I am happy, and I am victorious;
my obstructions have gone to destruction, and I have performed the relinquishment of everything.
Naked, with the quarters as my garment, and equal to the directions themselves, I stand here;
O son of a god, what else remains after such great renunciation? (11)
The various bonds are the objects of the senses, which are the causes of bondage. || 10 || 11 ||
Kumbha said:
"O King Śikhidhvaja, you have not renounced anything at all;
do not vainly pretend to the supreme bliss that comes from the renunciation of everything."

Unable to endure Kumbha’s performance of the pleasure of total renunciation—which was merely the abandonment of external requisites and was like the delusion of a child—Kumbha said: "All of it indeed. [This refers to] *abhinaya*, a specific expressive gesture. || 12 ||
Indeed, you still possess the supreme portion that has not been relinquished;
by renouncing it entirely, you shall attain the highest state beyond sorrow.
"Your," and so forth, as before. || 13 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O mighty-armed Rāma, lotus-eyed one, having heard this and reflected for a moment, that king spoke as follows.
Śikhidhvaja said: "O son of a deity, when I have renounced everything, only this body remains for me—a mass of senses like a swarm of vipers, and a form composed of blood and flesh. (15)

Then, having risen again, I shall bring this body— which is by nature subject to destruction— to its end by leaping from the Bhṛgu cliff without obstacle, and thus become one who has renounced everything.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having spoken thus, as he was making a hurried effort to rise in order to cast his body into the pit standing before him, Kumbha also spoke.
*Śvabhra* and *bhṛgu* mean a precipice. || 17 ||
Kumbha said:
O King, why do you abandon this innocent body in the great banyan tree?
For even a bull, when enraged, kills a young calf though it be ignorant.
[He killed] one who was blameless and innocent—a young calf, his own offspring—at the great banyan tree on the Bhṛgu mountain. || 18 ||
This wretched body is indeed dull, mute in nature, and miserable; it is not yours at all. Do not abandon this single form in vain. (19)
He demonstrates his very innocence with the word "insentient" (jaḍa). The words "it is your fault" are to be supplied as the ellipsis. || 19 ||
This silent self remains absorbed in meditation within itself alone;
it is moved only by another, just as a piece of wood is driven by a wave.
Another person alone, who is worthy of restraint, repeatedly and forcibly agitates him, just as a drunken thief disturbs an ascetic staying in solitude. (21)
He who, having committed an offense, points to another and causes agitation—he alone is worthy of restraint and should be punished. || 21 ||
For the body is not at fault for the arising of pleasure, pain, and so forth;
nor is the tree at fault when the self experiences its fruit through the movement of the self. 22.

One might object: "Since it is the locus for the arising of pleasure and pain, how can the body not be considered guilty? To this he says: "By pleasure... [and so forth]. By "bhūtyā" (by being), he means merely by being the place of origin. He provides an illustration for this: "Not... Just as when fruit falls from a tree laden with fruit due to a movement caused by the wind, the self who identifies with that tree does not become guilty. || 22 ||
The wind, throbbing, brings about the falling of fruits, heads, and flowers; what offense has the young man committed against himself by being virtuous? (23)

Since it is the very wind, as it blows, that forcibly causes the falling of the fruits, the sprouts on the tips of branches, and the flowers, it alone is the offender; likewise, what offense has been committed by the youth against the virtuous? Similarly, what offense has been committed by the body against the virtuous self? This is the meaning. || 23 ||
O lotus-eyed one, even though you have abandoned your body,
it is said that your renunciation of everything has not yet reached completion, for that is indeed difficult to achieve.

For this reason, that total renunciation becomes difficult and indeed hard to accomplish, because of the difficulty of obtaining a body qualified for it and the consequent difficulty of attaining knowledge; such is the meaning. || 24 ||
O Bhṛgu, you are pointlessly casting away this innocent body;
by abandoning the body, one does not thereby become a renouncer of that [the self]. || 25 ||
The meaning is that for one who does not abandon that ego which agitates the body, [liberation] will not come to pass, nor will it be accomplished. || 25 ||
If you abandon that evil by which this body is agitated, like a tree by a rutting elephant, then you are truly one who possesses great renunciation.
O King, when that [craving] is abandoned, everything beginning with the body is abandoned;
otherwise, even though submerged, this [craving] sprouts again and again.

Although this body and so forth are submerged and even destroyed by immersion in water and other such means, they sprout again from that very driver of the body, which constitutes the seed of birth and karma. (27)
Śikhidhvaja said:

By what is this body moved? What is the seed of births and karmas? When what is abandoned does everything, including the body and so forth, become abandoned, O handsome one? (Note: "sundara" is the reading found in the text).
Everything becomes abandoned, O handsome one. || 28 ||

Kumbha said: "O virtuous one, O King, the renunciation of everything does not occur through the abandonment of the body, nor by the relinquishing of a kingdom, nor by the withering away of one's hut and such."

When everything— whatever exists and from whatever source— is renounced within that single cause of all, and when everything has been completely relinquished, then total renunciation has been accomplished.

It is "all" (sarva) because it is the locus of all latent impressions; it is "from all" (sarvataḥ) because it extends toward all objects; and it is the "sole cause of all" (sarvaikakāraṇe) because it generates everything through volition.
Śikhidhvaja said:
"Everything is omnipresent, everything is to be abandoned, and everything must always be relinquished.
Tell me, O best among those who know the reality of all things, what is meant by 'everything'? (31)
The meaning is: "What is that which you describe as being 'to be abandoned everywhere,' 'to be relinquished at all times,' and 'worthy of being cast off'?"
Kumbha said:

O holy one, that which has an all-pervading form and is designated by names such as "jīva" and "prāṇa," which is neither inert nor non-inert, and which is deluded—that is traditionally known as the "all-encompassing mind" (citta). (32)
The subtle body (liṅga) is the mind; it is called "jīva" when consciousness is predominant, and it is called "prāṇa" and so forth when activity is predominant. || 32 ||
Know that the mind alone is delusion; know, O King, that the mind is the person.
Know that the mind is the web of the world; it is remembered that "all is mind. (33)
A man, that is, a person who engages in worldly affairs. || 33 ||

O Lord of the Earth, the mind is the seed of everything— whether it be sovereignty and the like, the body and the like, or the stages of life and the like— just as the seed of a tree is for the tree itself.

When the seed of everything has been completely abandoned, everything becomes truly abandoned; O King, through the realization of both the possible and the impossible, there occurs the renunciation of all. (35)
Because if that [ego] is abandoned, the abandonment of everything becomes possible, whereas if it is not abandoned, the abandonment of everything is impossible. || 35 ||
Whether it be all things or the absence of things, whether it be kingship or the forest, for one with a mind there is supreme suffering; for one without a mind there is supreme bliss. (36)
Whether all things such as dharma or adharma, or the places for enjoying the kingdom and its fruits, they are nothing but supreme suffering for one who possesses a mind. 36.
All this revolves as nothing but the mind appearing as the world, through the web of forms such as the body, just as a seed appears as a tree. (37)
It evolves; it undergoes transformation. || 37 ||
Just as a tree is moved by the wind, a mountain by an earthquake, and a bellows by the weight of its own contents, so too is this body moved by the mind. (38)
A leather bag for blowing [the forge] is like a skin-bag; it is filled by the smith with the weight of the bellows. || 38 ||
Know that the very firm mind of the great sages is the casket for all enjoyments of beings, as well as for old age, death, and birth. (39)
The phrase "of all beings" refers to the experiences well-known to all, such as old age, death, and other bodily attributes.

By the term "Great Sage," qualities such as tranquility and self-control are indicated. The meaning is that the mind itself, in which the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of these qualities have become firmly established in various instances, is their substratum. || 39 ||
All this proceeds as nothing but the mind in the form of the world;
through the web of forms such as the body, the mind becomes the living soul (*jīva*) consisting of thought (*manomaya*). (40)

The meaning is that the very same unpeaceful mind, through the act of thinking, becomes "mind-made" (manomaya); then, by means of internal vital activity, it becomes the individual soul (jīva), and finally, externally, it comes to exist through a web of forms consisting of the gross body and its various activities. || 40 ||
O Sage, that which is peaceful is designated by such functional activities as "intellect," "the great principle," "ego," and "vital breath," according to their respective functions. (41)

The meaning is that this very [Self], being internally tranquil, is designated by such functional expressions as "the Great One" (mahat), "the I-maker" (ahaṃkāra), "the vital breath" (prāṇa), and "the conscious self" (prājñātman), in accordance with its various activities. || 41 ||

They say that the mind is everything; when that is relinquished, O Lord of the Earth, the abandonment of all things is accomplished, marking the boundary beyond which all mental anguish and physical disease cease.
O best among those who know renunciation, the wise understand the renunciation of the mind to be the renunciation of everything;
when that is accomplished, O mighty-armed one, what truth remains that is not experienced? (43)
Why is Truth—not of the nature of ultimate reality, existence, and bliss—not experienced? The meaning is that it is indeed experienced.
When the mind is relinquished, duality and unity everywhere dissolve;
only that which is supremely peaceful, pure, one, and free from affliction remains. (44)
Duality is the succession of manifestations through the differentiation of effects; unity is the process of concealment within the cause, which undergoes dissolution and sublation. (44)
They know her mind to be the field for the continuous harvest of worldly existence; when the field has ceased to be a field, how could rice possibly arise? (45)
Mind alone, sporting with various forms of existence and non-existence, manifests as the appearance of objects, just as water manifests as waves. (46)
By way of being the object, that is, by way of the form of the referent of the word. || 46 ||
O King, by means of total renunciation, which takes the form of uplifting the mind,
everything is properly attained at all times, just as through universal sovereignty.
O King, just as there is another object for your total renunciation, so too do you become an object for another; you renounce, O King, yet you indeed take up again.
And with the intention that this renunciation of everything cannot be accomplished while there is a grasping at a limited self, he says: "All," etc.

O renouncer, O King, just as there is for you something else that is the object of your total renunciation, so too you yourself become the object of the renunciation of another who has renounced you. And thus, you grasp that which is to be renounced as being the self.
The meaning is that your renunciation of everything does not succeed. || 48 ||
By him who has renounced everything, the entire web of the world across the three periods of time has been contained within, like a pearl within its casing. (49)

But if the grasping of the Self is undifferentiated, then you alone are the Self of all; since it is impossible for you to abandon yourself through another, and since you—who are not included within the category of things to be abandoned—have brought everything under your own control by abandoning all, you have attained everything. Thus he says: "The Sūtra. (49)
By whom all has been relinquished, even in that void he remains established;
the entire world existing in the three times is situated within him like a string of pearls upon a thread. (50)

One might object: "By renouncing everything, has he not merely resorted to universal emptiness (*sarvaśūnyatā*); how then could he obtain everything under his own control? To this, he says: "by which" (*yena*). Although he has indeed renounced everything and entered into universal emptiness, nevertheless, because the world renounced by him finds no other substratum, it relies upon that very [emptiness] and attains existence and manifestation for as long as worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) continues.
The intended meaning is that, from the perspective of the conventional user, that very [reality] is called "all that is obtained throughout the three times. || 50 ||
By him who has abandoned everything like a lamp without oil, by him everything is illuminated as if by a lamp with oil. || 51 ||

For this very reason, he provides the analogy of an extinguished lamp for the light of the all-pervading essential nature from the perspective of non-conceptual vision— due to the abandonment of everything, the sublation of everything, and the absolute cessation of attachment—
while providing the analogy of a lamp with oil from the perspective of conventional vision, because it illuminates all worldly activity through that very light of the all-pervading essential nature.
Having renounced everything that remains, he who sleeps like an oilless lamp shines as a luminous self,
equanimous like a lamp with oil.
He clarifies that very point with the words: "It remains" (sthitam). || 52 ||
Just as you alone remain when all things have been removed, so too does primordial wisdom remain when every [dualistic] abandonment has been made. (53)

He prevents the attainment of emptiness through the renunciation of everything by saying "of all": that is, upon the removal—that is, the renunciation—of all things, such as the kingdom, the forest, and one's personal belongings. || 53 ||
Just as you are not like others even when all things have been consumed by fire, O King, so too, my dear, is Nirvana said to arise from the renunciation of everything.
Since the remaining aggregate [of elements] is distinct from oneself, what human goal (puruṣārtha) could there be for oneself therein? To this he says: "samasta... etc.
The meaning is that even though liberation (nirvāṇa) is the supreme human goal, it is nothing other than You. || 54 ||
For total renunciation is itself empty of self, yet it is the substratum for all infinite and sublime cognitions, just as space is for the inhabitants of heaven.

He says, "For the abandonment of all," because even though that [Self] is empty of all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), there is indeed the inclusion of all cognitions within it; thus, there is no attribution of insentience (*jāḍya*). [The phrase] "of the dwellers of heaven" refers to the sun, moon, stars, and so forth. || 55 ||
For one who drinks the essence of total renunciation, no fears of old age or death cause any affliction,
just as streaks of clouds do not affect the sky.

Just as when one drinks the essence of total renunciation, even if a slight taste of it is experienced, no "sky-scratching" or "hole-making" thorns—representing those who are unattached and indifferent—can cause any affliction; so it is in this case. || 56 ||
The renunciation of everything is the cause of greatness and stainless radiance; for if you renounce all, there arises the most expansive stability of intellect. (57)
From what source does such greatness arise, characterized by stainless radiance and the manifestation of one's true nature? To this he says:
"The renunciation of everything is supreme bliss; all else is most terrible suffering.
Having accepted this with the word "Om," do whatever you desire.
The word "iti" implies "having reflected thus. The explanation of "oṃ" is "urarīkṛtya" (having accepted). || 58 ||
For one who renounces everything, everything indeed comes to him;
just as water enters the fire, so too does it return to the ocean.

He prevents the loss of majesty even when there is total renunciation with the word "all": "All" means that the entire collection of possessions brought forth by *prārabdha* karma presents itself. The meaning is that just as water enters the submarine fire (*vaḍavāgni*) in the ocean, so too it continues to arrive from the rivers; it is exactly like that. || 59 ||
Within every act of renunciation lies the knowledge that brings clarity to the self;
indeed, it is like the space within a vessel where jewels and such are contained.
The meaning is that within the very abandonment of all ignorance and its effects, there must necessarily exist the knowledge that brings clarity to the Self;
for it is well known that the gems and such reside precisely in that part of a vessel which is empty of them. || 60 ||
Even in this Kali age, when everyone is under the sway of greed at the time of death,
the Śākya Sage remains as firm as Mount Meru, free from all fear.

The word "hatā" (slain) is used to illuminate the following point: if even a Śākya—who, being outside the Vedic fold, is most base—even during the Kali age, the most sinful of times, remained firm like Mount Meru by virtue of renouncing everything; then what need is there to mention you, who in the meritorious Dvāpara age, following the path of the Vedas and being most holy, remained as fearless as the sky? Thus it is said.
O Great King, the relinquishment of everything is the foundation of all prosperity;
for since he does not grasp at anything whatsoever, everything is offered to him.
He is the support and the dwelling place of all prosperities. || 62 ||
Having renounced everything, being peaceful, self-abiding, and equal to the sky,
O King, become of that very nature which is gentle.

Having renounced everything, O Great Being, you must now renounce that by which [renunciation] occurs; and having abandoned the stain of pride in renunciation, become one whose nature is liberated, O Protector of the Earth! (64)

O Great-Souled Protector of the Earth, having first renounced all that is to be abandoned by means of the mind, and immediately thereafter having cast off even that very mind by which you abandon, and subsequently having liberated yourself from the impurity of egoism characterized by the pride of renunciation—this is the meaning: become one who is liberated while living. || 64 ||
Thus ends the ninety-third canto, titled "The Awakening of Śikhidhvaja," in the first part of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*, composed by the sage Vālmīki. 93.
Thus ends the ninety-third sarga, titled "The Awakening of Śikhidhvaja," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The ninety-fourth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: While Kumbha was thus speaking repeatedly about the renunciation of the mind, [the Lord] spoke again.
Reflecting within himself, the gentle king spoke these words.
In this context, in order to relinquish the mind, one must purify its root;
by subverting the body and other objects of perception, the remainder that is the full consciousness is set forth.
The relinquishing of the mind and the means for relinquishing the mind. || 1 ||
Śikhidhvaja said: The bird of the sky of the heart, the monkey of the tree of the heart—
though repeatedly driven away, my mind indeed returns again and again.
"Cast away" means abandoned with the thought "this is not mine. The particle *hi* has the sense of "indeed" (*apyartha*). || 2 ||
I know how to seize this mind, like a fish from a tangled net;
yet I do not know how to relinquish it, for it is like a supreme substance within the mind, lacking any physical form.

(3) I know how to seize this mind—that is, to take possession of it through the sense of "mine"—just as one might catch a fish, because it lacks materiality. However, I do not know how to abandon it, as it is like a sublime, immaterial entity.
But I do not know renunciation, O Supreme One! || 3 ||
O Blessed One, tell me truly the original nature of the mind; thereafter, O Lord, tell me truly how to abandon that mind. (4)
The essential nature, which is worthy of being relinquished, is condensed into a universal form.
Kumbha said:
O great king, know that latent impression (vāsanā) alone is the very nature of the mind;
indeed, the word "citta" is declared to be a synonym for latent impression. || 5 ||

Kumbha states that very point: "It is simply the latent impression (vāsanā). This means the latent impression of passion (rāga-vāsanā). It is illustrated by common usage in the world; thus, worldly people say, "I have a latent impression for cakes," or "His mind is set on pancakes. || 5 ||
Its renunciation is exceedingly easy and simple to accomplish, even more so than the stilling of the mind;
it brings greater bliss than sovereignty and is more beautiful than a flower. (6)

"Easy to accomplish" means that its attainment occurs through mere indifference; this is the sense. "Even than sovereignty": as they have said— "Whatever sensual pleasure there is in the world, and whatever great divine pleasure there is, these do not equal even a sixteenth part of the happiness of the destruction of craving. "Sundara" means charming or pleasing. || 6 ||
But for a fool, the renunciation of the mind has indeed become difficult to accomplish;
it is like an empire for a commoner, or like Mount Sumeru becoming a blade of grass.
If that is so, why then is it not performed by everyone? To this he replies: "By the fool" (mūrkhasya). || 7 ||
Śikhidhvaja said:
"I know the true nature of the mind to be agitated and composed of latent impressions (vāsanā).
I consider its abandonment to be more difficult to accomplish than even swallowing a thunderbolt."

The meaning is: "I know by your words. It is even more difficult to accomplish than swallowing a thunderbolt; for when there is folly, it is precisely indifference that is hard to achieve—this is the intended sense. || 8 ||
Of the flower that is the fragrance of saṃsāra, and of the fire that burns with suffering;
of the lotus-stalk that is the world, and of the sky that is the wind of delusion.

The lotus, which is the characteristic mark of the world, belongs to that stalk (*mṛṇāla*). Even if the reading is *jāla*, its meaning remains the lotus itself, based on the etymology "that which arises in water" (*jale bhavam*). By all these synonyms, the Cause alone is indicated. || 9 ||
Tell me how the effortless relinquishing of the mind occurs— of that which drives the machine of the body and is like a bee within the lotus of the heart.

The suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*) [to the root *vah*] because it carries and sets in motion the machine of the body; "by which" means by whatever means it occurs. || 10 ||
Kumbha said:
O virtuous one, that which is the total destruction of this mind—the cessation of saṃsāra—is precisely what has been called "the renunciation of the mind" by those of far-reaching vision. (11)
The destruction of everything—the aforementioned roots, sprouts, branches, and shoots—is itself the exhaustion of saṃsāra;

that alone is the complete relinquishing of the mind, and not merely the turning away from the sense of "mine" as in the case of abandoning external objects. This is the meaning. [This is] by those of far-reaching vision, who perceive the undivided Self. || 11 ||
Śikhidhvaja said:
"I consider the destruction of the mind to be for the sake of perfect accomplishment through the renunciation of the mind.
How can its non-existence be experienced a hundred times over, as in the case of a disease?"
Reflecting upon the meaning thus stated and expressing his approval by way of restatement, Śikhidhvaja provides the supporting argument thereon, beginning with the word *citta*:

"The mind, indeed, is a disease. For the non-existence of a disease is not experienced even through a hundred acts of renunciation characterized by the abandonment of the sense of "mine-ness" (*mamatā*); rather, it occurs only through its eradication by means of medical treatment. Therefore, for the sake of its eradication—
The meaning is: "Tell me [of it] together with its roots, branches, shoots, and so forth. || 12 ||
Kumbha said:
The tree of the mind has the ego as its seed, with its branches, fruits, and sprouts;
uproot it along with its very root, and become one whose heart is like space.

Become one whose heart is free from obstruction and distraction—like the open space where that tree once stood—having uprooted that tree which has branches, fruit, and sprouts, and of which the "I" who is ignorant of the Self is the seed. 13.
Śikhidhvaja said:
O Sage, what is the root of the mind? What is its sprout? What is its origin? What are its branches, and what are its trunks? And how is it uprooted?
That in which something comes into being is "saṃbhava," namely, the field (kṣetra). || 14 ||
Kumbha said:
O high-minded one, know that this which arises as the sense of "I," consisting of the perception of the mind, is the seed of this tree of the mind. (15)

That which arises from the unawakened sense of "I" (ahamartha) is this well-known ego (abhimānin), whose nature consists in the cognition of the mind; the term "this very thing" refers to it by means of its causal sign (liṅga). The seed is the root. || 15 ||
The state of the Supreme Self is the field; that field belongs to the one composed of Māyā.
From this [field], which first sprouted forth, there arose a sprout in the form of experience.
He provides the answer to the question "What is its origin? with the words "the station of the Supreme Self" (*paramātmapadam*).

The station or nest of the Supreme Self is *māyā*; she alone is the field (*kṣetra*). Since she is the field for this entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*) consisting of *māyā*, the meaning is that she is likewise the field for the mind (*cetas*) as well. He provides the answer to the question "What is the sprout? with the words "from this" (*etasmāt*).

The meaning is that from this root which has first arisen, there is produced a sprout consisting of experience, characterized by the certainty "I am distinct," because it is permeated by the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa). || 16 ||
That which is of the nature of certainty and formless is called "intellect" (buddhi);
it is the swelling of this very sprout designated as intellect. (17)
He states that its transformation occurs through the very process of accumulation by means of the tree-like mind: "of this" (asya).

The connection with the subsequent clause is as follows: a fattening of such a nature arises, belonging to that which has the designation "mind" (citta) because of the recollection of the forms of the body and so forth, and the designation "intellect" (manas) because of the act of reflecting upon them. || 17 ||

Consisting of volitional constructs, she is designated by the names "mind" (citta) and "intellect" (manas). The individual soul (jīva), whose nature is false perception, is indeed empty in essence, like a stone. || 18 ||

He speaks of the life-force (*jīva*) of that tree, saying "the life-force. In the ultimate sense, because it is changeless, the Self is devoid of all modifications; therefore, it is like a stone—meaning it is the witness whose nature is the perception of the connection between the mind and its qualities, both of which are illusory. || 18 ||
This body is its pillar, composed of sinews, bones, and flesh;
the latent impression (vāsanā) is its temporal vibration, like the sprouting of a seed in another region. (19)
The trunk is the middle portion extending from the root to the end of the branches. This "body" is simply the physical frame.

Just as in the springtime and other such seasons, when one desires to initiate the growth of a sprout at the location of the sprout—that is, at the tip of the trunk in a different region from the base—in order for the trunk, branches, and so forth to grow there.

The meaning is that the "rasa" which vibrates at the time of the ripening of the karma that bestows various enjoyments—in the form of sprouts, shoots, and so forth, such as the activity of attachment and aversion—is none other than its own latent impression (*vāsanā*). || 19 ||
The branches of the tree of the mind are long, far-reaching, and spread out;
they are the sense organs, which yield meager enjoyment and have existence and non-existence as their source. (20)
The long, far-reaching, extended, and widespread branches of this tree of the mind are the sense organs (*indriya*);

existence and non-existence, births and deaths, are the sources of its thousands of misfortunes; and enjoyments are its great clusters of boughs, which are collections of intermediate branches—this is the connection with what follows. (20)
The great clusters of branches of this tree-like mind, which is of such a nature, are filled at every moment with auspicious and inauspicious fruits. (21)
"While pruning the branches, apply yourself to the scraping of the roots.
Śikhidhvaja said:
"I am performing the lopping away of the branches and so forth of the tree of the mind."

The meaning is: while performing the pruning of the branches, characterized by the severing of attachment to the enjoyment of sense objects, exert yourself with great effort—placing your primary weight—upon the scraping away of the root, which is characterized by the vision of the non-attached, non-dual Self.
Regarding that, the King asks about the means for both the pruning of the branches and the scraping away of the root, beginning with the words "citta" (mind). || 22 ||
"O Sage, how can I completely uproot the very foundation?
Kumbha replied:
"The various latent tendencies (*vāsanās*) are the branches, endowed with the movement of fruits and so forth. (23)
Then Kumbha spoke of the means for cutting the branches, namely: "Latent Impressions" (vāsanā). || 23 ||
Those who have not cultivated [the mind] are cut down within by the power of their own consciousness;
yet he whose mind is unattached, who is silent, and whose speech and deliberation are stilled—[is liberated]. (24)
They become severed by abandoning attachment through cultivation and by experiencing [the truth] through the power of internal investigative awareness.
He demonstrates this very point as a characteristic of those liberated while living (jīvanmukta) with the verse beginning "unattached" (asaṃsakta). || 24 ||
He who acts upon what has been attained becomes one whose mental creeper is severed within;
cutting away the web of the tree and creeper of the mind by means of human effort. || 25 ||

He says that when the practice of cutting away the branches and creepers has become firm, one becomes capable of scraping away the roots, in the verse beginning with "cittadruma" (the tree of the mind).
"Latājālam" means a mass of creepers, which is to say, a collection of branches. || 25 ||
He who remains would be fit for the testing of the root;
the cutting of branches is secondary, while the cutting of the root is primary. (26)
The secondary is the limb; the primary is the principal. || 26 ||
Therefore, O Great Sage, be intent upon scraping away the roots of the tree of the mind; for that purpose, thoroughly perform the burning of the root.

"By way of being primary" means by way of predominance; the sense is that if the principal element is not accomplished, there is the consequence of deficiency even for a subsidiary element that has been prepared with effort. || 27 ||
"Thus does the state of mindlessness arise for one who has severed the thorn of the mind.
Śikhidhvaja said:
"O Sage, [tell me] of the seed of the tree of the mind, which is the self-sense of 'I'."
Who could be an effective agent in this task called burning, which is like fire? || 28 ||

The syntactical connection with what precedes is as follows: "You, [O Fire], must perform a complete burning of the roots of the thorny grove of the forest of *karañja* trees, which is characterized by the mind (*citta-lakṣaṇa*). When this is done, the state of non-mind (*acittatā*) arises.
Since that burning cannot be accomplished by the well-known fire, one who desires to know another fire asks: "Of the self consisting of the sense of 'I' (*ahaṃbhāva-ātman*)."
One who brings about the purpose is capable. || 28 ||
Kumbha said:
O King, this inquiry into one's own self—taking the form of "Who am I?"—is known as the fire that burns the seed of the wicked tree of the mind. (29)
"Who am I?"—thus assuming the form of everything from inquiry up to direct realization. || 29 ||
Śikhidhvaja said:
"O Sage, I have reflected upon this many times with my own intellect,
as long as I have not [seen] the world adorned with the circle of the earth's forests."

"O Sage, although I have understood through my own intellect that external objects— ranging from the body to the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra)— as well as internal objects, are non-self and unreal, nevertheless, due to a lack of acquaintance with the reality of the Inner Self, the delusion of 'selfhood' regarding the inert ego-sense does not cease even though it arises again and again; thus, I find no rest," he said.

By these six [verses], beginning with "Thus," etc.; "as far as" (*yāvat*) signifies totality; the meaning is that the entire world has been investigated in many ways. He explains that very point in detail, starting with "I am not," etc. The concise statement is: "The world, adorned by the earth and the forest regions contained within it, is not I. (30)
Neither the mountain slope, nor the forest, nor the rustling of leaves and such;
neither the bodies due to their insentience, nor the flesh, bones, blood, and so forth. (31)
He explains that very point in detail with the words "not from the mountain," and so forth. "Because of insentience" is the reason applied in every case. || 31 ||
It is neither the organs of action nor the organs of perception;
it is neither the mind, nor the intellect, nor even the ego, because of its insentience.
Just as the state of being a bracelet exists in gold, so does the state of "I-ness" exist in the conscious self;
however, that which is insentient is non-existent by its very nature, and therefore it does not exist, O Sage. (33)

Warding off the doubt that there is no insentience (*jaḍatva*) in the ego (*ahaṃkāra*) by means of the reason of its being an illusory manifestation (*vivarta*), he states—beginning with "the state of being a bracelet"—that since an insentient thing cannot establish itself independently, its establishment through superimposition (*adhyāsa*) upon consciousness results in its falsity (*mithyātva*). Thus, the remainder is: "so too, the state of 'I' (*ahaṃtva*) is an illusory manifestation. However, insentient things such as shell-silver or a mirage are [falsely perceived] as having the nature of non-existence.

The word "well-known" (prasiddham) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. Thus, by that reason of insentience (jaḍatva), that "I-ness" and so forth does not exist; the meaning is that it is merely false. || 33 ||
In the supreme state, that which consists of the nature of arrangement and abiding, and which is the source of all objects and so forth, exists;
nothing else exists there because of its otherness, just as a great tree does not exist in the sky.

He states that [the world] is non-existent even because it is other than the true Being (*sad-rūpa*) which is the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the aforementioned insentient category beginning with the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*):

"It does not exist. If one asks why it is so, it is because the insentient category beginning with the cosmic egg is the support (*ādhāra*), consisting of the dwelling-place for the arrangements of the fourteen worlds and so forth.

He is the beginning, that is, the cause, of all objects such as sound and other sense-objects. Furthermore, the conscious self (cidātman) does not possess a differentiated nature, because its form is that of undivided pure existence (sattāsāmānya); this is the meaning. || 34 ||
"O Blessed One, although I know that you are the stainless cleanser of the 'I'-notion, I do not know the Inner Knower within; for that reason, O Sage, I have long been tormented. (35)

Thus, in this manner, although I know the cleansing of the impurity characterized by egoism, I do not know that inner consciousness which is the witness-consciousness (sākṣicaitanya), whose sole essence is the inward-facing Self. 35.
Kumbha said:

"O lord of the earth, if you are not merely this much—a mere collection of elements—then tell me, O sinless one of great intellect, who you truly are, for you are something more than that due to your dullness. (36)
Now, wishing to point out the witnessing consciousness (sākṣicaitanya) by means of elimination alone, Kumbha said: "This much" (etāvat).
This refers to the entire collection of objects of perception extending up to the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra). || 36 ||
Śikhidhvaja said:
"O best of the wise, I am pure consciousness, the clear self-awareness, in which those entities find their relish and by which they are determined. (37)
At the limit of the succession of internal sheaths (kośas), which are well-known as the knower, the enjoyer, and so forth, there exists the pure consciousness (cinmātra) whose sole essence is bliss;

therein, non-blissful and insentient entities such as the objects of sound and the rest find their relish, or by which [consciousness], when mounted upon the modifications of the intellect, they are determined through the distinction between the desirable and the undesirable. 37.
For one such as I, this clinging to the notion "I am" is surely either groundless or has some cause; yet I do not know that state [of its origin]. (38)

Upon reflection with the eye of discernment, I do not know whether this impurity—characterized by the conceit of identity (*tādātmyābhimāna*) in the form of "I" regarding my own collection of body and so forth—is possessed of a cause or causeless;
nor do I know that state which is Brahman. This is the meaning. || 38 ||
O Sage, because I am unable to wipe away this evil, non-self, and impure stain from my soul,
I suffer most grievously.
Kumbha said:
"Tell me, O mighty-armed one, what is this great stain clinging to you, by which you remain a transmigrating being, whether through that which exists or that which does not? (40)
O Being, by whatever stain—whether real or unreal, whether true or false—you have become a transmigrating being and remain so; [by that you are bound]. (40)
Śikhidhvaja said:
"The sense of 'I' (ahaṃkāra) is the seed of the tree of the mind and my impurity;
yet I do not know how to abandon it, for as soon as it is abandoned, it returns to me. (41)

I do not know whether that [ego-sense] is true or false; however, I know generally that it is the root of the tree of the mind which bears all manner of misfortune, and specifically that it consists of the notions of "I-ness" (*ahaṃbhāva*) and "mine-ness" (*mamabhāva*). Furthermore, I do not know the means to abandon or eliminate it. But surely, the well-known means for its abandonment is precisely the realization that "I am not" and "mine is not"?
"How can that which was previously shown by you yourself in the forests and other places be denied? To this he replies: "Abandoned, abandoned.

Thus, although it has been abandoned again and again, because its root has not been severed, it approaches me again and again. Therefore, the intention is: "Tell me its root and the means for its eradication. (41)
Kumbha said:
An effect arises from a cause; therefore, that which exists [as a cause] may be found everywhere.
But that which is otherwise is non-existent, like the appearance of a second moon; though seen, it does not truly exist.

In this regard, because the Real is immutable (*kūṭastha*), its status as a cause is simply impossible. As for the statement that the unreal is a cause, since it culminates in the sense that "an effect has arisen from an unreal cause," it results in the unreality of the effect itself; thus, it ultimately culminates in the identity of the Self. This is the secret, which is understood solely according to the capacity of one's intellect.

Intending to awaken Kumbha, [the Lord] said—through two verses beginning with "From a cause"—"Seek out by your own intellect and tell me the cause of the egoism that is well-known in the world. However, any other effect that has arisen without a cause, appearing like a double moon, is indeed non-existent; for if this were correctly perceived, it would not exist at all—this is the meaning. || 42 ||
"The effect arises from a cause; from the sense of 'I' (ahaṃbhāva) comes the sprout of worldly existence.
Having thus investigated the cause, tell it to me now. (43)

The meaning is: "Just as the sprout of existence, characterized by the mind and so forth, arises as an effect from the cause that is the sense of 'I' (ahaṃbhāva), seek out through your own intelligence such a cause for this very sense of 'I' and tell it to me."
Śikhidhvaja said:
"O Sage, I know that the cause of the fault of 'I-ness' is its perception;
tell me, O Lord of Sages, how that may come to rest. (44)

Thus questioned, the king searched for a long time with his own intellect; concluding that since the conceit of "I" (ahaṃtā) cannot apply to the sensation of the body's form and so forth when they are absent, the sensation itself must be the cause of that conceit, he replied: "O Sage! [iti].
"O Sage, tell me how this 'I' exists for the sake of suffering due to the mind's orientation toward objects of thought; speak of the cessation of those objects for the sake of its pacification. (45)
Because of its tendency toward the object of cognition (*cetyonmukhatva*), this body and so forth, existing as the sense of "I" (*ahaṃbhāva*), have become a source of suffering;
therefore, it is intended that the very objects of cognition—the body and so forth—are the cause [of suffering] for consciousness even in the absence of their actual perception.
With this in mind, he says "the object of cognition" (*cetya*) [in verse 45], asking: "Tell me the means for the cessation of the object of cognition in order to pacify that [suffering]. || 45 ||
Kumbha said:
You are a knower of causes; tell me quickly the cause of this sensation.
Then I shall instruct you in the sequence of causes and non-causes.

If you are a knower of causes, such that for the consciousness (vedana) being directed toward an object of cognition (vedya), the object of cognition itself is the cause, then quickly state what you intend. Thereafter, immediately following your statement, I shall enlighten you regarding the sequence by which that intended cause of yours becomes a non-cause; this is the meaning. || 46 ||

Tell me this: how has it come about that you, who are without cause, have become the cause for me—who am of the nature of the object of knowledge and the knower, and who consist of the thinkable and the thinker? (47)

He repeats the very same point once more to clarify it, saying "as the object" (*vedya*). The meaning is: just as you have intended—that which is an object (*vedya*), being false by nature both generally as the form of the object and cognition (*vedana-vedanarūpa*) and specifically as the un-conscious (*acetana*), is incapable of being a cause and yet has attained the status of a cause—so too [is this]. (47)

Śikhidhvaja said: O Sage, this existence of objects here, such as the body and so forth, which consists of the nature of the perceived and the perceiver and takes the form of the known and the act of knowing, has its cause in this [body].
Śikhidhvaja clearly stated what he intended when asked: "The object of thought" (cetya) refers to the existence of external and internal entities, such as the body and so forth. (48)
Sensation arises through the reality of the object as having a body and so forth;
it is like a vibration caused by the appearance of what is unreal, such as a streak of wind.

Regarding how the existence of the body and so forth can be the cause of cognition (*vedana*), he says: "The body... Since cognition itself arises in the form of the body and so forth, with the existence of the body and other objects serving as its instrumental cause—just like molten metal poured into a mold—it is impossible for the formless cognition to possess the form of the corporeal body and such.
Because it cannot be real, he qualifies it by saying "as an unreal appearance. || 49 ||
Just as I do not perceive the non-existence of the existence of things, so too does the seed of the mind—the perception of "I-ness"—become completely stilled. (50)

Just as the perception of "I-ness" within the seed of the mind is pacified, so too do I not yet understand the non-existence of the reality of the body and other such things. Therefore, the sense [of the request] is: "Please instruct me on how that non-existence may be understood. || 50 ||
Kumbha said:
If the existence of entities such as the body and so forth were real, then that [consciousness] would belong to you;
but since the existence of the body and so forth is non-existent, upon what is your perception based?

Thus questioned, Kumbha asserts the non-existence of the visible objects such as the body in order to dispel the delusion that consciousness arises in the form of its objects—stating, "It exists. If the existence of entities such as the body were real, then indeed your [opponent's] intended view—that consciousness takes on their form because of them—might hold;
however, that very thing is difficult to find. Thus, consciousness...
What is its smallest [state], and what is its object? The meaning is that it is indeed without an object. || 51 ||
Śikhidhvaja said:
How could that which has some perceivable nature consisting of conceptualization be of an unreal form? How could light be darkness?
The King asks, "How can there be a denial of the body and so forth, which are perceived through direct perception? [He answers with the verse beginning] "Of that which...
He further states, by means of an illustration, that a proposition asserting the non-existence of that which is perceived as existing is contradictory: "Like light..."

O Sage, how can it be that this body—which is endowed with hands, feet, and so forth; which possesses the manifestation of the fruits of action; and which is constantly being experienced—does not exist? (53)
Kumbha said:
O protector of the earth, that effect for which no cause exists does not exist here;
the cognition of such an effect is merely an illusion.

The existence of a visible object cannot be determined by mere non-perception, because there is deviation in the case of erroneous perceptions. Rather, when the causes are present, that effect which is perceived exists; however, he states that these [causes] do not exist for this [body]:
"Without a cause, the body, which is an effect, never exists."
Where indeed could that substance be produced whose seed does not exist?
But know that which is causeless yet appears as if it were an effect before one's eyes to be like the water of a mirage, arising from the delusion of the observer. (56)
Know that this which has arisen from false delusion is indeed non-existent;
even for one who exerts great effort, the water of a mirage cannot be obtained.
Śikhidhvaja said:
It is not logical to seek a cause for that which is non-existent, such as the double moon;
for whom does the decoration of all the limbs of the son of a barren woman shine? (58)
In that case, would this body and so forth be as utterly non-existent as the body of a barren woman’s son? Thus the King raises a doubt with the words, "If it were non-existent" (asataḥ). || 58 ||
Kumbha said: O King, know that this body, a cage of bones and so forth, is a mere effect without a cause; it is indeed non-existent because of its impossibility.

Kumbha says: "By means of a cause," [referring to] the scriptural passage beginning with "The bodiless dwells within bodies that are unstable," as well as the experience of the wise and the impossibility of determining a cause; thus, this is merely an accepted conclusion (iṣṭāpatti). || 59 ||
Śikhidhvaja said: O Lord of Sages, why is the father not considered the cause of this body, which is endowed with hands, feet, and other limbs, and is perceived as existing eternally?

The King raises an objection: "How can his father, who has been ascertained through tradition, inference, the testimony of reliable persons, and signs such as the similarity of physical form, be denied? (Verse 60).
Kumbha said:
O King, because of the absence of a cause, there is no such thing as a "father.
That which is born from what is non-existent is itself called non-existent. (61)
With the hidden intention that the same logic applies to its non-existence as well, he restates that very response:
"The cause of things that are effects is called the seed;
for indeed, my friend, no sprout can arise in this world without a seed. (62)
Therefore, for that effect whose cause is not found here to exist, it does not exist when the seed is absent; the cognition of it is merely an illusion. (63)
Indeed, that which is necessarily non-existent and seedless is a delusion of the mind;
it is like the appearance of two moons, water in a desert, or the state of a barren woman’s son. (64)
Śikhidhvaja said:
"Among the grandfathers, sons, and ancestors in the three worlds,
why is the Primordial Grandfather not the cause of the initial creation?"
Not understanding the hidden intention, the king suspects: "Of the grandfathers.

The first grandfather is Hiraṇyagarbha. Is he not the cause for the production of all individual and collective gross bodies—beginning with son, father, and grandfather—as well as their subtle elements and subtle bodies?

The meaning is "it may be so. Regarding the creation of the previous progenitors—Manu, Marīci, Dakṣa, and others—or regarding the production of a previous cosmic egg prior to their own respective effects. || 65 ||
Kumbha said:
O King, even he who would be the primordial grandfather does not exist at all;
for since there is no cause, nothing whatsoever can ever come into being eternally.
Since its cause, too, is difficult to specify, the same logic applies to its non-existence; thus, with a hidden intention, he gives the answer:
"It simply does not exist"—this is the meaning. || 66 ||
Because its cause—the seed of its own nature—is eternally absent, O Grandfather, that which is perceived as something else does not exist as anything other than a delusion. (67)
Is it not well known from such Vedic mantras as, "He who is the source and origin of the gods, Rudra, the great seer, superior to all—
may that God endow us with auspicious mindfulness," that the Lord is indeed the cause of his [Hiraṇyagarbha’s] birth, seeing him as he is born with a compassionate glance?
Dispelling the doubt as to how that [Self] could be denied, he reveals the underlying intention regarding the "house":
"Even though another is seen through the delusion of conceptualizing difference by means of *māyā*, that Grandfather (the Self) is not other than that [seen one].
Why is this so? Because it will be stated later that the true aspect of consciousness (*cid-aṃśa*), being unchanging, cannot be a cause."

By process of elimination, the insentient portion of *māyā* alone must be stated as its cause; and since that seed-like cause, which is of the nature of ignorance (*avidyā*), is eternally sublated by ever-arisen knowledge (*vidyā*), it is eternally absent in the Lord—this is the meaning. || 67 ||
It appears as a mere form of delusion, like the water of a mirage;
even its capacity to fulfill the purpose of a grandfather is of the nature of an error. (68)

By this, the appearance of the Grandfather’s (Brahmā’s) performance of purposeful action for the sake of the creation of the worlds and so forth is also explained; thus he says: “O [Lord], the dense persistence of that false notion within the Grandfather’s belly has indeed ceased for you; now I shall wipe away the rest. (69)

Thus, by the reasoning I have stated, the firm conviction that this entire continuum of the succession of effects— beginning with your grandfather and ending with your own body— is real, which was previously established as being extremely solid, has indeed ceased through the realization of its falsity. Now, [if you ask:]...
The meaning is: "I shall cleanse even that other remaining portion consisting of mere appearance by means of instruction culminating in the direct realization of reality. || 69 ||
