Therefore, O King, because he consists of consciousness, this God of gods eternally shines forth by himself within the self through the mind;
for that very reason, the Self has declared itself by itself as "the Lotus-born" and as its own essential nature—this entire universe is thus peaceful.

He concludes by summarizing the very point already stated with the words "Therefore" (tasmāt). O King, because that which is distinct from consciousness is non-existent according to the reasoning already set forth, this God of gods—the Lord previously mentioned—is Consciousness alone;
He is the Self who eternally shines forth in the form of the continuous succession of creations, beginning with Hiraṇyagarbha and extending down to a blade of grass.
By virtue of being of the nature of consciousness (*cidātmaka*), it shines forth within itself alone; it does not produce or become anything else, even to the extent of an atom.

Therefore, by its own self, it is the Self alone that is the essential nature (*svarūpa*). It is described through the conceptualization of names and forms such as "the Lotus-born" (*padmaja*) and so forth, according to such scriptural passages as:
"The Wise One, having willed all forms and made their names, then abides calling them by those names," and others. Thus it is.
Upon thorough reflection, the meaning is that this entire duality is quiescent Brahman alone. || 70 ||

Thus ends the ninety-fourth sarga, titled "The Awakening of Śikhidhvaja," in the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*, composed by Vālmīki, within the section on the means to liberation (*mokṣopāya*).
Thus ends the ninety-fourth sarga, titled "The Awakening of Śikhidhvaja," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The ninety-fifth canto.
Śikhidhvaja said:
"If this delusion shines forth, extending from Brahmā down to a blade of grass,"
And since it is capable of purposeful action, how could it be a cause of suffering? (1)
Here, the process of the subsiding of ignorance through the thickening and thinning [of consciousness] is described,
as well as the resting [in the Self] through the awakening of Śikhidvaja.

Regarding what was stated—that [the object] appears as a mere form of delusion like the water of a mirage—the King raises an objection, saying "From Brahmā down to... on the grounds that the example is dissimilar: because the water of a mirage and the like are not seen to possess the causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) for purposes such as bathing or drinking, and because they are observed to be causes of suffering such as drowning or death. Therefore, that [object] must indeed be capable of causal efficiency.
And how is it that this [self] is the cause of suffering? Such is the logical connection. || 1 ||
Kumbha said:
Thus, the perception of this wandering world is spread out,
like the hardness of water that has become solid through cold.

It is well known that even a false object, when made firm through the contemplation of a true resolve, possesses causal efficiency and becomes a cause of suffering—just as is evident in the case of the scriptures, weapons, elephants, horses, and armies created by the illusory power (*māyā*) of gods and demons;
what then need be said regarding the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) created by the *māyā* of the Lord of the Universe? With this intention, he provides the answer beginning with "Thus" (*evam*).

Since this world-delusion, which consists of creation, exists for the purpose of sentient beings experiencing the results of their karma, it possesses, in the manner you have described, the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*) and the quality of being a cause of suffering and so forth.
It is simply the manifestation of the Lord, whose resolve is true, extended out in the form of those various causal efficiencies and other attributes; just as by cold [one perceives heat].

The meaning is as follows: just as water that has become solidified over a long period of time undergoes a transformation into the state of crystal and so forth, whereby its dryness and its capacity for causal efficiency—such as serving as a seat or a vessel—are extended. || 2 ||
The wise know that ignorance is destroyed only when it has thus become slackened;
for there is no emergence [of knowledge] without the destruction of the displacement from its former state.

For this very reason, he says "ignorance" (ajñānam) to show that when the root ignorance becomes loosened through the process of maturing the practice of knowledge, the world is destroyed along with that innate ignorance precisely by the sequence of its transition into subtlety. He says "no" (na) to indicate that without the destruction of ignorance, there is no sublation of the world's structural existence. || 3 ||
Indeed, that very attenuation of all cognition is the cause for the attainment of the cessation of creation when one has entered the supreme state.

And since ignorance becomes slackened, he states that the thinning of the outward tendencies of the intellect through the practice of cessation (*nirodha*) is the cause: "When the thinning of that [intellect] is observed, for that person there follows, in due course, the dissolution of its former state, and thus tranquility (*praśama*) is attained. (5)

For this very reason, even in the world, the destruction of gross entities is well known to be preceded by attenuation (*tānava*), which is synonymous with decay (*apakṣaya*); thus he says: "attenuation. [This refers to] that body or other entity; "cessation" (*praśama*) means destruction. || 5 ||
In this very sequence, O King, you are thus the primordial person;
know that the arising of the form of delusion stands like the water of a mirage.

He says "by this" to show that, through the process of loosening ignorance in the manner thus demonstrated, the establishment of your own abiding nature as the Puruṣa— characterized by eternally perfected fullness— is achieved simply from the sublation of the world. Thus, even the previously mentioned state of the world remains merely an illusion, like the water of a mirage, according to this very principle.
He says that it is to be understood as "the arising of the form of delusion. (6)
Even in the absence of a grandfather, this lineage of beings is unreal;
for that which is established by what is itself unestablished can never be established.
Having concluded the response to the objection, he says "eṣā" (this) while concluding the very subject at hand. || 7 ||
For this perception of a real entity has arisen like water in a mirage;
through investigation, it dissolves just as the cognition of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell does. (8)
He shows its fruit with the words: "This... (verse 8).
As for the claim that an effect comes into being after having not existed due to the absence of a cause,
its nature cannot be established except through false cognition.
For this very reason, he states that the nature of the world is nothing other than mere illusion: "The cause... (verse 9).
That which is perceived through false views never exists at any time;
by whom have jars ever been filled with the water of a mirage? (10)
For this very reason, he says that what is seen as false, along with its causal efficiency, undergoes a state of being devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvarūpatā*):
Śikhidhvaja said:
"Why is the supreme Brahman not the cause of the primordial Creator?"
It is infinite, unborn, unmanifest, like the sky, peaceful, and immutable.

In that case, why is Brahman itself, as the grandfather (Pitāmaha), not the cause without distinction? Nor does it follow that Brahman would be impermanent due to being subject to transformation (*pariṇāma*), because its permanence is established—just like a genus (*jāti*)—by virtue of persisting through all successive transformations. Thus the King objects with the verse beginning "of the Creator" (*sraṣṭuḥ*). || 11 ||
Kumbha said: Because it lacks the state of being a cause, and likewise because it lacks the state of being an effect, the Self transcends non-duality; it is neither effect nor cause.
Kumbha says, "It is not so," because it contradicts scripture, reasoning, and experience; he states this with the words "as a cause" (*hetutve*).

For by the scriptural passage, "This Brahman is without prior and without posterior," there is a negation of causality—characterized by being a prior—and of effect-ness—characterized by being a posterior. This is further supported by the text, "There is not here any diversity whatsoever."

The meaning is that the Self is pure Brahman— transcending the entire phenomenal world (prapañca), neither an effect nor a cause— because scripture negates mere duality, because attributes such as succession (anuvṛtti) and so forth are impossible for one who is unattached (asaṅga)— as stated in such scriptural passages as "for this Person is indeed unattached"— and because transformation is incompatible with that which is immutable (kūṭastha). || 12 ||
How could Brahman, which is without agent, object, or instrument, without cause, and without seed; which is beyond reasoning and unknowable—how could it be an agent? (13)

Since no other agent (kāraka) is established, his agency characterized by independence as prompted by another is utterly dismissed; thus he says, "not an agent" (akartr). To illuminate that if an "agent to be employed" (prayojyakartṛ) is not established, then agency as an "employer" (prayojakakartṛtā) is also unattainable for him, he says "not an agent. It is "without cause" (akāraṇa), meaning devoid of a motive (nimitta); it is "seedless" (abījaka), meaning devoid of material cause (upādāna). || 13 ||
Because it is without cause, that world would be devoid of the nature of an effect;
it is non-dual unity, without beginning or end, the primordial perception.

If you imagine that because Brahman is devoid of all attributes (*nirdharmaka*), and precisely because it lacks causality, it must also be free from the attributes of being an effect, and therefore the world has come into existence as consisting of cause and effect— then that world [would be subject] to a real limitation characterized by duality and unity.

Contemplate also that the primordial reality, which is devoid of characteristics such as beginning and end and free from the limitations imposed by space and time, has become Brahman itself—the perception whose sole essence is consciousness. At that time, what room is there for the existence of the world, or for the relationship between cause and effect? Such is the intended meaning. 14.
How, for whom, by what means, as an agent, as an enjoyer, or at what time could that Śiva—who is inconceivable, unknowable, peaceful, and immutable—ever exist? 15.
In this very way, agency and enjoyership, which are brought about by the delusion regarding the state of being a living soul (*jīva*), must also be discarded; thus he says:
"Therefore, nothing such as this world and so forth has been created, nor does it exist.
You are neither an agent nor an enjoyer; everything is peaceful, unborn, and auspicious. (16)
He states the conclusion with the words "Therefore," and so forth. || 16 ||
Due to the absence of a cause, this world is not the effect of anything;
because it lacks a cause, know that this world is an effect only through delusion. (17)
And because it is not an effect, this creation does not exist; thus it is not found.
When the world is not the effect of anything whatsoever, then it is not a cause. (18)
He recalls what was previously introduced as being relevant to the present context with the words "yadā" (when). || 18 ||
The establishment of the non-existence of objects depends upon that [consciousness]; if that is established, what is there to be known?
Thus, in the absence of cognition, there is no cause for the sense of "I-ness. (19)
He concludes the subject at hand with the words: "But thus... (19).
"Therefore, you are pure and liberated; what talk can there be of bondage and liberation?
Śikhidhvaja said:
"I am enlightened, O Blessed One; what you have spoken is most excellent and endowed with reason. (20)
Having thus taught the means for dispelling the sense of "I-ness," he causes [the king] to experience the remaining reality of the Self—beginning with the words "Therefore" (ataḥ).
Rejoicing in the taught matter through his own direct experience, the king reiterates, "I am awakened," and so forth, stating that what has been taught by you is most appropriate. || 20 ||
Due to the absence of a cause, I know that this Brahman is not an agent;
because of the absence of an agent, the world does not exist, and therefore there is no perception of objects.
The perception of categories is the perception of name and form. || 21 ||
Therefore, the mind and so forth are not its seed; nor is there anything such as egoism (ahaṃtā) [derived from it].
This being the case, I am pure, I am awakened, or I am Śiva.

Having realized that "there is no self, nor any other object," and that nothing exists at all, the perception of objects appears thus as something non-existent. Through this, I am peaceful from beginning to end, like the expanse of space. (23)

"I have been enlightened by you that there is nothing whatsoever to be perceived other than the supreme nature of consciousness. Thus, through the reasoning taught by you, by means of the investigation (*vimarśa*) of all objects, [it is understood that] in the context of superimposition (*adhyāropa*), through the discernment (*viveka*) of the "I" and so forth, and in the context of negation (*apavāda*), the entire collection of perceivable phenomena (*dṛśyajāta*)—ending with the "I"—appears as non-existent, as not being at all. This is the connection with what follows. By this, through the sublation (*bādha*) of all duality—
One should sit calmly and undisturbed, like an empty treasury.

Alas! This vision of the world’s categories—the flood of places, directions, time, divisions, and actions—has been stilled after a long duration; only the peaceful Brahman remains, the imperishable Self.
Acting out that very state, he concludes with two verses beginning with "jagat":

"The perception of the world as a differentiation of objects, accompanied by the floods of place, direction, time, parts, and action, has after a long time become tranquil for me. Oh!—this exclamation expresses wonder—and thus the immutable Self, the changeless Brahman alone, remains."
The meaning is "the remainder. || 24 ||
I am stilled; I am extinguished; I am established; I do not go, I do not rise, nor do I set.
I abide—abide, O you whose self is established as it truly is! I am the auspicious, the beautiful, the purifying silence. (25)

"I abide everywhere in a state of fullness. I remain thus; you too, O Self, remain as the Self as it truly is, with the singular essence of inwardness. "O Yājñavalkya, may fearlessness come to you, since you, O Blessed One, teach fearlessness"—this was the king’s address to Kumbha, echoing the words of Janaka. In this state, I am indeed your very Self, the auspicious one.
The meaning is: "I am always that which is the supreme human goal, purifying, pure, silence, beyond the reach of speech, auspicious, and unsurpassed bliss. || 25 ||
Thus ends the ninety-fifth canto, titled "The Resting of Śikhidhvaja," in the *Pūrva-cūḍā* of the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki. 95.
Thus ends the ninety-fifth canto, titled "The Resting of Śikhidhvaja," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The ninety-sixth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Having thus attained repose in Brahman, that Śikhidhvaja—
For a moment, his mind became perfectly tranquil, like a lamp in a windless place.
Just as the existence of visible objects is completely wiped away for a king who has awakened,
so too is it described by Kumbha.

The meaning is that, by the arising of a mental modification (*vṛtti*) in the form of the indivisible Brahman, his mind became perfectly tranquil—characterized by the subsiding of external modifications—and thus remained motionless like a lamp in a windless place. || 1 ||
Intent upon non-conceptual meditative absorption and desiring to enter [the state] quickly, he was suddenly awakened by Kumbha with the words, "By my own play. || 2 ||

Then, when that king, having shaken off even conceptualization characterized by uninterrupted mental activity, had brought about the state of Brahman for his mind— like a drop of water fallen into the ocean of milk— and was intent on entering into a state of absorption through complete identity with Brahman, [the Goddess], perceiving his condition to be of such a nature, quickly [appeared].
The meaning is that he was awakened instantaneously by Kumbha with the intention of explaining the means for wiping away the perceived world, which will be described hereafter. || 2 ||
Kumbha said:
O King, awakened from the sleep of ignorance, you have become Śiva;
for you there is no purpose to be served by either setting or not setting [the sun].
"Is it not so that, with the subsiding of all objects of perception and even of the undivided mental modification (*akhaṇḍākāra-vṛtti*), I am desirous of entering the ocean of unsurpassed bliss?
Why then have I been hindered by you through this arousal? That state is difficult for me to attain again!
Perceiving the King’s intention to speak thus, Kumbha said: "O King! That state is difficult to attain only while ignorance (*ajñāna*) exists; once it is destroyed, it is no longer so."

Whether there be the cessation of all objects of perception through the knowledge of You or not, the point is this: that Reality, ever-shining as the Witness, is eternally unobscured and indeed easily attained. || 3 ||
O dear one, he whose self has shone forth once and for all, who has destroyed the nature of both the undesirable state and its opposite,
and who is liberated from the perception of parts, is now truly liberated while living.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Having been thus awakened by Kumbha, he indeed became enlightened;
having emerged from the casket of great delusion, he shone forth intensely.
With his intellect at rest in an instant, perceiving the non-existence of the object of perception, the liberated soul spoke thus with ease: || 6 ||

Even at the time of emergence from samādhi, perceiving the non-existence of the object of perception, he effortlessly engages in the play of testing the correspondence between his own ever-fresh awakening and the awakening of a jar long since matured.
Śikhidhvaja said:
Although this is already largely understood by me, let that which I ask be told once more for the sake of my refined awakening, O giver of honor, O bestower of joy! (7)
In the auspicious, peaceful, and non-manifest state, whose very nature is non-emergent, how could there be the cognition known as the seer, the seeing, and the seen—the self of the universe? (8)
In one whose self (*ātman*)—that is, whose true nature (*svarūpa*)—has not been manifested in reality (*tattvataḥ*), meaning it remains veiled by ignorance (*avidyā*);

how can there be a "cognition" (*pratyaya*)? For "cognition" (*pratyaya*) signifies both the object of perception and the act of awareness or consciousness. From what cause, or from what objective support (*ālambana*), could it arise? Is it from that which exists (*sat*) or that which does not exist (*asat*)? In the first case, modification (*vikāra*) and sublation (*bādha*) would be impossible.
The meaning is that in the second case, the appearance [of the object] as a real entity is untenable. || 8 ||
Kumbha said:
Well asked, O great king; you shine indeed with brilliance.
This alone remains for you to know—listen now to that.

Thus strengthened, Kumbha—intending to establish both [the Self and the non-Self] through meditative absorption (adhyāsa)—praises the question as being well-posed and the questioner as possessing the capacity to grasp the meaning of what is about to be taught, saying: "Excellent!
Having attained the reality of the Self previously taught, you shine brilliantly because the veil of ignorance has been dispelled.
"You shine; or rather, you reign like the sun"—in this reading, the word "vā" (or) has the sense of "iva" (like).
The meaning is: "After that awakening, you shine like the sun released from Rāhu. || 9 ||
Whatever is seen here in this world, whether stationary or moving,
all of it— abounding in every variety— is destroyed at the end of the kalpa.

In that context, in order to demonstrate the causal complex for superimposition (adhyāsa), and intending to show the substrate (adhiṣṭhāna) as variegated by ignorance accompanied by the latent impressions (saṃskāra) of what has been superimposed, he demonstrates the dissolution of the previous creation with the words "yad idam" [that which this...]. 10.
Then, neither light nor pervasive darkness remains;
at the end of the play of the great aeon, that which is the essence of existence alone remains.
The following passage, beginning with "tataḥ," demonstrates that remaining substratum. || 11 ||
Pure consciousness alone— stainless, tranquil, and appearing as the supreme ether—
is liberated from all mental constructs and united with the highest intellect.

The connection with the subsequent [verse] is as follows: that which is endowed with the supreme cognition of the direct realization of its own essential nature becomes uniquely arisen and utterly pure. || 12 ||
That which is manifested as singular, utterly pure, tranquil, pervasive, and radiant—the splendor whose nature is the Supreme Self, motionless and consisting of pure consciousness alone. || 13 ||
Inconceivable, unknowable, equal, auspicious, and blameless;
it is the fulfillment of Brahman, completely filled with fully arisen consciousness.
It is filled by consciousness that has arisen completely full, by one's own awakening. || 14 ||
He is the subtlest of the subtle and the most massive of the massive;
the heaviest of the heavy and the best even among the excellent. (15)
Such is that supreme, subtle reality, compared to which this sky appears as massive as Mount Meru situated beside an atom. || 16 ||

He clarifies with the following illustration that [the Self] is "minuter than the minute": "of such a kind. Even this sky, though renowned for being the most subtle among those things well-known to be progressively subtler in relation to the earth, [is surpassed by the Self]. || 16 ||
Such is that supreme gross [form], before which this world appears like an atom; it appears in some places, and in others it does not appear at all. (17)
And the phrase "the grossest of the gross" clarifies this very point in the same way—as being of such a nature. || 17 ||
Know that the manifestation of the universal self within the state of the Creator, who is beyond possibility, is the awareness of "I"; this is the Virāṭ self, established as the world. 18.

In such a state, variegated by illusion (*māyā*), which serves as the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*), there occurs—due to the awakening of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the previous world and in accordance with the respective karma of various living beings—that manifestation consisting of the universe through superimposition (*adhyāsa*). That very [manifestation] is the one from which the Creator (*vedhas*) originates; he is such that his birth is from *aḥ*, who is Vāsudeva.

Know that the superimposition of knowledge (jñānādhyāsa) of Hiraṇyagarbha is characterized by the "I-consciousness" (ahaṃvedana) and the sense of "I-am-ness" (ahambhāva). In that state, the world which exists as its object is that very Virāṭ-self; this is the meaning of the superimposition of the object (viṣayādhyāsa). || 18 ||
Just as no distinction exists between the wind and the movement of the wind,
so too there is no distinction between pure consciousness and the sense of "I," which are comparable to emptiness and space.

And in the case of superimposition (*adhyāsa*), since the existence of both the effect and the cause is established by the very existence of the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*), there is no inconsistency in their being perceived as existent, nor in their sublation by knowledge, nor in the reality and immutability [of the substratum]; with this intention, he states the non-difference of the superimposed from the substratum, along with an illustration: "Like the snake and the water in the rope and the mirage. (1.16) In the world, the snake is superimposed upon the rope, and water upon the mirage; yet, in reality, neither the snake nor the water exists apart from the rope and the mirage. Similarly, the entire aggregate of effects and causes—beginning with the intellect (*buddhi*) and ending with the gross body—is superimposed upon the Self, which is pure consciousness. Therefore, it does not exist apart from that [Self]. Just as the snake and the water do not exist apart from the rope and the mirage, so too the aggregate of effects and causes does not exist apart from the Self. Thus, because the aggregate of effects and causes has no existence apart from the Self, it is unreal; and because it is unreal, it is sublated by the knowledge of the Self. Furthermore, since the aggregate of effects and causes is unreal, its substratum—the Self—is real and immutable. This is the meaning. (1.16)

The bedstead and [the rope] are examples of the substratum because they are independent; movement and emptiness are examples of the superimposed because they depend on a location and a counter-correlate, respectively. || 19 ||
Just as waves and the like exist in water at the end of space and time with a cause,
so too does the world exist in the Supreme— which is beyond space and time— without a cause. (20)

Lest one fall into the view of the *asatkāryavādins* (those who maintain that the effect is non-existent [prior to its production]), he states a distinction by showing, through an illustration, that the effect possesses existence throughout the three periods of time within Brahman solely by virtue of the existence of its substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*). He says: "In water. That which has limits—namely, spatial and temporal delimitations—is such that, because water is an intermediate cause, it is by means of the very cause of water [that the effect exists].
It possesses a cause; yet, because Brahman is the root cause, it has no cause. || 20 ||
Just as bracelets and the like exist within gold at the end of space and time and possess a cause,
so too does the world exist within Brahman at the end of space and time and is without a cause.
Such is that most excellent kingdom of the world, which remains unimpaired;
it is non-dual, stainless, and peaceful, wherein the entire world is regarded as no more than a blade of grass.

And he clarifies this very point—that [Brahman] is the best even among all that is excellent—by means of superimposition (*adhyāsa*) itself, saying "of such a kind. That which has the world as its kingdom is "the world-kingdom"; that [Brahman], being the Great King, is "unharmed" (*ariṣṭha*), meaning the most excellent.
Since the world is superimposed upon it, it is as insignificant as a blade of grass; therefore, duality does not exist—it is non-dual (*advaita*). This is the meaning. || 22 ||
Such is that supreme good which exists in that Lord; when He exists, the splendor of the multitude of objects in the world attains its very being through the act of cognition.
Since that very [Self] is the substrate of all, the world acquires its existence solely through its existence; thus he says: "Such is this... (verse 23).
O King, that single essence alone exists here, all-pervading; it is the one, the sole beloved of consciousness, which, by virtue of its non-duality, is not even manifold.
Its nature is exclusively pure consciousness (*cit-mātra*). It is lovely (*kānta*), being the object of unconditional love. It is non-dual (*advitā*), meaning it cannot tolerate a second;
because there is nothing else to be excluded, even the number "one" does not apply to it, for the very number one would itself result in duality. || 24 ||
Therefore, no second conceptualization whatsoever exists;
the reality of the Self alone shines forth, which is both full and imperishable. || 25 ||
Filled on all sides. || 25 ||
Everything is eternally established as if arisen in every form;
because it is invisible and unattainable, it is neither effect nor cause.

The meaning is that, because it is invisible to the eyes and other senses and unattainable by the hands and other limbs, it is not an effect— lacking as it does a substrate for the excellence produced by knowledge and action— nor is it a cause, insofar as it does not bring about knowledge and action.
Because it is inaccessible to perception and the other means of knowledge, that supreme reality is indeed indescribable;
it is everything, the self of all, subtle, and consisting solely of pure experience.

It is something entirely distinct from objects established by worldly means such as direct perception; it is accessible solely through one's own experience, is supreme, consists of unsurpassed bliss, is itself the Self of all, and since all things have it as their Self, it is the Universal Self. || 27 ||

For that which has the nature of being both named and nameless, and which is like a vision of light devoid of appearance—whether it be existent or non-existent—how could it possibly possess causality? (28)

From the perspective of conventional discourse (*vyavahāra*), how could that which possesses the nature of both designation and the designated— the nature of all things consisting of words and their referents, or the nature of the manifest and the unmanifest— be the cause of itself? However, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), it is like a light devoid of appearance.
How could there be causality for that which is non-dual, whose nature is pure perception alone, undifferentiated by the radiance of appearances?

Furthermore, in conventional reality (*vyavahāra*), the non-dual is non-existent and duality is existent; whereas in ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), the non-dual is existent and duality is non-existent. The meaning is that it is impossible for anyone to assert a mutual relationship of cause and effect even between existence and non-existence. (28)

That which is indeed the seed of nothing whatsoever because it cannot be described, and which is not a cause—nothing at all arises from that, the Self who is the expanse beyond all means of valid cognition and the like. (29)

The world, consisting of the means of knowledge, the objects of knowledge, and so forth, is not born; for in conventional reality, it has the Self alone as its essence. The meaning is that the Self is not born from itself. || 29 ||
It is without agent, object, or instrument; it is truth, a mass of consciousness, and unimpaired.
It is the nature of the Self, without appearance, self-awareness, and indestructible. (30)
Therefore, O Sage, nothing whatsoever is born from the supreme Brahman;
how, what, or by whom could anything be obtained, since [the world] is like waves and other phenomena that possess a cause?

And thus, since under the theory of superimposition (adhyāsa) no modification such as birth occurs for anything whatsoever, he concludes that immutability alone is established: "Therefore" (tasmāt). As for that which I have described as having causes, such as waves and the like—even upon reflection, how can it be found to be distinct from water? Or rather, what is found? The meaning is: nothing at all, and not in any way. || 31 ||
"Others [say] that at the end of an improper place and time, the world is likewise without a cause.
Śikhidvaja said: "Indeed, that which consists of waves and so forth in water and the like does possess a cause."

Even though such a cause exists, when the relationship of cause and effect does not exist, then—because it is non-dual and because it is devoid of the limitations of space and time—it need hardly be said that this relationship does not exist in Brahman, which is itself without a cause. Thus he says: "In the supreme [Brahman]... Just as waves and the like, which possess a cause, exist within water, yet are limited by space and time; [so too is the case with the world].
"What you have just stated—that the world is without a cause because it does not exist at other places or times—is precisely what was previously asserted by me.
Regarding that, what is your intention in speaking of 'inequality'? Thus the King asks: "In water, etc. (verse 32).
"O others, I do not consider the egoism of the world and so forth to be without a cause.
Kumbha said:
"O Lord of the Earth, this truth has now been understood by me according to reality. (33)

Since the ocean is an effect produced from water that has undergone quintuplication (*pañcīkaraṇa*), the transformation of its water into waves and so forth possesses a cause, namely the elements such as air which serve as external instrumental conditions. In contrast, because no cause for Brahman is established and because it is non-dual (*advaya*)—and thus lacks any auxiliary causes—the transformation (*vivarta*) of Brahman is without a cause. This is the distinction intended by me. And that...

Because the possibility of even conceiving a non-dual reality does not arise prior to the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), it is impossible for the ignorant to understand; however, since you have thoroughly familiarized yourself with the non-dual reality through the sublation of all duality according to its true nature, it is easily understood by you—with this intention, Kumbha gives the reply beginning with "Now" (*idānīm*). || 33 ||
This world, consisting of "I-ness" and so forth, does not exist here at all;
devoid of the referent of the word "world," the world exists as being of the nature of Śiva.
If [the world] is without cause because all duality has been sublated, then what is the intention behind the statement that "the world exists" therein?
He states that: the meaning is that the intention is that [the world] indeed exists even when [duality] is sublated. || 34 ||
It is created within space itself, peaceful, and subtler than space;
just as emptiness exists in the sky, so does this world exist in the Lord.

Just as within space itself, a city of Gandharvas—created by the even subtler illusory space—is eternally quiescent due to its falsity, yet exists solely through the reality of space; and just as even in the non-empty sky there exists a voidness contrary to it, existing through that very reality; so too does the world exist within the Lord, Brahman variegated by Māyā. This is the meaning. || 35 ||
This world, when correctly known as being either identical with its own true nature or as having no form whatsoever, becomes auspicious.
When it is correctly known as being of the nature of consciousness alone, similar to its own essential form which is of the single flavor of consciousness;
or alternatively, when it is known as being merely void—not similar to any form whatsoever, whether conscious or insentient—it becomes indeed the auspicious Brahman. || 36 ||
By the power of right knowledge, even poison becomes like nectar;
but when wrongly understood, the world is supremely inauspicious and a source of suffering.
To the question, "How indeed can that which is inauspicious become auspicious?", he says: "Properly," etc. (37).
Even nectar, when consumed with the thought that it is poison, acts like the essence of poison;
and so it is with whatever this conscious Lord perceives.
Such a person may be accompanied by knowledge or accompanied by ignorance. || 38 ||
Śiva becomes exactly so, with such a form, instantly;
just as a flame, through delusion, gives rise to various illusory appearances.
Just as a flame, though appearing in various forms such as a mass of hair due to the delusions of ocular defects like cataracts, remains in its very own undifferentiated nature. || 39 ||
For the reality of Brahman indeed remains exactly as it is, without any change in its nature;
it abides within the self as the supreme, steady state consisting of the essence of consciousness.

That which is the Supreme Brahman, abiding as the very nature of consciousness, is itself [perceived] within the self as sluggish—that is, of dull awakening—by means of that very non-awakening as its cause. || 40 ||
By that [consciousness], the body, the embodied self, and so forth, as well as the world and so forth, are merely indicated; thus, only the supreme Śiva shines forth as the ultimate reality.
Therefore, it is not appropriate to raise questions regarding the world, the ego, and so forth;
for a question shines forth only with respect to a thing that actually exists. (42)
He says "Therefore" (ataḥ) to show that when there is firmness in awakening—[the state] being auspicious and tranquil—the very question you have posed has no scope at all.
Thus, the question itself—"Whence arises this cognition called the universe, consisting of the seer, the seeing, and the seen?"—is not appropriate. || 42 ||
As for that which has not been perceived, what is the use of an inquiry into its perception?
Just as the existence of gold is not found without its particular configuration. (43)

If the world does not exist at all, then one should not even raise the question, "How is it clearly perceived? To this he says: "It is perceived. The meaning is that since such a perception would lack an object, the very manner in which one could ask "how" would be non-existent. || 43 ||

Likewise, without the sense of "I" (ahaṃbhāva), the Lord has no existence; because He is without cause, this world does not exist as something other than Brahman, for it is Brahman alone that thus unfolds.
The establishment [of this] is worthy of inquiry; this is the ellipsis. || 44 ||
This world, which exists as if it were not even yawning [into existence], has its intentions mutually impelled by that very essence which consists of me alone. 45.

Now, if earth and the other elements do not exist at all, how is it that the Śruti says: "He who dwells in the earth, yet is within the earth, whom the earth does not know, whose body is the earth, who controls the earth from within—He is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal," and so forth? For [according to the scripture], all things are indeed impelled by the Lord as the Inner Controller.
Regarding the Vedic tenet that entities (*bhāva*) produce a marvelous effect in their respective functions, he says: "consisting of that" (*yanmayā eva*).

All entities consist of the Lord who is variegated by *māyā*; therefore, impelled by that very Lord variegated by *māyā*—and by *māyā* alone—to conjoin with one another as a causal complex (*sāmagrī*), they [produce] only something illusory (*māyika*) within the body composed of the five elements.

They produce the marvelous effect of their respective functions. Just as pairs of men and women, impelled by desire in their youth, produce wonder through mutual enjoyment and the procreation of sons and so forth;
or just as seeds situated in the earth, impelled by rainwater, produce wonder through the emergence of sprouts—such is the connection with what follows.
These states manifest as wonders within the pentad like a multitude of couples;
yet pure consciousness alone is perceived by pure consciousness through pure consciousness. (46)

Likewise, pure consciousness alone, being veiled by its own illusory power (māyā), becomes as if manifold through that very manifoldness; thus, it is perceived and delimited in the form of various effects. || 46 ||
Though not manifold, they appear as if manifold through their own nature as the knowledge of the Self;
from the Full, they draw forth full things, and from the Full, they have made full things.

Just as that very pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) manifests a wonder through its own nature as the knowledge of its own self, pervaded by its own ultimate reality, so too does Brahman manifest the illusory wonder of creation in the form of the world—which is itself Brahman—and the wonder of attaining its own ultimate essential nature through the knowledge of reality. "That is full, this is full... (*pūrṇam adaḥ pūrṇam idam*).

"From the full, the full is drawn out; having taken the full from the full, the full alone remains"—thus he cites the meaning of this Śruti with the words "from the full. At the time of dissolution (*pralaya*), when all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) have dissolved and only latent impressions (*vāsanā*) remain, the individual souls (*jīvas*) reach absorption even into Brahman as qualified by *māyā*. Then, at the beginning of a new cycle (*kalpa*), when the ripening of the *adṛṣṭa* (unseen merit/demerit) that impels experience occurs again, [they emerge].

In the act of creation, they extract their respective individual and collective limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) from the cause, which is the full and undivided Brahman; thus, through *māyā*, they bring forth effects that are themselves full and of the very nature of the undivided Brahman. Furthermore, during the period of maintenance, whatever collection of intermediate effects they fashioned—the means for worldly and celestial enjoyment as well as liberation—that too emerged solely from the Full.
And by means of illusion, they made them appear as if full. || 47 ||
From the full, full things arise; yet only the Full remains.
Only pure consciousness shines forth within the Self, which consists of nothing but pure consciousness.

The sense is that the intention of the Śruti is this: when they become liberated through the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), they also become full precisely because of the departure of *māyā* from the Full One; for when *māyā* departs along with the delusion of duality, only the Full remains. Furthermore, that perception of creation which is manifested within the Self consisting of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) is itself nothing but pure consciousness manifested within pure consciousness.
The syntactical connection here is with the word "kathitam" (it was told). || 48 ||
Without even conceiving that name, the perception of creation was conceived;
thus, at the beginning, Consciousness itself became, as it were, "I" through its own consciousness. 49.

Consciousness itself, whose nature is the inward Self (*pratyagātman*), at the beginning of creation, without abandoning its own form, becomes—by its own consciousness and of its own accord—as it were, the infinite form of the mind. (49)
Without abandoning its own nature, it remains indeed as form—consisting of light, without beginning or end, having the nature of mind, and infinite. || 50 ||
O Sovereign, you yourself appear as the very form of saṃsāra;
yet, because it is your own nature, you perceive this world as either truly existent or as being merely existence.
Through the power of mental conception, the visible world attains the state of reality and comes into being in an instant.

Then, through the conceptualization of grossness, that which is the self-existent (Sat) appears as the Universal Sovereign (Samrāj); by means of the state of Virāj, it becomes, as it were, the transmigrating world in the form of transmigration. Now, through the state of being an individual soul (vyaṣṭi-jīva), it perceives this world as "Being" (Sat) due to delusion;

however, in the ultimate sense, one perceives only the Being that is the substratum within the world—the meaning is that there is no delusion regarding that portion [of the Self]. [The text continues with: "the state of having become... (bhūtatām).
The state of being the fourfold collection of living beings. || 51 ||

This world, though appearing as a manifold expansion, is in truth quiescent; it is the single, ineffable reality, free from the denotations of words for its own nature, abiding as the essence of reality whose very self is the experience devoid of the world’s own inherent sound, consisting of the vision of its own innate wonder. || 52 ||

He concludes what has been said with the word "peaceful" (śāntam). In the manner thus described, it is peaceful by its very nature; it is liberated from both word and meaning, that is, from name and form. Therefore, it is indefinable. It is the single reality, the essence of the Self, which is self-luminous experience. This very reality, through its own inherent wonder, appears as the world in the form of Māyā and its manifestation.
The meaning is that it exists as if having become the world, by way of its nature as an expansion. || 52 ||

Thus ends the ninety-sixth canto, titled "The Awakening of Śikhidhvaja," in the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa*, the *Vālmīki Dēvamanuṣyamōkṣa*, in the *Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa*, in the *Pūrvārdha*, in the *Cūlikākāṇḍa*. 96.
Thus ends the ninety-sixth sarga, titled "The Awakening of Śikhidhvaja," in the first half of the Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The ninety-seventh canto.
Kumbha said:
"In gold, at the end of place and time, there exists such a sequence of produced and producer."
Nothing whatsoever is born from the peaceful, and nothing whatsoever is dissolved. || 1 ||
In the previous [verse], it was wiped away by the observation that no object of perception arises without a cause;
here, however, the consciousness's state of perceiving objects is diligently wiped away.

Thus, the analogy of the ocean waves mentioned in the twentieth verse has been established for its utility in removing perceived differences; now, in order to state that the analogy of the golden bracelet mentioned in the twenty-first verse and its internal distinctions should likewise be established, [the author proceeds].
Kumbha repeats: "It is gold. || 1 ||
Brahman, established in its own being, is neither seed nor cause;
it is pure experience alone, and nothing other than that exists. || 2 ||
"That which is the world, the ego, and so forth, is indeed that very same infinite [reality].
Śikhidhvaja said:
"O Sage, O Śivā, I know that the world, the ego, and so forth do not exist."

"Let it be that the object of perception is non-existent; but if that is so, how can there be the realization of pure consciousness as having the nature of cognizing that [object]? Thus the King asks with the words beginning "O Śivā," and so forth. (3)
"How does this perception of creation appear? Tell me this quickly.
Kumbha replied:
"That [reality], which is without beginning or end, exists as its own consciousness, appearing as an expansion."

With the intention that it is like the perception of the nature of the light of the sun spread across the sky as being the very form of the manifestation of a city of Gandharvas and so forth superimposed upon it, Kumbha gives the following answer:
"Vistāram" (the expansion). That which is expanded is the "expansion," which is merely the pure Being (*sanmātra*) that serves as its substrate.

The consciousness of that which is superimposed is consciousness itself, abiding like a manifestation. Therefore, the world superimposed upon that is nothing but the substrate, which is pure Being; thus, it is designated as having the form of the universe—this is the meaning. || 4 ||
Each respective world is utterly transparent; each is the world-body as that specific subtle element alone.
There is no object consisting of consciousness, nor is there an external object, nor is there emptiness.

In this regard, the Vijñānavādin maintains that objects such as the world and so forth are merely internal transformations of consciousness (*vijñāna-pariṇāma*), which, through conventional reality (*saṃvṛtti*), are perceived as if they were external objects. Gautama, Kaṇāda, Kapila, Patañjali, and others, however, hold that external objects consisting of the five elements—earth and so forth—exist as ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). The Mādhyamika, on the other hand...

It is only emptiness that manifests conventionally through the state of external and internal, grasped and grasper; there is no entity whatsoever that possesses substantial reality. Refuting those views, he says: "It is not composed of consciousness. (5)

Since its essence consists solely of feeling, it is said to have consciousness as its core; just as fluidity belongs to water, the state of being conscious or unconscious is not an inherent cause [of the Self].

To explain why that is so, he says: "feeling" (*vedanā*). The conceptual constructions (*kalpanā*) of all disputants are tenable only when feeling exists, not when it does not exist. Therefore, its emptiness, momentariness, producedness, perishability, or transformation cannot be asserted or established by anyone anywhere—listen to an illustration. Just as:

Just as liquidity is the essence of water, so too consciousness is the essence of all things. One should reflect on this: if the entity called consciousness did not exist, then, due to the absence of a means of realization, the entire world would be unfit for designation as either "existent" or "non-existent"—what else could it be? Thus, the point is that the lack of sentience in consciousness, which is of the nature of *rasa*, is without cause.
It can be determined by means of causes.
That [reality] is the self, the Lord, and infinite; it remains exactly as it is, established in its own state, because there is no exclusion of its opposite in either existence or non-existence. (7)
If it is asked how you can establish that the world is a manifestation of that [consciousness], he says: "In its own self" (*svātmani*).

That form of consciousness, whether manifesting in its own self as the form of the world or manifesting as the nature of ultimate pure consciousness alone, is capable (*īśam*) by means of its own *māyā*; therefore, it remains exactly as it is, whether accompanied by ignorance (*sāvidyam*) or free from ignorance (*niravidyam*).

The meaning is that it remains even through dependence (*pratītya*). If it is capable of existing in both the states of being clear and not clear, then from where does its exclusive establishment in the state of clarity arise? To this he says: "the counter-correlative" (*pratiyogī*). For the nature of pure existence (*sattvamātra*) is indeed the state of clarity; whereas the state of non-clarity is a state opposed to it. If that [non-clarity] were [to exist] in relation to its own opposite, existence...
Whether one performs a negation or does not perform it, in either case, [the object] is not established by itself;
for since there is no exclusion of the counter-correlative (pratiyogin) regarding existence and its opposite, impurity is non-existent.
Thus, the meaning is that in the supreme reality, which is an existent entity, the state of being established solely as pure nature is proven. || 7 ||
Because it is non-existent, the supreme state is established in its own pure nature; if there were a peaceful state capable of undergoing the transition into causality, [it would not be supreme]. (8)
Now, one might ask: why is the non-luminous nature [of consciousness] being utterly denied?

Why not simply postulate that the luminous nature of consciousness itself is capable of becoming the cause for the manifestation of the non-luminous world? To this, he says: [the verse beginning with] "bhāvaḥ" (verse 8).
How could that which is motionless, non-manifest, and beyond inference ever exist?
Therefore, Brahman is never a cause nor a seed at any time.
There is no creation of any effect whatsoever by that [cause];
nor indeed is any other mode of occurrence possible for this creation. (10)
He states that there is no possibility of the creation occurring by any other means apart from the practice of consciousness: "And not... (verse 10).
Apart from pure consciousness alone, no inert creation exists;
whatever is seen here has arisen as if it were a mass of consciousness itself.
As if arisen. || 11 ||
The coloring of the sense of "I," the world, words, meanings, and aesthetic flavors is not possible in the case of an entity, because of the absence of a cause. (12)
In that case, he refutes the position of the proponents of chance (yadṛcchāvādins), who claim that this world is indeed causeless, with the verse beginning "kāryam" (the effect):
"An entity consisting of duality, unity, and so forth, is like a flower in the sky; because it is established solely in destruction, it cannot logically be known by a wise person. (12–13)

If [the world] is of the single flavor of pure Being (*sanmātra*), then how is it perceived as having a dual nature consisting of both consciousness and insentience, as well as a nature of both duality and unity? To this he says: "Like a flower in the sky. The meaning is that the insentient portion is merely a mental construction (*vikalpa*), like a sky-flower. Let it be then that the world is of the very nature of consciousness; its cause would thus be Brahman, which is likewise of the nature of consciousness.

Nor is there an absence of distinction—such as "this is the effect" and "this is the cause"—in the case of identity with the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*), because birth and destruction themselves suffice to provide that distinction. To this, he says: "The entity," etc. Indeed, the worldly entity, such as a jar or a cloth, cannot logically be of the nature of consciousness, which is knowing. Why? Because it is restricted solely to destruction; that is, it is necessarily subject to destruction. For destruction does not belong to consciousness by means of consciousness.

It is established [that destruction cannot occur]. For at the time of the destruction of consciousness (*citi*), the statement of its destruction would be devoid of an object, since it is not possible for a non-conscious (*jaḍa*) entity to effect destruction even when consciousness is present; such is the meaning. || 13 ||
How can there be the destruction of that which has arisen, given that it is perceived? Or else, do you consider this [self] to be both eternally existent and eternally destroyed? (14)

But if someone were to say that the destruction of consciousness (*cit*), being of the very nature of consciousness itself, is independent of anything else in its manifestation to itself or others, to that he replies: "It is the cause of perception. The destruction of consciousness, being of the nature of consciousness, is the cause of the perception—that is, the illuminator—of its own birth or of its own counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*). Why? Because indeed not...

Its own origination can be perceived through the destruction of the consciousness that serves as its antecedent counter-positive; nor, in the absence of the perception of both [origination and destruction], can it be experienced that "its destruction has arisen by itself. Furthermore, there is no experience of those two by the Witness (sākṣin), because consciousness cannot be an object of consciousness; therefore, the origination and destruction of the world, which are objects of knowledge, [cannot be established].

The sense is that [the world] is indeed insentient (*jāḍya*). Thus, the insentiency of the world being established, since no cause can be specified, if there were production from a non-agent, there would be production at all times and destruction would be eternal, because there is no preventer of either. O proponent of *svabhāva* (inherent nature), if this world indeed possesses such a nature of eternal production and destruction, even though it is without proof and contrary to experience—
"Vetsi" means "he accepts. || 14 ||
Why is there distress over this flood of objects, even though it is thus of a single nature?
As for this perception that occurs, it is merely a marvel of the mind. (15)
In that case, what distress is there for you when that which is established by the scriptures, by the learned, and by experience—being of the nature of undivided, pure consciousness—is accepted?

The meaning is: why this pain? Now, if everything is of the single essence of consciousness, then how is the perception of the diverse categories of "conscious" and "unconscious" possible? To this he says: "But the perception... (verse 15).
Only the existence of the essence of consciousness exists; duality and unity do not exist at all.
Therefore, O King, while the existence of objective entities persists, [this is the case]. (16)
In that case, one might think that consciousness (cit) would have a second entity, namely the mind (citta); to this he replies with the words "Therefore," and so forth. || 16 ||
Since the cultivation [of ego] is impossible, there is for you no cultivation of "I-ness";
and because the state of "I" is impossible, what else can be called the mind? (17)
Thus, the great form of the mind does not exist, nor is there any difference [between them];
free from latent impressions, with a tranquil mind, silent, and composed of the supreme ether. || 18 ||

There is no differentiation—the distinction between the individual soul and Brahman, the distinction between consciousness and the unconscious, nor the distinction within consciousness consisting of the forms of the perceived object and the perceiving subject. || 18 ||
Whether with body or without body, even while situated amidst worldly existence, one remains like a mountain;
for, through the connection with the vision of pure consciousness, the non-existence of objective entities is established. (19)

The meaning is that because pure consciousness (śuddhacid) never attains a relationship with insentient objects, such objects are never established; consequently, even the form of the individual soul (jīva) characterized by the "I-notion" (ahaṃ), which is produced by the contemplation of those objects, does not exist at all, and thus the Self alone remains as a residue. || 19 ||

Through the cultivation [of the truth] within the mind that "I simply do not exist," and through the experience resulting from the contemplation of the meaning of the Vedas as "Brahman," and because the reality of the object of consciousness alone remains— where, indeed, can there be such a thing as thought? (20)
Such a Self alone is the truth: "Brahman is Being, Consciousness, and Infinite"; "Brahman is Eternal Consciousness and Bliss";

"This entire universe is indeed Brahman, the most excellent"—the meaning of all the Vedas is this, and it is attained through the contemplation (*bhāvanā*) and experience (*anubhava*) thereof. Therefore, the mental modification (*vṛtti*) characterized by the form of the undivided whole (*akhaṇḍākāra*), consisting of the thought of and the experience of That, is everything.

Fearing that [the thought] might remain as a residue after having sublated itself, he says: "cetita" (conceived). Because the object conceived through the contemplation of Brahman is the sole reality, even the mental modification consisting of such contemplation is sublated by the self-shining awakening;
thus, there is no possibility of anything remaining apart from Brahman—this is the meaning. || 20 ||
Therefore, you are that Brahman—stainless, causeless, liberated from the beginning, eternal, without end, both manifold and one;
it is the void, free from affliction, neither being nor non-being, without beginning or middle; it is the entire universe and consciousness itself, existing as that very Brahman just as it is.

He concludes the stated meaning by means of its result with the words "by that": "By that sublation of all duality, you are indeed Brahman. That Brahman has become entirely non-dual, one alone; and the entire world is unreal, a mere void.
Even consciousness, which is the form of its appearance, is simply Brahman as it truly is, unmodified and free from affliction."
The meaning is that only that [reality] remains. || 21 ||
Thus ends the ninety-seventh chapter, titled "The Awakening of Śikhidhvaja," in the Pūrva-cūlikā of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the glorious Vāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa composed by Vālmīki. 97.
Thus ends the ninety-seventh chapter, titled "The Awakening of Śikhidhvaja," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The ninety-eighth canto.
Śikhidhvaja said:
"May my understanding that 'the mind does not exist' become clear through reasoning."
Tell me that, or something else; the Buddha has not been understood by me with precision.

For the sake of strengthening the realization that "the mind does not exist," it is described in detail that because the object of thought is non-existent, that which is "no-mind" is indeed the existent Brahman.

Now, it may be argued that just as form and other objects appear only when there is light, so too the manifestation of consciousness—or anything else—occurs only when the mind exists, not when it is absent. Therefore, if the mind, which has taken on the form of Brahman through its mental modification (*vṛtti*), were to be sublated, then one would fall back into blindness, like the loss of a lamp. Furthermore, in the world it is well known that those who possess a mind are sentient, while those without a mind are insentient; thus, if the liberated-while-living (*jīvanmukta*) were to have their minds destroyed, they would likewise become insentient.

[If it were otherwise], they would become insentient like clay and other such substances; however, they are not seen to be so. Furthermore, when the mind exists, the supreme goal of human life—characterized by unsurpassed bliss—can be experienced as the fruit of the scriptures, but not when it does not exist.
Moreover, there can be no such thing as a "human goal" that is not being experienced. Furthermore, the mind itself takes on the form of Brahman.

Does it afflict itself or something else? Not the first, because of the contradiction of an action operating upon itself; for fire, while burning what is to be burned, is not able to burn itself. Nor the second, because that which is afflicted by the mind cannot logically be its afflictor;
furthermore, nothing other than a mental modification is recognized in the world as an afflictor, and thus the logic of "Sunda and Upasunda" does not apply here.

The King, desiring to strengthen his understanding by dispelling such doubts as—"Since Brahman is beginningless and the accomplisher of all things, it cannot possibly be their sublater; therefore, the sublation of the mind is useless, difficult to achieve, and contradicted by universal experience"—asks: "The mind... The meaning is: "State another argument that is applicable to that [case] and capable of removing all my doubts. "Nipuṇam" means firmly. || 1 ||
Kumbha said:
O King, the mind does not exist at all, anywhere, or at any time;
that which appears as if it were a mind is the imperishable reality known as Brahman.

In this regard, in order to state the reasoning that establishes the affliction of the mind by avoiding all faults, the author asserts the non-existence of the mind and the existence of Brahman alone as its substratum: "The mind... [verse 2]. At no time, in no place, and as no object whatsoever, does the mind exist as a self-entity.
Therefore, that which consists of ignorance does not exist as the world at all;
how then could there be imagined constructions such as "I," "you," "that," and so forth? (3)

He states that reasoning (*yukti*) with the words "therefore" (*ataḥ*). The meaning is: because the entire world, beginning with the mind (*citta*), consists of ignorance (*ajñāna*), it does not exist once ignorance has been sublated by knowledge (*jñāna*); therefore, for this reason.

This is the intended sense (*bhāva*): this contradiction regarding action within one's own self might occur if the sublation of the mind and so forth were something other than the sublation of ignorance through knowledge.

Indeed, the very sublation of ignorance consists in the cessation of everything—its effects, its relations, and its veiling and projection; and when that [sublation] exists, it is established as a matter of course that the mind simply does not exist, which is the very point asserted. For this reason alone, there is no further possibility of defects such as blindness, since ignorance itself has been eliminated.

This is because all causes of blindness have been removed, and because the unsurpassed human goal is accomplished through the remaining self-luminous, full-blissful state. Furthermore, consciousness does not depend upon the mind (*citta*), but rather upon the manifestation of consciousness (*cit*); and since that [manifestation] exists even in those liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*) despite the destruction of the mind, there is no possibility of unconsciousness. Nor is there any [defect] caused by the mind once the mind has been destroyed.

The manifestation of consciousness (cit) does not perish. Since non-manifestation is caused by the veil of ignorance (ajñāna), when that [veil] is removed, the manifestation of consciousness—being its very nature—is not subject to disappearance. For the manifestation of the sun, produced by the wind through the clearing away of clouds, does not perish when the wind ceases in autumn; thus, this is the resolution of all objections. || 3 ||
This world that has arisen as something whatsoever does not exist at all;
Brahman alone is everything here. By whom and how is that [Brahman] perceived? || 4 ||
Having concluded the first proposition which has been established, he introduces the second with the words "it does not exist at all.
To support that, he cites the scriptural authority: "But when for him everything has become the Self alone, then by what and whom should one see?"—using the word "by what" (kena). || 4 ||
This world was not produced anew at the beginning of the great dissolution;
rather, this designation "this" has been employed by me here for the sake of your understanding.
With the intention that even scripture (*śruti*) serves as authority for this—namely, "There is no cessation and no origination; there is no bound being and no seeker"—he says:
"Then the mind has indeed not arisen, so it does not exist at all. To the question, "In that case, how is it that you made the statement in your proposition, 'And this which appears as mind'?
he replies: "But as for the statement... (Verse 5).
Because causes such as the nature of grasping and so forth do not exist, and because it is impossible for all entities to be without a cause, [they do not arise]. (6)
With the intention that the previously stated reasoning is also capable of proving this, he says: "upādāna... (verse 6).
Thus, because the world is perceived by the intellect through ignorance, it does not exist;
therefore, whatever appears here is the radiance of Brahman and nothing else.
He concludes the second proposition with the words "Therefore" (tasmāt). || 7 ||
To say that "the Lord, who is ineffable and formless, creates this" is false;
such speech lacks logical foundation, it is not true, and it is not experienced [in reality]. || 8 ||

If it is objected: "But if there is no such thing as the beginning of creation, then what is the status of those scriptural and traditional declarations such as: 'He made himself by himself,' 'The one controller, the inner self of all beings,' 'He who makes the one seed manifold,' and 'The agent, the enjoyer, the Great Lord'?"—we reply:
not so.

With the intention that the purpose of the statement "not manifold" (*nānā*) is merely to establish non-duality by providing the object of negation required by that scripture—and thus it is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) rather than a statement of ultimate reality—he says: "In the inexpressible" (*anākhye*). This means: in that which is nameless (*nāmarahita*), formless (*anākṛti*), partless (*niṣkala*), and not of the nature of logical proof because it is devoid of reasoning.

Because it is contradicted by such scriptural passages as "devoid of activity" and by the experience of the wise, [the world] is not real; nor is it experienced as such even by worldly people. || 8 ||
"The Lord, who is inexpressible, non-obstructive, self-natured, and formless,
creates the world"— this statement is merely for the laughter of the unintelligent.

The construction of houses and such is well known for the purpose of warding off resistance from cold winds and the like; however, that the Lord—who is himself unobstructed—acts [in this way] is merely the statement of a futile exertion by an omniscient being, intended for the laughter of those whose intellects are devoid of the true purport of the explanatory passages (arthavādas). This is the meaning. || 9 ||
By this very practice, O King, the mind does not exist;
O virtuous one, the world itself is not real—how then could the mind and its derivatives, which are contained within it, exist? (10)

Thus, he states that when the creation of the world is not established, the intended thesis is proven, with the words "by this very [means]": the meaning is that when the world itself does not exist, how could the mind and so forth contained within it exist? || 10 ||

For the mind consists of nothing but latent impressions (vāsanā), and impressions exist only when there is something to be impressed. That which is to be impressed is the world, and that very world is non-existent; therefore, how can the existence of the mind be established? (11)
He states that since the world is non-existent, the non-existence of the mind is established because its objects are also non-existent: "For the mind... (ceto hi).
"In the object" (viṣaye) refers to the object of impression, which is the activity of latent tendencies (vāsanā). || 11 ||
That which shines as Brahman itself, by itself, within itself, is called by such names as "the mind" (citta) and so forth; it is created by that very [Brahman] through that very [Brahman]. 12.
If it is asked, "In that case, what is the object of the conventional usage of 'mind' and so forth?", he says, "That which is this," namely, Brahman itself as conditioned by Māyā.
A collection of names is "nāmaka. || 12 ||
This world-appearance is not something to be clothed [by a substrate], nor has it even arisen;
because there is no cause, it did not exist previously—so how, then, could there be the state of mind? (13)

He explains the verse beginning with "For the mind is merely latent impression" (ceto hi vāsanāmātram) with the word "the world" (jagat). The phrase "the visible is that which is to be perfumed" is intended to illuminate that latent impression follows from perception. The meaning of "due to the absence of a cause" is that when the object is sublated, it is impossible for a latent impression devoid of an object to persist. || 13 ||
Therefore, this very expansive awareness—whose nature is pure consciousness-space and which is named the supreme ether—is what shines forth; where, then, is the world? (14)

He explains even the verse beginning with "that which shines" (*kacati*) as being intent upon describing its fruit from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha-dṛśā*), starting with the words "therefore" (*ataḥ*). || 14 ||
Whatever slightly glimmers in the supreme space,
because it has not arisen in the mirror of consciousness (cid-ādarśa), there is neither mind (citta) nor the activity of the world (jagat-kriyā).

He explains the phrase "even from the perspective of the principle of Māyā" with the words "whatever it may be. In the mirror of consciousness, which is the nature of the supreme ether, there exists whatever indefinable form of Māyā; this is "slight," meaning extremely small. || 15 ||
This cognition of "I," "you," and "the world" is not real;
it appears falsely like a dream, surely bringing about my complete destruction. (16)

"This notion of mine that 'I am the world,' which brings about every misfortune—this appears to me, who am its witness, as nothing but false, like a dream. The word "nūnam" means "certainly" or "with certainty. || 16 ||
Since there is no world to be habituated to, and thus no latent impression (vāsanā) exists at all, what kind of mind could there be—composed of that [impression]—where, from whence, and how? (17)
This world, which is the visible object, is understood by the unawakened to be the mind;
yet that unreal mind is formless and was never produced in the first place. (18)

It has never arisen at any time, even at the beginning of creation, due to the absence of a cause; for such is observed through worldly experience, scriptural authority, and direct perception regarding any visible object. (19)

If it has not arisen, then why should the world not be beginningless and eternal? To this he replies with the word "loka" (the world). The connection with the subsequent clause is as follows: the beginninglessness of an object of perception, or its being devoid of transformations such as birth and so forth, or its immutability (kauṭasthya), is not tenable—neither from the perspective of common experience (loka), nor from the perspective of scripture (śāstra), nor even from one's own direct experience (svānubhava). || 19 ||
Neither beginninglessness, nor birthlessness, nor even stability is possible for this manifest world, which is gross and characterized by resistance. (20)

The logical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: it is not reasonable to deny the transformations of this world—beginning with the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*) and ending with the non-dissolution (*apralaya*), occurring in reverse order—which are established through worldly experience, scriptural authority, and direct perception as having form, being gross, and possessing a resistant shape;
for there is an absence of all grounds that could justify such a denial. || 20 ||
Furthermore, because of the absence of all causes—according to common experience, the scriptures, and direct perception—the great dissolution and other such events cannot be denied. (21)
Or else, based on the scriptures, personal experience, and the established tenets of the Vedas, even all three of them might say that dissolutions do not exist; such a person is indeed a madman.
He whose mind does not regard the world, the scriptures, and the Vedas as authoritative is more foolish than the wicked; therefore, a virtuous person should not take refuge with him.

He states that one who transgresses the boundaries of the world and the Vedas should be excluded by the cultured (śiṣṭa), saying: "The world... [verse 23]. He is even more foolish than the wicked—the Carvakas—who rely solely on worldly convention.
And for this visible object, which possesses resistance, an unresisting cause can never exist;
nor can that which is formless be the cause of that which has form. (24)
"In that case, let the position that Brahman is the cause as stated in the Śruti be accepted"; to this he replies: "And not so" (na ca). || 24 ||
O Sage, when perceived in this manner, each and every thing is thus constantly [existent];
and yet, it would not follow that this world is incapable of performing causal functions in this way. (25)

However, regarding the scripture that propounds Brahman as a cause devoid of form, it has already been stated that its purport lies solely in the world’s having Brahman as its ultimate, real nature, according to the logic of Bādarāyaṇa beginning with the sūtra, "Its non-difference [from Brahman] [is established] on account of words such as 'originating' (ārambhaṇa). Thus, when the world is perceived as being nothing but Brahman, in the context of worldly transaction—

Since its corporeality has not departed, it remains indeed capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*); thus, there is no contradiction with worldly experience. From the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), it has indeed become Brahman; therefore, it does not possess the form established by the vision of the ignorant, and consequently, there is no contradiction with the Veda either. With this intention, he says: "In this way" (*ittham*). "In this way" means having an unestablished form. (25)
Therefore, this [universe] arises from the partless sky of consciousness, which is of unobstructed form, formless, infinite, and because of its prior and ever-prior partlessness. || 26 ||

Now, he summarizes and concludes the purport of all the scriptures concerning creation and the scriptures that negate it—such as "not this, not this" (neti neti)—by means of three verses beginning with "Therefore" (tasmāt). [In the compound *pūrvātpūrvam*, the *samāsa* is formed because the word *pūrva* has a constant requirement for its correlative when construed with a portion of another word; alternatively, it is a case of the elision (*luk*) of the fifth case ending.]

And that [nature] is partless; the suffix *tasi* (in the form *tasya*) follows the previous word "partless" (*niraṃśa*), being applied to the genitive case-ending (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*) according to the rule for all case-endings (*sārvavibhaktika*). || 26 ||
That which is the equal [state] of Brahman— who possesses all forms and is peaceful and absorbed—
is the self-manifestation by its own nature, assuming the form of creation and dissolution.

The meaning of all the Śruti texts concerning creation is as follows: when the self-manifestation of Brahman—which possesses all forms and is of a perfect nature—occurs spontaneously, even without scripture, that very own body or essential nature (svarūpa) assumes the form of creation and dissolution for a moment, as long as there is the period of ignorance, appearing as if it were the world. That very essential nature [is what is meant].

In another moment, following the scriptures such as "That thou art," one realizes that the existent Brahman alone abides in its own nature, which is a self devoid of duality; this is to be understood as the intended meaning of the scriptural negation of duality, beginning with "not this, not this" (neti neti). || 27 ||
By that very [means], his own body was realized in an instant as being like the world;
yet, upon awakening in another moment, it remained as nothing but Brahman within the selfless state.
Therefore, all this is indeed Brahman; nowhere is there the notion of a world or the like.
Where could there be its beginning, where its end, or where the conceptualization of duality, unity, and so forth?
Therefore, [it follows] from the scriptural understanding. || 29 ||
Everything is without support, unborn, profoundly peaceful, and beginningless—this is the Self (ātman), existing as it truly is.
This, however, is neither manifold nor even non-manifold; remain as you are, in the silence of perfect stillness.

Thus, when all this world is known to be utterly tranquil, without support, without foundation, unborn, and existing exactly as it is—namely, as Brahman alone—it appears in the form seen by the ignorant; yet, because of its absolute non-existence, it is neither manifold nor non-manifold. Therefore, the meaning is: conduct yourself according to reality as it exists, remaining in the silence of the highest wood, devoid of the activity of speech and other such functions.
Thus ends the ninety-eighth chapter, titled "The Awakening of Śikhidhvaja," in the first part of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the glorious Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa composed by Vālmīki.
Thus ends the ninety-eighth sarga, titled "The Awakening of Śikhidhvaja," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The ninety-ninth canto.
Śikhidhvaja said:
"O great sage, through your grace, my delusion has vanished and my memory has been regained."
I stand firm, my doubts dispelled, my mind at rest, and possessed of the Self.
Even though the king has awakened, he is further awakened by Kumbha;
according to the maxim of "driving in a post," this is so that his awakening may become very firm.
