Thus, having awakened, the king declares that his own ignorance—the seed of all doubts and the like—has been destroyed by the knowledge born of instruction, showing this with the words beginning "it is destroyed. The direct realization of the Self, which had been forgotten, is itself called "recollection" (smṛti). || 1 ||
I am one who has known all that is to be known, a great sage of silence, having crossed the vast ocean of illusion;
I am peaceful, devoid of the sense of "I," a knower, established in a state free from affliction. || 2 ||
Alas! For how very long have I wandered in the ocean of existence;
yet now, I have attained this imperishable and unshakeable state.
O Sage, this being so, that triple world consisting of "I-ness" and the like does not exist;
I know that which appears as this foolish intellect is Brahman. (4)
This triple world, consisting of the ego and so forth, is perceived by the ignorant; in reality, it does not exist. || 4 ||
Kumbha said:
Where the world itself does not exist, there can be no manifestation of "I" or "you.
Thus, how, from where, of what kind, and in what manner could this world-expanse in the sky exist?
Kumbha, approving of what had been said, spoke as follows: "The world itself," and so forth. The "ether-world" (*ambarasaṃsāra*) refers to the conventional reality of a city of Gandharvas.
The interrogative particles (*kiṃvṛtta*) serve the purpose of negating the [usual] locus, cause, illustration, and mode [of existence]. (5)
O sage, remain as you are, conducting yourself with silence and a tranquil mind;
abide like the movement of a whirlpool within the belly of a gentle ocean.
Remain and abide like that peaceful movement of a whirlpool within the belly of a gentle ocean.
This peaceful form of Brahman exists thus as it is;
"I" and "this world" are essentially of the nature of space, consisting of the meaning of words.
But the nature of word and meaning, the very essence of word and meaning, consists of space and is indeed empty. || 7 ||
This entire thing, devoid of beginning and end— [the reading is "all of saṃsāra"]— which is called by the name "saṃsāra," shines as the sky of the Self, whose name is the wonder of consciousness.

That which is the nature of the Self, named the wonder of consciousness (*ciccamatkṛti*), is like the sky; it alone shines with its own shimmering brilliance, just as gold exists when the perception of its particular form has ceased.
Likewise, when the objects such as the world have subsided, this Brahman remains.

Just as when one perceives in the sky the form and arrangement of an inverted sapphire bowl, through the vision of discernment that [perception] subsides, yet the shimmering of the sun's light pervading it certainly remains—such is the meaning. || 9 ||
Just as the self-existent one is indeed called "volition" itself,
so too are bondage and liberation established as dependent upon one's own awareness.

Just as the self-existent (svayaṃbhū) is, by its very nature, mere volition (saṃkalpamātra) due to being the collective ego (samaṣṭyahaṃkāra), so too is the individual ego (vyaṣṭyahaṃkāra). These two— the bondage of the collective and individual [egos] and their liberation— depend respectively upon the identification with them and the relinquishment of that identification.
The conception "I am" leads to bondage that is utterly destructive;
the conception "I am not" leads to liberation for the pure-souled one.
He states that very point clearly: "It is 'I' alone," etc. (11).

The constant awareness of the true nature of the meanings of the words "bondage," "liberation," and "thought-constructs"—which are always [in reality] existent—is called both *sat* (Being) and *kaivalya* (Isolation). || 12 ||

What is that liberation? He explains it with the word "yat" (that which). The meaning is: the constant, sequential realization of one’s own true nature, which serves as the witness to the thoughts of bondage and liberation in those who exist—that very reality is called the True Brahman, Kevalatva, and Kaivalya.
The realization of "not-I" is perfection; the realization of "I" is calamities.
Thus, being one with the Self, he becomes pure awareness, realizing "I am indeed He, not this [limited self]. || 13 ||

Liberation is perfection; bondage is calamity. Therefore, become one who possesses the pure knowledge of the Self as absolute isolation (kaivalya), realizing "I am neither you, nor he, nor even this [ego]. (13)

Through the mere absence of volition, which consists in the arising of perfect knowledge, volition—which is by its very nature unreal—perishes of its own accord for the sake of spiritual accomplishment. (14)
And he says that pure awakening is accomplished through the destruction of volitional thought (*saṃkalpa*) with the words: "By non-volition" (verse 14).
For in the inconceivable nature of Śiva, there is no causality;
due to the absence of a cause, the category of an effect also does not exist. (15)

Because a pure entity cannot function as a cause, there is the non-existence of the objects of perception; from the ascertainment of that non-existence comes the cessation of mental construction (*saṃkalpa*);

from the destruction of mental construction comes the cessation of the sense of "I" (*ahaṃbhāva*); from its cessation comes the cessation of the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) consisting of the state of being a living soul (*jīvabhāva*) and so forth; and from that, [liberation].
He states the sequence [ending] with "only Brahman remains" through three verses beginning with "beyond reasoning. || 15 ||
When the non-existence of objective entities is fully established, cognition is no longer tenable;
due to the absence of its cause, the sense of "I" never arises again. (16)
In the absence of the arising of the sense of "I," whose is saṃsāra, and of what nature is it?
Due to the non-existence of saṃsāra, everything that remains is only the Supreme. || 17 ||
That which shines forth is indeed the Supreme Reality abiding within the Self;
the Supreme, being full of the Supreme, unfolds as the Equal within the Supreme.

Even previously, that which appears in the form of this world was, in ultimate reality, Brahman alone existing in that manner; and through the awakening to truth, nothing new occurs, but rather the Supreme itself, abiding in its own supreme nature, unfolds—that is, its very own nature manifests as something unprecedented by the Supreme, yet identical to it. || 18 ||
Know that by him everything has been rendered motionless, like a mountain strewn with stones; the world exists as Brahman, appearing as if composed of rays of light.

By that reason of being eternally of one single nature, it is strewn with diamond-stones, as dense and immovable as the interior of a diamond-rock, and firm. And whatever world is situated therein, that is like a thousandfold reflection consisting of the rays of diamond-jewels.
When the mental projector in front has perished, [what remains] of the city of conceptual construction...
Know that form of the world to be as pure as space, consisting of both being and non-being.
If that is so, how does it abide in liberation? To this he says: "In front" (pura). That which is real appears as unreal because of the non-perception of its reality. (20)
The world is quivering like a shadow-man, yet it is peaceful and devoid of mental construction;
he who sees the world as being devoid of the referents of the word "world" truly sees.

To the question, "How then can there be the perception of the world's vibration in that which is immovable? he replies with the word *chāyā* (shadow): Just as the reflected person within the interior of a diamond stone vibrates even while remaining motionless, so too does it appear to vibrate.
The wise know that Nirvana is indeed the realization of perfect knowledge, which consists of form, light, and mental attention, yet is devoid of the cultivation of scriptures. 22.

When the awakening of right knowledge has arisen, external forms and lights, as well as internal mental attentions, are perceived as sapless and devoid of essence; thus, through the authority of scripture, a firm cultivation arises, which the wise know as Nirvāṇa because it is the cause of Nirvāṇa.
Just as there may be a wind that is motionless, or as there may be even that which moves through the sky... [22]
Just as gold exists in the form of various ornaments, so does Brahman exist as the world.

He explains with illustrations that which was stated—that he who perceives the world as devoid of the referents of words truly perceives—[as follows]: "Gold exists apart from its arrangements such as bracelets and the like; likewise, it should be understood that Brahman exists as the world, though devoid of its [conventional] arrangements. This is the meaning. || 23 ||
These—form, light, and mental attention—which are sapless, appearing as unreal, yet producing the cognition of the world, exist as the very form of Brahman. (24)
He also explains this [phrase] "form, light, and mental attention" by saying "tasteless.
For one who has become Brahman through awakening whose nature is Brahman, the form, light, and mental attention that produce the cognition of the world are tasteless. What is the meaning?
The meaning is that they become appearances of what is non-existent. || 24 ||
Just as water, even in great quantities, is devoid of the meaning of the word "wave," so too is Brahman naturally devoid of the meaning of the word "creation."

Just as even many things such as waves in the ocean become mere water devoid of the meaning of the word "wave," so too, upon the arising of knowledge, even many objects become one with Brahman by their very nature; this is the meaning. || 25 ||
Emanation itself is the Supreme Brahman, and the Supreme Brahman is the vision of emanation;
this eternal meaning of the sentence is indeed devoid of the referents of the words "emanation."

To reinforce, through reciprocal identification, that there is indeed identity between the creation and the Supreme Brahman when the distinction between the meanings of the words "creation" (sarga) and "Brahman" is sublated, he says:
"The creation itself," etc. For this very reason, the meaning of Vedic statements such as "All this is indeed Brahman" is precisely this. || 26 ||

When the meaning of the word *brahman* was fully realized, the understanding of the meaning of the word *sarga* (creation) was established; when the meaning of the word *sarga* was perfectly accomplished, the understanding of the meaning of the word *brahman* was established. || 27 ||

In common worldly usage, the understanding of the meaning of the word *sarga* (creation) occurs precisely when the meaning of the word *brahman*— namely "expansion" (*bṛṃhaṇa*)— is established. Likewise, when the meaning of the word *sarga* is established as "the emission" (*visarga*) or "the relinquishing" (*tyāga*) of name and form,
it follows the meaning of the verbal root *bṛh* ("to expand") and thus constitutes the meaning of the word *brahman*, which is the cessation of the threefold limitation.
The meaning is that the two words "done" (kṛta) and "made" (kṛta) have indeed the same referent. || 27 ||
The pure sky of consciousness, which arises from the cultivation and non-cultivation of all words and their meanings, abides as that which is designated by the word "Brahman. (28)

To the question of how the word *brahman* can apply to a reality that is not a word (*aśabda*), he says: "The entire... (verse 28). The meaning is that if even a slight limitation were admitted, there would result a contraction of the root-meaning of "great" (*bṛhat*);
therefore, by the word *brahman*, exactly that same [infinite] reality is expressed, just as it is by the word *aśabda*.
When both have been realized through right vision and there is no longer any perception [of duality],
speech turns back from that which remains— ageless and tranquil.

Alternatively, the meaning is that just as with the word "jagat," once the direct denoted meaning of the word "brahman" has been known, when the perfect realization of the undivided reality is accomplished through secondary indication (lakṣaṇā), speech— even the word "brahman"— turns away from whatever remains as the ultimate reality. || 29 ||
The entire flood of sensations belonging to the self has been completely stilled; this is the singular nature of one's own true being.
It is the true nature of the entire world as it exists, like a stone, yet it is the supreme form of consciousness.
O King, all this world, in its true nature as it exists, whatever it may be,
is indeed the supreme Brahman-nature itself, being of the form of adamantine stone due to its extreme solidity;
even though this world has become one in which the entire flood of self-awareness is stilled by ignorance, nevertheless—
The meaning is that because the singular essence of one's own true nature exists as reality, there is but a single existence for both Brahman and the world; thus, nothing whatsoever is non-existent.
Thus ends the ninety-ninth canto, titled "The Awakening of Śikhidhvaja," in the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa* of the *Dehastha-mokṣopāya*, within the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki. 99.
Thus ends the ninety-ninth sarga, titled "The Awakening of Śikhidhvaja," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The Hundredth Chapter.
Śikhidhvaja said: "If it is so, O one of great intelligence, then tell me what that supreme cause is."
I know this very world to be precisely such an effect. || 1 ||
The existence of the world is sublated by the existence of Brahman, like that of a [superimposed] object;
untouched by transformations such as birth and so forth, it is declared to be Brahman itself, which is Being.

If there is but one single existence (*sattā*) for both Brahman and the world, then why should the world not also be ultimately real (*paramārthasatya*), just like Brahman? For the cause of a false thing is difficult to define, whereas for that which is real, Brahman alone can be the cause, since they are equal in this regard; thus the King raises the objection: "If it be so... (verse 1).
Kumbha said:
Where there is causality, there an effect is possible; but where that which is not a cause exists from the very beginning, how could an effect arise from that? (2)

The meaning is this: it may be that Truth, variegated by *māyā* and possessing the same level of reality (*samasattāka*) as the world through its own existence alone, serves as the cause of the world.

However, how could an effect arise from that which is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), which does not depend on another reality, which—due to its non-duality—is devoid of prior existence because there is no time prior to it, and which is changeless? For if an effect were to arise, it would have to possess the same level of reality as its cause.
Herein there is no cause whatsoever, nor is there ever any effect;
all this that exists is entirely peaceful, unborn, and the world itself.
Suppose it is argued that, in that case, the cause of the world is precisely that which remains there as variegated by *māyā*. To this, he says: "Not so" (*neha*).

Here, in the undifferentiated [Brahman], neither the cause variegated by *māyā* nor its effect, the world, exists. This is because the existence of *māyā*, its variegation, and its effects is admitted only from the perspective of *māyā*. However, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), all this—

The meaning is that the world is indeed peaceful and unborn. Thus it has been stated in the Vārttika: "The notion that 'ignorance exists' is conceived only by remaining within ignorance itself; however, from the perspective of Brahman, this ignorance is not in any way tenable. (3)
An effect arises from a cause, and thus it must possess the nature of that cause;
but for that which does not arise at all in this world, how can there be any similarity?
And since the consequence of similarity with that which is unborn would follow, he says: "It is born" (jāyate) || 4 ||
Tell me, how can that which has no seed at all be born?
And as for that which is inconceivable and inexpressible, how could it possibly possess the nature of a seed?

To the question "Why is it not born there?", he says: "It is the seed itself. To the further question "In that case, even in the absence of a seed, why could that very thing not be the seed?", he says: "It is inconceivable. || 5 ||
All things, by virtue of place and time, possess causes and are subject to valid means of knowledge;
how then can there be a cognition regarding Brahman as a non-agent with respect to these two causes?

If it is asked, "How can there be an absence of causes such as seeds and so forth in that [Brahman]? he says, "Because of the absence of a place and time suitable for them," which is established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). If it is then argued that the very cognition whose object is Brahman must itself have as its object the efficient and material causes therein, and that there is no contradiction, he says, "Non-agent" (*akartr-*) and so on. For that valid means of knowledge whose object is Brahman—which is opposed to all causal factors such as the agent and so forth—by that [means of knowledge], [the existence of such causes is negated].
The meaning is: how can it be said that valid cognition arises from both the cause (hetu) and the material cause (upādāna)? || 6 ||
In Śiva, who is devoid of agent, object, and instrument, there is no causality;
therefore, that which is known by the word "world" has no cause.
You are indeed Brahman; maintain that very nature which is eternally established.
That same [Brahman], when perceived by those of imperfect vision, is what is designated as the world.

Therefore, by means of the vision of reality, hold within your heart as "I" that very thing which is the true nature—resembling pure space and devoid of distinctions—and nothing else. And by the vision of the ignorant, that same thing is perceived in the form of the world; this is the meaning. Only that one, undecaying, and tranquil Consciousness alone is truly known.
By that very means, one perceives this world as the tranquil form of Brahman.

The world attains the state of Brahman through the very cognition of pure consciousness alone; yet, through the delusion of the mind which takes on unreal forms, Brahman appears in the form of the world. This he states in two verses beginning with "cinmātra" (pure consciousness). 9.
O Lord of the Earth, that very state of the mind which is otherwise is itself declared by the wise to be destruction, as it is experienced by them personally. (10)
Destruction is the loss of the essential nature of Brahman. || 10 ||
Know that the mind has the nature of destruction, O King, for it is essentially perishable;
since its destruction occurs in a single moment, it is designated by the word "mind" (citta) even in the context of an eon (kalpa). || 11 ||

He states that very point clearly with the words "the mind" (cittam). The meaning is that even a momentary loss consisting of forgetting one's own true nature is expressed by the term "mind" when it has been forgotten for as long as a kalpa. || 11 ||

By the mere absence of mental construction, which consists in the arising of perfect knowledge, mental construction—which is itself unreal by nature—is destroyed of its own accord for the sake of spiritual perfection. (12)

And that mind perishes through the knowledge of the finality of non-conceptualization (or, according to another reading, the knowledge of the finality of reality); thus he says: "By non-conceptualization" (asaṃkalpana). || 12 ||
O lotus-eyed one, if the universe is said to have its non-existence accepted by its very name alone, how could it possibly exist? Indeed! (13)

If it is asked, "Granted that the mental construction (*saṃkalpa*) is destroyed, how then does the universe (*viśva*) cease to exist?"—the answer is: "Precisely because it is false. It enters into the Supreme Self and becomes one with it; it does not remain as a separate entity.

Intending this etymological derivation (*nirvacana*) of the word "universe" (*viśva*), he says: "By its very name. That which does not enter [into oneness] when its own substratum is sublated [is what is meant].
The meaning is: how could that which exists [be so]? || 13 ||
How can he who, raising his hands, repeatedly declares with his voice, "I am a Śūdra," become a Brahmin? Of what nature, indeed, is his Brahminhood? (14)
In this regard, he establishes worldly practice by means of two [verses] beginning with "The hands": || 14 ||
Know that for one who, with his elements overturned, cries out loudly, "I am dead," while death has already arrived— indeed, his very life is but a delusion. (15)
One whose bodily constituents (dhātavaḥ) have become disordered and provoked through their combination—such a person is one for whom death is imminent.
Whatever exists here that appears in the form of an illusion is like a whirling firebrand, like a mirage, like a double moon, and like a child's ghost. (16)

If it is asked, "What then is the status of the experience that 'the mind and so forth exist'?", he says, with examples, that its status is simply being an error: "Having the form of an illusion," etc. (16).
How indeed could that which consists of the burden of exertion be real?
It is said that the mind itself is merely internal ignorance and delusion. (17)
"In that case, let it be that which consists of a mass of delusion; no," he says: "That" (tat).
The meaning is that it lacks any essential nature distinct from ignorance. || 17 ||
Ignorance is said to be the mind, which, though non-existent, appears as if existent;
it is non-perception and unknown, whereas knowledge would be perception.
Through the knowledge of the consciousness of the ignorant being—that is, through the realization [of its true nature]—there is destruction [of ignorance].
O virtuous one, the perception of water in the mirages of the desert is a vain delusion. (19)
"In that case, let the mind and so forth be real by virtue of having ignorance as their nature. To this he replies with the words "ignorance" (*ajñāna*).

The meaning is that because they are sublated by knowledge (*jñāna*), reality cannot be established even for that which has ignorance as its nature. He establishes this through two examples, beginning with "the cognition of water" (*jalajñāna*). || 19 ||
Through the realization that "this is not water," that mature ignorance which is the impurity of the heart— the notion that "this is the mind"— is dissolved by consciousness.
Through the knowledge that "the mind does not exist," it is destroyed along with its root, just as the state of being a snake in a rope arises from the delusion of ignorance. (21)

Just as the fear arising from the delusion of ignorance regarding the self perishes through the knowledge that "this is not a snake," which has taken firm root in the heart; so too does that which arises from the delusion of ignorance regarding the self perish.

The notion that "the mind does not exist" destroys the mind once it has taken root in consciousness through discernment; this persists as long as ignorance exists within the internal organ, [conceiving] "mind," "intellect," and "I. (23)
Up to the entirety. || 23 ||
There is no mind, nor indeed anything in this world joined with egoism and the like; there is only consciousness, absolutely pure. (24)

The phrase "something such as the body" refers to that which is joined with egoism (*ahaṃkāra*) and so forth. The particle *eva* is used in the sense of "even" or "also. If one asks, "What then exists? he says: "consciousness" (*saṃvit*). || 24 ||
By that deluded woman, the mind of volition and so forth had been created;
today, by the awakened one, everything has been abandoned through the absence of volition.
When he moves by means of volition,
O mighty-armed one, he goes as if by non-volition, like a mass of flames in a fire driven by the wind.
The entire world is pervaded by the reality of Brahman, which is a single, dense mass of the essence of the Self, just as the ocean is pervaded by water. (27)
Pervaded means swallowed. || 27 ||
I do not exist, nor does another exist; neither you, nor these [elements], nor the mind;
neither the sense organs nor space—there exists only the one, stainless Self. (28)
He states how it is swallowed: "Not I," [verse 28].
That very same [reality] is perceived in the form of jars and other objects;
what a deluded conceptualization it is to think, "This is mind-made" and "I am this"! (29)
In that case, what is perceived by those liberated while living (jīvanmukta) in the form of a jar and so forth? To this he says: "The jar, etc. (verse 29).
Nothing at all is born or dies in these three worlds;
this is solely the radiance of consciousness, appearing through the nature of conceptions of existence and non-existence.
Everything is the Self, the Supreme Brahman, eternally manifest and pervasive;
neither duality nor unity exists, nor is there delusion or confusion.
Agitation is the fear of death and so forth. || 31 ||
Therefore, O friend of great intelligence, you exist as the very form of the entire collection of sense-faculties; thus, you are not burned, nor are you stained anywhere.

Within the entire aggregate of the senses and even within the forms of fire and other objects perceived by them, you exist as the very nature of pure Being (sanmātra). Therefore, you are not burned by the causes of burning, such as internal and external states.
O friend, nothing perishes for you, nor does anything increase,
for you are of the nature of the stainless sky, whose form is the infinity of absolute liberation (kaivalya).
The two powers consisting of desire and non-desire, as well as that which is other than them, are you alone;
for the moon is not perceived apart from its rays.

The other, the power of action (kriyā-śakti), is also you alone; therefore, the particle *ca* is used to illuminate the meaning that for you there is nothing to be done, whether desirable or undesirable.
"Parts" (*aṃśavaḥ*) refers to the *kalās*; apart from those [powers], [there is nothing else]. 34.

That reality of the Self is unborn, undecaying, beginningless, and of an immutable nature; it is eternally pure, shining with a single form at all times; it is free from mental construction, yet its play is called the "parts" (kalās); it is ever-arisen, primordial, and unborn. || 35 ||

By the three steps of the *ajāpada*, birth, growth, and transformation are cast aside; by the phrase "always of one form," other modifications are excluded. It is that which shines forth once and is eternally manifest. By the measure of its own digits (*kalā*), there is an acquaintance with its own essential nature; such is its play (*līlā*). Being thus, it has arisen as pure existence (*sanmātra*). It is the primordial reality, established prior to all worldly transactions.
The meaning is that this very thing is the reality of the Self. || 35 ||

Thus ends the one hundredth canto, titled "The Supreme Awakening of Śikhidhvaja," in the *Pūrva-cūlikā* of the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa*, within the *Mokṣopāya* section of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by the sage Vālmīki.
Thus ends the one hundredth chapter, titled "The Supreme Awakening of Śikhidhvaja," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and first chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Thus reflecting upon those sincere words of Kumbha, the king—
In that very moment, he himself became transformed into that state of the Self. || 1 ||
In this context, the fulfillment of the king's purpose is described through the firmness of his knowledge;
furthermore, the state of being "liberated while living" (jīvanmukta), mindlessness (avacittatva), and abiding in reality (tattvasthiti) are discussed.
"Transformed" means having abandoned its previous state and attained that [new] state. || 1 ||
With his mind and eyes closed, the sage became silent;
with the form of his limbs motionless, he appeared as if carved out of the surface of a stone.
Like a statue or similar figure carved out of a stone surface. || 2 ||
Then, after only a moment, when he had awakened with his eyes twinkling,
Cūḍālā, who was in the form of Kumbha, spoke to him, O mighty-armed one.
Kumbha said: "Have you found rest in happiness upon this vast, pure, and expansive bed, which is free from conceptual construction for those who are free from mental constructs?"
In the state of unsurpassed bliss, which serves as a beautiful couch for non-conceptualizing yogins.
Are you awakened within? Have you abandoned delusion? Has that which is to be known been fully understood, or has that which is to be seen been truly seen? (5)
Śikhidhvaja said: "O Blessed One, by your grace, I have beheld a great station of immense splendor, situated above all things."

The stage characterized by that [state] is one of great majesty and unsurpassed bliss; it stands at the pinnacle of excellence, above all varieties of sensory bliss, beginning from that of ordinary beings up to the bliss of Hiraṇyagarbha. (6)
Oh, how wonderful! The association of the great-souled ones—who have realized that which is to be known—is composed of a unique and unprecedented nectar, bestowing the fruit of the essence. (7)

The word *bateti* expresses joy. "Unprecedented" means never before experienced in this beginningless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*). That which is "one immortal essence" (*ekāmṛta*) is the abundance of unsurpassed bliss; for that very reason, it bestows the essential fruit. || 7 ||
That great nectar which I did not obtain even by birth has today been attained by me of its own accord through association with you.

He explains in detail what was stated in general with the words "by birth": "By me, who am of the very nature of the Great Nectar, that [state] which had not been attained due to beginningless ignorance has today been spontaneously acquired without effort through association with you."
O lotus-eyed one, why was this infinite, primordial, and immortal state of the Self not attained by me previously? (9)
Kumbha said:

When the mind has attained tranquility and remains with the desire for enjoyments abandoned, and when the ripening of the internal impurities of the entire group of senses has been completed; || 10 ||

With the intention that previously this was not attained due to the absence of the ripening of the mind's impurities (*cittakaṣāya*), but now it has been attained through the ripening of those impurities by means of austerity (*tapas*), Kumbha gives the following reply beginning with "In the mind" (*manasi*) and so forth:
when the ripening of the impurities characterized by enjoyment belonging to the entire group of sense organs and the internal organ (*manas*) has been accomplished, and likewise...
"Mindfulness is the ripening of the impurities; actions lead to knowledge, which is the supreme goal. When the impurities have been ripened by actions, then knowledge is born. (10)
The stainless words of the Teacher find rest in the mind, just as drops of saffron water settle upon a pure white cloth. (11)
Today, the ripening has arisen for you of those infinite passions, accumulated within your bodies, which are of the very nature of your own latent impressions.
O lotus-eyed one, O virtuous one, all impurities fall away from the body over time due to ripening, just as fruits fall down from a tree when they have matured. (13)
From the body and from the subtle body (liṅgadeha). The impurities are the passions such as attachment and so forth, as well as sins. || 13 ||
O friend, when the impurities consisting of latent impressions have departed,
that which the Guru speaks within becomes stainless, just as an arrow enters a lotus stalk.
When the two lotus stalks were fashioned by the archer as his target. || 14 ||
Now that the ripening of the astringent has been perfected, you have been awakened by me today;
therefore, O one of great intelligence, the destruction of your ignorance has occurred this very day.
Today your impurities have been cooked away; today indeed you are fit for discourse on knowledge.
Today, with this instruction, you have become awakened right here and now.

The ellipsis [of the sentence] is that you have attentively grasped the discourse and instruction for the sake of knowledge. Because you have retained the meanings taught in your heart, you possess the instruction;
the meaning is that you have become awakened, one who possesses the knowledge of the direct realization of its fruit. || 16 ||
Today, the exhaustion of all auspicious and inauspicious karmas has been brought to completion through your instruction on the company of the virtuous. 17.
O Lord of the Earth, as long as this was the forenoon of that day,
so long did your ignorance regarding "I" and "mine" persist.
He says, "I have known that today, at the time of midday, your ignorance has been destroyed," beginning with the words "as long as... (yāvat). || 18 ||
Now, O King, since the destruction [of ignorance] has occurred in your mind through the awakening by my words, and it has been completely cast out from your heart, you have truly awakened. (19)
Now, in the latter part of this very day, when the mind has been completely relinquished from the heart and has reached its dissolution; || 19 ||
As long as the existence of the mind persists in the heart, so long does ignorance remain established.
When the mind is relinquished by means of the mind itself, the dawning of knowledge occurs. (20)
By means of the state of being without mind, that is, through the cognition of the absence of intrinsic nature. || 20 ||
The mind that perceives duality and unity is called ignorance;
the dissolution of these two perceptions is knowledge, which is the supreme goal. || 21 ||
Because of the manifestation of the Supreme Self through vision. || 21 ||
You are awakened, you are liberated; O King, the mind has been abandoned by you.
Indeed, the state of being composed of existence and non-existence—that unreal ground—has been abandoned by you.

Indeed, due to the mutual superimposition upon the Self, that which is called the mind consists of both existence and non-existence; it alone is the locus of the unreal world, the ground for conceptual construction.
Free from sorrow, free from exertion, unattached, without another [support], and possessed of the Self;
a sage of great exaltation, observing silence, abide in your own stainless nature. 23.
Śikhidhvaja said:
"Indeed, O Blessed One, the ground of the mind exists only for a foolish being;
for one who is awakened and knows that reality, O Lord, there is truly no such thing as 'mind'."

To ask by what internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) the accomplishment of worldly activity occurs for those liberated while living (jīvanmukta), once the mind has been relinquished, the King prepares the introductory framework with the words "For thus" (evaṃ hi). The word *kila* is used here in the sense of "if. || 24 ||
Tell me, how do these people who are liberated while living (jīvanmukta) wander about?
For men such as you and others likewise have no mind that exists.
He shows those who are to be questioned—namely, the "liberated while living" (jīvanmukta)—with the words: "That, then... (tat tarhi). || 25 ||
Thus, tell me everything without remainder with the rays of your own words;
in this manner, skillfully wipe away the darkness within my heart.

The ellipsis is "difficult for others to describe. Or, [it means]: "With your own rays of speech, which are distinct from the rays of the well-known sun and other luminaries, wipe away the darkness within the heart, which is distinct from the well-known [external] darkness. || 26 ||
Kumbha said:
O knower of reality, it is exactly as you say and not otherwise;
for the mind of those liberated while living does not exist, just as there is no sprout from stones.
That latent impression (vāsanā) which is capable of producing rebirth is called "dense impression" (ghanavāsanā);
it is designated by the word "mind" (citta), and it does not exist for one who knows that [reality].
Know that latent impression by which those who possess such knowledge engage in activities here to be what is called "sattva," which is free from rebirth. (29)

Just as parched and split grains of rice (lāja) are no longer denoted by the word "rice" (*vrīhi*) and so forth, nor are they capable of producing sprouts and the like; in the same way, the *sattva* that has been parched by the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) and is free from obscuration is no longer denoted by the word "mind" (*manas*), nor is it capable of rebirth—this is the meaning. || 29 ||
The great-souled ones who are liberated while living, established in purity and with senses restrained, move about free from attachment; they are never established in the mind.
He states that in the appearance of the conduct of one liberated while living, that very thing is the appearance of the cause: "The ones liberated while living" (jīvanmuktāḥ). || 30 ||
They say that the deluded mind is *citta*, while the awakened is called *sattva*.
Indeed, those who are unawakened abide in *citta*, whereas those of great intelligence abide in *sattva*.
The mind is born again and again, but the sentient being is not born again;
O King, bondage exists for the unawakened, but not for the awakened.
"You have become possessed of courage; you stand as one of great renunciation.
I know that today you have completely surrendered your mind. (33)
With the intention that your worldly affairs shall also succeed for as long as you live solely through the power of your inner strength (*sattva*), he says: "You are one possessed of *sattva*."
O King, being now liberated from all latent impressions (vāsanās), you shine this very day;
O Sage, I consider your mind to have attained equality with space.
You have attained supreme tranquility; you are perfected, established in equanimity toward all things.
This indeed is that great renunciation: that everything has been completely relinquished.
The meaning is this: that great renunciation which you previously intended to perform is precisely this very mind, having abandoned all its forms.
O virtuous one, heaven, liberation, wealth, and even the fruits of austerity and charity— all these are attained through awakened intellect, through the supreme awakening of the mind.

With the intention that all actions such as austerity and charity are included within the renunciation of the mind (*cittatyāga*), and their fruits—such as wealth, heaven, and liberation—are likewise included within its fruit, he says "svarga... [and so forth]. By means of an intellect (*dhī*) that is thus characterized by awakened intelligence (*medhā*)—the retention of the taught meaning—and is therefore possessed of supreme awakening (*paramabodhavatī*).
The meaning is that the very renunciation of the mind constitutes the wealth of heaven, liberation, and so forth. || 36 ||
How could austerity possibly bring about the destruction of even a limited measure of suffering, when the bliss that consists in equanimity is free from both decay and excess? (37)
With the intention that the fruit of knowledge is not included within the fruits of austerity (*tapas*) and so forth, he says: "Austerity, indeed... The meaning is this:

since the fruit of knowledge—namely, the bliss of liberation which is free from decay and excess—has come from equanimity (*samatā*), which consists of the renunciation of the mind; therefore, the suffix *mayaṭ* is used in the sense of "come from that," according to the rule *mayaṭ ca*. (37)
That reality is that very thing; it is something, yet not heaven or the like which is transitory.
It is mounted upon existence and non-existence, established as the realization of consciousness. (38)
With the intention that there is not even the possibility of including the real and the eternal within the unreal and the impermanent, he says: "That.

That fruit of knowledge is *sat*, meaning true; it is a *vastu* because it abides, and thus it is eternal. But heaven and such things are merely "that" (something), yet they are neither true nor eternal. They are "ascended upon"—that is, overcome—by existence and non-existence, by manifestation and disappearance.
The meaning is that the present alone—which was not seen in the prior or subsequent times—is apprehended as existing, having attained sensation and having reached perception, like a dream. || 38 ||
What indeed is heaven? It is bliss; yet even that remains situated within doubt.
Until the perfection of one's own Self is attained, the section on ritual action may be auspicious. (39)

With the intention that the trivial happiness of heaven and the like—which is easily obtained with great effort—is esteemed only by the ignorant and not by those who know the truth, he says: "Heaven," etc. The compound *svargo nāma* is a *kṣepa-samāsa* (a compound used for censure), meaning: "What is called 'heaven'?"—is it true bliss? Or is it merely trivial pleasure?
It is a compound in the sense of reproach.
Because it can be destroyed by even a thousand minor offenses such as the recitation of unavoidable dharmas, it remains in a state of uncertainty. || 39 ||
Would one who has not obtained gold ever abandon brass?
Through association with Cūḍālā and others, you shall attain the state of a knower with ease. (40)

With the intention that the pursuit of trivial things such as heaven is indeed appropriate for the ignorant due to the rarity of knowledge, he says: "By which... *Rīti* means brass. He says, "But for you, knowledge was not previously difficult to obtain; nevertheless, you have needlessly immersed yourself in the hardship of asceticism": "Cūḍāla... (verse 40).
Why then are you immersed in this calamity consisting of ascetic toil, for the sake of that evil deed which was to be accomplished through the various stages of life and other such distinctions? (41)

The "hermitage" (āśrama) refers to the forest-dweller's stage of life (vānaprasthāśrama). By the word "etc. (ādi), there are included the appropriate age, as well as other qualifying attributes that enable one to fulfill the duties suited to that stage.

Because it is bound by its very result—since it must be accomplished through thousands of fragments of distraction consisting of conceptualizations such as pride in that stage and anxiety over its means of accomplishment—it acts as a fetter.
Why have you been immersed until this very day in such misfortune—connected to despicable actions and abounding in the hardships of penances such as the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa*? || 41 ||
O wise one, its beginning and end are suffering; only the middle is happiness, for that is the time when it arises and when it passes away. (42)

To the question, "How can austerity, which is the cause of great happiness such as heaven, be considered useless?", he says: "The beginning and the end. O wise one, since the initial stage of this austerity—the state of its performance—and its final stage—the state of the exhaustion of its fruit—are both of the nature of suffering, while it is said that there is only happiness in the middle, during the state of enjoying heaven and the like; then what [is the point] for me?

He says "no" to the claim that the austerity performed was indeed useless: "Because... Since it is through austerity alone that the ripening of the impurities of your mind has occurred, the present moment has become the time for the awakening to reality (*tattva*). For this reason, all conceptual fragments consisting of austerity transform into that non-conceptual knowledge of reality (*avikalpa-tattvajñāna*), and they are indeed fruitful by virtue of that very fruit.
They come to be. || 42 ||
Establish your footing there upon those portions of conceptualization which are the form of austerity;
for all states of being have arisen from the sky of consciousness, which is clearer than the physical ether.

In that knowledge, take firm root and remain steadfast. The meaning is that the fruitfulness of your austerity comes solely through its result—knowledge—as indicated by such scriptural passages as, "They desire to know [Brahman] through sacrifice, through charity, and through austerity. By attaining the sky of consciousness, which is the fruit of knowledge, everything is indeed attained; for the intention is that the entire world arises from, subsists in, and dissolves into that very source, according to the scriptures. With this in mind, he says:
"Of the space of consciousness," [it is said]. || 43 ||
In that very same way, they are seen to have gone to dissolution right there;
the volitions "this is to be done" and "this is not to be done" are but droplets of Brahman.

Although everything—whether what is to be done (kārya) or what is not to be done (akārya), whether desired or undesired—is indeed but drops from the ocean of Brahman, nevertheless, because of their insignificance, all that is barren and fruitless; therefore, having abandoned it, one should take refuge in the undifferentiated [Brahman] alone, which stands in the place of the full ocean. Thus he says: "This... (44).
"O Śikhidhvaja, having abandoned the barren, take refuge in that which is full.
Ask for what is desired from me, just as one asks of a friend, my friend. (45)

With the intention that, because he is the object of supreme love and is of the nature of unsurpassed bliss, the prayer for the attainment of such a self is superior to the prayer for any other desired object, he says: "The desired.
Just as by a woman who has not yet obtained her beloved, another thing is requested of the beloved she is to obtain, saying, "Pray for what is desired by me."

In that very same way, why is he not himself entreated as the beloved? The sense is that when he is obtained through one's own power, all other things to be obtained which depend upon him are acquired of their own accord. || 45 ||
In the same way, how can he be thus entreated by a woman herself—these objects fashioned by her imagination, appearing so radiant as they come before her? (46)
Having accepted that things other than the Self are desired human goals, it was stated that they are not to be sought after precisely because they have already been attained.
But in reality, from the perspective of one who knows the truth, these are trivial and thus not to be grasped; this is what he says with the words "saṃkalpa... [and so on].
Like calamities, they are lusterless and unpleasing. (46)
The wise, being great-souled, do not grasp at anything whatsoever—even that which bestows fruits such as heaven and liberation—just as they do not grasp at reflections in water. || 47 ||

Just as one abandons the reflections of the sun in water once the actual sun has been reached, so too, with the intent that even the means to liberation (apavarga) are to be abandoned immediately after the attainment of knowledge—just like the means to heaven and other worldly goals—he says: "Heaven," etc. (Verse 47).
Having abandoned [all], become that very one who appears as equal to all;
indeed, being free from longing, let the essence be destroyed by the essence through destruction. 48.

In all objects, the existent aspect (sadaṃśa) is to be grasped solely as existence, while the non-existent aspect (asadaṃśa) is to be grasped solely as eternally vanished, without mental agitation; thus he says: "Existence" (sattvam). || 48 ||
Grasping this flood of objects, remain with a mind that is motionless;
for one whose mind is without movement, the cycle of worldly existence does not run here.
He states the purpose of saying "the ground of the unmoving mind" with the words "aparispanda" (without vibration). It does not run, nor does it reach [its destination].

The meaning is that just as misfortune, which arises from human error characterized by natural activity, does not reach the intellect when the dawn of discriminative knowledge has occurred, so it is here. || 49 ||
O virtuous one, misfortune is indeed considered to arise from human effort, just as it is in the mind;
whatever sufferings manifest here in the three worlds [are likewise so]. (50)
O Lord of the Earth, those various [faults] arise solely from the fickleness of the mind;
he whose mind is steady, peaceful, motionless, and free from fickleness is forever possessed of great bliss and is the fit vessel for universal sovereignty. (51)

He is called a "universal monarch" (samrāj) because he shines by virtue of having correctly shattered all obscurations; the meaning is that he is a vessel for the state of having realized the Self. || 51 ||
Therefore, O knower of reality, having brought both movement and stillness into a state of oneness within the mind, remain as you wish, having attained eternal unity.

The meaning is: having brought vibration and non-vibration to a state of unity by seeing them as merely the witness of that [witness], and having reached and attained the identity of the witness with Brahman-Atman, remain at will in the state of the bliss of the Infinite (bhūmānanda) through the fulfillment of all desires. || 52 ||
Śikhidhvaja said:
"O Lord, how have these two—motion and non-motion—attained oneness? O you who cut through all doubts, tell me this quickly. (53)
"How can there be a unification of these two opposites, vibration and non-vibration? the King asked. "How so?
[Kumbha] replied:
"The entire world is a single reality, pure consciousness alone, like water in the ocean."
That very [Self] vibrates through the intellects, just as pure water vibrates through its waves. || 54 ||
Although there is a contradiction between the two in their own essential natures, there is no such contradiction when viewed as the substratum, which is pure consciousness (sākṣi-cinmātra);
thus, revealing his own intention, Kumbha gives the following answer: "One," etc. Like water, it vibrates—that is, it manifests through the nature of vibration. || 54 ||
That which has been sung as Brahman, pure consciousness, stainless, and named "Being" (sattva), this very thing, O dear one, the deluded perceive as the world. 55.
That which is sung by such scriptural passages as "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite"—the word "aṅga" is used here as a form of address. || 55 ||
The vibration of consciousness alone is the entirety of creation; from that indeed arises the cycle of worldly existence.
For its supreme movement is equal to the movement of words such as "Vindhya" and the like.

He establishes the identity of vibration and non-vibration with the words "citspanda" (the vibration of consciousness). That which constitutes the very essence of all things in creation is nothing but the vibration of consciousness (*citspanda*).

In that regard, the physical movement (*parispanda*) of forms such as the Vindhya mountains is merely a second-order [phenomenon], equal to the vibration of sound (*śabdaspanda*). The word "equal" (*sama*) is used in the sense of "like" (*iva*) for the purpose of indicating its illusory nature. The meaning is that it is not a primary vibration of the Name itself. || 56 ||
If that very consciousness is conceived as both vibration and non-vibration through its single nature, then in that state lies this stainless Śiva.

"Let it be so; nevertheless, how can there be a unity between vibration (spanda) and non-vibration (aspanda)? To this he says: "Of consciousness" (citaḥ). The meaning is: if that very self which is the witness of each [object], being both the vibration and the non-vibration of consciousness, is contemplated as having a single nature, then in that state, only this auspicious (śiva) form of the Self remains. || 57 ||
Creation, whose essence is merely the vibration of consciousness, dissolves upon right vision;
it arises for those with false vision, just like the delusion of a snake in a rope. (58)
To the question of where that creation then goes, he says: "creation. For it arises through the delusion of those with incorrect vision. || 58 ||
The designation "mind" refers to that which is characterized by movement, whereas this [state] is pervasive and free from movement;
having ascended to the plane beyond the fourth (turyātīta), it cannot be expressed by words. (59)
That which denotes it is the denotation of emanation; however, that which is motionless has ascended to the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta). || 59 ||
Through the continuous practice of association with the scriptures and virtuous people, when the mind has attained purity over time like the risen moon, [wisdom arises]. (60)

When it has arisen in that manner, he says: "By the Teacher. Just as when the defect of cataracts in the eye is removed and it attains clarity, the eternally established oneness of the moon is realized; so it is here. (60)
This alone has appeared, extended through one's own experiences;
it is described by oneself, through one's own experiences, as one's very own form by means of the Self. (61)
If it cannot be expressed by speech, then how is it told by you to those like me? To this he replies: "This" (etad).
The meaning is that for those who have experienced it themselves, it is told by them personally through their own experiences, according to worldly convention. || 61 ||
You have attained the essence, which is without beginning or middle; remain right here, established in your own state.
O virtuous one, you have indeed become free from sorrow, for you are born as the great conscious self, whose nature is beyond the differentiation of forms.

"You too have indeed attained your own direct experience; however, by my word, merely establish firmness therein," he says with the words "You have attained. Because of the very absence of the body and so forth, which constitute the forms of duality, you are without distinction in all bodies. Therefore, through the awakening to reality (*tattva-bodha*), you have become the Great Consciousness-Self (*mahān cidātmā*); you have manifested from that very state, and for that reason alone, you are free from sorrow (*vīta-śoka*). In that state, what delusion (*moha*) could there be? What...?
The meaning is that this is according to the Vedic scripture: "Sorrow belongs to one who perceives unity. || 62 ||
Thus ends the one hundred and first chapter, titled "The Enlightenment of Śikhidhvaja," in the *Pūrva-cūḍā* of the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki. 101.
Thus ends the one hundred and first chapter, titled "The Enlightenment of Śikhidhvaja," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and second canto.
Kumbha said:
"Thus, O King Śikhidhvaja, everything has been told to you."
Just as all this has arisen, and just as it dissolves. || 1 ||
When the jar had vanished after being addressed, the king was filled with wonder;
having reflected for a long time, his rest in meditative absorption (samādhi) is described here.
I have explained to you the entire reality of Brahman, which is complete, by means of superimposition—how all this has arisen—and by means of negation—how it dissolves. || 1 ||
Having heard this, understood it, and reflected upon it, O Leader of Sages,
remain as you wish, now that the supreme state has been clearly perceived.

Having heard from the Guru and the scriptures, having reflected through your own discernment, and having correctly understood the supreme state— which is directly perceived and made manifest by the removal of veils— remain as you wish, whether primarily in meditative absorption (samādhi) or in worldly activity (vyavahāra). || 2 ||
"O sage Nārada, on this auspicious occasion, I am going to heaven;
you have arrived from the world of Brahmā in the assembly of the immortals. (3)
To heaven, to the assembly hall of Indra. || 3 ||
If he does not see me there, he becomes angry;
for a worthy disciple should never cause his gurus any agitation.
With all mental constructs abandoned and desiring nothing at all, you must always dwell [thus]; this very vision is purifying.
This is indeed what has been taught by me.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Even as Śikhidhvaja, with flowers in his hand, was about to offer this reply and perform a prostration, he vanished from sight.
He vanished before he could offer a salutation in reply,
because it is improper for virtuous women to accept a prostration made by their husbands.
Just as an object perceived through a flash of intuition is not seen at its conclusion,
so King Śikhidhvaja did not see the jar before him.
An object such as wealth appearing in a dream and so forth [is non-existent] at the end, upon waking. || 7 ||
When the jar had departed, the protector of the earth was filled with supreme wonder;
reflecting upon that very marvel, he became as if fixed in a painting.
It is wonderful and marvelous. || 8 ||
He reflected upon this wondrous play of Fate:
that under the pretext of a water-jar, I have been awakened for my long-delayed rising.
Or Brahman is that which has no rising, is eternally dawn, and possesses perpetual exaltation.
Where is Kumbha, the son of Nārada, and where am I, Śikhidhvaja by name?
By the mere power of time alone have I been fully awakened to that truth.
By means of the proper time and through the conjunction of the moment when fortune arises. || 10 ||
"Oh, how well-spoken by the son of the gods! It is indeed logical.
Oh, after a long time, I have truly awakened from the sleep of delusion! (11)
Where was I, submerged in the foul mud of the web of ritual acts, caught in the false whirlpool of delusions such as "this must be done" and "this must not"? (12)
"Oh, how cool, pure, and peaceful is this path of my own!
Its form, born of an elixir, cools my very being here. (13)
This is the state of universal sovereignty, in which the nature of the Self has been directly realized; it is the mind as pure being, free from latent impressions.
I am at peace, I am fully extinguished, and I abide solely in bliss;
I do not desire even the tip of a blade of grass; I remain established just as I am.
By that very [statement], he expresses his own state of having all desires fulfilled: "I am at peace. || 14 ||
Reflecting thus, the king, clearly intent on banishment, remained in silence alone, as if carved out of stone. (15)

Like a statue carved from a mountain, he remained composed, being silent—that is, devoid of speech and other such activities. The use of the *kvasu* suffix instead of the *liṭ* perfect tense is due to Vedic license (*chāndasa*). 15.
Then, having attained an unwavering firmness in that very silence— which is free from volition and without support— he remained like a mountain peak.
In silence, during the sage's activity of meditative absorption. || 16 ||

There, with his fear completely stilled, his mind at rest after a long time, and his self composed, he attained his own stainless nature after a long time; then, through yoga, he slept as one whose self was no longer subject to affliction.

That king, having attained his own stainless self-nature in that meditative absorption, being equanimous and of equal flavor, after his mind had rested for a long time, became instantly and without delay free from fear; with his self sustained by long-practiced yoga and his nature unimpaired, he slept—meaning, he rested as if in deep sleep. || 17 ||
Thus ends the one hundred and second chapter, titled "The Composure of Śikhidhvaja," in the *Pūrva-cūḍā* of the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa* within the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki. 102.
Thus ends the one hundred and second chapter, titled "The Consolation of Śikhidhvaja," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The One Hundred and Third Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Through unwavering meditative absorption, one’s state becomes like that of wood or a wall.
Thus has King Śikhidhvaja [spoken]; now hear about Cūḍālā. || 1 ||
Having gone to Cūḍālā’s supreme state, his return in three days,
the king's diligent awakening, and his discourse on reality are described.

In the manner thus described, King Śikhidhvaja became like a piece of wood or a wall due to his state of non-conceptual meditative absorption (nirvikalpa-samādhi); this is the implied meaning. [He told] Cūḍālā "that account," that is to say, her own history. || 1 ||
Having awakened her husband Śikhidhvaja by means of that disguise as Kumbha,
she vanished and swiftly traversed the sky.
He crossed over; he leaped. || 2 ||
In the sky, he cast off the form of a son of the gods created by his illusory power,
and assumed a beautiful feminine form, charming and innocent in appearance.
He assumed the form of a son of the gods, appearing in the guise of a water-jar, taking on a feminine appearance with the physical characteristics of a woman. || 3 ||
He reached his own city through the sky and entered the inner apartments in an instant;
he became visible to the world and performed the duties of a king.
The "king's duty" (nṛpakarma) means royal business, that is to say, the pleasing of the subjects. || 4 ||
Then, having returned to the sky after three days,
she became a water-jar through her yogic power and went to the grove of Śikhidhvaja.
Kumbha was the son of Nārada. || 5 ||
Likewise, while there on the forest ground, she saw that king established in unwavering meditative absorption (nirvikalpa-samādhi), like a tree carved in relief.
Like a tree carved out of wood, it was motionless, fashioned in the form of an image. || 6 ||
"Ah! Indeed, O friend, by good fortune this one has found rest within himself;
he stands self-abiding, equanimous, and tranquil," he said again and again. (7)
This is the king. || 7 ||
Therefore, let me first awaken him from this supreme state;
why indeed does he intend to abandon his body this very moment? (8)
Now, the intention is as follows: at the time when the remainder of *prārabdha* karma persists, for what purpose does one abandon the body? Or rather, let one not abandon it.
Let him enjoy for a short time either this kingdom or the forest;
once we have cast off these bodies, we two shall go together as equals.

Until the exhaustion of the karma to be experienced in the forest, or together with the forest—that is, at exactly the same time—we two shall go as equals, having an identical nature; "to liberation" is the understood remainder of the sentence. || 9 ||
His instruction is difficult and does not reach its fruition;
therefore, by means of this yoga of practice, I shall first awaken him.

The instruction previously given by me has not reached its full development—that is, its maturation—up until the stage of abiding on the seventh bhūmi; therefore, the sense is that he must now be awakened even for the sake of experiencing the bliss of liberation while living (jīvanmukti) at the very moment of casting off the body. || 10 ||
Having reflected thus, Cūḍālā let out a lion’s roar again and again before her lord, striking terror into the forest-dwellers.
Of the Lord, the Master. || 11 ||
When he did not move, even though that roar was repeated again and again like a boulder upon a mountain, she then caused him to waver.
He shook it by rubbing his palms together. || 12 ||
When the king was shaken and even cast down, yet did not wake up, Cūḍālā, who had assumed the form of Kumbha, reflected thus: (13)
"Aha! This venerable one has matured as a virtuous man in his own station;
therefore, by what means shall I now awaken him? (14)

It has matured up to the point of entering the seventh stage. "Aho" expresses wonder. Thus, the sense is: "My suspicion that his instruction is difficult and does not reach its fruition was indeed in vain. || 14 ||
Or rather, why should I awaken this Great-Souled One?
Having attained awakening, let him remain as he pleases, free from the body.
For this very reason he says: "Or else"; let the disembodied state (videha) stand aside. || 15 ||
I too, having abandoned this female body, shall go to the supreme state from which there is no rebirth; for what indeed is equal to this? (16)
I go along with them, at the same time; what greater happiness is there in this life?—this is the implied meaning. || 16 ||
Having reflected thus, the highly intelligent Cūḍālā, being intent on abandoning her own body, reflected once more.

By the word "Mahāmati," it is indicated that she, perceiving with her own intellect that even the remainder of his prārabdha-karma must necessarily be experienced, reflected upon it once again. || 17 ||
"I shall look upon this body of the lord of the earth for just this long, to see if there remains within his heart even a trace of vitality, the seed of awakening. (18)

If his mind, though devoid of latent impressions (vāsanā), remains as a mere residue in the form of subtle tendencies within the sky of the heart—specifically within the Brahman of the heart which is still veiled by a trace of Māyā remaining from past karma (prārabdha)—[then he is not yet liberated]. || 18 ||
At that time, this Blessed One will attain full awakening,
like a cluster of flowers resting within the sap-filled core of a tree.

"At the proper time," meaning at the moment of its arising; just as, at the onset of spring, within the root-cavity—the region of the roots of a tree—there is a subtle state of the remaining essence (*sattvaśeṣa*), like a future cluster of flowers latent within the earthy sap, so it is here. This is how it connects with what precedes. || 19 ||
Thus, even while living, one becomes truly liberated from separation;
if, on the other hand, one becomes liberated [in death], I consider that I shall go along with him.

In that case, being awakened by me and becoming liberated while living (jīvanmukta), he shall indeed wander just as I do. Furthermore, if he becomes liberated even from the obstruction of his remaining subtle body (sattvaśeṣa), then I too shall go to liberation together with him in equal measure. || 20 ||
Having reflected thus, the fair-complexioned Cūḍālā, observing her husband with both touch and reasoning, spoke apprehensively.

Having observed her husband with apprehension by means of his touch—the sign of bodily warmth—and by the signs to be described hereafter, she awakened him through the arising of the cause for consciousness; and she said, "There is indeed a remnant of life-force (sattva) remaining in his heart," which connects with the subsequent verse. || 21 ||
There indeed remains a residue of goodness in his heart, which serves as the cause for awakening; through the arising of the causes for awakening, he awakened that residue of goodness.

Śrī Rāma said: O Brahmin, how is one who possesses a deeply pacified mind, who remains like a piece of wood or a clod of earth, and who is absorbed in meditation, recognized as having only pure being (sattva) remaining?
Regarding what was stated as "by means of touch and by means of method" (naya), Rāma, desiring to know the meaning of the word *naya*, asks:
"Intensely" (*bhṛśam*). || 23 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: He who possesses within his heart the cause of awakening— a subtle form difficult to perceive— exists as a mere residue of being, like the flower and fruit within a seed.

To state the answer—that the non-arising of transformations such as growth, decay, and destruction in the body is a sign of the remaining pure being (sattva)—he restates the subject to be characterized (liṅgin) with two verses beginning with "prabodha": || 24 ||
For him who is free from the vibration of the mind, whose true consciousness is unwavering, who is devoid of duality and unity, and who abides equally and immovably; || 25 ||
Of that which is devoid of duality and unity, and is free from conceptual construction. || 25 ||
The body, being in a state of perfect equanimity, neither languishes nor exults;
it neither sets nor rises, but remains exactly even. || 26 ||
He becomes weary; he undergoes exhaustion. || 26 ||
The body of one whose mind vibrates with notions such as duality, unity, and so forth, undergoes change; but for one whose mind does not vibrate, it never does.
But for another, it is the opposite of that; thus he says: "Duality, unity, and so forth. (27)
For the vibration of the mind is the cause of the existence of the entire world and of all modifications of being, O Rāma, just as honey is the cause of flowers.

To explain why that is so, he says: "It is the vibration of the mind. It is the cause of all modifications of being (bhāvavikāra) which serve as the basis for the existence and worldly activity of the universe. || 28 ||
O scion of the Raghus, as the mind repeatedly departs from this body, joy, anger, and delusion no longer come under its control.

For this very reason, as long as the seed for rebirth exists, joy, anger, and delusion do not come under control—that is, they cannot be restrained—even when the mind, which is about to pass from this body to another body, is repeatedly suppressed with effort. This, then, is the sign that rebirth is inevitable. || 29 ||

When the mind has attained tranquility, that body which is devoid of [the notion of] a sentient being does not afflict it, just as the source of transformations of existence does not afflict the sky. (30)

He says "in the mind" because when modifications such as joy and the like are stilled in the mind, modifications in the body also cease. It is abandoned by *sattva*—that is, by a mind free from latent impressions (*vāsanā*)—and thus relinquished without further rebirth. The sense is that the very grasping of the body by the mind through the notion of "I" is the cause of modifications such as growth and so forth in the body. || 30 ||
Just as waves and the like do not arise from a continuous stream of water that is uniform,
so too no defect is perceived in a continuous stream of being that is uniform.
The defects such as bodily decay and graying hair, as well as the defects such as passion and so forth, are no longer seen. || 31 ||
There is no perception of a sentient being except through its cessation;
as long as reality appears as manifold, it subsides in its absolute state over time.

If it is asked, "For how long is existence perceived by those liberated while living (jīvanmukta)? he says: "Until the cessation of that [existence] through the exhaustion of the remainder of *prārabdha* karma.
Regarding the phrase "of existence" (*sattvasya*): it is "equal," meaning empty even of apparent diversity. "From time" means from the time of the exhaustion of the remainder of *prārabdha*. || 32 ||
But in that body where neither mind nor being is found,
O Rāma, it dissolves through the state of the five elements like snow in heat.

He says "in the body" (dehe) to show that upon the destruction of the *sattva*, the dead body dissolves. "Not the mind" (*no cittam*) refers to the death of the ignorant; "nor even the *sattva*" (*nāpi sattvam*) refers to the death of the wise. [This occurs] through death by way of the five elements (*pañcatva*). || 33 ||
This body of Śikhidhvaja is mindless yet exalted by its splendor; because it is endowed with a portion of pure being (sattva), it is not subject to exhaustion.
He states that she saw the signs of life in Śikhidhvaja’s body with the words "of Śikhidhvaja," etc.; by "tejas" is meant heat (ūṣman). || 34 ||
Beholding her husband’s body in such a state, that excellent woman did not abandon her own body, but reflected with haste: (35)
Having resolved the question, he connects the subject at hand with the words "him thus," and so forth: "while not having abandoned her own body. (35)
Having entered the all-pervading and pure essence of consciousness, I awaken it;
for I am established therein as that lovely awakening yet to come.

The reality of consciousness (cittattva) was previously described; that is the Brahman within the heart. Having entered by means of entering its body, and remaining there established in its very nature, she thinks:
"I shall awaken now itself my beloved, whose awakening will occur after a long time. || 36 ||
"If I do not awaken him, he will understand this by himself after a long time;
why should I remain alone?"—thinking thus, I awaken him.

"Surely he will understand by himself after some time; what is the hurry for me to inform him? To this she replies: "No. Her intention is: "Appointed as I am to the governance of the kingdom, I am not able to remain in meditative absorption like my husband; and having emerged from it, how could I possibly remain alone? || 37 ||
Having reflected thus, Cūḍālā abandoned her body, which is a cage of the senses, and attained stability in the principle of consciousness (cittattva), which is devoid of beginning and end.
The meaning is that, having abandoned his own body and entered that body, he attained stability in the principle of consciousness (cittattva) characterized as the Brahman within the heart. || 38 ||
There, having caused the conscious vibration within the embodied Lord, that consciousness entered its own body again, like a bird returning to its own nest. (39)

In that state, it is the vibration conducive to the separation of the intellect— which is permeated by the reflection of its own consciousness— from the consciousness that has become of one flavor with it, like milk and water, through non-conceptual samādhi. (39)
Then, rising up in the form of a water-pot, she settled upon a bed of flowers and began to sing the Sāman,
her voice resonating like the humming of a swarm of bees.
Hearing that sound of the Sāman chant, she, endowed with the quality of pure consciousness, perceived it within the king’s body as a lotus-pond perceives the springtime. (41)
The royal intellect, luminous with the reflection of consciousness, awakened through the reawakening of the latent impression of the ego-sense of Śikhidvaja;
it perceived the pervasion of the sense of "I" throughout the body, reaching even to the tips of the nails.
Then King Śikhidhvaja, having attained the perfection of inner strength, caused that vision to blossom like the sun causes the lotus.
Her eyes were closed in meditative absorption. || 42 ||
He saw a pitcher standing before him, intent on chanting the Sāman hymns,
endowed with a supreme form like another Sāmaveda.

In the word *gāyanam*, the absence of the substitution of *ā* for *i* (as in *gāyantam*) is a Vedic archaism (*chāndasa*). There is a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) that he is like another Sāmaveda endowed with a supreme, divine form. || 43 ||
"Oh, how blessed we are that the sage has come here of his own accord!"— uttering these words, the king gave a flower to Kumbha.
*Kusumam* means a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjalim*). By this, it is understood that due to the power of her asceticism (*tapas*), the flowers previously gathered do not wither.
"By good fortune, O Blessed One, we have been mentioned in your pure mind;
for what great beings indeed could possibly be situated within our own limbs? (45)

"By good fortune—that is, through the rising of my own merit—I have been raised up and have once again come within the range of memory as the fruit of the joy of seeing you. Or rather, what is the use of reflecting on my fortune? For the great are spontaneously intent upon bestowing grace upon others. With this intention, he says: "Who indeed... (verse 45).
The very purpose of your coming is to purify us;
if not, then tell me what the second reason for your arrival might be.
If the reason stated by me for coming here is not [the case], then what second reason could there possibly be?
The meaning is: "Tell me that. || 46 ||
Kumbha said:
From the moment I departed from your presence, O blameless one,
from that time forth my mind has remained here with you alone.
"Together with you alone" means that [the heart] remembers only you as its place. || 47 ||
I do not remain in the delightful heaven now, but am present near you;
O Lord of rising limbs, that which is desired stands before all beautiful things.

For this very reason, I do not remain even now in heaven, though it is delightful; rather, I stay in your presence. O dear one, because among many beautiful things, that which is most desired by the heart stands before one only when it is "udyat"—that is, attainable through effort and not without effort—it is solely by virtue of the effort toward beholding you that [I am here].
The meaning is "my arrival. || 48 ||
I believe that in this world there is no kinsman, trusted confidant, well-wisher, friend, companion, trustworthy person, or disciple like you for me. (49)
Regarding the question of what specific cause for your affection toward me might exist, he says: "one such as you. (49)
Śikhidhvaja said:
"Oh, how the trees of merit have indeed borne fruit upon our family mountain,
since even you, though free from attachment, desire union with us!"
On this Mandara, the king of mountains. || 50 ||
"This is the forest, these are the trees, and here am I, your devoted servant;
O Lord, if heaven does not please you, then please remain here. (51)
If, out of love for me, heaven does not please you, then stay here in my presence.
"O virtuous one, through the yoga-method bestowed by you, I have found rest;
I consider that there is no such rest in heaven as this. (52)

He says that even for him, who is satisfied by the bliss of meditative concentration bestowed by you, there is no desire for heaven: "by what was bestowed by you" (*bhavadvitīrṇayā*). "Bestowed" (*vitīrṇayā*) means given. || 52 ||
Relying upon that very same pure and luminous state,
sport here as you desire, whether in heaven or upon the surface of the earth.
Relying upon that very state of abiding in the bliss of plenitude (bhūmānanda) which has been taught to me—[a state] luminous and self-luminous. || 53 ||
Kumbha said:
"Have you found rest in the supreme state of great bliss?
Have you completely abandoned this suffering consisting of duality?"
O King, has your delight in those volitions that are pleasant only at first sight utterly vanished, so that you find only a lack of interest in worldly enjoyments? (55)
Is your mind established in tranquility, remaining equanimous in peace, beyond the states of what is to be rejected or accepted, and free from agitation regarding whatever has arisen? (56)
He abides in equanimity through tranquility. || 56 ||
Śikhidhvaja said:
"O Blessed One, by your grace, the state that transcends all objects of sight has been beheld;
the boundary of saṃsāra has been reached, and the certainty regarding what was to be attained has been gained. (57)
After a very long time, indeed after a vast duration, I have attained rest and am free from ailment;
having obtained everything that was to be obtained, I remain here for a long time, fully satisfied.
"From long ago" means after a great length of time; "after a very long time" means up to the limit of three days. || 58 ||
Nothing whatsoever needs to be taught to us;
I am entirely satisfied in every respect, I am established [in peace], and my fever has departed.

The known and the unknown, the unattained, the abandoned, the abandonable, and that which has been resorted to—the reality, the supreme, and the essence—none of these belong to me; they belong to myself alone. (60)

The word "attained" is to be understood as "not yet attained. Likewise, my being is free from latent impressions (*nirvāsana*), yet the mind has resorted to the state of otherness regarding this very self. || 60 ||
Free from worldly existence, devoid of delusion and fear, dispassionate, eternally risen, with an equanimous disposition toward all and entirely gentle;
