being the self of all, yet detached from all mental constructions, as pure as the expanse of space, I abide in perfect equilibrium.
If nothing whatsoever exists other than you, then what remains of you? To this he replies: "Devoid of transmigration" (niḥsaṃsṛtiḥ).
This is clear. || 61 ||
Thus ends the one hundred and third canto, titled "The Return of Kumbha," in the first part of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the glorious Vāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa of Valmīki, composed by the Sage. 103.
Thus ends the one hundred and third canto, titled "The Return of Kumbha," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The One Hundred and Fourth Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Thus, with these various discourses on the supreme self, the two conversed with one another.
The knower and the object of knowledge sat together in the forest for three muhūrtas. || 1 ||
In this [section], the king’s desire for sexual enjoyment with Kumbhīrāma is described;
following the pretext of heaven, there is the departure from the city and his dejected return.
Thus, as described, they were conversing with one another through various discourses concerning the self (*adhyātma*), the remainder of the sentence being "thus conversing. || 1 ||
Then, having risen, they sported upon a certain mountain peak abounding with lakes and cranes, and likewise in a lake and a forest, as if in the Nandana grove.

In which [place] there were delightful, glistening cranes and lotuses, as well as pairs of birds; in that Nandana, which bestows joy and protects the earth with fruits, roots, and other provisions—or rather, it is like the famous Nandana forest belonging to Indra—this is the implied sense. || 2 ||
By means of that conduct and those conversations,
they then spent eight days in the forest paths within those groves.

By that conduct renowned as being liberated while living; in the forest, meaning in the great wilderness; in the forest paths, meaning in the various divisions of intermediate woodland ranges—by this, it is indicated that there was no fixed abode, as he did not dwell in one place even for eight days. || 3 ||
Then Kumbha said, "Let us go to another forest on the mountain. Thinking "So be it," the king agreed, and they both set out.

The word *om* signifies what is intended. Just as in the case of a king, the Kumbha also possesses agency established by the facts of the matter; thus, by relying on the grammatical rule regarding the identity of the agent (*samānakartṛkatā*) between two actions performed by the same agent, the suffix *-ktvā* is employed in the expression "having thought" (*matvā*). || 4 ||
Forests of many forms, jungles, riverbanks, lakes, thickets of shrubs, peaks, and dense thickets. || 5 ||
Rivers, regions, as well as villages, cities, and forests;
Mañjughoṣa mountains, groves, sacred fords, and shrines.
Equal in every way, equal in affection, and united, the two remained together; with equal strength and equal energy, they always stood praising one another.
Being united and assembled together, they remained equally engaged even in their mental activity, praising and describing their mutual experience. || 7 ||
O Raghava, they worshipped the ancestors and the gods and partook of their meals;
they were equal-minded toward both what was heated and what was sprinkled with water.
"Sprinkled with water and moist" means in a cool place. || 8 ||
In the groves of *tamāla* trees and the thickets of *mandāra* blossoms,
that couple, whose hearts were tender and who were like dear friends, shone resplendently.
O Rāma, the mental construction of dualistic thought— “this is the home” and “this is not”— did not carry away those two, just as a whirlwind cannot move the mountain of the gods.
He states the characteristic of dwelling without a home with the words "this": conceptual construction did not captivate the minds of those two.
Those two friends roamed about, sometimes grey with dust,
sometimes their limbs smeared with sandalwood paste, and sometimes stained with ashes.
He states that even the conceptualization of the pleasant and the unpleasant did not arise for those two, by means of the verse beginning with "viceratuḥ" (they wandered). || 11 ||
In some places they wore divine garments, and in others variegated clothes;
in some places they were covered with sprouts, and in others adorned with flowers.
In just a few days, through that equanimity of mind and his exalted nature of purity,
the king shone like a water-jar [filled with water].
With courage, with a mind free from latent tendencies, and with nobility and excellence. || 13 ||
Then, seeing Śikhidhvaja, who shone like the offspring of a god and had attained such splendor, the proud Cūḍālā reflected:

Then, after the enjoyment of the *prārabdha* karma that brings about mutual enjoyment through the state of mere friendship, at the time when the *prārabdha* karma bringing about the state of husband and wife arises. || 14 ||
This husband is noble-minded, these forest lands are delightful, and this state of being free from exertion is one that has not been deceived by desire. (15)
They were not deceived by desire, which is a base dharma, nor by passion. || 15 ||
For those whose minds are liberated while living and who remain established in whatever enjoyment comes to them,
that which appears as one-pointedness is declared to be merely a trivial form of delusion.

For those who do not abide by the enjoyment as it is obtained and whose course is unceasing, that mental state which consists of an obsession—a persistent clinging—to the cessation of enjoyment in one instance is nothing but delusion. 16.
A noble-souled husband, freedom from anxiety, fresh youth, and houses filled with clusters of flowers—she is not a woman who does not desire these. (17)

One must indeed desist from enjoyments that arise from causes such as unrighteousness, disease, and exhaustion, for the sake of maintaining the world-order (*lokasaṃgraha*). In this regard, she who has no desire for her own husband is ruined if she is not yet liberated-in-life (*ajīvanmuktā*), by the sin of obstructing her husband’s enjoyment; if she is liberated-in-life (*jīvanmuktā*), she is ruined by the censure and so forth resulting from the failure to maintain the world-order—this is the meaning. || 17 ||

That beloved woman who does not take delight in a forest bower of flowers and creepers while her husband is at her disposal—she, being free from sorrow no longer, is indeed a ruined and wicked woman. 18.
He states clearly what has already been said: "In the forest," etc. (18).
Fie upon that wicked woman who, having obtained a lovely, handsome husband in a secluded place, does not take delight in him once she is married! (19)
If one who knows what is to be known always abandons even that which has been attained—blameless and of noble purpose—what could possibly have been accomplished by such a knower? (20)
What further fruit could be achieved by one who renounces their own blameless and noble wealth?
The meaning is: none at all. || 20 ||
Therefore, I shall quickly devise some artifice to display in the forest, by which this lord of the earth, my husband and bestower of honor, may take delight in me. (21)
By means of her insight—that is, by her own wisdom—she delights in me; she obtains the bliss of passion. || 21 ||
Having reflected thus, Cūḍālā, assuming the guise of Kumbha and standing within a forest thicket, spoke to her husband like a female cuckoo to a male cuckoo.
Kumbha said:
"This is the great first day of the bright fortnight of the month of Caitra;
today, indeed, the assembly of Hari in heaven begins its grand undertaking."
The assembly hall is the gathering of the divine sages; [it belongs] to Hari, that is, Indra. || 23 ||
I must remain present there before my father;
for destiny, as it has been ordained, must never be disregarded.
Of his father, Nārada. || 24 ||
"You must wait for me here in this forest region, sporting among the fresh blossoms without falling into agitation. (25)
My return must be awaited; it must be expected for this very month. || 25 ||
Today, at the end of the day, I come from the sky in a state free of conceptual thought;
indeed, association with you brings me even greater joy than creation itself.
"Non-conceptual" means free from the state of being subject to coming; that is to say, it is "certain. || 26 ||
Having spoken thus, Kumbha gave a flower-cluster to Mitra,
like one giving his own beloved wife born from the trees of Nandana, for the sake of mutual affection.
The beloved one is the heart-stealing [Nandana]; the Nandana tree is the Kalpavṛkṣa; [he saw] the cluster of blossoms produced from it. || 27 ||
"When you have spoken thus, O King, you must return very quickly";
having said this, he then leaped from the forest into the sky like an autumn cloud at its onset.
It is like a waterless cloud at the onset of autumn. || 28 ||
As he moved through the sky, he cast down a handful of flowers produced from a floral garland;
it spread abroad with the forest breeze like a snowy cloud in winter.

The *puṣpāñjali* (handful of flowers) is spreading and diffusing with the forest breeze. Regarding the formation of the word, since it is a neuter pronoun, the neuter gender—which had already been applied as an internal (*antaraṅga*) factor—is not set aside even when there is a connection with a specific masculine [referent]. Thus it has been illustrated in the Mahābhāṣya: "And by this [word], it is possible [to refer] even by means of dog-meat and so forth."
In that regard, a restriction is established to ward off hunger: "Five five-nailed animals are to be eaten. That which occurs in the winter season is *haima*. || 29 ||
Then Śikhidhvaja beheld him as he was departing until he vanished from sight;
like a peacock awakened at the sound of a cloud, for the affection of the wise is indeed difficult to abandon.
Non-perception extends as far as the range of vision; "cloud" refers to a rain-cloud. || 30 ||
At the end of Śikhidhvaja’s gaze, she who had the form of a jar abandoned herself in the sky;
like the beauty of water when its whirlpools have subsided, that charming woman returned to her own true form. (31)
His own form as Cūḍālā; he arrived, that is, he reached it. || 31 ||
By way of the celestial path, he reached his own city, which was as delightful as heaven, resembling a wish-fulfilling tree in full bloom, and adorned with fluttering banners. (32)
Because of that very [reason], its form—its configuration—is like that of a wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa) which has blossomed with clusters of flowers, having its banners fluttering. || 32 ||
Remaining invisible, she entered the inner apartments crowded with women,
like the great goddess of the spring season entering a tree adorned with shimmering creepers.
Having swiftly accomplished all the royal duties there,
he fell before Śikhidhvaja like a cluster of fruits and flowers.
Just as a fruit or a flower falls from a tree, so it is in that manner.
There, with an undaunted mind, she made her face— which had lost its luster (some manuscripts read *mlānadyuti*)— appear like the moon shrouded in mist, or like a withered lotus at nightfall.
There, in the presence of her husband, Cūḍālā, who was in the prime of her youth, made her face assume a dark luster.
Seeing him in such a state, Śikhidhvaja rose up;
his heart became distressed, and with great respect, he spoke these words.
Respectful means with reverence. || 36 ||
"O son of a god, salutations to you; you appear as if troubled in mind.
You are Kumbha; abandon your agitation and sit upon this seat. (37)

"You appear dejected, as if with a distressed mind"—this is the meaning, indicated by the sign of your withered face. "Agitation" (*saṃrambha*) refers here, by figurative extension (*lakṣaṇā*), to mental anguish. || 37 ||
Those holy ones who have known what is to be known do not resort to a state born of joy or sorrow;
established in their own nature, they remain like lotuses untouched by the moisture of water. (38)
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: When the king had spoken thus, Kumbha, entering his seat, spoke with a dejected voice resembling the sound of a broken bamboo staff. (39)
Because it arose from a throat choked with tears, it was like the sound of a cracked bamboo flute. || 39 ||
Those who, throughout the various states of the body, do not remain with equanimity of mind through their organs of action, are not knowers of reality; they are deceivers.

Regarding what was said—that persons who have known what is to be known do not resort to a state born of joy or dejection—Kumbha spoke, wishing to express a certain distinction therein: "As long as the body lasts," and so forth.
He meant that the very cessation of the activity of the organs of action—which is inseparable from the equanimity of mind induced by knowledge—is indeed the defining characteristic of the knower.

The intention is that those who know reality, though they possess equanimity of mind, appear as if empty [of action] only because of the fault arising from the mere activity of the organs of action impelled by *prārabdha* karma. || 40 ||
For those fools who do not know reality, O King, out of sheer childishness they flee from the states that are naturally grasped by their own nature. (41)

But it is not so for those who do not know reality; thus he says, "For those who... The meaning is that because they lack equanimity due to their childishness, they flee from—and fall away from—the states of restraining the various organs of action which were forcibly grasped through practice; since this occurs solely due to the nature of ignorance, there is a disparity. || 41 ||
Just as oil exists within every sesame seed, so does the state [of suffering] pervade the body;
he who does not succumb to this bodily state cuts through the sky with his sword.

With the intention that the state of joy or dejection of the organs of action, impelled by *prārabdha* karma, lasts as long as the body exists and is equal for both the knower and the ignorant, he says "as long as" along with an illustration. The ellipsis is to be supplied as: "the state—namely, the state of joy, dejection, and so forth of the organs of action—certainly occurs. He confirms this very point by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).
"—'yaḥ' (who). And thus, even for the knower, there is simply no transcending the state of the body; therefore, the sense is that my following after him is not a fault. || 42 ||

This renunciation of the suffering inherent in the state of the body is indeed unsurpassed; it consists in the equanimity of the mind through yoga, and not in the cessation of the activity of the organs of action. (43)

And thus, through the equanimity of the mind, the non-perception of the sufferings of the bodily state by virtue of samādhi is indeed their abandonment; the essential point is that this is not endurance through the forceful restraint of the organs of action. He states this with the words: "This... (verse 43).
As long as the body lasts, one who understands the ten limbs according to their proper conduct should remain active through the organs of action, but never through the organs of perception. 44.

For one who knows and understands reality, the only rule is that as long as the body lasts, one must remain within all circumstances acting exactly according to right conduct through the organs of action,
and never transgressing right conduct; likewise, through the organs of perception and the mind,
[one should act] with pure intentions, just as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and all the other supreme lords have declared.
They abide in various bodily states; such is the certainty of destiny.

He states that the continued existence of the body according to its natural state, unimpeded by the organs of action, is well-known among all those liberated while living (jīvanmukta), beginning with Brahmā—thus he says, "Parameṣṭhī. This is because there is no possibility of experiencing [the fruits of karma] otherwise than through the necessity of *niyati*, which is the necessity of *prārabdha* karma; such is the intended meaning. || 45 ||
Indeed, all this collection of visible phenomena, whether consisting of those who do not know reality or those who know it, runs toward destiny just as water flows toward the ocean. (46)
He says—starting with "The ignorant"—that no one at all, whether they be knowers of reality or ignorant ones, is able to transgress the necessity of *prārabdha* karma. || 46 ||
Those who know this [sustain] this unbroken destiny as long as the body lasts, through the equality of the intellect and other faculties, and by the movement of the hands and other limbs. (47)
If so, is there then absolute equality between the knower and the ignorant? No; he says: "The knowers of that" [referring to verse 47].
This lasts as long as the body is assumed, until the fall of that single body.

But the ignorant, O dear one, struck by states of pleasure and pain through universal agitation, pass their time under the sway of destiny, which is fragmented across hundreds of thousands of bodies. 48.
But the ignorant are not like that; thus he says: "But the ignorant... (verse 48).
If living beings here have thus understood that they must remain in this manner both in states of happiness and in states of suffering, then, O friend,
this fixed play of destiny— which manifests through the multitudes of both the ignorant and the wise— is indeed impossible to transcend. (49)

Having enacted the nature of *prārabdha-niyati* (the destiny of one's commenced karma), he demonstrates its inviolability by all; then, restating what has been said, he concludes with the words "ittham" (thus). Now, the address "anena aṅga" is used to address the King. By this means, [it is shown that] in this birth, this living being must remain thus amidst pleasures and in states of suffering.

Thinking, "One must remain thus," whatever mark on the forehead (fate) has been acquired or obtained by living beings according to their respective karma, that very thing manifests accordingly among the multitudes of beings— whether ignorant or wise; this is indeed the inevitable play of *niyati* (destiny), that is, of *prārabdha-karma*, which is difficult to transcend in the manner previously described.
This is the meaning. || 49 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and fourth canto, titled "The Exposition of the Conduct of the Liberated-while-Living," in the *Jīvanmuktiprakaraṇa* of the *Mokṣopāya*, within the *Vāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa* composed by the Sage Vasiṣṭha. 104.

Thus ends the one hundred and fourth canto, titled "The Exposition of the Conduct of the Liberated-while-Living," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa-tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and fifth canto. Śikhidhvaja said:
"O illustrious one, such being the case, how can there be such agitation?"
Even you, O god, have attained it; speak, O best among those who know what is to be known! || 1 ||
It is said that by night, due to the curse of Durvāsas, Kumbha attained womanhood;
and through their mutual reconciliations, the two remained in a state of affection.
Kumbha said:
Listen, O lord of the earth, to this matter in my heart;
I shall tell you everything regarding the creation that has occurred for me today.

Thus, since the multitude of living beings remains subject to the course of destiny, how did you, though being a god, come to experience such agitation caused by despondency? This is the meaning. || 1 || 2 ||
Sorrow disclosed to a friend reaches its greatest attenuation, just as a cloud, though thick, dull, and dark, does when it has released its rain. (3)
The neuter gender of the qualifiers "dense," "dull," and "black" is as before. Just as such a cloud, having released its rain, attains thinness, so it is here. || 3 ||
The mind attains clarity when questioned by a virtuous friend,
just as water quickly becomes clear through the application of clearing-nut (kataka) powder.
"By a friend who inquires out of a motive," and "by one who has approached for the sake of purity"—these are also qualifiers of the friend. (4)
Having first departed from here and given a cluster of flowers to your honor,
I have crossed the sky and reached heaven.
Then, having stood in due order in the assembly hall of Mahendra, he rose at the time for rising and was dismissed by his father.
The phrase "together with his father" is to be understood as the ellipsis. || 6 ||
Having abandoned heaven to come here, I have reached the sky;
I travel along the path of the wind together with the horses of the sun.
I carry [the wind] along the path favorable to myself, which is called Pravaha; by its very current, I flow as far as the desired destination—this is the meaning. || 7 ||
Then, while the sun had gone in one direction, I returned through the sky by another path, appearing like one who has fallen into the ocean.

Then, immediately after reaching the region desired by me, the Sun, being carried forward by that wind, proceeded along one path, while I came by another path; "having the appearance of having fallen into the ocean" means as if floating upon the sea. || 8 ||
Then, ahead of me along the path amidst clouds filled with water, I saw the sage Durvāsas approaching with great speed.
With its clouds as a covering garment and adorned by circles of lightning, the mountain—
with its sandalwood paste washed away by the rain— resembles a woman going to meet her lover.
He whose body-sandalwood paste (the cosmetic unguent applied to the limbs) had been washed away and cleansed by showers of spray. || 10 ||
He rushed with speed toward that river, which stood upon the surface of the earth providing excellent shade for its trees, like a beloved wife whose splendor is her asceticism.

He rushed with speed toward the river Gaṅgā— standing upon the surface of the earth, beautiful because of the excellent shade of trees growing upon her banks, and appearing like his own beloved Fortune of Austerity (tapolakṣmī) personified— fearing lest the time for the evening worship (saṃdhyāvandana) should pass him by. (Alternatively, if the reading is *āpayām*, it means "toward that beloved characterized as the Fortune of Austerity.")
He obtained his wife upon the surface of the earth; having brought her face-to-face, she seemed as if she were flowing toward him—this is a poetic fancy (utprekṣā). || 11 ||
Having paid him homage, I, traveling through the sky, said:
"O Sage, you are like a woman going to meet her lover, dressed in garments as dark as a blue cloud."
"You appear equal to a woman going to meet her lover in the darkness," so I said. || 12 ||
Having heard this, O giver of honor, he uttered a curse upon me:
"May she become a beloved woman, possessed of breasts and long hair, and playful with gestures and expressions. (13)
"Go; because of this ill-spoken word, you shall become a woman at night.
Having heard this inauspicious speech uttered by the decrepit Brahmin, [she was struck with fear]. (14)
The word *aśubham* (inauspicious) is the division [of the compound]. From the decrepit, aged Brahmin Durvāsas. || 14 ||
"O virtuous one, while I was reflecting for just a moment, the sage vanished;
thus, with a mind full of agitation, I have arrived here from the sky. (15)
One whose mind is such that it possesses agitation caused by what has been thus described. || 15 ||
"All this has been told to you; I have become a woman of the night. How shall I endure this state of womanhood at the end of the days? (16)
How can it be passed over? How can it be endured? || 16 ||
"Seeing a woman with breasts at night, what should I say to my father? Alas, how treacherous indeed is the course of destiny within this cycle of existence! (17)
The word "in the presence of his father" is to be understood as the ellipsis. || 17 ||
"Alas, that by fate I too have today become the prey of gamblers; through my being lost, a quarrel now arises. (18)

He clarifies that very logic—which makes young men an object of quarrel according to the maxim of vultures seizing meat—with the word "Alas! (kaṣṭam). The phrase "now" (adhunā) refers to a time proximate to this day, such as tomorrow or the day after. "By my abduction" (madapahāreṇa) means for the purpose of carrying me away; the instrumental case is used because the result is intended to be expressed as the cause, as in the expression "he dwells [there] for the sake of study" (adhyayanena vasati). || 18 ||
In heaven, for the divine youths whose minds were agitated by desire, and here on earth, for the gurus, gods, and twice-born brahmins whose souls were overcome by shame; (19)
"How should I properly conduct myself at first as a woman of the night?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Having spoken thus, she remained silent for a moment in the posture of a sage.
In the state of a sage, there is the concentration of the mind. || 20 ||
Relying on fortitude, Kumbha spoke here once more, O scion of Raghu: "Why do I grieve like one who is ignorant? What injury has been done to my self? (21)
"This body, composed of whatever has come together, will experience [its end] as something other than myself.
Śikhidhvaja said:
"O son of a god, what is the purpose of such lamentation? (22)
The meaning is this: "Womanhood, which has come about as a result of past actions (*prārabdha*), will be experienced by this very body alone, which is distinct from me;
therefore, what loss can there be for me, whose self is pure consciousness free from attachment? The king, approving of what was said, replied with the words beginning "By lamentation... (verse 22).
When it comes, let it come; the self of the body is not defiled. Whatever sorrows and joys are ordained shall come to pass.
All those [actions] belong to the body, and not at all to the embodied soul;
for even you, though unworthy of distress among such activities, are nevertheless distressed. (24)
Regarding the effects of the embodied self— the conscious soul characterized by the body— which must necessarily be accomplished as they are the fruits of past actions (*prārabdha*),

you ought not to grieve; yet if even you grieve, then who else could be a physician and a means for treating the grief caused by the lack of discrimination in others, such as yourself, who are adorned with the scriptures and skilled in realizing the true nature of the treatises?
The connection with the following verse is that "there would be no one who is a refuge. || 24 ||
"O you who are adorned by the scriptures, what other means could there be for others?
You have said something to the effect that, when one is weary, one should speak what is appropriate for weariness. (25)

"This is not your sorrow; rather, it is merely an expression appropriate for sorrow, intended to conform to worldly custom," he said. Regarding "sorrow": "Now, having attained equanimity, remain undistressed, just as you are. Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
With these and other such words, the two of them themselves offered mutual consolation.
Having stood there together, the two friends, tender as forest trees, were mutually distressed;
then even the sun, as if producing femininity in this pitcher, [shone upon it]. (27)
Then, after their mutual consolation. || 27 ||
The lamp of the world set like a lamp whose oil has been exhausted;
along with the weight of worldly affairs, the lotuses underwent contraction. || 28 ||
The roads, together with the travelers, and the hearts of the wives of those travelers,
were gathered together in one place by him, making all the birds like fish caught in a net.

The paths reached a state of contraction and lack of clarity due to the darkness; this means that the hearts of the wives of travelers and the travelers themselves were obscured by the darkness of grief at separation. The fishermen (*dāśas*) are those who dwell on islands in the ocean;
for they bind even birds with nets, catch even fish, and gather even jewels—likewise, [the world] is filled above and below with existing things.

The two worlds attained an equal state of similarity with one another through the gathering of birds and the abundance of the net of star-jewels; the suffix *ṣyañ* is used here in its own sense (*svārthe*), meaning they reached a state of equality. || 29 ||
The world, enriched by a net of star-jewels, attained a state of equality with the sky,
which, abounding in stars, seemed as if it were laughing at the lake of blooming night-lotuses.
The sky, rich with stars, went toward its destination like a laughing expanse of blooming night-lotuses—a multitude of *unnāda* cranes and swarms of wandering bees acting as its agents. || 30 ||
He went where the circles of *cakravāka* birds were crying out and swarms of bees were wandering;
then those two friends rose for the twilight prayer as the moon was emerging.
Having paid their respects and performed their recitations in that manner, they remained within the thicket;
then Kumbha gradually assumed a female form there.

Having bowed down again and again—*vandayitvā* being derived from *vand* with the causative suffix (*ṇic*) used in its own sense—he, manifesting (*abhyāharan*) this feminine form (*straiṇaṃ vapuḥ*), spoke to Śikhidhvaja who stood before him in faltering words:
"I seem to fall, I seem to throb, and I seem to melt away with my slender limbs. (32–33)
"Galadakṣaram" means with a faltering voice, that is to say, with a stammering or sobbing tone. || 33 ||
"O King, it is out of shame alone that I think I am turning into a woman;
behold, O King, these hairs of mine are growing long. (34)
The word "cities" (puraḥ) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. || 34 ||
Behold, these two breasts of mine, with their rows of shimmering nipples, appear upon my chest like the darkness at day’s end rising upward.

Because of the qualifying attribute of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*)—namely, "a garland of shimmering stars"—it is understood that the hair, which is the object of comparison (*upameya*), is likewise accompanied by garlands of pearls and other jewels. || 35 ||
Like two lotus buds on a lotus plant in springtime, facing upward toward the sky, my garments have become so long that they reach down to my ankles. (36)
Ambarāṇi means garments or clothes. || 36 ||
O friend, behold from the body itself, as if from a woman, the ornaments, jewels, and various garlands gradually [disappear]. (37)
The syntactical connection with what follows is that various kinds of garlands arise from the body itself. || 37 ||
Behold, my dear, how these [limbs] arise from one's own body like flowers on a tree;
behold, today this very person is as beautiful as the rays of the moon. (38)
From one's own limbs, such as the branches and so forth. || 38 ||
O giver of honor, a silken cloth has appeared upon my head like mist on a mountain; O bestower of pride, all the gestures of an embrace from my beloved have come to pass within me.
"Paṭṭāṃśukaḥ" means silk cloth. With the intention that one should understand that even in those regions thus covered, an exchange of gender has occurred, he says: "all," etc. (39).
"Alas! Woe is me! I am despondent; what shall I do? For I am a woman. Alas! Woe is me! O virtuous one, here I stand, truly a woman. (40)
The perfected one is established. || 40 ||
"O Kumbha, these buttocks and thighs within me are experienced by consciousness," having said this in the forest, he became silent and dejected.
Having spoken thus in the forest, Kumbha indeed became silent.
And the king, beholding him, was likewise dejected in spirit;
after only a moment, Śikhidhvaja spoke these words: || 42 ||
"Alas! This is that very same Great Being, and she has become a woman of excellent complexion.
O virtuous one, you have known all that is to be known; you understand the course of destiny. (43)
Do not let your heart be distressed by this inevitable matter; such various conditions inevitably befall even the wise, who possess nothing more than a physical body. (44)
They do not enter the minds of the wise who know reality, even when they fall upon the mere body.
"These [powers] do not enter the mind through the intellect, nor do they enter the body.
Kumbha said:
"So be it; I shall assume for myself the female form of a woman of the night."
But for those whose knowledge is accompanied by diligent practice, these ten stages affect the mind as well through its latent impressions (*vāsanā*), and not the body alone; this is the meaning.
I shall perform [them]; I shall follow [them]. || 45 ||
"I do not succumb to despair; by whom can destiny be transgressed?
Having thus resolved, the two of them brought that sorrow to a state of near-extinction.
They spent that entire night in silence upon a single bed;
then, at dawn, they cast off their female forms and their youth.

The king spent the night with long deliberation due to his anxiety over the calamity concerning Kumbha, while the queen passed it slowly out of longing for union with the king; both were deprived of sleep. [In the compound *yuvatyā idaṃ yauvanaṃ vapuḥ*,] because of the rule *taddhiteṣvacāmādeḥ* (Pāṇini 7.2.117), the *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine-like substitution) applies; however, since the suffix *aṇ* is not invariably present here, the *ṭilopa* (elision of the final vowel and following consonant) does not occur due to the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*). || 47 ||
She became Kumbha, possessing the luster of a jar and a form released from the pressure of breasts;
such was that queen Cūḍālā of excellent complexion. (48)
Resembling a water-pot from the previous day. || 48 ||
Having assumed the form of a jar, she later returned to her female state;
by night she sported in the forest regions like a maiden,
while by day she took the form of a jar and remained united with her husband, her friend.
A maiden who possesses the characteristics of a virgin is one whose conduct has not yet been defiled by marriage. || 49 ||
With her beloved, her friend, you, she wandered at will, adorned with garlands and necklaces, her yogic movement unimpeded across the peaks of Kailāsa, Mandara, Mahendra, Sumeru, and Sahya.
Regarding where, how, and in what manner she wandered, he says: "On the peaks of Kailāsa," etc.; that is, upon the plateaus of Kailāsa and the other mountains.

The connection [of the verse] is again made with the desire [to state]: "Cūḍālā, whose coming and going was unerring through the power of yoga and whose coming and going was characterized by the union of lovers, being adorned with garlands, necklaces, and bracelets, wandered at will together with her beloved—who was habituated to acting according to her own desires—just as she pleased. (50)

Thus ends the one hundred and fifth canto, titled "Kumbha’s Attainment of Womanhood," in the *Pūrva-cūlikā* of the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*, composed by Vālmīki according to the tradition of the Ṛṣis.
Thus ends the one hundred and fifth chapter, titled "The Attainment of Womanhood," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and sixth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Then, after only a few days had passed, she...
Assuming the form of Kumbha, the virtuous woman spoke thus to her husband.
Herein is described the marriage preceded by the sacred fire on Mount Mahendra and other sites;
as well as the union of the two in a golden cave upon a bed of flowers.
And she was Cūḍālā. || 1 ||
O King, whose eyes are like lotus petals, listen to these words of mine:
every night, I remain right here as a woman.
Therefore, I desire to perfect such a womanly duty:
I shall give myself to some husband through marriage. (3)
"To make proficient" means to make successful. "I give" means I shall give before long. || 3 ||
"Therefore, you alone are my chosen husband in the three worlds;
accept me through marriage as your wife for all time, even at night. (4)
O virtuous one, I wish to enjoy the pleasure of women together with my dear friend who has come to me unbidden; do not be an obstacle to me.
Do not create an obstacle by means of refusal. || 5 ||
What fault could possibly arise for one performing the task at hand—a pleasant and delightful undertaking that has been carried out progressively since the beginning of creation? (6)

The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: from the beginning of creation—that is, starting from the time of creation—up until the present day, among the gods, sages, and others, you have been performing this customary and current matter of marriage, which has proceeded in succession and is easily accomplished, having abandoned both desire and aversion toward it and its fruits; what fault, then, could possibly arise for you? "We" refers to the two of us, according to the rule *asmado dvayośca*.
The plural number. || 6 ||
Having abandoned desire and aversion toward all things on every side, we are neither desirous nor averse; therefore, we perform this desired act.
Śikhidhvaja said: "O friend, O one of great intelligence, by performing this deed I perceive neither good nor evil; therefore, do as you wish."
Therefore, for that reason. || 8 ||
With a mind that has attained equanimity, I perceive these three worlds as my very own nature; do as you wish.
I perceive my own true nature as being indeed identical with my very self.
Kumbha said:
"If it is so, O protector of the earth, then this very day is an auspicious moment for the wedding;
for yesterday, all of this was calculated by me during this full moon of the month of Śrāvaṇa."
Yesterday, as on the previous day, I calculated everything, including the auspicious time for the wedding.
O mighty-armed one, tonight when the moon has risen with its full and stainless digits, the wedding ceremony for both of us shall take place.
The marriage took place elsewhere; the meaning is that it occurred between the two alone according to the Gāndharva rite. || 11 ||
Today, on the delightful summit of the peak of Mount Mahendra,
in a jeweled cave-palace richly illuminated by jewel-lamps.
In a palace characterized by caves made of jewels.
It was resplendent with rows of lofty trees bent low under the weight of blossoms,
and enchanting with the dance of forest flowers and creepers like dancing women.
He shows the abundance of trees, creepers, and so forth by way of their serving as a gathering place for throngs of men and women suited for wedding festivities—thus: "A mass of flowers" (verse 13).
O you with eyes as long as the tips of your ears, let the stars in the sky at night, together with their lord, the full moon, gaze upon us both. 14.
The ellipsis implies: "May they behold the wedding festival. || 14 ||
"Arise for the sake of our own marriage; O King, let us prepare from the depths of the forest an abundance of sandalwood, flowers, and other materials, combined with precious gems. (15)
Having spoken thus, Kumbha rose up with that king and gathered flowers as well as a collection of jewels and other treasures.
Then, in just a moment, upon a level and auspicious jeweled peak, they both indeed made heaps of unguents and flowers.
"On a level, auspicious plateau abounding in jewels"—the word "in the courtyard" (ajire) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence].
"Anointing" (samālambhana) refers to the worship of the deities, the fire, the god of love, and so forth, as well as the flowers intended for that purpose. || 17 ||
Furthermore, heaps of necklaces, garments, supreme jewels, and other such things lay upon the ground;
they were like treasuries of good fortune accumulated by Time for the sake of Kāma.

From the statement "in the courtyard," it is understood that [the action] occurred previously as well in the courtyard. By time—that is, by the time of the ripening of the merit of the enjoyer—having thus prepared the wedding procession, those two great friends went to the river Mandākinī in the Golden Cave to bathe. (18–19)
There, Kumbha, preceded by auspicious rites, bathed the great king with great reverence—the king whose shoulders were like the frontal lobes of an elephant. (20)
Auspiciousness consists of curd, dūrvā grass, unbroken rice grains, white mustard seeds, and so forth, preceded by that [ritual].
He bathed Cūḍālā, his beloved wife who bore the form of a water-jar, assuming for himself the form of her future husband.
Having bathed there, they both worshipped the gods, the ancestors, and the sages;
just as they had no desire for the fruits of their actions, so too did they have no desire for the abandonment of those actions.

To the question of how there can be engagement in worship for those two who have no desire for the fruits of action, he says: "Just as," meaning just as there is [engagement] even when desiring neither [the fruit] nor abandoning the action. || 22 ||
While remaining established in the state of being never satiated by the essence of eternal knowledge and maintaining the stability of the world,
those two partook of a magnificent meal, each according to the other's desire.
The mutual enjoyment of food and other things provided by the power of their supernatural attainments (siddhis). || 23 ||
Having put on white silken garments from the wish-fulfilling tree and having eaten its fruits, the two of them proceeded in due order to the place where the bridegroom was stationed.

The fruits are the fruits of the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa). The place for the birth [of the deity] is at the base of the altar (vedi). "In sequence" means according to the order prescribed in the scriptures. || 24 ||
Then, after this much time had passed, while the two of them were longing for their wedding, the sun quickly entered the mountain of setting, as if to do them a kindness.
Then, when the twilight ritual had been performed and the recitation of the *aghamarṣaṇa* hymn was completed,
the sky became filled with a multitude of stars as if for the very purpose of witnessing the wedding.
In the sequence of the twilight rites, namely, in the procedure for the twilight worship (saṃdhyāvandana). || 26 ||
The night, the sole companion of the month of Mithuna, smiling with its clusters of white water-lilies,
arrived scattering a profusion of frosty nets.
Because it brings delight to couples, the three-watch night does not appear long to those who have but one friend.
On the mountain, Kumbha properly installed many jewel-lamps,
like the lotus-born Brahmā placing the luminaries joined by the sun and moon in the sky.
Brahmā is the one born from the lotus. || 28 ||
As night approached, she assumed the form of a woman and adorned the king with floods of sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, musk, and saffron.
With products derived from deer, such as musk and pauṣkalaka, and with saffron from Kashmir. || 29 ||
With necklaces, armlets, and bracelets, as well as garments from the wish-fulfilling vine, with garlands, elaborate wreaths, crest-jewels, and various other appropriate floral offerings; || 30 ||

With garments produced from the *kalpalatā* trees, with unrestrained garlands of exquisite beauty, with ear-ornaments such as clusters of jewels, and with necklaces and other floral wreaths suitable for various ornaments. || 30 ||
Likewise, with clusters of wish-fulfilling creepers, mandāra and pārijātaka trees, saṃtāna trees, and many jewels, and with a crown in the form of the moon; || 31 ||
By the word "mauli" (crown), the crest-jewel is indicated; by the term "indurūpiṇā," it means resembling the moon. || 31 ||
After this much time had passed, Kumbha attained the state of a young bride; burdened by the weight of his thick breasts, he quickly became full of amorous grace.
Possessing the playful charms appropriate for a bride.
He reflected thus: "I have attained the status of a bridegroom;
my very self must be offered for the sake of desire, for indeed, one's duty is that which is appropriate to the occasion. (33)
To Kāma, who can assume any form at will, the excellent one. || 33 ||
"Here I am, your lovely bride; you, my husband, stand before me.
O Kāma, take me! Come, for this is the time for your heart's desire. (34)
Therefore, having conceived her husband as an object of desire, she says in her mind: "This one... (34).
Having reflected thus, Rati approached her husband, who stood in the dense thicket before her like the rising sun, as she would approach Kama. || 35 ||
He was situated in a dense forest region located at the edge of the world. || 35 ||
"I am your wife, named Madanikā, O giver of honor;
this prostration at your feet is performed by me with affection. (36)
With affection and with passion. || 36 ||
Having spoken thus, she of faultless limbs, her face bowed down with shame,
prostrated before her radiant husband with her head and its dangling locks.
[She saw] her husband, shining and resplendent. || 37 ||
And she said this: "O Lord, adorn me with ornaments;
then, having gradually kindled the fire, perform my marriage ceremony. (38)
Having kindled [the fire], offered oblations, and performed worship. || 38 ||
O King, you shine exceedingly; you make me afflicted with love. Having surpassed Madana at the wedding of Rati, you stand triumphant. (39)
The meaning is that she surpassed Madana, who is well-known for his role in Rati’s wedding, by means of her own splendor. || 39 ||
O King, those garlands of yours are like the webs of rays from the moon,
and the necklace upon your chest bears the luster of the flowing current of the Gaṅgā on Mount Meru.

He describes that very splendor with the verse beginning "of the moon," and so forth: the necklace resting upon your chest bears the luster—the beauty—of the Ganges stream as it is renowned on Mount Meru. || 40 ||
O King, you shine with your locks of hair interspersed with mandāra flowers,
like a golden lotus whose filaments are inlaid with hovering bees.
With filaments inlaid and anthers joined together. || 41 ||
O Lord, with your jewel-like rays, flowers, beauty, stability, and splendor,
you stand surpassing Mount Meru, the abode of jewels.
The phrases beginning with "by the nets of jewel-rays" and so forth are to be applied by way of commonality to both the King and Meru. || 42 ||
Speaking in this manner, those two future husband and wife, who were formerly a married couple living in concealment, became mutually delighted. (43)
By the statement "those two speaking thus," it is understood that the king also described her beauty. || 43 ||
Seated upon a couch of gold, King Śikhidhvaja himself adorned the Great Queen Madanikā.
He was seated, having sat down upon a couch characterized by golden stones. || 44 ||
With ear-ornaments, as well as garlands, decorations of jewels and gems, garments, ointments, and flowers placed in beautiful positions. || 45 ||
[He was adorned] by those [ornaments] placed upon their respective locations suitable for each ornament. || 45 ||
Adorned, that slender woman shone— arousing passion and bestowing intoxication—
like Pārvatī longing for her wedding, or like a loving wife of Kāma.
She is like Rati, the beloved of Kāma. || 46 ||
The great king, having adorned the queen, said this to her:
"O fawn-eyed one, you shine like the newly risen goddess Lakṣmī. (47)
By the expression "newly arisen," the diminution of beauty due to the former splendor having become aged is suggested. || 47 ||
May that auspiciousness which belongs to Śacī with Śakra, which belongs to Lakṣmī with Hari, and which belongs to Gaurī with Śambhu, be yours. 48.
That is your auspiciousness; "together with me" is the ellipsis to be supplied. || 48 ||
With a heart like the bud of a lotus calyx, with eyes like trembling blue lotuses, and with the auspicious sound of *jhāṃ* arising from her fragrance, she remained seated there like a lotus pond.

The lotus-bud is like her breast, and the sprouts are like her passion within her heart; according to the opinion of Bhāguri, the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is applied after words ending in the consonant *h* (as in *āpaṃ*). She whose eyes are like restless blue lotuses, and who is auspicious with fragrances—the humming of bees—just as such a lotus-pond exists, so do you stand; this is the meaning. || 49 ||
With hands like deep-red sprouts and bearing the clusters of your breasts, I consider you to be the creeper of the wish-fulfilling tree of love, laden with manifold fruits. (50)
Now he describes her as being like a wish-fulfilling creeper (kalpalatā): "suraktā" and so forth. || 50 ||
With limbs as pure white as snow-cold frost and a smile that radiates like moonlight, you—like the splendor of the full moon—exert yourself to gladden us most fully, as if filled with joy. (51)
Expressions such as "cold as snow" and so forth are to be applied as common attributes shared by both the moon, which possesses the splendor of the full moon, and Madanikā. || 51 ||
"Therefore arise yourself, O lady of excellent hips, [and prepare] the wedding altar.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
"There, with networks of flowering creepers marked by stones at every step... (52)

The ellipsis implies "adorn it yourself. There, upon the altar (vedī), [it is adorned] with slabs of nine gems marked—i.e., characterized—by clusters of fruits corresponding to each section (kāṇḍa). || 52 ||
With heaps of pearl-garlands resembling clusters of flowers, and with four large coconut fruits placed in the four directions; || 53 ||
With full jars likewise prepared and filled with the waters of the Gaṅgā,
the two of them caused a fire to blaze up in its center using sandalwood logs.

The ellipsis to be supplied is that they both adorned the sacrificial altar with those prepared items. Having established the nuptial fire upon the center of that altar, they kindled it with sandalwood logs. || 54 ||
Having circumambulated the blazing fire with its flames kindled from the right,
he should sit facing east on a seat of leaves in front of the fire.

Having applied that fire—which was blazing with flames and situated on the right because its crest of smoke turned to the right—and having circumambulated it, the two sat down before that fire upon a seat of leafy sprouts; such is the connection with the subsequent verse. || 55 ||
Having directed the lovely couple [the meaning of the construction is:
he,
Śikhidhvaja, entered between those two children], he himself offered sesame seeds and parched grain (*lāja*) into the fire (the use of the neuter form *lājāni* is an archaic Vedic usage).
Śikhidhvaja. || 56 ||
Rising again and again, he took his beloved in his own arms;
they shone together like Śiva and Bhavānī in the forest.

Bhava and Bhavānī are "the two Bhavas. According to the rule *pumān striyā* (a masculine noun remains when joined with a feminine one), the masculine form alone is retained. They are Śivas, whose very nature is auspiciousness. || 57 ||
The couple performed a circumambulation of that fire,
offering their own hearts— the entirety of their knowledge, their love, and their fervor— as their sacrificial gift.
Regarding what gift they gave to one another when each surrendered himself to the other, he says: "their own inheritance" (svadāyam). || 58 ||
Having performed three circumambulations and offered parched grain into the fire, the two of them, whose faces were beautiful with the radiance of mutual smiles, gave [the bride] to one another.
The husband and wife, equally satisfied and with smiling faces, gradually released their hands,
as lovely as two newly risen moons.
With smiling faces, they remembered the presence of the time of their enjoyment together.
They both entered upon a new bed of flowers prepared beforehand;
in the meantime, the moon [descended] one-fourth from the surface of the sky.
Indicating that the first watch of the night has passed due to the activities of the wedding, he says "In this" (etasmin). "Caturbhāgam" means the fourth part. || 61 ||
He slowly advanced, as if to behold the beauty of these two,
and his gaze moved all around as if to find a flaw in that woman.
She moved her hands over that bed, just as the glance of a lover extends its own rays—the hands—everywhere about to look for a flaw in the woman. || 62 ||
Then, as the moon rose, the lover moved his hands through the bower of creepers with various new tales and conversations.
Those two lovely spouses sat together for a short while;
then, having risen, they entered a golden cave illuminated by blazing jewel-lamps.
The ellipsis "waiting for an auspicious moment for their union" is to be supplied. They entered a golden cave, a mountain cavern. || 64 ||
The two lovers entered the secret chamber they had prepared for themselves;
there they beheld a new couch fashioned of flowers.

Because even the moon was invisible, it was hidden; there they beheld the bed. He describes that very thing with three and a half verses beginning with "kalpitam. Regarding the form "dadarśatuḥ," the substitution of *guṇa* for the dual ending *-tustas* is a Vedic (archaic) usage. || 65 ||
It was completely covered on all sides by heaps of carved golden lotuses,
as well as by mandāra and other flowers that were entirely free from wilting.
Free from illness and unfading. || 66 ||
With flowers fashioned to a great height, perfectly uniform, resembling the long orb of the moon, and as cool as a bed of frost; (67)

The connection with the preceding verse is as follows: it was surrounded by flowers fashioned by Satya-saṅkalpa (the one whose resolve is truth) into the form of a long bed—flowers equal in size to a beautiful bed, raised very high, and resembling the orb of the moon elongated into the shape of a long couch. || 67 ||

Resembling a stream of milk from the ocean of Kṣīroda, beautiful as a mass of moonlight, it was like the reflection of the bodiless Cupid (or, according to another reading, of Ananta) resting upon a wall. (68) He further qualifies the bed itself with the words beginning "kṣīroda": *nata* means reflected. (68)
Fragrant, lofty, and lovely, that couple— having arisen after a long time as something distinct— sat down upon that pure heap of flowers on all sides,
like Mount Mandara in the midst of the milk-ocean of equal expanse.

That couple—the pair of woman and man—having long since, from the time of renouncing their kingdom, arisen through delusion as something other than husband and wife, sat down upon that heap of flowers as if upon a bed; the comparison to Mount Mandara is because the bed is crushed by the act of enjoyment. || 69 ||

Through those various playful exchanges of affectionate words, through those endearments suited to the occasion, and through their ever-new joys with their beloveds, that long night passed for the two of them as if it were but a single moment.

While those two were together with their beloveds, the time passed as if it were but a moment through various superhuman delights of affectionate speech, made charming by actions such as embraces appropriate for that occasion, and by the enjoyment of perfumes, garlands, and ointments.
Thus ends the one hundred and sixth chapter, titled "The Marriage of Līlā," in the Nirvāṇa Section of the *Mokṣopāya* within the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Valmīki. 106.
Thus ends the one hundred and sixth chapter, titled "The Marriage of Līlā," in the first half of the Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The one hundred and seventh canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Now, the interior of the world was colored by the pigment known as the sun.
In the morning, Śikhidhvaja’s wife Madanī took on the form of a water-jar.
The wandering among various mountains and monasteries, as well as the vision of Māyā and Indra,
and the summoning to heaven and so forth, are described for the purpose of examining non-attachment.
By means of dye—that is, by means of a coloring substance. || 1 ||
Thus, on Mount Mahendra, both Kumbha and Śikhidhvaja were married by their own selves; they entered [the marriage] and became a divine couple.
Because they were enriched with enjoyments similar to those of the gods, they were like a divine couple.
Every day they sported in the various forest groves,
which were laden with the weight of fully ripened fruits and abounding in flowers and tender shoots.
During the day, the two friends were more affectionate toward each other, and at night, the beloved couple remained united like a lamp and its light; they were never separated.
In the night; joined, that is, united. || 4 ||
They sported in forest groves and mountain caves,
in thickets of *tāla* trees and dense thickets of *mandāra* flowers.
And on the Sahya, Dardura, Kailāsa, Mahendra, and Malaya mountains; and on the slopes of the Gandhamādana, the Vindhya range, and the Lokāloka mountain.
The seven mountains beginning with Sahya [are as follows]. || 6 ||
When her beloved had fallen asleep after traveling for three days at a time,
Cūḍālā, having performed the duties of the king, returned once more.
"O beloved, having gone to your own city"—this is the ellipsis—while she had fallen asleep. || 7 ||
During the day, those two friends, the husband and wife who were kings of Kumbha,
stood together in mutual joy, adorned with various flowers.
For one month, they were honored by gods and kinnaras while staying in a cave-dwelling with jeweled walls on the delightful Mahendra mountain, which was thick with pine trees.
Regarding where, how many times, and for how long they stayed there, he says "for a month," and so forth; they were honored and praised. || 9 ||
Thus, on the ridge of Śuktimat, in a bower of wish-fulfilling creepers, [he dwelt] amidst garlands from the Mandāra forest that were within reach of his hand and were declared to be unfailing.

On the ridge of Śuktimat, a particular mountain, there was a forest garlanded with such *mandāra* trees— trees whose fruits, flowers, sprouts, and so forth had arisen and were ready to be grasped by hand, and which were unfailing in their power to remove hunger, thirst, disease, old age, and other afflictions. || 10 ||
For two months, on the southern slope of the mountain Pāriyātra,
in the Pārijāta forest within a pavilion of divine flower clusters, [he remained].
On Mount Maināka, which possesses wings, within a bower of flower-clusters fit for the enjoyment of the gods.
On the surface of Jambūkhaṇḍa, at the foot of Mount Meru, on the bank of the Jambū river,
he spent a month amidst vessels made of Jāmbūnada gold, with the juices and liquors of jambū fruits.

On the southern foot of Mount Meru, there is the well-known Jambu tree, the banner of Jambudvīpa; the two [daughters] stood upon the surface of a grove of Jambu trees growing from its lineage—this phrase is to be supplied everywhere [in the following]. By means of the liquors characterized by the juice of Jambu fruits, which are as large as elephants, they possess stable youth, being freed from perspiration, foul odors, old age, disease, and so forth.
It should be supplied as an ellipsis in accordance with what is well-known from the Purāṇas. || 12 ||
They spent ten days in the region of Uttarakuru,
and twenty-seven days in the northern Kosala countries.
They remained in the region of Uttarakuru for ten days. || 13 ||
Thus, in various other lands belonging to different rulers,
those two illustrious friends, husband and wife, stayed together during the night.
Then, after several months had gradually passed, Cūḍālā, who possessed the form of a son of the gods, reflected: || 15 ||
"I shall test Śikhidhvaja with a burden of beautiful objects, so that his mind may never again find delight in sensual enjoyments. (16)

"I shall examine; I will examine. The present tense (*laṭ*) is used here because of proximity to the present time. "Attachment" (*rati*) means devotion or clinging. The meaning is: "Having been made firm by this examination, he—being unattached—will never at any time experience attachment to enjoyments; indeed, he shall not experience it at all. (16)
Having reflected thus, Cūḍālā, by means of her illusory power, manifested in the forest region Hari, who had arrived accompanied by the gods and apsarases.
[He saw] Hari, Indra, dwelling together with the gods and the Apsarases. || 17 ||
Seeing Indra arrived with his retinue,
Śikhidhvaja, dwelling in the forest, honored him in the prescribed manner.
In accordance with the scriptures and as prescribed, [he should worship] with the ritual services beginning with water for the guest and water for the feet. || 18 ||
Śikhidhvaja said:
"O King of the Gods, you have caused me distress by coming from so far; it behoves you to tell me, out of your favor, how this came to pass. (19)
The meaning is: you ought to state the purpose—that for which, in whatever manner, and by what means this harassment characterized by your arrival and this exertion was performed. || 19 ||
Indra said: "We have come here from the sky because of the excellence of your virtues, which cling to our hearts like birds bound by a string while in the forest. (20)
From heaven (svarga). || 20 ||
Arise and come to heaven; there all the hosts of celestial nymphs stand, their faces turned toward you, filled with wonder at hearing of your virtues. (21)
Those gods and groups of celestial nymphs whose wonder and amazement were aroused by hearing of your virtues—[the compound *devāṅganāgaṇāḥ* means] the gods and the multitudes of their wives. || 21 ||
Furthermore, having taken these— sandals, pills, swords, elixirs, and so forth— by means of the path of accomplishment, take possession of the realm of heaven.

To the question, "How can there be my arrival in heaven for one who is devoid of the power to travel through the sky?", he says: "The sandals," and furthermore, "the other supernatural powers, celestial chariots, divine horses, and so forth. (22)
"Having arrived at the abode of the gods, you, being one liberated while living, must enjoy various pleasures; for that reason, I have come to you. (23)
Therefore, for the purpose of summoning you. || 23 ||
Virtuous men such as you do not despise the prosperity that has arrived with insults, nor do they long for prosperity that has not yet been attained. (24)
Observing that their refusal was held within their hearts, he said: "They treat with contempt... (24).
By your arrival today and by your dwelling in happiness without hindrance,
may heaven attain purity, just as the three worlds were purified by Hari.

Because of the well-known fact that Hari sports even in the netherworld (pātāla) for the purpose of guarding the gates of Bali and for the extraction of the six embryos, [the realm] is called "the three worlds" (jagattraya).
Śikhidhvaja said:
"O Lord of the Gods, I know the conduct that leads to all the heavens;
however, for me, heaven is not restricted to any single place."

"Equal to heaven" means that in which one dwells in happiness with conduct equal to that of heaven; or, it refers to that which possesses infinite happiness equal to heaven. [This applies to] every place. If it is asked, "What is the specific distinction in You that serves as the cause for such experience?", he says: "But rather... My intended heaven is indeed the earth itself, and its essence is present everywhere—this is the sense.
It is fixed and delimited. || 26 ||
For I am satisfied everywhere and I rejoice everywhere, O Lord;
because my mind is free from desire, I am full of bliss in all things.
He says "everywhere" to show that because his desires are fulfilled, he possesses happiness in all places. || 27 ||
"O Śakra, there is certainly a certain person here who is established in such merit for heaven; I do not know how to go there, nor do I carry out your command. (28)

I do not know how to go to, nor do I consider it possible to reach, that hollow heaven which is merely called "heaven. Thus, the implication is that while issuing a command regarding such an impossible matter is improper for you alone, my failure to carry it out is no offense. || 28 ||
Śakra said:
O virtuous one, for those who have known what is to be known and whose intellects are perfected,
I consider the enjoyment of pleasures to be consistent with the conduct practiced by the righteous.

For those of perfected intellect, the enjoyment of worldly pleasures and the non-enjoyment of them are equal. Even so, the enjoyment of pleasures is practiced by the virtuous for the sake of exhausting their *prārabdha* (karmic residue); therefore, I consider that [enjoyment] to be appropriate—this is the meaning. || 29 ||

When the Lord of Gods had spoken thus and the king remained silent, Hari said, "Why do you not depart from here? You shall depart. [The reading *nāpayāsyeṣa* found in the printed edition is to be considered doubtful.]

Even though the Lord of the Gods had spoken thus once more, when the king remained silent—having no desire to go to heaven—Hari (Indra), expressing his dejection, thought: "If you, being such a person, remain thus indifferent, then why do I not depart from here? For one whose purpose for coming has not been accomplished, departure alone is proper."
He spoke. || 30 ||
"I shall not speak [of this] at this very moment," said Śikhidhvaja;
"May it be well with you, O Kumbha," saying this, he vanished from sight.

While Śikhidhvaja was speaking with an unfinished sentence— intending to say, "I shall not go to heaven this very day; rather, once established again in my kingdom, I will return in due time as before for the purpose of destroying your enemies and so forth"—
Kumbha addressed him, saying, "O Kumbha, may that auspiciousness which the king desires, namely the restoration of his kingdom, be yours."
Saying this, Hari vanished from sight through his power of disappearance.
Then that entire host of gods, together with the Lord of the Thirty-three,
instantly became invisible there,
like a second ocean whose mass of waves has subsided when the wind is stilled, yet still shimmering with its schools of sea-monsters, foam, and great serpents.
When Indra had vanished, that second host of gods, accompanied by the lord of the thirty-three,
also became invisible in an instant; just as when the wind has subsided in the ocean, the turbulent masses of crocodiles, foam,
and great serpents that were surging within it likewise become unseen along with the mass of waves.
The meaning is "in that same way. || 32 ||
Thus ends the one hundred and seventh canto, titled "The Journey to Śakra," in the first part of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the glorious Vāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa composed by Vālmīki. 107.
Thus ends the one hundred and seventh chapter, titled "The Departure of Śakra," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and eighth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having brought that illusion to rest, Cūḍālā reflected thus:
By good fortune, this lord of the earth is not being led away by his desire for enjoyments. || 1 ||
In this context, for the purpose of examining his anger, the queen displays an association with a libertine through deceit,
while her own true form is revealed to the king in due course.
Having brought—that is, having withdrawn—that illusion in the form of Indra's arrival to a state of cessation, [the enemy] is carried away, that is, brought under control. || 1 ||
Tranquil—[the reading is *jñātaḥ*], with an even and equal enjoyment, he thus conducted his worldly affairs in the assembly of Śakra, free from agitation and without pride. (2)
Because he is eternally devoid of transformation, his physical presence—his facial features and bodily limbs—is equal to space and other such things.

He performed worldly acts of worship, such as offering water for the feet (*arghya*) and water for washing the feet (*pādya*), as well as appropriate words of greeting, all without agitation, fear, or negligence. || 2 ||
I shall once again reflect with respect upon this matter in detail, through the influence of a certain captivating [being] characterized by passion and hatred. (3)
The particle *eva* is used in the sense of "even" (*api*). By some manifestation (*prapañca*) dominated by passion and hatred, which captivates the intellect and agitates the mind. (3)
Having reflected thus, that virtuous Madanikā, assuming the form of a woman, went at night into the forest when the moon had risen. (4)
The connection of the words is as follows: "having assumed the form of a woman" [is linked] with the first two feet, and "imagined as her beloved" with the fourth.
While the wind blew, rich with blossoms and thick with sweet fragrance,
Śikhidhvaja remained on the riverbank, intent upon his evening prayers.

The connection with the following verse is as follows: when the Malaya breeze was blowing, he entered the inner apartments of the forest goddesses—a dwelling of *saṃtāna* creepers characterized by dense clusters of flowers—in that place abounding in blossoms and rich with flowering trees and creepers. || 5 ||
Intoxicated with passion, she entered the inner chamber of the forest goddesses— a bower of *saṃtānaka* creepers filled with dense clusters of flowers.
There, upon a flower-bed prepared in her imagination, she stood adorned with a garland of flowers,
holding to her neck the lover she had imagined— a wandering libertine.

There, having been garlanded and adorned with flower-garlands, she— by means of her illusory power (*māyā*)— created for herself a suitable young man in female form; one whose feminine characteristics such as the growth of a beard had not yet emerged, who appeared sixteen years of age, and who was therefore more beloved to Śikhidhvaja than even a bearded man.
The grammatical construction is: she stands having taken hold of the most charming *khiṅga* (paramour) or *viṭa* (lecher) by the neck. || 7 ||
Having arrived and searched through the groves, Śikhidhvaja beheld Madanikā in a bower of creepers with a charming libertine around her neck.

At the conclusion of his prayers, Śikhidhvaja emerged from the bower where he had been performing the twilight recitations; searching for Madanikā, he found her in the Kalpalatā bower, and beheld both Madanikā and Manorama around her neck.
His shoulders were draped with locks of hair, his body was anointed with sandalwood paste,
and his crest-jewel was disarrayed by being cast down upon the bed-curtains.
He describes the hero (nāyaka) with the words beginning "kun-tala" and so forth:

his shoulders are entwined by the locks of Madanikā as well as by his own locks; he is "samālabdha," meaning smeared or anointed; and his crest-ornament and topknot are disarrayed by being turned over, tossed about, or pressed down upon the bed.
(Note: there is a variant reading "niṣpeṣeṇa" for "āvṛtyā"). His hair-binding is in a state of disorder due to such tossing and casting down.
To him. || 9 ||
Upon a pillow formed by the arms of a girl with a golden luster and double-folded form,
his locks of hair were clinging to the surfaces of his ears, the corners of his eyes, and his cheeks.
Whose four ears and so forth were attached to a pillow and a cushion, characterized by the arms of children doubled over in a state of contraction. || 10 ||
He saw that couple, their faces smiling at one another,
their mouths joined together, and concealed by the garments of the kalpa-creeper.
A couple is a pair consisting of a woman and a man. || 11 ||
With their garlands and beds disheveled and agitated by the pangs of love,
they transferred their passion to one another under the guise of their limbs being entwined.
Under the pretext of the contact and union of their limbs, he offered [himself] and joined [with him]. || 12 ||
With faces turned upward in mutual joy, languid with unrestrained passion,
they struck each other with flowers while their breasts were pressed together against their chests.
Facing each other. || 13 ||
Beholding that with an unchanging mind,
Śikhidhvaja was fully satisfied and said, "Oh, how happily these two libertines are situated!"
Without change, meaning free from the transformation of anger. || 14 ||
"Stay, dear friend, as you wish and at your ease, just as you are;
do not cause us fear with obstacles," he said, and having spoken thus, he departed. (15)
"O dear one, since those two are afraid of seeing me, stay, stay as you wish! Having said, "I shall not create an obstacle," he went out. || 15 ||
Then, after only a moment, disregarding that elaborate display, she emerged,
revealing her own body which was blooming and agitated with passion.
"Having disregarded—that is to say, having withdrawn—that illusory proliferation; blossomed and agitated by passion (*rati*), that is, by the enjoyment of a paramour. || 16 ||
He saw the king seated upon a golden stone slab in a secluded spot,
established in meditative absorption, with his eyes slightly opened.
Having approached that place, her face bowed down with shame,
the woman Madanikā remained silent for a moment, distressed and withered.
In an instant, Śikhidhvaja ceased his meditation and,
with an undisturbed mind, spoke these exceedingly sweet words to her.
O slender one, why have you arrived so quickly with your joy obstructed?
Whatever beings there may be, they all strive only for the sake of bliss. (20)
"Whatever [there may be]" means all of them. || 20 ||
Go once more and satisfy that beloved with acts of affection;
for mutual love desired by both is indeed rare throughout the three worlds. (21)
"Mutually desired" means, that is to say, natural. || 21 ||
For this reason, O proud lady, I do not feel agitation;
for one who understands it thus, whatever is most dear in the world is exactly that.
The remainder of the sense is that a discerning person should understand that whatever is most dear to oneself is likewise to be enjoyed by others, such as you. || 22 ||
"O slender-limbed one, both Kumbha and I are free from passion, as is the other [your husband]. You, however, are a young woman born of Durvāsas’s curse; do whatever you wish. (23)

With the intention that "I have no lack of trust in my jar because of any fault of yours," he says: "I... The ellipsis is to be supplied as "...you are like anyone other than the jar. Therefore, do whatever you wish without hesitation. || 23 ||
Madanikā said:
"O illustrious one, such indeed is the fickle nature of women;
for the passion of women is eightfold, so you ought not to be angry. (24)
"O weak woman, while you were intent upon your evening prayers in this dense forest at night, I was here; what could I do, poor as I am? (25)
The ellipsis is "by him this was requested. || 25 ||
Neither a woman nor a maiden, out of intense longing, fails to place her lover—who is the very obstruction to pleasure—upon her own body. (26)

A woman who has been married is deprived of her independence due to her dependence on her husband; or a young maiden who is unmarried, having obtained a lover in secret, does not at all create an obstruction or hindrance to sexual pleasure. This is the nature of women. But by one whose lover has been abandoned due to weariness, or by whom an obstacle to pleasure has arisen through fate, [the desire is directed] toward one's own body.

The suffix *kta* is used here in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāve*). It means that [the mind] does not achieve stability; rather, having become exceedingly fickle in its mind and vital breaths (*prāṇa*), it suffers. || 26 ||
Women attain beauty only when they are not in the company of men; what will indignation, refusal, lamentation, or even chastity accomplish? (27)

For women, the sole reason for not uniting with men is the failure to attain a beauty capable of subjugating them; there is no other cause. If women were to possess such captivating beauty and appear before men in private, then there would be no reason at all for them not to unite.

One might object: "Are not the anger of a husband married in the presence of the sacred fire, the scriptural prohibition against union with another man, the outcry of public scandal, and the destruction of one's own wifely fidelity—when considered through the eye of discernment—not indeed reasons for union with a lover? To this, he replies: "Anger," etc. These [reasons] are overridden by the force of intense passion.
The sense is that she is capable of restraining the company of paramours. || 27 ||
"I am a weak woman, as well as young and foolish; I have committed an offense.
O Lord, you ought to forgive me, for the virtuous are indeed forgiving. (28)
Precisely for this reason, with the intention of asking for forgiveness, he says: "O powerless one" (abalā). || 28 ||
Śikhidhvaja said:
"No anger dwells within me toward this girl, any more than a tree exists in the sky;
yet, solely because she is censured by the virtuous, I do not desire you as my bride. (29)
Like a tree in its own open space, I do not desire a wife or a daughter-in-law. || 29 ||
O lady, as friends in these forest regions, let us always enjoy ourselves with equal pleasure, just as before, through our state of detachment.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: While Śikhidhvaja remained there in such equanimity,
Cūḍālā reflected upon him, her heart stirred by his virtuous nature.
By his being—by a mind examined through its emptiness of the latencies of passion and hatred—he was uplifted in intention and filled with joy. || 31 ||
"Oh, how wonderful! This Blessed One has attained supreme equanimity;
free from passion and devoid of anger, he abides as one liberated while living. (32)
The word division is "akrodha" (absence of anger). || 32 ||
Neither enjoyments nor even great supernatural powers (siddhis) carry him away;
neither pleasures nor pains, neither calamities nor prosperities do so either. (33)
Those enjoyments and supernatural powers sought by Indra were attained. || 33 ||
All these blameless women of great supernatural power, when thought of, come to this one man alone; I consider him to be like another Nārāyaṇa.

All those blameless and great powers (maharddhi) that I have contemplated—desirable to me and constituting the characteristics of one liberated while living (jīvanmukta), such as peace, forgiveness, fortitude, contentment, and so forth—all these converge upon and reach this one person alone; that is to say, they take refuge in him. || 34 ||
I shall cause him to remember this entire account of my own history;
having cast off this form as Kumbha, I shall become Cūḍālā once again. (35)
Because he is distinguished by such qualities, I shall remind him of this matter, as he is a fit person to be made aware of his own past history. || 35 ||
Having reflected thus, Cūḍālā,
her body uninjured, immediately cast off the form of Madanikā and revealed herself there in her own form as Cūḍālā.
Therefore, as if she had emerged from the body of Madanikā,
she appeared before him, joined with her, like a gem taken out from its casket.
Endowed with the concentration of yoga, she appeared as if emerging from a casket or a joined box.
He beheld her of faultless limbs, once again tender with affection,
his beloved Cūḍālā standing there like Madanikā herself.
In love—that is, in pleasing the heart of her husband—she was charming and clever; she was his beloved, his former beloved. || 38 ||

The king beheld his own beloved, appearing like a cluster of spring lotuses in full bloom, like the goddess Śrī descended from the surface of the earth, or as if manifested from an open casket of jewels. (39)

Like a *padminī*— a lotus plant— in full bloom during the spring (*mādhava*), or rather, like the *padminī* of Mādhava (Viṣṇu)— namely Śrī, who holds a lotus in her hand— manifested in her splendor or appearance;
she who, at the conclusion of Rāma’s incarnation, upon Rāma’s return to his nature as Viṣṇu, had previously entered the surface of the earth in the form of Sītā, and from there...
