The king beheld his own beloved Cūḍālā, who had risen again from the surface of the earth like the Goddess Śrī, or like the splendor of jewels manifested from a casket of gems; that is to say, he saw her before him. || 39 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and eighth chapter, titled "The Revelation of Cūḍālā’s True Nature," in the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa* of the *Mokṣopāya* within the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki. 108.
Thus ends the one hundred and eighth chapter, titled "The Revelation of Cūḍālā’s True Nature," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and ninth canto. 109.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Then, seeing his beloved, Śikhidhvaja, his eyes wide with wonder, spoke these words in a voice agitated by amazement.
Having seen this again and again, and having understood everything through meditation, the king was greatly amazed;
being pleased and praising Cūḍālā, he embraced her and spent the night there.
This is what is about to be stated. || 1 ||
Who are you, O lotus-petal-eyed one? From where have you come, O beautiful lady?
Why are you here, for how long, and for what purpose do you stay? (2)
"Are you indeed here in the form of a jar and so forth? For how long, or for what purpose, do you remain here in my presence?

Although the jar itself certainly knows the duration of its stay, the question "for how long" is asked because it is possible that it had been present even before arriving as a jar, due to its having been in another form. (2)
By your gestures, your conduct, your smile, and your conciliatory manner—
by these playful charms of a wife, you are perceived as such at that time.

By your limbs— that is, by the configuration of your members, by the conduct characterized by your gestures, by your affection— that is, by the manner of your continuous flow of loving words— and by the well-known grace of my wife Cūḍālā, you are perceived and seen as if you were her very form personified. || 3 ||
Cūḍālā said: "Know it to be even so, O Lord; I am Cūḍālā, there is no doubt.
Today I have been obtained by you in person with my natural body. (4)
By that which is uncontrived and innate. || 4 ||
It was solely to awaken you that this elaborate display of mine, consisting of the creation of bodies such as Kumbha and others,
has reached a hundredfold expansion here within the forest.
Ever since you abandoned the kingdom out of delusion and came to the forest for asceticism,
I have been striving for your awakening.
From that time forward; from that very moment.
By means of this pot-body, you have been awakened by me alone;
the creation of the bodies of Kumbha and the others was solely for the purpose of awakening you.
O Lord of the Earth, nothing such as a jar or other objects created by illusion is real;
therefore, you who have known what is to be known, perceive this unbroken [reality] through meditation.
Truth is non-conceptual; one should meditate upon it by means of the previously mentioned yogic concentration (dhāraṇā). || 8 ||
"O knower of reality, you see everything; behold [it] swiftly through meditation.
Then, being thus addressed by Cūḍālā, the king girded his loins.
"You see" means "you will see. "Apparatus" (parikara) refers to such things as a seat conducive to that kind of concentration (dhāraṇā). || 9 ||
Through meditation, he specifically beheld his own story with clarity, from the renunciation of the kingdom up until the sight of Cūḍālā. (Note: An alternative reading is *āssva rājye*.)
Above || 10 ||
In a single moment of meditation, he beheld his entire life story,
from the time of his renunciation of the kingdom down to the present moment.
In the phrase "the sequence of revolving moments," the prefix *ā-* is also drawn over here [from the previous rule]. || 11 ||
Having perceived everything, the protector of the earth ceased from his meditative absorption;
having emerged from samādhi, his lotus-like eyes blossomed with joy.
Quickly extending their arms, which had become radiant with horripilation,
they shed tears from limbs melting with intense affection, while their longing throbbed.

The arms, having attained a state of blazing with horripilation, are spread out and extended; "he embraced" is the connection with the subsequent [verse]. "With limbs dropping" means with severed parts. These four are adverbs (kriyāviśeṣaṇa). || 13 ||
Nakula embraced his beloved for a long time, as a male mongoose embraces a female;
and in that embrace of theirs, a certain state of being arose.

By the word *bhāva* (state), the stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) characterized by mutual passion, which has been manifested here, is intended. The grammatical connection is as follows: that Śṛṅgāra-rasa (erotic sentiment), which is beyond the reach of words, of such a nature, and consisting of supreme bliss, could not be described even by the tongues of Vāsuki. || 14 ||
He cannot be described even by the tongues of Vāsuki with such joy,
just as the bodies of those standing in heaven cannot be smeared with mud.
The moon and sun, stationed in the sky, appeared as if their bodies had merged through illusion, like two lumps of wet clay mixed with mud. || 15 ||
Like two mountains carved out of a single rock, the two lovers remained embraced for a long time;
in a moment, their bodies became heavy with perspiration and thick with horripilation.
May those two mountains remain for a long time joined and united, as if their forms were carved from a single rock in a mutual embrace. || 16 ||
Their two dear arms, whose hearts were filled with nectar yet resembled empty voids, slowly and slightly grew limp. || 17 ||
Due to the excess of bliss and the resulting numbness of the mind, no signs manifesting its actual existence are perceived; thus, they are like one whose heart has become utterly empty. || 17 ||
Having remained silent for a moment of intense bliss, his arms outstretched and his eyes fixed upon Lakṣmaṇa, he spoke with words tender with affection.
For the sake of steadying his gaze upon the object of focus, let him remain with his eyes fixed on that which is unobservable, due to the very state of mental numbness;
thus he spoke to his beloved in a manner tender with affection—this is the connection with the subsequent verse. || 18 ||
Placing his hand upon her chin, the king—lovely to the women of his own lineage and exceedingly sweet and affectionate—spoke to his beloved. (19)
And this merit, the outflow of your delight, is sweeter even than nectar; O slender-limbed one, how great must its measure be, since you are as charming as the young moon? (20)

The flow of passion (*ratiniṣpanda*), which is the essence of affection, is characterized by the four attributes beginning with "extreme sweetness" (*atyantamādhurya*); "how much" means how extensive it is. || 20 ||
For the sake of my husband, I have long endured terrible suffering;
thus, I have emerged from that cave of saṃsāra which is so difficult to cross.
For the sake of her husband, that is, for the purpose of accomplishing the goals of human endeavor, and for that reason. || 21 ||
By what can that intellect by which she was rescued be compared?
She is Arundhatī, Śacī, Gaurī, Gāyatrī, Śrī, and Sarasvatī. (22)
That intellect by which there is the thought of affection for one's husband—[that is the intellect]. 22.

O beautiful slender lady, by the splendor of your virtues, all things—intellect, fortune, loveliness, forbearance, friendliness, compassion, and the rest—become as insignificant as blades of grass. (23)

The connection with the following verse is as follows: "Dhīḥ, Śrīḥ," and so forth—the daughters of Dakṣa, who are renowned among beautiful women for their form and beauty—even among them, you are perceived to be the foremost and most excellent in virtue (satī). || 23 ||
Among beloved women beautiful in form, you appear as the very first;
by means of your supreme resolve, I have been awakened by you.
By what reciprocal service will your mind be satisfied, even though it has fallen from the beginningless thicket of delusion, which is infinitely deep? (25)

With what kind of return favor would your mind, having already achieved its purpose, be fully satisfied? The sense is that such a return favor by which it might be satisfied is difficult to find. || 25 ||
Noble women rescue one who has fallen through their resolve;
however, the meaning of the scriptures, the guru, and mantras are likewise incapable of such rescue. 26.
The statement beginning with "the meaning of the treatise" and so forth is a hyperbole intended for praise. || 26 ||

Just as these noble women of good family are full of affection for their husbands, so too are the friend, brother, well-wisher, servant, teacher, companion, wealth, and happiness [dependent upon them]. (27)
The scripture, the home, the servant, and everything belongs to the master;
noble women must always be honored with every effort. 28.
In these [states], all the bliss of the two-fold play is perfectly established, for she who is free from desire has reached the further shore of the ocean of saṃsāra. (29)
He says "niricchāyāḥ" (to you who are desireless) because he is unable to repay the favor of her who has accomplished all that was to be done.
How shall I repay this service of yours?
I believe that, because of you now, all noble women in the world have been surpassed.
"I consider you to be a woman of noble family"—this is the ellipsis. "All women of noble family renowned in the world have now been surpassed by you"—this is the ellipsis. || 30 ||
You shall become the subject of discourse regarding female excellence, surpassing the entire web of virtues of the Creator who fashioned you. (31)
In discussions regarding the excellence of qualities such as goodness in women, you shall be designated as the foremost. || 31 ||
I believe that Arundhatī and the other women must surely be provoked to anger, for you, O Satī, are a casket containing the jewels of beauty, goodness, and virtue.
The grammatical connection is as follows: they are enraged at the Creator for having fashioned you, who surpasses all others by means of a multitude of virtues, even in comparison to himself.
You alone are a *satī*, a devoted wife. || 32 ||
"Come, grant once more an embrace to me, who am exalted by your virtues.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Having spoken thus to that Cūḍālā, whose eyes were like those of a young deer, Śikhidhvaja—
Nakula embraced her again firmly, as a male mongoose embraces a female mongoose.
Cūḍāla said: "O Lord, while you were intent upon a web of dry rituals, your own self was agitated. (34)
Again and again, I have become deeply distressed on your account;
by that very means, my own purpose—whose essence is your awakening—has been accomplished.
"O Goddess, what honor do you show me in this matter?
Śikhidhvaja said:
"O lady of beautiful hips, it is just as you have accomplished your own auspicious purpose. (36)
"Now, let all these noble women accomplish that accordingly.
Cūḍālā said:
"O Beloved, O Lord, you have awakened and rested upon the shore of the net of the world. (37)

Or it may be an interrogative intonation (*kāku*) expressing a blessing: "May they accomplish [it]. The meaning is: "Are they unable to accomplish it? The syntactical connection with the distant word is as follows: "Having come to rest at the limit—the ultimate boundary—of the net characterized by the world, do you perhaps realize that in its true nature (*tattvataḥ*)? || 37 ||
Today you perceive that former delusion which persists in the form of the thought:
"I am doing this," "I am not doing that," "I have attained this. (38)
Do you perhaps regard that former delusion regarding the milk-vow, fasting, and so forth, as even slightly insignificant? (38)
Do you perhaps laugh inwardly at that state of your intellect which is as fragile as a blade of grass—those perceptions of trivial thirst and those wicked fabrications of mental constructs? (39)
The intellects, having their faults unripened, possess lightness and delicacy. || 39 ||
O Lord, today you are not seen, like mountains in the sky;
what has become of you now, my dear? Upon what are you established, and what do you seek? (40)
"O Lord, how do you perceive the subsequent sequence of bodily movements?
Śikhidvaja said:
"O you whose eyes possess the essence of garlands of blue lotuses filled with beautiful flowers! 41.

"How? Of what kind? Is it real or is it trivial?"—this is the meaning. O you with the crest-lock (cūḍāla), whose eyes are like a garland of blue lotuses filled with flowers, following along—that is, resembling—such [a garland]. 41.
Whosoever you may be within, to each of them I have presented myself;
I am effortless, I am partless, I am as pure as the sky, and I am free from desire.

You alone are that which has become my innermost self (*pratyagātman*); you abide as the internal illuminator of whatever there may be—whether it be delusion, discrimination, or the vision of reality—and within each of those, I too am established as the innermost self, situated in supreme proximity (*upa*). Thus, you see me now just as I am.
The meaning is that, just as he says "I see thus," my own state should also be understood through my own direct experience.
He demonstrates this very point by elaborating on it with the words beginning "free from effort" (nirīha). || 42 ||
I am peaceful, I am the nature of the ultimate reality (Artha), and I have long remained as the "I";
I have attained that state because my mind has entered the single path of the Self.

The meaning is as follows: having abandoned for a long time—the phrase "for a long time" (*cirāya*) meaning after a great duration—the delusion of "I" (*ahaṃbhrama*) regarding the body and so forth, which are not the "I," and having become that very "I" who am in reality the "I" whose nature is the ultimate truth (*paramārthasat*), I remain.

I am established on the single path of the mind directed toward the inner self (*pratyak*), and I have attained that state of unsurpassed bliss (*niratiśayānanda*) which— [Note: The provided text fragment ends mid-sentence; the translation reflects the available portion.]

Even Hari, Hara, and others, despite their great power, though they may attempt to prevent it through thousands of efforts, do not prevent it; they are unable to eliminate it. For the Śruti declares: "Neither the gods nor any other power can prevail against his non-existence (destruction), for he becomes the very Self of them. The sense is that it is impossible to discard the Self, which is by nature incapable of being discarded. || 43 ||
I am established in my own natural state, resting in pure consciousness alone, not even a fraction of which is denied by Śiva, Viṣṇu, and the other gods. || 44 ||
O lady with eyes like blue lotuses, I am now liberated from delusion and from saṃsāra;
I am neither pleased nor distressed, neither this [self] nor anything else.
This visible group of effects; the other is the cause. 45.
"I am neither gross nor subtle, O beautiful one; I am the Truth. I have come forth from the orb of light and have not yet fallen upon the wall. (46)

"Truth" (satya) refers to an uncontradicted reality. By means of light—that is, illumination—which has issued forth from a luminous orb such as the solar disc, has fallen upon a wall, and spreads through the mere expanse of space. || 46 ||
I am indeed equal through a radiance free from decay and excess;
I am tranquil, I lead to equanimity, I am established in my own self, and I am devoid of latent desires.
Having cast aside all the inequalities of the world, I shall lead it to equanimity; I am free from latent desires and devoid of a [discursive] mind. || 47 ||
O you who are devoted to your husband, I am indeed in a state of final nirvāṇa; I am like that which I am.
I am able to say only this, and nothing else. 48.

"O *pativrate*! In the reading *satīvrate*, the meaning is the same as *pativrate*, derived from the analysis: 'she whose vow is like the vow of virtuous women (*satī*)'. Alternatively, the meaning is: 'I am a husband whose character is similar to—that is, equal to—your own vow, which consists in abiding in your true nature (*svarūpa-niṣṭhā-lakṣaṇa*). || 48 ||
O you whose outer corners of the eyes are tremulous like waves, you are my guru; salutations be to you!
By the grace of the large-eyed one, I have crossed over the ocean of worldly existence.
I shall not take up impurity again, like gold that has been smelted a hundred times;
I am peaceful, self-abiding, gentle, restrained, free from passion, and possessed of indivisible wisdom. (50)

Just like gold that has been purified by being smelted in fire a hundred times; he who is thus intent, being exceedingly diligent in abiding in his true nature, whose intellect is partless and free from latent impressions (nirvāsana). || 50 ||
"Transcending all and omnipresent, I abide like the sky.
Cūḍālā said: "O Great Being, O Lord of Life, O beloved of my heart, since this is so... (51)
"Now, O Lord, tell me what pleases you, O high-minded one.
Śikhidhvaja said: "I do not know how to refuse, nor do I know what is desired. (52)
"This does not please me" means it is prohibited; thus, "prohibition" (pratiṣedha) is derived from the root with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of the object (*karman*). I do not know that. || 52 ||
"O slender one, whatever you do, I know that to be exactly so;
O beloved, may everything that is your wish be fulfilled without exception. (53)
Sometimes at the time of emergence; "mata" means desired. || 53 ||
I do not know how to pursue anything, O beautiful as the sky;
whatever you yourself know, O lovely one, do that very thing.
Like the sky, it is beautiful with its stainless equanimity and fullness; you know [it] as that which ought to be done—this is the ellipsis. || 54 ||
I shall maintain that very reflection, like a gem, with a mind free from desire, according to what has been attained and is beyond reproach. 55.

"I shall hold [it] in my heart" means "I shall fully comprehend it. Because the desired object—that which arises from its sphere—is dissolved by such [a mind], the mention of the "desired" (iṣṭa) is also an indication for the "undesired" (aniṣṭa). || 55 ||
"I neither praise nor blame; do as you wish.
Cūḍālā said:
"If it is so, O mighty-armed one, then listen to my thought. (56)
O soul liberated while living, having heard this, you ought to practice that very thing;
for you are endowed with the realization of universal unity, which arises from the destruction of ignorance.
To bring about; to perform. || 57 ||
We remain indeed free from desire, as clear as the sky; whatever constitutes our seeking, that very thing is our non-seeking.
Seeking (eṣaṇa) means the longing for the enjoyment of sovereignty and other such things. || 58 ||
Since no one at all practices here for the sake of attaining the vital breaths, who indeed is there that is merely consciousness?
Therefore, O Supreme Person, we are those who exist in the beginning, the end, and the middle.
He states the reason for that [non-attachment] with the word "yad" (since):

since, when the sense organs such as the eyes and the chief vital breath (*mukhya-prāṇa*) are seeking their respective appropriate objects, what excellence (*atiśaya*) is there in this Supreme Self? For, unlike the ignorant, the knower of reality does not have the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of identity with the internal organ, body, senses, and so forth, by which [the senses would be affected].

Through the repeated indulgence in sense-objects, there arises the possibility of defilement even for the Self. For the knower of reality—who is essentially actionless, unattached, and pure consciousness—what sense-object could he indulge in? The meaning is: none at all.
The substitution of the verbal suffix in the root *as* (to throw) is a Vedic anomaly. Therefore, [the Self remains untouched] except by the mere experience of *prārabdha* karma.

The meaning is this: because we are not attached to the impurity of addiction to those [worldly] practices, whether at the beginning of their enjoyment, at the end of their enjoyment, in the middle, or in the intervals between them, we—who possess whatever nature we have—possess that very same nature. Having exhausted the remainder of our *prārabdha* (karmic momentum) solely through experience and having come to rest, we have not become otherwise, nor shall we ever become anything else. || 59 ||
"Having set aside the one remaining [portion], we shall remain exactly as we are;
having spent this time with our current kingdom, we shall indeed proceed by stages. (60)
This remaining portion of time in the form of my life. || 60 ||
"O Lord, at some point in time we shall attain the state of being bodiless.
Śikhidhvaja said:
"Tell me, O fickle one, what will we be like in the beginning, the middle, and the end?"
Therefore, considering that there might also be another meaning for the phrase "in the beginning, middle, and end," and desiring to know it, the king asks: "We... (verse 61).
"Or how indeed shall we remain, having abandoned one of the remaining?
Cūḍāla said: 'O best of kings, we are kings in the beginning, the middle, and the end. (52)
In accordance with that very intention, Cūḍālā also describes the matter for his sake, beginning with "We... (verse 62).
"Abandoning delusion alone, we shall become yours once again;
remain as king in your own city, established upon your own throne. (63)
In that regard, he states another meaning for the word *śeṣa*: "delusion" (*moha*). || 63 ||
"Am I not indeed the ornament of lovely women? Shall I not become your queen, with the intoxicated citizens as your subjects and ever-new women dancing before you? (64)

I shall become the ornament—the very adornment—of the beloved women of the inner apartments. "In which [city] the inhabitants are esteemed and joyful" refers to the city-dwellers; these and other such epithets of the city serve to establish its similarity to the beauty of the creepers in the month of Madhu (spring). 64.

May that city—with its banners, sounding musical instruments, and strewn with heaps of flowers; with its shimmering creepers, its clusters of blossoms, and its garlands of humming bees—become equal for a long time to the splendor of the vine-like beauty of the month of Madhu. (65)
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Having been addressed thus by Cūḍālā, Śikhidhvaja laughed and spoke these sweet words, unperturbed and free from all distress.
"If it is so, O large-eyed one, then those splendors of perfected enjoyments are within our own power in the triple heaven; why then, my beloved, do I not dwell among them? (67)
"If you have a desire for enjoyments with me, then let only divine enjoyments, requested by Indra, be enjoyed; what is the use of human ones? Thus the king said: "If it be so," [verse 67].
Cūḍālā said: "O King, I have no desire for enjoyments nor for riches;
by the power of my own nature, I abide only in whatever comes to me. (68)
Neither heaven, nor sovereignty, nor even ritual action brings me happiness;
rather, I remain established as I am, undisturbed, with my conduct centered in well-being.
When the duality of "this is pleasure" and "this is not" has come to an end,
I abide here at ease in that very same state of perfect peace.
In the dual number, [the form is] *mithune*.
Śikhidhvaja said:
"O large-eyed one, you have spoken rightly with this wise mind.
For what purpose indeed could there be in either the seizing or the relinquishing of a kingdom?"
Having abandoned concern for states of pleasure and pain and being free from envy,
let us both remain exactly as we are, having attained composure.
According to its configuration, according to how it exists. || 72 ||
Thus, through their conversational discourse there,
the day drew to a close for those two lovers who had been husband and wife for so long.
Of an ancient couple, that is, of an ancient husband and wife. || 73 ||
Then, having risen, those two blameless ones, though full of longing, performed their daily duties as they occurred,
free from anxiety, being experts in what must be done.

The "daily conduct" refers to the evening twilight ritual (*sāyaṃsaṃdhyā*). It is considered a daily duty because it is said that the evening twilight should be performed while the sun is still visible.
Although they were full of longing for mutual union as they desired, they were without longing [for anything else] due to their state of being free from worldly desires (*nirvāsana*). || 74 ||
Disregarding the attainment of heaven, their minds remained full as they stayed upon a single bed with various acts of affection;
thus did that night pass for those two who were liberated while yet living.

As the two of them, longing for the supreme bliss of both worldly enjoyment and liberation, themselves expressed their desires through playful words of affection, that long night passed for them like a mere moment as it brought their yearning minds closer together. 76.

The meaning is that the night, though long, passed as if it were but a moment, bringing about— causing to reach— a state of longing and yearning in the minds of the two as they spoke, expressing their hopes so that the happiness of mutual enjoyment and liberation might be realized through the playful charm of their own words of love. || 76 ||
Thus ends the one hundred and ninth canto, titled "The Manifestation of Cūḍālā," in the first part of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the glorious Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa, a work of the Ṛṣis. 109.
Thus ends the one hundred and ninth chapter, titled "The Manifestation of Cūḍālā," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa-tātparyaprakāśa*.
The One Hundred and Tenth Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Then, when the sun had risen and the sky was free from darkness, it remained so.
As if from a casket, when that jewel of the world had emerged. || 1 ||
Having gone to their own city on the elephant of the army of mental constructs,
and having ruled the kingdom for a very long time, those two are described as being liberated.
When the sun had risen like a world-illuminating jewel emerging from its casket, and was established in a sky free from darkness;
The lotus-pond blossomed at the edge of dawn as if it were two eyes,
while the rays of the sun spread forth like the worldly customs of men.
When the lotus-pond of people blossomed at the edge of the dawn, as if it were their very eyes. || 2 ||
Having risen and performed the sequence of twilight rites, that couple remained seated upon soft and smooth leaf-mats in a lovely golden cave.
Then Cūḍālā rose up there and, standing before the jewel-pitcher,
her beloved, she mentally resolved that it be filled with the waters of the seven oceans.

She visualized a jewel-pitcher standing before her, filled with the waters of the seven oceans for the purpose of his royal consecration; with that auspicious pitcher, she, the wife, consecrated her husband in her own kingdom while he stood facing the east in a secluded place.
That king. || 5 ||
When he had arrived by her resolve upon a golden throne, consecrated and seated upon his own seat,
that slender Cūḍālā, possessing a divine form, spoke to him.
Upon a lion-throne, which was his own appropriate seat, having arrived by mere thought; || 6 ||
O Lord, having merely cast aside your silence, you ought to sustain this peaceful splendor which is the combined luster of the eight world-protectors.
This silence is suitable for a sage and is a peaceful splendor; casting that aside, you ought to assume the splendor appropriate for teaching, such as that of Indra and the other gods.
Thus addressed as "Cūḍāla" in the forest, King Śikhidhvaja, saying "I shall do so," attained the status of a great king. || 8 ||
Then he spoke to the proud woman who was standing in the position of a female doorkeeper:
"Today I shall consecrate you as queen in the position of the Goddess."
Because she lacks the ceremonial investiture (*paṭṭābhiṣeka*), she stands there out of discipline at the position of a *pratīhāra*, that is, the station of a doorkeeper;
[the other woman] has been placed in the position of a queen (*devī*), the station where the investiture has been performed. || 9 ||
Having spoken thus, and having bathed her in the lake and likewise consecrated her in the position of Mahādevī, the king addressed his own beloved wife: (10)
"O beloved, lotus-petal-eyed one, you ought to bring back that great and unrestrained wealth which arose from a mere momentary thought."
"Through the perfection of your yoga, by virtue of your power of true resolve (satyasaṃkalpa), [I shall bring about] your birth with great magnificence,
adorned with ornaments, jewelry, weapons, and missiles, and possessing a vast army numbering many akṣauhiṇīs.
Having heard these words of her beloved, Cūḍālā, of excellent complexion, [replied].
He marshaled his army, formidable like a cloud in the rainy season.
The two of them beheld that army, teeming with horses and elephants,
its banners filling the sky and making the forest appear dense.
By whom the forest was made dense and devoid of any open space. || 13 ||
The mountain caves and dense thickets resounded with the roar of musical instruments, while the great radiance of the crest-jewels pulverized the veil of darkness.
The mountain caves, dense thickets, and hollows of which resounded with the sounds of musical instruments.
There, upon that excellent Gandhadvipa, where the circle of the earth had been established and was protected by joyful vassal lords, the royal couple mounted [the elephant]. (15)
Because other elephants cannot endure his ichor, he is called Gandhadvipa.
Then King Śikhidhvaja, accompanied by his beloved queen,
led forth an exceedingly powerful army crowded with foot soldiers and chariots.
*Valaṃ* means an army. || 16 ||
Then he departed from that forest with his army, which moved like a shifting mountain,
as if splitting the earth and its mountains by means of a swift terrestrial wind.
With the earth-born [mudrā] and the rising [mudrā]. || 17 ||
Then that lord of the earth departed from Mahendra, the king of mountains,
beholding along the way various mountains, regions, rivers, villages, and wildernesses.
Showing that collection of his own life’s events to his beloved wife,
he reached his own city, which was as beautiful as heaven, in a very short time.
That collection of past events concerning himself, which had occurred previously on the road after he had emerged from his own body, along with the people of the countryside. || 19 ||
There, his neighboring kings, respectful of his arrival, understood his coming by the sound of "Victory! and went forth with uplifted hearts.
The ministers, appointed to the lordships of those various regions, were of noble intent and filled with longing. || 20 ||
Accompanied by those two armies, which had joined together and resounded with the blaring of trumpets, the king entered the city.
Showered by the multitudes of handfuls of parched grain and flowers from the city women,
he beheld the merchant's road, which was most excellent and unsurpassed.
With multitudes of handfuls of parched grain and handfuls of flowers, one after another, each succeeding one surpassing the last.
It was crowded with banners and flags, beautiful with networks of pearls,
filled with women devoted to dance and song, and stood immovable upon its own ground.
It stood immovable on its own ground and in its own place, as lofty as Mount Kailāsa. || 23 ||
Then, having entered the palace accompanied by various royal auspicious rites,
he properly honored the multitude of subjects who bowed before him.

Having celebrated a magnificent festival for seven days in the city with various items well-known in the world and in the scriptures— such as curd, dūrvā grass, unbroken rice, conch shells, lutes, umbrellas, and chowries—
the king performed his royal duties within his own inner apartments.
In the inner apartments, [he experiences] his own respective enjoyments of meditative absorption and so forth, according to his desire. || 25 ||
Having ruled the kingdom on the surface of the earth for ten thousand years,
O Rāma, he desisted from maintaining the body along with Cūḍālā.
The meaning is that, having desisted from maintaining a physical body, he became established in the bliss of disembodied liberation (videhakaivalya). || 26 ||
Having cast off the body like a lamp without oil, that one of great intelligence, O Rāma, attained Nirvāṇa so as not to be born again. (27)
He explains that very point clearly with the words "the body," etc., by this aforementioned method. || 27 ||
Having enjoyed sovereignty for ten thousand years with that equanimous vision, he attained the state of Nirvana.
Having ruled the kingdom and having enjoyed himself with that Cūḍālā, even after sporting with her on all sides; || 28 ||
Free from fear and despondency, liberated from pride and envy, performing his natural and innate duties, with a mind that has consumed all passion—
thus possessing an even and equanimous vision, the noble Mṛtyu then conquered ten thousand winters as a sole sovereign.
He did so. || 29 ||

He whose intellect was free from passion regarding enjoyed pleasures, and whose vision was equal toward all— even those who were equal— was that noble Śikhidhvaja. Having conquered death, characterized by desire, through the aforementioned awakening,
he exercised sole sovereignty (*aikarājya*) over Jambūdvīpa for ten thousand years, as indicated by the ten winter seasons.

Having enjoyed manifold pleasures on earth and having remained for a long time as the crest-jewel of all monarchs, he attained the supreme state of immortality with his essence remaining intact. Thus, following the course of nature that has come upon you, remain free from sorrow and arise to attend to the multitude of duties.
Or, experiencing for oneself by force the splendor of enjoyment, liberation, and so forth. || 30 ||
Having restated Śikhidhvaja’s state of abiding [in the Self] with the first half of the verse, the second half instructs Rāma on what must be done:

"Having enjoyed manifold enjoyments, he—remaining as the residue of that [experience]—attained the supreme state, which is immortal, ageless, and pure being (sattva) consisting of existence alone. O Rāma, you too, following the course of ordinary activities already begun and brought about by past karma (prārabdha)," [should act].

Free from sorrow, remain in meditative absorption (samādhi); or else, rising up while forcefully pursuing the splendor of the knowledge of enjoyment and liberation, remain in the state of emergence (vyutthita). The meaning is that there is no difference in the fruit between your meditative absorption and your emergence from it. || 30 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and tenth canto, titled "The Liberation of Śikhidhvaja," in the *Pūrva-cūḍā* of the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*, composed by Vālmīki and belonging to the *Ārṣa* tradition. 110.
Thus ends the one hundred and tenth chapter, titled "The Liberation of Śikhidhvaja," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The Cūḍālā episode—[also known as the Śikhidhvaja episode]—is completed.
The one hundred and eleventh canto.
The venerable Vasiṣṭha said:
Thus has this entire narrative of Śikhidhvaja been related to you;
traveling by this path, you shall never again be weary.
Just as a king [is deprived of his kingdom] by a queen, Kaca was made to renounce everything here by his father;
it is described that in the end, through the abandonment of egoism, he became perfect.
Going by this path, you will not grow weary; you shall become one for whom all weariness has ceased. || 1 ||
Firmly grasping this view which destroys passion and hatred, remain with a mind eternally free from passion, firmly established in that state.
By whom that state of perfect bliss has been grasped by the intellect, perceived as the ultimate reality, and taken as a support;
that [state] which abounds in both worldly enjoyment and liberation. || 2 ||
Just as Śikhidhvaja ruled his kingdom in such a manner, so too,
O Rāma, while conducting the affairs of the state, may you become one who possesses both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
O Raghava, understand it just as Kaca, the son of Bṛhaspati, attained awakening through the very method of Śikhidhvaja.
Just as Kaca attained awakening through the well-known process of universal renunciation practiced by Śikhidhvaja, so too should you awaken. || 4 ||
Śrī Rāma said: O Blessed One, please describe in brief how that venerable Kaca, the son of the blessed Bṛhaspati, attained enlightenment.
In brief, that is, in its entirety. || 5 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Listen, O illustrious King, to this story of how Kaca, the son of the divine preceptor, attained supreme awakening just like Śikhidhvaja.
Having transcended childhood and being intent on crossing over saṃsāra,
Kaca, who understood both words and their meanings, spoke to Bṛhaspati.

"Having crossed beyond childhood" means he has emerged from it; that is to say, he has merely reached youth. "A knower of words and their meanings" means one who is proficient in all branches of learning and a knower of the words and their meanings within the scope of the great sentence *tat tvam asi*. || 7 ||
Kaca said: O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, tell me how a living being, bound by the thread of life, may emerge from this cage of worldly existence.
By such a creature as I am, whose very life-force acts like a thread creating a thousandfold bond for itself.
Bṛhaspati said: "O son, by renouncing everything, one flies up without agitation from this ocean of saṃsāra, which is a house for the production of misfortune."

"It flies up" means it departs quickly; that is to say, by means of the renunciation of everything performed in such a way that there is no remorse or agitation regarding the objects once abandoned due to the firmness of extreme dispassion. || 9 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Having heard these most purifying words of his father,
Kaca abandoned everything and went to a solitary forest.
That departure of Bṛhaspati did not cause him any distress; for the great, being noble-minded, remain equanimous in both union and separation.
O noble-minded ones, you whose intentions are as steadfast as Mount Meru. || 11 ||
Then, when three or five years had passed,
that sinless Kaca again found his father in a certain great forest.

"In three and five years" means in eight years. The meaning is that, having recognized the varying degrees of maturity of their minds, he reached his father, who had come to make them abandon the remainder [of their worldly attachments]. || 12 ||
Having honored and saluted him, and having embraced his son,
Kaca again questioned the Lord of Speech with a pleasing voice.
Kaca said:
"Today it is the eighth year since I renounced everything;
yet even so, O father, I do not attain blameless peace."
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
While that kapiñjala was speaking these words of distress in the forest,
the Lord of Speech (Bṛhaspati), having said "Abandon everything," ascended to heaven.
The sky, the atmosphere. || 15 ||
When he had departed, Kaca likewise cast off even his deerskin garment and other belongings from his body;
he then became like the autumnal sky, from which the moon, clouds, sun, and stars have vanished.
"Gatendu" means the autumnal sky at the time when the sun has just risen; that is to say, the sky immediately adjacent to the rising sun. || 16 ||
Furthermore, after exactly three years, in a certain forest region,
he abandoned the raining of clouds and so forth, just as the sky [clears] in autumn.
The second half of the verse beginning with "punar" should be joined with the subsequent verse, from the word "dūyamānamanāḥ" up to the end of the previous one.

To explain how he became equal to the autumnal sky, the author says "tatyāja": in certain places, by taking refuge in mountain caves, he abandoned and avoided the rain from clouds and other such disturbances. || 17 ||
The lay disciple, breathing out his very essence as peaceful emptiness toward the horizons,
reached that very father and teacher with a grieving mind.

At the beginning of autumn, however, he dwelt for a while at the ends of the quarters. Thus, with a mind tormented by longing, after another three years, he encountered that very same father and teacher once again in a certain forest region. (18)
Having performed the sequence of worship with devotion and having embraced his son, Kaca questioned him again with a voice faltering from distress: || 19 ||
Kaca said:
"O father, everything has been renounced—even my patched garment, my bamboo staff, and so forth;
yet there is still no rest in my own true state. What shall I do? (20)
The staff is made of bamboo; by the word "and so forth" (ādipada), the water-pot, the grass mat, the deerskin, and others are also included. 20.
Bṛhaspati said:
"They say that the mind is everything; by abandoning it, my son, you shall shine.
Those who know all things understand the abandonment of the mind to be the abandonment of everything. (21)
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Having spoken thus to his son, the Lord of Speech (Bṛhaspati) swiftly leapt into the sky;
Kaca, however, with an undaunted mind, sought to abandon his consciousness.
He sought; he searched. || 22 ||
When he could not perceive his own mind even while reflecting in the forest,
he then reflected with his intellect and went [to him] by means of his thought alone.

When he neither knew nor had seen [the father], that is to say, prior to the elaboration of what is called "mind"—which is essentially the mind's own searching and its inherent instability—he went to his father with his intellect; that is to say, he reflected upon him. || 23 ||
The collection of objects, such as the body and so forth, is not called the mind;
why, where, or for what purpose should I abandon this which is useless and innocent? (24)

[Objection: "Surely, just as the Asuras [attained liberation] from the burning of Tripura, the abandonment of the mind will be accomplished simply through the abandonment of the body, the senses, and their objects. To this, he says:
"Since there is no certainty [that it would happen], why should I abandon—without fault—the body and so forth, which are free from the offense of providing a dwelling for the mind?
The meaning is that its abandonment is not appropriate. (24)
I shall go into the presence of my father to understand the mind, that great enemy;
having understood it, I shall quickly abandon it, and thereafter I shall remain free from fever.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Having reflected thus, Kaca ascended to the celestial realm;
having reached the Lord of Speech (Bṛhaspati), he affectionately paid homage and prostrated before him.
He questioned him in private: "O Blessed One, tell me, what is the mind?
Speak of the true nature of the mind, so that I may completely abandon it. (27)
Bṛhaspati said: Those who know the mind understand one's own ego to be the mind; that internal sense of "I-ness" which exists within a living being is called the mind. (28)

Those people who are liberated while living, knowing the witness of the mind by having separated the mind [from it]—[for us, it is required that the witness separates the mind; however, since the very expectation of the one who expects is itself not expected here, we hold that what has been stated exactly as it is is well-said and perfectly consistent. || 28 ||
Kaca said:
O high-minded one, tell me how this [happened] regarding the host of gods, which consists of thirty-three great crores, O Guru.
"O Teacher of the host of gods numbering thirty-three times ten million, O high-minded Bṛhaspati, tell me this:

how can it be that the very notion of 'I' (ahaṃbhāva) is the mind? For in the world, egoism (ahaṃkāra) is well-known as the self; thus, if it were abandoned, the abandonment of the self would follow, resulting in the consequence of nihilism (nairātmya). This is the intended meaning. || 29 ||
"I think that its renunciation is difficult and does not lead to perfection;
how indeed can this be abandoned, O best of yogis? (30)
Nor is the abandonment of the self possible, because its nature is such that it cannot be discarded; with this intention, he says: "I consider... (verse 30).
Bṛhaspati said: Even from the plucking of a flower or even from the closing of an eye, the abandonment of egoism is easily accomplished; there is not even the slightest difficulty in this.

With the intention that truth is difficult to abandon when the witness is unknown, but when the witness is known, it is easier to abandon than even the crushing of a flower, Bṛhaspati states the following answer: "Even... (31).
O son, listen as I tell you how this is so:
an object established solely through ignorance perishes through knowledge. (32)
Ignorance is delusion characterized by a lack of acquaintance with the pure Witness; it consists of entities such as the ego-sense, which are established solely through that [delusion].
And that [ignorance] is destroyed by knowledge, which is merely the acquaintance with that [Witness]. || 32 ||
In reality, O son, there is no such thing as egoism; it is a false delusion, appearing as if existent though non-existent, like a child’s phantom. (33)
Like a ghost imagined by a child, the object, though non-existent, appears as if it were existent, persisting through the vision of the ignorant. || 33 ||
Just as the state of being a serpent appears in a rope, and just as the notion of water arises in a desert, so too does the false manifestation of egoism flash forth as something unreal.
Likewise, the connection [of the verse] is that even the sense of "I" (ahaṃkāra) shines forth falsely. || 34 ||
Just as duality, though non-existent, is perceived in the moon due to delusion, so too does the ego-sense manifest; it is neither real nor unreal.
And it is neither existent nor non-existent; this is the remainder [of the verse]. || 35 ||
There exists the singular, beginningless and endless, pure consciousness alone, free from internal impurity; clearer even than the sky, it is the knower of all.

If all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) is false, what then exists? To this he says: "The One. Even if everything is false, the cognition of that [One] exists; for the non-existence of that [cognition] is unestablished precisely because there is no means of proof for it—this is the intended meaning. || 36 ||
That very same one shines everywhere, at all times, and in every manner among all living beings,
just as the single water reflects in the restless waves of the ocean.

He states that it exists because the manifestation of the world would otherwise be untenable in its absence—namely, with the words "everywhere. The phrase "as in water" is to be understood as the ellipsis. || 37 ||
In this regard, what is this sense of "I," from where does it arise, and how has it emerged?
Where is a mass of dust born within water, and where can water arise from fire? (38)

In this regard, between the seer (*dṛk*) and the seen (*dṛśya*), who is this ego (*ahaṃkāra*), from what cause, and how has it arisen—either from the union of the seer and the seen or by some other means? He states [the answer] with the word "where" (*kva*), implying that the very emergence of this entity, whose nature is distinct from both, is difficult to describe. A "mass of dust" (*rajo-rāśi*) is a heap of dry powder. (38)
"O son, abandon this vain notion of 'this is I,' which is trivial, limited in form, and subject to the constraints of space and time. (39)
"This body and so forth was born from my father and others; it is rendered helpless by space and time, and is subject to transformation through growth, decay, and the like. (39)
Unconditioned by space, time, and the like, transparent, eternally manifest, all-pervading, consisting of all objects yet having consciousness alone as its singular object—you are stainless. (40)

To the question "Then who am I there?", he replies: "The quarters" (diś). That which consists of all objects—appearing in the form of the transformations of all things—is in reality a single object, because it is not for the sake of another and is non-dual. || 40 ||
Like the sap of fruits, flowers, and leaves situated in every direction, you alone abide eternally within all worlds.
Being the stainless conscious self, forever infinite and without end, who indeed am I to you, O embodiment of pure being— what certainty can there be regarding "I"?

Showing another meaning—that it consists of all objects (*sarvārthamaya*)—as being the essence of all things, he concludes the present topic with an illustration: "Like the juice" (*phala*). Just as the juice within a tree is the cause and the essence of the fruits, flowers, petals, and leaves situated in all directions.
You are the cause of all worlds and their very essence, eternally abiding within as the most stainless, infinite Consciousness-Self; O Kaca,
for you whose form is existence and whose nature is the indivisible, non-dual Pure Being, what is this limited conviction of "I"?

The meaning is that there is no one [else like you]. Alternatively, the meaning is that you abide as the essence of the entire world, consisting of unsurpassed bliss, like honey—the sap that has attained a state of uniformity (*aikarasya*) in fruits, flowers, and so forth, situated in all directions. Therefore, you are indeed eternal (*ananta*).
"The self whose nature is consciousness alone is free from the stain of illusion," and so forth, as before. || 41 ||
Thus ends the one hundred and eleventh chapter, titled "The Enlightenment of Kaca," in the Story of Kaca within the Nirvāṇa Section of the Holy Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa, the Great Epic of Vasiṣṭha. 111.
Thus ends the one hundred and eleventh canto, titled "The Awakening of Kaca," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and twelfth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Having thus attained this supreme yoga, this unsurpassed instruction,
Thereupon, that son of the preceptor of the gods became liberated while yet living.
Indeed, here, following Rāma’s question after he was awakened by the account of Kaca,
the story of the illusory man Kāka is told for the protection of Khara.
Yoga is that by which the inner self (pratyagātman) is joined with and determined as one with the Supreme Self (paramātman) without division; [he requested] such instruction. || 1 ||
Free from possessiveness and free from egoism, with the knots of bondage severed and the intellect thoroughly pacified,
remain without modification, O Rāma, just as Kaca remained.
In that same way, you too should remain. || 2 ||
Know that the ego is unreal; do not resort to it, nor abandon it. For how can there be either the rejection or the grasping of that which is unreal, such as a rabbit’s horn? (3)

Regarding the phrase "mainam": the intention is that its abandonment consists merely in disregarding it with the cognition that it is false; it does not depend upon an effort capable of annulling one's ownership. || 3 ||
When egoism is impossible, where are birth and death for you?
Likewise, who could gather the fruit sown in the field of the sky? || 4 ||

If one does not prevent that [egoity] through effort, how can there be liberation from the fear of death and birth? To this he says: "asaṃbhavati" (it does not arise). This is a locative case within a negative compound ending in a present participle (*śatṛ*). Now, one might ask: why would death and birth not occur due to the power of the seeds consisting of desire, karma, and latent impressions (*vāsanā*)? To this he says: "nabhasi" (in the sky). Those seeds sprout only when the field of egoity (*ahaṅkāra*) exists, but not otherwise.
The meaning is: "when that [perception] is sublated. || 4 ||
Partless, with all mental constructs stilled, pervading and consisting of the essence of all beings,
subtler than even the most subtle atom, you are pure consciousness alone, yet composed of mind.
When the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) has been sublated, he states what remains: "I am partless" (niraṃśam). || 5 ||
Just as waves and the like arise from water, and bracelets and the like from gold,
so too does that very Self appear as something other, being conditioned by the sense of "I."
"How did I, being such as this, become permeated by the sense of 'I'? To this he says: "Just as...
The meaning is that although I was thus permeated by the sense of "I," I appeared as if I were something else. || 6 ||
Through lack of realization, the entire world remains as if composed of illusion;
through realization, O sinless one, everything becomes the very form of Brahman.
Regarding this, he states the reason: "by non-awakening. He also states the reason for its removal: "by awakening. (7)
Abandoning the notions of duality and unity, remain established in that which remains and be happy;
do not be miserable in vain like a deluded man.
The perception of duality is the observation of effects; the perception of unity is the observation of the cause.

Having abandoned those two and remaining after having set aside the pure Being (sanmātra) that permeates both, you shall become established and happy—this is the meaning. However, if you do not perceive [Being] in this way, the onset of suffering for you will be as unavoidable as it is for the person about to be described; thus he says: "Do not" (mā). || 8 ||
This worldly existence, which has become exceedingly difficult to cross and has reached a state of deep density,
quickly attains attenuation through awakening, like autumnal mist.
Diminution and decay. || 9 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
I have attained supreme inner satisfaction through the nectar of your knowledge,
just as a *cātaka* bird, overcome by the fear of drought, finds relief through the rain-cloud.
Like a *cātaka* bird overcome by the fear of drought—the obstruction of rain—[I am refreshed] as if by a sudden downpour of rain sent by fate.
(10) As if sprinkled with nectar, I enter into a state of coolness; yet I abide above all incomparable riches. (11)

The word "api" (also/even) serves to connect with the meaning of the preceding sentence. I abide in that which is characterized by unsurpassed bliss, standing above all incomparable riches, beginning with the attainment of Hiraṇyagarbha. || 11 ||
I do not reach satiety while listening to the words you speak, just as the thirsty cakora bird never reaches satiety with the rays of the moon. 12.
"By the tasting of your words"—this is the ellipsis. || 12 ||
O Lord, though already satisfied, I ask you this question once more:
who, even when satiated, would not drink the unswallowed nectar-liquor?
Although satisfied by the correct experience of the reality that is to be known, one should drink the nectar-like essence. 13.
O best of sages, why is that which is called the "false person" said to be both a reality and a non-reality? Tell me quickly how this entire multitude of worldly entities is so constituted.

To the Guru, who had been thus incited by praise, Rāma asks out of curiosity about the story of the "false man" (mithyāpuruṣa) previously indicated by the words, "Do not be sorrowful; you are like a false man in vain"—the meaning being, "Tell me that [story]. || 14 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāghava, listen to this beautiful narrative told by me for the sake of awakening the unreal person; it is a tale that produces laughter.
Which produces laughter for those who perceive reality. || 15 ||
O mighty-armed one, there exists a certain person made of illusion and machinery, whose intellect is as fragile as a child's and who is utterly deluded, concealed solely by ignorance. (16)

Like a child, he is deluded and distracted by a fragile intellect; hidden and enveloped by folly and ignorance, he is born somewhere in solitude and remains right there in that void, like a mass of hair in the sky or a mirage in the desert. (17)
He states that its nature is false even in its own form by saying "like a mass of hair" (keśoṇḍraka) in a secluded place beyond the range of people's vision. || 17 ||
Therefore, there is nothing else there; that which exists is only that itself.
And as for whatever else appears, it is a mere semblance of that, yet the dull-witted person does not perceive this.

In that place which is its locus, there is nothing whatsoever other than that false person (*mithyāpuruṣa*). Whatever is perceived as existing is that very [person] and not distinct from it; and whatever else he perceives, that is merely a manifestation of his own delusion (*bhrānti*), meaning that it is said to be "that very [person].
He does not perceive this entire invisible world as being himself, because he is of evil intellect (*durmati*). This is the meaning.
As he grew there, the thought arose within him:
"I am space, I am space, space is mine; I protect space," and he remained steadfast in this conviction.
I am dependent upon space; space is my means of subsistence. Therefore, I protect such space by pervading it. 19.
"Having established the sky, I myself shall protect the desired object with care"—
thinking thus, he built a house for the purpose of protecting the sky.
Having placed my own cherished object, the ether (kha), within some limiting adjunct (upādhi), I myself protect it with devotion. || 20 ||
He placed his trust in its interior, thinking, "The sky has been protected by me";
O descendant of Raghu, he was then satisfied with that space within the house.
In the inner treasury of that house; "this much space is mine"—such was his conceit (abhimāna). The word "became contented" is to be understood as the ellipsis. || 21 ||
Then, in the course of time, his house went to ruin,
like a cloud at the end of the season or a wave by the wind.
By another season, namely autumn. || 22 ||
"Alas, O space of the house, you are lost! Alas, where have you gone in an instant?
Alas, alas, you pure one, you are shattered!"—thus did he lament. (23)
This is space. || 23 ||
Having thus lamented a hundred times, the evil-minded one again dug a well right there for the sake of protecting his donkey, becoming intent upon the space of the well.
The other is attached to the space within the well through the sense of "mine-ness. || 24 ||
Then, in the course of time, even that well of his came to ruin;
when the space of the well had vanished, he became utterly immersed in grief.
Destruction means disappearance through being filled with dust, clay, and so forth. || 25 ||
At the conclusion of his discourse on the space within the well, he quickly fashioned a jar;
having become the space within the jar, he himself attained final liberation.
Nirvṛti is the pleasure derived from that conceit. || 26 ||
O scion of the Raghus, even Kumbha was brought to destruction in time;
for whatever direction an unfortunate person takes, that very direction perishes.
The justification for that [distinction] follows from the general statement "whichever [it may be]. || 27 ||
At the conclusion of his prattle regarding the space within the water-jar, he made a pit for the sake of donkeys;
likewise, by that act, he became intent upon the space within the pit. (28)
In the course of time, even his sacrificial pit met with destruction;
consequently, he grieved for the space of the pit as if it were darkness dispelled by light.
Due to some cause such as being attacked by wild elephants or buffaloes. || 29 ||
At the end of his grief, he built a great four-winged mansion for the sake of protecting the donkey; that mansion then became composed of space.

"Catuḥśālam" means that which has halls on four sides; [the house] in the middle is a large hall in the form of an assembly-hall (*sabhā*). Because it is not attached to that space, it is "consisting of that space," just as one says "a wretch consisting of women. || 30 ||
Time, which devours all creatures, swiftly snatched that away from him as the wind carries off a withered leaf; thereupon, he became consumed by grief.
At the edge of the sorrow of the four-pillared hall, he constructed a granary for the protection of his donkeys;
it was shaped like a cloud, and he remained there, intent upon the sky.
A *kusūla* is a granary for storing grain. || 32 ||
Time swiftly snatched that away from him as the wind carries off a cloud;
because of that, he was consumed by the grief over the loss of his granary.
In this way, with houses, four-sided halls, water-jars, sacrificial pits, and small vessels,
this endless time of his passes away.
Of that false person. || 34 ||
Remaining thus, powerless, he perceives the sky within the cave as his own home through a dense delusion of self;
bewildered by the cycle of coming and going, he moves toward and departs from a mass of suffering more intense than any other.

He concludes: "Thus. O Rāma, that illusory person (mithyāpuruṣa) exists in this manner, perceiving the sky within the cave—that is, within the interior of various [limited] houses—by means of houses that are dense and difficult to enter, and by means of adjuncts such as wells and jars; being deluded by his attachment to the coming and going associated with those [adjuncts], he remains engaged in the creation, preservation, and destruction of each of them due to his identification with them.
The meaning is that even from a denser mass of suffering, a further mass of suffering arises; it comes from there and goes forth, or departs.

Thus ends the one hundred and twelfth canto, titled "The Protection of the Sky," in the *Mithyāpuruṣopākhyāna* (The Narrative of the False Man) within the *Pūrva-cūḍā* (First Part) of the *Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa*. 112.
Thus ends the one hundred and twelfth canto, titled "The Protection of the Sky," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and thirteenth canto.
Śrī Rāma said:
"O Lord, why did the illusory man appear through his association with a false human being?"
This has been told by you; now what is being said regarding the protection of the sky?
The meaning of terms such as "false person" is here clearly stated,
just as the purport of a narrative is [determined] through the description of its similarities.

Considering that [the story] was of obvious meaning yet consisted mostly of the actions of a madman—something impossible for a discerning person—and concluding that its intent lay elsewhere, like a statement using a "false tale of a man" as an allegory (*anyāpadeśa*), Rāma asks him: "Mithyā... [The Māyā-puruṣa whom you described in connection with the false man (Mithyā-nara) is this...]
With what intention was that performed, and with what intention is the protection of the sky spoken of? This is the meaning. || 1 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Listen, O Rāma, as it truly is; I shall reveal this to you—the story of the account of the false man which has just been told.
As it truly is, as it exists. || 2 ||
O descendant of Raghu, know that this person who is said to consist of the machinery of illusion is that very ego (ahaṃkāra) arisen from the empty sky.
The empty sky is the illusory space; that which arises from it is [the same]. || 3 ||
O virtuous one, that infinite, unreal void within which this world is situated becomes, of its own accord, at the beginning of creation.
"At the beginning of creation" means prior to the act of creating. || 4 ||
Then, like sound from the ether, the ego arises from that Brahman which resides within and is extremely difficult to perceive,
just as vibration first arises from the wind.
Is it not the case that [the world] has arisen from a baseless illusion and remains therein? He says "within" (antar) to answer no.
It is not baseless; rather, it exists with Brahman as its internal substrate—that Brahman which is exceedingly difficult to perceive—and is of such a nature.
Now, how can the world, beginning with the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), arise from that which is beyond the senses? To this, he provides an illustration:

"Like sound from the ether. Intending that the ego (ahaṃkāra) is the subtle body (liṅgātman) and that it is indeed of the nature of Māyā, he states another illustration for that: "like vibration" (spanda iva). || 5 ||
Having increased and attained the state of being the self within the sky,
it then exerts itself through that which is called "the non-self as self."
The non-self itself, having through delusion attained the state of self, increases within its own cause, the sky;
through thousands of conceptual constructions, it imagines: "This is desired for me," "this is undesired," and so forth.
By means of that very imagined designation of "I" as the self, it strives for the attainment of the desired and the avoidance of the undesired. 6.

For the sake of protecting the self— which is non-self— this [ego], having fallen into agitation, repeatedly creates various kinds of bodies even though they are subject to destruction again and again.

Engaged in the protection of that self which is not its own body, it creates various successive bodies following each destruction of a preceding one, in accordance with the latent impressions of desire and karma. || 7 ||
That very person is a person of illusion; he is indeed a false person.
For the ego-sense, though unreal and purposeless, has arisen through māyā.
That is indeed the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra). || 8 ||
Having fashioned bodies such as wells, ponds, four-sided halls, and jars, he thinks, "The self has been protected," and thus his mental conception proceeds into that space.
He states that even by words such as "well" (kūpa) and "pitcher" (kumbha), various types of bodies are indicated through metaphorical indication (lakṣaṇā): "In that well," etc.
One develops the notion of self toward that [body] within the sky—that is, within the self consisting of Māyā delimited by that [body]. || 9 ||
O Rāghava, hear these names of this very egoism, by which delusions in the form of the world it causes one to be bewildered. (10)
These are names derived from yoga (connection) based on the distinctions of limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of action.
The meaning is that by whichever limiting adjuncts of action—namely, the delusions appearing as the forms of the world—this egoism (ahaṅkāra) deludes itself. || 10 ||
It is also well-known by the names Jīva, Buddhi, Manas, Citta, Māyā, and Prakṛti; and likewise as Saṃkalpa, Kalanā, Kāla, and Kalā. (11)
It is called the *jīva* because it sustains the vital breaths;
*buddhi* because it determines external objects; *manas* because it reflects upon them; *citta* because it thinks about them; *māyā* because it conceives of the unreal;
*prakṛti* because its nature is transformation; *saṃkalpa* because it forms intentions; and *kalanā* because it calculates the objects intended.

Because it is the cause of transformation and so forth, it is known as *kāla* (time); and because it is conceived as a partial differentiation therein, it is also renowned among the learned as *kalā*. 11.
Thus, through these and other such names that have become manifold,
the egoity (ahaṃkāra), possessing a thousand forms, expands by means of imagined objects.

By the word "etcetera" (ādi), all the names for the mind mentioned in the section on its origin are included; furthermore, through the multiplicity of its functions— well-known from various Vedic and Smṛti texts such as "Desire, resolve, doubt, faith, lack of faith, steadfastness, lack of steadfastness, shame, intelligence, and fear"— it has attained a state of manifoldness.
Within the vast and empty elemental ether, the world is certainly without foundation; the person remains there, experiencing pleasures and pains that are indeed illusory. (13)
Therefore, to superimpose upon experience that which was stated—that nothing else exists there, and that which does exist is that very [Brahman] itself—he says:

"bhūta... etc. When the full Brahman has first manifested as the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*) in its own nature, being pervasive and expanded, the world is imagined therein through the sequence of the conceptualization of air and the other elements, like a city of Gandharvas.

Through reasoning, it is ascertained upon reflection that [the space] is indeed devoid of any obstruction such as walls or the like. For how could space, which is a void, first arise within Brahman, which is without apertures? And how could that void-natured, vastly expanded, and motionless [space] become wind, whose nature is movement? Furthermore, how could that formless and non-hot wind become fire, whose inherent nature is the opposite of those?

It becomes that. And how can that [fire], which is hot and has the nature of burning, become water, which has the opposite nature of coolness and refreshing? And how can that [water], which has the nature of fluidity, evaporation, and lack of solidity, attain the state of earth, which has a nature opposed to it? Therefore, it is certain that the world is indeed without foundation. And in that regard, that person is entirely mistaken.
The meaning is that he remains experiencing pleasures and pains. || 13 ||
Just as a deluded man, fearing for his own self, might vainly try to protect the space within a jar, so too do you suffer; do not be thus afflicted.
And lest you become like that person of false understanding and deluded ignorance described as "one of evil intellect," who remains experiencing false afflictions, he says: "Just as... (verse 14).
Vaster even than space, pure, subtle, auspicious, and beautiful—how and by whom can that Self be grasped, or even protected? (15)
When the body, which is merely the space within the heart, perishes,
living beings grieve in vain, suspecting that the Self has been destroyed.
Upon the complete destruction of the body, its characteristics, its decay, and its dwelling place. || 16 ||
Just as space remains undivided when jars and other objects are destroyed,
so the embodied soul remains eternally untainted when bodies perish.
This pure Self, consisting of consciousness alone, is subtler than even space;
for it is merely a portion of one's own experience, O Rāma, and like the sky, it does not perish.
The aspect of one's own experience is the self-luminous consciousness (cit) extracted from the ego-sense; it is indeed that much alone. || 18 ||
Nothing whatsoever is ever born, nor does anything ever die;
it is only Brahman that expands in the form of the world's manifestation. 19.
Truth is the one peaceful state, devoid of beginning, middle, and end, and liberated from both existence and non-existence; having realized this, be happy. (20)

Having abandoned through awakening the entire state of egoism— which is the abode of all calamities, unstable, lacking self-mastery, prone to downfall, devoid of discernment, ignoble, and ignorant— you remain in the perfectly established state and attain supreme excellence.

Causing one to abandon the egoism whose nature as a false person has been described, he concludes by teaching stability in the remaining pure consciousness alone: "Of all calamities," etc. It is "dependent" because it brings about a lack of self-sovereignty; it is "such that a fall into hell and so forth is imminent," being opposed to all discernment; it is "ignoble."

The meaning is that if one abandons, by uprooting it from its very foundation through awakening, the entire state of censurable egoism— including all its constituent parts characterized by the body, the senses, and their objects— and remains firmly established with a well-fixed footing in the remaining, extracted pure consciousness alone, one shall attain the state of being supreme over all. || 21 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and thirteenth canto, titled "The Narrative of the Illusory Man," in the first part of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the glorious Vāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa, composed by the Sage. 113.
Thus ends the one hundred and thirteenth canto, titled "The Narrative of the False Man," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and fourteenth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Before the supreme Brahman, the mind first arose.
Consisting of reflection and characterized by enjoyment, it has attained its state while remaining established in that very [consciousness]. || 1 ||
Having distinguished here, by means of numerous examples, between the forms of the existent and the non-existent,
stability in the form of the existent is asserted through the elimination of the form of the non-existent.

Since the entire world consists of nothing but mental construction (*manovikalpa*), it is easy to dispel it by demonstrating the reality that is free from conceptualization (*avikalpavastu*); therefore, in order to explain this, [the author] first describes the mental construction regarding the supreme Brahman with the words "from the supreme" (*parasmāt*). Previously, at the time of creation and so forth, before all other constructions, that mind first arose within that supreme Brahman.
The meaning is that [the mind], existing as non-different from reality, has remained as such since time immemorial by serving as the cause for various conceptual constructions.
O Rāghava, the mind resides in Brahman like fragrance in the calyx of a flower, like a great wave in the ocean, or like a network of rays in the sun.
He provides examples for their existence in a state of non-separate reality with the words: "in the calyx of a flower" (puṣpakośe) || 2 ||
O Rāma, this world has come into existence solely through the forgetfulness of that invisible reality of the Self; it has not come from anything else, like a snake [seen] in a rope.
Having clarified the portion "remaining in that" through examples, he explains the portion "having come to abide," beginning with the words "tasya" (of that).
By means of ignorance (*ajñāna*) itself—which consists of non-recognition due to forgetfulness—it has come to abide as the root of the conceptualization of the entire world. || 3 ||
O Raghava, for one who conceives of this web of rays as distinct from the Sun, it appears as something other than that radiant one.

And so, he establishes through examples that when the world is meditated upon as something other than pure Being (*sanmātra*), whereas when it is meditated upon as being pure Being itself, it is indeed Brahman whose nature is Being—beginning with the words "The sun... and so forth. The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: for one who conceives this web of rays as distinct from the sun, this [web] would indeed appear as if it were other than that radiant sun. || 4 ||
For one by whom the armlet is conceived as being distinct from gold, that [armlet] is indeed merely an armlet for him;
it is not gold at all.
"Not his," [it is said]; the meaning is that the cognition of the identity of the object is already excluded by the bracelet alone. || 5 ||
He by whom the rays have been realized as non-different from the sun—that person is indeed the sun itself; he is called "non-conceptual."
Not distinct from the sun, it is free from conceptual construction, devoid of the conceptualization of distinctions among its rays. || 6 ||
For one by whom the wave is conceived as being distinct from the water,
only the notion of the wave remains for him, not the ocean.

Just as an object appears through the conceptual and non-conceptual forms [of cognition], so too the Person (puruṣa) becomes both with-mental-construction (savikalpa) and without-mental-construction (nirvikalpa) through the cognitions of conceptualization and non-conceptualization; thus he says, beginning with "In water... (salile...). 7.
He by whom a wave is perceived as not distinct from the water,
and who possesses the cognition of the commonality of water, is called "non-conceptual" (nirvikalpa).
He by whom the armlet is perceived as non-different from the gold,
possessing the great wisdom that gold alone exists, is called one who is free from conceptual construction (nirvikalpa).
For one who has cultivated the notion that the flame exists apart from the fire,
the cognition of "fire" dissolves, and only the cognition of the "flame" remains.
It flows, yet it does not arise. || 10 ||
That state is colored like a mass of flames or a streak of clouds;
the agitated mind, being absorbed in it, takes on that very same instability.

He says "jvālā" (flame), meaning that cognition, permeated by an imagined form, fixes its attachment right there and produces other conceptual constructions rooted in that [form]. It is like a streak of cloud; the mass of flames is like a streak of cloud, and it is colored by that very [streak].

That is to say, it has assumed the form of that [streak]. "Stability" (*sthiti*) refers to the modification of cognition (*buddhi-vṛtti*). "Contained therein" means contained within the mass of flames.
It assumes and fashions [the qualities] such as moving, upward motion, straightness, and curvature. || 11 ||
He who perceives the series of flames as non-different from fire possesses a single cognition of fire; he is called one who is free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*). (12)

He who is free from conceptual construction, who is exceedingly great, and whose vast intelligence is undiminished—he has attained that which is to be attained; he does not sink into material objects.

"Non-conceptual" means free from the two kinds of conceptualization regarding the grasped and the grasper as previously described. "In entities" means among conceptualized objects. "Plunges" means he becomes attached [to them] with the notion that they are real. (13)
Having abandoned all multiplicity within the hollow of pure consciousness alone,
remain established in the principle of awareness, which is utterly free from any object of perception.
He teaches the manner of abandoning the conceptual distinctions established in the illustration by applying it to the subject of the illustration—namely, "diversity" (nānātām).
The word *koṭara* refers to the inner, inward-facing reality. || 14 ||
When the Self, by itself and through itself, brings forth its own power called volition,
it is like the wind manifesting its power of motion through its own vibration.

The connection with the subsequent clause is as follows: when [the Self], by means of its own throbbing self-luminosity, brings forth the power called "volition" (saṃkalpa), then it becomes the mind (manas). || 15 ||
Then the mind, which consists of the fabrication of conceptualization, becomes like the universal self (viśvātmā), appearing as if separate while itself imagining its own form.
Meditating upon his own form as having all forms, the universal self becomes the collective mind. || 16 ||
The mind, which consists of volition, causes this entire world to exist; by whatever volitions it conceives, so does it become in an instant.
That collective mind, consisting of the volition of all forms, is of the nature of Hiraṇyagarbha. || 17 ||
It is the state of being an insect, the state of being born from a lotus, and likewise the state of being Meru or one of the Maruts;
it is that which is named mind, individual soul, ego, intellect, consciousness, and so forth. (18)
In whatever way one contemplates it, one analyzes and elaborates upon it as "the state of being a worm. || 18 ||
Through volition, the mind attains duality and unity and expands the existence of the world;
subsequently, within that very expansion, it itself undergoes manifoldness.
This expansive world that is perceived is composed solely of mental construction;
it is neither real nor unreal, having arisen like a web of dreams. (20)
The word "mithyā" refers to that which is false; the meaning is that it is indefinable, like a web of dreams. || 20 ||
