Just as a living being’s kingdom of the mind shines forth with its various undertakings,
so does this vast kingdom of Brahmā shine resplendently.
This belongs to Brahmā Hiraṇyagarbha; thus it is "Brāhma. || 21 ||
Because it is cultivated through the perception of things as they truly are, this [duality] dissolves;
for when seen from the perspective of ultimate reality, this is indeed nothing at all.

He says that [the world] dissolves in its illusory form precisely because, through the knowledge of reality, it is realized as being nothing other than Brahman-Ātman as it truly exists—by the words "as it really is" (yathābhūta). And thus says the Śruti: "By the mind alone is this to be attained; there is no diversity whatsoever here. (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.8) || 22 ||
But the visible world, though not ultimately real, branches out into a hundred forms, manifesting itself as the various configurations of water, such as waves and the like. 23.
He states what occurs in the absence of the vision of reality: "The visible" (dṛśyam).

Then, by the very power of not knowing the supreme truth, it proceeds to a hundred branches. Just as the ocean, though being merely water, assumes a form capable of the manifestation of waves, ripples, and so forth, and while shimmering, maintains the body of the ocean; so too [does the mind].

Even while performing thousands of actions, a person does nothing new— nor any modification or the like— to the immutable consciousness (*kūṭastha-cit*), other than the vibration of the mind which is joined with the reflection of consciousness (*cid-ābhāsa*). Therefore, you too, while abandoning even the slightest trace of duality and engaging in all worldly activities such as walking and so forth, do not create any new form of the world.

The syntactical connection extends up to the end of the fourth half-verse as follows: "There exists no truth whatsoever in the form of duality; rather, it is Brahman alone, established from the beginning, that exists as the ultimate truth—contemplate this. (23)
Just as the ocean naturally assumes its form, so too does consciousness;
for it performs thousands of actions without anything other than the vibration of the atomic consciousness.
He does nothing at all that was not already done; abandoning even the slightest sense of difference, he goes, hears, touches, smells, speaks, acts, and sleeps. (25)
Nothing whatsoever exists that is not already present; meditating thus upon the truth, know that whatever you do is but the pure, all-pervading consciousness alone. (26)
Brahman is of an expanded form; nothing other than that exists, since the entire multitude of objects remains composed of the essence of consciousness. (27)

Whether it be of the nature of expansion, of the nature of the unfolding of manifestation, or of the nature of the unfolding of its sublation, Brahman—which is described as being liberated from its own nature—causes one to reach the ultimate conclusion in the inner self (pratīci), by means of the words beginning with "padārtha" [and so forth]. || 27 ||
All this universe is indeed consciousness; there is no other conceptualization.
In this mere radiance of consciousness, which is named the "web of the world," [there is nothing else]. 28.

Whence arises the false apprehension that "this is one thing and that is another," given that consciousness alone exists in all its various forms? Since even the object of cognition does not exist at all, how can there be bondage and liberation? (29)
By the word "also" (api), it is implied that the cause of that [suffering] is also [to be abandoned]. || 29 ||

Forcefully casting aside all fruitless conceits regarding the thought that "this is liberation" or "this indeed is bondage," remain as one who is silent, self-controlled, free from pride and intoxication, a great soul performing his own duty, truly devoid of egoism.

O Rāma, having forcibly cast off with all effort every thought characterized by fruitless conceit—such as "this is liberation" or "this is bondage"—and having become silent through the mastery of all the senses beginning with speech, self-controlled, and free from pride and intoxication, remain as a great soul (mahātman) devoid of egoism while performing the duties of kingship and so forth appropriate to yourself; this is the meaning. || 30 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and fourteenth canto, titled "The Instruction on the Supreme Reality," in the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa* of the *Mokṣopāya* section of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa*, the work of the Sage. 114.
Thus ends the one hundred and fourteenth chapter, titled "Instruction on the Supreme Reality," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and fifteenth canto. Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
O sinless one, you are a great doer, a great enjoyer, and a great renouncer.
Having abandoned all doubts and having relied upon eternal fortitude. || 1 ||
Here, by means of explanations of such terms as "the Great Creator" and others, Śambhu describes the characteristics of those liberated while living for Bhṛṅgin, who requested them.
Having abandoned all doubts regarding merit and demerit, one should contemplate the self as the changeless, steadfast, and fearless reality.
Śrī Rāma said:
What is meant by "the great doer"? What is meant by "the great renouncer"? What is meant by "the great enjoyer"? O Lord, explain this to me correctly. (2)
What characteristics does one who has attained [this state] possess to be called a "Great Agent" (mahākartā)? This applies to all three cases as well.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāma, this triad of vows was formerly proclaimed by the moon-crested Lord [Śiva] to Bhṛṅgīśa, by which he became free from his fever.

With reference to the time of practice, these are called the three vows; however, at the time of fruition, these three characteristics become established just like [the qualities of] immortality and so forth. This one is Bhṛṅgīśa. || 3 ||
Formerly, on the northern peak of Mount Sumeru, which resembled fire, the bearer of the crescent moon stood together with his entire retinue.
O Rāma, the highly effulgent Bhṛṅgīśa, who possessed limited knowledge, stood before the Lord of Umā with palms joined in reverence and, bowing down, questioned him. || 5 ||

He possesses subtle consciousness, yet his self-knowledge is dull. Although he has attained omniscience at the very moment of attaining the state of a Gaṇapati, the statement is made by attributing dullness to his self-knowledge due to his attachment to worldly enjoyments, so as not to make it common with the knowledge of others. || 5 ||
Bhṛṅgīśa said: O Blessed One, Lord of the gods, omniscient Supreme Lord,
please tell me quickly and out of compassion that which I am about to ask.
O Lord, beholding this structure of saṃsāra, as flickering as a wave, I am utterly bewildered, being deprived of rest in the ultimate reality.
Fickle as a wave and perishable; even though the reality has been known, he remains devoid of rest due to attachment to enjoyments. (7)
Having accepted this beloved and well-established internal certainty,
I remain free from feverish distress within this dilapidated house of the world.
Delightful, pleasant with the joy of rest—may I remain, may I abide. 8.
Īśvara said: "O sinless one, casting aside all doubts and taking recourse in eternal fortitude, become a great enjoyer, a great doer, and a great renouncer."
Bhṛṅgīśa said:
What is meant by "the great doer," and what is meant by "the great enjoyer"?
What is meant by "the great renouncer"? O Lord, explain this to me correctly.
Īśvara said: O highly fortunate one, he who performs dharma and adharma as they occur, free from doubt and undecaying, is called a great doer.
In this regard, he explains the portion "having abandoned all doubts" with the words "dharma and adharma.

Because of the certainty that the Self is neither agent nor enjoyer, one is free from the suspicion of agency and so forth. It should be understood that this is a statement regarding the power of knowledge—similar to the verse "even having slain these worlds"—and not a permission for acting according to one's own whims. || 11 ||
He who acts without regard for passion and hatred, pleasure and pain, merit and demerit, or fruit and its absence— he is called the Great Doer.

By the terms "attachment," "aversion," and so forth, the activities that manifest them are meant. He who performs actions with a mind free from desire—regardless of fruit or non-fruit, that is, the desirable or undesirable—and with the sole purpose of maintaining the world order (lokasaṃgraha) [is a Sāttvika agent]. || 12 ||
He who acts with silence, free from egoism, pure, and devoid of envy, performing his duties without agitation— he is called a great doer.

Mauna is the practice of a sage, such as meditation (manana) and yoga; it is that action in which agitation has ceased—that agitation caused by the failure to attain results or by their being otherwise than expected.
He whose mind is not stained by doubts regarding dharma and adharma in matters both auspicious and inauspicious is called a great doer.

By means of dharma and adharma imagined through the false suspicion, "I am righteous" or "I am sinful," regarding actions such as the performance of a horse sacrifice or the eating of *kalañja* which have occurred by chance. || 14 ||
He who is free from affection toward all things and remains like a witness,
acting in his duty without desire— he is called a great doer.
Free from both agitation and joy, with an equanimous and pure intellect,
he who neither grieves nor exults is called a great doer (mahākartṛ).
He does not grieve over the causes of sorrow, nor does he rejoice over the causes of prosperity. || 16 ||
The wise sage whose mind is unattached at the time of action,
who abides in conduct appropriate to his task, is called a great doer.

At the time when the purpose appropriate [to him] has been brought about by his past karma (*prārabdha*), he abides in a conduct consistent with that task and possesses activities conducive to that purpose. 17.
He who, remaining indifferent while performing action as well as non-action, attains an absolute internal equanimity—he is called a great doer. (18)

While performing prescribed and prohibited actions— whether by his own volition or by chance— he attains equanimity toward both, through a firm internal conviction that the Self is not the agent, thereby relinquishing the sense of being the doer and the causal agency resulting from the instigation of others. || 18 ||
He who is peaceful by his very nature and does not indeed abandon equanimity, even while performing good and evil deeds—he is called a "Great Doer. (19)

He who, even while practicing what is beneficial toward friends and what is harmful toward enemies, does not abandon equanimity—because he is by his very nature peaceful; for his nature, which is like the moon’s quality of cooling, does not become otherwise. This is the meaning. || 19 ||
He whose mind remains exactly the same during birth, maintenance, and destruction, as well as during rising and setting, is called a great doer.

Among the five modifications of being—birth and so forth—namely arising, growth, setting, and decay—he is one whose mind remains equanimous toward bodies accompanied by these changes, due to his vision of the Self as pure Being, free from modification. || 20 ||
He hates nothing whatsoever, nor does he long for anything;
he partakes of everything as it comes to him—he is called a great enjoyer.

He states the characteristics of the Great Enjoyer with the words "nothing at all," etc. "The present" (prakṛtam) means that which is under discussion, brought forward by what has already begun. || 21 ||
He who does not grasp even while grasping, does not act even while acting,
and does not enjoy even while enjoying— he is called a great enjoyer.

Even while perceiving objects through the senses, he does not grasp them because he is established in the non-dual, unattached, and perfect Self. Even while performing actions such as grasping and moving with his hands, feet, and so forth, he does not act because of his realization that the Self is actionless.
Likewise, by seeing the Self as eternally satisfied and transcending hunger and other needs, he does not eat. || 22 ||
He whose intellect is unwearied observes the entire worldly transaction like a witness; he who is free from desire is called a great enjoyer.
The witness is likewise one who is indifferent and a direct observer. || 23 ||
He whose mind does not deviate because of pleasures or pains, through ritual actions or their application, nor by existence or non-existence which cause delusion— he is called a great enjoyer.

Through the application of activities such as victory and defeat, through existence and non-existence, and through gain and loss—the delusions being the distractions caused by these—he does not transcend [the Self] and does not become distracted. || 24 ||
He who perceives even old age, death, sovereignty, and poverty as truly delightful— he is called a great enjoyer.

It is beautiful through the vision of Brahman; the sense is that just as a golden tiger is beautiful through the vision of gold, so too is this [the world] beautiful [through the vision of Brahman]. || 25 ||
He who receives great joys and sorrows equally, like the ocean receiving its waters, is called a great enjoyer.
He accepts [them] equally, with impartial conduct, for the sake of enjoyment. || 26 ||
Non-violence, equanimity, and contentment are like rays from the orb of the moon;
because he does not consume [them], he is called the Great Enjoyer.
Because they have neither approached nor not approached. The word "and" (ca) serves to aggregate the multitude of qualities previously mentioned. || 27 ||
He who eats pungent, sour, salty, bitter, unrefined, refined,
and excellent food with equanimity— he is called a great eater.
Even food that is inferior, tasteless, and lowly. || 28 ||
He who perceives with equanimity the flavorful and the flavorless, as well as sexual union and its cessation—he is called a gentle and great enjoyer. (29)
One who has ceased from sexual pleasure, which is an obstacle to spiritual delight. || 29 ||
He whose equanimity remains steadfast toward alkaline substances and various kinds of sugar, as well as toward the auspicious and the inauspicious— he is called a great enjoyer.
In the sense of *khaṇḍaprakāra*, it refers to a variety of food items prepared with sugar. || 30 ||
Having abandoned the conceptualization that "this is edible" and "this is inedible," he who eats with all longing gone is called a great eater. (31)
"Unfit for food" means that which cannot be eaten, such as things that are tasteless or bitter; "conceptualized" means conceptualization itself. (31)
He who experiences adversity and prosperity, delusion and bliss, whether inferior or superior,
with an even-minded intellect, is called a great enjoyer.
The inferior consists of coarse grain such as kodrava, meager food, poor clothing, and so forth; the superior consists of excellent things such as divine food, clothing, and so forth. || 32 ||
He by whom merit and demerit, pleasure and pain, as well as death and birth, have been renounced through wisdom—he is called a great renouncer. (33)

Thus, by means of the intellect characterized as previously described—that is, by the intellect of the non-dual Self which is full of unsurpassed bliss—or else, by that [intellect] through which the false has been completely abandoned. || 33 ||
He by whom all desires, all doubts, all efforts, and all certainties have been relinquished through wisdom— he is called a great renouncer.
All endeavors—the activities of speech, mind, and body—have been completely abandoned on every side simply because of the obstruction of sense-objects by wisdom. || 34 ||
He by whom the very existence of the body, the mind, the senses, and the mental state has been truly renounced— verily, he is called a great renouncer.
By which false perception the existence of the body and so forth, along with their respective sufferings, has been abandoned and cast off. || 35 ||
"I have neither body nor birth, nor do actions—whether appropriate or inappropriate—belong to me.
One who possesses such internal certainty is called a "great renouncer. (36)
Whether in what is appropriate and inappropriate, or in what is prescribed and prohibited, or in the form of performing desired and undesired actions. || 36 ||
He by whom dharma and adharma, as well as the mental reflections and desires of the mind,
have all been completely renounced within, is called a great renunciant.
Dharma and adharma are bodily; mental deliberation is mental; and striving, such as speech and so forth, is physical activity. || 37 ||
Whatever extent of this entire perceived world is observed, he by whom it has been thoroughly renounced is called a great renouncer. (38)
It has been completely abandoned because it is sublated by perfect right vision. || 38 ||
Thus it was said by the God of gods to Bhṛṅgīśa; O sinless one, O Rāma, maintain this vision and remain free from all feverish distress.
He summarizes: "Thus," [it is said]. || 39 ||
Brahman alone exists—eternally risen, pure in nature, infinite, and primordial—not even a fraction of anything else can be conceived.
Meditate thus, having attained the state of stainlessness; reach Nirvana with all your mental fluctuations stilled and purified. (40)
He instructs Rāma in that meditation by which one effortlessly becomes a great doer, a great enjoyer, or a great renouncer— namely, "the eternally risen": "O Rāma,

having attained the state of the stainless (nirañjana) through the elimination of the five sheaths beginning with the body and the three states [of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep], you shall perceive the remainder."

Meditate thus: "There exists only Brahman, the eternally risen, stainless nature of the Self; there is no conceptualization of anything other than That. By constantly meditating in this way, through the manifestation of that state, you shall become one whose mental fluctuations have been stilled by the removal of the impurities of conceptualization; such being the case, attain—that is, reach—nirvāṇa. This is the meaning. || 40 ||
The Brahman is free from affliction, the sole seed for all the effects of every kalpa, and the very form of the Supreme Self;
it is vast, having expanded all states of being, and is that space which exists and shines here as whatever little appears, my dear.

O dear one, whatever appears here in this saṃsāra, throughout all the kalpas—that is, during the entire duration of time consisting of two parārdhas—is none other than Brahman, the Supreme Self; it is the single seed and the fundamental cause of all manifest effects, free from affliction, and itself devoid of the transformations such as birth and so forth. And that—
Even though all conceptualizations of existence are expanded by the various distinctions of vast creation, it remains only the void, the sky;
the meaning is that it is entirely devoid of all conceptualization. || 41 ||
"Nothing else whatsoever exists anywhere at any time; even that which appears to be real is actually unreal.
O virtuous one, remaining within with such a firm internal conviction, abide free from the play of doubt.

The sense is this: since nothing whatsoever—whether existent (sat) or non-existent (asat), gross or subtle, and by the force of the word "api" (also), even the cause—is possible as something other than Brahman, which is of a single essence; for if it were separate from the Existent, it would result in its being non-existent, and if it were not separate, it would result in the Existent being of a single essence, and no other alternative is conceivable. Therefore, O virtuous one, you...

The meaning is: having first established oneself through the power of the practice of samādhi with the firm internal conviction, "I am indeed the True Brahman," one should gradually ascend to the seventh stage (bhūmikā) and remain in that very state, free from the play of doubt.
Being inward-turned while constantly performing the entire multitude of external duties,
you never experience weariness and attain the state of one whose egoism has been cast away.

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: O holy man (*sādho*), if you, being inward-turned (*antarmukhaḥ*), attain a state where egoism (*ahaṃkṛti*) is cast aside, then even while performing the entire multitude of external duties, you shall never at any time experience weariness. 43.
Thus ends the one hundred and fifteenth canto, titled "The Description of the Three Vows," in the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*, composed by the sage Vālmīki. 115.
Thus ends the one hundred and fifteenth canto, titled "The Description of the Three Vows," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and sixteenth canto.
Śrī Rāma said: O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, within the mind known as the ego (ahaṃkāra),...
Or rather, what would be the mark of a being in a state of dissolution?
The constant melting of the mind in the fourth and subsequent stages,
as well as the characteristics of that which has melted, are described here from the perspective of the person who is the locus.
The mark (liṅga) or characteristic of the mind of a being whose latent impressions have been exhausted. || 1 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: For even when they arise by force, defects such as greed and delusion do not stain the pure heart, just as water does not stain a lotus.

Thus questioned, Vasiṣṭha first states that the primary characteristic of that [state] is indeed the destruction of defects such as greed and delusion—beginning with the word "by force" (*balāt*). "Produced" (*saṃjātāḥ*) means brought about; the sense is that they were produced even by force by another for the sake of testing and so forth. "Sita" means pure and bright. || 2 ||
The glories beginning with sympathetic joy (muditā) never abandon the face [of the practitioner], when the mind consisting of egoism dissolves and evil deeds dissolve. (3)

He states that constant cheerfulness of countenance and so forth is also a characteristic of that [state], saying "joy and so on. When evil deeds—the cause of despondency—dissolve through the fire of knowledge, [joy arises]. (3)
The knots of latent impressions (vāsanā) are completely severed and gradually snap asunder; anger becomes attenuated, and delusion indeed passes into weakness.
Elaborating upon what has been stated, he also mentions other characteristics, beginning with the words "vāsanā" (impressions) and so forth. || 4 ||
Desire goes to exhaustion and greed flees elsewhere;
the senses do not exult, nor does distress manifest intensely. (5)
Sufferings do not increase for him, nor do pleasures leap up;
equanimity arises everywhere in his heart, bestowing a cooling peace.
Coolness is the cessation of heat; she is the giver of that. || 6 ||
As for these things such as pleasure and pain, whether they are seen on the face or indeed perceived [internally], because of their insignificance, they do not smear the mind.

But surely, even in the case of the wise (*jñānin*), signs such as pleasure and pain, or clarity and turbidity, are occasionally observed on their faces— just as in the case of Śikhidhvaja upon hearing the curse of Durvāsas regarding the jar, or as in the case of Vasiṣṭha through Viśvāmitra’s deception of Hariścandra and the killing of his son. How then can there be [the states of] joy and so forth?

Regarding the characteristic that "the face of Śrī does not abandon [its natural state]," he says: "pleasure, pain, and so forth. Even if, due to the intensity of the *prārabdha* karma that brings about experience (*bhojaka-prārabdha*), there should occasionally arise the appearance of pain or the impurity of its signs, these two do not stain that mind, because they are sublated by the cognition of their falsity in the subsequent moment. Thus, it is not so.
The meaning is: the obstruction of the clarity of innate bliss and so forth. || 7 ||
As the mind dissolves, it becomes an object of longing for the hosts of gods;
the sage attains this state, and within him there arises an equanimity like the cool moonlight.
Thus the Great Body flows—tranquil and lovely, serviceable and unobstructed, restrained yet powerful, and pure. (9)
Unopposed means not obstructing the desires of others. Nibhṛta means modest. || 9 ||
Though it is contradictory as both existence and non-existence, though diverse, and though vast,
the delusion of worldly existence brings neither joy nor sorrow to the wise.
Though opposed by prosperity, adversity, non-existence, and poverty—conditions that are even uneven—for the virtuous whose egoism has dissolved, [all these are equal]. 10.
Fie upon that lowest of men who, out of delusion, does not proceed toward this reality— which is to be accomplished by the light of the intellect and is free from all calamities.

Now, demonstrating the extreme ease with which self-attainment is achieved and censuring those who do not strive for that purpose, he concludes with the words "by the light of the intellect" (*buddhyālokena*). This means by the illumination characterized as the intellect; or alternatively, *āloka* is the act of looking through a mind that is turned inward (*pratyakpravaṇā*), and when that [self] is attained—which is to be accomplished by that alone—the calamities (*āpadaḥ*) have set.
The meaning is: "Fie upon him who does not apply himself toward such a reality as the Supreme Self! || 11 ||

O friend, for one who desires to cross the ocean of birth—a mine of jewels of suffering—in order to attain the rest that is fitting after a long time, the thought "Who am I? How is this world? What might the beyond be? And what is the use of enjoyments?
is the supreme means. (12)

If it is asked, "In that case, what is the first means for its commencement? he replies: "Discernment and dispassion. [He says: "O dear one, for a person desiring to cross—that is, wishing to transcend—the ocean of saṃsāra, which is characterized by birth and death and serves as a mine of jewels of suffering, [there is the goal] on its further shore, whose nature is unsurpassed bliss."

"What am I? What is this world? And what might the supreme reality of the Self be like? What would be gained by these trivial enjoyments?"—this very mind, cultivated through constant practice in the form of inquiry and dispassion, is the primary intended means (*abhyupāya*) for attaining long-accustomed rest. Therefore, the meaning is that one should take refuge in that alone. || 12 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and sixteenth canto, titled "The Description of the Characteristics of the Dissolved Mind," in the *Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa* of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa*, composed by Vālmīki, according to the tradition of the Ṛṣis.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Characteristics of the Dissolved Mind," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and seventeenth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
"Your first ancestor was the king named Ikṣvāku."
Listen now to how he was liberated, O descendant of the Ikṣvāku lineage. || 1 ||
In this inquiry as to "Who am I? and "How is the world?", the discernment proclaimed by Manu regarding Ikṣvāku is now fully set forth as an illustration.
The meaning is: "Just as the Primordial Person, the Root Person, was liberated through a certain kind of inquiry and came to rest in the state previously mentioned, listen to that inquiry. (1)
A king named Ikṣvāku, while protecting his own kingdom,
once went into solitude and reflected in his mind.

"What could be the cause of this phenomenal world of appearances, which exists in a state of agitation through birth and death, and fluctuation through pleasure and pain?"—thus [he reflected] within himself. (3)
Thus he reflected within himself; this is to be connected with what precedes. || 3 ||
Though he reflected upon it, he did not discover the cause of the world;
then one day, he questioned Manu, who had arrived from the realm of Brahmā.
He did not perceive, through his discernment, his own father Manu who had come from the world of Brahmā.
To the Blessed Lord Prajāpati, who was seated in his own assembly and being honored,
Ikṣvāku said:
"O Blessed One, O treasure-house of compassion, you cause me to be joined with audacity."
Therein, he first turns Manu toward him by means of a prayer: "Me," etc. (verse 5).
This very grace of yours enables me to ask you directly:
from where has this creation come, and what is its true nature?
He indicates the portion to be questioned with the words beginning "Why? (kutaḥ) and so forth. || 6 ||
How much is this world, to whom does it belong, when did it arise, and by whom?
And how may I [be liberated] from this treacherous delusion of saṃsāra? (7)
By what number and what measure? For which enjoyer and which master? When and by whom was it composed?

These are explained by the Vedas and other authorities. Therefore, you must speak only that which is rooted in the authority of the Vedas and so forth, and has come down through the tradition of the lineage of teachers, and not otherwise.
It is indicated that something is to be conceptualized by means of reasoning. || 7 ||
"May I be liberated from this dense thicket like a bird from its net.
Manu said:
"Oh, how after a long time, through solitude, discernment has fully blossomed!"
In the expression "vimucyeya," the suffixes *ya* and *taṅ* are used in the sense of the reflexive agent (*karmakartṛ*).
You have asked an essential question that cuts through false and useless things:
"Whatever is seen here, O King, does not exist at all."

In this regard, he first provides the answer to the question concerning its essential nature (*svarūpa*)—namely, "What is the nature of this?"—by stating, "That which is this... Thus, the sense is that the world is false, having a non-existent nature, and is indeed unreal. (9)
Just as a city of Gandharvas, or as water in a desert, whatever is not seen by us does not exist at all. (10)

Now, do not the Sāṃkhyas say that the effect already exists within the material cause in an extremely subtle state and is merely manifested by instrumental causes? And do not the Vedāntins say that the existent Brahman itself becomes the world-form at the time of creation? How then can it be said that "it does not exist"? To this, he replies with the words "But that which..."—that which is not perceived by the witness-consciousness or by the senses.
The meaning is that not even the slightest thing exists within its own material cause, because there is no evidence for it. || 10 ||
That which transcends the six senses with the mind as the sixth, which is indeed nothing at all, yet is indestructible—that exists here and is called the True Self (Sadātman). || 11 ||
It might even not exist; the meaning is that there is not even the possibility of its existence. He states the second [point] with the words "indestructible."
But this succession of creations, O King, rich with all that is visible,
has attained its reflection in that very same great mirror.

Regarding the term "reflection": just as reflections are [perceived] through the superimposition of association with the existence of a mirror, let it be that the world is permeated by the existence of Brahman; nevertheless, its own inherent existence does not exist at all.
Thus, the statement that "it does not exist" is entirely logical—this is the intended meaning. || 12 ||
Luminosities, arising by their own nature, are the powers of Brahman’s manifestation;
some attain the state of the cosmic egg, while others become living beings.

If it is asked, "What then is the intention of the Śruti which declares that Brahman itself assumes the state of the individual soul (jīva) of the world after resolving, 'May I be many, may I procreate'?", he says: "Luminosity is its very nature," etc.
The powers of manifestation are the reflections of consciousness (cidābhāsa). "The state of the cosmic egg" means assuming that form through the identification with the gross aggregate.
The state of being an element (bhūtatā) consists in having the nature of earth and so forth through the conceit of identification with them. || 13 ||
Others undergo change; thus does the existence of the world persist.
There is neither bondage nor liberation; there is only Brahman, free from all affliction.
There is neither unity nor duality; it is the essence of consciousness that unfolds.

And otherness consists in the state of being the fourfold collection of living beings. Thus, he says, "There is no bondage," meaning that while the imagination of bondage and so forth occurs due to the delusion of the reflections of consciousness within false limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), in reality there is no possibility of such bondage. || 14 ||
Just as one and the same water manifests through the various breakage of waves, so too does consciousness manifest, yet it is nothing at all.
Cast far away the conceptualization of bondage and liberation; remain established in your own nature, free from the fear of becoming and non-becoming, for you are the very essence of fearlessness.
He concludes the answer to the second question with the verse beginning "ekaṃ": just as one and the same water [appears] through the distinctions of waves...
Just as a flame flickers, so too does consciousness (cit) manifest through the various distinctions of the world; yet, because these are merely illusion (māyāmātra), they are nothing at all.

Therefore, having cast far away the delusions of bondage and liberation, become one for whom there is no fear of worldly existence—this is the meaning: remain as the very essence of the fearless Brahman. || 15 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and seventeenth canto, titled "The Dialogue with Ikṣvāku," in the first part of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the glorious Vāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa composed by Vālmīki, belonging to the Ṛṣi tradition.
Thus ends the one hundred and seventeenth chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Ikṣvāku and Manu," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and eighteenth canto. Manu said:
When true consciousnesses, which are pure awareness consisting of nothing but consciousness, have turned toward the state of volitional intention (*saṃkalpa*), [the world appears].
O King, for those who live, their lives become like waves upon the water. || 1 ||
From what cause does creation arise, when, of whom, and by what means? To these questions, the means for perceiving the Self have been proclaimed here by Manu.
In that regard, he first states the cause for pure consciousness (*śuddhasaṃvit*) assuming the state of an individual soul (*jīva*): "By volition," etc.

For pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), which is pure awareness, there exist reflections within ignorance (*avidyā*)—which is variegated by various latent impressions (*saṃskāra*). When these impressions transform into the form of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), those [reflections] become individual souls (*jīva*) by being delimited by that [organ]. || 1 ||
Those living beings transmigrate here in this world that has arisen from before;
the delusion regarding the states of pleasure and pain exists only in the mind, not in the Self.

When the world has previously arisen as a limiting adjunct (upādhi) and manifests as the effect of the collective and individual minds—this being the case, he states the result that follows: "pleasure and pain," etc. (Verse 2).
Just as the invisible Rāhu is perceived by means of the eclipsed moon,
so too is the Self, whose nature is pure experience, beheld through that which is visible.
"But how can the invisible Self be seen in the visible mind—whether it be suffering from transmigratory existence or liberated from it, whether there is non-discrimination or discrimination?

To this he says: "Invisible [is seen] by the visible. This means: by the visible internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), and by its final transformation in the form of direct realization, acting as the instrumental cause. || 3 ||
The Supreme Lord is not seen through scriptures nor even by a teacher;
the Self is seen only by the self, through one's own intellect established in purity.
By abiding in the state of pure being (sattva), which is the state free from the notions of "I" and "mine. || 4 ||
Just as travelers on a road are seen by one who is free from attachment and aversion, so too should one's own senses and other faculties be viewed with such an intellect. (5)
He clarifies how the absence of "I-ness" and "mine-ness" regarding the body, senses, and so forth is to be perceived by means of an illustration: "Like travelers," etc. (Verse 5).
One should show neither respect nor contempt toward these;
let them remain at ease, occupied merely as objects.
Contempt is the infliction of suffering through fasting and other such means. || 6 ||
Having completely cast away from afar, by means of the intellect, all mere objects such as the body and so forth,
remain forever absorbed in the Self with an inner organ that is perfectly cooled.
Having completely renounced all mere objects—which are common to even indifferent things—he becomes identical with the Self, abounding in that state through the vision of the pure Self. || 7 ||
The notion that "I am the body" is the bond of saṃsāra;
indeed, this notion must never be accepted by those seeking liberation.
"I am of the nature of pure consciousness alone, consisting of nothing whatsoever, subtler than the sky"— this eternal realization is not a bond to saṃsāra.

There is not even the slightest thing wherein such [a state] exists; that which is pure consciousness (cinmātra) is of that very nature, subtler than even space. This means that it is neither the cause of bondage to saṃsāra nor the cause of liberation. || 9 ||
Just as light exists everywhere within and without clear waters, so too does the Self abide in all things. (10)
He provides a corresponding illustration for the manifestation [of the world] through the entry of the unattached Consciousness (asaṅga-cit) both within and without the insentient universe, saying:
"Just as... (yathā). || 10 ||

Just as gold assumes the various forms of armlets and other ornaments through a diversity of arrangement, so too does the Self assume the nature of the world and its like, being both identical to and different from itself.

Just as the forms of armlets and so forth are merely the variety of the arrangement and placement of parts belonging to gold itself, in the same way, the world is likewise [an appearance] of the Self within its source, which is Māyā; such is the meaning. || 11 ||
The waves of living beings, which are the ripples of the world-net, flow into the terrifying great ocean of desire, which is overwhelmed by the submarine fire of destruction. 12.

In order to represent himself as the Agastya who drinks up the ocean of time, he describes time as the ocean that is the place for the withdrawal of the river of the world—beginning with the words "vināśa" (destruction). It is distinguished by being pervaded by the submarine fire (*vāḍava*) which is destruction itself; and the "waves" of these [rivers] are the multitudes of living beings (*bhūta*). || 12 ||
Nevertheless, O King, always contemplate yourself as the great Agastya, who is the one that drinks up even this ocean of time which remains unfilled even today.
He is the one who drinks— that is, the consumer— of the ocean of time, which remains even today unsatiated and unfulfilled despite devouring the entire web of the world.
Having abandoned the notion of selfhood in this non-self— the web of visible things such as the body and so forth— and having ascended to pure being, remain hidden and abide as you please.
Sentient being is the state of being free from latent impressions. || 14 ||
Just as a mother weeps for her son, having forgotten him while he was sleeping in the hollow of her breast, so does this person weep for his own sake.
He says that grief arises from the delusion of non-attainment even though the Self is eternally attained: "In the hollow of the breasts... (verse 15).
Not realizing that the self is ageless and immortal, one weeps at the destruction of the body, crying out:
"Alas, I am slain! I am helpless! I am lost! (16)
Upon the expenditure of the body, that is, at the destruction of the physical frame. || 16 ||
Just as water appears in various forms through its own movement,
so too does the conscious Brahman expand by the power of volition.
It expands on all sides and increases through a succession of effects. || 17 ||

Having established your mind—freed from the stain of volitional construction—within the Self, and being as if completely stilled, remain here as if unmoved even during the vibration of thought; established in yourself, happy, rule this kingdom.

O son, having established in the Self a mind freed from the stains of volitional constructs, you remain as one who is virtually extinguished through the cessation of the entire cycle of existence along with its roots— remaining only as a residual appearance for the sake of experiencing the *prārabdha* karma.
Thus, even amidst the movement of the body and senses for the purpose of worldly transaction, because that movement is a mere appearance, you are here as the motionless Brahman itself.

Remain established in your own state and happy on the plane of worldly affairs; rule and protect this kingdom. [In the word "śādhi," the substitution of *dhi* for *hi* occurs because the substitute *śāsa* is not considered established (*asiddha*) due to its status as an augment (*ābhīya*). 18.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighteenth sarga, titled "The Dialogue between Ikṣvāku and Manu," within the Nirvāṇa Section of the Means to Liberation, in the Holy Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa composed by the Sage. 118.
Thus ends the one hundred and eighteenth canto in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and nineteenth canto.
Manu said:
The All-pervading Lord himself sports with the movements that constitute the creative emanations, like a child.
Then, having withdrawn [the universe] by means of his power of withdrawal, he abides within himself. || 1 ||

In this system, the independence of the person (puruṣa) with respect to liberation and bondage is described as resulting from the determination of the true and false nature of the self through the powers of knowledge and ignorance.

Regarding the statement, "Even while vibrating, remain here as if non-vibrating," the Lord Brahmā, having perceived through signs Ikṣvāku’s desire to know—namely, for what purpose the Supreme Self vibrates by means of *māyā* and how He remains non-vibrating—Manu spoke [the following verse]: "By means of those whose nature is creation... This all-pervading Supreme Self, through the power of ignorance (*avidyā-śakti*) which possesses the quality of procreation, [creates] for the ignorant...

It sports with vibrations consisting of successive creations; however, for the wise person, because it has been sublated by the power of knowledge (*vidyā-śakti*)—which consists of the dissolution of those [creations] and has eradicated creation along with its root—it always abides within the self, which is immutable and non-dual. This is the meaning.
In such a way that by it his own power arises through which he is bound;
in such a way that by it his own power arises through which he is released.

In this regard, he says "spontaneously" (svayam) [in verse 2], meaning that just as the power of creation arises for one who proceeds out of passion, so too does the power of withdrawal arise spontaneously for one who desists through dispassion.
Just as there are rays from the moon, the sun, fire, heated iron, and gems;
just as there are leaves and such from trees; and just as there are droplets from waterfalls. (3)

In that regard, when the Self is known as being contemplated in its nature as the universal commonality of existence (sattāsāmānya) shared by both the individual soul and the world, he provides examples for the conceptualization of the web of external and internal objects which constitute its particular manifestations: "Like the moon... and so forth.
Just as the various distinctions of rays—such as light, flames, and beams—are imagined, so too is the diversity of the world.

The logical connection (*anvaya*) is that the diversity of the cognitions and so forth that apprehend those [objects] is imagined. The mention of the seven metals is for the purpose of providing the illustration of the variegated illusion (*māyā-śabala*). || 3 ||

Likewise, this world, consisting of the intellect and so forth, is imagined within the expansive Brahman; it bestows suffering upon those who do not know It, appearing as if it were something other than That.
Oh, how wondrous is this illusion, my dear, which deludes the entire world,
since the self does not perceive itself even though it is threaded through every limb!

He says "Aho! (Oh! to express that it is indeed a marvel—due solely to the power of Māyā, which is capable of accomplishing the impossible—that there is no perception of the Self, which is all-pervading and self-luminous, yet there is a clear perception of the world, which is non-existent and lacks luminosity;
for [the Self] is woven within and without among all limbs, that is, among all external and internal entities that consist of parts.
Even though the Self is all-pervading, if one does not perceive it because of this [ignorance], [then one remains bound]. || 5 ||
He who remains with his desires stilled, contemplating that this entire world is composed of the mirror of consciousness, is happy, protected by the armor of Brahman.

He then describes that cultivation by which one may become happy upon seeing the Self, beginning with the words "consisting of the mirror of consciousness" (cidādarśamaya): the meaning is that one should cultivate the thought that the world is merely a phenomenal appearance within Brahman—like a city reflected in a mirror—and is not real. He is one for whom Brahman itself is armor, impenetrable by the arrows of delusion. (6)
One should contemplate that everything is empty, without support, and of the nature of consciousness, through a state of being free from the sense of "I" and devoid of objective form. (7)
"This is pleasant, this is not"—this is the seed of your continuous stream of suffering.
When that seed is consumed by the fire of equanimity, whence can there be any occasion for suffering? (8)
"Thus [is] the postulation of inequality"—this is the ellipsis. || 8 ||
O King, let the distinction between the pleasant and the unpleasant be swiftly severed within yourself by your own extraordinary human effort, using the weapon of non-conceptualization.

Non-cultivation consists in the forgetting of all objects of perception through the practice of samādhi. By means of that weapon characterized by such forgetting, the conceptualization of inequality—the notions of "dear" and "not dear" regarding pleasant and unpleasant things—should be cut down; for that [conceptualization] is the cause of attachment and aversion.
Let it be severed by the extraordinary effort of a person whose characteristic is the firmness of equal vision. 9.
Having cut down the forest of karma through cultivation by means of non-cultivation,
and having attained supreme attenuation, remain, O sir, truly free from sorrow.

By means of non-contemplation characterized by meditative absorption (*samādhi*), having cut down the contemplation of external objects and the forest of karma characterized by merit and demerit which motivates that [contemplation], and having attained a thinness and subtlety exceeding even the supreme ether, abide as one truly free from sorrow (*viśoka*) through its power upon the stain that is the cause of grief— this is the meaning. || 10 ||

Having filled the entire expanse of the world, yet remaining beyond all divisions; with the manifestation of the appearance of mental constructs dissolved, he possesses the splendor of discernment. Having attained the vibration of supreme bliss, he is for long free from affliction, his pure experience equalized through tranquility.
The embodiment of consciousness, free from the fear of worldly existence. || 11 ||
O son, you, having first possessed the splendor of discernment (*viveka*), through meditative absorption (*samādhi*) having dissolved the appearance of external mental constructions,
and having become one whose full Self fills the expanse of the universe, have attained the vibration—
the universal manifestation— of supreme bliss, which is the undivided bliss of Brahman.
Being of such a nature, excluded from that division, and having attained an indivisible oneness, he is thereby freed from the disease of saṃsāra;
having remained for a long time in the fifth and sixth stages,
he finally, in the seventh stage, becomes equanimous through the pacification of absolute distraction and unevenness, and white due to the fullness of his moon-like radiance.

The meaning is: "Obeisance to that fearless body of consciousness (abhaya-cid-vapuḥ) which is pure, having a clear manifestation (ābhoga-ākāra) due to the destruction of the impurity of knowledge caused by ultimate latent impressions (vāsanā). Alternatively, it should be understood that the four stages beginning with the fourth [stage] are shown in sequence by the four quarters [of the verse]. || 11 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and nineteenth sarga, titled "The Dialogue with Ikṣvāku," in the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa*, composed by Vālmīki, within the section on the means to liberation (*mokṣopāya*).
Thus ends the one hundred and nineteenth canto in the first half [of the work]. || 119 ||
The one hundred and twentieth canto.
Manu said:
First, one should increase one's wisdom through the study of the scriptures and association with virtuous people.
This is said to be the first stage of both yoga and the yogin. || 1 ||
Three stages belong to those seeking liberation; for one being liberated, there are the next [three];
and for one who is liberated, there are three further stages—thus seven stages have been shown.

Having reached the state where "extreme attenuation" occurs, he describes the various stages (*bhūmikā*) that serve as the means to that result which was previously stated as the fruit of practicing the stages of yoga, beginning with the words "In the scripture," and so forth.
Thus, the first stage is *śravaṇa* (hearing), accompanied by the fulfillment of the fourfold means (*sādhanacatuṣṭaya*) and aided by a guru, fellow students, and others.
The definitions of "stage" (*bhūmikā*) and so forth, which were already shown in the section on their arising, should be understood here as well. || 1 ||
The second is *vicāraṇā* (investigation); the third is *asaṅgabhāvanā* (contemplation of non-attachment);
and the fourth is *vilāpanī*, which consists of the dissolution of latent impressions (*vāsanā*). || 2 ||

*Vicāraṇā* is reflection (*manana*). *Nididhyāsana* is the mental cultivation of the non-dual, unattached [Self]. *Vilāpanī* is that which effects the sublation of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) consisting of ignorance and so forth through the direct realization of reality (*tattva-sākṣātkāra*). By the term "impressions" (*vāsanā*), the ignorance (*avidyā*) that is their substratum is understood. (2)
The fifth state consists of the bliss of pure consciousness;
here, the one liberated while living (jīvanmukta) abides with the appearance of being half-asleep and half-awake. || 3 ||

Pure, consisting of consciousness, and abundant with internal manifestation due to the maturation of samādhi—that bliss which is her very nature. He brings that state to the level of direct experience through an illustration: "half-... Just as a person who is half-asleep and half-awake at the end of sleep, even while hearing external sounds and so forth, remains internally attached to the bliss of slumber.
He does not desire such worldly transactions as giving a reply; likewise, the meaning is that even at the time of emergence, the yogi remains in this stage. || 3 ||
And the sixth stage consists of the nature of self-awareness;
it has the form of a single mass of bliss and is a state similar to deep sleep.

Self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) is that very state consisting of the mental modification (*vṛtti*) which has the form of Brahman, not diminishing by its own inherent nature; he states this very point with the word "bliss" (*ānanda*). || 4 ||
Then, with the fourth state stilled, there is liberation alone here;
equanimity, clarity, and gentleness—this is the seventh stage.
Now, when even that state (*vṛtti*) is exhausted, then Brahman alone remains, manifest as the full self-luminous reality;

such is the "seventh stage" for one who is still living. This very stage was previously described by me as "the enjoyment of pure clarity, equalized through tranquility" (*śamasamasita-svacchābhoga*). Since the first three stages are unified according to the method to be explained, the sixth is the fourth (*turyā*). || 5 ||
But the state beyond the fourth (turyātītā), which is supreme and of the nature of Nirvāṇa—
that seventh stage is fully matured and is not an object for those who still live.

With the intention that there is no difference between the seventh and eighth stages other than the mere fact of whether the yogi is living or not living, he says "turyātītā" (beyond the fourth). The meaning is that the seventh stage itself, when fully matured and designated as "beyond the fourth," becomes videhamukti; and that [state] would not be the domain of yogis who are still living. || 6 ||
In this context, the first three states are established as "waking" (jāgrat),
while the fourth is called "dream" (svapna), wherein the world indeed appears like a dream.
The fifth, called deep sleep (suṣupti), arises from the complete condensation of bliss;
then the sixth, characterized by non-perception, is designated as the state of Turiya.
The state beyond the fourth is the seventh stage, the supreme;
it is ungraspable by mind or speech, consisting of the nature of the self-luminous state.
He praises that very [state] with the words beginning "by mind and speech," and so forth. || 9 ||
If the object of thought is not perceived due to the power of internal withdrawal,
then there is no doubt that he is liberated by means of that great equanimity.

He states that absolute liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) results from the complete dissolution of all objects of perception into the inner self (*pratyagātman*) within that very state—referring to the seventh stage (*bhūmikā*) which is well-known by that name. || 10 ||

A person of such a mind—whether possessing a body or bodiless—becomes one whose full intellect has never before been touched by the portions of pleasure and pain arising from worldly enjoyments. || 11 ||
I neither die nor do I live; I am neither existent nor non-existent.
A man should remain delighting in the Self; that is declared to be liberation.
Regarding that state, he describes what kind of experience belongs to one liberated while living (jīvanmukta): "I do not die. (12)
Whether engaged in worldly affairs or tranquil, whether a householder or even a solitary mendicant, the living being does not grieve, having realized: "I am nothing but consciousness."
The ascetic who wanders alone is "ekaka. || 13 ||
Thinking, "I am untainted, ageless, free from passion, with tranquil latent impressions;
I am the stainless space of consciousness," one does not grieve. (14)
Thinking, "I am devoid of end and beginning, pure, awakened, undecaying, and immortal; I am peaceful, appearing as both equal and unequal," one does not grieve. (15)
Thinking that whatever exists on the tips of blades of grass, in the sky, in the sun, or among men, serpents, and gods,
is precisely that [same essence], one no longer grieves.

The meaning is: having realized the significance of the great, indivisible Mahāvākya—"I am that very Pure Consciousness (pratyak-cinmātra), which is the most well-known Pure Being (sanmātra) in the extremely minute tips of grass, in the exceedingly vast sky, and in the intensely luminous sun."
"My consciousness pervades horizontally, upward, and downward; knowing this greatness of that which possesses infinite manifestations, who indeed could suffer decay? (17)

"Knowing the greatness of that Supreme Self—that 'My greatness is all-pervading'—who, being subject to decay, would partake in the suffering of death and so forth? Thus says the Śruti: "This is the eternal greatness of the Brāhmaṇa; he does not increase by action, nor does he become smaller. Only he who knows His state, having known it, is not tainted by action."
"By an evil one," thus [it is said]. || 17 ||
An object that is pursued with habitual attachment brings pleasure;
yet that very same thing which leads to happiness quickly turns into suffering through its destruction. (18)

Since even for those liberated while living (jīvanmukta), their life depends upon the enjoyment of sense-objects, there arises the apprehension that they might experience suffering just like the ignorant when those objects perish. Anticipating this, the author speaks of the specific distinction by first describing the manner in which suffering arises for the ignorant upon the loss of sense-objects, in the verse beginning with "baddhavāsanam" (one whose latent impressions are bound). || 18 ||
The inseparable connection between pleasure and pain is well known; whether an object is pursued with intense desire or without desire, it results in the thinning of latent impressions.

The rule of coexistence is the state of being invariably concomitant. He describes the distinction of those who are liberated while living (jīvanmukta) as "having attenuated latent impressions" (tanuvāsana). In the fourth and subsequent stages, the latent impressions are attenuated, but in the seventh stage, they are entirely absent (vivāsana). || 19 ||
O sinless one, that action which is performed with an intellect whose latent impressions have been exhausted brings no pleasure, nor does it cause suffering at the time of destruction.
Thus, he says "kṣīṇa... [verse 20] to show that even their karma is non-adhesive.
Like a burnt seed, it no longer produces a sprout;
yet it is fashioned by the multitude of instruments, such as the body, senses, and so forth, through the agency of karma. (21)

Indeed, the taint of karma would occur only through the superimposition of identity with the body, senses, and so forth—which are distinct from the Self—and through the conceit that "I alone am the sole agent of the actions performed by them. Since such [conceit] does not exist for those who are liberated, he says, "by means of the body, senses, etc.," with this intention. || 21 ||
How, indeed, O dear one, can there be a single agent and enjoyer who has arisen, having completely cast off all mental constructions regarding all existing things? (22)
Having completely renounced the superimposition of "I-ness" and so forth upon all states such as the body and the senses, he has properly risen—that is, he has emerged [from them]. || 22 ||
Full and cool as the moon, he shines like the sun;
the beauty of the cotton-wool of karma, when being performed, has become [as light as] the silk-cotton tree of his body.
It has been made into a form that is accumulated. || 23 ||
Arising from the wind of knowledge, it flies up and goes away somewhere;
for every single art of a living being perishes through lack of practice. (24)
Fearing that even the portion of knowledge might perish over time just like karma, he says: "All indeed... (verse 24).
This digit of knowledge, once born within, increases day by day by its own power, like rice sown in a fertile field. (25)
The one Self, whose form is the universe, vibrates within all things, just as pure water exists within lakes and oceans;
O dear one, know that this entire world is nothing but the single portion of pure existence, in which the vast multitude of composite parts has been stilled.

Just as clear water alone shines through in lakes, rivers, and oceans, so too does the Self— whose nature is pure existence (*sanmātra*) and who is by Himself the universal form— shine through all illusory objects due to the superimposition of non-difference upon each of them. Therefore, O dear one, [realize] the entire world through the awakening to reality.

The meaning is: know that "I" am merely the residue of pure existence, which is the collection of the manifold variety of the world brought about by the cessation of the accumulation of delusion. || 26 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and twentieth chapter, titled "The Classification of the Seven Stages," in the *Pūrva-ārdha* of the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa* of the *Mokṣopāya*, within the *Vālmīki-digambara* version of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*. 20.
Thus ends the one hundred and twentieth chapter, titled "The Classification of the Seven Stages," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and twenty-first canto. Manu said:
As long as there is a desire for the enjoyment of sense-objects, so long does the designation "living being" (jīva) apply to the self (ātman).
For even that hope, when possessed by a lack of discernment, does not exist in reality.
That by which the individual soul is drawn downward, and that by which it is uplifted and liberated—
these two states have been correctly explained to you here by the Sage after having analyzed them thoroughly.

If the Self is indeed Brahman, which is unsurpassed bliss, then for how long does it bear the designation "jīva" due to ignorance? To this he says: "As long as... He further states that this [designation] is not real, saying: "...through non-discrimination. (1)
When hope comes to an end through the power of discernment,
then the self, having cast off the state of being a living soul (jīvatva), attains the state of Brahman, free from all affliction.
The destruction [of suffering] occurs through the destruction of ignorance; this is the refutation [of the opponent's view]. || 2 ||
Moving for a long time from above to below and again from below to above, do not become a water-jar on the rope of anxiety for the water-wheel of saṃsāra. (3)
He says "abandon that" because the very desire for enjoyment drags one toward heaven, hell, and so forth—referring to this with the words "from above.
The meaning is: do not become like a water-jar in the rope around the neck of the jar, which consists of the thought of enjoyment; do not be bound like a jar. || 3 ||
Those fools who, out of delusion, cling to this dense illusion of worldly convention— the thought "this is mine" and "I am this"— go downward from below to even further below.
He demonstrates the bondage between her and the objects of the senses, characterized by their mutual embracing of each other's necks, with the words "this" and so forth.
"‘This is hers,’ ‘this is mine,’ ‘this is he,’ ‘I am this’—
those by whom such delusion has indeed been abandoned through wisdom go higher and ever higher."

Having restated that very point, and thereby causing one to abandon both its root—the superimposition of identity—and its fruit, [the author] declares its result, which is supreme excellence, with the words "of this" (asya). || 5 ||
Relying without delay upon your own self-luminous Self, remain filling the entire space; O King, behold the worlds!
Behold the sky of consciousness alone, which fills all worlds on every side and is full without any intervening gap.
As soon as the form of consciousness is thus realized as all-pervasive and undivided,
at that very moment one has crossed over saṃsāra and attained the state of the Supreme Lord.
The extended is the full. || 7 ||
One should cultivate the thought: "Whatever Brahmā, Indra, Viṣṇu, and Varuṇa are prepared to do, I, whose body is consciousness, perform all of that. (8)
Now, one might object: "How can he who lacks the status of being the creator of the world and so forth have attained the state of the Supreme Lord?
To this, he says: "Brahmendra... (verse 8).
Whatever is proclaimed in whichever philosophical systems at whatever time, O dear one, all that is indeed true; for the play of consciousness is unrestrained.

If it is asked, "Since all activities are unreal, how can one who knows reality conceive of the self as an agent within them?"—this is not a fault. With the intention that the reality of all conceptual constructions is possible through the very existence of the Self, he says:
"In those... [verse 9]. That is, in the philosophical systems (darśana) and scriptures (śāstra).
By what can that supreme bliss be compared, which belongs to one who has become pure consciousness alone, who has crossed over death, and who is free from the mind?
Now, one might ask: what is the gain from crossing over saṃsāra? To this he says: "the state of pure consciousness" (cinmātratvam).
The meaning is that the gain is precisely the attainment of incomparable, self-luminous bliss. || 10 ||

Meditating on the world as neither non-empty nor empty, neither of the nature of insentience nor consisting of consciousness, neither of the nature of the self nor of another nature—be thus, O Bhava! (11)

If the world is non-empty by virtue of the existence of Brahman, then there is the consequence of duality. If it is empty because of the negation "not this, not this," then there is a contradiction of the Lordship characterized as the agency of all. Likewise, if the world is indeed of the nature of the insentient, then the manifestation of consciousness would also be impossible; for it is only that which is permeated by the luminous form through the process of triplication (*trivṛtkaraṇa*) that can be illumined by the illuminating light.

It is formless (*nīrūpa*). If, however, its being a modification of consciousness (*cid-vikāratā*) is accepted for the sake of its being permeated by consciousness (*cid-anuvedha*), then consciousness itself would incur the state of having modifications (*savikāratā*). Likewise, if it were not of the nature of the Self (*anātmarūpatva*), there would be no connection between the world and the unattached Self, and consequently, the world would fail to obtain existence and manifestation (*sattā-sphūrti*). But if it were of the nature of the Self (*ātmarūpatva*), there would be no sublation (*bādha*) by knowledge (*jñāna*), and so forth. To avoid such defects, he resorts to the doctrine of indeterminability (*anirvacanīyatā*): [The text continues: ...he avoids [these] defects by taking recourse to indeterminability (*anirvacanīyatā*).
Nor [is it] so, [it is said]. || 11 ||
Having attained this true nature, primordial matter (prakṛti) comes to rest;
there is no place called liberation, nor time, nor any other state.
How, then, is that [suffering] pacified? To this he says: "Having attained"—that is, having directly realized—this own ultimate nature of the Self. || 12 ||
Through the destruction of egoism and delusion, this nature—which is called "mental cultivation" (bhāvanā)—dissolves; this indeed is liberation. || 13 ||
*Prakṛti* is the innate nature of the Self. *Bhāvanā* is the reconnection with one's own nature that had been forgotten since beginningless time;
it is the final cognitive state (*vṛtti*) of direct realization, and because it enters into that [nature], it is designated by that name—that is, it is called "realization" (*sākṣātkāra*).
When this occurs, then this very well-known inner self (*pratyagātman*) becomes that liberation (*mokṣa*) renowned in the scriptures; such is the meaning. || 13 ||

With the fickleness of investigating the meaning of the scriptures stilled, with the curiosity for various poetic sentiments and dramas ceased, and with the turbulence of all conceptual constructions entirely dispelled, he remains at ease, equanimous, and established in his eternal nature. (14)
He explains how one liberated while living (jīvanmukta) abides through such direct realization with the verse beginning "praśānta":

all inquiry into the meaning of the scriptures, inquiry into the meaning of poetry, drama, and so forth, as well as the distractions of worldly dualities such as the pleasant and unpleasant, cease; thus he is equanimous (sama). || 14 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-first chapter, titled "The Dialogue with Ikṣvāku," in the *Pūrva-āśrama* of the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa* within the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*, the sacred work of the Sage. 121.
Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-first chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Ikṣvāku and Manu," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and twenty-second canto.
Manu said:
"Covered by whatever [it may be], and fed by whatever [it may be]..."
And wherever he may sleep, he shines like a sovereign emperor. || 1 ||
The conduct of the liberated ascetic here, who is established in the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta) through firmly rooted self-realization, is described by Manu according to its characteristics.

He elaborates upon that very state of the yogin which was described as "remaining happily in equanimity, with all disturbances of conceptual construction entirely cast aside," beginning with the words "by whatever [means]": "Covered" means clothed in garments; "fed" means nourished by food.
That yogin is like a sovereign emperor (*samrāj*), having reached the ultimate limit of human bliss. This comparison to a king is intended for those of inferior vision.

But from the perspective of ultimate reality, there is no comparison for that bliss; for, according to such scriptural passages as "from which words turn back," it is established that [this bliss] is limitless, being like a great ocean compared to the mere droplets of the worldly bliss that culminates in the bliss of Hiraṇyagarbha. || 1 ||
Abandoning the constraints of the scriptures regarding caste, duty, and the conduct of the stages of life,
he emerges from the snare of the world like a lion from its cage.

He describes the renunciation of the wise (*vidvatsaṃnyāsa*) as being established by implication for that [person]: "varṇa... and so on. It means one who is free from the restraint of the scriptures—that is, from being bound like a servant—and from the collection of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) such as agency and enjoyership regarding actions and their fruits in this world and the next, which are the cause of bondage in the world, like a net.
Thaḥ || 2 ||
Transcending the domain of speech and abandoned by the state of longing for sense objects, he attained an indescribable splendor, like the expanse of the sky in autumn.
It is the object of experience alone—the unsurpassed bliss that transcends speech; for this very reason, it is abandoned by the state of longing for sense-objects.
Profound and serene like a great lake in the mountains,
undisturbed by the flavor of supreme bliss, he rejoices in himself by means of his own self.
The "rasa" is the tasting of the supreme bliss, which is its continuous relishing; therefore, he is unagitated and undeviating. || 4 ||
Renouncing the fruits of all actions, eternally contented, and independent,
he is stained neither by merit nor by sin, nor by anything else.
And by other [states] such as joy, dejection, and so forth. || 5 ||
Just as a crystal is not stained by a reflection,
so the knower of reality is not stained within by the fruit of action.
By the fruit of karma—that is, by the pleasure, pain, and so forth brought about by *prārabdha*—there is "coloring," which is the attainment of another form. (6)
Dwelling amidst the multitude of people, he experiences neither weariness nor delight through the wounding or honoring of his body, as if these were occurring in a mere reflection.

He explains that very point clearly with the words "wandering" (*viharann iti*). Because one perceives [the body] as false—like a reflection of the body—through the piercing, cutting, and honoring of the body, it is said to be "as if occurring in a reflection" (*pratibimbagatair iva*). || 7 ||
He is beyond praise and free from transformation, devoid of both the worshiper and the object of worship;
yet he is both united with and separated from all methods of conduct and discipline.

"Though worthy of worship, he is not honored; though without praise, he does not seek commendation; and though devoid of worship, he remains unchanging"—in this *karmadhāraya* compound, the adjectives are to be understood in their respective order. The phrase beginning with "even when joined" (*saṃyuktaśca*) and so forth is an elaboration of this very point. (8)
Therefore, the world does not tremble before him, nor does he tremble before the world;
he is neither abandoned by nor joined to passion, hatred, fear, and joy.
It trembles and fears; by the terms "attachment," "aversion," and so forth, their objective causes are indicated.
At times, due to the force of *prārabdha* karma, it is joined with and abandoned from [the body]. || 9 ||
A person of noble disposition does not find pleasure in making anything an object of cognition;
yet one of pure intent can be made an object of cognition even by a child. (10)
Even for someone of virtuous intellect, [this person] does not truly ascend to or enter into the sphere of valid cognition (*prameya*);

that is to say, even those of refined intelligence are unable to ascertain him in reality. However, from the perspective of conventional practice (*vyavahāra*), he is made an object of cognition even by a child and is brought under control even with a slight degree of compliance; for this reason, he is one whose intentions are not evil.
The meaning is that he is "straight" because his mind is pure. || 10 ||
Let him cast off his body at a sacred ford or even in the house of an outcaste;
O King, let it never be otherwise, even at this very moment.

He says "tanum" (the body) to show that at the very moment of that knowledge, because of liberation and the sublation of the body and so forth, there is not even a thought regarding the abandonment of the body for the sake of further liberation through pilgrimages or the like— whether he should ever abandon the body at any time,
or whether he should abandon the body right now in this present moment; nevertheless, he [is liberated].
The connection with the subsequent [verse] is as follows: at the very moment of attaining knowledge, he is already liberated and bodiless (videha). || 11 ||
At the moment of attaining knowledge, he is liberated and freed from all latent desires;
for the delusion of "I" leads to bondage, while liberation is the destruction of that [delusion] through knowledge. 12.
To establish that, he states the nature of bondage and liberation: "The delusion of 'I'... (verse 12).
He is to be worshipped, he is to be praised, and he is to be saluted with effort; he is to be beheld and greeted by one who desires the fullness of prosperity.

"He is worthy of worship. And so says the Śruti: "Whatever world a person of purified being contemplates in his mind and whatever desires he longs for, he attains that world and those desires; therefore, one who desires prosperity should indeed honor the knower of the Self. (13)
O dear one, that supreme purity is not attained through sacrifices, sacred fords, austerities, or gifts;
rather, it is attained through devotion by the virtuous who know the Self and whose worldly ailments have been exhausted. 14.

He states that the worship of Him alone is also the cause of the knowledge that leads to the attainment of the supreme human goal—beginning with "na" (not so). O friend, for those who are *jīvanmukta*s, whose disease of worldly existence has been exhausted, that supreme state which is attained through devotion (*bhakti*) and worship by means of knowledge cannot be attained through sacrifices and the like; such is the grammatical connection. || 14 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Having spoken thus, the blessed Manu went to the abode of Brahmā;
Ikṣvāku also, having firmly grasped that vision, remained steadfast.
The abode of Brahmā is situated upon the summit of Mount Meru. || 15 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-second chapter, titled "The Awakening of Ikṣvāku," in the dialogue between Ikṣvāku and Manu, within the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*, composed by the Sage Vasiṣṭha.
Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-second chapter, titled "The Enlightenment of Ikṣvāku," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and twenty-third canto.
Śrī Rāma said:
"O Blessed One, such being the case, what unprecedented excellence belongs to one who is liberated while living (jīvanmukta) and possesses right-mindedness, O best among the knowers of the Self?"

For the Knower, in comparison to the ignorant who have attained other powers such as *khecarī* and *aṇimā*, there is indeed no desire [for them] due to his perfection; this is the distinction stated here.

Rāma, doubting whether there exists some unprecedented excellence—such as the attainment of powers like moving through the air (*khecarī-siddhi*)—in one who possesses the characteristics described for the "liberated while living" (*jīvanmukta*), as there is in those who have attained success through jewels, mantras, and so forth, asks: "Thus... (verse 1). That is to say:
when this collection of characteristics has been established in the form you have described.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
In some particular aspect alone does the intellect of the knower become preeminent;
ever-satisfied and with a tranquil self, he abides in the Self alone.

With the intention that the specific distinction lies solely in the experience whose object is the Self of unsurpassed bliss, which is not within the domain of other perfected beings (siddhas), he provides the answer with the words "of the knower" (jñasya).

The construction is as follows: for the knower, there arises an excellence of intellect regarding some portion of the supreme reality of the Self, which is inaccessible to others who have attained perfection. Alternatively, the particle *eva* (only) has the sense of "also": for the knower, [there is excellence] even regarding the portion of worldly perfections.

The construction of the sentence is: "The cognition of excellence does not arise with respect to any excellence whatsoever. To the question "Why is that?", he says: "He is eternally satisfied" (verse 2).

By means of those accomplished through mantras, those accomplished through austerity, and those accomplished through tantras—abundantly—such things as traveling through the sky have already been performed; what novelty could there be in that? (verse 3).

He states that there is nothing new for him regarding those powers such as *khecarī* attained by others through the realization that he alone exists even in the form of those perfected by mantras (*mantrasiddha*) and so forth— because he has attained them himself through the cognition that he is the self of all— with the words "by those perfected by mantras" (*mantrasiddhaiḥ*).
Alternatively, the word *apūrva* may be analyzed as that which has no prior cause (*pūrva-kāraṇa*).
