The knower of reality who has attained eternal and unsurpassed bliss alone is the primary [liberated one]. As for the collection of supernatural powers such as traveling through space and so forth, these are produced by means of mantra-perfection and the like, and are generated by one's own effort; therefore, the meaning is that they possess only prior existence (sapūrvatā) and not novelty (apūrvatā).
Even powers such as *aṇimā* have been attained in abundance by those very same [yogis], because they were accomplished through effort; yet these were not attained by one who perceives the Self.

Even if the meaning of the word *apūrva* (unprecedented) includes that which has not been attained by anyone else, nevertheless, since the collection of supernatural powers such as *aṇimā* and so forth has already been attained by many—such as those perfected through mantras and the like—it is not "unprecedented" in their case; thus he says:
"Even *aṇimā* and the rest. For one who is a knower (*jña*) who has become the Self of all, all worldly powers are [attained] by those very means through their respective efforts.
With the intention that there is no further purpose in proving again by oneself what has already been established, he says: "By effort" (yatnena) || 4 ||
This indeed is his distinction; he is not equal to those of deluded intellect.
Because of the abandonment of attachment everywhere, the mind of that great-souled one becomes passionless and stainless; he does not sink into worldly objects.

In that case, he states what the distinction of those who know reality is compared to others: "This very [knowledge]" (eṣa eva). The meaning is that the knowledge of reality itself is the distinction.
He mentions another distinction: "Everywhere" (sarvatra), which refers to all objects of experience. || 5 ||

This indeed is the very sign of one who has known reality—the one whose form is beyond signs, who is stilled from the long wandering of saṃsāra, and who is at peace: that for him, lust, anger, dejection, delusion, greed, and misfortune daily and skillfully diminish.

Describing the very fruits of dispassion as the characteristics of one who knows reality, he concludes with the words "etāvat" (this much): for one who is tranquil through the awakening to reality and thus liberated from long-standing delusion, the form is Brahman-consciousness alone— devoid of all attributes (*aliṅga*) and empty of all phenomena— whose essential nature is a single flavor like a mass of salt.

For one who is such as this, the sign or characteristic is indeed only this much: that there is a daily, skillful, and extreme attenuation—meaning a diminution—of calamities such as passion and the like. || 6 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-third canto, titled "The Specific Description of the Knower as Distinct from Ignorance and the Like," in the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa*, a work of the Sage (Ārṣa). Volume One, Part Two. Canto 123.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-third chapter, titled "The Specific Description of the Ignorant and the Knower," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and twenty-fourth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Just as a Brahmin, disregarding his own inner being (sattva), gradually [degenerates] through evil desire, so too does the world.
In that same way, the Lord accepts the state of being a Śūdra as well as the state of being a living being.
The causelessness of living beings, their bondage by attachment to objects of perception,
their forms, their states, and the fourth state (turya)— all these are taught as being like the deer and the hunter.

In order to establish the sense that the superiority of self-knowledge over other forms of attainment is due solely to its being the experience of eternal, unsurpassed bliss, and that the inner self (*pratyagātman*) possesses the nature of eternal, unsurpassed bliss precisely because it is of the very essence of Brahman, [the author] states— beginning with "Just as"— that Brahman itself attains the state of a living soul (*jīva*) by virtue of disregarding its own true nature. Just as...

Just as a certain Brahmin, desiring a Śūdra woman, gradually neglects his own appropriate nature— the *sāttvika* quality and the duty of a Brāhmaṇa— through the wicked longing for her company, sexual union, and cohabitation, and after a long time accepts the state of a Śūdra; so too does the Lord, through association with the intellect (*buddhi*) and the like, and by the desire for enjoyment prompted thereby, [neglect His own nature].
The meaning is that, setting aside its own nature of eternal purity, perfection, and bliss, it accepts the state of being a living soul (jīvatva). || 1 ||
Indeed, at every dissolution, beings manifest in two ways;
those born from the primordial vibration are indeed without cause.

These are of two kinds: those that are objects of enjoyment by virtue of the predominance of the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), and those that are enjoyers by virtue of the predominance of the limited self (*upahita*).

Following a beginningless succession of two types of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) residing in *māyā*, they are born from the first vibration of the nature of Hiraṇyagarbha and have manifested like a city of Gandharvas in *māyā*. Therefore...

Because they are false, they are causeless, being independent of any real causal complex (*sāmagrī*). The meaning is that a pot or other object in a dream does not depend upon a causal complex such as a staff, a wheel, and so forth, for its own production. || 2 ||
O dear one, having emerged from the Lord, living beings undergo further births and experiences solely through their own performed actions.

Indeed, in such scriptural passages as, "The doer of good becomes good, the doer of evil becomes evil; one becomes virtuous through virtuous action and sinful through sinful action; from that world he returns again to another world for the sake of action," it is understood that there is a beginningless mutual relationship of cause and effect between birth and action, like that of a seed and its sprout.

How then can it be said that the Lord, who is devoid of karma, undergoes birth in the form of a living being (*jīva*) during the first creation? To this he says: "From the Lord. [This means] by means of those actions performed by Himself and those performed by the conditioned [living beings]. The Lord has no dependence on karma for His state as a living being;
rather, after attaining the state of a living being, there is dependence upon the karma performed in successive prior bodies for the production of subsequent bodies and so forth. As, for example:

The meaning is as follows: just as the reflection of the sun depends upon the action of movement and so forth occurring in the water, and depends upon the action of the limiting adjunct (upādhi) for its transition into the various waves and for its experience of the modifications inherent therein, so it is in this case as well. || 3 ||
Such is this relationship of cause and effect between birth and action;
all living beings proceed from the supreme state without any [prior] cause.

He states that very point clearly: "the relation of cause and effect. And so it has been said in the *Vārttika*: "Just as the fullness of space arises for a jar solely in accordance with the inherent nature of the substance of space, and not from an agent, so it is with the cognitions of the Seer. (4)
Afterwards, they realize that their own actions are the cause of pleasure and pain;
for it is the volition arising from self-knowledge that is the cause of action.
How is it known that their actions follow later? To this he says: "From the knowledge of the Self.
Whatever kind of self one knows, one forms a volition corresponding to that, and one acts in accordance with that volition.
Indeed, without the notion that the body of a human being and so forth is the self, one neither forms the volition for nor performs meritorious or sinful deeds. And thus it has been said:
The venerable authors of the Bhāṣya have stated: "For no one acts by means of a body in which the nature of the Self has not been superimposed.
He further explains that even the superimposition upon the body is the cause for engagement in merit and demerit solely through the medium of volition (*saṃkalpa*): "Volition," [he says]. (5)

Indeed, the cause of bondage is the state of being possessed by volitional constructs (*saṃkalpa*); abandon that. Liberation, however, is the state of being free from volitional constructs; therefore, be intent upon its practice.

One who possesses *saṃkalpa* (volitional thought) is called a *saṃkalpī*; such a state is the cause of bondage through the continuity of merit, demerit, activity, experience, latent impressions (*vāsanā*), and so forth. || 6 ||
Be vigilant regarding the delusion of the grasped and the grasper,
gradually abandoning the states of conceptual construction at all times.

He states the means for the abandonment of conceptual construction (*saṃkalpa*) in the words "being attentive" (*sāvadhāna*). For when the delusion regarding the distinction between the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*) exists,

there arises a conceptual construction of activity conducive to rejection or acquisition, based on the consideration of favorability or unfavorability toward the object of grasping by the subject of grasping.

The sense is that by abandoning the delusion of the grasped and the grasper, and by practicing attentiveness characterized by one-pointedness toward its witness, the very root of volitional construction (saṃkalpa) is severed. || 7 ||
Do not become the nature of the grasped object, and do not become the nature of the grasper; having abandoned all mental constructions, become absorbed in that which remains. (8)
He states this very same point explicitly with the words "mā bhava" (do not be). That which remains is the nature of the witness;
one who is absorbed in that has that as their sole essence. || 8 ||
O sinless one, whatever object the group of senses constantly falls upon, there it is bound by attachment; there, through non-attachment, it is liberated.
Showing that when heedlessness prevails, attachment toward the desirable is unavoidable, he demonstrates the necessity of practicing detachment with the verse beginning "ajasram" (9).
If something whatsoever is pleasing to you, you are bound to worldly existence; if nothing at all is pleasing to the mind, then you are liberated from worldly existence.

Having distinguished the essential natures of passion and dispassion, he demonstrates that they are the indicators of bondage and liberation: "Therefore, among the entire collection of objects, including both the stationary and the moving—from a blade of grass up to the bodies of the gods—may nothing whatsoever be pleasing to you. (11)

From the lowest limit of existence, such as grass and the bodies of living beings, up to the highest limit, the god Hiraṇyagarbha, and from the entire collection of objects including his body and the forms of the objects he enjoys— may not even the slightest thing among them be pleasing to you.
Whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer in sacrifice, whatever you give, [or whatever you abandon—this is also a reading], and whatever else;
there, as neither agent nor enjoyer, the one whose mind is liberated is at peace. 12.

Now, one might raise this objection: "Even if the bondage of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtā*) has been conquered through supreme dispassion (*paravairāgya*), since actions such as bathing and eating cannot be abandoned while one is alive, the bondage caused by them will surely still exist. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "That which... In that regard, one whose mind is liberated (*muktamatiḥ*) is one whose intellect is fixed upon the immutable Self (*kūṭasthātman*). And so it was said by the Blessed One: "He who is disciplined [thinks], 'I do nothing at all.'"
One who knows reality should think thus. || 12 ||
The virtuous do not grieve for the past, nor do they worry about the future;
they embrace the present and perform their duty as it arises, without fail.
Fearing that attachment to bondage might arise through grief caused by separation from the beloved or the occurrence of the unpleasant, he says: "The virtuous...
(verse 13).
States such as craving, delusion, and pride are knotted within the mind;
O Rāma, the mind must be severed by the mind itself by one who possesses true knowledge.

Regarding the conquest of all bonds, the means is indeed the conquest of the mind, and that [conquest] is achieved by the mind alone and not by anything else; thus he says: "In the mind... (verse 14).
With the mind itself, as sharp as steel, cut through the mind by means of discernment—like iron [cuts] dross—for the sake of pacifying all delusion. 15.
He says that the conquest of the mind by means of the mind is achieved through discernment. || 15 ||
Those skilled in cleansing wash away impurity with impurity itself;
they ward off a weapon with a weapon and poison with poison.
With the mind, one who has conquered the mind avoids the fault of depending on the self—[the text says] "they wash away" [impurities] with dirt, alkali, and so forth. || 16 ||
The individual soul has three forms: the gross, the subtle, and the supreme.
Among these, worship that which is its supreme form; abandon the other two.

To demonstrate how much of the individual soul (jīva), which is conjoined with the mind, can be separated by the mind and thus severed, he analyzes the forms of the soul—beginning with "of the soul. Abandon them; sever them with the mind. || 17 ||
This body, composed of hands and feet, which moves about for the sake of enjoyment—this gross form exists here for the purpose of the individual soul's experience. (18)
He shows them with the words beginning "the hands," etc. (verse 18).

Know, O Rāma, that the mind— which consists of forms created by one's own volitions and which persists as long as saṃsāra exists— is the subtle, transportive body (ativāhika-rūpa) of the individual soul (jīva).
Know that which is without beginning or end, the truth, pure consciousness, and free from conceptual construction— that is the supreme third form, the universal form.
The metaphor for the universe is its defining characteristic; the meaning is that it bestows existence and manifestation. || 20 ||
This is the pure state of the Fourth (turya); take your firm stand here.
Having completely abandoned the first two, do not let your mind be fixed upon them.

Śrī Rāma said: O leader of sages, having distinguished it specifically, please explain the fourth state (turya), which remains present throughout all three states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, yet is unperceived.

The gross and subtle forms of the individual soul (*jīva*) during the waking and dreaming states are well known. Yet, even by abandoning those two alone, there is no complete purification of it; therefore, desiring to know that which transcends the three states, Rāma asks: "Waking... [and so forth].
It remains mixed and, for that very reason, clearly unperceived. "Specifically" means by way of excluding that mixture. || 22 ||

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having abandoned both the sense of "I" and the sense of "not-I," as well as existence and non-existence, that which remains unattached, equanimous, and pure is called the Fourth (turya).

The sense of "I" (ahaṃbhāva) is the distraction in the states of waking and dreaming; the absence of the sense of "I" (anahaṃbhāva) is in deep sleep. Their root is the veil (āvaraṇa). Both of these, in their individual forms, are the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of the individual soul (jīva); in their collective form, however, they are the existent (sat) and non-existent (asat), as well-known from such scriptural passages as, "In the beginning this was non-existent; from that, indeed, the existent was born. Having abandoned both of those—23.

That state which is transparent, equanimous, and peaceful—the established condition of one liberated while living—is the state of witnesshood; in common usage, it is called the reckoning of the Fourth (turya).
Among those liberated while living, she is established as the lowest state; in worldly affairs, during the time of practical conduct, she is well known as the state of being a witness. (24)
This is neither waking nor dreaming, because of the impossibility of volitional constructions;
nor is it the state of deep sleep, because of the absence [of consciousness], since there remains a state of insentience.
He prevents the confusion of that [state] with waking and so forth by saying, "Not this. "Inertness" (jaḍatā) is the veil; it belongs to ignorance (ajñāna), which persists therein.
To those who are perfectly awakened, this world remains as it truly is, peaceful;
yet to the unawakened, they say that which is actually the fourth state (turya) remains dissolved, appearing as something solid and stable.
Now, one might ask: how can the non-dual fourth state (turiya) exist even for those liberated while living (jīvanmukta) during the time of duality such as waking and so forth?
To this, he says: "It is peaceful. This means it is dissolved, having been sublated by knowledge. || 26 ||
When the subtle trace of egoism is abandoned, when equanimity arises,
and when the mind is rendered dissolved, the fourth state (turya) manifests.
When they have been rendered as fragile as salt dissolved in water, || 27 ||
Now, O wise one, listen to this illustration being told by me, so that even though you are already awakened, you may attain further enlightenment. (28)

With the passage beginning with "Now, this... (athemam), he dispels the doubt as to how the mind could be fragile while one is awake and engaged in worldly activity, by means of the illustration of the hunter. || 28 ||
Seeing a certain sage established in great silence within the expanse of a forest, the hunter asked him about this wondrous sight.
Great silence (*mahāmauna*) is the cessation of all activities such as speech through the realization of knowledge; he asked this which is about to be described. || 29 ||
"O Sage, having arrived later, I saw a deer fleeing, pierced by an arrow; struck by my shaft, the deer has come here. (30)

The deer, pierced by an arrow and fleeing, was pursued from behind by a hunter; this is the connection with what precedes. What did he ask? He states this with the words beginning "O Sage" (mune). || 30 ||
"Where has the deer gone? the sage replied to him:
"O virtuous one, we are forest-dwelling sages of equal character."
The repetition of the word "deer" is due to agitation. || 31 ||
We have no sense of "I" that is capable in worldly affairs;
for it is the mind, O friend, that performs all the functions of the senses. (32)
The phrase "in legal proceedings" is to be understood as "in those not previously practiced. || 32 ||
That [ego] of mine, consisting of the sense of "I," has surely flowed away for a long time;
I no longer perceive any states whatsoever known as waking, dreaming, or deep sleep. (33)
Consisting of egoism, abounding in self-conceit; for a long time, always. || 33 ||
"I indeed abide in the fourth state (turya); therein, no object of perception exists.
Having heard these words of the Lord of Sages, O Rāghava... (34)
The hunter, failing to recognize his true interest, departed for his desired destination;
therefore I say, O mighty-armed one, there is no state other than the fourth (turya). 35.

Therefore, because they are sublated by such experiences of the sages and by scriptural revelation, the states other than the Fourth (turya)— namely the waking state and so forth, as well as the gross state and so forth— do not exist.
For the fourth state of consciousness is indeed free from conceptual construction; that alone exists here and nothing else.
Indeed, the triad known as waking, dreaming, and deep sleep is merely a form of the mind. (36)

Because the three states are effects of the mind, which consists of the three qualities (guṇas) and is composed of Māyā, and because the mind itself becomes "dead" when Māyā is sublated, those states to be accepted [by the mind] are non-existent; thus he says with the verse beginning "jāgrat" (36).
The self-mind abides here as terrible, peaceful, and deluded;
the mind consisting of the waking state is terrible, while that which consists of the dream state is peaceful.
He shows the three states by dividing them into three types according to the predominance of the qualities (guṇas) such as rajas and so forth—beginning with the word "ghoram" (terrible).

Because it produces merit and demerit which are the causes of heaven, hell, rebirth, and so forth, and because of its excessive density, the mind consisting of the waking state—that is, the waking state itself—is "terrible," and so on; this is to be inferred for the others as well. || 37 ||
When the mind is deluded and situated in the state of deep sleep, devoid of the three qualities, it becomes as if dead;
and that mind which is "dead" remains there as pure *sattva* alone in equilibrium.
Indeed, all yogis strive with effort to achieve that very state.

Due to the destruction of *māyā*, which consists of the three qualities (*guṇatraya*), [the mind] is devoid of the three; when the mind of yogis has ceased, for the sake of experiencing the remainder of their *prārabdha* karma, only the *sattva* portion persists—like whiteness in ashes—and not even a trace of the portions of *rajas* and *tamas*. Thus he says: "And that which... Because it is not agitated by *rajas*, it is "even" (*sama*). In such a mind, due to the excellence of its purity, there is the bliss of one's own self (*svātmasukha*).
The meaning is that, because it is ever-manifest, one should diligently accomplish the practice of samādhi by ceasing all activities.
Remain in the fourth state (turya), the stainless self, which is free from the play of all mental constructs;
established therein, the great sages, with their distinctions stilled, are forever truly liberated. (39)
Therefore, he says—beginning with "samasta"—that you too, having cultivated such a mind, should remain resting in the fourth state (turya);
this is clear. || 39 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Hunter," in the *Pūrva-mārga* (First Part) of the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Valmiki, according to the tradition of the Rishis. 124.
Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Story of the Deer-Hunter," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa-tātparyaprakāśa*.
The one hundred and twenty-fifth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
"Indeed, the final conclusion of the spiritual scriptures (*adhyātma-śāstra*) is the negation of everything."
Here there is no ignorance, nor is there illusion; this Brahman is peaceful and beyond succession.
In that Fourth State (turya), which is the established conclusion of the total negation of all things and wherein disputants are deluded, steadfastness is taught along with its means.

The supreme conclusion of the scriptures— such as the Śruti, Smṛti, Itihāsa, and Purāṇa— which proceed with reference to the Self, is the negation of the entire range of duality, whether it be the manifestation of the three states of this [individual self] through innate ignorance (avidyā), or the manifestation of the world of ether and so forth belonging to the Lord through Māyā; it is not the revelation of a real entity.

He says, "In the Siddhānta," because the reality of the Self, being self-luminous, is established by itself; thus, no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) can operate toward its establishment. The meaning is that this Brahman—which is peaceful, free from all afflictions, and eternally immediate—is "not traversed" (*akrama*) by the scriptures, meaning it cannot be fathomed by them. And so says the Śruti: "From whence words turn back..."

"Not having reached [it] along with the mind. And likewise it has been said by the Draviḍācārya: "If Brahman is immeasurable, for what purpose is the scripture? [The answer is: "But it is established because it brings about cessation. || 1 ||
In the luminous consciousness alone— which is tranquil, pure, the self that is perfectly equal,
and inlaid with all powers— is the name "Brahman" conceptually imputed.

He states in two verses beginning with "The Peaceful One" that various conceptual constructions have arisen among those disputants who, due to their failure to understand the established conclusions of the Śruti and other scriptures, seek the root of the world through the power of their own intellect; these constructions proceed from the diversity of defects in their understanding regarding Brahman— the object denoted by the word "Brahman"— which is variegated by Māyā and possesses all powers.
Having determined emptiness, some [determine] mere consciousness, and others the nature of God; thus they dispute with one another. (3)
Having determined [the truth] according to their respective intellects, they have devised various differences in their established doctrines. || 3 ||
Having renounced everything, O sinless one, you have become a great silent sage—
possessing liberation, free from mental fabrication, with the mind exhausted and the intellect profoundly stilled.

Having abandoned the entire range of visible objects, which are all illusory, and having become a great silent sage through the cessation of the activities of all the senses along with the mind, being one who has attained liberation within the Self that is the nature of perfect bliss-consciousness—this is the connection with the subsequent [verse]: "Abide in the Self alone. (4)
Abide in the Self alone with a tranquil mind, like one who is mute, blind, and deaf;
remaining eternally inward-turned, let your intellect be filled within by the Self.
O Rāghava, remain in deep sleep even while awake and perform your actions;
inwardly renouncing everything, carry out your duties outwardly as they come.
Through the conquest of the fifth and subsequent stages, even while in the waking state, he remains as if in deep sleep.
The existence of the mind is supreme suffering; the non-existence of the mind is supreme happiness.
Therefore, O you whose nature is pure consciousness, bring the mind to its end through the absence of sensation.
Because there is no experience [of pleasure or pain], because there is neither affection nor aversion, and because there is no subsequent mental synthesis. || 7 ||
Whether one sees what is pleasant or unpleasant, one should remain as steady as a stone;
by such self-effort alone, the cycle of worldly existence is conquered.
He clarifies this very point [that it is] "due to non-perception" with the words: "Having seen," etc. (8).
Neither pleasure, nor pain, nor that which is between them is to be experienced;
by this much effort of the self, the infinite end of suffering is attained.
That which is to be experienced is to be contemplated. Unhappiness is suffering; the middle state is the means for both. || 9 ||
Like the full-orbed moon within [the sky], the knower of that [reality] attains happiness through the glorious elixir of rasa;
having realized the essence of all things in the three worlds, he does not even act, for he has attained the supreme state.

By whom the essence of all things in the three worlds has been realized; for that very reason, he is composed of that elixir—which is the nectar of unsurpassed bliss—and which is glorious, self-luminous, and radiant in every respect. And for that same reason, he is like the moon whose orb is completely full and nourished.
One who is like the full moon, having attained the Supreme Self which is beyond the beyond, and knowing that [Self], attains the bliss of liberation while living.

Even while performing the worldly activities brought about by *prārabdha* karma, he does not act; the meaning is that, as in the case of the movements of a reflection, he perceives no sense of agency in himself. || 10 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-fifth canto, titled "The Exposition of the Means for Stability," in the Fourth Part (Pūrva-ārdha) of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the glorious Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa composed by Vālmīki. 125.
Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-fifth canto, titled "The Exposition of the Means for Stability," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and twenty-sixth canto.
Śrī Rāma said:
How is the practice of the seven stages of yoga performed?
And what are the signs for the yogin regarding the stages?

It is said that regarding the characteristics of the sequence of practice for the stages of yoga, if death occurs in the interval, there is the enjoyment of experiences; thereafter, in another birth, comes victory.

"O Rāghava, perform actions while remaining in the state of deep sleep even while awake"— thus it was said that the state of the fifth and subsequent stages should be accomplished for Rāma, who had ascended to the fourth stage. Desiring to accomplish that,
Rāma asks about their characteristics and the sequence of their practice, in order to know the distinction between the stages already conquered and those yet to be conquered.
Since the designation *karmapravacanīya* for *prati* in the sense of repetition necessitates either reduplication or an *avyayībhāva* compound, their absence here is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*).
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
A person is of two kinds: the active (pravṛtta) and the withdrawn (nivṛtta).
Listen now to the characteristics of these two, who are oriented toward heaven and liberation respectively.

Desiring to explain the sequence of practice for the stages [of yoga] as requested, Vasiṣṭha first distinguishes between the two types of persons and promises to state their differing characteristics, in order to show the one qualified for this [path] as distinct from the one qualified for the scriptures of worldly activity (pravṛtti-śāstra).
He says: "The active person... A "person" (pumān) is an individual established on the path of the Vedas. || 2 ||
How small indeed is that so-called nirvāṇa; for me, transmigratory existence itself is better.
He who performs his duties is known as one who is engaged in worldly activity (pravṛtta). || 3 ||

In this regard, he first states the characteristic of one who has set out with a perverted intellect due to defects such as passion and the like, beginning with the words "How much" (*kiyat*). What indeed is that *nirvāṇa*, renowned for its emptiness of all objects? The meaning is that it is not highly esteemed by those who crave enjoyments. As they say: "May cyclic existence itself, replete with high and low enjoyments, be better for me. Furthermore:

"O Gautama, he would rather desire the state of a jackal in the empty Vṛndāvana than ever attain a liberation devoid of the sense-objects. Having thus determined, [he is] the performer of the collection of obligatory, occasional, and optional rites that ought to be done. || 3 ||
Like a tortoise inserting its neck through the hole of a yoke amidst the four oceans, a man endowed with discernment is born after the course of many births. (4)
Intending to characterize that which has ceased, he speaks of its rarity in order to describe the discrimination (*viveka*) that is the cause of cessation— beginning with the word *cala*:

"Just as within the interior of the two oceans, both eastern and western, which are exceedingly restless due to millions of swarms of aquatic creatures, fierce winds, the submarine fire (*vaḍavānala*), and the like..."

Just as for tortoises dwelling in water, there are countless entries and exits into their shells immediately upon even the slightest fear caused by the movement of waves, so too, at the end of countless births characterized by repeated entry into and exit from the mouth of death, there is only a rare individual who [attains liberation].

The meaning is that one becomes a man of discrimination (*vivekī*). Alternatively, just as the neck of the great tortoise dwelling in the salt ocean, though entering and exiting the opening of its throat many times, tastes only the flavor of the salt ocean and, esteeming only that, does not recognize the flavor of the milk ocean until the dissolution; yet at the end, at the time of the cosmic destruction (*kalpānta*), when the two [oceans] move...
Just as, at the time of the meeting of the salt-water and milk-oceans, when the neck enters the aperture characterized by the bellies of both,

it tastes the flavor of the milk, becomes a discriminator between the flavor of the milk and the flavor of the salt, and becomes attached to that [milk]; in the same way, the individual soul (*jīva*), having previously held only the flavors of sense-objects in high regard, at the end of many births—

The meaning is that through the dawning of good fortune, having tasted the flavor of the spiritual scriptures (*adhyātma-śāstra*), the discerning person becomes attached to them. Alternatively, just as when the gods and demons were churning the ocean to produce the nectar (*amṛta*), the Blessed One—who had become the tortoise supporting the mountain of churning—was both inside and outside [the ocean] because he is the belly that supports the entire universe; so too [is the case here].

When the gap appeared in the pair of oceans being churned, they proceeded to taste [the nectar] for the sake of examination as to where the nectar first arose; then, after many cycles of entering within and exiting without,
they drank it at that very spot— whether inside or outside— where the nectar had first emerged.

The meaning is that a person who has set out both externally through reflection (*manana*) and contemplation (*nididhyāsana*), and internally for the sake of discerning the reality of Brahman as the Self, finally— due to the force of practice over many lifetimes— either at the time of internal realization or during the occasion of external hearing, directly experiences unsurpassed bliss through discernment. Alternatively, [it refers to] the gap between the pair of two agitated oceans.

Just as when a tortoise enters a gap between the banks situated in the middle [of a river] using its neck as the means of entry, there is no rest whatsoever— whether in emerging on the other side, in withdrawing back, or even while remaining in the opening— so too, for the living being (*jīva*) who has abandoned the previous ocean of existence and desires to enter another state of existence, there is no rest anywhere.

For instance: in a previous birth characterized by a succession of sufferings such as old age and death, there is the continuous stream of suffering beginning with infancy; in the intermediate state, there is great suffering in the body of torment or in the womb.
Thus, at the end of many births consisting of nothing but suffering, a person eventually becomes discerning through the ripening of some merit.
Alas, the condition of cyclic existence is indeed essence-less; enough for me with it! What is the use of stale actions? The day is spent on those very things. (5)
He explains what kind of discernment arises for him with the verse beginning "asāra... (insubstantial, etc.). "Vividhā" means various and contradictory;

"vyavasthitiḥ" means state or condition; "asārā" means devoid of the happiness of rest. "Paryuṣitaiḥ" means by those whose transformations are improper [the reading is "aśucipariṇāmaiḥ" (by those with impure transformations)]. || 5 ||
"What could be the supreme rest, free from the excellence of action?"—he who possesses such certainty within is known as "one who has desisted" (nivṛtta). || 6 ||
The meaning is that it is "immutable" (kūṭastha), being free from the excellences resulting from ritual action—namely, origination, acquisition, modification, and purification.
Having reflected thus, he is one who possesses the firm resolve that this must necessarily be accomplished. || 6 ||
"How may I, having become dispassionate, cross the ocean of saṃsāra?"—
when the one of noble intellect is thus intent on reflection, (7)
He explains the sequence for attaining that first stage with the words beginning "How? (katham) and so forth. || 7 ||
Day by day he attains detachment within his meditations;
he proceeds toward noble deeds and rejoices daily.
He develops detachment—that is, a sense of distaste—for meditations on enjoyments and their means.

He applies himself to and becomes attached to noble practices that are conducive to the purification of the mind, such as ritual purity, association with the virtuous, worship of the Lord, and the chanting of mantras.
And through that daily accumulation of mental purification, he rejoices in the destruction of craving. (8)
He constantly doubts vulgar and dull-witted actions;
he does not utter words that pierce the vital points, and he devotes himself to meritorious deeds. (9)
He feels doubt and revulsion; he does not expose nor speak of the secret faults that are the vital points of others. || 9 ||
He practices gentle deeds that do not cause agitation to the mind; he constantly fears evil and does not long for worldly enjoyment. || 10 ||

He practices the duties of restraint (yama), observance (niyama), and so forth, which do not cause agitation to the minds of others or himself, which are gentle, require little effort, and yield great fruit; and he does not look toward worldly enjoyment, because evil is inevitable therein. || 10 ||
He addresses him with words that are imbued with affection and intimacy, charming, appropriate, and timely according to the place and occasion.
They are gentle, not causing agitation, appropriate, and characterized by truthfulness, kindness, benefit, and so forth. || 11 ||
Then he has attained the first stage;
with mind, deed, and speech, he serves virtuous people. (12)

He says "at that time" (tadā) to indicate the entry of a person distinguished by such qualities into the first stage, which is characterized by the qualification for hearing the true scripture; [he refers to] "good people" (sajjanān), who are endowed with tranquility, self-control, knowledge, and realized wisdom. || 12 ||
Bringing together treatises on knowledge from wherever they may be found,
he who possesses such an inquiry is intent upon crossing over the ocean of saṃsāra.
From wherever it may be, having brought the means such as wealth that are conducive to serving them, he serves them;
the meaning is that through their mouths he examines and hears the scriptures of knowledge, the Purāṇas, the Mokṣadharma, the Adhyātma-saṃhitās, and so forth. || 13 ||
He is said to possess the stages; the remainder is remembered as being for one's own sake.
He has reached another stage of yoga called "Investigation" (vicāra). || 14 ||
One who possesses the stages (*bhūmikāvān*) is said to have entered the first stage. As for the "remainder"—

meaning one who lacks the aforementioned attainment of the fourfold means (*sādhanacatuṣṭaya*) and so forth, and who, despite being attached to spiritual treatises (*adhyātmagrantha*), is self-interested and a deceiver because he subsists on his belly by deceiving unqualified people through passion and the like, and by means of acquisition and so forth— this is the meaning.

This is the first stage, known as *śubhecchā*. He describes the sequence of entering the second stage for one who has reached that stage in due order: "investigation" (*vicāra*), etc. One who has "reached the stage" is one who has descended [into it] by attaining the requisite qualification (*adhikāra*). || 14 ||

He honors eminent scholars who are renowned for their primary expertise in the study, recitation, retention, meditation, and performance of the rites prescribed by the Śruti, Smṛti, and the conduct of the virtuous.

Regarding what he does there, he says: "By the Śrutis... This refers to that Yoga-śāstra which is to be established through the Śrutis, Smṛtis, and the conduct of the virtuous (sadācāra), as well as through the means consisting of the practices of retention (dhāraṇā), meditation (dhyāna), and action (karma), and by means of the [eightfold] disciplines—yama, niyama, āsana, prāṇāyāma, and pratyāhāra—and by the goal, which is samādhi.

He resorts to—that is, goes for refuge to—renowned, excellent, and learned gurus, who are experts in teaching the experience of the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*), by means of their primary exposition, which is characterized by the performance of practice and the conferral of its fruits; the meaning is that he approaches them for the sake of inquiry through hearing, reflection, and so forth. And thus says the Śruti: "For the sake of knowing That..."
"He should approach a guru alone, with fuel in his hand, one who is learned in the Vedas and established in Brahman. || 15 ||

One who knows the classification of categories and has mastered what is to be heard understands the determination of what ought and ought not to be done, just as a master of the house knows his own home.

Being personally proficient in the auxiliary sciences such as grammar, and knowing the distinctions among the definitions and so forth of words and their meanings— including both the expressed (*vācya*) and the indicated (*lakṣya*) forms— a disciple who has mastered what is to be heard from the mouth of the teacher [discerns] that which is to be done (*kārya*), the goal to be accomplished which is the meaning of the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*), and that which is distinct from it: the already established (*siddha*).

The householder clearly understands the determination of the meaning of those two—the section on Brahman and the section on ritual—as one knows the division of the rooms within one's own house. || 16 ||
Like a snake casting off its skin, he even slightly abandons the excessive intoxication, pride, envy, delusion, and greed that have taken hold within him and even manifest outwardly.

Even though they are slightly dependent [on objects] in accordance with the worldly conventions of the external world, by this it is shown that for them there is internal cessation already in the very first stage. || 17 ||
One whose mind is thus disposed attains, through service to the scriptures, the teacher, and virtuous people, the entirety of this [teaching] along with its secrets, exactly as it is. (18)
One attains the secret of the scriptures—the ultimate purport—by dispelling doubts regarding the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
One attains the secret of the self, as esteemed by the guru and the virtuous, by dispelling doubts regarding the objects of knowledge (prameya). || 18 ||
Then that beloved one falls upon the third stage of yoga, named "Non-attachment," as if onto a stainless bed of flowers. (19)
Thus, for one who has conquered the second stage, he describes the entry into the third stage with the words "asaṃsaṅga" (non-attachment).
Thereupon, he falls—that is, enters—the third stage. || 19 ||
Having fixed his mind unwaveringly upon the true meaning of the words of the scriptures, through resting in the hermitages of ascetics and through the sequence of discourses on the supreme self; (20)
The two verses beginning with "yathāvat" are a restatement, as appropriate, of the two preceding stages. (20)
Likewise, by censuring cyclic existence and following the sequence of practices that produce dispassion,
he sits upon a stone bed and wears away his extended lifespan.
Dwelling in the forest retreat, which is graced by the tranquility of mind and characterized by the gentleness of unattached happiness, the wise man passes his time with propriety.

Because of the abundance of distractions in living in a village, one cannot successfully carry out the practice of meditative concentration; therefore, one should dwell in the forest retreat. || 22 ||
Through the study of excellent scriptures and the performance of meritorious deeds, this vision of reality becomes clear for a living being exactly as it is. (23)

In that regard, he shows that even at the time of emergence during mental clarity, the persistence of the factors belonging to the two preceding stages is also necessary—by the words "through practice" (abhyāsāt). || 23 ||
Having attained the third stage, the wise one personally experiences a twofold non-attachment; hear now this distinction regarding it. (24)
He explains the expression "by means of that which is gentle with unattached bliss" by analyzing it, saying: "the third," [verse 24].
This non-attachment is of two kinds: general and supreme.
[In the supreme state,] one is neither the doer nor the enjoyer, neither the afflicted nor the afflictor. (25)

It is common, being shared with the preceding stages. It is indifferent, being neither the agent nor the enjoyer of the actions and fruits of its own body. And it is unattached, being neither the victim nor the subduer regarding the actions and fruits of others. || 25 ||
Thus, the non-attachment to objects, which is called "general non-attachment," is entirely fashioned by prior karma and is dependent solely upon the Lord. (26)

Thus, by way of certainty: non-attachment (*asañjana*) toward objects that appear means the absence of clinging (*anabhiṣvaṅga*). To further strengthen this very lack of attachment to common things, he elaborates with three and a half verses beginning with "prākkarma": whether pleasure is being experienced or pain is being experienced, all of it is fashioned by prior karma, according to the view that one has independence over one's actions.

But according to the view that [the world] depends on the sovereignty of Īśvara, it is indeed dependent upon Īśvara. The word "or" (vā) is intended to indicate that the latter position is the authoritative one. || 26 ||
Whether it be happiness or suffering, what agency do I have here?
Enjoyments and non-enjoyments are great diseases; prosperities are supreme calamities.

The meaning is: since I lack independence in both alternatives, how could there be any "authorship" in the sense of the scriptural injunction that "the independent one is the agent"? There would be none at all. He shows other reasons for detachment—factors conducive to non-attachment toward worldly objects—which serve as grounds for indifference, starting with the verse beginning "pleasures" (bhogāḥ). || 27 ||
Unions lead only to separation; mental anxieties and physical ailments are but the workings of the intellect;
and Time is ever intent on swallowing all states of being without ceasing. 28.
That internal non-contemplation of phenomena which occurs through non-reliance—when the mind is fixed upon the meaning of the sentence—that is the common "non-attachment. (29)

He states that even this lack of attachment belongs only to one who is intent on knowing the meaning of the sentence through the assistance of hearing and so forth, and not to anyone else, for the sake of the bliss of non-attachment: "vākyārtha... (verse 29).
Through the yoga of various stages, through the union of great souls, through the separation from the non-existent, and through the practice of self-awareness; (30)
And this non-attachment should be properly practiced through means such as the company of the virtuous (*satsaṅga*) specifically on the two preceding stages;
thus he says, "by this. By the application—that is, the repeated practice—of the self-cognitions consisting of hearing (*śravaṇa*) and reflection (*manana*).
Accordingly, there is the aphorism of the venerable Bādarāyaṇa: "There must be repetition, because of the instruction given more than once" (Sūtra 4.1.1). || 30 ||
Through human effort and the yoga of continuous practice, when the object has become firmly clear—like a myrobalan fruit in the palm of the hand—[the goal is attained]. (31)

When the reality of the self has attained clarity—having dispelled the two types of doubt regarding the impossibility of the means of knowledge and the objects of knowledge—and has thus come within the range of conviction that "the reality of the self is exactly thus," [then... || 31 ||

On the far shore of the ocean of saṃsāra, in the essence that is the supreme cause, I am neither the agent nor the Lord; action or its fruit belongs to me only as a product of primordial nature (prakṛti).

The three words ending in the locative case are connected with what precedes; they qualify the word *vastuni*. He demonstrates the absence of attachment to excellence by means of the passage beginning with "I am not," etc. [He says: "I am not the agent, but the Lord alone is the agent. My action—whether previously performed or now being performed—"

Having cast far away even the cognition of the meanings of words—such as the conceptual constructions of "non-existence" and so forth, as well as their opposites—the phrase "that which is the state of silence" is to be construed with what follows. || 32 ||
Having indeed cultivated the contemplation of the meaning of words at a great distance, that silent and peaceful state of sitting is called the highest non-attachment. (33)

Mauna is that state of sitting or remaining still, devoid of all activity of speech, mind, eyes, and so forth, through the non-conceptual samādhi which is the fruit of the maturation of profound meditation (nididhyāsana). || 33 ||
That which is neither within nor without, neither below nor above, neither in the directions nor in the sky;
neither in an object nor in a non-object, neither in the insentient nor in the sentient.
That which consists of the state in which the mental fluctuations have dissolved into the single flavor of Brahman;

the meaning is that it is devoid of any objective support such as internal or external objects. "In consciousness" means in the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*). All [the following] are locative cases denoting objects. || 34 ||
It is seated, luminous, peaceful, and beyond appearance, equal to the sky;
beginningless, endless, unborn, and beautiful—that is called the supreme non-attachment. (35)
Because it is luminous, its nature is self-luminous consciousness; it is non-manifest, being devoid of any other illuminator. || 35 ||
Sweet with the fragrance of contentment, possessing the stainless sprouts of virtuous deeds, it is nestled within the tip of the stalk of the mind, though beset by the thorns of obstacles. (36)

And since this samādhi is the fruit of discernment (*viveka*) nourished by right conduct (*sadācāra*), he describes discernment through the metaphor of a lotus: "Contentment," etc. Its sprouts are virtuous deeds—namely, actions performed without desire for reward, as well as spiritual practice, service to the guru, hearing the scriptures, and so forth—which are clustered at the tip of the stalk characterized by the mind.
It is crowded and densely packed with the many thorns of obstacles arising from the latent tendencies of passion and other afflictions. || 36 ||
The lotus of discrimination, having taken root within and blossomed by the sunlight of inquiry, bears fruit in this third stage, which is characterized by non-attachment. (37)
Thus, he says that this very state of non-attachment is the third stage, referring to it as "the fruit. || 37 ||
Through the conjunction of pure associations and the accumulation of meritorious deeds,
the first stage arises by a chance occurrence, like the coincidence of the crow and the palm fruit.

If this very first stage, having sprouted by chance through the ripening of merits accumulated over many births as well as through the accumulation of merit in this life, is protected with great effort through association with the virtuous and other means, then if it is so protected,
the second and subsequent stages will be accomplished without effort; therefore, he instructs that one must apply even greater effort toward that very first stage.
"From association" means from the meeting of those who know reality and are pure, through means such as giving, honoring, and serving them. || 38 ||
That ground, as soon as it has been raised by them like a sprout of immortality, must be protected and guarded with great effort through the watering of discernment. (39)

He states what must be done by those [qualities] when combined: "The ground. For by those [qualities] when purified, that ground characterized as *śubhecchā* (the desire for the auspicious) has arisen; like a ground sprouted by clouds, through the daily sprinkling of the water characterized by the instruction of discrimination (*viveka*), it becomes *amṛtā*, meaning unfading.
Likewise, it means that [the intellect] must be protected and nourished—that is, it must be guarded with effort against obstacles such as negative tendencies.
(39) One should daily, with diligence, cause that very portion by which this [intellect] shines forth to attain growth through inquiry, just as a farmer tends to a sprout. (40)

This "desire for the auspicious" (śubhecchā), among the fourfold means [to liberation], should be brought to its arising and further growth through inquiry into whichever aspect first sprouts and shines forth, characterized by dispassion (vairāgya). || 40 ||
For this [first stage], which is the sole ground for the production of those whose inner selves have been polished, should diligently reach the second stage, and from that, the third. (41)
He says "eṣā" (this one) [in verse 41], meaning that one part has been increased and the other higher stages will be accomplished by herself alone.
For this third stage here is indeed the most excellent when fully attained; for the person becomes one who has completely abandoned all mental constructions and conceptualizations. (42)
He concludes the third stage, described along with its means and its fruit, with the verse beginning "The supreme" (śreṣṭhā). || 42 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
For one who is deluded, born of an ignoble family, engaged in base conduct, and who has not attained the company of yogis—how can there be deliverance? (43)
In this context, Rāma, out of compassion for those who are deluded in the interim, asks—"Of the deluded one" (mūḍhasya).

The meaning of the first question is: Is there liberation through some other means for that base person—one who lacks the specific qualifications such as noble birth, who is averse to discourse on the supreme self, and who is engaged solely for the sake of sensual enjoyment? Or is there not? || 43 ||
O Blessed One, what is the destiny of one who has died after having ascended to the first, the second, the third, or any other [level]? (44)

The second [question] concerns what kind of destiny awaits one who dies during the stages of being established in one, two, or three [levels], given that direct knowledge has not yet arisen within the first three levels. || 44 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
"Of the fool who has not ascended [to the higher state] and is possessed of faults... [Note:
In place of the two and a half verses beginning with "mūḍhasyārūḍhadoṣasya" and ending with "saṃgrahaḥ," this reading is found.]... "is the fool who has not ascended and is possessed of faults."

The cycle of worldly existence (saṃsṛti) extends only so long as the first stage has not been awakened here through hundreds of other births. Or rather, through association with the virtuous or by chance, detachment (vairāgya) certainly does not arise without an inquiry into the nature of worldly existence.
When detachment has arisen in a living being, the emergence of the stages [of yoga] is inevitable.

The cycle of worldly existence extends as far as it takes for [the soul], through hundreds of other births, by way of a chance occurrence like the "crow and the palm fruit," [to encounter the truth]. 45.

He provides the answer to the first question with the two and a half verses beginning with "mūḍhasya": the connection with the subsequent portion is that detachment does not arise—whether by chance (*kākatālīyayogataḥ*), through one's own inquiry, or through association with the virtuous. || 45 ||
Alternatively, if detachment does not arise through association with the virtuous,
then once detachment has arisen for a person, the emergence of the spiritual stages (bhūmikās) necessarily follows.
"Then cyclic existence is destroyed"—this is the summary of the meaning of the scriptures regarding an embodied being whose life has departed by means of the stages of yoga. (47)
He states the answer to the second [objection] with the words beginning "by the stages of yoga" (yogabhūmikayā) and so forth. || 47 ||
In accordance with the portions of the spiritual stages (bhūmikās), one's prior misdeeds are exhausted;
thereafter, one dwells in the celestial palaces of the gods and in the cities of the world-protectors (lokapālas). || 48 ||
Accompanied by his beloved, he delights in the groves and forest thickets of Mount Meru;
thereafter, [he experiences] the accumulation of his former good deeds and his evil deeds committed in the past.
It is understood by implication that he rejoices in accordance with the exhaustion of his evil deeds. The phrase "and in [the case of] evil deeds" is a reference back to what preceded.

For there is no experience of hell and the like for him, according to the Lord’s words: "O dear one, no doer of good ever goes to a miserable state. Alternatively, this refers to the experience of suffering as a secondary consequence even for those dwelling in heaven.
Because it is filled with thousands of physical, mental, and other forms of suffering. || 49 ||
When the web of enjoyments is completely exhausted, yogis are born on earth in the secret homes of pure, prosperous, virtuous, and saintly people. (50)

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: when the net of enjoyments is being consumed and the accumulation of merit (*sukṛta-saṃbhāra*) and demerit (*duṣkṛta*) have been exhausted; "of the yogins" is used in the plural to denote the class (*jāti*). || 50 ||
Having been born, these beings, permeated by yoga, devote themselves solely to yoga.
There, the wise, recollecting the sequence of the stages of yoga practiced through prior cultivation, leap far upward to the higher sequence of stages. (51)

"Only yoga"—for it is said in the words of the Blessed One: "By that very previous practice, he is carried along even against his will. He says the same thing: "perfumed by yoga. They fall and they ascend. || 51 ||
O Rāma, these three stages are known as the waking state;
this is perceived as the waking state because of the cognition of distinctions as they truly are. (52)
Having provided the answer to the two questions, he returns to the subject at hand with the words "the triad of stages" (*bhūmikātritaya*) and so forth.
He states the reason for applying the term "waking" (*jāgrat*) to the first three stages with the word "as it truly is" (*yathāvat*);
the meaning is that they possess a similarity to the well-known waking state by virtue of the quality of perceiving duality (*bhedadarśana*). || 52 ||
In this regard, for those engaged in yoga, there arises solely that state of nobility which, upon seeing it, the desire for liberation awakens even in those of deluded intellect. (53)
He states another sign as well—“it arises. Nobility (*āryatā*) means being worthy of honor, which is the excellence resulting from one's virtuous qualities.
“Having seen which” means according to the maxim: “Whatever the best man practices... (Gītā 3.21). || 53 ||
He who performs what ought to be done, refrains from what ought not to be done, and abides by the conduct of the common folk—he is remembered as an *ārya*. (54)

He first characterizes that very nobility which is distinguished from ignoble people with the words "that which ought to be done. This means all obligatory and occasional rites (*nitya-naimittika-karma*), as much as may be required. || 54 ||
He who adopts worldly conduct according to custom, according to scripture, according to his own mind, and according to what is established, is known as a noble one (ārya). || 55 ||

It should be according to custom, following the conduct of the elders; even there, according to the scriptures; even there, according to one's own mind—that is, only such conduct as, having performed it, one’s own mind becomes serene and does not feel remorse. This applies even to worldly social interaction. 55.
In the first [stage] it has sprouted; in the second it has blossomed;
in the third it bears fruit—thus does the state of a noble one (āryatva) come to be for the yogin. || 56 ||

That very state of nobility has sprouted in the first stage during the phase of "desire for virtue" (śubhecchā); it has blossomed in the second stage through engagement in hearing [the teachings] and so forth; and it has borne fruit in the third stage as a result of one-pointedness of mind—this is the meaning. || 56 ||
Having died while in a state of nobility, the yogi enjoys pleasures accumulated through pure intentions for a long time, and being possessed of yoga, he is born again. || 57 ||

Furthermore, for those who die in the interval [between lives] whose sins have been exhausted by the performance of desireless action (*niṣkāma-karma*), there is the enjoyment of the world of the gods (*devaloka*) and so forth— as well-known from such scriptural passages as "by action, the world of the ancestors; by knowledge, the world of the gods"— which,
because it is produced by virtuous latent impressions (*sadvāsanā*) instilled by pure intentions, is not like that of those who perform actions driven by desire.

With the intention that [the mind] is a cause for falling downward due to being filled with the evil latent impressions of passion and so forth, he says: "In the state of nobility" (āryatāyām). || 57 ||
When ignorance has reached its end through the practice of the three stages, and right knowledge has arisen in the mind, which is then comparable to the rising of the full moon; || 58 ||

When ignorance— the web of dualistic tendencies that opposes knowledge— and the defects of doubt and contrary conceptions have been destroyed, and when the non-dual, partless knowledge arises from the great Mahāvākya without obstruction, the yogis, having reached the fourth stage through the destruction of root-ignorance, perceive everything as...
The connection with the subsequent clause is: "they perceive [the world] as having the single flavor of bliss equal to the universe. || 58 ||
Those yogins whose minds are disciplined and who have reached the fourth stage perceive everything as equal—undifferentiated, without beginning or end. (59)
When non-duality has attained stability and duality has come to rest, those who have reached the fourth stage perceive worlds as if in a dream. (60)
The triad of stages is called the waking state; the fourth is said to be dreaming.
It dissolves away like the vanishing of scattered fragments of autumn clouds. (61)

The waking state (*jāgrat*) is so called because of the similarity in the manifestation of the world through empirical existence (*vyāvahārikasattā*); the dream state (*svapna*) is so called because of the similarity in that manifestation through illusory existence (*prātibhāsikasattā*). He shows the similarity with deep sleep (*suṣupti*), which is the basis for applying the term "deep sleep" to the fifth stage (*bhūmikā*), in the verse beginning with "disconnected" (*vicchinna*): "At the time of deep sleep, when everything has dissolved, one is overcome by darkness."

The meaning is that because it is well-known from the scripture stating "one attains the nature of bliss" (*sukharūpam eti*) that all things dissolve in deep sleep (*suṣupti*), there is a similarity here as well,

since even the residual illusory triad (*prātibhāsika-tripuṭī*) dissolves. It is like the dissolution of a detached fragment of an autumn cloud, characterized by the remaining of nothing but the pure sky.

The meaning is that one’s own nature, characterized by the remaining of pure consciousness alone, is dissolved— that is, it is attained through dissolution. Since, between the two parts of the verbal root's meaning— the result and the operation— the part consisting of the result is extracted and restated by the word "dissolution" (vilaya), and since that [result] stands as the object (*karman*) with respect to the part consisting of the operation, [the example] is "he cooks softly" (*mṛdu pacati*).

Just as in the case of adverbs, here too the accusative case is used; it is expressed by the verbal root of the finite verb that only the remaining portion of the activity dissolves, as in the expression "he grinds with water" (*udapeṣaṃ pinaṣṭi*). || 61 ||
Having reached the fifth stage, he remains as nothing more than mere existence;
having attained the fifth stage, which is named the state of deep sleep (suṣupta).
Existence is the existence of consciousness; she whose name "deep sleep" (suṣupta) is used figuratively because it is nothing but that [consciousness] remaining. || 62 ||
With all particular aspects stilled, he remains in non-duality alone;
with the appearance of duality dissolved, the awakened one rejoices within.
"Udita" means one whose true nature has become manifest. || 63 ||
Having reached the fifth stage from this point, he remains as one solidified in deep sleep;
though remaining inward-turned, he is yet engaged in outward activity.

With the intention that it is named "the state of deep sleep" (suṣupta) because of its similarity to the "mass of consciousness" (prajñānaghana) described in the scripture as "becoming one in the state of deep sleep, a mass of consciousness alone," he says:

"suṣupta. Furthermore, with the intention that it bears that name due to the similarity of tasting bliss for one who is inward-turned, as established by the scripture, "For [he] consists of bliss and is the enjoyer of bliss," he says: "ānandamaya."
"By way of being introverted. || 64 ||
Through constant tranquility, one appears as if perpetually asleep; practicing in this stage, one becomes free from latent impressions (vāsanas). 65.
"Free from latent impressions" (vivāsanaḥ) means being one whose latent impressions of self-assertion have been utterly severed. || 65 ||
He gradually ascends the sixth stage, known as the Fourth (turyā),
wherein there is neither non-existence nor the nature of existence, neither "I" nor even the absence of egoism.
Having described deep sleep (*suṣupta*), he states the characteristics of that which is designated as the Fourth (*turya*) by means of the passage beginning with "where... (verse 66).
With mere thought extinguished, he remains beyond both duality and unity;
free from knots, with doubts stilled, he is liberated while living, devoid of mental construction.
Since even the unity of dualism (dvaitavādaiikya) is a number that excludes other numbers, he is devoid of both.

Regarding this, he states the absolute breaking of the knot of the heart and all doubts by saying "nirgranthi" (without knots). The sense is based on the Vedic scripture: "The knot of the heart is broken; all doubts are cut asunder. (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 2.2.8) || 67 ||
Though not in a state of final liberation, it remains as if liberated, like a painted lamp;
empty within and empty without, it is void like a jar in the sky.

Though not yet extinguished and still maintaining a body sustained by *prārabdha* karma, he is extinguished and liberated. Just as a painted lamp is said to be "extinguished" because it does not burn even though its fuel is not yet exhausted, [the Self] is empty within and without of the nature of the inert world. 68.
Full within and full without, like a full jar in the ocean;
this has become something very slight, or rather, it is nothing at all.

By its very nature of unobstructed bliss, it is full both internally and externally. Since that non-dual form has never been realized during the state of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*), it appears as something unprecedented and supremely wonderful; yet from the perspective of ultimate reality, because it is eternally established, nothing at all has been produced. (69)
Abiding on the sixth stage, he shall attain the seventh stage.
Videhamukti (liberation while disembodied) is said to be the seventh stage of yoga; [the reading "not while living" is found].
If the seventh stage is fully matured, that itself is liberation; thus, that seventh stage, when fully matured, would not be an object [of further attainment].
The meaning is that it was stated previously, "for those who are living. || 70 ||
Inaccessible to words, that tranquil limit within the realms of existence is called "Śiva" by some and designated as "Brahman" by others. (71)

"Beyond the reach of words" means that it is accessible solely through the direct experience of the minds of yogis. One should not fall into the error of thinking that because the seventh stage does not exist for one who is still living, it is therefore inaccessible even to the direct experience of the minds of yogis; for that would contradict the statement that "it is the limit within the stages of existence," which describes it as the boundary marking the end of falling into the stages of existence (*bhavabhūmi*). Through the yoga of practicing these [stages]...

Furthermore, this is because it would contradict the statement that [the term] is to be practiced subsequently. The word "śivam" (auspicious) is used by the Śaivas; the intention is that this is in accordance with the Vedic scripture which says, "They consider the non-dual, the fourth, to be Śiva. The word "brahma" is used by the Vedāntins. || 71 ||

By some it was conceived as the discrimination between primordial nature (prakṛti) and the person (puruṣa); by others, in various other ways, through diverse distinctions imagined regarding the self. (72)
The Sāṃkhya and Yoga practitioners maintain that the state of prakṛti and puruṣa existing in an undifferentiated condition is what constitutes their "discrimination" (viveka).

Others— such as Jaimini, the Sāttvatas, the Māheśvaras, the Buddhists, the Ārhats, and so forth— hold views according to their own respective intellects, such as heaven, Vāsudeva, Maheśvara, unimpeded cognition, or unimpeded bliss, and so on.
Though it is eternally indefinable, it is taught in some manner.
These seven stages have been described by me to you, O scion of Raghu. (73)

If it is inaccessible to words, then how is it taught? To this he says: "Eternally. The meaning is: by means of certain methods characterized by the abandonment of parts [of the literal sense]. || 73 ||
Through the practice of these, no suffering is experienced;
there exists one who is utterly intoxicated with pride, moving slowly and languidly. (74)

He begins to describe, under the guise of the story of Mattakariṇī, that entry into the stages (*bhūmikās*) occurs only when there is firmness in supreme detachment (*paravairāgya*) and not otherwise: "There exists," and so forth. (74)
If that female elephant, intent on combat and displaying her great tusks—which surely brings about endless calamities—is slain, [it will be for our benefit]. (75)

"Always intent on conflict, ever engaged in battle, and possessing *śaṃsa*—which means praise or renown—by virtue of her two great tusks; let that be so. What follows from this? To this he replies: "If she... (verse 75).
Therefore, while all these stages remain intact, a man is victorious as long as that female elephant, intoxicated with rut, has not been overcome by his prowess. (76)
By this [knowledge], these stages (bhūmikās) are suppressed; therefore, the meaning is that not even a single stage can be conquered without slaying that [ego].
What warrior indeed [could prevail] in such fields of battle for prosperity?
Śrī Rāma said:
Who is this intoxicated female elephant, and what are those battlefields? || 77 ||

As long as she has not been conquered, what warrior indeed would be capable of even entering the battlefields—which, though they consist of the trivial riches of worldly existence, are already overrun by her? This is the meaning; the question is clear. || 77 ||
"How is this [desire] destroyed, and where does it find long-lasting delight?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
"O Rāma, desire is like a female elephant, whose form consists of the thought, 'May this be mine. (78)
In the forest of the body, she is intoxicated, bringing about various delights;
her fierce young elephants are the senses, and she speaks with the voice of a female elephant.
He provides the answer to the question "Where does she sport? with the words "in the forest of the body.

She is one whose nature is to cause the manifestation of various forms of wretchedness, running about, grief, delusion, and so forth. Her fierce and irascible young elephants are the intoxicated senses themselves. She speaks with the sweet trumpeting of her tongue-elephant calf. (79)
Hidden within the thicket of the mind and equipped with the two tusks of karma, her rut is the mass of latent impressions (vāsanā), her body spreading in every direction. (80)
He shows the two renowned tusks with the word "karma": action consists of the forms of the auspicious and the inauspicious.
He shows the intoxication mentioned in the phrase "intoxicated by pride" with the word "mada"; the same should be applied to what follows as well. || 80 ||
O Rāma, the various views of cyclic existence are its battlefields, wherein a person repeatedly experiences victory and defeat. (81)
This serpent of desire destroys the miserable multitudes of living beings;
it consists of latent impressions, longing, mind, consciousness, volition, mental cultivation, and yearning.
A female elephant is a *nāgī*. [She devours] collections of living beings, that is, multitudes of creatures. || 82 ||
May this multitude of names, residing within the treasury of her heart, [be subdued] with ease by the excellent weapon named Fortitude as it spreads forth. (83)

It resides within the treasury of latent dispositions (*āśaya*) and has entered the treasury of the mind; that is to say, it is impelled by the diversity of mental activities. To answer the question "How is this [mind] destroyed?", he says: "By fortitude," etc. (83).
One should conquer with one's whole being this desire, which is like a serpent and consists of all things, as long as it expands within [the mind] in the form "this is an object. (84)

[This state] consists of all things, having as its sphere of experience all objects of enjoyment up to the world of Brahmā; [it is attained] by means of a self that has been cultivated with the thought, "I alone am everything, in every way and by my very nature. For craving does not arise toward that which has been cultivated as one's own eternal essential nature; rather, it arises toward that which is seen as something unobtained, in the form of the thought "this [is mine]. Thus he says: "as long as... (84).
So fierce is the great cholera of the poison of saṃsāra;
indeed, this very mind which thinks "let this saṃsāra be" is itself the extent of that saṃsāra.
It is implied that craving, appearing in the form of the cholera-like poison of the great cycle of existence (saṃsāra), continues to manifest for that long. || 85 ||
The summary of this knowledge is that its pacification is liberation;
it is clarifying, pure, free from desire, and of stainless form. (86)

Craving itself is saṃsāra; its destruction alone is liberation (mokṣa), because it is the cause for the arising of the stages [of realization]. How is detachment the cause for the arising of the stages? He shows that: "By serenity... (verse 86).
The word of instruction comes to rest like a drop of oil upon a mirror;
by the mere absence of perception, the sprout of desire for existence does not arise. (87)

In a mind defiled by the human transgressions of passion and the like, the words of instruction from the scriptures and teachers do not adhere, just as a drop of water does not cling to a lotus leaf. However, in a mind endowed with the means such as dispassion, they do adhere—like a drop of oil on a mirror—and by wiping away the impurity of ignorance, they produce clarity: a state of transparency conducive to the manifestation of the form of Brahman.

The meaning is that it comes to an end. He states the means for the non-arising of passion and the like, as well as for the cutting off of what has already arisen, with the words "asaṃvedana" (non-perception).
The sprout of worldly existence, which consists of desire, does not arise merely by abandoning *saṃvedana*, which is the recollection of sense objects. || 87 ||
Desire, even when it has only slightly arisen, should be severed with the weapon of non-perception, for it brings about misfortune, just like a row of poison-sprouts.
Even if it has arisen only slightly, it must be cut away by the very weapon of non-perception. || 88 ||
The living being, though pierced by desire, does not abandon its state of wretchedness;
yet the effort of self-awareness remains silently seated within. (89)

*Vicchuritaḥ* means pervaded. *Dīnatām* refers to the wretchedness of attachment to enjoyments. He explains the nature of non-cognition with the words "svasaṃvedana" (self-cognition). Perfect non-cognition is *svasaṃvedana*; the effort of restraint conducive to that, as well as the effort of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*), and the posture (*āsana*) consisting of the mind remaining inwardly silent and free from activity. || 89 ||
Like a hundred corpses sleeping, utterly devoid of attention, catch that fish of desire with the hook of withdrawal (pratyāhāra). 90.

And that [state], which takes the form of attentiveness during the period of practice, but becomes naturally established—free from deliberate attention—during the period of perfection, as in the states of deep sleep and death; with this intention, he says: "By means of attention...
Seize and restrain that fish of desire which causes misfortune by means of the hook characterized by withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*).
"Bind [it]"—this is the response addressed to all listeners. || 90 ||
The supreme ones say that the agitation [of thought] "May this be mine" is conceptualization;
the non-contemplation of that object is called the relinquishment of conceptualization. (91)

[Objection: "But surely you have stated many times that liberation occurs precisely from the abandonment of prior conceptualization (*kalpanā*); why then is it now said to be from the abandonment of desire (*icchā*)?

To this he replies: "‘May this be mine’" etc. The meaning is that they call *kalpanā* the state resulting from conceptualization, characterized by the pursuit of objects, which is a running of the mind—that is, *saṃvega*. *Bhāvanā*... [is]... [cultivation].
Recollection. || 91 ||
Know that recollection is volition, while the wise know non-recollection to be Śiva.
In that state, both what was previously experienced and what was never experienced are contemplated.
With the intention that this very point is also the intended meaning of previous statements—that volition alone is the root of all misfortune—he says:
"Having forgotten memory, whether experienced or not experienced, like a piece of wood;
having quickly forgotten everything, remain hidden, O one of great intelligence. (93)

With the intention that—since even that which has not been previously experienced can be cultivated through mental resolve (saṃkalpa)—there is a distinction [between the two stages] despite their non-synonymity, and thus there is a certain specific difference in that they are both to be abandoned by those desiring to ascend to the higher stages; he says "the experienced" (anubhūtām) with the view that non-difference is intended here. || 93 ||
With arms raised high, I cry out this, yet no one hears it;
