freedom from volitional thought is the supreme good—why is it not cultivated within?

Now, the supremely compassionate Vasiṣṭha, wishing to reinforce—even through a cry of lamentation—the secret teaching of the entire Vasiṣṭha-corpus—that liberation is not achieved for all people without the renunciation of conceptualization regarding sense-objects, and that such renunciation must necessarily be performed—said: "With arms upraised. I cry out; I repeatedly call out in a loud voice.

Even when such abuse is being inflicted, some person hears it not, like one who is deaf, or as if asleep or intoxicated. Even among those who do hear it, there is the statement that they perceive no fruit from hearing it; why is this not contemplated within the heart? Why is it not reflected upon so that one might reach the state of having accomplished all that is to be done? For this is not [the case] for those of dull or middling capacity.
The meaning is that the accomplishment of the goal does not occur without correct reflection. || 94 ||
It is said,
O Rāma, that by remaining merely silent, that supreme state is attained, wherein even sovereignty over the entire universe is regarded as a blade of grass. (95)

That supreme state is attained by a person who remains silent, having indeed ceased all activity. The word "kila" indicates its well-known status in the Vedas. Thus says the Śruti: "When the five [sensory] knowledges, together with the mind, come to rest, and the intellect no longer stirs—that they call the supreme goal. Supreme...
The meaning is that even the bliss of universal sovereignty, extending up to that of Hiranyagarbha, becomes as insignificant as a blade of grass within that bliss of the Infinite (Bhūmā). || 95 ||
Just as the movement of the feet of a traveler who is intent solely on his destination is free from volitional thought, so too is the movement in one's own actions [when one is focused on the goal].

Now, one might object: "If all volitional thoughts (*saṃkalpa*) are abandoned in every respect, then since physical movement and so forth would be impossible and worldly activity (*vyavahāra*) would cease, how can there be life? To this he says: "As in the case of a traveler... Just as for a traveler whose stream of mental states is fixed exclusively on his destination, such as his own home, and who is thus free from volitional thought regarding his feet, a movement occurs at every moment; so it is here.

The meaning is that even for a yogin, activity will occur in regard to his own non-prohibited actions solely by the force of prior habituation and unseen merit (adṛṣṭa), even without volition. || 96 ||
What is the use of saying more here? This is stated in brief: conceptualization is the supreme bondage; its absence is liberation.
Seeing all this as thus unborn, peaceful, infinite, constant, and imperishable— the true nature of consciousness— abide in peace as you please.
He states that view by which non-conceptualization occurs: "All this," etc.
It is the nature of consciousness as the real object—the eternally established nature of consciousness as the ultimate reality. (98)
They know yoga to be non-perception, peaceful, seated, and imperishable;
established in yoga, perform actions without latent impressions, or else do not perform them at all. 99.

The knowers of Brahman understand that "non-perception" (*avedanam*)—through the transformation of such a vision—is precisely the forgetting of all superimposed distinctions of "I" and "mine," which is characterized as the union (*yoga*) of the individual soul and Brahman. This is because the Blessed One has explained it thus: "One should know that disjunction from the conjunction with suffering is designated as yoga. Therefore, [the Lord says], "Established in yoga, perform actions."

With the intention that those words were meant to prompt the performance of optional rites for one desiring to maintain social order, and not as a restrictive injunction, he says: "Established in yoga... Now, if you are intent upon samādhi, do not perform [these rites]. (99)
They know yoga to be the absence of sensation, the unconditioned cessation of the mind;
having become entirely absorbed in that, remain just as you are, O sir! (100)
"So be it, sir. The sense is that, upon the attainment of one's true nature as it actually exists, it is only fitting to remain established exactly as it is. || 100 ||
O Rāma, the constant contemplation of that which is auspicious, all-pervading, tranquil, consisting of pure consciousness, unborn, and pure— this is known as "renunciation of everything.
While contemplating this within yourself perpetually, perform your duties and actions.
He says that this very state is also the "renunciation of everything" demonstrated by Cūḍāla, because it consists in the cessation of all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*):
"It is auspicious. || 101 ||
One who perceives "I" and "mine" is not liberated from suffering; one who does not perceive them is liberated. Therefore, practice that which you desire [to attain]. 102.

Having extracted the reality of what is useless and the possession of the human goal as described at length, he concludes by showing them as clearly as a myrobalan fruit in the palm of one’s hand: "I" and "mine. 102.
Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-sixth canto, titled "Description of the Nature of Ultimate Reality," in the *Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa* of the holy *Vāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa*, a work of the Sage. 126.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Nature of Ultimate Reality," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and twenty-seventh canto.
Bharadvāja said:
Having heard all this ancient essence of knowledge spoken by the excellent sage concerning the illustrious descendants of Raghu...
The foremost of the clan, Vimalamati, asked something else: "Is he himself filled with equal happiness, established in perfect awakening? (1)
In this [work], Rāma’s repose, the words of Bharadvāja full of longing,
the characteristics of the waking state and the others, and the fourth state (turīya) are described.

Having thus far caused the dialogue between Śrī Vasiṣṭha and Rāma to be heard, and seeing that the Guru, Śrī Vālmīki, had become silent— having come to rest within the Self, which is full of unsurpassed bliss and brought near by the remembrance of Rāma’s repose— he [the disciple], even now, because he himself has not yet attained repose therein, [continues] further...

Eager to hear, Bharadvāja asks— "Thus," and so forth. O Sage of pure intellect, that Śrī Rāma, the foremost of the Raghu dynasty, was instructed and taught by the venerable Vasiṣṭha in many ways concerning this ancient (purāṇa), timeless (cirantana) [teaching] which has come down through the tradition of the great sages beginning with Brahmā.
Having heard and understood the essence of knowledge, he, desiring to know further, asked something more; or rather,

with all doubt and delusion stilled by this much instruction alone, he was himself filled with the bliss of the Self realized as it truly is— equal, devoid of the gradations caused by the diversity of sense objects.
Having become the very self of perfect enlightenment, he remains in that state; such is the ellipsis. || 1 ||
He is indeed the supreme yogi, worshipped by the universe, the Lord of the gods, free from birth and death, whose nature is pure consciousness,
a treasury of all virtues, and the very presence [of divinity].
The sovereign lord of Ramā’s creation, preservation, and grace of the three worlds.

One might object: "Since both you and Rāma have heard the same text, why is it that Rāma’s [understanding] is not determined by you through the very fact of whether or not his own doubts and delusions have been dispelled? This should not be doubted;
for he says, "He indeed," indicating that there is a great difference between him and me. He...

The Lord— who is celebrated in such scriptural passages as "His nature is consciousness, unobscured by the yoga of eternally perfected knowledge and sovereignty," "the controller of all," and "the ruler of all"— having descended for the protection of the world, and though he is the teacher of the universe, assumed through his own will the appearance of ignorance regarding himself in order to favor all people and set forth the science of knowledge, so that [others] might hear.
The sense is that there is a great difference: I, on the other hand, am a seeker of liberation from time immemorial, yet I am endowed with very few means. || 2 ||
Śrī Vālmīki said:
Having thus heard these words of Vasiṣṭha, which comprise the essence of Vedānta,
the lotus-eyed Rāma, who had mastered all branches of knowledge, [spoke].
Thus questioned, Vālmīki, supporting the second part of the inquiry with the remainder of the narrative, gave his reply, beginning with the words "Having heard this... (iti śrutvā). || 3 ||
By the power of the descent of grace (*śaktipāta*), the dense mass of pure consciousness manifested its unfolding;
for a moment, he became awakened as an ocean of the bliss of consciousness. (4)

The descent of power (*śaktipāta*) is the manifestation of the reality of the Self as eternal and unsurpassed bliss within the mental modification produced by the sentence of undivided form; by virtue of that, through the unfolding characterized by the bursting open of the sheath of ignorance, the pure mass of consciousness becomes manifest, and [the practitioner], piercing the six wheels (*ṣaṭcakra*) via the path of the *suṣumnā* by means of the *kuṇḍalinī*, [proceeds].

Or it is that which is well-known in the Yoga scriptures as characterized by the union of Śiva and Śakti through entry into the *brahmarandhra*; or rather, that which is well-known in the Mantra scriptures, whereby— through the Guru’s extraordinary grace toward the disciple— the [Guru] leaves his own body, enters the disciple’s body, and by means of purifying the disciple’s channels (*nāḍī*), effects the movement of the disciple’s Kuṇḍalinī through the seven cakras.
The descent of power (*śaktipāta*) that consists in the direct manifestation of the conduct of all worlds is not intended here;

for since Lord Śrī Rāma’s omniscience and other attributes are established by his own nature, he has no need for it, and through such [a descent of power] the benefit of the world would not be accomplished. [The term *udbuddha* means] awakened to one's own essential nature, alert, and blossomed. (4)
Free from the formal sequence of questions and answers and the like, his body was bristling with horripilation as he was filled with the nectar of bliss. || 5 ||

"Vibhāga" (discrimination) means the discernment of what has been stated and what has not been stated; by the word "ādi" (and so forth), the mere contemplation of external objects is included. He is devoid of those successions of mental states intended for that [contemplation], namely the operations of the mind, intellect, and senses. His vital breaths (*asavaḥ*)—that is, his life-forces (*prāṇāḥ*)—are filled with the nectar of bliss (*ānanda*). || 5 ||
Because it exists as the nature of the great universal (mahāsāmānya) and as the pervader of consciousness,
his desires for the eightfold sovereign powers are eternally regarded as being like blades of grass.

The Great Universal (*mahāsāmānya*) is pure existence (*sanmātra*) which underlies all things. Because its nature is realized through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it remains full, pervading consciousness everywhere. With the intention that this alone is the manifestation of unsurpassed bliss, he says: "eternal" (*nityam*). [This refers to] the eightfold qualities—the eight in number, beginning with *aṇimā*—which are the sovereign powers (*aiśvarya*).
One whose desire for acquisition is as abundant as grass.
Having attained and become established in the auspicious state, he said nothing at all.
Bharadvāja said:
"Oh, what a wonder for me! Rāma has reached the great state. (7)
"In the auspicious state, which is the reality of unsurpassed bliss, he has become transformed and attained a state of single essence.

Having thus described how Rāma, the person of the highest qualification, attains Brahman through hearing and other means, [the text now] describes specific forms of worship for those of dull and middling qualifications in order to purify their minds, by way of the three states [of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep].
Out of curiosity regarding Bharadvāja and others, the venerable Vālmīki describes [the events] to Ariṣṭanemi, beginning with the words "Bharadvāja said," and so forth. || 7 ||

O Leader of Sages, how can such an attainment be ours—how can those like me, who are fools, stubborn, and possessors of but little knowledge, and moreover sinners, [attain it]? Where is this state of Rāma, which is difficult to reach and sought after even by Brahmā and the other gods? (8)
"O Master, Lord of Sages, how may I find rest?
Tell me quickly how I may cross over this ocean of existence, which is so difficult to traverse. (9)
Of the ocean of existence which is difficult to cross, the water is delusion; this is the implied meaning. || 9 ||

Śrī Vālmīki said: O Lord, having reflected with my intellect upon the entire narrative of Śrī Rāma—from the beginning onwards—as it has been set forth in accordance with the words of Vasiṣṭha, please consider it; I too shall relate it to you here in that same manner.

Thus questioned, Vālmīki first teaches that the constant repetition of the study and reflection upon the sacred texts is established by the maxim "repetition [is required] because of the instruction given repeatedly" (*āvṛttirasakṛdupadeśāt*). He says: "O Śrī Rāma. The meaning is: "Listen; that which is to be told—such as the discrimination between the three states of consciousness—is being told in accordance with your own experience. || 10 ||
This is the manifold projection of ignorance; here there is not even an atom of reality. The wise discern this, while those lacking discernment engage in dispute.

He states, beginning with "of ignorance" (*avidyāyāḥ*), that because the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is the effect of false ignorance, its non-existence and the sovereignty of the non-duality of consciousness (*cidadvaita-sāmrājya*) cannot be understood by the merely intelligent. Now, if the phenomenal world is indeed the effect of ignorance, why do disputants (*vādin*) debate over it? To this he replies: "they dispute" (*vivadanti*). 11.
There is nothing whatsoever separate from consciousness; why do you obstruct yourself with conceptual proliferation?
O friend, become clear through the practice of the secret teachings. 12.
And he says that through false non-duality there is the loss of real non-duality: "It does not exist," etc. The address "O friend, O companion" is used out of affection.

Regarding the secrets—the meanings of the *praṇava*, the Great Sayings (*mahāvākya*), and so forth—and the meditations (*upāsanā*) to be described hereafter, become "clear," that is, pure in mind. 12.
The mental state whose object is conceptual proliferation is proclaimed as "sleep while awake"; but he within whom the stainless lamp of consciousness is fully awakened is truly "awake. (13)

Therein, first, he establishes the waking world (*jāgrat-prapañca*) as illusory for the sake of clearly discerning its witness, by means of the meaning of the first *mātrā* of the *praṇava*, starting with the words "the world" (*prapañca*). In the Śruti, it is proclaimed that "its three states are but dreams," and thus even the waking state is designated as sleep. (13)
O friend, this conceptual proliferation has emptiness as its root and emptiness as its summit;
because it is empty of essence, the wise have no reliance upon it even in the middle. 14.

It has emptiness as its root and false ignorance as its cause; it is such that its summit and peak—ignorance itself in the form of emptiness—is its very end. Even in the middle, when analyzed through methods such as the tripartition (*trivṛtkaraṇa*) and differentiation (*pṛthakkriyā*), its essence (*sāra*) or existence (*sattā*) is revealed to be merely phenomenal (*prātibhāsika*) due to its emptiness. Therefore, there is simply no concern for it.
The word "is appropriate" is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. || 14 ||
Due to the defect of beginningless latent impressions, this very [world], though non-existent, is perceived;
it is the cycle of existence, full of manifold delusions, appearing like a city of the Gandharvas. (15)

He says "beginningless" (anādi) because it is well known that even non-existent things, such as a city of Gandharvas, are perceived through ignorance accompanied by latent impressions (savāsanā-avidyā).
Why do you become deluded by cultivating the poisonous creepers of latent impressions (vāsanā), without practicing the auspicious kandalī-stalk of the nectar of consciousness? 16.
Why do you become utterly deluded, having resorted to and taken shelter of these poisonous creepers—the vines of latent impressions?
This waking state has not fallen below due to grasping at a support for knowledge;
for there are none above all these who possess consciousness free from support.

Through the vision of reality, by grasping the support—which is the nature of non-referential knowledge and serves as the cause for the stability of the mind—one falls below, into this waking state that existed previously during the stage of ignorance; however, in the higher fourth state (*turya*), even these three states do not exist. This applies to those yogis whose consciousness is non-referential.
The meaning is that this is established by the experience of all people. || 17 ||
The great river of consciousness, whose essence is nectar,
remains established in that state only so long as it is not plunged into its true nature by the skillful.

He says "tāvat" (for so long) to show that for as long as there is ignorance, for that same duration the river of consciousness possesses the growth of the tossing waves of the world, which are difficult to cross; thus, it is said to be "rūḍhā," meaning having the appearance of waves that are difficult to cross.
O friend, know that this entire world does not exist before, nor does it exist at the end;
even in the middle, it does not truly exist—this world is like the occurrence of a dream.

Since it does not exist at the times of its beginning and end, its non-existence in the middle as well must be inferred—just like a dream—because it is impossible for it to possess a nature that contradicts [the evidence]; thus he says, "prāk" (before), etc. That whose occurrence is like the occurrence of a dream. || 19 ||
All these diverse manifestations, whose source is ignorance, arise for a moment like bubbles and then dissolve into the single ocean of knowledge. (20)
Then, having recognized the river of very cool water and plunged into it,
let those who have wandered outside due to delusion emerge, their suffering now allayed.

That action in which suffering is experienced is "kalitam-asukha-duḥkham"; let them go forth in such a state. This expression is made by superimposing sentience upon even insentient things that are being heated. 21.
And one is the ocean of ignorance, which remains having submerged the world;
this is the eldest wave, "I am," born from the wind of nescience (avidyā). (22)

Now, the Blessed One, wishing to prevent his disciple from immersing himself [in ignorance], describes ignorance as the salt ocean with the words beginning "And one... Having flooded and pervaded the world, which is its own transformation, he shows that which was first born from its great waves: "The Eldest. This is the stream of nescience (*avidyā*), the beginningless latent impression of delusion. It is that very thing.
Wind arises from that. || 22 ||

The waves of the mind’s faltering and its fragmentation, as well as passion and the rest, are merely conceptualized; the whirlpool of the sense of "mine" proceeds of its own accord and at its own will. (23)

He shows the very small waves with the word "citta" (mind). The "āli"—meaning a row—of those various lapses and divisions of the mind toward their respective objects, as well as the causes thereof such as passion (rāga) and so forth, are conceived of as the even smaller waves; this is the ellipsis. He shows its whirlpool (āvarta) with the word "mamatā" (the sense of "mine-ness"). || 23 ||
Attachment and aversion are the two over-graspers; once one has been seized by them, who can prevent the subsequent fall into the abyss of misfortune? (24)

The phrase "two crocodiles set forth" is to be supplied by way of ellipsis. Once you have been seized by those two, who can prevent your immediate entry—being present and close at hand—into the mouth of death, that abyss of calamity?
The compound *gṛhītapada* (seized-footed), being semantically untenable, is a Vedic usage (*chāndasa*). 24.
Plunge into the ocean of pure nectar, which is tranquil with waves of immortality; why do you immerse yourself in the waves of the salt sea of the obsession with duality?

But if immersion in the ocean is necessary for you, then immerse yourself in the ocean of bliss; thus he says: "Who remains? Who has gone? What belongs to whom? By what has what come? Why indeed do you immerse yourself in illusion? Do not fall into it, but remain vigilant. (26)

He [Rāma] remains in saṃsāra, yet he has departed for me through the awakening to reality; thus he wards off the delusion that is the cause of grief, asking: "Who remains? You, being vigilant and discerning, must not fall [into such delusion]. // 26 //
They declare that this entire world is the single reality which is the Self;
therefore, O dear one, who else could there be beyond you that would be an object of grief? (27)
"When they declare" means when the Vedāntas clearly establish that "all this is this Self," and so forth. || 27 ||
To the ignorant, this entire world is a transformation of Brahman;
the wise, however, always abide in the untransformed bliss.
For those fools who possess ignorance, there is the illusory transformation (vivarta) of Brahman into the form of the world. || 28 ||
An undiscriminating person grieves and rejoices without cause; but the knower of reality remains smiling, for him delusion is a mere mockery. (29)

"Undiscriminating" means lacking discrimination. [Objection: But how is it that even those who know reality are sometimes seen to be deluded? To this he says: "Of him... It is a mere mockery, a simple imitation of the behavior of the ignorant. || 29 ||
And this subtle reality is concealed by ignorance;
just as people have doubts regarding dry land, water, and their own selves. (30)

But for others it is not so; for those whose selves are shrouded by ignorance, there is the delusion of selfhood in what is not-self, like the perception of land in waters. Thus he says: "And that. Just as ignorant people have the doubt that there is land in waters and the doubt that there is water in desert lands, so too [is there doubt] regarding the selves, even though they are imagined as distinct.
The meaning is that "saṃśaya" (doubt) is "bhrama" (error). || 30 ||
When this world, composed of the atoms of the great elements such as earth and the rest, remains [in this state], who then has departed here that one should be mourned? (31)

When, even according to the view that the world consists of atoms and so forth, there is no possibility of sorrow even upon such analytical discrimination (*viveka*), then in the doctrine that the world is composed of *māyā*, that sorrow is all the more remote; with this intention, he says: "Earth, etc. Who has gone? Who has perished?
Even in that [atomistic] view, since the body and so forth are not the Self, there is no destruction of the Self upon their destruction—this is the meaning. || 31 ||
There is no arising of the non-existent, nor is there the destruction of the existent, O friend;
these are merely the manifestation and disappearance of various forms.
For grief arises from the loss of what is dear. If that beloved one exists, then he does not perish; if he does not exist, then he was never present.
Since in both cases the loss of him is unestablished, there is no cause for grief—this is the intended meaning with which he says "of the non-existent" (asataḥ).
"Of entities" (saṃsthānām) refers to specific illusory configurations. || 32 ||
However, due to the intense efforts of many cities, he is approaching the enemies;
therefore, take refuge in the Supreme Lord, the Teacher of the World, who is endowed with full majesty.
Now, if the configuration of the body and so forth is indeed merely illusory (*māyika*), then let it appear as indifferent and detached, like the illusion displayed by a magician;
but what is the cause for its bestowing thousands of misfortunes such as grief, delusion, and suffering? To this he says: "But rather... This is true.

There is no cause for this in the present; rather, the cause is the manifold effort of a person—characterized by the activity of merit and demerit accumulated in the past—which is termed "merit and demerit. Therefore, this illusory body and so forth, for the sake of its experience, attains a poisonous nature, becoming the cause of thousands of calamities such as death and fainting, just like actual poison.
Even if the meaning of the scriptures of inner knowledge (*adhyātmajñāna*) is taught hundreds of times, it does not take root in the heart solely due to the power of sin;

therefore, he says "Worship" (*bhaja*), instructing one to perform the worship of the Lord with attributes (*saguṇeśvara*) for the destruction of that sin. [He is] "one by whom the fullness" (*ābhoga*)—the form to be described, such as the Ardhanārīśvara and others—"is perfectly assumed" (*saṃbharitaḥ*) for the sake of bestowing grace upon devotees. || 33 ||
All his misdeeds have certainly not yet been fully ripened;
for this god, the nooses have already become loosened.

"Even now they are not cooked"—the ellipsis implies "nor are they exhausted. The word *dhruvam* (certainly) is used here in the sense of deliberation (*vitarke*). It is precisely the karma—consisting of merit and demerit—performed by living beings that constitutes the nooses for binding the animal-like creatures of this Lord Paśupati;
let these attain *viśravatām*, that is, the state of being established through various means of valid cognition such as the Śrutis and others. 34.
Worship with form for as long as the mind is not yet serene;
thereafter, there is an unartificial state of stability in the supreme, formless reality.

The *sattva* (the mental essence) becomes serene and purified. From that worship, it follows—as the remainder of the sentence implies—that it will become "unartificial," meaning innate (*sahaja*), because it cannot be obstructed by impediments (*vighna*). And so says the Śruti: "Having meditated upon the Supreme Lord, the Master, accompanied by Umā, the three-eyed, blue-throated, and profoundly peaceful one, the sage attains [liberation]."
"The source of beings, the witness of all, beyond darkness. (35)
Having surely conquered this unrestrained darkness through the power of your being,
follow the path of Yama with a confident inner self.

Having conquered this well-known power of delusion belonging to unrestrained darkness— which is overcome by the force of a pure *sattva* purified through the worship of the Lord— follow with a mind endowed with faith in the instructions of the Guru and the scriptures the path of *Yama*, which consists of the restraint of the senses and the mind. 36.
Composing yourself for a moment, behold the inner self by means of the self;
let that night of your former ignorance clearly dawn as this manifest day.

Then, having composed yourself for even a moment—a twelfth part of a muhūrta—and having resorted to meditative absorption, may that night of yours, whose nature is the intellect shrouded by darkness, dawn through that vision of the Self; may it reach the state of daybreak. || 37 ||
That which is to be attained by men is obtained not merely through human effort and action alone, but only through the grace of Maheśa. (38)
Now, one might ask: since the purification of the mind is accomplished through the performance of good deeds alone, what is the purpose of the worship of the Lord? To this, he says:
"Maheśa... (verse 38).
Neither noble birth, nor conduct, nor policy, nor prowess—O friend, only ancient deeds alone are powerful. (39)

Now, it was previously established that the efforts of contemporary persons—such as noble birth, virtuous conduct, austerity, and ritual action—are more powerful than past karma; how then can it now be said that they depend upon the grace of God? To this, he says:
"Not [by] noble birth," and so forth.

The sense is that because past karmas are infinite and present human efforts are exceedingly small, the dependence on the Lord has not been abandoned; rather, it was established that the efficacy of prior and present-worldly effort is superior, but not to the exclusion of that [dependence on the Lord]. || 39 ||
Since there is no remedy for that which cannot be reasoned away, why do you despair in this way?
Even the Lord does not erase the line of letters inscribed upon the forehead.

If that is so, one might ask: "Should one then perform only the worship of God, and what is the use of restraints (yama), observances (niyama), knowledge, and so forth? To this he says: "Because it is beyond reasoning" (apratarkyāt).

Thus, even though you have taken refuge in the Lord, [you must understand] dharma and the rest—which are beyond reasoning (apratarkya), inaccessible to human logic, and knowable solely through the Vedas.

Why do you tremble? For even the Lord, propitiated by worship, does not erase the line of letters situated on the forehead with his own hand; rather, he does so only through the means of uprooting it by means of knowledge—this is the meaning. || 40 ||
Where is the speaker, where is his eloquence, and where is this creeper of delusion?
This destiny is inconceivable, for it has brought about this pair [of opposites]. (41)

The capacity of the teacher and the scripture to awaken the disciple, the disciple’s capacity for understanding through the purification of the mind and skill in reasoning (ūhāpoha), and the ripening characterized by the attainment of the fitness for the uprooting of attachment and other afflictions—this convergence of all these factors occurs solely by the power of destiny (niyati) characterized as the will of the Lord (īśvarecchā); thus he says: "Where? (kva).

Where is the Guru—the speaker whose mind is the indivisible Brahman-Atman, which is inaccessible to speech and mind—and where is the disciple’s cleverness or skill characterized by fitness for that realization? Where is this very creeper of delusion, which, through the sequence of tranquility, self-restraint, and so forth, has matured into one's own destruction? If all this equipment [of means] were to arise from her [the creeper of delusion]...

That destiny—the will of the Lord—which has come about as a mutual encounter of pairs, is inconceivable; that is to say, its power is such that it cannot be grasped by thought through the measurement of its limits. || 41 ||
O Bhāradvāja, clearly abandon your delusion through discernment;
you shall now undoubtedly attain extraordinary knowledge. (42)

For this very reason, when such a collection of circumstances has been attained, it is proper to exert oneself solely toward conquering delusion, rather than grieving in the interim; thus he says, "O Bharadvāja. "Asāmānyam" means uncommon or unique. || 42 ||
In times of great calamity, a king of great being exerts himself to the utmost;
for people of small being grieve even over a slight injury.

Furthermore, with the intention that grief is appropriate for one who lacks the necessary means even in the face of a great task, but not for you, O Great King, who are endowed with all such means, he says: "Far... A king of great being (*mahāsattva*), even when immersed in a great calamity such as war, [remains superior] because of his possession of wealth, servants, and other resources, unlike others.

The meaning is that although he is capable of performing tasks such as protecting the earth and suppressing the wicked while sustaining the virtuous by mere command— even those far beyond his desires— he is unable to do so when afflicted by calamities such as the loss of wealth, because of the absence of the necessary means, such as fortitude, required for overcoming them.
Awakening, which depends upon merit, unfolds over many lifetimes;
it may be inferred from its effects in the wise who are liberated while living. (44)

Taking those liberated while living as examples, and reasoning that "my awakening will certainly occur when the collection of merits is complete," one should first engage in acquiring the collection of merits with enthusiasm; with this intention, he says:
"Awakening... (verse 44).
"O son, by that very same action through which such bondage was incurred when it was hostile, you shall attain liberation when it has become friendly. (45)
Now, one might object: "Since even merit (puṇya) can be a cause of bondage, how can merit that has become an enemy be acquired? To this he says:

"by [merit] that has become an enemy. The meaning is that while merit becomes a cause of bondage when attachment exists, in its absence, it becomes a friend and is indeed conducive to liberation. || 45 ||
This agitation for virtuous deeds among the righteous, dispelling the ancient [tendencies],
extinguished the forest fire of living beings like a torrent of water.

He states that when past sins are destroyed by an excellence of merit, there occurs the pacification of the threefold suffering for those nourished by the nectar of tranquility, self-control, and so forth—beginning with the words "of the virtuous" (satām). The use of the past tense in "he sprinkled" (asecayat) is not intended to be significant. || 46 ||
O friend, having renounced all actions, become a lover of Brahman,
if you wish to bring to rest the whirling of the cycle of worldly existence.

He teaches what must be done once firm detachment has arisen following the acquisition of merit—beginning with "O friend": one who is a lover of Brahman, meaning one who is attached to Brahman through such means as hearing [the scriptures] (śravaṇa). || 47 ||
This world arises from conceptual construction only so long as there is grasping at external objects;
it is like a turbulent ocean when agitated by waves, yet merely water when the waves are stilled.

The meaning is as follows: external grasping and lack of devotion to Brahman are like the ocean when its waters are turbulent; it is hostile and rushes against the shore in a state of agitation. But when the water is still, it is merely water—nothing more. || 48 ||
Why do you embrace this grief that causes such blindness?
Let that very same unbreakable staff of wisdom support you. (49)

It causes darkness and obstructs the vision of discernment; therefore, until the opening of the eye of discernment for you who are blinded by grief, let the single staff of wisdom alone sustain you. (49)
Those who are carried away by the waves of joy and sorrow like blades of grass are never counted among the most exalted. (50)
By the waves of joy and sorrow, and by the destructions of auspicious enthusiasm. || 50 ||
O friend, this world has mounted the swing of the ten stages of life;
it is played upon by the six kinds of swings—so why, then, do you grieve? (51)
This world—the collection of living beings—is made to play by Time upon a swing characterized by states such as joy and sorrow.

It is played with by means of six kinds of swings or mechanical cradles, arising from the division of the six waves, the division of the six seasons, or the division of the six enemies beginning with desire (*kāma*). [The root] *krīḍ* is used here with the causal suffix *ṇic* because it is intransitive, according to the rule "gati-buddhi-... [Pāṇini 1.4.52].

By such statements as these, the agent is treated as the object, and thus the *la*-affixes (the verbal terminations) are applied to the object (*karman*). The meaning is that weariness is not appropriate regarding the conjunctions and disjunctions of objects fashioned merely for the sake of play and curiosity. || 51 ||
Time alone, full of curiosity, swiftly generates, withdraws, creates again, and destroys the worlds through many cycles. (52)
One who is curious is one who delights in play. || 52 ||
There is no perception of distinction whatsoever, nor is there any [discrimination] among living beings who are like food to be consumed by the serpent of Time as it advances. (53)

Having determined that, just like the bodies of all other living beings, one's own body and so forth are food for Time (Death), and that whatever is the food of a being must necessarily be consumed by it, he speaks with the intention of showing that there is no occasion for grief once the conceit of "I" and so forth has been abandoned therein:
"It is not well-known"—this is the meaning. Having begun [the discussion] regarding the serpent characterized as Time, who is the consumer...
"Forcefully seizing and devouring" means eating; [this occurs] among those living beings who have become the objects of that action. || 53 ||
What need is there to speak of mere mortal bodies that exist for but a moment? Even the hosts of gods have the misfortune of being subject to the sway of adverse time.
They are within the range of malignant time; that is to say, they have become [mere] food. || 54 ||
Why do you dance yourself in joy when your senses are impaired by calamity?
Sit motionless for a moment and behold the drama of saṃsāra.

Moreover, it is appropriate for you, as a witness, merely to observe the spectacle of the dance of saṃsāra, rather than to dance yourself through the transformations of grief, delusion, and so forth; thus he says, "himself" (svayam). He whose senses—the eyes and others—are "disabled" (vikalāni) in times of calamity—that is, during the destruction of wealth, mind, and so on—meaning they are incapable of discerning vision and are distorted by weeping and other such changes.
Being such as this, [he acts]. || 55 ||
O Bharadvāja, the wise man does not despond even slightly over this world, which consists of many waves and is subject to momentary destruction. (56)
The remainder of the phrase is "because of seeing [them] as subject to momentary destruction. A "manasvin" is one who possesses discernment (*vivekin*). || 56 ||
Abandon inauspicious grief and contemplate auspicious things;
and meditate upon the Self, which is pure and a mass of consciousness and bliss. 57.
Inauspicious, yet not deserving of inauspiciousness. || 57 ||
The grace of Maheśa shall be granted to those whose minds are made tender by the weight of faith in the gods, the twice-born, and the guru, and who take the true scriptures as their authority. (58)
He states which things are auspicious: "The deity," and so forth. Faith in the deities, the twice-born, and so on, are auspicious because they are means for obtaining the grace of the Lord.
The intention is that the grace of the Lord is the supreme auspiciousness, as it is a direct means to knowledge. And thus it has been said:
Only through the grace of God does the latent impression of non-duality arise in two or three men at most, as a protection from the great fear [of saṃsāra].
Thus [ends verse] 58.
Bharadvāja said:
By your grace, all this has been understood by me in its entirety.
There is no kinsman superior to dispassion, and no enemy greater than worldly existence.
Now Bharadvāja said: "I have understood the secret of all means condensed by you;

however, I have not yet understood the secret of the means for dissolving the expansion of the visible world and the secret of the means for the grace of the Lord, which were spoken by Vasiṣṭha in his detailed discourses scattered here and there, though now they have been condensed."
Demonstrating this both through explicit statement and by implication, he who desires to know it asks with the words beginning "It is known," and so forth. || 59 ||
Now I wish to hear the essence of knowledge as set forth by Vasiṣṭha, explained in its entirety through the text consisting of words.
Śrī Vālmīki said:
O Bharadvāja, listen to this great knowledge that bestows liberation;
by the mere hearing of which you shall not sink into the ocean of worldly existence. (61)

The meaning is: "I wish to hear the secret that has been stated in its entirety through a text consisting of many sentences, now condensed and extracted as a single word. In the reading *yadātmanā*, the phrase *yattātparyakeṇa* (that which has such an intended meaning) is an adjective qualifying the text. || 60 || 61 ||
Salutations to Him whose form is existence, consciousness, and bliss— who, though being one, exists in manifold ways through the distinctions of dissolution, maintenance, and creation.

In order to state the method of dissolution (*pravilāpana*), which is negation (*apavāda*), he pays homage for the sake of auspiciousness to the God who, though one, exists as manifold through superimposition (*adhyāropa*): "Saṃhṛti... (verse 62).
I shall explain to you, in brief, according to the teaching of the Vedas, the means by which reality shines forth once the phenomenal world has been dissolved.

He promises to provide an answer in accordance with the intent of the question, saying "kṛte" (in the Kṛta age). This is according to the instruction of the Śruti—that is, following the sequence stated in the Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad and other such scriptures. || 63 ||
How has your memory, which ought to discern what comes before and after, been lost?
By that very memory, everything is known by oneself as clearly as a myrobalan fruit in the palm of the hand.
(One should investigate this for oneself with one's own mind;

that by which one attains it, one no longer grieves. This should be contemplated again and again through the company of the virtuous, the study of true scriptures, discernment, and the possession of dispassion. || 65 ||
That which has been stated in a fragmented manner can be extracted and understood by those of subtle intellect through their own investigation of what precedes and follows;
yet, he rebukes [the opponent]—in order to focus attention on what is about to be explained regarding how that previously celebrated wisdom has now perished—with the words "pūrvāpara... (64–65).

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-seventh canto, titled "The Instruction of Bharadvāja," in the first part of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the glorious Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa, composed by the sage Vālmīki.
Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Instruction of Bharadvāja," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and twenty-eighth canto.
Śrī Vālmīki said:
He was tranquil, self-controlled, and withdrawn from prohibited and desire-driven actions.
And from the pleasure arising from the contact between the sense objects and the senses, he is endowed with faith. || 1 ||
In this [chapter], through the method of dissolution (*pravilāpana*), Bharadvāja’s fulfillment of his purpose is described,
as well as the sequence of the wise one’s duties regarding the restoration of Rāma.

In this regard, he begins to explain by means of describing the purport of the Śruti— namely, "having become tranquil, self-controlled, withdrawn, patient, possessed of faith, and concentrated, one sees the Self in the very Self"— the method for dissolving the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) which consists of its constituent parts and culminates in direct realization, starting with the words "tranquil" and so forth. Among those, the term "withdrawn" (*uparata*)...
He explains by way of distinguishing the objects [of the prohibitions], starting with "from what is forbidden" (niṣiddhāt). || 1 ||
Seated on a soft seat, having mastered the activities of the mind and the senses,
one should utter "Om" until the mind becomes serene.

In this context, describing the eight-limbed yoga beginning with posture (*āsana*) by way of the subject matter of meditative concentration (*samāhita*), he explains the term *titikṣu* (the patient one) through implication, starting with the words "on a soft seat" (*mṛdvāsane*). One should utter [the mantra] long, that is, recite it;
or, according to the method stated in the *Bhuśuṇḍopākhyāna*, one may recite it as extremely protracted (*plutatama*). || 2 ||
Then one should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) for the purification of the internal organ;
thereafter, one should gradually withdraw the senses from their objects.
Having understood that from which the origin of the body, the senses, the mind, the intellect, and the knower of the field (kṣetrajña) arises, one should subsequently dissolve them back into that.

Having known through scripture and other means that whatever has its origin—its birth—from whatever [cause], one should dissolve each of those [effects] back into their respective elements and deities. The meaning is that, according to the method stated in the passage beginning with "a mere modification of speech" (*vācārambhaṇa*), one should remember that nothing exists apart from those [causes]. || 4 ||
Having first established himself in the Virāj, and after that in the Self (Ātman),
he subsequently remained in the Undifferentiated (Avyākṛta) and finally rested in the Supreme Cause.

Having thus abandoned the state of the internal body, senses, and so forth, one first abides in the Virāj by means of the contemplation: "I am indeed the Virāj, whose meaning is the syllable *A*, and who is the collective totality (*samaṣṭi*) of the deities that constitute its cause. Thereafter, having dissolved the Virāj into Hiraṇyagarbha—which is the meaning of the syllable *U* and is the subtle causal aggregate of the elemental liṅgas—one abides therein.

The meaning is as follows: having first remained established in that cause—the unmanifest (avyākṛta) which consists of the three qualities (triguṇa), is conditioned by Māyā, and is the referent of the syllable *M*—one should thereafter dissolve even that unmanifest into the pure Brahman, which is characterized as the half-measure (*ardhamātrā*), which is the substratum of all, indicated as the root cause of the entire universe, and remain established therein. || 5 ||
One should dissolve the earthly portion, such as the flesh and so forth, into the earth;
the watery portion, such as the blood and so forth, into the waters; and the fiery portion into fire.

He further explains in detail what was previously stated regarding the dissolution of the body, senses, and so forth, each into that from which it originated—beginning with the words "flesh, etc. One should dissolve [them] by contemplating their reduction to their subtle essence (*tanmātra*). || 6 ||
One should cast the element of air into the great wind and the element of space into the sky;
having thus assigned the elements beginning with earth, one should then place the sense organs within the respective deities of the self.

The "etherial" (nābhasa) refers to the space within the body. In this manner, having cast away and dissolved the sense organs, such as the nose and others, into their own origins—the subtle elements of earth and so forth that serve as the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) for the deities—one should dissolve them. || 7 ||
One should assign the sense of hearing, endowed with its characteristic marks and so forth, to the directions for the sake of establishing the enjoyer's experience;
one should project the self's hearing into the quarters and the skin into the lightning.

According to the Vedic scripture, "Having become the ear, they entered the ears," and so forth, the deities of the quarters and other elements— having entered the physical spheres of the ears and other sense organs in order that the individual soul (the agent) might experience objects such as sound— became endowed with the nature of the senses characterized as the ear and so on, and [the soul] [resides] within those very deities respectively.
The word "should cast" (nikṣipet) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. He demonstrates that very sequence with the words beginning "In the directions," etc. (verse 8).
One should dissolve the eye into the orb of the sun, the tongue into the waters;
one should dissolve the vital breath into the wind, speech into fire, and the hand into Indra.
In the waters, [the deity] Varuṇa. || 9 ||
Likewise, he should place his two feet in Viṣṇu, his anus in Mitra,
and having placed his generative organ in Kaśyapa, he should fix his mind upon the Moon.
One should restrain the intellect within Brahman; these deities of the instruments are designated by the name of the sense organs. || 11 ||

"In Brahman" refers to the four-faced one (Brahmā). The mention of "intellect" (*buddhi*) is illustrative; in this same manner, one should dissolve the mind (*manas*), ego (*ahaṃkāra*), and consciousness (*citta*) into Candra, Rudra, and Acyuta respectively. He concludes with the words "these": recollecting the authority of Vedic statements such as "Agni, having become speech, entered the mouth," [the author shows that] it is the deities themselves who exist under the designation of the sense organs.

The connection with the subsequent verse is as follows: "I have not revealed these matters through my own arbitrary imagination; rather, they are taught by me for the purpose of dissolving [the notion of] the senses—which are indeed distinct entities—by means of instruction on reality. || 11 ||
Having recollected the words of the Śruti, one should not manifest [the self] by one's own power;
thus, having assigned the body to the Self, one should contemplate, "I am Virāj. (12)

Having thus explained the summary verse concerning the dissolution of the body, senses, and so forth, he clarifies the statement "having first remained in the Virāj" with the words "evam" (thus). || 12 ||
That Lord who resides within the cosmic egg as Ardhanārīśvara is the support of all beings; He is declared to be the Cause. || 13 ||

In the context of explaining the phrase "remaining subsequently in the indeterminate," it is stated that seekers of the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) should first meditate upon the Virāj— the self of the cosmic egg— who is identical with the illusory, variegated Brahman that serves as the non-different efficient and material cause of the entire world; she who eternally dwells within the heart-lotus of that Virāj, her body formed by half of the [divine] knowledge of Brahman.
Showing his own form, he says that he alone is the cause for all living beings in the form of their mother and father: "Within the cosmic egg... (verse 13).
That sacrifice, in the form of creation, is established within the functioning of the world;
outside the double-sized egg is the earth, and twice the size of the earth is the water.
Thus, by virtue of being the Father, he is established in the maintenance—that is, the means of life such as food and drink—of the world consisting of gods, humans, and others created by himself;

remaining within the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) in the form of the creation of Śrauta and Smārta sacrifices which nourish all through oblations, rain, and so forth. Having spoken this incidental matter, [the author] now speaks of the dissolution (*pravilāpana*) under discussion.

He states the coverings of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) with the words "twofold" (*dviguṇa*). Although it is heard in the Purāṇas that the egg is pervaded by these coverings increasing tenfold each time (*daśaguṇottara*), nevertheless, when encircling [an object] twice, as in the case of five *krośas* becoming twenty-five *krośas* through a fivefold [encirclement], a single fold becomes fivefold.

This should be understood with the intention that what is doubled becomes tenfold. Alternatively, there is no contradiction, as this refers to the covering of the unevolved elements (*apañcīkṛta-bhūta*), whereas the present statement refers to the evolved elements (*pañcīkṛta*). || 14 ||
Fire is twice the extent of water; wind is twice the extent of fire;
and space is twice the extent of wind—each increasing sequentially from the bottom upwards.
One by one, each subsequent [element] is superior to the preceding one. || 15 ||
The world is woven together by that which is both individual and collective, and all-pervading;
having dissolved the earth into water, one should cast the water into fire.

"Separately" means by that which has not been quintuplicated (*apañcīkṛta*); "collectively" means by that which has been quintuplicated (*pañcīkṛta*). For this very reason, he says "the earth," etc., [implying] that one should dissolve the innermost within the outer. || 16 ||
Having merged fire into air, one should cast air into the ether;
and the ether into the Great Space, which is the cause of the origin of all things.

Having caused [them] to enter and dissolve [into it], [he dissolves them] into the great space—the space of Hiraṇyagarbha—which is the cause of the arising of the entire gross phenomenal world. || 17 ||
Having remained there for a moment, O Yajña, he assumed a body consisting of mere subtle signs;
likewise, his latent impressions, the subtle elements, karma, and ignorance [remained]. (18)
What is that subtle body (liṅgaśarīra)? He says: "It is the latent impressions (vāsanā). || 18 ||
The wise know this—the ten sense organs, the mind, and the intellect—to be the subtle body (liṅga).
Then, having gone outside from that half-egg, one should contemplate: "I am the Self" (ātman) therein.

The *liṅga* is the subtle body (*liṅga-śarīra*). Thus, by the dissolution of the gross adjuncts, having become as it were half-formed, and having emerged from the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) through the abandonment of the conceit of being its self, he stands there within the collective subtle-body composed of the subtle elements, identifying: "I am indeed Hiraṇyagarbha, the presiding Self."
The meaning is that one should contemplate [it]. || 19 ||
This four-faced one is established at the forefront within the subtle elements;
the wise man, having placed the subtle linga in the unmanifest and the undifferentiated, [proceeds].

But surely, it is well known in the world that the four-faced body born from the lotus is Hiraṇyagarbha; however, this [Self] is the collective totality of the subtle elements of the gross elements and is not the four-faced one—how then can it be Hiraṇyagarbha? To this he says:
"The four-faced one. It is precisely this [Self], established through its presiding over the subtle elements of the gross elements, which is the foremost.

The meaning is that prior to the dissolution of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), for the sake of experiencing the sovereignty over the cosmic egg, he fashioned a body born from a lotus and became four-faced. After such contemplation on the nature of Hiraṇyagarbha,
he states what must be done next— beginning with the word "liṅga"— referring to that which is subtler even than the unevolved elements (*apañcīkṛtabhūta*).

The statement is made by dividing [the process] into two parts in order to indicate that the inert portion is dissolved into the inert, while the portion consisting of the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa) within the indeterminable illusory part—which is itself unmanifest as the form of the superimposed consciousness—is dissolved into consciousness. || 20 ||
Some call that in which the world abides, being entirely free from name and form, "Prakṛti"; others call it "Māyā," while still others call it "atoms."

Alternatively, with the intention that the designation differs for each [entity] based on the conceptualization of distinct causal factors (pravṛttinimitta) in the form of the fruit of an action—namely, that manifestation is the fruit of the act of verbal designation—he says: "Name," etc. The Sāṃkhyas call it *prakṛti*; the Vedāntins call it *māyā*. || 21 ||
Others, whose minds are bewildered by sophistry, revile ignorance;
having entered into that [ignorance], they all remain there in an unmanifest form. (22)

Other Buddhists [assert] that ignorance is of the nature of conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*). In that indeterminate time of dissolution, all entities, having undergone dissolution—the sixth transformation of state—remain in an unmanifest form, existing solely through the existence of that [ignorance]. || 22 ||
Then they arise again, devoid of connection and devoid of relish;
for they remain in that very nature as long as creation proceeds. (23)
He explains how they abide: "without connection" (*niḥsambandhāḥ*).
This means they are devoid of mutual contact and devoid of the relish characterized by being objects of consciousness. Why?
Because at the time of creation following dissolution, [they arise] from that very unmanifested state (*avyākṛta*), which is primordial nature (*prakṛti*). || 23 ||
Creation is said to proceed from the direct order (ānulomya), and dissolution from the reverse order (prātilomya).
Therefore, having abandoned the three states, one attains the fourth, immutable state.

"In accordance with the sequence beginning with space" means in direct order (*ānulomya*); "by way of reverse order" means by a sequence contrary to that of creation (*sṛṣti*). He explains this [statement], "He stands thereafter in the supreme cause," with the words "Therefore... The three stations—known as Virāj, Hiraṇyagarbha, and the Undifferentiated (*avyākṛta*)—consist of the gross, subtle, and causal forms.

Having abandoned the three states of collective waking and so forth— neither "consciousness within," nor "consciousness without," nor "consciousness both ways," nor "consciousness," nor "unconsciousness," nor "the mass of consciousness"— in accordance with the direction shown by the Śruti,
one remains in that which is their substratum, the single essence of pure consciousness alone.

One should meditate until its direct attainment—that which is invisible, beyond conventional usage, ungraspable, without characteristics, unthinkable, indefinable, the one Self, the goal of the Vedantic texts—as revealed by the scriptures. 24.
One should meditate upon the Liṅga for its attainment; having dissolved it, one should enter the Supreme.
The elements, the senses, the mind, the intellect, the latent impressions, karma, and the vital breaths—[all these dissolve]. (25)

By means of the final direct-apprehension (*sākṣātkāra*) vṛtti, kindled by meditation (*dhyāna*), one dissolves even the subtle body (*liṅga*), which consists of the agent and instruments of meditation, through the sublation of root-ignorance (*mūlājñāna*). Just as the space within a jar merges into the great space upon the breaking of the jar, one enters the Supreme Brahman, which is unsurpassed bliss; this is the meaning of his having achieved his purpose through liberation from the fetters of the subtle body. Now, [an objection]: [The text continues: "But surely..."

If it is asked, "Since no sublation of the subtle body (liṅga) is seen in scriptural passages such as 'not having consciousness within' (nāntaḥprajña), how can its cessation occur?", [the author] shows that the sublation of the subtle body is established by implication through the sublation of the three states, because the subtle body is established only in gross elements, subtle elements, the senses, and so forth: "gross elements, senses... (bhūtendriya...). || 25 ||
"And ignorance would be their foundation, with the unmanifest as the mark.
Bharadvāja said:
"Now I am entirely liberated from the fetters of the mark."

Now, how can ignorance be the support? To this he says: "The subtle body" (*liṅga*). For when the unmanifest (*avyākṛta*), which is the veil of ignorance, exists within pure Brahman, the subtle body arises by way of the subtle elements, and not without ignorance; therefore, that [ignorance] alone is the fundamental support of the subtle body, and upon its cessation—

The meaning is that there is the accomplishment of breaking the fetters of the [inferior] marks. Thus, having been awakened by Vālmīki through the means of elaborating upon the meaning of the *praṇava*, the enlightened Bharadvāja spoke—beginning with the words "Now," etc.—revealing his own experience for the sake of verification against the experience of the Guru. || 26 ||
Because I am a portion of consciousness, I have entered the ocean of consciousness-bliss;
being non-different [from it], I am the Supreme Self, devoid of all limiting adjuncts.
I am the immutable, absolute, and all-pervading possessor of the powers of consciousness and unconsciousness;
just as when a jar is absent, there is no distinction between the space within the jar and the space within the pot. || 28 ||

"I am consciousness (*cit*), but not the possessor of the power of consciousness (*cicchaktimān*). To the question of from what kind of non-difference you are the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), he says: "In the absence of the jar" (*ghaṭābhāve*).

This means when the jar has been destroyed. Just as for a single jar there is the conceptualization of different names such as "jar" and "pot," and for the space conditioned by it there is the conceptualization of different designations such as "the space of the jar" (*ghaṭākāśa*) and "the space of the pot" (*kalaśākāśa*).

In the same way, there arose the conceptualization of the various distinctions of names for the world from that single ignorance alone, as well as the conceptualization of the various designations— such as "individual soul," "Lord," "god," "man," or "elephant"— with respect to Me who am conditioned by that [ignorance]. Just as, through the breaking of a single jar, both [the jar and its space] cease and the unity characterized as pure space remains, so too, through the cessation of that single ignorance, [all distinctions cease].
The meaning is that through the cessation of distinctions such as all names and so forth, there is the sovereign empire of the oneness of consciousness. || 28 ||
Many scriptural authorities declare with such reverence that unity is indeed thus:
just as fire cast into fire follows after it by virtue of their equality. (29)

Intending thus to express this oneness, [the scripture says]: "Where one sees nothing else, hears nothing else, understands nothing else—that is the Infinite (Bhūman). But where for him everything has become the Self alone—by what and whom should he see?
They consider the Fourth State (Turiya) to be that which has the realization of the one Self as its essence, which is auspicious, peaceful, and non-dual; "In this, there is no diversity whatsoever."

The meaning is that many such scriptural passages (śruti) state this. With the intention of showing that such oneness alone is demonstrated by such scriptural texts as, "Just as water poured into water, milk into milk, or ghee into ghee becomes indistinguishable, so too does the individual self (jīvātman) [become indistinguishable] in the Supreme Self (paramātman)," he cites the example with the word "yathā" (just as).
Samānatva means oneness. || 29 ||
Having become one with that [state] and identified with it, it is no longer perceived as distinct;
just as grass and other things thrown into the *rumā* salt-mine turn into salt. (30)
Thus, he provides an illustration for how even the insentient manifold (acetana-prapañca), by being dissolved into consciousness (citi), attains its state—beginning with the word "yathā" (just as).
The insentient world, when placed within consciousness, becomes sentient, just as a lump of salt [dissolves] in the ocean or as rock salt [merges] in the sea. || 31 ||
"Placed" means dissolved. || 31 ||
Released from name-and-form, he enters into the state of the ocean,
just as water poured into water, milk into milk, or ghee into ghee.
These remain undestroyed and are not perceived as distinct;
likewise, I have entered into all things through my entire being whenever there is consciousness.

With the intention that even my suspicion regarding the destruction of the conditioned individual soul (*jīva*) has vanished upon the destruction of the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), he says: "They are not destroyed" (*avinaṣṭāḥ*). This refers to the conscious [Brahman], which is of the single essence of consciousness (*cidekarasa*). || 33 ||
In Him who is eternal bliss, all-knowing, supreme, and the ultimate cause;
who is eternal, omnipresent, peaceful, faultless, and stainless. (34)

He corroborates his own experience with such scriptural passages as, "partless, actionless, tranquil, blameless, and stainless" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.19), beginning with the words "eternal," etc. (verse 34).
I am that supreme Brahman, partless, actionless, pure, and higher than the high;
free from both the rejectable and the acceptable, the embodiment of truth, and devoid of senses. (35)
I am the supreme Brahman alone, whose resolve is truth, who is pure,
liberated from merit and sin, and the ultimate cause of the universe.
He whose will is true, whose very nature is reality, and who is capable of bringing about the existence of even the non-existent world by mere volition. || 36 ||
I am the non-dual, supreme light, Brahman, the imperishable bliss;
endowed with such qualities as these, yet devoid of the qualities of sattva and the rest. (37)
It is devoid of the illusory qualities such as existence and so forth. || 37 ||
One who performs their own duties should always meditate upon the entire Brahman as having entered [into all things];
for a person practicing in this way, the mind indeed sets there.

With the intention that even at the time of practice you have taught me meditation on this very [Self], he says "entered," and so forth: one who is devoted to performing his own duties, listening to the scriptures, and serving the guru, and who is steadfast in the duties of his own caste and stage of life (varṇāśrama-dharma). || 38 ||
When the mind has set, his own Self shines forth by itself;
when there is this illumination, there is the destruction of all sufferings and bliss within the Self. (39)
One realizes bliss by oneself through one's own self;
there is no other Lord besides me who consists of consciousness and bliss. 40.
Regarding how one should practice therein, he says: "Not intoxicated," etc. (40).
"I alone am the Supreme Brahman"—thus the Self shines within.
Śrī Vālmīki said:
"O friend, having renounced all actions, become a lover of Brahman. (41)

He states the meaning of the word "practice" (pratipatti) with the words "thus the Self. Having heard this experience described by Bharadvāja, Vālmīki, being satisfied, instructs him on the necessity of renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*)—established in such scriptural passages as "That which is to be known must indeed be abandoned; for the supreme state is directly realized by the one who has abandoned"—in order to stabilize that aforementioned experience. He addresses him as "Friend. (41)
"If you desire the cessation of wandering in the whirlpool of the cycle of existence," Bharadvāja said:
"O Teacher, all this knowledge spoken by you has been understood by me. (42)

It is called "delusion" (bhrama) because one wanders within the revolutions of the wheel of saṃsāra. If you do not lead [yourself] to peace—the happiness of rest—within the state of a householder, then, having renounced actions, become a lover of Brahman, remaining undistractedly attached to Brahman alone; for according to the Vedic scripture, "He who is established in Brahman attains immortality," one must do so through exclusive application.

The meaning is that it is only for renunciants (*saṃnyāsins*) who are devoted to Brahman that the cessation of delusion, together with its seed, becomes possible; "all" means complete, including every part. || 42 ||
The intellect has become pure and worldly existence no longer lingers;
now I wish to know what kind of action is performed by the man of knowledge.

The meaning is that this is based on the Śruti: "He shall not remain long by lingering; for him, it will be long only until he is liberated, and then he shall attain [the goal]. The first question is whether action must be performed or not by the knower who is liberated while living (jīvanmukta).
If it must be performed, then all action—whether obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), or optional (*kāmya*)—should be carried out exactly as before, in the form of active engagement.

The second question is whether one should perform actions, or rather, having desisted from desires, perform only those duties appropriate to one's own stage of life (*āśrama*). This is to be understood because the order of meaning (*arthakrama*) is more authoritative than the order of the text (*pāṭhakrama*). Now, [one might object]: "O friend, having renounced all actions, become a lover of Brahman"—having heard this, Bharadvāja [renounced] all actions.

Both questions are indeed untenable. Nevertheless, regarding those rites bound to be performed for as long as one lives by such scriptural injunctions as "One performs the Agnihotra as long as life lasts" and "Performing actions here, one should desire to live a hundred years," even though they have been relinquished at the time of initiation by statements such as "The initiated one does not give, he does not sacrifice," they must be resumed once the initiation has ended.

It is like possessing property. For that [property] must indeed be relinquished by one who renounces, as established by such scriptural passages as, "Desiring this very world, mendicants renounce their homes.

Thus, for those who have renounced for the purpose of the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*), once the purpose is fulfilled through the attainment of knowledge, the resumption of possession is established by logic. Nor does the injunction regarding the renunciation of the knower (*vidvatsaṃnyāsa*) imply a lack of possession; for that...

It should be understood that the two questions are appropriate because they are intended for those exceptional individuals who, by virtue of having practiced the renunciation of one seeking knowledge (*vividiṣā-saṃnyāsa*) in previous lives, have attained the dawn of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) while remaining in the stages of life such as that of a householder; thus, it is impossible for a rule to enjoin the preservation of the *vividiṣā-saṃnyāsa* already obtained to be directed toward those for whom the rule merely intends to prescribe a different, previously unobtained form of renunciation.
"Whether it be worldly engagement or renunciation, whether it ought to be done or not, O Lord," Śrī Vālmīki said:
"Therefore, that which incurs no fault when performed should be practiced by those seeking liberation. (44)
Thus questioned by you, Vālmīki himself first replied to your question— namely, "How is one who possesses knowledge to act thereafter?"—

by stating that the state of being a knower (*jñānitva*) must be accomplished through the study of the scriptures and the renunciation of those actions, both desirable and prohibited, which serve as causes for defects such as distraction that oppose knowledge. Following that, he himself gave the answer to your question regarding what his subsequent conduct should be.

"You will come to know [this]. He gives this answer with the following intention: because you will be able to experience the cessation of each respective karma precisely at the time when its corresponding stage (*bhūmikā*) has reached maturity; and because, given the diversity of *prārabdha* (projected karma) among the wise, it is observed that they do not remain in a uniform state, it is impossible to determine whether those karmas have already commenced or have already ceased.

— "Therefore": because you have understood my taught point— that devotion to Brahman accompanied by the renunciation of all ritual action is indeed the means for the knowledge that removes the delusion of saṃsāra— therefore,
O seekers of liberation like yourself, when whatever action [is performed]...
One should perform only that [action] which is free from the defects of obstacles to hearing and so forth, as well as the defects of mental distraction, impurity, and sin.

The meaning is that one must not perform actions that are motivated by desire (*kāmya*), those that are prohibited (*niṣiddha*), or—by the force of the word "and" (*ca*)—those that are means for producing perceptible distractions.

However, regarding the maintenance of the renunciation of the seeker (*vividiṣā-saṃnyāsa*), since it is impossible to resume what was abandoned according to the rule without a further rule, [it must be maintained].

The sense is that [the practice] will be established because of the hearing of faults regarding such a reversal— as in the passage, "But for him who, having ascended to the ultimate dharma, falls away again, I see no atonement by which that self-destroyer may be purified"— and because there is no purpose in taking up [the vow] again, and because it is censured by the learned. || 44 ||
One should especially not perform actions motivated by desire nor those that are prohibited,
when the individual soul is endowed with the qualities of Brahman and has abandoned the qualities of the mind.

However, his state of being a knower (jñānitva) can only occur upon the attainment of the qualities of Brahman—such as being of the singular essence of pure, non-dual, unattached consciousness and full bliss—through the renunciation of all mental attributes, and not otherwise; thus he says, beginning with "When... (yadā). || 45 ||

Then the entire collection of the senses becomes completely stilled; he is the all-pervading Lord, who is beyond the body, the senses, the mind, and the intellect, and who is higher than that which is high.
Beyond the four sheaths beginning with the physical body is the self consisting of the sheath of bliss; beyond that is Brahman, the substratum of that [bliss].
When one meditates thus: "I am that," then the individual soul (jīva) is liberated—freed from being an agent or an enjoyer, and divested of all limiting adjuncts (upādhi). || 47 ||

By the word "etcetera" (ādipadāt), the three triads—the agent, the action, and the instrument; the enjoyer, the object of enjoyment, and the act of enjoyment; and the knower, the knowledge, and the object of knowledge—are all included. When you shall become entirely free from all those limiting adjuncts such as the body which cause that [state], and from their fruits, namely pleasure and pain, then— || 47 ||
Then, liberated from pleasure and pain, he is fully released;
he perceives the Self in all beings and all beings in the Self. (48)
When one perceives [the Self] without differentiation, then the individual soul (jīva) is liberated;
when it has abandoned the three states known as waking, dreaming, and deep sleep.
When the individual soul enters the fourth state of bliss, it is then liberated;
and that which is called the fourth state of the soul is its abiding within the Supreme Self.
Free from states, seeds, sleep, and the like, consisting of the bliss of consciousness—this is the culmination of yoga, a great blissful experience. (51)

The seed of the waking and dreaming states is ignorance (*ajñāna*), along with its latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and karma. Sleep (*nidrā*) is a particular state of that [ignorance]. This very state, called the fourth (*turyā*), is the condition of the individual soul (*jīva*) resulting from the maturation of yoga—that is, non-conceptual meditative absorption (*nirvikalpa-samādhi*) born of profound contemplation (*nididhyāsana*); or, according to the word "or" (*vā*), it is for the primary qualified practitioner.
Or, *niṣṭhā* is the completion (*parisamāpti*) of the knowledge of direct intuition produced by mere reflection (*vicāra*). || 51 ||
When the mind has set for men, nothing else is perceived,
as they rest in the ocean of absolute nectar, whose waves are the tranquil nectar of immortality.

With the intention that for you who have found rest in that [state], there is no possibility of being attached to dualistic perception, much less the possibility of being submerged in the waves of the salt-ocean of karma, he says: "praśānta... (52).
Why do you wallow in the waves of the salt ocean of dualistic grasping?
Worship the Supreme Lord, the teacher of the world, whose fullness is ever-expanding. 53.

Having meditated upon the Lord as previously described, through His grace—whether by the path of knowledge taught by Vasiṣṭha or by the path of Yoga—when the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) is attained, there will be rest through the destruction of all doubt. This occurs because, through the knowledge of the One, there is the knowledge of all, and because the ignorance that is the root of all doubt is destroyed. He concludes with the verse beginning "Worship" (*bhaja*). 53.
Thus, O son, I have described to you in its entirety the instruction of Vasiṣṭha; by this path of knowledge and the path of yoga.
O Bharadvāja of great wisdom, you will certainly come to know everything through your mastery of the scriptures and by understanding the meaning of the teacher’s words. (55)

In this regard, he says "by means of reflection" (parāmarśena) [in verse 55], because one must determine the single-pointedness of the meaning of the scriptures, the teacher’s instructions, and one's own experience.
"Through practice, all perfection shall be attained; such is the instruction of the Vedas.
Therefore, casting aside everything else, make your mind steady in practice. (56)
Bharadvāja said:
O sage, since Rāma has attained supreme yoga within his own self by means of the Self,
how was he made by the divine Vasiṣṭha to be intent on worldly affairs?
Yoga is oneness through the abandonment of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). By means of one's own self—the inner self purified [of impurities]—[one attains this] in the Self, which is Brahman. || 57 ||
Having understood this, I shall likewise strive for the sake of practice, so that my worldly conduct during the state of emergence will also be exactly like that. (58)
Śrī Vālmīki said: When the noble-minded Viśvāmitra had become perfected in his own true nature,
he then spoke to Vasiṣṭha, the best of sages.
Rāma is high-minded, his mind possessing the form of Brahman that is undivided. || 59 ||
Viśvāmitra said:
O illustrious Vasiṣṭha, son of Brahmā, you are truly great;
your status as my guru has been demonstrated this very moment by the descent of your power.

The meaning is that by you, through the previously mentioned descent of power (śaktipāta) employed merely by a glance of grace, the state of being a Guru— characterized by the capacity to uplift the disciple— was demonstrated to us immediately, at that very moment, by means of the disciple’s transformation into Brahman (brahmīkaraṇa). || 60 ||
He who, through sight, touch, sound, or compassion, generates the Śāmbhava immersion within the body of a disciple—he indeed is a true teacher (deśika). || 61 ||

[The opponent asks: "But surely, having abandoned my own body and entered the body of Rāma, I did not perform the movement of Kuṇḍalinī and so forth; how then was the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) known by you? To this he replies: "By seeing" (*darśanāt*).
For those like you whose resolve is true, even by a glance of compassion, [the awakening] of the Kuṇḍalinī of a good disciple [is perceived].
