The meaning is that through the piercing of the six cakras, the descent of power (śaktipāta)—characterized by absorption into Paraśiva residing in the aperture of Brahma (brahmarandhra) and characterized by the soul’s (jīva) absorption into pure Brahman through the abandonment of its limiting adjuncts—is accomplished; [this is] the teacher, the Guru. || 61 ||
This Rāma as well, pure in soul and truly detached from his own self, desiring only rest, attained the supreme state through this dialogue. (62)
In this regard, he demonstrates Rāma’s status as a true disciple with the verse beginning "Rāma" (verse 62).
The disciple’s own wisdom alone is the cause of awakening through the words of the guru;
if the three impurities are unripened, how can they become ripened? (63)

The "three impurities" (malatraya) refer to those well-known in the Śaiva scriptures as consisting of the *āṇava*, *kārmika*, and *vāsanā* [impurities]. The ellipsis "how does he awaken? refers to the disciple. || 63 ||
This knowledge is indeed direct perception, serving the purpose of both teacher and disciple;
for both are qualified for all such [teachings]. (64)

He states that the fruit of the teaching is indeed visible among worthy disciples: "Knowledge," etc. The meaning is that if both the teacher and the disciple are qualified, they shall both become vessels for all human goals, even those characterized by liberation (kaivalya). || 64 ||
Now, out of compassion, you ought to bring about Rāma’s awakening;
for you have reached the final stage, while we are still occupied with our tasks.

Having thus praised Vasiṣṭha, he states the task at hand with the words "Now" (idānīm): out of compassion for those such as ourselves, you have reached the state [of perfection], meaning that you have accomplished all that was to be done. || 65 ||
O Lord, remember my task for the sake of which I have come, and how King Daśaratha himself was entreated by me with great difficulty. (66)

The connection is either with the preceding clause, "Remembering my task, you ought to bring about Rāma's emergence so that the success of the sacrifice may be free from obstacles," or with the following clause, "Do not let [this] be in vain. || 66 ||
O Sage, do not let all of this be in vain; perform the work of the gods with a pure mind, for there is another purpose for our incarnation. (67)
Furthermore, we shall carry out even the work of the gods by means of rousing Rāma. || 67 ||
I have led Rāma, the crusher of Rākṣasas, to Siddhāśrama; from there he will perform the liberation of Ahalyā and [the marriage of] the daughter of Janaka.

Demonstrating other tasks as well, he clarifies the mission of the gods with the words beginning "Siddhāśrama," etc.; the ellipsis is that he will bring about the liberation of Ahalyā—that is, her release from the curse.
Having resolved to marry her by breaking the bow,
he will surely restore the lost status of Rāma, the son of Jamadagni.
Or, "certainty" refers to the certainty regarding speech; "course" refers to the path to the next world. || 69 ||
Free from fear and devoid of desire, he [Rāma] has entered the ancestral kingdom of his father and grandfather under the pretext of dwelling in the forest, residing here in the Daṇḍaka wilderness.

Having abandoned the kingdom, he has departed; because he is liberated while living (jīvanmukta), he is fearless and free from desire. The connection with the subsequent verse is that he will deliver the sages dwelling in the Daṇḍaka forest from fear by slaying the Rākṣasas. || 70 ||
Under the pretext of the misery caused by the abduction of Sītā, he will indeed uplift various living beings and the sacred fords on earth from their state of lamentation. (71)

He will uplift various holy places (tīrthas) and living beings; that is to say, he will purify them. By means of the pretext of the distress caused by the abduction of Sītā—the mockery of grief, delusion, and so forth—he will, through the slaying of Rāvaṇa and others, demonstrate to all those attached to women on this earth their wretchedness and lack of composure; such is the connection with the following verse. || 71 ||
Through the slaying of Rāvaṇa and the others, he will demonstrate to all the instability of those attached to women, as well as the transformation of the monkeys and the rest. (72)
Now, by means of Indra’s boon, he will demonstrate the returning, the turning back, and the re-animation of the monkeys, bears, and others who have died in battle. || 72 ||
Seek the purification of Sītā and the approval of the world;
though liberated while living and free from desire, remain devoted to the performance of ritual action. (73)

Seeking to demonstrate his own purity through entry into the fire, he will show that Sītā is innocent and manifest his own conformity with public opinion and the conduct esteemed by cultured people. Then, having been consecrated in the kingdom, though he himself is liberated while living and free from desire, he will remain so as to observe the destiny of those authorized to perform rituals through their very performance of those duties.
The connection with the subsequent clause is: "in order to demonstrate [this], he will become devoted to the section on ritual action (kriyākāṇḍa). || 73 ||
The combination of knowledge and action will serve to reveal the destiny of those by whom [he] has been seen, or even remembered, or heard of, or awakened by. (74)

The remainder [of the intention] is that, in order to show the destination—such as the world of Brahmā—for those qualified for the combination of knowledge and action, he will also perform the combination of knowledge and action; here, "knowledge" refers to meditative worship (*upāsanā*). He is not merely beneficial to people existing at present by setting them on the path of action alone, but also for future times.

He states that [the Lord] bestows the bliss of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) upon his devoted followers who have taken refuge in him, by means of their remembrance, glorification, and awakening through His own deeds, and so forth—beginning with the words "by whom" (*yaiḥ*). || 74 ||
"Indeed, it will grant liberation while living (jīvanmukti) to those in all conditions;
for this is the task of the three worlds and of me as well, in its entirety. (75)
For those who have gone [to him] in all states of existence and follow him with devotion. || 75 ||
Homage to this high-souled man, Rāmacandra; by him all has already been conquered. May such a person as he prosper for a long time! 76.

The connection with the preceding is as follows: "By this great-souled Rāmacandra, in the manner described, the welfare of the three worlds—and thus my own—is to be accomplished. Now, Śrī Viśvāmitra, increasing the devotion of the audience toward Rāma, says:
"Salutations! O people, you all should bow down to this Rāma; by the mere act of saluting him—
The meaning is that everything must be conquered by you, yet it is as good as already conquered; no further means need be sought.

Among you, there is at least one preeminent man who, like Śrī Rāma, is liberated while living (jīvanmukta) and has long attained repose in unwavering meditative absorption (nirvikalpa-samādhi). May he prosper in happiness and increase [in virtue]. 76.
Śrī Vālmīki said:
Having thus heard what was spoken by Viśvāmitra,
all those perfected ones (siddhas) and the lords of great yogis, headed by Vasiṣṭha, spoke again.
Established in the reverent remembrance of the dust of Rāma’s lotus feet,
they listened to the story of the Lord of Maithilī, the account of which they had heard from afar.

Those by whom the story of Rāma—consisting of his later deeds (*uttara-caritra*)—was heard, though it was difficult to obtain even from afar, became such that they were always established in reverence for the dust of Rāma’s lotus feet (meaning: in prostration) and in the constant remembrance of Rāma; this is the ellipsis to be supplied. Vasiṣṭha, however, was not fully satisfied merely by hearing the story of the Lord of Maithilī.
He became satisfied. || 78 ||
The blessed Vasiṣṭha and the other great sages were not fully satisfied,
even as they spoke of and listened to the qualities of that treasure-house of virtues, which they had heard before.

In this way, the other great sages were not fully satisfied; the meaning is that they all became eager to hear more. For this very reason, hearing his qualities as spoken by others and recounting what they themselves had heard to others, they spoke [as follows]. The absence of the *laṅ* suffix (the augment *aṭ*) is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*).
The venerable sage Vasiṣṭha spoke to the sage Viśvāmitra.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
"O sage Viśvāmitra, tell me [of] Rāma, whose eyes are like lotuses."
Who was this wise one? Was he a human being or a descendant of Raghu? || 80 ||

"Speak clearly to the audience; tell them: who was this Rāma before his birth? Was he a wise deity, or was he a human being?"—this is a question posed in accordance with the perspective of ignorant people. (80)
Viśvāmitra said:
"In this very matter, place your trust; for He is that Supreme Person, who churned the ocean for the sake of the universe and whose domain is the profound scriptures. (81)

Viśvāmitra also gave an answer in accordance with the understanding of the ignorant people, saying: "Right here. O person, you should place your faith right here that this Rāma is indeed the Lord Vāsudeva himself. He is the ancient, supreme Puruṣa. Who is he?
He is the one by whom the ocean—the Ocean of Milk—was churned for the sake of the universe. Of those who are profound...
The meaning is that the domain of reality regarding the Upaniṣads, which are scriptures of hidden intent, is not accessible through any other means of valid cognition. || 81 ||
Rāma is the bestower of all things upon all living beings; he is perfectly full of supreme bliss, equanimous, marked with the Śrīvatsa, and well-pleased.
"He is the bestower of all human goals"—this is the ellipsis. "Propitiated by excellent devotion. || 82 ||
This one, when enraged, destroys; this one creates those who are unrighteous.
He is the origin of the universe, the progenitor of the universe, the Ordainer, the Sustainer, and the Great Friend. (83)

"Those who proclaim what is non-existent as existent" (the reading *asataḥ sataḥ kāyante* is also found); they are called *asatsakāḥ*—a Vedic usage, or one belonging to the *pṛṣodarādi* class. These are those whose objects are false. || 83 ||
This vast ocean of bliss is plunged into by those free from passion, who have transcended the deceptive and hollow world of saṃsāra.

The ocean of bliss is plunged into—that is, entered—by those ascetics who are free from passion, yet are rogues and deceivers of the world; for they have transcended [worldly existence], are repelled by reflection, are essence-less, and are soft, being bound to the cycle of cause and effect within saṃsāra. || 84 ||

In one place this person (puruṣa) is like a liberated soul abiding in himself; in another, he is designated as the fourth state (turya); in another, his nature is fully manifested; and in another, he remains established within that [nature]. (85)

He states that this very one exists in four ways—as liberated through knowledge (*jñānamukta*), eternally liberated (*nityamukta*), the controller of *māyā* (*māyāniyantṛ*), and bound within *māyā* (*māyāntarbaddha*)—in the verse beginning with "In some places" (*kvacit*). || 85 ||
This divine Being, composed of the three Vedas and transcending the thicket of the three qualities (guṇas), this wonderful Puruṣa who is the soul of the Vedas, triumphs with his six limbs. 86.

He consists of the three Vedas, has the Veda as his body, and possesses the ancillary sciences such as phonetics and ritual manuals; he is the soul of the Vedas, being their ultimate essential nature. || 86 ||
This one with four arms is the creator of the universe, the four-faced Brahmā;
this very one is Mahādeva, the three-eyed destroyer.
The four-armed protector is Viṣṇu. || 87 ||
This unborn one is born through yoga; ever-awake and great, the Lord, though formless, assumes this manifold universal form.
Due to yoga, that is, through connection with the power of māyā; because he is not shrouded by the sleep of delusion, he is ever-awake. || 88 ||
This man is carried away by Suparṇa, just as victory is by prowess, light by radiance, and the excellence of wisdom by sacred learning. (89)

Just as victory is carried forth—that is, attained—by valor and prowess; just as light, which is radiant in form, is carried forth—that is, maintained—by heat; and just as the excellence of wisdom is carried forth—that is, attained—by learning through the scriptures, in that same way, this [world] is carried by Suparṇa, meaning by Garuḍa. || 89 ||
Blessed is this Daśaratha, whose son is the Supreme Person;
blessed also is that Ten-necked one (Rāvaṇa), who is meditated upon in his mind by Him.
By this Rāma, he has become one who must be thought of—worthy of being considered—with the thought, "He shall fight against me. (90)
"Alas! Heaven is now empty because of him; alas! He has come here from the netherworld (pātāla).
By his arrival, this middle world has attained excellence. (91)

"Alas! Heaven is empty of this body of Viṣṇu; such is the meaning of heaven's lamentability. Here, the accusative case is used in the sense of the genitive (ṣaṣṭhī) according to the rule: "abhitaḥ, paritaḥ, samayā, nikaṣā, hā, and pratiyoge [also take the accusative]. Likewise, this Śeṣa-mūrti has come here from Pātāla in the form of Lakṣmaṇa; thus, the meaning is that Pātāla too is to be pitied. || 91 ||
This Supreme Person, who reclines within the ocean, has descended as Rāma;
this immutable Supreme Self is Rāma, a mass of consciousness and bliss.
Yogis who have subdued the collection of their senses know Rāma;
we, however, are only capable of perceiving his inferior form.
To be manifested, to be defined, and to be seen. || 93 ||
"We have heard that the Blessed One is the one who brings about the destruction of Rāghava;
therefore, O Vasiṣṭha, out of compassion, please act so as to bring him back to worldly affairs. (94)
He says that even Raghu’s lineage was purified by his incarnation with the words "raghoḥ" and so forth.

In the word "śuśruma," there is no insertion of the augment *iṭ* due to the rule governing roots ending in *krādi*. The absence of the substitution of *mā* for the suffix *mas* in the perfect tense (*liṭ*) is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*). || 94 ||
Śrī Vālmīki said:
Having spoken thus, the great sage Viśvāmitra remained silent;
then the highly effulgent Vasiṣṭha addressed Rāmacandra.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
O Rāma, Rāma, O mighty-armed one, O Great Being composed of consciousness!
This is indeed not the time for rest; be the bringer of joy to the worlds.
As long as the worldly attachment of the yogin has not been eradicated, so long will his state of firmly established samādhi never become stainless. (97)

The remaining portion [of the verse] implies that it is not logical as long as the worldly consensus, characterized by the fulfillment of its respective authority, has neither taken root nor been established. || 97 ||

Therefore, having observed that objects such as sovereignty are perishable, and [having laid down] the burdens of duties toward the gods and others, devote yourself to them, my son, and be happy. (98)

The meaning is: having observed for some time, having experienced the burdens of office such as the duties of the gods, and having further reflected upon them, one should thereafter resort to meditative absorption (samādhi). || 98 ||
Śrī Vālmīki said:
Although addressed in this manner, when Rāma remained silent and entered into dissolution,
he [the sage] also slowly entered his heart through the *suṣumṇā* channel.
When, although addressed by his guru as "Rāma," he had attained dissolution— the state of oneness with Brahman—
and neither spoke nor moved because of the absence of hearing external objects and the cessation of the activities of the vocal and other organs,
then Vasiṣṭha entered that body through his own volition via Rāma's suṣumnā channel.
It slowly entered the heart-lotus. Having entered, it condensed the subtle body (*liṅga*)—the limiting adjunct of the individual soul (*jīva*)—which had been dissolved there;
just as the wind that has entered the interior of a seed draws out the sprout within it, so did it draw [the soul] outward.
(Verse 99) The individual soul (*jīva*), whose nature is light, is the agent that brings about the connection between power (*śakti*), vital breath (*prāṇa*), and mind (*manas*).
With all his faculties fully nourished through the channels of the subtle veins, he slowly opened his eyes;
having beheld the eminent sages led by Vasiṣṭha, he remained standing, free from all desires, devoid of deliberations on what ought or ought not to be done, and awaiting them all.

Regarding the external extraction of that [light], he describes the sequence of the manifestation of the field, the illumination thereof, and the perception of external objects, through the process of the manifestation of the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) therein, by means of the word "power" (*śakti*). First, in the foundational power (*ādhāra-śakti*), which is the seed of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the rest; then, upon the manifestation of the vital breaths within them; and then, upon the manifestation of the mind (*manas*).

And "attachment" (*prasakti*) in that context means the entry [of consciousness] by way of being a reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*); thus, it is called "the instrument for effecting attachment to power, vital breath, and mind. For this very reason, the individual soul (*jīva*), whose nature is the light of that [consciousness] and who has that as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), enters through the gateway of the vital breath into all the apertures of the channels (*nāḍī*), and [perceives] all things—whether well-nourished or manifest.
Being one whose instruments consist of the organs of knowledge and action, he thus slowly opened his eyes and beheld the eminent and venerable sages, headed by Vasiṣṭha; for,
having himself accomplished all that was to be done, he was free from all desires, and therefore [regarded] both what must necessarily be done (*kṛtya*) and what ought not to be done (*akṛtya*).

The meaning is that, being devoid of deliberation upon worldly transactions that ought to be abandoned, of reflection on their merits and defects, and— by the force of the word "etcetera"— of the mental activities of rejection or acceptance prompted by them, he remained waiting for everyone, thinking, "What will they say to me? || 100 ||
Having heard the words of Vasiṣṭha as if they were the command of his own preceptor,
the venerable Rāmacandra, being composed in mind, spoke.

Immediately thereafter, having heard the words previously spoken by Vasiṣṭha—namely, "O Rāma, Rāma, O mighty-armed one," and so forth—which were once again made to be heard by him, and having heard the entreaties of his father, brothers, kinsmen, and others, [the Lord reflected: "This word of the Guru is not to be transgressed. Thus spoke the Blessed One, the Omniscient.
That is to say, he is one who knows the purpose of his own incarnation; the meaning is that, being composed by accepting that [purpose], he spoke. || 101 ||
Śrī Rāma said: By your grace, this [person] is no longer subject to injunctions or prohibitions;
nevertheless, your word must indeed always be carried out.
O great sage, in the Vedas, Āgamas, Purāṇas, and even in the Smṛtis,
it is declared that the word of the Guru is the injunction, and its opposite is the prohibition.

An injunction (*vidhi*) is a matter that must necessarily be performed; its opposite, namely its transgression, is a prohibition (*niṣedha*), meaning that which must necessarily be abandoned. || 103 ||
Having spoken thus, the soul of all beings, that treasure-house of compassion, placed the feet of the high-souled Vasiṣṭha upon his head and addressed them all.

Now, Śrī Rāma, seeing no other way to repay the service rendered by his guru— which consists of the granting of the supreme human goal— offers himself to his guru under the pretext of placing the guru’s feet upon his own head;
and for all people, he himself [proclaims] the greatness of knowledge and the greatness of the guru as being the most excellent of all.
He says, "Having spoken thus," [104], meaning that he taught what was directly perceived in order to strengthen one's conviction.
Śrī Rāma said: Listen all, may it be well with you; this is my firm and well-ascertained conclusion:
there is nothing superior to self-knowledge, nor even to the teacher who possesses that knowledge. (105)
"Knowers of that" (tadvidas) means "knowers of the Self" (ātmavidaḥ); this is an epithet of the Guru. It refers to those who know that reality of the Self through the Guru's instruction;
or it means that for such a disciple, there is no teacher superior to the Guru. || 105 ||
The Siddhas and others said:
"O Rāma, it is exactly thus that this has taken its place in the minds of all; and by your grace, everything has been made firm through this dialogue. (106)
"Stability" means certainty; "by way of correspondence" means by way of the characteristics of this text and by way of correspondence with what you have said. || 106 ||
"Be happy, O Great King Rāmacandra; salutations unto you!
Having been permitted by Vasiṣṭha as well, we shall now depart as we came. (107)
Śrī Vālmīki said:
Having spoken thus, they all departed, intent upon the praise of Rāma;
indeed, a rain of flowers fell upon the head of Rāmacandra.
Thus has this entire narrative of Rāmacandra been told to you;
by means of this sequential practice, O Bharadvāja, may you be happy. (109)
The *Saṃjīvana*—meaning the nectar of life—is characterized by the narrative dialogue extending up to Rāmacandra’s final repose in liberation while yet living (*jīvanmukti*). || 109 ||

Thus has the accomplishment of the Lord of the Raghus been proclaimed by me to you, variegated with a jewel-garland consisting of the rows of words from the excellent sage; it is a form to be served by the entire assembly of poets and yogis, and through the grace of the supreme guru, it bestows the path to liberation. He concludes [the work] with the word "iti": [this work], which is like a jewel-garland characterized by the rows of words of the excellent sage Vasiṣṭha.

The phrase "variegated and adorned" refers to the aforementioned form of the Lord of the Raghus' attainment of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti-siddhi*), which I have proclaimed to you in its entirety.

That state, which is to be served by all the assemblies of poets and yogins, when served through hearing and other means by the grace of the Supreme Guru, bestows—that is, places one upon—the path of liberation, namely the sequence of stages previously described. || 110 ||
Whoever should constantly hear this account of the ritual between Rāma and Vasiṣṭha,
even if in any state whatsoever, is liberated through hearing it and goes to Brahman.
The "method" (vidhi) refers to the manner of discourse.

Even a person who is possessed of all defects—such as delusion, impurity, attachment, aversion, major sins (mahāpātaka), minor sins (upapātaka), and so forth—is liberated from all those defects through mere hearing; and by means of attaining qualities such as tranquility (śānti), he goes to, that is, reaches, Brahman.
What, then, is the qualified person? This is the meaning. || 111 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-eighth sarga, titled "Rāma’s Awakening," within the section on the Vision of Brahman, in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa concerning the means to liberation, in the Bālakāṇḍa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, a compendium of thirty-two thousand verses spoken by the divine messenger. 128.
Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-eighth chapter, titled "Rāma’s Awakening," in the first half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.

Thus [composed] by the disciple of the mendicant named Śrī Gaṅgādharendra Sarasvatī, who was the disciple of the venerable Śrī Rāmacandra Sarasvatī, who was himself the disciple of the venerable Śrī Sarvajña Sarasvatī— the most eminent among the wandering ascetics of the Paramahaṃsa order.
Thus ends the first half of the Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa in the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*, composed by the mendicant named Śrīmad Ānandabodhendrasarasvatī.
This concludes the first half of the Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa.
Śrī. The Yogavāsiṣṭha. Accompanied by the commentary titled Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa.
The Latter Half of the Nirvāṇa Section, Chapter 6.
First Canto.
Śrī Rāma said:
Through the state of actionlessness and the abandonment of mental constructs, the body of the embodied one falls away.
O Brahman, how can this occur so swiftly while one is still alive?

I praise the God whose self is the wealth of incomparable awakening, who is auspicious, fearless, and an ocean of infinite bliss; who, with the web of delusion destroyed, is established as the beneficial one within the heart; and who is skilled in the arising, leading, and ceasing of the world.
Free from possessiveness, free from egoism, and devoid of volitional constructions and conceptual discriminations—
just as they live and act, such is the reasoning described for those who are liberated.

In the first half [of the work], under the guise of demonstrating Śrī Rāma’s samādhi, it is shown that for a person of the highest capacity, through the very ripening of the repeated practice of hearing [the teachings], the knowledge of direct realization arises, resulting in a permanent resting in the supreme state. Even if such a person should, by chance, emerge from that state again, he remains there without interruption.
Rest is accomplished without effort; thus, for the purpose of ascending to ever-higher stages, this second half [of the work] is commenced.

Here, at the beginning, it was stated: "O Rāma, one who perceives 'I' and 'mine' is not liberated from suffering; by not perceiving them, one is liberated; therefore, practice that which is desired. Regarding that which was stated there—namely, the total abandonment of all conceptual constructions—[the following is said]:

He raises the objection that the maintenance of the body and other worldly activities cannot be established if they depend on conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), stating: "Because of the state of actionlessness" (*naiṣkarmyāt*).

The meaning is: since all activity has ceased due to the abandonment of conceptual constructions such as "I-ness" (*ahaṃtā*) toward the body, vital breath (*prāṇa*), and so forth—i.e., because of actionlessness (*naiṣkarmya*)—how can the maintenance of the body and other worldly activities possibly occur? || 1 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
The abandonment of mental constructs is possible for one who is living, but not for one who is dead.
Listen now to its true nature, which is an ornament to the ears. (2)
Life is not dependent upon conceptualization (kalpanā), such that by abandoning it one would suffer physical death; rather, it is dependent upon the "experiencing" (bhojaka) prārabdha-karma.
On the contrary, the abandonment of conceptualization is itself dependent upon life. Thus, the renunciation of conceptualization does not contradict life;
rather, it is non-life itself that is contradictory. With this intention, the venerable Vasiṣṭha provides the resolution: "While living... (jīvataḥ).
The meaning is: "Listen as I describe, according to reality, the nature of this abandonment of conceptualization in such a way that it does not contradict life. || 2 ||
Those who know conceptualization say that the very cultivation of the sense of "I" is what constitutes conceptualization;
the cultivation of the space-like nature of objects is called the relinquishment of that conceptualization.

The contemplation of "I-ness" (*ahaṃbhāvanam*) is the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of limitation upon the body and so forth. The contemplation of "space" (*nabhaḥ*)—that is, the contemplation or constant recollection of that object which is the nature of Brahman as the unlimited ether—is called the renunciation of volitional constructs (*saṃkalpa*), because it effects the destruction of the superimposition of limitation. || 3 ||
Those who know the nature of conceptualization say that conceptualization is indeed the savoring of the objects of the world;
the abandonment of the mental construction of those objects is called the relinquishing of volitional intent.
The supreme ones say that the conceptualization "this is an object" is agitation;
the cultivation of the space-like nature of objects is called the abandonment of volitional construction.

This [notion] that all this visible world, beginning with the body, is ultimately real (paramārthasatya) is a state of agitation and conceit. Since it is a transformation of the four elements which are themselves products of space, in reality only the single object "space" shines forth; thus, there is the cultivation and thorough reflection upon this meaning. Although both of these [notions] contradict erroneous experience, they are not...
It is contrary to life; the sense is that the cessation of delusion is observed even while one is still living. || 5 ||
Know that recollection is volition; the wise know the absence of recollection to be Śiva.
That [recollection] is projected upon what was previously experienced as well as what was not experienced.
With the intention that the cessation of superimposition—which consists of recollection—is not incompatible with life, he says:
"It is merely an indication of the indirect mental modification. (6)
Having forgotten all memory—whether experienced or not—as if you were a piece of wood, and having quickly forgotten everything, remain hidden, O Great-minded One. (7)

Having forgotten all memory—recollection as well as other mental modifications such as inference and the like—and having merged into the form of the undivided Brahman, remain firm and supportless like a log of wood for a long time; thus live on! For in this way, the cessation of mental fluctuations through the state of being the Self that is Brahman is, rather than a cause for death, actually a cause for the prolongation of life for yogis.
The state of being. || 7 ||
Abide with a nature consisting solely of non-recollection regarding past actions,
like the movement of a half-asleep infant toward familiar occurrences.
However, at the time of practical application (*vyavahāra*), one must effect the cessation of mere memory; thus he says "all" (*sarva*).
With the intention that in a practice firmly habituated there is no dependence on the effort of remembering what precedes or follows, he says "half," etc.
"In cases where [the reasoning] has been practiced" (*abhyastopapattiṣu*) means in those instances where [the conclusion] is established by the mere force of prior practice alone. (8)
Just as the wheel revolves through a flow free from volition,
so too does it move by the power of its own momentum, its actions, and its stainless residual impressions (saṃskāra).

The meaning is that, just as a potter’s wheel, having completed its task, continues to vibrate and revolve due to the mere force of prior momentum until the exhaustion of its velocity—even in the absence of a further purpose or impetus—so it is here. || 9 ||
Being without a mind, you have entered into the conditioned formations of sentient beings;
move only within your own actions as they fall into the stream of continuity.

With the intention that his mind (*manas*), though its essence (*sattva*) is free from latent impressions (*nirvāsana*), follows the force of residual impressions (*saṃskāra-vega*) and thus remains in their wake, there is no possibility of unbridled activity due to the destruction of defects such as passion (*rāga*); with this in mind, he says: "The flow... (verse 10).
With arms raised high, I cry out, yet no one listens to me;
the absence of volitional thought is the supreme good—why is it not cultivated within?
Having thus resolved the objection, and following the maxim that "even though wholesome advice has been spoken many times, it should be repeated," he speaks again and again—

beginning with the words "With arms upraised"— proclaiming that the previously mentioned renunciation of mental constructs (*saṃkalpa*) and so forth is indeed the means for attaining the highest good (*śreyas*). || 11 ||
Oh, the greatness of delusion! That this wish-fulfilling gem called "discernment," which destroys all suffering, is abandoned by people even though it resides within their own hearts. (12)
Let there be neither sensation nor volition; become one with that very state. This much is the supreme good; let it be experienced by yourself.
The reality of the Self, which is devoid of sensation and free from the seeing of the visible, is itself the primary state of non-conceptualization. || 13 ||
It is said, O Rāma, that by remaining merely silent, that supreme state is attained,
wherein even sovereignty is regarded as a blade of grass.
Silently, without the activity of forming a mental resolve. || 14 ||
Just as the movement of the feet of a traveler who is focused solely on his destination is free from volitional thought, so too should you move in your actions.

He states another previously mentioned illustration regarding the establishment of worldly activity through the force of the momentum of actions impelled by prior volitions, which persists until that momentum is exhausted: "gamya... (verse 15).
Having forgotten the stain of the pursuit of the fruits of all actions, move without sensation in whatever task falls upon you like a natural flow, as if asleep.
That which was stated—namely, "non-perception and non-conceptualization"—is now established even from the standpoint of conventional usage: "All... (verse 16).
Without forming any deliberate intention regarding the throbbing [of the senses], and without contemplating pleasure or pain,
one should remain like a blade of grass released from its movement when caught in the current of a task.

Just as young grass or tender herb, being free from its own volition, vibrates when fallen into the flow of wind and other elements, performing actions such as contact with or separation from other blades of grass; so it is in this case. 17.
May the internal cultivation of aesthetic flavor (rasa-bhāvana) be the garland for your actions, as if you were a wooden mechanical doll performing deeds solely for the sake of others. 18.

Just as a wooden puppet or mechanical doll, standing like one performing dance and so forth for the sake of others' curiosity, has no cultivation of aesthetic sentiments (rasa) such as the erotic (śṛṅgāra) like an actual actor, so too for you who perform [these acts], let there be no cultivation of sentiment or sense of curiosity toward the pleasure of sense objects, as if you were a fool. This is the meaning. || 18 ||
May all perceptions of your senses be devoid of flavor, like creepers in the winter season, discernible only by their outward form. (19)
O you who quiver with the essence of the sixfold group [of passions] which obstructs the yellow sap of the tree of awakening—remain motionless like a vine clinging to a tree in winter. 20.

The sixfold group consists of the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa) conjoined with the five sheaths; the group of vital breaths along with the mind; the group of organs of perception; the group of organs of action; the fourfold internal organ together with the organs of perception and action;
and the body composed of the six sheaths. Enveloped by these six groups—as a tree in winter is entwined by a creeper—[the Self remains].
...as if devoid of sap. || 20 ||

By your own effort, quickly restrain the senses—even when they have set out toward external objects—so that they hold only the internal essence of consciousness, just as trees do during the winter season. 21.

Now, one might ask: how can the six groups [of senses], which are devoid of flavor (nīrasa), have life? To this he says: "Cid... Consciousness (*cit*), whose nature is unobstructed plenitude (*bhūman*) and bliss (*ānanda*), is itself the internal essence (*rasa*) that serves as the cause for their life, nourishment, and so forth.
Although they are naturally inclined toward the tasting of external flavors, one should restrain them by one's own effort and ensure they possess only the internal essence of consciousness.

The meaning is: "having performed [this], one should maintain it. The mention of the "senses" (indriya) is an elliptical expression for the group of six [internal faculties]. The meaning is that just as the winter season sustains trees through internal sap even in the absence of external water, so it is here. || 21 ||
Whether you restrain the activity of the senses or do not restrain them,
this caravan of worldly misfortunes will never come to rest.
Regarding what would happen if the functions of the senses were not restrained and remained full of worldly attachment, he says: "If they are full of attachment," etc. (Verse 22).
If you vibrate like the flame of a windless lamp or the movement of water from a machine,
then for the sake of infinite welfare, you are fashioned for the highest good.
O Maruts, if you move without any volition, just as there is movement in flame, in a machine, and in water, then you would be capable of being conceived [as a distinct agent]. || 23 ||
This alone is the supreme fortitude that wards off the fever of birth: the practice of agency in one's own actions while remaining free from latent impressions (vāsanā). 24.
Free from latent impressions and free from volitional thought, following whatever occurs naturally,
move gradually in your actions like the whirling of a potter's wheel.
The wheel revolves; thus, O expansion, like a configuration, move slowly, becoming ever more tranquil in your vibration.
Let there be no thought of the fruit of action, nor let there be your attachment to inaction;
either abandon both of these, or take refuge in both.

Do not be one whose intellect is attached to the fruit of action; likewise, let there be no attachment characterized by clinging to the fruit even in *akarma*—that is, in the renunciation of action. With the intention that when there is an absence of attachment to the fruit, there is no distinction between performing action and its renunciation, he says: "Both... (verse 26).
What is the use of saying much here? This is stated in brief: conceptualization is the bondage of the mind; its absence is liberation.
Here there is nothing whatsoever to be done, nor anything not to be done, anywhere at all.
Everything is Śiva—unborn, peaceful, and infinite; remain as you were before. (28)
That which is improper must be abandoned; as before, remain exactly as you are. || 28 ||
Perceiving inaction within action and action within inaction,
you whose nature is consciousness of reality as it is, remain at peace and at your ease.

"State of non-action" (akarmatvam) means the nature of the Self as the inactive Brahman. "Action" (karmatām) refers to the sense of duty—the necessity of performing action—within that state of abiding in such a Brahman-nature which is itself beyond action. || 29 ||
They know yoga to be the absence of sensation, the unartificial cessation of the mind;
having become entirely absorbed in that, remain as you are, O sir! (30)
Non-feeling has been explained previously. || 30 ||
In that which is equal, peaceful, auspicious, subtle, devoid of both duality and unity, pervasive, infinite, supreme, and pure—what indeed is distressed by what? (31)
He dispels the doubt that remaining motionless and silent might lead only to exhaustion, as if one whose entire body were numbed by rheumatism (āmavāta), by saying "on level ground" (same). || 31 ||
Let no resolve arise within you, like a sprout in a desert;
let no desire arise in you, O lady, like a creeper in the heart of a stone.
For one who is without sensation and at peace— whether living or even dead—
there is no purpose whatsoever here in what is done, nor any at all in what is left undone.
For one who lives by means of worldly or Vedic actions—whether performed or unperformed—there is no purpose, no human goal (puruṣārtha), either in this world or in the next. || 33 ||
In that which is tranquil within, whose form is eternal and non-differentiated, there is neither action nor inaction;
nor are there actions within action, nor even agency within the agent. (34)

To the question "Why is it not there?", he says: "yad" (because). Because, for that reason, even though you—who are the limit of the sublation of both action and inaction, who consist of both, and whose nature is eternal non-difference—manifest as the illusory nature of action (this refers to the word "karmaṇi" in the root text), in reality there is no state of being action.

[This meaning follows from the fact that the expression "in the action residing in the root" (*mūlasthakarmaṇi*) is a designation emphasizing the abstract state (*bhāvapradhānanirdeśa*). There is no agency even when [the self] undergoes transformation (*vivartamāna*) as such an agent-self; for one who possesses the notion of reality regarding the status of being both object and agent (*karmakartṛtā*), it is precisely for him that the fruit of the action exists—this is established by the scripture which prescribes the qualifications of the qualified person (*adhikāriviśeṣaṇa*), just like faith (*śraddhā*) and other such factors.
The meaning is "because of awakening. || 34 ||
Perceiving [things] as "I" and "mine," you are not liberated from suffering; by not perceiving them, you are liberated. Therefore, practice that which you desire.

For this very reason, since only one who possesses the cognition of "I" and "mine" with respect to the body and so forth has the authority to follow the scriptures of injunctions and prohibitions, it was stated previously that bondage is produced by karma for such a person and not for anyone else; thus he says: "I and mine... (35).
"I" and "mine" do not exist; that which exists is the supreme Śiva.
Yet this is even higher than the highest Śiva—beyond sound, yet having the nature of the ultimate reality.

The meaning is that this visible world, which appears as if it were an objective entity, is actually nothing but an unreal, illusory appearance—verbalizable yet indefinable—distinct from Śiva, who is known as the bliss of the supreme ground (pādbhūmānanda). || 36 ||

Whatever is seen here in this world does not truly exist; it appears like the state of being a bracelet made of gold. They know that its destruction is simply non-perception; thereafter, that alone remains as the truth and the ultimate reality.

He explains this very point clearly with the words "yad" (that which). "Something" (*kiñcit*) refers to that which is devoid of any defining verbal expression such as "it is thus" or "it is like this. The substratum of the sublation of this [universe] is, however, after the subsequent sublation of the ignorance regarding that [substratum], what remains—the non-cognition (*avedana*) which is the object of cognition itself; those whose final resort is experience know this to be of the nature of absolute truth, the form of the supreme human goal. This is the meaning.

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "Instruction on the Yoga for Treating Desire and Other Passions," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the glorious Vāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa composed by Vālmīki. 1.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "Instruction on the Yoga for the Treatment of Desire," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
PDF 157, p. 1071, Second Canto 2.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Non-dual unity is free from mental construction, peaceful, and established in the Self;
as is an army made of mud, so is the world composed of Śiva.
First, it is investigated here that the entire world is composed of Śiva;
likewise, having sought out the seed of karma, it is eradicated along with its root.

He promises to first establish here that which was stated [previously]: "All is composed of Śiva, peaceful, and infinite; let it remain as before"—namely, "non-dual unity. This exists within the Self, which is the ultimate nature, when viewed from the perspective of reality. (1)
And that very mind— consisting of the intellect (manas), ego (ahaṃkāra), cognition (buddhi), and so forth— is composed of that [consciousness],
joined with the arrangement of time, form, action, sound, and power.

For whatever is illumined by consciousness (*cit*), that is composed of consciousness (*cinmaya*) because it is an evolution (*vivarta*) of consciousness; thus, he demonstrates this sequentially regarding the fourfold internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) with the word "mind" (*manaḥ*). First, indeed, the act of thinking (*manana*), characterized by the mind’s orientation toward objects of cognition, is itself pervaded by consciousness; thereafter, its functions—such as egoism, determination, memory, desire, and volition—are likewise [pervaded by consciousness].

All things are pervaded by consciousness and are established through universal experience. Thus, time—characterized by the relationship between consciousness and its objects—and the entire process of the internal organ (antahkarana), including the forms of objects and their activities, can be understood as being composed of Śiva, because it is directly perceivable by the Witness (sākṣin). This is the meaning. || 2 ||
The sequences of form, perception, and mind consist of nothing but the mud of Śiva;
because they are identical with Him and because He is infinite, what is perceived by whom? (3)

Thus, even regarding external objects, the external perception mediated by the sense organs and their respective doors, the manifestation as immediate (*aparokṣa*) is brought about solely by the pervasion of consciousness (*cidvyāpti*). With the intention that even in those cases, the state of being identical with Śiva (*śivamayatva*) can be perceived by the discerning, he says: "Śiva... [and so on]. This includes the grasping of form and light.

This is also an elliptical indication (upalakṣaṇa) of the initial perceptions of sound and so forth; it includes the mental sequences and the external conceptual cognitions of rejection, acquisition, and so on, as well as their objects. Thus, he says "because of being composed of that" (tanmayatvāt) [in verse 3], meaning that when one perceives the state of being identical with Śiva, it is Śiva alone who manifests in the form of the entire triad [of agent, object, and action], and there is no other entity apart from Him.
The object of knowledge, the means of knowledge, the knower, and so forth; space and time, the directions and the like;
existence, non-existence, transformation, and all else—this world consists essentially of the mud of Śiva. (4)
He clarifies that very point with the verse beginning "mātra" (measure). || 4 ||
Since there is no essence other than the Supreme Lord apart from "I" and "mine," remain with an unattached mind, alas, like the silence within a stone!

Having subsumed all manifestations under the two forms of "I" and "mine," the author says "I" with the intention that, by reflecting upon the fact that consciousness pervades them, one's abiding in that state becomes easy, as nothing remains but the essence of that [consciousness]. It is like the silence found within a stone, characterized by the absence of activities such as speech; [it is] within that which consists of name, form, and action.

Since name and form manifest within phenomenal proliferation solely through the direct pervasion of consciousness, they are determined to be identical with Śiva; once this is ascertained, it is easy to abide in that essential nature by means of sublation [of duality] therein. || 5 ||
Śrī Rāma said: O Lord, for the wise man who does not contemplate the unreal nature of "I" and "mine," what is auspicious— through the abandonment of inauspicious actions or through their performance?

However, because actions characterized as merit and demerit—which have been accumulated over infinite millions of births—appear directly and are perceived, their sublation cannot be established merely by the vision of one's identity with Śiva. Therefore, as a means to remove them, the only remaining recourse is the renunciation of those actions, characterized by remaining in a state of motionlessness until death. For it is not the case that [this applies] to the knower (*jñānin*).

Is some fruit expected from the performance of ritual action, or not? Since there is no possibility of incurrence of sin (*pratyavāya*) in the abandonment of obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites, [the text] remains silent...
[p.1072 and 1073 are unclear].
By means of the non-perception of subtle consciousness, it is cut away by one's own effort;
that by which consciousness is investigated through its own non-perception by means of one's own effort. (45)
Therefore, with the intention that the means for abandoning karma is indeed what I have stated, he concludes with the verse beginning "sūkṣma":

by which [means] consciousness, whose nature is the reflection of the Intellect (*cidābhāsa*), is—along with non-consciousness, i.e., root-ignorance (*mūlājñāna*)—discerned through one's own effort; having realized the reality (*tattva*), it is "moved" (using *vicālyate* because of the non-distinction between *ra* and *la*), meaning it is displaced from its own nature. By that [means], its root...

Although these consist of the reflection of consciousness delimited by mental modifications (*vṛtti*) in the form of the perception of various objects, they are cut away precisely through the effort of the primary sublater—by means of non-perception and non-connection. The point is that no separate effort is required for their destruction. In some manuscripts, the second half of the verse beginning with "yena" is not read at all.

Then, by that knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna), the scraping away of the root—characterized by the sublation of everything—is extended for the tree of saṃsāra, by which it is cut down; thus it should be connected with the subsequent phrase [where "by the subsequent" is required to mean "by the former"]. || 45 ||
By that, the scraping away of the root of the tree of cyclic existence is carried out. || 46 ||
Inconscient space is non-dual and one; thus it exists, yet this [world] is devoid of objective reality.
Since that very form of space is such, they call it the stainless essence of consciousness. (47)
Where there is no volition and no reflection of consciousness,
such is the one, non-dual space, devoid of these objects of perception— distinct entities belonging to its own class;
that is Brahman itself according to the aforementioned vision, and it alone is the essence of all conscious beings, including ourselves.
The meaning is that those who know Brahman declare this to be the ultimate form. || 47 ||

Thus ends the second canto, titled "The Instruction on the Yoga for Burning the Seed of Karma," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, belonging to the *Ārṣa* tradition. 2.
Thus ends the second canto, titled "The Instruction on the Yoga of Burning the Seed of Karma," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa-tātparyaprakāśa*.
PDF 159, p. 1074, Third Canto (Tṛtīyaḥ Sargaḥ) 3.
Śrī Rāma said:
O Lord of Sages, how can there be the non-perception of that which is being perceived?
For there is no coming into being of the non-existent, nor is there the non-existence of the existent. (1)
When the object of knowledge has been thoroughly cleansed, that which is beyond cognition according to reality and free from activity is taught here as the means for the wise.

Regarding the statement, "They know liberation to be non-perception (*avedana*), the destruction of the mind, and the unconditioned (*akṛtrima*)," Rāma raises a doubt concerning the term "non-perception. He argues that this doubt cannot arise because it was already addressed previously: "Even though the nature of perception consists in being directed toward an object, when that state is abandoned, what remains is not 'perception'; that is called 'actionless' (*akarma*) and is known as the peaceful Brahman. Thus, there is no basis for this objection.
This is indeed possible. Nevertheless, by the statement that "at the end, it is cut away through the non-perception of consciousness," its destruction is asserted;
yet this contradicts the earlier statement that "that which is destroyed is called Brahman, the peaceful," because it is impossible for that which exists to become non-existent.
Thus, the question is certainly justified. [The text continues: "Having arisen from these elements, one perishes after them; one does not exist after death."
When it is said that "perception exists," [the opponent might argue] that this is just like Maitreyī’s question: "O Blessed One, do not confuse me; there is no perception after death. || 1 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
The non-existent has no being, and the existent has no non-being; when this is understood, then the perception and non-perception of [reality] becomes easy for oneself. (2)

For this very reason, Vasiṣṭha also provides a resolution—just as Yājñavalkya did when he said, "Verily, I do not speak delusion to you; this Self, O dear one, is indestructible and of an imperishable nature; its contact with the sense-objects is merely adventitious"—by stating, "Not of the non-existent.
These two terms, *vedana* (cognition) and *artha* (object), are comparable to the error of perceiving a snake in a rope.
Know that these two, when spoken of as unreal, are equal to the water of a mirage.

He explains how that is easily accomplished: "These two. These two are well-known in the state of saṃsāra. For in the Upaniṣadic texts it is said: "Where there is duality as it were, there one sees another; but where for him everything has become the Self alone, by what and whom should he see?
Where one sees nothing else, hears nothing else, understands nothing else—that is the Infinite (bhūmā)," and so forth.
The meaning is that this is because these two have been prohibited. || 3 ||
Non-understanding of these two is better; understanding leads to suffering for both of them.
Therefore, O Raghava, understand only that which is real; do not understand what is unreal.

For this very reason, with the intention that liberation consists precisely in the cessation of the threefold complex (tripuṭī) for the witness of the threefold complex—which includes the feeling—it is said: "But non-enlightenment... Understand that the nature of the Self is truly the eternal, indestructible, and immutable; do not understand the unreal—the reflection of consciousness conditioned by the mental modifications (vṛtti) and so forth contained within the threefold complex—to be the Self. || 4 ||
For a living being, the comprehension of the meaning of words regarding sensations causes supreme suffering;
having set aside the comprehension of the meaning of words regarding cognition, remain as you truly are.

He says "of the creature" (jantoḥ) to show that when that [body] is delimited, the very notion of it being the Self is the cause of all misfortune—for one must "uproot," meaning cut it away completely from its roots. || 5 ||
At the moment of universal awakening, when the meaning of the word "cognition" is realized here, let there be the supreme "Om," the arising of Nirvana; thus, be at peace.

To the question of how its cessation is to be effected at the time of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), he says: "All" (*sarva*). Even on the occasion of worldly transaction, which is characterized by the cognition of the triad [of knower, known, and knowing], there exists another, transcendent reality—the immutable pure consciousness (*kūṭastha-cinmātra*)—which, according to the context, is the ultimate referent of all objects and is denoted by the word "Om," which itself is the ultimate referent of all words.
Having recognized that very Self as the source of Nirvāṇa, one should become tranquil; this means one should conduct oneself without distraction.
One's own karma, consisting of both the auspicious and the inauspicious, must be destroyed by the discriminating person;
this is accomplished through the knowledge of reality, which realizes that such karma does not exist.

He states that precisely through such a conventional usage regarding awakening, the non-clinging to and the destruction of subsequent and prior auspicious and inauspicious [karmas] are established—thus: "Auspicious... (verse 7).
Through the complete wearing away of the root of karma, saṃsāra comes to rest;
for as long as karma has not been thoroughly investigated and sought out, it does not cease to exist.

He states that the very perception of the immutable Self (kūṭasthātman) constitutes the sublation of all karma by means of uprooting the ignorance that is the root of all karma—beginning with "Karma":
as long as all karma does not exist, along with its roots, its fruits, and its branches, twigs, leaves, and flowers. || 8 ||
When that which is of the nature of consciousness, situated within the core of the wood-apple fruit, assumes the designation of "mind" (citta) within itself,
it does not differ from the wood-apple even in the slightest degree.

Just as the pulp of a wood-apple (*bilva*) produces within itself the seed and so forth, yet the wood-apple itself does not thereby become divided, so too the Self, though its nature is consciousness (*cid-rūpa*), undergoes the designation "mind" and creates within itself the triad of action, agent, and object; yet that [Self] is not divided even slightly or in the least—this is the logical connection. || 9 ||
Just as a configuration is not separate from within another configuration,
so too space, objects, and the rest are not separate from the Supreme in the slightest degree.

Just as the configuration of Jambūdvīpa and the other continents, which are included within the configuration of the earth, are not separate from the earth; so too, space, the ether, and the objects consisting of the elements and worlds contained therein are not separate from the Supreme Pure Being (sanmātra).
Just as water itself is its internal fluidity and not separate from it,
so too is consciousness itself the mind, because the two objects are of that same nature.

Because those two meanings—the meanings of the words "citta" and "acitta"—are that very meaning, since they have as their meaning the root *cit* which signifies pure consciousness (*cinmātra*). || 11 ||
Just as liquidity exists in water and light in fire,
so too does the state of being Brahman and consciousness exist within the mind.
It is devoid of that state, being empty of the two properties of being a grasper and being a rememberer. || 12 ||
Volitional action is like a phantom that causes one to wander within its own interior;
it arises without a cause, for if it were not arisen, it would not exist.

Whence is that emptiness? To this he says: "consciousness" (*cetana*). For, by the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) that it makes known (*cetayati*), consciousness (*cit*) is understood as the activity or function (*kriyā*) of the intellect (*citi*), namely the illumination of objects. And that [illumination] is utterly rootless in the immutable consciousness (*kūṭasthā cit*); like a phantom produced by delusion, it is merely false. That which arises without a cause and in a false form has not truly arisen at all. Therefore, it is not [real].
The meaning is that the notion that "another form of action exists therein" is a mere conceptual construction; thus, the teaching is presented in that manner. || 13 ||
Volition is action, and this appears like the vibration of the wind;
it is without cause, being the self that exists both externally and internally as the consciousness of objects.

Thus, since there is no difference between consciousness and its activity, it is established that its objects are also not separate from it; this is what he states with the words "consciousness" (cetanam).

When the conscious action is without cause and non-different [from consciousness], like the wind and its movement, then in the external waking state, as well as internally in the states of dreaming and deep sleep, that very cognition of objects exists; therefore, the objects themselves are the Self alone and not separate—this is the meaning. || 14 ||
The body is the expansion of karmas; it is the self of egoism and the locus of saṃsāra.
Being insentient and devoid of egoism, you become tranquil like a windless breeze.

The expansion of all actions resides in the body alone; for there is a scriptural statement that "the self (ātman) is indeed the agent of actions. That very self is, at its root, the nature of egoity (ahaṃtā), while in its branches it is transmigratory existence (saṃsṛti). It consists of insentient matter and is characterized by activity whose essence is the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa). By means of non-egoity (anahaṃtva)—which has as its characteristic the sublation of such activity—one effects the uprooting of the root, thereby [destroying] that [transmigratory existence] along with its branches.
The meaning is that it becomes tranquil. || 15 ||
Having become infinite-souled through the absence of consciousness, though you are a knower, you have become like a stone;
now, like the tip of the snout of a boar, perform the uprooting of the very foundation of saṃsāra. 16.

One should not think that the destruction of the individual soul (*jīva*) has occurred through the annihilation of the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*); rather, having become the infinite Self by means of its nature as Brahman, it has accomplished the supreme human goal—the eradication of the root of its own suffering, which is *saṃsāra*. He says this with the words "from the insentient" (*acetanāt*). Just as the tip of the snout of a boar (*kroḍa*)—that is, a wild boar—is [the instrument of digging].
It acts in the same way as the decoction of the roots of mustā and other such herbs. || 16 ||
In this way, the relinquishing of the sheath of the subtle essence of the seeds of karma is accomplished;
not otherwise, O Raghava. May there be eternal peace for you, established forever. 17.
Not otherwise, O Rāghava; for this reason, may that which always resides within you—the nature of sensation rooted in karma—be pacified. || 17 ||
But when this minute portion of the seed of karma has been abandoned in the other self,
it no longer exists for the living being, according to those who know the reality known by the wise.

When this abandonment of the portion of the seed of karma has been accomplished for the living being (*jīva*), and when that which is other than the Self—namely, the self consisting of the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) distinct from the Brahman-Self, as well as the world-phenomenon (*prapañca*) perceivable by it—is no longer found to exist, then those who know That and are peaceful neither grasp at anything nor reject anything; such is the connection with the subsequent [text]. This is in accordance with the Śruti: "But where everything has become the Self alone for him, then by what and whom should he see? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.15).
The state of being. || 18 ||
Nothing is grasped by those who are tranquil, nor is anything renounced;
therefore, through their relinquishing and taking up, they are known as those of tranquil mind.
The wise, whose hearts are as empty as space, remain exactly as they are;
they act according to what arises, yet even that which they do is not truly performed by them.
Everything that has fallen into the stream vibrates even for one whose mind is peaceful;
thus their organs of action are like those of a child who is half-asleep. 21.

Just as grass, wood, and so forth fallen into the current of a river all move, so too their organs of action move—even without mental agitation—despite the mind being at peace; thus it is interpreted. 21.
When the state free from flavor is attained, even flavors become utterly flavorless;
they abide neither within nor without, like those who are expert in ignorance.

In that state which is devoid of expulsion, free from objects, and characterized by unsurpassed bliss, the functions of the senses—which are normally inclined toward enjoyment—become tasteless and void of passion; being thus, they become incapable of manifesting their respective objects through ignorance. || 22 ||
The experiencing of karma is its relinquishment, and that occurs through awakening;
since it is not a real entity, there is no purpose served by either what is done or what is left undone. (23)

The renunciation of action is precisely the experience previously described; [it is performed] by means of other action, namely that which consists of the movement of the body and so forth, impelled by the unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) of living. || 23 ||
That which is without sensation, beyond the reach of perception, free from latent impressions (vāsanā), peaceful, equanimous, and without mental delineation— that is called the renunciation of karma.
It is without delineation, being devoid of the synthesis of what has been done and what has not been done. || 24 ||
The complete non-recollection of long-forgotten karma—that is it;
established like the interior of a pillar, that is called the renunciation of karma. (25)
Those of futile understanding who regard non-renunciation as renunciation— those ignorant ones, like beasts, are devoured by the demoness of the abandonment of action.
"Non-renunciation" refers to that which is devoid of the renunciation of the root [of desire] and consists merely of the restraint of the organs of action. Thus it has been said by the Blessed One:
"He who sits restraining the organs of action but continues to dwell upon the objects of the senses with his mind, being deluded in soul, is called a hypocrite. (Gītā 3.6) || 26 ||
For those who have attained peace through the total renunciation of actions along with their roots, there is no purpose whatsoever here in this world in what is done, nor in what is left undone. (27)
Having completely uprooted even the slightest portion of the seed of karma along with its root, those who know that remain in eternal, one-pointed concentration; therefore, they abide in bliss. (28)
Thus, according to the method previously stated, having completely uprooted [it]. || 28 ||
When an action occurs by the force of circumstances, they move with only slight effort, lacking absorption in it;
they are as if reeling like drunkards, or as if driven by a machine. (29)

They are devoid of identification with those objects and free from the modifications characterized by egoism regarding them; they are like those intoxicated by liquor, or like wooden statues set in motion by a machine. || 29 ||
As if afflicted by a passion for the playful Goddess of Liberation, they descended to a certain earth with the appearance of those half-asleep and half-awake. (30)

"Afflicted by calamity"—that is, as if they had reached a state where they no longer identify with their own bodies and so forth due to an excess of attachment; this is a poetic conceit (utprekṣā). "A certain ground" refers to the fifth stage and those beyond it. || 30 ||
That which is abandoned along with its root is said to be truly abandoned;
that abandonment which lacks the uprooting of the root is like the mere lopping off of branches. (31)
The tree of karma has its roots and the tips of its branches uncut;
it grows again with a thousand branches for the sake of suffering. (32)
That from which the root has not been uprooted, yet whose branch-tips have been lopped off—such is it. || 32 ||
O dear one, the abandonment of karma is accomplished by that which is devoid of the nature of feeling; it is not achieved by any other means.
Therefore, strive for this alone.
Taking up [the practice] in the manner previously described and practicing it, remain steadfast. 33.
But those who, without thus renouncing action, perform something else, kill the sky—which is the nature of renunciation—by means of non-renunciation. 34.
Through the nature of awakening, the renunciation of action occurs spontaneously;
like a burnt seed, even intense desirelessness becomes non-action itself.

The activity of one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*), though it may involve the undertaking of great works, is indeed devoid of action because its seed has been burnt; for even a large appearance of cloth made from burnt threads does not become actual cloth—this is the intended meaning. || 35 ||
Action performed with the organs of perception is fruitful due to the cultivation of its essence;
it must be restrained like a rope, for any other movement born of the limbs is fruitless. (36)

When the sense organs are accompanied by the intellect, their activity—whether it be attachment to enjoyment or the cultivation of aesthetic flavor—is accomplished through purposeful effort. Just as a well-encircling wooden frame is made fruitful by the extraction of water and its subsequent irrigation (which results in the abundance of crops), and not merely through futile exertion; so too is another type of movement born of the body, which consists of mere physical exertion.
It is fruitless. || 36 ||

Established in the renunciation of action through awakening, liberated while living and free from latent impressions, he may stay at home or in the forest; let him remain tranquil or let him encounter rising activity.
Let him be pacified by the loss of wealth and other riches, let him become poor; or let him attain prosperity through their increase—he remains exactly the same. This is the implied sense. || 37 ||
For one who is tranquil, even his own home is a secluded forest;
for one who is not tranquil, even the wildernesses are crowded, and a city is no less so.

For the wise one whose mind is completely stilled, even in a dream, the forest ground— pure, expansive, and heart-pleasing— is as if not attained by human beings at all, yet remains as if within his own heart.
He explains the first half of this verse, beginning with "gehameva," by means of two verses starting with "pariśānta. (39)
For the knower, whose vision is liberation, the world itself is a great forest—composed of space, devoid of movement, and with all its particular objects stilled. (40)
Nirvāṇa is that for whom the visible world has ceased along with the fire of knowledge. || 40 ||
For the ignorant man who possesses infinite desires and whose heart contains the entire world,
the earth with all its oceans revolves within his very heart.
He describes the latter half of that [verse] with three verses beginning with "ananta": || 41 ||
For the ignorant and wretched person, the cluster of villages—with its various conflicts and hardships, its constant exertions, and its diverse forms—exists as if within the very heart. (42)

The earth—consisting of various states of activity and transformation, and including cities, towns, districts, and mountains—is reflected in the heart, just as it is in the bowl of a mirror; yet, while it remains pure in the former, it appears defiled in the latter.

[The reading is *bhayāratyādīti*. Always filled with various necessary tasks—such as earning, spending, travel, and quarrels—and characterized by states of transformation such as greed, delusion, grief, fear, and attachment;
*pura* means a branch-town; *pattana* means a great city; *maṇḍala* means intermediate regions; in the impure...
The meaning is that such an entire world becomes clearly reflected in the heart, as if in the interior of a mirror; thus, for the ignorant person, there is no peace even in the forest. || 43 ||

Thus ends the third canto, titled "Instruction on the Yoga for the Pacification of the Visible World," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa, within the Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa of Valmīki, concerning the means to liberation. 3.
Thus ends the third canto, titled "The Instruction on the Yoga of the Cessation of the Visible World," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa-tātparya-prakāśa*.
PDF 160, p. 1076. The Fourth Canto. 4.
The venerable Vasiṣṭha said:

When the world, beginning with the ego (sāhaṃtā), has been stilled within awakening—which is of the nature of the power of consciousness—renunciation, resembling an extinguished lamp, is perfected; it is not otherwise.
It is described that the very sense of "I" (ahaṃtā) is the root of saṃsāra;
its abandonment occurs through the cultivation of non-egoism (anahaṃbhāva) arising from self-knowledge (ātmabodha).

Liberation is indeed the relinquishment of all that is seen by the seeing Self; and that is accomplished through the destruction of attachment—like the extinguishing of a lamp—and through the sublation of ignorance, the root of all that is seen, by means of the realization of reality, and not otherwise. Thus he says:
"Renunciation is not the abandonment of action; renunciation is known as awakening."
He whose sole nature is the manifestation of the non-world, who is imperishable, and free from egoism and the like.

The meaning is that liberation is characterized by the relinquishment of everything; it is that state in which no appearance of the world exists, and only the singular Self remains as the primary reality. || 2 ||
Like a lamp without oil, when the supreme nirvāṇa has been stilled, that which remains is the awakened self, free from notions such as "this is I," "this is he," or "this is mine. || 3 ||

This [notion]—that the body and so forth, which are well-known even to common folk and are of the nature of the visible, are "I," and that the world consisting of objects of enjoyment connected to that body and so forth is "mine"—is a twofold bondage characterized by the superimpositions of identity and relation.
When this [bondage] has been extinguished root and branch, like a lamp without oil, there remains only the supreme awakening: that consciousness alone is the Self.
This very thing is the meaning of nirvāṇa and liberation. || 3 ||
For one who does not possess the knowledge that "this is he," "I am this," or "this is mine"— which is itself quiescent— for such a person there is neither peace, nor renunciation, nor liberation.
He confirms the stated point by means of the method of negative concomitance (vyatireka) as well: "This... (verse 4).

When there is the cessation of even this much—the notions "this is mine," "this is [mine]," and "I am this"—there exists nothing other than that auspicious and profoundly peaceful state which is the nature of awakening. (5)

The destruction of this [world] within this [consciousness], to the extent that it exists—this is expressed by the locative case used in the sense of the genitive. That [destruction] is indeed the nature of awakening itself;
the meaning is that what has been superimposed remains as nothing but its substrate once sublated. || 5 ||
When the portion of "I" has been dissolved, everything has indeed gone to destruction;
yet nothing whatsoever has been destroyed anywhere, for one remains as the single, solid mass of Nirvana.

"By means of the knowledge of reality (tattvabodha), [one realizes] that the entire world is a vibration of the sense of 'mine'. Regarding one who fears the loss of everything when all things perish, he provides the remedy with the words "nothing at all. In its ultimate form, everything indeed exists. || 6 ||
By the mere knowledge of "I am not," this [ego] subsides without obstacle;
since it is accomplished by this much alone, why is there such torment? (7)
He states the easy means for the destruction of the notion of "I" in the words: "by the knowledge of non-I.

Because of the state of being a non-I, that is, through the cultivation of the sense of non-egoity (*anahaṃbhāva*). Regarding the phrase "without obstacle": the meaning is that no obstacle is observed when the superimposition of silver is sublated by the cognition "this is not silver. This is liberation. This [liberation] involves such great hardship.
The meaning is: why, and for what purpose, is there such exhaustion from accomplishing so many means? || 7 ||

The delusion of "I" and "not-I" does not exist apart from consciousness (*cittva*). Since consciousness is as clear as space, where then can this state of delusion reside? [Note: *kvaiṣā* is also read as *kaiṣā*. But surely, the notion of "not-I" is also a superimposition (*adhyāsa*), just like the notion of "I," because it involves duality; by what, then, is it extinguished?

He states with supporting reasoning that, just as the *kataka* nut [clears] turbidity from water, that notion of "I" subsides by itself within the conscious self (*cidātman*) along with the mental impurity (*cittapaṅka*):
"I... Because of consciousness (*cittvāt*), that is, because of the nature of the ultimate consciousness (*paramārthacit*). "Without" (*ṛte*) means apart from it. || 8 ||
There is no delusion, nor wandering, nor indeed error, nor is there a deluder; this is merely non-perception, for through perception this [delusion] does not exist for you.

Since error, its means, its fruit, and its substratum are merely the manifestations of ignorance (*ajñāna*), there is no separate existence once ignorance has ceased; thus he says: "No. Non-perception is ignorance. (9)
Know that this entire expansion is merely consciousness alone, resembling the nature of the non-existent;
therefore, enough—remain in silence, for thus everything is nothing but nirvāṇa.
In that very same instant in which one perceives "I am," in that very same instant, having perceived "I am not," one no longer grieves. (11)

Whenever there is the occurrence of the rise of the sense of "I," at that very same time, a cognition of "not-I," which is its opposite, must be produced; thus he says: "By that very [means]," etc. (11).
Abiding firmly in that state, remain with the sense of "I" (ahaṃbhāva) dissolved like an arrow shot into the sky— either incessantly, swiftly, or until it is exhausted.
Thus, by means of a state of non-egoism maintained through constant vigilance, one should swiftly render egoism—

like a sky-flower or other such things— void of meaning, having brought it to a state where it is no longer fit for definition; then, like Arjuna’s arrow fixed upon his bow in battle, remaining never-turning-back, he becomes one who has firmly grasped and firmly taken hold of that state of Brahman.
O you who have destroyed the [defilements], remain eternally undecaying! 12.
O you who perceive thus without ceasing, may you attain the goal that is the very essence;
having crossed the ocean of worldly existence, remain unattached through all states of being. 13.

In the case of *samāna* followed by words beginning with *nabhas*, *artha*, or *sanabhas*, the vowel *a* of *samāna* becomes *o* according to the rule "in the Veda, *a* becomes *o* for *samāna* when it occurs before [words] beginning with *mūrdhan* or ending in *udarka*" (Pāṇini 6.1.220).
Thus: *sanabhorthām*. 13.
If one lacks the heroism to conquer even his own inherent nature, tell me, what talk can there be of that beast attaining the supreme state? (14)
Svabhāva is the sense of "I" (ahaṃbhāva) impelled by innate ignorance; [it is overcome] when that alone is conquered. || 14 ||
