He by whom the sixfold group has been previously conquered through his own superior knowledge is a vessel for great purposes; no other is such, being a mere human donkey. (15)
The group of six enemies beginning with sensual desire. || 15 ||
He whose internal mental activity is being conquered or has already been conquered is the object of the discerning; he is called a true man. (16)

For those of middling capacity, [the self] is being conquered; for those of superior capacity, it is already conquered. Such a person has made his human birth fruitful through the accomplishment of the goals of human life. || 16 ||
Whatever object falls upon you, like a stone into the ocean, flee from that very thing, contemplating only: "I am not this. (17)
Like a stone cast into the ocean, one should not think "I am this"; through the cultivation of the thought that the self is unattached, non-contact with it is itself the escape here. || 17 ||

Even though you have understood through reasoning that "I am not" (or, according to the reading, "it exists"), and even though you fully know that it is mere cognition, why do you become deluded like an ignorant person? (18)

Knowing and experiencing what pleasure is in the form of a formal request (jñapti) accompanied by logical justification, why do you become deluded? The meaning is: "You certainly do not become deluded. || 18 ||
In this world, the object of knowledge does not exist in reality, just as the state of being a bracelet and so forth does not exist in gold;
it is nothing but a delusion, and that delusion is stilled by the non-recollection of it.

The meaning is that it should be known through its actual sense and through logical reasoning; for you have understood the reasonings based on the principle of "merely a verbal handle" (vācārambhaṇa) and so forth. || 19 ||
Whatever state arises within you, like a vibration in the wind,
lead it to a state of supportlessness through the mental modification "I am not."
Alternatively, what is the use of thousands of arguments? He says, "Whosoever... (verse 20), meaning that the single practice of the realization "I am not" alone will eliminate all delusion.
Why does he engage in this useless and harmful act, since greed, shamelessness, pride, and delusion—which were conquered by him at the very beginning—have not been overcome? (21)

Thus, those who have not conquered themselves through such a state of egolessness (anahaṃbhāva) are ineligible for this spiritual science (adhyātma-śāstra), which is otherwise useless, fruitless, and leads to harm such as atheism and acting according to one's whims; why then would they engage in it? || 21 ||
That which exists within you as the state of "I-ness," like vibration in the wind, is not other than the Supreme Self; it is just as this vibration is not other than the wind.
Since you are the Supreme Self, this [universe] is not other than that.
Through the consciousness of non-creation, creation shines forth supremely within the Supreme;
indeed, even that which is of evil meaning appears beautiful through a particular arrangement.

Non-creation—having the nature of the immutable, non-dual pure consciousness—is dissolved (*asta*) into that Supreme Self through the realization of it; having attained that state and being merged therein, it shines forth. Just as an illusory snake or other harmful object imagined upon a garland is dissolved by knowledge into the garland itself, and when worn around the neck, it shines as a particular arrangement of the garland, so too is this case. || 23 ||
The Supreme Self, however, never rises nor ever sets;
and since there is nothing other than this, what could be either existence or non-existence? (24)

If it is accepted that through awakening there arises a specific manifestation of the form of the Supreme Self for both the world and the individual soul (*jīva*), then subsequent modifications of existence would also occur; and since those [modifications] would involve the destruction of the states of the soul and the world, a duality would result. To this he says:
"But the Supreme Self... The attainment of the nature of the substrate through the sublation of the imagined is neither origination nor destruction; rather—
Its very nature is eternally established. For action alone is the cause of modification and so forth, not knowledge; thus, there is no consequence of duality—this is the intended meaning.

"In the supreme, the supreme; in the full, the full; in the peaceful, the peaceful; in the auspicious, the auspicious. Only this much is extended: neither am I, nor is there a world, nor is there an intellect. (25)

When the triad beginning with "I" (the knower, the known, and the means of knowledge) is sublated, the state of being a living soul (jīvatva) occasioned by that [triad] ceases; thus, the referent of the term *tvaṃ* (thou) is indeed the Supreme, which is full, peaceful, and auspicious.

And that [Supreme] abides in its own nature as the Supreme, the referent of the term *tat* (that), which is full, peaceful, and auspicious. This much alone is revealed as it truly exists through the awakening to reality; it is not something new.
The meaning is that something has arisen. || 25 ||
In non-extinction there is extinction; it is peaceful within peace, auspicious within the auspicious.
Even extinction is non-extinction; it is neither an existent object nor is it not so.

[Objection: Surely it must be stated that the extinction of ignorance accompanied by its appearances—the fruit of knowledge—is accomplished, like the extinction of a lamp; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of knowledge being fruitless. To this, he says: "In non-extinction" (anirvāṇe). It is true that extinction is the fruit of knowledge; nevertheless, it is absolutely unestablished in the case of the sun, which is without rising or setting.
Just as there is no cessation of night when the sun rises, so too there is no "extinction" (nirvāṇa) in Brahman itself, which is eternally quiescent;

thus, the fruit of knowledge—namely, peace—is not a new state consisting of the cessation of evil. Likewise, since Śiva is eternally established in unsurpassed bliss, the fruit characterized by the attainment of auspiciousness and bliss is also not something new. Therefore, there is no emergence of duality through the fruit of knowledge. If...

If bondage were real in the inward Self (pratīc) and if objects such as space (viyat) and so forth were truly existent in Brahman, then its extinction (nirvāṇa) would be unprecedented, like the extinction of a lamp. But this extinction of the bondage of the inward Self is actually no extinction at all, being like the extinction of a snake [imagined] in a rope. Therefore, even that Brahman, for the sake of the unreal, is accompanied by the unreal objects such as space and so forth.
The meaning is that since it does not exist at all in reality, its cessation also does not entail the appearance of duality. || 26 ||
Blows from weapons are endured, and the pains of disease are borne;
what hardship is there in enduring this mere notion of "I am"? (27)
He refutes the claim that the cultivation of non-selfhood is unbearable with the words "the weapon. || 27 ||
The notion of "I" is the imperishable sprout from which the multitude of objects in the world arises;
when that sprout has been uprooted, the world itself has become uprooted.
Like a mirror soiled by vapor—even though that vapor is insubstantial—I appear as if substantial;
yet when that [vapor] subsides, it becomes perfectly clear.

The meaning is that the mirror of the supreme Self's characteristics appears turbid—meaning it is covered with impurities and stained—by the sense of "I" (ahamartha) and by egoism (ahaṃkāra), just as a common mirror is obscured by the breath from the mouth. || 29 ||
The referent of "I" resides in the supreme wind; when that [wind] is stilled, however, there is that which is indefinable, non-manifest, infinite, unborn, and immutable.
It is infinite, non-dual, and consists of space alone. || 30 ||
The object "I" (ahamartha) is that which presents the reflection of objects before consciousness;
when that [object] ceases, consciousness remains without appearance, infinite, unborn, and immutable.
He states that even in the perception of external misfortune, the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) alone is the cause: "The object of 'I'"—that is consciousness (*cit*). 31.
When the cloud of the sense of "I" has subsided, the autumnal sky of ultimate reality shines forth,
pure and radiant with the supreme, infinite, and translucent splendor.
O dear one, if the unmanifest copper, when freed from the impurity of the sense of "I," becomes the supreme, supremely luminous, and radiant gold; || 33 ||
O dear one, that very Brahman— which is unmanifest by nature, yet has long attained the state of a "living being" (jīva) through contact with the impurity of the copper-like ego-sense—
is indeed the Supreme when it is heated by the means of hearing and so forth and freed from the dross of the ego-sense, becoming like gold.

The meaning is that Brahman is endowed with gold—being supremely luminous, exceedingly radiant, and for that very reason beautiful—because of the Vedic scripture stating: "Having attained the supreme light, he manifests in his own true form. (33)
Just as the splendor of an object devoid of designation attains the state of being indefinable,
so too does this "I-ness" (ahantā), when free from the ego-sense (anahantā), attain the state of Brahman.

If it is asked, "Once the sense of 'I' has ceased, by what word can 'mine' be designated?", he replies with the words "Just as... (yathā), stating that just as the essence of a lump of rock salt dissolved in the ocean cannot be designated because the names "lump" and so forth have ceased, so it is in this case as well. || 34 ||
Brahman, though established in the state of "I-am-ness," appears as if it were a real object;
it shines as if it were tranquil and existent, and thus it possesses designations.

He states "It exists" to show that even the designation of that [Self] by names such as "Brahmā" and so forth proceeds by postulating an etymological ground (*pravṛttinimitta*)— namely, "bigness" (*bṛhattva*) characterized by the transcendence of the smallness defined as "I-ness"— just like other categories, and not according to its actual ontological status. For example, water is by its very nature devoid of waves and the like when it is perfectly calm.

The meaning is as follows: it is like [the ocean], which exists internally as if manifesting in the form of previous waves and so forth, partaking of the designations "wave" and "ocean," yet remains truly indescribable by its own nature as water. || 35 ||

If the sense of "I," which is the seed of the world, has been burnt away through non-contemplation, then what room is there for such notions as "this is my ego" or "this is the bondage of the world"? (36)
Because of the absence of cultivation, due to the destruction of the ignorance that is the root of cultivation; that, then, [is the case]. 36.
In the Supreme, which is the True Brahman, the Auspicious, and the Self, there is no stain of names;
yet the sense of "I-ness" arises, just as the forgetfulness of the clay-nature [occurs] from [perceiving] the state of being a jar.
In order to establish that the referent of "I" (*ahamartha*) is the seed of the world, he describes the manner of its emergence, beginning with the word "sat":
"Sat" means uncontradicted throughout the three periods of time. "Brahman" means the unlimited. "Śiva" means unsurpassed bliss. "Ātman" means the immediate, singular essence of consciousness.
In this nature of the Supreme, which possesses these four characteristics, "namanam" (bowing) refers to the [recognition] of all four of these natures.

By that contraction, she becomes stained and thus defiled; consequently, like clay that forgets its own nature due to being shaped into the form of a jar, the collective ego (samaṣṭyahantā) arises, devoid of the recollection of its fourfold nature. || 37 ||
From this seed, the "I-sense" (ahamartha), the creeper of existence has arisen;
upon it, infinite worlds come as fruits and pass away.
Therefore, from this seed which is the object "I," this tree of the objective world, characterized by the existence of the visible, has arisen;
in its state as individual manifestations, it is infinite and beyond numbering.

This world, consisting of mountains, oceans, the earth, and rivers, as well as this perception of forms and the desire for them, is the internal wonder of the "I-sense," which is like a seed of black pepper.

He elaborates upon that very point with the words beginning "sādrī" (together with mountains): "Sādryabdhyurvīnadī" means together with mountains, oceans, earths, and rivers. The perception of objects by the external senses is the "vision of form" (rūpāloka);
the mental modifications such as desire and volition directed toward those objects are "longings" (eṣaṇā), and it begins with these. || 39 ||
Heaven, earth, wind, space, mountains, rivers, and the directions—I am the fragrance of this blossoming flower of the Self. (40)
The pervasive sense of "I" reveals the world, just as the day, having commenced with the perception and reflection upon the form of existence, makes all things manifest. (41)

Just as on the far side of Mount Meru, day, being of the nature of existence (sat-rūpa), having spread forth, acts as the instrumental cause for the illumination and the perception of that which is indeed existent; so it is here. 41.
Just as the purpose of a day is made manifest by its progression,
so too is this unreal world instantly fashioned through the sense of "I-ness."
The object consists of form and so forth. The intention is that "creation" (nirmāṇa) refers precisely to the cultivation of a false object, as it is said to be "created. || 42 ||
A tiny drop of oil in the form of the object "I" has spread upon the water of Brahman; from that, this wheel of the three worlds has arisen and remains established.
A *lava* of oil is a drop (*bindu*). A *cakraka* is an appearance in the shape of a wheel. || 43 ||
Alas! By a mere opening of its eyes, the "I-consciousness" experiences the worlds;
it does not [require] a closing of its eyes, just like the eye [which sees] both what is real and what is utterly unreal. 44.
Like one with diseased vision, he experiences the worlds—which are non-existent and unreal—as if they were real; yet through their disappearance in an instant, he no longer experiences them. 44.
For when the referent of "I" has expanded, saṃsāra is indeed experienced;
but when it has ceased and dissolved within, it is no longer perceived, just as the pupil is not seen by the eye itself.

To further strengthen that very point, he says again: "In the sense of 'I'. [This sense of 'I'] is not experienced when it remains concealed during deep sleep, death, or fainting; nor when it has been fundamentally destroyed in liberation; or when it has merged within *samādhi* and been destroyed through direct realization. [The word] *tāraka* refers to the pupil of the eye. || 45 ||
When the portion of "I" has been rendered partless by eternal consciousness,
this mirage of saṃsāra subsides entirely.
Partlessness means the state of being without remainder. || 46 ||

In this supreme reality, which is to be accomplished through the mere cultivation of self-awareness, do not fall into distress or delusion regarding that which is spontaneously established within your own self. (47)
He shows the extreme ease of both the means and the result with the words "self-awareness" (*svasaṃvit*).

Self-awareness is the self whose nature is self-luminous consciousness; its cultivation is the mere accomplishment of a mental modification (*vṛtti*) in that form. Since it is to be accomplished by that alone, there is no requirement for effort to pervade a result as there is in the case of insentient objects; thus, the means is extremely easy. [This applies] to the self which is merely established.

Even regarding the fruit [of liberation], its extreme ease of attainment is indicated by the fact that it does not depend on the effort of production. "Bhramī" refers to the delusion of the sense of ego (ahaṃbhāva) and so forth;
the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied according to the rule *kṛdikārādaktinaḥ*. || 47 ||

O sinless one, I see no higher good for you than this: the realization of "I am not" (anahaṃvedana), which is to be accomplished through mere personal effort and requires no external means such as companions. 48.
He states its extreme ease of access by noting that it does not depend on external means such as other persons and so forth: "one's own" (sva). || 48 ||
Forgive me; remain as you are—you whose glory has spread forth, filling the entire universe;
whose pure self takes the form of the mountains on all sides, the intermediate space, the earth, the oceans, and the paths of the winds;
who are established in yourself, peaceful, free from sorrow, devoid of the slightest stain of the senses, and beyond all phenomenal expansion.
The essence of the established doctrine is that the nature of the mobile [consciousness] is both entirely pervasive and partially so. || 49 ||
Now, summarizing the essence of all teachings and established doctrines, he concludes with the verse beginning "having forgotten":
"O Rāma, first forgetting the individual sense of 'I', [be aware of] that which is renowned everywhere—
consisting of mountains, the atmosphere, the earth, the oceans, the wind (marut), and its path, the ether."

Having filled the entire universe and having extended your power, remain in the state of the universal totality (*samaṣṭi*). Thereafter, by sublimating the entire world— including both the moving and the non-moving— as being nothing but the undifferentiated Brahman,
you shall become established in yourself, peaceful, free from sorrow, and pure-souled, devoid of organs, impurities, and limiting adjuncts (*kalās*).

"Sit"—the meaning is that the essence of the established conclusion of all Vedānta is precisely the remainder of the self (ātman) which is free from conceptual proliferation (niṣprapañca), [attained] through both superimposition and negation. || 49 ||
Thus ends the fourth canto, titled "The Dissolution of Ego," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the glorious Vāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa, composed by the sage Vālmīki. 4.
Thus ends the fourth canto, titled "The Dispelling of Ego," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The Fifth Canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having first conquered their own inherent nature, those possessed of consciousness [should master] the senses.
For one who applies themselves to solitude, everything is swiftly accomplished.
"The scripture bears fruit only for those who have conquered their senses, and not for others"— thus,
after Vasiṣṭha had spoken to Bhuśuṇḍa, the story of the Vidyādhara is now told.

The meaning is this: having first conquered the inherent nature of the senses—which possess consciousness and a mind—to pursue their respective objects, he who subsequently applies himself to the means for discriminating between eternal and non-eternal entities and so forth, for him alone does the entire fruit of the instruction of the scriptures and the teacher become established, and not for anyone else. || 1 ||
For one of burnt intellect who has not conquered within himself even his own mere nature,
the attainment of the supreme state is as difficult to obtain as oil from sand.
The meaning is that listening and so forth, even when practiced for a long time, are as fruitless as the labor of squeezing sand. || 2 ||
For even a slight instruction, when given to one who is pure, takes root like a drop of oil on a clean surface;
it does not stick to those with upturned minds, just as a pearl does not adhere to a mirror.

It spreads and enters within like a drop of oil upon a clean cloth or similar surface; [this occurs] in those whose minds are superficial, lacking depth, and devoid of the four means of accomplishment (sādhanacatuṣṭaya). || 3 ||
In this very context, they cite this ancient history,
which was previously told to me by Bhuśuṇḍa on the summit of Mount Meru.
Long ago, on one occasion, Bhuśuṇḍa was questioned by me in a private conversation within a cave on the peak of Mount Meru.
In the course of conversation, during the introduction of a discourse on the inner self. || 5 ||
"O dear one, when I asked him, 'Whom do you remember as having lived for a very long time—someone of dull intellect who did not know the Self? he replied to me as follows. (6)
Thinking that a king of dull intellect, who has not conquered his senses, will inevitably come to grief through his efforts in vain, [the author] poses a question regarding such a person. (6)
Bhuśuṇḍa said:
"In former times, there was a Vidyādhara who was ignorant of the Self and afflicted by worldly pleasures;
he was noble, reflective, and dwelt on the peak between the Lokāloka mountains. (7)

"Thoroughly tormented" means afflicted by uncontrolled senses; for this very reason, he is "withered," meaning devoid of the rest that comes from relaxation. Alternatively, the connection with the following verse is that he is "withered" by austerity (*tapas*), observance (*niyama*), and restraint (*yama*). "Noble" (*ārya*) means endowed with virtuous conduct that is the cause for the increase of longevity. (7)
Through manifold austerities, self-restraint, and religious observances,
he remained with undiminished life-span for four kalpas in ancient times.
Then, at the end of the fourth eon, discernment arose within him,
just as a lapis lazuli gem from Vidūra manifests its brilliance upon the rising of the clouds through its inherent suitability.

Because of propriety, there is the necessary emergence of discernment (*viveka*) from long-practiced austerity, self-restraint, and so forth; just as the vaidūrya gem arises from a specific distant region when the clouds appear. || 9 ||
Reflecting upon death again, birth again, and old age as well, he thought, "I am ashamed; what single thing might there be that is stable? Thus he pondered. (10)

He demonstrates the very nature of discernment (viveka) with the word "again" (punar): "I am ashamed," reflecting that "may old age not come upon me. This means, in other words, that he is despondent. || 10 ||

Having cast off his own [worldly] city consisting of eighteen elements, he, with a detached soul and having realized the lack of essence in worldly existence, came to me to inquire [about the truth]. (11)

Having long supported his own city composed of eighteen elements—the five vital breaths, the ten senses, mind and intellect, and the gross body—and being weary from carrying it, he whose self and mind have become detached [from it]. (11)
Having approached me and performed a grand salutation, he,
being honored by me, spoke these blameless words at the appropriate moment.
"From the opportunity" means having reached the occasion for a question; such is the meaning. || 12 ||
The Vidyādhara said:
"One's own weapons and the senses are both soft and yet capable of causing intense heat; they are as firm and strong as stone, and are skillful in cutting and piercing. (13)

In this regard, intending to describe in detail later on the defects of the sense faculties and other causes of one's own exhaustion, he begins with two verses starting with "mṛdūni" (soft): because they enter quickly into their respective objects, they are "soft"; after having entered, they cause torment; and because they cannot then be moved, they possess a strength firmer even than stones.
The meaning is that the arrows and other weapons which have entered one's own body are equivalent to the sense organs. || 13 ||
Agitated, defiled, bestowing calamity, and possessing waves of suffering because they are like fires to the forest of virtues;
dense with the darkness of the heart and consisting of gloom—having conquered the senses, one attains happiness; so what use have I for worldly objects?

These sense-faculties are rooted in the heart, dense with darkness like a forest shrouded in gloom, and agitated by the monkeys of desire and the like. Within the vital breath, mind, body, and heart, they possess the six waves of hunger and so forth. Yet, by some stroke of fortune, there has emerged in them a grove of virtues such as tranquility and self-restraint.

Because they are purifying and burning, even though they possess waves, they are not cool. Having conquered such sense organs—and by the word "and," the mind which relies upon them—one attains happiness, not through enjoyments. Therefore, what purpose do I have with these objects characterized by the pleasures of the Vidyādharas? Thus, detached from them, he became desirous of knowledge.
The meaning is: "I have come for refuge. || 14 ||

Thus ends the fifth canto, titled "The Question of the Vidyādhara," within the Narrative of the Vidyādhara in the Nirvāṇa Section of the glorious Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa of Valmīki, composed by the Sage. 5.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Question of the Vidyādhara," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The Sixth Canto.
The Vidyādhara said:
Tell me quickly of that sublime state which is effortless, free from decay or excess, purifying, and devoid of beginning or end.
Long tested by himself while addicted to divine enjoyments,
the Vidyadhara here has described the wicked ways of the objects and the senses.
Therefore, he says "That which... [referring to the following verse], requesting: "Teach me, who am desirous of knowing Brahman and endowed with the fourfold means of qualification.

It is "exalted" (*udāra*) because it consists of unsurpassed bliss free from suffering, which removes all states of wretchedness. Speak quickly; for me, who am scorched by the threefold torments and who wish to plunge into the ocean of water like one whose head is ablaze.
The meaning is that there is an inability to endure delay. || 1 ||
"For so long a time I have been asleep, inert in nature;
now, O Sage, I am fully awakened through the grace of the Self. (2)

To the question, "In that case, why did the scripture not exist even earlier?", he replies: "For so long," etc. [This was due to] the grace of the self and the mind, characterized by the most intense dispassion. || 2 ||
The mind is greatly deluded, scorched, and agitated by the functions of ignorance; rescue me from this wretched state of "I" which persists through delusion. (3)

The mind is inflamed by desire, which is a great illusion; it is agitated by the evil tendencies that consist in the functioning of ignorance; it possesses activities and karmas whose ends are difficult to sever and whose fruits are bitter. He states the cause for this: "out of delusion.
This occurs in the form of the conceit of self (*ātma-abhimāna*) regarding that which is not the self, thinking "I am."

The meaning is: "from the cause of delusion," that is, from the non-recognition of one's own true nature (*svatattva*). Alternatively, the ablative case in "deliver me from delusion" (*mohād uddhara*) expresses the source as constructed by the intellect (*buddhi-kṛta-apādāna*). || 3 ||
Even in one who is illustrious, these—such as cowardice and the like—are swift destroyers;
even in one endowed with virtues and fierce prowess, they are like frost to a lotus.

Now, it is heard that the Vidyādharas—because they are the refuge of all sciences—are indeed capable of dispelling all suffering through the power of their knowledge alone, being endowed with the accomplishments (*siddhi*) of jewels, mantras, elixirs (*rasāyana*), and so forth, as well as the sovereign powers (*aiśvarya*) such as *aṇimā* and the rest; so why have these afflictions such as desire and other sufferings, along with defects such as cowardice and wretchedness, fallen upon you, who are so illustrious? For...

"Because you are the most venerable due to being born of the highest divine lineage, you have come for refuge even to me, who am of the lowly crow lineage, and you ask me about it. To this he says: "Even though she is glorious," meaning even though she is glorious through the perfection of all sciences and so forth, she is devoid of the knowledge of the Self (ātmavidyā).

The afflictions of desire, anger, envy, malice, and so forth, as well as defects such as cowardice, surely fall [upon one]; the sense is that this is due to the lack of control over the senses. In the case of the lotus, however, even though it is glorious—being the abode of Lakṣmī—and virtuous—possessing fibers of lotus-stalk—it has fierce leaves, harsh with their own moisture, because they are turned away from the affectionate water that is their support and cannot be smeared by its droplets.
For whom, even in such a state... || 4 ||
Only worn-out beings are born and die,
neither for the sake of dharma nor for the sake of liberation, like gnats in a lotus.

Indicating that in the absence of knowledge, even for those of divine birth, there is indeed equality with births such as mosquitoes due to the lack of qualification for dharma, he elaborates upon the perception of defects everywhere— which is the cause of his own dispassion— beginning with the words "They are born" (verse 5):
"By those very dispositions, those very mockeries of trivial pursuits..."
After a long time we have become weary, having been repeatedly deceived.

By means of those various objects such as sound and so forth, which have been experienced thousands of times before, for the sake of a most trivial fragment of pleasure—those who are "deceived" (*vipralambhāḥ*) by these "mockeries" (*viḍambanaiḥ*), characterized by the contact of the senses with their objects; [the word *viḍambanaiḥ*] is used in the passive sense (*karmaṇi*). Being thus deceived or cheated, [they are led astray]. [In the reading *tucchānnaiḥ*, it refers to] those things that are trivial...
The meaning is: "even by means of food that serves as sustenance for small creatures. || 6 ||
There is no end to this, nor is there a state of stability for one whose mind finds no rest as it wanders among the fragile enjoyments, like a traveler in desert lands.

As my mind remains restless, wandering thus amidst these fragile enjoyments that are subject to decay, there is no end to this path of saṃsāra for me, nor is there any stable abiding or state of steadiness. || 7 ||
The realms of sensory enjoyment are sweet at their onset, yet fragile and the causes of worldly existence; they undergo transformation in a short time and are ultimately terrifying. (8)
"O Father, I take no pleasure in this perverse woman who is intent on honor and dishonor, whose beloved is wicked pride, and who has destroyed the splendor of the Vidyādharas."
To the objection—"Surely you should find rest in the very wealth of a Vidyādhara, acquired through such vast merit"—he replies with the word "māna":

"by that which has pride as its primary [feature]," where "pride" (māna) is the conceit of establishing one's own superiority, and "disrespect" (apamāna) is the act of bringing about another's inferiority; "by that which is lovely" (ramyayā) because it belongs to those whose egoism is wicked. For this very reason...
By the left [hand] and by a discriminating woman who is adverse; even in that case, the qualifiers should be applied. || 9 ||
And he beheld the grounds of the Caitraratha garden, tender with blossoms,
where the splendor of every kind of wealth was provided by the creepers of the wish-fulfilling trees.
He reveals his distaste for everything because he has already experienced all enjoyments, beginning with the words "seen" (dṛṣṭāḥ) and so forth. || 10 ||
I have dwelt in the groves of Mount Meru and in the cities of the Vidyādharas,
amidst the rows of excellent celestial chariots and upon the ridges of the winds.
He found rest among the armies of the gods and in the vine-like arms of beloved women;
he found rest in the cities of the world-protectors, which were graced by the playful charm of captivating necklaces.
In which [cities] there are necklaces and other ornaments, and where there are playful movements and the wonders of strolling. || 12 ||
"Nothing is suitable or good; everything has been scorched by the heat of the poison of mental anguish and has turned to ashes, my dear father—I have realized this now. (13)

Mental anxieties are sufferings of the mind; it has now been realized—during this time when discernment has arisen—that [the self] was scorched by their feverish heat, whereas previously it was not known. 13.
By this eye, which is restless in its longing to behold forms and greedy for the faces of women, and which is accompanied by such radiance, I have been led to suffering for my own ruin. (14)

By what kind of discernment (*viveka*), and how was each [object] first known? This is shown regarding the eyes and other senses with the words beginning "form" (*rūpa*). By one who is "greedy" (*gṛdhnu*), meaning desiring; the suffix *knū* is applied to the root *gṛdh* according to the rule *trasigṛdhidhṛṣikṣipeḥ knuḥ*. "With that which possesses illumination" (*sāvabhāsena*) means accompanied by the external and internal light. For the sake of a fault (*doṣāya*).
For the purpose of corrupting the mind through attachment to its own objects. || 14 ||
Abandoning the conceptual construction that "this brings merit" or "this does not," [the mind] rushes even toward non-existent things because it follows after mere form. (15)

Regarding the body of a woman, having abandoned the discrimination and discernment that "only these things such as clothing, ornaments, and ointments are beneficial and produce beauty, whereas these things such as blood, flesh, bone, and hair are not," the eye runs [after her]— this is the ellipsis; it does not come to a cessation until it falls under the power of calamities.
The mind is intent on various attachments and is directed toward the welfare of others as its own end. (16)
A mind defiled by attachment to those objects and blinded by passion— like a moth blinded by the glow of a lamp—

becomes intent upon various evil addictions that lead to supreme misfortune such as death; thus, being directed toward them, it falls under the power of manifold bonds, slaughter, imprisonment, and calamities such as hell.
The meaning is that it does not reach cessation, that is, the state of desisting from activity. || 16 ||
This sense of smell clearly runs toward all manner of misfortune on every side;
O Father, I am unable to restrain it here, just as one cannot hold back a horse.
He demonstrates that the defect stated regarding the eye applies to the nose and the other senses as well, with the words: "The nose," etc. (17).
I have been joined with the sense of smell by my own excessive fault, which follows the breath from my mouth like a conduit for scented water and acts like an enemy. (18)

Just as someone who has been forcibly subdued by an extremely wicked enemy might be compelled to constantly move along a city sewer carrying foul-smelling water, so too am I compelled to remain within the nostril-passage, which is a conduit for foul-smelling fluids such as phlegm;
this is the meaning. || 18 ||
For a long time, I have been thoroughly struck by this tongue, devoid of discipline, against the mountains of suffering hidden within elephants and jackals. (19)

The system [of dharma] is a scripture primarily concerned with the distinction between what is fit to be eaten and what is not; by its neglect, one enters the mountains of suffering characterized by births as worms, insects, animals, and so forth. This is the sense, based on such Smṛti texts as: "Those who drink liquor become worms, and those who eat forbidden food likewise. In this regard, where even for the powerful there is an elephant...
"Since the jackal is the best among the intelligent, the guardianship belongs to those two alone and not to anyone else; thus it was said.
(19) "And I am unable to restrain the skin's greed for touch, just as one cannot [restrain] the heat of the sun blazing in the summer season. (20)
The sage’s powers of hearing, longing for the taste of auspicious sounds,
cast me into this perilous state, just as a deer’s desire for grass leads it to its ruin.
The "essence of sound" (śabdarasa) refers to the tasting of sound. In the case of the deer, it refers to a treacherous pit covered with grass. || 21 ||

The splendor of auspicious sounds was heard, consisting of the voices of women bowing down who were intent on doing what was pleasing, uttered by humble servants, and mingled with the resonance of musical instruments and songs.
"In that case, are the objects of your senses—from form (rūpa) to sound—difficult for you to obtain, such that you have encountered this misfortune for their sake?
To this he replies with the words beginning "praṇatāḥ" (bowed down): they are as if already bowed down simply because they are urged by submissive servants. || 22 ||

We have beheld the goddesses of Fortune, the women, the quarters of the sky, and the shores of the oceans and mountains— all of them captivating with their splendor and adorned with tinkling jeweled ornaments.
The four qualities beginning with glory (śrī), which are common [to all], should be applied as qualifiers. || 23 ||

For a long time, the six flavors—sweet, sour, salty, pungent, bitter, and astringent—endowed with excellent qualities, delightful with their charming aesthetic wonder, and brought by devoted beloved women, have been enjoyed. (24)
They possess the skill of blending and cooking the six flavors and various fragrances as appropriate. || 24 ||
In the expansive pleasure-grounds on all sides, they were touched without obstruction by breezes carrying the scent of silk garments, lovely women, pearl necklaces, and flower-strewn beds. (25)
Silk and the other six are objects of the sense of touch. || 25 ||
O Sage, the fragrances wafted by the gentle breeze—arising from the faces of brides, medicinal herbs, flowers, and unguents—have been experienced by you. (26)

The faces of the brides; the herbs such as sandalwood, uśīra, agaru, and so forth; the flowers; the unguents which are mixtures of camphor, musk, pauṣkalaka, and other substances; and the grounds from which those [unguents] originate. || 26 ||
That which was heard, touched, seen, tasted, and smelled again and again has become utterly parched and tasteless; tell me quickly, what more shall I pursue? (27)
Being served again and again, it has become as tasteless as a completely dried-up piece of wood; now that it has become mostly like vomited food, what shall I partake of there? (27)
Even after consuming this multitude of miserable enjoyments for thousands of years,
from the highest realm of Brahmā down to a blade of grass, no satisfaction arises.
He says "Having eaten," etc., to show that the desire to abandon that [pleasure] arises precisely from its lack of relish, and not from satiety. || 28 ||
Having ruled a universal empire for a very long time, having likewise enjoyed a multitude of wives, and having utterly crushed the forces of the enemy—what unprecedented thing has been attained? (29)
What is obtained? The meaning is: nothing at all. || 29 ||
Even those whose destruction there was not, by whom the three worlds were enjoyed—even they, all together, have in no long time gone to the state of ashes. (30)

The meaning is that for those such as Hiraṇyakaśipu and others, there was no means of destruction—that is, no instrument of their death—which had not already been well-known in the world; for, when he requested the boon beginning with "neither by the dry nor by the wet," all well-known instruments of slaughter were prohibited. || 30 ||
One should apply effort, even through arduous exertion, toward that which has been attained such that nothing further remains to be attained. (31)

This being the case, what is to be done? He says: "by one who has attained" (prāptena). Even by means of arduous effort—that which is accomplished through the exhaustion of restraining the senses, the vital breaths, and the mind—[one should strive]. || 31 ||
For those beings by whom desirable enjoyments have been enjoyed for a long time,
no tree or celestial balloon has ever been seen atop their heads in this world.

He says "by which" (yena) to show that even for men who have long enjoyed great pleasures, once the time of enjoyment has passed, no distinction whatsoever is seen compared to other men who have not yet enjoyed such pleasures: "By whatever [means] lovely women and most delightful enjoyments were long enjoyed, upon the head of any such man..."

The wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpataru*) has grown, yet it has not been seen by any living beings such that they might always rest in its shade with all their desires fulfilled; nor has a celestial vehicle (*vimāna*) or similar object, which glides through the sky, appeared upon its trunk such that they might always roam everywhere—this is the meaning. || 32 ||
For a long time, I have been deceived by my senses in these forests of sense-objects, which end in misery, just as a child is deceived by wicked boys. (33)
"Arbhakaḥ" (the child) is the subject; "sādhuḥ" (virtuous) is to be understood as the predicate. || 33 ||
Today, however, these enemies within my own domain, known by the name of the senses—though they are painful—have been fully recognized by me; yet they shall deceive me once again.

The syntactical connection is as follows: "Today I have fully understood those called 'senses' (indriya), which are the objects of their own respective domains; for they exist in the form of the ears and other organs for the sake of their individual experiences, by drawing out the very elements whose nature consists of objects such as sound from the mind toward the exterior. (34)
In the empty wilderness of saṃsāra, the deceitful hunters of the senses and their objects repeatedly console the scorched deer of humanity before they slaughter it. (35)
Among those who have not been burned by these venomous serpents— the objects of the senses which are like poisonous snakes— there are only two or three to be found even in this world.
By those venomous serpents whose very glance is poison—such men as have not been consumed by them are, it is implied, to be found only two or three in the entire world. || 36 ||
[It is] a snare trembling with craving, coiled by the terrifying elephants of enjoyments; it is filled with the fierce swords of greed and marked by the clusters of spears of anger. || 37 ||

In order to demonstrate that they must necessarily be conquered, he characterizes the senses themselves as an enemy army with three verses beginning with "Bhogā... [Verse 37]: "Enveloped by those elephants (ibha) which are the objects of enjoyment (bhoga). [37]
It was pervaded by the chariot of the net of dualities, protected by egoism,
crowded with the horses of active impulses, and tumultuous with the clamor of desire.
The pairs [of opposites], such as cold and heat; protected by the commander-in-chief, the ego (ahaṃkāra). || 38 ||
O dear one, those who have risen to conquer the army of wicked senses stationed at the very borders of the body—they alone are truly the noble warriors in this world. (39)
Having reached and occupied the boundary of the city characterized by the body, she stands there. || 39 ||
It is easier to pierce the temples of the intoxicated elephant Airāvaṇa than it is to restrain one's own senses when they have set out upon the wrong path.
The bursting forth—that is, the tearing open—of the frontal globes (kumbha) of the intoxicated elephant Airāvaṇa. || 40 ||
O virtuous one, the conquest of the senses is the ultimate limit even for those of great manliness, great being, and great fortune. (41)

Of the courage of a being; of fortune, that is, the perfection of repose; of the senses, the "assault" means victory; "the limit" means the boundary, that is to say, the highest pinnacle—even for the great who know the truth. || 41 ||
Even a man attains the highest status among the gods only so long as he is not dragged away like a blade of grass by his wretched senses.
Supremacy and honor. || 42 ||
Those on earth who have conquered their senses are the only true great beings; I consider all these others to be merely moving assemblages of flesh-machines.
O Sage, if I possess the effort to conquer this army of the five senses belonging to the mind-general, then I shall surely achieve victory.
If there is an effort and a means, then I shall conquer.
For those diseases of the most excellent senses, there are no medicines, no sacred fords, and no mantras for their pacification, except for the casting off of the desire for enjoyments.
He says, "I have known only one single means," [beginning with] the verse starting with "indriya" (verse 45).
I have been led to the utmost distress by my rushing senses, like a lone traveler in a great forest by bandits. (46)
The sense-faculties are like muddy ponds: they are turbid, devoid of clarity, possessed of great misfortune, and filled with the worthless moss of worldly fragrance.

From this point forward, he describes the sense organs through parallel attributes by way of their similarity to ponds and the like, beginning with the words "paṅkavanti" (muddy) and so forth. [He describes them as] "gandhibhiḥ" (fragrant), meaning possessing impurities similar to water-moss; and as "tucchāni," meaning contemptible. || 47 ||
The sense-faculties are like dense jungles, difficult to traverse, shrouded in mist, and generating a web of terror. (48)
"Thick with mists, dullness, and frosts"; "ātaṅka" means fear. || 48 ||
The lotuses have holes and their qualities are very difficult to perceive;
the lotus stalks have knots and inert limbs, and so do the sense organs. (49)

The qualities (*guṇas*), the latent impressions (*vāsanās*), and the threads (*tantavas*) are born from the mud of impurity (*paṅka*); because they are most subtle, they are very difficult to perceive.

They consist primarily of inert limbs, meaning they are like the parts of an insentient body; furthermore, due to the non-distinction between the letters *la* and *ḍa*, they may also be understood as having limbs made of water (*jala*). (49)
The sense-faculties are like the waters of the ocean: they are harsh, greedy for jewels, tossed by waves, and as terrible as crocodiles that are difficult to seize; they are full of salt water.
They are harsh because of their cruelty and because they are unpleasant to the touch. By "waves" is meant the six waves and the [ordinary] waves.
"Salt waters" refers to the waters of the ocean. 50.
The senses cause distress to one's kinsmen, bring about another body, and produce piteous lamentations at the time of death.
The senses are like dense, infinite, and empty forests; they are enemies to those lacking discernment, but friends to those possessing discernment. (52)
The forests are impenetrable, infinite and boundless, and devoid of any place for people to rest. || 52 ||
These sense-faculties are like terrifying clouds: they are solid yet hollow, impure and inert, and possess the fleeting brilliance of lightning. (53)
From which there are dense, crashing sounds like the thundering of clapping arms; [those things] whose flashes of momentary pleasure are like lightning.
In the alternative interpretation (pakṣāntare), this is clear. || 53 ||
Those seized by lowly creatures are avoided by the self-disciplined; likewise, those overwhelmed by passion and darkness, as well as the pits of one's own senses, are to be shunned. (54)

The sense-faculties are like pits, hollows, mounds, and ground occupied by lowly creatures such as insects who are attached to trivial pleasures; they are exclusively skilled at casting one down, filled with the venomous serpents of the afflictions, and bristling with hundreds of thousands of harsh thorns. (54–55)
The tops of the chasms are the openings of dilapidated pits. || 55 ||
One's own senses are like demons: they are self-centered, ignoble, delighting solely in rashness, and wandering in the darkness.
The sense-faculties are hollow within, lacking essence, crooked, and knotted; they are like ill-wooded timber, fit only for burning. (57)
Durdāruṇi refers to old bamboo and other such wooden materials. || 57 ||
The senses are like wretched cities: they are bound by dense delusion, difficult to traverse and deep, and though possessing great openings, they are utterly empty. 58.
Those wicked cities—cities of the unrighteous—are characterized by dense delusions and a persistent addiction to vices such as theft, quarreling, gambling, and the like. (58)
Among infinite objects, the causes in jars and the like are the whirling, mud-stained wheels and the sense organs. (59)
Cakrakas are potter's wheels. || 59 ||
O you whose nature is to rescue, lift me up with the dawning of compassion—me, who am thus sunk in calamity and utterly destitute.
For those few who truly prevail as saints in the worlds declare that association with them removes the greatest sorrow.

O you whose very nature is to rescue those who have fallen into distress, please lift me up— me, who am thus submerged in the ocean of calamity caused by the senses as described, who am destitute, who have abandoned all possessions, and who have come to you for refuge— by means of instruction in reality arising from compassion and mercy;
for whatever virtuous ones like yourself exist in this world, renowned as knowers of truth and compassionate, they are truly victorious.

The meaning is that all the scriptures and all people declare that association with them and taking refuge in them exist in a state of supreme excellence, and that this removes the greatest sorrow. || 60 ||
Thus ends the sixth canto, titled "The Description of Dispassion," within the Narrative of Vidyādhara, in the Nirvāṇa Section of the glorious Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa composed by Vālmīki.
Thus ends the sixth canto, titled "The Description of Dispassion," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The Seventh Chapter.
Bhuśuṇḍa said:
Then, O Brahman, having heard those purifying words of his, I—
This has been stated, exactly as asked, in words of very clear phrasing.
Brahman alone is not the world-suffering; rather, it is ignorance that has spread as the world.
Indeed, the tree of the world is seen here to have grown from the seed of the ego.
Of that Vidyādhara; this is the reply about to be stated. || 1 ||
Excellent, O Lord of the Vidyādharas! By good fortune you have awakened for the sake of prosperity;
after a long time, you desire to rise from the deep pit of the well of worldly existence.
By good fortune, through the dawning of luck. || 2 ||
Your purifying intellect shines with a dense form,
like a stream of molten gold purified by the fire of discernment.

The meaning is: she is pervaded intensely by a dense form through her discernment (*viveka*); just as a stream of molten gold pervaded by fire shines with an excellence of luster, so too does she. || 3 ||
He grasps the meaning of the words of instruction with effortless ease;
just as an object reflects without exertion in a stainless mirror. (4)
For this very reason, your mind will certainly grasp the meaning of my words of instruction; it will grasp them effortlessly, without exertion. || 4 ||
Whatever I say here, you ought to accept it all with the word "Om";
we have searched for this for a long time, so there is no need for hesitation in this matter.
"Oṃ" is uttered with the intention of acceptance. || 5 ||
Whatever tastes within you, awaken by casting off ignorance;
you do not exist as a separate entity even when sought for a long time within.

Therein, first, he briefly teaches the secret of all the Vedāntas—that the pure Brahman is the very nature of the Witness, distinct from all that is seen—in the verse beginning with "Whatever": "Whatever [object] such as the ego and so forth pleases you within your own heart and manifests as an object of perception, all that you are not. Among the categories of objects, there exists a certain Self."

The meaning is: thinking "I must find and obtain [it]," you have long gazed within and searched; yet it is you yourself who are found. Therefore, abandoning the non-intelligent (abodha) which is characterized merely as the object of sight, realize the Self that is its witness.
For you who are certain that "I do not exist, you do not exist, nor does the world exist," everything exists as Śiva; and that [Śiva] leads neither to suffering nor to pleasure for you.
Indeed, it is not the case that upon the abandonment of all objects of perception characterized by the seer and the seen one falls into nihilism;

rather, with the intention that everything continues to exist in its fullness through the state of the truly supreme and auspicious Brahman— by means of the cessation of the imagined portion of defects that cause the inequality of pleasure and pain— it is said:
"I am not," [he said]. || 7 ||
Whether the world was born from ignorance, or whether ignorance belongs to the world—
even after investigating thus, we do not know, because these two are essentially one.

He provides the justification for the statement that the mere object of perception is of the nature of non-cognition, asking: "What?"—that is, did the world characterized by waking and dreaming arise from the well-known ignorance (*ajñāna*) of deep sleep in its state as a solidified ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) and so forth;
or rather, is the ignorance of deep sleep derived from the world characterized by waking and so forth, which has dissolved like the hardness of lac?

Even though one might investigate [the matter] by thinking "they have arisen," because there is no decisive criterion (*vinigamaka*), we do not know how to establish a fixed relationship of cause and effect.
Therefore, the meaning is that, just as ghee remains a single entity despite its states of solidity and fluidity, everything is nothing but ignorance (*ajñāna*). || 8 ||
Like the water of a mirage, the universe, though existing, is non-existent because it lacks substantial reality;
that which shines here is Brahman, being neither nothing nor something at all.
The very perception of its illusory nature (vivartatā) is its abandonment; for when the world is sublated, it is realized as something trivial.
But when one realizes that the substratum (adhiṣṭhāna) is none other than Brahman, then everything is indeed Brahman—thus he says: "Like a mirage," etc. (9).
The universe does not exist, like the water of a mirage; nor do you exist, nor does even the appearance exist here, because of the absence of that [object]. Therefore, there is auspiciousness (śiva).
Clarifying the intended meaning, he refutes even its appearance with the words "like a mirage.

Because that [object] is absent, there is an absence of anything to appear; for the point is that when a jar is absent, even if light exists, the referent of the term "appearance of a jar" does not exist. || 10 ||
Know that you are the Great Ego (Ahaṃtva), the seed of the universe; for from it is born this world-tree, ancient and vast, with its mountains, oceans, earth, rivers, and islands as its roots.

Since it is impossible to refute the world— which possesses infinite forms— by means of its individual forms, he describes egoism as the seed and the world as the tree arising from it in order to state that its refutation occurs only through the burning of the seed, beginning with the verse starting "viśva" (verse 11).
From the subtle seed of egoism (ahaṃtva), this tree of the universe is born;
for its roots, which abound with the sap of the senses, are indeed the worlds.
The attachment to sense objects is the sap of the senses; the lower worlds, enriched by that [attachment], are the roots of that tree. || 12 ||
The clusters of stars are its buds; the multitude of constellations is its mass of unopened blossoms;
the spreading bunches of fragrance are its latent impressions (vāsanās); and the full moon is its abode of fruit. || 13 ||

The network of twenty-seven constellations beginning with Aśvinī is its primary cluster of buds; the multitude of other stars is a mass of subtle buds; the latent impressions (*vāsanās*) of living beings such as merit (*dharma*) and so forth are the clusters of flower-bunches; and the abodes of fruits are the bunches of fruit. || 13 ||
Heaven and the other great realms are its vast branches and hollows;
Mount Meru, Mandara, Sahya, and the other mountains are its rows of leaves.

The realms beginning with Svarga—namely the worlds known as Sva, Mahar, Jana, Tapa, and Satya—are the great divisions of the vast worlds, acting as the massive branches, hollows, and interior regions of the tree’s trunk. || 14 ||
The seven oceans are its prominent fibers; the netherworld is the hollow of its root;
the Yugas are the swarms of wood-boring insects; and the cosmic qualities (guṇas) are the rows of its joints. || 15 ||

The excellent sons are the irrigation trenches and moats; the Yugas, beginning with Kṛta, are the clusters of roots because they cause the sap of Dharma to flow out more and more. The series of qualities such as the years, solstices, seasons, and months of those respective Yugas are the joints from which the branches, roots, and so forth of the Tree arise (the reading "udbhedaparvāṇi" is also found). || 15 ||
Ignorance is the soil for birth; human beings are like millions of birds; perception is a massive pillar; and the forest fire is the bliss of nirvāṇa. || 16 ||

Human beings are living souls. Perception is merely delusive cognition, which is like a massive pillar—the central part that supports all its branches. From the realization of its true nature comes Nirvana; indeed, this very cessation is the forest fire that consumes the woods of worldly existence. 16.
Forms, light, and mental attention have various modes of activity;
the vast forest is space, and the surface of the mouth is a net of mother-of-pearl shells.

The perception of objects through the sense faculties—forms and lights—and the mental formations consisting of conceptualizations and discriminations regarding their spheres, as well as acts of attention, are the various modes of fragrance and the spreading of sweet scents from that tree. The unconditioned space is its vast forest; the lips, both upper and lower, are its facial skin and the sockets of its eyes.
The blossoming of flowers is like a multitude of pearl-oysters from which the laughter of the eyes has been released; that is to say, it is the binding of the fruit. || 17 ||
The seasons are its variegated branches, and the ten directions are its twigs;
it is a great flood of the sap of consciousness, with the movement of the wind as its circulation.

The flow of rasa, which is his own self-awareness, is the cause of his life; the movement of his vital breath is the very thread-self (sūtrātman), which functions through the conjunction of the sun, moon, fire, and other elements. || 18 ||
The rays of the moon and sun are flickering, intent on sinking and rising;
the flower clusters are beautiful, while the darkness is the wandering of bees. 19.

Its daily rising and setting are its immersion and emergence; the rays of the moon and sun directed toward it are its beautiful clusters of blossoms; and the wandering of the bees is the very circling of darkness along with the sun—the "bhramara-bhrama" meaning the bees that wander. (19)
Filling the netherworld, the quarters of space, and the intermediate region, that which is unreal stands as if it were real;
yet, when the seed of the ego-sense is consumed by the fire of non-egoity (anahantā), there is no further growth of it, even though it previously existed.

Such is this tree of worldly existence (*saṃsāra-vṛkṣa*): it fills the netherworld with its roots, the multitude of quarters with its trunk, the expanse of space with its top, and exists in reality as something unreal, appearing as real through delusion. When its seed—the sense of "I" (*ahamartha*)—is scorched and destroyed by the fire characterized by non-egoity (*anahaṃtā*), one attains the enjoyment of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*).

The meaning is that until the fall of that body, there is no further growth or sprouting of this tree of saṃsāra—even though it still exists—by way of mere appearance through rebirth and so forth. || 20 ||

Thus ends the seventh canto, titled "The Description of the Seed of the World-Tree," in the *Vidyādharopākhyāna* (The Story of the Vidyādhara) within the *Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa* of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa*, the Great Epic of Vasiṣṭha. Canto 7.

Thus ends the seventh canto, titled "The Description of the Seed of the World-Tree," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the glorious Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa, in its exposition of the essential meaning.
The Eighth Chapter.
Bhuśuṇḍa said:
"O Vidyādhara, you who are the support of the earth and whose dwelling is a mountain cave—"
Moving with swift motion through the expanse of the sky that reaches to the ends of the quarters.
In this world, the destruction of the tree of saṃsāra is understood to result from knowledge;
saṃsāra is described as being essentially a pavilion of volitional constructions.
Such is this tree of the world that it arises from the seed of the sense of "I";
when the seed is consumed by the fire of knowledge, nothing at all is born again.

He restates the tree of *saṃsāra* as it was described: "O Vidyādhara!"—that which has as its base and root-region the earth together with the seven lower worlds; whose caves are the mountain ranges reaching to the edge of the Lokāloka mountain, serving as its enclosures and sacrificial altars; and which, through its conduct, pervades the ten directions and the sky.

It is extremely restless, moving horizontally through its spreading branches, rising upward through the extension of its shoots, and shifting here and there with the movement of living beings. || 1 || 2 ||
And when it is being scrutinized, that "I-ness" (ahaṃtva) is indeed never found;
this much alone is that knowledge, and by this very [knowledge] it is consumed.

When this "I-ness" (ahaṃtva) is examined in its true nature—investigated like the examination of a gem as to what it might be—and is determined to be nothing but Brahman, that is [the realization]. || 3 ||
Because of the absence of the sense of "I," the sense of "I" exists as the seed of saṃsāra;
because of the absence of the sense of "I," the sense of "I" does not exist—this is the supreme knowledge.
Since this creation was indeed non-existent at the very beginning of creation, whence comes "I-ness," whence comes "you-ness," and whence arises the delusion of duality and unity? (5)
He states that for that which—whether non-existent or existent—origination itself is impossible, its continued existence is all the more excluded: "At the very beginning of creation," etc. (Verse 5).
Those who, having heard the words of their guru, strive by their own effort toward the attainment of the state,
conquering by completely abandoning all mental constructs (saṃkalpa) from its very root.

In order to strengthen the meaning already stated—that *saṃsāra* does not exist even in the three periods of time—the author prepares the introductory stage (*bhūmikā*) by describing the gambling hall of volition (*saṃkalpa*), beginning with the words "Having heard... and so forth. This is done so that one may completely renounce volition, including its very roots, as will be described hereafter and has been frequently described previously; [he approaches] the Guru, who knows the sequence of means for that [renunciation].

Having heard those words, those who strive by their own effort according to the method described therein, upon attaining the realization of reality, conquer that state known as Kaivalya, which is free from all volitional construction.
A cook attains victory through cooking when he has mastered his own craft;
likewise, a man of discernment attains his own state of discernment only through diligent effort, and not otherwise.

Just as a skilled cook, having thoroughly mastered the specific science of cooking according to his own treatise, attains victory over hunger, thirst, disease, old age, and the like, as well as excellence such as royal honor, through the preparation and cooking of various foods and diverse elixirs exactly in the manner prescribed therein— so too does the discerning qualified aspirant.

The meaning is that only through effort according to the path taught by the Guru and the scriptures does one’s own discernment triumph, leading all the way to liberation (kaivalya), and not otherwise. || 7 ||
Know that this world here is nothing other than a mere flash of wonder;
it exists neither in the quarters of space, nor outside, nor within—it is not found anywhere at all.
Since this saṃsāra is, like a dream or a magical illusion, merely the wonder of the unperceived Consciousness, it does not exist outside of Consciousness; thus he says: "Consciousness" (cid). || 8 ||
By the mere unfolding of its volition, the variegated world is perceived; yet upon the non-unfolding of that [volition], it dissolves like a painting on the mind of the painter.

He establishes that it is merely a flash of wonder (*ciccamatkāra*)—with the words "saṃkalpa" (conceptualization) and so forth. It is like a painting imagined in the mind of a painter (*citrakṛt*). || 9 ||
There is a pavilion with great pillars, fashioned from pearls and gems,
extending for many hundreds of thousands of yojanas and adorned with beautiful gold.

In order to strengthen the notion that the world is mere volition (*saṃkalpamātratā*), he imagines it to have the form of a pavilion for gambling with volitions, beginning with the words "the pavilion" (*maṇḍapa*) and so forth. || 10 ||
It was surrounded in front by a thousand jeweled pillars reaching up to Mount Meru,
and it was as beautiful as the clouds at the twilight of the kalpa, enriched with a thousand rainbows.
It was surrounded by a thousand jeweled pillars, each topped with a guggulu resin finial pointing downward like Mount Meru;
thus, it appeared in some places as if enriched by a thousand rainbows, and in others like the clouds at the twilight of the kalpa—
exceedingly beautiful amidst the women, children, men, and others of the residents moving here and there.
Where they were established for the sake of play amidst various artistic arrangements.

In that pavilion, for the sake of the amusement of the inhabitants—women, children, men, and others—there were placed here and there caskets and boxes shaped like various other worlds, such as the subterranean realms (pātāla) and the heavens (svarga).
Of what nature were they? Within them, by means of various arrangements of rivers, mountains, forests, elephants, horses, gods, animals, humans, and so forth.
They are joined. || 12 ||
Filled with the seeds of past beings and resounding with the humming of the enemies of darkness,
these are called the variegated manifestations of light and dark, acting as caskets for the transition between worlds.

The worlds are filled with living beings characterized by their respective seeds and the objects of their enjoyment; they are resonant with noise due to the activity of worldly affairs, which proceeds by means of the enemies of darkness—the slayers thereof—such as jewels, lamps, the sun, and the moon; and they possess various names and reputations because they are variegated by darkness in some places and by light in others. 13.

Fragrant with the scent of musk, their sprouts being the rows of moving clouds, the pleasure-lotus-pools of the women have had their wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpapādapa*) cut down. (14) [The reading *vilūnāḥ kalpapādapāḥ* is to be considered.]

In that pavilion, which was a source of the playful Lakṣmī (Līlāpadmā), trees were fashioned such that their ornaments— ear-pendants and other decorations— had been plucked and gathered for the adornment of women. || 14 ||
The great boundary mountains were balls set in motion by the breath of his tail;
the evening clouds were his ear-ornaments, and the autumn clouds were his fly-whisks.

They are so extremely light that they are moved even by the breath of children; such are the great mountain ranges (kulācala) which, for all practical purposes, have been turned into play-balls for children. The evening clouds have been made into ear-ornaments for the women of the quarters, and the autumnal clouds have been made into fly-whisks in their hands. || 15 ||
The clouds at the end of the eon have become the palm-leaf fans;
the surface of the earth has become the gaming board; and the starry sky has become the canopy. (16)
In that pavilion, the entire surface of the ground was made into a gaming board, and the sky, filled with stars,
was made into a canopy.
In the gambling match where the elements were the dice-sticks and the moon and sun were the dice,
the sky was the playing field for those dwelling in their homes, with the illumination of the world as the stake.

In that pavilion characterized by the sky, in the courtyard— the square where the very perception of the manifestation and disappearance of the worlds constitutes the stake in the game played by the inhabitants of the house, the lords of the pavilion, Brahmā and the others,
there [were] the pieces upon the chessboard, consisting of the essence of beings, the fourfold classes of living creatures.
In that game of dice characterized by wandering through repeated birth, death, and so forth, the nine planets, such as the Moon and the Sun, were made into the dice. || 17 ||
Thus, by long-term cultivation, mere mental resolve within the mind comes to attain, as it were, the status of reality, through its resemblance to the object perceived before one's eyes. (18)

Just as the mere mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*) of one who conceives that "there is such a pavilion" attains a semblance of reality through the analogy of an object perceived before one's eyes, so too does this pavilion in the form of the world, perfectly arisen through the volitions of the Creator (*dhātṛ*); such is the connection with what follows. || 18 ||
In the very same way, this world-form has arisen from volitions;
its essence consists solely of the wonder of consciousness, like a painting created by the mind of a painter. (19)
Everything that manifests is indeed unreal; it both exists and does not exist.
This world has arisen from the non-existent, as if having emerged from somewhere unknown.
It exists as a manifestation but does not exist from the perspective of ultimate reality; it arises from some cause like an illusory elephant or the like. (20)
Just as bracelets and such are nothing other than gold, so too this hollow interior of saṃsāra is merely the wonder of consciousness, brought to rest through the cessation of conceptualization.
In this hollow belly of saṃsāra, there is only such a wondrous play of consciousness.
Since this is entirely within your own power, do as you wish.
He who has shown disregard for the giving of food and drink—this is his final birth; he shall not abandon his [past] karma.

And thus, since for those who know reality, the manifestation and concealment [of things] through voluntary conceptualizations as well as non-conceptualizations is entirely under their own control, the meaning is: "Do as you wish.
This includes the provision of worldly means of enjoyment such as food and drink, as well as the provision of otherworldly means of enjoyment such as giving and sacrifice.
In both cases, there is a lack of attachment and no intentionality regarding the fruit.
O pure-souled one, you have attained the second stage of discernment, which is holy and sanctifies the three worlds;
I know that you will not fall again into sin with this mind, so abandon this stainless state of silence.

He consoles him—who fears the possibility of rebirth and so forth—by inferring that liberation is necessarily imminent through the very attainment of discernment (*viveka*): "You have attained," etc. O pure-souled one, O one of purified intellect, you have reached the path of discernment—which sanctifies the three worlds—in contrast to the path of non-discernment, which is the cause of falling.

Therefore, by means of this mind, I know—that is, I infer—that you shall not fall downward. For this reason, you should take refuge in the stainless state of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), which is silence devoid of the activities of speech and mind, and thereby [attain] the mind’s liberation.
Thus ends the section on the means to liberation in the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa*, second half, of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by the sage Vālmīki.
The eighth canto, titled "The Description of the Illusory Pavilion of the Vidyādhara."
Thus ends the eighth canto, titled "The Description of the Pavilion of Māyā," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.

1086, Ninth Chapter (9):
Bhuśuṇḍa said:
O sinless one, though you are of the nature of consciousness,
remain as a mass of peaceful consciousness, being unperceiving of objects like the reflection of the sun within pure water.
The manifestation, destruction, existence, appearance, and transformation of the universe are dependent upon consciousness;
here, the universe is described as the play of consciousness and as nothing but pure consciousness.
Just as bracelets and other ornaments are nothing but gold, so too this hollow interior of saṃsāra is merely the wonder of consciousness, in which all conceptualization has utterly ceased.

Having stated this, and wishing to demonstrate both points, he first teaches the method of non-conceptualization with the words "not perceiving. One who does not perceive— that is, one who, due to the sublation of the mind that performs the conceptualization of distinctions, does not perceive the object of thought (*cetya*) along with its actions, qualities, defects, and so forth, nor even the luminous nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*) which manifests them— is like one who has entered pure water.

Like the rays of the sun, remain with your heat subsided and nothing but pure luminosity remaining; the meaning is that even this state of the cosmic age (*kalpasthiti*) is the cause for the destruction of the conceptual constructions of the world. || 1 ||
The insentient exists within the sentient solely because of sentience;
even though it lacks similarity to its own source, it appears similar, just as fires exist within the ocean.

He demonstrates with reasoning, starting with the words "the insentient," that this very hollow interior of *saṃsāra* is nothing but the wonder of consciousness (*ciccamatkāra*). The insentient object of perception (*dṛśya*), although it possesses its own dissimilarity from consciousness—characterized by dullness, suffering, transformation, and so forth—nevertheless exists within consciousness itself, and nowhere else. Why is that? Precisely because of consciousness. Not otherwise.

For that which exists elsewhere cannot be perceived by a consciousness that is not connected to it; and nothing is established that is not being perceived. Nor is consciousness active in such a way that it could go and perceive. If it were all-pervading, then the thesis is already proven—this is the meaning. || 2 ||
The cause of both the conscious and the unconscious is likewise consciousness because it possesses consciousness, just as wind is the cause of both the extinction and the arising of a flame. (3)

Having thus established that all objects of perception exist within consciousness from the perspective of space (*deśataḥ*), he now indicates that they exist there from the perspective of time (*kālataḥ*) as well, thereby proving they are effects of consciousness—beginning with the words "sacetanā" (conscious). [This is a statement of the resultant meaning of the passage beginning with "the consciousness in the root-text"]. "Sacetanā" refers to those things which are the objects of the mental modification of "I-ness" (*ahaṃ-vṛtti*). "Acetanā" [refers to those which are not].

These are the objects of the notion of "this-ness. Likewise, as before, the cause is the illusory material substrate (*vivartopādāna*). The sense is that the very fact of consciousness undergoing illusory transformation is the wonder (*camatkāra*) of consciousness itself. || 3 ||
"I do not exist"—let this be your rest within consciousness, which is the very nature of consciousness. Therefore, remain as you are, exactly as you are.

In this regard, he says that by the very exclusion of the conscious portion [of the ego] through the negation of "I," the negation of both [subject and object] is established, resulting in the realization of abiding in pure consciousness:

"By the very destruction of the cause of conceptualization, let there be rest in this full Consciousness free from conceptualization"—this is the meaning. Thus, by you who have thus attained rest, then, after the exhaustion of the remainder of *prārabdha* karma... (4)
In the form of consciousness, you abide both within and without all things,
just as water exists both within and without a mass of clear water.

He says with two verses beginning with "cidrūpa" that, just as when water is removed from milk pervading it, only the milk remains, so too for You, only the incomparable form of Brahman remains. || 5 ||
O dear one, if the form of consciousness, which is "I do not exist," is fixed within consciousness itself,
and no other object is perceived, with what can that nature of Brahman be compared?
If Brahman, whose nature is immediate consciousness, becomes merged in consciousness and attains indivisible unity; || 6 ||
It was as if inhabited by the world of the gods, the asuras, the netherworld, and the earth;
it was as if agitated by various states of being, motion, stillness, activity, and time.
Just as the netherworld, the earth, and the heavens exist together with the gods and demons, this stage—

though crowded and filled with various states such as joy, delight, anger, battle, victory, and defeat, and with the swift movements of fleeing and pursuing— is like the very embodiment of time itself, manifesting through those corresponding actions.
The world is like a painting on a wall, remaining silent and devoid of activity, existing as the very nature of the wall;

likewise, the world, though composed of the variegated painting of the illusory intellect (*māyā-śabala-cit*), exists within the wall characterized by the space of pure consciousness (*śuddha-cid-ākāśa*) as that very self which is changeless and non-dual, and not as the world itself—this is the meaning. || 7 ||
Just as a painting on a wall appears as if it were silent,
so too is the world, painted upon the canvas of consciousness, situated within the void-wall of the Self.
That which is the mind, manifested from itself as manifold, exists as that very thing—whether insentient or sentient; do with it as you wish.

Whether it be the insentient form of the unreal world, or the sentient form of the Brahman that is ultimately real—whatever has manifested by itself, through its own inherent nature within consciousness, by that alone does it persist. Thus, since both states are under your own control, whether through the state of emergence or through meditative absorption (samādhi), do exactly what you desire; this is the meaning. || 9 ||
