These wonders of consciousness flash forth in the void as this world; like the rays of the sun, they do not obstruct [the vision] of those who have realized what is to be known, for they are transparent. (10)
This, however, is the distinction between those who know reality and the ignorant: just as in a desert, the rays of the sun, appearing in the form of a great river,
act as a barrier on this side of the bank for the ignorant— because they generate fear of drowning and death and because no means of crossing is seen— yet they do not [act as a barrier] for others.

The meaning is that for those who know the reality of the desert (*marubhūmi*), just as by a single cognition they truly know everything, so too for those who have known what is to be known—the knowers of reality—the wondrous manifestations of consciousness (*ciccamatkṛti*) appearing as the world-form are likewise unceasing.
And this has been established in detail in the *Līlopākhyāna*. 10.
Just as for those whose vision is overcome by cataracts, a mass of hair and other such things appear in the sky,
so too does the form of the world appear to those who abide in what is not the Self.

With the intention that [these teachings] are indeed the destroyers of ignorance for those who are ignorant, he says: "Timira... [and so on]. This refers to those ignorant ones who remain within the non-self, which is transmigratory existence itself. || 11 ||
Thus, that which consists of the awareness of "the world," "you," and "I" has arisen as a mere appearance, neither truly arisen nor unarisen;
it is like a city formed by the lattice of the sun's rays—here, walls and such exist as real, yet not in the sky like a creeper.
He concludes by describing the analogy "like the rays of the sun" in another way: "Thus...
It is merely an appearance, described as the mere wonder of consciousness; therefore, it is said to have arisen from the perspective of the ignorant, but not from the perspective of reality.
The two "ca"s (and) serve to include and exclude other modifications. The arrangement is produced by the very network of the sun's rays.

That whose manifestation is of such a kind as a city of Gandharvas—this world of walls and so forth on the plane of conventional experience—is like that [city] and does not truly exist in the sky, just like a creeper. Therefore, because it does not obstruct consciousness, the indivisibility of consciousness is established; this is the meaning. || 12 ||

Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Yoga of Consciousness-Shining," in the Nirvāṇa Section of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, within the *Dehātmabodha* (The Means to Liberation).

Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Yoga of the Shining-forth of Consciousness," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The Tenth Chapter.
Bhuśuṇḍa said:
Know that from consciousness alone arises both consciousness and that which is other than consciousness.
Just as fire [is not distinct] from water, consciousness is not even slightly different from insentience. || 1 ||
It is described that Brahman, which exists as it truly is, changeless and without cause,
never existed as the world anywhere at any time.

In order to establish the negation of the world within Brahman, [the author] makes manifest the conscious nature of that which is considered inert, so as to negate its inertia— beginning with the words "Know" (viddhi) and so forth. O Vidyādhara, know that the consciousness— the radiance— of the world, which is considered to be other than consciousness, arises from Consciousness alone.

For consciousness consists precisely in the nature of manifestation. If the world-form manifests, then it is indeed consciousness and nothing other than consciousness. Just as fire reflected in water is not a separate entity from the water, there is no insentience apart from consciousness;
just as the heat of the reflected fire is not distinct from the water's coldness, so too there is no dullness apart from consciousness.
The meaning is that there is nothing else besides name. || 1 ||
Since there is no difference between that [object] and the experience of it, remain established in your natural state—
unconstrained, like the cognition of a figure in a painting, or like the center of space.

He says "That" (tad), meaning: "Remain undistracted by the mere denial of insentience itself, since the denial of the world is thereby established"—that is, in such a way that it is free from restriction (*yantra*), which means limitation (*pariccheda*).
It is like the cognition of that [world] residing in the mental picture created by an artist, or like the space situated within an illusory city of the Gandharvas. || 2 ||
Likewise, due to the fact that all powers reside within Brahman, non-consciousness exists [within it],
just as a future fragment of foam exists within undisturbed, pure water.

However, as for those scriptural and traditional statements which maintain that even during dissolution the insentient world exists in a subtle form within Brahman, they do so with the intention that—because the Māyā-qualified Brahman possesses all powers—the existence of the world is asserted by way of superimposing the reality of Brahman even upon what is non-existent, just as one speaks of the "existence" of future foam-bubbles by means of the present existence of the water. Thus he says: "In Brahman... (verse 3).
Just as a fragment of foam does not dispel its cause— the water—
so too the creation and so forth do not dispel their cause, Brahman.

From the perspective of ultimate reality (*vāstava*), however, since *māyā* itself is non-existent, and because neither agitation nor its cause can possibly exist in that which is non-dual and changeless, the very emergence of an insentient creation and so forth is impossible;
thus he says, beginning with "no" (*na*) and so on. || 4 ||
And there is no cause here for this uncaused process of creation;
therefore, nothing whatsoever is born at the beginning of the world, nor does it perish.
Because there is absolutely no cause, the world is not born as anything at all;
like water in a desert, the world does not exist even though it is seen before one's eyes.
Brahman is infinite, unborn, and peaceful; therefore, this notion of creation does not exist.
Due to the absence of any cause, this is indeed the undivided Brahman alone. (7)
Therefore, you resemble a solid stone and yet are like the expanse of space;
because your form is the single, compact mass of Brahman, you are unborn and without parts.
Whether you know something or nothing at all, remain seated, free from doubt;
let the insentient mind subside within the Self by means of the Self in the reflection of consciousness.

It is "something" because it has the nature of the universal existence (*sattāsāmānya*) which follows all things while its specific distinctions remain unascertained. When those specific distinctions are sublated, even the nature of that universal which follows them ceases to exist;

furthermore, because it is ascertained as having a single uniform nature, it is "nothing. Wherein neither consciousness (*cetanā*), nor intellect (*buddhi*), nor the reflection of that [intellect] in pure consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) exists, [that is the state]. 9.
Because it is eternally blissful, the Unborn has no cause and performs no action;
since the creation and so forth are impossible, that which exists is therefore the unborn Śiva.
He states that there is no creation even due to the absence of dependence on a purpose, saying: "by virtue of being eternal bliss. The cause is the motive for action, which is the fruit. || 10 ||

But for those who revel in ignorance, for whom there is no unborn one whose nature is consciousness, what is there to be deliberated upon when the creation and destruction [of the world] have arisen? (11)

Having thus established the proof of eternal liberation through the vision of reality, he says "He is unborn" to show that for the ignorant, if this were not accepted, the consequence would be eternal bondage.
Since the fault of their lack of liberation would never cease, what further deliberation is there? The meaning is that the contemplation of the means to liberation is fruitless for them. || 11 ||
Wherever the Supreme Brahman exists, there indeed are worlds;
and such liberated beings exist in the form of the very meaning of the word "world. (12)
He describes the state [of the yogin] as seen from the perspective of one who is half-awake with the words "wherever... (yatra yatra). || 12 ||
In grass, in wood, in water, in a wall—in every place indeed the Supreme is situated;
and everywhere the flood of creation stands interwoven with one another. (Note: the reading "sthiro" is also found).
It is not appropriate to say what the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of Brahman is,
because in the infinite, supreme reality, the possibility of "belonging to oneself" or "not belonging to oneself" is utterly non-existent.

If it is argued that Brahman must therefore have the nature of a false creation, he says "no"—namely, "of Brahman. For *svabhāva* (intrinsic nature) is one's own state (*sva-bhāva*), that is, a distinguishing attribute; and its status as an attribute must be stated by way of its exclusion of what is not its own nature (*asvabhāva*). However, since in the non-dual Brahman both "own-ness" and "not-own-ness" are absolutely impossible, no other intrinsic nature can be defined.
This is the meaning. || 14 ||
Furthermore, because an entity that depends upon non-existence is impossible,
faulty expressions such as "intrinsic nature" do not find a foothold in the infinite.

Having stated that there is no composition with words denoting its own [negation] in the case of a differentiator (*vyāvartaka*), he also shows the lack of composition with words denoting positive entities (*bhāva*): "abhāva... (verse 15).

Since non-ownership and the absence of existence are absolutely impossible in that which is eternal and infinite, once ownership and existence are established, the expression "intrinsic nature" (svabhāva) no longer holds. (16)

He states that because the objects to be excluded are not established, neither of the two terms can apply there: "asvatva" (non-selfhood). He qualifies [the terms] with "eternal" and "infinite" to preclude the suspicion that they might be established at another time or in another place.
Furthermore, in common worldly usage, there is a description of the nature of things (*svabhāvokti*) regarding selfhoods and entities that are inherently established and non-excluding.
The employment of the word "intrinsic nature" (svabhāva) does not hold; the meaning is that it is unestablished. || 16 ||
O virtuous one, when examined through the light of the intellect, this "I-ness" cannot be found;
being non-existent, it has arisen from somewhere like a yakṣa seen by a child.

Just as creation and so forth are not established in Brahman, and thus non-duality [is proven], so too is "I-ness" and the like not established in the Inner Self (Pratīc); with the intention that through the purification of both, indivisibility is established, he says: "Not I-ness"—for that which is liberated from the meanings of the word 'I-ness' is the Supreme.
But when examined through the meanings of the words "I" and "mine," that which is joined [to them] dissolves. || 18 ||
Being observed through the scriptures, the teacher, and personal experience— just like the true nature of a jewel— and being seen with the vision of reality after having been examined.

The difference between the world and Brahman, and their non-difference, are like the playful manifestation of synonymous words and their meanings; they are said to be mere conceptualization and not real, just as [the difference and identity] exist between a bracelet and gold. (19)

With this perspective, in order to demonstrate that even the distinction between the individual soul and the world—just like insentience and the nature of consciousness—has attained a state of non-difference, he concludes with the intention that the previous examples of the non-difference between gold and its bracelets find their ultimate meaning: "Difference," as in "Rāhu’s head. This refers to the conceptual construction [of such a distinction].
The learned have stated that [the notion of] being a bracelet is merely a conceptual construction accompanied by verbal designation; "bracelet-ness" is simply the form of a bracelet. (19)

Thus ends the tenth canto, titled "The Instruction on the Yoga for Attaining Heaven and Liberation," in the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the glorious Vāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa, the great epic composed by the Sage. 10.
Thus ends the tenth canto, titled "Instruction on the Yoga for Attaining Heaven and Liberation," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa-tātparya-prakāśa*.
The eleventh canto.
Bhuśuṇḍa said:
Weapons, which were once his beloved limbs, remained clinging to his naked body.
He who, while perceiving, remains perfectly equanimous, is established in the supreme state.

It is described here that, through the conquest of the senses, one must firmly establish the mind in an immutable state and strengthen the vision that perceives the body and other objects as mere appearances.

He who remains perfectly equanimous— even while directly experiencing and perceiving weapons stuck to his own body in the open air, uncovered by clothes or other garments, as well as the breasts and limbs of his young beloved— is established in the supreme state.
The meaning is that, until such stability and perfection are achieved, one must firmly establish oneself in the conquest of the senses and in the Self. || 1 ||
One should apply effort through human exertion and fortitude in practice until the state of deep sleep arises with respect to the emergence of objective phenomena.

He states this very point clearly with the words "tāvad" (meanwhile): meanwhile, having rejected the arising of modifications from external objects such as weapons, beautiful women, and so forth, by means of the cognition of their falsity, one remains until that state of deep sleep arises which is characterized by resting solely in the bliss of one's own Self. || 2 ||
Just as waters do not stain even slightly a lotus, so too mental afflictions do not taint one who knows the reality of things as they truly are, even though those afflictions have come before him.
He states that the very definition of the establishment of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) is the absence of mental affliction (*ādhi*), saying "just as" (*yathā*).
The sense is that when mother-of-pearl is sublated, no mental affliction is observed regarding either the acquisition or the loss of the silver. || 3 ||
He who, being of tranquil soul, perceives weapons, women, and celestial realms as if they were not clinging to his limbs— though they are indeed clinging— truly sees.
The mention of "space" is for the sake of illustration; the meaning is that he is to be understood by the definition: "he sees" means "he possesses direct perceptual knowledge. || 4 ||
Just as poison, within its own interior, becomes a scorpion by itself, and this state of being a scorpion is nothing other than the poison itself; so it is here. (5)

The true, immutable nature of this [Self] is not lost by the existence as a living being (jīva) imagined through delusion; therefore, it is indeed logical that its attainment occurs merely through the sublation of that [delusion]. To establish this, he provides an illustration with the words "na ca" (and not): just as poison, though having undergone a transformation such as that of a wood-boring insect (ghuṇa-kīṭa), does not deviate from its own poisonous nature, and thus the state of being a wood-boring insect is not something other than the poison itself, so it is not [in the case of the Self].

Even though the Self is Brahman, it presides over the state of being a living soul (*jīvatā*)—which is a transformation (*vivarta*) into the form of a living soul and is sublated solely by the thorough knowledge of its own true nature; thus, one should understand that the state of being a living soul is nothing other than this. || 5 ||
Thus, without abandoning its own essential nature, it presides over living beings;
likewise, the Self [presides] over that [world], which is dissolved solely through the realization of it.

The individual soul (jīva) becomes difficult to discern, as if its very nature were subject to death [the lengthening of the vowel is an archaic Vedic usage]. Just so, without abandoning its own form, it attains a form that is both conscious and inert.

The meaning is that there is an illustrative example even regarding the aspect of contrariety: just as inert poison, which has the very nature of not dying, becomes the life of an insect whose nature is death without ever abandoning its own nature, so too does the consciousness of Brahman attain an inert form whose nature is death. || 7 ||
Though non-different from Brahman, he appeared as if different; though devoid of sound, a certain resonance arose within him.
Abiding in that very [Brahman], he remained as if not abiding there, appearing as the creator of the universe.
He says that even this world has arisen from the individual soul (jīva) like a [woodworm] burrow, in the verse beginning with "In Brahman" (brahmaṇi). || 8 ||
Just as a worm within poison does not gradually abandon its poisonous nature, so too [the self] is neither born nor does it die; yet even when it dies, it is born again.
Just as birth and death do not exist in a worm when viewed from the perspective of its poisonous nature, yet they do exist when viewed from the perspective of its embodied nature,

so too, he says in two verses beginning with "Poison," that birth and death do not exist in the individual soul (*jīva*) when viewed from the perspective of its Brahman-nature, yet they do exist when viewed from the perspective of its individual-soul nature.
By the very object of one's own consciousness, which has submerged its form within the meaning of the word, the ocean of existence is crossed like a cow’s footprint; it is not crossed by fate.

One who has not been submerged by attachment to the notions of "I" and "mine" regarding the body, senses, and objects, and whose true nature remains unobscured, crosses over by means of one's own self—by that very self which has as its purpose the realization of the Self accomplished through efforts such as hearing (śravaṇa) and so forth;
the meaning is that one does not cross by neglecting effort with the thought, "God will save me. || 10 ||
In that state which abides within all things, which transcends all states of being, and wherein there is inner coolness—what possible offense could there be against it? (11)

He wards off the potential neglect— that there can be no possibility of rest in that which is the solitary nature of the Self, remaining as a mere residue after the sublation of all objects of perception, and being utterly destitute— by saying "sarva" (all):
the internal state consisting of the essence of bliss of all things most dear to one is a creeper of inner coolness through the cessation of all feverish distress.
In that which is the nature of the full self. || 11 ||

When the existence of all objects in the world has been quickly contemplated in their general nature, what stain can there be for the pure Self, which is beyond mind, ego, intellect, and the rest? (12)

He states the means for the removal of the soul's stains, such as the mind and ego, with the verse beginning "The world": [the world] in its general form as Brahman, which is pure existence alone. || 12 ||
Just as you perceive objects such as pots and cloths, so too, O friend, perceive this body, as well as the "I-ness," the mind, the intellect, and the sensations. (13)

Just as you perceive objects such as pots and cloths from a detached standpoint, so first perceive the body from a detached standpoint, not with the conceit of "I-ness" and so forth; this is the meaning. || 13 ||

The entire flood of the world’s objects, as well as the mind, intellect, and so forth, are established within the Knower alone; therefore, remain as one free from objective consciousness, grounded in perfect steadfastness.

Immediately thereafter, O Knower, remaining as the witness of all, do not perceive the flood of external objects in the world nor the internal mind, intellect, and so forth; established in the state of pure consciousness alone, abide in your natural condition through perfected steadfastness. 14.
No one ever possesses any fault whatsoever, nor is there ever any quality here;
by means of pleasure or pain, or by existence or non-existence, there is neither an enjoyer nor any agency.
He says, "By nothing whatsoever," to show that in that state there is the accomplishment of the cessation of all distractions caused by virtues, defects, and so forth.

In that state, due to existence or non-existence, prosperity or adversity, or the pleasure and pain resulting from them—by no cause whatsoever and at no time for anyone—is there either defect or virtue. Since agency does not exist, therefore there is no enjoyer.

And [that duality] does not exist; for the meaning of such scriptural passages as, "But when for him everything has become the Self alone, then by what and whom should one see? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.14). || 15 ||

Thus ends the eleventh canto, titled "The Knowledge of Things as They Truly Are," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the Vāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa, a scripture of the Ṛṣis, within the section on Liberation (Mokṣopāya). || 11 ||

Thus ends the eleventh canto, titled "The Knowledge of Things as They Truly Are," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the illustrious Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa, within the Tātparya-prakāśa. || 11 ||
The Twelfth Chapter.
Bhuśuṇḍa said:
Just as there is the conceptualization that "the sky itself has become the firmament," [so it is with this].
The cultivation of the sense of "I" is likewise merely an illusion, having the nature of unreality. || 1 ||
The sense of "I" is mere delusion; the world-illusion is a transformation of consciousness.
Its root is ignorance (avidyā), and the sequence for its destruction is now set forth.

In order to establish the simultaneous eradication [of all duality] according to the sequence to be described, he demonstrates—through the passage beginning with "in the sky itself" (*kha eva*)—the unity of all conceptual constructions as being merely transformations of consciousness (*cid-vivarta-mātra*). He shows that it is precisely ignorance (*avidyā*) that exists in the form of the subtle world-process characterized by the sense of "I" (*ahaṃbhāva*), and that this very same [ignorance] takes on the form of the gross world-process. Just as in the sky...

Just as the mental conception that "another sky has arisen, produced within the very sky" is merely the delusion of duality regarding a single sky, so too, when the Self is unknown, the cultivation of the sense of "I"—which consists of the subtle phenomenal world—is a mere mental construction; such is the meaning. || 1 ||
Just as I am the one who imagines through delusion that "space has been produced," so too does the ineffable Self exist, though it is spread out as if it were non-existent.
But surely, in the illustration, there is a third person who is the imaginer; who then is that third? To this he says: "In the sky, the sky.

Because it is concealed by ignorance, the nature of the Self—which is indefinable, spread out as if non-existent, and for that very reason not accessible through words and the like—exists as a real entity; this is the meaning: the third [element] is the imaginer. || 2 ||
In the void, there exists only the Self, whose nature is consciousness; it perceives its own form as that which shines forth as "this-ness," yet it is neither "I" nor "not-I."

In the illustration, just as in the sky there exists only the non-dual sky-nature, whereas a second sky is merely the form of the body consisting of one's own volition— delimited by the volition of the *kalpaka-puruṣa* (the creator of the world)— and is perceived only after having been so imagined;
likewise, because the conscious Self, conditioned by ignorance, [imagines] its own...
The body itself, having conceptualized ignorance as the nature of the conceiving subject and the conceived object through the notion "I am this," appears;
therefore, there is no such thing as "I" other than ignorance, nor is there any form of the manifold world (prapañca) that is not of the nature of "non-I"—this is the meaning. || 3 ||
Therefore, there exists such a nature of consciousness wherein even the gross ether is fully contained within the atom, like Mount Meru; for that consciousness has indeed consumed the void.
For this very reason, he states that Brahman—which is supremely subtle and the substratum for the conceptualization of all gross things—exists as something to be discerned:
"From that [consciousness] arises the dense appearance of the insentient (acidābhāsa), which is even more minute than space;
that whose nature it knows exists as this creation. (Verse 5)
He establishes what has been stated regarding its supreme subtlety with the word "dense" (*ghana*).

The reflection of consciousness (*acid-ābhāsa*), characterized by ignorance (*ajñāna*) and an beginningless manifestation (*anādi-vivarta*), is even more subtle than the ether (*khāt*); yet, in comparison to the Self-consciousness (*ātma-citi*), it is "dense," meaning gross. Such is that which is supremely subtle.

Consciousness, through the beginningless latent impression (*vāsanā*) of the forms of "I" and "this," cognizes by means of the successive conceptualization of gross natures; this very [consciousness] is what is established as the manifestation of creation—this is the meaning. || 5 ||
For the knower of the Self, whose nature is tasted as "I-ness," the expansion of the world is like the spreading of the fluidity of water, such as its swirling into eddies and the like.

For the knower of the Self, the expansion of the consciousness of the Self—consisting of the internal "I-ness" (mahantā) and so forth, and externally the five elements such as space—is the emanation, the unfolding, and the manifestation of the world. || 6 ||
The expansion of the insentient is stilled, like water that has ceased to flow;
it takes on the form of windless air, resembling the heart of space.
The absence of the expansion of consciousness is the non-expansion of the insentient; it is the tranquil cessation of the world, that is to say, dissolution (pralaya). || 7 ||
And it is not possible [to perceive] within the expansions of the world such as space and time,
except for the emanation of pure consciousness, which is dense yet empty and devoid of appearance.

Thus, even regarding the expansions of the world—characterized by thousands of intermediate effects such as place, time, and so forth—which have been established in this way, no ultimate reality other than the expansion of pure consciousness (cinmātra) is logical or tenable. || 8 ||
When pure consciousness alone has expanded—whether in time, or according to the reading "in wood," or in space, on a boat, in water, or on land;
whether in sleep, in waking, or in dreaming—the world appears as if arisen.

He demonstrates the occurrence [of this state] therein with the words "in pure consciousness alone" (cinmātre). This refers to deep sleep, to well-known dreaming, to the waking state, and to dreams such as those of mental construction (manorājya) and the like. || 9 ||
For consciousness, neither expansion nor non-expansion is possible, because it is eternally more transparent than even space, and because it is unshakeable and so forth. || 10 ||
One might ask: why could it not be that consciousness itself is a real expansion characterized by transformation into the form of the world?
To this he replies with the word "prasaraṇa" (expansion). The meaning is that [consciousness] is devoid of all modifications, such as agitation (*kṣobha*) or movement (*saṃcalana*). || 10 ||
The Knower does not perceive objects of enjoyment and the like, nor does he conceive "I" within himself;
rather, established in the Supreme as non-dual, he exists like fluidity within water.

[Objection: "But surely modifications—consisting of the experience of the enjoyment of pleasure and pain, as well as the sense of 'I' with respect to the body and so forth—are observed in the conscious self (cidātman). To this, he says: "The Knower" (jña). [This refers to] the Supreme, whose nature is immutable (kūṭasthasvabhāva). Thus, the meaning is that the delusions of enjoyment and so forth belong only to the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa), and not to the immutable Self. || 11 ||

One who is free from conceptual construction does not perceive the group of qualities such as intelligence, modesty, prosperity, fear, mindfulness, fame, and splendor, just as one does not see the footprints of a snake in the darkness.

Regarding the point stated, he says "dhīḥ" (intellect) to show that the evidence for this matter is the observation of the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) with mental functions such as volition (*saṃkalpa*).
"Śrī" is a mental function consisting of reflection; "śrī" [in the sense of prosperity] is a mental function consisting of joy characterized by the conceit of wealth;
"kīrti" is a similar function produced by hearing the renown of one's own virtues; and "kānti" is desire. This applies to all cases.
By means of words that indicate mental modifications, their causes—the external objects—are indicated by implication. || 12 ||
The flow of the nectar-drops from the lunar rays of consciousness, shimmering within the orb of Brahma, is the creation;
because of the non-existence of space and time, this creation does not exceed the Lord.
The moon-disk is characterized by Brahman; from it flashes forth the moonlight characterized by the reflection of the individual consciousness (*jīvacidābhāsa*).

Since the nectar—which consists of cognitions such as visual perception—is dependent on a portion of that [moonlight], the creation, which is essentially composed of that [nectar], is not distinct from the Lord-Brahman. Why? Because space and time, which serve as its substrates, are partless and inactive.
Because it is impossible for [space] to exist within Brahman. For the time of creation could only be conceived through the movement of a material substance in a specific direction;

yet that direction does not exist prior [to creation]. This being the case, the production of space and so forth would have to be conceived as occurring at that time; yet it does not exist during the dissolution (pralaya), because there is no means of establishing it other than motion. Furthermore, motion is incompatible with that which is complete and immutable (kūṭastha). Nor can those two [space and time] exist while being non-existent.
The meaning is that since there is no room for anything else, there is no establishment of anything distinct from Brahman. || 13 ||
Thus, through the pride of self-identification, the mind— which is the primordial nature of the world— vibrates as a radiant manifestation within the Other, like a multitude of whirlpools in water.

When the Supreme Lord alone, in the manner described, manifests as the world non-different from Himself— shining forth as the universal essence of Being-Consciousness-Bliss (saccidānanda)— then, due to a particular misconception regarding the body and so forth, and by imagining things favorable or unfavorable to that [Self] as objects to be rejected or accepted, the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), consisting of the mind (*ādhimānya*), appears as if it were something other [than the Self].

The meaning is that all this—consisting of the conceptualization of the bondage and liberation of the living beings of the entire world—is merely the deluded mind itself, imagined like a whirlpool in water; there is not even an atom's worth of anything else. || 14 ||
With the sounds of plunging and emerging, and through the movements of turning, eddying, and swirling,
the river of creation appears to have long since been exhausted, yet it flows on without interruption.

He establishes the identity between the illustration and the illustrated by means of a metaphor—using the word "majjana" (immersion). Immediately thereafter, through the direct realization of reality (*tattva-sākṣātkāra*), the mirage-river characterized by creation is exhausted. || 15 ||
Just as water appears with whirlpools and smoke appears like a cloud, so too does this third creation exist between these two due to its insentient nature. (16)

Just as from a distance a mass of smoke appears like a dense cloud or a thick mist, so too this third creation—between these two, Brahman and the mind—appears as an object; that is to say, it appears as having an insentient nature through its manifestation as something real, and yet as having a non-insentient nature [in its essence]. This is the implied meaning.
Just as the grain, swirls, and so forth appear in wood when it is cut by a saw, so too does this creation—
consisting of both that which possesses the nature of the Supreme and that which does not— arise within the Supreme when He is not perceived.
It possesses both that form and its opposite; it possesses both the nature of the insentient and the sentient. || 17 ||
Apart from the sprout of volition, one finds no difference whatsoever between the plantain trunk of saṃsāra and a stone, even though the former is soft while the latter is hard. (18)

Because it is false by its very nature, even though it is soft, it does not possess even the slightest difference from a hard, solid stone— such as a crystal slab reflecting the trunk of a banana tree— when viewed with the eye of discernment; the distinction exists only due to the difference between the leaf created by one's imagination and the actual stone.
The meaning is that dissimilarity is nothing other than this. || 18 ||
It possesses a thousand hooves, heads, eyes, hands, and mouths;
it extends its various mountain-like bodies through every direction and region, measuring only a span across rivers.
Now he describes [the world] through its resemblance to a kingdom depicted in a painting on a canvas, with the four verses beginning with "Sahasra":

[the world] wherein his thousandfold activities—beginning from his hands and ending with his face—and his intentions (tadīhitāni) as well as his gestures (tadiṅgitāni) were inferred (ūhitāni) and conjectured;
wherein various mountains, bodies (tanavaḥ)—meaning the four kinds of physical forms—the quarters, regions, and rivers appeared as if they were merely the span of a finger (prādeśamātram).
Where [the object] is delimited. || 19 ||
Empty within and devoid of essence, it is stained by manifold passions; it is merely threatened by the cleansing brought about by manifest dispassion.

It is empty within, being devoid of internal parts; it is colored by many passions, desires, and dyeing substances. Dispassion (*virāga*) is detachment, a contrary color, and a cleansing agent; it is merely the act of cleansing prescribed for it, whose threat is the absence of expectation. 20.
[It pervades] the world including the gods, asuras, gandharvas, vidyādharas, and mahoragas;
it is stirred by the wind from inert matter, and it is perceived by the consciousness of others. 21.

It is characterized by motion through the inert wind, the thread-soul (sūtrātman), and the well-known vital air; it is perceived by the supreme Brahman-consciousness and the witnessing consciousness. 21.
The world, beautiful and radiant like a magnificent kingdom depicted in a painting on a cloth, is charming yet unable to withstand scrutiny; it is a mere manifestation of conceptual construction.
Apprehension is deliberation; it is an apprehension by means of another, and its non-tolerance is suppression. (22)
Falling into the aspect of conceptualization, which is unreal in nature yet possesses the essence of vibration, consciousness spreads through delusion like a drop of oil upon water. (23)

In the portion consisting of conceptualization—that is, in the mental activity of conceptual thought—they have fallen as reflections within the mind, which, being devoid of objective reality and subject to sublation, possesses an unreal form. || 23 ||
Through the spreading webs of heart-streaks that revolve in every whirlpool, and through the chewing of the dullness arising from the mixture of spreading affection; || 24 ||

He explains how that [mind] spreads: "Hṛllekhā," etc. Those which write upon—that is, agitate—the heart (the mind) are the *hṛllekhās*, namely the latent impressions (*vāsanās*) of desire. It is bound by the expansions—that is, the multitudes—of the net characterized by those [impressions].
It is mixed with the affection spreading toward children, wives, and so forth; thus it is inert due to its falsity and lack of awakening.

The meaning is that those objects such as sound, touch, and so forth are indeed unarisen; through their "chewing" or relishings, that very [consciousness] expands, which is described as the wondrous great kingdom—this is the nature of saṃsāra. || 24 ||
When [the consciousness] becomes oriented toward the form of "I" and so forth through conceptual construction,
it is not distinct from the Supreme, just as the nature of water is not distinct from water itself.

In this manner, although this primordial consciousness— turned outward by the conceptualization of "I" and having seemingly assumed the state of a living individual (jīva)— is not distinct from the Supreme Self, the meaning is that since the limiting adjuncts (upādhis) that create difference are mere conceptual constructs, the two terms "individual soul" (jīva) and "Supreme" (para) ultimately converge upon a single referent, just as the words "water" and "liquid" do. || 25 ||
The sun of consciousness, which is one’s very own self, is designated as "creation.
Having become [the ego] through the thought "I am," there is no other; indeed, neither creation exists nor a creator. (26)

He states that when the individual soul (*jīva*), which is the referent of "I" and the transformer of name and form through the entry of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), is realized as being nothing but Brahman, then even the meaning of the word "creation"—which is the object of its enjoyment—becomes Brahman alone; thus he says: "The Sun of Consciousness. (26)

Just as vibration exists within the essence of existence, like the fluidity of water, so too the conscious self, within its state of being space, does not perceive itself as "space-ness" and so forth. 27.

He establishes, by means of an illustration, that the world—like the head of Rāhu—is ultimately nothing but a mental construction of consciousness and nothing but ignorance: "In that which consists of vibration," etc. Let this be investigated: when it is said that "the water vibrates," does the water itself exist in the form of vibration, or is it something else? It cannot be the second case, because nothing else is perceived. [If it were] something else...
For if it were said that "it vibrates," there would follow the undesirable consequence that vibration lacks a necessary dependence upon water.

Nor can that necessity be established through inherence (*samavāya*), because inherence itself is unproven due to the infinite regress of relations. In the first alternative, however, it is untenable for water to be the agent of vibration; for that which is of the nature of vibration does not perform vibration, lest vibration itself become an agent.

Therefore, just as the fluidity of water is non-vibration within its own nature which consists of vibration, so the notion of vibration is a mere conceptual construction; likewise, although the conscious self (cidātman) creates the manifold world of space and so forth, it does not abide in the state of being space, nor is it the maker of space.
Thus, it is incapable of experiencing the state of being space, either for itself or for anything else.
The meaning is that it is merely a conceptual construction (*vikalpamātra*), just like the conceptual distinctions regarding the states of water as liquid or solid. || 27 ||
The experience of the Knower, preceded by the manifestation of space, time, and so forth, consists of creation;
therefore, its similarity to water and fluidity is not far-fetched. (28)

[Objection: Is it not the case that in the conceptualization of the distinction between the fluidity of water [in different instances], the distinction of space and time is the regulating factor? Water situated in a previous time and place is perceived at a later time and in another place. Since reaching another place in the case of arrows and the like is established as being preceded by action, a distinction in the action of flowing is likewise postulated for water. However, in the non-dual Brahman, there is no distinction of space or time; therefore [the objection does not apply].

He resolves the doubt that the analogy of water and clouds—which posits a causal basis for the conceptual differentiation of ether and so forth—is far-fetched—by stating "deśa" (space). Is this impossibility of the conceptual construction of the creation of ether and so forth being raised during the state of being the creation itself, or during the state of Brahman? In the second case, it is an admission of what we already accept; for we do not [assert the existence of such differentiation] in that state.

We admit some degree of conceptual differentiation (*vikalpa*) within the state of Brahman; however, during the phase consisting of emanation (*sarga*), we construct—through imagination—the division of time such as "this is the time of emanation" and "previously it was the time of dissolution," as well as the distinction between the regions of *saṃsāra* and non-*saṃsāra*.

Within that [constructed framework], we describe the experience by the conscious self (*cidātman*) of conceptualizations such as space (*viyat*) and so forth. Thus, there is no similarity with water and its fluidity.
The meaning is "going far. And so it has been stated in the Vārttika: "One imagines that 'ignorance exists' only while remaining within ignorance itself;
however, from the perspective of Brahman, this ignorance is in no way tenable. (28)
Know that whatever perception there is—such as the mind, the sense of "I," or the intellect—is ignorance; it is destroyed quickly through diligent human effort.

Even for the manifestation of space and time, there would be an infinite regress because it too would depend upon another space and time. Likewise, since conceptual constructions (vikalpas) are accomplished by the mind, the sense of "I" (ahaṃbhāva), the intellect (buddhi), and so forth, and since these are unestablished at the time of the conceptual construction of the various creations such as space and the rest, how could there be conceptualization? Such doubts and others are merely vessels for thousands of defects, such as logical inconsistency.
With the intention that [the objection] must be refuted precisely because [the world] is admitted to be mere consciousness (*vidyāmātra*), he says: "The mind" (verse 29).
Half [of the purification] comes from mutual conversation, a portion from investigations into the scriptures, and the remainder from self-realization; thus ignorance is brought to an end.
He explains by what specific human efforts and to what extent that [ignorance] is destroyed: "Half," etc.

Through conversation with those who know reality—who have been won over by discipline, prostration, giving, and honorable treatment—one practices until reaching the establishment of the first stage; then, through intense dispassion and so forth—

The meaning is that it perishes. Through the investigation of the scriptures by means of hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth, the fourth part of ignorance— consisting of the power of projection (*vikṣepa-śakti*), which takes the form of doubt regarding the validity of the means of knowledge and their objects, as well as the form of egoism (*ahaṃtā*) toward the body and other such things— is destroyed by the realization of the Self (*ātma-pratyaya*).

The meaning is that, through the direct realization of the self as Brahman— which begins from the fourth stage and increases further and further— the remaining fourth part, consisting of the power of obscuration, gradually ceases, just like darkness after the rising of the dawn.
When the fourfold division has been made through the gradual destruction of ignorance, that which remains simultaneously is the reality of the object, free from names. (31)

Thus, when the destruction of ignorance has been accomplished through the gradual process occurring simultaneously with the practice of the stages previously shown, that which remains—devoid of name and form and consisting of pure Being alone—is the supreme human goal; this is the meaning. || 31 ||

Śrī Rāma said: One part [of the fruit] comes from mutual conversation, another part from the investigation of the scriptures, and another part from self-realization; how then can that [fruit] be averted? (32)
Rāma, desiring to know what was stated in brief, asks for it in detail, beginning with the words "half," and so forth. || 32 ||
O Lord of Munis, what is it that is said to occur simultaneously and in succession?
Tell me: how can that which is non-existent be called "existent," and how can it be called both "existent" and "non-existent"? (33)

In the phrase "consisting of the reality of the non-apparent" (*anāmārthasat-mayam*), the suffix *mayaṭ* includes even the unreal portion; thus it is said to be both real and unreal. In that context, the meaning of "like that" (*tadvat*) refers to the unreal portion. || 33 ||

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: One who desires to cross over the cycle of worldly existence should deliberate upon the nature of saṃsāra together with a virtuous person who is dispassionate and with those who possess knowledge of the Self.

In response to the sequence of questions, Vasiṣṭha says: "With a good person," and so forth. Together with one who knows the Self—and by the use of the words *ca* (and) and *api* (also)—with another seeker of liberation as well, and by means of one's own intellect, one should investigate this transmigratory existence (*saṃsṛti*): what is it? What is its ultimate end? What is its root? What is its essence? And how is it to be crossed over? || 34 ||
Therefore, having sought out from wherever possible a person who is free from passion and envy, a virtuous man who knows the Self, a wise person should strive to propitiate him.

O best among those who know what is to be known, know that when the union with the virtuous one has been accomplished, ignorance has come to an end through the dawning of the supreme and most excellent state. (36)

The meaning is: "due to the arising of that state of being established in the first stage, which is superior to the other stages and more excellent than them by virtue of the attainment of the fourfold means. || 36 ||
Half of ignorance perishes through association with the virtuous;
a fourth part through the meanings of the scriptures, and a fourth part through one's own effort. (37)
"A fourth part" means a one-fourth portion. The ellipsis is to be supplied as "he should destroy it by his own effort. || 37 ||
A single desire arises which is restrained by enjoyments;
upon their exhaustion, one-fourth of ignorance departs through one's own effort. (38)

Therein, he establishes the first point with the words "If one": if a single longing characterized by an intense desire for liberation arises in this person, he is turned away from enjoyments and their means by means of the perfection of dispassion (*vairāgya*) and so forth;
the meaning is that, becoming free from the sense of "mine," he necessarily renounces. || 38 ||

Impurity is diminished by association with the virtuous, by the meaning of the scriptures, and by one's own efforts—either by each one individually, by all together, simultaneously, or even sequentially. (39)
When they are obtained simultaneously, it is at the same time; when they are obtained successively, it is also successively. || 39 ||
That which, being of the nature of the extinction of ignorance, is neither anything nor yet something at all—
that they call the Supreme, the nameless reality, which is both non-existent and existent.

He also provides the answer to the fifth question with the words "That which... (yad iti). The meaning is that it is non-existent (*asat*) because it is unfit for purposeful action and conventional usage, yet it is existent (*sat*) because it is the uncontradicted supreme goal of human life. || 40 ||
This Brahman is dense, ageless, beginningless, infinite, one, the vibration of volition, and indeed non-existent [as a separate entity].
Having understood this, with the delusion of the knower and the known dispelled, dwell in the sorrowless Nirvana, moving about at ease.
O Rāma, this remaining reality is Brahman alone—a single mass of bliss, devoid of transformations such as old age and the like.
As for the forms of the individual soul and the world, they are merely conceptualization, discursive thought, and its manifestation; thus, they do not exist at all.
Having realized the truth of the Self and the non-Self in this way, you, being free from the delusion of the triad beginning with the ego, shall attain liberation.
Having become Brahman itself, by virtue of its unsurpassed vastness, abide—meaning, remain free from sorrow while dwelling in all-pervasive expansion. || 41 ||

Thus ends the twelfth canto, titled "The Realization of the Unity of Volition and Creation," in the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the glorious Vāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa of Valmīki, composed by the venerable sage Vasiṣṭha. Canto 12.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Realization of the Identity of Volition and Creation," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The Thirteenth Chapter.
Bhuśuṇḍa said:
"For that which has the form of the expansion of the universe, no location is applicable."
There is no time for its retention, just as there is no obstruction of light in the sky. || 1 ||
It is described here that in the case of a magical creation (*māyākārya*), there is no dependence on place and so forth;
this is illustrated by the detailed narrative of Indra’s conceptualization of a kingdom within the interior of an atom.

The wise understand that perception is preceded by the creation of space, time, and so forth, because it consists of emanation (*sarga*); in order to establish this point which was stated, he prepares the introductory framework (*bhūmikā*) to recount the narrative of Indra and the *trasareṇu* (motes of dust), beginning with the words "the world" (*jagat*).
The statement "perception is preceded by the creation of space, time, and so forth" is a position accepted for the sake of argument (*abhyupetyavāda*); however, in reality...

According to the theory of "creation upon perception" (dṛṣṭasṛṣṭi), since the illusory creation in the form of the expansion of the world is sustained simultaneously along with space and time, a pre-existing location is not required. The meaning is that just as a pillar is not required for the support of light spreading simultaneously through the sky, so it is here. || 1 ||
These three worlds are merely a creation of mental ideation;
they are peaceful, subtle, light, and clearer even than the fragrance within the wind.
It has spread within the wind; because of its extreme subtlety, it is impossible even for the wind to sustain or shake it.
That fragrance—the light of fragrance, meaning the sweet scent—is "peaceful" (śānta), meaning it is withdrawn, subtle, fine, light, and clear. || 2 ||

For the holy man, who is indeed an atom of the world consisting of nothing but the wonder of consciousness, the fragrance within the wind and Mount Meru exist through the application of another's experience. (3)

O holy one, compared to the atom of the world perceived as mere wonder of consciousness, even a fragrance within the wind is indeed as massive as Mount Meru; for it is experienced by others through the connection with their own perceptions, meaning it is apprehended by others as well through the conjunction of their eyes, nose, and other senses. || 3 ||
That which does not arise as this creation is indeed what perceives it;
just as a person perceives their own dream-like configuration of objects.

However, since this phenomenal world (*prapañca*), which consists of "creation upon perception" (*dṛṣṭasṛṣṭi*), is not an object for any eye other than that of its own creator, it possesses supreme subtlety due to its uniqueness; thus he says:
"him [perceiving]... Just as an object of a mental wish (*mānorathika*) perceives its own configuration by itself through its own witness, so too does a person.
The meaning is that it is just as one perceives one's own dream by oneself alone. || 4 ||
In this very context, they cite this ancient history concerning what occurred long ago within the belly of a mote of dust belonging to the King of the Gods.

In this matter—concerning an object that is independent of previously established place and time, and which, by being the domain of non-dual experience, is of the nature of supreme subtlety—this [text] provides the proof. || 5 ||
At some time, in some place, on a certain branch of a certain world-age, within a certain wish-fulfilling tree,
there appeared a fruit which was the *udumbara* tree of the universe.

And "some" refers to that which is both a *kalpa*-tree and something; that is, in Brahman, which is variegated by *māyā* and the substratum of the fruits of all conceptualizations. At the junction of the two branches—that is, at the branch of the *yuga*—there is the fig fruit (*udumbara*) whose form is the world-egg (*jagad-brahmāṇḍa*). || 6 ||
It resounded with the humming of swarms of mosquitoes that were the hosts of gods, asuras, and spirits;
it had the mountains for its massive flesh and the netherworld, heaven, and earth for its formidable door-panels.

He describes that [city] with the words beginning "sasurāsura" and so forth: [it is a city] where the panels of the gates—characterized by the three worlds beginning with Pātāla—are thick, firm, fierce, and unassailable, [secured] by mountains serving as bolts.
Although the description of the inner panels in the form of an udumbara tree is not strictly necessary here, nevertheless...

This must somehow be reconciled by conceiving of a distinction from what is commonly known, on the grounds that [the fruit] follows the mental activity of one who desires the fruit of the wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpavṛkṣa*) or the fruit of the *udumbara* tree. || 7 ||

Exceedingly beautiful with the wonder of consciousness, thick with the essence of latent impressions, fragrant with the aroma of various experiences, and captivating as the relish of the mind. || 8 ||
It is beautiful (*cāru*) due to the wonder of consciousness and the variety of its creative power; it is lofty (*uccaiḥ*) and vast (*bṛhat*). || 8 ||
It reaches the millions of creepers of the mature existence of the vast tree of Brahman;
it has the great stalk of egoism and is brilliantly illuminated by perfect vision.

Within that vast Udumbara tree of Brahman described previously, there are millions of mature, manifested creepers of the subtle existence of the world; it is illuminated by the equal light of the witnessing consciousness residing therein.

Its mouth is opened wide as the gateway to liberation; it is covered by the rivers and oceans as its veins; it resides within the sheath of the five elements; and it sprays forth droplets like shimmering stars.
Knowledge itself is the blossoming mouth, which is the gateway to liberation. The *mātrās* are the subtle elements (*tanmātrās*).
In this [face], the stars themselves are the spray—either droplets of nectar or particles of frost—which float upwards as they cross over. 10.
Worn out at the end of an aeon, accessible now only to crows and cuckoos,
it has fallen into stillness and has gone somewhere to its final abode.

At the end of a great aeon (*mahākalpa*), [the world] becomes withered, ripe, and on the verge of falling away. Immediately thereafter, it is consumed either by crows or by cuckoos— just as the well-known *udumbara* fruit at its conclusion is eaten by crows or cuckoos, so too is this [world] consumed by the crow of ignorance (*avidyā*) following the harsh sounds of false scriptures, and by [the cuckoo] following the sweet sounds of the [true] scriptures.

The meaning is that it will either be swallowed by the cuckoo of knowledge, or it will reach its end somewhere—that is, it will attain the state of Brahman which is devoid of latent impressions (avāsana), characterized by the mere residue of residual tendencies (vāsanāmātra). || 11 ||
Therein was Śakra, the lord of the immortals and sovereign of the three worlds,
like a leader of small insects gathered around a jar of honey.
There, in that udumbara tree, [he saw] small honey-bees. || 12 ||
Through the instruction of his guru and his own practice, he became one whose veils were destroyed;
a great soul with a purified inner self, the best among those who know the past and the future. (13)
By whom the Self has been cultivated until the limit of all mental constructions is reached within. || 13 ||
Then, at one time, when Nārāyaṇa and the others who were endowed with prowess had for some reason retreated into concealment, he alone remained together with the lord of the gods.
He fought with the great asuras amidst the rising flames of their weapons;
being defeated by those of great heroism, he fled away in haste.

"Śastrajvālānalodbhārāḥ" means those who project the fire of the flames of weapons; [the suffix] *aṇ* is used here in the sense of an object (*karmaṇi*). Since the term "kṛt" (verbal derivative) includes that which is preceded by a prefix (*gati*) or an oblique case (*kāraka*), this forms an *upapada-samāsa*. "Āśu" means quickly or swiftly on all sides. || 15 ||
Chased by his enemies, he fled with great speed through the ten directions;
yet he found no place of rest, like a base man in the world beyond.
With great speed and exceeding swiftness; "the lowest" refers to an evildoer. || 16 ||
Finding a slight opening among those enemies whose vision was deluded, he brought his own internal and external mental volitions toward tranquility. (17)

When his enemies were slightly distracted in their vision, at that time—having brought that very opening, the opportunity for concealment, which was the form of his body, the conception of a gross form, to a state of quiescence within himself among the subtle elements (bhūtasūkṣma), and having dissolved it so as to become exceedingly minute—he entered some particle of dust (trasareṇu) outside; such is the connection with the following verse. || 17 ||
He entered a certain mote of dust situated within the rays of the sun,
just as a bee enters the interior of a lotus through the nature of consciousness.
By virtue of being of the nature of consciousness consisting of the volition to enter into that [interior]. || 18 ||
There he quickly found rest and, after a long time, attained relief;
then, having forgotten the battle, he returned to his composure.
"Nivṛtti" means the absence of going outward; or, one may divide the word as "anivṛtti. || 19 ||
Then, in that very moment, he experienced a mentally constructed palace;
in that palace, upon a lotus-seat, he took his delight as if upon his own throne.
At the end of the lotus, in the center of the lotus-seat, upon his own well-known throne, as if upon a lion-throne. || 20 ||
Then that householder Hari beheld a constructed city,
with walls and palaces made of jewels, pearls, corals, and other precious materials.
Then Hari, having entered the city, beheld the countryside,
resplendent with various mountains, villages, cow-pens, towns, and forests.
Cow-pens are *vrajās*. || 22 ||
Then, experiencing such delight, he perceived the universe—
extending to the mountains, oceans, earth, and rivers, along with its activities and the conception of time.
Such delight was produced by such a resolve. "The world" refers to the earthly realm (bhūrloka). "Rivers," "lords," and "kings" refer to the rulers;
"ends" refers to the boundaries of those respective regions, and it exists together with them. || 23 ||
Then Śakra, experiencing such delight, perceived the three worlds—
along with Pātāla, the earth, the sky, the celestial realms, the sun and other luminaries, and the mountains.
Then, the connection [of the verb] is to be drawn back, as in: "he remained there in the state of lordship over the gods. || 24 ||
There he remained in the sovereignty of the gods, adorned with the weight of enjoyments;
then a powerful son named Kunda was born to him.
Then, at the end of his life, having cast off the body, the blameless Śakra attained nirvāṇa like a lamp whose oil has been exhausted. || 26 ||
Having begotten his own son, Kunda, the king of the three worlds, at the end of his life's span, departed for the supreme state. || 27 ||
Then his son likewise, having installed his own son in the kingdom,
departed at the end of his life to the supreme, purifying state.
In this way, O handsome one, thousands of grandsons have passed away;
even now, a portion of the Lord of the Gods remains established in their kingdom. (29)
That lord of the gods had thousands of grandsons, among whom even today a king named Aṃśaka remains established in his kingdom.
Thus, for as long as the world is conceived, the lineage of Amareśvara alone occupies the station of Śakra;
even when that [lineage] is wounded, dissolved, slain, or lost anywhere in the sky, like a sunbeam purifying the atmosphere. (30)
In the manner thus described, from that time until the present day, within the world of atoms (trasareṇu) conceived by him,

his own lineage alone has occupied and protected the station of Amareśa, the sovereignty of Śakra; for even when some atom of the solar dust, purified by the sun's rays, is diminished, worn away, dissolved, or lost in some region of space, that kingdom does not [perish].
The meaning is "fallen away. || 30 ||

Thus ends the thirteenth canto, titled "The Description of the Multitude of Creations within a Single Atom," in the Indra-episode contained within the Vidyādhara-episode of the *Śrī-Vālmīki-Devī-Mahātmya-Nibandha*. 13.

Thus ends the thirteenth canto, titled "The Description of the Multitude of Creations within a Single Atom," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*. 13.
The fourteenth canto.
Bhuśuṇḍa said:
There was once a certain lord of the gods born in the lineage of that Śakra.
In that regard, his body was of excellent quality, glorious, and possessed of a beautiful posterior. || 1 ||
The world-renowned status of Śakra, born of that lineage, rests upon the lotus-fiber;
therein, within the vision of Brahman, the state of being the Sky-Śakra is perceived through every vision.
He was born into the family, that is, descended from the lineage, of that aforementioned Śakra. || 1 ||
Then, for that noble son of Indra,
there arose there an attainment of inspired knowledge as uttered by the words of Bṛhaspati.
There, by the words of instruction from his preceptor Bṛhaspati, there arose in him an inspired intuition (*pratibhā*);
that is to say, the realization of the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva-sākṣātkāra*), the attainment of knowledge whose nature is that [realization]—this is the ellipsis to be supplied. || 2 ||
Then, having realized that which is to be known and following the course as it had been attained, he,
the sovereign lord of the drinkers of clarified butter (the gods), ruled over the worlds.
Of the gods who drink the clarified butter. || 3 ||
He fought with the Dānavas and conquered all his enemies;
having crossed over the ocean of ignorance, he performed a hundred sacrifices.
Of sacrifices, namely the Aśvamedhas; for its fruit is the attainment of the status of Śakra within this Brahmāṇḍa upon the lotus fiber that is about to be described—this is the sense. || 4 ||
Out of necessity, she dwelt for a long time within the fibers of a lotus stalk,
and she experienced hundreds of other various adventures as well.
Within that lotus stalk was a fine fiber; and within that imagined fiber-stalk universe, he indeed experienced hundreds of other events, such as kingship, war, victory, defeat, and so forth. || 5 ||
Once, there arose in him, who was endowed with the power of awakening, the desire:
"Possessed of meditative concentration, may I perceive the reality of Brahman exactly as it is. (6)
The reality of Brahman has as its essential nature Brahman variegated by *māyā*.
Then, remaining in solitude with his mind stilled through the renunciation of all causes both internal and external, he beheld [the truth] by means of meditative concentration.
Through aspiration and meditative concentration, with a tranquil mind resulting from the abandonment of all causes of distraction. (7)
The Supreme Brahman is the source of all power; it pervades all things, consisting of all things;
in every way, at all times, it is everything, present everywhere, and accessible through all means.
With hands and feet everywhere, with eyes, heads, and faces everywhere,
and with ears everywhere in the world, He exists pervading everything.
"Endowed with hearing" means possessing the faculty of the ear. || 9 ||
It is free from the qualities of all the senses, yet endowed with the qualities of all the senses;
it is unattached and yet the sustainer of all; it is devoid of qualities, yet the experiencer of the qualities.

It is endowed with the qualities of all the sense organs, namely the capacities for perceiving form and so forth; yet, in the ultimate sense, it is unattached, while in the conventional sense, it sustains everything. The same applies hereafter. || 10 ||
It is both outside and within all beings; it is unmoving and yet moving.
Because of its subtlety, it is incomprehensible; it is far away, and yet it is near.
Everywhere it consists of moon and sun; everywhere it consists of earth;
everywhere it consists of mountains; and likewise, everywhere it consists of oceans.
The suffix *mayaṭ* is used in the sense of abundance.
Everywhere it is heavy with essence; everywhere it consists of space;
everywhere it consists of worldly existence; and everywhere it consists of the universe.

The designation "saṃsṛti" (transmigration) is used primarily because of delusion, while the designation "jagat" (the world) is used primarily because of the modifications of existence; such is the distinction in terminology. || 13 ||
Everywhere indeed it is the self of liberation; everywhere indeed it is the primordial consciousness;
everywhere it consists of all objects, yet from every side it is devoid of everything.

In a pot, a cloth, a banyan tree, a wall, a cart, and likewise in a monkey [the reading "man" (nara) also exists]; in a dwelling, in space, in a tree, in the mountain, in the wind, in water, and in fire; 15.
"In the abode" means in the splendor and in the house; "he beheld the three worlds"—thus is the connection with the subsequent verse. || 15 ||
He beheld the three worlds— even within a mere portion of a single atom— possessing various modes of conduct and behavior, and endowed with diverse activities.

In these [worlds] are found the various behaviors of living beings, both physical and mental, as well as the distinctions of actions; the cycles of returning from heaven, hell, and other realms; and even the parts of the atom—its upper, lower, middle, and so forth portions—even down to the level of the subtle elements (tanmātra). 16.
Just as sharpness exists within a mirage and emptiness within the sky, so too do the three worlds—both real and unreal—exist within the Self that consists of consciousness. 17.
When it exists, its nature is that of the time of manifestation; when it does not exist, its nature is that of the time of concealment. || 17 ||
Meditating in this manner with pure consciousness that was free from the sense of objective existence,
Śakra gradually became absorbed in meditation in that very same way.

"Contemplating" means seeing. The meaning is that Śakra [remained] as Śakra by means of that very body fashioned by prior latent impressions (*vāsanā*), through which his state as a living being (*jīva*) and his state of existence were maintained; it was not, however, by means of the state of being the Self of all (*sarvātmabhāva*) experienced in meditative absorption (*samādhi*). || 18 ||
Beholding everything as one through meditation for a long time,
that noble-minded one of great intelligence beheld this creation of ours.
In one place, within the Brahman variegated by māyā; this [creation], our own cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), which is being experienced by you and by me. || 19 ||
Then, wandering within this creation after Śakra had passed away, he attained the status of Śakra and exercised sovereignty over the worlds— a reign adorned with hundreds of historical accounts. (20)

Thereafter, in this creation, as he wandered mentally through the sequence of observing the worlds beginning with the netherworld (pātāla) and the earth, up to the end of Śakra’s world, the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of his identity as Śakra was awakened by the sight of Śakra; consequently, the inevitable fruit of his previous hundred horse-sacrifices manifested.
He performed the collection of taxes, their protection, and other such duties. || 20 ||
"Know this as it truly is: he is the sovereign of the Vidyādhara clans, the king of the gods even today, born into the lineage of that Indra. (21)

"Know that he is the sovereign lord of the Vidyādhara clan; in this manner, born into the lineage of Indra who was contained within a mote of light, he remains today even in this cosmic egg as the king of the gods. || 21 ||
Then, through the practice of yoga focused on the seed-syllable situated in the heart while facing eastward,
he experienced the account of his dwelling within the lotus fiber and so forth.

Then, immediately after becoming Indra, through the power of his former primary practice of the yoga of knowledge—which remained in his heart in the form of latent impressions like a seed—he experienced his previous life exactly as it had occurred, including his residence within the lotus fiber and so forth; that is to say, he remembered it. || 22 ||
Just as this Śakra has been described as having his abode within a mote of floating dust, so too this radiant one born of that lineage has his abode within the fiber of a lotus stalk. (23)

Since Brahman, who possesses all powers, exists everywhere as the reality of all things, one should consider that even thousands of such Śakras exist everywhere; thus he says with two verses beginning with "Just as" (*yathā*). The word *atha* is used here in the sense of "also. (23)
Likewise, hundreds of thousands of such transactions have occurred and continue to occur here and there in the sky. (24)
This river flows thus without interruption for a long time;
as long as it is seen as a mature stream, so long does one remain in those two stages: the ascended and the unascended.

When that state of Brahma exists as half-ascended and half-unascended across the stages beginning with the fourth and ending with the sixth, the realization and experience that "this is Māyā" occurs; this is to be connected with the subsequent [verse]. || 25 ||
Thus, this illusion is beginningless and long-extended, ever oriented toward its conditions;
it finds its sole delight in total dissolution through the mere perception of reality. 26.
O sinless one, this illusion arises from somewhere and appears anywhere; it is perceived merely as having come into being in whatever manner possible.
He says that because [the world] is of the very nature of illusion (*māyā*), one need not contemplate specific causes for its diversity; thus he states, "from whatever source.

By means of three interrogative verses (*kiṃvṛtta*) and three relative verses (*yadvṛtta*), he indicates that there is no necessity for restrictions regarding cause, time, place, action, or manner. || 27 ||
From the mere wonder of the sense of "I," like a mist from a cloud,
it arises instantly— vanishing upon the very moment of its perception.
Alternatively, he states that the superimposition of the ego alone (*ahaṃkāra-adhyāsa*) is the fixed cause for this variety [of appearances], beginning with the words "the sense of 'I'":
"Like mist, frost, and smoke... This is an illustration regarding its disappearance. || 28 ||
By which [cause], the manifestation whose nature is free from the long-desired seer, the act of seeing, and the object seen, is itself the Self;
and for that very reason, being devoid of all objects, it is of the nature of emptiness—a single void like the mere sky, consisting solely of the conceptualization of the "measurer" (mātra).
By which cause, the form of Brahman is the witness of all measurers, non-conceptual, and indeed entirely free from all conceptual constructions.

From the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), it is therefore by nature free from those things extended and expanded through the power of ego-grasping (*ahaṃkāra*)—namely, the mental constructions of what is desired, the perceptions characterized as the "threefold circle" (*tripuṭī*), and the sensory constructions;
that is to say, it is empty of the waking state. For this very reason, it is also empty of all dream-objects consisting of latent impressions (*vāsanā*). And for this very reason...

The meaning is that, because the counter-correlate (pratiyogin) is not established, and because of the ignorance of deep sleep characterized by universal emptiness, that which remains is the reality of the Self in the form of consciousness—a manifestation that is full like the void alone. || 29 ||

Thus ends the fourteenth canto, titled "The Demonstration of the Unity of Creation and Volition," within the narrative of Indrāṇī, contained in the Story of Vidyādhara, in the Nirvāṇa Section of the glorious Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa, according to the Holy Ārṣa tradition. (End of Utpatti-khaṇḍa).
The fourteenth canto, titled "The Demonstration of the Identity of Emanation and Volition."
Fifteenth Chapter.
Bhuśuṇḍa said:
"Where there is 'I-ness' and the world, [the Self] remains there, having arrived first."
Just as other supreme beings [exist] within the interior of a *trasareṇu* of Indra. || 1 ||
The sense of "I" (ahaṃbhāva) is described as both the seed and the form of the delusion of the world;
by its removal, the world is wiped away, and through the remaining purity, one's purpose is fulfilled.

To provide a justification for the statement that "the river of the visible world arises from the mere wonder of the sense of 'I', just as a vision arises from a cloud," he applies the story of Indra’s atom (indrāṇvākhyāyikā) with the words "where... Even in a brand-new dream-phenomenon, the statement "I see the world as already established" is made because it stands there having arrived previously, according to universal experience. || 1 ||
The primary root of this worldly delusion, which has arisen like the color of the sky, is declared to be the ego-sense (*ahaṃbhāva*), the self that conceives itself as an agent. || 2 ||
From this minute seed of the ego, drenched by the sap of latent impressions (vāsanā),
the tree of the three worlds grows upon the mountain of Brahmā in the forest of space.
In the forest—that is, the wilderness—characterized by the sky, which is the unmanifest space (avyākṛtākāśa). || 3 ||
It has the stars as its cluster of flowers, the dissolved mountains as its tender sprouts,
the rivers as the flow of its veins, and the essence of latent impressions as its fruit.

The clouds and mists have dissolved; the forest-covered mountains are [bare] save for their sprouts. The Ganges and other rivers are the essence; likewise, those enjoyments whose essence consists of the seeds of latent impressions (vāsanā) are its fruits. || 4 ||
This world is said to be the vibration of the water of egoism; it is the flowing liquid of spreading latent impressions (vāsanā), sweet with the wonder of consciousness.

Now, he describes the ego (*ahaṃkāra*) as a great body of water and the world as its waves and other effects, in five verses beginning with "I-ness" (*ahaṃtva*). This world is the vibration—the playful manifestation—of the water that is I-ness; it is where the wonder of consciousness takes the form of sensory pleasure, which is its sweet flavor (*mādhurya*). (5)
The stars were its spray of mist, it was dug deep into the infinite sky;
it possessed great whirlpools of existence and non-existence, and various mountains were its waves.

It is like the sky, infinite and unfathomable, possessing an interior cavity that cannot be delimited; therein exist both prosperity as "beings" and adversity as "non-beings," along with great whirlpools.
It was a wave that erased the writing of the three worlds, frothy with its flickering light,
bursting forth like a bubble from the cosmic egg, and thick as the pressure of a door-panel.

By the term "trilokī" (the three worlds), the people residing therein are indicated. It is that in which lines (*lekhā*)—appearing like painted figures (*citralekhyavat*)—are drawn; it is foamy (*phenila*) with the flickering lights of the sun, moon, and other luminaries; it is where the cosmic eggs (*brahmāṇḍa*) themselves are the bursting bubbles (*budbudodbheda*); and it is called a "door-bolt" (*kapāṭāpīḍa*) because, like a door-panel (*kapāṭa*), it presses against and obstructs entry into liberation (*mokṣa*).
By him, the bridge of delusion has become thick and fully grown. || 7 ||
Firmly rooted in the foam-mass of the earth’s surface, he is a water-bird within the density of consciousness,
characterized by the repeated immersion and emergence in the various states of swift motion.
The surface of the earth itself is a dense mass of foam, wherein the living beings— those manifestations of consciousness that are the density of *cit*—
are like water-crows; they possess various movements, consisting of rapid upward, downward, and transverse circling, as well as sinking and emerging.

It possesses the wondrous splendor of a mass of waves consisting of old age, death, delusion, and the like; it is uniquely beautiful with its multitude of drops—the bodies and other phenomena that arise and perish.
Let it be understood that the world is the movement of the wind of egoism;
let it be realized that the world is the fragrance of the lotus of egoism.
He describes the world through two other modes: "I-ness," etc. (verse 10).
I am never distinct from the world, just as wind is not distinct from its movement,
nor water from its fluidity, nor fire from its heat.
He states the conclusion resulting from this description: "Not so" (na). || 11 ||
The world exists within the sense of "I," and "I" exists within the heart of the world;
these two arise mutually, standing like the container and the contained.
He states their state of being mutual seeds: "The world," meaning that which arises from one another, whose nature is manifestation, and whose existence is dependent upon one another. || 12 ||
