He who, through awakening and the cessation of ignorance, wipes away the "I-ness" that is the seed of the world—by him the impurity of the world has been thoroughly washed away, as if by water. 13.
Therefore, he says "the world" [in verse 13], stating that from the cleansing of the ego (ahaṃkāra), the cleansing of the world is accomplished.
O Vidyādhara, that which is called "I" or "you" does not exist at all;
because it lacks a cause and is devoid of substantial reality, it is like the horn of a hare that has arisen [in the mind]. (14)
He states that, from the perspective of ultimate reality, the very perception of the non-existence of the sense of "I" (ahaṃtva) is its purification: "The sense of 'I'... (verse 14).
In that Brahman, which is pervasive, infinite, and devoid of the delineation of mental constructs,
there is never any reality consisting of "I-ness," because of the absence of its cause.
To the question "Whence is that so?", he says: "In Brahman. || 15 ||
At the beginning of creation, no cause is possible for that which is not a real entity;
therefore, "I-ness" and the like do not exist at all, anywhere, just like the son of a barren woman. (16)

Even if a cause were possible in the world, it does not apply to—that is, it does not operate upon—an insubstantial object (*avastu*). In the present case, however, at the beginning of creation, no cause is possible; the meaning is that even the possibility of such a cause does not exist. || 16 ||
Due to the absence of that [duality], the world does not exist; due to the non-existence of the world, there is only consciousness. What remains is indeed nirvāṇa; therefore, remain at ease in peace.
Nirvana is consciousness characterized by absolute isolation; only pure consciousness remains. || 17 ||
Thus, due to the absence of a basis for rebirth, the world, the self, and their respective identities do not exist;
for you, form, light, and mental attention are stilled, and nothing else remains.

Thus, because of the absence of both the world and the sense of "I" for one established in such realization, external transmigrations consisting of form, light, and so forth, as well as internal transmigrations characterized by mental attention, are all stilled. Furthermore, there is no other suffering to be abandoned apart from these two; therefore, the meaning is: "Remain in peace. (18)
That which does not exist simply does not exist; the remainder is peaceful, tranquil, and eternal.
You are now fully awakened; do not again entertain this rootless delusion.
It is peaceful, free from suffering and distraction. || 19 ||
Pure, with the stain of temporal succession removed, you are auspicious, you are peaceful, you are the eternal Lord.
Even the sky becomes like a mountain, or the entire world takes on the form of a single atom.
He from whom the stain—characterized by the conceptualization of external and internal objects of perception—is removed; for this very reason, he is pure.

The meaning is that in the context of superimposition (adhyāropa), even the void sky is compared to a mountain, whereas in the context of negation (apavāda), even the entire universe of Brahmā becomes like an atom, equal to space itself. || 20 ||
Thus ends the fifteenth canto, titled "The Liberation of the Vidyādhara," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the glorious Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa of Valmīki, a work of the Ṛṣis. 15.
Thus ends the fifteenth canto, titled "The Liberation of the Vidyadhara," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The sixteenth canto.
Bhuśuṇḍa said:
Even as that leader of the Vidyādharas was speaking in this manner, [the following occurred].
His consciousness was completely stilled, and he possessed the transformation of meditative absorption.
Having heard this, the meditative absorption (samādhi) of the Vidyādhara is described here;
it is a conclusion to the remainder of the narrative by means of praising the state of non-egoity (anahaṃbhāva).

He is one for whom the perception of the visible world has been completely stilled, and who possesses that transformation of the mind characterized by meditative absorption (samādhi), wherein consciousness attains a state of uniformity like milk and water. || 1 ||
Though being awakened by me again and again from this and that state,
he did not fall back into the visible world, having attained supreme liberation.
It did not fall upon the visible objects such as sound and so forth that lay before it. || 2 ||
He attained that supreme state through that much awakening alone,
O dear one, and not by any further effort of one desiring excellence.
Because he possesses primary qualification, he has attained awakening through my instruction alone;
he does not seek excellence in the repetition of hearing (*śravaṇa*), reflection (*manana*), and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*). "Aṅga" is an address to Vasiṣṭha.
Therefore, I said, "O Rāma, if the mind is indeed pure" (there is also a reading: *cetasi*).
Instruction spreads like a drop of oil upon water. || 4 ||

Now Vasiṣṭha, wishing to provide the example of the Vidyādhara’s mind regarding the point he previously stated, and hastening toward the description, bypasses Bhuśuṇḍa’s speech and says to Rāma: "Therefore," and so forth. (4)
"There is no 'I' within you; do not contemplate this for the sake of peace.
This alone is the supreme statement of instruction; indeed, there is nothing other than this. (5)

What is this instruction? He says: "I am not. Within the inner Self, which is of the nature of pure consciousness, there is no portion consisting of the "I" (ahaṃ). Therefore, do not contemplate this [ego] as existing; this much alone is the supreme statement of instruction, being the very essence of the summary. || 5 ||
This very [teaching], when it falls upon an unworthy mind, dissolves away,
like a pure pearl upon a smooth, upward-facing mirror.
But when the mind of a worthy person has become tranquil, it attains non-falling away by entering within that which is called "discernment," just as a ray of light enters a sun-gem.

It attains non-falling away; having entered within, it produces—this is the ellipsis—a crest of fire called "discernment" (vicāra), capable of burning the entire forest of delusion, just as the rays of the sun entering a sun-crystal (arkamaṇi) produce a crest of fire. || 7 ||
The intense conceit of "I" is itself the seed of the silk-cotton tree called suffering; likewise, the notions "this is mine" and "that is I" are the causes for the spreading of its branches.
In the same way, the notion "this is mine" (*mamedam-bhāvanā*), which is coextensive with the notion of "I" (*ahaṃbhāvanā*), constitutes the root and so forth of the tree of saṃsāra—

[the phrase "of the tree of saṃsāra" refers to the meaning of the passage beginning with "the root called suffering" found in the original text]; for it is from this that the spreading branches of passion and the like arise, [the phrase "the body as the root and so forth" refers to the meaning of the word "beginning" (*ādi*) at the start of the second half-verse].
The meaning is "the cause. || 8 ||
Beginning with "I" and ending with "mine," from that desire proceeds;
it brings about hundreds of misfortunes regarding this world's objects and is the bearer of worldly existence.

He says that very thing: "I" (aham). At the beginning, it functions in the place of the state of the seed; at the end, in the place of the tree which is its effect; and in the middle, the Will (icchā) functions in the place of the branches. || 9 ||
O best of sages, even such fools become long-lived; for indeed, O dear one, there is no fixed rule regarding the cause of longevity. (10)

Having thus supported what was stated previously by means of the consensus of the wise, Vasiṣṭha, continuing the narrative of Bhuśuṇḍa's words, concludes the story of the Vidyādhara with the words "of such a kind.
The ellipsis to be supplied is: "the cause of long life is indeed the knowledge of reality. || 10 ||
Those whose minds are inwardly pure, even if instructed only briefly, attain the supreme state from him who bestows fearlessness for a very long time. (11)
With the intention that there is indeed a rule stating that for internal purity, long-term practice alone is the cause of knowledge, he says:
"Internally," etc. Those whose minds are internally purified through very long practice [attain] the supreme state, which is knowledge. || 11 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having spoken thus to me on the summit of Mount Meru,
that lord of birds became silent, his soul liberated like a cloud over Ṛṣyamūka.
Bhuśuṇḍa was the lord of birds. On Mount Ṛṣyamūka, in the hermitage of Mataṅga, there is a well-known tradition that the clouds do not thunder out of fear of Mataṅga’s curse. || 12 ||
O Rāma, having taken leave of that accomplished Vidyādhara, I then returned once more to my own abode, which was adorned by a circle of sages.

First, having taken leave of that perfected one, Bhuśuṇḍa, and then having gone to the Vidyādhara to verify his words, and finally having taken leave of him as well, I, with my purpose resolved, went to my own hermitage, my dwelling place.
This method for the pacification of Vidyādharas, spoken by Bali and arising from a brief awakening, has been told to you today.
Indeed, eleven great ages have passed for me here during this assembly with Bhuśuṇḍa, the lord of birds.

O Rāma, by means of this brief and swift awakening, the pacification of the Vidyādhara has arisen; it was told to you today through the narrative of Bhuśuṇḍa, the crow. Once this meeting with Bhuśuṇḍa, the lord of birds, had been described by me, immediately thereafter, in this Kalpa, there were eleven great Yugas.
The meaning is that divine yugas have passed. || 14 ||

Thus ends the sixteenth canto, titled "The Liberation of the Vidyādhara," within the Narrative of the Vidyādhara, in the Nirvāṇa Section of the glorious Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa, composed by the Sage. 16.
Thus ends the sixteenth canto, titled "The Liberation of the Vidyādhara," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
Seventeenth Canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Thus, it is precisely from the non-perception of the "I" that [the mind] yields the fruits of both the auspicious and the inauspicious.
Surely, when desire ceases within, the fruit-bearing tree of saṃsāra withers away. || 1 ||

Here, through the fire of the realization of "non-I," which utterly consumes the seed of the notion of "I," the transmigratory cycle of the body and so forth is completely sublated; thus, its unreality is asserted.
Since all worldly existence has desire as its root, he first describes the cessation of that [desire] through the absence of the sense of "I" (anahaṃbhāva):
"Not-I" (anaham) || 1 ||
Through the practice of the realization of "non-self," having become one for whom a clod of earth, a stone, and gold are equal,
and having stilled the afflictions of worldly existence, a person does not suffer.
He states that through the cessation of desire, the destruction of defects such as greed, and the attainment of virtues such as dispassion, there is the destruction of all mental suffering:
"Driven by the power of supreme awakening which has flown out from the hollow of the ego-sheath, I know not where this stone of the object 'I' quickly goes. (3)

With the intention that, for one who possesses the means of practice (*sādhana*), the dawning of knowledge through the necessary hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth results in the sublation of the "I-sense" (*ahamartha*) as something distinct from Brahman, and thus its ultimate conclusion is sheer unreality (*alīkatva*), he says: "The I-sense" (*ahaṃtā*). Through the practice of churning knowledge by means of hearing and so forth, [the I-sense] arises from the very crucible of the subject-construct (*pramātṛ-yantra*) characterized as the "I-sense."

The stone of the objects of perception, such as the "I" (ahaṃkāra) and so forth—which was cast away, that is, expelled by the power of that awakening characterized by the direct realization of the Supreme Brahman which has flown up like a flame of fire—I know not where it goes; the sense is that it simply sinks into insignificance, like a stone hurled from a fire-engine. || 3 ||
Launched from the hollow of the ego-sheath, impelled by the strength of the hero Brahmā,
I do not know where this stone of the object "I" quickly goes.
With the intention that Brahman alone, when ascended upon by the final direct realization (*sākṣātkāra-vṛtti*), is capable of dispelling ignorance, egoism, and so forth, he says: "I-ness" (*ahaṃtā*).
Just as with ignorance and egoism, it is that very same Brahman which [dispels] the gross body, whether in its individual (*vyaṣṭi*) or collective (*samaṣṭi*) form.
With the intention that [the ego-sense] is not what brings about cessation, he says: "Ego-sense" (ahaṃtā) || 4 ||
Launched from the pouch of egoism and impelled by the force of the hero Brahmā,
I do not know where this stone of the bodily machine goes so swiftly.
Brahman alone is the hero (vīra), the valiant one (vikrānta) impelled by that power (bala).

In the compound *pūrvāpara-prathama-carama-jaghanya-samāna-madhya-madhyama-vīrāḥ*, the word *vīra* appears at the end [of the series] due to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*), even though it is a coordinate compound (*samānādhikaraṇa-samāsa*). || 5 ||
This object of the sense of "I" was previously enveloped by the non-"I," but now, as if flown away by the flame of consciousness, it has dissolved; I know not where it quickly goes.

Or rather, let there be the position that the destruction of the sense of "I" (ahaṃtā) is simply the consciousness reflected back by the mental state (*vṛtti*) consisting of the cultivation of non-"I"-ness (*anahaṃtā*); with this intention, he says:
"The flavor of 'I' has dissolved within by the flame of the consciousness of non-"I"-ness;
I do not know where it quickly goes, like sap from a leaf on a tree. (7)
From the "excellent color" (udvarṇāt), meaning from the superior caste such as the Brāhmaṇa who is qualified for the knowledge of Brahman, and from that which is white due to full ripening. || 7 ||
The intoxicating juice of the essence of egoism, once its sap has been completely extracted from the leaves of the body,
attains the state of transcendence by way of the sun of non-egoism.
Alternatively, with the intention that emptiness does not sublate the ego-sense (*ahaṃtā*) and so forth, but rather that they are indeed Brahman, he says: "The body... [and so on].

By means of the path of the sun's rays, which is characterized by non-ego (*anahaṃtā*), one attains transcendence—that is, the state of Brahman—and the state of being the subtle water-nature of its own cause. || 8 ||
Whether on a bed, in mud, on a mountain, in a house, in the sky, on dry land, or in water—
whether gross, subtle, formless, or even existing within another form— she is present.

However, without the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), there is never, at any time, nor in any state whatsoever, the absolute eradication of either the body or the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*). Because these two serve as each other's seeds and because they exist within one another, their arising is unavoidable everywhere in the form of the world-phenomenon; thus he says, beginning with "In sleep" (*śayane*). "In sleep" means on the bed.

The connection with the third verse is as follows: the seed of the banyan tree, characterized by the body—having reached twelve stages such as the gross state and so forth, and though situated here or there within the seven locations beginning with the womb—is such that the sprout of egoity (*ahaṃtva*) has arisen within it; being thus, in an instant it spreads this network of branches called "saṃsāra," which quickly pervades all directions. || 9 ||
Whether staying here or there, asleep, awake, or reduced to ashes;
whether held, led away, submerged, far off, or standing nearby—she is ever present.
The sprout of egoity, situated within the seed-vessel of the body, quickly spreads its network of branches known as this worldly existence in an instant. (11)
I am indeed a great tree whose body resides within the hollow of a banyan seed;
it spreads its multitude of branches throughout the cycle of worldly existence wherever it may be.
In this way, one should understand that the great tree of the body is situated within the banyan seed that is the characteristic of "I-ness" (ahaṃtva);
thus he says: "Ahaṃtva... (verse 12).
Indeed, a tree with its hundreds of branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits exists within the interior of a seed; it is perceived by the eye.
Likewise, the body exists within the atom of the "I-sense" (ahaṃtva), surrounded by the consciousness of all remaining objects of perception; this is seen only through the vision of the intellect.

He illustrates the point already stated by means of the example of the seed of a banyan tree (*vaṭa*) and others, beginning with the word "branch" (*śākhā*). Just as there exists a tree within the interior of whose seed hundreds of branches are present, along with shining leaves, flowers, and fruits— since that very being,
having burst through the seed-capsule, emerges in the sequence of sprouts and so forth, and is directly perceived by all people.

It is clearly perceived. The word "nanu" indicates what is well-known. Thus, the meaning is that the wise have seen—by means of the very vision characterized by subtle intelligence—that there exists a body enveloped by all remaining objects of perception within that "kaṇikā," which is characterized by the nature of the ego (ahaṃtva) and serves as the subtle seed. || 13 ||

Now, for one who has attained through inquiry the realization that the sense of "I" does not belong to the body, and whose form is thus purely the space of consciousness—for such a person, the tree of worldly existence does not sprout here from the seed-vessel of the unreal "I-ness," once it has been consumed by the great fire of awakening. (14) Having thus stated that the fruit of non-inquiry is the absence of liberation in all circumstances, he now declares that the fruit of inquiry is liberation, beginning with the verse: "dehād... (from the body...).

For such a person— whether it be a *jīvanmukta* whose bodily form consists of nothing but the space of consciousness (*cidvyoma*) due to the realization of reality through investigation, hearing, and so forth, yet who has not attained the sense of "I" or the conceit of identity with that body even while the body exists;
or else a *videhamukta* who is bodiless and firmly established in supreme, unsurpassed bliss— [the following applies].
Once the seed of the notion of "I-ness" has been consumed by the great fire of awakening, the tree of saṃsāra does not sprout from within it. || 14 ||
Thus ends the seventeenth canto, titled "The Instruction on the Union with the Non-existence of 'I-ness'," in the Nirvāṇa Section of the Holy Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa, composed by the sage Vālmīki. 17.
Thus ends the seventeenth canto, titled "The Instruction on the Non-existence of the Notion of 'I'," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The Eighteenth Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Death, which consists of the total destruction of everything, never exists at all.
The stability within one's own internal resolve is designated as death. || 1 ||
Indeed, it is described here how infinite worlds, containing the minds of living beings who have passed away, are carried everywhere in the sky by the winds.

Regarding what was stated—that "the body exists as the very atom of the 'I'-sense, surrounded by the consciousness of all remaining objects of perception"—and how it is seen solely through the vision of the intellect (*buddhidṛk*), he prepares the ground to establish both of these points by means of the exposition of the infinite world composed of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the living and the dead: [The text continues: "The body exists as the very atom of the 'I'-sense, surrounded by the consciousness of all remaining objects of perception; this is seen only through the vision of the intellect. Regarding that, [the author asks]: "How does it exist? What is that vision of the intellect like? He composes this introductory section (*bhūmikā*) to support both of those [questions] through the detailed explanation of the infinite world consisting of the latent impressions of the living and the dead.

Regarding "death": the ignorant believe that death consists in the total destruction of the mind, intellect, ego, and so forth. However, this is never the case, for it would entail such defects as the loss of the fruits of past actions (*kṛtahāna*). Rather, it occurs when the *prārabdha* karma that impels one to experience the state of having a human body or other forms ceases, and the corresponding volitions (*saṃkalpa*) vanish.
The meaning is that when the karma which brings about the ego-sense and so forth regarding the bodies of gods and others arises, there occurs a subsequent volition corresponding to that [body];
the stability of this [volition] until the exhaustion of the unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) that impels it, while depending upon the forgetting of the previous state, is designated as "death. || 1 ||
Behold, these mountains— Mandara and Meru— seem as if they are being carried away before me,
even though they have not been mounted by the winds of the quarters, like mountains reflected in a river.

"Let it be so; what follows from that? To this he says: "Behold! (paśya). And thus, the mountains such as Mandara and Meru, which constitute the world imagined by the volitions of those various individual souls, are being carried and driven everywhere by the winds of the quarters;
they are seen by me, and you too should behold them—this is the meaning. || 2 ||
Above and above, within, like the layers of a plantain leaf,
the successions of worlds exist in the sky, their natures both joined and unjoined with one another.

Higher and higher, further and further out, as many living beings as possess an equal unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) from their enjoyer, that many are conjoined—that is, merged in a state of unity; others remain in a non-conjoined state. || 3 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
"O leader of sages, I do not understand at all the unimpaired meaning of the sentence, 'Behold, they are being carried before me,' exactly as it is."
Rāma, unable to conceive of the meaning that had been stated, asks: "Behold!"—the sense being, "Tell me exactly how it is.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
The mind is within the vital breath (prāṇa), and the world is within the mind.
It exists in various forms, just as a tree exists within a seed.
It is well known from both worldly experience and the Vedas that the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) of deceased persons depart into the ether. Therefore, the meaning is:
if those vital breaths exist, then one should conceive that within the vital breath there exists the mind (*citta*), and within the mind, the entire world as well. || 5 ||
When a man has died, the vital breaths merge with the winds of space,
for they have flowed into the Self just as the waters of rivers merge into the waters of the ocean.

Granted that this may be so, he explains how they are carried away by the winds of the quarters: "When [the person] has died. When the person has died, the vital breaths (*prāṇavāyu*) that have departed from him merge with the full winds in the external atmosphere.
This is because those [winds] are also "swift" (*druta*), meaning they possess a liquid-like nature. Therefore, when things of a similar nature meet, there is only oneness.
The meaning is that it comes to be. || 6 ||
The worlds within them,
though consisting solely of volition, seem to move incessantly here and there, driven by the winds of the sky.

Therefore, the meaning of the statement that the worlds contained within those vital breaths—having been specifically impelled and drawn along by the winds of the sky—seem to move here and there, is that they appear as if they are being carried away. || 7 ||
I see all these directions filled on every side with winds accompanied by vital breaths, containing throbbing volitions within them.
Look here! Look! In the courtyard of the world born of volition, Mount Mandara and Mount Meru are being carried along before me by the vision of my intellect. (9)
I see it; you too should see it with the eye of the intellect.

Know that within the wind dwell the vital breaths whose life has perished; within the vital breaths dwells the mind; and within the mind, know that the world exists, like oil within a sesame seed. (10)
When there is wind in the void, the vital breaths of those who have died remain within. || 10 ||
Just as the vital breaths, which consist of mind, are carried along by the winds until they become equal to space,
so too are these limbs and even the worlds carried away.

Now, one might ask: "How can the worlds, being so heavy, be carried by winds? To this he says: "By the winds of space" (*khavātaiḥ*). Thus, just like the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the worlds—which are its limbs—are likewise light, equal to space, and are therefore carried along; this is the meaning. || 11 ||
Even the three worlds, along with their actual multitudes of sky, earth, and so forth,
are carried forward everywhere like a fragrance, even though they are not mounted [upon it].
They are real, accompanied by the four kinds of living beings; they are unmounted, not firm, and—so to speak—not established. || 12 ||

O descendant of Raghu, those things are perceived by the intellect alone and not by the physical eye; they appear before one in the form of mental constructs, like the cities seen in one's own dreams.
By means of vision, such as that of the eyes and so forth, it is like a city seen in one's own dream, or like such a city [seen while awake], or like the river-flood within such a city. || 13 ||
Everywhere and at all times, these [atoms] exist as something even more subtle than space;
yet, because their essence consists of mere conceptual construction, they are not perceived in the slightest degree.

Regarding the phrase "as if being carried away" (*uhyanta iva*), one should keep in mind that this was stated in the second verse of the current creation (*sarga*)—namely, "Behold these things being carried away as if.
To justify the meaning of the particle *iva* used therein, he says: "Because its essence consists of mere imagination" (*kalpanāmātrasāratvāt*). || 14 ||
Because of their firm nature, those very worlds are truly real for you within your own realms, just as they are for me, O Bhava, since the aspect of consciousness is all-pervading.
Although those [objects] do not exist at all because they are mere conceptual constructs and thus are not inferred [as real], nevertheless,

precisely because of their firm appearance within those respective worlds— such as heaven, hell, and the earth— which are to be experienced by those various living beings, they are indeed real insofar as they are capable of performing the causal function of experiencing pleasure and pain.
This is because the aspect of consciousness that constitutes the substratum (adhiṣṭhāna-cidaṃśa), which brings about its reality, is all-pervading.
The meaning is: just as you are real according to our perception, being present before us and capable of purposeful action such as hearing and retaining, so too is it. || 15 ||
Like cities in a reflection, they are carried along by the current of the river of life even before they have taken root; yet once rooted, they are no longer carried at all.

Those that are unrooted, being mere latent impressions (*vāsanā*), do not manifest; those that are rooted have manifested. Thus they are carried away, or rather, they are not carried away at all. || 16 ||
O Raghava, fragrances are gathered within the limbs of the wind;
the worlds reside within the vital breaths, yet they are essentially composed of space.
He states that the similarity to fragrance regarding subtlety and movement has been mentioned previously: "saurabhāṇi" (fragrances). || 17 ||
Just as there is no difference in the internal space when a jar is carried to another country,
so too there is no difference in the delusion of the three worlds within the mind, which consists of movement and other such fluctuations.

For this very reason, he says "in the jar" to show that even though there are distinctions in the movement of the mind—which consists of the wandering through the three worlds—these do not belong to the Self;
likewise, there is nothing else in the Self. This is the implied meaning. || 18 ||
Thus, this delusion of a real world, though appearing as if it were real, is entirely unreal;
it neither perishes nor arises, for it is of the very nature of Brahman alone.

Just as the dead are unreal because they are mere mental constructs of the world, so too is this world unreal for you; it is nothing but an illusion that has arisen. Even that illusion, from the perspective of ultimate reality, neither perishes nor arises; thus, from the viewpoint of truth, its nature is none other than Brahman—this is the meaning. || 19 ||
Or even when it has risen, its various movements are not perceived by the winds,
just as the movement within a boat is not felt by those situated inside its hold.

Now, one might object: "If the world or its delusion has arisen like the internal movement of air from the perspective of conventional experience, then how do we perceive the earth as being motionless? To this, he says: *yadi vā* ("or if"). It is not that it has not arisen at all; rather, even if the position that it has arisen is accepted, its various rotations and revolutions are produced by the winds.
The meaning is that it is not perceived by us who reside within the earth, just as the vibration produced in a boat is not perceived by men situated inside its interior compartments. || 20 ||

Just as the vibration of a bowstring attached to the body is not perceived by those situated within it, nor is it perceived by those on the earth—even though they are there—so it is, O Brahman, with those who dwell within that [Brahman]. (Note:
Although the reading "brahman tatsaṃsthaiḥ" is seen, the vocative "brahman" is inappropriate here as it is addressed to Rāma.)
[Aligned: By those established in that [state], and even by those consisting of that. || 21 ||

He explains that very point clearly with the words "Just as" (yathā). Just as the movement of a boat is not perceived even by those situated inside it—and by the word "also" (api), even by those who are identified with it, such as the rudders and so forth—so too [it is not perceived] by us who are situated on the earth, meaning even by those composed of earthly bodies and the like. || 21 ||
Just as a house one *yojana* in extent is experienced within a small space,
so too is the entire world contained within a single atom that serves as its pillar.

"Thus, look! These [mountains] Mandara and Meru seem as if they are being carried before us. Having thus justified his own statement to Rāma, and having further remarked that "the larger fits within the smaller like the interior of a plantain leaf," he first demonstrates the inclusion of the large within the small by means of the mental construction of the large as small, beginning with the word "yathā" (just as): "Just as a dwelling, though extending for many *yojanas*, [fits] into a small [space]..."

The meaning is this: just as the limitedness of a tree-trunk is experienced by the intellect of a craftsman striving to fashion it through the arrangement of various carvings and projections, so too is the world experienced through the mental construction of the world even within the most subtle atom. || 22 ||
For a person of feeble character considers even a vast thing to be small and a small thing to be immense; just as mice regard the contents of their own two palms as if they were fresh mud.

With the intention that the vast world cannot possibly be contained within an atom or the like—even by imagining them to be of maximum size—he says: "The thing" (vastu), etc. For example, mice who have entered a treasury of jewels, being themselves devoid of wealth, do not value the jewels highly; rather, they value even a mere handful of them.

In that state, they value even a mere commodity of grain obtained by chance as something great; or rather, just as children do not highly prize their own ornaments, however costly they may be, because they are experienced daily, but instead prize a fresh,
unprecedented lump of clay in the shape of an animal or bird, adorned with colors and the like, for the sake of play.
The meaning is that, being deceived by that gift, they think they are giving away even their own ornaments in exchange for it.

Even though this thing called the world has no real essence, it is a delusion for the wise; in this regard, the word "unrighteousness" (adharma) is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa) for both unrighteousness and righteousness.
"The fruits of dharma and adharma" has been explained; that is the meditation of Bṛhaṅga. 24.

Furthermore, while it may be true that the actual inclusion of the great within the small is impossible, it is certainly possible through delusion; with this intention, he says: "asatye va" (even though unreal). For one whose consciousness is veiled by ignorance (*ajñāna*), this world exists for the living and other worlds for the dead, even though these objects are unreal within the delusion called the universe.

The phrase "the fruits of dharma and adharma," and so forth, refers to that very cultivation (*bhāvanā*) in the form of mental construction (*saṃkalpa*), which serves as the nourishment for the expanding mind as it proceeds. The meaning is that this cultivation does not obstruct the fact that the object undergoes a change of state. The word *bṛhaṅga* [is derived] from the root *bṛh*; the suffix *ka* is applied in the sense of the abstract noun (*bhāve*) according to the rule "the application of *ka* in the sense of *ghan" (Pāṇini 3.3.58). Then, by the rule "it is seen in other cases as well" (Pāṇini 3.2.101), [the suffix is added].
Gamerḍaḥ | The augment num is applied by virtue of the rule of diversity (bāhulaka). || 24 ||
"To one who possesses the internal knowledge that 'this is to be abandoned' and 'this is to be accepted,' there exists delusion regarding existence, even if he is omniscient. (25)

Now, one might ask: "While the internal mental impression of the world's existence may belong to the ignorant, how can there be such an error regarding the internal existence of the world for those who are omniscient, such as yourself? To this he replies with the word "this" (*idam*). Even for an omniscient being like you, as long as the *prārabdha* (commenced karma) has not been exhausted, there persists a slight [impression] for the sake of worldly activity (*vyavahāra*).
The meaning is that delusion certainly exists. || 25 ||
For just as a conscious whole perceives its own parts,
so the living soul perceives the three worlds as spread out within itself.

For this very reason, he says "He who is conscious" (*sacetanaḥ*) to show that even for the omniscient Hiraṇyagarbha—the collective soul (*samaṣṭijīva*)—the vision of the three worlds occurs within his own interior, as if they were limbs. The "possessor of limbs" (*avayavī*) is the worldly person whose body is the self; the "individual soul" (*jīva*) here refers to the collective soul. || 26 ||
O friend, this consciousness— the supreme sky of the Self, infinite, unborn, and undecaying—
these worlds are but the forms of its constituent parts.
He says that the Lord, endowed with Māyā, perceives in this manner: "The Self of Consciousness. By the address "O," Rāma is reminded of that [Self]. || 27 ||
Just as an iron ball, though insentient within, perceives the razor, needle, and other objects [placed inside it], so too does the ignorant individual soul perceive the delusion of the three worlds.
Regarding how the Lord perceives the universe contained within Himself at the time of dissolution, he says this in four verses beginning with "sacetanaḥ" (conscious). The meaning is:

if a lump of iron were conscious, it would perceive, as its own future modification, the razor, needle, and so forth existing within itself in a subtle form; it is just like that. The individual soul (jīva), being endowed with all the latent impressions (saṃskāras) merged within itself... [28]
Just as a lump of clay, though insentient, is perceived by one as a bowl, a water-jar, and so forth, O dear one, so too does the living being perceive the world. (29)

Consciousness (cit) is designated as "insentient" (acid) when there is an intention to emphasize the form of clay and so forth superimposed upon it, by virtue of the predominance of the real nature of the substrate (adhiṣṭhāna).
The intended meaning (tātparya) is exactly as before. || 29 ||
Just as the sprout of consciousness and matter within the body conceives itself to be a tree,
so too this triple world is Brahman, devoid of the actual referent of the word "tree."

The sprout is insentient because its primary nature is that of earth and other materials superimposed [upon it]. Let there be this distinction: by means of a form qualified by the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the individual soul (*jīva*), one perceives the object denoted by the word "tree" along with that [sentience]; however, by means of the form of the Lord unqualified by that [individual soul], it is devoid of that [sentience], meaning its form is sublated by beginningless, established ignorance (*avidyā*).
The remainder is as before. || 30 ||
Whether conscious or unconscious, just as a mirror perceives a city— whether it is reflected within it or not— so too does Brahman perceive the three worlds, or perhaps does not.

Having stated the illustration regarding the perception of the world at the times of its creation and dissolution from the perspective of transformation (*pariṇāma*) concerning the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*), he speaks also from the perspective of illusory appearance (*vivarta*): "cidvā" (or consciousness). From the perspective of the vision conditioned by the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the *jīva* and *īśvara*, one knows;

but from the perspective of the unconditioned, pure vision, one does not know. The sense is that this is according to such scriptural passages as, "where one sees nothing else," and so forth. || 31 ||
The three worlds consist of nothing but space, time, action, and substance;
therefore, there is no difference between "I-ness" and the world, as these two are identical with the Self.

Having thus resolved Rāma’s questions and concluded all incidental matters, he now connects [the following] to support the previously introduced subject by another method, beginning with "deśa": "I-ness" (ahaṃtva) is also not distinct from the world, just as wind and its movement are not distinct. "I-ness" (ahaṃtvam api).
Because it consists of the conceit of identity with place, time, action, and substance, it is of that very nature;
thus, that which is taught by means of this imagined analogy—therein, through one part of the analogy, there is a commonality of properties with the object of comparison. (33)

He says, "By means of what is imagined," [meaning]: It is precisely in order to make this understood that both the Śruti and I have presented analogies such as clay and lumps of iron—even though they are insentient—by superimposing sentience upon them on the basis of partial similarity. || 33 ||
Whatever is seen here in this world, whether stationary or moving,
is known as the body of the individual soul (jīva), which does not abandon its supreme atomic nature.

The meaning is that the supreme atomicity (*paramāṇutva*), characterized by the state of being the real Brahman, does not abandon its subtlety (*saukṣmya*) even while appearing in the form of the gross world as a phenomenal manifestation (*vivarta*). || 34 ||
In that state which bestows pure vibration through the relinquishment of all perception,
there is not even the slightest difference, like a flawless gemstone free from attachment.

Therefore, he says "all" [in verse 35], meaning that when all illusory perceptions are sublated by the vision of the substrate (adhiṣṭhāna-dṛṣṭi), there is not even the slightest distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the world in the state of plenitude (pūrṇapada), which is the unimpeded expansion of the pure Self in every respect.
Whatever conceptual portion is projected, wherever, in whatever manner, whenever, and by whatever means— it is Consciousness itself that is thus projected.
But when there is no obstruction, consciousness always and everywhere evolves as the very self of all conceptual constructions; thus he says, "Whichever... whichever.

The ellipsis is to be supplied as "is given by the deluded one. The meaning is that consciousness, in that very manner, becomes possessed of such an evolution precisely in accordance with those conceptual constructions. || 36 ||
Because it lacks consciousness, there is no mental construction in the mind, just as a sprout cannot exist in the sky;
but because the mind possesses consciousness, know that here it is consciousness itself that constitutes conceptualization.

He states that even the mind possesses the power for diverse volitions only because consciousness has entered into it, and not by itself; thus, sovereignty over all transformations belongs to consciousness alone: "Because of its lack of sentience" (acittvāt). || 37 ||
That splendor of conceptual construction which arises for one of unawakened disposition is not composed of reality, because the sky of consciousness is all-pervading and infinite.
Just as the splendor of conceptual construction arises, it does not truly arise for one who is awakened;
because the sky of consciousness is all-pervading and infinite, that [construction] is not composed of reality.

Thus, although it has arisen for the unawakened, it has not truly arisen even when the reality is awakened to, because it is infinite and devoid of any limitation imposed by time or substance. || 39 ||
The notion that all mental constructions are real is unimpaired even from childhood;
for an object experienced internally in a dream or similar state can be obtained by someone [upon waking]. (40)
If it is composed of unreality (*asat*), then how is it that it appears as real even to children and cowherds? To this he says: "All," etc.

It is not only the mental construction of waking thought that appears as real, but rather everything in common with dreams and so forth. Furthermore, this must be understood through an implied question (*kāku*): no object such as an elephant or silver perceived in a dream or delusion can ever be obtained by anyone. || 40 ||
Volition, latent impression, and the individual soul—these three objects are inscribed upon consciousness;
though they are experienced, they are unreal, for they belong only to that which is non-existent, not to the existent.
[Objection: "But surely the world-process (*saṃsāra*) is real; how could it be unreal? To this he says: "It is volition" (*saṃkalpa*). Waking and dreaming are volition;

deep sleep is mere latent impression (*vāsanā*); and the individual soul (*jīva*), which is the form of consciousness reflected in both of those and the enjoyer of both—these three categories are painted upon the self by the real, immutable Consciousness, like a picture. This is that [reality].
The world, which is a conceptual construction of variegated appearances, is experienced as real by virtue of its existence as a substratum;

yet, because it belongs only to the unreal individual soul (*jīva*), it is unreal, and not so for that which is real as the substratum. The meaning is that [the world] does not touch that [substratum].
Just as horses in a painting, a reflection, or a dream are the vehicles only for unreal persons in a painting, a reflection, or a dream, [so too is the world].
The meaning is that it is the same for a truthful person as well. || 41 ||
When truth is expressed as non-truth, Śiva becomes truly liberated, possessing the blossoming of the complete dissolution of the subtle body (ātivāhika-deha). 42.

Let it be that, according to such scriptural passages as "In the beginning, this was indeed Brahman," the cycle of transmigratory existence arises from the lack of self-knowledge regarding Reality alone;

nevertheless, that [Reality] remains eternally liberated. For just as that Truth, Brahman, prior to the realization of its true nature, transfers its own reality to the world and thus becomes what is called the "reality" of the world, so too, subsequent to the realization of truth, [it remains liberated] from the sublated world.

When it withdraws its own existence into itself, that which is designated as "unreality" also ceases to be. Indeed, no other form of unreality can be properly described than the mere residue of the substrate (adhiṣṭhāna) remaining after the phenomenal world (prapañca).
For, upon the total destruction of one's own ignorance along with the subtle body (ātivāhika-deha), the liberated one attains expansion characterized by fullness.
The meaning is that the inner self alone becomes Śiva. || 42 ||
The worlds are carried by the winds through the sky like the cotton-wool of the silk-cotton tree;
yet they are not carried, like stones, nor do they exist at all except as a mental construction.
Therefore, he concludes by stating that it has been said: "The worlds are carried away only by the vision of ignorance, not by the vision of reality"—"jagantīti" (verse 43).
Thus, within this treasury containing the multitude of all objects, even in the exceedingly vast sky, there exist worlds—
some intermingled with one another, and some not intermingled at all.

In the manner thus described, within this void-like space— which is the treasury of the entire collection of objects, unknown in its ultimate reality as the Infinite Self (Pratīci), and vast beyond measure— there exist infinite worlds through the power of ignorance (*avidyā*). And these worlds, when the unseen merit and demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) of certain individual souls (*jīva*) is identical, during the state of waking, and when the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) is one, [exist] in mutual relation.
They are intermingled; however, in the case of their disparity—namely, when the cosmic egg is divided or in a dream—the meaning is that they are not intermingled with one another.
Because it is all-pervasive, the Supreme Consciousness manifests forms of infinite variety, filling the quarters with abundant beginnings;
these forms are as transient as the reflection of a city in shimmering water, yet they resemble the vast, dense cities existing within one's own heart. (45)

He specifies those very [powers] with the three [verses] beginning with "Because of being everything" (*sarvatvāt*): because the Supreme Consciousness, which is Brahman, is everything, possesses all powers, and lacks any limitation of measure, it has infinite forms— whether by quality,
substance, action, genus, and so forth— and is [perceived] by people situated in every direction through its abundance of initiating various effects.

They are gathered together; they are as transient as the reflection of a city in the hollow of a restless cloud. For this very reason, they possess as their likeness those great cities of the gods, Gandharvas, and others, which are situated within [the heart], densely packed, and filled with every kind of abundance. 45.

Though possessing stability, they are constantly perishing moment by moment; though their eyes are open, they are perpetually closed; though filled with light, they are surrounded on all sides by darkness—these are the surging waves of the ocean of consciousness.

Though they possess stability by virtue of their underlying continuous substance, they are momentary due to the modifications of their changing states; thus, even while the eyes are open during waking, they are in reality closed because of the absence of actual manifestation. Though they are illuminated by the light of the Self, they are shrouded in darkness because they are enveloped by the darkness of ignorance regarding that [Self]. (46)
The waters of the rivers, though distinct and mingled together in the ocean,
are like the lights of the stars, sun, moon, and planetary spheres risen together in the sky.

He provides two examples in sequence for the case where those situated separately become intermingled, and where those already intermingled become situated separately: "separately," etc. Though situated separately in the vessels of rivers, they become intermingled in the ocean. However, the light of stars and such that have risen simultaneously in the sky is such that one cannot say, "this is the light of that [specific star]."

Because they cannot be distinguished even though they are intermingled, and because there is no movement of one when the other moves, they are as if separate, and indeed like those [separate things]. || 47 ||

Thus ends the eighteenth canto, titled "The Instruction on the Yoga of the Similarity between the World-Web and a Treasure-Casket," in the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the glorious Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa of Valmīki, composed by the venerable sage Vasistha.

Thus ends the eighteenth canto, titled "The Instruction on the Yoga of the Similarity between the World-Web and a Basket," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The nineteenth canto.
Śrī Rāma said: O Sage, what is the nature of the individual soul (jīva), and likewise, how does it assume a physical form?
And tell me how he possesses the state of the supreme self, as well as what his abode is.
The true nature of the individual soul (jīva) in both its collective (samaṣṭi) and individual (vyaṣṭi) bodies is described,
along with its conceptualization, its abodes, the distinctions of its instruments, and its experience of enjoyment.
That which is form (rūpa) is that which is useful for scriptural discourse and that which is the ultimate form (pāramārthika-rūpa). Configuration (ākṛti) is the gross body;
its "grasping" (grahaṇa) is conceptualization (kalpanā). The "location" (sthāna) is the gateway for external worldly activity. || 1 ||

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: That which is called "the object of thought" (cetya) by its own volition (saṃkalpa), known by the alternative name "consciousness" (cit), is the infinite space of consciousness (cetanākāśa) that is designated by the term "jīva. || 2 ||

In this context, he first shows the collective individual soul (*samaṣṭijīva*), which is well-known from the scriptures on liberation (*mokṣaśāstra*) and is fit for purification through non-difference from Brahman, using the word "sva" (his own): "That very infinite space of consciousness which is Brahman—by its own volition as shown in the Śruti: 'Let me enter these three deities with this living self (*jīva-ātman*) and differentiate names and forms'..."

Because of entering into the subtle material adjuncts (upādhi) of its own objects of cognition (cetya), and because of sustaining the vital breath (prāṇa) which supports those [adjuncts]—in accordance with the meaning of the verbal root *jīv* (to sustain life)—it is designated as "jīva" by means of that vital breath which is its object of cognition. Furthermore, since it perceives (cetayati) through the doors of the eyes and other senses, it has another name, "cit" or "cetana" (the conscious one); the meaning is that such a being is expressed by the word "jīva."
Neither atom nor gross, neither void nor anything at all;
pure consciousness whose nature is self-experience, all-pervading—this is called the individual soul (jīva). || 3 ||
He states its ultimate nature: "No. There is no void, nor is there anything whatsoever contained within that space. (3)
The wise know that the life-force (jīva) is the subtlest of the subtle, the grossest of the gross, and indeed not even a mere atom; it is all-pervading.
Know that whatever state belongs to whichever object, that very state exists there as its manifestation, due to the exclusive realization of its identity with that [object]. (5)

He demonstrates its omnipresence with the words "of whatever [it may be]": whatever entity exists—whether it be a genus, a quality, a configuration, or some other unique form—it remains situated and present as that very entity, appearing as if it were that very thing.
Why is this so? Because upon seeing it again and again, it is perceived exclusively through that specific form.

The meaning is as follows: because of the restriction of manifestation, when there is a conjunction between the eye and the jar, the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) having emerged through the door of the eye, causes the radiance of the individual consciousness (jīvacit) delimited by the jar—which is pervaded by its own modification—to be experienced with necessity, precisely through identity with the nature of the jar, as "this jar manifests" or "this jar is manifesting. || 5 ||
O Rāma, whatever it conceives, wherever, in whatever manner, and whenever— indeed that very thing arises at that time, in that place, and in that way, as the nature of experience.

For this very reason, wherever and in whatever manner the universal soul (samaṣṭijīva) perceives, it becomes so there, because of its power of true volition (satyasaṃkalpatva). The individual soul (vyaṣṭijīva), however, perceives in whatever manner it exists in a particular place.
Just as there is vibration in the wind, so indeed is there objectivity (cetya) in the individual soul (jīva);
this is to be determined solely by one's own consciousness, and not through instruction, like a yakṣa.

And so, just as there is vibration in the wind that is the collective individual soul (samaṣṭijīva), the creation—which consists of the consciousness of the diversity of all things—is its own nature, established by one's own experience like the vibration of the wind; it is not produced by instruction and practice, like a child’s delusion of a ghost. Thus he says: "of the wind. Nor is it due to instruction...
We do not accomplish [it] by means of instruction; the substitution of the verbal suffix (vikaraṇa) in the root *diś* is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*).
Just as the wind, by ceasing its vibration, becomes the very essence of existence (sat),
even so the living being (jīva), through the cessation of consciousness, while still living, attains the supreme state.

For this very reason, he says "just as" (yathaiva) to show that in liberation, deep sleep, and cosmic dissolution, both external and internal objects, as well as the state of being a living soul (jīvatā), subside within consciousness. [He attains] the supreme goal, which is the state of Brahman. || 8 ||
Because the individual soul (jīva) is of the nature of a mass of consciousness and possesses the awareness of "I," it remains having fashioned the powers of space, time, action, and substance.

In order to describe the manner of grasping its form, he first shows the superimposition of the collective ego (samaṣṭy-ahaṃkāra), which is the root-pillar of all conceptualization and has manifested all powers—beginning with the words "the individual soul" (jīva). [The word] "having created" means having manifested. That indeed is his...
Rudra-hood is characterized by the perfection of omniscience and omnipotence. || 9 ||
[The power] which, though itself unconditioned by space, time, action, or substance, appears as if real despite being unreal, expansive, and having that [very appearance] alone as its body; || 10 ||

Then, with the two and a half verses beginning with "deśa," he describes the conceptualization of the collective mind (*samaṣṭicitta*), which is characterized by the manifestation of the subtle latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the elements: [he describes it as] "discussed" because of its slight manifestation in the form of latent impressions, and "undiscussed" because of its complete non-manifestation in a gross form. (10)
For with his mind he perceives within himself the form of non-existence, like a particle of frost,
as if it were his own self, resembling his own death in a dream.
By means of the mind—that is, through the state of collective consciousness—from the most subtle intermingling [of elements], it becomes like a mass of frost-molecules. || 11 ||
Perceiving her as being like the various parts of one's own body in a dream,
and forgetting the state of pure consciousness, one quickly returns to that very [objective] state of existence.

When one perceives in a dream the state of being a tiger or the like, that which is experienced as an unnatural appearance of one's own limbs, such as hands and feet— that collective consciousness (samaṣṭicitta) resembling it is Viṣṇu-hood;
this occurs precisely when there is forgetfulness of one's own nature as the Full Brahman.

He explains that through the conceptualization of gross existence, characterized by the state of the moon which consists of the collective totality of the mind (*manaḥ-samaṣṭi*), the form of the Virāj in the shape of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) manifests— beginning with the words "having forgotten," and so forth. Having forgotten consciousness (*cetanā*),
which is the reality of Brahman consisting of the single essence of pure awareness (*cidekara-sā*), one identifies [the self] as "I" with nothing but limited, insentient existence.
Beholding that very state, one quickly attains it.
Awakening in such a manner, he then perceives a swelling within himself;
he quickly beholds his own self like the orb of the moon. (13)

Through the process of quintuplication (*pañcīkaraṇa*), by attaining grossness, there arises an expansion in the form of the Virāj, who is the collective totality (*samaṣṭi*) of the gross elements. In that state, one perceives the mind—which constitutes the collective totality—as being swift and having a liquid nature due to the accumulation of time, like the disc of the moon;
this very perception is what is meant by its manifestation as Virañci, characterized as the collective totality of the intellect (*buddhi*). || 13 ||
Then, within the self— which is of the nature of the lunar orb— he himself perceives this fivefold consciousness,
which has arisen as if distinct through a chance coincidence.

Regarding the manifestation of the organs for the sake of experience within the body of Virāj, he describes the pentad of organs in the form of the sun and so forth, as well as the conceptualization of their distinct locations, starting with the words "ātmani.
Since the differentiation of the organs is conceived solely through the differentiation of the objects of consciousness, they are referred to as the "fivefold consciousness. || 14 ||
Then, he perceives those five distinct parts of the five consciousnesses, and he also experiences the apertures that have their form in them. (15)
Those forms are the gateways for the enjoyment of form and so forth, appearing in various forms according to their different locations. || 15 ||
He shines forth afterwards as the five-limbed Virāṭ Puruṣa,
whose consciousness has infinite forms, whose nature is unmanifest, and who is free from all affliction.
He shines while enjoying the five objects through the constituent parts located in the five senses—namely, the sun, the directions, water, wind, and earth.
Because he imagines infinite forms through mental constructs regarding those objects, there arises the perception of infinite forms. And this very [perceiver]...
Because the state of being an effect is unreal, it is essentially nothing other than the manifestation of its own cause; for this very reason, it is free from affliction. || 16 ||
This mind-made [body] has arisen from the Supreme; it is the first to emerge, as clear as space, tranquil, and consisting of the radiance of eternal bliss. || 17 ||

With the intention that even though he consists of mind (*manomaya*), because he is endowed with self-established knowledge, sovereignty, and all powers, he possesses both the state of a living being (*jīvatva*) and the state of the Lord (*īśvaratva*), [the author] says in two verses beginning with "He is mind-made" (*manomayo'sau*). || 17 ||
And he, though not composed of the five elements, is like one whose nature consists of the five elements;
he is the Virāj-self, the one Puruṣa, the supreme Parameśvara.
The single Puruṣa who is the collective form of all Puruṣas. || 18 ||
It arises by itself and quickly vanishes by itself;
it expands by itself and likewise undergoes contraction by itself.
He states that even regarding its own manifestation and disappearance, it possesses sovereignty by virtue of its nature as Īśvara, saying: "by itself alone" (svayameva). || 19 ||
By means of a flood of aeons created by his own volition, or in a mere moment,
he arises again and again at will, and having come into being, he subsides once more.
This body of primordial nature (prakṛti) has as its sole essence the form of mind alone;
it is called the "city of eight" (puryaṣṭaka), the subtle transport-body (ativāhika) of every being. (21)

This very body belongs to the Lord who is the material cause of all; it is likewise the [body] of the entire multitude of living beings in their individualized state (*vyaṣṭi*). The "eightfold city" (*puryaṣṭaka*) has been explained previously. 21.
Subtle and gross, this self of the ether is manifest and unmanifest, devoid of end; it is both outside and inside of everything, yet it is neither anything nor nothing at all.
And that [Self] is subtle within the subtle bodies of ants and the like, according to such scriptural passages as "equal to a gnat, equal to an elephant," and so forth.
However, from the perspective of ultimate reality (paramārtha), it is nothing at all; yet from the perspective of conventional usage (vyavahāra), it is indeed somewhat limited.
O Rāma, its eight limbs are the five [senses] with the mind as the sixth;
these are the organs accompanied by egoism (ahaṃbhāva), consisting of both existence and non-existence.

The five organs of knowledge, along with the vital breath accompanied by the organs of action, the mind, and the ego—these are the eight limbs. They consist of both existence and non-existence, and have the forms of the essence of the manifest and the unmanifest. || 23 ||
By him these Vedas were sung together with the conceptualization of words and their meanings;
by him was established the cosmic order (niyati), which remains even today exactly as it was fixed.
Having become four-faced by means of that [power], he sang these four Vedas; Niyati is the boundary consisting of scriptural injunctions, traditional conduct, and so forth. || 24 ||
His head is infinite above, and likewise his soles are below;
this universe-pavilion has the boundless sky as its belly.

The sky above is his head; the earth below is the soles of his feet; and the intermediate space between them is his belly. Of this very Self, Vaiśvānara, the head is indeed *Sutejas* (the Brilliant), the eye is *Viśvarūpa* (the Multiform), the breath is *Pṛthagvartman* (the Diverse-pathed), the trunk is *Bahula* (the Abundant), and the bladder is *Rayi* (Wealth).
The intention is that this is based on such scriptural passages as, "The earth itself is his feet," and so forth. The phrase "the body" refers to the pavilion of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍamaṇḍapa).
The infinite other worlds are its sides; blood is its water;
the mountains are its masses of flesh; and the rivers are its continuous veins. (26)

The *pārśvakas* are the ribs and other such lateral parts of the body. *Payas* means water; *kṣataja* means blood (and this also serves as an elliptical designation for urine). The *kṣitidharas* are the mountains. The *māṃsapeśyas* are the rivers; the *sirās* are the vessels or arteries. || 26 ||
The oceans are the reservoirs of blood, the islands are the entrail-wrappings, the arms are the vast quarters of space, and the stars are the mass of body hair. (27)
The blood-vessels are the muscles that collect the blood; the "enclosure" is the enclosure of the six sheaths; the "quarters" are the directions and the arms.

Although it is stated in the Chāndogya and other texts that the body hairs are the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), nevertheless, in accordance with another Śruti, they are here said to be the stars. || 27 ||
The forty-nine aggregates of wind are the vital breaths;
the fierce solar orb is the bile and the digestive fire of the stomach. (28)
The forty-nine winds, beginning with Āvaha and Pravaha, are the vital breaths (prāṇavāyu). "Caṇḍa" means cruel;
the word "eye" is to be understood as the remainder [of the compound]. The digestive fire (jaṭharapāvaka) is the submarine fire (aurvānala) and the bile (pitta). || 28 ||
The ten marks, the orb, the individual soul (jīva), phlegm, semen, the white, strength, the mind, the self whose sheath is volition, the essential self, and the supreme nectar. (29)

The group of six beginning with *jīva* is indeed the lunar orb itself. "White" means the absence of fat. "The self whose sheath is volition" (*saṃkalpakośātmā*) is a qualification of the mind (*manas*). "Supreme nectar" (*parāmṛta*) is Brahman itself, the essential self. || 29 ||
She is the root of the tree of the body and the seed of the tree of karma;
she is the source from which all states of being arise, and like the moon, she is the cause of bliss.
He states that even the state of being seeds and so forth belongs to the mind alone, beginning with the words "the root," etc.:
"Because it nourishes [the body] through the state of food and so forth, it is the cause of bliss. (30)
That which is called the lunar orb is said to be the sovereign living soul (jīva);
it is the seed, the root, and the cause of the body, actions, and the mind. (31)
With the intention that this very Virāj is the individual soul (jīva) within the cosmic body, because it sustains the collective vital breaths through its nature as food, he says:

"That which... It is the seed of the individual bodies composed of food, the root of all actions caused by the vital breaths, and the cause of the individual minds; for the moon, having become the mind, entered the heart.
The meaning is that this is because of such scriptural passages as these. || 31 ||
From this Indu-virāj-jīva, the individual souls, minds, actions, pleasures, and nectars spread forth throughout the three worlds. (32)
He explains that very point clearly with the words "from this": pleasures are enjoyments, and nectars are liberations. || 32 ||
O Virāja, these—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Hara, and the others—are his volitions;
the gods, asuras, and sky-dwellers are the wondrous manifestations of his mind.

Of Virāj, that is, of the Virāj-jīva. Since even the bodies of the four-faced Brahmā and others are of the nature of a transformation of the lunar nectar (amṛta), [it is said]: "Soma flows, the progenitor of thoughts, the progenitor of heaven, the progenitor of earth; the progenitor of fire, the progenitor of the sun, the progenitor of Indra, and the progenitor of Viṣṇu"—such is the meaning according to the Śruti. "Sky-goers" refers to birds.
This is an illustration representing all living beings. || 33 ||
When the conscious nature, while awakening, quickly contemplates the state of being like a particle of frost at the very beginning, it then remains right there.
He reveals the wondrous nature of the mind as a manifestation of consciousness (*cit*) conditioned by the mind, stating: "the very nature of consciousness.

When the Virāj, the Lord of Creatures (*Prajāpati*), perceiving through his witness-consciousness the extremely subtle state of the atoms of frost—essentially the nature of nectar—as being within the moon, then at the beginning of creation, he contemplates and conceives the form of the bodies of deities and so forth; at that time, therein...
The meaning is that, because of his power of true resolve (*satya-saṃkalpatva*), he exists as if already accomplished even while assuming such bodies as those with four faces. || 34 ||
Therefore, O scion of Raghu’s line, know that this alone is the abode of the living soul;
this body, consisting of five members, is what is experienced.

This very lunar orb is the body of that Virāj—the cosmic totality of all living beings—whose limbs are the five unquintuplicated elements; this is experienced by everyone as the waking state. || 35 ||
From the Virāj, from the Jīva, and from the Moon, the life-principles of embodied beings issue forth as food-born entities, in the form of a diffusion of frost.
He establishes what was previously stated regarding the emanation of the individual living beings (*vyaṣṭijīva*) from the Virāṭ living being (*virāḍjīva*), beginning with the word "Virāṭ.
The term "living beings" (*jīvabhūtāni*) refers to the means of life. It is by way of the moon's digits—the spreading of dew—that [the Virāṭ] flows forth into the medicinal herbs. || 36 ||
These very [elements], having become the mind, cause living beings to live within the bodies of embodied beings; they exert themselves through activity, being the cause of births in various actions.
The individual souls (jīvas) are the limiting adjuncts (upādhis) of the soul. || 37 ||
In this way, thousands of Virāṭs and hundreds of Mahākalpas have passed, and likewise will pass; they exist with various modes of conduct. || 38 ||
The words "thousand" (sahasra) and "hundred" (śata) refer to the innumerable; and they exist at present as well. 38.

By means of this existence, which consists of universal experience and is non-different from the supreme state, and by virtue of its union with the great body that is devoid of interior, he stands as the Supreme Person, the Virāj. (39)

From the supreme state of Brahman, by means of that very non-differentiated foundational reality (adhiṣṭhāna-sattā) which is thus devoid of end, limitless, and great in its bodily union— that is, its connection with individual and collective bodies—
the Virāṭ Puruṣa is its illusory transformation (vivarta), as described; thus, in every respect and at all times and places, here within Brahman veiled by Māyā.
"It remains" is the conclusion. || 39 ||

Thus ends the nineteenth sarga, titled "The Description of the Virāḍātman," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, according to the Ṛṣi tradition. 19.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Virāḍ-Ātman," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The Twentieth Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
This person of volition (saṃkalpa-puruṣa) indeed fashions whatever he himself wills.
Thus, in that manner, it becomes like the sky, consisting of the five elements.

In this world, the equality of individual souls (jīvas) with the collective totality is described through the creation of volitions that correspond to their latent impressions (vāsanās), karmas, and desires.
He states that Brahman assumes the form of an evolution (vivarta) following the will of the Virāṭ-puruṣa, whose resolve is true: "By his resolve" (saṃkalpa).
Whatever the Virāṭ-puruṣa, who consists of the five elements, resolves—"let this be thus"—that very thing becomes so, even as the void Brahman, the ether (kha). || 1 ||
O Rāma, the wise know that the entire world that has arisen is His volition;
it is spread out, possessing such a form, and directed toward the objects of the fivefold self.

The meaning is that, because of the latent impressions (vāsanā) deposited by his prior worship of Brahman, he assumed at the beginning of creation such a form as the Virāj, whose nature consists of the five elements; having become so, he became intent upon the enjoyment of the collective objects of experience consisting of the five great elements, which are the fruits of that worship. || 2 ||
The Virāṭ is the cause of the entire multitude of objects in the world;
therefore, effects are indeed equal to their cause. || 3 ||

The connection with what follows is as follows: because effects such as jars arise from causes such as clay with a nature identical [to that of the cause], for this reason [the effect is non-different from the cause]. || 3 ||
Just as this Virāj is indeed the Virāj within each individual self,
he expands within his own consciousness as one possessed of awareness, and not as one devoid of awareness.
The meaning is that even each individual soul (*vyaṣṭijīva*) is, within its own self, a cosmic being (*virāṭ*) capable of all creation.

Since, in accordance with the modifications of the mind, this [individual] also expands within its own consciousness in the form of external and internal objects—just like the cosmic being—it possesses the awareness of those respective objects and is not devoid of awareness; such is the sense of their equality. || 4 ||
Thus, from the subtle to the reptilian and up to the god Rudra, this world-appearance has arisen;
though it resides even within an atom, it expands like a tree within the seed-vessel.
From the lower limit of the scale down to the crawling insects, and from the upper limit up to Rudra, this very delusion in the form of the world has arisen;
that alone is creation. This is the logical justification for the nature of delusion even in the case of the atom. || 5 ||
From the crawling insect up to Rudra, the Virāṭ exists within each individual self;
yet even in the Supreme Self, this is due to the realization of the infinite Self, and not due to a lack of realization.
"Let it be so; what follows from that? To this he replies: "down to the crawling reptiles. Virāṭ is the creator. Thus, equality is established—this is the meaning. || 6 ||
Just as this expansion has come to be within the Virāṭ Self,
so too is it here within every single being, even one as small as an atom.
Even in an element (bhūta) as minute as a living being (jīva), whose body is limited to the size of a mosquito or a gnat.
In the ultimate sense, there is nothing whatsoever, whether gross or subtle, anywhere;
whatever is extended wherever it may be, that is experienced exactly as it is.
"Extended" means expanded through delusion. || 8 ||
The mind was born from the moon; the moon arose from the mind.
Likewise, the individual soul arises from the universal soul; indeed, this is but a single existence, like water and its fluidity.

[Objection: But surely there is a disparity because the individual mind (*vyaṣṭi-manas*) of Virāj and the individual soul (*jīva*) presided over by it both possess causal agency; how then can there be equality? To this he says: "The mind. Alternatively, since this very same Being (*sattā*) is one and the same in both the collective totality (*samaṣṭi*) and the individual (*vyaṣṭi*), there is no distinction at all; how then could there be causality therein? Such is the meaning of "no difference" (*aviśeṣa*). || 9 ||
They know the living soul (jīva) to be the essence of semen, resembling a drop of frost;
from that very source, the multitude of immovable mountains of bliss proceeds.

Having thus refuted the mind’s status as the cause through its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), he states the nature of the adjunct in order to refute the [Brahman’s] status as the cause with respect to the conditioned individual soul (*jīva*): "having semen as its essence" (*śukrasāram*).

First, it refers to that whose essence—the limiting adjunct—is semen itself. Then, from the very soul conditioned by that semen, at the time of the parents’ union, [the embryo arises] from the immovable...

Through the reflection of the Brahman of full bliss (*pūrṇānanda*) upon the mental modification (*vṛtti*) in the form of enjoyment, there arises the "outpouring" (*saṃdoha*), which is bliss characterized by complete fulfillment. This is the meaning of the Vedic scripture: "Other beings subsist on a mere fraction of this very bliss. One should then [perceive] that fullness, appearing as such, situated within the self, by means of the self in the mind.
Therein she assumes identity with that; by means of that, she takes on a form composed of that.

He perceives—that is, experiences through his own self—by means of his very nature as the seed, that bliss which is the characteristic manifestation of that Brahman, abiding within the individual soul (jīva) whose consciousness is delimited by the seed. As it were perceiving, he assumes an identity with that bliss in the form of the seed, thinking, "I am the most beloved bliss"; for from bliss alone [does this arise].
For it is stated in the Śruti: "Indeed, these beings are born from this. (11)
When this consciousness of the living being attains the state of the five elements (death),
there exists therein no cause whatsoever, nor is there any state of being an effect.
Immediately thereafter, this consciousness of the individual soul (jīva-saṃvit) attains identity with the fivefold state within it that has the form of the body.
That very [identity] constitutes its being conditioned by that [body]; and in that regard, neither Virāj nor any other [cause] is the cause. Thus he says: "Not there. (12)

Because there is no exclusion of a counter-correlate for its own nature and its essential character, the description of essential character (*svabhāvokti*) does not occur here in accordance with the actual meaning. (13)

If there is no cause for that superimposed form, then it would be non-adventitious and the very nature of living beings; and since the nature of nothing whatsoever can be lost, this would lead to the undesirable consequence of no liberation (anirmokṣa). Anticipating this objection, he says: "pratiyogī" (the counter-correlative). In this context, the expression "nature" (svabhāva) applied to the superimposed form is not meaningful or appropriate, because [nature] is defined by the meaning of the word "self" (sva).

The meaning of the word *bhāva* (existence) is intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). In this context, if the word *sva* (self/intrinsic) refers to something pure, then because that [pure thing] is non-dual, there exists neither a counter-correlative nor any exclusion of it; thus, since it is non-excluding, even the meaning of the word *bhāva* cannot be defined as "other than that. Consequently, the establishment of an object qualified by that [intrinsic nature] is far from being possible—this is the meaning. || 13 ||

The living being (jīva) exists as the state of being alive precisely because of its own nature as a living being; it is perceived internally and externally by itself, yet not [as a material object], like the wind.

Or, if the word "self" (sva-śabda) refers to that which is superimposed (upahita), even then it does not obtain a referent for the word "being" (bhāva-śabdārtha) that exists outside of itself and could qualify its own meaning; thus he says: "the living being" (jīva). Even the living being, though of a superimposed nature, is by its very nature a living being; and because it is of a superimposed nature, its state of being a living being is itself merely of a superimposed nature, not something distinct from it.
No other form, whether internal or external, which could constitute the referent of the word "being" (bhāva) and be fit to serve as a substantive, is perceived therein.
