Just as in the expression "the wind blows," the wind is essentially the action itself, yet it is designated as "it blows" by conceptually constructing a distinction through the discursive intellect (*vikalpabuddhi*), so too [is it said] "the living being lives" (*jīvo jīvati*) by means of the relationship between attribute and substrate (*dharmadharmibhāva*). This is the meaning. || 14 ||
Enveloped as if by mist, intent upon unreal objects, the self of the wind does not perceive the path, like one born blind. || 15 ||

If it is neither produced nor eternal, and not even its own inherent nature, then what is this form of the living being (*jīva*) that transmigrates? To this, he replies with the verse beginning "By mist" (*nīhāreṇa*), stating that it is none other than Brahman itself, veiled by indeterminable ignorance (*anirvacanīyājñāna*), whose transmigration is simply the perception of itself as something other than what it is. Thus, the "wind-natured one" (*mārutātmā*) is one who has attained identification with the insentience of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the senses, and so forth; for this very reason—
The meaning is that one does not perceive its true nature, as stated in such Vedic passages as: "You do not know him who generated these beings; another has indeed become the interval between you.
Enveloped by mist and prattling, the reciters of hymns wander about, seeking only their own breath. (RV 10.82.7). || 15 ||
Through the world-expansion (jagajjṛmbhikā), the individual soul assumes duality instead of its own unity;
like the wind enveloped by the power of vibration, it does not perceive its true self. 16.

Enveloped by the power of ignorance (*avidyā-śakti*), which manifests as the yawning and swelling of the world-form, he therefore imagines a duality—namely, the seer and the seen—within his own essential unity; having thus imagined it, he remains fixed and attached to it. || 16 ||
The dissolution of ignorance—the great knot, consisting of false objects of cognition, unreal, and having the form of the object "I"—is traditionally known as liberation (mokṣa). || 17 ||
For this very reason, since the destruction of ignorance is possible through knowledge, there is no fault of non-liberation; thus he says: "of ignorance.
The "tearing asunder" (bhedo) is the splitting open of the great knot consisting of the object of the notion "I. || 17 ||
With dense consciousness entirely dispelled, remain indeed without perceiving "I" on any side;
being of a single nature that is not dense with expressible consciousness, you shall be forever arisen as that which is neither existent nor non-existent, yet both existent and non-existent.

Therefore, O Rāma, you— being one from whom the dense cloud of ignorance has departed (*vyapagata-ghana*), thus being pure consciousness (*cetana*) consisting of the light of the Intellect (*cit-prakāśa-mātra*), and not perceiving the limitation imposed by the adjunct of egoism (*ahaṃkāra-upādhi-pariccheda*)— are one who has realized the purified meaning of the term "Thou" (*tvaṃ-padārtha*). Thus, you have attained [the state of] peace.
Remaining as that which is sublated— the formal (mūrta), the non-existent and formless (amūrta), and the root-ignorance (ajñāna) consisting of both existence and non-existence—

be thou completely full, being of the nature of that purified *tat-pada-artha*, a single mass of the essence of bliss like a solid lump of salt, a consciousness devoid of name due to the sublation of form, and identical in nature with that alone. 18.

Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "Instruction on the Yoga of the Extinction of the Living Soul," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa, within the Mokṣopāya section of the Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa composed by the sage Vālmīki. 20.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "Instruction on the Yoga of the Extinction of the Living Soul," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The Twenty-first Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
O Rāma, one should always be a man of knowledge, not merely a kinsman of knowledge.
I consider an ignorant person better than the state of being a kinsman through knowledge.
In this regard, the kinship of knowledge is twofold—both impure and pure;
it is described by its characteristics as that which is to be abandoned and that which is to be adopted with effort.

Therein, he first constructs an introductory framework (pīṭhikā) to describe those things to be abandoned, beginning with the words "only by the knower" (*jñāninā eva*). One must always be such a knower— whose characteristics will be described in the subsequent section of this work—
because, under the pretext of knowledge, one might otherwise obstruct virtuous action and devotion through a craving for enjoyment, [thereby harming] oneself and others.
And since it binds one with misfortunes, one should not be such a "knot of knowledge" (jñānabandhu); this is the meaning. || 1 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
Who is called a kinsman of knowledge, and who is called a knower?
What is the fruit of being a kinsman of knowledge, and what is the fruit of being a knower?

Having attained what characteristic is one called a "kinsman of knowledge" (jñānabandhu), and having attained what characteristic is one called a "knower" (jñānin)? Please tell me, O Puruṣa, regarding those characteristics and their results; such is the meaning of the question. || 2 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
He who explains and recites the scripture for the sake of enjoyment, like a craftsman, but does not strive in its practice, is called a "friend of knowledge" (jñānabandhu). || 3 ||
He who does not strive in the means for knowledge—namely, in practice, in the accomplishment of the fourfold qualification, and in reflection and so forth. || 3 ||
He in whom awareness is seen to bear fruit amidst the vibrations of karma is called a "kinsman of knowledge" (jñānabandhu), because he subsists by the craft of awareness. || 4 ||

He whose verbal understanding, acquired through the study of the scriptures, is not seen to bear fruit—through detachment, cessation, and other such results—in the vibrations of karma and in the visible affairs of worldly enjoyment; for his craft of understanding consists in the cleverness of deceiving others, as he subsists upon that very [learning]. (4)
Those who, satisfied with mere clothing and food, recognize the fruits of the scriptures as their kinsmen through knowledge— them one should know as artisans of the meaning of the scriptures.

One should recognize those who believe that the fruits of the scriptures consist merely of wealth, clothing, food, and gain as being like actors and other craftsmen who merely perform the drama of explaining the meaning of the scriptures. || 5 ||
He who abides in the Dharma characterized by active engagement as it is found in the scriptures is called a "kinsman of knowledge," because true knowledge is not far from him.
He indicates the second auspicious form of the kinship of knowledge by means of its characteristic: "in the characteristic of active engagement" (*pravṛttilakṣaṇe*).

This refers to the characteristic of active engagement consisting of desireless *agnihotra* and other such rites; it is appropriate for what has been heard—that is, for the knowledge of the meaning of the scriptures—and suitable for what is to be heard, namely the study of the Vedānta, by way of purifying the mind. Thus, it is "heard" (*śrute*) in the sense of being conducive [to that goal].

The meaning is as follows: [this practice] is appropriate because it is enjoined by the Vedas (*śruti*) and is consistent with the customs of one's own station and family; for the Veda states, "They desire to know through sacrifice, through charity, through austerity," and so forth. Furthermore, since the performance of virtuous deeds necessarily leads to knowledge through the sequence of purification of the mind—as understood from the etymological derivation that one is "bound" (liberated) by knowledge—it is understood that knowledge is not far off. || 6 ||
They know self-knowledge to be true knowledge; as for whatever other forms of knowledge there may be, they are merely reflections of knowledge, because they do not comprehend the essential reality.

Even those devoted to the study of treatises on non-self (anātma-śāstra) are seen to be connected with various cognitions of their respective objects; lest this [self] be like them, he demonstrates the distinction of the knowledge of the Self (ātmajñāna) with the words "the knowledge of the Self. Those [other cognitions] appear as if they were knowledge, but they are not truly knowledges. Why? Because of their essence (rasa), which is substantial and indestructible.
The two exist together with the Self that is unsurpassed bliss; thus they are "sarasau" (possessing essence), meaning the world and the individual soul are superimposed upon it.
Their state is "sārasyam" (essentiality), which is precisely the essence of Brahman as their substratum.
Due to the lack of realization of that [Brahman], and because only the objects of superimposition—which are sublatable—are perceived, [the world] exists merely as an illusion.
The meaning is: because it is merely a wave of ignorance. || 7 ||
Those who, failing to attain self-knowledge, are satisfied with a mere fragment of other forms of knowledge, are considered "kinsmen of knowledge" despite their arduous efforts.

For this very reason, he says "knowledge of the Self" to show that for those who are satisfied merely with the attainment of that [lower knowledge], there is only the bondage of the knowledge of impurity. They are satisfied in such a way that their actions involve painful exertions— characterized by the acquisition of defects such as false pride through the toil of practice, and resulting in worldly misfortune in the next life— and for that reason, they too [are bound].
The meaning is that they are remembered as kinsmen of the knowledge of the foul (aśubha). || 8 ||

O Rāma, one whose mind is not contented should not dwell here without the pacification of the expansion of that which is to be known through knowledge and its like; having attained the state of being a kinsman to knowledge, rejoice, and do not take pleasure in the diseases of worldly enjoyments.

For this very reason, he states "jñānādi" [and so forth] to show that one who desires liberation must not become complacent merely by reaching the stability of the seventh stage. "Jñāna" refers to the mental fluctuations (*vṛtti*) whose objects are both external and internal; by the word "ādi" (and so forth), their causes and their substratum—the cognizer (*pramātṛ*)—are included. Their "objects" (*jñeya*) are sound and the rest, and their "expansions" (*vikāśa*) are [the manifestations of those objects].

And because of their renown, one who desires liberation should not, with a mind satisfied by merely attaining an intermediate stage, think "I have achieved my goal" without establishing oneself in the identity of the Self with Brahman— which is self-luminous, of the sole essence of perfect bliss, and characterized by absolute peace.
One must never slacken the effort required to attain each successive stage. O Rāma,

although you are proficient in all branches of learning, you have nonetheless attained the status of a "friend of knowledge" by either neglecting the study of the science of the Self due to attachment to other fields, or by displaying skill in instructing those who are not yet qualified.
The meaning is: do not take delight in the diseases of worldly existence, which are characterized by enjoyments driven by fame, gain, and the like. || 9 ||
In this regard, one should perform blameless work for the sake of food; one should take food for the sake of sustaining the life-breaths.
The life-breaths should be sustained for the sake of inquiring into reality; reality should be inquired into so that there may be no further suffering. (10)

How, then, should one who desires liberation abide? To this he says: "In this regard" (atra). Regarding food—meaning the consumption of what is wholesome, moderate, and pure—one should perform the work of acquiring food and so forth by means that are irreproachable according to the Śruti, Smṛti, and the conduct of the wise, and by means appropriate to one's own caste and stage of life (varṇāśrama) for the sake of that [liberation], that is, for the attainment of its means. The rest is clear. || 10 ||
Thus ends the twenty-first canto, titled "The Investigation of Knowledge," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the glorious Vāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa of Valmīki, composed by the Sage. 21.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Investigation of Knowledge," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The Twenty-second Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Through knowledge, because of its abiding in the object of knowledge, that which is both non-mind and indeed mind—
He who does not perceive the fruit of action is called a man of knowledge.
First, the characteristics of the knower are proclaimed here with supporting arguments;
likewise, the nature of the individual soul, the world, Brahman, and so forth, are discussed as they arise in the context.

Having described the state of being a kinsman through knowledge (*jñānabandhutā*) and its fruit, [the author] now states the characteristics of the man of knowledge (*jñānin*) in order to answer the two questions: "What is called a man of knowledge? and "Even in the state of being a man of knowledge, what is the fruit? He begins with the words "By knowledge" (*jñānena*).
That person who, by means of knowledge fully ripened through the sequence of ascending the stages (*bhūmikā*), [rests] in the Knowable which is Brahman alone—

Because of his firm establishment in the Self, even while experiencing the fruits of prārabdha-karma, the wise one does not perceive as real the non-conscious objects such as sound—which are distinct from consciousness and transformed into various forms—nor the mind itself, which has transformed into various mental modifications such as desire and volition; for he understands that these are merely the persistence of what was previously sublated. Thus, he is called a knower (jñānī).
The meaning is that it is so designated by those who know the characteristics of the *tallaka*. || 1 ||
He who, having correctly understood the true instruction, perceives within all actions the nature of the self as being free from latent impressions— he is called a man of knowledge.

Likewise, for the knower—the cognizing subject who experiences objects such as sound and so forth—there is an authorization (*anujñāna*) regarding the objects of experience within the functions of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) in every act of cognition. This is an *avyayībhāva* compound used in the sense of repetition (*vīpsā*). Having correctly known, according to reality, that which exists as pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) by way of being the witness (*sākṣitayā*) in all the various modifications of perception such as sight and so forth, [one realizes that the ego-sense] is sublated.

The meaning is that he is a man of knowledge (*jñānin*) who perceives the visible world as being devoid of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), such that not even a trace of impression remains. Alternatively, having correctly understood that reality by knowing which the mind becomes free from impressions,
for that wise one who abides [in that state], regarding the actions of all living beings— that is, their activities according to their desires— [he remains unattached].
Only permission is seen in the form of the words "let them act as they please.
The meaning is that he who even approves of the activities of bandits—such as the seizing of their own wealth, killing, and imprisonment—is a man of knowledge (*jñānī*).
This, however, is well known in the case of Jaḍabharata and others. || 2 ||
He whose internal coolness is perceived by the wise amidst all desires, and who possesses a singular, unartificial peace—he is called a man of knowledge (jñānī). (3)
Of him who is at peace through a single, uncreated attainment of his own self, there is no striving in worldly activities. || 3 ||
That realization which leads to non-rebirth is what truly bears the name of "knowledge";
all else—providing clothing and food, as well as the regulation of one's livelihood through a craft—is merely a means of subsistence.

He states that only the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna) is true knowledge because it cuts off the ignorance that is the root of rebirth, and nothing else; thus he says: "for the sake of non-rebirth. The remaining skill in verbal knowledge other than that, which merely provides clothing and food—like any other craft—is only a means of livelihood and is not denoted by the word "knowledge" (jñāna). || 4 ||
He who remains with his heart like space, free from desire and volition, while engaged in actions that have fallen into the natural flow, is called a wise man.
He whose heart possesses an unobstructed radiance like the autumnal sky. || 5 ||
Entities appear as if they proceed without a cause;
though non-existent, they remain as if they were existent. (6)
In order to establish that the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna) destroys all latent impressions of duality (*dvaitavāsanā*) so as to fulfill the definition previously stated,
[the author] demonstrates the causelessness and non-existence of the world by showing that it is nothing but unreal ignorance (*asadavidyāmātra*),
starting with the words "without cause" (*akāraṇam*). Since they do not exist, they proceed without a cause— that is, independently of any cause.
They appear as if they arise, but in reality they do not arise; likewise, though non-existent, they remain as if they were present.
Through manifestations and disappearances, through existence and non-existence, and through becoming and non-becoming,
they subsequently become causes for one another through mutual causal activities.
With the intention that non-existence must likewise be understood in the case of the subsequent modifications of existence because they too lack causality, he says: "In manifestation...
Now, since the production of a sprout from a seed is directly perceived, how can it be said that they proceed without a cause?
To this, he says: "...subsequently. This is not possible at the beginning of creation, [as it occurs] during the dissolution (*pralaya*).
The meaning is that both the seed and the sprout would be non-existent; [this occurs] through the causal actions, that is, the operations of the causes. || 7 ||
Just as in the case of a non-existent hare’s horn or the water of a mirage—which cannot be obtained even by looking—what kind of cause could there possibly be for such things? (8)

Is the seed currently being perceived the cause of a sprout that already exists or one that does not exist? Not the first, because that which already exists has no need for a cause. It is not the second either; thus he says with two verses beginning with "asataḥ" (of the non-existent). 8.
Those who search for the cause of non-existent things, such as a hare’s horn, are reaching for the shoulder of the grandson of a barren woman’s son. (9)

They reach and ascend. For those who do not possess [the cause] and seek its means, the successive examples are the climbing onto the shoulders of sons, grandsons, and their respective groups. || 9 ||
For those things that appear despite being unreal, this alone is the swift cause:
namely, non-perception, which perishes in the very moment of perception. (10)

If, in order to avoid the consequence of non-liberation and to establish the authority of the scriptures on liberation, a cause must necessarily be postulated for the acceptance of the state of non-dual causelessness,

then that cause should be postulated as nothing other than false ignorance (*ajñāna*), which is removable by knowledge alone; it cannot be anything else of the nature of reality (*sadrūpa*), since such a thing cannot be removed by knowledge.
With the intention that, because it is impossible to turn back [the mind], there would follow the undesirable consequence of an eternal state of non-liberation, he says: "asatyā" (unreal).
Non-perception is ignorance. || 10 ||
When the individual soul perceives the insentient as its own, it becomes like the Supreme Self;
however, when it perceives the sentient as its own, it remains merely as the individual soul.
He demonstrates that bondage is the effect of ignorance and that it perishes in an instant upon the arising of true insight, stating: "The Supreme.

This individual soul (jīva), while perceiving the "Supreme"—that which is other than itself, insentient, and inert, such as the ego and the body—as being identical with itself, immediately acts like the Self due to the awakening of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of that superimposition of identity; this very process is its bondage.

The meaning is this: one who realizes the Self as the pure consciousness extracted from the conscious agent (*cetana*)—the individual soul (*jīva*) itself—remains as that very non-dual, unsurpassed bliss extracted [from all attributes], which, according to the direction shown by the scripture, "by which [the soul] knows and by which all beings live," is the cause of the sustenance of the entire world; that is his liberation. Alternatively, *cetana* refers to the intellect (*buddhi*), because by means of it [the object] is perceived (*cetyate*). Or, it refers to that in which [the object] is perceived.

The gross body is the conscious [entity]. Consciousness is the activity of consciousness, which is the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa). Realizing the Self as the immutable, non-dual pure consciousness that is devoid of those three, one acts like the Supreme Self and becomes the Supreme Self.
One remains established in the singular nature of non-dual, full bliss. Consciousness...

The meaning is that one who perceives the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth as the Self remains merely as a living individual (*jīva*) and does not attain the state of fullness. Alternatively, this living being [perceives] the conscious [Self] as being devoid of consciousness— that is, as if it were unconscious— by means of the mere pervasion of the mental modifications (*vṛtti*) regarding objects such as those seen by the eyes, and not by the pervasion of their results (*phala*).

Thus, one who perceives the self as being of the nature of self-luminous consciousness (*svaprakāśacidrūpa*) is indeed the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) and not the non-self (*anātman*), for not even an atom of the non-self can be perceived without being pervaded by the fruit [of consciousness]. However, when the conscious self perceives even an atom [of an object] in such a way that it is pervaded by a mental modification (*vṛtti*), it remains merely as the individual soul (*jīva*) and does not abide in its own true nature as Brahman.
The meaning is that he attains [it]. And thus says the Śruti: "He for whom it is not thought, by him it is thought; he who thinks he knows it does not know it.
It is unknown to those who understand it, and known to those who do not understand it. (11)
This very Supreme Self, while becoming conscious of the insentient, becomes a living being (jīva),
just as a mango tree itself attains the state of a *sahakāra* through the acquisition of sap.

He explains the first half [of the verse] with the words "the Supreme Self alone. This individual soul (*jīva*), perceiving within itself—according to the manner described above—that which is insentient and non-awakening, becomes the Supreme Self itself through the immersion into the essence of the Supreme Self; just as a mango tree, being almost asleep during the winter, [awakens] in the spring.

The meaning is that, like a mango tree (*sahakāra*) which, through the infusion of sap, becomes sprouted, flowered, and nearly fully awakened, it attains the designation of that [tree]; he explains the second half of the verse as well with the words "the conscious one" (*cetanam*). Throughout various births—that is, births in diverse wombs—the individual soul (*jīva*) remains as nothing other than the conscious one who is becoming aware.
The living soul is worn out by births and lives that have become decrepit through the process of living. || 13 ||
For those who have attained the supreme vision, their method is like that of water:
it is always a state of non-perception of form, a thoughtlessness, and a vibration that is truly non-vibration.

For this very reason, he says "those who... to show that the activities of those who know reality are indeed of a non-vibrant (aspanda) nature due to the absence of identification with them; [such activity] is devoid of identification with form, light, thought, or ego. The meaning is that it follows only what has been commenced by past impressions (prārabdha), just as water follows a downward slope. || 14 ||
For those who have attained the supreme vision and have seen beyond the splendor of the visible,
even that which exists does not appear as an extended perception to them.

Just as the sight of a burnt cloth is not the sight of a cloth but rather the sight of ashes, so too the sight of the glory of the perceivable world when it has been sublated is nothing other than the sight of the Brahman that transcends it; with the intention that they possess no perception of duality, he says: "Those who... (verse 15).
Know that for those who have attained the supreme vision,
all movement and non-movement here are like water, occurring solely through the power of non-perception.
For this reason as well, with the intention that their vibration is non-vibration even in the absence of the perception of form, he says "ye" (those who), using water as an illustration. || 16 ||
Unencumbered by the pursuit of form, light, or reflection, like one who has cast off a garland, the wise engage in actions just as the wind moves through the leaves of a tree. (17)

And for this very reason, he states that there is an absence of the bondage of the taint of karma for them: "formless," etc. Since they are not enveloped by the perception of form, they are like a bull that has cast off its tether; thus, the meaning is that they are devoid of bondage. || 17 ||
Those who have attained the supreme vision and see the further shore of saṃsāra do not praise ritual action, just as one living by a river does not praise a well.
With the intention that the expectation of results in the next world is utterly cast aside, he says: "Those who... (verse 18).
O sinless one, those deluded ones who possess bound attachments praise ritual action;
because of that, they proceed toward ignorance, even though it is consistent with the Śruti and Smṛti.

But for those who lack knowledge, action alone is their refuge; thus he says, "Those who... Without awakening—that is, due to the absence of the knowledge of reality—they proceed by that very action alone; the ellipsis is that they attain the experience of its fruit. || 19 ||
The senses fall upon an object like a vulture upon fallen meat;
having restrained them with the mind, one should sit disciplined and intent upon that [Self]. 20.
From where does their very action [arise]? To this he says: "The senses. That which has fallen away is that which has descended;
that is to say, the cause of downward descent. The sense is that when there is no support for virtuous action, the senses must effect their downward fall.
And thus says the Śruti: "Performing actions here alone, one should desire to live a hundred years. Thus...

"By you, there is no other way; thus action does not cling to the man. For this very reason, he says "those [senses]" (verse 20), meaning that even for the wise person, the establishment in one's true nature is accomplished only when there is restraint of the senses, and not otherwise.
There is no gold without its arrangement, nor does Brahman exist without its manifestation;
however, for one of disciplined intellect, the auspicious [Brahman] is described by means of the meanings of words such as "manifestation" and so forth.

Just as there is a similarity of arrangement between an unburnt and a burnt cloth, let it be granted that for the ignorant—and even for the wise—there appears to be a similarity of arrangement in the world; nevertheless, with the intention that for those who know, it is Brahman alone, he says: "not without arrangement.
When total darkness has set in at the end of the age, worldly activity [continues].
It is without division and without appearance, just as it is in the density of Brahman.

Since the meaning of the word "creation" (sarga) has been explained, he states that "dissolution" (pralaya) is the illustrative example—beginning with the words "eka... and so on. Likewise, the ellipsis is to be supplied as: "though non-existent, it appears as existent. (22)

Just as within the interior of a cloud there exists the nature of the wandering vapors, consisting of both motion and stillness, so too is the sovereign existence of all beings, which is essentially self-consciousness. 23.
To one who cannot conceive of the existence of vibration during the dissolution (pralaya), he provides an illustration with the words "within a cloud": just as within a moving cloud,

the existence of its constituent parts is conceived through the simultaneous presence of contradictory attributes— being devoid of motion due to their non-separation from the cloud, yet possessing motion due to the division of space— as established by the direct awareness of one's own experience.
In the same way, even at the time of dissolution, the existence of vibration within the Lord is to be conceived as being present in all beings; such is the meaning. || 23 ||
Just as within water there exists a vibration consisting of both duality and non-duality regarding the various portions of water,
so too does the perception of beings exist within Brahman as its own conscious self.
In that regard, he provides an illustration for the existence of the vibration of the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*), stating: "of water.

From the stillness of water—such as the water of a placid pond—the self-nature of one's own consciousness, which is the consciousness of Brahman, becomes the witness of beings (*bhūtadṛk*) and the appearance of various individual souls (*jīvābhāsa*); this state is difficult to describe in terms of either difference or non-difference (*bhedābhedābhyām*). || 24 ||

Just as the creation of the portions of the sky appears within the sky— which is both dual and non-dual by nature— as something non-different from it, so too does it appear within Śiva, who is without parts.
He provides an illustration for the existence of the differentiated world within that which is partless: "Just as," etc.
This refers to the portions of space (*ambarāṃśa*), which are the parts of the ether (*ākāśa*) appearing in the form of the various directions. || 25 ||
The world exists within the form of the "I," and the form of the "I" exists within the world;
they are interwoven with one another like the layers of a plantain leaf-sheath.
In this very manner, it may also be understood that the previously mentioned mutual inclusion of the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) and the world is possible; thus he says: "Of the world... (verse 26).
Through the apertures of form, light, and mental attention— as if situated outside [the reading is "as if situated outside by the blind"]—
the individual soul perceives the creation within itself, just as a mountain gazes upon a lake. || 27 ||
He provides an illustration for the individual soul (jīva), whose nature is ego (ahaṃkāra), seeing the world contained within itself as if it were external: "Like a form," etc.
Just as a mountain such as the Himavat sees the very water contained within itself emerging through its own cavities as the great lakes Mānasa and others, so it is in this case. || 27 ||
This living soul perceives itself as the world without cause, just as gold perceives itself as bracelets and the like; not perceiving that [gold], it does not perceive [the world]. || 28 ||

Just as the forms of bracelets and other ornaments, which existed in the past or will exist in the future, are perceived upon close examination within a lump of gold but are not seen when one looks only at the gold itself, so too is the world [perceived] within the living self (jīva). Thus he says: "The living self. This means that it is without cause, without basis, and exists only through delusion. || 28 ||
Though living, they do not truly live; though dead, they do not die.
Though existing, they are as if non-existent—those auspicious ones who know the near and the far shore.

For this very reason, he says—“They live”—that for those who perceive that [reality], the states of birth, death, and worldly existence do not exist at all, even though they appear real to others, for those who are liberated while living (jīvanmukta). || 29 ||
The awakened one, even while performing all actions, does not perceive them,
just as a householder engaged in domestic chores remains his mind fixed on the cattle-pen and its vessels.

One whose mind is attached to Brahman has no sense of agency regarding the activities of maintaining the body, just as one whose mind is attached to the household utensils has no such sense regarding domestic chores; thus he says: "The awakened one" (verse 30).
Just as the Virāṭ is in the heart like the moon, so does the individual soul (jīva) abide in every body;
it takes the form of a drop of frost—large when the body is large, and small when the body is small.

Having concluded the incidental discussion, he resumes the subject at hand with the word "virāṭ": Just as the Virāṭ-jīva, who is like the moon, resides in the heart of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), so too does the jīva, in the form of a drop of semen or frost, reside in the heart of every individual body;
this is the meaning. || 31 ||
I, the Self, undergoes the conceptualization of being a triangle;
though non-existent, the conscious body imagines itself to have the appearance of existence. (32)

He describes the manner of his taking on a body: "I am the Self. That living being (*jīva*), whose nature is the ego (*ahaṃkāra*), situated in the father's heart in the form of semen, is discharged by the father into the triangular womb of the mother; it then undergoes the conceptualization of being delimited by that triangle. There, it becomes mixed with the blood present therein.

The body, which is actually non-existent, manifests through the sequence of stages such as the embryo (kalala), the bubble (budbuda), and the mass (piṇḍa); yet, the consciousness conceives of it as "I," taking the form of something real. || 32 ||
In the treasury of karma and in the triangle, the Self abides as the essence of Śukra within the body, just as fragrance resides in a flower, thinking "I am the living soul. (33)

Thus, in the womb of the mother, characterized by its triangular shape, where semen alone is the essence, and wherein there is a solid portion such as bone and sinew—within such a body, which is a sheath constructed by one's own karma—one remains bound like a silkworm in its cocoon. "Svāmoda" means possessing a pleasant fragrance. || 33 ||
The consciousness situated in the seed-syllable *śukra* as "I" alone spreads from head to foot throughout the entire pavilion of the cosmic egg, like moonlight.

Even there, it is well known from one's own experience that, just as the digits of the moon reside within the lunar orb, there is a specific pervasion of the manifestations of the sense of "I" (ahaṃbhāva) within the drop of semen (śukrakaṇa) located in the heart; and through that, the manifestation of the general sense of "I" pertaining to the entire body occurs. Thus he says: "I... (34).
The water of sensation, discharged through the conduit of the apertures of the senses,
pervades the three worlds, just as smoke spreads through the sky by becoming clouds.

He states the gateways for that [consciousness] to perceive external objects with the word "akṣa" (the senses): "visṛtam" means spread forth or issued out; "vedanodakam" refers to the water of sensation characterized by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) together with its appearance (*ābhāsa*). "Trijagat" refers to those external objects situated within the three worlds that are in close proximity. Just as smoke pervades the sky by becoming clouds, so it is here. (35)
Although perception exists throughout this entire body, both externally and internally,
nevertheless, within this semen there is a dense latent impression (vāsanā).

He states—in the verse beginning with "dehe"—that the specific identification (abhimāna) residing in the semen located in the heart with respect to the entire body is established by experience; dense latent impressions (vāsanā) constitute this specific identification. || 36 ||
The individual soul (jīva) consists of mere volition; whatever volition it forms remains within the heart, and having become manifest there, that very same volition quickly and clearly flows outward.
For this very reason, he says "the individual soul" (jīva) to show that external worldly transactions proceed precisely preceded by volitions within the heart. || 37 ||
And apart from that state which is as it is, mindless, and like a mountain, the delusion of "I" is not pacified by any other state whatsoever. (38)

For this very reason, he says "as it truly is" (yathāsthitām), meaning that the ego-sense of the mind does not subside even by a thousand means without its abiding in the form of Brahman: "In the ripening of samādhi, through the stable state of oneness with Brahman, [the mind] becomes like a steady flame;
though it is the object of thought, it is to be contemplated as being like the sky."
Through the gradual pacification of the sense of "I," they [attain] peace. (39)

Therefore, O Rāma, even while the contemplation of Brahman is being pursued by you through reflection (*manana*), meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*), and so forth, it must be cultivated and accomplished as being comparable to the sky in the final stage, which brings about the absolute cessation of the sense of ego (*ahaṃbhāva*).
The meaning is that you should not stop with this much alone. || 39 ||
Those who know that reality conduct themselves here, free from the state of being and the process of contemplation, without form, light, or mental activity, remaining silent like logs of wood. (40)
If so, should that [meditation] also be practiced by you and others in that same way? He says "no," with the words "those who know that":
"In such a way as there may be no mental perception of external objects, free from the conceit of seeing what is seen by the mind;
and silence, which is devoid of the activity of the organs of action. (40)
He who is the cultivation of nothing whatsoever is said to be liberated;
while living, he is as clear as the sky, manifestly free from bondage. (41)
Free from bondage, as if released from chains and the like. || 41 ||
The consciousness situated in the seed-syllable "Ahaṃ" spreads from head to foot throughout the entire body, just as the light of the sun pervades the entire universe.
He states that even the pervasion of the sense of "I" throughout the entire body occurs solely by virtue of the pervasion of the seminal portion: "I... (verse 42).
"The eye is sight, the tongue is tasting, and that which is hearing becomes the ear"—binding oneself with these five such latent impressions (vāsanās), one sinks into them. (43)
He states that even the connection with their respective locations in the form of the sense organs, such as the eyes, belongs only to the *jīva* whose essence is semen:
"By means of all the senses, through the sight, touch, hearing, and so forth of women and others, because desire is ignited, one sinks [into it]"; this is the meaning.
Consciousness (*cidbhāva*) arises undivided, becoming the mind (*manas*) in a partial manner.
Just as the sap, though omnipresent, exists in the earth in the form of a sprout during the spring.

The meaning is that the very process of perverse conceptualization (viparītabhāvanā), belonging to one whose consciousness is veiled by ignorance, first becomes the mind; then, through the sense of "I" (ahaṃbhāva) and as an undifferentiated part [of it], it arises in the form of the various sense organs. || 44 ||
For one who contemplates the non-existence of entities that are not established here in reality, suffering will never cease for that person who lacks effort. (45)

For this very reason, he states that without the cultivation of the true reality which is opposed to that [ignorance], there is no cessation of that suffering—beginning with the words "He who": "He who," in this world of saṃsāra, regarding these well-established forms of the world consisting of mind, ego, body, and so forth—which are mere modifications beginning with speech, mere names, and for which it is said, "There is not even the slightest diversity here; therefore, the instruction is 'not this, not this'."

The meaning is that for one who does not contemplate the state of non-existence shown by such scriptural passages and who lacks effort conducive to liberation—that "male donkey" among men—the endless suffering of birth and so forth will certainly never subside. || 45 ||
Clothed in whatever [garment], fed by whatever [food], and sleeping wherever [he may be] in this world, he shines like a sovereign emperor. (46)

For one who meditates in this manner, even when there is a renunciation of all external possessions, there certainly exists the bliss of sovereignty up to the state of Vairāja, through the clothing, food, and other necessities provided by people drawn by past karma (*prārabdha*), as well as through the satisfaction of the nectar of internal bliss. Thus he says: "By whatever [means]... (46).
Though endowed with all latent impressions (vāsanās), he is free from latent impressions;
though empty within, his self is not empty, like the sky filled with breath.
By means of latent impressions—that is, by latent impressions of the form of Brahman, or by latent impressions of the world that resemble the form of burnt cloth and its threads.
Whether sitting, lying down, or traveling, he is not awakened by efforts;
like one who is drowsy, he is at peace, liberated from the mental constructions of the mind in nirvāṇa. || 48 ||
The meaning is that he is not awakened because he has already entered the sixth stage and those beyond it. || 48 ||
For the Puruṣa is pure consciousness alone; though all-pervading, he abides in the manifest essence of the body, just as fragrance resides in the filaments of a lotus. (49)
In the seminal essence that is manifest and essential. || 49 ||

They know the living being to be pure consciousness alone, and the world to be its outward expansion; the ground of instruction is that when one abides in the Self, one reaches the supreme state beyond the world.

Thus, applying the description of the individual and collective states of the living being (*jīva*) and so forth to the supreme subject at hand, he summarizes the entire essence of the instruction, saying:
"Pure consciousness alone" (*saṃvinmātram*). This is the supreme, most secret ground of instruction, the state of instruction. 50.
Become dispassionate toward all worldly objects, such as power and wealth;
making your heart like a stone, act in such a way that you may attain ultimate well-being.
In this regard, he states that the very secret of the means is the firmness of dispassion: "One who is tasteless," [verse 51].
O virtuous one, O Rāghava, let there be for you both the emptiness and the non-emptiness of the heart; for, being bodiless, you are like a stone due to the absence of consciousness.

He clarifies the intended meaning of the statement, "making the stone the heart," with the words "O virtuous one. Just as for a stone, whose nature is insentience, the hollow of the heart is well known to be non-hollow precisely because of that insentience— leaving no room for the entry of consciousness— so too, for you, whose nature is pure consciousness, the hollow of the heart in the form of the internal space (*daharākāśa*) [is likewise devoid of such a cavity].
The meaning is that his intention was: "Let this [body] be devoid of consciousness, crowded with non-consciousness, without any space, as if it were solid and without pores.

Or alternatively: "For so long a time, due to the conceit of being of the nature of the non-conscious, from your state of being non-conscious—that is, from ignorance—the collection of objects of enjoyment has been imagined within you, like the space imagined inside a crystal stone."

The meaning is this: the hollow of the heart—the cavity of the mind characterized by desire—which cannot be filled even by millions of gains such as wealth, has now been suppressed by the fulfillment of all desires through the attainment of the Self, which is eternally full and unsurpassed bliss;
thus, let it become a single mass of bliss, like the actual interior of a crystal stone. This is the intended sense.

Regarding all actions, whether existent or non-existent, there is no distinction whatsoever between one who knows that [reality] and one who does not, except for the state of being free from latent tendencies (nirvāsanatva).

For this very reason, he says "tajjña" (by the knower of that), [meaning]: even though there is equality in the cognition of both the knower and the ignorant regarding the activities of worldly transactions reflected in a crystal stone—as if they were real—the distinction is caused solely by the presence or absence of the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of reality. || 53 ||
This very consciousness, when it is open, becomes the world;
that supreme reality is spread out like the eye when it is closed, though it remains nameless.

And thus, just as the vision of a person looking at a crystal stone, the very existence of consciousness (*cit-caitanya*)—when opened up by latent impressions (*vāsanā*)—becomes the world; when closed by the absence of latent impressions, it becomes the pervasive, undivided reality known as liberation (*mokṣa*). This is the established conclusion. || 54 ||
The entire visible world perishes, and having perished, it is born again;
that which has neither perished nor been produced—that is the Real, and You are that.
For this very reason, he states that the existence of consciousness itself is eternity: "The visible," etc. (verse 55).
For the manifestation of existence is rootless; even when cultivated, it does not exist.
Like water in a mirage, it does not produce the sprout of existence. (56)
He says "bhāva... [verse 56]: when the root ignorance is destroyed by such awakening, even upon searching, the delusion of the world cannot be found.
The "cognition of existence" (bhāvajñapti) is the delusion of the world; it is "rootless," meaning its root has been sublated. It is "imagined" (bhāvitā), even though it has been searched for.
The cultivation of the thought "I am" is severed by the vision of things as they truly are;
even when perceived, it no longer sprouts within, like a seed that has been burnt.
Whether performing action or not performing it, the man who is free from passion, free from affliction, devoid of mental constructs, and eternally extinguished, abides in the Self. (58)
For this very reason, he says that for the wise there is no distinction between performing and not performing prescribed actions: "Action... (verse 58).
When the mind is stilled, the kinsmen of enjoyments are completely pacified for the sake of peace;
yet their own nature is not exhausted, for it is said that the mind is their mine.
To the question, "Why do even those yogis who possess mental tranquility (*sāmanasa*) not abide in the Self due to their peace and so forth? he says: "By the mind" (*cittena*).
Even those yogis who are peaceful through forceful effort (*haṭha*) become truly peaceful only when there is the cessation of the mind, and not otherwise;
for their "bonds of enjoyment"—that is, the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of enjoyment—do not become exhausted by nature because they continue to bind them through experience.
They are cut off at the root; for the reason is that their source—the mind in its state as a mine—still exists. This is the meaning. || 59 ||
The wise soul, free from all density and consisting of pure light alone, attains the Supreme;
it is both other than Him and not other, like the heat within the afternoon sun.

It is precisely the solidification (*ghanībhāva*) of the individual soul (*jīva*) in the form of mind, body, and so forth, that constitutes its differentiation and its state of suffering; in the absence of this, it is non-different from Brahman and free from suffering. Thus he says: "non-solid" (*aghana*). The non-solid, formless *jīva*—which is pure light of consciousness alone, the purified referent of the term "thatness" (*tattvam*)—is liberated. The meaning is that it becomes fit for non-duality with the Supreme.
On the sunny side, it is cloudless, free from the obstruction of clouds, and not rough. || 60 ||
The form that appears in the center of the mind of a person standing in one place who has come from afar— that form is the form of the Supreme Self.

That very [consciousness], being non-material and consisting solely of the light of pure consciousness, makes itself manifest to the self— this is what is meant by "in one part" (*ekadeśa*). Because there is no interruption in the midst of the mental modification (*cittavṛtti*) of the mind— which has traveled from the person's body to distant objects such as the sun and the moon via the doors of the eyes and other senses—
the [light] extends uninterruptedly from the body up to the lunar orb.

It indeed exists as manifested by immediate consciousness. Although that [consciousness] has objects in the region of the body and in the region of the moon, its well-known form in the interval between them is objectless;

it is precisely this form that is the entirety, the fullness, which is to be known of the Supreme Self—this is the meaning. And thus says the Śruti: "The wise ever behold that supreme abode of Viṣṇu."
"Like an eye stretched across the sky," thus [it is said]. || 61 ||
That which is the beautiful camphor of the sky, which itself causes wonder,
knows itself as the infinite, internally unmanifested world.

He says that this world is merely the wonder of illusion (*māyā*) within consciousness itself when it is devoid of objects—using the word "beautiful" (*cāru*). It is unmanifest (*avyakta*), meaning not yet fully revealed.
Having attained an imperishable peace, radiant with the cessation of wandering through existence, and remaining like a disregarded lamp,
a person who has followed the Lord of the World shines indeed with joy even while staying here in this world.

Thus, to those who know the reality of this world, it appears as the imperishable Brahman alone— shining with the cessation of worldly delusion and having attained the peace of nirvāṇa like a neglected lamp. But to the ignorant, however,
it appears in the sky as being followed by the Controller, the Lord, through all the established laws of destiny and through the joy of experiencing various enjoyments.
The meaning is that although it exists within the interior of space from the perspective of ultimate reality, it appears [otherwise]; thus, it is merely a difference in perception. || 63 ||

Thus ends the twenty-second canto, titled "Instruction on the Yoga of Happiness," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa, within the Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa of Valmīki, concerning the means to liberation. 22.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "Instruction on the Yoga of Happiness," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The Twenty-third Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
He whose worldly tendencies were entirely cast off by the latent impression of dispassion—
Arise and go away from this Prakṛti, marked like Maṅki. || 1 ||
In this [chapter], the meeting of Maṅkin with Vasiṣṭha in the desert wilderness is described;
furthermore, the instruction given to him, who was despondent and seeking to know the reality, is recounted.
To establish the necessity of what was stated— that one must become dispassionate toward all objects of existence, such as power and the like—
he begins the narrative of Maṅki with the words "virāga" and so forth.
Of this manifest primordial nature (*prakṛti*), which consists of innate ignorance and other such factors...
The meaning is: having arisen through the awakening to the reality of saṃsāra, go to the state whose nature is nirvāṇa;
"marked" means characterized by its specific signs. || 1 ||
Formerly, there was a Brahmin named Maṅki who was firm in his vows.
Listen to how he attained liberation after being enlightened by me.
He was awakened and instructed by me. || 2 ||
Once, having been invited by someone for the sake of your grandfather, I descended from the expanse of the sky to the earth. || 3 ||
Having been previously invited for the purpose of a sacrifice and other rites on behalf of your grandfather Aja, I was traveling across the earth and reached your grandfather’s city;
there I entered a certain vast and formidable forest of great heat.

Going toward the city of Ayodhyā, the capital of your grandfather, having reached the earth from the world of the Seven Sages; wandering, meaning moving about; *araṇyānīm* refers to a great forest—the suffix *ānuk* is applied by the rule *indravaruṇa-* etc., due to the greatness of both *hima* and *araṇya*. || 4 ||
O Rāma, it was indeed strewn with dust, its sands shimmering and heated,
its far shore and limits unseen, and in some places marked by footprints.
It was struck down and destroyed by a continuous flow of dust—meaning it was turned grey—and marked by wretched villages; this is the sense of the verse. || 5 ||
It was characterized by the tranquility of its unagitated winds, light, waters, and earth;
it was vast, empty, yet possessed of great power, like the stainless essence of Brahman.

It was radiant with the tranquility of the sky— which is unagitated by the absence of dust and the like— of the wind, of the gale-force breeze, of the light, of the sunlight, of the mirage-water, and of the parched earth;
it was characterized by great undertakings and efforts of those who travel there due to its inaccessibility, and it was stainless and free from mud.
This is clear in the case of the position that Brahman is the existent [cause]. || 6 ||
Like ignorance, it has reached a state of delusion and a mirage through error;
it is an expansive dullness, empty, and clouded by the mist of disorientation.
The phrase "having become insentient" is to be supplied [to complete the sense]. || 7 ||
Then, as I was wandering through that forest, I saw before me a traveler speaking from exhaustion.
Speaking clearly, articulating [his words]. || 8 ||
The traveler said:
"Alas! The sun, with its intense heat, leads only to exhaustion;
this wicked heat causes torment, like association with a villain."
Just as association with a wicked person leads to suffering, so too this sun, with its intense heat, leads to exhaustion; such is the meaning. || 9 ||
The vital points seem to throb as if with a burning heat; the forest ranges, their clusters of sprouts withered, are scorched by the sun’s glare. 10.
Therefore, I shall enter this village situated ahead;
having quickly dispelled my fatigue here, I will proceed swiftly upon the road.
Therefore, for that reason. || 11 ||
Having reflected thus, when he desired to enter the Kirāta village situated before him, these words were spoken by me: (12)

The meaning is: having recognized that time as the dawn of his good fortune, I spoke these intentional words about to be mentioned, which are intended to generate a desire for the knowledge of reality (tattva) in order to uproot the very foundation of all his exertion. || 12 ||
O friend who has not fully understood the path free from passion, you who appear beautiful;
O traveler on the great forest-path of the way of the gods, welcome to you! (13)

The literal meaning is: "By whom the path—well-known to those free from passion, belonging to those who possess nothing, fit for wandering, and provided by hospitable people—has been thoroughly understood. For this very reason, [he is called] "the traveler on the great forest-path of the gods" (*marumārgamahāraṇyapānthā*). However, the intended secondary meaning is clear: "O friend, welcome to you; may your arrival here result in the destruction of the root of all suffering through the sight of me. (13)
O traveler on the lower path, though you are weary, you shall not find rest for long upon this road through this desolate village in the land of men.
By the address "O traveler on the lower path," his own journey through the sky at that time is indicated.
The phrase "as it were in a deserted village" implies that he remained in a village devoid of hospitable people;
for although you have rested due to obtaining food, drink, shelter, and so forth in previous villages, you shall not find rest further ahead.

Such is the literal meaning. Regarding the intended sense: O traveler on the path of lower actions, even though you have rested here and there at various points along this road characterized by the southern and northern courses obtainable through ritual action and meditation upon the heavenly realms and other planes, [you remain like one who has reached] a deserted village—a place where the multitude of births has departed.
It should be construed thus: "In that way, like liberation, you will not find rest for a long time. || 14 ||
Resting in a village, which is the abode of the vulgar, does not occur at all;
indeed, thirst only increases further by drinking salt water. || 15 ||
It does not exist at all for common folk (*pāmaras*) because it is, on the contrary, caused by agitation through harsh words and the like; such is the literal meaning (*uttāna-bhāva*).

However, the intended sense (*āśaya-artha*) is as follows: in the village—that is, in the abode of the aggregate of agent and instruments, namely the bodies of gods, humans, and so forth, which are the abodes of common folk characterized by desire, hatred, and the rest—if you think that there is repose through the enjoyment of sense objects, he says in response: "Thirst" (*tṛḍ*).
And so it was said by Yayāti: "Desire is never extinguished by the enjoyment of desired objects; rather, like a fire fed with clarified butter, it increases all the more. (15)
These living beings take refuge solely in the village; like fawns, they tremble at the slightest movement and wander upon improper paths. 16.
"Pallavas" refers to specific tribes of Pulindas.
The literal meaning is that, because they are forest-dwellers, these people are afraid of the movement of the inhabited countryside and cannot endure the darkness [of night].

However, in the intended sense, these [internal states] such as desire and the like are "like shoots" (pallava) in that they possess affection, passion, and so forth; they are afraid of the movement of discernment and wander upon wrong paths.
Those who are inclined toward paths not sanctioned by the scriptures. || 16 ||
They do not quiver amidst anxieties, they blaze within their experiences, and they do not tremble before misconduct, as if they were made of stone machinery.
The phrase "they do not quiver," and so forth, is clearly applicable to both cases, like statues and the like made of stone or mechanical devices. || 17 ||

Those of burnt intellect, whose manly efforts are entirely devoted to passion for sensual objects and wealth, and who are full of hatred, take delight in actions that are sweet only at first sight. 18.
Noble by birth, expansive, cool, and rich in flavor—
wisdom does not find confidence here, just as a mass of clouds finds no rest in a desert.
Noble birth consists in the purity of both lineages; therefore, wisdom does not place its trust in people here on earth. || 19 ||
Better to be blind and dwell in a cave, better to be a worm inside a stone,
and better to be a lame deer in the desert than to associate with vulgar people.
It blinds, thus it is "blind" (andha); the cave is enveloped in darkness, and within it, his state is that of a python (ajagara). || 20 ||
Sweet with the taste of a mere blink, yet fading in the next moment;
solely intent on destruction, they are like vulgar droplets of poison. 21.
Poisoned grains are grains of poison mixed with honey. || 21 ||
In the dilapidated houses, the unrighteous winds of the villages blow, scattering clouds of ashes and busily tossing away grass, leaves, and forests.
Scattered with particles of ash and grey with dust, fierce winds blow and circulate, possessing the characteristics of those unrighteous people born in the village. || 22 ||
O sinless one, when he had spoken thus, I was addressed by him with these words,
which comforted me through his speech like one bathed in the waters of nectar.

Having gained full confidence that "by this Maṅki, who has been thus addressed and spoken to by me, my intention will be understood and he will rescue me," I spoke these words which are about to be related. || 23 ||

The traveler said: "O Blessed One, who are you? You are a perfected soul, a great-souled one; how have you become so self-possessed that you behold the world without agitation, like a wayfarer watching a village festival? (24)
"You are the full Self"—this is the ellipsis. || 24 ||

Have you drunk the nectar of immortality? Are you a sovereign (samrāṭ) or a universal monarch (virāṭ)? For even though you are destitute of all possessions, you shine for a long time as if you were completely fulfilled.
He reveals this very state of fullness through causal reflections: "But by you, O Emperor, lord of all worlds, you shine like the full moon. (25)
You are empty and you are full; you are as if whirling and yet you are steady.
You are not everything, and yet you are everything; you are nothing, and yet you are something indeed.

You are empty of the defects and sufferings of saṃsāra; you are filled with unsurpassed bliss and the qualities of one liberated while living. Because you do not identify with the body and so forth, you are as if reeling from intoxication; you are as if established in the ultimate reality (paramārtha). "Not all" refers to the views of superimposition and denial regarding the universal totality (samaṣṭi); "nothing at all" [refers to the same].
By means of the views of negation regarding individuality and superimposition. || 26 ||
O Sage, why is it that your form is both tranquil and lovely, radiant yet non-obstructive, withdrawn and yet majestic? 27.

If it is asked, "How were you known by me to be such?", [the author] says "He is tranquil" (upaśāntam), indicating that it was through the sight of his form. And thus the Śruti says: "This very form explains his majesty. || 27 ||
Though situated upon the earth, you stand as if above all the worlds in the sky; you are free from worldly attachment, yet you appear as if firmly established in profound absorption.
You appear as one who is firmly resolved upon the upliftment of those like me. || 28 ||
It does not extend into objects, nor indeed does it exist as the nature of objects;
for your mind, pure like the moon, remains composed of nectar. (29)

Like the pure moon, your mind consists of nectar; like the rays of the moon, it does not diminish upon contact with objects, nor is there any object—such as herbs, trees, soma, clarified butter, milk, or food—that can be consumed by it and cause it to waste away. Therefore, it remains eternally full; this is the sense that you surpass even the moon. || 29 ||
Possessing all arts yet free from blemish within, cool, radiant, and equanimous,
you shine like the full moon filled to the brim with the essence of elixirs.
He states another point regarding that similarity and its distinction: "The possessor of arts" (kalāvān), etc. (verse 30).
But by Your will, I perceive both existence and non-existence within Your consciousness;
this entire circle of transmigratory existence stands within it like a fruit within a sprout.
Thus, he says "In your will" to show that you possess both equality with Hiraṇyagarbha and a distinction beyond him:

"I see this entire sphere of transmigratory existence existing within your consciousness— your self— which is endowed with omniscience, omnipotence, and all other perfections, like the form of a tree beginning from the sprout and ending with the fruit, ready for manifestation."
I honor you. Regarding the purpose of that creation, however, I perceive and recognize the presence of both existence and non-existence within your will.
If you so desire, you too are certainly capable of creating the world; yet, the distinction lies in this: you do not so desire. This is the intended meaning. || 31 ||
"O Brahmin, I am indeed this man named Maṅki, born of the lineage of Śāṇḍilya; O highly fortunate one, I have come here in the course of a pilgrimage. (32)

Having thus drawn Vasiṣṭha toward him with praise, he proclaims his own lineage, name, and so forth, in order to demonstrate Vasiṣṭha’s fitness for instruction through his own perfection of the means such as dispassion:
"Having traveled a very long distance and having now seen the sacred fords (tīrthas)..."
After a long time, he prepared to go to his own abode. || 33 ||
And my mind being dispassionate toward home, I have no effort to go,
having seen beings within the belly of the world resembling flashes of lightning.
Resembling lightning, they are subject to momentary destruction. || 34 ||
O Blessed One, out of compassion, please tell me truly about yourself;
for the minds of the virtuous are indeed deep and serene lakes.

The literal meaning is: "Tell me of yourself by name, lineage, and so forth. However, by the force of the qualification "truthfully," the intended meaning is: "Instruct me regarding the Supreme Self. || 35 ||
In the presence of great beings who show friendship at the mere sight of others,
all living creatures blossom and find comfort like lotuses.
And I consider this mind of mine, born from the delusion of wandering in saṃsāra, to be incapable of abandoning it; therefore, may you [help me] through your compassionate awakening. (37)
He expresses that very intention clearly with the words "mama" (mine). The particle *ca* is used in the sense of "even.

Even this mind of mine, though possessing a slight degree of discrimination, due to delusion—that is, the predominance of ignorance and doubt—is unable to abandon the suffering born of the confusion of saṃsāra.
I have repeatedly reflected and concluded that it is not possible to eradicate [this ignorance] entirely by mere skill in one's own inquiry without the instruction of a guru; therefore,
you possess that aforementioned capacity for my rescue.

The remainder [of the meaning] is: "Make [this] capable of destroying suffering by cutting through delusion and doubt, by means of instructions that are compassionate and conducive to the awakening to the secret. || 37 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
"O one of great intelligence, I am Vasiṣṭha; I am a sage whose home is the sky. For some purpose, O royal sage, I have arrived upon this path."
Of the royal sage Aja; by some purpose in the form of officiating at sacrifices and so forth. || 38 ||
Do not fall into despair; you have entered the path of the wise.
You have, for all intents and purposes, reached the further shore of the ocean of saṃsāra. (39)
The further shore, the enemy of heroes. || 39 ||
Neither a mind magnanimous through the power of dispassion, nor speech such as this, nor a form of tranquil appearance belongs to one who is not a great soul. (40)

Regarding the statement "I have attained the path of the wise," he states the proof for this as follows: "through dispassion. [This applies] to one who is not a great soul—that is, one devoid of the fortune of being qualified for knowledge. || 40 ||
Just as a gem attains a state of stainlessness through gentle polishing,
so too does the mind attain discernment through the ripening of its austerities.

He says that even the arising of discernment (*viveka*) is a sign of the ripening of the impurities of your mind—referring to the "jewel" [in the verse]. By means of a sweet and gentle polishing (*kāṣa*), that is, by rubbing with a whetstone (*śāṇa*). || 41 ||
What do you wish to know? How do you wish to abandon saṃsāra?
I believe that what has been taught is accomplished through actions.

Since a disciple brings to fruition that portion of the meaning taught by the teacher which has been repeatedly understood through his own study—by means of such activities as further questioning and retention—you should therefore state that portion which remains unknown and desired to be known to you. This is the meaning. || 42 ||

One whose latent impressions are stainless, whose mind is supreme, and whose intellect is thoroughly secluded by the splendor of the people, is indeed fit for the stainless state free from sorrow; this is said of one who has resolved to cross over birth. (43)

Indeed, for this reason, that disciple whose latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are stainless— that is, devoid of the impurities of passion and so forth— and for whom, precisely because of that, the mind is endowed with the three means such as supreme dispassion (*vairāgya*),

and who likewise possesses an intellect that is thoroughly secluded and characterized by the discrimination between the eternal and the non-eternal, or the essential and the non-essential; he alone [is such].

By the power of the instruction of the venerable teacher (gurujana), it is fitting—that is, one becomes capable—to attain the state of the reality of the self (ātmatattvapada) which is free from sorrow; no one else [is so capable]. For this reason, it is said "this is for you" only to one whose qualification has been ascertained through conversation and testing, and who possesses the intent to cross over—that is, the desire to transcend—all sufferings such as birth and so forth.
Not for anyone else. Therefore, the meaning is: "Tell the account of your own past and future. || 43 ||

Thus ends the twenty-third canto, titled "The Liberation of Maṅki," in the *Maṅkyupākhyāna* (The Narrative of Maṅki) within the *Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa* (Section on Liberation) of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa*, composed by Vālmīki and belonging to the *Ārṣa* (Sage) tradition. 23.
Thus ends the twenty-third canto, titled "The Liberation of Maṅki," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The twenty-fourth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: When he had spoken thus, "It is mine," Maṅki fell at his feet.
Carrying these words along the path, he spoke thus with eyes full of joy.
Here, the flood of one's own worldly suffering, together with the body, senses, mind, intellect, defects, and so forth, is described in detail by Maṅki.

Having spoken thus, Maṅki fell at my feet and, with eyes filled with tears of joy, while carrying me along the path— meaning, while carrying my entire sensory apparatus (akṣa) filled with bliss— he spoke the following as he was about to say. || 1 ||
Maṅki said:
O Blessed One, my eyes have wandered extensively through the ten directions,
yet I have not found a virtuous man who could destroy my doubt.

O Blessed One, skilled in instruction for the severing of one's own doubts, while I was intent on seeking the true path, I wandered through the directions until my very vision whirled about as if in all directions. (2)
Today I have attained the fruit of the essence of all the essences of the body;
yet, O Blessed One, I am weary from beholding the conditions that bring forth the defects of saṃsāra.

"Today, by obtaining you, I have attained the fruit of my own body—which is the essence among all bodies, such as those of gods, asuras, and animals—namely, the excellence of the qualification for knowledge; this is the sense. (3)
Born again and again, and perishing again and again, there is constant wandering through pleasure and pain; for all things are inevitably characterized by suffering until their final end. (4)

He elaborates on distress itself along with its causes, beginning with the words "again," and so forth. "Born" refers to birth; "perished" refers to death. Now, one might ask: "How can there be a constant delusion of suffering, given that pleasures are also experienced in saṃsāra? To this he replies: "Necessarily," and so on. All [pleasures], even...
Pleasures are indeed nothing but suffering—extremely painful and utterly unbearable—because their end is inevitably suffering; this is the connection with what follows. || 4 ||
O Sage, pleasures are indeed extreme sufferings; therefore, sufferings are better than them.
Because they end in intense suffering, pleasures cause me pain.

Therefore, for these pleasures, sufferings alone are better. For a continuous succession of sufferings might—even through habituation—become endurable, like the cold experienced by aquatic creatures; however, that same succession becomes unbearable when interspersed with pleasure. Alternatively, because it is followed by such exceedingly powerful suffering, [pleasure] is [considered worse] in comparison to suffering, just as in the case of subsisting on *kodrava* grain.

Just as with the pleasure of tasting sweets mixed with poison, it is appropriate that there should be a greater degree of aversion toward the pleasures of enjoyment when considered in light of the succession of minor sufferings; thus he says: "Firm... (Verse 5).
In this way, O Rāma, my very suffering has turned into happiness;
it has reached a state of decay along with my thirteen teeth, body hair, and intestines.

"O Rāma! O gentle one!"—this is Vasiṣṭha’s address. The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "Pleasures distress me in such a way that my very suffering becomes a state of happiness. Now, he shows the useless decay of age and other factors that are not conducive to the knowledge of reality, and their status as seeds for a succession of misfortunes—age...
By such [statements] as these; "jarjaratām" means looseness or flaccidity. || 6 ||
The intellect, intent on falling from a high station, lacks resolute determination;
due to its evil intentions, it does not perceive the dense thicket of beautiful sprouts as luminous.

The intellect (*buddhi*), intent upon the desire for a fall from a high station—that is, a state of ever-increasing excellence in enjoyments—is not resolute in accomplishing the supreme human goal (*paramapuruṣārtha*). The mind (*manas*), however, is "well-sprouted" with the shoots of passion that grow ever higher; it is "dense" due to the evil volitions (*kusaṃkalpa*) of grief, delusion, and the like, which have as their object the infinite range of past objects of enjoyment.
Precisely because it is difficult to discern, it does not manifest through a discrimination that serves as a witness to one's own respective defects and so forth. || 7 ||

Like the hollow of a rotten tree in a wretched village filled with the droppings of woodpeckers, the mind is a state of constant evil, inhabited by vultures in the form of latent mental impressions (vāsanās). 8.

Regarding this, he provides an illustration with the word *pippala*: like the dense thickets found between wretched villages, filled with the floating heaps of dry leaves and such from *pippala* trees—such as the *aśvattha*—even their livelihood is [like that].
Because they carry various enjoyments, garments, and foul odors upon their bodies, they are thus called "those who carry bodily impressions" (*vāsanāṅgavaha*).
With senses that are like vultures or those who feed on vultures, it is always most sinful, like residing in a wretched village. || 8 ||
The intellect is as formidable and crooked as a thorny tree or creeper; it is like a night blinded by darkness, characterized by the exhaustion of one's lifespan.

And the intellect is formidable and crooked like the thorny creeper of the *karañja* tree; and life is wasted in vain—this is the connection with the following. Life is exhausted for naught by a constant preoccupation with sense objects that is wearying and shrouded in darkness, just as the eye is wasted for naught when it has not attained the light of the vision of Brahman, remaining like an eye in the darkness of night that has not reached the illumination of a lamp or other light. || 9 ||
One who is intoxicated by worldly affairs has not yet reached the light; though wasted by constant anxiety, he takes no pleasure in anything, and though already as good as lost, he does not perish.
Craving is like a withered creeper; it takes no pleasure in the taste of discernment. Because it repeatedly fails to bear fruit, though seemingly destroyed, it does not truly perish. (10)
For us, craving is neither flowering nor fruiting, like a withered creeper; action is submerged in action, that which is called latent impression (vāsanā) being itself non-action.
One might object: "Could not your liberation be achieved by actions alone? To this he replies with the word *karma*.

Whatever action—whether obligatory (*nitya*) or occasional (*naimittika*)—has been performed, it is merely submerged, meaning exhausted, by the destruction of only a small fraction of the mass of previously accumulated evil karma. However, that which is called the latent impression (*vāsanā*) for experience...
The seed [of ignorance] impels one toward optional and prohibited actions—which lead to further and further misfortune and result in non-action; this is the implied meaning. || 11 ||
The life of people has decayed, yet they have not crossed over the ocean of existence;
day by day, the hope for enjoyments swells, bringing only fear.
One's life is wasted through attachment to people such as sons, wives, kinsmen, and servants.
In one whose self is neither full nor empty, the great calamities of fortune—which cause the fever of anxiety and are like pits, thorns, and trees—are indeed destroyed. (13)

For the sake of acquiring fortune, great positions were attained; yet, when the self and the home remained unfulfilled, they were wasted and exhausted by the fevers of anxiety that cause such agitation. (13)
Though it was perfect and unblemished, she too yawned with longing,
like a dark cave resonant within with the brilliance of gems shimmering inside.

Lakṣmī, having repeatedly enticed even a man who is endowed with abundant wealth and the like and remains unharmed by weapons and such, draws him far away; by subjecting him to the power of enemies and robbers, she expands through deception, culminating in the destruction of all prosperity and the suffering of wounds from weapons and the like. As for example:

Just as one who has entered his own interior—a radiant hollow of a tree containing a dark pit, where a serpent is seen within and a jewel glitters—might yawn in delusion due to the bite of that serpent, so it is here; the word *vā* is used in the sense of *iva*. Alternatively, in the reading *rambhehaṃ*, it refers to a plantain tree with its fruit growing within.
Such an abyss serves as the illustration. || 14 ||
The wise do not touch me, who am like a desolate ocean—wretched, empty, and agitated by waves—intent solely upon the objects of the senses. 15.
