This mind, though called consciousness, is turbid and unclean due to the waves of a thousand desires; it is devoid of substance even when running everywhere, and for that very reason is like a parched ocean, difficult to fill and therefore wretched.
Consequently, those possessed of discernment do not touch me—one who is enslaved by the mind and solely intent on the objects of the senses—but rather disregard me. || 15 ||
Like a *śleṣmātaka* tree standing upon thorny filth,
this great undertaking is utterly unreal, like a wind-tossed arjuna tree.

Regarding this, he provides an illustration: "sakaṇṭakam" (thorny). Even the mind, when in a state of deliberation, is likewise [unstable], for from it arise great undertakings of action; just as the "Arjuna-wind"—a specific type of wind-disorder that constantly causes dizziness—moves within the body, so too does it [the mind]. || 16 ||
The mind, not having reached death, leaps toward suffering while it is still empty;
yet it bears the moon and stars of association with the scriptures and the company of the virtuous. 17.
Though death has approached me many times, it has not yet come; instead, my mind—devoid of its desired object—leaps and runs only toward suffering.
If you say, "Surely the mind should be restrained by means such as the study of scriptures and association with the virtuous," [I reply:
as long as the night of ignorance has not been exhausted by the rising of the sun of discernment, which is the fruit of knowledge.

With the intention that such things as study of the scriptures and association with the virtuous are not capable of destroying mental delusion absolutely—much like the moon and stars—he says "The scripture... in two verses (17).
The night of ignorance has not been exhausted by that yakṣa flourishing with the sense of "I";
it is rather the lion for the intoxicated elephant of the darkness of ignorance and the fire for the grass of karma. 18.
In which [state], the very sense of "I" (ahaṃbhāva), flourishing like a yakṣa imagined by a child, [is present]. || 18 ||
The sun of transformation has not yet risen, for the night of latent impressions (vāsanā) has not ended;
the elephant of the mind, though non-existent, is perceived by me as if it were a real entity. (19)
The senses cut me to pieces; I know not what will happen, for even that vision of the scriptures which the wise rely upon for crossing over has not been resorted to by me. (20)
That [delusion] too, like a lack of vision for one who is blind, brings about the onset of latent tendencies (*vāsanā*).
Therefore, O dear one, tell me— who am asking you— what action should be taken here in this terrible state of extreme delusion for the sake of future welfare.

The grammatical connection is as follows: "Even that which has not been resorted to by wise men through means such as service and the like—that very 'non-vision' (adṛṣṭi) of mine has resulted in blindness, as if it were an obstruction to vision. Thus, since I am submerged in extreme delusion due to the occurrence of misfortune from every direction in the manner described, tell me what must be done for my future welfare and liberation, so that I may cross over this state.
The connection [is established]. || 21 ||
The mists of delusion subside like autumn clouds when a virtuous person has arrived, and likewise all directions become clear;
may the word "Truth," sung by the company of the righteous, be realized through you, who have awakened me and grant peace from worldly existence. 22.

O Blessed One, it is well known in the world that when a virtuous guru— adorned with a multitude of luminaries such as stainless, pure knowledge and discernment— is encountered, like the autumn season in the month of Śarada, the mist characterized by delusion subsides in the disciple, just as it does in the sky; and all his desires, like the quarters of the horizon, become pure and free from the dust and stains of passion and other defilements.

The prayer is that the speech sung by virtuous people may become true—that is, its meaning uncontradicted—by means of what has been done by you, which brings peace to my worldly existence and awakens my understanding. || 22 ||

Thus ends the twenty-fourth canto, titled "The Dispassion of Maṅki," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the glorious Vāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa composed by Vālmīki, according to the Ṛṣi tradition. 24.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth sarga, titled "Maṅki’s Dispassion," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa within the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The Twenty-fifth Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Perception, ideation, latent impression, and mental construction—these are the names for it.
In this world, when the meaning of words is lost, that which is devoid of meaning proliferates to one's detriment. || 1 ||
The fourfold seed of bondage, arising from ignorance such as the sense of being a perceiver and so forth,
and the knowledge that destroys it within the Supreme Self— this is what is described here.
Thus, having described the misfortune of his own cyclic existence by Maṅki, and being asked about the means to eliminate it,

[the author] teaches— starting with the words "saṃvedanam"— in order to establish the fourfold seed of that [misery], explaining that the means for its removal cannot be accomplished without first fully understanding those seeds.

First, there is the experience characterized by the enjoyment of objects through the sense faculties; when the object has passed away, there is the repeated cultivation [of that experience] by means of recollecting its qualities. Through this, there arises in the mind a firm latent impression (*vāsanā*) marked by the form of that [object]; and by means of that [impression], even at the time of death and so forth, there occurs a mental construction conducive to the commencement of a future body and so on.

"Recollection of that" (tatsmṛti) refers to the fourfold [discrimination] which, in this cycle of existence, leads to misfortune; because it has as its object unreal things, and because it is itself unreal, it is devoid of true meaning. The meaning is that the referent of words, the referent of phrases, and so forth—which serve as the seed of all misfortunes—manifest through ignorance. || 1 ||
Know that sensation is the locus of all defects;
in it alone are calamities, just as creepers exist within sweet sap.
Regarding this, with the intention that the first two [types of objects] are absolutely harmful, while the last two are harmful by following upon them, he says:
"the perception" (*vedanam*). Furthermore, with the intention that the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) therein is a great harm, he says: "in that" (*tasmin*).
Just as a creeper, abundant with flowers, shoots, and so forth, exists when its sap has been set in motion by the month of Madhu (Caitra).
The meaning is that it is "like that" because the entirety of the creeper is a transformation of that [seed]. || 2 ||
On the dense path of saṃsāra, for those driven by the force of latent impressions (vāsanā),
a continuous succession of events unfolds through a diverse flood of occurrences.
For the discerning one, the agitation of saṃsāra together with its latent impressions (vāsanā) is exhausted at the end of Mādhava, like the moisture of the earth gradually [evaporates]. || 4 ||

For this very reason, he says "of the discerning one" (vivekinaḥ) to show that through the contemplation of the defects of sense-objects and the contemplation of Brahman, the entire cycle of worldly existence (saṃsāra), together with its latent impressions (vāsanā), is destroyed upon their cessation. || 4 ||
In this sal-lakī tree of saṃsāra, which causes the growth of latent impressions (vāsanā), she is like a streak of nectar on a wild banana plant covered in vines—she is the Mādhavī creeper. || 5 ||
But he says that for future rebirth, it is the latent impression (*vāsanā*) alone that is the activator—referring to "of this" (*asyāḥ*). A *sallakī* is a specific type of thorny shrub. || 5 ||
Due to the blindness of saṃsāra, the essence consisting of latent impressions (vāsanā) arises within consciousness,
just as the essence of the spring month remains upon the earth in the form of a forest.
In the *citau*, [it refers to] the living consciousness (*jīvacaitanya*) which is the substratum of ignorance (*ajñāna*). || 6 ||
Apart from the stainless pure consciousness, nothing whatsoever exists;
just as in the infinite sky there is nothing other than emptiness itself.

To demonstrate that ignorance (*ajñāna*) is the cause for the denial of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) and its obscuration, he first states the ultimate reality with the words "from pure consciousness" (*cinmātrāt*). The meaning is that apart from non-dual pure consciousness, the existence and manifestation of the world are established by the very existence and manifestation of consciousness itself, as this is proven by universal experience. However, [the world] does not possess existence and manifestation through its own inherent nature.
Nothing else whatsoever is established; the meaning is that just as in the sky nothing other than emptiness is established, so it is here. || 7 ||
The firm conviction that "there is no other self than sensation" is ignorance;
it is this delusion, and it is this that constitutes the pervasive cycle of existence (saṃsāra). || 8 ||

Thus, although it vibrates everywhere and at all times, that which is of the nature of pure consciousness and the essence of feeling is other than the body, senses, and so forth; yet it neither exists nor appears as such. That stable and beginningless manifestation (*pratibhā*) which causes the non-existence and non-appearance of the object is itself *avidyā* (ignorance), characterized primarily by its power of concealment (*āvaraṇa-śakti*), and [also] by its power of projection (*vikṣepa-śakti*).
The meaning is that saṃsāra is delusion appearing in the form of the fruit of both [ignorance and its opposite]. || 8 ||
Established through non-perception, it perishes by perception alone;
being unreal in nature yet appearing as real, it vanishes in an instant like a child’s phantom.
He shows the fruit of establishing that ignorance is the root: "By non-illumination," etc. (verse 9).

When all perceptions of the visible world are sublated, they attain oneness within the essence of consciousness, just as the full currents of rivers from the entire surface of the earth merge into the ocean. (10)
When the limiting adjuncts consisting of the perceived objects that cause differentiation are sublated, he shows the unity of all perspectives with the verse beginning "All" (sarva). || 10 ||

Just as a vessel made of clay is not perceived when devoid of clay, so too the object of cognition is not perceived when devoid of consciousness, because it consists of consciousness and the like. 11.

He establishes with examples that which was stated—that nothing exists apart from the stainless void of pure consciousness—beginning with the words "made of clay" and so forth; [he does so] by virtue of its being composed of consciousness (cinmaya) and, by the force of the word "etc.," also by virtue of its being composed of existence (sanmaya). || 11 ||
Whatever object is perceived within awakening is said to be awakening itself;
awakening does not perceive what is not awakening because of their dissimilarity, and therefore there is no otherness.

With the intention that the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of that which shines forth as consisting of consciousness culminates in nothing other than identity with consciousness, he says "bodha" (consciousness).

The meaning is: because of their dissimilarity—that is, because of their contradictory nature—manifestation cannot be established without non-difference from consciousness, and non-consciousness cannot possibly be non-different from consciousness. || 12 ||
In the seer, the seeing, and the seen, each is nothing but pure awareness;
that is their essence, and therefore there is nothing else apart from them, just like a flower in the sky. (13)

If one were to assert a superimposed non-difference through the cognition of the triad beginning with the seer, then—since that [triad] is unreal—it follows by implication that there is only the essential unity of the realization of the substrate; with this intention, he says: "The seer... (verse 13).
A homogeneous [cognition] attains unity with that which is homogeneous;
through this mutual experience, let there be the ascertainment of oneness. (14)
He states that the attainment of non-difference through mutual merging occurs only among things of the same class, just as water merges with water;

thus, if the world were merely the experience of that [consciousness], and if experiences were one, it would ultimately result in the established doctrine of the oneness of consciousness (*cidekatva*).
He says: "Of the same class" (*sajātīya*). || 14 ||
If wood, stones, and the like did not possess the nature of consciousness, then they would never be perceived, just as non-existent things are not. (15)

He states "If... (verse 15) because, if one does not admit the non-difference from the manifestation (*sphuraṇa*) of visible objects such as wood and so forth, they would be absolutely non-existent, like the horn of a hare.

But when this visible splendor is seen to have the single form of pure consciousness alone, then, being neither other than nor non-other than that consciousness, it is known by means of consciousness. (16)
But in our own established doctrine (siddhānta), this fault does not apply; thus he says: "When... (verse 16).
All that is visible throughout the world is pervaded by this alone—pure consciousness;
it is like the wind, which is merely vibration, or the ocean, which is merely water. || 17 ||

Likewise, he demonstrates the inference: "The world is consciousness alone, because its manifestation is not distinct from consciousness; for whatever has a manifestation not distinct from something else is merely that thing, just as the vibration of the wind. This is shown by the verse beginning with "sarvam" (all). || 17 ||
For even though these things, such as lac and wood, are mixed together, they are not mutually experienced [as one]; yet when there is mutual experience, they are indeed a unity. (18)

Now, one might object: "In the example [of fire and fuel], there is merely a blending through inherence (*samavāya*) between the action and the agent, or the part and the whole, but not absolute identity. Anticipating this, [the author] notes that while in the case of lac and wood there is no observation of blending despite their external contact because their distinction is still perceived, here [in the case of the self and the body], such blending is observed even though it is experienced.
With the intention that "because of the lack of uniformity, inherence is not established," he says: "they have become mixed. || 18 ||
For unity is indeed mutual experience, while unity is the mutual awareness of one another;
it is like that of two waters or two milks, and not like that of wood and lac. 19.

The meaning is this: just as there is indeed a unity consisting of the mutual experience of the nature of water and milk, so too there exists between the subject (the seer) and the object (the seen) such a unity characterized by mutual cognition; it is not merely a conjunction like that of lacquer and wood. || 19 ||
"I am" leads to bondage; "I am not" leads to liberation.
Since this much alone is required for liberation and it is within one's own power, why is there such incapacity?

Thus, when it is established that all objects of perception are nothing but pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), and that the consciousness which is the referent of the term *tat* (That) is eternally liberated due to its being unlimited, it follows that for the referent of the term *tvam* (Thou), the very notion of "I" as a limited entity is bondage, while the mere abandonment of that notion is liberation. This is what he states in the verse beginning with "ahamityeva" (It is only "I," etc.). || 20 ||
Like the cognition of two moons or the perception of water in a mirage, am I—who am indeed non-existent—arisen while remaining unarisen? (21)
He establishes that very point with the verse beginning "The moon": "How could I, who am non-existent, have arisen? It should be construed as: "I have not arisen at all. || 21 ||
"‘This is mine’ leads to bondage; ‘I am not [this]' leads to liberation.
Since these matters depend solely upon oneself, why this ignorance? (22)

With the intention that the bond of "mine-ness" (mamatā) departs of its own accord upon the abandonment of the sense of "I" (ahantā), he says: "mine. [This refers to] that which is dependent on the self, i.e., under one's own control. || 22 ||

The relationship between the pit and the jujube fruit, or the state of the jar and space—that very relationship does not exist as something other [than identity], for unity is indeed mutual awareness. (23)

He states that it is simply impossible for there to be either a concealment or a limitation of the real Self by an unreal ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), saying: "By whom. There is no such relationship by which concealment or limitation could be established for one who postulates an ego-sense that is absolutely distinct from [the Self]. Therefore, there is only actual identity.

The meaning is that, just as in the case of the double moon, the Self—which has a differentiated form imagined through ignorance—manifests by the power of its own self-luminosity, such that it appears as if there were a mutual cognition between them. || 23 ||
Mutual awareness is indeed a unity that persists even when divided into parts;
whether non-inert or inert, it does not abandon its single form.

However, for those followers of Jaimini who believe that the actual identity of insentience (*jaḍa*) and consciousness (*bodha*) is itself the nature of the Self (*ātman*), that identity— being insentient in its aspect of insentience and non-insentient in its aspect of consciousness— does not abandon even one of these two; thus, while it would not manifest in the aspect of insentience, it would manifest even in the aspect of consciousness.
The meaning is that if they were entirely devoid of objects, their mutual communication would be impossible, and thus there could be no unity between them. || 24 ||
That which is non-inert does not become inert, for intrinsic natures are immutable;
and where that which is non-inert is seen as inert, there is duality, not unity. (25)

To the question "Why does it not abandon [the other] there?", he says: "No. For indeed, because of that reason, only those properties (*dharma*) which are non-departing are called intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*). And as for that form of the Self (*ātmarūpa*) which is non-inert (*ajaḍa*) but was seen by you as inert due to being perceived as a distinct part—that is indeed dual and divided. In that case, there is no unity of the non-inert at all; thus, the meaning is that the establishment of a Self consisting of the identity of the inert and consciousness is impossible. || 25 ||
Enveloped by the onset of latent impressions (vāsanā) through hundreds of evil transformations,
they go lower and lower, like rocks falling from a mountain as they rush downward.

If this is so, how is it that disputants propound various mutually contradictory notions of the self? To this he says: "By the onset of latent impressions" (*vāsanāveśa*). The meaning is that they are enveloped and entangled by hundreds of evil transformations—their respective latent impressions and egoistic conceits—and thus, investigating reality solely through an outward-looking vision, they sink lower and lower. || 26 ||
For men who are scattered here and there by the winds of latent impressions (vāsanā), those sufferings descend upon them; it is impossible to describe them. (27)
Therefore, for those who have fallen away from the Vedic vision, who are driven hither and thither by the winds of their own respective latent impressions (*vāsanā*),
and who are like men made of straw, those various sufferings well-known in the world and in the scriptures— such as birth, death, and hell in diverse wombs— befall them. || 27 ||
Having wandered extensively like balls struck by the palms of the hand, people fall into the hells, impassioned by their cravings;
there, worn out by suffering, they eventually become like something else once again. (28)

Describing that very point, he concludes with the verse beginning "bhrāntvā": Driven by the passion and other emotions that follow from the pride of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), people—stained red by the juice of such attachment—wander incessantly like a ball struck by the palms of a woman's hands and fall into the hells. There, for a long time, having reached a state of utter exhaustion through the suffering of torments, they remain even after a great interval of time.

The meaning is that through births as stationary beings, worms, insects, and so forth, they become merely similar to others—just like them—and thus human birth is difficult to obtain once again. || 28 ||
Thus ends the twenty-fifth canto, titled "The Enlightenment of Maṅki," in the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the Mokṣopāya section of the glorious Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa, composed by the sage Vālmīki. 25.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth canto, titled "The Enlightenment of Maṅki," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The twenty-sixth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Indeed, for one who has fallen into the thicket of the path of worldly existence, calamities descend.
Like insects at the onset of the rainy season, they [perish] by the hundreds of thousands through their own conduct and circumstances.
In this world, misfortune is expanded through the coloring of the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) by means of mental cultivation;
yet, through discernment and the vision of reality, there is the complete cessation of desire and the pacification of misfortune.

Thus, for the individual soul (*jīva*) who has fallen upon the path of saṃsāra characterized by wombs such as those of immobile beings, hundreds of thousands of occurrences— consisting of cutting, piercing, burning, hunger, thirst, old age, fear, death, and so forth— that have occurred many times throughout beginningless saṃsāra, indeed recur once again. (1)
Indeed, all these phenomena are mutually unconnected, like stones in a forest; it is only through mental construction that a chain is perceived among them.
And in that regard, with the intention that non-cultivation (*abhāvanā*) alone is the root, he says "all" (*sarve*).
It is the cause for mutual binding, like a chain. (2)
Due to the dullness of the mind, it stands like a dense forest with the trees of worldly events; yet, through the coloring of aesthetic flavor, it is like a grove in spring within the world.

And the root of that [suffering] is the mind (citta), which is blinded by lack of discrimination, colored by the juices of passion, hatred, and so forth, and densely packed with the latent impressions (vāsanā) of past experiences; with this intention, he says "the mind. Here, "juice" (rasa) refers to passion and the like, as well as the [taste] of the earth. || 3 ||
Alas! How wondrous it is that, under the power of latent impressions (vāsanā), these helpless living beings experience pleasures and pains throughout their births. (4)
Alas! How extremely perverse is this latent tendency (vāsanā), by the power of which people experience within themselves this delusion regarding things that do not even exist. (5)
By means of objects existing in the form of a triple array (tripuṭī) which are indeed non-existent and false. || 5 ||
What difference is there between the moon and the wise man— both of whom are gladdening, as if restored from death, pure, illuminating, cool, and [active] toward all objects?
For this very reason, he praises those who have crossed over delusion and know reality as being happy, saying "delighting" (āhlādinaḥ).
The qualifiers here and in the two subsequent verses are to be applied equally to both cases. || 6 ||
What difference is there between a fool who desires whatever he pleases without considering what precedes or follows, and a child who lacks all restraint?
But he censures those who lack discrimination, saying: "The former and the latter... (7).
Tell me, what difference is there between a fish and a fool who, until the end of their lives, do not renounce the objects of sense—whether auspicious or inauspicious—that they have obtained? (8)

Sensual objects are like bait on a hook; death is the end of living beings. For those who do not abandon, who do not let go of these until that limit is reached, the "makara"—this term being an illustration for the species of fish—is indeed the one [who devours them]. 8.
Indeed, all these things— bodies, wives, wealth, and so forth—
are as fragile as a bowl of sand that quickly dries up and crumbles away.
Like a shallow bowl fashioned from sand that has not yet dried, they are fragile and destined for destruction. || 9 ||
Even as you wander through hundreds of wombs from the peak of Brahma down to a blade of grass until the end of the eon,
there is no peace for your mind except through tranquility.
Now, having awakened the very mind of the listener, he says: "From Brahmā... (verse 10).
Merely by reflecting upon it, even the slightest scent of bondage does not afflict one, just as the unevenness of a path does not trouble a traveler who keeps his eyes fixed ahead. 11.
Discernment is thorough reflection; by that alone [one is safe]. Observation is the looking at the ground where one places one's feet.
If your mind is not attentive while performing that, desire will swallow you up.
What can a demon do to one who is vigilant and awakened? (12)
"Attentive" means with discerning concentration; [this applies to] the Buddha, who is ever-watchful. || 12 ||
Just as the expansion of the eye consists merely in the perception of form,
so this world exists as the very nature of the expansion of consciousness, together with the sense of "I."

He says that the world, together with the ego, is merely the expansion of consciousness through non-discriminative attention—just as, for example, the expansion of the eye, which is the organ of sight, is nothing other than the mere perception of form, and no separate entity is established apart from it; so it is here. (13)
O Slayer of the Enemy, just as the closing of the eyes is the cessation of the perception of all forms, so too is the "covering of consciousness" the cessation of all that is visible. (14)

The restraint of the outward-turned consciousness—which destroys the sixfold group of enemies beginning with desire—by means of a mental state inclined toward the inward, is cessation within one's own self. || 14 ||
This world, though non-existent, I—the pure consciousness—manifests within the void;
by means of a slight expansion, it quickly vibrates, just as the wind does through a slight movement.

I, who am pure consciousness itself, expand this world together with the ego within the sky of my own essential nature—which is obscured by a slight diffusion caused by non-discrimination—just as one might fill the sky. || 15 ||
This very reality, though not performing any action, flourishes by means of another,
just as clay attains the state of a jar— an identity inseparable from itself— by means of gold.

From the perspective of the supreme reality of Brahman-consciousness, this world-form—which is indeed unreal—nevertheless expands and unfolds as if it were real, without ever having been made other than that consciousness. How is it known to be unreal? To this he says: "Like clay," etc. Just as the state of being a jar, which is imagined within clay or gold and is not obtainable as something separate from them, is set aside [as distinct].

Just as this world is impossible to obtain once it has been separated from consciousness, so too [the self] is impossible to obtain; the implication is that if it were real, it would be obtainable as something separate. || 16 ||
Just as the sky is mere emptiness, just as the wind is mere vibration,
and just as waves and the like are mere water, so too is the world mere consciousness.
Whatever is not obtainable as separate is devoid of separate existence; thus he demonstrates the pervasion (vyāpti) in gold and so forth with the words "merely void" (śūnyamātra). || 17 ||
Know that the three worlds are nothing but uninterrupted, partless pure consciousness—tranquil and like space within water, or as a mountain reflected in water. 18.

"Uninterrupted" (avyavacchinna) excludes differentiation within its own genus; "undivided" (nirbhāga) excludes internal differentiation. [The object] is either a mountain reflected in water, or a mountain-like great wave. || 18 ||
In the one who has attained Nirvāṇa and is stilled, there arises a coolness such that even these moons within him become like sparks of blazing fire. (19)

With the intention that one who knows the reality of the world in this manner is not subject to the torments of saṃsāra, he says: "Of nirvāṇa. That is the most excellent coolness, characterized by the subsiding of all torments and consisting of bliss; "where," meaning "by the sight of which."

In this world, which is void and devoid of light, how can anything be produced by anyone, in any way, within that Self which is of the nature of absolute peace, expansion, and auspiciousness? || 20 ||

In this regard, he states that there is no possibility of another light [being required]: "What? The meaning is: when the world is Śiva, who is void (śūnya), what is the nature of another light, by what means, and by what action is it produced? || 20 ||
That reality which is designated by the word "Brahman" is the innate form of everything;
wherein there is no contradiction whatsoever, everything is composed of that, and it is imperishable.
He states that this very thing is the uncontradicted intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of all entities with the word "yet" (verse 21).
As for this "objectness" which is experienced as being sublated in some cases,
and that sublation itself which is observed— we do not know what that is, for it is like a flower in the sky.
If so, what then is the nature of that which is sublated? To this he says: "That which... The state of being a category (padārthatva) is the condition of possessing name and form.

Having thoroughly reflected upon all of that—both its sublation and its sixfold modifications such as origination and so forth—we do not know it; the meaning is that it is utterly void, like a flower in the sky. || 22 ||
O Knower, remain as one whose internal mind has departed, peaceful like a great stone;
this is not the thinking mind, but the infinite, unborn, and imperishable Self.
And that form, being imagined by the mind, departs when the mind departs; therefore, [the text] says "be peaceful" and "be the Knower. [An objection:
Since the Knower will also surely depart with the departure of one's own internal mind, why is it said "be the Knower"? To this, he replies: "This one.
For when the mind departs, the mental activity consisting of name-and-form (nāmarūpa)—namely, thinking, conceptualizing, measuring, and [the functions of] the eyes and so forth—[also departs].
The meaning is that while the ignorant person departs, the knower does not; rather, he does not depart from Brahman itself, which is infinite, unborn, and immutable. || 23 ||
For one who abides in their own state, which is like space, the non-perception of the limbs occurs through the firmness of practice, just like the transformations in a dream. (24)

The meaning is this: for the knower who remains within his own body—which is like space—without mental affliction, there is simply no presentation or perception of name and form; because of the lack of firmness in the practice of abiding in that true nature, they arise in the mind like the transformations of a dream.
The Brahmanic agent perceives the variegated world even without any material cause or substratum; it is neither anyone at all, nor anything whatsoever.

How is it known that the world is merely a mental construction? To this he says: "without material cause" (*nirupādāna*). Since the mind alone—whether belonging to Brahmā or Hiraṇyagarbha—is the creator and fashioner of the world, and that [mind] produces the variegated world-picture even without a collection of material causes, being devoid of any apparatus such as coloring substances, brushes, or rollers, and even without a support, as if upon a wall-less void.

The meaning is that by mere volition one perceives and sees; there is no agent whatsoever apart from the mind, nor is there any object of action, as is observed in mental dreams and the like. || 25 ||
Since that which it expands is its very self, it remains established there in that manner;
because the visible does not exist, the visible is unreal—therefore, who, where, or what could act? (26)

And that mind, which stretches out—that is, expands—everywhere, as in a mental construction (*manorājya*) and so forth, exists there by its own self in the form of the appearance of this or that object. Thus, because of the absence of any visible object separate from itself, who can do what, to whom, and where?
The meaning is: no one does anything to anyone, anywhere. || 26 ||
"I am happy," and thus they are happy; "I am suffering," and thus they suffer.
All kings, though their true nature is that of space, remain established in their own essential form.

And thus, pleasure and pain, as well as the objects such as the earth and so forth that serve as their means, become either empty in form or identical with the nature of the Self when conceptual construction ceases; this he states with the words "I am. || 27 ||
The state of being material, as in the case of mountains in a dream, exists as a mere illusion for all entities, even those whose nature is the space of consciousness. (28)
He states that even for kings, the state of being non-kings can be conceived as being like a mountain in a dream, saying: "Of all... (verse 28).
Existence, when delineated by the sense of "I," is subject to the transformations of delusive states;
in the absence of that [sense of "I"], there is a state of rest characterized by tranquility, grounded solely in one's own true nature.
And this being the case, he states the result [of this] with the words beginning "by the delineation of 'I-ness'" (ahaṃtvollekhataḥ) and so forth. || 29 ||

Just as for you the meaning of the word "bracelet" exists as something distinct from gold, so too, for one whose self is tranquil, there exists no real ego-sense as something distinct [from the Self]. (30)
He is extinguished, free from mental activity, silent, both the doer and the non-doer, and cool;
he remains as pure consciousness alone, utterly tranquil, empty yet completely full.
Free from latent impressions and intent upon the motionless, like the limbs of a mechanical puppet,
that wise man remains exactly as he is, even while engaged in worldly activity.
Precisely because it is free from latent impressions (*nirvāsana*), it is supremely motionless and devoid of the conceit of movement,
like a body made of stone or other materials fashioned by a machine.
Just as the limbs of an infant lying on a couch throb or do not throb at all without any conscious effort of its own, so it is with one who has realized the Self.
He provides an illustration for the possibility of that [state] of non-vibration even during the state of bodily vibration, saying "just as" (yathā).
The meaning is that it should be understood as being like this: the limbs of an infant sleeping on a swinging cradle do not vibrate at all, even though the cradle itself is swaying. || 33 ||

For one who possesses the singular awakening that is free from [the notion of] awakening, who is devoid of hope, seeking, and desire, and whose nature is the peaceful and infinite Self—whence could there be any further mental pursuit? (34)

[Objection: Might not the very cognition of its own nature (svarūpa-jñāna) be the coordination with the body and so forth? To this, he says: "niḥsaṃbodha" (devoid of cognition). "Niḥsaṃbodha" refers to an outward-turned mental modification (citta-vṛtti), which is absent in that which consists of undivided consciousness (akhaṇḍa-bodha). There is a distinction between *āśā* (hope), which is the longing for an object yet to be attained; *sneha* (affection), which is [attachment] toward an object already attained; and *āśis* (blessing/aspiration), which is the praying for something through mental desires (*manoratha*).
For one who is neither a seer nor an object of sight, whose nature is not vision and who possesses no form—how indeed could there be any synthesis for such a witness who is independent? (35)

He states that there can be no synthesis for that [consciousness] even because of the sublation of the triad beginning with the seer (draṣṭṛ), by saying "of the non-seer" (adraṣṭuḥ); and [it belongs to one who is] "self-constituted and formless" (svarūpiṇo nirākārasya). || 35 ||
Expectation alone is dense bondage; equanimity alone is liberation.
For one who has come to rest within that state which encompasses all sounds, what remains to be perceived? (36)

The meaning is that equanimity (upekṣā) endowed with all sounds is indeed liberation through universal equanimity. When one has come to rest in that state of fulfilled desire, what is there to be looked for or expected? The reading "īpsyate" (is desired) is the correct one. || 36 ||
In this earthly body, which is as unreal as a limb in one's own dream and whose nature is mere delusion, from where, where, for whom, and what could there be any dependence? (37)
For everyone indeed depends upon a body; however, when that [body] is sublated—just like a dream-body or the like—it follows that no one at all has any need for it. This is the meaning. || 37 ||
With all worldly desires stilled, with every curiosity departed,
and with sensation cast aside, the wise one abides in pure, absolute knowledge.
He summarizes: "It is peaceful. || 38 ||
Then, by means of that which has been heard, even great delusion was entirely abandoned right there by the learned one, like skin shed by a snake. (39)
He states that due to Maṅkin’s status as the primary qualified recipient, delusion was removed by the mere act of hearing [the teaching] once:
"O Maṅkin," etc. (39).
Performing his duties as they arose in the natural course, with his latent impressions (vāsanā) cast aside,
he remained on the mountain in meditative absorption (samādhi) for the duration of a hundred years.
In that state, until now, the yogi remains with his faculties stilled, possessing qualities like a stone; yet, when being awakened, he becomes enlightened.
By this path of discernment, O Rāghava, may you attain peace and sport with a joyful mind;
let not your passion-laden intellect fall into despondency, for it would vanish in an instant like a cloudless autumnal bank of clouds.

Therefore, O Raghava, by means of this method embraced by the monkey [Hanuman], with a mind that has attained the excellence of knowledge through the faculty of discernment (*viveka*), attain peace so as to sport in the bliss of your own Self (*svātmānanda*). The meaning is: let not your intellect, while still possessed of passion, fall into a state of wretchedness—like a cloudless autumnal sky suddenly becoming devoid of clouds when its discernment has vanished. || 42 ||

Thus ends the twenty-sixth canto, titled "The Completion of Nirvāṇa" (or "The Perfect Attainment"), in the Nirvāṇa Section of the Holy Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa of Valmīki, composed by the Sage. [The perfect attainment is complete. Canto 26.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth canto, named "The Completion of Nirvāṇa," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The twenty-seventh canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Be extinguished, with a peaceful soul, following whatever has come to you.
O gentle one, he is equal to both the existent and the non-existent, as if fashioned from crystal and other such materials.
The manifestations of the universe arise from the delusion of the consciousness's vibration within the movement of the mind;
through the stilling of the mind alone, and thereby the stilling of that vibration, the abiding in one's true nature is proclaimed.

Just as a person fashioned from crystal, though existing, is like a non-existent thing because it does not obstruct the range of vision, so too [the Self], because it does not obstruct the range of the vision of the non-duality of one's own Self, is like that which is non-existent— [yet] all is established within that single, expansive Self.
Since it exists neither in a single thing nor in all things together, how can there be a perception of multiplicity? || 2 ||

The meaning is that prior to awakening, [the Self] exists as one alone in the form of the universal self; but upon awakening, it exists neither as one nor as all, because the states of being the individual (vyaṣṭi) and the collective (samaṣṭi) have been sublated. || 2 ||
Everything is devoid of beginning and end, a void filled with the essence of consciousness (cittattva).
In the arising and destruction of the body, what impairment can there be for the essence of consciousness?

An objection may be raised: "Since [the self] is experienced as being delimited by birth and destruction in each body, and by the measurement of seven spans, let it be manifold. To this he says: "Beginningless and endless... (verse 3).
For inert playthings manifest due to the flickering radiance of consciousness; through the absence of such flickering, they are not perceived, like waves in water.
The manifestations such as the creation of insentient matter are the play [of consciousness]; the mind is the wonder of consciousness, arising from its own restlessness.
Just as the suspicion that a white cloud is a cloth does not bear fruit,
so too this suspicion that "this body is I" is not real.

The suspicion that it is a cloth is a metaphorical imagination (*utprekṣā*) based on its appearance as cloth; it does not partake in the result of determining the ultimate reality. In this context, "suspicion" (*śaṅkā*) means delusion (*bhrānti*). || 5 ||

Do not remain submerged in that which is non-substantial, for it bestows manifold worldly existence; instead, for the sake of your ultimate welfare, contemplate today that which is substantial—the primordial, infinite bliss.
Do not become immersed in the conceit of "I" regarding the body and so forth, which are non-entities and illusory; [do this] for the sake of your well-being and liberation.
In this [reality], the infinite sky of consciousness alone constitutes the limit of the equanimous Self;
may that supreme reality be the ultimate reality for you. (7)
What is that reality which should be cultivated? He says: "The space of consciousness" (cidvyoma). The meaning is: may that supreme reality be the object of your mind. || 7 ||
Thus, you alone are indeed the stainless one who possesses such certainty;
the meditator, the object of meditation, as well as the act of meditation, and even truth itself, do not exist at all.

He states what the fruit of that is: "In this way. One might object that this certainty is not true certainty because it sublates the triad of meditation, the meditator, and so forth; anticipating this, he says "the meditator," with the intention that its very non-sublation is logical. To the question of why it is non-sublatable, he replies: "And it is real."
The meaning is that there is not even the slightest truth in the triad beginning with the meditator (the meditator, the object of meditation, and the act of meditation). || 8 ||
The seer, the seen, and the act of seeing are but the manifestations of consciousness alone;
apart from that awareness, there is no meditator and no object of meditation.
If it is then asked how the triad of perception and so forth can be sublated, since they share that same nature [of being dependent on the object], the author states the distinction:

"The seer," etc. For perception, being produced by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), is dependent solely on the object (*vastutantra*) and not dependent on the person (*puruṣatantra*); this is because, due to the predominance of the ultimate consciousness (*paramārthacit*) manifested through the mental modification (*vṛtti*), it brings about the cessation of ignorance (*ajñāna*).

The seer and the rest are merely manifestations (*vibhūti*) of the ultimate consciousness itself. Meditation, however, is not born of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), nor is it dependent on an objective reality; rather, it follows the will of the person. Therefore, because they are merely specific types of activity, the meditator and the rest are nothing but manifestations of ignorance (*avidyā*) and are thus to be sublated—this is the meaning. He states another distinction with the words "not that" (*atad*): "not that" means non-consciousness (*asaṃvit*).

The meaning is this: every insentient object is seen as distinct from that consciousness; therefore, the visible is necessarily dependent upon the act of seeing. However, the object of meditation (dhyeya) exists and shines even without the act of meditating (dhyāna); thus, it is not dependent upon meditation. This is the distinction. || 9 ||
When the moon of the first day of the lunar fortnight rises and the wind of universal dissolution blows, the reality of the self remains equanimous and serene; it neither agitates nor subsides.

He states that the changelessness of consciousness (*saṃvit*) is its distinction from everything else, saying "rising" (*udyatī*): just as the ocean is agitated when the new moon rises, or dries up when the wind of universal dissolution blows, the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*) is not like that; this is the meaning. || 10 ||
Just as a person traveling by boat perceives the shaking of stumps, trees, mountains, and so forth,
and just as there is the cognition of silver in mother-of-pearl, so too is the perception of the body and other objects for the mind.

If it is asked, "In that case, how is the triad consisting of the seer and so forth a manifestation (vibhūti) of that [consciousness]? the intention is that it is so only by way of illusory transformation (vivarta); with this in mind, he says "just as.
The meaning is that the error arises through the perception of the mind within consciousness. || 11 ||
Just as the body and so forth belong to the mind, so too does the mind belong to the body;
likewise, the individual soul belongs to the supreme state—therefore, whence can there be duality? (12)

In this way, the mind is also imagined through the perception of the body; the individual soul (jīva) is imagined through the perception of both; and through that [perception of the soul], both of those are imagined. Thus he says "as... (verse 12), meaning that all these are illusory manifestations (vivartāḥ) within pure consciousness.
All this is one, the peaceful Brahman, due to the expansion of consciousness;
there is no such thing as the world and so forth, nor does any other delusion exist. (13)
But from the perspective of Brahman, he says that it is indeed one, namely: "all. || 13 ||
Just as a forest does not exist in the sky, nor moisture in sand,
nor lightning in the orb of the moon, so too do the body and other such things not exist in the mind.
In the mind, regarding the vision of reality. || 14 ||
While this world-delusion does not exist at all, do not be afraid;
know this alone to be the supreme truth, O best among those who know the truth. (15)
Be afraid; experience fear. || 15 ||
That delusion of yours which held that "the world exists" has today been stilled by my instruction; what other cause for bondage remains? (16)
That delusion of yours which held that the world exists while the existence of non-dual Brahman does not exist, has now vanished. || 16 ||
Just as pots, water-jars, vases, and the like consist of nothing but clay, so this world consists of nothing but mind; and that [mind] is extinguished through analytical inquiry. (17)

In calamities and prosperity, in existence and non-existence, remain with a consciousness that is tranquil regarding desire, joy, and sorrow; liberated by the knower of the "I-notion" through gentleness, abide as you truly are and do not dissolve away.

O Rāma, being liberated from the affliction of egoism through my gentle instruction, remain as you truly are— equanimous amidst prosperity and adversity, with a consciousness of joy that has stilled its desires in times of fortune, and a consciousness of despondency that has stilled itself in times of misfortune, even amidst the fluctuations of power in this world of birth and death. Do not dissolve away by forgetting my instruction.
Do not remain, having abandoned the firm stability in your own true nature. || 18 ||
O Rāma, moon among the lords of your lineage, if you remain having realized the reality as it truly is, then remain free from joy, sorrow, desire, and aversion, or stay however you wish. (19)

Now, will there be a recurrence of bondage due to the fault of continuing in joy or sorrow—whether through negligence after the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), or due to the power of *prārabdha* karma? No, he says: "As it truly is.
O Rāma, moon among the lords of your own lineage, you [should realize] the reality of the non-duality of Brahman and the Self as it truly is, through direct perception (*aparokṣatayā*).

If you remain having correctly realized [the Truth], then either stay free from the defects characterized by joy, sorrow, and desire—which cause affliction to the mind—or else remain following them as you wish; this is the connection here with the word "or" (*vā*) from the previous verse. It was not said by me, "Remain dissolved," for the sake of your perceived happiness, but rather—
The meaning is that there is doubt regarding liberation only to that extent. || 19 ||
Thus ends the twenty-seventh canto, titled "The Instruction on the Principal Yoga," in the Nirvāṇa Section of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, within the *Deva-mokṣopāya*.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh sarga, titled "The Instruction on Primary Yoga," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa*, within the *Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The twenty-eighth canto.
Śrī Rāma said:
[Tell me] of the seeds and sprouts, and of human actions that bring about birth.
O All-pervading Lord, tell me again the true nature of those things associated with the meaning of the word *daiva*.
The true nature of seeds and sprouts, of human actions that bring about birth,
and of those things signified by the term "destiny" (daiva), is further described here.

The reality of all these factors— seeds as the material causes, sprouts as their effects, persons as the agents, and actions consisting of prescribed, prohibited, and indifferent deeds— which constitute the visible causal complex, and which, when joined with the unseen cause termed *daiva*, produce the misfortune of cyclic existence characterized by a succession of births.
The meaning is: "Although it was previously explained in a detailed analysis, explain it again by summarizing it into a single whole. || 1 ||

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: This very vibration of consciousness, passing through the successive stages of destiny, action, and so forth, from the state of a pot up to its final dissolution as a pot, has attained the status of a person in the world.

In this regard, first, the reality of destiny is action; the reality of action is the person (*puruṣa*); the reality of that [person] is the vibration of consciousness (*citspanda*) in the form of the mind; and the reality of that [vibration] is the conscious self (*cidātman*) itself.

That very conscious self, through the initial vibration of consciousness characterized by the primordial resolve, "May I become many; may I procreate," becomes the collective and individual mind (*samaṣṭi-vyaṣṭi-manas*). Thereafter—

Through the superimposition of the form of a body, the person (puruṣa) performs actions; thereupon, having attained the status of a deity in the form of unseen merit and demerit (adṛṣṭa), it undergoes transformation (*vivartate*) into the form of the world—consisting of substances such as jars for the sake of experiencing those [results]—and into the nature of qualities and actions residing therein, such as the universal "jar-ness" (*ghaṭatva*). Thus, it takes on the form of words denoting causes such as destiny and karma.

With the intention that things such as a jar, up to the limit of "jar-ness," and even the forms of words denoting effects, are in reality synonymous with the vibration of consciousness (citspanda), he gives the following answer: "By fate... (verse 2).
Apart from the vibration of consciousness, what could manhood or action possibly be?
For it is by this alone that the world—consisting of jars, pits, cloths, and so forth—is created. (3)
For this very reason, everyone experiences that human actions, jars, huts, and so forth, possess their existence and manifestation (sattāsphūrti) dependent upon consciousness;

however, if one does not accept them as transformations (vivarta) of consciousness, how could they exist devoid of existence and manifestation? The meaning is that they would simply be unreal (alīka). || 3 ||
The fortune of the world proceeds from the vibration of consciousness accompanied by latent impressions;
indeed, the cycle of existence ceases from the vibration of consciousness devoid of latent impressions. (4)
Since everything consists merely of the vibration of consciousness, he states the cause for its arising in diversity and its cessation with the words:
"it proceeds" (pravartate). || 4 ||
For they know that the vibration of consciousness which is without latent impressions (vāsana) is non-vibration;
even when vibrating, it is a non-manifesting vibration, by which one is not carried away as by a whirlpool or the like.

The meaning is that by which cause—such as a whirlpool and so forth—a wave, though possessing motion while being drawn into the interior, attains the state of being merely the internal ocean and is thus perceived (*asphurat*) as having no motion at all; that is, it is so inferred (*vitarkyate*). || 5 ||

O Rāma, there is not even the slightest difference between consciousness and its own vibration, nor between creation and the action of the person, except for the portion consisting of conceptual construction.

For this very reason, he states that there is a distinction between the vibration (*spanda*) and the person (*puruṣa*) through their mutual reflection: "even slightly" (*manāk*). It is precisely the vibration of consciousness (*citaḥ*) that constitutes the form of the person and so forth, while the cessation of that [vibration] is its formlessness; thus, the difference between vibration and the person arises from their reciprocal awareness. || 6 ||
Just as the duality of water and its waves arises from conceptual construction and is not real,
so too here are the living being and its karma, which consist of the vibration of consciousness.
He says "jala" (water) to show that there is even more certainly no difference due to the substratum: "jantuḥ" means a person. || 7 ||
O Rāma, action alone is the person, and the person alone is the state of action;
know that these two are non-different, just as coldness is inseparable from frost.
"In the undivided," so says the Śruti: "Now, the Self is the essence of actions; this is their *uktha*, for from it the actions arise. (8)
Just as that which is snow is coldness, and that which is coldness is snow;
so too is the action this living being, and the living being is that very action.
And thus, when merit and demerit are being performed, the meaning is that they exist in the prior state of the future body and its objects of experience. || 9 ||
Divine beings, actions, humans, and so forth are merely synonyms for the very essence of the vibration of consciousness; they do not exist as separate entities such as actions and the like. (10)
And thus, he says "consciousness" (saṃvit) to establish that which was stated: that [the term] is a synonym for destiny, action, and so forth. || 10 ||
Through vibration, consciousness becomes the seed of the world; through non-vibration, it attains seedlessness.
And that very [consciousness] is the sprout, because the beauty of the sprout already exists within it.
He provides the answer to the question regarding "the seed and the sprout" with the word "from vibration" (spandāt).
The meaning is that the very seed itself, having emerged in the form of subtle internal parts, is what is called the "sprout. || 11 ||
And consciousness, by its very nature, is in some respects motionless and in others mobile;
it is infinite, like a single ocean, established within the sequence of space and time.
The nature of consciousness is such that it undergoes vibration—established in the sequence of space and time—in some instances and not in others; this is the meaning. || 12 ||
The vibration of consciousness, possessing latent impressions, is here the seed;
though itself causeless, it becomes the cause for the series of sprouts such as the body and so forth. (13)
Having become possessed of latent impressions (vāsanā), even that which is not a cause attains the state of being a cause. || 13 ||
Even regarding the movement within the seeds of grass, creepers, vines, shrubs, and trees, the seed is nothing but the vibration of consciousness; for that [vibration], no seed exists.

With the intention that it is that very [seed] which, residing in the form of intermediate seeds, is the seed everywhere, whereas the intermediate forms serve to establish the specific arrangement of its effects as particular functional forms, he says: "tṛṇa... (grass, etc.). This is because the movement of other seeds proceeds toward their established effects. Now, one might object: in this way, there would also be another seed following after that [initial seed].
Fearing that this might lead to an infinite regress, he says: "Of that," [verse 14].
There is no difference between the seed and the sprout, just as there is none between fire and its heat;
know that the seed itself is the sprout, and know that action itself is the human being. 15.

If you think that the sprout is merely the power inherent within the seed, even then there is no difference between the power and that which possesses the power; with this intention, he says: "No. (15)
The consciousness, throbbing within the sheath of the earth, produces the sprouts of stationary beings—
whether gross or subtle, soft or hard— like bubbles upon the water.
[He creates] the sprout of stationary beings such as the banyan tree and others; [beings that are] cruel and hard. And thus they remember:
"The Maker of All, having entered the seed in the form of earth, water, and so forth, himself, in the form of Time, brings about the emergence of the sprout. (16)
Without the funeral pyre, who would be capable of causing sprouts as hard as adamant to emerge from the earth’s womb, which is exceedingly delicate? (The reading *aṅkurāt* is better. 17.
"Vajrasārān" means hard substances such as coral; who could cause them to sprout—that is, to emerge—from a much softer sprout?
Consciousness, which resides within the essence of the vital energy of living beings, expands the moving world;
just as the sap residing within a creeper produces flowers and fruit.
He states that this same principle applies even to the production of the body from semen and blood: "A living being," etc. (18).
If consciousness were omnipresent and not exceedingly powerful, then who would be capable of causing the agitation of gods, asuras, and mountains? (19)
This is the primordial seed of all moving and stationary beings;
as for this [seed], no seed exists other than the mere vibration of consciousness.
The vibration of consciousness is its throbbing. || 20 ||
There is no difference between seeds, sprouts, and conceptual constructions; nor between action, the agent, and karma; nor between waves, ripples, and billows—there is no distinction in reality.
Action is destiny; there is no distinction between them, nor is there any distinction in the underlying reality that serves as their substratum. || 21 ||
Salutations forever to that Great One, the wise Paśupati, for whom duality exists in the form of seed and sprout within both man and action. || 22 ||

He censures one who does not perceive this non-duality established in the Śruti with the words "dvitvam" (duality). "Dvitvam" means duality—that is, difference—even between those two, the seed and the sprout. Alternatively, the meaning is: "Obeisance to the Great Brahman," who exists as the Great Beast (*paśu*) by virtue of having that very nature. || 22 ||
That essence of latent impressions (vāsanā) which resides within consciousness—the seed of birth—causes the sprout [of rebirth] to flourish; burn it with the fire of non-attachment.
He says that its state as a seed, which is joined with attachment to latent impressions (*vāsanā*), departs when those impressions are burnt: "of consciousness" (*saṃvitter*), [verse 23].
The wise know that non-attachment consists in the mind’s non-immersion in auspicious or inauspicious actions, whether one is performing them or not. (24)
Alternatively, the eradication of latent impressions (vāsanā) itself is known as non-attachment (asaṅga);
by whatever means possible, you must indeed accomplish that within yourself.

If, however, you consider that attachment is indeed the latent impression (*vāsanā*) and that non-attachment is its very eradication, then [the author] says "Or else" (*athavā*), meaning: burn away that very latent impression through the practice of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*). || 25 ||
By that very same method and through human effort by which you understand this, the supreme Śiva is attained, wherein the sprouts of latent impressions (vāsanā) are utterly uprooted. (26)

By that very method—whether characterized by the previously mentioned *rājayoga* or by *haṭhayoga*—which has been long practiced through human effort, you shall easily attain the destruction of latent impressions (*vāsanākṣaya*); this is what is enjoined. This [destruction] is indeed the nature of the inner self (*pratyagātman*). || 26 ||
By means of human effort, or in whatever way you know how, restrain the portion of egoism;
this is the destruction of latent impressions (vāsanākṣaya). || 27 ||

Since the ego-sense (*ahaṃbhāva*) alone is the root of all latent impressions (*vāsanā*), being the very knot of consciousness, he says "by human effort" (*pauruṣeṇa*) [in verse 27], meaning that one should restrain that very ego-sense.

There is indeed no other way to cross over saṃsāra than through human effort—this effort which consists in the dissolution of the latent impressions (vāsanā) within this state known as the absence of egoism (nirahaṃbhāva). || 28 ||
In [the chapter] titled "The Exhaustion of Latent Impressions," which is the crossing over of saṃsāra. || 28 ||
Right from the beginning, consciousness alone exists here; that is the sprout, and it is the seed.
That is karma, and that is the person (puruṣa); that is destiny (daiva), and that is the auspicious and the inauspicious.

He states that the existence of sprouts, seeds, and so forth is due solely to the existence of the consciousness of the inner self (pratyagātman), which is without beginning or end, and not by virtue of their own nature—thus [he says]: "Ādyā... (Verse 29).
In the beginning, there is no seed other [than consciousness], nor a sprout, nor a person;
there is neither karma nor destiny and so forth, for it is Consciousness alone that arises. (30)
A man is a person. || 30 ||
O virtuous one, there is no seed, nor indeed is there even a sprout; neither is there karma, nor is there a person.
Rather, it is the single Consciousness that has arisen through this splendor of designations, like an actor appearing in the beautiful roles of gods, humans, and asuras.
[The meaning is: Since the seed and so forth are devoid of inherent existence, the one Self of Consciousness alone, having become the world through false forms such as seeds, dances.

He states the conclusion: "It is not the seed. Consciousness (*cit*) is the very nature of consciousness (*citsvarūpa*). The mention of the designation is for the purpose of recalling the scriptural teaching that "speech is merely a modification" (*vācārambhaṇa*). || 31 ||
Having cultivated this very certainty free from affliction, and having utterly abandoned the doubt regarding the deliberation of human effort,
remain— free from latent tendencies and liberated from all mental constructions— as the embodiment of pure consciousness, indeed, according to your own desired wish.

The meaning is: O healthy Rāma, having cultivated such a conviction that "you are indeed thus," and having abandoned the doubt regarding the investigation of unrealities such as human effort and action, remain—free from latent tendencies (nirvāsana), either concentrated or acting according to your desired will. || 32 ||
With all desires stilled and free from doubt, established in pure consciousness alone, you perform all duties;
delighting in the Self as your sole pleasure, with all desires fulfilled, O Rāma, be fearless and gladdened by tranquility. (33)
Clarifying this very point, he concludes with the verse beginning "praśānta" (33).
Thus ends the twenty-eighth canto, titled "The Exposition of the True Principle of Doubt," in the latter half of the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*, composed by Vālmīki. 28.

Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Exposition of Doubts and the Established Doctrine of Reality," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa within the illustrious *Vāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa-tātparya-prakāśa*.
The twenty-ninth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Remain eternally inward-turned, free from passion and devoid of latent impressions.
Contemplating everywhere that action is merely pure consciousness—stainless and tranquil. || 1 ||
In worldly conduct, one should follow the established customs of the people as they arise;
however, in one's true nature, constant steadfastness—this is what is taught here to Rāma.
He accomplishes and brings to fruition whatever action is appropriate in every case—whether toward enemies, friends, or neutral persons—cultivating it according to what has been attained. || 1 ||
Pure as the sky, wise, established in the singular density of pure consciousness, equanimous, gentle, and equal in bliss— he is Brahmā, whose mind is fully expanded.
O Bhava, may you be such that your intention (āśaya) is expanded and extended by that Brahmā whose essence is identical with Brahman. || 2 ||
In sorrows, in terrible calamities, in crises and in pitfalls;
in all circumstances as they arise—whether lowly or exalted. (3)
Regarding those things obtained— whether they be lowly or trifling, or exalted and great, such as sorrow and the like— he remains inwardly undistressed; yet,

following the local customs of each respective place, he undergoes in due order the suffering and the mockery of suffering, including everything up to weeping and wailing, as well as the pairs of opposites such as cold and heat.
And "perform the pleasures of enjoyment such as garments, garlands, sandalwood, and so forth"—this is the syntactical connection for both [verses]. || 3 ||
Without being distressed, inflict suffering upon them according to their sequence and location, including everything from weeping and wailing to the experience of dualistic pleasures. (4)
O gentle-souled one, enjoy the bliss found in the company of beloved ones, in festivals, and in times of prosperity, like one who is deluded and overcome by latent impressions.
He elaborates upon the very meaning stated in brief with the words beginning "In gatherings" (samāgameṣu):
"Those fools who are overcome by the latent impressions of enjoyment, just like those people devoted to ritual action (karmaṭha). (5)
Consume all beings in the affairs of death, such as battles and the like,
just as a forest fire burns up grass, like one who is deluded and overcome by latent impressions.
Beings who act contrary to the Dharma are to be punished.
Without becoming weary amidst those things that come in due course, acquire wealth through reflection like a crane;
yet remain like one who is deluded and overcome by latent desires regarding the tasks of amassing wealth.
In matters of acquiring wealth that are not contrary to the Dharma and have come down through traditional succession; "artha" means wealth. || 7 ||
O destroyer of enemies,
forcibly shatter all your foes like the wind disperses empty clouds, as if they were deluded by latent tendencies.
The enemies, the foes. || 8 ||
Maintain fortitude toward people who deserve compassion and toward great souls;
with a mind delighting in the Self, remain silent like one who is deluded and overcome by latent impressions.
Fortitude is steadfastness and magnanimity; being silent means not boasting. || 9 ||
Be joyful amidst pleasures, be sorrowful amidst sufferings;
show compassion toward the wretched, and be courageous among the brave. (10)
In joys, that is, in circumstances that are occasions for joy. || 10 ||
O sinless one, you are not the agent in that which is performed by one who is inward-turned, ever-blissful, endowed with delight in his own self, and possessed of noble tranquility.

In that regard, he wards off the consequence of the fault associated with acting like one who is deluded by stating "antarmukha" (inward-turned). The word "you" is to be supplied as the subject. || 11 ||
O virtuous Rāma, because you remain constantly inward-turned through self-cultivation,
even the vajra-thunderbolt, were it to fall upon you, would become blunted.
Even the edge of the thunderbolt hurled by Indra becomes blunted and rendered futile; for the meaning of the Vedic scripture is that neither the gods nor non-existence have power over him. || 12 ||

He who dwells at ease within his own self, delighting in the self alone, is the Great Lord (Maheśvara), situated in the hollow of pure self-consciousness, free from the movement of conceptual construction.
Within the hollow of one's own self-awareness, in the space of the heart.
Weapons do not pierce it; fires do not burn it;
waters do not moisten it; and winds do not dry it up. (14)
Embracing the unborn Sustambha, who is one's own self, ageless and immortal, remain firm-minded, supporting yourself as one supports a stable pillar within a palace. 15.
The mind firmly supports its own self, which is eternal, unsurpassed bliss; therefore, O wise one, remain motionless like a firm pillar within that well-supported temple of the Self. 15.

One should contemplate consciousness within consciousness— consciousness that is self-abiding, inward-turned, and infallible— and which possesses the supreme splendor of the fragrance of the flowers that are the multitude of objects in the tree of the world.

Taking refuge in the supreme consciousness of Brahman— which is like the glory of the fragrance of the flowers, namely the multitude of categories of existence, belonging to the tree characterized as the world— and having rendered all external cognitions inward-turned and unshakable, remain thus. 16.
For those who constantly perform their duties externally with an inward orientation,
no latent impression (vāsanā) arises even while they are alive, just as it does not arise in stones.
The activity of worldly affairs; the phrase "like stones" (dṛṣadām) serves as an illustration for the non-arising of latent impressions (vāsanā). || 17 ||
Furthermore, make the mind sleep within, released from its outward wandering;
performing all actions while remaining without activity, like the limbs of a tortoise.
Like the limbs of a tortoise, he remains inactive both internally and externally, devoid of mental fluctuations.
Perform your duties with a mind that is devoid of internal activity yet appears to possess external activity, as if one who has just awakened from sleep. 19.
He says that very thing: "Internal," etc. One who has awakened from sleep is half-awake. || 19 ||
Like the consciousness of a child, a mute, or others, your mind— having cast off internal latent impressions— is not defiled while performing its duties, remaining like the sky.
Remain free from feverish distress with a mind that has dissolved through the abandonment of worldly conduct, which spreads only slightly outward while remaining profoundly asleep within.

The abandonment of worldly conduct (*vṛttityāga*) consists always in the practice of the knowledge of non-conceptual meditative absorption (*nirvikalpasamādhi*). By that [knowledge], once it has dissolved—that is, having been sublated—it continues to manifest merely as an appearance, like a cloth that is partially burnt; or rather, it is as if one were in a state of deep sleep or dead. || 21 ||
O sinless one, remaining in pure consciousness— where the stain of volitional thought has vanished and where the mind arises as its own exhaustion through knowledge— do or do not act.
Moving through the activities of the waking state with a mental state like that of deep sleep,
take nothing at all, nor abandon anything at all.
Remaining awake and engaged in worldly activity even while walking, do not, through a state of mind like that of deep sleep, grasp at anything desired nor reject anything undesired. || 23 ||
If you are in deep sleep even while awake, and you are awake within deep sleep,
then because of the identity of waking and deep sleep, that [reality] exists as you, free from all affliction.

If you are in the state of deep sleep even during the waking state due to the dissolution of both gross and subtle adjuncts, then you remain awake even in that deep sleep because of the absence of the veil of ignorance.
When there is oneness through the sublation of ignorance and its effects— which are the differentiators between waking and deep sleep— that which remains as the residue is [the Self].
You are that which is pure existence alone. || 24 ||
Thus, by means of gradual practice, one should attain that state which is devoid of beginning and end, transcending all dualities and all objective entities. (25)
Having reached the certainty that the world is neither dual nor even unitary,
attain the supreme rest with a mind as clear as space.
Śrī Rāma said:
"If this is so, O tiger among sages, then tell me: why do you yourself remain here in this world, identified as Vasiṣṭha, characterized by the notion of 'I'? (27)

With the intention that, if all duality were sublated, even your state of being Vasiṣṭha, your sense of "I," and so forth would be left without remainder, and thus how could there be the conventional usage of being a speaker and so on, Rāma asks: "If it is thus... (27).
Śrī Vālmīki said:
While Rāghava was speaking thus, Vasiṣṭha, the best among those who speak,
remained silent for half a moment, his movements perfectly composed.
"O Vasiṣṭha, this sense of 'I' and so forth does not exist at all; it is merely grasped by my listeners through the lens of ignorance.
But once their realization of reality is perfected, silence alone is the answer"—with this intention, he resorts to silence, saying "O Rāghava. (28)
While that great assembly of courtiers remained silent,
having fallen into an ocean of doubt as to what might happen, Rāma spoke again.
Even though some of the chief authorities had attained knowledge, because the ignorance of all had not been eradicated, they fell into an ocean of doubt. || 29 ||
"For what reason, O Blessed One, do you remain silent like me?
There is no principle in the worlds that is not capable of providing an answer for the virtuous. (30)

Thinking that his teacher had reached a state of being unable to respond simply because his arguments were exhausted, Rāma asked: "For what purpose? [Rāma implied: "In the midst of the worlds, there is no such logic or reasoning to be put forward by disciples that cannot be countered by virtuous, learned gurus.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
O sinless one, it is not because of my inability to speak that my capacity for reasoning has come to an end; rather, regarding this question, the answer is simply silence.
Because the limit of this question is its ultimate extreme, silence itself is the answer. || 31 ||

The questioner is of two kinds: either one who knows the truth or one who does not. To the ignorant person, the answer should be given according to their ignorance; but to the knower, it should be given according to their knowledge. (32)
In order to demonstrate the very nature of the limit (koṭi), he prepares the introductory context with the words "of two kinds," and so forth. || 32 ||
For all this time, O Mahāmati, you remained ignorant of that state and were a vessel for the higher conceptualizations. (33)
Now you have become a knower of reality and are resting in the supreme state;
it is clear that you are no longer fit for further conceptualizations.
O best of speakers, whatever literary composition there may be—whether its meaning is subtle or ultimate, and whether it is extensive or very brief—[all of it is contained within this]. (35)
Verbal expression is the mention of that which consists of speech. || 35 ||

O virtuous one, all that— consisting of delusions such as the exclusion of counter-correlates (*pratiyogivyavaccheda*), number, and so forth, as well as delusions regarding the past and other times— is permeated by Him, just as light is permeated by motes of dust. (36)

The counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) is the defining characteristic; exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) is differentiation. Number (*saṃkhyā*) is enumeration. "Transcendent" (*atīta*) means that which has passed beyond all of that;

it is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), its means of accomplishment, the sublation of what is other than that, the cognition thereof, and its methods—the objects of cognition, the cognizer, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and so forth—are included. It is "endowed with the delusions" of these, that is, with the stains of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*).
Light is the sunlight seen through a lattice window. || 36 ||
O Sundara, one who knows that [reality] does not deserve an answer that is stained with fault;
yet there is no speech that is without fault, and you remain one who is even more proficient in knowing it. (37)
And I must speak to my wise disciples exactly as it is;
for those who know reality as it truly is understand that the silence of a log is devoid of an end.
Of the resident disciple; free from limits, devoid of the stain of all limitations. || 38 ||
They say that silence, free from deliberation yet accompanied by intention, is the supreme state;
that very thing has been granted to you, O beautiful one, who are a knower of that [reality]. (39)

They say that prior to the arising of the knowledge of reality, due to the absence of investigation (*avicāra*) and because of ignorance, there is a state accompanied by conceptualization (*sa-saṃkalpa*), which is the mental construction of the fitness for the activity of speech through instruction.
