However, they say that through investigation (*vicāra*), silence (*mauna*) is indeed beyond the reach of speech, as the scriptural passages such as "from which words turn back, not having reached it along with the mind" [Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.4.1] declare.
And the wise [also remain thus]; that is silence itself. 39.
For, my dear, whatever a person is composed of, that he speaks;
yet I am composed of pure knowability alone, established in the state beyond speech.

The speaker is the Puruṣa. That which is to be known is the non-conceptual reality accessible through the direct realization of the truth; it consists of that alone (*tanmātramaya*). The suffix *mayaṭ* is used here in its own sense (denoting identity). 40.
For how can one who stands in the state beyond speech grasp the impurity of speech?
Therefore, I do not speak that which is unspeakable; for speech is indeed marked by conceptualization.
For indeed, every word is marked by conceptual constructions such as the exclusion of its opposite (pratiyogivyavaccheda) and so forth. 41.
Śrī Rāma said: Disregarding those words that proceed from the mouth which cause defects, speak first by means of the exclusion of their opposites: who are you?

Disregarding—that is, not making the primary intended meaning the object—speak by means of the method of *bhāgatyāga-lakṣaṇā* (indication through the abandonment of a part). "Excluder" (*vyavacchedī*) means that which is excluded (*vyāvṛtta*). "Counter-correlate" (*pratiyogī*) means that which defines it. || 42 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
O Rāghava, this being so, hear this as it truly is:
who are you, who am I, or what is the world?—O best among those who know the reality. (43)
As it truly is, as it exists. || 43 ||
O dear one, I am indeed this stainless sky of consciousness,
devoid of the perception of objects of thought, and transcending all mental constructs.
I am the pure sky of consciousness, you are the sky itself, and the entire world is the sky; everything is nothing but the sky.

My self consists solely of pure knowledge within my own nature which is composed of pure knowledge; liberated from the perception of other consciousnesses, I do not know how to speak of anything other than myself. (46)

I do not know, nor do I wish to speak of anything else whatsoever, even as small as an atom, that is distinct from my own inner self (*pratyagātman*). Thus, relying on the maxim that "whatever a word aims at is its true meaning," the intended sense is: "Please realize the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) as an undivided, non-conceptual whole. || 46 ||
Those intent on manifesting their own faction lead even those striving for the sake of liberation to a hundredfold branching [of views], thereby increasing only the ego and the sense of self. (47)

How then is it that the effort of wise men who are free from egoism succeeds for the purpose of enlightening the ignorant and for victory over opponents? To this he says: "svapakṣa... (regarding their own position). For the sake of the liberation of disciples, for the removal of their doubts, and also for the sake of victory over opponents, the wise are diligent.

The meaning is that those who, by means of valid cognitions such as scripture and reasoning, are intent on establishing their own positions, further nourish the single entity—the "I-self"—even though it has been sublated, by means of a superimposed mental construct (āhāryāropa), and thus lead it to a hundred branches; they do not, like the ignorant, fall into delusion. || 47 ||
They say that the state of one who is living yet tranquil, and who engages in worldly affairs yet remains like a corpse, is the supreme state.

It should not be understood that for these [wise men], the mere practice of displaying their scholarship is the supreme goal; rather, it is something else entirely, as he says: "While living" (jīvataḥ). || 48 ||

That which has no external means of accomplishment, which is peaceful, which has no internal means of accomplishment, which is equanimous, and which is neither pleasure nor pain, neither "I" nor "another"—such is Śiva. 49.

He further qualifies the supreme state itself as "having no external means. Precisely because it is devoid of internal and external means, it is free from the states of being an agent or an enjoyer; for that very reason, it is free from the objects of enjoyment, namely pleasure and pain.
It is auspicious (*śiva*) because its nature consists of the abundance of self-luminous, unsurpassed bliss. || 49 ||
This "I-ness" of liberation is non-existence; where is there any cultivation of it?
To seek that very thing by means of that [cultivation] is like a person born blind looking at a painting. (50)

Now, one might ask: for what purpose is it said to be self-luminous? Why should it not be something merely to be enjoyed, like sensory pleasure? To this he replies: "Of liberation" (*muktatāyāḥ*). This very sense of "I-ness" (*ahaṃtā*) is the absence of liberation; it stands in the place of its prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*). Where is there any contemplation or experience of liberation through such a sense of "I"? For an absence cannot [be experienced] by means of its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*).
It is possible to experience [liberation]. Well then, let the contemplation of liberation be [performed] precisely as liberation itself; regarding that, he says: "by that very [means].
The meaning is that in both cases, the logic would be like a person blind from birth attempting to view a painting. || 50 ||
Know that state which remains like a stone, whether in vibration or in non-vibration, belongs to one who is not insentient; it is the ageless state of liberation.

In that case, one might ask: since [the Self] remains as motionless as a mountain or a stone during the movement or non-movement of the ego, the vital breath, and so forth—just like the movement or non-movement of trees and animals—why should it not be insentient (jaḍa) like them?
To this, he says: "In movement... The word *āsita* means "remaining" or "abiding. The suffix *kta* is used here in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāve*).

Because that nirvāṇa is ageless and devoid of modifications such as decay; for even in a mountain rock there is indeed movement due to decay, and thus there is no absolute immobility. The sense is that inertia resides only in things subject to change, not in the immutable (kūṭastha). || 51 ||
And that is not known by another; it is experienced by oneself, like the state of being a knower within one's own self by a wise person who is detached from worldly desires.

Therefore, he states "And that" (tacceti), meaning that self-luminosity is established by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*). The sense is this: the quality of being a knower (*jñatva*) well-known in the case of the empirical self is not cognizable by another cognition—just like the result of the manifestation of a jar or similar object—because that would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
In that state, there is neither "I-ness" nor "you-ness," neither non-"I-ness" nor otherness;
it is simply the state of absolute purity, stainless and auspicious Nirvana. (53)
That is there. || 53 ||
They say that the consciousness of this conscious being consists precisely in its orientation toward objects;
and this very state is transmigratory existence, bondage, leading to great suffering. (54)
He states that for such a one, the very state of being illuminated by another is transmigratory existence: "the orientation toward the object of cognition" (cetyonmukhatva).
Cognition (cetana) is the activity characterized by the pervasion of the object of cognition (cetya). || 54 ||
Know that liberation is the insentience of the conscious self, consisting in the state of being turned away from objects of thought; it is the supreme, peaceful, and indeed imperishable state. (55)
He states that the absence of consciousness due to the non-existence of such volition is indeed desired in liberation: "Of the conscious one... (verse 55).
When one abides in the peaceful Self, which is tranquil and unconditioned by space, time, and the like, an object of cognition is simply impossible; who could cognize what, and how? (56)
Now, one might object: "Let there be an object of cognition even in liberation. To this he replies: "The direction," etc. (Verse 56).

O kings, just as a mental construction within a dream-appearance would appear as something other than it is without the nature of pure consciousness, so too is it when that same construction has gone outside.

Having thus established liberation as self-evident through mere inwardness, [the author] demonstrates the expansion of the conceptualization of the world through mere outwardness with the word "saṃkalpa" (volition). "O kings! is an address to the listeners.

Just as in the world perceived in a dream, volition—which conforms to various latent impressions (*vāsanā*)—is contained within consciousness; and though it consists of consciousness itself, it appears as such.

The meaning is that if it were to abandon its nature as consciousness and become something else, then likewise, when this Self has gone outside and is turned outward, the Self itself would become like something else—the insentient phenomenal world. || 57 ||
These [entities] such as the mind (manas) and the intellect (buddhi) conform to pure consciousness alone;
however, when conceived through the referents of words such as "mind" and "intellect," they are of a material nature.

In this way, the mind, intellect, and so forth are also of an insentient nature only when directed outward; however, when directed inward, they follow pure consciousness and consist of the single essence of consciousness. || 58 ||
In pure consciousness alone—which is equal, clear, pervasive both within and without, and undivided—why does the notion of duality expand to such an extent, leading only to misfortune? (59)

Thus, since everything internal and external consists of the single essence of consciousness (*cit*), the notion of duality—characterized by the outward-turning of consciousness—is itself a single, useless cause of misfortune; thus he says: "In pure consciousness alone... (verse 59).
What is the difference between pure consciousness alone and the void? That difference which the wise know transcends the reach of speech. (50)
One should not think that pure consciousness (*saṃvinmātra*), which remains when all objects of perception have vanished and is like a void, is not a human goal (*apuruṣārtha*).
For its nature as unsurpassed bliss is experienced by the wise; thus he says:
"Of pure consciousness... It does not reach the range of speech, the domain of words. This is because of such scriptural passages as, "From whence words turn back," and so forth.
The state of being. || 60 ||
Just as some appearance, possessing both existent and non-existent forms,
is perceived with effort by one who looks into the darkness, so too is this world perceived within Brahman.
Then, how does the world appear from the perspective of one who possesses discernment and reasoning? To this he says: "having the nature of both real and unreal.
Just as when the eyes are directed toward darkness with effort, a reflection appearing to have the nature of both real and unreal is perceived, so it is in this case.
If I am pacified and free from latent impressions, I am indeed space itself; yet if you do not bind yourself with latent impressions, you remain as the very sky of consciousness.
The connection is: "If you also do not form a latent impression (vāsanā)... || 62 ||
Thus, one who possesses internal certainty and knows that [reality] appears like an ignorant person through conventional designation;
though existing as the very embodiment of consciousness, he himself becomes tranquil, as if non-existent.

Any other person as well who possesses the conviction "I am indeed this space" is a knower of that [Brahman]. Although he exists as if ignorant through conventional designation and worldly usage, being of the very nature of consciousness, he becomes tranquil as if non-existent even while the body and so forth exist. Thus it is said: "Whosoever among the gods awakened to this became that; likewise among the seers, and likewise among human beings."
The meaning is "from scripture" (śruteḥ). || 63 ||
The fire of ignorance, blazing within living beings due to the wind of nescience while their consciousness is concealed, is extinguished by that very same [wind] once they have attained awakening.

Now, does the ignorance of individual souls (jīvas) cease through the conscious self (cidātman) or through that which is insentient (jaḍa)? Not the first, because the conscious self, on the contrary, is not opposed to it but rather its very establisher. Nor the second, because that which is merely insentient is itself an effect of ignorance and thus cannot oppose it. Anticipating this objection, he says: "Of the individual souls... [and] "I am ignorant."

Because the witness-consciousness (*sākṣijñapti*) is the establisher of ignorance, the fire of nescience (*avidyā*) characterized as the transmigratory existence of living beings burns even while being fanned by the wind of that very consciousness; yet, for those who have awakened to the realization "I am Brahman," it is extinguished by the nature of their final direct-perception modification (*caramasākṣātkāravṛtti*).
The meaning is that [ignorance] is pacified by the very wind of ignorance itself, which has been transformed and remains hidden within as a witness; it does not require a third factor.
That ignorance of non-inert beings which subsides like [the darkness] of wooden pillars—they call that liberation, the unagitated, the seated, and the imperishable state. (65)

Now, is the world known by the liberated or not? In the first case, there would be no distinction between them and those in saṃsāra. In the second case, while you claim to have abandoned the single ignorance regarding the Self, you would have accepted infinite ignorances regarding the world. Furthermore, how could those who are like wooden posts (sthāṇu) possess liberation? To this, he says: "of the non-inert" (ajaḍānām).

Because their essential nature is unobstructed self-luminosity and unsurpassed bliss, those who are non-inert possess an ignorance that is devoid of worldly cognition; for this very reason, their state of abiding—which is undisturbed and free from the agitation of suffering—is called liberation. Furthermore, there is no consequence of infinite ignorance, since [all] is known through a single realization.

The meaning is that [the self] is distinct from the knowledge of reality because it consists of the destruction of all ignorance through universal consciousness, and because the absence of erroneous cognition constitutes its very nature, thereby lacking any differentiation from the knowledge of reality. || 65 ||
By attaining knowledge through knowledge, a human becomes a sage;
by falling into ignorance through ignorance, one descends to the state of a beast or a tree.

Furthermore, with the intention that it is only when fundamental ignorance (mūlājñāna) exists that its power causes the absence of knowledge regarding external objects to result in foolishness, whereas upon its destruction it results in the attainment of sagehood (munitva), he says: "By way of being a knower" (jñatvena). || 66 ||
The delusion consisting of ignorance—that "I am Brahman and this is the world"—is unreal;
when scrutinized, it is not found, just as darkness is not found by means of a lamp. (67)

Furthermore, with the intention that both the knowledge of Brahman and the entire delusion of the world are nothing but ignorance (ajñāna), and that the cessation of ignorance is not itself ignorance—such that liberation would not fail to occur—he says: "I... (verse 67).

Even though the entire collection of sense organs is present, one whose intellect is stilled—being free from volition and devoid of perception—experiences nothing whatsoever, whether internally or externally. (68)
In that case, since those liberated while living (jīvanmukta) perceive external objects through their senses such as the eyes, they would not possess liberation; to this he replies:
As in deep sleep, the dream dissolves into the state of samādhi;
so too, within the awakening of the Knower, the entire visible world dissolves, and only one's own Self is perceived again. (69)

When awakening has arisen once and for all through the knowledge of samādhi, whatever is seen as the visible world is perceived as one's own self alone; the meaning is that there is not even an atom’s worth of what is called "non-self" remaining for them. || 69 ||
Just as blueness exists in the sky, so does the nature of earth and the other elements exist in Śiva;
apart from mere delusion there is nothing else—just as the sky is, so is Śiva. (70)
If it is asked, "Where does it dissolve?", he says: "Because it is mere illusion"—namely, "the state of being blue. || 70 ||
Even though he is endowed with all latent impressions (vāsanās), he is free from latent impressions;
for his intellect is such that it regards all this as non-existent.

For this very reason, a latent impression whose object has been sublated is not truly a latent impression; thus, he says that the knower is indeed "without latent impressions" (*avāsana*), using the words "by means of latent impressions" (*vāsanābhiḥ*). || 71 ||

O noble one, just as the world-processes are like a marvelous dream, an illusion, or a magician’s trick within our mental constructs, what reliance indeed can there be on them once they have been seen for what they are?

One might object: "How can you deny—through such arguments as 'the world is merely an unreal mental construction'—this universe composed of diverse realms of gods, humans, animals, and so forth, which is governed by numerous injunctions and prohibitions? For surely such objects do not exist within mere mental constructs or daydreams. Anticipating this doubt, [the author] establishes the existence of marvelous objects even therein.
He demonstrates this with the words "In volitions" (saṃkalpeṣu).

O fortunate one, just as dreams, illusions, and magical displays are wonderful in the case of objects created by volition, so too are the cycles of worldly existence (saṃsṛti). The meaning is: what reliance is appropriate even for objects seen in dreams and the like that are directly perceived? It is the same regarding the cycles of worldly existence. || 72 ||
There is no suffering, no happiness, no merit, and no sin;
nothing whatsoever is lost to anyone, because neither an agent nor an enjoyer exists.

If there were a knower, then let there be the fixed rule of merit and demerit for the experience of all pleasure and pain by that agent and enjoyer; but since those two are impossible, what basis could there be for such a fixed rule? To this he says: "No. (73)
Everything is empty and without support; even this notion of "mine" is like the double moon or a city in a dream—for us, that [notion] also does not exist. (74)
This notion of "mine" does not exist, nor does that egoism for which it is the condition. || 74 ||
Whether remaining solely in the state of worldly convention or having attained the silence of wood,
by abiding like a piece of wood or a stone, one attains the state of Brahman.

Whether he remains as one who knows reality, solitary and devoid of all duality while engaged in worldly activity, or whether he remains motionless like a piece of wood or stone, established in samādhi and having attained the silence of wood (kāṣṭha-mauna)—in every way, he indeed attains the state of Brahman. || 75 ||
In this auspicious state, which is peace and the nature of consciousness, there is neither multiplicity nor unity;
as for the existence of a whole possessing parts, no other logical justification exists here.

Thus, by relying on the doctrine of illusory transformation (*māyika-vivarta-vāda*), the establishment of the knower of reality (*tattva-vid*) in the supreme human goal (*parama-puruṣārtha*) has been shown through the negation (*apavāda*) of the superimposed world (*adhyāropita-jagat*). As for those other logicians who formulate various doctrines in different ways, regarding their worldly dealings such as the origination of the universe and so forth, [and] concerning the supreme human goal characterized by...

And he states that there is no logical reasoning regarding the ultimate reality (paramārtha) with the words beginning "in its state of peace" (śāntatve). Here, in this auspicious inner self (pratyagātman), which—through identification with the vital breath, intellect, mind, body, and so forth—appears as a manifold self of diverse nature, crowded with hundreds of worldly misfortunes, and is directly perceived; [it is] in the state of peace resulting from the negation of that [perceived manifoldness].

In establishing that which remains as the non-dual form of freedom from suffering and unsurpassed bliss, there exists no reasoning shown by other disputants that transcends the logic of superimposition and denial (*adhyāropa-apavāda*).
However, when Śiva is accepted as being by nature eternally quiescent, he is immutable and unchanging.

If the mind were of a nature delimited by movement, then there would be no logical justification or proof for its transmigratory existence through various forms such as bodies and sense organs. However, if, for the sake of establishing that [transmigration], its delimitedness, mutability, and possession of parts were admitted,
then one would likewise have to admit that the whole (the self) possesses parts, whether those parts be conscious or insentient.

In that case, there is no logical justification for that whole (avayavin) to exist as such through parts that are either conscious or insentient. For if the parts were conscious, their disintegration would be inevitable due to the impossibility of unanimity, which would entail the destruction of the whole;
whereas if they were insentient, it would follow that the whole itself must be insentient. Thus, in both cases, there would be the production of something impermanent.

Because enjoyment [of fruits] cannot be established in the absence of prior merit and demerit, and for thousands of other such reasons; likewise, even though Śiva— the cause of the universe— is accepted as being peaceful, immutable, and eternally unchanging,
yet he possesses a mental faculty consisting of volitions conducive to the creation of the world, and is the impeller of that [creation] in the form of the manifold, diverse phenomenal world.

The meaning is that since no other logical justification exists for the earth and other elements contained therein being composite wholes, the doctrine of illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) alone remains as the refuge. || 76 ||

And since that which has attained its true nature through the object does not exist at all within this stainless, all-pervading Brahman, there is no expression of an intrinsic nature (svabhāva) therein. (77)

[Objection: "But surely, even though the Self is peaceful, since at the time of dissolution all objects are merged into Brahman, by the very power of the diversity of their respective natures resulting from that [merger], they will manifest at the beginning of creation endowed with a variety of states such as being consciousness, manifoldness, non-manifoldness, and having parts. To this, he says:

—Regarding the phrase "artha-āgata" (derived from objects): Is the nature that serves as the cause for the diversity of objects derived from those objects within the reality of Śiva, the Supreme Self, or is it self-established? In this regard, to say that its nature is derived from objects is contradictory; for one's own state is what constitutes "nature" (*svabhāva*).
How could that which is adventitious and dependent on another be considered "nature"? Likewise, because [Śiva] is unattached and non-dual, He is stainless.

Furthermore, a connection with impurity consisting of a diversity of natures produced by another is simply not possible. The first *ca* (and) is intended to indicate that those objects do not exist independently at the time of dissolution (*pralaya*), such that they might manifest as diverse solely through the power of their own respective natures. Therefore, by process of elimination, it must be stated that this is the very innate nature (*svasvabhāva*) of Brahman itself, which is not adventitious.

In this all-pervading Brahman, there is not even the possibility of stating that it possesses a nature that is the cause of diversity; for otherwise, it would follow that all things possess every kind of diversity. Indeed, in the case of an all-pervading Brahman, there exists no determining factor at the time of dissolution (pralaya) to establish that "this specific nature belongs to this very thing. Furthermore, if one were to admit that every variety exists everywhere, then diversity itself would be lost, for [otherwise]...

The meaning is that if dharma were common to all, then diversity would not exist, nor could any differentiator be established; for this would lead to the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that the entire world would be of a single uniform nature. || 77 ||
Nor is there existence of consciousness due to the perception of a nihilist, for it is not unarisen;
since the view of grasped object and grasping subject is impossible, nothing at all exists.

[Objection: But in that case, since even the diversity of the world, which is common to all people, cannot withstand logical scrutiny, why should its cognition not also be denied? For consciousness is not established in the absence of an object of cognition; thus, the doctrine of emptiness (*śūnyavāda*) would follow. To this, he says: "And not... [The existence] of consciousness [is not lost] even upon the denial of the object of cognition.

Nor can it be said that [consciousness] does not exist; for since only a nihilist who denies consciousness is ever observed, such a denial is impossible. For he would deny only the objects of consciousness—which are distinct from himself—and not his own self. When all consciousness is itself that [Self], then by denying the object of consciousness therein, one would be denying consciousness itself.

It indeed leaves a remainder. Furthermore, since a negation without a substratum is impossible, the negation must be stated with respect to a self-luminous substratum consisting of the non-apprehended and the non-apprehender, which serves as the locus for the apprehended and the apprehender. That very [self-luminous nature] is its essence; therefore, the conclusion is the demonstration of the impossibility of the views of the apprehended and the apprehender within that unborn self itself.
That which is peace—stainless, unassailable, cherished by the noble ones, auspicious, unborn, imperishable, seated, and equanimous; that is the unerring state.
Abide in that tranquility! Drink, sport, and enjoy, for this "you" does not exist. 79.

O Rāma, having become that very state which is cherished and served by noble knowers of Brahman, which is unassailable—meaning incapable of being taken away by others—which is auspicious, infallible, and the ultimate truth, and which is eternally established; abide in it from the perspective of the supreme reality. In worldly transaction, however, drink, eat, enjoy, and sport like other people; nevertheless, [remain as you are].
You are indeed liberated; for this reason, the meaning is that this bondage of the visible world does not exist for you. || 79 ||

Thus ends the twenty-ninth sarga, titled "The Exposition of Contemplation," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa, within the *Dehādvaita-mokṣopāya* section of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, which belongs to the *Ārṣa* tradition. || 29 ||
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Exposition of Contemplation," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The Thirtieth Chapter.
The venerable Vasiṣṭha said:
The very notion of "I" is the supreme ignorance that obstructs the state of Nirvana; that it should be sought after by the deluded is the behavior of a madman. (1)

That vision by which the wise man, through the pacification of the delusion of manifoldness arising from ignorance such as the sense of "I," becomes firmly established in Brahman— that very vision is what is being accomplished here.
With the intention that as long as egoity (*ahaṃtā*) is not abandoned, even the inquiry into Brahman does not arise, let alone its attainment, he says:
"Egoity itself... [verse 1]. It is supreme, being the root pillar of all causal ignorance (*avidyā*);
it is the obstructer and veil of the state of liberation (*nirvāṇapada*). That is the state of liberation. || 1 ||
Enough with this very egoism born of ignorance; it is the very illustration of one's state of being ignorant.
For in one who knows that truth and is at peace, the notions of "mine" and "I" do not exist. (2)

The very sense of "I" (ahaṃtā), which arises from ignorance, is the illustration and the mark of being ignorant, just as smoke is the mark of fire. He demonstrates its negative concomitance (vyatireka-vyāpti) with the words: "For not... (na hi). || 2 ||
Having cast off the impurity of egoism, the knower remains free from fever— extinguished like the stainless sky— whether still possessing a body or devoid of one.
Or rather, it means "sufficiently" or "completely," referring to the impurity characterized by the notion of "I-ness. || 3 ||
Neither the autumnal sky, nor the tranquil ocean,
nor even the center of the full moon shines as brilliantly as the Knower.
It describes that through the very departure of egoism, the wise one attains purity, non-distraction, and fullness—stating "not so" [in comparison to the ignorant]. || 4 ||
Just as there is an absence of agitation in an army engaged in a colorful battle,
even so is the equanimity of the wise man, despite his involvement in worldly affairs.

Just as in a battle depicted in a painting, although the armies strike one another and there is the appearance of agitation, there is no actual agitation; for the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*) according to the rule *yudhy-ādīnām agaty-artheṣv akarmakeṣu*. || 5 ||
For the knower who has attained oneness with nirvāṇa, even latent impressions (vāsanā) are no longer considered impressions;
they are like the lines drawn on the surface of water, whereas the waves and other phenomena of the ocean are not distinct from the water itself.

In this way, even the latent impression (vāsanā), which is inferred by the mark of the activity of worldly convention, is not truly a "latent impression," because it is like a web of threads on a burnt cloth— extinguished within through sublation and unified in nirvāṇa.
Just as the ocean, with all its surging waves, is nothing but water, so too Brahman— even when appearing as the swelling of the visible world— is Brahman alone and nothing else.
He clarifies the illustration beginning with "waves" by stating: "like a surging wave. (7)
He whose inner [mind] has set and is unagitated, whose outer [senses] have set and are tranquil,
yet who exists when impelled [by necessity], is said to be liberated.

If it is asked what the characteristic is when all internal and external latent impressions (*vāsanā*) have been sublated, the intention is that it is precisely unshakeable tranquility (*akṣobha-śama*) and so forth; with this in mind, he says: "Internally... [and] "arisen, ever serene. (8)
In the supreme consciousness which consists of consciousness itself, it vibrates in the form of the uncreated emanation like water within water; therefore, of what nature is this diversity?
In the supreme Self, which consists of consciousness, when it is unknown, [the world] flashes forth and evolves. || 9 ||
Just as elephants, chariots, and other formations appearing in the sky amidst spreading smoke are not distinct from that smoke, so too are all creations non-different from the Supreme State.

The various distinct forms and arrangements, such as elephants, chariots, and so forth, are merely the structured manifestations of mist and smoke shimmering in the sky in the form of fragments of clouds. || 10 ||

Through the investigation of consciousness and delusion, you who sport in the non-apprehension of delusion—be victorious! Do not fall into despondency, O knowers, for that very state of knowing belongs to you.

Now the venerable Vasiṣṭha, having awakened all the listeners, said: "Consciousness. O wise ones who have come here for the sake of hearing, do not despair; rather, through discernment, realize that according to the method I have explained, the entire phenomenal world—which is the cause of despair—is but an error of consciousness, a mere illusory transformation (vivarta).

In the investigation of error and its object, since errors would result in being devoid of any intrinsic nature (*niḥsvarūpatā*) and thus cannot be apprehended, you who are playful—that is, by nature inclined toward play—should prevail, meaning you should exist with supreme excellence; for, by my instruction, you possess knowledge of that [reality], and not ignorance. || 11 ||
Just as a sprout internally experiences the tree, its leaves, and its fruit,
so too does the Knower experience the world, the ego, his own self, and even the void of the self.

He explains what kind of delusion of consciousness that ignorant person experiences at that time: "Like a sprout. The ignorant person, though his own self is in reality like the void or space, experiences himself as the world within the state of "I-ness" (*ahaṃtva*).
The elided *saṃdhi* (sandhi) is an archaic Vedic usage. Just as a sprout [carries] within itself that which consists of latent impressions (*vāsanā*)...
The meaning is that it is like the state of a tree's leaves, fruits, and so forth. || 12 ||
Form, light, mind, and existence possess a stick-like nature within the flames, just as their rays;
yet even while existing, these do not truly exist, being like the illusory powers of a deluded mind. (13)

He explains what kind of inquiry (*vicāra*) is involved there with the words "rūpa" and so on: although external objects such as form and light, and internal states such as the mind, exist by virtue of being the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*), they do not exist in their own right (*svarūpeṇa*).

The meaning is that they are like the appearance of a staff, a wheel, or other shapes within the flickering flames of a whirling firebrand. These are merely the weak manifestations of the mind (*cittābalāḥ*).
Like beloved women imagined by a distracted mind. || 13 ||
"According to your pleasure, according to your undertaking, according to your destruction, and according to your arising;
according to the place and according to the time, may you, free from old age, remain in peace. (14)

Therefore, O listeners, having investigated— by means of the arguments set forth in the section on arising, persistence, and cessation— how this entire world arises, how it persists, how it undertakes its own functions, how it experiences pleasure and pain, how it perishes, and what its respective space and time are like; and having determined that it is false, remain in peace.

Even while engaging in worldly affairs, one who is tranquil amidst the attainment of the desirable and the undesirable experiences perfect nirvāṇa within, like a corpse, perceiving no other state. 15.
Like a corpse, he has attained nirvāṇa with a tranquil mind; therefore, he does not experience [sensation]. || 15 ||
That ego devoid of mental impressions, which sustains the world for a long time—whether one is living or dead—is the conscious soul; it is the supreme state.

The meaning is this: for those liberated while living (jīvanmukta), the egoity (ahaṃtā) remains devoid of mental impressions (vāsanā) until the fall of the body; that which sustains the world and that which is the living soul (jīva) who experiences it both exist for that duration as pure consciousness alone. There is not even an atom of an insentient part therein; thus, that state is indeed the supreme abode (paramaṃ padam). || 16 ||
For men bound by the noose, existence itself, carried away by the force of dullness, serves only as a burden of suffering, like young boats tossed upon the ocean. (17)

And thus, when one extracts the essential point, it follows that for both the individual soul (*jīva*) and the world (*jagat*), existence itself—consisting of a flow of insentient matter—is a misfortune; with this intention, he says:
"It should be construed as 'for the purpose of carrying the burden of merchandise consisting of suffering. (17)
Liberation does not resort to him as it does to the experience of ignorance and the like;
for how could one who is alive attain that which is said to be attained only by one who is dead? (18)

For this very reason, the state of liberation—characterized by the fullness of the uniformity of consciousness—does not resort to that ignorant person, as if due to the offense of his experience of the dullness born of ignorance. The meaning is that just as heaven and other realms attainable by one who has died through such acts as throwing oneself from a cliff do not resort to one who is still living, so it is here. || 18 ||
Whatever is conceived through volition, all that is subject to destruction by that very volition;
that wherein this [volition] does not exist is the true, imperishable state.

[Objection: "Let there be no liberation; let some eternal human goal (puruṣārtha) exist even within the fruits of heaven and so forth produced by mere volition. To this, he says: "Whatever [is desired]... The sense is that upon the destruction of that [volitional fruit], fear necessarily arises. What then is that which is fearless and imperishable? He says: "That is not possible"—this refers to such a volitional construction. || 19 ||
Become fearless through the meditation that "there is neither another nor am I";
this will become true and appropriate, just as even poison becomes nectar.

Although this absence of ego-inflation is improper to grasp from the perspective of the ignorant because it inspires fear, it is indeed proper to grasp it as true from the perspective of ultimate reality. The meaning is that just as nectar, which has been disregarded by a fool because he perceives it as poison, is proper for one with supernormal knowledge to take up. || 20 ||
Having investigated the entire body, from the inert physical form down to the mind, one realizes "I am not"; therefore, "I do not exist" is the truth.
He establishes its truthfulness with the verse beginning "insentient" (jaḍam) || 21 ||

For those in whom all particularities have been stilled through the investigation into the end of egoity—[the meaning is: liberation is that state in which there is an end to egoity]—liberation alone arises, but nothing whatsoever perishes. 22.

Therefore, since all things have been stilled, the stilling of the sense of "I" (ahantva) is the limit; that alone is liberation. And in that state, just as when the solidity of ghee dissolves, not even an atom of the ghee itself is lost, so too nothing whatsoever of the Self is destroyed.
With the intention that one should not fear this as a "total destruction," he says: "The stilled... (verse 22).
For in this matter, nothing other than the renunciation of enjoyments, discernment, and one's own manly effort is of use;
thus, O ignorant ones, bow down quickly to your very own self. (23)

In this regard, having determined that for this liberation nothing else is required but these three—the renunciation of enjoyments, inquiry, and the human effort of restraining the senses and the mind—it is said: "O ignorant ones who desire liberation, having abandoned the entire category of non-self, let your own Self alone be prostrated to; let it be taken as your refuge through the awakening to reality. This is the meaning. || 23 ||
They describe liberation as a state of mind free from latent impressions (vāsanā); that [liberation] does not occur without awakening.
The delusion of the world is [merely] a misconception; here, supreme awakening is not a matter of intellectual conviction, for otherwise there would be bondage for a very long time.
Thus, the cessation of all duality beyond the sense of "I-ness," characterized by the destruction of all latent impressions (*vāsanā*) such that there is no longer any residual impression—

this very state of the mind abiding as Brahman through contemplation (*manana*), which the Śruti texts and the wise proclaim to be liberation— that indeed never occurs at any time without awakening, that is, without the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*). And that [awakening]...
The supreme awakening, which is the cessation of the world-illusion, is indeed not non-existent as the ultimate reality; this is well-known here in the treatises on liberation (*mokṣaśāstra*).

However, for this reason—that is, because of the intensity of human defects such as passion and because of the firmness of the illusion regarding the reality of the world—there is no conviction or trust arising from such an awakening, even though it is produced by the Śruti texts beginning with "here there is no diversity whatsoever. Therefore...
The meaning is that, because of this cause, the bondage of saṃsāra continues for the living being for a very long time. || 24 ||
Having correctly realized that "the world is non-existent," one becomes entirely indifferent toward people, wealth, wife, and body;
for he indeed becomes the very nature of consciousness, which is like the infinite ether—certainly, there is no liberation otherwise. (25)

Therefore, through the firm conviction arising from the scriptures and other means, one should correctly realize through the practice of hearing (*śravaṇa*) and reflection (*manana*) that both "the world" and "I" are unreal and do not exist at all. Then, becoming indifferent toward kinsmen, wealth, wife, and even one's own body,

and having awakened to the ultimate reality (*paramārthatattva*), that individual soul (*jīva*)— which is the limited ether (*parimitākha*), consisting of the consciousness-space (*cidākāśa*) delimited by adjuncts (*upādhi*)— [realizes its true nature].
The world and the conscious being are pure consciousness (cinmātra); he becomes that very nature, and this alone is his liberation—this indeed is the means for it;
other than this, there is no liberation for him. This is the meaning. || 25 ||
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Ultimate Reality," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the glorious Vāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa, composed by the Sage. 30.
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Ultimate Reality," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The thirty-first canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Within the universal self, which is the manifestation of consciousness, that very [reality] is experienced instantaneously.
Whatever internal reality is experienced, whether it be a real entity or a non-entity.
Seized by consciousness, the formless [object] is neither non-existent nor existent;
that nothing has been lost—this is declared to be the state of nirvāṇa.

In order to experience the state of Nirvāṇa, characterized as the non-dual space of consciousness (cidākāśa) which is eternal, unsurpassed bliss, and full, he recalls the previously stated dependence of the perception of the visible world upon the practice of awareness: "In the Self of all...
[and so on]; that very [Self], through practice, was previously [experienced] in the form of the perception of external objects.
It appears as if vibrating externally; one's own dream is the illustration for this.
All this is of the nature of consciousness, and consciousness is clearer even than the sky; since consciousness alone gathers [all things], therefore this [world] is nothing whatsoever anywhere.

Let it be so; what follows from that? To this he says: "The nature of consciousness" (*cidrūpam*). All this is but the form of consciousness itself, appearing as various differentiated costumes through mental construction.

If so, what then is the real nature (*vāstavam svarūpam*) of consciousness? To this he says: "Pure consciousness" (*cidacchā*). Since consciousness alone gathers the world-form within itself—just as ghee gathers solidity within its own essence—it is therefore nothing but consciousness. || 3 ||
There is no destruction, nor non-existence, nor misfortune; there is neither birth nor death, nor space.
There is neither emptiness nor multiplicity; everything is indeed Brahman alone, and yet it is not even that.
Let it be so; what follows from that? He says: "No. The meaning is that, consequently, the desired non-duality of Brahman (brahmādvaita) is established. || 4 ||
Upon the destruction of the world, egoism, and the like, nothing at all is destroyed;
for indeed, even the non-existent—such as a dream—is not destroyed when it ceases.

[Objection: Surely, the destruction of the inert portion of the world, the ego, and so forth, through the realization of reality (tattva-bodha) is accepted; how then can that be denied? To this, he says: "In its destruction... The ellipsis is to be supplied as: "What even is this destruction? (5)
In a false appearance, such as a city of imagination, what destruction can there even be?
Likewise, in the case of the world, the ego, and so forth, no destruction exists for that which is unreal.
If it is asked, "Whence comes this reproach against the world?", [the answer is: that is directed toward a non-entity;
no determination is possible regarding things like sky-flowers—what can be said of them? (7)

If the world is indeed non-existent, then why is it criticized in the scriptures by describing it as being of the nature of misfortune, and why is it determined to be something to be abandoned? To this, the answer is: true. There can be no criticism of a non-entity, nor is its result—namely, investigation or determination—possible at all. The meaning is that just as no one would ever utter a criticism or a determination regarding a sky-flower, so it is with this case. || 7 ||

This alone is the final determination here: that one who does not bring anything to existence, remaining like a stone with respect to whatever has been eaten and whatever conduct has been practiced. (8)
If that is so, is the scripture then entirely useless? No; he says: "The determination.
It is not for the sake of establishing the abiding in one's own natural state that he says: "The determination.
Rather, for the sake of establishing the abiding in one's own natural state, [the scripture] employs censure and so forth by imagining even what is non-existent as if it were existent.

The meaning is that this very determination—that the means consisting of detachment, discrimination, and so forth, ending with the direct realization of reality (tattva-sākṣātkāra), is thus conceived—is the established conclusion (siddhānta). The meaning is: practice the sequence of stages (bhūmikā-krama) exactly as it exists, according to the scriptures, according to tradition, and according to the lineage (sampradāya). || 8 ||
In this delusion of creation, the firm conclusion is that this world, whose nature is mere conceptualization, together with its objects, subsides entirely in an instant.

Let it be thus regarding the determination of the nature of the Self; but what is the fruitful determination concerning the nature of the world, such as heaven and so forth? He states that [determination] with the word "jagat" (the world). In that regard, within the state previously mentioned, "artha" refers to the semblance of worldly human goals (puruṣārtha), and [the world] is endowed with that. || 9 ||
In creation, this [world] is indeed unrestrained and imperishable by virtue of its nature as Brahman;
otherwise, however, this creation neither exists nor does it not exist, or rather, it both exists and does not exist.

The nine creations perish by their own accord during deep sleep and cosmic dissolution; what then is the use of the thorough knowledge of them as being nothing but Brahman? To this he says: "All," etc. "Irresistible" means free from rebirth because its root has been severed. Otherwise, if there were destruction only at the time of dissolution and so forth, it would exist in the form of a seed but not in the form of an effect; or rather, they do exist even in dissolution, according to the manner described in the *Aindava* section.
The meaning is that his actions are performed through mere resolve, because they cannot be thwarted by others. || 10 ||
And for those whose creation exists like that of unreal men in a dream— that creation and those persons are like the waves of water in a mirage.
If that is so, how can there be dissolution when creation exists? To this he says: "Of those...

The meaning is that from the perspective of the one who intends the dissolution, since those [created things] do not exist [ultimately], the conventional designation of "dissolution" occurs simply because of the destruction of everything imagined by his own will. || 11 ||

We do not know how to reach a definitive conclusion regarding those who have attained a semblance of existence while remaining non-existent, just as one cannot resolve the words concerning the son of a barren woman.
For this very reason, he states that because the forms of the individual soul and the world cannot be determined, they are said to be indeterminable: "Of those that are non-existent alone," etc.
There is a certain unprecedented fullness, resembling a completely filled ocean;
for those who know that, they do not fall into the perception of the divisions of seer and seen.
For this very reason, he says "paripūrṇa" (perfectly full) to show that for those who know reality, there is always a fullness of non-dual consciousness-bliss;
for (*hi*) because they do not fall into, nor do they become attached to, the perception of the parts of the seer and the seen. || 13 ||
Like lamps in a windless place that remain motionless with equal radiance—
whether following conventional conduct or free from it— they abide in a state of perfect composure.
"Like immovable [mountains]," the ellipsis being "unshakable. "Sācārāḥ" (possessing conduct). The word "vā" is used in the sense of "iva" (like). || 14 ||
Resembling a single, overflowing ocean, an indescribable fullness has arisen within;
the realization of inner coolness is perceived by the knower as something truly unprecedented. (15)
In this world, the person is perceived as nothing but latent impressions (vāsanā), yet that [person] is not found; and since no one perceives it, from where has saṃsāra come? || 16 ||
He then states what the nature of ignorant persons is: "It is simply latent impression" (vāsanā eva). || 16 ||
That which is established as non-perceived by means of illumination does not exist [therein];
the non-apprehension of blackness and so forth is the clearly demonstrated example in this case. (17)
"Non-seeing" (anālokanam) means the non-manifestation of light. "Black darkness" (kṛṣṇam tamaḥ); by the word "etcetera" (ādipadāt), its effects such as thieves, yakṣas, and so forth are included.
The illustration is that these are not perceived when there is the manifestation of light. In the reading "thirst" (tṛṣṇā), it refers to a mirage.
"Clearly active" (spaṣṭaceṣṭitaḥ) means, that is to say, extremely clear. || 17 ||

The elements, the flesh of the body, and so forth, as well as that which is unreal and delusive and insentient—the intellect, ego, and mind—are composed of those [elements] alone and nothing else. (18)

He explains what kind of light it is with the words, "the elements" (*bhūtāni*). The five elemental principles (*pañcīkṛtāni bhūtāni*) are indeed the material cause of the gross body, consisting of the physical frame, flesh, and so forth. Likewise, the intellect (*buddhi*), ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), and consciousness (*cetas*) are indicative of the material cause of the subtle body (*sūkṣmaśarīra*). These too are composed of food, for, my dear, "the mind consists of food" (*annamayaṃ hi somya manaḥ*).
Based on such scriptural passages as these, they are indeed transformations of the unquintuplicated elements that constitute that [Brahman]. 18.
If the intellect, ego, and mind, having abandoned their nature consisting of the primary elements (bhūta-ādi),
attain an absolute state of stability, that is declared to be liberation.
Let it be so; what follows from that? To this he says: "The elements, etc.

Therein, the conscious self (cidātman), having entered through the sense of "I" into the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of the intellect and so forth—which are composed of the subtle elements—identifies, by means of that [adjunct], even with the gross body as "I" due to ignorance (avidyā). Through discrimination (viveka) of that [body] from the intellect, ego, and mind...

Having abandoned the state of being composed of the elements (*bhūtādimayatā*) by means of the method shown in the scriptural passage concerning "the origin of speech" (*vācārambhaṇa*), if one attains that state which exists as the nature of self-luminous pure consciousness (*cinmātra-svabhāva*)—then that alone is what has arisen as liberation, that alone has become manifest; this is the meaning of what I have called "light. || 19 ||
Since it is not established as a distinct entity, what such existence could there be here?
Therefore, what is the latent impression (vāsanā), from where, where, or of what nature could it be? (20)

Thus, when the light of the Self has thus expanded, even latent impression (*vāsanā*) is sublated; therefore, there is no possibility of bondage through it either. To this he says: "Consciousness" (*cid*). If the consciousness of the Self is joined with the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the subtle body (*liṅga*)—that is, merged through the superimposition of identity—then, because that [consciousness] is oriented toward objects of cognition, a corresponding latent impression is established as its very existence. And that [impression] here...
What is this state of liberation? || 20 ||
For whomsoever there is this delusion, that [delusion], being non-existent, appears as if existent through false perception;
like the water of a mirage, by that [delusion] what cycle of existence belongs to whom, from where, and for what reason? (21)
Furthermore, since the bound soul (*jīva*) itself is not perceived upon the vision of reality (*tattvadarśana*), he asks by whom and of what there could be the possibility of bondage, saying:
"Of whom... It is non-existent (*asan*), meaning false (*alīka*). And being non-existent, it is not observed through investigation, that is, through the vision of reality. || 21 ||
Therefore, in that case, whatever arising of thought there may be for him, that very same delusion of saṃsāra proceeds once again. (22)
However, if the light of the Self (ātmāloka) becomes dim, saṃsāra will surely arise again through the emergence of the mind;

therefore, one must ensure its firmness until the point where there is no further recollection [of objects]. Thus he says with two verses, beginning with "tadevam": "Therefore, in this way," and so forth.

For that reason, even for one who has thus engaged in the light of the Self, whatever emergence of the mind occurs upon the recollection of sense-objects, that very thing [leads back to saṃsāra] again.
Thus does saṃsāra proceed; thus would it proceed. || 22 ||
Therefore, without relying on anything at all, one should meditate upon that which is like space;
the highest good here is non-recollection, for it is supreme oblivion.
The remainder is that one should accomplish supreme non-forgetfulness through the practice of the stages (bhūmikā). || 23 ||
Here there is no seer, nor an enjoyer; there is neither existence nor non-existence.
This is as it is: peaceful, one, and eternally vibrating like the ocean.
To explain how one intent on that practice might perceive it, he says "not here," and so forth.
The cause for the activity of a diseased person brought about by the *prārabdha* (commenced karma) is [the body]; yet [the Self] is always full like the ocean. 24.
When it is clearly realized that the entire visible world is Brahman, which is Being, then,
like the drying up of water, the auspicious state arises upon the disappearance of both the reflection and the reflector.

The reflection (*bimba*) is the appearance of consciousness (*cid-ābhāsa*); that which possesses this is the "reflected" (*bimbī*), which is the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). Upon the destruction of both of these... (25)
Or rather, the conventional usage of "quiescence" is seen in one who has rested in the supreme reality and perceives with equanimity, being free from passion and hatred. (26)
Both tranquility and devotion to meditative concentration, or even conventional discourse, are observed as two [distinct states]. || 26 ||
Alternatively, only the state of peace remains for this nirvāṇa;
for how can the Sage, being truly free from latent impressions (nirvāsana), engage in worldly activity? (27)
As long as his nirvāṇa has not reached full maturity, he continues to engage in worldly activity, with the arising of passion, hatred, and fear still remaining. || 28 ||
He did not attain complete satisfaction until he reached rest upon the seventh stage. || 28 ||
Free from passion, fear, and anger, extinguished and with a tranquil mind, the sage remains forever like a stone that has become as solid as rock. (29)
Just as the entire lotus plant exists within the seed of the lotus in its sheath,
so too the delusion of dreaming exists within the self and is not external.

And thus, with the intention that— according to the perspective of inherent existence (*svābhāvikabhāva*), the world-form exists within Brahman, while according to the contemplation of scriptural reality (*śāstrīyatattvabhāvanā*), its ultimate form (*tāttvikaṃ rūpam*) also exists— one may easily obtain either misfortune or the human goal (*puruṣārtha*) as one desires, he says, beginning with "In the sheath" (*kośe*). "Externality" (*bāhyatā*) is the state of the world being established as other than the Self.
The meaning is "no. || 30 ||
Through the cultivation of externality, the external becomes [the self]; through the cultivation of selfhood, the self itself becomes [the external].
This occurs within the supreme reality, for that very cultivation is indeed that [reality] itself.

He says, "because of the cultivation of externality," [meaning] that the cognition "it exists outside" occurs only within the self due to the cultivation of externality, and not because there is another substratum.
Thus, with the intention of showing that it follows that externality and internality consist precisely in such-and-such a cultivation, he says, "cultivation. || 31 ||
That very same delusion which occurs internally, as in dreams and the like, is manifested here as being external;
there is not even the slightest difference between the two, just as there is none between the milk in two separate vessels.

For this very reason, he says "yet" to show that there is no difference between dream and waking based on their cognition; for there is no distinction or difference between them, just as there is none between milk contained in separate vessels. || 32 ||
In this same way, stability and instability here are merely delusion within the expanse;
those two, the container and the contained, are like water and its waves.

[Objection: Is it not the case that a difference in terms of stability and instability is directly perceived between the objects of the waking state and those of the dream state? What, then, is the resolution for that? To this he says: "sthairya... (regarding stability). Likewise, he says: "ādhāra... (regarding the substratum), meaning that even the perception of the dream as having the waking body as its substratum is not a differentiator. || 33 ||
In dreams and similar states, because one perceives the self as being other [than the body], there is the cognition of otherness;
however, when there is the realization of non-otherness, that [cognition] does not arise, for it is not other than that.
As long as the objects of a dream are not connected to their being nothing but the Self (ātma-mātratā), they appear as such;
however, upon connecting them with their nature as the Self alone, they are immediately sublated by waking, and thus their non-difference from the Self becomes established.
With the intention that this should be understood in the same way regarding the objects of the waking state as well, he says: "In dreams and so forth," etc. [The word] *udayi*...
And it is not like a separate manifestation. || 34 ||
That form of the Supreme Self which is free from temporal succession and is quiescent becomes such through its being that [very thing]; it does not become that through not being that. (35)
Therefore, it is established that even the real state of being Brahman is dependent upon its contemplation; thus he says: "Kalanā... (Verse 35).
When cognitions such as dreams have subsided, that pure, sovereign form exists;
it is not that it does not exist, yet it is not within the range of speech.

It does not exist because there is an absence of time, place, substratum, and so forth that could determine its existence. It is not non-existent because its own nature is uncontradicted. Therefore, the meaning is that it is beyond the range of words. || 36 ||
When delusion has utterly dissolved, one realizes [the truth] through yoga;
for that true nature is not the object of instruction for the wise.

How, then, is it taught by a teacher through speech? To this he says: "Absolute... One who is disciplined and established in samādhi realizes it solely through his own experience—just like the pleasure of union with a beloved—and thus it is not an object for instruction to another; nevertheless, the fruit of the instruction is simply to lead the intellect of the listener toward that state by demonstrating its means.
The state of being. || 37 ||

It is fitting to abide solely in that one, unborn Nirvāṇa—which is peaceful, free from fear, pride, despondency, greed, delusion, body, ego-sense, mind, and the dullness of the senses; which is the imperishable "I" (the Self), and in which all duality has been cast away. Therefore, O Rāma, having abandoned the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), [one should abandon] the eleven [faculties], beginning with dullness and ending with the senses.

In that [state] where one has become the one Nirvāṇa-Brahman—of such a nature, therefore, peaceful, unborn, undecaying, and with all distinctions cast aside—it is proper and fitting to dwell forever in samādhi, and not within the objects of worldly transaction; such is the meaning.
38. Thus ends the [section] in the *Ārṣa Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* by Vālmīki, in the *Dehātmabhāvanirākaraṇa* (or *Mokṣopāya*) section of the *Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa*. U. (Uttarakāṇḍa).
The thirty-first canto, titled "Description of the Instruction on the Logic of Nirvana."

Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Instruction on the Logic of Liberation," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The thirty-second canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
When consciousness expands, then there arises the delusion of "I" and the world.
That which is non-existent alone arises, as it were, and even from vibration, the state of air [arises]. || 1 ||
For one who possesses the practice of associating with the virtuous and reflecting upon the true scriptures,
liberation is brought within one's own control, as it is certain to occur in this very life.

Intending to describe how bondage and liberation depend upon one’s own mastery through knowledge and ignorance respectively, [the author] first shows that bondage—which depends on the expansion of consciousness—is under one's own control due to ignorance, beginning with the words "When... (yadā). The phrase "even from vibration" (spandād api ca) is for the sake of providing an illustration. The reading "iva ca" (as if) is clear. || 1 ||
Even when arisen, it does not lead to weariness because of the realization of its nature as Brahman;
however, it leads to supreme misfortune through the mental cultivation of the meaning of the word "world."
Just as the eye takes on the experience of form through its outward extension, so too consciousness, through its own expansion, assumes the delusion of the world.
That which spreads forth in vain is not real, because of the absence of any object of cognition;
how can that which is non-existent spread forth? Where does the son of a barren woman dance?
He establishes what was stated—that even when it has arisen, it does not lead to distress—by saying "yāsau" (that which...).

The meaning is that the nature of the immutable consciousness (*kūṭastha-cit*) as it flows outward, characterized by approaching external objects, simply does not exist either because of the absence of objects or by its own nature; therefore, since it is sublated by knowledge (*vidyā*), it does not lead to distress. || 4 ||
But this [self], though remaining in a state of experiencing only through experience, does so in vain;
for it does not experience that which is unreal, being like a child’s imaginary yakṣa.

This expansion of consciousness would be established through experience alone; however, that experience, being sublated by true knowledge (vidyā), does not perceive its unreal object and thus remains as something futile, like the experience of a child’s imaginary yakṣa—this is the meaning.

The sense of "I" (ahaṃbhāva) also exists for the sake of suffering, because there is the cognition "I am"; since there is no such cognition [in the absence of suffering], there is no "I. Therefore, bondage and liberation depend upon oneself.

Showing that the same logic applies even to the expansion consisting of the sense of "I-ness" (*ahaṃbhāva*), he states—beginning with the words "The sense of 'I'" (*ahaṃbhāva*)—that the fact that bondage and liberation depend solely upon oneself is established. || 6 ||
That indeed is meditation or that is concentration which consists in abiding without sensation—
like something insentient to those who are sentient, yet equal, peaceful, and free from ailment.
He establishes that liberation is dependent upon oneself with the words beginning "That," etc.

Through knowledge (*vidyā*), because the fundamental dullness is removed, there occurs the attainment of oneness with the conscious Self (*cidātman*); consequently, the non-consciousness of all things such as the mind and intellect—which are themselves non-inert—becomes motionless like an inert stone.
That very state of abiding, which is free from the notions of the object of knowledge and the act of knowing, is itself meditation (dhyāna) or concentration (samādhi);
it means that liberation is characterized by that. || 7 ||

O wise ones, do not despair like the ignorant through the distinctions between duality and non-duality, nor through the delusions of complex verbal compositions; for such things lead only to suffering. (8)

This very [teaching] is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) that serves as the cause of rest. With the intention that otherwise, by resorting to other conceptualizations, there would result only a futile parching of the throat for disputants through the mere culmination of quarrels, he addresses them and says:
"By means of the various conceptual proliferations such as duality (*dvaita*), and through the delusions of compositions of speech consisting of manifold quarrels..."
"Do not despair; do not undergo despondency characterized by the useless parching of the throat.
The meaning is: "Take refuge in this very established doctrine (siddhānta), which is the cause of the supreme human goal. || 8 ||
One who possesses dense latent impressions experiences suffering based on what is non-existent, like a dream,
[perceiving] forms, light, and mental attentions as if they were fashioned by conceptual construction.

For one whose latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are dense and whose mind is extroverted, even though suffering is unreal— just like the perception of forms and so forth— it is nonetheless extremely firm and difficult to ward off. However, for one whose latent impressions are attenuated and whose mind is introverted, even that suffering which is set in motion by past karma (*prārabdha*) and is being experienced at first glance is, as it were, already liberated, because it is concealed by the experience of one's own bliss.
To this he says: "It is non-existent," by means of two [verses]. It is "resorted to" (āśrāyate) means it is experienced (bhuṅkte). || 9 ||
He does not experience suffering at all, like one who is asleep, because his latent tendencies are attenuated;
he perceives forms, light, and mental attention as if they were devoid of conceptual construction.

The particle *eva* is used here in the sense of "even" (*api*). He does not eat—that is, he does not experience—even that suffering brought about by his past karma (*prārabdha*). Just as one who is asleep, whose mind is under the sway of the pleasure of slumber, does not perceive the pain of being bitten by mosquitoes, bedbugs, and the like, so it is in this case.

Through the conjunction of place, time, and action, even this latent impression (vāsanā) attains liberation by becoming utterly attenuated, just as the mental conception (bhāvanā) does with respect to an object.

Therefore, he says "absolutely" (atyanta) [in verse 11], meaning that through the very accumulation of latent impressions (vāsanā), just as there is the experience of saṃsāra, so too the experience of liberation is established through their gradual diminution over time and space.
When a latent impression (vāsanā) reaches a state of extreme attenuation, it attains liberation,
just as clouds and the like in the sky reach the state of emptiness through the transformation of their atoms.
By means of the final transformation, which is extremely subtle and ultimate, attained through a process of gradual diminution;
by the word "etcetera" (ādi), the inclusion of mist, smoke, and so forth is intended. || 12 ||

Through the cultivation of the sense of "I," the latent impressions regarding enlightenment undergo thickening or attenuation, just as ignorance results from the habitual lack of association with the wise, while wisdom arises from such association. (13)

If so, what is the means for the attenuation of latent impressions (*vāsanā*)? He says: "by the cultivation of the sense of 'I'. When the realization of "I am Brahman" increases in one's awakening, the latent impressions—becoming day by day more attenuated, that is, more subtle—result in liberation, just as it is for the wise (*vipaścit*).
The meaning is that just as foolishness, increasing from association with learning, reaches a state of attenuation and thereby results in wisdom, so it is in this case as well. || 13 ||
"By my reasoning, there is no certainty here that 'I exist'; rather, there is an internal state consisting of tranquility.
This is known as 'established awakening,' which exists whether one is living or not living. (14)

If it is asked, "For how long should awakening be cultivated? the intention is that it should continue until the state of firmly rooted awakening (*rūḍhabodhatā*) is reached. With this in mind, he states the definition of firmly rooted awakening: "I am not [this body]," and so forth. By means of the yoga of the inner self (*pratyagātma-yoga*), characterized by the contemplation "I am Brahman" according to my reasoning, whether for a yogi practicing while alive in this world or one who has departed to the next world after death— [The text continues: ...for such a person, there is no need for any other practice. This is because, through the constant cultivation of the realization "I am Brahman," the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of ignorance have been completely eradicated; thus, even though the body remains, the yogi is liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*). Therefore, there is no further requirement for him. This is the meaning. Furthermore, since the latent impressions of ignorance have been destroyed by the power of the aforementioned yoga, the yogi does not perceive the body as his own. Consequently, even though the body remains, he is liberated while living. Thus, there is no further need for him. This is the sense. Moreover, because the latent impressions of ignorance have been eliminated by the force of the aforementioned yoga, the yogi does not regard the body as himself. Therefore, although the body persists, he is liberated while living. Hence, there is no further necessity for him. This is the purport. And since the latent impressions of ignorance have been destroyed by the power of the aforementioned yoga, the yogi does not perceive the body as his own. The meaning is that one who possesses the internal certainty, characterized by tranquility, that the individual soul (jīva)—which is the referent of the word "I"—does not exist, is said to have "established awakening.
Just as a duality appears in the wind, so too this world and its like appear here;
yet through inquiry alone—asking "Who am I? and "How is this?"—it comes to rest.

Whether it be conceived as a compound (dvandva) of substance and action, or if the reading is "spanda" (vibration), it is clear; by the word "etcetera" (ādi), the individual soul (jīva) is included. || 15 ||
"Nirvana is simply 'I am not'—how much delusion is there in this? This is quickly understood through the company of the virtuous and through inquiry. (16)
Through association with those who know reality, the bondage of "I" is destroyed,
just as darkness is dispelled by light or the night by day.

"Who am I? How is this visible world? Who is the individual soul (jīva), and what is living?"—one should investigate these questions throughout one's life through association with those who know the truth. 18.

What is "living"? It is the maintenance of the vital breaths and so forth. The mention of "as long as one lives" (yāvajjīva) is an elliptical expression for [the duration] until liberation (āmokṣa). || 18 ||
The world shines as the individual soul (jīva), and from that, the notion of "I" perishes;
that Reality is attained by one through service to the sun of knowledge—let it be pursued.
With the intention that this investigation (*vicāra*) is accomplished quickly, reaching its fruit through service to the Guru, he says: "Life" (*jīvitam*).

For by serving—that is, through contact with—the Sun, whose characteristic is the Knower of That (*tajjña*), the Knower of Reality (*tattvavid*), the entire world (*bhuvanam*) shines as if revived by awakening; the darkness that veils the reality of all objects, namely the notion of "I," perishes, and the true nature of things (*vastutattvam*) [is revealed].
Therefore, since it expands in a single moment, that sun of the Knower of Reality (tajjña) should be cultivated; this is the meaning. || 19 ||
O friend, worship each and every one who possesses excellence in awakening separately;
for when they meet, the demoness of disputation arises among them. (20)

But when many learned men and logicians are present, and I am unable to determine whether or not this person is a knower of reality, what should I do? To that point he says, beginning with "Whosoever... [and so forth]. Now, why is it said, "Worship them separately"? What fault is there in worshipping them collectively? He states that fault in the verse beginning with "In their union... [and so forth]. Explain this.

The sense is that this is due to the statement of mutually contradictory arguments, according to the maxim: "On every head there is a different opinion; in every mouth there is a different eloquence. (20)
Even when the Lord of Yakṣas has risen, the delusion "I am" arises in the wise man just as it does in a child—a primary error, though it may appear to be well-reasoned. (21)

Let the demoness of disputation indeed arise; what is the fault in that? To this he says: "When the yakṣa of disputation. When the yakṣa—the demon characterized by disputation—has arisen, even for a discerning listener, my own nature as the primary subject (*aham-pratyaktattvam*)—which is not heard [by them], yet is being propounded by logicians through reasonings and arguments (the reading *yuktibhiḥ* is preferred)—is [misrepresented].

The delusion arises that "this alone is sufficient and adequate for me. Thus, by the maxim of the blind monkey and the cow-tail, the implication is that taking hold of such a thing would lead only to misfortune. || 21 ||
Therefore, a wise man should serve a learned scholar in private and alone;
having unified those matters taught by him, he should reflect upon them with his intellect. || 22 ||
One should serve [the teacher] by means of attendance and other forms of service, and having brought him under control, one should inquire. || 22 ||
One should reflect upon the meaning of that teaching with the intellect for the sake of increasing wisdom—[the reading "for the sake of purification" is correct].
One should attain absorption in that Reality which is free from all conceptual constructions. (23)

One should investigate through the means of scripture (*śruti*), reasoning (*yukti*), one’s own experience (*svānubhava*), and the consensus of the wise (*vidvad-antarasamvāda*); like examining the nature of a gem, one should scrutinize it until all doubts are severed for the purification of the intellect. Having thus stated that meditation (*nididhyāsana*) must be practiced once the intellect is purified by such reflection (*manana*), he says: "Free from all volitions" (*sarvasaṃkalpamukta*). That which is real is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*); [one should attain] absorption in that.
Then, from that non-conceptual samādhi, there is a state of unification. || 23 ||
Having brought the intellect to a state of supreme sharpness through association with the wise,
let that single creeper of ignorance be utterly reduced to fragments.
By means of that arising of the knowledge of reality, he demonstrates the destruction of ignorance with the words: "The wise one" (vipaścit). || 24 ||
This matter is indeed possible; therefore, I shall relate it.
We are children who have experienced this ourselves, and we do not speak what is improper. (25)
He says, "This is the meaning," [to show] that one should not entertain the doubt of its impossibility. || 25 ||

Just as the manifestation of clouds from the sky or the breaking of waves from the great ocean, neither arising nor perishing are possible for that which is devoid of mental construction; indeed, in this world, not even the slightest occurrence of destruction or origination is appropriate for it.

That which is liberated from all conceptual constructions is itself the Reality; upon attaining identity with that, even through all the worldly activities of the universe, there is for the wise person neither the destruction of the desired nor the arising of the undesired. Thus he says: "Of the sky," etc.
Just as [there is no change] for the sky due to the manifestation of clouds, mist, heat, and so forth, or likewise for the great waters of the ocean.
