Just as nothing undesirable arises nor does anything desirable perish through the dissolution of waves and the like, so too for the yogi who is free from mental construction (*nirmanana*) and free from volition (*niḥsaṃkalpa*), there is neither the arising of the desirable nor the destruction of the undesirable; such is the meaning. || 26 ||
For all this is like the water of a mirage within the undecaying, peaceful, and pervasive Brahman;
when investigated, even "I" does not exist here—how, where, and from what cause could there be the delusion of thinking and so forth? (27)

Since space and the ocean possess duality, there may even be a suspicion of their conjunction or separation; however, for the wise one, because his nature is that of the immutable, non-dual Brahman, there is not even such a suspicion regarding superimposed illusory transformations. With this intention, he says: "For this... When the stainless, pervasive, and full Brahman is investigated and realized, all this—

Like the water of a mirage, the separate form of a self as "I" does not exist. This being the case, for one who knows the reality here, from where, where, and by what means could there be the delusion of mental construction and so forth? Such is the meaning. || 27 ||
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Realization of Truth," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the glorious Vāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa composed by Vālmīki. 32.
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Realization of Truth," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The thirty-third canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
By one's own manly effort and by one's own intellect, which has been expanded through association with the virtuous...
If knowledge is not attained, there is no other means than that.
Herein is described the conceptualization of delusion, its counter-conceptualization, and the medical treatment for the next world, all through the prevention of the expansion of consciousness. (1)
Therein, at the outset, he prepares the introduction to state the counter-argument, beginning with the words "svapauruṣeṇa" (by his own human effort).

If a person (*puruṣa*) who has obtained a body suitable for qualification (*adhikāra-yogya-śarīra*) is led—that is, made to attain—*jñatva*, which is the knowledge of reality (*tattva-jñāna*), then [it follows that] it is not the other [the Self]. [Note: The verb *nī* is transitive; according to the rule *pradhāne nī-hṛ-kṛṣ-vahām*, the *la*-suffix occurs in the sense of the primary object. Thus, it is not the other.
The meaning is: "not otherwise. || 1 ||
That which is conceived as one's own and imagined through one's own conceptualization assumes a state of otherness,
just as nectar [assumes] the nature of poison.
He explains what kind of human effort (*pauruṣa*) it is by which one is led to knowledge: "One's own imagined [nature]" and so forth.
"One's own" (*sva*) means natural and not based on scripture. "Imagined" (*kalpita*) is used with repetition (*vīpsā*) to mean "all that is imagined.

Furthermore, that very root—consisting of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), ignorance (*avidyā*), and so forth—is [overcome] by its own respective scriptural counter-imagining (*pratikalpanā*); that itself is the state of being other (*anyatva*).

Having abandoned its status as a cause of bondage, it assumes utility for liberation. Just as poison, though by its very nature a cause of death, abandons its poisonous character through the application of methods prescribed in the science of alchemy (*rasāyana*) and becomes an elixir (*rasāyana*)—the means for immortality and the prevention of death—it is exactly like that. || 2 ||
Conceptualization ends in non-conceptualization; liberation is that which is non-conceptual.
And this is accomplished through the prior renunciation of enjoyment, and not otherwise.
If it is asked, "For how long should this practice of non-conceptualization (akalpanā) be performed? he says: "until the cessation of all conceptualization. Regarding the word *kalpanā*:

that which has the limit (*anta*) or boundary—the cessation of all conceptualization—is non-conceptualization; for by that reason, non-conceptualization alone remains as the liberation of the Self. In that regard, one must necessarily possess the state characterized by dispassion (*vairāgya*) and the state characterized by renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*).

He shows the initial conceptualization with the words "And this" (etacceti). The sense is that, as stated in the scripture: "Previously, at the outset, by the very act of renouncing enjoyments, that which is to be known is the supreme state of the Self within the individual who has renounced. || 3 ||
For one who dwells within, neither with speech nor with mind, while not conceptualizing words and their meanings, the cessation of mental construction gradually increases.

Then, having ascertained the reality of the Self through hearing and reflection, one should practice the cessation of thought characterized by the restraint of speech and mind; thus he says: "With speech... (Verse 4).
Apart from the notion of "I," there is no other form of ignorance;
when this [notion] is stilled through non-contemplation, there is no other liberation whatsoever.
Therefore, he says "having abandoned" to show that she (the state of liberation) is to be accomplished by means of the characteristic of non-egoity (*anahaṃbhāva*).

This is because of the direct realization of reality (*tattvasākṣātkāra*), which, through non-contemplation (*abhāvanā*), causes all contemplations to cease. When this egoity (*ahaṃkāra*) has been stilled—that is, sublated—[liberation occurs].
Then, as long as you do not abandon even a slight sense of "I-ness" (ahaṃbhāva) regarding the body, it perishes;
when that desire for the world and so forth is abandoned, you become tranquil and attain perfection.

Now, even after the direct realization of reality (*tattvasākṣātkāra*), if one who still possesses a lingering attachment to the former state of being a worldly soul should maintain even the slightest sense of ego (*ahaṃbhāva*) until the end of the physical body,
then, due to forgetting the nature of unconditioned, perfect bliss, one perishes as it were in the suffering of *saṃsāra*.
This means "like a cloth. When that sense of "I" is abandoned, you become tranquil and attain the cessation of all suffering;
furthermore, you are perfected through your own nature of unsurpassed bliss. || 6 ||
Salutations to that Great Soul, who is devoid of consciousness, by whom all this— though non-existent— is established as if it were existent, and who remains as tranquil as a stone.
Because it is not perceived by the outward-turned function of the insentient [mind]. || 7 ||
All this, being insentient, subsides like a mirage for one whose mind has dissolved into the supreme,
known as the Void, through the cultivation of the nature of consciousness.

For one whose mind is dissolved in the Supreme Brahman, for that very reason, all this visible world subsides— just like a stone— due to the absence of external consciousness, due to the internal cultivation of the state of pure consciousness, due to the absence of any supporting proof, and due to the presence of subverting evidence. || 8 ||
Whether this [external object] exists or does not exist, it is when it is perceived that it leads to an increase in suffering;
whereas when it is not perceived, it leads to internal happiness, for from the unperceived arises the unconscious state.
The existence or non-existence of the visible object (dṛśya) is not what matters regarding pleasure and pain; rather, it is the perception or non-perception of that object which does.
With the intention that therefore the mind alone—which has set out toward that [object] for the sake of consciousness—must be restrained, he says: "This...
The non-consciousness of the visible object, however, follows from the non-consciousness [of the mind] through the restraint of the activity of the mind.
The meaning is: solely by virtue of the counter-conception that culminates in the attainment of the form of Brahman. || 9 ||
There are two terrible diseases for embodied beings: this world and likewise the next;
by these two, one is afflicted by all manner of terrible sufferings. (10)
He begins to describe the treatment for the next world with the words "Two," etc. [by] all states, beginning with those that are internal. || 10 ||
In this world, the wise strive against disease with enjoyments that are like difficult-to-take medicines;
they apply treatment according to their ability for as long as life lasts, but not for any other ailment.

In this world, when afflicted by diseases such as hunger and thirst, people strive according to their ability with "difficult medicines" characterized by the enjoyment of food, drink, and so forth. However, in the otherworldly disease consisting of the succession of births in hells and the like—which is free from [ordinary] ailments—no cure can be achieved through such enjoyments;
this is the meaning. || 11 ||
Regarding the great disease of the next world, the best of men strive for its cure by means of the nectars known as tranquility, association with the virtuous, and awakening. 12.
The ellipsis is "in order to perform medical treatment. || 12 ||
Those who are vigilant in the treatment for the next world conquer through the power of tranquility the great desire for the path to liberation. 13.

Be vigilant in abandoning indolence and worldly enjoyment, and in partaking of the medicine of the company of the virtuous and so forth, by means of the power of the medicine called tranquility (śama). || 13 ||
He who does not seek a cure for the disease of hell while still here—once he has gone to that place where there is no medicine, what will he do, afflicted as he is by pain? (14)
[Objection: "Surely the treatment for the disease of the next world will be administered right there; what is the use of worrying about it here? To this he replies: "In this very world" (ihaiva).

[The state] is "devoid of medicine" (nirauṣadha), meaning it is a place such as hell or the station of immobile beings that is bereft of the medicines of the company of the virtuous, the true scriptures, and so forth. May life not go to ruin through the treatments of this world alone.
O ignorant ones, let the next world be treated with the medicines of self-knowledge. || 15 ||
They are ignorant. || 15 ||
Life is as fragile as a leaf tossed by the wind or a drop of water;
it is a great disease for the next world, so let it be treated with effort and speed. 16.
When the great disease of the next world is treated with effort and speed, the disease consisting of this world subsides of its own accord and quickly. (17)
He says that in this world, no separate effort need be made for the purpose of treating the disease of worldly existence: "In the other world... (verse 17).
They know that a living being is pure consciousness alone, and the world is its expansion;
even within the interior of a single atom, there exists that [consciousness] as vast as hundreds of mountains. (18)

Although there exist treatments for the disease of rebirth in other worlds—such as austerity, pilgrimage, sacrifice, charity, and expiatory rites—even so, these are not the causes for its absolute eradication; rather, it is only the knowledge of the Self (ātma-jñāna). And that [knowledge] arises solely from the cessation of the expansion of consciousness characterized by the practice of samādhi preceded by hearing (śravaṇa) and the other stages; with this intention [the author says]:

He prepares the introductory context for explaining the means to that [realization] with the words "pure consciousness alone" (*saṃvinmātram*). Because consciousness is full even within the interior of the atoms of that universe, it certainly exists there. || 18 ||
That expansion of consciousness which consists of forms, light, and the mind is experienced within space alone; therefore, the delusion of the world is not real.

"Expansion" means turning outward; that very [expansion] consists of forms and light as external objects, and the mind along with desires, volitions, and so forth as internal objects—this is the meaning. "In the void" means in the space of consciousness (cidākāśa). || 19 ||
Even when the cosmic dissolutions are observed, the delusion called the visible world neither perishes nor is born, for it consists solely of mere illusion.

With the intention that its cessation does not occur even through thousands of dissolutions because it is rooted solely in false belief (mithyātva), nor does its existence persist even through thousands of creations, but rather [its cessation occurs] only through self-knowledge (ātmajñāna), he says: "Even in dissolutions... The ellipsis to be supplied is "...it would not be born, even when creations are seen. He states the reason for this: "Because it is of the nature of mere delusion (bhrānti)"; the meaning is: because it is characterized solely by being nothing but an illusion.
If the self, submerged in the ocean of the mire of worldly enjoyments, is not rescued,
there is no other means for that than the marvelous power of one’s own human effort.
If it is asked, "What then are the means for the knowledge of the Self? [the author] says that the first is detachment itself: "In enjoyment... (verse 21).
A person who has not conquered himself is deluded and remains stuck in the mire of worldly enjoyments alone;
he becomes a vessel for calamities, just as the ocean is for waters.
Just as childhood is seen to be the beginning of life, so the renunciation of enjoyments, which brings about the pacification of passion, is the beginning of Nirvana. (23)
Of life, of the lifespan. || 23 ||
For one who knows that, the river of life, though full of waves, flows without agitation; it moves with equanimity and gentleness, as if devoid of flavor, like a figure in a painting.

He demonstrates the intended meaning of the qualification "the pacifier of passion" by describing the distinction between the river of life for one who knows that [reality] and for one who does not, beginning with the words "of one who knows that," etc. (verse 24).
But for the river of the life of the ignorant, the currents are extremely terrifying;
its whirlpools are the disturbances of worldly existence, and its waves carry one along with them. (25)
The *rasanās* are the sounds of wailing; they are exceedingly terrifying because of them. || 25 ||
The multitudes of created worlds surge forth as mere fragments of the expansion of consciousness,
like the illusion of a second moon, a child’s ghost, a deer in a mirage, or a dream.

He says "sarge" etc., [meaning] that for the ignorant, due to a lack of inquiry, there are mere fragments of the expansion of consciousness whose nature is the dispersion of appearances such as creation and so forth; they "pravalganti," meaning they spread forth. || 26 ||
Thousands of creations appear like a surging flood of waves upon the ocean of consciousness;
when investigated, they are unreal, yet they seem real due to the delusion of experience.
From the delusion of experience—that is, from erroneous experience. || 27 ||
Even within the hollow of space, the worlds are experienced as if they were real due to the delusion of the expansion of consciousness; however, they are not truly existent.
Even within the well-known expanse of space, worlds such as cities of the Gandharvas are experienced as if they were real. || 28 ||
The delusion of creation is a bubble in the water of the expansion of consciousness, possessing the form of the modifications of the existence of "I" and so forth. (29)
He possesses form through the six modes of being, such as "I" and so forth.
Consciousness is liberation; the world is the unfolding of consciousness.
It is neither internal nor external, neither unreal nor real—it is everything.
The nirvāṇa of consciousness is the absence of expansion; it is the non-world, the cessation of the entire world. Its blossoming is expansion. || 30 ||
The Lord is the nature of consciousness, unborn, unmanifest, one, and imperishable; He is Brahman, devoid of both selfhood and the state of being, and more tranquil even than the void.
The meaning is that Brahmā is the Lord (Īśvara), because he himself desires both the expansion and the cessation of his own [power]. || 31 ||
For Brahman, who is devoid of intrinsic nature, no external cause is required for the self-arising awareness of creation, just as no cause is required for the movement of the wind.
And he says—“of Brahman”—that this vibration is merely a transformation (*vivarta*) of false ignorance (*avidyā*), and not born from the true nature of Brahman. || 32 ||
Like the experience of a dream, these are delusions—the waves of Brahman within the ocean of Brahman;
yet in reality, there is neither dreaming nor the state of creation here.

And since they are non-avidyic, the states of creation are merely illusory transformations (vivarta) of Brahman; the waves [of creation] are nothing but an error. In reality, however, there is neither dream nor creation—this is the meaning. || 33 ||
This alone is non-manifest, mindless, non-inert, and equal;
it is neither existent nor non-existent, neither existent-and-non-existent, immutable, and non-dual. (34)

Then, as to what Brahman is like from the perspective of ultimate reality (paramārtha), he says: "It is indeed one alone. Its lack of consciousness means it is devoid of any other attribute known as consciousness. || 34 ||
He for whom, while remaining exactly as he is, there has arisen a cessation of consciousness that is non-perceptive in nature—him they call the best of sages. (35)
He states that for the yogin, abiding in such a state of Brahman is itself the pacification of consciousness and the state of a sage (munitva), with the words:
"of one who remains as he is" (yathāsthitasya). || 35 ||
He who, though existing, is like something made of clay— whose nature is non-perception of the world that has dissolved— that one they call the best of sages.
Such as I am, together with the state of being a living soul. || 36 ||
Just as a city of imagination subsides through the absence of volition, so too does this world,
which arises from perception, subside within consciousness through the absence of perception.

Just as the non-conceptualization of a creation produced by volition (*saṃkalpa*) is its cessation, so too for this "seen-creation" (*dṛṣṭasṛṣṭi*), its cessation is simply its non-appearance; thus he says:
"All verbal objects, with the exception of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), have causes.
But that which is the cause of intrinsic nature is liberation—the realization of that. (38)

The nature inherent in all insentient objects is insentience (*jāḍya*); that itself is root-ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*). With the exception of that single [ignorance], all words, meanings, names, and forms are accompanied by causes and have that [insentience] as their cause. The cause of even that nature—which establishes it by way of being its witness—is the realization of that [witnessing Self]; the meaning is that liberation consists in the attainment of one's own self as being nothing but That. || 38 ||
No object whatsoever possesses any inherent nature here;
all experiences are merely the flowing waters of the great ocean of consciousness. (39)

Since no insentience remains for anyone once ignorance has departed, the author states with the words beginning "Consciousness" (citi) that the world is of the single essence of consciousness for the yogin. || 39 ||
These very experiences are the vibrations of the great wind of consciousness; let it be understood that these are the emptiness of the sky of Brahman. (40)

The wind and its movement are non-different; so too are Brahman and the creation. Yet the perceived difference between them is unreal, arising from one's own delusion, like the experience of one's own death in a dream.
Error persists as long as the investigation into the true nature of reality remains unclear;
however, when the investigation becomes clear, error itself attains the very state of Brahman.
Regarding how long that error persists, he says: "But the error... (verse 42).
Error, however, is unreal; thus, upon investigation, no real entity is found.
Like the horn of a hare, it is utterly non-existent; therefore, Brahman alone remains. (43)

Now, one might ask: "How can error attain the nature of Brahman? To this he says: "But error... The meaning is that the aspect of existence and manifestation within error attains the nature of Brahman, whereas the other aspect simply does not exist; it was with this intention that it was so stated. || 43 ||

Without beginning, middle, or end, infinite, pure, equal, auspicious, eternal, and indeed one—having abandoned all delusion, the burden of the transformations of old age and ignorance, attain the state of space. 44.

Showing that Brahman remains as the sole residue after all delusions have been sublated, [the teacher] establishes Rāma in the state of being that [Brahman] with the words "beginningless," etc.: "O Rāma, having abandoned all delusion— the burden of modifications such as old age, delusion, and so forth— arising from attachment to the body (or, according to another reading, 'attachment to the body'), attain the state of the ether of Brahman."
The meaning is "you shall attain. || 44 ||

Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "The Exposition of the True Meaning," in the *Nirvāṇa* section of the *Mokṣopāya* within the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Valmiki, according to the tradition of the Seers. || 33 ||
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Meaning of Truth," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The thirty-fourth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
He who perishes when pleasures and pains arrive, he truly perishes.
That which does not perish is indestructible; it requires no instruction from the scriptures.

"The world is a creation perceived [only] through vision, and its dissolution occurs precisely through the non-perception thereof"— the logical proofs for this proposition, which has been introduced, are now described here.
Desiring to state the logical arguments for what was previously stated— that "the world arises from sensation and subsides in consciousness through the absence of sensation"—
the venerable Vasiṣṭha first distinguishes the imperishable Self from the perishable triads of experience consisting of pleasure, pain, and their perception.
Showing that by the mere sight of this [treatise], all the instructions of the scriptures have fulfilled their purpose, he says: "When [the truths] have been attained..."
For whoever there is an arousal of desire, for that person pleasure and the like necessarily exist.
If these are to be properly treated, then desire itself must first be abandoned. (2)

With the intention that whoever possesses desire and so forth is eternally miserable, and is not the Self, but rather belongs to the category of the disease of *saṃsāra*—which must be treated by means such as the renunciation of desire—he says: "And for whom... [In that state,] "I" and "this world" are but an illusion; they do not exist at all in the supreme state.
This is peaceful, without support, entirely nirvāṇa, and imperishable. || 3 ||
But as for that indestructible Self which possesses the conceit of desire and so forth, the world that is its object of conceit is simply not possible; thus he says: "I... (verse 3).
The delusion arising from the confusion of words such as "I," "Brahman," and "the world"—by whom indeed was this imagined within the all-pervading, tranquil space? (4)
And thus he says that words such as "I" are without an object there: "I" (aham). || 4 ||
Here there is no "I," nor the world, nor those things denoted by words such as "Brahmā" and the like;
since the one who is peaceful is everything, who here could be an agent or an enjoyer, and from where? (5)
In the absence of that [self], the discourse regarding an agent, an enjoyer, and so forth is cast far away; thus he says: "Not here" (neha). || 5 ||
Because he excels all teachers, this total negation of everything has been performed; and since that [negation] is itself of the nature of truth, he alone is distinguished as "I."

If it is objected that, in the case of the negation of everything, even the instruction and so forth would be negated, and thus the means for its realization could not be obtained— let it be so indeed. For even if there is a negation of everything, the Brahman to be taught remains un-negated, [distinguished] from all those things being negated which are unreal.

And because it possesses the excellence of the nature of the inner self (pratyagātman), which is the ultimate truth, and because after its realization there is no further need for means such as instruction by way of negation, he says "by instruction" with this intention:
it is distinguished, it remains as a residue, and it excels. || 6 ||
The movement of the Siddhas dwelling above is not perceived, nor is it harsh,
just as a man sleeping on one side does not hear the thundering of clouds in a dream.

Let it be so; nevertheless, how can the cessation of the perceptible be established by mere non-perception? To this he says: "In front," and so forth. Just as the movement and activity—though fierce and terrifying—of perfected beings (*siddhas*) or *piśācas* who remain in the space before one but are hidden by the power of invisibility is not perceived; or as [in the case] of a single bed-space...

The meaning is that just as the thundering of well-known clouds, though terrible, is not perceived by another person who is asleep—and from our perspective, that thunder does not even exist—it is exactly like that. || 7 ||
Since it does not exist in the state of being made known, the conduct of the perfected ones is not perceived;
for everyone experiences that which abides in its own nature as the state of being made known.
He states that very point: "In cognition," etc. The meaning is that it is a well-known fact of nature that everything is experienced by every observer as residing within their own cognition. || 8 ||
Even consciousness itself is essentially of the nature of the Self, for everything shines as being composed of that;
therefore, this entire world is non-different from the Supreme Self, which is "I."
Let it be so; what follows from that? To this he says: "Even cognition... (verse 9).
Pure consciousness shines as the world, just as in a mental construction or a dream;
it arises without diverse parts, just as water arises in the form of waves.
Although cognition itself possesses no diverse parts, it appears as the world with its diverse parts.
At the arising of cognition, that which is essentially one appears as if it has attained multiplicity;
yet, because it is unreal due to ignorance, it is not perceived when examined.

The single Self alone has come to appear as if diverse; this emergence in the form of a transformation occurs due to the ignorance of consciousness. However, because that emergence is unreal, it is not perceived when examined by one who sees reality.
Just as an aggregate might consist of all its own constituent parts alone, so too this world is nothing but Brahman—eternal, partless, and peaceful. 12.

The meaning is that just as this soul (*jīva*), though itself partless, becomes possessed of parts by imagining its own parts such as hands and feet in dreams, daydreams, and the like, so too is Brahman. || 12 ||
The brick of the nature of consciousness holds within it millions of vessels;
whatever that consciousness perceives, it knows as if it were the world and so forth.
The potteress, whose nature is consciousness, perceives and remembers the golden bricks.
Brahman alone shines forth as this world through its pure existence and its state as the universe;
because it is of the nature of consciousness and fluidity, it appears like waves and so forth from the ocean.
Whatever it conceives within, it perceives as if it were the world and so forth;
though formless, it perceives its own form, and that which it does not conceive, it does not perceive.
That which one does not will, nor superimpose upon, one does not perceive. || 15 ||

The statements regarding his being conscious or unconscious are made solely for the purpose of instruction, because he is the Lord even within his own body; they do not refer to reality in an ultimate sense.

Because of his lordship and because he is endowed with all powers through being variegated by *māyā*, [these qualities] reside in the *māyā* that has become his own body. However, this statement is not in fact concerned with the Real (*sat*), meaning it does not have the ultimate reality as its object. || 16 ||
The world is neither existent nor non-existent; it appears because of consciousness, for it does not shine forth from that which is unconscious.
Thus, what kind of apprehension of objects could there be for us here? 17.
Whether insentient or sentient, whether characterized by motion or stillness,
the Self remains independent, neither subjected to hardship nor remaining like a stone situated in well-being.

"Let it be so; what follows from that? To this he replies: "It is insentient. [This means] it is not dependent on itself—that is, it is not subject to its own control nor is it something to be accomplished through effort and toil. Just as for a healthy, motionless crystal stone, the movement or stillness of the thousands of reflections within it is not to be accomplished by effort, so too is it situated. || 18 ||
I do not know from where this Yakṣa—who has been gazed upon, yet for whom there is neither existence, nor support, nor cause—has arisen, thinking "I am he. (19)

With the intention that, by examining the single *ahaṃkāra*—which is the root of all conceptual constructions—and ascertaining its falsity, the falsity of the entire world is established, he says: "Of whom... (verse 19).
The very existence of this Yakṣa who thinks "I am his" does not exist in reality;
oh, how strange it is that you have been rendered powerless by him! (20)
In truth, in reality; existence means being present. || 20 ||
Just like the "crow-and-palm" coincidence, the delusion that "I shine within Brahman" appears;
it is merely one's own form appearing through a visual error, like a mass of hair in the sky.
It is accidental, like the maxim of the crow and the palm fruit. || 21 ||
I am indeed Brahman, and so too is this world; how then could there be destruction or origination?
Therefore, what basis can there possibly be for joy or sorrow? (22)
And thus, he states the result [of this] as "Brahman alone. What is its locus? It is both the object and the substratum. || 22 ||
Because the Lord is the sovereign of all, this world appears as perceived;
yet it does not appear as unperceived by Him. Therefore, let it be unperceived by you.

Having described the theory of "creation upon perception" (*dṛṣṭasṛṣṭivāda*), he states its result: "Because of being the Lord of all. Let there be for you the non-perception of the world, which has not been [previously] conceived; that very thing is liberation, whose nature is the cleansing of everything visible—this is the meaning.
Because the world arises from consciousness, Brahman appears as the void like the "crow-and-palm" coincidence; therefore, how could that [world] be distinct from it? 24.

According to the manner described, since the world also possesses consciousness (*cittva*), it is Brahman-space itself that appears otherwise suddenly—like a city in a dream or a mental construction, or like the "crow-and-palm" coincidence. In reality, however, how could that world be distinct from Him? For if there were such a distinction, it would follow that the world is unreal, as it would fail to obtain existence (*sattā*) and manifestation (*sphūrti*). This is the meaning.
Just as waves and such exist in water, or as a carved figure exists in wood,
or as jars and other objects exist in clay, so does the state of creation exist within Brahman.

The meaning is that it is like waves and so forth in water; like a carved figure on a tree or piece of wood that has not yet been chiseled out; and like jars and other objects in the earth that have not yet emerged. || 25 ||
That which is experienced within the pure, formless, and shapeless [reality] is precisely that;
therefore, what is called "I" and what are called "the worlds"? 26.
Regarding shape, which is partless; he will state later that it is "like a cloud" as an example. || 26 ||
Just as the Maruts possess the variety of movement through their very existence alone,
so too does the world, beginning with "I" and so forth, arise from Brahman, which is devoid of intrinsic nature.

He states that it is "nothing but that" (tanmātratva) because no difference from existence is perceived: "As in the sky... "Just as in the sky, which is devoid of intrinsic nature and free from ignorance, the state of being trees, elephants, horses, deer, and so forth is perceived;
likewise, others perceive the manifestation of creation within that which is non-existent in its arrangement and form. (28)
The forms of elephants, horses, deer, and so forth [are perceived] in the sky or in mist, which are devoid of such specific arrangements and shapes. || 28 ||
The entire creation appears as if possessing parts within the supreme Śiva;
know its likeness to be just like that of cause and effect.

Like a limb, like a branch of a tree; like an effect such as a banyan tree and its cause such as its seed—just as in the world there are well-known analogies for subtle objects, know that such is the analogy between those two, the creation and Brahman. || 29 ||

With a mind inwardly peaceful, effortless, free from limiting adjuncts, and devoid of delusion—since it is impossible for such a state to exist within the world—one should remain as equanimous as space. (30)
According to the manner described, since the world—other than oneself—is impossible, one should remain seated like space, free from all mental agitation. || 30 ||
Neither you, nor we, nor worlds, nor the elements exist;
this Brahman alone remains, entirely peaceful and full. (31)
"Nirbhara" means "excessive"; that is to say, "full. || 31 ||
In all things without exception, there is the state in which all particularities are stilled;
realizing "I am that very reality," abandon [the notion of self] quickly and cultivate this for the sake of liberation. (32)

Since no form apart from consciousness can be defined, and since all objects of experience remain indistinguishable [in their ultimate nature], one should abandon the delusion of distinctions and contemplate:
"I am that very consciousness, which is the supreme reality wherein all distinctions have subsided. (32)
Know sensation to be bondage; know non-sensation to be liberation.
Abide as you are, acting as you do, peaceful and free from sensation. 33.
According to the conduct of the wise, that is, the conduct of those who know, without transgressing the practice of the stages. || 33 ||
The seer does not become the object of sight, and consciousness does not become the object of thought. Since there is no object of thought in the non-world (ajagat), who could perceive what, and how?
He states that when there is firmness in the realization of reality, there is no possibility of attachment to insentient objects or sentient beings at all—namely, "the seer" (draṣṭṛ). || 34 ||
Due to the absence of the states of the seer and the seen, even while awake, remain as if in deep sleep—resplendent like the expanse of the autumnal sky and comparable to non-existence. (35)
It is like non-existence and similar to emptiness, yet it is not emptiness itself. || 35 ||

Likewise, within the single form of Brahman-consciousness, just as there is the movement of the wind, here non-consciousness is bondage (sarga) and consciousness is liberation (mokṣa); the realization of the oneness of Brahman is liberation.

The perception of difference within Brahman arises from ignorance, like the perception of movement in the wind; likewise, the very perception of a distinction between consciousness (cit) and the unconscious (acit) is creation, while the perception of their unity is liberation—this is the essential meaning. || 36 ||
The vibration of consciousness (citspanda) within the wind of Brahman is known as creation;
that which is the absence of such vibration of consciousness therein is declared to be nirvāṇa. || 37 ||
Just as a seed knows its own nature within itself as sprouts and so forth,
so too does the Great Consciousness know its own nature residing within it as the state of creation.
He establishes that the perception of difference itself constitutes creation by means of examples, beginning with the words "the seed," etc. (verse 38).
Just as a seed remains as leaves and so forth through the perception of those very leaves, so too does the supreme consciousness, through the awareness of creation, become the state of creation.

He states that even when its existence persists simultaneously with the sensation, the illustration is exactly the same: "Just as the modifications of existence appear as objects for the Supreme Consciousness, so too all seeds are illustrations; they are of that very nature and consist of that. (40)
He states that even the six modifications of being (*ṣaḍbhāvavikārāḥ*) are illustrations here, beginning with "Just as" (*yathā*).

The appearances of the modifications of being are sequential manifestations; because they are modifications of consciousness itself—which exists in the form of the seed and so forth—they consist of that [consciousness]. (40)
This entire world is composed of the changeless Supreme Brahman;
know it thus to be changeless, without beginning or end, and free from all affliction.

Consisting of nothing but one's own volition, this world— subject to decay through one's own volition and characterized by the transformations of duality and non-duality— is like a city created by imagination.
Just as you have understood the distinction between emptiness and space,
know that the distinction between Brahman and the creation is likewise devoid of self-nature.
That which was the tranquil existence of Brahman in the beginning, consisting of the form of great consciousness,
became this "I-ness" through its own lack of awakening, thinking "I am a human being."

The meaning is that she herself, who was previously established as the primordial reality, through lack of awakening, becomes both the ego-sense in the form of "I am the measurer" (mānava) and the state of the world. || 44 ||
In this Brahman, which is the form of the universe, nothing at all is born;
and even that which is born and then perishes does not truly perish, like a wave in water.
Even when born, it is not born; even when destroyed, it is not destroyed. || 45 ||
Brahman alone abides within itself in the form of the Brahman that constitutes all objects, just as a whole resides in its parts, or as space resides in space, or as water resides in water.
Brahman, which exists both as the form of objects and as the form of Brahman itself, abides within the Self whose nature is unchanging, just as a tree abides within its own parts. 46.
That form which exists within consciousness when one is situated in another place after half a blink of an eye—let that very nature be worshipped. (47)
He states that the actual state of consciousness is indeed objectless with the words "in a moment" (*nimeṣāt*). This has been explained previously. || 47 ||
The wise declare that the nature of consciousness is twofold: agitated and unagitated.
Be single-mindedly devoted to that by which you seek the highest good; do not be lacking in discernment.

O Rāma, the wise and discerning knowers of the scriptures proclaim that consciousness (*saṃvit*) is of two forms: one is the single, agitated nature of consciousness accompanied by manifestation (*savivarta*), which is established through the experience of the ignorant; the other is the unagitated, non-manifesting state, which is the eternally stable, full-blissful, singular essence. Between these two, [tell me] by which you are the higher...

You seek the highest good, which is the supreme goal of human life; therefore, be single-mindedly devoted to that alone. The meaning is: do not be one who grasps at whatever comes without examination—a person lacking wisdom and discernment. 48.

Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "Instruction on the Yoga of the Supreme Reality," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the glorious Vāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa of Valmīki, composed by the Sage. 34.
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "Instruction on the Yoga of Ultimate Reality," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The thirty-fifth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
For consciousness that has, in an instant, traveled from one distant land to another, [the transition is immediate].
That form which is stainless in the center is the supreme form of the Self.
For the sake of perceiving the indivisible unity of the reality that consists of both the manifold and the non-manifold,
the nature of Brahman— which appears as both the real and the unreal— is here elaborated.

Intending to elaborate upon Brahman— which possesses two forms, the agitated and the unagitated— by means of expressions that appear paradoxical, [the author] first recalls the unagitated form, which was previously familiarized through the aforementioned means, in order to enjoin steadfastness in it, beginning with the words "deśāt" (from space). This occurs during the interval between the two successive objects.
The meaning is that form which is devoid of objective referents is supremely undisturbed. || 1 ||
While walking, hearing, touching, smelling, opening and closing the eyes, and laughing—
be ever absorbed in this [Self] for the sake of attaining freedom from all affliction.
Become, indeed, one who consists of this, established in pure consciousness devoid of objects; this must certainly be so. || 2 ||
From that very reality which is free from appearances and devoid of latent impressions and desires,
she remains as she is, according to her nature and conduct, as immovable as the mountain of the gods.

Acting as one remains—without transgressing the state of one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*) and without overstepping one's own traditional conduct (*kulācāra*)—one is nonetheless "unwavering" (*acalā*); that is, one does not waver from such steadfastness. Here, the letter 'a' has the sense of a negative particle (*nañ*), yet it is not a negative particle [in the sense of negating the quality]; the meaning is that steadfastness in that very state is itself knowledge (*vidyā*). || 3 ||
This is the nature of ignorance: that it cannot be perceived.
If it were perceived, it would become supreme knowledge itself.

In order to define ignorance (*avidyā*), which is the opposite of that [knowledge] and is useful for what is about to be stated, he says: "This... It has been "examined," meaning it has been investigated by means of valid cognitions (*pramāṇa*). || 4 ||
Since the object of thought arises from ignorance, where and what could possibly arise within the state of no-mind?
How indeed can anything be perceived internally? Only peace has arisen with power.
The object of thought (*cetya*) and consciousness (*cit*) are non-different from one another; and since no difference exists, how could consciousness be perceived or exert itself within its own self?

Therefore, the meaning is that within reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), tranquility arises by force—the state of abiding in pure consciousness alone, wherein there is neither the object to be known nor the act of knowing. || 5 ||
Truth, Brahman, and the universe are one; though established as one, it appears as many.
Everything appears as if it were not everything; though pure, it is perceived as impure.

However, through the perspective of a discerning person who has ascended to the intermediate stage and whose vision is mixed with both knowledge and ignorance, Brahman— though fixed in a single form— appears as if it possesses various contradictory and unstable natures.
He elaborates upon this through apparent contradictions, based on means of valid cognition, reasoning, and experience, until the end of creation, beginning with the words "The True" (satyam).

Brahman and the world are real; from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), they are one and the same. It should be understood that this single reality exists as if it were manifold, appearing in forms that seem contradictory. The same applies hereafter. All is full (*pūrṇam*). 6.
The non-empty appears clearly as if empty, and the empty as if non-empty;
the expansive appears as if non-expansive, and the non-expansive as if resembling the expansive.
It is as if empty during the dissolution, yet as if not empty during creation; it is expansive in terms of both time and space.
Though changeless, it appears as if changing; though equal, as if uneven; though peaceful, as if unpeaceful;
though existent, as if non-existent; though visible, it has arisen as if invisible, and though it is that very reality, it has appeared as if it were not.
That which is invisible is impossible to see, as if it were non-existent.

Though indivisible, it appears as if divided; though devoid of inertia, it has become like inert matter; though beyond the reach of thought, it seems as if it were an object of cognition; though partless, it shines as if possessed of parts.
Shining brilliantly, as if possessing its own parts. || 9 ||

Though not the "I," it appears as if it were the "I"; though indestructible, it appears as if it were subject to destruction; though stainless, it appears as if it were stained; and though beyond being known, it appears as if it were the bearer of what is to be known.
As if subject to destruction, it carries the object of knowledge; by means of expansion, it brings it to completion, as if that were its very nature. || 10 ||
It was like light to the dense darkness, both new and ancient;
subtler than even an atom, yet containing within it the multitude of all worlds.
Light is self-luminous; [it is so designated] through the conceptualization of distinctions, as in the expression "the head of Rāhu. || 11 ||
Though it is the self of all, it is abandoned through great hardship;
though it is not a net, it is richly endowed with nets; and though it is without end, it is manifold in many ways.

By whom the multitude of visible objects has been abandoned through great human effort— consisting primarily of sacrifice, charity, austerity, purification of mind, detachment, hearing, reflection, and so forth— and which, though existing in manifold ways, is as if non-existent, being entirely devoid of any second remainder. 12.
Know that Brahmā, the lord of the wise, is free from illusion, yet possesses a pure solar orb of illusory rays; he is like the great ocean to the waters.

He possesses the form of a stainless sun, with a circle of rays and a web of light that has the nature of illusion; yet he is also "vit," whose essential nature is pure consciousness (*vedana-mātra*). The word *hi* is used in the sense of "also. He is the Lord (*nātham*), as if the sovereign, of all knowings (*vidām*), the Omniscient One. (13)
The great treasury of the jewels of the world is lighter than cotton on a scale;
even illusion and the moon of a mirage do not come within the range of his vision.
Though it is the great treasury of jewels that is the world in the form of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), when weighed on the scale of discernment (viveka),
it is lighter than even a fragment of cotton, because in that weighing, mere weight is nothing but falsehood.
Though infinite and shoreless, it does not abide anywhere;
intent upon the creation of forests and mountain ranges within space.
It is infinite in terms of time and shoreless in terms of space; nevertheless, it is not situated anywhere in space or at any time, even in the void of empty space. || 15 ||
The most minute among the minute, the largest among the large, the heaviest among the heavy, and the most excellent even among the excellent. (16)
Without agent, object, or instrument; without cause and without actor—this has been filled for a long time by inner emptiness alone.
It is filled with the causal factors, such as the agent and so forth. || 17 ||
The world-casket is eternally empty like a wilderness;
though as hard as infinite mountains, it is as soft as a fragment of space.
Day by day, for the most part, the ancient becomes fragile and new;
light appears like darkness, and darkness spreads as light. (19)

"Prati" means for each individual object; "prati" means every day or at every time. It is called "tamas" (darkness) because it causes the concealment of the world. The word "api" is used in the sense of "also. || 19 ||
Even that which is perceptible is difficult to discern, and even that which is beyond perception is foremost;
consciousness itself is inert, and the inert is of the very nature of consciousness.
I alone am the state of non-I, or the non-I is indeed I;
that which is other is I, and I am indeed that which is other. (21)
"I" is not for your sake; "this" is for another's sake—thus there is no tautology. || 21 ||
Within this full ocean, these three worlds stand as if shimmering, consisting essentially of their own inherent fluidity.
Intending to show that the aforementioned objects are mere illusion (māyāmātra), he states the supporting arguments beginning with "of this" (asya) and so forth. || 22 ||
It bears all that resides within its limbs like whiteness in frost;
indeed, everything shines by means of it alone, as whiteness does by means of frost.
Although this Lord is devoid of space, time, and parts, He extends the unreal world day and night, just like a wave upon the water.
In this vast forest of space, these worlds bloom as withered clusters of blossoms, spreading forth their five-fold leaves.
Those [energies] from which the five groups, characterized by the five elements, spread forth like petals. || 25 ||
This [mirror], possessing an extremely pure form, has itself become a mirror through its own desire to behold its own reflection. (26)
The state of being a mirror—that is, the nature of a reflecting surface—for the described reflection of oneself, which takes the form of the living world;

[this occurs] within the consciousness of the undivided Brahman. In that [consciousness], there is the "sky-udumbara tree" (the celestial fig tree of the sky), and from the luminous, blazing moon, sun, and other bodies—which are like the fruits of that tree and constitute parts of the three worlds fashioned by its own will—[arises the reflection].

The meaning is that the network of instruments, such as the eyes and so forth, which belong to the self that has become a living being (jīva), act as marvelous instruments for the perception of creation—that is, for the seeing of forms and other objects. || 26 ||
The radiant parts of this fruit of the tree in the sky, which are its own spontaneous manifestations, arise as the perception of creation and produce wonder within consciousness.
Through that which is internal and that which is external, by means of the manifoldness within the manifoldness of the Self,
this very [Self] shines both internally and externally through the manifestation of existence and non-existence.

This very Supreme Self shines by itself both internally and externally through the internal world of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and the external world consisting of the elements, appearing as manifoldness in the states of waking and dreaming, and as non-manifoldness in deep sleep, through the perception of existence and non-existence; the meaning is that there is nothing other than this, not even so much as an atom. || 28 ||

This splendor of objective entities, being of such a nature, produces wonder within this [consciousness] by its own will; for this very purpose, it remains coiled like a tongue within the cavity of its own mouth.
He elaborates on this very point with the words beginning "etadrūpa" (of such a form), etc. || 29 ||
That which is the fluidity of this water is called the world;
it possesses the whirlpools of the universe and is a constituent part of the experience of the sweetness of consciousness.
It is that whose subordinate parts—namely, the portions of form, taste, and so forth—are perceived in such a way that they become sweet through consciousness alone. 30.
In this [Self], the splendor of all objects whatsoever subsides within the Radiant One;
and from this very source it arises, like light from a luminous body. (31)

The splendor of all the luminous manifestations of the sun, moon, fire, and so forth—the beauty of objects such as form—subsides within this very Radiant One during deep sleep and cosmic dissolution, and from this alone it arises during the waking and dreaming states; just as the light and the circle of radiance belong to the sun and other luminaries. (31)
This entire world is indeed pure whiteness, just as whiteness resides in snow;
therefore, these [powers] proceed from it, like rays from the moon. (32)
This is Brahman. Therefore, from this Brahman, whose nature is consciousness, these glories of the objects of experience [arise]. 32.
From this bodiless aesthetic essence (raṅga), this variegated world stands; know it to be pervaded by that [essence], which is peaceful, being free from non-existence, modification, and the like. 33.

Know this to be composed of consciousness alone—devoid of the bodiless (Anaṅga), that is, devoid of parts, and devoid of the stage (Raṅga), that is, the coloring substance; and empty of the modifications of existence such as birth and so forth (the word "and so forth" including its own internal diversities). || 33 ||
From this forest-tree, which is firmly rooted in the courtyard of the sky, there extend visible branches that are clusters of the world’s network. (34)
Indeed, here on this immovable mountain flows a visible river characterized by both decline and rise, bearing various and infinite blossoms. (35)

If, on this unshakable and immovable mountain, there were a river characterized by visible features, possessing such rising and setting—that is, such decrease and increase—as that [of the ocean]. || 35 ||
On this stage consisting of the void, the dancer Niyati dances with incessant performance through the illusory movements of the drama of the worlds. (36)
By means of the watches (vāra), which take the form of various kalpas, and by means of the days, which are fixed festival days. || 36 ||
With the opening and closing of his eyes being the millions of worlds and the great kalpas and kalpas, he again performs the dance upon the canopy and generates the child of Time.

Upon the stage of Brahman, under the canopy of Māyā, by that dancing-girl Niyati, her own infant son characterized as Time is made to dance again and again; having been withdrawn, he is born once more. Of what nature is he? He for whom the millions of world-systems (brahmāṇḍas), both the great dissolutions and the intermediate dissolutions, constitute the opening and closing of his eyes.
Of such a kind. || 37 ||
Even while these worlds are arising, he remains entirely tranquil, like a mirror that does not desire the hundreds of reflections within it. (38)
Free from desire, he is devoid of transformations such as longing and the like. || 38 ||
He is the causeless seed of all beings—of those existing now and of those yet to come—just as the [primordial] cause is for all creations. || 39 ||
It is like the five elements, which are the cause of all material creations. || 39 ||
The opening of his eyes is the prosperity of the world, and their closing is the arrival of dissolution;
yet, being without such opening or closing, he abides in the Self alone. (40)
He for whom opening and closing [of the eyes] are equal is free from illusion; he is without opening or closing. For this very reason, he abides solely within his own self. || 40 ||
As these worlds— so very numerous, immensely vast, and subject to the states of creation, dissolution, and birth— arise,
this one whose nature is boundless remains entirely tranquil, like the wind itself amidst its own vibrations.

In terms of magnitude, those worlds— the cosmic eggs (*brahmāṇḍas*)— are great, and by virtue of the power of their temporal duration and so forth, they are exceedingly great; [the verse describes] their creation (*sarga*), non-going (*agamana* = *agamas* = *agamah*), maintenance (*sthiti*), and dissolution (*pralaya*),
as well as therein the birth of living beings, the assumption of bodies, the stages beginning with childhood, and the states beginning with waking.
The states of increase and decrease—all these arise within the space of consciousness (cidākāśa).

Having understood that all these are nothing other than the space of consciousness itself—which is boundless and of an undivided nature—just as the vibrations of the wind are nothing other than the wind itself, one should abide in peace; this is the meaning. || 41 ||

Thus ends the thirty-fifth canto, titled "Description of the Nature of the Supreme Brahman," in the Nirvāṇa Section of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, within the *Deva-mokṣopāya*.
Thus ends the thirty-fifth canto, titled "Description of the Nature of the Supreme Brahman," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The thirty-sixth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Then, misfortunes arise as wonders, like whirlpools in water.
All things have a single nature, just like the waves upon the water. || 1 ||
It is described that for one who is empty [of desire] and lacks longing, enjoyment does not lead to bondage;
indeed, desire alone is the supreme bondage, and liberation comes from its abandonment.

In this world, all objects appear both as multiple contradictory forms and as a single non-contradictory form. Among these, he shows that the first form—because it arises from passion, hatred, and so forth—is of the nature of misfortune (*anartha*) as a cause of suffering, whereas the second is conducive to liberation (*mokṣa*) through their subsidence: "They produce wonder. All objects are like whirlpools in water.
Diverse in form, they first produce wonder and cause the mind to wander by generating desires;

immediately thereafter, misfortunes in the form of attachment, aversion, hell, and so forth, result. Just as waves are nothing but water, so too those of a single nature neither produce wonder nor lead to misfortune—this is the intended meaning. || 1 ||
She is the form of both the knowable and the knower of this entire universe;
she is the nature of the supreme ether and rests upon ultimate tranquility.

What is that non-contradictory form by which all things are of a single nature? He shows it with the words "of everything indeed. That such a form is the supreme space (*paramākāśatā*) itself, whose nature is pure existence (*sattāmātra*), belonging to this entire universe. And that [space] is extracted from all objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) which have specific forms; it is therefore of the nature of that object of knowledge which is pure existence alone. For this very reason...
It is that which has as its support tranquility characterized by supreme meditative concentration; such is its nature. (2)
Just as a child’s imagination in the sky before me is nothing at all, so too is this universe in reality; yet it is real within the mind of a child.

He states that in the well-known case of space, the form terrifying as yakṣas, piśācas, and so forth—which is known by the intellect of a child—and its extracted, pure form—which is known by the intellect of an adult—are established as examples; thus he says, "bāla... (by a child). Just as for a child there is the thought [of a ghost], a form imagined through contemplation such as a rākṣasa or piśāca, yet by the vision of an adult nothing exists at all, so it is [with the self].
From the perspective of me, the wise one, the universe does not exist. || 3 ||
The mental engagement with form and light is like the army of a stone statue;
since the mental engagements with form and light appear [thus], what universality can there be here? (4)
The entire universe is merely the perception of forms and light, like an army of stone statues; from the perspective of the wise, what "universality" can there be therein?
However, from the perspective of the ignorant, the mental engagement with forms and light appears as real.
Apart from the essence of form, light, and mental attention—which is pure consciousness alone—that other [world] is not found; here, where else could there be the universe, except as space? (5)

He says "rūpa... [verse 5]: even when one scrutinizes form and mental attention from the perspective of ultimate reality, form is difficult to find as something distinct from pure consciousness; far less, therefore, can the manifestation of the universe be established through those two.

The world is an illusion for one who perceives it, but there is no delusion for one who does not perceive it; perception and non-perception depend upon you, just as your mind and its absence depend on you.

And thus, for the knowing person who is the knower, the very state of being a knower is the delusion of the world, while the state of not being a knower is precisely the absence of delusion, which is the cessation of all delusion; this is the established conclusion. And that [cessation] depends on oneself, like memory or non-memory—this is the meaning. || 6 ||
Because the sky of consciousness, whose form is expansive, is of the nature of the supreme ether,
no reversal of its own-nature can ever occur anywhere.

He clarifies what was stated previously—that it is "like the sky"—with the words "the supreme space" (*paramākāśa*). The intended meaning is that consciousness does not become inert, nor does the sky take on a material form. || 7 ||
For this universe, which consists of that [Brahman], no modification of its own nature exists even when observed; how much less, then, will there be any state of inequality? (8)
He states that the world is not a modification (*vikāra*) of Brahman because it is sublated by the vision of Brahman: "Of that which consists of That" (*tanmayasya*).
Whatever is not found even when being scrutinized in a certain place—that is sublated; how could such a thing arise, persist, or exist for him?
The meaning is that this is simply impossible. || 8 ||
All this is indeed the sky of consciousness; there is no such thing as "existence" or even "I.
No modification or the like exists within pure awareness, for that which is not awareness can never be found anywhere.
By the same logic used to refute the modification of the object of thought, the modification of the thinker must also be refuted; thus he says: "Everything.
Since neither modification nor sublation exists within consciousness—the conscious Self—therefore, everything whatsoever that is not consciousness is non-consciousness;
all is peaceful, auspicious, and pure. [This applies to] the delusion of "you," "I," and so forth.
I do not see anything at all, just as one sees a forest born of the sky.
Know this to be my word: that which is the emptiness of the space of consciousness abides of its own accord within you, in the space of your own consciousness, within the Self.
And thus, know that even these words of my instruction are of the nature of the void, which is the space of consciousness (*saṃvidākāśa*).
For these words abide by themselves within the Self alone, whose nature is the space of your own consciousness, and not within that which is insentient.
The sense is that even the reality of sound culminates in its extraction as being essentially the *sphoṭa*, which is of the nature of consciousness. || 11 ||
They say that the supreme state is that which consists in remaining without the arousal of desire,
like the sitting of a stone statue or one depicted in a painting.

Thus, when it is established that the object of knowledge, the knower, and the act of knowing are nothing but pure consciousness (cinmātra), then, due to the absence of objects of desire and so forth, that state of remaining—where no desire arises—is called the supreme state (paramaṃ pada). || 12 ||
With his mind at rest and observing silence, his movement in performing his customary duties was as effortless and undisturbed by desire as that of a wooden man.
He states that even in the absence of desire, the accomplishment of worldly activity for the sake of sustaining life occurs—namely, "he" (verse 13).
Empty within and empty without, tasteless and free from latent impressions—thus does life appear to the wise man who lives, like a hollow bamboo. 14.
Thus, he explains how the world appears to a wise person living according to worldly convention: "Internally," etc.
It is empty both inside and outside, like a bamboo stalk (*veṇu*). || 14 ||
He for whom the visible does not please, yet the invisible pleases within his heart—
he, being peaceful both internally and externally, has crossed over the ocean of worldly existence.
It does not taste good, nor does it please him. || 15 ||
Let the webs of words be uttered, like a bamboo flute whose latent impressions have vanished, through aesthetic flavor clinging to the god of love, with no other instigation than the subject at hand.

Elaborating upon the non-savoring (*asvādana*) of each sense-object, he demonstrates the state of having transcended them with the words beginning "Let [them] be spoken," and so forth. The subject at hand is the exhaustion of the remainder of what has been commenced (*prārabdha-śeṣa-kṣaya*); this is achieved through worldly activities devoid of the utterance of other words required for that purpose, remaining unattached to the limbs of the body (*anaṅga-lagna*).

The meaning is: let the nets of words be uttered—that is, let them be pronounced by the organ of speech—with a flavor (rasa), that is, with sweetness, devoid of the connection of "I-ness" and "mine-ness" toward the body and so forth which are merely limbs of worldly transaction, such that one's latent impressions (vāsanā) have departed like a flute made of bamboo. || 16 ||
Let the objects of touch be touched as they come,
without attachment, remaining unshaken like a peaked pavilion, without desire and without the arising of the mind.
Thus, with your sense of touch, you should remain without desire and without the arising of the mind, like a house inhabited by actors, soldiers, and courtesans.
And let things to be touched, such as garlands, sandalwood, and so forth, be touched. || 17 ||
Let the networks of flavors be tasted— free from desire, fear, and longing, devoid of attachment or craving— just as they are obtained, like [food] with a ladle.
Let the various arrays of forms be seen again, yet devoid of latent impressions, tasteless, free from mental conceit, and without pride, like a painted eye. (19)

Without flavor, without desire; the mind that is devoid of the web of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) by which the mind is measured or constructed, and which is free from pride—that is, devoid of conceit—is like the eyes of a person depicted in a painting. || 19 ||
Let those who are free from desire and latent impressions smell the fragrant flowers; like a forest wind, let them blow away the bonds of worldly agitation for the sake of renunciation.

"Let them smell"—the form *jighrantām* is a Vedic substitute for *ghrāyantām*; if the reading is *jighnantām*, it is a substitution of the verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa-vyatyaya*). [It should be understood that "brought by the apāna" refers to the scent, in accordance with the Kaṭhavallī Śruti: "The prāṇa leads upward, while the apāna moves downward. By means of vibration (*spandena*), [let them smell] the fragrance brought by the apāna.
It binds by means of unattached sin; thus, the bond of vibration is the olfactory sense, and those [objects] attached to it are for the sake of renunciation, not for the sake of passion.
If it is argued that, having been made aware of their lack of essence, the diseases of enjoyment have been treated [and thus cured],
then likewise there would be no way at all for their pacification.

Thus, in the manner described, having made the mind understand that even regarding the objects of the organs of action—which were not explicitly mentioned—the situation is the same as before, namely, that they are tasteless and devoid of essence just like the objects of the organs of knowledge; the meaning is that if the diseases of worldly enjoyment are not treated, then there is no way at all for the cessation of suffering, and rather, there is the arising of a succession of calamities. || 21 ||
He who, tasting the poison of sensual enjoyment, finds delight day after day, casts his own body into a blazing fire and abandons that which is imperishable, like dry grass.
He says that very thing with the words "yaḥ" (he who). *Kakṣam* means a bundle of grass. *Akṣayam* means unbroken; that is to say, incessant (*ajasram*). *Ujjhati* means he casts away. || 22 ||
Those adorned by the scriptures say that composure consists in desirelessness;
for the mind does not become tranquil through hundreds of instructions in the same way that it does through desirelessness. (23)
Therefore, he praises the fact that the very abandonment of the desire for enjoyments is the primary cause for the peace of the mind: "The state of being without desire... (verse 23).
Just as the arising of desire is suffering and the pacification of desire is happiness, so it is neither experienced in hell nor even in the world of Brahmā. (24)

Nor even in the world of Brahmā. Thus it was said by Yayāti: "Whatever sensual pleasure there is in the world, and whatever great divine pleasure there is in heaven—these are not worth a sixteenth part of the bliss that comes from the destruction of craving. (24)
The wise know that the mind is mere desire; its tranquility is called liberation.
Only this much is contained in all the scriptures, austerities, observances, and restraints. (25)
These [entities] terminate at just this much; they are limited to this extent. || 25 ||
To whatever extent and in whatever manner a living being’s desire arises, to that same extent a handful of seeds of suffering sprouts forth. (26)
To whatever extent a living being’s desire diminishes through discernment, to that same extent the cholera-like pains of suffering and anxiety are pacified. (27)
Just as the density of worldly passion increases according to one's desire, so too do the waves of the poison of suffering and anxiety grow ever greater. (28)
Of the world, that is, of the people. || 28 ||
If this disease of desire is not treated by the medicine of one's own effort, then I believe there exists here another, more powerful remedy. (29)

And regarding its treatment, he says that for the remedy there is only human effort characterized by fortitude, and nothing else: "If one is unable to effect the complete pacification of desire, even a small amount [of progress] must be pursued; one who stays on the path does not despair. (30)

"Even the slightest" means that one should strive for tranquility in every respect through the gradual practice of restraining even the most minor desires. "Abiding on the path" means having entered the true path. || 30 ||
But that lowest of men who makes no effort toward the attenuation of desire abandons his own self day after day in a blind well.
Day after day; every single day. || 31 ||
Desire alone is the seed of this transmigratory existence, which is characterized by the birth of suffering;
once burnt by the fire of perfect knowledge, it does not sprout again.
But he says that the obstruction of the desire for the ultimate [cessation] occurs precisely through knowledge by means of the destruction of its root: "suffering," etc. (32).
For saṃsāra is merely desire, while nirvāṇa is the non-perception of that; let effort be made toward the non-arising of desire—what is the use of vain delusions (or vain labors)? || 33 ||

The non-perception of that [nature] is its reduction to non-existence; for the verbal root *vid* means "existence," and the suffix *lyuṭ* denotes the abstract state (*bhāva*). What is the point of fruitlessly wandering through other efforts while disregarding the teachers of the scriptural instructions?
Why is it that you do not attain meditative absorption (*samādhi*) by following your own desire? (34)
He states that even the scriptures and so forth would be rendered useless if there were no effort to pacify desire—this is expressed in the verse beginning with "śāstra":
Why is *samādhi*—the means for the concentration of the mind—not attained? For what reason is it not resorted to? || 34 ||
For one for whom even the mere non-contemplation of their own desire is considered difficult to accomplish, instruction from a guru, the scriptures, and so forth are surely useless. (35)
From the self-discrimination of the intellect. || 35 ||
For men, birth in the wilderness is sufficient cause for the expansion of suffering, arising from a doe whose very nature is transformed by the poison of desire. (36)

In this cycle of existence, which is transformed by the poison of desire, death alone is the end for human beings; just as for a doe in a forest teeming with tigers and other predators, death is her only certain fate, so it is here.
If this [desire] is not made even slightly false for the sake of self-knowledge, let there be the pacification of desire; by that, it is fully attained.

If this "I" is not made childish—that is, if it is not made fickle like a child—by desire, then only a slight effort is required for self-knowledge; therefore, let the very cessation of desire be practiced, for by that alone is such knowledge attained. || 37 ||
Freedom from desire is indeed nirvāṇa, for desire itself is bondage;
one should conquer desire according to one's ability—what is so difficult in this? (38)
May the seed of desire, which is the root of the grove of karanja and khadira trees consisting of old age, death, birth, and so forth, be forever consumed within by the fire of tranquility. (39)
Let it always be consumed by the fire of tranquility through constant practice. || 39 ||
In whatever way desirelessness arises, in that very way liberation follows;
therefore, one should destroy every arisen desire, as far as it extends and according to its power.
Until the attainment of means such as discernment and dispassion; according to one's vital energy and according to the strength of one's fortitude and so forth. || 40 ||
From whatever direction one desires, from that very direction come the snares of bondage;
they consist of merit and demerit, and are vast heaps of suffering filled with intense affliction. (41)
Like one whose entire wealth has been plundered and stripped away by bandits and robbers. || 41 ||
When even a single moment of a holy man’s time passes, devoid of the fulfillment of one's desires, it is right to lament for a long time, like one who has been plundered by bandits. (42)
In whatever measure this man's inner desire is pacified, in that same measure his auspiciousness for liberation increases. (43)
The fourfold means of accomplishment are auspicious. || 43 ||
The fulfillment of the desires of a self that lacks discernment is itself the watering of the poisonous tree of saṃsāra. (44)
The fulfillment of the desire for the enjoyment of sense objects is precisely that [which has been described]. || 44 ||
Born from the tree of the heart, the seeds of one's own pleasure and pain— arising from the auspicious and inauspicious actions performed by the body, such as enmity and the like—
attain the flames of the fire of evil deeds and, becoming sharp-edged, crackle with the sound "chamaccham."
They destroy the male animal. || 45 ||
From the heart— the tree characterized as such, the support, and the fuel— arise the sharpened tips,

the flames of the fire of evil deeds whose nature is desire; these [flames] consume the male beast, the individual soul (jīva) characterized as a victim, which exists within its own support, the heart.
Having blinded [the mind] with the smoke of delusion arising from the fault of defiling its own substratum— whether it be the impure characterized by evil or the pure characterized by merit—
and having firmly bound it with the snares of affection, [it] approaches and casts down the seeds of its own pleasure and pain.

The two testicles, which are like the interior of a granary, are burned all over and roasted like eggplants (*vārtāka*—meaning *vṛntāka*). The onomatopoeia "chamacchamiti" imitates the sound arising from the burning of that fat. The "desires" are the agents; having reached and ignited the sheaths of those evil seeds with the flames of the fire of misdeeds, they burn them.

Or alternatively, "dahanti" means "they burn. Or the construction may be according to one's preference: "having reached the sheaths of the bad seed, they burn the male-animal (puṃpaśum). Regarding the form "puṃpaśum," when the word "pum" undergoes *rutva* (the substitution of *r*) by the rule "khayyampare," the substitution of *s* occurs by the rule "saṃpuṃkānām. However, the reading "puṃpaśum" is Vedic (*chāndasa*).

Thus ends the thirty-sixth canto, titled "The Description of the Seed of Saṃsāra," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa, within the Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa of Valmīki, concerning the means to liberation.
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Seed of Saṃsāra," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The thirty-seventh canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
The separation from the transformation caused by the poison of desire is what is called yoga.
For the sake of peace, listen once more to that which was clearly stated previously.
Just as desire itself may not arise, or even if it has arisen, it becomes nothing but Brahman—
so too is the yoga of knowledge further described here through logical arguments.
It is called "separation" because its fruit is separation; it is for the sake of pacifying all misfortunes rooted in desire. || 1 ||
If that which is distinct from the self exists here, let it be desired according to one's wish; but if it does not exist, why is this otherness from one's own self not desired? (2)

"Let it be desired according to one's wish"; the meaning is: "let desire proceed as one wishes. This is the same meaning even in the reading *icchatām* (where the change of verbal suffix is an archaic Vedic usage). And thus, as long as the Self is not known, the arising of desire occurs through the delusion that a second object is real; therefore, the yoga of self-knowledge alone [is the remedy].
The sense is that this is the means for its cessation by way of removing the objects [of the senses]. || 2 ||
The consciousness of space is partless, without components, subtle, and even more void than space itself;
yet, being that very same consciousness which takes the form of the "I" and the world, why is it sought as a separate reality? (3)
