But if you think that through knowledge the world has become truly Brahman itself and is not false, even then, since there is absolute non-difference, the desire—which consists of the triad of the seeker and so forth—is impossible; thus he says: "Nirbhāga" (without parts). That from which the "parts"—namely, the distinctions of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) that differentiate the triad, as well as the distinctions of divisible components—have departed. It is of the nature of "I" (*aham-ākārā*).
And that very same reality is the form of the world. || 3 ||
She is of the nature of space, indeed space itself, the knower and the known whose essence is space;
what object of desire could there be here for the appearance of the world, which is of the nature of space?

As for the claim that the relationship between the grasped and the grasper arises from something [external], we do not accept that; such a relationship does not exist for those who are utterly tranquil—those whom I do not know.

Since desire does not arise toward an object not grasped by the intellect, and since apprehension is impossible in the absence of the relationship between the grasped and the grasper, even for the wise there is no occurrence of desire; thus he says: "The grasped... For us who are tranquil, this relationship between the grasped and the grasper—which is established only through the perspective of the ignorant—does not exist due to any cause whatsoever, nor is it established by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
The logical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "For what reason is it desired that [it] does not exist? The meaning is: I do not know those ignorant ones for whom [it] exists;
even they are utterly unknown from the perspective of reality (*tattva*). || 5 ||
The relationship between the grasped and the grasper is not found even when it is considered to reside in itself.
How can that which is non-existent be obtained? By whom has a black moon ever been perceived?
The word "api" (also) is used in the sense of "even. Asita means dark-complexioned or black. || 6 ||
This indeed is the existence of the grasper and so forth: that they do not reside within themselves.
If they are real when their own nature is examined, I know not where they go. (7)

This alone is the existence of all triads, such as the subject and so forth. What is this? It is that which does not rest in the Self—that is, the lack of repose in the ultimate Self; in other words, it is ignorance. And as for those subjects and the rest, they are real only in relation to the non-scriptural view of inherent nature (*svabhāva*); when the scriptural vision of reality arises, where do they go?
I do not know. || 7 ||
This indeed is the true nature [of reality]: that the entirety of the seer and the seen is extinguished;
having realized that [the self] is unreal, one attains nirvana within the self through the cessation of the sense of "I."

This very same nature belongs to the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna) as well: that the unreal egoity, having known its own true nature through the scriptures, goes toward and departs from that Self. This is the meaning: it is the total destruction of both the seer and the seen, which is the distinguished Nirvana. || 8 ||
In nirvāṇa there is no object of perception and the like; in the object of perception and the like, there is no nirvāṇa.
There is no mutual experience between these two, just as there is none between shadow and sunlight.
He states that the mutual non-coexistence of the visible and nirvāṇa is also due to their very nature—namely, "in nirvāṇa.
Mutual experience means simultaneous experience. || 9 ||
Both of these are mutually unreal, and where there is unreality, there is no cessation; for from that [reality] comes Nirvana, which is experienced as ageless and free from suffering. || 10 ||
To the question, "Why is there no simultaneous experience [of both]? he says: "Both" (*ubhe*).

If these two were to exist together mutually, then both would be unreal due to their mutual sublation. To the question, "What is the fault if they are unreal? he says: "And if they are unreal" (*asatye ca*).
Thus, there is a contradiction with the experience of the wise; so he says: "Since" (*yataḥ*) || 10 ||
The world of appearances and so forth is illusory and never bestows happiness;
it is non-existent, so contemplate this and remain in the unborn state of Nirvana.

Now, lest one should harbor a lack of confidence, thinking that the great marvels of the visible world and so forth, well-known to all people, would be difficult to find in Nirvana, he says: "It is born of delusion. One should not contemplate—that is, one should not dwell upon—that which is unreal and harmful in nature, namely, the visible world and its like. (11)
That which is perceived as resembling the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell cannot be obtained;
since even the causal efficiency of the object does not exist there, what is the use of denial? (12)

That [world] which effects purpose—that is, which accomplishes the aims of human beings—does not exist at all. In this regard, the meaning is: what curiosity can there be in the negation of such a visible world? || 12 ||
From its presence comes great suffering; from its absence comes great happiness. Its non-existence, along with the logical proof for it, attains firmness through meditative cultivation.

The sublation consisting of non-existence, produced by verbal knowledge, together with its supporting reasoning and accompanied by reflection, results from the practice of meditation through the removal of that sublation. || 13 ||
Therefore, O lowest of men, why do you vainly apply cleverness to the Self for the sake of bondage?
For increase and decrease are clearly established only in an object that is not situated in the [Self], which is beyond such categories.

Now, the supremely compassionate Lord Vasiṣṭha, having forcefully rebuked his listeners— who are of inferior qualification and attached to the curiosity of the visible world— and seeking to make them abandon their attachment to the visible, said: "What then?"— O base ones, you [are attached] to the supreme reality, which is not the locus of the collection of transformations such as growth and so forth.

Since [the Self] is self-luminous and because of the instruction of the scriptures and the teacher, it shines forth as clearly as a myrobalan fruit in the palm of one’s hand; why then does this non-perception of reality occur? Have you not made that entire collection of objects of sight a means for binding yourselves? Is bondage itself what you are aiming for, such that you do not relinquish attachment to the visible world? This is the meaning. || 14 ||
When the entire world of cause and effect and so forth is indeed Brahman alone,
then Brahmanhood truly resides within this all-pervasive reality whose nature is pure consciousness.

When everything— including the relationship of cause and effect— becomes Brahman alone, then, through the disappearance of limitations such as the body and so forth, and upon attaining expansion within the inner self (pratīc) which consists of pure consciousness, the state of being Brahman is established; this occurs even when not the slightest atom of the visible world remains.
Enough with those deer seeking awakening;
for when the one all-pervading Self, whose nature is space, truly exists as the sole reality, what need is there for them? (16)

Therefore, since the Self is of the nature of space, full, and the soul of all, there is no need for those disputants who are like deer—whether they be logicians or disciples—who, while accepting the appearance of cause and effect and so forth, still search and seek out means for the awakening to Brahman; the meaning is that there is no purpose [in their efforts]. || 16 ||
What indeed is the sequence of those very utterances rich in cause and effect?
That which is the cause for the vibration of wind and for the fluidity of water. (17)

If a cause must necessarily be stated, then it is one's own ignorance (*svāvidyā*) which consists of the nature of all things; with this intention, he says: "O gentle one, when emptiness belongs to space, and the state of being the beginning of creation belongs to the conscious self (*cidātman*), and when the relationship of cause and effect and so forth—all of this is indeed Brahman. (18)

For this very reason, he states that for the learned, there is the fault of shamelessness in defining the cause of creation and so forth, because such [definitions] are sublated; thus he says: "kārya... (verse 18).
Then, within Brahman, the cause of all creations is free from shame;
there is neither suffering nor happiness, for the world is peaceful and composed of auspiciousness. || 19 ||
The expression of a reason for one's own conduct is called shamelessness (*nirlajjatā*). || 19 ||
Since there is no otherness from pure consciousness, how can there be the arising of desire? Just as in an army composed of clay bodies and clay weapons, there is nothing other than mere clay.
"There is no attachment to the visible world, to the ego, and so forth, nor is there anything other than Brahman.
Śrī Rāma said: "O Lord of Sages, if this is so, then let desire arise, or let it not arise. (21)

If everything is indeed Brahman alone, then desire is all the more Brahman; thus, from the perspective of the wise, Rāma raises an objection, wondering what loss there could be in its arising, with the words: "If this were so... (21).
"But she is indeed Brahman; what purpose could there be in her being enjoined or prohibited?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
"When she is known and fully awakened, the will is Brahman itself and nothing else."

"Let an effort be made to prevent desire from arising; what is the use of vain delusions?"—to such arguments that negate the previously mentioned injunctions and prohibitions regarding effort, [the author] replies with the words "When [it] is known," etc., stating that there is no harm whatsoever even if desire arises for the wise person, because its very emergence is impossible once it has been sublated by knowledge. || 22 ||
O Rāma, as the Fully Awakened One has spoken, that is the truth; however, listen to this:
whenever knowledge arises, at that very moment desire subsides.
Just as when the sun rises from its own essential nature, the night merely subsides and does not arise [again], so too do desire and the like [subside] within cognition and do not arise.

In the case of the rule *iṭakiṭakaṭī gatau*, the form *ayatī* is derived from the root *ī* (as it is *praśliṣṭa* [joined] therein) in its present participle (*śatṛ*) form in the seventh case singular; it is not derived from the root *ay*. This is because the latter is *ātmanepada*. 24.

To the extent that the rising of consciousness brings about the cessation of duality, to that same extent there is the dissolution of latent impressions; how, then, could the arising of desire occur? (25)
For such a person, this stainless liberation is said to arise through the subsiding of ignorance;
because of the distaste for all objects of perception, desire never arises in them anywhere.
With the intention that even from the cutting off of the root, there is no possibility of the arising of desire for the wise, he says: "Of that" (tasya). || 26 ||
Neither does detachment toward the visible arise for him, nor does attachment toward it;
rather, the splendor of the seer and the seen is experienced merely as it is, not by its own inherent nature.
It does not please him, nor does it appeal to him. || 27 ||
If, by some chance like the "crow-and-palm" coincidence, or through the instigation of another, he should at any time desire even a little [of this], whether correctly or not; (28)
The giving of food and so forth, which serves merely as a means for sustaining the body and is not prohibited by the authoritative scriptures, [is permissible]. || 28 ||
Therefore, whether he has desire or no desire, it is Brahman alone in this matter; of this there is no doubt.
Desire does not arise in the knower, either necessarily or otherwise. (29)

At that time, for this wise one, that desire—whether it be desire, non-desire, or both—is Brahman alone. Alternatively, for the knower, the wise one, a desire directed toward the wonder of new experiences certainly does not arise at all;
however, following what was previously practiced, it may be indeterminate. || 29 ||
If knowledge has arisen in a living being, then his desire subsides;
these two cannot coexist in one place, just like light and darkness.
Knowledge is the knowledge of reality; that [occurs] then. 30.
But for one who knows that [reality], the scope of prohibitions and injunctions does not exist anywhere;
for one whose desire for all worldly pursuits has been stilled, who would say what to him, and for what purpose? (31)

For this very reason, he says "pratiṣedha... [in the verse], stating that one who is free from passion (*nīrāga*) is not qualified for the scriptural injunctions that prohibit actions prompted by passion. For what purpose? For what motive? The sense is that it is not necessary for a person who is not blind to say, "One must not fall into a well. || 31 ||
This alone is the sign of knowledge: the extreme attenuation of desire, or else the experience of delight for all people. (32)

He states that the cessation of external desire and satisfaction through the experience of one's own bliss are the signs of the arising of the awakening to reality—this very thing [is it]—by means of which all people are gladdened through the granting of fearlessness. || 32 ||
When the object of perception has become tasteless and no longer brings any relish whatsoever, then desire no longer spreads; and at that very moment, there is liberation.
For one who abides in the peaceful non-duality that is the oneness of awakening,
all states such as desire and non-desire are of the nature of Śiva.
Through awakening, he has set aside duality; he is devoid of both non-duality and unity.
He is pure, free from agitation, tranquil, and established in the Self. (35)

The construction with the subsequent [verse] is as follows: "of Him who abides in such a way that He is devoid of non-duality (advaita)—which is a distinct entity consisting of the destruction of duality—as well as of oneness (aikya), which is a merging, and of the number one (ekatvasaṃkhyā). || 35 ||
For him there is no purpose whatsoever in action performed here, nor any in what is not performed;
nor does he have any dependence on any being for any object.
The attainment of the purpose is that which relies upon the meaning. || 36 ||
It is never [attained] through lack of desire, nor through desire; not by means of the existent, nor by the non-existent;
neither by oneself nor by another, nor by these [factors of] death and life. || 37 ||
"Not by lack of desire. The phrase "based on the meaning" is to be supplied everywhere [in the subsequent rules]. || 37 ||
And no desire arises in him who has awakened to nirvāṇa;
yet if a desire should arise in him, that very desire is eternal Brahman.
"There is neither suffering nor happiness; the world is as tranquil as a dog or a goat"—the wise know him to be truly awakened who remains inwardly like a stone with such a conviction. (39)

Making suffering into happiness through meditative cultivation, as if turning poison into nectar—having reached this certainty, one whose self is steadfast (or, according to another reading, whose self is formidable) is called "awakened. (40)

Thus, having ascertained the reality of the Self as previously described, he renders both suffering and pleasure like poison and nectar through the contemplation of his own nature as unsurpassed bliss. || 40 ||
That which exists in the sky is the sky; the peaceful in the peaceful, the auspicious in the auspicious;
the void in the void, and that which is real in the real—thus the world is situated within Brahman. (41)
He says "that" (tat) to show that the very state of all things conforming to the realization of that [reality] is the non-erroneous state, and not what is established by worldly convention:
"That" means at that time. || 41 ||
When it is established that "the universe does not exist" within the vast expanse of consciousness devoid of objective perception—
consciousness which is gentle, perfectly equanimous, peaceful, and auspicious— the delusion of egoism perishes.
Thus, in the manner described, when everything has become such that it is devoid of the world and free from the external universe; || 42 ||
Whatever is seen here in this world, whether stationary or moving, all that is the peaceful void, comparable to a city imagined by another's thought. (43)
The city of thought is like that city of the imagination. || 43 ||
Just as your coming and going are unimpeded within the center of the city of another's thought because of its emptiness, so it is likewise in this delusion of the world.

Just as for another person, the unimpeded coming and going within the city imagined by his own mental construction—in the midst of which there is no obstruction such as walls—is possible, so too it is possible for the wise man within this delusion of the world; this is the meaning. || 44 ||
Within the Self, which is utterly devoid of the beauty of oceans, heavens, earth, rivers, and mountains,
the faculty of seeing expands like the waves of water in a mirage.

To explain why that is so, he says: "The ocean," and so forth. Because within the Self, which is more void than the ocean and other such things, it is the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) of the seer itself that expands in the form of the splendor of the ocean and the like. Likewise, for a man who is thirsty and exhausted, the eye—the instrument of perception—expands in the form of waves of water in a mirage before him, even though that place in front is devoid of water.
The meaning is "in that same way. || 45 ||
Like a dream, a conjured city, a child’s ghost, or a palmyra palm;
regarding that which is seen here, what indeed could be other than unreal? (46)
What indeed could there be that is "other than" falsity which could be called truth? 46.
"I am indeed unreal" appears, yet it appears as real;
even without one who experiences delusion, this delusion flashes forth as something existent. (47)
He states that even the falsity of the one who experiences delusion arises from the delusion itself: "It is indeed unreal.

Since it is Brahman alone, which is reality, that appears as "I" and "this"—and yet this appearance is entirely unreal—therefore this delusion flashes forth even without one who experiences delusion; thus, the meaning is that it is unreal. || 47 ||
Neither existent, nor non-existent, nor both existent and non-existent— this world, which is beyond the reach of the senses and inexpressible, shines forth as undisturbed as the sky.

If it were absolutely non-existent, one would enter the position of the proponents of emptiness (*śūnyavādin*); if it were absolutely existent, there would be a contradiction with the non-dual scriptures and the experience of the wise. However, since being both is impossible due to contradiction, the conclusion is its indeterminability (*anirvacanīyatā*). He states this by means of elimination—like the case of [the gender] "masculinity"—saying: "It is not existent."
"Beyond the senses" (atīndriya) means a reality that cannot be determined by the senses. "Like the sky" (khavat) means like the senses;
or it is like the undisturbed space [that appears] in the form of a city of Gandharvas and so forth. || 48 ||
In this world, for the knower who has both desire and non-desire, equanimity is sufficient for peace;
nevertheless, I consider the arousal of non-desire to be clearly more conducive to the highest good. (49)
For the wise one who knows reality, the pacification of sense objects is sufficient through the power of the awakening to reality alone.

Although desire and non-desire are equal and yield the same result, nevertheless, I consider the arising of non-desire alone to be the clear cause for the manifestation of undisturbed happiness, leading to the highest good. The word "nanu" is used here as an address to Rāma. (49)

The cognition "I am the world" is situated in the void like the void itself within the void; it belongs to the conscious self (cidātman), just as vibration belongs to the wind, and there is no other cause for it here.

Just as the cognition "I am the world" is established in the unmodified space according to the sequence stated in the Śruti, beginning with "from space, air," so it is for the conscious Self (cidātman) when veiled by ignorance; no other cause need be sought here—this is the meaning. || 50 ||

That which is the mind's orientation toward objects of thought is itself the cycle of worldly existence (saṃsṛti). That same [orientation], when it is free from desire, is liberation. Having understood this principle, one should attain peace. 51.

And thus, it follows that the outward inclination of the conscious self (cidātman) is itself desire, the mind, and saṃsāra, while remaining established within its own nature is liberation; this is what he states in the verse beginning with "citaḥ" (51).
Whether there be desire or lack of desire, whether creation or dissolution— there is no harm whatsoever to anyone, for indeed nothing at all exists here [in reality].
And likewise, just as there is no gain or loss for Īśvara in creation and dissolution, there is no gain or loss for the knower in desire or non-desire; thus he says:
"Desire... The words "there is a result" are to be supplied. || 52 ||
Desire and non-desire, existence and non-existence, being and non-being, pleasure and pain—none of these conceptualizations can possibly occur within the void. 53.
He whose desires diminish day by day, and who is never satiated with discernment and tranquility, is said to be a partaker of liberation. 54.

He states the reason for arising therein: "desire and non-desire. "Kalanās" means conceptual constructions (*kalpanās*). Here, it refers to the void of the nature of the Knower of Reality, the space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*). || 53 || 54 ||
When the heart is pierced by the arrow of desire, a piercing pain arises;
where these [afflictions] prevail, neither jewels, mantras, nor medicinal herbs can conquer them.

By means of the *kṣurikā* characterized by desire (*icchā*), with its blade as sharp as a razor, [one cuts] the spear—the pain consisting of grief, delusion, and so forth—in which spear these world-renowned jewels, mantras, and medicinal herbs do not prevail; that is to say, they become blunted. Those very arrays of causal instruments (*kāryakaraṇavyūha*) which he had previously fashioned, [he now destroys].
I do not see [anything] through deliberate observation, except for the weight of false delusion.
The Creator fashioned the entire collection of medicinal herbs, mantras, yantras, and other instruments for the purpose of alleviating the suffering of living beings;
yet, though I have previously exerted myself in observing them many times for the sake of testing them,
I do not see those capable of treating him when he is attended by a person overwhelmed by false delusion.

If one were to engage in worldly activity by means of an unreal object that has become an object of delusion, then why is the mountain of another’s mind not turned into a woolen blanket (or, according to another reading, swallowed)?
[Objection: "Let there be the worldly activity of treating that [delusion], and so forth, by some means established through error. To this, he says:
Regarding the phrase "by that which has become delusion": *bhrama* is erroneous cognition; by that which has become [delusion], meaning by that which is established [as such].

When warding off the suffering established through another's delusion by means of a method established through our own delusion—such as [using] a mouth many yojanas wide imagined through our own mental wish-fulfillment to [remove] another's dream-mountain and so forth—[it is accomplished].
The meaning is that there would be the consequence of [the self] being subject to consumption. || 57 ||
If conventional usage were carried out by means of what is non-existent—which perishes upon mere inspection—then why is the sky not covered by a rabbit’s horn? 58.

Since that which is established through delusion lacks existence, it also lacks the capacity to prevent the suffering of others from an ultimate standpoint; thus he says, "because it is non-existent" (*asatā*). The word "is performed" (*kriyate*) connects with what precedes. Therefore, the meaning is this: for the removal of all his delusions and sufferings, the means is none other than Brahman itself—the ultimate reality manifested through the knowledge of truth belonging to him. || 58 ||
Due to the sense of "I-ness" (ahaṃbhāva) and through an excess of insentience, the space of consciousness instantly attains the state of a stone;
like water [freezing], it reaches the state of the mind and then the state of the body.
If the world is merely an immaterial mental delusion, how does it come to possess the state of material bodies and so forth? To this he says:

"From the sense of 'I'. From the sense of "I" which takes the form of the body and other such things; just as water, due to an excess of dullness, attains the state of stone, namely the condition of hailstones. || 59 ||

Because it is consciousness, it experiences this very state of being embodied even while it is unreal, just as the power of consciousness, remaining undestroyed, experiences its own death in a dream. || 60 ||

Even though the state of being an insentient body is imagined by consciousness as being equivalent to its own death, the real nature of consciousness remains entirely unimpaired; therefore, it experiences that [body]. Thus he says: "Because of its nature as consciousness" (cittvāt). || 60 ||
Just as blueness in the sky is unreal because it lacks substantiality, yet real because of its experience, so too this creation in this Lord is neither non-existent nor composed of existence.
He states that the insentient nature of the phenomenal appearance is indefinable because its existence is dependent upon appearance: "In the sky," etc.
Just as there is no difference between emptiness and space, or between movement and the wind,
so too there is no difference between the creation and Brahman, which are of one and the same nature.

For this very reason, because there is identity between the existence of the world and the existence of Brahman, he says that there is no difference, beginning with the words "Just as" (yathā). || 62 ||
Nothing here is born, such as the world and so forth, nor does anything perish;
it appears merely as a dream to one who has fallen asleep. (63)
He states that for an illusory object, like a dream-object, production and so forth are not established as anything beyond its mere appearance:

"When earth and the other elements do not exist, but consist of nothing more than appearance, what kind of exertion could there be in creation regarding taking up or discarding within the sky of consciousness? (64)
For this very reason, he states that attachment to the rejection or acceptance of that [object] is not appropriate, saying: "When it does not exist" (avidyamāne). || 64 ||
The body, composed of causes such as earth and the other elements, does not appear; there is only pure Brahman-consciousness alone, established within the Self itself. (65)

For the acceptance and rejection of objects such as the earth exist for the sake of the body; when both of these are non-existent because they are mere appearances (*pratibhāsa-mātra*), then those two are also non-existent—with this intention he says "no. [They do not exist] because they are merely appearances (*pratibhātaḥ*). 65.
Furthermore, the causality of the intellect and so forth is not real, because neither duality nor unity is possible;
however, this [causality] attains its validity through the possibility of the meaning expressed as "this is produced by that. (66)

In this way, since duality and unity, or difference and non-difference, are impossible even for the intellect and so forth in relation to the consciousness in which they themselves appear, the causality expressed in the conventional usage "this is produced by that" also turns out to be unreal; it pertains only to the existent reality, the ultimate entity, because only that is possible—this is the meaning. || 66 ||
In consciousness, the multitude of mental constructions and activities appears without cause and without sequence;
just as in a dream, death, birth, and so forth appear instantly to those who are impetuous.

Thus, [the author] says "without cause" (ahetu) to explain that Brahmās, kalpas, mahākalpas, and the multitudes of activities therein are indeed causeless and without emergence, yet appear as if they possessed causes and transitions; death, birth, and so forth are fleeting and devoid of long duration. (67)
The earth is indeed space, the mountains are space, and even firm walls are space;
the worlds are space, movement is space, and the perception of creation belongs to consciousness as space. (68)

And thus, it is established that everything is indeed the space of consciousness (cidākāśa); he states this with the words "only the void" (khameva). The meaning is that the perception of creation occurs within the very self of consciousness and nowhere else. || 68 ||
Upon the wall of the sky, the painting of the universe—composed of the stage of consciousness—is spread out;
it neither rises nor sets, it does not cease, nor does it weary.
In the water of consciousness, which takes the form of the fluidity of the lofty waves of the universe—what indeed has arisen, or how? What has been extinguished, when, and in what manner? (70)
He does not become exhausted, nor does he grow weary. || 69 || 70 ||
In the tranquil great space of consciousness, which is characterized by the emptiness of the world, since there is no possibility of an object of thought, how could there be rising or setting? (71)
"In that case, let the rise and fall of the world belong to consciousness itself. To this he says: "In the peaceful [state].

Since objects of cognition are impossible, when worlds themselves do not exist, how could there be the rise and fall of consciousness in the form of those [worlds]? The meaning is: from what could they be established?
Mountains appear like the sky, and the sky appears like mountains;
through the application of pure awareness, the state of Brahman remains as the manifestation of creation.

But if it is seen as resembling the play of illusion (*māyā*), then the fact that everything can assume every form is established according to one's desire; thus he says: "mountains. This is by means of the application of conceptualization (*saṃkalpa*), which is characterized by imagination following the diversity of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) within consciousness. || 72 ||
By the application of the powder of consciousness, yogis in half a blink of an eye turn the world into space and space into the three worlds.

For this very reason, he says "consciousness" (saṃvit), meaning that for those who have attained yoga, a contradictory conceptualization is accomplished at will in a single moment through the application of that elixir-powder whose characteristic is consciousness. || 73 ||
Just as there are countless cities of perfected imagination in the sky,
so too do thousands of creations exist within the sky of consciousness.

Just as in the well-known sky there exist infinite cities, fashioned by the will of perfected beings (*siddha*), which are mutually unattached and hidden from one another, so too do thousands of creations exist within Brahman. || 74 ||
Just as whirlpools in the great ocean, though mutually mingled, remain distinct from one another, so it is with the waters; they do not become anything other than water.
Regarding this, he provides an illustration: "In the great ocean," [verse 75].
The great cognitions and the great creations, though mutually intermingled, remain distinct; they are not separate from that [consciousness].

The words of the wise declare that the attainment of another world of the perfected ones (siddha) by an awakened yogi during the interval between one creation and the next is precisely this [state]. (77)

The declarations of the wise and learned are as follows: that very attainment (*prāpti*)—characterized by entering those worlds through the door of penetrating the minds of others, which occurs when a yogin, by means of the dissolution of his own limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) into the root-consciousness (*mūla-citi*), beholds other perfected worlds (*siddha-loka*) even when they are mutually hidden—is the same [attainment] when one beholds another creation from within one's own creation. It is exactly so.
The meaning is that this is because [the Lord] is described in such passages as the Līlopākhyāna (the Narrative of Divine Play). || 77 ||
The multitudes of creations abide without restraint within the imperishable, supreme Śiva, like the manifestations of emptiness within the sky. 78.

And thus, he states that the existence of all living beings and their objects of enjoyment as illusory manifestations (vivarta) within the eternal Brahman alone has been established: "indestructible" (avināśinī). || 78 ||
The innate delusions of creation, which possess the natural fragrance of the ultimate reality,
neither arise nor subside, like lines carved within a stone.

And so, he says "paramārtha... [and so forth], stating that the delusions of creation, which are like the natural fragrance of the ultimate space of consciousness (paramārthacidākāśa), are indeed of its very nature;
thus, these have no such thing as origination and so on—just like the lines seen within the interior of a crystal stone. || 79 ||
Just as the fragrances of flowers, though meeting one another,
remain unmixed even when blended, so too are these creations of the nature of space, each being a distinct ground of perfection for the *siddhas*.
The phrase "as if they were stages of accomplishment" is the ellipsis to be supplied. || 80 ||

Because its nature is the space of volition (saṃkalpa) and because it abides like all experience, the mental conceptions and expressions regarding the body, volitions, and delusions are indeed real. (81)

Therefore, from the perspective of common folk whose conceptualizations and delusions regarding the phenomenal world are gross, the world exists as a gross experience; whereas from the perspective of various types of yogis whose conceptualizations and delusions are subtle, subtler, and most subtle, it exists in a subtle and so forth manner.
He says that because they do not follow all [worldly] experiences, the descriptions of liberation for all beings—which follow their own respective experiences—are true:

the meaning is that the descriptions of the subtlety of the world, which are preceded by reflection, are true and should not be considered false on the grounds of contradicting the experience of common folk. || 81 ||
Neither the doctrine of knowledge nor the doctrine of external objects is true;
these perceptions bear fruit for you exactly according to how they are perceived.

For this very reason, the various conceptualizations of different disputants are true only in accordance with their respective latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and mental constructs (*saṃkalpa*), not in accordance with all mental constructs, nor from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). To satisfy them, he says "no. The position of the proponents of knowledge (*jñānavāditā*) is the doctrine that the ultimate reality consists solely of what is internally cognized; as for external objects of perception, they are worthless things that are causes of suffering.

The seven categories, beginning with substance, quality, and action, as well as the doctrine of their being mere mental constructs (tanmātra), are also true; for they bear fruit according to one's perception and intention, by virtue of their capacity to perform their respective causal functions. 82.

When it is contemplated that "the world exists within consciousness as the very nature of consciousness," then no distinction between them is possible, just as there is none between liquidity and water. (83)
What, then, is the authoritative position? He states it: "The power of consciousness" (*citīti*). Consciousness (*cittvam*) is the power of manifesting the threefold fold (*tripuṭī*).
The intended meaning is based on such scriptural passages as, "For [the Self] is unborn, both within and without," and so forth. || 83 ||
Time, the worlds, the universes, and I—the aggregate of sense-objects—you and those objects therein, and the notion that "it is so"—all this is one.
It is the space of consciousness, peaceful, unborn, and undecaying, the very self of the Lord; indeed, passion and the like do not exist at all.

Having restated what was said, he concludes by applying it to the subject at hand, beginning with the word "Time" (kāla): Time is the support of all; within it are the worlds, the cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas), and within those are the fourteen realms (bhuvanas).
Within those are the enjoyers, such as "I" and "you," and the group of senses (akṣavarga) which serves as the instrument for their enjoyment—all these [are contained therein].

The objects of enjoyment, such as sound and touch, as well as the diverse experiences therein—all this is, in its ultimate reality, nothing but the single, peaceful expanse of consciousness (*cidvyoma*), endowed with the Lord’s nature, consisting of illusory omniscience, omnipotence, and so forth.
When this is indeed firmly ascertained, no passions or other defects whatsoever can arise; this alone is the means for conquering all faults, beginning with desire.
The meaning is that it is the primary means. || 84 ||

Thus ends the thirty-seventh canto, titled "The Yoga of Instruction on the Visible," in the latter half of the *Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa* of the glorious *Vāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa*, composed by the sage Vālmīki. 37.
Thus ends the thirty-seventh canto, titled "The Yoga of Instruction on the Visible World," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
Canto 38.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Awakened by the realization of its own nature, consciousness perceives the world as false,
just as an eye smeared with the ointment of illusion sees mountains and other things within the sky.

In this context, by means of sound reasoning, it is established that consciousness alone is the world, through the dispelling of the delusion of difference caused by the contact between consciousness and its objects.

Desiring to establish through reasoning that this entire world of objects (*cetī*) is nothing but pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), he prepares the introductory framework with the word "Consciousness" (*cit*). "Awakened by false self-awareness" means distracted by the delusion of one's own non-Brahmanhood; just as the eye, when anointed with a special collyrium that causes the perception of illusion, sees mountains in the motionless sky.
The meaning is that he sees the intervening spaces—the slopes, plateaus, peaks, caves, forest thickets, and so forth—in exactly that same way. || 1 ||
The creation of Brahmā and the creation of the mind—these two are considered similar, because they both possess the nature of ultimate reality and are eternally undisturbed. (2)
This creation is imagined through delusion; like a painted creation, it appears as if agitated solely by the mental construction of the mind, but not in reality.
Thus he says: "Brahman... (verse 2).
Because it is of the nature of cognition, it is not external;
yet, because it is experienced as external, know that the form of external objects is real within reality. (3)

"Let it be so; what follows from that? To this he replies: "By knowledge," and so forth. Just as a painted creation on a wall is not external to the wall in its real nature as the wall itself, yet is external to it through the medium of deluded experience, so too the creation imagined within knowledge is not external to knowledge in its real nature as knowledge, yet is external through the medium of deluded experience. This being established, [it is concluded that] it is knowledge.
The meaning is: because it is of the nature of reality, know that even the form of external objects is real by virtue of having that [consciousness] as its essence. || 3 ||
For us, there is indeed an identity between the doctrine of external objects (bāhyārthavāda) and the doctrine of consciousness-only (vijñānavāda),
because the nature of cognition is always of a single form, whether it exists or does not exist.

And thus our view is not contradicted by either the theory of external objects (bāhyārthavāda) or the theory of consciousness-only (vijñānavāda), because there is harmony between both [positions] in this regard. The meaning is that we do not admit the existence of an external manifold distinct from consciousness, nor do we admit its non-existence as something internally cognized; for it is never established as such. || 4 ||
The very being of Brahman pervades everywhere—tranquil, characterized by the stillness of ether, air, light, water, and earth; vast, empty, and of great undertaking.

Since consciousness is eternally undisturbed and devoid of distinctions within the oneness of all, the pacification of the five elements such as space—which are subject to agitation—is established as a matter of course; thus, the result is the remaining of nothing but the existence of the full Brahman.
He states this with the verse beginning "undisturbed" (akṣubdha). || 5 ||
To him who is everything, from whom everything [proceeds], who is all that, and who is everywhere;
to him who is eternally composed of all things, to that Soul of All, obeisance!
Thus, he pays homage to that very world—which consists of all agents, actions, and fruits—having become one with Brahman, with the words "To him" (tasmai). || 6 ||

When the object of thought, due to its nature as consciousness, attains oneness with the consciousness of the seer, then this [object] is perceived by the consciousness through its very aspect as the visible; it is not perceived by consciousness otherwise.

He states that even at the time of empirical transaction (*vyavahāra*), the existence and manifestation (*sattāsphūrti*) of the object of cognition (*cetya*) occur solely by virtue of its attaining identity with consciousness (*cidaikya*), and not otherwise:

"Because it consists of consciousness" (*cinmayatvāt*). When the object of cognition, such as a jar, attains oneness with the witnessing consciousness—the subject-consciousness delimited by the visual modification (*vṛtti*)—through the mediation of the pervasion of that modification, because that object (the jar) consists of consciousness, [then it appears].
The meaning is that this jar and so forth are perceived by consciousness (cit) only when it is of such a nature—that is, when its visible limb, the body, is [present]; not otherwise. || 7 ||
When this entire world— consisting of the seer, the act of seeing, and the object seen— is nothing but pure consciousness (cinmātra),
then the experience of everything therein remains as a fully realized fruit.

Thus, since the seer, the means of that seeing, the act of seeing, and its fruit—all these have their establishment dependent upon identity with consciousness (cid-ekya)—when everything is indeed pure consciousness alone, then the ultimate result is established: that, in the highest sense, the very nature of the entire world remains as nothing but pure experience. This is the meaning. || 8 ||
If the seer and the seen were not one within the nature of consciousness,
then the ignorant person would not experience the taste of the seen, just as a stone does not perceive sugarcane even after seeing it.
He states the reasoning that supports the proof of the identity of the seer and the seen: "The seer and the seen...

If the seer and the seen were not one in essence within the conscious Self, the Witness, then a man engaged in eating sugarcane at a particular moment, even while tasting it, would be like a stone regarding the flavor of the object seen.

One who is ignorant of that sweetness would not experience it; for an insentient thing cannot experience rasa, nor will rasa manifest itself to an insentient thing such that it might experience it—this is the meaning. || 9 ||
Because consciousness is of the nature of pure awareness, the object of cognition sinks into that awareness like water into water;
through this, experience occurs, and not otherwise, as in the case of two pieces of wood.

If, however, one accepts that both [the subject and the object] consist of consciousness (*cinmaya*), then the object to be experienced must be experienced by the consciousness that is the experiencer.

Like a drop of water fallen into water, it sinks by merging into that [consciousness]; for that reason, experience becomes the entry into the manifestation of the "threefold set" (*tripuṭī*)—namely, "I am tasting the sweetness of the sesame"—and thus it is established. This is the meaning. || 10 ||

Just as wood does not perceive because of the absence of unity among its constituent parts, so too the observer, though non-inert, would not have known the object of perception had it likewise been composed of such parts. (11)

He establishes the similarity between the example and the case in point (the *dārṣṭāntika*) regarding their difference, as stated in the phrase "like two pieces of wood," by means of the term *sajātīya* ("of the same class"):

Just as a piece of wood (*kāṣṭha*), acting as the agent, does not perceive a second piece of wood—which is its object—despite their being of the same class as wood, because there is no identity of consciousness (*cidaikya*); so too the observer, though non-inert, [does not perceive] that which is entirely devoid of identity with consciousness.
He would not have known the visible world. || 11 ||
Wood possesses whatever kind of existence it has, yet it is insentient and does not know its own form; therefore, that which is visible is the insentient object of consciousness.
Furthermore, some do not perceive any distinction between the observer and the observed when both are insentient, like two pieces of wood; thus he says, "of whatever nature" (*yādṛk*).

This means: those things whose existence or state is of such a kind. The meaning is that no one perceives any other difference [between them]. Therefore, by the force of the reasoning already stated, the observer is the observed itself through the very nature of consciousness (*cid-rūpa*).
The meaning is that it is established that consciousness (cetana) is non-different from the conscious principle (cit); this is a *karmadhāraya* compound. || 12 ||
The states of water, air, earth, and stone exist only as the Great Consciousness-Self;
in these, there is no vibration, cognition, or the like, due to the absence of vital breath (prāṇa), the individual soul (jīva), and so forth.

Thus, since both the seer and the seen are of the nature of consciousness (*cid-rūpa*), the distinctions such as earth, wind, and water vanish from the world that is the object of perception; and since distinctions such as movement, intellect, and vital breath (*prāṇa*) vanish from the seer, it is established that the entire world is indeed one with Brahman. Thus he says: "By the Great Consciousness-Self" (*mahācidātmanā*). [This concludes] the section on the "stone-nature" (*aśmatā*).
In a collective dvandva compound, the neuter gender applies and the final vowel is shortened.

The vital breath, the intellect, and the other faculties attain their existence through the power of mental cultivation (bhāvanā). This mental cultivation is the wonder of consciousness itself, and it arises according to one's will.

He states that the distinctions such as the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) are also false because they are constructed through meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), beginning with the words "the vital breaths" (*prāṇa*). || 14 ||
The Self abides as the existence of Brahman through its state as the world and its state as peace; it has indeed attained the state of masculinity in both semen and the banyan seed. (15)

He states that the various distinctions of the world are false because they are merely the manifestation (*vivarta*) of the existence of Brahman—expressing this with the words "as the world" (*jagattayā*).

[The term] "in a state of peace" (*śāntatayā*) refers to the nature of deep sleep (*suṣupti*) and cosmic dissolution (*pralaya*). In the phrase "evātra," the division should be made as "ā iva. [The world] has arrived at, or is pervaded by, "masculinity" (*puṃstā*), which is the power of procreation; thus, "vaṭaka" means simply "the banyan tree" (*vaṭa*). || 15 ||

In the seed which consists of all the foremost atoms, that atom which is foremost among them becomes the respective foremost [seed]; and the seed remains established within itself. (Note: The reading "the seed remains established within itself" is found in the manuscript.)

In that regard, he demonstrates how the portion of Brahman—which is subtle, unmodified, and pervaded by masculinity—is present within the banyan seed and manifests as the unfolding of the banyan tree and so forth, with the words "sarvāgra" (the tip of all). The word "agra" refers to the essence (*sāra*).
Whatever is the most subtle atom (*aṇuka*) at the very tip, that is the Supreme Self; He alone [exists] in the sprout, the stalk, the branch, and so on.
The meaning is that, appearing before each successive subsequent effect, it becomes the foremost seed. || 16 ||
Brahman is the self of all atoms; because it is, in reality, subtler than the subtlest, whatever object exists becomes that very thing, yet as a reality, it remains Brahman alone. (17)

In this regard, with the intention that one should discern that whatever is well-known as subtle by way of being a cause belongs to the category of Brahman, and whatever is well-known as gross by way of being an effect belongs to the category of Māyā and is therefore false, he says: "Brahman.
The meaning is that when everything is thus characterized, only the reality of Brahman remains everywhere, and nothing else. || 17 ||
Just as a substance is indeed a substance— whether horizontal, upward, or downward—
so too is all this Brahman, in whatever manner and by whatever means it may be.

Just as each individual substance, such as a jar, from its base to its top is that very substance and not even an atom of something else exists therein, so too the entire universe, from its root to its summit, has been seen by this or that person through investigation to be Brahman alone in the form of pure existence (*sanmātra*), and not even an atom of anything else exists; such is the meaning. || 18 ||
Just as there is only the nature of gold and no otherness within a hundred forms of gold,
so too there is only the state of peace within the peaceful one, despite the multitude of created things.

He provides an illustration for its unchanging nature with the words "the state of being gold. "Emission" (sarga) refers to the state of the world; "I-ness" (ahantva) refers to the state of the individual soul (jīva), and [these occur] within its attributes. (19)
Just as no clouds in a dream appearing at one's side belong to you,
so too, for me, the tumultuous activities of creation and dissolution are nothing but the void-self.
He states that there is no comparison for its manifestations with the words "pārśvasthā" (situated at the side) [the reading is "alepa" (untainted)]. || 20 ||
Just as that army of sons and banners imagined upon the sky by one who is deluded is nothing but the state of peace— the sky itself— so too is this world.
Just as the imagined muddiness or impurity of the sky, and the army of banner-bearing sons of Gandharvas, are nothing other than the sky itself; so too [is this world]. // 21 //
The very delusion of mental construction, having flowered within, exists as the world—
like a tree at the end of an eon, whose seed was moistened by water and soil.

Having blossomed within the heart, it exists externally as the fruit of the world. Just as a seed of a banyan tree or the like, moistened and made wet by water upon the surface of the earth, develops and becomes capable of benefiting living beings through its provision of shade and so forth—becoming a great banyan tree or similar tree in this manner—it is called a "kalpa" (development). Thus it comes to pass. || 22 ||

For the wise one who is free from the sense of "I," who exists as the Self alone, and who remains in a state of oneness, even the powers such as atomization (aṇimā) are indeed like mere fragments of withered grass. (23)
Now, one might raise the objection: "If liberation is indeed abiding in that state of Brahman which is supremely subtle, then it would be equivalent to the supernatural powers such as *aṇimā*.
To ward off this doubt, he says: "from the perspective of the self that is free from egoism" (*anahaṃtātmanaḥ*). This means:
from the viewpoint of the knower in whom unsurpassed bliss has manifested through the removal of obstacles such as egoism. || 23 ||
In the three worlds, including the gods, asuras, and humans, I do not see anything that could cause even a single hair of that Great-Souled One to quiver with greed. (24)
Of such a great soul, for whom the entire universe is like a single hair on his body. || 24 ||
Whether remaining as one is or having gone anywhere at all,
for one who has realized the Self, the entire mass of dualistic conceptualizations does not exist.
For that Great Soul, the entire sky is indeed void;
how, for whom, and in what manner could there be any desire in him who is without a self? (26)
From that which is selfless (nirātman) and devoid of intrinsic nature (niḥsvarūpa), [arising] from causes such as enjoyment and so forth. || 26 ||
Who is capable of weighing existence and non-existence as equal for one in whom all distinctions have been stilled, by virtue of the distinction of being free from desire? (27)
Those who view existence and non-existence, as well as prosperity and poverty, as equal and alike—who is capable of fathoming their greatness? This is the implied meaning. || 27 ||
Nothing dies by means of the Maras, nor does anything live by means of living beings;
for this sky-like light consists solely of pure consciousness. (28)
With the intention that there is no possibility of joy or dejection for him even through the death or life of kinsmen, sons, and so forth, he says:
"By Māras..."—meaning by those who cause death, and by those who cause life. (28)
Birth and death appear falsely to the world through delusion,
even though they do not exist, just like the riverbank of a mirage which appears to one who is under an illusion.
Due to the delusion of the ignorant world, birth and death appear falsely within the self, which is itself subject to error and resembles the banks of a river of mirages. (29)
As long as it has not been correctly examined, there is neither delusion nor examiners;
indeed, there is neither birth nor death, but only the peaceful and immutable.
The meaning is that as long as we have investigated correctly, there is neither delusion, nor investigators, nor birth and death. || 30 ||
He who has attained detachment from the visible world and the like, who delights in the Self and has reached tranquility—
he, though real, appears as unreal, having completely crossed the ocean of worldly existence.
To the question, "Why is it said that they are not examiners?"—since there is no sublation for the examiner who knows reality—it is replied: "Because of the visible," etc.

The meaning is that although [the self] exists in the state of Brahman, it appears as non-existent through the nature of the examining self which is accompanied by the body, senses, and so forth. || 31 ||
They know that which is like the extinction of a lamp, in which the movement of the mind has set, which has attained peace within the self alone— that which is truly tranquil and stainless.
They know that very one who exists as the Brahman-self to be Nirvana, like the extinguishing of a lamp. || 32 ||
Those who are supreme call him liberated— he for whom the world of perception, beginning with the intellect, does not naturally appeal, just as it does not to the tranquil sky.
For this very reason, he says that saṃsāra does not taste sweet to him: "From the intellect onwards," etc. (verse 33).
"I" exists through non-investigation; through investigation, "I" does not exist.
Since the referent of "I" is absent, where is the world and where is transmigration? (34)
If one who knows reality is extinguished like a lamp, then how are you, Vasiṣṭha? To this he replies: "I... (verse 34).

The sky of consciousness perceives the world—consisting of forms, light, and mental objects—as existing in the very same manner as the cognition itself, through the act of conscious awareness alone, appearing with the forms of the intellect and so forth. (35)

To the question "How can there be non-existence there?", he says: "Consciousness" (saṃvit). It is the very reality of the sky of consciousness that, through the very perception of itself as otherwise, exists in the form of the intellect and so forth. || 35 ||
For you, whose mind is devoid of all objects and who are the Self of all, every single action is auspicious in every way, at all times, and in its entirety. (36)

He says—“sarvārtha” etc.—that when delusion is destroyed through the perception of reality as it truly is, even for you, whose mind is devoid of all objects, a state consisting of nirvāṇa alone will be established. || 36 ||
Whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer in sacrifice, whatever you give, whatever austerity you practice, and whatever you seek to destroy—all that is Śiva, the imperishable. (37)
He elaborates upon the entire practice with the words "That which... (verse 37).

That which I am, that which you are, hope, whatever [exists], as well as action, time, space, and so forth; that which the Lokaloka mountains are—that is the pervasive, auspicious expanse of consciousness.
With the intention that the mention of "conduct" (ācaraṇa) is an elliptical indication for the entire world, he says: "That which... Āśā means both desire and the directions. || 38 ||

Whatever consists of form, light, and thought; whatever is the world throughout the three periods of time; and whatever consists of the afflictions of old age, death, and so forth—that is the auspicious Great Space of Consciousness (Mahācinnabhas). 39.
Free from doubt, free from appearance, free from desire, and free from the mind—[the reading is "free from 'mine'"]—being a sage, selfless, and extinguished, remain as you truly abide. 40.

"Free from doubt" means either devoid of the search for means to pacify suffering, or being free from uncertainty. Alternatively, the reading "nirvikalpa" (free from conceptual construction) is clear.
Remain as you do when in the state of nirvāṇa. 40.
The state of being free from the thought of going and coming is peaceful, infinite, and beyond conceptualization;
whether there is worldly activity for you or not, it is like the wind through its movements and stillness.
Just as there is worldly discourse regarding the wind—belonging to the air—in terms of its movement and stillness, so too let it be for you. 41.
May there be for you that state of the Puruṣa which is free from latent impressions, devoid of parts, and tranquil—
like a wooden puppet moved by a mechanical device according to the instruction of a teacher.
Your manhood and manly conduct must be carried out and brought to completion by means of the engine-driven [chariot] characterized by the scriptures. || 42 ||
But the light of the elements is neither with affection nor without affection, being external;
let it be understood as the light that sustains the indefinable, like a multicolored lamp. (43)

O Rāma, may your outward gaze toward those who are your mother, father, kinsmen, and so forth, be neither full of affection nor devoid of affection; rather, may it be such that it bears no designation—that light whose manifestation cannot be designated by investigators as "existing" or "non-existing. And thus, by you—

Let it be like a painted lamp; let it remain so. For even that [lamp], because it is painted with oil despite being empty of oil in reality, provides illumination for living beings—beings who possess breath—and thus it is not devoid of light, nor is it lacking in luster, nor is it empty of that [light]. It is indeed illumination.
The meaning is that there is a similarity because light, like a painting, is not fit to be designated as either "existent" or "non-existent. || 43 ||

"Of one who is free from latent impressions (*nirvāsana*)" means: one who has become disenchanted with present enjoyments and is free from desire for those yet to come. "From the scripture" means from the true scripture (*sacchāstra*).

"Delight in reality" means repose in the bliss of the Self (*khasukha*), which is the cause [of liberation]. As long as the body is maintained, worldly activity (*vyavahāra*) is unavoidable due to its inevitable nature; therefore, by following the true scripture alone, one effects the removal of mental defects and the awakening of discernment (*viveka*) and so forth.

The meaning is that this is for the sake of establishing the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*). Therefore, even for that knower of reality who is free from intentional desire and is thus pure, his very nature—his unique defining characteristic—is simply his correct adherence (*samyaganuvartanam*) in his activities preceded by conscious awareness, in the meaning of the scriptures, in conduct appropriate to his own caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama*), and in tranquility, self-restraint, and so forth. This is his specific characteristic.

The meaning is that there is no acting according to one's own whims. Thus the elders have said: "If there were acting according to one's whims for one who has realized the reality of Brahman, then what difference would there be between dogs and those who perceive the truth, in the matter of eating impure things? (44)

Thus ends the thirty-eighth canto, titled "The Description of Nirvāṇa," in the latter half of the *Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa* within the *Mokṣopāya* section of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, according to the tradition of the Ṛṣis.
Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of Nirvāṇa," in the latter half of the *Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa* within the *Tātparyaprakāśa* commentary on the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa*.
The thirty-ninth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
A person in whom the conviction that worldly existence is inherently exhausted has arisen—
Being without conceptualization, it does not perceive conceptualization; therefore, it is indeed non-existent [in that regard]. || 1 ||
Whatever form remains when one has come to rest within the awakened Self—that is the true nature of the world; that is correctly described here.
Anticipating the objection that for a wise person there might still be an attachment to the volition that governs the observance of rules according to the scriptures,

he says: "saṃjāta..."— a person whose realization (pratyaya), which is direct intuition (sākṣātkāra), is of such a nature that it has arisen (saṃjāta) because its object is the reality as it truly is (yathābhūtārtha), and is thus unartificial (akṛtrima), and from which the cycle of transmigration (saṃsṛti) has been exhausted (kṣīṇa).
Even within the rules of scriptural convention, one remains in a state of non-conceptualization (*asaṃkalpa*).

For, seeing that the very self is the appearance of the conceptualization which is the cause for the appearance of those various conventional transactions, one does not perceive conceptualization. Since the existence of anything whatsoever is not established without such perception, the meaning is that this appearance of conceptualization is indeed unreal and false. || 1 ||
Like the fading of breath upon a mirror, that which stands as "I" from some unknown source is perceived by the Knower; yet, being seen without cause, it quickly perishes and is no longer found.

To explain the statement "he does not perceive volition," and with the intention that even due to the sublation of the superimposition of "I-ness" (ahaṃtādhyāsa)—which is the seed of all volitions—there is no possibility of volition for him, he says: "from breath" (śvāsāt).
Prior to awakening, the "I-ness" (ahaṃtā) arises as an exhalation from some indefinable cause, like a fading [reflection] in a mirror.
Established in the Knower of Reality, she perishes instantly without cause; though sought with effort, she is not found even when investigated.
He whose obscurations are exhausted, in whom all afflictions have been stilled and ceased,
and whose self is filled with the supreme nectar— he shines by his very being alone.
For attachment to volitional thought arises from desire, and that does not exist for one whose desires are fulfilled; with this intention, he says "of whom" (yasya).
[It is] by mere existence—that is, by the very existence of his nature as unsurpassed bliss. || 3 ||
By means of his brilliant intellect, which was like a wind for the mist of the dense darkness of all doubts, that region shone like the sky with a full moon.

With the intention that, just as there is no need for further effort regarding an object to be obtained once all gain has been attained through a single gain, so too there is no possibility of volitional construction (*saṃkalpa*) regarding an object to be known— due to the absence of delusion, doubt, and the like— once all is known through a single cognition, he says "all" (*sarva*). She is "luminous" (*bhāsvatī*), meaning she is the unobscured light of the Self.
By him who possesses such wisdom; for this very reason, he is like a wind to all the mists that cause the darkness of ignorance regarding the characteristics of the body.
The sense is that there is no possibility of his being affected by those [mists], as he is capable of dispelling the delusions and doubts of all people residing in that region. || 4 ||
Free from wandering, free from doubt, having attained light and being unobstructed,
the wise man is known as one who is pure as the autumnal sky and has realized that which is to be known.

The meaning is that since the wise who know reality consider the non-dual Śiva to be the fourth state, as stated in such scriptural passages as "He is the Self; He is to be known," it is understood that the Self alone is the object of knowledge. || 5 ||
Free from conceptual construction, without support, and tranquil, he bestows purity through his touch;
cool within, he is like the wind coming from the world of Brahmā.

Through contact—by means of prostration, service, and so forth—and through association with people, [he attained] purity, that is, freedom from sin, like the wind come from the world of Brahmā. || 6 ||
This nature of things belongs to those perceptions of non-existent forms,
such that the experience of heaven is like the perception of a dream or the son of a barren woman.

Having clarified that "he does not perceive volition," he now elaborates upon the nature of the perception of an unreal form in order to clarify the remainder of that statement—that "he is indeed unreal"—through four verses beginning with "asadrūpa. || 7 ||
This world that is experienced is indeed non-existent;
this very nature of things is the perception of what has no real form. (8)
Since these transmigrations are indeed unreal, how could there be any purpose [in them]?
The very words "creation" and "liberation" are like the son of a barren woman.
He demonstrates the similarity with the previously stated example—“like the perception of a barren woman’s son in a dream”—with the words “in the unreal” (*asatyeṣu*).

From what would it arise? From the real (*satya*) or from the unreal (*asatya*)? First, not from the real, because that is immutable (*kūṭastha*). Nor the second, because if the unreal were to arise from the unreal, it would follow that even the arising itself is unreal. Thus, let alone where [the effect] might abide...

The sense is that because the Real is unattached and non-dual, it is impossible for the unreal to serve as its substratum. Therefore, since even the words for "creation," "bondage," and "liberation from it" are like the son of a barren woman within these very unreal transmigrations, the establishment of their actual referents is far off—this is the meaning. || 9 ||
The world is real as Brahman—uncreated, unconditioned, and not established as anything else;
otherwise, it would neither exist for me nor be understood.
But even when the position is that the world is real, that [reality] must still be established through its non-difference from Brahman;

thus, the distinction between origination, persistence, and their determiners is entirely without foundation—this he states with the word "jagat" (the world). "Unmeditated" means not made an object of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*). And "not fixed in a particular substratum. Otherwise...
But if the state of being Brahman is not accepted, [then... || 10 ||
This nature of reality arises from resting in the intrinsic nature of the self;
it is the state of non-perception of "I-ness," creation, suffering, and so forth. (11)

Having described the nature of perceiving that which has the form of non-existence, he elaborates upon the nature of reality as resting in the essential character of perceiving that which has the form of existence, beginning with the words "Self" (*ātman*) and so forth.
"Non-perception" (*anupalambhatā*) means, in short, pure consciousness devoid of objects. || 11 ||
When the consciousness has reached another location, from a moment's time up to a distance of a hundred thousand yojanas,
that form of his which exists in the midst of the path is stainless.

Anticipating the objection that the absence of an object [for consciousness] is unestablished, he reminds [the opponent] of its establishment as shown in the verse beginning with "from one place to another" (*deśād deśāntaraprāptau*), by means of the words "in a moment" (*kṣaṇāt*). When the conscious principle—the consciousness delimited by the visual function—reaches, through the door of the eyes, a location such as the moon at a distance of hundreds of thousands of *yojanas* from its original location such as the branch of a tree; [therein lies the proof].

The connection with the distant [word] is as follows: they know that nature to be that which is established for all classes of living beings—the form consisting of consciousness (cinmaya) appearing as the void-receptacle (khakośābhāsa), which is unperceivable (acetya) by the moving (aya) consciousness (caitanya) that pervades [everything]. (12) It is like a windless breeze, consisting of consciousness appearing as the void-receptacle.
It is beyond conceptualization, peaceful, and exalted, like the blossoming of a creeper. || 13 ||
The wise know that to be the inherent nature of all classes of living beings;
for the discerning one who abides therein, the perception of creation dissolves. 14.
In deep sleep there is no cognition of dreams, and in a dream there is no cognition of deep sleep;
the delusions of creation and liberation are like those of deep sleep and dreaming.

Just as deep sleep (suṣupti) and dream (svapna) are mutually devoid of objects, one may consider that in the fourth state (turīya), consciousness (cit) is likewise objectless; thus he says: "In deep sleep... (verse 15).
This is the very nature of the object of delusion; it is neither dream nor deep sleep, neither creation nor nirvana—it is the truth, entirely peaceful. (16)

He states that even the distinction between dreaming, deep sleep, and so forth is merely an appearance within delusion and does not exist as an ultimate reality that constitutes the true nature of things—thus he says: "In delusion... (verse 16).
If delusion, which consists solely of the non-existent, is not found even when examined, how indeed can that which is unreal—like silver in a mother-of-pearl shell—be ever attained? (17)
To the question "Why is it not there?", he says: "Because it is an illusion" (verse 17).
That which is not apprehended does not exist; therefore, there is no possibility of delusion.
Apart from its own nature, there is nothing else to be apprehended for anyone at all. (18)
One might argue that even if the object of error is not apprehended by the error itself, it could still be apprehended by another perception; to this he replies:
"Because of its own nature" (*svabhāvāt*). Any other perception distinct from the error must be of the nature of valid cognition (*pramā*);
and there is no such thing as a witness-nature (*sākṣisvabhāva*) other than that of some object which is the domain of error. This is the meaning. || 18 ||
Indeed, the very nature [of reality] is always given as its own to everyone;
for it is non-dual yet appears as if dual—so let it be understood through these arguments. (19)

And thus, when correctly contemplated, the single witness-nature alone manifests within itself through the conceptualization of the threefold division (tripuṭī), and there is not even an atom's worth of anything other than this; so he says: "The nature" (svabhāva). It "tastes" (svadate), meaning it manifests as the object of supreme love. || 19 ||

"In the absence of intrinsic nature there is great suffering; in the presence of intrinsic nature there is only peace. Having reflected thus within with the intellect, let that which is desired be performed. (20)

He states that the conceptualization of something beyond its own nature is indeed the suffering of saṃsāra, while abiding in a state whose nature is non-conceptualized is indeed the bliss of liberation—expressed in the words "in what is not its own nature. Let it be prescribed; let it be adopted. || 20 ||
Just as a large tree exists within a subtle seed, so it is logically established that the world exists within Śiva; this is the supreme teaching: that the formless Śiva contains the formed universe.

If it is asked, "What is the means for grasping that [Self]?", the intention is that it is simply the vision of the universe superimposed upon it as being nothing but That (tanmātra). With this in mind, he demonstrates its non-separate existence from the time prior to its origination, beginning with the words "In the subtle" (sūkṣme). "Aga" means a tree. "Saṃkathā" refers to the discourse of the supreme ones—the knowers of reality—and of the Vedas.
The meaning is "a beautiful expression" (sadukti). || 21 ||
Form, light, mental attention, cognition, the sense of "I," and so forth are other [factors] that are essentially identical to its own nature, like fluidity is to water or space is to the sky. (22)

Thus, he states—beginning with "rūpa"—that even regarding the internal contemplation upon the inner self (*pratyagātman*), the non-separate existence [of its attributes] is established by the experience of all, because they are perceived as being of the very nature of that self. || 22 ||

Just as a corporeal being performs actions through its own constituent parts which resemble itself, so too the space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*), though non-acting, does so through the elements that have become one with it. 23.

Thus, he says "the embodied" (mūrta) to explain that the linguistic usage of the referent of the word *tat* (That), as well as the linguistic usage of the referent of the word *tvam* (Thou) at the beginning of creation, proceeds from the conscious Self (*cidātman*) through all objects which consist primarily of its parts, because they possess no existence apart from it— meaning, by means of those things that are similar to itself, consisting primarily of its own nature, and having no existence separate from it. || 23 ||
For those such as ourselves who have not attained liberation, there arises from the self the notion of "I" and so forth;
this sound, which is devoid of any objective referent, is produced in drums and other such instruments. (24)

He states that just as the transaction of objects, so too the transaction of employing words arises from the body, speech, and so forth—which do not possess independent existence—only when presided over by Consciousness; thus he says, "from that which resides in the Self. For those such as ourselves, who are non-transacting due to our insentience and are therefore incapable of activity by themselves, the sense of "I" and so forth arises in relation to the bodies of Vasiṣṭha, Rāma, and others.
It arises precisely from the conscious self (cidātman) residing within [the body] as its presiding principle.

The remainder of the sense is that just as various sounds corresponding to his intention arise from drums and other instruments when they are presided over by a man skilled in the rhythms, steps, and tempo of a dancer, so it is here. || 24 ||
That which appears does not exist upon examination; it is eternally non-existent.
The form of the world is formless by nature; Brahman abides within Brahman.

With the intention that, since all worldly transaction is sustained by non-difference from Consciousness (*cit*), there should be absolute non-difference alone—rather than accepting a difference consisting of the portion of insentience (*jaḍya*) established merely through a lack of inquiry according to the "half-old woman" (*ardhajaratī*) maxim—he says:

"That which... It appears at first glance; [it is negated] by "prekṣayā," meaning by the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) produced through inquiry. Therefore, it is of the nature of the portion of difference consisting of insentience.
The world, though appearing as form, is in essence formless and devoid of any intrinsic nature (niḥsvarūpa). Thus, Brahman remains established in Brahman, its own essential nature (svasvabhāva);
the meaning is that this very state is its abiding in its own true form (svarūpa). || 25 ||

For those for whom the world is a dream, they are mutually dream-people; indeed, they do not exist within themselves, nor do they exist in relation to one another, just like flowers in the sky as far as we are concerned. (26)
Now, one might object: "Let Brahman, which is non-transmigratory, indeed remain in its own nature; what benefit is there for transmigrating beings [in that]?

Anticipating this doubt, the author says "Of those who... with the intention that their concern for human goals (puruṣārtha) is as futile as a barren woman worrying about her son’s attainment of a kingdom. *Mithaḥ* means mutually.

Even from the perspective of deluded vision, whether in the waking state or within a dream, [these things] do not exist at all—like flowers in the sky—within ourselves, who are mutually and supremely one with Brahman; this is the meaning. The particle *hi* is used here in the sense of emphasis (*evārthe*). || 26 ||

In me, your Brahman is of a single form, peaceful like the expanse of space; and through worldly activities, which are non-different from it, you are likewise absorbed in me, as if by the vibrations of the wind.
He says, "In me," [meaning]: those [individuals] and their activities exist only within the insentient (jaḍa) portion of me, like a flower in the sky;
