however, in my sentient-consciousness (sac-cit) portion, they truly exist because of their identity with Brahman.

Those persons, along with their respective activities which are non-different from themselves—like the movement of the wind—truly exist in me, since both of these [the individual and its activity] are so.

The meaning is: that peaceful, existent Brahman, which is of the singular nature of the Self, exists within me as the essential nature of the inner self (pratyagātman). "But I am composed of existence (sanmaya) to them, like a dream to those who are dreaming;
whereas they are surely non-existent to me, like the dreams of one in deep sleep. || 28 ||

He states another distinction with the words "I, however" (*ahaṃ tu*). The sense is that from the perspective of one who is not awakened, the body of Vasiṣṭha is as real as the world itself. With the words "But they" (*te tu*), the sense is that from the perspective of one who is awakened, his body and so forth are sublated along with the world. || 28 ||
Whatever worldly transaction I have with them is Brahman established in Brahman;
let them see what they see, but for me, enough, quite enough of that!

The conventional activities such as favoring others and giving instruction—performed by me through those [beings] for whom the existence of truth is established by their own vision—are entirely useless for me.
The repetition "alam-alam" is used to indicate absolute pointlessness. (29)
I do not exist at all within myself; this pervasive reality of Brahman arises, as it were, for your sake—such indeed is this speech.

In my own self, in the state of being the body of Vasiṣṭha, I do not exist at all. This form of Vasiṣṭha and so forth arises, as it were, for your sake as the very reality of Brahman. This speech too, appearing in such a form for your sake, is merely a manifestation (*vivarta*) of the reality of Brahman;
however, from my perspective, its meaning is that it does not exist at all. || 30 ||

For one who knows that reality—the Self consisting of pure consciousness, which is both non-contradictory and yet transcends contradiction—neither the desire for worldly enjoyment nor the desire for liberation flashes within the heart. (31)

For such a knower of reality, even that which is contradictory—such as suffering and the like—is not contradictory, because he perceives all things as having the nature of a single flavor, namely bliss (ānanda). || 31 ||

Since this sequence of bondage and liberation for human beings depends solely upon one’s own nature, what a mockery it is—alas!—that through delusion one should experience the confusion of a sea even over a mere puddle. 32.

This torment of saṃsāra and this torment of practicing the sequence of means for liberation are well known to arise from delusion—that is, from the failure to recognize the Self as non-dual and unsurpassed bliss. || 32 ||
In liberation, which consists of the pacification of non-existence and is established as intrinsic nature, neither wealth, nor friends, nor ritual actions are of any help. (33)
In that which consists of the cessation of suffering, which is itself non-existent and of the nature of absence. || 33 ||
Just as a drop of oil, once cast upon water, spreads rapidly over the entire surface,
so too does consciousness, when fixed upon the conceptualization of an object, quickly become the world.
Just as a drop of oil fallen upon water becomes a circle of various colors, so it is. || 34 ||
Just as the persistence of dream-events possesses a certain flavor when one is awake,
so too does the existence of the ego and the web of the world possess that same flavor for the man of discernment.
But he says that the world, sublated by knowledge, attains a state of mere memory, like a dream—expressing this with the words "In the waking state" (*jāgrati*).
Whatever flavor and whatever kind [of experience] appears in memory... (35)
By that very yoga of practice, it likewise attains such thinness that neither "I" nor "saṃsāra" remains, and only peace is left behind. (36)
By that very practice of the stages previously described, let that web of the world reach attenuation, that is, its destruction. 36.
Whenever the sun of intrinsic nature (svabhāva) attains its station, at that very moment the darkness of worldly enjoyments (bhoga) dissolves; though it still exists, it is no longer perceived. (37)

With the intention that, through investigation with a vision inclined toward direct perception (*pratyak*), even now its diminution and sublation can be experienced, he says: "Whenever...". It "melts away" (*galati*), meaning it diminishes through absolute sublation; it is also experienced as being "not existent," meaning it does not exist even in the three periods of time. || 37 ||

Free from the great power of delusion, it vibrates at the time of death, becomes manifest, and likewise shines forth; for from it the collection of instruments such as the intellect arises, like light from a lamp. || 38 ||

Thus, when the darkness of enjoyments has ceased through death and destruction, the collection of instruments such as the intellect becomes free from delusion—that is, the obscuration of the self consisting of ignorance—and from the "greatness" of the superimposition upon the gross body and so forth. Consequently, it shines forth by means of the awakening kindled by the mental modification (vṛtti) in the form of Brahman; for from that shining, like light emanating from a lamp, [it manifests].
The meaning is that, having pervaded everything and become one with Brahman, he shines forth. || 38 ||

Thus ends the thirty-ninth canto, titled "The Instruction on the Yoga of Resting in One's Own Nature," within the *Vasiṣṭha-gītā* of the *Śrī-Vālmīki-Ārṣa-Rāmāyaṇa*, in the second half of the Uttara-kāṇḍa. || 39 ||
Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "Instruction on the Yoga of Resting in One's Own Nature," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
Chapter Forty.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
The perception of form, sight, mental activity, intellect, and so forth, as well as the experience of the senses—
They know the true nature of a thing that lacks inherent existence to be unfading.
In the state of transmigratory existence, Brahman does not shine, nor does transmigratory existence shine within Brahman;
it is described that for one liberated while living, both shine forth in alternation.

In this regard, first he states—beginning with the word "rūpa"—that the realized experience of the wise is that for external and internal objects which are devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), their only real essence is the witnessing consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*): "rūpa... [and so on]. "Unfading" (*amlānam*) means free from modification and blemish. || 1 ||
When the persistence of intrinsic nature expands through the attenuation of that very lack of intrinsic nature, then creation arises and appears like an illusion. (2)
Regarding this, he states the reasoning characterized by the positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) with that awakening in two verses beginning with "asvabhāva":

"When the pervasive, undivided, and real state of intrinsic nature (svabhāva-sthiti), which is without intrinsic nature [in its limited form], arises through the thinning of ignorance—which conceals it—by means of the limitation caused by that [ignorance] and by becoming its body; at that time... This is the statement of positive concomitance (anvaya). || 2 ||
When rest in one's own nature reaches a state of peace, then the world-appearance subsides like a dream in deep sleep. (3)
He states the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) with the words "when" (*yadā*). The phrase "by one's own awakening" (*svabodhena*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
Although there is a difference in that a residue of seeds remains, the illustration of deep sleep (*suṣupta*) applies to the aspect of abiding solely in the non-dual Self (*advaitātman*). || 3 ||
Sensual enjoyments are the great diseases of existence; kinsmen are a firm bondage; the attainment of wealth leads to misfortune. Therefore, let the self be stilled within itself.
For this very reason, he states that enjoyments and the like—which oppose repose in one's own true nature—are indeed misfortunes: "Enjoyments," etc. (Verse 4).
Creation is the state of being without intrinsic nature; Śiva is the singular essence of intrinsic nature.
Let there be the supreme ether; let there be peace; do not weary yourself here.

And thus, since those things dependent on oneself remain in their own nature, it is not logical for one to fall into misfortune; so he says: "May you endure. Here, in this saṃsāra, do not be distressed or weary. || 5 ||
I do not perceive a self, nor the visible world of delusion;
I have entered the peaceful Brahman—I am indeed Brahman, free from all affliction.

He demonstrates his own self-reliance through a dramatic representation of his own experience, saying "no"— meaning that he does not [perceive] himself as the primary observer within the triad of seer, seeing, and seen, which constitutes the life-force of Vasiṣṭha.
You alone perceive you, you alone perceive that being expanded by the meaning of words;
I, however, see only the peaceful, absolute, supreme ether.
"O Rāma, you are Vasiṣṭha"—thus, augmented by the meaning of the word "you," you see yourself as such; yet I see only the Peaceful. || 7 ||
Within the supreme ether that is Brahman itself, these delusions of yours— consisting of form, light, and mind— have arisen like the vibrations in the wind, appearing as if they were real.

For you as well, these delusions consisting of sound, meaning, and so forth, which are composed of light and mind, have not arisen in the ultimate sense; rather, they are merely produced by conceptual construction.
The Self as Brahman does not know the creation, nor does the Self as the creation know Brahman;
one in deep sleep does not know the dream state, nor does one in the dream state know deep sleep.

"My non-perception of duality is not due to an aversion toward duality, but rather because it is impossible to perceive both duality and non-duality simultaneously," he says: "Brahman is the Self. (9)
Awakened to the nature of Brahman and the world as being like the waking and dreaming states, the one liberated while living, with a tranquil intellect, perceives their form as pure light.

To the question of how instruction regarding that [reality] can be established when it is not perceived at all, he says: "the awakened one" (*prabuddha*). The intention is that the one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*) perceives both [aspects] alternately, and thus becomes an instructor. || 10 ||
The awakened one thoroughly understands all this as it truly is;
and with his self purified, he becomes tranquil like a cloud in autumn.
He says "as it truly is" (yathābhūtam) to show that this [ignorance] also subsides through the gradual non-perception of duality in the progressively higher stages. || 11 ||
Whether abiding in memory or abiding in conceptualization, the promise (saṃgara) is as it is described;
likewise, the delusion of "I" and the world consists merely in the error of existence and non-existence.
Having observed through that vision the increasingly fragile nature of duality, he expresses it by means of two examples, beginning with "smṛtistha" (situated in memory).
*Saṃgara* means battle. || 12 ||
For even in the self there is no seer of which nothing exists;
it is neither empty nor non-empty—this appearance is a delusion. (13)

This world-illusion (*jaganmāyā*), which is being perceived, does not exist even in the Self—which is the ultimate reality—nor, by the force of the word "even," in that which is absolutely non-existent, namely the void (*śūnya*). Furthermore, no perceiver of it exists, not even the individual soul (*jīva*). Thus, the meaning is that this delusion, distinct from both the void and the non-void, appears as something truly indefinable (*anirvacanīya*). || 13 ||

Thus ends the fortieth canto, titled "The Description of Resting in the Self," within the *Vasiṣṭha-gītās* of the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa* in the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*, composed by the Sage Vasiṣṭha. 40.
Thus ends the fortieth sarga, titled "The Description of Resting in the Self," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The forty-first canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
This entire perception of "I-ness" and so forth is by nature devoid of any inherent self-nature.
Let [the world] itself be brought to nirvāṇa by means of its own single intrinsic nature.
The dance of the daughters of the three worlds, by virtue of the nature of being without inherent nature,
and nirvāṇa itself are described here as having the single nature of inherent nature.

Ignorance (*avidyā*) is without intrinsic nature (*asvabhāva*), yet this Self (*ātman*), whose nature is that very ignorance, exists as the form of the entire world; being so, it does not perceive the dancing of the three worlds—consisting of the "I-ness" (*ahantā*) and other factors to be described—as dolls, and thus becomes possessed of the perception of egoism (*ahaṃkāra*) and the like.
In this way, this Self remains unliberated by itself.

When the non-dual, self-luminous, and perfect bliss—characterized by the manifestation of knowledge arising from scriptural means—is revealed, wherever that [realization] exists, there let there be light as it were;
and wherever the intellect is awakened, there let there be supreme distaste for sense objects. (2)

And with the intention that this knowledge is accomplished only through detachment born from discrimination in the company of the wise, he says: "Wherein..."—wherein there is no agent, object, or instrument, and where the seeing of the invisible seer arises as a painting on a wall-less surface, a mass of the world that cannot be grasped. (3)

In that regard, for the sake of dispassion, he describes the superimposition of the world-picture upon the pure [Self], which is by nature free from ignorance, in the verse beginning with "akartri" (the non-agent).
It is neither arisen nor anything whatsoever; it is not tranquil, yet it remains as tranquility itself.
It is the supreme Brahman, free from affliction, truth, and indeed immutable.
Having set that aside by means of the intrinsic nature of knowledge (*vidyā*), he demonstrates the true nature of *nirvāṇa* with the words: "And not... (4).
Who is able to count the painted figurines of the world in the sky, which are colored upon the stage of imagination and consist of nothing but the wonder of consciousness? (5)

Therein, he describes the first [aspect], whose nature is the absence of intrinsic nature (*asvabhāva-svabhāva*), as the infinite female figurines dancing within the three worlds, beginning with the words "the wonder of consciousness" (*ciccamatkāra*).

Those living beings whose essence consists solely of the wonder of consciousness—within the stage and theater of the dance, which is composed of mere mental construction—they are those who are colored by the various aesthetic sentiments (*rasa*) such as the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) and so forth; they are the painted figurines of the world in the void.
The connection with the subsequent word is "they dance. || 5 ||
Rich in aesthetic flavors (rasa), emotions (bhāva), and transformations (vikāra), they dance with ever-new gestures;
for the most part, being of the nature of space, they flash within the sky even in every single atom.

In such a way that it is enriched with the *rasas* such as the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*), with the *bhāvas*—both the stable (*sthāyin*) and the transitory (*vyabhicārin*) such as trembling, perspiration, and so forth—and with the *abhinayas*, which are gestures that manifest the forms of various objects; [this occurs] "atom by atom" (*paramāṇu-prati-paramāṇu*) even within the space existing in the subtlest particles, namely the sky of consciousness (*cidākāśa*). The word "mostly" (*prāyaḥ*) is used for the purpose of indicating probability. || 6 ||
Wearing all the seasons as their crowns, with the quarters of the sky as their many vine-like arms, with the netherworld as their vine-like feet, and the realm of Brahmā as their necks; (7)

Or, they are the "supporters" (dharā) of those "heads" (śirasaḥ) which are the Brahma-worlds; that is, they are the sustainers of the heads whose form is the Brahma-world. Or, "brahmaloka" refers to the neck (śirodharā), meaning they are the sustainers of those necks which have the Brahma-world as their form. || 7 ||
With the moon and sun as their rolling eyes, the stars as the hair upon their bodies,
the seven worlds as the creepers of their limbs, they have the vast sky as their garment on all sides.
Those whose body hairs were clusters of stars; those whose garment was the very sky—clear and transparent—pervading all directions.
The worlds, encircled by the oceans and the continents, with the Lokāloka mountain as their girdle,
possess life-breaths flowing through living beings that move under the weight of all creatures.
Those [rivers] whose flowing vital breaths (prāṇamāruta) move by reason of the burden—namely, the maintenance and nourishment—of the elements and their derivative bodies and so forth. || 9 ||
Adorned with the arrangement of forests and groves as their necklaces and armlets,
they have the words of the ancient Vedas for their speech and find delight in the fruits of ritual action.
The Purāṇas and the Vedas are their words; the various fruits of actions, pleasures, pains, diversions, and amorous sports are theirs.
Such are these daughters of the world who dance—this is the connection with what precedes. (10)
This dance of the daughters of the three worlds which is seen before us is the liquefaction of the waters of Brahman and the trembling caused by the wind of Brahman.
Abiding in the absence of intrinsic nature, it is the cause that constitutes the essence of the cause;
like a dream, it remains present even during deep sleep, as if it were real.

And for this dance, consciousness (cit) abiding in its own non-substantiality (asvabhāva) alone is the cause; for such a thing, being of the nature of a cause, is well-known in the scriptures. The meaning is that it is just like how, during sleep—that is, in the state of deep sleep (asuṣupta)—consciousness remains and is the cause of the dream, so it is here. || 12 ||
Abiding in a state of deep sleep even while not asleep, contemplate your true nature;
even while awake, remain free from agitation—do not take refuge in this dream.

Having thus described the nature of that which is devoid of intrinsic nature (*asvabhāva-svabhāva*), he now states the means for attaining *nirvāṇa* through the nature of the oneness of intrinsic nature: "asuṣupta" and so forth. O Rāma, by contemplating the ultimate intrinsic nature, even while awake, you shall reach the fourth state (*turya-pada*)—which is "not deep sleep" (*asuṣupta*) due to the destruction of ignorance, yet "deep sleep" (*suṣupta*) due to the withdrawal of all duality.
Be established in that. || 13 ||

Those who know reality understand that state which is deep sleep even while awake, devoid of desire and latent impressions due to awakening—that is one's true nature; liberation is the transformation into that state.
Taste, passion, and latent impression—this is what is empty of that. Its transformation is its final establishment in its own essential nature. 14.
Without agent, object, or instrument, without the seen, the seer, or the act of seeing,
and without form, light, or mental activity, Brahman exists as the world.

He states with the words beginning "without an agent" that even at the time of worldly transaction, upon reaching that final consummation, the world appears as having consciousness as its sole essence. || 15 ||
In the beloved, the beloved shines; in the full, the full is established.
Devoid of duality and unity, it appears as that which is free from both duality and unity.
When the inner self (pratīc) has been purified, being devoid of duality and unity, then Brahman—purified and free from both duality and unity—shines forth as an undivided, single essence. || 16 ||
It is truth, established in truth, peaceful, and itself the very self within the nature of creation;
it is like the hollow of space and resembles the interior of a stone.
Truth resides within the nature of creation; peace resides within the true Self, abiding by itself. || 17 ||
Having the form of a belly filled with excellent jewels, it is dense yet like the sky;
like a reflection, it is unagitated even when agitated, and is both non-existent and existent.
He dispels the delusion that its nature is like that of a stone's interior—lacking luminosity—by the words "O excellent jewel.
Therefore, although it remains as if agitated upon receiving the reflection of the world, it is in fact unagitated. || 18 ||
The city that was to be newly created existed as if within his mind;
it was Brahman, whose form was expanded light, with a mind rendered undifferentiated.
In which the mind has been rendered non-dual and made of a single flavor. || 19 ||
Just as a city of the imagination does not differ at all from the imagination itself, so too this appearance of the world does not differ from ultimate reality. 20.
Like a golden pedestal containing the arrangement of many future worlds, it was vast,
though perceived as tranquil and established in the imperishable.
The golden pedestal is square like a seat; it is a mass of gold, vast and of various dimensions, even as it is being perceived.
Rich with constant destruction and arising, yet uniform and free from affliction;
without destruction or arising, undecaying, and appearing as if manifold despite its splendor. (22)
Radiant and luminous. || 22 ||
Brahman alone shines forth, having entered into a state of dense tranquility, appearing through the emergence of creation that is devoid of rising or setting;
like the sky through its power of emptiness, it is indeed manifest by force to the awakened one, who has shed the perception of inherent existence. 23.
Indeed, O Rāma, when awakening has occurred, Brahman alone— having attained a state of intense tranquility—

shines forth by the very power of its non-dual nature, through the manifestation of creation characterized by the absence of rising and setting, and by the glory of its own sovereignty; just as the sky attains its true nature once it has shed all adventitious qualities and its obstructed form has been sublated.

The meaning is that, just as in the case of a tuft of hair, a city of the Gandharvas, a mirage, or impurity, there is a forceful and violent suppression of manifestation by means of one's own terrifying power of emptiness (śūnyatā), which shines forth. || 23 ||

Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "The Instruction for the Purpose of Dissolving the Delusion Regarding One’s Own Nature," in the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the glorious Vāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa of Valmīki, composed by the Sage. 41.

Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "The Instruction for the Purpose of Resting in One's Own Nature," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The forty-second canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: That which is the manifestation of the mind within the tranquil state is not distinct from that [tranquility].
Since it is indeterminate and stainless, how could there be the occurrence of creation and so forth from it? || 1 ||
Furthermore, the oneness of the universe with the Lord of the Universe is elaborated here;
and through discernment, one's own self alone is to be worshipped as the Supreme Lord.

In order to bring about the realization that the world is nothing but Brahman, as previously stated, he refutes the duality of consciousness (citi) which is the cause for the appearance of the diversity of the world, stating: "like the mind" (cittavat). That initial manifestation resembling the mind within the peaceful, immutable Self does not differ from that conscious Self whose nature is manifestation. Why? Because it is unmanifested (avyākṛta) and because it is stainless (amala). For instance:

For in the world, differentiation is well known to arise from the differentiation of name and form (*nāmarūpa*). And that [differentiation] is not possible in the mind (*citta*), which serves as the limiting adjunct for the entry [of the Self] prior to the evolution of name and form, because at that stage it remains undifferentiated (*avyākṛta*). Indeed, it was only after the creation of the subtle causal body (*liṅga*) consisting of fire, water, and earth that this Deity reflected: [“Let me enter these three deities with this living self...”]

"Alas! Entering these three deities by means of this living self (jīva-ātman), let me manifest names and forms"—thus is that manifestation heard [in scripture]. Furthermore, because it is stainless, consciousness (cit) is not distinct from it; for consciousness is stainless, and the mind (citta) is also stainless.
Nor can a distinction between two such things as these be perceived by anyone, just as in the case of light and space. [This applies] to the mind.
He states—“Where is this? (verse 1)—that by the very rejection of any differentiation within consciousness, the differentiation of the world dependent upon it is all the more rejected.

When the lamp of the mind has gone, the perceptions of form, light, and mental attention—like waves upon the water—go forth; yet they appear as if deluded while remaining in the sky [of consciousness]. (2)

This very point is clearly stated in the verse beginning with *cittadīpe*: "When the sun, which is the lamp that illuminates the mind, has set, the waves of water consisting of form, light, mental activity, and consciousness—which appear like the delusions of a mirage or a cloud—depart and vanish from the sky, that is, the immutable space of the inner self (*pratyagātman*). (2)
Just as the movement of the wind is independent of any instrument,
and just as the radiance of light is its own diffusion, so too is this world [manifested] within the Supreme.
He establishes through examples that the world is indeed Consciousness (cit) itself, because existence does not depend on any cause other than Consciousness—beginning with the verse "nirasta...
and so forth. That by which the dependence on instruments has been dispelled; "bhāsaḥ" refers to the spreading or expansion of light. || 3 ||
Just as liquidity exists in nectar, emptiness in the sky,
and vibration in the wind, so too does this something consisting of the Self exist within the Supreme.
In the nectar-like water; "consisting of the Self" means a transformation of the Self; "something indescribable. || 4 ||
In the great consciousness, within the great space, this world which shines forth is nothing but that very consciousness manifesting, like the purity [of reflection] in a gem. (5)

With the intention that, just as the manifestation of the mind and so forth occurs within the inward-facing [Self] during its two states, the manifestation of space and the rest within Brahman— though dependent on Māyā— is likewise non-different from It, he establishes this through those very same examples, beginning with "mahācitī" (verse 5).
Just as liquidity exists in water, as emptiness in the sky,
and as vibration in the wind, so does the universe exist within the Great Consciousness.
Just as the wind perceives its own vibration, so does consciousness perceive the world;
herein, not even the slightest possibility exists for distinctions such as duality or unity.

With the intention that even in its manifestation, consciousness is non-different from itself because it is independent of anything other than consciousness, he says: "He knows" (vetti). [This refers to] duality, unity, and the various distinctions among those objects of enumeration. || 7 ||
Through lack of discernment and discernment, the world appears radiant and fragile;
yet upon awakening, it is always of the nature of reality—non-radiant and indestructible.
Through lack of discrimination it appears radiant; through discrimination it is seen as fragile. But upon the realization of the ultimate truth, because it is nothing but Brahman, both are empty.
Apart from pure cognition alone—which is devoid of beginning, middle, and end—nothing else exists here; this is the certain conclusion regarding that whose nature is the Great Pure Consciousness.
He states what has been determined by awakening: "Cognition," etc. (verse 9).
To some it is auspicious and peaceful; to some, the eternal Brahman;
to some, mere emptiness; and to some, mere cognition. (10)

In that very context, he says "That" (tad) to show how various conceptual distinctions—both accurate and inaccurate—have arisen among disputants who investigate, whether they follow the Vedas or do not follow the Vedas. || 10 ||
Then, that consciousness whose nature is infinite, while contemplating as it were the state of being an object of thought,
undergoes, while remaining established in itself, the condition of being an object of knowledge as if it were ignorance.
In that very context, he states that there is a superimposition (adhyāsa) of the forms of the visible world, such as beginningless ignorance (avidyā), etc., by saying "that" (tad). || 11 ||

There is no existence without consciousness, nor is there consciousness without that [existence]; just as there is no wind without movement, so too is there no cause for movement without wind. || 12 ||

In this regard, because of the very power of consciousness, there is no existence of the object of knowledge apart from its manifestation as consciousness; and without that existence, the consciousness of that [object] does not belong to consciousness itself. The meaning is: just as there is no cause for wind without the sky—which is of the nature of emptiness and immutable—and just as there is no cause for vibrations without wind, so it is here. || 12 ||
Likewise, the great shadows of consciousness always possess existence or non-existence during the functions of the awareness of creation, because they do not depend on any other cause.

The meaning is that, since the appearances of creation possess their existence dependent upon the eternally existent Brahman, they have an eternal existence insofar as they depend on their substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*), yet they are eternally non-existent in terms of their own nature; thus, the scripture employs two designations—"Being alone, my dear, this was in the beginning" and "There is no diversity here"—because no other cause is required. The compound *asamarthasamāsa* (an irregular compound) is a Vedic usage. || 13 ||
If such were the meaning here, it would exist by virtue of duality, unity, and existence;
but who could conceive of duality or unity in the great void? (14)

The existence of the duality of the insentient and the unity that is its cause would be self-existent (svataḥ-sattā), for it is by virtue of that [existence] that the perception of creation occurs here;

such would have been the established meaning. But in the immutable, non-dual ether of consciousness (cid-ambara), who could conceive of duality or unity, or establish them through existence and manifestation? The meaning is that among insentient things, there is no such [agent]. || 14 ||

The state of being the infinite, singular, supreme expanse of space, encompassing the entire universe in every direction, is like the duality of wind and its movement; it exists only as a verbal designation and is not real.

And thus, just as the duality of space is unestablished and the distinction between motion and the wind is unestablished, it follows that the duality of the universe and its Lord is likewise unestablished; this is what he expresses with the verse beginning "viṣvak" (verse 15).
The duality of the Lord of the Universe and the universe itself is likewise of the nature of non-existence;
for that which is pure Great Consciousness alone cannot possibly possess duality.
This world-appearance is that very [Reality] itself; it is neither the universe nor the state of being the universe.
Just as gold possesses reality at some time through its possession of spatial and temporal attributes, [so too does this appear]. (17)

Alternatively, having raised the objection that even this unreal universe might possess reality by virtue of its pervasion over a greater extent of space and time relative to its own lesser space, time, and effects— viewing it through the perspective of Brahman—
he refutes this with the verse beginning "deśakāla... (verse 17).
Furthermore, since there is no possibility of duality or identity between the bracelet—which is distinct—and the universe as a whole, how can there be a relationship of cause and effect here? (18)
If the distinction between cause and effect were established, it would be so; however, that very [distinction] is not established. Thus he says: "By duality and unity... (18).
If it should be argued that this is merely a mental construction and not another real entity—just as emptiness is in the sky or fluidity is in water—[then we reply: 19.
If it is argued that a conceptual distinction between cause and effect is accepted, we say no; for truth cannot be established by means of such a conceptual [distinction]. Thus he says:
"syāccet" (if it were so). || 19 ||
The world’s primordial state is indeed non-different from the mere line in the sky;
whatever is the form of Brahman, that is the form of the world—so where is there duality or unity here? (20)

He says "in the sky" (khe) [in verse 20] to show that even though there is absolute non-difference, the conceptualization of difference is observed as a mere verbal construction (khalekha), and therefore the world might likewise be so.
Whatever is the nature of space, such indeed is the nature of the entire void, within that single, pervasive, pure, and all-encompassing essence of consciousness alone. (21)

The meaning is that the world has the same nature as Brahman—just as the space denoted by the term "line" (lekhā) is imagined to be distinct from the sky (kha), though it is not; such is the form of the world in relation to Brahman. This being the case, he says "in the single Self," and so forth, to show that even in Brahman, the status of being the cause of the world has vanished. || 21 ||
When [the self] remains like the stoneness in an army of stone statues, how and where could the diversity of cause and effect possibly exist? (22)
How could there be a state of non-voidness in the void, given that a second entity is impossible?
The creation shines as the very self of consciousness, consisting of light, within the Great Consciousness.
Like a daughter carved from stone, she is composed of that and has that as her essence due to being absorbed in it;
O virtuous one, when one understands the universe to be thus situated exactly as it is, it dissolves away. (24)
Having realized the true nature of reality exactly as it exists. || 24 ||
Only the appearance of worldly existence remains, resembling the silence of a wooden statue,
just as one with closed eyes experiences the mental delusion of perceiving forms.

Wooden silence (*kāṣṭhamauna*) is the state of being devoid of all external and mental activity; by such a state, the radiating Brahman remains after having cast off the phenomenal world (*saṃsāra*). He says that the entire delusion of the world, which is produced solely by the vibration of the mind characterized by conceptualization (*bhāvanā*), is shaken off merely by abandoning conceptualization and abiding in a state of non-vibration.
By the words "just as" and so forth. || 25 ||
Just as one who is awake in a dream perceives what is non-existent as if it were existent due to the power of mental conception,
so too for one with eyes open, there is a mental delusion regarding the perception of forms.
Even while awake and standing in the waking state, one is as if non-existent due to the mental conception of existence;
having brought about the cessation of such conception, one remains as one truly is, becoming firm like a stone.
Let the internal nature, which has become free from agitation, remain in equanimity through the offering of discernment and by honoring whatever objects are encountered as they arise. (28)
Resting upon an internal nature that has not become like stone—due to its being of the singular essence of consciousness (*cidekarasa*) and thus distinct from stone—one should remain.

He states that the practice of the means such as discernment (*viveka*) and dispassion (*vairāgya*), which are conducive to such a state, is the supreme worship of the Self, who is the Supreme Lord: "From discernment... (*āviveka*). That which is on all sides, from every direction...
Discrimination [is performed] by means of an offering characterized by that [discrimination]. || 28 ||
One’s own nature, the Supreme Lord, should be worshipped for the sake of awakening with the intellect;
one's own self, when worshipped through discernment, immediately bestows vast boons. (29)
He is called "Sphāravaraprada" because he bestows a vast boon characterized by unsurpassed bliss. || 29 ||
In this context, the worship of Rudra, Upendra, and others is regarded as a mere fragment of withered straw;
it is only the worship consisting of the flowers of inquiry, tranquility, and the company of the virtuous that is truly honored by a multitude of blossoms.
O virtuous one, one's own self is indeed the Supreme Lord, whose fruit is immediate liberation;
when worshipped solely through the mere perception of truth, he bestows the unsurpassed goal.
Where the Self and the Lord reside, what deluded person would seek refuge in another?
For one whose soul is honored by the company of the virtuous, tranquility, contentment, and discernment, [there is no need for another]. (32)
The sense is that [the opponent might argue for] a Lord who is distinct from the self and stands apart as an external entity;
for the Śruti states: "Now, he who worships another deity, thinking 'He is one and I am another,' does not know; he is like a beast to the gods.
One might object: "But surely the external Lord, being pleased by worship, will protect him from weapons, snakes, poison, fire, and so forth."

He will protect [the self] from all harmful things on every side; what then will the immutable self do? To this he says: "By association with the virtuous," etc. [Verse 32]: [This refers to] one by whom the self has been honored on all sides.
Weapons, snakes, poison, and fire become like *śirīṣa* flowers;
even acts such as worshiping the gods, performing austerities, visiting sacred fords, and giving gifts, though performed excessively, [become as harmless]. (33)
Furthermore, since faults are inevitable in the worship of deities and similar acts performed by the undiscriminating,
and since fruitlessness and even harm are certain to result from them, if even in those cases purity of place, time, materials, recipient, and agent—
as well as discernment, faith, devotion, tranquility, self-control, and so forth— are necessary, then how much more so in the vision of the Self, which is free from affliction and yields great fruit?
To the question, "Why then are these not employed [in this way]? he replies with the verse beginning "devārcana" (verse 33).
These [actions] turn to ashes due to their lack of purpose for those great-souled ones who lack discernment;
yet, even these very same actions are made fruitful through discernment.
Due to a lack of discrimination regarding place, time, recipient, and so forth; [this applies] to those who are not great-souled, the evil-minded. || 34 ||
Why then is discernment itself not clearly cultivated within, so that through the knowledge of things as they truly are, there may be the supreme cessation of latent impressions? (35)
He states what that discrimination is which is said to be the goal to be accomplished: "As-it-is," etc. (Verse 35).
The effort known by the word "discrimination" arises from the clarity of the self;
in that same measure, discrimination should be made to increase within by means of the nectar of tranquility. (36)

Regarding the word "effort" (yatna): the sense is that it thus comprises all the means [of yoga], such as detachment (vairāgya) and so forth. "From the serenity of the self" (ātmaprasādataḥ) means from the serenity of the mind achieved through sacrifices, gifts, and other practices performed without desire (niṣkāma). || 36 ||
Furthermore, to the extent that it undergoes drying up through no longer being deluded, by disregarding the existence of the body and through the vision of things as they truly are. (37)
By delusions, that is, by errors regarding sense objects. || 37 ||
One should conquer shame, fear, dejection, envy, pleasure, and pain with equanimity.
Since the world, the body, and so forth do not exist at all in the beginning, how could they exist today? (38)

He shows the method of reflection for disregarding the existence of the body with the words "jagadādi" (the world and so forth). At the beginning, the world—which is the primary cause of the body—and by the word "and so forth," its own cause as well, do not exist at all. That which does not exist in the beginning, how could it exist today?
This is according to the principle: "The coming into being of that which is non-existent is not possible. (38)
Even if this effect belongs to the cause, it is nevertheless nothing but Brahman;
it is merely a pure appearance, for objects such as jars do not exist apart from consciousness.
[Objection: "In the beginning, my dear, this was indeed Being alone" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1); thus, let the effect be Being itself in the form of Brahman at the outset.
To this, he says: "If it were an effect... Even so, it is nothing but Brahman alone and does not differ from it;
for if there were a difference from Being, it would result in its being non-existent. Since an effect that is non-dual does not obstruct the non-duality of the cause, [it remains identical].

He says that the appearance of difference is merely conceptual construction (vikalpamātra), stating: "It is only an appearance. The word "separate from cognition" (jñapteḥ pṛthak) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. || 39 ||
Intuition is indeed of the nature of knowledge; the entire world is nothing but cognition.
Even cognition, which is the glory of the reality of the Self, subsides when it is fully understood.

The meaning is that even the appearance of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) consists essentially of the knowledge of the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*); therefore, that alone is the entire universe. Furthermore, this cognition characterized as the reflection of consciousness subsides—like the beauty of a face seen in a mirror—for one who has not known the reality of the Self, once it is perceived merely as the innermost Self (*pratyagātman*) through the removal of the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) that cause differentiation. || 40 ||
But in the absence of the knowable, that which is inexpressible remains—the eternal, auspicious, bodiless, primordial, universal self; all this is pervaded by that Peace. (41)

Since, in the absence of the objects of knowledge that serve as limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), [the Self] is inexpressible as if separate from the original image (*bimba*), this connects with what precedes.

In this manner, when there is the state of the innermost self (*pratyagbhāva*)—that is, the state of Brahman which is bodiless and so forth—the meaning is that everything remains as the undivided, whole, eternal, and auspicious *Śiva*, characterized as "not the universe" (*aviśvātma*). || 41 ||
Free from the knower, the known, and the act of knowing, they remain like the silence of a stone;
with their inner senses stilled, they are established in themselves like the interior of a stone statue.
He says, "śānta... (verse 42), meaning that you all must accomplish the very state of abiding in that [peace].
Whether moving or causing others to move, remain as the very form of the Knower;
you are the nature of the knower of the unknowable, the essence of both being and non-being. 43.

He states that even though worldly convention (*vyavahāra*) is obtained as it is when those [entities] persist, there is no impairment, by means of the verse beginning with "moving" (*calanta*). || 43 ||
The stages of existence have become as clear as the expanse of space for you;
they remain just as they are, and beings pass away just as they came.
The wise attain the supreme state either by performing their single duty as it has been obtained,
or else by being radiant with an inner heart pacified through the renunciation of everything.
Or rather, he says "athavā" (or else), implying: "stay as you wish in meditative absorption. || 45 ||
Let all things remain in solitude, like figures depicted in a painting;
when conceptualization ceases, everything is always like a city of one's own imagination.

At all times—both during the state of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and during the state of worldly activity (*vyavahāra*)—for the awakened person whose awakening is uninterrupted, [the world] has always set because of its utter unreality, like a city of one's own volition (*saṃkalpa-pura*) or like a dream. 46.
Like one awakened from a dream, the world has always set for the enlightened;
yet, like one blind by birth, he perceives forms with his eyes through delusions.

And awakening, when possessed of the eyes, is firmly established like the experience of forms; it culminates in the experience of full bliss and is employed in *nirvāṇa*. It is not like the mental construction of forms by one born blind, nor is it a mere indirect cognition. With this intention, he says:
"He with the eyes," and so forth. (47)
Describing nirvāṇa through the instruction of conceptual fragments, the ignorant person is tormented within and does not find peace; such is the world, whose nature consists of ignorance. 48.
The ignorant person, merely by hearing a few statements, describes liberation while under the delusion that he has become a knower of reality;

like a person born blind describing the perception of forms by one with eyes, he is tormented within by honor and dishonor and the like, but unlike the knower of reality, he does not find peace. The meaning is that he does not experience the bliss of tranquility.

It is well known in the world that even those who are deceived by false teachings through the analogy of the "blind monkey" (the story of the blind men touching an elephant) experience the delusion of having achieved their goal; thus [the author] says: "The portion of conceptual construction... (verse 48).
Due to some ignorance, one who has not accomplished his purpose thinks, "I have accomplished my goal"; thus, deluded by folly, he perceives himself as having achieved what was unachieved. (49)
He will realize his failure to achieve his purpose through the torments of subsequent moments;
for the wise know that a means which is merely conceptual is no means at all. (50)
Therefore, he concludes by means of the experience of direct higher knowledge (*abhijñā*) that cognition consisting of conceptual construction (*kalpanātmaka-jñāna*) is not the means to *nirvāṇa*:
"the means" (verse 50).

Because it bestows suffering through the delusions of existence, non-existence, desire, and error, one thoroughly understands the world’s delusion; that state which is free from latent impressions (avāsana) and in which all sense-objects have become tasteless is indeed called Nirvāṇa. || 51 ||

Because it yields suffering through the delusions of desiring existence and non-existence in a mere moment, they know the conceptual mind to be a non-means; this is the connection with what precedes. Therefore, with the intention that the previously mentioned right knowledge alone must be made firm until the destruction of latent impressions (vāsanā), and that this alone culminates in liberation (nirvāṇa), he says: "The world... [and] "all things are tasteless."
In which the objects of experience end with the state of Hiraṇyagarbha.
Having attained the intuitive flash of meaning through this narrative, the essence of consciousness, being liquid by nature, will intensely experience the water of awareness;
seeing the entire stainless form of consciousness as that which is not an object of cognition, you shall attain liberation from the nature of the world. 52.

Therefore, O Rāma, you will not achieve your goal by merely attaining— that is, by understanding through an outward orientation— a meaning taught by me that is like the meaning of a narrative (*ākhyāyikā*), whether it be a worldly tale or one from the Purāṇas, which is indirect and consists of nothing but a mental construction (*kalpanāmātra*). Rather, [you must realize it directly].

Through the excellence of being filled by the mere latent impression (*vāsanā*) [of the world], you perceive and indeed see the nature of the world as a substance of fluidity whose very form flows all around— the water of insentience (*acid-vāri*). Yet, seeing with the inward-turned vision (*pratyag-dṛṣṭi*) the full, pure, and unknowable nature of consciousness (*cid-rūpa*), and experiencing it directly, you attain liberation, resting in *nirvāṇa*.
The meaning is "you shall become. || 52 ||
When, having set aside that which is understood through the scriptures as being of the nature of non-enlightenment— resembling the experience of forms by one born blind—
you fall into this internal awakening, O Bhavābhū, there arises direct experience.

Strengthening this point, he says: "jātyandhetyādi" (beginning with "born-blind"). That which is understood through the scriptures—that is, through instructional statements—due to being outward-looking, is like the experience of one born blind; it is indeed of the nature of non-comprehension (*abodha*), because knowledge of a thing that is directly present (*aparokṣa*) through indirect means (*parokṣa*) is merely an error. Therefore, having cast such a cognition underfoot, [one must proceed].

As if treading upon it with the foot, having utterly disregarded it—[the word] *adhaḥśirasī* [is used here] with the suffix *cvi* added to *pada* to mean "having placed below"—falling directly through immediate experience into this internal realization whose nature is the inner self (*pratyagātman*), which is manifest (*aparokṣa*), become that very experience itself, free from birth and its other states. This alone is your liberation (*nirvāṇa*); such is the meaning. || 53 ||

Thus ends the forty-second chapter, titled "The Instruction on Nirvāṇa," in the *Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa* of the *Mokṣopāya* section of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, according to the tradition of the Ṛṣis.
Thus ends the forty-second chapter, titled "The Instruction on Nirvāṇa," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The Forty-Third Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Through thorough knowledge, this world, beginning with the sense of "I," is realized as being unreal.
Through delusion, one proceeds with experience, perceiving even the truth as otherwise.
In this world, which is mostly like a city of the mind-yakṣas imagined through ignorance,
when it is wiped away by mere awakening, the state of abiding as one with Brahman is proclaimed.

The internal [world] such as the "I" and so forth, and this external world consisting of the enjoyer and the enjoyed—all of it becomes unreal through the thorough knowledge of the reality of experience, which is of the nature of the experience of that [Self]. For experience culminates in consciousness;
for experience is the enjoyer’s perception of a connection with the object of enjoyment, and by means of that perception, [it is known to be unreal].

For those deluded ones who, through ignorance and by means of a mistaken cognition involving the exchange of the self, possess the notion of "I" in the enjoyer alone, it is true that the self is not [perceived] by itself apart from experience; the meaning is that he is indeed Brahman. || 1 ||
For one who is freed from the fever of ignorance and whose self has been cooled by awakening, this alone shall be the sign: that the water of worldly enjoyment no longer appeals to them.
For this very reason, he states that those who know reality have no interest in the objects of enjoyment, beginning with the words "ajñāna" (ignorance). || 2 ||
Enough with other forms of thorough knowledge and the delusions regarding the signified and the signifier;
let Nirvana be contemplated as merely the absence of the cognition of "I. (3)

Thus, for those who are dispassionate toward objects of enjoyment, liberation—consisting of the residue of pure consciousness alone—is established merely by the abandonment of the portion of egoism within the enjoyer; so he says: "Enough! [with] the expressed form, the expressing name, and the forms of delusion regarding their objects. (3)
Just as objects experienced in a dream do not truly taste [to the senses] and do not exist, so too, in this delusion of "I" and this "world," they do not exist. (4)

He clarifies the statement "enjoyments are like water, they do not please" with the words "by one who has fully known" (*parijñāta*). Just as objects seen in a dream do not produce flavor (*rasa*), do not delight, and do not exist for a person who is awake, so too are the objects seen in the delusion "I am this world" [not pleasing] for the knower of reality (*tattvajña*); such is the meaning. || 4 ||
Just as a person with an eye disease sees a city with its inhabitants and trees as something unreal, so too does the individual soul perceive the cycle of existence.
He provides an illustration for this, saying "just as" (*yathā*): a *yakṣa* in the forest [perceives] a city fashioned by the illusory power (*māyā*) of a *gandharva*.

Alternatively, regarding the reading *yakṣatanau*, it should be explained thus: just as a man skilled in the arts of a *yakṣa*, having assumed the form of a *yakṣa* through his own mental construction (*svabhāvanākalpita*), perceives a city together with its inhabitants after having created it. || 5 ||
Just as a yakṣa that is of the nature of an illusion and the world of yakṣas are both real in form and well-established to one another, yet false, so too are the illusions of "I-ness" and the world.

In that regard, the *yakṣa* is of a delusive nature, its essence as an enjoyer being constructed by delusion; and the world of *yakṣas* and its city are of the nature of objects of enjoyment constructed by delusion—thus both do not exist at all. Nevertheless, the meaning is that they appear as if they were real entities because they perform purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) characterized by mutual enjoyment. || 6 ||
In the forest, because they are free from obstruction, the yakṣas take on bewildering forms;
just as these beings manifest, so too do these fourteen [elements].

With the intention that the cause for the appearance even of what is non-existent as real—both in the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*)—is indeed superimposition (*adhyāsa*) upon the unobstructed witness (*sākṣin*), he says: "due to non-obstruction. And by the number of adjuncts (*upādhi*) consisting of the worlds, there are fourteen. //7//
Having realized that "I am merely delusion and false," and contemplating this, the yakṣa becomes non-yakṣa; so too does this mind attain the state of the true nature of mind (cittattva).

He says, "It is mere delusion," because even when the error regarding the world is sublated, the very perception of its falsity is the cause—just as for a yakṣa, there is the withdrawal of his own imagined body, city, and so forth.
[This refers to] the state of the true nature of consciousness, which is its essential form as pure awareness. || 8 ||
Abandoning all suspicion regarding mental constructions, free from both rejection and acceptance, with no spreading desire for anything at all, remain peaceful and established as you truly are.
There are four adverbs of action. || 9 ||
This pervasive visible world, which arises from non-existence, is of the nature of the seer;
or else, if it is not of the nature of the seer, why does it remain as something that cannot be described as real? (10)
He states that, upon investigation according to reality, the object of perception results in being either nothing but the perceiver or in being insubstantial—thus he says, "non-existence" (*asattā*).
That which has no possibility or origination of existence (*sattā*) is not at all the nature of the perceiver. Why?
Because the ultimate reality of the perceiver is pure consciousness (*cit-rūpa*), which is inexpressible; how could it abide in the form of the object, which is insubstantial?
It is established; for it is impossible for anyone to bring about the state of non-existence for that which exists—this is the meaning.

Since the agent of the root *ās* (to sit) in its non-causative form becomes the object in the causative (*ṇyanta*) according to the rule "gati-buddhi... [Pāṇini 1.4.52], the suffix *la* is applied in the sense of the object. || 10 ||
Just as a cluster of branches and shrubs belongs to a spring overflowing with sap,
so too does the state of creation belong to consciousness that is filled solely by its own essential nature.

He demonstrates by means of an illustration that even though the seer lacks the nature of the seen, it is indeed possible for the manifestation of the existence of the seen to function as a support within empirical experience: "In spring... (verse 11).
This manifestation of the world is pure, a perception consisting of consciousness alone;
what room is there here for unity or duality? Let Nirvana, which is stainless, be attained.
But in the ultimate sense, even the possibility of the identity of the seer and so forth does not exist; thus he says: "That which is this... (verse 12).
Let there be dwelling in the space of pure consciousness; let the supreme nectar be drunk;
and let one remain without fear in the blissful grove of the joy of Nirvana. 13.
Now the venerable Vasiṣṭha, proclaiming for the benefit of all out of compassion, instructs them with the words beginning "Listen" (*bhūyatām*).
The supreme essence (*paramo rasaḥ*) is unsurpassed bliss, according to the Vedic scripture: "He is indeed the essence" (*raso vai saḥ*).
[This occurs] in the celestial grove (*svarvana*), the Nandana garden, which is characterized by the bliss of liberation (*nirvāṇānanda*). || 13 ||
Why do you humans, like deer driven by the wind, wander with deluded minds in these utterly empty wildernesses of saṃsāra? (14)
"Vātahariṇā" means "like one driven by the wind"; the word "iva" (as if) is to be understood as the ellipsis. The division of the words is "bhramatha u. || 14 ||
O you whose intellects are blinded and deceived by the mirage-water of the three worlds, do not run with agitated minds, for your intentions are ruined! (15)
With your intentions corrupted by desire and craving, do not run about in such a way that you, though free from agitation, fall into a state of distraction. 15.
O deer, do not waste your lives in vain exertion, drinking the water of a mirage consisting of forms, light, and mental attention. 16.

Forms and lights are external enjoyments; mental constructions are the enjoyments of the conceited. These very things are like the waters of a mirage—having undergone exhaustion, so it should be understood. (16)
Perish with the great pride that this world is a city of Gandharvas;
perceive these sorrows, which take the form of pleasure, as being for the sake of destruction alone.
"May you not perish through that pride which, like a city of Gandharvas in the form of the world, robs one of discernment"—the word "may [you not]" is to be supplied. 17.
Let me not be mistaken for a tuft of hair on the head of the world as I stand in the midst of the great sky; rather, let my true nature be perceived by those who are free from delusion. (18)

Do not look upon the great expanse of the Brahma-ether, nor upon the darkness of ignorance situated within it; rather, turn toward the unerring, true nature as it is seen in its actual reality. || 18 ||
O humans, do not sleep upon the beds of blind wombs, which are as fragile as water-waves and are reached through the high branches of the tree of desire.

O men! Do not sleep upon these beds of blind wombs, characterized by worldly existence, wherein human bodies are as fragile as the drops of dew that fall and scatter upon the high-hanging, wind-swaying leaves of the peepal tree. || 19 ||
Remain at rest in the peaceful, beginningless and endless nature without interruption;
let it perish through its lack of intrinsic nature due to the defects of the states of seer and seen. (20)

May [the Self] not perish—uninterrupted and unfragmented—in its own nature, which is the state of the ultimate Brahman; for, due to the defects characteristic of the states of the seer and so forth, there occurs a loss of its own nature through the exchange of its true form. 20.
Cyclic existence is understood through non-cognition; for it does not exist even in the slightest degree.
And as for that which remains—the Truth—its name is not found. (21)
Having forcibly snapped asunder the cage of saṃsāra, which is entwined with the iron chains of craving, remain above all like the king of beasts.

Having torn asunder with the power of knowledge the cage of saṃsāra— which is entwined and encircled by the iron chain characterized by craving— stand like a lion, the king of beasts, at the pinnacle of excellence above all. 22.
Liberation is merely the pacification of the delusion of grasping at a self and what belongs to a self;
for the yogin who abides in whatever manner that may be, that very state is his own being. (23)
The grasping at "self" and "mine"—the conceit of "I" and "mine"—is merely the cessation of the delusion characterized by that [grasping].

Liberation is nothing other than having that very state as its nature; it is the very existence of the self for the yogin. This is the meaning. Nirvāṇa is the state of being free from latent impressions (vāsanā), the supreme state, and the state of being free from suffering and ignorance.
For one weary on the path of saṃsāra, these are the peaceful grounds of rest. || 24 ||
Having conceptualized that very [state] as the distinct resting grounds for those weary from the road of saṃsāra, he says: "nirvāṇatā" (the state of nirvāṇa).

The word should be divided as "avāsanatā" (the state of being without latent impressions). "Parā" means supreme; "apatāpatā" means free from the three kinds of suffering (*tāpa*). These are the three stages beginning with the fifth. || 24 ||

That which is known by the wise is not known by fools, and that which is known by fools is not known by those who possess true knowledge; this purpose of the world exists as a mutual state consisting of inexpressible meaning.
It has already been stated previously that, for the ignorant person, the world consists of a flood of suffering, whereas for the wise person, it consists of bliss. || 25 ||
When all delusion has been completely stilled, that which remains is not even perceived;
it is like a doll made of water, enveloped by the waters of the great ocean.

Just as a doll made of water, appearing in forms such as the Gaṅgā, Godāvarī, and Narmadā, exists merely as a manifestation of the waters of the great ocean and is not perceived as such by those dwelling within the ocean, so too, when delusion has subsided, the universe is seen as such by the wise. This is the meaning. || 26 ||
When delusion has subsided for the awakened one who has attained nirvāṇa,
the world as it exists [in samsāra] has dissolved, yet it remains exactly as it is.
He explains that very point clearly with the verse beginning "bhrānti" (delusion). || 27 ||
Just as a line of ashes from burnt grass is carried away somewhere by the winds,
so too does the world vanish somewhere through the restful abidance in the true nature of the virtuous.
That arrangement of the categories of the world-Brahman is indeed supreme;
it has the nature of the referent of the word "Brahman" and does not partake in the function of the word "world. (29)
The meaning of the word *brahman* is that which has the nature of expansion (*bṛṃhaṇa*); its "arrangement" (*saṃniveśa*) is its specific form.

If this [form] is the inner self (*pratyagātman*), which is the primary meaning of the word *brahman*—being free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*), self-luminous, and unsurpassed bliss—that is the highest. As for the world (*jagat*), it is so called because it "goes" (*gacchati*), meaning it undergoes transformation through the sixfold changes.
The meaning is that if [the Self] were to possess the state of being an effect of modification—which is the cause for the application of the word "world"—then it would not be supreme. || 29 ||
Just as these objects appear to an ignorant child who does not understand them,
so too do they appear to the wise man who remains with his latent impressions (vāsanā) exhausted.
Since non-conceptual experience is well-known even in a child within this world, he states its similarity [to that experience] with the words "of the unknown" (*avijñātasya*).
This refers to a young child for whom no "vijñāta"—that is, specific or determinate knowledge—exists. (30)
That which is night for all beings, therein the self-controlled man is awake;
that wherein beings are awake is night for the sage who sees. 31.

He corroborates with the words of the Blessed One the statement—"Known by the knower of that, not by fools; known by the fool, not by those who know that"—which has been established: "That which is night," etc. (31).
That which is his waking state remains indeed uninterrupted, like deep sleep;
for him, the cravings for worldly pleasures during the waking state are like a painting being viewed.
This he explains with the words "remains as it is," and so forth:

because all people are enveloped by the darkness of ignorance, the reality of the Self remains for this knower of truth exactly as it is, like one in deep sleep; yet for him, there is no cessation—that is, he is devoid of cessation—and he is awake. Therefore, that which is night for all beings, in that [state] he is awake.

This is the meaning of what is said. Furthermore, because for this [sage], the "waking" states—well-known as the waking of deluded people, consisting of the pursuit of sensory objects and the tasting of sounds and so forth through the senses—are not present even when they appear before him like a painted performance of dance or battle, therefore that state in which "beings are awake" is called "night" for the sage who sees; such is the meaning of the verse. || 32 ||

To the knower, the perception of the world—which is like the experience of forms by one born blind, consisting mostly of error, and having the nature of the unreal—appears and yet does not appear. (33)

He explains the second half [of the verse] further with the words "jātyandha" (blind from birth): the sense is that if it shines, it is like a dream at night; if it does not shine, it is like deep sleep at night. || 33 ||
The three worlds are suffering born of delusion, and their objects are not real, being the domain of the deluded;
they are like the forms, perceptions, and mental activities in a dream once that dream is recognized as such.

The three worlds, which are established as suffering for the deluded, are indeed the object of the deluded alone and not the object of the awakened; this is because they do not truly exist. [Objection: If the knower has no enjoyment of objects, then by what means is he satisfied and how does he live?
To this, he says: "In a dream," and so forth. (34)
Just as they do not flow [in that state], so let them not manifest in waking or dreaming;
being undivided, fully composed, and having attained supreme non-contradiction. (35)

The connection with the subsequent verse is as follows: "Even though the experiences of waking and dreaming may not manifest during the waking state, nevertheless, the Knower remains extinguished, with an inner organ that is perfectly cooled. (35)
With an inner heart that has become profoundly cooled, the knower abides in nirvāṇa;
for one who knows that, whose mind is drawn away from objects and liberated, his state is one of equanimity even without formal meditation.

The outward attractions of the mind caused by the latent impressions of worldly enjoyments have been drawn away; for the knower of truth who is liberated from and abandoned by them, meditation becomes an even state of abiding without any effort to restrain the mind. || 36 ||
Without a low place, no flow of water is possible; likewise, there is no mental engagement without an object, and the mind itself is colored by the object. (37)

He establishes this by means of an illustration: "low-lying," etc. The meaning is that just as no activity such as flowing is possible for the water of a pond or similar body of water without a downward path such as a channel, so it is here. Now, one might object: if external objects are sublated by the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), let the external sense organs not function; however, [what of] the cessation of mental attention (*manaskāra*)?
To explain how this is established, he says: "The object itself," and so forth. (37)
This very manifestation consists of both the external and the internal;
it extends as far as the ocean and is composed of the confluence of hundreds of river currents.

This mental attention (*manaskāra*) itself is this appearance of objects. Just as all water—well known to consist of infinite distinctions such as river currents up to the ocean—is perceived as a single mass when united in one place, appearing only as the commonality of water; so too, the mind alone, together with its external and internal aspects, manifests as the form of all objects.
The subsequent [sequence] follows from another. || 38 ||

Just as the water of rivers flows from a single mass of congealed ice, possessing both internal and external forms and consisting of both the meaningful and the meaningless; so too does this world. (39)
It is the mind alone that vibrates as the appearance of objects, thus expanded;
there is no duality between object and mind, just as there is none between water and its waves. (40)

In the absence of one, there is the cessation of both, like that of wind and its movement; for in reality, this world is devoid of essence, and thus through the pacification of one alone, both are stilled. (41)

Let it be so; what follows from that? To this he replies: "One" (eketi). The meaning is that when the object is sublated by the knowledge of reality, the mind is likewise sublated, and thus there is no possibility of mental attention (manaskāra). || 41 ||
Because they are one, the object and the mind are both extinguished simultaneously and swiftly;
therefore, an object whose nature consists of conceptual construction should not be pursued by the wise man. (42)
And through right knowledge, the peace of both [the intellect and the mind] occurs;
for the knower, the object and the mind perish of their own accord when [the ignorance] is destroyed.
And this sublation of those two is like the destruction of a tiger in a dream; it is a destruction of that which was not [previously] destroyed. Thus he says: "When it is not destroyed" (43).
Just as one who knows [the truth] feels no fear toward an enemy made of clay when perceiving it as an enemy,
so too for the wise man, the object and the mind always remain exactly as they are.

The meaning is as follows: just as when an enemy who is one's own foe is imagined through delusion in a clay statue, and that [foe] is sublated by knowledge, the state of being an enemy and the fear induced by it perish; in that same way, [the world] remains exactly as it is, established in its ultimate nature as Brahman. || 44 ||
When that which is of the nature of pure existence has come into being, everything else becomes something entirely unprecedented;
even the time of the world and the meaning of the Vedic compendiums become ignorant, pertaining to the ignorant, and unreal.
Distinct from the form well-known in the state of worldly existence, there is another form consisting of perfect bliss;
when that [bliss] has become manifest as a positive entity, as the ultimate reality, and when it is joined and constituted through the relationship of cause and effect,
then the "object"— which is the experience of pleasure and pain and its means, namely the world and the three realms— is such that it constitutes the period of *saṃsāra*.

By the use of the word "api" (also), it is implied that the modifications of objects such as birth and so forth produced by time, the ignorant experiencer thereof, and even the objects of the senses such as sound and the rest—all these are unreal from the perspective of one who knows reality. || 45 ||

To the wise man, this world does not exist as something possessing consciousness, just as there is no dream for a man sleeping on his side, or as there is no malevolent yakṣa for one who is impotent; it is like the perception of a ghost held by a hero.
Regarding this, he provides two examples with the words "pārśva" and so forth. By the term "eunuch" (klība), one who is lacking in courage, such as a child and the like, is indicated;
[the situation] is like that of a yakṣa appearing before him. || 46 ||

The knower meditates upon the ignorant, and thus the ignorant grows for a long time, like a barren woman who increases [her lineage] as if she had attained the state of meaning, even though she lacks any knowledge of the meaning of words. (47)

Even a barren woman increases through the expansion of sons, grandsons, and so forth; "by that [expansion]" is the ellipsis. Now, what is the nature of the world that those who know reality (tattvajña) perceive? He states this with the words "even without" (vinaiva). The meaning of the word *jñāta* is being an object of knowledge (*jñānaviṣayatva*); even without that, it remains as if appearing as an object precisely because of its self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*).
The meaning is that they know the manifesting consciousness, which is without beginning or end, to be none other than Brahman itself. || 47 ||
They know the abiding consciousness, which is without beginning or end, as the nature that pervades all creation (or, according to another reading, "all-pervading").
It is the mind, devoid of word and meaning, and free from division and end. (48)

He states that the manner of experiencing described regarding external objects should also be understood to apply to internal mental ones: "The mind, sound, etc., are like the waves of the water of consciousness and the intellect within the pure mind; where indeed can they possibly exist internally, and what are these so-called object and mind? (49)

The word "they know" (viduḥ) is supplied [to complete the sense] as "they know it to be stainless. Thus, between these two ways of awakening the world—the ignorant way and the way of one who knows reality—which have been elaborated, he says "Where? (kvā) [in verse 49], meaning that only the second is to be accepted because it is true to reality, not the first.
Delusion is indeed purposeless; let one remain established in the nature of intrinsic being, like autumnal clouds in the sky, abiding in the nature of pure awareness.

When the state of abiding in one's own nature (*svabhāva*) is firmly established, the three states [of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep] attain the realization of being nothing but the fourth state (*turya*); since there is then no longer anything to be conceptualized, even the "mind-ness" (*manastva*) of the mind departs. Thus he says:
"Pure... [and so on]. [The comparison is] with autumnal lotuses, with lights, or with people. (50)
The nature of the mind is not experienced through the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep;
having shaken off infinite multiplicity and the unreal condition, [abide] in the one free from affliction.

Having shaken off the entire range of objects of knowledge— which possess infinite diversities through their internal divisions of states characterized by waking, dreaming, and deep sleep— just as one shakes off a superimposed snake from a rope, remain established in your own nature, which is free from all affliction. 51.
Know that everything without exception is like a rope; remain established in your own nature as the mass of consciousness.
It is cognition alone that presides over both the internal and external as the state of being an object. 52.
He presides over and sustains [it]. || 52 ||
Tell me, how can the seed, the branches, and the fruits exist? Where, then, are the object and the mind?
Since the knowable is non-existent, even cognition has reached the state that is beyond naming.
Cognition is a modification of the intellect.
Because its nature as all particularities has been stilled, the Residue (Śeṣa) exists as the reality whose essence is Being;
it is indeed the object, the mental attention, and that is an error consisting of non-existence. (54)

Self-nature (*svabhāva*) is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*). Since the object and the mind are defined in mutual dependence upon one another, it follows that if they were non-different, both would result in being mere illusion; thus he says, "the object alone," etc.
The sense is that because the external has the nature of being internal, and the internal has the nature of being external. (54)
The mind itself is the mental impression of objects, and that is an error consisting of non-existence;
because the Unborn One is the self of all, even this mind is without a cause.

"Arthasaṃskāraḥ" means that which is refined as an object (*artha*); because it ends in the suffix *ghañ*, it is masculine according to the rule "those ending in *ghañ* [retain] their gender. To the question, "What then are the object and the mind in reality? he says: "Because it is the self of all. Since the unborn Brahman is the self of all things, it manifests even in the form of the mind.
The sense is that even in its extracted form, it is merely void. || 55 ||
Due to the experience of delusion, an object appears as if it truly exists, though it is entirely false;
the mind itself shines forth as the manifestation of an object, even though it is without any external cause.
He says that even the mind, like Brahman in the form of the mind, appears without any external cause in the form of objects, stating:
"from the experience of delusion" (bhramānubhavataḥ). || 56 ||
Unstable and flickering like the flash of lightning,
you, whose nature is mere mental attention, cause delusion within the cycle of existence.

Through the thorough knowledge of the single nature [of reality], you neither exist nor do you wander in delusion; for the cycle of existence is [a product] of the mind alone, and it is stilled by the awakening to the Self. 58.
People suffer in vain through the form of the delusion of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell;
however, the state beyond existence and non-existence is the supreme nature of consciousness, free from saṃsāra.
Awakening is the state of being the non-existence of existence. || 59 ||
The delusion that "I am suffering" regarding any existence other than Nirvāṇa is like the water of a mirage; I am of the nature of the unreal and the void. (60)
