He states by what means, then, the other existence—the sense of "I"—is pacified: "Like a mirage.
The ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) is like the water of a mirage; it is pacified only when its nature is realized to be empty. (60)
Thus, through the thorough knowledge of the self, the notion of "I" itself subsides;
having known this and becoming composed of pure knowledge, one realizes the nature of all things, both external and internal.

Why is this so? To this he says: "Having known" (*jñātvā*). He who, at the beginning of that creation of Brahman, having known by his omniscience the objects to be created as being indeed his own self, becomes himself Hiraṇyagarbha—consisting of such knowledge—and according to his volition, he himself assumes the state of having both external and internal objects, without ever abandoning his own essential nature.
The meaning is "gone. || 61 ||
Just as water does not abandon its nature even when it has become a wave, and just as the existence of a tree extends from its roots to the tips of its branches. (62)
"Let it be so; what follows from that? To this he replies: "The root," etc.

From this, the following is established: just as there is but one single existence (sattā) extending from the root of a tree to the tip of its branches, so too, in this world consisting of the knower, the knowledge, and the knowable, there shines forth but one single existence—extremely stable and entirely changeless—that extends to the end of all objects of knowledge; there is no other existence.
The stainless, changeless reality shines as the single limit of the object of cognition within consciousness,
just as the one stainless sky appears to extend for hundreds of thousands of yojanas.
By the words "Just as... and so forth, he establishes the identity of existence through yet another example regarding the identity of existence. || 63 ||
In that same way, knowledge alone shines as undivided, reaching to the very limit of the knowable;
it is one and stainless due to its emptiness, just as space is all-pervading.
With the intention that this very same example applies even to its purity, he says: "Because of emptiness" (śūnyatvāt). || 64 ||
Likewise, having known that one stainless reality even within the states of both the knower and the known, the self becomes solidified like clarified butter and is turned into stone. (65)
In that same way, by the very act of being perceived, the Self itself is made into one's own mind;
thus, even without space or time, the Self attains the state of being the mind through awareness and non-awareness.
Through the non-awareness of one's own true nature, which is of the form of consciousness. || 66 ||
The non-awakened one is led by means of logical arguments, for this [Reality] alone is well-established.
Although here there is no possibility whatsoever of non-awakening or the like,
nevertheless, for the sake of mutual awakening, it is conceptualized right here.
He raises an objection—using the reasoning supported by the principle of parsimony (*lāghava-tarka*) and the scriptural indications that "He made Himself alone"—with the word "here" (*atra*).

"Here" means in the pure conscious Self (*cidātman*). He refutes this with the words "nevertheless" (*tathāpi*). "Right here" means precisely in this state of non-awakening (*abodha-daśā*), and not in reality (*na tattvataḥ*). And so it has been said in the *Vārttika*:
"It is only by remaining within ignorance that it is conceived that 'ignorance exists'; however, from the perspective of Brahman, this ignorance is not in any way tenable. (67)
Possessing great majesty and free from pride, they dissolve upon the pacification of the state of delusion;
being unerring and tranquil through their very infinity, they become eternally composed in meditative absorption.
He concludes that because their nature is impossible [to exist], all things dissolve along with ignorance upon the arising of the knowledge of reality:

"When the root ignorance, which is the state of delusion, is pacified by knowledge, they dissolve into one's very self like the solidity of ghee. Through that dissolution, being peaceful and free from error due to the state of being filled with unsurpassed bliss in its infinity," [he says].
The meaning is that they become intent upon that state of rest in *samādhi*, which is constant, uninterrupted concentration free from distraction.
Thus ends the forty-third chapter, titled "Instruction on One-Pointedness toward Brahman," in the *Nirvāṇa* section of the *Mokṣopāya* within the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki. 43.
Thus ends the forty-third chapter, titled "The Instruction on Being Constantly Absorbed in Brahman," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa within the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The forty-fourth canto.
Śrī Rāma said:
[I shall describe] that which, in due order, possesses the blossoms and fruits of the tree of meditative absorption (samādhi).
O Sage, speak of that Being who bestows rest, whose garland is made of flowers.
Herein is described the wish-fulfilling tree of meditative concentration, which is to be cultivated; and for the weary deer of the embodied mind to find rest, it provides its very base.
In due order, [he perceives] the seed, field, irrigation, sprouting, leaves, stalks, branches, flowers, fruits, and the expansion of shade;
likewise, creepers, branches, and wish-fulfilling vines (kalpalatās) together with those; that which provides rest for the deer of the mind; and existence (sattā), which is stability. || 1 ||

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Listen to the description of the tree of meditative absorption (samādhi), which rises ever higher throughout one's life within the forest of discerning people, and is endowed with leaves, flowers, and fruit. || 2 ||
It is called "ājīva" because it is lived by and subsisted upon with one's whole being; such is its nature. (2)
The wise know that the seed of this [renunciation] is the world-weariness arising from saṃsāra, which has somehow arisen either through suffering or spontaneously. (3)

The meaning is this: they know that the seed of the tree of meditative concentration (*samādhāna*) is supreme detachment (*paravairāgya*), which consists of an intense desire to abandon [worldly things]; and that this detachment has arisen in some manner—whether through suffering born of insults from enemies or kinsmen, by the power of destiny, spontaneously, or through other causes such as the instruction of virtuous friends. || 3 ||

The wise know his field to be that which is ploughed by the halter of the auspicious net, watered day and night with the essence [of dharma], and where the furrows are the flowing currents of the breath. [The reading "mano viduḥ" (they know it to be the mind) is more appropriate. || 4 ||
Disgust for saṃsāra is the seed of samādhi; it falls of its own accord upon the ground of the mind, which is secluded like a forest of those who practice discernment.

And that seed of samādhi, consisting of world-weariness, falls of its own accord upon the ground of the mind—which is like the Nandana grove in its characteristics of being a forest for those seeking seclusion, solitary, and adorned with discernment—or rather, there is no need to wait for it; such is the meaning. || 5 ||
The seed of meditative concentration that has fallen upon the ground of one’s own mind should be diligently watered with these consecrations by one of great intelligence, without weariness.

The seed of meditation, whose characteristics of detachment have been described, should be watered by a person of great intelligence with a firm mind intent on its cultivation, using these sprinklings whose characteristics will be explained hereafter; the meaning is that it must not be destroyed through attachment to enjoyments— as happens with the detachment born of mere exhaustion— by one who is weary from the force of desire, anger, and the like.
Exhaustion [is countered] by one who endures it. || 6 ||
With pure, gentle, and purifying words, sweet and beneficial to the self—
like the fresh milk from the company of the virtuous, or like the nectar of the moon.

In this regard, he says—through two verses beginning with "By pure"—that one should first be sprinkled with the nine kinds of milk characterized by association with the virtuous (*satsaṅga*), and subsequently with the nectar of the scriptures learned from their mouths:
"By those that bestow inner emptiness, yet are full; by those that are clear and cool as nectar."
By means of the excellent waters of the meaning of the scriptures, which are like channels of nectar flowing forth.
By means of [the words] "not this, not this" (*neti neti*), which negate all duality and bestow the inner Self that is empty of all worldly existence—

and for this very reason complete, sweet, and cool like nectar because they pacify all suffering— [these words] have issued forth through the gateway of exposition from the lake of Brahman residing in the heart of the Guru.

Recognizing with great intelligence that the seed— namely, detachment from saṃsāra— which has fallen upon the ground of one's own mind like a stream of nectar flowing through channels in the form of the meanings of the scriptures heard and reflected upon, must be protected with effort for the sake of meditation. (9)
The seed of meditation, which consists of world-weariness, must be protected. (9)

By means of various forms of austerity and giving, through the arrangement of ritual objects as desired, and by the planning of rest-houses at sacred fords and shrines and the expansion of groves; || 10 ||

What are those efforts? He states them as "penance" (*tapas*). Here, penance refers to that which is taught by the Blessed One—namely, the worship of the gods, the twice-born, teachers, and the wise; purity, straightforwardness, and so forth—which is threefold: physical, vocal, and mental, and characterized by *sattva*.

These are called "modes" (*prakāra*) because they are manifested through their defining characteristics. They are the "desires of the field" (*kṣetradohada*), meaning the objects [of cultivation] through the giving of those [efforts].
By means of the practice of humility and other virtues, supported by masters who have attained lordship, there is rest and residence in holy places such as sacred fords and temples;
this is achieved through the conceptualization of the expansion of its characteristics—the extensive layout of the enclosure consisting of walls, ramparts, and so forth. || 10 ||
A guardian named Contentment, whose disposition is disciplined and who is constantly accompanied by his beloved Joy, must be appointed as the protector of this [tree] once it has sprouted. (11)

Thus, for this seed that has sprouted and produced a shoot through means such as watering and the like, one must appoint a guardian— a man capable of protecting it— whose intention is trained in the methods of preservation, who is highly skillful, and who is accompanied by his beloved wife named Muditā (Joy), while he himself is named Saṃtoṣa (Contentment). || 11 ||
One should ward off from this [body] the birds of hope situated behind, the birds of excessive attachment, and the vultures of sensual pride as they swoop down.

From this protective cause, [one should protect] the birds characterized by hope who abide in former latent impressions (*pūrvavāsanā*), as well as the vultures of the group of desires (*kāma*) and so forth, which take the form of attachment— the affection directed toward others, namely those things other than the self such as children, friends, wealth, and the like.
One should ward off those who approach for the purpose of destroying the sprout of meditative concentration. || 12 ||
The dust and darkness [of the mind] must be wiped away from us by the gentle spears of virtuous conduct, by the rays of the sun of discernment, and by those which grant inconceivable light. 13.

Because non-violence is paramount, one should purify even the darkness of ignorance through gentle and virtuous practices—such as the restraints (yama), observances (niyama), postures (āsana), breath control (prāṇāyāma), and the worship of the Lord—as well as through discernment and austerity, which bestow the inconceivable realm of Brahman. || 13 ||
Prosperities and women are like waves, fragile in their enjoyment;
upon him fall the thunderbolts impelled by the clouds of his evil deeds.
In that sprout. || 14 ||

These [impediments] are to be warded off by means of fortitude, magnanimity, compassion, and mantras, as well as by recitation, ritual bathing, austerity, and self-restraint—by one who bears the trident that is the meaning of the *praṇava*. 15.
By means of the dissolution of the gross and subtle phenomenal worlds through the measures (mātrās) of the *praṇava*, beginning with *virāj*; that is to say, by the realization thereof.
Thus, from this seed of meditation which has been well-guarded, there emerges a new sprout called discernment—glorious, noble by birth, and exalted. (16)
He was exalted by his noble birth and by the excellence of his fullness and beauty. || 16 ||
By that, the ground of the mind shines forth, radiant and blossoming;
it becomes delightful with light, just as the sky is by the newly risen moon.
Therefore, from the sprout, both the leaf and the flower blossom of their own accord: the first is the study of the scriptures, and the second is association with the virtuous. (18)
He erects this pillar named Steadfastness,
reaching great height, wrapped in the bark of contentment and stained with the essence of dispassion.
*Stambhaṃ* means a trunk; *sthairyaṃ* means firmness of root; and *samunnatiṃ* means height. || 19 ||
One whose self is nourished by the essence of dispassion and who is endowed with the rains of the meaning of the scriptures attains supreme exaltation in a very short time.

Nourished by the essence of the meaning of the scriptures, the company of the virtuous, and dispassion, it does not tremble in the least from the disturbances caused by the monkeys of passion and hatred. (21)
Then, from that [source], whose form is adorned by consciousness,
these creepers, which delight in the play of sap, are born, spreading across vast regions.

Consciousness (*vijñāna*) is the knowledge born from hearing and mental application. These [faculties] to be described hereafter extend over vast regions, being widespread and pervasive, and they reside within undivided portions of their own self. (22)
Clarity, truthfulness, existence, steadfastness, non-conceptuality, equanimity, tranquility, loving-kindness, compassion, renown, and nobility. || 23 ||

Manifestness (*sphuṭatā*) is the becoming manifest of the reality of one's own self (*svātmatattva*), which is its sole truth. Existence (*sattā*) is abiding in that very nature. Fortitude (*dhīratā*) is being unshakable even therein. Equanimity (*samatā*) is the cessation of all inequality. || 23 ||
With these creepers— whose leaves are virtues and whose flowers are his fame— that ascetic’s mighty tree of meditation acts like the Pārijāta tree.
Those whose petals are virtues such as tranquility and the like; [this refers to] the ascetic, the renunciant (saṃnyāsin). || 24 ||
Thus, this excellent tree of knowledge, possessing creepers, sprouts, and flowers, will day by day yield the fruit of future wisdom. (25)
Future knowledge is the direct realization of Brahman, capable of uprooting fundamental ignorance, which culminates in rest upon the seventh stage. || 25 ||
Rich with clusters of flowers that are his fame, shimmering with sprouts that are his virtues, spreading the essence of dispassion, and having the form of blossoms that are his wisdom; (26)
Like a cloud in the rainy season, he cools all directions;
like the moon, he pacifies the heat of creation, as if it were the scorching heat of the sun.
The heat of creation is the suffering of worldly existence. || 27 ||
Peace spreads a cool shade like the arrival of the rainy season;
peace disperses the obstruction like a wind scatters a cloud.
Cessation is the steadiness of the mind. || 28 ||
It fastens itself as a pedestal, standing firm like a principal mountain;
it produces above the fruit a small vessel characterized by auspiciousness and other qualities. (29)

The *pīṭha* is the root-lock (*mūlabandha*). It fashions the vessel for the fruit called liberation (*kaivalya*), and it brings about the splendor of auspicious qualities such as peace and other blessings, beginning with the auspicious [day]. || 29 ||
But as the wish-fulfilling tree of discernment grows day by day, the forest of a person’s heart becomes enveloped by its spreading canopy of shade. (30)
The coolness that removes the heat from the soles of the feet proceeds forth;
it is a blossoming creeper of the intellect, as beautiful as the interior of frost.
It removes the well-known internal and other torments of the heart, which is the root-ground of the *tala*; its nature is such. 31.
In her, the deer of the mind—like a traveler worn out since birth and distressed by the clamor on the road—finds rest from its intermediate exhaustion. (32)
In the intermediate wildernesses of saṃsāra, the deer of the mind finds rest in her shade.

He describes that very deer of the mind—ending with the phrase "the charming fawn" (*manohariṇaka*) found in the penultimate verse of the creation—using numerous qualifying adjectives that establish the causes for its great exhaustion and so forth, beginning with the words "from birth" (*ājanma*). On the path...
The meaning is that even when the true path has been reached by chance, one is led astray while being agitated and distracted by the clamor of various disputants. || 32 ||
He was sought after by his enemies merely for the sake of his body, skin, and flesh;
he was on the verge of falling apart, worn out by the various essential forms of his secret practices.

By enemies—the hunters of the sixfold group of foes beginning with desire—he who is the embodied person (*śārīra-puruṣa*), whose nature is pure existence (*sattāmātra-ātman*), was watched for the purpose of seizing his characteristic skin; that is to say, he was pursued. Having repeatedly hidden himself within the thorny thickets of the body and so forth—which are characterized by multiplicity, insubstantial, and possessed of form—his own...
And he is one who, while concealing [the fault], has an upper face that is shattered by the thorns of that fault;
this is a *karmadhāraya* compound with a *bahuvrīhi* as its final member. || 33 ||
Driven by the winds of latent tendencies spreading through the forest of saṃsāra,
it is constantly scorched by the fire of the river of egoism.

By means of the river of asceticism characterized by egoism—which is like a mirage-river—there is constant running about; "dārada" refers to a type of poison, and one who has this is "dāradī," meaning one who, like someone overcome by poison, is agitated by internal burning, thirst, and the like. || 34 ||
Worn out by long-standing enmity and the wandering of accumulated essential wealth from afar,
he has fallen into a pit through the power of his obsession with sons and grandsons.

"Ādarī" means one who has regard only for extensive enjoyments; the sense is that he is not easily satisfied with little. For this very reason, even though the objects are far away, abundant, substantial, and consist mostly of green grass, he is "jarjara"—one whose limbs are worn out by wandering and running about. "Parāmarśa" refers to the protection [and care] of sons, grandsons, and so forth.
Due to the heat of the threefold forest fire—consisting of internal and other factors—instigated by that [passion], he fell into the pit of misfortune at the banyan tree. || 35 ||
His limbs were worn out by the hardships of wallowing in the creeper of Fortune;
grasping at the river of the glory of craving, he was struck far away by its surging waves. (36)
"Lakṣmī" refers to prosperity; "on creepers characterized by that" means by being entwined around the feet of trees.

"With limbs impaired" refers to the hardships of imprisonment, beating, punishment, and so forth, inflicted by enemies, thieves, kings, and others. "By waves" refers to the surges characterized by hunger, thirst, grief, delusion, old age, and death.
Devoted solely to flight due to the distress caused by disease and evil hunters,
he performed his actions with unhesitating resolve, as if fearing the fall of a hunter's arrow.
He by whom fate (daiva) was not suspected or considered as a governing principle is one whose actions are rendered fruitless and whose form is shrunken. || 37 ||
Apprehensive of the arrows of suffering that had reached the very seat of his knowable objects, he was intent on routing his enemies and marked by the carrying of stones. || 38 ||

He was apprehensive of the arrows of suffering arriving from the sources— the objects of perception such as sights for the eyes and other sensory organs, and the sounds of songs, the ringing of bells, sprouts, and so forth— which serve as the causes [of attachment], such as hunters, fields, and the like; as if from blows delivered by stones or weapons.
It is marked by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) resulting from the experience of suffering in each preceding [life]. || 38 ||
It was violently tossed about by the rising and falling of elevations and depressions,
and it was gradually pulverized by the impact of the stones of its own transformations.
By means of successive rising and falling in the high and low realms, such as heaven and hell;
regarding the phrase "marked by the fetching of stones," he shows the meaning of the word *dṛṣad* (stone) with the words "modifications" (*vikāra*).
Modifications are desire, anger, fear, and so forth. This occurs through succession, that is, in an uninterrupted sequence. || 39 ||
Wounded by being drawn into the net of the beautiful creeper of craving, his conduct fashioned by his own ignorance, he was thoroughly schooled in supreme deceit. (40)
Having come to the collection of the senses, he was intent on fleeing,
crushed by the fierce, thundering, and violent trampling of a great, most difficult-to-seize elephant-king.
Desire is a lordly elephant that is extremely difficult to grasp. || 41 ||
Fainted by the potent venomous hiss of the python of sensory objects, the lustful man is generally cast down upon the ground of women by his own passion. (42)
Crushed and trampled. || 42 ||
Burning with the bursting blisters on his back caused by the forest fire of anger, he is constantly tormented by the burning of many long-lasting sufferings involving repeated coming and going. (43)

Scorched and consumed by the forest fire of anger, he suffers an external burning as if from blisters on his back; meanwhile, due to constant coming and going— repeated wanderings among sense objects— he suffers an internal burning through the long-lasting miseries of endless anxiety, grief, and the like.
Afflicted by the defects of the partiality of desire clinging to one's own self,
he is long pursued by the jackals of the pleasures of enjoyment, greed, and vanity.
Chased by the panther of poverty, which is deluded by its own agency in action, his body tumbles into the pit of the mountain-peak of blindness caused by the mist of confusion. (45)

Pursued by the tiger of poverty, blinded by the mist of delusion characterized by attachment to wife and children, his body rolls upon deceptive pitfalls, mountain peaks, lowly deeds, and deep chasms. (45)
Distressed by the trembling of his heart at the sight of Mānasiṃha’s exultation,
he regarded death in battle as if it were a *vṛkapuṣpa* flower.

The trembling of the heart is fear; by that he is afflicted. By which [fear]—well-known as death, like a tiger in battle—he is seized, taken, or torn apart by the claws (varkāḥ) which are his own nails; he is seen as one whose happiness is being plucked away like a flower. 46.
He was avoided from afar by people because of his pride, as if he were a devouring fire;
on all sides, his desires were like the sprouts of barley spread out upon his tusks.
Because people were swallowed from afar by that great python of pride for the sake of its prey, it was frequented—meaning it was long awaited—in that vast forest.

By means of desires acting as instruments, the luster of his teeth, like barley sprouts, was spread out and expanded on all sides, as if by the gaping of his jaws due to wretchedness and the like. (47)
For a moment embraced by youth, his friend, he was then abandoned;
deserted by the winds of the groves as if they were enraged, leaving him to traverse difficult paths. (48)
For the sake of women, with youth as his companion and not acting on his own accord,

he was repeatedly abandoned and cast into the difficult-to-traverse wildernesses of the womb-destinies of hell-beings, stationary beings, and so forth, by the senses which are like violent gales. (48)
O King, sometimes that charming deer attains peace and tranquility under a certain tree, as if finding its livelihood in the sun.

"O King!"— this is an address to Daśaratha by virtue of his future state, or to Rāma. Such a charming young deer, at some time when the fortune arising from the ripening of merit accumulated over many births has dawned,

and during a birth as a qualified person, may it be described according to its characteristics in such a way that it is endowed with the means [of liberation], such as tranquility (śama) and the rest.

In the higher meditations, one attains *nirvṛti*, the bliss of rest. The meaning is that just as the multitude of living beings (*ājīva*), who are tormented by cold and darkness at night, attain *nirvṛti* when the radiant sun has risen, so it is here. || 49 ||

May that tree of tranquility grant you peace— the very name of whose bliss the deluded do not even know, though they rest beneath tāla, tamāla, bakula, and other trees and shrubs amidst the laughter of abundant blossoming flowers.

O listeners, for that which is called the "Ground" (*bhūmi*), the unsurpassed [state], whose semblance of transient enjoyments— resembling the playful smiles of abundant flowers— is found in the dwellings of the worlds from the earth up to the world of truth (*satyaloka*), which are like resting at the foot of trees such as the *tālī* and *tāla*.

The meaning is this: fools—people devoid of self-knowledge—do not even know by name such a bliss as the rest of liberation from which there is no return; yet your deer-like mind attains it from the wish-fulfilling tree of meditation, which has been nourished through the watering of the seed in the field and so forth, according to the method previously described. || 50 ||

Thus ends the forty-fourth canto, titled "The Description of the Misfortune of the Deer of the Mind," in the Nirvāṇa Section of the Liberation Chapter of the glorious Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa, composed by the sage Vālmīki.

Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Misfortunes of the Deer of the Mind," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa within the Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa.
The forty-fifth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Thus, O slayer of enemies, this deer of the mind has come to rest.
There alone he finds delight; he does not go to another branch. || 1 ||
The process of ascending the tree of meditation of the mind is described;
as one ascends through the successive stages, there is an ever-increasing excellence of bliss.
He is the Arhat; in that regard, [it is] precisely in the *Dhyānakalpataru* [that this is stated]. || 1 ||
Then, after this much time, that tree of discernment gradually and fully brings forth its fruit,
which is the supreme reality residing within.
By this much time— described previously from the beginning of the cluster (gucchārambha) up to its conclusion, and from the beginning of the mental deer’s rest up to its end—

that tree of meditation accompanied by discernment has been described; [and thus] the ultimate Self, the supreme reality, which resides within, which resides within the five sheaths, and which resides within the cluster, [is revealed as] the fruit of liberation, one's own true essential nature.

It brings to manifestation—that is, it causes one to directly experience—that which is being matured through the gradual process of ascending the stages (bhūmikās) that will be described hereafter. || 2 ||
That deer of his own mind, standing at the foot of that tree of merit which is the fruit of meditation,
gazes up at its fruit situated at the very top.

In this regard, first of all, he shows the door to the fourth stage—a direct realization consisting primarily of conviction—arising from the slight diminution of the defect of non-conviction, like a jar or similar object seen in dim light, by means of the verse beginning with "dhyāna":
"Prāntagatam" means situated at the very end, attached to the tip of a branch. || 3 ||
A man climbs a tree to taste its fruit;
he possesses an extensive resolve and abandons other groups of objects. (4)
The description as "a man" is used because his former animal form was no longer functional for climbing trees and because he had ceased from the nature of a fickle beast. || 4 ||
Having attained the elevated state, one abandons the worldly activities rooted in the earth, known as the "shadows of the tree of discernment," and no longer desires what is below.

He explains how one ascends: "By means of discrimination" (*viveka*). Having first become one whose foot is firmly established upon the tree of discrimination, he abandons the former tendencies—such as the notions of "I" and "mine"—which were rooted in the ground of transmigratory existence regarding the body and other objects. The elision of the word *pāda* (foot) [in the compound] is according to the rule *ahastyādibhyaḥ*, which prescribes the elision of the final member of the compound.
The meaning is that he does not look downward, because his gaze and mind are fixed with vigilance solely upon those parts of the trees that must be climbed and grasped. || 5 ||
Therefore, for the sake of the supreme fruit, having ascended the tree of discernment, he casts off his former formative predispositions (saṃskāras) just as a snake sheds its skin.
He abandons the formative predispositions; that is to say, he does not remember anything from the past. || 6 ||
Beholding himself ascended to such a high station, he laughs aloud, wondering, "What kind of wretched person was I for all this time? (7)
Sometimes, by chance, even while remembering [the truth], he laughs; the miser is wretched from his longing for mere fragments of sensual pleasure. || 7 ||
Wandering among those qualities such as compassion like one moving through the branches of a tree, he shines forth like a sovereign emperor, bringing the serpent of greed under his control.

"Compassion, pity for all beings"—from the first word onward, divine endowments such as fearlessness, purity of being, and steadfastness in the yoga of knowledge are understood. Wandering among the other branches of this tree characterized by those [qualities], he sports at the time of emergence like a sovereign whose desires are fulfilled. || 8 ||
Day by day, craving— the dark iron chain that is the row of throats for the moon of the heart and the mass of darkness for the lotus of suffering— is cast off.

As this heart-moon— the moon of right understanding— wanes, it is called "gala" (the throat), being the cause of the loss of its digits (*kalā*) due to the New Moon (*darśa*). This [state] is like a chain (*śṛṅkhalā*) fashioned from a particular kind of black iron (*kṛṣṇāyasa*), which is a series (*paṅkti*) of darkness (*timira*)— a specific eye disease— that causes the illusion of multiplicity in the lotus-like moon of suffering.

Such craving, which is the cause of bondage for living beings, begins to diminish day by day starting from the day of undertaking the desire for the auspicious, and it is completely abandoned at the fourth stage. This is the sense, based on the Lord’s statement: "Even his taste for worldly objects ceases upon seeing the Supreme. (9)
He remains equanimous toward what has not been attained and does not long for what has not yet arrived;
gentle as the moon, he becomes inwardly cool in all his mental states.
Seated upon the very sprouts of the meaning of the scriptures, he remains with his mind fixed there, looking down at the movements of the world as they rise and fall. (11)

The "scripture" refers to the spiritual science (*adhyātma-śāstra*), and its "meanings" are tranquility, self-control, contentment, and so forth; these are found in the "leaves," meaning the sprouts that characterize such teachings. When living beings follow the path according to other (worldly) scriptures, they rise as high as the world of Brahmā;
yet when following their natural inclinations, they descend as far as hell. Thus, the downward movements of the world occur only during the state of ignorance.
Beholding. || 11 ||
Beholding his own former grounds, which were bristling with heaps of flowers scattered by the terrifying trees and creepers, he laughs inwardly at their wretchedness.

Beholding and remembering those seven previously described grounds of ignorance— the terrifying and fearsome lands where the earth is made jagged by protruding clusters of poisonous flowers from venomous trees and creepers, appearing as if they stood with their high fangs bared— he gazed upon them.
Moving through those regions of the sky with a charming gait that alternates between soaring upward and swooping down,
he shines like a king among his subjects.

Having ascended the trunk-regions of that tree of meditation—which are distinguished by the successive higher stages—and having descended during the state of practice, he moves as if by flying and gliding; thus, he dwells with a mental state characterized by such a mode of being. || 13 ||
One perceives one's sons, wives, friends, and wealth—all together—as if they were produced in another birth, or as if they were born of a dream. (14)
Due to the great power of passion, hatred, fear, madness, pride, and delusion, these [afflictions] are seen in him whose mind is cool and pure, just as they appear in an actor. 15.
In worldly conduct, his activities are seen through a fabricated display of great passion and so forth, which, like that of an actor, is primarily intended merely to delight others.
The word "activities" (*vyavahārāḥ*) is to be supplied [as the object of "are seen"]. || 15 ||
The courses of the rivers of worldly existence, with currents as fickle as waves, appear before one like the behavior of a madman even as they laugh. (16)
Even when confronted by the courses of the mirage-rivers of saṃsāra, he laughs at them with the realization that they are false.
He does not direct his thoughts toward any desires for the world, wife, or wealth;
resting in a state never before attained, he is like one already dead while still alive. (17)
Having fixed one's gaze solely upon that solitary, pure, and most exalted nature of consciousness, one ascends to that supreme fruit. || 18 ||
The supreme is the state of the fifth stage. || 18 ||
Constantly recollecting his former states and nourished by the nectar of contentment,
he remains fully satisfied even when both gains and losses occur.
In legal affairs, in undertakings, and even in matters that bring about enjoyment,
he experiences supreme agitation, like one who was asleep and has been awakened.

Just as a sleeping person, upon being awakened, experiences distress due to the interruption of the pleasure of sleep, so too this [yogin], being awakened by others regarding necessary duties and worldly affairs, experiences distress due to the interruption of the bliss of meditative absorption (samādhi); such is the meaning. || 20 ||
Like a long-distance traveler who has been overcome by the fatigue of ignorance, he longs for rest— vast, uninterrupted, and eternal.

The meaning is that, having long ago been overcome by the weariness of wandering through the succession of births and deaths caused by ignorance, he now desires only the repose of meditative absorption (samādhi). || 21 ||
Even when awakened by exhalation, the fire within remains as if without fuel;
though equal to the mere breath, it subsides while still abiding inside.
Although equal to other people in mere breathing, he remained as if not at all present due to the internal conceit of the sense of "I"; thus, he comes to rest in the Perfect Self. || 22 ||
He is unable to ward off the dissatisfaction that descends with force upon objects,
just as one cannot turn back a vision that has already fallen away.

The sense is that he is unable to repel the aversion toward external objects—which arises through the force of previous habit—even when it falters or stumbles here among those external things; for it is as if he cannot reject the view of enjoying them as they happen to come, because it is not contrary to his disposition. || 23 ||
Proceeding toward that great state which bestows the fruit of the ultimate truth,
one also attains a stage that is beyond the reach of words.
The stage, namely the sixth stage. || 24 ||
When enjoyments arrive from some source entirely beyond one's own effort, by the power of destiny, one feels a distaste for them, just as a traveler feels toward the lands of a desert.
In the case of those things that are "unwrought"—meaning they are devoid of effort—yet have somehow come into being due to causes such as the effort of another. || 25 ||
Reeling as if exhausted, yet blissful and asleep to the activities of worldly existence,
with an inner mind full and observing silence, he attains an indescribable state.
Having attained such a state, he gradually reaches the proximity of that ultimate fruit, just as a bird reaches the path of the sky.
The bird has attained perfection; he has reached the path of the sky like a bird reaching the peak of Mount Meru or the top of a tree. || 27 ||
Then, having abandoned that entire intellect and becoming equal to the ether,
he grasps, tastes, eats, and finally becomes fully satisfied.

He describes his establishment on the seventh stage with the word "tataḥ" (then). By the phrase "having abandoned all intellect," he indicates the absolute destruction of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and the dissolution of the mind (*manonāśa*) therein. The ellipsis to be supplied is that he "attains the fruit which is the state of Brahman as the bliss of the Infinite (*bhūmānanda*). He attains it through the removal of veils (*āvaraṇabhaṅga*).

"Through unswerving radiance, he relishes; through a mental state inclined solely toward that, he enjoys; through a state of fullness in that very being, he is completely satisfied"—thus is shown here the attainment of the fruits of the fourth and subsequent stages. || 28 ||
The daily expansion resulting from the renunciation of objects of volition,
which is the resting in one’s own pure nature, is called the attainment of the ultimate reality.
He states the secret method for ascending all the stages: "By means of conceptualization," etc. (29).
When the cognition of difference has dissolved its object, non-difference alone remains;
the wise know that to be Brahman—pure, one, and without beginning or end. (30)

Regarding that, he states the means: "bhedeti" (by the dissolution of duality). When the cognition of difference—the witness-consciousness that perceives the distinction between the threefold set [of knower, known, and knowing]—has dissolved, and the objects (the distinctions of the threefold set) have likewise vanished, non-difference alone remains. And that is pure Brahman itself; this is the meaning. || 30 ||
One who is dispassionate toward the desire for worldly life, who has abandoned the desire for a wife,
and who is free from the desire for wealth— by such a person rests in that state.
He states the means for that as well in two verses beginning with "lokaiṣaṇā.
The intention is that by the very abandonment of the desire for a wife, the abandonment of the desire for sons is obtained by implication. || 31 ||
Through a subsequent transformation, the notion of difference between consciousness and ultimate reality dissolves, just as a streak of frost vanishes under the heat.

In the purification of the reality of the object, pure existence (*sanmātra*) is the ultimate truth; in the purification of the reality of the subject, pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) is the ultimate truth.

The meaning is that the final cognitive modification (*vṛtti*), which is the last direct realization, is the transformation of the mind into that supreme Self consisting of unsurpassed bliss, characterized by the indivisible unity of these two. || 32 ||
For one who knows that [reality], once drawn out and released, no state whatsoever can exist within the [conditioned] natures, except through a metaphor such as that of a garland of flowers. (33)

One might object: "When the mental modification (*vṛtti*) in the form of the undivided whole ceases—just as when a bow drawn and released [falls]—is it not inevitable that the mind returns to its previous state?
Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Of one who knows That" (*tajjñasya*).
For one who has attained direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*), [the mind] is like a garland of flowers, exceedingly delicate, unlike the harsh comparison of a bow and so forth.

Stability: Just as a garland fallen on the ground, when pulled up and set back down, remains exactly in that state—whether straight, curved, or otherwise—it does not return to its previous form like a bow; such was the meaning. || 33 ||
Just as a carved statue (śālabhañjikā) situated within a pillar has its limbs unmanifested,
being neither existent nor non-existent in the pillar, so too is the existence of the universe in the Supreme.
Is she dependent on herself, being of the nature of meditation? He says "no," with two verses beginning with "yathā" (as). "With limbs unmanifested" means having her parts unrevealed. || 34 ||
Meditation cannot be performed, nor is it of any use;
for one who has awakened through non-awakening remains right here by himself.

"Let it be so; what follows from that? To this he says: "Meditation. Thus, prior to awakening, because of the non-awakening to the nature of Brahman as being without phenomenal expansion (niṣprapañca-svabhāva) within Brahman which possesses phenomenal expansion (saprapañca), meditation cannot be performed at all. But one who is fully awakened, abiding in that very nature itself, how could he meditate upon it? For neither one who is dreaming nor one who is awake [can meditate on their own state].
The sense is that one is able to meditate upon the Self, thinking, "I am without sleep. || 35 ||
He in whom an absolute lack of relish for visible objects is perceived is a Buddha; for one who is not awakened, there is no power [to abandon the visible]. (36)

With the intention that one who knows reality, remaining vigilant, can only produce a state of absolute distaste for the phenomenal world by regarding it as worthless—just as one does toward the objects of a dream—he says: "Absolute... (verse 36).

The awareness of the visible object as being non-different from pure consciousness, which is never lost from that consciousness—this is designated by the term "samādhi" for one who is perfectly composed. (37)

If there is no meditation (*dhyāna*), then how can there be *samādhi* regarding Brahman, which is not its object, since it is a rule that concentration (*dhāraṇā*), meditation (*dhyāna*), and absorption (*samādhi*) must have the same object? For thus are the aphorisms of the venerable Patañjali: "Concentration is the binding of the mind to a place; meditation is the one-pointed flow of cognition toward that [place]."
"That very [state] which appears as the object alone, as if devoid of its own nature, is samādhi; the unification of these three is *saṃyama*.

Regarding this, he says: "Of the visible," etc. That which is the realization of the visible world—characterized by the triad [of knower, knowledge, and known]—as being nothing but the awareness of the nature of its witness (*sākṣin*), that indeed is [samādhi], well and perfectly, in its true essential state.

The term *samādhi* is expressed by the word *samādhāna* (establishment) through the analysis (*vigraha*) of the compound as "the correct placing (*samyaġ-ādhāna*) because of the cause of placing (*sthāpana*).

The meaning is that, according to the literal sense, the placement of that [reality] within its own true nature is accomplished, since it is from such a nature of awakening that the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) becomes non-perishing and eternal. || 37 ||
When the mental cognition takes the form of the unity of the seer and the seen,
it then naturally comes to rest in that singular concentration.

With the intention that even the statement of Patañjali—"it appears as the mere object, as if devoid of its own nature"—can be easily explained as having the purpose of dissolving the mind by effecting the identity of the seer and the seen, he says: "The seer...
[Verse 38]. The seer is the witness; the triad consisting of the seer, the seen, and the seeing is called *rūpa* because it brings about their unification (*ekatām rūpayati*).
For one who knows reality, the very essence of their own nature is the distaste for the perceptible;
the best of men say that the mere vibration of the perceptible is non-knowledge of reality. (39)

The state of the visible world being devoid of flavor consists in its opposition to the essence of consciousness and bliss, which is characterized by the absence of insentience, suffering, and other such qualities. || 39 ||
Objects of sense please only those who do not know that [Reality], but not those who know it;
for bitter sour gruel does not please one who has drunk nectar within. 40.

Objects have the nature of insentience (*acit-svabhāva*); they appear pleasing only to one who does not know reality, [appearing] as the self consisting of the body and so forth which are of the nature of insentience. [In the phrase "to him who knows that" (*tadvidas*),] the status of the recipient (*saṃpradānatā*) is established by the rule *rucy-arthānāṃ prīyamāṇaḥ*. [In the phrase "of him who knows that" (*tadvidaḥ*),] the genitive case is used because there is an intention to express the relationship of "remainder" (*śeṣatva*) toward that very same person. *Kāñjika* is a specific type of fermented liquor. (40)
For the wise man who is free from craving, established in the self, and has abandoned the three types of seeking,
meditation proceeds spontaneously even though he does not desire it.

But if you consider that meditation is simply the repeated contemplation of one's own true nature, then it is spontaneously accomplished for the wise person who remains vigilant, just as it is for the waking self; thus he says: "For one free from craving" (41).
Awakening flashes forth for one in whom that very thirst does not exist;
having abandoned his own nature, where could he remain, who would he be, and how? 42.
He reveals the intended meaning of the statement "of one who is free from thirst" with the words "bodhaḥ" (awakening).

It is well known that *bodhaḥ*—meditation characterized by the continuous contemplation of one's own true nature—shines forth, that is, it vibrates, as a cause for distractions such as craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and the like. This belongs to that knower of reality (*tattvavit*). And thus, by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣāt*), he states that there is the establishment of the contemplation of one's own true nature alone.
Regarding the word "tasya" (of that): interrogative pronouns (*kiṃvṛtta*) refer to the reflective awareness of the triad consisting of the visible object, the seer, and the act of seeing. || 42 ||
May that realization of the object of meditation, which belongs to the wise one who does not seek to propitiate [others], lead [him]—
for it is infinite for one free from thirst, arising spontaneously as undivided.

Alternatively, for the wise one who is free from thirst, that thirst is infinite and indivisible; for he has arisen as himself, being indeed of the nature of an undivided and unlimited self. Therefore, whatever kind of cognition of an external object—whether it be an object of meditation or something to be reflected upon—may arise, let him lead it into such a state of meditative absorption (samādhi) or worldly activity; nevertheless, he remains as he is.
The meaning is that one who does not propitiate it is incapable of fulfilling its thirst. || 43 ||
For one who is free from craving, meditation proceeds spontaneously and boundlessly,
like the steady stance of a mountain whose wings have fallen away.

Therefore, for one whose thirst for external objects has departed, since that very thirst remains only as the nature of eternal, unsurpassed bliss by process of elimination, infinite meditation characterized by the experience of that [bliss] proceeds spontaneously and does not depend on effort; this is the meaning. || 44 ||
Because it possesses the nature of knowing, the state of non-concentration arises within the pure self;
for a drop of clarified butter never remains in a well-kindled fire. || 45 ||

Therefore, the effort toward *samādhi* lasts only until the arising of pure awakening (*śuddhabodha*). The meaning is that when the nature of pure awakening is directly experienced, "non-concentration" (*asamāhitatva*)—which is the cessation of the effort for *samādhi*—is declared by those who know reality, precisely because it is contradictory to the state of being a knower (*jñatva*). He clarifies this contradiction by means of an illustration:
"Never," [it is said]. || 45 ||
Salutations to that Brahmin among men, by whom supreme detachment from sense-objects has been truly brought forth, and which is declared to be meditative absorption (samādhi). 46.

But the complete eradication of the defects such as passion and the like, which are the causes of distraction—that is true composure—and this belongs only to the wise; therefore, they are worthy of salutation. Thus he says: "The Supreme. It has been brought about, that is, accomplished. || 46 ||
Surely, when freedom from craving for sense objects has reached full maturity,
even the gods and asuras, including Indra himself, are unable to displace one's meditative absorption.

The meaning is that it is precisely because the gods are capable of creating obstacles by inflaming the craving of their own subjects—who are bound by the noose of craving—that they act in this way. || 47 ||
Therefore, let supreme detachment from sense objects and the diamond-like meditation (vajradhyāna) be accomplished;
once differentiation has dissolved through wisdom, what is the use of other meditations that are like mere grass? (48)

And since dispassion toward sense objects has as its ultimate effect the sublation of all objects through knowledge, that very state is also meditation firm like a diamond; thus he praises it with the word "supreme. || 48 ||
The meaning of the word "universe" resides in the fool, yet it is not likewise within the domain of the wise;
and so it is between the knower and the ignorant, as well as between the universe and the Lord of the Universe. (49)
For this very reason, he states that for the wise, the word "universe" (viśva) has its referent sublated, by saying "mūrkha... (foolish...).
The phrase "of the knower and the ignorant," etc., connects with the subsequent verse. "Of those two" refers to their respective knowledge or ignorance of that specific distinction. || 49 ||
O wise ones, rest there where all things shine as one—in the planes of awakening of the perfected ones, or in the objects of those who possess discernment. (50)

In that state of abundant bliss (*bhūmānanda*), it is said that there is a "shining forth as one" (*ekībhūya-kacana*) with the intention of subverting duality, but not with the intention of numerical oneness. For, among those who possess discrimination— whether they are seekers (*ārurukṣu*) on the stages of understanding through reflection (*manana*) and so forth,

or those who have attained realization (*ārūḍha*) on the stages of understanding through direct intuition (*sākṣātkāra*) and so forth— the existence or non-existence, and the duality or unity, of anything other than the Self [are understood accordingly].
And the grammatical connection is that [this] has not been determined by anyone at all. || 50 ||

Since existence and non-existence, as well as duality and unity, have been determined here by no one else, there is but one means: the purpose of the scripture and, secondly, association with those who possess knowledge. (51)

In that regard, he states the means for attaining rest: "The means" refers to the study of the scripture—that is, the repeated practice with reverence and continuity of the meaning of the scripture, which is the spiritual science (*adhyātmaśāstra*). || 51 ||
The third dhyāna is supreme in Nirvāṇa; therein, each succeeding stage is superior.
Through the mirror of the individual soul (jīva), one perceives the form of the other; this is the Great Body (Mahadvapuḥ).

It is superior due to the greater proximity to the fruit. Thus, in order to demonstrate that both the knowledge born of inquiry and dispassion are means to liberation and are established in mutual dependence,
[the text speaks] of passion and aversion, which are dependent on the limitation of the individual soul's adjuncts caused by non-discrimination.
He demonstrates the conceptualization of equality and inequality arising from contact with pleasant and unpleasant objects through the verse beginning with "jīva":
This Brahman-consciousness, whose body is great (mahadvapuḥ) and thus unlimited, which is eternally immediate,

appears mutually distinct from one another due to the influence of the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), which serves as a mirror for the reflection called the individual soul (jīva).
It grasps form. || 52 ||

In this world, from the friction of two things that are exactly alike, there arises no distinction whatsoever for one who has previously known the entire world situated like a chessboard of eight squares. (53)

In this world, due to the encounter with the pleasant and the unpleasant, it arises—without distinction—that is, pervading all specific entities from Brahmā down to a blade of grass—in various even and uneven bodily forms according to the diversity of one's own karma; such is the meaning. Thus, among the individual souls (jīvas) wandering through beginningless time:

The logical connection is as follows: through the dawn of good fortune for someone, in a birth suitable for the qualification of knowledge, by obtaining means such as the study of scriptures and association with the virtuous, one realizes that all previous and subsequent births and deaths are a wandering in delusion;
thus, when one of the two lamps—consisting of the awakening [to truth] and the thirstlessness [for worldly objects]—is established, both are established. || 53 ||
When one is established, both are established: the lamp of awakening and the lamp of dispassion.
Shaken by the whirlwind of the intellect in the sky of consciousness, everything is consumed by the fire of knowledge. (54)

Burnt by the fire of knowledge and reduced to ashes, the entire world-cotton, having been shaken off and blown away by the whirlwind of the intellect— characterized by the practice of higher stages within the space of consciousness—
I know not where it goes. 54.
I do not know where this world-cotton quickly goes into the supreme peace;
by that awakening, as if by a variegated fire, dullness is not extinguished.

He states that only a cognition capable of removing delusion is the cause for uprooting the dullness born of fundamental ignorance, and not mere superficial knowledge—by means of the phrase "with the variegated fire. Here, *jāḍya* refers to both ignorance and cold. || 55 ||
Even though the delusion of the world is rootless, it does not quickly dissolve; just as for the ignorant person, the perception of the world is intensified by their lack of knowledge. (56)

Just as the delusion of saṃsāra manifests through the increase of ignorance characterized by the insistence of the ignorant, so too, through the increase of thorough knowledge, ignorance is burned away more and more on the successive stages for one who knows reality;
thus he says: "Just as... (verse 56).
Likewise, through the thorough knowledge of the Knower, the non-perception of that [world] is illuminated;
for one who knows that, the perception of the ignorant world remains devoid of both word and meaning.
When ignorance is being consumed by fire, what kind of world appears to them? To this he says: "To the knower of that... (verse 57).
The cognition of the three worlds, just as it exists, has arisen like a painting;
it is fashioned by emptiness itself, as if constructed from sleep.
The luminous desire that is the cognition of the world shines within the mind of the knower;
indeed, for one who is undeluded in awakening, there is neither egoism nor the persistence of the world. (59)
The word "avimūḍhasya" (of one who is not deluded) is the division [of the compound]. || 59 ||
There is a certain state of being which shines as the form of supreme radiance; the mind, consisting of both consciousness and unconsciousness, appears like dry and wet wood.
He then states what that appears like for one who is half-awake: "bādha" (sublation), etc. || 60 ||
The world is one with consciousness, yet it does not attain selfhood due to its insentience;
through mutual consciousness, it disputes, but through the realization of consciousness, it resorts to friendship.
Like the two [natures], it possesses both natures. Through awakening, by virtue of its excellence in awakening, it practices supreme loving-kindness toward all beings;

the meaning is that it regards pleasure and pain with compassion as if they were its own. Or, through non-awakening, by way of its portion of non-awakening, it disputes or engages in worldly transactions such as contention. || 61 ||
The wise person remains identified with that very portion which is predominant; he does not perceive the true nature of the world’s existence and non-existence. (62)
But the wise person whose knowledge is fully matured does not at all perceive the true nature or reality of the world’s existence and non-existence, or its being and non-being. (62)

Just as one who has reached the fourth state (turya) perceives the nature of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, so too this mind, which is nothing but latent impressions (vāsanā), perishes through self-inquiry. 63.
Just as one who has mounted the seventh stage on a chariot does not perceive the nature of the waking state and so forth, so it is here;

thus, the simile is employed because of the conceptualization of difference. Now, since the resting of the deer of the mind upon the tree of meditation is the subject at hand, the attainment of the fruit of the supreme human goal must be described as occurring when that very mind ascends [to that height] in another form; therein lies the characteristic of the dissolution of the mind (*manonāśa*).
To the question of how liberation could be a human goal for such a person, he says: "It is merely latent impression" (vāsanaiva). || 63 ||
Therefore, because it is not a real entity, liberation does not proceed from the destruction of the self. || 64 ||

"Because it is not a real entity. Thus, the sense is that the description of the very Self—through its illusory and charming deer-form—coming to rest in misfortune and so forth, is what has been introduced. || 64 ||
Having gradually attained awakening from the tree of meditation, which had matured of its own accord over time into a great fruit,
and having tasted the elixir-fruit of supreme primordial enlightenment, the deer-like mind is released from its fetters.

Thus, he concludes that this destruction of the mind (*manonāśa*), described by means of the metaphor of the deer-like mind, has borne fruit as being equivalent to the liberation from the fetters of the Self— stating "meditation" (*dhyāna*) and so forth. Desiring liberation, the aforementioned deer-like mind,

having abandoned the vast forest characterized by the stages of transformation beginning with the sprout and ending with the fruit— namely, the root, stem, branch, leaf, flower, and fruit— [attains its goal].

The meaning is that by eating the fruit of the elixir, characterized by supreme bliss— which is the primary awakening from the tree of meditation, manifested through a mental modification in the form of the indivisible whole— one becomes liberated from the shackles of saṃsāra. || 65 ||
Thus ends the forty-fifth canto, titled "The Narrative of Manoharaṇikā," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the glorious Vāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa of Valmīki, composed by the Sage. 45.
Thus ends the forty-fifth canto, titled "The Narrative of Manoharaṇikā," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The Forty-sixth Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
When the fruit of the supreme reality has been known and has reached its culmination in liberation,
Even awakening quickly becomes non-existent; the deer of the mind is the ultimate reality.
The state of the mind when tasting the fruit of the tree of meditation, and the firm distaste for sense objects— just as it is, so is it described here.

When [the Self] is known—that is, directly experienced—the cognition, which is even the final state of direct realization (*sākṣātkāra-vṛtti*), becomes non-existent due to the sublation of its own material cause, ignorance; and the deer of the mind likewise becomes the Self alone, which is the supreme human goal. This is the meaning. || 1 ||
Somewhere that state of being a "deer" (or delusion) vanishes like a lamp whose oil is exhausted;
there remains only the vision of ultimate reality, shining forth infinitely.
That former state of being a deer, characterized by the nature of craving for sense objects and seeking them, passes away and departs. || 2 ||

When the mind has attained awakening through the fruition of the tree of meditation, it maintains a state of adamantine essence, remaining as motionless as a mountain whose wings have been clipped. (3)
Stability is the absence of wavering. || 3 ||
Mental agitation vanishes somewhere; pure awareness alone remains—unimpeded, undivided, and the essence of all that exists (or, according to both readings, "the soul of all"). || 4 ||

The state of mind is the nature of thinking about external objects; it is entirely full. For this very reason, the state of consciousness—which is pure awareness alone—remains uncontracted (or, according to both readings, "consisting of all"). || 4 ||
Through its state of perfect seclusion, the existence of the mind arises as awakening;
it is without beginning or end, and bestows the fruit of pure luminosity.

That very existence which was previously as if inert within the mind due to the lack of discrimination from the inert body and so forth, now stands as if arisen in the form of pure awareness because of its complete distinction from the body and so forth; for this means that it bestows the fruit of the manifestation of ultimate reality. || 5 ||
Then, there, by itself,
only meditation remains— devoid of all desires, without beginning or end, and effortless.
The meaning is that, since all desires have been cast aside, meditation on one's own Self alone is understood by way of elimination, because there is no other possible resort. || 6 ||

As long as Brahman has not been realized and one has not come to rest in the supreme state, so long is that [mental activity] understood as mere cogitation (manana) and not as meditative absorption (dhyāna).
When, then, is that mind not in meditation? To this he says: "as long as... That [mind], by virtue of its nature as a thinking organ—that is, by virtue of its pursuit of other objects. || 7 ||
Having attained oneness with the ultimate reality, I know not where the mind has gone;
where are the latent impressions, where are the karmas, and where are the perceptions of joy and anger? (8)
The yogi is seen alone, having attained exclusive devotion to meditation;
established in the diamond-like concentration (*vajrasamādhi*), he is like a mountain impervious to opposing forces.
Since his meditative absorption (*samādhi*) is also established by implication from his possession of meditation (*dhyāna*), he says "merely" in two verses: || 9 ||

For the yogi who has become dispassionate toward all enjoyments, whose sensory perceptions and consciousness are stilled, for whom every visible object is devoid of flavor, and who delights in his own self; || 10 ||
For one whose mental fluctuations have gradually dissolved and who has attained rest by force, who indeed could question the meditative absorption that has thus arisen spontaneously? (11)
Those of refined disposition cultivate a distaste for sense objects to such an extent that they do not perceive those enjoyments at all, just like a person in a painting.
He states that for such a person, even supreme detachment is established as a matter of course, saying "tāvat" (to that extent): "citranara" refers to persons depicted in a painting.
Not perceiving worldly objects due to the absence of latent impressions,
the self-possessed man is forcibly settled by another, as if in the concentration of a diamond.
In a concentration that is as indivisible as a diamond, one is forcibly established by another, as if by a restrainer, within that meditative absorption. || 13 ||
When that meditative absorption has arrived— like a river in flood during the rainy season—
my mind does not waver again, even though it was previously driven by force.
That samādhi which, having arisen as the singular essence of bliss, presents itself during the first stage—
tasting that one-pointedness which has arrived solely through the power of the object's own nature according to the analogy of the sugar-cane and the ant— the mind does not move away from it. 14.
When, through the cooling of all objects, one has arrived at meditative absorption by force, that dispassion toward sense-objects arising from knowledge is indeed *samādhi*, and nothing else. (15)

That very state of distaste for other objects which arises from knowledge and power is itself *samādhi*; for it is never observed that anyone achieves composure when the mind is being scorched by passion and the like. || 15 ||
The firm distaste for sense objects alone is declared to be meditation;
that very state, through its full maturation, becomes truly adamantine in essence.
In the same way, he states that rebirth in the meditative absorptions (dhyāna) also occurs only when there is a distaste for sense objects, and not otherwise: "Firmly," [verse 16].
This very freedom from craving for enjoyments is indeed the sprouting of meditation;
when that same [craving] is bound by the firming of the foundation, it becomes beautiful.

And thus, although there is no difference between them, the distinction in terminology is established: the absence of craving for enjoyments is the seed, *dhyāna* is its state as a sprout, and *samādhi* is its fully grown state. He states this with the words "tadetad" (this very thing). || 17 ||
Right knowledge, fully expanded and forever abandoned of latent impressions, becomes meditation; having reached the state of bliss, it is Nirvana. (18)

He says "samyak" (rightly) [in verse 18], explaining that Brahman itself, manifested through the mental modification of direct realization (*sākṣātkāra-vṭtti*), is designated as "knowledge" (*jñāna*) by virtue of destroying ignorance (*avidyā*), as "meditation" (*dhyāna*) by virtue of destroying latent impressions (*vāsanā*), and as "liberation" (*nirvāṇa*) by virtue of being the nature of bliss that destroys all suffering.
If there is freedom from craving for enjoyments, what else is needed with that "evil-mindedness" regarding meditation?
If there is freedom from craving for enjoyments, what else is needed with that "evil-mindedness" regarding meditation? (19)

All this is accomplished only when there is freedom from craving for enjoyments, and not otherwise; therefore, he praises that very state in order to strengthen it, beginning with the words "And it exists," etc. (19).
For the sage who has abandoned the enjoyment of the visible world and possesses perfect knowledge, non-conceptual meditative absorption proceeds without interruption. (20)

He for whom the visible world does not taste sweet is known as a perfectly awakened one (saṃbuddha); when enjoyments no longer taste sweet, perfect awakening (samyagbodha) is thus said to have arisen.
How can there be the state of an enjoyer for one whose nature is at rest?
For that which lacks intrinsic nature is indeed non-existence; when that is destroyed, how and from where could it [the enjoyer] arise? (22)

He states that the state of being an enjoyer (*bhogitva*), which is opposed to the nature of absolute non-duality (*pūrṇādvaya-svabhāva*), is possible only during the time when there is a perversion of nature caused by ignorance (*ajñāna*), and not after the destruction of ignorance—thus: "Of whom... (verse 22).
At the conclusion of hearing, recitation, and mantra-repetition, one should be devoted to meditative absorption;
when weary from meditative absorption, one should resort to hearing, recitation, and mantra-repetition.

What should be done by one who has emerged from meditation during the time of practice, or when should samādhi be cultivated? He states that sequence [in the verse beginning] with "śruta": *śruta* is the hearing of the Vedānta together with the guru, fellow students, and others; *pāṭha* is the repeated recitation of the Upaniṣads and so forth; *japa* is the silent repetition of the *praṇava* and other mantras. Thus it is said in the Skanda Purāṇa: "One who is weary from *japa*..."
When weary from meditation, one should meditate again; when weary from recitation, one should recite again. To one who is devoted to both recitation and meditation, the Supreme Śiva becomes gracious.

Thus, one should sit in liberation—free from all weariness, delightful through the subsiding of all doubts, as gentle as deep sleep, with a mind equally tranquil, and pure within like the expanse of an autumnal cloud.
With the intention that even there one must always cultivate the preeminence of meditative absorption (samādhi), he concludes with the words "Nirvāṇa.
This is clear. || 24 ||
Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Realization of Equanimity," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the glorious Vāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa of Valmīki, composed by the Sage. 46.
Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Realization of Equanimity," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The forty-seventh canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Exhausted by the burden of worldly existence, with his body rolling in calamities,
Listen to this sequence for one who desires rest. || 1 ||
Furthermore, as the detailed description of the sequence of the means to liberation is commenced,
it is here described up to the attainment of firm dispassion.

Relying on the maxim that "wholesome advice should be spoken even many times," the supremely compassionate Vasiṣṭha— having previously described the sequence of stages for the means to liberation beginning with *śubhecchā*, which are charming as they lead toward the cultivation, protection, and fruition of the tree of meditation, and provide refuge for the deer-like mind— now explains again, at various points, the attainment of specific qualities at each stage.
Desiring to describe this clearly by way of exposition for the awakening of those of duller faculties, he turns the disciple toward its hearing with the words "saṃsāra... (the cycle of existence).
[He describes] that whose bodies roll about in the perils of death, fainting, and so forth; [and] the sequence therein and there.
The sequence of attaining the excellence of qualities. || 1 ||
When, previously, a tiny spark of discernment arises within one’s own heart—consisting of world-weariness—whether from a specific cause or even without a cause; || 2 ||
In that regard, he shows which qualities are acquired upon the arising of the sprout of discernment (*viveka*) with the words beginning "previously" (*pūrvam*).
From a cause—that is, from worldly sacrifices, austerities, gifts, and so forth, which are causes for the destruction of sin; or from no cause—that is, in the absence of such [worldly] means.
For those whose sins have been exhausted solely by virtuous deeds performed in previous births, [these qualities arise] from childhood itself.

The meaning is that the dawn of discernment is seen even without any worldly cause. As soon as a tiny spark of discernment consisting of world-weariness (*nirveda*) arises, at that very moment the virtues to be described—being "well-expanded" or vast in their excellence—take refuge in him;
this is the connection with the following verse. || 2 ||

Then, scorched by the heat, they resort to those who possess good character and are exceedingly vast, who remove the fatigue of the journey, just as those tormented by the sun seek out trees by the roadside that provide cool shade.
In this regard, there is an illustration: just as men scorched by heat [seek out] shady trees along the road. || 3 ||
Like a traveler avoiding the sacrificial posts of the ignorant, he keeps those who lack knowledge far away;
following the gods, he performs ablutions, charity, austerity, and sacrifice.

Regarding this, he says "far away" (dūre) to indicate that the abandonment of association with ignorant people, devotion to sacrifice, charity, and so forth, and virtues such as the propitiation of the deities arise first. In the same way, the subsequent virtues are to be applied accordingly. || 4 ||
He maintains a conduct that is graceful, appropriate, and unartificial—a worldly delight that bears nectar like the orb of the moon. (5)
The lunar orb, acting as the agent, pours forth nectar as its object—nectar which is beneficial for the worlds through its transformation and provides immediate delight. (5)
Following the wisdom of others, capable, and fulfilling the welfare of others,
a certain gentle person proceeds, delighting in pure deeds.

Because he is free from attachment, greed, pride, and the like toward his own faction, and because he acts for the benefit of others, he follows the wisdom of others; for this very reason, he becomes beloved by all people, and thus he is "fortunate" (bhavya). Being gentle and superior to all people, he engages in and conducts himself through pure activities—those not forbidden by the scriptures—and takes delight therein. 6.
Like a vessel of fresh butter—clear, smooth, soft, and enchanting—her sweet new acquaintance brings happiness to people. (7)
The vessel of butter (*navanīta-sthalī*) is like the clear and smooth whey (*dadhi-maṇḍa*), which is the primary support; such is the common [simile].

"New acquaintance" (*nava-saṅgati*) means the first meeting. The adjective "new" (*nava*) is used to indicate that through the process of churning, separating, and ripening, a long-standing association becomes increasingly essential and thus a cause for obtaining a more delicious result. || 7 ||
The cool and pure deeds of the discerning person thoroughly refresh people, just as the clusters of rays from the moon do.
One does not rest so fearlessly in garden groves filled with heaps of flowers as one does in the company of the virtuous.
Like the waters of the Mandākinī, the associations of the discerning wash away sins and bestow purity. (10)
Among those who possess discernment, who are dispassionate, and who seek to cross over saṃsāra,
people find coolness as if in houses of ice and crystal.
In houses as if constructed from snow and pearl necklaces. || 11 ||
Indeed, that noble joy of love which exists in one who possesses discernment is not found even among the daughters of the gods and gandharvas, nor among human women. (12)
"It does not exist"—this is the ellipsis to be supplied. || 12 ||
The wisdom of one who performs appropriate actions gradually attains clarity;
it grasps the meaning of the scriptures within itself, just as a mirror reflects an object. (13)

From the cause of performing appropriate, desireless action (*niṣkāmakarman*) in due succession, wisdom attains growth, clarity, and purification. And through that purity, when the desire for knowledge (*vividiṣā*) arises, one internalizes the meaning of the scriptures heard from the mouth of the teacher;
the meaning is that one establishes it within the heart, just as a mirror-surface holds its own reflected object. || 13 ||

Abounding in the essence of the meaning of the scriptures, true wisdom attains its full development through the grace of one possessed of discernment, just as a plantain tree flourishes in a great forest. (14)
In the discerning one, within the abode of the heart possessed of discrimination; by means of playful expansion, such as the growth of roots and sprouts. || 14 ||
Wisdom, characterized by stainless purity, experiences all objects reflected within itself entirely, just like a mirror. (15)
That discerning wisdom experiences all objects as being nothing other than the internal play of the mind. || 15 ||
One whose soul is purified by the company of the virtuous and who has been cleansed by the meaning of the scriptures shines like a cloth purified by fire, its impurities removed.
"Purity in fire" refers to a garment that is purified by the burning away of its impurities, like a precious cloth;

for it is well-known in the scriptures that such a divine *siddhāmbara* (attainable garment), once the stains have been burnt, shines forth even more brilliantly when drawn from the fire, like a mass of lightning. || 16 ||
The virtuous person shines with his own splendor, which possesses the luster of glittering gold and produces stainless light, just as the world shines by means of the sun.
The virtuous one is discerning; by his own splendor, that is, by the internal light of the Self. || 17 ||
In this way, the wise person pursues both the scriptures and the company of the virtuous, so that through constant association he experiences those very two. (18)

Through the practice of the scripture and by serving the virtuous guru, he follows and pursues them incessantly; such that, through constant attachment characterized by an intense absorption in the meaning taught by them,
he experiences nothing other than contemplation of them and devotion to serving them even in his dreams, and never anything else due to such attachment even in his dreams.
The meaning is that one experiences only those two—being intent on reflecting upon Him and being devoted to serving Him—and nothing beyond them, not even one's own body and so forth.

Gradually attaining the state of a virtuous person and being permeated by the weight of the meaning of the scriptures, he shines while disregarding worldly enjoyments, as if having emerged from a cage. (19)

Through the gradual process of destroying defects such as passion, hatred, greed, and negligence, and accumulating virtues such as loving-kindness, one attains the state of a virtuous person—a state characterized by being free from faults and endowed with excellent qualities. || 19 ||
By him, who day by day cast off the misfortune of failing to obtain enjoyments,
