his family shone like the circle of stars with the moon.

The pursuit of enjoyments (*bhogābhigama*) is the act of approaching sense objects due to addiction; misfortune is characterized by that. A lineage (*kula*), meaning a family line and the social circle formed by it, shines forth. || 20 ||
No trace of miserliness regarding enjoyments ever arose in him; there was an unprecedented luster upon his face, like that of the moon when it is free from Rāhu. (21)
Free from the miserliness of attachment to enjoyments, a certain unprecedented splendor now radiates from his face;
it is as if he were liberated from Rāhu—meaning, like the moon when released from Rāhu. || 21 ||
To the great ones who treat the three worlds as mere straw, that wish-granting tree becomes an object of mention only in name,
like a celestial tree in the sky to the inhabitants of heaven.
The state of being expressible and praiseworthy; in the sky, that is, in heaven. || 22 ||
Feeling inward shame even in his mind due to his aversion to enjoyments, he is supremely satisfied even by the non-attainment of those enjoyments. (23)

The meaning is this: although one might feel satisfaction in renouncing enjoyments already obtained, yet even while feeling shame in one's mind—thinking, "How is it that I, who have abandoned all hatred, have felt hatred toward enjoyments?"—one is not truly satisfied. However, due to the non-attainment or lack of enjoyments, there is no occasion for such shame; therefore, one is supremely satisfied. The word *api* (even/also) is used in the sense of *tu* (but/rather). || 23 ||
The base man, his face smiling with exhaustion, mocks within himself those young women of restless movements, as if he were one who remembers his past births.

Recalling now his former young women—who were mature in passion and the like—and his own past actions, which were restless with a longing for enjoyment, he smiles inwardly with a face full of sorrow, as one might laugh at his own kind; the meaning is that it is just as when a low-born person, such as a Cāṇḍāla, having by chance regained the memory of his former births, laughs inwardly at his own previous caste. || 24 ||
Then virtuous people come to see him out of sheer affection, their eyes wide with wonder, like those who behold the moon risen over the earth. (25)
To see such a one; the virtuous are the perfected ones. || 25 ||
Having eternally disregarded enjoyment, he therefore does not highly esteem even the enjoyment that has been obtained through appropriate exertion, owing to his proper understanding.

Then, he did not highly regard the enjoyment of supernatural powers and the like—which, though unprohibited, were obtained from those gracious Siddhas as a fitting consequence of his spiritual endeavors. || 26 ||
First, for one whose inner self has arisen and whose dullness is worn away, a distaste for worldly existence arises from within, like the autumnal tree after its fruit has ripened.

If it is asked why he does not hold [the teacher] in high esteem, the intention is that this is because the means such as detachment (*vairāgya*) have already been firmly practiced even prior to contact with the teacher and the scriptures; with this in mind, the sequence of the arising of qualities is restated once more, beginning with the words "Previously," etc. (verse 27).
Thereafter, desiring his own well-being, he himself seeks association with virtuous people for the sake of future prosperity, just as one seeking health resorts to a physician. (28)
Therefore, having become noble-minded, he plunges into the meanings of the treatises, just as a great elephant enters vast, clear lakes. (29)
For a virtuous person, having rescued one standing near him from calamities,
establishes him in prosperity, just as the sun places all things within its own light.
Abstention from taking what belongs to others arises even earlier;
and for the discerning person, contentment with one's own possessions is born. (31)
Abstaining from taking what belongs to others and filled with the nectar of contentment, the discerning person gradually desires to even disregard his own interests. (32)
The sense is: if one disregards even one's own interests, how could one desire the welfare of others? || 32 ||
For even when asked for mere grain, oil-cake, vegetables, and the like, he gives them;
indeed, by that very practice, he eventually gives away his own flesh.
By that very yoga of the practice of renunciation, he gives even his own flesh to those who ask for it. || 33 ||
Surely, for those whose minds are dissolved and who pursue solitude,
their folly becomes as insignificant as a cow’s footprint when they are running.

He says "certainly" (nūnam) to show that for those whose minds are dissolving through the process of following discernment (viveka), ignorance (ajñāna) is destroyed by the daily accumulation of knowledge. Ignorance is delusion (maurkhya). "Lightness" (laghutvam) refers to becoming small through diminution.
Just as the footprint of a cow becomes insignificant—characterized by its being easily leaped over by running horses and the like—in the same way [ignorance] comes to pass.

Having first practiced with effort the abstention from taking what belongs to others— [the reading "parasvādāna" is consistent with the commentary]— one should then, through discernment, cultivate detachment toward one's own interests. (35)
Abstention from taking for oneself the wealth and so forth belonging to others; that is, cessation [from such taking]. || 35 ||
Then, through the renunciation of enjoyments, the wise gradually effect the abandonment of self-interest for the sake of supreme and perfect rest. (36)
There is no such suffering in this world, nor even in millions of hells, as that which consists in the lifelong pursuit of acquiring wealth. (37)
The administration of punishment directed toward the acquisition of wealth results in a multitude of sufferings pertaining to both this world and the next; such is the meaning. (37)

Whether on a seat, in bed, in a vehicle, while walking, or in the company of people, let the deluded indeed be intent upon mental anguish—or rather, as the reading goes, upon the pursuit of wealth. (38)

In this regard, although the ignorant do not remember the sufferings of the next world, he causes them to remember those of this world, which are well-known to all, by saying "on the seat. Let them know; let them remember. || 38 ||

Indeed, objects of desire are spread with misfortune; prosperities are continuous calamities; and enjoyments are the great diseases of existence—so they have been perceived by one who has cultivated the contrary view. (39)

The meaning is: if these [objects], which are well known to bring thousands of misfortunes to those seeking wealth—such as acquisition, preservation, expenditure, and [danger] from kings, thieves, and the like—are contemplated and reflected upon through discernment (*viveka*), which is the opposite of passion (*rāga*).

Alternatively, this is an expression emphasizing the abstract state (*bhāvapradhāna-nirdeśa*): although these are of the nature of misfortune, they have been perceived by people through delusion (*moha*) as their opposites.
This is the meaning. || 39 ||
The bitterness of enmity does not arise from the expansion of the objects of thought so long as one does not seek wealth— which is a great misfortune— for the sake of a trivial purpose.

As long as a person does not seek nor desire that misfortune characterized by worldly objects for the sake of tormenting them, so long does that person not undergo the bitterness of weariness—the withering caused by the threefold suffering. || 40 ||
May he for whom unsurpassed bliss has long been pleasing perceive the world as a mere blade of grass and attain peace. 41.

That person for whom the unsurpassed happiness called liberation is pleasing should view wealth—the very essence of the world—as something far more trivial than the tip of a blade of grass; the meaning is that the renunciation of the desire for wealth is his primary means to liberation. || 41 ||

The "caravan" (sārtha) is traditionally understood as the goal of those who undergo manifold transformations of state, the processes of aging and death, and the burning pains of wretchedness and wickedness. (42)

To further reinforce its worthlessness, he repeatedly censures wealth with the word "bhūri" (abundant): [the verse continues] "artha eva sārthaḥ. The meaning is that wealth alone is the "sārtha"—that is, the multitude—of emotional disturbances such as anxiety, grief, and delusion, as well as old age, death, evil deeds, wretchedness, and so forth. The word "sārtha" is applied even to that which is not a living being by way of metaphorical treatment, as if it were a living creature. || 42 ||
In this world, for living beings subject to old age and death, contentment is the elixir that makes one free from aging and death. (43)
He praises contentment, noting that it alone removes all suffering by establishing dispassion, with the words: "In this..."
Spring delights the garden, and the moon is said to delight the apsarases;
thus, on one side is the rising nectar of contentment. (44)

He states that he alone is also the cause of all happiness, beginning with the words "In spring," etc.; the grammatical connection is that they are "remembered as being on one side" [of him]. || 44 ||
Just as a lake is filled by the rainy season, so too was there a fullness through contentment;
it was profound, cool, heart-pleasing, serene, and rich in aesthetic flavor.
The ellipsis is that "fullness belongs to the person. The remainder [of the verse] connects with what follows. || 45 ||
Having attained vigor, the virtuous man shines through contentment alone,
like a tree in full bloom through the arrival of spring.
The virtuous person, having attained vigor through contentment alone, shines with the appearance of a forest in full bloom. || 46 ||
A person of base nature who seeks wealth strives like an insect crushed by the touch of a footstool; he goes from one misery to another. (47)

But he who is discontented and seeks wealth—touched by a footstool or a sandal, and by chance stepped upon and crushed like a worm—he, being of a base nature, thus exerts himself and strives. || 47 ||
Agitated by surging waves like those fallen into a turbulent ocean, suppliants with deformed appearances do not attain their own natural composure. 48.
Those who seek wealth are those desirous of riches. || 48 ||
Prosperity and women are as transient as high-arching waves;
what wise man would take delight in them, which are like the shifting shade of a serpent’s hood? (49)
What wise person would take delight in the shade of the parasols formed by the hoods of those snakes possessing such characteristics? The meaning is: no one at all. || 49 ||
That fool who, despite knowing the torment involved in the acquisition and preservation of wealth, still entertains a longing for it—one should not even touch that beast among men. (50)
He who cuts away both the external and internal undertakings of the mind with the sickle of equanimity and dispassion— his field shines forth.
The "field" (kṣetra) is either the external undertaking characterized by the pursuit of the senses, or the internal one characterized by volitional thought and so forth;
it is the place where the seed of knowledge germinates, or the place where the treasure of liberation is stored—namely, the heart. || 51 ||

The world-nature, which is unreal, appears as if real to the ignorant who have not awakened; even though the knower perceives it as such, that appearance is merely the manifestation of a lack of practice [in discernment]. 52.

Intending to conclude with the thought that the qualities enumerated up to "firm detachment" (dṛḍhavairāgya) establish knowledge only when they have been practiced, and not when they are pursued casually, he says: "The world-nature" (jagattvam). Although the knower knows that the world-nature—the manifold variety of the world's forms—which is perceived by the ignorant, is in truth non-existent even as its witness, yet due to the immaturity of his knowledge, he [remains] therein...

The meaning is this: although the world's diversity exists as if it were real, that which flashes forth and functions for the ignorant as if it had a true objective reality is actually a manifestation of the practice of the qualities culminating in dispassion (*vairāgya*). || 52 ||

Having attained a state of world-weariness toward saṃsāra, and having approached the company of the virtuous and the scriptures, one casts off enjoyments through the realization of the meaning of those scriptures; then, by means of the firmness of dispassion, one reaches the supreme reality.
First, having attained a state of world-weariness within saṃsāra, and through that having attained the company of the virtuous and the study of the scriptures,

one should— by means of firm contemplation on their meaning— cast aside all enjoyments; and through the firmness of non-attachment characterized as previously described, one [realizes] the supreme reality, which is one's own true nature.
The meaning is that one proceeds by way of the gradual ripening of the stages. || 53 ||

Thus ends the forty-seventh canto, titled "The First Introduction of the Seeker of Liberation," in the *Nirvāṇa* section of the *Mokṣopāya*, within the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki.
Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, titled "The First Approach of the Seeker of Liberation," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The forty-eighth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
When detachment from worldly existence has taken root and association with the virtuous is established,
When the meaning of the treatise has been contemplated by the intellect, and a lack of craving for enjoyments has arisen, || 1 ||
Those characteristics by which a person’s state is defined when supreme detachment has become firmly established,
and those described in the context of the establishment of knowledge, are here explained in detail.

In this regard, he first states those characteristics that arise when the eighth [stage], the state of being established in detachment, has been attained, beginning with the words "When [the power] has taken root" (rūḍhe), and so forth. || 1 ||
When distaste for sense-objects has arisen, when goodness has likewise emerged, and when the heart—having become oriented toward the Light—has attained its awakening; (2)
These two verses are a restatement of what was previously explained. || 2 ||
Wealth is not desired by a person of discernment, just as darkness is not;
even when present, it is abandoned like withered, impure leaves. (3)
Just as dried, impure, and unholy leaves from food remnants and the like are cast out from a house, so it is in this case.
Wives and kinsmen appear as a burden, like a traveler’s view of a heavy load;
yet they are indeed attended to according to one's ability and the proper time.

The meaning is that just as household goods and utensils, though useful for travelers' sight, are seen as a burden to be discarded because they cannot be carried, so too are wives and kinsmen viewed by one who is dispassionate.
The dative case is used here according to the rule *kriyārthopapadasya ca karmaṇi* (Pāṇini 2.3.14), [the suffix] *lakāra* [denoting the future].

Even though the objective power (*karma-śakti*) as defined by the action of seeing (*dṛśi-kriyā*) is expressed, that same power as defined by the action of abandoning (*jahāti-kriyā*), which is merely implied, is not expressed. If one asks, "In that case, are they abandoned all at once? he says: "according to their respective capacities" (*yathāśakti*). || 4 ||
Furthermore, even when the objects of the senses are present before the senses,
pleasures are certainly not experienced again and again due to the tranquility of the mind.
In solitary places, at the ends of the horizon, by lakes and in forests, in gardens, in sacred regions, or even in one's own home; (6)
He elaborates upon that very point with the verse beginning "In solitary places," and so forth. || 6 ||
One does not remain for long in the playful diversions with friends, in auspicious gardens, meals, and the like, nor in the investigation of the scriptures and logic. (7)
It is resorted to by one who resorts to it; it is inhabited; or, due to the absence of attachment, one does not remain there for long. || 7 ||
By one who is tranquil, self-controlled, delighting in the Self, and silent,
by the wise one who speaks only of realized knowledge, that which is already known is further investigated.

Even by one who has arrived there through destiny, it is the Knower alone, the perceiver of reality, who is sought after for the sake of strengthening knowledge. Alternatively, the meaning is that the Knower—the inner self (pratyagātman) who is the direct witness of the body, senses, intellect, and so forth—is sought after by means of the mind, and nothing other than that. || 8 ||
Thus, through the power of practice, the discerning person comes to rest in the supreme state by themselves, becoming tranquil like water flowing downwards. (9)

Thus, he says that through such uninterrupted inquiry, rest is necessarily accomplished by the vision of one's own Self: "Thus, both external and internal, it is Consciousness alone that has arisen as the object; no separate object is possible—this is the supreme state. (10)

"What is that state wherein he finds rest, and what is the nature of that certainty? To this he replies: "Both external and internal. Ignorance is simply one's own lack of knowledge (*svājñāna*) which arises in the form of the objective world; yet, since no separate object can possibly exist, that ignorance is "peaceful" (*śāntā*). That peace alone is the supreme state—this is the meaning. Alternatively:

The meaning is this: if the knowledge consisting of the certainty that no object exists externally or internally—this very state of the final direct realization (sākṣātkāra)—is extinguished within the conscious self like a fire whose fuel is consumed, then that alone is the supreme state. || 10 ||
"There is no perception of objects, nor is there emptiness apart from the nature of awakening"—thus they call that supreme state which abides in internal experience. (11)
Thus, the meaning is that that very state which abides as the ultimate limit of all sublation within one's own experience (*anubhūti*) is the supreme state (*paramaṃ padam*).
Know that supreme state to be neither a state of consciousness—due to the transformation resulting from its connection with a single awakening—nor emptiness, nor an object. (12)

Know that for that supreme state there is neither consciousness (*bodhatā*), nor emptiness (*śūnyatā*), nor even objectivity (*arthatā*). Why? Because it possesses an "excessive connection" (*atisambandha*)—an ultimate oneness-in-flavor (*atyantikaikarasya*)—with the single, non-dual consciousness (*bodha*) of the entire range of entities, due to its transformation into that very nature. Indeed, in the absence of an object of consciousness (*boddhya*), neither consciousness itself nor its exclusion can be designated. Nor...
The meaning is that its status as having that [object] as its referent can indeed be designated; nor does the mere absence of an object entail the emptiness of consciousness. || 12 ||
For the virtuous who are free from the mind and rest solely in self-awareness, sense objects do not provide pleasure, just as water does not moisten stones. 13.

He says "one's own" [etc. because absolute distaste for sense objects is not established until one rests in that [Self]. Just as milk does not taste good to stones that lack a mind, so it is in this case. 13.
Having attained the state of cessation, free from mental activity and slow with the silence of a sage,
he remains established in his very nature, like a self-possessed man depicted in a painting.

It is called "cessation" (nirodha) because it obstructs the outward-turning of minds that are inclined toward themselves, and the outward-turning of those resting within themselves; such is this state. It is made motionless, as if painted in a picture. || 14 ||
The heart of the knower of the known is the Great God himself—possessing all objects yet devoid of objects, like a supreme atom, and though non-empty, its very nature is emptiness. 15.
He explains what his mind is like at that time with the words "all objects" (*sarvārtham*).

For one whose nature it is to know—that is, to necessarily experience—the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*), which is the object of knowledge (*vedyam*), his heart, or mind, becomes "all-objected" (*sarvārtham*) even while being devoid of objects. This is because, in reality, everything is nothing but that [Self]. Likewise...
Because its form as Brahman is undifferentiated, that very Being (sat) becomes, like an atom, difficult to perceive as distinct from itself. || 15 ||
For the knower, the notions of "I" and "you," the activity of the world and so forth, as well as the divisions of space and time, and even knowledge and the void— none of these exist at all.

He explains the remainder of the statement, "the non-empty itself has emptiness as its nature," with the words "I-ness" and so forth. Since [the self] consists of knowledge and the like, it exists precisely as such; and since it consists of emptiness and the like, it does not exist. The underlying sense is based on the principle: "The being of the non-existent is not found, nor is the non-being of the existent found. || 16 ||
By means of knowledge abiding in the stainless state, just as by a lamp, the darkness within the heart as well as external darkness, along with passion, hatred, fear, and so forth, is dispelled. (17)
And whatever fear and so forth there may be, that too is dispelled. || 17 ||
One should bow to that Sun among men, who is free from all stains and directions, who has reached the further shore through his essence, and whose nature is devoid of the form of darkness.

In both cases, the qualifiers are clear: although [the Self] is concealed by the darkness of ignorance, it exists [as the witness], and thus it is "on the further shore" (pāram), meaning the far shore of the ocean of darkness. 18.
When differentiation has dissolved and the mind has attained invisibility, that state of one who has realized awakening does not come within the range of words. (19)
O one of great intelligence, the Supreme Lord, being propitiated by supreme devotion for a long time day and night, bestows this Nirvana.

The Supreme Lord bestows this Nirvana, characterized by the supreme state, as described above, through the power of austerity and the grace of the Deity; such is the meaning according to scriptural passages beginning with these words. || 20 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
O best of sages, who is the Lord, and how is he propitiated through devotion?
Tell me this in accordance with the truth, O foremost among those who know all principles. (21)
Rāma’s question is clear. || 21 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O one of great intelligence, the Lord is neither far away nor difficult to attain;
the Supreme Lord is one's very own self, whose singular essence consists of supreme awakening.
To him who is everything, from whom everything comes, who is everything, and who is everywhere;
who is within and consists eternally of all things—to that Soul of All, I bow.

For lordship (*īśvaratā*) is absolute independence (*svātantrya*) with respect to the object of rule (*īśya*). And since that [independence] is possible only for one’s own self in relation to everything and in every way, he states the logical justification with the words "To him" (*tasmai*). For everything insentient—such as chariots, houses, palaces, and so forth—is for the sake of a sentient being. Nor is there any other sentient principle apart from that [Self], according to such scriptural texts as, "There is no other seer but Him."
By this, his sovereignty over all forms of enjoyment has been stated. He says "from that" (*tataḥ*) to show that sovereignty over agency and so forth also belongs to him alone.

It should be understood that the suffix *tasi*—which takes the place of all case endings—is used here in its ablative, instrumental, genitive, and locative forms to illuminate his sovereignty even in the capacity of agent, instrument, cause, owner, and so on. He...

The word "all" (*sarvam*) is used to demonstrate His sovereignty (*svātantrya*) as the locus and substratum of all things. Likewise, the phrase "from everywhere" (*sarvataḥ*) should be understood as illuminating His sovereignty in defining all powers.
He states that "He is within" (*so'ntaḥ*) to show that even His sovereignty over subtlety, omnipresence, transformation, and so forth, belongs to Him alone.

Regarding the phrase "consisting of all" (*sarvamaya*): since he alone is in every way, at all times, and as the self of all, and because he is supreme in every respect, he alone is the Lord (*īśvara*) who is to be saluted. Thus, he says: "to him" (*tasmai*). || 23 ||
Therefore, these transformations of creation and dissolution are produced from that causeless Cause, like the various movements of the wind.
For this very reason, with the intention that its characteristic of being the cause of birth and so forth is well-known from the Śruti, he says: "Therefore" (tasmāt). || 24 ||
All these beings, both stationary and moving, constantly worship them by granting whatever is desired; thus, all those classes of living beings [do so]. (25)
He states that his alone is established as the state of being worshipped by all, saying: "unceasingly" (aniśam). || 25 ||
Throughout many births, according to his own desire and wish,
when he has been fully honored by him, he attains grace.
That Mahādeva, the Great Lord who is the Self itself, being well-pleased, swiftly dispatches a pure messenger with auspicious intentions for the sake of awakening [him]. (27)

That very Mahādeva, being pleased by auspicious intentions and well-performed deeds, sends forth—that is, dispatches—a pure, most refined messenger, who is about to be described, for the sake of awakening, which is the instilling of the knowledge of reality. || 27 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
O Sage, by whom is the messenger impelled—the Supreme Lord himself? And how does that messenger perform the awakening? Tell me this.
Tell me how he performs it. || 28 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
A messenger impelled by the Self, known by the name Viveka (Discernment),
dwells eternally in the cave of the heart, like the moon in the sky.

Impelled by that divine Self, the messenger named Viveka (Discrimination) comes and remains in the cave of the heart of the aforementioned qualified seeker until he becomes firmly established in knowledge. || 29 ||
This very [knowledge] gradually awakens the living being whose nature is latent impressions (vāsanā), and it delivers the undiscriminating person from this ocean of saṃsāra. (30)
The intention is that whatever that messenger of discernment awakens one to, that alone is his salvation. || 30 ||
This very self of awakening is the innermost self, the supreme, the highest Lord;
the syllable *praṇava*, approved by the Vedas, is the designator of this very one. (31)
This very inner self, which is established as the cause of the manifestation of the entire world, is the nature of awakening alone, not the nature of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
He alone is the supreme Parameśvara. The *praṇava* (the syllable Om), being its designator, becomes its name. || 31 ||
He is constantly propitiated by men, nāgas, gods, and asuras through the performance of recitation, fire-offerings, austerities, charity, study, and sacrificial rites.
The sky is his head, the earth his feet, the stars the rows of hair upon his body; the elements are his bones, and the supreme lord has the ether as his heart.

He shows that the form of Vaiśvānara, characterized by the gross manifestation (*sthūlaprapañca*), is to be meditated upon for the purpose of dispelling the delusion of the difference between the self, saying "The sky," and so forth. Thus says the Śruti: "Fire is his head; the sun and moon are his eyes; the quarters are his ears; the Vedas are his opened mouth; the wind is his breath; the universe is his heart; from his feet [proceeds] the earth."
"For he is the earth, the inner self within all beings. || 33 ||
Because it is of the nature of consciousness, it moves everywhere, wakes up, and perceives;
therefore, it possesses hands, feet, eyes, and ears in every direction.

With the intention that the harmony of such scriptural passages as "He whose eyes are on all sides, and whose faces are on all sides, whose arms are on all sides, and whose feet are on all sides" is found precisely here, he says: "Everywhere. He bears hands, ears, eyes, and feet on all sides; such is his nature. (34)
Having awakened the messenger of discernment and slain the demon of the mind, the living soul is led to some vast state of the Self. (35)
The remainder [of the sentence] is: "it is led by this. || 35 ||

Having abandoned the flood of all conceptual constructions—those transformations that are a mixture of misfortunes—one should, by one's own human effort, personally pacify the self within the thicket of grasping. (36)
In this darkness of the night of saṃsāra, which is agitated by waves like clouds and haunted by the demon of the wandering mind, one’s own self alone is the full moon.

In the darkness of the night characterized by worldly existence, which is agitated by clouds possessing the traits of the six waves—the great surges—he is his own Self, the full moon; that is to say, he is the light of bliss. || 37 ||
Within the hollow of this ocean, agitated by the waves of the deep whirlpools of death, flickering with the ripples of craving, and driven by the fierce winds of one's own mind; (38)
In order to state that discernment alone is the means of crossing over, he describes transmigratory existence as an ocean with the two verses beginning with "agādha" (bottomless). || 38 ||

In this vast ocean of worldly existence, which is filled with the afflictions of great dullness and is dense with the multitude of the senses—[where the reading "grāhagahane" (dense with crocodiles) also occurs]—discernment is the great vessel. (39)
In the support for the great masses of inert water-drops, which consist of all beings, both stationary and moving. || 39 ||

Having previously become well-pleased by worship according to one's desire, the Self, acting here as a purifying messenger, bestows discriminative discernment; and through association with the virtuous, study of the scriptures, and the supreme realization of the ultimate truth, it leads the individual soul to the one, primordial, and stainless state.
He concludes the question and answer briefly with the words "Previously," etc. This is clear. || 40 ||

Thus ends the forty-eighth sarga, titled "The Greatness of Discrimination," in the Nirvāṇa Section of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa*, composed by Vālmīki, within the section on Liberation (Mokṣopāya).
Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Greatness of Discrimination," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The forty-ninth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: For those whose discernment is fully matured and who have cast off the impurity of latent tendencies (vāsanā),...
Within the great, there arises a certain greatness that is truly unprecedented. || 1 ||
What kind of greatness belongs to those whose discernment is fully matured,
and how the universe appears to them clearly— that is described here.
An extraordinary greatness arises. || 1 ||
The fourteen worlds cannot fathom the minds of the great, which possess a vast and noble integrity and are beautiful in their profundity. (2)

He elaborates upon that very point with the words beginning "audārya" (magnanimity): "Of magnanimity," which is well-known throughout all the worlds through its various degrees, "the great ones do not fathom"—neither the fourteen worlds, nor the prosperities contained therein, nor the people—its sublime, excellent, and ultimate limit (*maryādā*) which, by virtue of its profundity, is beautiful like the intellect of the great. They do not [fathom it].
The meaning is that they are unable either to entice or to measure [him] by such a limited amount. || 2 ||
When the conviction has taken root among the wise that "the world is a delusion of the mind," then the crocodile-grasp of delusion, which moves both externally and internally, is stilled.

That which exists in the external objects characterized by sound and so forth is the "external" [grasping]. That which moves internally in the form of volitions, doubts, and the like, and is therefore primarily capable of moving between the heart, the interior, and the exterior, is the "grasping" (graha)—the collection of the senses together with the mind (samanaska-indriya). Its root cause is delusion (moha), which is ignorance (ajñāna).
By the use of the word "and" (ca), it is meant that latent impressions, desires, karma, and so forth are also pacified. || 3 ||
When the delusion of the world flashes forth like two moons, like heat-mirages, water, or a mass of hair in the sky, how can there be any basis for latent impressions?

As long as there is the conceit of reality regarding delusions, so long does their latent impression (vāsanā) accumulate; it is well known in the world that when those delusions manifest as such—that is, as delusions—their latent impressions are also destroyed because their root has been severed.
To demonstrate this, he provides an illustration with the words "like two moons": "In the delusion of the world, [one realizes] 'this is merely a delusion.'"
When the [insight] flashing forth from the awakening to reality is present. || 4 ||
When the causal condition of latent impressions (vāsanā) is empty, only the empty void remains;
since even that state exists when the mind is absent, how could it be abandoned by one who possesses discernment?

That state of the mind, which is devoid of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), is established only when the mind itself is non-existent. That state, free from impressions and free from the mind, is attained by the discerning practitioner in the seventh stage; how could it be abandoned? The meaning is that there is simply no reason for its abandonment. || 5 ||
But that state which is devoid of this triad through these three stages—
whether it be called "seeing" or even "not seeing"— is said to be the supreme state.

This triad of states—waking and so forth—is well known to all. However, that state which is devoid of these three, although not seeing because it is sublated by the root of worldly activity such as seeing and so on, appears as if seeing from the perspective of others due to the remainder of *prārabdha* karma which is the sole cause of mere living; yet, from its own perspective, it is the Supreme alone.
It is not grieved because it is not attached to the visible; such is the meaning. || 6 ||
Like a mass of rays from various jewels, the world consists of manifold forms;
it is a mere appearance, not a self, not a solid entity, and not composed of earth.

The meaning is that for such [beings], even at the time of emergence from meditative absorption, the world is neither the Self nor a solid entity composed of earth and other elements; rather, it is like a mass of diverse rays from jewels—a dense cluster of radiance—appearing as a mere semblance of solidity. || 7 ||
For the world that exists is merely the perception of forms and is indeed empty, arisen like a net of rays from a collection of various jewels in the sky. (8)
Here there are no real beings, nor is there the state of a world, nor even emptiness;
this is merely the unfolding of the net of light-rays from the jewel-lord known as Brahman.
Creations and non-creations, belonging to Brahmā, appear as manifold yet not subject to destruction; these dense masses of conceptual clouds shine forth as formless indeed.

Since there is no multiplicity, there are no creations; and since there is no destruction, there are no non-creations or dissolutions. Rather, the meaning is that these clusters of conceptual suns, being formless, appear as if they have become solidified. By the word "ark" (sun), its rays are indicated. || 10 ||
Thus, in this way, no substantial mass of form exists;
and in that which is conceptually constructed, only emptiness is perceived, like [the appearance of forms] in the sky. (11)

He says, "In this way, first of all," [verse 11], because it is well known that in the case of mental constructions such as daydreams, there is only emptiness for those forms whose shapes are imagined by conceptualization, and no apprehension of a solid mass.
Since that [bond] is a non-entity, how could there be a basis for bondage?
What bird could ever rest upon a tree in the sky? (12)
He states the fruit of establishing emptiness: "In that" (tasyām).
In that emptiness, how could there be the bondage of mental formations such as "I," "mine," attachment, and aversion? The meaning is that it is simply not possible. || 12 ||
There is no massiveness of the elements, nor does emptiness exist;
for this very reason, even the mind has set, and what remains is neither being nor non-being. (13)
Thus, having refuted the lump-like nature and so forth of the world, he says that pure Being alone remains as the essence:
"The state of being a lump," etc. He further states that this [Being] is impossible to deny: "And that is not non-existent. || 13 ||
Though possessing manifold forms, the awakened one remains truly non-different and equal;
with various objects dissolved within, he is like a mass of gold.

For this very reason, even while awake, one who knows reality remains as if in deep sleep, because the various appearances are dissolved within the Self that is pure Being; thus he says, with an illustration: "It is indeed equal to the non-dual. (14)

For one who remains as they truly are, the universe and the mind, along with the sense of "I-ness," dissolve; for the knower, there remains the inexpressible state of no-mind, which is the true nature of reality.

One might object: "Could it not be that for the Knower (*jña*), only that pure existence (*sanmātra*) remains, which is indeed the very nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*)? For it is well known that the manifestation of consciousness occurs when the mind (*citta*) exists, and that this is impossible when it has dissolved. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Of that which remains as it is" (*yathāsthitasya*).
If, while remaining in this insentience (*jāḍya*) that is contrary to its true nature, its egoity (*ahaṃtva*), the universe, and the mind were to dissolve, then—

[Otherwise] there would be a remainder consisting only of inert existence; but this is not so. Rather, for the knower who abides in the true nature of consciousness as a single essence, the "I-ness," the universe, and the mind dissolve through the vision of reality (*tattvadarśana*).

At that time, since it is impossible to speak of "mindlessness" (*acittva*) for one whose remaining essence is the single flavor of consciousness, the meaning is that the establishment of a remainder of existence as the single flavor of consciousness is proven.
The intellect is merely distressed by views that are higher and lower;
for the true object is understood through reasoning practiced even slightly. (16)

If it is asked, "If that is its very nature, then why is it not easily accessible to all?", he says—beginning with the words "is afflicted"—that it is because of the instability of the intellect due to its flickering among various high and low objects. || 16 ||
The Virāj is devoid of vital energy (ojas) through the relationship of cause and effect and so forth;
it is the source of the world-body consisting of the past, present, and future.
Showing that slight reasoning, he says "Virāṭ" to indicate that the fruit of such practice is characterized by knowledge:

by which qualified aspirant the birth—meaning the manifestation—of the world-limb, which consists of all things past, present, and future, is [perceived] through its causes and effects and so forth, according to the logic shown in the scriptural passage beginning with "a mere modification of speech" (*vācārambhaṇa*). By means of the Virāṭ...

The meaning of the verse is this: that which is awakened as the nature of indivisible consciousness, consisting of pure existence alone, and devoid of the gross manifestation (sthūlaprapañca), the subtle manifestation (sūkṣmaprapañca) which is the *pradhāna* in the form of the thread (*sūtra*) that supports it, and its power (*ojas*), he alone is the "knower" (*jña*) who knows reality (*tattvavit*). || 17 ||
He by whom the Buddha is perceived through the nature of awakening is designated as "the Knower. For that non-dual and quiescent one, the universe does not exist. (18)
All these aforementioned instructions and qualifications come to the experience of the knower spontaneously, like the words of a virtuous person.
He states that all instructions—which serve to eliminate respective portions of doubt regarding the impossibility [of realization]—culminate in such an experience: "The aforementioned... (verse 19).
There is no solid mass to the elements, for they are empty due to their non-origination;
therefore, the mind does not exist, and the remaining reality is your own abiding state.

He states another argument: "The state of being a mass (*piṇḍatva*)," etc. Since the four classes of elemental beings—the great elements such as earth and so forth—are seen when analyzed part by part and quality by quality, they do not even rest in the state of atoms; thus, first of all, there is no such thing as a "mass. Nor, moreover, is there emptiness (*śūnyatva*).

Because perception and the other [means of knowledge] are impossible, and because all conceptual constructions (vikalpas) have departed when both [perception and inference] are absent, even the mind—which exists dependent upon them—is no longer present. Thus, only the non-conceptual radiance (sphuraṇa), whose nature is pure existence (sanmātra), remains; that alone is your ultimate form, your abiding state, and your foundation—this is the meaning. || 20 ||
The consciousness of this internal conscious being consists precisely in its orientation toward objects;
that [orientation] which has arisen leads to misfortune, while that which has not arisen would lead to the highest good.
He states another argument: "The state of being directed toward the object of cognition" (*cetyonmukhatvam*).

For this inner conscious one, the *pratyagātman*, the very state of being directed toward the object of cognition is consciousness itself as the transmigrating self; it is awareness [in the form] of saṃsāra. || 21 ||
Having arisen, it attains externality; therein it reaches a state of massification.
By its own very self-awareness, due to its insentience, it becomes like water turning into stone. 22.
He states how that leads to misfortune: "It has risen," meaning it has attained the state of a mountain or the nature of a hailstone. || 22 ||
Just like the objects of a dream and so forth, consciousness assumes a state of solidification through non-awareness;
then, becoming the mind by way of grasping that [solidified state], it binds itself to a body.
Awakening is the conscious self; by non-awakening, that is, by one's own ignorance. || 23 ||
In all these states, no otherness arises within consciousness;
it is only through the conceptualization of words that difference is imagined. (24)
He states that even through thousands of such transformations, there is not even an atom’s worth of modification in consciousness;
thus, those [transformations] are merely a matter of words (*vācārambhaṇamātra*). He says this in the verse beginning with "etāvatīṣu" (in so many). 24.
Both externally and internally, it is the Self alone that appears through the perceptions of objects within consciousness;
it does not possess the nature of being internal or external in the manner of the mind.

Just as in the perception of a dream by the mind, it is the mind itself that appears modified through its internal and external aspects, so too the conscious Self (bodhātman) is not modified even when appearing through the perceptions of objects; this is the meaning. || 25 ||
Since consciousness is like space, time, space, and so forth are its very form;
likewise, all objects are one's own self, being like a dream—a void that does not possess the nature of external objects.

To the question "Why is it not modified?", he says: "of consciousness" (bodhasya). The meaning is that it is unmodified like time, space, and so forth. "Having the form of objects" (artharūpi) means undergoing transformation into the forms of objects. || 26 ||
The state of being an external object does not, by virtue of cognition, become internality;
for that which is insentient can never, anywhere, attain the nature of cognition, as it lacks similarity thereto.

"Let the insentient [self] not undergo modification by taking on the form of external objects; rather, let that very same insentient entity undergo modification by virtue of the realization of reality (tattvabodha) into the form of the internal consciousness.
To this, he replies with the word "bāhya" (external):
for the reason that the insentient is "asādṛśya," meaning it is utterly dissimilar [to consciousness]. || 27 ||
Awareness does not enter the state of the visible, nor does it even reach that condition;
it remains exactly as it is, without undergoing even the slightest change into something else.
Although that consciousness has reached the state of being an object through the power of phenomenal appearance, it remains exactly as it is, unmodified.
When the singular transformation of supremely pure consciousness has fully arisen,
even the hearing of words denoting "consciousness," "unconsciousness," or "objects" will set.
In the transformation and transmutation at the conclusion of the rest upon the seventh stage. || 29 ||
For those with subtle bodies, it is only their own minds that develop the perception of materiality through their own firm habitual tendencies. (30)
He states that the firmness of the perceived object arises through the very cultivation of the mind, and its loosening occurs through that same [cultivation],
by means of the verse beginning with "ātivāhika" (30).
This state of being composed of material elements is false, cultivated by subtle bodies whose minds are as clear as space,
just as the state of being a ghost is falsely assumed by actors.
Like a female demon conjured by actors for the purpose of performing in the guise of a demoness. || 31 ||
This delusion is known to be pacified through the practice of non-delusion;
indeed, madness is quelled by the realization, "I am not mad."
Through the thorough understanding of delusion by oneself, latent tendencies cease;
when one has realized a dream for what it is—a dream—of whom indeed could there be any [further] mental cultivation? (33)
Cultivation is the impression of the reality of the object. || 33 ||
Samsara is pacified solely through the thinning of latent impressions (vāsanā);
the wise are intent upon severing this very vāsanā, which is like a great female spirit (mahāyakṣiṇī). 34.
Others are intent upon its cutting and destruction. || 34 ||
Just as the madness of ignorance in men is cultivated through habituation, so too does it subside over time through the cultivation of awakening. (35)
That madness is impelled by knowledge. || 35 ||

Just as this subtle body (ātivāhika-deha) is led by those who know reality into a state of materiality through mental cultivation (bhāvanā), so too is it transformed by the grace of the existence of pure consciousness (bodhasattā). 36.

The meaning is that through the grace of that [realization], the existence of consciousness—made firm by practice—is stabilized; thus, the subtle body (*ātivāhika-deha*) is led to the state of pure ideation, which is the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of the realization "I am Brahman. || 36 ||
Just as the subtle body (ātivāhikadeha) leads one to the state of the individual soul (jīvapada), so too,
through firm practice of awakening, it should be led even to the state of Brahman.

Having brought it to the state of manifestation (bhāvanā), and having brought the state of the individual soul (jīva) to the state of living beings, it must then be led to the state of Brahman. || 37 ||
If origination, which is of the nature of consciousness, is understood through its own object, then how is it that the subtle body (ativāhikī) is also understood? (38)

How is the state of the individual soul (jīva) to be led [to its goal], and how is it then brought to the state of Brahman? To this he says: "like one's own object" (svavastuvat). For, by manifesting passion and other afflictions toward external and internal objects that have arisen, one carries oneself beyond; thus, the collection of latent impressions (vāsanā-saṅgha) is called the "conveyor" (ativāha). Indeed, the subtle body (liṅgadeha) arising from that is called the "conveying" (ātivāhika) body. In that regard, of all objects—

The first modification is origination (*utpatti*). If that is examined and understood—as one's own reality—to be immutable and consisting of pure consciousness (*bodha-mātra-rūpinī*), then by the same logic, one understands how and what the nature of the subtle body (*ātivāhikī-buddhi*) is. Indeed, the origination of any entity whatsoever cannot be established apart from the immutable nature of consciousness.

For instance: does that [change] qualify entities by arising itself beforehand, or without arising? In the second case, even a horn would qualify a rabbit. In the first case, being qualified by its own arising and so forth, it would be an entity itself rather than a modification of an entity. Likewise, its arising would also [require another arising], leading to the fault of infinite regress; if this is accepted, there would be nothing but an endless series of unchanging entities.

The meaning is as follows: since modifications such as arising and so forth cannot be determined by anyone in anything, those [entities] are indeed of the nature of immutable consciousness (*kūṭasthabodha*). Thus, who could convey what to whom? What would that conveying be, or what other cognition could there be? Even that [cognition] is cognized in its true essence. || 38 ||
If that knot [of ignorance] is not removed by the meaning of the counter-statement, it is like the word "pratipattr" (the performer) in the sūtra for the eradication of spirits. (39)

In this very manner, when the referents of the terms *tat* and *tvam* are purified, all the Great Sayings (*mahāvākya*) are capable of piercing the knots of all doubt by imparting the knowledge of the partless reality (*akhaṇḍārtha*). Otherwise, they would be entirely meaningless, like the words *huṃ*, *phaṭ*, and so forth found in mantras used for exorcising spirits.
He says "no cet" (if not) to show that it would have to be postulated that [the mantra] turns back saṃsāra by the power of mere hearing alone.
The ellipsis is: "Just as the words *huṃ*, *phaṭ*, and so forth, which constitute part of the practitioner in the case of a Sūtra or Mantra, so it would be [in this case]. || 39 ||
Having realized the oneness of the world with pure consciousness, that which is to be known remains untainted for as long as it is not itself perceived through ultimate transformation. (40)

In order to purify the meaning of the word *tat*, one first realizes the oneness of the consciousness that is the nature of the Lord, the cause of the world, according to the principle of "having speech as its beginning" (*vācārambhaṇa*); thereafter, for the purification of the meaning of the word *tvam*, one understands the inner consciousness (*pratyakcit*) to be non-attached and non-dual, following the direction shown by the scripture: "He pervaded all—pure, bodiless, and woundless."
It must be understood. Regarding how long one should remain intent on purifying the two categories of objects, he says: "Until the ultimate...

(atyanta-). The meaning is: for as long as that non-dual mental modification (*akhaṇḍākāravṛtti*) itself is not perceived through its ultimate transformation into the form of the sentence-meaning, which is an indivisible single essence (*akhaṇḍaikarasavākyārtha*), for that long [one should continue]. || 40 ||
When the mind, both external and internal, is stilled, its true nature shines forth;
resting in that very state, which is cool and radiant like the sky, may you find peace.
The man of knowledge, established in the sacrifice of knowledge and erecting the sacrificial post of meditation,
conquers the world and triumphs, having given the singular gift of total renunciation.

He states that this very person, known as the "Universal Consciousness," is the primary "sacrifice of knowledge" (jñānayajña) in the words "the one possessed of knowledge. Having firmly planted [the post] and raised it while weaving [the threads], and having become one for whom the sole primary sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is the renunciation of everything, he conquers the entire universe and remains victorious, abiding in supreme excellence. || 42 ||
Whether a rain of glowing coals falls or the wind of universal destruction blows,
whether he moves upon the earth or in the sky, the wise man remains ever equal within the Self.
He first describes supreme excellence itself through its unshakability by all calamities, beginning with the verse "He falls" (43).

For one whose mind is tranquil through freedom from craving and who has attained the purity of cessation, no state of stability is possible except through the adamantine concentration (*vajrasamādhi*). (44)

He also describes that [state] by means of its stability in the excellence of the bliss of peace and freedom from craving, which has the essence of a vajra, with the words beginning "freedom from craving" (vaitṛṣṇyam) and so forth. || 44 ||
The mind does not become so tranquil through treatises, compositions, instructions, austerities, or self-restraint as it does when there is freedom from craving for external objects. (45)
Among the means for achieving peace, he states the superiority of dispassion with the words "Just as" (yathā). || 45 ||
The fire of dispassion toward all objects has been kindled within the grass of the mind by the winds of total renunciation, through the contemplation that prosperity is itself calamity.

Thinking that "all prosperity is indeed calamity," he was awakened by the winds characterized by total renunciation amidst the heap of grass consisting of his mind; having understood the fire characterized by freedom from craving for all objects,
it awakened as the flame of the final direct realization, becoming renowned both externally and internally— that which is the darkness of delusion.

Impelled by that [consciousness], the grasping of the physical body—characterized by the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), the elements, and their derivatives—is equivalent to the conceptualization of thieves, yakṣas, and so forth;

and whatever perception of words and meanings occurs through the eyes and other senses impelled by that [body], all of it is nothing but consciousness, the very nature of the Self. Thus, it shines as an undivided, non-dual essence, just like a diamond or other precious gem.

The connection between the two [analogies] is as follows: just as [the sun], manifesting the multitude of objects reflected within it through its own unity, shines by itself, so too [is the case here].
Delusion both within and without, the grasping at a solid mass, and the perception of objects— all shine forth as mere cognition alone once one has known them within oneself, like a gem.
Through the perceptions of humans, serpents, asuras, houses, and mountain caves,
consciousness alone has spread forth, like smoke appearing as clouds in the sky.
It has spread out and attained various diversities. || 48 ||
The rivers of its own manifestations, flowing with the essence of the individual soul's power, tremble as they enter the inert vessel of the cosmic egg through their liquid nature. (49)

With the intention that all things contained within the vessel of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) are mere transformations of consciousness (cid-vivarta), because their movement is dependent upon the pervasion of consciousness, he says: "They tremble. [This means: they are full of essence (sarasāḥ), with essences flowing through the vital breath (prāṇa), which is the power of the individual soul (jīva-śakti). || 49 ||
The small fish of the individual soul, dwelling in the water of the sky,
is ensnared by the net of delusion and does not remember its own abiding state within the Self.

In that regard, he says "jīvakā" (the living soul) to explain how the fish-like individual souls (*jīva-śapharī*) fail to remember their own true nature due to being bound by the net of delusion within the rivers that are the manifestations (*vivarta*) of consciousness characterized by the fourfold body. || 50 ||

Having become condensed through its own density, the mass of consciousness (cidghana) flashes forth within itself, by means of its own self, in the courtyard of the sky in the form of various objects.

Within consciousness alone—the very Self characterized by its own essential nature—it is like clouds appearing in the courtyard of the sky; it manifests as the density of the earth and other forms, appearing in the shape of various objects. || 51 ||
All living beings are indeed equal in the absence of latent impressions (vāsanā); like dry leaves blown by the wind, they are inert, driven merely by the breath of life. 52.

In this regard, he says "all indeed" to show that although living beings possess an identical nature, the variety of suffering in saṃsāra arises solely from the diversity of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and not from anything else. Without latent impressions, they would be equal in all other respects;
it is only due to the disparity of their latent impressions that, like dry leaves blown by the wind, they are cast into the various divisions of the earth such as diverse heavens and hells.
They do not fall by themselves; for, due to the similarity of their inert limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), they are inert like bamboo flutes of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
Thus, even amidst the variety of sounds, they are incapable [of acting] without the variety of movements from the fingers of latent impressions (*vāsanā*)—this is the meaning. || 52 ||

Having summoned the powers of human effort, having conquered sloth, and having risen up, one should tear asunder with ease the dense cage of the snares of saṃsāra— having gathered the flood of latent impressions (vāsanā) through the threat [of discipline]— and then one must emerge on all sides like one who was previously ignorant.

For this very reason, one must cultivate unremitting human effort for the sake of shattering the vajra-cage of latent impressions (*vāsanā*); from that alone comes the accomplishment of the supreme human goal (*paramapuruṣārtha*). He concludes [the section] with the words "having gathered" (*āhṛtya*): first, having gathered the human powers such as hearing and reflecting upon the four means of attainment (*sādhanacatuṣṭaya*), and then [having removed] that which constitutes an obstacle to meditation...

Having conquered drowsiness through the practice of postures (*āsana*), breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), and so forth, and having risen from external perception by means of *samprajñāta-samādhi*, one quickly and effortlessly shatters the dense cage of the snares of *saṃsāra*— characterized by the mass of previously accumulated latent impressions (*vāsanā*)— precisely through entering the non-conceptual *asaṃprajñāta-samādhi*.

The meaning is: having shattered [all bonds] through the direct realization of reality (tattvasākṣātkāra), you should arise as the Self that is Brahman—the single essence of all-pervading, perfect bliss; you must not remain like an ignorant person dwelling within the cycle of transmigration (saṃsāra). || 53 ||

Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Peace of All," in the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa* of the *Mokṣopāya* section of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, according to the tradition of the Ṛṣis. 49.
Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Complete Quiescence," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa, within the Tātparya-prakāśa commentary. || 49 ||
Fifty-first Sarga.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: These multitudes of living beings that are seen extending throughout the ten directions—
Those designated as humans, nāgas, lords of the gods, gandharvas, and so forth—[if you say they are "gods" or "spirits," that is acceptable]. || 1 ||

The sevenfold classification of living beings, conceived through the distinctions of the firmness or looseness of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and their diversity, is here elaborated for the enlightenment of souls.
All living beings are indeed equal; it is only through latent impressions (*vāsanā*) that they are perceived as diverse.

Having stated that the diversity among living beings arises solely from the variety of their latent impressions, the author now promises to define that diversity by means of its sevenfold characteristics, beginning with the words "These...
The connection is: "those who are seen through the diversity of bodies such as humans, serpents, and so forth. (1)
Some are awake only in dreams, some are awake only in their mental constructs;
some abide solely in the waking state, while others remain established in that state for a long duration.
Others remain in dense wakefulness, while others are in the state of waking-dream;
some have their waking diminished—thus living beings are remembered as being of seven kinds.
Śrī Rāma said:
O Blessed One, let the distinction between these seven forms of living beings be told to me for my understanding, just as [the distinction] among waters in the oceans.
Just like waters in the oceans that have been perfumed by the distinct flavors of milk and other substances. || 4 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
In a certain former kalpa, in a certain world, somewhere, some living beings whose nature is to live remained asleep within their bodies. (5)
Therein, relying on the principle demonstrated in the narrative of Jīvaṭa, he defines the first [type] with the words beginning "In a certain... and so forth.
The syntactical connection with what follows is: "those who, possessing bodies and characterized by life, while being alive, perceive a dream. (5)
Know that this world is a dream for those who perceive it as a dream;
indeed, they are called the "awake in their dreams" (jīvikāḥ svapnajāgarāḥ).
This object before us is the dream that arose spontaneously for those who were fast asleep somewhere; we are but dream-men to them.

The meaning is this: when that dream-phenomenon which has arisen spontaneously for them becomes an object for us—due to the power of the arising of similar karmic impressions (vāsanā)—then we are their "dream-men. Indeed, this point was established previously in the narrative of Līlā. || 7 ||
Because of their long duration, that dream has attained the state of waking;
those living beings who were in the dream-waking state remain situated within it.

He provides the etymological justification for the term *svapnajāgaraka* (dream-waker) regarding them with the words "of them" (*teṣām*). The ellipsis to be supplied is: "because he has approached [them] from that [state]. || 8 ||
Because he is omniscient and omnipresent, everything exists everywhere for him;
therefore, we who exist like dream-people are situated within their dreams.
He also establishes what was said regarding their statement, "We are dream-men"—namely, that it is because [the Buddha] is omniscient (*sarvajña*).
Now, one might object: if the manifold world of our bodies and so forth existed within his mind in the form of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), then that very world would have arisen in his dream;
consequently, for us who are contained therein, we would indeed be his dream-men. However, this is not possible.

If you say this is not so, we reply: no, because by that very reason everything exists everywhere; for the all-pervading Brahman, variegated by *māyā* and the bestower of existence upon all things, is omniscient in all places.
Therefore, those dream-men are indeed situated within their own internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*) in the form of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), even while they are dreaming.
The meaning is that they manifest simultaneously due to the equilibrium of karma. || 9 ||
Śrī Rāma said: "In whichever kalpas they were born, those kalpa-constructions perish;
if that is so, how can there be a continued existence for those who have attained awakening?"

"Let there be a spatial [existence] everywhere; however, a temporal existence is not possible, because it is impossible for present objects to exist in past kalpas. Otherwise, all kalpas would result in simultaneity, leading to the undesirable consequence of a lack of distinction between them. With this intention, Rāma asks: "In which..."—meaning, in which kalpas previously [existed]. Those...

If the mental constructions of those living beings born and having attained birth— who are dreamers of our own conceptual proliferation— were to perish along with their bodies right now, then for those who have awakened from this dream,
no persistence in a past kalpa would be established; for indeed, by one who has awakened from a dream today, that which belonged to yesterday is not [perceived].
The meaning is that it is impossible for one who is awake to experience [the dream], as it resides far away in a previous kalpa. || 10 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Here, at the end of the delusion of their dream, they are either liberated from sleepiness, or,
having assumed bodies through volition, they fully resort to other such forms.

If those living beings happen by chance to attain knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) within this dream consisting of our own phenomenal world (*prapañca*), then they are indeed liberated; thus, there is no occurrence of this defect. However, if they do not attain it, then that particular kalpa has not passed for them, and [the dream] will surely arise again later, because only the passing away of those things imagined in other kalpas [is required]. This is held in the mind.
With the intention that even subsequent postulations regarding specific [individuals] remaining from that [previous] kalpa are possible according to the logic of the Aindava-episode,
Vasiṣṭha provides the resolution with the word "iha" (here). By the statement "they resort to others," he relies upon the doctrine of *dṛṣṭasṛṣṭi* (creation as perceived),
whereby even when there is the postulation of another body during daily waking, recognition occurs solely by virtue of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*).
This has been demonstrated. || 11 ||
In the same way, they perceive another world and its imagined constructs;
yet there can be no crowding in the sky of the manifestation of conceptualization.
Constriction is the state of having no space. || 12 ||
Those who are like worms in the decayed udumbara tree of the world—which is composed of mere conceptualization—are called dream-awakened; now hear about those awakened by conceptualization. (13)
Having concluded the description of the first group of living beings, he begins to speak of the second group with the words: "Listen" (śṛṇu). || 13 ||
In a certain former kalpa, somewhere in some world,
there were those who remained entirely sleepless within, devoted solely to their mental constructs.
Those who have cast off sleep through a mere fragment of wakefulness are intent on mental constructs, like the offspring of the moon.
Or else, having fallen away from meditative absorption, they follow the dictates of their own mental fantasies;
having attained the firmness of conceptual construction, their direct experiences have dissolved.

Alternatively, like the mendicant mentioned in the Jīvaṭa legend, they have rolled away or moved from meditation; their prior state has dissolved, as has their experience of the peak [of realization]. || 15 ||

For those whose state of waking consists of mere mental resolve (saṃkalpa) due to its long duration and partial manifestation, and for whom all activity has ceased therein, they are indeed "awake through resolve" (saṃkalpajāgarāḥ). || 16 ||

Those living beings whose very volition, having become solidified through long-standing persistence, constitutes waking—the state of being awake and the conceit of wakefulness—in which their mental activity has ceased with respect to purely volitional objects and is no longer capable of connecting the preceding with the succeeding; [these are the dreamless sleepers]. (16)
Upon the subsiding of their volitional constructs (saṃkalpa), they resort again to that [state] or another; within their bodies we, these persons of volitional constructs, remain. (17)

Whether that prior transaction was different or of a different character from that, according to their view, we are indeed persons born of volition (saṃkalpa-puruṣas), because they arise from an identical volition; this is the meaning. || 17 ||

These living beings dwelling in the world are said to be awake through their mental constructs (saṃkalpa) and sleeping through their mental constructs; they exist within the span of life. Now hear about those who are awakened solely by their own nature.

These are living beings; they go toward and enter into that which has its life in their own volition (saṃkalpa). Likewise, worlds such as our own are, from their perspective, merely waking states born of volition. He causes them to hear the third [state] by saying, "Listen. || 18 ||
They first descended from Brahmā, whose nature is expanded;
they are said to be purely wakeful, not yet unfolded prior to creation.

From Brahmā—whose self was expanded by the volition of creation and who possesses the form to be described hereafter—they descended for the first time in this kalpa, having obtained bodies; in that birth, because it was not preceded by a dream, they were purely waking beings, just like Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa mentioned previously, since they [possess those qualities]. Therefore, they...

The meaning is that [these dreams] are devoid of the characteristics of production and manifestation prior [to waking], because the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of a waking state belonging to another eon—which were exhausted precisely by the generation of the present waking state—cannot be conceived as the cause of dreams within this current eon. || 19 ||
Furthermore, those very same [entities], having passed into other births and remained awake for a long time,
are described as having reached maturity and moving through the process of cause and effect.

He speaks of the fourth [class] with the word "furthermore" (bhūyaḥ). They are those who, throughout various future births—successive series of births—have the nature of wandering among the two effects, namely waking and dreaming, as well as their cause, deep sleep. || 20 ||
Due to the penetration of those very evil deeds, they have attained the state of inert, immobile beings;
they are called "dense waking" because they have reached a state of density even among those who are awake.

He characterizes the fifth [category] with the words "ta eva" (those very same). "In the waking states" means during the conditions of wakefulness; "solidity" refers to the density of ignorance (*ajñāna*).

By the qualification "in the waking states," it is understood that even for stationary beings (*sthāvara*), there is sometimes the perception of human existence and so forth during dreams. Thus, the bound souls (*baddhajīva*) are divided into five types. || 21 ||

But those who have attained awakening, being enlightened by the meaning of the scriptures and by the company of the virtuous, perceive the waking state as if it were a dream; they become "waking-dreamers. || 22 ||
Intending to demonstrate the remaining two types of distinctions among those liberated while living (jīvanmukta), he states the sixth [verse] with the words "But those who... (ye tu).
This refers, that is to say, to those established in the fourth, fifth, and sixth stages (bhūmikā). || 22 ||
But those who have attained perfect awakening and rest in the supreme state,
for whom the stages of waking and so forth have ceased, have reached the fourth stage.
With the intention that those who have actually ascended to the seventh stage are alone "seventh," he says: "But those who... (verse 23).
Thus, the sevenfold division of living beings has been described to you by me, like that of the oceans; having understood this, become intent upon the highest good.
He is the supreme excellence, intent upon the ever-higher and more excellent stages.

Abandon the delusion consisting of the calculation of the world; you have attained the pure state of being a dense mass of consciousness alone. You are primordial, O Rāma, your body liberated from both duality and unity—free from emptiness and yet released from non-emptiness. The "calculation of the world" is the perception of it through the cognition of dualities such as the second object and so forth; abandon that very nature of delusion.

Relinquish [all notions], for you have attained a state of dense unity whose sole nature is pure awareness (*bodha*). Consequently, because there is no second or other, even the oneness that is distinguished from them is impossible; thus, your body is liberated from both duality and unity.
For this very reason, it is devoid of emptiness, yet even freed from the attribute called non-emptiness. It is primordial, transcending all conceptual constructions.
The meaning is that you remain as the primordial substratum, which is pure existence alone. || 25 ||
Thus ends the fiftieth chapter, titled "Description of the Seven Types of Living Beings," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa*, composed by Vālmīki. 50.
Thus ends the fiftieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Seven Types of Living Beings," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa-tātparyaprakāśa*.
The fifty-first canto.
Śrī Rāma said:
How can there be the state of being purely awake, which is without cause and devoid of purpose?
O Brahmin, it blossoms forth from the supreme, like a tree from the sky. || 1 ||
Just as the world arises falsely from the view of Brahman when the view of a self has not arisen, and is formless due to awakening— so too is it described here.

It has been stated that those [jīvas] who descended first from Brahman, whose nature is expanded, are called "purely awakened" (*kevalajāgaryā*); however, that is untenable. For it is impossible for there to be either a cause or a purpose for the descent of the immutable, non-dual Brahman as a *jīva* at the very outset, since the seeds—such as desire, action, and latent impressions (*vāsanā*)—exist only subsequent to the state of being a *jīva*.
Rāma suspects, asking: "How so? (1)
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O one of great intelligence, no effect is ever perceived without a cause;
therefore, for one who is merely awake, nothing at all can possibly arise here in this world.
This which has been said—that an incarnation of the individual soul (jīva) known as the "pure waking state" from the immutable non-dual reality is impossible—is too limited;
for the same logic applies to the impossibility of the incarnation of other souls rooted in that [reality] and of the world itself. Rather, it is from the immutable non-dual reality...

Vasiṣṭha gives the following reply, beginning with the words "Without cause" (*akāraṇam*), etc.: because it is impossible to give instruction without denying both the world and the individual soul (*jīva*), the conceptualization of the forms of the meanings of the words "individual soul" and "world" as belonging to Brahman itself has been fashioned in the Śruti, Smṛti, Itihāsa, and Purāṇas for the purpose of such instruction.
Because of its arising from that [source], all other varieties of living beings possessing life do not arise at all, being thwarted by the absence of their cause. (3)
They are shattered precisely because of the absence of a cause; that is to say, they are refuted. || 3 ||
Nothing whatsoever is born here, and nothing whatsoever perishes here;
the arising of the conceptualization of words and their meanings occurs only for the sake of instruction and the object of instruction.
Śrī Rāma said:
Who creates bodies through the consciousness of mind, intellect, and so forth?
Who deludes living beings with the bonds of affection, passion, and the like?

Let it be so; nevertheless, some creator must necessarily be asserted for the body and other bases of experience, whether directly or through the medium of karma and the like, because there is an invariable rule that every effect possesses an agent. Furthermore, having caused the individual soul (*jīva*) to enter [the body], there must be another who deludes it with sense-objects, for one observes no delusion of a conscious being without a deluder. And thus:

"Since the two—the deluded and the undeluded, known as the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*), who are distinct from consciousness—must indeed be accepted on the authority of scriptural testimony and reasoning regarding creation and so forth, Rāma again raises an objection: 'Who is it that acts?
(5) Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
No one ever creates bodies at any time;
no one ever deludes living beings at any time.

These two [theories] would be necessary if the agency of the body and so forth, as well as the relationship between the deluded and the non-deluded, were established as real by scripture and reasoning; however, since their unreality is firmly established by the scriptural passage beginning with "beginning with speech" (*vācārambhaṇa*) and by such passages as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), it is possible to account for mere appearance even through the illusory transformation (*vivarta*) of the immutable, non-dual Absolute. Thus, they are not required.
With the intention of showing the necessity of these two, Vasiṣṭha gives the reply beginning with "Not anyone at all," and so forth. || 6 ||
Awareness, whose nature is a manifestation without beginning or end, is established within the Self;
it appears in the form of various objects, just as [the one ocean appears] in the form of waves and so forth.
Just as water exists within itself in the form of waves and the like, so too does the conscious self exist within the Self. || 7 ||
Nothing external exists; it is consciousness that manifests as if it were external.
It arises from the heart of consciousness, like a great tree from a seed.
Now, one might ask: how can an external object be a transformation (*vivarta*) of the internal conscious self, given that they have different substrata? To this, he says: "The external...
[The external arises] from the very heart of internal consciousness, appearing as if external while remaining within. (8)
O scion of Raghu’s line, this entire universe exists within consciousness itself,
just as a carved statue is manifest within a pillar.
