Anticipating the objection that the analogy is flawed because a tree arises entirely outside of its seed, he states the following to show that the analogy is actually consistent: "Of consciousness... Alternatively, one might argue that if [the universe] were arisen within, it would have to remain only within; yet the universe exists externally.
To this, he says: "Of consciousness... (9)
May the world itself awaken—[the world] which is one with the self both external and internal, infinite in space and time, and the spreading fragrance of awakening. 10.
In reality, however, the entity of consciousness (cidvastu) is neither internal nor external; rather, it is infinite.
It is within that very [consciousness] that the conceptualization of the world—both internal and external—occurs, like a fragrance. Thus he says: "With the external... (sabāhya). || 10 ||
This very world is the highest world; let there be the exhaustion of latent impressions (vāsanā).
For one who has attained peace, what latent impressions indeed come from the state of the other world? (11)

If it is argued that if the world is merely a mental construction here [in this very body], then how is the other world—such as the realm of Brahmā (brahmaloka), which is accessible via the path beginning with light (arcirādimārga)—established as being so distant? [The answer is: It is due solely to the force of the continuous flow of such beginningless latent impressions (vāsanā). However, upon the exhaustion of these impressions, all of that becomes nothing but one's own Self and is thus extremely near. With this intention, he says: "This very [Self]... for the sake of the peaceful sage.
The meaning is that for one who exists here in this very world as the self belonging to the other world, the latent impressions (vāsanās) such as distance and so forth do not arise. || 11 ||
It is the locus of space, time, action, the world, form, mind, self, and existence;
yet it is devoid of the referents of words such as "space," "time," and so forth, and is not a mere void.

Now, if the inner self (*pratyagātman*) alone is the essence of all things—including the space, time, and so forth of the next world—then, when space, time, and the like are sublated, why would it not itself become of the nature of emptiness? To this, he says: "Space," etc. (Verse 12).
O Rāghava, the realization of that state occurs only for those who know the words and for those observers for whom the visible world has become stilled; it does not occur for others.

If it were not empty, then why would ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) not attain awakening in that state merely by the cessation of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*)? To this, he says: "In the state" (*pade*). || 13 ||
Those who have indeed taken refuge in the deep abyss of the greatness of instability—
none of them ever behold that light.
To the knower, this perception of the world—resounding with the fourteen kinds of infinite elemental beings—is comparable to the limbs of his own body. 15.
He then states what the perception of the world is like for one who perceives that [reality]: "fourteen," etc. (verse 15).
Due to the absence of a cause, creation neither arises nor ceases;
for whatever the nature of the cause may be, such is the nature of the effect.

To explain what kind of creation exists for them from the perspective of meditative concentration (*samāhita-dṛś*) and what kind exists from the perspective of conventional transaction (*vyavahāra-dṛś*), he says [the verse] beginning with "kāraṇa" in the first and second halves [of the stanza]. || 16 ||
If the effect were already present within the cause, what would constitute its causality?
Since only the effect is perceived, both [cause and effect] are non-existent, as they are not cognized as distinct entities.
Therein, he establishes with reasoning what was stated in the first half [of the verse], beginning with "If": "Why is it not established? To this he says:
"Because it is indeed the effect. The meaning is that since no other entity distinct from the earring is perceived, there is no other cause. || 17 ||
Just as waves, whirlpools, and the like exist within the tranquil ocean,
so do the world, the mind, and other phenomena exist within Brahman, which is free from agitation.
He also establishes what was stated in the second half of the verse by means of an illustration: "Of the gentle one," etc. (18).
The stainless Brahman, which is the self of all, exists as a single mass, just as gold exists within various vessels in the form of their internal shapes. (19)

Brahman exists as a single entity containing within itself various objects, like a lump of clay; it exists just as gold exists containing within it forms such as bracelets and earrings. The sense is that even the state of being a lump is an effect, and thus it is comparable to the state of being a bracelet and so forth. (19)
At the time of dreaming, it is indeed a dream, because one is not occupied with or grasping at the waking state;
at the time of waking, it is indeed waking, because of the realization of reality.

Just as it is established that at the time of the lump of clay it is merely a lump, and at the time of the jar it is merely a jar—such being the perception of one and the same thing—so too, regarding phenomenal expansion (*prapañca*), it is established that during the state of dreaming it is merely a dream within waking, and during the state of waking it is merely waking within a dream;
thus the knowers of the reality of the world perceive only a single [reality]. He says "in a dream" (*svapne*) [to illustrate this]. For one who is distracted...
Because the mind, which is attached to the expansion of latent impressions, is neither grasped nor restrained. || 20 ||
The Buddha exists as mind-only, like the water of a mirage;
when deprived of analytical investigation, he appears as the state of waking or dreaming. (21)

Even during the waking state, that which is examined as being merely the waking mind attains the very same nature as a dream; thus, the fact that the creation of the wise man is comparable to a limb of the body has been established. Concluding in this way, he states that even that [creation] is sublated along with its root in right knowledge, by saying "as being merely the mind" (cittamātratayā). || 21 ||
Through right knowledge, the elements, along with the body of the knower,
release their bond to the foundation, just as clouds disperse when their time has passed.
The meaning is that when the rainy season has passed, the clouds likewise relinquish even their state of mist, which was the very cause of their formation upon the surface of the earth. || 22 ||
Just as a dense cloud that has begun to dissolve returns to the state of the sky,
so too does the world, along with its grasping at a self, subside through the realization of truth.
It is accompanied by the grasping at a self, which is egoism; or, it is accompanied by the final state of direct realization. || 23 ||
Like autumn clouds that have been dispersed, or like the water of a mirage,
the state of being perceived falls away upon awakening, as if it were being touched once more.
Being touched by contact and so forth, it is indeed being experienced. || 24 ||
Just as gold, clarified butter, and fuel become one when absorbed in a blazing fire,
so too do the world, the mind, and perception attain unity within consciousness.
Through awakening, the sense of solid aggregation in the three worlds becomes attenuated,
just as the perception of a house as a demon vanishes for a child who has been awakened.
The "binding of the body" (piṇḍabandha) is the grasping of forms such as the physical form; its "attenuation" is its gradual dissolution. || 26 ||

Within consciousness, which is infinite in form, the appearance of the world, the mind, and so forth, occurs by itself within itself; indeed, the "binding of the body" (piṇḍabandha) is merely this [appearance] here.
And this dissolution does not depart due to the disappearance of its cause, as is the case with the dissolution of the hardness of lac;
rather, like the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, it is non-returning because its counter-positive is unreal. With this intention, he says: "of consciousness" (*bodhasya*).
Consciousness is that in which there exist no ends—that is, the three kinds of limitation (*pariccheda*)—nor forms—that is, distinctions of shape (*ākāra-bheda*).

The witness-consciousness itself, being without cause, appears as a threefold form: the world, the mind that conceptualizes it, and primordial ignorance; this occurs within this very awakening. || 27 ||
This world has arisen like the mind itself through the very act of awakening to non-awakening;
when that [mind] has set through awakening, what existence can there be for the bondage of the physical body? (28)
And thus, it follows that it is only false ignorance that expands through its state as the mind of the unreal world; so he says: "It is simply the non-perception of awakening. (28)
Through the awakening from waking and dreaming, it abandons the hardness of its mass and attains supreme lightness, like gold melted by fire. (29)

By this it is established what was previously stated: that even while awake, one abandons grossness during the time of dreaming and enters into a subtle state of the phenomenal world; and that the very delusion of the dream, through long-standing habituation, attains a density such that it appears as if it were the waking state. This he expresses with the words beginning "jahāti" (he abandons). || 29 ||
Awareness itself, as it truly is, attains a state of density,
as if creating space and time out of nothing, like gold.
Those two are waking and dreaming. || 30 ||
While one remains thus awake through inquiry, as the state that resembles a dream—fragile and now waning—attains thinness like the sap in the autumn season. (31)
Taste is the passion for enjoyment and water. || 31 ||
Though they persist, the splendors of the visible world have reached an extreme fragility;
like dreams, they no longer please the discerning man once he has recognized them for what they are. 32.
Frailty and insignificance. || 32 ||

Where indeed is the repose in one's own self, and where is this perception of objects? How could there be an identity between deep sleep and the waking state, or between the nature of delusion and non-delusion? (33)
With the intention that his disregard for sense-objects arises from being satisfied with the bliss of the Self, he says: "Where? (kva). The meaning is:
if sense-objects were to please even an ignorant person, then one might as well imagine an identity between deep sleep and the waking state;
likewise, one could not imagine an identity between a deluded self and a non-deluded self, or between a fool and a knower of reality. || 33 ||
When one abides in that which is mind-only, mere illusion, and essentially like a dream,
the notion of reality regarding the objects of this world ceases.
When the world is realized to be mind-only and established as having the nature of a mere dream, the notion of reality regarding objects such as garlands and sandalwood ceases here. || 34 ||
Whose untruths are pleasing, O Mahāmati? For how could they be so, when even those things that appear before one are like the waters of a mirage? (35)

To the objection that even non-existent objects of enjoyment might be pleasing to him, he says: "Of whom? The particle *eva* is used in the sense of exclusion (*vā-arthe*). The meaning is: how indeed could they be pleasing? || 35 ||
When the cognition of reality has dissolved, one of tranquil intellect perceives the world as having the nature of the sky— a single,
undifferentiated mass appearing like the web of rays from a window-lattice.

Just as one perceives the light of a mass of lamp-rays entering through a lattice window as having the nature of illumination yet being formless and of the nature of space, so too [does he perceive the Self]. || 36 ||

For one who is awake, the cultivation of the savoring of delusive forms— which consists of the delusion of the mind (or, as the reading *cittamātrātmanaḥ* suggests, which consists of the nature of mere mind)— ceases once that which is in reality empty has been fully understood. (37)

Therefore, the meaning is that it is well known that for a waking person, the experience and mental cultivation of dream-objects such as garlands and sandalwood—which are essentially mind-only—ceases once those objects are fully recognized as being empty (śūnya). || 37 ||
When something is known to be a non-entity, how can there be any value in adopting it?
Having recognized a dream as such, who would go after the gold seen in that dream? (38)
Who would go to obtain gold from a dream? || 38 ||
When the object of perception is thoroughly understood as being like a dream, attachment to it ceases;
then the severing of the knot of defects in the states of the seer and the seen proceeds.

Devoid of passion, with a tranquil mind, having extinguished the conceit of "I," and accomplished; free from attachment, effortless, and peaceful—the one with the intellect of a Buddha remains thus. (40)

Regarding how he remains when the senses have ceased their activity, he says: "tasteless" (nīrasa). This means he is without affection for kinsmen and the like, and free from passion toward sense objects. || 40 ||
When the flavor has become flavorless, latent impressions dissolve, just as the rays of a lamp vanish when its flame is extinguished. (41)
Through awakening, the sky appears free from clouds, shining with a mass of rays like a lamp;
the entire world is of the nature of delusion, like a city of Gandharvas. (42)

Once the reality is realized, the entire world, which previously appeared as a form of delusion, is no longer seen as a solid mass; rather, like the web of rays from a lamp, it is perceived as having the single flavor of light, being insubstantial and equal to space.
Seeing neither the self, nor space, nor emptiness, nor sensation—
through ultimate transformation— one beholds that state.
Then, how does it occur through the ultimate transformation characterized by abiding on the seventh stage? To that he says: "Not at all," [seeing thus] the knower of reality. (43)
Where there is neither self nor emptiness, neither the mental construction of the world nor the notion of the arising of the mind's objects— there everything exists just as it is.
The earth and so forth, though perceived by the ignorant, have set through knowledge;
for the wise person, they have become nothing but emptiness, and even while persisting, they do not exist.

By the ignorant, they are perceived as a solid mass; by those who have awakened through the knowledge that [the elements] such as earth and so forth are [merely] designations, they have reached their cessation. || 45 ||
He becomes one whose self is tranquil through single-pointed concentration and as stainless as the sky;
remaining free from attachment, he stays as if established, yet equal to the unreal.
With his mind set at rest, silent, and having attained the state of cessation,
he has crossed the ocean of saṃsāra and reached the end of all karmas.
Supreme ignorance is that which is intent upon the creation of the body, the world, the sky, and the multitude of mountains;
when that has dissolved, all this [universe], though still existing, dissolves away.

For this reason, the supreme material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) of the subtle bodies (*tanu*), the fourfold physical bodies, their supports— the worlds— their support— the ether (*gagana*)— the places of recreation, the mountain ranges, and the instruments that serve as their means, is none other than supreme ignorance, namely root-ignorance (*mūlājñāna*). Therefore:

When that primordial ignorance (mūlājñāna), which is the cause, has dissolved through knowledge, this entire world—including the body and the universe—though appearing to exist to the vision of the ignorant, dissolves; the meaning is that it becomes non-existent. || 48 ||

With his inner organ completely stilled, with conceptual constructions dissolved, consisting of the essence of his own true nature, and satisfied by the nectar of supreme peace, the wise one remains free from all veils. (49)

In this manner, the yogi whose conceptual constructions have dissolved, being composed of the essence of his own true nature, remains satisfied by the nectar of supreme peace—his own bliss—and abides in the nature of unobscured, infinite bliss; such is the meaning. || 49 ||
Thus ends the fifty-first chapter, titled "Instruction on the Yoga of Rest," in the Nirvāṇa Section of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, within the *Deva-mokṣopāya*.
Thus ends the fifty-first chapter, titled "Instruction on the Yoga of Rest," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The fifty-second canto.
Śrī Rāma said: O Sage, by what process does consciousness appear as if it were the world?
Speak that sequence step by step once more, for the sake of the cessation of further differentiation.

In this context, the existence of the world as indeterminable is established for the immutable reality through the refutation of various conceptual constructions arising from the logic of dialecticians.

Tell me again, through a process of supporting arguments and by refuting the various distinctions among the conceptualizations of other disputants, the sequence and manner in which consciousness—the immutable self of pure awareness—manifests. || 1 ||

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Just as with a tree that is utterly insentient, whatever is seen by its sight does not exist in its own mind; for one whose memory is extremely diminished, that which is not seen does not arise in the mind.

In order to support the point that this appearance of the world as the conscious Self (*cidātman*) is indeed indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*), he first demonstrates— relying on the doctrine of "creation upon perception" (*dṛṣṭisṛṣṭivāda*)— that its existence conforms to the presence and absence of perception, by means of the phrase "just like a tree. [This refers to] the tree of the Self belonging to one who is utterly deluded and ignorant.

The meaning is this: just as a world-form composed of various shapes—such as roots, wood, leaves, and sprouts—is established in one's own mind as existing only when it is perceived, and not otherwise; for this very reason, even the slightest thing that has been seen is remembered, whereas even a great deal that has not been seen is not, because its existence is not established. || 2 ||
A capable person perceives only the meaning of the scripture as it is connected from beginning to end;
he does not act upon whatever object merely falls within the range of his vision.

With the intention that the existence of the world is understood to be established solely according to each respective perspective—since a difference in action is observed between the learned and the ignorant based on their adherence to scripture or non-scripture—he says: "The fortunate one" (bhavya).
One whose vision is impaired does not perceive, even when it is close at hand, an object forbidden by scripture as something fit for enjoyment. || 3 ||
Being devoted to the practice of the teachings and with a mind focused solely on the meaning of the scriptures, become a sage and listen to this instruction, which is an ornament to the ears.

For this very reason, with the intention that you too are being enjoined to the hearing [of scriptures] and other practices solely by way of establishing the scriptural perspective, he says "bhāva" and so forth. *Bhāva* refers to action conducive to the purification of the mind. (4)
This delusion regarding the weight of the visible world is indeed called ignorance;
in reality, it does not exist, just as there is no water in a mirage.
He states that it is so because its status as ignorance is well-established: "This," etc. (Verse 5).
For the sake of the instruction and the one to be instructed, please listen for a moment to this, relying upon me as if I were Satī herself at my request. (6)
If that is so, how then is the instruction of the scripture and its fruit established? To this he says: "By means of instruction," etc. (verse 6).
Without raising the conceptual constructions such as "from where does this come" or "how is it so," you will yourself understand through awakening that "this is not theirs, nor does it exist."
However, at the time of attaining the fruit of the instruction, this delusion ceases entirely; with the intention that it is likewise [destroyed] even beyond that, he says:
"Whatever is seen here—this world, both stationary and moving, in all its manifold variety—all of it perishes at the end of the kalpa. (8)

Having thus demonstrated the theory of illusory manifestation (*vivartapakṣa*) as being grounded in direct experience, and desiring to state the defects in other positions, he first asserts the perishability of the world in order to state the defect that, for those who accept the non-difference of the world from Brahman—just as the branches are non-different from the tree—the infinity of Brahman would be lost: [He states: "The world is perishable."
That is to say: || 8 ||
The destruction of this [consciousness], consisting of the division of its parts, is necessarily unavoidable;
for when it is extracted through each individual *bindu* during awakening, there is indeed its cessation.

He establishes what was asserted with the words "of this": the destruction of this world—which consists of the division, that is, the disintegration, of its parts such as the earth and other constituents—is unavoidable upon awakening, that is, through reflection, because it possesses parts.
For, in the world, the destruction of water contained in a jar or similar object occurs when it is drawn out and separated drop by drop.
The meaning is that it is well-known to be like that. || 9 ||
This being the case, since Brahman consists of that very substance, upon the destruction of the substance, neither infinity nor existence can possibly occur at all. || 10 ||

Let there be destruction; what is the fault in that? To this he replies: "In this way. Just as a tree is destroyed when its parts such as branches are destroyed, so too, if substances such as the earth were to be destroyed, it would follow that Brahman is also destroyed; thus, the infinity taught in the Śruti would not be established. Furthermore, since a whole (avayavin) cannot exist when it is conceptually separated from its parts, its existence [as a distinct entity] is not possible.
The meaning is that Brahman, which is of the single essence of consciousness and partless, cannot logically become the world consisting of parts such as material forms and so forth. || 10 ||
The claim that "knowledge is like the power of intoxication" is not established for us;
for us, the body is [known] through consciousness as being like a dream, but not as a reality. (11)

Now, one might object: "Let it not be that the conscious self (*cidātman*) has the inert world as its constituent part; rather, let consciousness (*caitanya*) be a property of the very inert elements—earth and so forth—which have transformed into the shape of a body, just as the power of intoxication inheres in the constituents of wine. Having thus set forth the position of the Cārvākas, he refutes it with the words: "The power of intoxication itself... [is not established] among us, the believers (*āstikas*). It is not proven.

This means that it cannot be established against us by the Cārvāka. For, according to our view as authoritative proponents, the body—since its establishment is dependent upon consciousness—is not ultimately real, being like a body in a dream.
Indeed, there is no proof for the existence of a body apart from consciousness; and when the body is unestablished, [the Cārvāka’s argument fails].
The intended meaning is that consciousness ought to arise in the same manner as the power of intoxication. || 11 ||
The splendor of the visible world perishes; it is that very same splendor, neither something else nor not at all.
In this way, the scripture would be rendered consistent, and not otherwise.

Furthermore, if the non-difference of the world from Brahman were asserted [in a literal sense], there would arise the suspicion that Brahman is finite due to the destruction of the visible world. However, since this non-difference is merely superimposed (ādhyāsika), the destruction of the counter-correlate (the world) does not, in reality, touch Brahman—just as the counter-correlate itself does not—and thus that suspicion does not apply; moreover, the scripture achieves its purpose. With this intention, he says: "It perishes indeed. For, again:

The splendor of the visible world, having perished, arises again; it is that very same [splendor], not something else, yet it is not [that] either—it is indefinable, being mere ignorance (*avidyāmātra*). This being so, only when that [ignorance] is sublated by knowledge (*vidyā*) does the scripture become fruitful.
Otherwise, since the cessation of real bondage would be impossible, the scripture would be useless as a means; such is the meaning. || 12 ||
How could there be the possibility of a lost object if it were not grasped as "this is that very same thing"?
It would be more logical to say it is "different from that form," for we follow what has been experienced. (13)
He states that because it cannot be determined whether the world-structure, which was destroyed at the time of dissolution, is the very same as that which emerges again during creation,
or something else, it is indeed indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*), by means of the passage beginning with "that very same" (*saiva etīti*).
It is impossible to conceive without mention that "that which was destroyed is the very same [entity] returning," for [the world] follows upon what has been previously experienced.
The meaning is: we follow experience; we do not tolerate even the slightest thing that contradicts experience. || 13 ||
If it existed as space itself, then how could it be non-existent?
And if it remained as space in that very same way, then it has not undergone destruction. (14)

He clarifies precisely the failure [of the opponent's view] to ascend to experience with the words "that very same" (saiva). That very materiality (mūrtatā) existed at the time of dissolution (pralaya) as the state of space (vyomatā), that is, in an immaterial form; this is incorrect. For how can that very materiality be immaterial? If even as space it remained in that same previous state during dissolution, then it would not have undergone destruction, and thus the doctrine of dissolution would be abolished—this is the meaning.
When cause and effect are thus of one and the same nature, then, due to the absence of the relationship between cause and effect, their identity alone is our tradition. (15)

Thus, since the same logic applies to creation as it does to the state of dissolution, there would be the undesirable consequence that the effect—namely, creation—could arise from the unmanifest state of dissolution; this would result in the doctrine of an immutable [cause]. To address this, he says "kārya... (the effect...). The meaning is: "our scripture" refers to our own established tenet. || 15 ||
That which has reached the state of emptiness and non-apprehension is indeed destroyed;
tell me then, what other kind of destruction could there possibly be? (16)

Whatever entity has attained the state of being perceived yet has also attained emptiness—that is indeed destroyed. This is because its non-existence is admitted even at the time it is perceived; for the very attainment of non-existence is what constitutes destruction. If there were some other kind of destruction in the world, then let it be described as such. Nor can that which is destroyed be considered undestroyed merely by virtue of having been perceived.
It is so; for since even things that have perished are seen to be perceived in a dream, their non-perishing is not established. || 16 ||
When one perceives that what was lost has arisen again, who is it that perceives?
That which perishes necessarily gives rise once more to something else. (17)

If it is argued that because we observe a subsequent re-arising, the existence of [the entity] must be postulated even though it was destroyed in the interim, [we reply] that such is not the case, because arising is possible even through transformation (bheda), and because recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) and so forth are not observed; thus he says:

"destroyed" (*naṣṭam*). He recognizes (*pratyabhijānāti*) by means of cognition (*pratyaya*). The substitution of *pada* and *varṇa* in the form *ayateḥ* for *pratyabhijānāti* in the present tense (*laṭ*) is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*). || 17 ||

Since there exists a persistence of the seed-essence from the beginning until the body [is formed], consisting of various parts such as height and fruit at every stage, how can there be a relationship of cause and effect? (18)
Now, just as in a single tree, despite the various differences in hollows, trunks, branches, and so forth occurring here and there, there is a unity of the tree’s body from root to tip,
while only the branches and their effects are differentiated— so it is with respect to the various modifications such as origination, dissolution, and re-emergence.

If it is asked, "Why could there not be a single unity even from the world onwards? he says [in response]: "In the middle. Height (*utsedha*) means elevation; fruits, and by the word "etcetera," branches, sub-branches, the trunk of wood, leaves, flowers, and so forth—those parts which are individual yet pervasive, existing throughout the body of the tree as the undivided reality of the seed (*bījasattā*) itself—thus, in the vision of the unity of existence (*sattaikyadṛṣṭi*), that [reality] exists therein.
The meaning is that because the separate existence of branches and so forth is unestablished, the relationship between cause and effect would be destroyed. || 18 ||

Since the single seed exists here exactly as it is perceived—possessing its own specific place, time, and action—it performs only its own particular function; therefore, a jar does not perform the function of a cloth.
He demonstrates that the negation of cause and effect stated in the illustration applies to the subject of the illustration by saying "deśa" (space,

etc.): if one were to admit that the single seed is merely pure Being (*sanmātra*), whose nature consists of space, time, action, and so forth— pertaining to dissolution, creation, and the like— then, being such as it is, that single entity would not perform any action whatsoever, nor would it possess any action or its fruit.

Because of incapacity; for it is not the case that a jar, being incapable of the effect of a cloth, produces it—this is the meaning. Alternatively, that which is inherent in it must be stated to have a single nature, whether consisting of the locus of the seed, time, or action. For it is impossible for a single thing to possess multiple natures, since unity cannot be established when there is a difference in nature. And thus, if...

In that case, an entity possessing the nature of a single location would not perform an action at a different time; for it is never observed that an object having the nature of a jar performs the function of a cloth—this is the meaning. (19)
In the established doctrines of all philosophical systems, there is no difference regarding the ultimate reality;
since it consists of the supreme truth, what use have we here for dispute? (20)

With the intention of showing that one who asserts that a single entity possesses diverse intrinsic natures (*nānāsvabhāva*) would be a mere caviller (*vaitaṇḍika*) because he transgresses the tenets of all philosophical systems, [the author] says: "All," and so forth. In the tenets of all philosophical systems, there is no difference in effects when the entity is one.
Even regarding the nature of an entity consisting of ultimate reality, there is no difference or manifoldness. Therefore...
The meaning is: what is the purpose of engaging in a dispute with one who speaks in contradiction to all philosophical systems? || 20 ||

This is peaceful, without beginning or end, because upon investigation it is seen to be of that nature; it is like the sky, consisting of pure awareness alone, as established by the authority of direct experience. (21)

But by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), if there is only one single nature, then it is established that only the single nature of consciousness (*cit-svabhāva*), which is the foundational support, remains; thus he says, "This" (*idam*). The sense is that since all conceptual constructions have experience (*anubhūti*) as their essential core, and because it is impossible to deny that nature, by the method of elimination only the insentient nature (*jaḍa-svabhāva*) is discarded. || 21 ||
How this was not previously experienced, how it is now being experienced,
and how it attains perfection— all this is now explained in due order.
He promises to provide the proof for that with the words: "As follows. || 22 ||
When the entire visible sphere has perished at the end of a great eon,
including everything up to Mahādeva, along with their minds, intellects, and actions.

For this very reason, he says in five verses beginning with "At the end of the great kalpa" (mahākalpānte) that even when all distinctions have dissolved, only the nature of pure experience remains, unimpaired. || 23 ||
Even when the sky has reached stillness, when time remains unperceived, when the wind has departed, and when fire has utterly ceased to exist; (24)
When even fire has gone to destruction, when water and the other elements have long been exhausted,
and when the entire collection of words and their referents has reached its ultimate end— (25)
What remains is the essence of peaceful awakening, eternally pure, free from all that can be sublated, without beginning or end, gentle, indescribable, stainless, and immutable. (26)
Inexpressible, unmanifest, beyond the senses, and nameless;
the self of all beings, the void, both being and non-being—that is the supreme state. (27)
That is neither air nor space, neither intellect and so forth nor emptiness;
it is not anything at all, yet it is the self of all, another supreme sky.
One might ask: why could the remainder not simply be the nature of air and so forth? To this, he says: "That... (verse 28).
That is experienced by one who knows it, who stands upon that state, and who is liberated from it;
for others, it is described solely through the scriptures as they have been handed down.
He states that even now this is established by the experience of those who know it: "tadvidā" (by one who knows that). || 29 ||
There is no time, no mind, no self, neither being nor non-being, nor space or direction;
there is no middle between these two, no end, no awakening, and no unawakened state.

In this regard, he shows the meaning of such scriptural passages as "Time, inherent nature, necessity, chance, the elements, the womb, and the person—these are to be considered," by stating: "Not time. (30)

That which is somehow utterly transparent is realized by those who have reached the further shore of awakening, whose expansions of worldly existence have been stilled, and who have attained the supreme state. (31)

Thus he cites the traditional scripture (āgama) known by those who know the Self, beginning with "That which the knowers of the Self know," and says: "Something indeed... [referring to] that which is beyond the fourth state (turiya).
"But these objects which have been negated by me exist everywhere;
they are to be delimited by my intellect, like the waves of the gentle ocean. (32)

He says "they have been refuted" to show that these objects have also been repeatedly refuted by me, relying upon experience in accordance with the Vedas. Those very objects which exist as things to be prohibited throughout all the Śrutis are precisely what have been refuted by me.
Just as various carved figures exist uncarved within a great pillar, so do all phenomena abide there exactly as they are. (33)

In that case, what is the intended meaning of the scriptural passages on the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*), such as "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone"? He states it:
"as it truly exists. The purport of those [scriptures] is that the very existence of the world is the undifferentiated state of the nature of Brahman; such is the sense.
Thus, all entities exist there in that manner, and yet they do not exist in that manner.
That which is not the self of all is indeed the self of all; it is both that very thing and not that very thing.

For this very reason, with the intention that there is no contradiction between such scriptural passages as "Not here, not here" (*neha nānā*) and those such as "Being alone, my dear," both are designated in these two ways; thus he says, "In this manner" (*evam*). || 34 ||
Just as this state is the self of all and devoid of all objects,
so do those who are transformed into oneness perceive it therein.

He states that for yogins, the perception of both "it exists" and "it does not exist" is established there at will, like various figures carved upon an uncarved stone—thus he says: "The state" (pada). || 35 ||
Everything is indeed of the nature of everything, yet that primordial state is seen to be devoid of all objects, while simultaneously being completely full of all objects. (36)
O you of great intelligence, such perfect generosity as that which consists in the pacification of all objects has not yet arisen in you; here, doubt is the proof. (37)

"Up to this point" means up to the limit of the time of meditative absorption (samādhi) previously described. Here, "doubt" (saṃśaya) is the indicative mark (liṅga) for the non-arising of perfect knowledge. The sense is that, according to the scriptural statement, "All doubts are cut asunder," once the reality is ascertained, one no longer experiences doubt. || 37 ||
He who is awakened, who has attained the supreme radiance that is free from appearances,
and whose inner organ is pure and tranquil— he beholds that true nature.
"Non-appearance" means being free from the appearance of all that is visible; "supreme appearance" refers to the final direct realization. || 38 ||
This delusion of the world throughout the three periods of time—consisting of "this," "you," "I," and so forth—exists therein like a network of ornaments within a mass of gold. (39)
Within the mass of gold, there exists, as it were by imagination, a lattice—a collection—of silver coins and silver seals. || 39 ||
Just as a collection of various vessels is not perceived apart from a mass of gold, so too the world is not found to be distinct from the solid mass of ultimate reality.
If that is so, is the world real as a distinct entity, like a gold ornament? No; he says "from the lump of gold" (hemapiṇḍāt). This means it is not real as something various or separate.
For he whose self is always distinct from the perception of his own limbs as objects,
sees this entire world-duality as being like gold in the form of ornaments.
Although the unreal is not distinct from Being, nevertheless, Being is indeed distinct from the unreal; thus he says, "always.
The meaning is that the unreal is like a mere ornament upon the body [of Being]. || 41 ||
Devoid of the meanings of words such as "place" and so forth, this world—consisting of place, time, and action—is exactly as it is; therein, everything both exists and does not exist. (42)

It is empty—that is, devoid—of the objects of words such as "place" (deśa) and so forth, which serve as the grounds for their application (pravṛttinimitta), namely genus (jāti), quality (guṇa), action (kriyā), and the like. || 42 ||
Just as a painter creates a variety of objects upon a mass of clay, even though the water is uniform, so too does this [universe] abide within Brahman, like waves and the like in still water. (43)
Likewise, this [reality] here is neither different nor non-different; it both does not exist and exists.
It is eternally composed of that alone, pure, and likewise peaceful within peace. (44)
In the same way, he states that the unreal, whose nature is difficult to define due to its distinctions and so forth, resides within Brahman—using the word "tathā" (so too):
"When [the world] has been pacified by the knowledge of reality, it remains in Brahman as one whose self is pacified. (44)
This statue of the three worlds appears as if it were never carved at all; it has attained visibility within the wood of Brahman, as if by its own inherent nature. (45)

"Unplanted and uncarved"—this is as if the visibility of the artisan, who is his own essence and his own witness, [is revealed]. The metaphor "in the wood of Brahman" is a *vyastarūpaka* (distributed metaphor). 45.
The statues upon the pillars appear as if they were carved in stone;
within this very Akṣobhya, the waves of creative visions remain undisturbed. (46)
Regarding that, he states the distinction with the words "in this": in Akṣobhya, who is unchangeable, there are waves in the form of manifestations. || 46 ||
In the lake of supreme flavor, showers of the nectar of dense consciousness shine forth;
though undivided, they appear as if divided, and though unagitated, as if agitated.
Within the density of consciousness, the visions of creation appear to shine, though they do not truly manifest.

He explains this very point with the verse beginning "sarasī" (along with its half-verse): In the lake of consciousness (*citsarasi*), which is filled with the water of unsurpassed bliss (*atirasa*), the perceptions of creation—consisting primarily of the nectar-shower from the clouds of consciousness—exist as divisions even though they are devoid of any differentiating attributes;
they are agitated even within the unagitated, and while remaining unmanifest, they appear as if manifest. This is the meaning of the distinction. || 47 ||
In every single atom here, the entire circle of the world shines forth with radiant manifestation, yet nothing at all shines forth [as a separate entity]. 48.
In this regard, he clarifies the point that "those which were not manifest become manifest" with the words: "in the atom" (paramāṇau). || 48 ||
The collection of categories such as space, time, and wind constitutes its limbs, yet for that which is devoid of limbs, even these are not limbs.

Though it is the self of all and devoid of all modifications of existence, they call this the undecaying ultimate reality (paramārthatattva). [49] He concludes by summarizing the state of the world within the immutable (kūṭastha), beginning with "ākāśa": [He concludes by summarizing the state of the world within the immutable (kūṭastha), beginning with "ākāśa": "Space," etc.

Although this limbless and partless [Self] is described as having limbs in the form of the collection of categories such as space, time, and wind, even that is limbless and indeed partless, because it is false and because nothing remains but the underlying substratum alone.
Thus, although this undecaying reality of the Self is devoid of all modifications of existence, through the superimposition of everything upon it—
The meaning is that the Vedas declare [the Self] to be the essence of all. || 49 ||
Thus ends the fifty-second canto, titled "The Description of the Nature of Brahman," in the Nirvāṇa Section of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, within the *Deva-mokṣopāya*.
Thus ends the fifty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Nature of Brahman," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The fifty-third canto.
Śrī Rāma said:
Just as there is consciousness in the object of consciousness, and just as there is temporality in time;
Just as there is spatiality in space, and just as there is insentience in the insentient. || 1 ||
The reality of those objects of thought that have been superimposed, which possess their own individual distinctions,
is described as being none other than Brahman, whose meaning is established by the negative particle *na* and so forth.

When the process by which Brahman attains the form of the world— which is superimposed upon it and is inexpressible— has been described, Rāma, desiring to know in reality the nature of that which consists of universals (jāti) and so forth, which is inherent in certain individuals, distinguished from others, and denoted by abstract suffixes such as *tva* and *tal*, asks with the words beginning "Just as... (*yathā*).

"Cetya" means the object of memory; "cetanatā" is the state of being an object of memory. The suffix *lyuṭ* is used here in the sense of a locative substratum (*vaiṣayikādhāra*), resulting in the form *tal*. It is synonymous with "the state of being perceivable" (*cetyatā*). || 1 ||
Just as the nature of wind exists in the wind, non-existence in that which has not come into being, movement in that whose essence is motion, and materiality in the corporeal; || 2 ||
That which has not yet come to be is "present" according to the first term; therein lies its state of being unbecome, and by extension, it applies to that which is yet to be.

Just as there is divisibility in the divisible, just as there is infinity in the infinite, just as there is visibility in the visible, and just as there is the nature of creation in creations; || 3 ||
When the [mind] that possesses the conceptual differentiation of objects and so forth has ceased, it becomes infinite and empty of those [objects]. || 3 ||
O Brahmin, best among speakers, explain this to me in its proper sequence from the beginning; for those of limited understanding are made to comprehend only when taught in such a manner. (4)
Tell me, by means of the sequence of awakening methods, this very nature of all things which is unique to each;
[the author] reveals the intention behind the statement "by means of a sequence" with the words "from the beginning. || 4 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
That infinite great space is called the mass of great consciousness;
it consists of the nature of consciousness that is beyond being known, peaceful, one, and established in equilibrium.

Intending to provide the answer that the existence of the entities you have asked about— beginning with "that which was asked by you"— is the conscious Self alone, because its own superimposition of mutual identity upon those [superposed things] brings about the manifestation of their existence,
he begins to demonstrate its nature as eternally real with the words "That is infinite," and so forth. As for what was asked by you:
This is the meaning of "this very thing. || 5 ||

When the words "Brahmā," "Viṣṇu," "Īśvara," and so forth—ending with the one named the Great Dissolution (mahāpralaya)—have reached their conventional meaning, that which remains is the pure [reality]. (6)

Because it remains when everything else has perished, that alone is the true being (*bhāva*) of all things. With the intention of explaining that the word *bhāva*—derived from the root *bhū* with the suffix *ghañ*—denotes eternal existence, he says: "Brahman. [In this context,] "name and form" refer to the literal meanings of words; these have reached a state of "non-ascendancy," meaning they have become concealed. Through the dissolution of everything that is merely non-existent, the true referent of the word "Being" (*sat*) remains, and therein it attains its conventional usage (*rūḍhi*).
Or, [the meaning is] "having attained renown. || 6 ||
In that regard, no cause for creation is logically tenable—neither impurity (*mala*), nor form-seeds (*ākārabīja*), nor the like, nor *māyā*, delusion (*moha*), error (*bhrama*), and so forth. (7)

[Objection: "But let that [creation] also dissolve into its own cause; therefore, let it be non-existent there. To this he replies with the words "of creation" (*sargasya*). In that case, no cause whatsoever for the birth of creation is possible within the nature of the Real (*sat*). The sense is that impurity (*mala*), *māyā*, and so forth, have their establishment dependent upon that [Reality]. || 7 ||
It is exclusively peaceful, utterly pure, and devoid of beginning and end;
it exists even where space itself is as solid as a stone.
Since it is devoid of beginning and end, it exists eternally; thus, the meaning of the word *bhāva* is the sense of existence (*sattā*). This is the intended meaning. || 8 ||
When that which has the nature of consciousness exists, it is not proper to say that it does not exist;
nor is it proper to say that it exists, for at that time it is utterly tranquil and free from stain.

Therefore, when it is quiescent and free from impurity, it is not appropriate to say "it exists" according to the function of verbal expression; for in that state, it would be a potentiality (*bhavitṛ*) rather than an actual entity (*bhāva*). This is the meaning. || 9 ||
When self-awareness has reached a hundred yojanas in a mere moment,
that form which exists in the midst of it is the form of that state.

He prevents the notion that such a consciousness whose nature is devoid of objects is entirely unestablished by demonstrating its experience through the words "in the blink of an eye" (*nimeṣe*). At the moment of seeing the moon on a branch, in the very instant of a blink, when the perceiving consciousness has reached a hundred *yojanas* above the branch via the visual function (*cākṣuṣavṛtti*), [the consciousness] exists between that branch and the moon.
The meaning is that it has already been shown more than once previously that form is established as being devoid of an object. || 10 ||
When all external and internal delusions regarding latent impressions and objects have been stilled, for the awakened one who is free from all thought, it is as if it were midnight. || 11 ||

When the turbidity of the mind caused by sleep has been removed through deep slumber until midnight, that form becomes established as an experience for those yogins who have ascended into samādhi; thus he says in two verses beginning with "sabāhya... (11).
That form which is motionless, like the mind of a person abiding in peace who is free from both pleasure and pain— that is the form of that state.
The universal existence (sattāsāmānya) that extends through grasses, shrubs, sprouts, and so forth—that form which arises from its arising is the very form of that state. 13.

The meaning is this: regarding the emergence of all things—such as grasses, shrubs, sprouts, stalks, trees, branches, and so forth—that very pervasive and underlying form which is the general property of existence (*sattāsāmānya*) manifesting in connection with their emergence is what is meant by "the object of your cognition" (*tvatpratyayārtha*). Thus it is said in the *Vākyapadīya*: "That is existence; that is the Great Self."
The suffixes *tva*, *tal*, and so forth, are said to denote that [abstract quality]. || 13 ||
Within that state, this world-form which is clearly perceived—appearing as if it had a cause, as if formidable in its shapes, and as if possessed of distinctions—is [in fact] that very state. (14)

In that very form of the universal existence (*sattāsāmānya*), the nature of the world consisting of jars, cloths, and so forth—which is inextricably linked through identity yet appears as if distinct—shines forth as if it had a cause due to its adventitious nature, and as if it were formidable with forms such as the neck and the conch-shell. All of this is unreal; for this very reason, because it lacks a cause, it is neither born nor does it exist.
The subsequent [sequence] follows from another. || 14 ||
All that has not been born and does not exist due to the absence of a cause;
it is neither endowed with form, nor is it the world, nor is it joined with duality or unity.
That reality, being of the nature of existence, is not endowed with form; for this very reason, it is not the world, nor is it connected even with duality, unity, and so forth. || 15 ||
The existence of that which is without a cause is not tenable here;
for when an object is itself eternally experienced, who has the power to deny it? (16)
He asks "whence" regarding that, and says: "That which... In this matter, he states that everyone's own experience is the proof: "By oneself... (16).
Nor can that which is empty, without beginning or end, be the cause of the world;
for the formless Brahman cannot be the cause of the formed, visible world which does not have the nature of Brahman. (17)

"Let it be then that the cause of the non-existent world is emptiness (*śūnya*) itself. To this he replies: "And not [so]. With the intention that if emptiness were the cause, then because it lacks spatial and other limitations, everything would exist everywhere at all times, he qualifies it as "without beginning or end. For this very reason, even Brahman cannot be the cause; for [Brahman], being formless...
He states "Brahman" because it is impossible for [Brahman] to undergo transformation into a formal, embodied form (mūrtākāra). Thus says the Śruti:

"This very Brahman is without prior, without posterior, without interior, without exterior; this Self is Brahman, the perceiver of all. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.5.19) Therefore, when the form of the world appears therein, that [appearance] is indeed that [Brahman].
At that time, it shines by itself as the space of consciousness; thus it is established. || 18 ||

Therefore, regarding such Brahman, that which appears in the form of the world is Brahman itself appearing in that manner. He concludes—stating that "Brahman alone is the being (bhāva) of all things, the meaning of suffixes such as *tva* and *tal*"—with the words "Therefore" (tasmāt). || 18 ||
And because of the state of the world being Consciousness-Brahman, its appearance as such arises from delusion;
everything is one, unborn, peaceful, non-dual unity, and free from affliction.

Thus, since it is established that the appearance of the world as consisting of jars, cloths, and so forth is merely an illusory manifestation arising from its actual state as Consciousness-Brahman— which is perceived at first glance— it follows that everywhere everything is indeed one and the same.
From the full, the full flows forth; in the full, the full shines resplendent.
The full alone has arisen in the full, and the full alone is established.

He restates that the scriptural passage beginning with "That is full, this is full" (pūrṇam adaḥ pūrṇam idam), which was shown previously, applies both to the state of the world and the individual soul due to delusion, and to the state of being the real Brahman when delusion has ceased: "From the Full... (pūrṇād iti). || 20 ||

Peaceful, even, devoid of arising and passing away, free from form, unborn, as pure as the sky, singular, always existing as the self arisen through the unity of being and non-being—this is the primordial Nirvāṇa, the supreme nature of awakening. (21)

The meaning is that, according to the manner described, when everything is liberated from all forms and exists as the eternal Self arisen through the unity of being and non-being—that which remains, this supreme form of awakening, Brahman, is itself Nirvāṇa; such is the reality of the abstract suffix (bhāvapratyaya). || 21 ||

Thus ends the fifty-third canto, titled "The Description of Nirvāṇa," in the second half of the section on the Means to Liberation within the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, according to the tradition of the Ṛṣis.
Thus ends the fifty-third chapter, titled "The Description of Nirvāṇa," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The fifty-fourth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: That which is called the world is the pure sky; the existent Brahman abides within that sky.
This unborn world shines as the meaning of the word "space" within space. || 1 ||
Every entity abides in its own intrinsic nature; by its very nature, it is devoid of action and differentiation.
Therefore, being immutable, it is described as non-dual and pure existence alone.
The intrinsic nature or the difference of jars, cloths, and so forth cannot be defined without delineating their jar-ness, cloth-ness, and so on;

likewise, even the difference between a jar and jar-ness cannot be defined as having an unconditioned counter-correlativity (*anavacchinna-pratiyogitā*). Thus, in the act of isolating them, they must be apprehended in a non-conceptual manner (*nirvikalpatayā*).

Since the distinction between the state (*bhāva*) and the entity possessing that state (*bhavitṛ*)—which appear as identical—is merely conceptual, and since all things are thus nothing but their state, the extraction of the meaning of words such as "potness in a pot" ultimately results in "Brahman abiding in Brahman. He now begins to demonstrate here the result of this established extraction of the meaning of abstract suffixes (*bhāvapratyaya*): [The text continues: ...because the distinction between the state and the possessor of the state is merely conceptual, when one extracts the referent of words such as "potness in a pot," it culminates in the realization that "Brahman resides in Brahman. Thus, he begins to set forth the fruit of the extraction of the meaning of abstract suffixes that has been established here.

By the words "jagannāma" and so forth: when extracted from the entities such as potness and clothness, the world is well known to be as clear and free from the stain of differentiation as the sky. And in that [world], the entities such as potness and clothness exist as Brahman alone, according to the manner previously described. Thus, in this vision, within the entities such as "pot" and "cloth," there is only the sky.

In the ether, that alone shines as the referent of both the word "world" and words such as "pot" or "cloth"; and since that is unborn (*aja*), being devoid of modifications such as birth and so forth, there is no relation of cause and effect whatsoever for anything to depend upon. || 1 ||
The referents of words such as "you," "I," and "the world" are Brahman within Brahman;
they are peaceful, characterized by uniform radiance, and exist as that which is both situated and yet not situated.

He states this same point again more clearly: "Thou and I. Whether by distinguishing between the attribute and the possessor of the attribute, or even by perceiving absolute identity, [the Self] remains as an equal manifestation, existing separately due to its subtlety and other qualities; such being the case. || 2 ||
Even though this world consists of oceans, mountains, clouds, and the earth, it remains unborn; indeed, this universe abides as Brahman, like one observing the silence of a log.

Thus, although the world appears diverse—abounding in divisions such as oceans, mountains, and clouds, and manifesting through the various distinctions of agents, actions, and their fruits—in its final extraction, it remains as nothing but Brahman, which is devoid of activity, being the true essence of all those various states and their experiencers. This is the meaning. || 3 ||
The seer is the seer alone, established in his own self by virtue of the nature of the seen;
the doer is the doer alone, due to the absence of anything to be done and being devoid of causes.
That very [consciousness], abundant with the distinctions of the seer and so forth, is further elaborated among the various agents by extracting their respective states:
"Being situated [therein], he becomes the seer of that; likewise, he is the agent"—this is the meaning. || 4 ||
There is neither knowership nor agency, neither insentience nor the state of being an enjoyer;
here there is neither emptiness nor substantiality, nor even the nature of space.
He shows that by means of this view, the diversity of the entire world can be wiped away—stating: "No" (na). || 5 ||
Like the interior of a stone, it is truly one, dense, unborn, and pervasive; all is peaceful, without beginning or end, and one beyond both injunction and prohibition.
Because even the distinction between existence and non-existence has been wiped away, there is a single unity of both affirmation and negation.
Death and life, truth and untruth, as well as the auspicious and the inauspicious—
all are one, unborn space, like water consisting of a network of waves.
It is precisely through differentiation that the state of being an object of sight and the state of being a seer come into being;
and this conceptual construction is experienced in dreams, cities [of the Gandharvas], and the like. (8)
When there is a division [of Brahman] into the state of the individual soul (jīva), that which is one alone assumes the status of a seer through the predominance of its conscious aspect (cidaṃśa),

and by concealing its conscious nature through the predominance of the other aspect, it attains the status of the object of perception (dṛśyatā). This is just as, in a dream, when there is a division of the phenomenal individual soul from the illusory individual soul, the phenomenal individual soul remains concealed by sleep.
The meaning is that it becomes like the state of cities and other objects seen while living in a dream. || 8 ||
Thus, this world appears in the supreme ether like a city in a dream; from the very beginning, it is Brahman alone that exists in this manner. || 9 ||
That very Brahman, which is initially free from conceptual proliferation (niṣprapañca), exists in this manner as the world through its division into the individual self (jīvātman). || 9 ||
Know this to be such: everything that is of the nature of all things, which, upon the transition from one place to another, remains unmarked in the interval for the knower.

Therefore, know that this entire world-form, which is of the nature of the Self, exists as it was in the beginning— namely, as the very same non-dual (niṣprapañca) reality. It should not be argued that such a non-dual, unobscured form of consciousness is unknown or unestablished.

He says "from the place" (deśāt) because it has been stated more than once previously that the intermediate space between those two—the branch and the moon—is well-known as being manifested by consciousness (cit) through the functioning of the perception of both. It is "unmarked" (anaṅkitam), meaning not characterized by any specific object. || 10 ||
Thus situated within the center of the sky of consciousness—which is utterly tranquil—the world exists just like water in the form of waves and the like. 11.
Even now, when one reflects with inward vision, that form is easily perceived; with this intention, the illustration "just like water" is given. || 11 ||
That which arises has already arisen, and that which does not arise has not arisen;
for one who knows, there is no distinction between them in the interval when moving from one place to another.
He says that the entire world is indeed non-different from such consciousness devoid of objects, using the word "yat" (that which):

That which arises and has arisen in the form of an effect does not arise, nor does that which has arisen in the form of a cause arise. It is not differentiated, nor is it divided. [The suffix] *kta* is used here with the causative sense (*ṇic*) for its own sake. || 12 ||
Therefore, it is said that no cause for this creation is found, even when sought with great effort, just like the horn of a hare. (13)
"Let it be non-different; what of it? To this he says: "Therefore... (13).
That which appears without a cause is non-apparent and consists of delusion;
how can the reality of a delusion, which is itself unreal in nature, be asserted? (14)
To this he says "yad" (that which), asking what follows from that as well. || 14 ||
Indeed, how can there be an effect without a cause?
That which is the vision of a virtuous son by one who has no son is an illusion, not reality.
The meaning is that for one who has no son, the sight of a virtuous son in a dream is merely an illusion. || 15 ||
But that which appears without a cause is the manifestation of intrinsic nature (svabhāva),
appearing in every form like a mental construction or a city of Gandharvas.
The very nature of the seer, which is consciousness itself, manifests in that manner while abandoning its own [limited] form. || 16 ||
When moving from one place to another, the body of the Knower shines in the interval in an instant,
as if not abandoning its own nature, like a transformation of objects.

Where, then, does its own nature shine forth without abandoning it? To this he says: "From the location," etc. The meaning is that the manifestation of both forms is well-known there, just as in the case of the branch and the moon's location, which appear as a supreme illusory transformation (paramārthavivarta). || 17 ||
Awareness alone shines forth in the form of objects, and it is its own subtle essence;
the internal mountain of dreams and mental constructs is the experienced illustration in this regard. (18)

Even though an object does not exist, cognition appears in the form of that object; with this in mind, he provides an example even regarding the object itself, stating: "Cognition alone... (verse 18).
Śrī Rāma said: O Brahman, just as a future great tree exists within the seed of a banyan, why does the creation not likewise exist within the atom? (19)

Rāma raises a doubt: "Why is it postulated that consciousness itself shines in the form of objects? Why is it not instead postulated that the insentient phenomenal world already exists within consciousness—just as a subtle tree exists within a banyan seed—and is merely to be manifested? (Verse 19)
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Where there is a seed, there a branch of expansive form arises;
and that branch is brought forth by causal factors together with auxiliary conditions.

The reply is that this is an unequal analogy: for while a formless banyan tree existed previously within a seed that possessed form, and it manifested through the sequence of sprouts and so forth upon the convergence of auxiliary causes such as earth and water, nothing whatsoever possessing form exists during the dissolution of the entire world, nor are any auxiliary causes perceived. Thus, the two cases are dissimilar.
Vasiṣṭha said, beginning with the words "Where," etc. (Verse 20).
In the dissolution of all beings, what could the form of the seed be?
And what auxiliary cause arises for it, by virtue of which the world is produced? (21)
If it possesses a form, what could that form-possessing seed be? Likewise, what could its auxiliary cause be? || 21 ||
But as for that Brahman which is supreme and tranquil, what conceptualization of form could there be therein?
Even the connection with atomicity does not apply here; so what possibility is there for it to be a seed? 22.
[Objection: "But surely Brahman itself may be the seed there, containing within it the power of the world. To this he says: "As for that which...
The meaning is that even the connection with atomicity does not exist in this Brahman; the imagination of any form is cast far away. || 22 ||
Since a cause—such as a seed—that produces both the real and the unreal is impossible, how, by whom, from where, where, and of what nature could the existence of the world be? 23.
For this very reason, he states that the impossibility of a cause was mentioned previously: "of the cause," etc. Thus, by this method. || 23 ||
It is also not tenable that the world resides within the interior of the supreme atom; to claim that Mount Meru resides within a mustard seed is merely the imagination of the ignorant.

However, even if atomicity were accepted on the strength of such scriptural passages as "the subtle path, the ancient one" and "subtler than the subtle," the maintenance of the world therein would still be difficult to establish; thus he says: "The world... (verse 24).
When a seed exists, views of cause and effect proceed;
but for that which is formless, what is the seed, and where is the sequence of the produced and the producer? (25)

But if it were admitted that even the world is entirely formless, then, because seeds and the like would be utterly impossible, the result would be nothing other than such a Brahman alone; thus he says with two verses beginning with "satī" (25).
Therefore, that which is the supreme reality is itself this world as it exists;
herein nothing is manifested, nor does anything perish. (26)
It manifests, appearing and making its own nature known. || 26 ||
The sky of consciousness, by virtue of its own consciousness, perceives the delusion of the world within the heart-sky of consciousness;
it perceives the pure as if impure in the impure, and the pure in the pure. (27)
What then? He states that very point: "the space of consciousness" (cidākāśa). || 27 ||
Only its own form appears to it, like the movement in the wind;
for us, there are no conceptualizations whatsoever here regarding the word or meaning of "creation. (28)
Just as emptiness exists in space and fluidity in water,
so too does this pure creation, consisting of the nature of otherness, exist within the Self.
Self-nature consists in its own manifestations; it is the state of being other than itself. || 29 ||
This world, which is of the nature of light and profoundly peaceful, is indeed the Brahman spread out before us;
it is without beginning or end, the truth, and neither rises nor sets.
If it is thus non-retrogressive, what then is its nature? To this he says: "It is of the nature of light" (bhārūpa). || 30 ||
When one travels from one place to another, the body of the knower remains in the interval for a moment;
that which is thus situated within the self of space is called this "world. (31)
He reminds us that its non-establishment has been refuted many times with the words "deśāt" (from place). || 31 ||
Just as movement exists in the wind, fluidity in water, and emptiness in space,
so does this world appear within the Self, without any real connection to it.
It is devoid of connection—that is, contact—with any other distinct entity; in other words, it is unattached and non-dual. || 32 ||

"The sky of consciousness is indeed the sky of the world"—thus, where is there any rising or setting of the sun within the Self? For everything that constitutes its limbs is non-different from It. Cast away all conceptualization and remain as the mere sky. Having thus summarized and taught that the entire world is nothing but the nature of Consciousness, he concludes: The sky of consciousness is indeed the sky of the world; thus, where is there any rising or setting of the sun within the Self? Regarding the word "consciousness" (*saṃvit*): O Rāma, while the world remains established within the Self, which is the ultimate reality, it is certain—indeed, as a matter of certainty—that consciousness is nothing but the void, having attained emptiness; so why should it not be the sky itself? To this he replies with the word "the sky": [it is] without the sun, devoid of both its setting and rising, and established solely within the Self, which is its own essential nature.

In what sense is "the sky" (nabhas) well-known? For the sky is not well-known as being of the nature of existence and consciousness (saccit-svabhāva), nor even as devoid of the sun and other luminaries;

rather, it is known as inert and void. Furthermore, since all objects of perception appear as permeated by that reality which is of the nature of existence and consciousness, everything is known as being subordinate to that [reality], and not as subordinate to a void sky.

By which it would be merely that; therefore, it is non-different from that very Self consisting of Existence-Consciousness (saccidātman). Consequently, you too, being nothing but the sky of consciousness (cidambaramātra) with all objects of perception dispelled, remain—this is the meaning. || 33 ||

Thus ends the fifty-fourth canto, titled "The Exposition of Non-dual Unity," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa of the glorious Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa composed by Vālmīki, according to the Ṛṣi tradition. 54.
Thus ends the fifty-fourth chapter, titled "The Exposition of Non-dual Unity," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
Fifty-fifth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Existence and non-existence, grasping and relinquishing, the gross and the subtle, the moving and the unmoving—
For indeed, at the very beginning, at the start of creation, they were not produced without a cause.
Perceiving its own [nature] as something else through another mental cultivation, consciousness remains within the world;
yet, because it is not other than its own nature, the world consists of the ultimate reality.
Thus, since the world is absolutely non-different from Brahman, it follows that its non-origination is the established result; so he says: "bhāva... (verse 1).
For the formless element of consciousness can never be the cause of anything material;
it is incapable of being the seed of material things, just as the self cannot be the seed of trees.

But in the theory of origination (utpattivāda), a cause must necessarily be stated; however, as has been stated more than once, that [cause] is difficult to state—this he reminds us of with the words "na tu" (but not). || 2 ||
Constantly cultivating the very nature that consists of contemplation, the entire element of consciousness, possessing all experience, remains within the self alone. (3)
Therefore, the knower of reality, contemplating the entire world as having the very nature of consciousness, remains established in that state alone; thus he says:

"the very nature itself. However, if the reading is *sargānubhavavān*, it should be explained as follows: the ignorant one, the conscious element, contemplating within himself the very nature of creation, remains established as one who experiences it in that manner. || 3 ||
The element of consciousness, whose nature is like the sky, relishes whatever state it attains; through its own agitation, it experiences creation as a drunken man does through his own intoxication.
For this very reason, he says "he tastes" to show that a creation corresponding to the cultivation of his own nature has been obtained by him through his own ignorance;
just as one becomes intoxicated by oneself through the agitation caused by wine and the like, so too is the Self (khātmā) attained. || 4 ||
When all is unarisen and does not exist at all, yet is nevertheless perceived, then know this to be Brahman alone— equal, peaceful, and like unto the non-existent.

For this very reason, he says "yadā" (when), meaning: "Know that when there is the perception of the nature of another entity that has not arisen, there is the persistence of that [other] state. || 5 ||
Like the sky within the sky, or like liquid water within water,
that which shines forth because of its consciousness— by that very thing this world is created.
How, then, is the traditional teaching found in the Śrutis and other sources—that "this world was created by Him"—justified? To this he says: "In the sky of consciousness" (cinnabhasi).
Since this superimposed world shines forth by means of that causal Consciousness-Self, for that reason the world is indeed Brahman itself;
it is "created by Him" in the form of the world. This is the meaning of the traditional teaching; such is the ellipsis to be supplied. || 6 ||
Just as that very world arises in a dream as something pure, so too does it shine forth here in the void of creation, beginningless yet appearing with a beginning, like the shimmering of glass.

And this very [creation] belongs to the dreamer; as the Śruti says, "Then he creates chariots, draft-animals, and paths"—this is like the statement regarding his agency as a creator. Thus he says: "In a dream. Or rather, just as for one whose eyes are affected by a cataract, a tuft of hair and so forth appears in the sky, so too does this manifold form, beginning with creation, manifest within the space of consciousness (cidākāśa) when it is conditioned by the state of creation.
The meaning is "it shines. || 7 ||
Just as the world appears in a dream through the manifestation of one's own consciousness, so too this waking state is of that same nature; it exists as nothing but space.
Therefore, that is merely space, merely the sky of consciousness. || 8 ||
For at the beginning of creation, the dream of consciousness is designated as "waking";
today, the dream of consciousness during the night is likewise designated as "dream. (9)

If that is so, what then is the difference between the waking state and the dream state? He explains this with the word "ādau" (at the beginning). The dream of the intellect (*citi*) occurs in two instances: first, in the creation consisting of Hiraṇyagarbha which has already commenced; and second, in the creation occurring tonight, which consists solely of the transformations of the individual internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). || 9 ||
Just as the ripples on rivers, having set in motion from of old, remain established even today exactly as they were,
so too is the arrangement of objects within the range of vision.
The very volition of the initial creation is *niyati* (destiny), which establishes the nature and arrangement of all things until the great dissolution;

in accordance with that, the construction of objects as they exist even today remains established, proceeding just as before—just as the ripples on the waves of rivers are seen to be established in their course. This is the grammatical connection (*anvaya*). || 10 ||
Just as the beauty of water-waves is contained within the arrangement of rivers,
so too the immeasurable internal creation exists within the seed of consciousness in the sky of consciousness.

And likewise, just as the existence of the beauty of waves does not exist apart from the existence of water, so too that [existence] of the world does not exist apart from the existence of consciousness; with this intention, and with the view that there is a doctrine regarding Brahman being the material cause, he says: "Just as... (verse 11).
If death were absolute annihilation, then that would indeed be the bliss of sleep;
yet since cyclic existence arises again, that bliss is merely momentary.

Thus, since the world lacks separate existence, there is no possibility whatsoever of fear regarding birth and death; on the contrary, there is only happiness in both cases. This is stated in the verse beginning with "mṛtasya" (of the dead): even if the dead person is absolutely non-existent, nevertheless, because the existence of the bliss of Brahman alone remains as the essence of the existence of those respective [states]—both destruction and fear—in deep sleep (*suṣupti*), which is like sleep.

The meaning is this: having attained that very happiness which is renowned as unsurpassed bliss, even if saṃsāra should arise again through the body and so forth upon death, that very same happiness remains—even in its new form as saṃsāra—because there is no existence other than happiness; thus, there is no possibility of fear whatsoever. || 12 ||
If there is fear of evil deeds, that [fear] is equal both here and in the hereafter;
therefore, for all beings, death and birth are equal in their resulting pleasure.

Raising the objection, "Surely, for one who has died, there should be fear due to the possibility of suffering in hell and other realms resulting from evil deeds," he says: "From evil deeds...
