That fear is the same for one living here and for one dead in the hereafter; for since both hell and life lack any existence apart from the reality of the bliss of Brahman, so too does suffering.
The meaning is that because there is no distinction in its persistence by virtue of the very existence of pleasure. || 13 ||
Whether there be death or life, the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of these two is innate;
he whose mind rests in this [realization] is said to be "internally cooled. (14)

When both death and life exist as impressions in a subtle state of being, which is innate and of the nature of the self-evident bliss of Brahman, then, upon the cessation of all [empirical] consciousness, a certain kind of consciousness arises;
because one becomes identical with that very [consciousness], one is said to be liberated. || 15 ||
Therefore, by the departure of the separate existence of the visible bondage, he is said to be liberated. || 15 ||
Through the realization of absolute non-existence, the perception of all that is visible arises as something devoid of any object of cognition,
whether the world-creation exists or does not exist.

Thus, through the realization of the absolute non-existence of the visible world, whether a supreme existence as its creator exists or not, the perception of all that is visible arises as devoid of an object of cognition and free from the act of sensing; this is the meaning of the logical possibility of liberation. || 16 ||

Those who know that [reality]—which is neither an object of thought nor of the nature of consciousness, and which is unperceived even by consciousness—have attained identity with its being; they are peaceful, yet remain engaged in worldly activity.
Precisely because of the absence of an object of consciousness (cetya), it does not consist of the activity of consciousness (citikriyā) which is dependent upon that object. || 17 ||
That which is called "the world" is merely a shimmering play of consciousness;
in the utterly transparent supreme space, how can there be any such notions as bondage or liberation? (18)
That which shines repeatedly is *kacakaca*; the state of being so is *kācakacyam*. || 18 ||
The world, being essentially of the nature of the vibration of consciousness and of the nature of volition, consists only of the Real;
it never consists of earth and the other elements anywhere.
Here there is no space, no time, no substance, no action, and no ether;
everything appears as if real—whether expanded or unexpanded—and yet it is unreal.
Whether it be swollen by mere appearance or even not swollen at all, it is non-existent.
Thus, there shines here only the absolute, a dense mass of ultimate reality,
which is neither void nor non-void, and more transparent even than the sky.
Though possessing form or being formless, it is indeed non-existent yet exceedingly luminous;
it is the expansion of purely singular, utterly pure consciousness, like a city in a dream.
Thus is this Nirvāṇa spread out: within the sky of consciousness, it is both turbid and yet of an unturbid nature;
it appears as manifold, yet it has never been extended anywhere as manifold; it is emptiness, like fluidity in the ocean or like space in the sky.

O Rāma, the turbid form of the world belonging to the sky of consciousness (cidvyoman) is, in the manner described, actually its own pervasive, non-turbid form, which is nothing other than liberation (nirvāṇa). By this it is meant that this world has not spread forth anywhere at all; rather, it is spread everywhere. Just as emptiness is in the sky and fluidity is in the ocean, this world is not manifold, but is that very same reality. || 23 ||
Thus ends the fifty-fifth canto, titled "The Description of the World as Being Consisting of Ultimate Reality," in the Nirvāṇa Section of the Holy Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa, composed by the Sage. 55.

Thus ends the fifty-fifth canto, titled "The Description of the World as Consisting of Ultimate Reality," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the illustrious Vāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa-tātparya-prakāśa.
The fifty-sixth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Everywhere, in every way, everything, at all times, exists within the space that is composed of consciousness.
It is well that pure emptiness arises throughout everything, like the sky.
Since it is certain that consciousness alone is everything everywhere and everything is consciousness,
the story of the stone is related here for the sake of strengthening this conviction.
In the sky of consciousness, the space of Brahman, everything exists at all times and in all places through its reality as that [Brahman], by virtue of its uncontracted state of being;

and all that is always and everywhere purely transparent, for Brahman is not defiled even by a trace of its own apparent impurity. Just as the quality of emptiness in the sky remains the sky even when it appears in the form of blueness throughout its entirety.
"It vitiates" means it is like that [which is clear]; such is the meaning. || 1 ||
Wherever there is consciousness, there is the glory of creation—whether in the non-ether or within the ether;
because all things consist of consciousness, there is nothing unconscious anywhere.
He states the logical justification for what has been said: "Where," etc. "In non-space" means in earth and so forth. || 2 ||
Just as the collection of objects such as mountains and cities in a dream are nothing but consciousness alone—
the supreme ether— so too is the ground of waking objects.

Since it is well known that everything is pure consciousness (cinmātra) in a dream, he establishes that same state even in the waking condition by means of that analogy: "the entire collection of objects," etc. (verse 3).
O Rāma, listen here to this narrative of the stones, which is a veritable elixir;
it is that very wonderful and natural event which was previously witnessed by me alone.
The abode and locus of the various flavors (*rasas*), such as sweetness and the like, as well as the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) and others;
and that which is the medicine for the disease of delusion—this "wonderful" (*citram*) work, expanded by means of diverse narratives, is now being introduced and set forth in detail. (4)
Having realized that which is to be known, my mind is at times filled with fullness; desiring to abandon this worldly conduct, which is a dense delusion. (5)
Having attained one-pointedness through meditation, seeking solitude and proceeding toward tranquility, he gradually abandons both sluggishness and agitation for the sake of long-lasting rest.
I reflected thus while staying in a certain celestial abode,
observing the various transitory states of worldly existence.
Abiding in the abode of the immortals, I reflected upon this which is about to be spoken.
Truly, this worldly existence is devoid of essence, though beautiful at first sight;
I believe it never bestows happiness upon anyone, by any means, anywhere.
By some means and in some manner, at some place and at some time. || 8 ||
These perceptions of the visible world produce agitation within the observer, resulting from intense mental turbulence and distress, as they bestow both desired and undesired fruits. (9)
It does not merely bestow happiness; rather, it also brings about endless suffering. Thus he says: "Agitation," etc. (Verse 9).
"What is this that is seen? Or what does it perceive? Or who am I?"—all this is the peaceful, unborn, and space-like play within the Self, which is pure consciousness alone. (10)
"Alpaṃ riṅgaṇaṃ riṅgakam" means a slight turning or revolving. || 10 ||
Therefore, having gone from here to a most excellent region inaccessible even to all the Siddhas, Indras, gods, Daityas, and others, he concealed himself by means of his own self.

Therefore, since distraction and agitation must necessarily be abandoned, the meaning is "for the sake of their removal. Having concealed, hidden, and protected oneself—meaning one's own body—by means of such methods as invisibility through the self (the mind) alone. || 11 ||
Invisible to all beings, having attained the non-conceptual samādhi,
I abide in a state that is even, clear, and peaceful, free from all sensation.
In such a way that there may be a cognition devoid of external objects. || 12 ||
Therefore, what region indeed could there be that has reached absolute emptiness, where these five perceptions of external objects are not experienced? (13)
Agitated by floods of water and masses of beings within the forest of sound, the mountains, being themselves thoroughly disturbed, now cause me to tremble; therefore, they are my enemies. (14)

Now, one might ask: "Since many secluded places such as mountain peaks, plateaus, valleys, the depths of the ocean, its shores, and the caverns of the netherworld (pātāla) are well-known, why are they not resorted to for the sake of meditative absorption?
To this, he replies with the verse beginning with *śabda* and so forth: [one should avoid] forests, waters, oceans, and clouds, which abound in sounds that are causes of distraction.

The mountains, crowded on all sides by multitudes of lions, tigers, and other beasts, being themselves agitated, cause others to be agitated as well; therefore, they are adverse to me like enemies—this is the meaning. || 14 ||
The various regions, nestled between the lords of mountains and frequented by people, are indeed full of perils, for they are entirely infested by the snakes of sensual objects. (15)

The intermediate valleys were crowded with and surrounded by Kirātas and other tribes; the regions were like oceans whose depths are filled with aquatic creatures, for they are pervaded by people who are as treacherous as serpents due to their corruption;
and the cities were like those agitated by various undertakings, teeming with citizens.
"Agitated by various undertakings"—this applies to both [the subject and the object]. (16)
The shores of mountains and oceans, the cities of the world-protectors, mountain peaks teeming with living beings, and the caverns of the netherworld; || 17 ||
The slopes and peaks of the mountains and the oceans. || 17 ||
The caves and deep hollows of the lords of mountains sing with the humming of the wind, dance with their hands in the form of creepers, and laugh with their flowers.

"In that case, let mountain caves be resorted to. To this he replies with the verse beginning "gāyanti": "The lakes are indeed tasteless, echoing with the sounds of swirling waters; their deep hollows are filled with lions, serpents, and other beasts; and their lotuses—whose stalks tremble at the touch of silent fish and sages—are shaken by those very stalks. (19)
"In that case, let there be great lakes in the southern region known as the Sarayas, which serve as causes for meditative absorption on their banks. To this he replies:

"The silent one" (*maunī*). In those [lakes], the lotuses are swaying by means of stalks that are prone to trembling due to the touch of fish agitated by pride and fear, and of sages (*munis*) whose habit is bathing, through the disturbances of sporting, bathing, and so forth.
Such lakes, resounding with the whirlpools of their waters, were indeed distasteful to me because they were a cause for the interruption of my meditative absorption;
for at that time, due to my silence, I was unable to prevent them. || 19 ||
With its banners of grass and dust agitated by the touch of the wind,
even the earth of the mountain torrent roars with the whistling sounds of the breeze, unrestrained.
"Let it be then that the ground of the waterfall shall be the cause of your rest. To this he replies with the verse beginning "pavana... (wind...). "Unrestrained" means unregulated;
that is to say, characterized by unobstructed distraction. || 20 ||
Therefore, in some remote corner of the empty space, I shall remain here, supporting myself by means of the irreproachable method of yoga. (21)
By way of elimination, it is space alone that is the refuge because it is free from all causes of distraction; with this intention, he says: "Therefore..."
Having mentally constructed a small hut in one corner here,
I remain within it, silent and firm as the interior of a diamond.
"Solid as the interior of a diamond" is an adjective qualifying both the preceding and the subsequent actions. || 22 ||
Having reflected thus, I went into the stainless sky;
yet even there I beheld that entire expanse of space.
With its interior expanded and its core pervaded by thousands of causes for distraction. || 23 ||
In some places it had hosts of Siddhas wandering about; in some places roaring clouds;
in some places it was the support of Vidyādharas; and in some places Yakṣas were casting down ruined dwellings.
He elaborates in every way, through various qualifiers, the very abundance of causes for distraction, beginning with the words "In some places," and so forth. || 24 ||
In one place a preeminent city was wandering; in another, a battle had begun;
in one place clouds were rushing; and in another, yoginīs were leaping up.
Wherein there are yoginīs who are haughty and whose conduct is fierce with madness. || 25 ||
In some places it contained cities of Daityas and Gandharvas soaring upward;
in some places it had hosts of planets wandering about, and in others it was crowded with stars.
Where the cities of the gods, together with the Gandharvas, flew up from their seats in the form of Daitya cities. || 26 ||

In some places it was brushed by flocks of birds in the sky; in some places it was like a furious great wind; in some places it was enveloped by portents; and in some places it was adorned with circular patterns.
It was adorned with mandalas and encircled by garlands of clouds and other celestial phenomena.
In some places it was a flood of unprecedented beings, coiled like serpents;
in some places it was trodden upon by the chariots of the sun, and in other places it was crowded with the chariots of others.
In which [city] there were multitudes of beings and throngs of *piśācas* with unprecedented and wondrously diverse forms never seen before;
it was surrounded by *nāgaras*, that is, by groups of city-dwellers; and it was filled with the chariots of other planets such as the Moon and others. 28.
In some places it ends with the burning heat of the sun, in others it is endowed with the coolness of the moon;
in some places it is unbearable for base people, and in others it is difficult to traverse due to the intense heat of fire.
Where death is the end for living beings due to the burning heat from the proximity of the sun, and which is unbearable and loathsome because of base creatures such as bhūtas and pretas; (29)
In one place it was filled with frantic vetālas; in another, it was as terrifying as Garuḍa; in some places it resembled the clouds of the dissolution, and in others, the winds of the dissolution.
Then, having abandoned the hosts of spirits, I went from far to even farther away; I reached a solitary place that was empty and exceedingly vast.

Know that it is a place where the wind is utterly still, where no elements are encountered even in dreams, which is free from both auspicious and portentous omens, and which is inaccessible to the cycle of worldly existence.
It was free from auspicious signs, favorable omens, and ill-omened portents. || 32 ||
Then, I constructed there a hut with an open interior,
its walls solid and seamless, as beautiful as a lotus bud.
It was fashioned and created by one whose resolve is true. || 33 ||
Her body was as charming as the interior of the full moon's orb when bored through by woodworms;
she was adorned with the beauty of the calyxes of flowers such as the white water-lily, the jasmine, and the celestial *mandāra*.
"Pierced by wood-boring insects (ghuṇas)—that is, specific types of worms—and made full of holes, like the interior of a beautiful fruit; this is an 'unprecedented simile' (abhūtopamā). (34)
Having mentally resolved there that I was unapproachable by all beings, I then became inaccessible to all creatures. (35)

In that regard, having resolved in my mind that I was inaccessible to all beings, I remained established in the non-conceptual samādhi characterized by what will be described hereafter; this is the connection with the distant verb. || 35 ||
Seated in the lotus posture with a tranquil mind and observing the highest silence,
he determined his own time of rising at the end of a hundred years.
Established in non-conceptual meditative absorption, he appeared as if sealed by sleep; equanimous and dwelling in the gentle sky, he seemed as if carved out from the firmament.
Whatever the mind contemplates for a long time, it perceives that very thing instantly;
and when [the contemplation] is extended over a long duration, it is like the manifestation of the wind of hope.
Then, after a hundred years, the seed of awakening became enveloped within another husk in the field of my heart; it remained there for some time while gradually unfolding. (39)

Furthermore, he states the sign for emerging from meditative absorption (*samādhi*) after a hundred years with the word "for a long time" (*cira*). Then, when after a long period— at the end of a hundred years— the mind (*citta*), like a longing or like the wind, has become expanded, at that time the seed of awakening (*bodhabīja*), which is the karma that is the cause for emergence, remains for a certain duration within the field of the heart (*hṛdayakṣetra*), its inner middle portion being enveloped by expansion.
The connection with the subsequent clause is "it was of such a kind. In the reading *nāsāpavanavyaktivat*, the meaning is "like the manifestation of the vital breath" (*prāṇa*). || 38 || 39 ||
Then my vital breath became fully awakened, its consciousness restored,
like the sap of a tree whose limbs were withered by the cold returns in the springtime.
In the spring, during the month of Caitra. || 40 ||
Those hundred years passed for me there like a mere blink of an eye; even many successions of time seem but a moment to one whose mind is focused on a single point.
For one whose mind is single-pointed and focused, they become very slight, even minimal. || 41 ||
The sequence of my sensory perceptions has reached its full bloom and gone outward;
like the essence of intoxication in springtime, it has manifested for me in the form of flowers.
He states what happened to them immediately thereafter with the verse beginning "vikāsam" (blossoming).
The internal sap, which is the cause of the intoxication—the joy arising from the nourishment of sprouts and so forth—of the trees, [flowed] as if in the form of flowers. || 42 ||
The demon of the notion "I am" has emerged, having approached me— who am filled with vital breath and whose consciousness has arrived at its proper state—
and now, surrounded by the woman of desire, it suddenly assails me from somewhere, like a violent wind that causes a great tree to rise up and then bend down.

To explain what happened next, he says: "Mām... (Me...). Having perceived me—this body which is filled with the vital breaths (*prāṇas*), the five-fold winds, and the senses, and in which a portion of the consciousness of the individual soul (*jīvasaṃvit*) has appeared solely through their power;
having perceived me who had thus suddenly arrived—he was agitated by a woman characterized by desire, that is, by a *piśācī*.
The demon of egoism (*ahaṃkāra*), well known as "I am embraced," has emerged and arrived from some unexpected quarter;
the meaning is that it spreads just like a fierce wind, a gale that bends down trees such as the *śālmali* that were previously standing tall. || 43 ||

Thus ends the fifty-sixth sarga, titled "The Description of Vasiṣṭha’s Absorption in Samādhi," in the *Ākāśamandira* section of the *Pāṣāṇabhedaka* division of the *Nirvāṇa-Uttara-khaṇḍa* of the *Śrī-Vālmīki-Devarṣi-Mahāmuni-Rāmāyaṇa*, composed by the Sage.
Thus ends the fifty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of Vasiṣṭha’s Attainment of Samādhi," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The fifty-seventh canto.
Śrī Rāma said:
Śrī Rāma said:
O Sage, for the sake of pacifying my doubt, tell me: why does the demon of egoism afflict even you, in whom nirvāṇa has arisen?
In order to ascertain the distinction here between the knower and the ego-sense,
it is established that the object of perception, when sublated by knowledge, is pure consciousness alone.

Rāma asks— "You too..."— anticipating that even for Vasiṣṭha there might be the impermanence of the fruit of knowledge, since he understood that even he had been afflicted by the demon of egoism, as indicated by the statement "the demon 'I am [the owner]' has spread out" and by the illustrative example of the wind that rises and subsides. [The phrase] "whose root is the awakened knowledge of Nirvāṇa" refers to him whose foundation is the realized state of liberation.
Even you, who are of such a nature. || 1 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
In this world, the maintenance of the body for both the knower and the ignorant occurs without the sense of "I-ness" (ahaṃbhāva).
However, for that which is supported, a state of existence without a support is not possible here.

To demonstrate that the maintenance of the body— which is like a burnt cloth whose sole purpose is the enjoyment of the remainder of *prārabdha* karma— is not possible without the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), Vasiṣṭha provides the following answer by showing the specific absence of fault in the ego-sense of one who knows reality, beginning with the words "without the sense of 'I'": "Because the subsistence of the body is not possible without that [ego-sense] which is the substratum..."
The phrase "there is no existence without a substratum" is to be explained by the negation of the negative particle (*nañ*). || 2 ||
But listen to this distinction here, O you of tranquil mind,
by hearing which the demon of egoism shall find peace within you.
This demon of egoism, though non-existent within, has been imagined by this infant of ignorance; therefore, it persists.
It was imagined by a child, a fool characterized by ignorance; therefore, it exists solely through the power of ignorance. || 4 ||
Even ignorance does not exist at all when it is scrutinized and cannot be found, just as the nature of darkness cannot be perceived by one who possesses a lamp and investigates.

Let it be so; what follows from that? To this he says: "Even ignorance [is sublated]. The intention is that when ignorance is sublated by knowledge, the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), which exists dependent upon it, is likewise necessarily sublated. || 5 ||
Just as it is scrutinized, so it dissolves;
even this demoness of ignorance, when thus investigated, vanishes here.

And thus, it is well known that for the wise, there is an increase in the destruction of ignorance according to the degree of excellence in their experience; so he says: "In whatever manner... (verse 6).
Indeed, when ignorance exists, an eternal delusion of the intellect arises,
like a bodiless yakṣī appearing in the night.

For this very reason, he says "it is said" (kila) to indicate that ignorance is well-known as being restricted to the time prior to the attainment of knowledge; this ignorance is either the state of non-knowing or the causal avidyā. || 7 ||
If ignorance exists, its occurrence is possible, but not otherwise;
for when there is a second moon, only then does a second rabbit exist. || 8 ||

Thus, causal ignorance (*kāraṇāvidyā*) is also dependent upon that [consciousness], because its existence is merely a conventional designation for the time of the arising of the effect-ignorance (*kāryāvidyā*), and because it is knowable by the individual consciousness (*jīvacit*) conditioned by that [effect]. He says:
"But this creation, being unborn, does not exist as known by the ignorant."
It is not born because of the absence of a cause, being like a tree in the sky even prior [to its birth].
Let it be so; what follows from that? To this he says: "But the creation... (verse 9).

In the beginning of creation within the interior of the supreme space-receptacle, which is free from all affliction, what indeed could be the cause for the perception of earth and other elements? (10)
He establishes the non-existence of a cause with the words: "The supreme ether," etc. (10).

How can that which transcends the six senses including the mind be the cause of the self—which consists of those same six senses including the mind—and which possesses form, when [the former] is formless? || 11 ||

The meaning is this: because [the Self] is not graspable by the six organs including the mind, it is impossible for it to manifest itself without the establishment of those six organs including the mind;

and that which has not been manifested cannot be acted upon. Thus, the point is that for a formed object such as a jar, its production is appropriately by means of a formed agent such as a potter or a lump of clay, and not by one that is formless. || 11 ||
It is said that the effect, the sprout, arises from the cause, the seed;
but where even the seed does not exist, how could the sprout come to be? (12)
Without a cause, an effect indeed cannot arise;
when, by whom, or where has a manifest tree ever been seen or found in the sky? (13)
Just as branches and other objects are seen in the sky through mere conceptualization, so too that conceptualization itself becomes such [an appearance]; yet there is no substantial reality there.
If creation has not arisen at all, then what appears as such? He explains this with an illustration, beginning with the words "by volition" (saṃkalpena) and so forth. || 14 ||
Thus, this unimpeded persistence of creation which is experienced in the beginning of the emanation within the space of consciousness is like the form of emptiness in the sky. 15.

This unrestrained persistence of creation that is experienced at the time of the beginning of the world-cycle should also be understood as being like trees and other things in the sky, which are of the nature of emptiness. || 15 ||
The space of consciousness (cidākāśa) is indeed the same within the Self as it is elsewhere;
its very nature is what is called "creation," and because of its consciousness, that sentience is the Lord (Īśvara). || 16 ||
If so, does emptiness alone manifest in the form of creation? He says "no": "equal" (sama).
The meaning is that the Lord himself, being equal—devoid of the inequality of the form of creation—manifests in that manner. || 16 ||
The creation of dreams is the illustration here, which is experienced every day;
in the self-perception of a dream, the form of mountains and cities manifests.
He states that when the unmodified [Self] itself manifests as the world of transformations, its own self is the illustrative example, as in a dream—thus: "In a dream... (verse 17).
Just as in a dream one dwells within the nature of consciousness as if there were a creation,
so too did that which appears as a creation though it is not a creation previously exist in the great void.
The pure, singular, unborn, and undecaying reality shines forth as the unknowable knower;
that which exists at the beginning of creation, without beginning or end, is itself the creation in which we abide. (19)
And thus, he states that the true nature of the Self is exactly the same at the time of creation as it was prior to creation:
"The unknowable knower" (verse 19).
Here there is no creation, nor is this sphere consisting of the aggregate of earth and the other elements;
everything is peaceful and without support—Brahman alone abiding in Brahman.
That Brahman, whose essence is all-pervasive power, becomes exactly as it shines forth;
without abandoning its own pure form, it appears in such a manner.
Just as a city in a dream is a manifestation of pure consciousness alone for a living being,
so too is creation at the beginning of the world-cycle a manifestation of pure, stainless consciousness alone.
In the pure supreme space of consciousness, that which is established as the space of consciousness—this very creation is its own inherent nature, as conceived by that [consciousness] itself. (23)

And so, just as a variety of colors is perceived in the clear sky, Brahman itself shines forth by its own power through a diversity that is its very own self-nature; thus it follows that creation is nothing other than its own essential nature. He states this in the verse beginning with "svacche" (in the clear). || 23 ||

The intense cultivation of the stages of the object of meditation, the meditator, and the act of meditation—all this is nothing but the pure sky of consciousness, established by itself within itself. (24)

Now, in the word *svabhāva*, the term *bhāva*—being a noun formed with the suffix *ghañ*—denotes "becoming" (*bhavana*). This is the fruit of the activity of the agent (*bhāvaka*), residing in that which is to be brought about (*bhāvya*), and it is the activity of the agent conducive to the becoming of that which is to become (*bhavitṛ*). Since this activity is accomplished by means of the various factors of action such as the instrument (*karaṇa*), there is a single flavor within the three stages of the triad consisting of the object to be brought about, the agent, and so forth.

Regarding how [this] arises, he says: "bhāvya" (to be manifested). The sense is that a manifoldness of flavors is not imagined, because it would contradict the reality of a single uniform essence. || 24 ||
This being the case, whence is creation, whence is knowledge, and where is ignorance?
Brahman is all-pervading, peaceful, and solid; where can egoism and the like reside? (25)
When it has become stable through certainty. || 25 ||
This pacification of the sense of "I" has been described to you;
once fully understood, the sense of "I" subsides like a demon. (26)
Thus, it is concluded that the sense of "I" (ahaṃbhāva) obstructs ignorance, but not its knowledge; this he states with the words "the sense of 'I'":
like a ghost imagined by a child. || 26 ||
But when this entire sense of "I-ness" was fully understood by me in this way, then,
although it still existed, it became as fruitless as an autumn cloud.
By this, he shows that your question has been answered: "But by me... (verse 27).
Just as a painted fire is known to be fruitless when applied to things that can be burned,
so too the creation and other phenomena arising from the sense of "I" (ahaṃbhāva) become fruitless once they are understood.
Burning is the act of burning superimposed [upon the object]. || 28 ||
When there is equanimity for me toward both renunciation and attachment regarding this "I-ness," then my state remains constant in every creation, like the sky which is not [limited by] the non-sky.

The remaining part of the verse implies that "samā" (equality) refers to the state of the non-etherial [space]—which has been rendered without any room by clouds, thunder, heat, wind, and so forth—remaining constant during meditative absorption, renunciation, the time of worldly activity, and even amidst passion. || 29 ||
"I am not the ego-sense, nor is the ego-sense mine"— by this,
know that all this is but the cloudless expanse of consciousness alone.
With the intention that even by the mere relinquishing of [worldly] relations the sense of "I" (ahantā) does not persist—let alone when it has been sublated—he says:
"of the state of 'I'. "Utterly dense" means completely solid. || 30 ||
Just as it is for me, so it is for other awakened ones here;
this delusion of cognition does not exist, being like the fire-nature of a variegated fire. (31)

He states that there is a consensus regarding this point among the experience of all learned people, beginning with the words "Just as" (yathā). This refers to the sense of "I-ness" (ahaṃbhāva) and so forth. || 31 ||
"I am not, nor does another exist; everything is non-existent"—in this certainty, you, who are engaged in worldly activity, become like a stone, observing the silence of a rock.
He says, "I am not," meaning: "May you also become non-dual through the sublation of everything within, just as I am. One who engages in worldly activity is called *prakṛtavyavahāra*. || 32 ||
Remain for a long time with a form as clear as the expanse of space, free from all objective existence as taught;
indeed, from the very beginning until today, everything is nothing but consciousness, and thus the entire visible world is entirely Śiva.

The exposition is without scope, like a solid stone; "today" refers to the time of creation, and "from the beginning" refers to the period prior to creation. The suffix -tasi is used here in the sense of all case endings. || 33 ||

Thus ends the fifty-seventh canto, titled "The Investigation of Egoism by One Who Has Known What Is to Be Known," in the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa* of the *Mokṣopāya* section of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*, composed by the sage Vālmīki.
Thus ends [the fifty-seventh canto] in the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa*, in the latter half of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The fifty-seventh canto, titled "The Investigation of the Ego by One Who Has Known What Is to Be Known."
The fifty-eighth canto.
Śrī Rāma said:
"Oh, how vast, noble, stainless, expansive, and immovable it is!"
O Blessed One, for the sake of our welfare, you have once again proclaimed the Vision. || 1 ||
The splendor of all creation exists everywhere at all times, or it does not;
this point is described here through the illustration of the story of the stone, according to the difference in perspectives.

Once it has been established as a corollary that the egoism of one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*) is not an obstacle, the author prepares the introductory stage (*bhūmikā*) to ask about that very point which was promised to be supported by the story of the stone—the meaning of "everything, everywhere, in every way," and so forth—saying: "Aho! (Verse 1).
In every way, at all times, everything everywhere and always—this reality remains as "Being" alone, equal through the experience of sameness. || 2 ||

That which was proposed—that everything exists everywhere and in every way, and that everything exists everywhere and at all times—is found, when examined through experience, to result in nothing but the uniform, non-differentiated, single essence. This is because, in the case of all subjects and attributes, there is no establishment of exclusion or the state of being excluded in terms of space, time, or substance; such is the intended meaning. || 2 ||
O Brahmin, I have this doubt; dispel it for me.
O Blessed One, why is this narrative called "The Story of the Stone"? (3)

In this regard, he shows the portion that must be questioned with the words "this" (*ayam*). With what aspect is this story of the stone intended to have similarity? The sense is that similarity is well-known only between two things possessing distinguishing attributes (*vyāvartaka-dharma*) by means of a common attribute (*sādhāraṇa-dharma*). || 3 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
To establish that everything exists everywhere and at all times,
I shall relate this illustration of the stones to you.
This is of the manner that will be explained hereafter. || 4 ||
It is demonstrated here that even within the hollow of a stone whose body is entirely solid and without gaps, there exist thousands of creations; tell me, how so? (5)

The story of the stone is not commenced in order to assert that all phenomena are identical to a stone or that they are intermingled; rather, it is begun to demonstrate the possibility of the superimposition of the entire world upon Brahman—which is the substratum for the superimposition within the interior of the stone—precisely as something non-intermingled. He says: "nīrandhra" (solid), meaning "in the hollow" (koṭare) within.
In the space of consciousness, by means of this narrative story under discussion, this meaning is demonstrated. || 5 ||
In this great elemental ether, which does not abandon its own voidness, it is demonstrated that thousands of creations exist; thus it is shown.

Alternatively, with the intention that the superimposition of the entire world is possible even upon the consciousness that is the substratum of non-existence—which, like the space whose nature is emptiness, is as if fashioned within the belly of existence—the author says: "The elemental space... (verse 6).
It is demonstrated here that there exist thousands of creations of internal shrubs, sprouts, and so forth, as well as of living beings, wind, water, and fire; listen as they are described. (7)
With the intention that this principle should be applied everywhere, he says: "Inwardly," etc. (verse 7).
Śrī Rāma said:
O Sage, if it is said that floods of creations exist within walls and such,
then why is it not seen that those floods of creations shine in the sky?

Rāma said: "If the intended meaning of the narrative is that the superimposition of the entire world occurs upon consciousness (cit) as delimited by the absence of all things such as walls and so forth, then why is the position not adopted that the superimposition of the entire world occurs upon the pure space of consciousness (cidākāśa)? For by this, when the superimposed world is sublated, only the pure [consciousness] would remain, which would be more favorable."
He asks: "On a wall, etc. That, then, occurs in the sky, which is the pure space of consciousness. || 8 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāma, I have described all this to you in its primary essence:
this creation which is perceived is nothing but space situated within space.

"True, this very position is primarily what I intend to express. Since the pure space of consciousness (*śuddhacidākāśa*) cannot be comprehended all at once, with the view that even the conditioned consciousness (*upahitaciti*) may serve as a means to it, the superimposition of the entire universe upon each [individual] has been shown.
With this intention, he gives the reply: "This... [meaning] consisting of the very nature of the space of consciousness (*saṃvidākāśa*). (9)
For that which is perceived and appears here has never arisen even from the beginning, nor does it exist even now; it is Brahman, established within Brahman.
Thus, since the mere visible world is nothing but Brahman, non-origination alone is the established result; this he states with the words "from the very beginning.
The meaning is: from the perspective of ultimate reality (paramārthadṛṣṭi). || 10 ||
There is not even an atom of space that is not filled by creations;
nor do those creations exist anywhere as separate entities, for they are nothing but the ether of Brahman.

However, regarding the view of superimposition (*āropadṛṣṭi*), it is possible to perceive everything by superimposing the atoms that appear as its counterparts; whereas regarding the view of negation (*apavādadṛṣṭi*), it is the opposite. With this intention, he says "it does not exist," and so forth. There is not even an atom of earth that is not without gaps—that is, not densely packed; rather, the whole is filled with creation (*sarga*). This should be applied similarly in what follows. 11
There is not even an atom of space that is not filled by creations;
nor do those creations exist anywhere—[the reading "sargā brahma" appears in some versions]. That is indeed the void of Brahman alone.
That is fire. || 12 ||
There is not even an atom of space that is not filled by creations;
nor do creations exist anywhere, for they are nothing but the ether of Brahman.
That is he. || 13 ||
There is not even an atom of space that is not filled with creations;
yet those creations do not exist anywhere within space—that is simply the space of Brahman.

Since it is impossible for water to be excluded from the progression of the elements, and because there is even an atom of water in the interval between earth and fire, the verse beginning with "there is even an atom of water" (āpo 'ṇur apy asti) should also be inferred here. || 14 ||
There is no such thing as the state of the great elements that is not permeated by creations;
nor do creations exist anywhere—this is simply the void of Brahman.
"Great elements" (mahābhūta) is a designation for the five [factors] when they are combined as form (rūpa). || 15 ||
Among the mountains, there is not even an atom that is not solid by its creations;
yet nowhere do those creations truly exist—that is the very void of Brahman.
There is not even an atom of Brahman that is not filled with creations;
nor do those creations exist anywhere apart from it, for they are nothing but the void of Brahman.
Of Brahmā, the Golden Embryo (Hiraṇyagarbha), who has the subtle elements as his substrate. || 17 ||
In the creations, there is not even an atom that exists which is not always the very self of Brahman;
thus, "Brahman" and "creation" are such [terms]—this distinction exists in speech, not in reality.
Regarding those creations consisting of the worlds and the multitude of living beings produced by Him, he states what resulted from that being so: "Brahman," etc.
Creation itself is the Supreme Brahman, and the Supreme Brahman is the state of creation;
there is not even the slightest duality here, just as there is none between fire and its heat or the sun and its light.
It is like the heat of fire and the sun. || 19 ||
These creations and this Brahman appear like the sound of wood being split—devoid of any objective referent—since they are views that are ultimately inexpressible. (20)

Because "emanation" (*sarga*) arises from the act of creating (*sarjana*) and "Brahman" (*brahma*) from the act of expanding (*bṛṃhaṇa*), and because there is no mutual distinction between the two actions of creating and expanding, it is impossible to speak of a relationship between container and contained; thus, even action does not transcend the essential nature [of the agent].

Consequently, words such as "emanation" (*sarga*) and "Brahman" (*brahma*), being devoid of their own referents in the form of attributes that serve as the grounds for their application (*pravṛttinimitta*), [denote only the pure essence].

The meaning is that they appear as such—that is, they are perceptions (*dṛṣṭi*) or cognitions (*pratīti*)—from which, despite being devoid of actual referents (*arthaparivarjita*), there arises a figurative understanding (*lakṣaṇayā*) of something utterly inexpressible, just like the harsh sounds produced when wood is split by an axe or similar tools.
Alternatively, "wood" (*dāru*) is so called because it is split (*dīryate*); thus, the two words *dāru* and *vidārya* are essentially synonyms for the sounds (*ravau*) themselves.
The meaning is that, in the same way, they appear as devoid of distinct objects. || 20 ||
Where there is not even the slightest duality or unity, how, to whom, and in what manner could the meanings of words such as "creation" or "Brahmā" appear? || 21 ||

Let it be that there is no difference in meaning for them in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), because therein neither duality nor unity exists. But in conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), since there is a difference in meaning—namely, that Brahman is one while the creations are many—why should they not have distinct meanings? To this, he says: "Duality.
Even where duality and unity exist in conventional usage, the referents of words such as "creation" and "Brahman" do not appear even in the slightest degree. For these...
Whether the perceiver is dualistic in nature or non-dualistic in nature: in the first case, how can they appear to one who is ignorant?

In the second case, for whom would they appear, and what would they appear to be like, or of what nature? For it cannot be easily asserted that in non-duality there is any distinction between the manifestation and the object manifested; this is the sense. Alternatively, he reveals the very state of being beyond all verbalization through the word "dvaitam" (duality), wherein—
The syntactical connection (anvaya) is that in that reality there is not even the slightest duality or unity. || 21 ||
O dear one, for the knower, even while engaged in worldly activity, this state is peaceful, unique, without beginning or end, pure, and free from disease; his silence is as solid as a stone.
For this very reason, he says "it is peaceful" (śāntam) [in verse 22], meaning that even at the time of worldly transaction, reality remains for the knower of truth exactly as it is.
Thus, nirvāṇa is entirely like the sky, as are all visible things—yourself, myself, the masses of mountains, and the gods and demons.
Behold the world as being just like the network of worldly activities that appears within the mind of a creature in a dream of the body. (23)

He concludes the purport of the narrative concerning the stone, saying: "Nirvāṇam. O dear Rāma, behold the world in that same manner. That is to say, after waking, the web of worldly activity seen in the mind of a living being during a dream—even when slightly remembered—remains as nothing but the Self alone. || 23 ||

Thus ends the fifty-eighth canto, titled "The Exposition of the Brahman-nature of the Stone," in the *Uttara-pāṣāṇa* section of the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*, composed by the sage Vālmīki. 58.
Thus ends the fifty-eighth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Identity of Creation and Brahman," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The fifty-ninth canto.
Śrī Rāma said:
"O Sage, immediately thereafter, from the hollow of the cottage that is the interior of the expanse of the sky..."
What has happened during the hundred years since you awakened from your meditation?
Upon emerging from meditative absorption, the hearing of a subtle sound is experienced;
through the meditation that seeks its source, the manifestation of infinite millions of worlds arises.

Thus, when the incidental subject of the question has been described through these two chapters, Rāma, desiring to hear the remainder of the narrative, asks: "Immediately thereafter," etc. The question is: what occurred after the manifestation of the demon of egoism accompanied by the woman of desire previously described, once you had awakened from meditation at the end of a hundred years?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Then, awakened from my meditation, I heard a sound there— a soft, pleasant voice with distinct words, yet not following the path of ordinary speech.

"Niḥsvanam" means sound. "Mṛduvyaktāni" refers to syllables and words that are soft and indistinct, not too clear. Why is that? Because this sound follows the [mere] utterance; it is neither capable of conveying the meaning of the words nor capable of bringing about the understanding of the meaning of the sentence. || 2 ||
Whether it was soft and sweet like the nature of a woman, or resonant yet lacking full resonance due to its small physical frame—I inferred that speech from me. (3)

It resounds softly and sweetly, as if possessing a specific quality arising from its origin in a woman's throat; it is resonant by nature, yet because of its small size and lack of depth, it does not carry far—it is, in other words, audible only at a short distance. || 3 ||
It has the form of the humming of bees, is delightful with the resonance of lute strings,
is neither weeping nor recitation, and its sound is like that of a blooming lotus.
The *indindira* is a bee; its *ruta* is its sound, which takes that form. The *tantrī* is a lute; the *rañjana* of its resonance is that which bestows delight.
It is neither like the crying of a child nor like the recitation of the elderly; it possesses a sound equal to the well-known humming of bees within a lotus bud. (4)
Having heard that, I then quickly reflected upon this matter;
looking toward the ten directions with wonder, I gazed at those who were experts in grammar.

Because he observes—that is, investigates—the word-maker, the grammarian, he sees the ten directions; thus, [the term] "śabdadardura" is formed with the suffix *ṭhak*, meaning "one who makes a croaking sound regarding words. || 5 ||
This [region] is situated immediately beyond a portion of the sky measuring hundreds of thousands of yojanas, which is devoid of the paths traversed by the Siddhas.
From where [does he come], and why is he filled with wonder? Or what did he think then? He says: "Of the sky," and so forth.

The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: having traversed those hundreds of thousands of *yojanas* which are empty of even those paths suitable for the movement of the *siddhas*, this portion of the sky situated immediately above them exists. 6.
Therefore, how could there be the occurrence of such a word here?
Even though I look with great effort, I do not see any grammarian [who would have coined it]. (7)
In such a secluded place as this, [he heard] something like the speech of a woman;
[he sought] the author of the sound, the one who produced the word. || 7 ||
This infinite, empty, and stainless sky before me—though one strives to perceive what is real within it, nothing is seen here. (8)
A "being" (bhūta) refers to any living creature whatsoever; even when scrutinized and sought with great effort [it is not found]. || 8 ||
Thinking thus and looking again and again, when I did not see Śabdeśvara, I then reflected as follows: (9)
When I do not see Śabdeśvara, who is capable of uttering sound, then—
having become space itself and attained oneness with space—
I perform the functions of the objects of sound, which is the quality of space, within the treasury of space. (9–10)
Having first become the very sky of consciousness (*cidākāśa*) through the abandonment of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*),

and having attained identity with the unmanifest space (*avyākṛtākāśa*) superimposed upon it, I directly perceive— and that is to say, I shall experience— the quality of sound belonging to the elemental space (*bhūtākāśa*) which is its effect, as well as the objects corresponding to that sound, all existing within that sheath of space.
Having established the space of the body here in its natural state through meditation,
I shall attain oneness with the sky of the body of consciousness, just as water unites with water.
He states that very [method] along with its means, beginning with "the space of the body" and so forth. By "vyoman," he means the unmanifested space (*avyākṛtākāśa*).
It is like a drop of water [is absorbed] by water, as if by a commonality of water. || 11 ||
Having thought thus, I sat in the lotus posture to abandon my body;
with my eyes closed once more, I remained intent on entering meditative absorption.
Having abandoned the contact with external objects as well as those internal to the senses, I became the space of consciousness, whose very nature consists of the vibration of pure awareness.

Having abandoned the contacts with external objects pertaining to the senses and the non-senses through their cessation, and having also abandoned the internal objects of the fourfold internal organ—such as those to be reflected upon and so forth—through the cessation of reflection and the rest. || 13 ||

Gradually abandoning even that, I reached the state of the principle of intellect (buddhi-tattva); I have become the single mirror for the web of the universe within the space of consciousness (cidākāśa).

Having reached the state of the principle of intellect (*buddhitattva*), he abandoned even that and, abiding in the sky of consciousness which is his true nature, became a single mirror for the reflections of the web of the world superimposed upon himself. || 14 ||
Then, by that very nature, I attained oneness with the elemental space,
just as water merges with water or fragrance with fragrance.
"By water" means by the commonality of being liquid, like the water of the ocean and so forth. || 15 ||
Then, having become perfected, he pervaded the great space;
infinite and all-pervading, though formless and without support, he became the substratum of all objects.

Regarding that elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*), he states the conceptualization of its non-difference from the ether of consciousness (*cidākāśa*) for the purpose of perceiving the entire world, which is its effect, in the verse beginning with "become" (*saṃpanna*).

Thus, although I am without support due to being unattached and non-dual, I have attained the state of being the support of all things through my non-difference from the elemental ether, which is capable of being the support of everything. (16)
I behold the multitudes of the three worlds and hundreds of transmigrations;
therein, I see even countless millions of cosmic eggs.
There, in the space of consciousness established in that state. || 17 ||
The pure voids, unseen by one another, possess various modes of conduct and reflection, yet they are entirely empty of one another. (18)
Mutually, by virtue of seeing one another, the cavities—which are of the nature of mere unmanifest space—are therefore not seen by each other. 18.
Like the dream-forms of sleeping men occurring at the same time,
they were characterized by great undertakings yet were empty of one another.

Regarding this, he provides an illustration: "Like dreams," and so forth. Just as for people who have fallen asleep at the same time, there are dream-forms that appear to one observer as great undertakings, yet are perceived as vanished by another; therefore, they are both empty and non-empty.
Those being born perish; those growing do so in great numbers;
and those existing, as well as those past and those yet to be, all pass away in every way. (20)
Various networks of paintings, great walls,
and cavities have been fashioned by diverse people, as if they were formidable kingdoms created by the mind alone.
The cavities are like great walls with networks of many paintings, yet they are also without walls.
Forms that are unobscured, as well as those with a single obscuration;
those endowed with five obscurations, and those with six or one obscuration. || 22 ||

In that regard, within the "seen-creation" (dṛṣṭasṛṣṭi) models, which are like dreams, there is no fixed rule regarding the number or the nature of the cosmic egg's enclosures. With the intention of stating that for each individual, only a creation corresponding to the extent of their own manifested latent impressions (vāsanā) is imagined, he says "without enclosures," and so forth. [There are] five of the quintuplicated (pañcīkṛta) elements and five of the non-quintuplicated (apañcīkṛta) elements.

The ten variegated coverings (*daśāvaraṇacitrāṇi*). Together with those—[the portion beginning with "together with those" is to be examined]—there are sixteen coverings according to the Sāṃkhya conceptualization, consisting of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), the ego (*ahaṃkāra*), the Great Principle (*mahattattva*), and primordial nature (*prakṛti*).
By counting these very principles (*tattva*), there are twenty-four coverings. According to the Śaiva conceptualization...
And they are covered by veils that are like the sky, characterized by the thirty-six principles.
There are mandalas with ten enclosures, sixteen enclosures, twenty-four enclosures, and thirty-six enclosures. || 23 ||
They are empty, yet once filled with beings; composed of the five elements, yet consisting of a single element such as earth, or four elements such as earth and the rest. (24)
In these [atoms], there are only the individual elements, such as earth and the rest.
Furthermore, there are others such as the threefold earth and so forth, as well as the twofold earth and so forth;
likewise, there are the seven great elements, each consisting of a single genus.

In this way, there are also those composed of two, three, or four elements, such as earth and so forth; and since time and space possess parts, they are conceived as being elemental in nature, resulting in seven great elements (mahābhūtas). || 25 ||
But those regions which are utterly contrary to the full extent of experience such as yours,
being eternally dark and devoid of the sun and other luminaries— (26)

With the intention that the various conceptualizations of *siddhas*, *vidyādharas*, *gandharvas*, *yakṣas*, *rākṣasas*, and so forth—which are impossible even for the human intellect to conceive—he says: "O you who are like [them]! (*tvādṛśa*).
For those like you, in the fullness of experience (*anubhavābhoga*), these "excessive states" (*atiśayitadaśā*)—meaning states beyond measure—are contradictory and utterly inconceivable.
In these [elements], there are the various distinctions of the transformation of the subtlety and diversity of the primary elements (bhūta). || 26 ||
Likewise, they possess merged creations and are encompassed by a single lord;
they resound with various sounds from portions of the lords of subjects who are distinct from one another. || 27 ||

The creations, having closed their eyes as if in the state of cosmic dissolution or deep sleep, were at the beginning of each creation presided over and governed by a single Lord, such as Hiraṇyagarbha and others. They possess the diverse activities of the lords of creatures—the Prajāpatis—and of their respective classes of gods and other beings. || 27 ||
Likewise, there are treatises on world-weariness and those that are not treatises at all; they also contain worms, insects, and the like, as well as beings such as gods and other living creatures.
He elaborates upon that very point with the words beginning "tathā" (in that way):
beings such as gods and others possess life through undertakings similar to those of the worms in an udumbara fig tree. || 28 ||
But by their very nature, they possess a lineage through tradition and are endowed with conventional usage;
likewise, they are eternally luminous and consist of blazing fire. (29)

In some places, due to the disappearance of the Vedas and the scriptures since the beginning of the Kali Yuga, there are those who possess the conduct of Brāhmaṇas and other castes merely through convention, based solely on their ancestral lineage. || 29 ||
Likewise, those filled solely with water and those consisting solely of air remain motionless in the supreme ether and flow there perpetually. (30)
Some are fixed and motionless in the supreme ether, while others move and flow.
Some, as they are born, nourish others on all sides until they are fully developed; others move horizontally, being composed of the totality of all things.
They nourish and cause to grow all things that consist of every kind of enjoyment. || 31 ||
Some creations consist solely of gods, others consist solely of humans;
some consist solely of hosts of Daityas, and others are teeming with worms without any gaps.
Within, within that, and even within its own sheath, for every atom, there exist those already born and those currently being born, like the layers of a plantain leaf-stalk. (33)

The syntactical connection is as follows: even within the atom (*aṇu*), and even within the interior of that [atom], and even within the imagined sheath (*svakośa*) inside its interior, [the worlds] have been born, and so forth.
Indeed, the vast nets of dreams experienced by the soldiers were not seen by one another, nor were they mutually shared, as if they had arisen independently.
Like the dream-visions of soldiers, they were unseen by one another.
Though they are various and infinite, consisting entirely of the pure ether,
they do not function as one another, nor do they exist within one another.

The phrase "likewise, various kinds," and so forth, should be applied accordingly. This means that they possess different functions (*vṛtti*) and perform distinct purposeful actions (*arthakriyā*); that is to say, they do not exist in mutual dependence on one another, nor do they abide together as a single entity. || 35 ||
And those various scriptures which are mutually distinct from one another, those which are mutually infinite, those which have mutual arrangements, and those which are mutually diverse; || 36 ||

Those which are mutually infinite, having the nature of Brahman that is indivisible; or they are infinite because of the infinity of phenomena (*dharma*). Those whose arrangement is as if toward one another even in their difference, and which are mutually identical in recognition;
mutually otherworldly, and mutually established as ancient cities.
The great elements were of one kind, and the mountains of the quarters were of another. || 37 ||

Because those who have died in one place go to another, their respective worlds are mutually invisible due to the possession of the power of disappearance; thus, they are like cities of the perfected ones (siddhas) existing in relation to one another. || 37 ||

For those like you who possess such experience, even things that are inaccessible and have been newly encountered—though appearing inconsistent when described by people like me—are [clearly understood]. (38)

For this very reason, he says—“by one such as you”—that when another thing is described in another context, they appear in an inconsistent form because they are inaccessible to those of unsettled intellect. [The objects] are inaccessible to experiences, endeavors, and efforts; they have arrived, that is, they have come face-to-face. The meaning is: even though they are present nearby.
"In that case, they will be understood through the words of those like you"; to this he replies with the verse beginning "asamañjasā" (38).
In the sphere of the rays of the sun of consciousness, the rays of the ultimate glory [are] like earrings within the void. (39)

In the consciousness that pervades everywhere and consists almost entirely of the orb of rays of the Sun of Consciousness (*cidāditya*), there exist those things which are like the "atoms" well-known in the rays of the sun reflected in water; they are thus characterized by being sought out (*seṣyamāṇāni*)—[one should consider whether the reading is *seṣyamāṇāni* or *śeṣyamāṇāni*]. If the reading is *śeṣyamāṇāni*, it means they possess the quality of being residual. Likewise, of the ultimate glory...

In the sky—which is like the two earrings of the sovereign fortune of liberation—and in the unmanifest space as well as the elemental ether, they are like the rays of a network of various jewels. (39)
Some of those very same things, having come into being again and again, cease to exist;
others are born exactly like that, like the leaves of a forest.
And because they are mutually distinct, some are similar yet distinct, while others, though similar, remain entirely different for a certain period of time. (41)

Among these, some are similar even though they appear otherwise, because they all superimpose themselves upon the same single consciousness and thus lack separate existence, being identical with one another.
Likewise, even those that are similar may remain very similar for a certain period of time. Some others, however, are entirely dissimilar.
The sense is that this is because illusion (*māyā*) is exceptionally capable of accomplishing what is otherwise impossible. || 41 ||
Those fruits of the great tree of ultimate reality are infinite;
they are indeed non-different from it, yet different, for they are composed of that very essence.
Or rather, he states that the conceptualization of difference and non-difference therein is like that of the fruits of a tree: "The fruits," [he says]. || 42 ||
Some are for short eons, some for long eons;
others are for an indefinite period, while some are for a vast and definite duration.

"Indeterminate" (aniyata) means being devoid of restriction regarding place, time, object, or intrinsic nature; "abundant" (bhūri) means many. Some are "determinate," which means the opposite of that—this is the meaning. || 43 ||
Others, whose times of origin are unknown, arise spontaneously by the power of chance; they grow, become well-established, and remain steadfast. || 44 ||
Because of the absence of the sun and other [planets], the time is unknown. 44.
Those nets of emptiness have grown within the treasury of the supreme space, their duration unknown, rooted in that which is ignorant of its own defects.
Are these [notions] real? He says "no," using the word "tāni" (those). When, then, did they become established there?

To this he replies with "aparijñāta-": the meaning is that they are beginningless (*anādi*). They are established in the *pratīc* (the inner self) which is characterized by such a defect, namely, ignorance (*ajñāna*) that remains uncomprehended. || 45 ||
Enveloped by hundreds of oceans, suns, and skies from the very beginning,
the webs of dreams shine without obstruction within the sky of the wonder of consciousness.
In the sky of consciousness, which is of the nature of the wonder of pure awareness; "āvilam" means as if it were turbid, defiled by the qualities of *rajas* and *tamas*. || 46 ||
Because experience is of the nature of delusion and because causes do not exist,
earth and the other elements— being without cause— are both absolutely existent and non-existent.

Since the experience of causeless things such as earth and so forth is of the nature of an illusion, those worlds exist absolutely as the nature of the substratum, but do not exist in their own right.
Like the mass of water in a mirage, or like the description of two moons in the sky, things that have come into being are not real, even though they appear real through experience. (48)
Appearing in abundance like clouds in the sky of mental construction, these objects, driven by the wind of latent impressions (vāsanā), roll about through the activities of the self. (49)
And for this reason, he says "thus" (tathā): "the volition of consciousness" (citsaṃkalpa), etc. || 49 ||

The mosquitoes that are the gods and asuras find the fruits of the *udumbara* tree—abundant, filled with nectar, and swaying in the winds—only very rarely. (50) [Note: *bahuśodumbara* is an archaic sandhi.]
The gods, asuras, serpents, humans, and others are the gnats upon the udumbara tree that is Brahmā;
the various universes, filled with the essence of diverse enjoyments, are its fruits. (50)
For one whose nature is noble and who initiates creation,
these cities of imagination appear in the sky for that child-like pure consciousness.
Alternatively, the worlds are like cities of imagination created by the pure, solitary child characterized as the principle of consciousness (cittattva). || 51 ||
The notions of "you," "I," and "this" are rendered utterly powerless by the intellect, just as clay toys are overwhelmed by the brilliance of the sun. (52)

Regarding the cause for the solidity of these imagined cities, he says: "Thou... etc. By the force of the intellect consisting of the conceit of "I-ness" and so forth, they have become exceedingly firm (*alam*). They are like toys made of mud. The word "ca" (and) is intended to suggest other examples, such as pots of ghee [solidified] by frost. || 52 ||
The behaviors of those who are eternally satisfied by destiny, which is rich in aesthetic flavor,
are like forests filled with fierce fruits by the streaks of the essence of spring.

Constantly and repeatedly, by means of a craving—characterized by satisfaction, passion, and fluidity—their activities have been brought to completion, with their branches and sub-branches fully developed, through a necessity that ensures the inevitable occurrence of the fruits of karma. || 53 ||
The great agents are non-agents; they are either not created at all, like the voids, or they are created within the space of consciousness (*cidvyoman*) as forms spontaneously perfected.

From the perspective of the scriptural accounts of creation, those [worlds] have the Great Brahman itself as their agent; however, from the perspective of such scriptural passages as "without prior, without posterior," they are non-agents, meaning they lack an agent.
Even those things declared to be other than that are in truth composed of the ultimate reality;
though unobtained, they are as if obtained, and though always non-existent, they are as if existent.

Whether it be that or something else, or as if it were something else—the word "vā" (or) is used here in the sense of "iva" (like), as in the expression "maṇīvoṣṭrasya" (like the two jewels on the camel's hump). The phrase should be read as "sadā asanty eva" (they are always non-existent).
And there are the various classes of elemental hosts, numbering fourteen, ten, one, and so forth.
Furthermore, those very same things appear as both internal and external, each distinct from the other.

By the number of worlds, there are fourteen; by the mere number of divine origins, they are tenfold; by each single species beginning with humans, they are singlefold; and by the "and so forth" (ādi), there are groups of beings that, as appropriate, are fixed at two or more types. || 56 ||
Even hell, heaven, the underworld, enemies, and friends—
consisting as they do of great undertakings— are empty from the perspective of ultimate reality.
Like the waters of the milk-ocean, they consist everywhere of the essence of affection; they are as flickering as waves and are subject to movement both internally and externally.

"Sneha" means ghee and excessive affection; "sāra" means those things which possess it; "āvṛtti" means repetition, and "parivṛtti" means exchange; and [the suffix -mat] denotes that which possesses these qualities. || 58 ||
These forms, consisting of mere appearances, arose spontaneously from the light of the sun-like Self,
like vibrations arising naturally from the wind.
They are born from themselves, like the vibrations of the wind from the sky. || 59 ||
The forms of trees belonging to the intellect, ego, and mind— which are non-existent— are indeed non-existent, just like the men projected in a dream.

The forms of the tree that serve as the support for the leaves—which are the forms of the intellect (buddhi), ego (ahaṃkāra), and mind (citta)—are common even to non-existent perceivers distinct from themselves; yet they are truly non-existent, meaning they are objects of perception for non-existent men distinct from themselves, just as in a dream. || 60 ||
Upon the pillows of the conceptual constructions of the Purāṇas and Vedic doctrines, those who are fast asleep in deep slumber bear the appearance of corpses. (51)

In dreams that dwell upon the beds of the firm conviction that the fruits of vows, gifts, sacrifices, and so forth—well-known from the Purāṇas and other sources—are inevitable, they bear a state resembling death due to the absolute lack of awakening to the true nature of the Self; [the nasal vowel *ṇum* in *svapneṣu* is a Vedic archaism]. 61.
In the great forest of ultimate reality, within the dense self, there are indeed houses fashioned by the gandharva of consciousness, illuminated by the lamps of the sun.

The ultimate reality is Brahman; in that great forest characterized by it, there is a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) that these houses, illuminated by lamps characterized by the sun, were built by a Gandharva who is consciousness conditioned by *māyā*. || 62 ||
Then, as all beings were being born and dissolving pointlessly in the infinite sky,
I indeed beheld the worlds like the clusters of hair seen by one with cataracts in the eyes.

O Rāma, at that time during that state of samādhi, I saw—in the infinite sky of consciousness—worlds being born without cause and dissolving without cause, established through mere delusion like the clusters of hair seen by one with cataracts; the meaning is that I beheld them. || 63 ||

Thus ends the fifty-ninth sarga, titled "The Description of the World-Web," in the second half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the glorious Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa of Valmīki, composed by the Sage. || 59 ||
Thus ends the fifty-ninth sarga, titled "Description of the World-Web," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The Sixtieth Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Then, reflecting upon such a thing, I wandered about on all sides.
For a long time, he has attained the state of the space of consciousness, which is unobstructed.
In meditative absorption, the sight of a woman making a sound is prescribed;
disregarding her, one should again behold the manifold world.
Investigating—that is, searching for—such a cause of sound as previously described, he [attains] the state of unobstructed consciousness-space, which is the boundless space of consciousness. || 1 ||
Afterwards, I heard a sound resembling the tone of a lute; gradually it became distinct in its syllables, and from that it attained the status of an Āryā verse. || 2 ||

Nobility (*āryātva*) consists in being characterized by the definition of the meter known as *āryā*. As they say: "That [verse] in which there are twelve morae (*mātrā*) in the first quarter and likewise in the third, eighteen in the second, and fifteen in the fourth—that is an *āryā*.
Having cast my gaze toward the direction of the sound, I beheld a woman.
On her side, she illumines the sky with a radiance like molten gold. || 3 ||
One whose yogic vision is such that his gaze falls upon the source of sound—being thus—he [beholds] a woman, a lady; "at his side" is to be construed with what precedes and follows. (3)
Her garlands and garments were swaying, her hair was disheveled, and her eyes were restless; with her braided hair hanging loose, she appeared like another Goddess Śrī who had arrived. || 4 ||
He describes her with the verse beginning "ālolā" and so forth: she is one whose *dhammilla*—the binding of the hair—is *lolat*, meaning unsteady or wavering. (4)
Her limbs were as fair as lovely gold; she was in the fresh bloom of youth while standing on the path, beautiful in every limb and fragrant like a forest goddess.
Whose fresh youth was as if moving along the path. || 5 ||
She had a face like the full moon, a smile like a cluster of flowers,
a countenance exuberant with youth, and was graced with eyes possessing thick lashes.
Dwelling in the expanse of the sky, beautiful as the rays of the moon,
adorned with a string of pearls, she who is bent with humility follows after me.
She whose abode is the expanse of space—the elemental ether described previously—is one whose nature is to follow me. 7.
With a sweet voice, the noble and graceful lady,
gentle-smiling and tender toward me, recited this verse in a soft manner.
That beautiful woman, by my side, recited in a sweet voice, as softly as possible, the Āryā verse of the form about to be described. || 8 ||
O Sage, I take refuge in you alone, the tree on the bank that serves as a support for those who are being deluded in the river of saṃsāra by their improper, empty minds.

He cites that very noble verse: "Asat... O Sage, I am one whose consciousness—that is, whose mind—is devoid (rikta) of those faults such as passion, hatred, desire, greed, and delusion, which are appropriate for the wicked (asatām) and the base; likewise, I am a tree on the bank [of the river] serving as a support for those who are being deluded in the river characterized by worldly existence (saṃsṛti).
The meaning is that I bow to and praise only you, who have become the tree on the bank, and no one else. || 9 ||
Having heard this and having looked at her, whose face and voice were so beautiful, I thought, "Is she a woman? What is the use of her? and thus I departed, disregarding her entirely.
Having heard that, he says what you did in response: "Thus" (iti). || 10 ||
Then, having beheld that illusion consisting of the multitude of worlds, I was struck with wonder;
disregarding it entirely, I prepared to roam through the sky.
He clarifies what was stated in the second half of that [verse] with the words "tataḥ" (thereupon). || 11 ||
Then, completely casting aside that anxiety caused by her,
I, whose nature is space, set out to contemplate the world-illusion (māyā) as it abides in the sky.
He explains the words "anādṛtya" (disregarding) and "vihartum" (to sport): "tataḥ" [refers to her] who is situated in the sky (*khe*), which is of the nature of emptiness;
she is of the nature of space (*vyomātman*), having the form of the consciousness-ether (*cidākāśa*). || 12 ||
Just as all those worlds, however fierce they may be, and the entire sky are indeed empty—just as in a dream, a mental construction, or a verbal description—so it is here. (13)
He establishes the phrase "situated in the sky" with the words "as far as" (*yāvat*). The word *yāvat* is used here in the sense of "because. "In resolve" means in a mental construction;
"in narration" means in the manifestation of the meaning of a story. The word *tathā* is used in the sense of "and. || 13 ||
They never see or hear anything whatsoever,
even those things that have existed as a single entity throughout aeons, great aeons, and great births.

Precisely because they are empty in nature, those worlds do not see or hear anything whatsoever, anywhere, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). For this very reason, throughout aeons (*kalpa*), great aeons (*mahākalpa*), great births, and creations, they possess only equality—that is, a single uniform form. [In the formation of the compound,] by the rule *bahuvrīhau gostriyor upasarjanasya*, there is the shortening of the feminine suffix *ṭāp*; and by the rule *napuṃsakasya jhalacaḥ*, [the final vowel is shortened].

The word *numi* is again long. He begins to demonstrate, preceded by a description of the onset of dissolution, that those [elements] do not perceive even the onsets of their mutual dissolution, just as they do not perceive the onsets of their mutual production—starting with the words "Then," and so forth. || 14 ||

[He saw] the Puṣkarāvarta clouds acting like the intoxicated [beings], and the Utpāta winds like those who have lost their minds; the great mountains were shattered, while the pavilion of Brahmā remained constructed with a firm form.

The connection of all these words ending in the second case plural occurs in the fifth verse at the phrase *kalpāntānnavicetanti* (they do not perceive the end of the eons). [Note: From here, the fifth [verse] is to be understood as the twentieth śloka. || 15 ||
[He beheld] the abodes of the ḍākinīs, which were crackling and bursting like the blazing fire at the end of an eon,
and the twelvefold orbs of the sun, which were scorching like great cannonballs.
In which [worlds] the abodes of Aiḍabiḍa and the palaces of Kubera crackle and resound with the explosions of the fire at the end of an eon;
in which the orbs of the suns scorch and whirl in the sky like twelve-sided balls.

Resounding with the gurgling cries of lamentation from the vast throngs of the city of the gods as they rolled about, and formidable for swallowing the entire range of mountain ridges on the battlefield; (17)
Excelling in swallowing all the rows of mountain ridges as they resounded.
[He saw] the great roars of "paṭa-paṭa" from the blazing flames of the fire at the end of the eon,
and the great oceans of the sky agitated by the immense turbulence of their own destruction.
In which [waves], the sounds *paṭapaṭa* were clearly uttered by the bursting of joints in bamboos and other materials caused by the intense blasts of the fires blazing at the end of eons;
and which were agitated by the disturbances of the shoals of aquatic creatures, just like the great upheavals resulting from the loss of their own natural state.
In which the great oceans are the sky. || 18 ||
[He saw] the harsh, gurgling cries of gods, asuras, and humans,
filling the great flood of the seven oceans and overflowing the orbs of the sun and moon.
