Up to the limits of the celestial realm, the orbs of the sun and moon were filled by the great floods of the seven oceans, which had increased to the extent of the seven seas. || 19 ||
Thus, they did not perceive the end of the eons at all, as if they were sleeping together in a single house and experiencing the tumult of battle within a dream.
Even such world-ends occurring within each respective [world-system], all the worlds do not perceive one another.
There, thousands of Rudras and hundreds of millions of Brahmās were seen by me, as well as hundreds of thousands of Viṣṇus and numerous multitudes of Kalpas.

Having thus established the incidental mutual emptiness of the worlds, he speaks of the subject at hand with the words beginning "tatra": "There, among those worlds, [these things] were seen by me. (21)
There, in certain places where there is no sun and thus no ground of day and night,
the decline and emergence of the world occur through inference at the end of kalpas, yugas, and years.

In that world described in so many ways, it follows that in some particular conscious entity (cidvastu), both destruction and emergence are seen through conjectures and mere speculations alone. || 22 ||
In consciousness everything exists, from consciousness everything arises; consciousness is everything, and everywhere there is consciousness.
Consciousness is the reality that is the soul of all—this entire truth was perceived by me therein.
Let it be that the rise and fall [of the world] occur through mental constructs (*ūha*) alone; what follows from that? To this he says: "In consciousness" (*citi*).

The meaning is: "Therefore, I have examined and seen—through both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)—the previously mentioned heart of the story of the stone, in the form of 'all is in consciousness' and so forth. || 23 ||
If you say that there is "something" therein, then, my dear, it is as if there were something;
for she is emptier than space, yet she is not indeed nothing at all.

He illustrates what kind of inference there is regarding consciousness (*cit*), what its arising is like, or what its dissolution is like— beginning with the word "thou" (*tvam*). O Rāma, whatever form you conceive of and designate by name, such as "pot," "cloth," or "wall"— in that state,
consciousness (*cit*) appears just like that very thing you intend to speak of, assuming the nature of those respective names and forms.
That indeed becomes its arising. That very [arising], when intended as the emptiest even of space, becomes "nothing at all" and "no form at all"—this is the meaning of its cessation. || 24 ||
Therefore, this space shines forth as that which is designated as the "world";
for by means of that very space of sound, everything is indeed the supreme space.

Furthermore, that which is called the "world" shines forth as nothing but space (*ākāśa*), whose nature is empty of the conceptualization of name and form (*nāmarūpa*). This is because scripture declares that it is from space alone that the world evolves into its various forms through the sequence beginning with air. Moreover, since that space consists of the subtle element of sound (*śabdatanmātra*), it is also the commonality of the names of all things. By means of that very [space], [the teacher says]: "That thou art; I am..."

Through the ether that has transformed into the form of words such as "I am Brahman" and "there is no diversity here at all," the entire universe becomes nothing but the supreme ether of consciousness (cinnabha). This is the meaning of its absolute dissolution. || 25 ||
"This perception of the visible is an illusion, like a cluster of blossoms on a tree in the sky; it is merely a limb of the space of consciousness"—this I have experienced therein. (26)

Having thus reflected, he describes what kind of experience he himself had: "He saw," etc. O dear one, he experienced that which remains as the space of consciousness (*cidvyoma*) to be nothing but bliss—nothing but the singular essence of unsurpassed joy; this is the meaning. || 26 ||

By means of that which is of the single nature of the space of consciousness, all-pervading, and consisting of pure awareness—therein, by that which is infinite—this thought was experienced by me as "this has been thought by me. (27) [Note: Regarding the phrase *tatrānantena*, the commentators have analyzed it as *atra anantena na saṃkalpaḥ* ("here, by the infinite, there is no volitional construction"). This should be further examined by the wise.]

The intellect (*buddhi*) is the mental modification (*vṛtti*) consisting of the final direct realization; that which is the space (*ākāśa*) having that as its form—because of the manifestation therein of Me, who am of that same nature, all-pervading, full, infinite, and devoid of the three kinds of limitation—in that very state of meditative absorption (*samādhi*), there is no volitional construction (*saṃkalpa*).
(Note: Regarding the phrase *anantena nasaṅkalpaḥ*, the commentators have analyzed it as a word-split: *anantena* [by the infinite one] and *nasaṅkalpaḥ* [without volitional construction].)
This which is about to be described—experienced as being free from all conceptual construction—should be investigated by the wise. || 27 ||
The web of the universe is the Brahma-ether; the ten directions are the Brahma-ether;
and the divisions of time, space, substance, action, and so forth, are the Brahma-ether.

The meaning is that the web of the world—the collection of cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas)—the ten directions contained within them, and everything therein such as parts, time, and space, was seen to exist as nothing other than the very void of Brahman (brahmavyoma). || 28 ||
In that regard, O lords of sages, just as it appeared to me, hundreds of times throughout this cycle of existence, I have seen the most excellent sons of Brahmā named Vasiṣṭha. (29)
In that hundredfold cycle of worldly existence which appears through the emergence of the distinctions yet to be described, there were lords of sages like me whose forms were identical to mine;
O Brahman, all seventy-two *tretā* ages were accompanied by Rāghavas.
In that [cycle], a hundred *kṛta* ages and likewise a hundred *dvāpara* ages were witnessed.
It is implied that seventy-two divisions of the Tretā Yuga, including the incarnations of Rāma along with the descendants of Raghu, have been observed. || 30 ||
Indeed, those various states of creation are perceived through the emergence of differentiation;
yet, through awakening, that single, exceedingly pure Brahman is seen as the all-pervading sky.

The meaning is that through the arising of differentiation—that is, through the awakening of the latent impressions of duality—one perceives all this as nothing but the Brahman-sky, whereas through awakening, which is the vision of reality, one sees it thus. || 31 ||
This name "jagat" (the world) does not exist in Brahman; rather, this [world] is indeed within Brahman.
Brahman alone is unborn, without beginning or end; it is all that, including the word "tat" (That) and so forth.

And thus, he says "not this" (nedam) to show that the Brahman’s state of having phenomenal expansion (saprapañcatā) and its state of being free from phenomenal expansion (niṣprapañcatā) are not contradictory, depending on the difference in perspective;
for the word "this" (idam) is understood as a remainder [of the phrase]. A "foot" (pada) is that which is reached or attained through knowledge; it consists of that [Brahman]. || 32 ||
That which is like the silence of a stone, unuttered by anything whatsoever, yet shines as that "something"—that is remembered as Brahman, the world. (33)

Nothing whatsoever has been designated; it is empty of all names and forms. Its nature is light, its form is light. The meaning is that this very [reality] is remembered as being in the guise of the world. || 33 ||
The unperceivable consciousness alone shines within the space of consciousness as the world;
formless within the formless, it is like the experience of a dream. (34)
Even without an object of consciousness or the act of consciousing, the very existence of consciousness itself shines forth as the world of objects.
Brahman, which is non-different from the Self, is everything whose nature is mere manifestation;
like light, it makes things manifest, yet it does nothing at all.

Demonstrating that "it shines" (*vibhāti*) by showing its non-difference from the inner self (*pratyak*), he shows its nature as self-luminous (*svayaṃjyotiṣṭva*) with the word "ananyam" (non-other). "Ananyam" means non-other (*ananya*). The absence of the *adḍ* substitute is a Vedic usage (*chāndasa*). Brahman, whose form is pure light, performs everything and yet does nothing; just as light performs illumination.
And likewise, it does not act, because the manifestation of anything other than itself is unestablished. || 35 ||
Indeed, among those hundreds of thousands of worlds,
there are moon-disks that are hot and suns that possess cool forms.

If it is objected that if consciousness alone is the world, then the fixed order of necessity—such as that the moon is cool and the sun is hot—would be subverted, [the author] replies that this is an acceptable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*), because even the opposite is observed in the case of different cosmic eggs (*brahmāṇḍa*);
thus he says, beginning with "In those... (verse 36).
People see him in darkness, and they do not see him in light;
their conduct is like that of an owl, and their voices are similar to his. (37)
Of the owl, who is blind by day; those whose conduct—meaning their behavior such as seeing and so forth—is equal to that of the owl.
Since the meaning of the word *sama* (equal) is always dependent upon a correlative, the compound is formed because its syntactic capacity (*sāmarthya*) is not obstructed.
"By that very [conduct], with that very [owl]" || 37 ||
From here, some perish through merit and go to heaven by means of their sins;
they live by consuming poison and die from eating nectar. (38)
"Thus [it is said]"—this statement is due to the unrestrained nature of mental construction and not because of reality;
it should be understood that this is because it would result in the invalidation of the authority of the Vedas. || 38 ||
In whatever manner it is perceived in awakening, or in whatever way it arises spontaneously, whether it be real or unreal, that very thing immediately attains clarity in that same manner. (39)

To explain why that is so, he says: "That which... When an object is firmly established through long-standing practice within awakened consciousness, it arises exactly as it is perceived—as either a means to what is beneficial or harmful. Just as it arises, so too does it attain clarity at the time of experience. Whether the object exists elsewhere or not makes no difference; for it is Brahman alone.
The meaning is that it evolves in accordance with those latent impressions (vāsanā) and karma. || 39 ||
The forest in the sky swirls with trees that resemble vajras, appearing as masses of roots shaped like branches, and shining like leaves and flowers.

He says "viṭapaiḥ" (with branches) to indicate that this [tree] possesses a configuration of leaves and flowers opposite to those of the forests well-known in this Brahmāṇḍa, yet is endowed with functional efficacy as it is well-known in another Brahmāṇḍa.
Because one perceives masses of roots having the form of branches (*viṭapa*), it shines with leaves and flowers that are firm and beautiful like diamonds and jewels.
It is characterized by trees resembling leaves and flowers; the meaning is that it trembles. || 40 ||
When the sands are pressed, they yield an oily essence;
and from stone slabs, lotuses grow in abundance.

Thus, he says "grains of sand" (*sikatā*) to show that even a thousand things otherwise considered impossible may be possible elsewhere: "pressed" means crushed in an oil-press; they "flow" with the oily essence, which is oil. || 41 ||
In the wood, the stones, and on the walls, there are flickering statues that sing and converse together with celestial nymphs.
Living beings wear the clouds aloft like lofty garments;
every year, fruits of diverse kinds arise upon the mountain. (43)
Living beings, like clouds, clothe themselves—meaning they make a covering—as if with garments, upon the mountain-tree. 43.
With various limbs arranged in non-standard positions,
all beings move about upon the earth with their heads [downward].
Some worlds below are devoid of both scripture and the Vedas, utterly lacking dharma; they are inhabited by those who act on mere whim and are like animals. (45)
"Filled only with animals, beasts, and so forth" means [filled] horizontally. "Below" means in the lower worlds, such as the earth and those beneath it. || 45 ||
Deprived of the enjoyment of desires and devoid of women, some [cities] were pervaded by spirits with withered hearts, as if they were made of stone. 46.
For this very reason, because they are devoid of the experience of desire, they are born without women.
Some beings subsist on air, possessing jewels and precious stones;
they have not yet attained their purpose, yet they are free from greed and as if devoid of pride. (47)

Where all beings and living creatures subsist on air alone; where jewels and stones are equal; where things are unarisen and wealth is unproduced—that is to say, devoid of any worldly dealings involving riches—and for that very reason, free from greed; and like those who are free from pride, devoid of egoism—such were some of the places. 47.
In some cases, one perceives and attains the self as individual, and not otherwise;
for although the world consists of many elements, it is also composed of a single element.

In some places, he describes the conventional usage of the diversity of all bodies as being solely through identity with the Virāj-ego, without any distinction from the individual ego—this is expressed by the word "kvacit" (in some places). It does not attain any other self;

even there, the meaning is that it consists of many beings through the fourfold divisions of elements, and each single class of beings, such as those born from sweat and so forth, is filled with various elemental forms. || 48 ||
Just as [the self] is situated in the nails, hair, and so forth, so too is it situated elsewhere;
one should cultivate the realization that the self of all beings is one and the same as one's own self. (49)
In that regard, he shows what the contemplation of the self as one with the various parts of the body is like—by the words "not as," and so forth.

Just as when the nails, hair, and other such things are being cut or grown, one does not perceive the self’s own cutting, birth, and so on, but rather remains as if situated elsewhere; yet, in the enjoyment of pleasure such as their beauty and so forth, there is the contemplation of the self as one with them.
The meaning is that it is seen to be like this for him. For this very reason, the Śruti says: "Indeed, evil does not reach the gods;
he follows only after merit. (49)
In some places, there is only a vast emptiness, infinite, shoreless, and boundless;
through effort, one attains consciousness of it, yet at its end, the world does not exist again.

But in some places, because the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) for the diversity of creation have not arisen, it is perceived as being merely undifferentiated space (*avyākṛtākāśa*); thus he says, "infinite" (*ananta*). If that is so, how is it said that it is the self of all everywhere? To this he replies, "by effort" (*yatnataḥ*).
By means of the effort directed toward manifesting the object of the latent impression, while concealing the perception of its state of concealment (*tirobhāvāvasthā*), [it is realized].
By means of the limit of emptiness, through its transcendence, one again attains and perceives the world. || 50 ||

Some [beings] are neither awakened nor even capable of being awakened regarding the views on the meaning of the word "liberation," like the entire multitude of beings in a wooden mechanical puppet. (51)

The meaning of the word *mokṣa* (liberation) is the state of being the undifferentiated Brahman; for those who hold that view, all other things—which are utterly unreal—are perceived as such. However, when there is the perception of the intellect (*cit*) as distinct [from Brahman], all the multitudes of beings, like forms of elephants, horses, and so forth made of wooden machinery, are seen as if they possessed consciousness. || 51 ||
Some networks of spirits were devoid of the circle of stars and free from the reckoning of time; they consisted essentially of silent conventions.

The syntactical connection is to be understood through the following analysis: some [scriptures] are devoid of the cycles of asterisms and the cycles of luminaries, and for that very reason, they lack temporal calculation (*niṣkālakalanā*);

others are "essence-like" because, due to the absence of speech or the absence of ears, their practical application is accomplished through the conventions of gestures of the hands, feet, and so forth, as in the case of the mute. Thus, having distinguished them, the connection [of the verse] is established.
In the same way, it should be understood accordingly in what follows as well. || 52 ||
Some beings were entirely devoid of the perception of sight, sound,
and objects, their own radiant splendors rendered useless by the singular thought that they were but living entities.

By the word *netra* (eye), [it refers to] those things devoid of the eye, its object, the vision produced by it, and the perception of form and so forth; therefore, they are those in which the solar and other lights are merely a futile radiance. Thus, this state of the world has been described by me through "single-minded contemplation," meaning by means of the mental construction of one whose mind is concentrated in one-pointedness. || 53 ||
Some are devoid of the consciousness of vital breath and possess useless fragrance;
some are mute due to the futility of sound and are bereft of hearing.
The vital breath (prāṇa), the olfactory faculty (ghrāṇendriya), the odor produced by it, and the consciousness thereof—they are devoid of these and so forth, as described previously. || 54 ||
Some others are like the mute because they are devoid of the consciousness of speech;
some are like limbs of stone because they are devoid of the consciousness of touch. (55)
They are like stones or limbs devoid of the sense of touch. || 55 ||
Even some things that are seen consist only of pure consciousness;
though they function in worldly affairs, they are eternally ungraspable, like ghosts.

They consist of pure consciousness alone; that is to say, they are like a kingdom of the imagination. However, some, though participating in empirical usage, are not grasped by the senses because they are composed of subtle elements whose qualities have not yet manifested, like a piśāca;
the meaning is that they are cognizable by the witness-consciousness alone. || 56 ||
Some were made of earth and reached the very end; some were solid masses, while others were filled with water and some were filled with fire.
"Niṣpiṇḍāni" means devoid of solidification. || 57 ||
Some worlds are filled with wind and possess all possible forms, while others are of the nature of space; alas, they all shine there within the void!

This was spoken according to the mental conceptualization of one whose mind possesses the accomplishment of irresistible power—[a mind] which is of every form, capable of all effects, and consisting of all things.
Therein, "in the sky" means in the space of consciousness; "batā" expresses wonder. || 58 ||
While others remain in the various regions that fill the surface of the earth, embodied beings dwell there like frogs in the hollows of rocks or like insects within the belly of the earth. (59)

Regarding the phrase "only the earth" (bhūmayānyeva)—[here, as in the root text of the fifty-seventh verse, it should be read as "the earth and the others" (bhūmayānyeka)]—he removes the doubt concerning the impossibility of the existence of living beings therein by means of an illustration, beginning with the word "dhara" (earth). || 59 ||
The earth, its forests, and its mountains remain entirely filled with water; meanwhile, other beings wander within it constantly, like fierce fish.

Thus, it should be understood that the emergence of life occurs even in things filled with water and so forth; he says: "In water... [verse 60]. Just like a fierce fish or a crocodile, [life arises there].
In other places entirely filled with fire and devoid of water and the like, living beings—consisting purely of fire—throb intensely, like glowing embers. [verse 61]
Like a firebrand, they flicker and quiver like a whirling torch. || 61 ||
In other [beings] filled with wind, even those whose elements are otherwise diminished,
their limbs— consisting of nothing but wind— quiver like the wind in an Arjuna tree.

Arjunavāta is a specific type of disease; it is well known in certain regions that people afflicted by it wander about in the sky. (62) There are other living beings in the creations who consist of the mere void as their bodies and are of the nature of space; they engage in perception and worldly activity. (63)
Whether falling into the subterranean realms, soaring into the sky, or remaining in states of delusion within the quarters of the horizon—
in these various worlds, what indeed has not been seen by me among the flickering bubbles of the ocean of consciousness?
There, in that space of consciousness where the divisions of direction are imagined above, below, and all around, all manner of diverse things are floating.

He concludes by stating that he has seen the worlds and the objects contained within them: "In the netherworlds... etc. What indeed is there in the various worlds—which are like flickering bubbles in the ocean of consciousness—that has not been seen by me?
The meaning is: nothing at all. The sense is that there is no established object that lies outside the range of the witness of the Omniscient One. || 64 ||

Thus ends the sixtieth chapter, titled "The Description of the World-Web," in the second half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, belonging to the lineage of the Sages. 60.
Thus ends the sixtieth sarga, titled "The Description of the World-Web," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the glorious Vāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa-tātparya-prakāśa.
The sixty-first canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
From the space of consciousness, into the space of consciousness, [movements arise] like waves from water.
Because they possess consciousness, these living beings quiver; it is from this very source that our minds [arise]. (1)
When the heart of Brahman is unknown, the world remains imperishable even at the time of its destruction;
but when Brahman is known, the world has never existed, does not exist, and will not exist.
Brahman itself, which is beginningless and unknowable,

through the forgetting of its own nature as immutable, full, blissful consciousness, imagines another nature characterized by movement, limitation, and so forth; thus, by way of the sequence of mind, vital breath, and the rest, it becomes the individual soul (*jīva*) as the enjoyer and the world as the object of enjoyment, existing everywhere and at all times.
The notion that one transmigrates in every form implies that as long as ignorance persists, saṃsāra is of an eternal nature.

However, if that very [reality] is known through the instruction of the scriptures and the teacher, then it is realized as the single essence of full bliss and consciousness at all times, in every way, and in its entirety; consequently, there can never be, anywhere, for anyone, even the slightest trace of saṃsāra.

To demonstrate that it is possible to realize [the Self] and that its nature is indeed eternally liberated, Vasiṣṭha prepares the ground with the words: "From the space of consciousness" (*cidākāśāt*). Because it is consciousness, its nature is the single essence of consciousness that is unknown [to itself]. Living beings (*jīvas*)—delimited by the limiting adjuncts of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*)—manifest; they appear due to the arising of such beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*). Ta...

The meaning is that, through thousands of successive volitions and conceptual constructions, these minds—acting as the seeds of saṃsāra—attain, as it were, the state of being instruments within their own selves; thus they are called "minds" (manas). || 1 ||
Those very minds of ours have become the forms of the clear sky;
those infinite worlds have themselves spontaneously come into being all around.

He says "the worlds" (jaganti) to show that those very minds have become infinite worlds due to the expansion of the latent impressions of the world to be experienced within themselves into the form of a world. || 2 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
When the dissolution of all hosts of beings has occurred at the end of the great kalpa, by whom and how does the consciousness of creation arise once again? (3)

If this were so, it would amount to saying that Brahman alone, through its own ignorance, transmigrates as a single entity in the form of various individual souls (*jīva*) and various states of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*), and that through its own knowledge, it alone is liberated from all those states of worldly existence belonging to all souls; and thus, at the end of the previous elemental dissolution (*prākṛta-pralaya*), [it would follow that] Hiraṇyagarbha, who is the collective totality (*samaṣṭi*) of all souls...

With the thought, "Since the cessation of ignorance through the knowledge of reality necessarily entails the sublation of all states of being—both the individual souls and the world—which are rooted in that ignorance, the liberation of all must be asserted; yet, how could the cycle of transmigration arise again for the liberated Brahman through this succession of worlds and living beings? Rāma [spoke].
He raises an objection: the sense is that because liberation for all must necessarily be asserted, based on the scriptural statement, "And finally, there is the cessation of the entire māyā. (3)
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: At the end of the great dissolution, when the earth, water, wind, fire, and space— along with all their specific manifestations— have been destroyed,
and everything from Brahmā down to the stationary beings has reached liberation, this world is experienced once again in the same manner as it was before.

Listen. That which is indefinable, the solid mass of ultimate reality, which the sages call Brahman, pure consciousness alone—that is this world, its very heart; therefore, it is not distinct from it.
And that same Lord perceives His own heart, His own nature, as the world, merely for sport and not otherwise.
Upon investigation, we do not perceive anything whatsoever as a "world" in its true nature; therefore, what is destroyed and what is born?
Just as the supreme cause is indestructible, so too is that Heart (Hṛdaya) indestructible.
Even the great cosmic cycles (*mahākalpa*) and so forth are merely its parts; here, there is only a lack of full comprehension leading to mere differentiation.
Even that, when being examined, is simply not found. || 4 ||
Having restated the question, Vasiṣṭha promises to provide the answer in both prose and verse,

beginning with "mahāpralaya" and ending with "śṛṇu": when all specific manifestations up to and including space have perished, and the worlds of living beings— from Brahmā down to the stationary objects— have reached liberation, [there remains] the inexpressible Brahman.

Although it is said that "pure consciousness alone remains," nevertheless, this world is the heart of that undifferentiated Brahman-consciousness; therefore, the passage must be explained by completing it with the thought that [the world] is indeed non-different from Brahman.
This is the intended meaning: although from the perspective of one who is liberated, for one who is liberated-in-life (jīvanmukta), nothing whatsoever remains for anyone.

Nevertheless, because the dawn of the knowledge of reality has not arisen for each of the others individually, from their perspective their own respective ignorance has not been destroyed; thus, they continue to experience bondage. This is just as the moon’s small size—which is utterly non-existent from the perspective of those currently residing in the lunar world or those who have recently gone there—remains exactly as it is from the perspective of those standing on the earth.
"In that same way," he says this very thing with the words "that very deity," and so forth. One perceives [the world] through the bound perspective;
by the use of the word "and" (ca), one does not perceive it through the liberated perspective. If you are *jīvanmuktas*, then what kind of world do you perceive?
To this he replies: "Merely as a diversion. That is, merely as a diversion, in the form of curiosity regarding the persistence of what has been sublated.

The meaning is "like a burnt cloth. Therefore, since it is non-different even within these three views, what indeed perishes and what indeed is born in the world? If it is truly imperishable, then how can there be great kalpas, intermediate kalpas, and so forth? To this he says: "Great kalpas and so forth. For it is not possible to say that parts of that eternal reality are non-eternal; nor indeed...

The various divisions of the kalpas that have perished are capable of returning again and again. Therefore, the meaning is that it is precisely the existing divisions of the creation of the kalpas that revolve like the beads of a rosary, again and again, in the form of the wheel of time (kālacakra).
If one asks how there can then be a cognition of distinctions within past and future kalpas and so forth, he says:
It is merely a lack of full comprehension. || 4 ||
Therefore, nothing whatsoever ever perishes for anyone anywhere;
nor indeed is anything born, for the Brahman is peaceful, the unborn, and remains as the visible reality.
He concludes the matter established in prose with a verse: "Therefore," etc. (5).
That pure existence consisting of consciousness alone which exists even in a portion as small as a thousandth part of a space-atom; || 6 ||
Indeed, this world is the body of that Great Consciousness;
how could it perish while she remains undestroyed? And she, moreover, does not perish.

He states another argument for the indestructibility of the world: "Ākāśa... and so forth. The collective meaning is as follows: when it is established as a tenet that the world—ranging from space (*ākāśa*), which is the limit of the excellence of magnitude, down to the thousandth part of an atom (*paramāṇu*), which is the limit of the excellence of minuteness—exists only through the existence of the consciousness of Brahman (*brahmacitsattā*), then how can its destruction be possible in the absence of that [consciousness]? [The words] "body" (*vapuḥ*) and so forth [refer to this].
Verses || 6 || 7 ||
Just as the heart of consciousness appears in a dream in the form of the world,
so too does that which is of the nature of space itself shine forth from the very beginning of creation.
And since the state of being the heart of consciousness is well-known even in a dream, which has pure consciousness as its sole essence, he says: "Of consciousness... (verse 8).
Creation is a part of the void of consciousness; such are the destructions and arisings of creation. The entire sky—what is perishable and what is imperishable? (verse 9).
For this supreme consciousness is indeed indivisible, unburnable, undampened, and unsusceptible to drying;
it is invisible to those who do not know it. Whatever constitutes its heart, that remains exactly as it is.
Just as it does not perish, so too the experience of the world and all else existing within it neither arises nor perishes—it is simply [that].
By the power of recollection and non-recollection, it, as if by its own nature, conceives of experiences and non-experiences. || 10 ||
"In that case, let there be the destruction of consciousness as well. To this, he provides the answer in prose: "For this [consciousness]...

Just as this consciousness does not perish, so too the experience—the manifestation—of that which exists within it, which constitutes its very heart, namely the world and its cause, ignorance, neither arises nor perishes. If it indeed does not perish, then how [can there be] pleasure, pain, and so forth?
Regarding the experience of its occasional occurrence, he says: "Only... (verse 10).
Whatever reality has whatever as its nature, that remains inexhaustible without undergoing destruction;
therefore, know that the visible world, being of the nature of Brahman, is inexhaustible like Brahman itself. (11)
He states that the world is not perishable because it possesses a self through its eternal nature with the verse beginning "yadyad" (whatever...):

"Whatever..."—from this observation, the words "that very thing" (*tattat*) are to be supplied. Without the destruction of each respective thing, it is imperishable (*akṣayi*), meaning indestructible (*avināśi*). || 11 ||
The great dissolution and so forth are merely its constituent parts.
If the universe consists of Brahman, then why would there not be a plurality of Brahman due to the plurality of that universe? To this he replies:
"The great dissolution and so forth. These are indeed the limbs (parts) of that Brahman, whose nature is Great Time. || 12 ||
In the supreme void, which is pure consciousness alone, how indeed can there be existence and non-existence?
How can there be modifications of being and so forth in that which is as formless as space? (13)
If it be objected: "How can that which is composed of infinite parts such as insentient creation, dissolution, and so forth, be of a single uniform essence?"—

the author Padmapāda provides the answer with the words beginning "In pure consciousness" (*cinmātre*), intending to show that it is like a crystal slab, which, though composed of many reflections such as mountains, trees, and cities, possesses the single uniform essence of its own transparent substance.
"Nirākṛte" means "in the formless. The suffix *kta* is used in the sense of a state (*bhāve*), and it forms a *bahuvrīhi* compound. || 13 ||
Great eons and other such entities, as well as these worlds, are merely names;
they abide within this consciousness-Brahman solely by virtue of having Brahman as their self.

Just as various distinct reflections exist by virtue of the nature of the crystal itself, so too do the diverse states such as the great aeons (mahākalpa) reside within Brahman, whose single essence is consciousness; this is the meaning. || 14 ||
Having cast aside the impure and having conceived the visible world as being under the control of pure consciousness alone,
one attains that very state by which a yakṣa is fashioned within one's heart.

Just as yakṣa-cities, armies, and the like—which arise from mental volition—are merely mind, so too the world, which arises from the volition of consciousness (cit), is merely consciousness; with this intention, he says: "Formless" (nirākṛti). || 15 ||

Just as a tree, which is a composite whole, has branches, twigs, fruits, sprouts, flowers, and so forth as its parts, so too does the Supreme Reality— which is dense, formless even beyond space, indefinable, and devoid of dissolution, great dissolution, destruction, emergence, existence, non-existence, pleasure, pain, birth, death, and form— possess these as its constituent parts.
"Those," [it says]. 16.

If it be asked, "Granted that this is so, how then is there the non-destruction of the worlds?"—the author explains this through a prose description using the analogy of tree branches, with the intention that it is precisely because their constituent parts are indestructible. He begins with the words "Just as" (*yathā*), etc.: just as that whole (*avayavī*) whose nature is Brahman is indestructible and indefinable, even so are those parts, such as creation, dissolution, and so forth.
The meaning is: "for this reason. || 16 ||
Whether the part and the whole are both visible or both invisible, there is always only a single essence; there is never any difference between them. (17)

To explain why this is so, he says: "between the part and the whole. Now, one might ask: how can there be non-difference between that which is visible and that which is invisible? To this he replies: "or between two visible things. Even when there is non-difference, that very same thing becomes visible when there is grossness, but invisible when there is subtlety. The intention is that visibility and invisibility are not fixed by difference. || 17 ||

Just as consciousness is the root of a tree, so too is it the dense essence of ultimate reality; in some places there is a mere something, in some places the trunk of creation, in some places the branches that are other worlds,

in some places the established structures are the limbs, in some places the sprouts are the categories of objects, in some places the light is the flower, and in some places the darkness is the blackness.

In some places it is the hollow of the sky, in some places the shrubs of dissolution, in some places the shrubs of the great dissolution, and in some places the clusters of Hari, Hara, and the other deities; in some places it is the very skin of dullness—thus, this formless thing, which is of the nature of space alone, remains non-different from the Brahman within the self of consciousness due to its state of similarity with Brahman. || 18 ||

Therein, he establishes the non-difference between the part and the whole by means of an analysis of the similarity between a tree and its parts, beginning with the words "Just as" (*yathā*). Just as when a tree exists, consciousness of the tree itself is the root, so too, when the world—which is essentially pure Being—exists, consciousness alone is the root; this similarity is well-known. Thus, it is precisely because [the world] has consciousness as its root that...

In certain regions, it displays a certain variety just like a tree—this is indicated by the word "kvacit" (in some places). The trunk (*stamba*) is characterized by the primary creation (*sarga*). The branches (*viṭapa*) or trunks attached to that consist of the worlds beginning with the Earth (*bhūrloka*). Within those, the arrangements of Jambūdvīpa and so forth are the twigs (*śākhā*). Upon them, objects such as mountains, rivers, and provinces are the leaves (*pallava*). Upon those...

The light of the moon, sun, and so forth is its flower; the characteristic of darkness is the blackness of its green leaves; the characteristics of dissolution are its shrubs, which are the breaking of knots; the characteristics of the supreme deities such as Hari and Hara are its clusters and bunches; and the characteristic of the dullness of water-laden clouds is its bark. In this manner described, it is formless.

The meaning is that within the Brahman, which is consciousness itself, it exists as nothing other than the very nature of space, appearing through various forms due to its own essence being as pure as Brahman. || 18 ||
From this comes manifestation, from this comes existence, from this comes creation, and from this comes dissolution;
experience is indeed inherent nature—thus stands the immovable Brahman. (19)

He states the very same point in verse, beginning with "itara" (the other), etc. That which is to be (*bhāvya*) is a future object; that which exists (*bhāva*) is a present entity. This is also an elliptical expression for the past.

And all of that, because its establishment depends upon experience (*anubhava*), is nothing but experience itself. Furthermore, that which is one's own nature (*svo bhāvaḥ*) is the Self (*ātman*) itself.
The meaning is that Brahman alone is the one, immovable reality, which exists in this way through the conceptualization of manifold diversity. || 19 ||
Likewise, O dear one, there are no taints whatsoever in this supreme space of Brahman, just as there is only purity in the orb of the moon. (20)

If so, are the creation, dissolution, and so forth, which are the coloring of Brahman, real? He says "no"—"Thus" (evam). The grammatical connection is that none whatsoever exist at all. Just as there is no purity—that is, freedom from stain—in the orb of the moon, this is a comparison in some sense; or rather, the subsequent connection is with the word "nirmale" (in the stainless one). || 20 ||
In the stainless supreme space, where is there any coloring by existence or non-existence? Where are the conceptions of beginning, middle, and end? And where are the delusions of other worlds? (21)
In that case, only non-comprehension arises as a fault;
it is pacified simply by turning away from it through right observation. || 22 ||
If that is so, what is the cause of such delusion, or from where does its cessation arise? To this he says: "It is simply non-comprehension.
This is because of the vision [of reality] by means of an intellect turned inward, having abandoned the outward gaze and being inclined toward the inner Self—as stated in such scriptural passages as:
"A certain wise man, desiring immortality, beheld the inner Self with his eyes turned back."
The state of being. || 22 ||
Ignorance perishes when it is touched by the awakening of pure consciousness;
just as a lamp is extinguished by the very wind that caused it to flare up. (23)
He states the reasoning for how that which establishes ignorance—specifically, the final intuitive state (vṛtti) illumined by it—acts as its sublater:
"Ignorance," etc. (Verse 23).
When ignorance is fully understood, one realizes that it never existed at all;
having comprehended that everything is Brahman alone, there is neither bondage nor liberation.
It is well known that knowledge is the sublater of ignorance and its effects; thus he says: "Ignorance...
Having described the experience of Brahman as the remainder after sublation, he shows it: "...liberation from bondage. (24)
In this way, O Rāma, awakening and the rest, as well as liberation, are said to be known through one's own consciousness;
one who exerts effort in inquiry attains them—of this there is no doubt whatsoever. (25)

O Rāma, these means such as awakening (*bodha*) and the rest, whose nature has been thus described by me for the sake of liberation, are attained by a qualified person who exerts effort in the constant investigation of these very means. || 25 ||
Having seen here that this world-web, which is beginningless and unborn, appears as the object of Brahman,
the individual soul (jīva) remains within itself, perceiving through the vision of inquiry its own eightfold lordship as being like a blade of grass.

This web of the world is beginningless; it has never been born, nor has it ever arisen. Rather, it exists as Brahman itself appearing in the form of the heart of the world and so forth, for the purpose of seeking—that is, praying for—both enjoyment and liberation. This means that its own true nature is unknown. Thus, from the perspective of discernment, the individual soul (*jīva*) is the qualified seeker.

The meaning is that, through the vision of discernment, seeing even lordship endowed with the eightfold powers such as *aṇimā* as being essentially worthless because it is merely *māyā*, and regarding it as no more than a blade of grass due to the excellence of supreme detachment, one realizes "I am indeed Brahman, the unsurpassed bliss," and remains within one's own self with all desires fulfilled. || 26 ||
Thus ends the sixty-first chapter, titled "The Sole Awakening to the World as Space," in the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the glorious Vāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa composed by Valmīki.
Thus ends the sixty-first chapter, titled "The Sole Consciousness of the World-Space," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The sixty-second canto.
Śrī Rāma said:
"That which was seen by you at that time, with your body being the space of consciousness (cidvyoma)..."
How much more so, then, for one who dwells in only a single part of it, or even one who wanders through the sky? || 1 ||
O Sage, the observation of bodies and the world by a woman who is herself of the nature of space is described here,
as is her conversation with one whose form is space, like a dream.

Rāma, doubting whether that web of the world was seen by you while remaining with a limited sense of self and wandering in the sky like a bird, or rather through the nature of the unlimited space of consciousness, asks: "Is this...? Śrī Vasiṣṭha replied: "O Rāma, listen to what happened long ago in the past. There was a certain king named Mahābala, who was a great warrior and a master of all weapons. He had a son named Mahābuddhi, who was wise and possessed of great intelligence. Once, as he was wandering through the forest, he saw a beautiful woman who had been abandoned there. She was emaciated, her hair disheveled, and she was weeping piteously. Seeing her in such a state, the prince felt compassion and asked her, 'Who are you, and why are you weeping? She replied, 'I am the daughter of King Mahendra, named Indumatī. My father has banished me from the kingdom because I have fallen in love with a low-born man. I have no other refuge; therefore, O noble one, take me away from this place. Hearing her words, the prince took her with him and returned to his own city. There, he married her according to the prescribed rites, and they lived together in happiness. However, after some time, the prince became afflicted by a severe illness. As his life-force was departing, he called for his ministers and said, 'I am about to die; tell me, what shall I do? The ministers replied, 'O King, you have performed many meritorious deeds; therefore, you will surely attain a high state in the next world. But the prince said, 'I have not yet fulfilled my debt to this woman, who has placed her trust in me. If I depart without having honored her, I shall fall into hell. Therefore, I must first see her and settle my affairs before I leave this body. Having spoken thus, he summoned Indumatī and said, 'O beautiful one, I am dying; come here quickly so that I may see you one last time. She came at once, and seeing her, the prince’s mind became filled with passion. Overcome by desire, he forgot his illness and his impending death. He embraced her and said, 'O lovely one, I cannot bear to be separated from you even for a moment. Let us go together to a secret place where we may enjoy each other's company without fear. She agreed, and they went to a secluded grove. There, lost in the intoxication of their union, the prince passed away. When the ministers learned of his death, they cremated his body and performed the funeral rites. Indumatī, however, remained in that very spot, weeping and lamenting for her husband. She did not wish to leave, fearing that she would never again find such a lover. Thus, O Rāma, the mind of that woman was entirely absorbed in the thought of her beloved, and she remained there in that state until her life ended."* *(Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the full narrative continues with the prince being reborn as a bird due to his attachment, and Indumatī following him in death, eventually both attaining liberation upon realizing the illusory nature of their worldly bond.)*
At that time, I was indeed the infinite Self, all-pervading like the ether;
in such a state, what kind of coming and going could there possibly be? || 2 ||

In this regard, taking the second alternative, Vasiṣṭha gives the reply: "He is perfected" (saṃpannaḥ). In that state of infinity, there is no coming or going; this is merely an indication of all action. || 2 ||
I am not composed of that which abides in a single place, nor have I become composed of motion;
therefore, by me, this has been seen within my very own self.
The suffix *mayaṭ* denotes abundance. Therefore, for that reason, this world was seen by me within this very Self, which is immediate and not beyond perception. || 3 ||
Just as I perceive the limbs from head to foot as being the body itself,
so too have I seen this [reality] with the eye of consciousness, which is yet no eye.

He refutes the claim that the perception of the non-self as one's own self is unestablished—without resorting to the conceptualization of its abiding in a single location and so forth—by means of the introduction of examples, beginning with the words "Just as" (*yathā*). Regarding "in the state of being the body" (*śarīratve*), this refers to the perception of the body as the self.
"Limbs" (*aṅgāni*) refers to the hands, feet, and so on. Just as [the limbs] abide in a single part of the body even without the conceptualization of wandering within another body and so forth.
The meaning is: "just as I see with the eye of consciousness (cinnetra), even without the physical eye and independent of the eyeball. || 4 ||

Then, for that one whose nature is the stainless sky of consciousness, who is formless and established as partless, those worlds became like a lattice-work of limbs; yet they did not fall away from him of their own accord, nor did they lose their substantiality.
To the question of how the world could have become a constituent part of one who has become Brahman—which is unattached, indifferent, and partless—he says:
"anākṛteḥ" (of the formless). At that time, in that state of samādhi, even for me—who am the self of the stainless sky of consciousness and who abide as the partless formless—those worlds [appeared].
The sense is this: the network of parts arose in such a way that its own substantiality (*vastutā*) did not dissolve, nor did it cease to be substantial;

because it exists through my existence (*matsattayā sattvāt*), its substantiality did not dissolve. However, because its state of being my part is devoid of intrinsic existence (*svataḥ sattāśūnyatvāt*), it does not possess substantiality.
Thus, there is no fault in the fact that this [network] did not become a truly real (*vāstavī*) possession of parts. || 5 ||
In this matter, your authority is the delusion of the world seen in a dream;
for that which is perceived in a dream is experienced as such, yet it is nothing other than empty space.
Regarding the point already stated, he establishes the similarity between the dream-world and the waking world by means of a proof, [saying]: "The proof... (verse 6).
Just as a tree perceives its own leaves, flowers, fruits,
and so forth with the eye of self-awareness, even so have I seen this.
With the intention that the scriptural passage beginning with "But when for him everything has become the Self alone, then by what and whom should he see?

teaches the non-perception of the world specifically in the context of *nirvikalpa-samādhi* (non-conceptual absorption) and not in *savikalpa-samādhi* (conceptual absorption), [the author] provides another illustration—even without the instruments such as the eyes—for perceiving that [Self], saying "Just as... [a tree...].
The living being has become identical with the body of the tree. || 7 ||
Just as the ocean, whose nature is infinite, knows all aquatic creatures,
as well as its waves, whirlpools, and foam, so too have I understood this.
The ocean is the individual soul (jīva) possessing the conceit of being the sea. || 8 ||
Just as an embodied being perceives its own limbs within itself as non-different from its own self,
so have I understood these creations to be non-different from the Self.
What need is there for much? With the intention that such perception is well-known even among all living beings regarding their own limbs, he says:
"O Rāma, having attained oneness with pure consciousness, I still see those very same creations within my body, in space, on mountains, in water, and on land. (10)

He says—beginning with "Even today"—that it is not merely that I have had a vision of the world as being the heart within my own self at that very moment, but rather that it can always be seen with a gaze ever-inclined toward it. [The word] "even" (api) implies "also tomorrow. || 10 ||
Having attained oneness with pure consciousness, I perceive this entire universe before me— both inside and outside my house— as being filled with multitudes of worlds.
Just as water knows its own fluidity, just as snow knows its own coldness,
and just as the wind knows its own movement, so does one of pure intellect know this [the Self].
The words "water" (ambha) and so forth refer to their respective deities. || 12 ||
Whosoever indeed has become one with pure consciousness through the nature of discernment, he is equal to me as a single self; I know my own self to be such.

"Do you alone know this? To which he replies with "yo yaḥ" (whoever...). The intention is that everyone is of one essence with me; and since I know my own self to be such—that is, as being identical with their very self—the cognitions of all-knowing ones are simply my own cognition. Therefore, they are not to be sought separately. || 13 ||
For this vision,
there is no cognition whatsoever arising regarding a knower, a knowing, or a known object, since there is only the oneness of the nature of pure consciousness.

The meaning is that, due to the power of transformation (*pariṇati*) and maturation (*paripāka*), no cognition of the triad beginning with the knower exists as something distinct from its own self, because they have arisen as being of one essence with consciousness (*vijñāna*). || 14 ||

Just as one possesses divine vision to perceive objects situated on a mountain, so too does one know things extending for millions of yojanas; both external and internal, I have realized it to be thus.

If it is asked how there can be the vision of all things—both hidden and remote—by means of a single cognition, he makes this possible through an illustration: "As by divine... [The text continues: ...for a person situated on a mountain (adrisaṃsthasya), who has ascended a peak, because of being unimpeded by diseases such as cataracts or because of being refined by medicinal herbs and the like.

Because he is either born with innate perfection or is refined through yoga, he knows and perceives directly divine things—both external, pertaining to the physical world, and internal, pertaining to the self. "In this way" means "in that same manner. || 15 ||
Just as the earth-element knows all things such as treasures, minerals, and essences,
so too have I realized that which is identical with it— the non-dual reality that is nothing other than the Self.
By the term "the sphere of the earth," the individual soul (jīva) who identifies with it is understood. || 16 ||
Śrī Rāma said: O Brahman, since you experience it thus,
tell me, what did that lotus-eyed beloved do— she who was so proficient in reciting the noble verses?
Vasiṣṭha said:
Reciting that very same noble verse and likewise full of conciliation,
she remained near me with a body made of ether, like a goddess stationed in the sky.
It is endowed with *anunaya*, which is an activity that generates affection through praise and the like. || 18 ||
Just as my body is like space, so too is she of the nature of emptiness;
therefore, that woman was never before seen by me with this physical body.
If she were standing nearby, then why was she not seen by you previously, even without meditative concentration? To this he says: "Just as... (verse 19).
I am whose self is mere space, and she has a body that is mere space;
at that time, the web of the world existed therein as nothing but space.
There, in that space of consciousness; then, at the time of meditative absorption. || 20 ||

Śrī Rāma said: From what source does that speech arise, consisting of phonemes, which emerges from the body, its positions, its articulations, effort, and the vital breath— given that it possesses such a form?

Rāma asks: "If she is indeed of the nature of space (*ākāśa*), then how did she recite the *Āryā* verse in the absence of a tongue, palate, lips, breath, air, and so forth?"—this is expressed in the verse beginning with "śarīra... [referring to her having space as her body]. Thus, she is one whose body is space and who possesses such a form. || 21 ||
“From what do form, light, and mental attention arise, and how indeed do they belong to the selves?
O Blessed One, tell me the reality and the certainty as it actually occurred. (22)

With the intention that for you, who are thus merely space, even the contemplation of seeing such forms would be difficult to obtain, he says: "Tell me how he behaved and what his resolve was. This is the meaning. || 22 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Just as forms, perceptions, mental activities, sounds, recitations, and words exist in a dream within the sky itself, so too do they exist there in the ether.
To this, he gives the reply—stating that everything is logically established through the very example of a dream and by means of conceptualization—with the verse beginning with "rūpa":

"Through form, light, and mental attention, even in a dream, those [objects] arise in the sky of consciousness itself; just as they arise, so too does that which is seen therein abide as having the nature of space. (24)
Not only is that visible object so, but even this entire world which we perceive as an object is, for us, nothing but the pure void, just as it is.

To say that "at that time, that which is visible is of the nature of space" is to state too little. When investigated according to reality, this entire world is now likewise of the nature of space alone. He says "not only... to show that even here, the delusion of worldly activity arises solely through the error regarding the body and so forth—the grammatical connection being:
"we, our objects, and our field of perception, as far as they extend—all that is the world. (25)
The great ultimate realm, whose conscious body is liberated from all that is to be known, shines forth by itself in this very way; such is the certainty regarding its own nature.

The word "nāma" (by name) is used to indicate that this is well-known through scripture, the experience of the learned, and so forth; [it refers to] the nature, which is the nature of consciousness conditioned by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the world. || 26 ||
What proof do you have for the existence of the body, its location, and its organs?
Just as they possess a body and so forth, so too does this [body] exist for us. (27)

What proof is there for the cognition of its existence? The point is that this is sublated by such scriptural passages as, "It is bodiless, yet it abides within bodies that are themselves unstable," and so forth. || 27 ||
Just as that is, so is this; and just as this is, so is that.
The unreal has attained the appearance of reality, and the real stands as if it were unreal. (28)
The reality of the Self, which is existence without distinction, remains as if non-existent and as if utterly unestablished because it is concealed;
the word "and" (ca) serves to include by implication that there is likewise a transformation of its nature as consciousness and bliss. || 28 ||
Just as in a dream there is the activity of traversing the surface of the earth and other paths within space,
so too am I, you, she, and all this— everything is likewise space.

The activity of agriculture and the like on the surface of the earth, the activity of traveling and the like on the surface of the road, and the activity of sleeping and the like on the surface of a palace and so forth—all these take place within the sky of consciousness alone. || 29 ||
Just as in a dream, people experience the clamor of battle and the coming and going of others— though these do not exist— so too are the multitudes of worldly existence experienced.
If you say that the splendor seen in a dream is unreal, why is that so?
This cannot be stated [as a reason], for there is no other cause for the existence of experience. (31)

Even regarding the diversity of dreams, there is no room for the postulation of another cause; for, out of fear of defects such as infinite regress (*anavasthā*), all other disputants remain silent on that point. Thus, by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), it is established that this is simply the inherent nature of the conscious self (*cidātman*) as conditioned by ignorance (*avidyā*). This is my own position. He says: "Thou speakest"—that speech of yours is inconsistent.
For there is indeed no other cause for the persistence of dream-experience. || 31 ||
To the one who asks, "How is a dream perceived?", it is explained:
"It is just as you see it now"; this alone is the reason here, and no other.

The meaning is that for the questioner, the very experience of "just as you see" is proclaimed as the answer by all [the means of knowledge]; no other reason exists here to establish that [point]. || 32 ||
From the very beginning of the first creation, the Virāṭ Self shines like a creature in a dream within the sky;
in the void, it is merely the void itself, mutually [interpenetrating].

For instance, after a dissolution resembling deep sleep, from the very beginning of the first creation, the Virāṭ-self—consisting of mental construction like a being in a dream—expands as the sky of consciousness itself within the sky of consciousness; thus he says: "In a dream... [and so on].
These two exist in a state of mutual dependence as subject and object. || 33 ||
I employ the word "dream" for the sake of your understanding;
yet this visible world is neither existent nor non-existent—it is not a dream, but Brahman alone.
If so, is the world of the very same nature as the dream that serves as the illustration? No; he says "by the word 'dream'": || 34 ||
Then, O Raghava, that beloved woman, who was ever attached to me,
having entered into a conversation with me consisting of that [same essence], appeared in visible form and asked this.
Having thus resolved this intermediate question, he states the remainder of the narrative previously asked about, beginning with "atha" (now).

"Kānte" means in the beloved who is about to be described; "anuṣaṅgiṇī" means full of passion; "tanmayīm" means having as its primary focus the desire to know his intention—having formed such a mental resolve (*saṃkalpa-saṃvidam*). || 35 ||
Just as worldly interaction arises in a dream with those born of a dream, so too did my interaction with her arise at that time. (36)
To the question of how there could have been a conventional interaction such as questioning with her, given that you are bodiless, he says: "The convention... (verse 36).
Just as worldly activity is like a dream and is indeed empty space itself,
so too should you know this— me, the self, and the world— to be empty space.
He says that even my current dealings with you are exactly like that: "Just as... (verse 37).
Just as the form of the world in a dream is nothing but space, so too is this world;
for that which is a dream at the beginning of waking is the emergence of the world at the beginning of creation. (38)
To the question, "How then is there a difference in names such as 'dream' and 'the world'?", he says: "In the waking state and so forth," [verse 38].
This expansive manifestation of the world is a dream, or perhaps nothing at all, being merely the pure sky of consciousness; thus it is established as pure Being alone.
This hatred for the world is merely a dream of one's own self, or perhaps it is nothing at all.
The dream has a perceiver who possesses form, such as yourself and others;
however, the perceiver of the dream of creation is the stainless sky of consciousness itself, by its very nature. (40)
Alternatively, with the intention that some distinction can also be stated, he says: "Of the dream," etc.
It possesses form by way of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of "you" and so forth. || 40 ||

Just as the seer perceives the stainless sky, so too has the visible world become that very same thing; within this world, which is essentially like a dream, the stainless space is manifest as the world itself. (41)
The vision that exists within the interval between the seer and the seen is likewise just like space.
The dream that flashes forth spontaneously within the heart from the formless sky of consciousness—whence could there be a creation for it, and how could it possess form? (42)
For that dream which manifests, whence could there be creation or birth? And how could there be any form for this world, which is like the son of a barren woman? (42)
That dream-world which belongs to that which possesses form is but a pure void;
how then could the creation of the formless sky of consciousness not be a void? 43.

The meaning is: if even the world of dreams—which is unreal—is well-known to be such for you and others who possess form, then what need is there to say that the creation which is like a dream is likewise [unreal] for Brahman, who is formless? || 43 ||
Without any accumulation of material causes and upon no foundation at all, one perceives this world as a mental sky—an uncreated dream, yet appearing as if created. (44)
Although the pavilion of creation, with its windows of the senses, was fashioned by the Brahmin Brahmā in the void using the soft clay of the sky of consciousness, it was not truly created. 45.

Although the pavilion of the creation of the body and so forth was constructed by the Brahmin named Hiraṇyagarbha—wherein the senses themselves served as the lattice-windows—it was as if it had never been built at all. || 45 ||

There is no agency, nor are there worlds, nor is there any enjoyership; "it exists" does not apply, nor does "it does not exist," for nothing at all [remains] beyond this. Being wise, adopt the silence of a stone and practice conduct according to the natural flow of events—let the body remain here or let it not.
Therefore, through the cleansing of all that is seen, the wise one remains as the ultimate reality, being merely its witness. Thus, O Rāma!

Maintaining the silence of a stone within, perform your outward conduct according to the flow of worldly custom. In this regard, let your body remain as long as the residue of past karma (*prārabdha*) persists; beyond that, whether it exists or not makes no difference—this is the meaning. || 46 ||

Thus ends the sixty-second chapter, titled "The Unity of Consciousness," in the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa* of the *Mokṣopāya* section of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, in the *Uttara-pāśava* [portion]. 62.

Thus ends the sixty-second chapter, titled "The Unity of Consciousness," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the glorious Vāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa, in its elucidation of the essential meaning. || 62 ||
The sixty-third canto.
Śrī Rāma said:
How did it happen that she came to possess a body in the form of a woman?
How are the phonemes *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, and so forth, articulated therein? (1)
Within the non-knowing side, there exist within it infinite riches of creation;
yet in the side of the knower of Brahman, Brahman alone is proclaimed as a single mass of consciousness.

Although the activity of one who is bodiless— such as conversation and so forth— has already been established by the analogy of dream-activity, Rāma asks again, "Of you," for the sake of clear understanding by those of dull intellect: "O Sage, [was there] with that aforementioned woman of yours, who was not your true form (asvarūpa), being devoid of physical parts such as face and tongue, and consisting merely of latent impressions (vāsanā)?"
How did worldly discourse proceed with that body? In that state, how were the phonemes *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, *pa*, and so forth, uttered by you without a tongue? (1)
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: The letters of one's own body, such as ka, ca, ṭa, ta, and so forth, never arise at all within the [other] castes, just as [the characteristics of] corpses do not arise in anyone.

In the conventional activity of pronouncing phonemes and so forth, the body is not the cause, because such activity is not observed even when a corpse is present, and because it is observed even without a body during dreams; thus, there is a deviation from the rule of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Furthermore, if this activity were to have a [physical] cause, it would follow that the activity is real. Rather, it is mere conceptual construction (*kalpanāmātra*). And since that [conceptual construction] is easily available even then, Vasiṣṭha [says... with this intention.

He states the answer with the words beginning "In the phonemes" (varṇeṣu): according to the view of those knowers of reality for whom space alone is the body, those [phonemes] such as ka, ca, ṭa, ta, pa, and so forth, never arise at all;
the meaning is that they consist of mere conceptual construction. || 2 ||
If the pronunciation of the syllables had possessed a manifest meaning, then someone standing nearby, awake, would have experienced it within their dreams. (3)

Regarding the point already stated, he presents a reasoning (tarka) that is favorable to the [proponent's] position and unfavorable to the opposing position, beginning with the words "in the utterance of syllables" (varṇoccāre).

"Manifest meaning" (prakaṭārthaḥ) refers to the ultimate reality (paramārthaḥ). The reasoning is as follows: if the utterance of syllables in a dream were an ultimate reality, then it would be within the range of experience for a nearby listener to hear it. || 3 ||
Therefore, nothing in dreams is real; it is merely an illusion.
That manifestation of the space of pure consciousness is likewise produced by its own nature within the void.
That which is born of its own nature is not produced by the power of the nature of sleep. || 4 ||

In that state, the spaces of consciousness appear as if they have attained the nature of the moon, blackness, the void, the body, a stone, a song, and so forth; likewise, the body, sounds, and other phenomena appear in such a manner.
When this is so, what then [is the case]? He says: "At that time" (*tadā*).

At that time, just as the sky-space delimited by those objects—which have attained the status of illusory entities such as the blackness of the moon superimposed by one with cataracts, or the singing performed by stones possessing the form of space—[appears as real], so it is here.

The meaning is that it is established that even the dream-body, sounds, and so forth, are merely the space of consciousness (cidākāśa) as conditioned by the respective latent impressions (saṃskāra) of the awakened state, appearing in such a manner. || 5 ||
Know that what is called the manifestation of the space of consciousness during the experience of a dream is indeed space itself;
it is the manifestation of the ether, and nothing else.

"Let those very spaces of consciousness appear in that manner; what of it? To this he says: "That. Just as the manifestation of the sky in the form of material objects is nothing other than the sky itself, so too, know that which is commonly known as the world-form in the experience of a dream—the manifestation of that space of consciousness—is indeed the space of consciousness alone. (6)
Just as a dream is, so too is this waking state established before one;
just as space is non-space, so too is this [waking state].

Having thus established that the objects of a dream consist of nothing but the space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*), he says "just as" to show that, by virtue of that very same analogy, the objects standing before one and those perceived during meditative absorption (*samādhi*) likewise consist of nothing but the space of consciousness: "Just as...
That which was seen in meditative absorption. (7)
Just as that beautiful consciousness shines forth with such cleverness,
so too does it remain exactly as it is— this very reality, throbbing as if firm and stable.
And thus, he says "tathā" (so it is), meaning that all this is merely the wondrous manifestation of Consciousness itself, and there is not even an atom of anything that is insentient in nature.
The syntactical connection is as follows: "In such a way that this world flashes forth as if real and as if stable, so does that sentient Brahman abide with skill. (8)
Śrī Rāma said:
O Blessed One, how is it that this very dream has become the waking state? How can that which is unreal have attained the appearance of reality?

Rāma raises an objection, saying "O Blessed One," [arguing that] it is improper for the waking world, which is accessible through the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), to be equal to the dream state, which is inaccessible to them: "How could that which is truly unreal attain the status of reality—the state of being cognizable by the eyes and other senses? How could such a thing be possible? (9)
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Listen to how the worlds exist entirely as mere dreams;
they are not otherwise, nor are they real, nor do they abide with stability.

Granted that [the world] may initially appear as something accessible to the eyes and other senses; nevertheless, because it cannot withstand ultimate scrutiny and because it is unstable, it is indeed equal to a dream. With this intention, he provides the answer beginning with "Listen" (*śṛṇu*): like a dream, these [objects] are neither different from the Self nor are they real and stable like the Self; rather, being truly indefinable (*anirvacanīya*), they exist solely by virtue of the existence of the Self.
This is the meaning. || 10 ||
Experienced seeds are like a mass of seeds in the sky;
they are various and distinct, being both the same and not the same.

Thus, because they exist as mutual seeds and because they possess a nature that is a composite of contradictory difference and non-difference, he states their similarity to a dream: "Those experienced... (verse 11).
Likewise, many other various intermediate [worlds] have arisen individually, each unseen by the others. (12)

He states that they are indeed equal to a dream because of their falsity, which arises from the experience of them existing in an infinite succession between one another, like the arrangement of the layers of a plantain tree—this is expressed by the word "pratyekam" (each individually).
Furthermore, he says it is so because they are not perceived as distinct from one another, like a dream—this is expressed by the word "parasparam" (mutually). || 12 ||
All of them do not perceive anything at all of one another;
like inert masses, they even dissolve away like seeds.
He establishes that very point with the words "mutually": "Like seeds situated in a granary, they even waste away within. (13)
Because their nature is like space, they do not perceive one another;
though they possess the form of consciousness, they remain as if in a continuous state of sleep.

Even though they have dissolved, those entities remain in the form of consciousness; thus, unlike drops of water fallen upon a heated potsherd which, having attained the nature of the sky, become as if void, nor like ourselves who perceive and see one another, they—because their conscious nature is veiled by ignorance—remain as if in a continuous sleep and experience only a dream. This is the meaning. || 14 ||
Those who are asleep engage in the activities of the web of the dream-world during the day;
the asuras were slain by the gods while they remained within that dream-world. (15)

In this regard, he asserts that living beings who have fallen asleep, having encountered the web of the dream-world, become engaged in all worldly activities within that very imagined day— thus [he says], "those who have slept. Intending to prove this asserted point by means of a residue-inference (*pariśeṣānumāna*), since there is no other possible state for Asuras, humans, Rākṣasas, and others who are struck down in dreams, he first [examines] the case among the Asuras.
He shows this with the verse beginning "The Asuras," together with the following half-verse. || 15 ||
They have not attained liberation due to ignorance, nor have they reached a state of dullness due to inertia;
yet, being devoid of the existence of a dream-world, how can they be considered possessed of bodies? 16.

The Asuras and Daityas, having been slain by the gods during their sleep, remained within the very world of their own dream; for, due to the absence of knowledge, they did not attain liberation, nor did they fall into a state of insentience such as that of stones, nor did they become possessed of physical bodies. The meaning is: what else could they be, other than existing within the state of a dream-world? || 16 ||
Men who engage in their own customary conduct while asleep within the web of the dream-world are slain by other men, yet they remain situated exactly as they were. (17)
In this same way, men and humans also engage in worldly activity through their latent impressions (vāsanās) within the web of the world that is their own dream;
and when they are slain therein by other persons, they likewise remain situated within that very succession of dreams, just like the asuras previously described. (17)
Being devoid of liberation and lacking a body, yet possessed of consciousness and latent impressions, where else could they dwell if not within the perceived web of the dream-world? (18)

Since they too, due to the absence of knowledge, are without liberation and without bodies, they are incapable of waking; yet, being by nature disposed toward worldly activity through latent impressions (*vāsanā*), where else could such beings dwell apart from the web of the dream-world? The meaning is that for them, there is no other resort. || 18 ||
Those Rākṣasas who were slain by the gods while they were asleep, moving within the established conventions of the web of the dream-world, remained exactly as they had been situated.
With the intention that this principle demonstrated regarding the Asuras and humans should also be applied to the Rākṣasas and others, he says in two verses beginning with "suptāḥ" (19).
"O Rāma, tell me, what do those who have been thus slain do? If it is because of ignorance that they did not attain liberation, then why do they not remain as insentient stones? (20)
All this visible world, including the mountains, oceans, earth, and people, remains exactly as it is;
these beings experience it for a long time, just as we do with due respect.

He states that because their respective dreams persist for a long duration and are similar to our own experience, they become nothing other than the waking state itself: "The arrangement of the world and the eon for them is exactly as it is for us, and the arrangement of the world for us is exactly as it is for them. (22)
These very dream-men are we who stand here;
and those which are called "saṃsāras," they know this one alone among them. (23)

And thus, if the world as we experience it and we ourselves who are within it were seen by them, then our waking state would become their dream, and we would become their dream-people; so he says: "Of these... (verse 23).
Those dream-people are indeed real from the perspective of experience,
because the conscious self (cidātman) is all-pervading, whether it be one's own or that of another.

The meaning is that because the experience of oneself and that of another person are equal, their existence is indeed real; this is due to the equality of the conscious Self (cit-ātman), which is the substratum for the cause of that existence, by virtue of its omnipresence. || 24 ||
