Just as those dream-men are real within themselves, so too are others;
nevertheless, those dream-men are indeed real, and they are exactly like that.

The word *api* (also/even) is displaced [in the sentence]. Just as those dream-men are real, so too are the other men experienced by me in each respective dream; they are indeed real. In that same manner, you too should understand those dream-men. || 25 ||
Those citizens of your respective dream-cities whom you saw remain there even today in that very same way, because Brahman is the self of all.
For even upon awakening, dream-states are perceived as distinct according to how they existed;
likewise, they are experienced through their mode of existence either as the supreme Brahman or otherwise.

Just as those various dream-states are experienced as being broken apart and dissolved upon awakening—that is, upon waking—likewise, at the time of the dream, they are experienced precisely as persisting through their duration. And thus, just like their sublation, their existence also gains the force of experience and cannot be denied; this is the meaning. Alternatively, [it refers] to the very existence of Brahman.
With the intention that because it constitutes the very self of all beings, the existence of anything can never be denied, he says:
"as the Supreme Brahman. || 27 ||
Everything exists everywhere, at all times, as the self of all, just as in the case of others; for there is nothing that is not space, nor is it ever destroyed anywhere.
And thus, he says "all" to show that what was previously promised has been fulfilled:
just as the entire world, being an effect of space, is indeed space itself, and therefore nothing whatsoever is ever destroyed by it in its form,
so too within the Supreme Space— which is Brahman, devoid of beginning, empty of origin, continuous in the middle, and endless at the end— one is first delighted.

Therein, within infinite and incalculable aggregates of mind; therein, within those incalculable multitudes of worlds; therein, for every space; therein, for every cycle of saṃsāra; therein, for every world such as Bhūrloka and the rest; therein, for every continent; therein, for every mountain; therein, for every extent of every region; therein, for every village and every city; and therein, for every house.
Even there, for every individual being and throughout the time of each successive age and so forth, as many souls as have died—deprived of liberation—remain;
that many distinct and inexhaustible cycles of transmigration (saṃsāra) exist. Thus, these five [categories] share a single underlying connection.
In the boundless supreme space, in the boundless play, in the boundless mass of consciousness, and in the boundless multitude of worlds. || 29 ||

Corresponding to the treasury of every portion of space, corresponding to every circle of saṃsāra, corresponding to the form of every intermediate world, and corresponding to every island and mountain.
In every mandala, in every village, in every city; for every living being, in every house, in every year, and in every age. || 31 ||
However many living beings there may be who have died, being devoid of liberation, for that many separate and inexhaustible cycles of existence (saṃsāra) remain there. || 32 ||
They have their inner selves directed toward people; their minds are again directed toward the mind; the world is directed toward the world; and people are again directed toward people. (33)
With the intention that even by such a number there would be no rest for the number of worlds, and thus instability itself is the ornament of Māyā, he says "teṣām" and so forth. || 33 ||
Thus, this delusion consisting of the visible world is without beginning or end;
for one who knows Brahman, it is Brahman alone, and herein there is no limitation whatsoever.
Since pure consciousness alone exists within the wall, the sky, the stone, the water, and the earth—indeed, that is the entirety of this universe—wherever that [consciousness] is, there the world is;
so what counting can there be here? For those who know it, that supreme reality is all, whereas for the minds of the ignorant, it is merely the visible world.

O Rāma, whether in a wall, in the sky, in a clod of earth, in stone, in water, or on land—since nothing exists apart from pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), that alone is the entire universe; there is no other entity called "the world. That being so, because consciousness is omnipresent, the world exists everywhere, wherever one may be. In this world, how can there be any number? And that universe, for those who know it, is supreme and devoid of all distinctions.

Brahman alone is the singular essence of unsurpassed bliss. The word *atha* signifies the meaning of the word *tu* (but). For the ignorant, that very [Brahman] appears in their minds as the phenomenal world of objects (*dṛśyaprapañca*)—that is to say, in the form of misfortune. Thus says the Śruti: "In that very [Brahman], fear exists for the one who knows it but does not contemplate it. (35)

Thus ends the sixty-third canto, titled "The Exposition of the Unity of the Reality of the World," in the Uttara-pāda of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the glorious Vāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa of Valmīki, composed by the Sage.
Thus ends the sixty-third chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Unity of the Reality of the World," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The sixty-fourth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Then, she whose eyes were like garlands of *mālatī* flowers blooming with blue water-lilies (*kuvalaya*)—[the reading *kuvalayollāsi* is more easily explained].

Since there is also a word *kuvala* as a synonym for *kuvalaya*, it remains perfectly consistent even in its original form. Having gazed upon the charming woman, she was addressed by me with playful ease. (1)
For here, having been questioned by Vasiṣṭha, the Vidyādharī related in detail her birth in her own home, her past actions, and so forth, up to the end of the Vedas.

Having resolved this incidental question, Śrī Vasiṣṭha speaks the remainder of the narrative begun, starting with the words "Then" (*tataḥ*). "I beheld that woman whose eyes were like blooming blue lotuses (*kuvalaya*) and who spread forth like garlands of jasmine (*mālatīmālya*) through her playful side-glances; she was addressed by me with sportiveness and curiosity—that is, she was conversed with—and questioned."
Who are you, O lady with the luster of the interior of a lotus, and for what purpose have you come to me?
To whom do you belong, what do you seek, where have you come from, and what is your abode? (2)
"Whose daughter or whose wife are you?"—this is the remainder [of the question]. "What is her abode? means what is her place of residence. || 2 ||
The Vidyādharī said:
O sage, listen as I relate my own story exactly as it happened; you ought to question me with confidence, for I am distressed and a seeker of compassion. (3)

"Her own account" means her personal narrative. He dispels the suspicion that conversing with another's wife in private might be improper by saying "to ask. The syntactical connection is: "You ought to ask me, who am distressed and seeking a means to alleviate my suffering, with confidence out of compassion. And so it is said:
The meaning is that it is entirely appropriate for the virtuous to offer consolation to those in distress. || 3 ||
In some corner-cavity of the treasury of the supreme ether, this house of the world of yours is situated for the time being. (4)
Therein, he begins to state his own position first with the words "paramākāśa" and so forth. Regarding the phrase "in a certain [place]":
the intention is that this is based on such scriptural passages as, "All beings are but one foot of Him. || 4 ||
The netherworld, the earth, and heaven are here these three chambers;
a single maiden was fashioned here by the creative power of the Ordainer.

Here, in this house of yours, the world, the inner chambers are the private rooms within the dwelling. In these chambers, the state of being the Creator (dhātṛtva)—that is, the nature of Hiraṇyagarbha—is a single maiden known as the "imagination of the variety of creation" through the illusion (māyā) that takes that form; she has been fashioned for the sake of play. This is the meaning. || 5 ||
There, the surface of the earth— arisen from the *pāṭala* stone— is encircled by continents and oceans like bracelets,
appearing as if it were the forearm of the Goddess of the World’s Fortune.
Because it is encircled by continents and oceans as if by bracelets, it is therefore pale-red with their colors;
thus, it stands like the raised and elevated forearm—the base of the hand—of the Goddess of the World’s Fortune. This is the meaning. || 6 ||
Beyond the continents and oceans, situated in every direction,
there is a ground made of gold extending for ten thousand yojanas.
At the end of the seven continents and oceans, extending in every direction all around—that is to say, ten thousand yojanas in circumference and length. (7)
Self-luminous, bestowing the fruits of one's intentions, as pure as the sky,
composed of wish-fulfilling gems, and transparent, her own radiance surpasses that of the entire world.

He describes that earth with the words beginning with "svayam": it is self-luminous (*svayaṃprakāśā*), shining by itself even at night; it bestows the fruits of all desires through mere volition (*saṃkalpa*); it is as stainless as the sky; it abounds with *cintāmaṇi* gems; it is pure and free from dust; and by its own splendor, it has surpassed the worlds such as heaven. || 8 ||
It was a ground for the playful excursions of Apsarases, Maruts, and Siddhas,
beautiful with every enjoyment brought to perfection by mere thought.

That ground is fit for the playful excursions of Apsarases, immortals, and Siddhas— or rather, "that" and "ground" may be read as separate words. At the edge of that earth lies the world-renowned mountain Lokāloka,
bearing the appearance of a bracelet encircling the forearm of the terrestrial sphere.
On the outer edge, it stands encircling like a bracelet the surface of the earth, which is characterized as the forearm of the world’s Fortune.
In one place it is eternally pervaded by darkness, like the disposition of one with a deluded intellect;
in another place it is eternally of the nature of light, like the mind of those possessed of purity (sattva).
He describes that mountain with the words beginning "In some places" (kvacid), etc. || 11 ||
In some places it produces delight, like the company of the virtuous; in other places it produces distress, like association with fools. || 12 ||
In some places it reveals all its meanings clearly, like the mind of the wise; in others it is exceedingly profound and obscure, like the mind of a foolish Vedic scholar.
In some places it did not receive the rays of the moon; in some places it did not receive the light of the sun;
in some places it was filled with people by him, and in some places the horizons were suddenly empty.
"Consisting of the world" means abounding with people; however, in some places, its horizons are not empty of that world in their outer regions. (14)
In some places it was pervaded by the cities of the gods; in some places it was filled with the cities of the Daityas;
in some places it was as deep as the netherworld (Pātāla); and in some places its peaks rose high like necks.
It is as deep and difficult to enter as the netherworld (pātāla). || 15 ||
In some places vultures wandered in its chasms; in others it was enchanting with its peaks;
and in some parts, the interior of Brahmā’s city was reached by the summits of its ridges.
"With the tips of its peaks treading upon the interior of Brahmā’s city"—this is an exaggeration (atiśayokti) regarding the excellence of its height. || 16 ||
In one place, the winds of the end of the eon blew through vast empty forests; in another, hosts of Vidyādharīs sang amidst flower garden groves.
In some places it was terrifying with kumbhāṇḍas in caves as deep as the netherworld (pātāla);
in other places it was delightful with hermitages of sages, like the Nandana grove.
In caves as deep as the underworld, he was terrifying with various kinds of *kumbhāṇḍas* and *piśācas*.

In some places it was filled with clouds intoxicated by inexhaustible rain; in others, the clouds were difficult to find; and in other areas, its borders were dense with mountain caves, chasms, and thickets.
In which [place] there are inexhaustible [waters] ever-present, like roaring clouds intoxicated [with rain].
In some places, the earth was shaken by the agitation of the people;
in other places, the inhabitants surpassed the heavens through their innate goodness.

In which [city] the ground of the spirits—the abodes of *rakṣasas*, *piśācas*, and others—was utterly cleared away by the thrusts of swords, axes, and other weapons from people agitated and shaken by the turmoil of the countryside;
and by the benevolence of the multitude of its inhabitants, it surpassed the celestial realm (*triviṣṭapa*). || 20 ||
In some places, the mobile and immobile beings born from the flowing current are eternal;
in other places, the mobile and immobile beings are stable and liberated from all destruction.
Where the stationary and moving beings are born and manifested by winds that blow constantly and incessantly;

where they are entirely freed from all forms of decay arising from the various causes such as poison, weapons, fire, and disease; and for that very reason, where the stationary and moving beings remain stable for a long time. (21)
In some places it was terrifying with the whistling sounds released by the winds of the great desert; in other places it was adorned by the warbling of intoxicated cranes amidst the lotus ponds.
In some places it resounded with the gurgling of clouds amidst the surging waves of water; in other places it aroused the god of love through the playful swinging of intoxicated apsarases.
In some places its horizons were rendered motionless by being surrounded by piśācas and kumbhāṇḍas;
in other places its riverbanks resounded with the songs and dances of vidyādharīs and siddhas.
Its horizons were surrounded by Piśācas and Kumbhāṇḍas, and for that very reason appeared as if motionless. || 24 ||
In some places, its banks were washed by rivers flowing from clouds that were raining down;
in other places, it was adorned with various excellent cloths in the form of clouds constantly driven hither and thither by the winds.
With its banks tumbling and its embankments crumbling as it was struck by the arms of raining clouds—those very arms characterized by their river-like forms—it lay shattered. || 25 ||

In one place, his circle of meditation was situated within the interior of a lotus bud; in another, he served as the jeweled ornament for the teeth of the celestial nymphs and the beautiful wives of the Siddhas.

Where the circle of lotus plants (*sarojinī-maṇḍala*) has begun its meditation by means of the bee-eyes situated upon the mouths characterized as the buds of the *kamalinī* flowers; and which is so called because it adorns the teeth of the celestial nymphs (*apsaras*), the perfected beauties (*siddha-sundarī*), with betel—meaning, it is adorned with groves of betel vines (*nāgavallī*). || 26 ||
In some places it was beautiful with the conduct of people whose hands were like rays of heat;
in other places, intoxicated night-stalkers danced within the houses of the darkness of night.
In some places the earth was losing its people due to rising portents,
while in other places circles of cities were flourishing through the excellence of good governance.
In some places it was utterly empty, in others filled with inhabited regions;
in some places it was deep with interior chasms, and in others terrifying like the netherworld (Pātāla). || 29 ||
It was empty yet truly void; deep with water-filled chasms, yet terrifying as the netherworld (pātāla) where it was dry.

In some places there were great wish-fulfilling trees (kalpataru), in others moving creatures devoid of water; in some places there were herds of great elephants, and in others swarms of intoxicated lions.
In which there were intoxicated herds of lions, monkeys, and other such creatures.
In some places it was devoid of beings, in others it was filled with frantic rākṣasas;
in some places there were thickets of karañja trees, and in others great forests of palm trees.
He set out in such a way that the place became devoid of any collection of living beings; that is to say, his rising was in vain. || 31 ||

In some places it has lakes resembling the sky; in some places it is a vast expanse of desert; in some places there is dust constantly swirling; and in some places there are forests that flourish in all seasons.
In which [world] there are lakes comparable to the sky due to their purity, vastness, and other qualities; and in which there are forests where all the seasons are likewise present.
Upon its peaks are rocks resembling those of an ordinary mountain;
they are like well-established clouds, composed of jewels, and as pure as the sky.

Upon the peaks of that Lokāloka mountain, whose form has been described, there are common mountains such as Sahya, Malaya, and others, as well as rocks resembling them, all composed of jewels. || 33 ||
In these [cities], monkeys born from the lineage of Hari rest incessantly, like lions dwelling in forest thickets that are as white as the Milky Ocean, water, or the moon.

Like milk, like water, and like the sun, these are the origins—the causal sources—of other monkeys, including their sons and grandsons, upon the surfaces of those white, fair-colored rocks which are like the trunks of great forest trees inhabited by forest-dwellers; there the monkeys, lions, apes, and others rest. 34.
To the north of them, within the hollow of the eastern peak-rock,
I dwell upon a surface whose skin is equal to the indestructible essence of diamond.

"Among those rocks, on the northern side of that mountain, within the belly of that rock which belongs to the peak situated in the eastern direction, I dwell"—this is the answer to the question, "What is my abode? (35).
Bound there by fate, I dwell within this stone mechanism;
O Sage, I believe countless multitudes of ages have passed for me here.
Not only am I bound, but my husband there is also bound, just as a bee is caught within a lotus bud at evening. (37)
He begins to provide the answer to the questions starting with "Whose [son] were you? with the words "Not only... and so forth. || 37 ||
Together with that husband of mine, in the confinement of a rock-cavern,
many years have passed here over a long period of time.
"Even now, due solely to the fault of the self, we do not attain liberation;
we remain for a long time in that very place, with our dispositions still bound. (39)
Desire is the one fault; by it, the two—namely, mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and possessiveness (*mamatā*)—are bound. (39)
In that narrow space among the rocks, not only were the two of us bound,
but our entire retinue was likewise imprisoned there.
"Retinue" refers to the circle of attendants such as sons, grandsons, and servants; "nau" means "of us two. || 40 ||
"There dwells my husband, a twice-born ancient person who is bound;
though living, he does not move from that single spot for hundreds of ages. (41)
This husband of mine, though living for hundreds of yugas, does not move from his single spot nor does he rise from his own seat. || 41 ||
A celibate from childhood, learned in the Vedas, a reciter of scripture, yet free from indolence;
he dwells alone in solitude, straightforward in conduct and without fickleness. (42)

He is devoted to the three Vedas and habituated to the study of his own sacred texts; for this very reason, he is also a reciter of other [scriptures]. He is straightforward, possessing an honest livelihood, and free from fickleness, being devoid of sensory restlessness. || 42 ||
"O best among the knowers of the Vedas, I am his wife, fallen into distress;
without him, I am not capable of sustaining this body for even the blink of an eye. (43)
But he himself says that it is not so: "I" (aham). || 43 ||
Listen, O Brahmin, how I was obtained as his wife by him, and how this natural affection between us has grown to such an extent. (44)
*asmākam* means "of us" or "of the two of us. According to the rule *asmado dvayośca*, the plural ending is used [even when referring to two]. || 44 ||
Formerly, by that son born to me, my husband— who was still but a child,
possessed of only limited knowledge, and dwelling alone in his own pure abode— [this was accomplished].
He describes the manner of his own birth with the words "by him" (tena). || 45 ||
Having deliberated for a long time, he resolved: "From where can a wife worthy of my status as a Vedic scholar and endowed with noble birth arise? (46)
O lotus-eyed one, I, whose limbs are themselves faultless, have been brought forth by that Lord as if I were the stainless moonlight produced by the moon. (47)
Through my mind, I became the mental wife of Mandara, most beautiful of women;
from that, I grew like a flower-cluster in the springtime.
Clothed in her innate garment, she captivates the hearts of all beings;
with a face like the orb of the full moon, she is like the sky filled with pure stars. (49)
He describes his own [nature] with the words beginning "sahaja" (innate), etc. || 49 ||
With breasts as high as flower buds and endowed with every excellence, she was like a forest of choice creepers graced with sprout-like hands. (50)
They are called *rasas* because they are tasted (*rasyante*); she is *śālinī* by virtue of those qualities (*guṇas*). || 50 ||
She eternally captivates the hearts of all living beings; with eyes as dark and large as those of a doe, she bestows the intoxication of passion. (51)
She whose long eyes are like those of a doe. || 51 ||
She delights solely in playful pastimes, her eyes rolling with amorous sport;
she is ever fond of song and instrumental music, and insatiable in her passion.
He explains what was stated as "addicted" with the words beginning "līlā" and so forth; the meaning is that she is not satiated by enjoyments. || 52 ||
Supreme in the enjoyment of good fortune, she is the dear friend of both Lakṣmī and Alakṣmī;
she is inseparable from the nets of delusion and remains untroubled by both prosperity and adversity.
Because both fortune and misfortune consist of the mental constructs of her husband who perceives all things with equanimity, she views them with equanimity like a dear friend.
For this very reason, though not distinct from the nets of delusion, she remains undaunted by prosperity or adversity.
O dear one, it is not only the house of this twice-born man that I support;
indeed, I sustain this entire abode of the three worlds.
He states that because the husband consists of mind alone, even the sustaining of the three worlds imagined by him is dependent on me alone: "Not only... (verse 54).
I am a wife who brings honor to my family, capable of supporting a household; I alone bear the singular burden of maintaining the furnishings of the house that is the three worlds.
She is a lineage-maker, capable of producing a succession of sons and grandsons; she is a wife, and she is competent to support the circle of dependents. (55)
Then I became a young woman, with full and prominent breasts, radiant with the essence of grace like a flowering cluster on a swaying creeper. (56)
With clusters of flowers leaping up and bunches of blossoming fruits shining, she was like a creeping vine. || 56 ||
"Because of his prolixity, his status as a Vedic scholar, and his devotion to asceticism, my husband has not yet married me even today, out of some particular consideration. (57)

Although I possess such qualities and characteristics as these, that Brahmin husband did not marry me because of his procrastination— his inherent nature of being slow to act— due to some expectation of liberation which will be described hereafter. || 57 ||
Therefore, though I am endowed with youth and possessed of the essence of graceful charm, I burn with grief in his absence like a lotus plant in fire. (58)

To the question, "How can you be his wife if there was no marriage? she replies with the words *tena* (by him). The meaning is: "I chose him as my husband solely by my own desire; I am one who possesses that *rasa*—the longing for the objects of sensual enjoyment—which has been fulfilled through union with him during my youth. || 58 ||
Amidst the lotus ponds constantly stirred by cool breezes, he experiences a burning sensation in his limbs as if they were upon a bed of glowing embers. (59)
Like ground upon which glowing embers have been swept clean by the clearing of ashes. || 59 ||
All the gardens and groves are filled with showers of flowers;
even the desert lands, which were once barren sands, have become fertile.
The desert lands became such that they consisted of heated sands. || 60 ||
The lakes, tender with ripples of water and clusters of white and red lotuses,
though full of the sweet cries of cranes, have become tasteless to me.
Soft and pleasant to the touch due to the abundance of *kahlāra* flowers—a species of lotus—as well as *kamala* lotuses. || 61 ||
Though garlanded with clusters of lotuses, mandārakas, and kumudas, I experience intense burning as if tossed upon thorns.
To soothe her burning fever, she was adorned by her friends with heaps of lotus and other flowers, and as they fashioned swings and beds for her, she seemed to be swayed and rolled about.
The beds of white water-lilies, blue lotuses, white esculent lilies, and plantain trees, which rustled in the summer heat, are reduced to ashes through contact with my body. (63)
Due to the cause of contact with their limbs, [the leaves] are first dried up by the heat of the summer's scorching sun, becoming rustling (marmara), and thereafter they turn to ashes. || 63 ||
Whenever I behold that which is lovely, appropriate, sweet, diverse, and captivating to the mind, my long eyes become filled with tears within.
Dripping with teardrops scorched by the fire of calamity,
they fall and sink with a "chamaccham" sound into rows of lotuses and water-lilies.

The term *chamacchamīti* is used to indicate a resemblance to the sound produced by the falling of drops of oil along with the flames of a lamp as they fall; [this is formed] according to the rule *avyaktānukaraṇasyāta itau*, whereby the latter member of the sound-imitation takes the form of the following word (*pararūpa*). It should be understood that the prohibition [of this rule] stated in *nāmneḍitasyāntyasya tu vā* does not apply here because it pertains to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*). They "sink," meaning they enter within by means of their own heat (*svoṣman*).
They cause the lotuses and water-lilies to wither instantly, while they themselves also wither; such is the meaning. || 65 ||
In the cherished garden groves, by the playful swinging upon the trunks of plantain and kandalī trees, I cover my face and weep.

In the garden groves, while being fondled by my friends on swings made of fresh sprouts hung from the trunks of plantain and kandalī trees, I am unable to tell them of my own sorrow; instead, hiding my face out of shame, I weep. 66.
I see a pavilion of plantain leaves strewn with heaps of frost, casting off its heat and appearing as terrifying as embers of khadira wood.
Beholding the female crane, who rests upon a male crane amidst the swings of lotus stalks, I look upon her with a dejected face and inwardly reproach my own youth.
She was supported by her husband, the Sārasa crane, and remained united with him. || 68 ||
I weep when an object is pleasant, I become indifferent toward one that is neutral, and I rejoice over one that is unattractive; being thus distressed, I do not know what state I am in. (69)
I rejoice when there is that which is unwholesome, such as fainting or a state of stupor, because at that time I do not know what I am doing;
likewise, when the sense of "I" (ahantā) dissolves, I find rest because the suffering associated with it is no longer experienced—this is the meaning. || 69 ||
I have seen the kunda, mandāra, and kumuda flowers, as well as the snows,
scattered in every direction like the ashes of those consumed by the fire of passion.
"Towards every direction" means toward each individual quarter. The absence of reduplication in this compound is a Vedic archaism. || 70 ||

My days of fresh youth have passed in vain as I dried up my bed of dark-blue sprouts, lotus stalks, blue lotuses, white water-lilies, jasmine, plantain leaves, and *mālatī* flowers by the movement of my limbs.
(71) [Of] the dark-blue sprouts of the *tamāla* and other trees, of the lotus stalks, of the blue lotuses, and likewise of the white water-lilies and so forth...
And as I dried my bedsheets through the movement of my limbs and contact with my body, the days of my fresh youth have passed in vain. || 71 ||

Thus ends the sixty-fourth canto, titled "The Description of the Vidyādharī’s Misfortune," in the *Uttara-pāda* of the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa*, within the *Vāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa*, a work of the Sage (*ārṣa*). Volume 1, Part 2, Section on Liberation (*mokṣopāya*). Canto 64.
Thus ends the sixty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Vidyādharī’s Misfortune," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The sixty-fifth canto.
The Vidyādharī said:
Then, after a long time, that passion turned into dispassion.
It has come upon me like a bitter sprout at the end of autumn. || 1 ||
When her own passion had turned to dispassion with the arrival of the proper time, she,
having attained perfection through the practice of concentration (dhāraṇā), offered up her life-breath.
Just as a sprout, having become sapless at the end of autumn and the beginning of winter, attains a state of witheredness, so it is in this case. || 1 ||
My husband is old, living in solitude, devoid of passion, and lacking affection; he is straightforward-minded and silent. What do I think of my life? || 2 ||

He explains by means of the verse beginning with "vṛddha" what kind of sequence of reflection led him to attain detachment—the word "ajihmamatiḥ" meaning one whose mind is straightforward; the phrase "what is the fruit? is to be understood as the ellipsis. || 2 ||
Better is widowhood from childhood, better even is death,
better is disease or calamity, than a husband of an unpleasant nature.
This much is the fulfillment of life and unbroken good fortune:
that one’s husband is a youth, a connoisseur of aesthetic delight, and of graceful conduct. (4)
A woman is ruined who lacks a husband; the intellect is ruined that is not refined;
fortune is ruined when enjoyed by the wicked; and modesty is ruined when stolen by a prostitute.

If she is unrefined—devoid of the purificatory rites prescribed by the scriptures—and likewise if her modesty, which is appropriate for those of noble lineage and conduct, has been stolen away by harlots and unchaste women, then she is ruined. (5)
She is a true wife who follows her husband; she is true prosperity that follows the virtuous;
she is true fortitude that is sweet and noble; she is true goodness that possesses impartial vision.

That very intellect which is sweet through the perfection of tranquility, self-restraint, and so forth—that is wisdom (buddhi). Likewise, it follows that that alone is goodness (sādhutā) which consists in equanimity of vision. || 6 ||
Neither mental anxieties, nor physical ailments, nor calamities, nor misfortunes cause any affliction to the minds of a couple who are devoted to one another. (7)
Malignant calamities—excessive rain, drought, locusts, rats, birds, and kings who have drawn too near—these six are known as calamities. || 7 ||
The grounds of the Nandana gardens, with their blossoming flower-strewn meadows,
act like deserts for women who have lost their protectors and those whose lords are wicked.
They act like desert lands; that is to say, they cause torment. || 8 ||
All worldly states may be abandoned at will, even by a mere fraction of their qualities or through negligence; however, for a woman, her husband alone must never be forsaken.

For this very reason, he says "all indeed" to show that everything else is easily abandoned, whereas the husband alone is difficult to abandon: "All indeed... The things well-known in the world are houses, fields, kinsmen, wealth, and so forth. "On account of a mere fraction of quality" means due to a smallness of merit, or through negligence or lack of attention. The word "tu" (but) is placed out of its logical order; it means "except for the husband alone. || 9 ||
O leader of sages, behold the manifestation of misfortune: these sorrows have been endured by me, who possess eternal youth, for many thousands of years. (10)

The ellipsis "have been enjoyed by me" is to be supplied. In the word *varṣavṛndāni*, the accusative case is used according to the rule for expressing the complete connection (*atyantasaṃyoga*) between time and distance.
The ellipsis "is manifested by my misfortune" is to be supplied. || 10 ||
Then, in due course, my passion gradually turned into dispassion by that very [practice], becoming sapless like a lotus plant scorched by frost. (11)
Or rather, with the thought that "this is surely the dawning of my good fortune," he says, beginning with "atha": "Gradually becoming disenchanted, he attained detachment. (11)
Therefore, O Sage, through your instruction, I desire the extinction of my own self, which is the cessation of all attachment to worldly existences by means of the latent impression of dispassion.

Having attained the latent impressions of dispassion through the sequence described by him, I—who am thus characterized by a lack of attachment toward all things—now desire the liberation of my own self through your instruction. || 12 ||
For those who have not attained their desired goals, whose minds find no rest,
and who are being carried away by deaths, death is better than life.

Even at such a time, despite having obtained an instructor like you, my life is in vain because I do not desire rest; rather, death alone is better—with this intention he says "aprāpta" (not attained).
[He refers to] those being carried away by floods of deaths, that is, by streams of suffering equal to death. || 13 ||
Desiring liberation day and night, my husband, the king, strives to conquer his mind with his mind, as one king seeks to conquer another. (14)

He says in two verses beginning with "sa" [that] because women who practice the Dharma together possess conduct and propriety equal to that of their husbands, he will instruct me along with my husband: "Just as a king, with a royal ally, awakens to conquer a king— that is, becomes vigilant through the means taught in the treatises on statecraft— so too shall my husband [awaken] by means of his mind alone."
One awakens in order to conquer the mind; the meaning is that one remains vigilant regarding the means for solitude. || 14 ||
For the sake of pacifying the ignorance of that Brahman, my husband, and myself,
perform the remembrance of your own self through speech consistent with reason.
The recollection of the Self is like the awakening to a golden necklace forgotten around one's neck. (15)
When my husband remained indifferent toward me, disregarding me entirely, then his lack of passion brought a sense of distaste to my very existence in this world.

"Without regard for me," meaning having abandoned all consideration for me; "virāga" brought about a state of world-weariness, a lack of relish or tastelessness toward the condition of worldly existence. The transitive nature of the root *nī* (to lead) is well-established as taking two objects. || 16 ||
Therefore, having abandoned the influence of the latent impressions of saṃsāra,
I remained there after fixing my mind upon the intense dhāraṇā of moving through the sky as desired.
Now, with the intention that she possesses the qualification for instruction due to her mind being stabilized through the practice of *dhāraṇā*, he says:
"In saṃsāra... [verse 17]. This refers to the *dhāraṇā* known as Khecarīmudrā, which bestows the power of moving through the sky, as previously described.

Having thus acquired the power of movement in the sky through meditative concentration (dhāraṇā), I further practiced that concentration which yields the fruit of association with the perfected ones (siddhas). 18.
The "association with the Siddhas" refers to the discourse and other interactions with the Siddhas that bestow their fruits;
therefore, the sense is: "Having come to this secluded place, which is inaccessible even to others, I shall converse with you. (18)
Then, by observing the beginning and end of my own world-support,
I remained there having fixed my concentration (dhāraṇā), and she too attained perfection.

Having formed a meditative visualization (bhāvanā) in the form of my own world, my own abode, and the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa)—an entity composed of anterior and posterior parts—by beholding it as clearly as a myrobalan fruit in the palm of one's hand through the vision of the scriptures and the vision of yoga, she remained there.
Although she was common to all, she attained perfection for me through the process of conquering all beings within her constituent parts. (19)
Then, having seen his heart within my own world,
I, who had gone outside, beheld the massive rock of the Lokāloka mountain.

Having seen within my heart all things, I emerged outside it and beheld that stone of the Lokāloka mountain situated within this Brahmāṇḍa, which contains my own world as previously described. || 20 ||
O sage, even during all this time, we two, husband and wife,
never at any time had the slightest desire to see another.
But he says—“only this much”—that previously, at any time, this universe had never been seen by me or by my husband, because of the absence of that [divine] will. || 21 ||
"My husband, through his one-pointed contemplation solely on the pure meaning of the Vedas, knows neither what has passed nor what has come; oh, how he is free from all worldly desires! (22)

One who has understood the pure meaning of the Vedas, [yet] through one-pointed meditation on that [worldly object], does not know the past time—the time already gone—nor the future and present time yet to come, nor the objects contained therein, nor the reality of Brahman. || 22 ||
Therefore, although my husband was learned, he did not attain that state;
today, both he and I desire the supreme state through diligent effort.
By that revelation of reality; "today," meaning by the effort of hearing, reflecting upon, and so forth, your instruction, [the purpose is] to know the supreme state—this is the ellipsis. || 23 ||
Therefore, O Brahmin, you ought to make this request of mine fruitful;
for among the great, those who seek their aid never go empty-handed.
"In the presence of great beings such as yourself," [it is said]. "Those who are seekers" (arthinaḥ) are those desiring human goals (puruṣārtha).
The words *api* and *cana* are used here in the sense of "even. || 24 ||
O giver of honor, as I wander always in the sky among the hosts of Siddhas, I see nothing here but the forest fire of dense ignorance, except for you. (25)
To the question, "Why were other perfected beings (*siddhas*) not requested for this purpose?", he says: "Wandering" (*bhramantī*). || 25 ||
O Brahmin, since the virtuous fulfill the desires of those who seek their aid even without a cause such as compassion, you ought not to subject me—who have come to you for refuge—to rejection. (26)

Having thus related her entire life story and what she desired to know, and having sought refuge, she prays for herself not to be neglected, saying: "O Brahmin! For this reason—that the virtuous fulfill the desires of those who seek them even without being asked—therefore, [protect] me, who have come to you for refuge.
You ought not to yoke [this] by means of contempt and neglect; the sense is that for those who seek [help], neglect itself constitutes contempt.
Thus ends the sixty-fifth canto, titled "The Description of the Conduct and Birth of the Vidyādharī," in the *Nirvāṇa* section of the *Mokṣopāya*, within the *Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa*.
Thus ends the sixty-fifth canto, titled "The Description of the Life and Conduct of the Vidyādharī," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa-tātparya-prakāśa*.
The sixty-sixth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Then, having been thus addressed and questioned by me, she sat upon the prepared seat.
Seated upon the throne she had envisioned, she remained poised in the sky.
"How can there be stability in the airless space, or a house in the wind, or within a stone?"—
when asked thus, she then described the vast extent of the world therein.

She related her own history in the manner previously described, saying: "While I was situated in the sky above the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) as previously mentioned, and even there seated upon a mentally constructed throne, she too was seated upon a mentally constructed throne in that very same sky.
Thereafter, she was questioned. || 1 ||
O child, how could those like you exist within the interior of a stone?
How could there be movement there, and for what purpose would you have a dwelling place therein?

Being thus questioned, she said: "How? [The questioner asks: "How could there be a stay for those like you, who possess bodies and the like, within the interior of a stone that allows no space? And how could there be movement there? Furthermore, what is the purpose of your dwelling or home there, where even entry itself is impossible? To this, she replies: "In that very place..."
The meaning is that everything is absolutely impossible. || 2 ||
The Vidyādharī said:
O Sage, just as this vast world shines forth for you,
so too does our world exist there, joined with its creation and transmigration.
"Not only this much has been conceived by you as existing there; rather, even such another world exists"—thus he gives the answer to the Vidyādharī’s question with the word "O Sage" (mune). || 3 ||
The serpents quiver in the underworld, the mountains stand firm upon the earth,
the waters ripple and surge, and the winds blow through the sky.
He elaborates upon that very point with the verse beginning "sphuranti" (they quiver), etc.: "They quiver and make indistinct sounds;
the oceans shine with their waters; within them, living beings move slowly.
Beings are born incessantly and die without ceasing, just as [the waves do]. (5)
"With water" means with the flood; "they go" means they conduct themselves by way of movement and so forth—thus is the sense to be supplied as "just as here. (5)
The winds blow, the waters flow, and the gods shine and do not shine in the sky;
the mountains stand firm, the planets rise, and kings traverse the earth.
The successive traditions of worldly conduct among gods, asuras,
and humans have flowed restlessly until the end of the kalpa, like rivers into the ocean.
They shine in the form of constellations and so forth; they appear in the shape of their respective bodies. || 6 || 7 ||
The lotuses of the days of this lake on earth, possessing rows of flickering clouds, blossomed fully until the end of the kalpa, repeatedly closing and opening their petals.

"Until the end of the aeon" refers to time (*kālataḥ*); "until the sky" refers to space (*deśata�*). The prefix *āṅ* is used here in the sense of inclusion (*abhividhi*). The lotuses of the days—those very lotuses which are the world-sphere lake, blooming with bees whose nests are the flickering clouds—have been fully closed and then opened;
this intends to refer to the filaments and other parts contained within them. (8)
Creating moon-like splendor in the four directions with the sandalwood paste of his own luster,
he destroys even the darkness residing in the hearts of Rātri and Rohiṇī.

The Moon, applying anointing ointments in the form of moonlight—a sandalwood paste produced by his own radiance—in all four directions, destroys the darkness residing within and even that which has gone outside, both of the night and of Rohiṇī. || 9 ||
Delighting in tasting its own state, well-guided by the mechanism of the wind,
this lamp named the Sun shines in the sky, the dwelling place of heaven and earth.
Delighting in the consumption of the liquid essence— that is, the enjoyment of the oily substance— of the wick characterized by her own ten directions,
she was well-whirled and rotated all around by a machine characterized by the wind within the abode of the two worlds, heaven and earth. || 10 ||
Willed by Brahmā and obstructed by those who move with the flow of the winds,
the wheel of the stars revolves incessantly in the sky, turning upon the axis of the three qualities.
Now, he describes the celestial sphere as a grinding-mill by means of two verses beginning with "Brahmā":
"In the sky, the wheel of the stars—the celestial sphere—revolves by its qualities; thus the 'whirlpool of qualities' (guṇāvarta) grinds, that is, it revolves. And that..."
Revolving, it grinds from the time of creation until the end of the fourfold characteristics of the earth, like rice grains from the beginning of the cosmic cycle.
By which craftsman was this fashioned? He says: "It was fashioned by the volition of Brahmā. By what is it supported? He says:
It is held and propped up by the wind-rays that move with the circulation of the wind. Upon which pivot is it fixed? He says: [it is fixed] upon...
Resounding. || 11 ||
The pivot-pin, immovable by necessity, grinds the grain of living beings from the beginning of creation,
sounding like the rumbling of clouds against the door-panels of heaven and earth.
The surface of the earth was filled with islands, oceans, and mountains; the sky with celestial chariots and cities;
and the entire circle of the netherworld with multitudes of Daityas, Dānavas, and Nāgas.
He states that there too, as here, the worlds beginning with Bhūḥ are filled with continents, mountains, and so forth as is appropriate—namely, "with continents," etc.;
the sky is filled with cities fashioned from the arrangement of celestial chariots (vimānas). || 13 ||
The dark-blue orb of the earth’s surface stands as the earring of the Fortune of the three worlds,
shimmering with jewels like that of a woman whose conduct is fickle.
There too, the blue circle of the earth’s surface stood like a shimmering jewel-encrusted earring of the Fortune of the Three Worlds, ever-fickle in her conduct. || 14 ||
Taking up the subtle vibration of consciousness, which is devoid of intellect and the like and is like the wind, it is born as both the stationary and the moving.

Even there, the collection of living beings— both stationary and moving— is born, meaning it undergoes transformations such as birth and so forth, by taking up the internal, subtle vibration-consciousness called *prāṇa*, which is devoid of intellect (*buddhi*) and other faculties, just like the external, wind-like activity. || 15 ||

The Sage resorted to silence through his silences, steadiness through the waters, freedom from monkey-like fickleness through the winds, the quality of providing space through the skies, and radiance through his splendors. (16)

In that regard, the Sage (the Buddha) resorted to silence through the acts of a sage; the earth resorted to [supporting] oceans and so forth with its waters; the monkey resorted to fickleness through the winds; and space, though divided by various limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), resorted to the quality of providing room in accordance with those adjuncts. The meaning is that the inherent natures (*svabhāva*) of all things are fixed and uniform. || 16 ||

Within [this world], trees, the earth, oceans, mountains, and those who move in the sky—worms, gods, asuras, and aquatic creatures alike—are intensely throbbing with life, all facing death and rebirth. (17)

Therein flash forth those that move in trees, such as monkeys; those that move on the earth, such as humans; those that move in the waters, such as fish; those that move in the mountains, such as deer; and those that move in the sky, such as birds and deities. || 17 ||
Including the gods, asuras, and gandharvas, Time (Kāla) fashions all creatures with its arms—the kalpas, yugas, and years—just as a herdsman tends his own cattle. 18.

Time, together with the gods and other beings, is the Protector; like a man tending his own cattle with his arms, he governs and enjoys [the world] through his "arms" characterized by the cycles of the ages (kalpas), years, and so forth. || 18 ||
In the ocean of time, which is infinite, vast, unfathomable, and deep,
they are born again and again, only to dissolve through the turning of its whirlpools.
Those hosts of gods and aquatic beings, through the movement of time like the turning of whirlpools in the ocean of time, are born again and again and then dissolve. || 19 ||
The fourteen kinds of elemental dust, tossed about by the winds, dissolve into the space of destruction like the play of autumnal clouds. (20)
It is called "destruction" (nāśa) because things perish within it; such is the unmanifest space (avyākṛtākāśa). || 20 ||
Awakening the world with the fly-whisks of the rays of the moon and sun,
she stands with the sky as her garment and a crest of clusters of stars as her ornaments.

She whose garment is the very sky; she upon whose crest the clusters of stars serve as ornaments—such is the heavens, standing as if fanning the sleeping world with the fly-whisks of the rays of the moon and sun, awakening it. 21.
The quarters of the sky remain as if paralyzed, enduring wind, earthquakes, clouds, and heat, refusing to abandon their own regions.
There too, the quarters of the sky stood as if paralyzed, like immobile living beings, having become incapable of enduring wind, earthquakes, rain, and heat. || 22 ||
Through portents, the roar of clouds, earthquakes, and the seizing of planets—whether unknown or known—the movement of beings occurs. (23)

Furthermore, the course of living beings characterized by desirable or undesirable results arises even from omens such as portents, whether they are known by those skilled in the science of astrology or remain unknown to others. || 23 ||
The blazing submarine fire drinks up the waters of the seven oceans,
just as Time consumes the multitude of beings throughout the intermediate worlds until the end of the kalpa.
Just as Time drinks up the multitude of beings, the collection of living creatures within the fourteen worlds that constitute the various realms of the universe, so too [does he]. || 24 ||
The host of spirits enters the underworld, ascends to the hollow of the sky, and wanders everywhere throughout the circle of the quarters;
it traverses the circles of great mountains and oceans, as well as other islands, following the course of the wind.

Having stated everything, he summarizes it concisely with the words "pātālam" (the netherworld). There too, the host of beings—the multitude of living creatures—fit for the netherworld enters Pātāla. Those fit for dwelling in the hollow of the sky go to the hollow of the sky (*nabhibila*). Others, however, wander in the intermediate space within the circle of the quarters. This occurs according to the sequence of the movement of the winds (*marutaḥ*).
He traverses the circles of mountains and great oceans as if they were mere pathways, and he wanders through other continents;
thus, one should consider that every worldly transaction existing here also occurs there. This is the meaning. || 25 ||

Thus ends the sixty-sixth canto, titled "The Description of the Interior of the Stone," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*, a work of the Seers (*ārṣa*). Vālmīki’s Divine [Work]. Liberation. The Latter Part. 66.
Thus ends the sixty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Interior of the Stone," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The sixty-seventh canto.
The Vidyādharī said:
"O Sage, please show me favor and come to that world."
For when wonders occur, great men indeed become exceedingly curious. || 1 ||
Having gone to that stone out of curiosity, the world was not seen by the sage; then, being questioned by him regarding the greatness of his proximity, the Vidyādharī’s account is described here.
O sage, if you consider the collection of meanings spoken by me to be impossible, then come yourself and witness that creation directly in its entirety. || 1 ||
When he said, "So be it"— [the words "Śrī Vasiṣṭha said" being understood there]— I began to travel through the sky together with him,
like a fragrance carried by a whirlwind, or as one void moves with another void in the void.

When she had spoken thus, I accepted her request by saying, "So be it," and began to travel through the sky with her, just as fragrance travels with a whirlwind along with the scent of *campaka* flowers and the like. || 2 ||
Then, having traversed a long distance through the empty sky,
I reached along with her a multitude of beings situated in the firmament.
The aggregate of beings refers to the collection of living creatures, such as gods and others. || 3 ||
Having crossed that region where beings roam in the sky after a long time,
I have reached the white cloud in the sky above the crest of the Lokāloka mountain.
Emerging from that seat of clouds, white as the moon in the northern sky,
I was brought by her to that lofty stone slab fashioned like molten gold.
Emerging from below a cloud-seat as white as the moon, situated in the eastern portion of the northern direction. || 5 ||
As long as I beheld that bright stone, it was not this world,
but appeared like a lofty ridge of the world of fire made of refined gold.

The meaning is that although he searched thoroughly for that stone— which stood like the slope of Mount Meru and was visible from the world of fire, thinking "I am being watched by Agni"— and looked for it, he did not see the world described by her there.
Then I asked that beloved one: "Where is the ground of your creation?
Where are Rudra, the Sun, Fire, the Stars, and so forth, and where are the seven other worlds? (7)

"Where is the ground of your creation? And where are the Rudras, Arka, and others described by you?"—this is what was said by me; the connection with "everywhere" and "in front" [is understood] throughout. || 7 ||
Where are the oceans, the sky, and the cardinal directions? Where is the rising and sinking [of worlds]?
Where is the mass of the great ocean, and where is the grandeur of the starry firmament? (8)
The quarters are the directions; the emergence and submergence [of beings] are the birth and destruction of living creatures. (8)
Where are the ranges of mountain peaks, and where are the streaks of the great ocean?
Where are the seven circular continents, and where is the ground of molten gold? (9)
Where is the calculation of cause and effect, and where is the wandering through the worlds of the past?
Where are the Vidyādharas and Gandharvas, and where are humans, gods, and Dānavas? (10)
Where are the sages, kings, and seers, and where is the sequence of right and wrong conduct?
Where are the nights of the five-fold afflictions, and where is the wandering through heaven and hell? (11)
Where are those sages and kings, and where are the hermits among them? However, if the reading is *bhūpātālamunayaḥ*, it is clear [that they are all present].
The nights of the winter season consist of five watches. || 11 ||
Where is the reckoning of merit and demerit? Where are the play of parts and time? Where are the enmities of gods and demons? And where are the ways of hatred and affection? (12)
While I was speaking these words, that woman of excellent complexion,
her eyes as white as stone, looked at me with eyes wide with wonder and spoke.
While I was speaking thus, she said to me: || 13 ||
The Vidyādharī said:
"O friend, I see that everything here is not my own; I behold all people like cities and other towns reflected in a mirror. (14)

I, too, do not see as before; rather, the meaning is that I see all the aforementioned beings—gods, humans, asuras, and so forth—situated in the manner of reflections within a mirror, like a city other than the well-known city. || 14 ||
In this matter, O Sage, constant perception alone is the cause for me; I consider the absence of that perception to be the cause of your non-perception.
The absence of that [manifestation] is its concealment. The form "te" (in the sense of "you") at the beginning of the verse is Vedic (chāndasa). || 15 ||
Moreover, through this long discourse on monism,
we have both forgotten our state as the pure, singular, subtle spiritual body.

He says "and another" [to explain] that even due to the non-remembrance of the state of having a body consisting solely of pure mind, which is capable of grasping all subtle objects, your failure to see that [Self] or your indistinct perception of it occurs. || 16 ||
Since this world of mine has become like a creeper upon the sky—though it was practiced by me for an exceedingly long time—I do not perceive it clearly. (17)

The syntactical connection is as follows: "This world belonging to me, though it is my own, has almost perished; for, like a creeper in the sky long practiced [in imagination], I do not perceive it clearly. (17)
That which was previously my own world, appearing to me with extreme clarity, I now perceive as indistinct, like a reflection in a mirror. (18)
O Lord, through the mutual pain of our long-standing and futile conversation,
we have forgotten our own most pure and pervasive state of composure.

Well-being (*svāsthyam*) consists in the state of having a single, pure, *ativāhika* body established through the practice of the aforementioned meditative concentrations (*dhāraṇā*), and not in abiding in one's essential nature (*svarūpa*), because that would contradict the preceding text. (19)

That practice which shines forth from within through the essence of the pure sky of consciousness becomes identical with that very [consciousness] within, appearing as if it were innate from childhood.

By the word "practice" (abhyāsa), the firm latent impression (saṃskāra) produced by it is indicated. "Shines forth" (prakacati) means it becomes awakened and manifests. The particle "iva" (as if) is placed out of its logical order; [the sense is: "the internal mind (antaścitta) would become as if entirely composed of that. || 20 ||

Know that there is no branch of knowledge which cannot be mastered through the study of true scriptures nor by right reasoning; for what can fail to be accomplished through the practice of boundless exertion? (21)

For this very reason, he says "no" to indicate that for one devoid of practice, hearing and reflection are fruitless. The connection with the preceding verse is that "that power exists. He says "it does not exist" to show that there is nothing whatsoever that cannot be accomplished through practice. || 21 ||
"Surely this delusion of discourse has overwhelmed me through the power of long-continued habituation to my own world;
for between two [conflicting views], the stronger one indeed prevails. (22)

This delusion regarding the narrative of your conversation has overwhelmed and captivated me—who was already possessed by the delusion of my own previous world—by virtue of its continuous practice within my own world. The meaning is that, because of this, the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of the former [world] became as if obscured; for it is with the intention of stating that the present is stronger than a past delusion that he says:
"For there are two," so it is said. || 22 ||
O Sage, for those seeking their desired objects, there is no other refuge than the repeated performance of actions prescribed by one who knows them. (23)

For this very reason, for those who desire the fruits of worldly or Vedic arts and sciences, nothing other than the repeated practice of them according to the sequence taught by their respective gurus is the refuge; thus he says, "by the desired," etc. [Verse 23]: "By means of the action well-taught by gurus who know that [subject], and by the method of its performance."
This mature delusion of ignorance here, consisting of the sense of "I," subsides through the cultivation of knowledge; behold the manifestation of practice! (24)

If even the beginningless and endless misery of saṃsāra perishes through the practice of knowledge, what other undesirable thing could remain that would not be cured by such practice? To this he says: "This... Through the reflections on knowledge—that is, through the practices of hearing and so forth—I, a foolish young woman, see [the truth], yet you do not see it.
Even an omniscient one perceives the creation of stones as a manifestation of habitual practice.

It is said that proficiency through practice is seen even in children, whereas forgetfulness leads to confusion even for the great; in this regard, he says "I" to show that we two ourselves are the illustration: "Though I am but a disciple, I see the creation of stone; you, though the omniscient Guru, do not see it."
The meaning is that this is a marvel brought about by the power of practice. || 25 ||
Even the ignorant attains the state of the knower, and even a mountain is ground to powder;
even an arrow reaches its great target—behold the manifestation of practice! 26.
Even though an arrow is insentient, through the proficiency gained from the practice of aiming arrows, it reaches even a very large and extremely subtle target. || 26 ||
In this way, indeed, the fully matured cholera of false knowledge is pacified by inquiry; behold the manifestation of practice! (27)
O Sage, through habituation even a pungent substance becomes agreeable;
the neem tree is pleasing to one person, while honey is pleasing to another. (28)
To a Dravidian who has practiced the habit of eating neem, even the neem tree becomes pleasing. || 28 ||
One who has no kin becomes a kinsman through the practice of proximity; conversely, through the lack of practice, affection for kinsmen diminishes due to distance. (29)
The state of being a kinsman, which is affectionate like that toward a relative. || 29 ||
This subtle body (ātivāhikadeha), which is essentially the pure space of consciousness,
assumes the state of a material body through the power of the practice of mental ideation.
He states that even the delusion regarding the materiality of the body arises naturally from the habituation to it: "The subtle body... (Verse 30).
Through the cultivation of the practice of concentration (dhāraṇā), this physical body attains the sky like a bird; behold the manifestation of practice! 31.
He goes to the sky and attains the siddhi of moving through the air. || 31 ||
Meritorious deeds go to futility; mothers go to futility;
fortunes go to futility; but practice never goes to futility. 32.
Even by a slight offense such as [neglecting] *kīrtana* and other practices, even great merits, fortunes, and riches come to naught.
(32) Enemies who are difficult to subdue attain success, and they turn into friends;
even poisons turn into nectar through the yoga of constant practice. (33)
Poisons, when consumed through practice for the sake of medicinal purposes, become like nectar, serving as the cause of health and other benefits. || 33 ||
He who abandons practice regarding a desired object is the lowest;
he never attains it, just as a barren woman [never obtains] her own son. (34)
For this very reason, he says "by which" (yenā) [in verse 34], meaning that the practice of what is auspicious according to the scriptures must never be abandoned.
Even that object which is desired because it is acquired through one's own habitual practice must be abandoned with reasoned deliberation, just as one abandons life until death. (35)

In that case, one might argue that because they are prescribed by the scriptures, things such as wife, son, wealth, and the performance of virtuous deeds—which are highly cherished—should never be abandoned.

To this he says: "Even that which... Even those things such as a wife and so forth, which are extremely dear because they have been acquired through great effort and constant practice, should not be abandoned abruptly; rather, [they should be relinquished gradually].

Through the practice of dispassion (*vairāgya*), that which is joined with the conceptualization of mental fluctuations (*vṛtti*) and so forth should be abandoned by means of reasoning. The meaning is: just as even life, though extremely dear until death, is abandoned by yogis through reasoning, so it is here. || 35 ||
That lowest of men who does not practice toward a desired object obtains what is undesired in the undesired, passing from one hell to another hell.

However, the practice of the knowledge of reality must never be abandoned. With the intention that if it were abandoned, liberation would be impossible—since the practice of identifying with the body and so forth, which is inseparable from such abandonment, could not be prevented—he says: "In the desired... In the case of the undesired identification with the body and so forth, one inevitably obtains only what is undesirable due to the very nature of such practice; and consequently, one goes from one hell to another.
Those who indulge in the sapless flow of saṃsāra cross over the vast river;
they alone do not abandon the practice known as self-inquiry. 37.

The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: those persons who cultivate such discernment that they perceive *saṃsāra* to be essence-less, and who do not abandon the practice known as self-inquiry—they alone cross the vast river of *māyā*. || 37 ||
The appearance of repeated practice is fully capable of manifesting the desired object and brings it about without obstacle, just as the light of a lamp reveals a jar. (38)

Just as the light of a lamp reveals a jar to one seeking it and brings it forth without obstruction, so too does the illumination characterized by the practice of [repeated] hearing and reflection reveal the desired reality of the Self to one seeking that reality and brings it forth without obstruction. In this regard, the practice of hearing and reflection serves to dispel the darkness of doubt and incredulity.

It makes [the truth] manifest. The intention is that the practice of *nididhyāsana*, however, brings about [realization] by removing obstacles in the form of contrary mental impressions (*viparītabhāvanā*). || 38 ||
Just as the wish-fulfilling trees and creepers, and just as the true wish-fulfilling gems, bear fruit throughout the autumn months, even so do the stages of practice. (39)
The light of long-practiced familiarity with a desired object illuminates living beings;
thus they do not perceive the night of the earth known as the senses. (40)
Upon this earth characterized by the body, the desired object— the Self alone, which is the object of supreme love—
is illuminated by the radiant sun consisting of the practice of inquiry into that [Self],
just as subjects of noble birth, those persons qualified for action, [illuminate] what is called the senses.
The meaning is that they do not behold the night which provides the cause for the delusion of dreams consisting of thousands of misfortunes such as passion, hatred, birth, and death. || 40 ||
In the illumination of all objects for every class of living being, the sun of practice alone always triumphs supremely. (41)
However, among the fourteen kinds of beings born of the elements, no one achieves their desired object without natural, unartificial practice. (42)

The word *tu* is used in the sense of "even" (*api*). The meaning is that among all living beings, even those dwelling within the fourteen worlds, not even the slightest desired object can be accomplished by any creature without practice. || 42 ||
Repeated performance is called practice;
that alone is human effort (puruṣārtha) in this world, for without it there is no progress. (43)

He shows the nature of practice with the words "by repetition. This very human effort, which has been described many times previously in this treatise as having the supreme goal of man as its fruit, is what is meant here; without it, there is no progress or liberation, by means of one's own action known as "effort" and designated as "firm practice."
Success arises only from that which is born of one's own experience, and not otherwise.
One's own discernment is the perception of one's own nature, produced by that very [discernment] itself. || 44 ||
On this earth where the sun blazes intensely, there is nothing whatsoever that cannot be accomplished by a hero through practice;
through practice, even all the fears on earth become fearlessness, even in the most desolate mountain caves.

For a hero—a man who is a warrior in the conquest of the senses—when the sun of practice shines and blazes, there is nothing whatsoever that cannot be accomplished, whether it be on land, in the forest, in water, or in the intermediate space; nor do fears exist, such as tigers, serpents, and other causes of terror. 45.

Thus ends the sixty-seventh canto, titled "The Praise of Practice," in the *Pāṣāṇabhaṅga* section of the *Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa*, within the *Mokṣopāya* division of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa* composed by the sage Vālmīki. 67.
Thus ends the sixty-seventh chapter, titled "Praise of Practice," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The sixty-eighth canto.
The Vidyādharī said:
Then, through the pure concentration of awareness, [she perceived] her former practice.
By that [means], we shall bring about its manifestation, and the world will come to know it as residing in the mountain.
Here, by means of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) which dispels the delusion regarding the material body,
the reality of the subtle, transportable state (*ātivāhika-bhāva*) is established as true.

Since the delusion of materiality regarding the body and so forth does not cease, and the subtle spiritual state (*ātivāhika-bhāva*) does not manifest, without the effort of meditative concentration known as firm practice— and since, in its absence, it is impossible to perceive the persistence of another creation through direct witness— therefore, for this reason, [one should strive] toward the stainless Supreme Self with an inclination toward all-encompassing awakening.

By means of maintaining the form of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and practicing the prior state of the subtle body (*ātivāhika-bhāva*), through that method, the world spoken of by me—which resides in the mountain, that is, within the rock—will become manifest. || 1 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: When the Vidyādharī had spoken thus with logical reasoning upon the breast of the mountain,
I then sat in the lotus posture and became awakened in samādhi.
When that Vidyādharī had spoken such words, which were both logical and appropriate, I became intent upon ascending even to the plateau of Mount Dhara. || 2 ||
Having abandoned the cultivation of all objects and being devoted solely to pure consciousness,
I renounced that impurity consisting of the conceptualization of the meanings of previous discourses.

In that state of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), when all conceptualization of external objects has been abandoned, the meaning of the previous discourse—the mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of the physical body and so forth—is also relinquished; the sense is that one has even cast off the impurity of its latent impressions (*saṃskāra-mala*). || 3 ||
Then, having attained the state of the sky of consciousness, I reached the supreme vision,
just as the sky attains clarity upon the arrival of the autumn season.
This very point is stated clearly with the words "Now" (atha) and so forth. || 4 ||
Then, through the intense and singular practice of fixing my attention on truth within this body, my delusion regarding the material world has surely come to an end.
Freed from rising and setting, yet consisting of perpetual rising,
the great consciousness, as pure as the sky, then became as if manifest.
She consists of perpetual rising, eternally unobscured, and self-luminous.
Then, as far as I could see by the pure radiance of my own [vision], there was in reality neither sky nor stone; it was indeed the Supreme.
By the stainless light kindled by the mental modification (vṛtti) of its own witness alone; for the meaning is that the insentient mental modification lacks the power of vision by itself. || 7 ||
The ultimate reality is a dense, pure essence that shines forth in such a manner;
indeed, through such contemplation, my own self perceived it as being exactly so.
The meaning is that, through the cultivation of such perception, he beheld the stone—that very supreme reality which is the dense ultimate truth—as his own self. || 8 ||
Just as in a dream a very large stone seen within one's house is found to be nothing but empty space,
so too is the stone of the sky of consciousness utterly pure.
A man who himself possesses dreams enters into the state of being a dream-man for another;
in his essential nature, he is just like one who has awakened from ignorance within a dream.
If this worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) is indeed merely a dream, then how is it that there is the appearance of both self and others being awake? To this he says:

"By himself" (*svayam*). In a dream, by the very power of ignorance, one who has become another person seen in the dream—thinking "I am awake"—is himself, in his own essential nature (*svarūpataḥ*), just as he was when accompanied by the dream.
The meaning is that it appears as if one has awakened. || 10 ||
Those whose heads are severed while they remain in the state of dream are still situated within saṃsāra; indeed, what can they possibly do without the attainment of knowledge through time? 11.

For this very reason, he recalls what was stated previously by me: that in the *Sauptika*, since those who were killed while asleep lacked a body as a means for waking, there was no other alternative but to conclude that their state of wakefulness occurred within the dream itself—expressed as "of those in the dream-state" (svapnasthānām). || 11 ||
Awakening occurs in time even for those possessed of great delusion,
because there exists nothing whatsoever that is imperishable apart from the reality of Brahman.

Therefore, the primary awakening for this [individual] is indeed the realization of one's own true nature through the eradication of the sleep of root-ignorance; at other times, however, it is merely a dream, a vain conceit of being awake. Thus he says: "Awakening" (verse 12).
Therefore, I saw there that mass of consciousness, the pure Brahman-space, appearing like a solid stone; likewise, earth and the other elements were not found to exist anywhere there.

For this very reason, by me too, through the awakening to its true nature, that which was previously unseen as a stone-like form was seen as a pure mass of consciousness (*cidghana*), and not as a modification of earth and so forth; such is the meaning. || 13 ||
That which is pure and ultimate for all beings at the time of the first creation—
that very form of theirs remains attainable through meditation.

The beginning of creation is the "original creation" (ādisarga), meaning the time of the great dissolution (mahāpralaya). For these knowers of reality, it is attainable through meditation and reached by means of one-pointed concentration. || 14 ||
That which was pure and ancient at the first creation of beings, that very thing is today called the kingdom of the mind, known as *saṃkalpa*. || 15 ||

The Brahman-form alone is the body of all beings; it is the ultimate reality (pāramārthika-rūpa), yet it is described in the form of the world—this is the implication, referring to those who are deluded. || 15 ||
The body that carries the living being beyond is, in the ultimate sense, that which is supreme and directly perceived; it is the primordial manifestation of consciousness.

Let it be so; nevertheless, what is this *ātivāhika* (conveying) body, in whose presence the perception of the entire universe and the manifestation of the nature of consciousness—as previously described—occur? He states that [body] as "existence" (*sattā*). Brahman variegated by *māyā* is called "Being" (*sat*). Within that, the existence of the aspect of consciousness which is intermingled with the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the world is itself the *ātivāhika* body. However, the aspect of eternally immediate, pure consciousness— [The remainder of the text follows: —is the *nirupādhi* (unconditioned) Self.]
The meaning is: the manifestation of its own nature. || 16 ||

The first body of the living being (jīva), characterized by the initial emergence of the senses, is called "mental perception" (manaḥ-pratyakṣa); that very [perception] was just now [described] by the one of dull intellect. (17)

If so, how is it that the mind was previously described as the *ativāhika* (conveying) body of the individual soul (*jīva*)? To this, he says: "Arising," etc. That which consists of the nature of existence, arising at the dawn of creation as if taking on its form, becomes the first *ativāhika* body of the individual soul—whose nature is the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*)—in the form of the collective whole known as Hiraṇyagarbha, presiding over the sphere of creation. Furthermore, that...

The meaning is that it was previously stated that even the collective state (*samaṣṭibhāva*), when forgotten by the dull-witted, becomes the individual state (*vyaṣṭitā*) this very day; thus, the mind is perceptible to all people. || 17 ||
What has been called "yogic perception" is also called "mental perception";
that is merely the very nature of consciousness itself, which has needlessly undergone a change into something else.

Thus, it has also been stated that this very form of consciousness (cit) is perceived by yogis through direct perception in its collective form (samaṣṭi-rūpa), whereas it is perceived by the mind through direct perception as common to all people. || 18 ||
This so-called "present" arises from what is non-existent;
know, my dear, that this "present" is indeed a perception of the non-existent. (19)

In this regard, know that this present mental perception—which arises through the conceptualization of the body and so forth as being material—is indeed an unreal perception, since it has arisen in an absolutely non-existent form. O dear one, only the perception of the yogi is the primary perception, because of its immediate manifestation of the true nature of reality. 19.

Oh, how wondrous is this illusion! That which was previously perceptible has become imperceptible; yet when that very thing is determined to be imperceptible, the notion of perception returns to it. (20)
How then is it that all people experience that [reality] as being beyond perception while experiencing something else as being perceptible? To this he says: "Aho! (Verse 20).

Know that the nature of the subtle body (ātivāhika-deha), which was first described as being directly perceived, is real and all-pervading; whereas the material body (ādhibhautika) is merely illusion (māyā). 21.
