The phrase "first arisen" means that the superimposition of grossness is preceded by the subtle; for the Śruti declares: "That which is the red form of fire is the form of fire, that which is white is the form of water, and that which is black is the form of food; the 'fire-ness' of fire has departed; the truth is simply these three forms. Truth is all-pervading due to its nature as a collective totality (*samaṣṭi*), whereas Māyā alone is unreal.
Just as the state of being a bracelet does not exist at all in gold even when it has been experienced,
so too the materiality of the subtle body does not exist.
The living being perceives error as non-error and non-error as error; alas, this is surely a state of utter delusion, occurring without inquiry. 23.
This physical body is not found upon inquiry;
however, the subtle body (ātivāhika-deha) is indeed imperishable in both worlds.

By means of the previously elaborated investigation—such as whether the gross [form] is distinct or non-distinct from the subtle—what could its true nature possibly be? Because it facilitates all worldly transactions both here and hereafter, it is imperishable until liberation. (24)
For the material consciousness rooted in the subtle body is indeed false, just as a mass of water in a mirage is false in the desert. (25)
The manifestation of the materiality of the material consciousness has become established and has appeared. || 25 ||
The consciousness pertaining to the elemental (ādhibhautikī) arises within the sequence of the transportive (ātivāhika) consciousness;
through the power of the perception of a body, it becomes fully developed, just as the notion of a person arises in regard to a tree stump.
Just as there is the appearance of silver in mother-of-pearl, of water in a mirage, and of duality in the moon,
so too does the perception of materiality arise through Māyā in the subtle body (ātivāhika).
That which is unreal is made real, and that which is real is made unreal;
oh, how great is the power of delusion born from the lack of reflection in this living being! 28.
There exists only the perception of the yogi, yet there is also mental perception;
for the conduct of both worlds is established by these two alone. || 29 ||

Manifestation (*sphūrti*) and vibration (*spandana*) are the entire essence of worldly transaction. Since these two are common to both worlds, they ultimately result in the extraction of the subtle body (*ātivāhika-deha*) alone; thus he says, "the yogi," etc.
The word "mental" (*mānasa*) is to be supplied to "vibration. And that [mental vibration], because its establishment depends upon perception, exists only to a certain extent.
The sense is that the claim that it possesses an existence equal to that of direct perception is likewise nothing but false. || 29 ||
He who, having abandoned the primary means of perception, establishes himself in this truth,
remains happily after drinking the water of a mirage within that very perception.

And thus, with the intention that one should, by means of yoga, achieve stability in all common perception alone—setting aside everything else—and not in the mere perception of gross objects and so forth that is well-known only to ordinary people and pertains only to this world, he says: "The first."
That which they call happiness is in truth suffering, because it is experienced as perishing in every moment;
that happiness which is uncreated and without beginning or end—that alone the wise know as true happiness.

Likewise, regarding pleasure—which is common to all the world yet established as an experience for yogis alone—it is the supreme human goal for them, not for what is well-known among vulgar people; with this intention, he says "That which... [referring to the verse]. That sensual pleasure, which ends in suffering due to the experience of its destruction in a mere moment, and which was previously produced by thousands of sufferings—[is not the goal].
The meaning is that those who possess discernment call that very thing suffering. || 31 ||
Thus, let direct perception itself be examined by means of direct perception;
let that which is the primary direct perception be seen as real through direct perception. (32)
Desiring to further strengthen what has already been stated, he speaks again with the words beginning "by direct perception" (pratyakṣeṇa) and so forth. || 32 ||
There is no one more foolish than he who, having abandoned the direct experience of this world which yields enjoyment in the three realms, instead grasps that which is illusory in nature. (33)
For these beings, there exists only a subtle, transportable body;
the pervasive notion of a material body here is merely an unreal phantom.
How could that which consists of unarisen conceptualization be a real perception?
How could that which is not itself real produce an effect? (35)

He states [in verse 35] that for that which consists of false conceptualization (*mithyā-saṃkalpa*), even its birth is difficult to find, its existence is extremely difficult to find, and since it is non-existent (*asat*), its capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā-samarthatā*) is cast far away from even that—thus he says: "unborn" (*ajātā*). 35.
Where even direct perception itself is non-existent, what else could be existent there?
Where could that truth [or, according to another reading: where could that established thing] exist, such that an unestablished entity could be proven by it? (36)
[Objection: But how can the phenomenal world (prapañca), which is established by means of valid cognition such as the eye and so forth, be denied? To this he says: "Where...
The intended meaning is that [the world] is sublated even by the eyes and other senses because it is sublated by the direct perception (yogipratyakṣa) of the yogins. || 36 ||
If existence itself is directly perceived as having perished, where indeed could inference and the like be employed?
Where elephants are driven away, what talk can there be of camels?

When such is the case even with respect to the eyes and other sense organs, which directly establish their objects, then inference and the like, which are rooted in them, are also cast far aside; thus he says: "In perception alone... [The word] *ūrṇāyu* means "one who possesses wool"; the suffix *-yu* is used here in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*). (37)
Therefore, that which is established by valid means of knowledge—the object of perception—does not exist anywhere at all.
This alone exists as it were, the dense mass of Brahman, utterly solid.

Thus, he states the result of the cleansing of the visible world with the words "ananyad" (not other). The meaning is that this which appears as if it were a reality distinct from [Brahman] is, in fact, the solid mass of Brahman alone, like a single block of rock-salt; this is the established conclusion. || 38 ||
Just as in a dream, the mountain is only for the dreamer and not for anyone else within the house,
so too is that very stone a city for those two who possess the corresponding mental conception during their respective nights.

To the one seeing the mountain in a dream, that mountain is well-known even at that time, yet the space [in which it appears] is indeed empty; for at that very same time, for another who is either awake or dreaming, that mountain does not exist. Just as this is the illustration, so too the meaning is that for both of us—who possess the contemplation of the stone—that visible stone is also nothing but consciousness (citi). || 39 ||
"This is a mountain, this is the sky, this is the world, and this am I"— thus the Self, consisting of consciousness, spontaneously manifests as a wonder within the void.
It is wondrous; that is to say, it shines. || 40 ||
One whose self is awakened perceives this, never one who is unawakened;
the comprehension of the meaning of a story occurs for a listener, never for one who does not listen.
Only consciousness thus manifests, and nothing else; thus the awakened self alone perceives this, not the unawakened.
The meaning is that it is just as the comprehension of the meaning of stories such as the *Mahābhārata* belongs only to the listener thereof and to no one else. || 41 ||
"This is unawakened" is merely an illusion that has attained the status of reality;
to one who is intoxicated, even trees and mountains appear perfectly stable as they dance. (42)
Having realized the auspicious nature of consciousness— the direct perception that is unimpeded everywhere and of a single uniform form—
those fools who resort here to other, feeble forms of perception are as good as nothing, being as wretched as blades of grass. But those who,
even after realizing their own nature as the singular essence of full bliss through the direct perception of a yogi, still consider that realization to be sublated [by others]...

They tolerate even the feeble and hollow perceptions of the eyes and other senses as valid means of knowledge; enough of those deceitful, straw-like, and self-deceiving people! Since they lack confidence even in their own experience, how could they trust the words of others? They are simply beyond instruction.
This is the meaning. || 43 ||

Thus ends the sixty-eighth canto, titled "The Description of the Impossibility of the Perceptible World through the Non-establishment of Valid Means of Cognition," in the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, belonging to the *Deva-mānuṣa-nirvāṇa-upadeśa-pāda*.

Thus ends the sixty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Impossibility of the Objective World through the Non-refutation of Valid Means of Knowledge," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the illustrious Vasiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa.
The sixty-ninth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
The world is a limb of the Self, without appearance, invisible, yet existing as if visible.
When seen with the supreme vision, that very Brahman is perceived as free from all affliction.
Herein is described the entry into the stone cave, the observation of the local ritual there,
and the conversation with the sage who was seated there.

To demonstrate that Brahman, which is the substratum providing the manifestation and existence of the world, so that the reality of the world may be conceived within the interior of the stone, he says: "The limbs of the world," etc. Whose limbs are the worlds as it were; "without appearance," being beyond the reach of the lights such as the sun; "invisible," being beyond the reach of the eyes and other senses. || 1 ||
There, the delusions of mountains, river currents, worlds,
and the intervals between worlds appear reflected in that supreme mirror, the great void.
Then she entered that creation with unrestrained activity;
I too entered there along with her, consisting of mere volition.
She is that Vidyādharī; there, within the interior of the rock, she entered that aforementioned creation. || 3 ||
Then, having reached that world of Vairiñca,
she, being resolute and supremely beautiful, sat down before Viriñca.
Then, being diligent— meaning possessed of the effort to bring her there—

she reached the world of Viriñci situated there; while sitting before Viriñci, as she was about to speak words such as "This is my husband," the connection [of the narrative] occurs in the fifth [chapter], wherein it is said that a great dissolution (mahāpralaya) of the enemy [of the world] was imminent in this universe.
"O tiger among sages, this one says: 'This is my husband; he protects me. Long ago, for the sake of marriage, I was conceived by him in his mind. (5)
Even this ancient Puruṣa has not married me, though I have now reached old age; because of that, I have come to a state of detachment.
Even this seeker of dispassion desires to go to that state where there is neither the state of being a seer, nor the state of being seen, nor even emptiness.
Now that the great dissolution is imminent in this world,
he does not waver from his meditation, remaining as immovable as a mountain observing the vow of silence.
Again, she herself says this with the words beginning "saṃprati" and so forth. || 8 ||
Therefore, O Lord of Sages, having awakened both me and him as well,
establish us on the supreme path until the beginning of the creation at the end of the great kalpa.

Having awakened them through the instruction on reality, unite them with the path called Brahman— the fundamental ground— at the beginning of each and every well-known creation that occurs from now until the end of the great kalpa, the period of the final dissolution of all things.
Having spoken thus, he said this to me in order to awaken him:
"O Lord, this lord of sages has arrived at this residence today. (10)
For the awakening of that four-faced one, for his emergence from meditative absorption, and for his comprehension of the appropriate meaning. || 10 ||
"This sage is the son of Brahmā, now in another house in this world;
worship him, who has come to your home, with the hospitality due to a householder. (11)
Worship and please those who are worthy of honor in the houses of householders by means of appropriate offerings. || 11 ||
"Let the bull among sages be awakened and honored with water for the hands and feet;
for the great delight in grand offerings from those of noble soul. (12)

"Let this bull among sages be recognized by you as one worthy of worship; therefore, let him be honored with water for the hands and feet (arghya-pādya). For from great souls such as yourself, it is only a great fruit obtained through grand services that is pleasing, not a trivial one. [The fourth case ending is used here according to the rule *rucy-arthānāṃ prīyamāṇaḥ*. 12.
When she had said "So be it," he of great intelligence awakened from his meditative absorption,
like a whirlpool in the ocean arising from the nature of the fluidity of his own self-awareness.
Skilled in conduct, he slowly opened his eyes,
just as the spring season opens the flowers upon the earth when the cold has subsided.
The two eyes are comparable to two flowers; just as [the sun] causes them to bloom, so does sweetness. 14.
Gradually those limbs revealed their consciousness,
just as clusters of honeyed sprouts reveal their fresh sap.
The meaning is that the clusters of sprouts belonging to the spring (madhu) are like its own fresh essence. || 15 ||
Multitudes of gods, Siddhas, and Apsaras gathered from all sides,
like restless swans flocking to a lake blossomed at dawn.
He saw me and that playful woman arrived before him;
then the Creator spoke these words, beautiful with the sound of the *praṇava*.
In such a way that it is beautiful, with the vowels preceded by the syllable *praṇava* (oṃ). || 17 ||
The other Brahmā of the world said:
"O sage who has perceived the essence within the worthlessness of saṃsāra as clearly as a myrobalan fruit in the palm of one's hand, O great ocean of the nectar of knowledge, welcome to you! (18)
By whom the essence of the nature of saṃsāra—which is devoid of substance—has been seen like a myrobalan fruit in the palm of the hand. || 18 ||
We have reached this most distant path;
you are exhausted from the long journey, so please sit upon this seat. (19)
When he had spoken thus, O Blessed One, saying "I salute you," I sat down upon a jewel-encrusted seat that was pointed out by his gaze.
When a jeweled throne was indicated by her with a sidelong glance, I sat down upon it. || 20 ||
Then, the hymns, offerings, prostrations, and the rules for remaining [in his presence] were commenced, as uttered by the immortals, sages, gandharvas, munis, and vidyādharas. (21)
The principles of stability and the principles of appropriate worldly conduct. || 21 ||
Then, after only a moment, when the tumultuous clamor of all the hosts of beings had subsided, I spoke these words to Brahmā.
When all the hosts of beings, such as the gandharvas and others, had risen up, and the fervent outpouring of salutations with words and other gestures had subsided;
"What is this? [In this regard, the Sage said: "O Lord of the past and the future, since she has approached me and speaks with words of knowledge, you must diligently instruct us. (23)
The meaning is: "This Vidyādharī has approached me and says, 'You must enlighten us with words of wisdom'; is this appropriate or inappropriate? || 23 ||
"O Lord, Master of Beings, you have reached the further shore of all knowledge;
but this woman is a fool driven by passion—tell me, O Lord of the World, what does she say? (24)
Regarding the question "Whence does this doubt of yours arise?", he says: "You...

The sense is that since you have already accomplished all that was to be done (*kṛtakṛtyatva*), you have no need for my instruction; however, because she lacks the perfection of the means (*sādhanasaṃpatti*), she has no qualification (*adhikāra*). Thus, her request for instruction is logically inconsistent, and this is the source of your doubt. || 24 ||
O Lord, how was she, who was produced by you for the sake of being a wife, not brought here to the state of a wife; how was she instead brought to a state of bitterness? (25)
He shows another doubt with the word "how" (katham). Virasatām means despondency (nirveda). || 25 ||
Anyajagadbrahmā said:
O sage, listen; I shall relate this to you exactly as it occurred, for that which has transpired must be told in its entirety to the virtuous.

It is true that neither she nor I are worthy of instruction; nevertheless, by her own latent tendencies (*vāsanā*), she—imagining my own ignorance and her own entitlement—has thus petitioned you. Furthermore, every such conceptualization as "I have brought about her mere birth," "I am the one who begot her for the sake of a wife," and "I am her husband," belongs entirely to her.

It has come into being solely through its own latent impressions (*vāsanā*). Therefore, since it is false—being merely my own latent impression—its dissolution, along with the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) imagined by itself, shall now occur right before your eyes simultaneously with my attainment of disembodied liberation (*videhakaivalya*);
wishing to explain this further in detail, he makes a formal declaration, addressing him as "O Sage. (26)
There exists, indeed, a certain Reality that is unborn, peaceful, and undecaying;
from that, which has the singular nature of the manifestation of consciousness, I have emerged as a manifested being. (27)

In this regard, first, by way of an introductory preamble to what is about to be said, he states his own cause and the nature of his own birth in order to demonstrate that he possesses innate knowledge of reality— a fact well-known in the Purāṇas as the "fourfold [perfection] consisting of unimpeded knowledge, dispassion, sovereignty, and virtue, which are co-existent with the Lord of the World. He says:
"I exist" means: "I am present; I have become manifest. || 27 ||
I am always established in the Self, which is of the very nature of space;
when the creation is established, my name shall be Svayambhū.
To the question, "How can its own origination and the name associated with it be established when they are sublated by such knowledge of reality?", he says:

"Ākāśa... etc. When the creation of beings who engage in worldly discourse has arisen and persists, from their perspective, the name "Self-born" (Svayambhū) will exist as a conventional designation. || 28 ||
In reality, I am not born, nor do I perceive anything at all;
I am the space of consciousness, remaining unobstructed within the space of consciousness. (29)
But in reality, from the perspective of the ultimate truth: || 29 ||
That you say "this is mine" and I say "this is yours," this mutual discourse of ours is, in my mind, like one wave crashing against the crest of another wave.
To the question of what kind of discourse involving questions and answers occurs between us two who know reality, he says: "That which...
The sense is that just as the one undivided ocean displays a variety of sounds through the divisions of waves—which are fragmented and characterized by mutual collision—so it is here. || 30 ||
Thus, for me—who by the power of time have become indistinct in form—that maiden, who by her very nature consists of nothing but the reflection of consciousness within, [remains]. (31)

Thus, like a wave from the ocean, for that which— though its nature as the distinction between "self" and "other" is only slightly imagined and known through perception— is, by the power of time, slightly forgetful of its own true nature and possesses an indistinct form, there arises within it a latent impression (*vāsanā*) of "I am the inner controller" or "I am the ego," which consists of nothing more than a mere internal reflection of consciousness; this appears as something entirely different to another person, such as a young girl, but to me, it appears as non-different.
"She shines; she is both risen and unrisen, visible to us two"—this is the connection between the two [verses]. || 31 ||
That latent impression which appears here as "I" within me is distinct from yours, and yours is distinct from that of another; it is like the distinction between light and darkness within me.
I am the Self, established within the self, neither arising nor perishing; by my very nature, my form is unchanging, I delight in my own self, and I am the self-sovereign Lord.
Then, as for what you are like from your own perspective, he says: "I am that whose existence is indestructible," because I have not arisen [from anything else].
Due to that latent impression of the delusion "this is mine," which constitutes the existence of the world,
this presiding deity has come into being in the form of a body.

"How could she have arisen from such as you? And who was she there? To this he says: "Of him" (tasya). From the delusion of "I am" (aham), the form "ā" [is used]; in the case of recollection, the vowel "ā" is *pragṛhya* when preceded by the particle *aṅ*. Because it arises from the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of successive prior ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), the notion "I" is like a memory (*smṛti*).
The meaning is that this deity, who presides over delusion, the state of the world, and latent impressions (vāsanā), has become embodied through my own volition. || 34 ||
Thus she remains as the presiding deity of my latent impressions (vāsanā);
she is neither my wife, nor has she been honored as such. (35)

Having accepted the notion "I am the wife of Brahmā" through the power of the influence of her own latent impressions (*vāsanā*), she herself has come to this fruitless and extreme suffering; for indeed, this very thing is what constitutes internal latent impression. (36)
"In that case, why does she call you 'husband'? To this he replies with the word "sva" (one's own).

Because this very [consciousness] contains within it the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the entire universe, she has, by her own imagination, accepted the thought "I am a housewife," and thus has reached—meaning experienced—pointless and extreme suffering.
Thus it is said in the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* of Vālmīki, in the *Dehastha-mokṣopāya*, in the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa*. U. (Uttarakāṇḍa).
The sixty-ninth canto, titled "The Attainment of Creation by the Stone."
Thus ends the sixty-ninth chapter, titled "The Attainment of Creation," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The Seventieth Chapter.
Brahmā said:
Then I, who am the sky of consciousness, [perceived] a state consisting of another sky.
I desire to take another wife; for that reason, this period of decline has arrived here. || 1 ||
In this [work], the cause of world-weariness is described through the goddess Vāsanā:
namely, the dissolution of the world and its nature as mere false delusion.

"O Brahmin, how is it that she was produced by you for the sake of being a wife, yet has not been brought here to the state of a wife? Having thus stated the answer to this question, he now begins to provide the answer to the question: "How has she been reduced to a state of bitterness?"—I am of the nature of that space of the mind (*cittākāśa*), which is a manifestation of consciousness (*cidvivarta*); I am the Supreme...
The state of absolute liberation (*kaivalya*), which consists of unsurpassed bliss, is composed of another kind of space—the very essence of the space of Brahman.

For that reason, within this world fashioned by my own latent impressions (*vāsanā*), the fourfold dissolution well-known from the Purāṇas—namely, the eternal, the occasional, the daily, and the ultimate—is now imminent. || 1 ||
O Lord of Sages, at this time of the great dissolution, she was now abandoned by me; it is for that reason, surely, that she has become so bitter.

"To abandon" means to cause it to fall away from its own existence by cutting it off at the root. For that reason, when I become this primordial supreme space (*parākāśa*)—which is like the sky and so forth—characterized by a distaste for worldly objects and tending toward dissolution, then there occurs the state of the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*) and the total destruction of latent impressions (*vāsanā*). (3)

He states the reason for arising therein: "because of being space" (*ākāśatvāt*). This is a fifth-case ending used with the elision of a gerund suffix (*lyablope*). The meaning is: "when I, having abandoned the state of the space of the mind (*cittākāśatā*), become the primordial space of Brahman (*brahmākāśa*). (3)
Therefore, having become disenchanted with this world, she runs toward my path;
for what person of noble intellect would not follow their own creator? (4)
Here, at the end of the Kali age, the reversal of the four yugas has occurred;
today indeed has come the end of the subjects, the Manus, the Indras, and the gods.
The end of time (*kāla*) refers to the conclusion of the final aeon (*kalpa*), the final manvantara, and the final Kali Yuga. "Of them" refers to the subjects (*prajā*), Manu, Indra, and the gods.
This very day is the end of the eon and indeed the end of the great eon;
today is the end of my latent impressions and the end of the space of this body.

He states that today there is the simultaneous occurrence of the four kinds of dissolution: "This very day," etc. The phrase "within the latent impressions" (*vāsanānta*) expresses the absolute dissolution pertaining to higher knowledge (*vaijñānika-pralaya*). The phrase "within the space of the body" (*dehavyomānta*) expresses the dissolution pertaining to nature (*prākṛta-pralaya*). || 6 ||
Therefore, O Brahmin, this latent impression (vāsanā) is now prepared to reach its end;
for where indeed could a trace of fragrance remain when the lotus pond has dried up? (7)
By that collection of causes, such as the desire to perceive a self. || 7 ||
Just as a restless wave arises from the line of a dull ocean,
so too does desire arise in vain from latent impressions (vāsanā), even without a cause.

If it is asked, "How does the desire for this [intellect] to behold its own self arise when that very act is the cause of its own destruction?", he explains with justification that it arises from its very nature (svabhāva) alone, beginning with the words "Just as" (yathā). The meaning is that it occurs from its own nature, even without any other instrumental cause (apakāraṇa). || 8 ||
From the very nature of this latent impression (vāsanā) consisting of the conceited body, the desire for the vision of the Self arises spontaneously. (9)
Indeed, by means of the practice of concentration (dhāraṇā), she beheld the reality of the Self;
thus she saw this creation of yours, unrestrained and occupied with its various categories.

In that case, he states the reason for her interest in our vision of the universe: "The Self. The meaning is that for one engaged in the practice of *dhāraṇā* for the sake of self-knowledge, the attainment of such powers as traveling to other universes is an incidental result; thus, the desire to examine those very powers is the cause of her interest. She is "engrossed" (*vyagrā*) in the categories (*varga*), namely the fourfold aims of life beginning with virtue (*dharma*) and wealth (*artha*).
In whom the subjects are free from obstruction. || 10 ||
By her, who is intent on moving through the sky, the stone on the mountain peak was seen as being of the nature of space, serving as the support for our own world.
He states that even the previously mentioned vision of the stone occurs for her solely by the power of this [mantra], saying: "By this... (verse 11).

That in which this world exists is the "world-stone" (jagad-giri); that quality of being a world resides in the mountain of the world. Furthermore, within the objects of our world, there also exist other worlds.
We do not see those [realities], for these [others] abide in a vision of duality;
but having swiftly attained oneness with awakening, we see them through our insight.

Remaining in the state of emergence (*vyutthāna*) where dualistic perception prevails, we do not see [it]; yet, having attained oneness with pure awareness through meditative absorption (*samādhi*), we certainly perceive it by means of the yogic vision. 13.
In a jar, a cloth, a banyan tree, a wall, in the sky, in fire, in water, and in light—the worlds exist everywhere at all times, as if within a stone. (14)

The so-called "world" is indeed a vain delusion, comparable to a city in a dream; it is purely false—where is this "name," for that which is of the nature of consciousness neither exists nor does not exist? (15)

This world-illusion is indeed false. Where, indeed, is this false delusion? If it exists at all, then its nature is that of the underlying consciousness (adhiṣṭhāna-cidrūpa) and not the perceived form of insentient matter; such is the meaning. || 15 ||
Those for whom this [intellect], once fully understood, has attained oneness with the sky of consciousness, do not become deluded; but the rest remain vessels of error.
Then, O Sage, you were seen by her as she accomplished her own purpose through the practice of another concentration (dhāraṇā), which had been brought forth by the power of her own dispassion.
"What is this, O Lord of the past and future, that she has come to me?"—
thus he asks the reason for her capability to approach his presence, and provides the answer with the word "atha" (now).
"Now," meaning immediately after attaining the aforementioned detachment (*nirveda*), [she spoke] her own [thought] arisen through the power of her own dispassion (*virāga*).
By her— who, desiring to accomplish through your instruction that which she herself yearns for and which is conducive to self-knowledge, namely the approaching of a guru, hearing, reflection,
and so forth— there are [the powers] other than the aforementioned concentration (*dhāraṇā*) which is the cause for the vision of the creation of the world.

The meaning is this: by practicing the specific forms of concentration (*dhāraṇā*) described in the story of Cūḍālā—concentration which grants the power of moving through the interior of the universe as a sky-walker (*khecara-siddhi*) and the power of entering subtle objects imagined by the supreme mind—she recognized your place of meditative absorption (*samādhi-sthāna*), fashioned by your own volition; having gone there, she saw you even though you were hidden from view.
Thus the power of consciousness unfolds like an insurmountable illusion;
in this way, the stainless power of Brahman is without beginning or end.

In the manner thus described, the power of the individual consciousness (*jīvacicchakti*), which is ignorance (*avidyā*), expands like the illusion of a magician. And the power of Brahma’s *māyā* expands in exactly this same way. However, the distinction is that she [the supreme *māyā*] is "free from affliction" (*anāmaya*) because her veiling power has been dispelled;
such is the meaning. Alternatively, by the first half [of the verse], it is shown that she follows illusory limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) just as *māyā* does.

The statement that "the power of the individual soul (jīvacicchakti) unfolds" is the discourse of the ignorant; however, in the latter half [of the verse], it should be understood as the discourse of the knowers of reality, wherein the power of Brahman (brāhmīśakti) has manifested and the consciousness of Brahman itself unfolds everywhere. || 18 ||
No effects whatsoever proceed or cease here;
consciousness alone shines, illuminating substance, time, action, and the rest. 19.
They proceed, that is, they arise; they cease, that is, they perish. But it is consciousness alone that, like a substance, like time, or like action, shines, blazes, and vibrates. || 19 ||
Know that this—place, time, action, substance, mind, intellect, and so forth—is in fact nothing but the single body of the rock of consciousness, which is without rising or setting. 20.
*Angakam* is a replica of the limbs; the suffix *kan* is applied in the sense of "resembling" according to the rule *iva-pratikṛtau*. || 20 ||
This very consciousness remains in the form of stone,
bearing within it the web of the world as its limb, just as the vital breaths bear movement.
It remains, it abides. This is a Vedic transposition of word order. || 21 ||

One perceives the world as a self consisting of a mass of consciousness; though beginningless and endless, that consciousness appears to have a beginning and an end because of its nature as cognition—even though it is in truth nothing but pure awareness.

He says—starting with "vijñāna"—that this very perception of the contrary arises solely from the nature of the deluded mind: "having a beginning and an end" means being delimited by space and time; thus it has also reached a state of limitation created by such objects. || 22 ||
Though beginningless and endless, she is perceived as having a beginning and an end by those who understand her;
though possessing form, she is formless, established as the very limb of the universe. (23)
Though formless, she possesses forms; she whose limbs are the worlds—thus she exists in a state of apparent inversion. || 23 ||
Just as in a dream, consciousness itself perceives its own form as a city in the void,
so too does it perceive this world-body as a stone.

Just as in a dream the sky of consciousness itself perceives its own nature as a city, so too in the waking state the sky of consciousness itself perceives and sees the world—including even mountains and stones—as its own limbs. || 24 ||
In this state, rivers do not flow, the wheel does not revolve, and objects do not undergo transformation within; rather, it is this sky of consciousness that shines.
He shows the equality of sublation upon waking to that of a dream with the words: "They do not remember" (25).
In the sky of consciousness, the cognitions of the great eons and their endings do not exist as separate forms, just as one portion of water does not exist separately from another within water.
Just as waves and the like in the ocean are not distinct in form from the water itself, [so too are all things]. // 26 //
The worlds both exist and do not exist within the peaceful sky of consciousness, which is omnipresent and of a single form;
just as the spaces within various skies exist within the great sky, so too do all beings exist within the supreme void of consciousness.

This being so, he states the conclusion: through the perspective of superimposition (*adhyāropa*), when one observes, infinite worlds always and everywhere exist indeed by virtue of the reality of consciousness (*citsattā*); not even an atom-sized thing can be denied anywhere. Through the perspective of negation (*apavāda*), it follows that nothing whatsoever apart from the nature of consciousness can be established anywhere.

— "They move" (jaganti). Just as the spaces within pots and so forth exist within the great space by virtue of the existence of the great space, yet do not exist separately from it, so too these worlds, though they are the supreme ether and are empty, exist as reality through consciousness;
this is the meaning. || 27 ||
O Vasiṣṭha, O sage, go then; you too, upon your seat, attain peace this very moment.
Let the forms consisting of intellect and the rest proceed to the Supreme; we shall proceed to the state of the Great Brahman. || 28 ||

"O Sage Vasiṣṭha, go now to that world of yours; and there, upon your own ancient seat prepared in solitude, attain peace through meditative absorption—the bliss of undisturbed tranquility. Let these forms of the world, consisting of the intellect and so forth, fashioned by me, return to the supreme unmanifest through dissolution. As for us..."
The meaning is: by subverting the root-ignorance accompanied by the adjunct (upādhi) of Hiranyagarbha, we proceed to the supreme state known as Kaivalya. || 28 ||

Thus ends the seventieth sarga, titled "The Words of the Grandfather of the World within the Stone," in the Utpatti-prakaraṇa of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa, in the Vālmīki-Devarāja-muni recension of the glorious Vasiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa, a work of the Ṛṣis.
Thus ends the seventieth chapter, titled "The Words of the Grandfather within the Rock," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The seventy-first canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord Brahmā, together with the inhabitants of the world of Brahmā, [departed].
Having assumed the bound lotus posture, he entered into infinite meditative absorption. || 1 ||
Through the gradual cessation of the creative imagination, its causes, the architect [of the world], and volitional thought,
the process of dissolution of those beings imagined by that [imagination] is described.
Because there exists no end, no finality, nor any further emergence from it, that kind of concentration is "samādhi," and he is devoted to that. (1)

He whose mind was entirely stilled within the half-measure at the end of the first half of the syllable Oṃ— having the form bestowed by the act of writing, yet possessing unappeased awareness (or, according to the better reading, "unappeased latent impressions")— [remained] within those parts of the syllable known as Nāda, Bindu, Śakti, and Śānta, which constitute the latter half of the syllable Oṃ.
Through the gradual dissolution of the mind, at the end, one becomes one whose latent tendencies (vāsanās) are entirely stilled; this is the summary statement. || 2 ||
Following him alone, she likewise remained absorbed in meditation;
with all portions of her latent impressions extinguished, she became tranquil and took on the nature of space.
In her, the various seeds of memory did not remain as distinct parts; having become such, she was peaceful, having the nature of space, and possessed the essence of emptiness. || 3 ||
When that Parameṣṭhin,
free from all volition, had attained that state of attenuation, I beheld myself as the form of the all-pervading, infinite sky of consciousness.
Regarding how you perceived that inner secret of his, he says: "When she had reached [the state of] *parameṣṭhinī*.

When she—by means of the sequential dissolution of the *mātrās* of the *praṇava*, which are endowed with the meanings of the gross, subtle, and causal levels—had attained thinness (*tānava*) through the exhaustion of her own latent impressions (*vāsanā*), reaching the progressively subtler states up to *ā* (the supreme), then I too, through meditative absorption (*samādhi*), [perceived it].

Being that very one whose form is the all-pervading, infinite sky of consciousness, I saw all that. Now, [one might object]: "The suffix *kvasu* in *īyuṣī* indicates a remote past (*parokṣa*), while the expression 'I saw' (*apaśyam*) denotes immediate perception (*aparokṣa*); these two are contradictory. This is not a fault; for the remoteness is based on Vasiṣṭha’s state prior to the commencement of his meditative absorption (*samādhi*).

Because both [conditions] are established—namely, that one relies upon the state of having ascended to *samādhi* and that there is direct perception (*aparokṣya*)—there is no contradiction with the locative case (*saptamī*), which characterizes existence as indicating simultaneity.

This is because it is observed that one state of being can indicate another state of being even through an excellence of proximity; thus, its establishment is possible even by means of the metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) of simultaneity. || 4 ||
Just as his volition vanishes in an instant, so too does the earth, along with its mountains, islands, and oceans, quickly vanish in that very same way. (5)
From that very moment, as his resolve regarding that rite gradually became increasingly insipid,
so too did the entire capacity of the earth— with its mountains, islands, and oceans— to produce grass, shrubs, and other vegetation likewise fade away.
The connection with the subsequent [sentence] is: "the power of water and the other elements also began to set. (5)
The capacity for the growth of grasses, shrubs, creepers,
and rice began to gradually fade away entirely.
It is said that the earth bears the status of being a mere limb or part of that Virāṭ, who is the Self; for that reason, the [individual] consciousness of that [Virāṭ] does not arise [in her].

With the intention that for a dying person of knowledge who experiences sensations pervading the entire body, there should be understood a sense of distaste for the earth and other elements that constitute the limbs of the Virāj-body— much like the distaste for one's own limbs during their dissolution— the author says "kila" (it is said). Due to the cessation of those sensations— that is, the withdrawal of those perceptions— that consciousness, having become devoid of sensation, becomes tasteless and utterly worn out.
The connection with the subsequent verse is "it came to be. || 7 ||
Deprived of consciousness, she became tasteless and utterly decayed,
having fallen into a state of frailty through old age like a creeper at the end of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa.
Just as a finger becomes insensible due to our lack of awareness,
so too has the earth fallen into a state of distress due to the lack of awareness on the part of Viriñci.
He elucidates the illustration residing in the underlying intention with the word "just as" (yathā). || 9 ||
It was filled with a multitude of great calamities occurring together,
and its men were turned toward hell, scorched by the coals of their own evil deeds.

He elaborates on how [the world] became utterly decayed through fifteen and a half verses beginning with *saṃpanna*. In that context, with the intention that even the defilement of the Kali age is a cause for the destruction of human beings and so forth, he says *duṣkṛta* etc., while further elaborating upon that. || 10 ||
It was afflicted by famine, sudden calamities, instability, wretchedness, poverty, and misfortune;
it was filled with women of immoral character and crowded with men who lacked all sense of restraint.
By instabilities, such as calamities caused by kings, thieves, and the like. || 11 ||
The sun was grey with dust, mist, and pollen;
it was agitated by the suffering of those afflicted by pairs of opposites, fools, great misery, calamities, and disease. (12)
In that city, the sun was greyed by dust, mist, and pollen;

it was crowded with fools—who, because of the pairs of opposites such as cold and heat, were therefore great sufferers and addicted to evil vices—as well as with those afflicted by disease, all of whom were intent on the means of dispelling them. (12)
Its territories were devastated by fires, floods, and war;
its common folk were reduced to miserable straits due to drought and the failure of rain.
The city was struck by unexpected and great calamities as mountains fell upon it,
while its people wailed for the destruction of children, Vedic scholars, sages, nobles, and the virtuous.
In the midst of places where one would not expect them, deep wells have arisen;
the women of mixed castes are the ground upon which people become attached. 15.

In that city, due to the scarcity of water, people fearlessly dug reservoirs for water here and there in the middle of the dry land, resulting in deep wells everywhere; likewise, for the sake of intermingling castes, the inhabitants and the rulers were addicted to marriage and other unions among women without any consideration of lineage, sapinda-relationship, or those with whom marriage is forbidden. 15.
A city where all people have wealth as their only thorn,
where auspiciousness is the only thorn at its crossroads, where women have hair as their only thorn, and where the lords of men have their vessels as their only thorn.

In which [city] all people subsist upon *aṭṭa* (a toll-house) and *odana* (rice and other food), as well as upon *śūla* (stakes) through sale, seizure, and so forth; in which the crossroads (*catuṣpatha*) subsist upon *śiva* (the auspicious one) and that very *śūla* (toll/tax) as their means of livelihood; and in which [women] possess *keśa* (hair) and *bhaga* (fortune), and subsist upon that single *śūla* (phallus).

The traditional explanation (*saṃpradāyavyākhyā*) is as follows: *vanitā* means "women"; *pātra* means "head" and "hand"; and *śūla* means "that which is to be subsisted upon. Thus, it refers to those lords of men, the kings, in whose [realm] such [people] exist. Alternatively, from the root *aṭṭ* meaning "to transgress," *aṭṭa* refers to the transgression of the duties appropriate to one's own caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama*). *Śivā* refers to jackals; *keśāḥ* (hair) are well known.

The vessel, the courtesan, the dancer, and so forth—these are to be applied as appropriate, being the causes of addiction and lamentation for those [who possess them], just like the disease of colic (śūlaroga). The remainder is as before. || 16 ||

All people are afflicted by the pain of dualities, their conduct is characterized by the pain of suffering; women are the pain of unrighteousness, and the lords of men are the pain of intoxication. (17)
Thus, it is that [city] in which such social customs prevail, wherein sufferings themselves are like spikes that cause living beings to cry out; so too in what follows. || 17 ||

Enveloped by the trident of unrighteousness, possessing hundreds of tridents in the form of false scriptures, enriched with all the wealth of wicked men, and having destroyed the virtuous, [the Kali age has arrived]. 18.

It was surrounded on all sides by people intent on unrighteous abuse and armed with the spears of irreligion; it was pierced by hundreds of heterodox treatises outside the Vedas and cried out like one afflicted by disease. There, all the people—including wicked men, thieves, and slanderers—were rich in wealth. (18)
It was ruled by ignoble protectors of the earth who held no regard for the learned;
it was devoted to passion, delusion, fear, hatred, and lust—the dust of the disease of worldly existence. (19)
It was a place where men were destined for other realms, where virtuous brahmins were struck down by wrath,
and where commoners were intent on incessant lamentation.

Where men who go after others have abandoned their own duty and engaged in the duties of others; where the twice-born, who are instructors of their own dharma, are struck down by the wrath of anger; and where endless commoners are intent on the incessant wailing and weeping of others. 20.

It was a place where bandits had destroyed the cities, villages, temples, and the dwellings of the twice-born; its undertakings were sweet at first sight but resulted in suffering, and it was as fragile as a water-bubble.

In that [world], there are those who are fragile and short-lived, whose bellies are sustained by wealth acquired through unjust means—bellies whose undertakings are sweet at first sight but which result in suffering both in the end and in the next world. || 21 ||
Characterized by a failure of duty manifesting as the play of idleness,
it ends with the affliction of all calamities and, in due course, destroys the entire range of the quarters.

Wherein there are righteous people whose religious duties, such as the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyāvandana*), are neglected due to the manifestation of laziness; and wherein all calamities, afflictions, and diseases have come to an end. 22.
The cities and villages were reduced to ashes, and the entire realm was devoid of people;
the sky resounded with the wailing of jackals, while the clouds appeared like ash-colored earrings.
In which [city] the sky was as if terrifying due to whirlwinds that were wailing and roaring, filled with clouds of ash, and possessing earrings on both sides. || 23 ||
The belly of this wretched woman resounds with the loud cries of weeping as she begins her grand display;
she is a mere handful of people, yet she is attached to causing distress to the multitude.

She whose belly resounds with a loud noise (*ururavam*), abounding in sounds, due to the drumming and wailing of unfortunate subjects; and in whom the multitude of people (*janatā*)—that is, the mass of men—is equal in size to a handful (*muṣṭipramāṇā*) because of their plundering and theft. (24)
When the earth element has lost its sensation for Brahman, all regions become sapless to their very limits and are devoid of the qualities of all seasons. (25)

"Deprived of all the qualities of the seasons"—in the manner thus described, when the earthly element (*pārthiva-dhātu*) that constitutes the body of Virāj, the creator Brahmā, has become devoid of sensation (*gatavedana*) and its consciousness (*caitanya*) has been withdrawn, the earth became characterized by vast desolation (*pṛthu-vaidhuryā*); this is the syntactical connection with the following verse. || 25 ||
The earth, having become extensively distressed due to its imminent destruction, then the water-element, released from its consciousness, was on the verge of exhaustion. (26)

"From the imminent destruction," that is, from the dissolution (*pralaya*). Thus, he states with the words beginning "Then" (*atha*) that even from the watery portion, when the withdrawal of consciousness began, there was a lack of boundaries due to the agitation of the seven oceans. || 26 ||
When his mind was agitated, then, due to his transgression of destiny,
the oceans— having cast aside the boundaries of the noble and having their waters exposed— overflowed.
With their waters spread wide, they possess vast expanses of water. || 27 ||
Like madmen crying out, they have begun to undergo transformation;
by the shifting agitation of their waves, they shave away the forests on the shore.
They are the cutters of openings in the thickets of creepers. || 28 ||
The sky and the quarters of space were filled with towering waves whirling in eddies and surging upward through the tossing of the billows, while great clouds wandered about.
By which [clouds], with great, wandering masses and towering waves, the sky and the quarters were swallowed up. || 29 ||
The mountain caves were filled with a great gurgling roar and turbulent waters,
while the mountains themselves were enveloped by thick clouds amidst the vast onset of spray.

With great, gurgling whirlpools and thundering roars, their mountain caves resounded with the cries of fleeing creatures; their interiors were churned by trembling, restless heroic makaras, while their depths were filled with forests of trees overtaken by leaping sea-monsters.

Their interiors were agitated by heroic makaras that moved further ahead than the waves already moving forward, as those makaras sought to defeat the others by displaying the excellence of their respective speeds. || 31 ||
The aquatic creatures were struck down by lions fallen from mountain caves they had torn open;
the sky was made starry by the great jewels cast up by the waves.
The great clouds, moving through the sky and covered with leaping makaras,
produced harsh "bhāṅkāra" and "ṭāṅkṛta" sounds from the mutual clashing of their waves.
The sky-dwellers were covered by leaping and surging makaras, as well as by those who were massive and dense.
The trumpeting of the elephants, shimmering and rapid, washed out the sun;
meanwhile, the mountain walls were split asunder by the beasts busily tossing one another about.
The circles of waves were like plunderers of the mountain slopes on the banks,
and the intoxicated elephants were like those emerging clearly from the roaring mountain caves that served as their dwellings.
The kings, having invaded the cities of their enemies, stood as if clinging to them after slaying their foes;
they caused the sky-dwellers to flee from their mountain-like dwellings with the loud sound of their arrows.

By whom enemies—the forest fires of their own adversaries—were destroyed; and by whom the sky-dwellers, such as the gods, were driven from their homes by waves that crashed with a loud, high-pitched sound like the cry of *tāra*. || 36 ||
They plundered the forest groves and stripped the trees of their foliage,
filling the sky with waves that resembled winged mountains.
By those who, having plundered, uprooted, and raised up forest arrays, have made the sky—namely the atmosphere—as if it were a forest that had been cut down.
Shaken by mountain-like waves severed by winds of great roar, the waters resounded against the banks as they crashed against the multitude of trembling coastal mountains. || 38 ||

Like mountains shaken by waves severed and dispersed by the Maruts, the masses of mountains— with their roaring waters— had their ridges falling from the shimmering banks due to the radiance of gems, minerals, and other treasures.
The masses of sea-monsters were cast up by the surging,
vast whirlpools, while mountain caves were swallowed up as they sank into the flattened eddies.
Mountains and their caves were swallowed up by deep, bottomless whirlpools. || 39 ||
The jagged rocks, broken by the pounding [waves], formed uneven rows like teeth;
the waters were submerged within the caves hanging from the mountain peaks, where elephants were trapped amidst the surging waves.
They appear as if laughing, jagged with teeth of rock such as crystal that have been brought forth by the force of their bursting asunder;
they are those whose waves—water-elephants, a specific kind of aquatic beast—are submerged and entered into the long, hanging peaks at the edges of the caves. 40.
Turtles were impaled upon the branches of trees by the horses of Yama,
Indra, and the Guardians of the World, which were agitated with fear and pricked up their ears as they galloped along.
With the mounts of Yama, Indra, and Vasudhā—namely the buffalo-bulls, Airāvata, the elephants of the quarters, and so forth—with their ears pricked up and raised; || 41 ||
The sounds of the mountain ridges and slopes were heard crashing down as they fell;
the mountains, severed by the strokes of the fish's tail, were seen rapidly sinking and rising again.
The showers of cool rain, which had playfully cut through the forest thickets,
mingled with the masses of flames from the blazing submarine fire.
Whose [limbs] were cooled by the waters of the autumnal showers, as if resting within forest groves gently plucked by playful breezes. || 43 ||
With their great fires made suspicious by the destruction wrought by the Lord’s essence,
they fought against the elephants of the waters atop the crowning peaks that were gathering together.

From whom the great fires have vanished as if terrified—fearing the destruction of their own fuel, the abode of the Lord, by means of their own moisture and water; that is to say, those [clouds] who, meeting with the elephants of the dry land, are warriors whose nature is battle upon the peaks of the mountain ranges. 44.
As if dancing with the surges of their waves, piercing through the whirlpools of the water,
these mountains of water are experts at bursting forth from the mutual collision of the shifting waters.
The wise are experts in the mutual clashing and bursting apart of mountains by means of waters, and of waters by means of mountains.
Adorned by circles of living beings in the vast forests and groves,
they resounded with the beating of drums from the wild lordly elephants of the forest.

The connection with the following verse is as follows: "The sky is exceedingly (*alam*) agitated by the great waves (*kallolaiḥ*), which are like the *asura*s, resplendent due to the sounding produced by the striking of the tips of the waves against those *bherī* drums—characterized by the bloated bodies of dead forest elephants—which are leaping up wildly. 46.
Then there arose a sound like the trumpeting of the faces of the world-elephants with upturned trunks, which was exceedingly tumultuous with waves, like the netherworld with the Asuras.

Then, immediately after the agitation of the ocean, the roar of the world-elephants—the elephants of the quarters—arose; as they were floating there, their trunks were raised like upturned lotuses. || 47 ||
The earth, shaken for a moment by the fierce bursting and tearing within the cavity of the palate that reaches down to the bottom of the underworld,
trembled like a pillar set in unstable ground.

What kind of sound was it? It was a fierce and dense roar produced by the bursting, tearing, crushing, and compacting of the palate characterized as the surface of the netherworld (pātāla). And the earth, being overwhelmed by those thundering sounds, became such that its shifting mountain-pinnacles, Meru and the rest, were shaken from their positions in an instant.
And having been crossed by the surging oceans, she, being fickle, moved about like a trembling moss-creeper; this is how it connects with the subsequent part of the sentence.
Then, like a restless creeper of moss tossed by the surging ocean,
she was accompanied by a tumultuous roar as irresistible as a windless storm.

To explain what happened next, he says: "Then... (atha). The sky, filled with the tumultuous roars of irresistible clouds of dissolution that were like tempests, seemed to burst asunder while falling, accompanied by the sounds of echoes from the various directions. 49.
The sky seemed to burst as it fell with the shrieks of the lords of the quarters;
meteors, shaped like whirlpools and eddies, fell from the firmament.
Comets, appearing as portentous smoke-bannered signs, fell and flew upward. || 50 ||
Golden and jewel-encrusted pearls emerged from the quarters, the sky, and the earth like vermilion serpents, as the horizons were scorched.

In terms of color, they were like those made of gold and jewels, like pearls, and like cobras the color of vermilion; these are the comparisons for the rows of portents. The connection with the distant [verb] is that "rows of portents arose from the quarters, from the directions, from the sky, and from the earth. (51)
Rows of various portents, with masses of flickering flames for their matted hair,
were released from Brahmā on all sides toward the earth and other elements, as well as toward the Asuras and others.
Released by Brahmā— the Creator previously mentioned— and abandoned through the withdrawal of his sustaining resolve,
both types of great beings denoted by the word *bhūta*— namely, those beginning with the Asuras and those beginning with the earth—
fell into agitation. (52)
The two kinds of great elements were thoroughly agitated;
the moon, sun, wind, Indra, fire, and Yama were all thrown into a tumultuous uproar.
The lords who had reached the world of Brahmā were intent on falling;
with their trembling, rows of trees fell down with a *kaṭakaṭa* sound. || 54 ||
Having gone to the world of Brahmā, they were those whose power consisted in the fulfillment of their respective offices as lords. || 54 ||
The mountains experienced the intense swaying of the earth;
the caves of Kailāsa, Meru, and Mandara trembled from the earthquake.
Showers of red flower-clusters fell, released by the celestial *kalpa* trees.
As the cities, mountains, oceans, and forests from the various worlds were struck against one another by the apocalyptic winds of the kalpa,
the universe became a chaotic mass of scattered and shattered debris, like the overflowing waters of the full ocean at the destruction of Tripura.
The intermediate worlds, mountains, cities, oceans, and forests— all this world, ending with these,

was filled by the three cities as they were prone to falling from all sides due to the conflagration of Rudra’s arrows, amidst the tumultuous cries of people who, struck and being struck one another by the calamitous winds of the kalpa.
The meaning is that, like the host of Daityas in the city of Tripura, they were scattered and shattered in the full ocean. || 56 ||
Thus ends the seventy-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Disturbance at the End of the Kalpa," in the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the glorious Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa composed by Vālmīki.
Thus ends the seventy-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Cosmic Disturbance," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The seventy-second canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Now, when the Self-born One had withdrawn his vital breaths, the one born of space (the Wind) [arose].
In the printed manuscript, the reading is as follows:
"Abiding within the mass of wind, he abandoned his station within the Virāṭ self. (1)
Through the cessation of the vital breaths, the stability of the aggregate of wind within the elements is destroyed;
following that discussion, the state of the Virāj is described again as it was previously inquired about.

When the Self-born One, the Virāj, had withdrawn his vital breaths into his own heart-region and begun to dissolve them, the wind residing in the mass of air and born of the sky abandoned its stability— the boundary that supports the planets, the lunar mansions, the celestial chariots, and so forth. || 1 ||
For those, it is said, are his very vital breaths;
when they have departed, who else can maintain his station upon the wheel of the stars, which supports all living beings? (2)
Those layers of skin were the vital breaths of that Self-existent One; when they were traversed, they were withdrawn. || 2 ||
When the vital wind of Brahmā had ascended into the mass of wind, and [the world] having abandoned its equilibrium was entering into agitation, [the wind] moved along with it. (3)
When, having abandoned the previously mentioned state of stability, it becomes agitated in order to enter the state of equilibrium through withdrawal.
Supportless, they fell from the sky like sparks from a blazing fire driven by the wind, or like clusters of flowers from a tree onto the surface of the earth.
In the fire caused by the wind, the stars fell everywhere upon the surface of the earth like flying embers. || 4 ||
The rows of celestial chariots fell down— their roots shaken by the ripening of time, containing the fruits that are fragments of the world, and their supports the winds stilled.

The rows of celestial chariots (*vimānāvalī*), which were the abodes and places of enjoyment for the fruits of merit earned in the realm of the world, fell down; they were such that the roots of their enjoyment—namely, their *karma*—had become unstable and severed through the ripening of time. || 5 ||
When the fuel of Brahmā’s creative volition was on the verge of dissolution,
the paths of the perfected ones vanished like the flames of a blazing fire.
Of those who have attained supernatural powers and are radiant. || 6 ||
Wandering in the sky like bits of cotton driven by the winds of the kalpa,
the lineages of perfected beings fell silent as their own power waned.
Pointing out the perishability and insignificance of the *siddhis* such as *khecarī*, he says: "wandering about" (*prabhramantyaḥ*).
They are "mute," meaning incapable even of the activity of speech. (7)
The networks of wish-fulfilling trees and the cities of Indra and the other gods fell from the head of the mountain of the immortals, which was trembling from the earthquake.
The cities of Indra and the other gods, together with Indra and his followers, fell upon the heads and peaks of Mount Amabhūbhṛt, which is Meru. || 8 ||
Śrī Rāma said: O dear one, since the Virāṭ Brahmā, whose body is the universe, consists essentially of the creative will within consciousness,
what part of him is the earthly realm (bhūloka), what is heaven (svarga), and what is the netherworld (rasātala)?

Now, it may be argued that the gross body of Brahmā is the Virāṭ in the form of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), whereas the four-faced body residing in Satyaloka within it is merely a phenomenal appearance (*prātibhāsika*) fashioned by his mind. Nor is it logical to claim that even this latter body is his actual gross body, for it is impossible for one gross body to reside within another gross body; indeed, no one’s other gross body can ever exist inside their own gross body.

It may be possible to conceive of something seen or heard as being real; however, this being the case, how can there be a depletion of the masses of air and so forth—which serve as the support for the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) sustaining the cosmic body (*virāḍ-deha*)—through the mental resolve to withdraw the vital breaths from a mental body consisting of four faces, which is merely an illusory appearance similar to a dream-body? For it is not [the case] in a dream-body.

With the intention that, upon observing death through the withdrawal of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth, the destruction of the gross body well-known in the waking state is seen, Rāma raises an objection with the words beginning, "In consciousness, consisting of mere volition," and so on. Brahmā, the four-faced one, is consciousness; his essence is mere volition, which is the mind; and his body is the world-form, having the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) as its physical frame.

It is well known. Are the worlds, beginning with the earth-world (*bhūrloka*), the limbs—that is, the members—of that four-faced one whose nature is mere volition? For it is not possible for corporeal limbs to belong to an incorporeal mind. Even if they were possible, what limb would the earth-world be—is it the feet or something else? And what limb would heaven and the netherworld (*rasātala*) be?
"What limb? and "Which member?"—this is the inquiry regarding division. || 9 ||
O Brahman, how do these constituent parts abide within him, and how does he himself abide within his own body? (10)

Or even if he possesses a four-faced body that is corporeal, how could these exceedingly vast limbs— the earth and so forth— be contained within this body of such small dimensions? If it is argued that its extensiveness is such that it constitutes the very self of the universe (brahmāṇḍa), then how could he reside within his own body, inside this universe, in the world of Satya?
"Brahmā is essentially composed of mere volition and is formless; that this world exists is a certainty born within me—what else could I say? (11)

Furthermore, my conviction has arisen that Brahmā is composed of mere volition, formless and indeed bodiless, whereas this world exists with a definite form; therefore, if there is another way [of explaining this], please tell me. || 11 ||

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: First of all, this was neither non-existent nor existent; it remained free from all affliction, the supreme space of pure consciousness alone, filling the entire expanse of the quarters.

Therein, first, he establishes the introductory context by revealing the root [of the matter]—beginning with the words "In the beginning," and so on—in order to experience that the gross body is non-different from the mind-made body (*manomaya-deha*) and that its limbs are the limbs of that [mind-made body].
[He does this by stating: "Of hopes"—that is, of all desires—and "of directions" (the quarters) and "of treasuries."
Because its nature is the bliss of plenitude, the inhalation (pūraka) is indeed one.
It perceives this object of thought as being of its own nature, and it perceives this as being supreme;
never abandoning its own essential nature, it becomes conscious by virtue of its consciousness. (13)

This very supreme space (paramākāśa), without abandoning its own nature and without undergoing any modification or transformation, imagines its own spatiality as if it were a second moon; thus it perceives itself as a supreme object distinct from itself. || 13 ||
Know that living being (jīva) to be consciousness itself, which, due to its density, exists as the mind;
within this entire web of existence, nothing exists with a formal shape.

In that regard, know that the sentient being, the *jīva*, exists in the form of the mind (*manoveṣeṇa*) because it has become solidified through the cogitation of the triad characterized by the states of the object of awakening, the act of awakening, and the awakener; such is the nature of that consciousness.
He explains what was stated—that it does not abandon its own essential nature—with the words "to this extent" (*etāvatī*). To this extent...

Even though the web of existence has come into being through superimposition (adhyāsa) within the limits of the three folds and the locus of the individual soul (jīvabhāva), not even the slightest form possessing a mutually distinct shape exists there in ultimate reality; rather, it is only pure space, indeed a void—this is the connection with what follows. || 14 ||
The sky of consciousness (cidvyoma) remains within the Self as pure space, just as before;
yet that which appears here is nothing other than Śiva. 15.
What, then, is that which remains? He says: "the space of consciousness" (cidvyoma). || 15 ||
Then that mind, expanded, with its sense of "I" cultivated and throbbing,
remains as the ether consisting of volition— tranquil and imperishable.
Thus, because it is cultivated in the form of a conceit, even that which is non-existent flashes forth as if it were real; so he says: "Now," etc. (16).
The manifestation of consciousness as its own volition, conceived as "I am," experiences that which is utterly non-existent as a configuration within the void, like space within space.
He states with the words beginning "that" (tat) that even the conceptualization of the gross body is entirely unreal for him, following the conceptualization of the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra).
One knows, sees, and even experiences a manifested form;
yet it is established that this body is merely empty, consisting of nothing but mental construction.
Just as you perceive an imaginary city as being entirely empty,
so too the Unborn One perceived the body as nothing but space within space.
If the body is indeed empty, then how is it experienced as having form? To this he says: "It is indeed empty" (verse 19).
Because consciousness is pure, it experiences such and such an experience in this manner and then subsides by its own will.
He states that even the conceptualization of dissolution, liberation, and so forth is exactly like this: "of consciousness" (saṃvidaḥ) || 20 ||
When there is a thorough knowledge of reality for people such as ourselves, then know that this pervasive wandering of the world exists like a void, yet appearing as if it were real. (21)
When it is pacified, he says: "When" (yadā). In that case, the word should be split as "ātatam" (extended). || 21 ||
Through the thorough knowledge of things as they truly are, latent impressions (vāsanā) are stilled here;
from non-duality and the absence of ego, liberation remains as the final result. || 22 ||
Brahman is the ultimate truth as it truly is; through the thorough knowledge of that, false latent impressions are extinguished in this very birth. || 22 ||
In this way, he who is Brahmā is indeed this world that exists;
O Rāma, that body of Brahmā which is free from passion (viraja) is this very world.
"Let it be so; nevertheless, he says 'evam' (thus) to explain what has been asked regarding how this statement resolves the inquiry. || 23 ||
The delusion that arose from that [Self], which is of the nature of space and volition—that appears as this world; it is designated as the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa). 24.
And thus, even the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) possesses the nature of a gross body only through delusion; however, when investigated, it is found to be merely its mind.
Therefore, the intended meaning is that its dissolution is established by the dissolution of its constituent parts. || 24 ||
All this is indeed only space, consisting of the fabrication of mental constructs;
in reality, the world does not exist, nor do "you-ness" or "I-ness" exist anywhere at all.

Upon the orientation toward the waking state, there is a withdrawal of the dream-body and its limbs, just as there is a withdrawal of the dream-world and other realms; this occurs because both are essentially nothing but the space of volition (saṃkalpa). With this intention, he says: "Everything" (sarvam). || 25 ||
In some pure, subtle space, how or by what means could the world arise? What exists here, and what is the auxiliary cause? (26)
If it is asked how its unreality is to be known, [the author] says "Where? with the intention that it is because of its impossibility;
the five interrogative pronouns are used for the purpose of establishing its impossibility in every respect, such as place, time, and so forth.
Therefore, this has arisen as false; it is seen as false;
it tastes false; thus one perceives the void. || 27 ||

It tastes and expands through the states of the pleasant and unpleasant; by delusion, it perceives Brahman—which is beyond the world and free from conceptual proliferation—as the empty world, as a void like the sky, thus viewing it in the form of the universe. || 27 ||
By means of the primordial manifestation of the world, pure consciousness tastes itself spontaneously,
just as the wind moves within the sky of the Self through its own vibration, even in the midst of duality.

He states that very point clearly with the words "by [the power] beginning with the world. By the word "beginning" (ādi), its attributes—the ontological modifications such as origination and so forth—are included. || 28 ||
Know this world to be the sky of consciousness—neither something nor nothing, devoid of both duality and non-duality, empty, transparent, and free from affliction. (29)
By abandoning duality, there is something; by abandoning non-duality as well, there is nothing at all. || 29 ||
"O Raghava, I abide as one for whom all distinctions have been stilled;
being yet as if non-existent, remain likewise free from the sense of 'mine'."

Therefore, just like me, you too should exist as one who is truly real from the perspective of ultimate truth, yet appear as if unreal in worldly convention—like the body and so forth; however, the meaning is that you should remain free from the sense of "mine-ness" (nirmama). || 30 ||
Free from latent tendencies, with a peaceful mind, silent, and devoid of fickleness, do whatever comes to pass; or do not do it—what is the point of attachment here? (31)
Whether you are emerged from meditation, perform all worldly activities, or remain in a state of composure and do not perform them—what does it matter to a man?
The meaning is: why this insistence on one side? || 31 ||
That single experience which is beginningless and eternal is itself the visible; there is no other visible.
Those vast "great visions" of the visible are merely non-experiences within the true experience. (32)

Therefore, he concludes with the verse beginning "anādi" (beginningless), summarizing the essential point: that all which is perceived is Brahman alone, and the experiences of the perceived are merely instances of ignorance (*ajñāna*) transformed into the forms of delusion. The word *satye* (in the real) is formed with the suffix *kta* in the locative sense.
Thus, those non-experiences—that is, ignorances—within Brahman, whose sole essence is experience, are themselves [the cause] of the various diversities of delusion.
The meaning is that they are vast, great visions of the visible world. || 32 ||
Thus ends the seventy-second chapter, titled "The Description of Nirvāṇa," in the *Uttara-pāṣāṇa* section of the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa* within the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki.
Thus ends the seventy-second canto, titled "The Description of Nirvāṇa," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The seventy-third canto.
Śrī Rāma said:
The cognition of bondage, liberation, and the world is neither void nor composed of existence.
It is said that this primordial reality neither sets nor rises at all.
Here, the process of superimposition is further described for the sake of strengthening awakening;
following that is the answer to such questions as, "How are its constituent parts? and so forth.

Then Rāma, desiring once again to properly understand—both sequentially and according to the intended meaning—the manner in which the world is superimposed upon pure Brahman, which had been described as an introductory prelude to the answers to the three questions raised: "How is his earthly realm (bhūrloka)? How are these [subsequent worlds] his limbs? And how is his garment within?"—[proceeded].

In order to demonstrate, by way of a "lion’s glance" (siṃhāvalokana), the portion known to himself through the underlying intent (*tātparya*), he recalls the summary stated earlier in a distant passage with the words beginning "bandha" (bondage). [The intellect] consists of Being (*sanmayī*), having reality as its object. Precisely because it is the witness of all, it neither sets nor rises of its own accord. Therefore, this very intellect, which is the witness of all, performs some slight [function] in the cleansing of the object.

"You have taught, through the intended meaning (*tātparya*), that Brahman is primordial and inaccessible to speech and mind. The particle *kila* is used to dispel any suspicion of disagreement with the teacher's understanding. This connects with the subsequent phrase: "This has been understood by me. (1)
O Brahmin, this Brahma has been sufficiently explained by you to me;
however, speak further, for there is no satiety for me as I listen to this nectar. (2)
If that is so, should there then be a cessation of instruction? No; he says: "Furthermore" (bhūyaḥ). || 2 ||
O All-pervading Lord, for one whose vision perceives the turmoil of creation and so forth, as well as the vision of emptiness and so forth, none of these are real, nor are any of them unreal. (3)

The meaning is this: "true" refers to those things whose objects are non-sublated, while "untrue" refers even to those whose objects are sublated. This is because, from the perspective of various conventional agents, Brahman itself exists in such a manner; because there is no contradiction regarding causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*); because the position that the effect is non-existent (*asatkāryapakṣa*) is not accepted; because it is possible for even the power to bring about universal emptiness to exist within Brahman, which possesses all powers; and because all contradictions are resolved through *māyā*.
This being the case, I have indeed realized all that is true;
nevertheless, let the experience of creation be described further for the sake of even greater realization.

He says "Thus" (*evam*) to indicate that he has understood the reality of Brahman— which is eternally free and non-different from its substrate— just as one understands the majesty of Brahman as variegated by *māyā*.
Let the experience of creation, the sequence of the superimposition of the phenomenal world (*prapañca-adhyāsa*), be told again for the sake of many listeners.
"for the sake of awakening, or for the sake of an abundance of awakening. || 4 ||
