Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Whatever is seen here— the world, both stationary and moving— all of it, rich in every variety and possessing space, time, action, and so forth.
Upon its destruction— the great destruction known as the Great Dissolution (mahāpralaya)—
which brings about the transformation of Brahmā, Upendra, the Maruts, Rudra, and Mahendra.

When the gross [universe] consisting of the primary elements and their derivatives is destroyed within the subtle elements, it enters into the undifferentiated (avyākṛta) along with those subtle elements; that is to say, upon the destruction of the Great Principle (mahat), during the elemental dissolution (prākṛta-pralaya). [The term refers to one] in whom there is, or who is characterized by, the final modification of state (bhāvavikāra) of the bodies of Brahmā, Upendra, and others. || 6 ||
There remains something peaceful, utterly pure, unborn, and beginningless;
from which words turn back—what else can be understood? (7)
Then he describes that which remains, beginning with the words "it remains" (śiṣyate) and so forth. || 7 ||
Just as Mount Meru is of immense form in comparison to a mustard seed,
so too is space gross when compared to that which is the immediate void.
Space, though existing as extremely subtle and empty in relation to other things, is gross in comparison to that [which follows].
Just as these motes of dust are minute in comparison to the king of mountains,
so too is the gross cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) more minute in comparison to that [which it contains].
Likewise, even the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), which is gross and most vast in comparison to other things, is subtler and more minute in comparison to Him. || 9 ||
When that gentle time, devoid of measure, had long since matured,
he [remained] in that peaceful, supreme, primordial sky, which is of the nature of direct experience.

When the limiting adjuncts such as the sun— the cause of measurement— have dissolved, and in that period of dissolution which is reckoned without measurement, having long elapsed and reached its full duration equal to the lifespan of Brahmā, which is measured by two *parārdhas* [10].
Free from conceptualization, profoundly peaceful, and devoid of form in space and time, the great inner sky of consciousness perceives, as it were, the state of an atom.

The space of consciousness (cidākāśa), which is like deep sleep within the veil of māyā, perceives—as if reflecting upon—the state of atomicity consisting of the latent impressions (saṃskāra) of the world dissolved within itself, as if it were about to enter the dream state. 11.
Including that very non-existence within itself, like a dream,
it then knows by itself the meaning of the word "Brahman" as the pervasive nature of consciousness.

"Bhāvayan" means reflecting upon it. By reflecting upon that, one attains a slight degree of the appropriate state; because of this nourishment (*bṛṃhaṇāt*), it is known as *brahma*, which is the well-established meaning of the word *brahma*. Thus says the Śruti: "By austerity, Brahman is built up. (12)
The nature of consciousness experiences within itself its own atomicity of consciousness because it is consciousness;
then, as if seeing that very [atomicity], it remains as if it were the seer.

Since no cause other than the nature of consciousness (*cit-svabhāva*) can be established for the perception of that object—characterized by being its domain—he says: "The state of consciousness" (*cidbhāva*).
By this very fact, he demonstrates the attainment of the status of the seer: "That very [consciousness]" (*tāmeva*). || 13 ||
Just as in a dream one sees a dead person within oneself by means of the self alone,
so too the atomic consciousness, being itself dead, is the seer of death within the self.

If it is asked, "How can the relationship of the seen and the seer be established in a single locus when they are contradictory?", he replies, "Just as [in a dream]," because the contradiction is not fully considered—thus [he says] "yathā" (just as). || 14 ||
Thus, this single state of consciousness, though appearing as if it were duality within itself, remains in its own true nature, as if established as both the seer and the seen. || 15 ||
He states that even in such a conceptual construction, there is no impairment of actual unity, beginning with the words "tataḥ" (therefore). || 15 ||

Though entirely devoid of the nature of consciousness and utterly formless, it arises as if seeing a subtle body as though it were an object of sight; and at that time, like a seer, it perceives duality.
The explanation of "it is indeed empty" is "extremely formless. At that time, duality—consisting of both the perceived object and the perceiving subject—arises or is brought forth. || 16 ||
Perceiving itself as a subtle light through its own experience, it becomes conscious of its swelling, just as a seed becomes conscious of its state as a sprout.

And that seer, perceiving through the power of illusion his own self—which is of the nature of light—as an atom and limited, experiences and conceives, by the force of that perception, a state of swelling and expansion. 17.
Place, time, action, substance, the seer, the seeing, and the seen abide as entities distinct from one another, without their designations having arisen. (18)
At that very moment, because they are inseparable from it, conceptualizations such as the distinctions of space, time, and so forth also arise;
however, because there is no manifestation through speech and other means, these are said to be "unrisen designations. Thus he says: "Space," etc. (Verse 18).
Wherever that atom of consciousness shines, that place becomes perceived as space;
when it shines, that is time; and its shining is known as action. (19)

He clarifies the manner of conceiving its division with the words "the atomic consciousness" (cidaṇu). The sense is that it is impossible for something limited to be perceived as not being contained within space and time. || 19 ||
The perceived is known as the substance; the state of being a seer is the state of perception.
Illumination is the act of seeing; the eye is the cause of illumination. (20)

At that very moment, there arises the conceptualization of the distinctions among the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) that differentiate the threefold city (tripuṭī), as well as the witnessing consciousness (sākṣin) which serves as the cause for perceiving them;
thus he says: "It is perceived" (upalabdham). It is to be understood as the substratum for the conceptualization of substance, quality, action, and so forth. || 20 ||
Thus, swelling appears—either limited or infinite, according to the sequence;
though unreal, it is like the sky, having the very form of the sky, and emerging without exit.

In the same way, one should understand that in all cases there is the conceptualization of the distinctions of the threefold groups—such as the agent, the action, the instrument; the enjoyer, the object of enjoyment, and the act of enjoyment—as well as the witness thereof and its causality. With this intention, he says "evam" (thus).
[The world] is either limited by the delimitations of space, time, and substance, or it is infinite in terms of its countability and so forth. || 21 ||
The manifestation of the atom of consciousness appears within the body by means of its specific location;
that by which one sees is the eye—this is the summary of the functions of the sense organs. (22)

In this regard, he briefly demonstrates that once the triad of form and so forth is established, the conceptualization of the divisions of the instruments such as the eyes follows as a necessary consequence— by means of the words "of the conscious atom" (*cidaṇoḥ*). That through which the conscious atom— the individual soul (*jīva*)— sees the manifestation, namely the appearance [of objects] via the solar light and so forth,
through whichever cavity of the physical orb (*golaka*) and whichever supersensuous instrument (*atīndriya-karaṇa*), both of those constitute the eye.
This principle is the same for all perceptions through the senses, such as hearing and the rest; this is the summary, the concise statement.
(22) Within the manifestation of the atom of consciousness, first there is that which is devoid of name;
it consists of the mere sound of these [elements], and its nature is space. (23)

He says "the atomic consciousness" (cidaṇu) to indicate that the state prior to the conceptualization of the distinctions of name and form (*nāmarūpa*) regarding the objects of the five senses, such as hearing, is denoted by the term *tanmātra*. That which is the first, primordial nature of these five sense-objects, devoid of names— that is what the word *tanmātra* signifies.
The meaning is that because it is of such a nature, this very thing is of the form of space and is most subtle. || 23 ||
The mass of light that is the reflection of the atomic consciousness exists in a state of density;
when rendered helpless by the process of synthetic unification (*anusaṃdhāna*), it perceives the five sense organs which transcend the physical senses.

Thus, in this sequence, the atom of consciousness (cidaṇu), having become a dense state within space itself characterized by reflection, becomes a mass—the gross body; therein, by virtue of the pursuit of form and other qualities, the pentad of senses perceives—this is the summary. || 24 ||
In this way, the continuous connection of the atoms of consciousness sufficiently nourishes the visible world;
that very process is called "knowledge" (jñāna) and is designated as "intellect" (buddhi). || 25 ||

He describes the manner of conceiving the fourfold internal organ with the words "Thus" (evam). Through repeated experience of objects of perception such as sound and so forth, it attains nourishment and growth; therein, when the objects grasped by the senses are in the state of memory, that knowledge is called *citta*, and when they are in the state of determination (*adhyavasāya*), it is called *buddhi*. || 25 ||
Then the mind, having ascended that [state] and reached the stage of egoity (ahaṃkāra), accepted limitation by space and time as its own nature. (26)

Then, in the state of conceptualization and discursive thought (*saṃkalpa-vikalpa*), having ascended and become attached to that [consciousness] through the ego-inflation of the mind (*mano'bhimāna*) and the sense of "I" and "mine" (*ahaṃ-mamatā*), it reaches the stage of the ego (*ahaṃkāra*). He begins to describe the conceptualization of the divisions of space and time with the verse beginning "deśa... (verse 26), according to the method that will be explained below.
Wherever there is a fresh perception of this atomic consciousness, it will subsequently assign the designation of "prior" to that [moment]. (27)

He says "of the atom of consciousness" (*cidaṇoḥ*) to show that the conceptualization regarding that time and place proceeds only in dependence upon a subsequent conceptualization, as was previously described.
Of this well-known entity—the object such as sound and so forth—it is "fresh," meaning new; that is to say, primordial.
That atom of consciousness, the individual soul (*jīva*), in whom cognition occurs with respect to a substratum consisting of either space or time, is [the subject].

The meaning is that the atomic consciousness (cidaṇu), by means of the subsequent exclusion of that particular space and time, will assign or conceive the designation "prior" for what precedes; thus, this [designation] is indeed indefinite with respect to each individual soul and each object. || 27 ||
In another location, she will establish what is known as "upward";
in this manner, she will sequentially designate the names of the directions and so forth. (28)

Depending upon that conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), it will later designate only one [direction] as "upward" (*ūrdhvā*); however, the point is that there is a distinction in that there are many designations for the directions, such as upward, south, west, and so forth. || 28 ||
Although he will be as pure as space, he will himself come to perceive the meanings of words concerning place, time, action, and substance. (29)

Having thus conceptualized the distinctions of place, time, and object, as well as their respective names, for those persons who have grasped the linguistic conventions, it will be established by itself—through the very nature of the cognition of those various objects upon hearing the word; thus he says: "Place," etc. (Verse 29).
Thus, by its own experience, this internal body of consciousness— bearing the form of space itself— is established as that which is called the *ātivāhika*.

The meaning is that in this manner— the first being the subtle body (*ātivāhika-deha*) itself, then the differentiation of space, time, action, and objects, and finally the various distinctions of names— the entire body of the universe is produced, ending with name, in this sequential order. || 30 ||
And for a long time, through that very cultivation there, he grasps a full conviction regarding his own material nature. (31)

Thus, since the entire world consists of nothing but the mental constructions of the mind and is composed of parts of the subtle body (*ativāhika-deha*), how can there be a perception of it as being material? To this he says: "This very [body]... (31).
There is the delusion that it was fashioned by the pure sky within the sky itself;
it is like water in the river of heat, spread out by what is non-existent as if it were real.
Having the form of the sky, he assumes within his own body various mental constructions:
in some places he takes on the meaning of the word "head," and in others the meaning of the word "foot. (33)

That atom of consciousness, whose form is like the sky, assumes within its own body— which is itself a conceptual construct— the volitional ideation of the phenomenal world that is about to be described.
In some places it consists of the meanings of words such as "chest" and "sides," and is free from turbidity;
in other places it consists of the meanings of words such as "existence," "non-existence," "grasping," and "relinquishing."
Thus, it is said that the conceptualization of worldly transactions such as the rejection or acceptance of external objects should also be understood: "bhāva... (verse 34).
[She perceives] that which possesses a fixed form and configuration, constrained by space, time, and so forth;
which has become oriented toward objects, and which is pierced by the multitude of the senses. (35)
The determination of fixed forms such as "the cow has such-and-such a shape" or "the horse has such-and-such a shape," etc. (35).
Then Soṇu perceives his own form as imagined by himself,
composed of hands, feet, and other limbs, and endowed with the mental constructions of the mind and so forth.
In this way Brahmā is accomplished; in that same way Hari is accomplished;
in this way Rudra is accomplished; and in this way even a worm is accomplished.

He says that even for the lords, the conceptualization of bodies and so forth occurs solely through the power of volition, let alone for others: "Thus," he says—"nothing at all has come into being; it remains exactly as it is.
It is the void sporting within the void; consciousness expanding within consciousness. (38)
He says "and not" (na ca) to show that this entire conceptualization is indeed nectar. || 38 ||
Each chapter is the seed of bodies, the root of the creepers of the three worlds;
it provides the bolt for liberation and is a rain-cloud for the desiccation of worldly existence. (39)
He states that the Virāj, as the collective self (*samaṣṭyātmā*), likewise arises through conceptual construction, just like the individual self (*vyaṣṭi*): "In every bulbous root" (*pratikanda*).

The specific bulbous root for each individual body is the "pratikanda"; it is also the seed for the creeper-like three worlds that have it as their support. It provides the bolt of the creation of sense-objects, which acts as an obstruction at the gates of liberation. (39)
He is the cause of all effects, the leader in the performance of time and other functions; he is the primordial Person, acting according to his own will, both unarisen and arisen.
His body is not composed of the elements, nor are there bones in his little frame;
it cannot be grasped by the fist by anyone at all.
Precisely because there is no body composed of the elements and so forth, it cannot be grasped by a fist. || 41 ||
Therefore, by him whose soul was as powerful as the roar of a lion in battle amidst oceanic clouds,
he surely remained silent, like a man who is asleep.

Just as in a dream, despite the thundering roars of oceans, clouds, battles, and lions—which possess a powerful nature—a sleeping man remains in reality silent and without sound, so too did that king remain established in his own nature, which is free from phenomenal proliferation (niṣprapañca). This is the meaning. || 42 ||
Just as the experience of a wrestling match seen in a dream by one who is awake exists in memory yet is neither non-existent nor existent, so too does this [world] abide.

Just as the heroic prowess and clamor of warriors seen in a dream, when experienced by one who has awakened, enter the path of memory yet do not remain in an absolute sense, so too does this phenomenal world exist. (43)
Although his vast body measures many hundreds of thousands of yojanas,
he shines within a single atom, containing the three worlds within the pores of his skin.

With the intention that even a thousand things, though seemingly impossible, are indeed possible here because it is mere illusion (māyāmātra), he says: "Though his self consists of the multitude of worlds and possesses the qualities of the principal mountain ranges, the Unborn One does not fill even a nest the size of a grain of rice. (45)
Even grains, banyan seeds, and the like do not fill even that much of a hollow—a nest-hole—of a dwelling. || 45 ||
Although it is as vast as the expanse of hundreds of millions of worlds, in reality this [consciousness] does not occupy even an atom's worth of space, like a mountain in a dream. (46)
He is declared to be the Self-Existent (Svayambhū); he is called Virāṭ;
his soul is the cosmic egg (Brahmāṇḍa) and his body is the world, yet in reality, he consists of space.
He is called Sanātana and is also designated as Rudra;
he possesses bodies such as those of Indra, Upendra, the Maruts, clouds, mountains, and networks [of stars].
Having first conceived of the body as merely an atom of fire due to its being an object of thought, one gradually becomes established as the Great "I," which is expansive consciousness. (49)

Having stated everything, he summarizes it by saying "the fire" (*tejaḥ*). A mere atom of fire—the supremely subtle consciousness—first becomes the body of the mind (*cittavapuḥ*) through the act of cognizing. That very self of the mind, becoming expansive awareness through the described sequence, remains as "I am indeed the Great One, the Self of the Cosmic Egg. This is the summary of the meaning. || 49 ||
Through the perception of vibration, that which is called "vibration" is experienced;
it is that very same thing known as "wind" (anila) which exists in the form of the mass of air (vātaskandha). || 50 ||

For this very reason, his vital breaths are the masses of wind; with the intent that the destruction of those wind-masses was described by us through the withdrawal of that [breath], he says: "spanda... (verse 50).
The movement of the prāṇa and apāna is experienced through sensation;
by that [movement], this mass of wind which is described as being in space is [perceived]. (51)

He supports the previously stated claim—that "through the perception of vibration, the vibration of the vital breath (prāṇa) is experienced"—by means of what is well-known through universal experience, beginning with the word "prāṇa. The meaning is that this very vibration of the vital breath belonging to Him was previously described by us as the mass of wind within the space of that cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa). || 51 ||
Therefore, these [worlds] are imagined from the primordial mind by that [mind], just as a child imagines demons;
though they are non-existent, these particles of light have attained the state of celestial abodes.
The state of being a *dhiṣṇya*, that is, the status of being the abode of the sun, moon, planets, lunar mansions, and so forth. || 52 ||
The swing of the reversal of the prāṇa and apāna breaths, arising within its belly, bears the name "the mass of winds"; that great heart is the world.
The heart refers to the flesh, bones, and so forth located within the abdomen. || 53 ||
He is the primary seed of those whose bodies are according to their own desires, and of all those throughout the world who do not engage in conventional worldly activities for an eon.
The individual desires are the wishes for the differentiation of each individual life, pertaining to the separate bodies imagined by that [universal desire]. || 54 ||
Since those bodies arose from this [consciousness] as the self of the world through its desire to manifest, they exist such that their internal state is exactly like their external appearance. 55.

Regarding how bodies fashioned by imagination (paricchākalpitā) have attained the state of individuality (vyaṣṭitā), he says: "from the reflection" (praticchandyāt). That which exists as a reflection is *praticchandya*. The suffix *yat* is applied because it belongs to the *dig-ādi* group.
Because of that reason—since they have arisen from such a source—they consist of various latent impressions (*vāsanā*) corresponding to each individual body.
He says that the cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas) are to be understood in exactly this same way: "The bodies... (verse 55).
Just as the consciousness of that primordial seed was described previously,
even now it arises within the living being in that very same way, according to its own inclination.

In this regard, just as the existence of a single seed within another is inferred because we observe the successive emergence of a lineage of tree seeds, let it be inferred here as well; with this intention, he says: "Consciousness" (citiḥ). "Wished for by him" means desired by that Hiraṇyagarbha. || 56 ||
His phlegm, bile, and wind are the moon, sun, and wind;
his planets and constellations are his breaths and the droplets from his spitting. (57)

The phlegm, bile, and other humors belong to that Hiraṇyagarbha. For this very reason, the other planets, the hosts of stars, and the clusters of constellations are also his; when there is spitting or expectoration, their droplets are the drops of phlegm—this is the meaning. || 57 ||
We see his bones as mountain ranges, the masses of his fat as dense clouds, and we do not see his head, feet, skin, or body. 58.
The *jātikās* are like species born from fat; the *ghanas* are the clouds. Its head is the upper shell and its feet are the lower shell;
we do not perceive its skin or the coverings of the cosmic egg because they are situated at a great distance. || 58 ||
O limb of the world, know that the body of Virāj is indeed of the nature of conceptualization, for it consists of the imagination of that which is of the form of volition (saṃkalpa).
Therefore, everything—including the sky, mountains, earth, and oceans—is the tranquil space of consciousness (cidākāśa).

My dear one, know this world to be the body of Virāj. And that [body] is a mere mental construction (kalpanāmātra) belonging to that which consists of volition (saṃkalpa-rūpa) and has the nature of imagination;
it is not to be accomplished by external means, nor does anything consisting of mental construction possess any real existence.
Therefore, for this reason, everything—including the sky, mountains, and so forth—is entirely quiescent, meaning it is nothing but the space of consciousness (cidākāśa). || 59 ||

Thus ends the seventy-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Virāj-Self as a Stone," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the glorious Vālmīki’s *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*, a work of the Ṛṣis.
Thus ends the seventy-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Virāṭ Self," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The seventy-fourth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
In that kalpa, indeed, whatever form existed within his volition (saṃkalpa), [that was what appeared].
Listen to this established rule therein, which captivates through its diverse conduct.
Whatever limbs he has in this world, whatever his separate members,
and how he dwells within— all that is described here.

Now, in order to provide a detailed answer to the questions—"What part of him is the earth-world (bhūrloka)? What is heaven? What is the netherworld (rasātala)?"—and "How does he exist within it?", as well as the question—"How is it that this [universe], which is merely his mind, exists here without a physical form?", he first draws the attention of the listener with the words: "In that... (tasmin).

The meaning is: "Listen to this"—the arrangement of the division of the birth, activities, limbs, and so forth, of that body consisting of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) which existed within the volition (saṃkalpa) of that Virāj, which was seen as the interior of a rock and was of the nature of a Brahmā-kalpa; this is what will now be described. || 1 ||
That which is the supreme space of consciousness (cidākāśa) is the body of the Virāṭ Self;
its world-body, however, is light and devoid of beginning, middle, or end.

In this regard, he states that Brahman alone is his real nature, his primary and non-imagined form, whereas the Virāṭ-body is merely imaginary and, from that perspective, exceedingly insignificant—thus he says: "The supreme... (verse 2).
Brahmā, free from conceptualization, beholds that very space— resplendent all around his body— which is the egg of the universe consisting of conceptualization.
"How is it known that the nature of that [Brahman] is the space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*), devoid of beginning, middle, and end? To this he says:

"devoid of volition" (*saṃkalparahita*). Because that Brahmā, being outside the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) which is the body of his own volition, is—being devoid of volition and consisting solely of the space of consciousness as the witness (*sākṣi-cidākāśa*)—beholds his own egg, which is of the nature of volition; and that...
From the perspective of ultimate reality, the meaning is that it is simply space. || 3 ||
Brahman himself, possessing a radiant form, divided his own egg— which was of the nature of light— into two parts by his own volition,
just as a nourished bird divides its own body.

Therein, first, in order to describe his head, feet, and hips, he speaks of the division of the two upper and lower shells of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) with the words "Brahmā" and so forth. "Taijasam" means golden. Its form is luminous; its nature is that of consciousness presiding over the collective totality of the subtle bodies (liṅgasamaṣṭi). || 4 ||
He realized that one part of the cosmic egg had reached far into space,
while the portion situated beneath the earth was not distinct from himself.

"He perceived that it had gone far upward" means he conceived [it] as such; he conceived it as not distinct from himself and non-different. "The middle space alone" means the intermediate space within.
The upper portion of the cosmic egg is called the head of Virāj;
its lower portion is termed the feet, and the middle space is the waist.
The junction of the two distant fragments is extensive;
that infinite streak of sky appears dark and empty. (7)
The gap between the two halves of the skull is seen by people as a void, a dark line of the sky; the vast palate is the heavens, and the stars are drops of blood.
Consciousness is the wind within his body, and gods, demons, humans, and so forth are [the various elements]. || 8 ||
The palate is the uvula. "Portions" (lavāḥ) refer to the distinct modifications of consciousness and vital breath—that is, of the intellect and the life-force. || 8 ||
Within his body are worms, as well as *bhūtas*, *pretas*, and *piśācas*;
the various worlds are the cavities and hollows within his frame.

The spirits, ghosts, and demons are worms due to their greed for impurities such as blood and flesh. The other worlds—the realms of the sun, moon, and so forth—are the apertures of the eyes and other senses; the intermediate hells of Yama and others are the cavities below.
The base of his feet extends downward as the vast shell of the cosmic egg.
The hollows of the netherworld are the cavities beneath his knee-caps.
The earth, surrounded by oceans and islands, is unstable within its inner circle; it trembles with waters, hollowed with many cavities, and is ever-shifting.

*Tcalacalāyantī* means moving restlessly; *antarmaṇḍalī* refers to the circle of her middle, waist, hips, and buttocks situated therein; *lolā* means agitated by desire, disease, old age, death, and so forth; and she whose girdles, islands, and enclosures are like the inner garments, waistbands, and hip-bands [of the earth]. || 11 ||
The rivers, with their waters gurgling, are like veins carrying the essence of streams;
they flow toward Jambūdvīpa, which is like a lotus-heart of this [universe], with Mount Meru as its pericarp.
The *nāḍīs* are the vessels (*śirās*). By the word "rivers," their water is indicated; that is the nutrient-fluid (*rasa*) contained within those vessels. || 12 ||
The cavities are the quarters [of the body], empty; the liver, spleen, and so forth are the mountains;
the soft, unctuous, and banner-like structures are from fat, while the dense networks are the veins.

The *kukṣayas* are the abdominal cavities; the *kakubhas* are the directions; the *yakṛt-plīhādayaḥ* are varieties of flesh such as the liver and spleen; the *jālikās* are the membranous layers of the specific tissue *medas*; and the *ghanās* are the clouds. || 13 ||
The sun and moon are his two eyes, and the world of Brahmā is said to be his mouth;
his luster is declared to be the moon, and the snowy mountain (Himavat) is his phlegm.
Fire is semen. || 14 ||
Likewise, the world of Agni is his bile, which is exceedingly difficult to endure;
the great winds of the Vāta-sphere are the prāṇa and apāna breaths situated in the heart.
Within the masses of wind are the well-known great winds, such as Āvaha, Nivaha, Pravaha, and others. || 15 ||
In some places there are forests of wish-fulfilling trees and multitudes of serpents; there are infinite forests and groves consisting of networks of hair.
Other groves of wish-fulfilling trees, forests, and pleasure gardens are well-known in certain places such as Pātāla;
and the multitudes of serpents are his networks of body hair. || 16 ||
The entire upper portion of the cosmic egg became his vast head;
from it, a radiant flame arose, its light filling the cavity at the edge of the universe.

At the upper limit of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), there is a well-known aperture where a blazing flame shines; furthermore, it is established by scripture that "beyond this heaven, the light shines on the backs of all, on the backs of everything, in the worlds that are unsurpassed and supreme. This flaming crest or tuft is his radiant light. || 17 ||
Since this mind is itself [the agent], the mind is not employed by it;
indeed, the self alone attains the state of being the enjoyer—so who, how, and from what [could there be another]? 18.
Regarding the mind and senses of that creator who fashions such a body of Virāṭ, he says: "Himself" (*svayam*).

Since this Ordainer is himself the collective totality (*samaṣṭi*) of all minds, he is himself the mind alone. Therefore, no other mind is required for his various imaginings, as that would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress (*anavasthā*). If, however, the Self itself were the object of enjoyment for its own experience...
If you should think that [the Self] imagines [the world], that is not so; for it has the nature of being immutable and non-dual. Thus he says: "The Self alone...
The interrogative particles (*kiṃvṛtta*) are to be understood as before. || 18 ||
He himself has established the existence of these sense-faculties elsewhere;
for indeed, this entire collection of sense-faculties is merely a mental construction.

In this way, even his sense faculties are not applicable; for by him, the existence of sense faculties has been asserted and imagined in others such as ourselves. And in the imagination of sense faculties, they cannot serve as the causal basis, because that would lead to the consequence of infinite regress—this is the intended meaning. || 19 ||

Just as there is no difference between a part and the whole, so too there is not even the slightest distinction between the sense organ and the mind; for these two, which constitute a single body, possess complete identity.

If so, how then is the conventional distinction between the sense-faculties (*indriya*) and the mind (*manas*) maintained? To this he replies with the words "avayava... (beginning with "parts," etc.). The point is that there is indeed identity [between them], because the activity of the sense-faculties is seen to follow the presence and absence of the activity of the mind, and because in dreams it is observed that all the functions of the sense-faculties are accomplished by the mind alone. || 20 ||
Whatever activities there may be for the worlds, they are his very intentions alone; these move through the functions of the individual soul, though he is devoid of duality.
For this very reason, since all the activities of the entire world are indeed His own activities, even "activity" need not be asked about separately; thus he says, "of Him.

Since it is His own volition alone that moves as the essence of all worldly transactions—projected with duality and superimposed distinctions through the individual functions (*puṃvṛtti*) of all persons appearing in the form of the collective and the individual (*vyaṣṭi*). || 21 ||
When he awakens, his death and birth are to be known as nothing other than this;
he alone is this world, consisting of our own volitions, and nothing else.
In that case, the death and birth of this [Lord] would be identical to the death and birth of ourselves and others;

and thus there would be a contradiction with the well-known fact that His life-span lasts for two *parārdhas*. To this he replies: "Of the world" (*jāgate*). His death and birth are to be understood as the very death and birth of the collective world (*samaṣṭi-jagat*); they do not belong to Him in the sense of the individual (*vyaṣṭi*) manifestations known among ourselves and others. For...
This [universe] is the collective form (*samaṣṭirūpa*) in this world; it is that very same [Lord], whose nature is our own volition (*saṃkalpa*), and nothing else—this is the meaning.

Alternatively, according to the principle shown in the Purāṇas regarding "the fourfold [powers] being co-existent with that Creator," for one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*) through the knowledge of reality, [these powers exist] both in the time well-known as lasting until the end of two *parārdhas*, and in the individual manifestations (*vyaṣṭi*) such as ourselves that are well known.
Birth and death occur only within the world as conceived by our own vision, and not otherwise; the meaning is that they are established by one's own perception.

For he alone is renowned in this world. The meaning is that even our worldly activity, which consists of volition (*saṃkalpa*), is merely a form of him and nothing else. Alternatively, just as the senses and the mind [belong to him], so too do birth and death belong to him within the world.

There are no other objects of knowledge well-known to us and others; even his own mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*), which exists in a separate kalpa, is known in the world as being of the very nature of our own resolve. For he alone is all this, and there is nothing else whatsoever—this is the meaning. || 22 ||
The existence of the world depends upon its [the Self's] existence; by its death alone the world dies.
Just as there is a single existence for both vibration and the wind, such is the case for those two [the Self and the world]. (23)
From where [does it arise]? He says that this very [consciousness] is that: "by its existence" (tatsattayā). And [it refers to] those two: of that [consciousness] and of the world. || 23 ||
The relationship between the world and Virāj is like that between existence and its essence, or between the wind and its movement.
That which is the world is indeed Virāj, and that which is Virāj is remembered as the world.
The terms "Jagat," "Brahmā," and "Virāṭ" are synonymous;
they are mere mental constructs, whose true nature is the pure void of consciousness. (25)

These [entities], Virāj and Jagatī, are of the nature of pure consciousness alone; their resolution—well-known from such scriptural passages as "May I be many, may I procreate"—is merely volitional and devoid of intrinsic form (niḥsvarūpa). Thus, the final conclusion is that Brahman alone remains. || 25 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
By mere volition, that Virāṭ indeed became space itself assuming a form;
let it be so. But how can he remain as Brahman alone within his own body? (26)

Having accepted what was said up to the words "let it be so," Śrī Rāma recalls the remaining question with the words "within his own body" (*svadehāntar*). The meaning is: "Please state the answer to the question, 'How indeed does he abide within his very own form? || 26 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Just as you remain within your body through meditation,
so too does the Grandfather (Brahmā), whose nature is volition, abide within his own body.

Regarding the phrase "by means of meditation" (dhyānena): the meaning is that just as you experience it in mental worship—having seated the deity in an imagined jeweled pavilion within the heart and attending upon the deity with parasols, chowries, fans, mirrors, betel, and so forth, while remaining yourself in his presence—in that very manner [one should perform this]. || 27 ||
Likewise, for men and the foremost beings, the individual soul (jīva) resides within the interior of the city of Brahman;
its body, produced at birth, is like a reflection. (28)

Furthermore, he states—using the words "of men" (*nṛṇām*)—that the abiding of one's own subtle body (*liṅgadeha*) within the lotus of the heart of one's own gross body is established by the experience of all discerning people (*vivekin*).
[The term] "of men" refers to those who are primarily discerning. [It occurs] in the "city of Brahman," which is the body. It is the "daughter of birth."
Its form is that of a reflection corresponding to each respective body produced [by karma]; for this very reason, it is like a reflection within a mirror. || 28 ||
If even you are fully capable of remaining within the body, why would the all-pervading Brahmā, whose very nature is volition, not do so? (29)
He states, by means of the *kaimutika* (a fortiori) logic, that the Creator resides within His own body, in the verse beginning with "where" (yatra). || 29 ||
For the immobile resides within the seed, and the mobile resides within that object;
what then does not reside within that body, consisting as it does of the imagination of one's own consciousness? 30.

Where even stationary beings possess the capacity to abide within their own seeds and other bodies, what need is there to mention that [capacity] of the four-faced form, which consists of the conceptualization of consciousness whose every power has manifested? Thus he says: "The seed... (verse 30).
May he be with form, having the nature of space, or may he be formless like the void;
may he abide both outside and within, and yet be external to the distinction between the outer and the inner. (31)

And so, whether Brahmā exists with form as the architect of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), being of the nature of the sky of consciousness, or whether he exists without form as the collective totality of minds (*manaḥ-samaṣṭi*)—in either case, he abides both outside and within. This is merely a conceptualization of outer and inner; for [Brahmā] stands outside his own essential nature only in appearance, yet is not distinct from it. That which you imagine to be internal does not exist apart from him.
The meaning is that the nature of existence is differentiated. || 31 ||
Delighting in the Self, observing the silence of wood, he is not dull-witted yet is as inert as a stone;
though composed of "I" and "you" and other such notions, he abides within the Virāṭ Self.

Then, as to what he is like externally and internally, and in what kind of nature he abides in the ultimate sense (paramārthatas), he says: "delighting in the Self" (ātmārāma). Externally, he is the Virāj, whose self is the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa); internally, however, he consists of the individual and collective (vyaṣṭi-samaṣṭi) forms of the subtle and gross elements, such as the sense of "I-ness" (ahaṃtva) and so forth. But in the Self, he is one who delights in the Self.
Though he remains silent as a log, speechless and as inert as a stone, he does not abide as something insentient because his nature is the singular essence of consciousness.
Though his limbs are entwined like a creeper, discarded like grass or wood, and he utters cries like the rushing of water,
the knower of reality remains with a mind as tranquil as the interior of a stone, even while engaged in various kinds of worldly activities.
To show that such a state belongs not only to Virāja but to all who possess knowledge of reality (tattvajña),

he clarifies it through examples, beginning with "āveṣṭitā" (enveloped). A knower of that— that is, one who knows reality— is like a creeper, grass, a thicket, wood, a man, or an image, which was previously enveloped and bound by a rope or similar means in regard to the matter of enduring injuries from others.

Even when cast off and abandoned later on, they do not become angry; rather, they remain silent and still. Just as a torrent of water, though its flow is obstructed and its body is cut away, does not abandon its former state, so too, even while moving through a manifold web of activities, one whose mind is as tranquil as the interior of a stone remains in the very same state as before.
The meaning is that he is affected even slightly by anger, joy, despair, and so forth. || 33 ||

Thus ends the seventy-fourth canto, titled "The Description of the Virāṭ Self," in the Nirvāṇa Section of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa*, within the Means to Liberation (*Mokṣopāya*) of the *Ārṣa* tradition. Canto 74.

Thus ends the seventy-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Virāṭ Self," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa*, in its exposition of the essential meaning.
The seventy-fifth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Now, while Brahmā was absorbed in meditation, the world of Brahmā stood before him.
With my eyes cast down, I slowly looked in the directions and saw [him] before me. || 1 ||
While the Creator was absorbed in meditation, the fire of universal dissolution, born from the twelve suns,
is described as burning the entire world here.
Having concluded the incidental discussion on the question, he resumes the narrative at hand with the words "atha" and so forth. The connection with what follows is as follows:
"Then," that is, after seeing the cities of Indra and the other gods and the mountain peak of Meru, "I, having slowly cast my eyes in all directions, saw a second sun. (1)
At midday, a second sun clearly rose in the west,
like a conflagration at the face of the horizon or like a forest fire upon a mountain.
By the word "at midday," it is understood that the sun was situated in the middle direction. "In the directions" means among the cardinal points. "In front" means having gone forward;
"with the face toward the western direction" means facing west. The connection is: "I saw a second sun from the one standing in the middle. || 2 ||
Then, like the world of Agni in the sky or the submarine fire in the ocean,
I beheld the blazing sun in the direction of the southwest.
The similes beginning with "like a conflagration" (digdāham iva) are to be applied individually to each of all the suns. || 3 ||
The sun is in the southern quarter; the sun faces the direction of fire (the southeast);
the sun is in the eastern quarter; the sun faces the direction of Ishana (the northeast). || 4 ||
The sun was in the direction of Kubera, the sun was at the edge of the northwestern quarter, and the sun was in the region of the western direction; because of that, I was filled with wonder.
"In the direction of Varuṇa" is a restatement of what was previously introduced. || 5 ||
Just as I was quickly considering the chaotic deficiency of my ritual,
the sun rose from the earth like the Aurva fire from the ocean.
Deficiency in ritual performance and adverse fate. || 6 ||
In the eleventh [chapter], within the sky of the quarters, there arose a triad of suns that appeared like a reflection of all the suns.

In the intermediate space between the groups of directions, within the middle sky—where the compound is used with an irregular (asamartha) sense according to grammatical convention—it is understood that another sun has risen even above, because it is stated that there are eleven suns in the middle.
Among those, in the eleventh, the middle sun, three other suns appeared like a reflection within the interior of a mirror. For that indeed...

This single form of Rudra, consisting of the triad of Arka-s (the suns) arisen within the central sun, is composed of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva; it is this very "Raudra" body that is revealed by the Gāyatrī mantra as "that most excellent splendor of Savitṛ.
For this very reason, it is the source of the twenty-four thousand verses produced from the twenty-four syllables [of the Gāyatrī].

In the *Ādityahṛdaya*, which constitutes an essential compendium of the earlier *Rāmāyaṇa*, [the Lord] is saluted as the primordial Paraśiva of the three forms with the words, "Obeisance to the one who is Brahmā, Īśāna, and Acyuta, whose body is Raudra"; thus they say that He alone is the most excellent object of worship. || 7 ||
For that body there was fierce, and in its midst were three eyes;
it was a blazing mass of twelve suns.

There, in the midst of that sun, his fierce body—within which were three eyes—that very fierce body, having become a host of Vivasvats with the dimensions and form of twelve suns, "burned intensely," as the connection with the following verse shows:
"He burned intensely in every direction, like fire in a dry forest. (8)
Then there arose a summer day that withered the world into fragments.
O lotus-eyed one, that fireless conflagration, in which the clusters of firebrands suddenly became invisible,
was a burning by a fire that was not fire.
Precisely because of the invisibility of the firebrands and the thickets, a burning by solar fire occurred, even though it was devoid of any commonly known fire. || 10 ||
My limbs became as if scorched by a forest fire and exhausted;
then, leaving that region, I ascended far away.
He ascended high into the distant sky. || 11 ||
Standing in the sky, I beheld the one of fierce splendor risen like a ball struck by a firm blow of the palm, as if it were the very firmament itself.
He saw the twelve-fold host of Ādityas blazing even in all ten directions,
like the great, moving circle of stars with its constellations appearing as if on fire.

In that regard, the meaning is that I saw the stellar sphere—the wheel of constellations—moving in the form of whirlpools like a flame; it is called *satārāvā* because it protects or pervades (*avati*) the sky along with the stars in those directions. || 13 ||
It produced a great "kuha-kuha" sound, with the tumult of the seven oceans boiling; the interior of the worlds and the interiors of the cities were filled with dense masses of flaming firebrands.

From this point forward, all the words ending in the accusative case found within these twelve and a half verses are to be construed as adjectives qualifying the group of twelve Ādityas under discussion. *Kuhakuha* is an imitation of the sound of boiling.
The mountain was turned vermilion by the mass of flames acting as a thick cloth;
it had the great, blazing caverns as its steady lightning-streaked banners. || 15 ||

By him, the mountains were made the color of vermilion through dense masses characterized by flames and the billowing folds of red garments; and by him, the crests of the peaks became like steady flashes of lightning within the blazing palaces of the great world-protectors.

With its dense masses of stone, it produced columns of smoke rising from the earth, while the circles of cities were shattered with a crackling sound amidst the violent clashing of the trembling weapons.

The connection [of the verse] is as follows: it is as if it were creating, or performing, a pavilion characterized by the world's fire, which is rich with thousands of glass pillars in the form of smoke-sticks—that is, smoke shaped like staffs. || 16 ||
The pavilion that is the abode of the world was filled with thousands of pillars of glass,
and it resounded with a most ghastly gurgling from the cries of the stars— the great elements— boiling within.
With the loud cries and lamentations of living beings, of creatures, and of the great elements such as earth and the rest, it was exceedingly hoarse.
It was fierce with the crackling *caṭacaṭa* sound of the earth, worlds, and cities collapsing; it was a place where the surface of the jewel-bearing earth was scorched by the impact of falling stars.

It was intense with the crackling sounds of objects bursting on all sides due to the falling of beings, living creatures, worlds, and the cities contained within them; it was one by which the surface of the earth was rubbed by the gems [scattered] from the impact and collisions caused by the disintegration and falling of the stars, beginning with Aśvinī. 18.
In every place, the multitudes of people were moving about and being consumed by fire;
the quarters of the sky were filled with the foul stench of the hosts of spirits who were crying out in exhaustion and boiling in agony.

By whom the quarters were made foul-smelling and unfit for habitation by multitudes of beings—crowds of people moving, running, and burning in all places, dwellings, and their own homes; and by hosts of creatures and groups of living beings who were emaciated, dead, wailing, boiling, and being cooked. || 19 ||

The great ocean, whose waters were exhausted by the submarine fire, had its aquatic creatures distressed by the heated depths; the interiors of its cities were reduced by the burning of the fire of universal dissolution, leaving behind only wailing.
By which [fire], the interior of another city—a different town—was such that its cries had ceased and its weeping was stilled, being consumed by a fire spreading in all directions. || 20 ||
The mountain was propped up by the tusks of elephants of the quarters that had been split and scorched;
it was encircled by the vast circles of smoke rising from the deep fissures of the earth-supporting mountains.

By him, the mountains at the ends of the quarters were propped up and supported at their bases with the very tusks of the elephants of the directions—tusks that resembled pillars—as those elephants split apart, shattered, and were burnt. || 21 ||
The circle of cities was crushed and scorched by falling mountains,
while the great elephants and mountain lions let out cries of "paca-paca-paca."
The oceans and mountains were feverish with creatures rising up, tormented by the heat;
the women of the Vidyādharas fell down, their hearts bursting and their life-breath departing.
By whom the oceans and mountains were made feverish, as it were, with fevers arisen from beings tormented by heat who were rising up and leaping out. || 23 ||
The gods were forced to emerge from their heads, exhausted by the sound of wailing and lamentation;
the surface of the earth was scorched by the underworld, where the blazing flames of the world of the nāgas were erupting.

Some are exhausted by loud cries and weeping; others, having pierced the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra) through the power of yoga, emerge from the head, and for this very reason they are immortal yogins where [they go].
In that dried-up ocean, where the fierce aquatic creatures were constantly being cooked and tossed about,
the submarine fire (Aurva) seemed to fly up in a thousand directions due to the lack of fuel.
By him, the fierce and terrifying aquatic creatures such as crocodiles were always cooked and long-simmered in dry oceans through their violent churning and tossing about.
Having risen and danced as he went, seizing the courtyard of the sky,
there then arose [a fire] adorned with garments of blazing flames like *kiṃśuka* flowers.

By whom the celestial nymphs of the sky’s courtyard were seized—having thus described the host of the twelve suns, he describes the fire of dissolution arising from them as a dancer with the passage beginning with "atha" and ending with "naṭaḥ.
He is adorned with garments (*aṃśukaiḥ*) in the form of blazing flames, having the color of *kiṃśuka* flowers. || 26 ||
Like the fire at the end of an aeon for the sake of a wild dance, bearing a garland of flickering torches,
it was loud with the crackling of its flames, like a fierce warrior shouting as he fights.
Mālyavat was accompanied by flickering torches; it resounded loudly with bursting flutes and other instruments, and was filled with the grand display of various musical sounds.
With arms of blazing flames and hair of smoke, the actor who has worn out the world as his hut caused the forests, groves, cities, and towns to burn. (28)
The mandalas, islands, fortresses, jungles, and dry lands; all the cavities, the great space, the ten directions, and the summit of heaven. (29)

All cavities refer to the openings in the earth, such as the netherworlds (pātāla) and so forth; the great space above the earth is the sky; and the head, or upper portion, of heaven refers to the celestial realm (dyuloka). || 29 ||

With its precipices appearing as chasms, its waterwheels, towers, and cities reaching out toward the vast horizons; with its peaks, its throngs of perfected beings (siddhas), its mountains, and its oceans—(30)

Likewise, in some places the slopes of the horizon are vast and delightful, featuring chasms, water-lifting machines, mills, palatial mansions, and cities; likewise, there are mountain peaks, hosts of Siddhas residing therein, mountains endowed with them, and oceans and seas. (30)
Lakes, ponds, rivers, gods, asuras, humans, and serpents, along with the quarters of space, were filled with the sounds of "śana-śana" and with men worshipping Śiva’s flames.

The quarters and intermediate directions, together with the persons situated within them, blazed with the flames of Śiva’s radiance—the tongues of fire from Rudra’s eyes—with the sounds of "śana-śana"; this is the syntactical connection with the preceding verse. || 31 ||
The Rākṣasas, with their mouths emitting shrieks, had banners blazing with masses of flames;
they were terrifying with loud "bhaṃ-bhaṃ" roars and abundant ashes.

Furthermore, these quarters were ablaze with networks of flames; they were possessed of hair standing erect, and being such, they were tossing one another about with terrifying "bhaṃ-bhaṃ" sounds—well-known for their resonance—and with abundant ashes. Intent on the sport of *kṣveḍā* (mutual splashing of dust, water, and so forth), they were like the Kurākṣasas.
Flames issued forth from the caves of the chasms, mountains, and the earth;
all classes of living beings, reddish in hue, remained within the bellies of those flames.
The inauspicious [omens] brought about the beauty of the lotuses on land,
which resembled clouds of vermilion and instantly appeared as if dripping with blood.

Moreover, those quarters, devoid of splendor and wealth, immediately assumed the beauty of land-lotuses—their interiors occupied by swarms of bees—by means of masses of flames flashing with blood-red luster. || 34 ||
With masses of flames reaching out into the world and singing "dhagaddhag," the sky became strewn with red cloths, as if covered by the clouds of twilight.
There is an option between [the senses of] "knowing" and "imagining. || 35 ||
The regions were covered by forests of blossoming *kiṃśuka* trees that seemed as if they had taken flight,
while other places, filled with flowering *aśoka* groves, appeared as if enveloped by the submarine fire (*aurva*).
The phrase "the sky was covered" is to be supplied [to each clause]. The word *vā* ("or") is as before. Thus, the oceans were enveloped by the Aurva fire;

and the lakes—possessing blossoming aśoka groves—were as if surrounded by land-lotuses (*sthalābja*), or as if encircled by young suns (*ravirāḥ*), or as if pervaded by the rays of the rising sun. This is the connection with what follows. They are called *ravirāḥ* because they take in (*rānti*) or accept the suns (*ravi*).
The suffix *aṇ* in the word *rāvirāḥ* should be understood as having the sense of the base itself (*svārthika*). || 36 ||
Like lakes encircled by land-lotuses, like oceans filled with moonlight,
it possessed an arrangement of smoke and blazing flames of various colors.

Likewise, in the forests, the fire— possessing youthfulness, that is, the state of being young— seemed as if it were to establish, or bring about, a mature, actual fire upon the painted fire depicted on the surface of the palace; for it was a continuous arrangement, a series, of various colors, blazing flames, and patterns of smoke.
The connection with the following verse is as follows: he became exceedingly expansive, like Ananta, the king of serpents, who possesses a thousand-fold succession of hoods. || 37 ||
Like the fire of youth in the forest, he was like Ananta, having arranged [the trees] as if to place a kindled fire within the support of the painted mansion-like creepers.
Due to the rising and setting [of the sun], the Vindhya mountain fell into a state of distress,
as its branches became like glowing coals and it seemed to leap up from a forest of flames.

Furthermore, with the intention that the desire of the Vindhya mountain—which yearned for the absence of the rising and setting of the sun—has now borne fruit, he says: "From rising, setting, and so forth," in the half-verse; the words beginning with "aṅgāra" connect with what follows. (39)
Slowly, as if slightly agitated, it became unbearable;
it was garlanded by swarms of wandering smoke whose blackness shone intensely in its very center.
The Sahya mountain is famous in the southern region. It is garlanded by bees characterized by smoke, which possess a dark luster shining here and there;
and it is soiled by lotuses characterized by flickering flames mingled with smoke. Thus, the analogy of the sky to a lake is established.
The sky was seen like a lake, its lotuses darkened by the flames of the forest fire;
upon the mountain peaks in the air, the tips of the flames stood as crowning crests.

The directions are like female dancers characterized by death, whose crests are the mountain peaks, whose ear-ornaments are the tips of flames, and whose hair-like locks are the comet known as Dhūmaketu— a particular portent consisting of swirling smoke—
located upon the mountains' ridges, summits, and in the sky of the intermediate spaces.
And in a region of pure space, devoid of mountains and the like, the Truths, being tasteless—meaning empty of the flavors of compassion and so forth—danced.
The dancers, whose hair was like banners, danced without moisture;
the ground of the upper vault of the universe had the flames of fire placed upon its palms. 42.
The earth, which has the upper portion of the cosmic egg as its door-leaf and lid,

rests upon the surface of the world below; being such that it possesses the flames of fire in its lower part, within it the hosts of living beings— those multitudes of creatures who are like parched seeds— are leaping up due to threats and torments.
Such was the state of the frying-pan ground that it became a cauldron or a shallow pan; this is the implied meaning. || 42 ||
The ground was like a frying pan, where floods of spirits flew up in terror;
it resounded with rows of clanging sounds, possessed water, mud, and fire, and was reddened by faces of various colors.
Furthermore, at that time of dissolution, when the Earth was struck upon her breast by the Goddess of the World (Jagallakṣmī) as she wept,

this [Earth] became reddish-golden through various-colored faces— resembling crystals, gems, and gold— which were composed of earth divided into distinct continents, waters characterized by the seven oceans and so forth, and fires pervading them, all appearing like various jewels.
It became like a row of jingling bracelets. || 43 ||
Then, in the heart and forearm of the Goddess of the World's Fortune, [the weapons] became as if made of gold;
meanwhile, the mountains produced crackling sounds and the trees produced rattling noises.
Vidalana means being shattered or torn asunder. || 44 ||
The lands were utterly shattered by tumultuous outcries;
the oceans took on the appearance of boiling water, thick with frothy surges.
In this way, he imagines that the oceans also wept as if they had turned their faces toward one another—this is expressed by the word "abdhayaḥ" (the oceans).
[They wept] upon their own faces, which were adorned with the reflection of the sun as its tilaka. || 45 ||
In every mouth, they struck the face of the sun with the palm of their hands,
while the mountain took on the appearance of the earth’s surface with its waves tossing and surging against one another.
Furthermore, those oceans— mutually surging and joined by the clashing of waves, and thus exceedingly turbulent— carried away, that is, brought as their food,

the mountains which had attained the form of the earth's surface through the gradual leveling of clay, stones, and other materials; they swallowed them, meaning they reduced the enraged, dull, and foolish masses of clay, stone, and so forth to their own sustenance.
It is well known that they devour. || 46 ||
The dull-witted [ones], as if enraged by the waves of the Jahnu’s daughter (the Gaṅgā) upon their bodies—[the sense is that they have reached them;
the construction is "the mountain was reached upon the body"]—uttered deep roars from their caves, like those who feed on the sky of their hopes. 47.

And in some places, the fiery sound produced by the collision of the mountain slopes of Jvālātaṭa and Giritaṭa echoed in other regions the roars of those oceans emerging from the mouths of caves—sounds of the form "guhā-guhā"—just as the voice of a disciple mimics the words spoken by his teacher. This is the meaning. || 47 ||
A fire-born sound, arising from the crackling of flames, resounded;
the walls of the mountains, heated like glowing coals, collapsed upon the cities of the world-protectors.

Furthermore, at that time, with the cessation of the clouds of universal dissolution, all ten directions— having been released from rain and scorched by the falling showers from the cities of the ten world-protectors, their mountain walls filled with glowing embers— became truly like those of madmen and fell into a state of helplessness and agitation. (48)
Even the ten directions fell into a state of helplessness, behaving like those driven mad;
[the world] was filled with mountains, trees, houses, and caves dripping with molten gold.

Having become like molten gold, Mount Meru—possessing a beautiful form and accompanied by the surrounding mountains, Indra, trees, mansions, and cave-dwellings—gradually melted away in the heat, like snow. || 49 ||
Gradually, Meru, whose form was beautiful, became like frost in the heat;
in an instant, from that fire, Himavat was melted like lac.
Like lacquer or a seed of the *akṣa* tree, it is melted and dissolved. || 50 ||
Completely cool within and pure, like a virtuous man among the wicked;
even in that state, the Malaya breeze remains possessed of stainless fragrance. (51)
"Amalasaurabha" means fragrant—that is to say, possessing a pure scent. || 51 ||
The noble-minded person does not abandon their supreme quality even when facing destruction;
even while perishing, the great soul bestows joy and not sorrow. (52)
The Great Supreme Person. || 52 ||
Even when burned, sandalwood serves only for the delight of those who live;
a superior thing never becomes a non-thing.
Even when consumed by the fire of universal dissolution, gold does not perish;
nor do those two—the gold and the ether—perish within that fire of dissolution.
Though burnt, even while being burnt, he did not perish; he was not as one who has been destroyed. || 54 ||
The form of those two alone is praiseworthy, for they are indestructible even when everything else is destroyed;
the sky is indestructible due to its all-pervasiveness, and gold is imperishable due to its extraction from ore.

With the intention of praising the fact that only an indestructible entity is the essence, he says: "Of those two alone," meaning because they have been drawn forth—that is, extracted from defects—and purified. || 55 ||
I consider goodness alone to be happiness, neither passion nor darkness;
for they are like moving high forests showering down scattered embers. (56)

For this very reason, I consider pure *sattva* alone— extracted from *rajas* and *tamas*— to be the essence of bliss through its manifestation as the bliss of Brahman. Like a great cloud characterized by the fire of universal dissolution, which possesses massive flames of smoke and has burnt away the mountains in the form of clouds, it shines in the sky like lofty forests moving about.
The grammatical connection is that Aṛṣaṇa became one whose limbs were scattered. || 56 ||
The mountain of burnt clouds became a fire-cloud with great smoke and flames,
for those whose bodies were vast yet empty, suffering from the pain of forgetting the essence.

When the juices and waters have been utterly dried up, due to the total disappearance of even their residual impressions, the four kinds of beings—those born from eggs and so forth—become distressed by forgetfulness, empty, and their bodies become vast and desolate. || 57 ||
Of the dry leaves of the celestial trees, which had become like vessels for the clouds, and of those clouds themselves, which were scorched by the flames of the dissolution; (58)

Likewise, for those clouds that are dry and burnt— therefore resembling the leaves of trees in the sky, having reached a state of emptiness— or rather, for those very wet clouds forcibly burnt by the flames of universal dissolution;
O dear one, even their ashes are like the ashes of the defects of a knower of reality, which have been consumed by the fire of wisdom.
The logical connection is that it has not been observed anywhere. || 58 ||
O dear one, not even ashes are seen anywhere belonging to the Knower, as if he were free from all defects;
for the blazing fire does not leap over Mount Kailāsa.
He does not leap over nor does he overcome Kailāsa, the silver mountain. || 59 ||
At that moment, Rudra, enraged for an entire eon, consumed him with the fire from his eye;
there arose a crackling roar like that of trees and massive rocks bursting and burning under the heat.
That Kailāsa. Enraged for the sake of the cosmic dissolution (kalpa), he describes its burning as well, beginning with the words "dāha" and so forth. || 60 ||

The mountains, their edges trembling as they were adorned with the swelling masses of clouds that were like crests of flame, seemed as if they were fighting with floods of clubs, stones, and clods of earth.

The mountains were like so many foothills at his feet; moreover, those mountains, with their peaks—both the moving ones serving as ear-ornaments and the final, foremost summits—blazing forth in the sky, appeared as if they were forests of thick lotuses in full bloom. 61.
They became like forests of thick lotuses blooming in the sky;
the thought that "creation existed only at some time" passed into the realm of memory.
As if reminding the foolish that the end of the eon had arrived,
the fires— reaching their ultimate intensity through heat and torment and intent on total destruction— effected the disappearance of the worlds, just as they do for the wicked.
"Unrememberability" means being directly perceived [as non-existent]. The ellipsis is "reminding fools of the worthlessness of the world.
The "denial" of unrealities—of false things such as a hare's horn—is their absolute non-existence. || 63 ||

Their limbs tormented by the falling of thunderbolts, they resembled circles of thickets of flickering firebrands; like the winds at the time of universal dissolution licking up the fires at the end, the hosts of gods were scattered in the cataclysm.

When that dissolution had set in, the winds of the time of universal destruction— by which the branches of small trees (*gulma*) were tormented by falling thunderbolts, and by which the rows of immortals (*amarāvali*) were shattered and scattered as they resembled circles of blazing firebrands— issued forth from the midst of the flames at the end of the fire.
They blew as if licking the very quarters of the sky. || 64 ||

With flames white with glowing embers carried by the blows of wandering firebrands, their heat intensified by the ash rising from the forest of *dāladruma* trees bursting forth as they were violently shaken;
and darkened by the rows of flickering tongues of flame dancing amidst the falling peaks of the fire.
Winds blew with such speed, possessing a velocity like that of a well-praised fire that has consumed everything without remainder.

Furthermore, as to what kind of winds blew then, he says: *vyālolanti*. [The winds] were such that they produced clouds—that is, they filled the sky (*vyāpta-ākāśā*) or generated clouds—by means of the heat arising from the forests of fire-trees (*analā drumāḥ*), which were accompanied by ashes and were bursting open or blooming with the tips of their flickering flame-sprouts (*jvālā-pallava-koṭibhiḥ*). Likewise...

They were darkened by streaks of soot-laden flames— pale yellow in color and carrying glowing embers— which issued forth from them due to the striking and clashing of wandering torches; likewise, they were blackened by rows of smoky tongues of fire that fell and flickered amidst the crests of the fires, appearing like collyrium as they slipped down.
Likewise, when the entire world was set ablaze by the kindling of fires, winds possessing such speed as to be worthy of high praise blew with great force; this is the meaning. || 65 ||
Thus ends the seventy-fifth canto, titled "The Description of the Great Fire at the End of the Kalpa," in the Nirvāṇa Section of the Holy Vasiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa, composed by the Sage Valmiki.
Thus ends the seventy-fifth canto, titled "The Description of the Fire at the End of the Great Kalpa," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The seventy-sixth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Now, while the wind at the end of the aeon blew, shaking the mountains,
By the force of the ocean's waves, it caused whirlpools to form in the sky.
The rising of the Puṣkarāvartaka clouds is described here as occurring in the upward direction and the quarter of Varuṇa;
likewise, the withdrawal of the fire is described in the direction of Agni.
On Avadhūtācala, the mountain that trembles. || 1 ||
In oceans that are devoid of seals, in the dense transgression of boundaries,
among the poor and the wealthy alike, who are driven by the affliction of poverty and the lack of water.

When those who were without mudrās, devoid of marks, wealthy, or poor, had fled in haste due to the calamity of drought and the suffering of water-scarcity—this is to be connected with either "the cloud" or "the surface of the earth. (2)
When the surface of the earth was deprived of its share of living beings and scorched by fire, and even the netherworld had, in the course of time, sunk into the depths of Pātāla; (3)
Something entirely distinct from the well-known netherworld (pātāla), that is to say, destruction (vināśa). || 3 ||
Whether in heaven, or when the multitude of created beings has perished, in a world devoid of celestial light, or in the quarters of the sky which have become the abode of sorrow; (4)
In the world of the gods, the solar light situated in the sky becomes fire when it has attained that state.
From some part of the hollow of the sky, like hosts of arrogant demons,
the Puṣkarāvartaka clouds let out a deep gurgling roar.
"Guluguleti" is an onomatopoeic imitation of sound, intended to represent the first hearing of a high-pitched cry from a distance. (5)
It was formidable with the bursting of the walls of the cosmic egg shattered by Brahmā,
and it resounded with the tumultuous roar of the intoxicated ocean as its waves surged and dashed against one another.

He demonstrates its intensity through a sequence of proximity with the word "Brahmā": when the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) was split by Brahmā, there arose a fierce, supreme intensity, like the bursting of a wall—that is, the shell of the cosmic egg—due to mutual collisions.
It was turbid with the sound of those intoxicated oceans surging and leaping upward.

The description of turbidity arises from the superimposition of the "staining of the quarters and waters," which spreads simultaneously with the sound, onto both the object of comparison and the standard of comparison, even in the case of the word itself. || 6 ||
This [sound] is intense with a thick clamor vomited forth from the city of the ocean of the world,
and it rumbles with a fierce roar fixed upon the ridges of the boundary mountains.
In the worlds, the oceans, and the cities, it is rendered harsh and unbearable by dense, extremely high-pitched clamors arising as echoes;
and because these aforementioned sounds, issuing from the slopes of the great boundary mountains, are mingled with the fierce roars of the conflagration, it becomes a discordant din.
Slowly turning as it filled the interior of the conch-like cosmic egg,
it rose high with its dense clusters from the heavens, the earth, and the depths of the netherworld.

When the interior of the shell of the cosmic egg was filled, the sound waves— reflected back due to the obstruction of its walls— became slow and extremely dense; thus, from the world of the gods (Svarloka) and from the depths of Pātāla,
it reached an intensity such that it seemed as if accompanied by thickets and a multitude of branches.
It was capable of effortlessly crushing the walls of all distant directions,
and it possessed a thirst for drinking the wine of the great dissolution that had arrived.

It is as if it were abrasive, having the nature of scratching by playfully scraping against the walls of all the infinite and distant quarters; and it is as if it were thirsty, longing for the drinking and tasting of the beverage produced from the boiling together of the seven oceans at the time of the great dissolution. || 9 ||
It was amplified by the trumpeting of Indra’s elephant Airāvata, who was intoxicated during the spreading dissolution;
it gathered a roar like that of the ocean of clouds agitated at the end of an aeon.
It was like the thundering of the intoxicated Airāvata belonging to Indra, who had set out for victory in what is called the dissolution;

it was like the roar released all at once from the oceans characterized by clouds—which had been agitated by long confinement and had accumulated and stored up their sound until the end of the kalpa, the time of universal destruction. || 10 ||

It was like a water-wheel making a powerful roar within this formidable water-machine of the cosmic egg, echoing with the sound of churning the ocean of milk as it is agitated by the great dissolution.
Like a water-drawing machine, it is like a well-known water-wheel mechanism situated at an *āraghaṭṭa*, a place for a bucket-pulley (*ghaṭīyantra*). || 11 ||
Then, wondering how this cloud could remain while this fire of the kalpa was present,
I became filled with amazement and cast my gaze toward the nine directions.

Then, immediately after hearing the described sound of the clouds, I became struck with wonder and amazement; consequently, I cast my gaze—meaning I directed my sight—into the nine directions excluding the downward direction, in order to search for the clouds. That is to say, I exerted myself in looking about. || 12 ||
Until I see anywhere here in any direction nothing at all,
save for showers of firebrands like thunderbolts crossing over with flickering flashes.
"I do not see them"—the word "clouds" is to be understood as the ellipsis. What then did you see there? To this he says: "Only... They cross over;
they float in the sky. || 13 ||
By that blazing heat, objects within many millions of yojanas are reduced to ashes, even in all ten directions far away.
Immediately thereafter, in a moment, I experienced from afar in the sky a cool wind above and a heat like fire below. (15)
He experienced it with the sense organ of touch. || 15 ||
At such a distance in this vast expanse of space, the clouds of the kalpa remain; they are not within the range of the heat of those fires, nor indeed of those who possess true vision.

At such a great distance— that is, as far as that remote region extends— it is not within the range of the vision of those living beings who dwell there, even though they are subjected to the heat of the fires flowing beneath them.
Then, from the quarter of Varuṇa, there came a wind like that at the end of an aeon,
by which even the Vindhya, Meru, and Himālaya mountains were swept away like blades of grass.
Because of that, the mountains of flames, where embers flew like birds from the edges and which were overrun by forests of flickering torches, fled swiftly toward the direction of fire.
The mountains are characterized by flames and are immovable; there are two qualifiers that establish their status as mountains. (18)
Clouds of glowing coals rose with the appearance of twilight clouds;
masses of ash-like clouds and the dust of purified coals wandered through the sky.
The characteristics of the mass of ashes are like clouds because they bear the likeness of clouds; they are the dust of purified embers that have been cleansed by the wind. || 19 ||
Moving with a wind shimmering with flames, that wicked one approached the fire-eyed [Rāvaṇa],
appearing like a host of winged golden mountains melting away.
When the entire expanse of the earth and its mountain ranges had become a mass of glowing embers, and a multitude of wreaths of flames arose, shining with the brilliance of the suns; (21)

When the embers, which were gentle and flameless, had become composed of that [ash], and when the splendor of the twelve suns (the Ādityas) shone forth clearly due to the arrival of the *rajas* quality; [this is the implied sense]. || 21 ||
In oceans that were seas of fire, with waters boiling and surging;
in forests where leaves were no longer remembered, bearing trees with blazing fires.

In some places where the very waters were fire, and in others where the waters were boiling and surging—such as these, the multitude of clouds at the end of the aeon arrived; this is how the preceding words are to be connected with all those locative forms ending in -am. (22)
