When the lords dwelling in the Brahma-world and the cities of the Brahma-world— along with their women, children, and the elderly— were consumed by fire and fell into the sky.
In the Brahma-foremost lotus-lake, which was the lotus-pond of the fire at the end of the eon,
she remained with her seeds intact, adorned with sprouts of flame and glowing embers.

With sparks resembling filaments as its hair, by means of flaming torches composed of them, that lotus-pond— which possesses sprout-like flames, is characterized by the Brahman, is grown in a lake free from stones,
and takes the form of the fire at the end of an aeon— has taken root upon the Nāgas, who consist of wind and are dominated by the obstructive vital air (*viṣṭambhakavāyu*).

And while the mountains, in the form of serpents and mountains, had their roots sunk into the mire of glowing coals reaching down to the netherworld (Āpātāla)—this is the connection between the two [verses]. || 24 ||
When the Nāgas, whose very essence is wind, had sunk down to the netherworld (Pātāla) along with the mountains into the great mire of glowing coals; 25.
Perceiving the sky to be near at hand like a herd of camels in motion, a mass of clouds dark as collyrium arrived, rumbling loudly.
It was like that army [of the West], for in the western regions it is well known that camels carry water in leather bags (*carmabhastrā*). // 26 //
He is a mountain composed of lightning equal to the flames of the fire at the end of an eon,
upon a single corner of which rests the entire mass of the waters of the seven oceans.
He describes that very [state] with the verse beginning "stable," etc. (27).
The horizons were blocked by the weight of frost shining against the walls,
while [the wind] was expert at shattering the dense circle of the shell of the universe as if it were a mere wall.
He whose horizons were rendered irresistible and devoid of space by masses of mist as radiant as walls;
he who was an expert in the shattering of the dense terrestrial sphere up to the very walls of the cosmic egg;
and who, being himself dense, produced a sound resembling the bursting of the vault of the sky up to the walls of the cosmic egg.
Or "a wise man. || 28 ||
Like the ocean agitated at the end of an aeon, possessing the motion of circular whirlpools,
with lightning for its aquatic creatures and a deep roar, it seemed as if the sky itself had descended.

The poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) is that he has descended upon the sky as if mounted upon the very ocean agitated at the end of an eon. The epithets such as "possessing the circular halo of the twelve suns," which serves as the locus for his circular whirlpools, are intended to convey his supreme majesty. [He is] cooler than the moon by twice its measure when it is dead and burnt.
Having resorted to another form, he has come as if from the other world. || 30 ||

He shows another poetic fancy (utprekṣā) with the words "as if dead": having resorted to the other world, which consists of a supreme and exceedingly high region, he has arrived as if in another body characterized by a different form, namely that of a mass of clouds. || 30 ||
Like the entire Himalaya mountain in the form of a mass of gold, he bore all the quarters of the sky— water, fire, wind, and earth— as if they were entirely paralyzed by coldness.

Bearing, as it were, the Himalaya mountain—by which all waters without exception have been rendered motionless like wood through a coldness resembling a mass of lightning like a collection of golden ornaments—[the cloud]. || 31 ||
Then there fell a rain whose intensity was as hard as the bursting of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), filling the firmament; it was like a torrent of fierce frost that had previously been liquefied.

Then, immediately after the arrival of the clouds, rain fell. How? Such that the sky was fashioned by a thunderclap of hard adamant as fierce as the explosion of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*); in such a manner, first, violent hoar-frost (the meaning of *auṣāra* found in the root text) fell rapidly. Or else—
In accordance with this, one may assume that the reading in the root text is *udbhaṭanīhārā* (possessing fierce mist). [The direction] in which the quarters (*kāṣṭhā*) lie. 32–33.
Terrifying with the blazing of fire, the roar of the clouds, the sky, and the flashing of lightning;
with the bursting of the shell of the universe due to the crashing and clanging of thunderclaps.

He describes that very rain with the words beginning "like a conflagration": "Terrifying through the flashing of lightning between the forest and the sky, which resembles a fire-blast; with crashing *gaḍagaḍā* roars, it causes the shell of the universe to burst asunder. (33)
With a hundred rising sibilants of hissing sounds widely proclaimed, she possesses an inexhaustible roar;
she makes the sky into a wall of frozen spray and mist.
With showers of rain as brilliant as a multitude of vaidūrya pillars in a pavilion of clouds,
she adorned the mountains that bear the weight of the earth.

The two worlds, heaven and earth, were like the collection of beryl pillars for that pavilion characterized by such features; they were adorned with the strokes of axes upon the mountains—the draft-animals of the earth—which were rendered bright by the falling showers of thick, radiant torrents. || 35 ||
The city of burning coals was shattered by the crackling and snapping of the earth,
while the world was thrown into turmoil by the falling of beings due to the forceful onset of the thundering roar.
It is that by which the heaps of burning coals burst open the cities of charcoal.
Then she became like a playful mistress of the house that was the world of burning coals;
she was met by the earth with the splendor of her tears, which blazed like fire.

That rain, sporting in the house of the world which was filled with embers, was then met by the beauty of the earth's steam— though not yet flaming— as if by a female friend coming forward to welcome her.
The sky, with its display of leaping sparks of flame, appeared as if it were entirely covered by a mass of petals from a land-lotus;
there, the flickering clusters of cool spray droplets resembled rows of bees wandering amidst the flames. (38)
Then that sky, the atmosphere, became as if it were such a place where there was a profusion of leaping sparks of flame,
and where masses of petals from land-lotuses had grown and spread; therein, cool sprays of water droplets were shimmering like a mass of feathers.
The clouds, however, resembled a swarm of bees wandering amidst the flames. (38)

The terrifying collision of the discharge of water, filling the quarters with rising, vast *caṭa-caṭa* sounds, became like a fierce battle between the forces of great beings—battle that was as formidable as an irresistible enemy, where sharp weapons struck against sharp weapons. (39)
Furthermore, at that time, there was a convergence and meeting of water-bearing clouds and fires,
such that the quarters of the sky were filled with rising, great *caṭa-caṭa* sounds; being thus like an insurmountable enemy,
he was fierce, and in that state, his formidable weapons were struck by the missiles of great armies.
It became as terrifying and fearsome as a battle. || 39 ||

Thus ends the seventy-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Grandeur of the Puṣkarāvarta Cloud," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa of the glorious Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa, composed by the sage Vālmīki. 76.

Thus ends the seventy-sixth sarga, titled "The Description of the Splendor of the Puṣkarāvarta Clouds," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The seventy-seventh canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Now, at the end of the eon, when the earth, water, fire, and wind [dissolve]...
When that supreme agitation arose, these three worlds became [disturbed]. || 1 ||

In this [work], the world is described once again as it was when it was thrown into disorder by the torrents of rain released by the Puṣkarāvartaka clouds and shaken by the agitation of the seven oceans.
The meaning is: listen as I describe what the three worlds became when a supreme agitation arose among these four great elements—earth, water, fire, and air. || 1 ||
Resplendent with ashes like clouds rising from a *tāpiccha* forest,
it moved in the manner of a great whirlpool in the vast ocean, a swirling mass of smoke.
The grove of *tāpiccha* trees is a *tamāla* forest. || 2 ||
The playful, flickering blue flames roar with a soft *miṭi-miṭa* sound,
filling the spaces between the worlds with a mass of ash-clouds.
Upon the moist objects to be burned, it attained a playful and pleasing state characterized by the rising of blue smoke and flickering flames; it was prone to shrieking with long,
surging cries of "chamacchama" and "mayāmaya," while the sound of its victory resounded like a drum, spreading far and wide.

The long-continued sound of the *rut* [of the peacocks] was, as it were, a trumpet-sound rising up and striving to proclaim the widespread victory of the showers over the fuel-like clouds; such is the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*). 4.
It was like a mass of fierce clouds with spray tossed about by the delusion of vaporous clouds, resembling the agitation of great kalpa-clouds, dark as swirling clouds of ash and smoke.
The meaning is: "like a fivefold mass of clouds. || 5 ||
By the spreading gusts of wind, terrifying with the crashing roar against the walls of the cosmic egg,
the masses of the cities of Indra and the other gods were blown into the sky and consumed.
The eyes and ears were numbed by the clanging sounds produced by the violent friction of millions of stones bursting forth due to the surging of water, fire, and wind.
Its sense organs, such as the skin, were numbed by violent collisions; its hearing was deafened, with its ears rendered numb by the clanging sounds.
With incessant downpours of rain like pillars supporting the sky,
and with the dragging of the fires of cosmic dissolution, there arose a dense, thundering sound of "chamaccham."
By the "dragging" of the fires at the end of the aeons; that is to say, by their scraping, scratching, and tearing apart. || 8 ||
The entire ocean was being filled by hosts of rivers possessing waves like the Gaṅgā,
resembling clouds terrifying the sky.
Taraṅgikā consists primarily of individual waves. || 9 ||
The circle of clouds appeared as if its seat were licked by the scorching suns, resembling clusters of blossoms placed upon a mass of *tāpiccha* leaves.

The very same comparison that applies to clusters of flowers resting beneath *tamāla* leaves applies to the suns as well; thus, they are "compared to those. In this [description], the "circle of the world-system" (*kalpābhramaṇḍala*) has its base tasted—that is, it is almost entirely consumed—because the fuel-less suns act as its consumers. || 10 ||
It carried away the masses of mountains and rivers, the peaks, islands, and cities;
it crushed the mountains with the violent agitation caused by the winds at the end of an eon.
With fierce and agitated hosts of planets and stars, difficult to grasp due to their combative nature,
they fell like doubled whirling firebrands, descending in spirals.

By means of their physical forms, through mutual striking, and by means of difficult-to-grasp and difficult-to-restrain [missiles], they produced in the sky—indeed, as the remainder of the sentence implies—a twofold brilliance of firebrands (*alāta*) that was twice as intense as those on the ground; for this very reason, they were like whirlpools that fall and descend at the end. || 12 ||
It was struck by the impact of the collision between the great mountains and the rising waters,
like the rocky floor at the edge of a mountain overturned during the great dissolution.

It is called *āvaha* because it blows from all sides; it is a fierce wind, and where the mountains burst apart due to the collisions of massive waves—resembling water-mountain-kings—that arise from it, those are the *sphoṭa* mountains. || 13 ||
It was thick and sluggish with darkness that obscured the rays of the sun’s multitude, due to clouds of tears condensed into dense masses, as vast as the clouds at the end of an aeon.
By means of such clouds of vapor, in which the thick [particles] have been turned into droplets.
The ocean was congested with fragments of the shattered surface of the earth, with crumbling slopes, with mountains being carried away, and with falling peaks rolling along.
The horizons were shattered by the roars of the ocean, as deep as the sound of a thunderclap, and by gale-force winds that tore through dense clouds with rising pebbles.

The boundaries of the quarters were shattered by the winds of universal destruction—those voracious gales accompanied by clouds that had been torn asunder by upward-thrown stones tossed aloft by rising waves. || 16 ||
The single ocean resounded with the harsh clanging of the hammers at the very summit of the wall of the cosmic egg,
and with the crashing of the branches of the clouds at the end of the aeon.

With the slapping of his chest—the surface of which has the dimensions of the shell of the universe—by his arms that resemble the trees of the Kalpa age, and which produce harsh clanging sounds, he cries out with beating of his breast, as if the single ocean were being struck by one another; that is to say, he roars while weeping. || 17 ||
The sky was filled with fragments of heaven, the netherworld, and the earthly realm,
intermingled and remaining according to their own nature, along with the mountains and the base of the oceans.

Furthermore, with the fragments of the three worlds, beginning with the celestial realm, having flown up and remaining in the atmosphere according to their respective natures and degrees of heaviness, the lower portion—
devoid of water because it has not been touched by rainwater and because its watery component has been dried up by the wind— becomes like a desert.
By those whose base, root, or lower part [is such]. || 18 ||
With gods and dānavas whose limbs were dead, half-dead, burnt, or half-burnt,
their weapons whirled about as they were tossed by the wind from seeing one another.

Even though they share the same misfortune, because they look at one another with mutual enmity, they brandish their weapons against each other for the sake of killing. Thus, it is implied that even through thousands of calamities, the perception of enmity among the ignorant does not subside without [the cessation of] ignorance; therefore, that very ignorance is a greater calamity than all other misfortunes.
By the winds from the edges of the sky, which toss about the withered straws of other worlds,
pillars known as the Arjuna-winds were begun, rising up with clouds of ash.
"Arjunavāta" is the name of a specific type of wind-disease; for by that disease, the patients fly up into the sky and wander about.

However, since that disease does not possess the color of the *arjuna* tree, [the poet] began by whitening the wind with the ashes produced from the withered grasses of other worlds, so that the name might not be rendered groundless.
In this [verse], there is a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) suggesting that the pillar is the foundation and support of what is called the "wind of Arjuna. || 20 ||
The banks were being overturned by the impact of masses of rocks being swept away;
the world was falling apart, emitting the harsh, loud cries of a widespread and terrible calamity.
In which there was a widespread, harsh, and wretched state brought about by famine.
It resounded with the echoing roars from the caves of the mountain ranges shaken by the wind,
while the cities of the world-protectors were filled with swirling eddies created by falling [mountains].
It was resplendent with the whistling sounds from the caves of the mountain ranges, stirred by the surging and clashing of the wind.
It was surrounded by winds that produced harsh sounds like those of the Asuras, which carried away the forest groves and pierced through the windows.
In the sky, it bore a multitude of cities, mandalas, daityas, fires, gods, nāgas, and suns, like a swarm of gnats.
With the masses of the best of mountains perishing and the abodes of the gods shattered into fragments,
the water roared with gurgling sounds from its whirlpools, rising upward while fire blazed below.

The word *āvarta* means turning back; having uprooted [the clouds] like a *droṇa* measure and holding them in reverse, by means of that, with gurgling sounds, he held the rainwater above and the forest fire below without obstruction—this is the sense. || 25 ||
Crushing the cities of the world-protectors with the impact of its waters upon the mountains,
it caused the towns of the lords of gods, demons, siddhas, and gandharvas to fall.
The winds perform the pulverizing of mountains and other things that have become like extinguished embers, rendering material objects as insubstantial as dust. (27)
As if performing the pulverization of objects such as mountains, like [the grinding] of dust. || 27 ||
Shattering the ancient walls of the cities of the gods and demons as they whirl about,
the [waves] produce a clinking sound like gems striking the waters of the oceans.
Like the milks of water-laden clouds, they clink with the sound "khaṇa-khaṇa" due to their jewels, as they shatter the cities of the gods and the daityas. || 28 ||
The sky was filled with the falling temples of the seven worlds,
which, with their whirling forms, resembled the oceans of the gods as they revolved in a circular motion.
The sky was filled by such sevenfold mansions of the worlds, from which people were falling.
It was surrounded by objects, half-burnt and half-unburnt, whirling up and down as they were tossed by the gusts of wind, like clusters of withered leaves in the sky.
It was strewn with celestial palaces made of gold, crystal, lapis lazuli, and excellent gems,
which were falling from heaven with rising *jhaṇajhaṇa* sounds.
The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) of all the words ending with "ākīrṇam" is with the phrase "babhūvāsmiñjagattrayam" located in the first verse of the creation. || 31 ||
Clouds of smoke and ashes surged upward, while masses of rain fell upon the cities;
floods of waves rose up, and the mountains of the earth sank down.
By the water of rain falling day after day. || 32 ||
Roaring with the gurgling sounds of whirlpools and striving to crush one another,
the massive mountains whirled about like leaves scattered upon the ocean.
The world became difficult to behold, with the hosts of gods crying out, the living beings trembling, and hundreds of calamitous comets wandering about.
Wherein there are moving beings (*bhūtaka*), that is, living creatures possessing a slight degree of life; [the suffix] *kan* is used here in the sense of compassion (*anukampā*). 34.
The sky became completely filled with a continuous stream of living beings— some dead, some half-dead, and as flickering as the wind— resembling the color of withered leaves.
The world became filled with a torrent of massive streams falling from the peaks,
carrying hundreds of rivers swollen by the winds from the mountains and cities.
In which [battle] there was a downpour of thick streams of arrows, like mountain peaks falling down.
The fire, with its hundreds of branches of the sounds "śāmyat," "śama," and "śamā," caused the mountain ridges to tremble as they swayed and rocked from the surging and tossing of the moving ocean.
Intense with islands and oceans mingled according to the analogy of heaps of grass and rivers,
it is a forest capable of enduring the momentary flames of the consciousness-space that is exceedingly remote.

With the intention that it is not surprising that this world, which is to be consumed by the fire of the sky of consciousness ignited by the knowledge of reality, should be destroyed after a long time during its dissolution, he says: "absolutely" (*atyanta*).
The expression "absolutely distant" (*atyantadūra*) is used to highlight the rarity of the knowledge of reality. [The world] cannot endure even a momentary flame within the sky of consciousness.
One whose state of being is such as that [described above]. || 38 ||
The world, which had previously existed, was forgotten as to its creation; the gods fell amidst the fragrance of the ashes rising from the fire extinguished by the rain.
That which was previously existent, that which existed in the past— the world of moving and non-moving beings— is now one whose creation has been completely forgotten.

It possesses an unrestrained, surging resonance; it is the process of the cessation of creation; it is the remainder shining forth from the dissolution of creation; and it is entirely devoid of the dissolution of creation.

Wherein the sequence of cessation occurs through the dissolution of emanation; wherein, through the ultimate dissolution of emanation, the Supreme Self remains as the residual radiance; [that state] which is in reality devoid of both emanation and dissolution. (40)
It was cooled by winds that incessantly produce distortions [of perception], yet it was being filled again and again, like a heap of seeds. (41)
Or rather, with the intention that it is always distinguished by the elision of the *sarga* suffix (*-s*), he says: "anārata" (uninterrupted). || 41 ||
The hollow of the sky was revealed as a golden floor by the scattered dust born from the gold produced by the fire resulting from the mutual clashing of firebrands.
Where the hollow of the sky was like a floor paved with gold. || 42 ||
The surface of the earth was filled with vast fragments fallen along with their islands and oceans,
while the seven netherworlds were filled with rolling circles of the subterranean realms.
Upon which [mountains] there roll vast fragments of the earth's surface, such that they reach down to the other side of the netherworld (pātāla).
From the seventh layer of the netherworld up to the surface of the earth and its mountains,
reaching as far as the sky, it became a single vast ocean filled with the winds of universal dissolution.
The word *āḍaḥ* [is used] in the sense of pervasion. The seventh [level] is Sutala itself, which is *sutāla*, a synonym for *pātāla*; the lengthening of the vowel is Vedic (*chāndasa*). || 44 ||
Then the single ocean gradually and swiftly swelled with hundreds of rivers, its waves of water rising like the anger within the heart of a fool. (45)
First with a stream like a pestle, then with limbs resembling pillars,
and then with a torrent as forceful as the flow from a palm tree.
Āsāra means a shower; it is so called because of its pouring down. || 46 ||

Then, by means of that [weapon] which felled everything with a single downpour of fierce river-like waters, and which was like a thick cloud over the surface of the earth consisting of the seven continents; (47)

Then, immediately after the falling of the earth measuring [only] a palm-tree’s height, by her who alone causes the falling— that which is known as the fierce torrent of water from the peaks of Malaya and other mountains into the currents of the Tāmraparṇī and other rivers— the word "alone" (eka) here implying similarity— she whose emitters are clouds as thick as the entire surface of the earth distinguished by its seven continents. || 47 ||

Just as fire, which causes burning, is extinguished by rain, so too does one who has reached the depths of calamity find peace through the study of the scriptures and the company of the virtuous. (48)
Ignorance is like a state of dense suffering, thick with millions of miseries, the very ground for calamities, and the abode of all disasters. (48)

The hollow of the cosmic egg became desolate, its mass of objects situated above and below overturned, its mountain cores rattling with internal sparks, like a pure wood-apple fruit tossed about in the play of a mischievous child.
The meaning is that, like a trembling wood-apple fruit, it became distressed and ruined by the wretched, childish antics of bursting [the seed]. || 49 ||

Thus ends the seventy-seventh canto, titled "The Description of the World Disturbed by the Rain of the Puṣkarāvarta Clouds," in the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa*, the *Vālmīki Dēvamanuṣya Mānasa* [recension], in the *Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa*. || 77 ||

Thus ends the seventy-seventh canto, titled "The Description of the World Disturbed by the Rain of the Puṣkarāvarta Clouds," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The seventy-eighth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
When the surface of the earth was shattered by the falling of winds, rains, and snow-storms, [the world became desolate].
Jaḍavega attained growth, like King Kali in the [age of] Kali. || 1 ||
Filling the sky on all sides with torrents as vast as rivers,
the swelling single ocean is here described in detail.
Jaḍavega is Jalavega. || 1 ||
It was augmented by the falling torrents fallen from the current of the Gaṅgā,
and suddenly joined by thousands of rivers as radiant as Mount Meru and Mandara.

It is swollen by the falling streams of rain from the clouds that descend into the currents of the celestial Gaṅgā; or, according to the reading *vivarjitaiḥ*, it is swollen by thousands of rivers released and poured forth. It possesses waves as radiant as Mount Meru or Mandara suddenly rising up, which reach the path of the sun and carry away mountain caves along with them.
"There was a single ocean"—this is the connection between the two [verses]. || 2 ||
Having reached the path of the sun, the moon became dull and sluggish;
swollen like a single vast ocean, the lord was like a fool. || 3 ||
By the turning of its vast whirlpools, it has swallowed old mountain-grasses;
with the tips of its shimmering, lofty waves, it has swallowed the orb of the sun.

He further characterizes that very single ocean until the end of the dissolution with the words beginning "vipula" (vast): in which [ocean] the old grasses of the mountains were seized by the movement of vast whirlpools, and for that reason were tossed about—that is, being whirled around. || 4 ||
He is the aquatic creature dwelling within Mount Meru, Mandara, Kailāsa, Vindhya, and Sahya;
he is the lotus stalk whose serpent has slithered away and is hidden within the mud of the earth.

He imagines that very ocean to be a lotus-pond with the words beginning "galita" (fallen): it is one in which the fallen earth has dissolved into its mud, and within which the stalks of the divine serpents, such as Śeṣa and others, are submerged. (5)
With masses of half-burnt forest trees forming a thicket like water-weeds,
and mixed with the ashes of the three worlds, it became a loathsome mire.
The sky is its pillar; the great, lofty sun is its lotus; and the petals of the lotuses are dissolved in the great ocean of the mass of falling rain. (7)

In which [sky] the twelve suns— the Adityas— were like towering lotuses, with the pillars characterized by the sky as their stalks, the vast spaces as their pericarps, and the rays acting as seeds; and in which the great clouds, appearing as masses of falling rain, were like lotus petals that had become almost dissolved due to their contact with the waters above.
With intoxicated clouds roaring from the edges of mountains of foam,
it filled the cities and towns of Indra, Vāyu, Arka, and Indu as they wandered about.
The fierce multitude of gods and asuras was being swept away like logs;
gradually swelling in height, it licked the orb of the sun.
The great mountains were being swept away, rendered indistinguishable by the bubbles arising from the torrents of water that emitted the sounds "tara-tāra-tāra."
In that [ocean], where the great mountains being carried along were doubted on all sides as to whether they were mere bubbles or indeed massive peaks;
where the clouds of the end of the aeon, weary from wandering, found rest upon the whirling bubbles;
and where one beheld another ocean within those surging, supportless waters.

With those eyes whose pupils (*tārā*) were prominent due to the non-distinction between *ra* and *la* sounds—eyes resembling cloud-bubbles, devoid of support and lacking anything other than their own base, which is the face—he beheld another nearby cloud; such is the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*). || 11 ||
The sky resounded with the gurgling roar of the torrential flood of its great current,
while the principal mountain ranges of the heavens were swept away by that single mighty stream.
By which the sky was made resonant and filled with a humming sound; in whose single current the great mountain ranges along with the heavens were submerged.
With mountain-like masses of unprecedented water-torrents stirred by fierce winds,
it possessed a great, violent speed, roaring with deep, gurgling, and ghur-ghur sounds.
Rising up through the collisions and revolutions of the fragments of the cosmic egg,
it spread out and rose to heights of hundreds of thousands of yojanas.
He makes himself a hundred thousand yojanas wide and a hundred thousand yojanas high.
The mountain ranges, as if making the sun’s orb shatter with the blows of their stones, caused it to sway like blades of grass upon the waves.
In that vast nest of water-storms within the empty cosmic egg, he shattered the solar orbs with blows from stones by means of mountains swinging like blades of grass,
and carried away the dark mountain-crows with his nets of water.

Furthermore, in the vast nest—a hollow formed by a mass of water—within the great void characterized as the empty universe, he seems to seize and carry away the blue immovable mountains, which are like crows (kākolāḥ) or *droṇa*-crows; that is to say, the great water-fowls (*madgu*).

He appears to take them by means of nets consisting of the waters, having caught them with snares. [The form] "haran" is derived from the root *hṛ* with the suffix *śatṛ*, used according to Vedic usage.
The application of the properties of the optative (liṅvadbhāva).
They were agitated by the sinking and surfacing of great beings who were dead and yet as if immortal, appearing as if endowed with reflections of waves, sea-monsters, and whirlpools.
He qualifies the immovable *kākolā* with two adjectives, beginning with "dead" (*mṛta*). The word "as if" (*iva*) connects back to the preceding verse. || 17 ||
He bore the surviving gods, who had fallen from the city and were exhausted by the force of the waters, upon the edges of the mountain ridges of foam like so many mosquitoes.
Bearing [the weight] upon the slopes, edges, and peaks of mountains characterized by foam; [one should consider whether the word *asya* ends in a short vowel. || 18 ||
He perceived thousands of water bubbles, as vast as the space of the present sky, just as Indra perceives the eyes [of the world]. 19.
The vast and well-known space,

appearing like a silver bowl turned upside down— just as it is said that bubbles are "vast" when viewed from the perspective of the living beings situated within them; so too, the comparison "like the eyes of Vāsava" is made from the perspective of one looking from the outside.
With his eyes like shimmering bubbles, possessing the vast expanse of an autumn sky,
he seemed to gaze upon the streams of rivers and clouds filled with copper-colored water.
Those whose [streams] are like the currents of rivers. || 20 ||
With the many circles of waves from the Puṣkarāvartaka clouds,
which rose up like winged mountains, he seemed to be performing embraces.
Satiated by devouring the three worlds, he seemed to sing with his gurgling roars and to dance with his own fierce mountain ridges and the trees that were his surging waves.

"Those whose bracelets are indeed mountain ridges," or alternatively, "by means of bracelets that are mountain ridges. This is because, in the context of the compound (vṛtti), the word *adri* (mountain) refers to its ridges (*kaṭaka*), just as in the case of *śvamukha* ("dog-faced") or *kharamukha* ("donkey-faced"). || 22 ||
It was surrounded above by clouds that held streams of rivers, in the middle by mountains that had been burnt, below by mountains and serpents, and at the very bottom by those who dwell in the mud.
For whom there exists no support. || 23 ||
With the incessant downpour of streams filling the triple-pathed river (the Gaṅgā),
the mountain peaks were submerged and emerged again like masses of foam and bubbles.
The sky-dwellers cried out as fragments of heaven were being swept away and shattered;
meanwhile, the lotus-like faces of the throngs of Vidyadhara women were carried along, appearing beautiful within the current.
In that celestial realm, which is of a nature to burst asunder, the sky-dwelling deities characterized by swans and other such beings cry out;
for this very reason, its interior is as beautiful as a lotus pond. || 25 ||
When the great waters were being swept away during the destruction of the fragments of the three worlds, with a roar like a gurgling torrent amidst the floods of the single universal ocean; (26)
There was no protector whatsoever, and he was even slain by the power of Avīci; for who is able to protect one who has been swallowed up by Time? (27)
There was not even anyone who was not subject to the power of the waves—that is, who was not under their sway. "Hanta" expresses grief. || 27 ||
There was no sky, nor were there the quarters of space; there was nothing below, nor was there anything above.
There was no being, nor was there any creation; there existed only the supreme, absolute water.
This is clear. || 28 ||

Thus ends the seventy-eighth canto, titled "The Description of the Single Ocean," in the Nirvāṇa Section of the *Mokṣopāya* within the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, according to the tradition of the Ṛṣis.
Thus ends the seventy-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Single Ocean," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The seventy-ninth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: In the meantime, I, remaining in the sky, then cast my gaze [upon him].
In the great world of Brahmā, at dawn, it was like the radiance of the sun.
In this regard, the Nirvana of the Lord of the host of Sarṣi deities is proclaimed;
and its sublation by awakening, as if by the waking state of a dream, is likewise established.

Now, in the meantime, after the waters had filled everything up to the limit of the world of heat (tapoloka) as a single ocean, I, stationed in the sky adjacent to the world of truth (satyaloka), cast my eye upon the Great World (mahāloka)—the world of Brahmā (brahmaloka) abounding in light.
That is to say, I directed my gaze there for the purpose of seeing. || 1 ||
There I beheld the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin), established in meditative absorption (samādhi) with his principal retinue, appearing as if carved out of a mountain.

The principal retinue, having attained liberation such as *sālokya* through meditations on the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth, and desiring to enter the state of disembodied absolute isolation (*videhakaivalya*) along with Brahmā, constitutes his retinue of those liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*). Thus it has been said: "When the time of universal dissolution arrives, all those who have perfected themselves enter the supreme state at the end of the highest [Brahmā]. (2)
And there was an assembly of gods and sages of purified souls,
as well as Śukra, Bṛhaspati, Śakra, Vaiśravaṇa, and Yama.

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "There, I saw the assembly of the presiding deities, such as Śakra and others, as well as such sages as Śukra and others. He specifies some of them by singling them out with the words beginning with "Śukra. (3)
Then Soma, Varuṇa, and Agni, as well as other divine sages, and the leaders of the gods, Gandharvas, Siddhas, and Sādhyas. || 4 ||
The Vināyakas are the restrainers; that is to say, they are the masters. || 4 ||
All of them, their forms fixed as if by the hand of a painter, were devoted to meditation;
seated there in the lotus posture, they remained as if devoid of life.
"All were seen by me standing as if devoid of life"—this is the connection [of the sentence] through the transformation [of the subject]. (5)
Then those twelve Ādityas arrived at that very spot;
they stood there quickly, having assumed the lotus posture (padmāsana), just as he had done.
He states what occurred immediately thereafter with the words beginning "atha" (now), etc. || 6 ||
Then, in just a moment, I saw the Lotus-born [Brahmā] before me,
having become wide awake, appearing like something seen in a dream standing right in front of me.

The final moment of that [period], which measures the last muhūrta of the second half-parārdha, is a mere muhūrta; by means of that, through the awakening of Brahman-consciousness ignited by his final direct realization, he attained wakefulness— the state free from sleep— due to the sublation of the entire phenomenal world along with the body imagined by his ignorance.

The person perceives that which remains as the Self alone, sublated like the collection of dream-objects previously seen while dreaming; this very state is his disembodied liberation (videhakaivalya)—this is the meaning. || 7 ||
I did not see any of the inhabitants of the Brahma-world, as if they were merely the latent impressions of great beings, like one awakening from a dream-city while standing at its forefront.
He states that liberation occurred in exactly the same way for the people who were previously mentioned as his attendants by saying, "the people of the world of Brahmā.
This is another illustration: just as the prior latent impressions (vāsanā) of great knowers of reality are sublated by knowledge.
The rest is as explained before. || 8 ||
At that time, that contemplation of Brahman— which was accomplished through the resolve of Brahman— was as utterly empty as a forest,
like a city on earth suddenly destroyed by a violent calamity.

Then, at the moment of his final direct realization, that city of Brahmā or the cosmic egg was as empty as a wilderness, utterly devoid of householders and all others; it was devastated by a harsh, sudden, and unexpected cause of destruction. || 9 ||
At that time, none of them— whether sages, ascetics, gods, Vedas, [the reading is "siddhas"], or Vidyādharas and the like— were anywhere such as they had been before.
The connection [of the verse] is through the transformation that all those sages, gods, and others likewise were just such emptiness;
for the ellipsis is that they have not gone anywhere. || 10 ||
Then, while remaining in the sky, I perceived with focused attention that they had all attained nirvāṇa like Brahmā.

He demonstrates through self-experience that although [the self] is empty of the nature of name-and-form (nāmarūpa), it remains in its own essential nature as the very essence of nirvāṇa—thus: "It is known. [This is understood] through attentiveness and focused application. || 11 ||
When latent impressions have dissolved, they have come to non-appearance;
like dream-worlds for those who have awakened, they have returned to their own true nature.
With the intention that the very attainment of their true nature occurs through the removal of the forms imagined by latent impressions (*vāsanā*), he says:
"In the latent impression" (verse 12).
This body, though its very nature is space, appears clearly through latent impressions (vāsanā);
yet in the absence of those impressions, it does not appear, just as a dream does not appear to one who has awakened.
He establishes that very point with the words "the self of space," and so forth: for one who possesses awakening, that is, for one endowed with enlightenment. || 13 ||
Just as a body situated in the intermediate space is perceived in a dream,
nothing at all is observed upon awakening when those latent impressions have been stilled.
He has gone into the intermediate space; he possesses the power of moving through the sky. || 14 ||
Likewise, even while awake, when latent impressions (vāsanā) have been completely exhausted,
neither the subtle body (ativāhika) nor the physical body (ādhibhautika) is perceived here.

The distinction is that in the waking state, there is only the sublation of the objective (ādhibhautika) aspect of the dream, whereas upon the awakening to reality, there is the sublation of all three bodies, including the objective and the rest; with this intention, he says, "even in the waking state.

Since the awakening to reality—which is the cause for the exhaustion of latent impressions—can occur even while one is awake through the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), the expression "even in the waking state" is used.
This experience of a dream is pointed out here as an illustration;
it is well-established even among children, being experienced, heard, and remembered. (16)
And thus, even though the experience of sublation in a dream is similar only in one respect, it is cited as an example because it is well-known even to children; so he says:
"In a dream... It is heard in the Śruti that "he has three abodes there, which are dreams," and it is likewise recorded in the Purāṇas and other texts. || 16 ||
Furthermore, that rogue who denies his own experience must be abandoned; for who indeed would wake one who is asleep with falsehood? (17)

Thus, he says "he denies" (apahnute) regarding one who denies the sublation of dreams—which is established by the experience of both oneself and others—being a proponent of the reality of all perceived objects such as dreams; such a person is simply not to be awakened. [He is] one who mocks his own sleep under the pretext of a falsehood. 17.
If it is argued that a dream is caused by the body and is therefore not seen in the absence of a body, then it follows that for those without bodies, there can be no world beyond either. (18)
If it is argued that even so, the analogy of the dream is not tenable— because this [waking] body has the bodies of parents and so forth as its cause,

whereas the dream-body does not, and thus there is a disparity due to the absolute non-existence of the dream-body— then [the same would apply] to the heavenly body produced by sacrifices and the like.

He states [the following] because, due to the absence of the body being the cause [of the self], the consequence would be its absolute non-existence, which would result in the opponents falling into nihilism: "deha... (verse 18).
If this [creation] were to cease upon the dissolution of that body, then this creation would not exist; yet it does indeed exist at all times. (19)

Furthermore, if the body—which has the physical body as its cause—were absolutely non-existent, it would follow that even Hiraṇyagarbha, who consists of the collective aggregate (*samaṣṭi*) of subtle bodies (*ātivāhika-deha*), would also be absolutely non-existent. If that were the case, even the causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) for the purpose of creation and so forth would be utterly false.
Thus he says: "If this... That is to say, if this non-existence of yours were established in such a manner, then [the following would occur].

At the end of the dissolution of a previous creation, when all bodies have perished, this present creation would not have come into being at its initial time due to the absence of bodies caused by the lack of prior bodies. Yet, this very creation is clearly perceived.
With the intention of showing that the same could be argued for each preceding creation, he says: "always" (sarvadā). || 19 ||
Since destruction— which consists in the division of parts— is inevitable,
it is also untenable to claim that this world was never otherwise [than as it is].

[Objection: In that case, there is never a dissolution; for in this beginningless cycle of transmigration (*saṃsāra*), all bodies, possessing an uninterrupted stream and being the very causes of [future] bodies, will remain capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā-samartha*). Alternatively, one might postulate that the body of Hiraṇyagarbha arises from the preceding bodies of Nārāyaṇa and others. And thus, there has never been a time when things were not as they are now.

He refutes the view of Jaimini, namely that "the world [is eternal]," with the words "avayava" (having parts). For since the elements such as earth possess parts, their destruction is unavoidable because conjunction necessarily ends in disjunction. Thus, the doctrine that the world was never otherwise than it is now is unstable and lacks foundation; for when the earth and other elements perish...

The sense is that it is impossible for the bodies of the fourfold classes of beings to exist without a substratum, and because [if such a substratum were not the case], there would follow the consequence of the absolute non-existence of the body-form of Nārāyaṇa as its cause. || 20 ||
If you should say that there is never any destruction of the world, and that cognition arises from the qualities produced by the body, just as the power of intoxication [arises from wine], (21)
In this context, he restates the Cārvāka position in order to refute it as well, beginning with the words "never" (*na kadācit*).

Indeed, the world consists of nothing but the four elements—earth and the others—which manifest in the form of the four types of bodies and in the forms of jars, cloths, and so forth. And there is never any destruction of these [bodies] in their nature as the elements of earth and the rest; however, as for the body...

The aggregate of its properties consists precisely of such things as the genus (*jāti*), which arises from the conjunction of the elements and possesses emergent qualities such as cognition and desire, and is manifested by the specific configurations of limbs such as hands and feet. In that regard, although cognition is not observed in each individual element, nevertheless—

O Cārvāka, if you say that—just as the power of intoxication arises when the ingredients such as flour, water, alkali, and fermenting agent (kiṇva) used in the preparation of liquor are combined and undergo transformation through time and fermentation—the quality of cognition (jñapti) arises when the four elements have transformed into the form of the body, and therefore the body alone, possessing that quality, is the Self; then listen. [This is] the remainder [of the sentence], meaning: this is the answer to that. || 21 ||
Consequently, the Purāṇas, the Itihāsas, the Smṛtis and other such texts which teach the dissolution of all things, as well as the Vedas themselves, would become utterly meaningless. (22)

Therefore, that would mean the total destruction of all things— including the four types of dissolution known as *nitya*, *naimittika*, *prākṛta*, and *vaijñānika*— as well as the eighteen Purāṇas, the histories such as the Mahābhārata, the Smṛtis of Manu and others which teach the dharma and adharma pertaining to the welfare or harm of the self in the next world, and the conduct of the virtuous.
The meaning is that [the scripture] would fall into the error of being purposeless. || 22 ||
O Mahāmati, since these [reasons] lack validity regarding this matter, how could they possibly possess validity even in other cases, such as the case of a barren woman? (23)

If it is argued, "Let it be that the lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*) of the Vedas, Purāṇas, and so forth is precisely what the Cārvākas intend, and this has been established by you," he replies with the words "by way of being non-authoritative": if these Vedas, Purāṇas, and so forth—which are free from defects—lack authority regarding this matter characterized as the nature of *dharma*, *adharma*, and the self at the time of dissolution; [then...]

In any other [scripture] corrupted by thousands of defects such as passion for enjoyments, greed, hatred, and so forth—even in your own words—what validity could there be? [The suffix] *liṅ* is used here in the sense of possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*).
The meaning is that even the possibility of such [validity] is difficult to find. || 23 ||
And this is not accepted in the world because it would cause the destruction of the universe; but let that be aside for now, my dear friend, listen to this other thing of mine.
Furthermore, this lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*) regarding the Vedas, Purāṇas, and so forth, which you have asserted, is neither desired nor accepted by discerning people in the world.

This is because [such a view] would entail the faults of the loss of what has been done (*kṛtahāni*) and the acquisition of what has not been done (*akṛtābhyāgama*), as well as the impossibility of creation and so forth being without cause or purpose, leading to the consequence of the total annihilation of the world. Moreover, in the doctrine that the body is the self (*dehātmavāda*), are all the constituent parts (*avayava*) themselves the self?

Or [let us consider] the whole alone. In the first case, since there is no rule ensuring that many conscious beings always possess a single consensus, there would be the undesirable consequence of the body being torn asunder due to their disagreement. In the second case, if a single limb such as the hand were severed, there would be the undesirable consequence of the loss of life due to the destruction of the whole; and there are indeed thousands of other such refutations. Let this suffice.

By this, that which you said—that just as the power of intoxication arises in wine from a combination of fermenting agents, flour, water, and so forth, so too the quality of cognition arises in the aggregate of elements transformed into the form of a body—is already answered.
The meaning is: "Listen now to this further refutation that is about to be stated. || 24 ||

That state of becoming the body of a piśāca or other being for those who have died—which is observed in other regions through knowledge possessing the power of intoxication—is not established [as a valid proof]. (25)

If it is accepted that the self (*ātman*) has knowledge as its quality (*guṇa*), such that its very nature (*svabhāva*) is like the power of intoxication residing within the power of intoxication itself, then upon the destruction of the body—the possessor of the quality (*guṇin*)—the quality must necessarily perish as well. Consequently, for living beings who have migrated to other regions, there would be the total cessation of the body; thus, their arrival in their own original location by means of another body, such as that of a *piśāca* or similar being, would be impossible.

Furthermore, that purposeful activity which is well-known in the world—such as the recognition of former kinsmen and others, and conversing with them—through the entry into another body, would not be established [under your view]. || 25 ||
If it is argued that even this delusion is seen as long as the body exists,
then let that which is called "delusion" be considered by you as nothing other than the truth.

Now, if you should say: "That conceptualization of *piśācas* and so forth is also merely a vain delusion, because *piśācas* are not perceived, and according to the Cārvāka system there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) other than perception (*pratyakṣa*). Indeed, no means of valid cognition other than perception is possible; for even in the case of things whose concomitance has been observed hundreds of times..."
Because deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is observed in cases such as being earthen or being scratchable by metal in the case of diamonds and gems;

because the birth of donkeys and other animals from cows and others is observed at different times during portents and the like; and because the emission of smoke is observed even without fire from divine images and the like—therefore, there is a suspicion of deviation in all inferential marks (*liṅga*) across different places and at different times.

Because it is impossible to prevent [the occurrence of error], inference cannot be established as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, since the validity of analogy (*upamāna*) is not established when one considers the alternatives of similarity between the whole or a part, and because in common worldly usage no rule is observed for the determination of meaning in words that lack a basis in other means of knowledge, and because other words function merely as restatements (*anuvāda*), [scripture lacks authority].

Because verbal testimony cannot be a valid means of knowledge; because presumption (*arthāpatti*) and non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), which depend upon negative concomitance (*vyatireka-vyāpti*), share the same status as inference (*anumāna*); because possibility (*saṃbhava*) and tradition (*aitihya*) are mere probabilities;
and because [the other means] such as inference are themselves merely probabilities.

Because activity is established through the conceit of validity; and because, even when the result is doubtful, we observe a regularity of activity among those seeking an object—since certainty regarding the object is not an indispensable factor for activity—the entire course of worldly transaction is thus justified. Furthermore, even the verbal discourse of a Piśāca-possessed person continues only as long as the body exists.

If it is argued that [the ghost] is not seen upon death, and therefore the notion "I am possessed by a *piśāca*" is a vain delusion— like the delusion of one suffering from a derangement of the humors (*sānnipātika*) regarding their own body—

then everything you have said is indeed false and useless, because it is contradicted by your own words. For if everything other than direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) were invalid for the Cārvākas, [your own statement would fall under that same category].

Your statement would have to be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because it too is distinct from perception (*pratyakṣa*). Furthermore, if inference and the other means of knowledge were invalid, you would be unable to support the point you yourself have asserted through arguments; for arguments, being of the nature of inference, would themselves entail validity. Moreover, you possess no illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*).

Since similarity is apprehended through comparison (*upamāna*), it cannot be established if that means of knowledge is invalid. Furthermore, you are unable to put forward any reasoning (*tarka*) that is favorable to your own position or unfavorable to the opponent's position;
for reasoning is constituted by positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka-vyāpti*), and such concomitance is unestablished for one who denies it.

The meaning is that since the non-occurrence of either presence or absence would depend upon non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), if one were to accept that [non-occurrence], it would follow that one must accept the validity of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) and non-apprehension as means of knowledge; thus, even the sixfold set of means of knowledge would have to be accepted as real by the Cārvākas. || 26 ||
If this were so, would not even this cognition—that there is another world consisting of heaven, hell, and so forth—attain the status of truth? (27)

"Let it be so; what is your gain from that? To this he replies: "If it were thus. If the authority of sound and the other [sensory objects] were accepted, then for that reason—because the authority of the Śruti, which consists of flawless words, would necessarily follow—the other world produced by the Śruti, such as heaven, hell, and so forth, would truly exist.

Thus, why does this consciousness not also attain truthfulness and validity? For the validity of cognitions is inherent (*svataḥ*); it is only in certain cases that it is set aside by defects in the causes or by a sublating cognition (*bādhakajñāna*). Now, there is no defect in the cause here, nor is there any valid sublatting cognition such as "heaven, hell, and so forth do not exist"—this is the sense. (27)
For even the perception of a piśāca is not real for one who possesses the power of intoxication;
how then could the appearance consisting of the other world not be unreal? (28)
Now, he refutes what was stated—that it is also a vain delusion—with the word "no.

There is the valid cognition (*pramā*) regarding a *piśāca* in one seized by a *piśāca*, which is established through his own experience as the perception, hearing, and so forth of that *piśāca* residing in another body; and there is the valid cognition of our own kind of observers regarding the *piśāca’s* activity within that other body.

Furthermore, the truthfulness of cognitions is well-established in the world precisely because of their intrinsic validity (*svataḥprāmāṇya*). If even that were not true, then for this intoxicated person, the manifestation of the intoxicating power of substances such as wine—which possess the capacity to intoxicate—would likewise not be true. For those who deny objects established by the experience of one who is sober cannot reasonably deny the intoxicating power established by the perception of one who is intoxicated.

And thus, since your examples are unestablished and the quality of cognition as a property of the elements remains unproven, how could you possibly refute the existence of the next world consisting of heaven, hell, and so forth? This is the implied meaning. || 28 ||
If the cognition "a piśāca exists" is true because its object is real, then why is there not truth in the cognition that "there is another world for the deceased"? (29)

If, by virtue of that self-validity of cognitions which is universally established among all people, the cognition "the piśāca exists" is proven to have a real object through the force of experience, then why should there not be truthfulness in the cognition produced by scripture— such as "there is a world beyond for the deceased"— precisely by the force of that same [self-validity]? (29)

If a ghostly cognition exists within the body by chance, like the "crow-and-palm" coincidence, why is there no corresponding awareness of the objects of the next world, which must likewise have its cause? (30)

Furthermore, the cognition of one possessed by a *piśāca* is not born from a very firm means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) consistent with the Veda, but rather is accidental, like the "crow and the palm fruit" coincidence. Even if such a cognition exists as a valid perception because it cannot be denied by one's own experience, and if it has a cause—being accompanied by very firm Vedic testimony and so forth—then why does the cognition of the existence of the next world not exist? From what [source would it be denied]?
The meaning is that it is not a valid means of knowledge (pramā). || 30 ||
In whatever manner consciousness internally knows, it experiences that very thing accordingly;
whether it be true or false, it is established as such by virtue of experience. (31)

One might object: "Is it not the case that the existence of an object cannot be determined by the force of experience alone, since even in the experience of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, the existence of that object is not observed? Anticipating this doubt, he says: *yā* etc. That consciousness (*saṃvit*) which knows the existence of an object in a certain way experiences that existence of the object accordingly; such is the case with the consciousness of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell.

It [the initial cognition] apprehends the existence of the object as co-temporal with its own appearance. However, the subsequent sublation-cognition, "This is not silver," establishes the non-existence of the silver throughout all three periods of time. In this regard, let the existence of the silver and so forth be *prātibhāsika* (illusory) by virtue of the force of the first cognition;
or rather, let its non-existence be established by the force of the second cognition through direct experience (*anubhūti*). This is the nature of the object.
The meaning is that it is impossible to deny [this] without direct experience. || 31 ||
Knowing that there is a world beyond for the deceased, one should become composed of such [knowledge];
whether this body exists or does not exist, what is the use of that which is both existent and non-existent? (32)

In that case, if— whether while living with a body by the force of means of valid cognition such as scripture, or after death without a body by the power of mere appearance like a dream— there were necessarily to exist a consciousness of the nature of experience in the form "the next world exists," then what would be gained for one already living by that [experience] which is already established through experience?

The meaning is that it is impossible to deny either what is established by the experience of those who have died—that the unreal is unreal—or its opposite; thus, the authority of the Śruti and other sources is proven. || 32 ||
Therefore, the innate nature first flashes forth and perceives pure consciousness;
subsequently, having understood the cause to be latent impressions, it beholds the delusion.

If he should say that consciousness arises from the elements transformed into the form of the body, and therefore no trans-worldly consciousness will arise for one who is dead because the body has perished— then [we reply] that, on the contrary, due to the eternity and self-evident nature of consciousness, it is by the very power of its establishment that the subtle, transportive body (*ativāhika-deha*) consisting of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) [is established].

Since the gross body imagined by that [consciousness] and the external phenomenal world are established only subsequently, and since no other cause for the establishment of the visible world is established, it must be replied that there is no birth of consciousness from the body and so forth; indicating this, he concludes that reply: "When the latent impression has dissolved, it has reached the state of non-appearance."
With the words "Therefore," etc., he introduces the demonstration that the destruction of all objects of perception occurs solely through the exhaustion of latent impressions (*vāsanākṣaya*),
as previously set forth in the passage beginning with "Thus," etc.: because the authority of the Vedas and other means of knowledge,
as well as the self-validity (*svataḥprāmāṇya*) of cognitions, are established, the Supreme Self is of the nature of consciousness.

The meaning is this: because it is self-luminous (*svaprakāśatva*), one knows the consciousness (*saṃvit*)—which is one's own essential nature—as eternally established by itself prior to all worldly transactions; it does not depend on anything else for the fruit of that knowledge, just as fire [does not depend on anything else] for its nature of heat and light.

From that [consciousness], however, arises the subtle body (*ātivāhika-deha*), which is composed of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the entire universe and serves as the cause and material substrate for those impressions.

The point is this: at the very moment the waking state of creation begins, one awakens by the power of the nature of consciousness (*cit*) itself and subsequently perceives the delusion of the body and so forth; therefore, the establishment of consciousness, which is proven to exist prior to everything, is not dependent upon the body.
With the destruction of that [ignorance], the disease of the seer, the seen, and the seeing comes to rest;
with its existence, this demoness called "saṃsāra" arises. (34)

For this very reason, he states—“from its destruction”—that the destruction of all misfortunes is established precisely through the destruction of latent impressions (vāsanā), which in turn leads to the destruction of the subtle body (ativāhika-deha). || 34 ||
First, perception arises, and from that comes the latent impression (vāsanā) of Brahman;
know that the cessation of that [perception] is Nirvana, while its continued existence is the delusion of saṃsāra. (35)

In that regard, at the beginning of creation, or at the outset of Brahmā, there arises a perception consisting of the contemplation of the phenomenal world (prapañca) existing within latent impressions (vāsanā), according to the Vedic scripture: "He thought: 'May I be many; may I procreate. From that, the emergence of the previous worldly impressions occurs in the form of the world. However, upon the cessation of those impressions, [the world ceases] precisely due to the absence of its seed.
He says that "nirvāṇa" is established by implication from the non-arising of the world: "That," etc. (verse 35).
And that [power] has indeed arisen in the Supreme Brahman, since it cannot exist in anything other than the Supreme;
having arisen from the Samaya and so forth, it is none other than the Supreme Brahman itself, which is Reality. (36)
Now, from what is this latent impression (*vāsanā*) produced? It cannot arise from Brahman;

for its causality is denied by such scriptural passages as, "This Brahman is without prior, without posterior, without interior, and without exterior," and because of the scriptures concerning its being unattached, immutable, and non-dual. Nor can it arise from the world of a previous cycle.

Because that [cause], perishing by itself during dissolution, lacks the power to produce another; for is it not the case that it does not perish by itself, but remains having become subtle through its final transformation (bhāvavikāra), and that such a state of remaining is its dissolution in the form of latent impressions (*vāsanā*)? No, because as for this remaining of his during dissolution, is it by its own existence (*svasattayā*) or by the existence of Brahman (*brahmasattayā*)? In the first case, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (*sadeva somyedamagra*).

This is because it contradicts such scriptural passages as "In the beginning, there was only one, without a second. Furthermore, regarding the second alternative—that what is non-existent by itself persists through the existence of another—such a mere babble would over-extend even to the case of a falsehood; moreover, since there would be no distinction between creation and dissolution in either of these two positions, and since an "appearing existence" is unestablished, it cannot be said that "what has perished persists."
If you say it is because of contradiction, that is true; for that latent impression (vāsanā) must have arisen either at the beginning, during the dissolution (pralaya), or in the previous creation.
This is because you yourself have stated that it is impossible for it to exist in the non-dual Supreme Brahman, which is free from attachment.
Nevertheless, it serves as a means for awakening one to the non-dual Brahman.

Since the creation of the world without a seed (nirbīja) is impossible given the time of creation as conceived by the scriptures, it must be admitted that even that latent impression (*vāsanā*) arose due to some prior cause, persisting until the dawn of awakening. However, upon the dawn of awakening, the meaning is that the entire world is resolved as Brahman alone, and that latent impression is likewise resolved as the Supreme Brahman alone. || 36 ||
The wise know that thorough comprehension of this much is nirvāṇa;
know, O Rāghava, that lack of comprehension of this very same thing is bondage.

Furthermore, it is not possible for you to assert that the absence of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and the like in Brahman—which is unattached and non-dual—cannot exist unless that Brahman is first fully known through the scriptures; for if that is fully known, liberation (*nirvāṇa*) itself is attained through the destruction of ignorance, which is the seed of all doubt. Thus, [your objection does not apply].
With the intention of addressing the concern regarding the impossibility of the arising of latent impressions (vāsanā) and so forth, he says: "This much... (37).
This mass of consciousness alone, whose nature consists of both shining and not shining, shines by itself within, or indeed does not shine at all by itself. (38)

When one arrives at the conclusion through rational inquiry, it results that the world, its latent impressions (*vāsanā*), and its ignorance (*avidyā*) are none other than the unknown Brahman; likewise, the cessation of that [ignorance], which is knowledge (*vidyā*), and its fruit, which is liberation (*nirvāṇa*), are also none other than the unknown Brahman. With this intention, he says:
"By means of realization... [etc.]. Prior to the attainment of valid means of knowledge such as scripture, it does not manifest at all. || 38 ||

In that which consists merely of the transformation of the aspect of consciousness and is of a subtle nature, there is neither the vision of bondage nor the vision of liberation; how much effort, then, can there be for its attainment? (39)

Thinking of herself as bound by her very nature, she is herself her own bondage; yet, through valid means of knowledge, realizing "I am eternally liberated," she is herself liberation when this conclusion is understood. Thus he says—*saṃvidaṃśa*—"there is no difficulty whatsoever in the means of liberation. || 39 ||
Bondage lies in the awakening of consciousness; when that [awakening] does not occur, there is Śiva.
The world appears as real though it is unreal, for its interior is nothing but the awakening of consciousness. (40)

With the intention that this may be clearly perceived by investigators through the states of emergence and meditative absorption (*samādhi*), as well as through emergence and deep sleep (*suṣupti*), he says: "In the awakening of consciousness. This means in bringing about the outward orientation of consciousness. Śiva is liberation (*nirvāṇa*). It is precisely within the womb of the awakening of consciousness that the unreal world appears as if real.
Non-inert awareness while asleep is called liberation; that which is awakened is called [liberation]—take whichever you desire. 41.
Abide in that which is the latent impression of nirvāṇa—endless, beginningless, a continuous flow of pure awakening, unconditioned, and free from fear;
non-dual yet devoid of oneness, with emptiness cast out, and peaceful with a mind as clear as the expanse of space. 42.

With the intention that, between bondage and liberation— which are both optional— it is appropriate to adopt liberation alone because it consists of undistracted supreme bliss, the author concludes with the words "nirvāṇavāsanam":
"O Rāma, being Brahman itself, which is solely absorbed in pure consciousness, remain free from constraints and liberated from bondage."
The other qualifiers may be applied either to Brahman or to the action. || 42 ||

Thus ends the seventy-ninth canto, titled "The Exposition on the Absence of Latent Impressions," in the *Deva-mokṣa-nirvāṇa-upadeśa-pāda* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*, composed by Vālmīki according to the Ṛṣi tradition.
Thus ends the seventy-ninth chapter, titled "The Exposition on the Absence of Latent Impressions," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The Eightieth Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Thus, all those inhabitants of the world of Brahmā arrived.
The lamps have become invisible, like wicks whose oil is exhausted. || 1 ||
The sequence of dissolution has been described from the perspective of ultimate reality by the knower of science;
now another sequence of dissolution, pertaining to primordial nature and accessible to yogis, is being described.

The intellectual dissolution (*vaijñānika-pralaya*) is characterized by the sublation of that entire phenomenal world—including the elements, the worlds of gods, and all other realms—which is constructed by latent impressions (*vāsanā*), through a direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) arising at the moment the *prārabdha* karma is exhausted;
as expressed in such passages as: "Just as one who has awakened does not see the city seen in a dream, so [he does not see] what was before," and so forth.

The dissolution of the dream-like [world] has been described with supporting arguments from the perspective of one who is liberated. Now, however, from the perspective of one who is bound, the author begins to describe *pralaya*—dissolution characterized by the merging of the elements of the body, their constituent adjuncts (*upādhi*), and their respective senses back into their own causes within the *brahman* variegated by *māyā*: "Thus... (verse 1).
Then, when Brahmā had attained the state of Brahman, those twelve Ādityas,
with their radiant rays, consumed that world of Brahmā as they would the world itself.
In Brahman, whose body is that of the Creator, there is the state of Brahman as qualified by Māyā; [the world] is like the earth and other elements. || 2 ||
Having burned down the city of Virañca and entered meditative absorption like Virañca himself,
they too attained nirvāṇa, like ten oilless lamps.

He states that even for the individual souls (jīvas) presiding over [the realms] of Āditya and others, because their respective objective worlds were sublated by the final direct realization at the conclusion of their office-bound *prārabdha* karma, they likewise attained disembodied liberation (*videhakaivalya*); thus he says: "Vairiñca... (verse 3).
Then, the flood of the single ocean, possessing a hollow form, filled the interior of Viriñca’s city at night, just as darkness fills the earth.

He states what followed after that with the word "tataḥ" (then). It was the very same filling of the single ocean as previously introduced. According to the reading "mūrtimān" (embodied), it consists of water composed of the five elements. || 4 ||
From the world of Brahmā downwards, the universe was filled with that water,
just as it would be by a ripe grape fruit filled entirely with its juice.
With *arṇasā*, meaning with water; that refers to the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*). || 5 ||
Enveloped by flocks of birds from those various mountain-like waves,
the scattered clouds of smoke vanished right into the water.

By those various surging waves, by the masses of mountains, by the birds, and by the bodies of the gods, the aforementioned clouds of the kalpa—such as the Puṣkarāvartakas and others—were whirled about, shattered, and thus rendered barren, fragmented, and torn asunder. || 6 ||
In the meantime, I beheld from the sky something terrifying that had arisen from within the firmament; I was somewhat afraid.
In that interval, I saw a certain form rising from the sky—terrible and fearsome—but I did not specifically recognize it as Rudra; the meaning is that I was struck with fear at that moment. || 7 ||
Kṛṣṇa, whose form was like that of the world at the end of a kalpa and who filled the sky,
appeared like the darkness of night accumulated since the beginning of time, risen up in bodily form.
He describes that very form with eight verses beginning with "kalpānta," using extraordinary adjectives that serve as causes for fear:

"The darkness produced every night, accumulated and gathered together until the end of the aeon (ākalpa)— that is, until the conclusion of the two parārdhas— having arisen as if from his body, [belongs] to Aghora Rudra, the embodiment of withdrawal."
This is a poetic fancy (utprekṣā) based on the excellence of the color black.
Bearing a radiant splendor like that of a million rising suns,
it was as brilliant as three suns and intense with a mass of steady lightning.

He states that although his complexion was black, it was nonetheless radiant with splendor by saying "taruṇa... (youthful...). The word "dadhat" (bearing) is also connected to the phrase "bearing a radiant face" in the following verse. || 9 ||
With eyes whose faces were radiant, emitting masses of flames,
he had five faces, ten arms, three eyes, and held a trident in his hand.
"Vomiting forth a mass of flames" means emitting a heap of fire. || 10 ||
Though liberated from both beginning and end, you have assumed a body as vast in form as the sky and, like space itself, remain established within it, dark as a dense cloud.
It remained in the sky outside the cosmic egg, which was filled with the waters of the single universal ocean;
it was characterized by the arrangement of hands, feet, and so forth, like the sky itself.
He was like Govinda, who agitated the Milky Ocean with his staff-like arms, while [the other] had a single great ocean tossed by the reversal of the wind from his nostrils. 13.
The snout is the nose; by the reversals—that is, the turnings—of that wind, which is the breath-wind. || 13 ||
He was like the floodwaters of the ocean of the kalpa risen up in the form of a male,
possessing a physical body, the ego-principle (ahaṃkāra) itself, who had arrived as the primordial cause.
As if arisen in the form of a male, as if having come here embodied as the collective totality of all egoism; being the cause of all, he himself is without a cause. || 14 ||
Like a great multitude of mountain ranges taking flight,
it rose up with a display of majesty and filled the entire sky with its mass of wings.
Then, having recognized from afar that "this is Rudra" by means of his trident and three eyes, I paid homage to the Supreme Lord.

Then, immediately after seeing such a form, I recognized that this was Rudra, the Supreme Lord, the Sovereign of the Universe, by his well-known characteristics—the trident and the three eyes—and I paid him homage. || 16 ||
Śrī Rāma said: Is that Rudra of such a kind? Is he Kṛṣṇa? What is his great form? Why does he stand there with five faces and ten arms?

Now, an objection is raised: In such scriptural passages as "One should know Māyā as Prakṛti and the Great Lord (Maheśvara) as the wielder of Māyā," it is well known that the formless Maheśvara is indeed Brahman variegated by Māyā. For what purpose, then, does He assume a formal body (mūrti) characterized by five faces and so forth through various limiting adjuncts (upādhi), and how can this be consistent with His being the Self of all?

Desiring to know specifically what it means for his form to be "limited," Rāma asks: "Is he that [person]? This question—asking for what reason or by what limiting adjunct (upādhi) that Supreme Lord, renowned in all the Vedas, exists in such a terrifying form as described by you—is expanded into ten questions concerning the phenomenal world (prapañca), which constitute three groups.

They are independent. Even in the phrase "he remains," one should understand that the question regarding the substratum arises by supplying the word "where" (kva). Similarly, because the interrogative pronoun "what" (kim) is connected with each [term], there are two questions: "What is fierce? and "What is the Self? (17).
Was he three-eyed? Was he fierce in nature? Was he alone? What was his purpose? By whom was he impelled? What did he do? And what, O Sage, was his shadow? Tell me. (18)

Is he independent or dependent? If he is independent, then for what purpose does this one whose desires are fulfilled engage in the act of dissolution? If he is dependent, then by whom was he impelled? The meaning is: while that Lord exists in the form of Rudra, what was the nature of Māyā, which is his shadow-form, at that time? || 18 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
O descendant of Kakutstha, this one named Rudra arose as the ego;
his nature is the pride of being uniquely distinct, and his form is the pure sky.
