O Kākutstha, that Supreme Lord is the seed of all volitions, determinations, and the like, which govern the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe; He is the foundational pillar for the superimposition of the entire world, and He is the one who restrains all living beings and causes the afflictions of all those who have sought refuge in Him to vanish.

Having become the causal sign (*nimitta*), he arose under the name Rudra. In that state of weeping (*rodana*), he becomes one whose nature is manifold egoity (*viṣamābhimānātman*); but in the dissolving of suffering (*rugdrāvaṇa*), he becomes one whose nature is singular egoity (*ekābhimānātman*). That form of his was seen by me—you are the stainless sky, the very ether (*ākāśa*). || 19 ||
That Blessed One has the form of space, the color of space, and great splendor;
because his essence consists solely of the space of consciousness (cidvyoma), he is called the self of space (ākāśātman). || 20 ||
He states that by this [verse], the three questions—"Is he of such a kind?", "Is he Kṛṣṇa?", and "Is he of great form?"—are resolved: "The sky... (verse 20).
Because he has become the self of all beings and because he is omnipresent, his form is great;
those five cavities which are attached to him are indeed the sense organs.

He provides the answer to the question "Why five faces? with the words "Those which... Those who know reality say that the five organs of knowledge (jñānendriyas) which are attached to that ego (ahaṅkāra) in every body are the faces of that Rudra. || 21 ||
They say those ten forms of his are his mouths on all sides;
for the organs of action and their objects are his ten arms.
For this very reason, the organs of cognition are everywhere of the nature of heat and have light as their essential character.
When he was completely abandoned by all beings and men, together with Brahmā who had ascended to the highest realm,
he then returned to his own form.
He answers the question "Why does he have ten arms? with the words: "The vital points and the sense organs.

The five organs of action—known as speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals—are on the right; and their five respective objects—known as speaking, grasping, moving, excreting, and sexual pleasure—are on the left, in that order for him.
The meaning is that he has ten arms. If it is asked, "Why was he not seen even before in such a form?", [the answer is:

because his vision was deluded by the superimposition of the names, forms, effects, and shapes of the moving and unmoving world; for the Supreme Cause was not perceived apart from all the elements, the fourfold bodies, human beings, and their respective individual souls contained within Him.

When that [universe], variegated by Māyā, was abandoned by the four-faced Brahmā— who had arrived through the dissolution (*pralaya*) and whose own superimposed effect was like a cloth upon a thread— then he returned to his own previously described form, which consists of nothing but the remaining space, existing in the nature of the cause.
That is to say, it has become manifest. || 23 ||
And that [self], being of a single part and a single nature, does not exist, for it has no form;
nevertheless, it is perceived as having a physical body solely through delusion.

If he consists of space alone, then how was that formless being seen to have the bodily shape previously described? To this, he says: "And he... That Rudra is of the nature of that single part which remains as the cause after the dissolution of all specific effects; for him, that bodily shape described by me does not exist. Likewise, [it is not perceived] by the worshippers.
The meaning is that this [object] is perceived through one's own latent impressions (*vāsanā*). || 24 ||
He abides in the vast elemental ether that has become the space of consciousness,
and within the bodies of all beings, he dwells eternally like the vital breath, the Lord.
Regarding the statement "he abides in the questions," having supplied the word "where" (kva) to pose a question concerning the substratum, he provides the answer to that which was described:
"At that time, abandoned by all beings, possessing an ethereal form (khamūrtimān), agitating [the world] for a moment and then becoming diminished, he shall attain supreme peace. (26)
Those which are the qualities, forms, times, mind, ego, and intellect; those which are the syllables of the Praṇava, as well as the three Vedas; || 27 ||
He provides the answer to the question "What is the Three-eyed One? with the words beginning "ye" (those who). || 27 ||
By the arrangement of that Rudra’s eyes, he stands established;
by him, the triple world has been grasped within the hollow of his hand like a trident.

The meaning is that those five groups of three qualities and so forth are situated upon the five faces of Rudra, arranged respectively as the five eyes. Regarding the phrase "What is the fierce self? (*kim ugrātmā*), because the word *kiṃ* (what) is connected to each [member], two questions are described: "What is the fierce one? (*kim ugraḥ*) and "What is the self? (*kim ātmā*). Among these, the hidden meaning of the first is: "By what [means] is he fierce? By the weapon of the trident."
Proclaiming the omniscience of Rāma’s intended meaning, the Sage spoke this reply: "The trident," etc. [in] the hollow of the hand, that is, the cavity formed by the fist. || 28 ||
Since nothing else whatsoever exists apart from that [Self] even among the hosts of all living beings, therefore the body alone stands as the Self. (29)

He provides the answer to the second question, "What is the self? with the words "Because... This means that the self consists of the bodies of the entire multitude of beings. For this very reason, it is precisely through the meditation upon Rudra—who is of the nature of the *ahaṃkāra* (I-maker)—that all beings possess the conceit of identifying the body as the self.
And thus runs the aphorism of the venerable Bādarāyaṇa: "But [the self] is concealed by meditation upon the Supreme; for from that come its bondage and its opposite."
Thus [ends the section]. || 29 ||
Its purpose is a nature consisting of the perception of all beings;
this has been proclaimed by Śiva, who is of the form of the space of pure consciousness.

He states the answer to the question "For what purpose? with the word "sarva" (all). It is that which consists of the perception of all beings created by himself—namely, the experience of objects corresponding to their respective karmas—and which, through the gradual attainment of the means of knowledge, culminates ultimately in the perception of the reality of one's own Self. That [is the purpose].

That very [Brahman], whose nature is to bestow the fruits of actions prescribed or forbidden by the scriptures and of knowledge, is its "purpose" (*prayojana*) because it acts as the impeller at the beginning of creation. Thus it has been said by Gauḍapāda: "This is the inherent nature of the Divine; what desire could there be for Him who has all His wishes fulfilled? He answers the question "By whom impelled? with the word "impelled" (*īrita*).

By the Supreme Self alone—whose essential nature is auspicious, consisting of unsurpassed, infinite bliss beyond the reach of speech and mind, and whose form is the ether of pure consciousness—it is impelled; that is, it is urged toward the inclination for creation by the function of *māyā*, which consists of the volition "May I become manifold, may I be born. Thus impelled, it creates. || 30 ||
And being swallowed by that very [element], he attains supreme peace;
this Lord Kṛṣṇa is the self whose nature is the stainless ether. || 31 ||
The meaning is that, having been impelled toward dissolution, he swallows the universe in the reverse order of its process of creation and remains in the state of space;

then, being himself swallowed by that very Self in the form of Śiva, he abandons even the state of space and attains supreme peace, characterized by establishment in the nature of the bliss of the Infinite (bhūman). What [is this], O Kṛṣṇa?
Recalling that a reasoned resolution has been stated for all such questions as these, he concludes:
"Having brought about the dissolution of the entire universe and having drunk up that single ocean at that time, He attains supreme peace, so that there is no further return. (32)
Immediately thereafter, I saw him there;
with great effort, he began to drag that great ocean toward himself by the force of his vital breath.

Perceiving that the final question—"What did he do?"—was intended to elicit a desire to hear the remainder of the story, he provides the answer beginning with "Immediately thereafter" (*anantaram*). "With the force of his breath" (*prāṇavegena*) means by the force of the wind of his exhalation. "To draw out" (*ākraṣṭum*) means, that is to say, to drink. || 33 ||
Then his mouth opened wide, its interior filled with garlands of flames; like the great ocean drawn in by the vital breath, it entered as if into the submarine fire (*vāḍavāgni*). (34)
The phrase "filled with garlands of flames" is stated to indicate the absorption of water into fire. || 34 ||
Becoming that very submarine fire (*vāḍava*), Rudra, as the ego-principle (*ahaṅkāra*), drinks up all the waters in the ocean until the end of the kalpa. || 35 ||
With the intention that even at other times, when the water dries up, its reabsorption is well known to occur into fire alone, he says: "That very [fire]... (35).
Like water entering the netherworld, like a serpent its hole,
or like the five winds entering space, he entered that mouth with speed in an instant.

The fivefold wind is the fivefold function of the vital breath (prāṇa), like the space within the mouth of living beings. Since the downward breath (apāna) also has the nature of the vital breath, it is designated as having five functions. || 36 ||
Having approached, Rudra drank that milk in a moment,
just as the sun with its dark body consumes darkness, or as contact with the virtuous destroys vice.
The collection of faults consisting of the absence of qualities. || 37 ||
From the world of Brahmā down to the netherworld (pātāla), everything became peaceful and empty;
it was a uniform void, free from dust, smoke, wind, oceans, and the elements. 38.
It is equal, being entirely free from all inequality. || 38 ||
Only these four objects, as stainless as the sky, are seen there motionless; listen to them, O descendant of Raghu. (39)
These are the categories of objects that are about to be explained. || 39 ||
First, there was that one Rudra in the center, appearing in the form of black garments;
unsupported, he stood in the sky like a motionless reflection of a fragrance.
Āmoda means fragrance; its bimba is its essential nature, and it is like that. || 40 ||
The second part is situated far away, resembling the surface of the earth and the sky;
it is the portion of the abode of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) located below the seven netherworlds (pātāla).

Pervading the netherworld, the earth, and the heavens— including the great mountains and the celestial dwellers— he was composed of the earthly portion, consisting essentially of nothing but mud, yet he was his own sustainer.

Because the three worlds and the objects contained within them have been reduced to ashes, it is pervaded by the earthly portion which, through subsequent moistening by water, has become nothing more than mud; thus, being "possessed of self" (ātmabhāk), its essence is somewhat accumulated in comparison to its upper portions. || 42 ||
The third category of objects here was the region above the portion of the cosmic egg;
due to its extreme distance, it was beyond the range of vision and difficult to perceive as the dark expanse of the sky.
Because of the destruction of [wrong] views, the rays of vision do not extend there; the reason for this is "because of extreme distance. || 43 ||
That which lies between the two widely separated halves of the cosmic egg is space— beginningless and endless, the pure, all-pervading Brahman.
He states that the fourth category is simply the space between those two with the words "far away" (dūre). It is as stainless as Brahman.
At that time, I perceived this fourth category of reality;
there is nothing here other than these four, nor anything whatsoever apart from them.
This is the intermediate space. The grammatical connection here is that, among the objects situated before me, there was nothing at all other than this quartet. || 45 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
O Brahman, what exists outside the shell of the world-egg (Brahmāṇḍa), the abode of Brahmā?
Tell me, what are the coverings there, how many are they situated, and in what manner?

There are four questions: [First], what exists outside those two—the shell of the Brahmāṇḍa and the skull of the Brahma-abode (brahmasadmakaṭāha)—which are themselves enclosed? [Second], what are their enclosures (āvaraṇas)? [Third], how many are they? And [fourth], how do they remain situated without any support? || 46 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Beyond the two hemispheres of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), there is water ten times as vast;
beyond that lies the infinite twilight sky (saṃdhyākāśa), situated after having set aside that [water].

Regarding that, he states the first answer to the two middle questions: "Of the two halves of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*). And that water is infinite and extremely vast; it exists spread out only on the outside, excluding the space at the junction of the two halves within.
Although the space at the junction of the two halves is [discussed] in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka*: "As thin as the edge of a razor... [and so forth].

Or, as it has been explained, the space between them is as minute as the edge of a razor or the wing of a fly; nevertheless, previously here, the four-faced Brahmā split the two halves of the cosmic egg, and those two split halves went to a very great distance.
It should be understood that because it has been described in that manner, the infinite nature of the intermediate space (saṃdhyākāśa) is stated in accordance with that. || 47 ||
Then, in that very same way, the fiery energy consisting of flames remained tenfold;
then, in that very same way, the pure wind remained as wind. || 48 ||
In the very same way, like water, the wind—which purifies that water—remains as the wind or air itself, free from the impurity of dust. || 48 ||
Beyond that, the pure sky is said to be ten times [the size of the previous];
beyond that is the supreme, utterly transparent, and infinite space of Brahman (brahmākāśa).

"Nabha" means space (*ākāśa*). He provides the answer to the first question with the word "tataḥ": because of its extreme subtlety, it is exceedingly pure; the space of Brahman, variegated by *māyā*, remains there. (49)
Then, in various other places, his other infinite visions likewise shine in the sky; though situated far apart, they are mutually perceived as creations of their own selves.

[Objection: But surely in the Purāṇas and other texts, it is described that beyond space (ākāśa) is the principle of ego (ahaṃkāra-tattva), ten times greater than that; beyond that, the principle of the Great One (mahat-tattva), ten times greater still; and prior to that, infinite primordial nature (prakṛti). So how can this [account] be set aside? To this, he says: "Elsewhere," etc. In "elsewhere" means in the "sky" (khe)—that is, in the covered space of the essential nature (svarūpa-ākāśa)—of that Brahman variegated by Māyā.
In the various tantras such as those of the Yogins, Māheśvaras, Pāñcarātrikas, and Kāpilas,
infinite divergent views regarding the conceptualization of the coverings of the principles (tattvas) beginning with Mahat and Ahaṃkāra shine forth;
these creations of conceptualized views are proclaimed in the Purāṇas through mutual corroboration, but they are not found in the Śrutis.

The meaning is that we have disregarded [these] processes because they exist; or rather, the verse should be explained as being intent upon the vision of the differentiation of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*). || 50 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
O Lord of Sages, above the fragment of the cosmic egg and likewise below it, where, how, and by whom is that vast expanse of water and the rest supported? (51)
Recalling the fourth remaining question, Rāma asks: "Above...
[referring to verse 51], which describes a form of immense size, increasing tenfold in extent at each successive level even beyond the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa).
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
He remains amidst the objects of the earth like a lotus leaf;
toward him alone do those sons rush, just as children run to their mother.
They rush toward that king, taking him as their support and so forth, relying upon him as the very portion of the shell of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa).
The meaning is that just as the offspring of female monkeys, having firmly grasped their mother in the womb, do not fall even while leaping, so it is here. || 52 ||
O Atman, toward that very Great Body called the Cosmic Egg which is nearest, the objects of the world rush forth like thirsty people toward water. 53.

With the intention that this same principle—aided by proximity—is to be understood even regarding the non-falling of the water situated above the upper rim (*ūrdhvakharpara*), he says "ataḥ" (therefore). "Nedīyaḥ" means more closely situated; the substitute *nedas* is applied for the words *antika* and *bāḍha* when the suffix *īyasun* is added. || 53 ||
Relying upon that very [consciousness] while remaining within it, the faculties such as the taijasa do not abandon their own state of existence, just as the limbs [of a body remain attached]. 54.
Just as the limbs, such as the hands and feet, when joined with the body, do not relinquish their state of very firm connection, so it is in this case. 54.
Śrī Rāma said:
O Brahman, how can it be told how you two remain within the fragment of the cosmic egg? What are their forms, by whom are they supported, and how do they perish? (55)
Since the other two supports—the shell of the Brahmāṇḍa and the lower sphere—are exceedingly heavy, they must inevitably fall;
therefore, Rāma asks, "O Brahman," [inquiring] by what support do these two remain? By what foundation do they stand?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
That which was not held was indeed held aloft, and that which had fallen continued to fall;
the world, though formless, appeared as if possessing form, like a city in a dream.

This consideration regarding a substratum and so forth applies when things are seen as real; however, in the case of false perception, there is no restriction of substratum and so forth even for the most massive objects. Thus, Vasiṣṭha gives the answer by means of the analogy of a dream:
"unsupported" (adhṛtam). This means formless (anākṛti), that is, without material body (amūrtam). || 56 ||
What is its name that falls away, or by what is it sustained?
Just as consciousness manifests, so does this abide.
Just as a mass of hair appears in the sky, and just as emptiness exists in the sky, so too does the vibration of the wind exist in the space of consciousness, and so does the world. 58.
Upon the funeral pyre stands the city of imagination, the house of the world called the cosmic egg;
it is like space within space, formless yet appearing as if possessing every form.
For every form, it is as if each has its own specific, determined form. || 59 ||
That which arises from the consciousness of falling remains as "falling" day and night;
that which arises from the consciousness of going remains as "going" day and night.

He says "pāta" [in the verse] to establish that for all objects, their very nature—whether fixed or unfixed—is established precisely as it is perceived: "by one who goes," that is, by one possessing the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of going. || 60 ||
That which arises from stable consciousness remains steady day and night;
that which arises from the surging consciousness remains surging as it rises.

And thus, the two questions—"of what form [is it]? and "by whom is it sustained?"—are also effectively answered by implication: its forms, whether determined or undetermined, are imagined by one's own consciousness (saṃvit), and it is sustained by consciousness alone. || 61 ||
The knower of destruction goes to destruction through the perceptions of the great kalpas and so forth;
it is born through the perception of birth in the void by means of all primordial perceptions.
He provides the answer to the question "How does it perish? with the word "etīti" (it goes). || 62 ||
A multitude of pearls shines within the autumnal sky; though seen as unreal, they possess a form of supreme reality.
Just as it is impossible to count those shimmering in the heavens due to such delusion, who here in this world is capable of numbering these worlds? 63.

Just as a multitude of pearls appears to the vision of one looking into the expanse of the autumnal sky like the forms of jujube fruits falling [from a tree], so too, who is capable of enumerating the number, support, and other principles of these worlds shimmering through delusion in the sky of consciousness? The meaning is: no one at all. 63.
Thus ends the eightieth chapter, titled "The Demonstration that Error is Merely Illusion," in the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the Holy Vāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa of Valmīki, composed by the Sage. 80.
Thus ends the eightieth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Nature of Illusion," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The eighty-first canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Then, O Rāghava, at that time, in that great sky, he beheld Rudra.
I saw a mad elephant, with its body fully expanded, proceeding to dance. || 1 ||
Rudra, dancing at the time of dissolution, is described here as Bhairava;
and his shadow, the Night of Doom, dances with the universe as her body.

He begins the description of what remained as the answer to the question "What did he do?", namely Rudra’s dance in the space of dissolution, and the answer to the question "Tell me, O Sage, what was the shadow?", which is the nature of the dancing Night of Time (Kālarātri): "Now," etc. (1).
Like the sky having assumed a form without abandoning its own inherent pervasiveness, it was of vast proportions,
deep blue like a dense cloud, and filling the ten directions.
He describes his dancing with the verse beginning "Like the sky," and so forth. || 2 ||
With the sun, moon, and fire as its eyes, with the moving ten directions as its garment,
it was tethered by a dense and long-reaching mass of light from dark-blue flames.
Like a tethering post for the dark rays—that is, the binding pillar for the flames of blue luster. || 3 ||
Resembling the submarine fire, radiant with the weight of its surging waves like flickering arms, it rose up as if suddenly assuming a bodily form from the waters of the single ocean.
His eyes were like submarine fires; the phrase "as if arisen through the bondage of the body" (dehabandhena) is a poetic conceit (utprekṣā) regarding the assumption of a physical form.
Immediately thereafter, I saw that from his body there issued forth, like a shadow, something that followed the movements of his dancing. (5)
Following the dance, imitating the dance of Rudra. || 5 ||
Since the suns are absent and the sky is in great darkness, it is my thought: "How can this shadow exist? (6)
"Thus was my thought"—the word "was" (āsīt) is to be supplied—"such was my apprehension. || 6 ||
Just as I was quickly reflecting, there before him stood that vast Śrī Trilocanā, dancing.
She whose three eyes are glorious. (7)

Dark, emaciated, with limbs covered in veins, decrepit and stretched out in form, her head adorned with a mass of forest materials swaying in the fire filled with flames—[the reading "jvālākulānanā" is more appropriate].
He describes her with the verse beginning with "kṛṣṇā": "decrepit" means having loose or frail limbs; "lola" refers to the mass of forest materials...
She whose dark crest is adorned with flowers, sprouts, and the like, like the abundance of a forest. || 8 ||
Dark as crushed collyrium, she has assumed the form of the night;
the splendor of darkness, as if embodied, or rather, the radiance of the sky itself made manifest in a physical shape.
There are three poetic conceits (utprekṣās). || 9 ||
Exceedingly tall with a terrifying mouth, she seemed intent on measuring the sky;
with her long knees and arms, she appeared as if desiring to measure the quarters of the horizon.
To measure, that is, to determine by equality with its own length, and to compare. || 10 ||
Emaciated as if by many fasts, her great body was deeply sunken;
dark as collyrium, she was like a line of clouds tossed by the wind.
Whose great body was depressed all around and possessed of hollows. || 11 ||
When she was emaciated and unable to stand for so long a time due to fate, she was,
as it were, bound together by long, sinew-like cords.

When she became very tall and thin, and was perceived by the Creator to be unable to stand [erect], he then, as it were, bound her for the sake of firmness with cords in the form of veins; such is the poetic fancy (utprekṣā). || 12 ||
It was so exceedingly long that I could see its head and its hoof only with great effort, by repeatedly moving up and down for a long time.

She was so exceedingly tall that, through my effort and by the power of yoga, moving up and down for many thousands of years with the speed of thought, even after running back and forth for such a long time, her head-hooves— meaning the collection of her head and hooves—
and her toe-nails [remained as they were]. (The compound *śiraḥkhura* is a *dvandva* of parts of living beings.)
This is a case of singular collective treatment (ekavadbhāva). The meaning is that what has been seen by one cannot be seen by another. || 13 ||
With its head, hands, and hooves bound together by strings of entrails,
it was like a thicket of thorns entwined with cords from the very roots.

Whose clusters of limbs, beginning from the head down to the nails of the hands and feet, are bound together by intestines, networks of veins, and cords of entrails; who, like a thicket of thorns such as the *khadira* tree, stands rooted from the base up to the tips of the branches, entwined with threads from root to branch. 14.
She has clusters of lotuses on her head consisting of the sun and other luminaries possessing universal forms; she wears a garland made of pure light, and her borders consist of wind and fire.

She is adorned with garlands fashioned from clusters of lotuses formed by the heads of gods and demons, such as the Sun, which possess various colors representing universal forms; she whose borders and rags are composed of that fire which is kindled by the wind and possesses stainless light.
She had long, dangling ears like writhing serpents, wore earrings made of human flesh,
and possessed long, pendulous, dark breasts resembling withered gourd vines and large stones.
She whose ears were long and adorned with dangling serpent-earrings;
she who was like a dried gourd-creeper with hanging fruit; and she whose breasts were long, pendulous, and drooping as far as the joints of her thighs.
It was marked by the circles of Brahma’s locks of hair, which were like a flood of Kumara’s peacock feathers,
and by the circle of the skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga) upon the head of the exalted Lord of the Gods.

She is the one whose circle of skull-topped staffs (khaṭvāṅga) is such that it marks the lofty heads of the lords of the gods, Indra and the others, with the masses of peacock feathers from the young birds and with the circles of their own braided hair. || 17 ||
Pure like a garland of jasmine flowers due to the falling of stainless radiance, she was like an upward-stretching line upon the ocean of darkness, revolving within her circular whirlpools.
She is stainless by virtue of her moon-like row of teeth; for this very reason, she has increased in splendor through the force of their pure radiance.
Whirling with circular eddies, she stands like the upper surface of a dark ocean, appearing as its upward-reaching streak. || 18 ||
Resembling a dry gourd vine high upon the tree of the sky,
its knotty joints were tossed by the winds, making a "paṭa-paṭa" sound.
She stands upon a tree characterized by space and produced from space; in this same way, the two qualifiers should be applied to both [the tree and the woman] hereafter as well. (19)
With her great waves as upraised arms, she shone with dark splendor,
revolving in the cycles of her dance like a series of waves upon the single vast ocean.
In one moment she has the form of a single arm, and in another moment she is crowded with many arms;
she possesses a pavilion for the dancing of the world, cast forth by her infinite and fierce arms.
By her, the dance-pavilion of the world was seized and thrown into confusion by infinite, fierce arms.
Quickly she takes the form of a single face, quickly the shape of many faces; in an instant she has infinite fierce faces, and for a moment she is even faceless.
In one moment she is endowed with a single foot, and in another she is quickly endowed with hundreds of feet;
for a moment she is rich with infinite feet, and in a moment she assumes the form of being footless.
"I have inferred from her bodily appearance that she is this Kālarātri;
she is this very Bhagavatī Kālī—thus is she determined by the virtuous. (24)

Thus are the virtuous persons determined; since the root *nī* preceded by the prefix *ni* has the sense of "understanding," the suffix *kta* is used in the active voice according to the rule *gatyarthākarmaka-* (Pāṇini 3.4.72). || 24 ||
Her three eyes resemble a fierce well filled with blazing flames,
and the region of her forehead is like the peak of a mountain of burning sapphire.

He begins again to describe her from face to feet with the verse beginning "jvālā" and so forth. When the three hollows on the head-wood of a water-wheel (*āraghaṭṭayantra*) are filled with flames, that is to be understood as a comparison for her three eyes. She is like the plateau of a mountain of sapphire, which possesses a blazing foundation.
She whose forehead is vast. || 25 ||
Her two formidable jaws were like the terrifying abysses of the great sapphire mountain that illuminates the world;
she wore a cluster of pearl-like stars strung upon the thread of the wind-girdle.

Her two jaws, which are formidable because they are illuminated and yet unilluminated by the radiance of her earrings, are like the famous sapphire cavern at the base of Mount Lokāloka due to their downward slope. || 26 ||
In the sky, amidst the lofty radiance of arches as high as mountains of sapphire,
there was a terrifying crow, dark as a mountain of glass, perched upon her lap.

That [city] whose [gate] has a lofty archway—equal to a sapphire mountain, worthy of comparison, and fit for metaphor—adorned with the luster of rubies and other gems; and wherein the Lord Kāka (the crow), named Bhaga, rests established within the opening at the end of the gate like a downward-facing artificial glass mountain. || 27 ||
With the flowers of her dancing vine-like arms— the white circles of light from her nails—
she seemed to whirl hundreds of full moons across the expanse of the sky.
With their arms whirling and pervading the circle of the quarters like the clouds at the end of an aeon,
they rained down great streaks of light that resembled rows of stars from the extremities of living beings.
On the side of his arm-like wings, the stars—born of living beings and originating from elephants—shine with radiant luster like elephant tusks;

at their edges, they appear as rows of great streaks of light pouring forth. On the side of his arms, the rows of stars, born of living beings and originating from elephants and other sources, fall at the edge like pearls; and the rows of his nails, shining with great radiance, appear like a flight of stars.
By those who are raining down. || 29 ||
With their wandering tree-like arms, which were like networks of creepers with nails for flowers and fingers for tendrils,
those dark ones of fierce form made the entire expanse of the sky appear as a forest.

By those wandering tree-like arms— which, for that very reason, were of fierce form and dark, and which possessed clusters of creeper-like fingers with nails for their flowers— she made the entire expanse of the sky appear like a forest. 30.
Moving with a swaying gait, she traversed the ground thick with *tāla* and *tamāla* trees, which, scorched by great forest fires, resembled her own shapely thighs.

With its multitude of shanks moving restlessly in every direction, it imitates— meaning it resembles— the broad and lofty earth encircled by great forests of date palms and other trees that have been consumed by fire, which now consists only of the remaining burnt *tāla* and *tamāla* plants. || 31 ||
Even with its hair reaching the far shore of the infinite great sky,
it seemed to be spreading out a vast garment for the wandering elephant of darkness.
With her hair, she seems to be providing a dwelling in the sky for an elephant characterized by moving darkness. || 32 ||
By that breath-wind,
which resounds through the circle of the quarters, the village of the sky, and with a deep *ghuṃghuma* roar, even the Merus are carried away.

The connection with the following verse is as follows: he was as if in conversation with a dancer who, by his very nature of making proclamations, possessed a constant flow of breath-wind that was therefore continuous; this wind caused the entire circle of directions to resound with a dense *ghuṃghuma* noise through its echoes, within that village of the sky. || 33 ||
As it sang the song of its roar like a battle-shout amidst the blasts of the dense wind,
she was moved as if by a persistent and compliant entreaty.
Then, as her body grew larger through the intensity of her possession by the power of the dance,
she was seen by me with focused attention within the vast expanse of the sky.
As long as that garland, whose essence was playful undulations, remained encircling her body, it was encompassed by the Malaya, Kailāsa, Sahya, Mandara, and Meru mountains. (36)

He explains how she was seen with the words "yāvat" (up to). With her whose essence was the dance performed with ease and grace (*helayā vilāsena valanam*), a garland composed entirely (*yāvat-sākalyena*) of mountains such as Malaya, Kailāsa, and Sahya was fashioned upon her body; it was enveloped or, according to another reading, *dhṛtā* (worn) as an ornament. || 36 ||
The row of clouds at the end of the age was her silk headband;
and the three intermediate worlds were the mirror-circles upon her body.

Furthermore, with the intention of showing that the entire world became her constant array of ornaments, he says "There was," and so forth. At the end of the eon, the well-known garland of clouds such as the Puṣkarāvarta became a sash of sapphire cloth upon her chest; the three intermediate spaces between the worlds were upon her limbs, such as her hips and belly.
"Mirror-spheres made of jewels were present," and so forth; in all cases, the connection should be made by appropriately adapting [the phrase] through modification as required. || 37 ||
On his two ears are silver and golden rings shaped like the Himavat and Meru mountains;
he wears a great girdle around his waist, a garland made of the humming sounds of the cosmic egg.
The great boundary mountains are garlands, with their peaks, forests, and cities as their clusters;
the ancient cities, forests, islands, and villages are their delicate sprouts. (39)
Within her limbs are seen the ancient cities and towns, the three worlds as the seasons, and the arrangement of months, days, and nights. (40)

Regarding the word *dṛṣṭāni*, the neuter form remains by the rule "the neuter [remains] when combined with a non-neuter" (*napuṃsakamanapuṃsakena*); this is the rule for the remainder of the neuter (*napuṃsakaśeṣa*). || 40 ||
The pearl necklaces and other ornaments are the rivers such as the Yamunā and the Gaṅgā;
both merit and demerit are the ear-ornaments on his two ears. (41)
"In the ears of another" refers to the ears other than the previously mentioned ears, [specifically] those having the Himavat and Meru mountains as their earrings. || 41 ||
Her four breasts were flowing with drops of the milk of Dharma; they were the Vedas, with nipples established in the fourfold arrangement of the meaning of all the scriptures.
Those whose nipples—the tips of their breasts—are the four collections known as the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva Vedas, which contain the milk of the meaning of all the scriptures. || 42 ||
With tridents, sharp-edged spears, javelins, arrows, pikes, double-edged swords, and mallets,
she bears emerging masses of weapons like garlands of flowers.
The fourteen kinds of living beings, beginning with the gods, exist as the rows of hair upon her who possesses that body. (44)
Those well-known lines of hair are the "romāvalayas" (lines of body hair). || 44 ||
And as she dances, the cities, villages, and mountains lying within her body dance along with her; they do so for the sake of their own rebirth.
At that time, I realized that this entire world, including all that is moving and stationary, is but a single living soul; it dances, and thus abides in happiness in the next world.
Because everything in dance involves movement, it is non-static in nature; yet, because it was previously dead, it remains happily situated in the next world, characterized by that very body.
Having swallowed the world and placed it within her own body, she has attained satisfaction; intoxicated, she dances like a peahen that has digested an old serpent.

The female cātaka bird (cātakī) is one by whom the world is characterized—that is, an aged serpent or snake; here, by the word "cātakī," the peahen (mayūrī) is indicated, due to the similarity of being fond of clouds, and because she is well-known for both swallowing snakes and dancing. 47.
The entire universe appears as if situated within a mirror-reflection;
in her vast, essential body, it assumes a form identical to her own.
Assuming a form, he assumed a form similar to that of the previous world. || 48 ||
She does not dance; rather, this entire world—including its mountains, forests, and groves—dances, appearing in manifold forms as it dies and returns again. (49)

He said: "Once, even when she was not dancing, I saw that the world contained within her was dancing. That beautiful dancing of the world, reflected in the mirror of her body, was seen by me for a long time then, remaining undiminished and stable. (50)
The net of stars was flickering, the circle of mountains was whirling,
and the gods and demons were shaken by the wind like a swarm of gnats.
He describes that very dance of the world with the verse beginning "vicalat" (51).

The sky was encompassed by islands and oceans resembling the wheels released in battle; the earth, with its massive mountains, was like a blade of grass amidst the whirlpools created by his effortless tossing.

The sky was filled with those islands and other lands whose splendor resembled the whirling motion of wheels released in battle; in that [sky], mountains, earths, and grasses were carried away with great force by playful tossings and rotations, as if by whirlwind gusts. [In the word *prādūḍha*, the vowel lengthening occurs according to the rule *prādūhoḍho*. 52.
The sky resounded with the whistling of the wind as it was shrouded by garments of blue clouds,
while a loud "paṭa-paṭa" noise arose from the cracking and bursting of wood, bones, and other materials.
In which [place] the sky was made to resound with the *ghuṃghumi* sound by the winds amidst the shifting and turning of garments (*aṃśuka*) characterized like dark blue clouds; while below,
there was the cracking of joints through the friction of wood, bones, and other materials striking against one another.
It is characterized by sounds such as "paṭat-paṭa," which are worthy of imitation, and by specific rhythmic movements. || 53 ||
Just as a mirror is pervaded by various objects of the world, both mingled and unmixed,
so too was it pervaded by limbs that were coiled and hissing with sounds, and by limbs that moved about like illusions.
It was pervaded by worldly objects that were both mingled and unmixed, through their mutual collision and separation at every moment; likewise,
it was filled with limbs and whirlpools, and with swelling gurgling sounds like personified terrors.
Mount Meru dances, its great arms being the restless and lofty principal mountain ranges;
it is clothed in the swirling mass of clouds and possesses a fine body-hair of slender trees.
He describes that very cosmic dance of the world individually, beginning with the words "Meru" and so forth:
"That [world] whose [mountains] are joined by wandering masses of clouds, whose trees have bending trunks and fine foliage, and which possesses *kalpa* trees. (55)
The oceans, abandoning their seal of the shoreline, and the trees, [overstepping their bounds],
go from the surface of the earth to the sky, and from the sky they descend to the surface of the earth.
The sealing of the boundary is the regulation of the limit of the tide. || 56 ||
Cities are seen rolling below with gurgling roars, yet nothing—including the houses, watchtowers, and inhabitants—rolls down at all. (57)

The *vāstavyas*—those dwelling in houses and building sites—rolled about together with their tails so that they were covered [by her]. As she wandered skillfully therein, the moon, the sun, day, and night appeared like golden threads moving within the light of the lines at the tips of her claws. 57–58.

While that Night of Doom (Kālarātri) is wandering, the moon, sun, and other luminaries appear like long golden threads within the lines at the tips of her fingernails; the meaning is that they appear as if they were whirling firebrands. || 58 ||
Her creations shine like dewdrops upon a web of water, as she is clothed in dark clouds and adorned with frost.

The meaning is that the networks of water released by the clouds—the creations of that city of Hāravatī, which is charming with its mists and clothed in garments of dark-blue clouds—shine like drops of sweat on a hot day. || 59 ||
Her vast mass of braided hair became the sky;
her two feet were the netherworld (pātāla), her belly was the earth, and her arms were the quarters of space.
Now he describes how the entire world has come to be constituted as her limbs, beginning with the words "The sky itself," etc. (verse 60).
The continents and oceans are the coils of its intestines; all the mountains are its ribs;
and the series of vital breaths (prāṇa and apāna) are its swinging cradles, possessing the shoulders of the winds.

The continents and oceans became her bracelets together with the entrails; the masses of wind characterized as the Āvaha, Udvaha, Pravaha, and others became the towers and halls of her celestial palace; and the series of inhalations and exhalations became the swings for her.
Then, upon her expansive body as she danced,
he experienced the sensation of being rocked by mountains such as Himavat, Meru, and Sahya, which seemed to whirl like swings.

Therefore, there is a poetic fancy (utprekṣā) that the pleasure of swinging was experienced by Him upon His body, which was such that it was whirled about by the Himalaya and other mountains that had become its constituent parts through being attached to it as accessories for that very purpose. || 62 ||
As she twirled her garlands with her creeper-like arms, it was as if the cosmic dance of the end of the aeon had begun once more in playful sport. (63)

With that same *tāṇṭava* dance described previously—by which she causes the garlands, consisting of clusters and blossoms marked by stones, to float and turn about—it is as if a new dissolution (*pralaya*) has once again begun; such is the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*). || 63 ||
His body was covered with the hair-like forms of hosts of gods, asuras, and serpents;
unable to remain motionless, he whirled around like a wheel.

His tiny body was unable to remain motionless within her own body; being unable to do so, it wandered about—this is a poetic conceit (*utprekṣā*). The substitution of the verbal suffix (*vikaraṇa*) for the root *śak* follows Vedic usage (*chāndasa*). || 64 ||
Clad in the sacred thread of various manifestations of consciousness,
she moved through the sky, resounding with the deep roar of thunderclouds.

With the various states of existence as the fruits of karma, the consciousnesses that cause their performance as the threads, and the sacrifices consisting of their performance as the sacred thread— this goddess,

wearing the triple-threaded *yajñopavīta* and moving and dancing through the sky, was like a female religious student (*brahmacāriṇī*), resounding with the deep rumbling of clouds like the chanting of the Vedas. || 65 ||
In that state, the ground becomes space and space also becomes the ground;
it is a reflection within, and nothing at all undergoes transformation.

Alternatively, by that dancing there, neither the earth nor the sky changes or moves in the slightest; however, through the pretext of the wheel’s motion, by means of mutual reflection, each becomes a counterpart resembling the other:
in turn, the earth becomes the sky, and the sky becomes the earth. To those observing there, both appear together.
The meaning is that they merely revolve upwards and downwards by means of their own respective constituent elements; it is nothing but an illusion. || 66 ||
From the cavernous abode of his broad nostrils issued forth deep, rumbling sounds;
there, fierce winds blew, producing terrible whistling noises.
He describes those breath-winds [as follows]: "Vast," etc. (Verse 67).
With hundreds of rays that revolve in fourfold circles,
the sky shines as if filled with sprouts stirred up by a fierce wind.

Because of the resulting delusion regarding the multitude of worldly objects born from that limb [of mine], even my firm vision has faltered in this infatuation, like an army in the heat of battle. (69)

My vision, steadfast and firm, was like an army in battle; it became weary and its power blunted by the exhaustion arising from those wanderings which occurred together with the world-objects born of that [vision]. || 69 ||
Mountains are carried away like machines, sky-dwellers fall down,
and the abodes of the immortals roll about when the mirror of the body is turned.
When the mirror of her body was bent and turned over, || 70 ||
The Meru mountains were arrayed like leaves, the Malaya mountains like tender sprouts;
the Himalayas were like particles of frost, and the earths like lotus creepers.
The earth-born [beings] have become like water-lilies upon the broad earth—dispersed and shattered. || 71 ||
They were like birds on the Sahya mountain, like Vidyādharas on the Vindhya range,
and like royal swans wandering in the sky over the Vṛkṣāvarta region.

Like royal swans in the sky, they were circling within the whirlpool of trees; [the form] *antāḥ* [is derived from] *anta-* with a long vowel by the rule "when *ṇ* is elided after *ṛ*, there is lengthening. 72.
The continents were like blades of grass, the oceans like bracelets, and the abodes of the gods like lotuses within the waters of his body. (73)

In the water characterized by her body, it is understood that "the rows [of clouds]—the abodes of the celestial worlds—are like lotuses. Because of the placement of the rows within this poetic fancy (utprekṣā), the simile of the lake is established upon her body. || 73 ||
Upon her broad-thighed body, which resembled the clear sky, was like a city seen in a dream or through magic ointment, and possessed a luster equal to the orb of the sun.

The connection with the following verse is as follows: "On her body, which possessed a brilliance equal to the suns gathered together, all the mountains, beginning with Vindhya, attained mobility. (74)
Vindhya dances in the forest of the Golden Mountain; Sahya and the Sahya mountain, Kailāsa, Malaya, the peak of Mahendra, Krauñca mountain, and Mandara;
Gokarṇa, the courtyard of the sky, the earth, and the city of the Vidyādharas—all have attained mobility.
The forest-dwelling state was always present within her body. || 75 ||
In the forest upon the crest of the Golden Mountain, the Vindhya range dances as if seeking to avenge its ancient enmity;
the Sahya mountain, unbearable in its intensity, and Kailāsa and the others dance in the courtyard of the sky as if out of anger.
Out of partiality for them, the earth and the city of the Vidyādharas also dance. Thus, all the stationary beings—
The meaning is that they have attained the state of being mobile. || 75 ||

The oceans dance upon the mountain; even the mountain leaps high into the hollow of the sky; even the firmament, along with the moon and sun, has moved from beneath the earth. The multitude of forests, with their islands, mountains, and cities, is strewn with flowers in the heavens, like a tossing world in the ocean.
A blade of grass whirls about within the circle of the directions. || 76 ||

Moreover, this is another marvel: the ocean dances upon the mountain; and that mountain dances high up in the hollow of the sky. Even that sky, together with the moon and sun, having moved beneath the earth, is no longer known where it has gone. It is such that the mountains and continents, along with the islands, are strewn with flowers.
[The reading *pattanaḥ* is correct. The multitude of forests dances in the sky, in the celestial realm at the station of the sun and other luminaries.
Thus, the meaning is that the world, as unstable as a blade of grass, wanders within the circle of the quarters like one tossed upon the ocean. || 76 ||
Mountains, oceans, the ends of the quarters, other worlds, and circles of cities and towns wander in the sky,
like rivers and lakes within a mirror, by the process of the movement of grass scattered by a powerful wind.

Likewise, mountains wander in the sky, and oceans wander to the ends of the quarters; cities, towns, districts, rivers, and lakes enter other worlds from their own abodes like reflections entering a mirror. These are the strides and flights of grasses scattered by a powerful wind, as they are well known in the world.
The meaning is that they revolve according to that sequence. || 77 ||
Fish move about in the desert as if in excellent water; cities appear in the sky as if fixed upon the earth;
and mountains stand in the air like clouds at the end of an aeon, situated upon peaks whirled by the winds of cosmic dissolution.

Moreover, fish move upon the excellent waters as if in the ocean, though they are in a desert; cities appear fixed in the sky as if on the earth; mountains shine in the air; and the sky is filled with clouds that exhaust the waters—those clouds of universal dissolution—and the collection of these [phenomena] is situated amidst mountains whirled about by the winds of cosmic catastrophe.
The meaning is that this is the supreme marvel. || 78 ||
A multitude of stars revolves by means of a mechanical wheel of a thousand lamps, beautiful with the speed of a shower of jewels;
it is like a rain of flowers released out of affection by hosts of Vidyādharas and immortals both inside and outside, on every side.

Moreover, the cluster of stars, like a shower of jewels falling with great force, is beautiful and captivating as it revolves through the sequence of the thousand lamps' rotating mechanical wheels, both inside and outside the earth—
just as a rain of flowers was affectionately released by hosts of Vidyādharas and gods within and without your assembly.
In that same way, it wanders. || 79 ||

The multitudes of dissolution and creation, corresponding to the divisions of day and night, appear like drops of silver; the white and black masses of the day likewise shine forth in confusion on all sides, like the stainless white and black circles of a mirror.
Moreover, within that body, the contractions, dissolutions, and successions of creations flash forth during the divisions of day and night, and even within a fortnight;

that is to say, the days and nights are few in number. Likewise, the multitudes of days and nights—comparable to drops of the two colors, black and white—are extremely small in their manifestation. As for those pure fortnights, both dark and light, which surround it on all sides—
The meaning is that beautiful mirrors, white and black, fashioned from diamonds, sapphires, and other gems, shine like those maṇḍalas. || 80 ||
The orbs of the sun and moon, clusters of stars, and necklaces of shimmering circular luster serve as jewels;
the clear sky and the vast expanse of space act as garments, incessantly creating many swirling streaks like firebrands.
Thus, upon her body, the orbs of the sun and moon became jewels, and the clusters of stars...
The clusters of stars became necklaces possessing a shimmering, circular luster;

the clear skies became vast garments wrapped and draped about them; and within those, the whirling streaks of fire from lightning became lines of firebrands, emitting an incessant and abundant radiance.
The meaning is "they perform. || 81 ||

The various and virtuous ornaments, whose gems tumble through the three worlds at the time of the end of the aeon, emit a tinkling *jhaṇajjhaṇa* sound as they whirl about; their radiant splendors move upward and downward with a humming resonance.

During that dance at the time of the end of the aeon, as the three worlds rolled about, the jewels suddenly produced a "jhaṇajjhaṇa" sound through their revolutions; likewise, by means of that humming or resonance, various excellent ornaments such as anklets and bracelets moved upward and downward, reaching even the splendors of the sun and other luminaries— this is the meaning.

In these battles, where every day and its sunlight turn dark with the wave-like luster of the swords of intoxicated warriors, the clamor of the throngs of people is heard even as they roll about, though they remain steadfastly firm.
What is more marvelous? Among the intoxicated warriors in the battles—

The days, whose entire sunlight turns dark with the waves of radiance from [their] swords, and likewise the tumultuous clamor of the circles of heroes— firmly established in the Brahma-sthāna despite their rolling about during the Goddess’s *tāṇḍava* dance due to her whirling revolutions— is heard. (83)
Led by Brahmā, Indra, Viṣṇu, Hara, Agni, Ravi, and Indu, the gods and asuras rush forward in their revolutions;
they come and go in various ways, like gnats tossed about by the wind or like flashes of lightning.
There is yet another marvel: in the *tāṇḍava* of her whose body is composed of infinite millions of past and future creations and dissolutions,
the gods and asuras, beginning with Brahmā and Indra, though they are distinct from one another in their respective offices and activities,
are encountered and overwhelmed as if by well-known winds that shake away gnats or by thunderbolts and lightning flashes.
Through delusion—that is, through the play of instability—they come and they go. || 84 ||

In that [state], the phenomena of dissolution and creation, pleasure and pain, birth and non-birth, effort and lack of effort, prohibition and injunction, and life and death, always manifest together and separately; even though they have attained a state of intermixture within creation, they remain there as distinct entities.

Furthermore, another marvel: while her body was manifest, all states of being—such as creation and dissolution, which are mutually contradictory—always sported together with it yet separately, without touching one another; that is to say, even when they attained a state of intermingling, they continued to sport. || 85 ||

Of these illusory bodies shimmering in the sky— performing the arising, abiding, and destruction of existences, as well as the wandering through the worlds of creation and dissolution— not even the slightest trace of their number can be perceived here. (86)

Furthermore, what is the number—that is, the measure—of these phenomena within that body in the void of consciousness (cidākāśa), which manifest there as mere illusion? Precisely because of this, from the existence—that is, the presiding foundation—of those "void-bodies" (khaśarīraka) which are themselves empty, there arise: dissolution, creation, the delusions of worlds and lands, birth, persistence, calamity, destruction, instruments, the delusions of causal efficiency (arthakriyā), and transformations. Such is their enumeration.
It is not perceived even in the slightest degree. || 86 ||
Therein, portents, pacification, death, festivals, war, equanimity, hatred, passion, fear, trust, and so forth—
like a collection of jewels within a single casket— it shines as a succession of creations of various flavors that are unimpeded.

Furthermore, within that body, the various pairs of opposites—such as calamities and their pacification—shine together like a collection of jewels in a single casket; for the meaning is that his body is such that within it, successions of creations, though possessing diverse natures, exist without mutual obstruction. || 87 ||
Within her body, which consists of the ether of consciousness, the various states of the world—arising from the nature of indistinct experience—manifest everywhere;
yet, because they are subject to total dissolution, they shine forth like the appearance of a net of hair in the sky perceived by one with impaired vision.
Furthermore, within her body which is, in the ultimate sense, composed of the sky of consciousness (*cidākāśa*),
there exists an inherent state characterized by the obscuration of *māyā*— a state established by non-scriptural perception and consisting of an indistinct experience;
it is this state that brings about the various arrangements of the world and all its dissolutions, as perceived by those whose vision is clouded by the disease of cataracts spreading on all sides.
They flash like the shimmering of a tuft of hair situated in the sky. || 88 ||
The world, though agitated, is seen as unagitated, established in its state of stability; it remains unmoved, like a reflection in a mirror being shaken. (89)
The meaning is as follows: when the world is established in a state of pure existence through the sustaining power (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Immovable One (*Acalā*), it remains indeed undisturbed;

yet, from the perspective of the agitation of *māyā*, it appears to be agitated. For just as a mountain, which is itself immovable, appears to move when its reflection is shaken in a mirror, so too does the world appear while remaining exactly as it is. || 89 ||
With their inner majesty flashing through their dance, they abandon their state and assume it at every moment for the sake of the world, like the creations of a child’s imagination.

All objects of the world, situated within Māyā whose majesty flashes forth through her dance, abandon their prior state and assume another state at every moment due to constant transformation (*pariṇāma*). In this regard, the creation resulting from the imagination of children is the well-known illustration; thus say the Sāṃkhyas: "For all things undergo transformation at every moment."
"Existents," [it is said]. || 90 ||
The power of action, incessantly filling the interior of the body, becomes a mass and scatters the heaps of the world like a multitude of mung bean grains. (91)

The powers of the causal factors (*kāraka*) and of action (*kriyā*) are employed solely for the purpose of producing all things; however, the subsequent modifications of being proceed by themselves in the course of time. Just as the power of the causal factors and of action is employed in the heaping together of mung beans, but in their scattering and spreading, the cause is simply their own inherent nature of oiliness, and not anything else.
He says that the capacity for action belongs to other causal factors in the same way: "the capacity for action," etc. (91).
For a moment she is perceived as something, and for a moment she is nothing at all;
for a moment she is only the size of a thumb, and for a moment she fills the entire sky.
For that entire Goddess is the power of consciousness (saṃvit-śakti) consisting of the universe;
she is infinite, possessing a pure body that is the treasury of the supreme ether.
Because she consists of the world, which is insentient and subject to transformation, that Goddess is perceived as becoming different and different at every moment;
thus he says: "For a moment... (vv. 92–93).
For that Consciousness, which indeed exists within the three worlds situated in the three times, shines forth in that very manner— by way of a form that exists as it is,
like a web of the world-picture residing in the mind of a skilled painter, and by means of its flashing speed.
For that Goddess is the internal consciousness (citi) inherent within the three worlds, which abide in the three periods of time and possess the manifold variety of transformations of all principles.

For this reason, in the noble mind of the person— painted by the speed of consciousness as it flashes forth according to the maturation of various latent impressions (vāsanās) of desire and action, proceeding through its successive states (paryāya) exactly as they exist— [the universe appears].
The meaning is that the manifold web of saṃsāra, which exists as it is, shines forth in various forms corresponding to its actual state. || 94 ||
Because she is the single conscious self whose body consists of all things, and because she is the reality of the single conscious self whose body is the tranquil void;
thus bearing a form that is both closed and opened as one, she shines with an infinite and beginningless body.
If so, is she indeed possessed of manifold elaboration (*saprapañca*)? No; he says: "consisting of all" (*sarvātmakā*).

That Goddess, because her nature is the single consciousness (*ekacidātman*) veiled by ignorance (*avidyā*), exists as the body of the entire phenomenal world (*saṃsāra*), like a variegated wall. But when ignorance is dispelled by knowledge (*vidyā*), because her nature is the single consciousness free from ignorance, she exists as the tranquil void (*kha*), the ether, whose form is entirely devoid of manifold elaboration (*niṣprapañca*).

The meaning is that she shines, bearing a form that is in reality a single essence of consciousness, beginningless and endless; yet she is characterized by being accessible through the eyes of the bound and the eyes of the liberated, and through the closing and opening of the eyes, which metaphorically signify ignorance and knowledge respectively. || 95 ||
Within that infinite treasury consisting of the stone, the visible world shines forth like the carving of lines, lotuses, and wheels;
it appears within her whose body is merely the void of space, just as ripples appear in the expanse of the liquid ocean due to its consciousness.

Thus, for those liberated while living and for those established in reasoning, the world manifests within her through both the perspective of illusory transformation (*vivarta*) and the perspective of actual modification (*pariṇāma*).
He states two examples with the words "tasyām" (in that). Here, "stone" refers to a crystal stone (*sphaṭika-śilā*).
The portion ending with "having the sky alone as its body" is the explanation of the first example; the remainder is for the second.
"The great goddess Bhairavī, filling the sky while dancing," [is the second example].
That city belonged to that Rudra of another aeon, who possessed a terrifying form.
Having thus described the true nature of her and that dance, he further describes the dance through poetic fancy (utprekṣā) and other figures:
"Her forest-ground, its stumps scorched by the fierce fire resting upon the moon on her head, dances like a forest garland shaken by the winds at the end of an aeon. (98)

It was like that very earth whose forest ranges— like rows of groves— had been consumed by the fierce fire of the third eye located on the forehead of Rudra at the end of the eon, and which, for that reason,
were reduced to mere stumps; it was as if those forest ranges had been shaken by the winds at the end of the eon.
"It dances" is either a poetic fancy (utprekṣā) or a simile (upamā). || 98 ||
She carried a hoe, a mortar, a grass mat, a wooden board, a water-pot, and a basket;
she held a pestle, a ladle, a cooking pot, and a pillar, and wore garlands and strings of beads.
It is said—“kuddālā” (the spade)—that not only does she possess the garlands previously described, but also tools such as the spade, the mace, and the mortar. || 99 ||
Scattering such masses of flowers from the networks of garlands,
she seemed to be knitting together the earth, which had been wounded by the exhaustion of her dancing.
In the dance, she scatters that which was agitated, shaken, destroyed by decay, and broken, as if creating something ever new. || 100 ||
While being thus praised by her, Ākāśabhairava likewise,
with his form expanded in that very manner, danced exultantly.

May he protect us— he who dances to the sound of musical instruments, uttering "ḍimbaṃ ḍimbaṃ suḍimbaṃ paca paca sahasājhamya jhamyaṃ prajhamyaṃ," holding in his hand the great horn of Yama’s buffalo filled with the wine of blood, wearing a garland upon his chest and a crest of Tārkṣya feathers upon his head, while being praised by all.
Bhairava [is united] with Kālarātri through the joy of dissolution. || 102 ||
Holding in her hand the great horn of Yama’s buffalo, filled with red liquor,

she dances to the accompaniment of cymbals and other instruments marked by the sound of palatal consonants such as "ḍimba" and "ḍimbam"; making her own head a garland upon her breast, she wears a crest-ornament fashioned from the feathers of Garuḍa, having devoured the world at the time of universal dissolution.

May Bhairava, who is being saluted and praised by Muditā and Kālarātri, protect you—may this be a blessing meaning that he guards you by removing the defects that obstruct knowledge. Furthermore, the meaning of the passage beginning with "ḍimbaṃ ḍimbam" is as follows: O Bhairava, you [are the one who destroys] the *ḍimba*—the adjunct consisting of the experience of misfortune—for all living beings.

Having swallowed (*jhamya*) the expansion of the gross body and so forth— *jhamu* meaning "to eat"— and having likewise made the *ḍimba*, the expansion of the subtle body and so forth, the object to be swallowed (*bhakṣya*), one then, at the final direct realization, truly manifests and swallows (*prajhamya*) even the *suḍimba*, the causal body which serves as the fundamental limiting adjunct (*mūlopādhi*).

The syntactical connection is as follows: "May Bhairava protect you—he who, having made the food perfect by placing it upon the stages of yoga beginning with the fifth, quickly and suddenly cooks it, and having fully ripened it up to the seventh stage, causes it to decay through disembodied liberation (*videhakaivalya*), while being thus praised; or rather, he who is praised by you along with the dancing Kālarātri."

Thus ends the eighty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Night of Time," in the *Uttara-pāṣāṇa* section of the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki. 81.
Thus ends the eighty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Night of Doom," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The eighty-second canto.
Śrī Rāma said:
"O Blessed One, what is this that dances during the universal destruction, and by whom is she [made to] dance?"
What is the use of winnowing baskets, platters, jars, and so forth, when she wears a garland of wreaths?
Here, the true nature of Śiva, who possesses diverse forms, is extracted and described:
as long as it is not fully known, it is with parts (sakala); when it is thoroughly known, it is without parts (niṣkala).

The dissolution of the entire phenomenal world has been described in detail previously; furthermore, the existence of that dissolved world as ornaments and so forth upon the limbs of the dancing Kālarātri, as well as her dancing and whirling, were described. Thinking that this [reappearance] was an impossible resurrection of what had been destroyed, Rāma asks: "What is this?"

When everything has been destroyed, with which limb does that goddess dance? Since her winnowing basket, fruit, jar, and so forth have perished, how can the wearing of garlands by her—which was mentioned by you—be possible? This is the meaning. || 1 ||
What was lost has returned as the three worlds; what was situated within the body has been reclaimed by Kālī. How is it that Nirvāṇa dances and has once again arrived? || 2 ||

He explains that very point clearly with the words "What [is it]? (kimiti). The meaning is that if [the world] has perished and yet remains, how can there be liberation? And if the ceased world has returned, how can it dance again? Thus, it appears to be a contradiction. || 2 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
That was not a man, nor was it a woman; there was neither that dance nor those two individuals.
In such a state and with such conduct, there were no physical forms belonging to them.

If, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), you consider what I have said to be contradictory, then let it be so; for from the standpoint of ultimate reality, since the forms of the world such as male and female, and the distinctions between Rudra, the Goddess, and so forth— which are nothing other than pure consciousness, the single flavor of fullness, and pure existence— are absolutely impossible, there is no contradiction at all from the perspective of deluded vision (*bhrāntadṛś*).

Because it has been repeatedly stated that, since all things always exist through the reality of Brahman, it is impossible to define any distinction between their destruction and non-destruction; and because it is well known that even things destroyed in dreams or during insanity may reappear, and even those who have died and long since been reduced to ashes [may return].

Due to the power of the boons granted by Munisiddheśvara and others, it is well known that [the deity] will return; for as long as ignorance exists, the form of the world persists in the minds of all beings as latent impressions (*saṃskāra*). Thus, those who are utterly deluded—such as the worshippers of Rudra, Devī, and others—perceive [the deity] solely as the form of the world, as a single embodiment composed of the entire universe, and in such a manner.
With the intention that [the Self] can be seen through the power of the perfection of yoga, Vasiṣṭha gives the reply beginning with "nāsau" (not that). || 3 ||
That which is the beginningless sky of pure consciousness is the cause of all causes;
it is infinite, peaceful, a mere manifestation, immutable, and all-pervading.
That auspicious, true Śiva is directly perceived in the form of Bhairava;
established thus for the peace of the world, he is indeed the supreme ether itself.

Śiva is that very Brahman, whose sole essence is unsurpassed bliss; that Śiva, who is truly existent, is perceived by practitioners at the time of dissolution in the form of Bhairava, characterized by such features as having a blue throat and three eyes—this is the implied meaning. For, according to their latent impressions (*vāsanā*), that Supreme Space itself remains in such a form.
Because it possesses consciousness, it is not logical for that [self] to remain without the manifestation of such a nature, just as gold cannot exist without form.

Furthermore, the withdrawal of the world into the conscious Brahman is well-known in the Śrutis. Moreover, no formless conscious being is ever seen in the world; therefore, the Lord who withdraws [the universe], as established by such Śruti passages as "the Supreme Lord, the Master, accompanied by Umā, the three-eyed, blue-throated, and tranquil," should be conceived of in that very form.

With this intention, he says: "because of its being conscious" (*cetanatvāt*). The two genitive endings are used in the sense of the instrumental. The meaning is that just as it is not fitting for gold to remain in a formless state, so too it is not fitting for that [consciousness] either. || 6 ||
Tell me, O wise one, how can pure consciousness exist without a conscious being?
Tell me, O wise one, how can black pepper exist without its pungency? (7)

Just as in the case of gold or other substances there is a necessary rule that they must necessarily assume one or another form such as a lump or an earring, so too it is well-known in the world that consciousness must necessarily take hold of an objective form; thus, the position that only the formless remains is indeed [the correct one].
On the contrary, he says "how so? by way of a bold assertion (*prauḍhivāda*) regarding the impossibility [of such a thing]. || 7 ||
Consider how gold could exist without its bracelets and other ornaments;
how could the existence of an object occur without its own intrinsic nature? (8)
With the intention that the aspect (ākāra) is difficult to discard because even an unknown consciousness has the nature of possessing an object, he says:
"How [could it be] by its own nature," and so forth. (8)
Without sweetness, how can one speak of sugarcane juice?
That which is devoid of sweetness is not indeed that juice.
That which is mere consciousness (cinmātra) yet devoid of sentience is not called "mere consciousness";
nor is it possible for the space of mere consciousness to ever perish anywhere. (10)

Moreover, since even for things that have perished, their appearance is observed in memory, it is shown by the vision of consciousness (*cid-dṛṣṭi*) that the absolute destruction (*niranvaya-nāśa*) of anything is unestablished; thus he says: "And not... (verse 10).
Nothing other than its own mere existence is possible for it; indeed, it is impossible to maintain its distinctness from space, for it is said to be non-different from space. (11)

Furthermore, since no form of the world other than the mere existence of Brahman is established for that which is non-different from Brahman, the destruction of nothing whatsoever is established; thus he says, "His own. But [one might object]: "The defined and the undefined, the founded and the unfounded, consciousness and unconsciousness, truth and falsehood—all became the True"—this indicates that there is something distinct from the existence of Brahman.

The form is heard of and experienced even by common folk; regarding this, he says: "otherness. This Self, which is Brahman, thinking "May I be many, may I procreate," accepted otherness in the form of the universe. Therefore, according to the scriptural text, "From this very Self, space was produced," it first [produced] the sky, which is non-different from itself, being identical with the ether (*ākāśa*).
It is said that [the Creator] acts. If He creates space (*vyoman*) as non-different from Himself, then how could its distinctness (*anyatva*) be accepted?

Or, if its non-difference from the nature of existence (*sadrūpa*) is not established, how could space be said to have been created? For the very attainment of the state of being the Self of Existence is the "birth" of space and so forth; thus, it is neither defined nor undefined, according to the Vedic texts such as "that which is defined and that which is undefined," concerning the forms of the formed and the formless.
The meaning is that the difference from the nature of existence is not established. || 11 ||
Therefore, that which is its undisturbed state—mere existence, self-luminous, without beginning, middle, or end, and consisting of all powers—[is the Self]. || 12 ||

If it is asked, "What then is the nature of the world?"—it is simply the existence of Brahman (*brahmasattaiva*). For, in the absence of the means of knowledge that realizes reality, the world appears through the worldly perspective in the form of creation, dissolution, and so forth, just as a rope appears in the form of a snake; however, by the means of knowledge that realizes reality, it appears in its true form. He concludes this summary with the words: "Therefore... (verse 12).
Thus, this creation and dissolution of the three worlds— the sky, the earth, and the directions—
known as destruction and production, is nothing but the non-manifestation of space.

The meaning is that appearance without the manifestation of reality—that is, appearance by a vision corrupted by ignorance—is like the appearance of the moon, the sky, and so forth to one with cataracts; it is entirely devoid of any object apart from the pure existence of space itself. || 13 ||
Birth and death, illusion and delusion, dullness and unreality, as well as reality, discrimination, bondage and liberation, and the auspicious and the inauspicious—[all these are but the mind]. (14)

But from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), all this—birth and so forth—is the stainless space of pure consciousness (*śuddhacidākāśa*); such is the connection [of the text] in the fifth [chapter].
*Māyā* is projection (*vikṣepa*) and *moha* is obscuration (*āvaraṇa*); the combination of these two is [the term used here]. || 14 ||
Knowledge and ignorance, bodilessness and embodiedness, the momentary and the long-lasting,
mobility and stability, as well as "you," "I," and "the other"— all that is it.
Existence and non-existence, as well as both existence and non-existence, folly and wisdom itself, and the playful conceptualization of the reckoning of place, time, action, and substance— (16)
This world, consisting of form, light, mental attention, action, the intellect, and the sense organs, as well as fire, water, air, ether, earth, and so forth, is pervaded by that [Brahman]. 17.
All this is that pure space of consciousness, free from affliction;
not relinquishing its very nature as space, it thus abides as the self of all.
And all this is nothing but the pure space here; of this there is no doubt.
It is non-different from this [space], and the dream and other such examples are unimpeachable in this regard. (19)

With the intention that its non-difference from consciousness (cid-ananyatva) may likewise be conceived through the analogy of a dream—just as its non-difference from the seat [of perception] was—[the author] says: "All this... (verse 19).
That which I have described as the supreme ether consisting of consciousness—this very thing is called Śiva; he is the eternal one.

He is the Supreme Self, whose sole nature is Being-Consciousness-Bliss. The meaning is that I have presented this form of Rudra because He is indeed the eternal Śiva, as stated in such Vedic passages as: "Having abandoned everything else, one should meditate on the one Śiva alone, who brings about auspiciousness. Thus, this eternal Śiva is indeed Śiva. || 20 ||
He exists as this Hari; he becomes this Grandfather (Brahmā);
he is the Moon, the Sun, Indra, Varuṇa, Yama, Vaiśravaṇa, and Anala.

He alone remains in the guise of Hari for those who worship Him in the form of Viṣṇu and others; likewise, He becomes the Grandfather (Brahmā) for others. What need is there for more? He says "the Moon" to show that He also appears in whatever form corresponds to the mental impressions (*vāsanā*) of those whose intellects are permeated by the ideas of the moon, the sun, and so forth.
