And thus says the Śruti: "They call Him Indra, Mitra, Varuṇa, and Agni; and He is the divine, fair-winged bird."
Garutman: "The sages speak of that which is one as manifold; they call it Agni, Yama, and Mātariśvan. || 21 ||
The wind, the cloud, and the ocean—whatever object there was yesterday, that no longer exists;
thus these mere fragments of the space-treasury of consciousness flash forth intensely.

That very one is the wind, the air. "Yesterday" refers to the past day; this is an illustration for any measure of time. The meaning is that whatever object is conceptualized there as either existing or non-existing, all that is indeed this very one. And thus says the Śruti: "He is Brahmā, He is Hari, He is Indra, He is the Imperishable, the Supreme Self-ruler. He alone is Viṣṇu, He is Prāṇa, He is Time, Fire, and the Moon. He alone..."

"Having known that which is all—whatever has been and whatever is to be, the eternal—one transcends death; there is no other path to liberation. Thus have these entities, beginning with Hari and Pitāmaha, been described as portions and fragments of the Brahma-ether-receptacle consisting of consciousness, produced by the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of the qualities (guṇas) and so forth. || 22 ||
Through such designations, these things are falsely conceptualized;
however, by the realization of their mere intrinsic nature, they become exactly as they are. (23)

Through ignorance (*avidyā*), which causes one to perceive things otherwise by means of false conceptualization, [beings appear as they do]; however, through the awakening to the mere ultimate nature, these [beings] become such that their very nature is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*). || 23 ||
Non-awakening and awakening are thus nothing but the space of consciousness (cidvyoma) abiding within itself;
therefore, let there be peace, for neither difference, duality, nor unity exists at all.

And thus, Brahman itself remains for a certain time in the form of ignorance through the perspective of the ignorant, appearing as the individual soul (jīva) and the world; thereafter, through the perspective of the wise, it remains in its true nature in the form of awakening. The result is that there is nothing other than That at any time whatsoever—thus he says: "ignorance" (abodha). || 24 ||
For that long, this individual soul creates its own great ocean of saṃsāra consisting of waves;
but when it has attained identity with That, the soul knows the supreme, stainless nature. || 25 ||

And so, as long as the individual soul (jīva) does not know its own essential nature, which is the Supreme Brahman, it remains for that duration in the great ocean of saṃsāra, characterized by various waves such as birth, death, and wandering. But when it knows [that nature], then, having attained identity with That, it abides in That alone, free from all affliction.
This is the meaning. || 25 ||
But through knowledge, he attains peace in such a way that he is neither that ocean nor those waves;
for him, all this, as it truly exists, becomes the infinite Supreme itself, which is peaceful. (26)
He states that very point: "But when [it] is known," etc. (26).
Thus ends the eighty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Nature of Śiva," in the *Uttara-pāṣāṇa* section of the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*, composed by Vālmīki.

Thus ends the eighty-second chapter, titled "Description of the Nature of Śiva," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa*, in its elucidation of the essential meaning (*tātparyaprakāśa*).
The eighty-third canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
This which has been described by me as the supreme space of pure consciousness alone—
"This is that Śiva," so it was said, as Rudra then began to dance. || 1 ||
He is Śiva alone, pure consciousness; he is not Kālī or the form of Bhairava.
It is described that he appears as such through the conceptualizing vision for the sake of awakening.
O best among the accomplished, that form which belongs to him is not a form at all;
it is the sky of pure consciousness alone, and thus it shines forth in such a manner.

For this very reason, in order to dispel your ignorance and delusion and to reveal the vision of your true nature as Śiva, I have described my own experience of the dance of Rudra at the dissolution of the universe and so forth; however, one should not fall into the error of thinking that this alone is the ultimate reality.
Thus he says with the words beginning "cinmātra... (verse 1) and so on. (verses 1–2)
At that time, I saw that very space as having that form;
it was understood by me alone, for no one else perceives it in that way.
But by me, through the vision of reality, that form was seen as nothing other than the mere expanse of consciousness;
whereas another is devoid of the vision of reality. || 3 ||
Just as that end of the eon, that Rudra, and that Bhairavī are [mere appearances],
so too have I fully understood all this to be nothing but illusion.
By means of the vision of reality itself, I have fully realized that everything from the end of an eon onwards is merely illusion. || 4 ||
The supreme void is indeed the sky of consciousness;
through that particular configuration, it appears as such, having assumed the form of Bhairava.
Without the relationship between the signified and the signifier, no understanding arises;
therefore, what was perceived by me in you has been described exactly as it was seen.

Even though You are seen through the vision of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), the description before You is [necessary] because it is impossible to explain that which is devoid of distinctions without the conceptualization of the relationship between the signified (*vācya*) and the signifier (*vācaka*)—that is, words and their meanings.
He says "the signified," etc., meaning that this is for the purpose of explaining You by means of such conceptualization. || 6 ||
O Rāma, whatever has been expressed here is always for you;
for one whose perception of the material world is firmly rooted, this [world] attains the nature of illusion in an instant.
He says "yadeva" (whatever indeed) to show that the refutation of that [notion] is for the purpose of ensuring that no notion of reality arises regarding the imagined process:

"O Rāma, for you whose perception of the material world has long been firmly rooted through constant practice, whatever is mounted upon words immediately assumes the nature of illusion and falls into the delusion of reality. (7)
That is not Bhairavī, nor is he Bhairava, nor is there any destruction;
all of that is merely an illusion, for it is the space of consciousness alone that shines forth.
By the further negation beginning with "not Bhairavī" and so forth, all of that appears as nothing but an illusion, while in the ultimate sense it shines as the sky of consciousness alone. || 8 ||
Like a dream or a city of magical creation, like the force of a mental resolve, like the essence of the caravan of a story’s meaning, and like the play of a kingdom of the mind.
Just as a dream-city appears in the clear sky, just as the perception of pearls arises [in the air],
and just as a tuft of hair appears in the sky, so does the non-conscious (acid) appear within the dense mass of consciousness (cidghana).
In the same way, consciousness shines as if insentient within the mass of consciousness due to delusion. || 10 ||
The pure space of pure consciousness alone shines clearly by itself within itself;
thus, that which appears as such shines as the self in the form of the world. (11)
If that is so, how does it appear through awakening? To this he says: "It is mere consciousness" (cinmātra). || 11 ||
Just as the Self shines by itself within the sky of consciousness, so does it shine upon the canvas;
likewise, it shines there during the dance of the fire at the end of the aeon.
In that case, is there a distinction between the self-luminous conscious Self illuminating itself and illuminating others? He says "no," with the words "yathā" (just as). || 12 ||
O dear one, thus has the formless nature of the two Śivas been described.
Now listen; I shall tell you of the state of the dance as non-dance.

And so, having concluded that the only form remaining for Śiva and Śivā is the sky of consciousness (*cidvyoma*) itself—which is of a single nature of luminosity and devoid of distinctions, and is thus essentially formless—he says, "Listen to this portion being explained," namely that while the persistence of the dance is merely *māyā*, its true state is actually a state of non-dancing: Thus, having summarized that the only form remaining for the two, Śiva and Śivā, is the very expanse of consciousness (*cidvyoma*), which is of a single nature of manifestation (*kacanaikasvabhāva*) and devoid of distinctions (*nirviśeṣa*), and is therefore essentially formless (*nirākāra*);
he then says, "Listen," as he explains the point that the persistence of the dance is merely *māyā*, and thus its true state is a state of non-dancing (*anṛttatā*).
"Of the two Śivas," [so it is said]. || 13 ||
Volition cannot exist anywhere without some degree of contact with the element of volition, just as a thing cannot exist without being a reality. (14)

Just as an object such as mother-of-pearl, when perceived through delusion, cannot exist without the non-real [appearance] of silver, so too the conscious element cannot exist without some degree of vibration within consciousness;
this is because there is an identical rule regarding the nature of delusion to cause a reversal of reality. || 14 ||
Therefore, consciousness exists as Rudra by virtue of its own nature,
just as gold exists in the form of a statue through its artistic arrangement.

For this very reason, he states with the words beginning "by its own nature" (svabhāvāt) that Brahman, whose form is existence, abides as the substratum through the transformation of the entire universe into the forms of Rudra and the Goddess, who constitute His body. || 15 ||
Whatever is indeed volition, wherever it exists, necessarily possesses the property of movement by its very nature; for a thing arises from its own inherent nature. (16)
Reality is the state of being the substratum. || 16 ||

Whatever vibration belongs to this Śiva, who is a mass of consciousness, that alone shines forth for us as a dance itself, through the power of being possessed by one's own latent impressions (vāsanā). (17)
Therefore, know that when Rudra, who is auspicious at the end of the aeon, assumes a fierce form and dances swiftly, it is indeed his own vibration as a mass of consciousness.
Śrī Rāma said: From the perspective of valid cognition, this visible world does not exist at all in reality;
whatever appears as if it exists will all perish at the end of the kalpa.

From the perspective of valid cognition, [the world] does not exist at all; therefore, there is no question regarding that view. I ask, however, from the perspective of an invalid view: whatever exists as it were, all of that perishes at the end of the eon. (19)
In this supreme void, which is as utterly empty as at the end of an aeon, the mass of consciousness perceives, by some means, that which is indeed nameless and beyond the reach of thought.

That being so, how can there be that which is called "consciousness" (citta)—which is non-objective and devoid of objects? Likewise, in the absence of a substratum, how can there be a cognizer or an agent of cognition? And in the absence of any cognitive activity distinct from itself, how can the mass of consciousness (cidghana) cognize? The meaning is that the threefold division (tripuṭī) is not logically tenable. Furthermore, if it is ignorance (avidyā), then it is precisely because of that [ignorance] that the unreal visible world is made to appear.

If it were said that the accomplishment of the *tripuṭī* [the threefold union] occurs [there], then there would be no distinction between creation and dissolution; for neither that dancing nor the body of Rudra and the Goddess—which consists of the entire unconscious universe—is possible. The sense is that it is impossible to conceive of duality and unity simultaneously. || 20 ||
Śrī VasiṣṬha said:
Even then, my dear, this alone serves to pacify the ocean of duality and unity:
that in the sky of pure consciousness there is no object of thought whatsoever.

My dear friend, if you have such a doubt, even then, listen to this very answer for the sake of pacifying the ocean of your uncertainty regarding duality and unity. He says that very thing with the words "yadi" (if): if, at the time of universal dissolution, there were any object of cognition remaining for the sky of pure consciousness, then, precisely because of the absence of a second [entity], it could exist in some place or at some time.

At that time, no one perceives even the slightest thing; for the Śruti says, "But when for him everything has become the Self alone, then by what and whom should he see?"—this is the intended meaning. || 21 ||
Therefore, nothing whatsoever is perceived anywhere at any time;
everything is peaceful, a stone-like silence, a mass of consciousness, and the sky.

And thus, since you have proposed that this dissolution is precisely the nature of the eternally liberated self as established by the perspective of those who accept valid authority (*prāmāṇika*), the first alternative alone has been reached; so he says, "All... The implication is that, therefore, the question is not appropriate if one relies on the second alternative from the perspective of those who do not accept such authority (*aprāmāṇika*). || 22 ||
That which is called "the object of cognition" moves as its own nature;
for the tranquil nature of consciousness remains established in its own being. 23.

If, however, in order to distinguish [this view] from the first alternative, you admit that at the time of dissolution (*pralaya*) there exists some object of cognition such as ignorance (*avidyā*) and so forth, then by that very fact, the dancing of Rudra and the bodies of the Goddess within the triple-layered (*tripuṭī*) world will be established; thus, nothing I have said is impossible.
With this intention, he says "And that which is this... and so forth. [The term is] *svabhāvaḥ* (intrinsic nature).
Even during the dissolution (*pralaya*), the Goddess Rudra dances and manifests in the form of that dance of this Brahman whose essential nature (*ātmasvarūpa*) is not fully known.
He states that there is no loss of the true, immutable nature of consciousness (*citsvabhāva*) on account of this—thus he says: "of the nature of consciousness" (*citsvabhāvasya*). || 23 ||
Just as in a dream, consciousness itself appears internally like a city or a fortress, yet that city and so forth do not exist at all; it is merely the space of pure awareness.
He provides an illustration for the fact that even when there is an appearance of something otherwise due to error, there is no loss of its actual nature—beginning with "Just as" (yathā). || 24 ||
Having realized through the self within the self that both the knower and the object of knowledge are utterly devoid of consciousness,
it likewise understands its own manifestation from the very beginning of creation.

And thus, even though it has known all that is knowable by means of its own consciousness within itself, the Cit is always [aware] that the knowable is empty. Furthermore, from the moment of the beginning of creation until the moment of dissolution, even during the period of dissolution, it knows its own manifestation exactly as it occurred; therefore, the meaning is that Brahman is well-known as being eternally omniscient. || 25 ||
Shining by itself within the hollow of the sky that is its own nature, consciousness,
through its own imagination, sustains the delusion of the world— whether it be a mere moment or an eon.
For this very reason, it is also conceivable that even at the time of that creation, he perceives it together with all the thousands of past and future dissolutions;
with this intention, he says "himself," and so forth. || 26 ||
The sky of consciousness, whose luster shines within itself in the void of its own nature,
creates such conceptualizations as "this is he," "I am this," and "you are this."
Therefore, there is no duality here, nor unity, nor emptiness;
there is neither the conscious nor the unconscious, neither silence nor even that which is not silence.

For this very reason, with the intention that all objects of perception and their absence mutually negate one another, and thus serve as the limits for the negation of both existence and non-existence regarding the ultimate reality (*paramārthavastu*), he concludes with the words "Therefore," and so forth.
Furthermore, even the distinction between creation and dissolution is established by one's own experience alone; it cannot be denied by a simultaneous cognition.
The state of being. || 28 ||
Nothing whatsoever is perceived anywhere by anyone, because of the nature of the perceivable self;
therefore, even the perceiver does not exist, as it were, and only silence remains. (29)

For non-conceptual meditative absorption (*nirvikalpa-samādhi*) is the established conclusion in all scriptural traditions; that is the silence of a living rock. Therefore, one should remain simply silent. (30)
Performing your own natural duties according to the flow of worldly custom, remain steadfast in the silence of the ultimate truth;
free from pride, delusion, intoxication, and duality, with a mind as pure as the expanse of space and tranquil, abide as one whose life-force is the bodiless one (Kāma).
O Rāma, you too, like the Lord, appear as such through the eyes of the world, yet remain established in your own innate nature.

While carrying out the entire web of conduct for governing the kingdom and so forth according to the current flow, following the lineage obtained from his father and grandfather, he remained— by virtue of his own vision— in the silence of the ultimate truth,
free from pride, free from delusion, and devoid of egoistic distinctions between his limbs and the living soul that identifies with them.
Remain peaceful and undistracted, with a mind as clear as the expanse of space, free from all attachment. 31.

Thus ends the eighty-third canto, titled "The Vision of the Universal Form," in the latter half of the *Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa* of the *Mokṣopāya* section of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa*, composed by the sage Vālmīki. 83.
Thus ends the eighty-third canto, titled "The Vision of the Universal Form," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa-tātparyaprakāśa*.
The eighty-fourth canto.
Śrī Rāma said: O Sage, tell me what happened next; why was Kālī dancing?
Is she adorned with a garland made of winnowing baskets, wooden planks, hoes, pestles, and other such tools? || 1 ||
The innate nature of Śiva and Śakti is here described after having been analyzed;
their form as the winnowing-basket and so forth arises from the reflection upon the real and the unreal.

"What is that Kālī who dances, as described by you? What is her true nature?"—this is the meaning. Furthermore, "by what kind of garland made of winnowing baskets, planks, hoes, and so forth is she surrounded?"—the meaning is that you should explain both of these. Even in the reading "What is it like that Time (Kāla) dances?", the question concerns the very nature of Kālī, who is of the essence of Time; it is precisely about her.
Because of the description of dancing and the wearing of garlands with winnowing baskets, pestles, and so forth in the preceding and following sections of the text. (1)
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
That Bhairava, who is the space of consciousness, is designated as Śiva;
know that his non-different power of vibration, consisting of mind, is that [Śakti]. (2)

Since it is impossible to define the nature of Śiva’s power without first defining His own essential nature, he begins by defining both forms simultaneously with the word "He" (sa). [He is] the power of vibration (*spanda-śakti*) through the predominance of the *rajas* quality, whose inherent nature is motion,
and [the power of consciousness] through the predominance of the clarity of the *sattva* quality, by virtue of the pervasion of the reflection of consciousness everywhere.

The meaning is: know that Māyā to be non-different from Śiva, because it is composed of the impressions (saṃskāra) of the world, because it is the cause of the mental constructs of volition and doubt regarding creation and so forth—thus being identical to the mind—and because it is superimposed as identical with Śiva, and because its existence and manifestation are dependent upon Him. || 2 ||
Just as a single wind and its movement are one, and just as heat and fire are one,
so too pure consciousness and the power of movement are always of one essence.

He supports the non-difference [of the two] with two examples, beginning with "just as. The expression "always" is used with the intention that since all temporal activity is already concluded even prior to liberation, there is indeed pervasion by all time. || 3 ||
Air is characterized by its vibration, and fire is characterized by its heat;
pure consciousness, stainless and tranquil, is designated as Śiva.

Since the Śruti texts state, "From which indeed these beings are born; by which, once born, they live," and so forth—thereby defining Śiva, who is Brahman, through the very activity of the world's creation and the vital pulsation of living beings—it is said that [the world] is non-different from Him, as expressed in the following two verses beginning with "By the pulsation" (spandena). || 4 ||
That [Śiva] is indeed perceived only through the power of His own vibration (spanda-māyā-śakti), and not otherwise;
for the wise know Śiva-Brahman to be peaceful and inexpressible even to those who are masters of speech.
Now, one might ask: since the scriptures describe the characteristics of Brahman as creation and so forth, how can that [Brahman] be said to be Śiva? To this he replies with the word "Śivam.
Because all the scriptures and the knowers of Brahman understand Brahman to be none other than Śiva, the meaning is that there is no Brahman other than Śiva who is not auspicious (aśiva). || 5 ||
The power of vibration (spanda-śakti) extends that appearance of the visible world according to His will,
just as the will of a person possessing form creates a city of imagination.

In such passages as "He desired: 'May I be many, may I procreate,'" that very power of vibration (spanda-śakti) is said to be the will of Śiva; indeed, it is this same power that unfolds the universe like a mental creation for Him whose desires are ever-fulfilled. Thus he says: "The power of vibration. (6)
The Will of Śiva indeed acts; it acts this [universe] even though He is formless.

This very [Will] is called Consciousness (*cit*), because it is the life-force for those who desire life. [Following this: "Arising through its orientation toward the object of cognition (*cetya*), this same [Consciousness] is called by the name 'latent impression' (*vāsanā*), for it is the impression of the perception of the visible world. It is also called the 'portion of the individual soul' (*jīvakalā*)."
It is seen in some places. || 7 ||

This very power of consciousness (citi-śakti), because it is illumined by the reflection of consciousness (cid-ābhāsa) inherent within itself, is called the living consciousness (jīva-caitanya). || 7 ||
Having herself become the primordial nature (prakṛti) of creation by virtue of being that very nature,
she is called "action" (kriyā) because she brings about the manifestation and experience of the perceptible world.

By being the primordial nature (*prakṛti*), that is, by undergoing transformation into the form of the world. And thus says the Śruti: "One should know Māyā as the primordial nature, and the Great Lord as the wielder of Māyā.
[This refers to] the characteristics of arising, attainment, modification, and impression, which are experienced within the appearances of the perceptible.
Because of the production of the four kinds of fruits. || 8 ||
Because she dries up [all things] with a form like the crest of the submarine fire (vaḍavāgni), she is called Śuṣkā;
and because of her fierce nature (caṇḍitva), she is proclaimed as Caṇḍikā; and because of the color of the blue lotus (utpala), she is [called] Utpalā.

He states the reason for her well-known dryness in the Purāṇas— where she is described as being clothed in leopard skins, with parched flesh, and extremely terrifying— even by means of the word "vaḍavā" (mare-fire):

because she possesses a body that is the cosmic egg moistened by the waters of the ocean and other sources, she [is nourished] by the light of the summer sun and other luminaries, which have the form of the flames of the *vaḍavāgni* (submarine fire).
Because it is to be dried from its vicinity, it is therefore called "the dry" (śuṣkā). || 9 ||
She is Jayā because she is solely intent upon victory; she is Siddhā because she is the refuge of accomplishment;
she is called Jayantī because she is victorious; and she is Vijayā because she is the basis of triumph.

Since she is victorious (*jaya*), she is therefore called *jayantī*; thus, both names share one and the same ground for their application (*pravṛttinimitta*). However, the term *vijayā* refers to a distinguished victory. This should be inferred in the same way for what follows as well. || 10 ||
She is called Parājitā because of her valor, and Durgā because of her form that is difficult to grasp;
she is celebrated as Umā because she is the essential power of the syllable Om.

The meaning is that she is celebrated as *Umā* because the syllables *u*, *ma*, and *a*— which constitute the *oṃkāra*— are combined in reverse order (*u-m-a*) and the feminine suffix *ṭāp* is applied, thereby producing the word *umā*. However, in the reading "she is celebrated as *Samā*," it refers to her being the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), which is the essence of the entire phenomenal world (the gross, subtle, and so forth) and the fourth state (*turīya*) characterized by the *oṃkāra*.
She is called Gāyatrī because her nature is that of song; Sāvitrī because she abides as the source of procreation; and she is declared to be Sarasvatī because she causes all visions to flow forth.
They are singers and reciters because they consist of the supreme human goal;
for they are the refuge and the expansion for those who possess the vision of knowledge, meditation, and all ritual actions which are the means to attain heaven and liberation. || 12 ||
Gaurī, because her body is fair-limbed, is attached to the body of Bhava;
she resides in the hearts of those who are asleep as well as those who are awake through the mere utterance of her name.

Because the universe arises from him, he is Bhava, the Lord; Umā is that which is attached to his body. Furthermore, he explains the name Umā by another method: "Of those who are asleep... The word *atha* is used in the sense of *ca* (and). [She resides] in the heart of all living beings situated in the three worlds—both those who are asleep and those who are awake—in the form of the unstruck sound (*anāhatanāda*).

The crescent digit of the moon (*indukalā*) in the form of a *bindu*, which serves as an ornament upon the head of Śiva— known as the "inner space" (*daharākāśa*)— who resides in the shape of a *liṅga* within the cavity of the heart-lotus (measuring the size of a thumb) and who is called the "Word-Brahman" (*śabdabrahman*), consisting of the portion of the *praṇava*’s resonance devoid of the three measures beginning with the letter *a*, is called *Umā*. This is because she is eternally, at all times, uttered [along with him].

And so it is said in the Vāyavīya-saṃhitā: "Om is the single-syllabled Brahman, the designator of Brahman. It consists of the three measures—A, U, and M—and is followed by the half-measure (ardhamātrā). Among these, the letter A is situated on the right side of the flaming liṅga; likewise, the letter U is on the left, and the letter M is in its center. This [half-measure] consists of the half-measure."

"The sound is heard at the top of the *liṅga*. And in the *Haṃsopaniṣad*, after describing the various states of the individual soul (*jīva*) within the petals of the heart-lotus—beginning with "on the eastern petal, one of virtuous mind"—it states that deep sleep occurs in the *liṅga*. When the *haṃsa* abandons the lotus and dissolves into the *nāda*, that is the state beyond the fourth (*turīyātīta*). Thus, [the sound is heard] at the top of the *liṅga*, in that *nāda*.
The meaning is that it has been stated that the state beyond the fourth (turīyātītāvasthā) is the firm establishment in Brahman through the dissolution of all limiting adjuncts (upādhi). || 13 ||
The crescent moon is said to be the eternal essence of the beings of the three worlds;
because Śiva and Śivā possess the nature of space, their body appears dark.
Regarding the question, "Why does Kālī dance?", and intending the inquiry as to the reason for her name and color, he provides the answer:
"Of the two Śivas" (śivayoḥ). || 14 ||
For the sky is seen as flesh by these two eyes;
there is a sky within the sky itself, and those two are situated in that sky-of-skies.
Now, one might ask: how can Śiva and Śivā, who are of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*), possess the nature of inert space? To this he says: "The sky.

It is by these two, who are of the nature of consciousness, that their own body—consisting of flesh and appearing dark—is perceived through the vision of the creative resolve (*sargasaṃkalpa*); therefore, it is seen as if dark and as if inert.
He says "it exists" [verse 15] to show that even their existence without a substratum is to be inferred just like [the existence of] space.
Their limbs were as pure as the sky, appearing like the first-born [sons] of space;
yet, due to the distinction between the multiplicity and scarcity of their hands, feet, faces, and heads, they appeared diverse.

Their formlessness (*amūrtatva*) and transparency (*svacchatva*) should also be understood to be just like those of space; thus he says, "resembling the sky" (*nabhonibhau*). The phrase "like two elder brothers" (*agrajau*) is a poetic conceit (*saṃbhāvanā*) intended to strengthen the simile. If one asks how they can possess hands, feet, and so forth, as well as the wearing of ploughs, winnowing baskets, and garlands, given their formlessness, he provides the answer with the words beginning "hands" (*hastādi*).
"Hastapādāsyamūrdhnaḥ" is a collective dvandva compound treated as a singular.

The connection with the following verse is: "Listen to that manifold variety and diversity arising from the differences in the number [of limbs] such as hands and so forth, as well as [their functions] such as holding a plow, a winnowing basket, and wearing garlands. (16)
Listen to that diversity— the state of wielding plows, winnowing baskets, and so forth, as well as wearing garlands—
for she is the divine Action (Kriyā), whose sole form is vibration.
For indeed, that Blessed Lady, although she is the beginningless and endless power of consciousness (*citiśakti*), has by her own will and within herself assumed the form of all Vedic ritual action,
becoming the embodiment of the supreme acts of giving, bathing, and sacrificing prescribed by the Vedas, such as "one should give," "one should bathe," and "one should sacrifice."

Therefore, those various dances performed by the Goddess accompanied by manifold gestures (abhinaya) are to be understood as being of the nature of the fruits of Brahmā’s karma—the very patterns of the creation, maintenance, decay, and death of all living beings; such is the connection with the subsequent portion [of the text]. || 17 ||
"One should give, bathe, and offer oblations"—thus [it is said]; yet the primordial embodied consciousness, beginningless and endless, shines in this way by itself within itself. (18)
The beloved one, whose form is like space, is the visible splendor characterized by vibration;
for her, the goddess Kālī, there are various dramatic performances and dances. (19)
These are the modes of creation, old age, and death belonging to Brahmā;
this activity consists of the arrangement of villages, cities, islands, and provinces. (20)

Since this Goddess is Action (kriyā), and because action is not established as something partless, she—consisting of imagined limbs such as hands and feet for the very purpose of establishing her own essential nature—withdraws the villages, cities, islands, and mandalas into her body and performs vibrations through them; that is to say, she manifests her own nature as action. || 20 ||
She brings about vibration and holds it within herself, her nature consisting of imagined limbs;
she is Kālī, the lotus-like Kālī, the action that is the Time of the Cosmic Egg.

With the intention that even in the etymological derivation of the name Kālī, her nature as being solely action and her possession of all worlds as limbs by virtue of having the universe as her body are established, he says: "Kālī. For the words *kāla* and *kālī* are derived from the verbal root *kala*, meaning "to go" and "to count. Furthermore, it is said: "Kali is the wish-fulfilling cow (*kāmadhenu*)."

Grammarians state that the verbal root *kal* denotes all actions such as holding and so forth. Accordingly, this Kālī— being herself the action (*kriyā*) that impels, creates, sustains, and brings about transformations such as change within the seed-enclosures characterized as the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*)— is dark-blue (*śyāmalā*), like a lotus plant (*kamalinī*).

She is perfected. For this very reason, she holds within her heart this visible glory of the earth and other elements, which have become constituent parts of her own flowers and so forth; such is the meaning. Thus, even while bearing the world as her limbs, she remains without parts because her nature is that of Śiva, who is unattached and indifferent; this he states with the words, "never at any time" (na kadācana). || 21 ||
The Goddess of Consciousness holds within her heart this visible splendor which has become her own limb;
yet she herself never possesses any definable limbs anywhere.
Since there is no distinction from Śiva-nature, let Śiva-hood itself be seen in this way, just as, my dear, emptiness belongs to the sky and movement to the wind. (23)
He provides examples for the designation of a "limb" even when the limb itself is absent, saying: "Just as... (verse 23).
Thus, the visible aspect of consciousness is indeed the activity of the moonlight of consciousness;
know that which is auspicious, peaceful, effortless, immutable, and stainless. (24)

The limbs such as the night-lily (kumuda) are to be awakened by the moonlight (jyotsnā), that is, the lunar radiance (candrikā). However, if the reading is "jyotsnāṅgam indoḥ" (the limb of the moonlight belonging to the moon), it is clear. Having thus described her world-limb consisting of time, which is the nature of action, he describes her actual essential form with the word "śivam" (the auspicious). || 24 ||
In that state, there is not even the slightest inertia, for it possesses the nature of vibration;
when that very activity, being of such a form, comes under the influence of awakening, [it becomes liberation]. 25.

Regarding that, he states—using the word "she" (sā)—that the nature of action is unreal and visible only to the state of non-awakening, whereas its true nature as Śiva is real and visible to awakening. || 25 ||
When she remains in that very state through such withdrawal, she is then called Śiva;
for the activity of the power of consciousness (citiśakti), the Goddess, has its foundation within the self.

When, by virtue of awakening, one turns away from the nature of activity and abides in that very way through the real nature, then one is called Śiva. That which is the state of the immutable Goddess— who is of the nature of the power of consciousness— abiding within herself as an inert state born of adverse vibration due to the power of ignorance, that alone is called "activity" (kriyā).
That very state of abiding as it truly is is called Śiva;
it is the essential nature of the Goddess’s action, the power of consciousness, whose form is the Great Creation.
It is called "Śiva" precisely because, through knowledge, one abides in the true nature of pure consciousness as it is. || 27 ||
These worlds, radiant with light, consist of groups of virtuous beings; they possess no other limbs than those which bear the forms imagined [by her]. (28)

And so, in order to state that for her who assumes a body within the imagined world, just as songs are imagined in a dance, such ornaments as garlands of winnowing baskets, pestles, and the like are indeed appropriate, he prepares the introductory context with the words "kalpitākāra" (imagined form). Those in whom there are existing groups of people; these are all [the items] to be described hereafter. || 28 ||
The earths with their six continents and oceans, along with forests, groves, and mountains;
the three Vedas with their limbs (Aṅgas) and sub-limbs (Upāṅgas), together with the sciences (Vidyāsthānas) and songs (Gītis). || 29 ||

Sacrifices accompanied by ritual injunctions and prohibitions, involving conceptions of the auspicious and inauspicious, and consisting of sacrificial fees, the sacred fires, and the praise of the *puroḍāśa* cakes and other offerings—[all these are for the sake of the ignorant]. (30)

That which is the first edible thing in the form of the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) belongs to the reciter; it is to be determined by him, because sacrifices are defined by their materials and deities—this is the intended meaning. || 30 ||
There were battles joined with kings, mortars, grass mats, winnowing baskets, sacrificial posts, and so forth, as well as collections of weapons including spears, arrows, and javelins.

Since battles, like sacrifices, are prescribed actions that serve as causes for attaining heaven, prosperity, and so forth for the combatants, they are mentioned together with the constituent parts [of the sacrifice]. Adorned with garlands fashioned from trembling earth, mortars, and woven mats... (31)
Resplendent with spears, maces, javelins, horses, elephants, and warriors,
these are the fourteen kinsmen of the hosts of beings, beginning with the gods; likewise,
there are the fourteen oceans, islands, earths, and worlds.
The connection with what precedes is that all these [entities], ending with the fourteen worlds, are non-different from the limbs of the Goddess who assumes imagined forms. || 32 ||
Śrī Rāma said: O Sage, tell me:
do those conceptual constructions of the embodied consciousness—the various creations that reside within the body—abide in the Self, or are they unreal? Tell me this.

Thus, although you have resolved these two questions, a proper resolution has not yet occurred regarding my doubt concerning the impossibility of the simultaneous occurrence of duality and unity as established at the time of the prior creation;
for that which has perished and is non-existent cannot possess causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) by virtue of its own existence.

For the causal efficiency of causes consists precisely in the production of the existence of the effect. Furthermore, the destruction of the effect is the withdrawal of its reality by the material cause. It is not logically tenable that the existence of one's own effect should both be produced and withdrawn by the cause at one and the same time. Nor, indeed, [is this possible] during the dissolution (pralaya), when all things have had their existence withdrawn by the eternal nature of the universal cause.
With the intention that his own purposeful action might be possible, Rāma asks: "Of consciousness" (citer).

Regarding what you have described—that all past and future creations, cosmic cycles (*kalpas*), and dissolutions remain present before the consciousness embodied as Rudrakālī even at the time of universal dissolution—I ask this: as for those creations that remain...

The meaning is: "Tell me, do these things abide in a self that possesses a real nature capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsamartha*), or are they unreal, devoid of such a real nature, and like the water of a mirage? (33)
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
O Rāma, this is indeed the power of consciousness (cicchakti);
whatever is impelled by it is likewise perceived, and therefore all this appears as if real.
The dissolution of the world is never absolutely existent, nor is it non-existent;

rather, that which is conceived as "real" by the consciousness that conforms to its own true volition (satyasaṃkalpa) is real, and that which is conceived as "unreal" is unreal. It has no form of its own that would be fit for designation. Thus, even at the time of dissolution, the creations of the lunar realm remain.

With the intention that those things capable of causal efficiency exist through the vision of a mind of true resolve, whereas through the vision of another’s resolve they neither persist nor dissolve— as has already been described previously— Vasiṣṭha gives the reply beginning with "O Rāma":

"That which, by way of being a real entity, [is projected] by a mind of true resolve for the sake of creation through the sprouting of the seeds of karma and the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of various enjoyers..."
Or, it may have been impelled toward dissolution; thus, by those experiencers, it was merely conceived and experienced.
Therefore, from the perspective of its experiencer, all this appears as if real; yet from another perspective, because it is utterly unestablished, it appears as if unreal. || 34 ||
Reflected from the external [world] like a reflection in a mirror, that [object] exists truly within consciousness itself; it is not unreal in reality. (35)
He states why that [appearance] is as if real: "That," and so forth.

Since that [reflection] exists within that very [consciousness], having been reflected upon the consciousness of the witness (sākṣiciti) due to causes such as the latent impressions (vāsanā) of prior experience—just as a reflection appears in a mirror due to a cause such as an external object like a face—it therefore exists for that [witness] in reality.
Truth alone. || 35 ||
Nevertheless, for that which is of the nature of consciousness, there may still exist within it a city of real volitions;
but how could that [city] belong to a consciousness that has become purified through firm meditation? (36)

How, then, is it unreal? To this he says: "Of that which is of the nature of consciousness" (*cidrūpasya*). Thus, even if it were real by virtue of being experienced as such, because it is impossible for that which is of the nature of consciousness to enter into another thing of the nature of consciousness, it would be merely false, like a city of one's imagination. For this very reason, he says "firmly" (*dṛḍha*) to show that when latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are destroyed through the steadiness of meditation, there is no possibility of its occurrence at all. || 36 ||
Whether this creation exists in mirrors, in dreams, or in mental construction,
my conviction is that it is indeed real because it performs its functions within the self.

He states [the following]— beginning with "In mirrors" (verse 37)— that it is easy to assert the reality even of objects such as reflections and dreams merely from the perspective of the ignorant, because even they are seen to perform causal functions corresponding to themselves within that [consciousness].
If you say that he is not for my sake, how could that be?
For at this moment, all those who have gone to other lands are indeed for my sake. (38)

If you say that the jar and other objects reflected within a mirror are not capable of performing external functions such as carrying water, then listen: how could that which exists inside a mirror serve an external purpose? For it is not the case that something becomes non-existent simply because what exists in one place is incapable of performing functions like carrying water in another place. What does this matter to you?

The rhetorical question (*kāku*) is: "Are all those objects, such as jars, which have gone to another country, now capable of performing functions such as fetching water in this house? [The answer is no. He says "just as" (*yathā*) to show that while they may possess causal efficacy (*arthakriyākāritva*) in another location, even reflections and the like possess causal efficacy through mirrors, dreams, and so forth.
The state of existence [is] the state of being the perceiver of dreams and so forth. || 38 ||
Just as a village in another country serves a purpose for one who has gone there,
so too do all things serve a purpose for one who has attained that state, because of the certainty regarding their nature.
Whatever is seen to perform all its functions exactly as they truly are, that is real for itself; it does not become unreal for anything other than itself. (40)

Therefore, it is established that its reality is determined solely by the perspective of the observer who perceives those specific causal functions (arthakriyā), and not by the perspective of another; thus he says:

"That which... It is real for the self who is its observer, but it is certainly not real by the vision of another person who has attained a state other than that—that is, who is not its observer. (40)
Therefore, all successions of creation reside within the sheath of the power of consciousness;
they appear as real to one who has attained that state of being, but not at all to anyone else.
He concludes that the same [logic] should be applied to the present case as well, with the words: "Therefore... (41).
The multitudes of mental constructs and dreams situated in the past, present, and future are all real; for how could the Supreme Reality, the Self of all, be otherwise? 42.

Otherwise, if those [entities] were unreal, how could the Supreme Reality be the Self of all? For it is not established that what is absolutely non-existent can be either a reality or a self; such is the meaning. || 42 ||
Those [objects] are attained by one perfected in yoga who has entered into that state, just as mountains, villages, and regions are reached by another through travel to another country. (43)

For this very reason, he says "they are attained" (*prāpyante*), meaning that even objects such as the dreams of others are attained by yogins through their will and enjoyed. By means of another [power], namely the entry into another's body (*parakāyapraveśa*)—which is distinct from entering that person's dream-body—one enters that heart and assumes the state of that mind; thus, just as mountains and villages existing in another location are reached by going there, so too [is the dream-object attained].
In the same way, they are attained. || 43 ||
Just as for one who is deeply asleep and shaken, a city seen in a dream does not actually tumble even though it is clearly perceived as tumbling. (44)

He provides an illustration for the fact that even when Kālī moves by means of dancing, the earth and other elements situated within her body do not move, with the words "of that which has been moved" (cālitasya).
This refers to one who, though moved elsewhere from the place of rest by the gradual shifting of a couch to another location, [remains unmoved]. || 44 ||
Likewise, as she moved, the world situated within her body rolled along;
yet it did not roll at all, remaining fixed like a reflection in a mirror. (45)
He applies this to the case under discussion: "In the same way" (tathā) || 45 ||
That great undertaking of the three worlds, though real, is merely an illusion; tell me, what indeed can be said of the rolling or non-rolling of that which is merely an illusion? (46)
He states another argument for its immovability: "sa" (he), [verse 46].
When is the city of dreams real? When is the city of dreams false? When is the city of dreams destroyed? When is the city of dreams established? (47)
That very splendor of the visible world which stands before you is nothing but delusion; know that even this illusory fortune of the universe is unreal. 48.
This [teaching] is also for the present time. || 48 ||
In imagination, in the kingdom of the mind, in dreams, in conversation, and in delusion,
the experience of the three worlds is just like one's previous experiences.
In the same way, it follows that one should understand the experience of the three worlds. || 49 ||
This internal delusion, appearing as "I" and "the world," shines forth as it were from consciousness;
yet, when skillfully and thoroughly understood, it—known by the name of the subtle supreme space—is stilled.

In reality, neither the "I" nor the "world" exists within the consciousness; however, this delusion shines forth as a designation, just as space is said to be "thin. For there is no thinness or blackness in space;
that [notion] is indeed a delusion arising from ignorance. Therefore, the meaning is that through thorough and skillful understanding, it subsides. || 50 ||
Thus ends the eighty-fourth canto, titled "Description of Śiva and Śakti," in the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the glorious Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa of Valmīki, composed by the Sage. 84.
Thus ends the eighty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of Śiva and Śakti," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The eighty-fifth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Thus that goddess dances with the circles of her long, staff-like arms.
Making the sky a dense forest with their movements, which are of the nature of vibration. || 1 ||
Thus the gods dance, having seen and touched that Śiva;
because of their dissolution into His body through love, their state of oneness is described here.
Making the sky dense with the circles of her long, staff-like arms characterized by vigorous movement, that Goddess dances in the manner previously described. || 1 ||
In that same way, the stainless power of consciousness dances through its activities;
its ornaments are the winnowing basket, the spade, the mat, and so forth.
This very power of consciousness (citiśakti), whose own true nature is unknown, is action; and it dances in that manner by its very nature—this is the meaning. || 2 ||
Arrows, spears, clubs, darts, maces, and so forth, as well as rocks and the like;
the multitude of categories of existence and non-existence, the arts, time, sequence, and so forth—[all these are perceived]. (3)
The vibration of consciousness holds the world within itself, just as imagination holds a city within the heart;
or rather, that very [vibration] is the world, for it is nothing other than imagination, like a city [created by thought].

He says that the vibration of consciousness itself assumes the form of the world, just as the movement of a firebrand appears in the form of a wheel and so forth—thus he says, "the vibration of consciousness.

Just as the mere imagination of a kingdom of the mind assumes the form of cities within the heart, so it is here. Or rather, he says that the world is indeed that [consciousness] and not something different—thus he says, "that very same. (4)
Just as there is vibration in the wind, so is that will of Śiva;
just as the vibration of the wind is within it, so is Śiva with his will stilled.

Now, he states that this will of Śiva is non-different from Śiva by saying, "of the wind. To the question, "How can that which consists of will be non-different from Śiva, whose desires are fulfilled? he replies, "just as. Just as the internal vibration of the wind is not other than the nature of the wind itself—such that it is essentially non-vibration—so too the will of Śiva is non-different from Śiva, and is thus essentially non-will.
The meaning is: "by seeing that. || 5 ||
Just as the formless wind produces the vibration of sound and its display within the space of the sky,
so too does the will of Śiva create the universe.
To the question of how the form of the material world can belong to desire, which is immaterial, he says: "Immaterial. "Ānila" refers to vibration (spanda) resting upon the wind (anila). || 6 ||
Then, while she was dancing there in that supreme ether,
by the force of her own impetuosity, through a chance occurrence like the "crow and the palm fruit," [he fell].
When Śiva was touched by that intense agitation filled with love, he then began to return to his natural state; this is the connection with the distant [verb]. || 7 ||
Śiva, standing nearby, was touched by him as he approached;
yet the submarine fire, though flowing with a stream of water, does so for its own destruction.
The meaning is that, having slightly removed a portion of its own veiling power (*āvaraṇa-śakti*) which was nearby and like a cloud that obscures;
just as the submarine fire (*vāḍava-agni*) is touched by the flowing line of ocean water for its own destruction, so it is here. || 8 ||
As soon as she was touched by that Śiva, the supreme cause,
she began to gradually return to her original nature and likewise became attenuated.
The primordial nature in its unmanifest state. || 9 ||
Having abandoned her infinite forms, she became as large as a mountain;
then she became as large as a city, and thereafter she became Drumasundarī.

In this regard, first, by abandoning the infinite forms of the elemental derivatives (*bhautika*), he describes her state as consisting of the elements alone (*bhūtamātra*): "infinite" (*ananta*). Then, by abandoning the process of quintuplication (*pañcīkaraṇa*), she is like a city in the form of the subtle elements. Thereafter, because she possesses the sprouts and branches of various latent impressions (*vāsanā*) alone, she is beautiful like a tree. || 10 ||
Then, having assumed a form like the sky, she entered the very form of Śiva,
just as a river with its turbulence stilled enters the great ocean.
Its form is like the indeterminate sky. || 11 ||
Then he became truly one, separated from Śivā;
Śiva alone was Śiva, the peaceful one, the tranquilizer everywhere in the sky.
In the space previously described, Śamana, the destroyer of all, became the one auspicious Śiva alone through the pacification of all calamities.
Śrī Rāma said:
O Blessed One, why has that Śivā, the Supreme Goddess who was touched by Śiva, come for the sake of peace? Tell me this according to the truth.
For what purpose? For what cause? || 13 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
O Rāma, that is declared to be Prakṛti, the supreme will of Śiva;
it is renowned as the "illusion of the world," the uncreated power of vibration.
He is declared to be beyond primordial nature (prakṛti), the Puruṣa whose form is like the wind;
he bears the form of Śiva, is peaceful, and possesses the tranquility of the autumnal sky. || 15 ||
Prakṛti, whose nature is that of a bee, wanders through saṃsāra;
she is the will of the Supreme Lord, the power of consciousness (cicchakti), consisting essentially of mere vibration.
That is the will of the Supreme Lord. || 16 ||
As long as one does not perceive Śiva—the eternally satisfied, free from disease, undecaying, supreme, devoid of beginning and end, and transcending duality—[one remains bound]. || 17 ||
Thus, the sense is that for one who desires [the Self], movement continues only until the attainment of the desired object; but once that is attained, tranquility alone is appropriate. || 17 ||
Because pure consciousness alone is its sole substrate, through a chance coincidence, the Goddess Consciousness, having touched Śiva, becomes entirely one with Him. 18.
Having touched the Puruṣa, Prakṛti abandons its state as Prakṛti; having attained oneness within him, it is like the form of a river [merging] into the ocean. || 19 ||
The state of being primordial matter (prakṛti) consists in transformation into the form of an effect. || 19 ||
For a river consists of nothing but water; when it meets with the ocean, it quickly reaches that very ocean and dissolves right there. (20)
Regarding this, he states the justification: "The river," and so forth. || 20 ||
Consciousness is the will of Śiva; having reached that very God, it becomes stilled, just as a sharp-edged iron blade is blunted upon reaching the whetstone that is its place of origin. (21)
It is like the edge of iron, pertaining to iron products such as razors and the like. || 21 ||
Just as one's own shadow quickly enters the body of a man who has entered his own shadow, so too does Prakṛti enter Puruṣa. 22.
Just as when a person enters the shade of a forest, their own shadow enters their very body, so it is in this case.
Having willed its own conceived nature, which is eternal and designated as "person," it wanders further in saṃsāra; for it does not attain that true reality here.

In that case, one might argue that upon exiting the forest, just as there is shade again, so too would there be rebirth even for one who has attained Brahman; to this he replies with the words "cetitvā" (having perceived). The sense is that ignorance, which is the cause of returning [to saṃsāra], has been sublated. || 23 ||
The virtuous person dwells among a swarm of thieves only so long as he does not recognize them; once he has recognized them, he no longer finds pleasure therein. (24)
Furthermore, if there were a desire for saṃsāra, a return to it would be possible; however, once reality is realized, that very desire becomes difficult to find.
Thus he says: "One fully understands: 'This thief is harmful to me'; having recognized this, one no longer finds delight therein. (24)
As long as consciousness does not perceive the Supreme and become absorbed in It, it delights in and wanders within duality, which is essentially unreal. || 25 ||
That which is the nature of the supreme state, having the form of the extinction of consciousness,
one attains identity with that upon reaching it, just as a river attains the state of the ocean upon reaching the ocean.

Since the extinction of consciousness is the tranquil, supreme form—the state of unsurpassed bliss—therefore, even Prakṛti, though insentient, attains that very state by reaching it through knowledge. || 26 ||

Under the sway of delusion, consciousness wanders through those various states of birth within turbulent creations for as long as it does not behold the Supreme; then, having seen Him, it immediately immerses itself right there, like a female bee in thick honey.
He concludes by expanding upon the very meaning already stated with the two verses beginning with "tāvat. This is clear. || 27 ||

Who indeed, having attained it, would abandon that reality of the Self? And who, having obtained and experienced an elixir, would forsake it—by which, O Rāma, all incessant sufferings consisting of birth, death, and delusion are stilled? (28)

Thus ends the eighty-fifth canto, titled "The Description of the Sequence of Prakṛti and Puruṣa," in the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the holy Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa, a work of the Ṛṣis. Volume [Vā], Part [De], Section [Mo]. Canto 85.
Thus ends the eighty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Sequence of Nature and Spirit," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The eighty-sixth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Listen, O Rāma, how he remained situated there in that great space.
Having abandoned that delusion regarding the body, even he becomes Rudra and attains peace.
The disappearance of the body of Rudra, who devours the shell of the cosmic egg, into the space of consciousness due to its subtlety, is described here as being like that within a stone.
In other regions of that [Brahman], such as other stones, trees, grass, and so forth,
the observation of the diversity of creation is everywhere attributed to Brahman.

Therein, he first causes [him] to hear the sequence of the withdrawal of Rudra’s body, beginning with "Listen. The word *katham* is used here in the sense of "how" (*yathā*). He is the one whose power was previously described. || 1 ||
Then that Rudra, as if depicted in a painting, rendered those two fragments of the world motionless while I stood there watching.
Those two world-fragments, along with the upper and lower shells of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), were all then present in that sky, motionless as if fixed or painted in a picture. || 2 ||
Then, in just a moment, that Rudra beheld those two fragments in the midst of the sky, as if with his eye he were looking upon heaven and earth with the sun.

Like the two worlds, heaven and earth, by means of the sun—that is, by the gaze whose essence is the sun; or, if the reading is "koṇena," it should be explained as: by the side-glance, those two fragments of the world which have become heaven and earth. || 3 ||
Then, in the mere twinkling of an eye, having brought those two fragments along with his snout and breath, he cast them into his mouth as if into the interior of the underworld.
The "nose" (ghoṇā) is the nostril; by means of the breath drawn in through the mouth characterized by that [nostril]. || 4 ||
He remained all alone, like a single void within the entire void,
his circle of cosmic eggs having consumed the fierce fragments of the multitudes of universes.

By whom the two—the fierce [egg] characterized by the fragments of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), and the "cream" (*kṣīramaṇḍa*) as well as the "curdled mass" (*maṇḍaka*) and the "circumference" (*maṇḍala*)—have been consumed; or alternatively, the two, namely the fragments of the cosmic egg and the curdled mass-circumference, which are accompanied by the "milk-cream" characterized by the coverings of water and so forth, are to be explained. For indeed, together with the milk-cream...
A circle of pancakes is pleasing to their arms.
Then, in just a moment, he became light like a cloud;
thereafter he became the size of a staff, and then the size of a span.
He became as light as if he were bending; he was like a measuring-stick or a staff. || 6 ||
Then he was seen by me in the form of a speck of glass;
thereafter, having attained the state of an atom, he was seen by me in the sky with my divine vision.
A speck of glass is a minute fragment of glass; it becomes even more subtle than empty space.
Then, having become a subtle atom, he vanished;
thus he attained peace, like a fragment of an autumnal cloud.
"Even such a great undertaking [was destroyed] right before my very eyes"—
thus he spoke with a sense of concealment regarding those two panels of the cosmic egg.
When the leaf had been swallowed by the deer tormented by hunger,
the sky then became stainless, like the absolute Brahman alone, and all was stilled.
On a small leaf, on a tiny leaf; stainless, free from the turbidity of visible impurities. || 10 ||
"Without beginning, middle, or end, consisting solely of the space of pure consciousness—thus did I perceive there that vast delusion which lasts until the end of the eon. (11)

Indicating the conclusion of the narrative concerning the interior of the stone-like world, he concludes with the words "Thus I... [referring to] the end of the eon, the great dissolution (mahāpralaya). || 11 ||

Resembling a reflection in a mirror within the hollow of a stone fragment, he then remembered that woman, that stone, and that delusion— the conduct of Brahmā within the stone up until its dissolution, as well as her playful charms. (12)
That woman was a Vidyadhari. || 12 ||
Having arrived at the palace gate like a common villager, I was filled with wonder;
I gazed once more upon that slab of refined gold.
Like a person born in a village who has never before seen a city, he beheld that stone in various other locations as well, beyond the place where it had previously been seen. (13)
As long as all these creations exist here within this body like the limbs of Kālī,
they are perceived by the eye of the intellect, but not by the divine eye as they truly are.

The word *yāvat* signifies totality or the sense of "from which. In every part of Kālī’s limbs—that is, her body—as if they were previously seen, there exist creations (*sarga*). In the reading *kalpā iva*, the word *iva* should be explained as indicating unreality, meaning "the *kalpas* are like creations. These are the creations. || 14 ||
If that [vision] were indeed like the physical eye, then by it everything that exists everywhere and at all times would be seen as if from a distance, just as a stone is. (15)
If that stone is perceived at first sight as being exactly like flesh, like a distant object, then the logical connection is that it is indeed a single stone. || 15 ||
Only that single rock is seen, and not any creation or the like;
it remains as that very same rock, uniform in form and solid in its mass.
Then, vast and beautiful as an evening cloud yet composed of refined gold, I was filled with wonder and reflected upon it once more. (17)
She is beautiful like that [cloud], renowned for its golden hue, which is the cloud of twilight.
In the same way, with that supreme vision, I beheld the other part of the stone as well,
appearing as sluggish as the beginning of the world.

"Sluggish and afflicted by the beginnings of the worlds. However, in the reading "ambaram," it means that [place] in which the sky (ambara) is such that it contains the beginnings (ārambhāḥ) of the worlds. 18.
In that very same way, as if it were hollow in form and beautiful with various objects, I beheld yet another region just like that. (19)
Likewise, by means of a region seen previously, it appears beautiful with various objects within the form of a hollow; the word "iva" (like/as if) indicates its falsity. || 19 ||
Wherever I looked upon that region of the rock, it appeared everywhere to be just like that, filled with the intensity of the act of creation.
I beheld the world reflected therein like an image in a stainless mirror; then, with great curiosity, I examined all the rocks of that mountain.
The portions of prosperity, as well as the grasses, shrubs, and so forth,
were searched for everywhere, exactly as that world exists in its established state.
He is seen by the intellect alone, not with the eye, in various forms:
sometimes as the self of the first creation, or as the Prajāpati being born. (23)
By means of that supreme consciousness of "I" which is the witness of all and is free from the delusion of the state of a physical body;

he elaborates upon the specific features seen in various places with the words beginning with "kvacit" (in some place). In almost all instances, these are *bahuvrīhi* compounds. [The phrase] "jāyamānaprajāpatinā" refers to that [place] in which the Progenitor was being born.
Alternatively, it may be a bahuvrīhi compound containing a tatpuruṣa, together with the latter half of the following verse beginning with "kalpyamānarkṣa... || 23 ||
In some places, the stars, moon, sun, days, nights, seasons, and years were being reckoned;
in other places, there were circles of people endowed with prosperity upon the surface of the earth.
Wherein the circle of people on the surface of the earth has prospered.
In some places, parts of the four oceans were dug out but not yet filled; in other places, the gods had not yet appeared, while the dānavas had already been born.
Even today, that fierce place where the sons of Sagara have not yet completed their excavation of the four oceans remains there, where neither gods nor demons have been born.
In some places, it consists of virtuous beings whose conduct is that of the Kṛta Yuga; in other places, it consists of wicked beings whose conduct is that of the Kali Yuga. || 26 ||
In some places, it was difficult to traverse due to the array of cities and the battle with the Daityas.
In some places, the earth was entirely without gaps due to a vast network of great mountains;
in other places, it was the emergence of a single lotus, with its creation only partially completed.
In whom alone Brahmā, born from a lotus, exists. || 28 ||
In some places, the surface of the earth was inhabited by humans who were liberated from old age and death;
in other places, Śiva’s head was empty because the moon had not yet been born.
In which [place] Śiva has a head devoid of ornaments because the moon has not yet been born. || 29 ||
The ocean of milk had not yet been churned; it was filled with death, fish, and gods, but was devoid of nectar, horses, elephants, physicians, cows, lotuses, and poison.
The physician is Dhanvantari; the cows are the wish-fulfilling Kāmadhenus; Kamalā is Lakṣmī; and the poison is Kālakūṭa. || 30 ||
In one place, a host of gods was eager to destroy the great vidyā of Śukrāmara;
in another, the lord of the gods was intent on cutting off the limbs of a pregnant woman.
Where the host of gods was intensely eager to destroy— by creating obstacles to her asceticism— the Great Vidyā known as Mṛtasañjīvanī, which was being perfected by Śukra through his penance;
and where, aiming for the destruction of his future enemy, he entered the womb of Diti and [sought] the limbs of that embryo.
Wherein Indra, the lord of the gods, was eager for the act of cutting.
Because its nature is unfading, it is a self-luminous multitude of all things;
yet in some places, certain things abide in a sequence of arrangement different from what preceded.
That in which the state of things exists according to a sequence of arrangement different from the previously established sequence of arrangement. || 32 ||
In some places, the investigation into the practice and meaning of unprecedented Vedic scriptures remained as if it were the agitation at the end of a kalpa.
In some places, the abodes of the gods were being plundered by hordes of Daityas;
in other places, Gandharvas and Kinnaras were singing in the celestial gardens of the gods.
In some places, I have described the grand display of the world— past, future, and present— including the occasional friendship between the gods and the asuras that has been initiated.
It was there that the gods and the asuras, having commenced the churning for the sake of the nectar of immortality, displayed mutual friendship.
Then, within his body— which was the self of the great host of the universe— he experienced all at once the churning caused by the Puṣkarāvarta clouds agitated at the end of a kalpa.

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "At that time, within the Self of the great Viśvagaṇa, whose body is consciousness variegated by *māyā*, this manifold display of the world was experienced by me alone. He further elaborates upon that very display of the world with the verse beginning "In one place," etc. (36).
On one side, it was filled with the peaceful multitudes of all living beings; on the other, it was crowded with gods, asuras, and lords of men, both tranquil and agitated.
In one place, it was a mass of eternal darkness where light could not possibly exist; in another, it was lovely like the interior of a flame, where darkness could not possibly exist.
It is eternally dense with darkness that is indivisible and indestructible.
In one place, Madhu and Kaiṭabha were lying within the stalk of a lotus;
in another, the infant Brahmā was sleeping within a casket of lotuses. 39.
O Blessed One, it is there that Madhu and Kaiṭabha were hidden within the stalk of the navel-lotus.
In one place, Mādhava rested beneath a towering tree on the shore of the single universal ocean;
in another, the world was filled with the dense darkness of the void at the end of the kalpa-night.
Where Mādhava rested within the leaf-cup of the imperishable banyan tree—its top lofty and its summit elevated—in the cataclysmic dissolution of the single ocean;
a place agitated by a dense darkness devoid of light.
Motionless like the interior of a stone, it is like the vast expanse of space itself;
it has the form of the belly of deep sleep, unknown and devoid of defining characteristics.
Because earth and the other elements do not arise, and because only space arises, it follows that "space alone" exists in one place. || 41 ||
Inconceivable and unknowable, it was like a state of deep sleep on all sides;
in one place, the sky was filled with crows perched upon mountains shaken by the flapping of wings.
Because their wings were not yet clipped, they were agitated by their own flapping; like crows that are merely stones, they threw the sky into turmoil.
In one place, it was brilliant with mountains melting from the impact of thunderbolts; in another, mountain ranges were being swept away by the surging, intoxicated ocean.
On one side, it was tumultuous with the battle between Pura, Vṛtra, Andhaka, and Bali; on the other, the earth trembled from the intoxicated elephants of Pātāla.
Where the earth trembles from intoxicated subterranean elephants and the elephants of the quarters, crowded with battles against the ancient Tripuras, Vṛtra, Andhaka, and Bala.
In one place, Śeṣa’s head, upon which the earth rolls at the end of an aeon; in another, Rāma with his small form, having slain the Rākṣasa Rāvaṇa.
By Rāma himself, while still a mere child. || 45 ||
In one place, Rāghava was obstructed by the Rākṣasa Rāvaṇa himself,
who stood with his feet planted on the ground and his head resting upon the summit of Mount Deva.
Where Rāghava was struck down and deceived by the abduction of Sītā. || 46 ||
I see the sky pervaded in some places by Kālanemi,
and in others constantly protected by the Dānavas who are enemies of the gods.
By the Asuras, who had driven out the gods. || 47 ||
In some places it was protected by the gods who had cast down the demons; in others, it was guarded by Viṣṇu joined with Jiṣṇu, and by the Pāṇḍavas and Kauravas.

The victorious Arjuna was accompanied by Viṣṇu—here, in the compound *viṣṇunā*, there is a Vedic (chāndasa) compound because the word *viṣṇu* is a member of the compound and is construed with two instrumental-case qualifiers (*kṛṣṇena* and *guptena*). He was accompanied by Kṛṣṇa, who protects his own kin (*guptena*). || 48 ||
In one place, [he saw] a multitude of akṣauhiṇīs slain in the Bhārata war.
Śrī Rāma said:
"O Blessed One, tell me, who was I in a former life? (49)
Having heard [the words] beginning with "In some places by a small Rāma," Rāma, filled with wonder, asks: "Am I? || 49 ||
"If it did not exist, then by what means could it [be perceived] in this very arrangement?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
"O Rāma, all things indeed undergo transformation again and again. (50)
The meaning is: "Was I non-existent now with this currently visible arrangement of limbs and form, or was I otherwise? || 50 ||
Just as beans being filled may be done gradually by one [hand] or the other,
some [moments] are equal to all sequences, whether mutually by that same [sequence] or by another.

The meaning is: just as things being filled in jars, granaries, and so forth, revolve again and again through that [specific] sequence and arrangement, or by means of another form—either with that previous shape or by another appearance. || 51 ||
Certain states of being arise equal to their objects like waves in the ocean;
again you, again I, and again these people. (52)
Never indeed do others exist at all, for everything is the Supreme;
or else, those very [individuals] are others, just as waves are in the ocean—such is the conclusion. (53)

From the perspective of ultimate reality (*tattvadṛś*), however, he says: "never. From the perspective of illusion (*māyādṛś*), he says that there is simply no determination as to whether those very same beings are born again or others are born—hence, "ta eva" (those very same ones). The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is: "just as no determination arises. || 53 ||
Just as one is not born [in reality], so it is for beings wandering in saṃsāra;
infinite beings come and go here through their delusions of existence. (54)
Those very same ones and others besides, both equal and unequal;
they possess recurrence, and likewise others all around them.
Know that all beings are but sprays of water from the ocean of the world, distinguished by wealth, kin, age, action, learning, specialized knowledge, and effort. (56)
And reminding us that this has already been stated previously in the section on the conduct of those seeking liberation, he says the same thing: "Dhitta! etc.
By those very [qualities], some embodied beings are born again and again;
some are similar to them by half, and some are equal to them by a quarter.
Those living beings who possess different bodies become dissimilar from those [others];
some are equal in all these respects, while others are distinct by time alone;
some are similar in time and yet distinct from this [time]. (58)

He states that there is no fixed rule that bodies must be similar when the individual soul (*jīva*) is one, by saying "those souls" (*tajjīvāḥ*). With the intention of showing that there is likewise no fixed rule that they must be dissimilar when the individual souls are distinct, he says "by all" (*sarvaiḥ*), meaning "by this body. (58)
With restless movements over time, they go up and down like others; moreover,

weary from scratching their bodies, they repeatedly carry countless other and yet other elements and waters into that ocean consisting of worldly existence, which is as fickle as a whirling wheel— how could one possibly calculate them?
Enough of these sorrows! || 59 ||

For this reason, those living beings— becoming as if distinct from one another by assuming various diverse bodies over time through activities of diverse merit and demerit, which are agitated by defects such as passion, hatred, attachment to enjoyments, and greed—
go again and again to the lower worlds and upwards to the heavens and so forth. [The form] "adhordhvam" is used because the elision of the *y* in *adho-ūrdhvam* is established.

The sandhi here is archaic (ārṣa). Therefore, the meaning is: who is the person capable of correctly enumerating or determining those waters of the elements—which, like whirlpools in the restless ocean of saṃsāra, carry along all beings—whether they are similar or dissimilar, or whether they are the very same or different? || 59 ||
Thus ends the eighty-sixth canto, titled "The Description of the Unreasonableness of the World," in the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*, composed by Vālmīki.
Thus ends the eighty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Unreasonableness of the World," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The eighty-seventh canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Then, having a body of the space of consciousness, infinite and free from affliction, he pervaded [all].
Then, with my attention fixed upon his body, I beheld him somewhere.
In this context, Vasiṣṭha describes the universal manifestation within his own body;
for he himself is the self-born creator through the sequential emergence of his own limbs, senses, and so forth.
He says that "sargas were seen by me even in the limbs of my own body with attentive vision, as if in rocks, trees, grass, shrubs, creepers, and so forth," beginning with the word *tataḥ*.
*Tataḥ* means immediately after seeing the various creations within rocks, grass, shrubs, and the like. || 1 ||
To the extent that the internal creation remains established like a sprout—like a seed within a granary or a sprout in the heart once it has been watered. (2)

How is it like a sprout?
