To this he says: "Of the granary," etc. Just as within a seed soaked by rain in the heart of a granary, there is a swelling upward due to internal moisture, so too is the world—whether possessing form or being formless, whether conscious or unconscious—within [the Self]. (3)

The remainder [of the verse] is that the world exists—within all things, whether possessing form or being formless, having shape or being shapeless, conscious or unconscious, sentient or insentient—just as a sprout exists within a seed that has swelled after being watered from within. || 3 ||
Just as the splendor of the visible world manifests for one who has awakened from deep sleep,
or as it appears upon waking from a dream, so does it arise for pure consciousness through its own self-awareness.

Regarding how that was experienced by you in samādhi, he says: "Just as... (yathā). Just as for a person who is pure consciousness (cinmātra) and has attained awakening from deep sleep (suṣupti) to the vision of a dream, the splendor of the dream-objects manifests from his own consciousness;

or, when the dream has ceased and he has attained waking awareness, the waking world-manifestation (jāgrat-prapañca) manifests—in exactly the same way, [the Lord] appears before him. This is the syntactical connection with what follows. || 4 ||
In the very same way, within the Self, whose true nature is experienced at the beginning of creation,
the arising of creation occurs in the heart and not in any other form, because its nature is like space.
Śrī Rāma said: O you whose form is space, O Supreme Space, please explain further for the sake of precise understanding how the creation proceeds within space.

Addressing him with the words, "In the heart arises creation," you have spoken of the space of the heart (*hṛdayākāśa*) by the term "heart" (*hṛt*); and by the phrase "in the form of space," I have understood your intention to mean the space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*). Indicating this through his address, Rāma requests that [the teacher] explain it again in detail for the sake of clear comprehension: "O you whose nature is the space of the heart and the supreme space (*paramākāśa*)! (*ākāśa...*)
O Vasiṣṭha, how does creation proceed within you, who are of the nature of the space of consciousness? Let that be explained once more; this is the meaning. || 6 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Listen, O Rāma, to how I formerly experienced my own state of self-existence as something unreal yet appearing as real, like a city in a dream.

He promises to explain the matter asked about in detail: "Listen. His status as the Self-born (*svayaṃbhū*) arises from the creative conception of the entire world within his body; his status as the Supreme Lord (*parameṣṭhin*) arises from that same creative conception. || 7 ||
Beholding that great cosmic agitation, I, whose form is space,
caused consciousness to emerge within another part of my own body.

The meaning is this: having observed that great cosmic upheaval upon the golden mountain and other places as previously described at length, I—whose nature is the sky of consciousness—out of curiosity, caused consciousness to manifest through the volition of beholding creation, while it was situated in another part of my body. || 8 ||
The very moment that stainless consciousness remains with even a slight unfolding,
at that very instant I perceive myself there as if it were the nature of space.

In that regard, first he describes the conceptualization of space as an illustration of the sequence stated in the Śruti, "From this very Self, space was produced," beginning with the words "yadaiva" (at which very time). In the reading "yathaiva," the reading should be "tathaiva. || 9 ||

O Rāma, just as you perceive the sky of consciousness—which has attained its own true nature—as being equally dense when entering either the waking state or the world of dreams through sleep; so it is with this.

And this state of space is not a superior subtlety characterized by the attainment of an internal void within the mass of consciousness; rather, with the intention that it is actually grossness due to a preponderance of inertia relative to the subtlety of consciousness, he illustrates this through a simile:
"Gone," etc. O Rāma, just as you [previously] perceived the world of dreams and waking through sleep, or the dream itself—

The meaning is: just as when entering the world of a dream, you perceive that very self of yours as a uniform, dense mass which is the nature of its own support, so too should you conceive [of this]. || 10 ||

First there is the mere perception of space in the form of the directions, and then the cognition "I am. That [cognition] when solidified is called the intellect (buddhi); when that intellect is further condensed, it is called the mind (manas).

He states that the four internal organs, beginning with the mind (*citta*), which have that [space] as their object, are established through the very conceptualization of space—by the words "merely the directions" (*diṅmātra*).

That which measures the directions by way of its own movement and reflects upon them within itself is "merely the directions"; such space itself first becomes the conscious mind (*citta*). From that arises the cognition: "I am space."

That is egoism (*ahaṃkāra*). Because of the restriction that "that very thing is dense space" and because of the forgetting of its prior state, it is called intellect (*buddhi*). That same [intellect], becoming dense with the conceptualization of volition, doubt, desire, hesitation, and so forth, is called mind (*manas*; this is the meaning).
From that [mind] arise the subtle element of sound (*śabda-tanmātra*) and the other subtle elements (*tanmātrāṇi*).
From the grossness and other qualities residing therein arise the five sense organs; thus occurs the emergence of the group of organs. || 12 ||
Having thus conceptualized the objects, it also fashions the sense organs that grasp them; so he says: "That... (verse 12).
Just as for one entering the dream state from deep sleep, the world appears as a dense mass of visible objects,
so too at the beginning of creation does suffering manifest in an instant.

He states that it is solely due to that [power] that the self, which was previously free from suffering, undergoes the acquisition of the suffering of worldly activity as if in a dream: "From deep sleep... (verse 13).
Regarding this manifestation of the infinite web of the visible, which occurs simultaneously,
some speak of a sequence, while others do not speak of one.

Now, an objection is raised: "In a dream, there is no creation in the sequence of ether and so forth; rather, there is a sudden perception of the entire world all at once. Thus, there is a discrepancy. To this, he replies with the words "tulyakāla" (simultaneous). For in such scriptural passages as, "He thought, 'Let me now create the worlds,' and he created these worlds," and "Having performed austerity, he created all this," creation is heard of as being simultaneous.
The meaning is that even within the interior of a single moment, a sequence is possible through the conceptualization of temporal duration. || 14 ||
Within a lovely atom-sized particle,
I experienced the self as consciousness, which in reality is indeed the stainless void.

Just as one might conceive of temporal duration within the interior of a moment, so too, by conceiving of spatial extension even within the interior of an atom, he says— starting with "paramāṇu"— that through such imagination he himself beheld the conscious Self, which is the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa). || 15 ||
Just as the wind moves incessantly in the sky by its very nature, so too does one perceive a body everywhere by its very nature. || 16 ||
He states that the conceptualization of the body and so forth is the very nature of the mind, like the movement of the wind, by saying "just as" (yathā). || 16 ||
Whatever form has been willed by her through that supreme power, she is unable to make it otherwise, even with great effort. (17)

The meaning is that because this power cannot even alter itself by means of that initial power of mental conceptualization, it remains a fixed necessity throughout all subsequent conceptualizations. || 17 ||
Then, as soon as I saw that he had become minute in form,
by virtue of my own consciousness, I immediately became and remained in that very same state.

Therefore, he says "from that" (tataḥ) to show that although I am indeed unlimited, through the conceptualization of limitation created by that [intellect], I have become limited and assumed the form of an atom. || 18 ||
Then I perceived a form in the shape of a minute spark of light;
subsequently, while contemplating that very form, it appeared to me as if it had attained grossness.

The subtle *liṅgaśarīra* is thin and minute, having the form of a spark of light due to its pervasion by the reflection of consciousness; it assumes, as it were, grossness, that is, the state of a gross body. || 19 ||
Thinking, "Let me first look at something," he then, out of a slight awakening, set about to observe even a little and experienced [it]. (20)

In that regard, by means of the conceptualization of the doors of the eyes and so forth, the state of being the seer of forms and so on is accomplished for oneself; thus he says, beginning with "I see," etc. (20).
O descendant of Raghu, whatever little exists there, listen today to its principal names as they have been devised by those like you. (21)
That through which one proceeds to see is called the eye;
that which I see is the visible object, and the act of seeing is the fruit resulting from it. (22)
That which is visible is form. || 22 ||
When I see that it is Time, and when I see it as the Sequence;
when I see it as Mature Destiny, then that which I see there is the Void.

Following that, he says "yadā" (when), indicating that the determination of place, time, and so forth—which is both productive and inseparable from that [attainment]—has also been accomplished. || 23 ||
The conceptualization that "I am situated in this place" and so forth is merely a mental construction;
at that time, however, I am the cause consisting of those subtle elements, arising solely from the expansion of consciousness.
"Today" means at the time when conceptualization has become firm. To the question "In that case, what are you then?", he says:
"Then. The meaning is: from the perspective of that time, everything is merely the unfolding of consciousness (*cid-unmeṣa*); therefore, I am that alone which is the cause of it all. || 24 ||
Then, the thought "I see" arose in me as a slight awakening;
thereafter, through the two apertures, I saw that which is also unobstructed.
He says, "I see," [indicating] that this came about from the curiosity of seeing the arrangement of apertures such as the eyes within the body. || 25 ||
"Through those two apertures by which I saw, these two eyes are situated;
therefore, 'I hear something'—such is the consciousness that has arisen in me. (26)
Then I heard a very slight whirring sound,
like the sound of a blown conch shell, arising from the very nature of space.
He states the conceptualization of the object simultaneously [with that]: "From that," etc. (27).
Those two regions through which I then heard the far-reaching sound of the wind blowing— those very regions have now become these wounds upon my ears.
Those two regions from which the far-reaching sound was not heard are these [two ears]. The sandhi in *pragṛhyatve* is archaic (*ārṣa*).

*Śravaṇavraṇe* means the ear-cavities. The mention of "the wind moving" is intended to illuminate that even the functioning of the auditory organ and other senses is dependent upon the vital breath (*prāṇa*). || 28 ||
I have experienced some perception of touch here;
by that very region [of experience], the skin is designated as such. (29)
Thus, he says "the conceptualization of skin" (tvakkalpanā), beginning with the word "touch" (sparśa). || 29 ||
Whatever limb was touched by that, I experienced it as being of the nature of pure consciousness alone; this is known as "vāyu" (the vital air). || 30 ||
He states the conceptualization regarding that very [state] with the words "by which" (yena). The mention of "wind" (vāyu) is an illustration for the entire range of objects of the sense of touch.
"True consciousness" (satsaṃvedana) means one whose resolve is true; he is essentially composed of those subtle elements (tanmātra). || 30 ||
When I became aware that [the subtle element] was established as the subtle element of the sense of touch,
there then arose for me the sense of taste, which consists of the consciousness of tasting and its corresponding flavors.

Thus, according to the manner described, the statement "in me, the knower, the subtle element of the sense of touch (sparśanendriya-tanmātra) has become established" is a restatement of what preceded. He states the conceptualization of the sense of taste (rasanendriya): "Āsvādya... and so forth; it is drawn over [from the previous verse] that "the sense of taste, together with the distinctions of the flavors to be tasted, has become established. || 31 ||
From my vital breaths, the subtle element of smell has arisen, which is of the nature of space.
Thus, nothing at all has been produced; everything here has been accomplished for me.

From *prāṇa* [arises] the nose, due to the differentiation of the vital breaths drawn in by the volition of smelling; and from *apāna* [arises] its object, the subtle element of smell (*gandha-tanmātra*). The combination of these two is the "nose-and-subtle-element" (*ghrāṇa-tanmātra*). Demonstrating that this perfection of body, senses, and objects is indeed false because it consists of mere conceptualization, he concludes:
Thus [it is said]. || 32 ||
If the web of the senses and the subtle elements is thus situated therein,
then for that duration, the five powers have arisen from me by my very will.

Then he says "thus" (evam) to explain that the five-fold cognitions of enjoyment arise by force alone: "The cognitions of enjoyment," characterized by the manifestation of sound and so forth, are devoid of form precisely because they are false; they possess a nature that appears as such merely through delusion. || 33 ||
Having sound, form, taste, touch, and smell as their sole bodies, they are formless, yet appear as having specific natures, being essentially of the nature of delusion. (34)
"This net of such a form which I have cultivated and in which I abide—this, O people like you, is today called 'egoism' (ahaṃkāra). (35)
Cultivating [it] and conceiving it as such, he says "that" (tat) to show that from that very [cultivation] arose the conceptualization of egoism. || 35 ||
This very [consciousness], when condensed, is called the intellect (buddhi); that intellect, when further condensed, is called the mind (manas). || 36 ||
"Solidified" means made thick by firm resolve. It should also be understood that the mind (manas), repeatedly recollecting sense objects, becomes the intellect (citta). || 36 ||
Thus, I have established myself here as the very nature of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa),
having the subtle body (ātivāhika-deha) as my self and possessing the form of the space of pure consciousness (cinmaya-vyoma).
I am even emptier than the wind, consisting of nothing but pure space;
I am the void-form of all existents, offering no obstruction. (38)
Since I am of the nature of emptiness, for that very reason I am neither an obstructor nor a destroyer, nor a preventer of any of the entities that are being conceptualized. || 38 ||
Then, because I remained there for a long time through such meditation, the conviction arose in me that I was seen as possessing a body. (39)
When he had remained for a long time within that previously fashioned body whose nature is Brahman, then, at its conclusion, he saw himself possessing a four-faced body by his own power. || 39 ||
Then, by means of that notion of "I," he proceeded to make a sound,
just as a man who has fallen asleep in a void might cry out while dreaming of a man flying through the air.
Due to that perception of such a body, he began to make a sound, just as a man flying through the sky in a dream makes a noise as he moves about. || 40 ||
Then, because it was previously produced by a child, it was called "Omit"; subsequently, it attained further renown as "Oṃkāra. (41)

In that regard, since there is no determining factor for specifying a particular [meaning] among all possible expressions, he states—beginning with "Now" (atha)—that it was the syllable *oṃ* itself, which consists of the totality of words and possesses a meaning common to all, that was uttered first. || 41 ||
Therefore, know that whatever has been spoken by me is like the speech of a man in a dream; it is a discourse brought forth here only afterwards for renown. (42)
Whatever has been previously studied and recited, such as utterances, the Gāyatrī, the Vedas, and so forth—[that is what is meant]. (42)
I have become that very Brahman, the creator of the universe and the teacher of the world;
therefore, these creations were fashioned by me through the mind alone.
Brahmā is indeed four-faced; [it was] by me, through a mind-made body with four faces, [that this was done]. (43)
Thus have I arisen, yet I am not born to anything;
I have beheld the cosmic egg and that which lies beyond the cosmic egg, which is nothing at all.
The cosmic egg, together with its coverings, which constitutes his own gross body, extends to the end of the universe and exists even beyond the universe. || 44 ||
Thus, while this world of mine, composed of mind, has come into being, nothing at all has truly come into being there; it is merely empty space.
Thus, all this is indeed utterly empty, consisting of nothing but cognition;
for these entities, such as earth and the rest, do not exist even in the slightest degree. (46)
With the intention that this same principle should be understood to apply to all creations, he says: "In this way" (ittham). || 46 ||
The waters of the world’s mirage appear as consciousness within consciousness;
there is no external object, nor is there anything external, for that void remains situated like the sky in the sky. (47)
That sky is indeed the very space of Brahman, abiding in such a manner. || 47 ||
In a desert there is no water at all, yet consciousness perceives it as such;
being inwardly tormented and possessed by its own agitation, it experiences a baseless delusion.
Rootless and indeed causeless, she was as if inwardly tormented and agitated.
The world does not exist at all in Brahman; consciousness perceives it as such.
Because it is consciousness itself, the world is utterly rootless, and thus there is the delusion of error. (49)
Because it is consciousness, [it is] from the nature of consciousness that is unobscured by ignorance. || 49 ||
This entire world, though unreal, appears as if spread out within the heart alone, like a kingdom of the imagination or a dream-city. (50)

The phrase "just as a kingdom of the mind (manorājya) impelled by volition (saṃkalpana)" is to be applied separately [to each case]. In the reading *nṛmanorājyam*, it means "just as the kingdom of the mind of a person (*nuḥ* = *puruṣasya*) situated in volition. || 50 ||
Just as one does not perceive anything in the dream of a person sleeping on their side without entering that person's mind,
so too nothing is experienced without entering that mind.
Through the entry into another's body and the entering of the mind of the dreamer, this is experienced by yogis. || 51 ||
In the same way, the world enters into that stone and is experienced;
though it appears as a form reflected in a mirror, even when seen, it is otherwise non-existent.
That stone is the rock of consciousness which is the substratum for that conceptualization; otherwise, it would not be so, but rather even non-existent.
If it is perceived by the eye through its material nature, then nothing at all is seen; only the mountain itself is seen. (53)

For this very reason, it was stated that when viewing [the world] from the perspective of the material (ādhibhautika) level, only the Lokāloka mountain is seen, and not the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) contained within the rock; thus he says: "ādhibhautika... (verse 53).
If one perceives with the subtle body (ātivāhikadeha) through the vision of supreme awakening, the creation is seen as nothing other than the stainless Supreme Self. 54.
The meaning is that this creation is perceived by yogis as being none other than the Supreme Self itself. || 54 ||
Everywhere, both creation and liberation are perceived through the light of wisdom;
if it were otherwise, nothing at all would be discerned, for [all is] Brahman alone, which is the Self.
Regarding the vision through the perception of reality, he says: "In all cases. (55)
That which the pure intellect perceives through the investigation of reasoning,
that neither Śiva with his three eyes nor Indra with his hundred eyes can see.
He praises the vision of reality and the vision of the yogi as being preeminent in excellence—beginning with the words "That which... (verse 56).
Just as the sky is covered by creations, so did he perceive "the earth" (bhūḥ); then I became a meditator, endowed with the concentration on the earth-element.

In that regard, when a knower of reality perceives through the vision of a yogi liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*) that even the earth is pervaded on all sides by creations like the sky, and when the realization has arisen, then—
by means of maintaining the sense of "I" within each individual element such as earth— one sees whatever wonders exist therein.
Intending to describe all of that in detail, he first begins to speak of what was seen through the practice of earth-dhāraṇā, starting with the words "yathā" (as follows).
The meaning is: when I became aware of it, then I was endowed with the dhāraṇā of the earth. || 57 ||
By that act of supporting the earth, I assumed the form of the earth itself, yet without abandoning my nature as the body of the sky of consciousness, like a sovereign emperor. || 58 ||

Just as a universal monarch (cakravartin), without abandoning the sense of "I" limited to his own body, maintains a sense of "mine-ness" over the entire circle of the earth, so too I, without abandoning the sense of "I" that is Brahman whose body is the sky of consciousness, became the bearer of the form of the earth through the sense of "I" as the earth; this is the meaning. || 58 ||
And by means of the concentration on the earth element, having entered the interior of the earth-element, I experienced myself as the body of islands, mountains, grasses, trees, and so forth. (59)
The earth element is the living being who identifies with the earth; having attained identity with that intellect, he [enters] its interior. || 59 ||
Then I beheld the surface of the earth, endowed with various trees whose fibers were bent down,
pervaded by rows of diverse jewels, and adorned with various cities.

He speaks of what he experienced with the words beginning "it was accomplished" (*saṃpanna*) and so forth. From this point until the end of the chapter, the *bhūpīṭha* (the sacred ground) itself is described by means of its support, the body. || 60 ||

It is rich with villages, thickets, and mountains; its belly is hollowed out by the netherworlds (pātāla); it is embraced by the arms of the great boundary mountains (kulācala), and it is endowed with the circles of continents and oceans.
Abounding in grass, floods, bodies, and hair, with its mountain fragments and shrubs,
it was supported by the hundreds of heads of Śeṣa, which were like the frontal globes of the world-elephants.

Whose mountain fragments and mountain kadamba trees are like the swellings and knots of the *gulma* disease; by whom [the earth] was supported by his masses of hair—whereby "hair" (*kaṭa*) indicates his heads—and likewise supported by the hundreds and thousands of heads of Śeṣa.
Being carried away by rulers with splendid elephant-threads,
its body being enjoyed by living beings, it increases according to its established order.

By such rulers—whose [armies] were like the threads of a net, shining like the threads and knots of a military web—the [earth] was being carried away through mutual wars, according to the arrangement of regions such as Utkara and Nagara. 63.
With the Himavat and Vindhya mountains as its sturdy shoulders and Mount Sumeru as its noble neck,
its body resounds with the pearl-necklace-like flow of the Gaṅgā and other rivers.
It possessed caves, dense thickets, and marshy banks, with a circular expanse like that of the ocean;
it was beautiful with white sandalwood trees upon its desert and saline wastes, appearing as if draped in a garment of fine white silk.
In which [land] there are regions such as marshes and thickets hidden in caves; in which the oceans are like the surfaces of mirrors;
and which is beautiful with excellent garments that are white, characterized by the desert lands and the saline wastelands. 65.
Filled and completely purified by the great oceans of the past,
adorned with groves of flowers, and covered with masses of pollen. (66)
It was constantly ploughed by farmers, fanned by cool breezes,
scorched by the burning rays of the sun, and drenched by the waters of the rainy season.

Formerly filled to the brim by great oceans that existed in the past during the time of universal dissolution, it is therefore now as if risen after bathing, pure and sanctified on all sides; adorned with groves of flowers like garlands;
and anointed with masses of pollen acting as sandalwood paste.
A discrepancy between the readings of the root text and the commentary is observed in all available manuscripts. [End of verses 66 and 67. Liptam.
He has broad shoulders and a chest, eyes like lotus-pools,
a white and black cloud-like crown, and an abdomen as vast as ten directions.
Agrasthala is a level area of ground. || 68 ||
Terrifying with its formidable mouth formed by the great circular trench that encircles the world and the non-world,
it has as its sole consciousness the movement of the infinite multitudes of living beings.

Near Lokāloka, there is a great circular moat previously described; it is terrifying with its fierce mouth characterized by that [moat], and its consciousness consists of the very movement of beings, unified as a single movement. || 69 ||
It is pervaded both within and without by various hosts of beings, separately—
by gods, dānavas, and gandharvas outside, and by insects within.

It was filled with insects characterized by various groups of elemental beings; among them, the mention of "gods" and "dānavas" is a reiterative reference (anuvāda) made by way of exclusion (avayutya).
In the cavities of the subterranean realms and the apertures of the senses, there are multitudes of nāgas, asuras, and worms;
and in the treasuries of the seven seas, there are aquatic creatures of various species.
It was pervaded by floods of rivers, forests, oceans, the horizons of the quarters, mountains, islands, living beings, lands, and jungles;
it was filled with various rows and encircled by circular clusters, sections of lotus-beds, creepers, lakes, streams, enemies, hosts, and groups of lotuses.
Concluding by summarizing what has already been stated, he specifies it as follows: "pervaded" (vyāptam).
It is pervaded by islands within rivers and the like, by creatures that are the objects of experience for living beings, and by floods of terrestrial and forest-dwelling animals.
It is encircled by various successions of mountains, rivers, peaks, and so forth, as well as by rows of people, [forming] the circular enclosures (maṇḍalakośānām).
In which there were clusters [of lotuses]; likewise, it is understood that it was pervaded by creepers, lakes, rivers, hosts of enemies, and clusters of lotuses. || 72 ||

Thus ends the eighty-seventh canto, titled "The Exposition of the Infinity of the World Contained within the Earth Element," in the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*, in the *Vālmīkīya-Devarāja-Mokṣopāya-Nirvāṇa-Uttara-Pāda*.

Thus ends the eighty-seventh chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Infinity of the World Contained within the Earth Element," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The eighty-eighth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O descendant of Manu, after that, while I was there upon the surface of the earth, I—
This has been experienced through the state of self-awareness within the sounds of the rivers and streams. || 1 ||
The specific features situated here and there upon the surface of the earth, which has become like one's own body,
are described here out of curiosity as they were personally observed by me.

O Mānava, descendant of Manu, after I had become the surface of the earth as described, and following the manifestation of my own body composed of the general attributes common to all mountains previously described, I experienced each particular form— such as rivers, streams, and oceans— in accordance with my desire for individual perception, exactly as it was experienced.
"Listen to that"—this is the ellipsis to be supplied. || 1 ||
In one place, there was the piteous lamentation of women crying out at death; in another, the great bliss of a magnificent festival with women performing wild dances.
In some regions, there was the piteous suffering of women who were wailing due to the death of their husbands, sons, brothers, and so forth;
likewise, in almost all such places, the earth itself was the subject of description.
In others, there was great joy for groups of women and the like, due to grand festivals. (2)
In some places there was the ill-fated misery of irresistible famine and wailing; in other places, there was the deep affection resulting from an abundance of all kinds of crops.
Where, due to abundant harvests from bountiful rains and the resulting prosperity, all the multitudes of crops have ripened and friendships have become deep and enduring.
In some places, there was the terrible agony of bodies burned by great conflagrations;
in other places, fragments of cities and towns were swept away by surging floods.
They were not cut down by that flooding and submerging with water. There was a distinction between the city and the town due to the excellence of their warriors and merchants respectively;
in some places there was a circle of plundering made by fickle vassals, and in other places a circle of Rākṣasas and Piśācas of unrestrained wickedness.
In some places, the tips of its waves were bristling with joy at the splashing of the reservoirs of water;
in others, the clouds were being tossed about by the winds emerging from the depths of the caves.

Through the swelling and filling of reservoirs, and by the drenching and irrigation of fields, groves, and the like, the tips of the grain and shrubs stand bristling; this is the reason for [the description] "within the depths of the caves. || 6 ||

His own body, with its hair standing on end like sprouts arising from consciousness and awakening, had its surface deeply depressed by the agitation caused by the clouds (the bearer of water). [The reading "jalaṃ" is also found. || 7 ||

Where, through the awakening of consciousness and intense joy, they are uplifted and their limbs and hair stand on end as if sprouting new shoots; [this occurs] due to the agitation of the flow, which is the very vehicle for carrying the waters.
It contains cities, mountains, forests, and towns, including the abysses of Śṛṅgabhairava;
it possesses a gentle trembling marked by the lines of movement within the circle of consciousness.

It demonstrates the very unevenness of the ground surfaces with the words "saśṛṅga" (having peaks) and so forth. Where cities and other structures possess terrifying chasms that, due to large rocks and such things situated within them, appear as if they have peaks;
for this very reason, the "conscious ones"—meaning the people such as the citizens—experience a trembling of that region.
And where there is a gentle trembling out of fear that the marks of her footprints might fall [upon them]. || 8 ||
In some places, there was the withdrawal of armies agitated by neighboring vassals in battle; in other places, the entire circle of vassals was seated peacefully and calmly.
In one place, the forest was not entirely empty, resounding with the whistling of the wind; in another, the jungle was filled with crops that had been cut, sown, and fully ripened.
Wherein the grain was first reaped, then sown again, and subsequently grew to maturity.

In one place, there was a lake filled with swans and *kāraṇḍava* ducks and blooming lotuses; in another, there was a wind from the *nārjunī* forest that shook the thick trunks of trees in the desert wastes.
In that place, the winds—white with dust—are "thick-pillared" (sthūlastambhana), for they create massive pillars of dust when driven by whirlwinds across the desert wastes. || 11 ||
In some places, there was the gurgling sound of rivers and streams as they playfully erode their banks;
in other places, there was the swelling of seeds sown for the sake of sprouts.

For the sake of the effect that is the sprout, there is the unfolding of the rice seed and so forth located in the field—having been moistened by means of parts such as irrigation channels and water-wheels—into the state of a sprout and so forth. || 12 ||
In some places, there is the sensation of the soft movement of the mouth of a worm within;
it is as if an awakening, saying, "Recognize me at once here and save me! 13.
"O Vasiṣṭha, you alone must quickly perceive me, who am situated in the peril of rocks and the like, and rescue me"—it was as if I were being thus alerted by an insect; such was my state. 13.
In some places, it possessed the full expanse of its branches and secondary limbs, pressing down upon the surface of the earth;
in others, it supported its own network of roots while bearing forth its foliage.

In some places, in forests such as those of the *vaṭa* tree, the form of the surrounding branches is characterized by their tips touching the ground and being pressed down by the weight of the earth; and in other places, it has the nature of supporting the branches by firmly grasping a network of roots. 14.
In some places, the mountains, pressing against the borders of the quarters like limbs, struck one another;
in other places, they were densely packed with mountain bones, tossed about by the surging waves of the ocean.
In some places, the bones of mountains— dense trees that have completely crushed and clung to one another like rocks—
have been tossed and enveloped by the surging of the ocean, as if through the pressure of leaving no space for the limbs of the quarters of the horizon. || 15 ||
In some places, there was the crushing of limbs by the sun-like hands of the intolerant ones, which were tightly clenched around withered leaves, as they forcibly extracted the sap.

In some places, however, there was a forest where, because their own spreading [branches] had obstructed the ground, the intolerant and angry *arka* trees— with their rays of heat— having drawn up their own sap, caused the forest to suffer the contraction of withered leaves and the crushing pressure of dense limbs.

In some places, there was the harsh falling of thunderbolts upon trees, caused by the blows of elephants against temples and palaces, which resulted in the crushing and rigid stability of their massive limbs.
In some places, however, there were harsh falls of thunderbolts upon the mountain peaks, the temples of elephants, and the trees—those whose dense limbs possessed fierce stability.

The compound here is a *sāpekṣasamāsa* (a dependent compound), which is Vedic (*chāndasa*). In the reading "paruṣaṃ patanaṃ kvacit," [the meaning is] "in some places, there was a harsh falling by means of thunderbolts" upon the trees.
It should be understood that, due to the intense stability of my limbs being tightly bound, I experienced only a harsh falling in certain places. || 17 ||
In some places, there was a new blossoming of sprouts with extremely subtle outlines, which could not be approached by those whose bodies were composed of the bliss of closed eyes.

In some places, however, his eyes were closed; this indicates that he experienced a certain unprecedented and extraordinary thrill—the bristling of the hairs on his body—which, being perceived as such, suggests that he was experiencing a most subtle reality characteristic of those established in meditative absorption (*samādhi*) whose bodies are marked by such bliss. Or else, it means that in a certain sacred field (*kṣetra*), [he experienced this].

The meaning is that, like those who enjoy sense-objects with eyes closed and bodies characterized by bliss, they experienced a new wonder— a subtle and unprecedented manifestation of an inner bliss— as if the sprouting of a seed. || 18 ||
In some places it is like the dwelling of flies, lice, and mosquitoes; in others, it is like the effortless dragging away of a wall, a fragment of a jar, or a small bee by a plow.

A swarm of lice (*yauka*) resembles a soiled garment, which is their dwelling place; and because they crush those who sleep within the lotus-buds— namely, the "bad bees" (*kubhṛṅga*) that are fragments of walls or small bits of plaster fallen through negligence—
their enemies, the elephants, act like ploughs.

The dragging down of elephants and other such creatures by playful [elephants] is observed. If the reading is *kuṅmaleśa*, it should be explained as "the enemies of those bees who are sleeping in the best of buds, namely, the lotus buds. || 19 ||
In some places it was cold, with the skin of his body shattered and worn away by the chill, scattered like fragments;
in other places the water had turned to stone, and there was a harsh wind.
In certain regions of the Himalayas, there was cold; for embodied beings whose limbs were cracked by the chill, their skin was covered with frost.
Its soft limbs became like scattered cotton-wool as swarms of worms submerged within;
in some places, the roots of its body and other parts emerged as it sank into the water.
The *uddālana-mudrā* (the tearing-up gesture) and the *vidalana* (the splitting gesture) are those in which swarms of worms sink into the soft limbs of living beings;
in some cases, there is a separate connection with the experience of sinking into water. || 21 ||

In some places, there was the manifestation of rain, wherein water slowly seeped within, providing internal refreshment, while externally a mass of hair-like sprouts rose up from the moisture. (Note: From "bahiścarā" to "romaugham" forms a single compound word. However, in this context, we consider the semantic force to reside primarily in the two words "bahiśca" and "rasaḥ.")

In some places, the manifestation of the rain was seen within the seeds; thus, by the waters slowly entering within, they were brought to joy, and thereafter, a mass of hair-like sprouts rose up from the sap on the outside.
With the beds of tender lotus petals gently shaken by the subtle breeze,
the lakes have provided for me a wandering that is like liberation within my own limbs.

Furthermore, the meaning is that upon my limbs, with the coverings of soft lotus petals slightly trembling in the gentle breeze, a state of bliss consisting of unsurpassed joy— like a state of liberation (nirvāṇa)— has been established as if it were sport or play. || 23 ||
Thus ends the eighty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Particularities of the Earth-Sphere," in the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the glorious Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa, composed by the sage Vālmīki.

Thus ends the eighty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Particularities of the Earth's Surface," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa-tātparya-prakāśa*.
The eighty-ninth canto.
Śrī Rāma said:
Having established the earth-element concentration (*pārthivī dhāraṇā*), in order to behold the worlds...
This earthly world has been perfected by you; how much more so, then, the mental realm?
In this regard,
it is taught that through the power of that [meditative] retention, this very earth-mandala as well as the entire world is merely mind within the space of consciousness.

O Guru, having begun to observe the worlds within yourself out of curiosity, you established the earth-element concentration (*pārthivī dhāraṇā*); did this world— which is visible to us and others— become composed of earth, stone, and so forth, or did it become a mental world consisting of mind alone, like a kingdom of the imagination, not fashioned from clay and the like, but dream-like?
The Question. || 1 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
"I have become this mind and this vast earth;
yet in reality, I am neither this, nor the mind, nor indeed have I ever come into being."

Indicating that doubt is untenable because the distinction between two alternatives cannot be established—whether by the perspective of conceptual construction (*kalpanā-dṛś*) or by the perspective of reality (*tattva-dṛś*)—Vasiṣṭha gives the following reply: "And this... If he asks from the perspective of conceptual construction, then [the answer is] "this," which is well-known to you as being composed of clay and stone, and "that" is indeed the same.

Because it is a modification of the mind alone, the conjunction "and mental" (mānasam ca) is established. However, if you ask from the perspective of ultimate reality (tattvadṛśā), then the meaning is that neither of the two is established. || 2 ||
There exists no ground of the earth whatsoever that is beyond the mind;
whatever you perceive as either non-existent or existent, that is merely the mind alone.

He supports what was stated in the first half [of the verse] by means of the proposition (*pratijñā*) beginning with "amānasam" (beyond the mind). The intended meaning is that as long as the mind exists, the conceptualization (*vikalpa*) of "it exists" or "it does not exist" is observed therein. || 3 ||
I am the pure sky of consciousness; for me, who am that state of being, that which is the manifestation consisting of pure consciousness is known as this [universe] called "saṃkalpa. (4)
That mind, that surface of the earth, that world, and that Grandfather—
all this is the sky of the mind, shimmering in space like a city of one's own volition.
Thus, this entire expanse of the earth stands as nothing more than my own volition, spread out as a mere product of the mind, nourished by the practice of meditative concentration (dhāraṇā).
This terrestrial sphere is not that [reality]; indeed, it is something else, consisting of mind alone.
It is a mere manifestation within space, an unperceivable radiance of consciousness.

Since the common worldly notion that fire consists of clay, wood, stone, and so forth is negated by such scriptural passages as, "The fiery nature of fire has departed; only the three forms remain—this alone is the truth," the form perceived by one who knows the reality during meditative concentration (*dhāraṇā*) cannot be the same form established by the vision of the ignorant.
With this intention—that there is no synthesis [of the two views]—he says: "Not this. (7)
That very self, which is of the nature of pure space and has remained in such a state for a long time,
abandons its mental character because it has attained the realization of "this" (the ego).
If it is the case that space alone, being formless, manifests in this way, then how does it produce the cognition of "this" (idam-pratyaya) regarding that which possesses form?

To this he says: "That very [space]... In that case, does it abandon its nature as the mind (mānasatva), just as milk abandons its nature as milk when it becomes curd? No; he says: because earth and the other elements are perceived through the cognition of "this" just as in the waking state, they do not share the same status as milk, but rather—
The intended meaning is that this should be understood as being like water, gold, or cotton-wool, even though they exist in the form of waves, bracelets, or garments.
This firm, very hard, and expansive circle of the earth exists;
the notion that it "is" arises from long-standing perception, just as [the notion of solidity] arises regarding space.
Just as the cognition of blueness and so forth arises in the sky due to long-standing perception, [so too does this arise]. || 9 ||
By this logic, this surface of the earth did not exist as it does now;
and this very place alone has today become the first of the first creation.

However, according to the principle shown by the scriptural passage concerning "the beginning with speech" (vācārambhaṇa), in reality this surface of the earth does not exist in the form familiar to the ignorant; rather, it exists as that which has attained its state as the single, primordial, subtle form of the first creation in the form of Manu. The meaning is that this is what is indicated by the Śruti: "The three forms alone are the truth."
Just as in a dream it is consciousness alone that appears as the city within the void, so too at the beginning of creation, this world exists as consciousness alone. (11)
He clarifies the statement "because it is obtained through this condition" with the words "just as... (verse 11).
Know that the three worlds, as well as this entire visible realm beginning with the surface of the earth, are at all times the mental kingdom of the child who is consciousness. 12.
Of the four-faced one, whose nature is consciousness. || 12 ||
For the Self, whose nature is consciousness, there is no volition other than that which consists of it; the world is composed of that.
In reality, however, it has neither a true essence, nor a corporeal form, nor is it luminous.
The visible world exists when it is not fully understood; once it is fully understood, it is no longer found.
That very thing which you have been hearing for so long is what constitutes its full understanding.

With the intention that when the perspective of the ignorant is removed, the world is merely consciousness (cinmātra), but when the ultimate reality is extracted, it is only pure consciousness, he says: "The visible... The meaning is: "How is it that you do not awaken to this which you have been hearing from me for so long? || 14 ||
Everything shines by itself within itself as pure consciousness alone, perfectly tranquil;
it is the very nature of the terrestrial sphere and the nature of the visible world, entirely devoid of both duality and unity. 15.
Regarding what kind of thorough knowledge it is, he says there: "all" (sarvam). || 15 ||
Just as a gem, by its very nature, produces rays of light such as white, yellow,
and so forth even while not acting, so too does the space of consciousness produce the world.
A "jewel" refers to lapis lazuli and the like. "Not acting" means not being engaged in activity. || 16 ||
Since it performs no action and does not abandon its form,
therefore this mind does not exist as anything whatsoever upon the surface of the earth.
He concludes by reflecting on such scriptural passages as "Not this, not this" (neti neti), beginning with the words "yataḥ" (since). || 17 ||
The infinite space of consciousness alone shines forth like the surface of the earth;
within the Self, the sky exists as a stainless expanse, just as the netherworld (atala) exists within the sky.
Atala is empty of the nature of a foundation. || 18 ||
The manifestation of mere intrinsic nature is that very thing as it truly exists, like the surface of the earth, yet utterly transparent, entering into the midst of space itself. (19)
The meaning is that, by its own nature, it appears like the surface of the earth as it enters into the interval, the division, or the disappearance.
This terrestrial sphere and that [heavenly realm]—both of these are but the very nature of the Great Consciousness shining forth, just like a city in a dream. (20)

In this regard, he says "this" [in verse 20], meaning that this earth-mandala imagined through *dhāraṇā* and this actual earth-mandala are exactly equal in being manifestations of consciousness (*cidvivarta*).
This is of the nature of mere space, and that too is mere space;
through the thorough knowledge of the nature of ignorance, and through knowledge, neither this nor that exists anywhere.
It appears due to the thorough cognition of the Self as conditioned by ignorance; however, through knowledge, neither this nor that exists, being established in *dhāraṇā*.

The agitation of the nets of beings in the three worlds, occurring throughout the three periods of time, is like a dream or a mental construction when one abides in the state of a kingdom of the mind.
Agitation is indeed delusion; and that should be understood as existing within the state, the limit, and the similarity of the condition of a daydream (manorājya). || 22 ||
Those beings that have been, those that will be, and those that exist now—the spheres of earth they inhabit, my dear, have all attained a state of commonality in their existence. (23)

Because it is the common substratum of all, the very existence of the Self has attained a state of universality; for that reason, through the mental retention that "I alone am all those things and all the objects contained within them," they have been experienced by me with the mind and as the witness-consciousness, in their entirety and without exception.
The meaning is that they have been seen. || 23 ||
I alone am present within all of them;
therefore, they have experienced everything and seen it all in that same way.
This undecaying supreme reality of the Self is pure consciousness alone;
it sustains everything as it exists, including this world with its perceived distinctions, yet without ever abandoning its own nature as the pure Self.
O dear one, though awakened, it does not sustain even the slightest thing.

O Rāma, in the state of ignorance, He maintains the very reality of the Supreme Self (paramātmatattva) as if it had assumed the nature of the entire world residing within Himself—without ever abandoning its own pure self-nature (svaśuddhātmatā), making that which exists appear as if it had attained the state of His own self;
yet when awakened, He does not maintain even the slightest thing at all. This indeed is His liberation; such is the meaning. || 25 ||

Thus ends the eighty-ninth canto, titled "The Exposition that the Visible World is Merely Mind," in the Utpalapaṭala of the Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa of the glorious Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa, composed by the Sage. 89.

Thus ends the eighty-ninth chapter, titled "The Exposition that the Perceptible World is Merely Mind," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa*, within the *Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The Ninetieth Chapter.
Śrī Rāma said:
O Brahman, tell me what happened next; by you, the worlds were then [created].
They have been seen, or perhaps not at all, in the heart of some of the earthly realms.
In the Earth-heart [mantra], the vision of the infinite world is taught here;
and by means of the retention of water, all aquatic play occurs as before.

Just as there are many cosmic eggs (*brahmāṇḍa*) in the well-known world within various regions such as silver mountains and stones, Rāma—doubting whether they likewise exist in every object upon the terrestrial spheres seen through the power of *dhāraṇā*—asks [the following] immediately thereafter. The word "sphere" (*maṇḍala*) refers here to distinct regions. (1)
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Then, by me— who am the very essence of the multitude of worlds in the waking and dreaming states of the Supreme Self—
this was experienced within the heart and beheld with the supreme vision.
Through the support of the earth, by means of myself— who am the earth-mandala in the waking state and the earth-mandala in the dream state—

I have directly perceived, with my mind, reflected upon, and experienced that very heart of His, which is characterized by the various distinctions of those respective earthly regions, through the supreme vision of the Lord as witness. The mention of "dream" [is intended]...
This is for the purpose of demonstrating the possibility of infinite worlds even within the various locations such as one's own bedchamber and so forth. || 2 ||
To that same extent, the entire web of the world remains everywhere;
though everything composed of the visible is peaceful, it is nonetheless dualistic in nature. (3)
He states what was seen and experienced: "as far as" (*yāvat*).
Just like previously seen gold ore and so forth; "as far as" (*yāvat*) signifies totality. It is the peaceful non-duality, even though it consists of duality. || 3 ||
The worlds exist everywhere; everywhere Brahman is established.
All is void, supremely peaceful, and all is devoid of the agitation of worldly undertakings.
From where could there be that which consists of duality, or from where that which is peaceful? To this, he says: "The worlds," etc. (Verse 4).
Everywhere there exists the gross earth and so forth, yet that is nothing at all;
it is only the space of consciousness, like a city in a dream, unborn in the ultimate sense.
Here there is no diversity, nor is there non-diversity; there is neither non-existence nor existence.
Where even "I" does not exist at all, how could anything exist there, and what?
Even this which is experienced in the form of "I am" and so forth—whether it is read as *dṛśyakaṃ* (the visible)—does not exist at all; or, if it does exist, it is that unborn and painless Brahman.
Since this very world is like a city in a dream, existing within the sky of consciousness from the very beginning of creation—
what kind of existence or non-existence could there be therein, where, and from what source could it abide?

Since this [universe] was, prior to creation at the beginning of the cosmic cycle, nothing but the sky of consciousness (*cinnabha*), therefore, even though it is perceived subsequently within that sky of consciousness, it is exactly like a city in a dream. Thus, since the existence of its counter-positive is not established, its non-existence—its non-being—is likewise unestablished; so he says: "Existence... (verse 8).
Just as I had seen those worlds assuming the form of the earth,
so too did I see them become water in that very same way.
Having finished answering what was asked, he begins to describe whatever wonders were seen during the pouring of water, starting with the words "yathā" (just as), etc. (verse 9).
By means of the retention of water, having become water itself— though insentient as it were—
it made a prolonged gurgling sound within the depths of the ocean-abodes.

*gulagulāyitam* [is derived as follows]: from the imitation of an indistinct sound, or because it contains a meaning, the suffix *vayaṅ* is applied in the sense of "acting like" (*ācāre*), and the suffix *kta* is applied in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāve*). || 10 ||
It has ascended through the stalks and tubular vessels of the grasses, trees, creepers, shrubs,
and climbing vines— lightly perceived, as if by a louse upon your own limbs.
It was mounted in such a way that it was soft, gentle, and unobserved. || 11 ||

In the case of a pillar of grass and the like, when it is struck by my soft movement—just as one might pass through the ear of a serpent—the simile is that of everything rising up; [in other words,] when the pillar is cut, the simile is that of a bracelet. By my soft movement, as if passing through the ear of a serpent, [the effect on] the stalk of grass and the like is such that all [parts] rise up.

The "rising" (*utthāna*) of grass and so forth refers to their standing upright; it is "like that" (*tadupamā*), meaning it is similar to that, in the sense that they stand upright. When those grasses and so forth are cut, split, or divided at the joints, or when a hole is made in their interior, a "coil-like" (*valayopamā*) arrangement—one having the form of a coil—is produced or brought about; such is the meaning.
The interpretation should be made as follows: it should be understood that in the preceding verse, by the simile of the yoke, merely the act of mounting was established;

however, by the subsequent similes beginning with "like the ear," that same act is established preceded by the description of its specific form. [The arrangement is within the belly of the subject matter. 12.

Just as a snake in its ear [moves with a soft gait like the movement of a snake in the ear], so too, by means of a soft gait, there is an analogy for the rising of all grasses and the like—that is, the rising or upward standing of all those grasses and such; the meaning is that it should be directed so that they stand upright. This applies to the cutting or breaking of those grasses and the like.

The construction should be understood as follows: "In the division of the joints and in the division of the cavities within its belly, a 'valayopamā'—meaning a structure resembling a bracelet (valaya-ākāra-vatī)—was fashioned or produced. For while in the previous verse the mere act of ascending was established through the simile of a needle, here, by means of the similes beginning with "like an earring" (*karṇābhī*), the specific form [of the ascent] is established first.

This is what should be understood as having been explained: just as a particular kind of insect, resembling a fine thread, enters unobserved with a gentle movement as if merging into the ear, so too, in the cutting, splitting, joint-separation, or the creation of holes within the bellies of those grasses, shrubs, and so forth, such a mode of movement is natural; this is the meaning. || 12 ||
Having rested upon the sprouts and fruits of the *vallī*, *tamāla*, *tāla*, and other trees, she fashioned a design with lines through her well-nourished form. (13)

Having rested in the form of sap within the sprouts and fruits of creepers, climbing plants, and trees such as the *tamāla* and *tāla*, [the vital energy], through nourishment over time, produced the internal arrangement of veins and lines in the form of those respective leaves and other parts. || 13 ||
Having entered the heart through a mouth that bore the distress of the seasons,
the bodily constituents were stolen, impaired, consumed, and cut away from the bodies.

Likewise, at the time of drinking, having entered the hearts of living beings through their mouths, I— assuming the irregularities induced by the seasons such as spring— have at times sustained, at times disturbed, at times consumed, at times fully digested by the digestive fire, and at times lopped off the bodily constituents known as wind, bile, and phlegm.
The meaning is "broken. || 14 ||
He slept upon beds of tender leaves in all directions simultaneously and without weariness, appearing in the form of droplets of frost.
Taking up various lakes, rivers, and houses along his unceasing path,
he found rest here and there through the grace of his friend, the bridge.
Those houses of rivers, characterized by lakes, are resting places on the path for one who constantly grasps them along a road that never ceases its flow. (16)
Due to the lack of connection with consciousness, the insentient [mind] does not take refuge in that [consciousness];
thus, it manifests as various insentient forms, like a whirlpool in water. (17)
Because the non-conscious portion is perceived as an object by consciousness (*caitanya*), that conscious nature does not reside therein as a mere objective element;

therefore, being insentient—and for that very reason indistinguishable from water—I have surged forth through thousands of delusions, like whirlpools, within the receptacles of insentience, which are mostly composed of such receptacles. 17.
Like a wicked man, I have been shattered a hundredfold by falling into abysses, though situated upon the high rocks of the mountains that turn according to my own will.
Like a wicked evildoer who has set out for a leap from a precipice for the sake of atonement, I—
having become unsteady and shaken by the mountain torrents upon the high crags of the earth, have been shattered a hundredfold in the falls into the abysses.
Having emerged from the wood in the form of smoke into the ocean of the sky,
it remained within the blue sapphire-like star by means of the jewel of its particles.

In the ocean whose characteristic is the sky, those blue-colored *ṛkṣamaṇi* stars—jewels of the constellations—exist having become minute particles of gems (*ratnakaṇa*) within it. By the authority of Vasiṣṭha’s words, it is understood that although the blue-colored stars are invisible to those on earth, they do indeed exist in the heavens. (19)
It rested upon the beds of clouds together with its wife, the lightning,
like Śauri resting upon the remaining parts of Śeṣa, which are as dark as a split sapphire.
Even in a creation composed of atoms, it remains unperceived within the forms of composite objects,
like Brahman, the soul of all, residing within every entity.

Even in this creation, which consists of extremely subtle bodies such as those of insects and moths, I abide— as Brahmā does within water— within those most subtle constituent elements, such as the channels (nāḍīs), that exist inside the physical forms of various living beings. || 21 ||
Having attained union with the subtle tongue, the supreme experience was realized;
I consider this to belong solely to the self and to knowledge, not to the body.
Furthermore, having come into contact with the atoms characterized by his tongue through my own nature as the essence of sweet and other tastes,
I have produced in them that supreme experience characterized by the tasting of those flavors— an experience which I do not consider to belong to the body,
but rather hold to be the very nature of the Self, who is pure consciousness, manifesting in the form of the bliss of the object.
The meaning is that this is according to the Vedic scripture (śruti) which states: "Other beings subsist on a mere fraction of this very bliss. || 22 ||
That which has not been tasted by me, nor by the body, nor by anything else, yet is perceived as an object within—that too is unreal due to ignorance. (23)

In this regard, ordinary people (pṛthagjana) consider the object itself to be of the nature of bliss as it is being tasted; one should not understand it in that way, but rather [know] it to be of the nature of unreal suffering and truly untastable. Having distinguished it from that, he shows: "Not by me.
That which is of the nature of an object is neither "by me"—that is, by the consciousness (cit) which is its substratum—nor by the body of the person who tastes it.
Nor can it be experienced by any other living being, because such a being lacks even a trace of the bliss of the Self that has been tasted, and thus is unfit for such experience;
and that object of consciousness, which is revealed and manifested within by the Consciousness (cit), serves only for the ignorance and delusion of living beings.

Since that object of cognition is not [ultimately real], even that ignorance is simply non-existent; the meaning is that for a non-existent thing, it is only fitting that its referent should likewise be non-existent. || 23 ||
Having fully enjoyed various fragrances in all directions through the forms of the essences of all seasons,
he left behind the remnants of the clusters of flowers within his abode.

Even on the view that [objects] are to be tasted, one may entertain the conception that others taste only those objects already tasted by the Consciousness residing in the objects—objects which are, as it were, its leavings. With this intention, he says: "sarvartu... [and so on]. To the *alaya*, i.e., the bee. || 24 ||
In the joints of the limbs of beings of fourteen types, there dwells that which is insentient yet possesses a non-insentient nature, as if it were sentient. (25)
Even by one who is dull through conceptualization, [it is perceived] as having, in reality, a non-dull nature. || 25 ||
Having mounted the wind-god’s chariot in the form of a mass of spray,
he was as if fashioned by his own fragrance within the paths of the stainless sky.
Having ascended a chariot fashioned in the form of the wind, he engaged in play that delighted the people; this is the implied meaning. || 26 ||
O Rāma, in that state, this entire world, exactly as it exists, was experienced by him down to every single atomic particle. || 27 ||

In that regard as well, he says "rama" (verse 27), meaning that within every single object down to the ultimate atom, creations have been experienced in each individual thing, just as they were on the silver mountain.
By that net-like [intellect], which is non-inert yet as if inert and situated in equilibrium,
all internal objects abide as both known and unknown.
By that concentration (dhāraṇā), which is like a net (jālā) pertaining to water and is of a similar nature. || 28 ||
There, hundreds of millions of worlds, along with their hundreds of destructions and calamities,
were seen by me as they arose like the unfolding of plantain leaves upon a pedestal.
He says "of worlds" (jagatām) to indicate that within each individual object perceived, there are likewise situated within it other such worlds, seen one inside the other.
The meaning is that they are infinite, growing layer upon layer like the interior of a plantain tree. || 29 ||
Thus, whether it be the world or the non-world, whether with form or formless, everything is the sky of pure consciousness alone, more stainless than space itself. (30)
He says "evam" (thus) to show that even though the infinite world is thus imagined as pervading [the Self], there is not the slightest impurity in the consciousness that is the substratum. || 30 ||
Neither you nor this world is anything at all; this supreme, pure consciousness shines forth.
That too is nothing, yet it is not a void; you are like the sky itself—be at ease in this expansion.

Applying the aforementioned reasoning even to the world perceived by Rāma, he establishes Rāma in pure consciousness alone, which is the substrate of all, with the words "not anything" (*na kiṃcana*). "Not anything are you" is the negation of the body, senses, and so forth, along with the three states [of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep]. "And not anything is this" is the negation of the external phenomenal world, beginning with space. And that—

The realization characterized by the purified meanings of the words *tat* and *tvam* is neither of the nature of the visible, nor of the nature of the invisible, nor of the nature of the void of the invisible; rather, it is of the nature of the indivisible space (*akhaṇḍākāśa*). That alone you are. Therefore, expand [your consciousness] so that all contraction of duality is destroyed by the realization of the meaning of the indivisible sentence.
It would be so; the meaning is "let it be thus. || 31 ||

Thus ends the ninetieth canto, titled "The Description of the World of Water-born Creatures," in the *Uttara-pāśa* section of the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*, the sacred work of the Sage. 90.
Thus ends the ninetieth chapter, titled "The Description of the World of Water," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The ninety-first canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Thereupon, I became that light, kindled by the concentration of light.
It is endowed with diverse constituent parts such as the moon, sun, stars, fire, and so forth.
Having attained the state of radiant energy through the concentration on light (*tejodhāraṇā*),
the wonders of the sun, moon, fire, jewels, and so forth, manifest here before one's gaze.
Then, immediately after witnessing the curiosity of holding the water. || 1 ||

Because it is eternally dominated by *sattva*, it has the nature of light and pervades all things; yet, apart from that which is visible, everything is joined with the darkness of thieves and the heat of afflictions. (2)
It arrived, pervading the entire world, manifesting in the form of light. In the reading "rājavat" (like a king), the connection is as follows:

having abandoned all visible objects within the range of sight—just as they have been snatched away in sleep—and while the darknesses flee in every direction like thieves, it shines with majesty like a king. || 2 ||
With lamps and other offerings that were gentle, soothing, and shone for a thousand leagues,
he made every object visible in every house like a divine king.

Just as a good king, through hundreds of affectionate spies moving about in various disguises, personally observes the state of affairs in every house, so too [the lamp] has all its objects perceived by means of hundreds of wicks moving about in the form of flames and the like. In this case, "light" (*tejas*) alone is the recurring substantive throughout. || 3 ||
And in the Lokāloka mountain, he was embraced by the joyful rays of the moon, sun, and other luminaries, which act as his hair;
those rays, delighting solely in supreme illumination, have cast the garment of the sky far away. (Note: An alternative reading is *dūrotkṣiptāsitāmbaram*.)
Because they delight solely in illuminating others, they are exceedingly satisfied and thrilled by the light of the world, of people, and of the realms;

thus, by means of their body-hairs characterized by the rays of the moon, sun, and other luminaries, they appear to have cast far upward into the sky—the garment of darkness that covers all—like a cloth, which is the very nature of the firmament (ambaram)—such is the poetic fancy (utprekṣā). 4.
The visible world is the constant, true object of sight for everyone endowed with virtues, [serving] as a remedy against the darkness of wretchedness that destroys all good qualities. (5)

If it is asked for what purpose it casts darkness far away, he says in response: "of darkness. Because it destroys all existing qualities—such as form and the rest—and leads them to non-perception, such a state characterized by darkness is the object of wretchedness (*dainya*). And of everything...

The meaning is that for one who possesses virtues and is capable of removing the misery of others, it is indeed proper to remove that [misery], because this world—which is characterized by suffering—is truly excellent when free from wretchedness and is worthy of being seen. || 5 ||
It is the axe that fells the Tamāla tree of darkness, the state that effects supreme purification,
and the very life-sustenance for people through gold, gems, rubies, pearls, and the like.
Furthermore, what kind of splendor is it? It is like an axe for the *tamāla* trees characterized by darkness.
It is a "footstep" (*pada*)—meaning that by which the supreme, most excellent, and purifying [state] is reached.

It is the cause of respect for the life of those people characterized by being devoid of luster, such as gold and the like, due to their lack of regard for them; [it acts] in the form of gold and so forth.
Or, it is the means of livelihood for people. || 6 ||
The father who bestows bodies upon all castes— whether white, black, ruddy, and so forth— is eternally like a father to his sons, resting within the limbs of the moonlight.
The moonlight is the light for those lying upon its body; the meaning is that it is because the quality of light belongs solely to the form [of the moon]. || 7 ||
The essence of thick affection belonging to the earth protected it from the piercing of fire;
within the house, the little lamp-sons were surrounded by dense joys.

And this fire possesses a dense essence of moisture and an excess of affection together with the earth. Why? Because it has protected [the clay] from burning—that is, from being consumed by fire. Although fire is a burner of all things, it does not burn clay;
this is the mark of its affection. In this way, the earth also, in order to manifest its own characteristic of affection, [provided] a dwelling.

In every house, his little lamp was surrounded by the walls, palaces, and other structures out of an excess of affection born from the abundance of wealth, and it was protected from the impact of the wind. || 8 ||
In the netherworlds (pātāla), which consist of slight darkness, fire was seen;
and on the surface of the earth, which consists of dust and is garlanded by living beings, it was seen only half-visible. || 9 ||

He describes the gradation of the brilliance of light in the worlds such as Pātāla, which abound in *tamas*, *rajas*, and *sattva*, with the verse beginning "dṛṣṭam" (half-verse): "Slightly purifying" means slightly illuminating; "half-seen" means half-illuminated.
[In the worlds] consisting of *sattva*, there is great *sattva* and permanence in the abodes of the gods.
He is the lamp for the world’s dilapidated hut, and the great water in the well of darkness. 10.
The Great Being is a great luminosity; eternity is the state of being eternal. Like a deep, bottomless well within water and darkness, he swallows all within. 10.
It is the stainless mirror for the brides of the quarters, the wind that dispels the frost of night,
the very essence of the moon, sun, and fire, and the saffron unguent of heaven.

Like a stainless mirror for the brides of the quarters, he was a revealer who distinguished all things; like the wind that dispels the frost of night, he was the very essence of life for those whose being he could remove. 11.
The field of day-lotuses was a favor bestowed upon those swollen by darkness;
the water glistening from the washing of the great glass-vessel of the sky [was flowing]. 12.
The favor shown toward forms that have become swollen with darkness is like water for the purpose of washing a large glass vessel characterized by its transparency to the sky. 12.
Because it bestows existence upon objects and because it illuminates them as well,
it is like a younger brother born of the same womb as the ultimate reality that is pure consciousness alone.
Because the ultimate reality, characterized as pure consciousness alone, is inferior by virtue of its mere insentience, it is like a younger brother. || 3 ||
It is the sun for the lotus of action, the very life of the interior of the earth,
and the wondrous manifestation of the perception of forms and mental attention— just as consciousness is.

Through the functioning of visible form and light, as well as the mental attention directed toward them, there arises a sense of wonder characterized by the removal of the darkness that obscures the object, as if consciousness were ascending. || 14 ||
It is garlanded with the countless jewel-like stars situated in the vault of the sky;
it is foamy with the submarine fire and other elements, which increase with the days, seasons, and years.

Furthermore, to suggest that this radiance is indeed the great ocean situated within the cavity of the vast cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), he qualifies it with the attributes of an ocean conceived through metaphor: "the surface of the sky," and so forth.
It is augmented on all sides by the factors of time characterized by divisions such as days, seasons, and years.
It is foamy due to the agitation caused by the increased submarine fire and other such elements. || 15 ||
Dull with waves other than those of the moon and sun, vast and muddy,
situated within the cavity of the great cosmic egg, it is eternally a single, undecaying ocean.
Sometimes, by means of the dust particles spread within the waves characterized by the moon, the sun, and so forth, it becomes muddy even without water, though it is not insentient. || 16 ||

The state of being gold in things such as gold-ore, the primordial movement in beings such as men, the brilliance in gems and the like, and the manifestation in the rains and so forth—[these are the functions of that power]. (17)

Furthermore, how is it that this fire, being existent, has become the state of gold in gold and other substances? It should be understood that it has become prowess in men and others. *Kācakacyam* is a particular luster; *avabhāsanam* is the brilliance of lightning. || 17 ||
In the orb of their moon-like faces, there was moonlight; in their eyes with long lashes, there were marks [of beauty];
there was a flowing flood of the nectar of affection, and the radiance of smiles and friendship. (18)
The meaning is that while the moon-disks resembling his face possess only moonlight,

those moon-disks which are the marks of his face— marked by eyes with long lashes— possess not only moonlight but also a flowing flood of the nectar of affection, as well as a radiance endowed with laughter and friendliness. || 18 ||
Through his own invincibility, he became a playful lover among women, possessing cheeks, arms, eyes, brows, and hands that were like those of a formidable Kālāsaka.
Among women who desire me, I am renowned for being unconquerable; thus, my own natural amorous play has arisen. Of what sort is it?

It is a "lāsaka," meaning that which reveals the cheeks and other features through an excellence of beauty (*lāvaṇya*). In the reading *lāmaka*, it means the cause of transformations such as trembling and the like. || 19 ||

The valor that treats the three worlds as mere straw, which strikes down enemies with a slap, and which acts like a thunderbolt upon their heads—this is what dwells in the hearts of lions and the like. (20)

Furthermore, even for those powerful ones such as Vṛtra and others—who reduced the three worlds to mere straw and struck down their enemies with slaps—it was upon the heads of such heroes that the thunderbolt-strike, which acts like a thunderbolt, descended.

This may be construed either by applying the relationship of qualifier and qualified to each term individually, namely: "valor was produced in the minds of lions and the like," and "the thunderbolt-strike was produced [upon the heads of Vṛtra and others]. || 20 ||
The fierce battle raged among the warriors, who roared with sharp, swelling shouts as their swords clashed with a ringing *tāṃkṛta* sound against the hard armor of their enemies.

Furthermore, I am endowed with the prowess that, by implication, causes me to roam as a preeminent warrior among the soldiers upon the battlefields. Of what nature is that [prowess]? It resounds with a sharp and manifest arrogance, produced by the clashing of swords against the "biters"—that is, the iron armor (*kaṅkaṭa*)—which are harsh to the touch.
Having the habit of crying out. || 21 ||
Among the gods, he is the enmity of the Dānavas; among the enemies of the gods, he is the enmity of the gods;
among all beings, he is vigor; and among stationary things and the rest, he is height.
*Unnāma* is loftiness; or it is the power that causes one not to be bent even by the force of wind and other elements. || 22 ||
Then,
O lotus-eyed one, I experienced myself there as a radiant god among the gods within those world-ether-receptacles.

Now, within those cosmic receptacles of space fashioned by one's own concentration (*svadhāraṇā*), just as the well-known desert region experiences the mental construction of rivers and such within itself, so too did I, being radiant, experience everything that is about to be described within myself— this is the meaning. || 23 ||
With its mass of rays spread across the quarters of the horizon, it seized the world-bird;
like a village, it perceived the surface of the earth as its own limbs, thus assuming the nature of the sun.

He says that very thing with the words beginning "diganta": "I experienced the state of being the Sun. Of what nature was that?
