[It was] by means of the network of rays (karajāla) spread forth and extending to the ten ends of the quarters (diganta). It was grasping the bird (khaga)—namely the world—whose limbs (aṅga) or constituent parts were the mountains. Furthermore, of what nature was it? As small in dimension as a village (grāma).
Where the surface of the earth was visible. || 24 ||
He is the pericarp-wheel in the lotus of desire, the submarine fire in the ocean of darkness,
the lamp in the dwelling of the cosmic egg, and the tree for the multitude of fruits that are the days.
Furthermore, what is that solar nature like? It is the discus that serves as the cause for the closing of the buds of the moon-lotuses and the desire-lotuses.
The rest is clear. || 25 ||
The face of the sky is the moon, appearing like a pool of elixir;
it is the laughter of the night-demoness and the blossoming of the lotuses of the night.

Likewise, he experienced the state of being the Moon (*indutva*). What was that like? It had a form like a lake of *rasāyana*, the nectar of immortality; it was a face like the face of heaven; it was a smile like the smile of the night-wandering woman characterized as Night; and likewise, those who enter into the night engage in the activity of entering [it].
At the breaking of night, they cause those flowers to bloom with radiant light. || 26 ||
He is the locus of comparison for all the glories of the world's beauty, and the supreme beloved of the night, Rohiṇī, women, and white water-lilies.
The multitude of stars was like a cluster of flowers upon the celestial creeper of his face,
a soft swarm of gnats over the flood of heaven.

Likewise, because it is the cause of the joy and blossoming of the multitude of eyes and the faces of all living beings, the connection [of the verse] is to be understood by drawing in the phrase "supremely dear. Similarly, I have experienced the state of being a host of stars; this is an expression emphasizing the abstract quality (*bhāvapradhāna-nirdeśa*). And that too—

Of what sort? It stands like a cluster of flowers on a creeper characterized by the sky—that is, the firmament. It is soft and insignificant, like a swarm of gnats clinging to the flood of nectar consisting of the pleasures of heaven. || 28 ||
The quality of being a jewel was tested by the mere merchant as he weighed it in the balance held in his hand; the oceans, moreover, tested its worth by tossing it with the waves of their hands.

Likewise, I experienced the state of being a jewel; and that [jewel] was weighed by a merchant—thus it is called *vaṇiṅmātra*, "measured by a merchant"—in that marketplace (*vipaṇi*), it was shaken and tossed about by the hands of merchants on the scales. Furthermore, it had previously undergone tossing by the oceans with their hands of water-waves; this is the ellipsis (*śeṣa*). By virtue of the rule of diversity (*bāhulaka*), the suffix *lyuṭ* is used here in the sense of the object (*karman*). || 29 ||
In the water, a fish and a whirlpool; in the water, a cluster of lotus stalks;
at the beginning of the year, a forest fire; and upon his body, the flash of lightning. (30)

Furthermore, being the submarine fire (*vaḍavānala*)— so called because it "drinks" (*dhayati*) or consumes the waters (*ap*) of the ocean— I experienced the whirlpools, that is, the curiosity of circular revolutions, of the *śaphara* fish (small fish) who were terrified of me. Likewise, everywhere, the mass of *gomañjarī* plants is "water-drinker" (*abdhā*), so called because it "drinks" or dries up the water.

The meaning is that he experienced a radiance within his own body consisting of a mass of clusters of sunbeams; and at the beginning of the rainy season, having entered into clouds and mountains, he himself experienced a radiance within those respective bodies consisting of forest fires and lightning. || 30 ||
The blazing fire was spread wide, difficult to restrain as it split the wood;
it was auspicious for the burning of the sacrificial fire, yet its roar was harsh with crackling sounds.

Furthermore, having attained the state of fire, I experienced a blazing that was difficult to restrain for the purpose of splitting and tearing apart wood; therefore, I endured a conflagration spread in all directions, filled with the harsh roar of bursting logs. Likewise, as the sacrificial fire, I am auspicious in burning the various oblations offered in battle.
And the meaning is that he has experienced it. || 31 ||
The splendor consisting of glittering gold, rubies, pearls,
and gems has been reduced to a state of penance, as if its erudition were being snatched away by common folk.
Furthermore, in that state of fire, the great light— the splendor consisting of gold and other precious materials— blazing with an excellence of beauty,
was seized and overwhelmed by the conflagration of the treasury; having been reduced to ashes and the like,
it was brought to a state of suffering and torment for its owners, just as a single learned man is treated by many powerful commoners.

In the same way, one's scholarship, having been overwhelmed by contentious disputations, is reduced to a state of mere distress. Thus they have a popular proverb: "The scholar speaks of the *palāśa* tree; the fools chatter about the *pāṭala*.
But when tormented by blows from their fists, even the scholar says 'pāṭala! (32)
She rested upon the peaks of their breasts in the form of pearl necklaces belonging to the women of the leaders of the asuras, uragas, gandharvas, and men. 33.
Even though the state of liberation was introduced only as a secondary consequence, he describes what was experienced therein with the words "rested" (viśrāntam). || 33 ||
I have been trampled underfoot on the path, yet I have attained the status of a *tilaka* on the face of a bride by means of a firefly; behold the fickleness of my conditions! (34)

He speaks of what was experienced in the state of being a firefly: "The blow of a foot," and so forth. Having become a firefly while traveling on the road, I experienced that state of being a firefly by receiving the blow of a foot from people passing along the path; yet, upon the face of a young woman, I attained the state of becoming a decorative mark (*tilaka*). Thus, within the states of excellence and inferiority caused by differences in location—
Behold the fickleness and lack of constancy! || 34 ||

In some places, among those [clouds] situated in the sky— which were beautiful yet distorted and resounded with the whirling of waters— there was a flash of lightning, like that of a sapharī fish in the oceans.

While the clouds were in the sky, I have acted with beautiful, yet distorted movements, like a sapharī fish in the oceans flashing with lightning; this is described by the phrase "resounding with the whirlpools of water," which serves as an adjective for both [the ocean and my own state]. 35.
In some places, having been brought there as a lamp by women with limbs as tender as flower buds, she was gazed upon during the amorous dalliances within the inner apartments of beloved women. (36)
"Having been brought and stationed within the inner apartments"—this is the ellipsis to be supplied. || 36 ||
In some places, within its own hollow, it resembled a massive tortoise due to its contact with masses of soot that appeared like streaks of molten gold from its flames; thus it seemed weary.
Gold characterized by its flames is cut—that is, broken—into such a form [the compound *ākṛtam* is a *bahuvrīhi*:

*ākṛtam* means "form"]. By the mere contact with the mass of soot grown at the tip of the wick within its own hollow, I, through a lamp whose light is dim and weary, [assume] a form resembling a solid tortoise due to the contraction of the constituent parts of the flame and so forth.

The meaning is "it has been done. By me, having become the fire at the end of the aeon (*kalpāntāgni*), [the darkness] was dissolved into a certain part of the sky (*kha*)—black and dark with soot—from the great exhaustion caused by wandering through all the worlds at the ends of the aeons.
Just as lightning is dissolved into the cloud that serves as the vehicle for Rudra, the Cloud-Bearer (*Meghavāhana*), so it was. || 37 ||
At the end of the eons, due to the dense exhaustion from wandering through the entire world somewhere,
he is absorbed into the sky— which is as black as collyrium— like lightning into the cloud of Rudra’s elephant.
In some places, having drunk the waters until the end of the eon by means of the submarine fire,
he danced within the masses of water at the ends of the worlds and the skies.

When the masses of water had attained emptiness within the skies, I finally danced in the sky. Since the root *nṛt* (to dance) is transitive when its meaning involves the movement of limbs, it is here intransitive; therefore, the periphrastic perfect (*liṭ*) is used in the impersonal sense (*bhāve*).
In some places, with a mouth of firebrands, I appeared as one whose arms were flames,
with fierce locks of hair consisting of swirling eddies of flickering smoke, and possessing agitated energy.

In some places, while I was performing the act of burning ancient cities where thickets and ponds had grown, by means of my fiery energy— manifesting as fire with teeth of firebrands, arms of flames, and locks of hair consisting of the tips of flickering, swirling smoke— I was consuming materials such as wood that were fit for eating.
The connection with the subsequent clause is: "they were made fit for consumption. || 40 ||

During the burning of cities and marshes—[where "pallava" and "pallala" are also variant readings]—by him who has swallowed living beings, objects such as wood and other materials have been repeatedly fashioned as they were fit for his consumption. (41)

*Kṛtāṣṭa*: according to its etymology, this refers to one by whom the eight qualities taught by Gautama—beginning with compassion (*dayā*) and ending with freedom from desire (*aspṛhā*)—have been performed, that is, firmly established. || 41 ||
In some places, sparks and fragments of stone were spat out by the mountains as if by a person struck by weapons and stones, vomiting iron balls and the like in order to burn their assailants.

In some places, such as blacksmith’s workshops and the like, sparks (kaṇakāḥ) and fragments of stone were emitted from iron struck by weapons, iron hammers, and stones—that is, from the impact of metal being beaten; [the word *tal* is used here in the sense of a "collection," either because it is an archaic form (*ārṣatvāt*) or due to a grammatical split (*yogavibhāga*) allowing for the suffix *-tal* in the sense of "a group" in the expression *vāmajana-tal*]. 42.
In some great stone casket, by means of a stone-jewel,
I remained for hundreds of ages, invisible to all living beings.
It exists in the form of stones and gems, such as diamonds, lapis lazuli, and so forth. || 43 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
O Sage, bestower of honor, tell me for my enlightenment: in that state, was happiness experienced by you, or was it suffering? 44.
In that state of being a stone, a gem, and so forth. || 44 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Just as a man, though conscious, falls into a state of insensibility while asleep,
so too does the space of consciousness (cidvyoma) become an object of perception and thus experience its own dullness.

Vasiṣṭha prepares the introductory stage to provide the answer: "For me, who have become the Brahman that is the single essence of consciousness and bliss, there is not even a trace of suffering in the curious observation of the superimposition of the world's existence; rather, there is only happiness. (45)
When Brahman perceives itself as the earth and so forth, then it remains within as if asleep and inert; otherwise, this would not be the case.
The meaning is that since this Brahman’s true nature consists of existence, consciousness, and bliss, it could never otherwise be; thus, there is no possibility of suffering. || 46 ||
In reality, its earth and so forth are neither of the nature of non-existence nor composed of existence;
this Brahman remains uniform, appearing like the seer and the seen. (47)
To the question "Why would it not be so?", he says: "In reality... It is equal, that is, indeed unmodified. || 47 ||
For one in whom this unbroken thorough knowledge of reality has arisen, there are no five elements, nor is there the delusion of the seen and the seer. (48)
For if there were ignorance, there would be the occurrence of suffering, yet that [ignorance] does not exist; thus he says: "This... (verse 48).
Then, by me alone, who was pure and possessed the form of Brahman, that was performed;
for nothing whatsoever can be accomplished by one who is devoid of the form of Brahman. (49)
When all this visible world was realized as the untainted Brahman,
then, abiding in the state of Brahman, I perceived the Self in this very way.
But when I manifest myself as merely the five elements, being indeed insentient, then what indeed could I possibly perceive? (51)

With the intention that if there were no consciousness at all in my state as a stone, a jewel, or the like, then there would be neither the experience of them nor the memory of them today, he says: "When..."—that is, how could I perceive or experience these? || 51 ||
Even though he is conscious, having firmly conceived the notion "I am asleep," he attains a state of profound sleep-like dullness;
yet, even in that brilliance of stupor, he perceives something.

To the question of how there can then be the cognition "I did not know anything" during deep sleep, he says: "I was asleep. In that state, the dullness (jāḍya) brought about by the cognition "I did not know" is merely the ignorance (ajñāna) presented by sleep; it is simply the absence of [the perception of] the shining, self-luminous reality. Otherwise, [one could not recall] what was not experienced at the time of sleep.
The sense is: how could there be a recollection of sleep, ignorance, and so forth? || 52 ||
But for one whose self is awakened by knowledge, his body is merely material;
it subsides, and the stainless self of pure consciousness alone arises as the subtle, transmissible vehicle.

With the intention that, through the arising of knowledge, there is no possibility of insentience or suffering even because of the departure of the material state of the gross individual and collective bodies, he says: "But he who... (verse 53).

By means of that subtle body of transport, which is of the nature of consciousness and atomic, or by means of the expanded [body], he abides as one whose self is liberation, according to his will. (54)
One whose self is liberation is liberated while living. || 54 ||
By means of the body of awakening, he pierced the heart even of stones that were otherwise indivisible. [The masculine form is an archaic usage (ārṣa).
Alternatively, there is a reading "abhedi na," in which case the division is "abhedi na. *Na* here means "man.
It is inferred that *abhedī* is an adjective qualifying "heart."]
Having entered quickly, he emerges; he goes to the netherworld and to the sky.
Therefore, O Rāma, in the past, by me—
who was then infinite, consisting of consciousness and having the form of the ether of pure spirit— that was performed in such a manner.
And thus he concludes that there is no attachment to suffering for him: "Therefore," etc. (56).
For one who thus swiftly performs the coming and going through diamond, stone, the underworld, the sky, and space, no obstacle arises.
As long as it remains within insentient objects by means of its body consisting of pure consciousness alone,
so long does it abide there in that very state.
With the intention that there is no attachment to suffering even because of the curiosity created by one's own will, he says: "By one's own will alone" (svecchayaiva).

The meaning is: if one proceeds elsewhere by one's own will alone, just as there is no suffering [there], so too if one remains in that very place, it is likewise desired—not undesired—just as the return [to the original state] is desired. || 58 ||
If, having moved by its own will, it then proceeds elsewhere,
it returns to that very place in the same manner as it came.
They know the body to be merely consciousness, subtle, and imperishable;
now, as a wise one, you yourself experience that very same thing here.

Since you too, by virtue of your knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), can easily attain the state of a subtle body (*ātivāhika-deha*) and behold the wonders of the world's manifestation through various forms of concentration (*dhāraṇā*), he says—"It is mere consciousness"—with the intention that you should examine what I have said. The ellipsis to be supplied is: "If you so desire, you may experience that very subtle body and the manifestation of the world through concentration. (60)

Through the realization that "I am of the nature of the void of pure consciousness" regarding the sun and other objects, the self itself is brought to its setting; though existing, it becomes as if non-existent by its own nature.

He says "cinmātra" (pure consciousness) to show that those who know reality can, by mere will, dissolve the entire world—including the sun and other elements—into the state of being nothing but the Self.
The meaning is that while the world exists as the very form of the Self, it becomes as if non-existent through the sublation of its appearance as the world. || 61 ||
It remains in the world of dreams and the like, as if by darkness or as if by sleep;
it is as if veiled, unattainable to others, yet present for the vision of the wise.

If it is asked, "How can the world, which exists from the perspective of those like us, be as if non-existent? he says, "It is situated," meaning: just as the world existing for the waking person's vision is [regarded] as non-existent by means of darkness—that is, by way of ignorance—in the world of dreams and so forth well-known to a sleeping person.
The meaning is that it exists in a state of emptiness, as if veiled, or unattainable to other perceptions of those who are asleep, just like that. || 62 ||
With the river of charcoal clinging to her body like a wave-ripple,
she appeared as if suddenly born from the splendor of a kingdom of the mind.

Furthermore, just as a curious parrot, even when touched by the ripples of a river of glowing coals imagined through the glory of its own mental kingdom, remains entirely free from suffering, so too have I arisen through mere *ā-īhā*—that is, a slight desire—in the form of a stone, a jewel, or the like; thus, there is no possibility of being a parrot. This is the meaning. || 63 ||
The forest of fire, with its rows of soot-like smoke, took on the appearance of a blossoming land-lotus through the splendor of its flowers in the form of *kiṃśuka* and *aśoka* trees.
Having thus provided the answer to Rāma’s question, continuing with the subject at hand, he says:

*kajjalaiḥ*. By me, who have become fire itself, [the city] was filled with flames—blazing with fire—by means of that which is like collyrium (*kajjala*), namely the forehead-mark (*alika*) whose bees are swarms of bees; and likewise by that which is like flowers, namely the *kiṃśuka* and *aśoka* trees, which were thus kindled and radiant.
The forest was made to have the appearance of a blossoming land-lotus; this is the ellipsis to be supplied. || 64 ||
Though it was extensive in its undertaking and kindled by the high-flaming blaze of its flames,
O dear one, it perished like the fickle fortune of a wicked man.
O friend, having risen with my power, blazing like a flickering and radiant female fortune, and having suddenly attained its peak, it has instantly fallen away. 65.

O Rāma, in this very same way, I have seen the splendor of the universe here within the interior of even a single atom; yet that is not something other than the supreme sky of consciousness. In this regard, the multitude of mountains appearing in a dream serves as your illustration.

O Rāma, by my power, I have likewise seen the splendor of the universe (*jagacchrī*) in this very manner even within the interior of every single atom; and that splendor of the universe, well-known from your own time onwards as the "splendor of the world," is not other than the Supreme Ether of Consciousness (*cidambara*).
In this regard, for you, there is the group of cities and the group of mountains well-known in your dream.
The meaning is that "nidarśana" refers to an illustration (dṛṣṭānta). || 66 ||

Thus ends the ninety-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Fiery World," in the *Uttara-pāśa* section of the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa*, within the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, belonging to the *Ārṣa* tradition. || 91 ||
Thus ends the ninety-first chapter, titled "The Description of the World of Taijasa," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The ninety-second canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Then, out of curiosity to behold the world, he fashioned it from wind.
I have come here having extended my concentration through a steady mental state. || 1 ||
Through the retention of air (vāyudhāraṇā), the expansion of its functions occurs when it has become air;
thereafter, the state of universal identity with space (ākāśa) is described here.

The grammatical connection is as follows: having come to—that is, reached—that [space] which is spread out and extensive, extending as far as its establishment in the state of air (vāyubhāva), the wind has become [the wind], thinking "I am. || 1 ||
I am perfected as the wind, the dancer in the presence of the vine-like women;
I am the protector of the fragrance of the clusters of lotuses, blue water-lilies, kunda flowers, and the like.

He distinguishes himself by means of well-known attributes of the wind with the words beginning "vallī" (the creeper) and so forth. He is the "protector of fragrance" (*āmodapālaka*), meaning he protects fragrances by bringing them under his own control. || 2 ||
Intent on effortlessly carrying away sprays of mist like snow,
he is thirsting to refresh all the limbs of those exhausted by amorous play.
Skilled in the rhythmic dancing of the leaves of grasses, shrubs, creepers, and climbing plants;
adorned with the fragrance of flowers and the splendor of the fruits of vines and medicinal herbs. || 4 ||
The phrase "I have become adorned" is to be connected everywhere with the scents of flowers that are radiant with fruit. || 4 ||
Gentle during auspicious times, he was cherished by the gazes of women; yet during times of calamity, he was as terrifying as a massive mountain with its foliage.
At times of auspiciousness, it is endowed with softness, coolness, gentleness, and fragrance as a sign of future prosperity;

at times of rising (or upheaval), however, it is terrible because it is the opposite—rough, hot, and harsh; and at the time of dissolution, it is such that mountains have been blown away like leaves by its force.
In the Nandana grove, he was ruddy with the pollen of the nectar from kunda and mandāra flowers;
in hell, he was radiant amidst a mass of glowing coals like a great frost.
In the Nandana grove of heaven. || 6 ||
In the ocean, its movement was inferred by the lines of straight whirlpools;
in the sky, the mirror of the moon was polished and wiped clean by the passage of the clouds.
Its movement was inferred from the lines of ripples, which were like straight streaks;
it was as if the moon-mirror had been wiped clean by the removal of the clouds, yet then soiled again by their covering.
The chariot of Nakṣatra-kṣatrasainya was increased in speed;
it was capable of supporting the celestial palaces where the Siddhas of the three worlds travel.

The chariot, augmented and increased by the impetuous speed of the royal army—the warrior host characterized by the constellations—is beneficial and favorable for the movement of the Siddhas throughout the three worlds and for the support of the celestial chariots of the gods, according to the well-known tenets of the science of astronomy (jyotiḥśāstra), which states that the wind named Pravaha causes the circle of the stars to revolve. Thus it is [beneficial] even in the three worlds. || 8 ||
Because of the swift movement of his mind, he was as if a uterine brother;
though bodiless, he possessed all limbs, being a sandalwood tree of throbbing bliss.

He is free from the aging of the downy hairs caused by the falling showers of frost; he is the intoxication of the youth of fragrance, possessing the silence of maturity and the softness of childhood.
He was worn out by old age, with hair as white as frost and other such signs;
yet he seemed possessed of the intoxication of youth through the fragrances of flowers and the like, and his silence and gentleness were like those of childhood.
Sweet with the fragrance of the Nandana grove, possessing a sweet and noble course of existence,
released from the beautiful Caitraratha forest, and having removed the fatigue of passion in the wilderness. (11)
In the Nandana grove, it was noble and sweet; from Caitraratha, the garden of Kubera, it issued forth and spread abroad.
For a long time, he was weary from the constant swaying of his body upon the waves of the Gaṅgā;
yet, through ignorance of the true nature of fatigue, he had his exhaustion dispelled.

On the swings formed by the limbs of the waves of the Gaṅgā, he was as if fatigued by the swaying; yet, out of eagerness to ward off the fatigue of others and through his own lack of awareness of weariness, he warded off the vast and extensive labors of others. 12.

The creepers, like women of the spring forest, bent down under the weight of their flowers; with the touch [of the wind], they long made me tremble, their hands being the swaying leaves and their eyes the rolling blossoms.

The creepers stand like the women of spring; "capalayan" means having long made them tremble with playful touches. And "loladalahastāśca tā alilocanāśca" is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning those whose hands are trembling leaves and whose eyes are bees. || 13 ||
Having long enjoyed the tip of the moon’s orb, she slept upon the bed of full clouds;
then, having shaken off the host of lotuses, his fatigue from lovemaking was removed.
Having long enjoyed the foremost and most excellent nectar within the orb of the moon— whether it be one's own or that of another, resulting from the fatigue of amorous play—
he is the sole horse among all those possessed of passion, traversing the sky, and a great friend to the exultation of elephants intoxicated with the scent of rut. 14–15.
The cloud, acting as a cowherd, reached the peak of the lightning with its slow gait;
it was like an enemy to the dust-storms and a thread for the pearls of spray.

Having obtained a horn characterized by lightning—a well-known musical instrument of cowherd boys—the wise one, through its sound, became the protector of the cattle characterized by clouds, such as cows, buffaloes, and so forth;
that is to say, he was the dryer, possessing the nature of an enemy to the water-particles that cause the destruction of dust. || 16 ||
It is the fragrance of a flower in the sky, the twin brother of all sounds;
it is the water in the channels of the conduits, moving through the limbs and minor members of the elements.

The fragrance of the flower, which has the nature of space (ākāśa), has become the scent; for this very reason, it is a sibling to all sounds, which are its qualities. It exists within the limbs and minor members of living beings (bhūta/prāṇin), and thus it has become like water in the channels characterized by their respective veins—this is the meaning. || 17 ||
He is the sole soul who performs the work upon the vital points, the lion within the house of the cave of the heart;
he is the eternal traveler on the solitary path, the knower of the essence of the sacrificial fire.

Because all such beings are living entities, because they occupy vital points such as the heart, and because they perform functions upon those vital points (*marmas*), there is but one Self for them all. He is exclusively and invariably a traveler, whose nature is to move about. He is a "knower of the essence" (*sāravit*), for he knows the essence—the strength—of the fire-born (*jātavedas*); since he destroys that which is weak when it takes the form of a lamp or similar object, yet preserves that which is strong through his friendly disposition.
He causes to increase. || 18 ||
He is the plunderer of the jewels of fragrance, the ground for the city of celestial chariots,
the moon that cools the darkness of burning, and the milky ocean of cooling lunar light.
He is a plunderer of the jewels characterized by fragrance, forcibly untying the knot of the *Kalikā* to seize them;

he is the upholder of the earth, which is like a city characterized by a multitude of celestial chariots (*vimāna*); he is the fire that burns the darkness characterized by heat, yet he is the moon, the birthplace of coolness, just as the Milky Ocean is the birthplace of the cool-rayed moon. || 19 ||
By means of the rope of the vital and downward breaths, he is the driver of the machine for living beings;
he is both enemy and friend to the continents, delighting in their constant movement from one to another.
Because it breaks up the continents with its waves, it is an enemy; because it nourishes them with dust, it is a friend. || 20 ||
Though standing before one, its nature is invisible, resembling a city of the mind's kingdom;
it is like a palm-leaf fan, sesame oil, or a tethering post for a trembling elephant. 21.
In a single moment, he caused all the mountains to tremble,
acting alone like the flow of the Gaṅgā with its waves of various colors.
At the time of universal dissolution, he by whom all the mountains were shaken and uprooted in a mere instant;
and by whom the rows of letters of various colors—characteristic of the waves [of his speech]—were made into a single unity through their mingling with dust, like the flow of the Gaṅgā. 22.
He creates great whirlpools of water, smoke, clouds, dust, and rivers;
he is the torrent of the celestial river, the mass of clouds, and the swarm of bees upon the blue lotuses of the sky.
Furthermore, what kind of wind is it? It is the maker of great whirlpools for the smoke, the clouds, the dust, and the waters;
it is the bee upon the blue lotus characterized by the sky, wherein the flow of the celestial river is like a flood of water consisting of nectar. 23.
He was like a wind that fans away the old grass wrapped around his body; he was the sun to the forest of lotuses that were his throbbing limbs, and the sole rain-cloud for the downpour of his voice.

The wind is the cause of the slow movement of withered grass that has been released from the entanglement of a whirlwind. The sun is the cause of the blooming of the lotus forest, which is characterized by vibration—the general nature of action. And the cloud is the primary cause of rain, which is characterized by sound. || 24 ||
An elephant in the forest of the sky, a crocodile in the house of the body,
and the lover embracing the garlanded groves of kadamba trees in the dust.
In the house of the body, he is like a gargara—a specific kind of machine—constantly emitting sound;
he is the hero who embraces both the heroine known as the mass of dust and the heroines known as the garlands of forest flowers.
Through the qualities of solidifying, drying, supporting, moving, and fragrance... [25] ...he acts.
Through six cooling actions, he who has not yet found the opportunity [for liberation] attains imperishability.

Solidification, such as that of snow or ghee; the clumping together, such as that of mud; the drying up, such as that of clouds; the supporting, such as the holding up of grass and other things; the causing of movement; and the bringing of fragrances, such as coolness which removes heat—by these six actions, he has attained an inexhaustible moment that lasts until the final dissolution (*pralaya*).
That by which there is rest. || 26 ||
Constantly intent on extracting the essence like a brother of fire,
he effects the application of the bodily constituents that perform the functions of taking up and carrying away.
The "impeller" (cālaka) is that which effects the application of the hands and other limbs of those who perform the seizing and taking; that is to say, it is the mover. || 27 ||
In the city of the body, moving unhindered through the pathways of the channels,
he is the great merchant of the jewel of life, who turns over the vessel of vital essence.

He is unimpeded and free from obstacles regarding the sphere of movement; he is a great merchant concerning the preservation and expenditure of the jewel of life, which has been transformed into the form of prāṇa, apāna, and so forth within the vessel of the body composed of the essence of food.
He is solely intent on the destruction and reconstruction of the city of the body, and is skilled in separating the essence from the dross, the subtle portions, and the constituent elements. || 29 ||

He is skilled and proficient in separating the dregs of food-flavors from their waste products, and in distinguishing the six subtlest essential portions known as skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen, as well as the constituent elements (dhātus) known as wind, bile, and phlegm. || 29 ||
Then, within the body, I beheld the world down to its most subtle atoms;
therein I appeared clearly in this form, expansive and perfectly stable.

There, even within the state of air, down to the most subtle atom and reaching as far as the ultimate atom (paramāṇu), I have perceived the world in every substance and within every part of the body, just like a slab of gold. Within those worlds as well, I alone am thus the possessor of the form of the world consisting of earth and the other elements. || 30 ||
In this regard, the atoms are as if being carried away during the process of creation;
yet, truly, nothing at all is carried away—for what can possibly be carried away in that which has the nature of space?
But from the perspective of ultimate reality, nothing at all is perceived within the sky-like form that is empty in nature. || 31 ||
Together with the moon, sun, wind, fire, Indra, Padma, Vaiśravaṇa, and Īśvara;
along with Brahmā, Hari, Gandharvas, Vidyādharas, and great serpents. || 32 ||

He describes how the creations, as if being swept away, are joined with everything down to every single atom by means of three verses beginning with "With the moon and sun" (sacandrārka). In all instances, the *bahuvrīhi* compound is formed according to the rule *tena saheti tulyayoge* ("with that, in the sense of equal conjunction"), whereby the substitute *sa-* is used for *saha*. (32)
[He perceives] the oceans, mountains, islands, and the far reaches of the quarters as a vast expanse;
along with the intermediate worlds, the lords of those worlds, their activities, time, and the succession of its parts.

[He beheld] the worlds including heaven, the earth, and the depths of Pātāla, along with the intermediate regions, together with their presence and absence, their privations, and the turmoil of old age and death. (34)
Thus, O Rāma, at that time, I, assuming the form of the five elements, sported there within the interior of the lotus of the three worlds.

With the intention that, by means of this concentration on space (ākāśa-dhāraṇā), the experiences of the various manifestations of that [space] within the state of space should also be inferred, he concludes: "In this very way," etc. (35).
The taste of earth, water, air, and fire was drunk and experienced by me while dwelling among living beings as a network of roots for trees. (36)

He elaborates on how and in what manner he has moved about, beginning with the words "the sap was drunk" and so forth: "By me, dwelling within the bodies of trees—which consist of a combination of the elements of earth, water, air, and fire—the sap of the earth was drunk through my network of roots. (36)
They rolled upon bodies thick with elixirs, beautified by the liquid of sandalwood,
as if upon the lunar orbs or beds of frost.
Nectar, the elixir of immortality, was present upon his thick limbs, which were radiant with qualities such as coolness and whiteness like liquid sandalwood paste (37).
Having fully enjoyed the clusters of flowers born in all seasons and possessing manifold fragrances throughout the quarters, he offered the remains to the bees in his abode (38).
Various delightful clusters of flowers were enjoyed and experienced by me as I gave the nectar, the remnants of my own enjoyment, to the bees. (38)
On the courtyard of the sky, which was soft,
well-spread with clouds rising here and there, he slept as if upon beds of fresh butter amidst garlands of white clouds.
He was sleeping upon well-spread beds of white clouds in the courtyard of the sky, the arena of the firmament. || 39 ||
Upon the limbs of the celestial and Siddha women— limbs as soft as jasmine petals and radiant with the splendor of dark blue beauty— the latent impressions of passion have been cast far away.

"Like a leaf among the flowers of the *sumana* and *śirīṣa*, [you are] upon the soft limbs of the celestial and *siddha* women; why have you, a lustful man, slept there? To this he replies: "Stay far away! (40)
In the forest of lotuses— of white, blue,
and red varieties— a soft, playful clamor has been made by the female swans.
With the streams of rivers as their veins and the root-land as their foundation,
the mountains were like bodies inhabited by living beings, appearing as if they were the very abodes of hair.

Moreover, by me, who am the cosmic egg, the circles of worlds—whose living beings are radiant and which are supported by the earth-mandala that serves as the root for the flowing streams of rivers—are borne upon my limbs; likewise, the mountains, which are the abodes of hair, are borne upon my limbs like rows of body-hairs. (42)
The Khādiras were renowned for their long river-patterned garments, which, with their ocean-blue borders,
rested upon their limbs like mirrors reflecting images.

The meaning is that those things well-known in the world, such as food and so forth, along with long rivers, threads, and oceans, have come to rest within my limbs as if in mirrors accompanied by their reflections. || 43 ||
My body was at rest from the creation of beings, including the Siddhas, Vidyādharas, and others,
as if it were perceived by a fly that had taken the form of a bee.

But within my body, by the host of living beings beginning with the Siddhas and Vidyādharas—who were perceived as conscious and known [by me], yet who had assumed forms such as flies and beetles—it found rest. (44)
By my grace, the planets beginning with the Sun have obtained their bodies, which are joyful and colored black, red, white, yellow, and green, as if they were various types of emeralds.
In that case, what was attained by those who, like flies or lice, are terrified and distressed by being warded off at every moment?
He says "no," [but rather] "by my grace. This should be understood as a compound word beginning with *vapuḥ-kṛṣṇa*. [It means:
by means of bodies that are dark, red, and so forth, and which are firm like trees that are green and glossy.
The meaning is: "by those who are drinking deeply" and "rejoicing. || 45 ||
By means of the seal of the ocean, which consists of the seven continents and the sevenfold self, the earth was established in the forearm like a bracelet. (46)
The earth, renowned for its configuration and arrangement consisting of seven continents and sevenfold forms, has been placed by me in my forearm like a bracelet. (46)
By his own self, though unseen, he caused a thrill of horripilation to arise in the wives of the Vidyādharas, whose slender bodies had already been touched by him.
By means of those [rays], with my very self remaining unseen, I have brought about a thrill of horripilation in them through my own bliss. || 47 ||
The worlds themselves became the networks of my bones—vast, hollow, and filled with the pure, flowing essence of the rivers. || 48 ||

Within my body, the worlds—mountains and all—are situated as hollow and perforated structures, their interiors filled with pure and expansive fluids through veins possessing the characteristics of rivers; likewise, the networks of bones, flesh, and other tissues are established therein.
It dwells within my heart like gnats inside a fig tree, amidst countless sky-elephants with the moving chowries of the sun and moon.
By the elephants of the sky, such as Airāvata and others; in my heart, that is, in the space of the heart. || 49 ||
O Rāma, with all the netherworlds as its feet, supporting the belly of the earth,
and even the sky as its head, the state of being the supreme atom was not then abandoned.
He says "sarva... [verse 50] to show that even in the form of this exceedingly vast universe, my nature as the supreme subtle pure consciousness has not been lost.
It exists as the void-nature, acting everywhere, in all directions, at all times, and in every way; it is the universal self, yet it is not a [limited] whole.
In the form of emptiness—that is, in the form of pure consciousness alone, which is empty of all duality. || 51 ||
I have fully experienced you as something and yet as nothing, as having form and yet as formless, as possessing dullness and yet as consciousness. 52.

Then he says, "The state of being something" (kiñcit-tvam), meaning that at that time, the synthesis within its own self of all contradictory properties, such as being delimited and undelimited, is experienced. || 52 ||
"Indeed, thousands of creations of the ocean—so charmingly full and embracing Maināka—have been brought by me to rest upon the earth like motionless pillars. (53)

He says— beginning with "Maināka"— that even in regions such as the interior of the ocean, there exist infinite worlds upon the golden rocks, just as on Mount Maināka; and that he has experienced those as well, within the ocean which is charming, thick, and exceedingly vast due to the mountain rocks and other formations hidden within it, reaching toward every part of the earth.
"There have been thousands of creations that were like motionless pillars, and those too have been experienced by me"—thus it is connected by way of transformation. (53)
The worlds, whether hidden or manifest, were borne upon his limbs by Maya,
like cities of reflection in a mirror that is not insentient in nature.
Thus, by me, through my own nature as space, the states of water, wind, fire, and earth were created—alas, a manifestation of illusion, like that of consciousness in dreams. (55)
It was as if created by consciousness through its well-known power within dreams. || 55 ||
Moreover, in that state, I beheld countless worlds within the hollow of space, even within every single atom.
Space exists within every atom, just as a multitude of creations exists within every atom, like a city accompanied by other dreams within a dream. (57)
The sky exists thus expanded within every single atom, moving therein; and within every single atom, a multitude of creations exists. || 57 ||
I myself became this very earth-circle with its earrings of continents;
yet, even with my entire self, nothing whatsoever was pervaded by me anywhere.

I was merely my own superimposed nature as the Self. Thus, although I am the self of the entire universe, nothing whatsoever has been pervaded or touched by me; the meaning is that this is because of my non-attachment and non-duality. || 58 ||
By producing every sprout of creeper, tree, and grass, the earth has, through me alone, drawn forth the essences for the sake of those who bear human form. (59)

By me alone—who, for the sake of those bearing male bodies, such as men and others, produced in their entirety the creepers, trees, grasses, and sprouts—have the juices fallen from the rain been drawn up and drunk by the surface of the earth. (59)

When the time for awakening through battle—the most pure—has arrived [or, according to another reading: when I am composed of the time for pure awakening], millions of worlds exist and some do not exist. (60)
When I have reached the time of awakening— which is like a battle and which destroys all duality— millions of worlds exist for me and yet do not exist.
Those which manifest their own wonder within consciousness, being the wonders of the Self residing within, these are the perceptions of creation. (61)

If it is asked in what form they abide and in what form they do not abide, he says— in two verses— that they abide in the form of the mere wonder of consciousness (*ciccamatkāra*) and do not abide in any form other than that: "In consciousness" (*citi*), those internal wonders (*antasthāḥ svacamatkṛtayaḥ*) which, by their own nature, produce a wonder characterized by the manifestation of their own existence.
Having projected them onto the world, they manifest them in that form; the meaning is that these are the perceptions of creation. || 61 ||
Whatever suffering has been experienced or undergone, anywhere and in any measure,
nothing is found here apart from the wonder of the ultimate reality.
Each individual is of the nature of the universal form, the creator of all, and free from affliction;
he is awakened and of the nature of pure consciousness, since everything has Brahman as its essence. (63)

Therefore, because each [element] surrenders its own existence during superimposition (adhyāropa), the one awakened through the negation (apavāda) of the universal form is indeed the self of pure consciousness; such is the meaning. || 63 ||
All, everywhere, the self of all, all-pervading, and the refuge of all—this is the domain of the awakened; I do not know it as unawakened.

For this very reason, because of the superimposition of the entire world upon Brahman—which is within each and every object—Brahman is everything, is present everywhere, is the self of all, is all-pervading, and is the support of all; thus the nature of the world culminates in the domain of the awakened. However, he states that "the unawakened" [is not seen by the awakened], meaning that the form accessible to the unawakened cannot be perceived by those who are awakened. || 64 ||
Within the nature of consciousness, which is as clear as the expanse of space, this succession of creations shines forth eternally;
yet that [succession] is indeed within that very [consciousness], like internal heat within fire. This perception of duality does not exist; there is only the existent, the infinite.

And thus, regarding the non-dual conscious self (cidātman), the wise consider the conception of the "selfhood of all" everywhere to be mere conceptual construction (vikalpa); there is no object whatsoever existing apart from consciousness. He says this with the words "ākāśa" (space) and so forth. That [space] is within that very [consciousness]. Just as in the expression "the heat within the fire," there is no separate meaning for the word *tāpa* (fire), the word *tad-antara* (within that), or the word *ūṣma* (heat).

However, just as there is mere conceptual construction (vikalpa) from a sentence, so too is the perception of difference; thus, the meaning is that the world does not exist, but rather the infinite Reality exists. || 65 ||

Thus ends the ninety-second chapter, titled "The Demonstration of the Unity of Ultimate Reality and Creation," in the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the glorious Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa, composed by the Sage (Arṣa), in the Vālmīki edition, the Māhārāṣṭra recension. 92.

Thus ends the ninety-second chapter, titled "The Demonstration of the Unity of Ultimate Reality and Creation," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the illustrious Vāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa-tātparya-prakāśa.
The Ninety-third Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Then, having turned back from such a state of consciousness through diligent effort, [he remained].
I arrived at that place, the interior of a hut made of bark garments.
The beholding of the Siddha absorbed in meditation within Vasiṣṭha’s hut,
his fall due to the collapse of the hut, and his narration of his own history are described here.

Then, immediately after perceiving the world and my own body through the perfection of *dhāraṇā*, I turned away from that consciousness of curiosity regarding the aforementioned form and returned to my former place of meditative absorption, the interior of the celestial hut (*ambarakuṭīkośa*). || 1 ||
As long as I did not see my own body situated anywhere there, I saw only some other perfected being (siddha) standing before me. || 2 ||
Even though I have searched everywhere thoroughly, I do not see my own body anywhere. || 2 ||
Seated, established in meditative concentration, he had attained the desired state—
like the sun at its gentle rising, like a fire whose fuel has been consumed.

He who has attained the state of Brahman—the beloved object of supreme love and the station of unsurpassed bliss—is described by the verse beginning with "Like the rising of the moon" (saumyodayamiva) and so forth. || 3 ||
Seated in the bound lotus posture, peaceful, motionless in meditative absorption,
with the testicles positioned between the two ankles, he has transcended the objects of the senses.
By means of concentration, through the steadiness of the mind upon the desired object, it is motionless and unwavering. || 4 ||
His neck was beautiful with shoulders of smooth, gentle, and even proportions;
it was lovely with its broad, firm, noble, and well-rested posture.

Regarding the phrase "holding the body, head, and neck straight," he describes the characteristics of the bodily posture for meditation as taught by the Blessed One with the word "polished" (*mṛṣṭa*). His neck (*kandharā*) is beautiful due to his shoulders, which are polished by the lines of the sacred ash (*bhasma-tripuṇḍra*), gentle, lovely through their profundity, and well-proportioned.
Whose head is beautiful by its position—[the head] of that steadfast one whose mind rests upon a noble object, who is expansive and possesses a serene countenance? (5)
He was illuminated by the radiance of his two hands, which were extended upward near his navel,
as if by the splendors of the heart-lotus shining forth externally.

By the radiance of their two hands, which possess the splendor of a pair of blooming lotuses, there arises for them the poetic conceit (utprekṣā) that [the radiance] is indeed their own heart-lotus. || 6 ||
With its eyelashes closed together, having ceased all looking and attained a state of clarity, it was like a lake with its lotuses shut at the end of the day, as if asleep. (7)
One for whom all investigations and the activities of the external senses have ceased; at the end of the day, during the night. || 7 ||
With a steady disposition, he bore an inner core of the mind that was unshaken and profoundly tranquil, like the sky when all disturbances have subsided.
Not seeing my own body, yet seeing that sage before me, I then reflected thus there with a beautiful mind: (9)
This which is about to be stated has been reflected upon. || 9 ||
"Some great Siddha has arrived here in this region;
like me, he seeks solitude and desires rest in the vast sky. (10)
Formerly, like me, he was one who sought solitary rest. || 10 ||
With the thought, "May I find a solitary place suitable for meditative concentration," this hut was envisioned by him, who is endowed with the power of true resolve.
"I have come here with the thought that I might find a secluded place suitable for meditative concentration. With this in mind, he perceived that this hut was fit for his own meditation. (11)
Because he did not consider my arrival for a long time, he has cast off his own body, which has become a corpse, and established himself here. (12)

Then, because he had long neglected me, his own body remained there turned into a corpse; however, seeing Vasiṣṭha’s body there and not realizing that I would return again, he abandoned that corpse, cast it elsewhere, and took up residence here in this hut. || 12 ||
Then, having made the firm resolve, "I shall go now to my own world," just as I was about to depart, [it happened] due to the exhaustion of my mental constructs.

"Since my body here has perished and been destroyed, I shall go to my own world of the Seven Sages by means of the subtle body (ātivāhika-deha) alone"—having made this resolve, just as I was about to depart, [the Lord spoke]—this is the meaning. || 13 ||
That hut there vanished, and only empty space remained;
though he was a perfected soul, that meditator fell downward, being without support.

When that hut of my own volition was destroyed through the subsiding of my mental construction, it was like a city in a dream; this is the implied meaning of "like a city. This serves as an illustration for both the previous and the subsequent destruction of the huts. (15)
Then that meditator fell from there like a torrent of water from a cloud,
or like a cloud driven by the wind from the sky, or like the lunar orb at the end of an eon.
A flood of water is a downpour of water; it was like the orb of the moon at the time of destruction, the cosmic dissolution. || 16 ||
Like a meritless celestial being falling from his palace, like a tree whose roots have been severed,
or like a stone cast from a mountain peak, he fell then upon the earth.
"Meritoriousless" means one whose merit has been exhausted; "on the earth" refers to the golden ground that will be described hereafter. || 17 ||
While he was forming the thought, "As long as this hut exists, so long am I," once that [thought] was exhausted and the destruction of the hut occurred, he fell down, perfected in an instant. (18)
"When my resolve of truth—'As long as I remain here, let this hut remain and stand firm'—and my resolve to depart have both been exhausted," [so it was said]. || 18 ||
Then, as that perfected one was falling, out of curiosity regarding his noble character, I descended from the sky to the surface of the earth by means of my mind alone. (19)
Together with that perfected one, I went to the surface of the earth by means of that mental body, which is indeed a subtle transportive form.
He fell, by means of the circular whirls produced by the swirling of the mass of wind,
onto the pleasure-grounds of the gods at the edge of the seven continents and oceans.

The "balanam" (shaking) or turning of the masses of winds such as the Pravaha and others means that, by means of their whirlpool-like movements induced by those winds, water enters downward just as it does in a whirlpool; this occurs on the golden ground, the place of sport for the gods (gīrvāṇas). || 20 ||
Because his vital breaths (prāṇa) and downward breaths (apāna) were moving upwards, he remained suspended in the sky exactly as he was;
having previously cast his head upwards, he fell to the earth with his legs bound in the lotus posture (padmāsana).

He who was first created upon the earth and established there as the primordial portion of the foot, being thus one whose head is turned upwards— why is that? Because by means of the *prāṇa* (out-breath),
through the upward drawing of the *apāna* (in-breath), he moves upwards, just as the gourd of a water-jar descending into a well is drawn up by its rope, or like a fruit by its stalk.
The meaning is that because [the body] is held up by the upward and downward vital breaths (*prāṇa* and *apāna*), it is impossible for the head to be positioned downwards. || 21 ||
He did not wake up; moving about, he was unconscious, like a body made of stone, or as light as cotton wool. || 22 ||

Even upon encountering such a movement and shaking, he did not awaken from his meditative absorption (*samādhi*). For, because his mind was firmly attached elsewhere, he was as if insentient. If so, one might ask why he did not have his limbs broken by falling from such a great height; to this he says: "Like a body of diamond-stone. By the power of yoga, he was as firm as a mass of cotton.
Or indeed, it is as light as a feather. || 22 ||
Then, striving for the sake of awakening him, I assumed the form of a cloud in the sky and let forth a powerful roar and rain. (23)

For the sake of awakening and for the sake of emerging from meditative absorption, having assumed the state of a cloud—that is, having become a cloud—it rained; and there was a thundering that was intense and exceedingly powerful. || 23 ||
By that falling of hailstones within that region,
he awakened this [man] with his intellect, as the rainy season awakens a peacock.

Having become like a cloud, I—just as one might awaken a peacock during the rainy season—awakened this perfected being (siddha) through my own skill in intellect, by drawing him outward through that intellect or through my own awakened understanding; that is, I raised him up from his meditative absorption (samādhi). || 24 ||
With the beauty of his limbs illuminated and his eyes blossoming,
he became like a bed of lotuses in the rainy season, its very self in full bloom from the downpour of water.
When his vision had become perfectly tranquil, I questioned that awakened one who stood before me, whose mode of being was pure and who had desisted from the perspective of ultimate reality.
From the perspective of ultimate reality, it is for the sake of the meditative concentration that abides in the ultimate. || 26 ||
"Where are you situated, O leader of sages, and what are you doing?
Who are you, and why do you not fall from such a great distance even in your mind? (27)
He states what he asked: "Where? [meaning] why do you not perceive in your mind even the fall from a height, the downward plunge from afar? || 27 ||
Thus addressed, he looked at me and, recollecting his former state,
spoke these beautiful words, just as a cātaka bird addresses a rain-cloud.
The Siddha said:
"Wait for me while I recall my own history;
afterwards, I shall relate to you the account of my past life."
Wait; bide your time. || 29 ||
Having spoken thus and reflected quickly, he remembered his own conduct exactly as it had occurred and remained unimpaired, just as one remembers the day's activities at evening.

The past account of his own life, together with the accounts of his previous births, was told unimpaired and in its entirety—just as people remember their own deeds performed during the day in the evening. || 30 ||
Then he spoke these words to me— charming, cool as the rays of the moon,
gladdening, irreproachable, faultless, and resulting in happiness.
Because the speech about to be spoken is primarily concerned with discernment (*viveka*) and dispassion (*vairāgya*), it is praised through qualifiers such as "beautiful" (*cāru*) and so forth.
31. The Siddha said: "O Brahmin, you have now been recognized by me; I salute you."
This transgression must be forgiven, for forgiveness is indeed the nature of the virtuous.
Transgression is the offense characterized by failing to offer salutation upon first seeing [the teacher]. || 32 ||
O Sage, for a long time I have wandered through the grounds of celestial groves, deluded by the intoxication of sensual enjoyments, like a bee among lotus ponds. (33)
In this regard, since the question "Where do you reside?

cannot refer to the hut as a place of meditative absorption (samādhi) witnessed by direct perception, [the sage]—demonstrating his power of recollecting past births (jātismaratva) by declaring the various substrates prior to that—speaks of those common to other lifetimes, beginning with the word "O Sage" (mune). || 33 ||
Then, as I was being carried away by the whirlpools of the river of appearances, tossed about by the play of the waves of the water of the mind, I became distressed and thought: || 34 ||

Being deluded by the river of visible objects—which flows like a dream with the playful tossing of the waves of the mind—and consequently becoming weary of saṃsāra due to the arising of inquiry after a long time, he reflected as follows: || 34 ||
In the ocean of saṃsāra, I am agitated by the waves of visible objects; in time, I have fallen into distress like a cātaka bird during a drought. (35)
In the case of *avagraha*, which is the obstruction of rain. || 35 ||
In those things whose sole essence is pure consciousness, what indeed is there that can be called "enjoyment"? I shall remain solely in the sky of consciousness itself, free from all agitation.
He states what was intended by this: "merely consciousness" (*saṃvinmātra*). Among enjoyments, what indeed is delightful?

If it is only the pleasure manifesting there as the nature of consciousness that is delightful, then—since all other means of that [pleasure] are essentially suffering and thus have nothing but that [consciousness] as their core—one should abandon the entire portion of suffering and [rest] in that which constitutes the essence.
The meaning is: "I shall abide solely in the sky of blissful consciousness; what is the use of anything else that is essence-less? || 36 ||
Apart from the mere objects of sound, form, taste, touch, and smell, there is nothing else whatsoever here; why then do I take delight in this much? (37)
For it is not fitting to delight in a limited, calculated, and unpleasant state while abandoning the unlimited bliss; thus he says:
"All this is indeed the space of pure consciousness, or rather, it is pure consciousness alone.
Why then do I, with a ruined intellect, take pleasure here in an unreal form, like one who has lost his mind? (38)
All this—sound and the rest—is, by its own nature, nothing but pure consciousness (*cinmātra*). When it is perceived as distinct from that [consciousness], it is merely empty space;
yet when seen as non-distinct from it, it resolves into pure consciousness alone.
Thus, in either case, what is there to delight in within these forms of sound and so forth, which are essentially unreal? Like one whose mind is ruined, I am like a madman.
The meaning is "so it is. || 38 ||
Sense objects are like the unevenness of poison; they are deceptive and bestow the delusion of desire.
The flavors become tasteless once one has wallowed in them—who, having done so, has not been destroyed? (39)

Objects such as sound and the rest are like poison, being causes of death, madness, and other forms of imbalance. Women are treacherous. Passions are the causes of distaste even for a man who is full of flavor. Who is not destroyed by wallowing among these?
The meaning is that we see the slaughter, imprisonment, and so forth of deer, elephants, and others through attachment to even a single one of these. || 39 ||
The mind, which is like a decayed little water-flea in the mud of life, has quickly entered the body; now old age desires to seize it like a large crane.

Thus, he says "jīrṇā" etc., to show that attachment even to the body is not appropriate: "Old age has arrived swiftly like a large crane; thinking that this great minnow has been caught in the mire of life, she desires to seize—that is, to swallow—the body. (40)
This body is soon to perish, like a bubble in the ocean;
even while flickering before one's eyes, it vanishes like the flame of a lamp. (41)
It has various turbulent waves, it creates whirlpools and eddies, it has birth and death as its vast banks, and pleasure and pain as its ripples.

Thus, since hope for life is likewise inappropriate, he describes it as being like a river with the words beginning "vividha" (various): "that which has various agitated distractions as its waves. || 42 ||
Turbid with the effervescence of youth, frothing white with old age, and possessing bubbles of happiness produced by chance, like the falling of a palm fruit upon a crow— (43)
Thick with mud and turbid with mire. || 43 ||
It is filled with the clamor of the great current of legal disputes and the dull sounds of documents;
it is a place where passion and hatred flourish like dense clouds, and where the bodies of beings tremble upon the surface of the earth. || 44 ||

Agitated by the sounds of water—characterized by the "la" and "ḍa" sounds (which are indistinguishable from the "ra" sound) that signify worldly transactions and the prattling of fools—it surges and increases, accompanied by thick clouds characterized by passion and hatred. Thus it is described. (44)
Alas! This river called "life," which is cool with its roaring, possesses great whirlpools of greed and delusion, and causes one to fall, rise, and turn about. (45)

"Hā" expresses grief. "Nadana" means sounding; it refers to mere sound. The connection is that she carries [the water] which is cool only by that [sound], while in reality she is scorched by the threefold suffering (tāpa). || 45 ||
Just as waters enter the river of worldly existence, so too do riches come together and then depart entirely, both new and old. (46)
The unions with beloved sons, friends, and others, which have become like the waters of the river of saṃsāra, as well as former riches, pass away, while new ones arrive. (46)
Enough with those wretched beings who, having come forth, turn back;
for what kind of reliance can there be here upon those who proceed as never before? (47)
Regarding this, he says "pravṛttāḥ" (verse 47) to show that grief and joy are not appropriate for those who are departing or arriving.
The water of every river flows from the ocean and returns to it;
but the water of the river of the body, which is life, flows away and never returns again. (48)
He states the distinction of lifespan from wealth and other things with the words "of all" (sarvasyāḥ). [It arises] from a source such as a mountain or a cloud. || 48 ||
Hundreds of existences revolve for every single body at every moment; like the pots on a potter's wheel, all things spin within the ocean of existence. (49)
In every morsel of food, in every body, and at every moment, objects of enjoyment arise like pots, bowls, and other vessels mounted upon the wheel of a potter. || 49 ||
The four thieves, the enemies that are the turbulent sense-objects, roam about; they carry away the entire wealth of one's inner being. Am I awake here, or am I asleep? (50)
Existence is discernment; that is its defining characteristic and its very essence.
Fragments of life fall away again and again;
alas, no one perceives the days being consumed by Time.
"Today this is mine, and likewise this, and likewise this; this belongs to me"—by such reckoning, alas, the world does not realize what has passed or what has been attained. 52.
He does not realize that his lifespan has passed away and that death has arrived. || 52 ||
I have eaten and drunk, I have wandered through endless forest lands, and I have witnessed joys and sorrows; what else remains here to be accomplished? (53)
The other is unprecedented. || 53 ||
Because of the repeated experience of pleasure and pain, because of turning back again and again,
and because of the impermanence of all things, we remain free from longing.
Free from curiosity regarding enjoyments, they are devoid of longing. || 54 ||
Multitudes of enjoyments have been experienced and the extreme impermanence of things has been witnessed; yet, not even a slight rest is found anywhere here.
Having wandered through the lofty peaks and the grove-lands of Mount Meru, and having reached high into the cities of the World-Guardians, what uncreated [reality] have I found? (56)
What unconditioned and eternal thing has been attained? The meaning is: nothing at all. || 56 ||
Everywhere trees are made of wood, beings of flesh, and the earth of clay; since suffering and impermanence are likewise universal, tell me, how can one find consolation? (57)
Having analyzed it, he shows the worthlessness of all enjoyments: "In all [of them]," [verse 57].
Neither wealth, nor friends, nor pleasures, nor kinsmen are able to protect a person who has been seized by Time. (58)
Like water within the belly of a cloud, a person vanishes into the hollows of mountains; as fragile as a heap of dust, he sets away utterly empty.

Like a heap of dust, a fragile accumulation of soil, unstable and unfirm, a person—attached to the objects of the senses like water within a cloud fallen into the hollow of a mountain—is wasting away moment by moment and goes to its end in death, utterly devoid of the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*). [In the reading *jaraṭhajīmūta*... (Note: The phrase *jaraṭhajīmūta* refers to a "mature" or "old" cloud.)
Like an autumn cloud and water. || 59 ||
Sensual pleasures do not delight me, nor do magnificent riches; even this life of mine is as fickle as the flickering side-glances of an intoxicated woman.
O Sage, where, for whom, how, or from what source could there possibly be consolation?
For today or tomorrow, death—the wicked—places calamity upon one's head. (61)

The interrogative forms [kiṃvṛtta] imply the agent, the time, the manner, and the cause. The meaning is: since the evil and cruel Death bestows—that is, brings—calamity upon the head today or tomorrow. || 61 ||
The body falls away like a leaf; life is a state of decay.
The aesthetic flavors (rasas), seized by the lack of steadfastness of mind, have become flavorless.
My life has been spent merely through dry longings;
not even the slightest desired object has produced a sense of wonder for me.

My life has been spent with insipid enjoyments or merely through the desires for them; I have not accomplished even a single thing that would cause wonder—a true human goal—nor have I achieved what I truly desired.
Today delusion has reached its dullness; the body is of no further use here.
Indifference is the highest state; attachment to worldly standing is the lowest condition.
Non-attachment to sense objects; attachment to life—that is, dependence on worldly existence—is the lowest state.
Alas, this calamity has indeed befallen me, causing such delusion!
One must always think thus: "I am not attached here in this cycle of existence. (65)
For those who possess discernment, when prosperity and such are attained, it should be regarded as nothing other than a calamity that has befallen them. || 65 ||
By means of injunctions and prohibitions, both eternal and non-eternal,
the world is led according to its desires, just as water follows depressions and elevations.
He says that even the scriptures on action appear as mere delusions to the discerning person: "By injunctions," etc. (Verse 66).
The winds of the senses, like poisonous breezes, snatch from the heart’s flower-bud its entire essence—the fragrance of discernment—and, inducing a swoon, bestow [the objects of sense]. (67)
For this reason, [the author] says that [desire], having robbed the performers of action of their discrimination regarding worldly and otherworldly objects, leads them only to misfortune:
"Even that which is non-existent (asat) appears to have attained existence (sattvam) by being perceived as such;
just as the non-existent has become the form of the existent, so the non-existent itself is regarded as existent. (68)
In reality, however, the form of the object is non-existent; it appears to have attained existence when perceived through the cognition of existence, yet not in actual fact.
Just as that which is of the nature of existence becomes non-existent through obscuration, so too that which is non-existent becomes existent through projection (vikṣepa).
The meaning is that this is due to the power of Māyā, which is capable of accomplishing even the impossible. || 68 ||
Just as the wives of the ocean run along the earth, swaying their bodies back and forth, so do people run after sense-objects.
In this regard, he states that for those whose vision is turned outward, the inclination toward sense objects is natural, by saying "dolāyantyaḥ" (swinging like a swing).
Just as the rivers, the women of the ocean, swinging their bodies like a swing upon the ground of both banks, flow toward the oceans. || 69 ||
The arrows of the mind, once released toward their target, rush toward the objects of the senses;
they do not return again to their qualities, just as ungrateful people do not return to their former friendship.
The qualities such as discernment and dispassion, as well as the bowstrings. || 70 ||
A tempestuous wind is indeed death; friends are indeed enemies;
kinsmen are indeed fetters; and wealth is indeed the ultimate poverty. (71)
They are called *śatru* (enemies) because they cut [one down] through excessive attachment and affection; *naidhana* means that which brings about death. || 71 ||
Pleasures are indeed extreme sufferings; prosperities are supreme calamities;
enjoyments are the great diseases of existence; and delight is but supreme aversion.
Through the generation of attachment, there arise extreme sufferings; indeed, delight is attachment itself, while its opposite is aversion and agitation.
All calamities and all prosperities result only in suffering; life leads only to death—alas, this is the unfolding of illusion! 73.
Explaining what was previously stated, he says: "From calamities," and so forth. (73)
Beholding many revolutions of time, both desirable and undesirable, and even slight pleasures as well as separations from loved ones, a person reaches a state of utter decay.
Enjoyments consist of the indulgence in sense objects; they are like the hoods of serpents.
When touched even slightly, they bite; when looked upon, they vanish every moment.
The "enjoyments" (bhoga) of hooded serpents are their hoods themselves. He establishes this with the words: "they bite indeed. || 75 ||
Life passes away for those who are devoid of attaining the state free from exertion, through formidable and painful endeavors whose forms are fragile at their conclusion. (76)
For those bound by thirst for the hope of enjoyments, there is humiliation at every step,
like wild elephants tethered to a hitching post.
Of those who have despaired and been emaciated by fasting, eating, drinking, and so forth. || 77 ||
Prosperity and women are as transient as the crests of waves;
what wise man would take delight in them, which are like the shade cast by the hoods of a serpent? (78)
Not only are they transitory, but they also bestow immediate death; thus he says: "like the hood of a serpent. (78)
Truly, sensual pleasures are enchanting; truly, worldly prosperities are delightful.
But life is as fickle as the flickering glance from the corner of an intoxicated woman's eye. (79)
The two words "satya" (truth) and "śabda" (word) indicate acceptance and assertion; the meaning is: "let them indeed be pleasing to the mind. || 79 ||
Those who delight in sense objects that are charming only at first sight fall into hells whose ends are utterly devoid of flavor. 80.

"Āpāta" means the moment of sensory contact or lack of reflection. "They fall" implies that for those addicted to sense objects, demerit (adharma) is inevitable; this is the intended meaning. || 80 ||
Wealth, which is obstructed by the defects of dualities, difficult to acquire, unstable, and fit only for those lacking noble character, has never brought me satisfaction. (81)

He describes the defects of wealth as a means for those [ends] with the words "dvandva" and so forth. At the time of acquisition, they are obstructed by the defects of the pairs of opposites (dvandvas), such as cold and heat, hunger and thirst, and are difficult to achieve.
Even when acquired with great hardship, they are unstable because of destruction caused by kings, thieves, misfortune, negligence, and the like. || 81 ||
Sweet only at the first encounter and ending in suffering, fortune is a momentary plaything intended solely for the delusion of the world. (82)
Pleasurable at first sight but dispersing upon contact,
these associations bring about suffering and misfortune, just like dealings with the wicked.
The phrase "associations with wealth and so forth" refers to connections with the wicked; this should be applied by repeating the comparison as "like friendships. || 83 ||
The splendors of youth are as fleeting as the shadow of autumn clouds; sense-objects are pleasant at first sight but cause torment in the end. (84)
This verse, recited right here in the Kirātārjunīya, should be understood as follows. || 84 ||
The Ender (Death) stands as an obstacle even to the life of the great;
the lifespans of embodied beings fall away like water droplets hanging from the tips of branches. (85)
One who is obsessed is necessarily one who opposes; they waver and stumble. 85.
The hair of one who grows old decays; the teeth of one who grows old decay. Everything wastes away as one grows old; only craving alone does not grow old.
In the entire forest of the body, which is dense with the enjoyment and non-enjoyment of pleasures, the single uneven cluster of craving alone attains supreme blossoming. (87)
Now, he states that one must certainly not harbor the hope, "Having enjoyed pleasures now, I shall attain discernment, dispassion, and so forth in another birth":
"In the forest of the body," meaning even in the entire succession of future bodies. (87)
Childhood passes away like youth, and youth passes away like childhood;
thus, these two share a mutual relationship of both being the standard of comparison and the object of comparison, as well as a shared state of fragility.
With the intention that there is likewise no hope for freedom from craving even in states such as childhood, he says: "Childhood" (verse 88).
Life slips away quickly, like water from cupped hands;
once gone, it does not return, like the current of a river. (89)
To the question "Whence does it go there?", he says: "Life. Life means the lifespan. Of the flowing river. || 89 ||
The body arrives suddenly from somewhere, like the wind of Arjuna;
it sets even as one looks on, like a wave, a cloud, or a lamp. (90)
Whichever body has come into being goes instantly to its end and destruction while one is looking on, due to some cause, like a wave, a cloud, or a lamp-flame. 90.
In delightful things, unloveliness has been seen; in stable things, instability as well;
and in objects that are real, unreality. Therefore, we have become disenchanted with this world.
When the truths have been known as truths, they become tasteless, that is, free from passion. || 91 ||
When the mind has attained the state of pure being (sattva) through rest in the Self, that bliss which arises is not found in the netherworld,
on the surface of the earth, in heaven, nor in any sensory enjoyments whatsoever.
The state of being a sentient being is the state of being free from latent tendencies. || 92 ||
Even though their objects are not entirely delightful, these five functions of the senses still conquer me, just as variegated creepers captivate a bee.

He says "api" (even) to show that now, because my dispassion (*vairāgya*) is firm, even all the functions of the senses (*indriya-vṛtti*), though combined and accompanied by all objects of sense, are not able to conquer me even when acting together. By the particle "tāvat," the sense is that they do not conquer at all. || 93 ||
Today, after a long time, having become free from egoism,
I have attained through my intellect this state of being free from thirst for heaven and liberation.
For the sake of long-lasting, solitary rest, he came here to this region of the sky;
like you, I have arrived here and beheld that hut.
This, however, is the site for the construction of your hut. || 95 ||
Today this has been fully understood by me: that this is your hut, and that you will come here again; this was what I reflected upon there. (96)
The meaning is: "At that time, it was not considered that this hut belongs to you and that you have come to it; all of this has been fully understood today. || 96 ||
