Then, however, I realized here through inference that this was some perfected being (siddha) who, having abandoned his body, had attained liberation (nirvāṇa) by means of his own self. (97)
What, then, was known at that time? To this he says: "At that time" (tadā). || 97 ||
"O Blessed One, this is my life-story; who I am has been told by me to you exactly as it is. Having heard everything, do with it as you see fit. (98)

The meaning is that I have told you all this which was asked by you, beginning with "Where are you situated? and so forth; henceforth, do whatever you deem appropriate—whether punishment or favor—in regard to this offense. || 98 ||

O Sage, it is the very nature of even the minds of Brahmā and the other gods that as long as the remaining reality has not been investigated and determined by the perfected ones (siddhas) of superior intellect through focused attention, they know nothing at all regarding the calculation of the three periods of time.

O Sage, as long as even those such as yourselves, along with the Siddhas, remain intent on concentration and investigate every internal object with the highest intellect, yet do not reach a definitive conclusion, so long you do not possess even the slightest bit of perfect knowledge regarding the comprehension of events spanning the three periods of time. Is this not indeed the very nature of the minds of even the lotus-born Brahmā and others? What more need be said?
"Furthermore, regarding one such as I"—the meaning is: "forgive the offense of my ignorance concerning your history and my failure to offer you hospitality.

Thus ends the ninety-third canto, titled "The Description of the Meeting with the Siddhas in the Pavilion of the Sky," in the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa*, in the *Vālmīki Dīpikā* commentary, in the *Mokṣopāya* section, in the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa*. 93.

Thus ends the ninety-third canto, titled "The Description of the Verses on the Meeting with the Siddhas in the Pavilion of the Sky," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa within the illustrious Vāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa-tātparya-prakāśa.
The ninety-fourth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Now, upon that great ground which was as vast as the golden sky—
Out of friendship alone, I have spoken this to that Siddha.
In the world of the Siddhas, there are two types of vehicles, and the abode of the Piśācas is described as being for the deities, following solely the movement of the mind.
Upon the great earth, which is golden, vast like the sky, and situated beyond the seven continents and oceans;
out of friendliness—that is, from a state of friendship. || 1 ||
Not only by you, but even by me this has not been considered:
that for embodied beings there can be no such thing as being devoid of pervasion. (2)

He says, "By you," to show that this fault of failing to investigate belongs not only to you but is equal for me as well. Regarding that, he says, "Until pervasion," meaning that what you stated—that the perfected ones (*siddhas*) were not intent on focused attention—is indeed true.
For even among embodied beings, that is, yogins who possess bodies, there is "pervasion" (*āvyāpti*) regarding all objects through meditative concentration (*praṇidhāna*).
Cognition devoid of mental pervasion is simply impossible; there can be no awareness of objects past or future [without it]. || 2 ||
Why did I, after deliberating upon your condition, stabilize her in the sky? For had she not been a hut in the firmament, you would have remained in a state of fixed stability. (3)
He says that if it is possible, then that "hut of resolve" should be made firm so that your downfall does not occur; this is the intended meaning of "it must be forgiven. || 3 ||
Arise! Let us dwell as we are among the worlds of the perfected ones;
for those who abide in their own place, the gentle ones possess the excellent means for the realization of their own self.
The sense is that you and I must dwell in our respective abodes—I in the world of the Seven Sages and you in the Nandana grove of old.
To the question "For what purpose? he replies with the words "svāspada" (one's own abode): [it is] for the sake of one's own perfection, which is a state free from distraction. || 4 ||
Having thus resolved, those two, resembling stars,
soared high together from a single nest like stones released from a catapult into the sky.
High into the sky; they were released, having flown up together like two stones from a catapult, launched from a single mechanical device.
Then, having exchanged mutual salutations and taken leave of one another,
he departed for his desired destination, and I too went to my own desired place.
Regarding what they did after flying up into the sky, he says: "With prostrations... He [Nārada] went from the world of the Seven Sages to Nandana, and so forth. || 6 ||
Thus have I related this entire account to you, O Rāghava;
behold the wondrous and diverse nature of the cycles of worldly existence.

Thus, I have related to you the entire account of my own experience, including the story of the stone as it was described, as well as the account of the Siddha. He applies that account to the present context with the words, "consisting of wonders. (7)
Śrī Rāma said:
O Blessed One, this body of yours has become minute upon the earth;
with what body, then, did you wander through the worlds of the Siddhas?

It was stated by you yourself that your gross physical body, while situated in the hut, was cast away by the Siddha; furthermore, it was inferred by you that once discarded, the earthly body would, in time, become dust upon the earth. This being so, how could you—having gone to the worlds of the Siddhas with a body consisting of mind alone—have interacted with the people dwelling there?

He has engaged in worldly dealings (*vyavahṛtavān*). With the intention that one whose self consists of mind alone cannot engage in dealings with others, nor can others engage in dealings with him, Rāma asks: "O Blessed One," etc. "Atomicity" (*aṇutām*) means the state of being like dust (*pāṃsutām*). "You have wandered about" (*saṃcaritavānasi*). || 8 ||
The venerable Vasiṣṭha said:
"I have remembered it; now hear the account of me as I wandered through the dwellings of the world, among the hosts of Siddhas and the cities of the world-protectors."
The particle *ā* indicates recollection; it is the form *āṅ*. 9.
I reached the city of Indra, yet no one there saw me,
for I was devoid of a physical body and possessed only a subtle, transportive form.
O Rāma, at that time I indeed became one whose form was like the sky;
neither a support nor something supported, consisting essentially of the space of consciousness.
He has the form of the sky and is as non-material as space; he consists of that mind which is abundant with the ether of consciousness (cidākāśa). || 11 ||
For those like you who have realized the true nature of reality, there is neither a grasper nor an object to be grasped;
nor is there anything anywhere that can obstruct space or time. (12)
This applies to those like you who understand only gross objects, but not to yogins who perceive subtle realities;
for others, there has been no occurrence of such things as being sent on errands, waiting, or the transposition of space and time. || 12 ||
Consisting solely of the nature of mental ideation, devoid of earth and the other elements, having the form of a person created by volition, it is not an obstruction to objects. || 13 ||
It is non-obstructive because it does not come into contact with objects such as pillars, jars, and the like. || 13 ||
And being himself unobstructed by the flood of objects, yet oriented toward his own direct experience, he engages in worldly activity with such beings who are likewise composed of mind. (14)
One who engages in worldly activity through beings composed of one's own mind, like those in a dream or a kingdom of the imagination.
O Rāma, the experience of dreams is an unassailable illustration in this matter;
let there be enough for you of him who would deny such experience. (15)

"Experiences in dreams" refers to dream-experiences; the meaning here is that, in considering such a possibility, the entire unbroken set of examples should be kept in mind. As for the Naiyāyika, who [asserts] that in all cognition the body is a cause by way of the relation of delimitation (*avacchedakatā*), and that even the contact between the skin and the mind (*tvag-manas-saṃyoga*) is a cause in deep sleep—

He says: "Because in the absence of that [object], the absence of knowledge is established," and so forth—that fool merely prattles; he must certainly not be conversed with by you. He states this with the words "anubhūti" (experience), etc.: there is no purpose for conversation or the like with him. For even in deep sleep (*suṣupti*), since we observe such recollections as "I slept happily," the knowledge of happiness, sleep, and so on exists; thus, by means of dream...

"Having struck down the bodily [self], he, though not sleeping, looks upon those who sleep; taking the pure light, the golden person, the solitary swan, returns to his place"— because of the contradiction with such scriptural passages, and because I experienced suffering through the body cast off due to Nimi’s curse, I have, by the command of Brahmā, assumed this body born of Mitra and Varuṇa in order to prevent that [suffering].
The state of being. || 15 ||
Just as a dream-walker is not seen while transacting business within a house,
so too at that time I was not seen by those situated in the sky, even though I stood right before them.

The meaning is: just as a person who is asleep in a house and wanders about in a dream—a "dream-walker" (svapnacara)—though he is active in his dream, is not seen by others staying in that house; likewise, I too was not seen by the gods situated in the sky. || 16 ||
I see others shining with the forms of kings,
yet no one at all sees me, the subtle transmigrating self.
Śrī Rāma said: "If you are not seen because, being bodiless, your form is like the sky,
then how was it that you were seen by that Siddha in the Golden Forest?"

"‘No one sees me at all’—this contradicts your own statement, for you yourself previously said, ‘I was seen by the Siddha. Furthermore, ‘I see others’ is also inconsistent, because the mind lacks independence regarding external objects and one sees only things composed of one's own mind during a dream. With this intention, Rāma asks: “It is not seen. (18)

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Just as people such as ourselves do not obtain anything that has not been conceived by their own volition, because our bodies consist of the fulfillment of true desires born of that very volition. (19)

Vasiṣṭha refutes both [positions] by means of a system of perception that follows the principle of the realization of true resolve (*satyasaṃkalpa*), stating: "one such as us," etc. This refers to a person like us who has attained perfection through the yoga of knowledge (*jñānayoga*). || 19 ||
By a person whose pure self is immersed in worldly affairs, the subtle body (ātivāhika) of the self is forgotten in an instant. (20)
[Objection: But surely you have stated more than once that for those who have attained knowledge, there is always only the subtle body (*ativāhika-deha*) and not the gross one;
how then is it possible for them to perceive others, engage in social intercourse, and fulfill their true resolves through the notion of a gross body?
To this he replies: "In worldly transactions... This is true; however, such is indeed the case during the time of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and the discernment of truth (*viveka*).
The meaning is that since there is also a forgetting of the subtle body (ātivāhika-bhāva) at the time of waking and worldly activity, the possibility of its conceptualization exists. || 20 ||
At that time, he formed the intention, "May he see me";
therefore, he saw me, becoming the recipient of the object of his own resolve.

Thinking that this perfected one (siddha), being one whose resolve is true, might also be able to see me because he is perfected, [the Lord] distinguishes him [from others] by saying: "one who is the vessel for the objects of his own resolve. || 21 ||
An ordinary person, because of his fragile nature, is not a vessel for the objects of his own volition;
but this [Self], because of its indestructible nature, is a vessel for the fulfillment of true desires.

He states the distinction of the Siddha from other people with the word "jana" (person). Because he is one by whom duality—his own state of non-Brahmanhood—is made firm through long-standing latent impressions (*vāsanā*), and because such a state constitutes "worn-out duality"—meaning that his latent impressions of duality have been sublated—that very Siddha is a fit vessel, worthy of possessing the quality of having true desires. || 22 ||
When two [opponents] are both accomplished—one being established in what is contrary to the other's desire—the victor is the one who possesses superior purity of self and human effort. (23)

But then, where two accomplished beings (*siddha*) form mutually contradictory intentions—such as one intending, "I shall see this person," while the other intends, "May he not see me"—how is the matter settled there? To this, he says:
"Of the two. That intention is stronger which belongs to the one who possesses a greater degree of clarity in self-knowledge (*ātmajñāna*).

The meaning is as follows: just as when two princes strive for the sake of achieving a single kingdom, victory belongs to whichever one possesses a greater degree of valor and other such qualities; however, in the case of equality of strength, the attainment of both [results] will be explained in the section on the non-contradiction between boons and curses. || 23 ||
As I wandered through the cities of the world-protectors amidst the hosts of Siddhas, that nature of my self as a *ativāhika* being was forgotten due to the flood of worldly affairs. (24)

Let it be so; nevertheless, what is the case regarding the subject at hand? To this he says: "While wandering. The connection with the subsequent clause is as follows: when she was forgotten due to the floods of worldly activities (vyavahāraugha), which serve as causes, then she proceeded to engage in those very activities. || 24 ||
Whenever I then began to interact with others in the great sky, no one there perceived me as I moved about restlessly. (25)
O sinless one, even though I cry out incessantly, my voice is not heard by anyone in the worlds of the gods, like that of a man in a dream.
Crying out and shrieking. || 26 ||
For me, who has set out to grasp this [Self] and possesses a body consisting of the mind's reflections, nothing at all succeeds in grasping anything else. (27)

When I am intent on supporting another during occasions such as falling or climbing by giving them a hand or other limb to hold, not even a single hand or limb of mine becomes available for that other person’s support or grasping. || 27 ||
Thus, O descendant of Raghu, I have become a sky-demon;
this strange state of being a demon in a temple of the gods has been experienced by me. (28)
In this manner, he experienced the state of a piśāca in the temples of the gods. || 28 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
"Do piśācas exist in this world? What is their form, what is their abode, what is their lineage, what is their conduct, what are they like, and what is their disposition?"
The incidental inquiry regarding Rāma. || 29 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Hear what kind of piśācas exist in this world;
he who does not speak a word that has arisen in the course of conversation is no gentleman.

"Sabhyah" means worthy of an assembly. If the reading is "satyah," it means one who speaks according to reality; for the apprehension of the truth of a matter occurs through the authority of the listener. Moreover, when the listener has a desire to know a relevant matter, no valid cognition arises from the sentence regarding another matter that was not intended to be known; thus, one whose speech is not worth attending to should be disregarded like a madman. Likewise...
Vācaspatimiśra has said: "A speaker who explains a matter that is intended to be understood becomes one whose words are worthy of attention;
however, explaining what is not intended to be understood, he would be regarded as neither a worldly person nor an investigator, and would be disregarded like a madman. (30)
Certain Piśācas, possessing subtle bodies like the sky and endowed with hands, feet, and other limbs, perceive your form just as you do. || 31 ||
They possess subtle bodies, which are mental bodies; like dreams, they are endowed with hands, feet, and other limbs fashioned by the mind. || 31 ||
By means of their shadow, which elsewhere takes the form of a phantom causing fear, they seize the mind and awaken the disposition of men. (32)

If their bodies consist of nothing but mind, then how do they effect the possession of others? Since the mind lacks the capacity to project itself externally, he says: "by means of a shadow. Those *piśācas* [effect possession] in another person by means of a shadow that is actually a delusion of that person's own mind, and for this very reason, it is capable of instilling various fears.

The meaning is that, having entered by means of a reflection and attained a state of identity, as it were, within that person's mind, [the intellect] awakens his latent tendencies— such as karma, desire, and vāsanās— which result in the experience of suffering, in accordance with various deluded activities and the like. || 32 ||
They quickly kill, devour, and drink [the blood of] people of weak character and strength;
having assailed the mind, they destroy strength, character, and even the very lives [of beings]. (33)

When there exists a store of karma conducive to death, they kill [the victim] themselves and, according to the persistence of their own debts, devour the bodily constituents of that person and drink their blood and so forth; the ellipsis implies that they also exhaust his strength and vital essence. || 33 ||
Some are like the sky, some resemble mist; some have the form of men in a dream, while others, though possessing forms, are of the nature of the Self.

By this, the question "What is their conduct? has been resolved. He answers the two questions "What is their form? and "What is their lineage? with the words "Ākāśa... and so forth. According to their diverse karma, there is a gradation in the subtlety of their bodies, a gradation in their powers such as invisibility, and a variety of forms corresponding to their various latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
And the sense is that there is no remaining [in that state]. || 34 ||
Some resemble fragments of clouds, some have bodies of wind, and some are of the very nature of delusion; all are composed of intellect and mind.

"A fragment of cloud" (abhradalam) means a portion of a cloud. "Consisting of delusion" (bhramātmakāḥ) means, in other words, bodies that follow the illusion of being the person who is to be attacked. || 35 ||
They are not at all fit to be grasped, nor are they able to grasp;
having a nature as empty as space, they perceive their own form.
They see for themselves and experience [it]; and they see one another as well. || 36 ||
They experience pleasure and pain caused by cold, heat, and so forth;
yet they are unable to drink, eat, grasp, or even to will.
Endowed with desire, hatred, fear, anger, greed, and delusion, they are brought under control by mantras, medicinal herbs, austerity, charity, fortitude, and dharma. || 38 ||
To drink external water and the like; to eat and consume food and the like; and to act as one desires, engaging in activities such as giving and taking. || 37 || 38 ||
By means of a machine that subdues beings, or by means of a propitiated mantra, they are sometimes seen or even captured by someone somewhere. (39)

"By what means, then, are they seen by human beings? To this he replied: "By means of a *sattva*. *Sattvāvaṣṭambha* is a specific type of yogic concentration (*yogadhāraṇā*). A *yantra* is a device composed of seed-syllables (*bījākṣara*) conducive to the vision of the [deity's] true form, inscribed on a leaf of silver or other materials, and worn around the neck or elsewhere; by means of that, they are apprehended—that is, brought under control for service and so forth.
They are employed by some person who possesses the science of spirits (bhūtavidyā); the meaning is that this is well-known in a certain region. || 39 ||
For she is of divine origin; therefore, some are like gods, some possess splendor equal to humans, and some have the characteristics of nāgas. || 40 ||

Indicating that even the enjoyment of pleasure exists among them due to the gradations of sovereign powers such as *aṇimā* (minuteness) and others—since they are included within the eleven divisions of divine births—the author elaborates upon the distinctions of their species and forms, beginning with the words "The divine birth, indeed... Those [beings] possess a connection, that is, a similarity, with the *nāgas*, or serpents. || 40 ||
Some, resembling dogs and jackals, dwell in villages and forests;
others live in ditches, rubbish heaps, and streets, as well as in hells.

In hells, in places abounding in suffering, and in impure regions—this is their abode; such are the forms they are proclaimed to have. Piśācas are of such conduct; now hear this concerning their birth. || 41–42 ||
He states "this" (etad) to show that by this [verse], the questions—"of what form are they?", "what is their basis?", and "what is their conduct?"—have been resolved.

As for the question "of what kind are they?", even if it refers to birth, he provides the answer by teaching the reality of the world through its creation and so forth, beginning from its very root, with the words "birth" (janma) and so on. || 42 ||

Brahman, which consists of pure consciousness and is devoid of objects of thought, exists by its own nature as all-powerful; though it is already awakened within, it appears as if it were conceiving of objects of thought.
In that regard, first, understand the soul (jīva) to be the primary sprout of Brahmā as he assumes the state of a living being through the mind characterized by illusion (māyā).

Distinct from that [Brahman] and consisting of consciousness beyond objects of thought, it is the mind that, by conceiving of objects of thought, exists in the form of a sentient being like a person; know that very thing to be the soul, the first sprout.
Know that life-force (jīva) to be matured as what is traditionally called egoism (ahaṃkāra);
that same egoism, when fully developed, is designated as "mind" (manas) by those who have realized the Self. 44.

"Exalted" means strengthened by self-confidence. "By those whose Self has arisen"—that is, manifested—by means of the mental state (*vṛtti*) of the direct realization of reality (*tattva-sākṣātkāra*), for the sake of destroying the darkness of ignorance. || 44 ||
He alone is called Brahmā, whose nature is the space of volition;
he is the non-existent seed of the non-existent world, devoid of form.
That very living being (jīva) in the form of the mind, when considered as a collective whole, is called Brahmā; for this unreal world, the unreal mind alone is the seed.
Thus, though situated in the mind and possessing a body, Brahmā is like the stainless sky;
appearing in the form of a person in a dream, he is always existent yet his body is eternally non-existent.
Devoid of a physical form composed of earth and other elements, he possesses a subtle, transportable body (ātivāhika-deha);
for how indeed could earth and the other elements exist in the sky for a person created by mere volition?
Just as your mind perceives a city imagined in space, so too does it perceive the state of being Manu-Viraj imagined within itself. 48.
Whatever one knows as imagined, that one sees and even experiences as real;
why indeed should he not see that which corresponds exactly to his own measure? (49)

For this very reason, whatever Viriñca perceives through his own volition, he sees and experiences it in the form of that respective object. Whatever individual soul (jīva) is well-known, each and every one of them is indeed that very reality which is of the nature of consciousness; therefore, for what reason would that [consciousness], possessing the power of knowledge, not perceive? || 49 ||
Whatever he perceives is of that same nature: the self is empty, the sky is empty;
it is Brahman in Brahman, or Brahman itself—this is what is called this world.

That Brahmā, whose self is void and whose form is a formless mind, perceives within the sky of consciousness—that which is indeed the void itself—this very universe in the form of a cosmic egg; such is the meaning. || 50 ||
Likewise, at present, his manifestation—having become dense, stable, and nourished through long-term, singular contemplation—remains as beautiful as a very long dream. (51)
Because of his long-standing contemplation of that subtle body (ātivāhika-deha),
even though he is Brahman and of the nature of Brahman, he experiences the manifold creation of Brahmā.
Having attained the state of a physical body through the excellence of its manifestation, that very [state] is called "creation," shining with a continuous succession of distinctions. (53)

That Brahmā, whose self consists solely of Brahman, [remains so] regarding those two—the self consisting solely of Brahman and the world—which are both eternally unborn and identical with that [Brahman]. (54)
The individual soul and the universe are both of the nature of those two. || 54 ||
They dwell in a state of absolute non-differentiation, like emptiness and space,
or like the wind and its movement, existing through their very identity as one.
One perceives that state as consisting of the elements, yet it is entirely false and not real,
just as you perceive a person created by your own volition, whether they exist or do not exist.

He knows that [the world] consists of the elements such as earth and so forth; just as you know that for a person created by your own volition, even though it is non-existent, things such as cities consist of elements, so too [is this]. || 56 ||
Then, by him, the five designations beginning with earth were made for the elements of the body; nourished by consciousness (cit), they remained as that which is called the world. || 57 ||

By that Brahmā, names and designations such as "earth" and so forth were assigned to the constituent elements of his own body, which consists of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) and its solid, liquid, and other portions; these, in their collective form, exist as the world itself.
Just as this very resolve of yours was indeed unreal while that [other] was real,
so too did he experience his own resolve as being truly real.

Just as even that unreal mental construction of yours is experienced by you as truly real because it performs causal functions such as the curiosity of a kingdom of the mind, so too did that Brahmā experience his own mental construction as being truly real.

However, the distinction is this: because he is the collective self (samaṣṭyātman), the causal function arising from his mental construction is common to all people. This is the intended meaning. || 58 ||
He himself is the space of consciousness, and his volition is the sky of consciousness;
therefore, the entire world is a dream, wherein both creation and destruction reside.
He clarifies that very point with the words beginning "sa" (he) and so forth: In ultimate reality, that Brahmā is himself nothing but the space consisting of consciousness (*cinmaya-ākāśa*);
even his volition (*saṃkalpa*) is likewise nothing but the sky of consciousness. || 59 ||
Just as this mind is truth, so too its parts are indeed truth;
likewise, the rays of the moon, Rudra, and the sun are produced from that [truth]. (60)
How then is it that the moon, stars, and so forth produced by that [consciousness] become causes for all purposeful action? To this he says: "Just as...
Those parts of it and its functions are indeed truly capable of purposeful action, such as activity and so forth. (60)
This being so, the web of the world is called its mental kingdom;
and that is empty, without support, a manifestation in consciousness like the appearance of space. (61)
Just as a city in a dream, the sky, and the mountain of one's imagination are like space,
so too are Brahman and the world— space itself, pure and formless.
Thus, for that which is imperishable and shines incessantly as mere appearance,
the perceptions of creation, its middle, and its end have arisen here in vain and remain so.
The notions of birth, persistence, and destruction are merely perceptions of the beginning, middle, and end of creation. || 63 ||
O sinless one, tell me: in you, in me, or even in the world—which is but a small portion of the treasury of space—what could possibly be born or what could perish? (64)

Therefore, he says "What? to show that when one contemplates the nature of the Self as the space of consciousness (cidākāśa), neither for you, nor for me, nor for anyone else do creation and the other cosmic processes exist. The mention of "another person" (puruṣāntara) is intended to highlight that because the world is insentient (jaḍa), there is absolutely no possibility of the notion of birth and so forth. 64.
Tell me, for what purpose have passion, hatred, fear, and the like arisen—purposeless, meaningless, and futile, leading only to misfortune? (65)
In reality, my dear, there is neither creation nor beginning, nor is there non-creation;
this [reality] has always been thus, shining forth eternally as a single unity.

In reality, from the perspective of the ultimate truth (paramārtha), that which is the beginning and cause of creation, which has appeared once and attained manifestation such that it is never again concealed— this ever-fresh form is always that Brahman.
In the sky of consciousness—which is not empty, possesses vast expanse, is filled with the water of pure awareness, yet is turbid with the mud of mental constructs—it will come to be. (67)

Even though such a field of the ether of consciousness (cid-ambare kṣetre) is turbid with the mud of the conceptualization of ignorance, from that very seed of the Self (khātmanaḥ), this multitude of stones in the form of living beings will arise; the connection with the subsequent [verse] is that it was also born in the past. || 67 ||
In the inexhaustible field of the intermediate space, from the seed of the self which is of the nature of the sky,
there arose this vast range of mountain-rocks consisting of all beings.
There is no field here whatsoever that is sown, nor is there anything [that grows];
there is no seed, nor is anything born; yet everything remains established.
Regarding the removal of the mud of conceptualization, he says: "It does not exist. (69)
Those stone rings there that are well-nourished are the gods and others;
those, however, which are brilliant in color are the Buddhas, established in their own state with awakened intellects.

Thus, having explained the principle of creation (*sarga-tattva*) in the context of describing the various classes of *piśācas*, he now demonstrates the different species by way of the divisions of parts and so forth of the "stone" (*śilā*) previously described, in order to conform to the subject at hand— beginning with the words "yā" (those which). Therein,

in that field of the Self (*ātma-kṣetra*) which is fashioned from the mud of mental construction (*kalanā-paṅka*), those circles of stone (*śilā-valaya*) which are nourished and fully grown— those [are the species].
"Classes such as the *vibudhas* (gods) and others" is a general statement. He classifies them specifically with the words beginning "those which... and so forth.
Among them, those which are radiant due to their color and exceeding luster, being of the nature of jewels, are the classes of *buddha-buddhis*, such as the gods, sages, and so on. (70)

Those which are half-cooked become these species such as humans, nagas, and so forth; those which have become solidified and are free from passion (rajas) become worms, stationary beings, and the like.
The stones are half-baked and half-glittering with color; they are hardened yet withered. || 71 ||
But those that are heavy, devoid of fruit, empty in form, decayed and damaged, bodiless yet appearing as if embodied—these are known as piśācas and the like. (72)
"Weighty" means large and burdensome; "useless stones" refers to those devoid of fruits such as luster and radiance.
"Bodiless" means not having the form of a body, while "embodied" means having the form of a body—referring to [ordinary] stones. || 72 ||
For the will of one who intends is never subject to questioning;
such was the will of Viriñca, and thus were they born accordingly.
One might ask: why did Hiraṇyagarbha not form the resolve that only the jewels of the highest gods and so forth should arise in that field?
For what purpose did he instead form the resolve to produce the species of piśācas in the form of useless stones? To this, he says:
"Not indeed" (na hi). The desire of the Creator, the one who forms the resolve, is certainly not to be questioned or challenged.

The sense is that this is because they follow the prior karma and other factors of the individual souls (jīvas) to be created. Those desires of Viriñca arose in such a way, and in that very same manner, the various classes of Piśācas emerged. (73)
All classes of beings indeed consist of the form of consciousness;
they possess subtle bodies and are essentially devoid of earth and the other material elements.

By the poetic conceit (*utprekṣaṇa*) of their being stone, the materiality (*bhautikatva*) that might follow [for them] is precluded; he states this with the words "all indeed" (*sarvā eva*). || 74 ||
By virtue of long-term practice, they attained a consciousness of the material world through prolonged experience, just as one attains the waking state from a dream.
How then is there the experience of materiality in our body? To this he says: "tā" (verse 75).
Likewise, these beings such as Piśācas and others, who are of a similar nature and belong to the realm of living entities (adhibhautika),
remain with contented minds, sporting within their own respective cycles of existence.

The sense is that for those beings who have long practiced and thus attained a physical nature (*ādhibhautikatva*), their minds are satisfied with the enjoyments appropriate to their own species; consequently, even a body of a *piśāca* and its wretched enjoyments are dear to them and do not appear loathsome. || 76 ||
Some look at one another like village women looking at their fellow villagers; these classes of beings appear as if they were inhabitants of a world seen only in a dream.
They see one another and interact through sight and other means, like villagers (*grāmeyakān*).
The suffix *ḍhakañ* added to the word *grāmya* in the sense of the base itself is a Vedic (Chāndasa) usage. || 77 ||
Like a world created by the dream-magical power of many men, some do not see one another, though they are situated in various different forms. || 78 ||
For the most part, it is manifold. || 78 ||
Just as these base-born beings such as pishachas exist in the world, so too do these beings such as kumbhandas, yakshas, and pretas generally exist. (79)

He states that, just like the species of *piśācas*, the species of *kumbhāṇḍas* and others generally possess a *tāmasa* disposition regarding the activities and state of their subtle bodies (*ātivāhika-deha*), by saying: "They abide... (verse 79).
Just as water remains wherever there is a depression here on earth,
so too does darkness remain wherever Piśācas and other such beings dwell.

He states that, just as there is a gradation in the level of water according to the degree of depth, there is a gradation of darkness in those [hells] according to the degree of sin—beginning with "yathā" (as follows). || 80 ||
Even at midday, if a piśāca stands personally in the courtyard,
his very presence creates a profound darkness there.
Regarding the word "there" (tatra), the word "where" (yatra) should be supplied; that is, even if she stands in the courtyard (ajira) under the open sky. || 81 ||
The sun does not strike it down, nor does another perceive it;
he alone experiences it—behold the unfolding of illusion! 82.
The sun does not destroy that darkness; it is merely a demon.
Just as fire, the sun, the moon, and so forth possess a luminous sphere (taijasa-maṇḍala),
so too do piśācas and the like possess a dark sphere (tāmasa-maṇḍala) that is unproduced by external causes.

He says "of fire" (agner) to show that there exists a tamasic sphere, just as the orb of light from fire, the sun, and so forth exists for the sake of illumination for beings such as ourselves, while [there exists] a sphere consisting of the self not produced by fuel and the like for the sake of establishing the worldly activity of beings such as piśācas. || 83 ||
In light, one devoid of vitality proceeds, while in darkness, one whose nature is dominated by vitality does so;
that piśācas and others act like owls is a marvel arising from their very nature. (84)
Lack of vigor is weakness; this is indeed a marvel.
Thus, I have described to you this birth of one born as a Piśāca, consistent with the rules;
for it was in this context that I said, "I am born among the worlds of the guardians of the celestial realms, yet I am equal to a Piśāca. (85)

O Rāma, this birth of yours, who were born into the womb of a *piśāca*, has been declared by me according to your question. It is the tradition of teachers that what is asked at the proper time must necessarily be answered; it is not otherwise. By virtue of that—meaning, because of that tradition—I spoke when you asked in the context of my saying, "I am born like a *piśāca* in the worlds of the guardians of the celestial realm."
The meaning is "being existent. || 85 ||

Thus ends the ninety-fourth canto, titled "The Demonstration of the Identity of the World and Brahman," occurring in the context of the description of the Piśācas, in the *Niśvāsakārikā*, within the *Mokṣopāya* section of the *Śrī-Vāyavīya-Saṃhitā* of the *Ārṣa-Vāyupurāṇa*.

Thus ends the ninety-fourth sarga, titled "The Exposition of the Identity of the World and Brahman in the Context of Describing the Piśāca," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The ninety-fifth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Then, having the body of the space of consciousness and being devoid of the five elements, [he remained].
Dwelling even in the sky, I remained like a piśāca spirit. || 1 ||
Furthermore, his worldly interaction with people through the recollection of his power of true resolve (satyasaṃkalpatā),
as well as his attainment of names such as Ākāśa and Vasiṣṭha in this world, are described here.
Dwelling and wandering about. || 1 ||
Neither the moon, the sun, nor Śakra; nor Hari, Hara, and the others; nor the gods, Siddhas, Gandharvas, Kinnaras, or the hosts of Apsarases see me. (2)
"They do not approach me when I have approached them, nor do they listen to my words;
thus I have fallen into delusion, like a virtuous man who has been sold. (3)

Even though they have been stepped upon, ascended, and sat upon by me through the placing of my feet and so forth, they do not step back against me. Delusion (*moha*) is the failure to connect [the consequences of] one's prior and subsequent actions. (3)
Then I thought: "We here have our desires fulfilled;
let the hosts of gods behold me in that abode of the immortals. || 4 ||

He "thought" (cintitavān) means he remembered (smṛtavān) by means of his thought. "We are these whose desires are true"—this is an enactment of memory. And he "resolved" (saṃkalpitavān)—the word "resolved" being understood—that "let the hosts of gods behold me. || 4 ||
All those inhabitants began to look at me first,
and suddenly the city appeared before them like a tree conjured by magic.

They are called *vāstavya* because they dwell (*vasanti*) in front (*agre*). This is due to the supplementary rule stating that the suffix *tavyat* is added to the root *vas* in the sense of the agent, with the augment *ṇi*.
Then, having attained the status of one fit for social interaction among the abodes of the gods,
I remained conducting myself according to established custom, my actions free from hesitation.
He became one who engages in worldly affairs, being habituated to such activities as conversation and the like. || 6 ||
By those who saw me rising from the sacrificial fire-altar without knowing my history,
I am celebrated in the worlds as Vasiṣṭha, the son of a king.

I was first seen by them appearing in the courtyard on the square ground; they, imagining my origin to be from that very earth, proclaimed me throughout the worlds as "This Vasiṣṭha is born of the earth (pārthiva)," and thus I was brought to fame. The same logic should be applied to the subsequent cases as well. || 7 ||
By those who, traveling through the sky, beheld me in the firmament amidst the rays of the sun,
I am celebrated in the worlds as Vasiṣṭha the Luminous (Taijasa).
By those Siddhas dwelling in the sky who saw me arisen from the wind, I was addressed by the name Vātavasiṣṭha.
When I emerged from the water, those lords of sages who saw me said, "I am Vasiṣṭha of the Waters"; such is the continuity of my birth.
Thus, in this manner, it is solely by means of another's conceptualization that there is for me a continuous succession of births from the earth and other elements. (10)
From that time forward, I became renowned in the world as a king in some places; in others, I was perceived as consisting of water, or as fire, or as wind. (11)
Māruta is one whose body consists of air. || 11 ||
Then, in the course of time, within that very same subtle body (ativāhika-deha), the state of being a physical body (ādhibhautikatā) became firmly established in me, driven by the internal impulse.

In that very subtle body (ativāhika-deha), the state of being material (ādhibhautikatā) has become firmly established and manifested; it is impelled—that is, driven—by the internal mind (manas) which has been cultivated through long-term practice. Alternatively, it is impelled or proclaimed by other perfected beings (siddhas) who have ascended within. || 12 ||
That which is this state of transcendence and that which is the materiality of the body—
both of these, being of one essence within the body, shine forth from my consciousness.

In that case, did you become one whose self was merely the physical body like an ignorant person? No; he says: "This which... Since both of these are indeed the void, the ether (kha), and are thus in reality a single body-self—once this is thoroughly understood through the truth—then my consciousness alone shines forth as the state of the Self, not as the state of a body-self; such is the meaning. || 13 ||
Thus, my self is in some places space; though I am of the nature of light, I am also the sky.
I am indeed the supreme formless reality, yet I appear possessed of form within you.

In some places, I, whose nature is luminosity, appear in the form of the elements such as space (*vyoman*). Thus, the Self is of the singular nature of consciousness, the supreme ether itself, and not of the nature of the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*) and so forth. If it is asked, "How then do you appear to possess form?
he says: "In you" (*yuṣmasu*). The meaning is: for the sake of establishing the worldly transactions of instruction and so forth concerning you. || 14 ||
Acting while liberated in this life, he remains as one whose nature is the ether of Brahman;
likewise, even when liberated after the fall of the body, he persists as nothing but Brahman alone.
In reality, however, there is indeed an identity of form between liberation while embodied and liberation after death; thus he says: "liberated while living" (jīvanmukta). || 15 ||
Even through such conventional usage, my state is not devoid of Brahman-hood, because nothing else of that kind is possible; yet, among you and others, I am indeed "I."
The meaning is that, for the sake of instructing you and others, I have become embodied as Vasiṣṭha. || 16 ||
Just as an ignorant person perceives a dream-man as having birth and a physical form, so too do I perceive this world. (17)

To the question, "How then is the notion of materiality established in a body that is empty? he says: "Just as... regarding the world and other people (or, according to another reading, "other births"). || 17 ||
In this very way, all the self-existent ones (svayaṃbhū) and their creations appear;
yet they are not born, but proceed as if impelled [by a prior cause]. || 18 ||
He states that the bodies of Brahmā and others, as well as the creations produced by them, are likewise merely material from the perspective of another—namely, "in this very way" (evam eva). || 18 ||
I am that very same Vasiṣṭha here in the sky; today, through the practice of my own self, I have attained a state of fullness, or rather, your own state of being.
Your state of being is the state of a physical body that follows your own cognition. || 19 ||
All these are indeed of the nature of space and are self-existent;
for just as this is merely mind, so too are these creations.

He says "ākāśa... [and so forth], meaning that even for me, Hiraṇyagarbha, the world is, from my own perspective, essentially of the nature of the space of Brahman; however, from the perspective of an investigator, this is merely mind (manomātra).
This creation, of which I am the source, has—due to the fault of lack of discernment—attained for you the hardness of a diamond, like a vampire to children. 21.
Of you ignorant people. || 21 ||
But once fully understood, it subsides in a very short time,
due to the thinning of latent impressions, just like affection for a kinsman who has gone far away.
Just as affection for a kinsman who has gone far away subsides with the passage of time, so it is in this case. || 22 ||
Having attained density, the creation likewise subsides,
just as the notion of something to be grasped from the treasury of a dream ceases once it is fully understood.
The density and grossness that constitute the form of egoism are thus pacified; this is the cultivation of the state of being acceptable, the latent impression of what is to be accepted.
All views regarding the visible world subside when they are thoroughly understood,
just as the notions of grasping the water in the current of a mirage-river subside.
By merely perusing this treatise, which is like a great Rāmāyaṇa, this [liberation] is eternally attained; what is difficult in such a small matter? (25)
The word *prāya* means "resembling. This refers to the state of liberation while living (*jīvanmuktatva*) as described above. || 25 ||

If one's intellect is attached to the non-existence of the latent impressions of saṃsāra, that dull-witted person who has no longing for liberation is either a dog, a worm, or a mere human being. (26)

He censures one who is averse to the inner science (adhyātmaśāstra) due to excessive attachment to saṃsāra, beginning with the verse "saṃsāra...": That person whose intellect, by the power of worldly tendencies (saṃsāravāsanā), is attached to that which is non-existent and devoid of real nature—namely, the body, the senses, and objects of enjoyment—and who has no longing for liberation, is like a dog or a worm because of his attachment to impure enjoyments; he is certainly not [a human being].
"Human being": the meaning is that he is unfit for a human body which is suitable for the qualification for knowledge. || 26 ||
This very experience of enjoyment is indeed of one kind when experienced by one whose intellect is liberated while living, and of another kind when experienced by one who indulges in folly. (27)

Just as a single substance, such as food or an oblation like the *puroḍāśa* cake—which is of a pure form—is consumed by gods, twice-born brahmins, and others, while its impure forms, such as leftovers or excrement, are consumed by dogs, insects, and the like; so too, the enjoyment of sound and other objects is experienced by those liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*) as the nature of pure consciousness and bliss, whereas it is experienced by fools as the most impure form of sense-objects. With this intention, he says:

"—Regarding 'enjoyment' (bhogeti): What would the collection of enjoyments—the full experience of worldly objects—be like when experienced by one who possesses the consciousness of a *jīvanmukta* (liberated while living)?

And what would it be like when experienced by a fool, characterized by the habit of 'folly' (*maurkhya*), which is the perception of things otherwise than they truly are? This is the meaning of what should be reflected upon. || 27 ||
Merely by beholding this great scripture, which is like the Rāmāyaṇa,
an inner coolness arises that is like snow toward the interests of others.

Furthermore, he states that there is another distinction: for the ignorant, regarding objects of enjoyment, there arises only the torment characterized by thirst, anger, greed, and so forth—like fire; whereas for those of excellent knowledge who have studied the scriptures, a supreme inner coolness arises toward all objects. Thus he says: "In the Mahārāmāyaṇa... (verse 28).
Liberation is the state of a cool mind; bondage is the state of a tormented mind.
Even regarding this, people have no desire—oh, what delusion is this of the world!
Even though liberation is of such a nature, people have no desire for it; oh, what a wonder! (29)

This person, by nature enslaved by sense objects and mutually greedy for women and wealth, may become happy through the correct perception of reality and through the investigation of the meaning of the scriptures of those seeking liberation. (30)

This person, by nature and by very essence, is brought under the sway of sense-objects; for this very reason, he is greedy for them, even through mutual fighting, theft, plundering, and so forth, for the sake of acquiring women, wealth, and the like. Thus, constantly being scorched by the torments of delusion, he [should turn away from these] through means such as the investigation of the meaning of the scriptures of those seeking liberation and the practice of *nididhyāsana*.
The meaning is that one becomes happy, free from distress, and full of bliss only through the direct perception of things as they truly are, and not by any other means. || 30 ||
Śrī Vālmīki said:
When the sage had thus spoken, the day departed; the sun went to its setting for the performance of the evening rites.
Having offered salutations, the assembly departed to bathe; and at the end of the night, they returned along with the rays of the sun.
Thus ends the ninety-fifth canto, titled "The Description of Vasiṣṭha’s Body," in the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the Uttara-pāda of the glorious Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa, the work of the Sage. 95.
Thus ends the ninety-fifth canto, titled "The Description of Vasiṣṭha’s Body," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The ninety-sixth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
"O you who are skilled in action, this narrative of the stone has been told to you."
By this throbbing vision, these creations are brought forth, abiding in the sky.
The purport of the narrative of the stone is that the world-delusion is a transformation of consciousness;
here it is described that the Self is indeed consciousness, the bliss of Brahman, ageless and immortal.
He applies the story of the stone, which has been described in detail, to the supreme reality: "The story of the stone.

By means of this narrative, one should ascertain that all creations abide in the void—the sky of consciousness (cidākāśa)—through the flashing vision of the fullness of pure consciousness alone. || 1 ||
And yet, nothing whatsoever has ever remained anywhere at any time;
rather, Brahman remains as it is, unbroken within the density of Brahman.
In the nature that is of a single flavor, like a mass of Brahman or a solid block of salt.
Know that Brahman is pure consciousness alone, just as in the visions of dreams;
the city that appears never at any time differs from its own true nature. || 3 ||
He states that the world’s nature as a manifestation (*vivarta*) of pure consciousness is established by the experience of everyone in dreams, saying: "Brahman... [and so forth].

It never differs from nor deviates from its own nature as consciousness. Thus, the meaning is that the definition of *vivarta*—the appearance of another form while not deviating from one's own essential nature—is well-known in the world. || 3 ||
In the attainment of self-existence and likewise in the established state of the visible world,
the unborn space of consciousness remains, never abandoning its own essential nature.
He states that even in the case of creation, the nature of illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) should be understood, as in the phrase "in the attainment of self-existence" (*svayaṃbhūtvasamāpattau*).

"Self-existent" (*svayaṃbhūḥ*) refers to the collective individual soul (*samaṣṭijīva*); "in the attainment" means in its identification with the subtle adjunct (*sūkṣmopādhi*), and in the establishment of the gross objects of perception.
"Unborn" (*aja*) means changeless (*nirvikāra*). || 4 ||
There is no self-existent being, nor is there a world, nor even a city in a dream;
through this great vision of consciousness, all that exists is established as Brahman, which is pure awareness alone.
If the world is an illusory manifestation (vivarta), then what remains from the perspective of ultimate reality? To this he says: "No" (na). || 5 ||
Just as a city exists within one's own dream, abiding in the self as the form of consciousness,
so too does it remain undivided from the beginning of creation until the great dissolution.

He states that the same applies to the illustrative example as well, beginning with "yathā" (just as). The meaning is that just as the nature of indivisible consciousness remains exactly as it is, so too the form of the world—from its initial creation until the great dissolution—remains as that very same [consciousness]. || 6 ||
Just as no distinction whatsoever can exist between gold and a golden stone, or between a dream-city and consciousness, so too there is no distinction between consciousness and its creation.
He states that because all experiences of creation are permeated by consciousness, it is certain that consciousness itself exists in that manner—beginning with the word "hem" (gold).
This is well-known in the case of gold, stone, Mount Meru, and so forth. || 7 ||
There is only consciousness, no creation; there is gold, but no wave of it.
In the mountain of a dream, there is only consciousness, but no mountain-ness whatsoever.
Just as in a dream, that which is essentially pure consciousness appears like a mountain,
so too does the formless Brahman appear as the creation and nothing else.
This space is pure consciousness alone—endless, unborn, and undecaying;
throughout thousands of great kalpas, it neither arises nor ceases.
Space is clear, all-pervading, and untainted. || 10 ||
The person is indeed the space of consciousness; this Lord is the space of consciousness; I am the undecaying space of consciousness; the three worlds are the space of consciousness. 11.
The "Person" (puruṣa) is the living being (jīva). "Your Honor" (bhavān) and so forth are an elaboration of what has been stated. || 11 ||
Apart from the space of consciousness (cidākāśa), the body is merely a corpse;
that space of consciousness is neither to be cut nor to be burned, and it never perishes.
The corpse would indeed be devoid of life. || 12 ||
Therefore, nothing whatsoever dies, nor does anything whatsoever arise; because it is consciousness, the world is experienced as the manifestation of consciousness. (13)
If a living being, who is in truth nothing but pure consciousness, were to die, then his son would undoubtedly die upon the death of the father. (14)
He says "only consciousness" (cinmātra) because there is no proof for its destruction at death; otherwise, every instance of death would entail its [consciousness's] destruction.
The intention is that this follows from the scriptural statement regarding the non-difference of the father’s self from the son: "The self, indeed, is the name of the son. || 14 ||
If, when one living being has died, all others were likewise to die forever, then the entire surface of the earth would become empty of people. || 15 ||

For the Śruti states, "The single Self of beings is indeed established in every being"; thus, [the opponent] raises the objection that if one dies, it would follow that everyone dies. To this, he replies with the words "in one" (*ekasmin*).
Since no moment can be established as not being the locus of some individual death, the expression "at all times" (*sarvadā*) is used. The mention of "the surface of the earth" (*mahītala*)...
It is a secondary characteristic (upalakṣaṇa) for the world alone. || 15 ||
O Rāma, even now pure consciousness has not died for anyone anywhere, nor has the earth remained empty; therefore, the conscious person (cit-puruṣa) is imperishable.
He shows that the logical reasoning culminates in its opposite with the words: "And not... (16).
"I am indeed only pure consciousness; the body and so forth are not mine.
When this truth is thus contemplated, where is there room for birth, death, and the like? (17)
And thus, since the cessation of misfortunes such as birth and death is established through the thorough knowledge of the conscious Self alone, he says:
"One" (verse 17).
"‘I am pure consciousness alone, stainless’—those who destroy this self-experience of their own selves, being slayers of their own souls, sink into the ocean of calamity. (18)

Those who, by means of fallacious reasoning, negate—that is, destroy—the experience of the Self in the form "I am pure consciousness alone" (cinmātramaham), they alone are the slayers of the Self (*ātmahantāraḥ*). The change in word order is Vedic (*chāndasa*); or alternatively, the reading may be *apahatya*. || 18 ||
I am Consciousness, clear as the sky, eternal, infinite, and free from affliction;
what is life to me, or what is death, or pleasure and pain? (19)
"I am the conscious self whose nature is space; what are the body and other such things to me?"—fie on that destroyer of the Self who denies what has been directly experienced! 20.
He who denies with fallacious reasoning that experience which has been inwardly realized by the wise is a destroyer of his own self; fie upon him!
(20) The clear experience "I am the sky of consciousness" is manifest;
he from whom this has vanished is known as a fool—a living corpse. (21)
Those who know the truth recognize as a corpse— even while living— that fool for whom the experience "I am the conscious Self" has come to its end, having vanished.
"I am the self consisting of pure sensation; what are these bodies and senses to me?
Calamities do not overwhelm one who is thus clear and has realized the true self. (22)

Thus, the calamities of death and so forth do not destroy the Puruṣa, who has attained his true self through awakening and is rendered pure by the removal of the impurities of ignorance and the like. || 22 ||
For one who remains steadfast, having taken refuge in the pure Self which is pure consciousness alone,
mental agonies do not pierce him, just as arrows cannot strike a great boulder.
Those who, having forgotten their true nature as consciousness, place their reliance on this wretched body, have in effect abandoned gold and grasped ashes. (24)
In reality, having abandoned the gold, it was taken with the notion that it was ash and gold.
Strength, intellect, and vigor perish through the notion "I am the body," while these very same qualities arise from the firm conviction that "I am consciousness alone. (25)
This very [set] consists of strength, intellect, and so forth. || 25 ||
I am the pure space of consciousness; what deaths and births can there be for me?
This being so, where could greed, delusion, pride, and the like find their foundation? (26)
What would they be based upon? For at that time, they are not based upon the self, in the sense that by such a basis the self would be defiled; this is the meaning. || 26 ||

If one were to obtain some other essence distinct from the body apart from the space of consciousness (cidākāśa), then it would be appropriate to say of him that greed and the like exist; [but since there is no such essence, they do not]. (27)
One should attain and perceive the Self as the essence, distinct from the bodies known as the gross, subtle, and causal; for such a person, [the teaching is intended]—not for the deluded.
"I am not to be cut, nor am I to be burned; I am pure consciousness, as firm as a diamond.
For one who possesses this certainty that "I am not the body," even the Destroyer at the end of time is but a blade of grass.
Death is the bringer of an end. || 28 ||
Oh, how great is the delusion of those with the eye of knowledge, that they are utterly bewildered, thinking "we shall perish" when there is merely the absence of a fragment of a body! (29)
Even among the wise who possess the vision of knowledge, a state of delusion and confusion is observed;

for when the destruction—that is, the absence—of even a single portion of the body, which is but a fragment of the insentient category, occurs, they become bewildered and terrified, thinking "we are perishing"—this is the implied sense. || 29 ||
When the truth that "I am indeed the sky" is firmly established as a reality,
the falls of thunderbolts and the fires of the end of the eon are like heaps of flowers.
"I am not pure consciousness, nor am I immortal; I shall perish," she weeps.
Yet that body of hers has not perished at all; rather, a strange and unprecedented play has arisen.
"I am the immortal, pure consciousness; therefore, I do not perish"—when one weeps thus, one weeps for the Self which is actually imperishable.
From the perspective of the discerning, this is merely a mockery of weeping like that of an actor; it has become nothing but a novel performance of harshness and a game of ridicule. (31)
"I am this consciousness alone; I am not the views of the body and so forth"—he who possesses such certainty within never becomes deluded at any time. (32)
This eternally immediate consciousness, which is pure awareness alone, is indeed my very self.
I am the conscious space; destruction does not apply to me. The world is filled with consciousness; what doubt can there be for you in this matter? (33)
Doubtfulness is the uncertainty regarding birth, death, and so forth. || 33 ||
O you great fools, if you say anything other than "consciousness," then what is it that you are denying regarding your own self? (34)

Regarding the statement "the other two are different from volition" (*cetanā*), would it be spoken by those who possess volition or by those who lack it? Not the first, because those possessing volition—who experience their own volitional nature through direct perception—would be unable to speak in such a manner. Nor the second, because those lacking volition, being insentient (*jaḍa*), could not perceive, express, or deny anything by saying, "We are devoid of volition."
With the intention that it is possible, he says: "conscious" (cetana). || 34 ||
If that consciousness were to die, then people would be dead every day;
tell me, are you not dead, since that consciousness is indeed dead? (35)

Furthermore, if consciousness perceives its own death, then it would perceive it at all times; consequently, everyone who is living would experience death at every moment. To this, he says: "That... (verse 35).
Therefore, nothing whatsoever dies, nor does anything whatsoever live;
the consciousness thinks "I live" and "I am dead," yet it is never destroyed.

With the intention that, since death is thus unestablished, the conceptualization that "life" is its opposite is likewise futile, he says: "Therefore... [The Self] perceives—that is, it experiences delusion; yet it itself never perishes. And so says the Śruti: "For there is no loss of the vision of the Seer, because of its imperishability. (36)
Whatever it thinks, in whatever manner or whatever that may be, it perceives that immediately;
this experience exists even among children, and it never perishes anywhere. (37)
The experience of objects is established for all beings only in accordance with the imperishable consciousness and the sentient mind, and not by way of its opposite; thus he says:
"He perceives the cycle of existence, he perceives liberation;
he knows pleasures and pains, yet he does not differ from his own true nature. (38)

But from its own nature, which is the essence of consciousness, it does not differ even when there is a difference in the object of cognition, nor in difference of place, nor in difference of time. || 38 ||
When its true nature is not fully understood, it itself assumes the name "delusion";
but when its true nature is fully understood, it itself assumes the name "liberation. (39)
In that case, what causes bondage and liberation, or what is their distinction? To this he says: "By not fully knowing," etc. (39).
Nothing ever sets nor does it ever rise;
for everything is indeed pure consciousness, as clear as the sky. (40)
There is nothing that is not true, and there is nothing that is not false;
in whatever manner and by whatever means a thing is determined, it remains established for that person exactly in that way. (41)
And thus, he states that within the forms of the world, truth and falsity are determined according to one's own respective conclusions and are not real:
"That does not exist" (verse 41).
Whatever a conscious being perceives in the world in whatever manner, it experiences that very thing in that same way; this is established by experience.

It is observed that the multitude of objects is seen as either poison or nectar according to one's vision; thus it is well known that there is nothing that does not fall under the sway of consciousness.

Concluding by summarizing the point already stated, he says: "Whatever... The meaning is that it is well known that there is no object whatsoever that does not conform to consciousness—that is, no collection of objects whose diverse causal efficiencies (arthakriyā) are indeterminate, contrary, or fixed according to differences in time, differences in the enjoyer, and differences in auxiliary conditions, just as poison and nectar appear differently through such variations. || 42 ||
Thus ends the ninety-sixth chapter, titled "The Exposition of Immortality," in the *Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa* of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa*, composed by Vālmīki, according to the tradition of the Sages.
Thus ends the ninety-sixth chapter, titled "The Exposition of Immortality," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The Ninety-Seventh Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Because the world is composed of consciousness, it is like a dream of the Supreme Self.
Through the state of being the space of Brahman, everything is experienced as Brahman alone. || 1 ||
Because he possesses all powers, the truth of the arguments of all disputants is described [as being within him];
yet there is attachment to enjoyments for all others, while those who know reality remain rare.

Because Brahman possesses all powers, the arguments of all disputants are true; with this in mind, and for the sake of supporting the point to be stated in the penultimate verse of the section on creation—that "there is nothing which is not real"—the author prepares the ground by stating: "because it consists of consciousness. This refers to the world, which is like a dream, belonging to the Supreme Self.

The meaning is that because everything is Brahman alone by virtue of being the space of Brahman as ultimate reality (*paramārthasatya*), the entire world is experienced by all as nothing but truth; thus it is said that there is nothing whatsoever that is unreal. || 1 ||
Because delusion is extremely visible while the Great Consciousness is invisible, it is logical that the Self is like the power of intoxication; thus, its reality is also established.

If Brahman is real in its form as Brahman, how can it be real in its perceived form? For the snake superimposed upon a rope does not become real simply because the form of the rope is real. To this, he says: "Of the delusion... In that case, both the snake and the rope are objects of perception; since both are perceptible, the snake is unreal because it is sublated when the rope is seen. But here...

The meaning is as follows: since the delusion of the world is visible while its substratum, the Great Consciousness (mahāciti), is invisible, there is a disparity; thus, the conscious Self—like the power of intoxication—is itself invisible yet the cause of the error of the visible, manifesting its own existence only through the form of its effects. Therefore, the reality of this world-form is logical. || 2 ||
Because of the non-existence of sentient beings, because of the resting [of the mind] in the visible, because of the unattainability of the Great Consciousness,
and because of the absence of a perceiver, it is as if called "void," even though it truly exists.

In that case, how can the statement "there is nothing that is not false" be consistent, given that falsity is impossible for Brahman? To this he replies: "Because of non-existence. This means that at the time of bondage, because of the subsistence in the visible world, liberation—characterized by the cessation of all visible objects—is non-existent; that is, it has not been attained. Without that [liberation], [the statement holds].

The meaning is this: because the Great Consciousness (mahācit), which is the non-dual conscious self, cannot be attained even at the time of liberation—due to the sublation and consequent absence of the perceiving subject (pramātṛ), namely the jīva conditioned by the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), as well as the means of perception (pramāṇa) and so forth—it is as easy to speak of its being "void" (śūnyatva) as it is of something that is virtually entirely unestablished, even though it is the supreme reality. || 3 ||
The Puruṣa is pure consciousness alone and is a non-agent; from the Unmanifest, the world arises through their union.
This is true for one who perceives thus, because it is experienced as such in reality.

This being the case, intending to elaborate that the statement of every disputant is indeed true because it sets forth an object established by their own respective experience, he first demonstrates the truth of what was stated by the Sāṃkhya: "Consciousness alone" (*cinmātram*).
This world, being pervaded by the nature of pleasure, pain, and delusion...

From the Unmanifest (*avyakta*), which is the root cause known as *pradhāna* and characterized by the state of equilibrium of the three *guṇas*—the ultimate limit of such a succession of universals—the world emerges and manifests through the sequence of the Great Principle (*mahat*), ego (*ahaṃkāra*), and so forth. The Person (*puruṣa*), however, is pure consciousness and non-agent. For the sake of his experience (*bhoga*) and liberation (*mokṣa*), the process of creation proceeds; one who holds this view [is a Sāṃkhya].
The meaning is that for Kapila, it was likewise true in that very way. || 4 ||
Even for those who maintain that the visible world is an illusory manifestation (vivarta) of Brahman,
their doctrine remains untenable because objects possess such a nature as is experienced through perception.

But as for the Vedāntin who maintains that the world is an illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) of Brahman, his view is also valid; the meaning is that such objects are indeed experienced when one reflects upon them in this manner. || 5 ||
Even the view that the world consists of an aggregate of atoms is not real;
for whatever is perceived in whatever manner, it is experienced exactly as such.

Thus, he states that even the assertion of Kaṇāda, Gautama, the Sautrāntikas, the Vaiśeṣikas, and the Ārhats—that the world consists of a collection of atoms—is indeed true, because it conforms to experience: "paramāṇu... (verse 6).
Just as it is perceived, so indeed is this in this world and in the next;
neither non-existent nor existent—this is the mature, ultimate truth regarding the spiritual path.

Thus, for those who maintain the doctrine of *dṛṣṭasṛṣṭi* (creation upon perception), the world—both in this life and the next—is indeed indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*) and does not reside within either of the two categories of existence or non-existence; the nature of the world is merely a mental construction of the internal self, and even its comprehension is real. This is because they experience it exactly in that way. || 7 ||
Other truth-tellers claim that only the external exists and nothing else;
yet they do not attain that which transcends the collection of senses within their own self. (8)

In this way, those other Cārvākas who assert that only the four external elements—earth and so forth—exist, while no other internal form of a self exists, are also indeed speakers of truth; for, when they search within their own bodies for a self that transcends the collection of sense organs such as the eyes, they do not find it. || 8 ||
The cognition of momentary destruction is indeed logical for those who perceive it due to the incessant observation of error;
for that state is the primordial ground of all power.

Thus, for those who maintain the doctrine of momentariness, the cognition of momentary destruction is indeed logical; the meaning is that all entities, which undergo transformation at every moment, are constantly perceived as subject to change. || 9 ||
For those who know the Dharma, the principle is that "Dharma is like the kalaviṅka bird";
thus, because the Self is established in that way, there is no fault in its existence among the Mlecchas in their own lands. (10)

Just as a sparrow confined within a jar flies out when its opening is uncovered, so too the individual soul (*jīva*), which is a dharma delimited within the body, flies forth to the next world upon the exhaustion of karma; thus, even the Jain conception is true. Likewise, for the Mlecchas such as the Yavanas, the soul is merely the form of the body produced by God.

He remains in the places where the body was buried; then, after a period of time, being touched by the Lord, he is released by His will and is annihilated. Even the conceptualization that he is eternally established in heaven or hell is not faulty, as it follows from his own experience. || 10 ||
Even among brāhmaṇas, fire, poison, nectar, and death, those who know that [reality] appear equal;
for all this shines as the self of all for those who possess such knowledge.
Thus, for those who possess equanimity toward all things and have fixed their gaze upon the reality that is pure existence alone,

they appear as always even and ever-present, despite the fact that poison, nectar, death, birth, and so forth are universally known to be uneven and merely occasional. Since this entire universe is indeed Brahman and has Brahman as its self, therefore there is nothing here [that is not Brahman].
"Difficult to attain" means that even for all proponents [of various doctrines], there is the accomplishment of all their desired goals. || 11 ||

For those who know the truth, it is logical that this [omniscience] is established by its very nature; thus, even when investigated, the status of being the creator of all things does not reach the intellect of the wise.

Thus, the view of the Cārvākas—the proponents of *svabhāva* (inherent nature)—who know this, is indeed logical: that the entire world arises by its own inherent nature alone, perishes by its own inherent nature alone, and there is no creator of the world whatsoever. For while an intelligent creatorship is observed in the case of jars, cloths, and the like, it is not seen in the case of rain, wind, grass, sprouts, and so forth.

Even when thoroughly investigated, it does not reach attainment; for untimely rain, weeds, and the like, which arise from their own nature alone without a creator, do not—though they are undesirable to farmers who produce crops—permit the postulation of a creator. Indeed, there is no one who is the creator of all that is undesirable.
The sense is that the supposition—that there is a need for untimely rain, foreign fields, grass, and so forth—is possible. || 12 ||
"It is true that for those whose minds are absorbed in Him, He alone is the agent everywhere;
he who possesses this certainty attains Him here—this is unassailable. (13)

The conception that there is a single creator for every effect whatsoever, such as the earth, sprouts, and so forth, is also true; for it is observed that among those who possess such certainty and worship the Lord, there occurs purposeful activity (arthakriyā) such as the attainment [of the goal], grace, and the granting of boons.
Thus he says: "He is one. Those whose minds are absorbed in—that is, devoted to—Him, they are the worshippers, because He is thus [for them].

Thereupon, being possessed of certainty, he attains within himself that very object of his worship, the creator of all. For he does not consider Him to be sublated, as one might consider [the perception of] east and so forth [to be sublated by the perception of west]. This is because even untimely rain, weeds in a fertile field, and the like are not established as being undesirable in every respect;
and because there is no fault in the Lord—who bestows the fruits of all actions—acting to bring about the undesirable fruits of evil deeds. || 13 ||
This world and the next exist, as do bathing, fire-offerings, and so forth, and nothing else.
Know that such is the truth for one whose mental cultivation has been fully developed. (14)

For those who believe in the existence of the hereafter, just as this world exists, so too does the next world exist. Therefore, for those seeking the next world, bathing at sacred fords, the agnihotra sacrifice, and other such rites are not fruitless. Such a conviction of theirs, formed through their own contemplation, is indeed true. 14.
"That everything without exception is indeed empty"—this alone is the truth for the Buddhists; for through such investigation, one finds that there is truly nothing whatsoever. (15)

This cultivation [of the view] is also indeed true; for in the case of the doctrine of emptiness (*śūnyavāda*), which is itself devoid of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), it is possible to conceive of the emptiness of the objects of knowledge (*prameya*). This is the intended meaning. || 15 ||
Like a wish-fulfilling gem or a desire-granting tree, consciousness— being of the nature of space within the self— swiftly accomplishes whatever is desired by means of the inner self.
He states the logical justification for the establishment of each respective position desired by all disputants: "Consciousness," etc. (Verse 16).
This is neither empty nor non-empty; for those who know it, it is not a non-entity.
For that power is all-powerful; it does not exist as a [mere] thing.
