In this way, for those who maintain a third category that is distinct from both the empty and the non-empty—namely, the proponents of the "indescribable" (anirvacanīya)—that which they themselves intend as a non-existent unreality is not [ultimately] so. For that indescribable power of illusion (māyā-śakti) belongs to Brahman, who is all-powerful; indeed, it is not that the void exists, nor is it that Brahman, who does exist, is not [Brahman].
The meaning is that it is distinct from both. || 17 ||
Therefore, whatever one is established in as one's own conviction, one necessarily obtains the fruit thereof from that [conviction], provided one does not turn back out of childishness. (18)

The meaning is: if one does not turn back from a previous resolve due to childishness, characterized by distrust, or due to fickleness; or alternatively, if one does not turn back due to childishness, that is, ignorance—then, as long as self-knowledge (*ātmajñāna*) does not exist, those respective doctrines remain true. But when there is self-knowledge, the sense is that the Self alone is real and nothing else. || 18 ||
Having deliberated together with wise scholars upon a subject of supreme importance, the intelligent person should adopt that established conclusion; not otherwise, nor in any other matter. (19)
For this very reason, he states that the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) of anyone whatsoever should not be accepted without investigation: "having investigated" (*vicārya*). || 19 ||
One of supreme wisdom may arise from either the scriptures or from practical experience;
whoever is indeed learned in a particular field, one should rely upon him in that regard. (20)

He describes the characteristics of the most excellent wise man with two verses beginning with "saṃbhavati. From scripture (*śāstrataḥ*), from study (*adhyayanataḥ*), and from conduct (*vyavahārataḥ*, i.e., practice). "In which country" (*yatra deśe*). The word "namely" (*nāma*) is used to indicate his rarity and the difficulty of finding him. || 20 ||
Among the virtuous who may be disputing and who conduct themselves according to the true scriptures, he who is blameless and brings joy to all is the best; one should take refuge in him.
Blameless, he is free from the performance of prohibited acts that deserve censure. || 21 ||
All living beings constantly and by force run toward what is beneficial, just as waters flow downward; having reflected upon this, one should take refuge in that [the beneficial]. 22.

If one asks, "In that case, are all conclusions ending in different certainties merely fruitless? he says, "All indeed... *Śreyaḥ* refers to the desired goal corresponding to each individual's own conviction. They "run" means they attain it.
Having reflected on which among those might be the means for achieving the supreme human goal (*paramapuruṣārtha*), one should take refuge in the true scriptures and the true teacher alone. || 22 ||
For men being carried away by the great waves in the ocean of worldly existence, the days pass unnoticed like drops of water on blades of grass. (23)

With the intention that one should rely on those two quickly and not delay—since there is no basis for placing trust in life—he says: "By waves," etc. By "waves" (kallolaiḥ) is meant the ripples of a succession of desires; they are "unnoticed" (ajñātāḥ), meaning unperceived, like drops clinging to the tips of blades of grass. || 23 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
Even you, O Lord of the world, have come to rest in that expansive state;
through the investigation of what precedes and follows, who are those who perceive the absence of anything else?
Because of the intensity of thirst for enjoyments, those who are detached from them and seek liberation are themselves rare;
even among them, those who have realized the reality of the Supreme Self and possess the characteristics described by you—the best of the wise—are exceedingly rare.
Desiring to hear this very point in detail, Rāma asks: "The world... in the verse beginning with *vitate pade*.

The implication is that the thirst for enjoyment among living beings has come to rest in the vast expanse of the Brahma-ether, having first spread out like a network of thousands of world-trees. This being so, when one reflects upon the essential and non-essential nature of existence through an investigation into the true character of the worlds—both past and future—who are those "supreme scholars" mentioned by you, who see that ultimate reality (*paramārtha*)? Who are they other than yourself?
Or they may exist; the meaning is that they are exceedingly difficult to find. || 24 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: In every birth, only a few become truly distinguished— those whose days pass in radiance like those of the suns.

It is true that they are very difficult to find; nevertheless, since they do indeed exist among the various classes of beings—gods, asuras, humans, gandharvas, and so forth—they must be sought with effort. To this, the following answer is given: "In every birth," and so on. This refers to those designated by such scriptural passages as: "Whosoever among the gods awakened to this, he alone became That; likewise among the seers (ṛṣis), and likewise among humans. Etc.
They indeed come into being; they truly arise. || 25 ||
Running upward and downward through the revolutions and whirlpools of the cycle of existence,
all these deluded ones are carried away like blades of grass in the ocean of birth born of ignorance.
But all others, being deluded, are carried away like straws in the great ocean of ignorance by the waves of craving for sensual enjoyments. || 26 ||
Their own stability destroyed, the gods in heaven burn intensely amidst the fires of their enjoyments, like trees on a mountain being consumed by a forest fire.

He elaborates upon that very point regarding the various classes of beings, such as gods and others, with the verse beginning "naṣṭātmasthitayaḥ" and so forth. By "davena" is meant by the forest fire. || 27 ||
The Dānavas, filled with intoxication, were cast down by the enemies of the Dānavas into the terrible pit of Nārāyaṇa, like elephants deprived of their tethering posts.
The gods, with their showers of weapons, cast the Dānavas into a great pit, a deep abyss characterized by Nārāyaṇa. || 28 ||
Even the Gandharvas do not perceive the fragrance born of solitude;
their minds are intent on song and drink, and they wander like deer.

Even a mere trace of scent; that which is characterized as song, like wine when drunk, brings about being seized by others—the six internal enemies (ari-ṣaḍvarga)—who are thus "seizers" (parāmarśāḥ). Like deer, they hasten toward and enter the presence of the hunter Death.
And the Vidyādharas, deluded by their status as the repositories of sciences, show no respect even for those who have manifested noble [powers]. (30)

Because even the knowledge of Brahman is a form of knowledge, they do not show respect for the noble discernments that flash forth by the power of its fitness; the meaning is that they take delight only in those knowledges which are means to enjoyment. || 30 ||
The Yakṣas, who have shaken the earth, display their unimpaired dexterity toward those who are helpless— children, the elderly, and the sick— as if they were invincible.

Those by whom the earth has been agitated through the production of defects such as fear, fever, and madness, yet who consider their own bodies to be firm— as if they themselves were unharmed— display their own invulnerability toward children and others who are helpless, solitary, and devoid of the power of jewels, mantras, and the like. || 31 ||
Like intoxicated elephants pursued by the swift lion,
you shall bring about the destruction of the Rākṣasas, just as he has done.

However, the destruction of the Rākṣasas—who were intoxicated by the power of their desires, strength, and valor like elephants—was previously accomplished many times by Hari, who acted as their enemy in the form of a lion, namely Viṣṇu; and you shall do so again in the future.
Thus, he states that the fruit of their negligence is evident before their very eyes: "Of the elephants," etc. (Verse 32).
The piśācas see [him] intensely with the thought of devouring living beings,
like oblations seen by the flame through smoke, darkness, and wind.

However, because Piśācas are always afflicted by hunger, their thoughts are constantly occupied with the killing of living beings for food; thus, there is never any occasion for the application of discernment.
This is stated in the verse beginning with "piśācāḥ.
[The text continues: by that which, like a wind, produces the state of flames such as anger and violence within the smoke-and-darkness of ignorance...

The meaning is that, due to their constant preoccupation with eating living beings, the Piśācas see themselves as being perpetually consumed by smoke and flames, just as oblations fallen into a fire see themselves being scorched by the smoke and flame. || 33 ||
The lotus stalks of the Nāgajāla lake were submerged in the surface of the earth,
standing there as if they were the roots of mountains or as if they were utterly inert.

Thus, he says "the lineage of nāgas" to show that even among the species of nāgas, solitude is difficult to find: on the surface of the earth—that is, in the netherworld (pātāla)—they remain like the roots of trees (naga), inert, insentient, and devoid of discernment. || 34 ||
What talk can there be of solitude for those young asuras, who, like insects on the surface of the earth, have only a hole as their refuge? (35)
For the sake of even a tiny grain of rice, people generally wander day and night like ants;
indeed, human beings are for the most part of the same nature as ants.

With the intention of showing that if even those beings from the gods down to the asuras—who are endowed with such strength, vigor, power, and so forth—find it difficult to attain discernment (*viveka*), what need is there to mention others, he says "even by a mere trifle," and so on. "Persons" (*puruṣāḥ*) refers to human beings. (36)
For all living beings who are distracted by futile and long-winded pursuits,
their days pass away like those of drunkards, due to their wicked desires.
Pure discernment does not touch any person within, just as dust does not touch one who has fallen and is sinking in fathomless water. (38)
Just as dry dust does not touch the mud sinking in water, so it is in this case. || 38 ||
Men shaken by their restrictive vows are led away by the life-forces of men,
like heaps of pomegranate seeds purified by being parched in a frying pan.

Pride (*māna*) is the conceit regarding the body and so forth; by means of the winds characterized by that [pride], those who have been shaken—that is, moved away—from the restraints such as non-anger, are led into subjection to anger and the like. Just as heaps of chaff, blown up in threshing floors by farmers using winnowing baskets (*śūrpa*) that cause them to tremble, are tossed about for the sake of achieving the separation of the grain.
The meaning is that they are carried away by the winds like a collection of what appears to be pithless grain. || 39 ||
In the dense mire of drink and food, the hosts of yoginīs have fallen like common folk into a foul-smelling puddle. (40)

They have fallen into such a mire—a morass characterized by the drinking of wine and blood and the eating of meat—where there is the emission of a foul-smelling pool characterized by attachment to the enjoyment of the fruits of tamasic dharmas; that is to say, through lack of discrimination.
Only Yama, Candra, Indra, Rudra, Arka, Varuṇa, Anila, Jīvanmukta, Hari, Brahmā, Guru, Śukra, Anala, and others [are such]. (41)

Having thus elaborated upon the difficulty of attaining discriminative knowledge among the various classes of beings such as gods and others, he points out a few who are awakened among them, as if enumerating them, with the verse beginning "Only," and so forth. || 41 ||
The Prajāpatis, the Seven Sages, Dakṣa and others, Kaśyapa and others, Nārada and others, Kumāra and others, and the sons of the gods beginning with Sanaka; || 42 ||
Among the Dānavas were Hiraṇyākṣa, Bali, Prahrāda, Śambara, Maya, Vṛtra, Andhaka, Muci, Keśin, Putramura, and others. || 43 ||
Among the Rākṣasas were Vibhīṣaṇa and others, as well as Prahasta, Indrajit, and the rest;
among the serpents were Śeṣa, Takṣaka, Karkoṭa, Mahāpadma, and the others.
Among the snakes, among the *nāgas*. || 44 ||
Residing in the worlds of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Indra are those who have cast off their bodies,
as well as some who are liberated by nature, the Tuṣitas, the Siddhas, and the Sādhyas.

Those who dwell [there] are the *vāstavyas*. Those whose bodies have been cast off are the *jīvanmuktas* (liberated while living). The Tuṣitas and others are specific classes of divine beings (*devayoni*), but not all [beings]. || 45 ||
Among human beings, O scion of Raghu, kings, sages, and the most excellent brahmins who are liberated while living are indeed rare.
All beings are numerous in all directions, yet those endowed with awakening are rare;
indeed, while trees abound with clusters of fruits and foliage, wish-fulfilling trees (kalpavṛkṣas) are truly rare.
Likewise, although there are those liberated while living (jīvanmuktas) among all classes of beings, they are rare—this he establishes by means of this illustration:
"Beings"—this is clear. || 47 ||

Thus ends the ninety-seventh canto, titled "The Description of the Rarity of the Discerning," in the Nirvāṇa Section of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Valmīki, belonging to the Holy Tradition (*Ārṣa*).
Thus ends the ninety-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Rarity of the Discerning," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa within the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The ninety-eighth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Those who possess discernment, those who are dispassionate, and those who have found rest in the supreme state—
For them, the enemies such as greed, delusion, and the rest become attenuated.
The characteristics of the virtuous who know reality are described here;
having examined them and disregarded their faults, one should take refuge in them.

"Tanutva" means smallness or scarcity. Thus, the sense is: if even the mere scarcity of defects such as greed constitutes that characteristic, then what need is there to mention being entirely free from defects? || 1 ||
They do not rejoice, they do not become angry, they neither enter [into worldly affairs] nor seize anything;
they are not agitated by the world, nor do they cause agitation to the world.
They do not enter into any object, nor do they become attached to them; thus, they neither take up nor grasp any category of objects of enjoyment.
Neither from atheism nor from dogmatic faith were the Vedic practitioners of rigorous observances;
rather, they were of pleasing and sweet conduct, speaking with kindness and charm. (3)

Likewise, regarding actions pertaining to the next world as well, he says "no" to the idea that one should undergo suffering through stubbornness like a dry Vedic scholar, even when those actions do not entail extreme physical hardship. The meaning is: from the stubbornness prompted by the conceit of identifying with either of those two states—namely, an *āstika*, who holds the view that the next world exists, or a *nāstika*, who holds the view that it does not.
Like the rays of the moon, they gladden the hearts of those who associate with them;
they are discerners of affairs and reach a decision even in an instant. (4)

In the crisis of performing duties—both worldly and Vedic actions that ought to be done—which are fraught with mutual contradictions, they are the ones who distinguish between what should and should not be done, and who resolve doubts. || 4 ||
Their conduct causes no agitation, like that of kinsmen or citizens;
they maintain all outward social conventions while remaining inwardly indifferent toward all worldly objects.
The citizens were clever; they shared a common conduct that was equal for all.

They are connoisseurs of the meaning of the scriptures, knowers of those [scriptures], and have understood the higher and lower worlds; they discern what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, and they pursue their goals as they arise.
Those connoisseurs who have desisted from contrary actions abide in the state of the virtuous,
enjoying the happiness of others' stations through their unobstructed fragrance.
Regarding the conduct of the virtuous: "unveiling" means the opening of the treasury of the heart through instruction;

[the connection with the following verse is as follows: they honor the petitioner who has arrived with other "abodes"—meaning sources of support—consisting of the fragrances of the arising of knowledge produced thereby, and with "pleasures," meaning food and sustenance. || 7 ||
Like full-blown lotuses honoring a guest who has arrived, they— removers of the afflictions of the people— honor the seeker and win over the multitude.
In the case of the word *padma*, the phrase beginning with "unobstructed" (*anāvaraṇa*) is clear. They "attract" means they bring [beings] under their influence through their qualities. || 8 ||
Affectionate like clouds in the rainy season resting upon cool places,
the wise [kings] bring about the downfall of mountains and cause the agitation that leads to the ruin of nations.

Just as cool places such as gardens and the like are refreshing, so too do [these ascetics], being affectionate toward kings, restrain— by means of the power of their austerities, the performance of virtuous deeds, and the methods of conciliation (sāma)— the agitation of the people caused by famine, pestilence, foreign invasions, and the like, which brings about the ruin of rulers and the destruction of the country; they hold it back and prevent it by firmly obstructing it.
The positive concomitance is by means of another [instance]. || 9 ||
They restrain the agitation that has arisen, just as mountains withstand an earthquake;
they encourage one in times of adversity and bring comfort in times of prosperity.
With forms resembling the lunar orb, they were like wives who are mines of virtue;
their fame perfumed the quarters with its flowers, and they were the causes for future excellent fruit.

With the qualifying attributes such as "fame" and so forth, he poetically conceives the virtuous ones as the spring season, just as a devoted wife possesses the qualities of beauty, sweetness, love, and the like. || 11 ||
Like virtuous men who possess the melodious warbling of male cuckoos,
they [overcome] the ocean of delusion, which abounds with waves and whirlpools and is the abode of sea-monsters.
The *mādhavas* are the spring seasons. Words such as "billowing" (*kallola*) and so forth are adjectives qualifying the great ocean of another's mind. || 12 ||
Like the rolling winter season, it churns the abode of people;
the great ocean of another's mind is restless with the agitation of its waves.

It was agitating the lotus groves—which, like the human settlements of the countryside, were inhabited by bees, swans, and other creatures—as if it were the winter season itself rolling through them under the guise of waves tossed by an exceedingly cold breeze;

and it was likewise agitating the human settlements, which were the abodes of people, while its waves—the six worldly afflictions—were as fickle due to their turbulence and deluded by the well-known greed, hatred, and so forth. (The particle *ca* is used in the sense of "also.")

They are capable of restraining even such a great ocean of the minds of others, such as kings and the like, through conciliation, gifts, and other means, as well as through instructions on discernment. || 13 ||
And the virtuous mountains, standing on the shore, are able to restrain that [flood] during calamities, the loss of intellect, and amidst turbulent waves. (14)

"Standing on the bank" means remaining indifferent while staying near the shore. "Good mountains" is a metaphorical expression (*rūpaka*) and not a comparative compound (*upamita-samāsa*), because common attributes are explicitly employed. For this very reason, when calamities and the like befall the virtuous—those who possess discernment—the virtuous alone are their refuge, even amidst the turbulent waves characterized by the six surges: hunger, thirst, grief, delusion, old age, and death.
And also in places such as mountain clefts [the reading is *deśaviḍvarāhādiṣu*]. || 14 ||
In times of distress and calamities, the virtuous alone are the refuge of the good;
having recognized those of noble disposition by these and other signs, [one should honor them]. (15)
Now, regarding these [factors] just mentioned: the words "atha" (then) and "ca" (and) signify conjunction; [they refer to] these as well as others previously mentioned. || 15 ||
One who is weary from traveling the path of saṃsāra should resort to this for the sake of singular rest, because this serpent-ocean of saṃsāra is exceedingly treacherous. (16)
For the sake of resting in the one, non-dual Brahman; "the ocean of serpents" refers to the ocean that is terrifying with its serpents. || 16 ||
Without the company of the virtuous, it cannot be crossed by any other means;
let alone my own deliberation—whatever may happen, let that be mine. (17)
Thus, having encountered impurity within, one should not remain like a worm in a pit;
rather, one should abandon everything else for the sake of that single virtue which exists in another. (18)

"Kalka" means negligence. The syntactical connection with the following is as follows: even if only one of the aforementioned qualities exists in someone, one should, for that person's sake alone, set aside all other activities and take refuge [in them] in such a way that other faults are disregarded. || 18 ||
Disregarding other faults, one should rely on that [teacher] alone for the sake of discerning virtues and defects through one's own effort from childhood onwards. (19)

One should first develop one's intellect through the company of the virtuous and the study of scriptures as they become available; disregarding even the slightest trace of fault, one should constantly serve the good.
One should gradually and sequentially abandon gross defects that prevent liberation;
for even the beautiful becomes unlovely, and the stable becomes unstable.
One should gradually avoid—that is, abandon—a former retinue whose faults are gross and who has not attained liberation.

To state what the faults would be if one does not avoid them, he says: "It goes," and so forth. Even a mind that has been purified and made beautiful returns to ugliness, which is to say, it becomes defiled by passion and other afflictions. Even a blissful state of rest, though stable, becomes unstable due to interruption. || 21 ||
As it has been seen, I believe that a virtuous person may fall into wickedness;
this is indeed a most extreme calamity, when one who is virtuous turns toward evil.

If it is asked, "From where do you derive this conviction? he says, "Because it is seen so in the world," introducing the word "yathā" (just as). If it is granted that this is so, he asks, "What fault follows from that? and replies with the word "eṣaḥ" (this): an "utpāta" (portent) is an indicator of misfortune for the world. || 22 ||
Due to the influence of place and time, even great portents may be seen because of sins;
therefore, abandoning all other activities, one should seek the company of the virtuous.
This practice is free from obstacles and is the means for accomplishing the welfare of both worlds.

It is seen through the sins and misfortunes of people; for example, Viśvāmitra’s engagement in seizing Vasiṣṭha’s wish-fulfilling cow due to association with wicked ministers and others, and how, through the increase of mutual enmity, there arose a great deal of world-wide calamity ending in a battle between two cranes. Thus...

The meaning is that even the activity of Kaśyapa, Viśravas, and others in producing Daityas, Rākṣasas, and so forth— causes of misfortune for the world— through union with their wives, appears like well-known great portents such as comets, due to the influence of place and time.
Having restated what was said, he concludes with the verse beginning "All" (sarva). || 23 ||
One should never be far from a virtuous person; endowed with humility, one should serve the holy.
For the pollen of the flowers clinging to them, which causes [the senses] to bloom, touches those who are near them without even an effort.

And that association with the virtuous should not be interrupted until the attainment of the firm establishment of knowledge through the process of acquiring qualities; thus he says: "Not [so]. At no time whatsoever should one remain far removed from the virtuous teacher (*guru*);
endowed with the practice of humility, service, and so forth, one should always attend upon him. To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "They touch," referring to those [virtues].

By merely approaching the virtuous, the pollen-grains of their qualities—characterized by tranquility, self-restraint, and so forth—which spread effortlessly, touch one like sesame seeds infused with fragrance; that is to say, they necessarily transfer to them. || 24 ||
Thus ends the ninety-eighth chapter, titled "Praise of Association with the Virtuous," in the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the glorious Vāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa of Valmīki, composed by the Sage. 98.
Thus ends the ninety-eighth chapter, titled "Praise of Association with the Virtuous," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa within the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The ninety-ninth canto.
Śrī Rāma said:
"We possess the means for the destruction of our suffering—namely, the scriptures, the company of the virtuous, and reasoned inquiry."
They take refuge in mantras, medicinal herbs, asceticism, charity, sacred fords, merit, and hermitages. || 1 ||
Whatever kind of experience belongs to worms, insects, moths, and those born as animals or stationary beings within saṃsāra— all that is described here.

For extremely dull-witted creatures such as worms, insects, and moths, who lack any means to alleviate their immediate suffering, even mere survival is difficult to attain; moreover, they are incapable of knowing the means [to do so]. Being thus situated, Rama—desiring to understand the nature of their cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) and how they continue to live despite this—questions him regarding the persistence of their birth.

By the words "they exist" and so forth: for us, who belong to the human species, there exist means such as the scriptures for the destruction of suffering pertaining to this world and the next. But as for those such as worms and the like, how is their destruction of suffering [achieved], by what means, and in the absence of such [means], how do they remain and live? This is the logical connection. || 1 ||
How do worms, insects, moths, and other species of animals and stationary beings exist, what are their activities, and how can there be an end to their suffering? (2)
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: All beings here, both stationary and moving, are fully established and at rest within their own appropriate mode of existence.

In a state of existence characterized by pleasure that is appropriate for themselves and suited to their respective enjoyments; thus, even a mere fragment of the pleasure derived from objects to be enjoyed within their particular wombs appears to them as if it were the supreme human goal (*puruṣārtha*). The meaning is that, resting content with only that much, they live enduring even greater sufferings solely out of attachment to that [state]. || 3 ||
Even for beings as minute as atoms, desires are just like ours;
however, we are of little consequence as obstacles, while they are like mountains.

The implication is that there exist desires for the enjoyment of pleasures appropriate to one's own respective source; however, we have little interest in those enjoyments and face few obstacles. [In contrast, others face] great and numerous obstacles, resembling mountains in their immovability. || 4 ||
Just as Virāṭ exerts himself, so too do the Vālakhilyas in the sky;
behold the expansion of egoism even within a body as small as a child’s fist.

If it is asked how it is known that they have great attachment to enjoyments, the intention is to say: "From the sign of excessive effort," and thus he says, "Just as... Just as the individual soul (jīva), whose body is the cosmic egg (virāṭ), exerts itself for its own enjoyment through efforts to fulfill its own office, so too do those whose bodies are commensurate with the tips—the extremities—of the hairs of children.
Even worms, insects, mosquitoes, bedbugs, and the like likewise strive for their own space in the sky, even though their bodies are small compared to the opening of a child’s fist. || 5 ||
Birds are born and die in the supportless sky;
their sole domain is the void, and for them there is not a moment of true well-being.
"Khagāḥ" refers to the birds previously mentioned, namely those that fly in the sky. "Svāsthyam" means steadiness; that is to say, the cessation of effort. || 6 ||
Just as even a moment equal to our day is not sufficient for an ant, due to its activities such as seeking food, shelter, and kin; || 7 ||

With the intention that even from observing the great effort of ants and other creatures in gathering grains and the like, one can infer their great attachment to enjoyment, he says: "Of the ant. By the words *grāsa* (morsel) and *āvāsa* (dwelling), the efforts to procure them are indicated; and by the word *ātmabandhu* (one's own kinsman), the effort to nourish a family is indicated.

Even a period of time equal to our day is long for them; it is not sufficient, nor adequate, even for a moment, for their exertion in the acquisition of grain and so forth—this is the meaning. || 7 ||
A creature the size of a mote of dust, known as a *kṛmi-aṇu* or *timī*,
exhibits a restlessness in its movement comparable to that of Garuḍa.
There exists an extremely minute worm called *timi*.

Just as the world appears extensively to men through the conceptualization of imagined constructs such as "this is I" and "that is mine," so too does it appear to a worm through its own elevated qualities.

He states that the superimposition (adhyāsa) characterized by "I-ness" and "mine-ness" regarding the body and its objects of enjoyment is common to both humans and worms—expressing this with the words "This... [and so on].
Just as [the body] is expansive due to high qualities—that is, an abundance of excellence—and is fit for the application of great effort, so too is it for the worm. || 9 ||
Wasted away by the distractions of place, time, action, and material things, our life perishes like that of worms in a wound. (10)
He says—beginning with "deśa"—that the useless waste of life due to attachment to sense-objects is common to both us and even insects. || 10 ||
The trees are slightly awakening, while the stones remain in deep sleep;
even worms, insects, and the like experience dreaming and waking just as humans do.

"Slightly awakened" means being somewhat wakeful. They are called "awakened-in-dream" (svapnabodhin) because they possess both sleep and waking regarding their respective appropriate objects of experience and activity. || 11 ||
For them, the destruction of the body is currently a source of happiness, whereas for us, it would be a cause of suffering; yet for them, that very life is experienced as happiness.

For these worms, insects, and plants who are currently existing happily during the period of their bodies, it is only the destruction of the body that causes suffering, just as it is for us; their "life" consists merely in the persistence of the vital breaths within the body. (12)
Just as a person who has been sold to another island perceives the multitude of objects there, so too do beasts, deer, and other animals perceive the world of objects. 13.
He explains how they perceive our enjoyments—houses, palaces, wealth, jewels, and so forth—with the word "jana" (people).
The meaning is that they look upon the entire range of objects to be enjoyed by us with indifference and a clouded vision. || 13 ||
For animals, cyclic existence bestows pleasure and pain just as it does for us; they are distinguished from us only by their lack of discernment regarding the nature of things. (14)
By means of the classification of qualities, actions, utilities, and so forth, which serve as the causes for the cognition of the excellence, inferiority, and other attributes of things. || 14 ||
From the heart by means of pleasure and pain, and from the nose by means of the rope's tether, even commoners who have been sold are dragged about like cattle. (15)

He establishes the similarity between cattle and those who have been sold with the words "from the heart" (*hṛdayāt*). For cattle, such as oxen and the like, are pulled inward from the heart—that is, from the mind—by pleasure and pain;
and they are pulled outward from the nose—that is, from the region of the nostrils—by the master using the cords of the halter. Thus, in both ways...

The meaning is that there is a similarity between these two: even when dragged about by the power of others, those who have been sold in another land—like common laborers—are unable to avoid even the slightest of their own suffering, nor can they report it. || 15 ||
Just as we experience sensation when asleep, though our skin is clearly intact, so too do trees, shrubs, sprouts, and the like experience intense sensation. (16)
He also establishes the manner in which trees and other beings experience pleasure and pain in accordance with our own experience:
"For us, whose minds are overcome by sleep and who are tormented by excessive cold, heat, mosquitoes, bugs, and the like, [the state] during pleasant sleep is such as follows..."

The meaning is that it is an unrestrained sensation of suffering of such a kind. The mention of the "sprout" is for the purpose of highlighting the extreme intensity of the pain when one is bitten by worms, insects, and the like, due to its extreme delicacy. || 16 ||
Just as our cognition of objects is deluded for us who have fallen into this cycle of existence characterized by the sequence of desires, so too is that of animals, though it may appear unclouded.

He brings even that which was stated regarding the cognition of animals—which is devoid of the discrimination of objects—into the realm of experience through a supporting argument, beginning with the words "yādṛg" (of such a kind). "Īti" refers to the state of fleeing due to disturbances in the region;

for the sake of that, there is the cycle of saṃsāra consisting of running and other movements, as well as the sequential process of treading upon kusa grass, thorns, and hot sand, and the carrying of burdens.

The meaning is that for us, who are subject to falling, there is at all times a perception of objects characterized by fear and apprehension from every side, just as there is for birds, snakes, and other animals. || 17 ||
In the mere experience of delight, there is equanimity between Indra and a worm by virtue of their happiness;
this state is free from conceptual construction, whereas conceptual construction is nothing other than transgression.

If one is liberated from conceptual constructions and the experiences of distraction, then there is a similarity in the mildness— characterized by mental clarity— of both Indra and a worm regarding the mere joy that is common to all, namely the bliss of one's own nature, as well as the pleasures of food, sleep, and sexual union. However, for both of them, conceptual construction is indeed distraction, and it is difficult to transcend.
This is the meaning. || 18 ||
The pleasure and pain arising from passion, hatred, fear, food, and sexual union, as well as the suffering of birth, death, and so forth for animals, do not differ in any way. (19)
The remainder [of the phrase] is "it is known even among animals" (tiraścām indrasya ceti). It is not divided; it is not distinguished. || 19 ||
Apart from the understanding of objects that exist as actual entities and of things yet to come,
the rest [of their cognition] is equal to that of humans, such as mongooses, snakes, jackals, elephants, and so forth.
Objects of knowledge accessible through the scriptures include merit, demerit, the reality of Brahman, and so forth; past objects are those things that have already occurred;

and future entities are things such as the fruits of upcoming agricultural labor. Apart from the understanding of these—that is, excluding the knowledge of these—whatever remains of knowledge belongs to the mongoose (*babhru*), the mongoose (*nakula*), the serpent (*ahi*), the jackal (*gomāyu*), the elephant, and others.
The meaning is that all those [beings] are cattle, equal to men. || 20 ||
While the mountains and other beings remain experiencing their own existence, they perceive the trees as if they were composed of sleep;
yet others experience the undivided space of consciousness.

To the question of how mountains and the like experience [this], he says: "Sleep. Other [beings], such as mountains and stones, remain experiencing their own existence with a state of profound stupor, like trees that are abundant in sleep and situated in the state of deep sleep (suṣupti).

The meaning is that the Himalaya, Meru, and other such mountains are actually mountains of those who know reality; they experience the undivided sky of consciousness and remain forever established in samādhi. || 21 ||

Trees and other such things are in deep sleep; likewise, mountains abide in their own being. Moving beings [are likewise so]; there is never anything whatsoever called the "space of consciousness" (cidākāśa). 22.

And thus, the conception of the world is not from the perspective of living beings such as trees, because they are in a state of deep sleep; nor is it from the perspective of the species of living beings such as serpents, because they remain fixed in their own individual existence (*svasattā*). Even among the mobile species, it is not from the perspective of those who know reality, because they are nothing but the space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*); rather, it is from the perspective of certain ignorant mobile species.

And with the intention that this view is not capable of establishing the existence of the world—which would contradict many other views—he says: "Even the swollen... [āpīna-]. Those moving beings, the various classes of living creatures, even they are nothing but the space of consciousness (cidākāśa) during states such as deep sleep, death, fainting, and liberation; therein, for some at certain times...

The meaning is that it is logical that the world, which appears with partial expansion in a dream and with full expansion during the waking state, is nothing other than the space of consciousness (cidākāśa) itself, in accordance with the majority of observed perspectives. || 22 ||
The existence of mountains and other things consists of an undivided consciousness, as does the sleep of trees;
because it is free from the perception of duality, the world is therefore only the one space (ākāśa). // 23 //
In that state, the existence of mountains and such, as well as the sleep of trees, is nothing but space (kha) because they are free from the perception of duality;
therefore, from that perspective, the world is one, consisting of pure consciousness alone, conditioned by ignorance.
The entire world, as far as it is joined with ignorance, has been fully understood:
there is neither you nor I, nor indeed "is" or "is not," nor will there ever be.

As long as one's own true nature remains uncomprehended by another perspective, so long does the world persist. But once fully realized, there is neither "you" nor "I," nor existence or non-existence, nor being or non-being; it does not abide within any conceptual extreme whatsoever—this is the meaning. As it truly is, this [reality] is eternally silence itself, as solid as a stone.
Without beginning or end, uninterrupted, both sleepless and yet possessing sleep.
Thus, by the refutation of the world-appearance through its lack of established reality, he shows that Brahman alone remains, stating:
"as it truly is. The meaning is that, from the perspective of the ignorant, the diversity of the world is imagined within one's own self, as if by sleep, together with sleep itself. || 25 ||
Just as it was at the beginning of creation, so does it remain as one and the same;
even now and for infinite time to come, it shall be exactly thus.

But from the perspective of ultimate reality, it is always of a single nature; thus he says: "Previously. It exists just so at the present time, and it will likewise exist for infinite time hereafter—this is the grammatical connection. || 26 ||
Neither selfhood nor otherness, neither worldliness nor emptiness; neither silence nor the state of being silent—nothing at all is found here that can be established.
And since even its specific attributes such as selfhood (*ātmatva*) do not exist—because there is nothing from which they could be excluded—how much less so other [attributes]? Thus he says:
"Not at all" (*naiva*). || 27 ||
Remain exactly as you are; I remain exactly as I am.
In the peaceful, supreme space of bliss and non-bliss, there is nothing here at all.
Tell me, apart from the state of supreme space, what indeed exists in a city of dreams?
That which is known as peaceful is truly the stainless and healthy sky of consciousness.
In that regard, non-apprehension alone is what causes confusion;
yet once this is fully understood, even that [non-apprehension] does not exist anywhere. (30)
That non-cognition also does not exist, because it has been fully understood. || 30 ||
When the world is fully understood to be a dream, there is nothing whatsoever that is real;
what attachment, then, can one have for this [world], which is like a son born of a barren woman? (31)
Thus, regarding this world as a dream, why is there such grasping, such persistent attachment? || 31 ||
When it is fully understood that the world is like a dream within an atom of a dream, what worthiness of acceptance could there be? Upon awakening, this [world] is nothing at all.
It is to be understood that [this] is possible in each and every atom. || 32 ||
Wherein there is no awakening whatsoever, nor is there any lack of awakening anywhere;
whatever perception occurs at that time, it is simply that previous state as it was.
Regarding the objection that an object might be non-existent at the time of awakening yet existent at the time of non-awakening, he says: "That which... The prior state is simply ignorance;
the meaning is that it manifests in such a way through the nature of its own perception. || 33 ||
Presentness, as well as future and past states, awakening and non-awakening—none of these exist; indeed, every thing is peaceful.
In that case, is this ignorance regarding the three periods of time and its corresponding knowledge real? He says "no": "It exists" (vidyate). || 34 ||
Just as when one wave is struck by another wave there is no injury to the water, so too when one body is struck by the body, there is no injury to consciousness. || 35 ||

And likewise, he says "yathā" (just as) [verse 35], explaining that even when one's falsely conceived body and so forth are struck by falsely conceived enemies, there is no injury to the Self, which is the substratum of both.
The thought "I am the body" arises only within the space of consciousness;
therefore, when the body perishes, what indeed can perish? || 36 ||

Within consciousness itself, which is of the nature of space, the delusive perception that "this is the body" arises. Thus, when the body—which is of the nature of a delusive perception—is destroyed, what indeed is there that is destroyed? (36)
The world exists as the dream of the awakened space of consciousness (cidvyoman);
since it is devoid of earth and other elements, the world is therefore of the nature of a dream. (37)
At the beginning of creation, the cognition of objects such as the earth arises from the dream of primordial consciousness;
this delusion regarding the reality of dream-objects consists of nothing more than mere conceptual construction. (38)
[This occurs] from the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the dreams of successive prior consciousnesses. || 38 ||
While this dream, which is more ancient than the ancient, remains situated in its constituent parts—
even though it is unreal— the conceptualization of earth and the other elements has been fashioned.
Thus, while the dream—existing as an endless stream from the prior to the even more prior—is currently established only in an unreal form, fools nevertheless maintain the notion that it is real. (39)
And that delusion has become so firmly established that, though it is indeed unreal, it has attained a state of supreme reality; yet that [other] reality is utterly stainless.
That is the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya), meaning it is absolutely stainless and not defiled by dullness. || 40 ||
In reality, however, only the all-pervading Brahman, which is consciousness as it truly is, exists;
and therein nothing whatsoever is established—neither a rememberer nor a non-rememberer; what indeed is its nature? (41)

By using the word "as if" (*iva*) to suggest that a conceptualization has been made regarding something that is not actually real, it is shown that there is a resemblance between the conceptualization of delusion and the conceptualization of a real object. Anticipating the objection that this resemblance is only possible when real objects existed previously, when they were experienced, and when there is currently someone who remembers them—and not otherwise—the author says: "In reality" (*vastutaḥ*). That is, [the resemblance exists] with respect to that which has the form of reality.

Nor did anything such as the earth exist even previously; and since the experience of that [earth] is thus absolutely unestablished, what would the nature of the rememberer, the non-rememberer, or the forgetter be? (41)
Thus, in this case, the thorough knowledge of the measure itself is the awakener;
indeed, thorough knowledge in this very context is the opening of the door-panel.

If it is asked, "In that case, what is the indicator of similarity when [the object] is unreal and its reality is absolutely unestablished? [the author] says, "Thus, only the measure," meaning: it is simply the non-comprehension of the self-luminous, real nature [of Brahman] that constitutes ignorance regarding the world, which is actually nothing but the pure Consciousness-Brahman.

It awakens one to reality. Therefore, the full comprehension of truth itself is the opening—the removal of the covering—of the door-panel of ignorance and the door-panel of the distraction caused by the delusion of the world's reality. || 42 ||
By process of elimination, nothing such as earth or other elements exists anywhere;
that which is the seer and that which is the seen is only the stainless Śiva. (43)
When ignorance along with its effects is sublated, pure consciousness alone remains; thus, that which remains as pure consciousness is indeed Śiva. || 43 ||
Just as a reflection appears within a mirror from an original object, so does the world appear within the space of consciousness;
it shines forth by itself, reflected even though there is no external object.

A reflection (bimba) is a reflected image (pratibimba) derived from an external object (nimitta); however, the distinction—considering the case of a mirror—is that [in this context] there is a reflection even without an external object. 44.
Just as no reflection whatsoever is seen within a mirror even though it exists there,
so too the universe residing in the space of consciousness is not seen at all, even though it exists there.
What, then, is the intended point in the analogy of the mirror? He states it [in the verse beginning] with "In the mirror": || 45 ||
That which is obtained through investigation and that which exists as having a cause is the remainder of reality; but how could that which is mere appearance and non-existent be real? (46)
By means of *vicāra*—that is, by scriptural inquiry—that alone which possesses a cause and is supported by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is the Real, the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
The remainder, everything else, is a mere appearance (*bhāmātra*), a mere mental projection (*pratibhāmātra*), which has never existed even throughout the three periods of time. || 46 ||
Even something consisting of delusion might perform a purposeful action;
for even a woman in a dream brings about a real purposeful effect for men. (47)
If it were unreal, how could the world be capable of conventional usage and purposeful action? To this he says: "It would be...
[meaning] that when its own superior existence is present, it performs purposeful action characterized by the emission of the final element (the seed). 47.
That which is this manifestation is indeed the light of consciousness (cidbhā), and that is the supreme sky of consciousness (cidambaram).
Thus, where am I, where is the glory of the universe, where are you, and what are these perceptions of the visible? 48.

For the universal splendor beginning with "I" and so forth is established as being manifest; it cannot be otherwise. In that regard, that which is the manifestation is not some other thing, but is precisely the manifestation of consciousness, the light of the self’s own nature. As for the visible form that distinguishes that manifestation, if it were separate from the manifestation, it would be a void; if it were identical to the manifestation, it could not function as a distinguisher. Therefore, it is nothing but the ether of consciousness (*cidambara*). Thus.
The meaning is that by means of reflective discernment (vimarśa), some form of the world is established. || 48 ||
If there is rebirth after death, then what has been lost? Even if there is no rebirth after death, there is peace nonetheless.
If liberation exists by virtue of the vision of consciousness, then there is nothing at all here [elsewhere].
Suffering for one of noble intellect. || 49 ||

O noble one, if there exists for you—a person of exalted intellect—such a view of consciousness as has been demonstrated, then by virtue of that, since you consist of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), death through the departure of the body and the subsequent arising of another body would still occur; that is to say, there would be no liberation. Even so, what has been lost? What is it that [you have] destroyed?

There is no loss [of the Self], because the conscious Self—which is free from suffering and unsurpassed bliss—is untouched by either destruction or origination. Now, if there is no rebirth after death—that is to say, if liberation exists—nevertheless, there is simply the cessation of all phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*).
Therefore, the meaning is that in either of these two positions, not even the slightest suffering attaches here. || 49 ||
Only one who is ignorant knows what this state of a fool is like; indeed, we certainly do not claim to be experts in that matter.
For only the fish that dwells in the waters of a mirage knows the tossing of its flickering waves.

If it is asked how, then, suffering arises for a fool at birth and death, he says "of the fool" to indicate that the fool himself alone knows it. The meaning is this: just as the fish that experiences the state of being a fish, thinking "I am a fish," in the waters of a mirage-river (mṛganadī) is the one who knows the tossing of its flickering waves, but no one who is free from the delusion of the mirage-river knows them. || 50 ||
The single sky of consciousness alone shines as the self of all—within and without—as "you," "I," and so forth.

Like a wish-fulfilling tree whose body consists of branches, tips, boughs, leaves, and fruits, it has pure awareness as its sole essence. From the perspective of one who knows reality, that sky of consciousness is both within and without; it is "you," "I," and likewise the entire world.

Having become the essence of all, it shines and vibrates. The meaning is that just as the Self alone—which has the pure void of consciousness as its sole substance—manifests in the kingdom of the mind as the wish-fulfilling tree (saṃkalpavṛkṣa), possessing branches, their tips, their boughs, and their leaves and fruits, all within a single body; so it is here. || 51 ||

Thus ends the ninety-ninth canto, titled "The Exposition of the Ultimate Reality," in the Nirvāṇa Section of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa*, within the *Mokṣopāya* (Means to Liberation) of the *Vālmīki Deśika*.
Thus ends the ninety-ninth chapter, titled "The Exposition of Ultimate Reality," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*. || 99 ||
The Hundredth Sarga.
Śrī Rāma said:
"O Brahman, what kind of method might there be for the pacification of suffering within this worldly existence?"
Let those who hold this view be heard; let them then speak.
The reasoning is here set forth so that even those whose minds are entrenched in the doctrines of those who maintain the body to be the self may enter into the true reality.

In the course of describing how the arguments of those who maintain the reality of creation from the beginning are established by logic, it was stated that "this is indeed logical according to the experts.

But how can that which was described as the logicality of the Cārvākas' assertions be logical regarding their doctrine of the body being the self—a position that stands in opposition to all the schools of the orthodox (Sarvāstivādins)? And how, for them, could there be the attainment of the goals of human life?

Desiring to know this—namely, "how might it be so?"—Rāma asks: "The reasoning. Please listen with attention to this question of mine which is about to be stated, and then let the answer be given. || 1 ||
One should live happily as long as life lasts; death is not something that can be avoided.
Once one has been reduced to ashes and become still, how could there be a return? (2)

It is not within the sphere of experience; it is imperceptible. For one's own death is not perceptible while one is alive. Indeed, one's own death is inferred from seeing the death of others, yet inference is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for the Cārvākas, because they do not accept any means of knowledge other than direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). This is the sense. Or, let it be that [death] is merely the destruction of the body.
Nevertheless, since they do not accept rebirth, death itself—characterized by the cessation of all suffering—is indeed liberation;
with the intention that this is precisely what they desire, he says: "Of one who has been reduced to ashes.
"Of the peaceful one" means one who has attained the subsiding of all suffering. The phrase "of those for whom this is their position" connects with the preceding verse. || 2 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Whatever determination consciousness adopts, unbroken within its own interior, it experiences that very thing as a direct perception; such is the universal law.

With the intention that the very rule governing the experience of manifestations—which follow one's own internal conviction—is logically consistent even in the state of identifying the body with the self, and is likewise applicable to liberation, Vasiṣṭha begins to support that view with the words "yaṃ yaṃ... (whichever...). Thus, this is all-pervading, common to all people, perceptible, and established by one's own direct experience. || 3 ||
Just as space is all-pervading and tranquil, so too is the sky of consciousness all-pervading;
that alone is non-duality, for duality is utterly impossible since there is no other object.

The duality of the body and so forth imagined by the various proponents and common folk, as well as the unity established through the experience of learned Vedāntins and others, is that very same space of consciousness (*cidvyoma*); the meaning is that anything distinct from it is absolutely impossible. || 4 ||
At the beginning of creation, in that state characterized by the great dissolution, there is no other object apart from Him;
because it is devoid of space and time, this entire expanse is indeed Brahman alone.
He states the reasoning supported by such scriptural passages as "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 6.2.1), given that no other [cause] is possible:
"At the beginning of creation," etc. This means: at the beginning of creation—that is, in its prior state, during the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*) in the form of non-dual Brahman.
To the objection that there might then exist some cause of Brahman other than itself existing prior to it, he replies: "Because it has no cause. (5)
Those who do not accept the meaning of the entire body of Vedic scriptures, nor the great dissolution and so forth, are utterly deluded; being devoid of scripture, they are like the dead.

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that a Great Dissolution (*mahāpralaya*) in the form of Brahman is simply not admitted? Since the series of seeds, sprouts, and so forth is beginningless, and since the elements such as earth are beginningless in their flux, the world has never been otherwise than it is now. To refute this position of the "karma-dulled" ones, such as the Pūrva-mīmāṃsakas and others, he says: "The whole... [referring to the verse beginning with *samasta*]. "All the Vedas proclaim that state... (*sarve vedā yatpadamāmananti*).

Based on such scriptural passages as, "The Brahmins seek to know Him through the study of the Vedas," those who do not desire the meaning of the entire Veda and its auxiliary sciences— whereby the word "etcetera" includes the liberation of living beings characterized by the attainment of Brahman and the means thereto— are devoid of scripture; for, by parity of reasoning, the lack of authority of the scriptures on liberation would entail the lack of authority of the scriptures on ritual action as well.
From the perspective of us who know the truth, they are as if dead; the meaning is that they are not fit for discourse concerning the instruction of the truth. || 6 ||
For those who, through experience, have firmly established that "all this is Brahman" in a manner consistent with all scriptures— there is no further need for a sequence of discourse with them.
For those for whom the inner-self-consciousness (*pratyagātmacaitanya*) or the mind— which directs the body, senses, and so forth, which are the instruments of action— in all worldly transactions,

remains fully satisfied, complete in its desires, and accompanied by direct experience through the vision "all this is indeed Brahman" as established in all the scriptures without contradiction; even with such persons who have accomplished all that was to be done, there is no sequence of instruction or discourse.
The meaning is that the introduction of the discourse on instruction is intended solely for those who are seekers of knowledge (jijñāsus). || 7 ||
Whatever kind of consciousness arises perpetually and without interruption within the seat of the heart, by that alone the person becomes constituted; let there be a body, or let there be none.

Having concluded the incidental discussion, he resumes the main subject with the words "nitya" (eternal). Thus, even in the case of the identity of the body and the self as maintained by the Cārvākas, the meaning is that the cause—established through positive and negative concomitance—is simply the arising of a consciousness consisting of such firm conviction, and not the body itself, because the body is subject to deviation (*vyabhicāra*). || 8 ||
If that person were born from consciousness through awakening, he would be a sufferer;
for as long as there is a contrary perception, O dear one, the living soul remains composed of that.

For this very reason, although the Self is of the nature of a single flavor consisting of bliss, its state of being composed of suffering is established by all experience through the firm perception of contradictory suffering; thus he says, "Because of awakening," etc. The word "aṅga" is used as an address. || 9 ||

When it is contemplated that the world is merely the manifestation of the sky of consciousness, how can there be perception by the void? Whose awareness could there be, and from what source would it arise?

Thus, even for this world consisting of suffering, it is merely the manifestation of the sky-like consciousness of unsurpassed bliss; through such contemplation, when the reality of that state is seen, the nature of suffering imagined by delusion—as well as the grasped object and the grasping subject—subsides. This applies even to those who maintain the doctrine of the identity of the body and the self, provided they contemplate in this manner.

With the intention of establishing liberation (*nistārasiddhi*), he says: "The world... and so forth. The meaning is: how could that previously established experience of suffering and so on be perceived by the sky—the immutable, non-dual expanse of consciousness (*kūṭasthādvayacidākāśa*)? For whom would there be the perception of suffering and so on, or from what cause? || 10 ||
For men who possess the consciousness of a single certainty, neither pleasures nor pains run after them, just as dust does not cling to the skies.

He cites the meaning of the Śruti text, "What delusion, what sorrow can there be for him who perceives oneness? regarding the matter stated: "Not any... [etc.]. They "run forth," meaning they reach; that is to say, they smear. || 11 ||
Whether consciousness be real or unreal, such is the certainty;
this is established even among children—by whom and how could it be denied? (12)

In the experience of an object that conforms to one’s own firm conviction, neither the validity (*prāmāṇya*) of consciousness nor the reality (*satyatva*) of the mental modification (*cittavṛtti*) is required; for in the experience of the body as the self, the first [validity] is absent, and in the mental modification consisting of the direct realization of Brahman (*brahmasākṣātkāra*), the second [reality] is absent. With this intention, he says: "Consciousness" (*saṃvit*). Consciousness (*saṃvedana*) is *saṃvit*; it is true and valid (*pramā*).
"That by which something is cognized is consciousness (saṃvit)"—this statement expresses the absence of any restrictive rule regarding whether that consciousness is true or uncontradicted.
The meaning is: such a thing necessarily becomes the cause for the experience of objects, whether they be real or unreal. How can it be denied?
For it is not possible to deny an experience by resorting to something that contradicts that very experience; this is the meaning. || 12 ||
Neither the body, nor the person (puruṣa), nor even a distinct living soul (jīva) is perceived; consciousness alone is all this, and the world exists exactly as that consciousness perceives it.

For this very reason, with the intention that all disputants can be rendered satisfied by being made to understand that consciousness alone is the Self—being capable of accounting for the various specific notions of the Self held by each respective school—he says: "Not the body.
This refers to the "Person" (puruṣa) favored by the Cārvākas, the "individual soul" (jīva) favored by the Sāṃkhyas, or even that favored by the Mīmāṃsakas and others.

A separate experiencer, distinct from consciousness, is not perceived; therefore, all this that is the object of the disputants' conceptualizations is nothing but the consciousness of the body and so forth. (13)
Whether real or unreal, the body is experienced by that [consciousness] through its own autonomy,
just as in a dream, in the netherworld, in the sky, in water, or in heaven.
The meaning is: by its own independence, that is, by its own mere conceptualization, and not by dependence on causes such as earth and so forth. || 14 ||
Whether consciousness be real or unreal, the person is known as being of that measure alone;
whatever his conviction is, that is certainly his conviction of what is real. (15)
The person is the self; that is the real, which is capable of purposeful action. 15.
By this alone is the authority of all scriptures established;
it is my conviction that this is the final conclusion of all philosophical systems. (16)

Since consciousness alone exists in the form of the self and other entities favored by all disputants, it is ultimately real; and since the objects imagined by them are capable of performing their respective intended causal functions, the validity of all scriptures previously mentioned is established. Thus he says: "Validity," and likewise:

And he says that this doctrine of the non-dual nature of consciousness (*saṃvidadvaitātman*) is the crest-jewel of all philosophical systems, because it is the basis upon which all other disputants depend and because it is the cause of the supreme human goal (*puruṣārtha*): "all... (verse 16).
Therefore, that state of non-awakening which you possess is exactly as it is perceived;
it becomes pure in form and likewise partakes in its own fruit. || 17 ||
If so, does consciousness itself transform into the forms of the body and so forth as conceived by various disputants, in accordance with their respective determinations?

He says "therefore" (tasmāt) to answer no: that very ignorance (*avidyā*), which exists as non-cognition within consciousness, becomes manifest at the time of activity and so forth through such transformations, exactly as it appears to those various disputants. It is that very [ignorance].

The meaning is that when there is a transformation into the nature of the awakening to reality (*tattvabodha*), consciousness takes on a form of stainless purity and likewise becomes a partaker of the fruit of liberation.

However, that state of non-awakening which consciousness may occasionally possess—due to [limitations of] place, time, action, substance, the Vedas, the scriptures, desires, or delusions—is never destroyed. (18)

For this very reason, that state of non-awakening— arising from the delusions of desiring heaven, cattle, sons, and so forth through such actions as bathing and giving at sacred places, times, and so on, as well as through substances such as elixirs, mantras, and medicines taught in the ritual scriptures— is never destroyed, nor does the distracted consciousness induced by it ever cease. || 18 ||
If that [doubt], once diminished, should manifest again in an instant, then by what means and when indeed will the suffering of consciousness ever be pacified? (19)

One might wonder whether ignorance (*avidyā*), once sublated by awakening, could manifest again; however, this is not to be suspected, because there would be no seed for its recurrence and it would lead to the undesirable consequence of a lack of liberation. Thus he says: "It manifests. Even the suspicion of its recurrence has been exhausted through absolute sublation. If that ignorance were to manifest again after a moment, then [it would follow] from consciousness...
When or by what means indeed does the suffering of the living being ever subside? The meaning is: never, nor by anything whatsoever.
Consciousness alone is the life-force of men; as firm one's conviction is, so shall one become happy or miserable—this is the certainty. (20)
If there exists that realization for those who know it, it serves as a refuge for the destruction of worldly existence;
if it does not exist, then nothing remains but the deaf-mute blindness of a stone.

The consciousness of the nature of the inner self alone, when known in its true essence, removes bondage which is its own effect; therefore, that alone is the refuge for those seeking liberation. For in its absence, there would be nothing but blindness in the world, and any hope for liberation would be far off.
Thus he says: "Consciousness... [it] remains; by the method of elimination, it follows as the only possibility. || 21 ||
And that which is obtained through that very consciousness, through feeling itself—this internal insentience [is removed] by the knowledge of one's own nature, just as sleep is for a man. (22)

To the question "Whence does blindness alone remain there?", he says: "Since" (yat). Because, by that very consciousness of the inner self (*pratyagātma-saṃvitti*) which is self-luminous and reveals its own nature, this phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is apprehended by the person through a non-cognition (*avedana*) comparable to blindness—just as one's own dullness is [perceived] by sleep. Therefore, if that consciousness is denied, there remains only blindness, which is without a witness.
The meaning is: "by way of elimination" (pariśeṣāt). || 22 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
There will be no end to this [universe] in the cardinal directions or below, nor will there be the destruction of the world;
for one who has abandoned the notion of non-existence, it is realized that "it exists. (23)

Rāma, doubting whether there is a logical basis for the introduction of true knowledge in those who follow the firm conviction of the views you have censured—namely, those who, accepting that the world has never been otherwise than it is now, do not admit the existence of a great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*) and so forth, and who are like the dead, being devoid of the scriptures—asks: "In the directions... and so on.

In this cycle of existence (saṃsṛti), there is no end whatsoever in the nine directions—beginning with the east and ending with the zenith—and likewise in the nadir; even so, there is no decay or destruction of the world, as has been realized by that person whose mind has abandoned the three types of non-existence, beginning with prior non-existence (prāgabhāva). || 23 ||
"Surely he did not see that 'this is merely a mass of consciousness,' nor did he see, as it was actually seen, the destruction of everything. (24)

Furthermore, by what kind of person was this entire world perceived as being nothing but a mass of consciousness (*vijñānaghana*), seeing thus the ultimate reality (*paramārthatattva*)? This connects with the preceding [verse]. For one who sees the world exactly as it is seen as being real, what kind of reasoning regarding Brahman could there be for the destruction of mental distress (*ādhi*)?
Thus, sever my doubt for the further increase of my awakening. || 25 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
In this matter, first there is one appropriate response, and likewise a second;
listen now to this second reply which is logical and about to be spoken.

The previously stated [objection]—that "we are not like the dead, for whom there is no sequence of discourse"—is the very answer. Alternatively, the answer already given against each preceding proponent—that "whatever certainty one adopts is shattered by another consciousness," and so forth—is precisely what is appropriate. And thus, since such a certainty unpermeated by consciousness is unestablished, that too [is refuted].

The sense is that, having brought about an understanding of the dull consciousness by demonstrating that it is a transformation (*vivarta*) of the prior determination, one is able to lead [the seeker] into the experience of the indivisible unity of consciousness (*cid-akhaṇḍaikarasya*). || 26 ||
O Puruṣottama, that person whose nature has been described by you is experienced as being nothing more than pure consciousness. (27)

O Puruṣottama, regarding that person of such a disposition whom you described as possessing certainty in what was said: does he perceive the conscious self as distinct from the body, or does he perceive the eternal subtle body (*ativāhika-deha*) as the self, or does he perceive the gross body as the self, or does he perceive the pure consciousness as the self, or does he perceive the consciousness as veiled by ignorance, or does he deny consciousness altogether?

Regarding that, he first states [the position] in the first alternative: "He, for his part," and so on. If he accepts that when conscious cognitions of form and so forth are measured, that which remains is pure consciousness (*cetanāmātra*), whose nature is the manifestation of the Intellect (*cidābhāsa*), then the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*) is indeed experienced by him in succession; such is the meaning. || 27 ||
And that [body] is subject to destruction through the dissolution of its form; of this there is no doubt.
But if the body were indestructible, then what would be the point of the sequence of suffering here? (28)
He asks "whence" regarding that [state] and says: "And he" (*sa ca*). This particle *ca* is read here in the sense of *hi* (for/because).

For, by means of the destruction of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) consisting of the form of the body and so forth, he is joined with the Supreme Self; that is, he becomes one with it. Regarding the second case, however, he says: "Now" (*atha*).
When there is the notion of selfhood in the perishable body composed of food (*annamaya*), there is suffering due to the apprehension of total destruction on all sides.

But when there is the certainty that the nature of the self is indestructible, suffering does not follow merely through the fault of perceiving it as having the form of the body; thus, being gradually enlightened, he too will realize the truth—this is the underlying sense. Therefore, "krama" (sequence) means "prasaṅga" (consequential application).

The destruction of the self through the division of its parts would be unexamined; indeed, it is certainly the case that such destruction must inevitably occur for it—surely, this is the certainty. (29)
Regarding the third [type of] conceptualization (*kalpa*), he says "it might be" (*bhavet*). The division of parts (*bhāgavibhāga*) is the distinction between components;
that which is composed of these is the gross self (*sthūlātman*). For one who perceives that as the self, its destruction, though it occurs, has not been investigated.

And the destruction of that which possesses parts necessarily occurs. The word "kila" is used for the purpose of awakening [the listener]. There is also the conviction in a self distinct from that [gross body].
The meaning is that it is accomplished. || 29 ||
Once dead, because its nature is consciousness, it does not experience worldly existence (saṃsṛti) again;
for that consciousness which has been cleansed by knowledge does not remain in a state of non-transmigration.

Regarding the fourth alternative, he says: "dead" (*mṛta*). He is the seer of the Self as pure consciousness. Though liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*), seeing the world everywhere at all times as a mere play, he is "dead" in the sense of having attained absolute liberation (*kaivalya*) through the state of bodilessness (*videhatā*);

thus, he does not know the cycle of rebirth (*saṃsṛti*) again. The meaning is that he does not perceive it. Regarding the fifth alternative, he says: "knowledge" (*jñāna*). That which is consciousness...

If that [impurity] has not been washed away by the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), then because the state of being the seed of *saṃsṛti* (transmigration) has not been destroyed, one does not remain in a state of non-transmigration; the meaning is that one necessarily continues to transmigrate. Thus, the implication is that even for such a person, there may be liberation through the arising of knowledge in some future birth. Alternatively, if one possesses the certainty that "there is no consciousness" (*saṃvitti*):
Consequently, due to such a sensation, one indeed becomes as inert as a stone. || 31 ||
The sixth kalpa also says "or else": the meaning is that he remains for a long time indeed like a stone—insentient and devoid of specific cognition. || 31 ||

Just as the mind [withdraws] from objects according to their perception, when the body is destroyed and [perception] is lost, death alone is seen to be the supreme good, not further experience. || 32 ||

To address what or how the highest good (*śreyaḥ*) was seen by him there, he says: "according to his perception" (*yathāvedanam*). Following that very perception which has been made firm until death, immediately after the fall of the body, when the specific cognition (*viśeṣavijñāna*) within the intellect (*cit*) has been impaired and destroyed, that death itself becomes like a deep, dreamless sleep, resembling the liberation (*mokṣa*) of the Naiyāyikas.

The meaning is that because it is free from suffering, that fool perceived it as the supreme good; however, he did not perceive it as the supreme good through the experience of unsurpassed bliss. || 32 ||
Those who, being devoid of pure knowledge, become bodiless because of its impossibility for them, remain in a state of inertia; having become inert, they fall into an incurable blindness.

But as for those proponents of emptiness who possess a firm conviction in selflessness, he states their destination after death with the words "because of non-existence. Having died bodiless, they go there; and thus says the Śruti: "Those worlds called 'non-solar' are shrouded in blind darkness; to them go after death those people who are slayers of the Self. (33)
And for those who, being composed of consciousness, perceive everything like a city in a dream,
this entire web of the world proceeds as if it were real.

He says "And those who... to show that even for the Vijñānavādins, who perceive the world as consisting of momentary consciousness and as being like a dream, the establishment of conventional reality is the same. "Consisting of consciousness" means having the nature of a momentary, transforming conscious self.
What difference would there be in the intellect regarding the stability or instability of beings? (34)
Whether there is stability of the elements or lack of stability, happiness and unhappiness are indeed equal. || 35 ||

He speaks of the establishment of the worldly convention regarding the experience of pleasure and pain for both those who maintain the permanence of the world and those who maintain its momentariness: "Permanence... etc. What difference would there be in the novel view concerning the cognition of the diversity of worldly conventions? "Asukham" means suffering. (35)
Whether stable or unstable, even for the great elements such as earth and the rest,
this world appears as nothing but the light of consciousness as long as ignorance extends.
However, for those who know reality, there is no grasping at the momentariness or non-momentariness of the elements such as earth and the rest.

This is because, since that which is superimposed has as its true nature only the underlying substrate, Brahman, an investigation into it is as futile as an inquiry into the value of silver seen in a mother-of-pearl shell; with this intention, he says "stable. [This applies] even to the great elements such as the earth. (36)
Enough with those childish people who, having failed to pervade consciousness with the non-existence of consciousness, have either concluded or accepted that it is insentient. (37)

However, consciousness cannot possess momentariness; for it is impossible for its own non-existence—which is characterized as its own destruction—and its insentience (jāḍya) to pervade [consciousness], and since those two cannot be established without the pervasion of consciousness, there is no possibility of asserting such a thing.
