Thus he says: "saṃvidā" (by consciousness). Momentariness is the non-existence of consciousness in terms of time.

But insentience (*jāḍya*) consists in non-existence in some respects; and that [insentience], being neither pervaded nor touched by even that twofold consciousness which is claimed to be momentary, [remains]. This is also an indication of [the absurdity of] momentariness itself.
The meaning is: "Enough with conversing with such childish fools who have accepted [this view] after having determined it. (37)
Those supreme persons from whose bodies knowledge arises are worthy of worship;
enough with those lowest of men from whom knowledge arises only through their bodies.

For this very reason, those who maintain that the inert phenomenal world within the body arises as an illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) of the immutable consciousness (*kūṭastha-cit*) are truly fortunate; for by means of the principle of "originating from speech" (*vācārambhaṇa*), they perceive the unreality of modifications and thus attain the realization that only consciousness remains.

On the other hand, the Cārvākas, Kaṇabhakṣas (Vaiśeṣikas), and others who claim that consciousness arises from the inert body and so forth are fools, [for they would face] the destruction of consciousness.

With the intention that a residue consisting of insentient matter (jaḍa) would lack the status of a human goal (apuruṣārtha) and that there is an absence of any means of proof (sādhaka), he says: "Of those... The plural number in the word "vidbhyaḥ" is not intended to be significant. || 38 ||
The flood of the seeds of living beings, whose nature is consciousness, moves upwards, sideways, and downwards like a web of insects in the sky, as if filling itself by its own power. (39)
Or, the plural designation may be due to the multiplicity of the reflections of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) within Hiraṇyagarbha, who is the collective totality (*jīvasamaṣṭi*) of individual souls.

Thus, the conception that the single Hiraṇyagarbha, as the self of the collective totality, transmigrates through various individual souls by means of ascending and descending to higher and lower worlds, is also sound; this he states with the words "of the nature of consciousness" (*cidrūpa*). [The text continues with] "the worms of space."
Like mosquitoes and the like in a net; just as a flood of water being poured into a jeweled vessel or a flower-cup flows out sideways, upwards, and downwards, so it is in this case. || 39 ||
That by which another agent is perceived through the stream of seeds is that [Self] which is intent upon it;
likewise, it experiences within itself and vibrates of its own accord.

He states that even this collective totality (*samaṣṭi*) of various individual agents and living beings arises solely through the force of the mental attachment to its own conceptualization by the consciousness of Hiraṇyagarbha—expressed as "it is perceived" (*cetyate*). The instrumental case in the phrase "by the flood of seeds" (*bījaugheṇa*) denotes the manner of being (*itthambhāve*).

By means of that reflection of Hiraṇyagarbha’s consciousness (*cidābhāsa*), which exists in the form of the flood of seeds, he attains a state of collectivity at the beginning of a kalpa; and according to his own worship and latent impressions (*vāsanā*), another [being] likewise becomes manifold.

The individual agent, being distinct, perceives within himself that [object] to which he is devoted and attached; thus, he himself experiences within himself the form of various agents, and in that very way he leaps about and transmigrates—this is the meaning.
Whatever is perceived by whichever living being (jīva), that is immediately [experienced] by him.
This is established and remains unimpaired from childhood onwards, even by way of the nature of consciousness.

He says "yad" (that which) to show that by this manner also, exactly what was previously asserted by us is established—[namely] from childhood to old age, and unimpaired, meaning its accomplishment is unobstructed. || 41 ||
Just as there are various whirling eddies of smoke in the sky and of great waters in the ocean, so too are the diverse revolutions of transmigratory existence within the space of consciousness.

For this very reason, he says "as follows" (yathā) to show that because the variety of consciousness in the various transmigrations corresponds to the variety of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) within the living intellects, the variety of transmigrations is infinite. || 42 ||
Just as the city of the sky of consciousness appears to a person in a dream, so too has this very world existed from the beginning of creation. (43)
That very same space of consciousness (cidvyoma) exists having become this world.
Just as auxiliary causes do not exist at all in a dream, so too the elements such as earth and the rest did not exist at the beginning of the world's existence. (44)

He states that even because [the world] is established in heaven and so forth through mere appearance (*pratibhā*) alone, without auxiliary causes (*sahakāri-kāraṇa*), it is indeed identical to a dream—thus he says: "auxiliary," etc. "In the beginning" means at the start of creation. (44)
The various lands fashioned within the dream-city of the limbs are those very same ones that have attained fullness in the dream-city of the world. (45)

The earth is the successive division of the levels of the houses that constitute the limbs—the constituent parts—of the city. Those [levels] which were made delicate by half-blossoming have now attained fullness through their complete blossoming and consequent densification. (45)
These beings are nothing but the space of pure consciousness, devoid of both duality and unity; for what else could there be to color this space? Whatever appears in the sky is indeed the sky itself.
The word division is *yat* and *ābhāti*. || 46 ||
The moonlight of consciousness, cool and refreshing in the four directions, spreads the light of awareness; this world is its manifestation.

Because it pacifies the threefold heat, consciousness is cool; the manifestation of objects is its characteristic light. The shining forth of that light of consciousness in the form of objects [is what occurs]. (47)
Even today, at both its beginning and end, the vision of creation occurs within the space of pure consciousness;
through the opening and closing of the eyes of consciousness, the Self arises from the void and returns to it.

In the beginning, prior to creation, and at the end, during dissolution, within the void whose nature is empty of creation— the void consisting of consciousness— there is the well-known perception of creation even now, in this very present moment; and that is indeed the Brahman whose self is the void, arising by itself through the unfolding (*unmeṣa*) of its own consciousness in a limited form and through the closing (*nimeṣa*) of it in an unlimited form.
The meaning is that the essential conclusion is that [the world] arises and sets like a dream. || 48 ||
In whatever way one knows something, that very thing is experienced exactly as it is;
since everything is purely consciousness, what indeed is not found here? (49)
If one perceives the world as real by the power of its own existence, then it cannot be said that anything is non-existent; thus he says:

"That which... Because of that reason, whatever well-known real entity (sad-vastu) established by various scriptures one knows at the beginning of creation, even today one experiences it exactly in that same way. Therefore, since everything is indeed pure consciousness (cinmātra), what is not found therein?
The meaning is: "that which would be non-existent. || 49 ||

Those whose minds are gentle through consciousness remain like the autumn sky, pure and clear; the truly wise, having realized that supreme state, abide as non-existent [in the sense of being free from ego].
They are non-existent in a form separate from consciousness, but they are existent as the essence of consciousness. || 50 ||

Free from pride and delusion, having conquered the fault of attachment, and possessing their own purpose as it arrives in its natural flow, these people remain free from affliction, appearing like mechanical puppets in the sight of worldly affairs.

He makes their such state perceptible through a characteristic mark—“free from pride and delusion” (nirmānamohāḥ). Like mechanical figures of men, in that case, they possess their own movements and functions brought about by the force of the flow of water and so forth;
thus it should be understood that they remain as objects of the perception of others engaged in practical activity. || 51 ||
Thus ends the one hundredth canto, titled "The Refutation of Nihilism," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the glorious Vāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa of Valmīki, composed by the Sage. 100.
Thus ends the one hundredth canto, titled "The Refutation of Nihilism," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The One Hundred and First Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: The Puruṣa is indeed pure consciousness alone; it is that very same reality which exists in this manner.
Apart from pure consciousness alone, what else can possibly exist? || 1 ||
For one who always perceives everywhere the stainless oneness of pure consciousness,
the state of fearlessness is proclaimed because there is no attainment of causes for fear.

He constructs this introductory framework—beginning with the words "Consciousness alone"—to describe how all proponents of various doctrines likewise attain fearlessness and firm establishment upon realizing that consciousness alone is the ultimate reality.
Thus, by means of this [realization], one transcends the forms of permanence and momentariness imagined by various disputants, as well as the states of birth, death, fear, sorrow, and so forth. (1)
And that pure space is seen by the seer who consists of it;
since the world is merely that much, whence can there be the notion of what is to be rejected or accepted? (2)

Establishing that very point, he states its result: "And that" (tacceti). That pure consciousness (cinmātra) is also stainless and immaculate, like the sky itself. "Consisting of that" (tanmaye) means being a manifestation (vivarta) of that. || 2 ||
For that follower of Bṛhaspati who holds that there is no other world, what essence can there be beyond this life? For one such as he, how could passion and hatred ever cease? (3)

Even for the Buddhist who maintains the doctrine of the single aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-ekaskandha-vādin*), it is agreed that attachment and aversion arise from the absence of anything to be rejected or accepted;

however, his view must be disregarded because momentary consciousness is insubstantial—this is what the author states by saying "it does not exist. This refers to the Bārhaspatya proponent, a disputant who follows the teachings of the Buddha as formulated by Bṛhaspati.

Since no world or universe exists apart from momentary consciousness (*kṣaṇika-vijñāna*), for him there is no such thing as a "world. Therefore, because there is no objective referent (*aviṣayatvāt*), how could passion and hatred possibly arise? Indeed, what other essence—eternal and in the form of the goal of human endeavor (*puruṣārtha*)—could exist that the Knower (*vidas*) might desire, by the mere possibility of which his own eternity might be established? [This was said] regarding the sons of Raji and the Asuras.
It is well known from the *Matsyapurāṇa* and other sources that even Bṛhaspati composed a treatise on Buddhism for the purpose of deluding [people].

(3) O dear one, tell me: what is the nature of the defects of attachment and aversion arising from the perception of the desirable and the undesirable within this dream called the world, which consists of the expanse of pure consciousness? (4)

In our established doctrine, however, the world is a dream that is a manifestation (vivarta) of the immutable consciousness (kūṭasthasaṃvid) itself; therefore, there is no possibility of attachment or aversion at all. Thus he says: "Desirable and undesirable... (verse 4).
Whether this is to be abandoned or accepted, consciousness shines forth as pure within the pure self; what room is there here for the perception of "this" or "not-this"?

Or, even if there is the superimposition of conceptual constructions regarding what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted, nevertheless, there is no distinction whatsoever in the ether of consciousness; with this intention, he says:
"This [is]... (idam). "The views of that and not-that" (tadataddṛśau) refers to the perspectives of the desirable, the undesirable, and so forth. || 5 ||
Consciousness is the man, the immortal, and the serpent; consciousness is the stationary and the moving.
Existence, non-existence, and the like are the waves, whirlpools, and movements of this ocean.
Since everything consists solely of indestructible consciousness, even birth, death, and so forth cannot be conceived; thus he says:
"I, you, and all people are nothing but the space of consciousness. We never die at any time, for how indeed could consciousness ever die? (7)

For consciousness there is no object of consciousness; it has attained the state of being self-conscious. Therefore, O large-eyed one, because it is consciousness, where could duality or unity possibly abide? (8)

If consciousness is everything, no other object of cognition remains. To suggest that consciousness could be its own object of cognition is like the absurd notion of one's own shoulder climbing onto itself; thus he says, "of consciousness. If consciousness were to reach the state of being an object of cognition by itself, then, because of its nature as consciousness, there would be duality in the form of a distinction between the action and its object characterized by cognizability, which is other than consciousness.
Or where could that unity, excluded from those [other things], reside? (8)
Therefore, tell me: what entity can be said to exist apart from pure consciousness?
If it is said that such an entity dies, then why are we here today?
*Bhūtam* means the eternal, existent reality. The ellipsis is "from what do we, as living beings, live? (9).
Whatever those disputants— the Buddhists and others, as well as the Lokāyatas and so forth—
conceive of after setting aside the space of consciousness (saṃvidākāśa),
let that be stated. (10)

This being the case, it follows that for all disputants, it is consciousness-space alone that manifests in the form of the respective objects they intend; for there is no other alternative besides that. With this intention, he says: "of the disputants" (vādinām). || 10 ||
This very space of consciousness is called Brahman by some;
it is called knowledge by some, and it is called the void by others. (11)

He elaborates upon the stated meaning by means of two verses, beginning with "the space of consciousness," while placing the proponent of Brahman at the forefront: "Knowledge" (jñāna) is [ordinary] cognition; "higher knowledge" (vijñāna) is [liberating] realization. || 11 ||
By some it is called the power of intoxication (mada-śakti), by some the name "Puruṣa," by some the space of consciousness (cid-ākāśa), and by some Śiva and Ātman. || 12 ||

By some proponent of the body as the self; by the Sāṃkhya, as that which is called the *puruṣa*, consisting of the properties of the elements transformed into the form of the body and resembling the power of the intoxication of wine; by the Yogin, as the space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*); and by the Śaiva, as Śiva, Īśvara, the Self (*ātman*), the atom (*aṇu*), or the individual soul (*jīva*). || 12 ||
Even when described in this way, pure consciousness never undergoes any change into something else;
for it knows itself as such by its own nature, and not otherwise.

Even when there is such manifold conceptualization by various disputants, there is no injury whatsoever to consciousness (citi), because it is free from conceptualization (nirvikalpa) by virtue of being the witness of all conceptualizations. Thus he says: "Pure Consciousness" (cinmātra). || 13 ||
"May my limbs turn to dust, and may they become like Mount Meru;
what loss or what gain is there for me, whose body is of the nature of consciousness? (14)
Of me, who am such that my very body and essential nature (svarūpa) consist of consciousness alone (cidrūpa). || 14 ||
If our ancestors, beginning with the Grandfather (Brahmā), have died, yet she has not died even though she might die,
then that birth would not truly exist for us who possess the consciousness of death.
The bodies of our ancestors and others have died, but their consciousness has not died.

If that [consciousness] were also to die, then for them—whose consciousness is dead—there would be no rebirth; this is the meaning. Alternatively, the word "our" (asmākam) may be construed as intended to demonstrate that the same principle applies to us as well. || 15 ||
The imperishable space of consciousness is neither born nor does it die;
tell me, how could it be so? For how indeed could there be the destruction of space? (16)
Tell me, could there be a destruction of space, or how could it come to be? (16)
The indestructible sky of consciousness, whose sole manifestation is the form of the world,
remains solitary within itself, free from rising and setting.
Thus, since its destruction is impossible, the manifestation of the world-form is of the nature of appearance; that is nothing but consciousness, the indestructible sky, which remains. || 17 ||
Bearing the appearance of the world yet burning away its heat, the crystal mountain of the sky of consciousness—devoid of beginning, middle, or end—remains pure within the Self. 18.
The mountain of crystal, characterized by vermilion, itself bearing the appearance of the world within its own interior,

effects the burning away of that [appearance] by the fire of its own direct realization and remains in its own pure self. Just as a clear mountain of crystal, having previously held a forest of reflections within it, at some point [remains] as if in the state of the fire of those reflections.
The intention is that, having reached its own state, it burns that forest and remains in its essential nature alone; such is the case here as well. || 18 ||
Just as whatever is being looked at in darkness perishes, so too does this entire universe— which resembles a mass of clouds— vanish within the Self.
He provides an illustration for how, as knowledge becomes increasingly powerful, the world of ignorance is destroyed:
"Just as that which is being observed perishes completely in due course, so too does this entire universe created by the darkness of ignorance. This is the meaning. || 19 ||
Just as the ocean itself moves, yet while remaining still holds within itself its waters, whirlpools, and so forth,
even so the space of consciousness (cidākāśa) holds this entire universe as a limb within itself.

Just as a stream of water itself remains while supporting parts such as waves, whirlpools, foam, and bubbles, in the same way, the space of consciousness (cidākāśa) also remains within itself while supporting the world as its constituent part; this is the meaning. || 20 ||
The Puruṣa is indeed pure consciousness alone, and like space, he never perishes;
therefore, the grief that "I am perishing" is entirely futile.
When passing from one body to another, it is indeed a great festival;
why, O fools, do you grieve over that which is death itself, when it is a cause for joy? (22)
When death has arrived, which is the cause for casting off an aged body and obtaining a newer one, joy alone is appropriate, not grief; thus he says: "From the body... (verse 22).
If he does not die again, there will be great prosperity even here;
the fever of grasping at existence and non-existence, and of rejecting them, has been stilled. (23)

Furthermore, even if you harbor the delusion that there is no rebirth at all, despair is still not appropriate, because death itself prevents the attainment of all misfortunes; thus he says: "The dead... Accumulation (*upacaya*) refers to the excellence of the goals of human endeavor (*puruṣārtha*). || 23 ||
Since death and life are therefore neither suffering nor happiness, this very thing does not exist at all; it is indeed the space of consciousness that manifests in this manner.

With the intention that where there is no attachment to suffering even while birth and death exist, there can be no possibility of such attachment when those two are absolutely non-existent, he concludes with the verse beginning "Death" (verse 24).
If there is the acquisition of a body for one who has died, that is indeed a new festival;
for death is the destruction of the body, and that death is the supreme bliss. (25)

To one who thinks that fear of death arises solely from the doubt as to whether or not there is the acquisition of another body after death, he states the same point in a different manner, beginning with the words "mṛtasya" (of the dead).
For (*hi*) death is the destruction of the previous body, which is seized by old age, disease, and the like, and is comparable to a prison cell. || 25 ||
If death is absolute annihilation, then it is the destruction of the disease of worldly existence;
if there is the acquisition of a new body, then that is indeed a festival. (26)
For this very reason, he states that it is exactly the same even in the other alternative: "Death," [verse 26].
If you have fear of evil deeds, know that they exist both here and in the next world; therefore, O friend, do not commit them for the sake of attaining success in both worlds.

If it is argued that there is fear because of hearing of hells and other such states for evildoers after death, [the author replies: even for those who are still living, fear is equal because the results of extremely intense [evils] are seen right here in this world due to royal punishment and the like;
therefore, he says "from evil deeds" (*kukarmabhyaḥ*)—meaning: do not commit them, do not commit them.
The substitution of *a* for *i* is according to the Vedic usage (*chandasa*). || 27 ||
"I shall die, I shall die, I shall die"—thus you speak;
"I shall be, I shall be, I shall be"—thus you do not perceive. || 28 ||
Where indeed are birth and death? Where are the planes of existence and non-existence?
This entire world is nothing but the void of consciousness itself, revolving within the void. (29)
But from the perspective of ultimate reality, there is no occurrence of birth, death, and so forth; thus he says: "Where? (verse 29).
Your self is nothing but the space of pure consciousness; drink, eat, and remain without the sense of "mine.
For one who is as beautiful as the interior of the sky, how could desire ever arise?
He states that for those filled with knowledge, there is never any attachment to suffering because their worldly activity is free from desire:
"The space of consciousness... (verse 30).

The fearless and fortunate one experiences those states brought about by the power of his own mental flow and the influence of place and time—states which are purifying, even more so than the purifier itself. (31)

By the force of his own natural flow, through effort that is both spontaneous and disciplined, and by virtue of time and place, he experiences objects such as sound and the rest that have come to him; even among these, he experiences only those that are purifying rather than those that cause mental impurity or distraction—this is the meaning. In the reading "pāvanānpādapa iva" (like a tree [experiences] purifying [objects]), the sense is clear. || 31 ||
Disregarding the moderate defects that arise due to the influence of place and time,
he remains within himself, treating them with indifference like one whose intellect is asleep.
Even during times of regional upheaval, famine, and the like occurring from time to time, there is no occurrence of suffering for him;
for at such times, it is possible to disregard those circumstances by experiencing the bliss of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) in some solitary mountain cave or similar place. Thus he says:
"In the midst... His intellect is as if asleep within the internal, thought-free meditative absorption (*nirvikalpa-samādhi*). (32)
He does not come to suffering through death, nor does he come to happiness through life; he neither desires nor hates, for he remains then free from all mental afflictions.

Without reflecting upon death, life, birth, or old age, free from desire and devoid of latent tendencies, he who has known what is to be known dwells here like an ignorant man—fearless and as immovable as a mountain. (34)

He summarizes the matter stated in the section on creation with the verse beginning "maraṇa": the meaning is that one who does not reflect upon the decaying grasses characterized by death and so forth—though he has known what is to be known, he remains like an ignorant and utterly deluded person, dwelling as motionless as a mountain, free from fear. || 34 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and first chapter, titled "The Supreme Instruction," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the glorious Vāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa, composed by Vālmīki, according to the Ṛṣi tradition. 101.
Thus ends the one hundred and first chapter, titled "The Supreme Instruction," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and second canto. Śrī Rāma said:
When the supreme reality, which is without beginning or end, has been fully realized;
O Brahmin, tell me: what kind of person is a supreme being (puruṣottama)? || 1 ||
Furthermore, the series of characteristics of the reality of Buddhahood is described so that,
through the firmness of that practice, there may arise the consolidation of awakening.
Of what kind is he, and distinguished by what characteristics, does he become? || 1 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Listen, O best of men, to what kind of person becomes one who has known that which is to be known;
and how, throughout his life, does he abide and what is his conduct? (2)
Listen to how he abides, what his nature is, and what his conduct is.
Even stones are friends and kinsmen, as are the trees of the forest;
even for one dwelling in the midst of the woods, the young fawns are their own kin. (3)
In this regard, he begins to state first the internal characteristics that constitute its very nature, starting with the words "Even stones," and so forth.
The meaning is that there is an equal internal state of mind toward friends and others, as well as toward stones and the like, and toward union and separation. || 3 ||
To him, even a crowded place is as empty as a void; misfortunes are his greatest successes.
Even while established in a great kingdom, calamities alone are his festivals. (4)
A place crowded with people is one filled with a multitude of folk. Calamities are the destruction of wealth, kinsmen, and so forth.
Misfortunes are sufferings such as execution, imprisonment, and dependence on others. "Sūtsavāḥ" means like great festivals. || 4 ||
Non-concentration is concentration; great suffering itself is happiness;
even worldly activity is noble silence; and actions themselves are the state of non-action.
Verbal conduct consists of speech; actions consist of the body. (5)
Though awake, he remains as if in deep sleep; though living, he is like one dead.
He performs all customary conduct, yet he does nothing at all.
He is "established in deep sleep" because he abides in the non-conceptual Self which resembles deep sleep.
He is "like one who has died" due to his abiding in the state of the bodiless Self. Because he is established in the Self as a non-agent, he does not act.
A connoisseur of aesthetic flavor yet utterly devoid of taste; merciless yet affectionate toward kinsmen;
pitiless yet exceedingly compassionate; free from craving yet possessed by longing.

Even amidst the pleasures of sense objects, such a person is a connoisseur of the singular bliss of the Self; yet, through the perception of sense objects, he finds them utterly tasteless. Because he lacks the notion of "mineness," he is free from worldly attachment; but through the realization of the identity of all with his own Self, he is affectionate toward kinsmen out of unconditional love. Because he perceives no second entity as an object of compassion, he is without pity; for, by means of the analogy of his own body, he regards the bodies of others as his own.

Seeing happiness and suffering, he is possessed of ultimate compassion; thus, being full, he is himself free from thirst [for worldly things]; yet, because his nature is to uplift ignorant beings, he is endowed with a thirst for their welfare. (7)
His conduct is approved by all, yet he is excluded from all worldly conduct;
free from sorrow, fear, and fatigue, he appears as if possessed of sorrow.
To the question "In what conduct does he abide?", he states the external characteristics: "All," etc.
Because of seeing the suffering of ignorant people, he grieves for them and thus appears as if possessed by sorrow. (8)
Therefore, the world does not tremble before him, nor does he tremble before the world,
even though he has reached the highest agitation while still being a connoisseur of worldly existence.
He is not agitated and does not fear; "agitation" means fear. || 9 ||
He does not rejoice in what has been attained, nor does he long for what has not been attained; he remains equanimous amidst objects being experienced, neither elated nor dejected.
Even when an object that is a cause for joy or dejection is being experienced, no [mental state] belonging to those two [joy or dejection] exists [in them].
When others are suffering, he speaks of suffering; when they are happy, he speaks of happiness;
in all circumstances, he remains with an unconquered heart. (11)
"Unconquered by suffering and pain" means not overcome; that is to say, patient. || 11 ||
Nothing other than well-performed action pleases him;
indeed, for the great, it is their very nature not to act otherwise.
The word "nanu" is used as an address. That which is "not viceṣṭita"—meaning the avoidance of conduct not sanctioned by the scriptures—is indeed the very nature of the great ones.
In the reading "yatna-viçeṣṭitam," it refers to conduct prompted solely by effort in accordance with the scriptures. 12.
He never indulges in either aesthetic relish or insipidity;
though free from passion, he wanders among worldly objects as if possessed of passion, seeking his purpose yet remaining unattached to what is not beneficial.
He does not wander about among objects of wealth, having become a petitioner for riches, characterized by a lack of aesthetic appreciation and an absence of affection. || 13 ||

Just as one does not experience joy or dejection regarding the experiences of pleasure and pain that arise in succession according to the conventions of the scriptures, so too, even when the future arrives, one neither feels elation nor despair.
Though not yet arrived and untouched by pleasures and pains, it approaches as if it were touching them; consequently, it does not at all undergo joy or dejection.
They are seen to be greatly delighted, and likewise they are seen to be suffering;
yet these actors on the stage of saṃsāra do not abandon their inner nature. (15)

He explains with the presentation of their characteristics that which was stated—that they are as if untouched by pleasure and pain—by saying, "And being elated," etc. He also explains the statement, "neither joy nor dejection," by presenting the underlying reasons:
his intention is that the mere simulation of signs such as elation on their part results in a fruit that is equivalent to the performance of actors.
He distinguishes [them] as "the actors in the performance of saṃsāra. || 15 ||
For those who see reality, there is no attachment toward things considered "mine"—such as wealth and children—just as there is none for bubbles upon the water. 16.

Though indeed devoid of attachment, he whose heart is moistened by the most profound affection remains established in his proper order, demonstrating a disposition full of tenderness, like one who is wise.
Like those standing in the current of a river, fools vainly touch sense-objects;
poisoned by the very existence of the body, they dissolve within the belly of the senses.
But the ignorant do not know how to enjoy sense objects with the same detachment as those who possess true knowledge; thus he says: "Like winds.

For they, being deluded by their own existence—which is characterized solely by the body-self—become like those fainting from the heat of distress and, in order to pacify the distress of desire and the like, dissolve themselves with excessive attachment into the belly of the sense objects. And even though they have thus dissolved, [they do not find peace].

The hell-beings situated in the boiling current of the Vaitaraṇī river touch the objects of the senses—like winds—from above only slightly and in vain; the meaning is that they are unable to find rest by experiencing the objects of the senses in their entirety according to reality. || 18 ||
Outwardly engaged in all customary conduct, yet inwardly cool toward all objects of desire,
he remains eternally unpossessed within, as if possessed.

"Whose conduct is equal to all the disciplined (śiṣṭas)" and "in which all objects are cool"—these two are adjectives qualifying the action of abiding (sthitikriyā). The ellipsis is "the knower of reality (tattvavid) abides. || 19 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
"O leader of sages, who knows such a true nature of his?
Tell me, whether it be truth or falsehood; for even one who is ignorant may indeed be like this. (20)

Rāma raises a doubt: "The recognition of one who knows reality through the aforementioned characteristics is difficult to achieve, because these characteristics are seen even in fools, hypocrites, deceivers, and ascetics who have acquired them merely by rote. He says:
"Is such a nature—definable by the stated characteristics—real or unreal?"

Or who is able to discern whether [this] is imagined through hypocrisy and the like? For, since even an ignorant hypocrite in this world possesses such characteristics as you have described—this is the syntactical connection. || 20 ||
O Sage, those whose minds are not beautiful, though they practice celibacy like horses, become such as these for the sake of strengthening their false status as ascetics. (21)
Those whose minds are not pleasing [to others] resort to such imitation of the likeness of the learned, their hearts being dependent on honor, worship, and the like.
By the word "ascetic" (tapasvin), such a reputation is indicated;
the meaning is that it is for the sake of strengthening the fame of one's own asceticism, which has been falsely imagined. || 21 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Whether it be unreal or real, know that such a nature is excellent; for this is the experience of one's own inherent nature established within those who know the Vedas.

Even these characteristics, though cultivated for the sake of hypocrisy, result only in auspicious consequences; therefore, one should not disregard those who possess such marks. For, with the intention that by following such people one may—by the grace of destiny—encounter even a knower of reality (tattvavid) endowed with naturally perfected characteristics, Śrī Vasiṣṭha says:

He states the answer: "Or [it is] unreal. Such a nature, endowed with the aforementioned characteristics, is "excellent" (vara) because it is difficult to attain; however, for those who know the Vedas—that is, those who know the true essence of the Vedic meaning—this collection of characteristics exists and is established solely by the power of the experience of one's own nature, not produced by force. This is the meaning. || 22 ||

Though unpossessed by worldly passion, they act like those still possessed by it; though free from desire, they behave as if full of desire; devoid of laughter, they suddenly laugh at the ignorant, moved by compassion. (23)
Unpossessed means not being attached to the fruits of actions. || 23 ||
All that is seen as reflected in the mirror of the mind is but a deceptive floor;
perceiving it as unreal, one sees it like gold in the hand within a dream.
They perceive all that is visible as appearing within the mirror of the mind, like a deceptive mosaic, and as being unreal. 24.
No one perceives their inner coolness,
just as living beings perceive from afar only the fragrance of sandalwood trees.
But those who have understood what is to be known, whose intentions are thus purified—they know Him just as those without eyes perceive the feet of a snake within a hole. (26)
Although those who do not know the true nature [of reality] are unable to understand the essential form of the knower of truth, nevertheless, the knowers of truth certainly do know it; thus he says:
"But those who... [referring to] the "feet" as steps. || 26 ||
These unsurpassed ones conceal their supreme state;
for how could a priceless cintāmaṇi gem be found in a marketplace for common riches? || 27 ||

Hypocrites, however, proclaim their characteristics, whereas those who know the truth conceal them; with this distinction in mind, he says "the inner state" (bhāvam), intending that they may be recognized by this very difference. To the question of why they conceal it, he replies with "by the vulgar" (grāmyaiḥ):
like a wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi) that is priceless and impossible for the vulgar—those belonging to villages, cities, and the like—to purchase in the marketplace.
Who is extended? The meaning is: no one at all. || 27 ||
Since their being lies in that concealment and not in manifestation,
O dear one, they are indeed free from latent desires, free from duality, and free from pride.

With the intention that one should know, "This person is a hypocrite and not a knower of reality," by the sign of his public display of his own virtues—just as one knows "this is not a wish-fulfilling gem" (cintāmaṇi) by the sign of its being displayed for sale in a shop—he says: "In that... [tasmin]. Regarding those knowers of reality, their intent (bhāva), or rather their purpose (tātparya), lies solely in concealing their own virtues and such, and not in displaying them to those intent on seeing them.

Regarding their renown: because they are free from worldly existence (*nirvāsana*), being devoid of the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of pride, fame, and attachment; [the Lord] addresses them with "O friend" (*aṅga*).
But those who are free from solitude, pride, poverty, and the contempt of people—O Rāma, they bring such happiness as even those of great supernatural powers (*maharddhi*) cannot. (29)

He explains why they do not desire fame and the like with the verse beginning "ekānta": the sense is that when there is the abundance of fame, honor, wealth, and so forth, there arises distraction through thousands of misfortunes such as pride and attachment to social circles, which results in the interruption of the experience of the bliss of the Self.
*Amāna* is the avoidance of honor; *daurgatya* is the state of possessing nothing; *avajñaptayaḥ* are the insults from people. (29)
The state of having known what is to be known has as its essence that which is to be realized through self-awareness;
it cannot be shown, nor is it seen even by one who knows it.

That state of having known what is to be known is one in which the essence—the unsurpassed bliss—is to be experienced solely through self-awareness and one's own direct experience. This cannot be shown to another; for even by one who knows it, it is not seen—that is, it does not become an object of sight—but rather it manifests itself through its own self-luminosity. This is the meaning. || 30 ||
"May people know this merit of mine; may they offer me honor"—such is the striving of those possessed by ego, but not of those whose minds are liberated from it.

O Raghava, even for the ignorant, the fruits of ritual action— such as traveling through the sky of consciousness and so forth— are accomplished here in this world by means of mantras and medicinal herbs.

The fruits of practices such as the recitation of mantras, including the power of traveling through the sky and so forth, are accomplished even by the ignorant; the particle *cit* is used here to indicate their abundance. || 32 ||
Whoever is capable of depositing a particular kind of affliction, he necessarily reaps a corresponding fruit, whether he be enlightened or ignorant. (33)

Just as the fragrance of sandalwood exists within the sandalwood tree itself, so too does the fruit of spiritual vibration exist within the heart of everyone; indeed, it is certainly attained by one who possesses that vibration.

The fruit of all beings' performed and prohibited actions exists within their own heart alone as something of a previously non-existent nature; and that, having manifested in time, is fully attained. || 34 ||
He who possesses the latent impression of egoism and the sense of duality regarding the reality of visible objects accomplishes the fruits of actions such as traveling through the sky. (35)

The meaning is that he who possesses duality—characterized by the latent impression of egoism (ahaṃtā-vāsanā) in the form of the thought "I shall be the enjoyer" regarding objects perceived as signs of supernatural powers (siddhi)—achieves the fruits of actions such as the power of moving through the air (khecarī-siddhi). || 35 ||
He who knows that "this is nothing," or that it is "delusion" or "space," being free from latent tendencies, how could he perform actions driven by the whirlwind of karma? (36)

This collection of accomplishments is nothing at all—mere illusion, a mere delusion of the mind, or simply the sky, which is the space of consciousness as its substrate. He who, being wise and free from latent tendencies (*vāsana*), knows this to be so, is a knower of reality (*tattvajña*).

How could such a person perform the rites of mantras, herbs, and the like, which yield fruits such as the power of flight (*khecaratva*) that consists primarily in wandering about in the whirlwind of karma?
He has no purpose whatsoever here in this world through action, nor any at all through inaction; nor does he have any dependence on any being for any object of desire. (37)
There is nothing on earth, nor in heaven among the gods, anywhere at all, that can incite greed in one whose mental disposition is noble and who has realized the Self. (38)
For one for whom the entire world is but a blade of grass or even a speck of dust, what else indeed could there be that would become an object of desire? (39)

The particle *eva* is used here in the sense of "entirety. For that wise one to whom the entire world is nothing more than a blade of grass or even a speck of dust, what else that is not of the nature of the Self could have attained the status of being acceptable? That is to say, nothing at all. || 39 ||
Having brought the journey of the world to its conclusion, the sage, with a perfectly fulfilled mind, remains as he is and departs just as he came. (40)

He for whom the journey of the world has been brought to completion and whose activity for the sake of gathering people has ceased, follows—that is, conforms to—the conduct of the cultured as it has come down and as it was attained. 40.
Ever inwardly cool, silent, with the forest of his mind become a being of pure essence,
he has the appearance of a full ocean, his intention profound yet manifest.
Like a lake overflowing with elixir, it maintains joy within itself or bestows it upon another, like the stainless full moon.
It maintains its own bliss and brings it about for another as well. || 42 ||
The celestial realms, golden with groves of mandāra blossoms, do not gladden [the heart] as much as the intellects of the wise. (43)
He clarifies its quality of being refreshing with the words "Mandāra... etc. The celestial realms are Nandana and so forth;
"by those with the intellects of scholars" means by means of enlightenments. || 43 ||
With moon-like faces and with springtime, those of great and noble intent [attained] the essence among those who enjoy the world's fortune,
fragrance, and beauty.
For the discerning one who grasps the essence, like the fragrant summer season, takes the essence from those who enjoy light through the lunar orbs;

from those who enjoy fragrance, he takes the essence through the spring seasons; and from the great ones who know reality, he takes the essence through their unassailed intentions—intentions that are unhurt by passion and the like. Thus it is with respect to those things indicated by the copulative compound.
The connection is by way of transposition. The meaning is that its essence is obtained through those [means] alone, and not elsewhere by other means. || 44 ||
"This entire universe is mere delusion, a hollow illusion like a magician's trick"; having thus resolved, day after day, he abandoned his desires. (45)

If it is asked what essence the great ones have grasped from their inner dispositions, he says— in the verse beginning with "bhrāntimātram" (verse 45)— that first, through the vision of the world's falsity, they gradually abandon all worldly desires.
The wise person regards sufferings such as cold and heat, even when they have occurred within his own body, with indifference, as if they had occurred in the body of another.
Then he says—beginning with "cold" (śīta)—that one takes up the essence characterized by endurance toward the pairs of opposites such as cold and heat. || 46 ||
Through a disposition noble with compassion and through a conduct as steady as a creeping vine,
he who is devoid of worldly moisture attains a state of stability that possesses the essence of the essenceless.

Immediately thereafter, he takes up the essence of virtues such as firm reliance on the nature of compassion for all beings and contentment even with whatever water may be obtained; thus he says: "By compassion... In this way, being devoid of worldly flavor and dispassionate, he possesses through compassion a noble disposition—a vow to protect the distressed even at the expense of his own everything.

Like a creeper (*vratati*), by means of a steadfast mode of conduct that gathers the shade, fruit, flowers, and so forth— namely, the sole purpose of benefiting others— and which relies firmly upon its own tree,

he attains such a state of essence (*sāratā*) characterized by contentment with whatever is obtained, even water alone, as the cause of his satisfaction. Thus, through this mode of conduct, he moves toward that essential state in which even mere water serves as the basis for contentment.
Conducting worldly affairs as they arise in accordance with common human custom, he stands preeminent above all beings, both moving and unmoving. (48)
In the sense of elevation above, or in the sense of Brahman, whose root is directed upwards. || 48 ||
Having ascended the palace of wisdom, the wise man, who is beyond grief, looks upon grieving people;
like one standing on a mountain peak looking down at those on the ground, the wise man beholds all. 49.
He demonstrates that very state of being situated above: "Wisdom" (prajñā), [verse 49].
For a long time, the noble-minded one was tossed by the waves in the ocean;
but having reached the further shore, he attains supreme rest. (50)

At that very moment, he is liberated from the sufferings of distraction caused by long-standing passion and the like, and attains perfect rest; thus it is said: "For a long time... He was agitated and tossed about by the waves, namely the six internal fluctuations (ṣaḍūrmi). || 50 ||
With a peaceful disposition, he laughs at the worldly courses of former times; within him, the people remain as if smiling, yet they are shrouded in dense delusion.
"These perspectives on cyclic existence, which have drawn me down into the wilderness, are unreal yet they have captivated me"—thus he experiences wonder within himself. (52)
They are compared to those who, being blind, are lost in a wilderness due to straying from the path; they have carried [him] away, that is, they have deluded him. || 52 ||
"Even the eightfold sovereignty of vision, though undesired, is to me like a blade of grass"— thinking thus,
he approaches [his goal] with tranquility, and even while smiling, he feels no pride.
Having understood this thus, even while smiling or slightly laughing, he does not fall into pride or arrogance. || 53 ||
Some had mountain caves as their dwellings, some took refuge in holy hermitages; some lived the life of householders, while others remained wandering extensively.
He states that there is no restriction even regarding his place and so forth with the words "some person" (kaścit). The word division is either "aṭan" (wandering) or "raṭan" (shouting). || 54 ||
One was a wanderer for alms, another was a solitary ascetic; one observed the vow of silence, and another was devoted to meditative absorption.
One was renowned as a wise man, another was a listener of the Vedas and the Smṛtis;
one was a king, another a twice-born brahmin, and another remained like an ignorant man. (56)
One who has attained perfection through pills, collyrium, the sword, and so forth, moves through the sky;
another lives by means of crafts and arts; and another assumes the appearance of a commoner. (57)
One had abandoned proper conduct, another was a leader among Vedic scholars; one behaved like a madman, while another had taken up the life of a wandering mendicant.
The Puruṣa is neither the body and so forth, nor is he anything such as the mind;
the Puruṣa is that which is called consciousness, and it never perishes at any time.

Having heard the words "What kind of person is the Supreme Person (*puruṣottama*)" in Rāma’s question, and anticipating a desire to know its meaning, [the Lord] describes the Person and demonstrates His supremacy with the word "Person" (*puruṣa*). The meaning is that because He does not perish—due to His imperishability—He alone is the Supreme. || 59 ||
He is neither to be cut nor burned, neither to be moistened nor dried; He is eternal, all-pervading, stable, immovable, and ancient.
He says "indestructible" (acchedya) to show that this very [Self] is supreme even because it is untouched by causes of destruction such as cutting, splitting, and so forth. || 60 ||
Thus, for one who is perfectly awakened, let him remain wherever he may be in whatever manner;
what is the use of rules regarding place or non-place? (61)

It is precisely through the thorough knowledge of the reality of such a Supreme Person (Puruṣottama) that one becomes a knower of truth and a Supreme Person, and not merely by the observance of the boundaries of caste and stage of life (varṇāśrama). With the intention that his status as the Supreme Person does not depart even in the absence of those [observances], he says: "Thus," [referring to] the state.

The statement regarding the power of knowledge—"What could be accomplished by him through the restriction of abiding by the rules of the castes and stages of life?"—is as hollow as the claim, "I gave the Arunmukha ascetics to the jackals. || 61 ||
Let it enter the netherworld, let it traverse the sky and wander through the circle of the directions until it is ground to dust;
yet this pure consciousness is undecaying and shall not go to destruction—it is that peaceful, unborn, and auspicious state, like the expanse of space.
Reinforcing the very fact that he is an indestructible person, he concludes with the verse beginning "pātālam":

"Let him enter the netherworld by the power of one who knows reality, desiring his own destruction; or let him leap upward beyond the sky, or wander through the circle of the quarters—with whatever wandering he may do."
From the grinding against thousands of mountain rocks, such as those of Mānasottara and Lokāloka, only crushing or total pulverization is conceivable.
In the reading "let it go to pulverization," the meaning is: "let it cause itself to be ground by thousands of mountain rocks.
Nevertheless, this essential nature of the Knower of Reality—which is unattached, non-dual, pure consciousness, and ageless—does not undergo destruction.
The meaning is that, because it is like the expanse of space, it is auspicious, free from affliction, eternal, and of the nature of unsurpassed bliss. || 62 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and second canto, titled "The Instruction on the Non-existence of Death and Other Phenomena," in the Nirvāṇa Section of the glorious Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa, the Great Epic of Vasiṣṭha, composed by the Sage. 102.

Thus ends the one hundred and second chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Absence of Death and Other Phenomena," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the glorious Vāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa, within the Tātparya-prakāśa commentary. 102.
The One Hundred and Third Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
It is merely a state of being, or merely an appearance; it shines forth as nothing more than peace.
How and when could there be the destruction of that which is pure consciousness alone, without beginning or end?
The consciousness's eternity, unity, and sovereignty are established here;
furthermore, the greatness of this true scripture and its beneficial purpose are taught in this work.

In this regard, he first establishes the indestructibility of the universal consciousness (*cit-sāmānya*) by the force of universal experience, stating: "It is mere light" (*bhā-mātram*). Through direct perception, it is evident that for everyone, there exists a mere manifestation of light—either as the inner witness of the waking and dreaming states, or as the witness of ignorance, deep sleep, and so forth during the state of profound slumber; or else, it is merely the manifestation of objects. Thus, the mere light of the inner self (*pratyag-ātma-bhā-mātram*) indeed shines for all.

By the word "and" (ca), it is established through the evidence of worldly convention (*vyavahāra*), legal codes (*smṛti*), and so forth, that there exists pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) which is without beginning or end.

How could there be the destruction of that, and by what cause? For a cause not established [by valid means] is unproven, while a cause that is established cannot be the cause of its own destruction because it depends upon it. Thus, when could such a destruction ever occur?
The sense is that even such time, whose establishment is dependent upon that [consciousness], is dependent upon it for its very existence. || 1 ||
To that same extent, the Person (puruṣa) never perishes;
for pure consciousness (cinmātra) does not perish—how and how could it ever be born again?

"Let it be that pure consciousness alone is indestructible; what does that matter to the Puruṣa? To this he replies: "Only that much," etc. He says, "If [it were destroyed]," because if that were destroyed, there would be no creation hereafter, as a creation cannot exist without a witness. || 2 ||
And pure consciousness is never anything other than itself for anyone, anywhere;
when it is identical in the experience of all, what indeed can that "otherness" possibly be? (3)
[Objection: "Surely another consciousness will arise, and from that, creation will proceed. To this, he says: "Not so" (*na ca*).

Is the difference between the subsequent consciousness and the prior consciousness to be postulated because of an experience of interruption in the interim, or because of a difference in character? It cannot be due to an experience of interruption, because experience itself is consciousness; therefore, as long as that [experience] exists...

Because a disjunction [of the cognition] is not established; nor is there any difference in character, for that would result in the loss of its nature as consciousness. If the experience is similar in all respects during the preceding and succeeding times, what kind of "otherness" or "distinctness" could it possibly be? The meaning is that it would be unreal. || 3 ||
For everything, snow is cold, fire is hot, and water is sweet;
but what kind of difference can there be here for pure consciousness, which is ever-luminous?

Consciousness does not undergo differentiation due to differences among persons, just as it does not do so due to differences in time; for, just as there is no perception of distinct qualities in objects such as the coldness of snow, no such diversity is experienced even within consciousness—thus he says: "Of all [consciousness] indeed... (4).
If it is said that pure consciousness perishes upon the destruction of the body, then why is there despair at death—the end of worldly existence—which ought to be a cause for joy? (5)

Now, we do not admit a general consciousness (*citsāmānya*) distinct from the specific cognitions characterized by the experience of pleasure and pain. And for those who maintain that the body is the cause of specific cognitions through the relation of delimitation (*avacchedakatā-sambandha*), and that the destruction of cognition follows from the destruction of that [body]— [The opponent objects: "But surely, since the body is the cause of specific cognitions through the relation of delimitation, and you accept that the destruction of cognition results from its destruction, how can there be a single, eternal consciousness? [The proponent replies: This is not so. For even if the body is the cause of specific cognitions through the relation of delimitation, it is not the cause of the manifestation (*abhivyakti*) of consciousness itself. Otherwise, one would have to conclude that consciousness is non-eternal, just like sound, because it depends on a cause. Furthermore, the body is merely the cause of the manifestation of consciousness, not its material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*). Therefore, even if the body perishes, the destruction of consciousness does not follow, just as the destruction of a jar does not entail the destruction of the universal "jar-ness" (*ghaṭatva*). Moreover, since consciousness is eternal and all-pervading, it cannot be delimited by a substance such as the body; rather, it is the body that is delimited by consciousness. Thus, the relation between them is one of the container and the contained (*ādhārādheya-bhāva*). Consequently, the destruction of the body does not lead to the destruction of consciousness. Furthermore, the body is not the cause of the production of consciousness, because consciousness is eternal. Nor is it the cause of its manifestation, because the manifesting agent is the mind (*manas*). Therefore, the objection is invalid. As has been stated: "The body is the cause of the manifestation of consciousness through the relation of delimitation, but it is not the cause of its production. Hence, even upon the destruction of the body, there is no destruction of consciousness. Thus, the existence of a single, eternal consciousness is established. It is this very consciousness that, when associated with the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas, is designated by various names such as "soul" (*puruṣa*), "knower" (*jña*), "enjoyer" (*bhoktṛ*), (*draṣṭṛ*), "the one to be heard" (*śrāvya*), "the hearer" (*śrotṛ*), "the one to be thought" (*mantavya*), "the thinker" (*mantṛ*), "the one to be touched" (*spraṣṭavya*), "the toucher" (*spraṣṭṛ*), one to be restrained" (*niyamya*), "the restrainer" (*niyantṛ*), "the one to be governed" (*ś
Having raised the doubt of the Cārvākas, Vaiśeṣikas, and others, he refutes it with the words "the body" (*śarīra*). Regarding the phrase "in the place of joy":
for you, liberation is indeed the destruction of suffering that does not coexist with the prior absence of suffering;

and that [liberation] is established through the destruction of the body, because upon the destruction of the general consciousness (*citsāmānya*), there is subsequently no means of establishing the body, suffering, and so forth. For indeed...

There exists no means of proof for that [state] apart from consciousness (cit). Nor can a future body be established without a means of proof, and without that [body], consciousness cannot be established as its means of proof.
Therefore, the meaning is that for the sake of liberation, there should be joy at death and not despondency. || 5 ||
Indeed, the sky of consciousness does not perish upon the destruction of the body;
even when the body has perished, the state of being a *piśāca* was witnessed by the barbarians among the kinsmen.

Thinking, "Let it be so then," he cuts off the hope of one who opens his mouth in expectation with the words "and not. For generally, *piśācas* afflict only their own kinsmen; the mention of both "kinsman" (*bandhu*) and "barbarian" (*mleccha*) is intended to indicate that *piśācas* are seen in many forms only in border regions. || 6 ||
If it is said that as long as there is existence of the body, there is consciousness, then why does a corpse not move when the body remains entirely intact? (7)

Furthermore, the claim that "the destruction of consciousness follows from the destruction of the body" is entirely inconsistent, because it contradicts the observation that consciousness ceases even while the dead body still exists; thus he says: "As long as... [it] does not move, nor does it perceive. || 7 ||

If the experience of a piśāca were an inherent property of the living soul, why would it not see that [relative] at all times? And why would it see him in such a manner only when the relative has died? (8)
If some Cārvāka were to say that the vision of a *piśāca* while one is alive is merely the behavior of a living barbarian (*mleccha*),
and not caused by a *piśāca* existing there due to the residual consciousness of a dead barbarian— having raised this doubt,
he refutes it with the words "the experience of a *piśāca*": why does he not see that *piśāca* at all times, even when there is no death of a kinsman?
The meaning is that you must state the reason for the two-fold restriction: why one sees only when [the object] is actually present? || 8 ||

If the specific nature of the living being (*jīvadharma*) were truly such [as it appears], how could a man not perceive that state— even when he has died in another land— as a false manifestation like that of a *piśāca*? (9)
If that living being is distinguished by the knowledge of his relative's death, and his specific attribute is the vision of a *piśāca*,
and if such a rule holds true, then even so, why does a man not see that *piśāca*-nature when someone else, while he is still alive, falsely imagines him to have died in another land? (9)
Therefore, since it is the self of all, that pure consciousness is not restricted;
whatever it knows in whatever place and in whatever manner, it perceives that very thing there.

Therefore, since differentiation and destruction are impossible for consciousness (cit), its nature as the self of all things being established, it is not restricted even by the limitations imposed by objective reality. Thus, whatever object a thing knows in whatever place or time, it perceives that very object as its own self; the meaning is that there is no such knowable object existing separately from it. || 10 ||
Whatever kind of consciousness arises as entirely undisturbed and monolithic, experience is indeed of that very nature; its own intrinsic essence is the cause here.
And thus, at the beginning of creation, because of His desire for truth, consciousness—remaining uncontradicted—became exactly as it was by the nature of His own volition;
and even now, the experience of all people is precisely of that same nature. || 11 ||
Nothing else can possibly exist here as the cause at the very beginning of creation; tell me, what could that which exists now have been, and of what nature and how? (12)

The meaning is: apart from the knowledge of Brahman, whose will is true, no other cause such as Pradhāna, atoms, and so forth, is possible at the beginning of creation; for what kind of thing could exist apart from Brahman, and how could it be the cause?
Let the disputants now explain this before me through both scripture and reasoning, and I shall immediately refute it.
The splendor of conceptual construction never arose at the beginning of creation, nor does it appear now;
the manifestation of the world is merely the sky of consciousness shining forth.
What then is your established doctrine? He states it: "At the very beginning of creation," etc. (13).
One realizes that this visible world is merely a manifestation;
for apart from the realization that it is "visible," where could its visibility exist? (14)
If only the sky of consciousness (*cinnabhas*) shines, then why do all people perceive it as the "visible world" (*dṛśya*)? To this he replies:
"Where has the reality of this which is being grasped—such as nacre-silver, a mirage, or hair-nets—ever been seen apart from that sky of consciousness? This is the meaning. (14)
The cleverness of one's own wonder is beautifully awakened by consciousness through the sky of the mind;
it is perceived as the visible world through awakening, yet it is not perceived due to ignorance.

And thus, the meaning of the conclusion is this: the visible world is nothing but the cleverness of the wonder of one's own consciousness (cinnabhas); therefore, through the awakening of waking and dreaming, it is perceived by way of aesthetic relish (rasāt), whereas in deep sleep, it is not perceived due to the absence of such awakening. || 15 ||
Awakening and non-awakening are of that very same nature, likewise free from affliction;
here, the distinction exists only in words and not in reality, therefore there is no such thing as the state of being an object of perception.
If so, what are that awakening and non-awakening? To this he says: "Awakening. That is the very nature of the sky of consciousness (*cinnabhas*), not of the insentient.

Therefore, it is one and the same in its essential self. For the form of non-awakening cannot be established apart from awakening. And when awakening exists, the object of the sky there is difficult to find; thus, as in the case of "the head of Rāhu is indeed Rāhu," the distinction is merely verbal and not real.
The meaning is that it exists for its own sake. || 16 ||
Know that which was previously seen by them to be non-investigation;
since that has now been destroyed by investigation, where can it be seen? (17)

Alternatively, he says "yā ca" (and that which... [verse 17] to show that the very failure to investigate its own true nature is the objectivity of consciousness, and that this objectivity is destroyed by investigation.
In this very investigation into the knowledge of the Self, let there be an effort of the intellect;
through such effort, supreme practice is attained, which bestows the accomplishment of both worlds. (18)
Therefore, he says "In this very [investigation]" to show that I have stated many times that one must exert great effort in investigation itself.

He asks what will result from such effort in investigation and answers with "By effort": it bestows the attainment of knowledge either in this world or in the next. Thus, it is said in the Sūtra: "There is repetition, because of the instruction given more than once. And: "That which belongs to this life [is attained] unless there is an obstacle to its commencement."
"Because of the perception of that. || 18 ||
O virtuous one, although this subsiding of ignorance has arisen within you here, it will not attain perfection without practice. (19)

Now, one might object: "Since the instructional statement directed toward an eternally immediate reality will, by its single application, pacify ignorance and reveal that reality, what is the use of practice? To this he replies: "The pacification of ignorance... [and] "attainment" means the establishment in *jīvanmukti* (liberation while living). || 19 ||

Having completely abandoned agitation and having set aside [all distractions] for even a moment every day, let this scripture, which is beneficial and wholesome for both worlds, be reflected upon. (20)

To the question, "Then, relying upon which text should this inquiry be practiced, or by what means can awakening be swiftly accomplished? he says: "Not so. By a person endowed with the means such as tranquility (*śama*) and the rest, having abandoned laziness, discontent, agitation, and their causes—namely, eating at will and harmful associations—one should for a moment observe the discipline of service to the teacher and so forth.
Having taken up this scripture called the Mahārāmāyaṇa, let it be reflected upon daily by your command. || 20 ||
Even though it has been understood, this knowledge of the Self remains as if unknown for you highly fortunate ones, without collective practice.

And in that regard, he says "it is known" (*vijñātam*) to show that the collective practice of many fellow students together, through mutual verification of experience, is the cause for the immediate stabilization of knowledge. [For those who have] not known it, it is as if unknown due to forgetfulness;
[this applies to] those of great fortune who possess various kinds of misconceptions and the like. (21)
Whoever desires an object and strives for it in that manner will certainly attain it, provided he does not turn back out of weariness.
He says "yaḥ" (verse 22) to show that because knowledge is difficult to attain, one should not abandon listening out of a sense of agitation.
Therefore, turn away from this investigation of false scriptures;
you shall attain peace through the true scripture, just as one attains the fortune of victory from battle.
He states that those who have desisted from the study of treatises on the non-self should practice this [true] scripture, beginning with the words "Therefore":
"the glory of victory," meaning either the glory of victory over the earth or the glory of victory over heaven. || 23 ||
Whether in solitude or in the lack of solitude, this river of the mind flows;
wherever it is directed with effort, there it attains its stability.
"Through effort" means through the exertion of effort to block another, opposing stream. || 24 ||
Apart from this scripture, there has never been, nor will there ever be, a means to the highest good;
therefore, for the sake of supreme awakening, let this alone be investigated. (25)
The means for discernment is more excellent—that is, more praiseworthy. || 25 ||
By reflecting upon this oneself, the supreme awakening is experienced;
it removes the fatigue of the path of saṃsāra, unlike a boon or a curse.

The meaning is that by one who has personally investigated that scripture, the realization of the reality of the Self is experienced through direct perception (*pratyakṣatayā*), and not—as with a boon or a curse—delayed until another time. || 26 ||
That which was not accomplished by your father, nor by your mother, nor even by meritorious deeds— that supreme good, once fully understood, will swiftly bring you prosperity.

He says "that which" to show that this scripture is the most beneficial even in comparison with one's father, mother, and others—provided it is thoroughly understood through inquiry, or as it is said, "thoroughly understood [knowledge] is the highest good" (śreyas) when directly perceived. || 27 ||
O holy man, this cholera-like affliction consisting of the bonds of existence is treacherous;
without self-knowledge, it will never subside, however long it may last. (28)
This illusion, consisting of great delusion, persists as the false notion "I am";
through the contemplation of the meaning of the scriptures, may this state of supreme wretchedness be swiftly abandoned.
Let this illusion consisting of great delusion, which persists as the false notion "I am," and the supreme wretchedness brought about by it, be abandoned.
Go to the sky—which is of the single nature of space—[leaving behind] that which is sweet only at first sight;
like serpents licking their own insides, you have been licking the void wind within.

O wise ones, while tasting the multitude of sense-objects—which are sweet at first sight but empty like space—do not enter this endless cycle of existence that is of the same nature as space; do not be like greedy, hungry snakes licking the air, which is devoid of any essence.
Alas, your days pass away unnoticed as they come and go; for by those very same days, you are being led toward death while occupied with worldly affairs.
This consolation exists for you who are partakers of fear only so long as the limit of death has not arrived within a few days. (32)
As long as the limit of life in the form of death has not yet arrived, you possess the consolation that comes from being fit to rely upon the true scriptures. || 32 ||
When death approaches, you will experience bitter torment and anguish,
wherein there is the severing of limb from limb and the application of cool sandalwood paste.
Regarding what will happen after that, he says: "As they approach.

The meaning is that you shall experience such intense torment that even the severing of each and every limb must necessarily be endured as if it were the application of cool sandalwood paste. || 33 ||
Those deluded by wealth purchase status and riches at the price of their very lives;
why then, through their intellect, do they not purchase the ageless state according to the scriptures? (34)

The meaning is this: it is a marvel that foolish people, possessed by dense delusion, purchase wealth and the pride of victory even at the cost of their lives in battle and the like; yet, by means of the realization of reality attained through the methods prescribed in the scriptures—such as discernment, dispassion, and hearing—the ageless state of liberation, why do they not purchase it? This is truly astonishing. || 34 ||
How can those who, with supreme effort, place their foot in the sky, tolerate the foot of the enemy that is ignorance upon their own heads? (35)

How can those discerning ones— who, by the mere knowledge of their own true nature without effort, establish their station in the supreme, most excellent space of Brahman, the sky of consciousness, and who are capable of slaying the enemy of ignorance— tolerate the foot of that enemy of ignorance upon their own heads by neglecting the true scriptures and other means? || 35 ||
Having attained freedom from pride and delusion, go to that state which is not base;
by awakening to one's own self, the very root of great calamities is scraped away.

O people, since you have attained such firm discrimination from which pride and delusion have departed, realize the Truth and proceed toward the path of liberation; do not go toward the base path of worldly existence. || 36 ||
Having heard this, which I have been uttering day and night for your sake, let it be realized by yourself through your own self. (37)
"Vasiṣṭha has been engaged for a long time in awakening me in many ways;

let him be freed from the suffering of his parched throat. Out of compassion for me, or perhaps out of an excess of affection, thinking "having properly heard my words, let your own Self be awakened by you," he said: "To him who was prattling... [referring to] whom.

Having beheld me— who am world-renowned, intent on awakening you, prattling day and night for your sake, and constantly afflicted by the exhaustion of parching my throat and other such labors— having seen me clearly with compassion and having respectfully listened to these words of mine, [you should act] with your own awakened self.

The verb in the imperative mood (*loṭ*) is used here in the sense of a prayer: "Having abandoned the state of selfhood delimited by the body, senses, and so forth, let the true nature of Brahman as the Self be attained. || 37 ||
If one does not seek a remedy this very day against the calamity of death, what can that deluded person do when death has actually arrived? (38)
To those who think, "What is the use of self-knowledge right now? We shall do it later at some point," he says: "Right now.
(38) "Except for this book, no other book will surely be effective for the realization of one's own Self; it should be grasped like sesame seeds by those seeking oil. (39)

"No other exists"—this is the ellipsis. "Surely" means with certainty; he is to be accepted with the understanding that he is "one who accomplishes the purpose," i.e., one who fulfills desired aims. || 39 ||
This scripture illuminates the knowledge of the Self like a lamp;
it awakens one quickly like a father, and delights one exceedingly like a beloved wife. (40)
He states what its superiority is over other internal treatises: "knowledge of the Self. This means knowledge whose nature is the Self. (40)
Even though knowledge exists within them, that which has not been understood from the collection of scriptures is difficult to grasp;
yet they will understand it from this [work], which is sweet—of this there is no doubt. (41)
That knowledge which is their very self-nature—though existing and eternally attained—is not known through other scriptures;
they shall know it from this scripture. 41.
This supreme narrative, among the primary perspectives of the scriptures, grants awakening with ease; it is heart-pleasing and truly unprecedented. 42.
Among the principal narratives within the perspectives of the scriptures, this narrative is the most excellent.

In this narrative, there is nothing whatsoever that is unprecedented, nor anything fabricated by one's own imagination that is distinct from what is established in the tradition of those who know the beginningless reality; indeed, such a thing does not exist at all. 42.
One should contemplate this scripture with delight through various wonderful narratives; by doing so, a person attains the supreme state—of this there is no doubt. (43)
Even by investigating with diversion or curiosity, a person attains—that is, reaches—the realization of the Supreme Self. || 43 ||
For that awakening which has not yet been attained even now by unimpaired scholars is obtained from this [work], just as gold is extracted from sand. (44)

That realization which has not yet been attained even by the wise who are learned in all the scriptures is obtained from this treatise; just as gold is obtained from sand that has been sifted through washing at a gold mine, so it is here. 44.
One should never, at any time or place, revere the author of a treatise;
rather, one should always revere the meaning of the treatise itself, which bestows experience joined with reasoning. (45)

Now, one might object: "If knowledge is indeed derived from this very scripture, then from what scripture did its author himself know it? If we can know it from the very same source from which he knew it, then what hope is there for the arising of knowledge from this scripture for us, if he composed it without having known it himself? Anticipating such doubts, he says:

Regarding the phrase "the author of the treatise": if this treatise were not endowed with reasoning and culminated in direct experience, then one would have to reflect upon the author's cognition as the cause of the treatise's validity, thinking, "This treatise possesses validity rooted in the cognition of its author. However, since this treatise is inherently endowed with thousands of reasonings and is itself a source of direct experience, [such reflection is unnecessary].
