The meaning is that since all doubt is removed solely through one's own direct experience, it is always proper to immerse oneself in that very [experience]; therefore, one should never hesitate to plunge in due to any suspicion regarding the author of the scripture. || 45 ||
Oneness should not be practiced by those who destroy themselves—those who, out of ignorance, envy, and delusion, fail to reflect and disregard the meaning of the scriptures. (46)
For this very reason, he says "out of ignorance" (ajñānāt) to show that one should not cultivate friendship with those intent on disregarding this scripture. "Oneness" (ekatā) here means friendship.
The intention is that when the spiritual science (adhyātma-śāstra) is disregarded, the failure to attain self-knowledge (ātmajñāna) itself constitutes a "murder of the self" (ātmahatyā). || 46 ||
I indeed know these things exactly as they are—just as I am, as you are, and as these thoughts are;
for such is my very nature, awakened by compassion. (47)

"In that case, how do you maintain friendship with us and other ignorant ones, since you have engaged in teaching out of compassion? To this he says: "I know," etc. O Rāma, these rows of listeners are endowed with such specific qualifications as they possess, and you too—

I know all this: what specific qualifications you possess as qualified disciples; how your intellects have been made proficient through hearing, retention, and practice; and what kind of command I have received from my father for the purpose of instructing you and others.

Therefore, the sense is that I have proceeded to instruct you out of compassion awakened by the rise of such good fortune on your part. For indeed, my nature is such that compassion is always aroused toward the distressed; I am not cruel.
Thus, the meaning is: "O you who desire my welfare, respect my words as I am compassionate. || 47 ||
A mere fragment of your own pure consciousness stands here to speak thus:
"I am a man, not a Gandharva, nor a god, nor a Rākṣasa. (48)

Alternatively, I am indeed your very self; by the power of your merit, I have come to instruct you on your own pure reality. Since you are the object of my supreme love, as if you were my very self, I have attained a state of friendship with you—thus he says in two verses beginning with "yuṣmat. Lava is of the nature of pure consciousness (*saṃvid-rūpa*).
The subtle object has been purified, but not the body of humans, gandharvas, and so forth; such is the meaning. || 48 ||
For you are indeed pure consciousness alone; that state of yours is exceedingly stainless.
By your merits, it is said, "I am established"—yet I am not, nor is there another.
"I am not another, distinct from your own self. The word "nanu" is used here as an exclamation of address. || 49 ||
Until the days of death arrive, turning everything into gloom, let the essence be gathered while there is still a sense of relish in the perception of things. (50)

Therefore, let this first essential point—which I have stated as being from the most authoritative source and characterized by detachment toward the perception of all things—be gathered and retained. 50.
He who does not seek a cure for the disease of hell while still here—once he has gone to that place where no medicine exists, what will he do, afflicted as he is by pain? (51)
Afflicted with pain, he is tormented by the agonies of hell. || 51 ||
As long as a sense of distaste for all existing things has not arisen,
the contemplation of those things does not reach attenuation.

If it is asked why dispassion alone is the supreme essence, it is because without it the thinning of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) cannot be accomplished; thus he says: "O one of great intelligence, there is never any means whatsoever for the soul to extricate itself from impurity except through the thinning of latent impressions. (53)
To the question, "Why should there be such diligence toward the attenuation of latent impressions (vāsanā)? he says: "The self... (verse 53).
If entities were to exist, then there would be a cultivation of the reality of things;
however, these do not exist at all here, just like the horns of a hare and so forth.
[Objection: But how can the attenuation of those latent impressions (*vāsanā*) be established while objects (*bhāva*) still exist? To this he says: "But objects... (Verse 54).
If they existed as realities, then regarding those objects—specifically toward a beneficial thing that is favorable to oneself—the notion would arise: "This object is essential for me;
it must be acquired," and so forth.
All worldly phenomena indeed lack charm when scrutinized;
their true existence is non-existent, for they fall apart upon investigation. (55)
Those worldly phenomena which do not exist when investigations by authoritative means have been conducted—how can they exist, or what are they that exist eternally? (56)

Now, one might object: "Even if these entities do not exist within the investigations of the Vedāntins, they certainly do exist within the investigations of the followers of Kapila, Kaṇāda, and others; so how can their non-existence be ascertained? To this, he replies with the word *prāmāṇika*. When investigations conducted according to valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) have been performed, what are those things that are not found? What is their nature? Are they of the form of individual objects, or of the form of all objects? Or are they always [existent]?
Or perhaps it exists at some time; in any case, the meaning is that it has already been shattered hundreds of times before. || 56 ||
All worldly phenomena, due to the total absence of a cause, have never arisen even at the beginning of creation; that which appears here is the Supreme. (57)
In that state which transcends all the senses, there is no cause for entities whose nature consists of the mind and the six senses;
nor is there a cause consisting of the mind and the six senses.
The sense is that even at the time of dissolution, it is impossible to conceive of the causal state of those things perceivable by the senses within Brahman.
How can there be a causeless cause for entities of various designations?
How can there be unreality in a real thing, or how can there be non-voidness in the void? (59)

He states another argument—that even a cause devoid of name and form is not possible for a world possessing name and form—with the words "of entities" (bhāvānām). Thus, it is likewise impossible to say that a void is the cause of the non-void, because it is illogical for one thing to undergo the transformation into the nature of another; he asks "whence? (kutaḥ) to express this. || 59 ||
For that which has a form [arises] from that which has a form, like a banyan seed and so forth;
how else could that entity, being a seed with a specific form, arise as something different? (60)

Thus, it is also incorrect to claim that the formless is the cause of that which possesses form; so he says: "Of that which possesses form. "If there were not even the slightest seed possessing some form, then the claim that 'the world possessing form arises from that' is a mere mockery. (61)
"Farce" means devoid of meaning, just like the words of a farce; such is the sense. || 61 ||
In that supreme state, there is no such thing as the relationship of cause and effect;
whatever is imagined by means of verbal prolixity is nothing but ignorance.
By being talkative, that is, by speaking excessively. || 62 ||
For it is experienced even by children that in the absence of auxiliary causes, an effect cannot arise from a [single] cause; rather, something else [an assemblage of conditions] must occur. (63)

"Tell me, what further cause for earth and the other elements is there that results in the experience of those subtle elements alone? And tell me, how can there be shadow in the midst of sunlight? (64)
He states "tanmātra" (only that) because consciousness cannot be the cause of the world even on account of its being the knower of the world,
since it is observed that the knower of a jar is not the cause of the jar. In this context,
the word "mātra" (only) is used to avoid the objection of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), which might arise from the observation that the potter's cognition of the jar is indeed the cause of the jar.
With the intention that consciousness cannot be the cause even because it is impossible for it to abide in the state of non-consciousness, he says: "chāyā" (like a shadow). || 64 ||
The notion that the world is a collection of atoms is likewise unreal;
it is spoken of out of ignorance as being like a bow made from a hare's horn. (65)
For this very reason, the Buddhists and others who maintain that atoms are the cause [of the world] are also refuted;
for one does not observe that a collection of supersensuous things can be perceived by the senses. With this intention, he says: "paramāṇu... (verse 65).
If the world is produced by an aggregate of atoms coming together, then it would perish by mere chance in darkness, and [be formed] again by mere chance. (66)

If atoms were to combine and create the world, then—given that they are constantly seen flying up and falling down in the sky—one would expect every house to have a mountain peak added to it daily, or a pit to appear like a well; thus he says in two verses beginning with "paramāṇu": "If atoms were to create the world by combining, Then every house would daily become like a mountain peak, Or like a hollowed-out well, Because of their constant rising and falling in the sky. (66)
Then, in every region and every house,
there will always be a new mountain peak of dust rising up, or perhaps a pit,
on that day.
On the day. || 67 ||

The "limb" (aṅga) of that world—that is, its constituent part—is the dust; in every region and in every house, it moves ever anew and freshly, as if it were a horn or a pit. This is the meaning. || 67 ||
And yet, nothing such as that is seen; for whom could such an action belong? It would be in vain for one who lacks merit; atoms, however, are merely inert matter.

Furthermore, no substance called an atom (*paramāṇu*), which is partless, is perceived by anyone; for even in the rays of light passing through a lattice window, only dust particles (*rajas*) possessing parts are seen. If it is argued that a partless entity is inferred as the ultimate limit of the series of its parts, this is not so, because such an entity would necessarily lack substantiality (*adravyatva*) due to its incapacity for conjunction. Indeed, a partless thing cannot enter into conjunction with another.

This is because conjunction is necessarily restricted to residing in a single part [of its substrata]. Nor is there a contradiction in the claim that without such [conjunction], the establishment of dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth is impossible.

Furthermore, whose work would it be to construct the world by joining atoms that are beyond the senses and as unreal as flowers in the sky? Is it the work of one who is not subject to transmigratory existence (*asaṃsārin*), or of one who is subject to transmigratory existence (*saṃsārin*)? In that regard:

First of all, it is quite evident that transmigrating beings lack the capacity to construct the world from atoms; therefore, that task must be attributed to either an incapable being, or to a Lord who is subject to worldly existence (*bhava*), or to one who is insentient (*jaḍa*). Among these, for the first [type], the creation of the world would be both futile and purposeless; for a Lord who is eternally liberated has neither a need for nor any purpose in such a creation.
It is possible to establish [the necessity of an agent] for creation; the meaning is that insentient atoms are not capable of engaging in creation on their own. || 68 ||
O friend, no action whatsoever occurs for anyone without being preceded by intelligence;
for what madman indeed would perform an action intentionally that is purposeless? (69)
[Objection: Surely a conscious being requires a purpose when creating with prior intelligence, but not so when acting without prior intelligence. To this, he says:

"No. O friend, that work of creation—the world of beings consisting of the four classes of living creatures, whose structure cannot be conceived even by the mind—is not possible for anyone to perform without prior intelligence.
But what madman would perform a fruitless action intentionally? || 69 ||
For that which is insentient, there is no prior volition;
without that, a collection of atoms cannot come into being, nor can any other agent be logically established. (70)

By this, even the hope that "the wind itself will effect the accumulation of atoms, and the accumulation of atoms will occur without any intentional activity" is refuted; thus he says: "of the insentient. For the wind, being insentient, lacks intentional effort (*īhā*) or movement (*ceṣṭā*).

Without that, the accumulation of atoms is not possible. Furthermore, at the time of dissolution (*pralaya*), the entire class of living beings—which is distinct from both the insentient and the omniscient [Lord]—[does not exist].
The conclusion is that because of the absence of a body and so forth, [the cause] is indeed incapable; thus, no agent is logically possible at the beginning of creation. || 70 ||
We ourselves are indeed of such a nature, people whose self is empty and whose essence is empty; we stand just as the men in your dream appear to you in that dream.

Now, if the world has indeed not arisen due to the absence of a creator, then what is our nature, or how do we abide in this world? To this he says: "We... These "we" are of the nature of space (*khātman*), devoid of the formal corporeality of bodies and so forth, being nothing other than the conscious self (*cidātman*). In this same way, these people as well are of the nature of space. Nevertheless, just as in a dream there are dream-men for you, [so too are these beings].
The meaning is that they exist in that manner solely through our own conceptual construction. || 71 ||
Therefore, nothing whatsoever is born, nor does anything exist;
thus, the pure sky of consciousness alone shines by itself within itself.
Thus, he states that "therefore" the doctrine of the non-duality of Brahman is established without obstacle due to all the evidence presented: "tasmāt" || 72 ||
The entire expanse of space has attained universal rest within the space of consciousness,
just as vibration, fluidity, and emptiness reside respectively in wind, water, and the sky.

Just as movement and so forth in the wind and other elements are non-different from them and have come to rest everywhere, so too is the space of the universe within the space of consciousness; this is the meaning. || 73 ||

Know that the nature of consciousness which exists in the interval when one reaches another place from a very great distance in the blink of an eye— that very nature is the form of the space of consciousness (cidvyoman).
He causes one to remember that form of the sky of consciousness which is empty of the world—a form already illustrated many times through analogies—by the words "deśāt" (from space), etc. (74).
For that is the intrinsic nature of all things, and they are composed of it;
being such, they have the form of space, and therefore the universe is space.

The ultimate nature of all things is the very space of consciousness (*saṃvidākāśa*). For this reason, the universe is that [space] by virtue of its being that [consciousness], and not by virtue of being a void; such is the meaning. || 75 ||
The transformation of that intrinsic nature occurs very slightly and swiftly;
though it is indeed non-different from the intrinsic nature itself, it exists as this world. (76)

That which is the supreme transformation of the nature of that very space of consciousness (cidākāśa), inseparable from its own essence by way of illusory manifestation (vivarta)—that alone is this world; such is the position held by those who perceive only the superficial appearance.
Therefore, there is never any difference between the world and consciousness;
the form of the two is one and the same, like that of the wind and its movement. (77)

When one who knows [the truth] travels from one place to another, that form which exists in the interval—whose nature is the pacification of all particularities—the wise know that to be the primary [form], and nothing else. (78)
The meaning is that this is the primary, perfected illustration of experience, and not any other. || 78 ||
That is the inherent nature of all beings; therein the wise abide.
Therefore, these elements, such as the earth and the rest, do not deviate from their constant meditation.
This entire universe is nothing but the sky of manifestation, a mere radiance of light;
the wise know its nature to be immutable and devoid of form.
This entire universe is nothing but the space of manifestation; and its manifestation is mere light alone.
It is neither born nor does it die; having come into being, it never becomes anything else anywhere.
The world is not other than the space of consciousness, just as emptiness is not other than the sky.
The universe does not exist, nor did it ever exist, nor indeed will it ever come to be;
this which appears is the peaceful sky of consciousness within the Supreme Self. 82.
Just as pure consciousness alone shines forth as the world before one in a dream,
so too does it shine forth by itself in this state called waking, which is itself a dream.

Since entities do not exist even at the beginning of creation, how can there be a body? Therefore, how could there be the state of being a body for consciousness, which is like the sky in a dream? (84)
Since at the beginning of creation there is the non-existence of entities such as earth and the rest, how could this body composed of earthly elements and so forth exist?
Therefore, this appearing state of being a body belongs to consciousness—which is of the nature of space—only as a dream.
One's own body is called the Self-born (Svayambhū), the first dream of the Great Consciousness;
from that [body] we subsequently arise, moving from one dream to another dream.
"Prior" means the first. "Those of us whose emergence is from this body of the Self-Existent (Svayaṃbhū)"—the meaning is that we are like those who, after one dream, enter another dream. || 85 ||
Because of this very reason, our minds will not turn away from these pustules that have arisen upon the boil, even with the greatest effort. (86)

For this very reason, our mind, even when operating with the utmost effort, will not immediately reach Brahman; because of the firmness of the delusion regarding an obstructed connection—just as a pimple arising on the neck [is not felt] due to the obstruction by the neck itself. Thus he says:
"Of the cheek," etc. (86).
The person was indeed Brahman alone, yet he is experienced as if possessing reality;
from that moment on, he remained so, for this extended world is not unreal.

Just as the throat itself, having existed in the form of a goiter, exists also in the form of the pustule located therein—and though not separate, is experienced as if it were a distinct reality—so too, Brahman alone, having become the unreal person characterized by Hiraṇyagarbha and the individual souls (vyaṣṭi-jīvas), is experienced as if it were real through that very state. This is the meaning. From the moment Brahman became the individual soul...
From that time forth, this entire world has remained spread out as a falsehood. || 87 ||
The world, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, arises as something false;
just as in a dream, it is likewise false and thus quickly perishes. (88)
"False" means untrue. Thus, like a dream, it perishes quickly; that too is indeed false. (88)
Just as the very sky of consciousness, having assumed the state of the universe, perishes within a dream,
so too does it perish within that which is called the waking state, without the universe ever having truly arisen.
Without having risen, without even reaching its arising—that is, birth—[it perishes]. || 89 ||
Even that which is experienced as false remains false, yet it stands as if true;
for consciousness itself arises in the form of cities and such things, just as in a dream. (90)
If it is indeed false, then how was it experienced, or how did it stand as if real?
Since neither [experience nor reality] is observed in the case of a rabbit’s horn and the like, he says here: "It was experienced.
Even that which is false was experienced, and even that which is false stood as if real; for, according to our view, that is nothing other than consciousness itself.
The meaning is "empty. || 90 ||
Just as [a reflection] appears with form though it is actually formless, so does consciousness abide as the world;
the space of consciousness is subtler than space, just as an atom is subtler than Mount Meru.
It is subtler than even space. Regarding this, there is an illustration: just as an atom (paramāṇu) of Mount Meru is subtle, so too is it subtle. || 91 ||
If its name were "atom" (aṇu), how could it have the nature of space?
Since there is no other cause, its form cannot be established. || 92 ||

If that is so, is its property of subtlety (aṇutā) even greater than that of space? He says "no," using the word "kila" (it is said). From where or in what context is this property called subtlety well-known such that it could indeed be a property of that Brahman? Then, what is the intended meaning of the mention of "subtlety"? He states it: "because of the cause," etc. It is not possible for the world, which is other [than Brahman], to have a gross form.
The meaning is that its nature is stated in that way in order to say that such a cause is absent. || 92 ||
Since he was unborn even at the beginning of creation, how could this world be born?
That which is a city in the space of consciousness during a dream is precisely what we have here.

[Objection: But surely, since we observe the birth of cities and the like from bricks and other materials, let the world itself be born from the world, not from Brahman. To this, he says: "At the very beginning of creation. How could that city and so forth, which were unborn at the very beginning of creation, have been born from the world? Furthermore, in a dream, cities and the like are seen even without bricks and such materials. That which is the city in the space of waking perception—
That very point remains unestablished even in our own doctrine regarding the city in a dream; therefore, the contradiction therein is evident—this is the meaning. || 93 ||
There is no difference between the mountain in a dream and the sky of consciousness, any more than there is between the void and the atmosphere;
for that which is called the sky of consciousness is itself the city of the dream.

Thus, with the intention that since there is no difference between the objects of dreams and the waking state, and because dream-objects lack differentiation from the space of consciousness (*cidvyoma*), the non-differentiation of waking objects is likewise established, he says: "Just as that which is called vibration is nothing other than the wind itself, so too is difference [nothing other than consciousness]."
The self, whose nature is both movement and stillness, is like the wind and like space.

Having stated that there is no difference [between them], he says "yadeva" (that which... to provide the two examples of vibration and wind, as well as air and space—[the one] resembling space being non-different from space. || 95 ||
Therefore, this world is perceived as having the form of the sky of consciousness alone;
everything is empty, without support, a manifestation of the sun of consciousness.
All this is indeed quiescent, devoid of setting and rising;
it is once-for-all luminous, stainless, as silent as a stone, and free from ailment.
It is once-for-all luminous, consisting of indivisible radiance. || 97 ||

Therefore, tell me: how do entities exist? From where do entities arise? Where is the cognition of entities? Where is duality? Where is unity? Where am I? Where are entities? And where are mental constructions? (98)
And thus, the state of the consciousness being free from conceptual proliferation (niṣprapañcatā) is established; so he says: "Therefore," etc. (98).

Ever-arisen even while engaged in worldly affairs, changeless, with a mind liberated from duality and unity, supremely cool within, abide in nirvāṇa; having attained the oneness of pure awakening free from disease, my dear, no phenomena exist.
Therefore, my dear friend, having attained identity with that reality whose nature is stainless and pure awakening through the realization of that reality, you remain eternally risen;

even while engaged in worldly activity, because you lack any attachment to it, you are changeless. Being one whose mind is liberated from the two mutually contradictory states of duality and unity, you have become supremely cool within.
Abide in Nirvāṇa, which is the bliss of unsurpassed joy; for the meaning is that those states which are causes of distraction do not exist for you.

Thus ends the one hundred and third canto, titled "The Exposition of the Unity of Ultimate Reality through the Instruction on the Existence and Non-existence of All Phenomena," in the *Nirvāṇa* section of the *Uttara-kāṇḍa* of the *Divya* (Divine) *Mokṣa-dharma* in the *Śrī Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa*, according to the *Ārṣa* (Sage) tradition.
Thus ends the one hundred and third canto, titled "The Exposition of the Unity of Ultimate Reality," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and fourth chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Space is the subtle element of sound; wind is the subtle element of touch.
The manifestation of energy arising from the excellence of union with that [light], and its cessation—this is the nature of water. || 1 ||
Just as the state of air and so forth arises from space and so forth according to experience,
the state of the world arising from consciousness alone is established by experience itself.

Regarding that which was stated— that pure consciousness alone appears in the form of the world like a dream— that very point is what all those seeking to know the reality of things through valid means, based on direct experience,
must ultimately reach, even after traveling far through various successions of conceptualizations regarding the creation of space and so forth.

Desiring to describe that which is to be taken as a refuge, he states the nature and status of space and the other elements as established by the non-Buddhist outsiders (tīrthika), beginning with the words "Space" and so forth. From the excellence of their conjunction—that is, from the intensity of their friction—is born the subtle element of form (*rūpa-tanmātra*), which is fire; the "pacification" (*śānti*) of that fire occurs through the subsiding of its heat and dryness.
The meaning is that the state of the nature of water is the subtle element of taste (rasatanmātra), characterized by coldness, fluidity, and cohesion. || 1 ||
"Since the world appears like a dream, how indeed can there be a sequence of these [elements], for how could form ever proceed from the formless sky? (2)

But since it is earth (*bhū*) that brings these [elements] together, the *saṃgha* (congregation/assembly) is the cause of condensation in the process of unification; thus, the subtle element of smell (*gandhatanmātra*) is the cause for the manifestation of the world as a dream-like appearance within consciousness itself. This is the sequential state of things. Regarding this, we ask: how does the form, beginning with space and ending with earth, proceed from the formless void? If someone were to say that it is air alone—

First, from space (*ākāśa*), that which is primarily characterized by action and touch arises; and since it lacks form (*rūpa*), it is in some respects like space, yet because it possesses touch and action, it is in some respects also like a material object (*mūrta*).
Thus, it will produce a material fire (*tejas*) in which the subtle element of form (*rūpa-tanmātra*) predominates. That is not so, because [space] is partless and immutable.

Because wind itself is unestablished; for nothing that is inactive and partless is capable of either initiating or transforming anything. Furthermore, if it were to undergo transformation in its entirety, then, due to the absence of space (*ākāśa*), air and the other elements would have no room to exist.
If only half or a small portion were transformed, then it would follow that space itself possesses parts. Let it be so.

If it is argued that [the effect] also possesses parts, then it would necessarily possess touch and motion; consequently, the production of air and so forth would be purposeless, and there would be no room for its existence or for the existence of its parts. Likewise, the production of the *rūpa-tanmātra* (subtle element of form) from formless air—whether by way of *ārambha* (origination) or *pariṇāma* (transformation)—is difficult to establish. For the qualities of the cause...

[The qualities of the cause] initiate the qualities of the effect. Now, color (rūpa) does not exist in air (vāyu). For transformation occurs through maturation (paripāka), and there is no maturation without fire (tejas). This same reasoning should be applied to the two subsequent elements as well. || 2 ||

Even if this [object] is postulated as being extremely distant from cognition, then what fault could there be in this case for the object that exists from the very beginning, which is as stainless as space? (3)

But surely, on the strength of experience alone, we shall conceive that from the immovable ether (ākāśa) arose the mobile air (vāyu); from the formless air, the formed fire (tejas); from that tasteless [fire], the watery water (vāri); and from that odorless [water], the fragrant earth (pṛthivī). Indeed, it is the Blessed Lady, the cognition whose nature is experience, who is everything for us.
If it is argued that, having set aside contradiction, one will establish objects according to experience, he says in response: "Having gone...

If, even after going very far, consciousness alone is taken as the refuge, then that very consciousness—just as in dreams and the like—will suffice to account for this entire world through mere illusory manifestation (*vivarta*). Thus, since from the beginning Brahman alone exists as the nature of all objects, being stainless and free from all defects...
The meaning is: what fault is there in the established doctrine (siddhānta)? || 3 ||
Since it is pure cognition alone that shines as its own essential nature, that very thing is called the "world"; and because it is real, it is truly real.

"What is that final conclusion (siddhānta)? He states it: "It is consciousness alone. The meaning is that the secret of the final conclusion has been stated as follows: this very world is real, by virtue of the power of the ultimate reality (*paramārthasatya*) which is the substratum, and by the force of scriptural statements such as "All this, indeed, is Brahman," which speak according to the facts. || 4 ||
The five elements do not exist anywhere, nor do houses and such things;
yet they are experienced even though they do not exist, just as in the state of dreaming. (5)
Since consciousness alone is empty of the primary elements and their derivatives, yet it is established by universal experience as if those elements and their derivatives existed in a dream, he says:
"Nowhere... (Verse 5).

The very nature is pure, just as in a dream it appears like a city and so forth; likewise, this world shines forth even in the waking state, yet in reality it is space (the void). [Note: The printed reading "vastu tatsukham" is to be considered.]
Similarly, he says that even in the waking state, it is the very nature of consciousness that shines as the world: "The nature... (verse 6).
I am indeed the space of consciousness; this world that exists is that very same thing.
Thus, "I" and "the world" are one—the single void, as solid as a stone.
In reality, however, this [term] "space" clarifies that it is the space of consciousness (cetanākāśa). || 7 ||
That which produces the initial creation, that which brings about the evolution at the end of a kalpa,
and the very structure of the worlds— that indeed is the formless void.

He dispels the doubt that this creation might be such a primary creation as the initial creation of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), or a creation at the beginning of a kalpa, or even a transformation at the end of a kalpa, by means of the word "yat" [in the verse]. || 8 ||
Whether the body exists or does not exist, liberation is the state of being beyond suffering and pleasure, which is imperishable;
may there be complete rest in this stainless, enlightened nature here and now. 9.

This being so, he says "satī" [being] to show that there is no distinction whatsoever between liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) and disembodied liberation (*videhamukti*): when the stainless nature is realized, that which is the state of being free from suffering and pleasure—the imperishable form of the bliss of the Absolute (*bhūmānanda*)—is itself liberation;
and whether the body exists or not, that [liberation] is exactly the same. Therefore, let your complete, full, and intense rest be therein; by that alone, you are [liberated].
The meaning is that one has accomplished one's purpose. || 9 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and fourth canto, titled "The Exposition of the Non-existence of the World," in the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the glorious Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa, composed by the sage Vālmīki. 104.

Thus ends the one hundred and fourth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Non-existence of the World," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*. 104.
The one hundred and fifth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
The state of consciousness remains experiencing its own nature in the form of the world.
It is, by its own nature, non-different from the Self, like a dream, and is designated as "conceptual construction. (1)
Only consciousness appears as the waking state, and likewise only consciousness appears as the dream state;
it is described that there is no essential difference between waking and dreaming by their very nature.
To elaborate upon the previously stated analogy of the world to a dream, he prepares the introductory framework with the verse beginning "svabhāvam" (the inherent nature).
The "state of consciousness" (cidbhāva) is the self whose very nature is consciousness (citsvabhāva). || 1 ||
This world is indeed like the state of deep sleep even while awake, or like the interior of a stone;
it is like the void of space, yet it has not been abandoned by its nature as a universe.

The meaning is this: although this waking world has not been abandoned as such, it is in fact deep sleep; it is ignorance at its very root; it is empty space by virtue of its substratum, being like the void itself. || 2 ||
In this regard, the dream adorned with the circle of cities is the very illustration;
for in a dream, the world does not exist at all, yet it appears thus in its radiant splendor. (3)
He states that even a dream is exactly like this, and therefore it alone serves as the illustration here: "In a dream... (verse 3).
This triple world is indeed unreal, appearing just as it does in a dream;
likewise, in this waking state, it is exactly so, and not otherwise in the slightest degree.
Regarding that, he states in the third verse that the similarity to a dream is manifest: "The three worlds... (verse 4).
Neither in the waking state nor in dream is there any real existence of the world as an object denoted by the word "world";
rather, it is the manifestation of one's own conscious space that is perceived as the world.
With the intention that even in the second case, that similarity is easily understood by the discerning, he says: "No" (na). || 5 ||
The self-existent one, within the sky of consciousness, perceived his own creative wonder as the world— consisting of mountains and other forms— within the dream of waking.

He shows that [state] even in the first kalpa with the words "by the sky of consciousness" (cidvyomna). By the self-existent sky of consciousness (svayaṃbhuvā cidvyomnā), which exists as itself, there occurs within the void whose nature is veiled by darkness the self-manifestation (*svacamatkāra*) in the form of mountains and so forth;
that very darkness is perceived internally as the world in waking and dreaming. || 6 ||
This world is not anything at all, nor is consciousness (cid-rūpa) anything; these two—the sky, consciousness, and the world—appear as if they were something, but they are in vain.

Furthermore, he supports the third alternative with the word "the world" (*jagat*): If the world that is manifested were empty, then consciousness would have neither its own illuminating form nor anything else. These two—the consciousness and the world, which consist of the apprehended and the apprehender—are utterly non-existent like the sky;
they appear pointlessly within Brahman. (7)
Just as nothing exists in a dream, so too the three worlds appear;
thus, in the waking state as well, it is entirely empty and devoid of substantial form.
Therein he applies the illustration: "It has appeared as such. Thus, even in the waking state, the three worlds that have appeared are likewise bodiless and empty. (8)
O Great Sage, endowed with manifold emanations, in a dream indeed even undertakings are non-undertakings, and the unreal is spread out as if it were real.
The vast expanse beyond the limits of space is indeed the non-sky;
the multitude of various cities is indeed a mass of mountains, though it is but the sky itself.

The meaning is that it is a marvel that Brahman itself, which is non-ether (avyoma), has become the first ether (vyoma)—an exceedingly vast expanse whose nature is emptiness—and that this very ether, through the sequence of air and the other elements, has become the mass of mountains and the multitude of various cities; thus both are wonders. Alternatively, "non-ether" refers to mountains, the earth, cities, and so forth, while "ether" refers to the sky.
Thus it is: "The sky itself becomes the collection of mountains and so forth"—this is merely a formal proposition (pratijñā) according to what has been heard [in scripture]. 10.
Just as the roar of the ocean, the clouds, or the mountains may be nothing more than silence,
so too he standing nearby does not hear anything at all, even though he is fully awake.

Therein, he establishes the first [point] by means of an illustration with the word "api" (even). Just as the roar (*nirghoṣa*) of years (*abda*), oceans (*abdhi*), and mountains (*adri*)—though well-known to one who is asleep in a dream—is silence and mere emptiness (*mauna-śūnya*) for another;
so too are the years and other things in the waking state. To the question "Why is it silence alone in the illustration?", he says: "na" (not).
"He simply does not hear. For even another man standing nearby who is asleep does not hear at all any sound, such as that of the years or the oceans, even upon waking up. || 11 ||
Just as the son of a barren woman is born even though he was unborn, so too, even when born, one remains as if unborn when there is forgetfulness of the Self. (12)

He establishes the same point for the second time as well with the words "is born. Just as the son of a barren woman, though unborn, is born in a dream, so it should be understood here as well; that is the meaning. Likewise, even a person who has been born after dying remains as if unborn and unproduced—thinking "I am [unborn]"—when there is a forgetting of his own death; such is the meaning. || 12 ||
That which exists quickly becomes non-existent, just as the earth ceases to be experienced;
and everything is inverted, just as night becomes day. (13)
The meaning is that just as the non-experience of one's own bed by a person while asleep brings about the non-existence of that bed, so it is here. || 13 ||
Just as night quickly arises from day,
so does that which is impossible come to pass, such as the sight of one's own death.
He states that other misconceptions (viparyāsa) are to be established in the same manner, beginning with the words "non-existent" (asat), etc. (verse 14).
The impossible becomes possible, like the appearance of the world in the sky;
that which is accompanied by sleep is itself the great light of day. 15.
In sleep, darkness itself becomes light, as does the day during dreams; just as when falling into a pit or similar abyss, the very earth becomes like the sky.
For this reason, the sleep of owls and others is seen to have the day as its cause;
when one experiences falling into a chasm or the like in a dream, the very bed and the earth become the chasm and the sky. (16)
Just as the world appears in a dream as having no real form, so too does it appear in the waking state; there is not the slightest difference between them.
Just as two suns would be similar, or just as two men would be similar, so too are these two—the waking and the dreaming states; there is not even the slightest difference between them here.
There are two suns: that of yesterday and that of today; here, [the word] "of these" (anayoḥ) refers to those two. 18.
Śrī Rāma said: This is not so; for where there is a sublater, conviction arises immediately.
How could that [experience] within a dream, by its very appearance, be equal to the waking state?
Having raised an objection to the previously described similarity between waking and dreaming, Rāma, demonstrating their difference, suspects:

"This is not so. That which you have stated—that there is not even the slightest difference here—is not correct. Why? Because in that dream, by the perception of the waking cognition which arises quickly as a sublater, [the dreamer] himself internally...
Because one experiences its state as a mere appearance, how then could the waking state be equal to it? This is the meaning. || 19 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāghava, having sported in the dream-world together with his dream-kinsmen, that observer of the dream meets his death therein.

Disparity is not established by this much alone, because it remains unproven that a waking cognition occurring in a different location sublates a dream cognition. For in the place of the dream, the dreamer—possessing sleep and situated within the dream-body—perceives dream-kinsmen and others; whereas one who has departed from the dream-body, being free from sleep and situated within the waking body, [perceives otherwise].

One perceives the non-existence of relatives and others seen in a dream; yet, the non-perception of those seen in another body in another place, or their non-perception upon seeing something else in that same body or place, does not constitute their sublation.
For if it did, then the non-perception of relatives from a previous birth in this present life would also result in their sublation.
With the intention that there is no deviation from equanimity, Vasiṣṭha provides the resolution with seven verses beginning with "vihṛtya" (having withdrawn).
"Death" refers to the departure of the dream-body. || 20 ||
Having died in the world of dreams and being separated from the dream-beings,
the living being awakens here and is said to be released from sleep.
A sentient being is a living soul. || 21 ||
Having experienced many states of pleasure, pain, and delusion, as well as the reversals of day and night, the observer dies within the dream-like cycle of worldly existence.
He dies; he abandons the dream-body. || 22 ||
Because sleep has departed, the end of sleep subsequently arises here;
one should then become convinced that "this is not true. (23)
"Here," that is, in this place of lying down, "one is born," meaning one becomes connected with this body.
"Then," immediately thereafter, one should possess the conviction that "this [person] seen in the dream, such as a kinsman and so forth, is not real.
And the use of the optative (*liṅ*) in the sense of possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*) is intended to indicate that such a conviction is not capable of subverting the objects of the dream. (23)
Just as a dreamer, having met with death within the cycle of a dream, is born again to perceive another dream consisting of the waking state. (24)
The witness of the waking state likewise undergoes death within the waking world;
he is born again to experience another dream consisting of the waking state. (25)
Just as one does not consider a dream to be unreal while still in the prior waking state, so too,
having gone from one dream to another, one again takes up the conviction [of its reality].

Having died while awake and being born again within another waking state, just as one takes up the conviction that "the dream was unreal" with respect to the previous waking self by means of the phenomenal world, so too, having gone from one dream to another, one again grasps the conviction of waking in the subsequent dream. Therefore, the conviction of waking in the subsequent dream is as follows:

The sense is that, just as [the lack of perception] is caused by stupor, so too the non-apprehension of the dream-state and its unreality during the preceding waking state is likewise caused solely by stupor. || 26 ||
There, the person of deluded intellect again grasps the waking cognition;
furthermore, he then experiences there another vision of a dream.
Whether it be called "dream as waking" or "waking as dream," [the self] is neither born nor does it die;
yet, it is also born and it dies.

Furthermore, even there in the dream, immediately after the perception of the dream, one experiences the dream itself as being the waking state; this is the connection with what precedes. In this manner, in these two states named "waking" and "dreaming," this individual soul (*jīva*) is not born and does not die by its own nature.
However, it is through the assumption and abandonment of the identification with this or that body that one is born and also dies. || 28 ||
One who sees a dream and dies in that dream is said here to be awakened;
a creature who dies while awake in this world is said to be awakened elsewhere.

And thus, the meaning is that there is indeed equality between the two: one who sees a dream is said to have died in the dream and awakened here in the waking state, whereas one who dies here in the waking state is said to have awakened elsewhere in a dream. || 29 ||
From one dream-state to another dream-state, there is the manifestation of waking within dreaming;
for one who has died and awakened elsewhere, it becomes a waking-dream. (30)

And thus, when one moves from one dream to another, there arises a second dream-form which, because it is present relative to the former, is a superior perception—that is, waking. In this way, for a person who has died while waking and is awakened in another dream or another waking state, the previous waking or dreaming state necessarily becomes sufficient [as a basis for comparison]. || 30 ||
Both waking and dreaming consist of history (itihāsa) alone;
these two have become mutually related as the object of comparison and the comparison itself.

The meaning is that *itihāsa* (history/legend) consists of the narration of past events being celebrated; since the two [the king and the *itihāsa*] are composed of that or are similar to it—and not merely literal [identical]—they have become mutual objects of comparison (*upamāna* and *upameya*). In the reading with the long vowel, *itīhāsamayau*, the sense is: "thus here they have gone to what is unequal or uneven (*asama*)," meaning they are slightly distinct from one another. [In the variant] *itīhāsanmayau*.
The reading is correct. || 31 ||
Dream appears as if it were waking, and waking arises as if it were a dream;
yet in reality, both are unreal, and only the space of consciousness shines forth.
Furthermore, in the present state, even a dream appears as direct perception, just like waking; whereas the past, even if it were waking, is known as being like a dream that has arisen. (32)
The entire range of beings, both stationary and moving, without exception—what else can possibly exist apart from pure consciousness alone? (33)
He establishes the statement that "the sky of consciousness alone shines" with the verse beginning with "sthāvaram" (33).
Just as a vessel made of clay is not perceived when devoid of clay,
so too wood, stone, and the like are essentially nothing but the wonder of consciousness.
This entire collection of objects is exactly the same for us in the waking state as it is in a dream;
for the stone seen in a dream is nothing other than a wondrous manifestation of consciousness. (35)

Apart from the wonder of consciousness (ciccamatkaraṇa), what else could there be? O wise one, in this matter, deliberate with the learned through reasoning and determine it by means of discussion. The connection with the subsequent clause is as follows: in the vision of reality produced by inquiry, that very consciousness is well-known as the "dream-stone" (svāpnopala). || 35 ||
Tell me something more, O wise one: surely that [consciousness] must be nothing but consciousness itself;
for indeed, the very same undivided form which exists in a dream exists likewise in the waking state.
Therefore, the entire world that has arisen is pure consciousness, a fragment of Brahman;
therefore, the entire world that has arisen is pure consciousness, the very floor of Brahman. || 37 ||

Pure consciousness is indeed Brahman itself, which, through superimposition, appears fragmented and divided in the form of the world; however, through negation, the meaning is that the entire world has become the very floor of Brahman. || 37 ||
Just as a vessel made of clay is not perceived when devoid of clay, so too an object of consciousness is not perceived when devoid of consciousness. || 38 ||

He states that [the world] is indeed nothing but pure consciousness (cinmātra), because the world is not perceived apart from consciousness, by means of the verse beginning with "made of clay" (mṛnmayam).
Just as a vessel made of stone is not found to be empty of stone, so too the object of consciousness, which is composed of consciousness, is not perceived to be empty of consciousness. (39)
A stone is a part of rock; that which consists of it is "made of stone" (śaila). || 39 ||

Just as water is of the nature of fluidity and cannot be found apart from its fluidity, so too the object of consciousness (cetya) consists of consciousness (cinmaya), and nothing devoid of consciousness (cicchūnya) is perceived. || 40 ||
Just as fire in the form of heat is not perceived when devoid of heat, so too the object of consciousness, though consisting of consciousness, is not perceived when empty of consciousness. 41.
Just as wind consisting of movement is not perceived when it is motionless, so too the object of consciousness consisting of consciousness is not perceived when it is empty of consciousness. 42.
Consisting of vibration; having vibration as its essential nature. || 42 ||
If something is composed of a certain nature, how indeed can it be obtained without that [nature]?
Where can a non-empty sky be found, and where can a solid earth be found?
Non-obstructive and formless. || 43 ||

Just as objects such as pots and cloths are composed solely of the space of consciousness, so too these mountains and other things in a dream are merely the manifestation of the space of consciousness. 44.
In the same way, this waking state, including mountains and so forth, is also [unreal]. || 44 ||
O fortunate one, just as in a dream the sky itself appears as cities, mountains, and so forth, being composed of consciousness (*saṃvinmaya*), so too is it in the waking state.
Whether it be called "dream" or "waking," here there is indeed only the one, peaceful, infinite, pure consciousness; let there be no dispute over its name.
Clarifying what has already been stated, he concludes with the verse beginning "In a dream": "Just as in a dream, the well-known cities, mountains, and so forth..."
O fortunate one, even that which is renowned as the waking state—such as the eastern mountains and so forth—is nothing but the sky of consciousness;

likewise, it is nothing but the sky of consciousness. Thus, both "dream" and "waking" are but a single, residual pure consciousness, in which all conceptualization has ceased. Regarding such a reality, the disputants engage in futile debate without any actual object.
This is the meaning. || 45 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and fifth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Unity of Waking and Dreaming," in the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the glorious Vāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa, the scripture of the Sage. 105.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifth canto, titled "The Exposition of the Identity of Waking and Dreaming," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa within the Śrī Vasiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa.
The one hundred and sixth canto. Śrī Rāma said:
O Brahman, what would that supreme Brahman—the sky of consciousness—be like?
Speak further, for there is no satiety for me as I listen to this nectar.
Here, the sky of consciousness is further demonstrated through a flood of characteristics;
that very same thing is also further elaborated upon as being the world.

Through the detailed exposition of the world's similarity to a dream, one should realize that the reality is nothing but the space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*). Although its nature has been described hundreds of times previously, it is possible that those of dull intellect have not fully grasped it; therefore, out of compassion for them, [the author] speaks once more of that very same [reality].
Desiring to hear a thorough exposition through the distinctions between essential (svarūpa) and incidental (taṭastha) definitions, Rāma asks: "Of what nature is it? (1).

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Just as two names are assigned for the sake of worldly transaction to two identical twin brothers, so too are the two states of waking and dreaming established within that which is composed of stone.

Desiring to describe that which was asked, Vasiṣṭha reiterates the very theme already introduced—the similarity between waking and dreaming—as a prologue for that description, saying: "Of the two equal ones...

Just as the names of two twins born together are made distinct from one another, so too are the waking and dreaming states [distinguished] within the single, unbroken crystal slab of consciousness, which consists of that [reality] and wherein they appear like reflections.
The meaning is that two names are applied to the two similar types of conceptual proliferation (prapañca). || 2 ||
In reality, however, there is no difference between these two, like that of two quantities of milk;
both are indeed this one alone—the stainless sky of pure consciousness.
The form of consciousness that reaches from one distant place to another in a mere instant—that which exists in the interval between them—is called the space of consciousness (cidākāśa). || 4 ||

First, reminding us of the very definition of that space of consciousness (cidvyoman) which was stated previously, he says "deśāt" [from space]: the meaning is that it is the well-known form of consciousness which, in the midst [of all objects], is devoid of any objective content. || 4 ||
Just as the state of a tree standing [in stillness] while drawing up its pure sap is like the clarity of the sky,
so too is the sky of consciousness (cinnabhaḥ) traditionally described.

The meaning is: it is like that state of bliss, well-known from the Vedas, which exists in a tree as it drinks and thoroughly absorbs the water and sap drawn up from the root—a state characterized by growth and decay-free joy. || 5 ||
The state of the sky of consciousness is said to be exactly like the equanimity of a person whose every desire has ceased and whose mind is completely stilled.
The state that is equal and devoid of all inequality is the experience of the nature of innate bliss;
for in the state free from distraction, there is the universal experience: "I abide in bliss. (6)
That state of a healthy person which exists when sleep has not yet arrived and the objects of the mind have ceased is called the space of consciousness (cidākāśa).
Regarding the phrase "in the future": they say, "The state that arises at the beginning of sleep and at the end of waking—that state the yogi maintains, and he is not overcome by sufferings. (7)
That state which exists as the unmoving essence within grasses, shrubs, creepers, and the like when they reach their growth at the proper season,
is called the space of consciousness (cidākāśa).
In the rainy season, the monsoon, or autumn—such is the state of bliss in which all sense of "mine-ness" has been relinquished.
The state of that person who is liberated from form, light, and mental attention, and who is immortal, is like the clarity of an autumn sky; that is the ether of consciousness (cid-ambaram).
Of a man who lives by means of the nectar [of knowledge]. || 9 ||
That which has been created as the seat of wood, stone, and mountains, as well as of sentient beings— that essence of existence is called the space of consciousness (cidākāśa).

If that seat—the inactive state created by the Creator through its own nature—were the very essence of the existence and stability of conscious living beings, then it is called the space of consciousness (cidākāśa). And the sense is that this is realized only when the mind has been dissolved. || 10 ||
Know that the space of consciousness (cit-kha), from which the triad of the seer, the seeing, and the seen arises, and in which they set, is free from all affliction.
Because from that very witness of deep sleep arises the triad of the seer and so forth in both dreaming and waking, and in that same [witness] they reach their cessation. || 11 ||
That from which all diverse experiences of objects arise and in which they fully transform—that is called the space of consciousness (cidākāśa). 12.

From which all the diverse experiences of objects arise—that is, attain their emergence—and in which they successively transform through the states of perception, deliberation, determination, rejection, and acceptance. || 12 ||
That in which all is, from which all arises, who is all, and who is everywhere;
who consists of all and is eternal—he is called the space of consciousness (cidākāśa). || 13 ||
The two verses have been explained previously. || 13 ||
That which shines as the self-luminous space of consciousness— identical in name whether in heaven, on earth, outside, or within another— is called the sky of consciousness (cidākāśa).

That sky of consciousness, whose limbs are the universe, is that eternal and extended firm thread upon which the entire world—arising from both the existent and the non-existent—rests like a garland. (15)
In Him, whose every limb is the universe, the entire world—both existent and non-existent, embodied and formless—subsists like a garland upon a thread.
Since all transformations of creation and dissolution are produced from it,
and into it they are dissolved— whatever consists of that, it is the ether of consciousness (cid-ambaram).
He states the "indirect definition" (taṭasthalakṣaṇa) as expressed in the Śruti, "from which indeed these beings are born," with the words "from which" (yasmāt). || 16 ||
That from which the universe proceeds when sleep has ceased, and in whose tranquility it ceases, is called the ether of consciousness (cidambara). || 17 ||

When sleep—characterized by deep slumber and dissolution—has ceased, from that very source, by the power of its own capacity for projection (*vikṣepa-śakti*), the universe characterized by waking and dreaming, as well as that characterized by ether and the other elements, proceeds and manifests; and upon the pacification of that [sleep], that is, the cessation of the power of projection, it ceases. || 17 ||

Know that to be the sky of consciousness (cinnabhaḥ), which consists of self-experience and resides within oneself, by whose opening and closing [of its eyes] the existence and dissolution of the world arise. 18.

Unmeṣa is the manifestation in the mental state (*vṛtti*) of the final direct realization; by it, there is the dissolution of the existence of the world. Nimeṣa is the concealment of one's own true nature; by it, there is the emergence [of the world]. (18)
Having determined in every way that "this is not it, this is not it," that which is never anything at all, yet is everything—that is called the space of consciousness (cidvyoma). || 19 ||

Thus, he states that even "being the self of all" is its defining characteristic, up to the limit of the negation of everything—expressed as "not this": "That which is always everything, yet is nothing at all. (19)
That form of consciousness which exists in the interval when one has gone from one place to another,
even though it occurs at a distance in half a blink of an eye, is known as the form of pure consciousness alone.

"In half a blink" means without delay, for the sake of reaching another location; for if there were delay, it would be impossible to discern the pure sky of consciousness, either due to the interruption of the mental flow or due to the intrusion of other objects.
The repetition of what was stated at the beginning is for the purpose of indicating the conclusion. || 20 ||
This entire universe, exactly as it has come to be and as it exists, is indeed composed of that [Brahman];
even when joined with form, light, and mental activity, it remains of such a nature.

Having stated the characteristics [of the Self], he declares that the universe consists of that very essence in order to establish its non-duality, beginning with the words "the universe," etc. (verse 21).
Through a slight unfolding, this [reality], though non-different in form, appears as if it were something else—the pure-spatial expanse of being-consciousness (saccidvyoma) of stainless nature. (22)
To that [question], he says "īṣat" (slightly) [in verse 22] to explain how the manifestation of difference between the state of dissolution and the state of creation occurs.
Perceiving objects with the senses yet truly devoid of latent desires,
remain awakened and unified, as if established in the state of deep sleep.

This delusion of otherness arises solely through the power of latent impressions (vāsanā); therefore, it does not exist for one who is free from such impressions. Thus he says: "Even while seeing... (23).
Free from latent impressions, with a tranquil mind, speak, go, drink, or take; like a living stone, remain forever in profound silence.
This which you see before you as a visible object is not possible at all; it is like the water of a mirage, or like the appearance of duality arising within the moon. (25)
By the word "as if" (*iva*) in the phrase "as if it were something else," the falsity of otherness is stated. If one asks why that is so, he says: "Because it is simply impossible.
"This [effect] was originally unproduced because of the absence of a cause;
for indeed, an effect cannot possibly exist without a cause. (26)
Or rather, whatever arises is produced without a cause;
it is the supreme form as it truly exists that appears as if it has arisen. (27)

Or rather, whatever arises from a seed, such as a sprout and so forth, which is established through the observation of positive and negative concomitance—that too has its origin solely from the non-dual Brahman, which is itself without cause; such is the nature of that [universe]. Now, one might ask:
how can there be the emergence of a sprout and so forth from that which is changeless? To this he says: "as it is" (yathāsthitam). || 27 ||
Just as it exists, O limb, the prior form remains established;
it is indeed non-dual and pure, yet it is perceived through duality. (28)
The sense is that just as, even though the moon's orb is non-dual, it is perceived as dual during an optical illusion, so it is here. || 28 ||
In this regard, that mature experience which arises as a conviction based on "this" is known by the wise to be an adventitious delusion, equal to a woman seen in a dream. (29)
If that [object] is indeed such, how can there be the state of grasping it otherwise? To this he says: "In that case" (tatra). || 29 ||
Therefore, the visible object has not arisen, it does not exist, and it will not come to be;
nor does it perish—for what can perish that which does not exist? || 30 ||
If it is merely illusion, what is established? To this he says: "Therefore," etc. (30).
That very same supreme, tranquil expanse of consciousness remains thus:
unswerving from its own nature, established in itself, and serene, yet appearing as if the world has arisen.

That entire universe is the supreme, peaceful expanse of consciousness alone, existing in the guise of the universe. He says "not by transformation" (to answer the question) "how?"—namely, "from its own nature. || 31 ||
For that which was seen as the object of vision at the beginning does not exist as real at any time;
nor indeed is there a seer, for in the absence of an object to be seen, where indeed could there be the state of being a seer? (32)
If it is asked why [the Self] is not a transformation through modification (*pariṇāma*), he says: "For not... because it lacks the same ontological status (*samasattāka*) as that [modification].
For this very reason, even its being the seer (*draṣṭṛtā*) is not a transformation; for it is equal to that [Self], being defined by the object seen (*dṛśya*). Thus he says: "Nor... (32).
Śrī Rāma said: "If it is so, O Brahman, then tell me: what is this manifestation of the seer and the seen, and how does it appear? Speak further, O best of speakers. (33)

Rāma raises an objection: "If the seer and the seen are absolutely non-existent, then how can they appear? For that which is absolutely non-existent is never observed to appear. He says: "If this is so, then tell me again—even though it has been stated before—O best among speakers! (33)
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Since the visible world is always unreal by nature and lacks a cause,
even the bold assertion that "it possesses visibility" is utterly impossible.

Having accepted in the first verse the impossibility of the appearance of that which is non-existent, he states in the second verse the answer— that it is precisely the existent Supreme Self who appears in such a way through *māyā*— with the words "of that which is of the nature of the non-existent" (*asadrūpasya*). This is a bold assertion (*prauḍhivāda*) stating that because there is an absence of a cause, the very arising of that which is of the nature of the non-existent is impossible, and therefore its status as an object of perception is also [impossible].
The term *prauḍhivāda* (bold assertion) means that it is even more impossible because it is utterly inconceivable. || 34 ||
Whatever shines forth here, consisting of the delusion of the seer and the seen—the world and so on—know that to be the supreme form of the Supreme Self. (35)
For this very reason, he says that this seer and the seen do not have the nature of the non-existent, but rather belong to Brahman, which is ultimately real:
"Just as in a dream one remains as pure consciousness alone, like the sky or a forest, so too does pure consciousness itself shine within itself in the form of the world. (36)
If it is asked how it is known that this is indeed the form of the Supreme Self, he says: "In a dream," [referring to verse 36].
From the beginning of creation until now, there has never been any material cause whatsoever anywhere; thus, only the absolute Brahman shines forth.

If it is asked, "From what does its similarity to a dream arise?", the author says "here" (iha) with the intention that it arises from a dissolution (pralaya) similar to deep sleep (suṣupti), which is devoid of the entire collection of causes. || 37 ||
That which is the manifestation of the space of consciousness expanding by itself within itself—this very world shines as its own manifested form. || 38 ||
Intending to show that there is also a similarity with a dream because its manifestation depends upon the manifestation of the space of consciousness (cidākāśa), he says: "That which... (verse 38).

Just as there is the state of being for an entity, just as there is emptiness for that which is empty, and just as there is form for that which possesses form, so too is the world [the form] of the sky of consciousness. 39.

If it is asked how that consciousness-ether, which is devoid of all dharmas, can possess the nature of the world, [the author] says "just as" (yathā), establishing this through examples: "by the power of illusory conceptualization alone. [This refers to] that which has form, i.e., the embodied. || 39 ||
Know this to be the manifestation of consciousness, dense with the ultimate reality; know thus the manifestation of consciousness, dense with the ultimate reality.
Thus established, self-luminous, it consists of the seer, the seen, and the act of seeing. (40)

Know that which is like a solid mass of rock-salt, of a single flavor, the very density of ultimate reality, appearing as consciousness within illusion—thus existing in the form of the triple-fold (tripuṭī). || 40 ||
In reality, however, because of the absence of duality, there is neither appearance nor the act of appearing;
who can know this something indescribable as being either existent or non-existent? (41)
But when illusion is abandoned, since duality no longer exists, who knows whether it is real or unreal? The sense is that what has been sublated is unfit for further deliberation. || 41 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
If it is so, O Brāhmaṇa, tell me then how this distinction consisting of cause and effect and so forth has arisen, and how it has attained the status of reality? (42)

If, according to your own stated method, the ultimate reality (*paramārthatattva*) is devoid of both seer and seen—such that "thus it is not spoken, nor is there speaking"—then how can distinctions such as cause and effect exist? For nothing that lacks a seer can possibly be established; from what material cause (*upādāna*) or efficient cause (*nimitta*) could it have arisen? If you say that [these distinctions] are simply unreal, then...
The meaning is: how has it attained the status of truth, and how does it appear as truth to all people? || 42 ||

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: When the light of consciousness itself contemplates whatever appears according to its own manifestation, it immediately perceives its own self as that very thing; thus you have seen it.

Regarding that, he states the answer to the first question: "The light of consciousness" (*citprakāśa*). In reality, even one's own self is the Lord, the light of consciousness; whenever He, by His own will, manifests Himself in whatever manner according to the awakening of the desires, actions, and latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of living beings, and brings forth whatever exists through His power of true resolve (*satyasaṃkalpa*), then you immediately perceive it exactly as such, and that very same [Lord] is perceived by you as your own self.
The meaning is that because he has experienced the previously mentioned relationship between the seer and the seen, there is the accomplishment of this [state]. || 43 ||
This very form is but the sky of consciousness; it does not become deluded within its own void.
Just as one is not deluded in a dream, who indeed could pose a challenge to this?

He states the answer to the second [objection]: "It is the very sky of consciousness (*cidvyoma*) alone. This form consisting of the relationship between cause and effect and so forth is the sky of consciousness alone, just as a pot is nothing but clay; thus, the sky of consciousness alone is the material cause (*upādāna*), while delusion (*moha*) alone is its efficient cause (*nimitta*). How is this known? Because when one's own sky [of consciousness] is fully realized, one does not become deluded, whereas otherwise, one certainly becomes deluded. As it is said:

Just as one is deluded by oneself in a dream and abandons that delusion only through the awakening of one’s own self, so it is here. Now, [an objection is raised]: since the Lord is capable of knowing His own self, why does He become a living being (*jīva*) and become deluded, or for what reason does He not awaken? To this, he says:
"Who is this?"—meaning, why does the independent Lord become a *jīva* and become deluded?
"One who makes an inquiry" (paryanuyogakṛt) means one who raises an objection; the meaning is that there would be no such person at all. || 44 ||

When one state of being reaches another state of being, that form of consciousness which exists in the interval is the space of consciousness (*cidvyoma*); that alone is this entire existence, and nothing else. (In this context, the reading "all things" [*sarvaṃ vastu*] is more appropriate than "all" [*sarvam*]. 45.

He states the answer to the third [objection] with the words "because of existence" (*bhāvāt*). When milk attains the state of curds, or when a lump of clay attains the state of a jar, even though the prior state has ceased and the subsequent state has not yet arisen, there exists for a single moment in the interim that which is of the nature of pure being (*sanmātra*); this is well-known as the body, the very essence, of ultimate reality-consciousness (*saṃvit*).

That very same space of consciousness (cidvyoma) which was previously described by me is perceived as this entire existing reality; thus, the meaning is that everything has attained the status of being real. || 45 ||
Views such as the relation of cause and effect are but the manifestations of ignorance;
this [consciousness] constructs them just as it constructs the world—who is there to question it? (46)

He says—“kāryakāraṇa... (regarding cause and effect)—that just as there is no valid objection to the conceptualization of the Lord’s state as the individual soul (jīva), so too there is no valid objection to the conceptualization of the individual soul’s three states in the form of cause and effect through its own ignorance (avidyā). For indeed, no one can direct an objection toward their own self, asking, “Why do you act in this way?”
The sense is that he is capable of doing so. || 46 ||
If there were some other [entity] who is the seer, the enjoyer, or the agent, then how could it be appropriate to ask, "What is this visible world? and not otherwise? (47)

If the self were other [than the body], there would certainly be this objection regarding its being the agent or the enjoyer; thus he says: "The seer," etc. In this way, the objection would be appropriate. || 47 ||
Wherein, in the dream state, only the non-manifesting sky of consciousness shines forth—pure, one, yet manifold in nature—what could be conceptualized there, and where? (48)
It is conceptualized and subjected to critical inquiry. || 48 ||
This light of creation shines only within the Self-born One, who is pure consciousness;
yet, once fully known, it becomes Brahman itself in an instant.

The meaning is that the appearance of creation—the delusion of creation—shines forth from the Self-existent (svayaṃbhū) up to the Self-existent itself, due to a lack of thorough knowledge of reality. || 49 ||
This very same [reality], when not fully understood, is called delusion and illusion;
it is termed the world, and is described as the visible object. (50)
This very delusion of creation, when not understood in its true nature, is called "māyā" in the scriptures; in the world it is called the "universe" (jagat);
by the ignorant it is called "ignorance" (avidyā); and by those with discerning vision it is described as the "visible object" (dṛśya). || 50 ||

By the light of the sky of consciousness, the demon of the visible world is perceived by the mind as a mere phantom, just as a ghost is seen by a child— though non-existent, appearing as if it were real.
One's own mind is of the nature of consciousness; though non-existent as something separate, it appears as if existent—the Buddha is like a phantom appearing to the vision. || 51 ||
Although the world does not exist within the Self, it is experienced by the sky of consciousness alone,
just as in a dream the state of mountains and cities appears even though they do not truly exist, like a drawing on a limb.

He states that even though [the world] is non-existent and partless, the experience of it as existent and possessing parts must be explained here by analogy with a dream: "The world-appearance... and so on; "it is like a drawing of limbs, as if it were possessed of parts. (52)
"I am the mountain, I am Rudra, I am the ocean, I am the Virāj"—it is consciousness alone that perceives these in the void, just as mountains and cities appear in a dream. (53)
Therein, he elaborates upon experience through the superimposition of the ego-sense with the words "I am," etc. "Adri" refers to mountains such as Meru, Himavat, and so forth. || 53 ||
Due to the absence of a cause, no effect whatsoever has been produced;
thus does consciousness abide within the space of consciousness during the great dissolution, as this state of "this-ness."

"Why is it described that creation is merely the experience of consciousness (*cid-anubhava*), and why is it not described as having arisen from some other cause, such as *pradhāna* or atoms (*paramāṇu*)? To this, he says: "The shaper... (verse 54).
This world, which is merely the void of space, is experienced as such by the void; it is indeed without cause, a body of emptiness within the self of pure consciousness, in the conscious Self. (55)
The limb that is void is partless. || 55 ||
All living beings are indeed inert and worn out, like mirrors;
yet, for one who performs inquiry, the end [of suffering] occurs as soon as they have come near.
All living beings, though they possess within themselves the differentiation of the world imagined like reflections in a mirror,

are nevertheless inert and have wasted their lives in vain due to a lack of inquiry and the inability to perceive their own true nature. For the preeminent person who practices inquiry, however, the supreme goal of human existence is already present within, as it is the very nature of the innermost Self (pratyagātman).
The meaning is "thus. || 56 ||
Having abandoned those respective forms and realized that the world is the void of pure consciousness alone, one should remain as a conscious stone; there is no other superior state than this.
Having understood the true nature [of the self] through inquiry, he explains how one should remain therein with the words "tattat" (that-that):

having realized that the world is merely the sky—that is, pure consciousness (cinmātra) which remains after discarding each respective name, form, and individual nature—one should remain as motionless as a stone, which is itself a mass of consciousness (cidekaghana), by means of the conscious self; any other attachment to the body and so forth, which is illusory (māyikī), is not the highest state. || 57 ||
Just as the world-fluid, consisting of water and whirlpools, remains while moving the body,
so too does the consciousness remain as the state of being conscious through the perception of the world born of the mind.

To the question of how consciousness (cit) exists as the self of the world, he says: "Just as...
