Just as water, while moving its own body, remains as the world-fluid consisting of whirlpools and the like, so too consciousness (cit), having imagined within itself the nature of consciousness (cittva) in the form of the activity of cognizing, remains as that action perceived as the world. || 58 ||
Just as the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpadruma) grants one's desires and just as the thought-gem (cintāmaṇi) does,
so too does Consciousness (cit) instantly fulfill whatever has been cultivated within the mind.

With the intention that, if even those of little power such as the wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpadruma*) possess the capacity to fashion desired objects through mere volition (*saṃkalpa*), then what need is there to mention that for the Supreme Self who is all-powerful?—he says: "Just as... (verse 59).
Like a wish-fulfilling gem or like the tree of paradise, consciousness— being of the nature of space— swiftly accomplishes one's desires within the self by means of the inner self.
When one travels from one country to another, the body of consciousness remains in the middle region;
this visible world is composed of that very [consciousness], so whence can there be the delusion of duality or unity? (61)
Establishing that [the world] consists of that [Self] by means of drawing in its objects, he states the world's identity with it: "From space," etc. (61).
Thus, its own shadow shines forth clearly and infinitely from within its luminous interior;
though devoid of limbs, it is perceived like the blueness of emptiness within the sky. (62)
The shadow of consciousness—beauty itself—shines forth in the guise of the world; though it is empty and void of limbs and parts. 62.
The experience of dissimilar effects does not occur due to the absence of auxiliary causes;
therefore, at the beginning of creation, primordial consciousness alone is the perceived object, just as in a dream.

He summarizes the meaning established in detail with the verse beginning "visadṛśa": At the beginning of creation, the emergence—meaning the experience—of an effect that is insentient and dissimilar to consciousness (cit) is not possible, because of the absence of auxiliary causes that serve as the basis for such dissimilarity. However, in the case of something very similar...

The intention is that because there is no differentiator, the status of being an effect is not established. Therefore, the meaning is that it is proven by the analogy of a dream that this visible world is indeed primordial consciousness alone, and there does not exist even a single atom apart from it. || 63 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and sixth canto, titled "The Refutation of Cause and Effect," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa section of the Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa, composed by Vālmīki, according to the tradition of the Ṛṣis. 106.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixth chapter, titled "The Refutation of Cause and Effect," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa, in its exposition of the essential meaning. 106.
The one hundred and seventh canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: The universe, which is consciousness alone and devoid of any object of thought, shines everywhere as the sky of consciousness.
In this regard, this consciousness is the cognizer, and the object of cognition is likewise of the same nature. (1)
Here it is established that earth and the other elements lack substantial reality;
rather, the world is merely the manifestation of the jewel of consciousness itself, like a dream.

Having denied the existence of the object of consciousness (*cetya*) for the entire universe, he declares his intention to leave only pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) as the remainder: "not an object of consciousness" (*acetya*).

For the sky of consciousness alone shines everywhere; thus, the inference is shown that [the world] has its establishment dependent solely upon the sky of consciousness. Here, the meaning of the proposition—that the triad consisting of the conscious subject (*cit*), the act of consciousness (*cetana*), and the object of consciousness (*cetya*)—is composed of consciousness (*cinmayī*).

Thus he says: "In this [context]. The ellipsis is to be supplied as follows: "In this proposition, that which consists of pure consciousness (śuddhacidātmaka) is intended as the object of the proposition. || 1 ||
Therefore, everyone remains as if dead even while living;
"this one," "I," and "you"—though alive, you are as if dead.

The proof of the proposition results in two fruits: the cessation of the world-appearance for the world that already exists, and the cessation of the individual-existence appearance for us who are living. Thus he says: "Therefore... (2).
Even when engaged in worldly affairs, they are as if dead through the silence of wood;
indeed, all beings, whether moving or stationary, are like birds in flight. || 3 ||

He states that the fruit of this is the establishment of the immutability and formlessness of all things, using the word "kāṣṭha" (wood): "They have attained immutability, characterized by absolute inactivity, like wood; their movement in the sky is the attainment of an absolute state of formlessness. (3)
Whatever is spread out here, having the nature of a reflection in the glass of space, know that it is nothing at all;
for how could anything exist within the void?

He says "ākāśa... [and so on], teaching that one should understand the determination of non-existence even for that which appears, like the blueness of the sky; "kācakacyam" means a blueness that shines like glass. || 4 ||
Like a tuft of hair, the current of a river, a column of smoke, or a pearl,
that which shines as space has no reality even when it is experienced.

In the very same way, within this sky of consciousness called the world, which shines as consciousness itself, there is nothing but absolute emptiness; even when experienced, what basis for stability can there be, and who could provide such a basis?
And thus, it follows that attachment to worldly enjoyments is as improper as a desire for pearls in the sky; he states this with the words "tathaiva" (in the same way).
What entity could there be that serves as the basis or the producer of such attachment? || 6 ||
In the web of the imagination of the Child of Consciousness, which is void in essence and purposeless;
in earth and the other elements, which are non-substantial and arise like a mere sky of delusion.
"Children, tell me: what is the basis for this 'I' and 'mine'? Enough! Now it is understood: only a child delights in the conceptual constructions of a child. (8)
If attachment is indeed improper, then what is the reason that people still place their attachment there? To this he says: "Ah, it is understood!
This particle *ā* is used in the recollection of a cause. "It is understood" means it has been remembered. The meaning is: their childhood alone is remembered as the cause of that attachment. (8)
O timid one, through futile investigations into the unreality of earth and other elements, your life will pass away in vain; you will know nothing at all, being intent on washing the sky.

For this very reason, those who have attained even a slight degree of discrimination should abandon the inquiry that causes vain birth and destruction—being the cause for the acquisition of non-existent things such as earth—and instead rely upon the collection of means beginning with dispassion (*vairāgya*), which brings about the meaningfulness of birth. With this intention, he says: "Earth, etc. Just as:

The meaning is as follows: if one, driven by the desire for greed for gold, jewels, and the like, abandons the washing of the site where those [treasures] are located and instead endeavors to wash the sky, one will obtain or see no fruit whatsoever, despite great effort; it is just like that.
Since causes such as auxiliary factors (*sahakārī*) and others are absent, how could that which has never arisen even at the very beginning exist now? (10)

He states that the non-existence of earth and the other elements has already been established previously through their lack of causality, their being unproduced, and so forth: "The auxiliary... (verse 10).
Those fools who deal with an object that is unborn and non-existent are like those who cherish a son who is either dead or yet to be born. (11)
For this very reason, he says—beginning with "by that which is unborn"—that the attachment of the learned to worldly convention is a source of laughter. || 11 ||
Whence [arise] the earth and the other elements; by whom, what indeed, and how have they arisen?
This peaceful expanse of consciousness shines thus by itself within itself. 12.
Relying on the experience that earth and the other elements are absolutely non-existent from the perspective of ultimate reality, he says: "From where?"
For those whose minds are agitated by the conceptualization of cause, effect, time, and so forth, the earth and other elements exist in such a manner; enough of this talk with such fools. (13)
He says "kārya... [verse 13] to show that we have no authority regarding those of deluded views.
The world called "jagat" consists both of that which is not earth and so forth, and that which is composed of earth and so forth;
thus it shines as the form of space, like the jewel of consciousness in dreams and other states. (14)

And thus, the meaning of the proposition is established; so he says: "not-earth-and-so-forth" (*apṛthvyādi*). The word "indeed" (*nāma*) indicates what is well-known. Both that dream-world which is not-earth-and-so-forth, and the world well-known in the waking state which consists of earth-and-so-forth—both of these are of the nature of space (*khātmaka*), that is, of the nature of the sky of consciousness (*cidākāśātmaka*). What then is this world that shines forth? To that he says: "it shines forth" (*kacati*). || 14 ||

That which is the limb of this consciousness-ether, formless yet inferable through one's own experience, appears in the form of the surface of the earth and so forth, given the designation "the knowable. (15)

That which has its authority followed by one's own direct experience (*svānubhava*)— namely, this formless and shapeless limb or body (*aṅga*) of this sky of consciousness (*cidambara*), meaning its very nature (*svarūpa*)— is that which, existing as such,

always shines forth having been made into a verbal designation (*abhidhāna*) in the form of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), appearing as the object of knowledge and perception in the form of the surface of the earth and so forth.
The meaning is that it does not manifest as another entity, nor as a non-entity. || 15 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and seventh chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Nature of Ignorance," in the latter half of the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*, composed by Vālmīki. 107.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventh chapter, titled "The Exposition on the Non-existence of Ignorance," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and eighth canto.
Śrī Rāma said:
"He in whom this ignorance exists, manifesting in the form of the visible world,"
Like a city in the sky or a dream-city, it is empty even while being perceived. || 1 ||
As long as ignorance has not been destroyed, there is never an end to the world.
To this point, a detailed and wonderful exposition of what is called ignorance is now set forth.

Rāma, harboring a doubt as to whether or not there can be an end—defined as the non-existence of ignorance throughout the three periods of time—even in the absence of sublation by the knowledge of reality, regarding that ignorance which has been described as having the nature of *saṃsṛti*, asks:
"Ignorance... This city of dreams in the sky of consciousness, though existing, is essentially void and yet appears in a visible form.

The connection of the two [verses] is as follows: "For that ignorant person in whom ignorance exists, shining forth because it has not been sublated, for how long a time would it persist? What would its form be, and what would its nature be? And to what extent would it exist in terms of space? Please tell me this again. (1)
O Sage, please tell me again: for how long does that ignorance persist, what is its nature, and of what magnitude is it? || 2 ||
Regarding that conduct of Vipaścit, the report concerning the emergence of his enemies in the four directions is here related from beginning to end.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
For those ignorant ones in whom ignorance regarding the earth and so forth exists, there is no end to it, just as there is none to Brahman; hear now the story concerning this. (3)

Thereupon, Vasiṣṭha, adopting the second alternative of the doubt, first causes Rāma to attend to the story of Vipaścit in order to establish that [point], saying: "Avidyā. Just as there is no end to Brahman in terms of space or time, so too there is none for this [avidyā]. Just as there is no end to Brahman in terms of space or time...
In this case as well, it does not exist. Regarding this matter, listen to the illustrative story that is about to be told:
"Somewhere in a corner of the sky, there exists a world similar to this one;
some portion of the triple-world exists by means of this very same arrangement. (4)

He introduces that very point with the words "something similar": in some corner of the sky of consciousness (*cidambara*), where there exists a certain substance resembling a mirror-slab of gold from the Lokāloka mountain, and even in some part of that, there is something similar to this world— the triple world—
by means of this very well-known arrangement of the three worlds, including its continents, regions, times, and so forth.
It exists by way of a limit. || 4 ||
There is a certain region that is an ornament of the earth;
therein lies a city named Tatamiti, whose fame is clearly manifest upon the world.

In that regard, there is a certain portion of the earth which serves as an ornament to the terrestrial expanse characterized as Jambūdvīpa; and within that, on such level ground— a land where, due to the absence of irregularities caused by mountains, embankments, sand, and the like, the activities of movement and other functions of men, elephants, horses, chariots, and so forth can occur with great clarity.
The meaning is that there is a city well-known by the name Tatamiti. || 5 ||
In that place there was a certain king, renowned as Vipaścit,
who shone by virtue of his wisdom in an assembly of excellent courtiers.
In that city, in such an assembly where the members were distinguished, he shone because of his wisdom—that is, his learnedness in all the scriptures. || 6 ||
He shone in that assembly like a royal swan among lotus plants, like the moon, the lord of stars, amidst the circle of constellations, and like Mount Sumeru among the range of mountains.
He describes his splendor even through his majesty and beauty as he shines there, saying "the royal swan":
in the *abjinī*, that is, in the lotus-filled lake; like the moon, the lord of the stars (*uḍurāṭ*), amidst the circle of bears (*ṛkṣacakra*), that is, the host of constellations. || 7 ||
Since their speech turns back from describing his qualities due to its own inability,
the light of the poets becomes as motionless as a mountain.

The speech of poets, which is intent upon describing the ever-increasing excellence of qualities everywhere, turns back from its description due to the inability to describe [further] because of the infinity of qualities and their incomparability—starting from that wise man;
nevertheless, poets continue to honor him. For, from that wise man...
From the presence of poets, there shall arise an unshakable, stable prosperity—a radiance brought about by the excellence of their qualities and fame.
For he is like Mount Meru, the bearer of the earth, who, by his own light, turns into gold the men, deer, grass, shrubs, and other things that depend upon him;
such is the meaning. || 8 ||
From whom, who blossoms every morning and strives to illuminate all directions,
glory born of his majesty arises as if from a lotus.
*Śrī* means prosperity; in the case of the lotus, it refers to the beauty produced by its heat and sunlight. || 9 ||
Proud and devoted to Brahman, he worshipped Agni alone as the presiding deity;
with equal devotion, he honored him and knew no other god.

His mind was devoted to Brahman and intent on the welfare of Brāhmaṇas; for this very reason, because Agni is a Brāhmaṇa among the gods, he worshipped Agni alone as the presiding deity among the gods. Accordingly, there is a mantra in the *agnyupasthāna* (the ritual attendance upon the fire): "Among the gods you are a Brāhmaṇa, and I am indeed a Brāhmaṇa among men."
"He runs up to the Brahman with the words, 'I run up to you. Regarding this, it is said in the Vājasaneyaka: "By means of Agni alone, he became the Brahman among the gods. (10)
They were arranged in arrays of fish and sea-monsters, accompanied by multitudes of elephants and horses;
they were enriched with whirlpool and wheel formations, and garlanded by the force of surging waves.

Among his ministers were four wise and fearless ones, preeminent in the strength of their arms, and superior in both their own power and their military forces; these four ministers, like the four great oceans, were appointed and engaged in protecting the boundaries of the country by warding off enemy armies from the four directions—this is the connection between the two [verses]. In that regard, they were like the oceans.

The ministers, accompanied by multitudes of elephants and horses, formed arrays like those of fish and sea-monsters; the oceans were rich with whirlpool formations, while the ministers were rich with circular (cakra) arrays. The oceans were garlanded with billows, and the ministers were garlanded with armies. || 11 ||
Devoted to the maintenance of boundaries and possessing strength greater than Akampana,
he had four ministers who were like the oceans situated at the four quarters.
The oceans are superior in strength to the immovable mountains. || 12 ||
He was a conqueror difficult to defeat, who, like a wheel of false doctrine, illuminated the earth as the hub for the entire circle of the quarters.

With those ministers, that king became the center and support of all the circles of quarters, like the nave of a wheel; like the Sudarśana discus, he was difficult to conquer, invincible by his enemies, and himself a victor. || 13 ||
Once, a swift messenger arrived from the eastern direction;
he spoke these words in secret, with rapid speed and terrible syllables: ||| 14 ||
A wandering spy arrived; he was one in whom terrible syllables resounded because of his irrepressibility, like the force of the speed of Time.
"O Lord, you who have not fallen from your vow to bind the earth-cows that had rested upon the wicked tree!
Listen to me; after hearing from my mouth, let what is appropriate be done. (15)

O Acyuta, because the earth has been bound by the resting of your two arms, it is never displaced; that is to say, the earth is forever supported by your arms. Here, through the pun on the word *acyuta*, the attribution of the nature of Viṣṇu is also implied. 15.
The vassal king of the eastern quarter has set due to fever;
I believe he has gone to conquer Yama, having been challenged by you, the conqueror of enemies. (16)

The vassal who was appointed by you to the eastern quarter to maintain the boundary—the aforementioned minister—has met his end through fever. Regarding this, the poet offers a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*): "I believe" (*manye*) that he, having been appointed and set forth by you, the conqueror of enemies, for the purpose of world-conquest, has gone to defeat Yama, the lord of the southern quarter. || 16 ||
While he was attempting to conquer it from all sides, the leader of the southern region was struck down by his enemy after being assailed by two armies from the east and the west.

When he had died, your vassal, the leader of the southern region, set out from all sides to conquer the eastern and southern directions; he too was attacked and slain by an enemy with forces from both the east and the west. || 17 ||
When he had died, the Lord of the Western Quarter arrived and, having assembled his forces, came with intent to seize those two quarters.

When he has died, his vassal, the lord of the western quarter (the direction of Varuṇa), having arrived with his forces and being intent on seizing the eastern and southern quarters, will be slain in battle midway by enemies—the kings of the eastern lands together with the rulers of the southern region. This is the connection between the two [verses]. || 18 ||
Together with the kings of the eastern regions and the monarchs of the southern path,
he was slain in battle by his enemies right there on the road.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
While he was speaking thus, another messenger, distressed by haste,
arrived at the palace like a mass of dull, surging waves.
He indeed entered. || 20 ||
Another wanderer, as if distressed and tormented by haste, entered the palace; he was like a well-known torrent of water, a deluge of dull matter, during a cataclysmic dissolution.
The spy said: "The commander of the northern quarter, harassed by the enemies of the gods, approaches from here with his army, like a flood of water breaking its dam. (21)
O God! 21.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Having heard this, the protector of the earth, considering the delay to be unreal,
spoke these words as he was departing from the excellent palace.

Considering the things of this world and their foundations to be harmful and unreal, he spoke even as he was departing from his excellent palace, addressing the men standing nearby. This is the meaning. || 22 ||
Let the king’s vassals be mobilized and let his ministers be brought forth; let the armories be opened and let the terrible weapons be distributed. (23)

What did he say? "Having equipped the king, as well as the vassals and ministers—with the act of equipping meaning 'having made them ready for battle'—let all of them be brought here. Since the object of the action expressed by the *lyap*-suffix is not already expressed [by another word], the second case (*dvitīyā*) is used, just as in the example: *paktvaudanaṃ bhujyate* ("Having cooked the rice, it is eaten"). However, in the usage *paktvaudano bhujyate*, since the primary object of the action is already expressed [by the nominal suffix], only the nominative (*prathamā*) is used.
In the case of an action ending in the suffix *ktvā*, however, the connection is implied rather than expressed by the words themselves. Let the halls—the armories—of weapons be opened. || 23 ||
Let armor be fastened upon the bodies; let the foot soldiers assemble; let the armies be quickly counted, and let the excellent battle arrays be formed. (24)
They possess excellent dispositions and provide support for the best of warriors. || 24 ||
"Let the commanders of the forces be appointed, and let spies be dispatched in all directions.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: While the king was speaking thus with haste and agitation, [the sage intervened]. (25)
The doorkeeper, having entered with a hurried and bowed mien, spoke thus:
The doorkeeper said:
"O Lord, the commander-in-chief of the northern quarter stands at the gate."
He longs for a vision of the God of gods, as a lotus longs for the sun.
Of you, the god of gods, the king of kings. || 26 ||
The king said:
"Go, then, without delay and bring him in.
We shall learn what has occurred at the ends of the earth by hearing his report."
"By hearing the account— that is, by listening correctly to it— we shall know what has occurred in the farthest quarters," said Śrī Vasiṣṭha. Thus addressed,
[he spoke to] the Lord of the North, who had been ushered in by the doorkeeper.
At that moment, the king beheld the commander of the forces standing before him, intent on prostration.
When the king had spoken thus, he beheld Uttaraśeṣa, who had been ushered in by the doorkeeper, standing before him intent on prostration.
With every limb mangled and wounded, his body covered from head to toe with arrows,
gasping for breath and vomiting blood, he was yet unconquered by his enemy through his fortitude.

Every limb and every minor part was covered with arrows; thus, it was rendered powerless and consequently conquered. The word "by steadfastness" (dhairyeṇa) is to be connected with what follows later. || 29 ||
Having prostrated, suppressing his bodily pain while breathing with continuous gasps, he quickly spoke these preliminary words with urgency.
Steadying his bodily pain with fortitude and bowing down, he spoke these words, which constitute the commencement—that is, the opening statement—as follows. || 30 ||
The Commander of the Forces said:
"O Lord, all three guardians of the quarters, accompanied by a vast army,
have gone to the city of Yama solely by your command in order to conquer Yama."

Those three previously mentioned guardians of the quarters, acting as vassals, went to the city of Yama—that is to say, they died—under your command; this is a poetic conceit (utprekṣā) suggesting it was as if to conquer Yama himself. || 31 ||
Consequently, many kings have arrived here with force, pursuing me, who am incapable of protecting that region and other such duties.
This great enemy force has reached the territory of Your Majesty;
let it be dealt with accordingly, for there is nothing that is unconquerable for Your Majesty. (33)
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Now, while he was speaking thus, distressed and seeking a livelihood,
another man suddenly entered and spoke these words.
The enemy force has arrived; let it be dealt with so that our own army, which has fallen into a miserable state, may be victorious. || 33 ||
O Lord of Men, the vast forces of the enemy stood on high in the four directions around this circle with the grace of spreading petals.

O lord of men, by the well-known playful trembling of the leaves of the *aśvattha* and other trees belonging to this realm—which are like man-eaters—the vast and extensive forces of the enemy stationed on high in the four directions were overwhelmed. (35)
Is the earth not surrounded by our enemies—whose splendor is like a forest of swords, maces, spears, and javelins—as if it were encircled by the ridges of the Lokāloka mountain? (36)
Our land is surrounded and encompassed by enemies. || 36 ||
There, chariots with banners as weapons and warriors for their limbs, crowded with moving attendants, rush forth like the mass of the three cities flying up into the air.
Those whose limbs are banners, weapons, and warriors. || 37 ||
Raising their trunks like trees in a forest of flesh within the sky,
the arrays of elephants trumpet like masses of rain-clouds in the monsoon.
With their trunks as their tips, they roar and trumpet like masses of well-known clouds during the rainy season. || 38 ||
Making the earth rise and fall with their galloping,
the throngs of horses neighed like a great ocean tossed by the wind.

By means of their galloping, they produce rises and falls similar to the undulations of the earth; neighing like the great oceans tossed by the wind, they are called "wind-tossed" (vātaspanda). || 39 ||
The horses neighed as they fell into foamy whirlpools on all sides,
forming circles like the waters of the salt ocean.
They resound and roar; moreover, they are frothy and whirlpool-like, meaning they descend while spinning. || 40 ||
With armor as radiant as the sky, army after army rises up in every direction with massive waves, like the flood of the ocean at the time of universal dissolution.

An army, distinguished by armor, weapons, and other equipment, and possessing a clarity and luster like that of space, rises up in every direction; the reversal of the distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) is a Vedic archaism. 41.
The luster of the arrows, missiles, weapons, armor, crowns, and ornaments upon their bodies shines like the flames of the fire of your majesty. 42.
The splendors of their strength, consisting of arrows, missiles, weapons, and the like, flash like the flames of the fire of your majesty.
With arrays of fish and sea-monsters and the circular movements of whirlpools, the masses of troops rise up like the surging waves of the ocean. (43)

They are accompanied by arrays in the forms of fish, sea-monsters, and so forth; this is clear in the case of the ocean. "Waves" refers to both large billows and the various divisions of the advancing army. 43.
Through their mutual contact, the rows of weapons such as spears and the like blaze and roar with fierce *huṃkāras* born of anger and other emotions. (44)
With fierce *huṃkāras*, consisting mostly of *huṃ* sounds, and with the clanging of *jhaṇatkāras*.
"O Lord, I have been thus commanded by my master to make this request:
therefore, please depart after clearing away the shrubs and other obstacles at the boundary of the maṇḍala. (45)
Your lord, your vassal, has been spoken to and dispatched by you to your presence. || 45 ||
"O Lord, I am going there, equipped with my spear, sword, and arrows;
everything has been reported by me here, and the Lord knows what must follow. (46)
"Armed and clad in armor, I am going toward that sender, equipped with spears, swords, and arrows.
All of his words have been reported and made known here before you. Beyond this, what ought to be done, the Lord knows; I do not—this is the meaning. (46)
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Having spoken thus and offered his salutation, he departed in haste,
making a gurgling sound like a wave of the ocean that has subsided.

The king's palace— filled with a multitude of bewildered ministers, kings, warriors, officials, elephants, women, chariots, horses, attendants, and citizens, and with its collection of weapons shaken by their own fear— became like a great forest agitated by a fierce wind.

In which [city] there were ministers, kings, warriors, officials, executors of royal commands, elephants, women, chariots, horses, attendants, those who perform services, and throngs of citizens; where caravans—consisting of multitudes of living beings whose weapons were raised out of fear of him—were present; and in the reading *alihatetisārtham*, it means that they were struck down like bees.

The meaning is that the king’s palace—where calamities and multitudes of misfortunes had arrived—was like a great forest agitated by a fierce wind; it was comparable to such a state, being utterly distraught. || 48 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and eighth canto, titled "The Description of the King’s Fury upon the Rejection of Ignorance," within the "Instruction of Vipaschit" in the "Discourse on Ignorance," in the *Śrī Vālmīki-Devarṣi-Maharṣi-Nibandhana-Upanishad* (or *Uttara-Khaṇḍa*) of the *Ārṣa*.
Thus ends the one hundred and eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the King’s Resolve," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and ninth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
In the meantime, all the ministers approached the king.
The sages [sought him] as Vāsava [seeks the heavens] when the firmament has been assailed by the Daityas. || 1 ||
In this context, having heard the words of the minister, the king’s immediate rising from the fire with four bodies is described.

When the Daityas had assailed both the sky and the earth, he [protected them]; for him, the world of heaven (svargaloka) was "nabhobhūḥ"—meaning that which exists in the sky (*nabhas*)—just as the sages [protect] Indra (*vāsava*). || 1 ||
The ministers said:
"O Lord, we have reached a conclusion: as long as the enemies remain within our territory, let the fourth expedient, force (*daṇḍa*), be employed against them among the three [other] means."
The word "yāvat" signifies totality; the meaning is that it has been determined after investigating everything. What was determined?
That [the enemy] is not within the scope of any of the three expedients—conciliation, bribery, and sowing dissension. || 2 ||
O Lord, as for that request or penetration which was never made before, what talk can there even be now regarding it among them? (3)

*Praṇaya* is affection shown through gifts, honors, and the like. *Anupraveśa* is the infiltration of one's own partisans into the enemy ranks under the pretext of seeking refuge—following the maxim of the crow and the owl—for the purpose of their destruction.
What need is there even to mention the employment of such methods among those enemies who rob one of one's reputation? (3)
The wicked Mlecchas, wealthy and hailing from various lands, are well-united;
having found many vulnerabilities, these enemies are not susceptible to conciliation and the other [strategic means]. || 4 ||
"Among those who are somewhat trustworthy yet not wealthy, there is scope for employing the means of conciliation and bribery; however, these [enemies] are not of that sort," he said:
"Aside from this, there is no other remedy; this alone is a matter of great urgency. Therefore, let preparations for battle be made immediately. (5)
"Let the command be given to the heroes; let the chosen deities be worshipped;
let the vassal lords be summoned, and let the drum of battle be struck. (6)
"Let the warriors arm themselves completely and go forth to battle;
let the quarters of the sky be made radiant, thick with clouds like the trembling of Time."

Let the soldiers arm themselves; then let them go forth into battle. Let the quarters of the sky be made to shine by the herds of elephants, as if by dark-colored clouds at the end of an aeon. || 7 ||
Let the bows be strung loudly; let the rows of bowstrings twang; and let the quarters of the sky become dark as rain-clouds with the circles of [shattered] fragments. (8)
The rows of qualities are the series of bowstrings; by means of bows resembling half-moons, that is, semicircular in shape.
May the clouds of heroes— whose lightning is the vibrating bowstring, whose thunder is their deep roar,
and whose earrings are their flashing bows— release showers of iron arrows.
May those heroic clouds, who possess deep thundering roars like the lion’s cry, release showers characterized by iron arrows; they whose earrings are their gleaming bows. || 9 ||
The king said:
"Go quickly; let the preparations for battle be made.
Having bathed and worshipped the fire, I shall depart for the field of combat."
Arrangement refers to the planning of city protection, military formations, and so forth. || 10 ||
Having spoken thus, the king, though engaged in great undertakings, was bathed in an instant by jars of Ganges water, like a new garden in the rainy season by clouds.

"Like a newly blossomed garden in the rainy season, he was bathed in an instant"—by the phrase "even though it was a great undertaking," it is understood that he abandoned even other necessary duties. (11)
Then, having entered the fire-chamber and worshipped the consumer of oblations with devotion according to the scriptures, the protector of the earth reflected as follows.
He reflected upon the matter that is about to be described; this is the meaning. || 12 ||
His lifespan has been brought to its end through the splendor of effortless luxury and majesty;
he has granted security from fear to his subjects, sealed as far as the ocean.
It was sealed, accompanied by the seal of the teaching. || 13 ||
Having trodden upon the surface of the earth, his enemies were placed beneath his footstool;
the ten directions were bent down like creepers weighed down by the burden of their fruit. 14.
Even the ten directions were made to vomit forth the fruit of their hands, like creepers laden with fruit. || 14 ||
His bright fame is inscribed upon the moon-like faces of his subjects;
the creeper of his glory has been planted upon the earth and flows toward the three worlds.
It was inscribed—that is, set down and filled—in the moon-disks which bear the characteristics of the minds of the subjects.
Although not explicitly stated, the equality of his fame in its various digits is understood. The Gaṅgā, flowing through the three paths, is characterized as a creeper of fame;
by the metaphor of her flowing through the three paths, it is implied that the creeper of fame increases even in both the upper and lower worlds.
The pervasion of extension is understood. || 15 ||
Friends, companions, noble ones, and kinsmen were filled with jewels as if they were treasuries;
on the shores of the ocean, the fermented liquor of coconut sap was drunk.
The noble ones are the venerable Brāhmaṇas. By the expression "on the shores of the ocean," the conquest of the quarters extending to the limits of the four oceans is understood.
The lives of my enemies have become as tremulous as the skin on the throat of a frog;
marked by my command, they have become like the mountain ranges of other continents.
The vital breaths—the lives—of his enemies were like the skin of frogs, well-known for its location in the throat at the time of their croaking, which trembled [in fear]. || 17 ||
It has roamed through the Siddha armies across the nine regions at the ends of the quarters;
it has rested upon the peaks of the mountains at the earth's edge with the grace of a cloud.
In the far reaches of the horizon, there are nine famous and unprecedented lands of gold and other precious substances;
and there are the kings of the frontier regions—both the sovereigns of intermediate lands and those whose realms extend to the very edge of the Lokāloka mountain.

By means of his intellect alone—filled with wisdom, characterized by absolute virtue, and accomplishing desired ends—he acquired kingdoms that remained undestroyed and were established in high positions. (19)

He states another illustration with the words "by the intellect alone" (dhiyeva). Just as [the world] rests in the high station of Brahman by means of an intellect full of knowledge and habituated to solitary concentration, so too have I—acting for the desired welfare of my subjects—preserved, increased, and acquired the kingdoms. 19.
Even the unruly Rākṣasas were bound with heavy fetters;
and Dharma, Artha, and Kāma existed among one another, free from mutual increase or decrease.
Even the Rākṣasas dwelling in Laṅkā and other places, who were undisciplined and possessed of no self-restraint, have been bound by me with firm fetters.
My youth has been spent by me without interruption, drinking in great fame;
now it is radiant with a heavy burden of frost resting upon the young grass.

My life has been spent upon dharma, artha, and kāma, which were pursued without mutual conflict, free from both accumulation and depletion—that is to say, in balanced measure. Now that my fame has been fully drunk up, I have become white with old age;
like a great mass of frost resting upon the tips of young grass shoots, this radiant whiteness of senility has arrived.

The connection [of the word] is with the subsequent [term]. In the reading *śakyaviśrānta*, it should be explained as "resting upon those things such as straw that are capable of becoming solidified. || 21 ||
Old age has arrived, sweeping away the fervor for all enjoyments;
upon it, fierce and powerful enemies seeking battle have descended.
Upon that old age; that is to say, while it exists. || 22 ||
Having assembled from all sides, victory remains uncertain;
therefore, let us offer this very fire here to this god who bestows victory.
"Raising up this very oblation of my head, I indeed offer it.
The King said:
"O God Agni, this head of mine has become an oblation for you. (24)
O Lord of Gods, previously I offered [this] like a sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa);
if you are pleased, O Blessed One, by this act performed by me. (25)
Just as in previous sacrifices the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) was offered, now this head is being given. If you are pleased with me, then [let it be] by virtue of this performed deed. || 25 ||
"O Lord, let four bodies arise for me from the sacrificial pit—powerful, radiant with splendor, like the arms of Nārāyaṇa. (26)
"O Lord, may four [sons] arise for me from your own body out of the sacrificial pit. || 26 ||
"O wise and all-pervading Lord, may I slay my enemies in the four directions without obstacle;
and you must grant me your vision. (27)

"I am to be slain" (*vadhyām*); the elision of the *s* is a Vedic archaism (*chāndasa*). "O you who possess intelligence," [I speak] with the desire to see you, that is, with the intent of remembering you.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Having spoken thus, that protector of the earth took up his sword and swiftly severed the head— tremulous like a lotus— as easily as a child might playfully pluck one.
With ease, like a child plucking a lotus, that protector of the earth severed his head. || 28 ||
As soon as he had offered the severed head to the one whose path is black (Agni),
that king fell into the fire along with his body.
To the one whose path is black, whose track is black; together with the body, the headless trunk. || 29 ||
Then, having consumed it, the fire gave that body back to him fourfold;
for that which is consumed by the great increases immediately. (30)
"Having eaten" means having utilized as an oblation; "consumed by the great" means accepted by the great—this is the meaning. || 30 ||
Then, O lord of the earth, the king arose from the fire in four forms,
blazing with masses of splendor like Nārāyaṇa emerging from the ocean.
Those four bodies of his shone with radiant splendor,
adorned from birth with excellent crests, ornaments, weapons, and garments.
For them, the most excellent ear-ornaments, decorations, weapons, and garments were born simultaneously [with their bodies].
All of them were high-minded; all women wore breastplates and helmets, along with crowns, bracelets, armlets, and the full expanse of earrings.
All men likewise wore armor and helmets, together with crowns, bracelets, armlets, and large earrings.
By the word *mauli* (crown), its ornaments such as crest-jewels (*śiroratna*) and so forth are indicated. [The term] *sarvāḥ* means "those who protect all" (*sarvān avanti rakṣanti*).

According to the rule *verapṛktalopāt*, there is the elision of the suffix *vali* by prior application of the rule for the elision of the suffix *apṛkta*; thus, when the *vali* is elided, the long vowel of the same class as the preceding one (*pūrvasavarṇadīrghaḥ*) is substituted. || 33 ||
All were of identical appearance and possessed similar limbs; they stood there like jewels among horses, resembling the swift and noble Uccaiḥśravas.
They are established and mounted. || 34 ||
Those noble-minded ones possessed quivers filled with golden-tipped arrows;
they were auspicious, equal in their physical forms, and possessed bows of identical quality. || 35 ||
It is connected with arrows and quivers, along with golden ornaments. || 35 ||
That man—whether on an elephant, a chariot, or a horse—upon whom they mount, becomes entirely inaccessible to the faults of enemies. (36)

He describes another extraordinary quality: "They ascend. Those bodies which ascend upon that person—whether he be a palanquin-bearer, an elephant, a bull, a chariot, or a horse—that man and all such [beings] are not at all accessible or reachable by the defects of the spells, mechanical devices, sorcery, weapons, missiles, and so forth employed by enemies.
It comes to be. || 36 ||
Having drunk and held them for a long time within the womb, they were heated by the masculine fire,
like oblations poured upon a sacrificial altar being consumed there by the submarine fire.

Did your four bodies first drink the waters of the oceans with the submarine fire as their mother, and then, having been held for a long time within the womb, were brought to manhood—that is, the form of a man—and subsequently placed upon the sacrificial altar of the fire-pit, as if they had been born? This is a poetic conceit (utprekṣā). || 37 ||

With their bodies filled with heaps of jewels, horses, gold, and flowers, illuminating everything with smiles as bright as the moon, those four— whose forms were auspicious like lions or oceans, or like the Vedas— issued forth from the fire fed by oblations, just as the Haris themselves or the oceans might emerge.

Moreover, upon the bodies of horses adorned with jewels and which were themselves like jewels, their forms filled with heaps of flowers, they illuminated the quarters of the sky with moon-like smiles; those four wise ones appeared like the four Viṣṇus— Haraṇas— emerged from the fire of the *āhuti* oblations as embodied manifestations of the Good, or like the oceans themselves having taken on physical form.
Or rather, they rushed forth and emerged like the Vedas. || 38 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and ninth canto, titled "The Attainment of a Body through Entering the Fire," in the *Nirvāṇa* section of the *Mokṣopāya* within the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by the sage Vālmīki.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninth chapter, titled "The Regaining of the Body through Entering the Fire," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa within the illustrious Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa.
The One Hundred and Tenth Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
When they had reached the outskirts of the city from the four directions along with their enemies, [the following occurred].
In the meantime, a fierce battle commenced there.
A fierce battle that commenced as the enemies from the four directions reached the vicinity of the city is described here in detail.
A battle commenced with the enemies who had arrived at the vicinity, that is, near the city. || 1 ||
Villages and cities were plundered, along with common and noble families;
bodies were ablaze from conflagrations, and everything was shrouded by masses of smoke like clouds.
Wherein the lineage of living beings is greatly agitated.
The sun was obscured by the great smoke of the net of arrows, appearing as if shrouded in darkness;
now the sun was suddenly visible, and now the solar disc was suddenly invisible.
Where the sun was obscured by nets of arrows and great clouds of smoke, and darkness prevailed. || 3 ||
The forest of leaves was scorched by the great heat of the fire’s burning; the sky was filled with stones and the spears and clubs of flickering tongues of flame.
Where the forests have their leaves scorched and drying up, and where the sky is filled with flickering firebrands and flaming creepers.
With a double blaze of weapons arising from the reflection of the fire of his own flames,
he attained the nectar of Indra’s consorts through the great heroes who had been broken in battle.

Wherein weapons blaze with double intensity and shine with double brilliance; where the celestial nymphs, the consorts of Indra, and nectar are attained by great heroes who have been defeated in battle.
It resounded with the cries of wild elephants, bringing joy to those eager for battle,
and rained down a shower of *bhuśuṇḍīs*, discuses, spears, tridents, and javelins.
It brings joy to the heroes who are eager for battle and longing for combat.
It caused the hearts of the base and ignorant to break with the joy of the soldiers' clamor,
and it blocked the path to heaven with clouds as white as masses of dust.
Where cowards and commoners die from the mere hearing of the soldiers' tumultuous clamor due to their hearts breaking;
where there is the blocking of the path of the sky, that is, the obstruction of the celestial path. || 7 ||
The villages were fleeing at the cries raised by the vassal kings agitated by death,
while the people fell here and there, struck down as if by lightning.

Where the herds, moving in such a way as to let out cries from their neighbors who were distraught at the prospect of death, and where the creatures were struck down by a portentous fire born of lightning; || 8 ||
The house was like a cloud of fire, abandoned by one whose dwelling had been consumed by flames;
it was like a cloud consisting of countless showers of arrows that bestowed the joy of death.
Where the smoke-clouds, consisting of fire and raining fire, were abandoned—that is, released—by the falling houses consumed by flames. || 9 ||
It surpassed the waves of the ocean with its surging horses,
and was harsh with the loud *kreṃkāra* sounds produced by the clashing tusks of elephants.
It was filled with fierce, true warriors who were like thorns upon the walls and huts of millions upon millions of fortresses;
it was a mass of dancing, leaping, and rushing, where the tips of their weapons struck and blunted against the peaks of the watchtowers.

Where, at the millions of fortresses and at the crossings of millions of passes, there were formidable and excellent warriors stationed upon the walls of the huts—walls that were like thorny shrubs; or, according to the reading *kaṅkaṭodbhaṭa*, where excellent warriors were resplendent in their armor (*vārabāṇa*); [and] while they were being enveloped by fire, which was thus flaring up...
Where masses of fire danced upon the moving turrets of the watchtowers, atop the bridges, and on the summits of the battlements as they became blunted.
With battle-axes flashing with the grand display of rolling, falling, and striking, and with the "paṭa-paṭa" sound of banners and flags fluttering in the sky; 12.

Where there are battle-axes (paṭṭiśa) rolling about— crushing, striking, severing movement, and bursting forth with arrogance— and where there are towers (aṭṭa) upon which the banners flutter and swirl in the sky, resounding with the "paṭat-paṭa" noise.
The celestial elephant was summoned by the high-pitched shrieks of "tāra," the "kreṅkāra" sounds, and the "huṃkāra" roars produced by the friction of its tusks against the stones of its weapons.

Where the celestial elephants— the world-guardian elephants (diggajas)— seem as if summoned by the white tusks of the elephants [of the quarters], by the discharge of weapons, by the grinding and clashing against stones, and by the loud *kreṅkāra* and *huṃkāra* roars that generate martial fervor. 13.
The great ocean of the sky was filled with the flood of the river of falling arrows,
and it was harsh with the crocodiles of the edges of whirling discuses, spears, and swords.
Where the great ocean, characterized by the sky, was filled with the surging floods of autumnal rivers.
The circle of continents was joined together by the fierce clanging of the armor of colliding warriors and by the brilliant *jhaṇajhaṇa* sounds.

Where the circles of islands were formed and pervaded by the loud shouts of roaring warriors and by the brilliant, jingling *jhaṇajhaṇa* sounds produced by the clashing of armor and mail-coats. || 15 ||
The ground was turned into mud by the arrows crushed under the falling feet of the warriors;
chariots and elephants were being swept away by the force of the flowing rivers of blood.
With double-edged spears and sharp-edged axes falling and rising with the ease of Garuda’s flight,
it was a sea where weapons served as aquatic creatures, broken and distressed by the waves of arrows that warded them off.
Where the aquatic creatures of weapons were shattered by the waves of arrows that resembled reeds for those who were distressed. || 17 ||
The sky was set ablaze by flames emerging from the friction of the weapons,
while heroes, freed from wrinkles and grey hair, had ascended to the third heaven.
Wherein the heaven of the gods (triviṣṭapa) was occupied by heroes who, having attained the state of divinity, were free from wrinkles and grey hair.
The earth became the support for those fighting in a battle where the sky was devoid of any space due to weapons, while the lightning-like flashes of discuses gleamed amidst the clouds of pale dust.
Where, amidst the pale, dust-marked clouds that carried the water, there were flashes of lightning bearing the mark of the wheel;
and where the surface of the earth, rendered gapless and without space by weapons, became a supportless ground for the combatants' blows.
It was fierce with the loud clamor of rival warriors shouting in the arrogance of their fierce battalions;
it was filled with the clattering of colliding carts and the rolling of chariots crushed by the impact of splintering wood.

Where carts, crashing against the earth as they crowded together, crushed the wooden frames of other chariots; and where those chariots rolled about amidst the clamor of shouting rival warriors—warriors who themselves rained down arrows from their bows like thunderbolts. || 20 ||
It was crowded with thorns consisting of headless trunks, soldiers, and vetālas;
and its lotus-hearts were the foremost corpses being devoured by vetālas for their flesh.
The thorns that are enemies, mixed with Kabandha and others—by them, it is a crisis difficult to penetrate. || 21 ||
The sky was turned into a forest by the swaying tree-like arms of headless trunks (kabandhas), whose heads, half-heads, hands, hooves, and thighs had been severed by heroes.
"Śirārdham" means half a head, severed by heroes; the lengthening of the vowel is Vedic (*chāndasa*). It refers to that place where heads, hands, and so forth [were scattered].
The chests were struck by the laughter of Vetālas with trembling faces, while it was terrifying due to the frowns of soldiers who were fiercely arrogant in their armor. || 23 ||

There, chests and their own baskets were filled with corpses struck by Vetālas— leaping, floating, and with trembling faces— who laughed out of sheer joy; it was terrifying with the frowns of fierce and haughty warriors armed with armor.

It is exclusively for killing and exclusively for dying; it is exclusively an ornament [for the brave], yet it is a transgression beyond limit through the wretchedness of both inflicting and receiving blows. (24)
Where both the certainty of striking and the certainty of dying are the singular ornaments of heroes;
where meanness and incapacity in both the giving and receiving of blows are the boundless defect and reproach that dries up the rut-fluid of the elephants among the best of warriors.
It nourishes the joy of Kṛtānta (the God of Death), who finds sole delight in slaughter. || 25 ||
For those who do not boast and remain concealed, there is the proclamation of victory;
for those who are not brave but remain concealed, there is the supreme proclamation of their power.

By not boasting— that is, by not proclaiming one's own valor through one's own mouth— there is the proclamation of victory for hidden or secret heroes by those who have witnessed their valor in battle through the mouths of others, as well as the proclamation of the lack of valor for hidden non-heroes before the lord. || 26 ||
The awakening of their own dormant virtues, such as valor and the like, is the wealth of those strong-armed men who serve as the foundation for kingdoms. (27)
Therefore, for those endowed with strength—brave men who serve as the support for the weak within kingdoms—wealth is as dear as life itself. (27)
It shattered the temples of elephants with its thundering, as they were mounted by riders on chariots;
it warded off the rut-fluid of all intoxicated, musth-elephants.
In that battle where chariots mounted by tuskers clashed against one another, the elephants had their temples shattered;
there was a complete warding off and drying up of the rut-fluid from all those intoxicated scent-elephants, the enemies of the Dānavas.
The intoxicated elephants were released by the surrounding vassal lords who were crying out like cranes;
the army’s strength was exhausted, and they suffered the pain of sword-blows inflicted by that host.

Where intoxicated elephants, even as they fled, were released by the young vassals with cries of "Sāra-sai!"— just as cranes cry out when they have entered a lake filled with intoxicated elephants; and where, thereafter, the knowledge of swordsmanship was mastered even by the aged through their ranks of *āsīkas* (swordsmen),
those for whom the sword (*asi*) was the chosen weapon.
The manifestation of that state occurs therein—meaning that even the aged, though experts in swordsmanship, displayed their proficiency in their own science through the force of possession.
The suffix *īkak* applied to *śakti* and *yaṣṭi* is formed according to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*), hence the absence of the augment *se*. || 29 ||
Like the day for the sun, it became the refuge of the king—
a place where men were half-crushed and half-dead by the throngs of soldiers yet to arrive.

In some places, even when no troops had yet arrived, men fled in the mistaken belief that they were coming; there, crushed by one another’s soles, they were nearly half-dead. For this very reason, they have gone for refuge to the feet of the king, as the day goes to the feet of the sun.
It was a new marketplace for wealth, whose very life-force is traded as merchandise, where the striking of the hammers began as men, intoxicated by the power of their vital breath, bowed down.

It was a city where, by the force of the wind of madness characterized by pride and arrogance, those who were themselves bowed down began to strike others; it was a town that served as a new marketplace for wealth whose currency was human lives. 31.
With the multitude of cloth-bound banners acting as moving tree-like arms,
he was like a coral ornament for the Fortune of the Three Worlds, owing to his radiant redness. (32)
The expanse of the sky was filled with a multitude of weapons and richly adorned with flowers, covered by parasols as beautiful as the waters of the Ocean of Milk churned by Mount Mandara.
The intention of the hero was made into a song by the hosts of gods and gandharvas;
his weapon was the Hālāhala [poison] held at the tip of his flickering palm.
In that place, the intentions and enthusiasms of heroes were sung by the Gaṇas, Pramathas, Gandharvas, and Gīrvāṇas;

and there, because of their intoxication, the warriors became like Halāyudha (Balarāma) through the splendors of those Gaṇas, Gandharvas, and others, as well as by their shimmering tips of palm trees, the tops of banners, and their weapons. (34)
Having devoured the yātudhānas—who were striking at the Saṃgha with a clanging of weapons—and having filled the mountain-cave dwellings with unprecedented, hideous trees; 35.
Having himself eaten those countless *yātudhānas*— who took pleasure in attacking the Saṅgha as a group— and having made them silent with the clattering sound of *ajhaṇajjhaṇa*,
he led them away as a burden of corpses and others, and filled his own home, characterized by mountain caves, with them; indeed, all others without exception were fed there.
Where the trees are difficult to climb, consisting mostly of poisonous trees, and where there are *yātudhāna* demons. || 35 ||
The sky was filled with heads and hands whirled about by the clashing forest of spears,
while the quarters of the horizon were submerged in a flood of stones hurled from slings.
The sky was filled with shimmering groves of spears resembling vast forests of spears, and with scattered heads and hands severed and cast down by those wielding spears. || 36 ||
The great trees were bursting and melting with a massive *caṭacaṭa* sound,
while the women’s shrill cries of lamentation filled the city and its palaces.
Where there are many trees whose sounds seem to burst forth with great *caṭacaṭa* noises produced by the slapping of their branches.
Abandoning their multitude of weapons, which shone like a forest fire amidst the clouds of *mandāra* flowers,
they left behind their wealth and homes, while their subjects fled far across the earth.
Because it bore weapons on all sides, it was abandoned by those who sought to witness it face-to-face;
it was shunned by the timid, just as a flock of birds is avoided by serpents.
Because the weapons and missiles were being carried and hurled from all sides, it was abandoned by the spectators on every side out of fear. || 39 ||
It was crowded with excellent warriors crushed by the tusks of elephants,
like a machine for pressing grapes made of men situated on the very threshold of death.

Where there was a perilous situation for the brave warriors, who—like grapes remaining after being crushed by the tusks of elephants upon a mat of hide—were being ground down on the temples of those very beasts that resembled the very jaws of Death. || 40 ||
The weapons within its waters were ground to powder by the collision of mechanical stones;
its caverns were made resonant by the deep trumpeting of herds of elephants that roared during battle.
Amidst the mountain caves, their thundering roars were echoed back;
they had acquired and amassed that which constitutes the very essence of their life-force.
Where the roars [of the elephants], having reached the mountain caves, were filled with echoes and reverberations;

and where they, by means of great effort, displayed—by spending—the entirety of their life-force and the entirety of their strength acquired since birth. [This is the form of the root *ṛj*, meaning "to go."]
The grammatical connection here is that the battle, which had commenced, was fought by heroes. || 42 ||
He was scorched by the burning of weapons and by incessant fires,
and he was never at rest due to those very same battles and others as well, fought in pairs.

Furthermore, he describes what kind of battle that was as it proceeded, beginning with the words "scorched" (bharjita) and so forth: "uncompleted" (aniṣṭhita) means not having reached its conclusion or end. || 43 ||
It was surrounded by elite groups of surviving warriors,
who were like pure Kailāsa mountains that have become the support of the Lord.

He clarifies this very essence through a simile: "as if with Kailāsa mountains. [This refers to] groups of excellent warriors who are completely pure, who do not deceive their master, and for that reason alone have attained the status of being the support for the Lord within their hearts. In the case of the Kailāsa mountains, two points are clear. || 44 ||
Overwhelmed by those noble ones— who are themselves the death of even Death—
death became their life and life became their death in battle.

For those warriors for whom death in battle is as dear as life, and for whom living by fleeing is as loathsome as death—by such noble men even the three worlds have been traversed; that is to say, they have conquered them. They become the very death of Death itself, having attained the supreme state. As it has been said: "These two are the [true] men..."
"In this world, two are piercers of the solar orb: the wandering mendicant absorbed in yoga, and he who is slain facing the enemy in battle. (45)
In that battle, in the sky where the excellent elephants were severed like lotuses,
the exceedingly formidable warriors shone like cranes in a lake.

With the whizzing sounds of stone-tipped projectiles launched from machines, with the hissing of rivers of arrows swiftly traversing the sky, with the roars of soldiers whose heads were suddenly struck,
and with the clanging of weapons in the heavens—
With the sounds of galloping horses, chariot wheels, and elephants, that [noise] reached its ears— already worn out and hardened by the interior of stones with no joints— and passed away.

Describing that very battle, he concludes with the verse beginning "yantra-": by the *ghūtkṛta* sounds— specific types of noise— of the rivers characterized by the streams or flows of *yantrāśman* (stone-missiles),
and likewise by the *phūtkṛta* sounds of the heads that were suddenly (*drāk*) severed and flew up, traversing and moving through the sky.
That battle was pervaded by the sounds of hissing breaths, by the roars of soldiers discharging showers of arrows,
by the clanging of weapons spreading through the sky, and by the neighing and trumpeting of horses and elephants;
it was such that the ears of those present were worn out and rendered deaf.
It was as motionless as the interior of a stone, its joints and bonds completely severed. || 47 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and tenth canto, titled "The Description of the Battle between the Ignorant and the Wise," in the *Nirvāṇopadeśa* of the *Mokṣopāya*, within the *Vālmīkīya-uttara-rāmāyaṇa*, the holy *Ārṣa-śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa*.
Thus ends the one hundred and tenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Battle," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*. 110.
The one hundred and eleventh canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Thus, during that tumult of battle which was like the end of a kalpa, you—
As the armies were falling and leaping up, they shone forth in the battle.
As his own army was being routed there, the king emerged and the destruction of his enemies in the four directions is described as having been brought about by his Vāyavya missiles.
Those [actions] which were set in motion—these are to be construed with the word "udabhūt" (arose) in the fifth verse, following all the locative forms denoting states of being. || 1 ||
While the celestial drums, kettledrums, great conchs, and swords resounded in the sky,
and while the twangs of the heroes' bows produced piercing shrieks, || 2 ||
While the three types of musical instruments, such as the *tūrya*, resounded with echoes in the sky, and while the swords there rang out with sounds imitating the piercing cries of heroes, || 2 ||
In that mass of soldiers, formidable with the mutual clashing of their armor, making a loud *kavaṭ-kaṭa* sound in their display of pride, and with their mail coats fiercely struck together; || 3 ||

In the troop of soldiers (*bhaṭapeṭaka*), while there was the clattering sound of armor being struck harshly, the suffix *śatṛ* is used here in the sense of the root *ku-śabda* (the sound "ku"). || 3 ||
In that battle,
as the armies of the wise king’s faction were being broken and overcome by dejection, they appeared like creepers being torn away.
In which fainting fits, as they enter, there is a state of stupor.
The drum for the king’s departure resounded, filling all directions with a sound as deep and full as the roar of clouds at the end of an eon when struck by the fourfold thunderbolt.
Simultaneously with the bursting of the great mountain ranges,
it was fierce, its deafening *caṭacaṭa* explosions numbing the entire expanse of the quarters.
Manifest simultaneously; rendered inert, made motionless. || 6 ||
With his four forms like the world-protectors, or like the four arms of Nārāyaṇa, that lord of the earth went forth in the four directions.
With four bodies possessing forms, like the four arms of Nārāyaṇa. || 7 ||
Surrounded by a great fourfold army,
he emerged with difficulty from the city, passing out through the circle of watchtowers.
He beheld his own army depleted and the circle of enemy forces powerful,
roaring with a form of destruction like a terrifying ocean agitated by battle.

He saw his own strength depleted, but he saw the circle of enemies powerful and exultant. He describes that very circle of enemies as being like the ocean, beginning with the words "roaring," and so forth. (9)
It was dense with the spray of arrows, crowded with arrays of crocodiles,
encircled by arrays of elephants, and expanded with arrays of waves.
Generally, metaphors occur everywhere. || 10 ||
Its interior was filled with waves of battle-formations flowing like the whirlpools of a river;
it possessed hundreds of whirling chariots for its eddies and a multitude of banners for its surging billows.
Its interior was filled with military arrays moving like whirlpools and with waves of people.
Rich with the foam of shimmering parasols, resounding with the neighing and whinnying of horses,
possessing the water of gleaming weapons, it was a supreme, surging torrent of flowing streams.
Where the neighing of horses is the very sound of the aquatic creatures' shrieks, it is a mine of shimmering streams. With the surging waves of the multitude of elephants and horses leaping about,
the water of weapons reflects the gleaming weapons, while its depths resound with the rising gurgling noise.
Wherein the wicked Mlecchas, gleaming and manifesting themselves in the waters that possess the characteristics of a mirage, act like black serpents;
and whose interior resounds with the rising tumultuous noise of the reports concerning the warriors of Draviḍa and other regions.
Resounding with a humming noise produced by winds agitated by the shattering [of mountains],
its body was characterized by great tremors that caused the lords of mountains to rise and fall.
In which [ocean], the great surging characterized by the sinking and emerging of the lords of mountains was produced by the bending and rising of elephants; such was his vast body. 14.
In which the great waters were beautiful with waves of overflowing floods wandering boundlessly, and in which mountains were easily struck down by my elephants and horses as they plunged through. 15.
He whose great waters are shoreless, surging with armies at their forefront, and are fully adorned with waves.
It had the dense form of the onset of a world-ending dissolution at an untimely hour,
a single great ocean of blood that filled the entire space between heaven and earth.

Its form was like the gathering of clouds at the onset of the dissolution of the eon out of season; the compound *rodasīrandhra* (the space between heaven and earth) is an archaic usage where the elision of the case-ending is not applied;

its interior was filled with heaps of necklaces, weapons, and fragments of gems scattered by the flight [of birds], and it contained stones for hurling from moving mechanical engines within shifting battle arrays.
Its interior was covered with heaps of glittering weapon fragments serving as identifying marks and with scattered gems flying upward;

as the military arrays moved, the stones used for hurling from siege-engines were scattered about—the sense being that the use of stones for hurling from engines by seafarers on ships is well known even in the ocean. || 17 ||
In some places it was bent by clouds of twilight and masses of mist that were like sprays of jewels;
in other places its clouds of rays were swallowed by a torrent of dust.
Beholding him, he thought in his mind, "I shall become for him an Agastya for the ocean of battle," and thus resolved to drink up that vast sea.

Beholding that ocean of the enemy's forces—the cause of the battle described in such a manner—Vipaścit thought, "I shall become Agastya for the drinking of this," and he recalled the Vāyavya weapon to drink up that sea of troops. (19)
He recalled the Vāyavya weapon and aimed it in the four directions upon his bow,
which was as firm as a mountain peak, like the one raised by Tripurāntaka.

Just as Śiva, intent on the destruction of the three cities at their end, fixed his weapon upon the bow characterized by Mount Meru, which served as the support for its peaks, so too [did he act]. || 20 ||
Then, for the welfare and peace of his own country and army, he paid homage to Anala and, having quickly recited the mantra, he abandoned that terrible fire.
In the reading "for the pacification of enemies," the word "having paid homage" is understood, with "to the Fire-god" as the object; he then released that weapon. || 21 ||
Just as in that very instance, he released the Parjanya weapon, the lord of great weapons, to assist him in quelling the heat of his enemies.
The meaning is that just as he discharged the Vāyavya weapon, he likewise discharged the Parjanya weapon for his assistance;

therefore, [the arrows] emerged from that terrible bow wielded by the one who possesses weapons, filling the hollows of the quarters in all four directions of the eight-formed Lord (Aṣṭamūrti). || 23 ||

From that eight-formed one, who possesses two weapons [the bow and arrow] directed toward the four quarters, streams of arrows and other missiles issued forth from the bow; such is the connection with the following verse. || 23 ||
Rivers of arrows issued forth, as did rivers of tridents; likewise, fierce rivers of spears and rivers of *bhuśuṇḍī* weapons flowed out.
There were rivers of mallets and rivers of spears flowing with speed; there were rivers of wheels and the swift currents of rivers of battle-axes.
The rivers of tomaras became great torrents of bhindipālas, and the streams of stones were winds foretelling the end of the eon. || 26 ||
And the winds are fierce gales. || 26 ||
There were rivers of thunderbolts and likewise rivers of lightning;
there were floods of rivers consisting of streams of water, accompanied by showers of swords.
The great showers of iron arrows, thick with the joy of their arising like portents,
were like the offspring of the king of mountains split asunder at the end of an eon by the serpents.
Driven by great winds, the thick, robust, and well-nourished elephants and serpents emerged like massive portents of calamity,
as if born from the great mountains split open at the end of a yuga.
By the force of that shower of weapons, that ocean of the enemy's army was instantly swept away,
not by time, but all around like a heap of dust.
By the force of that shower of fiery weapons, that ocean of the enemy's army was not merely dispersed by the passage of time, but was instantly scattered like a heap of dust blown away. || 29 ||
Like lakes whose embankments have burst apart, the armies fled in all directions due to the showers of water, thunderbolts, and weapons, as well as the fierce winds.
That flood of troops, consisting of the four divisions, turned its back and fled in all four directions,
rushing away like the great torrent of a mountain river during the rainy season.
Fleeing in haste, he went in all four directions. || 31 ||
The trees of its banners and standards were broken and carried away by the wind;
the forest of its sword-blades was shimmering and variegated with the flowers of its rays.
He describes that very flood of troops as it flees, employing a comparison to a mountain river and so forth, beginning with the word "vahat":

"Where the banners and standards themselves were like trees—large and broken—carried along by the force of the wind and drenched with sweat; and by which the forests of sword-blades were variegated and flickering with the flowers of its rays. (32)
The ground is covered with the liquid blood from large rolling stones;
it is enough to break one's heart with its terrible, gurgling roars. (33)

Those stones characterized by their stoutness which were rolling about due to the inability to flee—by the drops, that is, the droplets of liquid blood from them, it was difficult to speak; for those who had fallen there and fainted, the terrible *ghuraghura* sounds caused a breaking of the heart, meaning they were terrifying. || 33 ||
The thundering clouds were intimidated by the crackling *caṭacaṭā* sounds produced by the collisions with the tree-like tusks of the massive elephants being swept along. || 34 ||
He establishes the specific characteristic of the mountain river through the metaphor of a cloud with the word "being carried away" (uhyamāna). || 34 ||
It resounded with the jingling of flowers produced by the violent clashing of weapons and movements;
it was filled with the surging waves of horses that were leaping, trembling, and neighing.

The fierce clashing of stones and other weapons that occurred in battles is itself present here in the "jhaṇajjhaṇa" humming sound of bees produced among the flowers on the trees along the riverbanks.
It was thick with the roar of "Śilārka" from the multitude of chariots and the throngs of warriors,
and it was congested by the clashing of foot soldiers, chariots, elephants, horses, and boulders.
The deep and resonant sound produced by the chariots and the throngs of soldiers amidst the rocky precipice was thick and robust, like the warbling of cranes and other birds. || 36 ||
It was thick with harsh clanging and shrieking sounds, and filled with a dense clamor as they cried out, "We are dead! We are dead! (The reading *ṭaṅkāra* also occurs). || 37 ||
He says that very thing: "Bitter," etc. (37).
It had the gurgling roar of moving great whirlpools in the waters of the army;
it was a canopy of twilight clouds formed by the mist of blood-sprays.
The clouds, dwarfed by the waters severed by the waves of the thunderbolt, adorned the surface of the earth—which was like a bank—by breaking it with the mud of their rain. (39)

Where the clouds—stunted and bowed by the waters, as if cut down by the currents like banyan trees—are adorned by being shattered for the purpose of clearing a path on the muddy surface of the earth. (39)
It was wondrous with spears, pikes, maces, and javelins held aloft like palm leaves;
it scorched the timid folk who cried out in distress, like a young deer.
With those fleeing while wielding spears and other weapons, it was as wondrous as a palm grove where the palm leaves are being carried away.
It was densely covered with the withered leaves of the multitudes of dead elephants, horses, and warriors; it was filled with the mud formed from the mire of crushed bodies, fat, and flesh.
The riverbed was thick with the sand of massive bones ground to powder by hooves;
it was perilously rugged with the tips of wooden beams and boulders being carried along by the current.

The distinction is that bones reduced to powder are somewhat coarse sand, whereas those crushed by hooves are extremely fine sand. The expression "kaṭaṅkaṭa" (a harsh, jagged noise) is a figurative attribution of a specific sound based on the mutual clashing of surging masses of stones and the tips of trees. || 42 ||

With oceans roaring like those at the dissolution of the world, with winds blowing like those at the dissolution, with torrents falling like those at the dissolution, and with the perils of thunderbolts at the dissolution; || 43 ||

The words ending in the third case, such as "udgarjatpralayāmbhodaiḥ" (with roaring clouds of dissolution) and so forth, are syntactically connected in the fifth verse with the phrase: "In this way, the armies of the kings flee and perish like swarms of mosquitoes. || 43 ||
The entire surface of the earth was mired with mud, its lands inundated by water,
while the sky-cages were formed by rain-showers that had frozen due to the intensity of the cold and whiteness.
That whiteness which is sharp and cool, by virtue of it, [the sky appears] with cage-like structures formed from streams of water that are neither solidified nor dried up, suspended in the void.
By the fires blazing through the entire city, village, and houses, and also by the gurgling cries of the subjects, horses, elephants, and foot-soldiers; (45)
With the rumbling of chariots like clouds in the sky and on the earth,
and with the fourfold loud cries of the stars in all four directions, [the world was filled].
On earth with the rattling of chariots, in heaven with the thundering of clouds, and in the four directions with the fourfold twanging of the bow of the wise Tāra— (46)
By the friction and clashing of the expansion of circles of lightning, and by the raining down of arrows, spears, clubs, darts, slings, and other weapons; || 47 ||
By the collisions and friction of clouds that cause the expansion of circles of lightning. || 47 ||
In every direction, the countless forces of the powerful kings fled swiftly and perished like swarms of mosquitoes. (48)
By the falling showers of thunderbolts— which were like a mass of clouds containing weapons resembling unrestrained forest fires—
the armies became as agitated as the waters of a restless ocean, as if entering the submarine fire.
