The armies of the frontier kings were like creatures entering the submarine fire; for they were overwhelmed by the fires of weapons resembling unrestrained forest conflagrations, and by the falling showers of thunderbolts that distressed the people, while their weak forces, being boiled like aquatic monsters in the turbulent waters of the ocean, perished.

Thus ends the one hundred and eleventh sarga, titled "The Flight of the Armies in the Four Directions," in the *Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa* of the *Mokṣopāya*, within the *Dehajanmavibhāga* section of the *Vālmīki-ṛṣi-viracita Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*. 111.

Thus ends the one hundred and eleventh chapter, titled "The Flight of the Armies in the Four Directions," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the glorious Vasiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa, in its exposition of the essential meaning. || 111 ||
The one hundred and twelfth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
[Consider] the world as a forest of sandalwood trees, with its serpents being the necklaces and garments of people.
Cut by the edges of axes, it fell into the southern ocean.
In this work, all the enemy warriors in the four directions are described exactly as they perished, wherever and in whatever manner they were targeted and fled.

Therein, he first describes the manner of the destruction of the Cedi warriors with the words beginning "loka-": the sandalwood forest, characterized by the Cedi warriors, having been cut down by axes, fell into the Southern Ocean. He qualifies it with the word "loka-" in order to justify the well-known fact that sandalwood trees are entwined by serpents.

"Lokas" are those which are looked upon; it is that [city] in which there are beautiful necklaces and garments, and serpents. Here, in every instance, it should be understood that the mention of "Bhaṭa" is by way of the name of the place itself. || 1 ||

Like leaves swept away by a flood, the Pārasīkas, striking one another in their confusion, were destroyed in the Vañjula forest. (2) [Note: By interpreting the gerund *prohya*—meaning "having carried away"—as "having reached" (*pravahaṇaṃ prāpya*) in the sense of "that which is to be swept away from its base," this result is achieved.]

The Persian soldiers, being carried away like leaves by the flood of weapons— [this is the result of interpreting the gerund *prohya* as "having reached a boat" from its base meaning "to carry"]— perished in the region of the Vañjula forest while striking one another in their confusion. (2)
On Mount Dardura, in its depths, the Daradas— whose hearts were torn by fear—
lay hidden within the hollows of caves like Dānavas.
Likewise, the Darada warriors were hidden in the deep caverns of the Dardura mountain. || 3 ||
The winds, bearing a mist of powder from the tips of the streams of their four weapons,
were encircled by lightning and caused the clouds to whirl with their uplifted arms.

The winds, set in motion by the Varuṇa weapon, were encircled by flashes of lightning and carried a mist consisting of the powder from stone armor and other materials produced by the edges and tips of the four weapons characterized as arrows, spears, swords, and axes; their weapons whirled about. || 4 ||
With their bodies crushed by the mutual clashing of tusks,
the elephants became like morsels of food for the belly of Death, who devours his prey whole.
When they had set out, he describes what occurred at that time with the verse beginning "dantinaḥ" (the elephants).

With their tusks broken by one another's blows, and their bodies overwhelmed by a flood of blood, the elephants became like morsel-sized lumps filling the belly of Death—filling it to its capacity. The repetition [of the word "dantinaḥ"] is intended to indicate their great number. || 5 ||
Those Raivatikas, born of that [lineage], were struck by fierce tomara-spears at night;
their limbs were devoured and divided into portions by Rūpikā Piśācīs.
Some of those born in the Darada region are known as Raivatikas, who dwell hidden on Mount Raivataka; they are accompanied by Rūpikās—female demons who deceive men with their own forms.
In the dense thickets of *tālī* and *tamāla* trees and in the withered forests of Daśārṇa,
they were placed on the necks [of lions] and, having been torn apart within, they lost their lives.
The Daśārṇas are the warriors born in that region. || 7 ||
On the shore of the western ocean, in the land of coconut trees,
the Yavanas were deprived of life, swallowed by swarms of sea-monsters.
In the coastal forest where coconut trees grow. || 8 ||
The Śakas could not endure even for a moment the dark shower of iron arrows;
their lives were made to dance like beds of blue lotuses trampled by the Ramaṭhas.
The Śakas could not endure that mass of dark iron arrows; likewise, the Ramaṭhas, their lives trembling like clusters of lotuses struck by the wind, were left breathless.
Mount Mahendra, with its peaks reaching toward the ears of heaven,
appeared as if surrounded by dark masses of clouds scattered across the sky.

Mount Mahendra, whose form was like the expanse of the Śravaṇa constellation with its three horn-like peaks, appeared as if enveloped by a net of clouds because it was surrounded by the fleeing dark-blue armies moving through the sky. || 10 ||
The army of the Taṅgaṇas, possessing the excellent form of refined gold, was shattered;
their garments were stripped away by thieves, and they were devoured at night in a secluded place by night-stalkers.
The army of the Taṅgaṇa warriors, whose garments had first been plundered by thieves and who was subsequently violated in a secluded place by night-stalkers, perished.
At that time, the surface of the earth became like the sky due to the showers of meteors,
as flaming weapons whirled about and flashed on all sides.

At that time, during the devouring of the Taṅgaṇa army, the surface of the earth there shone with a splendor like the sky, filled with night-stalkers who were wandering and moving about on all sides, bearing flaming weapons and torches,
and thus gleaming like a multitude of stars or a mass of bears.
Resounding with the deep humming of echoes from the hollows of the clouds and the earth, the sky, like a cave within the house of the world, seemed intent on singing a song as thick as a rain-cloud.

Moreover, in that victory of Vipaścit, the entire world became his inner chamber; thus the sky, with the deep rumbling of thunderclouds echoing from the cavities of the earth, was like the sound of thick mṛdaṅga drums, as if it were striving to sing of his dense fame. (13)
The people of other lands, shattered by the wheels, gave up their lives like old fish in a waterless swamp of mud and dried flesh. 14.
Like fish in a muddy swamp that has become a forest inhabited by aquatic creatures—a stagnant pool of moss that has, by fate, run dry—they are left without refuge.
Having conquered as many islands as could fit within their bellies, they rested for seven days on the Sahya mountain with equal forms and proceeded slowly due to exhaustion.
As many as there were islands and as many as there were soldiers born in those islands, they hid on the Sahya mountain and rested for seven nights;

then, their wounds having been healed through medical treatment and other means, and being of uniform appearance, they returned slowly and with great effort to their own country, drenched by heavy rains. || 15 ||
Heaped up in the groves of *gandhamādana* and *puṇnāga* trees,
these *gāndhāra* [sandalwood] trees are guarded by the daughters of the *vidyādharas*.
By those showers of discuses released by the Hūṇas, Cīnas, and Kirātas, their heads were severed by the headwinds and fell like lotuses. || 17 ||

The heads of the Hūṇas, Cīnas, and Kirātas were severed by the showers of discuses released by Vipāścit—discuses that were thus impelled by headwinds and possessed great velocity—as if they were lotuses. || 17 ||
Like thorns upon the stalks of lotuses, they remained motionless; out of fear of him, those made of wood dwelt for a long time within every tree.
The Bhaṭas, who were called Nīlīpas because they were born in a region with that name, lived there as tree-like beings, consisting mostly of wood. || 18 ||
Upon the mountain and forest lands, which were the playgrounds of beautiful deer,
there arose a dense agitation in all four directions caused by their sudden descents.
In the mountain and forest regions that served as playgrounds for deer, antelopes, and birds, the agitation caused by the sudden attacks of that Vipaścit became exceedingly intense.
Those named Kaṇṭakasthala, who were as harsh as thorny ground and who dwelt upon thorny ground,
resided within the region of Kaṇṭakasthala.
In that region, a district of thorny ground like a forest of *karañja* trees, those who dwelt in the thorny places—hidden within forests of *karañja* and other such trees—were harsh robbers. || 20 ||
The Persians, having reached the further shore of the ocean by means of boats, fell down, purified by the winds, like stars at the time of universal dissolution. (21)
Winds, striking the ocean and marked by the ridges of rocky peaks, blew forth, plundering the forests in every direction, as if portending the dissolution of the world.
Marked and bearing signs by the blows of boulders upon the mountain ridges, they were made objects of apprehension regarding the dissolution of the world. || 22 ||
Dense with the force of rain-showers, drenched in muddy water, and filled with deep rumbling sounds,
they became invisible in all ten directions due to the winds of many agitated weapons.
The ten directions, having become as intense as heavy downpours due to many agitated weapons and winds, became invisible, submerged in mud and water.
With winds that produced a roar and carried the sound of "chapa-chapa," mists spread across the earth like the currents of the great ocean.

Driven by the winds, the mists flowed forth with a "chapachapa" sound; this is an onomatopoeic imitation of the indistinct noise produced by the impact of the mist. Even the great ocean currents, when impelled by the winds, are well known to those who have experienced them to flow with a "chapachapa" roar.
Standing at a distance from their chariots and making whistling sounds like the waves, they fell with the breezes from the lake waters like bees from lotuses. (25)
Carried away by the winds and situated in a distant region, the chariot-warriors fell into the lake-water like waves, uttering cries of distress. || 25 ||
Even amidst a flood of weapons, the infantry force, turbid from the multitude of discuses, fled like a mass of dust in a heavy downpour, being unable to stand its ground.

Although their infantry force possessed a multitude of weapons, they were unable to withstand the downpour of the shower of discs; with eyes clouded by tears and turbid from the mass of dust raised during the flight, they were as incapable of fleeing as a thicket of chaff before a torrential rain.
The Hūṇas are submerged up to their heads in the sands of the northern ocean;
drenched right there within the mud, they are like impure spikes used for filling.
Just as an iron spike becomes soaked when it is covered with mud and becomes stained by the earth filling it, so too are they drenched. || 27 ||
On the borders of the cardamom groves along the eastern ocean, the Śakas were captured and held for a day; though released, they did not depart, nor did they go to the abode of Yama.
The Śaka soldiers, having been led by Vipaścit to the rows of cardamom forests on the shores of the eastern ocean, were bound for only a single day;
subsequently released out of compassion, they did not go to the abode of Yama—meaning, they did not die. || 28 ||
Gently crying out from Mount Mahendra, they fell from the sky;
they were comforted by the best of sages like the deer of their own hermitage.
From the mountain peak, as high as heaven itself. || 29 ||
Having entered into a request on Mount Sahya, two items were obtained from the Surabhi cow;
sometimes, through an adverse circumstance, a benefit comes about by chance, like the falling of the palm fruit upon the crow.
The soldiers, having entered the Sahya mountain into the presence of Mūkāmbikā on its peak named Kuṭajāḍhya,
obtained— by chance entering a divine cave— the fulfillment of their desired goals as a result of their petition for both worldly and otherworldly benefits.
For instance, at a time of rising fortune, even through some accidental occurrence (*kākatālīyanyāya*), one may obtain something even from what was not intended.
The goal, the aim of man, is attained; for by those who entered the cave of the gods—which was fit for death—the *siddhis* were obtained. This is the meaning:
the Daśārṇas fell like withered leaves in the Dardura forest;
having ignorantly eaten poisonous fruits, they died right there of their own accord.
The soldiers of Daśārṇa, having fallen in the forest of Mount Dardura, entered [the cave]. || 31 ||
Having eaten the *viśalyakaraṇī* herb by a stroke of chance,
the Haihayas went home on the Himalayas like Vidyādharas.
The warriors from the Haihaya country, having consumed the *viśalyakaraṇī* herb on the Himalayas, became sky-goers like the Vidyādharas and returned home. || 32 ||
Having returned home with bows whose flowers have withered on their backs,
the Vaṅgas are not seen even today, as if they have attained the state of Piśācas.

In this way, the Vaṅgas too, having consumed the medicinal herbs of the Himalayas, returned home appearing like men who have become withered with their floral ornaments fallen from behind; being thus distinguished only by their bows due to the exhaustion of their arrows, they are not seen even today because of fear, as there is no possibility of their venturing outside. || 33 ||
Having consumed the forest fruits that bestow the status of a Vidyādhara,
the Vidyādharas remain in heaven and sport with Vidyādharīs.
Having become Vidyādharas, they remained in heaven. || 34 ||
Falling upon the groves of *tālī* and *tamāla* trees with their limbs shattered,
the Pārasicas fell into a swoon like celestial beings (*vaimānika*) reeling from a fall.
The Pārasīkas, having fallen into the regions of Tāla and Tamāla trees, were struck down by their enemies as soon as they entered;
with their limbs shattered, they fell into a state of delusion and swoon, and there, through their confusion, they became like celestial beings in aerial chariots.
The fourfold army of the Kaliṅgas was destroyed, its elephants with trembling temples having fallen upon the courtyard of Taṅgaṇa, while their limbs were crushed by the limbs [of the enemy]. 36.
That fourfold army of the Aṅgas and Kaliṅgas, consisting of swift and powerful elephants, having been struck down by his limbs, fled and fell upon the courtyard of the Taṅgaṇas. || 36 ||
As he advanced against the enemy forces, the Sālvas fell into the interior of the mountain of his arrows along with their lord; even today, they remain there like stones. (37)

While the enemy force—consisting of Sālva warriors, arrows, mountains, heaps of stones, and waters within its belly—was thus advancing and attacking, they fell together with their lord; even today, having become stones and images, they remain as the local village deities of that region. || 37 ||
Countless men fled in every direction, and they met their destruction in oceans with surging waves. (38)

Who is capable of counting the fallen bad fruits in fields, forests, cities, waters, lands, mountains, riverbanks, canals, villages, rivers, oceans, cliffs, and trees; or in hamlets, market-towns, mountains, wells, caves, and houses?
Not only in the oceans, but also in fields, forests, cities, waters, dry lands, mountains, riverbanks, canals, agrahāras, rivers, seas, cliffs, trees, as well as in villages,
market-towns, toll-stations, hills, wells, caves, and houses— their remains, fallen and deceased, [were found].
Who is able to measure or count [them]? The meaning is: no one at all. || 39 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and twelfth canto, titled "The Loss of Strength," in the *Ārṣa* Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa of Valmīki, within the Section on the Departure of the Sons, in the Sub-section on the Descent of the Sons, in the Book on the Instruction of the Sons. 112.
Thus ends the one hundred and twelfth canto, titled "The Fall of Bala," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and thirteenth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Then, as the enemies were thus fleeing while their forces pursued them, [the following occurred].
Those four wise ones reached a place even more distant than the distance [they had already traveled]. || 1 ||
In this work, the pacification of enemies by means of missiles, the exhaustion of the means of accomplishment,
and the manifestation of the oceans are described in detail.
Pursuing and chasing after the forces of the enemies of the gods. || 1 ||
Sent forth by the one Lord, who consists of all powers,
they all set out for the conquest of the directions with equal resolve.

They were dispatched for the conquest of the quarters, sent forth by the Lord—the single Consciousness who consists of all powers and is endowed with all powers, residing within all bodies; they were of equal disposition and identical intent. || 2 ||
Your forces pursued you from afar without interruption,
as far as the shores of the oceans, like the currents of rivers.
They followed in such a way that they were continuously interwoven with the enemy forces without interruption. || 3 ||
By means of their long and weary journey, all their resources—
both their own and those belonging to others— were exhausted like the water of a wretched river.

As those armies of the wise marched on with unceasing travel over great distances, all their well-known means of livelihood and warfare— wealth, missiles, weapons, and so forth— were exhausted day by day through consumption,
like the water in small irrigation channels.
Having fully beheld their own and others' powers,
they were like those seeking liberation who flee from both merit and sin as if from exhaustion.
As those wise ones fled, their own and others' armies—worthy of being beheld like the merits and sins of those seeking liberation—were utterly exhausted and vanished without remainder. || 5 ||
Then, as if because there was no longer anything to be consumed, the flames of the fires and the weapons in the sky became extinguished of their own accord, having accomplished their purpose.
In their dwellings— consisting of chariots, horses, elephants, trees,
and crowds— the weapons lay dormant, like birds that have settled for sleep at the end of the day.
Hidden within their respective places, such as quivers and scabbards in armories, or within chariots and the like, they remained motionless, as if asleep. || 7 ||
Like waves within water, like mists within a cloud,
or like fragrant clouds in the wind, they vanished into the sky.
The aquatic creatures of his weapons have become still, clinging to the mud of the streams;
he is now entirely free from the misty showers of iron arrow-sprays.

In the fourth verse, there are qualifying adjectives that establish the metaphor of the ocean: "one upon whose surface, covered with mud by the falling torrents of rain, the aquatic creatures such as fish and crocodiles—characterized by their weapons [the teeth]—are hidden and thus stilled; likewise, one who is entirely devoid of the misty showers of spray characterized by arrows. These are the qualifiers that justify the ocean imagery.
The syntactical connection here is that "the sky became a single ocean. || 9 ||
Released from hundreds of whirlpools, it was endowed with clarity and gentleness; the violent agitation of the clouds having subsided, its high waves ceased their heavy downpour.
In which [sea] there were showers of rain, calmed though once impelled by the fury of clouds, rising even higher than the waves.
The vast ocean of the sky became stainless, with its waters of emptiness, wherein the submarine fire of the sun was situated at the edge amidst the mass of the jewels of the stars submerged within.
In which [ocean], masses of jewels characterized by stars were submerged; in one corner or region of which was situated the submarine fire (vāḍava) characterized by the sun;

and in which emptiness itself was the water—such a vast and expansive single ocean, characterized as the sky, became manifest at the time of dissolution as the famous "single sea" (ekārṇava). || 11 ||
The sky shone, luminous, profound, serene, and exceedingly radiant; free from dust, it was like the mind of the great. 12.

The sky shone like the mind of the great; it was profound due to its vast and expansive self-luminosity and the light of the sun, and it was free from the quality of passion (rajas) as well as from dust.
Then they beheld those oceans, like younger brothers of the sky—
vast, pure in appearance, and filling the entire expanse of the quarters.
He begins to describe the oceans until the end of creation with the word "atha" (now). || 13 ||
[The rivers] were filled with the great gurgling roar of waves, droplets, and surges,
and their bodies were made beautiful by the captivating mist of abundant spray.
Their bodies are charming and captivating because of the many clouds that are as lovely as sprays of mist;

here, the possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*) must be justified even after a *karmadhāraya* compound, by the intention to express an intensification of meaning through constant association (*nityayoga*). || 14 ||
They stood upon the ground, having spread out their own bodies like those afflicted by disease—
breathless with distress, their bodies trembling, and their great arms tossing like the waves of a whirlpool.
Having spread out his own body upon the ground; "vivartāḥ" means those whose great arms are like waves being tossed up. || 15 ||
Though inert, they were composed of movement, with millions upon millions of waves and hollows; like the vast expanses of worldly existence, they were agitated by the conditions of whirlpools.
On the side of saṃsāra, there are waves—the six surging afflictions—by which the crooked reservoirs of water are struck and filled with hollows. || 16 ||

The sun was made to appear more massive by the radiance rising from the slopes of the heaps of jewels; the deep humming sounds were intensified by the noise of the wind entering the piles of conch shells. (17)
At the time of sunrise, the sun was made to appear as if swollen or thickened by those mountain ridges which were illuminated by heaps of jewels;
and from whose [caves], as the wind entered the masses of conch shells, there arose a threatening *ghuṃghuma* sound—a menacing roar.
The vast expanse of the sky resounded with the gurgling roar of masses of fleshy waves,
while coral trees whirled about within the expansion of circular eddies.
With the roars of massive, swelling billows, they possess a grandeur that makes the sky rumble like thunderclouds.
Resounding with the gurgling roar of the Makara-array,
it produced the cries of sinking ships shattered by the lashings of fish-tails.
With the lashing of their tails and the tips of their tails, they made a great clamor as the ships, cut in two by those very [tails] and thus sinking, cried out. || 19 ||
With throngs of men swallowed by upturned tortoises and sea-monsters,
they resembled the sky filled with the sun and its seven-horsed chariot reflected in the waves.

In which [mountains] there were multitudes of men wearing woolen garments (*aurṇāmbara*), who had been swallowed by sea-monsters such as whales, tortoises, and crocodiles; the adjective "woolen" (*aurṇā*) is used to indicate that the maritime people generally wear woolen clothes. 20.
The wind produced a whistling sound as it blew through the jars struck by the falling attendants,
while the clusters of jewels tossed up by the waves made a jingling "jhaṇ-jhaṇ" noise through their power.

In those [ships] where the vessels—vastly spread out, falling as they move along due to winds that produce a whistling sound, and expanded by their own prosperity—are "udghaṭāḥ," meaning they strive and exert themselves upward;
[this occurs] by the force of the impact from falling violently. || 21 ||
With their powerful arms, they playfully touched the solar orb with various nets [of light], while the circles of rubies and gems upon them caused rays of light to rise and fall.
In some places, with the upraised trunks of elephants, they momentarily turned the waters into groves of bamboo, featuring rising whirlpools of frothing foam and swarms of sea-monsters.
By the upward thrusts of the trunks of elephants, they were made to resemble a forest of bamboo.

In some places, he saw Mādhava with his followers, who were like creepers clinging to trees, with their palms pressed against their backs; in other places, he saw Mādhava resting in the interior of caves together with his entire retinue.

[He saw] those whose tails were like creepers upon the waves; [he saw] the multitude of elephants' backs, which were like rows (*āli*) characterized by that [back], where the *mādhava* trees—like the spring season (*vasanta*)—were in bloom with masses of foam, as if in Śvetadvīpa or similar realms. (24)
[He saw] countless various abodes of asuras and suras situated in one place, with the sky made jagged by the mass of waves of descending stars. || 25 ||
[The compound may be analyzed as] a *dvandva-garbha-ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* ending in a *catuṣpada-bahuvrīhi*: those by whom the sky was mocked—
that is, rendered jagged— by a flood of ever-new waves resembling reflections, foam, and stars, which served as the abodes for various kinds of *asuras* and *surās*.

He reduced the coastal mountains to extreme smallness by means of the surging masses of his water-waves, making those mountains— which were as tall as trees— seem like mere pits to one terrified by a gnat in a cave.

Like mosquitoes dwelling in a cave, they are settled in the pits of the underworld, fearing exit to the outside; for this very reason, they are as motionless as branches rooted in the base. [The Lord] brings them to a state of dwarfishness (kharvatā) in relation to the tide and so forth;
the sense is that he does so by producing the great height of the masses of waves. || 26 ||
The sprouts of the paths of light from many jewels planted in the field of the sky, with their sandy banks interspersed by pearls released from the mouths of pure oyster shells; 27.
The paths of the rays are the expansions of the rays; those [beings] by whom sprouts possessing those characteristics have been planted in their own field are [the ones referred to]. || 27 ||
Like cloths variegated with threads of various gems and silken fabrics, rippling and entering from the ten directions, they were strewn all around.

Variegated with silken threads marked by the rays of various jewels, they were such that rivers themselves entered them like threads being drawn into a shuttle; they were completely surrounded on all sides by the quarters of the sky, which had become their fringes, and thus stood as if they were woven cloths.
In some places, marked by hundreds of pearl-oyster shells scattered upon its sapphire slopes,
it displays the beauty of the fingernails of a beloved woman, like a hundred lovely moons.
In one place, they display the beauty of their fingernails as if they were a hundred moons beloved by the god of love. || 29 ||
Intertwined with the lattice of jewel-rays and reflected upon the surface of the waves, the blossoming rows of palm groves on the shore appear to be whirling about.
They reflect the rows of palm groves on the shore within the various directions and locations of the waves, and as the waves turn back, they cause those reflections to turn back as well. || 30 ||
Desirous of seizing garlands of cardamom, cloves, and kaṅkola fruits fallen from the creepers of the coastal forest, the aquatic creatures had resumed their predatory habits.

[The waves] in which water-dwelling creatures, desiring to seize garlands of *āmalaka* and other fruits fallen from the creepers of the coastal forest, have seized [the fruit] and whose movements along the shore have been turned back. || 31 ||
The aquatic creatures, deceived by the birds reflected [in the water] as they were about to feed on the tips of mango, nīpa, and kadamba flowers, let out a sudden snap.

In those [sounds], there were the *ācchoṭas*—the snapping sounds made by aquatic creatures who, under the pretext of showing food, drew [the fish] near the waves and devoured them; such were the sounds prevalent therein. || 32 ||
In an instant, the water-dwellers, fleeing here and there at the reflection of the sky-goer, broke the great embankments of their bonds.
He saw those four formless beings, who were like Nārāyaṇas, vast as the sky and situated in the cardinal directions, appearing as reflections within his heart where the three worlds reside.
By virtue of their common characteristics, such as being formless, they stood like four Nārāyaṇas in the cardinal directions. || 34 ||
Having swallowed the sky with its qualities of extreme depth, purity, vastness, and splendor, he displays it as if reflected from within his own heart. (35)
The sky, reflected in the waters of the aquatic birds,
bore within its depths the lotuses that were its own essence, like bees clinging to themselves.
They bore it within their intentions and hearts, residing within their own selves like a treasure held in a casket.
Their garments were struck by winds from the tossing of waves,
and they resembled the clouds at the end of an eon with the deep resonance of sounds echoing from their mountain caves.

"By means of the deep [sounds]" is an expression where the abstract quality (bhāva) is emphasized. By means of the depths of the caves—which are to be inferred from the outbursts characterized by the entry and exit of the wind within the mountain caves—one [perceives] those which have become the abode of the clouds at the end of the eon. 37.
He intensely contemplated those [mountains], terrifying as thunderbolts with the deep rumbling echoes from their caves, appearing as if they were being devoured by the Agastya and Aurva fires.

In the caves, with the gurgling sounds of their swirling currents, they were as terrifying as thunderbolts; they seemed to imagine that the Agastyas who consume their own food and the Aurva-fires within the depths of the caves had been violently swallowed up.
The sky was filled with forest-like masses of water, where abundant spray was the blossoming flowers, the surging waves were the trees, and the ripples were the clusters of blossoms.
Likewise, [the clouds] remained as if contemplating the waters and forests that had reached the sky. Of what sort were those waters and forests?
They were such that their flowers were abundant droplets of spray; their trees were the masses of waves; and their blossoming clusters were the surging billows.
With their nets of waves shimmering and living beings leaping within them, they appeared below as if they were fragments of the sky fallen there due to delusion. (40)

Likewise, they saw the four oceans—networks of waves surging along, filled with leaping creatures such as fish—as if they had fallen downward because they were fragments when the expanse of the sky was split by weapons; this is the connection with the preceding verse, for one who perceives them through such a delusion. || 40 ||

When [the chariot] reached the long shore of the salt-water ocean, its tip shattered by the dancing leaves of cardamom, cloves, bakula, myrobalan, tamāla, hintāla, and palm trees, a line appeared upon the mountain-peak of the sky that resembled a swarm of bees. (41) By the aforementioned means, as the waves fell and the long shores of the salt-water oceans rose up in response—

When Vipaścit’s army had arrived, the dark forest line—resembling a swarm of bees and divided into sections by the dancing leaves of cardamom, cloves, and other trees upon the mountain peaks that reached toward the sky along the long shoreline—shone forth; that is to say, it was beautiful. || 41 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and thirteenth canto, titled "The Description of the Ocean," in the *Ārṣa* Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa of Vālmīki, within the section on the liberation of Devarāja, in the discourse on the non-existence of duality. 113.
Thus ends the one hundred and thirteenth canto, titled "The Description of the Ocean," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The One Hundred Fourteenth Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Then, at that time and place, he showed them various things to them.
The forest trees, the oceans, the mountains, the clouds, and the forest-dwellers were at his sides.
From this point forward, those [beings] shown by the wise— namely, forest trees, oceans, mountains, clouds, and forest-dwellers— are described for the sake of the discerning.

The word "atha" (then) serves to indicate the commencement of the detailed description of the forest and so forth. Subsequently, after reaching the vicinity of the ocean, the ministers and others who were at the side of those wise ones showed them various wonderful things, such as forests, trees, and the like; the meaning is that they did so for the sake of their curiosity. || 1 ||
"O Lord, behold this peak of the mountain that scrapes the clouds,
which has come from the midst of the Maruts and other regions to reach this land of stone."

O Lord, from regions such as Madhyadeśa— including its valleys (*upatyakā*), peaks (*adhityakā*), and plateaus (*prastha*)— this mountain has gradually reached the land of Aśmaka, a region abounding in stone; its summit (*agrabhūmi*), which is sky-scraping and exceedingly high, and for that very reason possessed of much wind (*samarut*) and frequented by wandering gods, *gandharvas*, and others— that summit...
The meaning is "behold. || 2 ||
These ranges of forests, teeming with *bakula*, *punnāga*, and coconut trees, waft winds laden with various fragrances. (3)
Behold also these enclosures of groves, from which the wind has vomited forth and disgorged various fragrances.
The ocean mows down the foothills, with rows of rocks as its rice-fields,
using its waves as sickles, cutting away the forest groves along with their fruits and sprouts from root to tip.

The forest fire, with its sickles in the form of surging waves, mows down the foothills—the ground near the mountain—as well as the circles of rocks that look beautiful upon the tranquil mountain; furthermore, it mows down the forest rows covered from root to top with fruits and sprouts—meaning, behold this! || 4 ||
The young ocean shakes off the rows of clouds upon the mountain ridges as they dance with their own waters,
like a line of smoke from a house.

The ocean shakes with the wind the rows of clouds resting upon the plateaus of the mountains— clouds adorned with droplets of its own water that resemble beads of sweat, as they dance through gestures such as the arms of tree-creepers trembling in the breeze;
just as a child fans away a column of smoke from his own house with the wind from a fan.
See it in that same way. || 5 ||
These trees on the banks, their branches like conch shells submerged in the full flood of the ocean of the full moon,
shine like wish-fulfilling trees bearing the lunar orb as their fruit.

Look! On full-moon nights, at the time of the rising of the full moon, these trees on the bank—whose branches are filled with conch shells by the surges of the overflowing ocean—shine like *kalpa* trees, bearing white fruits as bright and full of the essence of nectar as the lunar orb. The word "look" (*paśya*) is to be understood as connected to every [verse]. 6.
The trees, accompanied by their wives in the form of creepers, seem to worship you with hands made of red sprouts laden with a profusion of jewel-like flowers.

The trees, accompanied by wives in the form of creepers and filled with clusters of flowers resembling jewels, appear as if they are honoring you—the guest who has arrived at their home—with hands characterized by red sprouts; that is to say, they seem to be scattering [offerings]. || 7 ||
With its cave-mouths containing stone-teeth that swallow crocodiles,
Mount Ṛkṣavat roars with a gurgling sound like a bear.
Mount Ṛkṣavat bears the name Ṛkṣavat because it possesses caves characterized by mouths with teeth of white and other colored stones that swallow crocodiles and sea-monsters,
and which produce a growling sound like that of bears and wildcats. || 8 ||
The mighty Indra, the lord of battle, overpowers the roaring clouds with his thunderous roars,
just as a powerful man overcomes his adversaries with those who are dull-witted.
This Mount Mahendra, from its heights, hurls thunderbolts downward at the roaring clouds with its own deep roars, as if to threaten them;
just as a powerful warrior skilled in battle hurls insults at his enemies with harsh words. || 9 ||
Smeared with sandalwood paste and glorious, that lofty Malaya mountain stands as if prepared like a wrestler to conquer the surging waves of the ocean.
This wrestler, characterized by the Malaya mountain, is as if prepared to conquer the tossing of the wave-arms of the ocean, his rival wrestler. 10.
The ocean, eternally shimmering on all sides with waves of jewels,
is perceived by those traveling along the path of the sun as if it were the jeweled girdle of the earth.

This ocean, adorned on all sides with waves filled with jewels, is constantly gazed upon by sky-dwellers moving along the path of the sun, who—mistaking it for the jewel-garlanded circle of the earth—think, "In some places it is radiant. (If the reading is *kacidaujaskam*, it should be construed as a single compound used as an adverbial modifier. || 11 ||
The mountain peaks, with their jewel-like summits and filled with forest groves, sway in the gusting wind like serpents with their raised and lowered hoods. (12)

The "forest-fillers" (*vānapūra*) are small mountains that are filled with forests, which are collections of woods; when the forest is shaken by the wind, these moving [mountains] glide like serpents. "Jewel-headed" and "wind-drinkers" are common epithets [applied here]. By means of various gaits consisting of rising and falling movements... || 12 ||
Wandering upon the crests of the waves, the sea-monsters, with their formidable trunks, scatter sprays of water like clouds driven by the wind.

Wandering upon the crests of the waves, sea-monsters like makaras and wild elephants roam about with their fierce trunks and gaping mouths as the wave-crests surge forth and subside, seeking to seize one another; pursued by the clouds that scatter spray like water-releasing rain-clouds, they captivate the minds of those who watch them with wonder.
The remainder. || 13 ||
An elephant with a trunk shaped like a whirlpool, scattering sprays of water in all directions,
and whose head is unable to lift due to its fullness, dies from excessive rutting.
In that place, behold: one elephant, by fate caught in a whirlpool in bottomless water, his form thus overturned;
with the quarters of the sky strewn by the masses of spray he emits, and being unable to raise his head because it is submerged in the flood of water, he dies with his trunk held aloft. 14.
Just as all the oceans are filled with various living beings and contain waters, mountains, and high and low elevations, so too are the lands of the continents.
The meaning is that one should understand that just as those oceans exist with water and are uneven due to mountains being high and low, so too do all the lands of the continents exist. || 15 ||
Though they are non-different from one's own self, these whirlpools appear as if they were other;
though unreal in nature, they are perceived as being clearly visible.
"The ocean, as it were, bears whirlpools within the world of Brahmā"—this is the syntactical connection between the two.
The qualifiers such as "though non-different from itself, yet as if different" and so forth are to be applied in common to both the whirlpools and the worlds. || 16 ||
Just as Brahmā supports the worlds, the ocean bears its own waves— which are unstable, restless within, and insentient— yet which are continuous and never-ending.
Just as the ocean holds many sun-gems that shine like Indra immediately after [the churning],
so too does it possess those whose entire wealth was seized by Mantha, which were protected for the sake of the gods.

At that time, when the ocean had been stripped of all its wealth by the gods and demons during the churning, the sun conceals within himself those many sun-gems which he had protected and hidden from the gods. Just like Indra, who, while guarding the gems from the demons, conceals them; in that same manner. || 18 ||
From the great splendor visible there, as well as from the netherworld (pātāla),
he perceived [the beings] as if they were hidden yet real within, through the analysis of their reflected images.

Likewise, because they possess such great splendor and form, he holds within himself those jewels which are clearly visible even from the netherworld (pātāla), having rendered them as if unreal through the artful play of their reflections. || 19 ||
If one were to cast a single hair from among them into the western ocean every day for the purpose of disposal, I believe that by that means the days would be numbered.

From among those jewels, I imagine that on each day he casts one jewel into the sky for the purpose of depositing it in the western ocean, and by that means the day comes to pass—this is a poetic conceit (utprekṣā). || 20 ||
In the ocean, there is no meeting of virtuous people from various directions and regions, which is otherwise filled with the mutual clamor of people during a pilgrimage. // 21 //
Anticipating a cause for the appearance of the ocean's dark hue, he says: "nānā... (verse 21).
Indeed, at the confluence of the ocean and the sea, the battle between the foremost aquatic creatures, characterized by their mutual tossing and dashing against one another, never ceases.
"Among those possessing enthusiasm for battle, aquatic creatures alone are the best"—this is a conjecture (*nūnam*). Why?
Because at the confluence of the two oceans, the eastern and western seas, their constant mutual tossing never allows the battle to subside. (22)
The wind approaches, whirling with the grace of dancing waves whose tips are exhausted by fatigue,
scattering pearl-like spray as it blows.

Behold, the Lord Wind approaches like a master, encircling with his rewards—pearls accompanied by sprays of water—which he has vomited forth; these pearls are for the whirlpools that appear like the confusion of dance on the crests of the waves as the timi fish, a species of large fish, faint and weary from exhaustion. 23.
The long, shimmering lordly pearls situated within the pearl-necklace-like waves of the ocean jingle "khaṇa-khaṇa" as they move restlessly in every direction.

An imaginative conceit (*utprekṣā*): situated here and there amidst pearl necklaces characterized by their brilliance are lordly gems, the finest of jewels, marked by the color of clouds; hanging down from the ocean’s throat on all sides, they produce a *khaṇakhaṇa* sound due to their mutual collision. || 24 ||

Resounding with the roar of the earth as it reverberates through the cave-dwellings of Mount Mahendra, these sounds bring great happiness to the Siddhas and Sādhyas whose paths have been turned back from the ocean.

Furthermore, what kind of wind is it? Having reached the earth—which causes distress to those who frequent Mount Mahendra—the wind turns back toward the paths of the ocean for the sake of delighting the Siddhas and Sādhyas (distinct classes of divine beings) who, out of aversion to that place, have retreated into the dwellings of mountain caves. (Note: The change in case ending is Vedic.)
It brings great happiness by dispelling the fatigue of passion. || 25 ||
Mandara, its forest expanses shaken by the gusts of wind emitted from its caves, spreads clouds of flowers across the sky.

Another [verse] describes Mandara, showing it as follows: "Mandara. By means of the outpourings of the wind (mātariśvan) issuing from its caves, it spreads (tanoti)—that is, expands—clouds raining flowers in the sky; that is to say, it fills with flowers the clouds that have ascended to its plateaus. || 26 ||
The cloud-deer, with eyes as flickering as lightning, enter the caves of Mount Gandhamādana, which abound with the fragrance of mango, nīpa, and kadamba trees.
The winds, emerging from the caves of the Himalayas, move as if performing a dance upon the coils of creepers; they carry with them the waves of the oceans and clouds that have been rent asunder.
The years are distinguished by masses of ocean waves; these are adjectives that provide qualities such as coolness, gentleness, and fragrance.
O dear one, the breezes from Mount Gandhamādana, fragrant from their contact with the tops of the mango and kadamba trees, cause the waves of the ocean to curl.
Enveloping the clouds that have become like the curls on the forehead of Alakā,
the wind approaches from here, creating a cloud of flowers along the forest paths.
Having attained the state of *alaka*—that is, having become the curls of hair—of Alakā, the city of Kubera. || 30 ||
There he perceived breezes, languid with the sweet fragrance of clusters of kunda and mandāra flowers, mingled with sprays of frost.
Here, on this Gandhamādana, perceive and touch the breezes.
Behold, the winds from the city of the Persians are about to blow, having acquired a bitter fragrance from the dancing of coconut and palm trees. 32.

Behold how, in the past, those [trees] gradually acquired a pungent smell from that liquor and a sweet fragrance through the rhythmic swaying of the coconut trees and the jasmine creepers respectively. 32.
Shaking the camphor-clouds from the blossoming groves of Īśāna and stirring the lotus-pools of Kailāsa, the winds blow.
Shaking the clouds that are fragrant with the kadalī and karpūra from the blossoming pleasure-garden of Īśāna.
These winds from the caves of the Vindhya mountains, their forms sluggish with the ichor flowing from the temples of lordly elephants, rustle like parrots.

"Śuka-śukāyante" is an imitation of the indistinct sound produced by a clump of *vīraṇa* grass; or else, because they emerged together with the parrots (*śuka*) of the Vindhya mountains, they "śukāyante"—that is, they appear green, possessing that color. || 34 ||
On the mountain, where the bodies of the Śabara women lie amidst heaps of withered leaves,
the forest row, with its leaf-clad hunters pierced by iron arrows, acts like a city.

On the slopes of the Malaya mountain, where the heaps of withered leaves serve as garments for the bodies of the Śabaras, and which is filled with Śabaras clad in leaf-vestments and their iron arrows, the forest groves— where herds of deer and flocks of birds remain but few—
behave like a city; indeed, they act as a city.
The quarters of the sky, whose bodies consist of the oceans, mountains, rivers, clouds, and forests, seem to laugh at you with their rays of sunlight through the force of your majesty. 36.
In the forest groves of Mount Atri, they describe flower-beds prepared by Vidyādharīs;
there, charming women, having turned their positions on both sides, engage in the role of the man upon the ocean that has rolled back.

In this region, they describe and indicate flower-beds prepared for pleasure by Vidyādharīs in the forest avenues near the mountains. From what sign do they indicate this? He says: "From the side... [and so on]. From the mark of a foot-print (*padāṅka*) situated on both sides of the ocean—which is accompanied by a seal of red lac (*alaktaka*), turned over, and perfectly formed—[they indicate] a man.

The meaning is that, when she was exhausted from passion, these [marks] indicate the "manly acts" (*puruṣāyita*)—the behaviors characteristic of a man—performed by the innocent woman as she turned over from her lower position. || 37 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and fourteenth canto, titled "The Vision of the Directions," in the *Vāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa*, the sacred work of the Sage, within the section on Liberation (*Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa*), in the *Mumukṣu-vyavahāra* division, in the *Upadeśa* portion, concerning the *Avikalpa*. 114.
Thus ends the one hundred and fourteenth canto, titled "The Overview," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*. 114.
The One Hundred and Fifteenth Sarga (115).
The attendants said:
Here, in these bowers of vine-circles with their most excellent interiors, playful and restless women perform songs.
Having rested, the hosts of kinnaras, having forgotten their worldly activities due to the intense flavor of their unrestrained emotion, [sing] with sweet, melodious warbling. || 1 ||
Here, forests, mountains, trees, rivers, oceans, winds, birds, villages, clouds, and so forth, are described in the four directions.

O noble-minded one, on this mountain, groups of Kinnaras— whose playful movements are characterized by the attachment of beautiful women— having forgotten the activities of the day (the passage of time) through their unrestrained transitory emotions (*saṃcāribhāva*), aesthetic sentiments (*rasa*), and the erotic sentiment of union (*saṃbhoga-śṛṅgāra-rasa*), have now rested and [performed] the arts.
They experience—that is, they sing and they listen to—a song characterized by such *kākali* notes. || 1 ||

These mountains—the Himalaya, Malaya, Vindhya, Sahya, Krauñca, Mahendra, Madhu, Mandara, Dardura, and others—though situated far away, appear in the sight like white clouds, resembling lumps of earth marked by fragments of withered leaves.
(2) He says that even very lofty mountains, when seen from afar, appear small: "these. These...

Behold! The Himalaya, Malaya, and other great mountains, though situated at a great distance, appear to the spectator's eye like clods of earth marked with dried leaves and fragments—possessing a resemblance to them. || 2 ||
These mountain ranges, which bear the likeness of the city walls before them with their series of great ridges separated by distant valleys,
appear like rivers agitated as they enter the ocean, clinging to the edge of a cloth-painting.
Like fringes made of very fine white threads.
Furthermore, these mountain-peaks, which are like distant watchtowers, possess a light that reaches far;

being thus situated with their intervening paths and spaces between them obscured from others, they appear on all sides joined together and assume the form of ramparts before one's eyes. Likewise, they seem to enter the ocean...
And the rivers, agitated by the speed of the entry, appear like the fine white threads of the fringe caught within the edge of the cloth.
O King, those ten directions, covered on all sides by clouds dark as rain-clouds atop the mountains,
filled with the warbling chatter of birds,
and adorned with creeper-like arms— the beautiful forest-belts— smiling with flowers released from their vines, shine like the ladies of your palace.
In front. || 4 ||

O King, those [women] were like dense clouds, dark-hued and enveloping the mountains on all sides; their warbling was like the clamorous chatter of birds; they were distinguished by flowers released from creepers;
and they possessed lovely, shining vine-like arms characterized by forest-garlands.
The ten directions appear like the queens of the forest-dwellers, smiling as it were before you. || 4 ||
The shimmering forest, its lofty peaks crowded with *tālī*, *tamāla*, and *bakula* trees appearing as a single mass,
shines forth like a dense network of moss clinging to the shore, struck by the restless waves of the ocean.
It is a place where lofty mountain peaks are crowded with palm trees and the like;

and upon those mountains that appear from afar like ramparts, the forest— shaken by the wind and struck by the surging waves of the ocean— shines forth with a unified form, resembling a dense mass of moss clinging to the shore.
Because similarity is understood through the suffix *kalpa*, which indicates slight incompleteness, this is an implied simile (*gamyamānopamā*).
Here sleeps Keśava; here his enemies’ kinsmen; here also rest the winged mountains seeking refuge;
and here too is the submarine fire along with all the clouds of universal destruction—oh, how vast, powerful, and capable of bearing the weight!
The body of the ocean. || 6 ||
The winged mountains—those possessing peaks—lie down, that is, they sleep; [this is from] the root *śīṅ* with the augment *ruṭ*.
The body of the ocean, vast and expansive, is powerful, capable of bearing weight, and able to sustain a great burden; oh, it is wonderful, meaning it is incomparable. || 6 ||
O King, these entire villages, forests, cities, plains, mountains, trees, pillars, settlements, and mountain ranges along the banks of the Jambūnadī shine with the rays of the sun;
licking the interior of the sky encircled by garlands of flames, they emit light on all sides.
Thus, this abundant [place] is to be resorted to by the immortals here, not by humans. || 7 ||

Someone, pointing out the golden banks of the Jambū river at the foot of Mount Meru to Vipaścit as he was setting out toward the northern direction, said: "These..."— meaning these banks of the Jambū river, in which all the villages and other settlements consist of gold, shine forth on all sides, pervaded by the rays of the sun.

The virtuous, licking the very ends of the sky which is encircled by garlands of flames, emit light on all sides. O King, in this state, the entire earth is fit to be resorted to and enjoyed by the immortals—the gods—but not by humans; such is the meaning. || 7 ||
These clouds, following the path of the sun, appear like a blanket of *kadamba* groves as they move along;
may the slope of this mountain be for you like the earth itself—do not harbor the fear that it is a mass of clouds in the sky obstructing the sun.

Carrying a blanket of *kadamba* groves that resembles clouds, these plateau regions following the path of the sun shine forth upon this mountain. Therefore, let there be the thought that "this too is a shore," just like the earth (*vasudhā*) itself, in these regions; the meaning is that one should not harbor the suspicion that these are masses of clouds situated in the sky obstructing the sun. || 8 ||

This is that very Malaya mountain, where the trees are made to dance upon its face by the three [fires], their intensity drenched by the intoxicating abundance of the thick fragrance of sandalwood trees shimmering with the fierce *lavalī* creepers;
a dance provoked by the rising heat from the cheeks of the eye-possessing [fire] situated within the blazing conflagration.
Just as grains of hot sandalwood are held by the thumbs and fingers of women until they are heated. || 9 ||

Another [verse] describes the Malaya mountain to the wise man who has set out toward the southern direction: "This is it. This very Malaya mountain, visible nearby, possesses such power that even other trees, through the intense intoxication of the fragrance from the sandalwood trees shining with excellent *lavalī* creepers upon its peaks, are filled with sap.

Having become like sandalwood, they are made into forehead-marks (tilaka) upon the lotus-face by the three classes of beings—gods, humans, and asuras—as if they were bees. Furthermore, from the intoxication of this fragrance, there arises a blazing heat on the cheeks of Rudra, who possesses a flaming fire situated in his third eye; [this occurs] in such a sublime [place].

The meaning is that those who are intent on the *tāṇḍava* dance, though heated, become like warm drops of water—just as the drops of sweat produced by the fatigue of lovemaking on women are made exceedingly cool; such is the power of this [mantra]. || 9 ||
This is the mountain named Malaya, whose slopes are washed by the ocean and where sandalwood trees are encircled by the coils of the lord of serpents;
its entire rocky surface is turned to gold by the mass of radiance from the lotus-faces of the Vidyādharīs.
It was such a place where, upon its shores washed by the waves of the ocean— shores made of *kaladhauta* (silver) and *suvarṇa* (gold)—
there appeared sandalwood trees entwined by the coils of the bodies of lordly serpents; likewise,
other [trees] were turned to gold by the masses of radiance from the lotus-faces of the Vidyādharīs.

This mountain standing before us is of such a nature that even its rocks are entirely [fragrant]; it is named Malaya. The meaning is that its name is significant (anvarthanāman), for Lakṣmī (the Goddess of Fortune) "lies" (līyate) within it. The shortening of the vowel occurs according to the rule *ṅyāpoḥ*. 10.
In this place, where the bamboos create a tumultuous display with the whistling of the rivers in the thickets of warbling bowers,
the serpents coil upon the trunks of ancient *rohaṇa* trees, agitated by the cries of the moving peacocks. (11)

By the grand display of song from the hollow bamboo stalks— which were accompanied by the warbling of thickets, the rattling sounds of riverbanks such as rugged rocky ridges and caves, and various types of rhythmic clapping—
the bees dwelling in the buds became mute and silent through their absorption in listening to that sound.

In that family, there is this mountain named Krauñcācala; on this mountain, the serpents—a specific class of snakes—are agitated by the cries of peacocks, whose beloveds are the dark clouds accompanied by excellent, rhythmic cranes as they move about. [They hear] the ancient, long-standing [sound of] Rohaṇa.
The meaning is that they appear upon such hollow, decayed trees; they "undulate" upon the trunks—that is, the inner heartwood—climbing up and hiding themselves by contracting their coils. || 11 ||
On this bank, listen to the widespread nectar for the ears produced by the swaying bracelets of women sporting in their dwellings of tender golden creepers. 12.

O King, here on this bank of the Krauñca river, in a bower of dwellings fashioned from tender golden creepers, listen to the widespread, impassioned tinkling of the bracelets of beautiful women sporting with their lovers— a sound that is like drinking an elixir for the ears. 12.
This mass of water-drops in the ocean, drenched by the ichor flowing from the temples of elephants and surrounded by swarms of bees like flickering waves,
seems to cry out as if it were being chewed and tormented.
Because it is enveloped and mixed with the ichor flowing from the temples of elephants, the mass of water-drops in the moving waves seems to be chewed by swarms of bees;
thus there is a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) that it cries out in the ocean.
Behold the dark moon, surrounded by beautiful women whose bodies are like fresh butter of nectar!
She performs water-sports upon the lap of her father, the Ocean of Milk.

He offers this poetic conceit (*utprekṣā*), showing the reflection of the moon in the ocean: "Behold! O King, the stainless moon, possessing a body like the fresh butter produced from the churning of the nectar of immortality, surrounded by the beautiful women of the stars, [dwells] in the ocean of milk.
Reflected in his father’s lap, he performs water-sports—playing in the water; the meaning is: "Behold this wonder!
(14) On the pure slopes of the Malaya mountain, behold the young creepers dancing, accompanied by the sweet warbling of intoxicated cuckoos;
they possess eyes in the form of swarms of restless bees and hands in the form of flowers with reddish petals. [The compound *lokālī* is a bahuvrīhi where both members serve as qualifiers.]
This is a *karmadhāraya* compound: [the women] possessed of particular charms for the festival of honey (*madhūtsava*). || 15 ||

Another person somewhere in Malaya displays the dance of the creepers, saying: "They dance. They have eyes in the form of swarms of restless bees; they possess flowers upon their hands in the form of reddish leaves; and through the playful festivities of spring, they are distinguished by the pollen as if by decorative forehead marks (*viśeṣaka*). || 15 ||
Those drops of rainwater which, at the proper time, enter the hearts of bamboos, into the joints of mountains, into the depths of the ocean, or into the hearts of pearl-oysters seeking water,
they attain the state of pearls within the frontal globes of elephants— or else, they become something else entirely, provided they are pure.
These three types of pearls possess excellent qualities, just like [other] pearls. || 16 ||
Someone describes three supreme pearl mines and the production of pearls of the highest quality within them,
beginning with the words "of the bamboos" (vaṃśānām). Within the hollows of the joints of various types of bamboo on the mountains,
as well as in the hearts of pearl-oysters seeking water in the ocean during the time of the Svāti constellation, there are drops of rainwater.

They enter [the pearl-oysters] and attain the state of being pearls. But there is another, a third kind of pearl, which occurs on the frontal globes (kumbhas) of scent-elephants (gandhahastins). Of these aforementioned types of pearls, there are three well-known varieties; they are excellent in quality by virtue of the purity of their source and the excellence of the size of the pearls.
The meaning is that they come into being. || 16 ||
O Lord, gems of various forms appear in mountains, oceans, men, the earth, clouds, frogs, stones, and elephants; yet their functions—
delight, expulsion, killing, fever, fear, delusion, illumination, blindness, exhaustion, and burning— are not found in those [other] things.

Thus, it is well known in the *Ratnaśāstra* that the origin of gems as well as the diversity of their qualities and functions varies according to the difference in their mines; hence he says: "In the mountain," and so forth. Listen to their respective functions:
[they bring about] refreshment, the alleviation of heat, the expulsion of enemies, killing, fever, fear, delusion, and blindness.

[The powers are] weariness and purification. For the Master of Jewels, the manifestation of hidden and remote objects, the power of moving through the earth, the power of traveling great distances, or the power of moving through the sky by diving into the ground, are well known;
as are the vision of the past and future, the destruction of disease, famine, and so forth, and [protection from] poison and sorcery employed by others.
The meaning is "and the countermeasures such as mechanical devices. The word *tathā* is used in the sense of conjunction (*ca*). || 17 ||
When the moon has risen, the cities here chant through the mouths of their windows, balconies, lattices, side-doors, and main gates;

just as Mount Mandara, with its multitude of chasms, clouds, caves, caverns, forests, and bamboo thickets, [sang] the ocean of nectar for the moon, so too does another city, at the rising of the moon, produce a clamor from the people at the windows and other openings, set in motion by great joy.

And imagining the sound of the abysses and so forth through the relationship of the object compared and the standard of comparison, he imagines the moon as the recitation of its own praise—beginning with "vātāyana":
"In this place, when the moon has risen, the cities, acting as agents, [sing] with mouths characterized by the interiors of their windows and so forth... regarding Mount Mandara.

The mountain, as it were, through the multitude of its openings—its chasms, clouds, caves, caverns, forests, and bamboos—is reciting and praising the moon, which has become a veritable ocean of nectar; such is the poetic fancy (utprekṣā). || 18 ||
The wind carries away this peak—
what is it?— thus watched with startled apprehension by the innocent wives of the Siddhas looking upwards;
the thunderbolt-pillar soars high above the clouds, leaping up from forest to forest along every slope of the Snowy Mountain.
As if for the sake of lifting the earth up toward the surface of the sky. || 19 ||

Observing the rising of clouds from the slopes of the Himālaya mountains as if they were being lifted up by the wind—which acts like a hand—imagining them to be pillars raised from the earth toward the sky and the netherworld (pātāla), someone says: "This [is it].
It is as if for the purpose of testing the excessive weight of the sky and the sutala region, [the mountains] have been lifted up. || 19 ||

O King, behold the slopes of Mount Mahendra, cooled by the spray from the waves of the Ganges, with their beautiful rocky surfaces inhabited by Vidyādharas, and their flowering forests enshrouded by clouds of blossoms. 20.
Having seen forest regions spread across other lands, flower-filled grounds, groves, and cities,
as well as the waters that purify the world at sacred fords (tīrthas), the fear of misfortune departs with swift speed.
(21) He states that the cessation of misfortune is a great fruit resulting from the sight of most meritorious lands, forests, sacred fords, and so forth:
"In other regions" means that it moves away swiftly, being impelled—that is, joined—with speed. || 21 ||
Beholding the mountain peaks whose summits fill the entire circle of the horizon, which are crowded with chasms, clouds, caves, and thickets,
and seeing the oceanic coils that resemble the very sky, even the greatest of one's evil deeds melt away.
Having beheld the peaks of Śrīśaila and other mountains; the quarters of the sky filled with virtuous people; the hollows of holy fords, wells, ponds, and the like;
the cloud-filled caves of the Himavat and other ranges; the groves of Campaka forests and similar places crowded with clusters of bowers;
and the ocean-ringed continents, pure as the sky, containing holy sites such as the Setubandha—[having seen these], for living beings...
Even the most extensive evil deeds, such as the killing of a Brahmin and others, dissolve and perish. || 22 ||
For on Mount Malaya there are beautiful groves of sandalwood; on Vindhya, elephants blinded by rut; on Kailāsa, O King, gold from the foot of the mountain and moonstones;
on Mahendra, divine medicinal herbs; and on the snowy peak, all kinds of jewels indeed exist everywhere—yet this man is like a blind rat.
In a dilapidated house, a person decays in vain. || 23 ||

With the intention that the eyes of men would indeed be rendered useless if they were not to behold those great mountain ranges (kulaśaila) which abound in various excellent objects, he says: "Delightful" (*ramyā*). O King, gold is the best among things born from the earth;
*candra* is a particular mineral of the mountains; on the snowy peak, the Himavat; and in all these other places as well, there are jewels.
Even though this was so, this unfortunate person, not seeing them, was both blind and a mouse; thus he wastes away in vain within his dilapidated dwelling. The meaning is: "How wonderful! || 23 ||
The world, like a lake whose banks have been submerged by darkness, appears as if overflowing with water;
and these flickering lightning-flashes tremble like darting minnows, as if at the end of an eon. (24)

Someone describes the quarters of the sky shrouded in darkness as being filled with water: "It is elevated," he says. Enveloped by the darkness of clouds, these directions—the entire world up to the limits of the celestial realm—appear as if they have become a single lake, overflowing with water at the end of the age (*yugānta*). Therein, the flickering lightning flashes like little fish (*śapharikā*) in that lake.
They quiver like small fish. || 24 ||

O, how the monsoon winds blow with a rising roar, drenching the clouds that pour forth streams of dew, frost, and mist; they stir a profusion of intense horripilation from the cold, bringing forth a tumultuous sound.
They cause the clouds— which themselves emit streams of mist and frost, which have become congealed upon the earth and other surfaces,
and which have been thinned by evaporation— to become intoxicated; and they are such that, through their cool touch, they bring about an intense proliferation of horripilation among people.
The monsoon winds blow so as to produce a rising sound; "aho" expresses wonder. || 25 ||
Alas! The wind blows, following the expansion of dark clouds, scattering clusters of blossoms from the sprouts of trees;
it is beautiful as it moves through the interior of the forest of majestic, excellent trees, carrying the essence of a multitude of spray-drops from the heavy downpour.

Following the expansion of dark clouds, moving through the interior of forests of sprouting trees, beautiful and endowed with qualities such as fragrance, the steady wind—more essential than even the essence itself—blows, scattering the clusters of sprouts and blossoms from the trees; "Alas! is the cry of distress uttered by one afflicted by the cold or by a lover separated from his beloved. || 26 ||
These breezes, fallen as it were from heaven, increase in strength and carry a fragrance through the sighs of lovely women overcome by passion.
Living beings fallen from heaven are like the mere roots of the latent impressions of their former merit. || 27 ||
These breezes blow, soft as they strive to break the sprouts of blossoming blue-lotus creepers, yet capable of rending thick cloth; they have shaken the groves. (28)

These fragrant breezes blow, intent upon the blooming of the *kuvalaya*—the blue water-lilies—upon the orb of the earth; likewise, they are skillful in splitting open the buds of flowering creepers. These winds, capable of rending thick garments, are cool. (28)
In the sky, the winds, with their gentle trembling, carry along fragments of twilight clouds;
they are like excellent servants in the king’s courtyard, which is perfumed by variegated patterns of flowers.

These winds in the sky approach the fragments of twilight clouds with a gentle, soft trembling—a slow movement—just as excellent servants move through a royal courtyard scented by the variegated patterns of flowers, without crushing those flowers; such is the meaning. || 29 ||

In some places the mountain peaks carry winds fragrant with flowers, in others scented by clusters of lotuses; in some places they bear rains of blossoms and scatter lovely filaments, while in others they blow white as snow, or green, yellow, and dark blue.
[They are] destroyers of the slow-moving dharma of the gods. || 30 ||

Those winds, whose fragrance is like that of flowers—compounded with the word "like" (iva) because it precedes the object of comparison—or in some cases, those whose fragrance is like the scent of clusters of lotuses; white with snow, yet possessing the colors of mountain minerals such as green, yellow, and dark blue; these winds, associated with the mountain peaks, blow during lovemaking for those who are languid and weary, cutting through their sweat. 30.
In some places, with his rays making sounds like "hum" and "kāṃ," the sun scatters heaps of glowing coals through his attendants, as if he were one who associates with fools.

With his hands, he scatters heaps of glowing coals, which are characterized by the *huṃkāras* and *kāṃkāras*— the sounds of wailing— of living beings being burned in caves and other places by sun-crystal gems (*sūryakāntamaṇi*) that act like servants (*kiṃkara*) obedient to his command. || 31 ||

When she approached in her physical form— a woman who had attained liberation through the elixir of human essence and whose modesty was dissolved by intoxication— she could not be endured, as if by a spreading paralysis caused by the stupor of poison.
When a man— a person—

approaches her with his body, embraced by a young woman who has cast off shame through intoxication precisely because she is insatiable, being free from satisfaction regarding that elixir of love which is to be tasted upon union; then, for the sake of ceasing the sexual act, there arises a protracted [interruption] characterized by the description of some other necessary duty.
The meaning is that deceptive speech, when employed with the stupefying power of poison, cannot be endured, just as one's own death cannot be. || 32 ||

The winds from the forest regions before them, which bend the red lotuses, carry soft sprays of water and part the waves of moonbeams; yet to women separated from their lovers, they seem to possess fire and consist of heat.

The meaning is that even though the forest winds are endowed with all excellences such as causing the lotuses to turn, they act like fires—causing burning—to women separated from their lovers. || 33 ||

Behold, here on the slope of the shore of the eastern ocean, how do the Śavara women—clad in garments of broad leaves, with hips like the slopes of mountains, and resting in the vigor of youth and fresh intoxication—proceed? 34.

O King, here in this low-lying depression characterized by the shore of the eastern ocean, there are women whose forearms are adorned with bracelets made of bell-metal and other materials well-known among the Śabara tribe;
whose garments consist of broad leaves of the Nirguṇḍī plant; and who possess fresh liquor as their intoxicant.
Observe and see how the Śabara women, who are the very embodiments of youth, move with that graceful gait of theirs. (34)

With a mind distressed by the fear of the exhaustion of the night— the essence of the nectar of the nine sentiments— this woman does not abandon her lover even slightly, as if she were being pursued swiftly from behind by serpents.
This woman— because she is fresh like the essence of celestial wine, and because she possesses such an intoxicating enjoyment as the very quintessence of liquor—

does not, due to her distressed state of mind caused by the fear of the passing of such a night, quickly abandon her beloved even slightly, despite his state of moistness. Here before us, she is seen enveloped by the rays of the moon.
The meaning is that she is like a sandalwood creeper. || 35 ||
Like a woman who has been threatened by days made resonant with the morning trumpets, she now lies hidden upon the chest of her beloved, yet remains vividly manifest within his heart.
This forest range on the shore of the southern ocean, with its blossoming *kiṃśuka* trees, appears as if ablaze;
it is drenched repeatedly by the ocean with its waves of water. (37)
"Like [something] set ablaze"—this is a poetic conceit (*hetūtprekṣā*) regarding the repeated sprinkling. || 37 ||
From her, the clouds of black filaments emerge with the winds like columns of smoke; the flowers issue forth like sparks from her limbs, and the birds and bees resemble extinguished embers.

From this forest of blossoming *kiṃśuka* trees, dark clouds—those whose upper portions consist of filaments like smoke—are emerging like smoke. In this way, the *kiṃśuka* flowers emerge like glowing coals, and the birds and bees emerge like extinguished embers. "Behold! refers to the meaning previously stated.
Rebirth. || 38 ||
Behold this very forest range, ablaze with the fire of truth;
yet on the peak of the mountain in the northern direction, it is carried far into the sky by the winds.

Having shown a row of forest trees with imagined flames, he shows that same row to the north as having actual flames, saying, "It is just like this. It is being blown and shaken in the sky by the winds. || 39 ||

Behold this scene upon the Krauñca mountain, where peacocks are made to dance by the deep and piercing roar of slow-moving circles of clouds; see how the forest, with its flowers, fruits, and sprouts, is shaken by the tumultuous, agitated rain and wind.

O King, on the ground of Mount Krauñca, where the peacock-feathered flocks of peahens were made to dance by the deep and piercing cries of the slow-moving and sluggish cloud-circles, there arose a towering mass whose flowers, fruits, and sprouts were shaken about by the agitated rains and winds.
Behold this forest grove, a collection of woods. || 40 ||

Upon the western mountain, its beautiful joints shattered and worn out by the impact of the peaks of vast golden summits, that chariot of the Sun falls down; hear, this is the sound of its creaking wheels and the loud rattling of its pole! 41.
This very chariot of the Sun, having struck against the rugged and uneven golden peak— the summit of the Sunset Mountain—
has its beautiful joints shattered and worn away by the impact; thus,
emitting a piercing creaking from its wheels and a loud rattling sound from its pole, it has descended into the low-lying terrain.
"He used to fall" means "he used to descend"—this is an exaggeration (atiśayokti) intended to express his extreme loftiness. || 41 ||
On the mountain that serves as the rampart for the abodes of the world, the moon—the drum-beater—has blossomed; the swarm of bees, terrified by its light, has taken refuge nearby.
Yet, there exists here no object among the worlds more excellent than this; could even Fate, though thwarted, create anything superior?
That which was defiled in an instant. || 42 ||

Upon the mountain Mānasottara—which serves as the rampart for the abode or house characterized by the world—and upon the peak of the Sunrise Mountain (Udayagiri), there is the moon; on that [peak] is the *meruka* flower, a species of tree well-known in certain regions as auspicious (*māṅgalika*). Because it indicates good fortune, it is afraid of inauspiciousness and impurity (*mālinya*).

It blossomed with radiance on all sides; yet even such a flower as this was approached by a bee characterized by impurity—a stain brought forth by a destiny that ordains misfortune. This being so, there exists nothing whatsoever in this world, among the things of the universe, that is not struck down in an instant by adverse fate.

One should not allow oneself to be stained. The meaning is: if such is the condition even of the moon—which, though situated on a mountain peak or in the sky, does not touch the earth—then what need is there to speak of others? || 42 ||
This is Maṅkola, the great abode of the world, the loud laughter of the Lord of the Three Worlds;
it is the flood of milk and water, the lunar light from the ocean of the sky. 43.

He imagines the moonlight, spreading everywhere in three ways—as "tribhuvana... and so forth: this lunar radiance from the ocean of the sky is the loud laughter (*aṭṭahāsa*) of Rudra, the destroyer of the three worlds, as he dances at the time of dusk; or else, it is the whitewash (*maṅkola*) upon the great mansion that is the world; or else—
The pure, forward-flowing surge of water possessing the characteristics of milk [appeared]. || 43 ||

Behold the quarters of the sky, their bodies filled with masses of radiance, like the spreading floods of a fierce river, resembling the waves of milk surging from the ocean of the moon as it was churned by Mount Mandara at the onset of night.
He was being churned by Mount Mandara, which, at the onset of night, was colored by the hues of twilight;

he was like the Ocean of Milk characterized by the moon, with spreading masses of light resembling the breaking waves of milk surging forth; and he was like the fierce Śiva, with the spreading floods of the river Gaṅgā released by him.
Behold the quarters and directions, their parts completely filled! 44.

O incomparable one, these hosts of Guhyakas, surrounded by a swarm of young Vetālas who are fierce with their clapping hands, descend by night by force to consume the cities of the Lord of the Hūṇas— cities from which all peace has been cast out and which are devoid of the auspicious sounds of the Vedas.
