O incomparable and peerless one, these hosts of Guhyakas, accompanied by groups of Vetālas as terrifying as palm trees, descend— meaning they go— to devour the people living in the cities of your enemy, the lord of the Hūṇas; for at night, all rites for peace, recitations of auspicious prayers, and auspicious observances have been cast out from those cities, and thus they are rendered destitute by portents.

The full moon shines in the sky only so long as the face of the bride does not emerge outside the house; once the moon-like face of the young woman has risen in the courtyard-sky, what difference remains between it and the moon, that mere fragment of a white cloud?
The face of the young bride does not come to the courtyard outside the house, which is open and unobstructed.

When the moon-like face of the frail woman rises into the sky of the outer courtyard by means of her departure, what difference is there between that moon and a fragment of white cloud, both of whose splendor has been eclipsed by her beauty? "None at all"—this is the speech of the lover. (46)

These peaks of the Lord of the Snowy Mountains have ancient moonbeams for their fresh garments; their rocks are washed by the torrents of the Gaṅgā; they are covered with snow and possess fierce creepers for their matted hair. (47)

Someone describes the peaks of the Himalayas, pervaded by the rays of the moon, as "grown old" (*vṛddhāni*). Here, "growth" (*vṛddhi*) refers to length. *Tuṣāraśaileśvara* is the Lord of the Snowy Mountain, the Himalayas; its "heads" (*mastakāni*) are its peaks (*śikharāṇi*). || 47 ||

This very Mount Mandara, the ornament of the Mandāra forest, where breezes spread the songs of celestial nymphs on swings, is seen in the sky in some places variegated with the diverse luster of jewels. (48)
The wind there is characterized by its spreading the songs of the apsarases who have mounted the swings and hammocks;
because of its extreme height, it is visible in the sky. 48.
These great mountains, bearing dense flower-offerings in vessels upon their thick, blossoming *śilīndhra* trees that are ever-awake and without gaps,
possess the splendor of the sky filled with stars within their deep interiors that resound like thick clouds.
Those very *śilīndhra* trees, which are full-blown, dense, and laden with flowers, bear offering-bowls filled with thick blossoms; such great mountains (*mahīdhra*) as these,
with their deep valleys (*droṇī*) in their cavernous interiors resounding with the thick roar of clouds, together with the bears (*ṛkṣa*) and the stars (*nakṣatra*).
That which is the present intermediate space (antarikṣa) bears and sustains that glory. || 49 ||

From here, Mount Kailāsa appears as if it were the paved courtyard of Śambhu’s son, measured by a vast stream of radiance that fills the sky; and even the moon seems as if it had entered the Ocean of Milk.

Look toward the north from here; behold that famous Mount Kailāsa. Of what nature is it? By its immense and measured flow of radiance, the sky appears below like the paved floor of a pleasure-house made of powdered pearls belonging to Śambhu’s son, Skanda; yet even the moon [is surpassed] in its upper regions.
It appears just as if it were submerged and immersed within the ocean of milk. || 50 ||
O Vāsava, behold how he joins together tree trunks whose branches have been severed and even those made of clay, though they lie far apart, as if their crests were set in motion by the winds.

O King, the curious Indra, having created with his rains— as if they were released flames— saplings upon tree-stumps whose branches had been severed by axes, and upon earthen walls whose foliage and branches had been consumed by fire, even though these objects were far apart from one another, caused them to grow on both sides by means of the winds.
Behold, it joins them together as if for mutual interweaving. 51.
These winds, fragrant with the scent of *kadamba*, *kula*, and *kunda* flowers, besmear my sense of smell with the richness of a rain of nectar;
darkened by swarms of bees, they are like clouds of antimony that stir up the sky with dense masses of fragrance.

Likewise, these fragrant breezes, scented by *kadamba*, *kula*, and *kunda* flowers, become dark as swarms of bees due to their thickness from drinking the rain of nectar; having churned all the perfumes,
they— dense like masses of clouds— smear even the nostrils of people with those fragrances that resemble a canopy of clouds.
The meaning is "behold. || 52 ||

In forest regions where the petals of the buds remain unfaded, in jungles thick with shady meadows, and in villages crowded with trees that bear fruit continuously, prosperity itself seems to dwell as if for the sake of making them its home. (53)
During the rainy season, he dwells in four locations such as forest groves for the sake of his own residence, as if to display an extraordinary beauty. || 53 ||
With winds carrying the filaments of the *kośātakī* flowers from the palace chambers— covered by creepers reaching through the windows—
the village of these forest deities shines forth, its courtyards strewn with buds up to the ankles.

This village standing before us has its flower-strewn courtyards— strewn up to the ankles— with flowers and their filaments brought by the winds that enter through the windows and doors and fill the palace chambers with *kośātakī* creepers.

Thus endowed with such courtyards and open squares, that city of the forest deities shines forth, where women swing upon the swings of creepers among blossoming, pure campaka trees; where the flows of murmuring waterfalls resound and the tāla trees in the vicinity are in full bloom.
The mountain villages are delightful, with peacocks sporting in vine-arbors cooled by blossoming, radiant clusters of flowers, and with clouds hanging from the tall *sāla* trees on their slopes.
In which [gardens] women play, swaying upon swings made of creepers belonging to stainless *campaka* trees that are in full bloom;
where the waters of mountain torrents coo;
where, all around the precincts, *tāla* trees stand in full flower; and where vine-cottages are adorned with white, radiant clusters of blossoms.

In these mountain villages, peacocks are dancing with joy; on their elevated perimeters are walls or trees where clouds hang like long garlands—or rather, where the *sāla* trees themselves are like long, swaying clouds. Such mountain villages are delightful. (55)
Whose nectar-like pavilions are these, with their blue grounds filled with creepers of variegated leaves swaying in the wind;
where flocks of quails, ruddy geese, and wild cocks warble; where Pulinda women sing;
where young calves are restless; and which shine with the drinking of curds, honey, milk, and clarified butter?
Delightful mountain villages have been constructed. || 56 ||

Likewise, those [forests] whose grounds were filled with green meadows where creepers—variegated with leaves such as sprouts and the like—were swaying in the wind; where *lāvaka* birds, a species of small fowl with sweet voices, [dwelt];
where the women of the *pulinda*s—a specific class of barbarians (*mleccha*)—were singing; and where the young calves were untroubled because they were being tended by their tails.

In those [villages], there are calves; likewise, those very same young ones—unagitated and like little kids—are radiant from drinking curds, honey, milk, and clarified butter as appropriate, and such flowers are found therein. The meaning is: for whom would such mountain villages not be delightful for rest? They appear like pavilions constructed and filled with nectar. || 56 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and fifteenth canto, titled "The Description of the Nature of Objects as Emulated by Vipaścit," in the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*, the *Vālmīki-Divya-Mokṣopāya-Nirvāṇa-Uttara* [section]. 115.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifteenth canto, titled "The Description of the Nature of Objects as Emulated by Vipaścit," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa within the Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa.
The one hundred and sixteenth canto. The attendants said:
"O Lord, behold here the mountain ranges that form the boundary where the battle has commenced."
The masses of weapons flash and the forces disperse. || 1 ||
The grandeur of mountain ranges separated from the sky of battle,
the clouds in mountain caves, and even foolish crows have all been described [by him].
Therein, first, he introduces the description of the battle with seven verses, beginning with "O King": "The fourfold forces" refers to the four constituent parts of an army. || 1 ||
Behold, behold! Having repeatedly lifted up heroes by the thousands—both those slain and those standing firm before them—the celestial chariots of women are ascending to the sky. || 2 ||
The women were celestial nymphs; [they traveled] by means of chariots and celestial palaces. || 2 ||
Furthermore, for one desiring victory, when a crisis has arrived in an open battle,
a righteous war shines forth like amorous dalliance in youth.

When a powerful seeker of victory encounters a manifest and perilous crisis from his enemies in battle, their slaughter through unrighteous means does not shine; rather, a righteous war—one that does not deviate from dharma—is what truly shines forth. This is the meaning. || 3 ||
Fortune unblemished by the world, health endowed with prosperity,
and righteous battle for the sake of others— these are the supreme fruits of life.
He asks why that is, and says: "by the worlds. The meaning is that these alone are the supreme fruits of life, and not such things as censurable wealth and the like. || 4 ||
That hero who, without violating the law (*dharma*), slays one who has come before him in battle according to the rules of combat, attains heaven; no other does.
"According to the warrior's status" means as follows: in the case of a single warrior, he is exactly like himself—when with a mount, he is with his mount; when with a bow, he is with his bow;
when with a sword, he is with his sword; and when unarmed, he is indeed unarmed, striking while engaging in hand-to-hand combat.
Here, the arrival of night occurs through the thick dust raised by horses, dark like a garland of blue lotuses or a fine sword held in the hand.
Behold how he strides, adorned with the weight of uplifted weapons— the very ornaments of Fortune! O King, in this heroic man who bears these uplifted (pronnāma) masses of weapons as his decorations,
he is darkened by the garland of blue lotuses in the form of the sword held in the hand of the Goddess of Battle.

How can the arrival of night, characterized by the darkness created by the thick dust arising from the horses, proceed upon this battlefield? The meaning is: "Look with curiosity to see whether she will choose him herself in this night's svayaṃvara or not."
These shine forth, filled with arrows, spears, maces, *bhuśuṇḍīs*, tridents, swords, lances, sharp *tomaras*, and discs;
like masses of lordly serpents leaping upon the earth with their bodies as the ocean—trembling with its surging waves and dancing hair—quakes in its agitation.

These warriors, bristling with weapons such as arrows and spears, shine like forest fires blazing upon the mountain, which is shaken by grass and wood resembling their dancing hair. And amidst them, the masses of arrows, spears, and other missiles flash like the hosts of serpent-kings on the earth when the ocean leaps up with its body. || 7 ||
Behold the sky, filled with powerful oceans of clouds; behold the sky, a shimmering necklace of radiant stars;
behold the sky, its essence obscured by dense, clinging darkness; behold the sky!
Sprinkled by the rays of the clear moon. || 8 ||

From here onwards, he describes the sky in the four directions with the words beginning "Behold" (paśya). It is "very dense" (*sughana*) because it is thickly attached; thus, by such darkness, it is "of one essence" (*ekasāra*), meaning its essence is identical to that [darkness], namely, blue. || 8 ||

In that sky, where the multitude of abodes for many gods and asuras has become the stars, and which is the dwelling place of the constellations and of all things that spread upward— yet even now the notion that it is "empty" has not vanished; who else but you could wipe this away?
A person should endure the public censure fabricated by the ignorant. || 9 ||

In that sky, where the multitude of celestial chariots and other abodes of numerous gods and asuras has taken the guise and pretext of being called "stars"; and in that sky, which is the dwelling place of the constellations beginning with Aśvinī,
and the motionless expanse of all the lofty luminaries such as the moon and the sun— even though that sky is completely full on all sides.

The notion that [space] is empty has not ceased even now among the ignorant; since even the great and capable sky is unable to wipe away this denial of emptiness fabricated by the ignorant, what else could possibly be capable of doing so?— this is the meaning [of the verse] regarding the massing clouds.

Even today, the sky has not reached its natural limit despite the conflagrations of universal dissolution, the blows from the wings of mountains, the floods of stars, and the tumultuous battles between gods and demons; yet, the greatness of those who possess internal qualities of profound essence is not perceived by such [external] means. || 10 ||
The limit of the greatness of those who possess the quality of essential resolve is not seen. || 10 ||

O virtuous one, you repeatedly embrace with your lap the sun in the sky, Nārāyaṇa, the moon, and likewise other radiant splendors such as the brilliant lightning; yet it is a marvel that even so, you do not abandon your inner blindness.
O virtuous one, you have made the sky your constant abode, Nārāyaṇa your sun, all the gods your attendants,
the moon another planet, and likewise other radiant splendors such as lightning;
yet even so, you do not abandon the internal darkness characterized by the gloom of ignorance within your heart.
"Citram" means "wonderful" or "marvelous. || 11 ||
O Sky, you shine where the orb of the moon appears; yet it is stained by the blackness of the soot-like darkness scattered by you.
That you do not lead it to total blackness through such contact is truly a great marvel; for who indeed would defile another with their own internal impurity? 12.
O Sky, you are stained! For where the orb of the moon was scattered by you, whose nature is full of holes, it became filled with soot-like darkness;

in that place, under the guise of a spot, you appear visibly as something defiled—the meaning being that you are indeed seen as such. This being the case, since the full orb of the moon [became so] through contact with you...

That you do not lead it to blackness—that is a great marvel! Or rather, through association with the soiled, that which is already foul within comes to acquire external dirtiness as well; but as for the internal impurity, who indeed could defile it? The meaning is: no one at all. || 12 ||

I believe that for one who is ever unchanging despite being filled with the defects of the world— just as space remains unaffected— the happiness found in the emptiness of all objects is like that of a wise man.

Alternatively, even if all defects such as impurity and the like were to exist, nevertheless, by the power of being changeless alone, the happiness of being free from all misfortunes caused by them is easily attained; with this intention, he says:
"Even for one who is full," meaning for the wise one who knows reality. || 13 ||

You shall be the creator and the sustainer of the elevation of the aeons, clouds, trees, and creepers, as well as of the sky, the moon, the clouds, the sun, the kinnaras, the winds, the mountain ranges, and the gods; for you,
whose intention is unconfused and whose nature is equally pure, everything is beautiful.
But this very quality of burning, my dear, alas, leads to our primary distress. (14)

O noble one of unconfused intent, O exalted intellect, O sky! You are the creator of elevation by granting space to those who, beholding and desiring the height of trees, shrubs, and creepers, look toward such loftiness— just as the moon [is to the night-blooming flowers].

You were the sustainer and support even of these— the clouds, the sun, the kinnaras, the hosts of Maruts, and the immortals— and thus every action of yours, whose nature is perfectly pure, was indeed beautiful. However, that which constitutes the burning nature and the scorching quality of fire and the sun, by providing heat and space, is a source of primary distress to us.
But it is not for the sake of pleasure; this is said by one who is tormented by forest fires, heat, and so forth. || 14 ||
O Ākāśa, you are pure, transparent, and brilliantly shining; by virtue of your loftiness, you are the supreme support for the most excellent things.

Yet, alas, this dense mass of hailstones (karakā-ghana) grinds upon the world; because of that, you are surpassed by those who are low. O Ākāśa, you are stainless, clear [devoid of obstructions such as clouds], and radiant.

You are radiant and, by virtue of your loftiness, the supreme support for the highest beings such as the gods; yet, having come upon and taken refuge in you—who are sparse and full of empty space—this cloud raining hailstones crushes the world, that is, the people.
Therefore, because of that fault, you are "paraḥ," meaning lowly and utterly inferior. || 15 ||
O Sky, I consider your very nature to be that of a whetstone; I believe you have long been honed, yet nothing else has been added to you.
You are empty, for you carry and shine with the clouds, stars, celestial chariots, the moon, the sun, and the wind, yet you are not devoid of purpose.

O Ākāśa, it is only on you—your very touchstone, the place for testing gold—that long-standing friction is appropriate; the meaning is that there is no other locus for your examination. For although you are empty, you nevertheless bear and shine with clouds, bears, celestial chariots, the moon, the sun, and the winds.

The meaning is that it is neither meaningful nor purposeful for you—who possess every golden quality—to say "it does not exist," because it is only fitting that the very place where its qualities are examined should serve as the locus for the examination of those qualities. || 16 ||

By day you are luminous with a red body, at the end of the day you are black during the watches of the night, and yet you always carry nothing at all that truly exists; even the wise do not understand this illusion of yours, nor how you act like the void.

In the phrase *he vyoma*, the prohibition of the elision of *n* (by the rule *na ṅisaṃbuddhyoḥ*) has not been applied, either because it belongs to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*) or because it is non-obligatory (*anitya*). You are luminous and brilliant-hued during the day; at the end of the day, you possess a body reddened by the glow of twilight; and in the "watches" (*yāmāsu*)—referring to the three watches (*triyāmāsu*) by mentioning a part of the name—you are black. And furthermore:

The meaning is that because you do not carry even the slightest real entity within you eternally, you are empty of all things; thus, no one perceives even the activity of those knowers of reality who understand your *māyā*. || 17 ||
Even one who possesses nothing accomplishes his tasks with a humble disposition;
even the sky, though empty within, is the cause of the elevation of all things. 18.
He was one whose intentions were expansive, possessed of exceedingly vast intellect, and a knower of reality.
There is no grass or water, no village nor even a name for a town, no tree with dense shade from its abundant foliage, and no virtuous water-stall;
yet the sun travels the path of the sky day after day— that which has been undertaken, however difficult it may be.
Those of virtuous nature do not abandon that. || 19 ||

In the path of the sky, there is neither grass nor water to provide rest for travelers; there is no village at all, and neither a town nor a city exists—meaning they are utterly non-existent. There is not even a tree with lush foliage and pleasant shade, nor is there a lovely *prapā*, a public water station. And yet, the sun—

Day by day it travels along the path of the sky; likewise, those who are *sāttvika*—possessing the quality of purity (*sattva*)—do not abandon what they have begun, even if it is difficult or impossible for others to accomplish; rather, by their own power, they certainly bring it to completion. This is the meaning. || 19 ||

The Yama-gods adorn themselves with the veil of darkness; the moon with its cool rays as if with floods of camphor; the day with the new garment of sunlight; and the sky with the clusters of star-flowers.
Thus, all these seasons together adorn the world with clouds, frost, water, and blossoms.
In the three worlds, the courtyard of the sky belongs to the two Lords, whose nature is Time and its divisions.

The day adorns itself with the fresh garment characterized by the light of the sun; the sky adorns itself with the clusters of flowers consisting of the multitude of stars at night; and all the seasons, beginning with spring, adorn themselves with water-flowers characterized by rain-clouds and frost. All these together—

The meaning is that they adorn the courtyard of the sky, which is the playground of their two lords, the Moon and the Sun, who are the masters of the three worlds and whose nature consists of time and its divisions. || 20 ||

The atmosphere does not abandon its natural state even through the disturbances caused by smoke, clouds, dust, darkness, the sun, the moon, twilight, stars, celestial chariots, Garuḍa, mountains, gods, and demons; oh, how wondrous is the exalted and elevated stability of one of great soul! For the stability of a great-souled person is seen to be marvelous, risen high, and manifest. Since the atmosphere—[remains unchanged] even by the agitations of smoke, clouds, dust, darkness, the sun, the night-maker (moon), twilight, stars, celestial vehicles, Garuḍa, mountains, gods, and asuras—oh, the stability of a magnanimous person is indeed marvelous, arisen, and lofty! Since the sky [does not change], [so too the mind of the noble]. (Note: The commentary explains that just as the sky remains its natural self despite various upheavals, so too the mind of a "mahāśaya" remains in its natural state of equanimity regardless of external disturbances.)
Even through the agitations of the thirteen [energies] beginning with Dhūmā, it does not abandon its nature, which is its prior state. || 21 ||
This world has the quarters as its walls, the sky as its upper surface, and the earth’s surface as its vast storehouse of dense cities and mountains;
it is filled with the nets of Vidyādharas, gods, and great serpents, and teeming with the swarms of ants that are the multitudes of beings wandering through the cycle of existence.

Another person describes the three worlds as a single dilapidated house: "The walls of the quarters," and so forth. The very directions are its walls; by them it is bound, and the sky above has become its upper floor. The earth itself is its lower floor. The dense ancient mountains are its abundant household utensils.

In which [city] there were weavers such as the Vidyādharas and others, and in which there were spiders like the *ūrṇanābhi* insects; likewise, it was filled with "ant-colonies" characterized by the floods of worldly beings—the fourfold classes of living creatures. || 22 ||

Time and action, the world and its dwellings, as if for a long time presiding over a blossoming grove—though it is suspected every day that it has surely perished, it does not perish even now; oh, what a wonder is this illusion!
(A pair of verses.)

This world, this abode, and Time and Action— this couple presides over and protects it for a long time, just as a florist couple presides over a blooming garden. Although it is not presided over by Time and Action day by day, and indeed its destruction is feared at every moment, nevertheless, even now—
It perishes—and because of the word "and" (ca), it does not perish; nevertheless, it continues by way of its stream. Thus, even while perishing, it does not perish;

such is the nature of its contradictory attributes—oh, what a *māyā*! The meaning is that this is like a magician’s trick (*indrajāla*). And so says the Śruti: "Why do they not perish, though being eaten all the time? The Person (*puruṣa*) is indeed the imperishable; for he [sustains] this food through his intellect."
"He generates [it] through intellect and by means of actions," so it is said. || 23 ||
I consider that space restrains the excessive height of trees and other things;
for even in the Great One who is not an agent, agency arises through His majesty.
"I think" (*manye*) is used here in the sense of poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*). By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), all things characterized by growth are included. Now, one might object:
since space (*kha*) is devoid of any activity of obstructing, it is indeed a non-agent (*akartṛ*) with respect to obstruction; how then can agency, which is its opposite, be poetically fancied?
To this he says: "of the non-agent itself. This is as in the expression: "the mountains block the path of travelers."
The state of being. || 24 ||
That space in which millions of worlds do not exist and yet arise is called the void; fie upon this unbroken "wisdom"! (25)
Someone, refuting the proponents of the voidness of space through reasoning, censures them with the words "of the worlds" (*jagatām*). [The worlds] do not exist;
they dissolve and they arise. || 25 ||
They dissolve into space alone and emerge from space;
those who fall into this madness have created a distinction where none exists regarding the Lord.
Another, perceiving the characteristics of the Lord in space alone, censures the proponent of its difference from Him, saying: "In space alone.
This distinction—that space is other than the Lord—was made by the proponent who has fallen into madness;
for all worlds dissolve into space alone, emerge from space alone (the word *ca* implying that they also abide in space alone).

The meaning is that the definition of the Lord established by the scripture—namely, "He from whom the birth, etc., of this [universe proceeds]"—is seen in space alone; therefore, space itself is the Lord. In the reading "names such as 'Lord' have been applied," the sense is that by the disputant who falls into the delusion of madness—that is, the error consisting in the notion of something else—due to the aforementioned understanding of the meaning, [the names] are applied to space.
Thus, names such as Īśvara and others have been established. || 26 ||
The splendors of creation come, go, fall down, and likewise rise up like droplets of water rising from a fire;
that which is stainless therein— I consider that alone to be the beginningless and endless space (ākāśa), and not a cause called by the name of Īśvara.

If you consider the birth and so forth of the universe to proceed from space itself, according to the analogy of sparks from a fire, then that space is not inert; rather, it is I myself in the form of the consciousness-space (*cidvyoma*). For the Śruti declares: "In me alone has everything been born; in me everything is established;
into me everything goes to its dissolution; I am that non-dual Brahman. Thus, I alone am that Lord (*īśvara*).
The position of an *īśvara* who is merely external (*taṭastha*) is alone worthy of refutation; regarding this, a certain knower of reality says: "They come," etc.
[Verse 27]. This refers to the one called *īśvara* as an external agent, as maintained by the Naiyāyikas and others, and not [to the *īśvara* as the inner self].

I consider myself to be the Supreme Consciousness alone, whose body is space, which possesses an infinitely vast support for the jewels of the three worlds and contains within its limbs all things without exception; it is in this very space that this delusion of the world undergoes its rise and setting. (28) That which is immeasurable and contains all things within its limbs, the infinitely vast support for the jewels of the three worlds—that is indeed space.
I consider that the supreme Brahman alone is the very embodiment of consciousness. || 28 ||
In the forest groves, where the trees are dense and enchanting, the song of the lovely women wandering in the woods is heard;
from here, on the mountain peak, it is perceived by this traveler on the road who is overwhelmed with longing.

Someone, displaying a particular curiosity regarding the mountain, says: "In the forest-glade... On the peak of the mountain, in the forest-glade, a song is being sung by a charming lover wandering in the woods amidst dense, enchanting trees. Hearing that song while traveling along the path below, this separated man [listens] so as to become overwhelmed with emotion (*rasākula*). That singer—
It is gazed upon from above. || 29 ||
Having sighed with longing, a Vidyādhara woman, stricken by separation, sang this song with a voice choked in her throat from within the hollow of a high branch’s tender leaves;
O Lord, hearing that name here, this traveler listens with a deep breath, as if swaying on a swing.
It does not pass away because of a flickering mind, nor is it uttered repeatedly. || 30 ||
Another [poet], displaying a similar marvel, says with the words beginning "The song": O Lord,

in a grove resembling a cluster of leaf-buds belonging to a tall tree on a mountain peak, a Vidyādhara woman— stricken by separation and filled with longing— having sighed, sang a name with her voice clinging to her throat.

Thus, as this traveler goes downward here, listening with a sigh of relief, he does not proceed further because his mind is wavering like one on a swing; it is a marvel that even his followers do not urge him, saying, "Go! || 30 ||
On a tree atop the mountain peak, within a hollow of leaves, this Vidyādharī, distressed by separation and her face clouded with tears, sings with a sweet, low melody before me: "O Lord,
remembering and relishing your smiling kiss upon the couch of your lap— your chin held in my hand— I am overcome."
"These elixirs have been brought by me, having had their impurities destroyed. || 31 ||

That Vidyādharī, overwhelmed with tears, sang in such a way that her forehead mark (*atilaka*) and decorative tilaka (*viśeṣaka*) were blurred. What she sang is stated as follows: "O Lord, remembering the elixir (*rasāyana*) characterized by your kiss—accompanied by a slight smile and with my chin resting upon the lap of your home—I [suffer]."
Tasting them again and again, he sings here: "I have spent these years, which are as despicable as those whose lives are destroyed. || 31 ||
The husband of this woman in her previous birth was turned into a tree by a sage’s curse; counting those very twelve years, she remains right here,
singing with longing for that beloved while clinging to that tree on the path of travelers.
O King, this was heard by me from his own mouth.

To explain why she remains right there singing, he says: "asyāḥ" (of her). That husband, who was a *vidyādhara* youth, became her lover in a previous birth (*prāgbhava*); however, due to some offense committed against a certain sage, he was transformed into a tree by a curse for twelve years. Counting those very years, she remains right here, longing and full of yearning (*utkalitā*).
Taking refuge in that very tree which she holds so dear, she sings: "O King, this was heard by me on the road from the mouths of those traveling along the way. (32)

Look! There is that Vidyādhara, his curse pacified by our gaze; having released the girl from the tree, he—who possesses the clear laughter of blossoms—now embraces her neck with those very arms that were previously a deceptive disguise as the branches.
And that sage made our very sight the end of his curse; therefore, this Vidyadhara, who had become a tree,

having his curse pacified by our mere glance, has cast off his state as a branch and, with those very arms disguised as branches, [embraces] that young Vidyadhara maiden, whose blossoming flowers are her manifest smiles.
Behold, being such as he is, he embraces those who have attained perfection and places them upon his neck. 33.
Upon the trees with their blossoming foliage, the heap of flowers upon the elephants that resemble mountain peaks shines;
for this peak possesses the appearance of frost, like the play of stars fallen from the sky.
Another describes the mountain peaks: "Of the elephants characterized by their tusks (śikhariṇām)," and so forth.

Upon the summits of the elephants characterized by their tusks—which possess clearly visible bristles like branches—the heap of flowers, resembling the frost of spring (vāsantika-himakaraṇa), shines with the play of stars fallen from the sky. || 34 ||

Ah, the Kāverī shines forth like a woman clad in a white garment of flowers; her banks and marshes are crowded with flocks of fearless cranes, while she is made formidable by the cries of female ospreys fluttering as they are struck by the waves tossed up by the impetuous leaps of schools of fish.

Another describes the Kāverī: "With its banks made formidable by shoals of fish darting with impetuous leaps that stir the water-waves, where playful and crying ospreys sport, and which are crowded with various deer and young elephants wandering without fear; [the river] possesses flower-white garments."
The Kāverī, whose marshes and water-abundant regions are of such a nature, shines forth; "aho" expresses wonder. || 35 ||
Behold here, on the ridge of Mount Suvela, a golden rock shining with entirely stainless splendor by the light of the sun;
it resembles the sparks of the submarine fire cast about by the breaking waves of the ocean tossing against the shore.
O King, here on the ridge of Mount Suvela, the entire golden rock shines forth, being illuminated by the sun;
it appears as if it were the very sparks of the submarine fire— the Vāḍava fire— of the ocean, which remains unagitated at its shores yet is scattered abroad by the breaking waves.

Behold the splendor of the cowherd settlements on the mountains, whose dwellings are surrounded by nearby, thick clouds; where the trees in the forests at the outskirts of the houses are in full bloom; and where the sky is veiled by masses of *palāśa* flowers. (37) Thus, on those mountains, the dwellings are encircled by nearby, dense clouds, and at the *gehopaśalyas*—the boundaries of the houses—the trees in the forests are blossoming.
Behold the splendor of the cowherd villages, the dwellings of the Ghoṣas, where the forest trees are in full bloom and the sky is veiled by masses of palāśa blossoms.

Victorious are these villages, where clusters of flowers are bright white like blossoms in full bloom; where the banks are lined with baskets of mandāra flowers and peacock feathers; where the play of water-weeds in the cascades provides musical instruments; and where the people sing amidst the depths of caves from which spirits leap forth.
Likewise, those [banks] possess flower-gardens whose clusters of blossoms are intensely white and exceedingly bright due to flowers that have fallen away;

likewise, those marshy banks (kaccha), being the sites for the dancing of various peacocks, are like caskets for them, as they contain Mandāra trees which are like baskets holding a great abundance of flowers.

Victorious are such mountain villages, which possess regions of coolness; where, in the waterfalls, the playful splashes of masses of water falling from above serve as musical instruments for the dancing of peacocks; where the caves seem to leap with echoes;
and where the songs of people who dwell in such dense thickets prevail.
"Heaven" is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. || 38 ||

I believe that the satisfaction which the gods here derive from intoxicated bees—blinded by passion—humming as they hide among the petals of blossoming kandalī flowers, is not equal to the joy found by men dwelling in mountain caves within the cowherd settlements (gokula). 39.
He clarifies that very point with the verse beginning "unnidra": here, in the mountain villages and cow-pens,

by the intoxicated bees— blinded by passion— who are humming and hiding within the interior of the buds of the *kandala* plants that have blossomed all at once (*unnidrāṇa*), even the most vulgar folk (*pāmarāḥ*) are made frantic, their desire being kindled.
I believe that the joy which belongs to men dwelling in mountain caves with their pairs of mates is not even attained by the immortals sporting in the Nandana grove. (39)
With their eyes fixed upon the faces of Pulinda women singing amidst the forest thickets where the creepers are swayed by bees,
do these Kirātas— restless in their play and pitiless in mountain caves— slay the innocent deer as if they were an enemy? (40)
In the mountain caves within that forest, where the groves were filled with creepers swaying like swings and frequented by bees,
the Kirātas— distraught with amorous gestures as they cast their eyes upon the faces of singing Pulinda women— regarded the innocent deer as a pitiless enemy.

"Where, what, and how do they strike so mercilessly? Alas! That those whose gaze is fixed elsewhere and whose minds are on something else possess such skill in piercing moving targets, and yet exhibit such extreme cruelty even at a time like this—this is the meaning. Or rather, [it refers to] the faces of the Pulinda women, who resemble creepers swaying under the weight of bees."

The poetic fancy (utprekṣā) is: "Because they have granted their eyes to the innocent deer, and because they are constantly mindful of how they have stolen the beauty of the Pulinda women's eyes while eating the sprouts of the creepers, do they regard [the hunters] as enemies and thus strike them mercilessly even at a time when they ought to be objects of compassion? || 40 ||

Victorious are the villages within the depths of the great mountains, which delight the moon; their travelers' limbs are cooled by the swaying of vine-leaves that have acquired the essence from heaps of various blooming flowers, and their flowing waters spread with surging waves.
Furthermore, they possess the essence—such as coolness, fragrance, and pollen—obtained from various clusters of blossoms.
The limbs of travelers were cooled by the swaying of creepers and leaves caused by such winds;

those waters, along with their quality of coolness, are celebrated as "possessing water" (*sāmbhaḥ*). Through the spreading of such winds, there are villages where the reservoirs have waves surging upon them.

They surpass the moon by virtue of their superior quality of fragrance; thus, the intended meaning is that even compared to the gods residing in the lunar orb, the inhabitants of the village possess greater happiness. || 41 ||
With the warbling of birds, with the spreading and blossoming *tāla* trees, with the canopy of the sky formed by the swaying creepers laden with flowers and shoots playfully tossed about,
and with clouds hanging from the tall *sāla* trees on their slopes— these delightful mountain villages, where the earth is measured by the *candra-aśvattha*, [are now reached].
Like the garden districts of Śaśipura. || 42 ||

The first three quarters [of the verse] have been explained. Such mountain villages are like portions of the gardens of Śaśipura—that is, the city of Candra situated in heaven—and they surpass the earth of the world of Brahmā (brahmaloka), which is measured by the *aśvattha* tree known as Somasavana, according to the Vedic scripture (*śruti*) that it "sheds lunar nectar. This is to be supplied to complete the sense.

Victorious are the villages, where flocks of peacocks dance to the deep, rumbling roar of nearby clouds like thick yellow thunderheads, scattering their soft plumage from their tails— plumage that resembles a multitude of flying moonstones.
Furthermore, these mountain villages are near such clouds that have drunk the lightning and possess deep, rumbling sounds;
and in the fresh dances of the peacocks dancing to those sounds,
the clusters of gems characterized by moon-spots have flown away along with the soft fragments of the plumage scattered from the flocks of their tails.
The meaning is that those who are such as described triumph, as previously stated. || 43 ||

Where could that playful splendor found in villages on mountain slopes—adorned by beautiful moon-discs resting at their sides and shielded by heavy clouds like elephants—be found even in the wealthy kingdoms of Brahmā? 44.

Furthermore, what kind of playful splendor exists in those villages situated on mountain slopes—slopes where the beautiful lunar disc rests upon one side as their very ornament, and where clouds, heavy with water, find rest upon the other side—that same splendor, how could it exist even in the prosperous kingdoms of Brahmā? The meaning is that it is difficult to find elsewhere. || 44 ||

May I delight in the mountain caves, beautiful within the Nandana grove with its own fragrance, where bower-thickets laugh with clusters of *saṃtānaka* flowers, and where the thick *pāribhadra* trees are filled with bees humming softly as they awaken.

In those mountain caves where there are groves possessing the nature of *saṃtānaka* clusters—those belonging to a species of wish-fulfilling tree—which mock the interior of the Nandana forest with their beauty; where the dense trees, in the form of *pāribhadra* and *nimba* trees, are in full bloom, covered with bees buzzing with deep humming sounds, and are wide awake. In such mountain recesses, I...
May you rejoice! || 45 ||
In the mountain villages, delightful with the cries of does and charming with beautiful *hārīta* birds, men find pleasure as if they were in the cities of the God of Love. (46)
Like the flower-arrowed Manmatha in his own cities. || 46 ||
Behold these peahens dancing in this mountain glen of the village, where the waters of lovely waterfalls cascade down crystal pillars.
In which [gardens] there were delightful, cascading waters from mountain torrents that resembled masses of crystal pillars. || 47 ||
There, crested and playful creepers, bent low under the weight of their flowers, dance within the groves to the sound of the resonating waterfalls. 48.
In this mountain cave, where the waterfalls and lotuses resound—that is, where the waters of the cascades ring out.

In these village settlements hidden within mountain caves, where the trees of the groves are green with the brilliance of emeralds and the pure, sweet warbling of birds resounds from the ponds— I believe that this god of love now sports there with joy according to his own nature.

I believe that in these village settlements— hidden and concealed by mountain caves, where the garden trees are green and captivating with various birds such as *hārīta* parrots, and where there are pure, melodious warbling (*kākalyaḥ*) characterized by the cries of swans, cranes, and other waterfowl in ponds of great measure— this Kāma, renowned throughout the entire world, sports with joy according to his own natural inclination. 49.

O Cloud, you are the ornament upon the crests of the mountains—those lofty forms that dispel the heat of the great sun with their glorious foliage—and you are the sole abode of the essence of the earth.
Yet this one thing causes distress to the minds of all: that while you rain down, O Cloud, [the parched lands] are being consumed.
Out of joy, the process of distributing water proceeded among the saline soil, the ponds, the dry land, and the trees. || 50 ||
From this point until the end of the creation, the descriptions are generally to be understood as indirect (anyāpadeśa).

O Cloud, you who possess a character like that of the wealthy—namely, great magnanimity—and who, being desirous of protecting the world, are high-minded; you whose form and body are lofty, elevated, and deep, providing shade from the heat.

You are the ornament upon the crests of the mountains, the bearers of the earth; likewise, you are the sole abode of the essence—of water—for the sake of providing the prosperity of fields, groves, and the like to the world. Thus, although you possess a thousand virtuous qualities, by raining out of joy upon unworthy recipients such as saline wastelands and mere puddles...
Furthermore, regarding the thorny trees and others found there, you have adopted a method of distributing water based on the analogy of fertile fields;
however, this failure of yours to discern between worthy and unworthy recipients would weary and afflict the minds of the virtuous.
The implication is: if even great men such as yourself do not honor the excellence of the qualities of a worthy recipient, then who else will? || 50 ||

Established in a high station, you constantly bathe in the vast waters of sacred fords; being pure, you dwell upon the forest floor having undertaken a vow of silence. Even when empty, an exceeding luster is observed residing in your body; yet, rising up, you discharge the thunderbolt.
What is this trivial exertion of yours? || 51 ||

With the intention that harsh, bitter, and ear-piercing speech at the time of beginning a gift is a great and most unbearable fault for donors, he says: "Always," etc. O Cloud, you always bathe with the masses of water from excellent holy sites such as the ocean and the Gaṅgā; likewise, being established in a high position, you give water to all living beings, and thus you are an *ambuda* (water-giver).

Furthermore, being pure, you have undertaken the vow of silence associated with sages and thus dwell in the forest; moreover, even though you are empty in the autumn, an extraordinary white luster is seen residing in your body. Even so, having risen for the sake of giving, you [emit] lightning—
Preceded by lightning and fire, you produce a harsh sound; what is this trivial activity of yours, fit only for the base?
The meaning is that it is entirely improper. || 51 ||
Everything, whether auspicious or inauspicious, becomes vast when it reaches its proper place; yet water, upon reaching the site of a dark cloud, turns black.

The bystander says: "A thing," etc. Even a beautiful thing may become unwholesome when situated in an unsuitable place. The word *vāri* (water) should be read as a separate word [in the verse]. || 52 ||
"Oh, how the cloud has released its water! Oh, how the earth has been filled with that water!
Oh, how the wretched one on the ground has been nourished by those waters, like a poor man by a wealthy benefactor! (53)
The wretched and the poor, like a loving friend, and the withered crops and other things were all completely satisfied upon the earth. || 53 ||
Cruelty, instability, impurity, wandering the streets, and utter contemptibility—was this indeed received from dogs by fools, or from fools by dogs? I do not know. (54)

In the context of praising qualities such as generosity and magnanimity, someone censures fools who possess the opposite traits, such as cruelty, by demonstrating their doubt regarding an exchange of qualities with dogs: "Cruel... (verse 54).
Even one who possesses many faults may indeed become acceptable to someone on account of just a few virtues—such as valor, contentment, and devotion. (55)
If a fool is indeed only contemptible, then why do kings accept him? To this he replies with the words "by virtues" (guṇaiḥ).
Even a fool, like a dog, becomes acceptable to someone such as a wicked king through qualities such as valor and the like. || 55 ||
Having cast his form into the pathways of sense-objects— running, falling, and rushing about like one insane, intoxicated, or on the verge of death—
he regards as a mere fragment of straw that being who seeks liberation; let it be considered whether this is his dullness or his true nature.
Having cast his form— that is, having projected his body— into the pathways of sense objects and into successions of enjoyments, the fool, greedy for sense objects,

[beholds] those who are intoxicated by consuming substances such as *dhattūra*, those who are drunk with wine and the like, those on the verge of falling into wells due to the onset of negligence, anger, and possession, and those running about due to possession by *piśācas* and other spirits; [he beholds them] through the excellence of his knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*).

Because he has forgotten the limitations of the body and so forth, and because he is established in the supreme authority of the realization "I am Brahman," he considers those who have ascended to the sixth stage and beyond—who are superior to all means of knowledge—to be mere straw by attributing his own self-knowledge to them. O tip of a blade of straw, you yourself observe this man who is greedy for sense objects: is his nature one of desire, or is it rather one of dullness?

Let that secret be reflected upon: if it possesses consciousness (*sattva*), then it is equal to a dog; if it is insentient (*jaḍatva*), then because its attachment to sense objects and other defects exceed even those of a blade of grass, it is itself lower than that, and thus even the comparison to grass will be difficult for it to attain—what then need be said of its inferiority compared to madmen and the like? This is the result of such reflection.
The meaning is that it is to be expressed. || 56 ||
Even though they share the same animal nature, the clamor is endured in one way by lions with agitated minds and in another way by dogs with eyes closed.

The tumultuous roar of thunderclouds and the like is endured with indifference by lions whose minds are unperturbed, with their eyes closed; yet it is endured out of fear by dogs whose minds are agitated, with their eyes closed. Thus, the sense is that there is a difference between the two cases. || 57 ||

O you who are ever impure, devoted solely to barking at those dear to others, and who spend all your time wandering through the alleys—alas, I think you have been taught by some fool whose disposition is truly equal to that of a dog! 58.

"O dog, by some fool who—due to a disposition and mental state similar to yours—regarded you as fit for instruction in his own virtues, you have been taught your own qualities such as perpetual impurity and so forth. The word "I think" (*manye*) serves as a resolution to the doubt previously expressed; for if that were the case, it would be logical to observe that the teacher possesses greater virtues than the pupil.
The state of being. || 58 ||
The Creator, constantly fashioning this entire world as something incomparable, has made everything equal in this dog, his own grandson:
its dwelling is a hole in a foul midden, its food is excrement and pus, and its conduct is lewdness in the sight of all.
The body is entirely censurable. || 59 ||

By the Creator, who fashioned this unequal world through partiality by performing dissimilar deeds, everything that is about to be described has been created equally for the sake of observing all similar and corresponding qualities in this dog— the offspring of his daughter Saramā, known as Devaśunī, and thus a grandson of his own. What [is it]?

He says all that with the word "dwelling" (*vāsa*). In an impure place, within a hollow or a burrow made by itself—that is, a nest in a pit—it takes excrement, feces, and pus as its food. It is observed by all people; thus, "the whole world" refers to the street or path.
In that [place], there is a loathsome, long-knotted pleasure, namely sexual intercourse; the "craving" (*kurati*) for that object is a wicked desire. Likewise, the body is censured by all.
And "all this" is the meaning. || 59 ||
To him who had asked, "Who is more base than you?", the dog replied with a laugh: "He who indulges in folly, impurity, blindness, and inauspiciousness more than I am superior.
For those qualities—valor, unfeigned devotion, and fortitude—which constitute my glorious virtues, are not found even in a fool."
Though sought with a multitude of efforts, it is not obtained. || 60 ||

To the man who had spoken thus and questioned him, the dog spoke with a laugh, as it were. "Folly" (*maurkhya*) means ignorance. "Impurity" (*amedhya*) refers to the conceit of identifying with the body and so forth. "Blindness" (*āndhya*) is the lack of the eye of inquiry. Then he stated by which qualities his superiority over that fool consists:

Regarding "valor": steadfastness is contentment with little. This collection of virtues, even when sought for a long time, is not found in fools upon observation; therefore, the meaning is that he is inferior to me. || 60 ||
He eats filth and constantly delights in filth within the great heap of refuse; he silently devours that which has consciousness and cuts down that which is unconscious.
When all have come together for pleasure, he is pelted with clods of earth by people like a dog; thus the Creator has established his existence as one joined with play.
In the world, he is not made by a lord. || 61 ||

In the word *avaskara*, [the suffix] *suṭ* is applied according to the rule "in the sense of excrement, [it is called] *avaskara*. Having by chance obtained even a conscious and living creature such as a mongoose or a mouse, he eats it silently while it is still innocent. And having found something insentient and weak, such as a goat or a calf, he cuts or bites it silently while it is still innocent. When a dog and a female jackal are engaged in sexual union, all people come and—

He is beaten with clods of earth. Thus, it is enough; the Lord is not powerless. The meaning is that he was made by the Creator (Dhātṛ) to possess a life-span endowed with "khela"—that is, play, sport, and the curiosity of mischievous frolic—for as long as his life lasts. In the reading *śveva samanvitasthitiḥ*, it means one whose status is like that of a dog, namely, a servant who is not independent. || 61 ||
Above the linga, this crow, cawing loudly, reveals itself, saying:
"Behold me, who have ascended from all the lowest sins to the highest state! (62)

Seeing a crow cawing loudly above a Śiva-liṅga on the bank of a certain river in order to eat the offerings and unbroken rice grains (akṣata), someone imagines the intent behind its cawing: "Of the liṅga... It shows, that is, displays itself. Why does it display itself? He says: [it is] of all sins, which are the causes for downward descent.
"Look at me, who has become a crow, standing directly before you, having taken refuge in the Śiva-liṅga which is the highest point in the center for the consumption of Śiva's food. || 62 ||

O crow, you who have swallowed the mud of virtues with your harsh and bitter cries while wandering in this lake, you now obstruct the humming of the bees; therefore, you have become a fruit upon my head.

Another person, pointing toward a crow that was crying out and wandering about in the lake, said: "Kākaka!"—O vile crow, Kākaka! You, by whom the virtues of the swans, cranes, and others have been swallowed up with harsh, deceitful, and hypocritical cries, you who wander in this muddy lake, drown out the sound of those drinking honey.

Because you conceal within yourself your own bitter and harsh nature, for this reason you are like a thorn—the very cause of pain upon my head—and as such, you swallow up the multitude of hells while the crow rejects the lotus stalk.
Therefore, let there be no pride in you; that which is well-practiced always tastes sweet.

A certain friend says to him: "He devours. The crow—that is, the raven—devours the various kinds of impurities found in the multitude of hells, yet he avoids even a lotus stalk when it is within reach; therefore, let there be no pride or astonishment [at this]. For if even something contemptible is habitually consumed due to addiction, that very thing alone is always sought.
It is palatable; that is to say, it is like a dish prepared with garlic for those who eat it. || 64 ||
At first he was seen like a swan with a body white as the filaments of various forest flowers;
then, as he swallowed a mouthful of moist worms, he was recognized as a crow. (65)

With its body glowing from the filaments and the pollen situated upon those filaments of various forest flowers, the crow was seen by mistake to be a swan; this is the sense in which the word *iva* (as if) is used. Then, immediately thereafter, as the crow swallowed a mouthful of a swarm of worms that were soaked in moisture, it was recognized [as a crow]. 65.
When joined by cuckoos of similar color and plumage, by what means is a crow distinguished, unless it speaks for itself? (66)
A crow perched on a stump watches the earth of the forest,
just as a thief from a shrine looks toward the ten directions when people are asleep at night.

Just as this crow, perched upon a pillar made of clay from the earth of the great forest Araṇyānī—a pillar that is like a wall or a column worn out by age—spies the ten directions at night while people are asleep, so too does he (the king) spy;
such is the meaning. || 67 ||
In this lake, beautiful with the nectar of lotuses blooming amidst the vigorous movement of cranes, how is it that a crow wanders here, its shoulders grey with a mass of shimmering droppings? (68)

In this beautiful lake, where the lotuses (*puṣkara*) are being torn asunder by impetuous cranes and the honey of the lilies (*padma*) is present, how does a crow—its body grey with the dust stirred up by the blowing wind—wander about? The meaning is that this is utterly improper. || 68 ||

Alas, what a tragedy! Behold this crow, a demon with a face fit for striking with a whip, who has perched upon this lovely lake—the very heart of blooming white lotuses—and performs all manner of antics alongside the royal swans.
(69) [He sits] in the heart (*kośa*) of the blooming (*sphuṭa*) white lotuses (*puṇḍarīka*), within the lake that possesses a desirable form (*iṣṭavapuṣi*).

Alas, what a pity! O King, look: this crow, a mere demon, having sat down upon this small pool with a beak suited for pecking at stones—stones so called because they "scratch" (kaṣanti) along with royal swans—is performing various antics to mock the royal swans. 69.
O crow of harsh cry, marked by a single saw-like scar! Where has such self-confidence of yours gone today?
Why is this fruit of the cuckoo so useless to you? For even that [fruit] was intended for the hope of a mother with an only son, yet it has served only to bring you ridicule.

Fearing that a virtuous person might obtain through righteous means his share of wealth and possessions that were acquired through deception, theft, and the like, someone speaks under a pretext to a wicked man who is crying out harshly in royal assemblies to thwart him, saying:
"O crow! That which is characterized by a harsh cawing—a saw that tears at the ears of the listener—is itself a single [saw].

O you who possess such a mark— having always called out only to the crows with the apprehension that "may a non-crow not eat my portion of the crow"— where indeed has that self-doubt of yours gone today? Why do you,
for the sake of the hope that "my only son may live," vainly and pointlessly seek the protection of the young cuckoo?

You nourish [it], for because of that delusion, the nurturing of a sweet-voiced cuckoo—though performed by one whose sole habit is harsh speech—will not lead to the fulfillment of your desires, but rather to ridicule; such is the meaning. || 70 ||

Beholding a crow, resembling a dark stain, crying out loudly and full of insolence within the lotus grove—he whose every movement has been destroyed by hundreds of cries of "Alas! Woe!", let him be torn apart with a saw so that he does not weep! (71)

Having observed the crow, someone says—this is the ellipsis—what does he say? He says: "Alas! O crow, that man who, having heard hundreds of harsh and cruel cries from you or from villains, does not weep because his resolve has perished through distress—let that man be torn apart by you with your sharp, curved beak! But as for me, I am not like that; why [then do you attack me]?
The meaning is "you roar. || 71 ||
If there were restless owls and crows in this pond, which is filled with fragile reeds and dense with cranes and water-fowls, then this assembly would be complete. (72)
In an assembly of the wicked, only the wicked themselves are fit, not even a single virtuous person; with this in mind, he says by way of an indirect illustration (anyāpadeśa):

"viśarāru... etc. If in a shallow pool (palvala) thick with moving, fragile, and predatory birds—abounding in herons (baka), cormorants (madgu), and water-crows (jalakāka)—there are fickle owls (kauśika) and crows (kāka); [then...]

In that case, this assembly, which is like a mere puddle, would have to be endowed with those worthy of a formal court. In the expression "kauśikakākāḥ" (owls and crows), although there is a contradiction, it is not intended to be expressed; therefore, the rule for the singular form of a *dvandva* compound—namely, "the *dvandva* of those who are in a state of eternal enmity"—was not applied.
However, the singular form of a *dvandva* involving birds is optional. || 72 ||
A cuckoo, possessing a form indistinguishable from a flock of crows,
becomes manifest through its song, just as a scholar reveals himself in an assembly. (73)
He whose wings—his coverings that conceal the body—are equal in color, and whose shape and configuration are such; [he was recognized] by the spoken words, that is, by distinct speech. || 73 ||
The flowering creeper is able to endure the pecking at its tender flowers, sprouts, and leaves by the cuckoo,
but not by the heron, vulture, cormorant, crane, cock, crow, and the like.

With the intention that even the offense of the virtuous can be endured, but the very association with the wicked is unbearable, he says "mṛdu" (soft), etc.; the words "even the touch of crows and the like" are to be supplied as the ellipsis. || 74 ||
O sweet-voiced cuckoo, who here hears your melodious song— a festival for the ears and a messenger for the union of lovers?
My hearing has grown deaf from the harsh, gurgling cries of crows and the quarrels of owls in these thickets.

In an assembly of the wicked, someone said to a person eager to present true knowledge: "O *kalakaṇṭha* [sweet-voiced] cuckoo, who here, during the reconciliation of a couple in a lovers' quarrel caused by pride and the like,
would not listen to your cry— which is sweet (*kala*), and therefore a festival for the ears, acting as a messenger for their union?"
He hears. For here, among these groves of *picumanda* trees, there are crows who are always at strife with owls;
by the shrieking and gurgling cries of such crows, the hearing—the faculty of the sense of hearing—of everyone has reached its end, meaning it has departed outwardly. || 75 ||
While the young cuckoo, with its soft voice, tells auspicious stories with such sincerity that it wins over all those who are full of passion, the crow,
swooping down into the grove with incessant and terrifying "drāṅkāra" cries, [shouts], "This is my son!"
All [beings] have been rendered sapless by the sky. || 76 ||

In the grove, before those who were full of passion and possessed of a longing for his song, the young cuckoo— having delivered a discourse like a great festival of auspiciousness with its tender voice— was just then captivating and delighting the minds of all the listeners with its sincerity, when a crow swooped down upon it. This...
With terrifying cries such as "The young cuckoo! My son! My child! He was nourished by me! He was brought to life by me!", all the listeners were rendered tasteless and devoid of enthusiasm. || 76 ||
O cuckoo, why do you warble so rapidly with such exuberant joy? Withdraw your voice back into the hollow of your throat; let there be no more of this delusion for long.
This is not the manifestation of spring, but rather the dense, continuous display of winter with its blossoming flowers.
These trees have been withered by masses of frost.

To someone who, out of a delusion regarding their own fitness and the like, is eager to display their virtues to unworthy listeners at an improper time, another says: "What? What? O cuckoo, why do you warble so rapidly out of joy, prompted by an eagerness to proclaim your own merits, without even considering the fitness of your listeners? This is because there is no obstruction [to your hearing].

[The word] *dvirvacanam* [is used]. Let it enter back within after having been emitted and made to resound with joy from the hollow of the throat; let there be no delusion that this is merely the time for the introduction of qualities or that these are fit only for hearing. This is not merely the blossoming of the spring (*madhu*) with unrestrained flowers, but rather—
These trees have been withered by the winter with its masses of frost; thus, there is no fruitfulness for your words regarding them—this is the meaning. (77)
O cuckoo, warbling so sweetly with your melodious notes, you of auspicious form, by whom have you been taught this ill-fated speech that brings such sorrow?
In the month of Caitra, amidst the wonderful new sprouts, a woman separated from her lover says to you: "Whose honey is this, O spring?"—it is because of this that it belongs to you.
"Yours," he said, and quickly [climbed] very high up the tree. || 78 ||
In such a month of Caitra, when fresh sprouts are variegated, she who is separated from her lover speaks. What does she say?

"O warbling cuckoo, this spring month of Caitra is always auspicious for love-making; for whom is it not so? Thus, from my question, you must quickly and loudly proclaim [the name] of your own *madhu* tree, saying "yours, yours."

Who has taught you this soft yet painful, ill-spoken, and false speech with its sweet warbling? (The word *vata* expresses grief. Indeed, it is not spring that causes me pain through separation; rather, it is you alone who sing so melodiously with your beloved. Thus, while I should have said "my, my," your false claim of "your, your" is intended solely to torment me.
The meaning is "of yours. || 78 ||
Even though they share the same silence, movement, dwelling, color, and form, this cuckoo— resplendent with beauty— is recognized from afar amidst a flock of crows;
for everyone indeed attains greatness when situated among fools, like a scholar in the midst of the ignorant, distinguished by his own noble appearance and refined conduct.
Because of the wonder within a similar mind. || 79 ||

Even though there is a similarity in silence, movement such as the flapping of wings, behavior, color, and physical form between this lovely cuckoo and a flock of crows— that is, a multitude of crows— it is recognized and distinguished from afar as "not a crow," like a wise man among fools. For indeed, every person reveals his auspicious actions through his own outward appearance.
Through the internal wonder arising from a statement that is appropriate to its subject, even what is hidden attains expansion and renown. (79)
Brother cuckoo, enough, enough with your warbling! Your priceless quality does not come forth; remain silent in some hollow cave concealed by a mass of withered leaves.
This is now the season of winter, crowded with rows of harsh-cawing crows in the caverns of the wild trees.
This spring festival was celebrated with his friend. || 80 ||
O friend, O brother cuckoo, this is the season of winter, crowded with flocks of harshly cawing crows; it is not the festival of spring.

At present, your precious quality of warbling does not come to fruition; therefore, enough, enough with your warbling! Remain silent in some cave within the hollow of a wild tree, covered by a mass of withered leaves.
"This young cuckoo has abandoned his mother and gone to a crow; surely she is pecking at him"— while I was thus reflecting for a moment,
he too quickly embraced his mother-like [crow] with delight, and toward whichever direction he goes, he grows.
That very [nature] is his innate beauty; it is that which bestows his greatness.

Therein he shows wonders, beginning with "The marvel": first, it is a marvel that this young cuckoo has departed, having abandoned its mother, the female crow; second, it is another marvel that this very mother-crow now pecks at this young cuckoo with her beak and claws—while I was reflecting thus for a moment, that young cuckoo also...
Furthermore, it is a marvel that he became intent on increasing [his stature] like his mother through his essence (*rasa*) and his energy (*utsāha*). For indeed, the meaning is this:
whatever direction a person who is naturally handsome and fortunate may go, that very direction becomes endowed with greatness because of him. || 81 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and sixteenth canto, titled "The Description of Verses Addressed to Dogs, Crows, and Kokilas," in the *Ārṣa* [work], the *Śrī Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa*, in the *Bālakāṇḍa*, in the *Māyāmoha* section, in the *Uttarakāṇḍa*, by the learned sage Vālmīki. 116.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixteenth canto, titled "The Description of Verses on the Dog, the Crow, and the Kokila Bird," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and seventeenth canto.
The companions said:
"Behold the sky reflected as if upon a mountain peak before us—that which has Māra at its vanguard."
It was surrounded by birds of various beautiful calls, sporting upon the swaying stalks of clusters of white, red, and blue lotuses. || 1 ||
In this work, a lake adorned with lotuses, kumudas, and utpalas is described;
in connection with that, the lotuses, bees, swans, and other creatures are also described.

Therein, at the outset, he begins to describe the lake primarily through thirteen verses, starting with "Behold" (paśya). O King, here before you, upon the mountain peak, the lake is pervaded by birds that sport and warble melodiously among the stalks of clusters of white, red, and blue lotuses for the sake of their lotus-fibers; thus it appears as if possessed of wings in the form of stars, being reflected [therein].
Behold the lake standing like a mirror! That mountain ridge, by its extraordinary beauty, is as if the vanguard—the foremost servant—of Māra, because it kindles his passion. || 1 ||

With its blossomed thousand-petaled lotus as its sheath and a majestic royal swan stationed upon it, and frequented by bees as its seat and birds as its people, it was like the palace of the Lotus-Seated One [Brahmā] upon the earth. || 2 ||
He further distinguishes that very lake with twelve verses beginning with "vikāsita":

where royal swans (*rājahaṃsa*), exalted and bearing the burden of its beauty, reside upon the calyx-bases of the thousand-petaled lotuses (*sahasrapatra*)—a variety of lotus—whose stalks are erect and blossomed; and which is likewise filled with bees (*dvirepha*), acting as the pedestals for [the lotuses] which are like sapphire thrones (*indranīla-pīṭha*).
It was frequented and inhabited by cranes, curlews, and other birds, as well as by Brahmins and common folk, standing upon the earth like the very abode of Brahmā. || 2 ||
With the quarters of the sky made formidable by scattered spray, pale with the pollen from the interior of clusters of blooming blue and white lotuses,
and filled with the songs of bees and birds intoxicated by the fragrance, it moved along like a canopy borne through the heavens.

By which [wind] the quarters of the sky were made formidable by dense sprays of frost; it was whitened by the pollen residing within the mass of blooming blue and white lotuses; it was sung to by the songs of bees and birds intoxicated with fragrance; and it rose upward like a canopy reaching into the sky under the guise of the reflections of clouds, mist, and other such things.
"Carrying the one who carries. The masculine gender is a Vedic archaism. || 3 ||
In one place, it was broken by waves of shimmering red lotuses; in another, it resounded with the many humming bees that were its enemies;
in some parts, it slept in deep, pure water; and in others, it was hidden by the brilliant blossoms of the lotuses.

In some places, the waves break like stars as they cross over; in others, bees, hostile to one another due to the excess of their intoxication, are making a great humming sound. Deep with its pure water, it is as if asleep because of its stillness;
covered by lotuses with radiant blossoms and lilies, it is as if hidden or obscured. || 4 ||
On its shores, it was thick with masses of heat like pearls released from atoms; on its banks, it was dense with beautiful creeping vines;
its fierce marshy edges were shaken by waves; and its boundless marshes were like the very sky upon the surface of the earth.
It is called *tāpaṭāla* because it dispels or removes heat (*tāpa*) by means of water droplets that have become like fine particles and are almost like pearls.
On its banks, due to the fear of another lion reflected in the water, the lions are hesitant to drink;
in some places, this is indicated by beautiful creepers hanging from the tops of trees down to the water's edge.

It is so called because it thoroughly shatters [the mind] by the cessation of the perception of reflected images. Likewise, its marshy banks (*kaccha*), which consist mostly of water, have their rocks washed away by waves and are thick with mud. Furthermore, with its infinite marshy banks formed by endless clouds, it stands upon the surface of the earth like the sky descended to the ground. || 5 ||

With the luster of the pollen rising from the lotuses shaken by the clouds— pollen whose interior was illuminated by flashes of lightning— the sky’s expanse, its one portion consisting of darkness, appeared like the dim twilight sky.

By such a wind—one from which the clouds have been driven away—the multitude of lotuses (*abjajāta*) has been shaken; with the luster of the pollen rising from that, its interior appears as if illuminated by lightning. For this very reason, one part of it consists of a profusion of water droplets, while another part consists of dense darkness.

For him, such an expanse of the sky at the time of twilight shines forth on all sides like the very station of space; thus it is "āprakāśa," meaning either shining intensely or slightly shining. || 6 ||

With his limbs covered by swans whose shoulders were weary from devouring glistening lotus stalks— swans that resembled fragments of autumn clouds scattered by the wind, filling the sky with only the air remaining, or like the lunar discs gathered together by Time— [he appeared] like the sky itself.

Their bodies were covered by swans whose shoulders were heavy from the weight of broad lotus-stalks— characteristic mouthfuls being carried toward their nests for the nourishment of their young— and who, having gathered together in one place over time like so many moon-disks, were scattered by the wind.

The meaning is: even the sky alone, which consists of many fragments—namely, pieces of autumnal clouds—is moving along with the wind; how much more so, then, the wind endowed with all excellent qualities? || 7 ||
With the skill of tearing open the pods of mud by means of a wind fierce with fragrance and abundant nectar,
the rising streak of clouds seems to weave a great cloth, as a rain of flowers falls from the creepers inhabited by agitated birds.
As if from the abundance of fragrance of this lake, by means of gentle yet formidable winds moistened through contact with nectar, the mud-encrustation—
consisting of portions of mud mixed with water— is shaken; its "tearing" (*pāṭana*) consists of the separation of the mud from the water by drawing it downward.

In that region, the row of waves— characterized by a great "paṭapaṭa" sound arising with speed due to its proficiency— seems, as it were, to weave or extend a rain of flowers dropped by the creepers on the banks inhabited by birds agitated by their own cries, for the sake of increasing the cloth of the lake; such is the meaning.
Alternatively, by resorting to the *bahuvrīhi* compound beginning with "kṣubhyat" (turbulent), it is either a separate, independent qualifier of the lake. || 8 ||
Fanned by the great lotus-leaf fans of swaying lotus shoots, with the beautiful foam of whirling chowries,
resounding with the songs of bees and cuckoos, and possessing a multitude of lovely women who were like graceful lotus-stalks of virtuous conduct, it appeared as a sovereign king.
He describes that very lake by way of a comparison with a king: "velladbhiḥ" and so forth. It was fanned by moving palm-leaf fans (*tālavṛnta*) in the form of large lotus petals;
it possessed beautiful foam like waving chowries (*cāmara*); it was celebrated by the songs of bees and cuckoos; and it was of virtuous conduct (*sadvṛtta*).
The multitude of women belonging to him was lovely, rounded, possessed of virtuous conduct, marked by the signs of lotus-stalks, and graceful; for this very reason, it appeared like a king. || 9 ||

Its waters were enchanting with the captivating songs of bees at the tips of the reeds and turned tawny by the scattering of pollen from the lotuses; its banks were adorned with groves that served as ear-ornaments, beautified by clusters of white lotuses as pale as masses of foam.
In which [lake] there was a captivating and enchanting song from the foremost vessels characterized by bees— the finest and most beautiful cups—
and which was likewise strewn and pervaded by the friction and crushing of the pollen of lotuses; for this very reason, its water was yellowish-brown, appearing like masses of foam.
It was beautifully adorned nearby by clusters of exceedingly white lotuses;
it was the crest-ornament of the forest on its bank, possessing a mass of flowers upon its head. || 10 ||
With its lotus-heart secluded and supremely gladdening the heart, this lake shines with a flavorful sweetness, comparable to the company of the virtuous. 11.
This lake of such a nature shines like the company of the virtuous; the qualifying attributes are to be applied to both. (11)
O gentle one, this [palace] shines spotless through its mirrored sky, like the mind of the great, purified by the mastery of the meaning of the scriptures. (12)

"Like the Maru desert," meaning by a waterless sky, that is, by the autumnal sky; "O gentle one," [it is attained] through the transformation into the form of that—the Brahman which is the meaning of the scripture—by means of the final cognitive state (vṛtti) of direct realization. 12.
Seeing this lake, with its clear water and cranes, and where the wind was harsh with droplets and no visible target could be found, it appeared like a cloud of snow.

Then, regarding what the essence is like in winter, he says: "something. Because it is covered on all sides by mist, it is barely visible; due to the mist, its own color has been brought into conformity [with the surroundings], so its dark hue has vanished. || 13 ||
Just as this visible world of Brahmā is nothing other than his own unchanging nature—O King, like waves and such appearing as if separate from the water—so it is. (14)

There is no modification (*vikāra*) or transformation (*pariṇāma*); by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the notions of origination (*ārambha*), aggregation (*saṃghāta*), and manifestation (*vivarta*) are included. There is nothing else that is immutable; rather, it is Brahman alone. Just as waves and so forth in the water of a lake are nothing but water, such is the meaning.
