[This refers to] those things being carried along by the Self itself, which produce whirlpools and eddies.
Alas, for those of dull intellect, there is a treacherous succession of waves! 15.
Of those being carried away by the very waters of their own selves; "hā" expresses wonder. This [term] "chāyayā" (by means of a shadow/reflection) should also be applied to Brahmā. || 15 ||
Just as a difference is observed between a well, a pond, a lake, and the ocean, so too should the difference between women, men, and water be understood. || 16 ||

Just as there appears to be a gradation in water due to the difference in limiting adjuncts such as wells and ponds, so too is there a perception of gradation in the Self due to the excellence of bodies such as those of women and men; thus he says, "In a well," etc.
"Antaram" refers to the gradation of excellence and deficiency. || 16 ||

Who indeed is capable of counting the lotuses of this mind—which, like that of a living being, has long been bound by the ties of worldly existence—as it whirls incessantly in the rotation of the eddies through the tossing of its dilapidated waves? (17)

"Jale-jāti" refers to those such as lotuses and water-lilies whose birth (*jāti*) or origin is in the water. Due to the non-distinction between *la* and *ja*, "jaḍāt-jātayaḥ" also refers to various species born from the dull or inert (*jaḍa*).

Through their connection—that is, their association—with the binding of these [beings], for this lake—as for the mind of a living being that has grown old—the waves (*laharī*) which culminate in a state of decay, as well as the enthusiasm for enjoyment (*bhoga-utsāha*), belong to the lotuses and so forth, and to their respective bodies.

Who indeed is capable of counting the countless lotuses that are like whirlpools—continuous revolutions of the fluctuations of desire, aversion, and so forth, intensified by delusion? The meaning is: no one at all.
Oh, how strange is the manifestation of association with the dull-witted! For even this lotus considers its own virtues to be as if they were non-virtues.
She hides it within herself by tucking it against her throat, yet she displays to everyone the entire mass of her wretched thorns.
He begins the description of the lotuses with the words "It is a marvel," and so forth. From this point onward, the verses are for the most part *anyāpadeśas* (indirect descriptions).

Oh, how wonderful is the manifestation of the union with the dull—meaning both the contact with water and the association with fools! Why is that? Because this [lotus] is renowned as a supreme treasury of excellent qualities.

The lotus, too, while remaining in bud, places its own qualities—such as fragrance, beauty, and nectar—within its throat, concealing them deeply as if they were defects; meanwhile, it displays to all people its wretched mass of thorns on the outside. || 18 ||
Enough with qualities that are full of holes, unstable, subtle, concealed, and joined with dullness— even if they are numerous, they are as worthless as the fibers of a lotus.

However, as a corollary, he says "with holes" regarding those threads of the lotus which are denoted by the word 'qualities' (guṇa)—meaning qualities similar to them that are always accompanied by defects—and that such [defective] qualities should be disregarded everywhere. The meaning is: because they are corrupted by defects such as having holes, they lack any worthiness to be accepted and are therefore to be disregarded. || 19 ||
Even Vāsuki does not have the power to enumerate the majesty of those great lotuses of noble families who are endowed with the beauty of virtuous qualities.
By the fragrance of the fame of those who proclaim their lineage—the lotuses of noble families—even Vāsuki, the serpent Śeṣa, [is surpassed]. 20.
Since even Lakṣmī, who rests upon the chest of Hari, holds a lotus in her hand merely for the sake of beauty, what other hope could be greater than this? (21)

What further praise or aspiration could there be for that lotus—beyond its being the source of beauty even for Lakṣmī, the presiding deity of all loveliness? Or, if the reading is "tatsāmyaṃ kasya vā bhavet" (with whom could it have equality?), then the meaning is clear. || 21 ||

There may indeed be dissimilarity between a cluster of white lotuses and a cluster of blue lotuses due to their white and black forms; however, these two are equal insofar as both are insentient. (22)

In these two clusters of lotuses and water-lilies, the dullness of the water and the dullness of consciousness—characterized by the folly of aversion toward the moon and the sun—are equal; however, it should be understood that there is only a dissimilarity or distinction between them due to their white and dark colors respectively. || 22 ||

The newly arisen splendor of the blossoming lotus grove does not attain equality with the lakes through the flowering forest, nor with the sky through its stars, nor even with the clusters of moons— [the reading "indubimbeḥ" is preferred by the commentator]— but rather with the beauty of the faces of dancing women smiling in mirth. (23)

The newly arisen splendor and beauty of this lake with its grove of fully blossomed lotuses does not equal the likeness of a forest of blooming *mandāra* trees and the like; it does not even equal the likeness of the sky filled with stars. Nor does it equal the likeness of the lunar discs gathered together in one place. Rather, it is [only] comparable to the laughter of dancing young women.
"By the beauty of her face, she attains equality"—this [statement] rejects a previously unestablished standard of comparison for the sake of the injunction. (23)
Those bees whose entire lives have passed with undivided minds on the taste of flower-creepers—they alone are the most fortunate of beings. (24)

In this context, he describes the bees by means of the verse beginning with "yeṣām": those bees whose long life has been spent tasting the flowering creepers—they alone are the most fortunate; or, "O fortunate one," may be read as a separate word. || 24 ||
Only those bees that wander among the lovely wonders of the mango tree possess true aesthetic wonder; others merely fill their bellies with the common species.
The bees and cuckoos partake of—the sweet nectar-juice of the mango tree, fragrant and full of lovely charm, as well as the astringent taste of its fresh sprouts. (25)
Those [lotuses] which resound upon their stalks with the intoxication of honey-fragrance mock the bees who, though satisfied by other flavors, wander about. (26)

He says "mattāḥ" (intoxicated), as if the bees tasting the lotus-buds were mocking other bees attached to the interior of the forest. The word "janma" (birth) is to be supplied, or there is an intention to express the object of the action [of laughing]. || 26 ||

Alas, how will that very same bee now feel toward the tasteless flowers of the trees in this cold season— he who dwelt, sported, frolicked, and slept within the bellies of the lotuses, which were as soft as the hollows of the moon?
That very bee...
How will the bee, in the cold season, maintain its affection or delight in tree blossoms that have lost their flavor? || 27 ||
The bee upon the magnificent, unopened bud of the jasmine flower appears like Andhaka impaled on a trident by Kālarudra. (28)

Since the state of not being in full bloom is already established by the word *mukula* alone, the word *aphulla* is used for the purpose of establishing a similarity with a trident (*śūla*) by excluding those [buds] that are about to blossom. || 28 ||

O bee, though you constantly wander through all the mountain vine-cottages tasting the honey of various flowers, you are still not satisfied; why is this, my friend? I think you are full of evil intent, for you do not perceive the true essence within the forests.

O friend, O bee, while tasting the honey of various flowers and wandering constantly through all the mountain bower-vines, why are you still not satisfied? Because of your greed for sweetness, you are full of wicked desire;
even now you do not obtain the essence from the forests. "Kaṣṭam" expresses sorrow; "manye" indicates deliberation. Indeed, [this would be so] were the essence not obtained.
The sense is that it is even possible to conceive of either dissatisfaction or wandering [as occurring]. || 29 ||
O bee, skilled in devouring the multitude of lotuses, do not go to this lake;
rather, make your body torn by the saw-like thorns in the pits of the jujube trees.

O bee, skilled in the art of tasting, go to a lake, a lotus-pond where there is a cluster of lotuses— a place for devouring, that is, for the enjoyment of nectar. Do not subject your own body, which has grown robust and nourished by nectar, to being torn apart by the saw-like thorns within the hollows of jujube fruits.
When the flax flower, the circle of blue lotus petals, and the *tāpiccha* tree are in full bloom, a wise man, like honey among them, possesses a distinct excellence. || 31 ||
O honey-bee, even during those portions of time such as the late autumn and early winter when you find no lotuses,

spend the remainder of your life with honey as appropriate upon the flax flower which resembles your color, upon the blossomed circles of blue-lily petals, and upon the *tāpiccha* and *tamāla* trees. Just like a wise man.

The meaning is that, just as one who fails to obtain an assembly of masters suited to oneself does not dwell even among the learned for the sake of attaining true scholarship if he lives under a dissimilar master, so it is in this case. || 31 ||
Behold this pure row of swans, like a creeper nourished by the beauty of the filaments of the navel-lotus, resounding with the chanting of the Sāmaveda.

In this context, describing the row of swans, he shows it by saying, "Behold! O King, behold that stainless creeper characterized by a row of swans, which is nurtured by the beauty—the splendor—of the filaments of the lotuses in the lake's center, possessing a color and form identical to them; and which possesses a deep warbling like the chanting of the Sāmaveda. This is the meaning.

In the word *gāyanam*, the absence of the *ātva* change (the substitution of *ai* for *e*) is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*). Alternatively, it may be explained as referring to a row of Brahma-swans seen by chance: one whose warbling is truly a song of praise (*sāmagāna*) protected by the beauty (*śrī*) of the filaments of the Lord’s navel-lotus. Thus, it should be interpreted as being devoted to the swan-like hosts of Brahman. || 32 ||
Seeing his mate reflected in the sky while she sits within the lotus-nest of the swing,
the swan follows her through the circle and is not conscious of this world.

Here, in this lake, the male swan, following his mate through the sky, beholds her reflected in a lotus nest that resembles a swing; seeing her there, he loses consciousness out of fear that she might fall or drown. The meaning is that he fell into a swoon.
O King, let no one ever fall into such extreme misfortune;
behold this swan, who followed his mate as she was reflected in the water and perished.
He censures such addiction to women, saying "let it not be so. The particle *eva* is used here in the sense of "even" (*api*). || 34 ||
The sweet warbling produced by the royal swan with effortless ease is something that the crane cannot learn to produce even in a hundred years. (35)
Although their origin, form, birth, behavior, food, and so forth are identical,
there is a vast and absolute difference between a common swan and the royal swan.

*Ākara* means place of birth; *ākāra* means physical form; *aśana* means food. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), names, colors, and so forth are included. There is an absolute difference, a disparity, and a vast distance between the other swan and the royal swan (*rājahaṃsa*). For the former plays in the Mānasa lake amidst forests of golden lotuses, while the latter, having plunged into the ocean, emerges as pearls.
They eat from that which is accessible to all winged creatures and they move in the upper reaches of the sky; no others do so—this is the sense.
As for the royal swans (*rājahaṃsa*), they are white with red beaks and feet. (36)
Established in the sky during the bright fortnight, illuminating the beds of night-lotuses,
he gladdens the hearts of all like a swan-like moon that has risen.
The moon is like the white fortnight; the swan is like both white fortnights, stationed in the sky.
The moon is the illuminator and bloomer of the source of night-lotuses, while the swan is the cause of beauty; such is the similarity between the two. || 37 ||
What other bird can attain the splendor of the swans sporting in a forest thick with lotus stalks, lotus stems, and plantain trunks? (38)

The literal meaning is as follows: "In a lotus-forest consisting mostly of plantain groves, crowded with plantain trunks characterized by stalks that are actually [the upturned] stalks of those lotuses (*unnālā yā nalinī*), let the swans sporting therein enjoy their beauty and splendor. But according to the intended sense (*tātparya*), it refers to the heart-lotus (*hṛdayapadma*) which, through yoga, has its stalk turned upward (*ūrdhvīkṛtanālā*).

Through the expansion resulting from the practice of *prāṇāyāma*, that which is like a plantain tree is withered; this "stambha" (stump) refers to the aforementioned forest characterized by the three heart-lotuses. In that forest, let the *haṃsas*—the ascetics who always sport there by tasting unsurpassed bliss free from the three-fold afflictions—attain the sovereign fortune (*lakṣmī*) characterized by the imperial sovereignty of the bliss of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*).
"Khaga" means "who goes" (ka eti), even though he is a god; such is the meaning. || 38 ||
She is encircled by waves, captivating with her mass of shimmering spray, and beautiful with an abundance of kumuda, utpala, and kahlāra flowers. (39)

Now, describing that lake through a comparison with a woman, he utters this poetic fancy (utprekṣā) beginning with "taraṅga": "That which has waves for its bracelets; charming with shimmering clusters of spray, it is as if adorned with necklaces. (39)
Her creeper-like locks of hair trembled like bees; her tinkling girdle and anklets resounded;
her navel was deep and whirling; and her eyes were like moving waves.
She whose creeper-like tresses are as fickle as bees. || 40 ||
Like a woman awaiting her beloved who bestows the essence of pleasure,
the lake shines with its two beautiful swans.

Its essence is desire and its water is fulfillment; awaiting the mountain that holds the rain which brings it about, she gazes directly toward him. [She is adorned] with two swans, two anklets, and two young swans. 41.
O swan, do not dwell alone and incessantly in this lake whose essence consists of water-fowls, cormorants, cranes, and ravens;
even in times of adversity, association with those of one's own kind—possessing similar character, age, and speech—yields the fruit of well-being.
In this context, someone addresses another under a different pretext, saying: "O Haṃsa!

O Haṃsa, do not make your dwelling alone in that lake which is filled with the essence—that is, dominated by—those cruel predators such as the *madgura*, the water-crow, the crane, and the common crow; for even here, in times of calamity...

The meaning is that association only with one's own kind—those who are like oneself in conduct, age, and speech, being like swans—is conducive to the fruit of excellence and results in future happiness, whereas association with others is not. || 42 ||
This very bee— who once stood upon the temples of great elephants trampled by his feet, whose sole abode was a lotus pond,
and who possessed the fortune of enjoying the fragrance of white, blue, and yellow water-lilies, jasmine, and campaka creepers— now,
by the power of fate, in the cold season, tastes only clods of earth and grass in the freezing chill.
Alas! Seeing this withered crane, my mind is cast into dejection by this calamity. (43)

Another [author], by way of a digression, says: "With his feet," etc. Though this bee possesses such power—having trampled the frontal lobes of great elephants with his feet, having the lotus-pond as his sole abode, and being full of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) in enjoying the vine-wives such as the white water-lily (*kahlāra*)—yet, by the power of fate (*vidhi*), he [seeks] clods of earth and grass during the cold season.
Though tasting [objects of pleasure], he does not truly taste them; he acts like a withered crane—he "cranes" (bakati). The suffix *kvip* is applied according to the rule:

"The suffix *kvip* should be prescribed after all nominal stems to denote habitual action. The exclamation "Aho! expresses sorrowful wonder. Even by great calamities, the mind is cast into dejection (*dainye*). 43.
O friend, as I wandered through the dense thicket of lotus stalks shaken by the shoulders of a swan, I long remembered the shimmering, sparkling luster within the heart of my son's leaf-cup;
at midday, that cool, blooming flower scatters its own spray of water drops like the white pollen-essence of a lotus.
Let it be seen clearly, bursting forth suddenly upon the head. || 44 ||

O King, when I had entered the thicket of stalks, the forest of lotus fibers, driven from the shoulders and wings of the swan, I heard the words of a young swan— seated within the radiant interior of a lotus petal— who was swimming out and crying out in a loud, piercing voice toward his father.
[The memory] is recalled through the conjunction of a perception that awakens a similar impression. What was that speech? He says:
"O Father, the lotus (abjinī) scatters its own mass of water-drops like a shower of white pearls;
even at midday, it suddenly blossoms with cool, clear frost upon its head (mūrdhni)."
"Let it be seen directly. || 44 ||

As the swan glides silently for a long time through the sky— which is like the gentle waters of the moon— the drops of water that fall upon him from his lotus-bud-like beak, as it moves without trembling due to the pressure of his shoulders, are like the waters of the Gaṅgā falling here from the hollow of Brahmā’s lotus-hand.
The aquatic creatures, being delighted, drink them quickly. || 45 ||

O King, here in this lake, in the sky— that is, in the atmosphere— as in the presence of the moon, within the clear and serene water, from the Brahma-lotus cup, by means of the vibrations caused by the striking of the lotus stalks against the shoulders (wings) of a swan moving silently along, [the sound arises].
Those drops of water that fall upon him from the lotus-bud of the seat of Hiraṇyagarbha, aquatic creatures such as fish drink them up quickly with joy, just like the waters of the Gaṅgā. || 45 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and seventeenth canto, titled "The Description of the Lotus, the Bee, and the Swan," in the *Avidyā-praviveka* section of the *Vālmīki-nirvāṇa-upadeśa* within the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventeenth canto, titled "The Description of the Lotus, the Bee, and the Swan," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and eighteenth canto.
The male and female companions spoke in turn:
"Let this one virtue of this meritless crane be observed."
By saying "prāvṛt" and "prāvṛṭ," he causes one to remember the rainy season (*prāvṛṣ*).
In this work, the conduct of cranes, peacocks, travelers, separated lovers, fish, and cātaka birds is described.
"Prāvṛṭ, prāvṛṭ"—this is an imitation of the indistinct sound of a crane, expressed here using distinct phonemes. (1)
Like a crane, you appear like a swan dwelling in a lake while maintaining friendship with water-fowl;
yet, having abandoned both cruelty and [harsh] speech, become clearly a swan indeed.
Here too, as before, there are statements of indirect instruction (*anyāpadeśa*). O crane (*baka*), you appear like a swan (*haṃsa*) by your color;
the meaning is: "Having abandoned the three defects such as friendship with water-fowl (*madgu*), become a swan. || 2 ||
Those clever and skillful ones, who repeatedly entered the deep interior of the water filled with swimming creatures and,
with their beaks piercing [their prey], devoured even the most dexterous fish;
they have today, by some stroke of fortune, been brought to the state of dead whales by the power of Time when it has arrived, and they do not attack.
These lame and intoxicated ones, though standing in order, do not perceive even that which is easily grasped before them.

Having repeatedly entered— that is, having entered again and again— the interior of such water wherein there are clever and skillful cormorants (*madgu*) who are experts in the art of catching fish, they,
with their beaks pierced by the fish at the time of swallowing, devoured the fish.

By some power of destiny or fate, these cranes, having fortunately consumed [the fish], were brought to a state where their throats were pained by dead *timi*— a species of fish— and thus, at the time of an attack driven by extreme hunger,
they stood in succession in a row on the shore; yet even so, they could not overcome the prey that had come to the edge of the bank, however easy it was to seize.
Being lame, they do not step upon the fish; the meaning is that this is wonderful. || 3 ||
Demonstrating that "the world is thus ruined by its own self-interest," the wicked man praises me, saying, "My teacher has attained the status of being my teacher. (4)
He expresses, in an indirect manner, that wicked people learn from the water-crow (*madgu*) how to achieve their own ends by harming the world:
"In this way," and so forth. Just like the water-crow, the world is harmed—that is, it is fit to be harmed—for the sake of one's own desired ends.
Demonstrating this point, he says: "The water-crow (*madgu*) is my teacher (*guru*); having attained the state of being such a teacher, [I have become] a 'Madguru'. Thus.
A wicked person praises and extols a fool.
"This is a swan in the sky, with its neck outstretched and its broad, pure, beautiful wings spread"—thus was it perceived by people.
But when it seized a small fish from the water of a pond, it was then indeed recognized by the world as "this is a crane.
Here, in the sky, it has its neck upraised and its broad, stainless, lovely wings extended.

When this crane—which was previously recognized and certain by people to be none other than that very swan dwelling elsewhere—seizes a small fish from the water of a pond here on this earth, then it is known by the world as "this is a crane. || 5 ||
Beholding the swans wandering for a very long time,
the women on the bank were amazed at these rogues who, under the guise of asceticism, remained right there in the dense darkness.

Having observed for a very long time in a pond or similar place fish that were restless for the sake of food, and having likewise observed in this very lake herons who were restless through the hypocrisy of asceticism, a certain woman on the bank— having recognized the conduct of rogues— beheld elsewhere as well those who were restless through their craving for sensual objects due to the hypocrisy of asceticism, for a very long time until the end of darkness, reaching even to the rising of the sun.
The meaning is that she was struck with wonder upon seeing the rogues waiting there. || 6 ||
"Look! These playful women in the water are carrying away the white lotuses.
Do you wish to follow them? I am not your beloved; I am going," she said. (7)

A traveler’s wife speaks to her husband as he gazes upon the women who steal the lotuses: "O beloved, these village women disregard the frost—that is, the cold—in this water; indeed, they are like that (heya-antī). [The word *hī* is a separate particle, or it may mean *mehalā*, 'girdles,' implying they are truly women. They carry away the white lotuses, yet you desire to follow them; therefore, I am your beloved."
"I am going for the reason that they are not dear to me. || 7 ||
O leader of men, behold on the path in the forest at the edge of the pleasure-grove of flowering creepers this traveler, who is intent on his efforts to appease his beloved wife who has become angry.

To her who speaks thus in anger, this traveler on the road, intent on effort, seeks to appease his beloved in a bower of flowering creepers within a grove at the edge of the play-lake, saying: "O leader of men, look!"—such is the connection between the two [verses]. 8.
"O King, look at this excellent woman as she performs these gestures of coquetry, expressions of emotion, playful movements, glances with suppressed anger, and smiles. (9)
He shows this courtesan to the king as she speaks with boldness about this very traveler’s conduct as a couple—thus [it is said]. || 9 ||
Even among cranes, frogs, and crows, who always dwell in the same place,
there is a mutual confusion of their cognitions, unlike that between fools and the learned.
Of the hunters, the predators, such as the Niṣādas and others; "confusion of intellect" means their mingling, that is to say, their friendship. || 10 ||
At the tip of the lapwing’s beak, a worm squirms;
it stands like a raised and lofty banner for ancient misfortune.

The "kīṭa" here refers to a moth (*pataṅga*). It cries out "kiṭikaṭī," thus it is said to *kiṭikiṭāyate*. From a word ending in the suffix *ḍāc* used in the sense of "like" (*iva*), the suffix *kyaṅ* is added in the sense of performing an action. At the tip of its beak (*cañcvagra*), it *kiṭāyate* (makes a *kiṭa*-sound) or *keṭati*; thus, a *kiṭa* is one that is trembling. It acts like such a [trembling] creature. It is like a raised banner on the high, upper part of the ancient, previously accumulated misfortune or sin. || 11 ||
While the restless crane cries out shrilly at the tree on the riverbank, and while the frog leaps up in the muddy puddle of the cow’s hoofprint,
the minnow—
plunging as if into the breast of her beloved— is skillfully saved from fear by the breaking of its own heart.
For in this world, there is indeed nothing other than death that bestows such happiness.
As long as that crane was crying out, shimmering upon a tree on the bank of a pond; as long as he was warbling in the water-muddy puddle of the pond, slightly moistened by water;

"as long as" (yāvat) here signifies totality, meaning with all one's might. By [the crane’s] death, the minnow—plunging into the breast of her lover as if out of passion, yet out of fear—saved her own body even at the cost of her life. In this world...
When a great calamity has arrived, there would be no other refuge that bestows happiness than death through the breaking of the heart;
and thus, even by dying, the protection of her own body accomplished by her was indeed appropriate—this is the meaning. || 12 ||

That state of composure which exists in the hearts of creatures such as the *baka*, the *ajagara*, and the *madgu*—those who have swallowed things without chewing—I consider it to be truly like sleep. (13)

The state of mind—the stability of consciousness—of creatures such as fish that have entered the hearts or bellies of crocodiles and the like, remaining there unchewed and swallowed, is like sleep; I consider it to be similar to deep slumber or even fainting. || 13 ||

The fear that arises for those dwelling in the water upon seeing nearby water-fowls, herons, vultures, cats, or snakes—compared to that, the destruction caused by a lightning strike is like a blade of grass; this was told to me long ago by a wise man who remembered his past lives. (14) [Regarding the phrase "of those dwelling in the water": it refers to fish and other aquatic creatures. The fear that arises for them when they see nearby water-fowls, herons, and so forth—compared to that [fear], [the destruction by lightning is as insignificant as a blade of grass].

The destruction caused by a thunderbolt strike before one's eyes is like a blade of grass compared to fear; this secret was previously told to me by a wise man who remembered his past lives and recalled the sufferings of births in the wombs of fish and other creatures from his own experience—it should not be considered untrue. This is the meaning. || 14 ||
Look here, at the foot of a flower-laden tree on the shore of this lake, upon the dust of the world before you, where innocent deer are forcibly covered by fresh blue lotuses and *ketaka* blossoms.

Behold—that is, show to the world—the beloved women as they gaze upon those charming deer, who are such that fresh blue lotuses and *ketaka* flowers have been perfectly scattered [as ornaments] upon them by the power of the beauty and strength of their eyes and ears, which are like bees. 15.
Because of his exalted mind, Barhi entreats Indra for water;
the Great-Souled One fills his entire earth with it.

The peacock (*barhin*), because of his lofty mind and noble disposition, begs Indra for water. Since the verb *yāc* (to beg) is transitive, Indra is also the "unexpressed object" (*akathita-karman*). Indra, being well-pleased by that quality of his lofty mind, fills the entire earth with water for his satisfaction; for he is a Great Soul (*mahātman*) who is exceedingly generous.
This is the meaning. || 16 ||
These peacocks follow the clouds like suckling infants; thus it is inferred that the dark one is indeed the son of the dark one. 17.
They are like calves who drink from the udder; thus, they are called "breast-drinkers" (stanapa). || 17 ||
Beholding the deer and thinking of the eyes of his beloved, the traveler became like a mechanical doll before the objects standing before him. (18)
"Equality with a puppet fashioned by a machine," that is to say, "state of being devoid of movement. || 18 ||
The peacock does not drink water, yet he forcibly devours the serpent from the earth;
I do not know whether this wickedness belongs to the serpent or to the peacock.
I do not know whether it is the wickedness of the serpent or the wickedness of the peacock. || 19 ||
Having abandoned the great lake that resembles the bed of a virtuous person, the peacock drinks water spat out by clouds; I believe this is out of fear of bowing down.
Behold the peacocks dancing like clouds formed from their shimmering plumage; shaking the moon-like luster of their tails, they resemble the young calves of the rainy season.
That bowing—the bending of the head—which was directed toward that lake, [occurred] out of fear of it. (20) (21)

In this excellent grove, the ocean itself seems to sport here among the peacocks— whose tails spread with the forest breeze like beautiful, flickering ripples of moonlight— by means of its scattered pearls.

The meaning is: "Look! In this forest, it is as if the ocean itself—by virtue of having spread forth, bestowed, and released [the clouds]—is the playful dancer who causes the peacocks to dance, and not a mere cloud. || 22 ||
Walk on grass, drink water on the forest floor, and take rest in the grove of plantain trees;
for excessive pride, O startled Cātaka bird, scorched by the fire of affliction, does not lead to happiness.

O startled cātaka bird, in this forest expanse during the summer, scorched by fire and filled with the threat of flames, your persistence in dwelling within the hollows of parched trees—though signaled by your great pride—is certainly not for your happiness.
Feed upon the cool, green grass near the plantain groves; drink the water from the irrigation channels and such; stay in the plantain forest.
"Take rest"—this is a pretext for something else. || 23 ||
O peacock, this is not a cloud, its belly filled with the waters of the ocean, ascending into the sky;
rather, this is a circle of smoke rising from the mountain, emerging from the hollows at the tops of forest trees consumed by a wildfire.
This peacock seen here before you, desiring to ascend into the sky—

let there be no delusion in you that this is a cloud, its belly filled with the waters of the ocean, the abode of sea-monsters; rather, it is a circle of smoke-rings rising from the fire within the hollows of forest trees consumed by a forest fire, emerging from the mountain and appearing thus out of place.
The meaning is that they were in a state of agitation at the commencement of the dance. || 24 ||
If the peacock, who satisfies himself with water even during the autumn season, were not to fill the lake even during the rains,
it would be fit for the minds of children; yet, seeing his own undertaking,
the virtuous person would be distressed by laughter, as if out of self-pity, thinking, "The peacock will be in a wretched state."
He was fully intent on passing the entire duration of time. || 25 ||
Someone describes the disposition of a peacock that drinks terrestrial water during a drought with the verse beginning "yena":

"That cloud by which the peacock was satiated with waters even in the autumn season would not fill a lake even during the rainy season"— such conduct is fit only for petty people like children, not for one so great.

Seeing that this [display] undertaken even at a time suitable for grandeur was lacking in magnificence, the company of virtuous people would become distressed and sorrowful due to the laughter provoked by the vulgar; reflecting thus, the peacock is intent—meaning, he is prepared—to spend his entire life solely upon his own thirst. || 25 ||
Having drunk the water as pure as crystal that has issued from the belly of a cloud, the peacock does not again drink water on the path, even when agitated by thirst;
remembering it intensely again and again, he quivers with joy, yet he does not perish, for the person of virtuous character is like that water.
Even the exertion of those who hold fast to their hope brings happiness. || 26 ||
In that case, is the peacock acting improperly? No; the author says: "as pure as crystal.

Even when agitated by thirst, the peacock first drinks water that has emerged from the interior of a cloud, which is as pure as crystal, and does not subsequently drink muddy water on the path. If so, why does he not die of thirst? To this he says: "he sparkles. He...

Even when remembering a dense cloud, one may quiver and rejoice, yet one does not perish—that is, one does not die. Therefore, for those whose hopes are bound to a virtuous person, even their toil brings only happiness and not suffering; this is the meaning. || 26 ||
Here, at the onset of the rainy season, these travelers generally pass the hardships of the road through stories,
just as those who are deluded pass their lives.

Just as travelers separated from their beloveds pass the time during the rains with some difficulty through conversation and the like, so too do fools devoid of self-knowledge pass their lives; thus he says: "Here," etc. These are the travelers.

"Look here, O Lord! Having taken loads of lotuses, water-lilies, night-blooming lilies, lotus-roots, and stalks, as well as white lilies, leaves, and water from this lake, these young girls have set out. (28)
Taking loads of milk placed in lotus leaves, young girls and maidens set out. When asked by them, "O Lord, look! Why are you carrying this? they replied to him:
"O traveler, we are but childhood friends to her who is tormented by the fever of calamity. (29)

When asked by those young girls, "What is this collection of burdens, and for what purpose do you carry it?", they gave this answer to the questioner: "O traveler, we are the companions of a young friend who is tormented by the fever of the affliction of separation;
thus, we carry loads of lotuses, water-lilies, and so forth for her treatment. This is the meaning. || 29 ||

Then, their hearts colored by passion, their forms graced with charm and playfulness, and their breasts full and swelling, the beloveds staying in their own homes once again brought the travelers back to the path of memory. (30)

Then, thereafter, with their hearts colored by passion for their own lovers, those women—while the travelers looked on—brought their beloveds staying at home to the path of memory. The sense is that the sight of something similar serves as an awakener of latent mental impressions (*saṃskāra*). || 30 ||
Surely my beloved, seeing the sky so dark with thick,
glossy clouds and as desolate and dense as a void, laments, falls to the ground, and falters.

In this regard, a certain traveler, remembering his beloved, says: "She... Having seen the sky darkened by the dense clouds—characterized by those very clouds—which are as black as thick darkness and as deep as a dense forest, my beloved laments, falls upon the ground, and stumbles as she walks.
The word "nūnam" is used here in the sense of probability or supposition. || 31 ||
Ah, the breeze blows, intoxicated by drinking the honey of the lotus-stalks stirred by the cups of lotuses encircled by rows of bees and blue water-lilies;
it possesses the quality of songs from the charming sounds produced by the dancing of the sprouts of the trees on the banks.
It was stirred by a drinking vessel marked with a lotus, which was encircled by rows of bees and blue water-lilies;

it was intoxicated by the drinking of that lotus-nectar, and thus it sang— that is, its state was made known— by a collection of soft, low-toned, and charming sounds produced by the swaying of the sprouts of the trees and creepers growing on the bank.
The wind blows, possessing qualities such as coolness, gentleness, and fragrance; "hā" expresses the sorrow occasioned by the intensification of separation. 32.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Deer, Peacock, Crane, Fawn, and Others," in the *Ārṣa-śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa*, in the *Vālmīkīya-devarāja-mokṣopadeśa*, in the *Nirvāṇaprakarana*, in the *Uttarakāṇḍa*. 118.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Deer, Peacock, Crane, and the Simpleton," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The One Hundred and Nineteenth Sarga (119).
The companions said:
"Look, this traveler is speaking in the thicket of Mount Mandara."
[He related] the account of their separation concerning his beloved, whom he had regained after a long time.
Having regained his beloved, the traveler described before her his former state— born of separation from her— which had ended in the cremation ground.
O King, look at this traveler in the bower-thicket of Mount Mandara; before his beloved, whom he has found after a long time, he recounts the story of their own past during their separation. || 1 ||
Listen now to this supreme wonder that occurred in one place:
filled with anxiety, I said, "I shall send a messenger to your presence. || 2 ||

He begins to describe the account of his separation as it was related by him to his beloved, starting with the words "ekatra" and so forth: "O beloved, listen to this wonderful event which occurred to me on a single day during the state of separation from you— the account of my own circumstances that I shall relate in your presence."
Reflecting on whom to send as a messenger, I, filled with anxiety, spoke these words: || 2 ||
In this separation, which is like the time of the great dissolution of the universe, who could it be that goes to my home for me with her?

There is no one in this world who would strive so continuously, simply, and with such affection for the sake of pacifying the suffering of another. He said this at that time: "In this," etc. In this separation characterized by the features of the great dissolution...

In this great calamity, who could be such a compassionate messenger that he would come to my house to honor me by delivering news of her while she remains here? He who would joyfully and with simplicity strive incessantly for the sake of alleviating another's suffering—such a person does not exist at all in this world. (3)

Behold, this cloud upon the mountain peak stands like the horse of Smara joined [with its rider]; encircled by the playful vine of lightning, it remains there as a true connoisseur of aesthetic delight.

Ah! Now I remember: this cloud visible upon the mountain peak before us is constantly endowed with qualities such as the alleviation of others' suffering; like the horse of Smara, it is capable of swiftly reaching my home. Delighting in the service of others, it is embraced by a playful maiden in the form of a streak of lightning.
The meaning is that he remains present. || 4 ||

O brother Megha, cast your gaze upon the rainbow of Mahendra as a fitting necklace for her neck; roar softly for a moment and show her mercy, for that young girl, her body as tender as a young lotus stalk and slender, is not able to endure it. Go to her, O Sugata!
He comforted himself with the drops of water falling from his throat and with his own breaths.
Thinking, "Therefore, I shall entreat him alone," he says: "O brother!"— O Cloud,

you who possess a string around your neck (*kaṇṭheguṇa*), having taken up that great bow of Indra which is fitting for you who are endowed with such virtues, go, O you who travel beautifully through the path of the sky (*sugata*), to my beloved.

First, comfort yourself with drops of water from your throat and with your own breath; then, in order to deliver my message, thunder softly and gently for a moment and show mercy. For that slender young woman, whose body is as delicate as a young lotus stalk and whose eyes are filled with tears from the pain of separation from me, will not be able to endure your deep thundering.
Forgiveness. || 5 ||
Having been drawn in the sky with the brush of my mind and embraced,
O cloud, I know not where my beloved has gone from here this very moment.
O cloud, having drawn that beloved in the sky of my heart with the brush of my mind, I embraced her; I know not how she has now departed from here. || 6 ||
O slender one, while my mind was thus overcome by anxiety, my memory of you vanished somewhere as my mental faculties were withdrawn within;
I have become one whose body is subject to another, with limbs like wood or a wall— who indeed could endure such a collapse?
He is capable of [enduring] that which is called the suffering born of separation. || 7 ||

O slender one, having thus addressed the cloud, my memory— that well-known faculty capable of synthesizing the past and the future— has gone away somewhere with you, as my mind’s movement has dissolved within me while I am overcome by thoughts of you. Then...

Due to the loss of mindfulness, I have become one whose body is subject to another's will, such that my limbs have become like wood or a wall. For who indeed is able to endure the collapse born of the pain of separation and such humiliation?
The meaning is: no one at all. (7)
Thereafter, a tumultuous clamor arose among the continuous caravan of travelers as they addressed the cloud with piteous cries, distressed by their calamity: "Alas!
The traveler is dead!"—a cry of "Hā hā! accompanied by great exertion.
[He was] struck on the broad chest by the women of travelers who had just set out [on their journey].
Thereafter, he beheld me in such a state when a caravan of travelers—a multitude of wayfarers—had gathered together with great activity, amidst which there arose cries of "Alas! Alas!
and widespread beating of breasts by the wives of the travelers as they arrived.

In that place where such a traveler had died and a clamorous outcry—a sound of tumult—had arisen, some people, distressed by their calamity, with faltering voices and piteous words, both addressed and reviled the cloud. (8)
Thinking "he is dead," the world, with eyes filled with tears, performed the funeral rites for me;
having gathered wood,
I was led away to be burned, which caused me great fear.
The cremation ground is terrible with the loud, crackling sounds of the bursting of clearly visible cloths arising from the blazing funeral pyres.
He tells what happened there next with the words "by the people": then, having determined that "this man is dead," those travelers,

with eyes filled with tears, performed for him the funeral rites (*śāvī*)— the form of worship consisting of ornaments such as perfumes and garlands appropriate for a corpse— and gathered wood (*dāru*).

Having been seized, I was led to that terrifying cremation ground which inspires extreme fear, where there are such blazing funeral pyres and endless, rising, loud crackling sounds from bursting flames— a place fierce and full of agitation. || 9 ||
There, O lotus-faced one, I was placed by some of them— whose eyelashes were drenched with tears— upon a funeral pyre strewn with the ashes of the gathered people;
I rested upon the head of the intoxicated Death, thick with dense masses of rising smoke, like a supreme crest-jewel.
In the case of fire and gold, which are visible only as a minute fraction [of their essence]. || 10 ||
O lotus-faced one, there I was laid upon the funeral pyre by those travelers with eyes filled with tears;
there, amidst the dense,
matted mass of billowing smoke that formed a line like a swarm of bees surrounding it, I rested upon the head of intoxicated Death, which resembled a famous and excellent crest-jewel.
When the gold, characterized by fire, becomes manifest and visible even in its smallest fraction, || 10 ||
At this moment, a line of smoke, as delicate as a *kuvalaya* lotus-stalk, has begun to enter my nostrils and soft throat;
it is hot, black, and moves swiftly like a young snake pursued by a mongoose entering a hole in the ground.
She is far-reaching, long, contracted, and humpbacked.

At that time, like a *kuvalaya* lotus— tender, soft, yet hot and dark, and bent by the contraction of its length— a streak of smoke, possessing all the aforementioned characteristics, terrified by a mongoose, entered my soft throat-cavity, the nostril,
like a slender female serpent entering a minute hole in the earth.
She proceeded with the firm resolve to enter. || 11 ||
Armored by the nectar of your resolve, I was not pierced by that firm-falling volley of spears, like a vajra-bodied being;
plunging into the river of passion within the house of my heart as you drew near, I even revelled amidst the severing of my vital organs.
I did not know those feelings. || 12 ||

O beloved, I am armored and enveloped by the nectar of your form; thus, I have not been pierced nor afflicted by that line of smoke. Just as the unborn Brahmā, whose body is like adamant, was not pierced by the firm-falling spear-line of Death, so am I. Furthermore, you are the river of Love dwelling within the chamber of my heart.
Even while plunging into the fire, though the piercing of my vital organs was being performed, I did not perceive those manifested pains that had arisen;
how much less, then, the mere smoke? This is the meaning. || 12 ||

O slender one, for this long time, I have experienced within my heart, together with you, that which is appropriate— an eternal immersion in You, restless with inner play. Upon seeing which, the enjoyment of sovereignty is like emerging from a lake of nectar.
The thought arises that it is like a mere trifling slaughter. || 13 ||
"O slender one, during this much time, such a bliss was experienced by me within my heart together with you while in this state of swoon. He describes what that [bliss] was like: 'In which,' etc.
Just as when one emerges repeatedly from a pool of nectar, so too, when that bliss was seen, this well-known..."

The meaning is that even the enjoyment of sovereignty—the happiness of lordship over the three worlds previously described—is perceived as being utterly trivial and insignificant, like a minor pain compared to the agony of a mortal wound. || 13 ||

That playfulness of yours, those graceful gestures, that speech of yours accompanied by smiles, those side-long glances— joyful, infinite, and worthy of their full expansion as the sole ornament of the inner self;
those movements agitated by the speed of laughter and the shifting of necklaces at the moment of their removal— what indeed is that which is not yours?
When remembered, it brings an inner delight like the taste of nectar. || 14 ||
O beloved, that peerless play of yours—which consists of unsurpassed bliss accessible only through direct experience—is exactly such;

those playful gestures of yours, such as the movement of your eyebrows, are exactly such; even your speech is exactly such, and your smile is exactly such, as are your side-long glances. And far away [is] that single-string necklace (ekāvalī), which is the preeminent ornament among all ornaments, made of jewels, upon whom [you rest].

Such was that [experience] which, during the flow of immediate bliss—that is, of sexual union—was appropriate for the act of embracing; those various efforts such as scratching with the nails and other gestures; those sounds such as the cries of passion; those playful laughter-filled moments filled with the essence of such things;
and those states of mental agitation caused by the force of movement—all these, when remembered, do not produce the internal joy of nectar.
What indeed is that? Nothing at all; the meaning is that everything indeed produces the delight of the nectar of immortality. || 14 ||
O young girl, through the elixir of the bliss of love in union with you, I was so utterly satiated that I became overcome by exhaustion;
I remained there upon the soft surface of your bed, like one resting upon the orb of the moon with its autumnal, cool, and stainless radiance.

O child, immediately after that, in union with you— wherein the very bliss of amorous sport was my elixir— I, afflicted by exhaustion and sluggish from extreme satiation, remained there upon a soft bed, like the orb of the moon in autumn amidst cool rays. 15.
In that interval, suddenly, like a thunderbolt from the long, moon-like fragment of sandalwood paste that was cool,
I beheld a fire blazing upon the surface of the earth, resembling the submarine fire (vāḍava) of the Ocean of Milk, as it emerged from its own bed.
In this interval, at this very moment,
like a thunderbolt from a long crescent moon cool with sandalwood paste, an utterly inconceivable fire rose from his own bed, blazing with sound upon the surface of the earth within his own body.
The submarine fire associated with the Ocean of Milk—that Vāḍava fire resembling it—was seen. || 16 ||
The companions said:
When her beloved had spoken thus, the innocent girl, crying out "Alas, I am ruined!", stood there in a swoon due to her naivety, suspecting that the groom was turning away.

When her beloved had spoken this story, that innocent woman, having heard it, became so bewildered by her own simplicity that she stood there in a swoon, fearing that the "āvarta" (whirlpool) was actually the "saṃvarta" (the fire of cosmic destruction). || 17 ||
Consoling her who was in such a state with water from the hollow of a lotus leaf, he remained there, holding her against his neck.

This beloved, fanning that beloved lady who was in such a state with lotus leaves and refreshing her with cool waters while dispelling her fainting spell, remained here in this Mandara grove, holding her by the neck. || 18 ||
Questioned again by her, he says: "Behold that very same conversation;
here he is, having taken his beloved by the chin as she stands at his side. (19)
He speaks—that is, look—of that very same conversation previously mentioned; in other words, he speaks of the remainder of the story. || 19 ||

"Alas, alas! O Fire!"—just as I, somewhat overcome with distress, was saying this in great haste, that funeral pyre was suddenly plundered by those gleaming travelers, who in an instant made it resound with harsh, grating cries. He speaks to her: "Alas, alas!"—O beloved, I, having become somewhat overcome with distress, [cried]
Even as I was speaking, that funeral pyre— already crowded with those travelers who were gleaming with joy and making harsh,
grating sounds— was suddenly overwhelmed by them and plundered by the removal of all the torches.

Then all the travelers, embracing me— whose body was covered with abundant garlands and who stood with my posture raised by the playful music of swaying palm leaves— surrounded me on all sides and shouted, sang, laughed, danced, and leaped about.

Then, out of joy at the resurrection of one who had died, all the travelers, surrounding me and embracing me— my body filled with many large, auspicious crest-ornaments made from clusters of tree-blossoms like the playful music of trembling palm-clappers— stood encircling me.
Out of joy, they wept, sang, laughed, danced on all sides, leaped about, and moved forward; such is the meaning. || 21 ||

Then he beheld the cremation ground, which grants happiness even to the formidable Vināyakas, winding with heaps of ashes, snakes, and human heads, and possessing bones and skulls as white as the moon— a body, as it were, of the Fierce One.
Then I beheld a cremation ground, as terrifying as the very form of Saṃhārarudra;
the descriptive epithets are to be applied equally to both. || 22 ||
Stealing away the shadows from their sides, spreading the scent of shifting, crumbling, and moist skeletons,
and wafting forth a dense mist of widespread ashes,
the rays of the moon— shaped like arrows fallen from the moon’s mouth— shake the hair upon the skulls of the bones belonging to Śiva in the expanse of the sky.
There, winds blow that produce harsh sounds with a whistling noise.

There, in that cremation ground, winds blow. Of what sort are they? They are shifting and spreading, carrying away the green shadows of the forest on its flanks with showers of ashes; they extend a widespread mist—a veil of frost—composed of abundant ashes and the odors of decaying skeletons that are being torn asunder and moistened by the corpses.
Shaking their hair, they were like arrows fallen from the moon into the quiver whose nature is the sky;
likewise, they were such that harsh and rough voices were produced by the *ṭāṃ* sound— the clanging noise— of the bones of Śaṅkara, which are fit for his ornaments.
This is the meaning. || 23 ||

With its trees and leaves withered by the heat driven forth by the winds from the streams of blazing funeral pyres, that land bears the likeness of the pleasure-houses of Agni, Vāyu, and the Son of the Sun (Yama). 24.

That cremation ground was such that its trees had their leaves withered by the heat of the blazing fires, while being struck by a wind carrying streams of smoke and sparks issuing forth from those pyres;
it belonged to the fire Jvalana, the wind Pavana, and Śanaiścara, the son of the Sun.
It bears characteristics resembling that house which is fit for pleasure; it is an imitation of it. || 24 ||

He beheld that cemetery, thick with the foul-smelling remains of endless, terrifying skeletons; it was made dreadful by the shrieks of intoxicated jackals, crows, herons, vultures, piśācas, and vetālas.
Such was that cremation ground seen: thickly crowded with endless, terrifying skeletons and half-burnt corpses, and emitting an extremely raw and foul stench. (25)
The bowers of the horizon resounded with the wailing of kinsmen and traveling companions who had arrived, crying out over various corpses;
there were clusters of burnt trees where strings of wet tendons and entrails, pulled down by birds, were still attached.
Furthermore, what is that cremation ground like? It is one in which the horizons and groves resound on all sides with the wailing of the circles of kinsmen who have arrived for various corpses;
it is a place where the quarters are mostly burnt out and bound together by wet veins and strings of entrails dragged out by birds.
In which there were clusters of trees and networks of creepers. || 26 ||
In some places it was illuminated by the agitation of funeral pyres; in others, it was filled with masses of clouds formed by great locks of hair;
and in other parts, the setting mountain resembled a thundering cloud at night, with the earth’s surface spread out as if drenched in blood.

The earth’s agitation was its trembling; by that, light was produced through the kindling of flames. There, a multitude of clouds was formed by the great locks of hair, as if they were a mass of rain-clouds. In some places, however, it stood like a canopy over the earth, smeared with blood and appearing like a mountain cast down from the setting sun; at night, it was like a thundering, roaring cloud.
It remains. || 27 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and nineteenth canto, titled "The Description of the Travels of the Separated Lover," in the *Ārṣa* [work], the *Śrī Vālmīkiya Vālmīkīya Devatāmaya Muni-nirmita Utpatti-vipatti-pathikavirahavṛttavarṇana*. 119.

Thus ends the one hundred nineteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Wanderer’s Conduct and Separation," in the latter half of the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa* within the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The One Hundred and Twentieth Sarga.
The companions said:
"Behold this great couple as they engage in such conversations."
O lotus-eyed one, drink this water which has flowed from the udder. || 1 ||
Winds, trees, bees, forest groves,
celestial nymphs, ocean waves, and birds such as the golden-crested one (Jatayu) are described therein.
"O lotus-eyed one, behold this aforementioned couple—a pair of man and woman—engaged in conversation as previously described, now proceeding to drink the finest essence, the wine.

This concludes the narrative of the couple; the substitution of *enat* for the neuter pronoun in the sense of a subsequent reference (*anvādeśa*) is prescribed by the rule "the neuter *enat* should be used. || 1 ||
Various winds blow, skilled at snapping the clusters of plantains and kandalī flowers as clear as crystal, and adorned with the filaments of blossoms. (2)
Someone describes the winds with the verse beginning "kadalī" and so forth: "They are experts at snapping and unfolding clusters [of flowers]."
The winds blow, rich with the manifold fragrances wafted from the forests;
they have drunk the drops of perspiration and have brushed against the tresses of beautiful women.
The playful movements of the women’s dangling locks of hair as they sway and toss about are truly charming. || 3 ||
The winds from the salt ocean, rising from the caves and dwellings of the mountain ranges and stirring the lions within, blow with the fury of demons.
Like lions, the lords of beasts, who have emerged intent upon entering and roaming through the cave-dwellings of the boundary mountains,
they move forward with the fury of demons, exerting themselves to scale the peaks of Mount Meru.
They were cherished by the playful, swaying motion of *tāla* and *tamāla* creepers, and their tender sprouts were tossed upward by the waves of the water stirred by the wind. || 5 ||
By those [birds], who, like restless young children, were rocked by playful swings among the *tamāla* and *tāla* trees, and who, leaping from the waves of water,
had alighted upon the tender sprouts at the tops of the trees.
In the gardens, the winds blow like kings in intoxication, grey with the pollen of flowers vomited from the undulating creeper-like lips.
The lakes were covered with the pollen of flowers blown forth by those swaying young creepers. || 6 ||
This forest breeze, resting upon the bamboos, has begun to sing sweetly,
as if it had been instructed by the women of Pāṇḍu’s city.
He rested in the bamboo thickets and groves of kīcaka reeds; it is well known that in the city of Pāṇḍu, Hastināpura, the women are skilled in the art of singing. || 7 ||
When an insult was offered to the wind by the Karṇikāra tree,
even the bees avoided it from afar.
He imagines the reason for the bees' avoidance of the *karṇikāra* tree from afar: "It is an insult" (*nikāra*).
An "insult" (*nikāra*) is a contemptuous disregard resulting from the failure to offer fragrance, pollen, and so forth. || 8 ||
The palmyra tree yields neither fruit nor even a sprout to the seeker;
for it is merely a trunk, like a formless beginning devoid of shape.
This palmyra tree, being like a mere pillar and difficult to climb, yields neither fruit nor foliage to the seeker.
For indeed, the reason is that even its lofty form does not shine at all—meaning it is as if formless—without the undertaking of fulfilling the desires of those who seek. || 9 ||
For passion alone serves for the beauty of those who are devoid of merit and dull by nature;
O King, it is by passion alone that this *kiṃśuka* tree shines like a king. (10)

The meaning is that for those who are dull-witted and foolish, devoid of qualities such as nobility, passion for the ostentation of clothing, ornaments, and the like serves only to color the body for the sake of beauty, and nothing else. The *kiṃśuka* is the flowering *palāśa* tree.
"Come! This *karṇikāra* is merely a vessel for transformation."
What joy is there in this, which is like a living being devoid of virtue? || 11 ||
"This pursuit of transformation was in vain" refers specifically to the mental affliction characterized by despondency. || 11 ||
The dark Tamāla tree, standing amidst a mass of swaying flower-clusters like flashes of lightning,
vainly causes the Cātaka bird to mistake it for a rain cloud.
The dark *tamāla* tree, standing there with its mass of flower-clusters resembling flashes of lightning, creates the illusion of a rain-cloud for the *cātaka* bird;
this is done in vain, that is, pointlessly. || 12 ||
With leaves like dense masses of clouds, providing shade that covers the mountains, these lofty bamboo-like lineages are worthy of great virtues. 13.

They were adorned with leaves, feathers, and vehicles; they possessed a dense, impenetrable mass; they were surrounded by excellent shadows, or by kings who had been chosen for the sake of providing shade to the virtuous; and they were the bow-strings of virtues, such as honor and the like. || 13 ||

The foremost cloud, resting upon the golden mountain ridges and dwelling on the slopes of the Vātavyādhi mountains, wears a yellow garment of lightning; agitated—[in the case of the sky, agitated by lightnings;
in the case of the garment, moving and shimmering]—it is like Hari at his manifestation (udbhava).
In one sense, he possesses supreme sovereignty in the higher realms. || 14 ||

The cloud rests upon a seat characterized by golden ridges, while Hari rests upon one resembling golden ridges; for this very reason, Bhava (Śiva) is foremost (agrya). On the slopes of that cloud, there is a disease characterized by wind (vāta-vyādhi), and in the vicinity of Hari, there is the disease of wind (vātavyādhi) on the shore. The cloud bears the sky, which has been turned yellow by lightning.
Hari wears yellow garments, like lightning.
With birds and bees busily engaged in entering and exiting,
the blossoming *kiṃśuka* tree shines like a hero drenched in blood.
Whose arrows—like bees and like birds darting in and out—are restless as they rush forth;
that hero, a warrior, is "red" (rakta) with blood, as if stained by a stream of gore. 15.
In the palace of clouds, tawny with clusters of mandāra blossoms,
upon the peak of Mount Mahendra, the intoxicated Gandharva lovers slept.
On the summit, the peak of Mount Mahendra, they slept, intoxicated by drink. || 16 ||
O King, behold the travelers—Siddhas and Vidyādharas—who, having found rest under the extensive shade of the forest of wish-fulfilling trees, sing their songs. (17)
They were accompanied by those excellent instruments, such as the vīṇā and others. || 17 ||
Behold, in this forest, upon every single sprout of this wish-fulfilling tree, celestial beauties rest, sing, and laugh. (18)
This is the temple of the noble sage Mandapāla on Mount Mandara, whose soft abode is a bower; he whose wife is that female bird.
That well-known female bird named Jaritā was a vulture belonging to the sage Mandapāla, who is famous in the Mahābhārata and other texts. || 19 ||
Behold this series of hermitages belonging to sages, filled with trees flowering in all seasons, where lions and elephants, mongooses and snakes, sport together in mutual friendship. (20)
A series of hermitages belonging to sages, wherein lions, elephants, and other animals—having abandoned their innate enmity toward one another—engage in affectionate play. 20.
These water droplets, reflecting the sun, glisten upon the sprouts of the creepers on the ocean shore, which are intermingled with coral trees.

These drops of water (udabindavaḥ)—wherein the sun is reflected in the tender shoots of the creepers (vīrudhaḥ) standing on the ocean shore, which are intermingled with coral trees and entwined together—shine forth.

[In this context], the substitution of "uda" for "udaka" occurs according to the rule: "In the words mantha, odana, saktu, bindu, vajra, bhāra, hāra, vīvadha, and gāha, 'uda' is substituted for 'udaka'. (Pāṇini 6.1.159). || 21 ||
The waves play among the spots of gems and rubies with their whirling eddies,
like playful women sporting upon the chests of lovers.
The waves sport and play repeatedly with their circular revolutions in the places where rubies and gems are found, as if they were young, playful women sporting upon the chests of their lovers.
Listen: the divine jingling of ornaments, arising from the coming and going of women from the world of the Naga kings, is heard from the sky. 23.
With the sounds of intoxicated female bees falling from the vicinity of their ears,
the mountain caves seem to sing of the bathing grounds of Airāvaṇa.

Behold these caves of Mount Airāvata, the bathing ground of Airāvaṇa; they seem to be singing with the sounds of intoxicated female bees, whose honey-drops have fallen from their temples near the tips of their ears.
As the ocean daily diminishes during the dark fortnight, the lines marking the end of the dark phase are seen upon its emaciated body like rows of seashells.

During the dark fortnight, as the ocean recedes following the moon, rows of black streaks are seen on the shore—the dwelling place of the Vāstu—forming the shape of the dark line [of the moon]. || 25 ||
Breathing with the fragrance of incense, providing cool shade, her limbs were cool to the touch; she revealed her form in solitude and was filled with various flowers. || 26 ||

Someone describes the forests themselves in the form of a woman with two verses beginning with "āmoda. All the adjectives should be applied by unifying them as they intend two meanings through devices such as *śleṣa* (punning). She is one whose breath (*śvasana*)—meaning the wind—is endowed with fragrance (*gandha*), which is the very scent of the forest (*vanāmoda*). || 26 ||
Clad in the arrangement of forests, laughing with the purity of waterfalls, with carpets of strewn flowers spread out—blessed is she who sports in the forest. (27)
A playful woman has the characteristics of a forest. || 27 ||
Those of noble intellect do not delight in the Nandana grove as much as they do in the pure forest lands where all sounds have been stilled. (28)
The gods and others possess exalted intellects. || 28 ||
The delightful, solitary forest lands bring equal delight to the mind of the sage who is utterly dispassionate and to the seeker of sense-objects who is full of passion. (29)
The dispassionate mind of the sage and the passionate mind of the lustful seeker of sense-objects both find equal delight in them.
(29) The feet of the mountains on the shore of the ocean, whose slopes are washed by the waters, shine and resound with their masses of jewels, as if wearing anklets. (30)
The feet are the peripheral mountains, and they are likewise characterized as the [Buddha’s] feet. || 30 ||
Resting upon the Puṃnāga trees, those birds with lovely golden luster and golden crests shine like hosts of gods in the sky. (31)
Behold, the forests of blossoming campaka trees—dense with bees, clouds, and smoke—are trembling in the wind like mountains set ablaze. (32)
Rich with smoke from bees and clouds, they appear as if ablaze because they tremble. || 32 ||
Embracing her beloved cuckoo as it swings upon the tips of the *karavīra* creepers, she makes him utter sweet, trembling notes.

The topmost creeper of the *karavīra* tree, its branches reaching upward, serves as a swing; upon it, the female cuckoo embraces her beloved male cuckoo as he swings, and she addresses him with a sweet series of songs. || 33 ||
Behold these shores of the Lāvāṇa and Saindhava oceans, filled with kings whose hands carry offerings, making a resonant clamor like that of cranes.

O King, behold these riverbanks of the salt ocean (Lavaṇasindhu), belonging to Lāvāṇa and Saindhava; here, by the rule "hṛdbhagasindhvante pūrvapadasya ca," there is vowel strengthening (vṛddhi) in both members of the compound. See how the lands along the shore are filled with kings holding tribute in their hands, amidst a resounding clamor.
Let the kings remaining after the battle with the gods— from the eastern salt ocean to the western, and from the northern to the southern— be made footstools for you;
and let weapons be bestowed according to the scriptures in every direction of the mandalas for the protection of the earth.
For a long time, preceded by patience, you have taught the teachings with incomparable power and tranquility. || 35 ||
From this eastern salt ocean to the western salt ocean,
and likewise from the northern to the southern salt ocean— the prefix *ā* here denotes a boundary—
let all those kings who remain, however many they may be, in this Jambūdvīpa, be made into footstools upon their heads in this exalted battle.

In short, let them be favored by the placing of [Your] feet upon them. Furthermore, for the long-term protection of those various mandalas in every direction, let edicts be issued according to the scriptures—in the manner prescribed in the treatises on statecraft (nītiśāstra)—preceded by patience and composure, and with a peaceful mind. Following that, let garments be granted; and after that, let military force, namely Your own army, be dispatched.
Let it be given. || 35 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and twentieth canto, titled "Description of Vāyu and Others Residing in the Various Quarters," in the *Avidyopākhyāna* of the *Nirvāṇa-khaṇḍa*, within the *Vāyustuti-mahātmya* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*, composed by the Sage. 120.

Thus ends the one hundred and twentieth chapter, titled "Description of the Wind and Other Elements Moving in Different Directions," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and twenty-first canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Then, upon those shores of the ocean, these Vipaçcits [remained] upon the earth.
Having sat down, they deliberated upon all these matters concerning the administration of the kingdom.
Having established the boundary of the mandala here, for those who have approached the fire,
an effort is undertaken to see the ends of the directions by means of a boon from the fire.

Then these aforementioned wise ones, having sat down on those shores of the ocean, carried out this purpose previously announced by their ministers: the establishment of the boundaries of the sacred circle (maṇḍala). || 1 ||
Then, having established their place of residence right there, they remained in due order and fixed the boundaries of the maṇḍala so that it was protected.
They themselves remained there and established the boundaries of the maṇḍala. || 2 ||
Then, as if to describe his majesty,
the glorious sun entered the interior of the ocean and departed for another world.

The majesty of those wise ones [was such that] they entered another world—according to the astronomical school (jyotiṣamata), the netherworld (pātālaloka); according to the Purāṇic school (paurāṇikamata), another region situated on the northern part of Mount Meru. The phrase "having entered into the midst of the ocean" is an expression from the perspective of people standing on the seashore. || 3 ||
The night arrived, dark as a streak of cloud, having become slender;
they, having completed their daily duties, remained upon their own beds.
*Tānava* means expansion. They are the wise ones (*vipaścit*). || 4 ||
Like the currents of rivers reaching as far as the ocean, they arrived from afar;
with their minds overwhelmed by wonder, they accomplished this task.
They brought to mind—that is, they reflected upon—this which is about to be stated. || 5 ||
"Oh, how we have reached this distant path without effort, by the power of the god of gods, Agni, and through our own divine vehicles! (6)
How vast must this expansive beauty of the visible world be!
Here is the ocean, and beyond that, the land of the islands, with its lordly sea.
He states that very point with the words "How great would it be? and so forth: beyond this Jambūdvīpa is the Salt Ocean;
after that is the land of Plakṣadvīpa, and then the Ocean of Sugarcane Juice. This means that the lordly [ocean] is twice the extent of the Salt Ocean. || 7 ||
From here is an island, from there an ocean; what might lie beyond that? How great and of what nature is this formless illusion? (8)

Beyond this ocean of sugarcane juice lies Kuśadvīpa, and beyond that is the Suroda ocean. In this sequence, what might exist at the end of the seven continents and oceans? And what might lie even beyond that? How vast is this formless Māyā, and of what nature is she in her manifold variety of objects? (8)
Therefore, we pray to the god Hutāśa for those boons;
meanwhile, let us gaze tirelessly at all the directions until the very horizon.
To see all of that, we pray to the god Hutāśa; let us pray. || 9 ||
Having reflected thus, they all remained in their respective places and simultaneously invoked the blessed Agni.
They were stationed simultaneously and at the same time upon the shores of the four oceans, each in its proper place.
Then the blessed Fire-god became visible to them;
assuming a physical form, he said, "O sons, choose a boon."
The Vipaschitas said:
"O Lord of the Gods, one reaches the end of this visible world composed of the five elements by means of the body,
then by the mantra-body, and finally even by the mind."

As long as it is possible to go with this body, so long [one should go] with this very body; when that is unattainable, then by means of this very body consecrated by the power of Vedic mantras; when even that is unattainable, then by the mind.
"O Lord, let this supreme boon be granted to us: that we may behold [Thee] as far as there is perception, as far as there is existence, and as far as there is the self. (13)

"Up to the limit of perception" refers to all objects suitable for direct perception; "up to the limit of possibility" refers to those accessible through inference; by the second [term] there is the mention of everything subtle; and by the third, the mention of the entire expansion of causes. Thus, let this boon be granted to us. || 13 ||
O Lord, may we see with our physical bodies that path leading to the unattained goal;
then, at its end, may we behold the visible [reality] with the mind alone.

Those yogins are perfected; "accessible to those who have attained perfection" means that which is to be reached through the power of yoga. "With this very body" means with this physical form itself. Now, "at its end, it is inaccessible to them"—this is the meaning. || 14 ||
May death not befall us on a path that has not yet been traversed;
rather, let our mind alone proceed, leaving behind the body which cannot accompany us on the journey. (15)

The phrase "for those traveling on the path" is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. On a path where a body is impossible—that is, on a path consisting of the southern and northern solstices and so forth, which can only be traversed after death. || 15 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Then, having said, "So be it," the Fire-god departed instantly,
as swift as the ocean hurrying to assume the form of Aurva in a single moment.
Then, immediately after that request for the boon, as if in haste to go to the ocean in the form of Aurva—that is, as the submarine fire (vaḍavāgni).
Then Agni departed and returned; the night lingered and then passed away;
the sun also appeared and then set; and their desire to cross the ocean of wisdom continued unabated.

Having thus granted the boon, Agni departed. Then night arrived; that night also passed after lingering for four watches (yāmas). Then the sun appeared, and the desire of those wise men to cross the ocean of the intellect also arrived. (17)

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-first chapter, titled "The Determination of Vipaścit," in the *Vipraparinaya* of the *Uttarakanda*, within the *Nirvana* section of the *Mokshopaya*, in the *Dehalinga* of the *Vasishtha-maha-Ramayana* composed by Valmiki, according to the tradition of the Rishis. || 121 ||
Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-first chapter, titled "The Determination of Vipaścit," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and twenty-second canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Then, at dawn, having firmly established the proper order for the earth according to the scriptures, he—
As if their bodies were possessed by that aesthetic flavor (rasa), they seemed as though they were being restrained by the chief ministers. || 1 ||
The wise ones who travel here upon the waves of the ocean,
having emerged after tearing through whirlpools and sea-monsters, have been well described.

Having established the regulations for the division and protection of the kingdom, as well as the instruction on the means [of governance], according to the scriptures— that is, without transgressing the treatises on political ethics (nītiśāstra)— they were, as it were,
possessed by spirits due to an intense longing to see the ends of the earth.
The word "iva" (as if) is used because the chief ministers, being unable to forbid him directly, were forbidding him by means of gestures. || 1 ||

Having restrained his entire retinue who were wailing and weeping with their faces upturned, and having cast aside pride, envy, greed, the afflictions, and desires through his lack of attachment; || 2 ||

Having warded off his entire retinue and all his attendants; "overpowering" (*abhibhava*) refers to the defeat of enemies, while "seeking" (*eṣaṇā*) includes the pursuit of kingdom, women, sons, and so forth, as indicated by the word "and the rest" (*ādi*). Alternatively, "overpowering" may refer to being insulted by enemies who mock him, while "seekings" are those previously mentioned, and by the word "and the rest," one includes kingdom, wealth, and other such things.
Having cast aside, having abandoned. || 2 ||

Having surveyed the horizon and saying, "We shall arrive at the far shore of the ocean in an instant," they entered the sea on foot alone by means of the supreme power of their own mantras. (Note: The printed reading *adbhiḥ* is to be considered doubtful.)
Having said, "We shall return in an instant, swiftly, after having surveyed the horizon on the far side of the ocean," they departed— this is the ellipsis to be supplied—

to reassure their attendants; [they attained] excellence and perfection through the mastery of the elements such as earth and water by means of the power of mantras which have fire as their source of grace.
The meaning is that at that time, the ocean was entered by them using those very footprints alone, and not by means such as a boat. || 3 ||
Vipaścit, followed by some servants and by many others who were entering the ocean in every direction,
proceeded as if treading upon water with his feet.
