Followed by some servants who, out of excessive affection, entered the ocean with them, they proceeded on foot alone. || 4 ||
Having set foot within the mass of waves, as if upon the surface of dry land,
those four, though joined one by one, were utterly separated from their own army.

He explains how they went: "Upon the waves," etc. Having placed their footsteps, as if upon the surface of dry land, within the multitude of waves; they were "yuktāḥ," meaning prepared or diligent. || 5 ||

Following that very sequence, those Avalokitas entered deep within the great ocean until they reached a state of invisibility to those standing on the shore, like fragments of clouds in the autumn sky.
The servants standing on the bank watched them for as long as it took for them to become invisible, like fragments of autumn clouds in the sky. || 6 ||
Then, with their resolve firmly established, they traversed that path on foot across the ocean,
as if they were tigers with girdles fastened for a great exertion.

Driven by their expanded resolve and firm determination—acting like elephant-drivers—those wise ones carried that bound load across the waterway, just as such elephants would traverse it; they brought it safely to the other side.
By ascending and descending mountains with their rises and falls,
those forms of Hari steal away the splendor of the waves of the waters.

By means of ascents and descents—elevations and depressions—that were like mountains, they themselves, by assuming that very state, carried away the beauty and splendor of the water-waves; for this reason, their forms were like the form of Hari (Viṣṇu).
Indeed, even the form of Hari, at the time of churning the ocean from Mount Mandara, [assumed the form of the mountain].
The intended meaning is that it is well known that Fortune (Śrī-Lakṣmī) abandons one who is raised up and cast down by ascents and descents. || 8 ||
Like blades of grass whirled in eddies, they wandered for a long time without agitation amidst those [clouds] which shone like circles of moons, flickering and intoxicated.
They wandered for a long time like blades of grass within the whirlpools, which shone as they were entered by them, just as the moon’s orb shines when it has entered a dark cloud. || 9 ||
Invincible by virtue of the power of mantras, sciences, and vital energy, they held weapons in their hands;
in some places, their bodies were swallowed and then disgorged by careless sea-monsters.
Those whose bodies were first swallowed and later vomited out due to the inability to digest them. || 10 ||
Their forms driven by winds resting upon the waves of the water,
they were carried back and forth in a mere instant for hundreds and hundreds of yojanas.
By virtue of her body being as lofty as the elephants amidst the waves of the water,
she possessed the splendor of standing upon the backs of the state elephants.
By means of the elephants characterized by the waves of water, which possess towering bodies and a height that is unprecedentedly marvelous.
Like winds, they displayed the emergence of water from the clouds through their skill in rending the city with the broad, continuous bands of breaking waves.

Displaying their skill (*pāṭava*) in splitting— meaning the cleaving and rending— and in overturning— meaning the turning face-downward— of vast stone slabs characterized by masses of waves, the winds, fanned by the Maruts, show forth their emergence from the ocean characterized by water, like flashes of lightning. || 13 ||
Struck by the surging mass of waves from the leaping elephants, they did not abandon their own fortitude, like the excellent shores of the sea-beach. || 14 ||
Though struck by the surging masses of waves as if by restless elephants, the famous excellent shores, like stone ramparts, did not abandon their inherent steadfastness. || 14 ||
Reflected in the circles of pearls and rubies from the great waves,
they appeared as if surrounded on all sides by a multitude of men, even though they were alone.
Reflected in the great waves and in the circles of pearls and rubies, they appeared as if surrounded by a multitude of men—a collective human presence (*pauruṣeya*). || 15 ||
Making light steps upon masses of pale foam,
they assumed the beauty of royal swans gliding among white lotuses.
The splendor of a royal swan that has alighted after wandering among white lotuses.
The mountains were not terrified there by the roar of the ocean, which was as terrifying as the crashing of thick clouds and resounded with a tumultuous gurgling from its swelling against the shore.
"Nirghāta" means a thunderclap. The term "bhūbhṛtaḥ" is a pun; because they were *bhūbhṛtaḥ* (mountains), they were not afraid. || 17 ||
Struck by the falling and crashing of great water-bearing mountains that scraped the very clouds,
they descended to the netherworld (pātāla) in one moment and ascended to the abode of the sun in the next.
Struck by the falling and rising of those lordly mountains composed of water that lick the clouds; || 18 ||
Covered by the falling torrent of water rising unexpectedly,
they were as if shrouded by a canopy collapsing during a sudden calamity.
They were as if covered by the canopies of clouds falling down upon the occurrence and arrival of a portentous calamity. || 19 ||
They have entered the ocean together with their companion crocodiles; they are surrounded by brave sharks and crabs, and their swirling eddies are filled within with sprays from the water-trees,
as if making their bodies endowed with splendor.
At every step, it was filled with flowers made of shimmering rubies and pearls whose rays were both manifest and latent, and with other abundant clouds in the form of vapors.

Adorning their bodies, which were endowed with splendor, as if with clusters of rubies, pearls, and flowers that were thick, abundant, cloud-like in form, and possessed both manifest and latent rays of light; likewise, they had companions— makaras— that were whirling everywhere within the eddies filled with brave crocodiles, kulīras, and crabs.
Those wise ones of such a kind set forth—that is, they moved—into the ocean, the reservoir of waters. || 20 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-second canto, titled "The Fall of Bala," in the *Ārṣa* Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa of Valmīki, in the *Deva*, *Mokṣopāya*, *Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa*, *Uttarārdha*, *Avimukta*.
Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-second chapter, titled "The Fall of Bala," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The One Hundred and Twenty-Third Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Thus ends the investigation into ignorance in its form as the visible world.
They set out on foot, traveling toward the islands of the ocean. || 1 ||
The various conditions encountered by wise travelers who have set out upon these islands and oceans, beginning from the western regions and proceeding in order, are here described.
In this manner, these wise ones set out on foot to investigate the very limit of ignorance in its visible form. || 1 ||
From ocean to island, from island to ocean, and from island to mountain and forest,
they leaped with agility, free from any cutting or piercing.
Because of lightness and swiftness. || 2 ||
The learned Pītā was defeated by the fish Mīna, who considered himself immortal,
born of the lineage of Viṣṇu-Mīna, and possessed the power of the vehicle Vitastā.

There, a scholar who had set out to see the western horizon was swallowed— that is, engulfed— by a fish possessed of the conceit of thinking itself to be an immortal god; for that river Vitastā is renowned for its extreme rapidity, possessing a vigor even swifter than the vigor of its vehicle, such as a boat.
By such [a person]. || 3 ||
Having reached the Ocean of Milk, it was vomited up by that fish;
having crossed the Ocean of Milk, it went far away to another region.
"Sudurjara" means incapable of being digested. || 4 ||
In the city of the Yakṣas, Dakṣiṇa beheld an ocean of sugarcane juice; having been cast into it by a Yakṣiṇī skilled in her arts, he was made her lover.

He tells the news of the second [son] with the words beginning "In the south," etc.: while staying in a city of Yakṣas situated upon the ocean of sugarcane juice, he was observed by a clever Yakṣiṇī skilled in the training of the science of subjugation; having been drawn there by the power of her lore, he was made her lover. || 5 ||
When he had previously attacked Makara and cut him down, he was then brought by the Gaṅgā and cast ashore at Kānyakubja.

He tells the account of the third [Vipaścit] with the words "In the east" (*pūrve*). When Vipaścit, proceeding in the eastern direction, was gradually beholding the confluences of the thousand mouths of the Gaṅgā, he once, desiring to swallow a *makara*, forcibly seized it;
then, having brought the Gaṅgā for its extraction, he cut it open—that is, he tore it asunder. At that time, that Vipaścit...
Having been brought back by the Gaṅgā and turned around, he was abandoned and left behind in the city of Kānyakubja. || 6 ||
But Uttara, having propitiated the people of Uttarakuru, attained prosperity;
therefore, the fears of death do not afflict him even at the ends of the earth.

He tells the account of the fourth [son] with the words "But Uttara": having propitiated the Lord (Īśvara) who was sporting with the Goddess in Uttarakuru—referring to Uttarakuru by metonymy—he obtained prosperity (*śrī*), that is, the sovereign powers such as *aṇimā* and the rest.
Therefore, even though this Vipracitti had spread his fame to the ends of the earth through that very prosperity, death (*mṛta*) and the fears caused by it did not overcome him.
They cause suffering; the meaning is that he became immortal. || 7 ||
Having assumed a form that was repeatedly swallowed and disgorged by the sea-monster Makara-mātanga,
he traversed many principal mountain ranges of other continents.
By her, that is, by Śrī herself; the meaning is: by her power alone. || 8 ||
Placing him on his back, the western bird Hemacūḍa swiftly carried Kuśāṅgaśrī across the oceans to Kuśadvīpa.
Again, he speaks of the news from the west—referring to "the western" one. By *hemacūḍa*, that is, by Garuḍa;

for it is well known that Garuḍa, stationed upon a *kuśa* blade in Kuśadvīpa, when propitiated by worship and other means, delivers that island and its oceans. His bodily splendor—the beauty of his form—is like that of a golden *kuśa* blade. || 9 ||
On the mountain of Krauñcadvīpa, he was swallowed by a rākṣasa in the forest;
that rākṣasa was torn apart by him with the cutting of his entrails in the heart.

Again, he tells the news of the east: "In Krauñca... In the well-known Krauñca-dvīpa, [the sage] was swallowed by a *rākṣasa* on the mountain that marks the boundary of the region (*varṣasīmācala*). Then, that *rākṣasa* was split open and torn asunder by Vipaścit with his rending of entrails; in an instant, [the demon], who had become a *yakṣa* due to the curse of Dakṣa, became [righteous] again.
In Śākadvīpa, he attained liberation after one hundred years.
Again, he speaks of the account of the South, beginning with "Dakṣiṇa"; "mokṣam" means liberation from the curse. || 11 ||
Uttara, who had crossed over the excellent river of stars (the Milky Way),
became a stone upon the earth due to the curse of a Siddha, even though he possessed the gold of the great ocean.

By his very speed and force, he crossed over the great stars, the small ones, the minor ones, and the rivers—[here there is a *ekaśeṣa* compound referring to both feminine and masculine forms]—as well as the surging oceans; beyond the great salt ocean, upon the celebrated golden earth, he reached the state of stone, becoming a rock. 12.
Then, after a hundred years, through the grace of Jātavedas,
he was released by that very Siddha and attained delight there.
Having been liberated from that very curse by the same Siddha who had bestowed it, he attained delight and mental satisfaction. || 13 ||
Varṣa was the king of the inhabitants of Nālikera for eight years;
he was exceedingly righteous and subsequently regained his former memory.

Again, he relates the former account with the words "years" (*varṣāṇi*). The meaning is that, having gone from the land of Kānyakubja toward the northern direction, he became the king of those dwelling in a region where coconut trees predominate. "Prāksmṛtiḥ" means the recollection of the former account. || 14 ||
In the forest of wish-fulfilling trees to the north of Mount Meru, he dwelt for ten years with an apsaras, subsisting on coconut fruits.
Knowing the truth regarding the respiration of birds, he lived for many years in play within the nest of a female bird on a Śālmali tree in Śālmalidvīpa.

Again, he tells the news of the western direction with the verse beginning "vihaga" (bird). He was an expert in the *tattva*—that is, the secret—concerning the subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*) and comforting of birds; for this very reason, it was previously stated that he was carried across the oceans after being mounted on the back of Garuḍa.
The meaning is that he dwelt for ten years playing together with her in the nest of a female bird. || 16 ||
On Mount Mandara, in a bower of Mandāra trees upon soft ground,
a Kinnarī named Mandarī attended [him] for one day.
Immediately thereafter, on Mount Mandara, a Kinnarī attended upon that learned Paścimavipaścit who had gone there for one day.

Then the first [Purūravas], agitated by desire, passed seventy years together with the Apsarases, who were like the deities of the Nandana grove and the rows of kalpavṛkṣa trees in the forest on the shores of the Ocean of Milk.

Then Pūrva, having gone from the coconut grove to the shore of the Ocean of Milk, spent seventy years there, agitated by desire, among the rows of kalpavṛkṣa groves together with the celestial nymphs of the Nandana garden.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-third chapter, titled "The Roaming in All Directions," in the *Vasiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa*, the holy work of Valmiki, belonging to the *Deva-mānasa* lineage of the *Mokṣopāya*.
Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-third canto, titled "Wandering in All Directions," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and twenty-fourth canto.
Śrī Rāma said:
All of them consist of a single consciousness, even though they possess distinct bodies.
O Brahman, how did various desires come to arise within those who possess but a single body? || 1 ||
The worldly activity of even a single [Buddha] is accomplished through four bodies;
likewise, the monasteries of the wise are established upon various mountains throughout the continents.

Rāma raises an objection, stating that if there were four bodies in one and a single living soul (*ekajīvaka*), it would be impossible for them to have different desires—this is expressed in the verse beginning with "eka-": "Since there is but one consciousness—that is, the single witnessing-consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*)—and since they consist of that, there is but one body which has manifested in four ways; thus, those wise ones (*vipaścitaḥ*) possess but a single body. Furthermore, they possess but one embodied soul (*dehī*). Thus it is said.
The meaning is that, without a distinction between the living beings, a simultaneous difference in desire is untenable. || 1 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Though it is the single, dense space of consciousness, all-pervading and indeed without diversity, it has itself become as if manifold, like the mind within the Self during sleep.

Since even for a single *jīva*, through ignorance (*avidyā*), there is seen in dreams the conceptualization of various bodies and so forth, and since within those [bodies] there is seen the manifestation of diverse desires through the conceptualization of the states of enemy, friend, or neutral, Vasiṣṭha gives the following answer— “*ekasaṃvid*... (the single consciousness)— with the intention that at the beginning of creation, even while Brahmā is awake as a *jīva*, everything is possible provided such karma exists.
Because of its transparency, the Self itself is reflected within the Self in that manner;
for such a being, it is as clear as a stainless mirror.

Because that sky of dense consciousness is clear—being as exceedingly transparent as a mirror—the Self reflects itself within itself as if it had attained a state of manifoldness, just as the great space containing mountains, rivers, and so forth is reflected in the space within the belly of a mirror; such is the meaning. Even for one who is so clear, [it appears] in such a manner.
The remaining sense is that, just as in the case of a mirror, it is precisely its stainless transparency that is the cause for the manifestation of the various forms of the world. || 3 ||
Just as mirrors made entirely of the same metal reflect one another, so too do these ultimate entities reflect one another. (4)

[Objection: But surely the world, too, is in reality nothing but consciousness (*cit*). If that is so, how can there be a reflection of consciousness within consciousness itself? [Response: Listen to the illustration; thus he says, "one," etc. The meaning is: even though they are ultimately of the nature of consciousness (*paramārthataś-cidrūpāḥ*), because the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of *māyā* possesses inconceivable power, it is like [the appearance of] a city of Gandharvas on the surface of a crystal wall in the sky.
And the sense is that it is because the reflections of the moon, the sun, clouds, and the great sky are seen [in water]. || 4 ||
Therefore, whenever and whatever object appears before anyone,
it is appropriate that it serves that person's purpose,
because its sole intrinsic nature is the mass of consciousness. (5)

For this very reason, he says "by that" (*tena*), explaining that Brahman— which has the form of the superimposed world of objects of enjoyment— reflects within the consciousness of the individual soul (*jīvaciti*) as delimited by the intellect (*buddhi*), in the form of the experience of pleasant and unpleasant objects when there is contact between the sense organs and their objects. Whatever object of enjoyment comes before one and attains proximity, by means of that object, the soul is joined with it— that is, it becomes fit for its experience.
The meaning is that if the object of enjoyment were not reflected in the intellect (*buddhi*), then enjoyment itself would not be possible. || 5 ||
Thus, this is non-different even while being different; in reality, it is both different and non-different.
It is neither different nor non-different, and therefore its nature consists of both difference and non-difference.

If it is argued that the state of being both manifold and non-manifold in one thing is contradictory, and how this could even occur through *māyā*, and that therefore a logical justification must be stated for that—then he says: "Not so" (*na ca*). If there were merely a negation of manifoldness, then it would necessarily be of a single, uniform nature.
However, because the attribute of non-manifoldness is also negated, it is possible to conceive of it even as manifold; thus, there is no contradiction.
The meaning is "logical reasoning. || 6 ||
Therefore, whatever object first appears before a wise person,
he attains a state of pure consciousness through it and comes under its influence.

For this very reason, when the ripening of karma that grants the simultaneous enjoyment of various objects located in different directions occurs, the fourfold nature of a single body and so forth, as well as the simultaneous reflection of the objects of those respective locations within the intellect, are accomplished. With this intention, he says: "By that... (verse 7).
Though situated in a single place, yogins perform actions by pervading everywhere; they also experience all things throughout the three periods of time.

When it is well known that even for yogis such as Agastya and others—who reside eternally in a specific, fixed location like Mount Malaya—there is the capacity to experience everything through their presence in various places and times, past, future, and so forth, by the power of yoga;
then what need is there to mention this for wise men who have traveled to different lands? With this intention, he says:
"Regarding 'a single part' (ekadeśa): || 8 ||"
Time, though being a single entity possessing pervasiveness, performs distinct actions at the same time;
by means of that [pervasive] foot, it both produces and experiences delight.

He states that when a single entity simultaneously performs different actions in various locations, it is merely its pervasion of those respective places that is required, not a plurality of souls— thus he says, "The cloud" (*abda*). Just as a cloud (*abda*), which brings delight (*āhlāda*) to those afflicted by the heat,
due to its very greatness, simultaneously possesses pervasion over various cities, mountains, rivers, fields, and so forth;

Just as one who identifies with them performs distinct actions— such as washing a palace, breaking a peak, filling a reservoir, or nourishing crops— at the same time through various parts of his feet, and the individual soul (jīva) identifying with those [feet] experiences "these actions have been performed by me," so too should the logical consistency of this case be understood here. || 9 ||
Simultaneously and in incalculable numbers, those who are rivals to the Lord create and experience the web of karma that constitutes the world. (10)
Due to the attainment of powers such as atomization (aṇimā) and others, yogins become like unto the Lord.
Viṣṇu alone, by means of his four own arms or bodies,
protects the world while performing separate activities and enjoys excellent women.

Performing distinct activities—sometimes entering yogic sleep with four bodies, sometimes practicing asceticism, sometimes providing assistance as the younger brother of Indra, and sometimes enjoying various pleasures in Vaikuṇṭha—he protects the world; he enjoys, that is, experiences, beautiful women. || 11 ||
When he, possessing many arms, effects the gathering of two purposes with two hands,
he constantly engages in battle with many hands.

When there is the possibility of including two objects with two arms, then he includes them; and when there is the possibility of including them all together with all the hands, he does that as well. || 12 ||
In that very same way, by those wise ones who remained thus in every direction—even though they consisted of a single consciousness—transactions were conducted accordingly. (13)
He applies the analogies to the subject at hand with the words "in the same way": "The pleasure, pain, and so forth that were obtained... (is the ellipsis). 13–14.
By them [the senses], while asleep, pleasure was enjoyed upon beds of earth, and in other continents;
they roamed through forest groves and wandered across desert lands.
"Prakrāntam" means moved away. || 14 ||
He dwelt among the mountain ranges, wandered within the depths of the oceans,
rested upon the coastal strips, and hid himself amidst the thickets of clouds.
He remained hidden, stationed upon mountain peaks covered with dense rows of clouds. || 15 ||
They sported amidst the rising garlands of waves and the gusts of wind, upon the ripples of the water, on the shores of mountains and oceans, and within cities.
"Rūḍham" means manifested. || 16 ||
On the shore of the Sunrise Mountain in Śākadvīpa, he had slept for seven years within a dense thicket in the eastern interior,
deluded by a yakṣa;
having forcibly drunk the water of the rocks there, he turned into stone and remained situated within it.
Seven equal [periods] by natural birth of the earth. || 17 ||

Likewise, in the past, on the slope of the mountain Udayagiri, which is famous in Śākadvīpa, [the sage] Pūrvavipaścit slept for seven years within the thicket of a leafless *sruhī* tree, having been rendered unconscious by a yakṣa through the power of a deluding spell (*saṃmohana-vidyā*). By that same Pūrvavipaścit, having drunk somewhere on this mountain water containing pebbles—
Having been forcibly brought by power to the state of a stone— a condition of rock— and having become of the same nature as the earth, he remained within it for seven years.
In Śākadvīpa, on the summit of the Sunset Mountain, in a cloud-cave dwelling, the western [king] was made a lover for a month by a Piśāca-Apsarās. (18)
In a cave-dwelling sheltered from the clouds. || 18 ||
In that region of Śāntabhaya, on the great mountain Jaladhāra,
in the Harītakī forest, the eastern [Vidyādhara] attained invisibility.

In the region called Śāntabhaya, due to the curse of a certain sage regarding a division of land, he attained the state of a harītakī tree and became invisible to people; this lasted for seventy years. || 19 ||
Here, on Mount Raivataka, in the region named Śiśira,
there was a lion for ten nights who had previously been brought under the power of a Yakṣa.
There, having become like a frog in a cave of the Golden Mountain and other peaks,
he lived for ten years, deceived by the illusory power of the Piśācas.
In the caves, he took on the state of a frog—that is, the condition of a *bheka*. || 21 ||
Having reached the northern shore of Mount Śyāmā in Śākadvīpa during his youth,
the blind man lived at Andhakūpa for a hundred autumns.
He speaks again of Uttara’s end with the words "kaumāram" (childhood). Śyāma is from the Blue Mountain; "blind" means being like a frog. || 22 ||
In the year Marībaka, he spent fourteen years here;
subsequently, through the science of the Vidyādharas, he attained the state of a Vidyādhara.
He tells the news of the western region, beginning with "Marīcaka," by means of a mantra-lore that grants the status of a Vidyādhara. || 23 ||
Having embraced the breeze from the coastal forest, which is moistened by the spray from the gradual movement of the goddess Lakṣmī’s tremulous limbs—
she who is weary from the fatigue of her dalliance with the Enemy of Tripura (Śiva)— and which bears the fragrance acquired from embracing the cardamom creepers.
He states what he took as his support to attain the state of a *vidyādhara* at that time: "By means of *rata*," etc.

It was sprinkled—that is, permeated—by the droplets arising in succession from the lines of her limbs, which were trembling due to the excellence of her beauty (*lakṣmī*) and the exhaustion of Śiva (*purāri*) caused by the fatigue of sexual union (*rata*, i.e., *surata*). Likewise, it acquired the fragrance through embraces with the creepers of cardamom (*elālatā*) belonging to the coastal forest (*velāvana*).
"Taking hold of the wind that carries fragrance" means relying upon it as the cause of bliss. || 24 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-fourth canto, titled "The Description of Other Islands," in the *Vāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa*, the *Arṣa* [scripture], in the *Mokṣopāya* section of the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa*. 124.
Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-fourth sarga, titled "Description of Other Continents," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa-tātparya-prakāśa*. 124.
The one hundred and twenty-fifth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: On the mountain Jaladhāra, during the year known as Śāntabhaya, beneath a tree—
Drinking such water from the river Kartari while staying in Śākadvīpa, he remained there. || 1 ||
In this [work], the mutual assistance of the wise even in times of adversity,
as well as the universal performance of purposeful action by those liberated while living, is described.

There, having observed through signs Rāma’s doubt as to whether wise men wandering in different directions possess mutual awareness of one another and mutual assistance in times of calamity or not, Vasiṣṭha, desiring to dispel that doubt, first [described] the former case in the "Chapter on the Allaying of Fear," within the context of the "Harītakī Tree" section.

He speaks of the favor bestowed at the end: "In the year named Śāntabhaya" means in that year which is well-known by that name; here, in this year Śāntabhaya, on the mountain Jaladhāra—the mountain mentioned in the previous creation—within the Harītakī forest, he was in such a state, having become a *harītakī* tree.

Drinking with his roots the water connected to the rocks within the ground that resembled a pair of shears, the eastern Vipaschit remained there; then the western Vipaschit, having learned of that situation, arrived at that place, propitiated the sage who had pronounced the curse,
and by means of the lore granted by him, he cut off his state of being a tree as if with a saw.
The connection with the subsequent phrase is: "liberated from the state of being a tree. || 1 ||
Then, after seventy years had passed, he was released by the western [king] who came and,
like a tree cut down by the saw of knowledge, he emerged unharmed.
A person from the West who has turned to stone during the year of Śiśira was quickly liberated by one from the South through the application of beef and other such substances. (3)

In the same way, the western [prince] also, having turned to stone due to the curse of the lord of the Piśācas during the year known as Śiśira, approached from the south and, by means of the offering of beef and other substances, propitiated the lord of the Piśācas and was liberated. || 3 ||
When Śiva was situated on the far side of the western mountain (Asta), year after year,
one [demon] was liberated by coming from the south, while another was turned into a bull by the Gopi-Śākinī.
Having been turned into a bull by a Piśācī in the form of a cow through the Piśāca-vidyā, he was turned into a bull-Piśāca; then, from the west, he was liberated by the one from the south. || 4 ||
In this very Kṣemaka year, on the tree at Mount Āmbikeya, the southern one attained the state of a Yakṣa and, through that Yakṣa, obtained liberation. || 5 ||

The state of being a *yakṣa* implies a specific division among the *piśācas*. Since there is no purpose in liberating one who already possesses the nature of a deity or a *yakṣa*, [he was liberated] by means of the Lord of *Yakṣas*, who had been propitiated later by the *yakṣa*. || 5 ||
In this very Vṛṣaka year— [the reading "in the Kṣemaka year" also exists]— on Mount Kesara,
the former one who had become a lion was liberated by the latter.
Here, in this very Śākadvīpa.
Śrī Rāma said: O Blessed One, how is it that yogis, though situated in only one place, perform all actions throughout the three periods of time by pervading everywhere?
The meaning is that one must state the justification for how [the Lord], having pervaded everywhere and attained various [states], performs actions such as bestowing grace and so forth. || 7 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
O Rāma, let that which belongs to the unawakened in this world suffice for us;
however, hear now that which pertains to the awakened as it is being told.

With the view of yogis— that all phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*) is merely mind (*manomātra*), and that even when the mind functions simultaneously in all mental activities, its unrestricted sovereignty remains unimpaired, thereby making all actions possible— Vasiṣṭha gives the following reply,
beginning with "In this world" (*iha*): "O Rāma, from the perspective of those who are not awakened in this world..."
Since there exists a gross reality consisting of the elements and their derivatives, enough for us who are awakened with logical reasoning.
However, that which is pure consciousness or mere mind according to the vision of the awakened—that reality is capable of purposeful action everywhere;
listen to how this is established. This is the meaning. 8.
For those who know that [reality], there is no self other than the universal existence of pure consciousness alone;
for when the realization of the absolute non-existence of the visible occurs, the perceptions of creation and non-creation come to an end.

Regarding the view that the reality is consciousness alone (*cinmātra*), he states—beginning with "consciousness alone"—that for one who is the Lord of all, the performance of all purposeful actions is possible everywhere, just as it is for the Universal Lord.

For those who know that [reality], the knowers of truth, from the perspective of their vision, there exists nothing other than the universal existence of pure consciousness; that which has no self (or *ātman*) as its own nature is "non-self" (*anātma*). Here, the word *na* is not the negative particle *nañ*.
That is to say, it is devoid of intrinsic nature. || 9 ||
For one who rests incessantly in the universal commonality of the existence of pure consciousness alone,
there exists here at all times both the state of being the Lord of All and the state of being the Self of All.
Tell me: by what, how, where, when, and like what is anything obstructed?
For you are all-pervading and the self of all; tell me where, when, and in what manner [this obstruction] appears.
The interrogative particles (*kiṃvṛttāni*) are as before. It is "obstructed" (*rodhyate*), meaning it is prevented everywhere in the sphere of all purposeful activity (*sarvārthakriyā*).

Even by adopting the position that the world is created through perception (*dṛṣṭasṛṣṭipakṣa*), he states its non-obstruction with the word "all-pervading" (*sarvaga*). The word "now" (*atha*) serves to indicate an alternative position. 11.
When that shines forth then and there as the Self of all, what is there for us that is not [included]—the past, the present, and the future, the gross and even the subtle? (12)
"What do we have? What is that which, because of this, does not attain existence?"—this is the meaning. "The past," and so forth, is the elaboration of that point. || 12 ||
Likewise, distance and proximity, a moment and even an eon—these always remain within the universal [the general form], never abandoning its own nature. (13)
In the general [category], that is, in the generality of existence (sattāsāmānya); those [qualities] are the past and so forth. ||13||
Behold the manifestation of Māyā, which resides within the Self of all—unborn, unceasing, and established exactly as it is. 14.
Unceasing and undestroyed. || 14 ||
Therefore, these three worlds are indeed a single mass of consciousness;
and while not abandoning its nature as space, it remains as space itself, the self of all.
Precisely for this reason—that its existence is dependent upon the universal of being (sattāsāmānya)—it favors the unmodified Self, which is like the sky. || 15 ||

The Self of the world, appearing in the form of the world as the seer and the seen—since that which is the very vision of the Universal Self is the body itself, what could exist, by what means, in what manner, or at what time? 16.

For the Self of the world is variegated by *māyā*, and it is that very [Self] which arises in the form of the world through the relationship of seer and seen. But as for that body of the variegated Universal Self which consists of pure consciousness alone (*dṛṅmātra*), by what means, in what manner, at what time, or how could it exist? The meaning is that transformation (*pariṇāma*) or illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) and so forth are impossible in the case of the Pure [Self]. || 16 ||
O knower of reality, speak of that which is difficult to accomplish, for you understand the nature of both the achievable and the unachievable;
therefore, [speak] regarding this one, constant, and wise royal consciousness.

The meaning is that for the variegated [reality] which consists of both the achievable and the unachievable, there is nothing whatsoever that is difficult to accomplish; thus, the performance of all purposeful actions is always and everywhere possible. || 17 ||
For one who is following toward awakening but has not yet attained the supreme state—whether she be single or manifold—everything is applicable everywhere. (18)

He concludes by applying the resolution of Rāma’s question to the present context with the words "Therefore" (tasmāt). The meaning is that since the individual soul—such as Vipaścit and others—is merely the Lord’s consciousness appearing as distinct due to the difference in limiting adjuncts (upādhi), it is logical that everything can be produced everywhere; for although the consciousness is one, it assumes manifold states through the multiplicity of its adjuncts, just like fire and other elements. || 18 ||
For what indeed exists in the Supreme Self, whose very nature consists of both awakening and non-awakening?
Until supreme awakening is attained, it is only natural that there should be a confusion regarding objects. (19)

In that which is variegated (*śabala*) and whose nature consists of both awakening and non-awakening, what indeed could there be that is unattainable? This is the implied meaning. He states another argument for that very point:
"of that which has not been attained" (verse 19).
For one who has entered into some degree of awakening, that state of perfection is indeed appropriate;
thus, all those situated in every direction are entirely interconnected with one another.

He states the logical justification for the fact that yogis possess established perfection characterized by the capacity for purposeful action according to their will—beginning with the words "something" (kiñcit).
Because it is possible for there to be an intensification of freedom from desire through the progressive stages of awakening, there follows an excellence of bliss produced thereby;
thus, they treat—that is, they counteract—the disease of misfortune. || 20 ||
They perceive, experience, and quickly treat the crisis;
yet if the space of awakening were to deviate even slightly from its own nature, it would do so instantly. (21)

Regarding the view that for the awakened, all things are merely mind, the intention is that in such a conception, the performance of all purposes (arthakriyā) everywhere is even more appropriately established as being like a kingdom of the mind; with this in mind, he says: "In the space of awakening" (bodhākāśe). The sense is that, as has been explained many times in the section on origination, the state of mind is nothing other than a slight deviation from one's own true nature. || 21 ||
"Even though it remains exactly as it is, it assumes, as it were, the state of being something else.
Śrī Rāma said:
"If the wise are truly awakened, how could they assume the form of lions, bulls, and so forth? (22)
Even though he is well-established in his true state, because of the slight defect of deviating from that nature characterized as the state of the mind,

he simultaneously assumes otherness— the form of the world. Thinking that the wise ones are also awakened, Rāma [speaks] while the simultaneous accomplishment of all purposeful actions for awakened yogins has been described in the context of the wise one.

He raises an objection with the words "the wise" (*vipaścitaḥ*). The sense is that for those who are awakened, because they possess independence regarding all purposeful actions, there is no possibility of being constrained by dependence on others such as the bodies of lions or bulls; therefore, the statement regarding mutual assistance is inconsistent. || 22 ||
"O Brahmin, tell me quickly for the sake of my understanding: why do they go in all directions?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
"O noble one, those whom I have described as awakened are indeed yogis."
To the question, "How do yogis perform actions while being pervaded by you?", I have here described the awakened ones as yogis;
however, Vasiṣṭha clarifies that not even the wise are considered awakened yogis in this context, stating: "The awakened ones."

O mighty-armed one, the wise are not awakened by means of a logical consequence (prasaṅga) or through another form [of argument]; those who are truly wise are not awakened by you, for you are not skillful.

The meaning is that, for the sake of answering your question, [these matters] were told to you, the yogi, by way of an internal discourse with Vipaścit; however, they were not told even to Vipaścit himself with the intention that he was already awakened. || 24 ||
For they remain suspended, swinging between the two views of enlightenment and non-enlightenment; the signs of liberation are seen on one side, and the signs of bondage all around. (25)
If so, are they utterly deluded? No; he says "awakens" (bodhayati). This means those situated on the second stage (bhūmikā).
The signs of future liberation are discernment (viveka) and so forth; the signs of bondage are attachment (rāga) and so forth. || 25 ||
For those wise ones who are awakened to the eternal Dharma through that suchness,
the yogins do not go beyond by means of their retention.

The meaning is that by means of such a meditative concentration (dhāraṇā), which has been described as being of that nature and characterized by oscillation, yogis do not, however, attain the supreme state. || 26 ||
For those yogins of concentration have attained the perfections of concentration;
they have reached supreme awakening, in whom ignorance no longer exists.

The meaning is that for the practitioner of *dhāraṇā*— who attains perfection through the restraint of the mind upon the deity of fire in regions such as the heart— the ignorance (*avidyā*) has not been destroyed, unlike those who are practitioners of *jñāna-yoga*.
O lotus-eyed one, why do they look upon ignorance?
For these practitioners of concentration have indeed attained supernatural powers through their boon. (28)
If they are practitioners of the yoga of knowledge (*jñānayogin*), why would they look upon ignorance?

The meaning is that this very desire to see it is the sign that their ignorance has not been severed. At the conclusion of the ripening of their meditative concentration (*dhāraṇā*), they have attained supernatural powers (*siddhi*) through a boon born of the grace of the deity.
Ignorance exists for them; therefore, they do not investigate that [reality]. Listen to something else, O Rāma, concerning those embodied beings who are liberated while living (jīvanmukta). (29)

Those "wise ones" (vipaścitaḥ) do not investigate that [Reality], being devoid of inquiry into the Self. He declares another distinction between them and those liberated while living (jīvanmukta), for whom there is only the appearance of the body and so forth during the time of worldly activity, whereas in samādhi there is indeed equality with the liberation of the disembodied (videhakaivalya), by saying "and another," and so forth. || 29 ||
In the realm of conventional usage alone does the cognition of distinct objects exist;
even liberation is a property of the mind, and it abides in the mind itself. (30)
"In worldly activity" means precisely at the time of emergence [from meditation]. Why is it that they possess such a state only in meditative absorption? To this he says: "Liberation.

For liberation is the cessation of bondage for one who is bound. Since it is the mind alone that is bound, not the Self, liberation is also a property of that [mind] alone. Therefore, that liberation exists only when the mind is absorbed in samādhi, and not in the body, nor in the state of emergence when the body has come into being.
This is the meaning. || 30 ||
The mind does not possess the attributes of the body, nor does it ever depart from the body;
once liberated, the mind is never bound again.

"Not in the body" connects with what precedes. The meaning is that while worldly activity—which is a property of the body and dependent upon the existence of the body—does not cease even for one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*), this does not preclude his awareness of other objects. If it is then argued that the mind of the one liberated while living would also be bound as long as the body exists, he says "never" to refute this. || 31 ||
By what effort can a fruit fallen from its stalk be bound again? Even for those who have attained liberation while living, the body remains subject to the laws of the body.

A fruit that has fallen, having slipped from its stalk—by whom, even by one who is capable, could it be bound to the stalk again as before? By no one at all; this is the meaning. For this very reason, he says "But the body... (verse 32), [explaining] that for both the liberated and the unliberated, the persistence of the attributes of the body is equal, but not the persistence of the attributes of the mind.
Their mind, being focused on that, is indeed unshakable;
for liberation is not to be known by another, unlike the practice of concentration (dhāraṇā) and so forth. // 33 //

For this very reason, these [practitioners] cannot be recognized by others as being "liberated while living" (jīvanmukta), whereas those who have attained perfection through *dhāraṇā* and other means can be so recognized; thus he states another distinction in the verse beginning with "mokṣa. || 33 ||
This [self] is indeed self-cognizable, like the pleasure derived from tasting honey and the like;
it is that which, joined with pleasure and pain, personally experiences bondage. (34)

It is asked: how is it said that liberation, which is a property of the mind, is self-cognized? To this, he says: "self-cognized. The meaning is that, just like bondage, liberation—which likewise resides in the mind—is established solely through the direct experience of the witness (sākṣin). If both bondage and liberation are properties of the mind, then why is it that in the scriptures the Self is conventionally described as "bound" or "liberated"?

Regarding this, he says: "by means of pleasure and pain. The connection [of the verse] is as follows: this Self, which bestows its own experience, when joined with the mental attributes of pleasure and pain becomes the individual soul (jīva) who personally experiences bondage; when that mind is liberated, he is said in the scriptures to be liberated. || 34 ||
When that [state] is liberated, he is said to be liberated; indeed, he who bestows his own experience and whose mind is inwardly cooled is designated as "liberated. (35)
If this were the case, then the body and so forth would also be conventionally designated as "bound" or "liberated" by those two mental states;

to this he replies with the word "internal" (antar). It is proper—both for the sake of what is established by experience and for the sake of conventional usage—to accept that the superimposition of internal joy and suffering occurs only upon the internal conscious self (cidātman), and not upon external objects.
The intended meaning is "in the body and so forth. || 35 ||
Bondage is said to be a "heated mind"; it is not seen in the body and such.
Whether the body is cut into pieces or the kingdom is bestowed [as a gift], [the mind remains unaffected]. (36)

The reading *saṃtaptacitte* is an archaic sandhi (*ārṣa*). With the intention that, when the mind is disciplined, there might arise the misconception that liberation—a quality of the mind—resides in the body, just as bodily qualities do, he says: "in the body. *Kṛtte* means cut or severed. || 36 ||
For one whose mind is liberated while living, whether weeping or laughing, neither sorrow nor joy arises within; that state remains established.
That [state] is established as being connected to the body. || 37 ||
Even for one who grasps it, this experience exists only therein and not elsewhere;
scholars are seen broken, having undergone a transformation of form. (38)

[Objection: But surely people perceive mental states such as pleasure and pain even with respect to the body, as in "there is the pain of a thorn in my foot" or "there is the pleasure of sandalwood on my body. How then can it be said that the superimposition (adhyāsa) occurs only upon the Self? To this, he says:
"gṛhṇataḥ" (of one who perceives). Even for a person who perceives pleasure, pain, and so forth in the body through the relation of delimitation (avacchedakatā), [the sense of] "I..."

Since the experience "I am happy" or "I am suffering" culminates in the self alone, this conceptualization exists only there and not elsewhere, such as in external things like the body. For this very reason, those who do not accept superimposition upon the self—
namely the Cārvākas, Naiyāyikas, Sāṃkhyas, Buddhists, and Vaiśeṣikas— have arrived at different positions due to their misconception of the body and so forth as being the self.

It should be understood that those [other] scholars are seen to be broken and defeated because they have not found the means to liberation; or else, they are seen to be broken and vanquished by Vedāntins in the course of a debate. || 38 ||
For those liberated while living (jīvanmukta), by their very nature, there is never [attachment] to the body and so forth;
even when dead, they do not truly die, and even when weeping, they do not truly weep.
Or, even if there were some kind of experience of bondage—such as pleasure, pain, and so forth—even in the body, such an experience certainly does not exist for liberation.

This is because it is clearly experienced by those liberated while living (jīvanmukta) during samādhi when the body does not appear, and it is experienced, though faintly, by those of dull or middling knowledge at the time of emergence (vyutthāna) when the body does appear; with this intention, he says: "The body and so forth..."

"By its own nature" means by its nature as the eternal, bodiless Self. And thus says the Śruti: "The wise man does not grieve, having realized the great, all-pervading Self, which is bodiless and yet abides within bodies that are themselves unstable. For this very reason, he states that the Self is not joined with the attributes of the body, such as death, by saying: "Even when dead," etc. (39).

Laughing, the liberated one who has attained great prosperity does not laugh at all; those free from passion appear as if possessed by passion, and those without anger appear as if filled with anger. (40)
He states their lack of connection even with mental objects (manodharma) by saying: "those free from passion" (vītarāgāḥ). || 40 ||
Even those who perceive reality appear shrouded by delusion due to their lack of wisdom;
for such notions as "this is pleasure" and "this is pain" are merely mental constructions. (41)
Enough of those [theories] which have gone too far, like sprouts growing from the sky;
for the Self of the world does not exist at all, yet it is that of which everything is one.
The self of the world, whose very nature is the world—and by the use of the word "ca" (and), for whom that root-ignorance does not exist at all;

and for whom everything exists as the One, a single essence—such a one who is liberated while living: for him, the claim that pleasure, pain, and so forth exist, is like the statement that there are branches on the sky; such is the connection of the words. || 42 ||
The claim that "pleasure, pain, and so forth belong to him" is like a tree in the sky;
it is only those who are truly sorrowless who grieve, for the liberated while living are endowed with victory.
"In that state, what delusion and what sorrow can there be for one who perceives oneness?"—according to this Vedic scripture, they are endowed with the conquest of sorrow and delusion. (43)
Those who perceive reality see that the head of the Lotus-born [Brahmā], which is intensely devoted to chanting the Sāman hymns, appears as an undivided single entity. (44)

Even when their heads and other limbs were severed, they remained uncut, being of a single state of being and a non-dual self-nature. Where was that seen? He illustrates it with the word "head. In the word *gāyanam*, the absence of the substitution of *ā* for *i* is a Vedic (Chāndasa) irregularity. || 44 ||
Hara severed it with his fingernail as if it were a delicate lotus;
yet Brahmā, though capable, did not produce that head again.
The oneness of this space of consciousness with the [outer] sky is achieved through the head alone; what is the use of anything else?
For him, there is no purpose whatsoever here in what is done, nor in what is left undone. (46)

The meaning is: since this lotus-born one possesses oneness with space—that is, equality with the sky—what purpose is served by another, fifth head which is false and illusory? If so, for what reason does he perform the instruction of the Vedas with four heads? To that, he says: "Not at all" (naiva). || 46 ||
Whatever has attained its name according to its nature, let it remain so; what is the use of anything else?
Hara bears upon his body the fawn-eyed woman and the unceasing tears of Śarada, just as the Ocean of Milk bears the hidden digit of the nectar-moon.

"It has come about through the power of the karma of living beings"—this is the implied meaning. He states that even the Lord's activity follows solely the karma of living beings and is not for His own sake by saying "Hara": he bears the fawn-eyed woman on half his body from the god of love (Manmatha) when he is favored and his arrows are not exhausted; but when [he is] restrained...
"And because of the onset of an unimpeded samādhi, he bears tears of joy upon his body;
it is as if [he bears] a hidden digit of nectar—thus there is a double simile. (47)
Although capable, this noble-minded one does not abandon his state of passion;
for the virtues of dispassion were witnessed by him at the time of the burning of the five-arrowed god. (48)
He has no purpose whatsoever here through action, nor any through inaction;
nor does he have any dependence on any being for any object of desire. (49)
The attainment of the purpose is that which relies upon the meaning. || 49 ||
Let this [world] be full of passion for him; what is the use of another state, such as dispassion?
Whatever has come to pass in whatever manner, let it remain so; what is the use of anything else? (50)
The meaning is: whether by non-attachment or by another form of attachment, what gain or what loss is there? || 50 ||
Janārdana, though liberated while living, intensely acts and causes others to act, dies and is even killed; he is constantly born and grows. || 51 ||

He performs the subjugation of asuras and other such acts himself, or causes them to be done through Indra and others. He dies, accepting death at the conclusion of his incarnations; moreover, he is even put to death by those favorable to that end, such as the śarabha and the hunter.
And although he is capable of abandoning the state of being either slow or swift, he does not do so;
for by that which is abandoned there is no purpose for him, nor indeed by that which is resorted to.
Driven by the power of the karma of living beings, he is unable to abandon this state of constant coming and going and the preoccupation with worldly affairs. || 52 ||
"Let it remain exactly as it is here"—thus is the cessation of latent impressions (āśraya-parāvṛtti).
Hari remains entirely free from desire, bearing the nature of pure consciousness alone. (53)
The sun constantly and eternally swings his own self, which has become a ball of time, upon the courtyard of the sky within the house of the world. (54)

He states that even the sun and other celestial bodies, though devoid of desire, fulfill their respective offices solely in accordance with the karma of living beings—beginning with the words "the self" (ātmānam). He causes it to oscillate, that is, he causes it to revolve. || 54 ||
The Lord of Day is not capable of obstructing the body;
yet, though devoid of desire and extinguished, he remains exactly as he is.
One who is liberated while living is as if in nirvana. || 55 ||
The moon undergoes incessant waning in vain until the end of the kalpa;
yet, being liberated while living, it remains as it is, free from distress.
"Until the end of the eon" means up to the limit of the kalpa's conclusion; "decay" refers to consumption (rājayakṣmā). || 56 ||

Just as one liberated while living maintains his composure through his natural state, so does the fire remain steady, though it is exhausted by consuming the oblations of Marutta, Gaurīśa, Vīrya, Grāsa, and others.

During Marutta’s sacrifice, for a period of twelve years, the Lord of Gaurī was afflicted by indigestion caused by the consumption of oblations consisting of a continuous stream of clarified butter falling like the trunk of an elephant; consequently, when the gods attempted to create obstacles at the confluence of the Gaurī at the time of Skanda’s birth, he was shaken from his place.

By the command of the Brahman Vīrya, there was consumption and drinking [of the waters] through the internal burning induced by him; and by means of the carrying of oblations, the seizing of the gods' property, the hiding in the waters, and so forth—[the reading being "by the carrying of oblations, the seizing of the gods' property," etc.]—the gods were tormented day and night. || 57 ||
Though they were liberated while living, their two gurus, Śukra and Bṛhaspati, remained in this world like wretched men, occupied with many desires for victory.
By means of desires for victory, that is, by mutual wishes for conquest. || 58 ||
The sage Janaka rules the kingdom with a mind liberated while living, wearing down his body in fierce battles upon this earth. (59)
In battles, that is, in wars. || 59 ||
Nala, Māndhātṛ, Sagara, Dilīpa, Nahuṣa, and others—
liberated while living— ruled their kingdoms for a long time as if they were free from all agitation.
In worldly affairs, the ignorant and the wise are indeed exactly the same;
for it is only the presence or absence of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) that is the cause of bondage and liberation.
Bali, Prahlāda, Namuci, Vṛtra, Andhaka, Mura, and others—
liberated while living and free from passion— maintained their worldly positions as if they still possessed passion.
Therefore, whether there is non-existence or existence, and whether there is the destruction or arising of passion and hatred,
there is not even the slightest difference regarding the nature of the cognizer, who is of the nature of pure consciousness.

Demonstrating that by this the doubt regarding liberation— even when there is the appearance of passion and aversion in those liberated while living— is dispelled, he concludes with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). With reference to the sky of consciousness (*jña-kha*), which is the space of consciousness of one liberated while living,
whether passion and aversion have ceased or arisen, whether they exist or do not exist— that is, whether they are present or absent— [the state remains unchanged].
Whether in the state of misconduct or in liberation—which is the manifested true nature—there is not even the slightest difference or doubt.
For those who, through knowledge as pure as the sky, perceive all phenomena to be like the ether, how could there be any notion of duality in those who are liberated while living? (64)
"If the notion of duality, 'I am not Brahman,' were present, there would indeed be doubt regarding liberation; however, He says that such a notion does not exist for them:

those beings who—by means of the knowledge consisting of the final direct realization (*sākṣātkāra-vṛtti*)—maintain their bodies, minds, vital breaths, and so forth, perceive them as being like the sky, in the state of the non-dual, full Brahman which is unattached and similar to space."
For those who are liberated while living, since the ignorance that causes the delusion of duality has been destroyed, from where could the notion of duality arise again?
The meaning is: from what cause could it possibly be conceived? || 64 ||
Just as the radiant bow of Indra appears as if manifold though it is empty,
so too this delusion consisting of the visible world is a mere appearance.

If it is asked, "By the direct realization of reality (*tattva-sākṣātkāra*), how is the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the world (*jagat*) sublated?"—with the intention that [this distinction] is established as mere illusion (*bhrānti-mātra*), he establishes its lack of substantial reality (*avastutā*) by means of an illustration, beginning with the words "luminous" (*bhāsvara*). "Śakra’s bow" (*śakrakodaṇḍa*) refers to Indra’s rainbow. "The rays of the sun situated within a mass of clouds" (*megha-paṭala-sthāḥ sūrya-raśmayaḥ*).
It is well known that they are seen in the form of Indra’s bow (the rainbow). || 65 ||
Just as various colors shine in the expanse of the sky within a rainbow,
so too are the atoms of the cosmic egg essentially empty by nature.
Atoms have the nature of the cosmic egg.
This world appears as non-existent yet manifests as if it were real;
it is unborn and unceasing, just like emptiness in the sky.
Manifestation means being made evident. Unborn means unarisen. Unceasing means undestroyed. || 67 ||
Though having a beginning and an end, it is without beginning or end; though not empty, it is empty.
Thus the world is both born and unborn, unobstructed and indeed obstructed.
The word *tathā* is used here in the sense of "even" (*api*). Even that which is born is as if unborn; that which is obstructed is as if unobstructed; that which is destroyed is as if undestroyed.
The meaning is that even when perceived as the world, the reality—which is eternally immutable, unattached, and non-dual—is not subject to beginning, end, or the like.
Thus, Brahman, appearing just like the sky, shines forth as if born and as if obstructed.
Just as a pillar is made of wood, so too is its carved figure.

If it is argued that, just as the state of the world exists, so too the state of its birth and cessation is established in Brahman through conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), then this is an accepted consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*); for immutability (*kauṭasthya*) is not impaired by mere conceptual construction—with this intention, he says "jātam" (it is born). Just as a pillar made of wood is indeed wood, so too the statue (*śālabhañjikā*) situated in one part of that pillar is also indeed wood; such is the meaning. || 69 ||
One should know that the world is composed of that which is free from all temporal divisions, equal, sleepless, and the seat of the solitary space of consciousness. || 70 ||
He says—beginning with "samasta"—that one should superimpose upon experience, through the vision of samādhi, the non-conceptualization that the world is indeed Brahman alone:

"By means of samādhi, when there is a state of equanimity free from all mental constructions and devoid of sleep—an abiding as the Self alone—one should know that world to be composed of that, consisting of nothing but that. (70)

One should know that the form of consciousness which exists in the interval when moving from one place to another, being without expansion, is the space of consciousness; the entire world is composed of that. || 71 ||

Even in the case of not being in meditative absorption (*asamādhi*), when one perceives the moon on a tree branch through a mental modification (*buddhivṛtti*), and as that modification moves from the location of the branch to the location of the moon, there occurs in the interim a state of consciousness whose nature is manifested by that modification and which is devoid of objects; one should know that the world consists of this.
Thus he says: "From the location... (verse 71).
In that regard, as for that non-duality or unity, I consider even that not to exist at all;
it appears as mere space, and I consider even that not to exist at all.

In that such Self of Consciousness (*cidātman*), whatever duality appears in the form of particulars, and whatever unity appears in the form of a universal—that too, I consider through reflection and determine by means of contemplation, to be none other than that very nature of the space of Consciousness; it does not exist at all. Even that which appears as mere void or emptiness is likewise not real, for [the Self] is of the singular essence of full bliss (*pūrṇānandaikarasa*).
The meaning is that even emptiness would be untenable. || 72 ||
This very world is indeed the ether of consciousness; it exists within the Self by the Self alone.
Though clearly perceived and vast as a city yet to be built, it remains manifest [as such].

In the world, emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and fullness (*pūrṇatā*) are well-known as being relative, such as when one says "the jar is empty of water" or "the jar is full of water. That [kind of relativity] does not apply to the Self; rather, because this world—the state of being a world—is absolutely unestablished, its emptiness is simply that "this is just space. In this way, the Self alone is within the Self.

"Established" (*saṃsthita*) means fullness that is independent of anything else. The meaning is as follows: just as a city yet to be built is seen now as a vast expanse of space, time, and so forth, through a voidness that is independent of any counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), and just as [that space] is clearly seen as fullness independent of any counter-correlate, so it is here. || 73 ||
The entire range of perceivable phenomena remains as silent as the self, as tranquil and solid as a stone, with an intention as clear as the expanse of space.
Alas, what a delusion is this *māyā*—that by bestowing upon it the name "world," this very Self seems to be deluded! 74

O Rāma, that collection of visible objects—which, though appearing as solid as stone, remains as tranquil Brahman alone, like the vast expanse of space within a clear-minded person—exists merely under the name "the world," which is in fact his own self; yet, having fashioned this designation, he stands as if deluded.
Oh, how truly wondrous is this illusion! This is the meaning. || 74 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-fifth canto, titled "The Consideration of Liberation while Living," in the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa*, the *Arṣa* (sage-authored) work, in the *Vālmīkīya*, *Devarāja*, *Mokṣopāya*, *Nirvāṇa*, *Uttara*, and *Avimukta* sections. 125.
Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-fifth canto, titled "The Attainment of Liberation while Living," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa-tātparyaprakāśa*.
The one hundred and twenty-sixth canto.
Śrī Rāma said:
"O best of sages, what did the Vipracittas do immediately after that?"
They resided in those quarters of the world, including the continents, oceans, forests, and mountains.
For all those who have died here, the delusion of cyclic existence within their own minds is described as ending with the vision of the northern pit of darkness.
Having gone to those directions beginning with the east, what were those wise ones doing? || 1 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Listen, my dear, to what happened there to these wise ones as they wandered among the islands, mountains, and forests thick with rows of palm and tamāla trees.
What is their conduct? Their history. || 2 ||
A certain wise man on the western shore of the mountain of Krauñcadvīpa was crushed by the elephant against the mountain slope,
like a lotus crushed by its stalk.

Among them, one wise man was crushed—meaning ground to pieces and killed—by an elephant on a rampart-stone at the edge of a mountain on the western shore of the region famous as Krauñcadvīpa. At the time of requesting a boon, he had said: "May death come to us upon a path that cannot be traversed even by the Siddhas."

Thus, because of the context of the limit (*avadhi*), it is understood—even though not explicitly stated—that "the path (*adhvan*) is to be realized through the Siddhas" after that; this should be understood similarly in what follows as well.
The second, his limbs mangled by the Rākṣasa, was carried through the sky and cast into the Vāḍava fire,
where he was reduced to ashes.
The second, Vipaścit, his limbs wounded in battle by the Rākṣasa, was carried through the sky via the celestial path and cast into the submarine fire; there he was reduced to ashes. || 4 ||
The third was indeed led by a Vidyādhara to the realm of the Thirty-three;
having gone there, he was reduced to ashes by the curse of Indra, who was angered by his failure to prostrate.
He went to the thirteenth region, the assembly hall of Indra; and there, due to his failure to bow down and offer salutation, he was reduced to ashes by the curse of the enraged Śakra. || 5 ||
The fourth, traveling swiftly, was torn into eight pieces by a crocodile difficult to resist on the bank of a mountain in Kuśadvīpa, at the edge of a river.
The fourth, Vipaścit, was cut into eight pieces by a crocodile on the bank of a mountain in the marshy region of Kuśadvīpa; the meaning is that he died. || 6 ||
Thus those four kings, like the world-protectors, met their destruction when the four quarters were overwhelmed, their minds agitated in every direction.
Thus, in this manner, those four wise kings met their end in death, just as at the dissolution at the end of a kalpa, the four world-protectors (lokapālas) go to their destruction. || 7 ||
Then, due to the impressions of his former consciousness, he perceived for those who were of the nature of space within the sky itself the circle of the earth as being of the nature of space.
Then, immediately after death, their self became the consciousness-space (saṃvidvyomātmā) and, within that very space, beheld the terrestrial sphere just as before. || 8 ||
It possesses a girdle of seven islands and oceans, adorned with cities and ports;
it is the pedestal for the summit of the divine mountain and the crest-jewel of the world of Brahmā.
He describes what kind of earthly realm he saw at that time, beginning with "saptadvīpa" (the seven islands): "The mountain of the gods" refers to Meru;
it is that whose height is like a throne for the head. "Brahmaloka" here refers to the abode of Brahmā situated upon Meru. || 9 ||
With the orbs of the moon and sun for its eyes, a cluster of stars for its necklace of pearls, the flickering clouds for its garment, and various forests for its body hair; (10)
She perceived the bodies of those four wise ones,
as pervasive as the sky and the horizons at the end of an eon, just as they had been before.
A *kalpa* is a dissolution; upon its reversal, at the time of the commencement of creation, the term "heaven" (*dyau*) refers to the *prajāpatis* who were created first therein. (11)
Due to their experience of the subtle body (ātivāhika), those whose nature was like space perceived before them the manifestations of the gross physical body within that very void.
Then those wise ones perceived that the appearance of space within the non-spatial self, which is consciousness itself, is of the very nature of that self;
for, regarding the phenomenal body— which is the object of a mere mental appearance arising from the knowledge of the subtle body—
they beheld before them the states of grossness, inertia, and so forth, which are caused by its being a physical body.
In order to examine how great this ignorance might be in its nature as the self,
all four of them proceeded forward by the force of their mental impressions.

While this very body is thus determined [to be non-self], the Self remains unknown; yet, when that [body] exists as the self, they proceed—driven by past impressions—to investigate how much and of what measure this ignorance, consisting of the visible earth and so forth, might be. || 13 ||
Seeking to perceive the ultimate nature of the experience of the earth's circle as both the seen and the seeing, they wandered through other continents out of ignorance.

In order to perceive the limit—the delimitation by way of measure—of the culmination of ignorance, which takes the form of the experience of the terrestrial sphere situated between the seen and the seeing. || 14 ||
Having crossed seven continents and seven great oceans,
the wise Vipaścit reached Janārdana in the land of Ghanabhūmi.
Among them, the last, Vipaścit, by the power of the rise of his fortune, reached and beheld Janārdana playing upon the Ghanabhūmi, the ground previously described as being like solid gold.
Therefore, having attained incomparable knowledge in the various directions,
he remained in that very state of meditative absorption for five years.
Therefore, having obtained incomparable knowledge—the science of Brahman—from Janārdana, he remained for five years in that very region, absorbed in meditative concentration (samādhi). || 16 ||
Then, having abandoned the body once consciousness had attained its true being,
that very vital breath of his entered the supreme space of ultimate liberation.

Having abandoned the body and the sense of being a body—according to the method described in the narrative of Vītahavya—he attained the existence of consciousness in the mind as the nature of pure Being (*sanmātra*), or rather, the reading may be "non-existence" (*asattā*). That wise man attained supreme *nirvāṇa*, which is absolute liberation (*kaivalya*), just as his vital breath attained the state of space (*ākāśa*); this is an illustration for all sixteen digits (*kalā*). The digits have departed.
"Establishment is fifteenfold," according to the sacred scripture. || 17 ||
Having long contemplated his body situated at the side of the moon’s orb during the full-moon festival, he remained in the city of the Moon with his physical form vanished.

The wise man, having previously set out toward the eastern direction on the full-moon day (rākā), remained for a long time beside the orb of the cool-rayed full moon—that is, in the presence of the moon—contemplating his own body as being like that of Indu until the dawning of its true nature; thus, with his physical body dissolved, he came to abide in the city of the Moon. But is this not improper?
For indeed, among all four bodies, there is but one conscious individual soul (*vipaścij-jīva*) residing in a divided state, as in the case of the yogic multiplication of bodies (*kāyavyūha*).

When that soul attains liberation through knowledge by virtue of Viṣṇu’s grace within its final body, who else could then go to the world of the moon from the previous body of Vipaschit by means of the meditation on the moon? For it is not possible for two [different] bodies of the very same single soul [to have separate destinies].

In some cases liberation and in others bondage would both be simultaneously and equally valid, which would entail that the fruit of liberation is partial and limited. Nor is it logical for one [individual] to assume four bodies and thereby become four distinct souls, or for another soul to arise [from him]. In the first case, regarding the fourfold division, the original soul— [The text continues: ...would be subject to the aforementioned defects. Furthermore, if the soul were to undergo such a transformation, it would result in the loss of its essential nature as a single, indivisible entity. Thus, the doctrine of the soul's division into multiple parts is untenable. Moreover, if the soul were to remain one while manifesting in four forms, it would contradict the scriptural injunctions concerning the unity of the self. Therefore, the theory of the soul's division must be rejected. Instead, the appropriate view is that the soul remains one, and its apparent multiplicity is merely an illusion caused by the limiting adjuncts (upādhis). This preserves the integrity of the soul and avoids the logical fallacies of partiality and limitation inherent in the theory of division. Thus, the soul is eternally one, and its liberation is absolute and universal. Any notion of partial liberation or limited results contradicts the fundamental principles of Vedānta. Consequently, the soul does not become fourfold; rather, it remains a single, undivided reality throughout all its states. This conclusion is consistent with the teachings of the Upaniṣads and the authoritative commentaries thereon. Therefore, the hypothesis of the soul’s division into four parts is logically and scripturally indefensible. The soul is one, and its manifestation in various bodies is a mere appearance, not a real fragmentation of its essence. This establishes the unity of the self as the final truth. Any other position leads to contradictions in both reason and revelation. Hence, the soul is not divided, but remains eternally one and whole. This is the correct understanding of the nature of the individual self. The notion that the soul becomes fourfold through the assumption of four bodies is a misconception. The true state of the soul is unity, and its liberation is complete and unconditioned. To suggest otherwise is to undermine the very foundation of spiritual liberation. Because [otherwise] there would be the consequence of universal destruction. Even in the second case, since there would be an absence of the seeds—such as the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of desire and action—for those newly arisen [beings], the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) would not occur. Furthermore, it is impossible to account for the diversity of bondage and liberation through actions or through *māyā* without contradicting [the principle that] the diversity of experience is [already] established by them.
If it be argued that this is because liberation does not depend upon action and because it contradicts scriptural texts regarding the cessation of universal illusion (*māyā*), we reply: True.

However, the intention of the venerable Vasiṣṭha appears to be this: there is no such thing as a "living soul" (*jīva*) distinct from the space of Brahman (*brahmākāśa*). For Brahman itself, through *māyā*, is divided within the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the internal organs.
That which appears as if wandering in accordance with the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of desire and action residing therein is called the *jīva*.
In that state, when many internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*) congregate like lamps, there arises both unity and an increase [in capacity].
And for a single [organ], by virtue of causes such as the grace of a deity or yoga, multiple contradictory locations [of consciousness] may occur simultaneously.

When there arises, through the convergence for the sake of that experience, a latent impression (*vāsanā*) of karma characterized by identical desires and a capacity for enjoyment pertaining to the same place and time, then there occurs the state of being a single living being (*ekajīvatva*). Due to parsimony (*lāghava*), until the emergence of karma caused by experiences in contradictory places, there results a single body as the locus of experience. This is just as the life-force (*jīva*) of Yudhiṣṭhira [was shared] by Dharma and Indra.

Just as there is one single life-force (*jīva*) through the union of Bhīma with Vāyu and Indra; or as Arjuna’s life-force becomes one through the union of two Indras and Nara; or as there is one life-force for Nakula and Sahadeva through the union of Indra and the two Aśvins; so too, Draupadī has one life-force through the union of the portions of Nārāyaṇī, Lakṣmī, and Gaurī.

This is well known from the consideration of the narrative of Pañcendra and others. Or, for example, it may be inferred that Agni and Vāyu became a single soul through their union during the incarnation of Agastya as a result of Indra’s curse. Furthermore, when a single soul is divided by various limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), there is also the state of being many souls. [Thus, Indra obtained] a son from Kaśyapa who was the slayer of Indras in the womb.
When Indra first cut the embryo— which had entered the womb of Diti while she was sleeping in a state of impurity—
into seven parts, there were seven living beings; then, when each of those was again cut into seven, fifty-nine Maruts were produced, resulting in fifty-nine living beings.
