Furthermore, in the case of plants such as the banyan tree, sugarcane, and dūrvā grass, which grow from stems and branches, we observe life through their continuous sprouting from every branch and every stem; thus, the division of a single living being into multiple individual selves due to limiting adjuncts (upādhi) is even more well-established.
And so, in the present case as well, as long as the four living beings arise with identical desires and actions, they exist as a single body.

Whether one conceives that the governance of a kingdom and the movement to other regions through the division of bodies and so forth occurs upon the arising of activities to be enjoyed in hostile or divided lands, or whether one conceives that a single *vipaścit* soul becomes four souls like the wind due to the division of its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), there is no consequence of universal liberation following the liberation of one; nor is there [any such fault].
If a single soul were produced by the union of many [souls], that new soul would lack karma, and thus transmigration would be impossible;
for according to the theory of *ārambhavāda* (the doctrine of new production), the arising of a brand-new soul is not admitted.
Even when the Gaṅgā and Yamunā rivers meet and attain oneness, there is no notion of a "new Gaṅgā" arising, but rather the recognition: "This is that very same [river]."

Just as there is no contradiction in two things existing as a single entity through the recognition "This is the Ganges," so too there is no contradiction in the two beginningless living beings (jīvas) existing as one;

for when the two limiting adjuncts (upādhis) merge into oneness, the merging and oneness of that which is conditioned by them (the jīva) is established by all experience. This is so even in terms of their unity.

This is because of the possibility of experiencing the fruits of past karma. Thus, when one person exists as four living beings, since there is non-difference from the previous single living being through recognition, the heaps of desire, karma, and latent impressions residing in that [being] are established as divided fourfold;
consequently, the occurrence of transmigration is possible there, such that even when one is liberated, another remains bound.

Furthermore, the occurrence of saṃsāra is due to the absence of knowledge. Nor does this entail the contingency that the fruit of liberation is either partial or limited; for even when individual (vyaṣṭi) jīvas are liberated, it is logically consistent—just as in the case of liberation at the end of one's office—that the universal (samaṣṭi) Hiraṇyagarbha-jīva remains [in its state] until the conclusion of its authority. Indeed, [this is not so] for the universal self...

The knowledge of reality belonging to Hiraṇyagarbha results in liberation that is limited and occasional for individual souls (vyaṣṭi) when liberation is otherwise absent; whereas in a case where liberation occurs even while existing [in the world] through the non-difference of the individual and the universal (samaṣṭi), there is a merging of liberations— this being so when a present distinction of individual souls exists, [liberation is attained] merely by virtue of the prior non-difference from Him.

There is no occasion at all for the contingency of a confusion of liberations (*mukti-saṃkara*). Furthermore, the scriptural statement, "And finally, there is the cessation of the entire *māyā*," is intended to mean the cessation of the seeds of all the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) belonging to each respective individual soul (*jīva*). Otherwise, by the liberation of a single person, it would follow that all other souls—even those devoid of knowledge—would attain liberation. As it is said: "Whosoever among the gods awakened, he alone [became immortal]."

Furthermore, this would render void numerous Śruti and Smṛti passages such as: "Thus it was for the sages, and likewise for men; many, purified by knowledge and austerity, have attained my state. Nor can one [be motivated] by the hope of liberation attainable through many future births for those of dull faculties in the present age.

It should not be argued that there would be no performance of the means of attainment (sādhana) because of the doubt that if one single self were many individual souls, there would be the persistence of bondage and the non-cessation [of it] even when liberation occurs for some; for such a doubt regarding the impossibility of liberation would not be removed. This is because one engages in the practice of the means to liberation [precisely] because even a small portion of this dharma protects one from great [evil].

"O dear one, no doer of good ever goes to a miserable state because of fear; rather, having attained perfection over many births, he then goes to the supreme goal"— in accordance with the authority of this *smṛti*, there must necessarily arise knowledge either gradually or all at once in all cases, whether through the non-distinction or the distinction [of the self] as various individual souls (*jīvātman*) in subsequent births, occurring together with the purificatory impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the means of realization.

For it is possible to engage in the performance of the means [of liberation] by means of inference; indeed, this has been described in the *Bhikṣu-Jīvaṭa-upākhyāna* regarding how, at the end of his state as various living beings—which he had attained through a casual resolve despite being one who performed the means—a mendicant came to possess the nature of Śatarudra. All [the souls]...

The liberation of the individual souls (*jīva*) who have been so divided consists in the attainment of knowledge. Nor does this entail the undesirable consequence of the liberation of all souls, for such a consequence is accepted [as our position]. From the perspective of *māyā*, because of the infinity of *māyā*, its form is not perceived here in that way; it has neither end nor beginning, nor does it have a fixed foundation; it is eternally the very embodiment of the world, and by it all this [is pervaded].

This is because it is established by such Smṛti texts as "It is spread out" (*tatam*). However, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*tattvadṛṣṭi*), for one who holds that the individual soul (*jīva*) does not exist at all, liberation would be impossible.

Nor is there a contradiction with the Śruti text, "Other than this, everything is afflicted" (*ato 'nyad ārtam*), since that Śruti is consistent even if interpreted merely as the affliction of individual manifestations;
for even though the stream [of manifestations] is infinite, there is no contradiction, as the destruction of the final manifestation alone constitutes the destruction of the stream.

Since the final individual instance of the saṃsāra of all living beings is not established, its destruction is likewise unestablished. In the present case, however, because of the grace of the Lord arising from the ripening of devotion to Him, a single late-born wise man attains knowledge, but not others; thus, liberation is possible for that one alone. || 18 ||
In Śālmalidvīpa, the southern king, having destroyed his enemies, still exercises sovereignty today, for he has not forgotten his former resolve toward the virtuous.

Now, it is said what the wise one on the right did there: "The right one," etc. Being such that his enemies were destroyed, he was one by whom the determination of other [external] objects—the ascertainment of external things—was forgotten due to the attainment of the *sat*, the ultimate reality; yet he was not [simply] one who had forgotten it. || 19 ||
In the seventh ocean, where the waves were tossed by violent surges,
he dwelt for a thousand years within the belly of a sea-monster.
In the seventh ocean, the salt-water sea, having been swallowed by a makara, he dwelt for one thousand years within the belly of that sea-monster.
Feasting on the flesh from the belly of the Makara when the lord of the Makaras had died,
he emerged from the depths of the ocean like a Makara itself.
Regarding that, he states what his food was there: "In the belly of the sea-monster," etc. (verse 21).
Then, having crossed eighty thousand yojanas of the dense earth— the belly of the ocean of water that resembles snow— he reached the very thick interior.

Then, having crossed eighty thousand yojanas beyond the ocean of sweet water whose waters were like snow, he reached a great golden land characterized by a very dense and vast foundation; such is the connection with the subsequent verse. || 22 ||
Having reached the great earth, ten thousand yojanas in extent,
he died upon that golden ground which is the path frequented by the gods.
And in that state, and in its midst, Vipaścit attained the state of being unmanifest;
like a piece of wood placed in the middle of a fire, he instantly attained the nature of fire itself.
Then, having died on that ground, that Vipaścit attained the supreme state of a god, the condition of being a celestial being;
just as a piece of wood situated in the midst of fire attains the state of fire in an instant, so it was with him. || 24 ||
Having become the Pradhāna-god, he went to the Lokāloka mountain,
which stands like a basin for this tree that is the terrestrial globe.

That wise and preeminent deity, having become the best of gods, went from there to the Lokāloka mountain due to his latent desire (*vāsanā*) to travel toward the previously mentioned horizons. Of what nature was the Lokāloka mountain? To the north of it, at the base of this terrestrial sphere—which, because of its height, is mostly covered with trees—is a peak of Mount Meru that serves like a basin or a dam.
It is established. || 25 ||
It rises fifty thousand yojanas high;
one part of it is rich with light, the world, and conduct, but not the other.
Of this Lokāloka mountain, one—the first—portion is rich with the light of the sun, with the conduct and the social dealings of people; the other, however, is not.
Having reached the summit of the Lokāloka mountain and remaining within the path of the stars,
they saw him situated below, suspecting him to be a lofty constellation.
By ascending Mount Lokāloka, he reached its summit; the people remaining below beheld that divine Vipracitti, suspecting him to be a star.
Beyond that region, on the other side of that great mountain,
lies a vast chasm extending in all four directions— a void like the sky, infinite and empty.

On the far side of that great mountain, in the region beyond, there was darkness. On all four sides, surrounding it, was a vast trench in the form of a moat—a pit as infinite as the sky, devoid of all living beings, and extending for many yojanas. || 28 ||
Then this terrestrial globe is indeed completed in its spherical form;
beyond it is the void of space, a great abyss filled with darkness.
In that state, know that there exists neither darkness blue as collyrium or the interior of a tamāla tree, nor earth, nor anything moving;
nor does any object whatsoever exist as a support, even in the slightest degree, at any time. (30)

O Rāma, in that pit there is only blue darkness, like a bee, like collyrium, or like a tamāla tree in the midst of the sky; there is neither earth nor any moving living beings; there is no support and no refuge; and you should know that no collection of objects whatsoever ever comes into existence there. This is the meaning. || 30 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-sixth canto, titled "The Deeds in Previous Births of the Wise Vipaścit," in the section on Nirvāṇa, within the Mokṣopāya of the glorious Vāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa of the Holy Vālmīki, composed by the Sage.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Conduct of Vipaścit in a Previous Birth," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa within the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The one hundred and twenty-seventh canto.
Śrī Rāma said: "O Blessed One, tell me this: how is the terrestrial globe situated?"
How does the host of bears travel, and how is the Lokāloka mountain?
The stability of the earth, the stellar sphere, and so forth,
as well as the space beyond them and the stability of the pair of hemispheres of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), are described here.

This is a supplementary inquiry regarding Rāma: How does the terrestrial globe remain without a support? How do the host of stars and the circle of constellations move and revolve without a support? And what is the reason for the name of the mountain Lokāloka as described by you? (1)
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Just as a ball fashioned by the imagination of a child remains in the sky,
so too does the earth imagined by the Child of Pure Consciousness exist in the void.

Regarding that, Vasiṣṭha first gives the answer to the initial question with the words "Just as... (yathā). A *vīṭā* is a ball. The meaning is that even the earth, imagined by Hiraṇyagarbha—who is but a child of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*)—stands thus in the sky, the ether, and does not fall. || 2 ||
Just as those with cataract-afflicted eyes perceive hair, moons, and so forth,
so too, at the beginning of creation, the space of consciousness perceives the earth and other elements.
He says "yathā" (just as) to show that the possibility of falling due to false views must be prevented. *Timirika* means "one who has *timira* (a visual disorder).
The suffix *ṭhan* is used here in the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*). || 3 ||
Just as a city of imagination, though being maintained, is not seen,
so too the experience of the earth is maintained and maintained by the consciousness.
Being supported by some substrate, it is not seen nor experienced as being so supported;

for although it is supported by pillars, walls, and so forth that are purely conceptual (*sāṃkalpika*), nevertheless, because such conceptual pillars and the like lack substantial reality, it is not truly supported—nor is it supported at all. This is the meaning. || 4 ||
In whatever manner and to whatever extent consciousness manifests, by virtue of its own nature as consciousness,
it manifests in that very way and to that same extent, being of that very essence in each respective instance.

With the intention that since the establishment of the intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) of all things depends upon consciousness (*cit*), one might infer that the earth—which is established by consciousness in the form of a globe—is possessed of such an intrinsic nature itself, he says: "Whatever [is] as [it is]" (*yadyathā*).

"Of that nature" (*tadātmakam*) refers to the intrinsic nature of the thing; "in that manner" (*tathā*) refers to its specific mode of being; "for so long" (*tāvat*) refers to the intrinsic nature of its lifespan and destiny (*niyati*).
It is grasped. || 5 ||
Just as one whose eyes are afflicted by cataracts perceives a mass of hair in the sky, so too does the globe of the earth appear to pure consciousness; yet it remains exactly as it is.
Regarding the phrase "the perception of hair, a moon, and so forth," he clarifies the perception of hair with the words "in darkness" (*timira*), etc. Thus, it exists solely through delusion. (6)
Rivers flow upwards and fire burns beneath them;
if such things appear upon the funeral pyre as in a dream, then they must exist exactly so.

If even a nature contrary to the natural downward flow of rivers and the like were to be manifested by Consciousness (cit) somewhere, then the cognition would be "it exists" and not "it does not exist," as in a dream; thus he says: "Upwards.
If, at the beginning of creation, a fire with flames directed downwards were to shine within those [rivers] below, that would be perceived.
Even now, this very state of inversion remains as it is; it has not ceased to exist.
Therefore, when the earth appears as falling, the world indeed falls incessantly;
but when consciousness appears as rising upward, it likewise becomes manifold in nature.

For this very reason, with the intention that the various conceptualizations of the disputants—such as the earth’s incessant falling, upward movement, revolving, or leaping—are indeed real by virtue of the existence of consciousness delimited by their respective cognitions, he concludes with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). To explain:
some disputants maintain that the earth actually falls incessantly into the great ether due to its weight.
Furthermore, because there is no spatial limit below the sky, its fall never comes to rest anywhere;

and because that fall is so vast, it is not perceived by us. Moreover, the circle of luminaries is bound on both sides to the two poles attached to Mount Meru, and thus falls along with them. And that—

Some maintain that because it is exceedingly light, the earth revolves due to the force of its own falling from time immemorial. Others, however, hold that based on the Vedic scripture, "He who knows the ship established upon the waters stands firm," there exists an ocean as the support of the earth;
thus, like a ship not moored therein, the earth remains revolving, and during the dissolution (pralaya) it sinks back into that very place, while at the time of creation it emerges again.
"It rises upward according to the analogy of the water-lily. Others, however, maintain this view:
there is only water, unconfined above, below, and all around the earth. Within the cavities of that earth exist the seven worlds, their intermediate spaces filled with air. Within those...

"Due to the extreme lightness of the wind, it moves constantly upward like a gourd fruit submerged in water," so they say. Others, however, believe that it is indeed in space all around the terrestrial globe; and because of its infinity, and because the southern portion—due to the weight of Mount Meru—is the downward direction from the perspective of the gods situated upon Meru, it therefore always falls toward the south alone. Still others are the proponents of the Asura view.

Considering Pātāla itself to be the upper region, and imagining the direction favored by the gods (the zenith) to be downward, they believe that the earth falls toward the north due to its weight. Following this very same logic, those in the east and west also consider their own respective regions to be above, and thus they perceive the sun to be in the east and the west respectively. Others, however—

The circle of luminaries does not rotate; rather, it is the earth itself that rotates upon its own axis. Failing to perceive these two [motions] as distinct, we—like those standing on a ship—perceive the circle of luminaries as rotating, just as we perceive the movement of the boat. Others, however, maintain that the earth alone is situated at the bottom of all things, and that from the perspective of people standing around it, the various points of the sky are defined by their respective positions relative to the zenith.

All directions are indeed upward. Among them, because there is no determining factor (*vinigamanā*) to establish that a specific direction is "down"—such as gravity—whereby one might imagine the earth falling toward it, that direction does not exist in a determined form. Thus, since it does not fall anywhere, it remains stable in its own place.
For those various disputants, everything is real through the existence of consciousness delimited by their respective intellects; but in itself, it is not so.
The sense is that even a slight degree of truth [would apply]; likewise, according to the appearance of each respective thing, it would necessarily be of a manifold and contradictory nature. || 8 ||
Appearing as if motionless, she remains fixed; yet, while possessing light, she is luminous.
Devoid of light, she abides within the self of those who perceive that which is beyond light.

It appears motionless and indeed as if stunned. To those living beings whose eyes are unobstructed day and night, it is always full of light (*sālokā*)—that is, luminous—from their perspective. Likewise, to those born blind who dwell in darkness, it is always devoid of light (*nirālokā*) from their perspective. [This occurs] within the Self (*ātmani*), which is consciousness (*cit*) delimited by the intellect (*buddhi*). (9)
Following the singular manifestation of consciousness alone, the circle of stars and likewise the earth—
this entire world, though non-existent, appears as if existent and remains undivided.

Thus, for those who argue regarding existence and non-existence, he says—starting with "cidbhāna"—that nevertheless, the circle of stars and the earth remain exactly as they are, in accordance with the manifestation of consciousness. || 10 ||
Then there was light upon light, and from that arose the vast hollow of the sky;
thereafter, darkness remained there in various places, appearing like a single ocean.

The answer to the third question begins once the answer to the second question has been completed: "Ālokāloka. This earth stands pervading the Ālokāloka, which itself pervades the Lokāloka; it extends only that far. Beyond that, there is the void in the form of space (*kha*), a hollow (*khāta*) or pit shaped like a ring (*valaya*), and therein is the Great Darkness (*mahattama*), which has the appearance of a single ocean (*ekārṇava*). By the expression "here and there" (*kvacit kvacit*),...
It is understood that there is even a slight entry of sunlight within the space between those two peaks. || 11 ||
Due to the distance of the circle of stars and the formidable height of the great mountain,
there was darkness in some places and light in others, even right there in that very courtyard.

He states the cause for the non-occurrence of the term "lokāloka" regarding that mountain: "due to distance," and so forth. Because the circle of stars (ṛkṣacakra)—that is, the circle of constellations—revolves far beyond the sky, and because of the formidable nature of the mountain, there is darkness in some parts. By the word *catvara*, the plateau (*adhityakā*) is expressed through figurative usage (*gauṇyā vṛttyā*). "Up to the plateau" means reaching the edge of the plateau.
The meaning is that because there is light in some part [of it], it is called Lokāloka. || 12 ||
From the sphere of the sky situated beyond the Lokāloka mountain,
the circle of constellations revolves at a vast distance in the ten directions.
He demonstrates the very nature of its distance with the words "lokāloka" and so forth; it revolves, that is, it turns around. || 13 ||
That circle of stars, bound between the netherworld and the heavens,
spreads through the sky in the ten directions, falling everywhere except for that which is above.
Regarding how far it extends below and above, he says: "From the netherworld (Āpātāla) to heaven. Except for Dhruva at the very top, everything else falls and revolves. 14.
The earth-world itself, together with the netherworld and the circle of constellations, revolves at the edge of the Lokāloka mountain; it is nothing other than a conceptualization of consciousness.
This entire circle of constellations, together with the netherworld (pātāla), revolves around and circumambulates the terrestrial world (bhūloka);
and that [circle] is nothing other than a construction of the intellect (cit-kalpanā). || 15 ||
Immediately after the sky, which is twice the size of the worlds of Sālōka and Bhūloka,
the circle of stars remained like the parched kernels of ripe walnuts.
It is like the kernel within the shell of a ripe walnut, which is the very essence of the seed.
Twice the extent of the sky is the thickness of the stellar wheel (ṛkṣacakra),
which extends in the ten directions and stands like the bark of a wood-apple (bilva) fruit.

Therefore, the thickness of the stellar sphere (ṛkṣacakra) in the sky is double that of the earthly realm; this is the extent of its internal diameter. (17) Just as the manifestation of the dense mass of consciousness is of a conceptual nature, so indeed is this worldly condition through such an arrangement. (18)

The meaning is that the very manifestation of the variegated Brahman—which is a mass of consciousness and whose nature consists of the realization of true will—is itself the worldly state, existing in this manner as the cosmic egg and its constituent parts. || 18 ||
Beyond the circle of the constellations, there exists another sky twice its size;
that [sky] is in some places rich in light and in others composed of dense darkness.
Beyond that, there exists another space, distinct from the previously mentioned space. || 19 ||
At the extremity of that sky stands the shell of the cosmic egg;
one is above, the other is below, and the space between them is the middle.
It is a hundred million yojanas in extent, nourished, firm as a diamond,
established in the sky as consisting of consciousness, and having the nature of space itself.

He states the measurement of the petals within that [lotus] with the words "of yojanas. That which consists of consciousness, whose form is mere conceptualization, and which in the ultimate sense is the sky—the modification of space resulting from the fivefold elements—is indeed the sky, the very expanse of consciousness (cidākāśa). || 21 ||
In the great sphere of the sky, which faces all directions, there are its own stars;
what here could be above or below, or is everything both above and below? (22)
In the sky, which is in the form of a great sphere, the circle of luminaries—including the sun and the stars—remains situated facing all directions.

This being so, what here in this circle of luminaries could be "above" and what "below"? If such distinctions were to exist, then everything would be above and everything would be below; by the use of the word "ca" (and), the meaning is that everything might also be to the south, north, east, or west. || 22 ||
Falling, rising, going, staying, and consciousness—these are mere vibrations, not a real entity.
There is no falling, nor rising, nor going, nor coming, nor even staying. (23)

The falling, rising, moving sideways, standing, and remaining stationary of all objects— which appear to exist— is merely the vibration and manifestation of the mind, which is the inner self (*pratyagātman*). In reality, however, there is no falling,
no rising, nor any going, coming, standing, or remaining stationary whatsoever.
The meaning is that it would contradict the state of non-duality. || 23 ||
Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-seventh canto, titled "The Determination of the Earth's Globe," in the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*, the *Vālmīki-Divya-Moda-Nirvāṇa-Uttara-Artha-Vibhūti*.
Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Determination of the Earth's Globe," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and twenty-eighth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
For people such as ourselves, this is perceptible through direct experience, not merely inferential.
By means of a body of pure consciousness, not one consisting of material elements. || 1 ||
Having crossed over the darkness, the chasm, and the enclosures of the cosmic egg,
the wandering of Vipaschit within ignorance is here described.
By what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) have you understood this—the dimensions and other characteristics of the wheel of light (*jyotiścakra*)? To that he replies:

"Of people like us. For those who are not yogis, it is not by means of the subtle body (*ativāhika-śarīra*), which is dominated by that pure realization of reality—the direct perception of the truth of the entire universe—that has been purified through the practice of yogic knowledge.
The meaning is: "in the form of the gross, pertaining to the elemental world" (ādhibhautika). || 1 ||
I have described this world-dream to you; it is not so for others.
In the world-dreams of others, there exists likewise another state of affairs. || 2 ||
This arrangement of the Lokāloka mountain, the Jyotiścakra, and so forth, which has been described by me, is stated as it is well-known within the dream-world of our own universe;

however, it has not been described regarding other [universes]. The meaning is that in other dream-worlds characterized as different cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas), the situation is generally the same, though in some cases it may be otherwise. || 2 ||
What is the use of describing other arrangements regarding the dreams of the world?
For the wise, there is no discourse that is more useful than this. (3)
In that case, state that as well; regarding this, he says: "The world," etc. (Verse 3).
Meru is to the north of all [continents], and Lokāloka is to the south; by this inference regarding the entire multitude of lands, the wise [determine their locations]. (4)

O wise ones, by that very principle, among all the cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas), Mount Meru is to the north of all the continents and oceans, while Lokāloka is to the south; thus, for those who have a desire to know the entire multitude of worlds, let inference proceed as inference. This is the meaning. || 4 ||
This is directly perceptible to others, wherein those other delusions of the world exist;
for they do not exist in that manner within our own domain, which is beautiful in its established order.

However, those intermediate distinctions are perceptible only to the inhabitants of that [region] and not to those here; thus he says: "Perceptible to all [is Meru in the north and Lokāloka in the south];
this is the certainty for the inhabitants of the seven continents, and not for others. (6)
Of others who have gone outside the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa). || 6 ||
Listen now, O Rāma, to the subject at hand: that shell of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), and the water situated outside it, which is ten times its extent. (7)
The lid of the cosmic egg consists of the two halves of the shell previously mentioned;
measuring as previously stated at one hundred million yojanas, beyond that, on the exterior, there exists a tenfold layer of water, the watery covering.
That shell of the cosmic egg, however, naturally holds water like a blade of grass or a jewel that grants all desires, remaining so eternally like a wish-fulfilling gem.

Now, one might ask: what is its support? To this he says: "That" (tat). That very shell of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍakavāṭa*) supports that water by virtue of being a portion of earth and through its power of attraction. Just as a "grass-gem"—a specific type of magnet for grass—supports grass by means of its inherent nature consisting of the power of attraction.
Or rather, the meaning is that it is just as the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa) holds the jewels desired by those who seek them. || 8 ||
The earthly element remains present in all things like a wish-fulfilling gem;
because of that, these [substances] fall down here in abundance at all times.

In that case, water droplets released from clouds and the like would not fall into oceans, rivers, and so forth, because of the absence of an attractive force in the water; rather, even from afar, they would approach the shoreland itself and fall there. To this, he says:
"Of all... These refer to the rainwater and other such things. (9)
Outside the water, there exists a fuel-less fire ten times greater;
it is as clear as space and resembles the interior of a tranquil, motionless flame.
Outside of the water that forms the covering of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), as previously described.
Therefore, the expansive wind is situated ten times greater in the exterior;
and the stainless space stands ten times greater than the wind in the exterior.
Beyond that is the infinitely vast, peaceful space of Brahman;
it is neither light nor darkness, but the imperishable, solid mass of great consciousness.
The space of Brahman is the space of Brahman variegated by ignorance; it is a mass of consciousness, a solid mass of wisdom, resembling deep sleep.
In that great sky of Brahman, which is without beginning, middle, or end; which is called the Great Consciousness, the Self of all, and whose nature is unborn liberation.
Like an iron hammer, it is of the nature of flawlessly indestructible nirvāṇa. || 13 ||
Far and far away, again and again, millions upon millions of such cosmic eggs flash forth and cease to exist.
They shine forth and arise; they cease and dissolve. || 14 ||
Nothing whatsoever shines forth here within this even [reality] whose nature is shining;
being composed of that very essence and possessing such a form, it is established solely within itself.
What is that cause which causes millions of cosmic eggs to manifest? To this he says: "Nothing at all.
Rather, it is that very Brahman itself which, through ignorance (avidyā), exists within itself as being of such a nature. || 15 ||
This entire sequence of the experience of the visible world has been told to you;
now hear what happened concerning Vipaścit on Lokāloka.
Having concluded the dialogue of questions and answers, he causes the subject at hand to be heard: "This," [he says]. || 16 ||
Impelled by his shining certainties and driven by previously well-practiced mental impressions,
he fell into the dark abyss from the summit of the Lokāloka mountain.

Impelled by such a resolve, he whose latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) from former efforts to see the ends of the quarters had been well-cultivated, fell— that is, entered— the previously mentioned abyss of darkness beyond the summit of the mountain Lokāloka. || 17 ||
There he beheld a body resembling a mountain peak,
its mind and form mangled by birds, yet extending forth according to his own thought.
And there he saw his own natural divine body torn apart and devoured by very large birds such as vultures, which resembled mountain peaks;
immediately thereafter, he saw his mind-body proceed toward the vision of the ends of the quarters, just as it had been conceived in his thought.
Because of the holiness of that region, he, being pure in disposition, did not bring about the perception of his subtle body (ativāhika-deha) as being material (ādhibhautika). || 19 ||

Because that place of death was meritorious, he did not lose the state of the *ātivāhika* body— that is to say, the impressions (*saṃskāra*) pertaining to the sphere of the gross body were awakened by the fourfold assembly of elements and so forth. || 19 ||
Having attained only that much awakening and not reaching a higher realization,
he reflected upon his dark deeds and became devoted to the welfare of Prakṛti.

One whose awakening has such a limited scope—that it concerns only the self as distinct from the gross body—is a "wise man" (*vipaścit*) in that sense; however, he has not yet attained a higher awakening whose scope is the pure consciousness-self alone, transcending the three bodies. Therefore, having reflected upon the task characterized by seeing to the ends of the quarters—a task that is unblemished and inexhaustible—[he proceeds].
The meaning is that he was beneficial—that is, favorable—to Prakṛti, whose nature is to approach [the Puruṣa], and did not cease. || 20 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
O Sage, how does this mind, which is bodiless, extend into its object?
What kind of superior awakening arises from the consciousness of the subtle body (ātivāhika)?

"But how can the mind, which is without a body, move or go outside? Even if that were admitted, O Rāma, previously he possessed a divine body with unimpeded movement through the path of the sky; therefore, when that [divine body] was destroyed, what difference was there for him as he traveled along the celestial path by means of a mental body—a body consisting of mind alone—compared to his former physical body?"
He asks: "bodiless"? || 21 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Just as one who dwells within the inner apartments travels upon the path of mental constructs, so does this mind of his proceed once it has been set in motion.

Regarding that, he states the answer to the first question with the words beginning "saṃkalpa" (volition) and so forth. The meaning is that the movement of volition upon its path does not depend upon the movement of the body. || 22 ||
Just as the mind extends itself toward delusion, dream, mental projection, false knowledge, or the hearing of stories, so does that extended mind [perceive]. (23)
When they fall, that body is called the *ativāhika* (conveying body);
through forgetfulness, the notion of it being a material (*ādhibhautika*) body arises here at that very time.

He states the answer to the second [objection] with the words "they fall" (*patanti*). The word *tu* (but) is intended to highlight the distinction from the *ādhibhautika* (material) body. The meaning is that the body in which those [experiences], such as delusion, dreaming, and mental fantasies, fall—that is, manifest—is the *ātivāhika* (subtle) body. In this very *ātivāhika* body, due to the forgetting of one's true state...
The statement that "the notion of materiality arises" is a restatement of what was previously mentioned, intended to demonstrate a specific distinction. || 24 ||
Then, when this physical body— comparable to the delusion of a rope-snake— has vanished,
only the subtle body (ātivāhika) remains.

When, then, does the remainder consisting of the subtle body (ātivāhika) remain through the cessation of the perception of the material (ādhibhautika)? To this he says: "Those, at that time. The word "those" (te) connects with the preceding verse. When, through inquiry, the delusion of the material has vanished, then the subtle body remains. || 25 ||
O dear one, let this subtle body be carefully investigated;
for here, there exists nothing else whatsoever apart from pure consciousness alone.

With the intention that even when only pure consciousness remains upon the cessation of the subtle body (*ātivāhika-deha*), inquiry alone is the means [to liberation], he says: "The subtle body... By the means for perceiving reality shown in the scripture, "Seek, my dear, the root of Being with the sharp tip of fire," [one attains this]. || 26 ||
That form of consciousness which exists in the interval when one reaches another place from one place—that is the true nature of this infinite, singular Consciousness-only. (27)

With the intention that the well-known [existence] of pure consciousness devoid of objects has already been refuted many times before, he recites again the half-verse previously cited—beginning with "deśāt"—with the ellipsis: "its nature is indeed well-known."
Where is duality, and where is aversion? Tell me, where indeed are passion and the rest? All is Śiva, without beginning or end; it is remembered as supreme consciousness. (28)
And in that state, there is no possibility at all of an object characterized by duality, nor of the attachment, aversion, and so forth caused by it; thus he says: "Where? (verse 28).
The supreme awakening is the state of abiding in peace, free from the mental constructions of the mind;
one who remains within the subtle body has not yet attained that awakening.

That state which is free from the mind and mental conceptions, and which is established in stillness—that alone is the supreme awakening. However, the wise man (vipaścit), while residing in the subtle body (ātivāhika-deha), had not yet attained that awakening; rather, his awakening consisted merely in the realization of the self as being nothing more than the subtle body.
Therefore, the connection with the subsequent verse is: "For this very reason, he saw the mind expanding forth. (29)
Awakened by the wisdom of Vipaścit, he beheld his expanding mind—
that darkness resembling the dwelling in a womb— through the realization of the subtle body (*ātivāhika*).
And he beheld a darkness resembling dwelling in a womb. || 30 ||
At the end of the darkness, there was the ground formed by the breaking of the shell of Viriñca’s egg,
consisting of gold with the essence of diamond, extending for ten million yojanas.

The surface of the earth is of the nature of that which is like a split or a fragment of the shell of Viriñca’s egg; that is to say, it constitutes the joint of the division between the two halves of the cosmic egg. || 31 ||
At its end, he reached water eight times greater than that;
it stood level with the surface of the earth and the door-panel, like the surface of the ocean.

Following that, he describes the attainment of its enclosure with the words "at its end": situated at the edge of the island, it stands like the surface of the ocean, equal to and coextensive with the ground of the door-panel itself. Since water cannot exist without a support, it rests upon the fragment of the shell of the cosmic egg (aṇḍakapāla), remaining divided just like that [ocean].
The state of being. || 32 ||
Having passed beyond that, he then reached a mass of splendor terrifying like a multitude of suns,
radiant with a hollow interior filled with dense flames like the fire of universal destruction.

However, since the luminous (taijasa) and subsequent coverings do not require a supporting medium like water, there is an absence of joints or divisions; thus it is described as being radiant, like the interior of a solid mass. || 33 ||
With a mental body free from burning, grief, and the like,
as he was traveling there, he recognized the vehicle in which he had previously resided.
While traveling there through the fiery enclosure, that Vipaschit perceived himself being carried upward into the enclosure of wind.
Being carried along, he perceived himself as having a subtle, transportable body (ātivāhika); he even wondered, "How is it that my own self, which consists of nothing but mind, is being carried? (35)
He states that the intended meaning of the phrase "he understood" is that this [experience] of his was essentially like a mental construction in a dream and not real: "being carried away," etc. (35).
Thus, through his awakening, the wise-souled one crossed that ocean of wind and reached the vast sky extending ten times beyond it.
He states that the crossing of the wind-obstacle occurs solely by the power of such a sensation: "Thus," etc. (36).
Having transcended that, he reached the infinite space of Brahman, wherein is all, from whence is all, which is nothing and yet is everything. (37)
The Brahma-ether is the Brahma-ether variegated by ignorance. || 37 ||
Wandering there in his mind, he went further and further away;
by him were seen the earth, water, fire, air, and likewise the entire world.
The meaning is that it is seen [to occur] by the power of mental formations (saṃskāra). || 38 ||
Again there are the structures of saṃsāra, again the creations, again the directions;
again the mountains, the sky, again the gods, and again human beings. (39)
Furthermore, people become attached [to them] through the transformation [of thought], thinking, "The men have been seen. || 39 ||
Furthermore, within the limit of the five great elements, there is the cloudless Brahman;
again therein are the worlds on high, again the creations, and again the directions. (40)
It is solid, yet it is without solidity. || 40 ||
From that [state] comes the ether of Brahmā, and from that, other creations yet to be established;
thus, sporting for a long time, he remains even today. (41)
They are unestablished and unsettled. || 41 ||
Indeed, because of his long-practiced self-certainty, he does not attain cessation;
for there is no end to ignorance, since that [ignorance] is itself the reality of Brahman. 42.
Because of the certainty [of non-duality], from the certainty that the world is unreal; if one thoroughly investigates reality—that is, the true nature of things—it is indeed Brahman alone.
(42) In reality, there is no ignorance here within Brahman, whose self is free from conceptual construction.
This visible world and this so-called "ignorance" are merely the expansion of the Self. (43)
He asks why that is so, and says: "In reality... (verse 43).
Just as you have seen, see, or will see in waking or in dream,
so indeed has Brahman— real, peaceful— been, is, and will be.

That Brahman which you saw previously in the waking state and in dreams—according to the arising of such-and-such latent impressions (vāsanā)—and which you see now, you will see before you as well; that Brahman has been exactly thus, it is so now, and it will be so in the future. || 44 ||
This great, sequential manifestation of the world is a revolving wheel for observing the darkness of the forest;
by virtue of this nature of manifestation as the Supreme, it is neither existent, my dear, nor does it have the form of non-existence.
For this very reason, he says that this world is indeed indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*), being distinct from both the existent and the non-existent: "Thickly heated," etc.

This manifestation of the world—appearing as "it was," "it is," and "it will be"—which is endowed with temporal sequence, is merely dense darkness, nothing but ignorance (*avidyā*). It appears vast, like a circle of hair seen by one with blurred vision when the eyes are closed. And that [darkness] is, in reality, the Supreme Self, which is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*).

It is not real by way of that [nature], because it lacks the nature of appearing; yet, by this [nature] established through the perspective of the ignorant, it is not unreal in form. Therefore, since both perspectives possess validity, the meaning is that it is simply indeterminable (anirvacanīya). || 45 ||

Even now, O Rāghava, because the true nature of those worlds has not been realized, he wanders like a fawn through the high mountain ridges— those very same worlds, which are exceedingly subtle within the womb of Brahman and situated at a vast distance from us.

O Raghava, that wise one, even today, because the reality [of his own nature] remains unrecognized, wanders like a *raṅku* deer—a specific kind of wild animal—within the bellies of Brahmās and Virājs, within the well-known worlds, and within forest tracts; these being merely subtle impressions (*vāsanā*) of those previously seen, or of others similar to them, and thus exceedingly slight. He does so due to the great height of his own latent tendencies.
"Baṃbhramīti" means he wanders again and again. [This form arises] from the root *bhram* when the *yaṅ* affix is elided, with the augment *nuk* applied to the reduplicated syllable. (46)

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Vision of the Brahman-Ether, the Vipaścit, and the Moon of the World," in the *Brahmagītā* of the *Śrī Vāyavīya Saṃhitā* of the *Skanda Purāṇa*.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-eighth canto, titled "The Vision of Brahma, Space, Vipaschit, and the World-Moon," in the latter half of the Nirvana-prakarana of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and twenty-ninth canto.
Śrī Rāma said:
O best of sages, what happened after that between those two?
Afterwards, when those two Vipashchits were indeed obstructed by him, [the other] Vipashchit spoke.
Here, the remaining two sons of Vipaścit are described;
for one of them, having ended his life as a deer, there is likewise a reunion with Rāma.

Having heard that one wise man, having attained knowledge through the grace of Viṣṇu, was liberated, while the second still wanders in ignorance even today, Rāma asks about the conduct of the remaining two with the words "of those two," [referring] to the world of the Moon and the kingdom of Śālmalidvīpa.

After those two wise ones—the eastern and southern Vipaschits—who had been restrained by enjoyments and who were well-acquainted with the worthlessness of worldly pleasures, what other conduct, distinct from that previously mentioned, arose in connection with that excellent one who beheld the ends of the quarters? This is the question. || 1 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
One of those two, rendered helpless by long-practiced latent impressions (*vāsanā*),
wandered through various islands with a multitude of bodies and eventually reached that very same path.

The meaning is that while the northern wise man has reached the path of Brahman—which is variegated by the transcending of the shell of the cosmic egg—the southern wise man has gone only upon the path characterized by wandering through hundreds of millions of cycles of worldly existence. || 2 ||
In that very same way, having cast off all veils within the hollow of the supreme ether,
he remains even today beholding hundreds of thousands of worlds in saṃsāra.
The passage beginning with "tathaiva" (in the same way) is an elaboration of what has already been stated. || 3 ||
Of those two, the second, due to his long-standing habit of initial non-attachment, has abandoned wandering bodies; today he remains as a deer on the mountain.

The second, Vipaścit, being previously wise, abandoned those [bodies] after having been characterized by them— bodies that appeared month after month along with the moon due to the power of his attachment, specifically his excessive affection for the deer in the moon, which he had cultivated through proximity to it.
Today, having become a deer, he remains on the mountain.
Śrī Rāma said: O Brahman, there is but one single latent impression (vāsanā) that is ever-present for the four [orders];
how has it attained such diversity as to yield both inferior and superior fruits? (5)

Rāma raises the doubt that if the latent impression (*vāsanā*), the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), and the body were of a single form, then a fourfold division of them—or even a distinction between inferior and superior fruits arising from the differentiation of impressions—would be impossible; he does so with the verse beginning "ekaiva" (5).

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: The latent impression (vāsanā) well-practiced by a living being undergoes a change in its degree of subtlety or firmness due to the influence of place, time, and action; it does not become something else through the intensity of its firmness.

Regarding that, he states the answer to the first question: "svabhyasta... [and so forth]. It is "tender" due to slight firmness; it has "become extremely firm through full maturation" due to dense firmness. This is the division of the other [state]. || 6 ||
Place, time, action, and so forth, as well as the unity of latent impressions—whichever of these two is more powerful, that alone triumphs in an instant. (7)
Regarding the cause for the unification or differentiation of latent impressions (*vāsanās*), he says: "Space," and so forth.

When there is a unity of the causal complexes of space, time, action, and effort that are conducive to the fruits of experience, then the unification of the latent impressions—which share the same objects and are conducive to those [fruits]—is also accomplished. But when there is diversity [in the causes], then there is differentiation.

But when two latent impressions (*vāsanā*) arise—one having a location, time, action, and result identical [to another], and the other having a different location, time, action, and result—then between those two, whichever is stronger prevails. The point is that this strength is to be inferred from the result. || 7 ||
Thus, through this distinction, these four are established here:
two are dragged away for the sake of ignorance, while another is liberated and the last is like a deer.
In this manner,

these four Vipaschitas remain situated together, existing as distinct entities due to a division of their substrates caused by the division of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) for experiencing objects in mutually contradictory locations that have arisen simultaneously. Among them, three— including the first two who are for the sake of ignorance and the other who is a deer— are all drawn away.
By means of latent impressions; however, one other is liberated. || 8 ||
Even now, those of deluded intellect have not reached the end of ignorance;
this ignorance is infinite, being nourished by lack of knowledge.
By those three [ignorances], it is surrounded, increased, and augmented by thousands of delusions. || 9 ||
When the light of wisdom has arrived, it quickly becomes pacified;
it dissolves away without root—[or with root, according to the reading]—just as the splendor of darkness vanishes at sunrise. 10.
It dissolves entirely, leaving nothing behind and without root. || 10 ||
Listen to the account of Vipaschit, born in another world at a later time;
in that very distant region, amidst the delusion of worldly existence.

"In a short time" connects with the preceding verse. Now he relates again by which conduct liberation was attained by the later scholar (*paścimavipaścit*): "In another," etc. It occurred in another world-system (*brahmāṇḍa*) imagined by his own latent impressions (*vāsanā*). In that world-system, in a very distant region of the earth characterized by color, situated on the far side of the Sweet Ocean (*svādūdadhipebhāga*). || 11 ||
Somewhere in the great void of Brahman, within some sphere of the visible,
he— though appearing in the form of the visible— is in reality of the nature of Brahman.
Regarding whether [the world] rests upon some visible sphere within the great void of Brahman, or whether it is real, he says:
"He alone, through auspicious association, having entered into the midst of the wise, and having understood the visible world as it truly is, has attained the stainless state of Brahman. (13)

Through his association with the multitude of auspicious qualities such as tranquility, self-restraint, and devotion to the Lord, he was the last among the wise, the sole one among the learned who were liberated while living.
Through the swift and thorough knowledge of that very [reality], both that ignorance and that body—
which were governed by passion— attained quiescence, like the water of a mirage.

Regarding where that ignorance in the form of the world and that body go after liberation, he says: "In that very place. They have reached the cessation of hope and destruction, because passion and desire are dependent upon them, their existence being subject to them. And thus says the Śruti: "When all the desires that dwell in his heart are cast away, then the mortal becomes immortal; here [he attains Brahman]."
"He attains Brahman," so it is said. || 14 ||
Thus, I have clearly related to you all the activities of Vipaścit;
for this ignorance is infinite, since it consists of that very [Brahman], just like Brahman itself. (15)

He concludes the current discussion with the word "iti" (thus): This ignorance, which is the ignorance of effects, is infinite even today in all directions because its end is not seen by them, just like the causal Brahman. || 15 ||
Wherever one may travel for hundreds of thousands of years, in each such place, something is perceived by its own inherent nature. (16)

He states the intended meaning of the illustrative example—that it is "like Brahman"—by saying that its infinity arises precisely from the infinity of the consciousness (citi) unknown to the creator of that [world]: "By which... (verse 16).
That very same [reality], when not fully understood, is called false knowledge;
but when fully understood, it is peaceful and is likewise called Brahman. || 17 ||
He states the intended meaning of the expression "consisting of that" as follows: "That alone," meaning that very Brahman. || 17 ||
There is no duality; this so-called duality is that of which it consists—namely, Brahman itself as the manifestation of consciousness. For even differentiation is of the very nature of consciousness.
Now, if there is a distinction between "ignorance" (avidyā) and "Brahman," how can it be said that they are one and the same? To this he says: "The distinction.

This distinction is not a [real] distinction, because it consists of that; it consists of ignorance alone, and that ignorance is indeed Brahman itself. Furthermore, since it is illuminated by consciousness (cit), the distinction is not other than consciousness; thus he says: "That" (tad). || 18 ||
The end of this pavilion of the universe was reached after hundreds of ages by the unwise who wander therein; it was not reached by the wise one, because of ignorance.
But by one who is devoid of knowledge and lacks discernment, the end of ignorance is not attained even in a hundred yugas; thus he says:

"The Cosmic Egg," etc. In this manner, by the wandering, undiscerning, and ignorant person, the end of ignorance is not reached even in hundreds of yugas, whereas by the discerning one [it is reached]. || 19 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
"O Brahmā, best among speakers, why was that door of the cosmic egg not reached by Vipaścit? You have described this, yet you did not mention it."

With the intention that it is impossible for there to be a "twilight sky" (*saṃdhyākāśa*) at all—since no cause is mentioned for the destruction of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*)—Rāma raises a doubt regarding how Uttara-vipaścit could have exited through the path of the twilight sky at the seam of the shell of the cosmic egg, saying:
"He... [and] "Why did he not reach the very leaf of the cosmic egg's shell? and thus, "In that case, him..."
Why was it not told by you that he emerged after having broken through? (20)
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Long ago, as soon as he was born, Viriñca split open the sphere of the cosmic egg with two of his own arms— one below and one above.

Vasiṣṭha recalls what was already stated previously in the account of the stone—that he was the cause for the separation of the two halves of the cosmic egg—by saying "jātena" (by him who was born). || 21 ||
From that point, one part has gone upwards to an exceedingly great distance;
another part has gone downwards to an even more distant interval. 22.
Or, it is something else that is exceedingly distant; that is, it has reached a limit that is an exceedingly distant interval. || 22 ||
Depending upon those two, the coverings of water and the other elements remain;
they alone are their support, hanging and situated within those two.

Those two parts, like the water and other coverings, remain supported by those very [elements], though they appear divided. It has already been established that while their coexistence is common to all, the state of being divided belongs specifically to the water covering alone. || 23 ||
Know that the space between these two halves of the cosmic egg is the sky,
which appears as this dark blue expanse, without shore or limit.
There, the coverings of water and the other elements do not adhere and do not exist;
for that is stainless, void, and the support fashioned by the constructions of the aeon.

In that context, the description of space as "boundless" is for the purpose of demonstrating its vastness in comparison to the other elements; otherwise, it would be impossible for the external space-enclosure to have a magnitude ten times greater than the preceding enclosure. Furthermore, it would be inconsistent with the subsequent description of the Brahma-space (brahmākāśa). It is the tethering post (*ālāna*), the support for the other elements, until the dissolution of the world (*pralaya*).
By means of the conceptualizations of the duration of the aeons. || 25 ||
Proceeding by that path like a wise leader of a host of bears,
he remained intensely dedicated until liberation for the sake of examining ignorance.
He was as if having taken the initiatory vow, being exceedingly consecrated for the purpose of scrutinizing ignorance from every side. || 26 ||
This ignorance is indeed Brahman itself, since it consists of that;
therefore, when unperceived, it exists, but when fully perceived, it does not exist.

If it is asked, "In that case, why did he not see the end of ignorance despite the uninterrupted and most intense effort of the person? [the author] says, "It is Brahman itself," because in reality it consists of the infinite Brahman-Atman. Then, if so, how is its end seen by those who know the truth? To this he says, "When fully known. || 27 ||
Having reached the state of the All-Seeing (Vipaścit) far, far away in the supreme ether,
others wander among certain other forms of the world which are products of ignorance.
Within certain forms characterized as the world, which are [manifestations] of ignorance... (28)
One deer was liberated, another remained, and even today those two wander somewhere,
rendered helpless by their abundant past habitual tendencies (saṃskāra).
Śrī Rāma said:
O Sage, if you have compassion for me, please tell me: in what kind of worlds, and at what distance, do those Vipracittas wander?
Rāma’s questions are clear. || 30 ||
O Sage, over what extent of time have you been born in those various states of existence?
This which has been told by you here is a great marvel for us. (31)
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
O Rāma, those two worlds in which both Vipaschit and I were situated have passed beyond our range; even with effort, we can no longer perceive those worlds.

Thinking that this question regarding the world—like a question asking how far from here a village seen for the first time in a dream is located—is not fit to be answered by stating a number of *yojanas*, Vasiṣṭha provides an answer that indicates his own intention under the guise of admitting ignorance of that [distance], beginning with the words "In their state... (*sthitau*). Even upon careful reflection, those worlds of ours...
It has not entered the range of our intellect, nor become an object of it. || 32 ||
The third has become a deer where the wise one dwells; at times, accompanied by the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), he remains within our range of perception. (33)

That cosmic egg, together with the worlds contained within it and their respective transmigrations, does not remain within the range of our perception—that is, within the domain of the intellect. || 33 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
O Vipaschit, that world in which you, having become a deer, were situated—where is that world, O one of great intelligence? Tell me this exactly as it is.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Having gone further and further away into the great sky of the Supreme Brahman, there is a deer named Vipaścit in that world; hear now about that world.
Know this: that deer is situated here within these three worlds;
this is that supreme ether, which stands far, far beyond the world.
It was situated far, even further than the birthplace of the ancient Vipaschit. || 36 ||
Śrī Rāma said: "How is this consistent? This Vipaschit, having attained that state from this very world, has been born here today as a deer; how can this be? (37)
How can it be consistent that one who has gone on a journey to see the ends of the earth should be born as a deer right here?
The meaning is that birth as a deer here is impossible without returning from that journey. || 37 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Just as the whole always knows all its parts,
so do I know all things established within the Brahman-self.
"Far, and even farther," and so forth—all such [expressions] belong only to those who perceive the Self as limited.
However, for those who perceive the Self as unlimited, everything is indeed most proximate, just as the parts are to a whole.
With the intention that this statement is based on one's own direct experience, he provides the answer: "the parts," meaning "all the cosmic eggs."
The remainder. || 38 ||
He saw those many [beings] in various forms, still unfinished and being withdrawn;
they were interwoven with one another and visible to one another, appearing as if they were earthly beings in their own essential nature.

With the intention that, from the perspective of Brahman, even those who are most remote in time are actually most proximate, and thus nothing is distant in terms of time, he qualifies them as "unestablished" (*aniṣṭhitān*). This means they are currently unestablished—meaning not yet manifest—due to occurring at a later point in time; likewise, [he qualifies them] as "accompanied by dissolution" (*sasaṃhārān*).
These [objects], though produced in former times and accompanied by their dissolution, possessing various and diverse forms, and though invisible to one another,
appear as if mutually interwoven due to their superimposition upon a single consciousness—
just like the nature of threads and cloth which are modifications of the earth. || 39 ||
O Rāma, whatever occurred on that certain other path while it stood just like this one has been related by me to you.

The meaning is this: although that which occurred in a certain other Brahmāṇḍa situated on a path within that [other] Brahmāṇḍa—just like what occurs here in this Brahmāṇḍa—I have described it to you right here as if it were this very Brahmāṇḍa, both in its reality and its mode, because there is no difference between them. || 40 ||
While those wandering through other worlds in various bodies roamed across the quarters of space,
he, with an unwearied mind, remained for that same length of time in the infinite sky of the firmament.

Deluded by those aforementioned various directions—which are conceived through their own respective latent impressions (*vāsanā*) within diverse cycles of existence—they are in fact wandering with such very same bodies; the connection is that Vipracitti, who was previously [there], has now been born here as a deer. || 41 ||
Having wandered through the vast delusions of many worlds by chance, he was born right here as a deer in a certain mountain cave. (42)
Wandering far through the worlds, he perceived that this creation— in which a deer was situated—
existed in the void by mere chance, like the "crow-and-fig" coincidence.
In the sky, that is, in the space of Brahman. || 43 ||
Śrī Rāma said: If it is so, O Brāhmaṇa, tell me: in which direction, in which region, on which mountain, and in which forest does that deer reside? (44)
In the quarter of Kakubh. || 44 ||
What does he do, and how does he, dwelling upon the fertile earth, chew the dūrvā grass? When will that man of mature wisdom remember his former noble birth? (45)

When will that deer—whose dwelling is on a fertile land rich with crops, and who possesses a "jaraṭha-jñāna" (a wisdom as frail as that of an old man)—ever remember his former birth, his existence as a learned man? || 45 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Know that the pet deer which was given to you by the lord of Trigarta, and which remains in the pet-deer house, is none other than Vipaścit.
The Trigartas are a specific region; the king who is their lord gave you a pet deer as a tribute.
That pet deer is now staying in the cage for captive animals. Know that deer to be Vipaścit.
(46) Śrī Vālmīki said:
Having heard this, Rāghava, filled with wonder in that assembly,
dispatched many boys to bring back the deer.
Then that innocent deer, having been brought in, entered the vast assembly hall;
he was beheld by all the members of the court, appearing both well-nourished and joyful.
Emulating the sky with the drops from his body joined with the stars,
he threatened the beautiful women with showers of blue-lotus-like glances.
With the drops and droplets situated on his body, he imitated—that is, he emulated—the sky filled with stars and dots. || 49 ||
With their eyes blue as the luster of emeralds, they were regarded with both respect and disregard by the spectators;
they ran about restlessly in their desire for grass, casting charming and startled glances.

By those with startled glances and fearful sidelong looks— who, though respectful and full of reverence for the sight, were themselves treated with disregard— the dark-colored pillars and other parts of the assembly hall, shimmering with the luster of emeralds inlaid therein, were being run toward to seize, out of a desire driven by the delusion that they were blades of green grass.
With his ears pricked, eyes raised, and neck outstretched, he agitated the members of the assembly with his swift movements, which were momentarily unstable due to their flickering nature.

With his ears, eyes, and neck held erect, he agitated the members of the assembly who had gathered there— distressing them with such momentary, unstable, low, and irresistible postures, as well as with such speeds, through their longing to see him and their fear of being overtaken. 51.
Upon seeing that deer, the people—including the king, the sages, and the ministers—were for a long time filled with wonder, exclaiming, "Alas, this is infinite illusion! (52)
They were filled with pride and astonishment, and thus became agitated. || 52 ||

With all the people utterly amazed by the tasting of such wonders, and as the assembly gazed at Kṛṣṇa— who was showering a thick rain of blue lotuses upon everyone and was covered in a lattice of jewel-rays— it seemed like a lotus-pond drawn in a painting.

Beholding that deer— which appeared as if turned black by the dense and thick showers of blue lotuses characterized by the glances of all the members of the assembly, and which was fashioned and adorned with the networks of rays and masses of luster from various kinds of jewels— the assembly experienced the savoring of wonder, that is, the aesthetic relish of the marvelous sentiment (*adbhuta-rasa*).
Because all internal objects of cognition had dissolved away, there was an inner tasting [of bliss]; by that, all the worlds were utterly amazed, rendered motionless by wonder.
Being thus, she was fashioned like a lotus grove, depicted in a painting. || 53 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-ninth canto, titled "The Acquisition of Mṛgalābha by Vipaścit," in the section on the liberation of Avindhya, within the Mokṣopāya of the Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa, composed by the Sage.
Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Attainment of the Deer by Vipaścit," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and thirtieth canto.
Śrī Vālmīki said:
Then Rāma said to this sage, "By whom was Vipaścit [created]?"
Through skillful means, there may be an end to suffering by virtue of the arising of the primordial self. || 1 ||
The entry of the deer into the fire produced by Vasiṣṭha’s meditation,
as well as the recovery of his former memory through the acquisition of Vipracit’s body, is described here.

The construction of the sentence is as follows: "The former self was the body of Vipaschit; from its arising—that is, from its renewed manifestation and from the manifestation of the real self through knowledge—[the body perished]," thus spoke Rama. || 1 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
For whomsoever by whom [the mind] has been aroused, for that person there is no progress without it;
it is neither beautiful, nor pleasant, nor conducive to welfare, nor does it yield good fruit.

For whatever person, by whichever deity long worshipped, success in their repeatedly desired goals first arose, for that person, even without that deity, future progress and the attainment of desired success do not occur; even if they were to occur, they would not be auspicious; and even if they were auspicious, they would not yield happiness in the end. Even if some happiness were somehow attained, it would not be beneficial for the next world.
It never happens otherwise. And thus says the Śruti: "He who sacrifices beyond his own deity falls away from his own deity;

he does not reach the higher one, but becomes worse off. And the learned say: "O Blessed One, that twice-born man born in a family who would sacrifice beyond his ancestral deity falls away from both."
That fool would perish like the *abhyudayeṣṭi* or the *upāṃśuyāja*. Thus [ends the section]. || 2 ||
Fire is the refuge of the wise; by entering it, this deer regains its former form, just as gold becomes stainless.
He is the refuge, the protector by granting desired objects; his former form was his previous body as a wise man. || 3 ||
"I shall do all this; let it be seen, for I shall show it to you.
Here, this deer is now entering the fire before us. (4)
Śrī Vālmīki said:
Having spoken thus, the sage Vasiṣṭha, whose conduct was most excellent,
sipped water from his own water-pot according to the prescribed rule.
Having touched water and sipped it, he should touch his head, eyes, nostrils, ears, and heart, not transgressing the rule stated in the Śruti: "in the proper manner. (5)
He meditated upon the fire as being without fuel and consisting of a mass of flames;
by that meditation, a web of flames rose up from the midst of the assembly hall.
From the central area of Daśaratha’s assembly hall. || 6 ||
Having the appearance of being devoid of embers, free from fuel, clear, crackling, smokeless, and without soot. (7)
Regarding the word *dhamadhamāyantam*: from the imitation of an indistinct sound (*avyaktānukaraṇa*) [“dhamadham”], by the rule “*ḍāci bahulaṃ dve bhavataḥ*” (Pāṇini 6.1.98), there is reduplication;

then, by the rule “*lohitādiḍājbhyaḥ kyaṣ*” (Pāṇini 3.1.13), the suffix *kyaṣ* is added; and from this *kyaṣ*-ending form, the present tense marker *laṭ* is replaced by the suffix *śatṛ*. The term *apakajjalam* means *akajjalam* (without collyrium). || 7 ||
With a most charming and shimmering splendor, beautiful as a golden temple,
it rose up like a blossoming *kiṃśuka* tree or like an evening cloud.
Beautiful like a golden palace, its splendor shining with a most charming radiance. || 8 ||
Beholding that mass of flames from which the assembly had long since fled,
the deer, out of his former devotion, began to frolic with glances.

Since the courtiers had moved far away, that deer, beholding such a mass of flames, rejoiced and was filled with joy by those respectful glances which had previously been cast upon him with feelings of devotion. || 9 ||
Beholding that fire and desiring to enter it, his evil deeds exhausted,
he quickly retreated to a distance, springing back like a lion.
In the meantime, having reflected in meditation, that bull among sages spoke,
purifying the deer with his glances as he looked upon it.
He spoke; the ellipsis implies "to the fire. || 11 ||
O Lord, O bearer of oblations, remembering our former devotion,
out of compassion grant favor to this wise deer.
While the sage was speaking thus, a deer, having run from afar into the assembly of kings, entered him with great speed like an arrow released with force hitting its mark.
Having entered the mass of flames, he was seen with his body clearly visible, like a reflection in a mirror, or like evening clouds come to rest.
"He was seen by people"—this is the ellipsis to be supplied. || 14 ||
Then, even as the members of the assembly were looking on, the deer attained human form,
just as a fragment of a cloud assumes a different shape within the belly of a flame in the sky.
The state of being a man is the human form; a fragment of cloud in the sky has the form of a deer; "another form" means the human form, just so. || 15 ||
Then, within the flame, there appeared a man of invisible form, possessing the luster of gold within, pure in appearance, and beautiful with lovely limbs. (16)
He is beautiful with limbs that are lovely and radiant. || 16 ||
Like the sun in the orb of the Arka tree, like the moon in the lunar disc, like Varuṇa in the great waters, or like the moon amidst the twilight clouds. || 17 ||
The series of similes beginning with "like the orb of the sun" [is as follows]. 17.
Within the sockets of his eyes, like reflections in a mirror, in water, or in a gem, the fire of devotion shone with the luster of the sun. 18.

The phrase beginning with "the eye" is a *mālopamā* (string of similes). He whose support is fire, like a reflection within the sockets of the pupils of the eyes, stands as devotion itself, like a person (*puruṣa*). The connection with the preceding verse is: "The sun-like person was seen. || 18 ||
Immediately thereafter, like a lamp struck by winds in the midst of an assembly,
he vanished somewhere with his mass of flames, like an evening cloud from the sky.
Immediately thereafter, struck by the winds, that mass of flames vanished somewhere like a lamp; it was as if it were extinguished. || 19 ||
When the walls of the hut had collapsed, a man stood there like a god reflected [in the ruins], having emerged from the cloth like a dancer appearing on stage.

When the walls of the temple chamber have crumbled, the immortal one situated within—appearing in the form of Viṣṇu and other deities—is like a reflected image or a statue; he is like an actor who has emerged from behind a curtain or a screen. || 20 ||
Wearing a rosary of beads, peaceful, and possessing a golden sacred thread,
he was clothed in garments purified by fire, appearing like the moon that has just risen.
He whose purity and stainlessness consist solely in being burned by fire, yet who is covered with such garments as these; || 21 ||
Because he shone with that attire while the members of the assembly exclaimed, "Aho!
Bhā!", he was called Bhāsa, possessing a vast splendor like the sun. (22)
"This one is called by the name Bhāsa," so it was said by the people. || 22 ||
"He will become known by the name Bhāsa because he appears like a personified form (mūrta)";
thus it was said by some members of the assembly, and for that reason he is called Bhāsa. (23)
Then, having sat down right there, Bhasa remained absorbed in meditation and recalled his entire previous history within that body.
The account of one's own previous history or life-story. || 24 ||
While the assembly remained motionless and he himself stood with a smile within himself,
Bhāsa saw in just a moment that his own story had remained unharmed.
Having seen and remembered with a smile— a look of wonder (the reading *smitena* appears in the printed edition)—
he arrived from his former births and awakened from the light of meditation. Rising up, he surveyed the assembly in due order.
The phrase "he came" is explained as "he awoke from the light of meditation," occurring respectively in the order of the king of sages, the vassal, and so forth. || 26 ||
Having arrived, he joyfully prostrated before Vasiṣṭha and declared:
"O Brahmin, you who are the life-giving sun of knowledge, salutations be unto you! (27)
That wise man named Bhāsa uttered, that is, spoke. || 27 ||
Vasiṣṭha also spoke to him, touching his head with his hand:
"O King, may the destruction of your ignorance finally come to pass today. (28)
May there be today the destruction of that ignorance which has been visible for so long. || 28 ||
Then Daśaratha, rising slightly from his seat, spoke as if smiling to him who was bowing and crying out, "Victory to Rāma! (29)
To that Bhāsa, who was clearly crying out "Victory! toward Rāma and bowing down in salutation. || 29 ||
Daśaratha said:
"Welcome to you, O King; please sit upon this seat. You who have wandered through the accumulation of many births, may you rest here."
Śrī Vālmīki said:
While Daśaratha was speaking thus, the wise one named Bhāsa entered,
bowing to the sages headed by Viśvāmitra as they sat upon their seats.
Regarding the word *viṣṭara* as a seat or a tree-seat, the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* occurs according to the rule "in the case of *viṣṭara*, when meaning a seat or a tree. || 31 ||
Daśaratha said: Alas! For a very long time, the wise Vipracitti has experienced suffering through ignorance, like an elephant bound by a tethering rope.
Like a tethering post, that is, like a binding pillar. || 32 ||
Alas, what a perilous course results from false awakening and distorted vision!
This [ignorance] displays the tumultuous spectacle of creation within the very void. (33)
How many are these worlds within the expansive Self?
They have been spread out for a long time and have been scrutinized by the wise man.
How many delusions have been entertained by the wise man regarding his own expansive self? This is a marvel! 34.
Oh, what manner of greatness is this of the self-nature of the void-like consciousness!
For within the dense sky of the Supreme Self—which is itself a void—these various worlds shine forth in such a way.
