This manifestation, which is the very nature of Māyā and consists of the activity of the conscious self, is in reality of the nature of space.

What kind of majesty is this, even of the void? "Aho" expresses wonder; "nu" indicates deliberation. That majesty which, being the void itself, exists within the dense mass of the Supreme Self—which is as unattached as the sky—and having become these various and manifold worlds of the aforementioned kinds, shines forth. The meaning is: this is truly a great marvel. || 35 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and thirtieth chapter, titled "The Entry of the Deer into the Fire," in the *Videhamukti-prakaraṇa* of the *Mokṣopāya*, within the *Nirvāṇa-kāṇḍa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by the sage Vālmīki. 130.
Thus ends the one hundred and thirtieth chapter, titled "The Entry of the Deer into the Fire," in the *Tātparyaprakāśa* commentary on the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa*.
The one hundred and thirty-first canto.
Daśaratha said: "This wise man is distressed by that which is the object of ignorance, as if he were unwise."
Therefore, I consider that to be mere exertion; what is the use of clinging to a thing that is not real? (1)
Having been prompted by Kauśika after he had told the story of the prince Vaṭadhāna, Vipaścit related his own delusion in detail.

I consider all that which this wise man, being afflicted, has experienced as afflictions directed toward ignorance— that ignorance characterized by looking toward the ends of the quarters and consisting of what is not a human goal—
to have been merely the delusive and futile exertion of one who is unwise, ignorant, and devoid of self-knowledge; for [it is directed] toward a non-entity.

The meaning is: regarding the illusory curiosity of seeing the ends of the horizon and so forth, there is a contemptible obsession; "kiṃgraha" refers to a stubborn persistence (*durāgraha*) such as "I must certainly achieve this," which is painful and results in affliction (*kleśa*). || 1 ||
Śrī Vālmīki said: At that moment, Viśvāmitra, who was standing by the side of the king, spoke these words which arose in the course of conversation.

Having heard the king’s words, Viśvāmitra—whose latent impressions (saṃskāra) regarding the prince were awakened by the mention of the Buddha’s birth—is described by Vālmīki as saying that story, which he deems not to be neglected because it serves as a cause for strengthening the purpose of describing the current account of the wise man: "In this... (verse 2).
O King, for many who have not attained supreme enlightenment, there arise in great numbers various kinds of obstacles to that which is to be known through enlightenment. (3)

O King, you have spoken most correctly; for those who have not attained supreme awakening— that is, the knowledge of reality— for such people as these, there arise many such extraordinary, diverse, and manifold cognitions consisting of delusion, or rather, objects known through them which consist of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and take the form of infinite millions of worlds.
The composition of the introductory framework for the narrative to be related hereafter. || 3 ||
Today, having wandered in this very manner for seventeen hundred thousand years with their resolve unshaken, these seeds of the banyan tree remain situated upon the earth.

Therein he introduces the narrative with the words "Today," and so forth: even the princes named Vaṭadhāna, who are to be described later, have likewise remained wandering for seventeen hundred thousand years from the present day until the end of time, just as Vipaścit did. || 4 ||
Even now, they have set out for the purpose of seeing the end of the earth, free from agitation; like the currents of a river, they do not turn back.
Indeed, this great world is circular, situated in the sky;
it is like a tree born of the imagination of a child, yet established by the resolve of Brahmā’s own volition.

He begins the description of that very earth with the words "This" (ayam). This well-known great world—the aggregate of the fourteen worlds beginning with Pātāla and Bhūmi—is spherical due to the spherical intermediate spaces (antarikṣa-loka), and it is situated in the sky surrounding the earth. And that [world] belongs to Brahmā...

The Hiranyagarbha is nothing other than the very determination of volition (*saṃkalpa-niścaya*), which cannot be otherwise defined. This [Hiranyagarbha] is indeed that which is renowned in the science of astronomy (*jyotiḥ-śāstra*) as being situated in the sky or ether like a tree of a child’s imagination—consisting of the terrestrial globe, the great worlds, and the fourteen realms inhabited by beings who depend upon it as their support; for this too is of the nature of Brahmā.
The meaning is that it is simply the determination of one's own volition. || 6 ||
When the ball is confined within the void, ants wander in all ten directions;
in this same way, living beings, which are always supported by that [body], wander perpetually.

To the question of how that which is itself without support can be the support of all beings, he says: "In the ball" (kanduke). Just as ants swarm in the ten directions around a ball smeared with honey, even so, all beings who depend upon Him wander in the ten directions all around Him; such is the meaning. || 7 ||
The lower portions of the terrestrial globes and their upper parts are its limbs;
then the elements abide there, and having entered them, they revolve.

Having entered those limbs of his which are situated on the lower part of the earth-globe and those which are upward-facing and above, whatever beings reside there at any time, they then wander about in those very places. || 8 ||

Having entered that very [space], the constellations of stars, along with the moon, the sun, and so forth, revolve continuously at a great distance from the rivers, moving aloft without ever touching them.

The rivers such as the Mandākinī flowing through the atmosphere, and the circle of constellations which is the form of the celestial sphere, revolve high above that very terrestrial globe, held at a distance by the power of the binding wind and moving without contact [with it].
The feminine ending for the neuter is a Vedic archaism (chāndasa).
Right here, the sky stands encompassing all directions;
above that is the space extending in every direction, and beneath it is the surface of the earth.

That sky, together with its light and its wheel, having encompassed the earth, is situated here within this very earth; and therein, space exists in all directions, meaning that [the zenith] is directly above and the surface of the earth is directly below. || 10 ||
The elements fall and run toward its lower part, reaching every limb;
that from which they spring upward and depart is designated as "above."

Now, one might ask: how can the sky beneath the terrestrial globe be considered "above," and how can the surface of the earth be considered "below" in relation to it? To this, he says: "bhāvāḥ" (entities). Those entities or objects that move beneath that surface of the earth reach every limb—that is, every part—of it, falling upon and arriving at their respective locations.

They go, they move about. In whichever space birds and other creatures fly as they rise up, that very place is designated as "upward" (ūrdhva), and not as "downward" or "sideways"—this is the meaning. || 11 ||
In a certain region there, O King, were those known as the Vaṭadhānas;
among them, three sons of kings were born in former times.
In that terrestrial globe, in a certain region, there exists a place called Vaṭadhāna, as well as its sovereign Kṣatriyas; in their lineage, three princes were born in former times. (12)
For they, being thus of one mind, having firmly resolved to go forth for the sake of sport, wondering what the end of the visible path beginning with the earth might be, set out.

Those princes, like Vipaścit himself, possessed a single resolve and firm determination, thinking, "What might be the end of this world consisting of the earth and other visible paths? We shall see it," and they set out to behold it. || 13 ||
Again water, again earth—these long assailed them;
for those who had newly acquired bodies, a vast period of time passed away.

The meaning is that for those who, traversing the various islands and oceans again and again— alternating between water and land in succession— obtained new bodies through death at intervals, a long period of time elapsed. || 14 ||
Moving here incessantly according to the analogy of a ball and a swarm of bees, they do not reach the end, yet they perceive it as something other [than themselves]. (15)

Those ant-insects clinging to the clear ball wander about according to that same principle; in the reading "by the principle of the anthill" (*valmīka-nyāyena*), the word *valmīka* indicates by implication (*lakṣyate*) the very ant-insects who construct it. "Being elsewhere" (*anyatvam*) means being in another location.
O King, they remain even now as restless as ants chasing a ball tossed into the air, yet they do not succumb to weariness.
And whatever region of this terrestrial globe they reach, there too, just as here, the directions—upward, downward, and across—are likewise perceived. (17)
Whichever lower region or lateral direction they reach, they behold the quarters; this is the ellipsis to be supplied. || 17 ||
They said, "O Great King, since we have not yet reached the end despite our efforts, we shall proceed further from here. (18)
"By those with uplifted weapons" means by those who have exerted effort. || 18 ||
Thus, this entire display of Brahmā’s creative resolve is nothing at all;
it is a mere mental construction, an infinite ignorance, like an object seen in a dream. (19)
Having concluded the narrative, he applies it to the subject at hand: "In this way," [verse 19].
Conceptualization is that supreme Brahman, and the supreme Brahman is indeed conceptualization;
there is no difference between their nature as consciousness, just as there is none between emptiness and space. (20)
Since the conceptualization of mental constructs has consciousness as its substrate, he confirms through a reciprocal exchange that pure consciousness alone is the reality:

"Whatever appears as pure consciousness, like a transformation of a flowing stream of water—how could that which is of such a nature appear as something else? For it is impossible for one thing to be another. (21)
The "flow" (vāha) is the current of water; it is like the transformations found therein, such as whirlpools, waves, and bubbles.

While in the case of whirlpools and the like, there might somehow be an appearance of something else due to their resemblance to the hollow of a navel and so forth, here, however, since nothing else—whether similar or dissimilar—is absolutely possible, how could there even be an appearance of something else? This is the meaning. || 21 ||
Non-existence in the sky, and this very sky at the beginning of creation is the supreme ether;
it appears as if it were the world itself, for there is nothing else in dissolution or creation.

At the beginning of the creation of this world, there was non-existence; therefore, space (*kha*) is indeed the void (*śūnya*). Thus, it is beyond dispute that at that time it was the supreme ether, the very space of Brahman (*brahmākāśa*). And so, according to the view that even now it is that very same [Brahman] which appears as the world by itself, there is no other [reality] apart from dissolution and creation. (22)
Just as it grinds against the nature of consciousness, so too does it attain delight therein;
thus it remains for a long time within its own cycles of existence, both seen and unseen, for as long as it lasts.

And that consciousness-nature (cidrūpa), in accordance with the latent impressions (vāsanā) of desire and karma, however it undergoes modification and embraces conceptual construction (kalpanā), in that very way it attains delight and attachment therein,
through seen and unseen, knowable and unknowable, and insentient and sentient forms superposed upon one another as being identical in nature.
Just as it existed for a long time previously through its own successive births, so too does it remain for a long time hereafter.
This single form, whose nature is the visible, is thus one and imperishable;
it shines by itself as unborn, such that nothing at all appears to shine.
By explaining that these two possess the nature of being seen and unseen, he demonstrates the inexhaustibility of the second, stating: "That which consists of the visible. || 24 ||

Within the belly of the atom of consciousness reside all atoms of experience—[the reading *anubhavārṇavāḥ* (oceans of experience) is to be considered doubtful]—transparent like stones within the interior of a mountain, being of the nature of space within the self that is space. (25)

He says that within the belly of the atomic consciousness (cidaṇu), the atoms of the experience of the world remain, delimited by the respective latent impressions (vāsanā) of their forms—thus [he states] "of the atomic consciousness" (cidaṇoḥ). || 25 ||

They abide in the ultimate state of intrinsic nature— [here the reading *svabhāvabhūtāḥ* would be more suitable for the commentary]. Yet they do not truly abide in that which is of an indeterminate nature, because they have not yet turned away from the supreme state.

He says "no" to the question of whether [these] exist within the belly of the pure conscious atom, stating "svabhāva... etc. Those who have become that [consciousness] possess their own nature (svabhāva), which is the veiled form of the Self. However, they do not abide in the supreme state—that is, in consciousness free from ignorance; indeed, they do not exist there at all. The meaning is that since no other form to be excluded is established there, they would be non-excluded and thus absolutely non-different [from that consciousness]. || 26 ||
Therefore, that very Brahman, which is of the nature of light and all-pervading, is called the "world" by those of subtle intellect when they skillfully reflect upon it from beginning to end. (27)

Since they are not excluded from that [reality], therefore it alone is the world and nothing else; this I have stated with precision through a careful consideration of what precedes and follows. O you of subtle intellect! (27)
This is most wonderful: though he has not fallen from the supreme abode itself, the living being (jīva) suffers by means of the notion of diversity, thinking "I am [a separate] individual."

Thus, even though this individual soul (jīva) has not perished nor departed from the abode of the Supreme Self due to its identity with pure consciousness, the fact that it suffers and languishes with the thought "I am a jīva" because of the notion of multiplicity is truly a great wonder; such is the connection [of the verse]. || 28 ||
"O King Bhāsa, you who are named Vipashcit, speak! How much of the visible world have you seen, how much have you wandered through, and what do you remember? (29)

Having thus corroborated the account of Vipaścit as told by Vasiṣṭha with his own words, Viśvāmitra spoke in order to corroborate it also with the words from the mouth of Bhāsa, saying: "Let it be told. "O Vipaścit, also known as Apara, O Bhāsa, how much of the visible world have you seen, and how much of it have you wandered through? Of that, what do you remember? Tell us that in brief."
Let it be stated. || 29 ||
Bhāsa said:
Much that is visible has been seen by me, and much have I wandered without weariness;
indeed, I remember having experienced many things in many ways.
O King, having reached that infinite great void, I have for a long time experienced, in bodies of various kinds and at a vast distance, immense joys and sorrows throughout endless worlds. (31)
Having reached that great expanse, the unmanifest space.
O Great-Souled One, by means of the power of boons and curses, I have witnessed infinite manifestations with diverse bodies—
the revolutions within the whirlpools of successive births— through my mind being firmly fixed on the boon granted by Agni.

It follows that with a mind firmly fixed on the range of vision of the horizon, I have experienced there, during the revolutions of other births, infinite transformations arising from the boon of the Sun. || 32 ||
For the sake of examining the limit of this earth-bodied form, which is of the nature of the visible and perceived through the eye of ignorance,
I formerly exerted constant and intense effort with body after body toward every world until the dawn of memory.

The meaning is: although I wandered through every universe, body after body, without any distinction between different bodies, I nevertheless remained—through the cause of remembering my former firm resolve—with intense effort and speed, for the purpose of examining the end of that vision of ignorance which consists of the nature of the earth and other elements, and whose essence is the visible world. || 33 ||

For a thousand years I was a tree, inward-minded and experiencing the suffering of consciousness; yet, without a mind, amidst the expansion of flowers, fruits, and branches, I was like a bulbous root, colored only by the sap of its own body. (34)

Then, at the time of death, by the force of the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) directed toward the sight of that tree, I—possessing an attachment (*rāga*) toward taking up a body in a limb [of that tree]—became a branch for a thousand years; the suffix *aka* here has the sense of possession (*matvarthīya*), thus I was a "branched one" (*viṭapī*). Of what nature was I? Because the movements of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which are the external causes of activity, were not manifested, I existed only within.
The meaning is as follows: that which possesses a mind (*manas*); where suffering is experienced by the conscious living being (*jīva*) who identifies with the body of the tree;

and likewise, without the *citta*—which is the cause for the prior and subsequent reflection—there is a bulbous root (*kanda*), a specific type of root, in the spreading or the production of flowers, fruits, and so forth, which functions according to the principles of earthly sap, time, and other factors. || 34 ||

For a hundred years I was a deer on Mount Meru, golden-hued, with ears like tree leaves; devoted to tasting blades of dūrvā grass and listening to songs, I lived as the youngest among the forest-dwellers. (35)
He who possessed a firm attachment and a constant craving for tasting the sprouts of *dūrvā* grass and for songs;
who was the smallest among the forest-born deer, having a small body and little strength; and for that very reason, he did not harm anyone. (35)

With my back covered by eight rows of feet, having brought about my own death through the distress of the waters when they were dying, I was a Śarabha for fifty years in the golden caves of Mount Krauñca. (36)

Even when walking on all fours behind the Śarabha species, since even the region of its belly can become its back, he whose own back was encircled by eight feet; yet, when death was imminent, he prepared to fight with the cloud, using the hailstones falling from the roaring clouds as his weapons.
He who brought about his own death through the very suffering of leaping and falling from the mountain peak. || 36 ||

On the peaks of Malaya and on Mount Mandara, within the bower-houses of Mandāra, sandalwood, and kadamba creepers, I have drunk the nectar of the arts of love from Vidyādharī maidens, carried by the breeze entwined with black aloe-wood trees and vines. (37)
Therefore, the genitive case in "me" (of me) expresses the residual relationship (*śeṣatva*) of the agent. Having attained birth as a Vidyādhara, I— on the ridges of Malaya and Mandara,
embraced by the creeping vines of black aloe trees and thus [surrounded] by a breeze that was cool, gentle, and fragrant—
drank and experienced the nectars characterized by the various arts of the Vidyādharīs during their amorous dalliances.

Tawny with the nectar of golden lotuses, these waters were drunk by me for fifteen hundred years on Mount Meru; there, as the son of the swan of Brahmā, I sported upon the banks of a mountain torrent.

I, the son of Viriñca’s swan, having obtained the birth of a son, have drunk the waters turned tawny— stained with the nectar of golden lotuses— while sporting on the banks of the river Mandākinī atop Mount Meru. (38)

For a hundred years, I have heard the song of the beautiful women of Mādhava, which removes both grief and old age, while their dark tresses of hair were stirred like the fragrant breezes from the forests on the shores of the Ocean of Milk.
On Mount Kālañjara, amidst a forest of Karañja and Guñjā trees in full bloom, I took on the form of a jackal.
There, a certain elephant was crushed by a lion; that elephant was seen by me, who had died for his sake.
Then, on Mount Kālañjara, in a forest abounding in *karañja* and *guñjā* trees, I attained birth as a jackal, reaching the state of a *sṛgāla*.
There too, when my own body was crushed and ground to pieces by an elephant, while I was half-dead, I saw that very elephant who had crushed me killed by a deer, which was itself a lion. || 40 ||
On a certain ridge of the Sahya mountains, which laughs with rows of *saṃtānaka* flowers, there lived a celestial nymph with a face like the moon of another world;
and then, due to the curse of a *siddha*, I myself became that solitary woman in her dwelling made of clusters of *kalpa*-tree blossoms during half of the Kṛta Yuga.

Then, on a ridge of Mount Sahya that shone as if laughing with clusters of *saṃtānaka* and various *kalpavṛk�sa* trees, I, a moon-faced celestial woman, remained for half of the Kṛta Yuga due to a curse incurred by a perfected being (*siddha*).
In one place, I spent another hundred years with a fearless mind in the hollows of great mountains and among the thickets of karavīra creepers;
elsewhere, on the distant sovereign mountain, I dwelt alone and constantly in the form of a bird, like Vālmīki.

Then, by the power of my proximity to Sahya, the king of mountains, I brought a hundred birds of the species known as *vālmīka*— which are ever-crying and habitually vocal— to the interior regions of the branches and creepers of *karavīra* trees growing in the marshy coastal zone; thereafter, in that grove of *karavīra* trees...

When his wife, sons, and others had perished, and while the world remained otherwise far away, he spent the remainder of his life alone on Mount Indragiri, the Mahendra mountain, deeply afflicted by separation. || 42 ||
Elsewhere, on the mountain ridges, I beheld women hanging from creepers entwined with shady sandalwood groves;
they were like fruits adorned with charms, enjoyed and even carried away by the wandering Siddhas. (43)

Thus, after being released from the curse of the Siddhas through two births, and having myself become a Siddha solely by the grace of the Siddhas, I beheld women upon another ridge of Mount Mahendra— which was encircled by groves of fragrant sandalwood trees— swaying with the playful grace of hanging like the fruit of creepers upon swings; though they were carried off by traveling Siddhas, they were enjoyed by me as well.
Elsewhere, on the slopes of a mountain and in the thickets of kadamba trees, those days were spent in the highest state of asceticism;
yet within, my mind was afflicted by the cholera of obsession with a single object, and thus, though possessing great intelligence, I remained one of little wit with a weary soul.

Immediately thereafter, by me— who was thus characterized by a mind seized and brought under control by the cholera-like affliction of *abhiniveśa* (clinging) directed toward a single object that is defined by ignorance and false vision, and who was for that very reason one whose intellect was weary and distressed— having attained inner disillusionment, [I turned] elsewhere.
Days were spent in the state of an ascetic on the marshy banks of the Kadamba groves at the mountain’s slope. || 44 ||
There exists another [world] filling the entire universe, consisting of all the oceans and the regions of every direction;
it possesses fire, ether, wind, and existence, with its ground being merely the forms of beings dwelling in water. (45)

Thus, amidst the description of the succession of his own births, he begins to speak with longing of certain most wonderful events that were forcibly remembered, starting with the words "Brahmāṇḍaiḥ" and so forth: "O Sage, there is another single marvel; listen to it. Of what nature is it? It is filled with infinite cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas)."

[He describes it as] "where all beings situated in the extremities of every direction [are like aquatic creatures]. Explaining the intended meaning of the simile "like aquatic creatures," he qualifies [the world] with the word "saṃdigdha" (doubtful): "in which the existence of the three great elements called fire, ether, and air is doubtful. [It is] "situated in water, as if in water."

The meaning is that this very Brahman exists as a most wonderful reality, in a state where name and form are only slightly differentiated—that is, a ground whose nature consists merely of such a form, like a being reflected [in a mirror]. || 45 ||
In one place, I beheld a certain woman; within her body, the three worlds shone as if reflected inside a perfect mirror, complete with the sky, mountains, the cardinal directions, and all else. (46)

And another marvel I have seen there is that, according to the analogy of gold dust on a stone, the entire universe is present in its entirety within every single object, including the bodies of women; to express this, he cites a certain woman with the words "In one place" (*ekatra*). Within the body of that woman, as if in a beautiful mirror...

The meaning is that it is an utter marvel how the three worlds—including space, mountains, and so forth, as well as the directions, time, living beings, and the rest—appear as if they were reflected therein. || 46 ||
"O lady of excellent limbs, when asked by me, 'Who are you, and what is this body of yours?', she replied:
'I am the pure Consciousness here; these limbs of mine are the great worlds.'"

Then that woman was questioned by me: "O lady of excellent limbs, who are you? Why is this body of yours fashioned like this, encompassing the three worlds? Thereupon she replied to me: "O dear one, I am that pure Consciousness which illumines everything within this collection of objects. And these great worlds are my own body, consisting of both the manifest and the unmanifest."

The body. The intention is that this is based on such scriptural passages as: "There are indeed two forms of Brahman, the formed and the formless; all beings are the body of that [Brahman]," and so forth. || 47 ||
Just as I am, so too is this daughter of Smaya; it is exactly like that, my friend, for there is nothing wonderful in this.
When others do not perceive their own nature as pure, then, my friend, they see things in this way.

My dear friend, just as I—who have been seen by you—am a source of wonder (*smaya*), astonishment (*vismaya*), and amazement (*āścarya*) because I possess a body suited to that [wonder] due to being composed of the entire universe; so too is this entire collection of objects, such as pillars, jars, and the like, truly a most wonderful and marvelous thing because it is composed of the whole world. Therefore, even by other ordinary people (*pṛthagjana*), all...

To the question "Why is the object not seen in this way?", he says: "By others. The sense is that when the nature of each individual thing is not known in this manner, then one does not see it as such; however, when it becomes known through the firm conviction that it exists merely as a subtle body (*ātivāhika*), then they too will certainly see it. || 48 ||

By all beings in the world, even without the aid of the Vedas or other scriptures, this sound—which declares "this is to be done" and "this is not to be done"—is heard constantly from the very walls of their own bodies. 49.
Is this not indeed inconsistent?

Since I do not experience my own body as being composed of the entire universe, if you claim that the world is not seen there because the eyes and other senses do not enter within the body, then it would follow that one could never hear the Vedas, scriptures, and so forth located therein with the ear.

Perceiving my lack of conviction through various signs, she spoke to me with two verses beginning with "aveda" in order to inspire confidence in me: "Even by all beings, including yourself, though it is not accepted as being outside the scope of the Vedas and Śāstras,
there exists within the body another world distinct from the external one, which is limited to the portion residing within your own body."
From its own respective location within the ear-cavity (*karṇa-śaṣkulī*), which constitutes a single part [of it], the eternal *anāhata* sound—

which consists of the *nāda* that is the common form of all sounds such as the Vedas and the Śāstras— is indeed heard by itself. For that very [sound] is this [source of] obligatory and occasional ritual action, as well as the means for knowledge such as tranquility (*śama*) and self-control (*dama*).

The meaning is this: since everything that is to be enjoined (*vidheya*) must necessarily be performed, it contains within it all injunctions; and since this [prohibited act] such as the eating of *kalañja* is not to be enjoined, it contains within it all the prohibitions of the Vedic scriptures. Therefore, by the mere hearing of that [sound], one should conceive that the entire world—which is the object of those injunctions and prohibitions contained therein—exists within the body, just like the scriptures of injunction and prohibition themselves. || 49 ||

The very nature of the existence of things is such that even walls, mountains, and the like speak to me here as if in dreams or illusions; therefore, it is not inconsistent for them to address you. (50)

With the intention that, by the logic already stated, the existence of the entire world may likewise be conceived even in the case of pillars, jars, and so forth, he says: "The unstruck sound (*anāhatadhvani*) has the nature of the universal of sound;
indeed, its nature is such that it is the very nature of the universal composed of the entire world. This is because it is well-known in this world for that reason.

Even walls, mountains, and so forth are that very existence of Brahman (*brahmasattā*). One should not fall into the error of thinking that walls and such do not speak and are therefore merely insentient;

for even now, they speak words before me, just as in the well-known illusions of dreams and the like. This is because even in walls and other objects renowned for being utterly inert, there exists the sentience that comprises the entire universe.

There was no inconsistency then even among you who consist primarily of consciousness; it is all the more so that there was no inconsistency in your bodies, beginning with those of yours—this is the meaning. || 50 ||
While wandering through this world devoid of women, I once beheld a being from whom many beings were emerging and into whom many beings were entering. (51)

Having described the wonder characterized by conversation with women that he himself had witnessed, he describes another such wonder in the verse beginning with *astrīka*: "In some place or time, there exists a world (*saṃsāra*) where no women are found; while I was within that world, I did not perceive any other desire whatsoever among the entire multitude of living beings."

If it is observed that someone possesses a desire for such a transformation, then how can there be a connection with sons, grandsons, and so forth, or the death of ancestors therein? To this he says: "The elements," etc. (Verse 51).
O you of vast limbs, I have clearly seen clouds in the sky emitting a rattling sound;
they fall on all sides as rain and become sharp weapons for men in their fragments.
He speaks of another marvel: "ekāni" and so forth. "Āñjasāni" means independent of omens such as portents.

Other single clouds were seen in the sky; and they produced a "jhaṇajjhaṇa" sound through their roarings, which resembled the noise of clashing weapons. From those [clouds], by means of rain, those things such as lightning that fall like water fell in fragments.
From their own fragments, the weapons of people come into being. || 52 ||
"Elsewhere, as far as the eye can see through the sky, blind people here go toward village houses;
they enter them there, while here it has become your village—this very same one obtained from another place. (53)

Elsewhere, another marvel was seen. What was it? In this world, as many villages and houses as there are, all of them travel through the sky—the path of the atmosphere—by means of a blind darkness that impairs the sight, and enter there into the distant horizon; yet that very village has become here, and that same [village] was found by me in quite another place.
This means "it is a marvel. || 53 ||
Apart from the distinctions of humans, gods, and serpents, all beings are equal;
they arise from space alone and at that same time, they do not go to dissolution.

He speaks of another wonder seen elsewhere, beginning with the words "nara" (men): these men, these gods, and these serpents—by those intermediate distinctions of the inhabitants of the three worlds, they are abandoned; for that very reason, they are equal.

I remember that certain world, the sole beloved of all, which is devoid of moon, stars, and sun, yet free from darkness; a collection of all beings self-luminous, resembling the interior of a flame, and liberated from day and night. (55)
Elsewhere, he states another marvel: "without moon," etc. The reason for the absence of darkness is: "self-luminous."

I remember infinite great worlds containing unprecedented beings such as Daityas, serpents, humans, and gods, with unprecedented trees and cities, and possessing unprecedented activities in other realms. 56.
He states another marvel: "Apūrva" (unprecedented). Unprecedentedness consists in being distinct from the conventional usage of well-known forms.
There is no direction that has not been traversed by us, nor indeed is there any region that has not been seen;
there is no task that has not been experienced, and nothing else remains except for reflection upon another [state]. (57)
What need is there for more? There is no direction in which I have not wandered; there is no land that I have not seen;
and there is no activity or curiosity that I have not experienced—by virtue of my own reflection, discernment, and experience, I am the witness of all.
There is nothing else that exists apart from this— neither another locus, nor another substratum, nor anything distinct and separate from it.

(57) I remember the jingling sound produced by the armlets on Upendra’s arms as they struck together in one place, created by the friction of the tips of the jeweled peaks of Mount Mandara when it was whirled in the ocean of milk.
By one who was alarmed by the roar of a thundercloud. || 58 ||

Fearing the deep thundering of the Lord Upendra’s armlets— which produced a jangling resonance as they were struck and sharpened by the sharp, whetstone-like tips of the peaks of Mount Mandara (which had been rotated for the purpose of churning the ocean of milk)— [the clouds fled].

This is the conclusion of the expressions of wonder, beginning with "I remember," regarding that sound heard by the people as being most extraordinary due to their suspicion that it was the roar of a cloud. || 58 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the World-appearance," in the *Vasiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa* of Valmiki, belonging to the Holy Arsha tradition, within the section on the Ultimate Reality, the Liberation of the Disciple, and the Instruction to Bharata.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Illusion of Saṃsāra," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and thirty-second canto.
Bhāsa said:
On Mount Mandara, in a soft *mandāra* bower, [he saw] the one named Mandarā.
Embracing an Apsaras, he was carried away like a blade of grass by a river while asleep.
Here too, Bhāsa describes at length the wanderings through successive births,
numerous wonders, and the essencelessness of worldly existence.
He resumes the narrative concerning the succession of births in the fire, which had been interrupted by descriptions of wonders,

beginning with the words "on Mandara": having attained perfection through the experience of the ascetic life spent for many days in the thickets on the slopes of the mountain, he [dwells] in the soft bower of Mandāra trees on Mount Mandara.

Having embraced me while I was asleep, embracing the Apsaras named Mandarā, the river about to be described carried me away like a blade of grass fallen into its current; that is to say, she swept me along. || 1 ||
Then, having been questioned by me and comforted while she was distressed with water, that girl with tremulous eyes said, "O child, what is this? (2)

The word "mām" (me) connects with what precedes. Immediately thereafter, that Apsarā, distressed and agitated by the water, was consoled by me and questioned: "O young woman, for what reason has this sudden drifting of our two vessels occurred upon the river?
Then, her eyes trembling with fear, she spoke. (2)
Here, at the rising of the moon, these rivers born from the slopes of moonstones rejoice at the arrival of night, like beloved women.

To explain what was said, he says: "Here. O beloved, here in this region, when the moon has risen, these rivers—which are the offspring, that is, the progeny, of the mountain ridges consisting of moonstones—rejoice and swell with their flowing waters, just as those who are fond [of their loved ones] rejoice at the arrival of their beloved at the onset of night.
In the same way, women, when united with desire, become intoxicated. || 3 ||
"Surely that was forgotten under the influence of the intense passion for union with you.
Having said this, she took me up and flew into the sky like a bird.

To the question, "Why then was this matter not reported by you to me even before sleep came? he replies with the words "tvatsaṅgame" (at the time of union with you). The word "nanu" is used as a gentle address. The ellipsis is "I forgot it. Just as a female bird staying upon a golden lotus on the Gaṅgā flies up into the sky taking her companion, the bee, with her; so [did I forget].
"Taking hold of me, she flies up into the sky"—this is the connection with what follows.
I remained for seven years as a bee on the peak of Mount Śṛṅgavat, upon the golden lotuses of the Gaṅgā, drenched by that [water] even though it was not submerged in mud.
Drenched by that water, I thereafter remained for seven years with her on the peak of Mount Mandara, which was stainless and free from mud. || 5 ||
Furthermore, I have seen another world devoid of the circle of stars,
filled with people who are self-luminous and belong to a single birth while remaining within the womb of the womb.

Then, he describes the vision of the interior of the world with its wonders in another birth: "Another," etc. It was devoid of the circle of stars, the *jyotiścakra*. It was filled with people of a single lineage who, like the inner core within the layers of a plantain tree, dwelt within a womb and were self-luminous. (6)
Therein there is no division of directions, nor days, nor indeed treatises, nor Vedic doctrines;
nor is there any distinction between Daityas, gods, and others—that world which is composed of me, self-luminous in such a manner.
To the question, "In that case, how does the engagement in worldly and Vedic activities proceed there?", he says: "No; [it is] illumined by the Self alone, shining forth. (7)
On the slopes and thickets of mountain ridges that scraped the clouds— lands where Vidyādharas and gods dwell in their celestial chariots—
I, named Amarasoma, lived for seven years as an ascetic on the shore of another sea, my mind equanimous in the midst of battle.

Then he describes another birth: "Vidyādhara... and so forth. On the shore of the ocean—that is, in a place adjacent to the ocean—on the slopes of a multitude of mountain ridges that were cloud-kissing and exceedingly lofty, I was a Vidyādhara named Amarasoma; for fourteen years (seven plus seven), I remained there as an ascetic. || 8 ||
It was surrounded by many clouds that served as bodies for horses with various wind-like movements,
and by elephants, deer, lions, trees, creepers, antelopes, mountains, serpents, and birds.

Then, by means of the supreme power of the Fire-god, desiring to behold ignorance everywhere in the world, I saw those whose bodies were like clouds— possessing various excellent horses of noble breed moving like the wind in the form of currents through various arrangements of gait.

The connection between the two verses is as follows: having ascended from the earth into the sky—which is filled with such people, elephants, deer, lordly bulls, trees, creepers, and other wild animals, mountains, serpents, and birds—and which is an infinite treasury, Garuḍa, the devourer of snakes, rushed forward with force and speed, having spread himself out like that. || 9 ||

Having ascended from the earth into the sky by the supreme power of the Fire-god, I moved forward like Garuda, desiring to behold from every side the infinite expanse of the world and forcibly dispel ignorance.
At one time, having emerged from the world, I fell into a vast single great ocean; there, white as the sky and dwelling within it, I experienced that fall according to the cosmic law.

Therefore, having emerged from that world, I fell into the sky, which is as vast as a single great ocean; there, bound within the white cluster of stars that resembled an abode, I experienced time consisting of days, nights, months, seasons, and so forth, as well as falling and moving in all directions. || 11 ||

For me, who was exhausted and whose sole activity was the experience of falling through the expanse of space, sleep then provided a resting place within; and thereafter, in that state of deep sleep, the entire universe was perceived by me as a dream within that very self,
according to the manner described— wherein the primary experience was indeed the act of falling and moving through the void of space.
Then, immediately after my exhaustion from such a long fall, sleep took its place within my heart. While I remained in that state of deep slumber well-known to all people,
thereupon, when the dream-like waking state had commenced, [I saw] right there within myself.
The entire universe has been perceived and seen within oneself. || 12 ||

Furthermore, like a bird upon a creeper, he was tossed about by the unceasing force of the wind— the instability of the world consisting of the quarters, the heavens, the gods, and Mount Mandara— and thus fell into those various caves of the universe.

Even there, being tossed about like a bird by the creeper of the world— which is restless due to its wandering through the various quarters of space and the universe, and which possesses the strength of an inexhaustible wind— I fell into those caves of the world characterized by the "mās," which are the measures (māna) or limitations (iyattayā pariccheda) of those aforementioned visible objects. 13.
As long as there was hope for sense objects, I went [to them] in an instant;
yet seeing the visible world exactly as before, I went again and again.

The meaning is: as far as the range of my vision—the eye—extended toward objects, for that same extent of space, having gone there in an instant, I went again and again to behold the sight out of curiosity for that vision, even while continuing to look on in that very same manner. || 14 ||
Thus, as I traversed with speed regions both visible and invisible, as well as those accessible and inaccessible, many years passed for me.

In this manner, while traversing with speed both accessible and inaccessible regions— directed toward objects that can be perceived in waking and dreaming states as well as those that are distinct from them and imperceptible— many groups of years have passed for me. (15)
I have not yet reached the end of that ignorance called "the visible," which has taken root in my heart as something false, like a child [fearing] a demoness. (16)
Although one remains established in the experience of inquiry, thinking "this is not it, this is not real," nevertheless, the false vision that "this is this" does not cease. (17)

The sense is this: although I remain established in the experience of inquiry, thinking "this is not real" and "this is not real," nevertheless, a false perception persists regarding each object, thinking "this is real" and "that is real," because the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of the long-practiced reality of duality is so powerful. || 17 ||
Moment by moment, through pleasures and pains, and through encounters with places and times, all things are as unstable as the waters of a river; they come anew and pass away.

Even though false views have been dispelled by investigation, they arise anew again and again— like the waters of a river— due to pleasures and pains that recur at every moment, due to differences in place and time, and due to encounters with liked and disliked people. || 18 ||
I remember a certain mountain peak, towering with *tālī*, *tamāla*, and *bakula* trees, its summit unsurpassed in height, where the wind roars with great force;
it is devoid of the sun and other celestial bodies, yet it makes the entire universe—including all moving beings, mountains, and forests—manifest by its own radiance.
Regarding that one marvel, he says: "Tālī... And that peak, even though it is devoid of the sun and others...

Shining manifest by its own luster, the universe—consisting of both the stationary mountain slopes and the moving beings—is like the plateau of that peak; thus, Brahman alone, as the substratum of all, is indicated here as the wondrous peak. || 19 ||

That which is captivating for solitary dwelling, spontaneous, peerless, immeasurable, and free from fear—nowhere among the beautiful worlds have I seen its equal; even the splendor of the king of the gods is not its match. (20)

This peak, which is captivating and enchanting for those knowers of reality who dwell in solitude— being independent, singular, immeasurable, free from the fear of transformation, and devoid of the threefold limitations— is seen here and there among the beautiful worlds within the circles of the knowers of Brahman, as well as by the king of the immortals, Indra, and by Hiraṇyagarbha.
And his fortune (lakṣmī) is not equal to, nor can it be compared by measure with [the former]; the sense is that this is because the blisses ending with that of Hiranyagarbha are limited. || 20 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-second canto, titled "The Description of His Own Succession of Births as Narrated by Bhāsa," in the *Ārṣa-Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*, within the *Vālmīkīya-Daivatarāmāyaṇa*, in the *Mokṣopāya*, in the *Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa*.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-second chapter, titled "The Description by Bhāsa of His Own Succession of Births," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and thirty-third canto.
Vipaścit said: "Listen, what wonder have I seen in some other unprecedented world? Tell me."
That which was forcibly brought about by ignorance, resembling the state of the great narrative of Gha. || 1 ||
A most wonderful event, seen somewhere, is described here by Bhāsa:
the falling from the sky of a corpse as large as the seven continents.

In this explanation of ignorance, he introduces the narrative of the corpse through the mouth of Bhāsa by way of a discourse on most wonderful descriptions, beginning with the words "In a certain...": "O Sage, in a certain unprecedented world other than this one, I beheld this marvelous and exceedingly wonderful thing which I shall describe; listen to it."

That which was most loathsome—even equal to the conditions experienced in hells such as Raurava, which are the fruits of great sins like the killing of a Brahmin—was performed and brought about by me, blinded by ignorance, through the power of my petition for a boon from the Fire-god; that is to say, it was experienced. || 1 ||
Somewhere in the sky, inaccessible to you, there exists a world with a wondrous creation of blazing light;
yet even such a thing is like another city within the void, as unreal as a dream-city appearing in the mind during the waking state.

In some part of the sky that is inaccessible and impossible for you to reach, there exists a manifold creation illuminated by the blazing light of the moon, sun, and other luminaries. That [creation] is of such a configuration, resembling this cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), yet it is indeed different from this one because, when viewed from the perspective of space, it is devoid of substantiality. An illustration for this is as follows: just like a dream.

The meaning is as follows: a city seen in a dream, although similar to a city seen while awake, is indeed different because it appears in the mind as empty from the perspective of waking reality; such is the case here. || 2 ||
While dwelling there, I cast my eye toward the quarters of the sky in search of the object held within my heart;
as I looked, I beheld the shadow of the mountain upon the earth, darkened by swarms of bees, wandering about.

While dwelling in this world, I cast my eye toward the faces of the quarters—the very limits of the horizon—to seek that object of my heart’s desire which was situated within me; that is to say, it was sent forth. As far as I looked with curiosity among them, I beheld upon the earth a vast shadow, dark as a swarm of bees, resembling a mountain, wandering restlessly to and fro.
It wanders. || 3 ||

"What is this? Is it merely a marvel? In the twinkling of an eye, while I was still casting my gaze upon the world, I suddenly beheld a mountain of incomparable size in human form falling from the sky with whirling circular motions. (4)

Then, reflecting upon whether this shadow-form was appropriate given its immense size and wondering what kind of marvel it might be, as soon as I cast my gaze upward toward the sky, I suddenly beheld a being in human form falling through the atmosphere with whirling circular motions, possessing a scale equal to the measure of the mountains.
Who might this man be, as heavy as a mountain, a cosmic Virāṭ perhaps, whose body falls suddenly like a toppled peak;
he whose form fills the sky and reaches the highest heavens, yet does not shine at all, having obscured the beauty of the entire day? (5)

"Who is this man falling with a body as heavy as a mountain, filling the entire sky? Is he Brahmā, the Virāṭ whose body is the cosmic egg?"—such was the conjecture. For even by him, the sun, though renowned throughout the highest heavens, ceased to shine, its entire splendor of day obscured. || 5 ||

Just as I was thus reflecting upon such a thing with a slight measure of thought in my heart, Vivasvān suddenly fell from the sky with a speed that possessed a deep roar like the crashing of the shell of Brahmā’s egg when it is overturned by the winds at the end of an aeon.
Just as I was reflecting upon such thoughts for a moment, suddenly the sun, Vivasvān,

fell from the sky with a thunderous roar and great velocity, like the falling of the upper shell of the Grandfather’s cosmic egg (Brahmāṇḍa), which had been turned over by the winds at the end of an aeon.
As that terrifying being, whose body is as vast as the ocean, falls,
he fills the earth with its seven continents in an instant.

To the question of what you did then, he replies with two verses beginning with "tasmin": when that object in the form of a person, possessing a terrifying nature, fell upon me, I, fearing the inevitable destruction of my own body due to its crushing impact, then entered the fire standing nearby.
The lineage of both. || 7 ||
Fearing the destruction of my own self along with the worlds and their continents,
I then entered the fire that was inevitably standing by my side.
That venerable Jātavedas, who had been worshipped through hundreds of previous births,
spoke to me with his body as cool as the moon, saying, "Do not fear."
That Blessed One, who has been worshipped for hundreds of previous births, who is like fire yet as cool as the moon, said to me, "Do not fear. || 9 ||
Victory to you, O God! You are our supreme refuge in every birth;
since an untimely end of the aeon has occurred, protect me, O Lord! (10)
Then he speaks his own prayer to Agni, beginning with "Jaya": [Agni] has been born, [that is,] has become manifest. || 10 ||
When this was said, the Fire spoke again: "Do not fear!
Arise, come, let us go to my world, O sinless one."
"O sinless one, let us go to my world, the world of fire; you must come," he said. || 11 ||
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One then placed him upon the back of a parrot;
having burned that being which clung to a portion of his body, he leaped into the sky.

Having placed me upon the back of his own vehicle, the parrot, he burned that previously mentioned "pātobhūta"— meaning a corpse (pāti) because it falls (pāta)— in a certain part of the body, pierced it, and soared into the sky.
Immediately thereafter, having reached the sky, I beheld that terrifying being of hideous form,
who was a source of fear and such a great portent involving a falling of living beings.
As he fell with great speed upon it, the earth—along with its oceans, mountains, forests, cities, and vast wildernesses—trembled;
it created rivers flowing with water from the two mountain-like peaks, and it formed deep chasms from the terrifying wounds where his body had been torn asunder.

When that great corpse fell with such force, the earth, together with the ocean and other realms, trembled. The rivers, their waters stilled and the flow of water obstructed, created two precipices—two waterfalls—on both banks of the mountain streams as the water flowed through alternative channels. Water poured down.
They created pits of terrifying appearance and fearsome form— distinct from ordinary bodies—
that were unlike the ponds, wells, and such things produced by the tearing of the earth through the bodies of humans and other beings;
[in the variant reading *vidhuradehavibhedakartṝn*, it means] those which cause the breaking of one's own body through a disordered and distressed shattering of the earth.
The meaning is that he performed the cutting of the embankments and other such tasks. || 14 ||
The earth resounded; the northern quarter resounded and the southern direction resounded loudly.

The sky resounded and the entire world, including its mountains, resounded intensely, terrified by the agitation of the dissolution. He speaks again as to what else occurred then—beginning with "the earth": the earth is the ground; "from the north" means the northern quarter, and likewise the eastern [quarter].

The southern and western quarters, as well as the sky along with the mountains and all beings, being terrified by the agitation of the dissolution, shrieked, roared, and wept aloud. The repetition of the verbal root [in "rarāsa," "dadhvāna," and "ruroda"] is intended to indicate the distinctiveness of those various sounds. || 15 ||
The broad earth resounded with a roar, a sound that terrified the entire expanse of the quarters with its impetuous and violent force;
even the sky was filled with an insurmountable, tumultuous *ghuṃghuma* din.
Fierce in its power to cause the flight of the hosts of enemies of the Nāgas. || 16 ||
Having already stated this, he says it again more clearly with the word "urvī" (the earth). Regarding the support of the corpse fallen upon the ground:
with an intensity of pitch, he produced an exceedingly loud *ghuṃghuma* sound that could not be surpassed by other sounds;
it was fierce and unbearable, as if during the flight of the enemies of the serpents—the Garuḍas—out of fear. || 16 ||

A thunderous roar arose on all sides, portending terrible fear; born from the violent splitting of mountain caves, it delivered a threatening challenge like the sound of the clouds at the end of an eon, stirred by the fierce and terrifying gale of a cosmic portent.

An earthquake—a crashing sound caused by the violent shattering of mountain caves—arose for the purpose of terrifying and striking fear, and it manifested as a cause of dread that split the ears and hearts. Of what nature was it?
It was like the clouds of the cosmic dissolution (*kalpa*), which were agitated by the end-of-age winds that, possessing a terrifying force, draw everything in like a net.
One by whom threats and rebukes have been bestowed and issued forth from the roars of the clouds of universal dissolution. ||17||
As it fell with such speed, the earth resounded and the quarters of the sky went deafeningly silent as if pierced by a hundred bolts;
there, the great slopes of the principal mountain ranges shattered, and the peaks of the Himavat entered the realm of Pātāla.
Upon that corpse, he attained—that is, reached—a penetration a hundredfold greater than before; [this occurred] there, in that penetration. || 18 ||
The descent of him, who was like a rock from Mount Meru, caused the shattering of mountain peaks and the rending of the earth. (19)
The fall of that corpse was of such a nature. To describe what it was like, he says: "shattering," and so forth. || 19 ||
The agitation of the masses of waters, the casting down of mountains upon the earth,
the oppression of all living beings, and the sport of those seeking universal dissolution.
"Depositing on the ground" means the means of leveling it; [this refers] to the hosts of Rudras who seek dissolution. || 20 ||
The casting down of the sun to the earth, the obscuring of the succession of continents, the pulverizing of the mountains, and the shattering of the terrestrial mandala. (21)
Sthaganam means covering. || 21 ||
The sky-dwellers beheld it as if it were a second terrestrial surface, like another half of the cosmic egg, or like the sky itself fallen down in form.
By form means by way of a manifested shape. || 22 ||
Then I beheld that mountain composed of flesh;
not even a single limb of his could be contained within the earth of the seven continents.
Having beheld him, O Lord, I approached the deity who was established in grace; I then questioned the blessed Fire-god, "O Master, what is this? (24)
How did that fleshly Arka fall from the sky together with him?
For he could not be contained upon the surface of the earth, including its mountains, forests, and oceans.
"How did this body made of flesh fall? And how did that celebrated Arka fall along with him?"—this should be applied by repeating [the question] for each. || 25 ||
Agni said:
"Wait for a moment, my son, without haste, until this fault has been pacified; then I shall explain it."
They [depart] from there. || 26 ||
Wait, wait; until this fault of its falling is completely pacified—[the reading "śāmyati" occurs in both places]. || 26 ||
Then, even as he was speaking thus, all the sky-dwellers belonging to that web of worlds arrived from every direction, having come through the atmosphere.
For whom the entire sky and the world are their garments, ornaments, garlands, and so forth.
Siddhas, Sādhyas, Apsarases, Daityas, Gandharvas, Uragas, and Kinnaras;
Ṛṣis, Munis, Yakṣas, Pitṛs, Mātṛs, and immortals. || 28 ||
Who are those who move through the sky? He says: "The Siddhas," and so forth. || 28 ||
Then all those sky-dwellers, with their heads and bodies bowed low in devotion, offered praise to the goddess Sarveśvarī, the refuge-seeker, the Night of Doom (Kālarātri).
The sky-dwellers said:
Having tied the great mass of matted hair of the lotus-born Brahmā to the prong of his skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga),
and having fashioned a garland for his chest and a crest for his head from the severed heads of the foremost Daityas with the feathers of Garuḍa;

May that Goddess—who, having consumed the universe, drinks up this entire world including its mountains and the surface of the earth; she who is stainless and possesses a formed body like a creeping vine—protect those who are worthy of her protection. 30.

That Goddess who, at the end of the great kalpa, having bound the mass of Kapila-colored matted locks of the withdrawn Padmayoni (Brahmā) upon the tip of her khaṭvāṅga staff, and having made a garland for her breast from the severed heads of the Daityas,
and likewise fashioned a crest-ornament and ear-pendant from the wings of the withdrawn Tārkṣya (Garuḍa);

Having consumed the entire universe—the multitude of living beings—she, being such as she is, drinks up this world consisting of mountains and the surface of the earth. Thus, even during the dissolution of the entire world, because she is untainted by even a trace of fault, she is stainless and her nature is pure consciousness alone; yet, for our sake, she has assumed a slender form, having taken on a physical body.
May he protect—that is, guard—us, who must necessarily be protected by him. || 30 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-third canto, titled "The Description of the Great Corpse," in the Section on the Instruction of Nidāgha, within the Sub-section on the Liberation of the Corpse, in the Dialogue between Vasiṣṭha and Rama, in the Great Epic Poem of the Auspicious Vāsiṣṭha-Rāmāyaṇa, composed by the Sage. 133.
Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-third canto, titled "The Description of the Great Corpse," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and thirty-fourth canto.
Vipaścit said:
"In the meantime, that man falling from the sky was [seen] by me."
He was seen in the form of a corpse, covering the entire surface of the earth. || 1 ||
Now, the body of the Goddess who has manifested here is described,
as well as her devouring of the yellowish-red corpse by her attendants.

In the meantime, at the moment when the gods had begun their hymn of praise to the Goddess, I beheld— that very man described previously— falling down in the form of a corpse, lifeless, such that he completely covered and concealed the entire surface of the earth. || 1 ||
That portion of his body known as the belly,
by which even the earth with its seven continents was covered, was vast like a mountain and immeasurable.

The meaning is this: that portion of the corpse by which even the earth of seven continents was covered—that very part, known as the "belly" (*kukṣi*), resembling a mountain and possessing a vast interior, belonging to that corpse which had not yet reached its full measure of size upon the complete earth, was seen by me. || 2 ||
Vahni said: "That [Ananta] is infinite; each of his arms, thighs, and heads has reached the further shore beyond Lokāloka, which is indeed outside the range of human perception. (3)
"In that case, how did you know that his arms, thighs, and head were far away? To this he replies: "By fire. "Then where did it fall? To this he replies: "From Lokāloka. || 3 ||
Then, while the assembly of sky-dwellers was praising the Goddess with reverence, she manifested from the sky; had she not been dry herself? (4)
She herself becomes withered and devoid of blood; "nu" is used here for deliberation. || 4 ||
Followed by hosts of pretas and cherished by the circle of Mothers,
she made the sky starry with a multitude of kumbhāṇḍas, yakṣas, and vetālas.
He describes what that [night] was like with the words beginning "by hosts of pretas": she by whom the sky was made *tārakita*, as if stars had appeared within it. (5)
With her veiny, long, staff-like arms she made the surface of the sky appear like a forest;
with the falls of her glances, she scattered suns that set the quarters of the horizon ablaze.
By her, the vault of heaven was made to resemble a forest with her long, sinewy, and veined staff-like arms;
she scattered and dispersed the suns with the glances of her eyes.
Resounding with the jingling *jhaṇajhaṇa* sound produced by the flashing forms of various weapons,
she reduced the host of birds within the hollow of the sky to a hundred fragments.

With the forms of various flashing weapons, she was shattering the host of birds—that is, the multitude of winged creatures—into a hundred fragments within the hollow of the sky, producing a resonant *jhaṇajhaṇa* sound as they struck. || 7 ||
With bodily limbs rich with the heat of the glow of her body's fire,
she radiates splendors extending for ten million yojanas, appearing like a vast forest of tall bamboos.

With her bodily flames, the heat of her gaze, and the intense warmth of the fires in her eyes—endowed with such abundant qualities of her physical limbs—she radiates and scatters splendors extending for millions of yojanas, resembling a vast forest of tall bamboos. || 8 ||
The quarters of the sky were bathed in milk by the moon-like luster of her teeth;
her body, though slender, was exceedingly tall and broad, filling the entire expanse of the heavens.
Supportless and without abode, like a vast garland of clouds at twilight,
she is mounted upon the seat of a *preta*, yet firmly established in the supreme state.

In the case of the garland of clouds, it is that whose support is the sky (nirālamba-ambaram-āspada). In the case of the supreme state, Brahman, she is well-established (suṣṭhu rūḍhā), having manifested therein. || 10 ||
Trembling and blazing in form, the twilight was as red as a rain-cloud,
bearing the splendor of the submarine fire within the ocean of the sky.
Bearing the splendor of the submarine fire, the *vaḍavānala*.
Scattering garlands, she was restless with corpses and severed limbs, with pestles, spears, lances, maces, stools, mortars, and ploughs.
Bṛsikās are seats. || 12 ||
Carrying her offspring through the courtyard of the sky with the clattering roar of her limbs,
she resembled a mountain in the rainy season with the gurgling sounds of falling stones.

With the clattering sound of her teeth—imitated by the word *kaṭakaṭeti*—and with their haughty displays and grandiose movements, she carries the multitude of living beings, the bodies of men, across the courtyard of the sky; just as a mountain torrent in the rainy season carries a series of rocks upon its own body through its gurgling waterfalls. || 13 ||
The gods said: "O Goddess, O Ambikā, this one has been offered as a sacrifice;
let him be brought here quickly along with his own retinue. (14)
The gods said to that goddess: "What did they say? 'O Ambikā, this corpse has been offered as a sacrifice by us together with our retinue; let it be taken quickly and eaten,' thus they spoke. (14)
While the host of gods was speaking thus, the Goddess proceeded to swiftly extract the essence of blood from that corpse by means of her vital breath.

Since the Goddess herself is the power of all vital breaths (prāṇa) and because blood is the substratum of the vital breaths, she proceeded to draw out that essence of blood by means of the vital air itself. || 15 ||
Drawn in by her breath, that blood entered the mouth of the Goddess like a mass of evening clouds entering the interior of a cave on Mount Meru.
While she remained in the sky, she drank that blood drawn from his life-force until,
being satisfied and full, the goddess Caṇḍikā stood there with her body restored.
Having been dry before, she became satisfied, and subsequently, having become plump and nourished, she remained so. || 17 ||
Then she became one whose body was swollen with blood;
red as a row of rain-clouds, her eyes flickered like lightning.
Just as during the rainy season a red-colored mass of clouds stands with eyes as flickering as lightning, so it was. || 18 ||
The Blessed Lady has a protruding belly and is adorned with venomous serpents;
she is intoxicated by the wine of blood and bears all types of weapons.
She began to dance in the sky, which was half-filled by her own body,
while being watched by the gods stationed upon the peaks of the surrounding mountain ranges.
Having filled half of the sky with her own body, she began and commenced her dance;
it was watched by the gods stationed upon the peaks of the rows of summits of the Lokāloka mountain that forms the horizon.
Then the great hosts of Piśācas, Kumbhāṇḍas, Rūpikas, and others obstructed the corpse, just as clouds shroud a massive mountain.
That mountain of corpses was seized by the Kumbhāṇḍas from its waist,
by the hosts of Rūpikās from its belly, and by the Yakṣas who had been mangled by elephants.
Starting from one belly to another; meanwhile, the yakṣas seized him by the remaining sides and back, which had been spared from the wounds inflicted by their own elephant tusks. || 22 ||
Since his other limbs, such as his arms, thighs, and neck, have reached the furthest limit of the universe, they are exceedingly vast. (23)
Now, one might ask: why were they not perceived in parts such as the arms, thighs, and neck? To this he replies with the words "bhujorvi" (arms and thighs).

Since they had reached the farthest shore of the shell of the cosmic egg—the region of the enclosures of water and so forth—for that reason those aggregates of beings remained at a great distance in the extremities of space; thus they were not perceived there, but rather [perceived] right there by means of time.
The connection between the two [verses] is that they were composed by himself. || 23 ||
Then those hosts of spirits remained at a distance in the far reaches of the quarters;
indeed, they did not reach that very place, for they were themselves overcome by time.
While Caṇḍikā was dancing in the sky amidst a host of spirits crowded with corpses,
and while the gods remained upon the mountains, the world then became [as follows].
The mass of quarters was enveloped in a foul stench from the collection of funeral cakes;
it blazed with fires of khadira wood, appearing like masses of clouds with crimson interiors.
He describes what it was like at that time with the words beginning "piṇḍa":

it was such that the masses of quarters (the directions) were enveloped, covered, and pervaded by heaps of raw, foul-smelling flesh, fat, and so forth, which were being brought in, eaten, and carried away. || 26 ||
It resounded with the "sha-va-sha" cries of corpses rising up in the frenzy of chewing flesh, and it echoed with the loud "kaṭa-kaṭa" noise of large bones being shattered by creepers.

"Śava-śava" is an imitation of the sound of gnawing. It is the *bībhatsa* (disgusting) sentiment. It is that in which a great *kaṭakaṭa* (crunching) sound has arisen and spread through the sky from the snapping of sinews and bones, as if they were creepers. || 27 ||
It possessed a terrifying roar due to the clashing and separation of the hosts of beings,
and it was filled with mountains of bones as vast as the Himalayas and Vindhya ranges.
The surface of the earth was smeared with flesh cooked by the flames of fire from the Goddess’s mouth;
the mass of directions was made vermilion-red by the mist of sprays of blood.
The quarters of the horizon were surrounded on all sides by gods acting as spectators,
while the earth with its seven continents had become a single ocean of blood.
Where the quarters of space appeared as if surrounded by a wall and encircled by a rampart. || 30 ||
The entire circle of mountains had completely vanished from sight,
and the women of the quarters were clothed in garments consisting of masses of clouds with a crimson luster.

Where the entire circle of mountains, including their peaks, has become completely hidden— having attained invisibility through the entry of living beings and the covering of bones and other things; where the quarters of the sky, as if young women draped in crimson garments, are dyed by masses of clouds reddened with a glowing hue.
The surface of the sky was covered by weapons whirled by arms moving in circular and oscillating motions,
while the circles of cities and towns were reduced to the distant range of memory.
Where the surface of the sky was covered by weapons—the missiles and armaments of that host of goddesses.
It consists of all things, both stationary and moving, whose forms are absolutely impossible [to conceive],
and it is the singular meeting place of infinite kumbhāṇḍas, rūpikas, and other beings.
It is a place where there is a single assembly and gathering of infinite kumbhāṇḍas, rākṣasīs, and others.
With the masses of birds moving about, their forms like those of dancers,
he was as if fashioning another world with the measuring lines of the Creator.

Those beings who are devoted to dance— those among the hosts of spirits who possess the forms of performers— their characteristic birds, for the purpose of encircling and binding them, appear like nets spread across the sky by the Creator as he fashions another world;
they stand like the measuring lines of his mind, extending from the earth up to the sun.

At that time, the world— the triple universe— became as if measuring the interior of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) with threads characterized by entrails, which were brought there by the *piśācas* from the side, while extending upward and downward as far as the path of the sun and across the ten directions in the form of bowers; such is the connection established by the initial construction of the two [verses].

With intestines as threads brought from the earth up to the sun, the Piśācas seemed to be measuring the world— across, upwards, and downwards— with the hollows of the quarters as their measuring rods.
Having beheld the world thus submerged by the flood of calamities that had arisen, and having turned the surface of the earth—which had once been his own domain—into an ocean of blood; (36)

Beholding the world submerged by a rising flood— its oceans turned red by those who once stood upon the surface of the earth in former times— the gods took their stand upon the summit of the Lokāloka mountain, which remains unassailed by the wretched limbs of that corpse even as far as the edge of the seven continents.
"were more exhausted"—this is the connection between the two [verses]. || 36 ||
On the summit of the Lokāloka mountain, at the edge of the seven continents,
the gods remained deeply distressed, unassailed by his limbs.
Śrī Rāma said: O Brahmā, since your limbs have extended even beyond the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), why has the Lokāloka mountain not been obstructed by them?

"How was the Lokāloka mountain not obscured— that is, not covered— by such a great corpse, whose limbs such as hands and feet were so exceedingly long that they extended even beyond the cosmic egg? Thus Rāma questioned Vasiṣṭha alone, the omniscient one, and not Bhāsa, because his vision did not extend as far as the Lokāloka mountain.
The meaning is: because of the certainty that he is ignorant of that. || 38 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
O Rāma, within this [universe] consisting of seven continents, his belly is situated;
while his head, hooves, arms, and other limbs are situated beyond the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa).

For this very reason, Vasiṣṭha himself stated the answer to that [question] with the verse beginning "dvīpa" and so forth: "O Rāma, his belly—the central body characterized by the belly—is situated in the midst of the seven continents; and his feet, characterized by the head and the hooves, as well as his limbs such as the arms, are situated beyond the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa). Thus, what was spoken by Bhāsa is indeed true. || 39 ||
From his two sides, from the middle of his thighs, from both sides of his waist,
and from the middle of his two shoulders, that Lokāloka mountain is perceived.

Nevertheless, because the peaks are not covered by the two sides of the corpse, from between its two thighs, from both sides of its hips, and likewise from between its two shoulders, that Lokāloka mountain is seen— meaning it is indeed visible— above. || 40 ||
Seated there upon the mountain peaks, those gods appear like clouds free from water, possessing a most pure luster due to their heat.

Having thus stated the answer to the question, Vasiṣṭha himself relates the remainder of the story—which Bhāsa did not know—beginning with the words "There... and so forth. [The word] *tāpāt* means from internal anguish as well as from the heat of the autumnal sun. || 41 ||
With its limbs outstretched and its face turned downward,
that fallen corpse was devoured by a multitude of spirits while the Mothers danced around it.
While that corpse, with its face turned downward, is being devoured by the multitude of spirits, [the practitioner should visualize it]. || 42 ||
As streams of blood flowed and the stench of fat intensified, the gods, each individually distressed, reflected as follows: || 43 ||
He reflected upon this which is about to be stated. || 43 ||
Alas, what misery! Where has the earth gone? Where have the masses of water gone? Where have the multitudes of people gone? Where have the mountains gone? (44)
He states that very point with the words "Alas, what misery! and so forth. || 44 ||
Alas, where has that Malaya mountain gone—the pavilion adorned with groves of sandalwood, mandāraka, and kadamba trees, and [filled] with heaps of flowers? (45)
Malaya stands like a pavilion made of heaps of flowers. || 45 ||
Even those vast, lofty, and pure regions of the Himalayas were quickly reduced to a state of mud by their own blood, as if through a sudden rage of whiteness turning crimson.

With blood as the agent, as if out of anger (ruṣā) toward the whiteness produced by snow, for the sake of overcoming that [whiteness], he assumed his own state of mud—his own condition as mire. || 46 ||
Even that great wish-fulfilling tree (kalpadruma) which stood on the surface of Krauñca-dvīpa,
with its branches reaching up to the world of Brahmā, has been reduced to dust.
On the slope of the mountain Krauñca, beneath the island named Krauñca, there was a wish-fulfilling tree (kalpadruma). || 47 ||

Alas, O Lord of the Ocean of Milk, master of the *pārijāta* tree, the lotus, the moon, and the nectar! Alas, O Ocean of Curds, whose coastal forests sprang from the peaks of butter! Alas, O Ocean of Honey, you who possess coconut mountains and are served by the sovereign yoginīs! Where will you now go, and where is my beloved?
They have become like mirrors for all directions. || 48 ||

O Lord, O Master, O Ocean of Milk, you who are the source of the *pārijāta* trees, of the lotus, of the moon, and of the nectar; O Ocean of Curd, whose coastal forest has emerged from those peaks filled with fresh butter (*navanīta*); O Girika, you who dwell on the shore, who are preeminent among coconut trees, who are worthy of compassion, and who are served by Yogeśvarī!
O Madhvarṇava, the meaning is that each one of you is to be pitied. Now, where will you go?
Where have you gone, having lost your status as mirrors for the women of the gods, for celestial nymphs, and for the quarters of the sky—mirrors made of crystals and other precious gemstones?
Alas! O mountain with joints as firm as the golden, stainless creepers of the wish-fulfilling tree;
