O Krauñcadvīpa, dense with the lotus-lake of Brahmā’s swans and the network of the quarters; where have you gone, leaving the Vidyādhara women resting here in the caves of the Kadamba forests?
O Puṣkaradvīpa, you are the celestial abode of city-dwellers skilled in the arts of play.

O Krauñcadvīpa, you are such that the Krauñca mountain within you is bound to it by a connection so seamless and unconditional as to be like a wish-fulfilling tree joined with spotless golden creepers; likewise, you are such that the expanse of the quarters is densely filled and rendered without gaps by the swans of Brahmā and the lotus-beds. Furthermore—

O Puṣkaradvīpa, you who serve as the home for the Vidyādharīs resting in the groves of Kadamba trees and in the caves—those skilled in the amorous sports of love—as well as for the Nāgas and the immortals; where have both you and he gone from here? Where have you two departed? (49)
Merely by remembering the forests of Svādūdaka, which possess fierce heat and are filled with flowers that purify the earth;
the caves of Gomedha-dvīpa, beautiful with wish-fulfilling trees and golden creepers;
and the white mountains of Śākadvīpa, adorned with groves of celestial trees—merit arises.
It bestows the bliss of the state of the gods upon new men. || 50 ||

[The rays] encircle and restrain the intense heat of such forests as are sanctuaries for the earth covered with flowers belonging to that ocean of sweet water; likewise [the heat] of the Gomedha island, of its kalpa-trees, of the golden creepers found there, and of those beautiful caves. And likewise—

Merely by remembering these nine objects—the forests of immortal trees (amaratara) and wish-fulfilling trees (kalpavṛkṣa) that have been revealed; those [forests] clothed in their flowers; those mountains together with Krauñcadvīpa that are white with those flowers;
and [the remaining ones]—merit arises for human beings which bestows the bliss of the divine state, heaven (surapada). 50.

Alas, I know not how the people will find consolation when all those forests—whose every quarter was illuminated by the expanse of young creepers with sprouts swaying in the gentle breeze—are utterly destroyed. (51)

All those forests, whose every quarter was illuminated by clusters of celestial *kalpa* trees—trees endowed with young creepers whose sprouts were caressed by gentle breezes—have been devastated and destroyed. "Alas! expresses grief. Beyond this, for people such as ourselves, there is no further consolation.
"How shall one attain rest and the concentration of the mind? I do not know"—this is the statement of someone regarding that matter. || 51 ||
When indeed shall we behold again those groves on the shores of the sugarcane-ocean and upon the grounds of Mount Khaṇḍa, as well as the jaggery-sweets and even the sugar-candies for children? (52)

On the shore of the ocean of sugarcane juice, where sugar has solidified into rock, and where the lands are adorned with mountains composed of that very substance—when indeed shall we see, behold, or witness those well-known sweets, the *guḍa-modakas*?
(The variation in verbal suffixes is Vedic. Likewise, when shall we see the little figurines made of sugar for the purpose of play?
We shall see. || 52 ||

When indeed shall we behold the dance of those beautiful sandalwood women in their golden dwellings, upon the mountain of the groves of *tālī* and *tamālī* trees, cooled by *kadamba* and wish-fulfilling trees? (53)

Seated upon golden platforms cooled by rows of palm trees, groves of *kadamba* trees, and celestial *kalpa* trees, they will at some point behold the dance— previously experienced many times— of beautiful Apsarases anointed with sandalwood paste,
or perhaps the dance of beautiful sandalwood creepers.
"May we now behold [him]. The suffix *liṅ* is used here in the sense of hope (*āśaṃsā*). 53.

Alas, those fruits at the very top of the Jambu tree have passed into the state of mere memory—even those fruits whose juices cause this river Jambumatī, which girdles the island with its ocean, to flow. (54)

Those supreme fruits of the Jambū tree—renowned for their elephantine size, their nectar-like flavor, and as the source of Jāmbūnada gold—have attained a state where their very form is now only a memory. "Alas" (*kaṣṭam*) expresses grief. By the juices of those fruits, [the land] became a river whose islands and oceans served as its girdle. Such was that [land].
The earth, in the form of Jambudvīpa, bears [the name] Jambumatī. || 54 ||

Remembering again and again the shore of the celestial ocean, where the songs and dances of intoxicated celestial women resound within the dense caves of the Śilīndhra mountains, I feel as if my heart is bursting, just as the earth once burst forth with its primordial lotus.

Furthermore, having repeatedly recollected the shore of the ocean of wine (suroda), which was such that within the caves and hollows of mountains rendered gapless and devoid of space by *śilīndhra* trees, there was dancing accompanied by song performed by celestial women intoxicated with honey-wine (*madhu*). Prior to this...
In the morning, like a lotus, and now, like the earth, I am rent asunder by my heart; that is to say, I undergo tearing apart. || 55 ||
Behold, upon the surface of the ocean of blood, the peaks of hundreds of golden mountains shine with radiance;
reddened by the twilight, they appear like the buds of the rising moon in the quarters of the sky at the lands of sunrise and sunset. (56)
O friend, upon the head— the upper surface— of that fresh, newly arisen ocean whose waters are blood-red,

the crest-tops and peaks of hundreds of golden mountains such as Meru stand toward the directions of the north and others, reaching the lands of sunrise and sunset, the regions adjacent to where the sun rises and sets.
Look at them: reddened by the two twilights, they shine and gleam like slightly risen crescents of the moon with their radiance. 56.
I know not if there exists another land adorned with such an expanse of ocean waters, a region where the sky is filled with masses of clouds resting upon lofty mountain kings like blue lotuses,
and which is clothed in rivers, deserts, forests, formidable cities, villages, and agrahāras, and abounding in trees, sprouts, and shoots.
Alas, where has the earth gone? (57)
She whose girdle consists of those masses of water—the oceans—which have been described as being of such a nature;

she who is adorned by various other islands (dvīpāntara); and she who serves as the ground for the garlands of blue lotuses, which are the clusters of clouds resting upon the exceedingly lofty mountain-kings that resemble her breasts.

"Adorned by that" means up to this point. Where has that earth now gone—I know not—whose streams, rivers, jungles, forests, cities formidable with warriors, villages, agrahāras (brahmin settlements), and even the very garments [of its surface] were adorned with trees, sprouts, shoots, and the like? "Alas! expresses grief. || 57 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-fourth canto, titled "The Description of the Lamentation of the Gods," in the *Śavopākhyāna* (Episode of the Corpse) within the *Uttarakāṇḍa* of the *Devamānuṣasaṃvāda* (Dialogue between the God and the Man) in the *Bālakāṇḍa* of the glorious *Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa*, composed by the Sage. 134.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Lamentation of the Gods," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and thirty-fifth chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: [Bhāsa said—both readings exist here:
"When the corpse had been reduced to a mere remnant by a troop of intoxicated spirits," he spoke.
Then, on the mountain, the gods together with Indra spoke thus once more in all directions.
When the flesh was eaten here by the hosts of spirits and the blood was drunk, the earth was formed from the fat;
from the remainder of the blood, an ocean of wine was created.
While the Lokāloka mountain stood in all directions, the gods situated there spoke these words that are about to be related.
Even upon the grounds of the celestial chariots where the Vidyādharas and gods dwell, the spirits have spread out vast nets of fat to cool the earth;
these resemble fragments of pure clouds driven by the wind, filling the sky.
In the sky, which is the sphere of movement for the celestial chariots of the Vidyādharas and the immortals seeking recreation,

the hosts of elemental spirits and goddesses created a thick mist to counteract the heat; thus, the vast intestines became equal to the sky, which was filled with abundant, pure fragments of clouds driven by the wind.
They have been spread out. || 2 ||
Behold, across all seven continents, the waters of fat have been spread out by living beings; flesh has been eaten and blood has been drunk. Now, let the earth itself be examined.
(3) Let it be seen—that is, let its true nature be observed. (3)
Now the earth, its entire body enveloped in layers of fat, stands in distress;
the forests appear as if covered with blankets by the masses of autumn clouds composed of fat. (4)

The earth, which once bestowed joy upon all living beings, now stands in distress, her entire body enveloped in layers of fat. And the forests appear as if wrapped in grey blankets, covered by masses of autumn clouds composed of that very fat. || 4 ||
Behold these bones of his, which have become great mountains,
standing like the peaks of the Himalayas, covering the very horizons.
The bones of that corpse. || 5 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: [The reading "Bhāsa said" occurs in both versions.
While the gods were speaking thus, that host of beings, having made this earth a mass of fat, danced wildly in the sky in a state of intoxication.

That multitude of beings, that host of goddesses, being satisfied, made this earth smeared with fat by means of the networks of fat remaining after they had drunk [the blood]; and being thus gratified, they danced in the sky. The word *heti* is used as a particle of renown. || 6 ||
While the hosts of spirits were dancing, the remaining blood from the earth was cast by the gods into the ocean in a single stream.
By means of a single stream created through volition, it was cast into the ocean, the abode of sea-monsters, which is one among the seven [oceans].
The gods formed the resolve that this very [ocean] should be the ocean of wine;
from that time until today, it has remained the ocean of liquor.
Having resolved that very ocean to be the ocean of wine, they transformed it into a sea of liquor. || 8 ||
Having performed a dance in the sky, those beings drink that wine;
then they dance again in the sky within the temple of bliss.
They drink that local wine there. || 9 ||
Even today, spirits drink from the ocean of wine as if it were that very same [liquor],
and they dance in the sky together with hosts of yoginīs.
Even now, those beings of the present day drink wine from that ocean of liquor and dance in the sky, just like those [beings] of old. || 10 ||
Then those networks of fat from those beings, spread out and dried upon the surface of the earth, remained there; hence the earth is called Medinī.
The networks of fat from those beings, which remained after they were drunk, dried up upon the surface of the earth; for this reason, the earth remains known by the name Medinī.
Thus, when Śiva had gradually attained peace and the succession of day and night began once more, the Lord of Creatures then created new beings; thus the creation here became as it was before.

Thus, indicating that the sun was likewise restored to its own place by the gods as before, and that the mountains and other features were established as previously ordained, he says: "iti" (thus). When, according to the sequence described, the night has reached its end and dissolution (*kṣaya*), and because the sun has been restored to its own station and Meru and the others have been raised up, the sequence of day and night begins once more; then—
Prajāpati created new beings; there on this earth, that creation occurred as before. || 12 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-fifth canto, titled "The Pacification of Śava," in the *Uttarakāṇḍa* of the *Devarāja-mokṣa-nirvāṇa*, within the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-vālmīkīya-ārṣa*, composed by the sage Vālmīki. 135.
Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Pacification of the Corpse," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and thirty-sixth canto.
Bhāsa said:
Then I asked that great god, the Purifier (Agni), this:
O Lord of the Earth, listen to that which is situated at the corner of a parrot’s wing.
Questioned here by Agnibhāsa regarding the account of the corpse from the beginning,
he described [the events] starting with the asura, the mosquito, the deer, and the hunter.
O Lord of the Earth, Daśaratha, he is situated at the corner of the wing-root—the base of the wing—of Śuka, whose vehicle is fire. || 1 ||
"O Blessed One, Lord of all sacrifices, Master of Svāhā, Consumer of Oblations!
What is this that has occurred? Tell me, what is this corpse?"
"What was this that has now become what is called a corpse, and for what cause did it previously come to be so?"—these are two questions. (2)
Vahni said:
Listen, O King, as I describe to you in its entirety and exactly as it happened the indestructible account of the infinite corpses that illuminated the three worlds.
Therein, Vahni proclaims the answer to the first question, beginning with the words "Listen" (śrūyatām) and so forth. || 3 ||
There exists the infinite, formless, supreme space consisting of consciousness,
wherein these countless worlds are like mere atoms.

In this regard, he first demonstrates that Brahman alone is the ultimate root of the superimpositions (adhyāsa) of consciousness, existence, and so forth, which are about to be described—beginning with the words "It exists" (asti). The term *apasaṃkhyāni* means those from which number has departed (*apagata-saṃkhyāni*). || 4 ||
In that all-pervading, pure, and infinite space of consciousness alone,
which is the self of all, there arose spontaneously a consciousness consisting of the act of knowing itself.
Cognition is knowledge possessing the form of the object; she consists of that.
Under the influence of that sensation, she perceived the state of being atoms of light,
just as one who has realized the nature of his goal perceives himself as a traveler in a dream.
And she, by virtue of being the object of her own perception, saw the state of light-atoms solely through the power of her own nature as consciousness;
just as you, while dreaming and imagining a traveler, see your own self as that traveler. || 6 ||
Because it lacks consciousness, the atom itself did not perceive its own atomicity—
that luminous state, which is like the pollen of a lotus and consists of the nature of conceptualization.
Due to its lack of consciousness and because its mind is veiled by ignorance, the atom [perceives] the radiant, clearly manifest [light] as being equal to the dust arising from a lotus. || 7 ||
Cultivating the state of being hollowed out by grief, she once again became herself;
she spontaneously experienced the sense organs, such as the eyes, within her own body.

And that luminous subtle state, by its expansion, manifesting as the swelling of the void, experienced—that is, it became aware of—the other senses such as sight; thereafter, it experienced them as being attached to the body. || 8 ||
And the Eye of the World saw before him the primordial source, which by its very nature consists of the elements like a container and its contents, resembling a city in a dream.
And first, with his eyes and other senses, he beheld the world consisting of the elements, like a container and its contents, which possesses qualities such as sound and touch. || 9 ||
There was a living being there named Asura who was indeed conceited;
his very nature was a manifestation of untruth, and he was the father, mother, and grandfather [of that state].
He begins to describe the succession of causes regarding the subject of the second question: "Asura.

In that context, among the aggregates of the body and its organs—which consist of superimpositions ranging from sensation to the objects of the senses—there was a certain living being belonging to a specific class named Asura. And he, by his very nature as an Asura, became proud and full of conceit.

Indeed, did he not have fathers, mothers, and grandfathers? They certainly did exist; however, the meaning is that they were like the ancestors of Vidūratha and others—consisting of unreal appearances for him. || 10 ||
When, intoxicated with pride, he trampled the hermitage of a certain great sage— a vessel of peace— there, || 11 ||
Precisely because he was an asura, due to his arrogance and swelling with pride like a soaked chickpea, [he became bloated]. || 11 ||
The sage pronounced a curse upon him: "Since you have destroyed my hermitage because of its great size, die and become a lowly gnat! (12)
By "of great form" is meant having an excessively large body; "inferior" means excessively small. || 12 ||
Then, at that very moment, the fire of that curse reduced the asura to ashes,
just as the Aurva fire reduces the waters to ash.
Formless, supportless, and like the power of space, the mind—though essentially consciousness—became as if something insentient and devoid of objects of thought. 14.
To the question of what that insentient consciousness was like at that time, he says: "formless. The mind was unperceivable, as if in deep sleep or a swoon. || 14 ||
That consciousness attained oneness with the elemental ether due to their similarity;
then it attained oneness with the wind, which has that ether as its substrate.
That unmanifest form, together with consciousness, attained oneness with the elemental ether; and that elemental ether, in turn, attained oneness with its own substrate, the wind.

He was endowed with consciousness and the nature of wind, becoming the first among living beings; he was pervaded by passion (rajas), water (payas), fire (tejas), space (nabhas), and the subtle atom (aṇu). (16)

The vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the wind of volition (*cetanavāta*); its essence is that very [volition], and it becomes known as "life-force" (*prāṇin*) upon the acquisition of a body. The earthly portion is *rajas*; it is pervaded by the four primary elements starting with earth. By the subtle (*aṇu*), meaning unquintuplicated (*apañcīkṛta*). || 16 ||
Consisting of the five subtle elements (tanmātras) and being a minute atom of pure consciousness,
it attained vibration by its own nature, like a particle of air in the sky.
In that regard, he describes the manifestation of the power of action (kriyā-śakti) with the words "He" (saḥ). || 17 ||
Then that consciousness, situated within the vital air, became awakened,
just as a seed on the earth produces a sprout through the action of time, wind, and water.

By means of *spanda*, he describes the manifestation of the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*) within the subtle body (*liṅgadeha*): "Now" (*atha*). Just as a seed that produces a sprout is awakened by the state of swelling through the prior time of the rainy season, the wind, and the water of the rains, so it is here. || 18 ||
His consciousness, having become aware of the pure curse within his heart, perceived the limbs of a mosquito;
having known them, he became a mosquito. (19)

Knowing the curse of the pure sage, she was pierced by that pure curse; remaining until the end of her life in the form of a mosquito, her consciousness was permeated by the impressions of that [curse], and having perceived the limbs of the demon—the wings, feet, and so forth—she herself became a mosquito. || 19 ||
The lifespan of that mosquito here, which is born from sweat, possesses a tiny body, and whose form collapses with each breath, consists of only two days.

He states what its origin is and how long its life lasts with the words "of the sweat-born" (svedajasya). Its body falls and flies up even by a mere breath; its life is two days—this is to be supplied as the maximum lifespan. || 20 ||
Śrī Rāma said: O Lord, for all living beings here, does their origin arise solely from another womb, or can it also be otherwise? (21)

"The waking state is just like a dream"—this has been stated repeatedly by the Blessed One. Now, while the origin of a body in a dream is not seen to arise from a womb, the origin of the waking body is indeed seen to do so; suspecting that by this analogy, the origin of bodies everywhere might likewise proceed solely from a womb, or perhaps otherwise, Rāma asks Vasiṣṭha in the course of their conversation:

Regarding "of living beings": in the aspect of the material cause as illusory manifestation (*vivarta-upādāna*), it consists of Brahman; in the aspect of the material cause as transformative modification (*pariṇāmin-upādāna*), it is born from a womb. || 21 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
The origin of all beings, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, is twofold.
One is composed of Brahman; the other is born of delusion. Listen to these two. (22)
Because of the coloring by the subtle elements (tanmātra) of the world-delusion previously established, the birth of beings is said to arise from delusion, joined with the visible [world]. (23)
Therein, he defines the second [type of birth] with the words "pūrva" (formerly) and so on.

That which is the arising of beings—of living creatures—from those various elements and subtle essences (*tanmātra*) by means of being colored by them, due to a firm delusion of identity with that body rooted in the experience of its womb in a previous life, is "born of delusion. Having emerged from these elements...
The meaning is that they perish along with those very [elements], according to such scriptural passages as, "In whatever they become, that they then become. || 23 ||
When the delusion of the world has ceased, he who exists as the being of reality by his own nature is declared to be composed of Brahman; his manifestation is not born from a womb.

The meaning is this: although the world-delusion has never appeared at any time within the eternally liberated Brahman, that which—by its own nature as a phenomenal manifestation (vivarta)—comes into being at the beginning of creation in the form of the individual soul (jīva), consisting of the fourfold states of beings, is identical with Brahman.
This being the case, O Rāma, listen to the sequence of that gnat's actions: it arose from the power of worldly delusion, not from Brahman.

And that [state] is experienced only by those perfected from birth, such as Kapila, Sanaka, and others, and not by the ignorant, such as mosquitoes; thus, with the intention that the arising of the mosquito is merely born of delusion, he says "In this way. Vasiṣṭha himself, out of enthusiasm, relates the remainder of the story begun by Bhāsa: "Of him... (verse 25).
Humming amidst clusters of wild rice, sugarcane, young grass, and thickets,
he spent half his life for a single day, wandering about and consuming everything.

On the earth of Kṣamā, among the sugarcane thickets, young grass, tender blades of grass, and clusters of *kāśa*, *muñja*, and other weeds, there are mosquitoes that hum— that is, produce an indistinct sound; by means of such a mosquito, who himself hums, makes such a noise, leaps about, and plays, half of its own two-day lifespan— one full day— is entirely spent.
Eaten. || 26 ||
He himself has long engaged in the sport of swinging upon a cradle made of the heart of a grassy meadow, together with this very female mosquito as his child-playmate.
Next, he describes the activities of the second day with the words beginning "śādvala-": together with his wife Maśikā. || 27 ||
While he was resting somewhere there, exhausted from the journey on the swing,
he was crushed by the fall of a mountain brought down by the tip of a deer's hoof.
The deer saw only the tips of his feet with the vision of a gnat, and the mountain [was shaken] by that fall.
Because she had surrendered her life upon seeing the face of Hari,
he, having taken up his eyes according to the previous sequence, consequently became a deer.

By the mention of the "face," the complete form of Hari is indicated. That which is the "vision" (*saṃdarśa*) of Him—the thorough contemplation at the time of death—by that [vision] the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is abandoned; by whomsoever this is done, such is the state. By the very same sequence as was previously described regarding the assumption of the body of a mosquito, the other senses are withdrawn.
By which the external and internal organs [are governed]. || 29 ||
While dwelling in the forest, a deer was struck by a hunter with a bow;
because his gaze fell upon the face of the hunter, he was reborn as that very hunter. (30)
While wandering through the forests as a hunter, he arrived at the grove of sages; having rested there, he was awakened to truth by a sage through their conversation.
From association—that is, from the good fortune of attaining the company of the virtuous. || 31 ||
"O deluded one, why do you kill deer with your bow for the sake of this long-lasting suffering? Why do you not protect the sacred law (tantra) in this fragile world? (32)
To what [objection] was he awakened? He says: "O deluded one," and so forth.
Why do you not protect the *tantra*—the established order of the scriptures concerning non-violence, the granting of fearlessness, and other such practices which yield great fruit? (32)
Life is as fragile as water hanging from a mass of clouds torn asunder by the wind; enjoyments are as flickering as lightning flashing amidst a canopy of clouds;
the caresses of youth are as unstable as the current of a river; and the body perishes in an instant. My son, being seized by fear, [one should seek liberation].
Let nirvāṇa be sought by one who is under the sway of saṃsāra. || 33 ||

The livelihood obtained through the traditional custom of the hunter tribe is the killing of deer; if that is abandoned, how will one live, or how will there be the attainment of enjoyments? To this he replies: "Life... Neither life nor enjoyments are the true human goal (*puruṣārtha*). For if these are procured through violence and the like, there is the inevitable occurrence of future-world misfortune to be experienced for an infinite time. [The word] "life" does not...

There is no stability therein by which its non-occurrence might be avoided; for life is as fragile as the water in the mass of clouds shattered by the wind. In that context, sensual enjoyments are as flickering as the lightning flashing amidst a canopy of clouds. Likewise, the indulgence and amorous play of youth are like the swift current of a torrential stream.

Fickle! The body and the sphere of enjoyments are subject to ruin in an instant, fraught with the possibility of falling into miserable states. Therefore, my son, having become terrified by the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*)—characterized by a succession of future misfortunes in the next world—you must strive for the attainment of eternal, unsurpassed bliss, which is marked by the cessation of all ultimate suffering through means such as the gift of fearlessness and non-violence.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Enlightenment of the Mosquito Hunter," in the *Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa*, the *Vairāgyaprakaraṇa*, within the *Mumukṣuvyavahāra* section of the *Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa*. 136.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Awakening of the Mosquito and the Hunter," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and thirty-seventh canto.
The hunter said: "If it is so, O sage, tell me: what is the means for the complete destruction of suffering?"
The course of one's conduct should be neither harsh nor overly mild. || 1 ||
Questioned here by the hunter, the sage himself, through the practice of dhāraṇā and by means of entering another's body, related that dream he had seen.
If such practices as violence are indeed causes of suffering, then tell me: what kind of course of conduct would serve as the cause for the complete destruction of that suffering? || 1 ||
The sage said:
"Having now completely cast aside your bow along with your arrows, and having adopted the practice of silence, remain here with your suffering stilled."
With the intention that the very sequence of conduct of the sages is the cause for the destruction of suffering and must be learned by living in their company, the Sage gives the following reply:

"Right now," etc. He refers to *mauna* (the state of a sage), which is well-known among sages, by relying on the conduct of restraints (*yama*), observances (*niyama*), inquiry (*vicāra*), and so forth. (2)
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Having been thus enlightened by him, he cast aside his bow and arrows and remained right there, following the conduct of a sage, subsisting on food obtained without asking.
There, in that very hermitage. || 3 ||
Then, remaining silent, he entered into a state of discernment through the scriptures by means of his mind,
just as a flower enters the heart of a person with its fragrance in a few days.

Then, through association with the virtuous, he entered into that disposition of discerning the essential from the non-essential which is well-known in the scriptures; just as a flower, gladdening the minds and hearts of men by means of its fragrance arising through the sequence of budding, ripening, and blossoming, enters into them, so it was with him. || 4 ||
Once, O subduer of enemies, he questioned that tiger among sages:
"O Blessed One, how is it that a dream is seen both internally and externally? (5)

Having thus attained detachment, that hunter once asked that tiger among sages: "O Arindama"—this is an address to Daśaratha—"he said: 'O Blessed One, how is it that a dream residing within living beings appears externally, as if waking? And how is it that what resides externally..."

How is the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), being a dream, perceived internally? How, and by what means, is a dream—which exists within living beings—perceived? In this way, how is the phenomenal world, which exists both internally and externally, perceived as a dream?
If the phenomenal world is indeed a dream, then how is it perceived as existing in two ways—as internal and external?
Thus, these five questions, condensed from many doubts, have been addressed by means of the *tantra*. || 5 ||
The sage said:
"O virtuous one, even for me, who am discerning, this very same doubt previously arose in my mind from some unknown source, like a cloud appearing in the sky. (6)

Having heard the question filled with many reflections, the Sage [thought]: "Such a reflection occurred to me as well during my stage of tender discernment; and by means of the practice of *dhāraṇā*, through entering another's body, I myself repeatedly observed his dreams and so forth, examining them for a long time through positive and negative concomitance."
Having understood the reality and being composed, the Sage begins to explain the answer to the third question in detail, starting with the words "mamāpi" (even for me), by means of a narrative.
Then, desiring to behold this, I practiced concentration and became steady within that consciousness, having assumed the lotus posture.

I became firmly established in that very consciousness which is well-known to all people as the Self, by one who has practiced the external retention of breath (bahiḥ-kumbhaka) conducive to entering the bodies of others.
Remaining there, I drew back my own heart, which had been cast far away, just as the sun at evening draws back its radiance by means of its own light.

Abiding there in that consciousness, I withdrew my mind, which had been scattered far away, by means of that very consciousness; just as the sun at evening withdraws its heat by its own radiance, namely the splendor of its orb, so it was with me. || 8 ||
Then, by means of the agitation of sensation, that vital breath, accompanied by the mind, was emitted by me from the body into the external world, like fragrance from a flower.

Feeling (vedanā) is the mind, accompanied by the limiting adjunct of the individual soul (jīvopādhi), which— through the agitation of the mind and by means of the effort well-known in the Yoga Śāstras that is conducive to the soul's exit from the body along with the vital breath— is expelled (recita) by exhalation (recaka) into an external location beyond the body. || 9 ||
That vital breath (prāṇapavana), which had been drawn into my heart situated in the ether, was directed by me into the breath of the creature standing before me, located at the tip of his mouth.

Then he describes the method for entering another's body that he himself composed, beginning with the words "vyomastha" (situated in space). "By means of the mind situated in the external space, conjoined with the limiting adjunct of the individual soul (jīva), that vital breath (prāṇapavana) was directed and merged by me into the breath of a certain living being—a student—standing before me in front. (10)

The vital breath (prāṇa), which is enveloped by the individual life-force (prāṇavat), was led into the interior of the heart; indeed, it was tormented by its own desire, like a serpent by a young elephant. || 11 ||

The life-breath of that creature who is bound by my own life-force has led me into the interior of his heart; just as a camel or a bear, having forced its face into a hole, draws in its own food— a snake— by means of its own exertion characterized by the inhalation of breath through its mouth, and then, once it has entered its own mouth, devours it.
In the same way, he is led back to his own heart. || 11 ||
Then, by means of the horse of my vital breath, I entered his heart; standing in that narrow space, I followed those two within with my own intelligence.

With that horse whose characteristic was his very life-breath, I followed those two life-forces as they were intermingled with one another; having entered the interior—that is, the middle—of his body, I remained there, situated in the perilous situation about to be described, by means of my own intellect. This is the sense of the verse. || 12 ||
It was surrounded on all sides by many channels flowing with the juices of autumn,
like the entire surface of the earth encircled by large and small irrigation canals.
The abode of the living soul is crowded with the cage of ribs, the spleen, the liver, blood, and other such masses, like a dwelling filled with household utensils and furnishings.
He elaborates upon its state of confinement with the words beginning "parśukā" (ribs) and so forth. *Parśukāḥ* are the ribs;

in the cage characterized by them, there are the *plīha* and *yakṛt*, which are specific types of flesh. *Ḍimbakaiḥ* means by lumps or masses. That body is the dwelling place, the house, of the living soul (*jīva*). || 14 ||
It was covered with all its limbs hissing and hot,
like the ocean heated by the rays of the summer sun and filled with networks of waves.
"Śala-śala" is an imitation of the sound produced by the boiling of the digestive fire within the stomach. || 15 ||
A fresh and ever-new coolness, consisting of consciousness, emanates from the tip of the nose;
for the sake of life, it is incessantly and unceasingly led forth by the mind-wind.
Furthermore, of what nature is that abode of the living soul? It is perpetually elevated by the vital breaths (prāṇa) and other winds through the mind for the sake of non-extinction.

Within it, as the downward-moving breath (apāna), whose essence is Soma, enters from the tip of the nose into the interior, there is ever-new external coolness entering within; therefore, it is of the nature of consciousness. || 16 ||
It was slippery with the flow of blood, pus, phlegm, and fat;
thick with darkness, hot, and as confining as hell. || 17 ||
It is red, and it is slimy with the secretions of those food-essences and phlegm-like humors that are crushed and severed from the channels. (17)
Through the distinct or indistinct sounds of the winds associated with the conjunctions of rising and falling [breaths],
and due to the irregularity of their duration and cessation, it indicates future ailments.

Through the play of the vital winds, such as the *prāṇa* and others— some of which are manifest due to the ease of their movement within certain branches of the seventy-two thousand channels of blood, lymph, phlegm, and bile, and some of which are unmanifest due to the obstruction of their paths— and through the destruction of the extremities and their dissolutions situated within the seven bodily constituents (*dhātu*).
It is an indicator, through dreams and other signs, of the onset of future disorders and diseases resulting from an imbalance.
It resounded with the wind blowing through the openings forced by the violent pressure of the earth,
while the submarine fire of the ocean blazed within the conduits of the lotus-stalks.

The apertures such as the nostrils and others, which open with great force, produce sound through the air exiting from them; within that cavity—the channel of the heart-lotus stalk—blazes the digestive fire (*jāṭharāgni*), like the *vāḍava* fire in the ocean. Thus it is said in the *Mahopaniṣad*: "It resembles the interior of a lotus bud..."

Beginning with "And the heart is downward-facing," [it continues]: "At its end is a subtle cavity; in that, everything is established. In the middle of that, a flame of fire, extremely fine, stands directed upward. (19)
It was densely packed with objects meeting one another, white and clear along with the winds;
in some places it was tranquil, and in others agitated, like a city at night beset by thieves.

It is densely packed and made solid by the objects consisting of latent impressions (vāsanā) that arise; it is covered and bound by the sense organs along with the vital breaths (prāṇa). Yet, by its nature as the witnessing self (sākṣyātman), it is transparent. Due to the various modifications of the mind (cittavṛtti) and its different locations, it is sometimes calm and sometimes agitated. || 20 ||
It was surrounded by winds moving through the channels of the nāḍīs, traveling along the path of the Vidyādharas, and singing songs with melodies that were half of a half-mora in length. 21.

It is filled with winds moving through the channels of the vessels—winds intent upon the resonance and humming of the food-essences situated within the stomach, and for this very reason resembling travelers who are *vidyādharas* singing along those paths;
those winds whose movements in song consist of two-mora *akāra*s, half of that (one-mora), and half of that again (half-mora). Of the measure of the song...
The meaning is that it is because [the condition] is curable by means of wind (vāta). || 21 ||
Then I entered the heart of that creature, which was filled with poison within, just as a superior man enters a dense crowd of men crowded together limb to limb. || 22 ||
Just as a superior and excellent man enters a crowd of men that is so crowded and devoid of space that there is no room for him, even so [is it with the Self]. || 22 ||
Immediately thereafter, I attained the element of fire within my heart,
which, though situated at a distance, was perceived with effort like the moon at night or the light of the sun.

I have attained with effort the fire-element (*tejodhātu*), which is the essence of the fire characterized by the digestive heat (*jaṭharāgni*). Because it must be reached through the pathways of many channels, even though it is nearby, it is as if far away—just as the sun’s rays reach the moon at night. And so says the Śruti: "This indeed is the Brahman that shines forth, which is seen as the sun."
Now, that which dies and is no longer seen—its radiance goes to the moon alone. Thus [it is said]. 23.
Since it is the mirror of the three worlds and the lamp for all things in the triple universe,
the living soul (jīva) abides therein as the existence of all entities.

To the question of how that [Self] possesses the essence of radiance (*tejaḥsāratva*), he says "yasmāt" (because): because the Jīva—the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) who is its very nature—is present within that radiance; for it is the cause by which even the three worlds are internally illumined, acting as a mirror for the objects of the triple world and shining like a lamp. And so it is said:

The Śruti says: "In the center of that, a flame of fire stands upwards, extremely subtle; in the center of that flame, the Supreme Self is established. He is Brahman, He is Śiva, He is the Unborn, He is the Imperishable, the Supreme Self-ruling Lord. (24)
The life-force pervades the body just as fragrance resides in a flower;
likewise, vitality exists within the filaments, and coolness within the mouth by the sun. (25)
[Objection: But surely, in such scriptural passages as "He has entered here even to the tips of the fingernails," the individual soul (*jīva*) is heard to pervade the entire body;

how then can it be said that it resides only in the element of fire (*tejo-dhātu*)? To this, he says: "In the body" (*kāye*). Although the self, being the individual soul, has entered the body up to the tips of the fingernails and is thus omnipresent, it nevertheless resides specifically in the *ojas*, which is the element of fire. Just as...

The meaning is as follows: just as the fragrance and coolness of a flower, though present everywhere, reside especially within its mouth (the interior) when it is opened by the sun and characterized by its filaments, so it is here. || 25 ||
I have entered unobserved into that vital energy (ojas) which is the support of the life-force,
protected on all sides by the vital breaths (prāṇas) like a covering.

It is protected on all sides by the deities who preside over the senses and the vital breaths at all four gates; just as the light of a lamp covering a jar is protected by the winds entering through the minute holes of that jar, so it is here.
The sense is that if the openings were closed entirely, the destruction of the lamp's light would be observed. || 26 ||
Then I entered him directly, as fragrance enters the wind, as the hot-rayed sun enters the moon, or as water enters an earthen vessel. (27)

Then I directly and immediately entered that very bliss-sheath (ānandamaya-kośa), which is the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of that living self (jīva) and is permeated by the sheaths of mind (manomaya) and consciousness (vijñānamaya).
He states the analogies for this with the words "like fragrance," and so forth. || 27 ||
Resembling the rays of a second moon, as delicate as a fragment of white cloud, resembling fresh butter and molasses, and as beautiful as a bubble of milk. (28)
In that regard, because affection and bliss are seen to arise from themselves alone, they are like fresh butter and molasses [where *guḍa* means a ball]. || 28 ||
Standing there, free from the agitation of entering, I beheld the entire universe as if dwelling within my own vital energy, like a dream. (29)

Abandoning the agitation and exhaustion associated with entering former states, I abide composedly within the vital energy (*ojas*) residing in my own heart; like one in his own dream, I behold the entire world in its undivided form as the dream-form of that [Supreme Being], including the sun, the mountains, the oceans, and all gods, demons, and humans. (29)
[He beheld] the expanse of the city and its forests, together with the intermediate regions and the quarters of the world. || 30 ||
He specifies that very universe with the words "together with the sun," and so forth. || 30 ||
[He saw] the ocean of the seven continents and seas, together with the sequence of time and its instruments,
along with all the kalpas, moments, and seasons, including all things mobile and immobile.
That vision in the dream remained steady and constant there;
I truly abide even at the end of sleep, because sleep has not yet arrived.

Firmly established in a beginningless flow, it exists as the very same as the well-known world; I dwell exceedingly within that waking state at the end of sleep, because sleep has not arrived at all at the conclusion of waking. 32.
"O hunter, while I was reflecting, 'Am I seeing a dream even though I am not asleep?', this was realized by me as I became fully conscious. (33)

Nevertheless, while reflecting, "What dream am I seeing?", O hunter, immediately thereafter, by me—who was awakened, that is, possessed of discernment—this which is about to be told was understood. || 33 ||
Indeed, this very nature of the impact of consciousness is its divine essence, which it designates for itself as the sky-like substance known by the name "the world. (34)

What was known then? He says: "Now," etc. The word "nāma" (by name) indicates what is well-known among the discerning. This divine form belongs to this conscious essence, the inner self (*pratyagātman*). Of what nature is it? This Lord (*īśvara*) designates for himself whatever name and form—whether as "the ether," or "this pot," or "this cloth," or "the world," or "the non-living"—and by that very name, he [appears] as that world.
It comes to be. || 34 ||
Wherever the element of consciousness resides,
there it perceives its own form as the world, yet without ever abandoning its very nature as space.
He says "no" to the question of whether it abandons its true nature, stating: "the state of space"; that is, it does not abandon it at all. || 35 ||
Aha! Today this has been understood: that this world which is seen in such a way is called a dream, being nothing more than the manifestation of one's own consciousness.
"Ah! Today I have realized that this very thing is called 'a dream' by people"—here, "ā" is used for recollection, and "aṅ" is an interjection. || 36 ||
That which is the manifestation of the element of consciousness is called "dream" in one sense and "waking" in another;
yet waking and dreaming are not two distinct things.
He says—beginning with "of the element of consciousness"—that even when examined from the perspective of ultimate reality, waking consciousness culminates in this very same [conclusion]. || 37 ||
Dream is a dream within waking; yet in that dream, there is waking. Dream is indeed waking—thus waking itself exists in a twofold manner.
He states that, from the perspective of one another, these two are merely dream-states, yet from their own respective perspectives, they are indeed waking states—thus he says:
"In a dream... The meaning is as follows: In a dream, this waking state is itself a dream; however, a dream is itself waking from its own perspective.
When it is perceived from its own perspective, it results in the conclusion that waking itself exists in a twofold manner. || 38 ||
O one of great intelligence, since the person is indeed consciousness, when even hundreds of bodies have perished, how, whose, and at what time has he died? (39)

Now, one might ask: "In that case, would death not be something distinct from both dreaming and waking? To this he says: "The conscious one" (*cetana*). There is no such thing as "death" at all. Because the *puruṣa* is consciousness—here the suffix *-lyuṭ* denotes the abstract state—he is pure consciousness alone. And even though hundreds of bodies have died, when has he ever died? Of whom has he died? How has he died? In all three ways, [he remains].
The meaning is that because of its non-establishment. || 39 ||
That consciousness exists as space itself, appearing like a body;
it is infinite, undivided in nature, and consists of both the resistant and the non-resistant.
Having provisionally accepted that body, this "death" has been described; however, in reality, neither of those two exists, as he says with the word "that.

The meaning is: "pratigha" refers to that which is struck or obstructed, i.e., a material form; "apratigha" is its opposite, and it is through delusion alone that [the self] appears to have that nature. || 40 ||
The world is known as the marrow of the atom called consciousness, which is by nature non-obstructive and whose self is eternally and infinitely arisen. (41)

In that regard, the nature of that which is non-obstructive by essence is the very marrow and core of the atom called consciousness; through delusion, even the world is remembered as being like the body. (41)
All atoms of experience shine within the belly of the sky of consciousness, just as the various atomic parts appear within a whole object. 42.

He establishes the very nature of the marrow itself with the words "of the sky of consciousness" (cidvyomnaḥ). The individual souls (aṇavaḥ) are characterized by the experience of the delusion of the world. 42.
Withdrawn from the external, the individual soul (jīva), abiding in the heart which is the support of the soul,
perceives its own form as this creation of a dream through the radiance of consciousness.
The first and third questions have been resolved; he now resolves the second question with the words "nivṛtta" (having ceased).

Having ceased from the external waking state—that is, upon the exhaustion of karma that produces the enjoyments of the waking state—one remains in one's own true nature, yet, in accordance with external latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), perceives the external objects as the dream-heaven itself, namely, as the shimmering of consciousness (*cid-ākacā*) or the transformations of consciousness (*cid-vivarta*). || 43 ||
This living soul perceives its own externally directed form, which is manifested outwardly and designated as "waking"; it likewise perceives that which resides within as "dream. (44)

When the mind is directed outward, then its own form shines forth as what is called the waking state; when the mind is situated within, then this living soul perceives its own form as the dream state. (44)
Heaven, earth, wind, space, mountains, rivers, and the quarters—life has spread forth and stands as a single essence both within and without. (45)

He provides the answer to the fourth and fifth questions with the word "dyau" (the sky): "The individual soul (*jīva*), which is essentially one, has spread out externally and internally as the sky, the earth, and so forth. (45)
Just as the sun, though situated within its own orb, remains here [on earth] by means of its radiance,
so too the individual soul (jīva), though taking the form of the universe, is established both outside and inside.

If one knows, "I alone am both the internal dream and the external waking state," being of the nature of consciousness and perceiving things as they truly are, one is liberated, free from latent impressions.
Therefore, since the state of being the self of all is the only reality, one is liberated through that very thorough knowledge; thus he says: "internally," etc.
"As it truly is" means according to reality. Being free from latent impressions (*avāsana*) through the gradual ripening of the distinctions between the stages (*bhūmikā*), one is liberated. || 47 ||
This living self (jīva) is neither to be cut nor to be burned; yet, speaking otherwise, one is surely deluded by the yakṣa of dualistic conceptualization, just like a child.

The individual soul (jīva), though inwardly directed toward the inner Self, dwells as if outwardly directed when it perceives the external world; thus, while within itself, it experiences both dreaming and waking in the form of the universe.
Seeing his own inner self as the form of the internal world, he remains in a state of dreaming; likewise, seeing the external world as its form, he remains awake.
These two alone constitute his dreaming and waking states.
As I was reflecting thus, the thought occurred to me, "What would deep sleep be like? Consequently, I became intent on investigating the state of deep sleep. (50)
In this context, he states the true nature of deep sleep (suṣupti) and the fourth state (turīya), even though they were not asked about: "Thus" (iti).
Thus, as I was reflecting upon waking and dreaming from the perspective of reality, the thought characterized by the inquiry, "What might deep sleep be? arose within me. || 50 ||

As long as one remains silent for a long time within the state where the seen and the seeing have ceased, there arises the realization "I am mindless"; this tranquility is nothing other than deep sleep.
"What is the use of seeing what is seen? I shall remain silent for a long time, devoid of thought.
As long as there is such internal awareness, characterized by both tranquility and non-tranquility, that state is deep sleep; otherwise, it is not so—this is the meaning. || 51 ||
Just as the nails, hair, and so forth in this body are both known and unknown, so too,
within the conscious Self, there is neither the insentient nor the sentient during deep sleep.

Fearing that in the absence of mental pervasion and the non-manifestation of consciousness, there would be insentience like that of a jar or similar objects, [the author] states: "Even though it is not specifically known as 'I', because it is known in a general sense—like nails and hair—it consists of both the known and the unknown. That deep sleep is not insentient; and yet it is indeed insentient, shining within the conscious Self, its witness. Thus he says: "Nails... (Verse 52).
"By what consciousness am I weary? The mind has resorted to peace.
Because of this single transformation, there is no other state than deep sleep.

"I am afflicted by fatigue from wandering through the states of waking and dreaming; what is the use of my particular consciousness? Let me remain peaceful for a short while"—in this resolve, deep sleep is simply the transformation into a single state of profound slumber and nothing else; such is the meaning. || 53 ||
This state, thick with sleep, occurs spontaneously even while awake;
through the practice of not thinking of anything, it becomes uniformly tranquil. (54)
He says "this" (etad) to show that even while a person is awake, this state of deep sleep occurs during the condition of abandoning all thought.
When this state reaches density, it is then released;
that subtle state is designated by the term "sleep" (nidrā) and by the term "dream" (svapna). || 55 ||

By etymological derivation, "sleep" (nidrā) refers specifically to deep sleep (*suṣupti*) because it is "extremely firm" (*nitarāṃ dṛḍhā*); however, that which is "slight" (*tanvī*), being lax due to a slight degree of distraction, is referred to by the term "dream" (*svapna*). This is the meaning. || 55 ||
Having determined that this is deep sleep, I have set out to seek the fourth state; I am prepared to act and am intent upon it with the highest intelligence.
Just as light cannot be found apart from darkness, so too, apart from pure perfect awakening, not even the slightest trace of the fourth state can be obtained. (57)
The full form of the Fourth State (turīya) cannot be attained without perfect awakening. || 57 ||
This universe, as it exists, dissolves through perfect awakening;
yet it remains exactly as it was, and nothing at all is dissolved.

Therefore, right awakening alone is the fourth state (*turīya*). For in that state, the universe, having dissolved away, remains in its ultimate non-dissolution; thus he says: "as it truly is" (*yathāsthitam*). || 58 ||
Therefore, dream, waking, and deep sleep exist within the fourth state (turiya);
this world exists exactly as it is, yet truly nothing at all exists.
For this very reason, he says "ataḥ" (therefore), meaning that the three states are included therein. "Sayathāsthitam" means accompanied by the world as it exists. || 59 ||

The world has arisen from a cause; Brahman does not exist in this manner as the world. When the unborn and tranquil state is realized as pure consciousness, that indeed is the fourth state (turiya). || 60 ||

The meaning is that the state of being always in the fourth (turya) state consists precisely in the realization that the world has not arisen from a cause of the world, but rather that Brahman itself exists in this manner as the world. || 60 ||
Due to the impossibility of the causes for manifestation, nothing at all called "creation" is born;
for the consciousness of creation is grasped by consciousness itself, just as fluidity is inherent in water.
Describing this further, he concludes with the words "because of the impossibility": "Sambhava" means birth;

because that [birth] is impossible for its causes within the non-dual Brahman, no second thing whatsoever is born. Rather, the consciousness of creation is itself grasped by the consciousness itself in the form of the world, just as liquidity is grasped by water.
The meaning is "in that same way. || 61 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-seventh canto, titled "The Description of the Waking, Dreaming, Deep Sleep, and Fourth States," in the *Ārṣa* [work], the *Śrī Vālmīki-Devarāja-Mokṣopāya*, within the *Avadhūta-vijaya*.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Waking, Dreaming, Deep Sleep, and Fourth States," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and thirty-eighth canto.
The ascetic said:
Having thus reflected on going, I then attained a state of unity with that consciousness.
And having set out, he was like a fragrance following the fragrance of a supreme lotus.
"When the universe is doubled by the union of the individual soul (prāṇijīva) and the supreme soul (svajīva),
and when they are in unity, I have seen it as one"— thus and so forth is spoken by the Sage.
Having thus investigated the reality of the states beginning with waking and ending with the fourth (turya), immediately thereafter,

I set out to attain oneness— the state of identity— with the consciousness of that living being, characterized as the reflection of pure awareness (cidābhāsa), just as the fragrance belonging to a blossoming mango tree is carried by the wind to a lotus pond and merged with the lotus-born [bee].
The meaning is that it proceeds in the same manner as [the fragrance] moves toward becoming one with the scent residing in the air. || 1 ||
As long as that consciousness of his does not abandon the element of tamas and ojas,
it proceeds toward external perception through the cognition of all the sense organs.

The meaning is this: while I had not yet abandoned that previously mentioned element of vitality (*ojodhātu*) in order to enter the consciousness—that is, the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*)—of that living being, my own consciousness, characterized by all the senses, forcibly engaged in external perception, that is, in outward-directed activity. || 2 ||
Grasping consciousness with consciousness, both externally and internally, in an instant I spread forth there like a drop of oil upon water.

Then, while forcibly restraining those external perceptions of the senses by means of an internal perception characterized by effort, I instantly spread even within. To explain how I spread there, he provides an illustration: "like a drop of oil. (3)
Then, while I was thus transforming within that consciousness,
I beheld the entire world existing exactly doubled in size.
Thus, through the door of the pervasion of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), as long as I transform by merging with the consciousness of the reflected consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) of that living being,
during that interval of time I beheld the entire world existing as doubled, appearing within both the impressions of that [world] and the impressions of the non-dual [Self]. || 4 ||
The quarters of the sky became doubled as both suns blazed;
two terrestrial spheres were produced and two heavens indeed arose.
He elaborates upon this very state of being doubled with the verse beginning "diśā" (by the directions), etc. || 5 ||
Just as two reflections of a face appear reflected in a mirror, so do these two— the world and consciousness— appear merged together.
And when these are mixed with that, the world-mind is increased twofold.
Just as oil appears within two sesame seeds contained in a shell,
so too does the dual world appear, thoroughly intermingled, within that [consciousness].
That which shines like oil within the two seeds of consciousness, residing in the sheath of the intellect—

within those two reflections of consciousness (cidābhāsa) situated in their combined limiting adjuncts— that very world appears doubled and thus intermingled; for those two sheaths of consciousness, though mixed, remain unmixed.
Both of them shone like two equal oceans of milk and water. || 8 ||
Because there is no mixing of latent impressions (vāsanās), they are unmixed. || 8 ||
Then, by a mere glance in an instant, she— consisting of that consciousness—
was led entirely into the state of his own self, as if by the consciousness itself measuring her out.

That consciousness, which is the reflection of the consciousness of those living beings, having been measured and delimited by its own self-consciousness, is brought to the state of oneness—that is, to the state of a single identity—by means of effecting the unification of the two limiting adjuncts (upādhi). This is the meaning. || 9 ||
She was like one season following another, like a small river following a great river,
like a streak of fragrance carried by the wind, or like a trail of smoke from a cloud.
He states the examples for establishing the nature of the self: "The season," etc. (Verse 10).
Through the rapid realization of oneness, the world attained unity for me,
just as the moon, which appears double due to faulty vision, attains oneness through clear sight.
There, through the unification of even the latent impressions (vāsanās) and the absolute oneness of consciousness, the world—which had previously become twofold—attained unity. (11)
Then, as I remained within that consciousness and did not abandon my own state of discernment, my own volition diminished and came to abide in that [universal] volition. (12)
He has reached—that is, attained—a state that conforms to the volition of that living being, which consists of his own discernment and reflection upon what precedes and follows. || 12 ||
Then, observing the external world solely through that mental activity,
he performed his daily routine without ever abandoning those various states of mind.

There, by means of that very mental state of his, I perceived the external objects of enjoyment, such as sound and so forth, without ever leaving his heart; I experienced (abhuñji) his daytime conduct characterized by waking activity—that is, I underwent it. [The use of the *ciṇ* affix in the sense of the agent is Vedic. || 13 ||
Then, by chance, he gradually became overcome by sleep,
like a lotus that has drunk water and eaten its food at evening, becoming weary.
Then that creature, having eaten food and drunk water, became overcome with sleep due to the fatigue that had arisen, falling asleep quite by chance. || 14 ||

He withdrew his mind that had spread through the forest thickets of the quarters, performing the activity of perceiving forms, just as the sun at evening withdraws its radiance from the outside world.
Regarding what his vital breath did at the onset of sleep, he says: "It has spread forth" (prasṛtam), etc. || 15 ||
Together with his mind, all those functions of his sense organs entered the cavity of the heart, withdrawn like the limbs of a tortoise.
He then states what occurred after that: "Together," etc. (verse 16).
Sealed within the form of the heart, those [senses] such as the eyes became like lumps of clay—
mere dead matter, as if fixed in the work of a painter.

The eyes and other senses, being sealed, remained in the form of heart-lotuses; at death, in the moment of passing away, they became as if slightly like clods of earth or like figures depicted in a painting—devoid of all activity. || 17 ||
By that very movement of his mind, I suddenly rose up and remained there;
because of my conformity with his mind, I entered into each of those hearts.

I too, conforming to that mind, abandoned those physical seats of the senses along with the very fluctuations of that mind and entered his heart through the respective channels of those nerves. || 18 ||
Having withdrawn my external perceptions into that inner vital energy,
I experienced for a moment a void-like deep sleep upon the softness of the bed.
In the sheath consisting of bliss, which is as soft as a couch, possesses the aforementioned luster within its essence, and resides therein. || 19 ||
Due to an abundance of fatigue, food, and drink, even when the channels are congested,
the wind either does not exit at all or moves only through those that are hollow.

At that time, when the vital air called *samāna* is obstructed here and there by the abundant transformations of the essence of food and drink within the hollow, perforated channels (*nāḍīs*), it does not indeed emerge outward;
nevertheless, it moves and circulates by means of an extremely subtle course. 20.
Whenever one is solely intent upon the Self that is identical with that [Reality], one renders this mind— which by its very nature seeks its own ends— subordinate, as it abides within the heart.

When deep sleep occurs in this manner, what does this vital breath (prāṇa) do with the mind and its senses? To that he says: "When [it is] thus. When it is so, then the vital breath—being of that nature—is the one, non-dual, perfectly serene Self;
being intent solely upon That, having entered the heart within the pericardium (purītat), it swallows this mind which is situated together with it and renders it subordinate.

He makes [it] his own. Why is that? Because of its nature as one's own object (*svārthasvabhāvataḥ*). "One's own" (*svaḥ*) refers to the inner self (*pratyagātman*); that alone is the "object" (*artha*), the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), and the goal of human endeavor (*puruṣārtha*). It is because of that very nature that there is an inclination toward resting in the bliss characterized by the state of being the remainder (*pariśeṣalakṣaṇasukha*). This is the meaning. || 21 ||
Today, for him, there is only his own self-interest; no one else's task shines forth within him, because this very body exists solely for the sake of its own purpose.
Granted that it is intent upon its own object, why then does the mind not also perform the functions of other organs such as the senses?

To this he replies with the words "svārtha" (its own object). The meaning is that in deep sleep—which consists of the existence of one's own object in the form of unsurpassed bliss—it is precisely this body of unsurpassed bliss that shines forth, and not even a trace of the suffering of distraction. || 22 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
O great sage, does the mind think solely by the power of the vital breath?
Since the mind has no inherent form of its own, what then is it in its absolute state?
Regarding what was said—that the *prāṇa* swallows the *citta* and renders it subordinate—Rāma raises a doubt with the words "the mind":

"The mind (*manas*) and the *citta* are one and the same. O Great Sage, even now the mind performs activities such as thinking only by virtue of the *prāṇa*. Therefore, if it has been rendered subordinate by the *prāṇa*, it would not think."

What does it think even now? Since there is no essential nature of the mind apart from the vital breath (prāṇa), what is there that is merely devoid of the vital breath? The meaning is: nothing at all. The particle "ca" serves to aggregate the preceding question. || 23 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Even this body, though experienced as one's own, does not exist here at all;
this form is merely a product of the mind's imagination, like a mountain in a dream.
When separated from the mere existence of the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*), there is nothing whatsoever in the form of the body, vital breath (*prāṇa*), or the world;

however, when not separated from it, everything exists indeed by virtue of its existence. With the intention that your doubt—that the mind separated from the vital breath does not exist as a single entity—is trivial, Vasiṣṭha gives the reply beginning with "The body... and so forth.
Since this body is of the nature of mental construction, the meaning is that there is no body separate from the mind. || 24 ||
That mind also does not exist at all, because it is joined with the absence of an object of cognition;
for at the beginning of creation, there is an absence of a cause, which is the reason for the non-arising of the visible world. || 25 ||

In the same way, since the mind too is defined by its objects of cognition, it can also be rightly said that in the absence of those objects, its distinct intrinsic nature does not exist; thus he says: "That... If it is argued that each preceding object of cognition is the definer of the subsequent one, he says in response to that:
"Therefore, when all this is Brahman and that [Brahman] is the self of all..."
Then this entire universe remained just as it was, as if it had never been.

Since Brahman is the self of all, when its existence is asserted, it implies that all things such as the mind and the body indeed exist; thus he says: "For those who know It, the mind, the body, and so forth are none other than That Brahman itself. However, in whatever manner these appear to those who know them [as separate], they do not exist for us in that way within our sphere of experience. (27)

Since everything such as the mind and body exists for those who know that [reality], it is indeed Brahman itself. However, for those who do not know Brahman, this mind, body, and so forth—whatever they may be like—do not exist within the sphere of our knowledge of reality.
Just as this Brahmā is the triple world, so too is he of manifold nature;
in this regard, O Prince, listen to this sequence as it is being described. (28)
O Prince Rāma, listen to this description of the process of superimposition and so forth, explaining how these three worlds are indeed Brahman alone; such is the meaning. || 28 ||
There exists pure consciousness alone, stainless and having the nature of infinite space;
it is at all times the self of all forms, neither the world nor the state of being an object of perception.
Therein, he first indicates the basis: "It exists" (asti). || 29 ||
But because of its omniscience, this state of mind was perceived by it through itself—pure, awakened, and free from mental afflictions—without abandoning its own essential nature. (30)
Therefore, this state of mind was first conceived and superimposed; and because of that, there is no absence of another appearance for the substratum—thus he says: "form. || 30 ||
O upholder of the earth, know that this very vital breath (prāṇapavana), which is conceived by the mind as one's own refuge, is indeed that [refuge] for those who know what is to be known.
Refuge means wandering. || 31 ||
Just as this vital breath is experienced by him as if it were imagined by him,
so too are the senses, the body, and the like, as well as the perceptions of space and time.
Thus, this entire universe is the undivided, all-pervading mind alone; and the mind is the supreme Brahman, which is consciousness. Therefore, this whole expanse is Brahman.
Formless, without beginning or end, without appearance and without affliction, peaceful, consisting of pure consciousness and pure existence—this very Brahman is the body of the universe. 34.
The Supreme Brahman, who possesses all powers, exists through the power of the mind;
wherever it may be, it fully experiences its own form in that very way.

Since it possesses all powers, therefore, by its primordial mental power, it experiences its own very nature—which exists as it was previously established—as the world-manifestation, whether in waking or in dreaming, exactly as it is. || 35 ||
The mind, whose essence is volition, is Brahman; whatever it conceives in whatever manner, that very thing it experiences accordingly.
This is established as a fact even for children.

The mind, which consists of volition (saṃkalpa), is indeed the effect-Brahman (kāryabrahma); for in whatever manner it conceives of the worlds beginning with Bhūḥ and other things, in that very same way it experiences them. And this is established as being such even among children, including infants. 36.
Indeed, this very Self has been made into a living being by its own mind; it has been made into a body and even made into the three worlds. It is not that the first [Self] was made into a body;
rather, it is like the void being made into a body or the sky being made into mountains—this has been experienced in dreams within imagined cities.
"O Rāma, is it not so that the very void-body itself is the conscious self, the primordial person, the first living being endowed with breath?

It was made such by consciousness alone; likewise, it was made embodied, and likewise, it was made into the three worlds. All of this has been experienced by everyone within their own imagined cities—their own bodies—just as in dreams; that very thing should be taken as the illustration. This is the meaning. || 37 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-eighth canto, titled "The Exposition of the Universal Nature of Consciousness," in the *Ārṣa* [text], the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa*, within the *Mokṣopāya* section of the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa*.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Mind as the Universal Self," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and thirty-ninth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: The mind alone is the creator of the world; in whatever manner it conceives, so does it become.
Non-existence, existence, and both existence and non-existence—thus does his reality abide. || 1 ||
For here, the primacy of the mind over even the vital breath is described;
[this is shown] through the sage’s observation of dissolution in detail as he passes from deep sleep to the attainment of the dream state.
Having accepted that the mind is always dependent upon the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and having established the priority of the superimposition (*adhyāropa*) based merely on its initial occurrence,

the question of Rāma was resolved with the intention that both waking and dreaming possess equal primacy, whereas in deep sleep (*suṣupti*), primacy belongs to the vital breath alone. Now, however, because the mind alone possesses independence in the creation of the entire world, including the vital breaths and so forth, its primacy [is established].

However, at the onset of deep sleep, because it is exhausted and incapable of functioning, the mind accepts the predominance of the vital breath (prāṇa) for the sake of its own rest; with this intention, he begins the resolution [of the objection] with the words "the mind alone," etc. "Non-existent" (asat) means false (alīka). "Existent" (sat) means empirical (vyāvahārika). "Both existent and non-existent" (sadasat) means apparent (prātibhāsika). Of that...
Of the mind-self. || 1 ||
By him the vital breath was conceived with the thought, "The vital breath is my refuge";
therefore, without it, I do not exist, for he is devoted to each respective [function] through that.

"The mind is the sustainer of all my worldly activities; without that vital breath (prāṇa), I neither come into being nor remain. For this reason, that mind is said to be dependent on the vital breath, having it as its ultimate resort. || 2 ||
"Surely I shall remain deprived of life for some time;
I shall certainly not exist again"—thus was it conceived. (3)

Anticipating the objection that the resolve "I do not exist" might be fallacious—since mental activity is observed even in the absence of breath in bodies well-known from dreams, daydreams, and the like—he says: "I... (verse 3).
O dear one, wherever that [mind] goes, there the body is instantly raised by the vital breath;
in a moment, the mind perceives it as an expansive city of illusion.
Wherever he has fashioned a body with his mind together with the vital breath, there he perceives it as having arisen in an instant. || 4 ||
"I shall not exist again, deprived of life and body"—
when the consciousness possesses such a firm resolve, it does not arise once more.

Immediately after the conceptualization of the vital breath and the body, the individual soul (jīva) becomes possessed of an extremely firm conviction that it shall never again be separated from the vital breath and the body; however, the Consciousness (cit), whose very nature is pure consciousness, does not possess such a firm conviction. || 5 ||

Swinging back and forth due to doubt, he dwells in suffering with an uncertain mind; because of such conceptualization, this [suffering] of his will not pass away by means of a small amount of knowledge.
For this very reason, there is no liberation from ignorance that arises from slight reflection and is mostly accompanied by doubt;
for a firm contrary conviction does not cease without a firm conviction in accordance with reality. Thus he says: "it is wavering.
In this way, this most firm erroneous cognition will not pass away through a slight conceptualization [based on] the knowledge of reality. (6)
For one who possesses the notion "this is mine," that [suffering] does not subside;
indeed, by no means other than through the realization of the self (ātman) can it be so.
Knowledge does not manifest anywhere other than through inquiry into the means to liberation;
therefore, one should diligently investigate that very means to liberation.
But when the knowledge of reality has become more firmly established, this very manual (*grantha*) is the means; thus he says: "Not elsewhere" (verse 8).
Indeed, this notion of "I am this" does not exist as ignorance anywhere;
apart from the means to liberation, this [ignorance] cannot be removed by anything else.
Ignorance exists in only two ways: "I" and "this. The word "other" is the understood remainder. It departs, meaning it goes away. || 9 ||
Thus, whatever has been practiced and perceived by the mind remains exactly so;
therefore, because my life is my vital breaths, my mind is established in the vital breaths.

Because it has been firmly cultivated by the mind that "my very life-breaths (prāṇāḥ) alone are my life" and "the object of supreme love is form," for this reason the mind remains fixed upon the life-breath, being dependent on the life-breath. || 10 ||
When the vital breath (prāṇa) is established calmly within the body, the mind becomes possessed of its own reflective nature;
when the breath is agitated, seeing the agitation inherent in the breath, one perceives nothing else.

Thus, he states that the mind is dependent upon the body—beginning with the words "In the body": when the body is agitated, the mind, perceiving that agitation as residing in the vital breath (prāṇa), perceives neither anything else nor the discernment of the reality of the Self. || 11 ||

When the vital breath (prāṇa) becomes intensely preoccupied with the vibration of its own activity, then the breath, being occupied with that which it seeks, does not exert itself for the sake of the Self. || 12 ||

For this very reason, he says "when" (yadā) to show that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) does not become oriented toward the knowledge of the Self without the practice of restraint; [the mind] is distracted by the activities of that [breath]. 12.
