For these two, the vital breath and the mind, are like a chariot and its driver; indeed, who would not follow the mutual lead of the chariot and its driver? (13)
He asks "Why so? and answers with the verse beginning "These... (verse 13).
Thus, at the beginning of creation, one's own self was perceived by the Supreme Self;
therefore, even today, this law of necessity does not cease for the ignorant.

To the question "Whence is that?", he says: "Thus" (iti). Thus, in this manner, at the beginning of creation, the Self was perceived—that is, willed—by the Supreme Self in the form of prāṇa and manas, which are by nature mutually interdependent. || 14 ||
Through place, time, action, and substance, the mind, vital breath, and the embodied self of those who have not yet ascended to the supreme state pass away even while within their bodies. (15)

For those who have not ascended to the supreme state, who are unenlightened, and whose minds, vital breaths, and bodies remain within physical forms, worldly transactions—engaged with space, time, action, and substance—proceed and continue to function within their bodies. || 15 ||
When the individual's vital breath and mind remain in equilibrium, they perform action while abiding [in the state of waking];
when they are in disequilibrium, one [of them] becomes irregular; and when [the mind] is stilled, that stillness is the state of deep sleep.

In that regard, as long as the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the mind (*manas*) remain in a state of equilibrium while performing their respective functions, so long does the even activity known as waking proceed. When the vital breath ceases from impelling the senses and falls into a state of disequilibrium, then the uneven, solitary mental activity known as dreaming proceeds. And when the mind is stilled...
The meaning is that a state of deep sleep, characterized by the subsiding of all mental distractions, proceeds. || 16 ||

When the life-force (prāṇa), being dull and massed together somewhere within the channels obstructed by food and other such things, remains in a state of quiescence, then deep sleep (suṣuptatā) arises.
When, then, does the mind become tranquil? To this he says:

"When... When the channels are obstructed by food—meaning by the essence of food (*annarasa*) and, by the word "etcetera," by bile (*pitta*) and so forth—the vital breath (*prāṇa*), becoming condensed, dull, and moving slowly, remains somewhere; then, through the tranquility of the mind, deep sleep (*suṣupti*) arises. || 17 ||
When the channels are filled with food or likewise exhausted by fatigue, the vital breath remains motionless; then the state of deep sleep arises.
He states the cause for even those who are hungry and so forth falling into deep sleep due to exhaustion: "Or when [the breaths] have dwindled," etc. (18).

Due to the softness or the fullness of the channels within the interior of the wound, when the vital breath (prāṇa) remains or dissolves somewhere, they become motionless; that is the state of deep sleep (suṣuptatā).
He states that even the softening of the channels (*nāḍī*) through massage and other means is a cause of deep sleep, saying "of the channels.
Likewise, he states that being filled with arrows, wounds, blood, and so forth is also a cause of it, saying "due to fullness. || 19 ||
The ascetic said:
Then, he into whose heart I had entered became, during the night,
deeply absorbed in a heavy sleep and satiated with food.

Having thus concluded the incidental discussion regarding Rāma’s question and answer, Vasiṣṭha resumes the very speech of the ascetic that was introduced, beginning with the words "atha" (now) and so forth.
The statement, "that living being, being fully satiated by food, became desirous of the dense sleep of deep slumber," is a restatement of what was previously mentioned. || 20 ||
Together with him, having attained oneness of mind with him, I experienced a profound, dense state of deep sleep, becoming as if a mere subordinate quality.
Having become subordinate, it has abandoned its independence. || 21 ||
Then, as the internal channel-path of this blind man became clear and the natural movement of the vital breath (prāṇa) was established, his deep sleep (suṣupta) grew thin.

Then, when the food (*andhas*) within the belly of this living being has been digested, and when the vital breath (*prāṇa*) has begun to throb—that is, is moving—within its natural, innate channel-path; [the suffix] *kta* is used here in the sense of the agent according to the rule *gatyarthākarmaka-*; [the breath] reaches a state of thinness, that is, minuteness.
When deep sleep had become attenuated, I beheld right here a world containing the sun and other luminaries, as if it had emerged from my own heart.
Then he says, "In deep sleep," [meaning] that the expansion of his dream was seen by me. || 23 ||
And that [ocean], being filled by the great waters rising from the agitated sea,
was like one where clouds have been released at the end of an eon, with its waves scraping the very heavens.

And I saw that world being filled by a great flood of water arising from oceans agitated at the time of dissolution. He distinguishes that very water with the words "as if released": "by the clouds of the kalpa" means by those released—that is, poured down—from below in streams as thick as pestles. The word "as if" (iva) [indicates a comparison].
The indicator of falsity (mithyātva) is to be applied everywhere. || 24 ||
It was swept away by a mountain-flood roaring with great whirlpools,
filled with rows of forests and rich with grassy meadows, uprooting elephants along its course.

By a whirlwind (*vātyā*)— characterized by a row of forests (*vanālī*) carrying [the wind] and by mountains rich in thickets of grass (*tṛṇyā*, a mass of grass)— or, according to the reading "filled with grass and the like," clearly by such a whirlwind; [a whirlwind] by which trees (*aga*) and mountains have been uprooted, and which has already scorched the three worlds (*trilokī*) with its flames of fire.
The connection with the subsequent [verse] is: "with fragments, [and] with the whole. || 25 ||
Even before the three worlds had been entirely consumed by fire,
they were filled on all sides with vast fragments of their cities, mountains, and lands.
The cities of the gods, asuras, and others are well-known in the sky, consisting of those [elements] beginning with that [ether]. (26)
I saw myself right there, in a certain dwelling, in a certain city, staying in a house as the son-in-law of someone. (27)
And at that time, I see myself situated in a certain dwelling place, in a certain city there, and even in a certain house there, together with my wife; such is the meaning. || 27 ||
Together with my wife, my servants, my sons, and my kinsmen, along with my goods, utensils, and house, I was swept away by the waters.
And in such a state, I was carried away and swept along by that flood of the waters of dissolution. || 28 ||
That house and that city were being swept away by the waters of destruction,
overwhelmed by trees taking the form of mountains, and filled with floods of water.

He describes that house and that city in such a state with the words "being carried away" (*uhyamānam*). By the waters of destruction, that is, the waters of the dissolution; by waves having the form of trees. || 29 ||
Raising a great clamor like one striving to conquer the ocean,
its inhabitants were utterly agitated and paid no heed to their children.
The inhabitants of the site—that is, those belonging to the ground of the dwelling—are called *vāstavya*. || 30 ||
It was crowded and agitated by movements rich with the tossing of whirlpools,
and it was terrifying with the mire of people crying out and beating their breasts.
It was filled and driven along by the currents of its waters, and it was terrifying with its mud and mire.
With walls crumbling and beams snapping with a rattling sound, it was filled with a terrifying roar; the faces of the women remained visible through the windows as the roofs and awnings fell down.
Where a loud, piercing sound was produced by the snapping pegs. || 32 ||
Thus, while I was looking on for a moment and had attained that state of mind, I wept piteously as my whole house [fell into ruin].
Divided fourfold by the breaking of the walls and accompanied by the old, the young, and women,
it flowed in a hundred streams like a mountain torrent over a rock.
By means of the breaking and splitting of the walls. || 34 ||
Then, I was being carried away in the waters of the dissolution, my mind having abandoned all concern for wife and kin, intent only on preserving my life. (35)
Cast by the mass of waves from one league to a multitude of leagues,
he was shattered as the tips of trees being carried along were torn away amidst the intervening flames.
The trees being carried away there by the flames of the fire of dissolution were shattered by those movements passing through its midst;
or rather, [they were shattered] by the obstacles encountered along the way. || 36 ||
Struck by the harsh clashing against wood, walls, banks, and seats,
he went to the depths of the underworld and after a long time emerged again.

Struck and battered by unbearable collisions with wood and other materials, he went to the depths of the netherworld during the whirlpools and dances of the churning, and after a long time, he rose up. || 37 ||
In the water, which was filled with the gurgling roar of shifting currents, surges, and ebb-tides, he was submerged and emerged again and again amidst the many great waves.
For a moment, he was submerged in water made turbid by the collision with the lord of mountains,
like an elephant sunk in a puddle, before being lifted out by the pure waters.
I became submerged therein; there, by chance, I was raised up again by pure water that had arrived. || 39 ||
Just as I was quickly recovering my breath upon the foam-peak of the mountain,
I was suddenly struck by the rushing water as if by an enemy.
While I was resting and finding respite upon a mass of foam, a fragment of a mountain, or even on a piece of driftwood, I was struck by a great wave of excessive water. || 40 ||
At that time, by me— who was of the nature of suffering— there was no sorrow that was not experienced, as I was beset by a mass of water with its various tossing waves.
What more need be said? He says, "of various kinds," [meaning] that at that time all suffering was experienced by me. || 41 ||
In the meantime, there, at that time, the dark-eyed ascetic addressed the hunter,
due to his lifelong practice and because he was conscious of the danger. (42)

"In the meantime, I recollected my former self whose nature consists of meditative absorption (samādhi)"—this is the connection with what follows. In the reading "tāmarasekṣaṇa," it is Vasiṣṭha addressing Rāma while repeating the words of the sage [Viśvāmitra]. || 42 ||
"I have recollected my former form, which consisted of meditative absorption.
Oh, how strange! While the world has taken on another form, I remain here as an ascetic. (43)
He says "ā aho" and so forth, as if mocking memory itself. Since *ā* is not a part of a suffix (*anāṅ*) when used in memory, it is treated as a *pragṛhya* by the rule *nipāta ekājanāṅ*. 43.
"I have entered here with the desire to see the dream-vision of another; thus, I perceive this delusion within a dream. (44)
In the recognition "this is I," [the self is perceived]. || 44 ||
Even while being carried away by the waves within this self consisting of false knowledge and firm habitual tendencies of the present, I remain happy because of that [realization]. (45)

I, who am currently existing in this body—the self consisting of false knowledge produced by the firm habitual practice of one's own mental proliferation—even while being carried away by the waves [of worldly existence], [attain that state] immediately after remembering it. || 45 ||
Or rather, I saw this as water, with the mountains, cities, villages, tracts of earth, and trees being swept away by the churning of the ocean at the time of universal dissolution. (46)

Those possessing the qualifiers to be mentioned hereafter are like the transformations of the ocean at the time of dissolution. This is well known: that which is the water of the mirage in the desert is [perceived] as such;
that is to say, it is in its falsity. || 46 ||
The women of the lord of the gods, men, and sky-dwellers were being swept away,
as were the cities and abodes of the world-protectors, along with their great undertakings.
Then, repeatedly beholding the destruction of the world— characterized by waves of water mixed with mountains and the crashing together of those mountains— I reflected upon what would follow.
It is a marvel that even this three-eyed one is being carried away like withered straw in the ocean;
alas, for cursed fate, there is indeed nothing that cannot be done.

He said, "What did I think then?"—namely, "It is a marvel. Here, it is a marvel (citram) and a wonder that even the Lord (Īśvara), who possesses three eyes characterized by the three states within this great ocean of Māyā, becomes a living being (jīva) and is carried away like a withered blade of grass. It is a marvel regarding the destruction of Fate (vidhi), that is, Destiny (daiva). 49.
By breaking through the four walls, I manifest my inner intent;
the rays of the sun reveal the houses within the water like lotuses. (50)

Just as at dawn the rays of the sun cause the lotuses to bloom and reveal them, so too do the houses, by the splitting open of their four walls, display the beauty of their revealed inner chambers [this is the realized meaning of the word *maha* found in the root text]. They show themselves in such a way that this occurs. || 50 ||
Wondrously, in the undulations of the waves, the women of the Gandharvas, Kinnaras, humans, gods, and Nāgas shine forth;
like lotus ponds filled with bees that form necklaces of swarms, they are all truly moving lotuses known as "the stainless ones."
And these lotus-ponds— characterized by numerous whirlpools, eddies, and ripples, bearing necklaces in the form of rows of bees white with pollen,
and possessing lotuses in the form of their faces, hands, and feet— are indeed well-known as *hradinyaḥ* (river-like ponds), yet they are neither entirely pure nor are they [all] rivers.
These are called "mobile"; however, these [others] are the opposite of that. Therefore, the grammatical connection is: "as if variegatedly flashing forth amidst the undulations of the waves. || 51 ||

The wall-sections of the great mansions of gods, asuras, and nagas— possessing the splendor of lattice-windows made of jewel-nets that form the boundary of moonstone enclosures entwined by the vine-like arms of vidyadhara women— wander amidst the mass of waters like a multitude of golden ships.

In those [clouds], the wall-sections of the great mansions of gods, asuras, and serpents— wherein the splendor of jeweled lattice-windows shines like the divisions of courtyards within moonstones entwined by the vine-like arms of vidyādharīs— wander amidst the mass of the waters of universal dissolution like a multitude of golden ships.
Here, Indra— exhausted by the fatigue of love-making— rests upon Śacī’s breasts, which are as expansive as the frontal globes of an intoxicated elephant and marked with saffron;
clinging there as if out of pleasure, he moves back and forth on the swings of the waves while remaining within his palace of shimmering jewels.
Indra, situated within a palace of shimmering jewels, became weary and exhausted by the fatigue caused by amorous play with Śacī,
the daughter of Puloman; being drenched in this mass of dissolution-water clinging to her expansive and broad breasts, which were marked with saffron like the frontal globes of a rutting elephant,
he sought relief from that exhaustion through the pleasure of sporting in the water (the infinitive *krīḍitum* being implied).
The fifth [verse]: She makes the swings of the waves as if for the sake of the pleasure of sporting in the water. || 53 ||

Alas! The winds blow, swirling through the sky with the waters and scattering heaps of flowers shaken from the stars; they seem to carry handfuls of parched grain toward the falling celestial mansions whose peaks are strewn with jewels, as if entering the hollows of gardens.
In such a manner that the sky was enveloped by the swirling currents of waters; likewise,

winds scattering showers of flowers characterized by stars and constellations fell upon the jeweled peaks of Mount Meru, where they had gone into the hollows of its groves, while celestial mansions and palaces were falling [from the sky].
Having entered for the sake of auspiciousness, they blow like people scattering a rain of excellent flowers along with parched grain; "hā" expresses grief. || 54 ||

This lotus of the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin), who is solely intent on meditation and whose pericarp is covered by petals, rises in the sky like a golden stone produced by a machine; its form is water, tossed upward by the crests of formidable waves from the agitated mountain, and it revolves in the heavens.
This water, tossed upward by the crests of terrifying waves as formidable as agitated mountains in the sky,
resembles a golden stone hurled from a machine;
its form in the heavens of the Brahma-world is like that of the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin), who is absorbed in meditation and seated upon the pericarp, surrounded by petals and leaves.
Having reached the lotus that serves as its seat, it turns away; the meaning is that it does not turn back in the interval. || 55 ||
Like clouds, terrifying with their exceedingly thick and rumbling roar, these masses of waves— lightnings over the city of gold—
wander through the sky, possessing bodies equal to elephants, horses, lions, serpents, trees, mountains, forests, and the surface of the earth.
With bodies resembling elephants, horses, and other such creatures, and terrifying with the exceedingly dense *ghuṃghuma* sounds,
these masses of waves— within which golden cities of gods and asuras appear like lightning— wander through the sky like clouds. (56)
Being carried away by the waves that possess the beauty of flax flowers,
even this Yama is led away as if by another Yama in the form of the flood of water.

The meaning is that, being carried away by the flood of water upon such a wave in the ocean of dissolution, he— possessing a splendor like the flax flower— appeared as if even Yama himself were being led by another Yama. || 57 ||
All these guardians of the world, along with the serpents, mountains, and cities numbering in the hundreds of thousands, are sinking into the waters;
their submergence is made manifest by the gurgling roar of the mass of water as it swirls within the cavernous womb of the ocean, the source of fortune.

All the world-protectors and the nāgas, together with their own abodes—the mountains such as Meru and the cities—are sinking and submerging. There, the flood of water that has entered or gone into the mountain-womb caves, which are mines of wealth such as treasures, is characterized by the gurgling sounds of the wind emerging for the purpose of turning back that flood; these are the ones whose filling [is thus marked].
Being such as they are. || 58 ||

When the netherworlds, the earth, the vault of heaven, and the horizons were completely filled by the swirling of irresistible waters, the multitudes of Indra, Yama, Yakṣas, gods, and asuras—along with their villages, cities, celestial chariots, and mountains—wandered about like fish.
This is clear. 59.
As Kṛṣṇa was being carried away, his very body, having taken the form of water,
became a source of suffering by turning into a bond— like the mother’s shank becoming a tether for her calf.
The meaning is that at the time of milking, the calves were tied by the cowherds to their mothers' shanks. || 60 ||
"Ah! As they grapple with one another, the gurgling roar of the gods and demons is heard, mingled with the tumultuous cries of their own women."
It was tumultuous with shouts of "halahala," as if for its own sake or for the sake of women. || 61 ||
In the quarters where the mass of waters is agitated by the speed and force of the preeminent city filled with clamor,

and which seem to envelop the sky with dense clouds of wandering water, this solid wall-structure consisting of water is clearly perceived through the velocity of the tumultuous cries of the gods and demons of those foremost cities.

With the quarters of the sky filled by masses of water agitated by the falling drops, and with clouds wandering amidst them like dense nets of mist, a solid wall of water is clearly perceived. || 62 ||
Alas, what a tragedy! This one has been swiftly swept downward by the water through the whirling motion of the eddies;
distressed by the masses of water-clouds, these—Kubera, Yama, Nārada, Vāsava, and the others—are giving up their lives. (63)
This sun, well-known to all people, has been effectively drawn downward by means of its circular and revolving motion;
the distressed ones are unable to survive. 63.

The wise, having abandoned pride, carry this body— which is being borne here as something utterly inert— as if it were a corpse; for by the impact of the waters from the fragments of the cities of Brahmā, Indra, and Viṣṇu, they see it as being violently crushed.

Seeing the violent crushing of the ancient cities of Brahmā, Indra, and others by such a flood of turbulent waters— those among them who are wise and knowers of reality perceive their own body, which is peaceful, dead, and therefore inert, being carried away here in the water.

Pride is that sense of "I-ness"; having abandoned it, the virtuous carry themselves as if they were corpses. Therefore, the meaning is that they are not tainted by the sufferings of cutting, piercing, striking, and so forth. || 64 ||
A multitude of women comes here, half-crushed; alas, what other fool is capable of protecting them? For this mass of people, being chewed by the teeth of Death, is not able to save one another.
Who is capable of protecting this group of women, who are as dull-witted and foolish as the earth itself? "Janatā" means a multitude of people. || 65 ||
Vast masses of water, surging against mountains and slithering along like serpents, flow on;
upon them, like boats, the cities of the gods, having raised their bodies aloft, quickly descend below.

They strike against and shatter mountains, thus they are "mountain-shatters. Those vast masses of water, the billows, which possess a gliding motion like that of snakes, surge forth. Upon those billows, the cities of the gods first raise themselves up like a ship, and immediately thereafter descend rapidly; that is to say, they sink. 66.

The three worlds— filled with continents, mountain kings, gods, asuras, serpents, and humans, along with nāgas, apsarases, and cāraṇas, appearing like lotuses whose roots have been severed by the surging waters— now stands as a single ocean-lake; uprooted by Time, alas, where have you gone?
The gods, who possess great supernatural power and majesty, are the leaders of the world. || 67 ||

In the course of time, the three worlds were uprooted by the great islands and mountain-kings tossed about by the waves; filled with gods, asuras, serpents, men, nāgas, elephants, apsarases, and celestial bards—all of whom were like lotuses with severed roots—the world remained as a single lake characterized by the one ocean. "Alas! expresses grief. Great indeed...
Where have those leaders of the world—the gods such as Indra and others—gone, whose sovereign power was derived from supernatural might? (67)

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-ninth canto, titled "The Description of the Destruction of the World," in the *Ārṣa* [text], the glorious *Vālmīki-Devarṣi-Mahāmuni-Nirvāṇa-Uttara-Avirodha-Viśada-Śata*, [the Uttarakāṇḍa]. 139.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Destruction of the World," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The fourteenth hundredth canto (140).
The hunter said:
"O Blessed One, how did you come to such a state as that?"
How is it that he did not then attain tranquility through the practice of meditation? || 1 ||
The receding of the ocean of dissolution, the abiding of a twice-born in a village,
and the outward departure of the sage who is the very life-breath— these are described therein.

The word *ca* (and) is used for the sake of emphasis. How did even one such as you—who had attained perfection in the yoga of knowledge—fall into those various states of delusion previously described in many ways, such as being submerged in the waters of dissolution?
At that time, [you were unable to do so] despite the application of the limbs of yoga characterized by meditation, which is the means for perceiving all things past and future.
How has he not reached, how has he not attained the cessation of all delusion? || 1 ||
The Sage said: At the ends of the kalpas, the worlds— which are of the nature of illusion— perish through various forms of destruction, like mere appearances in the sky.
Sometimes destruction occurs gradually at the end of a kalpa;
sometimes it happens suddenly and unexpectedly all at once through a single transformation.

In the case of a gradual dissolution, there would be an opportunity for the contemplation of past and future events through yoga; however, in the case of a sudden dissolution, no such opportunity was obtained by me—intending this as his reply, he demonstrates the two-fold nature of dissolution with the words "kadācit" (at one time). This refers to the transformation characterized by the simultaneous and singular disappearance of the seven oceans. || 3 ||
Then, at that very moment, when the water was thus transformed,
as soon as they began to flow away, the gods were carried off by the waters.
Just as the gods were rushing—desiring to go—to report this to the primordial Hiraṇyagarbha, they were carried away by the waters.
Thus, the meaning is: "If even the gods have met with such negligence there, what need is there to speak of me? (4)
Furthermore, O Lord of the Forest, time indeed erases everything;
whatever is destined to happen at a particular time, that will necessarily come to pass then. (5)

Or, due to the overwhelming power of time, my meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) and concentration (*dhāraṇā*) did not manifest at that moment; thus he says, "Furthermore" (*anyacca*). O Lord of the Forest, O Hunter! *Sarvakaṣaḥ* means that which wears away or destroys everything. The meaning is: whatever is destined to happen at a particular time occurs exactly so. || 5 ||
When the time of destruction has arrived, strength, intellect,
and splendor are everywhere and in every way overturned, even for the great.
He elaborates on that very point: "Power," [verse 6].
Moreover, O Lord of the Forest, this which has been described by me to you was indeed seen in a dream; for what is there in this world that cannot possibly occur within a dream? (7)

Furthermore, he offers another resolution to the objection: "What is this that was seen by me in a dream, following the thoughts of another, wherein even for the great, the absence of discernment is well known? He says, "Moreover" (*anyacca*); the meaning is: what is not well known here among all people?
The hunter said:
O All-pervading One, if this is unreal, being merely a delusion of a dream, then what is the purpose of this narration, O Knower of the Auspicious? (8)

That which has the delusion of a dream as its measure is "mere dream-delusion. What, then, is the purpose of this being told to me? The vocative address, "O you who are skilled in auspicious matters," is used to indicate that such speech of meaningless words is not to be expected from you. (8)
The sage said:
O intelligent one, there exists here a great task consisting of awakening you;
you perceive this as being of the nature of delusion, but hear the truth from me.
Revealing his skill in what is auspicious (*kalyāṇakovidatva*), the Sage gives the following reply: "Consisting of your awakening.

It is "great" because it culminates in liberation (*mokṣa*). For you understand that even this which is currently perceived is illusory in nature, through the realization of the similarity between this world and the described cosmic manifestation (*prapañca*).
Since everything that is merely perceived is of the nature of delusion, you alone remain as the true form of the Seer.
Therefore, the meaning is: "Listen from me to this means of purifying [the Self] through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), which is the remainder of the discourse. || 9 ||
Immediately thereafter, within that [ocean] possessing the force of a single intoxicated sea, I,
remaining as the vital energy (ojas) of the creature, wandered and beheld a wandering dream.
Meanwhile, the entire body of water was about to flow out somewhere,
like a multitude of great winged mountains terrified by a turbulent thunderbolt.
Regarding how long he observed that delusion, he says "yāvat" (as long as). "Sasakalam" means existing together with all [the phenomena], such as whirlpools, waves, and so forth. || 11 ||
Being carried along, I reached some shore by the power of destiny;
I remained there, clinging to it as it resembled the edge of a mountain peak.
Supporting myself against that bank, I took refuge there and stayed. || 12 ||
Then, in an instant, that water emerged entirely,
while the sky became starry with deities whose forms were revealed by the crests of the waves.
He describes that water with the verse beginning "vīcyagra... and so forth:

by which [water] the sky has become starry—having acquired stars—in the form of droplets of water bursting from the crests of the waves, appearing as the planets, lunar mansions, and other deities. || 13 ||
Its interior was composed of jewels by the clusters of stars situated in the netherworld (pātāla),
and it was filled with vast old mountain grasses whirled around in its eddies.
By certain clusters of stars situated in the netherworld, it was as if its interior were made of jewels. || 14 ||
It was filled with celestial palaces resembling the islands of gold,
and was garlanded by clusters of lotuses where the swarms of wandering celestial nymphs settled.
It was garlanded by clusters of lotuses that possessed the hidden characteristics of celestial nymphs.
It possessed a network of blue moss-like clouds being carried along in the midst [of the sky],
and it was filled with lightning like yellow gorocana and dark lotuses like the blue clouds.

It was filled with blue lotuses characterized by clouds—dark as the clouds at the end of an aeon, appearing like clusters of moss, while their filaments were like lightning and their pollen like yellow orpiment; it surpassed all else in its abundance of such features.
The edges of the quarters were filled with clouds of mist from shimmering spray,
and the multitude of Kalpa trees being carried along was indistinguishable from the surging waves.
Its banks in all directions were formed by clouds, mountains, and mists emitting shimmering sprays of water.
Then that ocean-bed became a parched hollow;
in some places the Sahya mountain had crumbled away, and in others Mount Mandara was completely withered.

He describes even the excavation of the single ocean with the verse beginning "śuṣka" and so forth: it is that place where Mount Mandara—or perhaps another—is subject to doubt as to whether it is Mandara or something else, due to its being withered and decayed. || 18 ||
In some places, the moon, Yama, Indra, and Takṣaka were submerged in mud;
in other places, there were clusters of wish-fulfilling trees whose branches were sunk deep below the mire.
In some places, his hands were strewn with the heads of world-protectors like lotuses;
in other places, he was crimson with pools of blood resting upon the lotuses.
It was crimson with pools of blood that resembled lotuses resting upon the surface.
In some places, groups of Vidyadhara women were submerged up to their necks and crying out;
in other places, it was filled with fierce buffaloes that struck terror by means of elephants killed in dreams.
He was surrounded by dead elephants like dreams, by the fierce buffaloes that are the mounts of Yama’s messengers, and by the steeds of Yama himself.
In some places it was a formidable mountain of great-bodied Garuḍas, and in others, a great bridge of intoxicated [beings] trodden upon by the staff of Yama.

There stands the immortal mountain, possessing the characteristics of a great-bodied Garuda; there, as if intoxicated by the staff of Yama fallen upon the earth, stands a great dam, incapable of being breached by the waters.
In some places, the ground was mud mixed with the laughter of swans that were the gods of Brahmā;
in other places, the celestial elephants had half their bodies submerged in the mire.
In the meantime, having reached a mountain peak there at the hermitage,
when I rested from my fatigue, sleep came over me intensely.
When I had rested in the hermitage of a certain sage on a mountain ridge, a region of level ground, then sleep came upon me intensely. (24)
Then, at the end of that deep sleep, accompanied by that same latent impression (vāsanā),
I perceived that very same end of the kalpa while remaining established in my own vital energy (ojas).
Remaining in my own luster, I beheld that very same being who had been seen within me during the interval between deep sleep and the subsequent onset of sleep. || 25 ||
Seeing that double the suffering, I remained agitated here for a long time;
then, having awakened, I beheld that very peak situated within his heart.
I beheld him with favor, seated within the heart of this living being. || 26 ||
Then, on that second day, I beheld the world, beautiful with the rising sun, together with its inhabitants, its sky, its earth, and its mountains.
"Heaven, earth, wind, space, mountains, rivers, and the directions"—this has arisen in my mind like leaves and such from a branch. (28)
It was born and produced from the mind itself, just as leaves and such are produced from a branch, which in turn arises from a tree. || 28 ||
Then, when that ground was thus seen by those objects, I engaged in worldly activity, my intellect somewhat clouded by forgetfulness. (29)
The ellipsis is "engaged in acting. [He is one] whose intellect has forgotten something regarding an object previously experienced here, or who is urged by one whose intellect has forgotten. || 29 ||
"Today I am sixteen years old;
this is my father, this is my mother, and this is my home"—such was the joy that arose within me. (30)
And there, a certain unprecedented intuition regarding worldly activity arose within him as if it were already established; thus he says: "Of one who is born" (*jātasya*).
"Abode" (*āspada*) means a home. || 30 ||
I saw a certain village and a certain hermitage of Brahmins; likewise, I saw a certain house and a certain kinsman in a certain hermitage.
In that regard, the ellipsis implies that "someone was a kinsman. || 31 ||
Then, as I remained in the village house together with my kinsmen,
as days and nights passed by, that very same reality [remained] even while I was awake and so forth.

The ellipsis is to be supplied as "experiencing the distinctions between the states of waking and so forth. That very village and such [was experienced]; it became real, as if according to its true nature.
Then, by the power of time, my former consciousness of awakening was forgotten there due to such habitual practice—oh, how like the state of being a fish! (33)

The meaning is that, although Kaṭa had previously been described as one who was free from worldly attachment (nirvāsana), due to his long-standing habit of living with fish, he forgot his former realization; thus, like a fish, he became a resident of the village. || 33 ||
Thus, at that time, I became a village-dwelling Brahmin,
whose concern was bound solely to the physical body and who had cast far away the ground of discernment.
He elaborates upon that very point with the words "iti" and so forth. || 34 ||
One who is attached only to his own body as the self, whose soul is colored only by his wife, whose essence consists only of latent impressions, and who is solely intent upon wealth alone; || 35 ||
One for whom the self, the inherent nature, or the body has as its essence nothing but latent impressions (vāsanā). || 35 ||
His only wealth was a worn-out cow-hide; he had planted a fence of creepers;
he had gathered fire, earth, and living beings; and he had acquired a water-pot.

By him the growth of niṣpāva beans and other creepers was planted in the courtyard of his house; by him fire, the earth—meaning fields and other lands—and living beings such as cattle were accumulated. The absence of the letter *n* (in *agniśca*) is a Vedic archaism.
His gaze was fixed upon a swaying young tree, and he was ever devoted to worldly customs;
his dwelling was situated on a patch of dark-green grassy ground near the side of a house. (37)

He places his reliance on fleeting trees such as the *tulasī*, which live for only a short time; he delights in the customs of the world, in the local laws of nations and villages; and his dwelling is upon small plots of land covered with dark green grass situated near houses.
He spent his days engaged in the cultivation of vegetable gardens and groves,
and was devoted to bathing in rivers, lakes, streams, holy fords, and ponds.
By him were spent the days in the cultivation and adornment of gardens of long-stemmed vegetables and groves;
[the compound] "of the lakes" (*saronām*) is treated as a singular collective dual. || 38 ||
He collects cow dung, food, water, firewood, and stones with great hardship, rendered helpless by the two snares of "this must be done" and "this must not be done. (39)
The bricks are desired; he is one whose nature is to collect cow-dung and other materials with great effort. || 39 ||
Thus, as I lived there, a hundred years passed by;
once, a self-controlled ascetic guest arrived from afar.
The self-possessed one is the knower of the self. || 40 ||
Having been honored, he rested in my house after first bathing;
having eaten and retired to his bed, he recounted a story during the night. (41)

During a certain course of conversation, charming with the worldly affairs of various directions, countries, mountains, and lands, and resting upon manifold aesthetic sentiments (rasas), [he spoke]. (42)
In a certain course of conversation, he awakened me; this is the connection with the distant [verb] "iti" (thus). || 42 ||
All this is indeed nothing but pure consciousness—endless and changeless;
though it remains exactly as it is, it shines forth as the world.
Thus instructed by him, I attained a state of pure, undivided consciousness;
by the power of dhāraṇā, I remembered that entire account in its entirety.
That account of his own past experiences, such as entering the bodies of previous living beings. || 44 ||
Having remembered my own history— that I had dwelt within his womb—
I suspected him to be Virāṭ and prepared to depart from him.
Suspecting that living being to be the Virāṭ form because it contains the belly of the entire world, [he emerged] from its belly.
Then I did not know that mouth was the gateway for departure, when within that vast world filled with lands, oceans, mountains, and rivers, [I wandered]. (46)

When I was wandering in that vast world within the belly of a living being, I did not know that its mouth was the door for my exit; at that time, even without leaving that place, I entered the vital breath (pavana) of that being so as to go outside—this is how it connects with the following verse. || 46 ||
At that time, without abandoning that place crowded with kinsmen, I entered his vital breath in order to exit as the external wind. (47)
"Remaining here, I perceive everything—both the external and the internal, as well as that which is born of another—as belonging to this Virāj; having thus resolved it to be so," (48)

The connection with the following verse is as follows: "Remaining here, with the thought 'I shall behold all this—both that which is external to this living Virāṭ and born of another, and that which is internal and produced within the Virāṭ'—and having established a meditative concentration (dhāraṇā) upon that [Virāṭ] which conforms to it, consisting of the ego-identification with its vital breaths, I did not leave that place. || 48 ||
Having bound myself to that region through the power of meditative concentration (dhāraṇā), I did not abandon it;
along with my vital breaths, I departed like fragrance from a flower. 49.
Having reached the mass of air and entered the hollow of its mouth,
I emerged by means of the chariot of the external wind and beheld what was before me.
Having gone outside in a chariot possessing the characteristics of wind, he saw before him what is about to be described. || 50 ||
Meanwhile, my body remained exactly as it was, seated in the lotus posture,
while somewhere in a mountain cave a hermitage protected by disciples stood.
Somewhere outside, in a mountain cave, there is a hermitage of sages; there, my entire body remains seated in the lotus posture, exactly as it was previously experienced.
While they stood before me, intent on the task of protecting me,
a period of time lasting but a single moment passed for those dwelling at the end.
That man, with whom I have entered his heart,
lies happily satisfied, as if satiated by food obtained through the joy of a festival, even though he is merely on his back.
That living being, a male disciple, having become satiated with the fine food obtained during some festival in a village, lies comfortably on his back with his back [exposed]. || 53 ||
Having seen that marvel, I said nothing to anyone;
out of curiosity, I entered his very heart once again.
Driven by that latent impression, I reached that region of vital energy within his heart in order to behold those kinsmen of mine.

The connection with the following verse is as follows: "As soon as I reached that previously experienced region of vital energy (*ojas*), which is a portion of the three sheaths beginning with the *ānandamaya*, the end of the Yuga commenced there. (55)
When the exceedingly terrible end of the Yuga had set in there,
that world, along with its established order, underwent total transformation.
It has come to, or reached, a state of inversion together with the established order of dharma and adharma. || 56 ||
The mountains there are indeed different, and the earth is situated differently;
the divisions of the quarters are distinct, and likewise the arrangement of the worlds is otherwise. (57)
He elaborates upon the very reversal of the world with the words "another" (anya). || 57 ||
Those kinsmen, that village, that stretch of land, and that region of the horizon—
I know not where it all has gone, as if swept away by the winds.
Having arrayed and having gathered together. || 58 ||
Then I beheld another world situated as far as it extended; with its unprecedented configuration, that universe appeared as if it were something entirely different.
As much as has been done. || 59 ||
The twelve Ādityas scorch, the ten directions blaze,
and the mountains, like ice and congealed water, have begun to melt away by force.
Like water that has become congealed and solidified by cold, they began to melt away. || 60 ||
On every mountain and in every direction, the forest ranges are ablaze; all those things that were like jewels have been consumed by fire and have become mere objects of memory.
All the oceans have dried up, and the great winds stand before us;
the entire circle of the earth has become a heap of glowing coals without exception.
They stood up, positioned in the eastern direction. || 62 ||
Then, flames began to issue forth from the netherworld, from the earth, and from all directions;
instantly, the entire universe became a single circle of fire, like the clouds at twilight.
First from the netherworld (pātāla), then from the surface of the earth, and immediately thereafter from all directions, flames began to issue forth;
the entire universe quickly became a single circle of fire, turning as crimson as the clouds at twilight.
Having entered that abode of flames like a wandering bee into the calyx of a golden lotus,
I did not suffer the pain of the transformation caused by burning, for I approached it from afar with the gait of a moth.

Having entered that abode of flames, which was like a golden lotus-bud with wandering bees, I did not experience even the slightest suffering from the affliction of burning, despite being constantly exposed to it; for my conviction was that I possessed only a subtle, transportive body (ātivāhika-deha). This is the intended meaning. || 64 ||
I wander within that great cloud composed of flames like a flash of lightning driven by the wind;
my body flickers with the movement of the fire, possessing a beauty like that of a bee hovering over a cluster of land-lotuses.

Through the practice of breath-control (*aniladhāraṇā*), my self has become composed of air; thus, like lightning in that great cloud consisting mostly of wind, I move perfectly within it. The meaning is that, with a body trembling amidst the flickering of flames, I have come to possess a beauty resembling the bees that wander among clusters of land-lotuses. || 65 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and fortieth chapter, titled "Description of the Mental Construction of the Heart," in the *Ārṣa-Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*, within the *Vālmīki-Daivata-Mokṣopāya-Nirvāṇa-Uttara-Arṣa-Viśeṣa*.

Thus ends the one hundred and fortieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Construction of the Heart," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and forty-first canto.
The sage said:
Even while being consumed there, I did not become a partaker of suffering.
Even one who knows in a dream, "This is a dream," does not fall into the fire. || 1 ||
In this world filled with the flames of fire, the emergence of fierce wind is described here as a cloud of flames rich with scattered showers of glowing embers.
Though being scorched and pervaded by fire on all sides. || 1 ||
With all the circles of newly rising masses of flames, I wandered alone through the entire sky,
as beautiful as a whirling firebrand.
With circles of newly risen masses of flames, I whirled through the entire sky like a firebrand.
While I, possessing knowledge of reality, remained undaunted in mind and soul and investigated that forest fire,
the wind arrived.
His soul exhausted by wandering, his mind slightly fatigued. || 3 ||
Uttering a sigh of deep distress resembling the roar of clouds,
he was surrounded by the objects of the world, which were revolving and being swept away.

He describes that very wind with the verse beginning "sītkāra" and so forth: *sītkāra* refers to a particular sound resembling the hissing of fire; it is surrounded and pervaded by worldly objects such as stones, glowing embers, dust, and ashes being carried along. || 4 ||
In the forest, with the force of great *ghuṃghumā* sounds, the clouds were doubled;
it was like a mass of suns gathered in rotation, mingled with whirling firebrands.
By whom [the sky] was filled with fire-wheels (alātacakras) intermingled with the twelve suns—the twelve Ādityas—arranged in arrays, set in motion, revolving, and whirling about. || 5 ||
With masses of flames like clouds at twilight, hundreds of great rivers of fire,
and mountain-like fragments of land twice the size of mountains, it was a city of both Dānavas and gods.
By him were set in motion hundreds of great rivers of fire, characterized by flames and resembling masses of twilight clouds;
in that [conflagration], fragments of land twice the size of mountains, as well as the clods of earth and the cities of the Dānavas and the gods, were consumed.
The multitude of vessels, doubled by the spirits wandering within the belly of the sky,
were burning, unburnt, and half-burnt as they struck one another.
By him, the previously mentioned multitude of vessels consisting of hundreds of rivers was doubled by the spirits wandering within the cavities of the sky.
With fragments of fire-tongues doubled by the falling celestial women,
it was jagged with sprays from the mass of falling streams of glowing coals.

In which [cloud] the crests of fire are doubled as flames, and the twilight clouds are like drops of water; it stands as if its teeth were protruding, made jagged by the torrents of its water characterized by falling embers and by droplets characterized by sparks of fire. (8)
Shaking off circles of fierce, glowing embers like whirling firebrands and lightning,
he veiled the face of the withered upper direction with the darkness of smoke.

Shaking—that is, causing to tremble—those fiery whirling circles of his firebrands, which were like fierce circles of glowing coals from which the ashes had been cast away; and covering—that is, obscuring [the sky]. || 9 ||
From the earth, from the sky, and from all directions, clouds like the twilight of flames issued forth;
by them, the seven worlds, together with the sky and its inhabitants, came to stand as nothing more than a single mass of flaming mountains.

From the earth, as well as from the sky and from the quarters of the horizon, those clouds of twilight— characterized by flames and appearing in the manner described— emerged. By means of those clouds, the seven worlds (*saptalokī*)— together with the gods and others who dwell in the sky and on earth— became nothing more than a single mass of flaming mountains and remained so.
In one place, with his mass of hair blazing tawny like scattered sparks of fire from a leaping flame; in another, with walls shattered and pale as a heap of ashes, skilled in harsh shrieks;
and in yet another, wearing a mass of flames that falls all around him as he seizes it—thus does the Fierce One act.
Then that wind, like Hara, began his dance-playful movements.

Then Hara, who was like the fierce wind previously described, began to perform the playful dances of Kālāgnirudra. In what manner? In some upper region, his dwelling of hair was filled with tawny, blazing sparks of fire scattered by his upward leaps; and in some lower part, [sparks] were as if flown up by the striking of his feet.

[He is one] by whom walls [are made]; skillful (*paṭu*) in that harsh (*kaṭu*) and unbearable (*duḥsaha*) rattling; whose limbs (*aṅga*) are massed together (*saṃpiṇḍita*) and covered (*avaguṇṭhita*) with ashes; wearing—that is, putting on—the mass of flames (*jvālāpaṭālī*) that falls all around him somewhere in the middle part; such being his state—this is the meaning.
The qualifiers are to be applied to both cases. || 11 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-first canto, titled "The Description of the End of the Kalpa," in the *Ārṣa* [work], the glorious *Vāsiṣṭha*, composed by Vālmīki, in the *Deva-mānasa*, *Mokṣopāya*, *Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa*, *Uttarārdha*, *Aṣṭamabhāga*, *Vibhūti-sthiti*, and *Śata-sahasra-saṃhitā*. 141.
Thus ends the one hundred and forty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the End of the Kalpa," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
Chapter One Hundred Forty-Two.
The Sage said: While that painful and intense agitation was then occurring, the sage spoke.
Being carried along, I experienced extreme exhaustion. || 1 ||
In this context, the reality of the world of dreams and so forth is proclaimed to be Brahman;
and from the perspective of that reality, the absence of karma—the seed of the world—is established.
Kheda is dejection characterized by exhaustion and fatigue. || 1 ||
I thought: "This is a dream within the heart of another; therefore, I shall attain final nirvana. Why should I pointlessly behold this suffering? (2)
Then, out of weariness, I thought: "Why do I behold this suffering of a vain bad dream? Therefore, by abandoning this vision, I shall awaken; that is to say, I shall attain peace. || 2 ||
The hunter said:
"Was it merely a dream? Indeed, in order to quell my doubt, you entered his heart; what did you determine there? (3)

The hunter asks—"What indeed?"—inquiring what you determined after entering another's body to observe a dream of another in order to ascertain the true nature of a dream, and whether, upon seeing it, you desisted from that inquiry. What did you determine regarding that dream in accordance with reality? (3)
What is this that you have seen? Where in your heart is the great ocean?
Is the wind of the cosmic dissolution in your belly, and how is it that the fire of the cosmic dissolution is in your heart?
Have great oceans and other such things ever been seen within another's heart? (4)
Heaven, earth, wind, space, mountains, rivers, and the directions—tell me how that which is called the "world" exists as it truly is within the heart. (5)
The meaning is: "Please explain the reality of how the name 'Jagat' (the world) exists in the heart, exactly as it is, according to your own established conclusion. || 5 ||
The Sage said:
Because there is no cause for it, and because its non-arising at the very beginning of creation is evident,
the word "creation" and its referent do not exist even in the slightest degree as unknown entities.

Thus, having examined through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)—by means of observing one's own and others' dreams and so forth—that the world, consisting of words and their referents, is unreal across the three periods of time when viewed from the perspective of sublation (*bādhadṛśā*), its reality is precisely its non-existence. However, from the perspective of the remaining substrate (*pariśiṣṭādhiṣṭhāna*), which is Brahman, that very [non-existence] is the reality. With this intention, the Sage provides the answer beginning with "Because it is without cause" (*akāraṇatvāt*).

Because it lacks a cause, that is, because it is impossible for it to have a cause. To explain: a cause must be either immutable (*kūṭastha*) or subject to modification (*vikārin*). It cannot first be immutable; for since that which does not act cannot logically be an agent, it would be unfit to be connected with an effect.
Furthermore, its nature would be indeterminate as it excludes the state of being indifferent, and since no change in its intrinsic nature occurs, causality is impossible.

Furthermore, which part of that which is subject to transformation and composed of various undetermined parts could be the cause? For, in the case of a lump of clay undergoing transformations such as a jar, is the non-arising form of the lump the cause, or the arising form of the jar, or the form of the clay and so forth that persists through both? Not the first; for that which is incapable of even self-preservation and does not endure until the time of the effect cannot be the cause.

Furthermore, it is impossible for that [cause], which does not serve as a substratum for the operation toward the effect, to possess the status of being a cause. Nor is the second [alternative] tenable, because no other effect can be established. Nor is the third, because if it were of a non-productive nature (*akurva-d-rūpa*), it would be immutable (*kauṭasthya*); whereas if it were of a productive nature (*kurva-d-rūpa*), it would entail the consequence of an infinite number of jars, since that which is capable cannot be delayed.

Because it would follow that all effects would arise simultaneously, resulting in the absurdity that the lump, the jar, the shards, and the powder would all occur at once. If it is argued that this order is maintained by a fixed arrangement of connections with other auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*), we say no; for if that connection is itself an effect of the clay, it must be produced at that very same moment. If, on the other hand, it is an effect of something else, then the same consequence of simultaneous production of all its effects would apply to that as well.

Since at that time the relation itself would also have to be produced, and because this same fault would not be avoided even when it is conjoined with a third auxiliary cause— due to the lack of a determining factor (vinigamanā), there would follow either the simultaneous production of everything or the non-production of anything due to mutual obstruction. Therefore:

The meaning is that, since the position of there being no cause for creation and so forth remains as the only alternative, it has been determined as the truth that the word "creation" and its referent do not exist even in the slightest degree. || 6 ||
And both these—the word and its referent—are unknown within the Supreme Self;
for that state consists of both ignorance and knowledge, and is free from affliction.

How then are the meanings of the word "creation" (sarga) well-known in the world? To this he says: "And these two... These two meanings of the word "creation" are well-known only when known in their true nature as belonging to the Supreme Self; for these two are indeed that form of the Supreme Self which is unknown [in its true nature]. An objection is raised: "If they are unknown, then they must simply be unestablished, not well-known. To this he replies:

—Regarding the word "yataḥ" (since): this would indeed be so if the world were merely ignorance (*ajñāna*). But since that [world] is the locus of the Self (*ātmapada*) when unknown, it consists of both ignorance and knowledge due to its variegated nature (*śabala*). Therefore, by taking the aspect of ignorance, it is "unknown," and by taking the aspect of knowledge, it is "well-known"—this is the meaning. || 7 ||
Therefore, O fortunate one, since awakening has occurred within your own position according to this established doctrine,
there is the cessation of ignorance in that supreme, most purifying state which is without beginning or end.
If [the world] is well-established, then the very meanings of the words "creation" and so forth do not exist; how then can you speak of them? To this, he says: "Therefore," etc.

O fortunate one, when the truth of the world—beginning with dreams—is understood according to your own position (tvatpakṣe), and when ignorance (maurkhya) has been stilled, by abiding in the supreme, most purifying state of the ultimate doctrine (paramasiddhānta), this...

I state the proposition that the word "creation" (sarga) and its referent do not exist at all. The connection with what follows is as follows: "I do not perceive this existence of words and their referents within the consciousness of the deluded, because it is absolutely impossible. (8)
I speak this regarding the consciousness of the deluded: that which appears here, I do not know it as such;
this all-pervading expanse is mere awareness, appearing as both the real and the unreal.
Where is the body, where is the heart, where is the dream, and where are the waters and such?
Where is awakening, where is the cessation of awakening, and where are birth, death, and the like? (10)
But in the established doctrine (siddhānta), there is no such well-known entity as a body and so forth; thus he says: "Where? (kveti) || 10 ||
There exists here only pure consciousness, which is translucent;
in comparison to it, even the gross sky is like a mountain in the presence of atoms.
What, then, is it? He says: "It is transparent" (svaccham). || 11 ||
By its very nature, that sky of consciousness perceives something through thought;
though its body is space itself, it perceives that very space as the world.
Regarding what the vision of the world is like for the Lord and for those who know reality, he says: "By its own nature," etc. (Verse 12).
Just as in a dream it is consciousness alone that appears in the form of a city,
yet there is no city or such thing at all— so too this world is nothing but pure consciousness in the void.
This is peaceful, unmanifest, and non-dual; it does not exist within the self.
It appears to you in consciousness, in vision, in darkness, and in space, like a wheel or other such illusions.
Then, how does it appear from the perspective of the hunter? He says: "In consciousness" (citi).

The meaning is that when there is darkness—in the form of the eye of consciousness (cidrūpāyāṃ dṛśau), which is the disease of cataracts characterized by ignorance—it appears just as wheels and other such things appear in the sky. Thus, it appears in that manner.
But for us, there is neither non-manifestation, nor non-existence, nor existence, nor space;
it is the singular, formless, beginningless and endless sky of consciousness alone. 15.

But according to his own view, he says: "Of us. That which is unreal (*asat*) is the apparent (*prātibhāsika*); that which is real (*sat*) is the empirical (*vyāvahārika*); and the void (*kha*) is the absolute sky of consciousness (*cidvyoma*). The word "shines" (*bhāti*) carries over from the previous verse. || 15 ||
In a dream, the pure seer alone shines forth without a cause;
therefore, in this case, there is an absence of a cause, neither a seer nor a seeing exists.

By that reason—namely, that which appears as if causeless, being determined in the dream state to be the pure seer alone, devoid of the triad [of subject, object, and means of knowledge]—it follows that here in the waking state as well, the absence of a cause has been previously established; thus the meaning is that the triad beginning with the seer does not exist at all. || 16 ||
That something pure shines forth, clearly experienced by oneself, which is inexpressible, without beginning or end, one, and devoid of both duality and unity. (17)
Even though it is experienced by oneself, it is inexpressible, like the pleasure of a maiden; it is impossible to describe. || 17 ||
Just as a single time may be a kalpa, and light may possess a dual nature,
so too is Brahman, whose essence is everything, like a seed that culminates in fruit and flower.

Where has the existence of that which is devoid of duality and unity been seen as having the nature of both duality and unity? To this he says: "As one. Just as the cosmic cycle (*kalpa*)—which consists of both dissolution (*pralaya*) and manifestation (*prakāśa*) or creation (*sarga*)—is of a dual nature; or just as a seed itself remains present through its own being until it culminates in sprout, stalk, tree, branch, leaf, fruit, and flower, so too [is the Self].
The meaning is that Brahman is the self of all. || 18 ||
That which is a massive wall to one person is seen as pure space by another;
this is observed within the realms of stable dreams, mental constructs, and delusions. (19)

In that case, one might think that Brahman is like duality-and-unity (dvaita-ekya) itself, rather than being devoid of them; to this he says: "That which... (yad iti). The sense is: if it were, in the ultimate sense, like duality-and-unity, then it would appear so to everyone, but it is not perceived as such by all. || 19 ||
Then that single Self shines forth as pure, like the space of consciousness alone;
just as the waking state appears in a dream, so too does the dream appear in the waking state—it is not otherwise.
Just as the Self, being nothing but the void of pure consciousness, appears as if waking within a dream, so too does it appear within the dream that consists of the waking state;
yet not even an atom’s worth of difference appears between the waking state and the dream. Thus, even now, its non-duality remains exactly as it was—this is the meaning. || 20 ||
Just as an invisible fragrance resides within the invisible wind, so too does the non-obstructive universe reside within the non-obstructive pure consciousness alone. 21.
Now, one might object: "Since this world does not exist during dissolution or deep sleep, how can it be said that this [Self] is always of a single nature?

Anticipating this doubt, he says "in the invisible" with the intention that it cannot be determined that the world was non-existent at those times merely because it is not seen—just as, for example, even though the wind is invisible to the eye, such fragrance as belongs to it remains present.

Just as it is determined by the experience born of the sense of smell, so too the meaning is that the world—which is invisible even to a person experiencing deep sleep or cosmic dissolution—nevertheless exists from the perspective of another person. || 21 ||
When all mental constructions have been abandoned, you are that which you are— free from affliction,
the infinite Self both within and without, eternally and perfectly established.

By abandoning the mental conceit of "I," one realizes that in the vision [of reality], the world has never existed, does not exist, and will never exist; rather, the non-dual Self alone is eternally and perfectly stable. Thus he says: "All... (verse 22).
The hunter said:
"O Blessed One, for whom indeed does past karma exist here? For whom does it not exist? Tell me that; how could it be otherwise even without you? (23)

"In that case, since the mind thinks only according to past karma and not otherwise, it follows that karma alone is the seed for the bondage of saṃsāra. Therefore, for those in whom that [karma] has been destroyed without remainder, the abandonment of all mental activity is accomplished.
Thinking thus, the hunter asks—"O Blessed One, for whom does this exist, and for whom does it not?"—referring to those for whom...
They do not possess that karma; even without mental engagement, how could it arise for you upon its abandonment? 23.
The Sage said:

Those self-born beings, such as Brahmā and others, who shine by themselves during the creation and other cosmic phases, possess bodies consisting of mere cognition; for them, there is neither birth nor karma.

For those for whom the fourfold [aim] is established by the very principle that it is included within the fruit of the meditation that brings about their qualification, and who possess innate knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), action does not exist; thus the Sage gives the answer: "In the creation and so forth.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), Sanaka, Kapila, and others are included. The mention of "taking birth" is according to the analogy of a burnt cloth.
This is for the purpose of demonstrating the maintenance of the body. || 24 ||
For them there is no saṃsāra, no duality, and no conceptual constructions;
they possess bodies of pure knowledge and abide eternally as the self of all. (25)
Because they possess selfhood, all things have the Self as their essence. || 25 ||
At the beginning of creation, no prior karma exists for anyone here;
at the beginning of creation, Brahman alone thus expands itself in the form of the creation. (26)

Having raised the doubt as to how those who are empty of action can be the selves of those possessing action, he says—in the verse beginning with "sargādau"—that from his perspective, action belongs to no one at all. || 26 ||
Just as Brahmā and the other gods appear at the beginning of creation in the form of Brahman,
so too do other individual souls (jīvas) appear by the hundreds and thousands.
However, those born of the *sattva* quality perceive themselves as distinct from Brahman;
whereas those lacking true knowledge, having perceived this duality called "the insentient," consider it to be themselves. (28)

To whom, then, does karma belong? He says: "But those who," etc. Those who, being unawakened—meaning shrouded by ignorance—do not realize their own nature as Brahman, but instead perceive themselves as other than Brahman, thinking "I am not Brahman."

The connection with the subsequent clause is as follows: those living beings (*jīvas*) whose origin is from that which is *asāttvika*—meaning a transformation of *sattva* mixed with *rajas* and *tamas*, distinct from a transformation of pure *sattva* alone—perceive this duality called "insentient matter" (*acid*) as real; being permeated by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of that [belief], they die in the five elements (*pañcamṛta*), and their birth, accompanied by their *karmas*, is seen at a later time.
In a subsequent time, their birth is seen through those very actions;
having become such [beings] themselves, they have resorted to the state of being non-entities.
The meaning is that because they themselves, having become identified with insentient bodies and so forth, have forgotten the supreme reality and resorted to the state of being unreal. || 29 ||
But those by whom no difference from Brahman has been perceived within the Great Self that is consciousness—
these, namely Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Hara, and the others, are here beyond reproach.
But those by whom the Buddha has never been perceived are faultless, being devoid of the fault characterized by the bondage of karma. || 30 ||
The transparency of all-pervading consciousness is established solely within the Self that is Brahman;
it perceives itself as appearing in some places like a living soul (jīva). || 31 ||

The remainder is that transparency is its inherent nature (*svābhāvika*). For Brahman is established in itself, in its own essential nature (*svasvabhāva*), even when [associated] with some impure limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). || 31 ||
Wherever one perceives the state of being a living soul (jīvatva), there ignorance (avidyā) persists;
therein, the Self assumes a form established as such under the name of transmigratory existence (saṃsṛti). || 32 ||

He states [the following] in the verse beginning with "yatra" (wherein), showing that even ignorance exists only through the limitation of the adjuncts of the individual soul (jīva) and not in the pure [Self]. || 32 ||
For, having by itself in due time realized its own true nature,
it becomes by itself Brahman alone, established in its own essential form.

"By oneself alone," etc. The meaning is that this is based on such scriptural passages as: "In the beginning, this was indeed Brahman; it knew only itself, thinking 'I am Brahman'; therefore it became all that exists"; and "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman indeed. || 33 ||
Just as water, due to its fluidity, appears as if it were moving in whirlpools within itself,
so too this world-appearance appears as if it were creation because of the consciousness of Brahman.

He states that for one who does not know Brahman, the delusion regarding creation is indeed its very nature—beginning with the words "Just as" (yathā). The ellipsis to be supplied is: "creation is the nature of this [ignorant person]. || 34 ||
This creation consists of the manifestation of Brahman; it is neither dream nor waking.
Whose are the actions here, what are they like, or how many are they? (35)
The remainder [of the question] is: "What is his course of rebirth? || 35 ||
In reality, there is no action at all, nor is there ignorance, nor the notion of creation;
through self-awareness, everything proceeds as nothingness alone. (36)
It proceeds; it expands. || 36 ||
Brahman alone is the creation, the self of all beings, and the notion that it is "action" or "birth";
acting by itself, it appears as such, partaking in the imagined objects due to its omnipresence.
Because of its sovereignty, because of possessing all powers, and because of having true resolve. || 37 ||
At the beginning of creation, no action whatsoever exists for the individual soul;
later, having fashioned its own action through conceptualization, that consciousness experiences it.
Subsequently, after the conceptualization of remaining within ignorance, [the Lord], having fashioned and produced [the world] by means of bodies and so forth... || 38 ||
Tell me, what is the body of a whirlpool, and what are its actions?
Just as a whirlpool is nothing but water, so too the world is nothing but Brahman. (39)
But when the state of Brahman is perceived, there is not even the possibility of karma; thus he says: "Like water" (jalavat). || 39 ||
Just as for men who have seen things in dreams, there is no prior karma,
so it is for living beings in the primal creations, whose nature consists of pure consciousness alone.
In the primordial creations, within bodies that were pure and characterized by sattva. || 40 ||
When creation has become established as a process of creation, the conception of prior karma arises;
subsequently, these living beings wander, brought under the sway of the fetters of karma.
Why is it not there? He says: "In creation" (sarge). The meaning is that it is simply because they lack the established status of being a creation. || 41 ||
This so-called creation is not truly a creation; Brahman indeed abides thus.
Wherever it may be, what actions are there, or whose are they? (42)
That which is merely the lack of full knowledge of the Supreme Self indeed leads to bondage; for one who knows that [Self], it subsides. (43)

And thus, bondage is not caused by karma, but rather is caused solely by ignorance; therefore, let it be designated as that alone—the seed of karma—and nothing else. Thus he says: "It is merely non-comprehension. (43)
To the very extent that a wise person's thorough understanding proceeds, to that same extent his karmic bondage is immediately stilled. (44)
For this very reason, because karma is also of the nature of ignorance (avidyā), it diminishes in proportion as knowledge increases; thus he says: "As long as... (verse 44).
What trouble can there possibly be in the pacification of that which, as it were, does not exist at all?
Apart from the ultimate reality (paramārtha), no such thing as bondage exists whatsoever. (45)
Anticipating the objection, "How can a thing be destroyed by mere knowledge?", he states that action itself lacks the status of being a real entity:
"As long as one does not possess that wisdom by which one does not fall again into the wheel of saṃsāra, so long does māyā continue to cause fear of worldly existence."
Therefore, one should exert effort without ceasing toward wisdom, which is sublime through the stainless knowledge of the Self; otherwise, fear will never find peace for you.
Therefore, he concludes that effort must indeed be made for the sake of wisdom alone, because without it there is no peace from fear:

"tāvat" (so long). As long as wisdom does not exist, for that duration alone Māyā causes the fear of worldly existence (*bhava*). This is not an instance of the suffix *khaś* [as in *bhayaṅkara*], according to the rule *meghatribhayeṣu kṛñaḥ*; for the prohibition of the extension of a grammatical operation to a stem ending in a specific suffix applies here, since the nominal base (*prātipadika*) already includes the sense of the suffix.

That alone is true wisdom by which one does not fall again into the wheel of saṃsāra; the meaning is that the wisdom of dry logic and the like is of no use here. For this reason, one should make an effort in hearing [the scriptures] and so forth toward a state of scholarship that is vast with stainless knowledge without ceasing. Otherwise, your fear will not find peace through any other means. He—

The meaning is that this is according to such scriptural passages as: "That which is unknown does not nourish one; it creates a separation within the belly, and then fear arises for him," and so forth. || 46 ||
Thus ends the one hundred and forty-second chapter, titled "The Determination of Karma," in the *Vasiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa*, within the *Mumukṣuvyavahāra* section of the *Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa*.
Thus ends the one hundred and forty-second chapter, titled "The Determination of Karma," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The one hundred and forty-third canto. The sage said:
Of all dharmas, of all karmas, and of all sources of happiness—
The wise man is the ornament of the white lotuses, like the sun.
The praise of wisdom here consists in this vision of pure consciousness;
that "consciousness alone is the world" is further established through reasoning.

Only a scholar— who, by severing the knots of doubt, expands the intellect of listeners regarding the determination of all dharmas, the determination of worldly actions not contrary to dharma, and the determination of the relative gradations of the fruits of both (namely, happiness in this world and the next)— is the true ornament of an assembly, just as the white lotus is among lotuses.
The meaning is that, just as the sun is the ornament of the firmament when it shines forth, so too is he. || 1 ||
To that destination which those who know the self and are skilled in the ways of the world attain,
there, O Śakra, even royal splendor appears like a mere fragment of withered grass.
He says—starting with "By the knowledge of the Self"—that even all the happiness of the next world is far lighter than a mere spray from the ocean of self-knowledge attained by the wise. || 2 ||
Whether in the netherworld, on the surface of the earth, or in heaven, I do not see any happiness or sovereignty whatsoever that surpasses wisdom. (3)

The meaning is that [he attains it] from wisdom and from the bliss which is the fruit of wisdom, according to the Vedic revelation: "Other beings subsist on a mere fraction of this very bliss. || 3 ||
The wise person’s vision of things as they truly are becomes serene, like the sight of the moon with its entire, stainless orb in a cloudless sky. (4)

The vision of the wise person—one who possesses knowledge born from the investigation of authentic scriptures—finds clarity and rejoices within its own self, just as the eye finds delight in the stainless orb of the full autumn moon. (4)
This visible world, whose nature is ignorance, becomes Brahman in an instant;
through the awakening of the wise man, it subsides like the appearance of a snake in a garland.

For the wise and enlightened one, the entire collection of perceived phenomena, such as the creation of the body, which is like a serpent imagined upon a flower garland, subsides through awakening. || 5 ||
That Brahman which is established in Brahman has its reality established by that very fact;
notions such as the creation, destruction, and so forth of the body are of the nature of its own inherent essence alone.
In that case, one might ask: does the cessation of the creation of the body and so forth arise as something other than the nature of Brahman? He says "no"—"yad" (that which).

By means of the knowledge of its own true essence, that which abides in Brahman within its own nature—precisely for that [Brahman], designations such as the creation and dissolution of the body have been made by that very [knowledge] as being of one essence with that nature. The meaning is that this is the truth, the ultimate reality. || 6 ||
This creation indeed exists where nothing at all [of duality] is found;
its properties, its actions, and even the sequence of syllables do not exist there.
If it is asked, "Why is this so? [the author] replies: because the remaining Brahman is devoid of the activity of attributes known as the destruction of the visible world.
"If earth and the rest were to come into being, let them have a cause;
but where that [world] does not exist at all, what could be its cause? (8)
He states that because the visible world is non-existent throughout the three periods of time, its status as having a cause is refuted: "Earth and so forth... (verse 8).
That which has manifested from Brahmā is called this world;
by that very [manifestation], how could these things such as earth and so forth exist, and where would there be a cause? (9)
