"Pratibhāna" means manifestation. The point is that a pot which is merely a manifestation does not require causes such as a staff or a wheel. || 9 ||
Just as for a dreamer, the objects seen by men are merely imaginary and not real, so too for men in the waking state, there is no prior desire that is real. (10)

The meaning is that just as there is no real, but only a conceptual, cause such as a father or other [relative]—referred to as "prior desire" (pūrvakāma) because one desires what was previously experienced—so it is likewise in the dream-state which has the form of waking. || 10 ||
Just as prior karma and masculinity do not exist for men in a dream, so too they do not exist for men here in the waking state, even though these things appear to them.
He states that action, like the father and so forth, is likewise unreal, saying "yathā" (just as): [in the state of] *puṃstva*, that is, in the condition of being a male person and so on. || 11 ||
In all creations, the individual soul perceives all dream-objects mutually as unreal,
according to its prior karma and its latent impressions.

The ellipsis "they look at one another" is to be supplied. And in these creations, within the false worldly transaction that occurs according to one's latent impressions (*vāsanā*), even the existence of prior karma is itself false according to those impressions; such is the meaning. || 12 ||
At the beginning of creation and at the end of the body, living beings appear to one another like the objects of a dream;
according to their respective perceptions, they are both existent and non-existent.

Living beings, the creation, and the creation of the elements and worlds—from that beginning until the attainment of the body—appear within the cycle of existence (saṃsāra) exactly according to their own respective perceptions, without overstepping the limits of individual experience, like the objects of a dream. Therefore, the meaning is that these things exist and are present in the aspect of perception, like dream-objects, but they do not exist in their other aspect. || 13 ||
Therefore, for one who meditates, all things appear according to their perception;
they exist within the self, just as in a dream, mutually providing objects as if in the waking state.
Since things appear in accordance with how they are meditated upon, they exist even in a dream; they are mutually capable of providing objects and are thus endowed with causal efficiency.

Because it rests upon an object situated at the forefront of the consciousness of volition, the fruit obtained by you in a dream is indistinct; for it is indistinct due to its lack of foundation in the external world.

Just as in your dream, even without an external object, the very consciousness of the intention to eat results in the fruit of satisfaction through the sequence of the consciousness of cooking and so forth—because it is of such a nature that it culminates in the actual substance of the food being swallowed before one—so too is the consciousness of intention in the waking state. Dream is indistinct; [waking is] distinct.
The meaning is that the only distinction is this much: [the state of] being awake. || 15 ||
Pure consciousness, abiding in its own nature, shines forth by itself as luminous;
it is to this very shining of that [consciousness] that the designations "waking" and "dreaming" are applied. (16)
Whatever manifests by itself, whether clearly or indistinctly, for each such manifestation the names "waking" and "dreaming" have been assigned in the world. (16)
Just as that cognition which appeared at the beginning of creation or at the end of the body remains exactly so until liberation, this is what is called "creation. (17)
The meaning is that until liberation—that is, up to the limit of liberation—it remains exactly as it is in the form of a continuous flow. || 17 ||

There is no difference between the collection of objects in the waking and dreaming states and consciousness itself, which is of an unobstructed nature, just as there is none between light and its illumination. (18)
The meaning is that there is no difference between those objects well-known in the states of waking and dreaming and the consciousness of them, which is of an indistinct nature. || 18 ||
Just as between fire and its heat, or wind and its motion, or water and its fluidity, or even between coolness and the breeze that brings it; || 19 ||
Or it is like two masses of liquid water that remain without interpenetrating one another, even though they occupy the same space down to the very bottom of the Avīci hell.
The entire world, born as something insubstantial, is entirely non-obstructive and peaceful;
thus, it exists only as being (sanmaya), and is not endowed with any objective reality (artha). || 20 ||

Because it is of the nature of non-obstructive, formless consciousness, it is incapable of resistance; yet, insofar as its essential nature is that of the foundational consciousness (*adhiṣṭhāna-cit*), it exists as pure being alone. It does not exist in the sense of a negation—either by the negative particle (*nañ*) used in the sense of "not" according to the Śruti texts such as "not this, not this" (*neti neti*), or by way of being a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*).
And it is conjoined. || 20 ||

Having emerged from Brahman and having passed away, that which consists of the experience of the visible world is, in truth, nothing but pure consciousness—indestructible, peaceful, one, and stainless. || 21 ||
Brahman, having arisen as the self of the world and having "died" through its nature as dissolution,
appears in the empirical usage of universal identity as both the form of the experience of the visible and the form of the non-experience of it; yet in the ultimate sense,
it remains as one alone, immovable.
Just as the causal relationship of objects is conceived within the heart by Brahmā, even as it was by Puruṣa, so too is it within the city.

The discourse regarding the causality of objects such as earthen walls within a city—which is imagined by Brahman in the same way as [the causality] of space, wind, and so forth with respect to a person—remains exactly so. The meaning is that this scripture is not intended to subvert the principle of necessity (niyati), but rather to subvert the notion of their reality, duality, and so on. || 22 ||
This creation exists within the heart of Brahmā, just as a dream-city exists within your own heart;
therein, the relationship between cause and effect remains exactly as it has been described.
He says "of Brahman" to show that when its reality is sublated, it culminates in pure consciousness alone, just like the necessity of objects in a dream:
"Just as the dream [reality] has been described, so too [is this]. (23)
Within the interior of the density of consciousness, the relationship of cause and effect exists;
it stands exactly as it has been projected by you or by him, like a city of imagination.
Just as she was meditated upon and envisioned at the beginning of creation. || 24 ||
In this creation, which is a city of volition,
that entire order consisting of cause and effect has been established by you alone through your own nature of volition.

Having taken for granted that you too have firmly established a system in the city of your own volition, consisting of causes and effects according to your will, he says: "The Intellect" (citi). || 25 ||
That which is the manifestation within the mind, whose very nature is one's own self, is indeed space;
because it is a fixed arrangement, that which is within it is called creation. (26)

It is established by one's own experience that both the city of imagination and the order existing within it are nothing but the manifestation of the space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*). Furthermore, this currently perceived creation is also said in the Śruti and Purāṇas to be included within the "creation of imagination" (*saṃkalpasarga*), because it is born from the imagination of Hiraṇyagarbha.
The meaning is that he is outside of that. || 26 ||
Those states of consciousness that exist within the city of mental constructs in the heart—
this very thing is the self-established nature, consisting of the categories of cause and effect.

That state of consciousness belonging to the sun of pure awareness (cidāditya), characterized by self-luminosity, which always resides within the city of the mental constructs (saṃkalpa) in the heart—this very state is the inherent, naturally established nature of the entire collection of causes and effects; the meaning is that it does not differ from that even by a minute atom. || 27 ||
In the beginning, whatever appears exactly as it is, that very thing exists here as consciousness;
it is to that alone that the designations "necessity," "time," "space," and so forth, have been applied. (28)

He establishes that very point with the words "Firstly": according to such scriptural passages as, "He uttered 'Bhūḥ' and created the earth," at the commencement of creation within the heart-consciousness of Hiraṇyagarbha, that consciousness which shines forth and manifests itself in the form of the earth and so on, through modes such as smell and solidity, exists even now in exactly that same way. Of that very [consciousness], in that manner...

The meaning is that for that which exists in the form of the earth with the fixed nature of smell and solidity, water with the fixed nature of fluidity, fire with the fixed nature of heat and light, air with the fixed nature of motion and subtlety, and so forth— and which exists in the form of past, future, and other times, as well as in the form of directions such as east and west— names have been assigned accordingly. || 28 ||
Just as the emptiness of the space of consciousness appears instantly according to its name,
so too does it exist as a reality based upon the relationship of cause and effect.

He says, "That which is called... in order to show that this should be understood in the same way for all cases, such as cows, jars, and so forth: just as a cow is the cause of milk, and a jar is the cause of its containment. (29)
In this mere flash of consciousness, which appears as creation yet consists of pure being,
first the entities come forth, and afterwards the wise apply the designation "creation."

For according to the Vedic scripture, "Whatever one conceives with the mind, that one speaks with speech," the conceptualization of form occurs first in the mind, and subsequently the conceptualization of name; thus he says, "the wonder of consciousness. Mental state (*bhāva*), creative contemplation (*bhāvanā*), and volition (*saṃkalpa*)—these, being its very form, exist as the voidness that takes the form of the three worlds, abiding thus within the sky of consciousness.
They are non-different from the gentle wind, just as their own vibrations are inseparable from it. || 31 ||
He demonstrates by means of an illustration that whatever conceptualization exists there, even though it is empty, is of the nature of that [emptiness] alone—namely, "emptiness.

Just as the existence of the movement of the wind is devoid of any essential nature distinct from it and is non-different from it, so too, within the space of consciousness (*cidvyoman*), the emptinesses that take the form of the three worlds are likewise [non-different]. This is the meaning. || 31 ||
Just as the lack of density due to its emptiness exists in the sky as "blue," so too does the density of consciousness manifest as creation within the Intellect.

And thus, he says—beginning with "In the sky"—that for those of deluded vision, the very density of consciousness flashes forth as the world. Regarding the phrase "the density of its own voidness": the meaning is that in a sky pervaded by smoke, dust, and so forth, one does not perceive the blueness [of the sky]. || 32 ||
When this [universe] has already appeared as manifest, the state of being a creation is realized only with great difficulty,
just as one realizes again the true nature of the rope in what was perceived as a snake in the rope.

When, however, is the state of emission (visargatā) realized within Brahman? To this he says: "When the creation has appeared" (ābhāte)—that is, when the creation has appeared, meaning when it has manifested as the very nature of pure consciousness devoid of the threefold limitation. "With difficulty" (kṛcchrāt) means through the hardship of practicing the spiritual means. || 33 ||
Having died, he perceives the entire world as distinct, like a dream;
that [world] is one thing and this [reality] is another, while the sky remains eternally unobstructed.
He says that the creation of the world beyond (pāralaukika) is just like this worldly creation (aihalaukika): "When dead... and so forth.

That [world beyond], which is other than this and subsequent to it, and this [world here], which is other than that and pertaining to this life—all of it is nothing but the unobstructed, formless sky of consciousness (cidambara). || 34 ||
The hunter said:
"How is it that this body comes into being for the sake of pleasure and pain from another source? What is its cause, and what are its auxiliary causes? (35)
After the fall of this body, how is another body produced? "Cause" refers to the material cause (upādāna); "causes" (hetavaḥ) refers to the instrumental conditions (nimittas).
If they produce dharmas and adharma by means of that [body] which consists of resistance, then it is illogical to say that they produce its non-resistant form. (36)

Regarding those who believe that all phenomena (dharmas) and non-phenomena (adharmas) perform everything solely for the sake of one's own enjoyment, there follows the undesirable consequence of no liberation, because they do not perceive the cessation [of suffering] through the knowledge of what is produced by karma. Thus he says: "they perform. For one who exists in the form of a body and so forth as something characterized by resistance (pratigha), actions [cannot produce] that non-resistant, eternal form which is called liberation.
The claim that they "act" is inconsistent; the intended meaning is that what is produced cannot avoid impermanence. || 36 ||

The Sage said: "Dharma and adharma, latent impressions (vāsanā), the agent of action (karmātmā), and the individual soul (jīva)—this burden of synonymous terms is merely conceptualized here; it is not real. (37)
Dharma and adharma are said to be the performance of prescribed and prohibited acts existing in the form of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*).
The mind, which consists of a collection of such impressions, when pervaded by the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*), is the individual soul (*jīva*).

Because it is characterized primarily by the activities of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth, it is the "agent of action" (*karmātmā*); that very soul, according to its own latent tendencies (*vāsanā*), [assumes] bodies and the like.

Thinking "that self becomes as if [identical with those objects]," all these various manifestations are indeed of consciousness alone; therefore, let them be imagined there at will according to one's desire, for in their ultimate result there is no difference. With this intention, the Sage first gives the answer to the second question, beginning with the words "Dharma and Adharma," etc. "The burden of sound" means a mass of sounds.
The meaning is that there is no real distinction between objects. || 37 ||

Because it is of the nature of consciousness, through its own imagined state of mind, these names have been created within the self—which is like the sky of consciousness—by means of the thought that "someone exists. (38)

Someone, by means of the mind—which is imagined as the nature of consciousness (*cittva*) and consists of the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*)—conceives that this manifold expansion of the visible body and so forth exists; and within the Self, which is the sky of consciousness (*cinnabhas*) and whose own nature is space itself, he has himself fashioned these names such as merit and demerit, as well as their fruits, pleasure and pain. "The Wise One, having envisioned all forms, [gave] names... (Rig Veda 10.82.2).

The intention is that [the disciple] remains after having performed [the prostration] and offered salutation, according to such scriptural passages as "having done so, he remains," and so forth. || 38 ||
The self, whose nature is consciousness, by virtue of its own cognitive power, perceives the body within itself as if it were space within space—
just as one perceives a real entity after death, or as in the case of volitional imagination and dreams.
He resolves the first question: "The Self is consciousness. (39)
To one who has died, the perception of the next world appears like a dream;
he beholds it for a long time, yet even there, there is no reality.
He states that even the conceptualization of a body and so forth after death is just like a dream—“by oneself” (svayam). || 40 ||
If another were to fashion a dead body, how could there be memory for it?
Or how could it be that very same person? Consciousness would be like the empty sky.
He dispels the delusion that a father or some other lord creates the dead once again—by the word "the dead.

If another were to create [it], how could that [other] be the very same person? For it is heard in scripture that the creator himself enters [it]: "Having created that, he entered into that very thing"; and because that [creation] is his own self. If one accepts this as the desired conclusion, then for him...
Otherwise, how could there be the memory conducive to activities such as suckling at the breast?
The meaning is that even that established consciousness which is firmly rooted in the very self previously proven would be as empty as space. || 41 ||
Therefore, upon death one is not born again; rather, by the mind alone, he perceives here in this manner that which consists of latent impressions (vāsanā) within the void.
Repeating the answer given to the first question, he concludes: "At death... [and so on]. He is not born, that is, he does not undergo birth;

rather, it is only by means of the mind that he falsely perceives through imagination, thinking "I am thus born here," within the Self which is like the sky and devoid of transformations such as birth. || 42 ||
Having long practiced his own very nature, he remains experiencing it; possessing a clear conviction therein, he understands it fully as "this is indeed the truth. (43)

He says—“It is its own [nature]”—to show that the worldly and Vedic conventions regarding birth and so forth arise from the manifestation of that very entity as a clear cognition, and not from an objective reality. || 43 ||
The Self, being space itself, perceives the visible world as a dream within that very space;
it then experiences its own death, followed by rebirth and the world once more.
While bringing [the materials] and placing [them upon the fire]. || 44 ||
Seeing this very net of falsehood in the sky, each one remains established therein;
they see, they practice, and they consume, yet nothing belongs to anyone.

Abiding in the state of individuality, it perceives its own superimposed effects and causes through its mere presence and impels them toward objects; it consumes [them] during the waking and dreaming states, and [it "consumes"] during deep sleep, dissolution, and liberation. But in the ultimate sense, nothing is to be consumed by anyone, nor is there anything that consumes.
The meaning is that someone eats. || 45 ||
Thus, there exist millions upon millions of worlds;
yet they are known by Brahmā alone, while to others they appear otherwise as mere objects of perception.
Otherwise, if it remains uncomprehended, it is merely an object of perception; the sense is that according to the Śruti, "As long as he is unknown, it does not benefit him. || 46 ||
Nothing whatsoever is obscured by them, nor do they exist [as external objects];
yet each one among them perceives this very world as being solely its own. (47)
By those millions upon millions of worlds—does this Self among them perceive each individual living being as "this very world" and nothing else? || 47 ||
The elements abide in each of those [powers] and likewise in one another;
they are truly real when viewed through the perspective of unreality, yet through the perspective of reality, they are the unborn state.

The meaning is that for those millions of worlds, the five elements beginning with earth and the fourfold classes of living beings—each residing within their respective worlds conceived as being inhabited by individual souls—are likewise not dissimilar. And these are real from the perspective of conventional truth (*vyavahāra-dṛṣṭi*), which is unreal; however, from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-dṛṣṭi*), which is real, they are unborn.
The meaning is that it is indeed the state of Brahman. || 48 ||
That which is non-existent for the ignorant is inexhaustible for one who has known what is to be known;
that which is non-existent for the fully awakened is clearly existent for the ignorant. (49)
For this very reason, he states that for the knower and the ignorant, truth and untruth are mutually opposed, saying: "That which is real... (verse 49).
Whatever appears to the consciousness in whatever manner, that is real in that way;
for this reason, all these beings are mutually of the nature of reality. (50)

Alternatively, because it is of the nature of manifestation within the consciousness of ultimate reality (paramārthasatya), everything is indeed true; thus, he says "of consciousness" (citeḥ) to indicate that there is no contradiction whatsoever. || 50 ||
Therefore, those various [objects] are eternally true to one another, precisely because their form—which is indeed to be determined by consciousness—is non-obstructive. 51.

Alternatively, he states that truth is established as follows: "that which appears as the world to someone at a certain time is true for that person at that time"—this is expressed by the word "eternal" (*nityam*). Since the determination of whether the form of the world is real or unreal must be made solely by means of true consciousness (*satya-saṃvid*), if that blessed Consciousness determines it to be truly real, who else could possibly establish the opposite?
The sense is that one should accomplish it; "unobstructed" (apratigha) means incapable of being resisted by anyone. || 51 ||

Since the distinction between "otherness" and "non-otherness" is to be determined solely by consciousness, where can there be any talk of duality or unity when the multitude of objects appears exactly as they are perceived? 52.

"How can there be otherness and non-otherness, or non-suchness and suchness, between those two? This principle should be applied to the distinction and non-distinction of entities, to duality and unity, and so forth," he says: "according to how they are perceived. (52)
"This is that very thing" arises from cognition; "this becomes that very thing" is sufficient [for its establishment].
Yet, "this is that very thing, this is that very thing" would occur only because of the unreality of cognition. (53)

"Let it be so; what follows from that? To this he says: "That very [knowledge] itself. Because of the realization of the non-difference between knowledge and the object of knowledge—that this which is to be known is indeed that knowledge—this entire collection of the visible becomes that very knowledge. The sense is that by that much alone, through the swallowing up of all objects of perception, the non-duality of consciousness (*cidadvaita*) is established. But [one might object]: "In this way, by the denial of knowledge..."
To the question, "Why could it not be that only the object of knowledge remains? he replies: "That very thing is this. That knowledge is indeed this object of knowledge.
Thus, the claim that only the visible (the object) remains would be possible—that is, conceivable—only if consciousness were unreal.
The implication is that if that were the case, there would be no establishment of the object of knowledge at all, as it would be devoid of consciousness. || 53 ||
If that object is identical to its cognition, then it does not exist apart from that cognition;
but if the object exists as something distinct from the nature of cognition, then it would follow that this [cognition] is devoid of cognition [of that object]. (54)
Therefore, by process of elimination, if this entire manifold (prapañca) is indeed the object [of cognition], it does not exist apart from that consciousness (jñapti).

Thus, when every object is established as being of the nature of consciousness, this seer (draṣṭā)—through non-cognition, that is, through ignorance (ajñāna) of that—might depart from, or fall away from, the essential nature of consciousness; yet the meaning is that this does not occur in reality. || 54 ||
That which is knowledge is itself the object of knowledge, for it is not separate from the object of knowledge due to the non-existence of anything apart from it;
thus, as knowledge, it expands itself by means of itself.

And thus, it follows that ignorance itself expands the state of the knowable world within the Self by means of the Self; this is the established conclusion, which he expresses with the words "Knowledge" (jñānam). || 55 ||
Even though they see and even though they meet, those of separate creation are nothing at all;
for the wise man who knows the unreal as being only real, I do not know them as objects of knowledge for the ignorant.
And thus, for the wise knower of reality who perceives the creations as existing only as the nature of cognition while being non-existent separately,

it is the truth that the creations of the eyes and other senses— which they see and grasp— and even the creations of form and so forth which meet with them, are nothing apart from cognition. However, I do not know the creations known by the ignorant.

From the perspective of awakening, all are but the void of the Self consisting of pure consciousness; yet through manifold perceptions, that very same [consciousness] appears as a thousand entities composed of both the conscious and the insentient.
Of ignorant living beings whose nature is subject to rebirth. || 57 ||
In the same way, that which is a single pure consciousness exists as a hundred thousand-fold self within a dream;
then, from that dream, it remains as a single hundred-thousand-fold self in deep sleep.

He states that it is well known that the single conscious self (cidātman) possesses the nature of hundreds of millions of selves in a dream, while possessing the nature of a single self in deep sleep: "One" (ekam), etc. (verse 58).
That which is the perception of a dream within the sky of consciousness is called the world;
deep sleep is declared to be the cosmic dissolution (pralaya); therefore, this very principle is the correct one.

The principle stated regarding dream and deep sleep applies equally to creation and dissolution as well, because there is no difference between them; thus he says: "In the sky of consciousness," etc. (59).
Consciousness alone undergoes the states of manifoldness and human-hood,
as well as emptiness and objective reality, just as in dreams and mental constructs.
There is diversity in the form of the objects of enjoyment, and the state of being human in the form of the enjoyer. || 60 ||
All this, they say, is non-obstructive and consists of nothing but cognition;
it is pure, and in whatever manner it appears in a given place, it becomes exactly so.
At the beginning of creation, there is only one consciousness;
it becomes fire, water, ether, earth, and so forth for the purpose of creation, just as in dreams and mental constructs. (62)

For the sake of creation, for the purpose of accomplishing creation, the earth and so forth first come into being. The use of the particle *vat* is for the purpose of indicating its unchanging nature:
that which is called "earth" and so on shines as nothing other than the very form of the space of consciousness (*saṃvidākāśa*).
That which is indeed this void (*kha*) alone appears as this world. (63)
He states that very point clearly: "Consciousness," etc. (verse 63).
Consciousness appears as having resistance, and likewise it appears as being without resistance;
yet in reality there is no resistance, for consciousness ceases at the end.

That which possesses resistance appears as perishable and material, while that which lacks resistance appears as eternal and immaterial; yet in reality, there is neither resistance nor destruction. For when that resistance is brought to an end, it ceases, and once ceased, pure consciousness alone remains. 64. You go to the eastern and western directions, knowing them for a long time as one who knows.
For you there is no such thing as resistance, nor are you ever possessed of resistance anywhere. (65)

This very absence of resistance (*apratighatva*) establishes the nature of consciousness (*saṃvit*); thus it says, "You go... You travel for a long time with the mind to the eastern and western directions, and there, knowing the objects that have been seen, heard, inferred, and so forth, you yourself know them.
In that regard, for you whose nature is consciousness, there is simply no such thing as resistance; therefore, consciousness is never obstructed anywhere.
The meaning is "it is accomplished. || 65 ||
He who practices for a long time whatever object he has seen or conceived will certainly attain it, provided he does not turn back out of weariness.

If it is argued that the futility of many volitions of the living consciousness is observed, and that very futility constitutes its resistance—meaning it possesses the quality of being "with resistance" (sapratighatva)—to this he replies: "It is seen. That person who practices for a long time, continuously, and with persistence toward an object intended by the will that is established by valid means of knowledge, necessarily attains it.

And thus, the futility [of an action] arises precisely from the lack of firmness in the resolve; for the mere fact that what is not firm is incapable of producing its effect does not imply that consciousness possesses resistance (sapratighatva), as that consequence would otherwise apply everywhere—this is the intended meaning. || 66 ||
Whether one goes to the eastern or western direction, knowing it for a long time,
he who sits there and moves about abandons that very state and not the other.

Alternatively, an unstable resolve performs only an unstable journey to distant quarters, such as seeing the objects located there, which is merely a product of imagination (*mānorathika*). But when it is firm, it is indeed firm; thus, with the intention that even for the latter there is no futility, he says: "You go"—you go with your mind to the eastern and western directions.

In that state, he who remains as the one who wills, having known those various objects for a long time, goes—according to his own volition—to the nature of those very things, such as the travel to the ends of the directions and the objects located there, which he himself has willed. For another person, however, having abandoned that volition, does not go to another direction even with the mind. It is by this very distinction [that they differ].
In that context, the meaning is that consciousness is unimpeded. || 67 ||
For one whose consciousness is unwavering in the thought "May I become the object seen and conceived," both [subject and object] arise;
for another whose consciousness is unwavering, both perish.
From the resolve of one whose consciousness is unwavering, such as Aindava and others, "May I become the object intended," a twofold manifestation first arises:
it is *prātibhāsika* (illusory) when the resolve is weak, and *vyāvahārika* (empirical) when the resolve is firm; this meaning has been observed.
This applies even to another person who does not form the resolve, or to one whose consciousness is unwavering regarding their own self or other objects.
The meaning is that even those two perish and are no longer perceived. || 68 ||
For one whose consciousness is unshakable, there is the thought, "I am going from the south to the north";
for another whose consciousness is unshakable, both [the subject and object] arise and both perish. (69)

Thus, for one whose consciousness is unshakable, when thinking "I am going from the southern region to the north or another direction," there arises a duality consisting of both the mental and the physical; and the two movements toward the east and west likewise perish.

For one whose consciousness is unwavering in the thought, "May I be a city in the sky" or "May I be a deer on the earth," both [the city and the deer] would come to be, while the other two perish; such is this world.

From the perspective of awakening, everything is but pure consciousness, which is essentially the void of the Self; yet, through manifold perceptions, that very same [consciousness] appears as a thousand entities consisting of both the conscious and the insentient.

The meaning is that through the awakening to reality (*tattvaprabodha*), everything is indeed one, being pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) alone; yet through the lack of such awakening, that very same [consciousness] becomes a thousand individual souls (*jīva*) consisting of both conscious and insentient natures, due to manifold perceptions. || 71 ||
Whether the body be non-obstructive or indeed obstructive, this cycle of existence for the living being consists of the nature of a dream, both here and in the hereafter. (72)

Now, if consciousness itself exists in the form of the body and so forth, then because that [body] possesses resistance (*sapratighatva*), it would follow that consciousness also possesses resistance.
To this, he says: "The body. Let the body be non-resistant in its nature as consciousness, or let it be resistant in its other form; there is no fault whatsoever in this.
The meaning is: because of being presided over by and corrupted by the qualities and defects pertaining to false objects. || 72 ||
This is directly perceived through the sight of those who have died in lands such as those of the Mlecchas, and through their recounting [the event] with full recollection. (73)

If it is asked how it is known that the soul is not destroyed along with the destruction of the body, he says: "This [is known] from perception and from scripture. In regions such as those of the Mlecchas, when those who have died arrive here in the form of Piśāca bodies, they are perceived directly by those who are experts in the science of spirits (bhūtavidyā).

Furthermore, because they describe their own domestic affairs and activities from before the time of [the soul's] departure with full recollection, the existence of the living consciousness is directly experienced. || 73 ||
Those who have died and been reduced to ashes in the lands of the Mlecchas return once more;
having explained the matter, they depart, being of an unimpeded nature.
If this were the law for one who is alive, then why would it not apply when a person has gone to another land, even though one perceives that person as being dead? (75)

He refutes the Cārvāka hypothesis— that this delusion of seeing and conversing with a *piśāca* belongs only to a living person such as a physician of spirits, and not to the arrival or conversation of one who is dead— by the word "this" (*eṣa*). In reality, even when the object is non-existent, such worldly activity as seeing and conversing occurs through the error of perceiving what is dead as being alive.
Why does it not proceed? || 75 ||
If that [nature] is indeed the property of the living, why is it not also the property of the dead?
For such is the experience when these two identical logical positions are established. (76)
Furthermore, if that [speech] is an illusion belonging to the nature of the living, then why is conversation with the dead not also real?
For those who rely on experience for the establishment of truth, whatever kind of experience occurs when someone is alive is exactly the same when they are dead.
Thus, since both lines of reasoning are equal, what is the distinction? This is the meaning. || 76 ||
The appearance of the world is like a dream; thus, when this [view] is established as true and unimpaired, it stands in agreement with the noble experience and the scriptures. (77)

Thus, since experience establishes the existence of an object, the capacity to establish an object remains equal for both waking and dream experiences so long as no sublation occurs; and through awakening, there remains only the experience itself. Therefore, that which was proposed—that the appearance of the world is just like a dream—is now seen to be unrefuted and firmly established. And by this—

There is a state of mutual agreement and a focus on a single meaning between this [text] and the experiences of the wise, as well as such scriptural passages as "He has three abodes and three states of sleep," "Modification is a mere verbal handle, a name; there is not the slightest diversity here," and so forth. This is what is meant by the term "upapannā" (established/consistent). || 77 ||
Just as the net of vision for the multitudes of people beholding the moon’s palace is unimpeded,
so too is the world, consisting of both the existent and the non-existent.
The meaning is that just as the network of eyes of the multitudes of people beholding the orb of the moon in the palace of Indra is non-obstructive—
devoid of mutual resistance and consisting of both being and non-being, such that it is "being" for some and "non-being" for others— the world itself is likewise non-obstructive. || 78 ||
It conforms solely to pure existence, consisting of nothing but clear experience;
it is pure consciousness, whose nature is mere manifestation, being the self of all objects yet devoid of any object.

Everything that is apprehended as an object is apprehended by consciousness as mere measures (mātrās)—that is, as distinct portions of pure Being itself. And the subject is nothing but pure, transparent experience. Furthermore, pure Being does not establish itself merely by appearing; therefore, it is indeed existent. And that very [Being], although devoid of objects, consists of all objects.
"It vibrates" means that everything is non-obstructive and quiescent. || 79 ||
The entire world is non-resistant and peaceful within the single sky of consciousness;
let it rest by itself, within itself, unmoving and without appearance. 80.
He teaches the means to realize the meaning already stated: "unwavering" (aniṅgana). || 80 ||
To whatever extent one makes consciousness itself steady and immovable, to that same extent it quickly becomes so—whether it be unreal or even real. (81)

"In whatever manner one remains having made the mind steady, in that very manner it quickly becomes so"—this is the connection with what follows. [One should consider either that the word "pareṇa" (by the following) is redundant, or that a half-verse has been omitted from the preceding section. || 81 ||
Now, regarding bodies, actions, sufferings, and pleasures—whatever they may be as they exist, whether they persist or pass away—whose is the grasping for them, and what is there to grasp? (82)
Of what is there grasping, and what is its object? It is appropriation. (82)
"Let it be thus, or let it be otherwise; let it not be, or let it come to pass—what concern is there in this?
O Phalguna, abandon the fruit that brings further fruit; you have understood, so enough with these wanderings. (83)
Abandon that effort which brings fruit, which necessarily yields its result.

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-third canto, titled "The Instruction on the Awakening of Nirvāṇa," in the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa*, the Great Epic of Vasiṣṭha, belonging to the *Ārṣa* (sage-authored) tradition.

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-third canto, titled "The Instruction on the Awakening of Nirvāṇa," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa within the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and forty-fourth canto. The Sage said:
"In all states of being and non-being, which consist of the nature of dream-experience,"
Among forms that are eternal and non-obstructive, what is bound and what is liberated? || 1 ||
Just as the world appears as consciousness alone, and consciousness itself appears as the world,
so too is Brahman, endowed with all powers, established through logical arguments in this regard.
He states that if the visible world is nothing but pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), even the contemplation of bondage and liberation disappears, with the words "in every way" (*sarvathā*). || 1 ||
Just as there is a shimmering of visual appearances in the sky, so too is the world;
though it is incessantly changing, due to lack of awakening it is perceived as stable. (2)

Just as in the sky there appears through the transformation of the rays of vision a constant shimmering of falling jars, water-pots, pearls, locks of hair, and so forth, so too does the world incessantly undergo transformation; yet, due to the lack of discernment regarding its substratum, it is perceived as stable by virtue of that [substratum’s] stability. || 2 ||
Just as the configuration of a city gradually undergoes change into something else,
so too does the world incessantly transform, like the shifting of whirlpools in water.

He experiences the very subversion [of reality]—namely, that which is well-known as the configuration of the front [object], just as over time it undergoes alteration, that is, the state of becoming a different configuration. (3)
This world of earth, water, sky, mountains, and so forth, becomes non-existent in an instant;
yet within that very same instant, names such as "yuga" and "kalpa" are assigned based on the passing of moments.
At the very moment it occurs, the learned have applied designations such as "yuga" and "kalpa" to its constituent parts—kṣaṇas, lavas, truṭis, and so forth. || 4 ||
The entire world is experienced like a dream, though it is non-existent;
if that which does not exist were entirely absent, then consciousness alone would thus shine forth abundantly. (5)
If it is denied that the world exists, then it is consciousness alone that shines forth in its entirety.
Just as this world of ours exists, so too do hundreds of worlds exist in the sky;
let them behold those [worlds], yet their experiences are not mutually shared.

Let them perceive and acknowledge that this world of ours is as it is well-known to us, and that there exist hundreds upon hundreds, even tens of thousands, of other worlds and other men in the sky; yet, for them, the experiences of one another are not directly perceived, because of their lack of fitness [to do so]. || 6 ||
The frogs in lakes, oceans, and wells are each seen in their respective abodes;
they do not know one another, nor do they ever perceive any other restriction regarding what is visible and so forth.
By words such as "lake" (sara), the creatures residing therein are understood. "Another" means one distinct from its own respective location. || 7 ||
Just as the dream-cities of hundreds of people appear within a single house, so do the worlds shine in space; they are neither existent nor non-existent.
Because they are experienced by one [person], they do not exist [for others]; because they are not experienced by others, they do not exist [for them]. (8)
Just as hundreds of dream-cities shine within a single house,
yet do not truly shine at all, so too do worlds exist and yet not exist in the void.
He states that very point clearly: "They shine," etc. (9).
One's own body, which is the non-dual visible world, is merely the wonder of consciousness;
it is both with form and formless, and both with cause and without cause.

It is like a limb or a constituent part of its own self. While for one it is with form (*sarūpa*), for another it is without form (*nīrūpa*); and even for the same thing, at one time it is with form and at another time it is without form. However, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*tattvadṛśā*), it is always without form—this is the meaning.
Thus, that which has a cause is also without a cause. (10)

Although designations such as "conditioning factors" (saṃskāra) and so forth are applied to that which possesses the nature of bestowing [results], these conditioning factors and the like are not distinct from the presiding image. 11.

In this regard, one might raise the doubt: "Do these world-constitutions of living beings reside in the body or in consciousness? If they reside in consciousness, then they would be visible to everyone. If they reside in the body, then they would be destroyed upon the departure of the body. Anticipating this, he says: "Dadhantyā" (by her who bears).
It is neither in pure consciousness nor in the mere reflection of the body, but rather in that which undergoes transformation into the forms of those various objects of perception.

Even though it possesses the nature of consciousness, it is the intellect itself—by means of its pervasive manifestation—that receives the designations of "mental impressions" (saṃskāra) and so forth;
for it is through the power of the intellect, which is inherently potent, that these [impressions] are empowered.

Memory occurs regarding things never before experienced, as do dreams and the perception of objects of one's own volition; furthermore, memories and perceptions arise regarding things similar to those previously seen. (12)

If the world is merely a transformation of the intellect (*buddhi*) which sustains the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the world, then the experiences of objects in one's volitions would necessarily be nothing but memory; to this he replies: "Because of novelty" (*apūrvatvāt*). Even in the case of experiences of objects in volitions that resemble things previously seen, they are indeed memory; yet because of their novelty—that is, due to the loss of the element of "that-ness" (*tattā*) pertaining to what was previously experienced—they are like a dream.

It occurs as follows: although [objects] such as one's own death have not been experienced in this life, they have certainly been experienced in other lives; thus, they are superimposed upon that which possesses those very latent impressions (*saṃskāra*). This is the meaning of the distinction. || 12 ||
At the beginning of creation, this [universe], whose nature is emanation, unfolds like a reflection;
consisting solely of the light of consciousness and being transparent, no other name for it is possible.
This world, whose nature is the creation of the waking state, unfolds at the beginning of creation like a dream. || 13 ||
By this aforementioned statement, "The world shines as Brahman alone," it follows that what appears is not something new; therefore, it is established that this is indeed Brahman.

Having condensed the ultimate purport of the various modes of expression beginning with "in all ways, in the existence of non-existences," he says: "Brahman alone. And that [Brahman] does not appear as something new, nor was it previously unmanifest; rather, its nature is beginningless light. The intended meaning established here is that this world, having attained identity with that, is beginningless Brahman alone.
The meaning is that it has reached its conclusion. || 14 ||
That which is called the cause is the prior [state], and it is distinguished as the effect; because it is a refinement (*saṃskāra*), this refinement is said to be an action (*kṛti*). || 15 ||

It has been stated that the Supreme Self alone is both the cause and the effect; for He Himself is the prior—the cause in its general form—and He Himself is differentiated as the effect in its specific form. Since a seed is the cause because it is the substratum of the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the effect and properly produces the effect—according to the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) of the word *kāraṇa*—it is said that this very Self is the impression. In that regard:

*Kṛti* is effort conducive to action; it is the meaning of the verbal root *kṛ*. By the etymological derivation that "proper cause" (*saṃskāra*) means "that which effects thoroughly" (*samyak-karaṇa*), this *saṃskāra*, characterized by effort, is also said to be the Self itself. || 15 ||

That unprecedented object which appears as an example in dreams and the like is designated by such terms as "mental impression" (saṃskāra) and so forth; there is no external object present within the mind.

In that regard, the object which appears in dreams and so forth—unprecedented and distinct from waking objects, serving as the very illustration for waking objects—is itself, due to its subtle nature, called by names such as "subtle impression" (*saṃskāra*), "latent tendency" (*vāsanā*), "attachment," "aversion," "desire," and so on; the meaning is that there is no other external object whatsoever residing in the mind under the name of "impression. || 16 ||
The object is both seen and unseen, yet it exists like consciousness in the sky;
by its own nature, even that which is of the nature of space shines forth and expands as if it were seen.

Furthermore, that entity called "formative impression" (*saṃskāra*), which is seen in a dream but not seen in the waking state, should not be considered non-existent merely because it is not perceived [in the waking state]. For it always exists within the space of the mind (*cittākāśa*) like consciousness itself. And that, though being of the nature of the void, shines forth in the dream due to its nature as the witness (*sākṣi*), and expands and spreads out even more than the objects seen in the waking state.
The non-existence of the previous creation, which consists of the meaning of the Vedānta, proceeds;
thereafter, the wise establish the order of the objects of knowledge for the sake of accomplishing their own purpose. (18)

Having ascertained that very nature— which is the non-dual inner Brahman characterized by the absence of attributes, determined through hearing accompanied by the perfection of the means— wise scholars, for the sake of their own goal, the supreme human aim,
and for the sake of establishing it even among disciples, [realize] that the world-process is none other than the Self previously unknown.
The meaning is that once [reality] has been correctly investigated and known, the established position in the scriptures is that non-dual Brahman alone is liberation. || 18 ||
However, those who know the truth maintain that the impression of waking within a dream is something newly produced by that waking state; it is not truly waking, yet it appears as waking. (19)
Now, having restated another theory regarding the manner in which dreams are produced, he refutes it with the verse beginning "In a dream...

(svapne tu). The meaning is that some who know [the truth] maintain that what appears in a dream is the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of the waking state; that is, a form produced by the waking state which is a new *apūrva* (unprecedented), and though it is not actually waking, it appears as waking because it was produced by the experience of the waking state. || 19 ||
Therefore, like the vibrations of a lute, mental phenomena abide in the mind by their own nature;
they proceed spontaneously of themselves—what role for a creator of formative forces (*saṃskāra*) is there in this? (20)

That is not so; for just as vibrations exist inherently in the wind, the states of being dreams and so forth abide by their own nature. And these proceed by their own nature in the form of dreams; therefore, what role could there be for the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of a waking person therein? This is the meaning. || 20 ||
In this same way, the single pure consciousness exists as a hundred thousandfold self within a dream;
and since that dream of a hundred thousandfold nature arises from it, there remains once again the state of deep sleep as the one.
That very perception of a dream within the space of consciousness is called the world;
deep sleep is declared to be the cosmic dissolution (pralaya); therefore, this alone is the correct principle.
The single expanse of consciousness alone assumes manifold forms while not abandoning its own nature; that which appears as this world is like a dream.
How is it known that all entities reside in the mind? To this, he says: "The one," etc. (vv. 21–23).
Thus, this world-existence stands within the atoms of consciousness;
it is non-different from them, yet it does not possess their nature, like reflections in the surface of a dream.

By the reasoning thus stated, that [object] is non-different from consciousness; the meaning is that just as in dreams, or as faces, forests, mountains, and so forth seen upon the surface of a mirror are non-different [from the mirror], so it is in this case. || 24 ||
That which is the sky of consciousness, consisting of pure awareness alone, as vast as an atom and devoid of beginning, middle, or end—that very thing is called the universe. (25)
It is as extremely subtle as an atom, yet it is pervasive and vast; in terms of time, it is likewise without beginning, middle, or end. || 25 ||

Therefore, wherever the infinite space of consciousness (cidākāśa) eternally abides, there the appearance of the world exists; for that appearance is not of a nature other than its own limbs [i.e., its own parts].
It is like its own limb, having no form other than that; or "aṅga" is an address of endearment. || 26 ||
"The world is indeed pure consciousness; you, I, and the universe are composed of consciousness.
By this principle, the unborn universe enters even into the interior of a single atom. (27)

Through the thorough understanding of the collection of logical methods taught by the Guru and the scriptures, according to right principle, the world—even though it exists within the belly of an atom—attains grossness [only to] abandon that and reach the state of pure consciousness, which is supremely subtle; such is the meaning. || 27 ||
Therefore, I am the supreme atomic self, possessing the form of the entire universe;
I abide everywhere, even within the interior of a single atom.
He demonstrates, through the expression of his own experience, what that thorough understanding according to the principles taught by the Guru and the scriptures is like:
"This very Self of the universe, though consisting of the supreme atom of pure consciousness, is like space;
wherever I abide, there I behold the three worlds. (29)
I am indeed of the nature of a conscious atom; by that conscious atom, through the act of beholding it, I have attained oneness with it, just as water merges with water.

I am the self of the atom of consciousness (*cit-paramāṇu*), which is the purified meaning of the term *tvaṃ* (Thou). Through that atom of consciousness—the purified meaning of the term *tat* (That)—which is Brahman, I have attained oneness with it by means of its perception. And so says the Śruti:
"Just as water poured into water, milk into milk, or ghee into ghee becomes indistinguishable, even so is the individual self (*jīvātman*)."
In the Supreme Self. Thus [ends the section]. 30.
Then, having entered its vital energy (ojas), I remained as if experiencing it,
possessing the form of the three worlds within me, just as a seed exists within a sprout.

Having thus explained the secret of self-knowledge through a series of questions and answers, he resumes the narrative at hand and says, beginning with "tadoja" (then its vitality): "Like that" refers to the experience of the world consisting of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) contained within the vitality (*ojas*) of those living beings;
this is a statement intended to reconnect with the remainder of the previous story. Just as [the future] exists in a subtle form within a lotus sprout, so too does it exist here.
The meaning is that it is like a seed which contains within itself the manifold variety of thousands of potential states. || 31 ||
Therein, the form of the three worlds shone within me in my own self;
thus it existed there, but it does not exist externally anywhere for anyone.

There, within my very self, the entire form of the three worlds consisting of latent impressions—belonging to him, to me, and to others—shone forth within the self as the inward consciousness. Not even the slightest trace of that world-form exists externally; the meaning is that an external location itself is absolutely non-existent. || 32 ||
Wherever and whenever that which appears— whether in a dream or in this waking state—
is perceived as the external or internal visible world, it is nothing other than one's own manifestation of consciousness.
When the world, spread with bliss, appears to a living being in a dream,
that manifestation belongs to the atom of consciousness itself, as the Self in its essential state.
By way of that state, [and] by way of the state of dreaming. || 34 ||
The hunter said:
"If the visible world were without a cause, how could it be established?
If the visible world has a cause, then from where does the notion of creation and so forth arise in a dream? (35)
How is it established? For we do not observe the establishment of the intrinsic nature of things such as a rabbit’s horn that lack a cause.

If [the world] has a cause, then for one who doubts—asking from what cause the cognition of creation and so forth arises in a dream, given the absence of causes such as the staff and the wheel used for the creation of jars and the like—the question is posed. || 35 ||
The Sage said:
This creation proceeds at the beginning without any cause, because the sky of consciousness, which is the self of creation, is devoid of all causes. (36)
Supporting the very position that [the world] is without a cause by concluding with the non-duality of Brahman, the Sage gives the reply: "It is indeed without a cause. (36)
Since entities devoid of causes are absolutely impossible here, no creation whatsoever can exist anywhere that possesses resistance. (37)

A gross creation that is characterized by resistance cannot exist without a cause; however, the point is that for that which is illusory and false, there is no rule requiring it to have a cause. || 37 ||
This Brahman shines thus, luminous by its very nature as consciousness;
it is synonymous with terms such as "creation" and so forth, yet it is devoid of beginning and end. (38)
Thus, in this causeless creation which shines forth as the form of Brahman,
there appears the reflection of the limbs of the Supreme, through the nature of the limbs of the eternal Self.

Thus, since creation in the manner described is entirely impossible as being without a cause, and since the appearance of parts in the Supreme—which is of the nature of Brahman—is but the consciousness reflected in Māyā; and since, although the eternal Self is non-dual in its essential nature, its apparent multiplicity due to limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) is utterly illogical; so it is that within Brahman—which is not non-Brahman, which is formless yet appears with form, and which is unobstructed—it shines forth as such.
When manifestation occurs, that very Brahman—which is formless because its nature is consciousness—appears as if possessing form through its vibrating body;

having become the Self, it sequentially assumes the forms of gods, seers, and sages, as well as the stationary and the moving, and performs all destiny, including injunctions and prohibitions. This is the summarized meaning; such is the syntactical connection of the four [verses]. || 39 ||
Though it is non-dual and yet appears as diverse, though it is Brahman and yet takes the form of non-Brahman,
though it is formless and yet possesses forms— it shines forth unimpededly toward every object.

That very Brahman, being formless yet possessing a radiant body due to its nature as consciousness, appears as if it were possessed of form, having become the self of all things mobile and immobile. (41)
He assumes the form of divine sages and seers, and sequentially ordains destiny, as well as injunctions and prohibitions regarding place, time, action, and so forth. (42)
Existence and non-existence, grasping and abandoning, the gross and the subtle, the moving and the unmoving—all these objects deviate; therefore, not all of them are subject to fixed necessity.

He says that precisely because [the world] was created by Brahmā, even though there may be deviation regarding objects such as existence and non-existence, there is no deviation from the necessity [of its being his creation]:
"From that time forward, without having a cause, the arising of entities is impossible, just as the production of oil from sand and the like is impossible. (44)
Therefore, from the postulation of necessity (niyati) onwards, there is no possibility of the existence of entities without a causal relationship characterized by specific necessity. || 44 ||
Fate and the Leader likewise, as limbs of Brahman by means of the Self,
restrain themselves by their own limbs, just as one hand restrains its own hand.

Of that Brahman, there is Niyati (the principle of necessity), its ordainer, the leader, and the individual soul (jīva) as the enjoyer; this movement proceeds from Brahman by itself, through its own self, like the bending of two hands. That Brahman, with that one limb, restrains and governs the other, just as one hand restrains the other hand. || 45 ||
And even without prior intention or desire, it proceeds in this very manner, like the "crow-and-palm" coincidence, or like eddies in water arising from a movement. (46)

Therefore, for the individual soul (jīva) alone, this creation characterized by waking and dreaming proceeds like the "crow-and-palmyra" coincidence—without prior intelligence and without desire. || 46 ||

For the structural arrangement is indeed destiny; without it, Brahman would be unable to exist even as the emergence of resistance, and that [destiny] is imperishable because it constitutes the nature of all things.

The necessity regarding the specific arrangement of an effect as determined by its cause is precisely what constitutes *niyati* (destiny). Without that necessity of arrangement, Brahman cannot remain even for a moment in an unmanifest state;
the sense is that it is just as [clay] cannot exist without assuming one of the various arrangements such as powder, a lump, a jar, or a shard.

And that maintenance of the structural arrangement (saṃniveśadhāraṇa) continues until liberation—that is, it persists until its absolute destruction by means of knowledge through the entire self; such is the meaning. || 47 ||
Thus, at all times, the entire visible sphere is accompanied by its cause; for whomsoever it is created, from whatever time it begins, it remains so for that person. 48.

Thus, by the postulation of necessity (*niyati*), everything has a cause; for whatever person and from whatever time onwards necessity has been operative in a creation, it applies only to that person and not to another person or to objects occurring at a different time.
Brahman shines as causeless even to the unawakened, who [perceive it] as the nature of creation;
and for that very person, this delusion of the vision of cause and effect appears. (49)
Brahman, though devoid of causality, appears even as the nature of creation to the unawakened and ignorant. || 49 ||
When creation exists by chance, like the "crow-and-the-palm-fruit" maxim,
this principle of necessity (niyati) remains established, such that "this is thus" and "this is not thus," just as in the case of recurring patterns.

From the perspective of one who possesses discernment, when the world exists by chance like the "crow-and-palm" coincidence, there arises— through the mere observation of the rule of temporal sequence and through reflection that "this jar and so forth was produced from such a collection of causes as a staff, a wheel, and clay," and "this cloth and so forth was produced from such things as a shuttle and a loom"— a certainty regarding the words and sentences of the eternal Veda, as if it were established by grammar.
The meaning is "established. || 50 ||
Since all entities necessarily possess causes when a temporal sequence is involved,
waking and dreaming perceptions cannot occur here without a cause.

For one who maintains that produced entities necessarily possess a temporal sequence of priority and posteriority, and thus must have causes, no causeless things can exist for such a person regarding the waking and dreaming states. Indeed, there are no causes for the arising of the waking world immediately following either the dream or the deep sleep state. Likewise, [there are no causes] immediately following either the waking or the deep sleep state...

Even regarding the arising of the manifold world of dreams, causes cannot be determined; thus, that [dream-world] also does not exist [as a real entity]. Nor does the dream-manifold persist in exactly the same state as it was when interrupted by the waking state, such that it would not require a new creation.
The meaning is that the waking manifold, which is interrupted by the states of dreaming and deep sleep, is likewise [not inherently existent]. || 51 ||
Just as in a dream, due to the agitation of water, the delusions of universal dissolution are seen;
hear and experience the cause that lies therein. 52.

"Just as I myself saw living beings in a dream, pervading the entire earth and deluded by the dissolution [of the world] due to the agitation of the waters—what is the cause of that which is seen by you?
Or rather, let it be heard from scripture, or experienced through other means of valid cognition; for this is a matter of possibility."
The imperative mood (*loṭ*): the meaning is that nothing at all is possible. || 52 ||
In all things, logical arguments always shine forth like crystals or shells;
yet it is the experience of meditative cultivation itself that is truly powerful and victorious as the very essence of life. (53)

The arguments demonstrating the identity of Brahman and the phenomenal world (brahma-prapañca-aikya), as described above, flash forth spontaneously to the intellects of the wise regarding all things that are investigated, just as crystals or mother-of-pearl shine by themselves through their own luster when light is present; therefore, in every determination, [this is the case].

That very experience, born from the cultivation of reasoning in accordance with the scriptures, is renowned as victorious; it is itself possessed of the power to determine all principles and constitutes the very life-force of all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). The meaning is that it exists with supreme excellence.

Thus ends the "Investigation of the Nature of Things" (*Padārthavicāra*) in the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa*, in the *Vālmīkīya Deśika-mokṣopāya-nirṇaya*, in the *Upadeśasāra*, in the *Avadhūtaprakaraṇa*, in the *Śataka*, [chapter] named... (Note: The final portion of the title appears to be incomplete or corrupted in the source text.)
The one hundred and forty-fourth canto.
Thus ends the one hundred and forty-fourth chapter, titled "Investigation of the Meaning of Words," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and forty-fifth canto. The Sage said:
"By means of the external senses directed outward, and by the internal senses directed inward, one perceives what is external as well as the dream-like state within."
The living being perceives both [pleasure and pain] through two [types of karma] that possess extremely intense momentum. || 1 ||

The various types of dreams experienced by a living being whose body is filled with phlegm, bile, and wind are described here; likewise, the external delusions perceived through the senses are explained.

This living being perceives an external dream through the external senses; it perceives an internal dream through the internal senses; and through the senses that abide in both the external and internal realms—extremely intense and impetuous for the sake of accomplishing activity in both—it perceives both. || 1 ||
When the senses remain externally distracted,
then the object of one's volition is experienced as something withered.
In that case, when one engages with external objects through the external senses, is there then no internal engagement at all? He says "no"—"when.

It certainly exists, but it is experienced as being like a daydream (*manorājya*), characterized by a faded experience of objects accompanied by volitional constructs (*saṃkalpa*); the meaning is that it is not experienced with the clarity of a dream. || 2 ||
But when the senses are indeed turned inward, then the world,
though no larger than an atom, is thoroughly known by the individual soul within its own body.

Because it consists of nothing but latent impressions (vāsanā), even though the dream-world is extremely subtle—being merely an atom in size—he thoroughly understands it and perceives it as if it were gross; this is the meaning of "his own unfading experience. || 3 ||
The world is never at any time anything that possesses resistance;
the vision of the eyes of living beings—which are themselves non-resistant—is what constitutes the non-resistant world.

The external or internal world, though possessing resistance and appearing gross, does not exist in reality. When one conceives of the grossness of the *jīva*’s organs of sight—the senses that serve as the instruments of perception—that very vision which is non-resistant and unimpeded is what is meant by the "gross world. (4)
When the senses, which are the life-breaths and eyes, are entirely external in nature,
then the living soul perceives within consciousness the world-body as being essentially external.

For this very reason, it is said that wherever the senses extend, whether externally or internally, there alone the world is perceived as something gross: "The aggregate consisting of the ear, skin, eye, nose, and tongue, which is active in nature, is called the *jīva*; it is of the nature of consciousness (*cid-rūpa*) and possesses the form of air (*anila-mūrtimān*). (Verse 6)

The mention of the ears and so forth is also indicative of the organs of speech and the rest. "Possessing a form of wind" means composed of the five vital breaths (*prāṇas*). "Consisting of what is desired" refers to the fourfold internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) dominated by desire; the aggregate whose nature is that [organ] is the subtle body (*ātivāhika-deha*).

The meaning is that this very [body], through its conjunction with the reflection of the immutable consciousness (*kūṭastha-cidābhāsa*), is called the individual soul (*jīva*), which is of the nature of consciousness. || 6 ||
Everywhere and at all times, the living soul (jīva) exists as composed of all the senses;
because it is the imperishable space of consciousness, it perceives everything everywhere.

Such a living being (jīva) may indeed perceive the world consisting of its own latent impressions (vāsanā) within; but how does it perceive the world consisting of those impressions externally, given the absence of such impressions there? To this, he says: "Everywhere. In that regard, the immutable consciousness (kūṭastha-cit) itself, appearing as the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa), being of the nature of the universal space (samaṣṭi-vyoma), exists everywhere, at all times, and consists of all the sense organs.
The meaning is that, since it abides as the substratum of all latent impressions (*vāsanā*), the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of the external world upon it is indeed logically established. || 7 ||
When the inner life-force is filled with the essence characterized by phlegm,
then that subtle self, in the form of an atom, perceives within those very sensory organs.

In that regard, he elaborates upon the fact that for the *jīva* who has entered the vital energy (*ojas*) during the perception of the manifold variety of specific internal dreams, the cause is precisely its entry into the channels (*nāḍī*) filled with specific essences of food such as phlegm (*śleṣman*),
beginning with the words "by means of the nature of phlegm" (*śleṣmātmanā*). When its expansion of the organs has been withdrawn, it becomes subtle (*aṇu*) and [pervades] in a thousandfold way.

The meaning is as follows: your *jīva*, capable of moving within extremely subtle channels (*nāḍī*) whose dimensions are equal to the parted strands of hair, becomes filled by the essence of food in the form of phlegm (*śleṣman*) that has entered those channels; at that time, within each respective atom (*akṣāṇuka*), it experiences dream-delusions in the manner to be described later regarding those very channels.
It was like the Milk Ocean surging at the rising of the moon in the sky,
with lakes filled with blossoming lotuses and entwined with white water-lilies.
Having himself become as if flown up into the ocean of milk, he attains the sky accompanied by the rising of the moon; this is to be supplied everywhere. || 9 ||
With clouds of flowers as their canopies and sung to by bees,
the inner gardens of the springtime palaces arose in the sky.

The lakes, which served as substitutes or counterparts for the divine clouds made of flowers, were the gardens that formed the inner apartments of the King of Spring; they arose in the sky, the space of the living. || 10 ||
[He saw] festivals filled with auspiciousness, groups of women restless in their play,
and courtyards of houses completely filled with the splendor of various foods, edibles, and drinks.
Bearing flowers, laughing with foam, and possessing tremulous, restless glances, the rivers— intoxicated by their youth— approach the ocean with playful grace.
The fish are tremulous; those whose eyes are tremulous with that same quality are women. || 12 ||
The palatial mansions, exceedingly cool and white as the peaks of the Himalayas,
with their walls washed in plaster, appear as if they were fashioned from the very surface of the moon.
The palaces seem as if they were constructed with floors made of moon-stones. || 13 ||
And [he saw] lands covered by the clouds of the dewy season, the cold season, and the rainy season,
as well as grounds abounding in blue lotuses, creepers, and green meadows.
The grounds of the city gardens were covered with scattered heaps of flowers, where deer and travelers rested in the shade of trees with glossy leaves. (15)
Where the deer and travelers alike have found rest.
The flower-filled grounds were radiant with the nectar of the kadamba, kunda, and mandāra trees, and with the luster of the moon, while their seats, locations, and structures shone brightly.
Those whose configuration is like that of one appearing while seated upon a throne. || 16 ||
He saw dark-blue lotus-ponds entwined with creepers, bearing clusters of flowers,
and rows of forests as tender as the clear sky from which the clouds had dissolved.
Like an autumn sky, free from clouds and stainless, [the rays] are soft and lustrous. || 17 ||

They wore crests fashioned from plantains, kandalī, kunda, and kadamba flowers; they were garlanded with mountain ranges and were as delicate as the swaying, beautiful, playful sprouts [of their arms]. (18)
*Kadali* and *kandali* are species of deer; *taru* and *gulma* are types of trees and shrubs; and *girimālā* refers to ranges of mountains. || 18 ||
With their creeper-like mālatī garlands loosened from their hair-braids as they turned playfully, those slender-limbed young women performed a dance like youthful maidens. 19.

With their braided hair gracefully swaying, the young women stand like *mālatī* creepers whose branches have been released and spread out; as they perform their dance, they captivate the heart. || 19 ||
The assembly halls of the king resembled blossoming white lotus ponds,
covered with hundreds of beautiful chowries, golden water-pots, and canopies.
Their limbs were gracefully entwined in the playful arrangement of circular vine-circles;
their forest garlands possessed the soft, melodious resonance of shimmering water-channels.
The forest garlands are the rows of groves; they are deep and melodious with the warbling of birds in the channels and irrigation ditches of shimmering waters. 21.
The ten directions held clouds whose forms were formidable as they bore the weight of the earth,
and their interiors were like necklaces of spray and mist.

The ten directions were such that the mountains—the bearers of the earth—were joined with clouds, those "terrible-limbed" (karālāṅga) rain-bearers who, through their showers, possessed the power of supporting and filling the burden of the earth. || 22 ||
When the inner life-force is filled by the rasa whose nature is bile (pitta), then the ojas,
which consists of the subtlest atoms, finds itself right there.

Having elaborated upon the specific types of dreams seen when the channels are filled with phlegm (*śleṣman*), he describes those seen when the channels are filled with the essence of bile (*pitta-rasa*) by means of the verse beginning with "pittātmanā" (23).
Beautiful with *kiṃśuka* trees dried by the movement of the wind,
the rows of flames were as delicate as the petals and sprouts of a radiant lotus.
"He finds" means that he sees rows of flames. || 24 ||
The streams of rivers were like showers of scalding sand, and the quarters of the sky were darkened by the smoke-blackened crests of forest fires. || 25 ||
He further characterizes the rows of flames as "scorched" (saṃtapta): [the land] from which rivers—characterized by vapors and tears—issue forth, along with the sprinklings of heated sands. || 25 ||
The rays of the sun were harsh like fire, possessing the brilliance of sharpened sword-edges,
and acting as mines for the perverse flavors of forest conflagrations and the onset of poison.
Whose rays are sharp and keen like the edges of a wheel; from whom the reservoirs of water, whose forms are liquid, have become pervaded and especially inverted.
He made the ocean hot with his sweat, as if the entire circle of the three worlds were perspiring;
he caused even the salt marshes and dense forests to seethe with boiling brine.

"Sweat" (sveda) means moist with heat; "perspired" (svinna) means moistened by sweating. "Thickets" (pratarda) refers to the extreme density of trees, shrubs, grasses, and so forth; the dense forests are also characterized by such density. || 27 ||
It appeared like the water of a mirage shimmering in the morning, like a flowing stream, and like lakes;
it was lands never seen before, yet appearing as if they had existed for ages.
It was beautified by cranes moving through the lakes, appearing like water in a mirage as they flew forth at dawn.
To the traveler, who was dusted grey by heated dust due to the intensity of his haste,
the roadside tree with its lush shade appeared from afar like nectar.
Agitated by fear, he sees himself running along the paths due to its influence;
what was seen like nectar becomes even more highly esteemed through that very vision. (29)
The world, its form set ablaze by fever, was heated like fire;
the regions were struck by dust, as were the quarters of the sky and the intermediate spaces.
The planets, villages, oceans, mountains, forests, skies, fires, and directions—[all those] formidable as the jars of infinite, countless clouds that consume frost and food—[were destroyed]. 31.

He beholds the quarters of the sky, from the houses up to the ends of space, as being ablaze with fire.
