He sees clouds of infinite number—terrible like jars containing that fire which consumes (jahati) and releases (muñcati) the "snow-eater" (tuhināhāra), namely Agni, who brings and devours cold snow—and [he sees] autumns, summers, and springs [produced by them]; such is the connection with the following verse. || 31 ||
He saw the autumns, summers, and springs, which inflict the torments of heat; he saw the earth covered by masses of clouds, heaps of grass, leaves, and creepers, and the warmth [of the sun].
The earth—the various regions of the ground—was covered and concealed by grasses, leaves, masses of creepers, heaps of clouds, and vapors. || 32 ||
The surface of the sky, the earth, and the horizons became golden;
likewise, the vast lakes and the regions of the snowy mountains were heated.
He beholds vast and numerous lakes, the plateaus of the snowy mountain, and various regions that have become scorched. || 33 ||
When the vital breath (jīva) is filled by the wind once the fluids have been depleted, then that self, whose essence consists of subtle atoms, perceives the vital energy (ojas) right there. || 34 ||

When the individual soul (jīva), whose nature is atomic in size, has entered the region of the channels— which is emptied of the bodily fluids, food-essences, phlegm, bile, and so forth, and is filled solely by the wind— and is then itself filled with that wind, it experiences the dream state described below within the *ojas* mentioned previously. || 34 ||
Because his consciousness was agitated by the wind, he saw an unprecedented surface of the earth,
and unprecedented circles of cities, villages, mountains, oceans, and forests.
The unprecedented is that which is distinct from what was previously seen. || 35 ||
He saw himself flying up like rocks from mountain peaks,
emitting deep and resonant roars, and performing such feats as whirling about on a wheel.
With the deep, humming roars of the clouds, he made the regions resound with noise, and even without a potter’s wheel, he caused the rotation of water-wheels and the like. (36)
There was the mounting of vehicles such as horses, camels, garuḍas, clouds, and swans,
and the coming and going and movement of yakṣas, vidyādharas, and others.

The vehicle ending with the swan (haṃsa) refers to the act of going and its descent; likewise, the "goings" and "comings" refer to movement from afar and movement within one's own place. Alternatively, *gati* may be treated as a separate word. || 37 ||

There was a trembling of the mountains, the heavens, the earth, the rivers, the lords, the forests, the lands, the villages, the cities, and the directions— like bubbles in the ocean— as their bodies turned toward fear.

[He caused] the trembling of the forest lands—consisting of trees and so forth—which arise in the woods together with mountains, the vast sky, rivers, and rocks; as well as the trembling of villages, cities, and regions, and of humans and others whose limbs were turned toward fear. 38.
Or one who has fallen into a blind well, or into a vast calamity;
or one who perceives oneself as having ascended a tree or a mountain that reaches the sky. (39)
He measured and delimited the sky with the luster of that tree and mountain, which possessed such beauty of form.
When the living soul is filled with wind, bile, and phlegm,
it then becomes afflicted, having come under the power of the portions of wind.

Having described the dreams visible when each individual portion of a channel is filled, he now describes those visible when all three are filled, beginning with the words "vāta" and so forth. || 40 ||
Pārvatī fell amidst a perilous rain of fine stones,
where the sounds of crumbling towers and ramparts resounded and the circles of trees were whirled about.
The circle of wandering trees resounded along with the echoes from the clear palaces and the mountain ridges. || 41 ||
With its forest arrangements swirling about, it made the clouds appear indistinct; the quarters of the sky were rendered continuous by lions, elephants, and rain-clouds.
The middle of the quarters was filled without interval by lions, elephants, and rain-clouds.
It was crowded with rows of palmyra, tamāla, and hintāla trees blazing with fire,
and it resounded with the deep, gurgling roar of echoes from within its caves.
He specifies that very other direction with the words "tālī" etc. || 43 ||
The cave was beautiful with the continuous sound of the gentle churning of Mount Mandara,
and it was struck by the irresistible mutual clashing of the rocks as they were being split apart.
He beholds a cave that has been struck by a mutual collision which is difficult to withstand in its crushing force. || 44 ||
Resembling the clashing of mountain peaks, harsh with a multitude of "kreṃ-kreṃ" cries,
the sky was filled with falling rivers that resembled shimmering strings of pearls.

Between two mountain peaks, he beholds those rivers whose sounds of flow resemble the clashing of the two summits; which are harsh with the multitudes of *kreṅkāra* cries from ruddy geese and other birds; and by whose falling [waters] resembling strings of pearls, the vault of heaven appears as if adorned with garlands of flowers. (45)
The great ocean, its waters filled with fragments of rock, filled the sky;
it struck against the shell of Brahmā’s cosmic egg with the force of dense, surging forest fires.

Indicating that even his own dream-vision of the ocean of dissolution and so forth arises from this very cause, he says: "śilāśakala... [and so on]. He sees the great ocean, its expanse filled with waters (arṇas) full of fragments of stone.
He describes that very ocean with the words beginning with "vahat... [and so on]: of the forests and thickets being carried away...
By him the Brahma-maṇḍala—the world of the seven sages—was struck and shaken by blows. || 46 ||
It was jagged with the mutual rubbing of their ten eyes and teeth,
and it resounded with the distinct *kaṭakaṭa* clattering of their snapping armlets.

It stood as if laughing with jagged peaks, displaying the ten directions washed and polished by the mutual splashing of waves; it appeared as if marked by the blows of chisels, for the mountain ridges were splitting with a *kaṭakaṭa* sound that filled the quarters and enveloped them.
[He saw the mountain] where the forest creepers were stirred by the winds shaken by the falling rocks,
and which bore lotuses variegated by the dust of its own clashing stones.
"Khapāta" means that which falls from the sky; by that wind (pavana), the forest was shaken (adhūta).

In that [forest], there arose the dance of creepers (latālāsya) following the breeze. It has the habit of bearing lotus-born things such as moss (śaivāla) and the like, which possess variegated colors (karburavarṇa) due to the pebbles (dṛṣaccūrṇa) produced by itself as it crashes against them. 48.
With deep "maramara" sounds arising from the piercing cries of formidable jackals, the three worlds appear as if illuminated by cruel lamentations. (49)

The meaning is that at that time, the three worlds appeared as if resplendent with the deep, resonant sounds of the palm groves and other forests— sounds that had arisen like the mutual rending of fierce warriors (bhaṭodbhaṭa) at the end of the eon when they first began to invade the ocean, resembling the cries of cruel creatures in distress. || 49 ||
Thus, when the individual soul (jīva) has been rendered inert, it remains utterly oppressed, surrounded by those [elements]: wood, stone, clay, fire, wind, and the body. || 50 ||

In the channels filled with the three elements, the individual soul (jīva), being obstructed by those aforementioned and universally known factors— whether wood, stone, mud, water, wind, or soldiers— remains utterly tormented and rendered inert within the dream state. || 50 ||
Like an insect within soft earth, like a frog inside a stone, like an unformed fetus within the womb, and like a seed within a fruit. || 51 ||

In the third [meaning—that is, the third of the subsequent triad]—the connection is with all [the preceding terms]—one experiences [it] like an insect inside clay or like such stones and the like. || 51 ||
Like a sprout within the belly of a seed, like an atom within a mass of matter, or like the body of a wooden puppet situated within an unceasing pillar and its casing. || 52 ||
Due to the impossibility of any cavities, it is devoid of the movement of the vital breath;
it is threatened by a surging mass of stones and a flood of pebbles.

He then explains when and by what cause this [jīva] experiences deep sleep (*suṣupta*): "By means of a cavity" (*sauṣiryāt*). When this jīva has entered the *purītat*—the cage of channels characterized by the knot of the heart-bone formed by the tips of all the ribs—at that time, because a cavity is impossible in that region for the purpose of further movement, [he remains there].

Being devoid of the vibration impelled by the vital breath (*prāṇapavana*), he is as if obstructed in his cavity by a mass of ribs—the side-bones—rising up like a heap of stones; thus threatened and rendered incapable of activity, how could he exist? At that time, he is like a mountain-casket or a stone-womb, containing within it the very energy (*tejas*) previously described as "extremely dense vitality" (*nibiḍataraujaḥ*).
The connection between the two [verses] is that one experiences deep sleep as being like the interior of a blind well, due to the density of ignorance that has that [sleep] as its appearance.
Then, as if within a dense mass of light, one experiences deep sleep itself, which resembles the interior of a mountain cave or the depths of a dark well. (54)
When that transformed effort again attains a state of vacuity, then the living soul, awakened by the vital breaths, experiences a dream once more. || 55 ||

Then, as to how one returns there again in a dream, he says: "When... When the food that was eaten has been transformed by digestion, and when the channels through which the essence of food enters have once again become hollow due to the removal of the obstruction, then the individual soul (jīva), having attained the effort for exit by means of the movement of the vital breath (prāṇa), is awakened again by the vital breath.
He knows that which is without dream. || 55 ||
When those portions fall into the interior parts of that region,
transforming within the body, that indeed is the excessive raining upon the mountains.

When those food-essences, undergoing transformation within the body, fall from one part of the channels to other parts along with the *jīva*, he then perceives the internal showering of *ojas*. || 56 ||

Due to an excess of fire, one perceives much even with a small amount [of fuel], and due to the conjunction of wind, bile, and other humors, one experiences agitation both externally and internally. (57)

Because of the great fire—that is, being pervaded by an excessively intense digestive heat—and due to the combination of wind, bile, and other humors, one perceives a great deal of agitation both externally and internally;
thus, this introductory section is composed to describe the perception of delusion even in the external world. 57.
Just as this individual soul, having been brought under control within, perceives this,
so too does it perceive or experience [external objects] when enveloped by wind, bile, and other humors.
He begins to describe that very [state]: "He sees," "he knows by means of the organs of perception," or "he goes by means of the organs of action. (58)

When agitated both internally and externally by wind, bile, phlegm, and so forth, one perceives this visible world as very small and slightly distorted; when these elements are in equilibrium, it is perceived as even.

When the humors such as wind (vāta), bile (pitta), and phlegm (kapha) are agitated by even small amounts of food-essence, one perceives external and internal objects of sight very faintly due to delusion; when they are balanced, one perceives objects of sight clearly and correctly;
and when they are excessively agitated, it follows by implication that one perceives objects of sight with extreme delusion. || 59 ||
Enveloped by these agitated elements, this individual soul perceives externally the movement of the earth, mountains, and sky, as well as the blazing of masses of fire.
[The fault] arises from these [faults] when they coincide with causes such as gems, mantras, medicines, and so forth. || 60 ||
Traversing the sky, as well as the rising moon and the Himalayas;
the dense thickets of trees and mountains, and leaping through the heavens over the oceans. (61)
He elaborates upon the objects perceived through external delusion, beginning with "traveling through space" and so forth. || 61 ||
Diving and surfacing in the ocean, amorous dalliance in the celestial abodes, and frequent resting upon mountain slopes, groves, white clouds, and mountain peaks. (62)
Resting upon the seats of white clouds and sitting amidst the masses of white clouds. || 62 ||
There was the crushing sound of massive saws, the delusion of experiencing hellish torments,
and rows of palm, tamāla, and hintāla trees revolving in the sky.
There was falling by means of whirlwinds and sudden leaping into the sky;
even in empty space there appeared a multitude of people, and even on dry land there was immersion in the ocean.
In the dead of night, the diverse and contrary activities of worldly life are as difficult to discern as the light of the sun during the day, or as darkness during the day.
Like the light of the sun at night, as if it were day.
One perceives the surface of the earth as being in the sky, solid ground within the construction of a wall, walls within the open space of the sky, and friendship toward an enemy. (66)
Within the dense wall-enclosure, there was a vast open space free of walls.
One should perceive others in one's own kin, and goodness in the wicked;
one should see level ground in a pit, and the nature of a pit in level ground. (67)
[The temples] were filled with soft, melodious songs, washed with nectar, and beautifully decorated;
they were either composed entirely of white [stone] or made of fresh butter.
[They are] made of white crystal, silver, and so forth. || 68 ||
In dwellings formed by clusters of leaves from *kadamba*, *nīpa*, and *jambīra* trees,
women find pleasant rest, just as bees find it among lotuses in heaven.

For these functions of the senses, when closed within, see [the internal objects], but when opened, they see [external objects]; thus, due to the imbalance of the bodily constituents (dhātus), the sensory activities produce error.
These sensory functions, when closed by internal sleep, perceive these delusions; but when opened by waking, they perceive them externally in such things as magical illusions.
Those whose constituent elements are unbalanced see and experience many such things as these,
even though they are external, just as in a dream.
Those persons whose wind and other elements are unbalanced are [as such]. || 71 ||
Both externally and internally, many contrary effects are seen— extremely terrifying deeds performed by living beings with imbalanced bodily constituents.
Within these equal elements, this inner life-force itself experiences this uniform state of worldly activity, just as fire existing within [fuel] experiences its own condition.
This well-known established state of worldly and scriptural convention. || 73 ||

He saw the continuous succession of cities, villages, towns, and forests as they truly were, along with the pleasant waters, the shade of trees, the various regions, and the coming and going of travelers on the roads.
Adorned with pleasant sunlight, the moon, the sun, stars, and the cycle of day and night—thus this unreal appears as if it were real. (75)
The perception of the visible within the nature of consciousness is like a vibration in the wind;
though non-existent, it appears as existent, remaining undivided yet appearing as if divided.
From the peaceful void-self, the entire universe arises; yet from that which is peaceful, nothing whatsoever arises, nor does it arise as "existent.
Such a sky-like state shines forth within the body of infinite consciousness as mere light, an expansive and infinite form.

The entire world arises from Brahman alone, which is peaceful and free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*); yet, nothing other than that peace exists. For that which is called "existent" does not arise in the form of a produced effect perceived by the senses, nor indeed is it ever born. Therefore, in the body of infinite consciousness—which is like the sky—it is merely a manifestation of light.
The meaning is that the world shines forth as infinite in form as mere appearance; there is no other reality. || 77 ||
The one hundred and forty-fifth canto, titled "Description of the Waking, Dreaming, and Deep Sleep States," from the Mahārāmāyaṇa of Vālmīki, in the Uttarakāṇḍa.

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of Waking, Dreaming, and Deep Sleep," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and forty-sixth canto.
The hunter said:
"Immediately thereafter, O best of sages, within that heart and that vital energy..."
O you who are illusory in form, what has happened to you while remaining thus? Even by name alone, you are a delusion.
At the conclusion of the dream he has just experienced, his deep sleep is described;
then, through the further occasion of dreaming, the non-duality of Brahman is explained in detail.

Having heard this incidental account, the hunter asked again for the remainder of the previous story, beginning with "Immediately thereafter": "O you whose form is illusion, what kind of experience—such as seeing dreams and so forth—occurred before you while that creature’s vital energy remained present? (1)
The sage said:
Listen now, my dear, to what happened there immediately thereafter,
concerning him who was seated within the element of fire, his form enveloped by that vital breath.
That form, the subtle body (*liṅgadeha*), of mine is enveloped and permeated by that life-force (*tajjīva*). || 2 ||
At that time, while that terrible agitation at the end of the aeon was occurring,
the wind of dissolution blew, carrying away even the great lords of mountains like blades of grass.
Suddenly, a rain of mountains arrived from somewhere,
carrying away the expanse of forests, peaks, villages, and cities.
When that [rain] reached his interior and was then transformed, at that moment I, in my subtle form, beheld that very downpour of rocks. || 5 ||
When that vital energy of his was transformed within me by means of my own living self (jīvātman), then I beheld that very downpour of mountains which had arrived there. || 5 ||
Compressed by that flood of food-particles as high as a mountain peak, I became dense with a profound, dreamless sleep, like the state of deep slumber.

By that mountain-high flood of food-essence, which had entered the channels of that living being and consisted of minute particles of food, I became compressed, formed into a solid mass, and rendered motionless; thus, I experienced deep sleep, which is mingled and blended with the blindness characterized by ignorance.
Then, after experiencing that state of deep sleep for some time,
I gradually became inclined toward awakening, like a bed of lotuses at dawn.
When the food essence that obstructs the path of excretion had been digested, then at dawn I became intent on awakening, like a bed of lotuses. || 7 ||
Just as a vision in long-standing darkness appears in the form of a wheel,
so too was that very state of deep sleep transformed into the state of dreaming.

Just as the vision, closed by darkness, after a long time shines forth in the form of the radiance of a circle of light, so too the very state of deep sleep (suṣupta), which is the nature of the Self, has come to the state of dreaming; this is the meaning. || 8 ||

Likewise, from the repose of deep sleep, I entered into sleep within the dream; I beheld the visible world within my own vital energy, just as the ocean perceives its own waves as its own form. (Note: The reading is *svamūrtitvam*.)

From the state of repose in deep sleep (*suṣupti*), I entered the sleep of dreaming (*svapnanidrā*). The absence of the augment *aṭ* is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*). Just as the ocean perceives its own form as being filled with a thousandfold dispersion of waves and the like, so too did I perceive a thousandfold internal dispersion of that energy (*ojas*); this is the meaning. (9)
The visible world, which consists of the treasury of consciousness, has thus come to me;
it is like the vibration within the motionless wind, which is not other than it.
Just as heat exists in fire and the like, as fluidity exists in water and the like,
and as pungency exists in pepper and the like, so too does the world exist within the space of consciousness.
Because its nature is solely that of consciousness, the world-appearance is spread out as that very [consciousness];
it has issued forth from that deep-sleep self as an object of perception, like the son of a child.
That world is his dream; it was born from the womb of the Seer, who is in the state of deep sleep, like a young son.
The hunter said:
"Since it is designated as 'the visible object of that one whose self is in deep sleep,' tell me, O best among speakers, what do you mean by 'the visible object of deep sleep'? (13)

For deep sleep (*suṣupti*) is well known as the dissolution of all that is visible; having heard it stated that even in that deep sleep there exists a visible object belonging to that self in deep sleep—as expressed by the words "of that" (*tasya*) and "from the visible" (*dṛśyāt*)—the hunter, unable to conceive of such a thing, asks: "That... By the use of the pronoun "that" (*tat*) and the word "visible" (*dṛśya*), the visible object of deep sleep is designated.
The meaning is: "Intending that something exists, you say it; tell me what that is. || 13 ||
From that deep-sleep self, which is the object of perception, or even from the deep-sleep self itself, what other produced thing could possibly arise, or else what other state of deep sleep? (14)

Furthermore, from that living being whose self is in deep sleep, or even from your own self which is in deep sleep, what other world-like object of perception could possibly be born? What is this birth that serves as the cause for such otherness? Or, upon the dissolution of all objects of perception, is there some other state of deep sleep? || 14 ||
The Sage said:
"The jar and so forth, as well as the world and its like, are born, they shine, and they manifest"—this is a conceptual outpouring of those tormented by duality. (15)

"Do you ask whether this birth and so forth are seen from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), or from the perspective of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*)? Regarding the first case, because they lack the nature of a real entity, the Sage gave the answer 'nothing at all' with the words beginning 'it is born' (*jāyate*). The meaning is that I have merely repeated the conceptual chatter of fools who are tormented by duality; this is not a discourse on reality. || 15 ||

For the word *jāta* is heard as a synonym for mere existence (*sanmātra*); how so? It is said that *jan* denotes manifestation (*prādurbhāva*), while *bhū* is the very form of that manifestation. (16)

In the investigation of the wise, however, the meaning of words such as "born" (*jāta*) and so forth is Being alone (*sanmātra*), and not this [world]; thus he says: "The word 'born'. The meaning is: "How is it a synonym for Being alone? Listen, and I shall demonstrate it. The verbal root *jan*—as in *janī prādurbhāve* ("to be born" means "to manifest")—is stated by Pāṇini and others to have the sense of manifestation. In that context, *prāduḥ* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*).
The root *bhū* itself, while indicating the manifestation of the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), is its subordinate body; that is to say, it is its primary form. || 16 ||
The root *bhū* is said to have "existence" (*sattā*) as its sole meaning; therefore, that which has arisen from it is called "born.
When it is said "born from creation," it is designated by the term *sansarga*.
"Let it be so; what follows from that? To this he replies: "The meaning is existence" (*sattārtha*). For the verbal root *bhū* is taught by Pāṇini and others as "being" (*bhū sattāyām*).

Therefore, arising from the word *bhāva* together with the prefix *pra*, it is called "manifest" (*prakaṭa*) when it has the sense of existence. One should understand that because it resembles a prefix (*upasarga*), it functions as a prefix. That...

And the meaning is that [it] is indeed the eternally established, self-luminous conscious Self (*svaprakāśacidātman*). Even if the word *prāduḥ* has the meaning "from creation" (*sargataḥ*), there is no defect whatsoever; for even in the case of the word *sarga*, when the suffix *ghañ* is added to the root *sṛj* in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*), and that abstract state in the form of existence (*sattā*) is construed non-differently with the object of the root *sṛj*, the meaning is that what is designated as "creation" (*sarga*) is precisely that which exists (*san*), and nothing else. || 17 ||
For the wise, such as ourselves, nothing at all is born, nor does anything perish; everything is peaceful, unborn, and real.

This being so, he says "of the wise" (budhānām) [in verse 18], meaning that from the perspective of the learned, birth and so forth, which are well-known among ignorant people, do not belong to anyone as established reality.
Brahman consists of the existence of all beings; the world consists of the existence of all beings.
Tell me, what injunctions and prohibitions could possibly apply there? (19)
Thus, since Brahman consists of the essence of all beings, there is no room even for the affirmation or negation of things—such as "it exists" or "it does not exist.
To this effect, he says: "All... (verse 19).
Whatever power there may be exists both in that very [Brahman] and does not exist [therein];
for that Brahman is of the nature of that, and likewise the self is of the nature of that.

Then, showing what is the object of the worldly convention of "existence" and "non-existence," he says in the second [verse]: "That which is called... (*yā nāma*). This refers to the power of *māyā*. Because that Brahman is variegated by it, it is the self of the ignorant; he explains the term "its self" (*tadātma*) with the words "just so" (*tathaiva*). In whatever manner the power of *māyā* unfolds, in that very same manner is the Self.
The meaning is that the referent of the word "ātman" (self) is that whose essential nature is constituted by all powers, being of the nature of each and every one of them. || 20 ||
For the wise who know the ultimate reality of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and so forth, nothing at all exists as it appears to be situated. // 21 //

But for those who know reality—who are always established in the fourth state (turyapada)—the states of waking and so forth do not even exist, let alone injunctions and prohibitions; thus he says, "waking," etc. "Of the knowers" means of the wise. (21)
Just as there is not even the slightest form existing in dreams or in cities of the imagination, despite their state of being experienced, so it is with the world at the beginning of creation.
He dispels the doubt that it is difficult to deny what is directly perceived by those who have experienced it, by means of two examples, beginning with the words "In a dream" (svapne). || 22 ||
Indeed, in this world, the individual soul (jīva) arises as the witness of this dream-vision;
yet at the beginning of creation, consciousness shines forth, clearer than even the sky, being itself beyond the object of cognition.

In that case, just as the seer of dreams and mental desires is the individual soul (jīva) possessed of vital breaths and so forth, so too at the beginning of creation, Brahman would be established as possessing vital breaths and so forth, rather than being without attributes. To this he says: "The seer. Since those two [dreams and desires] occur after the creation of the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of the individual soul, the soul is possessed of vital breaths and so forth as their seer; however, prior to the production of vital breaths and the rest, the seer of the creation and so forth remains as pure [Brahman].
The meaning is: "Thus, consider it so. || 23 ||
Here there is no seer, nor is there an enjoyer; everything here is of such a nature that it is neither something nor nothing, being both silence and yet beyond all speech.
Having provisionally accepted creation, the purity of its observer was stated. But in reality, the entire threefold division (tripuṭī) ceases right here in the Pure One;
thus he says, "not here. Such is that which consists solely of the essence of consciousness. 24.

At the beginning of creation, due to the absence of any other cause, whatever is manifested in consciousness remains for a long time in that very form, just like the cities of dreams or mental constructs.
He says that even at the beginning of creation, consciousness itself shines forth in the form of the creation and remains exactly so until dissolution: "At the beginning of creation," etc. (25).
Thus, from this conscious non-duality, one either fears or does not fear,
just as a person himself does not fear his own form depicted on his body.

Thus, in the manner described, one fears duality—which is essentially non-different from the conscious Self—due to the delusion of otherness arising from ignorance. Or, through the realization of reality, one does not fear. The word "vā" (or) signifies a fixed alternative. The meaning is that just as a child fears a painting of a tiger, a snake, or the like on his own limb, whereas an adult does not fear it, so it is here. || 26 ||
Without beginning, middle, or end, infinite, one, and utterly transparent, yet appearing as manifold through extreme transformation;
though it exists as it is, radiant yet unappeased, this entire universe is indeed perfectly tranquil.

In reality, Brahman alone—which is without beginning, middle, or end, and is utterly pure—appears through delusion as manifold and subject to great transformation, even though it remains exactly as it is. The meaning is that this world, though appearing unpeaceful, is in truth perfectly tranquil through awakening. || 27 ||
Thus ends the one hundred and forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Investigation of Deep Sleep," in the *Vasiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa*, the *Vālmīkīya-deśopadeśa-mokṣopāya*, within the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa*.
Thus ends the one hundred and forty-sixth chapter, titled "An Inquiry into Deep Sleep," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and forty-seventh canto. The Sage said:
"O mighty-armed one, immediately after I had emerged from deep sleep..."
In a dream, this visible world emerged as if from the ocean. || 1 ||
In this context, the process of emerging from sleep is described through analogies with deep sleep,
and therein the reality of perceiving one's former family and so forth is explained.

It is like waves, gems, pearls, and so forth, emerging from the ocean; here, wherever it is possible, this should be understood as a simile (upamā), and where it is impossible, as a poetic fancy (utprekṣā). || 1 ||
As if carved from the limbs of space, as if carved from the earth, as if carved from the mind, or as if carved from the very sight itself. (2)
"Engraved" means manifested by means of cutting with a chisel and so forth, like a stone image. (2)
It was like a blossoming from trees, like a creation arisen in the beginning, like a mass of waves on the shore of the ocean, or like a manifestation of visions. || 3 ||
The meaning is that he was already arisen and pre-established from before, not something produced at that moment; thus he appeared.
He was like a mass of waves from the ocean near a riverbank or shore, or like the shimmering of eyes through the appearance of optical illusions such as clusters of hair or double moons. || 3 ||
It was as if it had descended from the vault of heaven, as if it had come from the cardinal directions,
as if it were carved out from the mountains, or as if it had arisen from the earth.
It has arisen from the earth, like a wall or an anthill.
It seemed as if it had emerged from his heart, entered into the clouds,
been produced from trees, or grown from the earth like a crop.
It was as if the sky had entered the clouds through a transformation into a strange form, like a crop.
As if emerging from his limbs, as if carved out by his senses,
as if manifested from a cloth, or as if issued forth from his very palace.
It was as if engraved in the directions by the sense-faculties acting like chisels, as if produced by carving, or as if spread out;
it was like a painting manifested upon a cloth. || 6 ||
Existence (saṃsāra) is as if it has fallen from somewhere, as if flying down from the sky,
or as if it were a gift received in another world.

It was like a tribute brought by the subjects for kings; it was like merit accumulated in this world appearing as its fruit in the next world; or it was like a treasure-trove extracted from the earth through means such as digging.
It is like a flower of the Brahma-tree, or a wave of the ocean of speech; it is a beautiful statue within the pillar of consciousness, made manifest without being carved.
Like a flower brought forth in due time from the tree that bears the characteristics of a Brahmin, such was the statue— a manifestation made manifest without even being carved out.
The infinite walls are made of clay from space, and the city is within space;
the mind is like an intoxicated elephant—thus is the false life of the living being.

The wall is an infinite and incalculable transformation of clay possessing the nature of space; it is the playful sport consisting of the elephant-like mind; it is one's entire life and all that one possesses. (9)
And there was a variegated painting in the sky without a wall, the entire wealth of a certain Śambareśa known as Ignorance (avidyā). 10.
Śambara’s magic is the entire treasury of illusion belonging to a certain magician named Avidyā, who is capable and powerful. 10.
Though it involves great exertion and is steadfast, it is devoid of space and time;
though it appears manifold and richly diverse, it is non-dual; and though it seems to possess many selves, it is nothing at all.
Because it is seen to possess extension and duration even while its spatial and temporal subtlety remains, it is devoid of space and time.
The analogy of the city of the Gandharvas is also equal [to the dream] in its lack of reality; for even that which is an illusion is indeed perceived during the waking state. (12)

Whatever is perceived even during the waking state as an error—such as a snake in a rope, water in a mirage, and so forth—it is understood by implication to be equal to that [dream experience]. || 12 ||
Consisting of pure consciousness alone, though unoriginated, it remains as if originated,
joined with space, time, action, substance, and the processes of creation and dissolution.
It was as enchanting as the womb containing the embryos of gods, demons, and men,
like a pomegranate filled with a multitude of seeds situated within separate compartments.
It is as charming as the trunk of a plantain tree, with its internal cavities— the supports of the three worlds characterized by gods, demons, and others— and their own further cavities; moreover,
because of the conception of infinite Brahmāṇḍas within those intermediate cavities, it stands like a pomegranate fruit filled with a multitude of seeds situated in separate compartments.
It was filled with rivers, mountains, forests, and the like, crowded with the sky, stars, and clouds;
it resounded with the humming of the wind, enriched by the singing, oceanic chanting, and recitations [of the Vedas]. 15.
He elaborates on that very point with the words "the river," etc.; the sense is according to the analogy of a slab of gold. || 15 ||
Then, as I looked there at that circle of visible objects,
I beheld that very same village, my former dwelling place.

I saw—that is, I beheld—that village seen in the dream of my previous entry, as well as that former dwelling-house there; [this is expressed with the present tense] because of the rule regarding the particles *yāvat* and *purā*. 16.
He saw all those very same kinsmen standing in their respective positions,
those same sons, that same wife, and that very same house at that time.
"Of such a form" means having the configuration of the physical state and arrangement previously experienced; [he saw] a woman, that is, his wife. || 17 ||
Seeing that former rustic impression, she forcibly seized it,
just as a wave in the great ocean seizes a bystander whose limbs are being overwhelmed.

In the great ocean, the wave forcibly seizes and brings back the former shore-dweller who was deluded and agitated—as if it were his own body—the former vulgar latent impression (*vāsanā*) consisting of the conceit of ownership regarding house, field, sons, kinsmen, and so forth;
this is the specific qualification of "kinsmen, sons, wife, and house. In that regard, according to the rule *napuṃsakamanapuṃsakena* (Pāṇini 1.2.69), [the singular form is used].
In the case of a remainder consisting of neuter nouns, there is a singular collective form.
Then I was there, blissful from that embrace; surely, with my latent impressions grasped, I had forgotten my former memory. (19)
He was satisfied and happy by the embrace of those sons of his kinsmen. || 19 ||
Whatever object stands before it, that very reflection it assumes;
in its very nature, this mirror of consciousness is just like an ordinary mirror. (20)
In this context, he elaborates upon the natures of the unexamined and examined consciousness through the verse beginning with "bimba" (the original object),
and so forth: Just as a well-known mirror takes on the reflection of whatever stands before it, even though it is itself [unmoving],
so too the mirror of consciousness subsequently assumes the appearance of the forms of whatever was previously present, brought forth by latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
The meaning is "he grasps. || 20 ||
But he who possesses the realization that "all is the sky of pure consciousness" is not awakened here by duality; O dear one, he remains as the absolute alone.

But for one whose consciousness has been thoroughly investigated, this is not his true nature; thus he says, "But he who... He is not awakened by duality consisting of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), such as the grasping of reflections and so forth. The intended meaning is based on the principle stated by the Blessed One: "That which is day for beings is night for the sage who sees. Alternatively, the reading *bādhyate* (is sublated) may be used. || 21 ||
He whose stainless memory, endowed with awakening, does not perish—this demon of duality does not afflict him even in the slightest. (22)
He states that very point: "No," [verse 22].
For those through whose practice of yoga and association with holy persons and excellent scriptures the awakening intellect arises, which, once arisen, never again forgets its emergence. (23)
If that awakened intellect, once arisen, does not forget its own arising, the meaning is that it remains forever in the nature of constant contemplation of Brahman. || 23 ||
At that time, my intellect regarding awakening was immature, and it was by that [ignorance] that I was struck down;
who today could possibly destroy my intellect, even if they were a malignant planet? (24)
If that is so, how can he be a knower of reality? To address the doubt that he might still be deluded, he says: "aprauḍha" (immature).

If his intellect (*dhī*) was immature and thus struck down by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of relatives and the like, then one might ask: is his intellect of awakening still immature even now? He answers: "adya" (now). "Durgraha" refers to the accumulation of difficult-to-eradicate latent impressions. || 24 ||
O hunter, know this: even your intellect, being devoid of the company of the virtuous, will attain peace only with great difficulty through the arduous realization of duality.

"O hunter, because even your intellect is devoid of the company of the virtuous, it does not attain peace right now; rather, after attaining knowledge through the hardship of dualistic perception—by means of the bodily growth, death, and rebirth resulting from the austerities to be described, and through the exertion of practicing the spiritual means—you will eventually reach peace. (25)
The hunter said:
"O sage, this is true;
yet even by such purifying instructions of yours, my mind does not find rest in the state of the virtuous. (26)
Consenting to what was spoken by the sage, the hunter said: "It is even so. || 26 ||
The web of doubt—whether it might be thus or not so—does not subside even today regarding this reality, despite its being directly experienced by oneself. (27)
Alas! This ignorance, though it exists only as a latent tendency, has been made so firm by habit that, though already stilled, it does not subside. (28)
Being always non-existent, it is eternally quiescent and yet does not cease.

It is my firm conviction that this delusion of the world comes to rest through practice— by means of association with the virtuous, by an intellect awakened to the words and their meanings, and by limbs [of the mind] made charming through inquiry into the true scriptures and the authentic path— and not by any other means whatsoever. (29)

Consenting also to what was said—that [the path] is "devoid of association with the virtuous"—he says: "Through associations with the virtuous. By means of delightful components such as sacred scriptures (*sacchāstra*), the authentic sequence (*san krama*), the lineage of the Guru (*gurusaṃpradāya*), and inquiry (*vicāra*), there arises a single-minded cognition of words and their meanings born from association with the virtuous; and from the awakening to reality produced by the repeated practice of that, this [realization] occurs through the gradual stages (*bhūmikākrama*).
The delusion of the world comes to rest; it does not come to rest by any other means whatsoever—this is my firm conviction, meaning my certain resolve. || 29 ||
Thus ends the one hundred and forty-seventh canto, titled "The Perception of the Dream," in the Śava-upākhyāna of the Bālakāṇḍa of the glorious Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa, composed by the Sage.
Thus ends the one hundred and forty-seventh sarga, titled "The Perception of Dreams," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and forty-eighth canto (148).
The hunter said:
If this is so, O best of sages, how can there be truth and untruth?
This very great doubt remains within me regarding one who stands as a dreamer. (1)
In this [work], the reason for the truth or falsity of dreams is investigated;
it is endowed with the unity of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, as well as the purity of the unity of the all-pervading consciousness.

If the established doctrine is that both dream and waking are merely consciousness-experience following from latent impressions (*vāsanā*), and that the waking state is indeed a specific kind of dream, then [one must conclude]: for a dreamer, a certain dream—such as riding an elephant seen at dawn—is real because it indicates a result such as gain;
whereas another dream—such as wandering through a forest—is unreal because no such result is observed. Thus it is with dreamers.

How can reality and unreality be logically established? Thus, even within the waking world, this very great doubt remains before me: "The creation devoid of the mind of Hiraṇyagarbha is real because it is capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), whereas our own creation is unreal. [To this, the reply is: The reality of that which is superimposed is due to the reality of the underlying substrate-consciousness (*adhiṣṭhāna-cit*); its unreality, however, is intrinsic.
The sense is: if it is indeed equal in both cases, then what is the reason for the discrepancy? || 1 ||
The Sage said:
That consciousness which arises with certainty through place, time, action, and substance,
appearing as if by chance like the "crow-and-palm" coincidence, is known as a true dream.
That dream-consciousness which occurs in a place such as the presence of the Mistress of Dreams (Svapneśvarī), at a time such as dawn,

and which is determined by scriptural authorities and so forth to have a specific result for such a dream— due to practices such as the worship of deities, austerities, and vows, and through materials such as sacrificial offerings and mats of kuśa grass— is necessarily of that nature.

That consciousness arises—like the bird that happens upon the fruit of the "crow-and-fig" coincidence—and because of the certain attainment of the result at a later time, it becomes what is called a "true dream. || 2 ||
Cognition arising from gems, mantras, medicinal herbs, and substances is in some cases non-deviant and in some cases deviant; it is known as "true dream" (satyasvapna). (3)

The meaning is as follows: although that which arises through causes such as gems and mantras is unfailing when directed toward a person suitable for it, yet even if it is fallible when directed toward one unsuitable, it is nevertheless remembered by the name "true dream" in both cases, because it does not transgress the boundaries established by the scriptures. || 3 ||
When such a state of true dreaming exists among the worlds, then,
by the logic of the crow and the palm fruit, no other [state] is obtained.

In this regard, since the "crow-and-the-palm-fruit" maxim (*kākatālīyanyāya*) is the only refuge in both cases, and no other regulating factor can be perceived or formulated, he says with this intention: "satya... (Verse 4).
Whatever determination consciousness adopts when its own certainty is not firm,
it becomes exactly like that, by virtue of having a nature conjoined with the fruit.

The consciousness of Hiraṇyagarbha and others, being born from the ripening of previous meditative practice (*upāsanā*), consists of a firm conviction in the form of true resolve (*satya-saṃkalpa*); thus, whatever determination it adopts, it becomes exactly so. This is stated in the words "whichever [determination]... (*yaṃ yam*).
By virtue of his own nature, which is impelled by the fruit of his former worship. || 5 ||
But if another person were to subvert that very certainty of hers,
how could that mature certainty be considered a valid object of perception?
To the question, "Why is she not thwarted by another's true resolve that is contrary to hers? he says: "That very [resolve]...

If someone else were to subvert her certainty regarding the creation and so forth, then the mature conviction held during the time of her previous meditation—"I am the creator of the world"—which arose at the time of her departure, is indeed the conqueror of this world.

How could one who partakes in the fruit of his own specific goal, as established by such scriptural passages (śruti), be otherwise? Therefore, the intention of other perfected beings (siddhas) arises only in non-contradiction with that [scriptural authority], and not in opposition to it; this is the intended meaning. || 6 ||
Nowhere do any objects exist either externally or internally;
consciousness alone, according to its own will, remains manifest in the forms of the world.
And thus, he says "no" [in verse 7] to show that the sovereignty of consciousness remains entirely unimpeded.
When this dream is spoken of with the internal conviction that "this dream is true," it immediately becomes so; likewise, through doubt, it shall lead to doubt.

Through the certainty produced by the authority of the scriptures and other means of valid cognition; however, from doubt regarding the authority of the scriptures and so forth, one would incur doubt regarding the result. || 8 ||
Even when a result is obtained from another source, because of the conceptualization of its truth through a dream, this person understands it simply as "this result was indicated by a dream. (9)
He explains what was stated as "like the maxim of the crow and the palm fruit" with the words: "from another [cause]. || 9 ||
All things in the three worlds, though firm and superior in their own consciousness,
deviate from their state due to time, place, or effort— whether after a long duration or in an instant.

Thus, he says "all indeed," meaning that even the cognitions of jars and so forth, which are well-known during the waking state, are merely accidental (kākatālīya), because it is observed that even regarding those objects, they undergo transformation due to differences in place and time. These [cognitions] are surpassed by their own respective individual cognitions, having been long cultivated through purposeful action and the like.

Even all entities whose natures, such as that of a jar, have been rendered firm, undergo alteration in terms of place, time, and through efforts such as the blow of a mallet; thus, they deviate from their previously determined nature. (10)
At the very beginning of creation, the world appears as an unobstructed manifestation within the sky of consciousness;
therefore, consciousness alone, assuming form, extends its own substantial existence as it desires.

He states the established conclusion (*rāddhānta*)—namely, that because consciousness does not deviate from its own intrinsic nature, it is non-deviating and has a non-obstructive (*apratigha*) nature; thus, while being real, it assumes the form of the unreal and obstructive world of hatred. He says this in the verse beginning with "at the beginning of creation" (*sargādau*). || 11 ||
Know that, excluding the one Brahman which is pure consciousness alone, everything else—
whether existent or non-existent, fixed or unfixed— is always situated as such.

For this very reason, he says "pure consciousness" (cinmātram) [in verse 12], meaning that pure consciousness is restricted to being the sole reality, whereas everything else is restricted to having a non-real existence.
Since Brahman alone is the self of all, being one and truly existent and nothing else, what then could possibly be real, or what could be unreal? (13)
Since the existent Brahman alone is the single Self of all, what else—whether real or unreal—could one conceive apart from it?
The meaning is: nothing at all. || 13 ||
Therefore, a dream is sometimes real and sometimes indeed unreal;
for the unawakened it is not of the nature of non-existence, nor for the awakened is it composed of existence.

Thus, upon such investigation, even a dream is sometimes true and sometimes untrue; yet, in its nature as consciousness (*saṃvidātman*), it is true, while in any other form it is untrue—so he says: "Therefore," etc. (14).
This delusion of consciousness appears under the name of the world as its very nature;
and since it itself declares, "I am a delusion," who here can be certain? (15)
Svarūpiṇī means possessing form; niścitā means corresponding to reality. || 15 ||
It is consciousness alone that, for a long time, causes this mind to shimmer;
when it is like water within the Self itself, this world flows forth as a liquid.
The word "having become mind" is to be understood as the ellipsis. That which flickers and vibrates with appearance—that alone is this world. || 16 ||
Just as, having perceived a dream, deep sleep is experienced, so too, having perceived the waking state, sleep is experienced. (17)

He prepares the introductory context (*bhūmikā*) to demonstrate that waking, dreaming, and deep sleep are indeed non-different from one another, like solidified ghee and melted ghee—thus he says, "Just as" (*yathā*). Here, *nidrā* refers to dreaming. || 17 ||
Therefore, O high-minded one, know this waking state to be indeed a dream;
and know that dream to be waking—these two are one, unborn.

"Let it be so; what follows from that? To this he replies with the word "ataḥ" (from this). The meaning is: just as ghee that is slightly melted becomes solid again once it has been slightly melted, there is no difference between them because of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*); it is just like that. || 18 ||
This entire expanse is but the manifestation of the one, non-objective pure consciousness;
what are called waking, dreaming, and deep sleep are merely sequential arrangements within it. (19)

And thus, deep sleep alone—which is of the nature of pure consciousness veiled by ignorance—should always be regarded as being like clarified butter (*ghṛta*); the result is that all distinctions of name and form are merely its various arrangements. He states this in the verse beginning with "just as the sky" (*vyomaiva*). || 19 ||
In this [dream-consciousness], there is no such thing as necessity, nor is there any lack of necessity.
Tell me, what kind of necessity and lack of necessity exist within the consciousness of a dream? (20)

He says "not so" (neha) because the necessity and non-necessity of the results of dreams and the like do not exist apart from that [reality]. He further says "necessity and non-necessity" (niyatyaniyatī) because they do not exist apart from that even due to their falsity. || 20 ||
To whatever extent there is an appearance in a dream, to that same extent there is that very constraint; the sage alone can effect the regulation of the appearance of consciousness.
Consciousness (cit), when veiled by ignorance and uncontrolled, constitutes the states of waking and dreaming; when controlled by causes such as fatigue, it is deep sleep (suṣupti);

and when controlled by effort, it is meditative absorption (samādhi). Upon the destruction of ignorance, that very consciousness is liberation (mukti). This being so, during the time that consciousness appears in the state of dreaming—which consists merely of mental activity through the cessation of waking—it is that same consciousness [that persists].

The interval between external activity and its restraint is the interval of sorrow; however, as long as there is restraint of the manifestation of consciousness, so long in deep sleep that very Self is the end of all sorrow. Having understood this, the sage, desiring rest in the bliss of sorrowless samādhi, should practice restraint alone—this is the meaning. || 21 ||
Just as the movement of a gust of wind is independent, so too is consciousness; O dear one, since it is entirely without cause, what could destiny be, and of what nature?

Now, one might object: "Consciousness cannot be restricted, because its manifestation in the forms of dreams and so forth is as unpredictable as a gust of wind. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "At its own will" (*svacchandam*). The manifestation of the form of an object is not the inherent nature (*svabhāva*) of consciousness, since it is not observed during deep sleep. Nor [is it the nature] in a dream...
Thus, it is impossible to determine another cause for such manifestation upon which "niyati" (destiny/fate) would depend;
the meaning is: what is this "niyati," and of what nature is it? || 22 ||
Now, whatever name such as "A" (ākāra) and so forth is imagined as the cause of consciousness, that is itself causeless; for the creation is not other than consciousness. || 23 ||

[Objection: "But surely, in relation to its own connection, it is the very form of external objects such as jars and cloths that is postulated as the cause for consciousness having its own form. To this, he says: "Now (atha). This would indeed be so if some other cause for creation could be determined; however, when—by the reasoning previously stated—creation is shown to be without cause, then form and the rest are not other than consciousness, but are [identical] to consciousness.
The meaning is that it would simply not be a cause at all. || 23 ||
In this matter, such is the very nature of necessity:
that whatever appears in whatever manner, to the extent that it has manifested as a perception, it is exactly so and not otherwise.

If so, has all necessity (niyati) been destroyed? No; he says: "only to this extent. The meaning is that whatever consciousness manifests in whatever manner at whatever time—that object is then real, whether ultimate (pāramārthika), empirical (vyāvahārika), or apparent (prātibhāsika);
thus, necessity exists indeed as long as worldly transaction (vyavahāra) persists. || 24 ||
Sometimes there is truth in a dream, and sometimes there is untruth;
due to the very absence of fixed necessity, that is merely a "crow-and-palmyra-fruit" coincidence.

He states that the certainty regarding the truth of dreams is already explained as being like the "crow-and-the-palmyra-fruit" maxim—occurring everywhere simply by virtue of following the scriptures—in the words "kadācit" (sometimes). || 25 ||
That which shines by its own nature through the essence of gems, mantras, and medicinal herbs—whatever is indeed fixed as such—is seen even in the waking state. (26)

He states that even in the case of waking cognition, the certainty regarding the truth of what is employed by means of gems, mantras, and medicinal herbs is established through convergence, saying "That which... [yad iti].
Waking and dreaming are merely the manifestation of consciousness; what difference is there here?
In the waking state, the city of dreams is of a similar nature because it is perceived as such.
For this very reason, it is said that there is no difference between waking and dreaming because both consist of pure consciousness (cinmātra). Thus he says: "jāgrad... [and so forth].
He states that for one who experiences them, the nature of the object of knowledge (vedya) or the nature of the knowing (vedana) is exactly the same in both states: "jāgrati... || 27 ||
That which is designated by the word "waking" does not exist at all as waking;
the form of the world is merely a dream of the Self, even though that Self is truly sleepless. (28)

For this very reason, since there is a deviation in both cases regarding the self when it is free from sleep, he states that [the self] is indeed non-existent by means of the two verses beginning with "jāgrat" (while waking).
Indeed, that which is called "dream" does not exist at all;
it is simply the nature of consciousness of Brahman, whose single form is both sleeping and non-sleeping. (29)
These states of waking, dreaming, and so forth do not exist at all times;
one perceives the visible world only momentarily, immediately following the delusion of death.
This being so, with the intention that even deep sleep (*suṣupti*) does not exist for one who is sleepless, he says: "jāgrad" (waking).
Likewise, he says that even death—in the form of the absolute non-perception of the visible world, or in the form of the annihilation of the self—does not exist:
"Just as for an infinite time, without interruption, the waves of spray [continue to rise]..."
These very [entities] flash forth intensely as non-different from one another, like clouds that are not distinct from one another.

Just as in a cloud-like delusion of the quarters, the directions (āśā) and the points of the compass (diśaḥ) appear as if they were other than what they are; though non-different, they manifest as if different. The term "ananyāḥ" is a bahuvrīhi compound. || 31 ||
Likewise, other creations, whether manifest or unmanifest, do not exist as something separate from Him;
what then is the difference between waking and sleep there, which are like lines within the interior of a stone?
Having the nature of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the fourth state; devoid of form yet possessing all forms; bearing the body of creation while transcending all mental construction;
pervaded by the body of consciousness yet hollow with the void of the objective world—this is the sky of pure consciousness.
Furthermore, it is not even slightly different from the mere space itself.
This nature of the Self—consisting of the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, as well as the state of the Fourth (turya) which is their opposite;

devoid of form yet possessing all forms; transcending the calculation of time, yet bearing a body delimited by time in the form of creation—is, by this very void of consciousness and this very void of the nature of the visible, nothing but the void of space itself.

Although it is hollow, empty, and pervasive, nevertheless this is pure consciousness (cinmātra), whose nature is space (kha) or ether; the meaning is that it is not even slightly different from the form of mere space (nabhomātrā). || 33 ||
At the beginning of creation, it contains within itself the sky, wind, fire, water, earth, and the clouds at the ends of the worlds;
yet, because it does not experience any external cause, it consists solely of the nature of consciousness.
It is devoid of even a name, ultimately joined with the very form of awakening, pure, and consisting of nothing but pure awareness.
The entire visible world is not a separate entity.

Furthermore, since no other cause for the visible world—including all elements such as space and their derivatives—is perceived through any means of valid cognition even at the time of creation, the entire world is essentially of the nature of the mind of Hiraṇyagarbha. And thus, because that which consists of the mind lacks names and forms as found in a mental fantasy, it is indeed devoid of name. By virtue of its conscious nature...
It is indeed conjoined with the witness of the mind; ultimately, upon the dissolution of the mind, it is pure awareness alone and not a separate entity—this is the meaning. || 34 ||
Thus ends the one hundred and forty-eighth canto, titled "The Determination of the Dream," in the Uttarakāṇḍa of the Nirvāṇa section of the Arṣa Śrī Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa.
Thus ends the one hundred and forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Determination of Dreams," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and forty-ninth canto.
The hunter said:
"O Sage, next tell me that true reality of yours concerning the world."
What is the conduct of one for whom the cycle of worldly existence has been extinguished by hundreds of great accounts? || 1 ||
In this context, what was heard from the mouth of the sage who had come to his house regarding that dream-incident—
namely, the cause of the equal suffering and so forth experienced by many— is now being related.

O Sage, you whose worldly existences have been extinguished along with hundreds of vast events such as dissolution within the bodies of living beings—tell me that reality which pertains to the worldly occurrences experienced there [in that state] following your dwelling with wife, kinsmen, and others in your home. This is the grammatical connection. || 1 ||
The sage said:
O virtuous one, you who long for the conduct of the righteous, listen then to what unprecedented event occurred at that time within the vital energy of his heart.

O virtuous one who desires good conduct, listen to that unprecedented event which occurred thereafter within the vital energy of that living being's heart. The use of "ya" (who) in the sense of "ka" (what) serves the purpose of inquiry and restatement. || 2 ||
In that same way, for me— who remained there, having forgotten the wonder of my own self—
time passed in the form of seasons and years.
For me, whose mind was captivated by my wife, sixteen years passed there while I remained in the householder stage of life, devoid of wisdom.
Of one who lacks wisdom, that is, one who is devoid of self-reflective contemplation. || 4 ||
Then, on one occasion, a sage of fierce asceticism, venerable, possessed of great awakening, and wise, came to my house as a guest.
Once, the wise sage came to my house as a guest; "so it was," [meaning] he followed up with an affirmative reply. || 5 ||
Thus honored there, he was pleased; then, having slept and awakened, O dear one, he reflected upon the conduct of the people and spoke this as he was questioned by me.

That is to say, he first ate and then slept; the multitude—that is, the mass of people—having reflected upon and considered the sequence of the occurrence of similar pleasure and pain for itself. || 6 ||
O Blessed One, you possess vast awakening and you know the destinies of the world;
for this reason, anger is never seen in you, nor do you take delight in pleasure.
In happiness, [they find] delight and attachment toward a mere fragment of sensual pleasure. || 7 ||
For those devoted to action, pleasures and pains arrive through their deeds—
whether auspicious or inauspicious— just as crops come to those seeking fruit in the autumn season.
Why do all these creatures perform equally unwholesome karma, since their faults, such as greed and the rest, manifest equally? (9)

Since these "all-eaters" (sarvādyaḥ)— referring to calamities such as famine— consume and cause all people to eat everything, whether edible or inedible, do they perform their inauspicious causal karma simultaneously when these misfortunes occur at the same time? || 9 ||
Why do famine, drought, and portents arise simultaneously for everyone? Whose similar misdeeds bear fruit upon the masses of people alike? (10)

If that which proceeds as equal were to be the same for everyone, then what would constitute a "bad action" (duṣkriyā) for whom? The meaning is that it is impossible for all to simultaneously perform actions that are conducive to such [a result]. || 10 ||
Having heard this and gazed upon him, as if smiling with a mind uplifted in ecstasy,
he spoke these venerable words, beautiful as a flow of nectar.
Smiling, as if filled with wonder, with his mind uplifted, or perhaps laughing slightly. || 11 ||
Another sage said: "O virtuous one, well done! Tell me, by what cause do you know whether this visible world is real or unreal, since your inner mind is so purified?"

Thinking that it is impossible to resolve doubt without first eliminating ignorance—the seed of all doubt—that sage questioned me for that purpose, in order to explain the reality of the Self and the falsity of the visible world:
"Tell me, by what cause do you know whether something exists or does not exist? How do you know it? You say, 'I know'."

The ablative case in the word "kasmāt" (from what) is used as a causal ablative to indicate that the pure witness, being distinguished from the aforementioned cognizer, is the object of the inquiry. || 12 ||
"Remember your entire self: who are you, and where do you stand here?
Where am I, what is this visible world, and what indeed is its essence? (13)

Seeing me there, having become silent due to my inability to discern [the truth], he said, "Remember," so that I might remember myself as the witness of all previous events along with those occurrences: "O friend, why do you not know that this which appears is merely a dream—something trivial and indeed devoid of essence? (13)
I am a man in a dream, and you are like a man in a dream. [The reading "mama" is also found. || 14 ||
It reveals its very lack of essence with the words "merely a dream. This is because of the reason [indicated by] "yad" (since). || 14 ||
Formless, inexpressible, beginningless, and beyond conceptualization—this world exists as a mere shimmering reflection within the mirror of pure consciousness. 15.
Kācakacyam is a particular kind of luster. || 15 ||
Such is the innate form of this pure consciousness alone:
that which is omnipresent, whatever exists wherever it may be, that very thing is its form there.

In this regard, he says "rūpam" (the form), meaning that the uncreated nature of pure consciousness (cinmātra) brings forth the qualities of sattva and so on within its own superimpositions, according to how they are perceived. || 16 ||
By conceiving of him as having a cause, everything becomes possessed of a cause;
by conceiving of him as being without a cause, everything becomes without a cause. || 17 ||

For this very reason, he states that even the doctrines asserting that all things possess causes and so forth are established in accordance with that conceptual construction: "sakāraṇatva... (verse 17).
But for us, these creatures, that Virāṭ is the pervasive Self;
we abide within His heart, and He [abides] here by the power of our consciousness.
He says, "Of these," [to show] that even the conceptualization of the collective and individual states depends solely upon our own consciousness.

In the heart—that is, in the vital energy (*ojas*)—of whichever living being we reside, he is our *virāj*-self. And he has attained the state of *virāj* solely through the power of the conceptualization of our own consciousness; yet, by his own conceptualization, he is common to others as well.
The meaning is that it is indeed the individual manifestation. || 18 ||
He alone shall become another Virāṭ-ātman for the other women;
he is the cause of their pleasures and pains, and of their actions consisting of existence and non-existence.
It is conceivable that another living being, like this one, may become the Virāṭ-self for other classes of beings;

however, it is established that within that particular body, that very being alone is the cause through its status as the enjoyer of pleasure, pain, and so forth, and not any other—this is the meaning. "States" (bhāvāḥ) refers to prosperities; "non-states" (abhāvāḥ) refers to calamities; and "actions" (karmāṇi) refers to deeds.
Their good and evil deeds [follow them]. || 19 ||
Through the transformation of the elements of Virāj, by means of irregular throbbing and so forth, there arose simultaneously this multitude of people from the limbs and members of his body. (20)

Regarding the common sufferings of people, such as famine and drought, he states in two verses beginning with "Virāṭ" that the cause is simply a particular modification of the elements belonging to that Virāṭ, who is the gross universal aggregate (sthūla-samaṣṭi-rūpa) of each individual. || 20 ||
Whether it passes beyond the calamity of famine or comes to rest,
that which is the existence of Virāj is the very nature of this creation.
Famine, drought, the passing away [of prosperity], and destruction—their combination arrives or subsides according to the circumstances. To the question "Why is that? he says: "Because... (verse 21).
O virtuous one, like the "crow-and-palm" coincidence, suffering and other misfortunes fall equally upon certain people who have committed evil deeds, just as a thunderbolt falls upon trees.

It is said that even for those beings, there exists the ripening of their corrupt karma at the same time; thus: "By the chance occurrence of the crow and the palm fruit (kākatālīya), consciousness becomes a partaker of the fruits of its own karma through the conceptualization of karma;
when released from the conceptualization of karma, it is not a partaker of the fruits of karma. (23)
If such karma too was previously fashioned by consciousness alone, then it is that [consciousness] which partakes of its fruit and not anything else; thus he says: "Karma... (verse 23).
Whatever conceptualization arises in whatever place, whether slight or excessive, that very [conceptualization] remains there in that very way, whether it has a cause or is causeless. (24)
A conceptualization that has a cause exists as something that has a cause; however, a conceptualization that lacks a cause exists as something that lacks a cause. || 24 ||
In the city of the causal body and so forth, which is like a dream, there exists no auxiliary cause whatsoever;
therefore, that is the beginningless, auspicious, conscious, undecaying Supreme Brahman.
Nor does the causality of jars and other things exist in a dream merely by the conceptualization of having a cause;
thus, because a causeless world is not established, he says "it does not exist at all" (nāstyeva) to show that Brahman alone, which is pure consciousness, exists in the ultimate sense. || 25 ||
This so-called delusion of dream appears as something causeless;
some appear to have a cause, being empty and consisting of both the existent and the non-existent. (26)
Since it consists of both the existent and the non-existent, it is therefore empty and illusory. || 26 ||
All cognitions of dreams appear like the "crow-and-the-palm-fruit" coincidence;
because they are perceived as being identical to those [waking cognitions], this extended world is nothing other than them. (27)

He states that the principle explained regarding dreams should be understood as applying equally to the waking world as well, because the perception [of both] is identical: "It is like the maxim of the crow and the palm fruit.
There is nothing other than the consciousness (cit) or from the dream. || 27 ||
That which is established here by way of having a cause is "with cause";
that which is established here by way of lacking a cause is "without cause. || 28 ||
He states that even the established notions of having a cause and being without a cause are settled here just like in a dream: "By way of having a cause... (verse 28).
This world, arising through the sequence of cause and effect consisting of action and agent, is merely the manifestation of consciousness, like a dream;
it is the very nature of that which is called the Great Waking state. Therefore, the wise know all this to be the supreme peace.

The conclusion that what arises in a dream through the sequence of cause and effect is essentially nothing but the manifestation of consciousness (*citibhānamātra*) applies equally to this great, gross world known as the waking state; this is the remaining point. For that reason, the knowers of Brahman understand everything to be peaceful and supreme—this is the meaning. || 29 ||
"O Mahāmati, listen to which entities have no real cause:
what is the cause of intrinsic natures, and what is the cause of space here? (30)

[Objection: "Surely, let Brahman alone be the cause of all entities; and since they have a real cause, let them too be real. If that is so, how can everything be Brahman, or how can there be the non-duality of reality? To this, he says: "Those which have a real cause," etc. "O Mahāmati, in response to this doubt, I shall tell you the answer. You—"

Listen! What are those entities that you consider to have true causes, O long-lived one? Is truth the cause of things that are themselves real by nature? Or is truth the cause of things that are unreal by nature? And are they of the same class or of a different class? In the first two cases, from Brahman only Brahman would arise, not the world; in the second two cases, it would not [arise at all].

If the establishment of the reality of that which is born of Brahman results in its being causeless in effect, what would you have proven? Furthermore, we ask regarding all the Kalpas: what is the cause of space here?
In the first two Kalpas, there is no proof of a difference in the delimitors (avacchedaka) of the denotation of the word "space," and in the latter two, there is no proof of its reality.
Furthermore, what is the cause of the creation of the dense mass of the earth and other elements?
What is the cause of ignorance, and what is the cause of the Self-born (Svayambhū)? || 31 ||
He states that this same principle should be applied to earth and the other elements as well: "Of earth, etc. (verse 31).

At the beginning of creation, what could be the cause of the winds and of the fires? What could be the cause of the waters, which consist of mere sensation, and of that which is of the nature of space? (32)

Because its own nature cannot be defined apart from sensation, and because there is no means of proof for those things whose form is merely sensation, they are unestablished; thus, the void is of the nature of space. || 32 ||
What is the cause for the grasping of a physical body and the acquisition of a form by those who have died?
In this very manner, all creations proceed from the very beginning. (33)
In this very way, they proceed and revolve within the world,
like wheels in the sky when viewed for a long time by the eye.
Therefore, by the method of elimination, it is established that [these appearances] are causeless and consist of mere illusion; thus he says: "In this very way.
"Long observation" means experience over a long period of time, and [the phrase "seen through the vision of illusion"] refers to the perception produced by that. || 34 ||
In this very way, by means of the emanation proceeding in the form of Brahman,
the designations of earth and so forth were subsequently applied to that very same form of his own.
In the form of Brahmā, having the appearance of Hiraṇyagarbha, he himself gave the names "earth" and so forth to his own self, which consists of earth and the other elements. || 35 ||
In the prior sky of consciousness, creations appear like the movement of the wind;
they themselves bring about the conceptualization of the causes of the body. (36)

For this very reason, at first they form conceptions such as the body, karma, and so forth—which are extremely subtle like a kingdom of the mind—only after long practice do they become gross. || 36 ||
In whatever way it is imagined, Destiny assumes that very form as its body;
for this is the innate nature of the imagined consciousness.

In that regard, according to the first hypothesis, whatever is imagined in a certain way, its body becomes determined accordingly. And this is established by one's own experience regarding objects imagined by oneself; thus he says: "Of the imagined... (verse 37).
Whatever form consisting of light was first perceived by consciousness, that remains even today exactly as it was, being inherently nothing other than myself within consciousness itself. (38)
The altar prepared for the creation is the altar of Hiranyagarbha, which is conducive to the act of creation. || 38 ||
Furthermore, by another effort that is superior to it, that very consciousness is capable of being altered from that state once again by means of a great effort. (39)

He says "again" to indicate that even for the great, a change from their original conception occurs only at some time through very great efforts; the sense is, as in the case of Nandin, Nahuṣa, and others, who attained the state of gods, serpents, and so forth. (39)
Wherever a cause is conceptualized, there the essence belongs to causality;
that wherein no cause is conceptualized by the wise is the non-cause.
In some cases, such as with milk and the like, causes such as churning and heat are postulated for the transformation into curds and so forth;
however, he states that even such a postulation is impossible for [the transformation] of air and the like into solid or liquid states—thus: "is postulated" (kalpyate). || 40 ||
This world first appeared spread out like a whirlwind;
though it appeared as if real, it remains even now exactly as it was—unreal. (41)

In that regard, the appearance of the non-conscious (acit) within the conscious (cit) is not an effect, but rather an object of knowledge; however, because it was primary, he says it persists even now:
"like the whirlwind" (vātyāvarta). || 41 ||
Some, acting together, perform their own actions— both auspicious and inauspicious— and they obtain a fruit corresponding to those deeds;
