yet others encounter suffering that is entirely without cause, like a falling rock or a thunderbolt.
Numbering one thousand. || 42 ||

Regarding that which was asked by me—namely, whether all these beings perform equally unwholesome karma—he provides the answer and concludes with the words "saṃbhūya" (having come together): some individual souls, even when acting together, perform both wholesome and unwholesome karma, and they experience the fruit of that karma only after having come together; however, others...

Because they are devoid of the conceit of agency (*kartṛtvābhimāna*), even though they are non-doers, those thousands of *jīvanmuktas* encounter suffering that is indeed causeless; the meaning is that it is just as a rock on a mountain peak, though not having committed any evil deed, nevertheless experiences the fall of a thunderbolt. || 42 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Investigation into Causes," in the *Ārṣa* [text], the *Śrī Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa*, in the *Bālakāṇḍa*, in the *Māhātmya*, in the *Nirvāṇa*, in the *Uttara*, in the *Avimukta*, in the *Vasiṣṭha*, in the *Śata*, [chapter]. 149.
Thus ends the one hundred and forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Investigation of Causes," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and fiftieth canto.
The sage said:
By such a means as this, that sage then [acted].
Thus, having awakened, I have gone to that state by which the knowable has been fully known. || 1 ||
Through those words, there is here the awakening of one's own self and the co-existence of that [self] with the body;
until the capacity to leave the body is attained, the burning of the corpse and so forth are prescribed in response to the inquiry.

I, this very person, was thus awakened by that Sage through the reasoning previously described in such a manner that, by that awakening, at that very moment I attained the state of one who has known what is to be known—the knowledge of reality. || 1 ||
Therefore, because of her long-standing entreaty, he was not abandoned by me;
he dwelt there with him even after [the other] had died, and remained exactly so.

Captivated by her long-standing aspiration, her devotion, her compliance, her service, and that collection of virtues such as humility, he continued to dwell in that very house even while I was dead—being, as it were, already dead, due to my lack of self-reflection. And so it has been said by the elders: "Whether one is walking or standing, whether one is awake..."
"Or even while sleeping, he whose mind is not intent on inquiry is said to be dead. (2)
Behold this best of sages standing by your side— he by whom these words, auspicious like the rising of the moon, were spoken.
He shows that such a compassionate sage, my instructor, is currently right here by your side with the words "by whom" (yena). || 3 ||
By him, who destroys delusion, who knows the past and future of all that is visible, and who is like a sacrifice incarnate, this was spoken even before it was asked.
By Yajña, who had assumed a physical form—standing as if he were my own meritorious deeds such as sacrifices personified. || 4 ||
Agni said:
Having heard those words of the sage, the hunter then became as if visibly struck by the creation of a dream; why was he thus dejected, as if with a smile? (5)

Having heard those words of the sage, the hunter became as if dejected by his astonishment and doubt, wondering: "Is this creator of my dream, the sage who gave me that instruction, now actually present before my eyes? || 5 ||
The hunter said:
"O Sage, oh, this great wonder is difficult to bear in the mind;
it has been told to me today by you, who remove the torment of worldly existence."
He clearly expresses this very lack of confidence with the word "Aho" (Oh!). || 6 ||
That which was described in a dream is now being presented as a waking reality;
and yet it is actually obtained—O Sage, this is indeed wonderful! (7)

"What is that wonder which I have described? To this he says: "That which... The meaning is: that the sage who was described by me as my own teacher in a dream is now perceived directly while awake, and that I perceive him directly myself—that I know to be a wonder. || 7 ||
O Lord of Sages, how is it that this great person seen in a dream has become as stable even while awake, like [the conviction] of one with a child's intellect?
A vetāla that has come into being. || 8 ||
Tell me this wondrous narrative in due order:
from where, for whom, and what is this? For it is indeed a supreme marvel.

"Let this wondrous narrative be told to me in its entirety and in due order. From what cause did this vision of the man in the dream arise? To whom does this vision belong? Is it a dream, or is it waking reality?"
The sage said:
"Therefore, O illustrious one, listen to this wondrous account of mine;
I shall relate it to you in brief, so do not make me wait in haste. (10)
By this [means], that was then described there for my enlightenment;
and by those great words, I quickly became wise.
By this sage standing at your side. || 11 ||
Then, by these words, my own innate nature was first remembered by me—
pure as the clear sky at the end of the summer heat by means of that which is pure.

The former [self] has the nature of pure existence established from beginningless time. At the end of the heat—that is, at the end of the month of Māgha, meaning the end of the cold season—he thought:
"Oh, how wonderful! I have become that sage. Thus, with his heart expanded by this rising aspiration, he remained bathed in wonder. 13.
Then he says "Aho! because even his former state as a sage has come back to him through memory. Out of wonder at this, he was as if bathed and moistened in his heart. 13.
Through this attachment to enjoyments, I have reached this state like an ignorant traveler, running about afflicted by fatigue and seeking water in vain through a mirage. (14)

He laments that state with the verse beginning "This... and so forth: "Like a traveler afflicted by fatigue and seeking water, I have reached this state through a craving for enjoyments that is as futile as a mirage. (14)
Alas! Even the wise man is deceived by the perception of objects—which exist as mere illusion—just as a fool is deceived by a phantom. How strange! (15)
"Alas! How strange it is that by this dancing, false knowledge—devoid of all reality—I have been led to such a state! (16)
Or rather, even this "I" of mine is mere delusion and not composed of reality; nevertheless, it is called a hundredfold variety because that which is unreal is being feigned.

Alternatively, that which is the object of the recognition "I am he"—namely, the "that-ness" (*tattā*), the "I-ness" (*ahaṃtā*), and so forth—that too is mere illusion. Thus, one should not ask whose wonder it is; nevertheless, the meaning is that there is indeed a hundredfold wonder regarding that which is manifested as having a non-existent form by the Witness (*sākṣin*). || 17 ||
"I am not" [and "this is not I" is also a reading], nor indeed is this "this is not," for even that is an error; wonderful how all this is false, yet everything stands as if it were real. (18)
What should I do now here, since the destruction of my bonds is at hand? There remains for me only this sprout to be cut; therefore, I shall abandon it. (19)
That internal specific modification of consciousness (vṛtti) in the form of Brahman, which is called the "breaker of bonds" because it shatters bondage, is the sprout that exists;
since even that is indeed to be cut away, I shall therefore completely abandon it. 19.
Let this ignorance be; it is of a useless nature—what is the use of it? This delusion, which is unreal in form, has now been abandoned by me. (20)
Since the delusion of the world is non-knowledge (*avidyā*), it is severed by the very functioning of knowledge (*vidyā*); therefore, it need not be abandoned now.
Thus he says: "Let it be" (*āstām*). || 20 ||
"This teacher is merely a sage; here there is only delusion.
This form appears like me, yet it is Brahman alone, as transient as a cloud in the sky by day. (21)

The meaning is that even this instructing sage appears as Brahman itself, just like myself as a disciple; thus, there is no difference to be abandoned, as in the case of a person seen in a cloud during the day. || 21 ||
"Thus, having first declared the knowledge that has arisen, I shall speak of the Great Sage";
having reflected thus, that sage was addressed by me there as follows.
Since knowledge has arisen from that great sage, the Guru, I shall thus declare the knowledge of my own intention as it is about to be spoken. || 22 ||
O Leader of Sages, I am going; I go to see this body of mine, and I have also set out to behold that body which I have come to perceive. (23)
The meaning is: "I am now intent on seeing both that body of my own which resides in the hermitage and this body of a living being; therefore, I shall go outside to behold them. || 23 ||
Having heard this, that best of sages then said to me with a smile:
"Whence did those two bodies of yours come? They have gone to a very great distance."
From where do those two bodies come to exist? For they have gone very far away due to being reduced to ashes by cremation; such is the meaning.
Go yourself, O you who are skilled in conduct, and observe the events;
first see what has transpired, for having seen it, you will understand the illustration for yourself. (25)
Or go there yourself and observe the situation firsthand.
Having reflected thus, I abandoned that body— which was composed of the elements of earth and stone—
and, as the conscious self, I joined its vital breaths with the wind.

When he had spoken thus—the word "iti" being understood as "having said"—I, desiring to go there after reflecting upon that former body, abandoned my own consciousness, which had been imagined through the existence of the dream-ground as a form consisting of my own earthly body with the thought "I am this very [earthly] body. Then, the conscious self (cidātman) supported by the vital breaths—my own living soul—was joined to the mass of wind (pavanaskandha) from those vital breaths, which served as the gateway. || 26 ||
"O sage, as soon as I have looked upon my former body, you must remain right here until I return"; having said this, I departed for the wind.
Having said what to the sage, did you then enter the wind? To this he replies: "The former," etc. "Gataḥ" means entered.
Then, mounted upon a wind-chariot, I wandered through the sky;
having traveled for a long time with great speed, I reached the infinite expanse like the fragrance of a flower.
Then, after wandering for a long time, even as I moved toward the opening of his throat,
I did not find anything while remaining within his belly.

Then, having wandered for a long time, I did not find the exit door of that living being—namely its throat-passage—or any other door; thus, the connection with the following verse is: "At that time, remaining within the belly of the wind-eater, I fell into distress. (29)
Then, having returned once more, he fell into the utmost despondency:
"This very web of the world is my own tether. (30)

The sequence of the meaning is as follows: having returned once more to his own home—which was the supreme tethering post for him, serving as a pillar of bondage—he then perceived this unsurpassed sage, his own guru, standing before him. || 30 ||
Having first obtained this here, I then questioned that unsurpassed sage with one-pointed concentration; thus did I ask him while at home.
This is what is about to be stated. || 31 ||
"O Blessed One, best among those who know the past and the future, tell me what this is; for you see exactly how it occurred with your supreme eye of knowledge. (32)
I have entered whose body, and he has likewise entered my own body; where have those two bodies gone, and for what reason are they not found? (33)
And that is a living being. || 33 ||
For a very long time, I have wandered through the expansive circle of saṃsāra;
from the stationary beings up to my own self, why was that opening of the throat not attained? (34)

The word division is *ā ātmanaḥ*. The syntactical connection is: "From the self down to the stationary beings (*sthāvara*), the vast circle of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāramaṇḍala*) has wandered as an object of experience. (34)
When asked, "Having gone there, what did that sage, the high-souled one, say? the lotus-eyed one replied, "O lotus-eyed one, why do you ask as if you yourself already know it? (35)

Then he said to her, "Do you know?"—meaning, why do you know by yourself, through your own intellect alone, that which occurred previously regarding your body and so forth, without the means I have described? By the address "O lotus-eyed one," it is indicated that this cannot be seen merely by the beauty of the eyes. || 35 ||
If you perceive this yourself through the singular consciousness of yoga,
then you will see it entirely, as clearly as a lotus in the palm of your hand.

If one asks what the means for seeing that is, he says: "This. If you behold it with consciousness one-pointed in yoga, then indeed you shall see this entirely and in its completeness through the eye of knowledge. || 36 ||
Nevertheless, if you have a desire to hear my words, then listen to this as I shall speak it exactly as it occurred, without omission. (37)
If you desire to hear it only through my words and do not wish to see it, then I shall relate it exactly as it happened; listen. || 37 ||
As long as you do not exist, there is no one like you— the sun of asceticism, the source of the lotus of auspiciousness, and the navel of Hari from which the lotus of knowledge springs.

Thinking, "In this regard, first understand the reality of your own self; then I shall tell you the account of your previous body," [the teacher], relying on the principle shown by the Śruti—"The three forms are indeed real, while the state of the individual soul (vyaṣṭi-jīva) is false, and the state of the collective whole (samaṣṭi) alone is true"—said: "You are this... [tapaḥ].
He does not exist as a specific individual soul (*vyaṣṭi-jīva*) experienced by you; rather,
he is the sun that causes to blossom the lotuses of the meritorious deeds of all living beings,
and he is the collective totality (*samaṣṭi*), like a bed of lotuses, for all auspicious joys ranging from human bliss to the bliss of Prajāpati.

You are indeed Hiraṇyagarbha, the navel—the pericarp—of the lotus-navel of Hari, whose nature is knowledge, and who is the self of the aggregate of all individual souls resting upon that [lotus]. || 38 ||
Once, while you were established in austerity, desiring to see a dream,
you entered the heart of a certain living being with a fully awakened consciousness.
If so, how did my state as an individual (vyaṣṭi-bhāva) come about there, and how did these particular delusions arise? To this he says: "But you...
You became an ascetic (tāpasa) in that hermitage, established in a mental vision consisting of a kingdom of the mind, out of a desire to see the dream of individual existence.
There, through the nourishment of the consciousness of individuality and out of a desire to witness the wonders of dreams within other bodies and so forth, [the delusions arose].
He has entered the heart of some living being. || 39 ||
Because you have entered the heart, you have seen here this entire triple world, with its vast expanse and the great interior of heaven and earth.
While you were thus long occupied, his body likewise remained in that great forest, lying there with the appearance of one fast asleep.

In this manner, while you were long occupied with seeing a dream within another's body, your own body remained there in that great forest in the form of one who had fallen asleep; meanwhile, that living being who had entered you remained there, and his body—as well as your hermitage together with the cottage of your hermitage—was consumed by that fire. This is the syntactical connection with the tenth verse. || 41 ||
The fire of the onset was like smoke-colored clouds, veiling the vast expanse of the sky;
it contained whirling, powerful, and flickering circles of firebrands that resembled the orbs of the sun and the moon. (Note: The reading *sphuradbala* is more suitable for the commentary.)
There, in that great forest, a fire broke out. He describes that very fire with the words beginning "dhūmadhūmrābhrā... [and so on]:
it is one by which solar discs and lunar discs have been produced by means of whirling circles of firebrands (alātacakra) that flash and move with force. || 42 ||
The sky was covered by clouds of smoke filled with the ashes of burnt clouds,
appearing like blankets as white as the petals of a dark-blue lotus.

The quarters of the sky, darkened by black blankets characterized by smoke and clouds—blankets filled with ashes from the burnt clouds—protect the regions of space with their covering; thus the heavens were overspread by such [clouds]. 43.

He filled the quarters of the sky with the roar of a lion emerging from its mountain cave, threatening all, and with the loud crackling sounds of his snapping that deafened the space between the directions. || 44 ||
He has rendered the quarters of the sky motionless and deafened the space between the directions. || 44 ||

Like a dense mass of clouds, he produced crackling sounds with his blows, as the rows of *tāla* and *tāla* trees were reduced to the state of fire-trees by the falling sparks resembling the flames of a cataclysmic conflagration.

The forest was filled with the crackling and tumultuous sounds of rows of *tāla* and *tamāla* trees, which had become like fire-trees due to being enveloped on all sides by flames; these trees were bursting apart like a cataclysmic fire and roaring like portentous clouds. || 45 ||
To those who had traveled to distant lands, he showed the sky as a floor paved with molten gold, which they perceived through the mistaken notion that it was a steady flash of lightning.
Having made the floor appear as if it were coated with the liquid flow of molten gold from the sky, he displayed it. || 46 ||
With his lovely grains, he made the clusters of stars in the sky appear doubled;
he was the delighter of the eyes of the young women resting upon his chest.

Making the host of stars appear doubled by means of his sparks and embers, he delighted the sky with those very sparks, acting as the glances that bring joy to the eyes of the young woman characterized by the flames residing within his chest. || 47 ||
The interior of the sky was filled with the roar of crackling flames, while wild forest-dwellers,
startled awake, fled in confusion from their cave-dwellings.
The lions, deer, hunters, and birds were fleeing while half-burnt; the fierce forest-dwellers were blinded by the boiling waters of the lakes and the currents of the rivers.
By whom the fierce forest-dwellers—such as hunters, tigers, and the like—and the aquatic creatures were tormented and cooked. || 49 ||
The tips of the beautiful yak-tail fans were set ablaze by the flames of the forest fire;
the clouds were enveloped by the stench of the fat of living beings from the burning woods.
By this forest fire, leaping like the fire of cosmic destruction, your hermitage has been consumed as if by a spreading serpent. (51)
By that forest fire of the kind described by him, your hermitage together with your hermitage, as well as his body and the body of that living being, were burnt. || 51 ||
The hunter said:
"O sage, what was the natural cause for that fire which consumed him? And how was that entire forest, along with all those excellent young brahmins, destroyed?"
What is the cause for this common occurrence? Those excellent youths have entered bodies such as that of a brahmacārin;
how is it that everything was destroyed simultaneously? || 52 ||
The Sage said:

Just as the vibration of the mind that forms intentions is the cause for the arising and destruction of intentions and the like, so too, when devoid of vibration, the three worlds quickly cease to exist.

Just as the vibration of the mind of an individual who forms a resolve is the cause for the arising and cessation of that resolve, so too, for the Creator who conceives the three worlds, it is the very vibration of His mind that has arisen in an instant which constitutes the three worlds; therefore, the meaning is that in their arising and cessation as well, this vibration of His mind is likewise the cause. || 53 ||
Just as there is vibration in the heart and at the edge of the forest, whether causing agitation or its absence,
so too, O Spanda, is the vibration of these three worlds here.

Just as in the heart, agitation or its absence is the cause of immediate vibration during states of fear and so forth, so too in the three worlds and in the forest, that very same [vibration] is the cause of agitation or its absence; this is the meaning. || 54 ||
The world is a city of mental construction within the *dhātu*; its vibration here is the cause of the arising and destruction of beings, as well as of disturbances such as rain and drought. (55)
Even that mind of Brahmā and the others exists within this [consciousness], and that too exists elsewhere in the sky of consciousness;
thus, this movement within the sky of consciousness is one, peaceful, and without end.
Brahmā, the mind-composite cause of this world, is himself imagined elsewhere in another mental sky;

he too is imagined elsewhere, and he too elsewhere—such is the course of the consciousness-ether variegated by Māyā, a succession of conceptualizations that is endless. The meaning is that it is indeed unstable. || 56 ||
In the sky of consciousness, the splendor of the sky of consciousness shines forth as stainless for the wise;
but for the ignorant, whether it appears thus or otherwise, it does not truly exist here as that [reality].
But when the vision is refined, it is the splendor of the sky of consciousness alone that shines within the sky of consciousness; such is the stainless vision of the wise.
For the ignorant, however, this vision consists of superficial perception—whatever appears, they take that to be real.
But in this ultimate reality, that which appears is not truly existent; the meaning is that it is merely false. || 57 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and fiftieth chapter, titled "The Supreme Instruction," in the *Vasiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa* of Valmiki, belonging to the Holy Vālmīki, the Great Epic of Rāma, in the Section on the Final Liberation, in the Book of Nirvāṇa. 150.
Thus ends the one hundred and fiftieth chapter, titled "The Supreme Instruction," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and fifty-first canto.
Another sage said:
"There, those cities, those houses, and those trees are yours."
In an instant, everything was reduced to ashes, like dry grass. || 1 ||
The subsiding of the fire whose body was the burnt hermitage by means of the winds and ashes is described; therefore, this principle [applies] to the state of waking within a dream. || 1 ||
Not only the hermitages and such, but indeed everything, including the cities and so forth, was reduced to ashes. || 1 ||
While you were thus asleep and your two bodies had been reduced to ashes,
those great stones were likewise split asunder by the intense heat.

Likewise, while you were dwelling in that hermitage which was split open by the intense heat, those two bodies of yours, being asleep, attained the state of ashes in the manner described; such is the grammatical connection. || 2 ||
That fire, having consumed the forest entirely, gradually subsided;
it went out like Agastya after he had drunk the ocean.
Like Agastya who drank the ocean, he was first extinguished with only his embers remaining; thereafter, he went to his setting, beyond sight. || 3 ||
When that fire had gone out, the wind blew away all those ashes, which were thoroughly cooled,
scattering them bit by bit like a heap of flowers.
First blazing and later becoming perfectly cool, the wind blew—that is, it shook [it]. || 4 ||
Consequently, it was no longer known where the hermitage had been, nor where those bodies were; where that multitude of chests had gone was as unclear as a dream upon waking.
That city was like a casket containing a multitude of people. || 5 ||
When your two bodies have thus come to non-existence,
for you who are sleeping and deluded, it is consciousness alone that unfolds.
Therefore, where is that throat-pit, and where are you, the Virāṭ-ātman?
You are burnt, and the body of one who is burnt possesses vital energy; yet the body of one who possesses vital energy is likewise burnt.

Fearing that his vital energy (*ojas*) might remain as a residue even when the body is burned, he says: "endowed with *ojas*" (*saujaska*). Only the body of that sleeping one, while it was still possessed of *ojas*, was consumed by fire. || 7 ||
O Sage, it is for that reason that you have not obtained two bodies;
rather, you remain here in the endless dream-saṃsāra as if in a waking state.
You abide in the waking state, which consists of the cycle of dreams.
Thus, this very dream has attained the state of waking;
we are all here, O observer of noble vows, but dream-beings belonging to you.
And with the intention of showing that what was previously stated—that there is no difference between waking and dreaming—is indeed demonstrated here, he says:
"Thus, in this way" (tadevam) || 9 ||
You are our dreamer, and we are the men in your dream;
this very space of consciousness (cidākāśa) is forever established as the Self within the Self. || 10 ||
At all times, even in the three states, the self is non-dual by its very nature. || 10 ||
From that time forth, you became a man in a dream; and being possessed of waking cognition, you became a waking man, well-established in the householder’s life.
Although you were previously a man in a dream, from that time forward you have become a waking man, firmly established in the life of a householder.
All this has been told to you in its entirety, exactly as it occurred;
it was experienced and clearly perceived, and you see it now through meditation.
In case of doubt, you too shall see all this spoken by me through meditation; [the future tense] "drakṣyasi" is used in the sense of the present because of its proximity to the present time. || 12 ||

Thus, devoid of beginning or middle, this one of infinite forms, a mass of pure consciousness, shines in the void like the brilliance of gold; its body flickering upon its own forehead within itself, the self consisting of consciousness expands through creations that are both dark and white.

In the sky, there is a golden heat; like that [heat], that which shines is its plowshare (phāla), which is the exuberant power of its own radiance. By means of that, the Self, whose essence is consciousness and whose body is restless, is densely packed within itself with manifested states consisting of creation—states that are the fruits of evil karma and are black, those that are the fruits of good karma and are white, and those that are the fruits of mixed karma and are variegated. It is a mass of consciousness.
The meaning is that it alone shines, and nothing else. || 13 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-first chapter, titled "The Vision of Non-existence," in the *Ārṣa* [scripture], the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha*, composed by Valmiki, in the *Deva-muni-nirvāṇa-upadeśa*, in the *Avimukta-viśeṣa-śataka*.
Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-first chapter, titled "The Vision of Non-existence," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and fifty-second canto. The sage said:
Having spoken thus, that sage remained silent there upon his own bed during the night.
And then, out of astonishment, I felt as if I were being carried away by a current. || 1 ||
Having dispelled the sage's doubt regarding the reality of dream-objects, the other sage began to state the reason for the hunter’s status as his teacher in this world.
Then I was carried away like one swept off by a whirlwind. || 1 ||
Then, after a long time, O excellent sage, I said to him:
"O Lord, it is my conviction that every such dream possesses a real form."
By the statement, "My mind is such that it perceives reality as it truly is," astonishment is expressed through the impossibility [of such a thing]. || 2 ||
Another sage said:
"Where something else arises from that which is real, there it is appropriate to consider 'this is real.
But where this very thing itself is the reality, what proof can there be for its being even slightly less than real? (3)

If some other waking object were possible as real, then it might be appropriate to feel astonishment—that this dream and so forth could be real. But since even this waking perception is, by its very nature, meager in existence, insubstantial, and false, what proof can there be for reality in a dream? The meaning is that it is all the more utterly false. || 3 ||
Just as a dream, so too does this initial creation appear;
though devoid of earth and the other elements, it stands as if established by earth and the rest.
Thus, from this present dream, the dream of creation is of a pure nature;
listen, O lotus-eyed one, O sage, O great teacher, O hunter! (5)

Thus, even compared to our present dream that is currently being perceived, the dream of creation—which is renowned as being the waking state—is composed solely of pure consciousness. The meaning is that even such a degree of existence for that [waking world] is difficult to find. O Great Teacher Vyādha, O Sage with eyes like lotus petals, hear the reasoning here; even in comparison to you—
The address [“O Lotus-petal-eyed One”] is used in this way to indicate that at the time of awakening the dull-witted hunter, you will understand the effort involved in providing [this instruction];
the intended meaning of this address has already been explained previously. (5)
Today, for those who have perceived the objects [of the dream], the dream belongs to the dreamer;
yet the dream of creation shines first in the void as an object already perceived.

He states the justification for what was promised to be said: "Now," etc. In this waking state, because the words and their meanings perceived during the day deposit their own impressions (*saṃskāra*) in the intellect, it is possible—even for you who experience dreams—that the word and its meaning appeared during the night in a dream;
for that causal complex consisting of impressions and so forth exists there, and thus it might be considered real.

The dream of creation, well-known at the time of the beginning of the universe, shines forth in the sky of consciousness (*cidākāśa*) exactly as it was previously perceived; yet, because a long period of dissolution has intervened, the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of that prior experience and so forth have been severed, and thus it is utterly insignificant even when compared to a dream of the present day.
The meaning is that it is logically established that [the effect] cannot even be considered to possess an existence equal [to that of the cause]. || 6 ||
Why do you speak as if it were doubtful, saying "thus it is a real dream," when it was clearly experienced? How could there be an effort toward meditation on a real dream? (7)
"Since the waking world is thus more intensely false, O All-pervading One, it is my conviction that the entire dream is of the nature of reality (*sad-rūpa*).

By using the word "conviction" (*mati*), you seem to suggest something as if it were doubtful; what is this you say? Even though this own home has been clearly experienced as real through my instruction, how did the effort to meditate upon it as a dream arise in you again? It is not so.
For the sense is that a certain dreamer perceives at that time, "This dream is false."

O Sage, when this world of dreams—which is experienced as being thus and is clearly manifest—is indeed experienced by the living being along with the gods, how can there be any doubt regarding it? (8)
Furthermore, he says "this" (idam) [in verse 8], meaning that for you who experience the world as existing, there is not even a seed for doubt regarding its non-existence.
Then, as he was speaking thus, I interrupted his speech and asked: "Tell me, what is this state of being a hunter-master? (9)
He interrupted, having obstructed [the discourse] by posing another question. || 9 ||
Another sage said:
"Listen to this other narrative which I shall relate to you in brief, O highly wise one; there is no end to my detailed account."
I am indeed one whose ascetic penance has been long, while you are exceedingly righteous;
having heard these true words of mine, you shall find delight right here.
"As long as you remain the master of hunters, I shall stay right here. O leader of sages, having heard these words of mine, you too shall find delight right here in my home. (11)
"You shall not abandon me while I remain here;
it is my firm resolve that I shall dwell together with you. (12)
And you shall not abandon me while I remain here.
O virtuous one, after some years have passed from now,
the destruction of all your kinsmen will occur here due to famine.
And at that very moment, due to a conflict over the boundaries and the surrounding areas of the village, this entire hamlet, along with its inhabitants, will perish from their homes. (14)

Due to conflict with neighboring petty kings and vassals stationed on the borders who are intoxicated by their own power—such as through the engagement of mutual warfare—the living beings therein have become diminished; such being the case, this village will perish from its home, that is, it will flee. 14.
Then, no longer perceiving suffering, they rested together for a long time;
being tranquil through the knowledge of all that is to be known, they were equal and free from desire for any object.
Then he said, "What shall we two do?"—this is expressed by the following two verses beginning with "tataḥ" (15).
Right here, in some single thicket of trees,
we two shall dwell together in solitude, like the moon and the sun.
In time, this excellent forest will arise in this wilderness, its entire ground covered with a network of *śāla*, *tāla*, and creeping vines. (17)

From our dwelling, an excellent forest—a thicket of trees—will arise in the wilderness. He elaborates upon its excellence with the verse beginning "śāla" and so forth, consisting of one and a half verses. || 17 ||

With its quarters adorned by the dancing of the leaves of *tāla* and *tamāla* trees, with blossoming trees worthy of praise from the groves of full-blown lotuses, and with lovely creeper-thickets where flocks of *cakra* birds warble, it shone like the Nandana garden descended from the sky. (18)

Where the blossoming trees, being worshipped by flowers as if they themselves were worthy of worship because their feet rest upon beds of blooming lotus groves, stand like the celestial Nandana grove descended from the sky or heaven and become stationary; this completes the connection with the preceding verse. 18.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-second canto, titled "The Description of the Dialogue between the Sage and Rātri," in the *Ārṣa-Śrīvāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*, within the section on the Liberation of Devasena, in the *Mokṣopāya* portion of the *Vālmīki-Rāmāyaṇa*.
Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-second canto, titled "The Description of the Sage’s Nightly Discourse."
The one hundred and fifty-third canto. Another sage said:
"As the two of us were practicing asceticism for a very long time in that forest,"
A hunter, exhausted from pursuing a deer, will arrive. || 1 ||
In this [work], the weightiness of that [scripture] is established through reasoning such as the arrival of hunters;
and at the proper time, the knowledge arising from discernment and the identity of all things as one are described.
In that forest, whose qualities have been described. || 1 ||
You shall awaken him with discourses on the merit of one's own true nature;
then, detached from the world, he will practice austerities in that very forest.
Then, in the midst of those practicing ascetic disciplines, desiring to know the self and wishing to understand dreams, he will inquire about the discourse on dreams.

Following the perfection of the means such as tranquility and self-control through the practice of the conduct of ascetics, that hunter, desiring to know the Self and wishing to inquire about dreams by way of an introductory illustration, will pose a question concerning dreams. (3)
"You shall speak to him the unbroken knowledge of the Self under the pretext of a dream; therefore, he will become a fit recipient."
Then, through the context known as "The Dream," you will discourse upon the knowledge of the Self.
"In this manner, you shall become his guru;
therefore, my dear, I addressed you with the words, 'O teacher of hunters.'"
For that reason. || 5 ||
Thus I have explained to you everything: how this wandering in saṃsāra occurs, who I am, what you are like here, and what will become of you.
Having completed the answer to what was asked, he concludes the preceding [section] with the word "iti" (thus). || 6 ||
Having been addressed thus by him, my mind was filled with wonder;
after deliberating upon this matter together with him, I attained the height of amazement.
This is the collection of all that is visible. || 7 ||
Then, when the night had passed, at dawn that great sage,
having been honored by him in such a manner, found delight in that very place.
Delight and joy. || 8 ||
Immediately thereafter, O firm-minded one, we remained in that house and likewise in every village house, having established a mutual bond of affection.
Having fixed their hearts upon him while he was staying in that forest-dwelling, as well as upon that former village-house, they were bound by affection.
Then this time, consisting of seasons and years, flows on;
I remain like a mountain, abandoning and taking up the states of being as they arrive.
[He endures] entities that are undesirable, desirable, or mixed; in the case of the mountain, [these are] forest fires, rain, and so forth. || 10 ||
I do not long for death, nor do I long for life;
I remain just as I am, free from all feverish distress.
Then, I reflected there upon that circle of the visible world: "What could be the cause of this? What does he perceive with his mind? (12)
What is this collection of objects, and what indeed is its cause, within this vision of a dream whose sole nature is the sky of consciousness? (13)
What is the cause or the motive for this? || 13 ||
Heaven, earth, wind, space, mountains, rivers, and the directions—
these are merely the sky of pure consciousness, manifesting while established within the Self.
And within the Self, whose nature is a single mass of consciousness, there exists only the sky of pure consciousness. ||14||
That which spreads its radiance throughout the four quarters like the light of the moon—
this very world appears as a variegated, non-obstructive form within the void.
In the sky of consciousness (khe cidākāśe), because of the absence of grossness, its nature is such that it is incapable of resistance; it is non-obstructive by essence. || 15 ||
These are not mountains, nor is this the earth, nor is this the sky, nor even am I;
only this manifestation of the void of pure consciousness shines forth as the absolute.
But surely, since mountains and the like possess resistance, how could they be non-resistant? To this he says: "Not these" (neme). || 16 ||
Alas, what indeed could be the cause of this entire collection of objects? For without a cause for their aggregation into a mass, no such thing as an object could possibly exist. (17)
If it is merely the manifestation of pure consciousness, then there is no cause at all, because neither the grasping of a solid body nor its cause can be established; thus he says:
"If this were mere delusion, what indeed could be the cause of that delusion?
Who is the seer and the thinker of the delusion, or what kind of cause for it exists, and where? (18)

Anticipating the objection that "in that case, let this [appearance] simply be an illusion," he states—beginning with the word "bhrānti"—that even in that case, the cause, the observer, and so forth are difficult to specify. || 18 ||
He in whose vital energy, consisting of pure consciousness alone, I dwelt—
that very one has indeed been reduced entirely to ashes along with me.
I am pure consciousness alone, who, having entered his body, dwelt within the vital energy of his heart; that living being, along with my own body, has been reduced to ashes by me.
Therefore, this is the beginningless and endless sky that is mere luster of consciousness;
it is the form of the mass of consciousness, devoid of agent, object, and instrument, and free from succession.
Therefore, because that body, my body, and so forth do not exist, all this is merely the radiance of consciousness, nothing but the sky.

This manifestation of the sky of consciousness—consisting of jars, pits, cloths, and so forth—is clearly evident; from what else, then, could these jars, pits, cloths, and the like have been produced? (21)
From where indeed was the manifest form of jars, wells, cloths, and so forth produced according to their shapes? The meaning is: from nowhere at all. || 21 ||
Nor is pure consciousness a mere manifestation, nor is it a solitary void;
for what is its manifestation, of what nature is it, how does it manifest, and what is this "sky"? || 22 ||

The notion that "it is the manifestation of pure consciousness alone" is also a mere conceptual construction, like the expression "the head of Rāhu," because the distinction and the relationship required for a genitive *tatpuruṣa* compound are unestablished; with this intention, he says: "Nor even...
(verse 22). Is this foam something new from the ocean of consciousness? What is its manifestation?
This very infinite mass of consciousness remains as the nature of pure light alone. || 23 ||
Like foam, it is foam. || 23 ||
Pure Brahman, the expansion of the mass of consciousness, is the manifestation of pure consciousness alone;
it appears as if this world, but where is the object of sight, and from where could there be the state of being a seer? (24)
Brahman is eternally the solid mass of expanded consciousness.

Devoid of beginning and end, immeasurable, without beginning or middle, the one all-pervading Lord—[the masculine gender in "vibhum" is a Vedic archaism]—who is free from the existence of cause and effect; who consists of pure being (*sattāmaya*); who is the universe, the mountains, the quarters of space, the manifold and the non-manifold; he alone is some kind of consciousness that is everything. (25)

In terms of time, it is devoid of beginning and end; in terms of space, it is likewise without beginning or middle; and in terms of substance, it is one. For this very reason, it is free from cause and free from effect, and its existence is independent of anything else. It is primarily characterized by its own intrinsic existence, for it alone brings about the existence of the worlds and all other things through its own being.
Thus, while appearing as both manifold and non-manifold, it is something that transcends the reach of speech and mind.
The meaning is that whatever is conscious is indeed all [of reality]; there is not even an atom's worth existing apart from it. || 25 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-third canto, titled "The Exposition of the Universal Unity of the Self," in the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha*, in the *Vālmīki*, *Devarāja*, *Mokṣopāya*, *Nirvāṇa*, *Uttara* [part], in the *Avadhūta* [section], in the *Śata-sāhasrī*.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-third chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Universal Unity of All," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa-tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and fifty-fourth canto.
The sage said:
Having thus reached a definitive conclusion regarding this visible world, I remain free from all feverish distress.
Free from passion, free from fear, liberated, and devoid of egoism. || 1 ||
The state of liberation while living (jīvanmukti) arising from discernment (vicāra), which is innate, has been described here by the Sage;
however, for the hunter who lacks practice, there is no such stability.
The sage elaborates upon the fruit of his own inquiry and his state of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) with the words beginning "Thus," and so forth. || 1 ||
Without support and without that which is supported, free from pride and without dependence, abiding in its own nature, self-peaceful, the essence of creation, it is manifest in every way. || 2 ||
Free from pride, he is devoid of conceit. || 2 ||
I am the agent of what is attained; yet I am never an agent at all. For how can there be agency in that which is itself like space? (3)
He who [is like] space itself, which is inactive. || 3 ||
Heaven, earth, wind, space, mountains, rivers, and the quarters—all this is the single-souled sky, whose sole conscious body is the entire web of beings. (4)
The one Self is existence, the sky of consciousness alone. || 4 ||
I am stilled, I am completely extinguished, and I abide solely in bliss;
for me there are neither injunctions nor prohibitions, neither the external nor the internal.
Thus, as I remained here established in my natural state,
you have today arrived before me by chance, like the falling of a palm fruit upon a crow.
"O hunter, it is you who have arrived here today."
Thus everything has been explained to you: how the dream is, how we are, how the world is, how you are, and how this visible world is.
To you who have thus attained [this state] and ask, all this is as it has been described. He elaborates upon that very point:
"And what you are, and what this visible world is, how this is seen before you; how things are, how Brahman is, and how these multitudes of people are before you. (8)

And you are the seer, such as you are; this internal, spiritual object of perception consisting of the body, senses, and so forth, as it is; and this external, material object of perception appearing before you, as it is; and the states within them, such as attachment and aversion, or rejection and acceptance, as they are. (8)
Having understood this, O hunter, O hunter, be at peace;
for this very existence is peaceful, consisting of the void of pure consciousness alone.
"O hunter, O hunter!"—this repetition is used out of respect. May you become peaceful, realizing that all this is false;
for this very existence of the self shines forth as inherently tranquil and naturally extinguished (nirvāṇa), not as unpeaceful.
Nirvāṇa shines by itself, or rather, nothing at all shines. The hunter said:
"If this is so, then you, I, and all the gods and others—" (10)

He demonstrates the very nature of peace with the words "not at all" (naiva). The meaning is that peace is precisely the absolute non-appearance of the visible world. By means of an ironic intonation (*kāku*), the hunter speaks—suggesting that it is inconceivable for such clearly manifest beings as humans, gods, animals, and immobile things to be merely like a dream—saying: "If this were so... (10).
"All these dream-men are mutually composed of both the existent and the non-existent.
The Sage said: "It is so; all this stands in relation to one another like a dream. (11)
The ellipsis is to be supplied as "they would indeed consist of clay. With this admission of the opponent's position, the sage gives his reply: "It is so. (11)
In this way, both the existent and the non-existent are experienced by one another within the self;
whatever the visible object is perceived to be by someone, it is experienced by that person exactly in that manner.

The meaning is that while it exists in the self, it does not exist in others, precisely because it is experienced by all in that way. He states that it is so also because its status conforms to consciousness: "the visible" (dṛśyam). || 12 ||
Therefore, an object is neither manifold nor one; it is neither existent, nor non-existent, nor something intermediate between them.
In the waking state, it is merely a perception, like a city in a dream.

Because an object is neither manifold nor one. For example, a single jar consists of a manifold reality—comprising various shards, fragments, a succession of parts, and ultimately atoms—yet it is also of the nature of a single entity because it is perceived as one. In this regard, for those who perceive its manifoldness, the "one" is non-existent; for those who perceive its oneness, [the manifold is non-existent].

The notion of manifoldness (*nānātva*) is non-existent. For those who perceive both [existence and non-existence], both existence and non-existence are partial and contingent. However, for those who know reality, there is only pure awareness (*vedanamātraka*); thus, not even one [of these] exists—this is established by experience, such is the sense. That which is situated in the middle is neither existent nor non-existent. (13)
"It is like a city seen from afar that was never seen before;
thus everything has been told to you, and you have been awakened without interval. (14)
"You are yourself wise and you understand; do as you wish.
Even though you have been thus enlightened, O hunter, such is your mind. (15)
The connection with the subsequent clause is as follows: "In your view, the mind comes to rest only in the delusion that the world is real, but it does not come to rest in the supreme state. (15)
For a moment they rest in awakening, yet they do not rest in the supreme state;
without practice, this awakening does not take root in the heart of the mind.

To explain why that is so, he says: "No. This awakening, without reaching a state of supreme transformation through practice, does not go—that is, it does not enter—into the heart of the mind. Just as, in the task of holding water, water does not enter into a piece of wood unless it has been transformed by cutting and other means into the supreme form of a water-pot or similar vessel.
The connection with the subsequent [verse] is "in that same way. || 16 ||

O wise one, through the practice of resting in awakened consciousness by relying solely on the Guru and the scriptures, the mind reaches a supreme transformation— like wood in the holding of water— and, through the pacification of the perceptions of duality and non-duality, it is said to attain Nirvana. (17)
When, through practice, the resting within awakening has been accomplished, that very mind is called "nirvāṇa" by those who have experienced it; thus he says: "Through practice... (17).
Free from pride and delusion, having conquered the fault of attachment, ever established in the inner self, with desires turned away,
and liberated from the dualities known as pleasure and pain, the undeluded go to that imperishable state.
He shows the concurrence of the Blessed One’s words regarding the matter stated [in the previous verse] with the words, "Free from pride... and so on. Internally free from pride and delusion;

externally having conquered the defect of attachment. Internally free from pride and delusion; externally having conquered the defect of attachment. Constantly established in the inner self both internally and externally; their desires have ceased because they have attained the Self which is full bliss in every respect.

Those who possess correct knowledge regarding pleasure and pain—being thus liberated from the pairs of opposites such as the pleasant and so forth, and being undeluded knowers of reality—go to that supreme state of Viṣṇu called Nirvāṇa;
the meaning is that they experience it. || 18 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-fourth canto, titled "The Description of Things as They Truly Are," in the *Ārṣa* [text], the glorious *Vālmīki-Rāmāyaṇa*, in the *Bālakāṇḍa*, in the *Māhātmya*, in the *Nirvāṇa*, in the *Uttara*, in the *Avimukta*, in the *Viśveśvara*, in the *Śata* [section]. || 154 ||
Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of Reality as It Is," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and fifty-fifth canto. Agni said:
Having heard this, that hunter then, in that forest region—
He remained motionless with wonder, as if his form had been fashioned by a painter. || 1 ||

It is declared by the sage that through the hunter's foolish asceticism and long suffering, there shall be movement through the sky by virtue of a boon from Fate, as well as the increase of his undertakings and his death.
With his form rendered like a painted image, he was made motionless and paralyzed by astonishment. || 1 ||
His mind found no rest in that state without his own habitual practice;
he felt as if bewildered, as if being swept away upon the ocean.
He did not rest; he found no repose.
As if mounted upon a wheel, he was carried away by the wheel of his own asceticism;
deprived of prowess, he was as if seized by a crocodile. || 3 ||
As if carried away by the wheel of a whirlwind through the power of his own asceticism, by some perfected being (siddha). || 3 ||
"Is this Nirvana, or is it something else?"—from such doubt, he did not attain peace, like a fool in the prime of youth. (4)
Reflecting thus: "This visible world is indeed created by ignorance," the notion that "the world is ignorance" does not firmly take root in the heart of one who is skillful.

Since the meaning that "this world is indeed nothing but ignorance" does not enter his heart, he remains thinking that this world was created—that is, produced—by the power of Brahman known as ignorance (avidyā), and is therefore truly real. || 5 ||
"How far does this visible world extend? I shall observe it from the beginning.
Thus he thought, having acquired a body through asceticism and standing at a great distance and height.

To what extent does this visible world reach, and how far does its limit extend? Having obtained this body through the power of austerity, I shall go from the beginning, starting from the earth, and having traveled upward with my body to that great distance, I shall see it—I will behold it. || 6 ||
One dwells eternally in bliss at the end of this world, which consists of both existence and non-existence;
therefore, even space exists, and where that is not, there I shall go.
At the end of this visible world, which consists of both existence and non-existence, I shall dwell eternally in bliss in that realm beyond saṃsāra. || 7 ||
Having thus resolved in his heart, he became a mere fool;
for even such a thing as has been said here is reduced to ashes without practice.

The meaning is that such an exceedingly extensive teaching of the Sage, though supported by both illustrations and logical proofs, goes in vain—like an oblation poured onto ashes—if it is devoid of practice. || 8 ||
From that time forward, together with those very sages,
he abandoned his state as a hunter and prepared to practice asceticism.
By that very same determination. || 9 ||
Dwelling forever together with those beings in that world,
he performed very great ascetic penance for many thousands of years.
By those characteristics and signs well-known among ascetics.
While performing austerities, he once again questioned that sage, "When will there be rest for my self? Thereupon, the sage replied: ||| 11 ||
He asked, "When shall I find rest within my own self, which is free from affliction? Thereupon, the sage replied to him. 11.
The sage said:
"That knowledge has been taught to you; it remains in your heart like a small fire with withered wood, but it is not appropriate for it to proceed until it has consumed what is to be burned."
By the statement "it remains like a small fire with withered wood," it is indicated that it will attain awakening in another birth.
At present, although it is proper to burn the fuel and capable of burning even the visible misfortunes, it does not remain so, having failed to overcome them. (12)
Without practice, you have not yet come to rest in the auspicious knowledge;
however, through practice over time, you will attain complete repose.
After a long time. || 13 ||
Now listen to this future account concerning yourself, a wonder of the earth that will serve as an ornament for my ears as I describe it. (14)
It is most wonderful, for it cannot even be conceived by anyone on earth, even with the mind. || 14 ||
One whose self is not awakened by this essence of knowledge, though it has been praised, possesses a consciousness that vacillates; such a person is neither a fool nor a sage.

He was prepared to understand that essence of knowledge, renowned among the wise, by her; yet, because he had not realized the Self, he was of such a nature that his consciousness was consequently oscillating. The compound "asamartha-samāsa" is a Vedic usage. || 15 ||
"What is the measure of this world, which is insatiable and consists of the nature of ignorance?"—with such a conceptualization regarding the self, you have set out to perform ascetic penance. (16)
By means of the conceptualization of a self, which is merely the imagination of one's own desires. || 16 ||
"In this manner, O broad one, you must perform severe penance for a hundred yugas;
then the Supreme Lord, being pleased, will approach you along with the gods. (17)

"In this manner," that is, by the very method being performed at present; "for a hundred ages" means, since the livelihood of a hunter is impossible [in a single life], effectively through many births. (17)
"You shall seek a boon from that giver of boons; choose a boon!"—this is an address to the hunter, because he has applied himself to asceticism by abandoning the violence inherent in his own species.
This [use of the neuter gender is archaic (ārṣa), or there is a variant reading "idam"].
"Devoid of doubt and uncertainty" (*saṃdehasaṃśayam*): "Doubt" (*saṃdeha*) refers to that which was mentioned immediately above as being of the nature of ignorance (*avidyā*), and so forth;

"certainty" (*saṃśaya*) means its complete resting or cessation. That in which this [doubt and uncertainty] exists is "devoid of doubt and uncertainty"—this is a qualifying attribute of the boon (*vara*). || 18 ||
In the presence of that Creator, the bestower of boons, you will seek a boon fashioned by your own desires due to your unrestrained wickedness; that is to say, you will pray for one. 18.
O God, while this visible form is perceived and the delusion of ignorance persists, there exists nowhere a reflection free from impurity, as in the case of a mirror. (19)

He says, "Listen to what you shall request," addressing him as "O God": "O God, O Creator, since this visible form is perceived, and while the delusion of ignorance persists like a mirror, there is no spot in Brahman free from the stain of reflection where, having gone, I might abide in an undistracted state. This is the meaning. || 19 ||
In this mirror of the sky of consciousness, which has the form of an atom yet is situated within [all things], this [universe] is reflected, whether it be here or there.
To the question "Why is it not there?", he says: "Of the mirror of the sky of consciousness.
Because this mirror of the sky of consciousness, though situated within even that which has the form of an atom, reflects this form of the universe here and there. || 20 ||
Therefore, how infinite can this visible world, which causes suffering, be?
And what might lie beyond its limit? That too is merely the visible sky.

Since this state of the intellect exists because of ignorance (*avidyā*), how far could this visible world, produced by ignorance and causing such misfortune, extend? How far, indeed, might that infinite, ignorance-free Brahman lie beyond this visible world— Brahman which, like space, is devoid of *saṃsāra* and of which I am composed?
That which is to be seen must necessarily be gone to and indeed be seen; in the case of a necessary duty, the suffix *kṛtya* is used. || 21 ||
For this purpose, I pray for this boon;
listen, O Lord of Gods, and grant it to me quickly and without obstacle. (22)
In order to know and directly experience such a matter as this, I pray for the boon that is about to be described. || 22 ||
May this body of mine be free from disease for a long time, possessing the power to die at will,
and endowed with Garuḍa-like speed as it travels through the sky.
May this body of mine be free from disease, subject to death at my own will, endowed with a speed equal to that of Garuḍa, and capable of traveling through the sky. || 23 ||
May this [space] increase by one *yojana* in each individual channel, gradually becoming of the nature of space on the exterior of the world. (24)
Furthermore, may this body of mine increase by a *yojana* in every channel, at every moment, and in every limb; and in the course of time, may it extend beyond the three worlds of the universe,
becoming as vast in form as space itself.
O Supreme Lord, may I obtain the end of this visible world which appears to have space;
let it be my supreme boon that [this] infinite [world] should thus come to an end. (25)
May I reach the end of this visible world within this space. || 25 ||
When you have thus spoken, O virtuous one, the Lord of gods,
the sovereign master, will say, "So be it for you," and the Lord will vanish from sight.
When that Great God, the Lord of Heaven, has departed along with the gods,
your body, emaciated by asceticism, shall become as radiant as the moon.
In the great god Vedhas, or alternatively, in Mahādeva because of the non-difference between the three forms (trimūrti); he shall become one whose splendor is like the splendor of the moon. || 27 ||
Having paid homage to me and taken leave of me at that very moment,
he will leap into the sky out of a desire to behold the object situated within his mind.
At that very moment following the attainment of the boon, you shall leap from my hermitage and ascend upward into that sky. (28)
Like a second moon, like a second sun, and like a second submarine fire, he has arisen in rivalry with the moon and the sun. (29)
Then, with the speed of Garuḍa, he sought to reach the end of the visible sky through the force of his flight, as one might seek the end of the world or of rivers.
As you proceed, your body will grow until it reaches the end of the world—the end of the three worlds—just as rivers reach their terminus; this is how the subsequent clause connects. || 30 ||
Then his body will increase incessantly until the end of the world,
filling the shoreless sky like the ocean intoxicated at the dissolution of the aeon.
Even for the boundless sky, filling it results in the production of a state where there is no space left. || 31 ||
Then, increasing in size with a vast body within the great void, you shall behold [it] through the continuous progression of the sky, which is an unobstructed support for all creation.
By gradually traversing that infinite space which serves as the foundation, being unobstructed and indeed without impediment.

They are like wheels of wind within the emptiness of the great space of ultimate reality; they are like waves upon the ocean of consciousness, arising from the impulse of the fluidity of intrinsic nature.

He further qualifies the creations themselves with the words beginning "paramārtha": they stand like whirlwinds of wind impelled by the emptiness (*śūnyatā*) of the ultimate great space (*paramārthamahākāśa*).
Their nature (*svabhāva*) is the state of being unknown (*ajñātatā*); [this refers to] the fluidity characterized by that [nature].
These waves of the ocean of consciousness, which have arisen from the impulse and the swelling [of energy].
Just as cities and other things appear in a dream— which is a mass of consciousness— as being of the nature of space,
so too will these unrestrained multitudes of creations manifest for you then.
"They will come within the range of vision"—this is the ellipsis to be supplied. || 34 ||
Just as masses of leaves flash in the great sky, stirred by agitated winds,
so too shall you, with unshaken resolve, behold infinite creations.
"Just as they flash forth," the word "flashed forth" (visphuritān) is to be understood as the ellipsis. || 35 ||
Just as a net of rays from eyes fixed on an assembly, though existing, is as if non-existent,
so too the world-self within the space of consciousness, though existing, is as if non-existent.
Just as for women staying in a palace, the observation of a dancing assembly outside through the lattice of a variegated window-paned balcony is what pleases them and nothing else—
for such people, that variegated lattice of windows, though existing, is as good as non-existent; so too,
for those who know reality and whose consciousness is the space of the Intellect (*cidākāśa*), the variegation consisting of the world exists therein [in the Intellect] as if it were non-existent.
The meaning is that even though it exists, it is as if non-existent. || 36 ||
Just as the entire world appears as a web reflected upon the moon's orb when it is fixed there, so too is the non-duality of the Self established when the world is situated within it.

Just as the mass of smoke, mist, dust, and so forth—which are seen by all people standing on earth as being attached to the lunar orb—is utterly non-existent from the perspective of a person situated within the lunar orb, so too the entire world, having attained non-difference from the Self, is likewise utterly non-existent for one who knows the reality (tattvavid). This is the meaning. || 37 ||
"Again creation, again the void; again creation, again the sky—while you perceive it thus, a long period of time will pass here. (38)
Then, after a long time, upon this leaf-like creation that is quivering,
you yourself shall experience agitation in the vastness of the sky.
Trembling and moving through the sky, that is, the unmanifest ether. || 39 ||
Then you will experience a sense of agitation as you reap the fruit of your asceticism;
at that time, you will cast off this body which fills the infinite sky.
You will explain it, you will see it, and you will speak of it.
What is this wretched body of mine that stands like a burden, wherein even a hundred thousand mountains such as Meru seem like a blade of grass? (41)
He states that very point with the words beginning "What is this? and so forth. || 41 ||
This body of mine is immeasurable; the entire sky is pervaded by me.
Even now I continue to fill the void, and there is no end to what is yet to come.
It is immeasurable and infinite; whatever is destined to be does not come to pass, nor is it known. || 42 ||
Alas, this terrible ignorance is immeasurable and endless;
it cannot be measured by anyone at all except through the knowledge of Brahman. 43.
This is the form of the visible; it is measured, experienced, and indeed measured—defined by its limits—or destroyed. 43.
I shall surely abandon this very body, whose interior is laid bare; for through it I do not attain anything, such as the company of the virtuous or the true scriptures. 44.
With this body of mine, now so greatly increased, I do not attain association with holy men or good scriptures, nor any other means for liberation. || 44 ||
What is the name of this body of mine, which is boundless, shoreless, and limitless, whose abode is the supportless sky, and which brings about the attainment of goals so difficult to reach? (45)
For the association with the noble ones who know reality is very difficult to attain. || 45 ||
Having reflected thus, and having performed the concentration (dhāraṇā) that expels the vital breath from that body,
you shall cast it off like a bird leaving a withered fruit after it has been enjoyed.

One exhales the breath, meaning one leads it out from the body, having performed a concentration characterized by that [exhalation]. Just as a bird, such as a parrot, discards the dry, sapless portion—the seeds, skin, and so forth—from a fruit it has eaten, such as a pomegranate, in that same way [one should discard the exhaled breath]. || 46 ||
Having abandoned the body, the living soul, endowed with its vital breaths,
shall abide in that space of yours, as subtle as the wind yet moving like the wind.
With its wings severed, the body will fall like Mount Mahāmeru;
there it will pulverize everything, including the world of mortals and its mountains.
In that [context], therein, in that world. || 48 ||
Then the Goddess Śuṣkā will devour his body along with the circle of his mothers;
by that means, the earth shall become free from blemish.
The goddess Kālī, who was previously described as withered and bloodless, together with her circle of Mothers and the Gaṇas, will devour that body in the manner previously described. || 49 ||
"Thus, O observer of noble vows, you have heard my entire life story;
having performed penance in the Tālīvana forest, do as you wish."
The hunter said:
"Alas, O Blessed One! I must endure inexhaustible suffering for that which was sought after by me with wealth for no purpose and to my own ruin."

Having heard that this is the fruit of one’s own firm resolve regarding the future, the hunter becomes despondent and asks—beginning with "Alas!"—whether there is a means to avoid it or not: "For what reason (yataḥ), by means of wealth (arthena)—that is, through the delusion of regarding it as a human goal (puruṣārtha)—only suffering was sought and established by my resolve. || 51 ||
"O Lord, is there some reasoning for this excellent state of affairs?
If the matter must be otherwise, then let it be told. (52)

"O Blessed One, most excellent one, this very state of future events has been described by you. If there exists some reasoning by which this destined event might be otherwise, please tell us whether such a reasoning exists or not. (52)
The sage said: An event that is destined to happen can never be made otherwise by anyone; for that which is ordained does not fail, despite all effort.
Because of that, it does not flow away nor perish through present effort. || 53 ||
Just as a man has no power to effect a reversal of his left and right hands or feet, so too he has no power to bring about a change in the nature of things as they exist.

Just as a man lacks the power to effect a reversal—that is, to transpose—the left and right sides of his own body, or the head and feet, so too there is no power to establish future objects in a state other than how they actually exist. || 54 ||
Through the knowledge of the meaning of the science of astrology (jyotiḥśāstra), there occurs here the cognition of future events;
however, nothing else whatsoever that is unprecedented ever comes to pass.
He states that its thorough comprehension occurs solely through scriptural means and not otherwise: "By means of the science of light," etc. (55).
Victorious indeed are those primal deeds by which, having reached their present state,
they sleep as Brahman itself— possessing consciousness that remains unaltered even through the burning of the body.
Anticipating the objection that liberation would be impossible due to the infinity of past karmas resulting from firm resolutions, he says:

"They conquer. By those preeminent men who, having attained the means such as tranquility and self-control through their past merits, [employ] the methods of consciousness (*saṃvinnaya*) which lead to the realization of Brahman-consciousness.

The meaning is this: having attained the knowledge of reality through means such as hearing (śravaṇa) and so forth, those best of men sleep as Brahman alone and do not wake with the perception of the world; they conquer all their former karmas and the painful impressions of evil volitions—even though these were extremely firm—by cutting them off at the root, whereas others do not. || 56 ||
Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-fifth canto, titled "The Description of Future Attainments," in the *Vasiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa*, within the *Mumukṣuvyavahāra* section of the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa*.
Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of Future Attainments," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and fifty-sixth canto.
The hunter said:
"Thereafter, O Blessed One, [I beheld] those who dwell in the vast expanse of space."
What will become of me there when my body has fallen down upon the earth? || 1 ||
Abiding in the wind, that hunter, having become a kinsman, killed Vidūratha;
how he heard his own true nature from the mouth of a minister is described here.

"Having abandoned the body, the living soul, endowed with its vital breaths, shall abide in that sky, becoming like the wind—subtler than even the wind. Having heard what was thus said, the hunter asks for the answer regarding his own future: "Immediately thereafter," and so forth. (1)
The sage said: Listen attentively, O auspicious-souled one, as to what will happen when that body of yours has perished within that supreme ether.
When [the world] has been thoroughly examined and has perished, [it remains] in the supreme kāmbara, the unmanifest space. || 2 ||
When that body has fallen away, the living soul, joined with the vital breaths,
will become a mere fragment of wind in the vast expanse of space.
In that moment of mental clarity, you will see the visible world situated before you within the heart;
you will behold the surface of the earth as non-expansive, just as one perceives the world in a dream.

In that very moment of the wind's arrival, he will perceive the vast world—consisting of latent impressions (vāsanā), situated within his own heart and mind, and characterized by the surface of the earth—as it rests there. || 4 ||

Then, due to the expansion of the mental fluctuations, the individual soul (jīva) will perceive those [objects] as "I am the king upon the surface of the earth," thereby experiencing the objects of its own volition.
Since it is the mental modification itself that has attained greatness by appearing in the form of the universe, the individual soul (jīva) will perceive within it: "I am the King there. || 5 ||
There, a sudden flash of intuition will arise within him spontaneously:
"I am the illustrious King Sindhurāja, highly honored by name. (6)
He was exceedingly honored and worshipped by his vassals. || 6 ||
When my father had gone to the forest at the age of eight,
the kingdom of the earth bounded by the four oceans, bestowed by my father, came into my possession.
The sovereignty over the earth bounded by the four oceans, which was granted to me by my father, has now come to pass.
At the border there is a king known as the enemy Vidūratha, who cannot be conquered by name alone without diligent effort. (8)
Whatever enemy exists cannot be conquered without effort.
While I have been exercising this kingship, a hundred years have passed;
oh, what happiness has been enjoyed by me together with my multitude of servants and wives!
"Alas! This sovereign of the bordering land has grown powerful;
a terrible battle with him is now at hand. (10)
As he was thinking thus, King Vidūratha [reflected]: "A great battle will take place here, destroying the fourfold army. (11)
A battle will take place with King Vidūratha. || 11 ||
Through that great battle, you shall slay Vidūratha,
even though you yourself are deprived of your chariot, having severed his shanks with the blade of your sword.
You shall slay Vidūratha.
Then, you shall become a sovereign of the earth bounded by the four oceans, whose commands will be honored by the guardians of the quarters who are overcome with fear.
Whose teaching is honored even by the guardians of the directions, who are overcome by fear.
Having become like an ocean and having attained the entire circle of the earth,
you shall engage in these conversations together with your learned ministers.
By the wise who know the reality of the scriptures; these [teachings] which are about to be described. || 14 ||
The minister will say:
"O King, this is most wonderful,
that Vidūratha was thus defeated by Your Majesty in battle and led away to the abode of Yama."
In this regard, some mantra-master who knows reality will say: "This is most wonderful! (15)
"You shall say:
'O virtuous one, tell me why King Vidūratha, the enemy of this wealthy man who is as swift as the ocean at the end of an aeon, is so difficult to endure. (16)

Precisely because I possess an army and the strength of my own arms, which have the speed of the ocean at the end of an eon, for what reason and by what force has King Vidūratha become difficult to withstand? Tell me that—this is the meaning. || 16 ||
The minister will say:
"He has a wife named Līlā, by whom the stainless Goddess Sarasvatī, the mother and sustainer of the world, was acquired through extreme asceticism. (17)
The mother has been won over by means of the attitude of a mother; that is to say, she has been brought under one's own control. || 17 ||
Once she has been accepted as his daughter, that progenitor of the world effortlessly accomplishes for him all his tasks, even those such as liberation.
He says that very thing: "Of her who has been accepted. Sarasvatī accomplishes even such tasks as liberation and so forth for this Līlā, who has been accepted as his daughter. || 18 ||
By a mere word—a mere sound—she turns even the world into a non-world in an instant; when she brings about the destruction of existence, what difficulty can there possibly be for her? (19)
When she is destroyed by you, what kind of incapacity could there be—consisting of humiliation, torment, and the nature of affliction? (19)
Sindhur will say:
"What you have said is indeed appropriate; if it is so, then Vidūratha is invincible, and his slaughter in battle is a marvel."

This has been stated appropriately and logically. If this is so, then that Vidūratha was indeed impossible to conquer; therefore, his slaying in battle which has occurred is a marvel—meaning it is inconceivable. || 20 ||
Thus, being endowed with such serenity toward the Blessed One, why did the king not achieve victory in that battle? (The connection is: "in this battle," "in that battle. || 21 ||
The minister will say:
"O lotus-eyed one, the Goddess was entreated by him with unwearied devotion at all times, saying: 'May there be liberation for me from saṃsāra. (22)
O Lord, by that very cause—through that unfailing consciousness—he was brought about;
thus, by King Vidūratha, defeat in battle was secured for him who relied upon it.
By that goddess, who possesses unfailing consciousness and whose resolve is true, liberation itself was accomplished; thus, he himself incurred defeat. || 23 ||
Sindhu will say:
"If this is so, then this goddess is always worshipped by me;
why does this Supreme Goddess not grant me liberation? (24)
The minister will say:
"For this is the petition that always resides within the heart of everyone;
that very Goddess, whose nature is consciousness, is called Sarasvatī. (25)
Jñapti is designated as Parā; it is the seed of all sounds, culminating in Vaikharī.
In whatever manner one's own [nature] is desired by each individual, it bestows that very thing immediately of its own accord; therefore, it is experienced as consciousness.
"Belonging to oneself" means beneficial to one's own self. Therefore, through that gift, his very consciousness of true resolve is experienced in the form of the fruit of the boon. || 26 ||
