O crusher of enemies, this [knowledge] was not sought by you for the sake of liberation;
rather, it was your own consciousness that was sought by you for the sake of subduing your foes. (27)
Sindhu will say:
"Why was this Sarasvatī not sought by me?
Why was pure discernment (*saṃvit*) not sought by me here for the sake of liberation? (28)

One should supply the word "iva" (as if) and construe it thus: "Why was he not requested by this Vidūratha for the sake of the kingdom, as if it were me? Or why was liberation not requested by him, as if it were me? || 28 ||
O dear one, why does this Sarasvatī, who has entered my heart and granted me this realization, not act—even though she is of auspicious form—for the sake of my liberation? (29)

Fearing that this question directed at me might be improper given your own inclination to act according to your own will, he reveals its true intent with the words "madāśaya" (my intention). "Āśaya" means the mind; even though this [will] residing therein is identical with my own self, why does it not grant me the cognition characterized by the desire for liberation and bring about my liberation through the perfection of the necessary means?
"It acts" means "it intends. || 29 ||
The minister will say:
"O Slayer of Enemies, you possess an inauspicious habit from your former lives;
therefore, O Lord, although this [meditation] leads to liberation, it was not requested by you after your prostration. (30)
Having bowed, that is, having paid homage. || 30 ||
"Since it is established from the very beginning of the world that a living being becomes what its mind is made of, who—starting from childhood—is able to act otherwise? (31)

The gods do not bestow grace independently, but rather solely in accordance with the disposition of the devotee's mind; with the intention that the Vedic scripture, "Whatever one’s mind is set upon, that one becomes—this is an eternal secret," serves as the authority for this meaning, he says, "whatever the mind.
Nor is this unknown even in the world, as he states, "from childhood onwards. || 31 ||
Whatever is internally realized by one whose self is stainless through stainless practice—
that very thing, my dear, becomes the unimpeded reality, whether it be existent or non-existent, by the total sublation of all else.
By whatever person, through stainless knowledge— that is, through consciousness— the kingdom of the stainless self-nature within one's own mind is realized,

whether it be liberation or something else, and having made it consist of practice, abundant with firm habituation, that which is then experienced— be it existent at that time or non-existent, or otherwise characterized— it is that very thing [which remains] through the destruction of all other latent impressions.
The person himself necessarily becomes free from obstacles; the meaning is that there is no other whatsoever who is the result of that [state]. 32.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-sixth chapter, titled "The Instruction to Sindhu," in the *Yogavāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa*, in the section on the *Vālmīki* tradition, the *Dehalī*, the *Mokṣopāya*, the *Nirvāṇa*, the *Uttara*, and the *Ardhaka* sections. 156.
Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-sixth chapter, titled "The Address to Sindhu," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and fifty-seventh canto: Then Sindhudvīpa will say:
"Who was I in the past, possessing both noble and ignoble forms and lacking right understanding?"
By whose power does this former latent impression (saṃskāra) of mine exist, which brings about further existence? (1)
The birth of Sindhujīva is described as being of the most tamasic nature;
yet, by renouncing his kingdom, he attained liberation in the end through discernment.
"Ārya" is an address to a minister. || 1 ||
The minister will say:
"Listen to the secret, O King, being intent on attentiveness for a moment;
being urged, join this today which destroys all infirmity."

Endowed with a mind intent on attentiveness—being thus "intent on attentiveness"—you, being impelled and urged by me today, shall place and maintain in your heart these words of mine, which effect the destruction of dullness and ignorance. (2)
There exists here something devoid of beginning and end,
real and free from disease, which abides in forms such as "you" and "I," and is designated by the word Brahman.

To explain the former state of the one who lives by the ocean (Sindhujīva) when questioned, [the author] first shows his existence in the nature of Brahman—intending to describe the state of being a *jīva* through connection with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*)—with the words "kimapīti" (something indescribable). He declares his universal identity with the words "sthitam" (it exists). || 3 ||
That Brahman itself, having assumed the consciousness "I am the conscious one," remained as if having attained the state of a living soul; having become the mind, it cast off its [prior] body.

Thinking, "I too shall move from here," and having attained the consciousness of volition, he became the collective and individual mind; then, as if attaining the state of a living soul within that limiting adjunct, he remained without casting off the limiting adjunct of the body.
Know that the mind is the body, whose nature is as pure as the sky and which is of a subtle, transportable form;
that alone exists here, and nothing else such as a material physicality.

What is that body which he abandoned when it had become lifeless? To this he says: "But the mindless... [referring to verse 4]. Then, what is this gross body? To this he says: "That very same... [verse 5].
This mind, though formless, exists as if possessing forms;
through mental constructions such as the next world and so forth, it alone is real, like dreams and the like.

That very mind, though formless, exists as if it were the world with its forms, through volitions such as the next world and this world, dream and waking, life and death, enjoyment and liberation, and so forth.
The wise know that this world is the mind itself, which, though formless, is all-pervasive—
just as that which is called "wind" is nothing other than its own vibration.
"This secret is known by those who know reality, and not by others," he says: "It is formless. (7)
Just as the world and the mind are one within the emptiness of space, so too,
in this unimpeded form, there is not even the slightest difference.
In this mind, which possesses unimpeded power to conceive the forms of the world within its non-resistant nature. || 8 ||
The web of the world residing in the heart is nothing at all;
know that the world is formless, being merely the mind and not real.
Due to delusion (*mithyātva*), nothing exists within the heart; rather, the entire web of the world remains merely as a latent impression (*vāsanā*), appearing as if it were something external.
That very body of goodness (sattva) which previously arose from the station of Brahmā has now become this one who is the most tamasic of the tamasic (tāmasatāmasa). || 10 ||

In the first creation, because it was composed of the nature of sattvic deities, that very *sattva* known as Hiraṇyagarbha arose from the state of Brahmā as his collective body (*samaṣṭivapuḥ*). This same collective entity, upon entering into individual manifestation (*vyaṣṭibhāva*),
[becomes the ego] through attachment to tamasic objects, according to the method described in the section on origination.
According to the sequence of the thirteenfold division beginning with the *rājasa-sāttvika*, that soul of yours has today become *tāmasa-tāmasa*.
Sindhu will speak:
"O illustrious one, what is being said? Tell me, who is the most tamasic of the tamasic? By whom were these designations first established in the supreme state? (11)
The question is clear. || 11 ||
The minister will say:

"Just as in this world a sentient being who possesses parts has parts such as hands and so forth, so too does the subtle body (ātivāhika) of the Self, though itself partless, possess such [parts]. (12)

With the intention that it is precisely the undivided Self which, through the delusion (*māyā*) of being divided by way of the state of Hiraṇyagarbha, creates all designations, he gives the answer: "of the living being" (*jantoḥ*). In this same manner, subsequently, that very Self will itself create various designations within itself.
Those named "pertaining to the elemental" (ādhibhautika) consist of earth and the other elements, while those in the subtle body (ātivāhika) are as follows.

In Himself, He will apply designations to His own individual souls (svavyaṣṭijīvas) as being the very Self of the aggregate (saṃmāṣṭyātman). If there is an elision [of the suffix], then according to the rule "tathā ātmeti soci lope cet pādapūraṇam," there is the elision of *sa*. Likewise, when His own aggregate subtle body (ātivāhika-svadeha) has been made into a material body (ādhibhautikatā) through quintuplication (pañcīkaraṇa), He will apply the designations of earth and the other elements to its constituent parts. || 13 ||
In this appearance of the world, which is like a dream, he himself will engage in worldly activity through his own volition, which is of the nature of the Self,
by means of that very form of the Self known as consciousness.
Having thus conceptualized name-and-form, he himself will engage in worldly activity as an individual entity.
Because that which has manifested as a new form of the subtle body (ātivāhika) has been called "this birth" (jāti), it is designated as such even though it is characterized by great darkness.

In that regard, when the individualized state was being conceptualized, Hiraṇyagarbha—by means of a creative resolve directed toward you and through his individualized nature—perceived [you] as "this one is of great darkness" (mahātamaska). For that reason, the meaning is that your species, characterized by a subtle body (ativāhikākāra), was given the name "Mahātamaskī," which signifies the darkness of darkness (tāmasatāmasī). || 15 ||
For the Lord Brahmā, who is changeless though appearing as if subject to transformation,
various castes have been fashioned under diverse names upon his assuming the state of individual souls.

This is not the only designation; rather, he states that when Brahman exists in the state of the individual soul (jīva), thirteen designations—such as *rājasa*, *sāttvika*, and so forth—are made according to the qualities of their respective limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*): "Of Brahman... (verse 16).

When Brahman itself, through its very primacy, assumes as it were the state of a living being, at that very moment it becomes the enjoyer by means of the intellect; such a class of beings is the most refined among the sattvic.

In this context, demonstrating that the conceptualization of the different classes (*jāti*) of living beings is due solely to the virtues and defects of the mind which cause the swiftness or delay of liberation, he classifies and defines those five classes beginning with the words "by being foremost" (*prāthamyena*). If, at the beginning of a kalpa,
[the individual] first attains the state of being a living being within Brahman, then, in that very birth—
One who is an enjoyer of sense objects through an intellect endowed with innate knowledge and sovereignty is liberated in that very birth;
such is the most sattvic of sattvic births, as in the case of Sanaka and others. 17.
O giver of honor, that birth which is endowed with auspicious qualities in the present existence is declared by the best among those who know births to be purely *sāttvika*. (18)

The meaning is that if, while existence and its cause— ignorance— persist for some time, one becomes endowed with auspicious qualities such as knowledge and sovereignty in that very birth and is then liberated, it is said to be purely *sāttvika*. || 18 ||
If, through many births, one becomes a partaker solely of both worldly enjoyment and liberation,
that is called by the virtuous who know the truth "the most excellent among the rajasic" (rājasarājasī).

That birth which, though newly manifested at the beginning of a kalpa, becomes—after many births have been spent in experiencing worldly enjoyments—gradually destined for liberation alone, is called *rājasarājasī*; such is the meaning. || 19 ||
O giver of honor, that which is devoid of auspicious qualities in the present existence is declared to be purely *rājasa* birth; it may occur even in a short lifetime.

Even after fifteen births within that same kalpa, if one who has little existence is devoid of auspicious qualities such as discernment (*viveka*) and the like, they will undergo a succession of many more births; however, if they eventually attain auspicious qualities, it means that [the previous state] was purely *rājasa*. || 20 ||
If one proceeds toward liberation through an extremely great number of births,
that is called by the wise and the virtuous "Tāmasatāmasī" (the most ignorant among the ignorant).

The first type, beginning from the start of the kalpa, consists of those who are extremely numerous—such as stationary beings, insects, and kirātas—and who only at the very end become partakers of liberation; this is the meaning of the "tāmasa-tāmasī" (the most ignorant among the ignorant). || 21 ||
In general, those who possess the lot of liberation after many births are declared by the experts in the classification of castes to be of the purely *tāmasī* class.
If she were merely of a purely tamasic nature, she would generally belong to many births among rākṣasas, piśācas, śūdras, and so forth, which are neither superior nor conducive to liberation. (22)
By this sequence, there is a manifold conceptualization of the divisions of castes;
you have been born, O giver of honor, into this most tamasic of those castes.
Among those classes of beings, you have been born into this most tamasic class. || 23 ||
"O hero, many births of yours have passed away—those various and manifold ones I know, but you do not. (24)
You know us. 24.
But especially by you, who possess a body like that of a great corpse yet are capable of traveling through infinite space, this time has been spent in vain.
Thus, when you were born from a lineage that is even more *tāmasa* than *tāmasa*, then liberation for you from the cavern of *saṃsāra* is difficult to attain. || 26 ||
The word "iti" marks the conclusion of the question and answer. || 26 ||
Sindhu will say:
"Noble sir, tell me by what means this base birth may be overcome?
As long as it remains thus, tell me that which would purify it. (27)

By what means is this wretched, most ignorant species of living beings—characterized by past [karma]—conquered or overcome? O Noble One, explain that means! If there should be such a purifying and cleansing method by which I may remain, for as long as I have a body, in that very manner according to your instruction, then tell me that. || 27 ||
The minister will say:
"O one of great intelligence, there is nothing whatsoever in these three worlds that cannot be attained by a man who is free from despondency. (28)
By *pauruṣa*, meaning by human effort (*puruṣaprayatna*). || 28 ||
Just as yesterday’s misconduct attains splendor through virtuous action today,
one should therefore strive with effort this very day to perform good deeds for the sake of the future.

Just as yesterday’s misconduct attains beauty and excellence through virtuous action this very day, so too, by that same effort, conquer your past [misconduct] and become one who performs good deeds. 29.
Whoever strives for a particular goal in accordance with that which they seek, will certainly attain it, provided they do not turn back out of exhaustion. (30)
In whatever way one constantly strives, whatever one cultivates, and whatever one is composed of, and however one desires to become—that is how one becomes, and not otherwise. (31)
Not a person. || 31 ||
The sage said:
Thus addressed by him with a resolute mind,
he will then and there completely abandon that kingdom under such a name.
Having been addressed thus by that minister, [she], with her burden of sovereignty cast off, became resolute. || 32 ||
For even though entreated by his ministers, he will go to the distant forest;
he will not again resort to that kingdom from which all enemies have been eradicated.
He will not rely upon it, nor will he accept it. || 33 ||
As he remains in the midst of the virtuous, through the power of those discourses on discernment, discernment will arise within him, just as fragrance arises from contact with flowers. (34)
Just as fragrance arises in oil and other substances through contact with flowers, so shall discernment arise. || 34 ||
Then, by means of continuous inquiry as to "How has this birth come about? From where has this saṃsāra arrived?", he will attain liberation.
The state of liberation, that is, liberation while living. || 35 ||
Then, becoming constantly devoted to inquiry, that Sindhu will, through the company of the virtuous, attain the purifying state where no fortune whatsoever—
like a leaf shaken by the wind— attains any reality.

That King Sindhu, being constantly devoted to inquiry through association with the virtuous, will then attain that purifying state known as liberation; in that state of liberation, even the splendor extending up to the sovereignty of Hiraṇyagarbha does not attain the status of a reality or worthiness of acceptance, but rather becomes like a dry leaf shaken by the wind. However—
The meaning is that it becomes utterly empty. || 36 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-seventh chapter, titled "The Liberation of Sindhu," in the *Śavopākhyāna* (The Narrative of the Corpse) within the *Upadeśaprakaraṇa* of the *Mokṣopāya*, in the *Vālmīkīya-uttara-pāda* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa*.
Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-seventh chapter, titled "The Liberation of Sindhu," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and fifty-eighth canto. The sage said:
"All this has been told to you, concerning the future as if it were already past."
"O hunter, now let it be properly done just as you wish."
Having heard the words of the sage, the hunter performed austerities; by a boon from Brahmā, he leaped into the air, became a corpse, and fell down—thus it is described, and so forth.
Because it is a fact, like a story of the past. || 1 ||
Agni said:
Having heard these words of his, his mind overwhelmed with wonder,
both the hunter and the sage remained still for a moment and then quickly went to bathe.
Having stood for a moment, he reflected; that is to say, until he had reflected.
Thus both of them, the hunter and the great sage, who had become friends without cause, wandered there, engaged in asceticism and the investigation of the scriptures.
Then, in a very short time, the sage attained nirvāṇa;
having cast off his body at the end of his allotted span, he reached the supreme transformation.
The intention is that "in just a short time" implies that even a much longer duration of time appears brief while the sage is in meditative absorption (*samādhi*).

Although, according to the literal reading of the text, it appears that the sage’s abandonment of the body occurred first and the arrival of the Lotus-born One (*Padmaja*) to grant the hunter his desire occurred later after a long interval, nevertheless, previously...
In the sage’s book of prophecies, it was stated that after the hunter received the boon,
he would say, "Having taken leave of me and paid my respects, at that very moment you shall leap up into the sky,
desiring to behold the object situated within your mind. Because of this statement by the sage, the sage remained alive at the time of the hunter's upward ascent.
It should be understood that "it remains as it is" means that the abandonment of the body occurs only later; [this happens] at the end of the lifespan that was specified as the pretext. || 4 ||
Then, after a long time consisting of hundreds of ages had passed,
the Lotus-born One arrived to grant the hunter's desire.
The hunter, unable to restrain the onset of his own latent tendencies,
requested the boon previously described, even though he already knew it.
Although he knew that it had previously been described by the Sage as being useless, he nevertheless requested the boon.
Having said, "O Brahmā, let it be so," he departed in his desired direction;
the hunter, to enjoy the fruit of his asceticism, leaped into the sky like a bird.
With his ever-increasing body, he filled the great sky beyond the world for an incalculable time with speed, like a mountain.
Beyond the world, above the three realms, is the great space, the unmanifest ether. || 8 ||
As he filled the sky— sideways, upwards, and downwards— with the great speed of a garuḍa, a vast amount of time passed.
Then, after a long time, when he did not reach the end of that delusion of knowledge, he fell into a state of agitation.
Agitation and the world-weariness induced by it. || 10 ||

Then, out of agitation, having bound his breath through the practice of *prāṇarecana-dhāraṇā*, he abandoned his life-breaths in the sky; his body became a corpse, falling downward. [In the reading *adhobhuvi*, the word *vapuḥ* must be supplied. || 11 ||
The mind, endowed with the vital breaths, went into the sky and there attained the state of the ocean—
that very [ocean] which was the form of Vidūratha’s enemy and the protector of the entire earth.
The state of being a river (sindhutām) means the sovereignty over the Sindhu country; the enemy of Vidūratha was his foe, that is, Drupada. || 12 ||
Becoming bodiless like a great corpse with the form of a hundred Meru mountains,
he fell from the sky like a thunderbolt or diamond, resembling a second earth.
Having abandoned his body, he fell through the path of the sky.
It is like a covering for some path upon the earth,
or like a tuft of hair appearing in some part of the sky, or like a whirling dizziness within some worldly delusion.

In a certain delusion of the world belonging to some Brahmā, appearing like a tuft of hair [seen by one with an eye disease], the path of the earth stands there in the midst of space like a vast covering. || 14 ||
O best of the learned, I have thus described to you that great corpse, which filled the entire circle of the earth and its mountains with its physical form.
O best of men, O wise one, I have thus related to you this great corpse along with its history exactly as it happened. || 15 ||
In this world, upon the circle of the earth, wherever a corpse has fallen, this entire world appears to us like a city in a dream. (16)
It has appeared in our minds, manifest and vibrating with clarity. || 16 ||
Having tasted this corpse, the goddess Caṇḍikā— once lean, now full, and possessing a large belly— became red and filled with red entrails.
Being filled with blood and entrails, she became red, that is, possessed of a red color. || 17 ||
The earth has become "Medinī" because it was filled with the fat (medas) of this corpse;
it is filled with a form never seen before, possessing the appearance of the Himavat mountain.
By means of a form never seen before, which was truly marvelous. || 18 ||
At that very moment, this great fat attained the state of the element of earth;
in time, the earth once again became composed of clay.
Forests have once again sprouted upon the earth, and villages have been established along with cities;
those mountains have emerged from the netherworld, and the prosperity of worldly commerce has begun to flourish.
Previously, because the forests and other things had been destroyed by the corpse, the forests grew forth once more; the villages were re-established;
and those crushed mountains rose up properly from the netherworld (pātāla) just as before. Thus, the meaning is that the prosperity of human worldly activity then commenced. || 20 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-eighth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Corpse," in the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*, in the *Vālmīkīya-Devarāja-Mokṣopāya-Nirvāṇa-Uttara* section, within the *Avimuktaka-Viyoginī-Śataka*.
Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-eighth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Corpse," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and fifty-ninth canto.
Agni said:
"O best of the wise, O virtuous one, go now to the direction you desire."
Furthermore, the circle of the earth remains stable, as it does in its natural course of worldly activity.
Having taught here Agni’s journey to Indra for the sake of the wise one,
many wonders are described at the end, as well as the reality of Brahman.
O most excellent Vipaschit, having once again reached the circle of the earth with stability, as if engaged in your ordinary affairs, proceed toward your desired direction. || 1 ||
"O Śakra, you have been summoned by a mantra to perform a sacrifice for the multitude of subjects in heaven on the hundredth day; O knower of ways, I am going there. (2)
Śakra has begun to perform a sacrifice in heaven; I have been summoned there, so I am going. || 2 ||
Bhāsa said:
Having spoken thus, the blessed Agni vanished right there,
like a flash of lightning moving across a cloudless sky.
He disappeared in the form of a physical body; however, in the form of fire, he moved through the sky like a flash of lightning. || 3 ||
In the same way, I too, carrying my own past [deeds] by means of the mind,
remained wandering in the sky in order to determine my own karma once again.

Carrying with him the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) regarding the objects of perception from his previous ignorance, he acts to determine and accomplish his own movement toward the furthest reaches of the quarters. || 4 ||
Once again, I beheld countless worlds in the sky,
possessing various modes of conduct and reflection, and existing in diverse forms.
In some places, O King, bodies made entirely of umbrellas appear as a single mass;
they shine, they seem conscious, they move, and they captivate the heart.

He describes those very worlds as he has seen them with the words beginning "In some places" (*kvacit*) and so forth. "United" (*ekībhūtāni*) means joined together with one another. "O Lord of the Earth" (*bhūpate*) is an address to Daśaratha. They "move slowly" (*copanti*) and they "steal" (*haranti*) the hearts and minds of the beholders. (6)
In some places, O Rāghava, all beings with bodies made of clay appear,
perceive, and move about, resembling mountains.
In some places there appear beings with limbs made of wood;
in other places there are numerous beings with bodies of stone.
Somewhere in the world. || 8 ||
In some places, beings were seen in the sky remaining together for the duration of their lives like solid rocks, their activities consisting of mere words.

For as long as life lasts, like a stone statue or an image; they engage only in verbal interactions such as mutual conversation, but do not possess activities such as going or taking things; "in the sky" means within the space of one's own mind. || 9 ||
Thus, for a very long time, though I watched with a focused mind, I did not perceive the end of ignorance; consequently, I became distressed by that state of vision.
Being of the nature of mind, like a dream, with a body consisting of mind alone; therein, within the sphere of ignorance—the objects of the various classes of perceptions—I became distressed. (10)
While he was intent on performing austerities for the sake of attaining liberation somewhere, Indra said to him: "Indeed, there is another deer-species for me in the sky."

Thus, being deeply agitated, I sat down in a certain secluded place and became intent on performing austerity—the contemplation of the reality of the Self—for the sake of attaining liberation. Then Indra spoke to me. What did he say? "O Vipaścit, in the sky of the mind (*khe*), this great interval between my birth and yours has arrived; therefore, this is not the time for the contemplation of the reality of the Self."
This is the meaning. || 11 ||
Overcome by the delusion of heaven and enslaved by my former habits,
I was indeed wandering in the sky there in the grove of Mandāra trees.

[The opponent objects: "Surely, for me of little merit, it is possible that some evil deed might lead to birth as a deer; but for you, who possess great merit, how could such a possibility exist? To this he replies with the word *pravṛtta* ("engaged"): "I too was engaged in the delusion of heavenly enjoyment due to the offense against Durvāsas; where, however, was your engagement in such a thing? He answers this with the word *mandāra*. (12)
When I said "So be it," he replied, "O Lord, I am weary of worldly existence;
may I be liberated quickly. Having heard this, he then spoke to me.
When that Indra had spoken thus, [it happened]. || 13 ||
When the Fire-god said, "I am the pure self and formless;
choose a boon," I then requested another [boon] from him. || 14 ||

He states what he said at that time: "Purified," and so forth. Liberation quickly occurs only through the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), namely: "I am indeed the pure Self, devoid of form—that is, free from the three states as well as from the forms of the manifest and the unmanifest.
The remainder of the sense is that you have already heard this previously from Hutāśana during the context of describing the dialogue with Vyādha.

When Indra said, "Therefore, choose another boon," I requested of him another boon in the form of complete knowledge regarding what would happen to me in the future during my state as a deer. || 14 ||
Indra said:
"This consciousness of yours has wandered for a long time within the womb of a deer;
I have perceived that this purpose of yours was destined to come to pass. (15)
He transmigrates, or he desires to transmigrate. || 15 ||
Having become a deer, he has reached that highly meritorious assembly hall,
wherein this unerring knowledge spoken by me shall lead to awakening.
To that assembly of the son of Daśaratha, he of pure soul spoke my words, namely: "I am formless. || 16 ||
Thus, O deer, afflicted by worldly existence, you will remember all this fruitless account of your own life here on the earth of saṃsāra.
Having been thus addressed, Hariṇa gradually reached the assembly hall and, through the grace of Vasiṣṭha, related his entire account— his own life story.
It is like a dream or an illusion, comparable to that which is fashioned by all conceptual constructions;
it resembles the meaning conveyed by a story about an object experienced in another world.
He elucidates this very state of barrenness through examples, beginning with "In a dream... (verse 18).
But when you become a man released from the state of a deer, then,
at the end of this body consumed by the fire of knowledge, that [truth] which resides in the heart will flash forth.
"Will I remember [it] by means of the deer's body alone? To this he says "no": "When... (verse 19).
Therefore, having abandoned that long-standing delusion called ignorance, you will become fully extinguished, like a wind whose movement has ceased. || 20 ||
By that radiance of the reality of the self, he is completely liberated, that is, released. || 20 ||
When that god had spoken thus, at that very moment an intuition arose in her, certain of this: "I am this doe in this forest. (21)
When that lord of gods had spoken thus, that prior mental impression— "I am a deer"— arose, now confirmed, capable of purposeful activity for the sake of worldly transaction.
From that time forward, I became a deer right there in that inner corner on that excellent mountain, feeding upon blades of grass and sprouts of dūrvā.
Right there, in a corner within the Mandāra grove. || 22 ||
Then, once upon a time, seeing a forest-dweller who had come to the border of my territory seeking game, I became afraid and intent on flight. || 23 ||
Then, O scion of Raghu, having approached him and led him home, he kept him there for three days and brought him here for your pleasure.
O sinless one, I have related to you this entire account of myself,
which is like the illusion of saṃsāra and filled with various wonderful flavors.
It is comparable to the illusion of a magician well-known in the world of saṃsāra. || 25 ||
Thus, this ignorance is infinite, flourishing with the spreading of its branches;
it is never extinguished by anything at all except for the knowledge of the Self. (26)
Śrī Vālmīki said: When Vipaścit had spoken thus and remained silent for a moment, Rāma, whose intellect is beyond reproach, then addressed him with these words.
This is what will be stated hereafter. || 27 ||
Śrī Rāma said: "O Lord, tell me: how did that which is without volition perceive itself as another volition within the Self, such that it became the object of sight in creation, like a deer? (28)

If this deer, which consists of another's volition (*saṃkalpa*), has become an object of perception for us, then it follows that even a person who is himself devoid of volition perceives the multitude of objects existing within the creation of another's volition. Explain how this can be logically established.
This is the meaning. || 28 ||
Vipaścit said:
Regarding that great corpse which fell upon the earth in this world—formerly, as Indra was traveling there out of pride in his sacrifices, [he encountered it]. (29)

To provide the answer— that even an object imagined through the volition of another, such as by the curse or blessing of a great sage (*mahāmuni*) or a deity, becomes fit for the practical activities of seeing and so forth even for those who did not form that volition— the author introduces the previously mentioned corpse as a further illustration, beginning with the words "a great corpse" (*mahāśava*), etc. Previously...

Before the corpse was cast down, Indra— blinded by the pride of being the sacrificer in the Mandara forest due to his performance of sacrifices toward that ground, and failing to recognize that this was a sage, mistaking him for one whose life had departed— struck Durvāsas with his foot out of contempt. || 29 ||
Struck by his foot in the sky while absorbed in meditation, Durvāsas—
unaware that he had passed away— became enraged and cursed him.
O Śakra, this corpse, which resembles the cosmic egg and is as vast as the surface of the earth,
will before long crush you, O most terrible one, into powder.

In the phrase "Śakra, Śakra," the word *śakra* is repeated twice following the vocative particle because of the rule stating that repetition occurs after a vocative when expressing envy, approval, anger, contempt, or threat; here it is used in the sense of anger and so forth. [If you go,] the surface of the earth, which you desire to reach, will be pulverized. (31)
"Since you have passed me by, regarding me with the notion that I am a corpse, you shall therefore quickly reach the earth through my curse. (32)
Just as that sage had previously done for the sake of the deer, O Goddess,
so too by that conversation she was brought at once into the range of his vision.

By that sage Durvāsas, together with Vipaścit, for the sake of Śakra’s state as a deer, you likewise became a divine deer at the same time as Vipaścit; by the word "Vipaścit," just as even the deerhood mentally conceived by Vipaścit became real and capable of performing causal functions such as being seen by others, so too did he.

The word "cursed" (śapta) is to be understood as the ellipsis. Therefore, by that very account of Indra’s curse, through the power of the sage’s words, even the deer-form of Vipracitti—which was produced merely by his will—became an object of perception for those like you at all times; that is, it attained the status of being perceived. || 33 ||
In reality, however, it is neither one, nor a second, nor even non-existent;
that manifestation arises in such a way—so, is it existent or rather non-existent? (34)

Having thus resolved Rāma’s question from the perspective of worldly consensus (*jagatprasiddhadṛśā*), he resolves it from the perspective of ultimate reality (*tattvadṛśā*)—beginning with "In reality, however" (*vastutastu*). Upon investigation, even that one empirical world is not real; nor is the second, the conceptualized world, unreal. Because both are equal, he says: "That" (*sā*) || 34 ||
Furthermore, O Raghava, listen to another argument from me for the sake of a very clear understanding of this composition. (35)
He states that there is no contradiction whatsoever even because Brahman possesses all powers and is the self of all, beginning with the words "Moreover... and so forth;
*nayāḥ* refers to logical arguments, and *tāsāṃ saṃdarbhe* means in their systematic arrangement. || 35 ||
O highly fortunate one, in that Brahman wherein all exists, from which all proceeds, which is all, and which is everywhere—in that, indeed, what is there that cannot come to be? (36)
It is logical that what is born of conceptual construction does not meet with another; it is also logical that what is born of conceptual construction meets with another. (37)
The meaning is that both [the notions] that what is born of volition (saṃkalpa) does not meet with another and that it does meet are possible within the All-Powerful One;
thus it is understood that what is born of volition meets with one another.
For in the Self of All, wherever there is shadow, right there is also sunlight. 38.
It is directly perceived in cases such as the sight of a deer; and since there is a logical justification for this, he says: "in every soul."
If that [universe] were not possible, how could it attain the state of being the self of all?
Why is it true that a city of one's imagination does not coalesce with another? (39)
If contradictory attributes cannot coexist in one place, then the very nature of Brahman as the Self of all would be contradicted; thus he says, "No.
And this point has already been explained extensively on many previous occasions. || 39 ||
And thus, even as it embraces itself within that which possesses all forms,
there is nothing that is not real, and there is nothing that is not false.
Everywhere, in every way, everything, at all times, in every form—alas, how treacherous is this illusion that brings delusion to the mind! 41.
Because *māyā* is capable of bringing about the impossible and is thus of a most wondrous nature, everything is possible; thus he says:
"Affirmations and negations both find their place in one and the same [reality].
Such is this existence of Brahman, that by itself it manifests itself as itself. (42)
He states that such majesty belongs not only to illusion (māyā) but also to the existence of Brahman (brahmasattā): "Such is... (verse 42).
By that [ignorance], it is experienced as both beginningless and having a beginning;
for if the three worlds were merely pure consciousness, this would not be so. (43)
By that reality of Brahman. || 43 ||
How could the creation of those things destroyed at the end of the great kalpa occur properly?
How would there be the existence of fire, how of wind, and how of earth? (44)
Therefore, apart from the mere manifestation of its own nature, there is no other world;
this is the conclusion of the scriptures, of experience, and of the people who maintain their doctrines until the end of the great aeon (mahākalpa).

The world is nothing other than the mere manifestation of its own nature (*svabhāva*). This is established by the Vedānta and other scriptures, the experience of the wise, and worldly well-known examples. The meaning is that there is no point in conversing with those fools for whom these are not authoritative means of knowledge. || 45 ||
For those for whom not everything is an authoritative means of knowledge, enough with those [means] praised by the virtuous;
by this very vision of realization (*jñapti-dṛṣṭi*), everything becomes an authoritative means of knowledge in an instant. (46)
By means of the praiseworthy, [which by] the logic of contrariety [are actually] censurable; by the vision of pure consciousness, that is, the vision of the play of *cit*. || 46 ||
The wise know that essence is not other than that very body;
it is pure consciousness, the existence of Brahman, yet [it appears otherwise] due to the thought "I am ignorance."

However, through any other view, it does not become authoritative; rather, it becomes thin and insignificant. For that reason, the wise know the essence to be established solely by the vision of knowledge (*jñānadṛṣṭi*). How they know this, he states with the verse beginning "pure" (*śuddha*):
"This world-form flashes forth like the beauty of wind from its vibration. (47)
No one here dies, and no one at all is born.
The very notion that "I am dead" and "this exists" is of the nature of consciousness.
If death were absolute annihilation, then it would be like sleep, comparable to bliss.
If the absolute disappearance [of the world] is the non-perception of the visible, that is deep sleep, comparable to the bliss of that state. (49)
If there is again the perception of the visible object, then surely that is life itself;
therefore, there is no death here, nor is there any life here at all.
In some mere manifestation, there may be duality, or there may be none at all;
that which is perceived exists as duality, while that which is not perceived does not exist as duality.
"In which one?"—the elision of the vowel *e* is a Vedic (archaic) usage. He states the justification for this with the words "it is perceived" (*cetitam*). || 51 ||
And that which is perceived is one alone, the infinite well-being of consciousness;
tell me, what indeed is life apart from pure consciousness? 52.

Therefore, the meaning is that for consciousness (*cit*), which is the witness to the existence and non-existence of duality, there is always its own well-being and security. For a life free from suffering is indeed desired by all as happiness, and since that [happiness] is nothing but pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), that alone is the supreme human goal (*puruṣārtha*). Thus he says: "Pure consciousness... Because it is imperishable, it is free from suffering; therefore, where and for whom could there be suffering?
Where everything, including both the expressed and the expresser, is nothing but the space of consciousness.
In which vision of reality all that is expressible form, together with its expressive name, [is subsumed]. (53)
It is both different from that and non-different from that; what then are unity and duality there?
Just as whirlpools and the like exist in water, so do bodies and the like exist in the Supreme.
Anticipating the objection that "is it not the case that the body and so forth are themselves suffering?", he says: "āvartādi" (beginning with whirlpools), etc. || 54 ||

The world is nothing but the unagitated manifestation of consciousness—unobstructed like space itself—whose nature consists of the presence and arrangement of that [consciousness], and which is non-different from its cause. 55.
Because it is not distinct from its cause, it consists of the very nature of all causes; it is unimpeded and stainless.
It is a marvel that a substance which is very dense, agitated, and characterized by resistance remains;
likewise, there is no ground for such an experience, nor is there a ground for experiencing the present.

That which exists as a dense, distinct, and resistant substance is itself a marvel! Just as there is no objective domain for existence (bhū) in the past—that is, in what has passed and is known—likewise, even in the present, there is no objective domain for existence in experience;
that is, the domain of experience does not exist [as a separate object]. || 56 ||
In that regard, let it be understood that through delusion this Piśāca appears as the "self in the void";
for just as this is space, so too is this space—this remains as space.

In that experience of the present, let it be understood that this void-self appears as a visible phantom, having become the void-self itself. Just as this sky is being perceived here, so too is this sky whose nature is the space of consciousness (cidākāśa); for this very sky, recognized as the space of consciousness, remains as a void. || 57 ||
Thus, from this [consciousness] has arisen the world, and from this [world] arises that which is other than it—the supreme void.
That which is the light of consciousness is itself the world; herein there is neither unity nor duality.

Likewise, the meaning is that in this lower region there is earth, in another region there are the elements such as air and space, and in these directions and intermediate points there is something else; thus, while appearing in manifold forms, it is only the supreme ether (khama) that shines, and nothing else. || 58 ||
There is neither any resistance nor any lack of resistance;
for one who sees the reality of things as they are, everything that is perceived is non-resistant. (59)
In this context, neither the knowledge of that nor the lack of knowledge of it exists, nor do they exist as non-existent;
since both existence and non-existence are unreal, therefore everything is the silence of wood.
He states that even the distinction between knowledge and ignorance vanishes in the vision of fullness: "tajjñatā" (that knowledge), etc. || 60 ||
Whatever is perceived as the infinite Brahman—that alone is the supreme state;
all this is established as being nothing but the Supreme Brahman. || 61 ||
And thus, he says "That which... [verse 61], meaning that all that is perceivable has indeed become Brahman itself.
Thus this element of consciousness shines forth within itself;
its shining is the world, the unobstructed form of space.

From the beginning of creation, there have been innumerable births and deaths for living beings at every single finger-breadth; these are infinite in number, invisible, and do not obstruct one another.
He says that creations exist everywhere: "beginning with creation" (sargādyāḥ). And this has been established in detail previously by Vasiṣṭha. || 63 ||
Those perfected beings, having reached their own respective worlds, are gathered together;
though they remain joined with one another, they do not see each other.

The worlds of the perfected ones (*siddha-loka*) become increasingly subtle, having attained their own essential nature, wherein they merge into Brahman. This is described in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* in the questions of Gārgī: "In what, indeed, are all these things woven warp and woof? "In water, O Gārgī. "In what, indeed, are water woven warp and woof? "In wind, O Gārgī. "In what, indeed, is wind woven warp and woof?"
"Beyond this world, O Gārgī, and beyond the intermediate worlds," and so forth. (64)
This splendor of the visible world exists as nothing but space, having the nature of the sky;
it is of the form of consciousness, perceived by none other than itself, and is the seer of its own self, like a dream.
In reality, however, with the intention that the existence of a seer distinct from the Self is itself unestablished, he says: "it becomes.
Since this splendor of the visible world exists only within the space of the Self, it is therefore seen by none other. 65.
For when this is thoroughly understood, it remains just as it is:
its nature is the extinction of mere appearance, a state of rest devoid of the form of conceptual manifestation. (66)
He says, "For this indeed," because its very nature is the sky of consciousness (cidgagana), its form is realized merely through full knowledge.
Its form is like the form of darkness—that which is called "non-appearance" (apratibhā)—at the end of night, at dawn. || 66 ||
The entire web of the world, whether existent or non-existent, which remains as it is with its nature of all-pervading tranquility, is stilled through perfect knowledge. (67)

If it remains as it is—established as having a nature in which all particularities are stilled—then whether this world be real or unreal, it is sublated by ignorance; there is no loss whatsoever. Thus he says: "Stilled," etc. (67).
Just as there is a momentary separation and union of drops of ocean water,
so too is the mutual [separation and union] of the atoms of consciousness (cidaṇu) as they flash forth within the ocean of Brahman.

Let it be so with this web of the world; now he describes the state of the living beings bound within it in relation to Brahman—beginning with "yathā" (as). This means: as long as ignorance persists, they exist in the relationship of part and whole. || 68 ||
At the beginning of creation, the splendor of the world appears like a dream, consisting of the sky of consciousness;
therefore, it is logically established that all this is the peaceful Brahman. || 69 ||
He explains how the splendor of creation appears to them at the beginning of creation with the words: "Like a dream" (svapnavat). || 69 ||

I have seen worlds of infinite splendor and experienced them as they unfold through the transformation of karma; I have wandered through the ten directions for many eons, yet the defect of the visible world does not come to an end except through knowledge.

I have beheld worlds of infinite splendor; I have experienced the fruits of pleasure and pain, which are the manifestations resulting from the transformation of my own past actions (karmas). I have wandered through the quarters for many ages—to the extent that it can be fully stated—the meaning is that the defect of the visible world does not reach its end except through knowledge. || 70 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-ninth canto, titled "The Description of the Delusion of Saṃsāra," in the Mahārāmāyaṇa of Vālmīki, in the Uttarakāṇḍa, in the section concerning the liberation of Vipracitti.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-ninth canto, titled "The Description of the Delusion of Saṃsāra by Vipaścit," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the glorious Vāsiṣṭha-tātparya-prakāśa.
The one hundred and sixtieth canto.
Śrī Vālmīki said:
While Vipaścit was speaking thus, in order to observe the details of that event, [Rāma]—
Like the sun proceeding to another world, he went with his feet stretched out far ahead.
In this [chapter], the rising from the assembly in the evening, the return on the following day,
Bhāsa’s state of liberation while living, and ignorance are described.
Having heard the former account of that Bhāsa, as if to witness it directly with its rays for feet, the drum at the end of the day arose, filling the quarters;
and a roar of "Victory! Victory! was released by the directions, as if they were delighted. (2)
The quarters are the directions; the drum that signaled the evening—the end of the day—was sounded. "With contented [voices]" is a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) regarding that.
To the wise one, Daśaratha gradually bestowed his household, wives, wealth, and so forth—a prosperity commensurate with his kingdom—as he rose up from his seat. (3)
Conceptualizing and establishing. || 3 ||
Having mutually taken their leave and performed the rites of worship in due order, those [sages] headed by Rājarāma and Vasiṣṭha departed for their own abodes.
Their own abodes are their respective homes. || 4 ||
Having bathed, eaten, and passed the night, they returned at dawn;
that assembly hall remained established in that very same arrangement.
In that very same previous arrangement, in due order.
Then, like the moon emitting the delight of nectar through the radiance of its face, the sage gradually spoke that story which had been introduced.
Uttering words that bring delight, as the moon gladdens with the radiance of its face like nectar, he spoke.
"O King, this is ignorance; it persists as if real though it is unreal.
Even with such effort, this has not been definitively resolved by the wise. (7)
Thus, by means of the methods of description employed by Vipaścit, it is meant that ignorance, which consists of the delusion of the visible world, has not been determined as having an end. || 7 ||
Thus, ignorance, when not fully understood, appears as long-lasting and endless;
but when fully understood, it does not exist at all, like a river in a mirage.
Being unrecognized as being nothing other than the Brahman that is the substratum, it remains for a long time, infinite in terms of time, space, and substance. || 8 ||
O you of great intelligence, you yourself have indeed witnessed this life-story of the wise Bhāsa, who was their minister.
The phrase "those ministers saw" is drawn back [to the previous context] by means of ellipsis (vipariṇāma). || 9 ||
Through these discourses similar to those [you have already given], he will come to know that supreme state;
and when ignorance has been stilled, he will become liberated while living (jīvanmukta). || 10 ||
After this, through these supreme discourses, having realized the truth and with ignorance stilled, he will become a liberated-while-living (jīvanmukta) equal to you. || 10 ||
Consciousness is sustained by Brahman within the self through its own existence;
yet, due to that delusion, even what is non-existent appears to it as if it were real.
Since consciousness was held by Brahmā under the name "ignorance," therefore, through that very delusion, its unreal form appears as if it were real. || 11 ||
When this ignorance consists solely of Brahman and not of anything else,
then, whether it is uncomprehended or comprehended, it does not differ.

And thus, because this [avidyā] lacks any nature apart from Brahman, its existence lasts only as long as it remains uncomprehended; its cessation occurs through mere comprehension. He states this with the words "When... (verse 12).
Thus, this ignorance is infinite, abounding in manifold productions;
it is insentient yet charming, a flower-cluster of the springtime of delusion, full of aesthetic flavor. 13.
He describes that very ignorance with the words beginning "avidyā" (ignorance) and so forth. In all cases, the qualifiers are to be applied to both [ignorance and spring].
It is "rasamayī," meaning it causes attachment; it is a "mañjarī" (cluster of blossoms) in full bloom during "mohalakṣaṇe mādhave," that is, in the spring season characterized by delusion. || 13 ||
Hollow within, knotted, smooth, yet possessing its own sprouts and thorns;
dull, full of sap, and long—she is like a forest bamboo creeper.
Smooth at first sight, yet possessing sharp thorns in every bud at the time of experience—she is like a forest-creeper grown upon a wild bamboo, resembling its branch. (14)
The hope for fruit is in vain, utterly fruitless, and captivating to the mind; like a garland of flowers out of season, it is not welcomed by that which is auspicious. 15.

In which [hope] there was a suspicion that the fruit would exist only in vain; it was not welcomed by the wise, who are most excellent in discerning what is beneficial, like a garland of flowers out of season appearing as an ill omen. 15.
It was not at all corporeal or solid, yet it filled various worlds;
crowded with living beings and devoid of light, it was like a vast expanse of darkness.
It was crowded with spirits, living beings, and piśācas, like a night consisting of darkness.
Like the illusion of a tuft of hair, it is a complex entanglement of various knots;
appearing falsely in the sky, when scrutinized, it is nothing at all.
Lacking variegated colors and devoid of qualities, it is an expansive form within the void;
consisting of dull vibrations and upheavals, it is like a streak of Indra’s bow in the sky.

It is defective, devoid of qualities, and lacking its string; in the case of the bow of the wheel, it is the dull movement, the movement of water, and rain—its portents are the distorted rays of the sun that indicate these calamities. || 18 ||
Abounding with dull waves, frothing with the rising of turbidity,
and consisting of an inexhaustible succession of whirlpools, it is like a river in the rainy season.
It is like hundreds of mirages in a world that flows ceaselessly toward emptiness;
consisting of masses of dust, it is harsh and as ill-fated as a cremation ground.
"Śavabhūḥ" means like a cremation ground (śmaśānabhūmi). || 20 ||
Just as one who wanders for a long time in a city of dreams does not reach its end,
so too it is in this city called "waking," wandering therein for a long time.
Wandering means roaming about. || 21 ||
Those nets of conceptual constructions which have fully attained a firm foundation belong to those of steady mind who have abandoned the body situated within the net of the single perceived object.
For those living beings who have abandoned their bodies in one place within this phenomenal world of visible objects, at the time of death,

those very networks of mental constructs— which had become solidified through minds firmly fixed on the form of this world— attain a stable existence in the form of this world, body, and so forth. || 22 ||
Those jewels within the casket of the sky of consciousness remain in an unconfined state; thus established in the form of celestial chariots, cities, lands,
and so forth, they shine within the void as the abodes of the *siddhas*, each in relation to the other.
Even those things that are unseen and innumerable, though they do not exist, are well-perceived. || 24 ||

There are also those not seen; and there are those that, though well-reached, are not truly seen even by those with right vision. These are the abodes of the Siddhas and the worlds of the Siddhas. || 24 ||
And there were lakes made of gold, gems, rubies, pearls, and lapis lazuli,
as well as lakes of elixirs rich with various kinds of foods, edibles, grains, and drinks.
He describes those very abodes of the Siddhas with the verse beginning "suvarṇa" and so forth. || 25 ||
And [the regions] were filled with streams of honey, wine, curd, milk, and ghee, and were surrounded by women whose forms were composed of elixirs. || 26 ||
The elixir of rejuvenation is the moon, surrounded by women whose forms consist of that very essence. || 26 ||

They were filled with flowers, fruits, and sprouts of every season; their dwellings were crowded with women moving about playfully; and by the mere act of volition, they were at all times teeming with an abundance of every kind of wealth.
[The worlds] possess flowers, fruits, sprouts, and river currents that are well-known in all seasons. Regarding the word "by mere volition" (saṃkalpāt):

the meaning is based on such scriptural passages as, "If he becomes desirous of the world of the ancestors, by his mere volition the ancestors arise for him; endowed with that world of the ancestors, he is magnified," and so forth. || 27 ||
Some [forms] consist of a thousand lunar disks and a hundred suns;
some consist of gold, nectar, clothing, and water. (28)
Those whose attire is like gold and like nectar, and those beings consisting of water who dwell within them.
Some were self-luminous like darkness or light, consisting of eternal bliss, being led along,
and as light as a tuft of cotton.
Being carried by the wind to whatever place is desired. || 29 ||
Some [beings] undergo arising and destruction in every moment due to the power of *kalā*,
while others possess infinite food and drink and are free from old age and death.
Appearance and non-appearance [of objects] are due to the uninterrupted succession of their arising and destruction. (30)
They possess diverse architectural arrangements and manifold splendors;
they are delightful with the qualities of all seasons and consist of everything that fulfills every desire.
Since those nets of conceptual constructions arise from the performance of virtuous deeds, how could they possibly serve as a wall for minds that are steadfast? (32)

Through the performance of auspicious deeds—that is, through the practice of virtuous actions prescribed by the scriptures—there occurs a transformation of those respective minds into the forms of the fruits thereof, which remain stable in the form of various worlds and their enjoyments. But how could such a gross foundation come to be? (32)
O dear one, nothing else whatsoever exists here within the Self, which consists solely of Brahman;
therefore, let it be said: what could this possibly be made of? (33)

Since mental transformations such as desires and the like are seen to exist solely as pure consciousness (cinmātra), this entire world, being composed of nothing but Brahman, makes everything I have said possible along with its supporting reasoning. O dear one, if there were another way [of explaining it], then let it be stated by the disputants: of what would this world be composed? This is the meaning. || 33 ||
At the very beginning of creation, even this "beginning of creation" does not exist at all;
since there is an absence of a cause, of what nature could this world possibly be? (34)

Although one might now imagine that [the world] consists of the elements (*bhūta*) and is composed of elemental matter (*bhautika*), nevertheless, because of such scriptural passages as, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second," no other cause can be conceived; thus, he states—by saying "at the very beginning of creation"—that if the world were not Brahman, it would be absolutely non-existent, being without a cause. || 34 ||
Just as those endless things are conceptualized within consciousness, so do they appear; tell me, what is the wonder in this? (35)
If they are absolutely non-existent, then how do the worlds appear? To this he says: "They are conceptualized.
The sense is that even for things that are absolutely non-existent, such as a hare's horn or a flower in the sky, their appearance is observed when they are conceptualized. || 35 ||
Even now, O virtuous one, you or others as well— anyone at all—
[should know that] cities of intense, fervent resolve exist in this very same way in the sky.

If it is asked, "In that case, why is our resolve and so forth barren? it is simply because of a lack of intense spiritual urgency (*tīvrasaṃvega*). However, through intense spiritual urgency, you or anyone else can indeed create cities even in the sky; and by means of the practice of single-minded absorption, they attain those [cities] according to the analogy of the city of the moon (*aindavanaya*). Thus he says in two verses beginning with "Now" (*idānīm*). || 36 ||
If, indeed, by practicing with single-minded focus, they perform these [austerities] by chance,
they shall soon attain this very body in the sky after casting off their present one.
But he who follows these two imagined entities obtains [the fruit] like heaven and so forth; indeed, one whose intellect is focused on each [object] attains only that one.
This world consists of two manifestations: that which is already established and that which is imagined by oneself through practices such as meditation.

One who follows these with the firm conviction that both necessarily exist—just as a performer of sacrifices and other rites inevitably attains heaven and so forth—will likewise attain both in due course. However, he who holds that one of these two is the truth...
The meaning is that he of firm intellect attains only the One. || 38 ||
Just as the Siddhas always shine forth in this way by the power of internal conceptualization, so too do the sufferings of hell and other realms appear through conceptualization. (39)

He states that the principle taught regarding the worlds of the perfected ones (*siddhaloka*) applies equally to the conceptualization of the fruits of sin, such as the hells, by saying: "The perfected ones.
However, this much is the distinction: the fruit of meditative worship (*upāsanā*) occurs only when there is a firm practice of its reality through diligent effort;
whereas the fruit of merit, provided both faith (*āstikya*) and performance exist, is real even without such practice.

The fruit of evil becomes firm; the sense is that even in the absence of faith (*āstikya*) and practice (*abhyāsa*), the conviction "this is indeed true" becomes firmly established through the mere performance of evil. || 39 ||
Whatever is perceived in any way is experienced exactly as it is;
whether this body exists or not, it is the mind-made body alone that experiences it.

But since the state of following consciousness is common everywhere, he says "whatever [is perceived]" (*yadyat*). It is in the body alone; the particle *eva* (alone) implies entirety. The meaning is: in the entire body. || 40 ||
When the living being abandons one cognition consisting of the body upon the occurrence of a certain state,
it immediately perceives another cognition consisting solely of that same state right there.
For this very reason, he says "the living being" (jīva) to show that the living being, following the mind alone, abandons one body and takes up another body—right there in that same space. || 41 ||
Pure consciousness perceives pure worlds, while impure [consciousness] perceives impure ones;
being of the nature of space, it experiences for a long time only those things that are of the nature of space.
The auspicious one is the performer of merit; the inauspicious one is the consciousness of the living being that has committed evil. 42.
When pure, consciousness perceives and even experiences the cities of the perfected ones;
when impure, it perceives forms that are full of suffering within the hells.

But she who is purified by ritual action and meditation perceives the extremely subtle cities of the perfected ones belonging to others, and experiences her own as well; she perceives and experiences even the greatest sufferings. (43)
There is the grinding by the revolving wheels of twin mountains of whirling stones, and the falling into blind wells from which there is no further rescue. (44)

He elaborates upon those things which one sees and experiences in hell with the verse beginning "ghūrṇat" (rolling), etc. "Ghūrṇatpāṣāṇe" means being crushed by two mountain-circles—the two wheels of the Yama-mountain—which are shaped like the grinding-stones of a wheat-mill; this occurs in that hell. || 44 ||
By the terrible, extreme cold, his body has become like stone;
his form has become a dwelling place for endless desert paths consisting of living coals.
One's own and others' bodies are like travelers on that path—the infinite, waterless desert abounding in spirits, *piśācas*, and glowing embers. (45)
It was a rain of glowing coals falling from clouds composed of purifying charcoal,
and it was as terrible as a harsh downpour of a multitude of heated iron arrows.
Let there be a rain of embers falling from the clouds composed of those very embers which were once purified and had their ashes cast away. || 46 ||
It carried stones, wheels, swords, rivers, and moved through the sky;
it shattered [enemies] with blows from axes that resembled clouds raining pearls from their chests.

Moving through such a sky where rivers of stones and other debris were being carried along, they caused the splitting of chests by the impact of axes shaped like clouds that fell upon their chests as pearls; this is the analysis of the compound according to the alternative reading *vṛṣṭyāmuktānām*. (47)
There is immersion with the sound "cham-cham" from contact with the rough surface of heated iron,
and crushing by weapons and machines accompanied by loud *kaṭakaṭa* clattering sounds.
The embracing of heated iron balls, tridents, and the like, as well as sinking [into them] with a loud sound. || 48 ||
A rain of wheels, vajras, clubs, darts, spears, swords, and arrows;
the seizing of thorny silk-cotton trees, the binding with nooses, and the piercing with hundreds of sharp javelins.
The seizing and embracing of the thorny silk-cotton tree. || 49 ||
It was a sinking into the underworld caused by the falling of heaps of heated sand;
it held the terror of fire concealed by lamps, and it was being chewed by large crows.
There is danger from the fire of a meteorite concealed in the guise of a lamp; there is the devouring and the prodding by large crows. (50)
There was the entry of emaciated coals and great coals through openings that had no exits,
as well as the piercing with arrows, spears, clubs, darts, *bhuśuṇḍīs*, and discuses.
There, hosts of hungry ghosts, harsh with the agitation of hunger, gnawed at one another’s limbs, while others were cast down from palm-tree heights onto extremely rough stone surfaces. (52)
Even from a palm tree that is exceedingly tall, there is a falling upon the surfaces of massive rocks from a high elevation. || 52 ||
It is crowded with rivers of pus and the like, mired in the mud of blood and impurities;
there, one is crushed by stones, weapons, horses, elephants, trees, and rocks. (53)
The multitude of people was scratched by owls from the abysses and struck by clubs;
circles of vultures gathered there, scavenging for fragments of heads, hands, hooves, and shoulders.

In regions resembling chasms, there is the tearing apart of bodies, inscribed by owls; there, circles of vultures are intensely eager for the fragments—the severed pieces of heads, hands, feet, and so forth.
From the cultivation of the thought, "This fruit arises from this very evil deed," one sees it thus—firm in its location, non-contradictory, and extensive. (55)

The meaning is that, due to repeated experience in such places prior to the ascertainment [of truth] from the scriptures through meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), one's very own self has expanded out in the form of those various hells. || 55 ||

Whatever name there may be, whatsoever it be, whenever it appears in the sky of consciousness—or rather, does not appear, or is indeed unprecedented—that arises from conceptual construction and is composed of that very [consciousness]; therefore, it moves for a long time by its own spontaneous will alone.

Having summarized what was said, he concludes with the words "yannāma" (whatever it may be): Whatever name there is—be it any conscious body and so forth—that has ever appeared in the sky of the mind (*khe*), or even that which has not appeared because it is yet to come, as seen in dreams, or even that which is entirely unprecedented—all that shines forth from conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) in the form of the delusion of volition (*saṃkalpa-bhrānti*). All of that is composed of that; it is composed of the mind alone (*manomaya*).
Therefore, it is established that because of that state, one moves by mere chance after having experienced for a long time, and not even by hundreds of efforts; such is the meaning. || 56 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and sixtieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Perception of Heaven and Hell," in the *Vasiṣṭha-uttara-rāmāyaṇa*, within the *Mokṣopāya* section of the *Vāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa*. 160.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixtieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Perception of Heaven and Hell," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*. 160.
The one hundred and sixty-first canto.
Śrī Rāma said: "This account of the sage and the hunter, which contains hundreds of various conditions..."
Could this have another cause, or is it born of its own inherent nature? (1)

The manifold world, which has no other cause and consists of the manifestation of pure consciousness alone, appears as the universe due to lack of awakening; upon awakening, it is described as Brahman.

Is this hundredfold sequence of states such as pleasure and pain that occurred for the sage and the hunter, as described by Bhāsa, caused by no other cause— like a dream seen every day— or is it like the transformation of Lavaṇa, Gādhi, and others into outcastes, which was due to causes such as the power of a magician or a divine boon?
The meaning of Rāma’s question is: "Does it arise from the intrinsic nature of another sign? || 1 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Such whirlpools of creative intuition arise incessantly by themselves within the great ocean of the Supreme Self, being of the nature of space within their own self.

In this regard, let there be another cause or not; Vasiṣṭha gives the answer with the words beginning "of such a kind," stating that as long as the Self remains unknown, such delusions always persist until liberation.
Just as from the wind, whose nature is vibration, incessant streaks of movement arise,
so too from the existent consciousness within the sky of consciousness, [mental states] arise endowed with manifestation.

The meaning is that just as, whether other causes such as a fan are present or absent, minute vibrations and fragments of movement always arise within the wind, so it is here; "pratibhā" refers to the manifestation of the form of the object. || 3 ||
In whatever manner a radiance of intuitive insight (pratibhā) arises from this [Self] as its own inherent limb,
it remains exactly so here, unimpaired, as long as it is not struck down by another.

The meaning is that [the previous form] has not been struck down nor destroyed by another form—that is, by the manifestation of a different state—just as, for example, the form of a lump of clay is destroyed by its transformation into the form of a jar or the like. || 4 ||
Just as there is here only one single whole (avayavin) possessing various parts, so too this single space of consciousness-Brahman (cidbrahma) is of the nature of manifestation. || 5 ||

And he says—“not manifold” (nāna)—that within those infinite appearances, Brahman, whose nature consists solely of pure existence, remains as the underlying substrate, pervading them just as a tree pervades its branches and so forth. || 5 ||

Some [mental constructs] in Brahman are stable and some are unstable, appearing like objects through their own luminosity; they abide within the Self, just as bodily states reside in the Self, which is established in the Self that is Space.

In that regard, some states—such as those of the earth, the atmosphere, the directions, and so forth—are stable due to their persistence over a long period; others are unstable, remaining for only a short time. This means, for example, the states consisting of the body’s forms such as the torso, hands, and feet, as well as states such as the closing and opening of the eyes. || 6 ||
The manifestation within one's own self, like a city in a dream, is the wonder of consciousness.
What is essential and what is inessential? What might be real, or what might be unreal? (7)
He states that for the deluded, the apprehension of essence and non-essence within those [perceptions] is entirely in vain: "In one's own self," etc. (verse 7).
All this has been fully understood as being nothing but the expanse of consciousness;
the visible world has been realized by you as neither existent nor non-existent—how can it be described? (8)
As long as you, being ignorant, have not [realized] the Buddha. || 8 ||

In this auspicious world, which is everywhere a mere manifestation of the sky of consciousness, what room is there for attachment or detachment? Those who know it remain established in things exactly as they are.

"Abiding," meaning remain established, by taking as your object the intrinsic nature (svarūpa) exactly as it is configured and exactly as it exists. This is a Vedic substitution of verbal endings (tiṅ-vyatyaya). || 9 ||
The manifestations of creative intuition arise from themselves, like waves from the ocean;
they are identical with their own self, emerging from the divine Self which shines forth as the perception of cause and effect.
From itself, from its own self, the forms of intuition arise, produced by intuition, through the mode of being the seer of cause and effect. || 10 ||

Just as one's own creation arises from one's own volition within the vast and supreme ether, so too is the world perceived by that [consciousness] alone; for what are earth and the other elements here?
That very expansive manifestation which is like one's own volition and like one's own creation is perceived by him as the world. || 11 ||
Thus this appearance shines forth, yet nothing at all shines;
it is Brahman itself, established in Brahman alone, which by its own nature is designated as "ignorance."
That world [arises] from itself, not from another cause. 12.
In this world, the entire universe is nothing but the sky of consciousness through its density as the mass of consciousness;
such is the supreme awakening, and the perfection of this is liberation.

In this state, density belongs to the mass of consciousness alone, and not to any other form such as earth and so forth; proficiency is the firmness attained through practice on the stages (bhūmikās). || 13 ||
The appearance that is spread out as the mere form of the emptiness of the sky of consciousness shines forth simply as this world—unobstructed and tranquil. (14)

The remainder [of the meaning] is that form (rūpa) exists as if it were the blueness of space within emptiness, having ignorance as its objective support; "appearance" (ābhāsa) means delusion (bhrama). || 14 ||
For one who meditates, whose body has been dissolved, and whose vision remains fixed for a moment in meditation—apart from pure consciousness alone, what power could possibly be said to exist? (15)
And he says "dhyāyinaḥ" (for those who meditate) to show that this is established by the experience of meditators:

for one whose body has been dissolved through establishment in non-conceptual samādhi—that is, for one whose sense of bodily existence has been severed—what capacity could there be for seeing the world, given that his nature is pure consciousness as the witness? What power of perceiving the universe could possibly exist?
Therefore, the meaning is that its capacity [to produce cognition] must belong to ignorance alone, as this is the only remaining possibility. || 15 ||
In whatever manner a portion of the space of the element of consciousness appears within [a particular object], it remains there in that very manner, as long as it does so by its own nature. (16)

And thus, he states the established principle—that Brahman alone appears as the world when conditioned by the mind of the ignorant, whereas elsewhere it appears as pure consciousness—by saying: "The element of consciousness... [verse 16]: "...due to its nature as both awareness and non-awareness."

For one who lacks analytical investigation, the delusion regarding the visible world—which is actually composed of space—does not subside, just as the defect of seeing two moons due to ophthalmia does not cease for those born with that condition. (17)
Of one born with *taimirika*, that is, a person whose eyes have been afflicted by the disease of cataract from birth. || 17 ||
Whatever is seen here is indeed Brahman alone, free from affliction;
it is the beginningless and endless space of consciousness—how could it, or what, be pacified? (18)
But he says that the world, having attained the state of Brahman, does not perish: "That which is this... (verse 18).
That which is the manifestation of one's own self—like a dream—without abandoning its own nature as pure self-awareness, is what is called this world. (19)

Thus, he states that even in the state of ignorance, the world is merely a transformation of the consciousness of dream (*svapna-cid-vivarta-mātram*), using the word "its own" (*svam*): the meaning is that a transformation (*vivarta*) is the appearance of the unmodified as otherwise, and this definition applies here. || 19 ||

When, through the meanings of the scriptures and with a sharp intellect, one does not engage in mutual conceptualizations, one makes oneself as if asleep; then one is awakened by someone who is enlightened. (20)
