This consciousness, which is the firmly rooted notion that "this is ignorance," is indeed unerring;
for you, however, it simply does not exist, just as there is no dust in rivers.
That which has become established for you in the form of the world does not exist at all for us.
Just as in a dream the earth does not exist anywhere even though it is experienced by oneself,
so too this state of being visible does not exist, for although it is experienced by oneself, it is composed of unreality.
Now, one might ask how experience itself is perceived; to this he says: "Just as... (verse 22).
Just as in a dream, objects appear as mere fire within the void of consciousness, so too in the waking state, fire is perceived as nothing other than one's own self.

The meaning is that, just as in a dream the sky of consciousness alone shines—possessing the objects such as form and the fire that illuminates them—so too is the fire of one's own waking witness perceived as being incomplete and consisting solely of the nature of self-luminosity. || 23 ||
There is no distinction whatsoever between "this is waking" and "this is dreaming," because both are experienced as entirely equal within the reality of the ultimate truth. (24)
The meaning is that the distinction which appears through experience between those two times does not exist at all. || 24 ||
"Just as the cognition 'this is not so' arises upon waking from a dream, so too does the cognition of one who has died and awakened in the next world arise while in the waking state. (25)

The meaning is that even for one who has awakened in another body, while still in the womb and possessing the memory of past lives (*jātismara*), the well-known cognition experienced while awake is likewise sublated by the realization, "This is not so. || 25 ||
In this world, the cognition that "this is a short time" or "this is a long time" arises regarding both dreaming and waking;
for these two are equal insofar as they consist of the experience of the present. (26)
If it is asked, "How then does the perception of inequality arise among people? [the author] says, "Time," meaning that they do not perceive it due to the brevity or length of time. || 26 ||
Externally, because all qualities such as "thus it is" and so forth are entirely equal,
neither of the two states— waking nor dreaming— is superior, just like the case of twins.

Nor is there a distinction such that waking occurs externally and dreaming internally; for dreaming also occurs externally. Since everything in that dream is exactly like waking, the meaning is that because one experiences an equality of qualities in both states regarding all things, neither one is superior to the other. || 27 ||
"That which is waking is this dream, and that which is dreaming is indeed waking"—the thought "this is certainly not so" arises for both states over time. (28)
The intellect is the intellect that investigates. || 28 ||
Just as hundreds of dreams are indefinite until the end of one's life, so too are hundreds of waking states indefinite until great awakening and nirvana. (29)
In the great sleep of ignorance, for the soul that has not attained nirvāṇa. || 29 ||
Just as many dreams that have arisen and perished are remembered, so too are hundreds of births remembered by the Buddhas and the Siddhas. (30)
By the Buddhas, the fully awakened ones, and the Siddhas who possess the yogic power conducive to the recollection of past births. || 30 ||
Thus, when there is complete similarity in the nature of all experience, the waking state shines like a dream, and the perception of a dream is like the waking state. (31)
Just as the two words "the visible" and "the world" have always attained the same meaning, so too are these two— waking and dreaming— considered to be of the same nature.
To explain how, then, there is a difference in names in that regard, he says: "Just as... (32).
Just as a vast dream-city is nothing but the sky composed of consciousness, so too is this world; therefore, where is ignorance seen, and from whence could it arise? (33)
He shows the purpose of demonstrating the similarity to a dream with the words "In this way" (evam). || 33 ||
If that very self which is pure space is called ignorance,
then when it exists, that alone is my bondage, consisting of its own mental construction.

If that very Brahman is denoted by the word "ignorance" (avidyā) just as it is by the word "dream" in such scriptural passages as "That indeed is a dream," then we do not dispute over the words; however, our position is simply this: that which remains when all illusions have subsided is the Self alone, whereas bondage previously consisted merely of one's own mental constructs—and this is already established. This is the intended meaning. || 34 ||
Therefore, do not act in this way; this is the bondage of one who is truly unbound.
What difference can there be between the stainless sky and the formless self consisting of consciousness? (35)
When this is so, then for the eternally liberated Self, the very delusion of bondage should not arise; thus he says "that":

what difference, what distinction, can there be between the stainless sky and the formless, consciousness-natured [Self], such that the verbal argument might proceed that "the sky is not bound, but the conscious Self is bound"?
The meaning is that both are absolutely identical due to their being formless, non-adhesive, most subtle, and so forth. || 35 ||
In this manifestation of the space of pure consciousness, where indeed there is no objective form, how could there be bondage or liberation, known as the "visible" or "ignorance"? (36)

The meaning is: while this manifestation of the space of consciousness, known as ignorance, exists as the so-called visible world, from what cause could there be either bondage or liberation? || 36 ||
Ignorance does not exist by name; there is no bondage for anyone.
There is no liberation for anyone, and as for liberation, it is sufficient to say that "it exists" and "it does not exist" do not apply.

Just as that which is called ignorance does not exist, then bondage is not bondage; likewise, liberation is not liberation. The meaning is that since nothing other than Brahman exists, it is impossible for anything to be fit for the conventional usage of "is" or "is not. || 37 ||
Neither knowledge nor ignorance exists at all; this unborn Consciousness alone shines forth.
Like the sky appearing as the form of the sky, it manifests as the creation within its own body, like a dream.
Like a dream, consciousness itself, having assumed its own body in the form of creation, shines forth. || 38 ||

The nature of consciousness that exists in the interval when one has gone from one place to another is precisely the form of what is perceived in waking and dreaming; this is the certain conclusion. (39)

One must reach the firm conviction that the very nature of consciousness, which is well-known to be devoid of objects in the intermediate state, is itself the ultimate reality of the perceived world established in the waking and dreaming states. || 39 ||

The form of that single person who sleeps peacefully amidst all external and internal objects of perception is the same as the form of those seeing the waking and dreaming states here in the night. (40)

The meaning is that the very nature (*vapus*) or essential form (*svarūpa*) of the self-luminous Self—which is ever-awake for the purpose of illuminating both external objects of perception and internal objects of perception, such as the senses, the mind, and their modifications—is the true, ultimate form of those who perceive the waking and dreaming states. This is according to the Vedic scripture: "Unsleeping, He beholds those who sleep. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.11). || 40 ||
Know that this very perception of difference is of that same nature; for once one has reached the limit of consciousness, what else indeed could there be in the perception of difference? (41)

Therefore, know that even the conceptualization of "the perception of the distinction between waking and dreaming" is of that same nature—that is, it is simply the nature of the witness-consciousness (sākṣi) of both; it is not the perception of a distinction within consciousness itself. For what other [consciousness] could have come into the interior of the witness-consciousness—which is continuous through the three states—to perceive a distinction in consciousness? This is the meaning. || 41 ||
The sky of consciousness alone is the perception of non-duality, and the sky of consciousness alone is the perception of duality;
both duality and non-duality are one and the same—thus peaceful and indivisible.
The words "this being so" (tathā sati) are to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. || 42 ||
Just as the perceiver is composed of both consciousness and its object, so too is that which is seen; thus, the experience of non-duality is a single unity.

Just as within the aspects of Being, Consciousness, and Bliss belonging to Brahman, the aspect of Being (*sadaṃśa*) is non-different in both its nature as consciousness and its nature as being graspable by consciousness, so too the aspect of Consciousness (*cidaṃśa*) is non-different, in that duality and the cognition thereof are one and the same; for those very things which are the seer are the same as those objects made the objects of seeing.

These are called "the visible" (dṛśya). Furthermore, no one is able to define the relationship between object and subject as anything other than identity with the mind (cittādātmya); that is the meaning of the word "tasmāt" (therefore). || 43 ||
They know that Brahman as the void; it is duality, non-duality, and indeed absolute non-duality.
Emission itself is the supreme Brahman; it is both duality and non-duality, being the Reality.

When a single existent reality alone manifests as the nature of all duality, then Brahman itself is both dual and non-dual, and non-different from non-duality. The meaning is that nothing whatsoever is established apart from it. || 44 ||
Having determined through "not this, not this" that it transcends everything,
one should thereafter abandon even that [determination] and remain here, making the space of consciousness one's own bedrock.
In that case, should Brahman be understood as consisting precisely of the union of duality and non-duality? No; he says: "Not so" (*neti*).

Previously, at the very beginning of creation, the Supreme Brahman was indeed both dual and non-dual. (Note: The reading *sat* here is correct, as it is read likewise in the forty-fourth verse; thus, a confusion with the end of the preceding half-verse is easily conceivable.)

Having thus determined that the expansion of the manifest and unmanifest is of the nature of Brahman, one subsequently abandons all duality in its entirety by means of the negation "not this, not this" (*neti neti*). Then, even though the inner self— the sky of consciousness— has become manifest here, through the practice of successive stages (*uttarottara-bhūmikā*), [one attains liberation].
Having made yourself into a solid stone, as dense with the single flavor of bliss as a block of rock salt, remain seated. || 45 ||
O fortunate one, proceed, drink, eat, and feed others according to their sequence, as they are situated, as they abide, and as they arise;
being free from mental longing and without movement, become a stone upon the supreme path consisting of pure consciousness. 46.
O fortunate one, you have thus attained the supreme state within the Brahman that consists of purity; therefore,
without transgressing the sequence appropriate for your own caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama*), and without overstepping the established order of the world as it exists,
go to whatever desired place or region according to your inclination and in accordance with your own means, sport, drink, and enjoy.
And feed the groups of your twice-born friends; if the reading is *anīpsitam*, it means "in such a way that they have no desire [for more]. || 46 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-first chapter, titled "The Description of Liberation," in the *Videhamukti* section of the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa*, within the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Valmiki, according to the tradition of the Rishis.
Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-first chapter, titled "The Description of Nirvāṇa," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and sixty-second chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
This world exists exactly as it is, because all objects have the space of consciousness (cidvyoma) as their ultimate reality.
Even the perception and reflection upon forms and light are merely the sky of consciousness. || 1 ||
In this [work], the removal of ignorance is established through beneficial teachings that describe the entirety of duality as being nothing but Brahman.

He states that because everything visible flashes forth as the very object of the sky of consciousness (*cidvyoma*), there remains nothing but that alone— thus he says, "the sky of consciousness. The entire collection of visible things, both external and internal, accompanied by the perception of external forms and internal reflection, consists of objects such as cows and grass, which are essentially of the nature of the cow and so forth.
The meaning is that the sky of consciousness, which is the object of experience, remains as nothing but the sky of consciousness alone. || 1 ||
Since nothing else exists apart from the nature of the city of the mind in a dream, the world is therefore the peaceful void; herein there is not the slightest diversity.
By what illustration is it established that the object of consciousness (cidbhogya) results in nothing but pure consciousness (cinmātra)? To this he says: "In a dream...
Because, for that reason, in a dream there exists nothing other than the consciousness itself which is the enjoyer of the city, since it takes the form of the city;
therefore, the waking world as well is as tranquil as the sky. He shows the agreement with scripture regarding the aforementioned inference: "Not here..."
"There is nothing whatsoever. || 2 ||
The manifestation of consciousness alone appears as if manifold, through its own non-duality;
it perceives itself as the non-self by means of the self, as in the cities of the sky within a dream.

If multiplicity does not exist, then what is it that appears as if multiple? To this he says: "The manifestation of consciousness" (cidābhāsa). That which is multiple is indeed non-self and devoid of intrinsic nature; it manifests itself by means of its own witness, the Self. The meaning is that it is like objects in dream-cities, cities in the sky, and cities of Gandharvas. || 3 ||
Like the world at the beginning of creation, this universe is a city in the sky of dreams within the space of consciousness;
it appears as if real, yet it is certainly unreal, though it remains as if truly existent.

He clarifies that very similarity with the words "At the beginning of creation" (sargādau). The meaning is that the similarity consists in the fact that even now, at the beginning of creation, the world appears as if it were unreal—just like a city in the sky seen in a dream—just as it was during the time of dissolution. || 4 ||

The meaning of the word "creation" (sarga), which consists of both the real and the unreal, exists for the wise as something known through ignorance, and for the ignorant as something known through wisdom; it does not exist for those who are neither.

He states that the world is thus even because there is a contradiction with the experience of the knowledge of that [world], just as in the case of the "finger-breadth of the moon" (*candraprādeśika*): "tajjña" (by the knower of that).

The word "ajñāta" (unknown) is to be construed with both [terms]. Alternatively, the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) cannot be established by following the experience of either the ignorant or those who know it.
The meaning is that because of their mutual contradiction, the truth remains unknown by both of them. || 5 ||
But regarding that which remains within the internal cognition of those two— the one who knows it and the one who does not— they are unable to understand or express it to one another.

To explain why that is so, he says: "Of the knower and the ignorant. For those who possess only the internal vision are the knowers (*tajjña*), while those whose vision is directed solely outward are the ignorant (*ajña*). However, regarding the nature of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) which stands in the interval within the mental modification (*buddhivṛtti*) during internal apprehension, neither of them knows how to perceive it for themselves, nor are they able to describe it to one another. || 6 ||

In their own minds, the meanings of the word "heaven" are mutually distinct; indeed, for these two, there exist stability and instability within their waking consciousness, like that of a sober man and a drunkard.

He provides the justification for what has already been stated with the words "in one's own intellect" (*svabuddhau*). It is undisputed that the meaning of the word "creation" (*sarga*) flashes forth only as it exists within its own respective intellect and not otherwise; in this regard, between these two—the non-deluded and the deluded—like those who are sober and those who are intoxicated, each respective form of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is "internal" (*antaḥstha*), because it resides within the internal intellect. The particle *kila* indicates what is well-known through reasoning.
In this regard, because the intellect of the wise person is always awake to stability, he perceives only the stable reality of the Self.

Because the intellect of the ignorant person is awake to instability, he perceives only the unstable external world. However, the nature of the phenomenal expansion (*prapañca*) residing within the intellect is neither entirely internal nor entirely external; thus, it belongs to neither of the two.
The meaning is that there exists the thorough knowledge of that. || 7 ||
Just as waves in the water of a river attain a state of fluidity, so too do the waves of creation, through consciousness, attain a state of stability within the Intellect.
If the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) cannot be perceived by either [the self or the other], then how did it come to have its existence? To this he says:

"Like liquid... The meaning is that, relying solely upon the nature of consciousness which is not [otherwise] known, they have attained their existence in the interval through the very being of the Self (*ātman*), just as waves exist through the liquidity of water. || 8 ||
That which is of the nature of consciousness (cidrūpa) is nothing at all, yet it remains as this "something";
though invisible, it appears as if visible, like cities in a dream.
For this very reason, he says that the world is merely the wonder of consciousness: "The form of consciousness" (cidrūpa). || 9 ||
This shadow called the "world" shines forth;
indeed, though it is formless, it appears as if possessed of form, like a shadow cast by a material object.

Alternatively, he states "the shadow of consciousness" (cicchāyā) to show that the very reflection which exists within Māyā manifests in the form of the world—or as another reading has it, in the form of the individual soul and the world—just like the shadow of substances such as jars and cloths appears in a mirror. || 10 ||
This is merely the body, consisting of nothing but delusion and composed of unreality; it is a firm seat of illusion, for the most part like the appearance of a phantom in one's confusion. (11)
In this regard, he states that the very delusion of identifying the body with the self is the root of all exertion: "The body... (verse 11).
Like a kingdom of the mind, it is unreal; like a dangling drop of water, it is flickering.
Since it is thus experienced by these two [perceptions], how can there be any selfhood in that which is non-existent? (12)
He dispels the delusion that "the body alone is the self" with two verses.

The meaning is: when even that which is examined by means of the two types of experience previously described—those of the wise and the ignorant—is found to be unreal, how could there be any possibility of it being the self? || 12 ||

Like the sounds of splitting wood or the roar of wind upon the waves, sounds in the sky appear as the bursting forth of the wind; so too do objects appear through the arising of latent impressions (*vāsanā*). (13)
To explain how linguistic conventions regarding the body and the self—such as "I am Rāma" or "you are Vasiṣṭha"—arise in that context, he says:

"Having split open," and so forth. Just as when thick bamboo or wood is split in the earth, the sound residing within it appears as if it were emerging outward, yet that sound neither remained inside nor actually emerged; so it is with water.

Just as from waves, from flames and the like in fire, and from the wind, sounds such as echoes appear to have emerged from the sky, and as the phonemes, words, sentences, and *sphoṭas* appear to have issued forth from the regions of the throat, palate, and so on— yet these do not exist within them beforehand— in the same way, objects consisting of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) also appear as if they have emerged from the Self during waking and dreaming, like sparks from a fire.
The meaning is that they appear, yet they do not exist there. || 13 ||
From the beginning of creation, one’s own conceptualization shines forth like a mountain in a dream;
yet in reality, there is no word, no object, and no state of being visible.
One's own self-consciousness is one's own experience. 14.
Whatever exists here and whatever appears—all that is ultimately real;
because no other cause exists, it was not produced at the beginning of creation.
However, a form different from reality—that is, distinct from Being—has never arisen at all; because of the absence of a cause, it was not produced even at the beginning of creation.
With the distinctions of words and their objects cast aside, yet with all objects uncast aside, let it be understood: "I am at peace, I am fully extinguished; I am indeed like space. (16)

Therefore, one should understand that "I am indeed the ever-constant, single-natured, and truly existent space," which is of the nature of supreme peace and liberation; thus he says: "With [all] cast aside... (verse 16).
Let that state of agitation, which has arisen from the unreal and is produced by the self within the living soul, be abandoned through resting in the self, whose sole nature is pure awakening. (17)
In the living being (jīva), "ajava" refers to the state of being swift, which is the distraction of the mind. || 17 ||
For the self alone is the friend of the self, and the self alone is the enemy of the self;
if the self is not protected by the self, there is no other means [of protection]. 18.
For this very reason, he says "the self alone" (ātmaiva) [in verse 18], meaning that one should uplift oneself by means of one's own discernment alone.
O Mother, as long as this youthfulness of yours remains, cross over this ocean called saṃsāra by means of the boat of pure intellect. 19.
As long as youth remains, cross over to the further shore of the ocean called saṃsāra by means of the boat of wisdom.
Do this very day what is for your welfare; for when one has grown old, what will you be able to do? Indeed, even one's own limbs become a burden in such a reversal of fortune.
In the reversal of age, that is, in old age. || 20 ||
Childhood, old age, the state of being an animal, and even death—these are merely the youth of the living soul, provided that one possesses discernment. (21)

Childhood and old age should be understood as being incapable of producing knowledge, just like the state of an animal. Regarding the phrase "if it is discriminative": the implication is that if it lacks discrimination, it is even more base than the state of an animal. || 21 ||
Having entered this saṃsāra, which is as flickering as a flash of lightning,
one should extract the essence from the mud through contact with true scriptures and virtuous people.
From the mud—namely, the mud of delusion—he [extracted] the essence, which is the Self. || 22 ||
Alas! How cruel are these men; what will their destiny be?
They seek their own advancement even while they themselves are submerged in the mire.
Vasiṣṭha laments: "What will be the fate of those who, even though their very selves are submerged in mud, do not employ the means taught in the scriptures as a way to raise themselves up? (23)
Just as an assembly of clay ghouls causes fear to a rustic, yet for one who understands the reality of the matter, that which is merely made of clay causes no fear. (24)
To a rustic person who is unacquainted with clay [as a building material], the thought "I have seen an assembly hall containing real vetālas" is a delusion;
[the hall] is "bhaṅgadā," meaning it causes suffering such as fear, fever, and so forth. || 24 ||
Thus, for the ignorant person, the visible splendor consisting of Brahman brings about destruction;
however, when there is the realization of the true nature of reality, it remains as Brahman itself and does not bring about destruction.
This very same unpeaceful world becomes peaceful; though it remains, it dissolves through the thorough knowledge of reality. While being seen, the visible object is no longer seen.
To the question "Why does it not perish?", he says: "It subsides" (śāmyati). || 26 ||
Just as in one's own dream-time, even a vivid experience attains the state of reality only through the realization that it is unreal. (27)

Now, one might object: "Since the world has attained the state of reality through its clear experience, how can it become non-existent merely through knowledge? To this, he says: "Clear," etc. Just as during the time of a dream, even though the dream-world is clearly experienced, it ceases upon full realization—that is, upon waking—so too [the world], while being experienced...
Even though it has reached the state of truth, the "experience of creation" is connected with what follows [in the next verse]. || 27 ||
Even while being experienced in that way within the sky of the consciousness of creation,
when one realizes the true nature of reality, only emptiness remains in that which consists of pure consciousness.

In the wilderness of life, scorched by the fever of birth, these senses have grown old through the process of being carried away like deer by the wind; having conquered them—driven by the gusts of the intoxicated mind—attain victory and abandon rebirth. (29)
Showing that this knowledge is not obtained without the conquest of the senses along with the mind (*manas*), he concludes with the verse beginning "jāti":

"In the jungles of life, which are ablaze with the fevers of birth— that is, the fevers consisting of birth— and ignited by the forest fires of desire, anger, and so forth, the manner of gathering grass, leaves, and the like of the wind-deer (the deer of the vital breath) is only occasionally found."

Do not think "never"—by conquering these senses, which are joined with the outward movement (saṃcāra) of the vital breath (prāṇapavana) and the intoxicated mind, and by means of which they have become worn out and slackened, attain through knowledge the victory over ignorance. And being liberated by that, abandon—meaning, cast off—rebirth; that is to say, restrain it. || 29 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-second chapter, titled "The Dispelling of Ignorance," in the *Vāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa* of Valmiki, belonging to the *Arsha* tradition, in the section on the *Nirvāṇa-upadeśa*.
Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-second chapter, titled "The Dispelling of Ignorance," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The one hundred and sixty-third canto.
Śrī Rāma said:
Without the conquest of the senses, this state of ignorance does not subside.
Therefore, O Sage, tell me how those senses are to be conquered. || 1 ||
Here, the means for conquering the senses, the restraint of the mind within non-dual consciousness,
and the practice of this scripture are proclaimed as the causes of awakening.

Having conquered the senses, attain victory; abandon rebirth—since Vasiṣṭha has thus stated the necessity of conquering the senses, Rāma asks about the means for doing so with the verse beginning "vinā" (without). || 1 ||
Śrī Vasistha said:
Neither in abundant enjoyments, nor in manhood, nor in life,
nor in the liberation of the senses does [the mind] find a lamp for its vision, just as one with weak sight [cannot see a lamp].
Expressing his approval by saying, "The question you have asked is appropriate," Vasiṣṭha elaborates on the inquiry with the words "Not so" (*na ca*).
Just as a lamp, though blazing brightly, is of no use for perceiving subtle objects to a person of limited vision or weak sight,
so too [the senses] are of no use to one who is attached to abundant enjoyments, nor for achieving excellence in manhood.

For one who is attached—not even to life itself, but to the means of living such as the acquisition of wealth—the practice of the scriptures and other disciplines is not useful for the realization of Brahman; likewise, it is not useful even for those intent on the conquest of the senses. This is the meaning. || 2 ||
Therefore, listen to this complete method for mastering the senses;
by means of this body, one attains perfection through one's own effort and with ease. (3)

Therefore, because the conquest of the senses is indispensable, by this reasoning stated by me, even a slight accumulation of means (*sādhanasaṃpat*) attains—reaches—perfection, which is the attainment of the fruit of liberation, through one's own effort. || 3 ||

Know that the Puruṣa is pure consciousness alone; from consciousness arises that which is called the individual soul (jīva). Whatever it perceives within, it becomes identified with that in an instant.

Because volition (cetanā) illuminates the object presented by the mind; that is to say, because it is dependent upon the mind. Whatever one wills—having pervaded it through a mental modification (cittavṛtti) and making it manifest—one becomes identified with that and becomes attached to it, just as in the expression, "the fool is possessed by women" (strīmaya). || 4 ||
Having conquered the intoxicated elephant of the mind by pulling it with the sharp goad of awareness, effort, and awakening, one triumphs; not otherwise.

This being so, he states the reasoning: that by the effort of withdrawing the mind through its internal attraction, one suppresses its external form; and through the practice of awakening to the form of Brahman, the sense organs—though inherently lame—are naturally conquered as a matter of course. Thus: "Consciousness... (Verse 5).
The mind is the leader of the army of the senses; victory comes from conquering it.
For one whose feet are hidden by shoes, is not the entire earth effectively covered with leather? (6)
To the question "Why is that so?", he says: "The mind. [The mind] is the leader, acting as both the motivator and the restrainer by virtue of its status as the master.
With the intention that just as all thorns are conquered by covering only the feet with shoes, all the senses are conquered by covering only the mind, he says: "The shoe. (6)
Having planted consciousness within the space of consciousness, for one who remains thus in the heart,
the mind itself subsides like autumnal mist.
If so, what is the means for the pacification of the mind? He says: "the consciousness" (saṃvidam).

Having established the consciousness—the individual soul (jīva) which is consciousness delimited by the mind—within the space of consciousness, that is, within Brahman, and having unified them. || 7 ||

O dear one, the mind becomes tranquil through the restraint of effort regarding one's own consciousness in such a way as it does not through a multitude of austerities, pilgrimages, sciences, and sacrificial rites.
Through the effortful absorption of one's own consciousness and the consciousness of the individual soul into Brahman, as previously described.
Whatever is experienced, that very thing is surely made forgotten through conscious effort within consciousness; thus, there is mastery over enjoyments.

Whatever is experienced or forcibly remembered, that very thing is surely and certainly caused to be forgotten through the consciousness of dissolution within the consciousness of Brahman as its substrate; by the eradication of its latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), it is rendered incapable of being remembered again. By that means, there is thus the conquest of enjoyments, the causes of enjoyment, and the objects of sense. || 9 ||
Through the effort of self-awareness, consciousness is somewhat restrained from the bait of sense objects;
by that, the state of the gods is attained.
When consciousness is restrained by this means through the mind, the state of self-sovereignty—which is established by experience for the wise who know reality—is attained by the gods. || 10 ||
"Whatever comes to me through the practice of my own dharma—that alone pleases me, nothing else. With these words, become as firm as a diamond.

Thus, he states that firmness in being solely devoted to one's own duty (*svadharma*) is also a cause for the conquest of the senses by way of achieving freedom from craving (*vaitṛṣṇya*): "One's own duty... (verse 11).
He who avoids the engagement of consciousness with conflicting objects, and remains established while cultivating tranquility and contentment, is one who has conquered his senses.

I desire the engagement of consciousness—that is, the will—toward objects that are contrary [to dharma], such as food and other things that serve merely as the means for maintaining the body, which are themselves opposed to one's own duty. 12.
The mind of one who experiences neither agitation toward the internal relish of consciousness nor toward its states of insipidity becomes tranquil. (13)

For one whose mind does not succumb to world-weariness or aversion while practicing both internal delight in the essence of consciousness and external insensibility toward objects, that [distraction] subsides for him. 13.
Through the restraint of consciousness and effort, the mind abandons its own habitual tendencies; freed from the fickleness of the intellect, it pursues discernment.
The pursuit of sense objects is its evil addiction; that very thing, when abandoned, is its freedom from fickleness. 14.
One who possesses discernment and a noble soul is said to have conquered the senses;
he is not deluded by the force of the waves of latent impressions in the ocean of worldly existence. 15.
Through constant association with the virtuous and the continuous study of authentic scriptures, one who has conquered the senses perceives the world as it truly is, in its reality. (16)
Thus, having conquered the senses, he perceives the world as it truly is: as the reality that is nothing but Brahman. || 16 ||
Through the contemplation of truth, the turmoil of saṃsāra comes to rest;
it is like the perception of water in a desert, which causes the suffering of falling into what is false. 17.
It brings suffering by causing one to fall into and run after false objects. || 17 ||
This world exists as nothing but pure consciousness, devoid of objective reality;
for one who possesses such true awakening, how can there be the notions of bondage and liberation? (18)
Just as water that has been dried up and is without form does not flow again, so too the visible object, when severed by knowledge, does not sprout forth because it lacks a cause. (19)
Formless, its material form severed by drying up. || 19 ||
Feeling is merely space, assuming forms such as "you" and "I";
setting this aside, everything else that exists as "I" and so forth is the world.

Since consciousness alone, whose nature is that of pure space, assumes forms such as "you" and "I" through its own ignorance, this world—consisting of the superimposed notions of "I" and so forth—is abandoned and wiped away by knowledge; thus, there remains only the substratum, which is distinct from what was superimposed. || 20 ||
This entire world, beginning with the notion "I am," is merely ignorance;
it rests within the space of consciousness alone, peaceful, and having emptiness as its sole body. (21)
It is peaceful; being inherently peaceful due to its freedom from false reality, it abides in the very form of the true reality, which is the sky of consciousness.
This world appears as the shadow of consciousness within the sky of consciousness;
it is certain that this consciousness is utterly void, being itself nothing but emptiness.
Having seen that this world is empty even by means of the "not-empty," the firm conviction that it is indeed empty is the established tenet. || 22 ||
By whom indeed can the analogy of seeing a dream be refuted here?
For that which consists of the unreal is experienced, and even what is personally experienced consists of the unreal. (23)

If it is asked, "Where is the emptiness of both established? he says, "In the perception of a dream," using the word *svapna*. "Consisting of the non-existent" refers to emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and "experienced" refers to the emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyaśūnyatā*). He states that even though what was experienced consists of the non-existent, that very same example applies:
"Even though it was personally experienced... (verse 23).
Just as that [Self], whose essence is pure consciousness alone, is magnified as whatever kingdom it may be,
without being agent, object, or instrument— so too is the form of the world for Consciousness.

O dear one, that whose very nature (*svarūpa*) consists solely of the consciousness of its own dreams is such that whatever kingdom or power it becomes and is thereby magnified, each of those is but a form of consciousness itself;
for that form is independent of the factors of agency, such as the doer, the object, and the instrument. The waking world is likewise.
The meaning is "that which is to be awakened. || 24 ||
I am devoid of agent, object, and instrument; I am pure mass of consciousness alone.
This world is indefinable, characterized solely by self-awareness. (25)

Whatever is independent of agent, object, instrument, and so forth, that is merely the mass of consciousness, which is none other than I. It has been established previously that this world, at the beginning of creation, cannot be described as possessing an agent and the like;
therefore, the meaning is that it is simply the nature of my own self-luminous Self. || 25 ||
Just as death experienced in dreams does not exist,
so too this ignorance— the desire for water in a desert— though appearing present, does not exist.

And thus, although ignorance exists as an appearance—like a dream, one's own death, or water in a mirage—it does not exist because it is sublated by knowledge; this he says with the word "yathā" (just as). By the term "desire for water," the delusion of water is indicated. || 26 ||
At the beginning of creation, that which was perceived within the void by the consciousness-ether as its own shimmering reflection became,
by itself and without root, the world— occurring quite spontaneously, like the coincidence of the crow and the palm fruit.
That which is perceived and conceived within the void of one's own self. || 27 ||
This appears entirely rootless, appearing as if luminous even though it is without light; therefore, the wise know that whatever is luminous here is that very state.

The meaning is that they know that very thing to be the supreme state, which is eternally immediate, because this world exists as something luminous and directly manifest due to it being the causal ground of the light of consciousness (citprakāśa). || 28 ||
However, that which appears here as the manifestation of living beings and so forth is precisely that [emptiness];
emptiness itself becomes the sky, just as whirlpools are nothing but water. (29)
Just as the form of a whole possessing parts would be one and yet possessed of parts, so too Brahman, though partless, has the individual soul (*jīva*) and other such things as its parts. (30)

Or rather, he states that the identity of the individual soul and so forth with Brahman is to be realized by means of the conceptualization of the relationship between part and whole, beginning with the words "Just as... (yathā). || 30 ||
The object of sight is a mere appearance; it is pure consciousness, peaceful and immutable.
Since it remains as it is—[the reading "sthitamaccha" is more appropriate]—what is there to be deliberated upon within this own nature? (31)

He states that the world should be understood as appearing within Brahman, like the reflection of a mountain river and so forth within a crystal slab—thus he says, "merely an appearance" (ābhāsamātram). And with the intention that it is the very nature of its own transparency that appears in the form of the world, he says, "in its own nature" (svabhāve). The syntactical connection is: "What is being investigated? (kiṃ vicāryate) || 31 ||
In the supreme state, there are no internal mental constructions whatsoever, neither beginning nor end;
this very nature is ignorance, yet here no "ignorance" exists as such.
There is neither beginning nor end, nor even an end; there are no conceptualizations whatsoever of intermediate regions.
Whether entering from dream into the waking state, or from the waking state into dream, or whether awakened or even unawakened, the living being remains in a single uniform nature. (33)

He states that the pure reality of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the world (*jagat*) is to be known through the investigation of their presence and absence during dreaming and waking, or by means of purification:
"The *jīva*... [This is so] because both in the state of awakening and non-awakening, they possess the single nature of manifestation. (33)
When deep sleep and the fourth state (turya) are present, they always exist; likewise, dream and waking exist.
However, one whose intellect is awakened knows waking and dream as being truly one with the fourth state.

The Self in deep sleep is veiled by ignorance; the fourth state (turya) is the pure Self. Just as the end of the illusory snake resides within the rope, so do the ends of the states of dreaming and waking reside within the rope of ignorance and the pure rope [of the Self] respectively. || 34 ||
For the awakened one, waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and everything else are the fourth state (turya);
for him, no ignorance exists, and though he remains within duality, he is indeed non-dual.

"Of the awakened one" means of one who possesses the realization of reality (*tattva*). The particle *eva* is displaced [in the sentence]. It means: "even though situated in duality, he is indeed non-dual. || 35 ||
"Duality and non-duality, 'I' and 'this'—how could such conceptualizations exist for one free from ignorance? And how could there be even space? (36)
Thus, how could there be even a trace of conceptualization for one free from ignorance? Whence can there be talk of space or emptiness? (36)
Through the distinctions between duality and non-duality, and through the confusions of various verbal compositions, the ignorant play like children; those who are mature in wisdom laugh at them.
Unawakened and unenlightened, children and fools play. || 37 ||
This sprout from the sky of the heart, which puts an end to the dispute between duality and non-duality—without it, the cleansing of the sky of awakening does not arise here. (38)
To the question of how even those awakened in the scriptures still desire disputes regarding duality, he says: "Dvaita... etc.
This is a cluster of blossoms, superimposed upon the space of the heart, which has the fruit of awakening the disciple as its result. (38)
Having become friends through debate, we engaged in an inquiry into duality and non-duality;
this has served as a broom for sweeping away the dust of ignorance from within the house of the heart. (39)

For this very reason, he says "as a friend" (suhṛd), meaning: "Having accepted this inquiry into duality and non-duality out of friendship, I too shall now cast it aside once its purpose is fulfilled, like a broom after the house has been swept. || 39 ||
With their minds fixed on that and their lives dedicated to it, awakening one another and constantly speaking of it, they find contentment and delight.

When the ashes of ignorance have been wiped away, those who possess the qualification—whose minds are fixed on That, whose minds are Brahman, and whose vital breaths are absorbed in Brahman—delight and find joy as they awaken one another. || 40 ||
For those who are constantly disciplined and who worship with love,
that yoga of wisdom arises by which they go to that state. (41)
For those who thus constantly practice this yoga of the Buddha taught by me while engaged in inquiry, it becomes firm in time,
whereby they then attain that state which is the Self and is called liberation.
If one protects even a mere blade of grass with such effort, how can the protection of the multitude of the three worlds be accomplished without effort? (42)
The word "kila" reveals the intended meaning of the statement "for those who are constantly engaged," which refers to the necessity of exceptional effort.

Indeed, even for the concealment and protection of something as small as a blade of grass from water, fire, cattle, and so forth, it is only a means accomplished through diligent effort that is beneficial, not one accomplished through negligence. This is because [the same applies] to the attainment of the state of Brahman for the entire host of the three worlds.
How can the knowledge of reality, which consists of absolute protection in the form of concealment, be accomplished without effort? || 42 ||

Though she is situated within the heart, she is free from internal afflictions; though she is the lowest and powerless, even the entire world becomes an object of ridicule for her when she abides in the highest state. 43.

For one who, in order to enjoy a progressively hundredfold superior bliss— beginning from human bliss up to the bliss of Hiranyagarbha— is spread across the fourteen distinct worlds of that supreme state characterized by unsurpassed bliss, yet remains unable to conquer the base desire residing within the heart.
"Incapable" means, that is to say, "struck by desire. The word "also" (*api*) implies "even the entire world. The meaning is:
since the whole world—the totality of living beings—is an object of derision due to its attachment to worthless enjoyments, how is it that such a supreme state does not deserve effort? || 43 ||
What indeed is this so-called happiness that sprouts forth as kingship and the like?
When one finds rest solely in the knowledge of reality, even the status of the king of the gods is but a blade of grass.
He demonstrates the worthlessness of enjoyments by means of a specific illustration, saying: "What indeed... (verse 44).
Just as those who are asleep and awake perceive the visible world and take delight in it,
so too do the peaceful and virtuous, being detached from the visible world, perceive that supreme state.

The meaning is this: while people, sleeping in the slumber of ignorance and attached to the enjoyment of sense-objects in the visible world, perceive that which is seen with extreme attachment, those who are peaceful and knowers of reality—being unattached to the visible world and as if in deep sleep—awakened, perceive that state of unsurpassed bliss. Thus it has been said by the Blessed One: "That which is night..."
"The self-controlled one remains awake during that [state] in which all beings sleep; that in which beings are awake is night for the sage who sees. (45)
Without a heavy burden of effort, this is never accomplished;
know that the supreme state is the fruit of the great tree of practice. 46.

"How could such a state of liberation—consisting of eternal, direct perception and unsurpassed bliss—be accomplished without a great effort? Thus, he speaks of the necessity of practice, beginning with the word "vinā" (without). || 46 ||
"This has been said much; what is the use of this?"—thus thinks the evil-minded one.
Even when so much has been spoken, the one of ignorant intellect neither grasps it nor accepts it. (47)

For this very reason, so that you might achieve firmness in practice, I have repeatedly spoken of this very same point many times—through various modes of expression, through different arguments, and through extensive discourses and narratives. And yet, by you, this very same thing has been stated again and again by the Blessed One; indeed, by means of this text, which is expanded by thousands of repetitions despite its already being much spoken.
Therefore, one should not adopt the inferior intellect characterized by lack of faith, which asks, "What is the purpose of this laborious practice?

For a person of superior knowledge and exceptionally skillful intellect, there is no dependence on practice; however, the dull-witted mind does not grasp this extremely subtle reality of the Self in its heart, even through such an extensive exposition of the instructional statement.

Therefore, the meaning is that practice characterized by repetition and so forth is necessary for that [knowledge]. And thus is the aphorism of the venerable Bādarāyaṇa: "There must be repetition, because of the instruction being given more than once. (47)
If this is tasted repeatedly over a long time through constant turning back [to it], then whether it is heard or spoken by one who knows it or by one who does not, it becomes that very thing. 48.

For this very reason, he says "again and again" (*bhūyobhūyaḥ*), indicating that this text should be savored by those of dull or mediocre faculties through repeated hearing and so forth until the dawn of knowledge. The meaning is: "Even by one who is ignorant, by means of this practice of repetition, this scripture spoken by me will certainly become known; there is no doubt in this matter. (48)
But that lowest of men who, having looked at it but once, should discard it thinking "it has been seen"—he indeed gains from the scriptures nothing but ashes. (49)

But for one who is intent on non-practice, there is no attainment of this fruit; thus, he censures him with the words "He who... From the scriptures—that is, from those treatises that do not concern the inner self (anadhyātma-śāstrebhyaḥ). || 49 ||
This supreme narrative should always be studied like the Vedas; it should be explained and honored, for it bestows the fruits of the goals of human existence. 50.
Whatever is obtained from this scripture is likewise obtained from the Veda;
when this is known, both ritual action and knowledge attain purity. (51)

He demonstrates its supreme excellence by showing that it supplements the direct Veda and serves as the means for attaining the entire fruit of both sections [of the Veda]—this is expressed by the word "yat" (that which). Ritual action (*kriyā*) is the subject matter of the first section; knowledge (*jñāna*) is the subject matter of the latter section. Both together constitute the whole.
Purity, which has as its fruit the complete removal of impurity. || 51 ||
When this is known, the established doctrine of Vedānta and logic is understood;
this supreme narrative has been explained according to the perspectives of the scriptures. (52)

The particle *ca* (and) is displaced [in its logical position]. The word *tu* (but/however) is for the purpose of highlighting the specific [criteria], such as the introductory passages (*upakrama*) and so forth, which are conducive to determining the intended meaning (*tātparya-nirṇaya*) as shown by Bādarāyaṇa and others in the Vedāntas. It is described as being distinguished among the various forms of scriptural vision (*śāstradṛṣṭi*).
It has been explained as being "renowned for its excellence," which means it is celebrated as such. || 52 ||
I say this out of compassion for you, not out of deceit; but you yourselves perceive it as a deception—let this be reflected upon. (53)
I do not speak out of illusion or deceit, but rather out of compassion.

Since you will understand from this excellent scripture, when it has been investigated, that this entire collection of the non-real is illusion and is false, therefore let this scripture be investigated. 53.
From the understanding born of reflecting upon this supreme treatise, all other scriptures appear like side dishes seasoned with salt. (54)

The meaning is that the understandings which arise from the investigation of this supreme treatise cause other scriptures to appear as delicious as seasoned condiments; thus, this [treatise] is the sustenance for all other scriptures. || 54 ||
Disregarding this narrative as ignoble because of your perception of the visible world, do not become destroyers of yourselves by partaking in worldly existence. (55)

Unnoble because it is mere poetry, it is unworthy of honor. Those whose intellects are attached to visible enjoyments—here, the long vowel in place of the case-ending is either a Vedic archaism according to the rule *supāṃ suluk* (Pāṇini 7.1.39), involving the substitution of the preceding vowel, or a transposition of case-endings (*sub-vyatyaya*). This refers to those who are "slayers of their own selves" (*ātmahantṛ*); that is, they fall into the pit of delusion, which is the cause for repeatedly attaining a succession of deaths.
And consequently, those who partake in birth shall no longer be subject to repeated becoming. || 55 ||
"Thinking, 'This is my father's well,' base men drink its salty water;
may you who possess discernment never, even for a moment, fall into such ignorance. (56)
"Is it not the case that in our lineage the ancestors were devoted solely to asceticism, ritual action, and the like, and not to devotion to Brahman?
Our ancestors were Mīmāṃsakas of ritual action; our ancestors were logicians;
our ancestors were Sāṃkhyas; our ancestors were Tantrikas, accomplished in mantras, and accomplished in yoga?"

Mocking those people who say, "They were perfected through elixirs such as *auṣadha* and *rasāyana*; therefore, we too, being of their lineage, shall follow only that path and not the science of the inner self (*adhyātma-śāstra*)," [the author] prevents seekers of liberation from entering that path by saying, "of his father," and so forth. Those of "crow-like" character, due to their false pride, [ignore] even what is close at hand.

The meaning is: just as people disregard the waters of the Ganges and drink salt water instead, so too you should not—by constantly engaging in various contradictory deliberations—become vessels for ignorance through the succession of repeated births, nor seek after folly for the sake of attaining only folly. 56.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-third canto, titled "The Description of the Treatise on the Means for Conquering the Senses," in the *Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa* of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa*, composed by the sage Vālmīki.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Treatise on the Means for Conquering the Senses," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The one hundred and sixty-fourth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
The atoms of living beings within the world are like the rays in the orb of the sun of consciousness.
Since those parts are identical [in all things], therefore there is the nature of being partless.
Through the cleansing away of the states of the individual soul and the world by means of the arising of the state of Brahman,
the state of essential identity between the individual soul, the world, and Brahman is accomplished here.

Therein, he begins first to investigate the nature of the individual soul (*jīva*), starting with the words "the atoms of souls" (*jīvāṇavaḥ*) and so forth. Within the orb of the sun of consciousness (*cidāditya*), which is completely full on all sides, there shines forth that world wherein those well-known atoms of souls reside.
They are equal to that sun of consciousness, possessing a nature of light similar to it, like sparks from a fire; for that reason [they are called *jīvāṇavaḥ*].
The partless nature of the sun of consciousness (*cidāditya*) is established; for, since hands, feet,

and other limbs are seen to possess mutually distinct forms and intrinsic natures, and since the whole (*avayavin*) is seen to have a form and configuration different from them, the distinction between them and the relationship of part and whole (*avayavāvayavibhāva*) are well-known in the world, but [such distinctions do not apply here].
The meaning is that this is because they are absolutely identical. || 1 ||
Having attained supreme awakening, everything abandons its own objective form;
yet, because it is once again in a state of oneness, there would be nothing else whatsoever.

Now, one might object: "In that case, since the stars in the sky are also observed to possess a uniform nature of luminosity, why should there not be mutual non-difference and partlessness among them as well? Furthermore, the rebuttal based on their occupying different locations and the variation in their degrees of luminosity applies equally to individual souls (jīvas). Anticipating this doubt, he says: "All... [The meaning is: the difference among souls is not like the difference between stars; rather—

Like the division of space within a jar, a water-pot, and so forth, [this division] is adventitious (*aupādhika*). And all those limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*)—the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and the rest—which cause that division, upon attaining the realization "I am Brahman," which is supreme, partless, and immediate, cast off and abandon their own nature as limiting adjuncts and the state of division they themselves created. And when the distinction of the limiting adjuncts has vanished...

The meaning is that the thesis is established. Alternatively, previously, through ignorance (*avidyā*), living beings manifested mutually contradictory attributes; due to the severance of their unity with Brahman, there arose, as it were, difference, bondage, and misfortune. Now, having dispelled ignorance through knowledge (*vidyā*) by means of the removal of those contradictory attributes—

Furthermore, since the unity of expression with Brahman has been established, what other differentiator could there be by way of the relationship between part and whole and so forth? This is the meaning. || 2 ||
In all these states, however, that which is the object of the knower of reality is the supreme, stainless Brahman alone; it is never anything else at any time.

If so, were the individual souls (*jīvas*) previously distinct during states such as ignorance, the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), and the body, and have they now been brought to oneness with Brahman through knowledge? He says "no"—"in all [these states]" and so forth. As for that Brahman which is the object of the knower of reality, it remains in all these very states entirely devoid of the impurity of difference and so on, being of a single essence (*ekarasa*). Never at any time is there even the slightest stain of duality.
In this context, the meaning is "it exists. || 3 ||
That which pertains to one who does not know reality, only he knows that;
but we know neither "I," nor "you," nor the one who does not know reality, nor that object.
How then is there the prior perception of impurities such as "I-ness" (ahaṃtva)? To this he says: "And that which..."—we do not know that stained object. || 4 ||
The notions "this is that," "I am this," and "this is real" do not arise in one who knows reality, just as a mirage does not appear on Mount Meru.

From where do we know this? To this he says: "This [is it]. For the appearance of a mirage is well-known to those whose vision is clouded by thirst and fatigue; however, on Meru, which is like heaven, no one possesses thirst, fatigue, or the like—this is the sense, and thus the mirage is not established there. || 5 ||
Just as when the mind is fixed upon one object, cognitions of other objects do not arise,
so too other cognitions do not abide simultaneously.

Just as when a person has reached a certainty regarding the true nature of a single substance—such as "this is indeed a post" or "this is indeed mother-of-pearl"—other cognitions contrary to that, such as the doubt "is it a post or a person? or the erroneous cognition "this is silver," do not arise; likewise, when the supreme reality is ascertained, other cognitions of the delusion of duality do not occur.
They remain. || 6 ||
This world was never non-existent, nor has it arisen; it does not exist, nor will it ever come to be. It is Brahman alone, whose nature is reality, established in this very manner. (7)
Having thus wiped away the state of being a living soul (jīva), he likewise begins to wipe away the state of the world—referring to "this" [world].
By wiping it away in this manner, the world remains as Brahman alone. || 7 ||
The vermilion hue and the shimmering of the glass reside within its own self;
that which is called "the world" is perceived therein solely through the knowledge of that [self]. (8)

Thus, when the sky of consciousness—which was perceived as the world during the act of cleansing—is purified, it abides in its own self as the state of pure Brahman. In that state, for those liberated while living (jīvanmuktas), that very thing is perceived through the knowledge of "that" (tat) alone as the world; the meaning is that nothing insentient is perceived. || 8 ||
Just as in dreams and in cities of imagination there is nothing else at all— save for pure consciousness, which is like the clear sky—
and likewise in formless things there is neither form nor even the absence of form, so it is now with this world called the waking state.

Just as in dreams and in cities imagined through the power of the mind, there exists nothing other than the one stainless pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), so too in this present world called the waking state, there is no form of limitation whatsoever apart from pure consciousness. Thus, by the removal of limitations, there is no other form within these formless individual souls (*jīvas*); this is the state of oneness with consciousness (*cidaikarasya*).
The meaning is that it is established. || 9 ||
It is said that something previously arises called "this," yet it does not truly exist; rather, it is beginningless space itself appearing as such because of its nature as consciousness.
Since there is neither a primary cause nor a cooperative condition for that which appears, what kind of statement is this: "Therefore, the entity arises by itself"? || 10 ||

"O Somya, in the beginning this was Being alone, one only, without a second"—according to this Śruti, since prior to creation there was indeed neither a transforming material cause (*pariṇāmy-upādāna*) nor a cooperative instrumental cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*), from what then does this world arise? Therefore, nothing at all arises here; that which appears as if it has come into being is merely an appearance.
The meaning is that it is established that this beginningless Brahman is indeed the void itself, appearing as such by its own nature of consciousness (citsvabhāva). || 10 ||
Therefore, nothing here comes into being by itself; indeed, from the beginning, Brahmā and the others were unknown to the ignorant and do not even exist as such.
This all-pervading space is this very Self-born One; thus, the sky of consciousness alone shines forth through consciousness. 11.

Reinforcing this very point, he states it again more clearly with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). Brahmā and the others, known by the ignorant as individual and collective *jīvas* along with their limiting adjuncts (*upādhis*), do not exist at all. Rather, this self-existent one and this phenomenal world (*prapañca*) are such that, from the perspective of Brahman, this expanse is merely the void of space—the sky of consciousness itself.
The meaning is that it is established that [the world] shines forth as one's own mind. || 11 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-fourth canto, titled "The Instruction on the Experience of the Unity of the World and the Supreme Self," in the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa*, the *Vālmīki Devarṣi Mokṣopāya*.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-fourth chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Experience of the Identity of the World and the Supreme Self," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The One Hundred and Sixty-Fifth Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
In the dream within the waking state, the dream itself assumes the nature of waking;
and in the waking within the dream, the waking attains the state of dreaming. (1)
Because of their mutual interpenetration and because they arise from one another,
the identity of waking and dreaming is asserted in order to strengthen the realization of pure consciousness alone.
Waking, dreaming, and deep sleep are each threefold through mutual interpenetration: waking-waking, waking-dreaming, waking-deep sleep;

dream-waking, dream-dreaming, dream-deep sleep; and deep-sleep-waking, deep-sleep-dreaming, deep-sleep-deep sleep. These are indeed [discussed] in the *Sureśvaravārttika*, in the section on "Prior Origination."

These [examples], established here through various illustrations, are taken as already proven. In that regard, because objects in the waking state and in dream-imaginations are independent of the activity of the senses and consist solely of the mind, the waking state attains the status of a dream by virtue of its similarity to a dream. Likewise, even in a dream, one thinks: "For this long I was asleep; now I am awake."

The meaning is that, because they are established through common experience, both dream and waking are proven; however, it is established by one's own direct experience that the waking state itself becomes a dream. || 1 ||
Dream enters into waking, and from dream one awakens to waking;
waking enters into dream, and the awakened one [emerges] from the waking-dream.
He states that there is a mutual causality between these two, like their mutual interpenetration, saying: "In a dream.

The meaning is that even from the state of waking which has the form of a dream, when one is awakened, the Self enters the very state of waking as if it were a dream; thus, mutual causality is also observed. || 2 ||
For one who possesses both waking and dreaming, the dream state is designated as "dream";
for one who possesses both dreaming and waking, the waking state is designated as "waking. (3)
He states that even a confusion of designations between these two is observed—namely, "waking-waking" and "dream-dream"—by means of a double expression through repetition (*vīpsā*) in both cases. (3)
In this world, that which arises in the waking state is indeed waking, and never a dream;
in a dream, it is a dream while awake, and never waking at any time.

In that regard, even within a dream, one who experiences it as if waking here—just like being awake—is indeed in the waking state and not in a dream. Likewise, in the "waking-dream" of mental projection (*manorājya*), one who experiences it as such is in a waking-dream itself and not in the waking state; this is the meaning. || 4 ||
For sleep always consists of a short duration within the waking state, and the waking state likewise always consists of a short duration during the time of sleep. (5)
He states that the short duration of dream and the long duration of the waking state would be reversed if they were mutually interpenetrating:
"having the nature of a short time" (laghukālātmaka). || 5 ||
There is never any difference whatsoever between waking and dreaming;
for one, there is no opportunity in the other, nor are both composed of reality.
Thus, regarding what is established when there is mutual intermingling, he says: "No. For neither of the two has an occasion for entry into the other;
their mutual penetration is not logically possible as being composed of reality (*sanmaya*).
At the time of awakening from death, the waking dream subsides;
and upon the realization of the experience of that dream, there remains only the exceedingly luminous void.

An objection is raised: "Surely, a dream ceases upon waking, and the objects of the dream remain utterly void during the waking state; this is not so for the waking state, which does not cease, nor do its objects appear as non-existent. To dispel this doubt regarding the dissimilarity with a dream, he says: "At death" (*mṛtau*). This waking-state dream also [ceases] at the time of death, which is the awakening to the next world.
Furthermore, the awakening to reality, characterized by the death of absolute duality, indeed subsides at that time.

The meaning is that there is only a similarity, not a difference, in that one remains in a state of voidness during the time of perceiving dream-objects—which is characterized by the daily experience of dreams—and, as indicated by the word "and" (ca), also during the state of deep sleep. || 7 ||
For one who is alive, during the time of dreaming, nothing whatsoever pertaining to the next world is perceived as a waking reality, except for the arising of the cognition of death.

One might raise the objection that there is a disparity between the two cases: objects experienced today in a dream are indeed non-existent in tomorrow’s dream, whereas objects experienced today in the waking state persist in tomorrow’s waking state.
He dispels this doubt by demonstrating the lack of persistence across different births with the words "jīvataḥ" (of one who lives), [meaning] until the dawning of the realization of death.

Since there is an absence of anything perceivable upon awakening from death, not even the slightest waking state consisting of another world is seen; while this empty waking consciousness, whose nature is manifold illusion, persists,
no dream consisting of another world is seen at all.

This being the case, while one lives in this present dream—which is devoid of all dream-objects such as life and the like—merely through delusion, there arises the consciousness of living, thinking "I live" within a self that is manifold and illusory; yet, since the dreams of tomorrow and yesterday are essentially of the nature of the next world, not a single object belonging to those [past or future] states is seen to persist here. This is the meaning.
Just as the three worlds appear in a dream as consisting solely of the wonder of consciousness,
so too do they shine forth in the waking state, from the very moment of creation, within the heart.

And since the nature of being merely the wonder of consciousness (*cic-camatkāra*) is equal for both, he says: "Consciousness" (*cid*). [This occurs] in the heart, that is, in the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).
Even though they appear vast, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), these things are indeed non-existent.
This possession of form does not exist at all in the waking state, just as it does not in the earth of a dream. (11)

Since the waking state is one with the dream state, it is clear that for those two, the eyes and other [senses] are formless and unreal, just like dream-objects; thus he says: "They indeed exist" (verse 11).
Just as the world, though appearing diverse and radiant, is empty in a dream,
so too in the waking state this entire universe is but space, consisting of the nature of consciousness.
Then he says—“Not the self”—to show that even the state where only pure consciousness remains is established. || 12 ||
For this is the very nature of the sky of consciousness that this world appears here in the expanse of space in such a vast manner, like light from a luminous source. (13)
It is like the light or radiance of fire, the sun, and so forth. || 13 ||
This wonder named "the world" shines forth intensely from the City [of the Heart], being innate in the sky, on the wall, in the atom, on land, and in water. 14.
Innate means belonging to the essential nature. || 14 ||
While this delusion, which lacks any real form, persists as if it were a real entity—having a body that is nothing more than empty space—who indeed would have any attachment toward it? (15)
What persistence or insistence can there be regarding this delusion of the world? The meaning is that it is entirely improper. || 15 ||
The world, consisting of the nature of the grasper, the grasping, and the grasped, is indeed empty; let it be existent or let it be non-existent—my friend, what is the point of clinging to it? (16)

The world, which consists of the triad beginning with the grasper (the subject), is empty and non-existent. Indeed, [it is] "hy" (for) and "arte" (in this matter). By virtue of the existence of the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*), it may be considered existent; or rather, let it be non-existent. In this regard, what is the purpose of "graha"—that is, the stubborn insistence on establishing one side or the other? This is the meaning. || 16 ||

"Let this be so, or let it be otherwise; let it not be, or let it come to pass—what cause for agitation is there in this? What attachment to the fruit is there in a fruit that is insignificant? That has already been understood; enough with these conceptual constructions. (17)

From a lack of understanding, there arises the delusion of partiality toward one side or the other. Now, since you have understood the truth in its essence, what attachment can there be to the status of being a "fruit" regarding this inferior fruit—both in establishing the reality of this [world] characterized by enjoyment included within that [truth], and in the other [state] characterized by water? The meaning is that such an attachment is entirely improper. || 17 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-fifth canto, titled "The Instruction on the Unity of Waking and Dreaming," in the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa*, in the section concerning the Ultimate Reality (*Nirvāṇa*), within the portion dealing with the Liberation of the Disciple (*Mumukṣuvyavahāra*).

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-fifth chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Identity of Waking and Dreaming," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The one hundred and sixty-sixth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
[Know that state] which is devoid of the meaningful word "self" (ātman) and the word "renown" (khyāti).
Know this to be the theory of self-manifestation (ātmakhyāti), as solid as a stone's core.

In this context, the specific nature of self-apprehension (ātmakhyāti) is explained, as well as the existence of other theories of error; furthermore, the illustration of the "blue stone" regarding Brahman is stated along with a series of questions and answers.

Having observed through his signs that Rāma’s inquiry was as follows— "Regarding what was said, 'This wonder called the world shines intensely,' by which of the four types of cognition (khyāti) accepted by different schools of thinkers— namely, non-apprehension (akhyāti), apprehension of the non-existent (asatkhyāti), misapprehension (anyathākhyāti), or self-apprehension (ātmakhyāti)— does that [world] shine for the wise?"— the sage [responded].

In this regard, intending to refute even the four types of erroneous cognition (khyāti) postulated by various disputants—which, from the perspective of the wise, are as non-existent as a hare’s horn—he begins to explain the fifth type, the extraordinary *ātmakhyāti*, which is accepted by the learned:
[the meaning is] "that which is indicated by two words whose referents are indivisible. It is as solid and continuous as the interior of a stone slab, as will be described below.
The dense one. || 1 ||
From the very beginning of creation, the sky of consciousness alone has been thus expanded;
that which shines within itself is, by that very fact, its state as a creation.

Regarding the co-referential connection (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the two terms "the Self alone" and "manifestation" (*khyāti*), in response to the inquiry—"What is this Self, and of what object does that manifestation consist?"—he says: "From the first creation," and so forth. Since that Self, by its own power of consciousness, has manifested the state of being the creation within itself alone as something perceived, therefore, this very Self is the subject of the manifestation whose object is the state of being the creation.
The meaning is "manifestation. || 2 ||
In this [reality], rivers do not flow, nor is there here the act of emerging from or submerging in water;
the sky shines within the sky itself, and likewise the form of consciousness shines forth, utterly motionless.

In the term *cidvyoma* (the ether of consciousness), which is intended as an explanation of the word *ātman*, the meaning of the word *vyoma* is simply the emptiness of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*). Therefore, by the phrase beginning with "they do not flow," he demonstrates that the meaning of the particle *eva* (only/itself) is that the phenomenal world and its manifestation are the Self alone. It "shines" (is manifested); it is "unmoved" (devoid of action). || 3 ||

They know this as *ātmakhyāti* (self-apprehension), which is devoid of any mention of gold and entirely free from conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), occurring without the object that serves as the subsequent term.

The meaning is as follows: by the word "khyāti," which denotes "appearance" (*kacanavācaka*), and by the latter member of the compound—the word *khyāti*—the wise know [this doctrine] as *ātmakhyāti*. This is because, even without that [external] object or its meaning, the self alone shines forth, consisting of the manifestation of the creation that is identical with itself. Thus, they understand it as the "manifestation of the self. || 4 ||
This entire world is indeed the Self alone, wherein there is no such thing as manifestation;
for that which is unmanifested by name is never manifested anywhere through manifestation.
Thus, he states that in a creation whose nature is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), terms such as "non-apprehension" (*akhyāti*)—which are favored by opponents—are inapplicable:

"The Self alone... and so forth. When this entire world is the Self alone, and that Self is self-luminous, it has never been made manifest by an apprehension distinct from itself; therefore, the verbal formulation "it is unmanifested" (*akhyāta*) might apply there. However, it is not "non-apprehension" (*akhyāti*).
The meaning is that, in that context, it is possible to connect a word ending in a *ktin* suffix which has the sense of a verbal root (*bhāvārthaka*). || 5 ||
In this matter of "manifestation" and "non-manifestation," the verbal formulation is unreal;
for what indeed could manifestation be there, or likewise, what could non-manifestation be? (6)
To explain why it is not possible [to negate it], he says: "manifestation" (*khyāti*). For the root *khyā* has the meaning of "becoming known" (*prathā*).

The suffix denotes "being," which is existence (*sattā*). Thus, the meaning of the word *khyāti* is existence whose nature is manifestation. Since this Self is precisely such a manifestation, it cannot be connected with the meaning of the negative particle; therefore, it is called "non-non-manifestation" (*akhyāti*).
