The meaning is that the verbal formulation favored by the opponent is unreal in that context. [The opponent] might then argue: "Let there be a *ktin* suffix here after a causative (*ṇic*) root; since the form *khyātiḥ* is established there by the elision of the *ṇic* according to the rule *ṇeraniṭi*, the intended meaning of the opponent will be established through the etymological derivation: 'that in which manifestation (*khyātiḥ*), i.e., making known, does not exist, is *akhyātiḥ*'. Anticipating this objection, he says: "What is that?"—referring to the insentient (*jaḍe*).
For if creation (*sarga*) is accepted as something distinct [from the self], then in that case, its manifestation (*khyāpana*) or non-manifestation (*akhyāpana*) by another agent would be applicable.

But when the self itself, being self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*), is the creation, then—just as one lamp cannot manifest or fail to manifest another lamp therein—what purpose would manifestation or non-manifestation serve? It serves none at all. Thus, the meaning is that in every respect, the position favored by the opponent is untenable. By this, the theories of *asatkhyāti* (the apprehension of the non-existent) and *anyathākhyāti* (misapprehension) are also refuted.

The meaning is that once the alternative views have been rejected, the meanings of the words *asat* and *anyathā*—just like the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*)—are likewise unfit for syntactic connection with the referent of the word *khyāti*. || 6 ||

Non-apprehension (akhyāti), misapprehension (anyathākhyāti), and the apprehension of the non-existent (asatkhyāti)— these others are merely the wondrous manifestations of the mind, appearing as objects to that which is of the nature of pure consciousness.

But if you accept that non-apprehension (akhyāti) and the other theories are merely the wonders of consciousness, consisting of nothing but imagination and equal to other objects of perception such as dreams and mental fantasies, then let it be so; we have no objection at all. Thus he says: "Non-apprehension... (verse 7).

In whatever manner, whenever, and whichever they may be, those pure rays of consciousness shine forth from the sun of the sky of pure consciousness; at that time, each one appears exactly in that manner.
The "portions of consciousness" (cidaṃśavaḥ) are conceived parts of consciousness, like sparks from a fire. || 8 ||

Self-manifestation (ātmakhyāti), non-existent manifestation (asatkhyāti), non-manifestation (akhyāti), and otherwise-manifestation (anyathākhyāti)—these are the wonders of consciousness, the manifestations of self-manifestation. (9)
This being the case, he states—"Self-apprehension" (ātmakhyāti)—meaning that those [theories] favored by you are in fact merely manifestations of my own theory of self-apprehension.
The meaning of the term "self-manifestation" (ātmakhyāti) is devoid of the state of self-manifestation;
it is without beginning or end, beyond description, and exists as this single, solid mass. || 10 ||

Concluding the description of *ātmakhyāti*, he begins to explain the phrase "solid as a stone-womb" (*śilājaṭharanirghanām*) by means of the narrative of Śilā: "Of the term *ātmakhyāti*... (verse 10).
In this regard, listen to this great narrative, which is an ornament for the ears, a refutation of dualistic views, and an illumination of the sun of awakening. (11)

In that regard, concerning the subject of the explanation of the term "solid as a rock-mass" (*śilājaṭharanirghana*), which is indicated by the phrase "standing as a single compact mass" (*ekaghanaḥ sthitaḥ*). || 11 ||
There is a rock, vast and stainless, as hard as a wall of sapphire, measuring thousands of millions of yojanas in extent.
If the sky itself, blue on all sides, were to become a wall, it would be as hard, pure, and vast as that [wall]. (12)
Its joints are not tight, yet it is as solid as adamant;
it is expansive, with an utterly nourished and firm belly, and pure like the sky. || 13 ||
In which there are no joints—that is, no joining together of parts—and this word [sandhi] is not the negative particle *nañ*.
It is "visāriṇī," meaning expansive or widespread. || 13 ||
Possessing a solid body that remains indestructible throughout a multitude of incalculable kalpas, she of lovely limbs appears like the very form of space due to her stainless purity. 14.

Regarding the phrase *kalpanicayam*, the accusative case is used according to the rule *kālādhvanoratyantasaṃyoge* (Pāṇini 2.3.5), just as in the example *krośaṃ giriḥ* ("the mountain extends for a *krośa*"). 14.
Its birth is indeed known, yet its specific nature is not known by anyone;
as to how, where, and when it occurs, that is never truly understood. (15)

Since another entity of the same class is not established, that specific genus—which is excluded from what is of a different class—is not known by anyone at all. Likewise, its location, time, and mode are also entirely unestablished; thus he asks: "How? (15)
Within her heart, however— which is devoid of the elements of the physical world—
there exists [a nature] that is dense, infinite, firm, possessing the essence of a diamond, and indestructible.

The connection with the subsequent clause is as follows: within her womb, which is devoid of the elements of existence, the great elements, and the fourfold classes of living beings, there exist lotus-networks and the like, consisting of inscriptions resembling lines within crystal slabs.
There exist in great abundance various marks consisting of lines that have become his very own limbs, such as clusters of lotuses, conchs, maces, discs, and so forth. (17)
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), there is the inclusion of the sword, the skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga), and so forth. || 17 ||
Space, wind, water, fire, and earth—these were the names assigned;
however, among those self-written [scriptures], there was no mention whatsoever of a "jīva. || 18 ||
In that case, within the interior of the stone, there was no such thing as space, air, and so forth;

rather, the designations "space," "air," and so on were merely applied by that stone to its own inscriptions which appeared in that manner. And by that [stone], the designation "living being" (jīva) was likewise applied to its own bodily inscriptions—this is the meaning. || 18 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
Tell me, how does this stone possess consciousness?
How can that which is called an insentient stone indeed act? (19)

"Now, this stone is indeed insentient precisely because it is a stone; 'nāma' (by name) refers to worldly convention. And how could there be consciousness—that is, cognition—in it? If it is indeed insentient, then how does it assign names such as 'space' or 'wind' to its own inscriptions? For the act of naming is well-known to have a conscious agent," thus Rāma raises the objection with the word "śilā" (stone).
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: That vast and radiant stone is neither conscious nor inert;
who knows its genus, and what else exists therein?

Vasiṣṭha answers the question with the words beginning "No," etc., resolving that this very inquiry has already been answered by the previous statement: "Its origin is known, but its distinction is not known by anyone. The meaning is: "Who else exists who could know its origin?"
Śrī Rāma said:
"Who sees those lines within her womb, and how?
Or how and by whom was she broken, and at what time? Tell me this. (21)

If no one else exists there, then who perceives those lines situated within its belly— those described by you as having the forms of space, wind, and so forth? And by whom were they carved with various internal line-patterns using chisels?
"Since it is impossible for it to have entered the interior of the anvil or elsewhere, how could it be broken? Tell me, when indeed was it broken?"—this is the explicit question of Rāma. || 21 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
It is not possible to pierce that fierce [intellect], nor does a piercer exist;
likewise, everything is enveloped by her who possesses a body of infinite extent.
He provides the answer by way of denial to those who have been questioned, beginning with the words "yat" and so forth. "Ugrā" means exceedingly firm. "Āvṛtam" means pervaded.
The sense is based on the Śruti passage: "There is nothing whatsoever not pervaded by it, nothing whatsoever not enveloped by it."
Within that hollow there exist infinite networks of trees and mountains, as well as cities and towns, all composed of written records. (23)
Among them, there are those made of writing bearing the names of gods and dānavas;
they are subtle and yet not subtle, formless and yet appearing as if they had form, like little figurines.
The figurines and images are both subtle and non-subtle. || 24 ||
There exists a line named Ākāśa, possessing great breadth;
and within it there are secondary lines named after the moon and the sun. (25)
Śrī Rāma said:
O Brahmā, tell me, by whom were those lines seen there, and of what nature were they?
Tell me also, how are they seen while remaining within the hollow of a solid stone?
Those which reside within that stone-casket, which is exceedingly solid, compact, and extremely dense, [are the elements]. 26.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
"O Rāghava, those such scribes were seen by me there;
if you also have the desire, then you too shall see them."
You see it; you shall behold it through meditative concentration. || 27 ||
Śrī Rāma said: Such a stone, as hard as a diamond, cannot possibly be broken;
nevertheless, how was it that you saw those lines within its interior?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
O Rāma, I am situated as a mere line within her womb;
therefore, staying there, I see that entire network of lines unimpaired.
Even though I am the body of Vasiṣṭha, I reside within her womb; for that reason, she bears only a mere line [of hair]. || 29 ||
"Who else besides me is capable of shattering that stone?
Standing within it, I beheld all of that which was inside it. (30)
Standing within it, I beheld that entire collection of writings existing inside. || 30 ||
Śrī Rāma said: Who is that stone, and who are you? Tell me, where are you situated?
What is this that you say? Speak; what is it that you have seen? (31)
Now, desiring to know that stone and Vasiṣṭha in their true nature, Rāma asks: "What is this?"—that is, what do you mean by this so-called "stone"? (31)
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: This great reality of the Supreme Self has been described by me to you through this very turn of speech; it is not, however, a massive stone.
By this turn of phrase in the narrative concerning Śilā. || 32 ||
We are within the belly of the stone of the supreme Self’s great existence;
these [beings] are merely the flesh of that stone, entirely devoid of any cavities.
The meaning is that we are like the flesh on a stone—that is, we are of the very same nature as the stone itself. We are these [very ones]. || 33 ||
Know that the limbs of that stone are the sky; those limbs of the stone are the ever-moving wind;
those limbs of the stone are actions, sounds, latent impressions, and the conceptualization of time.
He elaborates that the entire world is indeed that very stone-body with the words "that stone-body. "Sadāgati" means wind;

this is an indicative term for the five elements. Likewise, the mention of action-words is also an indicative term for the qualities of all the elements and elemental products, such as wind, space, and so forth. "Vāsanā" is an indicative term for the qualities of the mind.
Earth, water, fire, air, ether, mind, intellect, and ego—these are declared to be the various components of that stone. (35)
Having already stated it, he says again more clearly: "The ground" (bhūmiḥ) || 35 ||
The Supreme Self is the Great Being, the rock, and we are the flesh;
therefore, although we are all non-different from it, we perceive ourselves as different. (36)
"But we understand 'others' through delusion. (36)
This exceedingly vast stone is indeed of the single nature of pure consciousness; apart from this, where could it be? Tell me, what else could there be? (37)
If there exists anything apart from this [consciousness], tell me where it is and what it is—state both of these. || 37 ||
This entire world, consisting of jars, pits, cloths, and so forth, is nothing but pure sensation;
it appears just as [objects appear] in a dream, or as water appears in the form of waves. (38)
One might object: "Is it not the case that the ground, the jar, the tree, the cloth, and so forth are well-known as being distinct from that [Brahman]? To this he says: "Pure" (śuddham).
The meaning is that none of these exists apart from it. || 38 ||
This entire Brahman is a solid mass, an expansion consisting solely of pure consciousness;
the wise know it all to be a single, solid mass—tranquil and the essence of ultimate reality.
All this is but one great mass of consciousness, like the interior of a stone, entirely devoid of cavities, without end, and without beginning or middle.
By that very Self, through its own nature as the power of manifestation (*kalana*), this creation—known by the name of the "world" or the "universe"—has been fashioned.
The entire world is but one Brahman, like the interior of a stone; and that [Brahman] is devoid of cavities, meaning it is without the state of being hollow or pierced.

Devoid of the far shore, infinite, and likewise without beginning or middle— by that such Brahma-self, by his very own self, the creation— the world, the universe, known also by these synonymous names— is "kalitā," meaning it was fashioned or assumed as that which is called the visible manifestation. || 40 ||
Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-sixth canto, titled "The Story of Śila," in the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa*, the *Vairāgyaprakaraṇa* of the *Mokṣopāya*.
Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-sixth chapter, titled "The Legend of Śila," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The One Hundred and Sixty-Seventh Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Self-apprehension, the apprehension of the non-existent, the apprehension of what is not apprehended, and otherwise-apprehension;
To one who knows that [reality], these views regarding words and their referents are like the horns of a hare.
Here, from the perspective of one who knows that, the fourfold renown of the disputant is set aside,
and the reality of the self, free from the three states, is described.
The term "anyathākhyātiḥ" (apprehension otherwise) is to be construed with the preceding word that is separated [from it]. || 1 ||
O friend, at some time indeed no [objects] whatsoever arise;
the knower remains as the peaceful, indefinable Self, with all activity having subsided. (2)

For if the appearance of the world were real, there would be occasion for such conceptual alternatives as: "Is it *ātmakhyāti* (the theory that the self is perceived) or *asatkhyāti* (the theory that the non-existent is perceived)?
But if that [appearance] does not exist at all, then of what could there be these four varieties? With this intention, he says: "Never... [referring to the verse]:
"When the limbs have set, [he is] devoid of the mental activity that is the root of conceptualizations such as appearance. (2)

These perceptions, such as the manifestation of the self (ātmakhyāti) and so forth, arise from pure consciousness alone; and that [consciousness] is the most pristine ether, perceived as being identical with it.

The "views" (dṛśaḥ) are erroneous perceptions. And that pure consciousness, from the perspective of ultimate reality, is the most pristine void, empty of all conceptual constructions. Every conceptual construction whatsoever is seen by me as being composed of that very [consciousness];
for the meaning of the Vedic scripture is: "That which consists of this, consists of that, and consists of all. || 3 ||
The internal delusion of conceptualization that "this is the Self" and "this is manifestation" cannot possibly exist; therefore, having abandoned this word, become a partaker of the ultimate reality.

"Having abandoned the word"—the meaning is that for this very reason we have stated that it is "devoid of the meaningful word 'self' (ātman) and the word 'manifestation' (khyāti). It possesses the object; it possesses the ultimate reality. || 4 ||
Whether walking, standing, or even eating, everything is therefore peaceful;
it is like the silence of space—pure, uninterrupted, and devoid of activity.

In the phrase "gacchan tiṣṭhan," there is a Vedic (chāndasa) transposition of genders. Therefore, from this observation of the meaning, the sense is that even while the world is moving, standing, giving, or eating, it appears as motionless, devoid of all activity. || 5 ||
Though filled with various great sounds, it remained as silent as a stone; though moving without ceasing, it stood like a mountain, like the sky.
This very point is clarified by the passage beginning with "not manifold" (nānā) and so forth. || 6 ||
Though it possesses various kinds of undertakings, it is the great void, unmarked; though composed of the five elements, it is like space, having not attained the state of the fivefold [senses].
Though crowded with objects, it is empty and consists of pure consciousness alone;
like a great city seen in a dream, though perceived, it is composed of pure, stainless awareness.
Whether with effort or without effort, it is like a city of one's imagination;
it is mere space, consisting of delusion, and comparable to union with a woman in a dream. (9)
It is merely space, utterly empty. || 9 ||
Even though experienced, it is as useless as a woman who is a mere reflection;
for an entity constructed from various perceptions is, in reality, empty. (10)
Śrī Rāma said:
I consider this world to consist of waking and dreaming, perceived through memory alone;
here, memory produced by external objects that possess the nature of reality is the very cause.

If this world, consisting of the waking and dreaming states, which does not exist at all, is seen merely through mental impressions (*vāsanā*), then I consider that it is seen by means of memory alone. In this manifestation of the world, memory itself is the cause, not delusion (*bhrānti*).
For that [memory] is devoid of causes such as a defective substrate, similarity, or sensory contact, and its object is external and real in nature.
The meaning of Rāma’s question is this: "Those objects which do not exist—does consciousness have as its domain that which consists of them alone? (11)

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: That which, through the shimmering of the crystal of consciousness, appears as the body of all things by chance— being of the nature of space, the mere existence of phenomena, and without any supporting wall— is the Self.

Vasiṣṹṭha provides the following resolution with the underlying intention that this [cognition] is indeed an error based on that [substratum], and not memory; for it arises from defects such as the sleep of ignorance (avidyā), and because there is no application of contact with self-luminous consciousness (cit). Furthermore, since all prior experiences would likewise be equivalent to the present one, they would result in being classified as memory, which would lead to the undesirable consequence that the original experiences upon which they are based could never be established. Vasiṣṭha says: "O noble one, what you have said is true; however, it is not memory. Why? Because it is born from the defect of the sleep of ignorance and the like, and because there is no application of contact with self-luminous consciousness. Moreover, if it were memory, then all previous experiences, being equal to the present one, would also be memories; consequently, the original experiences that serve as their basis would remain unestablished."
—By the words "That which... and so forth. Therein, he demonstrates the existence of the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) with the words "That which...":
the meaning is that this very world is that which, being of the nature of space (*vyomātman*) and pure existence (*sattāmātra*), appears as a shimmering reflection (*kācakacyena*). || 12 ||
This very [nature], whose essence is indestructible, exists at all times within the omnipresent Supreme Self, just as ripples exist within calm water. (13)
This very state, which is signless and consists of its own essential nature, exists within the Supreme Self—
the Self of all, within Nirvāṇa, within the Self that is space, and within the Selfless.
Whenever and by whatever means it appears,
in whatever manner and at whatever time— whether always or never, wherever or nowhere— it is nothing at all.

In that which is produced by ignorance (*āvidyaka*), there is no dependence on fixed defects and the like; however, with the intention that indefinite defects (*aniyatadoṣa*) certainly do occur, the expression "by this or that" and so forth is stated. (15)
Of that very radiance of Brahman, by means of that very self which is Brahman, [it perceives] its own nature, which is inherently pure and does not abandon its own essential being.
If so, by whom were these names such as "the world" and so forth created for this delusion? To that he replies with two verses beginning with "tasyaiva" (of him alone).

"This is waking, this is dreaming, this is deep sleep, and this is the fourth"— these names are merely applied by the mind to itself, just as one applies the name "Brahman" or "Self" to the Self because of its own consciousness.
In reality, there is neither dream, nor waking, nor deep sleep;
there is no fourth state (turiya), nor that which transcends it—all is the supreme, peaceful ether. || 18 ||
Therefore, what has passed is redundant. || 18 ||
Or rather, all this is always of the nature of waking, or it is always a dream, or it is always deep sleep. (19)
The intellect (citta) is always in a state of waking because it never sleeps; it is always a dream because it is mere illusion;
and it is always deep sleep because it is merely the veil of ignorance. || 19 ||
Or perhaps it is always the fourth state (*turya*), or always within that;
or it is this very thing which we, whose forms are the inner quarters of space, do not know.

The meaning is that, because it always and indeed transcends the three states by its very nature, it may even be called "the Fourth" (turya) at all times. Since those three are not established [as real], we do not know the non-existence of that Fourth within, nor do we know any conceptual construction (vikalpa) such as "this is it" or "that is it," for it is beyond conceptualization. || 20 ||
This is neither foam nor anything at all, nor is it a bubble nor anything whatsoever; it is the sky of consciousness within the great belly of the ocean in the waters of emptiness.
Whatever is perceived in whatever manner, that is experienced in exactly that way;
whether it be real or unreal, it exists in the dream just as both the real and the unreal exist in the sky.

But regarding the perspective of conceptual cognition and perception, one should simply be satisfied with the fact that whatever is experienced by someone, in whatever manner, and at whatever time, it is exactly so for them at that time; thus he says: "In whatever manner" (yathā). || 22 ||
This manifestation of consciousness shines forth according to its appearance—
space within space, the nature of consciousness within the nature of consciousness, within the pervasive Self.
And that consciousness, whose essence is the midst of the sky of thought, is always of such a nature;
it neither sets nor rises, for this world is its own limb.
Since the world is nothing but consciousness, it neither sets nor rises.
The great dissolutions, creations, and so forth, as well as the nights of the great dissolution,
have become constituent parts of her alone, like hair, nails, and the like.

One should understand that the divisions of time beginning with the great dissolution and creation consist of nights characterized by the great dissolution and days characterized by creation. || 25 ||
Its manifestation or non-manifestation, its radiance or its dullness, is nothing other than the Great Consciousness itself, just as movement is nothing other than the nature of the wind. (26)
Is it the luminous form of consciousness, or is it the dull form of māyā? || 26 ||
Therefore, what indeed could be called waking, what dreaming, and what deep sleep? What is the fourth state (turya), what memory, and what desire? These are all empty, false perceptions. (27)
He concludes: "Therefore," etc. (27).
Since internal consciousness shines as its own external object, where is duality and where is the wealth of objects? Thus, how can there be such a thing as memory? (28)
This being so, from what would memory arise? || 28 ||
This very thing shines forth without a supporting wall, manifesting by its own nature;
it is like the luminous form of the sun in the sky, devoid of any material elements.

That which shines as non-different and non-distinct from itself is self-luminous; that luminosity is of the very nature of the Self and is not distinct from it. The meaning is: just as the sun in the supportless sky has a luminous form that is its own shining and does not depend upon an object to be illumined, so it is here. || 29 ||
If an external object exists as a real entity, then let memory arising from it serve as the cause for the existence of this world, beginning with names and so forth. (30)

Let it be granted that [this world] arises from that and has that as its cause for experience; however, this does not apply to the first state of the world's existence at the time of creation. || 30 ||
However, this external object does not exist, because it is utterly impossible for the five elements to have existed at the beginning of the first creation, due to the absence of any causes.
Just as a rabbit’s horn does not exist, just as a tree in the sky does not exist, just as the son of a barren woman does not exist, so too a black moon does not exist. 32.
Likewise, an object that appears to the ignorant—such as the world, the ego, and so forth—exists when not scrutinized; yet when scrutinized, it does not exist at all, for nothing real remains.

At the beginning of the world, at the time of creation and so forth, objects such as the "I" (aham) appear to the ignorant; however, if examined from the perspective of reality, they are not seen to exist, whereas if examined [with wisdom], they do not exist. || 33 ||
Just as this great form exists, yet is not any material form at all— being the domain of those who know reality— so too, O Rāma, does this undivided reality exist.

The meaning is that there certainly exists an undivided reality, which is not an object for those who know the truth, which has no form whatsoever, and which is devoid of both embodied and unembodied forms, being a single solid mass of pure consciousness alone. || 34 ||
Whenever the marrow of the sky, which is the density of consciousness, arises,
it is designated by the conventional expression "eternally arisen" as having imagined settings and risings.
Though eternally risen, she is conceived through metaphorical usage as having both setting and rising in worldly transaction.
At various times, it perceives within the void itself as if it were earth and so forth;
thus, due to its own manifestation, it assumes the conceptualization of earth and other elements. (36)
Whenever the ignorant person vainly perceives the sky itself as being earth and so forth, at that very moment he conceives the conceptualization of earth and the rest.
The unborn Great Consciousness, which is its own manifestation and nothing but space itself,
subsequently designates itself by the designation of "earth" and so forth.
The Great Consciousness itself subsequently designates—that is, refers to—its own self-nature by means of the designation "earth" and so forth, using the names "earth" and so on. || 37 ||
Just as a child [perceives] a city of the imagination, so does pure, immutable consciousness maintain its own awareness that "this earth is indeed space. (38)
The imperishable, pure consciousness, which is like space, maintains within its own self the self-awareness that "this earth exists. || 38 ||
One should not conceptualize what its manifestation might be or what its non-manifestation might be;
know that it has the nature of both vibration and non-vibration, like the wind in the sky. (39)

If it is pure consciousness alone that appears in the form of this world, then what could its non-appearance be? Such a doubt should not be entertained, nor is it to be conceptualized. Know this: by means of its vital power (*prāṇa-śakti*), it has the nature of vibration (*spanda-svabhāva*); by means of its consciousness-power (*cic-chakti*), it has the nature of non-vibration (*aspanda-svabhāva*). || 39 ||
Just as the space of consciousness shines, so does this world appear;
it is formless space within space itself, and these elements such as earth and the rest do not exist anywhere as reality.
In whatever manner it appears and flashes forth through the arising of latent impressions (vāsanā), in that very same manner this world manifests. || 40 ||
Just as it shines, because its nature is the space of consciousness, though it appears fully, it is neither existent nor non-existent; it is nothing at all, yet it is not nothing.

Just as it appears, so let it be called "existent. Yet, even though it appears, because its nature is the space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*), it is neither truly existent nor non-existent. The meaning is that this form of phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*) is not anything at all, but rather something entirely indefinable. || 41 ||
Whether it be thus or otherwise, whether existent or non-existent, as it truly stands—
the wise man understands the history of the world’s various transformations, and no one else.

That very [consciousness], through the perception of the visible world manifesting within the space of the heart, perceives the external cosmic egg exactly as it is situated—whether as real or as unreal. (43)

The meaning is this: since that very wise one dwells as the Self within the space of the hearts of all, it is by means of the perception of the visible—which shines forth in His own form—that the designation of distinctions such as "this internal body" and "this external universe" has been made. || 43 ||
What here is external, or what is internal? What is the visible, and what is its visibility?
All is auspicious, peaceful, and yet unpeaceful; let all be stilled in "Om."

Having dissolved everything by means of the conceptualization of its non-difference from the *mātrās* of the *praṇava* as "Oṃ," let there be peace. In the reading "mā mā," the meaning is "having cast it away" through the repetition of the negation "mā mā. || 44 ||

Investigation free from the perception of the signified and the signifier does not come about; and that [investigation] is accomplished through the nature of conceptual construction. Furthermore, no realization whatsoever is possible without that, just as there is no perception by the eyes at night without a lamp.

With the intention that the injunctions for hearing [the scriptures] and so forth proceed only by provisionally accepting the conceptual distinction between the signified and the signifier—even though such a distinction is ultimately unreal—as long as there is investigation, he says: "No. An investigation into the meaning of the scripture is not possible without recourse to the perspective of the signified and the signifier; and that investigation consists precisely of the object of inquiry (*viṣaya*) and the doubt (*viśaya*), both of which are composed of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

"The prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), as well as the final conclusion (*uttara*), the purpose (*prayojana*), and [the subject matter and connection]—they know that a topic (*adhikaraṇa*) in the scripture consists of these five limbs.

Thus, what is composed according to this well-known five-limbed structure leads to success. Without such investigation, success is simply not possible. The meaning is: just as visual perception does not occur at night without a lamp, so it is in this case. (45)
Therefore, having cast aside with a supremely pure intellect the internal web of manifold conceptual constructions and mental imaginings,
and having made the mind fixed upon the great meaning of all the scriptures, fly up and go to the supreme state, established in the One.
Therefore, with an intellect purified by correct inquiry, having cast aside the vast web of conceptual constructions characterized by internal volitions,
and having made the mind fixed upon that non-dual Self which is Being-Consciousness-Bliss— the great goal established as the quintessence of all scriptures—
one becomes intent solely on That; thus, having flown out from this cycle of transmigration, one reaches the supreme state known as liberation.
The meaning is "go. || 46 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-seventh chapter, titled "The Exposition on the Absence of Waking, Dreaming, and Deep Sleep," in the *Mokṣopāya* section of the *Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa*, within the *Vāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa*.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-seventh canto, titled "The Exposition on the Absence of Waking, Dreaming, and Deep Sleep," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and sixty-eighth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Just as a fault committed entirely without prior intention results in a variety of branches [of consequences],...
Thus the Unborn performs various appearances of creation, like space within space.
In this context, the superimposition of creation is described as being not preceded by intelligence;
and since that which consists of pure consciousness is devoid of change, it is excluded from the category of consciousness [as a subject].
He supports the idea that the creation was not preceded by conscious intent (*abuddhipūrvakatva*) with examples in order to establish its falsity,

beginning with the words "without conscious intent" (*abuddhipūrvam*). Just as a tree (*ago vṛkṣo yathā*) produces a variety of branches without conscious intent— that is, without the prior thought "I am creating this variety of branches"— so too does the Unborn (*ajo*), the Supreme Self (*paramātmā*) who is devoid of transformations such as birth and so forth, [manifest] in the sky (*khe*).

In its own self, which is like space, it produces various and manifold appearances of creation—the superimposition of the phenomenal world—within that void which is of the nature of emptiness. Now, [it is said]: "He thought, 'Shall I create the worlds? "He desired, 'May I become many;
may I procreate. "He performed austerity. "Having performed austerity, He created all this. "By austerity is Brahman built up."

If it is argued: "Since such scriptural passages as 'From that, food is produced' proclaim that creation is preceded by intelligence, how can it be said here that creation is not preceded by intelligence? This contradicts the direct scripture (pratyakṣa-śruti). Listen!
This would indeed be so if the scripture’s primary intent (tātparya) were to establish the origin of creation; however, that is not the case.
Because there is no purpose [for it]. Indeed, no purpose for the knowledge of creation and so forth is heard in the scriptures.

For the knowledge of the non-dual Brahman as the Self is introduced as having a purpose in all the Upanishads. Since that [knowledge] possesses a fruit, the creation and so forth—heard in its proximity but being themselves fruitless—attain the status of being subordinate to it when they require a purpose.

And this [injunction] of his, which is intent upon the rule for tranquility as an ancillary to the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā—in the passage, "All this is indeed Brahman; because it is born from that (tajja), dissolved in that (talla), and breathes in that (tadan); therefore, being tranquil, one should meditate"—[explains that] since this entire world is born from that, it is "born from that" (tajja). Because it dissolves in that, it is "dissolved in that" (talla). Because it breathes, lives, and exists by means of that, it is "breathing in that" (tadan); thus, its existence at the times of origin, maintenance, and dissolution is dependent upon that. Therefore, all this is indeed...

Because the status of creation and so forth as auxiliary to knowledge is established by the Śruti itself—on the grounds that they serve as means for demonstrating the non-duality of Brahman through the statement "That [world] is indeed Brahman"—and because it is impossible to reconcile them otherwise;

and because this is supported by thousands of arguments elucidated in the Sūtra-bhāṣya and other works, beginning with the aphorism: "Its non-difference [from Brahman] is established on account of the words concerning 'origin' and so forth."

Furthermore, since the purport of the creation-śrutis has been determined to be the elucidation of the reality of the Self as Brahman— devoid of phenomenal proliferation (*niṣprapañca*)— through the methods of superimposition and negation (*adhyāropa-apavāda*), based on thousands of corroborating sources such as the *Smṛtis* and *Purāṇas*,
it is observed that superimpositions such as those of a snake upon a rope, silver upon mother-of-pearl, a mirage in the desert, or a dream, are invariably devoid of prior conscious intent.
Since no instance of superimposition (*āropa*) preceded by conscious intent is observed anywhere in the world,
the venerable Vasiṣṭha establishes here that the creation is not preceded by conscious intent, so that no one might suspect that there is any superimposition in the process of manifestation.

As for the mention in the Śrutis of [the creation] being preceded by "seeing" (*īkṣaṇa*) and so forth, this is intended to establish Brahman’s omniscience, its nature as pure consciousness, and other such attributes.
This [argument] culminates in the refutation of the Sāṃkhya and other schools' assertion that the material cause (upādāna) is a conscious principle such as *pradhāna*;

for the sūtras beginning with "Because of seeing, [Brahman] is not that which is not based on scripture" (*īkṣaternāśabdam*) describe the purport of the Śruti in exactly that way. As it is said: "He has three abodes and three states of sleep; as hair and body-hair arise from an existing person, so does this universe arise here from the Imperishable."

This is because it is consistent with such scriptural illustrations as these. Since desire, volition, and so forth—which precede the emergence of the principle of the intellect (*buddhi-tattva*)—are merely modifications of *māyā*, it is logically possible that although they are preceded by that [intellect], they do not have the intellect as their substrate (*dharmin*). This is because [the intellect] is a superimposition (*adhyāropa*).

Furthermore, since it is only for one who is established in the referent of the term "thou" (*tvaṃpadārtha*) that its refutation through negation can logically result in liberation, there would be no purpose in teaching the superimposition of the world upon the referent of the term "that" (*tatpadārtha*). Moreover, if the phenomenal world were the effect of ignorance inherent in itself, its refutation would be logically possible through its own knowledge.
And within itself, there occurs only a superimposition of the three states that is not preceded by conscious intent; for example:
"Just as the ocean, through its own nature, produces whirlpools and the like without conscious thought, so does the Self in the void—the Lord of all—produce all perceptions. (2)
Being devoid of cognition and not preceded by cognition, [he perceives] all sensations and the appearances of the world. (2)
From those very self-cognitions, he himself then creates various designations such as "mind," "intellect," and "ego. (3)

The meaning is that, at the beginning of creation, these self-cognitions, which take on the forms of the world, themselves assume names such as "mind" (manas) and "intellect" (buddhi), according to the sacred scriptures. || 3 ||
The manifestation of the nature of consciousness occurs spontaneously and without prior intention;
when conceptualized as the intellect and so forth, it is like the waves and such arising from the ocean.

From the manifestation of intellect (*buddhi*) up to the attainment of perfection, there is an undertaking that occurs spontaneously and without prior conscious intent (*abuddhipūrva*). However, that undertaking which is conceived after the intellect has attained its realization is "with prior conscious intent" (*buddhipūrva*), beginning with the intellect itself.
In both cases, "the wave and so forth" (*taraṅgādi*) serves as the illustrative example. || 4 ||
In the same way, the mind, intellect, and other faculties proceed from pure consciousness alone,
just as whirlpools, spray, waves, and billows arise from the ocean.
Just as a mere wall is nothing more than the appearance of a painted world, so too consciousness—
whose nature is the mere space of consciousness— is nothing more than a mere manifestation.

That which is perceived is "light" (āloka); just as a world painted in a picture consists of nothing but that [canvas], so too this world, being manifested within consciousness, is "appearance" (ābhāsa) consisting of nothing but that.
Thus, this world is essentially nothing other than the void of consciousness (cidvyoma). 6.
An undertaking that is not preceded by conscious intent, yet possesses a fixed structure, comes to pass within the course of existence;
so too does that which consists of creation arise within consciousness.

Just as in the previously mentioned accounts of trees, oceans, and so forth, even though the commencement of branches, whirlpools, and the like proceeds without prior intelligence, they nevertheless come to possess a uniform configuration through necessity; likewise, the manifestation of the form of creation within consciousness will also possess a uniform configuration. Therefore, [the objection] for that purpose is also not valid.
The meaning is that it depends upon being preceded by intelligence. || 7 ||
Just as another person applies designations such as "cluster" (gulucchaka) to a tree,
so too are names assigned to the flowers and other parts of the tree of consciousness, as well as to the earth and other elements.

However, the earth and so forth— which are like the flowers and fruits of the tree of consciousness— occurring subsequent to the collective intellect (*samaṣṭibuddhi*) and other such factors, should be understood as having names assigned and designated by Hiraṇyagarbha and others, who are essentially the collective intellect of those distinct from pure consciousness. || 8 ||
Just as flowers, leaves, and so forth are not different from the great tree,
even so this world is indeed non-different from the supreme self, the sky of consciousness.
Non-different means undivided. || 9 ||
The other [the individual soul] assumes various designations among the constituent parts of the tree;
though existing within the self of the space of consciousness (cidvyoma) in all things, it appears as if distinct from the selves that are like space. 10.
Becoming like another individual soul (vyaṣṭijīva), He assumes various designations and names for all His sons and other diverse purposes. || 10 ||
The creations are but the sprouts of the tree of consciousness; by virtue of being consciousness itself, they do not exist at all.
It is that very consciousness which appears of its own accord, like a dream, in the form of cause and effect.

Having thus elaborated upon the superimposition (*adhyāropa*) of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), he now begins the refutation (*apavāda*) with the verse beginning "The tree of the mind" (*cittaroh*): "That is indeed the tree of the mind. (11)
If you say, "How is it that this is experienced in vain?", who would deny the creation at the beginning of time, or [the experiences] in dreams and the like? (12)

If creation and so forth do not exist at all, then it follows that consciousness experiences them pointlessly in the other world, the hereafter; but that is not tenable, because it would entail the impossibility of the fruits of performed prescribed and prohibited actions. If you say, "How could this be? and thus object, then [consider] among these well-known experiences in dreams and the like—such as the rope-snake and the mirage—what is the case?

Who indeed would resort to denying [the efficacy of] karma on the grounds of its futility? For even in that case (the dream state), there is no difference in its being the fruit of karma that produces dream-enjoyments.
And if you claim that karma is effective there merely through the manifestation of a semblance of enjoyment, then the same applies to the present case as well; such is the intended meaning. || 12 ||
Just as this conceptualization was fashioned for a tree that possesses form,
so too has this conceptualization been made for consciousness, which is nothing but space.

However, this much is the distinction of consciousness (citi) from all [objects] in the case of superimpositions possessing form (sākāra): that while those superimpositions possessing form occur upon what possesses form, the superimposition of the world occurs upon consciousness which is formless. With this intention, he says: "tarau" (on the tree). || 13 ||
Just as fragrance and so forth exist in a flower, and emptiness and so forth in space;
just as motion and so forth exist in the wind, so do the intellect and its functions exist in the Supreme.

Just as fragrance and other qualities reside in a flower, and emptiness and other qualities in space, and just as movement and other qualities reside in the wind, so too do these creations reside in consciousness. 15.
The created things, such as the earth and so forth, are also [included]. || 15 ||
Just as one perceives the emptiness, movement, and fragrance of space, wind, and flowers,
so too does consciousness experience the creation and maintenance of the world as being empty in nature.

Just as the perception of emptiness in space, the perception of vibration in the wind, and the perception of fragrance in flowers—though experienced—are in their true nature devoid of being separate from them, so too is the existence of creation within consciousness; this is the meaning. || 16 ||
Emptiness is not separate from space, nor is fluidity separate from water;
fragrance is not separate from the flower, nor is motion separate from the wind. (17)
He states that very point clearly with the words beginning "no," etc. (verse 17).
Heat is not separate from fire, nor is coldness separate from snow;
likewise, the world is not separate from the Lord, who is the pure, singular essence of the space of consciousness.

That which is seen in the sky at the very beginning of creation, as well as in the heart through dream—that is without cause; for how indeed could it be anything other than the space of consciousness? 19.
To the question "Why not separate from that?", he says: "At the very beginning of creation. Since it is without cause, therefore it is not separate; this is the meaning.
Without a cause, how could the immutable consciousness (cit) be anything else? Let them say so—this is the sense. The particle *kila* is used here in the sense of an inquiry. || 19 ||
Let the dream itself, which is constantly observed here, be considered as the illustration;
apart from pure consciousness, what essence can be said to exist therein? (20)
This traditional teaching (smṛti), beginning with "this [world] is perceivable through the impressions of the intellect," is not possible;
how then could it speak of that which is the ultimate reality? || 21 ||

But surely, dream is nothing but memory. In other memories, which arise from latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) and are devoid of an external object, the aspect of "that-ness" (*tattā*) appears. However, here [in a dream], due to the defect of sleep, although there is an awakening of the latent impression regarding the aspect of being within the range of "this-ness" (*idantā*), because of the loss of the aspect of "that-ness," "this-ness" appears. Thus, this very thing—the object visible through the latent impression produced by cognition—is one and the same in both cases, and so forth.

But such a doubt is not possible. For if that which is "thatness" (tattva) were to become "thisness" (idantā), how could it be so? Indeed, "thisness" is well-established only in relation to what is immediately present; however, in memory, the object is not proximate and is therefore indeed remote. Thus, the meaning is: "Tell me, how can this be consistent? || 21 ||
If that which was seen there were to exist here at the time of recollection, then it would not have been experienced there; for how could a single thing have a twofold existence?

Now, one might argue: "At the time of dreaming and recollecting, the tiger and so forth seen there in the forest and other places are brought into proximity here in the place of the dream by means of sleep; thus, if 'this-ness' (idantā) were present there [in the dream], then that tiger and so forth would not have been experienced as different from those [tigers] in that forest. If it is argued that "by means of sleep, a single tiger is established in two ways," he says in response: "How indeed? (kaiva) || 22 ||

Therefore, this world appears in consciousness by way of a revolving process, like the "crow and the palm fruit" coincidence; subsequently, this conceptualization of dreams and so forth arises therein.
Therefore, since the experience of dreaming cannot be denied, the illustrative example certainly exists;

thus he concludes that his own statement is established with the words "tasmāt" (therefore). Following the establishment of the experiences of waking and dreaming—"paścāt" means after the accomplishment of the creation that occurs without prior conscious intent—just as waves and so forth [arise].
Subsequently, its arrangement and stability are likewise established by itself.
That which is born is not truly born, for that which is born does so without a cause;
since it is unborn, it is the primordial, and it remains established as such, equal [to itself].
For this reason, there is a word-break as "ajātam" (unborn). || 25 ||
Just as the rays of jewels and other such things arise without prior intention,
so too does the very existence of these perceptions of the world [arise] through its particular arrangement.
The implication is that the very being of Brahman alone manifests through the arrangement and appearance of those who perceive the world. || 26 ||
In whatever manner this world first comes into being,
it subsequently assumes a fixed order within itself, like a whirlpool in the ocean.
In some way or other, solely by the power of an indeterminable illusory cause, [it produces] necessity—that is, reality characterized by the necessity of causal efficiency. (27)
In the sky of consciousness, dream-networks and the worlds of consciousness proceed and cease without cause, even though they are essentially void and empty. (28)
Until finally, after a long time, everything becomes the cause of everything else;
thus, for them, entities such as God and the rest are merely empty in nature. (29)
Regarding the phrase "Īśvara and so forth": the intended meaning is that even the state of being Īśvara (the Lord) possesses a nature that is dependent upon Māyā. || 29 ||
This very emptiness arises, and emptiness alone grows;
indeed, through emptiness itself, it perishes utterly as emptiness. (30)
Empty means non-existent. || 30 ||
That person of base intellect who denies the dream as an illustration—wherein the empty appears as if non-empty—is like a beast that denies its own master. 31.

In this regard, he who denies or repudiates his own experienced dream—which serves as an illustration for the manifestation of even that which is non-existent—is a person of base intellect; being like a shepherd (*meṣapāla*), he [denies] the "kuka" (the act of seizing) by the wolf (*vṛka*)—that is, the seizing performed by the wolf—which he himself directly witnessed from the Great Ram (*mahāmeṣa*), the Lord of Beasts (*paśubhartṛ*).

[The word *kuka* is derived from the root *kuk* in the sense of "seizing" (*ādāne*), with the suffix *ka* used in the sense of the suffix *ghañ*. Thus, it refers to the seizing whose agent is the wolf.
The meaning is that one might even deny that [the self]. || 31 ||
This world appears as if it were real, yet it is merely an illusion, a highly fabricated construct;
for the knower, it is nothing but the wonder of consciousness, while that which is truly real is the uncreated, pure Being.
The meaning is that for the knower, that very thing whose self or essential nature is the wonder of the illusory power (māyā)—which is uncreated and pure existence—is not the world. || 32 ||
This long-standing conceptualization is the delusion of creation and dissolution;
knowledge is the radiance of one's own nature, while ignorance is the unfolding of error.
This realm of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) consists solely of long-standing volitional constructs; it is nothing other than the delusion of creation and dissolution.

It should be understood that the manifestation of its true nature is knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), whereas its expansion in the form of error is ignorance (*ajñāna*). This is the meaning. || 33 ||
The visible world arises instantaneously from Brahman as its self, appearing without cause like a dream arising from deep sleep in the sky; subsequently, it comes under the sway of necessity.

It is observed that the Self, which is Brahman conditioned by *māyā*, suddenly becomes the visible world and arises without any prior cause; just as a dream is seen immediately after deep sleep within the Self, which is devoid of the visible,
so too does it subsequently attain the necessity of causal relations and the determination of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*).
He goes. || 34 ||
Due to its nature as consciousness, the object of perception appears within consciousness like the "crow-and-palm" coincidence;
it exists by itself, established in its own nature, just as whirlpools and the like exist in the ocean.
He says that there is no dependence on a cause for the sudden manifestation of the visible world: "It is like the 'crow-and-palm' [coincidence].
It resides in its own nature, being based solely upon the nature of consciousness. (35)
Such indeed is this element of consciousness, consisting of mere space;
that this body of consciousness shines forth in this manner as the form of the world. (36)
He clarifies the very nature [of this] with the words: "such as this" (īdṛśa). || 36 ||

Thereafter, by that conscious form, designations consisting of the conceptualization of memory and so forth, as well as earth and so forth, and intellect and so forth, were imagined within itself, which is the object of vision.

First, due to the appearance of the form of the visible object prior to any conscious intention, that very Self of Consciousness, having become the visible object, subsequently conceives within itself various designations:

those consisting of the conceptualization of memory and so forth when [the object] appears as "past," and those consisting of the conceptualization of earth and its corresponding perceptions when it appears as "present. And thus, all of this—
The meaning is that, within the undivided appearance at that moment, the distinction between cognition and so forth is merely a conceptual construction. || 37 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
"This being the case, O Blessed One, you have stated that memory arises from the impressions of the intellect;
tell me then, what is attained if there is no memory when one is fully awakened?"

If the world is merely a conceptual construction of distinctions and differences within appearances that exist only for a moment, then it follows that the world—which lasts only for the duration of its appearance—does not exist at all during the time it is not appearing. Consequently, since the world would perish upon the destruction of its appearance in the subsequent moment, this leads to the undesirable consequence of the doctrine of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅgavāda*). Let it be so.
If it is argued that for the knower of Brahman (*brahmavid*), there is likewise no purpose in establishing the permanence of a world that is illusory (*māyāmaya*) by nature, we say:

no; for if that were so, the authority of the Vedas, the scriptures, and so forth would be undermined, as they depend on the rule that memory, recognition, and other such cognitions must have previously experienced objects as their domain.
With the intention that this would result in the root of the doctrine of Brahman being undermined, Rāma raises an objection: "This being the case.

That is to say, if the world exists merely as a temporary mental construction according to the manner you have described, then memory and recognition would arise from the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the previously arisen cognition born of authoritative experience.

If it is not accepted that memory and recognition—which have as their objects things previously experienced—are fully awakened [cognitions], then tell us: how is the rule established and obtained, which is proven by the experience of all cultured people? This is the meaning of the request for an answer. || 38 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Listen, O Rāma, and split this question as a lion splits an elephant;
I shall establish a single non-duality, just as the sun establishes a single light.
Thereupon, the Blessed One Vasiṣṭha, regarding the objection as significant, promises a resolution:
"Listen. I shall resolve this objection—the question—by means of reasoning; I shall split it open. Non-duality, the reality of the Self, exists:
this visible world is the Self of the universe within the hollow of pure consciousness.
Like an uncarved wooden statue remaining within a tree in the forest. || 40 ||

This fault would arise if one were to accept the Buddhist tenet that the world, being previously non-existent, arises simultaneously with its momentary appearance; however, we do not accept it in that way. Rather, the world is of the very nature of the eternal existence of Brahman, and though it is always capable of manifestation, it appears only through an appearance whose essence is eternal consciousness.
Through the wondrous variety of the powers of obscuration, veiling, and projection caused by ignorance, it sometimes appears as if manifested and as if vanished;

as if possessing specific forms such as jars and cloths; as if cut, as if divided, as if produced by causes, as if perceptible, as if one, as if many, as if both different and non-different, and as if momentary.

Because it manifests through various wonders— such as being past, present, or future— which are both determinate and indeterminate, as well as similar and dissimilar, since it is a permanent substrate (*sthāyin*), everything such as memory, recognition, and so forth, is indeed logically consistent therein; with this intention, he begins the resolution with the words "it exists," and so on.
The phrase "dwelling in the forest" is used to indicate infinity. || 40 ||
A carpenter might once extract a carved statue from a tree;
but who can carve such a figure from a single, solid pillar of consciousness? (41)

Just as one would reveal [an image] by removing the fragments of wood that conceal it, who else besides that [Supreme Being] could properly carve out this world-statue from the pillar of consciousness—which is non-dual and devoid of agents such as a creator? The meaning is that, because it is not dependent on any other agent, its manifestation does not occur [in the way one might think], like a wooden statue [carved by a craftsman]. || 41 ||

In a pillar, that [consciousness] becomes manifest through dullness because it is not carved out here; but in consciousness, being internalized, it shines forth sufficiently within itself alone by virtue of its very nature as consciousness.
To the question of how, then, that [object] becomes manifest, he says: "But in consciousness" (citi tu).

When the obscuration of the consciousness that serves as its substrate is removed, by the power of such consciousness alone, it shines forth fully within the Self—that is, within the conscious Self—just as Rāhu appears within the moon; this is the meaning of "becoming manifest. || 42 ||
Though appearing, she is as if her body were not carved out;
she is of the nature of space, never fallen from her own essence, and remains within the self as pure consciousness alone.

If it is asked, "In that case, why does she not appear even during dissolution and deep sleep?", [the author] replies, "But while appearing," [meaning] she indeed appears as the essence of universal existence (*sattāsāmānya*). The word "but" (*tu*) is intended to highlight the distinction from the time of creation. || 43 ||

At the beginning of creation, that [consciousness], possessing the power of ideation, brings about the processes of creation by its very nature as consciousness, just as one experiences what has arisen today within the dream-self in the void of the self.

Even at the beginning of creation, that consciousness (cit), first possessing the previously mentioned state of non-conceptualization, subsequently performs various acts of world-creation through mental constructs arising in accordance with the impelling unseen force (adṛṣṭa).
The connection with the following verse is that it conceives these in the heart, just as one conceives a construction arisen today within a dream. || 44 ||
In the heart, which is indeed space, the statue of consciousness, taking the form of the supreme space, imagines various mental constructs within herself by means of herself.
"This is a fraction of Brahman; this here is indeed the manifestation of pure consciousness (cinmātra).
This is the intellect (citi), this is the individual soul (jīva), and that is the ego (ahaṃkāra). (46)
He elaborates upon how and in what manner He conceives the various distinctions at the beginning of creation through the passage beginning with "This" (*iyam*), and so forth:

"This is a portion (*kalā*) of Brahman, whose nature is universal existence (*sattāsāmānya*), and which serves as the seed of the universe. Within this very portion of Brahman, there is this manifestation of pure consciousness (*cinmātrakalanā*), which is eternally unobscured by nature; it is this consciousness that is the reflection of That. This indeed is...

The individual soul (jīva) is that which is conjoined with the vital breaths (prāṇa) and so forth; this [jīva], however, is primarily characterized by the function of egoistic conceit (abhimāna), whereas the intellect (buddhi) is primarily characterized by the function of determination (adhyavasāya). This and other such points are to be inferred accordingly. || 46 ||
This is intellect, this is mind, this is time, and this is space;
this is that "I," this is action, and this is the pentad of subtle elements.
This collection of the senses is known as the "city of eight" (puryaṣṭaka);
here, this is the subtle body (ativāhika-deha), as well as the physical body (ādhibhautika). || 48 ||
Herein lies this aggregate; this is composed of the fivefold elements.
I am Brahmā, I am Śaṅkara, I am Upendra, and I am Ravi;
this is the external and this is the internal, this is creation, and this is the world.
This entire web of conceptual constructions, beginning with such [distinctions], is nothing but the utterly pure sky of consciousness.
Therefore, where are these multitudes of objects, where is memory, and where is duality or unity? (50)

The meaning of this and all such passages is that the entire web of mental constructs (*kalanājāla*), being utterly pure, is nothing but the sky of consciousness (*cidvyoma*); there is not even an atom’s worth of anything other than that.
Therefore, where can these masses of insentient objects imagined by the ignorant possibly exist? || 50 ||
The fragment of the world's expanse is indeed without cause;
at the beginning of creation, it appears like a dream, as the void itself appearing as if subject to transformation within the void.
Thus, in this manner. || 51 ||
For that which is of the nature of consciousness shines within the space of consciousness, like space within space;
when it is realized by that very [consciousness], where is that world, since it has been dissolved through awakening?
Where is memory, and where is dream? Where are times and what are mental constructions? This manifestation of consciousness shines, peaceful like the void in the sky.
When there is only the single expanse of consciousness (*cidvyoma*), it follows that the various divisions of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) do not exist at all; thus he says: "Where? (*kva*).
Whatever exists within the mass of consciousness has attained the state of being outside;
yet in reality, there is nothing external nor internal, apart from pure Being alone.
That which exists within; the meaning is "that essence which is internal. || 54 ||
How could those who are blind otherwise maintain that an element which arises from that which is devoid of parts, tranquil, and ineffable, could be without a cause? (55)
Those blind speakers [assert] that which has arisen as an effect from no cause; how could that be? And how could that which is immutable be otherwise, subject to modification? (55)
Therefore, as is the supreme Brahman, so is this supreme visible world;
just as the sky of consciousness is in a dream, so too is the city of the dream.

Therefore, having abandoned the nature of insentience and so forth belonging to the world—which is grasped through one's own delusion—one should accept the nature of pure consciousness alone; thus he says: "Therefore," etc. (56).
This visible world does not exist even in the slightest degree;
for where is there dust in the full ocean, and where is there a visible object in the supreme ether? (57)
Even a speck of dust from the waters is but a mere atom.

If this which appears as something whatsoever shines forth, it is merely consciousness (cinmātra), devoid of an object of cognition; though appearing as if manifesting, it is utterly tranquil, established thus within the Self.

For this reason, being devoid of an object of cognition, it does not shine; indeed, even while not illuminating anything else, it remains established as the illumination of its own self alone. || 58 ||
From the Full Brahman, the full is indeed drawn out, yet remains undrawn;
this world shines as the form of light, a manifestation whose essence is the Supreme Self. (59)
To recall the scriptural authority for the stated meaning, he cites the Śruti: "From the Full [comes] this Full. Thus, the Supreme Self alone is that which consists of the Supreme Self. || 59 ||

While I am thus speaking, alas, how great is the inner delusion of people, for even though they experience [the truth], they do not even now suddenly abandon the notion that the world-body is real while awake, despite knowing it to be like a dream. 60.

Having observed through various signs that certain people of dull faculties remain unawakened despite this instruction—which is so extensive and repeated daily—the Blessed One, feeling compassion for them, said:
"In this manner... [referring to] the reality of the Self being experienced by me within myself in such a most vivid way.

Again and again he speaks with great vehemence; even though the delusion within the minds of those who hold office is dull, they still do not abandon the conviction that this world-body—which is like a dream—is a waking reality. "Vata" expresses grief; even though the official knows [the truth], he does not abandon that [conviction] immediately or suddenly. "Nāma" indicates the well-known intensity of his delusion. (60)

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-eighth chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Statues," in the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*, in the section concerning the liberation of the sons of King Ambarīṣa, within the *Mokṣopāya* of the *Vālmīkīya*. 168.
Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-eighth chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Statues," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The One Hundred and Sixty-Ninth Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: For him for whom pleasure does not lead to happiness, and for whom pain does not lead to suffering—
One whose mind is eternally turned inward is said to be liberated. || 1 ||

The characteristics of one whose mind is repeatedly and profoundly at rest, who is liberated while living, and who possesses self-mastery, are now described, as well as his constant state of deep sleep.

If you have characterized the lack of awakening in those of dull faculties by certain signs, then by what signs is the departure of that lack of awakening known? To Rāma and others who desire to know the characteristics of liberation, the venerable Vasiṣṭha speaks of those [signs] beginning with "na sukhāya" (not for pleasure). "Sukham" refers to pleasure and the entire collection of objects that serve as the means to pleasure. "Antarmukhī" (inward-turned)...
One whose mind is attached to the inner self. || 1 ||
He whose wisdom does not flicker, remaining unmoving within the sky of consciousness even amidst spreading enjoyments, is said to be liberated. || 2 ||

It does not quiver, it does not move. "Prajñā" means intelligence (buddhi). The meaning is that just as the intelligence of the ignorant does not move away from its attachment to expanded enjoyments, so too [is this]. || 2 ||
He whose mind is unwavering, resting in the Self which is pure consciousness alone,
and has attained delight in that very state, is called one liberated while living.
He clearly states the meaning of the two verses [beginning with] "In the self that is pure consciousness" (cinmātrātmani) as follows: || 3 ||
He whose mind, having found rest in the Supreme Self, does not turn back to wander again in this visible world, is called one liberated while living.
He explains the meaning of the restrictive particle "eva" in the phrase "tatraiva" by saying: "in the Supreme Self. (4)
Śrī Rāma said: O Sage, I consider that man to be merely inert and devoid of consciousness, for whom pleasure does not lead to happiness and for whom pain does not lead to suffering.

He raises the objection that the definition stated in the first verse is subject to deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of those who are insentient, insane, or unconscious—stating: "Not for the sake of pleasure," etc. (Verse 5).

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: He who, by virtue of being established in the absolute solitude of the sky of consciousness, does not experience pleasure even without effort because his nature is pure awakening— he is called one who has attained rest.

With the intention that no fault exists because the deviation [from the rule] has already been excluded by the very qualification "of one whose mind is turned inward" (*antarmukhamateḥ*), Vasiṣṭha provides the answer, clarifying its purport with the words "the sky of consciousness" (*cidvyoma*).
With the intention that the phrase "not for the sake of pleasure" (*na sukhāya*) should be further qualified by "without effort" (*vinā prayatnena*), he says: "with effort" (*prayatnena*). || 6 ||
He whose doubts regarding all things have indeed been completely exhausted through discernment is at rest in the supreme state.
He states other characteristics with the words beginning "all indeed," etc. Regarding the phrase "in all objects":

the sense is that since all doubts are rooted in ignorance (*ajñāna*), it is logical that all doubts are destroyed by the destruction of their root, which is ignorance. And thus says the Śruti: "The knot of the heart is severed, all doubts are cut asunder, [and karmas] are exhausted."
And his actions [are destroyed] when that which is both high and low has been seen. || 7 ||
He who possesses no aesthetic relish (rasikatā) toward any object whatsoever,
even while engaged in worldly affairs, is said to have attained inner rest (viśrānta).
Sensuality is the state of possessing passion. || 8 ||
He whose every undertaking is free from desire and volition, who dwells in whatever comes to him, is known as one who has attained rest.
He who has attained rest within the Self—by virtue of its being consciousness—amidst the long path of saṃsāra, which is without support and knows no respite, is victorious. (10)
Because it is consciousness, due to the perception of its being pure consciousness alone. || 10 ||
Those who, having run for a long time, have finally attained rest and remain still,
appear as if asleep, even though they are engaged in worldly activity.

Having run for a long time and wandered about, they appear as if asleep in order to dispel the fatigue of running; thus, the sense is that the very absence of running toward sense objects is clearly their defining characteristic. || 11 ||
For they shine with radiance in the sky of the manifestation of consciousness and its objects;
like risen suns, they shine eternally, yet they do not abide anywhere here.

The object and the subject—the perceived and the perceiver—are the appearance of consciousness and the intellect; these shine forth as risen suns of pure consciousness, radiant within the sky of one's own mind, which is the ether devoid of both, in this world of saṃsāra. || 12 ||
Even while engaged in worldly affairs, these superior ones appear as if asleep and as if their faculties were dissolved; though they seem dull, they are not actually dull-witted.
They appear as if wasted away like the Videhas; they are dull and resemble those who are bewildered. 13.
Those who abide in the city of dreams, as if asleep upon their beds here,
are called "asleep," yet they have not fallen into a state of insentience.
He explains the intended meaning of the word "asleep" with the passage beginning "as if asleep," continuing until the end of the chapter. "Inertness" refers to being under the sway of sleep. || 14 ||
He who, having rested from the long journey, does not speak even when addressed, is said to abide in the blissful silence; he is not of dull appearance.
If it is asked, "In what respect, then, is there a similarity with deep sleep? he says, "By means of rest and silence," beginning with the word *dīrgha*.
Having ceased from wandering, he is at rest; being rested and free from fatigue, he does not give—that is, he does not utter—[the teaching] to those whose faces are turned outward. || 15 ||
That which is night for all beings, consisting of the setting of ignorance—in that [state], he is established in equanimity; it is supreme awakening and supreme peace. 16.
That which is night—consisting of the setting of that [sun]—for all beings who, like owls, conduct themselves in the darkness of ignorance, is supreme awakening; it is equal and of one flavor. 16.
In this visible world which brings suffering, wherein all beings remain awake, he remains perpetually asleep; thus, he does not perceive it and is happy.

The explanation of the word "asleep" (supta) is "he does not see that. Thus, the intended meaning is that the Blessed One has shown two characteristics in the verse beginning with "That which is night" (yā niśā) in the Gītā. || 17 ||
O scion of Raghu, he who disregards the flood of karma and abides solely within his own self is called one who delights in the self (ātmārāma); he is not a dullard.
He states that even the renunciation of all actions is its characteristic: "He who... (verse 18).
Having transcended this suffering and reached the further shore of the ocean of existence, that fortunate one remains within himself, experiencing the bliss of rest. (19)
Exhausted on the long journey by the four objects of the senses for a long time,
he is afflicted by the nature of enjoyments and beset on the path by cruel and terrifying calamities.

He elaborates on the meaning of the verse "having run for a long time" with the words beginning "dīrghādhvanī" (on the long road): "By objects that are clever at deception, and by long-lasting, terrifying disturbances of the country, as if by the plundering of the equipment for enjoyment, [the mind] has been aroused and set forth. (20)
Repeatedly frozen by the thunderbolts of the frost of old age,
this deer of human existence wanders in vain agitation through the wilderness of birth.
Rendered inert by the frost-like thunderbolts characterized by old age, he has been made incapable of worldly activity. || 21 ||
The traveler on the path of saṃsāra is encompassed by the Supreme Self amidst the perilous thicket of the thorns of suffering, where the shade of happiness is extremely difficult to attain. (22)
But he himself, alone and without any companion, has wandered forth and set out. || 22 ||
Having made his provisions from evil deeds, he stumbles and is worn out at every step;
rendered helpless by paths consisting of gain and loss, which are fraught with perils. (23)
With wealth acquired through evil deeds and sin, he is diminished at every step; having fallen, he rolls along the ground.
Having reached the further shore of the ocean of saṃsāra, which is devoid of [the notion of] beings, that self-possessed one, free from desire and awakened by supreme knowledge, lies down in bliss.

Thus, though exhausted by fate, this man—having awakened through the attainment of the means, the grace of the true scripture and the true guru, and through the direct realization of reality (tattva-sākṣātkāra)—having reached the further shore of the ocean of saṃsāra, that self-possessed one sleeps happily, being "without a bed" (aśayya), meaning even though he is without a physical bed. This is the syntactical connection for all [the verses]. || 24 ||
Having cast off wandering, being without dreaming or deep sleep, awakened yet not externally asleep—alas, the self-possessed one sleeps happily! (25)

"Creeping things" (*sarpāṇi*) refers to houses, inner rooms, palaces, couches, and so forth, because those who seek rest crawl upon them and creep away from them. "Free from those" means being such that these are absent; "devoid of movement" means being such that activities such as breathing have ceased;
and "awake" means being such that there is alertness within the true nature of the Self.
And he sleeps in such a way that he is devoid of any other entity called "sleep" that exists outside his own essential nature; "hā" expresses wonder.
Like a noble horse, though born here as a mere beast, moving, breathing, and speaking, alas, the self-possessed one lies happily in the midst of the world, as if in a great forest.
For it is a worldly proverb that a noble horse, while eating, walking, standing, and sleeping, remains awake only in battle; thus, there is the expression "like a noble horse. || 26 ||

For those who perceive reality, there is a certain profound sleep, utterly unprecedented, which is not disturbed by the roars of clouds at the end of an aeon nor by the laceration of their own limbs. (27)
"Unprecedented" means extraordinary; the proof for this is as follows. || 27 ||
That profound sleep of the perceivers of reality is truly unique;
for even though they are awakened, it causes their eyes to close.
The meaning is that she causes even the vision of the awakened ones—who perceive pure consciousness—to slumber;
