or rather, she causes the vision of the external senses—the perception of forms and so forth—to slumber, that is, she conceals it, even for those who are awakened in worldly affairs. || 28 ||
He whose entire universe dissolves while his eyes remain unblinking is truly intoxicated in the ultimate sense; alas, that self-possessed one sleeps in bliss! 29.
In the ultimate sense, he is intoxicated, yet not intoxicated by liquor. || 29 ||
Having swallowed the entire universe and attained supreme fullness,
he who possesses the Self sleeps happily, having drunk nectar to his heart's content.
Amṛta is the essence of unconditioned bliss. || 30 ||
Free from worldly joy yet possessing great bliss, experiencing unchanging and undecaying happiness;
free from light yet possessing great illumination—alas, the self-possessed one sleeps in peace! 31.
He is one for whom there is a great light, an illumination, within his own self, which is devoid of external light yet appears as another light. || 31 ||
With the cessation of the darkness of greed, having transcended attachment to the world, and possessing a fullness that is not material density—alas, the self-possessed one sleeps in happiness! (32)
In its state of density (*aghanatva*), it is that whose fullness (*ābhoga*) and relish (*āsvāda*) consist of the essence of formless bliss (*amūrtānandarasaghana*). || 32 ||
While the world remains in a state of unpeaceful and endless suffering that is never stilled, alas,
the self-possessed man sleeps happily, his enjoyment turned inward.

"Enduring suffering" means experiencing pain; "peaceful" and "ceased" refer to that [suffering] having subsided. "In the state of people" refers to the conduct appropriate to the social classes (*varṇa*) and stages of life (*āśrama*), which he maintains for the sake of sustaining the world (*lokasaṃgraha*). "Not outward-turned" means unattached to external objects; it is one who enjoys internal bliss. All these are adverbs. || 33 ||
Making himself the smallest of the small and the largest of the large, having made the sky his bed, alas, the self-possessed one sleeps in happiness. (34)
Having made his bed even in the sky, that is, in the firmament itself, in such a manner... [34]
Within every single atom, even hundreds of millions of worlds are contained;
alas, the self-possessed one rests happily within that body which holds both the minute and the massive.
Due to its subtlety, it resides in the atom, and due to its omnipresence, in the gross body of consciousness; holding and supporting infinite millions of worlds within every single atom. || 35 ||
Whether performing the floods of dissolution and creation or not performing them in any way at all, alas,
the self-possessed one rests happily upon the bed of supreme light.

Having fully understood the dream of the accumulation of saṃsāra as a state of deep sleep, and leading [his vision] toward the vast expanse of the manifest directions, alas, the self-possessed one sleeps happily! 37.
The directions were made manifest by the full radiance, meaning they became long and, as it were, limitless. || 37 ||
Having attained the state of universal existence common to all objects in the world,
he who is more pervasive than space, the self-possessed one, now lies happily.

Because it follows through everywhere in the form of existence (*sadrūpa*), it possesses the nature of the universal "Being" (*sattāsāmānya*). Regarding the phrase "from space": the intention is that [the Self] is greater than space, according to the Vedic scripture, "Greater than space. || 38 ||
Having made the sky perfectly clear and having turned the world itself into a void, he who possesses the Self sleeps happily—alas!—with all sound and breath stilled. (39)

First, by means of dissolution, having rendered the world into the sky—that is, having brought it to the state of space—and having made the sky of consciousness (cidambara) even clearer than the unmanifested (avyākṛta) space that covers all; [he performed] that action in which both sound and the supreme exhalation (praśvāsa) were stilled. The "sky" (ambara) is like a covering cloth, clear and transparent.
Having made the entire world into a garment and a cloak, and having covered it all, he sleeps with his breathing and the sound of snoring stilled; such is the plain meaning. || 39 ||
Beholding this world of ours within a mere corner of space, alas,
the self-possessed one— whose nature is the treasury of the clear sky— lies happily.
Seeing this world as a dream, like a mere appearance within a dream, in a corner of that space of consciousness which is himself, the innermost self; || 40 ||
Just as one who has rested upon a bed of grass in a place delightful with the flow of worldly activity—alas, such a self-possessed man sleeps in happiness! (41)

In the definition of conventional usage (*vyavahāra-lakṣaṇa*), from "delightful" (*manorame*) up to "rested upon a mat" (*kaṭe viśrāntaḥ*)—referring to a heap of grass (*tṛṇyā*) as a mat (*kaṭa*) for spreading—that entire sequence constitutes a single compound word. || 41 ||
Through supreme personal effort characterized by thorough knowledge,
one perceives the living being as if by a dream-vision— like the sky within the sky by means of the sky itself.

Just as for one who is awake, a dream experienced during sleep acquires a nature suitable for recollection through supreme effort and subsequent investigation, so too, by some means through supreme effort— namely, the effort of oneself and others— the mind is turned slightly outward, and through the thorough understanding of external activity, [recollection arises] at first sight.

The meaning is as follows: by means of a body and so forth that possess their own specific nature (*svarūpa*), the living being (*jīva*) exists; just as space (*kha*), which is unable to remain in a place without room, finds its scope and attains existence within space—its own essential nature—as if it were a second space imagined through that very nature, so it is here. || 42 ||
Through wisdom that is like space, having realized all phenomena as being similar to the sky,
the Knower, by means of diligent effort, has attained the state of the supreme ether.

By means of the knowledge of one's own true nature, which is like space, he who has perfectly awakened (*saṃbuddha*)—having fully realized through effort—that the phenomena characterized as the individual soul and the world are utterly non-existent and comparable to the sky, by means of the state of being a knower produced through exertion; for the suffix *kta* is used here in the sense of the agent in the roots *man* and *budh*. (43)
Awakened while asleep, and even asleep while awakened, he rejoices incessantly;
having become as if in deep sleep, he then awakens along with his friend, the object of his dream.

Having thus described the sleep of the one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*) with respect to the domain of ignorance, he speaks of his perpetual awakening in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*): "The awakened one is asleep. One who knows reality (*tattvavid*), though always asleep in this manner, is both awake and asleep according to worldly convention regarding the well-known states of waking and sleeping; yet, even while experiencing the objects of the waking and dreaming states, he remains as such.
He sports incessantly with a friend who will be described as his companion; therefore, the meaning is that while he is in deep sleep, he is indeed in deep sleep together with him. || 44 ||

Having spent all his days with that ancient friend—whose affection is sweet with a variegated persistence born of the long-term desire to dwell together through many lifetimes—he shall attain rest for a long time in the supreme state. (45)

Having sported with that friend for as long as the experience of *prārabdha* karma lasted, [the author] speaks of his liberation without a body (*videhamukti*) at its conclusion, beginning with the words "in other births" (*janmāntare*). That one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*), having abandoned all sense of personal distinction with an even-mindedness— as if due to the excess of affection resulting from long cohabitation— [remains] as one throughout other births.

With an even mind, and thus through various manifestations of tranquility, self-restraint, endurance, knowledge, dispassion, contentment, and so forth— sweet and ancient as a friend to be described hereafter— he should spend all the remaining days of his life together with that [friend].
Having been led by the rapture to be described hereafter to the supreme, unsurpassed bliss—the state of disembodied liberation (videhakaivalya)—he will find rest;
that is, he will attain it. || 45 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Rested Mind," in the *Ārṣa* Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa of Valmīki, in the section concerning the liberation of the mind, within the ultimate instruction on the nature of reality.
Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Tranquil Mind," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and seventieth canto.
Śrī Rāma said: "O Brahmā, tell me who his friend is, with whom he takes delight?"
What would the nature of pleasure be? Is it of the same essence as passion, or is it something else? (1)
Accompanied by friends, his own kinsmen, sons, wives, and servants,
his virtues are described therein, as well as his delightful and bliss-inducing dalliance.

Is this delight of the one liberated while living (jīvanmukta) with that friend his very nature, or the abiding in the essential form of his own self, or rather "rati"— meaning a joy characterized by the inclination toward sporting in delightful places of enjoyment? || 1 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: His own natural flow is indeed his well-wisher; his own inclination is his well-wisher; and his own past actions are his one uncontrived friend.

Innate action is that which is performed spontaneously as part of one's natural flow; prescribed action is that which is performed for the sake of maintaining the world order; and action practiced through personal effort is that which is cultivated through one’s own exertion, consisting of the study and reflection on the sacred scriptures, the company of the virtuous, tranquility, self-restraint, forbearance, withdrawal from sense objects, purity, contentment, and devotion to the Lord.
It is designated by three names according to the distinction of its limiting adjuncts (upādhi); for this very reason, there is the statement that "friendship is one."
It provides consolation like that of a father, restraint like that of a wife,
and is ever-faithful during calamities that are difficult to endure.
He describes the virtues of that friend with the words "like a father" and so forth: "In matters of what ought not to be done, there is a restraint born of shame that is unfailing. (3)
He who acts without causing apprehension, who brings about perfect peace, and who bestows the nectar of winning over others by remaining unprovoked even in the face of anger. (4)
By whom the nectar characterized by conciliation, which bestows attraction and brings about composure, was bestowed. || 4 ||
Dedicated to the removal of faults that are difficult to cross, difficult to traverse, and difficult to restrain,
it is a treasury of all the jewels of trust, inhabited since childhood.

Thus, while [the world] was prone to sinking into difficult places, impassable paths, and faults such as irresistible enmity and strife, [He] remained intent on its upliftment; for, due to the continuity of practice through many lifetimes, He had dwelt [therein] since childhood. (5)
Having been together since childhood, playing in the dust, he was a companion from his very youth; his wicked impulses were restrained, and he was intent on protecting him like a father.
Intending exactly that, he says, beginning with "saha" (together), etc. || 6 ||
Like heat is to fire, like fragrance is to a flower, and like the day is to the sun, pure [conduct] is eternally inseparable [from it]. (7)
Always delighting solely in nurturing, solely devoted to protecting, and ever intent on guarding against the onset of every calamity. || 8 ||
Like fire for gold, this [treatise] bestows purity upon the body in all its states;
it is solely intent on revealing what is to be abandoned and what is to be accepted.

Even for one in every state—meaning even for one in an impure state due to touching or eating impure things and so forth—in the act of seeing, that [perception] follows immediately upon the discernment and demonstration [of the object]. || 9 ||
Like a city [delighting its citizens] with blameless stories,
it was a temple containing a multitude of vessels made of the jewels and rubies of virtuous conduct.

"Nāgara" means one born in the city, that is to say, one who is clever. "Sacceṣṭāḥ" refers to auspicious activities of speech, mind, and body; the treasury house is the repository for the collection of vessels made of gems and rubies characterized by those [activities]. || 10 ||
Just as the sun constantly reveals what is unpleasant, like darkness,
she revealed only what was dear, like a devoted great lady.
"Not displaying" means casting [it] away from afar; "mahelā" means like a woman. || 11 ||
He made the people speak kindly by acting only in a pleasing manner; he was graceful, sweet, affectionate, unperturbed, and possessed a joyful disposition.
One whose intention has arisen should be vigilant.
He who brings benefit to the world, who is worthy of worship, who speaks with a smile, whose desires are stilled, whose nature is virtuous, and who is the sole cause of the ultimate truth. (13)
He was a benefactor and a servant to the world’s virtuous people; because he was tranquil regarding sensual desires, his form was like that of the truly good—thus he was "Sad-rūpa" (of noble form).
In that battle born of ignorance, he was previously intent on striking;
his locks of hair were like playful women engaged in the sport of creating unprecedented wonders.

In a battle that arose by chance against ignorant people— where he was previously intent on striking and possessed of supreme heroism— he was, through his unprecedented and world-transcending playful compositions such as jests, laughter, and curiosities, as well as through his graceful dalliances with women, a caresser who brought delight. 14.
He is the protector of those whose essence is virtue, of their wives, and of their lineage;
he is the nectar-like medicine for a mind overwhelmed by mental and physical afflictions. 15.
It is like nectar for reviving life and like medicine for removing disease. || 15 ||
A source of diversion through discourse that was distinguished by specialized knowledge and eloquence, it stood as if divided into two parts because of their shared lineage and character. (16)

Especially through his learning, cleverness, scholarship, and debates, he provided entertainment that aroused wonder for his venerable and eminent masters, teachers, honored elders, and others; at times, due to their shared family and character, it was as if they were divided into two distinct parts. (16)
He always caused devoted kings, virtuous men,
and generous donors to perform sacrifices, acts of charity, austerities, pilgrimages, and to be intent upon the pursuit of justice and wealth.

"Having made the king and others devoted, liberal, and exuberant in giving"—the word "always" (sadā) is connected to both [parts of the sentence] according to the maxim of the 'lamp on the threshold' (dehalī-dīpaka). 17.
Together with his sons, wife, twice-born men, women, servants, and kinsmen, he enjoyed auspicious food and drink and the most excellent and praiseworthy company. (18)
By whom association with the most excellent, praiseworthy, and great [is sought]. || 18 ||
It wards off the state of being bound by craving for enjoyments and the like, which brings suffering;
it is noble, filled with affectionate conversation, and the supreme refuge for consolation. (19)
Endowed with such a friend in himself and united with his wife,
he rejoices through the name of his own karma, impelled by his very nature.
By its own nature, through its innate functioning alone; the meaning is that it is not impelled or prompted by anything else. || 20 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
O Lord of Sages, what is the wife of this friend, and what is her form? Tell me that briefly. (21)

"Kalatra" refers to the group of dependents, such as wife, sons, and so forth. The meaning is: what is the wife of that friend who is accompanied by them—that is, his own—and what is her form, and of what kind of qualities is she possessed? || 21 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
O high-minded one, his sons are named Snāna, Dāna, Tapas, and Dhyāna; they are great-souled beings who are devoted to all the subjects.
Therein, first he spoke to his sons, beginning with "snāna": those whose entire subjects are completely devoted to them because of their virtues. || 22 ||
Like a crescent moon, she brings delight to the eyes of the world;
she is his inseparable wife, joyful and full of affection for him.
He describes his wife along with her virtues: "Like a digit of the moon," and so forth; she is *muditā*, ever-contented. || 23 ||
Her companion, who is never-failing, is filled with the wealth of compassion, captivating to the heart, and a producer of bliss for him. (24)
Compassion is pity; because of that, she by whom wealth is scattered, dispersed, and strewn all around. || 24 ||
Equanimity is considered his constant beloved dwelling in his heart; she stands before him as a female doorkeeper, bowing low and bestowing happiness upon his face. (25)
The beloved wife named Samatā was dear to his heart; the female gatekeeper was the door-warden. || 25 ||
O virtuous one, that intellect which is always fixed upon fortitude and righteousness runs ahead of this wise, preeminent, and fortunate man.
That intellect which is directed toward the objects of fortitude and righteousness is [the intellect]. || 26 ||
This bow, ever present upon the shoulder of that one of great majesty, is like a friend bestowing counsel for the king’s victory over the enemies that are the sense-objects. (27)
This king has another wife named Maitrī, who bestows counsel regarding the conquest of the enemies that are the sense-objects; she is always equally and firmly attached to his shoulder. 27.
The noble boundary of all duties is the teacher that possesses wisdom;
for this venerable one, truthfulness is the bestower of his own true purpose. (28)
Regarding the matters of noble conduct and duty, his teacher is his instructor; regarding truth that bestows one's own welfare, his treasurer is his overseer. (28)
Thus, with such a retinue, friend, and counselor,
conducting himself according to his own duty, he neither rejoices nor becomes angry.

One who possesses such a retinue and circle of dependents, acting everywhere through his own work with such a minister and friend, is liberated while living; he neither rejoices in gain nor is angered by loss. || 29 ||
That sage remains exactly as he is, with a mind extinguished like a lamp,
appearing as if fixed in a painting even while constantly engaged in worldly affairs.
Like a warrior depicted in a painting, even while engaged in activities such as combat, he remains exactly as he is. || 30 ||
In debates devoid of substance, he was like one made of stone, mute; regarding words that served no purpose, he had reached a state of supreme deafness. (31)
He was like a mountain, having the form of a stone statue. || 31 ||
Regarding all rites that contradict worldly custom,
as well as those concerning the conduct and deliberations of the noble, Vāsuki or Bṛhaspati is the authority.
A corpse is one who is like the dead. || 32 ||
Engaged in meritorious discourse, he was eloquent in countering the crooked;
in a mere moment, he could determine the truth and swiftly speak of many matters.

He is one who possesses eloquence regarding the crookedness and other defects of himself and others; he is a speaker who, having reached a definitive conclusion, explains even a subject that is difficult to grasp or a point of doubt. (33)
He was even-sighted, noble-minded, generous, and sharing;
he was gentle, affectionate, sweet, handsome, and one whose fame was meritorious.
This indeed would be the nature of those with awakened intellects, yet they do not become such through effort;
for the moon, the sun, fire, and so forth, are never illuminated by the instigation of another. (35)
This collection of qualities described belongs to those of awakened intellect as their very nature (*svabhāva*).

Such persons do not become possessed of such qualities through effort; rather, just as the moon, sun, fire, and so forth shine by their own nature and not through the instigation of another, they are likewise [self-luminous]. This is the meaning. || 335 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and seventieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Conduct of Those Who Know Reality," in the *Śrī Vālmīki Mahārāmāyaṇa*, composed by the Sage, in the Bālakāṇḍa, in the section concerning the *Mokṣopāya*, in the *Nirvāṇopadeśa*. 170.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventieth chapter, titled "Description of the Conduct of the Knower of Reality," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and seventy-first chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
This world shines as the manifestation of the space of consciousness.
In reality, there is neither the world, nor non-existence, nor emptiness, nor even consciousness. || 1 ||
For the sake of establishing liberation while living and for the pacification of all doubts,
the cleansing of the visible world is performed once again through the instruction on the ultimate reality.
In reality, however, there is neither the world nor the appearance of the world, nor is there appearance itself, nor is there emptiness, nor even the consciousness of mental modifications. || 1 ||

That which shines as the sky of consciousness called the "world" is not distinct from that [consciousness]; it does not exist as something other than it, just as emptiness is not other than space, nor is anything else established as separate.
From the perspective of the ignorant, although it appears as something else, it is not other than that space of consciousness;
just as emptiness is not other than space, so it is in this case.
In the interval between the departure from one place and the arrival at another, that which is the form of consciousness appears as this visible world; no other visible world exists. (3)

And thus, consciousness itself is indeed objectless; the meaning is that it appears as the "visible" (dṛśya) precisely when it is well-known to exist in the interval between the attainment of one object and another. || 3 ||
Indeed, when the great dissolution has occurred, how can there be a primary creation again from a supreme cause, given the absence of any cause for the manifestation of the visible world? (4)

"In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone. "When there was darkness, there was neither day nor night, neither existent nor non-existent; Śiva alone was the absolute. From such scriptural passages, we hear that after the occurrence of the Great Dissolution (mahāpralaya), characterized by the remaining of pure Being (sanmātra), the initial creation takes place once again. In that context, because of the restrictive emphasis in the phrase "Being alone" (*sadeva*), [there is nothing] other than the supreme, which is devoid of modification.
In the absence of a cause, how could this visible world possibly come into being? || 4 ||
For then not even an atom of the seed of the visible world exists,
since this wheel proceeds once again in a formal, embodied state.
In that regard, he states "tadā" (then), because there is no room for the postulation of other causes such as atoms due to contradiction with scripture;
[the world] would proceed, or rather, it proceeds. || 5 ||
Therefore, this visible world is not at all produced as something material;
like the son of a barren woman, it does not exist at all, and thus the cognition of the visible is likewise non-existent.
To this he replies: "It is indeed produced. The meaning is that the purport of the scriptures concerning creation lies precisely in establishing non-origination. || 6 ||
Whatever appears here as the visible object standing all around,
the wise know that to be pure consciousness alone, like the clear sky, the supreme state itself.

Regarding the question of what becomes of the appearance of the visible world when [the Self is realized], he says: "And that which... The word *viduḥ* means those who know the purport of the Śruti. || 7 ||
Just as one who goes from deep sleep to dreaming enters a state of instability, yet does not abandon its own pure,
stainless, and healthy nature— which is mere consciousness— so too [is the case here].

He states that the manifestation of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) in the form of the visible world is well-known upon passing from deep sleep to the dream state, using the word "just as" (*yathā*). || 8 ||
In the beginning of creation, in this very same way, the Self alone, by itself, within itself—
being of the nature of space and appearing as consciousness— manifests as the visible world.
He states that the transition from dissolution to creation should be understood in the same way as the transition from deep sleep to dreaming: "Of creation... (verse 9).

"Just as the mind appears in the form of a city, sluggish with its own volitions, so too at the beginning of creation, the supreme sky of consciousness appears as if it were the visible world. (verse 10)
Just as movement exists within the wind and strives like the circling of a whirlpool, so too,
at the beginning of creation, the sky of consciousness remains, abiding as the very appearance of the visible world.

Just as a dark whirlwind, being in motion, stirs within itself like a vortex or a gale, so too the sky of consciousness, when unperceived, remains within itself as the very object of perception. || 11 ||
Therefore, it is known that the visible triple world is indeed non-manifest;
this supreme Brahman alone shines, established thus within its own self. (12)
Therefore, if the visible triple world is known [as it truly is], it does not appear at all; rather, only the Supreme Brahman shines forth. || 12 ||
There is never anything whatsoever, such as the earth or other elements, that possesses form;
whether it be formal or formless, this is Brahman alone that shines forth.
The essential meaning is this: whether viewed by the ignorant or by the wise, whether manifest or unmanifest, it is Brahman alone that shines forth in such a manner. || 13 ||
Just as at the time of awakening, the mountain of dreams is nothing but formless space,
so too, upon awakening, these three worlds are but the void of peaceful pure consciousness.
Awakening means waking at that time; "in awakening" means in the awakening of the Self. || 14 ||
To the awakened, this world is the supreme Brahman, undifferentiated;
yet even the wise do not know that which is this state of non-awakening.
Even though the wise reflect upon it, we do not know what this "non-awakening" is like. || 15 ||
That form of consciousness which exists in the interval when one has gone from one place to another is indeed the true nature of all beings; that state is the Supreme Self.
He states that for all beings, the very nature of one's own self is nothing but consciousness devoid of objects, beginning with the words "deśāt" (from space). || 16 ||
That form of consciousness which exists in the interval when one has gone from one place to another—that is the supreme space (*paramākāśa*); in this, everything is established. (17)
Regarding this: the meaning is that even the substratum of all is consciousness alone, devoid of objects. || 17 ||
As is that state, so is this [world], consisting of both the existent and the non-existent, wherein nothing whatsoever exists apart from the five categories of objects. (18)

He states that this superimposition (adhyāsa) conforms to its substratum (adhiṣṭhāna) with the words "of such a kind" (yādṛg). To which aspect there is similarity, he explains with the words "by which" (yena): by which reason nothing other than the fivefold objects—the five elements—exists;
thus, the meaning is that its similarity to Brahman consists precisely in its being devoid of any effects distinct from itself. || 18 ||
The wise know that form, light, and mental attention are this very state;
these are the whirlpools of fluidity within this great water of the state. 19.

The manifestations of objects produced by the external senses, such as forms and light, as well as mental attention directed toward internal mental cognitions—all these are indeed this very state. || 19 ||
In the movement from one place to another, that which is the form of consciousness in the interval—apart from this, there is no such thing as the world at all. (20)
And thus, it is well known that there is no state of being a world apart from objectless pure consciousness; so he says: "From space," etc.
"The state of being a world" means the condition of being the world. || 20 ||
States such as passion and hatred, as well as views regarding existence and non-existence—without relinquishing this very form, they remain as its constituent parts. (21)
This form is the form of existence and the form of manifestation. || 21 ||
Having abandoned the prior and posterior limits, that which is the form of consciousness in the middle is to be known as the supreme nature, designated within the ocean of the world.

In the perception of the moon reflected in a branch, the branch is the prior limit and the moon is the subsequent limit; having set those aside, that well-known objectless form of consciousness which exists in the middle is its true nature.
That very nature is designated as the substratum for the world, which is like the water in a mirage in the desert—this is the meaning. || 22 ||
Know that the intermediate consciousness occurring when one has gone from one place to another is the other name for the world, belonging to the Self which never falls away from its own true nature.

Intending precisely this, I have repeatedly proclaimed—in the verse beginning with "from place to another place"—the universally recognized fact that immediate consciousness is objectless and all-pervading;
with this intention, he says: "From place... [and so on]. Because of its immutability (*kūṭasthatva*), the Self does not deviate from its own nature.
That very form of consciousness which exists in the state of deep sleep midway between reaching the place of dreaming from the place of waking;
that form of consciousness which exists during the dissolution (pralaya) midway between reaching a new creation from the place of the previous creation;
and that form of consciousness which exists in the state of fainting midway between reaching the place of the next world from the place of this world.
In that very same way, it exists eternally; the meaning is that "the world" is merely another name imagined by the ignorant for that very [reality]. || 23 ||
From the very beginning of creation, the visible world has never actually arisen for us;
that which is said to exist here is merely the deceptive display of illusion.

This being so, he states the conclusion that follows: "From the first creation," etc. The intended meaning is that the conclusion reached is that this world, characterized by illusion (māyā), is merely the display of a magician (śambara) who is like Indra’s conjurer. || 24 ||
Alas, that which is visible does not exist at all, yet it remains established as if it did;
and that supreme Brahman which truly exists, alas, remains established as if it did not exist. (25)

And thus, due solely to the misfortune of the deluded, this error of inversion has arisen—like the delusion that there is no gem but only glass. He says "Alas! (kaṣṭam) to express this; the word *kaṣṭa* is used here in the sense of lamentation. || 25 ||
Where shall I go, for this world has become perverted? That which is unreal is called real, and thus Brahman itself is not understood. (26)
"But I—where shall I go, where shall I find this world which is non-Vedic (*abrahmaṇya*), devoid of the nature of Brahman (*brahmabhāva*), and contrary [to it]?
By the deluded, that which is unreal is called 'real'; yet even by them, Brahman alone is thus reached as a name, not the visible [world].
The meaning is that it is impossible to go to what is unreal. || 26 ||
Nothing whatsoever that is visible has ever arisen, nor does it appear anywhere;
that which appears here is Brahman alone, shining by itself like the sky.
Just as a gem shines by its own radiance which is not distinct from itself,
so too is the sky of consciousness illumined by a creation that is non-different from itself. (28)
The explanation of the term "non-distinct" (*avyatirikta*) with respect to the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*) is "not other than its own self" (*svātmano 'nanyayā*). || 28 ||
Within that very same peaceful state, this sun shines;
it is indeed a part of that [state], for there is no other sun by name. (29)

If it is asked, "How is this to be understood? [the author] says, beginning with "In that very... (tasminneva), etc., because the world, such as the sun and so forth, is experienced as having the nature of existence (*sadrūpa*) precisely by virtue of being for the most part a portion of the universal of existence (*satsāmānya*). || 29 ||
Even though situated there, neither the sun nor the moon shines;
rather, this Lord illuminates the sun, but the sun does not illuminate that Lord.

Just as the sun and other luminaries depend on that [Brahman] for their illumination, Brahman does not depend on the sun and others for its own illumination; thus he says: "Even though situated... It "shines," meaning it illuminates. And so says the Śruti: "The sun does not shine there, nor the moon and the stars, nor do these lightnings shine, much less this fire. Everything shines only after Him who shines; by His light all this is illumined."
It shines forth. || 30 ||
By its radiance this entire visible sphere shines;
it is the illuminator of all things, including the moon, the sun, and fire. (31)
The conceptualization of the meaning of words as being "with form" or "without form" is, for those who know the truth, non-existent in nature like a flower in the sky; it does not occur.
Because the objects do not exist, [the cognition] is of a non-existent nature. || 32 ||
Just as a single atom, together with its constituent parts, shines within the light of the sun of the individual soul (jīva),
so too do the suns and other luminaries neither shine nor appear there at all.

Just as a single minute particle shines within the mass of light of the sun when one observes the world as its living soul, so too do these suns and others shine—or rather, they do not shine—within Brahman, which is the undivided radiance of consciousness; this is said with a sense of disregard for their apparent existence. || 33 ||
Tell me, how could those manifestations—the sun and the rest—be distinct from that jewel of the space of pure consciousness? (34)
For that reflection is not distinct from the jewel. // 34 //
That state is devoid even of pure consciousness, yet free from emptiness;
it is empty of all selves, yet endowed with all objects.
Since there is no object to be excluded if "non-acid" were not established, it would also be devoid of pure consciousness alone. (35)
Even the earth and other elements do not exist there; nothing whatsoever exists there.
Furthermore, no living beings exist there, even those who are alive.
Not abandoning the grossness of duality, these are atoms therein;
yet, not abandoning its own nature, there is no duality or unity whatsoever here.

Without abandoning their grossness as resulting from the combination of two parts, these [entities] such as the sun are, within that consciousness-light (citprakāśa), supreme, partless atoms (paramāṇu). Their own nature is existence (sattā). || 37 ||
"Something here is indeed nothing; it is neither something nor nothing.
The conceptualization that 'it is neither something nor nothing' is far removed from this. (38)

"Something" (kiñcit): the sense is that if mere worldly convention (*vyavahāra*) were negated, then both contradiction (*virodha*) and non-contradiction (*avirodha*) would likewise be negated therein. || 38 ||
The very existence of the sky of pure consciousness—unitary, uninterrupted, infinite, and eternally expanded by its own nature—abides within itself under the name of the world. (39)
For one who has abandoned one object of consciousness and has not yet attained another,
that which is the nature of consciousness is the very nature of this world, even though it appears as manifold.
He describes the meaning of the verse beginning with "from place to another place" as being established therein by means of the word "one": "ekam" || 40 ||
This manifold world is indeed not manifold; it is the expanse of consciousness alone, spread out in the form of the five elements, existing like consciousness in a dream. (41)
The city is like the consciousness of a living being; and thus is the aphorism of the venerable Bādarāyaṇa: "And so it is in the Self, for [the powers] are manifold. (41)
Just as consciousness, while remaining in the state of deep sleep, enters into a dream,
so too does it attain this state of creation while remaining exactly as it was.

And thus, he says—in the verse beginning with "suṣuptāt"—that just as from deep sleep one perceives a dream, so too from dissolution (pralaya) consciousness alone appears in the form of creation. || 42 ||
Just as deep sleep is, so too is dreaming, and likewise waking; and the fourth state is exactly like this. Therefore, the world is equal to the infinite void.
He clarifies that very point with the verse beginning "yādṛg" (of whatever kind). || 43 ||
Waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the fourth state—all these exist as that alone.
I do not know that which the knower of reality perceives, for the fool is rooted in the notion of "I."
The lineage of the knowers of reality is the tradition of the knowledge of Brahman; however, regarding that subject, I do not know what an ignorant commoner knows. || 44 ||
He who is the incessant and imperceptible transformation of all objects, both insentient and sentient, yet remains internal and devoid of mind, intellect, and the like; || 45 ||

Abiding within both insentient worlds and sentient living beings as their inner controller (*antaryāmin*), He transforms the world in such a way that He Himself remains imperceptible; thus, the Lord is the one whose transformation is imperceptible. He alone is the ultimate reality of the purified individual consciousness (*jīvaciti*). Since all objects of the world are composed of Him, He Himself appears in the form of the world.
The meaning of the two [verses] is that "it is established" is the essential conclusion. || 45 ||
The form of the perfectly pure consciousness is the objects of experience, and they are composed of that [consciousness];
they do not exist as having a real nature, for it is that [consciousness] alone which exists in such a state.

Therefore, O sinless one, for those who perceive the meaning of words such as "transformation" (pariṇāma) and so forth, not even a trace of this [teaching] exists here among the utterances intended for instruction. (47)

Now, if objects such as earth and the rest are indeed of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*) and do not exist apart from consciousness, then how can there be the agency of transforming them by way of being their inner ruler (*antaryāmin*)? To this he says: "Because of transformation, etc.
This means that for the sake of instruction, there is no contradiction in the statements of those who proceed by accepting worldly transformation, even though it is [ultimately] unreal.
The meaning is that, from the perspective of ultimate reality, it is intent upon transformation. || 47 ||
From the very beginning of creation, within the Self by means of the Self, there exists the one Great Soul—the supreme space of pure consciousness. || 48 ||

Where, then, lies the intended meaning? He states it: "From the first creation," etc. The proof for this is the experience—the direct realization—of the Great-Souled One, the knower of reality, within the perfectly full single Self; this connects with what follows. (48)
In the perfectly full, singular Self, that consciousness which is all-pervasive is manifest; by means of that [consciousness], designations such as "the world" are made within the Self itself. (49)
These designations were made for the sake of those who lack knowledge. || 49 ||
Just as when a dream is fully understood, pleasure becomes true pleasure through its acceptance, and pain becomes true pain in an instant through its non-acceptance. (50)
And thus, upon awakening, whatever Self remains as the sole reality, by accepting that, all the various wonders of the world that were previously experienced become nothing but happiness.
But in the absence of awakening, when that [Self] is not accepted, everything that is experienced— birth, death, old age, disease, and so forth— is accompanied by suffering.
"All that becomes nothing but suffering, like awakening from a dream or not awakening," he says: "When fully understood" (verse 50).
Whether walking or standing, waking or likewise sleeping,
for one who knows that and is peaceful, there exists a constant, singular state of meditative absorption.
For this very reason, because those who know that [reality] are free from suffering and distraction, they possess only the constant bliss of meditative absorption; thus he says: "As they go... (51).
For the wise one who, despite difference, abides in non-difference; who, even in suffering, remains established in happiness;
and who, though existing, is as if non-existent—what else remains for him? (52)
Since he is liberated within even while existing externally in saṃsāra, he is as if non-existent there; what else remains to be accomplished or abandoned? || 52 ||
Even while engaged in worldly affairs, he neither abandons nor grasps at anything;
though his actions are external, he remains inwardly in a state of non-action.
Even while engaged in external affairs, he does not, in his heart, abandon or acquire anything; rather, he remains established solely in Brahman, which is beyond all action. || 53 ||
Just as coldness belongs to snow and heat to fire, so too would such a nature of his be eternal; it would not be an acquired quality of his. (54)
And such a state of his is indeed his very nature, not a quality that must be acquired or produced through effort. (54)
But he whose nature were this [desire] would not truly be a knower of reality;
for this alone is the mark of ignorance: that desire is other than one's true nature.
"Other than primordial nature" means having as its object that which is distinct from the self. || 55 ||

With an inwardly comforted mind, with diminished conceptual constructions, consisting of the essence of his own true nature, and satisfied by the nectar of supreme tranquility, the wise one remains free from all veils. (56)

The wise one who is free from worldly attachments remains forever satisfied by the supreme nectar of tranquility; his inner organ is at peace, his mind is always composed, his conceptualizations of enemies, friends, and the like have perished, and he abounds in the essence of the bliss of his own Self. || 56 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-first chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Yoga of the Stainless Unity and Duality," in the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa*, the *Vālmīki* version, the *Devarāja* recension, the *Mokṣopāya* section, within the *Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa*.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-first chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Yoga of Non-duality, Unity, and Freedom from Affliction," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and seventy-second chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Thus, the primordial Lord of Creatures was devoid of earth and the other elements, being nothing but space itself.
I consider myself to be mind alone, like a tree whose branches are volitions.
In this context, the Creator is composed of mind alone; the delusion of the world is his volition.
He has neither a body nor memory; thus is the true nature of memory proclaimed.

Now, one might object: "The world is heard to have been created by a Creator; for it is said, 'The Ordainer fashioned the sun and moon as before, as well as heaven, earth, the intermediate space, and the sky. How then can it be described as a mere manifestation of consciousness, like a dream?
To ward off this doubt, [the author] establishes that the Creator's volitions and the world composed of them are indeed nothing but pure consciousness.

He begins the description with the word "evam" (thus): Thus, precisely because he is a beginningless one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*), even Prajāpati Virāj is devoid of earth and the other elements, being nothing but the unobstructed space (*kha*)—the very sky of consciousness (*cidākāśa*).
And I consider that [space] to be merely Hiraṇyagarbha, the collective totality of the mind (*manaḥ-samaṣṭi*); and the mind, like a tree whose branches are volitions (*saṃkalpa*).
The meaning is that since the mere shining of consciousness is well-established, its state as pure consciousness (cinmātratva) is proven. || 1 ||
By the designation "mind," a subsequent attachment was subsequently fashioned,
just as a whirlpool, having arisen through the turning of a current, continues its whirling.

Regarding how this is well-known, he says: "The mind. Because of the conceptualization of the form of thinking, that which was previously nothing but pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) is subsequently designated by the name "mind" after the conceptualization of the form of thinking;
thus, its identity with the intellect (*citta*) is imagined through superimposition (*adhyāsa*). It is just as a whirlpool, having itself arisen in the form of a revolving eddy within water alone—
In the same way, a whirlpool was fashioned by him. || 2 ||
How indeed can cognition and the other faculties belong to that which consists of mere existence?
For when earth and the rest do not exist, what dust can there be in infinite space? (3)
For this very reason, he states that even its [the Self's] intellect and other faculties do not exist apart from consciousness: "Existence" (sattā). || 3 ||
For him there is no body, mind, and so forth, nor sense faculties, nor latent impressions; although these exist, for him they are eternally nothing at all.

Thus, he says "not of him" to show that even the body and so forth do not exist. Although they appear to exist for the sake of carrying out the semblance of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*) nothing at all exists. || 4 ||
O wise one, since the former lord of subjects has attained liberation, how indeed could there be rebirth again? There is neither memory nor rebirth.

If it is asked why it does not exist, it is because of the absence of a cause at the beginning of the initial creation (*ādisarga*). Nor is the previous Prajāpati himself the cause of the subsequent one, because he attained liberation (*mukta*) at the conclusion of the previous two *parārdhas*. Thus he says: "of the previous one" (*prāktanasya*).

[The portion of the commentary beginning with "because of the absence of a cause" (*kāraṇābhāvāt*) and continuing with "because of the absence of a cause again" (*kāraṇābhāvād bhūyaḥ*) has been interpolated by someone.]
This appears so because it contradicts the primary commentary; for there is no cause for the apprehension of the body, intellect, and so forth [by such a being].
Therefore, the meaning is that the possibility—that is, the occurrence or birth—of a memory conducive to the creation of the world by a newly arisen Prajāpati is not possible. || 5 ||
There is indeed no recollection of saṃsāra nor any further arising of a body for the liberated.

Just as for living beings in saṃsāra who are subject to the cycles of rebirth, there is no such thing for the liberated—those who have attained disembodied liberation (videhamukti)—either in another place or at another time. There is simply no recollection of saṃsāra and no further arising of a body.

The meaning is that because there is no returning again—based on such scriptural passages as, "They do not return to this human whirlpool," and "He does not return again"—[the liberated soul does not return]. || 6 ||
Or if there should be some body and so forth belonging to him through memory,
that too is quiescent, being like a subtle city of imagination, not distinct from earth and the other elements.

Or even if, by the force of the latent impressions (saṃskāra) produced by the ego-identification with Hiraṇyagarbha— which were formed during a previous kalpa belonging to that Prajāpati— some such thing as his body and so forth should arise through memory in that very manner,
it would still be due solely to the impressions arising from mental construction consisting of meditative worship (upāsanā).

The meaning is that the body, which is produced solely from the mind and not from earth and other elements, is subtle, utterly insignificant, resembling a city of imagination, and is indeed false; yet that it is real is the establishment of our own philosophical tenet. || 7 ||
Just as the form of a mountain created by mere thought, though clearly visible,
is devoid of earth and other elements, so too is the body of Virāj.

Now, one might ask: "How can this Virāṭ-body, which consists of the cosmic egg and is perceived as being composed of earth and other elements, be devoid of them? To this, he says: "Just as... (verse 8).
And memory indeed never arises at all;
that which exists through worldly intellect does not exist through the intellect of the wise.

Now, it may be objected that in the previously cited scripture, "Heaven and earth, the intermediate space, and also the sky," its form is heard to consist precisely of the earth and so forth; and since [the text continues], "The Creator fashioned them according to their prior state," it is understood that they were created based on prior memory. To this, he replies: "And memory... regarding this.

In the original creation of Prajāpati, memory is simply not possible due to the absence of prior experience. As for this [memory] which is understood through the authority of scripture, it is presented by the Śruti in accordance with the understanding of ordinary people who perceive the world as real and are ignorant [of its true nature],
solely for the purpose of setting in motion the flow of the path of karma established from time immemorial.
Because of that awakening, that memory does not exist in the intellect of that Prajāpati who knows reality.
Śrī Rāma said:
O best among those possessed of memory, why is it that memory does not arise for these [beings]?
And why, in the absence of memory, is there still merit, O mine of all virtues? (10)
Now, one might object: in a previous kalpa, during Prajāpati’s state as a practitioner of meditation (upāsaka), he certainly had the experience of earth and the other elements;

for in their absence, how could he have meditated on himself as "I am the Virāṭ body composed of earth and the rest"? Consequently, by the power of that [previous experience], at the beginning of this kalpa, through the recollection of earth and the rest, he [attains] the Virāṭ body composed of them, which was obtained through the power of his meditation.

Rāma raises a doubt as to how all the qualities of the previous cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), which were established by the Vedic revelation stating "He fashioned [the world] as before," could be realized in this present cosmic egg; thus he asks, "How?
He addresses Vasiṣṭha as "O mine of multitudes of virtues. || 10 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Indeed, this nature of cause and effect exists within the realm of the perceivable;
however, memory—which is characterized by the presence and absence of that [perceivable object]—cannot exist [in the absence of the perceivable].

We do not deny memory that arises from the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of conceptual error and is devoid of an object; rather, we deny that which arises from impressions produced by the experience of a real object. For when that [memory] exists, there occurs—by way of the impression of the experience of its own object and the memory thereof—the [recognition] of the class of real objects that were the domain of the prior experience.
By postulating positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) regarding the objects of this current kalpa, the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is established;
however, if this world—whose existence is obtained through the existence of its own constituent causes—were real, it would contradict the monistic doctrine of Brahman (*brahmādvaita-siddhānta*).

Therefore, the presence and absence of those [objects] refer to the perceived earth and so forth belonging to the previous kalpa, which are real from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārthataḥ*).

The positive and negative concomitances (anvaya-vyatireka) of those [cause and effect] are established by virtue of that [recollection]; this causal relationship, which is well-known through worldly reasoning, is possible only by means of recollection. However, that recollection which serves as the medium itself is not possible. || 11 ||
From the realm of Brahmā down to a blade of grass, not even the slightest visible object exists;
how, where, of what kind, and from what cause could the arising of memory possibly occur?

To explain why it is not possible [for duality] to exist there, he says: "From Brahmā down to... "In this, there is no diversity whatsoever; it is one only, without a second. "Now, therefore, the instruction is: 'Not this, not this. "Where one sees nothing else, hears nothing else, understands nothing else—that is the Infinite (bhūman).
"This very Brahman is without prior, without posterior, without interior, without exterior; this Self is Brahman, the perceiver of all."

Because all objects of perception are negated by such scriptural passages as "modification is a mere verbal handle, a name," and because it is likewise the experience of the wise, it follows that— according to the direction shown in the Smṛti text, "the fourfold [set] is established simultaneously"— the prior phenomenal world of Virāja, which was sublated by the knowledge of reality, becomes purely illusory for the knower of truth by virtue of its innate nature.
The meaning is that it is not capable of establishing a memory corresponding to reality, nor, by means of that, of becoming a cause for a real creation. || 12 ||
For memory is said to be the recollection of an object that was previously perceived;
where the object of perception itself does not exist, how can such mental constructions arise? (13)

The meaning is as follows: memory (*smṛti*) is defined by those learned in the scriptures as the recollection at a later time of that which, having come into being—having arisen in the ultimate sense—and existing as a real entity, was experienced through the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). However, there is no memory of that which is non-existent, imagined through delusion, or sublated by the awakening to reality. || 13 ||
Indeed, there is always an absolute non-existence of this visible world;
since "all is Brahman" is the true meaning, how can there be any mental constructions based on the memory of that [world]? (14)
Therefore, memory is simply not possible for Prajāpati at the beginning;
how could there be any possession of form for him whose nature is pure consciousness? (15)
Indicating the very intention already stated, he concludes the resolution with the words: "Memory" (smṛtiḥ). || 15 ||
That which is to be remembered exists by virtue of its own being; worldly memory does not exist at all.
But there is another meaning of "memory" which is the true Self; listen to this from me. (16)

In his previous birth, there was a contemplative practice consisting of the meditation on himself as the body of the universe; by virtue of that, for the sake of attaining the fruit of such worship, he must necessarily remember, "I am the body of the universe. However, that [memory] which is known in the world—such as the memory "she is my mother" or "she is my daughter"—which is produced by the cognition of an object, does not exist for him at all. It belongs to others...

The meaning is that while worldly objects of memory, such as one's mother, daughter, and so forth, exist in the house, there is no object for meditation comparable to those of one's mental fantasies; thus, there is a disparity. How is it that they do not exist? Listen to this matter. (16)
The recollection of a thing that has existed is called memory;
yet such a thing does not exist at all—it has neither been, nor will it ever be. (17)
In common worldly usage, *smṛti* (memory) is said to be the internal recollection of an object that has already come into being or has passed away, by virtue of its latent impression (*saṃskāra*).

However, in the case of Prajāpati at the beginning of the *kalpa*, there is no existing object, nor was there any that had come into being, nor will there be anything that exists in the future, of which he could have memory; this is the meaning. And so it has been stated in the *Sureśvaravārtika*:

"Merely through the arising of correct knowledge produced by sentences such as 'That thou art,' along with the destruction of ignorance, [the world] did not exist, does not exist, and will not exist"—thus says the Śruti: "This very Brahman is without prior, without posterior, without interior, and without exterior. (17)
For indeed, this Brahman is the supreme and immovable from which [all things arise];
since it is without beginning, middle, or end, how could there be memory and the like therein? (18)
Immovable and unchanging. || 18 ||

Because it is the self of all things, that which is the essence of all objects and the ocean of the sky of consciousness is, even in worldly transaction, perfectly tranquil; it is by means of remembrance that it has been designated by me with words.
If it were argued that because [the Self] is the self of all, even the nature of memory is Brahman, and thus it is spoken of from the perspective of being the self of all, then let it be so;

thus he says: "Because it is the self of all. Having this very point in mind, I too have said: "Or if there should be something such as the body and so forth, that belongs to it through memory"; thus he says: "Even in empirical usage... (19).

This so-called "recollection" (smaraṇa) is indeed the manifestation of its own nature. Therefore, an external object that has been previously experienced appears [in memory] due to its similarity [to the original perception]. (20)

For one who does not know the true nature of Brahman, its manifestation occurs only as something remote; yet, when that [manifestation] is repeatedly practiced through the form of meditation (*upāsanā*), it appears as the very Self of Brahman—due to the similarity with the form imagined by meditation—just like an external object that has become the fruit of that meditation. 20.
Whatever is experienced, that [experience] makes its own nature its own; therefore, whatever object appears by means of that [nature], it is designated as "memory. (21)
Whatever is perceived by the individual soul (jīva)—who is Brahman conditioned by ignorance—either through delusion or through a succession of memories, is based solely upon its own nature.

That which exists as its own nature appears at a later time as an object characterized by "that-ness" (tattā) in that very form; the designation "memory" for this is applied by the mind to itself alone. This is the meaning.
Just as the visible world appears though it does not exist, such is its state;
it appears yet is non-existent, like a rising mirage.
Just as in the experience of delusion an unreal object appears as if it were seen, so too should its persistence be understood in the case of memory.

Those excellent cognitions which, being established in the true universal self, shine forth—when their objects become firmly rooted through repeated practice, they are called "memories" (smṛti) due to their similarity [to the original experience]. || 23 ||

Through the habitual practice of error, these [cognitions] become firmly established as real objects; they are called "memories" because of their similarity, characterized by having the same object as the experience of that error. || 23 ||
In the Supreme Self, all excellent cognitions appear like the "crow-and-palm" coincidence;
being one's own limbs, naturally established in themselves, they are designated as "memories. (24)

Those cognitions which appear by virtue of an accidental awakening—like the "crow-and-palm" coincidence—are, though seemingly external objects, as if they were limbs of one's own body or parts of consciousness itself; although they are unstable due to their externality, they are stable and unmodified in themselves because of their intrinsic immediacy. || 24 ||
Whatever aspect of one's own nature shines forth by itself as having the form of reality— [the reading "cidrūpa" (having the form of consciousness) is also found]—
that is called "memory" by the wise, due to its resemblance to an object previously experienced. (25)
Whatever appears within experience, by virtue of its similarity—namely, its having an identical form—with the object previously cultivated [in meditation], [it arises]. || 25 ||

Whether the cause has been attained or not attained, for the wise, those very [mental states] which have become firmly established through practice are termed "memories" (smṛti) because of their similarity [to past experience], just like the movement of the wind. || 26 ||

Whether the awakening cause is obtained or not obtained, just as the movement of air occurs whether the cause such as a fan is obtained or not, so too those cognitions (vidas), characterized by the function of experience, become memories at a later time. || 26 ||
Those designations called "memory" appear by chance, like the coincidence of the crow and the palm fruit;
just as these limbs of yours shine forth and yet do not shine forth. (27)

If consciousness were composed of parts, then why do they not manifest at all times, just like those parts? To this he replies: "Like the 'crow-and-palm' maxim" (*kākatālīyavat*). The sense is that the convergence of the factors that awaken [consciousness] occurs only occasionally. Just as the parts—the hands, feet, and so forth—manifest when the mind is directed toward them but do not manifest when it is directed elsewhere, so it is in this case. || 27 ||
In that same way, all cognitions, which consist of every thing, abide within the Self alone,
just as objects such as jars and cloths consist of false knowledge.

The syntactical connection is as follows: just as jars, cloths, and so forth in dreams, magical illusions, and the like consist of false cognition, one should investigate what the basis is for such an error, which is the object of memory. || 28 ||
In the same way, why is the object of memory analyzed as an error?
For the knower, since the visible object is impossible, memory does not exist at all in reality. (29)
For this very reason, there is no such thing as memory for the non-deluded, wise Prajāpati. || 29 ||
Because the existence of the world is thus a single mass and consists of the space of consciousness,
this visible world exists exactly as it appears right now for the ignorant person.

The knower of reality remains exactly as before, entirely unchanged; the meaning is that from his perspective, the existence of the world is nothing but the space of consciousness (*cidvyoma*). But for the ignorant, it is the opposite; thus he says: "as it stands. (30)
I do not know the teaching on the means to liberation nor its established nature;
yet, as if out of doubt and desiring to know, the discourse on liberation is now being told. (31)

To the question "Why is that so?", he says: "No. This refers to the state of that knower of reality. For this very reason, once he has obtained the fourfold means [to liberation] through destiny, as long as he remains like one desiring to know (*jijñāsu*) due to doubts and the like, the discourse on liberation is spoken to him by the Guru. || 31 ||
As long as the object of perception, memory, and recollection cease for him, due to the absolute non-occurrence of ignorance, folly, and delusion; (32)
Just as the ignorant do not know the state of one who knows reality, so too we who know reality do not know the conviction of the ignorant; thus he says: "Of ignorance... (verse 32).
The certainty residing in the state of ignorance is never within our range;
and that which does not exist within a particular object, that he (the ignorant one) does not experience at all. (33)
Tell me, my dear, how can there be the experience of night for the sun?
For that which shines as the very nature of an object is nothing other than pure consciousness itself. (34)
Now, in order to wipe away the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) which is the cause of memory, he states its essential nature with the words "that which has appeared" (*bhātam*).
Whatever external object, in its own nature, has appeared within the pure consciousness conditioned by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*),
and if that has been repeatedly practiced through worldly usage or has perfumed the mind through similarity to such an object— [that is the nature of the latent impression].
The meaning is that it is known as its "refinement" (saṃskāra). || 34 ||
Due to the similarity with an object previously practiced, that mental impression (saṃskāra) is remembered;
this applies even to those things that are of the nature of the Self and consist of the form of the space of consciousness. (35)

In that regard, because all imagined external objects—which have become one's own nature—are sublated by the knowledge of reality, they persist only as a semblance; yet, according to the analogy of a burnt cloth, they do not exist in reality. Thus, for those who know reality, no latent impression (saṃskāra) can arise, because the mind has been cleansed of any resemblance to them. This is the remainder [of the argument]. || 35 ||
Since all imagined things remain unestablished even in their appearance,
in this way, no world whatsoever can ever possibly exist.
And thus, he states the result [of this] with the words "evam" (thus). || 36 ||
It is seen like water in a mirage, yet it does not exist in ultimate reality;
when this is so, then it appears likewise in dreams and at the beginning of creation. (37)
And thus he says that what was promised is established: "But when... The meaning is that this point is established; this is the ellipsis to be supplied. || 37 ||
The supreme expanse of consciousness alone exists within itself as the various manifestations of creation;
thus appearing as the expanse of consciousness, it has not fallen away from its true nature as pure being. (38)
Whether as form within itself or as if established in the nature of existence,
it remains falsely manifested even while it is being manifested from the very beginning of creation.

The connection with the preceding verse is: "Thus manifested by itself within itself. Alternatively: "Having become Brahman, which is of the nature of the unreal, the form of the world remains as something false, like a reflection in a mirror. (39)
Therefore, how could there be the appearance of anything to be rejected or accepted anywhere?
This [consciousness] is not something possessing form, nor is it ever of the nature of memory.
Due to the absence of a cause, the true nature of the Supreme Self shines forth;
and whatever suffering would arise from having a formal shape occurs only in memory. (41)
But why is its nature as memory also rejected? To this he says: "If it possessed a form" (ākāravattve).
The sense is that even through the memory of the death of a wife, son, or others, suffering is observed. || 41 ||
Since this duality does not exist, that which is called "bondage" is not found;
it remains exactly as it is, as a mere void within the space of consciousness, which resembles the elemental ether. (42)
The connection with what follows is as follows: "It remained as it was, suitable for worldly activity throughout the lives of those liberated while living.

(42) "The world—consisting of the earth, sun, mountains, and so forth—remained without abandoning its own nature; it did not relinquish its own form, including its fixed directions and time, however intense they may be. (43)

The city of the dreamer’s dreams consists solely of the knower, whose nature is nothing but his own self-experience; it exists within the belly of the space of consciousness, never abandoning its own form. (44)
He states that the analogy of the dream-phenomenon is also very appropriate in this context: "It is [the Self] itself," etc. (44).
Since there is no earth or other elements there, tell me, how could earth and the rest exist?
That which shines there is merely the peaceful space of consciousness (cidākāśa), and it is likewise within the Self.
He establishes this very equality with the words: "not earth, etc. (45).
At the very beginning and at the time of sleep, from where could the earth and other elements arise?
They emerge, as it were, from the reality of Brahman—which is of the nature of the Self—within the Self, appearing in the form of the world.
It subsequently produces designations such as "earth" and so forth, which appear as if they were bestowers of real objects;

yet it is neither of the nature of memory nor possessed of form, because earth and the like are impossible [in that sense]. It is neither an illusion nor a transformation; the world is solely of the nature of Brahman. (47)
Brahman shines forth as this beautiful form of the world, yet it is one alone, established in the nature of both manifestation and non-manifestation;
though appearing as the visible, it is pure like the tranquil sky, eternally risen, and its very essence consists in the emergence and dissolution of creation and destruction.

This very Brahman shines forth as the beautiful form of the world; and yet, in its shining and non-shining—its creation and dissolution—it remains established in its own unchanging nature within itself. It is of one single form alone, appearing as the visible world yet remaining stainless like the sky, eternal from beginningless time.
The meaning is that it is delighted by the arising of the nature of dissolution and creation for those who are ignorant. || 48 ||
Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-second chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Brahman-nature of the World," in the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa*, the *Vālmīki Dēvamanuṣyamōkṣanirṇaya*.
Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-second chapter, titled "The Exposition of Brahmanhood," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and seventy-third canto.
Śrī Rāma said:
"This [state] belongs even to him who is the nature of all experience and likewise the self of all."
Since the reality of the Self is infinite, why should there be the grasping of "I" even with respect to the body? || 1 ||
Just as the body and so forth, though conscious, are perceived as having inert states and activities,
and just as [the Self] possesses the nature of being the soul of all, so too is that demonstrated here.

If the world is nothing but the wonder (*camatkāra*) of self-luminous consciousness (*cit*), then, since consciousness is uniform everywhere, the grasping of the sense of "I" (*ahambhāva*) would be equally appropriate [everywhere]. Here, *graha* means seizing, insistence, or attachment. Why is there this restriction—that the intense grasping of the sense of "I" occurs only with respect to the body and not elsewhere? This is the first question. (1)
How could consciousness become like stone or wood in dreams and such states?
And how is it that these things, such as stone and wood, neither exist nor do not exist? (2)

Secondly, how could there be a non-apprehension of insentient entities such as stones and wood if consciousness alone were thus accumulated? This is because it is impossible to abandon the nature of consciousness, and it is impossible to accept that which is insentient.
Thus, if consciousness alone possesses universal selfhood (*sārvātmya*), how can this non-existence of stones, wood, and so forth occur? For the denial (*apahnava*) of consciousness is impossible.

Thus, there are two questions: how can non-conscious matter (acidrūpa), such as stone or wood, which is opposed to consciousness that is the self of all, exist at all; and by what means could [the world] possess the nature of being the self of all? || 2 ||

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Just as there is a grasping at the state of being a hand within the hand of an embodied being, so too is there a grasping at the state of being a body within the body of the Universal Self.

Just as when the manifestation of "I-ness" (ahantā) is equal across the entire body, the specific determination of "hand-ness" residing only in the hand and "foot-ness" residing only in the foot— and not elsewhere— is apprehended through the fixed arrangement of genus, action, configuration, and so forth,
by virtue of the beginningless impressions (saṃskāra) of those respective forms and nothing else; so it is with the body.

With the intention that one should understand the lack of grasping (*agraha*) regarding the state of being a body, the sense of "I," and so forth, he answers the first two questions by elaborating on the examples, beginning with the words "of the embodied one" (*śarīriṇaḥ*).

Words such as "the state of being a body" (*dehatā*) and "the state of being a tree" (*vṛkṣatā*) refer to the respective senses of "I" (*ahantā*). In all these cases, there is a superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of the object upon the subject.

It should be understood that in the case of the superimposition of knowledge, the superimposition of knowledge is the illustrative example; thus, two pairs of the words "yathā" (as) and "tathā" (so) have been employed. || 3 ||
Just as there is a grasping at the state of being a leaf in a single leaf of a tree, so too there is a grasping at the state of being a tree in the tree as a whole. || 4 ||

Even in the case of trees, the sky, and so forth, superimpositions based on those respective perceptions are cited because the individual soul (jīva) possessing the conceit [of being one with them] exists therein. || 4 ||
Just as there is a grasping for emptiness within the voidness of space, so too is there a grasping for substantiality within the substance of the universal self. (5)

In the case of a substance— such as wealth consisting of gems, pearls, gold, and so forth— and in the state of being a substance, which is characterized by the fitness for being acquired through effort;
just as there is a grasping of form in a dream-city appropriate to that dream,
so too is there a grasping of the Self as such in the states of dreaming, waking, and so on.

Since it is appropriate for the dream-city to be formless because it is produced by the appropriation of a formless mind, the dreamer nevertheless maintains a persistent attachment to its having form and possessing specific features throughout the three states, beginning with the waking state and including the dream state itself.
Just as that same perception occurs regarding a stone, a tree, water, and so forth in relation to Mount Aṅganda,
so too does that same perception occur regarding the state of being the city of Aṅganda in relation to the Universal Self.
The meaning is: even while a non-agent and a pure [nature] exist, such as in a stone and so forth, there is that well-known insistence;
that is, the insistence of those who identify with them regarding their state as mountains and their state as cities. || 7 ||
Just as there is a perception of the body in things such as hair and nails, so too there is a perception of the Universal Self in wood, stone, and the like. (8)

He also answers the final two questions with the words beginning "of the body" (*śarīrasya*). Just as there is a non-apprehension of consciousness in the hair, nails, and so forth of the body—even though it is intended to be conscious—so too there is a non-apprehension of consciousness (the non-apprehension of its being insentient) in wood, stone, and the like, even though they are of the nature of consciousness, because the Universal Self is of the nature of consciousness. This is due to the non-apprehension of consciousness by the intellect (*citā cittvasya*).

The meaning is that the impossibility of abandoning [the world] and the impossibility of accepting the lack of consciousness must be resolved by the fact that Māyā brings about the formation of even that which is not formed through its two powers of concealment (āvaraṇa) and projection (vikṣepa). || 8 ||
Just as consciousness itself appears as wood, stone, and so forth in a dream,
so too does the space of consciousness possess parts and the like at the beginning of creation.

He states that one must accept that even for the partless consciousness (*cit*), the possession of parts arises solely through the force of dream-experience—just as the state of being non-conscious (*acittva*) arises as something opposed to it—by saying "of the consciousness itself" (*cita eva*). That is, from the standpoint of the consciousness itself. || 9 ||
Just as the body of a person is a single entity consisting of both conscious and unconscious elements,
so too is it radiant in its form, characterized by nails, hair, water, and space.

Furthermore, with the intention that it is not contradictory for that which is variegated by *māyā* to initiate both types of conventional usage—since it is a single entity consisting of both the sentient and the insentient—he says: "The sentient... and so forth. Nor is there any contradiction. || 10 ||
The body of the Universal Self is likewise a single entity consisting of both conscious and unconscious;
it comprises all that is mobile and immobile, yet it is eternal and formless.
For one who possesses perfect knowledge, this world subsides as it truly is,
just as the delusion regarding objects seen in a dream ceases for one who recognizes the dream as such.
For this very reason, he says that through the knowledge of reality, all contradictory attributes are pacified: "As it truly is" (yathāsthitam).
"This is only the space of pure consciousness; there is no seer, nor is there anything seen. This silence is sufficient; that which belongs to the dreamer is his state of awakening. (13)
That state of awakening which is well-known in the morning for the dreamer is itself [the truth]: there is neither a seer nor a seen;
rather, when there is the certainty that all this is merely the space of pure consciousness (*cinmātra-ākāśa*), it is sufficient—meaning it is fully capable [of liberating one]. || 13 ||
For thousands of millions of kalpas, creations come and go;
