they are both these very ones and others, like whirlpools of water in the ocean within the sky of consciousness.
He states that even if there were to arrive a thousand times ten million such superimpositions (*adhyāsa*), there would be no impairment to the singular nature of the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*):
"even for tens of millions of kalpas," etc. (14).
Just as the ocean produces various shimmering forms such as waves and the like,
so too does Consciousness produce the designations of creation and so forth within its own self-consciousness.
"He creates water"—this is the ellipsis; [he does so] within his own conscious principle, which is consciousness variegated by *māyā*. || 15 ||
This universe, as it exists, is always Brahman itself,
free from all affliction— except for the conviction held by those ignorant of reality regarding one who knows the truth.
"I am not a wave; I am water"—by such reasoning, if a wave has realized this, how can it possess the state of being a wave? (17)
By the rule *taraṅgena*. Regarding the rule *prātipadikāntanumvibhaktiṣu*, since the phrase *pūrvapadāt* is also understood here, one must consider how its application occurs in this example.
Furthermore, in the case of *ca*, because the word *aga* is understood from the rule *pūrvapadātsaṃjñāyām*, there is no substitution of *ṇa*. This applies even to that which is insentient.
This statement is based on the superimposition of sentience. || 17 ||
Since this [world] appears as a wave of Brahman, therefore the two powers of Brahman—being a wave and not being a wave—attain their respective states. (18)
The word "wave" refers to the world which is similar to it. || 18 ||
O Rāma, this very mind— which, without abandoning its nature as the sky of consciousness, experiences manifold perceptions like a dream— is indeed called Brahma, the Grandfather.

That form which consists of the aggregate of minds, wherein the individual perceptions have been reversed through the mutual exchange of their functions and the states of consciousness are inverted, was designated by the words "Mind" and "Brahman" by the Grandfather. || 19 ||
Thus the primordial Lord of beings is formless and free from affliction;
his nature is pure consciousness alone, devoid of the causal city of conceptual construction.
By this, Hemāṅgada indeed realized that there is no such thing as being an "armlet" (aṅgadatva);
for how could he possess the state of being an armlet? His nature is purely that of gold.
Today, within this body of the sky of pure consciousness whose nature is mere volition,
that which appears as "I," "you," "the world," and so forth— that is indeed That alone.

Since the totality (*samaṣṭi*) is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), it follows that for its individual manifestations (*vyaṣṭi*), such as ourselves, this is established even if not explicitly stated; thus he says: "In the unborn" (*aje*).
Those voids that shine as the wonder of consciousness within the space of the intellect—these are the very perceptions of the intense activity of creation, maintenance, and dissolution. (23)
This very manifestation of the sky of pure consciousness is itself [the world];
appearing like a dream, it is nothing but the state of the mind—this is what we must understand. (24)
The great-grandfather is Hiraṇyagarbha. || 24 ||
Just as a wave incessantly surges in that very form or another,
so too does this delusion of creation and dissolution, which has neither beginning nor end, manifest itself.
The beautiful manifestation of the sky of consciousness, which is designated as Virāj,
would indeed act through its mind just like a city of one's own volition.

He states that Virāj is also like that: "of the consciousness-ether" (cidvyomnaḥ). The meaning is that whatever that Virāj might do—such as the mind, Hiraṇyagarbha, the worlds, or the multitude of beings—that too is like a city of one's own volition (saṃkalpa-pura). || 26 ||
Creation is a dream, and the waking body is indeed just a dream;
deep sleep is like dense darkness, just as consciousness may appear through such states. (27)

And thus, that very Virāj is the creation; he alone becomes the dream, and the dream itself becomes the individual and collective body of the waking state. Just as a person in deep sleep might experience a dream due to the visual impairment characterized by excessive drowsiness, so too at the time of dissolution (pralaya), the Self, veiled by the darkness of ignorance, becomes the perception of the world—this is the meaning. || 27 ||
The night of another aeon arose as his hair;
light and darkness were known as the joints of his limbs, called the "end of time. (28)

He describes the entire world as being the limbs of Virāj, beginning with the words "of him" (tasya). Of that Supreme Self in the form of Virāj, the intermediate dissolutions at the end of kalpas are the night of the four-faced Brahmā;
these appear as his hair because they arise first. Light and darkness—day and night—are the joints of his limbs. || 28 ||
Fire was his mouth, heaven his head, space his navel, and the earth his feet;
the moon and sun were his eyes, and the quarters of space his ears—thus was this conceptualization expanded. (29)
In this manner—identifying the eastern and western directions with the two ears—the very imagination of the mind unfolds in the form of Virāj.

Thus, when correctly perceived, the Virāj—the self whose nature is space, whose form is expansive, who resembles the mountain of our own volitions, and who exists in the form of a dream—is seen as such. (30)
Thus, its similarity to our own dream is established, and therefore the ultimate reality is indeed the state free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*). To this effect, he says:
"Whatever shines forth by itself within the space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*), that very thing is experienced by it as 'this world'; thus, it is the Self alone that is experienced. (31)
And this [Self], having attained the state of a living being consisting of consciousness, shines forth by itself, blazing intensely.

[The form] *kacakāyate* is derived from the root *kac*, meaning "to shine," with the suffix *ac* (by the rule *pacādyac*), followed by the suffix *ḍāc*; then, after reduplication, since the word ending in *ḍāc* is considered to belong to the *bhṛśādi* group, the suffix *kyaṅ* is applied. || 31 ||
Thus the Virāj-self shines as the pervasive space consisting of consciousness,
a city of dreams that is its own nature, composed of mountains and serpents.

In this manner, the Virāj-self shines as nothing but the pervasive space consisting of consciousness; or rather, in such a vision, it is the Virāj-self that appears as the space consisting of consciousness. || 32 ||
The experiencer alone experiences the experience as real, even though his own self is as if unreal;
he experiences it as having a limited extent, just as an actor in a dream experiences the location of that dream.

The experiencer is indeed the conscious self (*cidātman*), whose own nature is the singular essence of experience and who is Truth; yet, due to the veil of *māyā*, it makes even its own self appear as if non-existent and experiences it as a limited phenomenal world,
just as an actor in a dream perceives his own self as a dream-land filled with an audience of spectators distinct from himself.
The meaning is that, just as one experiences one's own dance there after having danced it, so it is in this case. || 33 ||

The views expressed by the Vedāntins, the Arhats, the Sāṃkhyas, the Sugatas, the Triad of Gurus, and others, are merely the manifestation of Brahman itself through its own power of self-limitation; for that which is eternal is essentially identical with the Self.
And for those who know the Self, all their actions result in heaven as their corresponding fruit, because they are one with this Brahman.
Such indeed is the majesty of that body which is the self of all.

He says "vedānta... because in this sense there is no contradiction with the established tenets of all disputants, and the attainment of the results sought by all is achieved precisely through this. The Vedāntas are those devoted to pure Brahman, those devoted to the omniscient Lord, and those devoted to meditation. The Ārhatas are the Digambaras. The Sāṃkhyas are the followers of Kapila, as are the Yogins. The Saugatas are the Buddhists.

The Sautrāntikas, Vaibhāṣikas, Yogācāras, and Mādhyamikas—those whose teachers are Vyāsa, Arhat (Nirgrantha), Kapila, Patañjali, and Buddha; or Tryakṣa, Paśupati, or Bhairava, the authors of various Āgama scriptures; and, by the use of the word "etcetera," the Vaiṣṇavas, Hiraṇyagarbhas, and others who are the authors of the Āgamas.

Viṣṇu and others are included. Whatever [conceptions] have been well-spoken—that is, propounded in their respective scriptures—by them, all of those, having become [the Brahman], are none other than the Brahman favored by us, manifesting through its identity with those various latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
And for those disputants who know the Self, heaven manifests in accordance with their own respective certainties.

The meaning is this: all fruit—whether of the nature of happiness in the next world or entirely of this world—is that very Brahman, because its nature is identical to the Self; thus, it is hoped that "may the fruit be so and so. Such is the well-known majesty of this Brahman, since from Brahman...
Thus, his body has a nature variegated by *māyā*; the meaning is that it consists of all things. || 34 ||
Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-third chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Supreme Reality," in the *Brahmagītā*, within the *Vasiṣṭha-vākya-darpaṇa-mokṣa-nirṇaya-upadeśa* of the *Ārṣa*.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-third chapter, titled "Instruction on the Supreme Reality," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa within the illustrious *Vāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa-tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and seventy-fourth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: At the beginning of creation, consciousness alone shines forth through the perception of a dream.
Just as the world appears [as such], therefore the three worlds are indeed Brahman alone. || 1 ||
When the visible world has been wiped away by means of awakening, as in the case of a dream,
that which remains— the single conscious self— is here described as the supreme state.

Since it has been established that at the beginning of creation, pure consciousness alone appears as the world through the perception of the dream-knower, therefore, upon awakening to the realization that the three worlds are indeed Brahman, liberation (kaivalya) is attained; this is the meaning. || 1 ||
The creations are the waves of the ocean of Brahman; within them, consciousness is the fluidity.
Another creation consists of pleasure and so forth—where else could there be duality, unity, or anything other than that? (2)

The creation, which is established by the ignorant and consists of the nature of suffering, has been wiped away by awakening. However, that which remains even thereafter for the worldly dealings of those liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*)—being of the single essence of bliss, existence, and consciousness—is indeed another creation;
how could it, being other than that [true creation], consist of duality, unity, and so forth, or take the form of unhappiness? This is the meaning. || 2 ||
Just as the self in dream and deep sleep is of the very nature of sleep,
so too the sky of consciousness consists of the single essence of both the seen and the unseen.
Since their such creation does not disturb the state of uniformity (*ekarasya*), he provides a more well-known illustration from the perspective of the ignorant, beginning with "just as" (*yathā*).
Just as in a dream, even though there is an appearance of a distinction between deep sleep and dreaming, the uniformity of sleep is not disturbed;

likewise, even though there is an appearance of a distinction between liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) and disembodied liberation (*videhamukti*), the uniformity of bliss is not disturbed—this is the meaning. || 3 ||
Just as one perceives a city in a dream while awake, so too is this world;
once it is fully understood as such, how could a person of discernment have any attachment to it?

If it is asked, "Why is there no suffering? [the author] says: "Because for the wise person, when an object has been sublated, there is an absence of attachment," beginning with the verse "jāgrati... (IV.4).
At the beginning of creation, because of the perception of creation and the knowledge of things as they truly are,
the world is just like a city in a dream experienced while awake.
Of whatever kind it is, and how it has been sublated. || 5 ||
Just as various impressions of a city in a dream are not real even though they appear real while one is awake,
so too are the impressions of the waking state not real.
With the intention that their persistence as mere latent impressions (*vāsanā*)—like that of a burnt cloth—is incapable of producing suffering, he says: "While awake" (*jāgrati*).
This means they have manifested for the sake of the appearance of enjoyments while one is awake. || 6 ||
If a cause were postulated here for [the cognition] arising otherwise, then why is such an error not likewise postulated as being closer at hand? (7)

One might object: "If the world were merely an illusion, then through the realization of reality (*tattva-bodha*), the ignorance that is its root would be destroyed, resulting in its sublation (*bādha*).

However, if one does not conceive of it as an illusion because it can be explained otherwise by means of other causes such as *pradhāna* or atoms (*paramāṇu*), then no sublation would occur, and consequently, suffering would indeed persist. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Otherwise" (*anyathā*), having established [the point].

Having established this: because it is more well-known in the world of dreams, because of parsimony (*lāghava*), because of such scriptural teachings as "modification is a mere verbal handle, a name" (*vācārambhaṇaṃ vikāro nāmadheyaṃ*);

"therein are his three abodes, which are dreams" (*tasya traya āvasathāḥ svapnāḥ*); "one should know Māyā to be Prakṛti" (*māyāṃ tu prakṛtiṃ vindyāt*); and "furthermore, at the end, there is the cessation of the universal Māyā" (*bhūyaścānte viśvamāyānivṛttiḥ*), this [theory] is closer than other conceptualizations.
The meaning is: since it is more proximate due to its rapid manifestation, why not simply assume that the world is nothing but an illusion?
(7) This very illusion is indeed experienced, just as in the worlds of dreams;
however, a cause must be established through inference—where, then, does inference have authority beyond direct experience? (8)
Furthermore, when one reflects according to the principle demonstrated by the scriptural passage on "the beginning with speech" (*vācārambhaṇa*),
one perceives directly that since pots, cloths, and so forth are not observed apart from clay, threads, and the like, this is merely one's own individual delusion regarding them;
and where could an inference possibly possess greater force than direct perception?
The meaning is: by the power of which [perception], primary matter (pradhāna), atoms (paramāṇu), and so forth, would be established. || 8 ||
Even that which has been seen exists, though it is not under one's own control nor has it been examined by the self;
because it cannot otherwise be accounted for, it is of the nature of an internal delusion, like a mountain in a dream.
Furthermore, there is also a perceptible sign (*pratyakṣa-liṅga*) here, seen in the fact that the world is like a dream or a mountain [seen] within [a cave], due to internal delusion.

For this reason, this person is not able (*na īśe*), nor is he capable, to create what is desired within himself, nor to ward off an undesired creation. The change of person (*puruṣavyatyaya*) is Vedic; or rather, one may supply the words "I am not able" (*ahaṃ na īśe*) as being experienced.
Furthermore, it is not the case that what was previously deliberated and determined by him is seen [to occur] suddenly through the perception of some random object;

for if creation were dependent upon other causes, people would surely produce what is desired through the accomplishment of such causes and avoid what is undesired, and they would not perceive anything appearing spontaneously.
The meaning is that, because the three gender-markers would otherwise be inexplicable, it is established that this is indeed an illusion, like a mountain in a dream. || 9 ||
The non-conceptual state is supreme insentience, whereas the conceptual state is transmigratory existence;
therefore, no meditation or concentration whatsoever is possible [in that state]. 10.

For this very reason, he says "nirvikalpam" (beyond conceptualization), stating that even yogins—who believe they can achieve liberation without the sublation of the world through mere meditation culminating in non-conceptual samādhi—are refuted. For to yogins, the Self, though directly experienced as a form of consciousness devoid of bliss, is not a human goal; thus, the postulation of such a direct realization [is rejected].

Since there is no purpose in that which is eternally inferable according to the Bhaṭṭa theory of knowledge, and which is eternally beyond direct perception, only insentience remains. In that state, even if the mind achieves a non-conceptual absorption (*nirvikalpa-samādhi*), it results in nothing but supreme dullness.
But if a conceptual absorption (*savikalpa*) is achieved, it is merely worldly existence (*saṃsṛti* or *saṃsāra*). For that reason, that meditation [is not the goal]. By that...
The meaning is that even if concentration is accomplished, it cannot in any way constitute the goal of human life (puruṣārtha). || 10 ||
Samsara is meditation accompanied by mental objects; however, the state of a stone is meditation without mental objects.
Liberation is not a manifestation like that of a stone, nor is it of the nature of conceptual construction. Therefore, [it is non-conceptual]. 11.

He clarifies that very point with the words "sacetyam" (along with the object of thought). That knowledge which is devoid of bliss (*anānanda*), as postulated by others, and which remains as a residue in liberation, is not liberation as a specific human goal (*puruṣārtha*).
By this, the liberation favored even by the Vaiśeṣikas and others—who do not accept that the self has the nature of consciousness—is utterly [rejected].
Refuted! The meaning is that if the object of cognition were of the nature of conceptual construction (*vikalpātmaka*), then liberation from that would not be different from bondage. || 11 ||
And indeed, by means of the non-conceptual meditative absorption (nirvikalpa-samādhi) that perceives nothing, nothing else whatsoever is attained; what is gained by one's own sleep? 12.

To the question, "Why can liberation as you define it not be obtained through the practice of the meditative absorption (samādhi) favored by yogis?", he replies: "And not even that... If something other than what is favored by the Sāṃkhyas—that is, something other than what we favor—were to be obtained, then it might as well be obtained through one's own sleep; for in both cases, there is equality regarding the cessation of mental agitation and the non-cessation of the veil of ignorance.
The state of being. || 12 ||

Therefore, for the discerning person, through right thorough knowledge, there arises the state of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*), because of the absolute non-existence of creation, which is nothing but an illusion. (13)

Therefore, since the positions asserted by others entail the defect of non-liberation, and because there is no liberation [in those views], the world is mere illusion. The Self is indeed of the singular essence of existence, consciousness, and unsurpassed bliss. Through the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), when the veil of ignorance—the cause of illusion—is destroyed, the illusion ceases; that which remains is the supreme human goal. Thus, our position alone is [the truth] for all.

He concludes with the words "therefore" (*tasmāt*) and so forth: the state of being liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*) is itself non-conceptual absorption (*nirvikalpa-samādhāna*), and that indeed is infinite liberation (*nirvāṇa*); such is the connection with what follows. || 13 ||
Non-conceptual concentration is here called infinite;
it is the seat that remains as it is, undisturbed, and illuminates all things.
That which is called infinite deep sleep is known as the Fourth (turiya);
it is declared to be Nirvana and designated as Liberation (moksha). || 15 ||
That which is the state of being a single mass of perfect awakening is known as meditation (dhyāna);
they call that awakening, whose nature is the absolute non-existence of the visible world, the supreme state.

The meaning is that this is what the scriptural passages beginning with "Where one sees nothing else, hears nothing else, understands nothing else—that is the Infinite (bhūmā)" and others say, as well as those who know reality. || 16 ||
And that state is not a dullness marred by obscuration, nor is it like deep sleep;
it is neither free from conceptual construction (nirvikalpa), nor possessed of conceptual construction (savikalpa), nor is it non-existent. (17)
And that [state] is not like the liberation accepted by Gautama and Kaṇāda, which is a dullness marred by defects;
nor is it like the state of deep sleep found in the dissolution of *prakṛti* as accepted by the followers of Hiraṇyagarbha;
nor is it merely a state of non-conceptuality like the liberation accepted by the Pātañjalas.

It is not a state of liberation characterized by conceptual construction, as is the case with the liberation favored by the Pāśupatas, the Pāñcarātras, and others; nor is it a void characterized by non-existence and selflessness, as is the liberation favored by the Buddhists. || 17 ||
That very primordial consciousness is indeed the nature of the absolute non-existence of the visible;
it is all that, yet it is nothing at all, and it knows itself in that very way, my dear. (18)

What, then, does he say about that? He says: "is seen. That alone is everything. The meaning is based on the Śruti: "In the beginning, this was indeed Brahman; it knew only itself, thinking 'I am Brahman'; therefore, it became all.
And according to such Śruti passages as "where one sees nothing else, hears nothing else," there is nothing at all. || 18 ||
Through perfect awakening, that supreme nirvāṇa is proclaimed;
herein this universe, as it truly exists, has reached its ultimate dissolution.
He states the reasoning for both "being everything" and "not being anything" with the words: "as it stands. || 19 ||
Therein there is neither diversity nor non-diversity, neither nothingness nor something;
it is declared to be the ultimate limit of all that exists and does not exist.

Regarding the term "limit" (*sīmānta*): just as the thread is the limit of the conceptualization of whether a cloth exists or does not exist; the cotton is the limit of the conceptualization of whether the thread exists or does not exist; the seed of that [cotton] is the limit of the conceptualization of whether the cotton exists or does not exist; the earth, whose nature is clay, is the limit of the conceptualization of whether the seed exists or does not exist; and it [the earth] is the limit of the conceptualization of whether it exists or does not exist.
From those [elements] comes water; from that, fire; from that, air; from that, space; from that, the unmanifest (avyākṛta);
and from that, the limit of the conceptualization of existence and non-existence is the pure conscious Self alone—this is the meaning of "the limit" (sīmānta). || 20 ||
Know that the visible world is absolutely non-existent, and that which remains as nirvāṇa—pure, the arising of awakening, and peaceful—is the supreme state. (21)
Know that very Nirvana—which is free from all distraction and is an abiding state seated in the nature of unsurpassed bliss—to be the supreme station and the highest goal of human endeavor. || 21 ||
And that pure awakening, the unsurpassed meditation, is attained by one whose intellect has been awakened through the study of the treatise and who understands the words and their meanings. (22)
And regarding the attainment of that [liberation], he says that this work titled *Mokṣopāya* is the means, stating: "And that... (verse 22).
This scripture, titled *Mokṣopāya*, should be read constantly by a person possessing pure intellectual means, and by no one else whatsoever. (23)

The meaning is this: "intellect" (buddhi) refers to the knowledge born from the study of the spiritual scriptures; by that specific means, and not by any other alternative means whatsoever, [the Self] is attained.
This is because of such scriptural passages as, "Having known Him, one transcends death; there is no other path for liberation. || 23 ||
Neither by sacred fords, nor by charity, nor by ritual bathing, nor by knowledge;
neither by meditation, nor by yoga, nor by austerities, nor by sacrifices. (24)
He elaborates on that very point with the words beginning "not" (na) and so forth. By "knowledge" (vidyayā) is meant knowledge other than the knowledge of Brahman. || 24 ||
This is indeed mere delusion; though non-existent, it appears as if existent. Like a dream within a wakeful sky of consciousness, the void itself takes on the form of the world. (25)

He asks "from where [does it arise]? and answers with the words "merely an illusion" (*bhrāntimātra*) and so forth. Since it is merely an illusion, therefore it is not pacified by asceticism or sacred fords; this is the connection with what follows. || 25 ||
Delusion is never pacified by austerities or sacred fords;
through austerities, sacred fords, and the like, the heavens are attained, but not liberation. (26)
Delusion is pacified by correctly perceiving the meaning of the scriptures through right understanding;
this occurs here in this very life solely through the means to liberation consisting of self-knowledge, and not from anything else.
All delusion caused by darkness is completely pacified by the stainless light of the meaning of the scripture itself, which acts as an intense illumination. (28)
By the light of the rising sun; like a dark night of the waning moon. || 28 ||
The appearances of creation, dissolution, and maintenance shine within the sky of consciousness, like vibrations in the wind or states of fluidity in water. (29)
"Configuration" (saṃsthā) means stability (sthiti). "Appearances" (bhāsaḥ) means manifestations (pratibhāsāḥ). || 29 ||

Just as the innate wonder of a substance resides within itself, or as the movement of the wind is constant, so too does this creation exist; its very being is a dissolution within the sky, possessing no form other than that.

Just as the wondrous capacity to assume the form of a banyan tree resides within the substance of a banyan seed, or as the wondrous capacity for vibration resides in the wind, so too does this creation of the world exist within the sky of consciousness variegated by *māyā*; its existence and persistence are of no other nature than that [consciousness], and it will likewise go to dissolution—this is the remainder of the sense. || 30 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-fourth chapter, titled "The Instruction on Nirvāṇa," within the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa*, in the section concerning the teachings of Brahmā, belonging to the *Vālmīki* recension, the *Devarāja* version, the *Mokṣopāya* (Means to Liberation), and the *Nirvāṇa* division. || 174 ||
Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-fourth chapter, titled "The Instruction on Nirvāṇa," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa within the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and seventy-fifth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: The primordial sky of consciousness, which is like a dream, is the cause of the perceptions of the body.
Since the possibility of any otherness from the visible world is impossible for the sky of consciousness, how could it have a physical form? || 1 ||
As long as ignorance appears as consciousness itself without cause,
so long is it described here that when that ignorance is removed by the scripture, one is liberated.

By stating that "this creation and its existence are non-different from [Brahman]," the author refutes the objection that might arise— that the manifestation of consciousness is merely the body— by saying "resembling a dream. For the primordial space of consciousness (cidvyoma), having become like a dream through its own ignorance,
wanders in the state of a living being (jīva) with such notions as "I am a god" or "I am a human."

The cause of the superimpositions (adhyāsa) of identity with various bodies—acting through desire, karma, latent impressions (vāsanā), and so forth—is established prior to the formation of the individual soul’s limiting adjuncts (upādhi). However, during the great dissolution (mahāpralaya), when the state of dreamlessness is attained, the existence of other objects of perception is impossible; yet, since the instrumental causes and so forth must still be established, how could that visible world, which constitutes the creation, be the body or form of that space of consciousness (cidvyoman)?
The meaning is that it would arise from a cause (nimitta). || 1 ||
O sinless one, at the beginning of creation, everything is of the nature of a dream-cognition;
without it, neither this creation nor the world beyond is established, even though they appear to be perceived.

He states that the establishment of creation and so forth occurs simultaneously with the state of being a living soul, precisely in the form of dream-consciousness, and not from any other cause: "At the beginning of creation," etc. (2).
This world appears exactly as it is experienced—namely, as non-existent;
it is merely the peaceful, absolute expanse of consciousness, like union with a woman in a dream. (3)
Nor does the consciousness-space (*cidvyoman*) possess a real state of being a living soul (*jīva*) or a state of being the world (*jagat*), by which the world could become its body; thus he says:

"It is indeed non-existent" (*asadeva*). The experiencer (*anubhū*), whose sole essence is experience—the conscious Self—appears through its own ignorance (*svāvidyā*) having become this very world, though it is non-existent. (3)
There exists such a consciousness-element (ciddhātu), beginningless and endless, stainless;
though its nature is void and its form is transparent, it manifests as the world.

If so, is even experience non-existent? He says "no"—"it is thus named. That which appears as the world exists as the very essence of the void, transparent in form, the element of consciousness (cid-dhātu). || 4 ||
This impurity (mala) is [only] non-existent when not fully understood; once fully understood, it becomes the Supreme.
For how indeed could there be impurity in the Supreme Space, which is without beginning or end? (5)

This very Supreme Self, as long as it is not fully known, is impurity; indeed, it is ignorance itself. In that state, while transmigrating, it becomes as if separate, like a *jīva*. But when fully known, it becomes none other than the supreme, stainless Brahman. The sense is based on such scriptural passages as: "He who knows that supreme Brahman becomes Brahman itself. Regarding its state as Brahman:
He states that there is no possibility of such a fault at all, asking "Why?"—the sense being that [the world] is sublated by awakening, just as a dream is. || 5 ||
This very pure perception is itself the city of a dream; that alone is the world. At the beginning of creation, how could there be the arising of earth and the other elements? (6)

The similarity to a dream, however, has already been established many times due to the impossibility of a [real] cause; he restates it with the words "That which... and so forth, in order to further reinforce it. || 6 ||

The conceptualization of earth and the other elements, as well as that of the mind, intellect, and so forth, was fashioned from the sky-like radiance of the self of consciousness, which takes the form of creation.
Like a whirlpool in water or like the movement of the wind,
the appearance of the world in the sky of consciousness occurs without prior intention and without a supporting wall.
Subsequently, by that very same [being], proclaiming its own sovereignty,
there was fashioned a conceptualization of intellect and so forth, as well as earth and so forth, consisting of both the existent and the non-existent.

Subsequently, after the manifestation of the world, having entered it in the form of the individual soul (jīva), Hiraṇyagarbha performed the act of conceptualization characterized by the differentiation of names and forms— beginning with the intellect and ending with the earth— thereby proclaiming his sovereignty as "I am the creator of the universe. This [differentiation] consists of the union of the existent and the non-existent, abounding in both the formed and the formless, and taking the nature of the coupling of truth and falsehood.
This great consciousness of one's own, which is utterly transparent, shines by itself;
that which is called "creation" is merely its own space, and nothing else.
This great consciousness, which is both transparent and yet non-transparent, shines forth by itself in the form of the world; therefore, the world is nothing other than the sky of consciousness.
And yet, my dear, not even the slightest thing shines forth; it is remembered as being purely transparent.
It is the singular perception of pure consciousness alone, fully expanded within itself by itself.

Through this reflection, O dear one, nothing at all shines forth; for that which is characterized as pure consciousness alone—that single, unique reality—is thus spread out within the Self as its very manifestation.
This very body of its own impurity is the space of consciousness within the space of consciousness;
the mind appears as if it were an object of perception, existing just as it does in a dream. 12.

One's own body is inherently full; that very same thing is one's own inherent form, or rather, it is that which is unknown as one's own inherent body. It is like the mind and like that which is perceived. 12.
Because it cannot be otherwise explained and because there is no other cause for the object— meaning,

because there is no other cause for the real object— it perceives its own self as the visible world by itself; at the very beginning of creation, the sky of consciousness perceives its own self as the visible.

Because it is impossible for even thousands of disputants to establish creation through any other means, since it cannot be accounted for otherwise, [the conclusion follows] by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*).
And that [reality] is devoid of attributes like a dream; it does not differ in the slightest.
Therefore, the space of consciousness is the space of consciousness—emptiness like the sky and so forth. (14)
Having concluded the refutation of the world’s having the nature of a body that was established [earlier], he summarizes the remainder: "Therefore," etc.
The repetition of the term "consciousness-ether" (*cidvyoma*) is for the sake of emphasis. (14)
That which is the supreme Brahman, devoid of all forms—that alone is the one, existing in such a manner as the universal whole. || 15 ||
This is experienced in a dream, for the dream indeed shines as the Self alone;
though appearing as manifold cognition, it is truly nothing but the stainless Brahman.
Having extracted what was already stated and restated it once more, he provides another illustration with the words beginning "In a dream" (svapne), etc. (16).

Brahman itself, through its state as consciousness, imagines within itself the condition of being a living soul (jīva); without abandoning its own pure form, it appears to attain the state of the mind.
This entire [universe] seems to expand from that, yet it is indeed the void whose nature is space;
though changeless, it appears as if it undergoes transformation into the form of the world.
And that [Self], in the form of the collective totality of the mind, as it were, extends this entire universe. || 18 ||
The mind itself is Brahmā; abiding within the heart of creation, it incessantly performs all things and also perpetually withdraws them.
Brahmā is Hiraṇyagarbha. || 19 ||
In that [state], which is devoid of earth and the other elements and lacks even the charming parts of the body,
the other three worlds appear as formless, just as in a dream.

Devoid of earth and the other elements, that Brahmā in the form of mind dwells within his own heart—which is itself devoid of limbs—as the heart of the universe; therefore, having become the three worlds, he shines forth as something other than himself. || 20 ||
I am the one, formless, and infinite self; through the forms of bodies and worlds, I abide as the mind, which is both consciousness and unconsciousness, and the supreme dissolution.

Having undergone the defeat of its full being through its own ignorance, that very mind, assuming the form of "I" and becoming the infinite self in the form of the body and the world, remains as both consciousness and unconsciousness; thus he says: "The body... (verse 21).
Here there is no earth or other elements, nor a body, nor indeed any other object of perception;
it is only the void of the mind that flashes forth as the world.
When viewed through the perspective of discernment (*vicāra*), even this does not exist as anything at all;
rather, only pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) alone shines, denseless, by itself within itself.
Concluding the description of the alternative perspective, he applies it to the subject at hand with the words "having investigated": "nirghana" means extremely dense. || 23 ||
From which words turn back, silence alone remains;
though engaged in worldly activity, one's own self remains like a mute.

Through the attainment of unsurpassed bliss that transcends the domain of speech and mind, there is silence and immobility. He states—by the words "even while engaged in worldly activity"—that this immobility does not depart even during the time of conventional worldly interaction. || 24 ||
Boundless, shoreless, and limitless, with pure consciousness as its supreme foundation, this Supreme Person remains awakened, having become silent. || 25 ||

The meaning is that the supreme brick, characterized as pure consciousness alone, becomes itself the mass of unsurpassed bliss which is the object of supreme love. Or, because it has become firm through the ripening of the fire of knowledge, it is indeed the "brick" (iṣṭakā) that has become Brahman;
just as moss and other things float unintentionally upon the water.
In the same way, the insentient [factors] such as the mind (citta) and the intellect (buddhi) are likewise created by Brahman. || 26 ||

Thus, in order to preclude the possibility of bondage again for one who is liberated through the process of creation and so forth at another time, he shows that creation is preceded by ignorance with the words "abuddhipūrvam" (unpremeditated). "Abuddhi" refers to ignorance (*ajñāna*), which is to be destroyed by enlightenment (*bodha*); "preceded by that" means [creation occurs] for the very Brahman-consciousness veiled by *avidyā*.
Because water and the like possess various conceptual distinctions such as whirlpools by virtue of existing in the form of water and so forth, they serve as examples. || 26 ||
Just as movement is produced by the wind without prior intention,
so too the intellect and other faculties are produced by the Supreme Self, being non-different from it.
Just as the imperishable vibration is not different from the wind,
so too pure consciousness is not different from the Supreme Self.
All are pure consciousness alone; the individual souls, characterized as manifestations of consciousness, are non-different from the Supreme Self, which is the innermost form of the Self. 28.
"O best among the wise, the sky of consciousness, Brahman, pure consciousness alone, the Self, and the Great One in consciousness—these are to be known as synonyms for the Supreme Self. (29)

For this very reason, with the intention that the nature of the individual souls (*jīva*) is also understood as being synonymous with Brahman, he says: "The ether of consciousness" (*cidvyoma*). || 29 ||
Like the wind, whose nature consists of both movement and stillness through the opening and closing of the eyes of Brahmā,
the world is such that its manifestation is exactly like its dissolution.

For Brahman, veiled by ignorance, is like an eye characterized by opening and closing, or like the wind characterized by movement and stillness. The meaning is that its very nature of closing, which consists of dissolution, is identical to its nature of opening, which consists of creation; that is, it is the world. || 30 ||
The manifestation of the visible is its opening, and the absence of the visible is its closing;
this is one and formless, because both of these states are ultimately exhausted.
Just as the eyeball is common to both opening and closing, since the opening and closing are contained within it alone, so too is Brahman; thus he says: "This is one. (31)
The Supreme is considered to be of one and the same nature throughout both closing and opening [of the eyes];
therefore, that which is perceived as "this exists" or "this does not exist" is always Consciousness itself, being both being and non-being.

Therefore, since the manifestation of the visible world as "existent" or "non-existent" arises solely from consciousness (citi), the meaning is that the visible is both existent and non-existent, whereas consciousness itself is always of the singular nature of pure existence. || 32 ||
For Brahman, whose body is creation and who consists of both closing and opening [the eyes], there is no closing other than opening, nor is there any opening other than closing. (33)

He states that even opening and closing the eyes are non-different from one another, being essentially the variegated Brahman residing in the eyes along with the eyelashes which are their cause—thus: "Nimeṣa" (verse 33).
Know this world to be exactly as it is: entirely peaceful, unborn, undecaying, like the sky, gentle, and perfectly equal. (34)
He states what is established by this view with the word "that" (tat).
"Equal" (samam) means having a single flavor (ekarasa), being identical with the nature of Brahman which is common to both the closing and opening of the eyes. || 34 ||
The void whose nature is consciousness and non-consciousness shines forth as form;
that which is called "consciousness" appears as this very world, for such is its body. (35)
Just as the sky, though superimposed with the form of blueness, shines with a shimmering luster, so too does Consciousness shine with a shimmering luster, as if it were of an inconceivable nature.
The visible world neither perishes nor arises, nor is it experienced;
rather, pure consciousness alone, being itself, brings about wonder within itself. 36.

The light of the jewel of the great space of consciousness, though appearing as non-different from its own source despite being designated by the name "the visible," shines forth like heat from the radiance of the sun.
The radiance of the great jewel of the sky of consciousness is non-different from the jewel itself, its own source.
Deep sleep appears like a dream, and Brahman alone appears like a creation;
everything is one, auspicious, and peaceful, yet it vibrates as if existing in manifold forms.
Whatever is perceived—of whatever nature, whether existent or non-existent, in whatever manner, and at whatever time—it is experienced in that very same way; whether it be real or unreal.

Whatever exists in the form of an objective entity, in whatever manner it is perceived and manifested by consciousness, in that same way it is experienced through the reflection of consciousness. || 39 ||
If a cause is postulated on the grounds that it cannot otherwise be explained, then this world-appearance must be like a dream, for it cannot be explained otherwise. (40)

If it is argued that, because the insentience of the world cannot otherwise be accounted for, a primary cause such as *pradhāna* or atoms (*paramāṇu*) must be postulated accordingly, then that [cause] appears in a dream; thus, the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is "dream-like," since it is impossible to establish it through *pradhāna*, atoms, or the like, and it is the Self itself that, having abandoned its own nature, assumes the state of the world.

The meaning is that this is not tenable. In that case, if one accepts that the Self alone assumes the state of the world, then by that same logic, Brahman itself will assume the form of the world even at the beginning of creation; thus, the postulation of primordial matter (*pradhāna*), atoms (*paramāṇu*), and so forth, is contradicted—this is the sense. || 40 ||
Since the universe has arisen as non-different from that which transcends the subject, therefore nothing whatsoever that transcends the subject has arisen apart from it. (41)

And this being so, since the world is superimposed upon Brahman—which is not an object of the means of valid cognition—the world will also be established as having an indefinable nature, characterized by its form being undeterminable by the means of valid cognition, just like a dream; thus, because it does not contradict non-duality, he says that this is further favorable: "Because it transcends the means of valid cognition" (pramātītāt). || 41 ||
Whatever the mind finds to be its object of relish, toward that it moves accordingly;
therefore, the mind that finds its sole relish in Brahman attains that very state.

For this very reason, he says—beginning with "yasya"—that for those who relish Brahman, the mind perceives the world as Brahman itself, and thus an experience corresponding to that [realization] has also arisen. || 42 ||
Whatever a person’s mind is focused upon and whatever their life-force is directed toward at all times, that they perceive as "this is the reality"; thus, they clearly know that very thing. (43)
Whatever the mind may be intent upon as having the single flavor of Brahman, that very thing it becomes in an instant; whatever its heart finds flavor in, by that it perceives that alone as real.
For that person whose mind has indeed come to rest in the ultimate reality,
he performs other actions for the sake of worldly convention, following right conduct though devoid of its [worldly] flavor.

For whatever being’s mind rests upon something with firm resolve, that very thing is for him the ultimate reality (*paramārthasat*). Therefore, even a knower of Brahman who is an atheist, when he performs sacrifices, gifts, and so forth as determined by his own [conventional] conviction, does so solely for the sake of maintaining worldly order (*lokasaṃgraha*); he performs them merely as a social convention, without any savor for them and without desire, as if by force. This is the meaning. || 45 ||
No conceptualization of duality, unity, or the like exists here; this vision is pure existence alone, and if it is perceived as such, that is sufficient. (46)
If the world is viewed from this perspective of the means I have described, then all this is mere existence; it is only this vision itself. Here, no notion of duality or unity exists at all.

In this world, for the perceptions of the invisible and the visible, the existent and the non-existent, the embodied and the formless, there is neither an agent nor an enjoyer anywhere, nor indeed is there not. (47)

For those who perceive that the invisible Brahman itself is the visible—both as the existent and non-existent, and as the embodied and the formless—for them there is no individual soul (*jīva*) here who is either an agent or an enjoyer, nor indeed is it non-existent; for its very nature as Brahman remains as the final residue.
This world, which is thus without beginning or end, is a mere transformation within the Self.
He stood like a pillar on the path, as the single, solid mass of Brahman, utterly tranquil.
Like a tree stump standing on a path through a wilderness, it presents itself to ignorant travelers who, due to the presence of thieves, doubts, and delusions, mistake it for something else.
That which is Brahman, consisting of the intellect and so forth, is indeed this very stainless one;
know that which is the peaceful, empty sky to be that very same thing. (49)
The world, beginning with intellect (buddhi) and the like, and including Hiraṇyagarbha as the collective totality of intellects, [arises from that]. || 49 ||

Just as tufts of hair and the like in the sky consist of both existence and non-existence and appear as if they have attained duality, so too do the intellect and other faculties appear within the Supreme.
Likewise, intellect and so forth, the body and so forth, sensation and so forth—whether higher or lower, many yet non-different—are all voidnesses, just like space. (51)
In Brahman, which is both transcendent and immanent and whose nature consists of all commonality, there are all the voids—the absences of jars, cloths, and so forth. (51)

Just as for one whose nature is singular sleep, there is no duality or unity when entering from deep sleep into a dream, so too for Brahman, even while abiding in creation, there is neither duality nor unity.
For one who exists within creation, as well as for one who exists within a dream-creation, there is neither duality nor unity, because that which is to be excluded is unestablished.
In this very way, this clear reflection of one's own great consciousness shines;
yet, my dear, nothing at all truly shines, for it remains established as sheer clarity alone.
Shadow, luster, or ignorance. || 53 ||
For in the sky of consciousness, the sky of consciousness itself is one's own stainless body;
it appears as the object of thought, like the visible world, just as things appear in dreams according to their state. 54.

Due to the impossibility of any other explanation and because there is no external cause for objects, the self, which is the sky of consciousness, first perceives itself alone as the visible world. (55)

The meaning is that, because it is impossible for anything other than an existing reality to be established even by thousands of disputants (*anyathānupapatti*), and because there is no other cause, the position that the sky of consciousness (*cidvyoma*) perceives itself alone as the visible world at the beginning of creation is firmly established. || 55 ||
At the very beginning of creation, the visible world appears as the formless void-self alone;
this delusion arises on all sides, just like in dreams, mental constructs, and false cognitions. (56)
It is formless, devoid of material shape and its specific characteristics; yet that manifestation is a complete delusion, a total confusion on all sides. (56)

And that [universe], like a dream, is devoid of intrinsic properties (nirdharma) and does not differ in the slightest from the reality of the space of consciousness (cidvyoma), even though it appears as a modification and seems to possess properties due to impurity.

And that which is perceived is, like a dream, devoid of objective properties (*nirdharma*) and empty of all phenomena (*sarvadharmaśūnya*), being nothing but the space of consciousness (*cidvyoma*). For not even the slightest property exists therein. The meaning is this: although the space of consciousness, which is the ultimate reality, is changeless and devoid of properties, a form possessing properties is perceived due to the impurity of ignorance (*avidyā*). || 57 ||
Having the form of that city in a dream, it possesses the nature of reality yet is devoid of such nature;
thus it remains eternally non-different from Śiva. 58.

Although it possesses the same nature [as Śiva], through common perception it appears as having a different nature; yet, being non-different from Śiva—the pure substratum—it remains thus, incessantly, in the form of the world for those of ignorant vision. (58)
The visible world is as transparent as a mountain in a dream; it does not differ from it even in the slightest.
Therefore, the voidness of the sky of consciousness is like that of the physical sky.

It does not differ from one's own self-abiding state (*svādhiṣṭhāna*). Therefore, the meaning is that since what remains is merely the space of consciousness (*cidvyoma*), it is established that this space of consciousness is even more empty and more subtle than the physical sky. || 59 ||
That very Supreme Brahman, which is devoid of all forms,
exists in this state as the creation itself.
This is experienced in a dream, for in a dream it is the self alone that shines forth;
it does not exist as a city or the like constructed by others at that time.

Now, one might object: "Let it be that during the time of a dream, the city and so forth are created by the living being (jīva) as something real; for the scripture states, 'He indeed creates chariots, horses yoked to chariots, and paths, for he is the creator'. Anticipating this objection, [the author] says: "But not there... In dreams, there are no chariots, no horses yoked to chariots, and no paths;
they are mere illusion (māyāmātra), because their true nature is entirely unmanifested—according to such scriptural passages and sūtras regarding dreams.
The meaning is that this is because of the negation of creation and the demonstration that [the world] is mere illusion (māyāmātra). || 61 ||
Furthermore, in dreams, there is no existence of recognition, mental impression, or memory, because the object "this is that which was seen" is utterly impossible [in that state]. (62)

[Objection: "Surely this is that very Devadatta," or "This is that same house seen before"—let objects in dreams be real on account of such uncontradicted recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) and other [cognitions]. To this, he says:
"And in a dream... Regarding the object such as a house which is being recognized as "this is that":
The point is that because recognition is absolutely impossible in locations such as the heart, the throat, the channels, or the apertures, it cannot occur;
and since the object itself is impossible, the latent impressions and memories directed toward it are likewise clearly impossible. || 62 ||
Therefore, having abandoned these three, that which is the manifestation of the consciousness of Brahman—
because of its similarity to objects perceived by the senses— is attributed by the deluded to memory and so forth.

Therefore, precisely because [the former] is impossible, one must set aside well-known memory and so forth; rather, one should postulate that the very consciousness of Brahman undergoes a transformation due to defects such as sleep, and that this [transformation] possesses a similarity to objects perceived in the waking state.

Having thus postulated a resemblance to memory and so forth—just as there is an appearance of the experience and its linguistic usage—one may also [conclude] that it has the nature of memory and so on.
The remainder [of the sentence] is that it must be accepted as having been inferred by the deluded. || 63 ||
Just as a wave goes again and again to that very place from which it arose in the water, so too does the world go to that same non-dual, supreme void.

He says "just as" (yathā) because it is well known that errors of recognition—such as "this is that very same wave" or "this is that very same flame of a lamp"—occur even due to similarity. [The verse states: "In the sky which is the locus of imagination, i.e., in the realm of the space of consciousness, [the world] is not other [than that], and likewise even in a dream. The meaning is that at the beginning of creation, the universe should be understood in the same way. || 64 ||
All injunctions and prohibitions whatsoever, whether always distinct or mixed together, exist in the Supreme, yet do not exist [as separate entities]. (65)

Precisely because it is mere conceptualization (*kalpanāmātra*), there is no contradiction in the coexistence of scriptural injunctions regarding the world—such as "He, the Brahman, supported this earth and yonder sky; in whom the heaven, the earth, and the intermediate space, as well as the mind together with all the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), are woven"—and scriptural prohibitions regarding the world—such as "There is not even the slightest diversity here. *(Note: The original Sanskrit text provided by the user appears to be a fragment from a commentary on the *Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad* or a related Advaita Vedānta treatise. The translation reflects the philosophical context of reconciling positive cosmological descriptions with ultimate monism.)*
He says: "They obtain," namely, the injunctions. || 65 ||
Therefore, since the existent Brahman is the self of all, what indeed is not found here?
That very existence is the self of all, and this [world] also has that as its essence.
That very existence is the existence of Brahman; that alone is the Self of all. Thus, all this is of the nature of that, of the nature of Being, and of the nature of the All. || 66 ||
Just as the spinning of a person who is dizzy does not cause the earth itself to spin,
nor does it cease for the knower [of the truth] without practice, so too in this case, the vision [of reality] does not become steady without cultivation.

For this very reason, with the intention that the inclusion of all disputants and even all conceptual constructions occurs without contradiction therein, and that liberation for one who has abandoned conceptual construction is thus established, he says: "Of the deluded one. This refers to a child wandering for the sake of play together with groups of trees, mountains, rivers, and so forth.
The meaning is as follows: while some maintain that the earth rotates and others hold that the earth does not rotate at all, both views are essentially real.

Just as a child’s perception of the earth’s rotation does not cease even for a cognizant person who lacks the practice of stability—having been acquired through habituation—likewise, the perception of the world’s illusory rotation does not cease [for one lacking spiritual training]. 67.
But for this treatise, there is no other practice than its recitation by which the cessation of the visible world will have occurred or will come to be. (68)
Regarding the question of who should practice what for the purpose of pacifying the delusion of the visible world, he says:

"Of the scripture" (verse 68). Without the practice of hearing preceded by the mastery—through service and other means—of this scripture which is the means to liberation, by winning over a teacher who knows reality through instruction and exposition, there is no other [means].
The mind, being neither living nor dead, does not undergo cessation within saṃsāra;
because it is inseparable from the body, it does not perceive this [cessation] through awakening.

Now, one might object: "What is the use of this study of scripture? For the attainment of the desired goal—characterized by the non-perception of the visible world—occurs simply through the cessation of the mind (*cittanirodha*) as established in the Yoga scriptures. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "No.

This would indeed be so if the cessation of the mind were possible; however, that mind, because its very nature is inseparable from transmigratory existence (*saṃsṛti*), [is bound] by both waking and dreaming.

Because it dissolves during deep sleep while one is alive, or because it cannot be restrained even with effort when one is dead, this [ego] does not cease; rather, it is only through the awakening dependent on the study of the scriptures that this [ego] is sublated and no longer perceives saṃsāra—thus, the meaning is that the practice itself is the means. || 69 ||
The mind is always inseparably connected with the body and its objects of perception;
yet here and in the hereafter, it subsides of its own accord at the end of awakening. (70)
Just as the mind is inseparable from saṃsāra, so too is saṃsāra, in the form of the visible world,

inseparable from both the mind and the body. And these two— the visible world and the body— subside either in this very life through the practice of this scripture and the realization of reality when there is no obstacle, or else in another life hereafter if an obstacle exists.

It subsides through the arising of enlightenment upon the destruction of obstacles; and thus there is the aphorism of the venerable Bādarāyaṇa: "That [result] belongs to this life when there is no obstacle to what has been commenced, for that is seen. (70)
The three bodies, which are the objects of the mind's vision, are stilled through awakening,
just as the winds, their movements, and armies cease for want of a cause.

The meaning is that just as the wind and its movement, as well as the armies of clouds produced by them, subside when the causes that impel them—such as the setting or rising of Venus—cease, so it is in this case. || 71 ||
The sole cause of this is ignorance, and that is pacified for those of somewhat refined intellect simply by reading this very scripture. (72)

What, then, is the cause of this triad beginning with the mind? He states it: "The cause" refers to ignorance (maurkhya), which is the nescience (avidyā) that obscures the nature of Brahman as the Self. || 72 ||

For one who understands the text, what was previously unknown is indeed understood from the subsequent [parts] of the book; knowing both the words and their meanings, such a person does not turn back due to weariness. (73)

[Objection: But how can its entire meaning be understood through mere recitation? To this he says: "if it is not understood. The words "it does not cease" are to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. || 73 ||
Therefore, know that this very scripture is the means for the destruction of delusion;
it is experienced as having attained a state that is not shared by any other.
Therefore, one should investigate this great treatise according to one's ability—whether two parts or one part; by that, the destruction of suffering shall occur. (75)
One part, or half a chapter. || 75 ||
"This is of non-human (āruṣeya) origin"—[in many manuscripts, the reading "āṛṣeya" is found;
in both cases, the status of being of sage-like authority (ārṣatva) is the same]. If it does not please you due to some oversight, then one should examine some other treatise on self-knowledge. 76.

Thinking, "This treatise was composed by a seer (ṛṣi) in the form of a Smṛti, and since Śruti is the source of Smṛti, we shall investigate Śruti itself," if this treatise does not appeal to you due to some oversight, then you should instead investigate another scripture in the form of Śruti, such as the commentaries on the Upaniṣads, which constitute the science of self-knowledge.
The meaning is that our intention here is not that one should become averse to one's own scriptures, nor is there an insistence on this alone. || 76 ||
One should not reduce one's life to ashes through harmful lack of discernment;
rather, by means of awakening—the essence of knowledge—one should assimilate the visible world into the Self.

By means of the essence of knowledge—that is, by some method such as hearing [the scriptures] and so forth, through the awakening to reality in whatever way possible—all that is visible must be surrendered to the Self;

it must be made one's own. In other words, it must be swallowed by the Self through the process of sublation (*bādha*). The suffix *sāti* is used here according to the rule "deye trā ca" (Pāṇini 5.4.55), as in the expression: "this food must be made [the property] of a Brāhmaṇa" (*brāhmaṇasāt*). || 77 ||
Not even a single moment of life can be obtained for all the jewels in the world;
alas, what a great delusion it is that one should lead such a life in vain! 78.

In that regard, he urges the indolent on with the words "of life. The ellipsis is to be supplied as follows: even with all the jewels together with heaps of gold and so forth, his [the indolent person's] negligence remains. || 78 ||
And yet, this world, though experienced and accompanied by the seer, appears as if it were a dream, our own death, or the weeping of kinsmen—though manifest, it is as if unreal. (79)

The meaning is this: although this visible world is perceived directly and experienced by the individual soul (jīva) as conditioned by the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), even when one's own death is seen by chance in a dream and the surrounding kinsmen are weeping, it appears as if real;
yet, though it shines as if existent, it is not real—it is merely false. This is the drum-beat of the conquest of the quarters by non-dual Brahman (brahmādvaita). || 79 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-fifth chapter, titled "The Argument for Non-duality," within the *Paramārthagītā* of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa*, in the section concerning the liberation of the sage, in the *Mokṣopāya* of the *Vālmīkīya*. 175.
Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-fifth chapter, titled "The Argument for Non-duality," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and seventy-sixth canto.
Śrī Rāma said:
"There have been, and there will be, worlds beyond count."
O Brahmin, how is it that you awaken me with discourses on those very things? || 1 ||
"At the beginning of creation, universes appear like dreams within the atomic consciousness of Brahman.
To explain this matter, the narrative known as the *Brahmāṇḍa* is now related as spoken by Brahmā.

If the goal of human endeavor (*puruṣārtha*) consists solely in the remaining of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) through the sublation of the visible world on the grounds that the visible is non-existent, then it is only the cleansing of the currently existing world— the very world of bondage together with its roots— that is useful, and not the cleansing of past and future worlds that are not presently perceived. For they do not even exist as objects of perception.

With the intention that, because it is impossible to define [the world] as a bond, its mention in the scripture would otherwise be entirely useless, Rāma raises an objection with the words "jaganti" (the worlds). || 1 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:

You have understood the relationship between words and their meanings within the dreams of the world; it is not merely a name, nor is it meaningless for the world to speak of it. Thus, [your inquiry] is not in vain. || 2 ||

Your objection—that only that which is currently perceived is fit for presentation, and nothing whatsoever, whether past or future—is reduced to its logical conclusion. However, that is not tenable; for the relationship between words and their meanings, the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*), and the establishment of examples and so forth, all depend upon past linguistic usage, and thus cannot be accomplished without the presentation of such [past] things.
Because it is impossible for a treatise consisting of deliberation to function [in that manner], therefore past and future world-systems (*brahmāṇḍa*),
as well as other present world-systems,
need not be introduced, since they are of no use in the apprehension of the relationship between words and their meanings; this much is the objection that can be raised.

As if accepting with indifference by saying, "If it is logical, let it be so," the venerable Vasiṣṭha gives the reply beginning with "In the dreams of the world... and so forth. By "the world" (lokena) is meant the people qualified to hear the meaning of this scripture. || 2 ||

That discourse which is expressed by means of words and meanings understood by those who have realized the Self is not cognized internally by others; it is that very [discourse] which functions here in worldly convention.

The meaning is that you have rightly raised an objection by considering the matter solely according to ordinary worldly intellect—that for those who have understood the self and ascertained the relationship between signifier and signified, it is only this [conventional usage] that is employed in linguistic practice, and no other. || 3 ||
When you have known that which is to be known and possess stainless vision of the three times,
then you shall perceive those very things through direct perception itself.

If you were to reflect upon the vision of the three times as it is well-known among those who know reality, then, because you alone would be the seer of everything, there would not be even the slightest distinction between this present universe and the infinite past, future, hidden, and remote universes; therefore, this objection of yours does not hold.

With the intention that [the opponent] ought to rise up, he says: "When... Even though the vision of reality is present, because it is rendered futile through a lack of reflection, the statement is made by superimposing futurity—saying "you will become" and "you will perceive"—as a form of derision. || 4 ||
Just as in a dream, pure consciousness alone shines forth by itself as the world, so too it is at the beginning of creation; nothing else is logically possible here.

With the intention that those who know reality must certainly be cited in the scripture—even those currently existing within other cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas) and those yet to come in future cosmic eggs—in order to eliminate their apprehension of rebirth and to demonstrate the sublation of even their worlds by awakening them to the root ignorance through the analogy of the phenomenal world being like a dream, he says: "In a dream... (svapne).

"At the beginning of creation" means at the beginning of all creations, past, future, and so forth; this much alone is applicable there, and no other variety of that [creation] is appropriate here as being relevant to the subject at hand—this is the meaning. || 5 ||
There exist in the sky worlds numbering more than an anāvanā;
who indeed is capable of enumerating the floods of their worldly activities?

If it is asked why that is so, the intention is that because they are innumerable, it is impossible to describe the extent of their variety in the scripture; with this in mind, he says: "In every single atom... (6).
In this very place, it was previously told to me by my father, the lotus-born Brahmā;
listen as I relate to you that narrative known as Padmareṇumatākhyāna.

In this regard, regarding the matter mentioned as being "countless upon countless," listen to the account told to me by my father, whose body was covered with lotus pollen, as he was considered [as one] amidst the dust of lotuses. || 7 ||
Formerly, I asked Brahmā: "How vast is this web of the universe, and where does it appear? Tell me. Thereupon, Brahmā spoke to me.
The venerable Brahmā said: O sage, all this that appears as the world is indeed Brahman;
it is infinite for the virtuous through its true being (sattva), yet it appears as the world to those who are untruthful.
Listen to this auspicious narrative of mine, an ornament for the ears;
it is called the *Brahmāṇḍapiṇḍa* as well as the *Brahmāṇḍākhyāna*.
He states two names for that narrative: "The Cosmic Egg" (Brahmāṇḍapiṇḍa). It is well known as being designated by a name that corresponds to its actual meaning. || 10 ||
In the void there exists the Self, which is non-different from the void itself, a supreme atom of consciousness;
it is pure like the form of emptiness in space, and like vibration in the wind. 11.
He begins to explain that very point with the words "It exists," and so forth: "Like pure vibration in the wind, it is the cause of the activity of the universe by its mere existence. (11)
He perceived within himself, as if in a dream, the state of being a living soul;
it was like the voidness of space or the vibration of the wind.

That atom of the supreme space of consciousness, under the influence of the sleep of not perceiving its own true nature, perceived its own state as a living being (*jīvatva*) and as the collective living being (*samaṣṭijīvatva*), just as one might perceive a dream; just as one might perceive the voidness of the sky—which is actually a real entity—as non-existent in a dream; or just as the wind perceives its own vibration. || 12 ||
Without ever abandoning its nature as space, the living being (jīva) then spontaneously perceived a form consisting of the word "I," which was itself of the nature of space.
In that case, is it subject to transformation? No; he says: "having the nature of space.
This means having the nature of space—unchangingness, non-attachment, fullness, and subtlety.
Having the nature of space, resembling space, the individual soul (jīva) perceived its own form as simply "I am. || 13 ||
He perceived within himself the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), which is the very notion of "I";
it is composed of the construction of a single resolve and conforms to the nature of Māyā.

He, in the form of egoism (*ahaṃkāra*), perceived within himself the form of the intellect (*buddhi*). And that intellect consists of the construction of a single certainty; it conforms to *māyā* because it causes delusion regarding unreal objects—this is the meaning. In a dream, the intellect perceives the mind as "I am," which is composed of unreality.
They direct themselves by means of themselves, using conceptual constructions toward that which is free from conceptual construction. || 15 ||
By means of conceptual constructions—through the imposition of the appearance of concepts upon herself—she bends herself, that is, she makes herself subservient. || 15 ||
Then, in that dream, he saw his own mind within the body as possessing five senses;
though formless, it appeared to have a solid form, just as the ignorant intellect perceives a mountain in a dream.
That mental body beheld a form consisting of the three worlds;
it was the self of space, yet it was space itself—devoid of any foundation, yet spread out, radiant with the appearance of foundations.
Thus, that atom of the supreme ether of consciousness, existing as the collective self of the mental body, beheld the cosmic form of Virāj, which consists of the three worlds.
It is composed of many elements, consisting of various stationary and moving beings;
it is fashioned by the reckoning of time, and its mutual conjunctions are imagined. || 18 ||
He describes the body of Virāj with the verse beginning "aneka" (verse 18).
In this dream, one perceives each [element] individually, like the city of the three worlds reflected in a mirror, enchanting with its ninefold colors. (19)

By means of the conceptualization of the distinction between the individual soul (*vyaṣṭi-jīva*) [and the universal soul], he provides an illustration for the state of being a witness to each of the three worlds, saying:

"In a dream... (verse 19). It is captivating because of those three triads: the seer, the seen, and the seeing; the enjoyer, the object of enjoyment, and the enjoyment; and the agent, the action, and the instrument.
Then, even here, each individual perceives within his own heart the three worlds, enchanting with their ninefold colors, as if reflected in a mirror. (20)
He states the application of that analogy with the word "atha" (now): [it applies] to each individual living being. 20.
Within the interior of every single atom,
there exist vast worlds that are not minute at all, appearing as if they were dense masses.

Thus, within the extremely subtle belly of every single atom of consciousness—which is distinct from the individual soul—there exist worlds that are imagined to be non-subtle and vast, according to the manner described; these too are as if dense with massive living beings and dense masses of earth and other elements. 21.
This ignorance is infinite; when it is perceived as ignorance, yet fully understood as Brahman, it becomes the stainless Brahman.
And all this is indeed ignorance, characterized by the lack of knowledge regarding one's own true nature; if that is removed by knowledge, Brahman is stainless.
In this way, even the seer perceives nothing at all within the web of dreams;
who here is the seer, whence is the seen, where is duality, and where is the cause? (23)
When the world, which is like a web of dreams, is seen as Brahman, even the seer is nothing at all.
Everything appears as utterly tranquil, the void-self without foundation and absolute;
it abides within the Self of Brahman, pure and devoid of beginning or end.
Brahman, which is without foundation and without division, abides within the self in its own essential nature.

The multitudes of millions of cosmic eggs are eternally situated within the Supreme Self; though they appear distinct, they are not separate from it, just as these collections of water-atoms exist as a surging mass due to the unrestrained force of spreading waves within the water.

And so, as long as the sleep of ignorance persists within the Supreme Self, there exist within that Supreme Self multitudes of millions of cosmic eggs; according to the manner described, though they are eternally non-different from it, they remain as if distinct. Or, for example, just as in the ocean there are innumerable collections of water-atoms, which—due to the cause of the unrestrained force of spreading waves—remain in a state of agitation within the water that is otherwise still.
The meaning is that they remain in that same manner. || 25 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-sixth canto, titled "The Narrative of the Cosmic Egg," within the *Brahmagītā* of the *Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa*, in the *Mokṣopāya* section of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa*, a work of the Sage. 176.
Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-sixth chapter, titled "The Narrative of the Cosmic Egg," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and seventy-seventh canto.
Śrī Rāma said:
This world arises without any cause from Brahman, the supreme state.
If it indeed proceeds, like a dream, a mental construction, and so forth. (1)
The world is with cause through conceptual construction, but in its actual reality it is without cause;
like a dream, it is described as "Brahman" through awakening from delusion.

Regarding what has been stated many times—that this creation is indeed causeless and like a dream—Rāma raises the objection concerning the logical consequence of production (*utpattiprasaṅga*), namely: "If that were so, then even effects such as grain and crops would arise even without causes such as agriculture and rain. [The distinction between grain and crops is based on their being with or without husks. Thus he questions the possibility of production occurring without a cause.
"Without cause" [is established] by two [verses]. || 1 ||
Since it is established that [an effect] arises without a cause, why would another thing not arise as causeless anywhere, at any time? (2)

The meaning is this: if, by the mere absence of a cause, the attainment of all that is desired were possible, then why would other things such as grain and crops not also arise for farmers without any cause—namely, without the causes consisting of plowing, rain, sowing seeds, and so forth? || 2 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
In whatever manner something is imagined by someone, he perceives it exactly in that way;
