otherwise, there could be no different conception, for that would entail a departure from its very cause.

We do not deny the conceptual relationship of cause and effect— such as that between a seed and a sprout— which establishes conventional usage; rather, we reject that which is non-Vedic, such as *pradhāna*, atoms (*paramāṇu*), and so forth, which are distinct from Brahman, because they lead to the contingency of the world being real and thereby render the knowledge of reality purposeless.

We refute the cause imagined by the disputants with the intention that, through the establishment of the world as being merely a transformation (*vivarta*) of Brahman, and through the sublation [of that world] by the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), the attainment of liberation (*kaivalya*) may occur. To this, Vasiṣṭha replies:

"Whatever, in whatever manner... In beginningless worldly discourse, whatever has been imagined by someone through a firm superimposition (*adhyāsa*) in whatever manner, that remains for him exactly so.

One perceives everything as either effect or cause; otherwise, even in worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), if the conventional rules were disregarded, no conceptual construction whatsoever would be possible, and thus, through mere lack of practice, the undesirable consequence of universal liberation would follow—this is the meaning. || 3 ||
Just as this imagined object of perception is perceived by one mind in a certain way,
so too does that [mind] perceive it exactly as it was imagined by another.
For this very reason, he says "just as this" (*yathedam*), meaning that an object is experienced precisely as it is established according to the conceptualizing intellect (*kalpakabuddhi*).

And thus, in the *Bhaṭṭavārtika*, while concluding the discussion on the doctrine of non-objectivity (*nirālambanavāda*), it is cited: "In the body of a single woman, there are three perceptions—a corpse for a wandering mendicant, a mistress for a lustful man, and food for a dog."
"Conceptual constructions," thus [it is said]. (4)
That Brahman is by its very nature a single unity consisting of both conceptualization and non-conceptualization;
such is the nature of conceptualization for a living being, just as it possesses hair, nails, and so forth.

If that is so, is conceptualization (kalpanā) then entirely without an objective basis? No; he says: "The nature of conceptualization and non-conceptualization. In this regard, the insentient portion is of the nature of conceptualization, while the sentient portion is of the nature of non-conceptualization; this world is composed of both. The meaning is that it is just as a conscious living being, a person, is perceived as being composed of insentient things such as hair and nails. || 5 ||
The state of being a causeless entity and the state of being an entity possessing causes—
both of these exist in Brahman, because it is the self of all powers.

Therefore, from the perspective of the reality of things, Brahman is a causeless entity, while from the perspective of conceptual construction, it is an entity with causes; thus both [states] exist in Brahman without contradiction.
If there were ever, anywhere, anything other than Brahman, then its conjunction with a cause would be possible through the conceptualization of such a cause. || 7 ||
If Brahman is of a dual nature, then why was the position that it is causeless alone established by you? To this he says:
"Because... The sense is that since the knowledge of reality alone possesses purpose, that [position] was established out of partiality toward the view of reality alone. || 7 ||
Where everything—without beginning or end, appearing as manifold and diverse—is in truth only the peaceful Brahman, the single Self; there, what could be the cause of what? (8)
Nothing here proceeds, nor indeed does anything cease;
Brahman alone, which is of the nature of space, remains as the one without beginning or end.
What is the cause of what? By what means, for what purpose, or where might it come to be?
What is the cause of what? By what means, for what purpose, or where might it not be? (10)
He states—“What of what?”—that actual causelessness is not in contradiction with either the non-arising or the arising of an imagined effect. || 10 ||
In this Great Emptiness, there is neither emptiness nor non-emptiness, neither existence nor non-existence, nor a middle state; there is nothing that exists, nor "not this," nor "not not this. (11)
In the Great Void (mahāśūnya), because it is the voidness of both the dual aspects of void and non-void, its conceptualization is "not this, not this" (na neti na neti). || 11 ||
This is nothing, or it is something; whether it exists or does not exist, know that all is Brahman alone—whether it is thus or otherwise.

He says "this" (idam) to show that everything is indeed emptiness (*śūnyatā*) precisely because of its identity with Brahman, and not because of an identity with emptiness alone: for this reason—that Brahman, due to its being all-pervasive, is thus [in the state of superimposition], and due to its being excluded from everything, is not thus [in the state of negation]. || 12 ||

Śrī Rāma said: O Brahman, regarding an effect that arises from a cause within the domain of those who do not know [the Truth], how could it be of the nature of being without a cause? Or how so? Tell me this, O Lord. (13)

Rāma raises an objection: "But why is the occurrence of cause and effect as formulated by the Pradhāna, atoms, and so forth not accepted, just as superimposition (adhyāropa) and negation (apavāda)—which concern those who do not know reality—are accepted by those who know reality for the sake of instructing them? He asks this with the words "atajjña" and so on. [The answer is: In the case of the effect characterized by earth, water, fire, and air...

The meaning is: since atoms—which are the ultimate limit of the subtlety of that series of parts, or which are the causes consisting of the qualities such as *sattva*—exist, how could the produced substance be without a cause, or how could there be the remainder of the non-dual Brahman? || 13 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
For one who knows that [Reality], there is simply no such thing as an "ignorant person. Therefore, what kind of inquiry can there be regarding a non-existent tree in the sky? (14)

This would indeed be so if a creator of the primary matter (pradhāna), atoms (paramāṇu), and so forth—distinct from Brahman and ignorant of that [Brahman]—were established. However, according to the direction shown by the Śruti: "In the beginning, this was indeed Brahman; it knew only itself, 'I am Brahman'; therefore, it became all," it is Brahman alone who, due to its own ignorance, is ignorant of that [Brahman], and for whom the knowledge of reality is necessary.

With the intention that the scripture is useful for the knowledge of reality precisely through the method of superimposition and negation (*adhyāropāpavāda*), and not by means of conceptualizing [entities] such as *pradhāna* or atoms, Vasiṣṭha replies with the verse beginning "One who does not know that" (*atajjña*). || 14 ||

Consisting of a single awakening and having the nature of a mass of tranquil consciousness, those who know that [reality]—how could they have any deliberation regarding objects that are unreal in form? (15)

To the question "Why does it not exist there?", he says: "Consisting of a single awakening. The meaning is that this is according to the Śruti: "Just as a mass of salt has no interior or exterior, but is entirely a mass of taste, even so, my dear, this Self is indeed a mass of consciousness, a mass of wisdom. || 15 ||
And that state of not-knowing appears within awakening as its constituent part,
just as the nature of sleeplessness alone remains within the states of dreaming and deep sleep once they have passed.

One might object: "How can it be possible that there is no one other than Brahman who is ignorant of It? For both logicians and common folk experience through direct perception within their own selves both the state of being ignorant of reality and the state of not being Brahman, thinking, 'I am not Brahman' and 'I am not a knower of Brahman'? Anticipating this objection, [the author] proceeds by the very force of such experience even with respect to those souls...
He establishes the nature of Brahman with the words "the state of being ignorant of that" (*atajjñatvam*).

For the state of being Brahman consists in being pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) which serves as the substratum for the superimposition of the entire world, beginning with ignorance. And this [nature] is unavoidable in the case of the self of the logician (*tārkika*), who experiences "I am ignorant," because ignorance resides in that which is of the nature of awakening.

It shines within the Self. Moreover, if this Self were insentient as imagined by the Vaiśeṣikas, how could it experience ignorance within itself? Therefore, its nature as consciousness—the substratum of ignorance—is established by this very experience. And the world...
Since it has attained the status of being a limb of that [Self], it is nothing but ignorance itself; just as in dream and deep sleep,
which have become limbs of internal sleep, there is only sleep and no nature of those two states exists apart from sleep—
likewise, ignorance, which is contrary in nature to the Self whose essence is knowledge, cannot exist in that Self except through superimposition.
It must be so, because it is from this very experience that [the world] is known as the substratum for the superimposition of the universe consisting of ignorance and the like;
nevertheless, even while granting the conviction of the ignorant, it is said:
"Because this entire self of mine is the subtle, untainted Brahman. (17)

One might raise the objection: "If being the Self of all—in the form of being the substratum of the world consisting of ignorance and so forth—is the definition of Brahman, then upon the removal of that [ignorance] through knowledge, it would follow that it is no longer Brahman. Anticipating this, he says: "Even so" (*tathāpi*). This has been stated by me for the purpose of instructing the ignorant, following the perspective of the ignorant mind, in order to explain the pure Brahman.

The incidental definition (taṭasthalakṣaṇa) of Brahman is being stated. However, its essential definition (svarūpalakṣaṇa)—its state of being the single essence of pure, untainted bliss—does not enter the path of experience for those lacking knowledge; such is the meaning. || 17 ||
Entities exist as those without cause and likewise as those born from causes;
for just as consciousness perceives them, so are they conceptualized and so are they obtained. (18)

And likewise, although one might accept that at the beginning of the Brahma-kalpa the world was created as if it were something else in accordance with the understanding of the ignorant, and thus [Brahman] is the cause—according to the maxim "the offering corresponds to the deity"—nevertheless, since such Māyā alone is the cause of this illusory phenomenal world (prapañca), there is no damage to actual non-duality; with this intention, he says: "They exist," meaning they are without a cause.

Regarding mother-of-pearl appearing as silver, a mirage, a rope appearing as a snake, and so forth: among these, those imagined as being produced from causes are "with cause" (sakāraṇaka), whereas those imagined otherwise are "without cause" (akāraṇaka).
He states that the distinction between them is established solely according to the nature of the imagination, just as there is a relationship of mother and son between a clay Gaurī and Gaṇapati.
It is consciousness. || 18 ||
When all causes have completely subsided for those endowed with every experience, there is no cause for creation; therefore, creation is indeed without cause. || 19 ||

But from the perspective of the vision of reality (*tattvadṛśā*), there is always only undivided, non-dual pure consciousness (*cinmātra*); since there is never even an atom’s worth of error, it is impossible for anyone to determine a cause for creation. Thus he says:
"Of all... [referring to] all those who possess experience and know the reality (*tattvavidaḥ*). || 19 ||
Whatever is postulated here, such as a Lord (Īśvara) and so forth, which lacks the quality of being heart-pleasing—that which is somewhat unpleasant or useless—is merely a web of words. (20)

In this world, which is like a dream, a city of the Gandharvas, or a mirage in the desert, those such as the Vaiśeṣikas— who, through their obsession with establishing the reality [of things], postulate a transcendent Lord (taṭastheśvara), primordial matter (pradhāna), or atoms (paramāṇu) distinct from Brahman as conditioned by Māyā— a Māyā well-known from such scriptural passages as "One should know Māyā as Prakṛti and the Great Lord as the wielder of Māyā"— [are mistaken].

Any cause that might be imagined is contradicted by perception, scripture, and the experience of the wise, and is refuted by the arguments well-established in the Vedānta scriptures; furthermore, it is useless because it would result in a bitter, unpleasant creation for either the Lord as creator or the individual soul as enjoyer, failing to achieve any human purpose.

Therefore, because the higher knowledges (abhijñās) reach the heart, that which lacks such heart-reaching quality is abandoned; the meaning is that it is merely a web of words that causes the throat to wither in vain. || 20 ||
Apart from the perception of appearances as in a dream, there is no other visible nature of the object of sight consisting of a gross form, precisely because it cannot be established otherwise. (21)

He states—“by way of its being otherwise inexplicable” (anyathānupapattyā)—that because the world can only be accounted for as something sublated by awakening, it is indeed like a dream; therefore, there is no room for the postulation of a cause. || 21 ||
In the experience of the dream-earth and so forth, what cause is there for one who is not awakened? Speak apart from the nature of consciousness: what indeed is the so-called object of a dream? (22)
He clarifies that very point with the words "In a dream," etc.: [it belongs] to one who is unawakened, that is, one who has not attained enlightenment. || 22 ||
For the object of a dream, when not fully understood, bestows a great burden of delusion; yet when fully understood, it leads to no more delusion—just as it is with the process of creation itself.
Whatever cause is postulated—whether through the obsession with dry logic and dogmatism, or even that which is devoid of direct experience—that is merely an adherence born of ignorance. (24)
The heat of fire, the coldness of water, and the luminosity of all radiant things—these are the inherent natures (svabhāva) of all objects; what need is there for an unawakened cause? (25)

If a cause must necessarily be postulated, then let it be the very nature of the Self, which is unawakened and conditioned by ignorance; with this intention, he says: "Of fire... The ellipsis is to be supplied as: "or the nature of the Self, which is unawakened and conditioned by ignorance, is the cause. (25)
What is the cause of a single object of meditation being perceived by a hundred meditators?
And what is the cause for the walls in a city of the Gandharvas? (26)

With the intention that even because it possesses forms established according to the differences among perceivers—like a city imagined by one's own desires—it is not easy to maintain that there is a single cause common to all, he says: "What? (verse 26).
Since dharma and the like are formless, they cannot be the cause of the embodied body in the hereafter;
what then could be the cause of the body for one who experiences the fruits of creation and so forth? (27)

Furthermore, because merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) are formless, they cannot possibly serve as the material cause for a corporeal body and so forth; thus, he refutes even the conception of the Karma-Mīmāṃsakas with the words "merit and so forth" (*dharmādīti*). [The result] occurs "there," that is, in the next world. || 27 ||
For the proponent of cognition (*jñānavādin*), what is the cause for cognitions—which take forms such as walls or non-walls, which are infinite, and which repeatedly arise and perish? (28)

Even in the Vijñānavāda system, it is difficult to explain how formless and momentary consciousness can have material and momentary things as its material cause (*upādāna*); thus he says: "walls," etc. "Walls" refers to thick walls and the like; "non-walls" refers to atoms, which are distinct from them. By the expression "of those that perish as soon as they arise," [he implies] the activity conducive to the effect and the connection with the effect.
And it has been indicated that [causality] is impossible in the case of momentary things. || 28 ||
Even when it is said that "this very nature is the cause of nature," that is merely a figurative construction (paryāyokti) regarding nature. (29)

He refutes the view of the Cārvāka, who maintains the doctrine of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), with the words "of intrinsic nature" (*svabhāvasya*). Regarding the statement made by the Cārvākas that the cause of the intrinsic nature of the sprout and so forth is the intrinsic nature of the seed and so forth when conjoined with time, field, water, and other factors—

that assertion is also untenable because no distinction in meaning can be established between the two uses of the term "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*) in the phrases "seed-intrinsic-nature" and "sprout-intrinsic-nature."

The meaning is that such a statement is pointless because: (1) even the relationship denoted by the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhy-artha-sambandha*) would be difficult to establish; (2) if there were multiple meanings, simultaneous usage as synonyms in both cases would be impossible; (3) a universal (*sāmānya*) characterized by a nature common to all [individuals] is not established;

(4) it would entail the failure to refer to the specific individual forms (*prātisvikarūpa*); and (5) the unity of meaning (*ekārthya*) would be unattainable. Thus, the statement is devoid of purpose. || 29 ||
Therefore, error is without cause, yet entities appear as if they were caused;
for the ignorant, however, every effect is established as arising from a cause.

Therefore, by means of the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), he demonstrates that which is established according to his own view with the words "tasmāt" (therefore): "Therefore, all entities and their cause—all this is merely an illusion (*bhrānti*) without a cause for the ignorant; but for the wise, the effect exists as nothing other than the Self which is Pure Being (*sanmātra*). From that very cause, it manifests and withdraws in the form of the wonder of consciousness (*ciccamatkāra*)."
The meaning is that there exists not even an atom's worth apart from that. || 30 ||
Just as one does not experience suffering in a dream due to the loss of wealth by thieves when the dream is fully understood, so too is life [without suffering] through the vision of reality.
For this very reason, he says "just as... to show that even by millions of offenses committed by the ignorant, no internal suffering arises for the knower.

Just as the beating, binding, and so forth inflicted by thieves who steal property in a dream do not cause pain—that is, do not produce affliction—for one who has awakened due to their full realization of the falsity of the dream; [so too is it with the knower].

Similarly, after the vision of reality, even living does not result in making [life] a source of suffering; this is the meaning. The suffix *ḍāc* is used here according to the rule *sukha-duḥkha-tat-kriyāyām*. || 31 ||
From the very beginning of creation, this visible world was never produced; rather, it is the sky of consciousness itself that appears like a dream in its own nature—nothing else is possible here.
Suffering is one thing, and its cause is another. || 32 ||
No other conception is seen to be supported by reason;
why, apart from this logic, should Brahman alone be the ground of experience? (33)

Apart from this principle, there is no other conception; that is to say, the various conceptions of disputants are of a different nature. Therefore, the meaning is that this construction of the world is nothing but the very ground of the experience of Brahman. || 33 ||
Just as waves, whirlpools, fluidity, and so forth appear in pure water or a cloud,
so too does this succession of creation manifest within Brahman as Brahman itself.
Just as the movement of ripples, whirlpools, and eddies appears within a pure wind,
so too does this vibration of creation manifest within the wind of Brahman.
Just as infinity, porosity, emptiness, and so forth exist in the great sky,
so too does this supreme creation exist as the nature of consciousness, being neither existent nor non-existent.

The meaning is that he by whom the self of awakening is thus proximate is well-known as being truly existent, and is therefore just like space; if the reading is "na san" (not existent), the sense is clear. || 36 ||
Even when these states, such as sleep and the like, are clearly perceived, they are essentially non-existent, because they do not possess an independent nature of their own. (37)
From where [does he know] that they are indeed existent? To this he says: "In these," meaning because they have existence as their non-different essence. || 37 ||
Thus, within the Self— which is a mass of consciousness, serene, pure, and dense with sleep— the structures of creation and dissolution appear like the states of dreaming and deep sleep.
Just as a human being passes from one dream to another within sleep,
so the Unborn (aja) remains within its own existence, passing from one creation to another.
The unborn, who is devoid of birth and other such states, the Supreme Self, remains by Himself as the essence of one creation after another. || 39 ||
Although this space of Brahman is devoid of earth and the other elements and is free from affliction,
it appears as if possessing those very things, just as in dream-experiences.
Just as sounds such as "pot" and "cloth" remain present while I am perceiving them—
whether already arisen or yet to arise— so too do all creations abide within the non-dual Great Consciousness.
In her who is the vision of the present, whose nature is all-seeing, those born in the past have arisen, and those yet to be born are unborn.
Just as the Paśyantī [level of speech] shines forth while being perceived by the Paśyantī itself, so too do the worlds shine;
for within consciousness, the creations are nothing but consciousness, consisting of consciousness alone.

When there is no difference [between them], then the statement that "words and the creations that constitute their objects exist in Brahman" results in a metaphorical relationship of container and contained within that which is non-different; it culminates in the figurative expression that "Paśyantī abides in Paśyantī itself. Thus he says: "In Paśyantī itself. (42)
What is the use of treatises or the investigation of their discourses? Liberation is simply life lived free from latent tendencies (*vāsanā*).
Since creation is unreal due to its lack of a cause, it does not exist even while appearing to exist; indeed, there is no such thing as "creation" at all. (43)

When words and creations are indeed composed of consciousness alone, then even the scripture (*śāstra*), having accomplished its purpose, ceases—because there is no longer anything to be taught (*śāsya*), because the fruit of liberation does not exist separately [from that state], and because there is no longer any bondage of phenomenal expansion (*prapañca*) to be discarded. Thus he says: "What? That is, what is the use of the scripture itself, or of the discourses and investigations concerning it?

What [is the result]? Since the fruit of the scripture is established as liberation—which is life itself free from latent impressions (nirvāsana)—in the manner described above, because creation is without cause and thus non-existent, the construction of the manifold phenomenal world (nānāprapañca) is entirely wiped away; that is to say, it is not something perceived as real, nor is it simply non-existent. This is the meaning. || 43 ||
And this very latent impression (vāsanā) established here is indeed that single, uninterrupted reality which is pure consciousness;
though devoid of multiplicity and variety, it appears as the city and other forms within a dream, for here it is consciousness alone that takes on such shapes.

And this which appears here as "imprint" (*vāsanā*), being the seed of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), shines as the very reality of consciousness (*bodhasattā*) itself, devoid of multiplicity despite appearing as multiplicity;
the meaning is that it is just as consciousness alone shines in the form of houses and so forth in a dream that is directly perceived here. || 44 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of Truth," in the *Brahmagītā* within the *Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa* of the *Mokṣopāya* section of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa*, composed by the Sage. 177.
Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of Truth," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and seventy-eighth canto.
Śrī Rāma said:
"In the three worlds, objects are of two kinds: the formed and the formless."
In which some things possess resistance, while others are without resistance.
Here, the reasoning for the movement of the material by the immaterial consciousness is stated;
it is clear from the narrative of Indu that the world is nothing but immaterial consciousness alone.

Having heard the statement that "because dharma and so forth are formless (amūrta) in the hereafter, they are not the cause for the movement of the embodied (mūrta) body," Rāma— desiring to know the logical justification for the movement of the embodied body and its like by means of the formless conscious self (cidātman)— prepares the introductory stage to demonstrate its lack of justification,
beginning with the words "padārthāḥ" and so on. Herein is shown the distinction between the embodied and formless Brahman.

It is not that [the distinction] is intended [as intrinsic], but rather it is produced by the difference in limiting conditions (upādhi) consisting of the capacity for resistance and the lack thereof; with this intention, he specifies:
Those which do not obstruct one another and do not move against each other are said here to be non-obstructive; those which do move against one another are said to be obstructive.

Lest it be thought that because objects such as flowers, cotton, and butter are softer than hard substances like stone and are thus unfit for resistance (*pratighāta*), they might be considered formless (*amūrta*), the intended meaning of the qualification is revealed through two characteristics: "tāni" (those) and "vellayanti" (they move/intermingle). [The former] refers to those [objects], while [the latter] means they intermingle or come into contact. || 2 ||
In this world, mutual displacement is observed among things that possess resistance;
however, there is no such thing at all for any entities whatsoever that lack the nature of resistance. (3)
Thus, he clarifies this by means of what is well-known in the world, beginning with "In this world" (iha). || 3 ||
In this regard, that which is called "perception" is as follows: everyone experiences how this [light] falls from here toward the lunar orb without obstruction. (4)

Let it be so; what [is the point] regarding the subject at hand? He says: "In that case" (*tatra*). In this context, that which is known as "cognition" (*saṃvedana*) is indeed non-obstructive (*apratigha*). For this reason, for a person seeing the moon, there are cognitions delimited by that [moon], together with the mind following the visual rays from this location.

They fall upon the lunar disc without resistance and indeed without any contact; therefore, the meaning is that everyone who beholds the moon personally experiences these [rays] as being formless. || 4 ||
Accepting this [view] as constructed from the non-duality of conceptualization and discrimination that is only half-awakened, I speak thus; however, it does not abide in the state of true awakening.

Now, is this objection [of yours] from the perspective of one who has awakened, or from the perspective of one who has not? In the first case, it is unestablished that the embodied [self] is [the agent]. In the second case, it is unestablished that the formless consciousness impels the body and so forth, because worldly people experience only the collection of things beginning with the body and ending with the ego-sense as the self. Anticipating this doubt, he says:

—*Ardheti*. I speak—that is, I refute—having accepted this world as it is imagined through the duality of conceptualization and discursive thought by those who are half-awake, situated in the interval between the third and fourth stages.
However, having accepted that which remains when viewed from the perspective of awakening—the pure consciousness alone—I do not refute it; such is the meaning. || 5 ||
"O Lord, tell me: what vital breath (prāṇa) situated within the body generates agitation, consisting of inhalation and exhalation, and how does it do so?"

Although it is easy to say that the corporeal vital air (prāṇamāruta) itself, when agitated by the distinction between the functions of inhalation and exhalation, impels the body, nevertheless, who produces the agitation of that vital air? || 6 ||
How can that which is called sensation be non-resistant while having resistance as its nature?
It moves this body just as a bearer carries a load.

[Objection: But surely the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa), which constitutes the individual soul (jīvātman), will produce that [body]; to this he replies with the word "how" (katham). "The body" refers to everything from the vital breaths (prāṇa) up to the end of the body. || 7 ||
If a resistant object moves while that which is non-resistant by nature does not, then why does a mountain not leap up for a person through mere consciousness alone? (8)

If consciousness alone—which is non-resistant by nature—can, having pervaded it, cause that which extends from the vital breath to the body to move despite being resistant, then why is a mountain not moved by the mere conscious volition of a person, thinking "the mountain moves"?
The meaning is: what is the difference between an external object like a mountain and something like the body? || 8 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: When the tube situated here in the heart undergoes expansion and contraction,
then the vital breath (prāṇa) comes and goes through its interruptions.

Just as external air acts as a mover by means of its entry and exit through the bellows of a blacksmith, so too the vital air (prāṇavāyu) acts as the mover of the body and other organs through its entry and exit—both of which are inferred from the contraction and expansion of the cavities of the channels such as the throat;
this is indeed directly perceived. It should be understood that the same applies even during entries into the heart and other locations, as stated in the aforementioned passage.
Vasiṣṭha, with a hidden intention, responds with two verses beginning with "vikāsam" (expansion). [The word] "chedaiḥ" means by cuts or apertures. || 9 ||
Just as air, whose nature is to occupy space, enters and exits an external tool such as a bellows,
so too does vibration occur here within the heart.

Space is the cavity; wind, whose nature is to circulate within all substances that have it as their locus and support, moves through it—just as [air] goes out, enters, comes in, and goes out from an external bellows used by a blacksmith. || 10 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
An iron-smith employs an external bellows by means of contraction and expansion;
but who is the mover who sets the internal channel in motion?

It may be argued that while it is true that the wind moves [things], it moves them only within a bellows presided over by the intelligence of a blacksmith or similar agent, and not elsewhere; therefore, it must necessarily be stated that consciousness alone is the cause of the regulated activity and movement of the unconscious. In this context, the meaning is that some conscious being, having entered through the channels (nāḍī), sets it in motion. || 11 ||
How can a hundred become one, and how can one become a hundred?
How is it that these pieces of wood, clods of earth, stones, and so forth possess consciousness? (12)

But surely, in the scriptural passage, "There are a hundred and one channels of the heart," a hundred channels spreading in all directions are heard of; and there it is also stated that there are one hundred and one channels, and that from each of these seventy-two thousand branches, thousands of channels arise, within which the *vyāna* breath moves. In that case, [the question arises] regarding the movement of the *vyāna* in all those channels.

If [the vital breath] were the cause of the movement of the body and so forth, there would always be a movement of all the limbs, rather than the specific raising of a single hand, foot, or other limb. If it is argued that when the movement of each individual limb occurs, one hundred channels become concentrated in that particular limb, whereas when the movement of all the limbs occurs, even a single channel becomes pervasive throughout all the limbs; [this is not tenable].
Regarding that, he says: "A hundredfold. Furthermore, there is no actual contact of formless consciousness even with the body.

Moreover, since the relationship of superimposition (*ādhyāsika-sambandha*) is equally present in pieces of wood, clods of earth, and so forth, it would follow that these too must be said to possess consciousness; and how could that be? This is the meaning. || 12 ||
Why does a stationary object not tremble even when it is moved? Tell me, why is it that only a moving object here is considered to be "moving" by its very nature? (13)

Likewise, if stationary objects such as trees, creepers, wood, and stones were sentient, why do they not move? Why are they not, like the body, animated by the experience of enjoyment? And why do they not move at fixed times, being governed by a measure and presided over by a potter or similar agent, like a wheel and its apparatus? || 13 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Just as a blacksmith in this world moves the bellows externally, so does that which is called internal consciousness move the coiling of the entrails through external activity.

In that [state], where there is the superimposition of identity— impelled by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of desire and action brought forth by the beginningless stream [of existence]— upon the consciousness of the *jīva* as the experiencer and the mistress of cause and effect; and in its movement,
there is independence through the connection with the vital breath (*prāṇa*) which possesses the superimposed identity of "self," while elsewhere there is dependence.

With a hidden intention regarding the established order (*vyavasthā*), Vasiṣṭha gives the answer beginning with "within" (*antar*). "The intestinal coil" (*āntraveṣṭana*) refers to the collection of channels (*nāḍī*) related to the intestines (*āntra*); the ellipsis is that it is precisely by following those [channels] that everyone in the world performs external movement. 14.
Śrī Rāma said:
O Sage, everything residing within the body—such as wind, fire, and so forth—is possessed of resistance;
tell me, how can consciousness, which is without resistance, cause it to move?

Having avoided [the objection] by means of an explicit meaning and a hidden intention, using his own seed of doubt as the basis for the avoidance, Rāma, maintaining that very same hidden intention, restates his own doubt once more: "Vāyu... (verse 15).
If consciousness, which is non-resistant in nature, could move that which is resistant in essence, then it could, by its mere will, move even distant water. (16)

He states the fault in the opposite case with the words "saṃvit" (consciousness): "In that case, then, even water situated far away would go [to the thirsty person]; thus, the thirsty traveler would have moved by his own will, or it would have come to him spontaneously. || 16 ||
If there were mutual movement between two entities, one with resistance and one without resistance, then what would be produced by the agent, the object, and the sense organs, and where? (17)

And likewise, since all activities of all living beings in external worldly affairs would be accomplished by will alone, the organs of action and instruments such as jars would become useless; thus he says: "sapratigha" (possessing resistance). The implication is: "In that case, will alone shall perform external functions such as speaking, grasping, moving, and excreting. (17)
Just as there is no union between that which is resistant and that which is non-resistant externally, I consider it to be exactly the same internally; O Sage, tell me the rest. (18)

"Even if there is no cohesion externally, let there be cohesion internally"; to this he replies: "possessing resistance" (sapratigha). Thus, when your arguments for a resolution have been refuted, state whatever other argument remains; do not state again and again that which has already been refuted—this is the meaning. || 18 ||
Just as this is experienced within oneself by a yogi, so too, for me, let there quickly be a swaying of the formless by means of the formed. (19)

Alternatively, the meaning is: just as this movement of the formless by means of that which possesses form—though extremely unestablished in the world—is experienced within [the heart] by you, a yogi, through the power of yoga and by whatever means, so too [is it here]. || 19 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Listen to these words, which are an ornament for the ears and serve as the scraping away of the roots of all trees of doubt, for the sake of experiencing the unity of all things. 20.

Thus challenged, Vasiṣṭha— considering that although he had previously offered an answer based on his hidden intention, it was rooted merely in the delusion of external and internal limitations, was consumed by an infinite regress, and was incapable of withstanding scrutiny; and further considering that Rāma, though he had understood and exposed it, would surely still refute it— set that aside.

Relying solely upon the established conclusion (siddhānta), he resolves everything with a single statement: "All... Since all doubts are rooted in the ignorance of reality, they are resolved by the experience of the oneness of all things.
[The verse continues: "In this world, there is no object whatsoever that possesses resistance anywhere."
At all times, all this is indeed peaceful, non-obstructive, and pervasive.
All this mass of objections of yours would hold true only if one were to accept a real manifold of resistant objects;
however, when consciousness alone— which is non-resistant— manifests through the power of ignorance as the illusory self of the distinction between external and internal things,
then, in accordance with how it appears, within the aggregate beginning with the vital breaths and ending with the body...

The intended meaning of the whole is that it is accepted as an established principle—and not as a confusion—that the superimposition of movement and so forth upon external objects like a jar depends solely on internal consciousness, whereas [the perception of] the hand's grasping and so forth depends on the physical support of the hand itself. // 21 //
The entire collection of objects, beginning with earth, is pure, consisting of consciousness alone, peaceful, and non-obstructive in nature, like those in dreams or mental constructs. (22)
This entire world does not exist at the beginning nor at the end due to the absence of a cause;
though appearing in the present, its nature is illusory, like a dream within consciousness.
Heaven, earth, wind, space, mountains, rivers, and the quarters—through a great multitude of causes, they know his unimpeded awakening. (24)

Therefore, the knower of reality, having wiped away the embodied form along with its latent impressions by means of a great flood of causes— achieved through the effort of discrimination, dispassion, renunciation, hearing, reflection, and meditative absorption— the entire world, including heaven, earth, air, and so forth, becomes non-obstructive.
The meaning is that they know it as mere consciousness (bodhamātra). || 24 ||
Know that everything—whether the internal organ, the elements, or earth, wood, stone, and so forth—is either void or non-void; it is consciousness and nothing else. (25)
"Cetanam" [is formed] with the suffix *lyuṭ* in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāva*). || 25 ||
In this regard, listen to the narrative of Aindava, which is an ornament for the ears;
it was previously told by me, and now another portion of it is being described.

In order to reiterate the previously mentioned narrative of Aindava—that the entire world is pure consciousness alone and that nothing possesses material form—he makes the following promise: "Therein... Previously, it was stated that the world is mind-only (*manomātra*) in order to demonstrate its origin; here, however, it is shown that the world is simply pure consciousness (*cinmātra*).
The meaning is that it is praised for the purpose of extracting [the essence of] nirvāṇa. || 26 ||

Nevertheless, listen to that [explanation] so that you may understand the question just posed regarding the present, and thereby realize that all this—the mountains and so forth—is indeed consciousness alone. (27)
He states that even due to the difference in purpose between the question at hand and its resolution, repetition does not constitute a fault, saying "nevertheless" (*tathāpi*).

You will understand the resolution of the question simply as "the intellect is formless" (*amūrtā cit*); here, the future tense suffix *lṛṭ* is used in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi*), with the augment *sya* and the substitution of *bhaṣ* for *c*.
O Brahmin, in a certain former cycle of the world, there was a twice-born man known as Indu, who was the very foundation of asceticism, the Vedas, and sacred rites.
In the specific web of the world, according to the manner described in the previous section on the process of origination.
He had ten sons who were like the horizons of the world—noble-minded, great-souled, and the refuge of the great and the virtuous. (29)
The ten horizons of the quarters are like the boundaries of the space within the interior of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) of the world; they are the foundation and the support. || 29 ||
In the course of time, their father passed away,
like the Lord Rudra, the eleventh among ten, at the time of universal dissolution.
At the time of destruction, that is, at the great dissolution (mahāpralaya). || 30 ||
His devoted wife, fearing widowhood,
followed him like the twilight follows the day, her eyes like stars.
Their two sons, overcome with grief, went to the forest;
having performed the funeral rites and abandoned worldly affairs, they remained in meditative absorption.
They are conceived of as, or pervaded by, the suffering of separation from suffering. || 32 ||
Among all the *dhāraṇās*, which one bestows the supreme accomplishment? By means of which *dhāraṇā* may we, being perfected beings, become lords of all? (33)

The meaning is: among the various types of *dhāraṇās*, characterized by the steadiness of the mind taking on the specific form of an object, which one would be the supreme *dhāraṇā* regarding what object? All the lords are those who have become Hiraṇyagarbha. || 33 ||
Having thus reflected there, those ten, having assumed the lotus posture (padmāsana) within the interior of a cave free from obstacles, meditated upon this: || 34 ||
"Free from obstacles" means devoid of harm caused by wild beasts and the like. || 34 ||
Abiding by means of sustaining the entire world presided over by Padmajā, may we remain without obstacle as the form of the world united with Padmajā. (35)
Remaining motionless, they abide with the conviction: "I am that very same entire universe, the cosmic egg, presided over by the four-faced one born from the lotus. || 35 ||
Having reflected thus for a long time with the intent of sustaining the world together with Brahmā,
they stood with eyes closed, as if they were figures in a painting.
Then, with their minds fixed in concentration (dhāraṇā), those embodied beings remained there for eighteen months without falling away.
The "unfallen" (acyuta) are those who have not undergone a fall by means of maintaining another state of mental activity. || 37 ||
Dried up and reduced to skeletons, their limbs chewed by carnivorous beasts,
they met their destruction there like patches of shadow under the scorching sun.
The state of being a skeleton and the state of being a corpse. || 38 ||
"I am Brahmā, and this world, along with this creation consisting of the worlds, is mine"—as they perceived this, a long period of time passed by. (39)
And this world is myself, for those who perceive and meditate thus. || 39 ||
Those ten mind-bodies, through the unification of the ten meditative absorptions,
then became the worlds themselves as ten distinct physical bodies.

The meaning is that ten minds, ten bodies, and ten worlds in the form of cosmic eggs were accomplished through the ripening of meditation, according to the principle of "as is one's resolve" (*tatkratu-nyāya*). || 40 ||
Thus, their desire for consciousness was fulfilled as the entire universe;
yet it remained in a state that is utterly transparent in nature and devoid of form.
Consciousness itself, having become desire, has become the world. He says "not so" [to the objection] that this might involve the loss of its own nature, by the word "absolutely" (atyanta). || 41 ||
Because the worlds consist of consciousness, know that everything—the earth, the mountains, and so forth—is of the nature of consciousness; if it were not so, what else could be said? (42)
And thus, he states that what was proposed as the thesis is established: "Because it consists of consciousness. (42)
It is said: what indeed is the nature of that web of the three worlds? It is nothing other than the emptiness of the space of consciousness; it is not anything else.

The connection with the preceding [verse] is as follows: "Is it not the case that for these [beings], this tenfold web of the three worlds is [real]; or rather, what is its nature? Let that be told by you. He states what is said by you: "Consciousness" (saṃvit) [is it]. || 43 ||
Just as no wave exists apart from water, so too movement and the like do not exist apart from the reality of consciousness. 44.
The connection [of the phrase] "motion and so forth do not exist" is to be understood by drawing it over from the previous context. || 44 ||
Likewise, these worlds are composed of consciousness within the void;
similarly, even wood, clods of earth, stones, and so forth, are composed of consciousness within them.
He states that the similarity between the lunar world and the world under discussion should be understood even though the latter is the subject at hand: "aindavāni" (etc.). || 45 ||
Just as the volitions of Aindava attained the state of the world,
so too has this volition of the Lotus-born come to the state of the world.
He demonstrates this very equality with the words: "Just as... (yathā). || 46 ||
Therefore, these mountains here, the earth, the trees, the clouds, the great elements, and everything else—all this is spread out as consisting solely of pure consciousness (cinmātra). || 47 ||
The tree of consciousness, the earth of consciousness, the sky of consciousness, the ether of consciousness, and the mountains of consciousness—
nothing whatsoever exists that is not consciousness, just as in those worlds of the moon-god (Indra).
By the potter that is the void of pure consciousness, upon the revolving wheel of its own body, this creation is incessantly fashioned from the clay of its own form. (49)
"Why?"—this expression of impossibility is for the purpose of highlighting falsity. (49)
If, in a creation fashioned by volition, stones were not sentient, then tell me: what is this [sentience] in clods of earth, mountains, and the like? (50)
With this intention—that by this [explanation] the question of how these pieces of wood, clods of earth, stones, and so forth can possess consciousness is also resolved—he says:
"Conceptualization, memory, and latent impressions do not hold an object within their interior;
rather, they belong to another class of things that possess the capacity for objects, which have already been purified of conceptual construction and the like. (51)

Temporal succession, experience, memory, the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) that produce them, and—indicated by the word "and" (*ca*)—desire and volition: these are indeed particular states of consciousness whose objects are external things, for it is within these that external objects manifest. Moreover, these [states] contain within their own interior nothing but pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) manifested; they do not contain an insentient object. Therefore, he says that objects are in fact of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*).
Regarding the term "kalanā" (mental construction): he asks, "Whence [does this arise]? and answers, "Previously," etc. For we have already deliberated upon this:

that the state of mental constructions (*kalpanā*) and the like, which are devoid of objective referents (*arthaśūnya*), is one thing; whereas the wonder of those who possess a portion of the objective reality (*arthakalāvatām*) and who are endowed with the aesthetic power of penetrating the ultimate principles (*tattva*) is quite another. Alternatively: "But surely..."

Since the clay clod and other such objects are determined to be of an insentient nature by virtue of their uniformity with the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the memory of being a "clod" and so forth, how can they be described as sentient? To this, he says: "Kalanā... [and so on]. Since the processes of *kalanā* (differentiation) and the rest cannot fathom the reality of the clay clod, the mountain, and so forth—which is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*)—held within its womb, therefore those who possess even a fraction of that object...

The phrase "it exists even prior to the arising of conceptualization and so forth" means that it has been thoroughly examined and reflected upon. For, regarding an unknown object, there is the conceptualizing by the eyes and other senses; regarding a known object, there are memory and mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), both of which have the same object as the [original] cognition.
Therefore, the point is that the establishment of the unknown object must necessarily be stated as preceding those [mental functions]. Nor is it of the nature of the insentient (*acid-rūpa*).
It is possible to speak of grass, wood, mountains, and so forth as being "unknown," because there is no purpose for the obscuration of ignorance (ajñānāvaraṇa) regarding insentient objects.

Therefore, the reality of grass and other such things is the very existence of Brahman itself, which is distinct from the insentient; it is this [Brahman] that is mistakenly perceived as insentience through the conceptualization of its otherwise nature and through the latent impressions of memory—this is the meaning. || 51 ||
Just as a gem [shines] within a heap of gems in the abode of consciousness,
so too does some object arise sufficiently within the mind, which is the self of all.
For this reason as well, he says "that" [in the verse] to show that even wood, clods of earth, and so forth are sentient:

because that supreme abode of consciousness itself, shining intensely like a gem within a heap of gems, remains within the collective and individual minds—the abode of all consciousness—and emerges as some object such as grass, wood, or stone; having entered into that, it became both the manifest (*sat*) and the unmanifest (*tyat*).
The meaning is "because of scripture" (śruteḥ). || 52 ||
The purpose of performing what ought not to be done is nowhere different from Brahman;
since it is its very nature, the certainty is that all this is Brahman. (53)

Furthermore, grass, wood, and so forth are sentient, because there is the creation of that which is incapable of action [if they were not]; just as the radiance of the sun is of the very same nature as the sun itself and is not of a non-luminous form, in that same way, all this is the sentient Brahman alone—this is the meaning.
53 Just as the water of consciousness, having set out, flows and whirls upon the earth;
By one's own exceedingly intense effort, without [relying on] another, oneself, or one's kin. || 54 ||

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: just as water flowing on downward-sloping ground revolves by its own effort and of its own accord—without any other cause—into various diversities such as whirlpools, currents, and waves (regarding itself and others as "self"), so too does consciousness (*cit*). || 54 ||
The worlds shine forth like the play of a lotus from Brahman, who is pure consciousness; they are not even in the slightest degree other than his own self.

Just as in the Padma Kalpa the playful lotuses from the Lord’s navel shine forth as if they were the world itself, so too do the worlds manifest from Brahman, who is pure consciousness; therefore, they are not even slightly different from Him.
Unborn and unceasing, pure existence, Brahman whose nature is space;
peaceful, the middle between being and non-being—this world is nothing but the light of consciousness. 56.
He states what follows from their non-difference: "unborn. Because both existence and non-existence—being and non-being—are wiped away, it is the middle. (56)
One who says that mountains and such things, which exist within the world of mental construction as consisting of consciousness,
are instead "not consisting of consciousness," is laughed at by the wise as an ignorant person.

For this very reason, he says "that which... [verse 57], meaning that those who regard grass, stones, wood, and so forth as insentient are fools who are ridiculed by the wise; the word "speaker" (vaktā) should be understood as "ignorant" (ajña).
Just as the Self knows these worlds in the sky as consisting of its own volitions,
so too does Brahman know this world, which is of the nature of space, as born of its own volition.

Since the four-faced Brahmā is born from his own volition (saṃkalpa), one may infer that he is pure consciousness (cinmātra) just like a kingdom of one's own imagination; thus [the author] says: "The worlds... [and so on]. The Self is just as it is itself. 58.
To the extent that this vision is observed more and more rapidly, to that same extent this suffering dissolves more and more rapidly. || 59 ||
To the question, "For what purpose is this very view being supported again and again through various modes of expression? he says:

"As long as... This view of the phenomenal world (*prapañca-dṛṣṭi*), when observed for as long as it is by means of the strengthened vision of consciousness (*ciddṛṣṭi*), for that long this suffering dissolves. || 59 ||
To the extent that this view is scrutinized, before long it becomes a heap;
to that same extent, this suffering becomes dense and solid. (60)
For those long deluded by evil deeds and lacking this vision, this cycle of existence—hard as a diamond—is never stilled. (61)
Here there is no form, nor birth and destruction arising from existence and non-existence; there is neither being, nor indeed is there such a thing as non-being.
Only the supreme, peaceful reality shines thus within the Self, or rather, even this "shining" does not exist here at all.
Therefore, because it yields such great fruit, one should firmly establish this very view—thus he concludes with the words "neha" (not here). Here...
In the world, conceptual constructs such as form and so forth do not exist. Existence (*sattā*) is the second transformation of being; non-existence (*asattā*) is its absence.

Thus does [reality] shine within the Self, whose nature is ultimate consciousness. Alternatively, even a shining that transcends Brahman is utterly non-existent; the meaning is that there is no basis for the operation of the verbal root *kac* (to shine). || 62 ||
Devoid of beginning and end, it is the creation of the root and the tip of the unattainable creeper;

it is entirely pure, encompassing all, containing within itself the multitude of children who are the creations of the spaceless void; indeed, it stands eternally as a solid mass, free from birth and destruction.

He describes what kind of Brahman remains even in the absence of the golden egg: "Beginningless and endless," etc. That Brahman is like a crystal pillar; within it exists the entire multitude of the creation of the world, which is like a collection of puppets made of empty space.
Unattainable are the creepers of the world—their tips, their roots, their productions, and the enclosures and entrances into the earth that serve as the roots of those roots.

In that [state] wherein such [a reality] exists—devoid of beginning and end, free from birth and destruction even in terms of time, entire, pure, exceedingly transparent, a single solid mass of consciousness and bliss, and eternal; this is the meaning of *kaivalya* (isolation). || 63 ||
I am indeed this entire reality— pure existence alone, devoid of internal distinctions, with all its manifold manifestations, free from limitations and beyond calculation,
unconditioned in form, having the self and space as its essence, well-supported, unborn, silent, and sufficient unto itself, free from conceptual constructions.

When this very [Being] was in the aforementioned state, it was then devoid of internal distinctions, innumerable, entire, and pervading everywhere; it possessed hands and all other limbs—eyes, ears, heads, throats, bellies, feet, and so forth—which were beyond counting even at their extremities, being truly incalculable; such as this, it was all that existed.

The meaning is: "I myself have become this very form of a beautiful crystal pillar—liberated in nature, consisting of the self and the ether, the form of a firm pillar, pure existence (sanmātra), unborn, and silent; therefore, enough with further conceptual constructions, for there is no purpose [in them]. || 64 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-eighth chapter, titled "The Legend of Indu" within the *Brahmagītās*, in the *Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa* of the *Mokṣopāya*, in the *Vālmīkīya Devarāmāyaṇa*, the great *Ārṣa* epic of the venerable *Vāsiṣṭha*.
Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-eighth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Aindava," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and seventy-ninth chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Thus, the three worlds are nothing but pure Being, which is solely Consciousness alone.
No beings whatsoever arise here that are devoid of consciousness.
Since the entire universe exists as nothing but pure consciousness and is non-obstructive, it is stated:
"What occasion is there for the aforementioned doubt?"
The elements, as perceived by the ignorant through their resistance and materiality, do not exist here [in this ultimate sense]. || 1 ||
Therefore, from where could a body or any other object possess resistance?
Whatever is seen here is entirely non-resistant and all-pervading.
The non-resistant Brahman alone is spread out. || 2 ||
The sky of consciousness abides in the sky of consciousness; the tranquil abides equally in the tranquil. Space abides in space; cognition unfolds within cognition. (3)
It is equal, being entirely free from all inequality. || 3 ||
Everything consists of consciousness and is peaceful, existing in the waking state like a dream;
it abides in an unobstructed form—where, then, is this state of obstruction?
The meaning is: where is that "resistance" (sthiti) spoken of by you, in which your doubt might spread? || 4 ||
Where are the limbs of the body, where the wrapping of the entrails, and where the cage of bones?
Know the body to be like space, unimpeded, though it appears as if possessed of resistance.

However, from the perspective of one who is awakened, the body, its limbs, and so forth, are nothing but pure consciousness (cinmātra), just like a dream-body; therefore, the doubt regarding them arises only from the perspective of the ignorant, not from the perspective of the knower of reality. Thus he says: "Where? (kveti).
As for the phrase "resembling a tangible dream-body," it must be explained in some way [as figurative], since tangibility is not established [for a dream-body]. || 5 ||
The hands are consciousness, the head is consciousness, and the entire collection of sense organs is consciousness;
all is peaceful and unobstructed, for indeed nothing exists that is obstructed.
Because the existence of the world has the nature of being like a dream within the ether of Brahman,
all this comes into being— both with cause and without cause.
One should not think that it is an act of rashness to deny the embodied form and so forth, which are established by perception and other means of knowledge; thus he says:

"Of the Brahman-ether. [This refers to] that which, though established by valid means such as perception and accompanied by causes, is here said to be without cause and without proof, and though possessing a cause, is without a cause. Of that, there are three abodes, three dreams; "here there is no diversity."

The sense is that because the world is negated by the very scripture beginning with "Where one sees nothing else, hears nothing else... therefore the instruction is 'not this, not this' (neti neti)," [the world does not exist]. || 7 ||
It is logically untenable that an effect can exist without a cause;
for whatever is determined by someone in a certain way, it is characterized by them accordingly. (8)

From the perspective of ultimate reality (*tattvadṛśā*), because Brahman is changeless and non-dual, and because there is no other cause for the world, its non-arising alone is logical; thus, its denial [as a real entity] is justified. However, from the perspective of delusion (*bhrāntidṛśā*), because it is beginningless and because a succession of causes is possible, the world arises from Brahman.
Without a cause, an effect appears as if it were real; consciousness undoubtedly attains that very object exactly as it has been conceived. (9)

However, from the perspective of reasoning, he states— beginning with the words "by a cause"— that this world, having arisen without a [material] cause and being obtained as the very nature of consciousness, is neither absolutely non-existent nor absolutely existent, but rather exists as if it were real. || 9 ||
Just as everything exists everywhere and in every way within a dream according to its possibility,
so too in the waking state there exists the nature of being the self of all, because it consists of consciousness alone.

In the state of Brahman, which is the self of all, there exists existence— both that which is without cause and that which is born from a cause— even though it abides in various and non-various forms.
But in the doctrine of Māyā, everything is consistent; thus he says: "In the Self of all," etc. (verse 11).
Just as these sons of Indu became one thousand,
so too did they attain the state of being hundreds upon the earth along with hosts of worlds born of their own volition.
For in that same way, when there is a thousand cognitions,
there would be a single body through the emanations [of the Lord] in union with Cakrapāṇi and the others.

The meaning is that, through the phrase "of Cakrapāṇi" and so forth, there occurs the attainment of oneness by way of the merging of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*)—in the case of union (*sāyujya*) with Brahmā, Rudra, Indra, the Moon, the Sun, and others—in accordance with the direction stated in the summary of the narrative of Vipaścit; for the Śruti says, "He attains union with Indra, or the same world as him," and so on. || 13 ||
The ocean remains but one, even with hundreds of rivers;
time remains but one, despite the multitude of seasons and years. (14)
He says "eka eva" (is indeed one) because the attainment of oneness of being between two distinct beings is well-known even in the world;
[this applies] even though [the year] is divided by the excellence of the seasons and years. 14.
This body has arisen like a dream within the very space of consciousness;
it is formless like a mountain in a dream, even though it is made manifest by one's own experience.
Likewise, he says "the space of consciousness" (saṃvidākāśa) to show that the one and only Self appears as if it has attained multiplicity through the body and so forth due to delusion. || 15 ||
Consciousness alone exists by virtue of its own experience; yet that very consciousness is not of the nature of an object of experience.
Through the triad of the seer, the seen, and the act of seeing, it shines as the single sky of consciousness; therefore, the world is one with it.
By means of the vision of the seer, the seen, and the seeing—a vision that perceives through delusory divisions—(16).
Feeling and the feeler are one, like sleep, dreaming, and deep slumber;
like wind and its movement, they are non-different. Therefore, the world is the one space of consciousness.
Just as sleep is one and the same, yet it consists of two types—being of the nature of sensation in dreaming and of the nature of non-sensation in deep sleep—so too is that [the Self]. || 17 ||
The seer, the seen, and the act of seeing are the manifestation of consciousness, the ultimate void;
like a dream within emptiness, the world appears as nothing but the single expanse of consciousness. 18.
O Lord of the gods, this entire world is indeed non-existent; through delusion it appears from the first creation, but like fear in a dream, it subsides when fully understood.
Since the world is indeed non-existent, its manifestation—like the fear of tigers and such in a dream—is pacified the moment it is fully understood. || 19 ||
Just as a single consciousness appears in various ways within a dream,
so too at the beginning of creation does it appear in the form of manifold objects within the void.
In the sky, in Brahman. || 20 ||
Just as many shadows appear as one in a house with many lamps,
so too the single power of the All-Powerful shines forth in manifold ways.

He states that even for a single power of illusion (*māyā-śakti*), a manifold appearance is possible, just as the light of many lamps appears as one; thus he says, "In many lamps. Here, *chāyāḥ* means splendors. || 21 ||
That manifestation which is the shimmering of spray in the ocean known as Śiva is like the shimmering of a cluster of trees in the sky;
yet this cluster of trees in the sky has a distinct form, whereas in the ocean of Brahman, it does not exist even in the slightest degree.
The Drop of Emanation || 22 ||

Just as a cluster of trees appears in the sky through delusion, so too this creation is merely the flashing of spray upon the ocean called Śiva. However, there is this distinction: whereas in the sky the cluster of trees appears as if it were an entirely separate form—due to its being permeated by the sky’s own nature of emptiness—in the ocean of Brahman, [it is not so].
The meaning is that even though the drops of emission (sargabindu) are quivering, they do not possess even the slightest degree of separate form. || 22 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-ninth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Nature of Being Consisting of Brahman," in the Section on the Attainment of Liberation through the Knowledge of Brahman, within the Section on the Realization of the Self, in the Discourse between Vasiṣṭha and Arundhatī, in the Holy Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa of the Sage.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-ninth chapter, titled "The Exposition of Being Consisting of Brahman," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa-tātparyaprakāśa*.
The one hundred and eightieth canto. Śrī Rāma said:
O Blessed One, dispel this doubt of mine, which is like darkness before the sun.
Just as for the world, it serves for the correct perception of the true nature of all things. || 1 ||
Here, in this narrative of Kundadanta composed by Rāma, the story of the ascetic hanging from a tree on a mountain is related, ending with his attainment of a boon.

Having himself awakened through his long-standing desire to know reality, and having asked the Guru about his own doubt— namely, whether or not the Brahmin named Kundadanta, who had taken refuge in him, attained awakening to reality upon hearing the instruction currently being presented— Rāma, wishing to resolve that matter, spoke this most wonderful narrative to Vasiṣṭha.

Preparing the ground, he entreats that Guru with the words "this" (*imam*). This refers to what will be stated at the conclusion of the narrative. The meaning is: just as the light of the sun cuts through the darkness so that the true nature of all things in the world—the universe—may be correctly experienced, so too [is this work]. || 1 ||
Once, while I was sitting with one-pointed attention in the assembly of the learned at the house of knowledge, a certain ascetic arrived.
He begins the narrative to show the seed of doubt, starting with the words "kadācit" (once upon a time) and so forth.
The phrase "yāvatsthitastāvattasminkāle" means "as long as he remained, at that time. || 2 ||
A learned and illustrious preeminent brahmin from the region of Videha,
possessed of great ascetic power and radiant with beauty, was as difficult to withstand as Durvāsas.
Having entered and quickly saluted the assembly hall of radiant splendor, he sat upon his seat; while remaining there, he was saluted by us.
To the assembly, the assembly of the twice-born. || 4 ||
Having gathered together the doctrines of the Vedānta and Sāṃkhya systems, I asked this of that most excellent man as he sat comfortably at ease and rested.
There, having set aside the doctrines of the Vedānta and Sāṃkhya systems as they were being taught to me, I asked that ascetic the following question. || 5 ||
Exhausted by the long journey, you appear as if burdened by great effort;
speak now, O best of speakers, from where have you come? (6)
You appear as if making an effort, striving to acquire or understand some particular matter. (6)
The Brāhmaṇa said:
"It is even so, O highly fortunate one; I am indeed possessed of great effort.
Listen now to the decision regarding that purpose for which I have come here. (7)
The meaning is: "my words" refers to the definitive conclusion that removes your doubt. || 7 ||
There is a land named Vaideha, endowed with every auspiciousness,
like a reflection upon the earth of heaven situated in the sky.
Upon the ground, which was like a floor of crystal.
There I was born as a brahmin and remained one who had attained his learning;
because my teeth were as white as kunda flowers, I was known as Kundadanta.
There, among the Videhas. || 9 ||
Then, having become detached from worldly desires, I set out to wander for the sake of allaying the fatigue caused by the agitation of gods, brahmins, and great sages.
The ellipsis implies "the abodes of the gods, the twice-born, and the lords of sages. || 10 ||
Once, I reached Śrīparvata, which is unbroken [in its sanctity];
there I dwelt for a long time, performing gentle and protracted penance.

"Unbrokenly here" (akhaṇḍeham) connects with what precedes; or it means "I dwelt there unbrokenly. It is "gentle" (mṛdu), meaning not harsh, and "long" (dīrgha) because of its duration over a long period of time. || 11 ||
There is a well-known forest there, free from grass, woods, and the like;
it is like the expanse of the sky over the earth, from which light, darkness, clouds, and so forth have departed.
Regarding the aspect of emptiness, there is the illustration of the surface of the sky. || 12 ||
In the midst of that place stands a small tree with delicate foliage;
it is situated in the empty sky like the sun with its rays dimmed.
A *viṭapin* is a tree with many branches. || 13 ||
Upon its branch hangs a person of dwarfish form,
like the sun held by its rays within the sun, appearing as if knotted together.
Bhānu is the sun; as if caught by its own rays within the sun—that is to say, with his feet bound by ropes—his feet are held fast by the ropes that bind them. || 14 ||
With his feet bound by a girdle of muñja grass and his head perpetually downward,
he appeared as if bearing the state of a "great-knee" upon the great-kneed śālmali tree.

He states that very point clearly: "mauñjeti" (with the girdle of muñja grass). It is as if it were assuming the state of being a knee-bone (*aṣṭhīlatva*), that is, the condition of having long, knotted joints.
Having reached that place, I once saw that man;
I examined him closely as he stood nearby with his palms joined in reverence at his chest.
It has been investigated by the mind and reflected upon. || 16 ||
For as long as he lives, that brahmin sighs with his form unharmed;
he experiences all the sensations of cold, wind, and heat produced by time.

He states that very reflection clearly with the word "yāvat" (as far as). The word "yāvat" is used here in the sense of deliberation (*vitarka*). The meaning is: "Surely he lives, because he breathes. || 17 ||
Immediately thereafter, I did not attend to many others;
instead, through the fatigue of the day's heat, he was gradually brought to a state of confidence. (18)
This man who was hanging there alone—I, having attended to him for many days by enduring the exhaustion of the sun’s heat, gradually brought him to a state of relaxation and confidence. || 18 ||
And he was asked: "Who are you, O Blessed One? For what purpose do you perform this terrible austerity, O large-eyed one, with your very life barely visible? (19)
With his own life barely perceptible due to breathing only after long intervals. || 19 ||
Then he said: "O ascetic, what kind of object could it be?
For the desires of embodied beings regarding an object are never very extraordinary. (20)

"What is the purpose, what is the motive for you to have this thorough knowledge of my lineage, country, ascetic practices, and so forth? For indeed, an inquiry into a matter that serves no purpose is not possible"—this is the meaning. || 20 ||
When he was questioned by me with such effort and persistence,
he then gave me this reply.
When that ascetic had spoken thus and was questioned by me with effort and persistent affection, he then said this to me, which is about to be told.
I was born in Mathurā and grew up in my father’s house;
standing between childhood and youth, I am a knower of words and their meanings.
He who knows the words [of grammar] and the treatises on word-meanings [of lexicography] is a knower of words and word-meanings (padapadārthavid). || 22 ||
"A king becomes a treasury for the accumulation of all happiness"—having heard this, I, seeking enjoyments and in the prime of my youth, went there. (23)
I have heard that the king, as the lord of the earth, serves as the repository for all complete accumulations of happiness and the requisites of enjoyment, like a treasury. (23)
Then, I, noble-souled as I am, reflected for a long time: "May I become the lord of the earth, as vast as the seven great continents. (24)

Then, immediately after hearing that, I—the lord of the earth extending over the seven great continents—reflected for a long time, thinking, "May I likewise be such a noble-souled one, capable of fulfilling the desires of those who seek my help"; that is to say, I formed this wish. (24)
Having arrived at this region for this purpose,
O giver of honor, I have remained here for twelve years.
For this very purpose and for this reason, he came to and remained in this region of Śrīśaila. || 25 ||
Therefore, friend, go quickly to whatever desired place you wish, as if it were no concern of mine;
and I too shall remain thus firmly established until the attainment of my own desire.

Therefore, since I have explained the matter you asked about, you—a friend without cause—should go quickly to your desired destination; for if you travel slowly, you will not reach distant villages or cities and would consequently be exposed to the night in the forest. As for me, however, until my goal is attained, I shall remain thus firmly established in asceticism.
Having been addressed by him in this manner, I spoke to him thus: "Listen;
the mind of a wise person does not feel distress upon hearing something wonderful. (27)
"O virtuous one, as long as you have not obtained the bridegroom of your choice, I shall remain here for the sake of guarding and serving you. (28)

"For that duration, I too shall remain for the sake of your protection, performing service and attending to you"—this is the meaning. (28) When I had spoken thus, he became like a stone, silent and composed; with eyes closed, his form diminished, and externally devoid of movement. (29)
His form is like that of one who has wasted away and died; for he is without conceptualization regarding external objects. || 29 ||
Thus I dwelt before him, who observed the vow of silence like a log of wood,
for six months, free from agitation and enduring the impulses brought about by time.
Enduring the onsets of cold, heat, and other conditions brought about by time. || 30 ||
Once, I beheld a man, radiant as the sun, who had emerged from the solar disc and was standing in another region.
In that other region, he saw a man as radiant as the sun standing before that ascetic.
While he was being honored by him with mind and deed, as well as by me,
he then spoke words as beautiful as a flow of nectar.
While that man was being honored by the ascetic along with me, he spoke.
O Brahmin, O long-lived ascetic intent on hanging from a branch, withdraw your penance; O destroyer, accept the boon you desire.
Withdraw your ascetic penance; accept a boon that is perfectly captivating, enchanting, and desired.
"You shall rule the earth, encircled by the seven oceans and continents,
for seven thousand years with this very body, in accordance with righteousness."
"By means of this body, you shall perform penance and dharma; you will not protect [the world] with this body," for that would contradict the subsequent text.
(34) Having thus granted what was desired, that second Sun, having risen from where he had come, entered the solar ocean to go to his setting. (35)
For he, having himself arisen and emerged from it, entered that very ocean in the form of the sun to go to its setting, which is invisibility.
When he had departed, I spoke to that wise ascetic of the Śākha lineage, who was a supreme granter of boons whose excellence had been heard of, seen, and experienced.

He by whom that foremost and most excellent giver of boons—the solar person (ādityapuruṣa)—who is heard of in the scripture, who is seen directly, and who is experienced through the practice of granting boons, has been encountered; [this refers to] that ascetic of the branch. || 36 ||
