O Brahmin, having attained your desired goal, abandon this asceticism of hanging from the branch of a tree and conduct yourself according to the worldly life as it naturally presents itself.
O Brahmin, that penance of yours which took the form of hanging from the branch of a tree has now reached its desired goal;
since it has become such as you intended, you should now abandon your asceticism and engage in the activities appropriate to your station, such as returning to your own home. 37.
When he had thus consented, I then released his two feet from that tree, as if from a tethering post, like an elephant at the appointed time.
The two [elephants] at that time were related to the young elephant, as if [released] from their tethering post—that is, the pillar to which they were bound. || 38 ||
Having bathed with purified hands, he performed the *aghamarṣaṇa* recitation;
then, by means of the merit obtained from its fruit, he broke his vow at the tree branch.
By means of merit and the power of success in asceticism, he broke his vow together with me by eating the fruit obtained from that very branch. || 39 ||
By the power of that merit, we remained there for three days, refreshed and undisturbed by those sweet fruits obtained from the tree.
Having performed penance with his body suspended from a tree with feet upwards, the brahmin sought to enjoy the entire earth— its quarters sealed by the seven continents and oceans—
and having obtained the desired boon from the Maker of Day for three and a half days of the universe, he [departed].
He set out to go to his own home with his dear friend. || 41 ||

He concludes the very story already told by means of a summary: "saptadvīpa... etc. Having obtained the desired boon from the Maker of Day (dinakṛt), that is, from the Sun-purusha, and immediately thereafter having rested for three days at the foot of the tree—after the fatigue of my feet had ceased—I myself, together with my friend...
He set out to go to the palace situated in Mathurā. || 41 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and eightieth chapter, titled "The Narrative of Tāpa," in the *Brahmagītā* within the *Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa* of the *Mokṣopāya*, in the *Vāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa* composed by the Sage. 180.
Thus ends the one hundred and eightieth chapter, titled "The Narrative of the Ascetic," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa-tātparyaprakāśa*. 180.
The one hundred and eighty-first canto.
Kundadanta said:
With joyful countenances, we two set out to go to our dwelling.
The city of Mathurā was like the city of Indra, frequented by the moon and the sun. || 1 ||
As they were traveling to Mathurā, they lost their way and arrived at the Gaurī forest;
there, their conversation with an aged ascetic is described here.

Just as the moon and the sun set out in the evening to go to their well-known dwelling in Indra’s city in the east, so too have we two, having set out from here, proceeded toward our dwelling in the interim. || 1 ||
Having reached the village named Rodha and rested on the mountain of mango groves,
they dwelt happily for two days in that city of Sālīsa.
He describes the locations for residence in sequence, beginning with "having reached" and so forth: on a mountain abounding in mango groves. (2)
With our hearts gladdened by the journey, we passed the second day [among] forest trees with cool waters and lush shade. (3)
On the second day, having crossed over such ravines, marshy grounds, and forest lands where there are cool waters and forest trees with lush shade—thus [is] the connection on the fourth [day]. (3)
White with heaps of flowers fallen from the creepers on the riverbanks,
they gladden travelers with the singing of the gurgling sounds of their surging waves.

He specifies those very lands with the words beginning "on the riverbank," and so forth. Regarding the form *gāyanam*, the absence of the substitution of *āt* for *aś* is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*).
The shadows of the lush forest trees resounded with the cries of deer and birds;
on the tips of the branches of thick grass, dewdrops hung like pearls.
On that day, they completely traversed forests, mountains, cities, villages, ravines, marshlands, plateaus, and plains, as well as river currents and lakes.
In some places the lands became deserts, in some places mountain ranges, in some places cities and villages, in some places chasms, and in some places low-lying marshlands.
We spent the night in a dense grove of plantain trees,
exhausted and chilled by the frost, upon a bed made of plantain leaves.
On the third day, we arrived at a forest region adorned with clusters of thickets— [the reading *abjaṣaṇḍaka* is questionable]— which, being devoid of people, appeared like the sky itself.
It was adorned with clusters of lotuses and thickets of shrubs;
it was divided by gaps created by those who gathered grass, wood, and other materials; and it was fashioned as if the sky itself were partitioned on all sides by the breaks between clouds.
There, abandoning the path he had been following and entering another forest, he spoke these words regarding an improper act: (9)

Now, because his brother and the other sages whom he wished to see were absent from Gauri’s hermitage, and because it had been forbidden that "the brother should not go anywhere intent on searching [for them]," his speech constitutes a failure to act, since the unnecessary delay of time would have interrupted the primary task of returning to his own home. 9.
"Let us go to this hermitage, adorned by a circle of sages,
where my seven brothers remain in the forests seeking their goals in this very manner."
"We eight brothers were born through that singular birth; we are composed of one consciousness and possess one and the same resolve. (11)

He clarifies the statement "thus indeed [we were] seekers" with the words beginning "O brothers. By virtue of having many desires born from that previously described longing for the enjoyment of sovereignty over the seven continents, all eight of us brothers became intent on austerity, consisting of a single consciousness and characterized primarily by a firm resolve of one form. || 11 ||
Therefore, they too, having come here and relying on their own resolve for asceticism,
remain here, their sins destroyed by various forms of penance.
"Previously, I came here with those brothers and dwelt for six months in the hermitage of Gaurī; it was there that he was seen by me. (13)
"Here in Gaurī’s hermitage; for that reason, he who was previously seen is this very same person seen before us"—such is the expression of recognition (pratyabhijñā). || 13 ||
In the shade of the trees within the flower groves, the young fawns slept peacefully;
at the entrance of the leaf-huts, the parrots perched rested, reciting the insights of the sacred scriptures.

He describes that very hermitage with the word "puṣpa" [etc.]: where even the parrots, resting upon the tops of the leaf-huts (uṭaja), have recited—that is, presented—the perspectives of various scriptures. || 14 ||
Therefore, come for the sake of prosperity to this hermitage of sages, which resembles the world of Brahmā;
let us go there, for our minds will become exceedingly pure through its merits. (15)
There, our minds will become exceedingly clear through the destruction of all defects. || 15 ||
For even among the learned, the steadfast, and those who know reality,
the mind of men indeed hastens toward the perception of the conviction that "enough."

The meaning is: when even wise men have their minds stirred upon beholding those sages whose thoughts are stilled by the vision of reality and whose hearts are full, how much more so must it be for us two? || 16 ||
When he said, "So be it," we two reached that hermitage of the sage;
and there, in the great forest, we beheld the horse in its true form.
The internal withdrawal of that [world] by means of its very form; that is to say, the hermitage becomes empty of its formal appearance. || 17 ||
Neither a tree, nor a hut, nor any shrub, nor a human being;
neither a sage, nor a child, nor anything else, neither the sacrificial altar nor a twice-born brahmin—[he did not spare any of these]. 18.
He states that very point with the words beginning "not a tree," etc. (18).
That infinite forest was nothing but pure emptiness;
scorched by heat on all sides, it was like the sky resting upon the earth.
While he was saying, "Alas, what misery! What has happened here?", we wandered for a very long time and then saw a small tree in one place.
In that ascetic who was my companion. || 20 ||
With glossy skin and dense luster, cool like a rain cloud,
an aged ascetic sat established in meditative absorption beneath him.
We two sat for a long time on a grassy spot in front of that sage, beneath his shadow, until he turned away from his meditation.
Then, after a long time, out of agitation and impulsiveness, I spoke these words loudly: "O Sage, awaken from your meditation! (23)
From fickleness, that is, from a fickle nature. || 23 ||
Awakened by my loud voice, the sage—
like a lion at the roar of a cloud— yawned and spoke.
"Who are you two holy men? Where has that hermitage of Gaurī gone?
By whom have I been brought here, and what time is this that prevails? (25)
Here, in this empty wilderness. || 25 ||
When he said "So be it," I also replied: "O Blessed One, know that it is thus;
there is nothing [unknown] to us, so why does even the Buddha not know it himself? (26)
"O Blessed One, regarding this which you have asked, we two do not know anything at all"—this is the ellipsis. Therefore, you alone must know.
Even though you are the Buddha, the omniscient one, why do you not know it yourself through the power of yoga? || 26 ||
Having heard this, the Blessed One once again became absorbed in meditation;
he beheld the entire account of us as well as of himself.
After awakening from meditation, the sage spoke after only a moment:
"Listen to this marvel, for you two, noble ones, are knowers of what must be done."
O virtuous ones, behold this young Kadamba tree, which is my dwelling place in the wilderness and appears like a flowering braid of hair. (29)
This [body] is my abode and my own dwelling place; for this very reason, because it is to be pitied, it is called "little son" (putraka). || 29 ||
For some reason, while he was present, the virtuous Vāgīśvarī dwelt there for ten years, experiencing all the seasons.
Having become Satī Gaurī Vāgīśvarī, she dwelt here as Satī Sarasvatī. || 30 ||
Then, by him, a vast and dense forest was created here,
renowned as Gaurīvana, adorned with flowers and the seasons.

Adorned and embellished by all seasons, in which flowers predominate—at that time, for that reason—[it was] with the playful, swaying songs of female bees, captivating to the minds of people, and the gazes of sweet-voiced birds.
(Note: there is also a reading "viloka" for "vilola").
The sky was canopied by hundreds of moons and clouds bearing flowers, while the quarters of space were strewn with particles of pollen from excellent lotuses.

He describes that very place as follows, beginning with the words "bhṛṅgāṅganā" and so on. The term "aṅga" is an address to both [the speaker and the listener]. It is a place where the sweet-voiced birds, the cuckoos, are restless with the charming songs and playful movements of the female bees; likewise, it is filled with trees that resemble clouds and shower down flowers.
There was a canopy for the sky adorned with a hundred moons. || 32 ||
The quarters were made fragrant by the nectar of mandāra and kunda flowers;

it was filled with heaps of blossoming flowers reaching to the moon; it was beautiful with the blooming smiles of clusters of santānaka blossoms; and it possessed a multitude of vine-like women exhaling the scent of perfumed breezes.

By which the quarters and directions were made fragrant with the nectar of mandāra and kunda flowers; wherein there was the perfection, splendor, and abundance of moon-disks characterized by heaps of blossoming flowers that were fully and beautifully exhaling [their fragrance] on all sides. 33.
The city of Puṣpākara resounds with the songs of bees and abounds in pavilions formed from clusters of flowers frequented by female bees; there,
throngs of celestial nymphs and Siddha women dangle upon flower-swinging cradles as tender as the web of moonbeams.

It stood like a city of spring, the season that brings forth flowers, enriched with pavilions formed from clusters of blossoms frequented by female bees; there, throngs of celestial and Siddha women swayed upon delicate flower-swinging cradles that were like nets of moonbeams on all sides.
Its banks were crowded with flocks of hārīta ducks, swans, parrots, cuckoos, ruddy geese, crows, cakravāka birds, bhāsas, and sparrows;
it was delightful with the playful sport of bheruṇḍas, wild cocks, piñjala birds, golden-crested pheasants, peacocks, and cranes.
His limbs were crowded with flocks of birds such as the hārīta; the *hemacūḍās* are partridges, and the *rāḍhas* are a species of bird.
The window possessed a cluster of lotus-stamens formed by the crowns of Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Suras, and Siddhas rubbing against its lotus-feet;
it held the fragrance of the multitude of golden, tender Campaka flowers, like a mass of clouds in a sky filled with stars.

In that place stands the Kadamba-Sarasvatī, whose lotus-bases (the two feet) are rubbed by the crowns of Gandharvas, Yakṣas, and others; it is likewise a dwelling for fragrant breezes, and thus its scent is like gold, having been taken from the clusters of tender Campaka flowers by the starry clouds.
It was cooled by the rays of the sun hidden by the arrangement of young creepers and sprouts shaken by a gentle breeze,
and it was sipped by the floods of pollen from the clusters of flowers of the kadamba, karavīra, coconut, tālī, and tamāla trees.

It was cool within because the rays of the lord of day were obstructed by the arrangements and expansions of young creepers whose sprouts were shaken by the gentle breeze in the hidden groves; likewise, it was yellow, being drenched by the floods of floral pollen from the kadamba and other trees.
It abounds in clusters of white, night-blooming, blue, and red lotuses, and resounds with the calls of cakoras, cranes, ruddy geese, kadamba ducks, and swans;
it possesses diverse powers dwelling within the cavities of *tālīsa*, guggulu, sandalwood, *pāribhadra*, and auspicious trees.
In those lotus-pools strewn with white water-lilies and interspersed with night-blooming lilies and blue lotuses,
where cranes and other flocks of birds frolic in joy; and wherein dwells a wondrous power that fulfills all desired objects, sporting within the hollows of palm trees and other such trees.

For some reason, Gaurī, whose face is like the orb of the bright moon, remained for a long time in that forest as Kadambavāgīśvarī, who shares half the body of Hara. She was like a digit of the moon upon the head of Śiva among all the riches of the forest.
Regarding the cause for this, he says: "In that forest..."—in that forest, Gaurī, who shares half the body of Hara...
For some reason, having become Kadambavāgīśvarī, she dwelt there for a long time; the meaning is that she alone is the cause of the forest's abundance. || 39 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-first chapter, titled "The Description of Gauri’s Hermitage," in the *Tāpasopākhyāna* of the *Brahmagītā*, within the *Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa* of the *Mokṣopāya* section of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa*. 81.
Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-first chapter, titled "The Description of Gaurī’s Hermitage," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and eighty-second canto.
The aged ascetic said:
"In this very *kadamba* tree, I have spent ten years according to my own will."
Having stayed there, Gaurī then went to the palace that is half the body of Hara.
In this [chapter], the meeting of Kadamba-tapas with his brothers,
as well as the fulfillment of the causes for the boons and curses within their homes, is described.
In this very Kadamba tree, my own abode, whose virtues have been thus described. || 1 ||
Sprinkled by the nectar of her touch, this young kadamba tree,
as if seated upon her lap, does not at all succumb to old age.
Sitting upon his lap like a child, he does not at all undergo old age or decrepitude.
Then, when Gaurī had become purified, that great forest became like an ordinary forest,
subsisting upon the crowds of people.
Sustained by the masses of people with offerings of grass, wood, fruits, flowers, and the like, it attained a state of commonality with other forests. || 3 ||
There is a country named Mālava; there I was the lord of the earth.
Once, having abandoned the glory of sovereignty, I was wandering through the hermitages of sages.
Now the Sage tells his own life story, beginning with the words "In Mālava," and so forth. (4)
Having arrived at this place, I was honored here by the inhabitants of Āśrama; remaining beneath this kadamba tree, I became established in meditation. || 5 ||
Then, at a certain time in the past, you arrived at this hermitage for the sake of asceticism together with seven brothers.
Those eight ascetics lived there at that time in such a manner that other ascetics were held in high esteem by them as true ascetics.
Those eight ascetics then lived as ascetics in that manner;
the meaning is that they became honored and worshipful even to other ascetics. || 7 ||
In due course, one of them went immediately to Śrīparvata,
while the second departed for ascetic penance to [the presence of] his lord Kārtikeya.
After some time, among them, you alone went to Śrīparvata; likewise, the other three also did so. 8.
The third went to Vārāṇasī, while the fourth went to the Himālaya.
Here itself, those other four wise ones performed supreme penance—meaning they practiced intense asceticism. The absence of the augment *aṭ* is an archaic (Vedic) usage. || 9 ||
And for each one of all these, this was their individual desire: "May I become the lord of the earth of this entire world consisting of all its continents. (10)
Then this desired object was accomplished for all of them by means of excellent boons granted by their chosen deities, who were pleased by their ascetic penance.
With the most excellent boons. || 11 ||
Then, having enjoyed the Dharma-yuga upon the earth, those brothers went to their own abode, just as Brahmā goes to the city of Brahman.

They remained performing penance as if they were burning [with fervor]. The genitive case here is used in the sense of disregard (*anādare*), according to the rule for the genitive denoting a characteristic state (*bhāvalakṣaṇe*).

Having enjoyed—that is, experienced—the Kṛta Yuga, which is characterized by righteousness, upon the earth, at its conclusion, the four-faced Creator [Vedhas] went to the city of Brahmā, as it were, the world of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*). || 12 ||
O noble one, at that time, during the ritual for granting boons, those brothers of yours diligently entreated their own chosen deities as they were prepared to bestow boons.
O fortunate one, you have requested this boon that is about to be spoken. || 13 ||
O Goddess, while we all remain as lords of the seven continents,
may all these subjects, including those dwelling in every stage of life, abide in truth.

The expression "lord of the seven islands" (*saptadvīpeśvara*) is a designation emphasizing the abstract state [of sovereignty]. May all subjects, who are the people born of the lineage, be truthful, having abandoned falsehood. Likewise, may all inhabitants of the seven islands abide by the duty (*dharma*) of their respective stages of life (*āśrama*). This also implies a prayer for the fulfillment of the duties of the social classes (*varṇadharma*). || 14 ||
Having respectfully accepted that purpose of their chosen deity,
the Goddess said to them, "So be it," and vanished from sight.
That chosen deity, having accepted—that is, having consented to—each respective object thus requested. || 15 ||
Then those residents of the hermitage all went to their own dwellings;
they have all departed, and I alone have not gone.
I alone have not gone. || 16 ||
I alone, with my mind focused solely on meditation in a solitary place,
stand like a mountain at the foot of a cluster of Vāgīśvarī trees.
To the question "Why is that so?", he says: "I... (verse 17).
Then, as this time flowed on, consisting of seasons and years, this entire forest was cut down by people living on its borders. (18)
"This is that very Kadamba tree"—thus is the analysis of the compound.
People worship this unfading Kadamba tree intensely, as well as me alone, because it is the abode of Vāgīśvarī and because we are attained through the same single meditative concentration. (19)
And they worship me alone. || 19 ||
"Now that you two long-lived ascetics have come to this place,
I have related all of this in its entirety, as it was perceived by me through meditation."
Therefore, having risen, O virtuous ones, go; you have arrived at home, where all your brothers are assembled together with their wives and kinsmen.

"Having come here, you two may now go home. Those brothers of yours have already been reunited with their wives and kinsmen; for all eight of you, there shall be prosperity in your own abode, like the gathering of the high-souled Vasus in the world of Brahmā. (22)
"There will be a meeting for all eight of you with the eight Vasus in the world of Brahmā, the world of the gods.
When he had spoken thus, I questioned that supreme ascetic: "Noble one, because of my doubt regarding this marvel, I shall now describe it to you."
"O noble ladies"—this is the address to Rāma's assembly. || 23 ||
"O Blessed One, this earth indeed consists of only seven continents;
how is it that eight lords of the seven continents can exist simultaneously? (24)
The Kadamba ascetic said:
"What has been stated so far is not even inconsistent for us;
however, hear from me this other matter which is even more incoherent. (25)
"This much alone is inconsistent and incoherent"—this is what we [say].
However, listen to me as I speak of and cite something else that is even more incoherent and utterly inconsistent; this is the meaning. || 25 ||
These eight brothers, having become ascetics there at the dissolution of their bodies,
will all become lords of the seven continents within the interior of their home.
These two verses are a restatement of what was previously said, intended as a prelude to what is about to be explained. || 26 ||
Listen to me: these eight kings shall become lords of the seven islands here upon these very seats of the earth and in these very palaces. (27)
It is said that these eight have eight blameless wives,
as constant and radiant as the eight stars in the various quarters of the sky.
The comparison "like a group of eight stars" for the intermediate directions, such as the East and so forth, is a poetic conceit (utprekṣā). || 28 ||
When they had departed for long-term asceticism, those eight wives became sorrowful,
for separation from men is difficult for women to endure.
For this reason, separation from my husband is as unbearable as a serpent. || 29 ||
Suffering on account of those conditions, they performed severe penance;
by their performance of a hundred cāndrāyaṇa fasts, Pārvatī became pleased with them.

When there was repeated recollection of those husbands through faith, those women, being distressed, performed severe penance. As for what that penance was named, he says: "the hundred Cāndrāyaṇas. || 30 ||
At the time of worship in the inner apartments, that invisible Goddess, the Sovereign, spoke these words to each of them individually.
The Goddess said:
"O young girl, let a boon be accepted for the sake of your husband and for your own sake;
you have long been emaciated by asceticism, like a flower-cluster withered by the summer heat."
By the heat of summer. || 32 ||
Having heard these words of the Goddess, Ciraṇṭikā, having offered flowers,
began to offer praise to the Sovereign Goddess according to her own latent impressions.
Gaurī, having offered flowers, and Ciraṇṭikā, a married woman, having presented a handful of flowers at her feet. || 33 ||
Speaking softly, Ānandamantharā addressed these words to the goddess stationed in the sky, as a peahen might address a line of clouds: 34.
Slow due to joy, with a faltering voice; or perhaps it is the name of the eldest [daughter]. || 34 ||
Ciraṇṭikā said: "O Goddess, just as you have love for Śambhu, the God of gods, so may I have love for my husband; may he, my husband, become immortal. (35)
May he be immortal, free from death. || 35 ||
The Goddess said:
"From the beginning of creation, due to the firmness of destiny, immortality cannot be obtained.
Therefore, O lady of virtuous vows, choose another boon than this through penance and gifts. (36)
Because of the firmness of destiny—the command of the Lord—which has been operative since the beginning of creation, starting from the first creation, it is impossible to break it. || 36 ||
Ciraṇṭikā said:
O Goddess, let this not be unattainable for me; let not the life-breath of my husband depart even for a moment from within his house to the outside. 37.
Even from a moment, and even from a long time, because of the word "api" (even). || 37 ||
"O Mother, let this boon be granted to me: that when my husband's body falls [into ashes] within my own home, may it happen then. (38)
The Goddess said:
"So be it, O daughter! Even though your husband has gone to another world, you shall become his beloved wife after the end of this body; of this there is no doubt. (39)

Perceiving that foolish woman’s lack of skill in requesting a suitable bridegroom, the Goddess herself grants another boon, saying: "And you... [referring to] sovereignty over the seven continents in another world. (39)
Having spoken thus, that voice of Gaurī ceased within the belly of the sky,
like the sound of a mass of clouds rising faultlessly and powerfully.
Blameless and faultless, she is intent upon bringing joy to the world.
After the queen had departed, after some time, their husbands all returned from the various quarters, having obtained great boons.
From the quarters, from the intermediate directions. || 41 ||
Today let this husband also go to his wife's side;
let there be a mutual reunion between brothers and kinsmen. (42)
Now hear of this other matter, a strange and confused account concerning them—an extraordinary event that obstructed the noble task. (43)
He also cites another instance of impropriety with the words "this": it is an obstruction to the noble deeds, which are the fruits of virtuous actions. (43)
While these [sages] were performing their austerities, their parents, accompanied by their daughter-in-law,
went forth filled with sorrow to visit the series of holy fords and hermitages of the sages.
Accompanied by and together with their daughters-in-law and granddaughters. || 44 ||
Disregarding their own bodies and desiring the welfare of their sons,
the two of them made every effort to go to that village of Kalāpa.
By the word "body" (śarīra), the pleasure to be enjoyed by it is indicated through its independence [from that body]. That well-known sacred site (tīrtha) called Kalāpagrāma—|| 45 ||
As they proceeded along the path to the village of sages, they beheld a white man,
tawny, short, with limbs smeared with ashes and hair standing erect.
They saw on the path a man who was tawny in complexion and short in stature. || 46 ||
When the two of them disregarded the scattering of dust, suspecting him to be an old traveler,
he spoke to them with mounting anger.

Then, suspecting those two—the parents of the eight—to be some old travelers, they disregarded the sage and offered him no respect, nor did they perform salutations, worship, or praise; on the contrary, in their haste to depart, they even kicked up a cloud of dust over him as they went. At that offense, he was filled with wrath.
The sage said: || 47 ||
"O great fool with your wife! Seeking a sacred ford, you go past me, Durvāsas, without having offered the prescribed salutation. (48)
He states what he said at that time: "savadhūka" etc. "Avihitānatiḥ" means one who has not performed a prostration. || 48 ||
As you depart, even the great boons obtained through your ascetic penance will turn adverse for both your daughters-in-law and your sons. (49)
The boons acquired through austerity will instead become contrary and result in suffering. || 49 ||
While he who had spoken thus was being honored by the king together with his wives and daughters-in-law, the sage suddenly vanished from sight.
Then those two parents, accompanied by their daughters-in-law, returned home deeply distressed, emaciated, with dejected faces and devoid of hope.
Becoming despondent, they turned back and returned to their own home. || 51 ||
Therefore, I say to you: not even one of their names is improper; rather, there are hundreds of thousands of improper things, like pustules bursting upon a boil. (52)
Therefore, I say that it is not merely one inconsistency they possess, but rather hundreds of thousands of inconsistencies;

for the conception of a kingdom over the seven continents inevitably entails the conception of the mountains, peaks, and so forth contained within them. The sense is this: just as there is a goiter on the neck, and upon it there are boils, and those are clearly manifest.
The meaning is that if these [faults] manifest, an undesirable consequence follows; and upon that undesirable consequence, yet another undesirable consequence arises, and so on. || 52 ||

In this great city of the mental constructs of the consciousness-ether, such diverse and incongruous things come into being, even though it is of the nature of emptiness— just as the manifestations of visible objects appear in the sky, which is itself invisible.

Thus, he says "the sky of consciousness" (*cidvyoma*) to show that in this world composed of illusion (*māyāmaya*), hundreds of thousands of inconsistencies likewise arise. In this great city in the form of the world, constructed by the volitions (*saṃkalpa*) of the sky of consciousness,
millions of such diverse and inconsistent things come into being, just as they do in the [physical] sky.
The meaning is that, just as manifestations such as cities of the Gandharvas, comets, headless trunks, and meteors occur due to the force of portents, so it is in this case. || 53 ||

I0 Śrī0 Vā0 De0 Mo0 Ni0 U0 Br0: Within the *Tāpasopākhyāna*, this is the one hundred and eighty-second canto, titled "The Description of the Lord of the Seven Continents," belonging to the *Saptadvīpeśvaropākhyāna*. 182.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Lord of the Seven Continents," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and eighty-third canto.
Kundadanta said:
Then, I questioned that ascetic there at Gaurī’s hermitage.
His hair was withered and matted by old age, like the tips of *darbha* grass dried out by an ascetic’s heat.
Here, the mutual victory of those possessing inner essence, despite their conflicting boons and curses, is correctly determined based on the words of the Four-faced One (Brahmā).
His hair, worn out by old age, was like the tips of darbha grass that have withered in the summer heat and become entangled with one another. || 1 ||
There is but one earth consisting of seven islands;
how is it that you eight have become the supreme lords of those seven islands? (2)
Being asked "What?", he replied: "It is one alone. (2)
How can that living being, who has no exit from his dwelling to the outside,
achieve world conquest as the lord of the seven continents?
He states the second question: "Of whom... (verse 3).
How can those curses, which were granted by boon-granters as boons, turn into their opposite? For how could a shadow ever become heat? || 4 ||
He states the third question with the words "by whom": how do those [trees] with cool shade come to possess the heat of the summer sun? || 4 ||
How can two properties that are mutually incompatible abide in one place?
And how can the substratum itself become the superstratum within its own self? (5)
He states that it is difficult and impossible for a single fruit to possess the dual nature of both a boon and a curse by saying "mutually" (*mithaḥ*).

How can two contradictory properties—defined as the specific delimiters of the fruits of a boon and a curse, namely auspiciousness and inauspiciousness—possibly abide in one and the same substratum? This is because it is impossible for them to reside within a single substrate.
Let there be a mutual dependence between those two factors; regarding that, he says: "The support alone... (Verse 5).
The ascetic of Gaurī’s hermitage said:
"O virtuous one, listen further:
when this eighth [day] has fully arrived, you will see him in that region along with his kinsmen."
The ascetic Kadamba gave the answer to all these questions by means of a narrative account, saying:
"Do you see? O virtuous one, what do you perceive here that is contradictory or inconsistent?
Listen now to what happened thereafter; by that very account, your resolution will be attained—this is the intended meaning.
When this very day, the eighth from today, has arrived, you two will reach that region of Mathurā together with your kinsmen; this is the implied meaning. || 6 ||
Having reached that place from here, you two will dwell in happiness; remaining in the comfort of your own kin, you shall abide thus for some time.
Then those eight brothers will die one after another at home;
thereafter, their kinsmen will consign their bodies to the fire.
That is to say, they will purify by means of cremation in those respective fires those who have been established in various fires and are dependent upon them, through their funeral rites (antyeṣṭi).
Their respective spaces of consciousness, situated separately,
shall remain for a mere moment like those in deep sleep, as if insentient.
Living beings are the space of consciousness. || 9 ||
In the meantime, those actions of theirs— consisting of boons and curses— will, by the nature of things,
converge together in the sky.

He begins to explain the resolution of the contradiction regarding karmas with the words "In this... (etasmin). "By nature" (dharmataḥ) means by the essential character of the necessity of power. "In one place" (ekatra) means in the ether (khe) delimited by that particular mind. || 10 ||
Those karmas, in the form of presiding deities, will produce separate bodies of boons and curses as a collection. || 11 ||

Those presiding deities, who bestow the respective fruits of those actions, will assume those forms and separately fashion individual caskets—closed boxes composed of collections corresponding to each [karma]. Thus, the boons and curses, having been thus encapsulated, will manifest as distinct bodies. || 11 ||
The fortunate ones who possess lotuses in their hands, whose weapons are the staffs of Brahmā, whose limbs are white as the moon, and who have four arms— these excellent beings shall go there.
He describes their distinction of dress with the words "excellent" (varāḥ): they will go, that is, they will attain [the goal]. || 12 ||
There, curses shall manifest as three-eyed beings holding tridents;
they will be terrifying, resembling dark clouds, two-armed, and with faces knit in frowns. (13)
Because Durvāsas is a portion of Rudra, and because he is intent on bestowing the fruits of evil deeds and possesses a terrible form, they have three eyes and hold tridents in their hands. || 13 ||
The excellent ones will say:
"Go far away! The time for our curses has arrived;
who is capable of transgressing it, just as one cannot bypass the arrival of the seasons? (14)
Like the seasons beginning with spring. || 14 ||
The curses will say:
"Go far away, O excellent ones; our time has arrived, just as the seasons do. For who is capable of transgressing that? (15)
They will speak thus:
"Sirs, we have been made by the Sage; we have been made by the Maker of Day (the Sun), since the Lord was formerly superior even to the Munis. || 16 ||

In this regard, the excellent [sages] demonstrate their own superiority through the excellence of their source, saying "O venerable ones. For it is understood that the Creator (Dhātṛ) created the Blessed Sun for the sages in ancient times. || 16 ||
While the excellent ones were thus speaking, the curses of those with angry minds toward the excellent ones were uttered by Vivasvat:
"You have been made from a portion of Vivasvat, and we have been made from a portion of Rudra."
"Rudra is superior to the gods; the sage is born from a portion of Rudra.
Having said this, they raised their peaks against them like mountains.
Having spoken thus, she raised her uplifted [weapons]. The substitution of *aḍ* for the case-ending follows the Vedic rule *supāṃ suluk* (Pāṇini 7.1.39), as in the expression *tā tā piṇḍānām*.
"Horns" refers to the tips of the tridents. || 18 ||
While the enemies stand with their horns raised in curses, the excellent ones,
laughing, will proclaim the certainty that has been made an object of direct perception.

O Śāpas, having abandoned your wickedness, let the end of this matter be deliberated upon through correct investigation preceded by internal means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), regarding the object of knowledge (*prameya*) that has been determined as your own interest.
That very matter which is to be settled at the conclusion of the quarrel should be investigated from the very beginning. (20)
"Pāpatā" means the performance of what is improper; the remainder of the sense is that "that very thing should be done first. || 20 ||
"Having gone to the city of the Grandfather (Brahmā), a decision must be made by us at the end of this dispute; why is this not arranged here at the outset? (21)
Having heard the words spoken by the boons and curses, he accepted them, saying "So be it.
For who, even if a fool, would not accept a statement that is endowed with sound reasoning? (22)
Then, along with the boons, the curses shall go to the supreme state of Brahmā;
for the goal of those of great majesty always leads to the destruction of doubt.
The goal is the refuge. || 23 ||
Having first offered salutations, they will relate all that occurred to one another;
and having heard it, Brahmā will speak to them.
Brahmā said:
"O lords, those who possess internal essence triumph over both boons and curses."
"Let us surely investigate among ourselves which of us possesses inner substance. (25)

Victorious are those who possess internal essence—that firmness of the cognition of forms produced by both the study of the scriptures and steadfast practice. Let this be sought; let it be thoroughly examined.
Having heard this, they entered in order to examine the essence of boons;
for curses are the heart of boons, and boons are the heart of curses.
The expression "they have entered the belly" is a figurative statement; it means that they deliberated within one another. || 26 ||
Having searched for one another and personally realized the essential truth of their own hearts, they will come together and speak to the Grandfather.
By means of a union characterized by mutual harmony. || 27 ||
The Śāpas will say:
"O Lord of Subjects, we have been defeated because we lack inner substance;
only those with inner substance are truly excellent, remaining as immovable as pillars of diamond. (28)
"O Blessed One, these boons and curses are indeed always [mere] mental constructs for us;
surely our bodies are nothing other than composed of consciousness. (29)

In this context, they show the fundamental consciousness (*mūlasaṃvid*) in order to state that the firmness of the forms [of objects] through the intense practice of cognition constitutes their predominance—expressed as "We, indeed. Here, "body" refers to one's own essential nature (*svarūpa*). || 29 ||
For that very consciousness of the granter which remains as "the boon has been given," remains for me, the petitioner, as "this boon has been obtained. (30)
They establish that very point with the words beginning "of the Giver of Boons" (varadasya) and so forth. || 30 ||
The body is the manifestation of representation-only (vijñaptimātra); from that, it itself is the fruit.
Through the delusions of hundreds of places and times, one sees, experiences, and consumes [it]. (31)

For the fruit of merit is the body, which is the locus for the enjoyment of pleasure; and that body is the manifestation of mere-cognition (vijñaptimātra) consisting of mental construction. Therefore, that very cognition, having assumed the form of a body, perceives and experiences various objects of enjoyment through hundreds of delusions consisting of the conceptualization of space, time, and so forth; therein it eats what is to be eaten.

Because it is grasped by the self that bestows boons, when this consciousness is accumulated over a period of time, it then becomes invincible due to its internal essence; however, that which arises from a curse is not so.

In that regard, because it has been received from the Bestower of Boons (Varada)— who is the self of consciousness (saṃvidātman) brought under control by a firm resolve formed during the time of scriptural austerity— the mental construction of the boon (varakalpanā-cit), when it has become perfectly nourished and strengthened at the stage of its fruition at a later time, then and there becomes possessed of internal essence (antaḥsārā). || 32 ||
When the granting of boons has been practiced for a very long time by givers of boons for the sake of those seeking boons, then that becomes the essence of all boons.
Whatever consciousness one practices for a very long time, that alone quickly becomes its essence; it swiftly comes to be, and one quickly becomes identified with it.
To the question "Why is that so?", he says: "That very... (verse 34).
Among cognitions, that which is pure is indeed perceived as extremely pure, while that which is impure is perceived as impure; there is no equality between them over time.
Regarding that, they say that because it is scriptural, there is a greater strength in its purity; thus [the text says] "of the pure ones.
The genitive case in "saṃvidām" (of consciousnesses) is used for specification (*nirdhāraṇa*). Therefore, even in the result, there is no equality. || 35 ||
Even by a mere fraction of a moment, that which is superior is fulfilled through its own logic;
pride is not able to exert any other logic regarding the matter. (36)
They say that even due to seniority (*jyeṣṭhatva*), there is strength in a superior cognition, stating: "even by a moment's portion.

The sense is that because the senior [cognition] has not yet encountered opposition, it is firmly established. For indeed, the seniority of that which arises from non-valid cognition (*apramāṇaja*) is the determining factor for its being sublated; as, for example, in the case of the delusion of silver regarding an object confirmed by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

It is well known that for a cognition that is not dependent [on another], its seniority (jyeṣṭhatva) is the determining factor in its sublation; no other principle is capable of making this curse more powerful—this is the meaning. || 36 ||
An object situated at both extremes together becomes a mixed entity that is neutral, like milk mixed with water through the play of a blessing and a curse. (37)

For this very reason, he says "by that which is equal" (*samena*), meaning that where there is an equality of strength between two opposing actions—whether they be boons or curses—or an equality in the practice of means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and so forth, the result is necessarily a mixture of both. It stands on the boundary of both the auspicious and the inauspicious, such as the human body. || 37 ||
Or rather, through both blessings and curses,
consciousness itself experiences its own dual nature, as if it were a city within dreams.

Just as at one and the same time two equal things—a boon and a curse—are to be experienced in different locations, there, according to the principle stated in the *Vipaścit* narrative, the single consciousness of the individual soul (*jīvacit*) attains a dual form through the division of its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) due to the difference of bodies; thus he says: "by the two equal [things]. Just as in dreams, consciousness consists of cities.
In that same way, it undergoes a division as if through the differentiation of the bodies of the city's inhabitants. || 38 ||
O Lord, that very thing which was taught by you has been recited by me back to you in reverse; we shall depart quickly—salutations be unto you! (39)
Reflecting that such audacity in proclaiming the truth before the Lord was improper, they said, "It has been learned.

"That which was learned from you alone has been recited again before you; because it brings forth audacity, it is contrary and opposed [to your presence]. Therefore, forgive our offense of audacity. Thus, let there be salutation to you; we shall depart quickly."
Let us go to our own place. || 39 ||
Having spoken thus, that self-imposed curse, along with its host of curses, vanished somewhere,
like a hair-tuft seen in the sky when the darkness has subsided.

Cursing himself out of shame for having needlessly exerted himself and for manifesting his own folly, he departed for some unknown place; this was a "self-curse" (svayaṃśāpa). Just as when the disease of cataracts is cured, the illusory cluster of hairs seen in the sky vanishes somewhere, so it was with him. 40.
Then another series of boons, which obstructed his departure from the house,
fulfilled him with a corresponding purpose, like a command that fills one's station.

Thus, when Durvāsas’s curses had passed away, there arose another obstacle to their departure from their home— a rival for sovereignty over the seven continents— and yet another, a multitude of boons granted by Gaurī to their wives,
like a grammatical substitute (*ādeśa*) taking the place of the original element (*sthānin*) in the system of Vaiyākaraṇa, which led to disputes with the excellent sons of Sūrya.
He fulfilled the place of the curse; for he too was "samāna," meaning one whose purpose was of such a kind that its fruit was contradictory at the same time. || 41 ||
Those residing in the place of the curse will say:
"O Lord of Gods, we do not know the exit of the living beings of the seven continents from their abodes of death, just as one does not know the waters within a blind well. (42)
Those stationed at the place of the curse, the *śāpasthānakas*, who have chosen their wives, will speak to Brahmā. What do they say?

"O Lord of the Seven Islands (*saptadvīpeśa*)": O Lord of the Gods, we do not know the exit from the abode of the corpses of these living beings who are considered future lords of the seven islands; for we have obstructed it. This is the meaning.
From a blind well, from an empty well. || 42 ||
These excellent and noble heroes cause these lords of the seven islands to perform conquests of the quarters in battle within their dwellings on these islands. (43)
Therefore, O Lord of the Wise, since this conflict is thus unavoidable,
command us what must be performed by us for the sake of our welfare.
"Command that which is to be commanded for our welfare and success; that is to say, give us your orders. || 44 ||
Brahmā said:
"O you who are the lords of the seven islands, O you who are the bestowers of boons and the protectors of the home!
Your desire has indeed been fulfilled here, as it has for all of you."
The desire of all of you has indeed been fulfilled. || 45 ||
Depart from this state of dependence; for even those who were lords of the seven continents have remained in their homes for a long time, indeed for ages, yet they too perished in an instant. (46)
To explain how this was accomplished, he says: "Go! You must go toward this mutual dependence.

For although you eight brothers did not desire it for a long time—even when separated from each other's will—immediately after death, you remained for a long duration right in your own home, having become lords of the seven continents. || 46 ||
Immediately upon the falling of their bodies,
all these lords of the seven continents became supreme and most excellent beings in their own abodes.
He states that very point clearly: "immediately after" (samanantaram) || 47 ||
All will say:
"From where have these eight circles of the earth and the seven continents with their riches come?
Here, only a single terrestrial plane has been heard of and seen, and nothing else. (48)
Whence come these beings and their respective powers? They are "heard," well-known in the Vedas; they are "seen," well-known even in the world. || 48 ||
And how do these remain within some small chamber? How do great elephants appear within the subtle calyx of a lotus seed? (49)
Brahmā said:
It is fitting that you and we [should know] that the entire world is of the nature of space;
situated within the supreme atom of consciousness, it is experienced like an internal dream.

He offers the reply that this is not contradictory, as it is like a dream, stating: "It is logical. Since the entire world, consisting of both individual and collective forms, is of the nature of space, and everything down to the ultimate atom exists within [the Self], it is experienced as an internal dream; therefore, that which exists even within an atom appears inside one's own house.
The subsequent [inference] is by way of positive concomitance. || 50 ||
What wonder is there that it shines within the interior of its own home, inside the supreme atom? What cause for pride is there in the process of nature? 51.
So what is this unprecedented wonder? What is this pride or amazement? || 51 ||
Immediately after death, this world appears exactly as it is;
at that very moment, the consciousness itself manifests as a dense form within the void.
Demonstrating precisely this similarity to a dream, he clarifies what was stated with the words beginning "mṛteḥ" (after death), etc. || 52 ||
Even within an atom, the entire world is contained; what wonder is there that the earth with its seven continents shines within the interior of a house? (53)
That which appears as this mind-essence and the state of the world is never the world anywhere;
it shines as pure consciousness alone, like the sky through its emptiness.

That which appears as this world is indeed Consciousness itself. Since it appears as nothing but pure Consciousness, there is no material world-form anywhere that would not shine within it; this is the meaning. || 54 ||
Thus were those boons proclaimed by Brahmā, the giver of boons;
having then completely abandoned those bodies which consist of the delusion of the material world (ādhibhautika), [they attained liberation].
Having completely abandoned those previously imagined bodies—which consist of the delusion of the physical realm—through inquiry into reality, they became possessors of subtle (ātivāhika) bodies;

then, having bowed to the Unborn (Aja), they went together with him, without opposition, to the dwellings and treasuries of the respective gods within the seven continents fashioned by each one's own mind. This is the connection with the following verse. || 55 ||
Having prostrated before the Unborn One, those possessing subtle spiritual bodies (ātivāhika-deha) departed together;
they went to the seven islands and to the houses and treasuries of the gods, as well as to the people.
Meanwhile, those eight kings who were there—rulers of the seven continents, beloved and prosperous—remained for eight days. (57)

The word "yāvat" signifies totality. Those eight brothers were in that house, nourished by their kinsmen through auspicious rites such as sacrifices and the like; they belonged to the lineage of the first kings—the Manus, sons of Svayambhū—during the eight days of Brahmā, which correspond to the eightfold divisions of the world. This is the implied meaning.
The meaning is that they became sovereign rulers of the seven continents. || 57 ||
Unaware of one another and ignorant of each other as their own kinsmen, they dwell in one another's territories and seek the welfare of one another's intended objects. (58)

Because each one is imagined as being accompanied by his brothers, they are mutual kinsmen; yet, due to the division of the kingdom, they are ignorant regarding their respective shares of sovereignty. For this very reason, they are intent on each other's welfare and do not act with hostility. Among them, a certain one, beautiful in his youth, remained within the house itself.
He dwelt in happiness in the great city of Ujjayinī, the royal capital. || 59 ||
He describes the conceptualization of the different conducts for each of them with the words beginning "of those" (teṣām), etc. (verse 59).
A certain inhabitant of Śākadvīpa, intent on conquering all directions, wanders within the belly of the ocean with the desire to overcome the world of the Nāgas.
In the capital city of Kuśadvīpa, a certain king, having conquered all directions and being free from anxiety toward his entire subjects, lay asleep while supported by his beloved.
In the lake at the city atop the head of the lordly mountain of Śālmalidvīpa,
a certain [being] was engaged in water-sports together with a host of Vidyādharīs.
On the summit of the king of mountains, in the pleasure-lake of the city situated there. || 62 ||
In Krauñcadvīpa, at Hemapura, which is expanded by seven islands,
a certain king began to perform a horse sacrifice for eight days.
In which [the earth] was increased by those who brought great supernatural powers from the seven continents.
In Śālmalidvīpa, someone prepared for battle with a wanderer from another continent, having uprooted the great mountain ranges by pulling them with the tusks of world-elephants.
He was one who, prepared to fight with the king wandering through other continents,
had drawn up the great boundary mountains (kulācala) by means of the uprooted tusks of the elephants of the quarters. 64.
A certain king of Puṣkaradvīpa, Gomedadvīpaka, went forth by his power to bring back a daughter; Kaṣatsena became the eighth.
Gomedadvīpaka was his dwelling place; [he went] to conquer and bring him back to marry [her]. "Under his control" means under the sway of desire.
He whose army, while "rubbing away"—that is, crushing—the territories of his enemies, was such that he who formerly was the eighth among his brothers became [the ruler]. 65.
A certain king of Puṣkaradvīpa, the lord of the earth who possessed the Lokāloka mountain as his domain,
set out with a messenger, desiring to behold wealth and land.
It was a land of wealth, a place where treasures were stored, and he went there out of a desire to see it.
Thus, each of these [kings], exercising sovereignty over their respective islands within the space of their own homes, beheld what was appropriate to their own creative imagination.
Having abandoned the form of egoistic conceit, those excellent ones are then of two kinds;
through their consciousnesses, they attain oneness within the houses, just as the voids [merge] with the voids.

The connection with the subsequent verse is as follows: those by whom the form characterized by egoism has been abandoned even within the form of the subtle body (ātivāhika-deha), being of such a nature, they shall attain oneness with the consciousnesses of the eight living beings. || 68 ||
They shall go and become, for a long time, lords of the seven continents, having attained their desired goals; indeed, all eight of them shall be contented and possess great joy.
The meaning is: "having obtained a kingdom accompanied by contentment. || 69 ||

Thus, those of expanded intellect shall attain these goals through their austerities, for the very same reality that flashes within the consciousness of the wise also manifests externally; indeed, by whom has that not been attained through appropriate actions? (70)

He summarizes what has been stated with the word "iti" (thus). Thus, these eight brothers—whose purpose for action consists of the boons previously mentioned and who have blossomed through their austerities—will attain sovereignty over the seven continents.
That which flashes forth within the consciousness (*vit*) of the inner self as a firm resolve, that alone manifests externally.
By what [means] has that not been attained through appropriate acts such as austerity and recitation? The word "kila" indicates renown. || 70 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Seven Continents and Eight Mountains," in the *Brahmatapa* section of the *Mokṣopāya*, within the *Vāsiṣṭha* of the *Ārṣa*. 183.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Seven Continents and the Eight Mountains," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and eighty-fourth canto.
Kundadanta said:
Having been thus questioned, that ascetic dwelling at the foot of the Kadamba tree spoke as follows.
How could those eight earths, consisting of seven continents, appear within houses? || 1 ||
Even though millions of worlds may arise within the interior of a single house,
it is described as such because that which is merely unawakened consciousness appears in that manner.

When I asked him, "How can those grounds, each fifty crores of yojanas in extent, appear within houses that have so little space? he—the ascetic dwelling at the foot of the Kadamba tree—gave the following reply. || 1 ||
The Kadamba ascetic said:
This very element of consciousness is such that, although it has the nature of space, it is all-pervading;
wherever it resides, there it exists within itself by its own power.

The connection between the two [verses] is as follows: although he is of the nature of space and devoid of conceptual proliferation (prapañca), the Self perceives itself—either in the form of the three worlds or in another form such as deep sleep or the fourth state (turya)—without ever abandoning its own true nature. || 2 ||
In this way, he perceives his own self— whether in the form of the three worlds or in some other form— without ever abandoning its essential nature as space.
Kundadanta said:
How can a manifold diversity, established by its own nature, exist as real within that one, stainless, peaceful, auspicious, and supreme cause? (4)
The meaning of the doubt is that multiplicity in a single [locus] is contradictory. || 4 ||
The Kadamba ascetic said:
"Everything is the peaceful space of consciousness; there is no multiplicity here whatsoever.
Even that which appears so vast is like a whirlpool within water."

This diversity is not real, but is produced by delusion; and since that [diversity] is not contradictory even in the case of a single moon—just as there is an appearance of duality [in it]—he gives the answer with the words "all" (sarvam), intending this. || 5 ||
That in which these non-existent objects appear as if they were real entities is the sky of consciousness, whose nature is like dream and deep sleep; that is its own pure, innate form.
Like dream and deep sleep, one's own innate body—the very nature of the self—is unknown because its true essence has been forgotten. || 6 ||
For even that which is in motion is motionless, and even a mountain is not a mountain;
just as the nature of consciousness appears in dreams, so too does its nature appear as residing in external objects.

Thus, he shows that there is no contradiction: "saspanda" (with vibration). The meaning is that the nature, which is the essence of pure existence (*sanmātra*), is to be understood as being exactly the same even when it pertains to imagined objects. || 7 ||
Neither intrinsic natures nor objects exist for that which is appropriate to the nature of all things;
whatever form was manifested at the beginning of creation remains exactly as it is.
In the appropriate, real form of that which is the self of all, there is neither the nature of creation and so forth, nor the objects produced by it. || 8 ||
Indeed, there is no other form whatsoever that consists of shining or non-shining;
for thus, the self of substance and consciousness—the consciousness-space—stands as nothing but this alone.
Nor is it insentient even by way of its substantial nature.
Just as the one consciousness alone shines forth clearly in a dream as if it had become a hundred thousand people in an army,
so too does its state of being objects appear.
That which is the sky of consciousness, shining brilliantly by itself within its own pure self, is experienced as the world, appearing in that very form through that [consciousness] alone. (11)
Just as the cognition of heat appears even when fire is absent, so too does an object appear as its own illuminator within the void that consists of pure consciousness alone. 12.
Just as in a dream, even though fire is unreal, the consciousness of the dream itself manifests as heat. || 12 ||
Just as in a dream one perceives the nature of a pillar in the sky even though no pillar exists there,
so too this manifoldness of it, though non-different, appears as if different.
At the beginning of creation, the nature of all things was indeed the cessation of their own inherent nature;
whatever was perceived by the space of consciousness (cidvyoman) in whatever manner, that it experiences even today in that very same way. (14)
How, then, is there a necessity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) in that case? To this he says: "At the beginning of creation" (*ādisarge*). || 14 ||
Just as the tree itself exists within its flowers, leaves, fruits, and trunk,
so too does the Supreme, which is the Self of all, exist everywhere as both the transcendent and the immanent.
Likewise, there is another world. || 15 ||
The succession of creations is but water in the ocean of the ultimate sky;
emptiness is the consciousness of creation within the great space of ultimate reality. (16)
The cognitions of creation are the appearances of creation. || 16 ||
Ultimate reality (paramārtha) and manifestation (sarga) are synonyms, like the words "taru" and "vṛkṣa.
Through awakening one realizes this; through lack of awakening, however, duality leads only to suffering. (17)
The ultimate truth is this certainty alone: that this entire world is one.
Indeed, through the awakening brought about by the study of the inner science (adhyātmaśāstra), this very state constitutes liberation. 18.
Brahman is the body of volition for that which has the form of conscious volition;
that very thing is the form of the world. Therefore, the world has Brahman as its essence.
Regarding this, he says "of the conceptualization" (saṃkalpasya) to explain how there is only one [cause] therein. || 19 ||
From which words turn back, or perhaps do not turn back at all—so too do injunctions and prohibitions, as well as the views of existence and non-existence. (20)
Because all words are restricted to those subtle elements (tanmātra), they do not cease at all—or rather, they do indeed cease. // 20 //
That which is non-silence yet silence, the individual soul (jīvātman) whose state is like that of a stone,
which is being itself yet appears as non-being— that is called by the name Brahman.
The meaning is that it is real yet appears as unreal, according to such scriptural passages as "It moves, and it does not move," and so forth. || 21 ||
In the entirely single, dense, and stainless Brahman alone, what is activity and what is cessation? What are entities such as existence and non-existence?
Activity is creation; cessation is dissolution. || 22 ||
When within a single, undifferentiated state of deep sleep, the delusions of dreaming appear as if variegated and continuous; (23)
In this very existence of the sky of consciousness, which is itself undifferentiated, many primordial creations appear as if variegated and continuous, though they are not so.
Roots are the seeds, the states of dissolution, and the states of creation. || 24 ||
Just as one substance joined with another substance brings about a different effect,
so too does the internal vibration, whose essence is consciousness, mutually manifest in such a manner.

He explains how it shines forth with the words "in a substance" (*dravye*). Just as when one substance, such as curd and the like, is joined or mixed with another substance, such as sugar and the like, it brings about a different effect—distinct from its individual effects—such as the effects of relish, nourishment, or the pacification of bile; so too [does it act] within the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) of living beings.

The meaning is that the essence of the cognizer’s consciousness, having become manifest and having emerged through the external doors of the eyes and other senses, becomes conjoined with the mental modification (*vṛtti*) taking the form of a jar or the like; then, by the removal of the veil over the consciousness that underlies each respective object such as a jar or cloth, it brings about the mutual manifestation of the triad (*tripuṭī*).
All objects are always nothing but the essence of consciousness and are non-obstructive;
they appear exactly as they do because of their identity with pure consciousness alone. (26)

For this very reason, he says "all" to indicate that even objects such as jars possess existence and manifestation only by depending on the consciousness (cit) that is their own substratum; thus, they consist essentially of that [consciousness] alone. Just as they appeared at the beginning of creation, so do they appear now as well. || 26 ||
Because their sole essence is the one self that is pure consciousness, the powers of the substances manifest— remaining as they are perceived, motionless and free from mental construction.

Their persistence, too, is precisely according to their perception. Because they have as their foundation the motionless consciousness (niḥspanda-cit), all the powers of substance do not move from their own substratum nor do they diminish; thus he says: "motionless" (niḥspandāḥ). They are devoid of mental activity (manaskāra)—that is, the mental grasping of dualistic forms. || 27 ||
This entire world—including Rudra, Upendra, and the Lotus-born Brahmā—is seen and experienced even though it does not exist at all, like a dream. (28)
And thus, with the intention that the world is merely phenomenal because its entire nature depends solely upon appearance, he says:
"It is indeed non-existent. (28)
Indeed, various modes of vibration are seen within the water of consciousness, manifesting as the mobile and immobile self arising from joy, indignation, and despondency. (29)
Indeed, for this reason, various modes of movement arising from joy, anger, and dejection are seen to be just like those in a dream. || 29 ||
Alas! How widespread is the diffusion of the frost-like clouds of consciousness-rays, which, stirred by the wind of intrinsic nature, produce the wondrous spectacle of the web of the world! 30.

Its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is established in an unknown form; it is that which, being shaken by the wind consisting of *vikṣepa-śakti* (the power of projection) alone, possesses the wonder of the world-web as its form. Such [a nature] manifests through the light of the quality of *sattva* characterized by consciousness (*cillakṣaṇa*), through the dust-cloud of the quality of *rajas*, and through the predominance of the dullness of obscuration belonging to the quality of *tamas*.
In the sky whose nature is like that of clouds and mist, there is a pervasive expansion—an extensive diffusion. "Hā" expresses grief; the meaning is:
how has it come to consist of thousands of millions of calamities such as birth and death?
"Pāṃśu" is simply "pāṃsu," for it is established in the lexicons that "śamba," "śūkara," and "pāṃśu" may belong to both the palatal and dental classes. || 30 ||
Just as a tuft of hair appears in the sky to one with blurred vision,
so does this delusion of the world appear in the void to one who does not know the Self.
For one who does not know the Self, whose vision of consciousness is veiled by ignorance, [it is as if] in the sky—that is, in the space of one's own Self. || 31 ||
To the extent that it is conceived, it appears exactly as it was conceived;
just as this city of imagination shines forth, so does this world appear.

And he says that the determination of its time and mode occurs solely in accordance with one's intention—expressed by the word "yāvat" (as far as/as long as)—in whatever manner (yathā) and by whichever means (yena yena prakāreṇa). || 32 ||
In a city of one's own imagination, as long as the entire existence of that imagination persists,
it remains indeed unreal in nature, yet it stands as if real within the experience.
He clarifies this in the example: "In the city of imagination. Though its nature is unreal, it exists as if real. // 33 //
Destiny, which bestows its ordained objects, indeed flows on;
both the stationary and the moving remain exactly as they are in their proper order. (34)

That very element, whose form is volition (saṃkalpa), as destiny (niyati), flows even now and will continue to flow in the future; by that alone the entire range of living beings, from the immobile to the mobile, remains fixed in their respective orders. || 34 ||
The mobile arises from the living, and the immobile even from the immobile;
by necessity, water flows downward and fire ascends upward. (35)
He states that even the determination of their birth, karma, and essential nature is by that very same [process]: "is born" (jāyate).
From the *jīva*, which is clearly living and mobile (*jaṅgama*). (35)
The bodily machines carry [the breaths], the luminaries blaze,
the winds move eternally, and the mountains and other things remain fixed.
Consisting of light, revolving, and having turned the sky into a downpour of rain,
the wheel of time (kālacakra), which is the essence of the ages, years, and so forth, proceeds.
The wheel of time, consisting of light, revolves by way of the southern solstice during the rainy season, filling the sky with torrents of rain; this occurs through that very same necessity. || 37 ||
The arrangement of the earth, the oceans, and the mountains remains distinct;
and the power of substances, consisting of the grasping and abandoning of existence and non-existence, persists.
And upon the surface of the earth, the arrangement of the various continents, the oceans, and the mountains— interspersed one by one— proceeds as if established, remaining fixed in its course.
Kundadanta said:
A thing previously seen comes to memory because of one's own volition;
but in the first creation, whose perception of what was previously seen could there be? (39)

Now, one might object: "Let the worldly transactions of all people, including ourselves and others, be established by *niyati*, which is the nature of the Creator’s volition (*dhātṛ-saṃkalpa*). But how can the very establishment of the Creator’s volition be proven? For, since there is no possible cause other than impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by prior experience, and since prior experience was impossible at the time of the first creation, how could it be established? Thus, Kundadanta raises this doubt with the words: "Previously seen... (*prāgdṛṣṭam*).
Therefore, there arise self-conceptions following that [prior state]. From these self-conceptions, a fixed creation shines forth.

However, this is applicable to a creation in the second kalpa and subsequent ones; for in the first creation, whose prior manifestation of creation is well-known, such that one might ask about it or remember it oneself? This is the meaning. || 39 ||
The ascetic said:
"Everything appears as unprecedented, just like one's own death in a dream;
yet, due to habituation, there arises the recollection that 'this was seen before' right within that very experience. (40)
The volition of the Creator is not dependent on memory;

rather, it is dependent on the vision of all things past and future through divine knowledge. This is according to such scriptural passages as: "He thought, 'Shall I indeed create the worlds? He created these worlds," and so forth. And at that moment, everything past and future [was present].

The world is seen as something entirely unprecedented, and a purely volitional creation, which is a manifestation (*vivarta*) of consciousness, proceeds in accordance with what has been previously perceived. In that very context, the notion "this was seen by me before" is superimposed in some cases; thus the ascetic explains [the matter] with the words beginning "unprecedented" (*apūrva*). (40)
Because it is consciousness, the city of the world’s conceptualization shines within the sky of the intellect;
therefore, this [world] is neither existent nor non-existent, since it appears and does not appear by its own nature.
For it appears at one time and does not appear at another.
If even the city of one's own volitions is experienced through the clarity of consciousness, how could the pure sky of consciousness—the city of volition—possibly not be remembered? 42.

For memory would only be postulated if there were an incapacity for perception; however, since we observe that for consciousness (*citi*), which is capable of perception through mere imagination in a dream, memory is likewise postulated, he says: "by the clarity of consciousness" (42).
Free from joy and resentment, and from both suffering and happiness, the wise proceed by the natural path alone, like wheels on a journey. (43)

For this very reason, because they do not recall virtues, faults, and so forth, those who know reality—being devoid of joy and resentment—continue to revolve solely by the momentum of their *prārabdha* (commenced karma), like a potter's wheel; thus he says: "joy... (verse 43).

Know that the delusion of the three worlds is just like the city in a dream when sleep has passed away, or like [the appearance of objects] in memory; it is the supreme, whose nature is the space of consciousness. 44.
And he states that what is called "sublated memory" is not actually memory, but rather the perception of the mere residue of the substratum—using the word "sleep" (nidrā) as an illustration: || 44 ||
Know that which is designated as the "world" to be nothing but the appearance of consciousness;
it is the utterly tranquil void of consciousness, absolute and nothing else. (45)
Know that to be like the utterly tranquil sky. || 45 ||
That in which all exists, from which all proceeds, that which is all, and which is from every direction;
that which is all by way of being all—that all remains forever as all. (46)
Since it is precisely from that [source] that everything has become completely stilled, he says "in which" (yasmin) [to explain this]. || 46 ||
How this Brahma-cycle of transmigratory existence will come to be for you, and how the appearance of the visible world occurs—all this has been explained by me. || 47 ||
"All this has been told by me to you"—this is the conclusion. || 47 ||
"Arise, go to your own desired abode this very day; let it be accomplished quickly, like two bees toward a lotus.
I remain here, established in a state where even suffering is pure, O dear one; I shall enter into meditative absorption once more for a long time."
I enter. || 48 ||
"Come now, O twice-born ones, arise! Like two bees to a lotus at dawn, go to your abode, your home. There, let your desired virtuous deeds be performed.
As for me, I shall now remain in a state of profound exhaustion, established in my meditation, so that there may be utter misery."
Therefore, in order to avoid that [fault], the meaning is: "I shall once again enter into meditative absorption (samādhi). || 48 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-fourth canto, titled "The Instruction of Kundadanta," in the *Brahma-tattva-prakaraṇa* of the *Nirvāṇa-upadeśa*, within the *Mokṣopāya* section of the *Vāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa*, a work of the Sage (*ārṣa*). 184.
Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-fourth chapter, titled "The Instruction of Kundadanta," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa-tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and eighty-fifth canto. Kuṇḍadhāra said:
Having spoken thus, "Even an aged sage," he closed his eyes in meditation.
His breath and mind were motionless, as if fixed in a painting. || 1 ||
The arrival of those two at his house, the gradual destruction of his brothers there,
and the eradication of Kundadanta’s delusion through the attainment of Rāma are described.
He whose vital breath and mind are motionless. || 1 ||
Although he was entreated by us again and again with words full of affection, he,
being ignorant of the world, did not grant us an answer.
Although he was entreated by us with words full of affection, he did not grant his reply;
for, having ceased from external activity, he neither perceived nor took account of the world—this is the meaning. || 2 ||
Having departed from that place with slow and eager steps, we both reached our home—where our kinsmen were filled with joy—in just a few days. (3)
Anxious due to separation from the Sage. || 3 ||
Then, having held a festival there and recounted ancient stories,
we remained for as long as those seven brothers were present.
There, in that house, having performed a festival consisting of the worship of the family deity, the feeding of married women, Brahmins, and other such rites; || 4 ||
Gradually they have reached dissolution like oceans at the time of universal destruction;
only this one friend of mine remains liberated, like a single vast ocean. || 5 ||
At the onset of the dissolutions, due to the heat of the twelve suns, they were like the seven oceans [drying up]. || 5 ||
Then, in the course of time, he too set like the sun at the end of the day;
my soul overwhelmed by sorrow, I fell into a state of supreme despondency.
He is my friend, even though he is the eighth; [I feel] distress at the separation from my circle of friends. || 6 ||
Then, being even more distressed, I went to the ascetic at the Kadamba tree, intent on asking about that knowledge in order to destroy my suffering. (7)
Thus has been declared the knowledge of the Self as it was spoken.
There, after three months, he became free from that meditative absorption;
then, being questioned by me with deep reverence, he spoke as follows.
The Kadamba ascetic said:
"I am unable to remain for even a moment without my meditative absorption;
I shall quickly enter into that very absorption with all haste. (9)
O sinless one, this instruction on the ultimate truth does not take hold without practice;
therefore, listen to this supreme method and then act accordingly.
Even though it was performed by me now, it does not affect you; [therefore, I shall explain] another method, a means for attaining knowledge. || 10 ||
There is a city named Ayodhyā; there dwells a lord of the earth named Daśaratha, and his son is known as Rāma. || 11 ||
Go there into his presence; for it is said that the best of sages named Vasiṣṭha, the family preceptor, will speak in the assembly.
He will discourse on the means to liberation.
O twice-born one, having heard that divine discourse on the means to liberation for a long time,
you will attain rest in the supreme, purifying state, just as I have.
Having spoken thus, I entered this region, which is a great ocean of the elixir of meditative absorption, having approached your presence. (14)
