"Into your presence"—this is the reply directed toward Rāma. || 14 ||
I have related this entire account to you—exactly as it occurred, exactly as it was seen, and exactly as it was heard, without omission. (15)
Unbroken and complete. || 15 ||
Śrī Rāma said: From that time forward, he— expert in narrating stories such as those of Kundadanta— remained constantly by my side.
This very twice-born man named Kundadanta, who stands here by my side,
has heard this Saṃhitā called "The Means to Liberation" in this world.
Here, in this assembly hall. || 17 ||
"This very brahmin named Kundadanta, who has come to my side, has today become free from doubt; let him be questioned as to whether this is so or not. (18)
Having thus described the introduction to the question, he states the subject matter to be asked: "He" (saḥ) || 18 ||
Śrī Vālmīki said:
When Rāghava had spoken thus, the best of speakers, that most excellent sage Vasiṣṭha, looking toward Kundadanta, replied. (19)
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Kundadanta, best of the twice-born, O sinless one, tell me what has been understood by you from my supreme, liberating discourse, which is to be known by one who has heard it.
Kundadanta said:
"The very mind, which cuts through all doubts, is my victory;
the cutting through of all doubts is known, and the object of knowledge is realized as indivisible. (21)

The ellipsis is that "the severance of all doubts has occurred," because the reality of Brahman—which must necessarily be known, which is undivided, and which is devoid of the divisions characterized by the internal self—has been realized. || 21 ||
That which was to be known has been known as the stainless; that which was to be seen has been seen as the unimpaired;
that which was to be attained has been attained in its entirety; I am now rested in the supreme state.

He declares that one has accomplished all that was to be done because, through the mere knowledge [of the Self] and the consequent cessation of delusion, there remains nothing further to be known, nothing further to be seen, and nothing further to be attained—thus he says: "It is known. || 22 ||
All this that is yours is the Buddha, a dense mass of ultimate reality;
it has blossomed from the non-dual Self within the void in the form of the world. (23)
"This self-consciousness has been realized by me from you, from you"—how was it realized? To that he says: "All this," and so forth.
Because [the Self] consists of all things, possesses all forms, and is the universal soul, that which is non-universal arises abundantly everywhere, at all times, and by means of everything. (24)
Worlds arise within the hollow of a single grain of mustard seed, and yet they do not arise; this has been known in its entirety. (25)

Siddhārtha is white mustard; even within the hollow of its seed-particle, worlds arise through the vision of Māyā, because the consciousness of the substrate (adhiṣṭhāna-cit) is filled with the power of all conceptualization.
Yet, from the perspective of ultimate reality (paramārtha-dṛśā), they do not exist anywhere at all.
Within the house, the earth with its seven continents truly exists;
yet the house remains empty—this is the truth, without a doubt. (26)

Whatever object appears here at any time with whatever nature described, and is experienced by living beings, all that exists as the dense mass of Brahman; thus Brahman exists, free from beginning and end.

In this regard, he extracts and summarizes the essential reality of Brahman with the words "whatever...": the meaning is that the conclusion is this—the Self alone is the "all-in-all" (sarvaghana), existing as every possible object of cognition for all people at all times; not even an atom other than that is ever experienced by anyone at any time. || 27 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-fifth chapter, titled "The Awakening of Kundadanta," in the *Brahma-tattva-prakaraṇa* of the *Nirvāṇa-upadeśa*, within the *Mokṣopāya* section of the *Vālmīki-devarṣi-mahārāmāyaṇa*. 185.
Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-fifth chapter, titled "The Awakening of Kundadanta," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa-tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and eighty-sixth canto.
Śrī Vālmīki said:
While Kundadantā was speaking thus, the venerable sage Vasiṣṭha [spoke].
The one of irreproachable soul spoke these words, which were appropriate for the ultimate truth.
The established doctrine that "all is Brahman" is rendered unshakable through logical arguments;
likewise, the fulfillment of boons and curses arises from the Creator’s conscious volition.

Having first firmly established the nature of Brahman as variegated by *māyā* as described by Kundadanta, Śrī Vasiṣṭha proceeded to describe that which is free from *māyā* and pure; thus he says: "O Kundadanta... (Verse 1).
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Ah! Rest in discernment has arisen for this great-souled one;
he perceives the entire universe as Brahman, like a myrobalan fruit in the palm of his hand.

The word *batā* is used here in the sense of compassion (*anukampā*). Regarding the reading *jñāta*: through what is known—that is, by means of the fruit of direct realization (*sākṣātkāra-jñāna*)—there is the repose or fullness (*viśrānti*, *pūrṇatā*) of discernment (*vijñāna*), which is the knowledge born from hearing the scriptures. The phrase "like a myrobalan fruit in the palm of the hand" is a vivid illustration of that very point. || 2 ||
It is said that this entire universe, whose nature is mere illusion, appears as the unborn Brahman;
yet that illusion is Brahman itself, and Brahman is the one, peaceful, and untainted.
Error is the apprehension of things otherwise; since the entire universe consists of that [error], it appears as Brahman, and because even error itself appears as Brahman alone. || 3 ||

In whatever manner, by whatever means, wherever, of whatever nature, to whatever extent, at whatever time, and from whatever source something exists; in that same manner, by those same means, in that very place, with that same nature, to that same extent, at that same time, and from that same source, it exists.

He states that what has been described by him through the perspective of extracting the variegated Brahman (*śabalabrahma*) is also entirely correct, beginning with the words "yad" (that which). || 4 ||
It is auspicious, peaceful, unborn, silent yet beyond silence, undecaying, all-pervading;
it is both perfectly empty and non-empty, non-existent, without beginning or end, and eternal.

And that [consciousness] is pure and non-contradictory, because it manifests diversity even without undergoing modification; with this intention, he says: "Whichever state is filled with the intensity of consciousness, that very state attains a thousandfold branching, just as a creeper does through sprinklings. (6)
By consciousness, which is a mind variegated by illusion; "burden" refers to an excess of volition. || 6 ||
Since the supreme cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) is but an atom situated within the space of consciousness (cidvyoman),
and since the cosmic egg is indeed a single atom containing the entire world within it.
The entire universe is but a supreme atom; likewise, the supreme atom itself is the universe, for within it resides the world. (7)
Therefore, this entire universe is the space of consciousness—without beginning or middle, indivisible, and serene.
It is Nirvana, wherein the bond of birth has ceased; remain as you are, O healthy-souled one.

If the world is indeed Brahman itself, then he states the result of that [realization] with the words "Therefore" (tasmāt). Having become one whose bondage—consisting of birth and the diversity of the body and so forth—has set, remain as you truly are, having become Brahman itself. || 8 ||
Itself the object of sight, itself the seer, itself consciousness, itself inert matter;
itself something and itself nothing—Brahman alone is established within the Self.

In the realm of conventional discourse, Brahman itself exists in the form of the visible and so forth; however, from the perspective of ultimate reality, it exists only as the Self, whose nature is non-dual, self-luminous, and of the single essence of bliss. || 9 ||
Just as this world, being itself Brahman, becomes merged within the space of the Self—remaining peaceful and not abandoning its own nature—so it is there. 10.
Wherever and by whatever latent impression (*vāsanā*) something is accomplished, it remains there in that very manner; this is the underlying principle (*anukarṣa*). || 10 ||
The Brahman is never perceived as a duality of "the seen" in its true state;
know that the oneness of these two is like that of emptiness and space. (11)
The visible world has arisen through the *māyā* of Brahman; by this much alone, one should never conceive of duality, for it remains exactly as it is, without any modification. || 11 ||
The visible world is indeed the Supreme Brahman, and the Supreme Brahman is indeed the state of being visible.
This is neither tranquil nor untranquil, neither manifold in form nor devoid of form.
Just as dreams and the like appear upon awakening, so too is the body formless;
its essence is pure consciousness alone, it is non-obstructive, and though experienced by oneself, it is composed of unreality.
To the question of how the perceived form of the body and so forth can be denied, he says: "Of whatever kind... (verse 13).
Just as a living being composed of consciousness remains in a state of sleep and becomes inert,
so too does this consciousness, having become inert, abide in that which is called "stationary" (sthāvara).
He provides an illustration for consciousness existing in an insentient and stationary state with the words: "consisting of consciousness" (saṃvinmaya). || 14 ||
Due to its immobility and insentience, consciousness attains the state of a sentient being from the mobile;
thus the conscious soul, whose nature is deep sleep, experiences the dream and the waking states through hundreds of worlds.
He provides an illustration for the manifestation of consciousness (*cid*) in the state of mobility following its state of immobility:

"From the state of being stationary," etc. The meaning is that just as the soul (*jīva*), while in deep sleep, experiences the dream and waking worlds through hundreds of mental constructs, so it is here. || 15 ||
Until liberation, this existence of the individual soul appears as a dream-like manifestation of millions of worlds through earth, water, air, fire, ether, and the self. (16)
Regarding how long the state of existence as stationary and moving beings lasts therein, he says: "until liberation" (āmokṣam). || 16 ||
Just as a person in a state of sleep accumulates dullness, so too does consciousness accumulate inertia;
yet consciousness does not truly become subject to that inertia.
It accumulates and superimposes. Nevertheless, its nature as consciousness remains unimpeded; thus he says, "it accumulates.
Due to the power of the inertness superimposed upon it, it does not accumulate inertness; in reality, it does not indeed partake in inertness. || 17 ||
By consciousness, the body is made stationary for the knower of sensation;
by consciousness, the body is made mobile for the knower of sensation. || 18 ||
Just as a stationary body is fashioned for the individual soul (jīva), which experiences the sensation of dullness, so too is a moving one. || 18 ||
Just as a man’s nails and feet are one and the same body,
so too the stationary and the moving are one and the same non-obstructive consciousness.

Even when this is done, there is no difference in consciousness; rather, he says "yathā" (just as), explaining that everything—both the insentient and the sentient—is superimposed upon the Great Consciousness and is merely a limb of it, like the nails and feet [of a body]. || 19 ||
That form of consciousness which, at the initial creation, appeared and remained like a dream as "the world," is said to be exactly the same at the end.

In the primordial creation—that is, in the volition (*saṃkalpa*) which was the cause of the first creation—whatever form first appeared remains exactly as it was even now. Thus, although it has long remained in an insentient form, because it consists of consciousness (*cinmaya*), it is unobstructed and tranquil; the subsequent connection is that the end of creation is described by means of the negation (*apavāda*) of that [insentient state]. || 20 ||
And that very [reality] is non-obstructive, peaceful, abiding exactly as it is;
nothing has come into manifestation, nor was there anything unmanifested that was beneficial. (21)
Since it has never been unmanifested while not existing, this alone is beneficial.
This appears as the beginning and this as the end of creation,
emerging from the chamber of dreamless sleep within the profound slumber of consciousness.

Thus, since the entire creation is non-existent throughout the three periods of time, even the conceptualization of its beginning and end is likewise false; this is what he says with the words "this" (ayam).

The meaning is that just as the state of a dream-phenomenon—from deep sleep up to the point of awakening—is conceptualized only within the interior of the "womb" of sleep, and not within the interior of the "womb" of waking, so it is here. || 22 ||
For I am established as one, without beginning or end, a solid mass of ultimate reality;
therefore, even the name of dissolution, maintenance, or creation does not exist for me.
To the question "Whence [is that]?", he says: "Abiding. The meaning is that for me, who am awakened, even the name does not exist, let alone the form.
The visible world, consisting of dissolution, maintenance, creation, and so forth, does not exist;
nor is it anything other than the Self, just as a painted woman is nothing other than the painting itself.
Just as the painting to be produced does not differ from the canvas,
so too the various perceptions and the absence of perception are themselves the state of emanation within the nature of consciousness.

Just as an army depicted by a painter does not differ from the painting upon which it is conceived, so too the various manifestations of resistance, though appearing as formalized creations, are neither manifold nor non-manifold within the creative consciousness of the Creator.
Even though it is devoid of division, this [Self] is robbed of its liberation from deep sleep by the dense slumber of consciousness; however, the dream is merely a product of the mind.

Even by ignorance (*avidyā*), which is a dense sleep of consciousness (*cidghana-nidrā*) and is devoid of differentiation, the well-known portion that constitutes liberation—the very essence of one's true nature—is stolen, plundered, and denied, as if from deep sleep (*suṣupta*). On the contrary, having become a mere mental state (*cittaka*), this waking portion and dream are displayed; such is the remainder of the sense. However, in the reading "liberation is extracted from deep sleep" (*suṣuptāt sodyate mokṣaḥ*), [the meaning is as follows].
The distinction is shown that liberation belongs to the person who is engaged in the effort of hearing, reflection, and so forth;
however, it should be explained that in another case, having become one with the mind, two kinds of dream are manifested. || 26 ||

This is dissolution, this is creation, and this is a dense dream—all these are but the manifestations of consciousness, which possesses the brilliance of a thousand suns and an unimpeded form. || 27 ||
The "dense wakefulness" belongs to the sun of the Self, which possesses the brilliance of a thousand consciousnesses and whose nature is deep sleep characterized by the density of wisdom;
such are the manifestations, the various modes of light. || 27 ||
The dream-like portion of the sleeping consciousness is declared to be the mind (citta).
That very same thing, when awakened, is called the living being (jīva), which perceives gods, asuras, and so forth. (28)

In that regard, that very self which consists of manifested latent impressions (vāsanā) is, through the predominance of its conditioned aspect (upādhi-aṃśa), called the mind (citta); and through the predominance of its conscious aspect (cidaṃśa), it is called the individual soul (jīva).

When that same [self], perceiving itself as the bodies of gods, asuras, humans, and so forth according to its respective capacities, shakes off sleep through the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna), it is liberated. || 28 ||
When this very state is fully realized by itself as deep sleep, then it is called liberation by those who long for liberation. (29)

He says that very thing: "This indeed... That which was fully understood in the fourth and fifth stages becomes deep sleep (*suṣupti*) in the sixth stage; in the seventh stage, it is called liberation (*mokṣa*). || 29 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
The mind consists of gods, asuras, and so forth; the sleep of the mind is the vision of one's own Self.
O Blessed One, what is its measure, and how does the universe exist within its belly? (30)

The meaning of the question is: what is the measure and what is the configuration of the mind (citta) as divided into gods, asuras, and so forth; and within its belly, what is the measure and for how long does the world exist during its sleep? || 30 ||

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Know that the mind is the man, the god, the asura, the immobile being, the woman, the serpent, the mountain, the piśāca and so forth, the bird, the insect and so forth, and the rākṣasa. (31)
Regarding that, he states the answer to the first [objection] with the words beginning "Know" (viddhi) and so forth. || 31 ||
Know that his measure is infinite, wherein this entire world—from Brahmā down to a blade of grass—attains the state of being mere dust by the thousands. (32)
Taking the state of dust and the state of the ultimate atom as the limits.
That which moves upward from the path of the sun is this consciousness;
it is the realized mind, possessing an infinite and stainless form.
It also brings the excellence of its vastness into direct experience— namely, that when the eye is directed upward,
whatever visual cognition extends even to the region above the path of the sun, including the realm of perpetual darkness and so forth,
the mind (citta) has become of such a measure, infinite and pure in form.
The meaning is that this is established by all experience. || 33 ||
This is the formidable form of consciousness (citi); within it lie the prosperities of the worlds.
When these come forth, then the creation is said to have emerged from consciousness.

It is "fierce" (ugra) because of the abundance of the unbearable sufferings of saṃsāra. When the prosperities of the worlds within this very collective self emerge through the conceptualization of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) and so forth, that is called "creation" (sarga); and we say that it has come from the mind.
They know the mind alone to be the living being (jīva), which is devoid of beginning and end. || 34 ||
Like space within jars, it exists within bodies or does not exist according to its own will.

The all-pervading Lord is devoid of beginning and end; for this very reason, He dwells within all bodies in the form of the individual (vyaṣṭi), yet by the will of the Creator, He does not remain [in that state] once He has departed from the body—this is the meaning. || 35 ||
Just as the current of a river takes up and abandons the low and high parts of the earth, O dear one, so does the mind take up and abandon bodies. (36)
In this regard, he provides an illustration for the taking up and casting off of the body, beginning with the word "nimna": "O dear one (aṅga)! [36]
But for him, through the thorough knowledge of the Self, this delusion regarding the body and so forth is quickly pacified by awakening, just like the perception of a mirage.
In that [state], the world is as minute as an atom within the mind;
for the person (puruṣa) is indeed always of that same measure. Therefore, the world resides within the persons. (38)

Thus, he states that the mind, which contains the entire universe within it, is of the nature of an atom: "In the world... etc. That which is known as the most subtle atom in its magnitude, such as the mote of dust seen in a sunbeam through a lattice window, is the measure—the dimension—of the mind. And that very [atom] is the person, the individual soul (*jīva*). [As it is said: "Of the hundredth part of the tip of a hair, and that again divided into a hundred parts... [that part is the soul].
The meaning is that this is according to the Vedic scripture which states: "He is to be known as the individual soul (jīva), and he is capable of attaining infinity. || 38 ||
Whatever is seen here is but the mind, like things in a dream; that very mind is the person (puruṣa). Therefore, what difference is there between the world and the Self? || 39 ||
And thus, he says "as far as... (yāvat) [in verse 39], indicating that even the distinction between the individual soul and the world has been wiped away.

This entire flood of objects is indeed consciousness alone; there is no "object-ness" existing as something separate from it, just as in a dream, or as the state of being a bracelet and so forth does not exist apart from gold. (40)
He states that since there is no difference between the living being and the world, the world’s nature as pure consciousness (cinmātratā) is also established—namely, "consciousness alone" (cideva).

The meaning is that if anything else were admitted to exist apart from consciousness, it would lack both existence and manifestation; consequently, by falling into unreality, no distinct category of object could even exist or be established. || 40 ||

Just as waters, though distinct, manifest everywhere throughout the ocean in every single part, so too do the objects of perception, which are non-different from Brahman, eternally abide within consciousness as its very nature.

Just as waters that exist in a single mass within a portion of the ocean manifest separately, so too do those [powers] whose nature is the visible world [manifest] within Brahman; such is the meaning. || 41 ||
Just as liquidity exists in the ocean and the waters contained within its belly manifest, so too do all other multitudes of objects appear, though they are non-different from the Knower.
Regarding non-difference, he provides the illustration of its fluidity with the words "just as" (yathā). || 42 ||
This pillar of consciousness, which assumes the form of space—the carved figures of the world as it exists—is motionless and remains devoid of beginning or end. (43)

And thus, the pillar of consciousness itself— possessing the form of that absolute emptiness which is the ethereal nature of the figures carved upon it, and characterized by the world as it truly exists— remains motionless and immovable.
This entire universe, as it exists, is established within the sky of consciousness;
remaining peaceful and not abandoning its own nature, it is like the entirety of a dream-world.

There is equality, reality, existence, oneness, and immutability between these two—the universal consciousness and the substratum—and there is a mutual relationship of container and contained between them. (45)

He explains how it is peaceful and how it did not abandon its own nature with the word "samatā" (equality). Because the distinction [between them] is not perceived in five ways, it is "peaceful"; yet, because there is a slight appearance of difference in worldly transaction due to the relationship of container and contained—like a pillar and a statue carved upon it—it did not abandon its own nature. This is the meaning. || 45 ||

In this world, between the visions of dreams, mental constructs, saṃsāra, boons, and curses, there is either no difference at all, or else there is a difference—just as there is among the waters of lakes, oceans, and rivers. (46)
Regarding this, he says "In a dream," etc., to show that while the distinction is merely apparent, in reality there is no such thing.
Just as for Nandin and Nahuṣa there was an appearance of being a god or a serpent due to a boon or a curse, there is a distinctness capable of functioning in worldly affairs;
however, from the perspective of ultimate truth, it does not exist at all.
Śrī Rāma said:
How can there be the relationship of cause and effect regarding the perception of the purpose of boons and curses?
It is said that an effect cannot exist without a material cause; please explain this. (47)

In the case of Nandin, there is no taking up of a divine body within a human body, nor is there any portion of lunar nectar; likewise, in the transformation of the lunar nectar into the divine body of Nahuṣa, there is no taking up of a serpent body, nor any egg and so forth.
Since in this world no effect ever exists without a material cause (*upādāna*), how then is the manifestation of the divine and serpent bodies established in both those cases?
The meaning of Rāma’s question. || 47 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: The world is said to be the manifestation of the sky of one’s own pure consciousness,
just as the movement of whirlpools occurs within the surging waters of the ocean.

Vasiṣṭha prepares the ground to offer a response to this objection by means of the theory of illusory manifestation (*vivartavāda*), stating: "The consciousness of the Lord Rudra, whose knowledge is free from obscuration, and that of Agastya and others—consciousness itself, as delimited by true volition (*satyasaṃkalpa*)—manifests there in the form of the bodies of gods and serpents. He begins with the words "svavadātā" and so forth.
I have stated repeatedly that the manifestation of that sky of consciousness—which is perfectly pure because it is refined by the knowledge of reality—is in accordance with its true resolve. 48.
Objects whose nature is consciousness shine like the roaring waters of the ocean;
the wise call their names "volition" and so forth. (49)

The states of the world within the consciousness of the Creator’s own self appear spontaneously as being of the nature of consciousness itself; regarding these appearances, the wise and the seers cite such scriptural passages as "He desired," "He reflected," and "Heaven and earth were fashioned," and they speak of them by names such as "volition" (saṃkalpa) and so forth. || 49 ||
Through time, through the practice of yoga, through impartial inquiry, or by virtue of a sattvic birth, one becomes sattvic with a stainless soul. (50)

In that regard, in order to show that the manifestation of the meaning of an object for those whose consciousness is free from obscuration is itself "the realization of true intent" (*satya-saṃkalpa*), he states the causes of such consciousness, beginning with "by time," etc. [The phrase] "by time" refers to things such as the *karkaṭī* fruit.
"By equanimity" refers to the vision of equality toward enemies, friends, and so forth. For the gods, however, it is due to their birth being characterized by *sattva*. (50)
For the wise one who possesses right knowledge and perceives reality as it truly is,
the intellect becomes pure consciousness alone, free from both duality and unity.
She consists of consciousness free from all veils, having the nature of Brahman; she is pure awareness whose sole body is light, devoid of any physical form.
Thus he perceives everything without exception, as far as it consists of mere volition; he sees his own self-manifestation as peaceful and non-different from the ultimate reality.

This very person, whose consciousness is free from veils, perceives whatever exists as mere volition; since he perceives all that as non-different from himself in the ultimate sense, the truth of his volition is established. || 53 ||
For this entire world is indeed nothing but her mere volition,
just like a city of imagination or a great city in a dream.

The word division is *asya ā idam*. The meaning is that this entire world, which is perceived all around (*ā*) this Hiraṇyagarbha who is of such a nature, is nothing but his mere volition (*saṃkalpa-mātra*). || 54 ||
The self is the master of its own volitions and is self-luminous; in whatever manner it conceives, so does that become for it.

In this way, another [being] as well, whose own will is sovereign and who is himself free from obscuration, perceives whatever he wills merely through his volition; in that very manner, it comes to be. || 55 ||
Just as a child in a city of imagination perceives the levitation of stones as real, so too does one, through experience, quickly realize the constraint of one's own volitional actions.
Where there is control and restraint that is subject to and dependent upon the self. || 56 ||
In these three worlds, which are composed of his own volition, the Supreme Self knows that granting boons,
pronouncing curses, and so forth, are truly non-different from himself.

In that regard, he who is the self of unobstructed consciousness, beginning with Hiraṇyagarbha, knows that fruit which consists of boons and curses as being truly non-different from his own self. || 57 ||
Just as oil is produced from sand through the power of one's own volition, so too,
by the creative wills of the world-creation, do boons and other things arise here from the Self.

And because the world consists of His volition, even for the self of Hiraṇyagarbha and others, purposes such as boons and curses are accomplished—though lacking any material cause—just as oil is produced from sand by a child within a city created by his own volition. || 58 ||
Since the cognition of differentiation does not arise because of the unobstructed nature of consciousness, which is inherently peaceful,
therefore, for one who [realizes] the non-duality of conceptual construction, even the attainment of boons and the like is not established as a goal.
He demonstrates the purpose of the qualification "unobstructed" (nirāvaraṇa) with the words "not unobstructed" (anirāvaraṇa): for this ignorant person, the boons and so forth do not succeed. || 59 ||
Whatever mental construction has become established remains so even today, unless it is reversed through effort by means of another conceptualization. (50)
He says "yet" [in verse 60] to show that for those whose knowledge is free from obscuration, conceptualization does not cease until the arising of another such conceptualization.

Just as there is a sequence of various parts within a reality that possesses parts, so too, when the two states of duality and unity are released from their constituent parts and remain stable in Brahman, [there is a similar sequence].
Regarding how the conceptualization of boons, curses, and so forth—which are contradictory to it—can persist within that which is partless and whose nature is unobstructed knowledge, he says:
"In Brahman" (verse 61).
Śrī Rāma said:
O Brahman, tell me how those who practice dharma solely out of unobstructed ignorance bestow curses and the like. (62)
Then, with the intention that for those who possess unobstructed knowledge and are solely fierce ascetics, boons, curses, and the like would be rendered futile, Rāma asks: "anirāvaraṇa... (verse 62).
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Whatever indeed Brahman conceives within itself at the beginning of creation, that very thing it experiences, because nothing else exists therein. (63)

Vasiṣṭha prepares the introductory framework—beginning with the words "saṃkalpa" (volition)—to provide the answer that even the boons and curses of others possess reality because they arise solely from the Creator’s volition at the beginning of creation, and thus they are not in vain: "When he knows himself as Brahman, this Prajāpati is that Brahman; there is nothing else that can obstruct that."
And that [Brahman] is not distinct from us, just as liquidity is not distinct from water. (64)

The power of the Creator (*dhātu*), however, is established precisely because he is a knower of the Self as the True Brahman; with this intention, [the author] says "Brahman. Since that Prajāpati, the Creator, knows Brahman for that reason, he is indeed Brahman himself.
The sense is based on such scriptural passages as: "Whosoever among the gods awakened to that, he alone became That" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.25.2). || 64 ||
Whatever indeed that first Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati) conceives, that very thing immediately comes to be; this world is his mental construction.
Supportless and without a basis, having the nature of space, it shines within space,
like a mass of hair seen by one with impaired vision, or like a string of pearls perceived by the sighted.
He states what that conceptualization is like: "without support" (nirādhāram). || 66 ||
By him were conceived the progeny, righteousness, charity, austerity,
the qualities, the Vedas, the scriptures, the five elements, and the instructions on knowledge.

By that Prajāpati, there are five [traditions]: the four Vedas and the Smṛtis; or alternatively, the Trayī (the three Vedas), Sāṃkhya, Yoga, the doctrine of Paśupati, and the Vaiṣṇava [doctrine]. These are the teachers of knowledge (*jñānopadeśanāḥ*). [The suffix] *yuc* is applied after the causative form of the root *diś*. 67.
Whatever ascetics might say without delay through their discourses, and whatever those learned in the Vedas might declare, he then established that it should be so.

Then, that Prajāpati conceived and resolved thus: "Whatever those who know the Vedas, whether through their discourses or by their innate nature—as indicated by the word 'and' (ca)—may say, all that shall necessarily come to pass. || 68 ||
This Consciousness-Brahman has thus conceived [the elements]: space as the aperture, air as motion, fire as heat, water as fluidity, and earth as solidity. (69)

Thus, he says "this" (*idam*) to show that even the distinctions between the natures of all things are imagined by that very [consciousness]: "This is Brahman, whose nature is distinguished from the conscious and the insentient; space (*kha*), whose nature is that of an aperture; air (*vāyu*), whose nature is motion;
fire (*agni*), whose nature is heat," and so forth. (69)
Such is this element of consciousness that whatever it perceives as being of the nature of space,
it immediately experiences exactly as such— whether as "you," "I," or "he"— as does everything else.
Thus, he states that "this entire conceptualization is a conceptualization of the very essence of consciousness (cidghātu) appearing in the form of Prajāpati"—namely, "the essence of consciousness.
The intended meaning is that it experiences [these forms] because of its nature of having true volition (satyasaṃkalpatva). || 70 ||
In whatever manner the sky of consciousness perceives a thing, it becomes exactly that;
for even the eternal Self appears as something non-existent, like "you" or "I" in a dream.
Just as a stone falsehood becomes true within a city of one's imagination, so too,
within the city of the world's imagination, that which is desired by Brahman is true.

Therein, he clarifies the state of being the eternal Self by means of an illustration—namely, "the stone" (śilā). It was desired by Brahmā Prajāpati for the sake of experiencing the *prārabdha* karma that had commenced within his office. || 72 ||
Whatever has been awakened by means of the pure nature of consciousness, and whatever it is like—that an impure being is unable to alter is just as [impossible] as for a worm [to do so]. (73)

To the question of why that which is born from a superior resolve is not rendered otherwise by people through a contrary resolve, such as a superior curse, he says: "By the nature of consciousness" (citsvabhāvena). || 73 ||

Consciousness perceives that which has been frequently practiced as large, while it perceives the other as small; and when the state of waking occurs, it perceives everything as real, even in a dream.

With the intention that even for those who are impure, the independence of contrary conceptualization does not arise due to the firmness of the habituation to non-independent conceptualization, he says: "It is practiced.
For one who possesses very firm waking impressions such as "I am bound by chains," [this occurs] even in a dream.
The meaning is that this is because one experiences only the state of dependence resulting from being bound by chains. || 74 ||
Always within the sky of consciousness, this one innate form of the sky of consciousness—consisting of the seer and the seen—shines forth as it perceives itself, and nothing else. (75)

Thus, even when consciousness manifests in the guise of the imagined triad [of knower, known, and knowing], it always continues to manifest by its very nature as a detached witness; this he states with the word "always" (sadaiva). The mention of the seer and the seen is an illustration for the entire triad. || 75 ||
Since the sky of consciousness is all-pervading, being both the single seer and the seen,
therefore whatever is perceived anywhere as desired is always real there.
He states that the establishment of the existence of those threefold categories (tripuṭī) occurs solely through the power of their pervasion by the witness-consciousness (sākṣicin): "One" (eka).
It is called "one" because it subsists upon the existence of the single consciousness. || 76 ||
Just as the state of fluidity resides in water which is a limb of the wind, and as the nature of Brahman resides in Brahman, so too does the world reside as a limb of the Unborn (Ajā). 77.

He states, with an illustration, that this world is indeed a limb of Him (the Creator), because its existence and manifestation are dependent upon the witness-consciousness of the Creator: "Like the wind... etc. The meaning is: "Just as [the wind]" refers to His state of being Brahman and His possession of the power of Māyā which causes the expansion of the world-form. Of the unborn Virāj. (77)
I am indeed Brahman, the Virāj-self; the world is the body of the Virāj-self.
There is no difference between Brahman and the world, just as there is none between emptiness and the sky. (78)
It has been stated repeatedly that the world is superimposed upon Brahman from before; how then is it now said to be "situated within the limbs of the Unborn"?
To this, he says: "Brahman alone... (78).
Just as from a waterfall various rows of water droplets fall and spring up, reaching diverse places and times. (79)
At a precipice, on the edge of a mountain peak, at the place where the Gaṅgā and other rivers fall downward. || 79 ||
Having dissolved even the single [notion] of "I" along with mind, intellect, and so forth, for as long as an eon, those whose consciousness is Brahman shine as the Self within the Self alone. (80)

The meaning is that just as [the waters of the Ganges] fall for an entire kalpa in a single stream, yet become divided into thousands of millions of distinct drops, and then, returning to oneness, shine within their own single continuous flow; so too should the various distinctions of the world be understood as being the manifold cognitions of Brahman. || 80 ||
Having themselves fashioned the conceptual constructions of intellect and so forth within their own bodies, they embraced the splendor of creation, just as water assumes the state of fluidity.

However, this is the distinction: whereas the rows of skulls are devoid of mind, intellect, and so forth, those Brahma-consciousnesses themselves, having fashioned within their own bodies the mental constructs of mind, intellect, and the rest, have accepted the glory of creation as an object of enjoyment. || 81 ||
Thus, this world exists for those of poor understanding; but for me, it is indeed causeless, non-dual, unborn, and pure action alone. (82)
With the intention that, upon the abandonment of conceptual constructions such as the mind (manas) and intellect (buddhi), the world ultimately resolves into mere ignorance, he says:

"Thus, in this way. By my vision—which is free from the difficulty of understanding characterized by the distracted ignorance of the mind, intellect, and so forth—this entire world, including the mind, intellect, and all else, has not been born at all throughout the three periods of time. || 82 ||
Whatever kind of existence is experienced in this body as being eightfold, such is the insentient existence of the Supreme Self in stones and other such objects. (83)

The meaning is this: just as the state of death in this body is experienced as a condition devoid of mind, intellect, and so forth, and just as the insentient existence in stones and the like is of such a nature, so too the non-disturbed existence of the Supreme Self should be understood as being likewise devoid of mind, intellect, and so forth. || 83 ||
Just as both deep sleep and dreaming exist within a single state of sound sleep,
so too do these appearances of creation and dissolution abide within Brahman.
And thus, he states that both creation and dissolution are merely internal distinctions within the sleep of ignorance: "Just as... (84).

"Just as light and darkness appear during deep sleep and dreaming, even though they occur within a single state of sleep; so too, O Supreme One, do creation and non-creation [occur] within the one [ignorance]. (85)
[Objection: But then, since the light of the sun and other luminaries exists during the creation, how can they be distinct from the dissolution which consists of darkness? To this he says:
"In deep sleep... (verse 85).
Just as a man experiences the state of a stone while asleep,
so does the Supreme Self experience this state of insentience.
He states that even in the conceptualization of the distinction between the insentient and the sentient, the dream state itself serves as the illustrative example: "Just as... (verse 86).

Furthermore, when there is no contact with wind or other such things by means of the thumb or a finger, that experience which occurs to one whose mind is directed elsewhere toward a stone or similar object belongs to the Self. (87)

He refutes the objection that the experience of insentience is not established in the case of consciousness with the words "of the thumb" (*aṅguṣṭhasya*). It is well known that when a person whose mind is distracted by another object experiences the touch of wind, heat, dust, or the like on his thumb or another finger, the resulting experience—though it has occurred—is as if it had not occurred; such an experience is exactly the same [as the one in question] regarding a stone or similar object.
The meaning is that even though it exists, it is as if non-existent due to its insentience (jāḍya). || 87 ||
Just as there are bodily experiences for the sky, stones, water, and so forth, so too are there various experiences today for us who are without minds. (88)

Thus, he states that even for the insentient, there is the well-known experience of the state of sentience—beginning with the word "space" (*vyoma*). Just as experiences occur within the body, whether in the form of the Virāṭ-body or in the form of the bodies of the respective presiding deities, so too do experiences occur today at the time of creation for us who were unconscious during the dissolution; this is the meaning of the reading "of you and us."

The words beginning with *tyad* (demonstrative pronouns) are always [retained] when combined with all [other words]; in the case of the mutual co-utterance of words beginning with *tyad*, that which is subsequent remains, and thus the absence of *ekaśeṣa* (the retention of one of several identical words) is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*). || 88 ||
Just as the perceptions of day and night manifest throughout the ages (kalpas),
so too do countless perceptions of creation and dissolution manifest in the Supreme.

Just as our perceptions of day and night appear within the undivided time consisting of the various Kalpas that are the divisions of Brahma’s day, so too do countless perceptions of creation and dissolution appear within the Supreme Self. 89.

Just as eddies, waves, and circles manifest spontaneously within a dense mass of water, so too does this multitude of creations and dissolutions manifest within the Supreme, which is peaceful and free from light, form, thought, experience, seeking, and desire.

Just as in the ocean— which is a mass of water possessing a single nature— whirlpools, waves, ripples, and so forth manifest from its very nature, so too, within the Self which is therefore free from distractions such as seeing (the act of perceiving), the object of that sight (the form), the mental reflection upon it, the experience characterized by enjoyment thereof, the desire for it, and the subsequent longing to obtain it, all arise within the supreme, tranquil state. This [is the case].

The meaning is that the multitude of dissolutions and creations vibrates by its very nature, and not through any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), once the vision of reality (*tattvadarśana*) has been attained.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-sixth chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Yoga for Establishing that 'All This is Indeed Brahman'," in the *Brahmagītā* of the *Śrī Vāyavīya Saṃhitā*, within the *Mokṣopāya* section of the *Ārṣa*.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-sixth chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Yoga for Establishing that 'All This is Indeed Brahman'," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
Chapter One Hundred and Eighty-Seven (187)
Śrī Rāma said:
From where does the necessity (niyati) of these diverse and innumerable states arise?
How is it that the inherent nature (svabhāva) of these states remains uniform and immovable? (1)
In this [work], the intrinsic nature of all things,
destiny, origination, the attainment of the state of a living soul, the causes [of bondage], and the purity of Brahman are described.

What is the cause by which *niyati*—the fixed order of cause and effect, as well as the unchanging and infallible nature of fire, water, and so forth, such as their heat and fluidity—remains established in the world?
The implication is that this is because such things are not observed in other false objects, such as those in dreams or mental fantasies. || 1 ||
Among the innumerable gods, why is it that the sun alone possesses such fierce radiance? Furthermore, what causes the lengthening and shortening of the days? || 2 ||
By whom was it made? What was made? || 2 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: That which appears in the Supreme by itself as if by chance—existing exactly as it is and in its true form—is called the world. || 3 ||

In the original creation, whatever appeared through the principle of "chance" (*kākatālīya*)—in whatever manner it manifested—it remained fixed in that very way by its causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*) and so forth.
In this regard, the will of the Creator (*dhātu*) alone is the cause for its non-deviation; this should be understood to apply equally to the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of things.
With this intention, Vasiṣṭha provides the answer to the first two questions, beginning with the words "by chance" (*kākatālīya*), etc. [The rest follows].

The meaning is that the manifestation at the beginning of creation, which was determined by the Creator as if by chance (kākatālīya), exists even today in the very same form and in the same manner of cause and effect as it did then; thus the world is described. || 3 ||
Whatever appears as any particular form of the All-powerful is real in that very way;
since its essence is consciousness, how could that which has appeared ever become non-existent?
Or, with the intention that destiny (*niyati*) is unfailing because it is impossible for the power of the Lord (*īśvara-śakti*), which is fixed, to undergo change, he says:

"of all-powerful" (*sarvaśakteḥ*). This means that because its essence is consciousness (*saṃvit-sāratayā*), the consciousness of His true resolve lacks the insubstantiality found in the consciousness of the dreams and mental fantasies of beings such as ourselves. || 4 ||

Since Brahman has existed as it is and has shone forth for all time due to its consciousness, its manifestation— which appears as non-manifestation— is precisely what is designated as "Niyati" (the principle of necessity).

It should be understood that just as there is the appearance of that which resides within the womb of Māyā at the time of creation, so too at the time of dissolution, through the attainment of subtlety, that very same thing becomes as if non-apparent;

thus, the causal efficiency (*arthakriyā-śakti*) of all things is indeed beginningless, and it is this very power that is designated by the name *niyati*. This is what he states with the words: "as it truly exists" (*yathāsthitam*). || 5 ||
That which shines forth as "this is thus" and "this is so," being itself Brahman,
is declared to be that which is called Niyati (Destiny), assuming the form of creation and dissolution.

Or rather, he states that the establishment of the foundation of necessity (*niyati*) consists in this: Brahman itself, which is capable of performing all determined causal functions, assumes the form of the universe—thus [he says] "this" (verse 6).
That which is known as waking, dreaming, and deep sleep is the self-manifestation within consciousness;
it is non-different from that [consciousness], being as singularly transparent as liquidity is to water.

Alternatively, because the three states have the nature of the Self as their unknown essence, the establishment of the non-deviation of necessity according to what is perceived is stated: "Waking... (verse 7).
Just as emptiness is in space, as fragrance is in camphor,
and as heat is in sunlight— and nothing else exists apart from them— so it is with the waking state and the others within consciousness.
He supports its having that as its intrinsic nature by means of examples, beginning with "just as" (yathā). || 8 ||

It is established solely within the Self of Brahman, which is the single sky of pure consciousness, existing as a non-different reality within the single continuous flow known as creation and dissolution.

The meaning is that because [the world] exists within the single Self of Brahman— which consists of the sky of pure consciousness— through a single stream of existence that is non-different [from it], like the sequence of seed and sprout, and through the beginninglessness of the stream of creation and dissolution, therefore the accomplishment of determined causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is established. || 9 ||
That momentary manifestation of consciousness which is perceived as "this creation" is that same momentary manifestation of consciousness perceived as "this eon. (10)

For this very reason, the entire system of regulation follows solely from the manifestation of consciousness (*cit*). With the intention that even a single moment is a conceptual construction (*kalpa*), and because there is no other means to prove its non-conceptual nature within the manifestation of consciousness, he says: "This is creation" (verse 10).
That time, that action, that space, and those objects, places, and arisings, are merely the manifestation of pure consciousness by its own nature, just as in a dream. (11)

For this very reason, he states with the words beginning "That" (tad) that consciousness itself, manifesting as the various entities such as time, action, place, and substance, constitutes both the intrinsic nature of all things and necessity (niyati). || 11 ||
Form, light, mental attention, place, time, action, and so forth—
that which is called "consciousness" shines within the space of consciousness by itself, being inherently devoid of name and form.
Just as whatever time has been conceived and whatever has been imagined,
by that very means this necessity (niyati) is indeed of the nature of space.
Thus, even that which appears as such is merely of the nature of space and not real; this is the meaning. || 13 ||

That which is called a moment (nimeṣa) lasting until the end of an aeon (ākalpa), and that which is a manifestation of a single form—those of expanded intellect call that inherent nature (svabhāva). (14)
Now he answers the question, "What is the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of entities? with the verse beginning "called the aeon" (ākalpākhya).

Those who know the reality of intrinsic nature—the proponents of svabhāva—declare that the uniform manifestation of entities, which persists throughout the duration of what is called an aeon (kalpa), which is a single blink of Brahmā's eye, and which is restricted to each individual object, is precisely what they call svabhāva. 14.
In that same way, there is a hundredfold variety of objects within the single pure consciousness,
just as this form of each respective portion of consciousness does not abandon its own nature.

The meaning is as follows: even though a single entity such as fire appears in manifold ways due to differences in place and time, that which is its single, underlying nature—consisting of heat and luminosity—is precisely that inherent nature which persists through those various manifestations. Just as the nature of the individual soul (*jīva*), which is a portion of consciousness, is the very essence of consciousness that pervades all [states], so it is here. || 15 ||

In that which consists of consciousness, those [powers] which shine forth as if within the supreme consciousness—by means of them, that differentiation of their own bodies was performed by those [powers]. (16)

Even within the various modifications (vṛtti-bheda) that abound in consciousness, those cognitions of the reflection of consciousness which seem to flash forth are the very nature [of the Supreme]. In the Supreme, regarding its objects such as earth, water, fire, air, and so forth, among those various modifications— which are like one's own body— whatever specific configuration of form belongs to whichever particular modification, that is [the nature of the Supreme].
That which is made is its form; this means its intrinsic nature (svabhāva). || 16 ||
Consciousness, the earth, water, fire, motion, and even emptiness—
each of these is a mine [of manifestation], yet they are like dreams within the sky.

Having cited these very distinctions of various forms, he shows that the ultimate nature of them all is indeed the foundational space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*)—thus he says "consciousness" (*cit*). Each of those elements, such as the earth and so forth, is a mine (*ākara*) or source for its own effects. The earth is the inherent nature pervading all earthly objects; likewise are water and the others. And for all of them, the sky of consciousness (*cidambara*) is the source.
The meaning is that Brahman itself, variegated by *māyā*, is the source. || 17 ||
In this regard, O King, the surface of the earth—resistant, solid, and the support of all people—shines forth, preeminent among kings. (18)
He elaborates on what has already been stated with the words beginning "Therein" (tatra) and so forth: like a king, he is the bestower of life. || 18 ||
The ocean is the primary essence of waters, the sun is that of all luminous bodies;
the wind is the essence of motion, and space is that of the void pervading the world. (19)
Everything in the world is permeated by its respective specific qualities within the primary elements, such as the Ganges and so forth, as well as fire and so forth;
there is a singular collective expression (*ekavadbhāva*) due to the retention of a single neuter form (*napuṃsakaikaśeṣa*). || 19 ||
"Of the five"—that is, because consciousness is the mine of the elements, those five are appropriately called "Brahmic. What question is there regarding the Sun? (20)

He clarifies the portion concerning their "sky" with the word "five": those five great elements are indeed the consciousnesses of Brahmā manifested in that manner; thus, the meaning is that Brahman alone is the true nature (satsvabhāva) pervading them. With this intention, he states that by this, the question—namely, how it is that among the countless gods, the Sun alone possesses fierce radiance—is also resolved.

—Regarding the word "question": the meaning is that since it has already been resolved by the very answer to the question concerning intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), there is no separate question. || 20 ||
This consciousness is called "Buddha," all-pervading and possessing all forms;
by its own majesty, it is experienced everywhere by everyone. || 21 ||

Because she illuminates everything, the wise know her to be omniscient; because she possesses all forms, she is known by all the realized ones as the supreme nature, the supreme form, and the supreme destiny, solely through the majesty of her characteristic of self-luminosity. || 21 ||
This Brahmātmā, the child of Brahman, possessing the form of the sky, expands this manifestation of his own self-awareness, which is named the earth, the silken garment of the ether.

This youth named Caturmukha-Brahma, being himself of the nature of Brahman, is already of the form of the "Brahman-cloth" (brahmāmbara); thus, he makes vast— that is, he causes to expand and extend— within himself that which is called Bhū, which possesses a covering of linen (kṣauma) consisting of space (vyomātmaka), [space] being the vibration of the consciousness that is his own self.
The verbal root *nāmadhātu* [is derived] from the root *sphurati*; by the rule *vā cisphuror ṇau*, there is the substitution of *ā* for *i*. || 22 ||

When she thus brings this and that to rest through her unborn consciousness—[the reading "viramati" is preferred]—then the flickering [senses], such as the sun and so forth belonging to her limbs, are neither produced nor do they arise. (23)
When that variegated illusion (*māyā*), together with the consciousness of the four-faced one who is unborn from the consciousness of the Omniscient One,

devours this gross and subtle phenomenal world (*prapañca*) and withdraws it into its own self, then the flickering, rotating nature of the form of the sun and other [luminaries], which are limbs of that four-faced consciousness, is no longer produced.
Since that is so, therefore, from this summary, the meaning is that the individual self (ātman) attains the state of the Supreme Person alone. And thus says the Śruti:
"Then, having risen up from there, he neither rises nor sets; he remains alone in the center. || 23 ||
Preceded by volitional thought, this wheel of celestial abodes, like a net of spiders,
appears within the space of consciousness as if it were a visible object, revolving in the manner of a whirlpool.

To indicate that the question— "What causes the length and shortness of the days?"— is answered simply by the well-known distinction between the sun's movement on its southern and northern paths within the celestial sphere (*jyotiścakra*), he displays that celestial sphere:
"Constructed like a net for catching mosquitoes, fashioned by the Creator as a mere creation of his will..."
The stellar wheel of Śiśumāra, which consists of the planets, constellations, and other celestial bodies, is indeed well-known from the treatises on astronomy (jyotiḥśāstra) and similar works.

By means of the Sun, which revolves along the paths of the southern and northern solstices, this shortening and lengthening of the days that you have asked about appears as a fixed phenomenon, corresponding to those respective revolutions. This is the meaning. || 24 ||
In that regard, some objects appear luminous, some appear slightly luminous, and some appear non-luminous; thus do things manifest in various forms. (25)

To the question, "How is it that among the countless gods, the Sun alone possesses fierce radiance?", he shows those many gods who were mentioned as existing in the form of constellations and so forth within the wheel of light (the zodiac), beginning with the word "Therein" (*tatra*). Non-luminous beings such as Rāhu and others, as well as the previously mentioned dark constellations, [are included therein]. || 25 ||
This entire collection of objects has neither been born nor is it seen;
to the knower, this unborn world appears as the void-self, like the objects seen in a dream. (26)
Having thus resolved these questions, he returns to the subject at hand and says: "The aggregate of objects" (padārthajātam) || 26 ||
The Self is pure consciousness alone, the Lord of all, and everything indeed appears as if it were an object of sight;
yet in its own disembodied state, it neither shines nor perishes.
You, I, and everyone else appear as well-known entities, like something beyond the visible; yet when the person has died and become bodiless, they seem to perish.

That which appears like a dream-vision within the sky of consciousness in the ether of consciousness—apart from its nature as the sky of consciousness, whence could there be any other form for this world? (28)
Form is the ultimate nature. || 28 ||

In whatever manner that [reality] vibrates as a vibrating body throughout the full extent of existence, it is here described by such terms as "intrinsic nature" (svabhāva) and "necessity" (niyati). (29)

That very nature of ultimate reality, while superimposed upon the jar and so forth, remains manifest as identical with them for as long as they exist; that same [reality] is designated by such terms as "intrinsic nature" (svabhāva) and "necessity" (niyati). || 29 ||
The existence within the body of space, through the conceptualization of the subtle element of sound, remains in an unmanifest form, like a seed within a granary or a sprout [within the seed]. (30)

Therein, that Brahman-existence remains unmanifest within its own first-born limb, which is of the nature of space, abiding as a conceptualization of the subtle element of sound (śabdatanmātra); like the power of a sprout not yet manifested in seeds contained within a granary, it exists in the form of hope as the potentiality of the seeds of the world, such as air and the rest. || 30 ||
"This was accomplished from that" — such is this effort at composition;
it has been composed in vain by fools for the enlightenment of the simple-minded, as the reading "kṛtā saṃmugdhaḥ" conforms to the commentary. (31)

Therefore, this conceptualization— that from her (Māyā) this world, consisting of the elements and elemental derivatives characterized by air, fire, and water, arises in succession— was formulated by the Śrutis and the sages with the desire to explain the construction of the universe for the sake of awakening the truth in those who are deluded and ignorant; it is not that creation itself is ultimately real.

[This is] for the sake of demonstration. If that were the case, this account of creation would have been composed in vain by fools alone. For the sense is that no purpose whatsoever—either seen or heard—is observed for anyone in knowing that creation is not real.
"Nothing here ever sets, nor does anything ever rise."
Like the interior of a stone, this [world] is eternally peaceful; though it exists, it is non-existent.

Since that true form of Brahman neither sets nor rises, therefore this form of the phenomenal world is real by virtue of the Supreme Being's existence, but is non-existent in itself; such is the meaning. || 32 ||
Just as the atoms that are the parts of a whole never cease to exist within it,
nor do they rise or set, so too the worlds do not rise or set within the state of the Self.

He says "yathā" (just as) to show that, since the world does not have an existence separate [from Brahman], it is essentially comprised of parts within Brahman and is thus devoid of rising and setting. The first negative particle (*na*) is for the purpose of negating separate existence. || 33 ||
The world-space exists within the space of Brahman, just as one void exists within another void;
how then can that which is utterly pure ever set or rise? 34.

He states—“Brahman in the void”—that when the existence of the world apart from the existence of Brahman is denied, the world resolves into Brahman alone as pure; thus, its manifold variety, such as rising and setting, comes to an end. || 34 ||
Of that gem of consciousness, whose nature is infinite light and which is all-pervasive, there is a manifestation consisting of pure existence alone, occurring incessantly by its very nature. (35)

Thus, having established that upon the thorough investigation of the reality of the world it is nothing but Brahman, he begins with the words "Of that... (tasya) and so forth, in order to explain how the very Brahman, through forgetting its own true nature, undergoes the transformation into the form of the world. || 35 ||
Then, by means of that [intellect], it itself appears as if becoming slightly objectifiable;
though its nature remains ungrasped, it indicates the movement of reflective awareness within consciousness. (36)
Because it has not yet grasped its own nature, it is therefore initially unknown; otherwise, it would indicate deliberation and reflection due to its transformation. || 36 ||
Through the perception of future objects, its form is slightly inferred;
it is subtler than space, pure, and the awakening to all that is yet to be.
The manifestation of that [Supreme Reality] in a form conceived by you arises from the contemplation of the future phenomenal world. || 37 ||
Then that supreme Being, being oriented toward consciousness, becomes fit for the name "Citi" (consciousness) by virtue of its being slightly attainable through that [orientation]. 38.

When that [intellect] has reflected upon its objects and becomes oriented toward right cognition (*samyakcetanā*), it cognizes; thus, by obtaining the occasion for the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) as "that which cognizes" (*cit*), it becomes fit for the name "consciousness" (*cit*). || 38 ||
Following from that dense perception, there arises a conceptualization of a self called "living being" (jīva) and so forth; yet, as this occurs, it becomes the supreme state.
He states what occurs after that: "Dense," etc. Being thus present, when one attains birth as a qualified candidate (adhikārī), it becomes the supreme state once again. || 39 ||
Having internalized the state of being covered by the sky of consciousness (cidākāśa), she remains as the inexpressible;
now, however, she is of a non-dual nature with the utterly pure plane.

Is it not the case that she is always the supreme state? To what excellence does her verbal expression lead, given that one attains knowledge through a body qualified for such practice? He says: "having internalized" (*garbhīkṛtya*). Since she remains in the state of individual life (*jīvatva*) having internalized the ignorance (*avidyā*) that veils the space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*), she is therefore "inexpressible" (*anākhyā*)—her nature as the supreme state being unmanifested—at the time of the attainment of knowledge.
The meaning is that now, for the pure state, which is of no other form, there occurs the attainment of indivisible oneness alone. || 40 ||
At that time, these [faculties], intent on a cycle of existence whose essence consists solely of the singular contemplation of the self,
follow that [self] through their inherent inseparability.

Then, in the state of being veiled (*āvṛtatā-daśā*), through the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of identity with the Self (*ātmatādātmya*)—which consists essentially in the mere contemplation of that [Self] as one with itself—the soul becomes intent on transmigratory existence by means of the body, senses, and so forth. "Separation" (*vinābhāva*) is the dissociation from its true nature (*svarūpa-viyoga*); the "afflictions caused by that" (*tatkṛta-tāpāḥ*) are the sufferings resulting therefrom. It undergoes these: *tam* (in the sense of exhaustion), *glāniḥ*, *tamanam*, *tāmaḥ*, and the actions (*karmāṇi*) caused by them; these are the "afflictions" (*tāpāḥ*). In the reading *tābhimāḥ*, it refers to those [afflictions] characterized by egoistic conceit (*abhimāna*).
These are well-known as the Abhimānīs and Anabhimās; the sandhi is archaic. 41.

The single self-existence, whose nature is emptiness, yet contains within it the qualities such as sound and so forth, is fully perfected through the cultivation of consciousness; this is the state of being the referent of future designations.

That single self-existence (svasattā), which is by nature devoid of any other entity, contains within it the qualities such as sound and the like; through the error of conceptualizing consciousness (savikalpacidbhāvanā), it becomes fully manifested.
It serves as the ground for the application of the names of the five future elements, beginning with space (ākāśa), and constitutes their objective referent (arthatā).
That is to say, consisting of subtle elements. || 42 ||
Immediately thereafter, it arises together with the very existence of time;
for you, that [seed] is the primary cause for the future state of the world's persistence. (43)
By that [verse], he describes the conceptualization of the subtle body (liṅgadeha) as being dominated by the sense of "I" (ahaṃkāra): "The state of 'I'... etc.
Through the existence of time brought about by the activity of the vital breaths (prāṇa), which constitute the subtle body, there arise those two: the state of "I" and the existence of time. (43)
The net of the world, which is unreal in nature, is merely the self-perception of the supreme power of consciousness; through that consciousness, it appears as if real. (44)
In that regard, he states—“of the power of consciousness” (citiśakteḥ)—that the delusion of the world arises therein through the manifestation of the living consciousness. || 44 ||
Having such a nature, that consciousness is the seed of the tree of volition; conceiving it within as something not previously seen, it itself becomes this [world] in an instant. (45)

This very thing called the "living soul" (jīva) now wanders within the state of the Self through the whirlpools of the fluctuations of existence and non-existence, like water moving in the form of waves within water. (46)
In the state of the Self, which is Brahman variegated by Māyā. || 46 ||
When consciousness possesses such a state of contemplation regarding the subtle element of space, it gradually solidifies by itself and perceives the subtle element of ether (ākāśa-tanmātra).

He describes the conceptualization of the gross five elements as the collective totality (*samaṣṭi*) of that [unmanifest] in the form of Hiraṇyagarbha, beginning with the word "cid" (consciousness). Having condensed—that is, having made dense—the subtle ideation of the space-tanmātra, [one obtains] the gross ether, which is the self-tanmātra. || 47 ||
That seed of the tree of the flood of words is the form of future objects;
it undergoes transformation into the meanings of words, sentences, the means of valid knowledge, the Vedas, and so forth. (48)

Therefore, the entire glory of the world shall arise from the reality of sound (śabdatattva), spreading forth through the transformation of the multitude of objects fashioned by the flood of sound. (49)

"Therefore," etc. The meaning is based on such scriptural passages as: "He uttered 'bhūḥ' and created the earth; 'eta' indeed did Prajāpati create the gods; 'asṛgram' [did he create] humans; 'indavaḥ' [did he create] the ancestors," and so forth. || 49 ||
That consciousness, characterized by such a resolve, is designated by the word "jīva";
it is the seed of the tree that is the multitude of past beings, through the web of future words and objects.
The meaning is that it is Brahman-consciousness itself—possessing such resolve and such diverse volitions—that is designated by the word "jīva," and nothing else. || 50 ||
From that, the fourteenfold collection of living beings, which envelops the sky and fills the ears of the world's interior, will spread forth.
Not yet having attained the designation or activity [of a formal being], it is conscious by virtue of its livingness;
like the "crow-and-palm" coincidence, it itself perceives as mere vibration-consciousness (spandacinmātra). 52.

He describes the manner in which she conceives of the collective skin and other sense organs for the enjoyment of the elements and elemental products created by herself, beginning with the words "asaṃprāpta" and so forth. Being such that there is no verbal designation—that is, no linguistic usage—and no practical activity—that is, no worldly conduct—by means of the body and so on, she perceives and conceives of that which is to be described for that purpose. || 52 ||
The seed of the tree whose form is the aggregate of wind, and whose bark and touch are its nature, is this;
from it, the vibration of the activity of all beings shall spread forth.
In that regard, whatever experience of light occurs as the play of consciousness,
that is the subtle element of form (*rūpatanmātra*), which will provide the objects corresponding to their designations.
Luminous consciousness is light; that light cannot be produced by anything else.
Tactile sensation is touch; it does not arise from any other touch.
He establishes that the very nature of the experience of light is the subtle element of form (*rūpa-tanmātra*) with the words "prakāśacetanam" (light-consciousness).
He states that touch and the others should be understood in the same way with the words beginning with "sparśa" (touch). || 55 ||
The perception of sound is sound itself; it is experienced by itself alone, just as space is perceived by space within its own cavity. Indeed, there exists nothing else that produces sound.

Just as space, having found its own scope within its own sheath which is of the nature of space itself, remains there and not by means of anything else, so too consciousness is produced by sound and perceives sound through sound alone, which is its own essence; the meaning is that there is nothing else [besides this].
Indeed, in that state, who else could be the creator of sound?
Just so, even today, duality and unity are utterly impossible.

It should be understood that just as at the beginning of creation it appeared in its collective form (*samaṣṭi*), so too now, in its individual form (*vyaṣṭi*), it is consciousness itself that, having superimposed the forms of various objects upon itself, appears in the guise of the world and nothing else. Thus he says: "it is said" (*kila*).
Just as it was then, so it is even today. Furthermore, this must necessarily be accepted by all disputants; otherwise—

This is because the determination of objects for cognitions is established [only through them]. Indeed, the very identity with consciousness (*saṃvit-tādātmyam*) is the object-nature (*viṣayatā*) of objects, and no other [nature] can be established even by thousands of arguments. Furthermore, an identity characterized by oneness with consciousness is not possible for sound and the like if they were not of the nature of consciousness; with this intention, he says: "of duality and unity" (verse 57).
For in this way, the subtle element of taste and the subtle element of smell, though entirely unreal, are perceived as if they were real, like a dream. (58)
The principle demonstrated regarding sound should be understood to apply to taste and the other [objects] as well; thus he says: "For in this way... (58).
The seed of the tree of light is the splendor [of consciousness] manifested through the sun and other luminaries;
from that, through the differentiation of forms, the cycle of existence will expand. (59)
Having concluded the incidental discussion, he speaks of the subject at hand: "Fire," etc. For the eyes were split open;
from the two eyes came sight, and from sight came the sun—so says the Śruti. (59)
Then, the relishing of that which is called "the future," which is non-existent like the sky or like a self, is termed the subtle element of taste for that assembly. (50)

From that which is non-existent and devoid of modification, like space from the sky; "svadana" is the consciousness of sweetness; [it arises] from that aggregate of food, drink, and so forth, which has been quintuplicated (pañcīkṛta). || 60 ||
This entire group, consisting of the mental construction of future forms, is of the nature of volition; it then perceives the subtle elements, such as odor and the rest.
This entire group, consisting of the collection of causes and effects, is the individual soul (jīva). || 61 ||
From that seed of the tree of form, which is the soul of all supports and exists as the future earth-globe, this cycle of existence will expand forth.
Though unborn, that host of mere elements has come into being;
though formless, it has become possessed of form through the power of conceptual construction.

This group of subtle elements (tanmātras), by its own nature like the "crow-and-the-palm-fruit" coincidence, perceives form through a particular location; that [location] is called the sense-organ (akṣi). (64)
He states the conceptualization of the locations of the eyeballs and so forth with the words beginning "This," etc. (verse 64).
That region by which one perceives sound is called the sense of hearing;
that region by which one perceives touch is the tactile faculty (tvagindriya). || 65 ||
That part by which one perceives taste is the gustatory faculty;
that part by which one perceives odor, however, is the olfactory faculty.
Due to the distinctions of space and time, this individual soul has assumed a limited form;
because it lacks the nature of being the Self of all, it does not know everything with all its limbs. (67)

He describes this [individual soul's] conceptualization of distinctions of space and time, which is conditioned by the sense of "I" directed toward the body that possesses the two-fold discernment—beginning with the words "space" (*dig*).

The ellipsis to be supplied is: "it performs the reckoning of space and time. Furthermore, it does not perceive all objects such as taste and smell through every limb, such as the eyes and ears; likewise, as an individual entity (*vyaṣṭi*), it does not perceive the entire range of objects of experience through its whole body.
The meaning is: because of the fault that [the self] would not be the universal self (asarvātmatā). || 67 ||
Thus, the infinite reckoning of the self—immanent, inferable, non-different, and identical with the Self—neither rises nor sets; it remains as solid and profoundly silent as the interior of a stone.

In this manner, although it has not been explicitly stated, the infinite worldly conditioning (*kalana*) that exists within each individual soul (*jīva*) is to be inferred from its very infinity; because of that infinity, it is impossible to describe it individually.
Furthermore, that infinite conditioning is non-different from the Self, being of the very nature of the Self. Therefore, in the ultimate sense (*paramārthatas*), it does not arise at all.

Nor does it go to setting or destruction; rather, like the interior of a gem, it remains as a single, solid mass of being, consciousness, and bliss, entirely devoid of activity—this is the meaning. || 68 ||
Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-seventh canto, titled "The Exposition on the Existence of Living Beings," in the Holy Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa, the Forest Book of the Southern Recension.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-seventh chapter, titled "The Exposition of the State of Being a Living Being and of Transmigration," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and eighty-eighth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
This which has been described is the state of having a beginning belonging to this mental construction (kalanā).
The reality that is non-dual with respect to another is not real for the sake of awakening.
