The individual soul is indeed Brahman; this "birth" of his is merely figurative, occurring through the delusion of the subtle body—this is clearly established here.

The production of the living being (*jīva*) was established by the passage beginning with "subsequent to the dense perception [of the elements], there arises that which is named 'living being' (*jīva*)," and so forth. However, that is not tenable; for since a newly produced living being lacks the desires, karmas, and latent impressions (*vāsanā*) that cause *saṃsāra*, *saṃsāra* would be impossible for him. Consequently, he would fall into the state of falsity (*mithyātva*), like a jar or a cloth.

Lest the doubt arise in Rāma that liberation is unattainable because of the impossibility of identifying with the nature of Brahman, the Blessed One himself stated its intended meaning: "The state of having a beginning," etc. This refers to the *kalanam*—the differentiation of the individual soul (*jīva*), which consists of the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*).
That differentiation is non-dual and non-distinct from the supreme Brahman; this is for the sake of your understanding, and not because there is actual origination or the like in reality.
The meaning is: with the intention that "the living being exists. || 1 ||
Such an innate modification of the Self, which is the reflection of consciousness directed toward an object of thought, is designated by the term "jīva. || 2 ||
By what method is it taught that [the Self] is non-dual with respect to anything else? To this he says: "of such a kind.
That manifestation (*kalanam*) of the Self, which is Brahman, is "of such a kind" as an adventitious limb or member; for this very reason, it is uncreated (*akṛtrima*).
The phrase "turned toward the object of cognition" (*cetyonmukha*) is a restatement of what was previously mentioned. And thus, it is indeed adventitious.

The meaning is that the intention [of the author] is this: the state of being separate and the distinction of names such as "living beings" (jīva) and so forth, which are applied to it, belong only to the Supreme; just as the distinction of names such as "the space within a jar" (ghaṭākāśa) and "the space within a hut" (maṭhākāśa) belongs only to space itself. || 2 ||
O descendant of Raghu, listen to these many diverse names of this *kāla*, which is the conscious self (*cidātman*) oriented toward objects of thought (*cetyonmukha*). (3)

By the passage beginning with "of the reckoning" (kalanasya), [the text] declares the various names of the individual soul (*jīva*), which arise from its adventitious modes of activity and the distinctions caused by those very modes. || 3 ||
From its being the living principle, the conscious one is called "jīva" (the living soul);
and by its orientation toward objects of consciousness, the mind is designated as "citi" (consciousness). || 4 ||

It is called *jīva* because it sustains the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the organs of action (*karmendriya*), and consciousness; and it is called *citta* because of its orientation toward objects previously experienced, past, and future, and it is called *cit* because of its orientation toward immediate objects. (4)

Because it possesses clear cognition of "this is such-and-such," it is called *buddhi* (intellect) here; because it conceives through imagination and knows by reflecting, it is designated as *manas* (mind).
Because of its conceptualizing and volitional imagining, and because it knows deliberation, reasoning, and refutation, it is called the mind (manas). || 5 ||
The internal ego is said to arise from the notion "I am," while the mind, rich with consciousness, is called the immortal by those who investigate the scriptures. (6)

The expression "I am" (asmīti) refers to the manifestation of ego-conceit (*abhimāna*). Through the common understanding of ordinary people (*pāmara*), the term *citta* was previously explained as "mind. However, according to the consensus of scholars, based on the etymology of the verbal root *cit* in the sense of "to perceive" (*saṃjñāne*), those who investigate the scriptures have stated that the primary meaning of the word *citta* is the Self (*ātman*) itself—the supreme reality (*paramārthavastu*) which is Truth (*ṛta*) and enriched by the consciousness of its own true nature. This is the meaning. || 6 ||
From the web of mature volitions, it is known as the "eightfold city" (puryaṣṭaka);
because it is the primary cause of transmigratory existence, it is known as "primordial nature" (prakṛti).
The meaning is that they are called *puryaḥ* because the individual soul (*jīva*) is filled (*pūryate*) by them through volition and so forth; thus, the term refers to a group of eight (*aṣṭaka*).
This is because they are "under discussion" (*prakṛtatvena*), having been introduced at the time of creation and so on, and therefore they are primary. || 7 ||
"Because it does not exist from the perspective of awakening, it is called 'ignorance' (avidyā) by the wise.
Thus have these names for this conceptualization been told to you. (8)
Because, through awakening—that is, the vision of reality—it does not exist in its conditioned form. || 8 ||
This [Self], which is without beginning or end, formless and free from disease,
is designated by the wise through the term "subtle body" (ātivāhika-deha).
Thus, the delusion of the three worlds—appearing as a substantial body yet performing functions—is like a city in a dream or a mental construction; it is empty and non-obstructive in nature.
The two goals are enjoyment and liberation; even their cause is a formless body.
Thus has the subtle body (ātivāhika-deha) been described, O best of embodied beings;
this mental body is the sky of consciousness, more void even than space.
The ground of consciousness is the single source of the fourteenfold creation of beings; it neither sets nor rises within the world until the realization of liberation.
He states for how long he remains there: "until liberation-consciousness. The ground in the form of the mind (*citta*) is the place of growth for the creation of the elements. (12)
In this regard, hundreds of thousands of cycles of existence will come to be and are currently coming to be;
they have also existed in the past, like fruits according to the arrangement of time. (13)
This body, composed of mind, exists both within and outside the worlds;
it is as empty as the sky, like a reflection in a mirror. (14)
Just as a mirror holds reflections of worlds both within and without, yet the sky remains truly empty—this is the meaning.
(14) When the great dissolution has occurred and all destruction is firmly established, one abides in the exalted state of the Great Void, the stainless Self of Brahman. (15)

Regarding the question "From what time has he been supporting the worlds?", he says: "At the end of the great kalpa," that is, at the final moment of the primary dissolution (prākṛtapralaya). || 15 ||

Being by its own nature a mass of consciousness and lacking the state of being an insentient object, this manifestation of consciousness belonging to the Self perceives, through this sequence, as if it were a subtle, transportable body (ātivāhika-deha).
Due to the absence of consciousness, from the cause which is ignorance that veils consciousness; by this aforementioned sequence. || 16 ||
That subtle body, impelled by that light, is called "Brahman" by some and remembered as "Virāj" by others. (17)

That very soul is the subtle body (ativāhika-deha); its light, which consists of the perception of the universe, has set in motion a certain portion that is described in the scriptures as the four-faced Brahmā, saying "I am. || 17 ||
One was known by the name Sanātana, another was named Nārāyaṇa;
one was celebrated as Īśa, and another was called Prajāpati. || 18 ||
The mention of Sanātana is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa) for the sons of Brahmā, such as Sanaka and the others.
The five cognitions of one's own sense-faculties appear like the coincidence of the crow and the palm fruit;
wherever and in whatever manner they abide, there they remain exactly so. (19)
In whichever part the perceptions of one's own five senses appear, there the corresponding objects are likewise situated. || 19 ||
Thus, when this vast and fully developed delusion of the visible has arisen,
not even the slightest thing has truly come into being, because everything is pervaded by emptiness.
The reality of the Self is pervasive and vast, because it is empty of all that is perceived. || 20 ||
The supreme Brahman, which has no beginning, is said to be neither being nor non-being;
it is that very same reality, without beginning or end, existing thus as non-cognition.

The existent is that which has become manifest; the non-existent is that which has become concealed. For that very same non-cognition, being devoid of the direct realization of its own nature, thus exists in the form of both the existent and the non-existent. || 21 ||
As that subtle body experiences it for itself,
the dream of one who is thus afflicted attains fullness, like a beloved woman approaching her lover.
This conceptual proliferation reaches full development for one who is distressed and addicted to the pursuit of a beloved, like a beloved in a dream. || 22 ||
Even though it is empty and formless, the form of a jar is experienced, just as in dreams and mental constructs one experiences one's own body and the world.

He states another illustration for the appearance of the void world itself in the form of the world: "Even though empty," etc. The meaning is that there is an illustration for how one's own body and the world appear as if they were inherently real, even though they are [actually] void. || 23 ||
It becomes exceedingly high as an object that fulfills purposes, like an object in a dream within the space of consciousness;
though its nature is purely that of space, it appears like a formidable material entity. (24)
He says "it exists" to show that even for such [a thing], the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*) is well-established in that very [place]. "Ugra" means harsh or rigid. || 24 ||
This subtle body (ātivāhikadeha), though formless, empty, dream-like, and non-existent, experiences by itself in succession, yet remains present.
The collection of bones, including the consciousness, constitutes the gross series of limbs such as the hands, which exists as an arrangement of three types of hair, veins, and sinews. (26)

And that *jīva*, in the form of the subtle body (*ativāhika-deha*), [perceives] the gross body— which consists of a collection of bones, the spine of the triple-jointed [back], and the hair through its various arrangements as warp and woof,

or through the distinctions of the limiting conditions of the flesh enveloping the bone, and the distinctions of the veins and sinews existing as their particular configurations— within the sphere of space, time, sequence, posture, sound, and other sense objects.
The logical connection is that it moves for the sake of enjoyment. || 26 ||
It is the locus of birth, action, and experience, established in transformation and age;
it is the delusion of arising for the sake of objects and states, through the sequence of place and time.
And within that body, its arising—that is, its birth—he perceives as a delusion.
It encompasses the progression through the ten directions of the sphere of birth, old age, and death;
it is the state of knowledge, the object of knowledge, and the knower, as well as the perception of beginning, middle, and end.

Likewise, it perceives old age and death, the imposition of qualities and defects, the traversing of the ten directions, the sequence, the wandering, the triad of knowledge and so forth, and the perception of the beginning, middle, and end of all states of being. || 28 ||

The ancient Puruṣa perceives his own body as consisting of the earth, water, sky, sun, people, worldly transactions, cities, and mountain peaks, composed of both the support and that which is supported. (29)

Thus, the ancient Puruṣa, having become the subtle body (ātivāhika-deha), by means of the causes consisting of the individual and collective gross bodies imagined by himself, being himself the self of everything from the earth up to the peak of Meru, perceives the dream of saṃsāra—which is composed of delusion—in which the earth and other elements are his supports and he himself is supported by them. This is the meaning. || 29 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-eighth canto, titled "The Description of the Nature of the Living Being," in the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* of Valmīki, belonging to the *Divya*, *Mokṣa*, *Nirvāṇa*, and *Upadeśa* sections.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Nature of the Living Being," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and eighty-ninth chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
This is the subtle body (ātivāhikadeha) of that first Prajāpati.
If one thinks that consciousness and so forth occur by chance, like the "crow-and-palm" coincidence, then [the following applies]: || 1 ||
In this world, the delusion of materiality is described with respect to the subtle body, the self, the progenitor Prajāpati, and mental desire.

The connection with the subsequent clause is as follows: "Whatever [the mind] perceives in whatever manner, that very thing attains stability in that same way," according to the detailed modes described in such passages as "One is called Brahman" and "Another is remembered as Virāj. || 1 ||
Thus, by its very nature as consciousness, it remains for a long time in that state;
alas, this entire universe appears [as such]—how can there be any astonishment at this which is unreal? (2)
This entire universe has appeared by virtue of the very nature of consciousness, which possesses the power of true volition; "batā" expresses lamentation. || 2 ||
The seer is unreal, the seeing is unreal, and that vision is pervasive;
or else, everything is indeed real, for by virtue of that [vision], all is Brahman as the Self.

Therefore, because it is mere illusion, the triad beginning with the seer—the seer, the seen, and the seeing—is unreal; "seen" refers to the object, and "seeing" refers to the mental modification (*vṛtti*). || 3 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
Thus ends the account of the world of the subtle body belonging to that first Prajāpati.
How did it attain such solidity? And how can there be reality in a dream?

Thus, in this manner, if the vision of the *ātivāhika* (subtle body) is merely a perception consisting of delusion, then how can it possess solidity—that is, the state of being stone and so forth—or reality—that is, the capacity for causal efficiency regarding results in the next world and the like? (4)
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
The subtle, transportive light is experienced by itself alone; because it is always and incessantly so, that very light shines forth as if fully nourished.
"Always" means continuously. Likewise, through long-term practice, it appears as if it has become nourished and solidified. (5)
Just as the fullness of a dream, when experienced for a long time,
appears as if it were perfectly real, so too does its subtle, ethereal nature appear.
The meaning is that it is just as the dream of Hariścandra and others possessed a richness appropriate for being experienced over a long duration. || 6 ||
When the subtle body (ātivāhikadeha) has long experienced its own nature,
the notion of materiality arises within it, like water in a mirage.

The world appears as a delusive manifestation like a dream, existing like the water of a mirage; though it is entirely non-existent, it shines forth even while producing the conviction that it is real.
The materiality of the subtle bodies (ātivāhika-rūpa) is itself unreal;
yet it is sought by those of limited vision as if it were real, though it lies far away.
By those of limited vision and lack of discrimination; "desired" means accepted through attachment. || 9 ||
"This is I," "this is mine," "these are the mountains, the sky, and the directions"—thus this false delusion appears like a mountain in a vivid dream. (10)
This subtle body (ātivāhikadeha), fashioned by the primordial Creator,
perceives this material form as having the nature of a physical aggregate.
This is the form of a physical body, such as the earth-body and so forth. || 11 ||
Having abandoned the consciousness of the intellect, one perceives, "I am Brahman";
yet, one binds oneself with the notion that "this is the body" and "this is the support. || 12 ||

Having abandoned the correct cognition that "I am Brahman," one perceives, "This body, a human being and so forth, is I; this earth and so forth are my support," and therein one fixes one's mental cultivation and attachment. || 12 ||
By meditating on the unreal with the conviction that it is real, one becomes bound;
by repeatedly cultivating this internally, one pursues manifold diversity. (13)
It runs after; it pursues. || 13 ||
He produces sounds, conventions, designations, and vibrations;
when "Om" is uttered, he then chants forth the Vedas, the masses of sacred words.

First, he produces and creates Vedic and worldly words; he establishes a convention for them with respect to objects possessing their respective limiting adjuncts (upādhi), and by means of that convention, he creates designations. He describes the manner in which words are produced: "When 'Om' is uttered," and so forth. || 14 ||
By means of those very [concepts], the mind quickly constructs worldly discourse here and there; for the mind indeed conceptualizes that which it perceives.
For how can that which consists of something not perceive it?
Thus, the unreal delusion of the world has reached such maturity. (16)
"Consisting of that" means "attached to that," just as in the expression "a fool consisting of women. || 16 ||
"Everything up to Brahmā appears in vain, like a long dream or a magical illusion.
Thus, this [notion] of the subtle body (ātivāhika) being composed of material elements (ādhibhautika) is appropriate. 17.
In this manner, from Brahmā down to a tiny insect, materiality—characterized by solidity and other such qualities—is entirely appropriate and not improper. || 17 ||
There is no materiality whatsoever anywhere at all;
through practice, this [body] attains the state of pure subtle spirituality.
This is the contemplation on the elemental (ādhibhautika) nature. || 18 ||
"Since it has arisen thus from the very root, this delusion consisting of false experience belongs to Brahman alone"—this is the conviction of the great-souled ones. (19)

The meaning is this: since this delusion of such a nature has arisen from the very source of the Creator, Brahman, who is its root, this error consisting in the perception of the world persists even for the great-souled knowers of reality as long as their *prārabdha* karma is not exhausted.
Thus, O Rāma, in this state, where can there be any "solidification" (*piṇḍabandha*)?
All this is either merely an illusion, or it is Brahman alone that appears as such.

Where could such a miserable state exist for Brahman, whose sole essence is consciousness? Rather, all this—beginning with the miserable state of saṃsāra—is merely an illusion. Or else, Brahman itself has appeared in the form of the world, living beings, and so forth, out of a sense of playful curiosity (*kautuka*). For one’s own nature cannot be a miserable state for oneself. Thus ends [the section].
And this is a demonstration of the definitive extraction of the distinction between bondage and liberation. || 20 ||
There is nothing here other than the eternal; there is no cause apart from that which is indeed devoid of being an effect.
Since the possibility of being an effect or a cause does not exist in the Untainted (Anāmaya), what then is this that has been so extensively spread out?
There is no cause for the world other than the eternal Brahman; and that [Brahman] cannot be a cause without being an effect.
In the flawless, immutable, non-dual Brahman—which is consciousness and bliss—the possibility of being either an effect or a cause does not exist at all.
Therefore, for this reason, this world-form is merely an expansion of some delusion; it is not a real entity.
The meaning is "the extraction. || 21 ||
Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-ninth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Oneness of Brahman," in the *Mokṣopāya* section of the *Vāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa*, the sacred work of the Seer (*ārṣa*).
Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-ninth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Unity of Brahman," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and ninetieth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: The state of knowledge becoming an object of cognition is designated as bondage.
The pacification of the very knowability of that [object] is designated as liberation. || 1 ||
Having completely cleared away all doubts concerning the past and the future through logical reasoning,
the pacification of the knowability of knowledge is established here as liberation.
At the conclusion, he has demonstrated the definitive analysis of bondage and liberation by stating that "all this is either merely an illusion or it is Brahman alone appearing as such.
Having refined that point, he says: "Of knowledge... (Verse 1).
Śrī Rāma said:
O Brahman, how does the peace that comes from the cessation of the objectivity of knowledge proceed? And once that [peace] has taken root, how is the notion of bondage here turned away?

In this context, Rāma, desiring to reveal the sequence of resolutions by unfolding the sequence of answers to questions—even those doubts previously raised—for the benefit of all, first asks about the means [thereto] with the words "of knowledge" (*jñānasya*). "Rūḍhā" means firmly practiced. "Katham" means by what means? 2.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Through perfect knowledge— that is, through the awakening of right understanding— the dull-witted person is turned away from ignorance.
Thus, liberation itself proceeds as formless, innate, and peaceful. || 3 ||

Through awakening characterized by firm and well-practiced right knowledge, accompanied by the means such as tranquility and self-control, the delusion of the dull-witted mind is removed. And when the dream of delusion has vanished, liberation in the form of peace—such a state of knowability—proceeds to manifest through the gradual ripening of the stages [of practice]. || 3 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
What is that which is called perfect knowledge— bodha in the form of absolute liberation—
by which this living being is completely released from bondage?

In the case of objects such as jewels, which possess numerous specific qualities, even when some of those qualities are known, there may be another correct cognition produced by repeated reflection for the sake of knowing other remaining qualities. But in the case of an entity devoid of specific qualities, what other correct cognition could there be— beyond the initial superficial cognition— by means of which its bondage might be removed?
The meaning is doubt. || 4 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Knowledge has no object of knowledge; it is merely undecaying knowledge.
That internal realization which is inexpressible is remembered as perfect knowledge.

Since that which consists of pure consciousness as the substratum (adhiṣṭhāna) possesses no objectivity (jñeyatā) even throughout the three periods of time, the direct realization of reality (tattvasākṣātkāra) culminates precisely in the sublation of all that is perceivable; however, superficial knowledge is not so—this is the meaning of the subsequent verse. || 5 ||
Śrī Rāma said:

O Sage, tell me: is the knowability of knowledge distinct [from knowledge], or what is it within? Furthermore, is the word "knowledge" (jñāna) to be understood in the sense of an action (bhāva), or rather in the sense of an instrument (karaṇa)?

Since the Self is of the single essence of consciousness, how could there be within it a state of being an object of knowledge distinct from that? Likewise, the question regarding the word "knowledge" (jñāna) is whether it is to be derived in the sense of an action—as something to be produced or explained—or rather in the sense of an instrument—as something by which one is explained. This is the meaning of the inquiry. || 6 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Knowledge is merely awakening, consisting solely of the means to realize existence.
There is no difference between knowledge and the object of knowledge, just as there is none between the wind and its movement.

The word "knowledge" (jñāna) is to be derived as denoting the very state of being; and the fact that the world of objects is the form of knowledge itself is merely a figurative conceptualization (vikalpa), not something that destroys its essential unity—this is the meaning of the subsequent verse. || 7 ||

Śrī Rāma said: If this is so, then how has this delusion of knowledge and the knowable come to be established— this which resembles the horn of a hare, yet is perceived as the past, present, and future?

If this is so, then how can that conceptual construction—which is like the horn of a hare—appear as something capable of functioning through the divisions of past, present, and future by means of perception and the other sources of knowledge? This is the meaning of the question.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
The deluded intellect described here is to be understood as arising from the error regarding external objects;
for neither an external object nor an internal one exists at all.

Non-existence is not the determining factor for the absence of manifestation or the capacity for causal efficiency; for even a thousand non-existent things are seen in dreams and erroneous cognitions. Rather, sublation is the determining factor. And that [sublation] certainly exists here—both as a logical inference for those who investigate and as direct perception for those who know reality. This is the meaning of the subsequent verse. || 9 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
O Sage, tell me how this object which is perceptible to the senses—this self that consists of "you," "I," and so forth, as well as the elements and the like—is not existent for me? 10.
The meaning of the question is: how can that which is established by means of worldly perception and so forth be denied? || 10 ||

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O sinless one, even at the very beginning of the primary creation, no object whatsoever was born as the primordial Virāṭ-ātman; therefore, there is no possibility of anything that can be known.

The intended meaning of the subsequent portion is as follows: since at the initial creation of the world no causal complex other than *māyā* can be satisfactorily described, and since it must necessarily be admitted that [the world] is mere illusion, the same must be asserted even now; thus, while worldly perception and the like fulfill their purpose through the mere non-contradiction of empirical usage, they are sublated by reasonings concerning reality and by the Śruti scriptures. Likewise:
And scripture says: "There is neither cessation nor origination, neither one bound nor a seeker of liberation, neither one desiring release nor indeed release—this is the ultimate reality. (11)
Śrī Rāma said: O Sage, this vision of the world—which exists in the past, present, and future—is constantly being experienced; why then is it said that it has not arisen?

The meaning of the objection is: how can there be a sublation by a single cognition of reality (tattvajñāna) of the infinite perceptions and other means of knowledge that have as their objects all things—past, future, and so forth—which are infinite and common to all people? || 12 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Like the objects of a dream, the water of a mirage, the moon in the clouds, or a mentally constructed object,
the world and the sense of "I" (ahaṃtva) appear falsely, like the optical illusion of a hair-tuft.
The meaning of the latter part [of the verse] is that even for such dream-cognitions, sublation is observed by a single waking state. || 13 ||

Śrī Rāma said: O Blessed One, how was it that at the beginning of creation, even the interior of the universe— consisting of "I," "you," "this," and so forth— did not arise as an object of experience?
The meaning of the question is: by what reasoning is there sublation? || 14 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
It is a certainty that an effect arises from a cause and not otherwise;
yet, in the universal quiescence and the subsequent emergence of worlds, there is no cause.
The meaning of the subsequent [verse] is by means of the reasoning of the absence of a cause. || 15 ||
Śrī Rāma said: O Sage, that which remains at the occurrence of the great dissolution— unborn and immutable— how indeed could it not be the cause of creation?
The meaning of the question is: why could Brahman itself not be the cause? || 16 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Whatever effect exists within its cause, from that it proceeds;
for nothing non-existent is born, O Rāma, nor does a cloth arise from a jar.
The meaning of the latter part [of the verse] is that because Brahman consists of the single essence of consciousness (cidekarasa), the power of the seed of the world cannot exist therein. || 17 ||
Śrī Rāma said: When the great dissolution has arrived, the world remains within Brahman in a subtle form; therefore, it proceeds forth once again.
The meaning of the question is: "In that case, let the world exist at that time in a subtle form within Brahman, just as it does within the *guṇas* favored by the Sāṃkhyas."
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
O sinless one of great intelligence, by whom was the existence of creation experienced at the end of the great dissolution? And what is that state like which resides therein?

The intention of the subsequent [verse] is that it is impossible to accept [that position], because there is no proof for its existence and because it is contradicted by the scriptural texts on non-duality (aikarasya). || 19 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
The Śrī (glory) residing there is experienced as being of the nature of consciousness;
however, that which is of the nature of space cannot exist, for it is neither being nor non-being.

In that case, let its existence at that time consist solely in self-luminosity through its nature as pure consciousness (*jñapti*); it cannot, however, be of the nature of the illusory space (*māyākāśa*).

For, since that [illusory space] culminates in emptiness (*śūnyatā*), it is impossible for what is non-existent to come into being as something existent. This is the meaning of the question; for indeed, what is non-existent does not attain existence. || 20 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
If this is so, O mighty-armed one, then the three worlds are nothing but consciousness.
For one whose body is pure knowledge, how can there be death or birth?

If it were thus, the world would consist of nothing but a single essence; and since there would be no basis for differentiation, what then would be the referent of the word "world"? This is the intended meaning of the reply. || 21 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
"Thus, since from the beginning there was no creation, from where and how has this delusion come about? O Blessed One, tell me."
In that case, the meaning of the question is: "What is the cause of the delusion of the world? || 22 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Due to the absence of the relationship between cause and effect, neither existence nor non-existence truly exists;
for whatever is perceived here is merely that which one's own self perceives as its own thought-construct.

There is no real cause, nor is there a world consisting of effects; rather, by means of *māyā*, Brahman alone assumes the guise of those various triads. This is the meaning of the latter part [of the verse]. Whatever is perceived, whatever is perceived as an object, and whatever perceives—all three are one's own self; this is the meaning. || 23 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
If the conscious perceiver perceives the machine, and the Lord is the seer who becomes the object of sight, how does this come to be? And how indeed could wood ever burn fire? (24)
Is this not, indeed, a contradiction? For if the aggregate of cause and effect, which is like a machine, is insentient, yet it perceives;

and if the Lord, who is the seer of all, being of such a nature, becomes an object of perception that is insentient—then how could he ever burn anything, for how could wood, having itself become the burner, turn fire into something to be burned? This is the sense of the doubt. || 24 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
The seer does not become an object of sight, because the object of sight is impossible;
therefore, the seer alone shines, as the singular, solid form of the Self of all. (25)

We do not maintain that the seer becomes an object of sight; rather, our position is that the triad beginning with the object of sight is, in its true nature, nothing but pure vision—the absolute isolation (*kaivalya*) of the seer—which shines forth as a single, undifferentiated mass. Thus, there is nothing at all contradictory here, but rather the cessation of all contradictions; such is the intended meaning of the reply. || 25 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
That pure consciousness, which is without beginning or end, then perceives the object of perception.
From where could this appearance of the world arise, given that the object of perception itself is impossible?

Since at the beginning of creation the appearance of an unperceived world is not established, one must necessarily admit that at that time pure consciousness alone perceives its own object of perception (*cetya*). In that case, the meaning of the question is: "How could such an object of perception possibly exist? || 26 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Indeed, because of the absence of a cause, nothing whatsoever exists as an object of cognition;
and due to the absence of such objects, the state of liberation for consciousness is eternally inexpressible.
If the object of cognition (*cetya*) had come into existence at the beginning of creation, then there would be occasion for the question, "From what was it produced?

However, since that which is absolutely unproduced is like the son of a barren woman, what is the use of a desire to know its logical justification? Thus, the meaning of the reply is that the Self must be understood as eternally liberated. "Inexpressibility" (*avācyatā*) means the state of being unfit to be spoken of. || 27 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
If this is so, then how does this object of cognition, such as "I-ness" (ahaṃtā) and the like, arise? Whence does it come?
How is there the perception of the world, and how is there the perception of movement and so forth?

The underlying concern of the doubt is this: if there were eternal liberation, the manifestation of the ego and so forth would never occur at all, which would render the teacher, the scriptures, and other means futile. || 28 ||

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Since no cause is possible, nothing whatsoever was produced in the beginning; therefore, from where could the object of thought arise? Thus, all is peaceful, and creation is but an illusion. (29)

The intended meaning of the subsequent portion is that the fruit of the scriptures and so forth is precisely the cessation of the delusion of worldly bondage through the awakening to eternal liberation—the realization that nothing at all has ever arisen. || 29 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
In this [reality] which is devoid of mental constructs, beyond the reach of thought, immovable, and so forth—
pure and ever-shining— who could have what kind of delusion?

"Give me an answer to this"—this is the ellipsis. In Brahman, which is devoid of mental constructs (*vigatollekha*), inaccessible to speech, eternally manifest once and for all, self-luminous, and perpetually liberated—of whom could there be delusion (*vibhrama*), from what cause, of what nature, and of what kind?
For in that non-dual reality, even a trace of duality cannot be tolerated; such is the meaning of the question. || 30 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
O Rāma, due to the absence of any cause, delusion truly does not exist at all;
everything—“you,” “I,” and so forth—is peaceful, one, and free from affliction.

Granted that even an error is untenable from the perspective of one who has realized through scripture the truth of the non-dual Brahman; yet, it is not for this reason alone that the scripture is rendered fruitless once its task is accomplished—such is the intention of the subsequent [verse]. 31.
Śrī Rāma said:
O Brahmin, having fallen as if into delusion, I do not know how to ask anything further;
nor am I entirely awakened, so what should I ask here now?
Thus rendered speechless by Rāma, yet his doubt not yet dispelled due to a lack of firm awakening, he demonstrates his own inability to ask further questions, saying, "O Brahmin! (32).
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Ask about the very touchstone of causality until the cessation of causelessness;
you will yourself attain rest in the supreme, ineffable nature.

O Rāma, do not cease from questioning me merely because you have been rendered speechless by my lack of ready wit; rather, do not question me without cause until you have removed all doubt, using me as a touchstone to examine the strength or weakness of the seeds of your suspicions. Then, gradually, [you shall resolve] the doubts that are the causes of your questions.
And through the complete destruction of that ignorance which is its cause, you shall find rest in the supreme nature. || 33 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
I believe that, due to the absence of a cause, the state of creation did not exist even previously; therefore, whose is this delusion of the sentient and the insentient? (34)

I certainly understand and accept your stated conclusion that, due to the absence of a cause, the state of being a creation was not manifested prior to the very beginning of creation; nevertheless, my doubt as to whose this delusion of the perceived and the non-perceived is does not depart, and the intent of my question is: what is the reason for that? || 34 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Because it is without cause and because it is everywhere peaceful, delusion does not exist;
it simply does not find rest due to the lack of practice.

The purport of the reply is this: if you know the doctrine (siddhānta) stated by me, then, due to a lack of practice, your failure to attain firmness in that knowledge—and consequently your lack of rest—is in vain and serves as the cause for various doubts. || 35 ||
Śrī Rāma said: From what would non-practice arise, and from what would practice arise?
From what has this delusion, consisting of practice, now reappeared? (36)
The meaning of the question is: where there is not even a cause for the delusion of the world, from what cause could a delusion consisting of habitual practice arise? || 36 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Because the Infinite is infinite, there is no delusion at present;
all that is the delusion of practice, yet it is the undivided mass of the Great Consciousness.

"Let there be no delusion whatsoever; nevertheless, for those liberated while living (jīvanmukta), there is still worldly interaction with all things, which are essentially composed of pure consciousness.
Śrī Rāma said:
"In the matter of the teacher and the teaching, and so forth, by means of this wealth of words..."
O Brahmin, tell me something else: when everything has become stilled, what remains? (38)
When the delusion of the entire world has subsided for those who are liberated while living, such as yourself and others,

[this occurs] through this abundance of words in the form of spiritual scripture (adhyātma-śāstra) for the sake of instructing those like us who are worthy of instruction, by means of the descent of power (śaktipāta) and other factors that enable the entry into the body of the teacher.
The question is: what else could be the cause for the worldly activity of awakening? || 38 ||

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Brahman, consisting of both the teacher and the teaching, is established within Brahman itself; it is the certain conclusion that in the nature of pure consciousness there is neither liberation nor bondage. (39)
For those [enlightened ones], Brahman alone—existing as the self of all worldly transactions such as instruction and so forth—is established within Brahman;

for from the perspective of the vision of reality (tattvadṛśā), other kinds of bondage, liberation, and their means are absolutely non-existent. This is the purport of the subsequent [verse]. || 39 ||
Śrī Rāma said: For those whose minds perceive distinctions of place, time, action, and substance,
how can the existence of everything be established when nothing at all is possible?
Then the question arises: for what reason does the existence of the world, established by the perspective of the ignorant, appear? || 40 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
For those whose minds perceive distinctions of place, time, action, and substance, there was no other existence in the past than that which arises solely from ignorance. (41)
The answer is: "Precisely because of the cause of ignorance. For prior to liberation while living (jīvanmukti), there is no other existence of the world established by experience for us.

Śrī Rāma said: O Brahman, since there is no possibility of the relationship between the object of cognition and the cognizer, how can there be the state of being consciousness? Since duality and unity are impossible, and since a cause is likewise impossible.

The meaning of the question is this: since, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*tattvadṛśā*), neither duality nor unity is possible, there can be no occurrence of the relationship between the object of knowledge and the knower; therefore, how could there even be the "state of being a cognition" (*bodhatā*) for the cognition of reality? For indeed, the word "cognition" (*bodha*) is not known in the world as being devoid of an object (*akarmaka*). || 42 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Through awakening, one attains the state of being awake; however, the word "awakening" refers to the state of being awakened.
This [instruction] is appropriate only for those like you, and not for people such as us.

For that which is unawakened attains the state of being an object of awakening—the status of being an action upon which awakening acts—by virtue of being the locus for the fruit of the destruction of one's own ignorance through the awakening to Brahman.

By that very fact, the word "awakening" (bodha) also attains transitivity, characterized by the possession of the fruit of awakening, which is the state of having an object to be awakened. All of this applies only to those who are possessed of ignorance.

The meaning is that, in the case of those liberated while living (jīvanmukta) such as ourselves, because ignorance is absent, it is impossible to characterize awareness as having an object (sakarmakatā). || 43 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
When consciousness itself attains the state of "I-ness," then there is the appearance of something other than consciousness.
How could this [otherness] exist in the supreme, infinite, stainless, and exceedingly pure [consciousness], which is like water?

By saying "not in those such as ourselves," you have shown that even in those liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*), there exists an egoity (*ahaṃtā*) which serves as the ground for the application of the term "we. And that [egoity] is not the effect of ignorance (*abodha*), because ignorance is not established in them. Therefore, by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), it must be said that consciousness itself undergoes a transformation characterized by egoity. In that case, its difference from consciousness would be unavoidable; yet this is that very egoity.

Indeed, this person called the "living soul" (jīva)—where could it exist within you? For you are the Supreme, infinite, devoid of the three kinds of limitations; therefore, you have transcended all water, being beyond even water, and are the stainless essence of pure consciousness. How [could it exist] in you? 44.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
That which is the very nature of consciousness as consciousness is called "I-ness" (ahaṃtva).
Here, duality is described as being like the relationship between the wind and its movement, or between the eye and its sight. (45)

The meaning of the latter part [of the verse] is this: that which is the nature of consciousness belonging to those such as ourselves—whose essence is solely consciousness—is what we call "I-ness" (ahantva) through a figurative designation, like the movement of the wind; it is not by means of the individual soul (jīva-puruṣa), whose primary characteristic is the conceit of an ignorant person. || 45 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
Just as the waves and other phenomena within the gentle ocean take on their respective forms,
so too has the awakened one realized that the nature of consciousness is to be understood as consisting solely of its own essential form.

If this is so, then by the analogy of the waves of the ocean, it follows that for those liberated while living (jīvanmukta), the world—including the ego and so forth—and the triad consisting of the object of knowledge, the knower, and the act of knowing, are nothing but pure consciousness; such is the purport of the question. 46.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: If this is so, then who could there be, and what fault could arise from defects such as duality,
within that infinite, singular, peaceful, and perfect supreme state?

If, in this way, persistence alone is the reality, then, O Brahman, since duality and unity are impossible through that [persistence] and a cause is likewise impossible, how could the defect characterized by the loss of non-duality—which you have raised based on the contingency of duality and so forth—possibly exist? What indeed would it be?
Therefore, one should not think in this manner; rather, take recourse in pure non-duality (śuddhādvaita) alone—this is the meaning. || 47 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
Who here is the one who imagines "I-ness"? Who is it that experiences, and who is the experiencer? What is the root from which this infinite delusion of the world expands? (48)

In that case, within the doctrine of pure non-duality (śuddhādvaita), who is it that experiences worldly activity by imagining the conceptualization of "I-ness" (ahaṃtva-vikalpa) as being like the vibration of the wind? Furthermore, if the conceptualization of the world's delusion were likewise dismissed [as unreal], then the very distinction between bondage and liberation would also cease to exist—this is the meaning of the question. || 48 ||

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Indeed, when the reality of that which is to be known is realized, bondage no longer exists at all; since consciousness itself is the form of all objects, whence can there be bondage or liberation? (49)

For if there were an adherence to the reality of the objects of knowledge (*jñeyārtha*), bondage would again ensue. But for those who know reality, the existent object of knowledge does not exist at all in the ultimate sense, because it has been sublated by the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*). Indeed, for them, pure consciousness alone appears in the form of all objects for the sake of experiencing the remainder of their *prārabdha* karma; therefore, there is no possibility of the conceptualization of further bondage and so forth—this is the meaning of the latter part [of the verse]. || 49 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
Just as blue and other colors appear from a lamp, the external object appears from consciousness;
yet surely there exists an external object of a real nature, for it is perceived through direct observation.

Is it not the case that cognition (*jñapti*) does not possess the form of all objects? For, just as the appearance of blue, yellow, and so forth proceeds from a lamp which is the illuminator, the existence of external objects such as jars and cloths proceeds and attains manifestation by virtue of cognition alone. And thus, the external object—which is perceived through observation and established by means of perception and other proofs—is established as having an existent nature solely through the power of cognition.
The meaning of the doubt is: how can it be possible for you yourself to deny that very [point]? || 50 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: This reality of external objects, which are effects without a cause, consists solely of the nature of delusion; it is nothing else.

When it has been previously established that the external object, being devoid of causal efficacy, is like the son of a barren woman, then its apparent reality—which is well-known through superficial observation—is merely of the nature of an illusion, like the reality of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell; it is not such that it possesses as its supporting factor another cognition that is consistent with reality. However, for those who know the truth...
The meaning of the latter part [of the verse] is that, because the ignorance which is the root of delusion has been destroyed, there is no possibility of its occurrence at all. || 51 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
Whether a dream be true or false, it nevertheless bestows suffering;
likewise is this delusion of the world—tell me, what is the remedy for this?
Let it be real by virtue of its capacity for causal efficiency at that time, or let it be unreal because it is sublated upon awakening;
in this regard, the question "What is the means for its medical treatment? is clear. || 52 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Thus, if this state of the world is exactly like a dream,
then the entire perception of objects as solid masses has arisen solely from delusion.

Once the similarity between waking and dreaming has been established, the subsequent intention is that the very sublation of the grasping of objects as solid masses through the awakening to reality (*tattvabodha*) is the means for the pacification of all suffering. Therefore, by implication, it follows that the grasping of objects as solid masses is nothing but an illusion (*bhrānti*). || 53 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
When all this has been accomplished, what dear thing remains to be achieved?
And how is it that the state of objects as solid masses ceases, even in dreams and the like?
Without understanding the underlying intention, the question is clear. || 54 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Through the reflection upon what precedes and follows, the sense of substantiality in objects subsides;
when this is so even in a dream, gross conceptualization ceases.

Thus, when stability is established through the reflective awareness of the preceding and succeeding [states], the gross conception of dreaming necessarily ceases upon the arising of awakening. || 55 ||
Śrī Rāma said: For one whose mental conception has become attenuated, what does he perceive?
How is this wandering in the cavern of saṃsāra stilled for him? (56)

The question is: what and of what nature does that one who is liberated while living perceive the world—he whose contemplation of the world's grossness has been attenuated through inquiry into its prior and subsequent states? || 56 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
One who is free from latent desires perceives the world as a mere semblance of unreality, like a city arisen in a dream, or like a painted scene washed away by rain. (57)
The answer is clear. || 57 ||
Śrī Rāma said:

What then happens for him when the attenuation of latent impressions has been established, when the grasping of material objects has ceased, and when the existence of the world is seen to be like a dream? (58)
Thereafter, immediately following that. || 58 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:

Through the gradual dissolution of the world, which is of the nature of mental construction (saṃkalpa), his latent impression (vāsanā) also vanishes; by that means, he quickly becomes free from impressions and attains extinction (nirvāti).
Through the gradual process of maturation across successively higher stages. || 59 ||

Śrī Rāma said: How is this terrible latent impression (vāsanā), which has grown deep over many births, which abounds in branching offshoots, and which causes the bondage of worldly existence, to be pacified?

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Through the realization of things as they truly are, when the mere delusion is established within the Self, this wheel of the visible world, being devoid of solidification, gradually comes to an end.

The meaning is that when this wheel of the visible world—which consists of nothing but delusion—stands like a burnt cloth through the knowledge of reality as it is and the consequent abandonment of grasping at a solid body, even that [remaining karma] is exhausted through the sequence of experiencing the residue of what was already begun (*prārabdha*). || 61 ||
Śrī Rāma said: O Sage, when this wheel of the visible world has been gradually liberated from the grasping of the physical body (piṇḍa),
what else occurs, and how is peace produced?
Furthermore, the question is: what becomes the means for accomplishing non-distraction? || 62 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
When the delusion of grasping at a solid body has subsided and the mind has realized its nature as mere consciousness,
the world’s existence comes to rest, liberated from the weight of suppression.
The answer is that the tranquility resulting from detachment from enjoyments is what is termed "supreme dispassion. 63.
Śrī Rāma said:
While this radiant world exists in the form of a child’s imagination, how can there be the pacification of attachment? Why should a man [cling] to such suffering?
Since the world exists as a mere form of the imagination of the ignorant, being exceedingly fragile, how can there be the cessation of the presence of the causes of suffering?
If that is so, then why does even a child—a person whose imagination is likewise extremely fragile—suffer? The meaning is: how is it that one is seen experiencing suffering? || 64 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
When that which is accomplished by mere volition has perished, how can there be suffering?
Let that which is merely the mind of volition be investigated for a moment. (65)

Even for a child, suffering arises simply from a lack of investigation and a failure to understand its insubstantiality; however, when that [insubstantiality] is understood through investigation, there is no suffering resulting from its destruction and so forth. Thus, he gives the answer: "By conceptualization... (verse 65). He says, "You too must investigate."
Śrī Rāma said:
O Blessed One, what is the nature of the mind, and how is it to be investigated? Furthermore, tell me, what is attained when it has been properly investigated? (66)
The question is clear. || 66 ||

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: That state of consciousness which is directed toward an object of thought is called the mind (citta). This very inquiry is its remedy; by means of this, its latent impressions (vāsanā) are pacified.
This very act which you are now performing by placing me at its head consists precisely in the listening to the Great Rāmāyaṇa.
Śrī Rāma said:

O Brahman, how much indeed must there be of the absence of the mind's orientation toward objects for the state of non-mindfulness to arise in the consciousness, thereby bringing about liberation? (68)
As long as the mind continues to exist, how long will that state of consciousness directed toward the unobjectifiable—which is to be accomplished through its cessation—persist?
Therefore, the meaning of the question is: "Please explain the very means for the destruction of the mind. (68)
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: An object of consciousness cannot possibly exist; what, then, could consciousness perceive, and from where?
Since an object of consciousness is impossible, the existence of the mind has long since ceased to be.

The meaning of the latter part [of the verse] is that the very cleansing [of the mind], through the vision of the impossibility of the "thinkable" (cetya), is the means for the destruction of the mind. || 69 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
How can this object of cognition that is being experienced not exist? And how can such a denial be made regarding what is directly perceived?
The intended meaning of the question is: "If the object of cognition (*cetya*) is in no way possible, then what is the object of its experience? || 70 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
To the extent that the world is an object for the ignorant, it possesses no reality;
yet to the extent that it is an object for the knower, it is that which is inexpressible and non-dual.

The meaning of the latter part [of the verse] is that when there is a denial of what has been fully known through ignorance, the object of that [denial] is, by implication, the reality itself, which transcends name and form as understood by one who knows the truth. || 71 ||
Śrī Rāma said: What is the nature of the three worlds for those who lack knowledge? Why is it not real for them?
And why would it not be appropriate to describe what the world is like for those who possess that knowledge?
The question is clear. || 72 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: For those who lack knowledge, there is duality between beginning and end; for those who possess that knowledge, it does not exist.
The world does not come into being, for it is eternally unarisen from the very start.

The meaning is that this world—characterized by a duality consisting of limits imposed by space and time, as well as limits imposed by substantial reality—is currently non-existent for those who possess such knowledge, nor could it have arisen from the beginning; thus, it is eternally unproduced, resembling a hare's horn or the son of a barren woman. || 73 ||
Śrī Rāma said: How can that which was unproduced from the beginning, which never comes into being,
which is non-existent in form and without appearance, be experienced?
The question is: if it were absolutely non-existent, how could it be experienced as capable of causal efficiency? (74)
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: That which is unreal, yet appears as real, unarisen and without cause,
arises like a waking dream and is experienced as if it were a functional object.
The answer is that even such [an entity] is experienced like waking and dreaming. || 75 ||
Śrī Rāma said: That which is perceived in dreams and in mental constructions arises from the latent impressions (saṃskāra) of the waking state, resulting from past performance and experience.
"In imagination and so forth" means in mental fantasies, discursive thoughts, and the like. "Practice" refers to waking-world activity;
the meaning is that it arises from the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of that same nature produced by the experience thereof. || 76 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
O Rāghava, tell me this: is that which is experienced in a dream of the nature of waking, or is it something else—namely, [the nature of] volition and the kingdom of the mind?
"Does one experience in a dream an object already well-known from the waking state, or something else? Tell me this"—such is the meaning of the question.
Śrī Rāma said:
"In dreams, in mental constructions, and the like, it is the waking state itself that appears."
And it is eternally characterized by the nature of conditioned formations within the delusions of mental fantasies. || 78 ||
Thereupon, Rāma, adopting the first alternative, replied with the verse beginning "In dreams": "jāgrat" refers to the very object well-known in the waking state. || 78 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
If that very dream appears due to the impressions of the waking state,
then how can a house that was crushed in a dream be recovered in the morning?

"Luṭhitam" means fallen; "geham" means house. The sense is that, since there is no difference in meaning, the falling [of the house] in a dream is of the same nature as the falling [of it] while awake. || 79 ||
Śrī Rāma said:

That which does not shine in the waking state shines in the dream; that is indeed Brahman and nothing else. How is it that this, though understood, appears as something different and unprecedented? (80)

When the first alternative was refuted, Rāma resorts to the second alternative—saying "no"—[arguing that] the object of the waking state does not shine or appear in the dream, but rather something else; and that [something else] is indeed Brahman itself, as you intend, which I have understood. However, this much doubt remains: that this other Brahman appears like a world that has never existed before (*apūrva*). || 80 ||

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: An object, whether previously experienced or not experienced, appears in the mind; however, that which has been well-practiced appears throughout the beginning, end, and middle of creation.

It is not a fixed rule that [an object] must appear as if entirely unprecedented; rather, some objects appear as "unprecedented" because they have never been experienced before, while others appear as "not unprecedented" because they were experienced previously. Furthermore, in whatever form an experience was habituated during the beginning, end, or middle of creation, it appears in that very form. In this regard:
The meaning is that when the practice of the form of Brahman is well-mastered, it will manifest in exactly that same way. || 81 ||
Śrī Rāma said: "O Brahmin,
having understood that this world appears as consisting of dreams,
how is this dream-demon, which is like a planetary affliction, to be treated?"
Thus awakened by you, I have realized that even this waking world appears as nothing but a dream;
yet, even though it is such, this yakṣa of the world afflicts me like a seizing spirit—therefore, how is it to be treated? (82)
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
What could be the cause of this dream of worldly existence?
Reflect upon this: it is observed that the cause is not distinct from the effect. (83)
With the intention that he must be treated by examining the cause, Vasiṣṭha asks about that cause, beginning with the words "yo'yam" (this which...). || 83 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
The mind is the cause of the perceptions in dreams; therefore, that very mind is the universe—devoid of beginning or end, essence-less, and free from affliction.
The answer is clear. || 84 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O one of great intelligence, the mind is thus nothing but a mass of great consciousness;
as it exists in that state, there is no dream or anything else of a different nature.

It has been stated more than once that consciousness itself, when oriented toward the object of thought, is what we call "mind" (citta); thus, that mind is indeed a mass of great consciousness (mahācidghana). And so, it is established that this very [consciousness] exists as if in the form of the world—this is the meaning. || 85 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
Just as there is a distinction between a part and the whole, so indeed is He [distinct from the world].
Yet, within that partless Brahman, there is oneness with the world and all else.

Rāma then raises an objection: "In that case, why is it not simply said that the world exists within Brahman through both difference and non-difference, according to the analogy of the tree and its branches? Why is it denied that 'nothing at all, such as a dream, exists'? He asks this with the words beginning "avayava" (the parts).
Just as there is a distinct state of oneness characterized by identity between the parts, such as the branches, and the whole, the tree; [so too might the world be related to Brahman].

Likewise, let there be a difference that tolerates division even between the mind and the world; therein, by means of the "world" and so forth—which is the collective mind—let there be oneness with Brahman, which is partless. This is the meaning. || 86 ||

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Thus, it is simply not possible that the world exists as something eternal, unproduced from the beginning; rather, the entire universe is undecaying, peaceful, unborn, and entirely free from affliction.

He refutes this with the words "thus" (*evam*). Such a conceptual construction is simply not possible. Because, upon initial investigation, the world is eternally unproduced within Brahman due to the absence of a cause. Indeed, the relation of part and whole, or difference and non-difference, does not arise through mere illusory conceptualization; for even in the case of a mirage, a city of Gandharvas, and the like, [such relations would absurdly follow].
The meaning is that [otherwise] there would follow the consequence of it having parts, such as rays of light, space, and so forth.
"Unpierced" means unbroken, that is to say, undivided. || 87 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
I consider the delusions of creation, its end, and so forth, to be like the "crow-and-palm" coincidence;
they, along with the states of being a deluded seer and an enjoyer, exist within the supreme state.
Thus composed, Rāma, relying solely on the established conclusion of the Siddhānta, said:
"It is like the maxim of the crow and the palm fruit" (kākatālīya). || 88 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
There is a certain ever-new vision of poets, active with aesthetic flavor for those who know flavor; and there is the vision of the wise, which unfolds upon the subject matter of established truths.
Supporting both of these, the entire universe is perceived as tranquil; so long as there are no perceptions for the sight to grasp, there is neither emptiness nor delusion. (89)

Vasiṣṭha concludes by addressing Rāma, who has thus determined that the world is merely an illusion, stating: "That illusion too has been dispelled by me through scriptural inquiry rooted in two perspectives.
For indeed, three kinds of perspectives are well known.

There are three perspectives: the perspective of the ignorant, the perspective of the dialectician, and the perspective of reality. Among these, the first is to be refuted by the [following] two, while the second is to be refuted at the end by the third; with this intention, I have described this entire universe in its true nature by relying on those latter two perspectives. What are those two? They are the essence of the essence even for those who know the essences, arising from the aesthetic flavor (rasa).

One [type of vision] is that which is novel because it consists of an extreme refinement, characterized by the operation of most acute inquiry, belonging to poets who are capable of discerning through churning [the depths of truth] and are skilled in examining the principles of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the objects of cognition (*prameya*).
And the other is that which is perfected by the full maturation of hearing, reflecting, and meditating upon all the treatises of inquiry.
The object whose nature is the supreme reality is the "unfolding" (*unmeṣa*)—the manifestation through direct perception—of the objective world which consists of those [five] elements alone;

that such a vision exists within the final intuitive state (*caramasākṣātkāravṛtti*), and that it is well-known among the wise (*vaipaścitī*), namely among the liberated-while-living (*jīvanmukta*); relying upon these two perspectives, [it is explained] to what extent the universe [extends] in this treatise.

He states that which was described by the word "yāvat" (as far as): "As long as those views and the individual souls who hold them do not exist even in the three periods of time; and as long as neither the emptiness of the world nor delusion has been conceived—this means until one reaches the state of abiding in the single reality of the Self, which is Brahman, eternally immediate and supreme bliss. || 89 ||
Thus ends the one hundred and ninetieth chapter, titled "Rāma’s Rest," in the Nishchaya-Upanishad of the Vālmīki-Delivered Mahārāmāyaṇa of the Holy Vasiṣṭha, according to the Ṛṣi tradition.
Thus ends the one hundred and ninetieth chapter, titled "The Resting of Rāma," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and ninety-first chapter.
Śrī Rāma said:
"O best of sages, if this world is thus composed of the ultimate reality (paramārtha),..."
The self of all existents, being eternal, neither arises nor ceases. || 1 ||
Just as Brahman alone appears in the form of the world due to lack of awakening,
its complete extinction through mere awakening is here described correctly.

Thus enlightened, Rāma adopts the established philosophical position and declares it with the words beginning "If this is so": "The manifestation of the supreme reality consists of the ultimate truth. (1)
This very delusion appears in the form of the manifestation of the world;
or rather, it is not even delusion at all, but solely the existence of Brahman itself. (2)

Ignorance (avidyā), which consists primarily of the power of delusion and distraction, does not exist at all from the perspective of logical reasoning, nor from the perspective of the vision of reality.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Just like the "crow-and-palm" coincidence, when Brahman appears as if by itself within the Self,
one understands through that very self that it is the Self alone which is the world.

Expressing his approval of what Śrī Rāma had said, Vasiṣṭha spoke as follows: "Like the maxim of the crow and the palm fruit" (kākatālīya). This means that by means of inconceivable ignorance (avidyā), through the Self which has become the individual soul (jīva)—that very Brahman itself—[the world appears]. || 3 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
O Sage, tell me how it is that at the beginning of creation and elsewhere,
the light of a lamp shines even without walls, and how it shines so brilliantly beyond all directions?
At the time of the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*),

as if unable to conceive of a world devoid of its own objects of perception, spatial divisions, and so forth— a mere undifferentiated radiance of consciousness— Rāma asks with wonder, "How? [referring to] the beginning of creation at the time of dissolution, being without space or spatial divisions.

And how does it shine and manifest in liberation hereafter? "Aho" expresses wonder. By means of a support (*ālambana*), that is, by depending upon one; for just as light cannot exist without a support, so too it is impossible for the conscious self (*cidātman*) to exist in such a way [without a support]. This is the meaning. || 4 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
This world shines in such a form as the radiance of the light of consciousness;
behold, it is that very consciousness which abides as the Self through its own manifestations of light and so forth.

He provides the resolution, stating "of such a form," [implying]: even though this is something never seen elsewhere and is most wonderful, it must be accepted as possible solely by the force of the experience of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). For the scripture says: "This is of such a form and is indeed most wonderful," and "He is all-pervading, consciousness-bliss, formless, and marvelous," and "Someone beholds him as a wonder."
And because of the words of the Blessed One: nevertheless, one should not entertain doubt. Having examined it through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), you should see this:

for that very same light, which is of the nature of consciousness, remains manifesting itself alone during the time of darkness even in the presence of the light of the sun and other sources; yet, after sunrise and so forth, it remains together with the [external] lights such as that of the sun. || 5 ||
Light appears as if on a wall; that wall and its illumination [are likewise unreal].
Since the visible object is impossible from the very beginning, let the speaker and the seer be seen [as equally unreal].

Even the light of the sun and other sources, while possessing a nature of illumination that is independent of walls and the like, appears as if it were on a wall; for its luminosity is certainly not caused by the wall. On the contrary, both the wall and its manifestation occur solely through the power of that [light’s] own self-luminosity, because the wall is manifested precisely through its identity with the light. In this regard:

Just as light is seen in the sky before it comes into contact with walls and other objects, so too at the beginning of creation and even during dissolution, this Self—both speaker and listener—should be seen as being without an object; such is the meaning. || 6 ||
Therefore, there is a seer, but this visible world does not exist at all; this is the state free from affliction.
The radiance of consciousness itself, by its own nature, becomes both the wall and the illumination.

Thus, because the possibility of consciousness (*citsaṃbhāvanā*) being without an objective support (*nirālambana*) is established, he says "therefore" to suggest that it is this very [consciousness] which, at the beginning of creation, has manifested in the form of the world: "Just as a wall is a physical support for a reflection, so too is the radiance of the sun and other lights. (7)
The single reality, consisting of both the seer and the seen, shines forth by its own self alone;
just as it does here today in dreams and other states, existing as the very nature of the seer and the seen.
He states that the triadic nature of a single consciousness is well-established even in dreams and similar states, saying: "The seer... (verse 8).
For at the beginning of creation, consciousness alone shines; shimmering, it appears as if it were the creation itself.
It is both the object to be manifested and the act of manifestation, its very nature being self-luminous.
In which, at the time of creation and so forth. || 9 ||
At the beginning of creation, Consciousness alone, having become a triad, shines as if it were the creation itself;
this very nature belongs to her, that she shines thus as the Radiant One.
Intrinsic nature is the power of illusion. || 10 ||
This is indeed experienced within cities of dreams and mental constructs;
thus does this first-arisen radiance of consciousness shine forth. (11)
It shines and illuminates. || 11 ||
Just as the form of the sky appears within the sky itself, so does this world shine;
it is without beginning or end, and its various creations are merely the manifestation of the nature of that creation.
Its manifestation as the nature of creation is simply its own manifestation; that manifestation itself is the creations.
To us great-souled ones, however, this appears as our very own nature;
the consciousness of the perceived and the perceiver, which was manifested through [dualistic] intuition, has vanished.
He says, "This appears as something wonderful only to the ignorant, not to us," by stating, "it is one's own nature.
Even though it may appear suddenly, it perishes instantly through the investigation of reality. || 13 ||
At that time, indeed, at the beginning of creation, there was neither the object of illumination nor the illuminator;
it was solely due to false knowledge, just as the cognition of a person arises with respect to a post.
How is there an investigation into reality? To this he says: "But then... (verse 14).
Thus, because duality appears within the self, there is the manifestation of duality in the mind;
yet at the beginning of creation, there is neither an object to be manifested nor a manifestor.

But there is certainly no such thing as a non-existent illuminating self; it must necessarily exist. The word "vā" is used in the sense of conjunction (or, according to another reading, "in the case of an alternative").
Due to the absence of any cause, non-duality alone shines as the sky of consciousness;
tell me, what indeed could be the cause in reality at the beginning of creation within consciousness? (16)
Due to the absence of perceptions of objects, consciousness alone shines forth in this manner;
that which is this appearance of the world is neither waking nor deep sleep.

He states that even because the manifestation of the world at the beginning of creation is not included within the three states such as waking and so forth, it is the fourth consciousness (*turyacid*) alone that shines forth in this manner: "Because of its non-existence" (verse 17).
It is not a dream, because it is impossible [for a dream to exist]; rather, it is Brahman alone that shines as the visible world.
Thus, from the very beginning of the creation within the void of pure consciousness, it manifests with such splendor.
That which knows its own body as the world, though it is not composed of the world,
shines forth in this manner as an unfolding from the very beginning of the creation of the space of pure consciousness.
"Causing to blossom" is to be construed with what follows. || 19 ||
That which is called "the world" is indeed like emptiness and space.
The blossoming of the conceptual construction of difference between emptiness and space. || 20 ||
And having realized this, one should remain endowed with one's own direct experience, free from conceptual construction;
for the "silence of stone" spoken of by the base person should not be accepted, as it is merely the speech of an ignorant man who has eaten and then spoken.
He concludes the method for investigating reality described above with the words "having understood" (*buddhvā*).

By means of this method of investigating reality as stated by me, having understood reality, one should proceed until it becomes firm— endowed with one's own direct experience— through the gradual ripening of the stages (*bhūmikā*), so that one may be liberated from conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

One should remain in non-conceptual samādhi, observing the silence of a stone with all verbal and other activities restrained. Even if a wicked person says, "Eat," one should not accept the collection of external objects—which have been experienced again and again by oneself and others, ignorant as we are, throughout beginningless saṃsāra, but which are now abandoned and relinquished through the excellence of dispassion. This is because of the grasping for sense-objects.
The meaning is that because it is a cause for craving enjoyments, it obstructs the bliss of meditative concentration. || 21 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-first chapter, titled "The Great Awakening of Discourse" (or "Investigation of Reality"), in the *Arṣa* [text], the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa*, within the *Vālmīkīya Deśopadeśa Mokṣopāya*.
Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-first chapter, titled "The Enlightenment of the Great Discourse," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and ninety-second canto.
Śrī Rāma said:
"Alas! For a very long time, we have been utterly bewildered within."
Merely by not fully understanding [this] within the supreme sky of saṃsāra. || 1 ||
Having awakened here, Rāma explained in detail to his guru how his own awakening was such that this entire world is nothing but pure consciousness.

With all his doubts dispelled, Rāma, having become perfectly awakened, remembered the delusion of saṃsāra as if it were the error of a dream upon waking from sleep, and spoke with a sense of wonder, beginning with "Aho!"— referring to how for a very long time he had remained within that supreme, boundless space characterized as saṃsāra, and even therein, within its interior, in this single portion of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa).
We have been deluded by the reality of the self merely through its non-recognition. || 1 ||
O Buddha, this so-called delusion of the world is nothing at all;
it has not existed, it does not exist now, nor indeed will it ever come to be. || 2 ||
Regarding the word "buddhe" (in the enlightened), the term "yāvat" signifies totality. Thus it has been stated in the *Sureśvaravārttika*:
"Merely by the arising of the perfect knowledge produced from such statements as 'That thou art,' ignorance, along with its effects, has not existed, does not exist, and will not exist. (2)
