Everything is peaceful, without support; consciousness alone remains—endless, a mass of pure awareness, like the sky, free from passion and devoid of conceptual construction.
Because it is devoid of conceptual construction, and precisely because of that lack of conceptualization, there is an absence of passion for it; thus, it is free from attachment.
This very supreme space, merely through being unrecognized, has—as it were—fallen into the state of saṃsāra for us; how wonderful, indeed, O friend! (4)
Thus this duality appears: these worlds, these mountains;
yet it is nothing but the pure supreme ether, appearing as if impure.

At the beginning of creation, in the next world, in dreams, and in mental constructs, it is consciousness alone that appears as the object of cognition; for how indeed could there be any other notion of a visible object?
"Kalpanā" means poetic composition; by the word "etcetera," the inclusion of mental daydreaming (manorājya) is intended. || 6 ||
If one has the thought, "I am situated either in heaven or even in hell," then for that person,
the end of that hell is seen as consisting of pure consciousness.

The intellect is delusion (*bhrānti*). By virtue of that delusion, there is for those men the "end" (*anta*)—meaning bondage—of that hell (*naraka*). [The word *anta* is derived from the root *at*, meaning "to bind," with the suffix *ghañ*. 7.
This is neither the visible object nor the seer; there is no creation, no world, and no consciousness.
There is no waking state, no dream, no attainment, and so forth—none of this exists at all, for even that [perceived reality] is unreal.
The intellect is the reflection of consciousness. || 8 ||
If it is asked, "O Sage, from what does the occurrence of this illusion arise?",
we reply that even this is not tenable, because of the experience of the absence of illusion.
Since error has the nature of non-existence, even the consideration of its cause is entirely improper; thus he says: "From what? [It is] seen, that is, perceived.
Error is simply not possible in the changeless state of pure consciousness.
As for this cognition of "error-ness," that is itself [the consciousness]; it is not something other than that.
Knowledge is the cognition of reality; that resides in its own state.

In the uninterrupted, beginningless, and endless void, or within the interior of a mountain, how could there be anything that conceptualizes duality, given that the locus of consciousness is immutable? (11)
In a mountain interior that is continuous and devoid of any intervening space, or within the heart of a crystal rock. || 11 ||
The experience of delusion is indeed false, like one's own death in a dream;
that which is called "non-perception" ceases through right perception.
Just as the delusions of a mirage, a city of Gandharvas,
and a second moon do not exist upon investigation, so too this delusion of ignorance is not found when subjected to inquiry.
The ellipsis is "just as the delusion of two moons. || 13 ||
For even when one is awake, this delusion—like that of a child seeing a ghost—is not true knowledge;
having taken root through lack of inquiry, it is pacified by inquiry. (14)

"Waking" (*jāgaraṇa*) is derived from the root *jāgr* with the suffix *ka* in the sense of the *ghañ* affix. Even when perceived through direct experience during such waking, knowledge is not [necessarily] according to reality.
(14) O Sage, the question "from where did it arise? does not apply here;
for through inquiry, there is gain only of that which exists, not of that which does not exist. (15)

The question, "From what cause did this delusion arise? is also not appropriate here; for a question is intended for the sake of inquiry, and that inquiry would be fruitless in this case. The meaning is that it is impossible to determine the non-existent ignorance which is its root. || 15 ||
That which is not found when scrutinized through valid investigation is simply non-existent; therefore, the experience of that [non-existent thing] is an error. (16)

He states that the non-existence of ignorance follows precisely from its being unobtainable through investigation preceded by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), saying: "by means of valid knowledge" (*prāmāṇika*).
Ignorance is the root of the primordial world. For that very reason, it is indeed an error (*bhrama*) because of that [apparent] experience. || 16 ||
How can that which has been determined by the means of valid cognition as non-existent, having been thoroughly investigated like a sky-flower or a hare’s horn, be obtained from what exists? (17)

To the objection, "Why might ignorance and its effects not have Being (sat) as their very root? he says: "That which... Even when examined from every perspective by means of the instruments of valid knowledge—namely, the scriptural texts such as the *vācārambhaṇa* [the reading is *vācārambhaṇa-śrutyādibhiḥ*]—that which is found nowhere at all.
What kind of existence could there be for that which has the form of the son of a barren woman? (18)
In that case, why might the world itself not also be real? To this he replies with the word "sarvataḥ" (from all): from some cause and from valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Therefore, no delusion whatsoever can ever possibly exist;
this entire expanse is indeed nothing but a mass of unobscured consciousness. (19)
Whatever appears here in this world today, that is indeed the Supreme;
the Supreme abides as the full within the Supreme, which is the supreme plenum.
When the supreme nature of Brahman is filled with unsurpassed bliss, that very Supreme remains established in its own majesty. || 20 ||
Nothing here has ever appeared, nor has anything ever not appeared;
this body of the world remains thus, transparent and utterly tranquil. (21)

Unborn, immortal, unassailable, cherished by the noble, supremely unchanging, entirely free from affliction, the lotus of my state is indeed arisen, pervasive, pure, egoless, manifold yet non-dual, and fully blossomed. (23)
He describes what kind of state that abides in: "unborn" (aja). It is "irremovable" (ahārya), meaning it cannot be taken away by others.
It is "cherished" (juṣṭa) by the noble ones (ārya), the wise; it is "all-pervading" (samanta-pūrṇa); it is "I myself," being devoid of ego (nirahaṃkṛta) and arisen from awakening (bodha).
Through the destruction of veils and limitations, it expands in every direction. || 22 ||
Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-second canto, titled "The Description of Attaining Rest," in the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*, the *Vālmīki-Divya-Moda-Nirvāṇa-Upaniṣad*. 192.
Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-second chapter, titled "The Description of Attaining Rest," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and ninety-third canto.
Śrī Rāma said:
Neither the gods nor the sages know that which is without beginning, middle, or end.
That state which shines forth—where is the world, and where is the visible?
Here, Rāma, through awakening, spoke of the state of the eternally abiding Self in which all duality has been wiped away, occurring in an instant upon the exhaustion of the sleep of ignorance.

The gods are perfected through ritual action and worship; the seers (*ṛṣi*) are perfected through austerity and yoga. Alternatively, in this context, the "gods" and "seers" are simply the external and internal organs, such as the eyes and so forth. Regarding them, the gods brought forward the *udgītha*, according to the scriptural passage beginning:
"These two, Gautama and Bharadvāja," and so on. (1)
Enough for us with the delusions of doubt arising from statements concerning the distinction between duality and non-duality; [we seek] that primordial, healthy form which is perfectly tranquil.

Enough of our verbal discourse, doubts, and delusions arising from the mental agitation caused by the investigation into duality and non-duality; the meaning is that there is no purpose [in them]. This entire world is that very form established by the Śruti in the beginning of all things: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second."
The word "shines" (bhāti) is carried over [from the previous sūtra]. || 2 ||
Just as the appearance of space within the sky is utterly tranquil,
so too is the manifestation of the vast space of the three worlds within the sky of consciousness.

He now describes what kind of appearance of the world has come about at present: "In the sky," etc. [This refers to] the appearances in the sky such as hair-nets (*keśoṇḍraka*), strings of pearls, cities of the Gandharvas, and so forth. (3)
Just as the nature of space resides in space,
the nature of stone in stone, and the nature of water within water, so too does the nature of the world reside within the density of consciousness.

Just as [the quality of] "space-ness" (vyomatva) and so forth exists in space and other things through non-difference, as a universal form, and as that very essence—so it is here; this is the meaning.

Know that this visible world, beginning with the sense of "I-ness" (ahaṃtā), though spreading out to the sky of hope, is the belly of the Great Consciousness—a peaceful void arisen from emptiness. || 5 ||
Spreading through the quarters, the intermediate directions, and the sky, it is vast beyond measure; yet, being appropriate as emptiness, it arises from emptiness. || 5 ||
In this Supreme Being, whose manifestation is immeasurable, the demon of transmigratory existence— which though flickering within the deluded individual soul— is brought to rest.
When this supreme Brahman, of infinite manifestation, is merely perceived, the demon of the individual soul’s transmigratory existence is extinguished.
Even for one engaged in worldly activity, the perception of duality completely vanishes—
just as it does for the insentient, or indeed for the sentient— as when waves dissolve within the belly of the water.

How does it become pacified? To this he says: "The perception of difference. Because there is no distinction between the letters *la* and *ra*, [the word] *jalasya* (of water) also applies to the side of the waves.
When the sun of ignorance has gone anywhere—even into the mine of majesty and so forth—the day of the existence of saṃsāra goes to its setting; that is the arrival of night. (8)
When the threefold torment— beginning with the internal (ādhyātmika) and so forth— and, by the word "etcetera," the thirst for sense objects,
go to their setting, that is, become invisible, it is the arrival of night, which is the cause for resting in the bliss of liberation.
Regarding existent and non-existent effects— namely, old age, death, and birth— the knower, though remaining amidst the state of constant flux, does not truly abide therein.
In the state of constant flux and in the distraction of worldly discourse. || 9 ||
There is no ignorance, no delusion, no suffering, and no arising of happiness;
for "knowledge," "ignorance," "happiness," and "suffering" are nothing but the stainless Brahman alone.
When this is fully understood, it is indeed the stainless Brahman alone;
as long as it is not fully understood by us, there exists no self that is other than Brahman.
Of us who know the reality. || 11 ||
I am awakened; all my false views have been stilled.
I behold this triple world as peaceful, even, and as the void, which is myself.
Equal, devoid of all duality and inequality. || 12 ||
This entire world has been rightly known as nothing but Brahman alone;
that which was Brahman with an unknown Self has now become established in the known Self. (13)

"I was not anyone previously, nor am I anyone else now; rather, I am Brahman itself. Previously, the Self was unknown, by which [ignorance] I became such [a person]; but now that the Self has been known, I abide in my own true nature. (13)
Brahman alone is thus undecaying, appearing neither as the known nor the unknown;
it is one, just as the sky is one in its nature of emptiness, unity, and blueness.

"Without appearance" means it is devoid of the appearance of knowledge or ignorance that is distinct from itself; the meaning is that it is like the single sky, which remains one whether it is devoid of blueness or possesses blueness. || 14 ||
I abide free from doubt in the radiance of nirvāṇa; I abide without effort in supreme bliss; I abide eternally and infinitely as it truly is; thus abiding, how could I not be at peace? 15.

Therefore, through that awakening, I remain as one who has attained *nirvāṇa* itself. Through the very cessation of ignorance, all doubts have ceased; thus, I remain free from doubt. I remain in supreme bliss—the bliss of the Self which is free from distraction—so that here and now my mental state may flow in an uninterrupted stream (*dhārāvāhika*). Thus awakened, I remain absorbed in the universal Self.
"How did he remain in Brahman?"—the meaning is: "because of the sublation of those causes for the falling away from that state. || 15 ||
I am always everything, the infinite One; or rather, I am nothing at all, being utterly tranquil.
I am everything and yet nothing, I am the eternal One, and yet I am not—I, indeed, am this peace! (16)

I am always everything, or rather, I am utterly tranquil, free from all disturbances, and nothing at all—I alone am the One Reality. Or else, because no locus of space or time can be established, I am nowhere at all. This state called Nirvana, this total peace—oh, how it is of a most wondrous nature! Such is the meaning. || 16 ||
That which was to be realized has been realized; that which was to be attained has been attained by others; this entire multitude of things has reached its end.
Such is that state of arisen, exultant awakening, wherein even the mere name of rising and setting no longer exists.
It does not exist. || 17 ||
That which was fit to be attained and known has been attained and known; that which is of the nature of the supreme human goal has been realized.

That liberation-sukha, inaccessible to others and difficult to reach, has been obtained. This entire collection of things, consisting of the miseries of saṃsāra, has come to an end. Such [a state] is characterized by the awakening arisen from the final direct realization.

My own true nature has been declared; in that true nature, there is not even the name of further occurrences of setting and rising—that is, of death, concealment, suffering, and other such misfortunes. The word "name" (*nāma*) is used here to indicate what is well-known among the wise. || 17 ||
Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-third canto, titled "The Narration of Rest," in the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa*, the *Vālmīki Dīpikā* commentary by Mōkaṇa, in the *Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa*.
Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-third chapter, titled "The Attainment of Rest," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and ninety-fourth canto.
Śrī Rāma said:
By whomsoever, through whatever means, and whenever, in all beings and in all states of being—
Just as self-awareness shines forth, so does it experience itself.
Rāma himself, having realized here the true nature of the self and the true nature of the world as the means to nirvāṇa, communicated it to his guru.

In that regard, he describes the nature of the Supreme Self when it is not recognized: "The Self of all. Whenever, by whatever means of experience, and in whatever manner, the self-luminous conscious Self (*svaprakāśacidātmā*) shines—that is, manifests as a transformation (*vivartate*)—it does so by itself alone within all selves (*ātman*), that is, all individual souls (*jīva*), and within all states of being, which are the various modifications of the mind.
It experiences itself through the state of being various individual enjoyers; the meaning is that it manifests by its own māyā in the form of the triple fold (tripuṭī). || 1 ||
Even when combined, the creations remain as their own inherent nature;
here too, they are accepted just like the various rays of light from gems.

Because all individual souls simultaneously superimpose themselves upon the one partless and supremely subtle Brahman, even though they are combined, the infinite creations— each vast with its own distinct cosmic eggs, worlds, and so forth—
exist within the very nature [of Brahman] without being mutually connected. This is because they reside here within such a Brahman, despite its being partless.

The meaning is that [the powers] have been accepted through the superimposition of identity (*tādātmyādhyāsa*), made one's own, and rendered extremely subtle; thus, there is no lack of space or mutual obstruction within one's own self. The sense is that just as the subtle rays or beams of various gems, even when meeting in a single house, remain unrelated and unmixed, so it is here. || 2 ||
Here, the seen and the unseen enter into and pass through one another,
like a world that is a mass of light-rays yet a mass of various jewels.

He clarifies that very point with the words "herein" (*atre*). The world—both the seen (*dṛṣṭa*), which is proximate and perceptible, and the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*), which is remote due to the intervention of space and time—enters into this Supreme Self (*paramātman*) as a dense mass of rays;
it enters, moves, and circulates therein without mutual obstruction. It is like a dense mass of various jewels.
Just as a web of rays, so it is. || 3 ||
Just as among many burning lamps, some have mutual perception while others do not, so it is with these creations. || 4 ||

In this regard, with the intention that there is mutual experience among those living beings whose superimposition (adhyāsa) is caused by similar karmic impressions (*karmavāsanā*), but not among those different from them, he says: "of some. In the case of the lamp, this refers to those with sight and those who are blind. || 4 ||

Just as there is essence in every drop of water, and whirlpools in the ocean, and delight in the earth, so too within that creation there is [essence] in every atom; yet even in that, there is no such sequential order of creations.

Just as there is a taste such as saltiness in every single particle of water within the ocean—the place of sport and the playground of the whirlpools—so it is in reality: there are no creations, nor even their sequence. || 5 ||
Everywhere, in every way, and eternally, there is the perception of water by one who is a mass of consciousness;
by whom could the successions of creations and their supports be numbered? (6)
The sensation of water is like the taste of a single water atom.
Just as the possessors of parts are never distinct from their parts except through a difference in terminology,
so too the subsequent states of creation are not distinct [from the primordial nature] except through a difference in terminology.
Because there is no cause for that which is singular and yet of infinite forms,
the world and its origins, by their very nature, neither arise nor pass away.

The beginning and the substratum of the world—which, through the illusory power (māyā) of the one Self alone, possesses infinite forms—is that very Self; because it is of that nature, it neither arises nor does it set. || 8 ||
This very cognition, though itself devoid of agency, while shining forth, renders this undivided state of the knowable manifest, just as the rays of the sun produce visible light.
Shining and quivering; "samālokam" refers to the illumination of objects such as jars and cloths. || 9 ||
Through the absence of thirst for all states of existence, by the very completion [of all things], that concentration which is itself imperishable is attained; that is called nirvāṇa.

When, then, does that addiction to superimposition (adhyāsa) abandon its hold, and by what means? To this he replies: "Through the cessation of thirst" (vaitṛṣṇyāt). Because all objects are sublated by the knowledge of reality, through their very completion [and disappearance], the self becomes liberated from the superimposition of identity with the perishable body and so forth; that which is such a true nature is itself [the goal].
The meaning is that because all causes of distraction have been exhausted, its state of being composed is called "nirvāṇa" due to its nature of cessation. || 10 ||

Awakening is not awakened by the intellect; because awakening is non-intellectual, it is not awakened [by anything]. Nor is it awakened even by that [awakening]; how then could awakening be something to be awakened? || 11 ||

Only upon the complete cessation of the succession of superimpositions does one’s own supreme human goal remain as a residue; for how could that which is not being experienced be a human goal, given that only that which is experienced by the intellect constitutes a human goal? Therefore, it is the experience itself that serves as the motivator for the status of being a human goal.

Anticipating the objection that since the final intuitive cognition (*caramasākṣātkārabuddhi*) is necessary for liberation, it is not logical to accept the cessation of all existents, he says: "No. Enlightenment, which constitutes the supreme human goal, is not cognized by the final intuitive modification (*vṛtti*) of the intellect as the Supreme Self; for that [intellect], being insentient, lacks the power of consciousness, whereas enlightenment is [of the nature of] consciousness.

And because it is impossible for [the Self] to be an object of the intellect (*buddhi*). If that is so, let the Supreme Self, which possesses the power of consciousness, be awakened—like a sleeping king by bards. To this, he says: "Because of being conscious and unconscious" (*bodhābuddheḥ*). It is not awakened either. Why? Because of being conscious and unconscious. Having perceived that the king is asleep, the bards proceed to awaken him; however, the one who is asleep is not awakened by the intellect.

The meaning is: how could that [cognition] proceed toward awakening him, who is called "Buddha"? If it is argued that awakening should be awakened by awakening itself, he says: "No. Awakening is not awakened even by that [other] awakening. Why? He says: "Because it is that which is to be awakened" (*bodhya*). How can awakening itself be the object (*karman*) of awakening? For an object is that which serves as the locus for an excellence produced by an action. Indeed, in the case of awakening...

The meaning is that neither action, nor the excellence produced by it, nor the state of being its substratum is possible [in Brahman], because it is devoid of action, devoid of modification, and because action is contradictory to its own nature. || 11 ||
Though already awakened, self-awareness awakens as if it were asleep;
even in the absence of space, time, and other conditions, it is like the heat of the sun at midday.

Therefore, this process culminates of its own accord through a succession of transformations ending in the final direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) that terminates the series of superimpositions. And when that [process] has reached completion, the Self, being self-luminous, is indeed awakened— just as the sun, which had become as if asleep due to the onset of mist, shines forth once the mist has entirely vanished at midday.

And like the sun, he awakens as it were; with the intention that this very state is his supreme human goal, characterized by the manifestation of unsurpassed bliss which is eternally attained, he says: "He is indeed awakened. || 12 ||
For the virtuous who are free from craving for all actions and who desire peace, through awakening, nirvana occurs even though they do not will it.
By the word "karma," the fruit pertaining to this world and the next is indicated. || 13 ||
With awakened consciousness, established in meditation, and abiding in the absolute nature,
he grasps nothing at all and relinquishes nothing at all.
He whose conscious self is awakened from the sleep of delusion, who is established in meditation with external mental fluctuations restrained. || 14 ||
He who remains exactly as he is, inactive like a lamp while observing, is without mind, without measurement, and without mentation—even though he possesses the mind that performs mentation. (15)

Then, how does he abide at the time of emergence? To that he says: "He who... Even though possessing the mentalizing of the mind (*manomanana*), because of the absence of attachment to sense objects, he is one whose mentalizing of the mind has ceased; for this very reason, although illuminating like a lamp, he is inactive.
At the time of emergence, [his state] is called "the form of the universe" (*viśvarūpa*); elsewhere, it is designated as "Brahman."
Pure consciousness, whose nature consists of both creation and non-creation, shines as the reality everywhere.
Established in the experience of one's own nature, which is non-different from the form of pure consciousness,
he who perceives both while emerging from meditation and while restrained attains peace.
He who, whether emerged from meditation, in a state of cessation, or established in samādhi, possesses undivided awakening;

he who, remaining fixed in that very experience of his own true nature as the Reality (Sat), perceives both cessation and emergence with an attitude of indifference—he alone is stilled from the distractions of saṃsāra, and no other. || 17 ||
Apart from being solely established in pure consciousness, there is no other existence for the multitude of objects in the world, just as there is no existence of space other than its emptiness. (18)

He describes that state of abiding in the experience of such a true nature with the word "jagat" (the world). The meaning is that this state consists in the realization that there is no other reality or ontological status apart from the condition of being solely consciousness (*bodhamātra*), which is the single, ultimate foundation and the true form of all things. || 18 ||
For those of expanded awakening, only infinite consciousness remains;
yet even that, through its own further transformation, reaches a state beyond description. (19)

If it is asked, "How can there be no other existence?", the intention is that when the form of the world is sublated through the direct realization of reality (*tattva-sākṣātkāra*), only the existence of the pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) that witnesses it remains; with this in mind, he says: "It remains. This refers to those of expanded awareness—those possessing an awakening characterized by the vast expansion resulting from plunging into the undivided Brahman. That...

Even such consciousness, whose nature is the inner self (pratyagātman), attains the state of being inexpressible and the state of being indicated by sentences denoting the undivided reality (akhaṇḍārtha) through a supreme transformation characterized by the remaining of only Brahman-as-Being (brahmasanmātra). || 19 ||
Upon its coming to rest, does the supreme being remain or not remain? It is some indescribable state of ultimate peace that does not fall within the range of speech.

When there is rest in that and one abides in its state, that condition enters the range of neither "it remains" nor "it does not remain," nor even both; it transcends the reach of words altogether. || 20 ||
That which is the ultimate limit of equanimity is itself the essence of awakening;
therefore, creation consists of that alone, and thus everything is peaceful and immutable.

The ultimate limit and supreme boundary of Being-in-general (*sattāsāmānya*), which is the purified nature of the referent of the term *tat* (*tatpadārtha*), is itself the ultimate limit of Consciousness, which is the purified nature of the referent of the term *tvam* (*tvaṃpadārtha*). Since creation—characterized by ether and the other elements, as well as by the three states [of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep]—is experienced by all as "it exists" and "it shines," it consists essentially of Being and Consciousness. This being so:
He states what has been brought to fruition with the words: "the whole" (sakalam). || 21 ||
Even Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara always long for that being who is free from craving for nirvāṇa and whose consciousness is clear and cool. 22.

Because that very [Self] is the most beloved even for Brahmā and others, it is Nirvāṇa, whose nature is unsurpassed bliss; thus he says, "for Nirvāṇa. All living beings—even by the force of the word "api" (even)—aspire to its existence, thinking, "May I always exist, may I never cease to be. || 22 ||
The conscious principle alone, which is the self of all objects, exists everywhere, at all times, and in every way as arisen; it is pure, and its destruction is not possible.

That very Reality—which is the object of desire for all at all times, which arises in every place and at every time as the essence of all things, which is consciousness itself, spontaneously radiant in form, and pure—is indeed that; its destruction, or its non-appearance, is not possible even for a moment. 23.
Samsara is extremely hot, while Nirvana is exceedingly cool;
it is indeed exceedingly cool, and heat itself does not exist there.
Heated [existence] consists of unsurpassed suffering; the extremely cool [state] is the absolute cessation of suffering. || 24 ||
Just as statues carved within stone perceive according to their capacity even though they are not themselves carved,
so too does Brahman perceive this undivided universe.

Just as figures carved within stone remain uncarved from the perspective of the artisan's intellect yet manifest and vibrate according to their own nature, so too Brahman—though imparted with existence, undivided, and uninterrupted—perceives and vibrates in the form of this world; such is the meaning. || 25 ||
Just as the circle of waves is perceived within a reservoir of gentle water,
so too is the imperishable Great Consciousness perceived as the object of thought within the sheath.

The "gentle treasury" refers to a reservoir of water, and that which resides therein; or, "treasury" refers to the sheath consisting of food and so forth, and that which resides therein, as well as that which resides within the treasury of the cosmic egg—the object of consciousness—having itself become that very thing, it perceives and vibrates. || 26 ||

It is undivided, yet as if divided by those who abide in division— those who are peaceful, infinite, expansive as the sky of ultimate reality, and yet sluggish due to their lack of realization of the nature of the Self.

The Self, which is unawakened and shrouded by ignorance, is [described] as being "by way of its state" (*tadbhāvena*)—that is, by those who are sluggish and mostly inert through artificial guises that are but the expansive manifestations of the sky of ultimate reality, which is pure existence (*sanmātra*). The third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used here in the sense of "being in such a state. The connection with the following verse is: "by whichever living beings it has been cultivated in whatever manner, in that very way it is perceived. (27)
In whatever way each [individual] has long internalized and contemplated the Self within themselves,
for each of them, [the teaching] has arisen accordingly amidst the various distinctions of worldly enjoyment and liberation.

Just as the designation "real" does not arise for one who awakens from a dream regarding a kinsman who was either dead or alive within that dream, so it is for the knower of truth regarding objects of perception.
Just as for a person who has awakened from sleep, the notion of truth—the perception of reality—does not arise regarding a kinsman in a dream, whether that kinsman is dead, not dead, or even living;
likewise, for one who knows the Truth (tattvavit), no such notion arises regarding any perceived objects. The meaning is that, consequently, there is no attachment to joy or sorrow. || 29 ||
Since all this, such as the visible world and so forth, is indeed quiescent and entirely auspicious—whether it be cultivated or realized within—whence can there be the arising of delusion? (30)

The syntactical connection is as follows: even when all that consists of the threefold form of the perceived object and so forth has been inwardly contemplated and correctly understood as being quiescent and auspicious (śiva), what could possibly arise thereafter from delusion? || 30 ||
In every respect, a lack of thirst for all things numbered among the body arises when perfect awakening occurs, just as one feels toward objects of desire and the like in a dream. (31)

When realization has occurred, by what sequence does delusion cease to arise? He explains this with the words beginning "in every way" (*sarvathā*). "Those which are correctly perceived as the body" (*dehasaṃkhyāḥ*) refers to such things as one's own objects and the means to enjoyment. || 31 ||
Through the absence of craving, awakening increases; through awakening, the increase of the absence of craving occurs.
These two manifest mutually, like a wall and its light.
Let it be so; what follows from that? To this he says: "Because of the absence of thirst" (vaitṛṣṇyāt). || 32 ||
That awakening by which there is freedom from craving for wealth, wife, children, and so forth—even one's own body—such dullness remains established in that very state. (33)

To explain why that is so, he says: "by which" (yena). By whatever cause—whether it be freedom from craving (*vaitṛṣṇya*), wealth, wife, and so forth—it is by the very awakening characterized by adherence to reality (*tattvābhiniveśa*) that [the state] becomes well-established, non-deficient, self-sufficient, accumulated, and perfected; and even dullness (*jāḍya*), whether it is opposed to or conducive to that [awakening], likewise [becomes so] in accordance with that respective adherence.
The meaning is "established. || 33 ||
This alone is the true nature of awakening: freedom from craving.
That which lacks freedom from craving is merely what is called "learning," yet it is actually ignorance. (34)
But those two, not rich in the awakening of thirstlessness and not mutually nourishing, are indeed non-existent; they are not lost, like a painted fire. (35)

The meaning is that one should not think that even though those two have mutually increased, they are merely incapable of producing an effect—like a variegated fire—and thus are as good as destroyed; rather, they remain truly existent. || 35 ||
The supreme attainment of dispassion toward awakening is called liberation;
and one who dwells in that infinite, peaceful state does not grieve. (36)

To the question of why it should not be so considered, he says: "Supreme," etc. Because liberation (*mokṣa*) is defined as the unsurpassed attainment of both enlightenment and freedom from craving (*vaitṛṣṇya*), since it consists of unsurpassed bliss and the total destruction of the causes of suffering.
For ignorance alone is the root of bondage, and craving itself is bondage; thus, liberation consists of the cessation of both these states.
The meaning is "because of this logical justification" (upapatti). || 36 ||
That which was to be traversed has been traversed, that which was to be done has been done, and that which was to be seen has been seen in its entirety;
for everything is Śiva—peaceful, one, primordial, and free from affliction. (37)
Therefore, he says "it has gone," and so forth, to express that he has lived his life having accomplished his purpose through those two very [qualities] once they have increased:
"that which was to be traversed" (gamya) means that which was to be eliminated; "gone" (gata) means it has been eliminated. || 37 ||

For one who delights in the Self, who is peaceful, free from craving, and devoid of egoism, there arises a state of non-conceptualization, as pure as the sky. (38) [Regarding the term *vaitṛṣṇyasya*: the suffix *ṣyañ* is used here in its own sense (*svārthe*), meaning "one who is without thirst" (*vitṛṣṇasya*). Alternatively, that very reading may be supplied.]
From among thousands and thousands, some valiant person arises and tears asunder the web of latent impressions, just as a lion rends its cage.
He says that those who sever the bonds of thirst and delusion are rare, using the words "from among thousands. This means: from among those who are striving. || 39 ||
Having attained purity through the awakening of light and possessing supreme inner radiance,
the mist-like [ignorance] quickly subsides of its own accord, like the frost in autumn.

He by whom the realization and knowledge of the self as light, as well as the sun and other luminaries, have been attained, and by whom the mist—the portion consisting of the latent impressions of dullness—is dispelled. (40)
But he who has known what is to be known is free from volition, his mind transcending all volitional constructs;
being devoid of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), he may engage in worldly activity or remain still like the wind.

The *āśaya* (inner disposition) of one who transcends—that is, surpasses—his own volitions (*saṃkalpa*) is free from latent impressions (*avāsana*). Such a person is liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*); he may either engage in worldly activity or not engage in it. The meaning is that he rests solely in meditative absorption (*samādhi*). || 41 ||
Through firm mental attentions and because of the certainty that there is only delusion,
that state which is everywhere like space— that is dwelling without latent impressions.

In all places and regarding all things, through mental attentions and reflections on reality, that state which arose from the steadfastness of the wise—one in which there is the certainty that it is mere delusion—is itself the state of abiding without latent impressions (*avāsanamāsitam*); this is the meaning. || 42 ||
When the noble-minded being has been expelled from existence and the awakened one perceives the visible world as a mere barren wasteland like the sky, then,
within the conviction of the singular, stable Nirvana, there arises the infinite tranquility known as liberation.
When a person of noble being and pure inner heart has arisen as a state devoid of latent impressions (*nirvāsana*) in the manner described,

and when he has awakened to the realization that "the entire visible world is indeed Brahman," and his mind is fixed in the singular extinction (*nirvāṇa*), then for that man there arises the cessation of all saṃsāra— which is designated as "infinite liberation" (*ananta-mokṣa*)— spontaneously by itself.
The meaning is that it becomes manifest. || 43 ||
Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-fourth canto, titled "The Attainment of Rama’s Rest," in the *Nirvāṇa* section of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa*, composed by Valmiki.
Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-fourth sarga, titled "The Attainment of Rama's Rest," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa within the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*. 194.
The one hundred and ninety-fifth chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
"O Rāghava, how truly awakened you are! [This is] the destroyer of the sins of sinners."
This speech of yours is accomplished, yet it is full of mockery toward those who are awakened. || 1 ||
Having himself praised the auspicious words spoken by the awakened Rāma, the Guru then presented these questions, which were formulated by Rāma for the purpose of examination.

Therein, at the outset, Vasiṣṭha praises the words spoken by the awakened Rāma, rejoicing in them, beginning with "Aho" (Oh!): "O Rāma, these words of yours destroy the sins of the unawakened; among the awakened, however, because they repeat matters established by experience and because they are endowed with reason, they are not objects of ridicule, but rather cause the face to beam with the smile of great joy."
It is accomplished. || 1 ||
This world shines forth as non-existent and is stilled by the absence of volitional construction;
this peace is Nirvana—such is the ultimate reality.
The extraction of the nature of bondage is this: this world, being indeed non-existent, appears as if it were real due to the volitional construction (saṃkalpa) induced by ignorance.
The extraction of the means to liberation is this: it is pacified by the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna), which culminates in the firm cessation of such volitional construction.
The extraction of liberation is this: its very pacification is nirvāṇa. This is the meaning: that alone is the ultimate reality (paramārtha). || 2 ||
In the conceptualization and non-conceptualization of form, there is only the nature of the other and not that of the one;
just as in the case of the movement and non-movement of wind, there is neither unity nor duality here.

And thus, the conclusion that bondage and liberation—consisting of conceptualization and non-conceptualization—are both the very form of Brahman for the unawakened and the awakened respectively, has also been established; he states this with the words: "Conceptualization and non-conceptualization. (3)
The state of a person who has awakened, which is like that of a stone within its interior,
whether in a state of tranquility or in worldly activity, is called stainless liberation.
In tranquility and meditative absorption. || 4 ||
Abiding in this state which destroys the suffering of the descendants of Raghu, we remain thus established,
equal in both tranquility and worldly activity.
He states that abiding in this very state is the condition of equal form for both samādhi and its emergence for those like us who are liberated while living (jīvanmukta): "We... (verse 5).
In this very state, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Hara, and the others always abide; though engaged in worldly activity, they remain peaceful and possess the nature of pure consciousness.
Those who possess the nature of knowledge are awakened.
For us awakened ones who dwell within the womb of the mountain, that state is indeed free from affliction; having attained it, let this [body] remain here.
"Since this state is unshakable like the interior of a mountain for those who abide therein, it cannot be attained by you any more than it was by us or others;
therefore, dwell here in this state of liberation while living (jīvanmukti), from this day forward. This is the meaning. || 7 ||
Śrī Rāma said: O Brahman, in this way this world appears as something unreal in nature, unproduced, non-luminous, without beginning, and indeed formless.

Thus, having been established in the state of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) through the words of Vasiṣṭha, Rāma describes how the world appears to those who are liberated while living in two verses beginning with "tatpraṇīti": "Because it has never arisen, it is luminous yet does not appear as something separate. (8)
It is like the water of a mirage, like water in waves and whirlpools,
like the gold in a golden ornament, and like mountains created by dreams and mental constructs.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: If you have understood this, O Rāma, then for the sake of increasing your own awakening,
resolve the doubts of me, your questioner, as I ask them.

Now, Vasiṣṭha, in order to establish Rāma in the state of liberation while living (jīvanmukti), has placed him in the position of the speaker according to the analogy of the yoga-band; he himself, like a disciple, says: "You have understood," [and continues], "I ask you so that I may sever my own doubts. || 10 ||
Thus, although this manifestation called the "world" is constantly experienced, though situated upon one's head, and though exceedingly radiant, how indeed could it not exist? (11)

Because it is confirmed by means of valid cognition such as direct perception and because it is non-contradictory in terms of causal efficiency, it is treated as true, even though it is almost as if situated upon one's head. || 11 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
"In the beginning, this was indeed unproduced; at no time did anything exist.
Therefore, the existence of this son of a barren woman has no reality apart from conceptual construction."

In this regard, Śrī Rāma provides a resolution using the very same arguments previously stated by his guru, beginning with the words "pūrvam eva" (already before). The meaning is that [the world] has not arisen because of the absence of a cause; [it exists] only through mental construction, that is, apart from delusion. || 12 ||
What could possibly be the cause of this delusion of the world, from which it has arisen?
For nowhere does any effect ever come into being without a cause. (13)
He demonstrates the very absence of a cause with the words "What, like what? and so forth; [for] from what could it have arisen? || 13 ||
And no cause whatsoever here can possibly exist that is both subject to modification and free from decay, unless it is itself subject to modification and destruction. (14)

He states that there is no possibility whatsoever of Brahman being a cause: "And not... The meaning is that nothing characterized by modification is established apart from the exhaustion of its prior state. || 14 ||
This very Brahman, whose nature is indefinable, expands as the cause;
so where, for whom, and how indeed can there be the cognition of the meaning of the word "world"? (15)

If it were said that the unchanging *sat* alone, as the material cause of the world-illusion (*vivarta-upādāna-kāraṇa*), unfolds in the form of the world through *māyā*, then the referent of the word "world" would not be found to be real; thus he says: "The cause..."—[meaning] the cognitions of consciousness are in accordance with reality. (15)

Then, for some brief duration, the bearer of the subtle body (ātivāhika-deha) remains in that peaceful, ineffable state, having experienced consciousness for the first time after a long interval. (16)

The meaning is that the first volition, known as Hiraṇyagarbha, which lasts for a certain fraction of time measuring two *parārdhas* and exists in the form of a phenomenal manifestation (*vivarta*) as a subtle body (*ātivāhika-deha*), appears as if it persists; thus, he becomes the object of the world-illusion (*jagad-bhrānti*).
Just as you perceive a year within a single moment in a dream, so does he perceive it.
There he sees the moon, the sun, and other celestial bodies, as if by chance, like the "crow-and-palm" coincidence.
At that very first moment of consciousness, one perceives the illusion of the expansion of time, such as years and so forth; just as you perceive it in a dream, so do you see it now. || 17 ||
For him, whose very self is volition (saṃkalpa), the world— endowed with space, time, and action— shines forth by itself, as if entirely within the void.
When he has been ordained through a false procedure, that false man, performing his conduct falsely, revolves [in saṃsāra] accordingly. || 19 ||
The practice of the creation of those elements, worlds, and so forth. || 19 ||
It moves from below to above, and again from above it goes downward;
thus arises the agitation caused by the perceived multitude of objects, both meaningful and meaningless, which are as infinite as they are imagined.

That very [Self], through its individualized living soul (vyaṣṭijīvātman), is born and wanders as if in delusion within the various worlds imagined by itself, in order to experience the results of its evil deeds and so forth, both below and above.
If that resolve of his had come to pass by mere chance, like the "crow-and-palm" coincidence,
then even today it would remain as firm and stable as it was then.

If, by mere coincidence—like the "crow and the palm fruit"—the state of that resolve remained even today exactly as it was previously, then, having recognized [it] from that very source, he took hold of a stable position in the world, though grasped through delusion. || 21 ||
Just as one might say that a stone performs the coloring of the face of a barren woman’s son with powdered sky, so too this world has appeared falsely.

Thus, this false world, having arisen in such a manner through delusion, is a mere conceptual construction—just like the meaning of a sentence such as: "A stone becomes a woman in love, and she, being the son of a barren woman, applies a tilaka of celestial powder to the face and forehead of her lover, thereby creating an extraordinary beauty. This is the intended meaning. || 22 ||
This is indeed reality, or else how could it be falsehood?
It is neither falsehood nor reality; it is that unborn, all-pervading something.
If, however, one considers that even the property called falsity (*mithyātva*) is unestablished because it is absolutely non-existent,

then [the opponent] says "it is indeed real" (*satyameva*), on the grounds that it is merely the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*). But if, due to the non-establishment of the falsity to be excluded, even the conceptualization of reality as the excluding factor (*vyāvartaka*) is not possible there—
When that is investigated, because the flow of words for its definition has ceased, this remains something indefinable. || 23 ||
This inexhaustible world is as clear as the expanse of space, as dense as the interior of a stone, and as tranquil as the silence of a rock. (24)
Within the subtle body of the Virāj-ātman, which consists of all volitions of pure consciousness alone, the perception of space and the world appears. 25.

The meaning is that the space which is of the nature of pure consciousness (saṃvedana) within the subtle body (ātivāhika-deha)—the Virāṭ-ātman, which is of the form of all-pervasive ideation (sarvākāra-saṃkalpa) belonging to the illusory self (cidātman)—is what appears as the world. || 25 ||
Thus, this Brahman is indeed the great space; where is there any talk of a world? It is peaceful, an even and uniform expansion, one and devoid of beginning or end.
This being so, he states the result: "In this way" (evam). Even among equals, it is one whose manifestation (ābhoga) is equal, meaning devoid of ultimate disparity. || 26 ||
Just as the waters do not become something other than water due to the rising and falling of waves within them, so too the Supreme is not made other by the presence or absence of other phenomena.
In the supreme Brahman. || 27 ||
Some who know the higher and the lower, within this supreme state,
dissolve internally like a drop of water in water.
Those who know the higher and the lower, and who discern the essential from the non-essential, reach a state of transformation into absolute uniformity. || 28 ||
To others, this appears as something other, as if it were of the nature of another;
yet in the stainless and peaceful [reality], neither worlds nor their activities exist.
This other world, appearing in the form of individual souls, shines forth like a disguise, an effect, or a limb of the Supreme Brahman.
Yet, when investigated according to ultimate reality, it is found to be the Supreme alone; worlds, their activities, and worldly transactions do not truly exist.
When a dream is known as a dream, and when the visible world is likewise realized as Brahman,
who would cultivate the notion of reality regarding the water in a mirage?

When the water in a mirage is thoroughly understood as being something else, as something different, and as nothing more than barren soil, who would cultivate the mental impression—that is, the notion of its reality—once again? || 30 ||
Without the internal experience of the wonder of ultimate reality,
one person does not know another, just as a bird cannot perceive the taste of wine.

The awakened one does not know any other taste of enjoyment within the manifold expansion of impurity; the meaning is that it is just as a twice-born Brāhmaṇa does not know the sweetness of liquor, such as the flavor of *sīdhu* wine. || 31 ||
Having attained liberation, this very Self, having turned back and looked within,
abandons its orientation toward objects of thought and abides peacefully in the Self.
This innate Self, having turned away from external perception and abandoned the state of being oriented toward objects of thought, becomes extinguished in meditative absorption (samādhi).
When beheld by the final cognitive modification of direct realization, it abides in the Self that is peaceful, auspicious, and eternally liberated.
As the Śruti declares: "A certain wise man, desiring immortality, beheld the inner Self with his eyes turned inward. (32)
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Since the visible world exists within the causal Brahman like a sprout within a seed, why is the reality of creation and so forth not logically established here? (33)
Thus composed in meditation, Vasiṣṭha again raises the doubt regarding the reality of the world within Brahman by means of the analogy of the seed and the sprout.
Śrī Rāma said:
"The sprout, though residing within the seed as a sprout, is not perceived."
But whatever being exists within the seed, that indeed would be the seed itself. || 34 ||

He provides the resolution: "The seed. If the sprout were existent, then it would have to be situated within the interior of the seed and emerge by breaking through the outer shell of the seed; however, that is not the case. For when the seed is split open, no sprout is perceived residing within its interior as a sprout. As for that existence of subtle parts within the interior of the seed, that is merely the seed itself, not the sprout.
This is the meaning. || 34 ||
Thus, within Brahman, it is the world itself that is perceived as the world;
if that [world] exists, it must be eternal, for that is Brahman itself, which is changeless. (35)

If it is argued that there is a discrepancy because the existence of the world within Brahman is not perceived as such, but rather only the world itself is apprehended—and that this remains the same at the time of dissolution—then that [world] must be Brahman itself; since Brahman is changeless, the logic of the seed-and-sprout analogy does not apply here. This is the meaning. || 35 ||
"That it arises from that which is changeless and formless as something characterized by transformation and form—this we have neither seen nor heard. (36)

"Let it be that Brahman is changeless; what follows from that? To this he replies: "Because of being changeless. The syntactical connection is as follows: it has never been seen or heard anywhere that something subject to modification arises from that which is changeless, nor that something possessing form arises from that which is formless. || 36 ||
Furthermore, this [world] cannot exist within that which lacks form;
nor can it reside within an atom, for Meru mountains do not fit inside it. (37)

Thus, he states—beginning with "from that which is formless" (anākṛtāt)—that even the existence of something gross, which possesses form and parts, within that which is formless and partless is contradicted by all means of valid cognition. || 37 ||
The world exists within Brahman like a jewel in a casket;
to say that the Formless possesses a great form would be the speech of a madman. (38)
In a small box, in a casket. || 38 ||
The Peaceful and the Supreme shine as the support of that which possesses form;
yet it is impossible to say where the indestructibility of that which possesses form resides. (39)

It does not seem appropriate to say that the supreme Brahman, which is peaceful and characterized by the cessation of all [phenomena], is the substratum of the formed [world] through identity with it. (39)

Even through the conceptualization that "this form is indeed consciousness," the intellect is not perceived by means of the unprecedented, firmly established worldly states (saṃsāra), just as in a dream. [In accordance with the commentary, the reading "ākāraiḥ" is required. || 40 ||

This being the case, he states that even the Buddhist conception—that momentary consciousness alone arises with forms (ākāra) that are unprecedented and firmly established like those in a dream—is untenable: "Consciousness itself... (verse 40).
This creation that is being experienced is indeed an unprecedented dream;
for a dream is seen only as an object previously experienced and thoroughly practiced.

To the question "Why is it not possible?", he says there: "Because it is unprecedented" (*apūrva*). For this creation is like a dream; it is experienced through the means of valid cognition, such as the eyes, as something entirely unprecedented—that is, an object never previously experienced. A dream, however, consists of objects experienced during the waking state that appear by means of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) alone; specifically, an object well-practiced during the waking state is what is seen in a dream. This is the sense of the word "kila" (indeed).
Established for all people. || 41 ||
That which is waking is the same as dreaming—this is not tenable here.
How could a person who has been burned in a dream be seen in the morning? (42)
For this very reason, he states that the Buddhist claim regarding the non-distinction between waking and dreaming is also inconsistent for them—beginning with the words "yadeva" (that which...).

A person who has died in a dream is led to the cremation ground and consumed by fire. Therefore, the analogy of the world to a dream, based on the conceptualization of consciousness as having form, being momentary, and so forth, is contradicted by all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
The point is that it is established [as being like a dream] because, by virtue of being superposed upon the immutable Brahman, it is sublated; thus its similarity to a dream is proven. || 42 ||
The claim that there can be no dream for one who is bodiless is also not tenable;
for piśācas and other such beings do exist, and their state of being is like that of a dream. (43)

In this regard, he resolves the objection raised by the Cārvāka: "Of one who is bodiless" (*aśarīrasya*). The meaning of the portion of the objection is as follows: since a dream is not observed for one devoid of a gross body, the statement that the three states and the dream are superimposed upon the bodiless Inner Self (*pratyagātman*) is not tenable. The remainder is clear. || 43 ||
Therefore, like a dream, that manifestation is established within the self of consciousness;
the Supreme Self, though formless, appears through various forms such as creation and the rest. (44)
Therefore, by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), he states with the verse beginning "Therefore" (and the following half-verse) that his own position alone remains faultless:

the meaning is that the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is firmly rooted—that the formless Supreme Self (*paramātman*) alone exists, appearing through various forms such as creation and so forth, which are of the nature of illusory manifestation (*vivarta*). || 44 ||
In a dream, consciousness itself abides within the self in the form of mountains and other objects;
this entire world is the Brahman-self, liberated from [the notion of] "other," even if it were created by another.

He says "brahmātma... [etc. because, upon the awakening to the oneness of Brahman and the Self, the phenomenal world (prapañca) is sublated like a dream; thus, being unfit to be described in terms of either existence or non-existence, its mere insubstantiality (tucchatā) remains. This inner Self (pratyagātman), liberated from all bonds, is indeed Brahman. And this phenomenal world was created by another—namely, ignorance alone—just like a dream.

The connection with the subsequent part of the verse is as follows: when such a Brahman-self has been realized according to the established doctrine (siddhānta), existence, non-existence, and so forth are no longer experienced here in this phenomenal world; thus, only sheer emptiness remains. 45.
In this state, neither existence nor non-existence is perceived in what is apprehended;
there is neither the state of being an experiencer nor the sequence of experiencing. (46)
This something indescribable is experienced by the Buddha alone; it is to be known through self-reflexive awareness, the unfolding of both existence and non-existence. (47)

When one is awakened, the world is not experienced at all; yet even in the state of non-awakening, the world remains truly indefinable. This is stated in the passage beginning with "svasaṃvedana" (verse 47).
Entities whose nature is non-existence appear as existence, and those whose nature is existence appear as non-existence;
at all times and in every way, all things shine forth, having attained luminosity. 48.
Brahman expands within Brahman, and the void increases within the void;
yet no expansion of Brahman within the void is possible.
The expansion—the growth of Brahman in the form of the world—is not possible within the ether. || 49 ||
This delusion of creation and so forth, consisting of the seer, the seen, and the act of seeing, is my own self;
it is the expansion of the tranquil sky of consciousness, and no such thing as a wall or the like can exist within it.
Just as a city created by one's own imagination does not exist as a wall or other such structures, so too is this world; it is peaceful, one, and free from affliction.
Just as a city created by one's own imagination is not real, so too are the walls and other structures therein all the more unreal.
For this entire [reality] is full, supremely peaceful, undivided, motionless, non-manifesting, without beginning or end, and beyond cognition. (52)
I have realized my own state, which is free from birth and death, peaceful, without beginning or end, great, devoid of limiting adjuncts, and formless.
That very consciousness which vibrates within attains the state of speech;
for indeed, that seed which is latent in the earth comes forth as a sprout.
He states with supporting reasoning that his own statement is indeed true because it is not based on mere experience:
"I am the one Self consisting of pure knowledge, entirely devoid of both duality and unity;
I do not know even in the slightest degree the artifice of the conceptualization of duality and unity. (55)
I do not know even a fraction, a trace, or the slightest bit of the conceptualization of duality and unity. || 55 ||
All these people, being liberated while living, were entirely composed in silence;
with all their worldly impulses stilled, they remained as if established in the void of their own true nature.

All these people, though living, are like me due to their own ignorance; because they are nothing but Brahman, they are eternally liberated, abiding in their own nature like emptiness in the sky. || 56 ||
Though it involves the great activity of touching the world, this [universe] remains silent;
it is like a painting executed on a wall, or like a kingdom of the mind brought forth. 57.

Likewise, that world which is to be enjoyed, because it consists of the great activity of touch and is perceivable by the senses such as the skin, exists as a mere appearance—variegated and distinct, yet like a painting on a wall. || 57 ||
It was as if carved from a mountain, as if described in a narrative, as if fashioned by Śambara, or as if arisen in a dream within the sky. (58)
It is like a carved image and so forth. || 58 ||
Indeed, this world which appears right from the beginning of creation like a dream—being without a foundation and unimpeded—what reality could it possibly have? (59)
Since, at the beginning of creation, it appears without walls and without support, what reality can it possibly possess? (59)
To one who possesses full realization, this world perceived by the intellect is false;
it is Brahman, whose essence is Brahman—tranquil within tranquility, the supreme ether.

And so, he says "the world" to show that the world has become fourfold through the difference in perspectives: this world is real from the perspective of the ignorant who possess the notion of a world; it is false from the perspective of the discerning one who possesses thorough knowledge;
it is Brahman for one who sees it as having Brahman as its essence; and [it is peace] in the person who is tranquil through the sequential ascent of the stages [of yoga].
The meaning is that, like darkness, having gradually subsided, it results in nothing but the supreme sky of emptiness. || 60 ||
All these entities indeed, together with the stationary and the moving—ourselves and others, as well as space and the objects of the world-knower’s domain. (61)
Regarding that, he states that the fourth form has as its object those who know reality: "All indeed... (61).
I am space, you are space, consciousness is space, the world is space, and even space itself is space;
having attained oneness with the space of consciousness, abide in the nature of the single void.
O Guru, for the sake of the test I have spoken, assume the form of a single space.

I pay homage to that best of bipeds, who, through awakening, has realized his own self as being like space—identical with the object of knowledge and non-different from it—by means of a gnosis resembling the sky. 63.

To you, the best among bipeds, who abide in such a state as the expanse of Brahman (brahmākāśa), I bow with salutation in the dual form— having awakened through self-knowledge that is like space, recognizing you as the universal Self, comparable to the sky, and non-different from the one Brahman which is full bliss and the object of knowledge. 63.
Because its nature is consciousness, this world arises within it and dissolves right there;
it is without cause, internal, and like the supreme, stainless ether.
Anticipating the objection that it is contradictory to say "it is the self of all" and "resembling the sky," he says:
"Because its nature is consciousness. (64)
Having attained that state which transcends all words, surpasses all scriptures and arts,
and is free from dualities, you have become one whose nature is like space.

Having attained that state which transcends all the arts and sciences as well as all scriptural reasonings—therefore being "beyond all arts and sciences"—you too have become the sky, the sky of Brahman, whose essence is that; you have always been so, or rather, you are devoid of worldly existence (*bhava-śūnya*). || 65 ||
Neither I nor the world, nor feet, hands, and so forth, nor jars and the like exist;
everything is space, and that space alone is the pure, subtle consciousness.

I am Rāma; his limbs, feet, hands, and so forth, as well as external objects such as jars and the like—the world as it is commonly known—does not exist at all for us, because everything is indeed only space (ākāśa). || 66 ||
This total negation which I have shown to you is censurable in the debates of disputants, yet it shines forth in the knowledge of the Self. (67)

And although this total denial (sarvāpahnava)— like the statement "my mother is barren" or "there is no tongue in my mouth"— is censurable in the debates of disputants such as logicians because it incurs faults such as self-contradiction and cavilling (vaitaṇḍika), and thus does not shine in their assemblies; nevertheless, when many disputants have proposed various [objections] regarding the knowledge of the Self, [this denial serves its purpose].
In the midst of an assembly of investigators, it shines forth as to what knowledge would culminate in the supreme human goal; for indeed,
without the total negation [of the world], there can be no establishment in unsurpassed bliss characterized by the cessation of absolute misfortune.
The meaning is that it is accomplished. || 67 ||

When, in the context of debate, one does not employ the "silence of wood" (kāṣṭhamauna) which consists in the total denial [of all positions], then through that [denial] self-knowledge does not become clear in debates. || 68 ||

The word *yataḥ* is used here in the sense of "because. Because [the self] culminates in absolute silence (*kāṣṭhamauna*), it is of the nature of that silence; thus, the negation of everything (*sarvāpahnava*) is simply not possible in verbal debate, and so it is not performed. By not performing that [negation], the knowledge of the Self—which is the non-dual Self—does not become clear or arise through debates due to a lack of familiarity; this is the meaning. || 68 ||
How can that Brahman, which is ungraspable by means of perception and other proofs, unmarked [by attributes], and born of one's own direct experience, be attained through mere words? (69)
To the question "From what does it not arise? he says: "Perception," etc. (69).

Transcending the meaning of all scriptures, signless, pure, one, unborn, primordial, and devoid of name and form— there exists here that which is pure, consisting of consciousness, mere experience, whose conceptualization as "peace" is sufficient to dispel any suspicion of impurity. (70)

Having stated the essence, he summarizes it concisely with the word "all": "All" refers to those various scriptures and divisions of treatises; from their meanings, there arises a direct experience (*anubhūti*) which is the measure (*mātrā*) or means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
That in which such [experience] resides is the signless (*acihna*), and for that very reason, it is free from the conceptualization of names, pure, consisting of consciousness (*cidātman*), and one.

Since there exists only the space of Brahman and not even a particle of anything else, there is no need for any suspicion of impurity (*mala*) therein; that is to say, it is sufficient and there is no purpose [for such a doubt]. || 70 ||
Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-fifth chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Yoga for Illuminating Awakening," in the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa*, the *Vālmīki Dēvamanuṣyamokṣanirṇaya*.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-fifth chapter, titled "Instruction on the Yoga for Illuminating Awakening," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and ninety-sixth canto.
Śrī Vālmīki said:
Having spoken thus, O one of great intelligence, the lotus-eyed Rāma—
Having rested for just a moment and remained silent in the supreme state.
Just as Brahman is attained here through means such as the Guru and the scriptures,
so too is the narrative of the wood-carriers described in brief.
"O you of great wisdom"—this is an address to either Bharadvāja or Ariṣṭanemi. || 1 ||
Having attained supreme satisfaction and resting in the Supreme Self,
he questioned the sage once again, even though he already knew [the answer], as if in sport.
[This was done] playfully, through the mouth of the Guru, out of a curiosity for hearing [the teachings]. || 2 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
O Lord, O lord of sages, you are like the autumn season to the clouds of my doubt;
now this subtle doubt has arisen in my mind. (3)
Thus is this great wisdom, which carries one across the ocean of saṃsāra;
it stands having completely transcended the entire web of speech.
In order to connect the question about to be asked with what precedes it, he restates what was said before: "Thus," etc. (Verse 4).
O giver of honor, that which is indeed the true Brahman, determined as mere self-consciousness, is said to be inexpressible even by the words of the great.

The meaning is that it is inexpressible because of the Vedic scripture stating, "From which words turn back, together with the mind, having failed to reach it," and because it is devoid of those attributes (dharmas) that serve as the grounds for the application of words. || 5 ||
This being the case, the supreme object of knowledge is free from all conceptual construction;
it is attainable solely through one's own fourth state of consciousness (*turya*), and thus remains difficult to fathom.
That which is the nature of self-consciousness—the fourth state (turya) transcending the three states—is a self-luminous reality attainable only through that [self-consciousness] alone;
for this very reason, because it cannot be reached by the guru, the scriptures, or other means within the waking state, it has become difficult to comprehend.
How indeed can that which is sought through the exclusion of counter-correlates and distinctions of number be attained by means of the trivial, conceptual words of the scriptures? (7)

Because [words] such as *tuccham* (insubstantial) depend on the exclusion of a counter-correlate that is even more insignificant (*kṣudratara*), they are incapable of conveying that [reality]. || 7 ||
Knowledge is not attained through scriptures consisting of words and other elements whose essence is conceptual construction;
so for what purpose, and to what end, have teachers, scriptures, and the like been imagined?
It leads to the misfortune of a succession of delusions resulting from the continuous pursuit of thousands of conceptual constructions. || 8 ||
Is there a cause for the realization of the Guru, the scriptures, and so forth, or is it without cause?
O Brahmin, best among speakers, tell me the certain conclusion regarding this.

Therefore, in the matter of the knowledge of reality (*tattva-vijñāna*), the teacher, the scriptures, and so forth, are either the cause or not the cause; the meaning is: "In this doubt, please state the certainty. || 9 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
"It is even so, O mighty-armed one; scripture is not the cause of knowledge.
Scripture consists of various words, while the supreme state is nameless."
Vasiṣṭha, concurring with Rāma’s apprehension, provides the resolution with the words "It is thus," and so forth. Regarding the term *anāma* (nameless):

because it is devoid of the attributes that serve as the grounds for the application of words (*śabdapravṛttinimitta*), and because it is unconditioned (*asaṃsṛṣṭa*), the Supreme State is neither the meaning of a word (*padārtha*) nor the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*). This is the sense. || 10 ||
Nevertheless, O best of the Raghavas, listen to me as I explain in brief how this has become the cause of the supreme awakening arising from the scriptures and other sources.

Even though this is so, nevertheless, listen to how and in what manner this scripture and the rest have become the cause of supreme awakening and its fruit, which is liberation, by means of the illustrative story of the wood-carrier (kāṣṭhavaivadhika) that is about to be told; such is the meaning. || 11 ||
In some places there are porters and wood-gatherers who have long been unfortunate;
having arrived with great hardship, they have withered like old trees in the summer heat.

He says that very thing with the words beginning "There are" (santi) and so forth. The words *vivadha* and *vīvadha* refer to a particular kind of wooden pole used for carrying loads on the shoulders, with baskets tied to both ends; those who carry such loads are the *vaivadhikas*, namely the *kīrakas*, a specific class of Śūdras or those born in a particular region.
*Śoṣam* means emaciation. || 12 ||
By this endless poverty, which reduced them to the state of mere rags,
their lotus-like faces lost all hope, as if water had been drained from them.

A patched garment (*kanthā*) woven from rags (*paṭaccara*), serving as a covering by that very means; or, according to the reading *kathā-saṃsthāna*, it means that which serves merely as a basis for talk concerning previously experienced new clothes and such. Like lotuses by water flowing out from the breaking of a dam, their faces and hopes were dejected. (13)
Tormented by poverty, they thought about their livelihood:
"By what means can we fill our bellies? (14)
They are tormented by misfortune and poverty. || 14 ||
Having reflected thus according to the prescribed rule, day after day until the end of the day, they remained resolved: "We shall live by selling loads of wood. (15)

"Day by day" means every single day. "By the end of the day" means that which is accomplished at the conclusion of the day, at the end of the day's fatigue; such is their established or settled conviction. || 15 ||
Having reflected thus, they went into another forest for the sake of wood;
for whatever means one employs for livelihood is the very same that shines forth in times of adversity. (16)
Thus, going daily to the forest, those wanderers of the wilderness would fetch wood, sell it, and thereby maintain their bodies.
Wandering through existence, they are habituated to eating lotuses obtained on each respective day. || 17 ||
For whatever they go to the edge of the forest, all those things—whether hidden or unhidden jewels, woods, and gold—are indeed present there. (18)
The jewels and other objects, whether concealed, unconcealed, or manifest. || 18 ||
From among those burden-carriers, some indeed obtain gold and jewels from the forest after a few [days].
Some are fortunate. || 19 ||
O giver of honor, some Cirakīras live by selling sandalwood logs, some flowers, and others fruits. (20)
Flowers such as the *ketakī* and *campaka*; *cirkīrakas* are those whose livelihood as *kīraka* ascetics has been made firm through long-standing practice. || 20 ||
Some of evil intellect, having failed to obtain anything at all, live as those who subsist on forest paths, taking and selling even difficult wood that is hard to work with.
Some unfortunate and dull-witted people, whose intellects are unskilled in seeking out the essential, carry away only the worthless timber. || 21 ||
All of them, having set out for the sake of wood and reached the great forest,
some arrived and remained there, all suddenly freed from their feverish distress.
Some, having obtained jewels and other riches, remained in such a state that the fever of poverty was gone. || 22 ||
While they were thus incessantly enjoying that great forest,
from one particular region, the wish-fulfilling jewel (cintāmaṇi) arrived.
By chance, a gem called the *cintāmaṇi* was obtained. || 23 ||
Therefore, having obtained all the splendors of prosperity from that wish-fulfilling gem,
they attained supreme happiness and remained there in bliss.
Having set out for the sake of wood and obtained a jewel that grants all desires,
they dwell in happiness, free from the pairs of opposites, like the best of gods in heaven.
Free from the pairs of opposites, they have cast off the sufferings of cold, heat, hunger, thirst, and the like. || 25 ||

Because they were completely filled with the essence of all purposes, those great jewels attained through their exertion upon the wood remained—having attained equanimity, with minds slow with bliss, and with fear, delusion, despair, and suffering stilled.
He concludes the narrative with the words "sarvārtha" (all purposes): those *kīraka* birds had indeed attained [the jewels] through their exertion upon the wood.

Those virtuous ones who have obtained the true jewel, the wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi), having become full through all the essences of wealth— that is, supreme riches— as described by her, and having thus become slow-witted with bliss such that fear, delusion, despondency, and suffering are stilled, attain equanimity toward other gains, losses, and the like.
They remain in peace. || 26 ||
Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-sixth canto, titled "The Acquisition of the Cintāmaṇi," in the episode of the Wood-Carrying Porter within the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Uttaraprakaraṇa*.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-sixth chapter, titled "The Attainment of the Wish-Fulfilling Gem," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and ninety-seventh canto.
Śrī Rāma said:
"O best of sages, act in such a way that the order of the carriers of the burden is maintained."
O giver of honor, I understand this correctly and without doubt.

In this work, the causality of the teacher, the scriptures, and so forth with respect to the knowledge of the Self is clearly described through a process of explaining the intended meaning of the narrative concerning the carrier of burdens.
