"Act according to the commentary in such a way that I may understand it through its essential meaning"—this is the request. || 1 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
O Rāma, those who are carriers of burdens on this earth are indeed human beings;
the misery of their poverty is the great penance of ignorance.
Those whom I have described as porters (vaivadhika) should be understood as being similar to these human beings; this applies everywhere in the subsequent passages as well.

That which I have called the suffering of poverty is their ignorance, and the great heat resulting from it is the threefold torment (trividhasantāpa). Alternatively, in the reading "that gift is great austerity" (tattu dānaṃ mahātapaḥ), [ignorance] is that which motivates the practice of giving and austerity.

The desire for enjoyments pertaining to this world and the next is expressed here by way of indication (lakṣaṇā). The intended meaning is that those who are seekers of enjoyment are intent upon the means for attaining it. || 2 ||
That which was called the "Great Forest" (Mahāvana) refers to the lineage of the Guru and the scriptures;
for those people were indeed seekers of enjoyment, rising up for the sake of devouring [the world].
May floods of enjoyments come to me; may I be a person free from miserliness, engaging in the study of the scriptures and other such pursuits without regard for the fruits of my actions. || 4 ||

Thinking, "May floods of enjoyments come to me," a person who is utterly wretched and miserly—being one by whom other purposes are disregarded—[exerts himself] toward the beginning of the scripture and toward the means rooted in that scripture. || 4 ||
Even one who has set out for the sake of enjoyment attains, through gradual practice,
the very first stage he had envisioned, even while remaining subject to the power of others.

Although this person has engaged in the scripture solely out of a desire for enjoyment, nevertheless, that scripture—by the maxim of the "sugar-coated pill"—first entices him with the tasting of results and ultimately leads him indeed to its own intended goal, the supreme state; thus he says: "For the sake of enjoyment. By means of first obtaining the fruit of enjoyment according to the scripture...

Through the gradual strengthening of that conviction, by the practice of the means taught therein, and by ascending the sequence of the different stages (*bhūmikā*), one contemplates the supreme goal of the scriptures—the primordial state known as liberation, which is Brahman. || 5 ||
Just as one intent on obtaining wood may happen to acquire a jewel,
so too does this person who has mastered the scriptures attain the ultimate state for the sake of worldly enjoyment.
"Bhāva" refers to the investigation and search for what is essential and what is non-essential; one who possesses this is a "bhāvī," namely, a porter. (6)
Thinking, "What could possibly come from the study and investigation of the scriptures? someone may proceed with a playful indifference toward doubt; yet later, they attain the supreme state.
With a playful curiosity prompted by doubt. || 7 ||

One who has not perceived the supreme reality of the meaning of the teachings proceeds to the beginning of the treatise; out of doubt and for the sake of experiencing its purpose, a person attains that state. (8)
It is called an "object" (artha) because it is sought after; it is the objective domain for the sake of enjoying it. 8.
Otherwise, people proceed according to the scriptures and their latent impressions;
they obtain something else entirely, just as porters might find a jewel instead of their load.

The meaning is that people, imagining the fruit of the scripture to be of one kind or another according to their own respective latent impressions (*vāsanā*), engage themselves in it; however, regarding the aspect of attaining that other fruit—which is beyond the reach of speech and mind, objectless, and unsurpassed bliss—the example of the porters (*vaivadhika*) is presented. || 9 ||
He who by his very nature proceeds without ceasing to help others is called a virtuous person; indeed, his conduct is the authoritative proof of this.

Since, for all people, the very sight of virtuous conduct is the root for engaging in the true path, he speaks—preceded by a demonstration of the characteristics of the virtuous—with the words "In helping others," etc.; the phrase "the authority for all the world" is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. || 10 ||

Due to the influence of virtuous conduct, people act toward the beginning of the scriptures with the hope of attaining enjoyments, as well as out of doubt, being ignorant of the ultimate reality. (11)

"Let it be a means of valid knowledge; what of it? To this he replies: "Well said. The world, being ignorant of reality, has doubt regarding the fruit of the scripture; thus, even while doubting, one proceeds with the hope of attaining enjoyment. || 11 ||
Having set out for the sake of enjoyment, he obtains both enjoyment and liberation;
therefore, he attains them just as one seeking firewood finds a wish-fulfilling gem in the forest.
Some obtain sandalwood logs, some the cintāmaṇi jewel,
and others ordinary gems, as they find them in the forest.
He states the intended meaning of the passage beginning with "secret and non-secret" (guptāguptāni) by means of the words "some" (kecit) and so forth. || 13 ||
Some obtain desire, some wealth, and some the three [goals] including dharma;
likewise, some obtain liberation entirely through the teaching.
O Raghava, indeed, instruction regarding the three groups (vargas) exists in the scriptures and other texts;
however, because it is inexpressible, the attainment of Brahman does not exist even in those teachings.

The triad of goals—dharma, artha, and kāma—exists as its primary function; likewise, in his teachings and even in those scriptures devoted to Brahman, the attainment of Brahman and the realization of Brahman occur primarily through the medium of words and sentences. || 15 ||
She alone, the glory of time, is understood through the resonance of all the meanings of the words, just as she herself is perceived through her own manifestation by means of direct experience. 16.

The splendor of the seasons beginning with spring is manifested—that is, indicated—by the blossoming of various seasonal fruits, flowers, and so forth; in the terminology of the Alamkarikas, this occurs through the function known as *vyañjanā* (suggestion), whereas in other systems, it is by means of *lakṣaṇā* (indication). || 16 ||
In the scripture, there exists the knowledge of Brahman, which transcends all objects;
it is all-pervading and pure, like the luster of beauty in a woman.

He says "sarvārtha" (pertaining to all objects) to show that although the scripture lacks the capacity to bring about understanding through its primary mode of operation (*mukhyavṛtti*), it certainly possesses the capacity to bring about understanding through means such as secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*); thus, there is indeed knowledge of Brahman for those qualified [students], and so there is no futility.
It has transcended all objects—that is, the category of the visible (*dṛśyavarga*) or the three aims of life (*trivarga*)—and has reached the pinnacle of excellence.
The meaning is that in a woman who is a jewel among women, there exists a loveliness (*lāvaṇya*) that surpasses all beauties found in jewels, mirrors, the moon, and so forth. || 17 ||
This supreme awakening, which transcends all states, is not attained through scriptures, nor by the words of a teacher, nor by giving gifts, nor by the worship of the Lord. (18)
The meaning is that it is not directly attained. || 18 ||
O Rāghava, listen to how these very non-causes have attained the state of causality solely by resting in the one Supreme Self. (19)
They have become causes by means of the progressive accumulation of a succession of means, beginning with the purification of the mind. || 19 ||
When the mind has attained purity through the practice of the scriptures and disciplined application,
it beholds the purifying state swiftly, even without desiring it.

Desiring nothing and thus liberated from all desire for enjoyments, the mind—turned inward and inclined toward the inner reality in this very way—perceives that state, which is Brahman, day after day. || 20 ||
From this scripture, the sattvic portion of ignorance is described;
through its sattvic part, the tamasic part of it comes to total destruction. (21)

It is said that it is led to excellence (*utkarṣa*). From the word *ucca* (high), with the causative suffix *ṇic* in the sense of "he causes that to be done," followed by the present tense marker *laṭ*, the *yak* affix, and the elision of *ṇi*. || 21 ||
Surely, by washing away impurity with the primary means in the form of the scripture,
a person attains supreme purity through the inherent power of reality.

Washing with the primary water that takes the form of the scripture, [he does so] by the power of the reality, that is, from the inconceivable influence of the scripture and so forth, and also from the capacity of the reality of the eternally pure self which is to be understood through it. || 22 ||

Just as in the case of the seven-horsed sun and the ocean, which are themselves desireless, their third state was previously unseen; yet, by the power of their own nature— [the reading "the third, however,
by the power of its own nature" is consistent with the commentary]— it arises spontaneously.

Just as, in the proximity of the seven-horsed Sun and the ocean, a reflection—which was previously invisible—arises as a third [entity] by virtue of its own nature of clarity and luminosity; so too, through the mere mutual connection between the seeker of liberation and the scripture, the knowledge of the Self arises. Thus is the conjunction of these three. || 23 ||
Merely by its own presence, the reflection proceeds as something expansive, consisting of both the existent and the non-existent, and appearing as it is known. 24.
That which has such a manifestation—meaning, one whose appearance is known, established through experience, and perfectly radiant—is described as being "of such a kind. || 24 ||
Thus, through this very mutual relationship between the seeker of liberation and the scripture, the knowledge of the Self—which transcends all states of consciousness—comes forth. (25)

Just as discrimination arises regarding these two upon close observation, so too does the knowledge of the objects of cognition arise from the natural discrimination [brought about] by the scriptures. (26)

Just as from the observation of these two— the sun and the ocean— there arises a discrimination characterized by the realization of their absolute difference and so forth, so too from the discrimination produced by the scripture, there arises in the body the knowledge of the second object of knowledge (the Self) as unassociated with all limiting adjuncts. || 26 ||
Just as a child washing one clod of earth with another in water gains supreme cleanliness for his hands through the destruction of both clods, so it is here. (27)

He provides an illustration for the attainment of self-purity through the cleansing of conceptual constructions born of delusion by means of the analytical arguments formulated by the authors of the treatises: "By a clod of earth," [verse 27].
Likewise, the wise man, washing away conceptual constructions through his own inquiry by means of the floods of scriptural distinctions, attains supreme purity. (28)
Furthermore, by means of volition, he is washing [himself] through the repeated investigation of the true nature of the self. || 28 ||

The knowledge of one's own self, which is the natural outflow of the meaning of the Great Sayings (mahāvākya), is attained through one's own experience, just as sweetness is obtained from sugarcane juice through the scriptures and other means. (29)
To the question of by what means and how this is investigated, he says: "By the Great Sayings" (*mahāvākya*).

From the scriptures and so forth—namely, from the Sūtras, the Bhāṣya, their commentaries, the *Mahārāmāyaṇa*, and other such texts—one obtains the essence resulting from the purification of the two referents of the terms *tattvam* and *tvam*. This [essence] is the indivisible meaning of the sentence (*akhaṇḍavākyārtha*).

The meaning is that just as the tasting of sweet, delicious sweetness is obtained through one's own experience from the sugarcane juice extracted by means such as pressing machines, so it is in this case. || 29 ||
Just as light is perceived through the close proximity of a luminous object and a wall,
so too may the knowledge of the Self arise from the association of one who has heard the teachings with one who has not.

Just as light, though diffused throughout the sky, is clearly perceived when manifested through its contact with a wall and its radiance, so too the knowledge of the Self—though its nature is eternally self-luminous—is clearly experienced through the conjunction of the hearing [of the scriptures] and the qualified seeker; this is the meaning. || 30 ||
That sacred learning which serves only for the accomplishment of the three aims of life and not for liberation is,
among the discussions of vast learning, as insignificant as if it were never heard at all.

In this regard, he states that listening to other treatises or possessing expertise in them is simply of no use, with the words "trivarge" and so on. Those of vast learning (*vipulaśruta*) are those who have heard much; they are knowers of reality (*tattvavidaḥ*). Regarding their discussions on the means for awakening to reality, that which has been heard there is as good as unheard—it is merely ignorance—because its subject matter and fruit are false and therefore trivial. This is the meaning. || 31 ||
That which was heard for the sake of making it known is that very knowledge by which there is equanimity;
that equanimity is where the state of deep sleep arises even while one is awake. || 32 ||
Therefore, with the intention that the sacred teaching (śruta) must be accepted as culminating precisely in abiding in the nature of non-conceptuality, he praises it with the word "that" (tat).
In this state, even while awake, the non-conceptual abiding in one's own nature arises, just as in deep sleep. || 32 ||
For in this way, all of this is obtained from that scripture and so forth;
therefore, with every effort, one should undertake the practice of the scripture and other such means. (33)
He states that this [work] is necessary because it is entirely dependent upon the scriptures, using the word "evam" (thus). || 33 ||

O Rāma, through the power of contemplating the meaning of the scriptures, by the words of the gurus, by association with the virtuous, and through discipline and tranquility, that supreme, primordial, and beginningless bliss—the Lord of All, which transcends all states in the entire universe—is attained.
O Rāma, it is more exalted than and surpasses even the sovereign happiness of all states in the universe, up to the world of Brahmā; it is the purifier.

The meaning is that the Lord of All, known as liberation—an eternal bliss—is attained solely through the words of the gurus by virtue of understanding the meaning of the scriptures, and that [understanding] is obtained through association with the virtuous and so forth. || 34 ||
Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-seventh chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Scripture," in the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* of Valmīki, belonging to the *Divya Mokṣa Nirvāṇopadeśa*.
Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-seventh chapter, titled "The Greatness of the Scripture," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The one hundred and ninety-eighth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
O scion of Raghu’s line, listen once more to something for the sake of further refined understanding.
That which is stated again and again remains [impressed] even upon the ignorant. || 1 ||
Herein is described the cause for the enlightened ones' abiding in undistracted bliss:
the vision of equality everywhere, which is like a dam for waters.

To prevent the objection—"Why is this secret, which has already been described at the beginning of the *Upaśama-prakaraṇa* and elsewhere for the sake of subtle awakening, for the cause of strengthening that awakening, and for the attainment of non-distraction (*nirvikṣepatā*), being described here again?"—he says: "Again and again" (*punaḥpunaḥ*). || 1 ||
O Raghava, I have first explained the section on the maintenance of the world,
by which it is understood how this universe was produced in this manner.

When it has been understood—through the chapters on Origination and Persistence—that the world thus produced is merely an illusion, the vision of equality (*samadarśana*) was described in the chapter on Quiescence (*upaśama-prakaraṇa*) for the sake of establishing that vision of equality; that very same [vision] is now described again here for the sake of establishing the bliss of *jīvan-nirvāṇa* (liberation while living). Thus he says, beginning with "O Rāghava," etc. (Verse 2).
"Therefore, it has been declared by me through the methods of tranquility that one born in this world ought to be characterized by supreme peace. (3)
Having attained supreme tranquility through the methods of pacification taught in the Chapter on Tranquility, one should dwell here free from the fever of worldly passion.
In this context, it refers to the bliss of nirvāṇa which is to be established by this treatise. || 4 ||
Just as one who has attained what is to be attained and knows it should conduct himself amidst the views of cyclic existence,
so too is there something very little remaining for you to hear.

Regarding how one should conduct oneself within the worldly views and conventional activities of saṃsāra—whatever secret there is concerning that which must be heard from our mouths by you—that is what is being stated; such is the meaning. || 5 ||
Having attained birth in this world, one should understand this worldly condition exactly as it is even while still a child, and then dwell here free from the fever of passion.
Having understood the condition of the world to be like a childhood playmate, one should dwell without distraction in the manner that will be described. (6)
O sinless one, relying upon the pure equanimity that generates universal goodwill and provides solace to all, you should conduct yourself here in this world.
Equanimity— that which will be described as the vision of the single self (aikātmya) in all beings, characterized by the absence of inequality consisting in the perception of virtues and defects,
the view that their pleasure and pain are equal to one's own, and the vision of Brahman devoid of all differentiation. Enough.
Firmly. || 7 ||
It is blessed with every prosperity, it increases all good fortune,
and it is the purifying fruit of the beautiful creeper of equanimity.

The fruit consists of the form of loving-kindness toward all beings. The distinction is that "prosperities" refers to external things, while "good fortunes" refers to states of good fortune and "auspicious qualities" refers to virtuous attributes. || 8 ||
O Rāghava, for those who dwell in the auspiciousness of equanimity and perform their natural duties in due order,
this entire fortune of the world becomes their servant.
He reveals that very twofold fruit with two verses beginning with "samatā": "Those whose efforts and activities are auspicious through equanimity and beneficial to all beings. (9)
Neither from the attainment of a kingdom nor from union with beloved women is that enduring,
essential happiness obtained which is gained through equanimity.
Know, O Rāghava, that equanimity is the ultimate limit for the subsiding of dualities, the destroyer of the fever of agitation, and the cloud that rains upon the heat of all suffering. (11)
He says "dvandva... [verse 11] to show that by means of that [knowledge], the pacification of all suffering and its causes is also accomplished.
A person who has made all enemies his friends, who perceives things as they truly are, and who consists of the nectar of equanimity, is rare to find among the worlds. (12)
Having tasted that equanimity— the outflow of the moon of one's own awakened mind, which is sweeter than nectar— all beings, such as Janaka and others, truly live.
Explaining the intended meaning of the phrase "consisting of the nectar of equanimity," he cites such people as examples with the words "of the awakened one.
They live by tasting it; that is, they subsist upon it. || 13 ||
For a person practicing equanimity, even his own faults turn into virtues;
suffering constantly becomes happiness, and death becomes like life itself. (14)
One's own faults, such as anger, greed, and so forth, gradually transform through the states of tranquility, magnanimity, and the like, and thus act virtuously; they become virtues. || 14 ||
Women such as Muditā and others, lovely with the beauty of equanimity,
constantly embrace that Great-Souled One, just as those addicted to vices embrace their own addictions.

Joy and the others—namely, loving-kindness, compassion, equanimity, and so forth—are well known in the Yoga treatises. They are "addicted" because, by virtue of their longing, they are as if possessed by a passion for union with their Lord. 15.

He is always equanimous when things arise, and his intellect is forever equanimous when they do not; indeed, for one who is equanimous, there are no such things here as "prosperities" that could disturb him. (16)

He is endowed with auspicious qualities and all perfections; he has attained perfect worldly prosperity and has reached the state of ultimate perfection. He is one whose intellect and thought have not arisen [in the sense of being distracted by worldly things]. His supernatural powers are his riches. 16.
Men and gods alike desire one who is virtuous, equal in all undertakings, engaged in natural conduct, and as noble as a wish-fulfilling gem. (17)
Men and gods alike desire a man who is impartial toward all tasks—whether his own or those of others—who is virtuous and patient toward offenders, and who is noble and generous. (17)
O Rāma, neither fires burn nor do waters drench a man who acts rightly, who is exalted, joyful, and even-minded.
They drench—that is, they cause the suffering of distress—to one who acts rightly and performs good conduct for the benefit of all people. || 18 ||
Whatever is done and however it is seen, exactly as it is, who is capable of weighing that which is free from both joy and agitation? (19)

Whatever is appropriate to be done in whatever manner, that is performed by him in that way; he who is free from joy and agitation, from elation and resentment, has accomplished everything with equanimity, by whom all things are seen as such. || 19 ||
Friends, kinsmen, enemies, kings, and litigants—all these trust in one who acts rightly and knows the truth, provided they are themselves of great intelligence. (20)

Those who know reality and possess equal vision do not flee from the undesirable, nor do they feel satisfaction upon attaining the desirable; rather, they proceed according to the sequence of nature as it unfolds.
O Rāma, having abandoned all blameless states that are unworthy of being grasped,
they maintain an excellent mode of conduct characterized by equanimity and freedom from suffering.

What are those who know reality like? Having abandoned even all blameless things—such as houses, fields, and other possessions—which others desire to acquire, they maintain the supreme mode of life characterized by freedom from greed and contentment; free from affliction, they laugh at the web of the world and sustain it.
They, whose intentions are equal and joyful, are honored by all the wise.
They give life; that is, they revive by means of instruction in discernment and so forth. || 23 ||
A person whose disposition maintains only composure upon the moon-like face, even when it has reached its natural state of anger, becomes like gentle nectar to people.

The meaning is that if even a person of equanimous disposition, for the sake of another's welfare, should maintain anger upon his moon-like face when it has arisen according to the circumstances, that too would be like nectar itself; it would not cause distress to anyone. || 24 ||
Whatever he does, whatever he eats, whatever he steps upon, or whatever he censures—
this multitude of people always praises him with an impartial vision.
Whatever action people condemn as improper, he avoids it; thus, he praises all of his virtuous conduct. || 25 ||
Whether it be auspicious or inauspicious, whether done long ago or this very day,
people rightly rejoice in that which has been performed with an even mind.

They do not even rejoice over an unwholesome fault committed through negligence, whether it was done long ago or just today; for those with an even vision, there is not the slightest bitterness toward terrible and continuous sufferings, however great they may be. (27)
Toward pleasures and pains—whether terrifying, formidable, continuous, or long-lasting—one should maintain a sense of detachment and mental composure. || 27 ||
King Śibi, with a joyful mind and this very same impartial vision, gave his own flesh, cut from his body, to the pigeon.
Now, he illustrates those who are steadfast through their equanimity even amidst great sufferings, beginning with the verse starting "Śibi":

For the sake of the dove—that is, to protect the life of the dove that had come for refuge—he gave his own flesh by cutting off a portion of his body as a substitute for its meat. This is well known from the *Mahābhārata* and other sources; the same should be inferred for the subsequent examples as well. || 28 ||
O dear one, even upon seeing his beloved— dearer than life itself— lying before him in such a state, the king, being of equanimous mind, did not lose his composure.
In front, in her own presence, she was humiliated and tormented by her enemies. || 29 ||
With a mind full of regret, the Lord of Trigarta gave to the Rākṣasa his son— who had been obtained through hundreds of desires— as he had been lost in the wager.
In a wager of words—a game of dice—the Rākṣasa lost his own side and was defeated.
Whether the city was burning, adorned for a festival,
or in its ordinary state, King Janaka, the best among rulers, remained entirely equanimous.
The king of the Śālvas, who perceived all things with equanimity, quickly cut off his own head— which had been sold according to the law— as easily as a lotus petal.
"Having sold [him] by promising, 'I will give you whatever sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) you desire,' he was practically sold to the Brāhmaṇa;
having cut him up, he gave him [to him]. || 32 ||
With his intellect, Sauvīra abandoned that mountain-like king— who, at the sacrifice, shone like a sacrificial fire-pit and was as white as a pale mountain— just as one discards withered grass.
Having recovered Airāvata, who stood like Mount Kailāsa white with snow, from Indrajit, he gave him back to Indra at a sacrifice at the request of the officiating priests.
Constantly performing his own ritual sequence with a focused mind,
one named Mātaṅga Kuṇḍapa attained the station of a celestial being in a divine chariot.

A certain outcaste named Kuṇḍapa, performing his own daily routine for the sake of maintaining his body with a mind fixed on the conventional path, hired a cow as his wages; having rescued five cows of a Brahmin that were mired in mud,
he gave the cow he had hired as wages back to that Brahmin at the lotus-pond with a mind fixed on the conventional path.
Immediately ascending a celestial chariot that had arrived, he attained the status of a god, the state of dwelling in a vimāna. || 34 ||
Through extensive practice of equanimity, the Rākṣasa of the Kadamba forest abandoned his demonic conduct, which causes the destruction of all living beings.
Although born of Bālacandra, he was dull-witted due to his equanimity; like one who eats molasses and sweetmeats, he consumed fire as if it were a matter of course.
The dull-witted one is Jaḍabharata. "Obtained by right" means obtained in the manner of alms within his begging bowl according to the rule of mendicancy. || 36 ||
Through equanimity of mind, even while devoted to cruel conduct, the Dharma-hunter cast off his body and went to the supreme state. (37)
Even while residing in the Nandana grove, the man Kapardana did not lust after the celestial women, even though they were full of affection for him. (38)

The royal sage named Kapardin, though a man capable of enjoying celestial women by virtue of his masculinity, did not lust after his own beloveds even when they were full of passion for him; the meaning is that he did not fall under the sway of desire. || 38 ||
Possessing equanimity of mind, he remained motionless even in thickets of *karañja* trees;
having renounced his kingdom, he dwelt for a long time in the marshy forests of the Vindhya wilderness. (39)
Having renounced his kingdom, he himself dwelt for a long time motionless even in the thickets of *karañja* trees within the marshy glades of the Vindhya wilderness.
The ṛṣis and munis, as well as those perfected ones (siddhas) worshipped by the gods,
were not agitated by those vows and supernatural powers because of their equanimity.
They are undisturbed by their equanimity toward vows, the hardships of austerity, supernatural powers, and enjoyments. || 40 ||
Kings, commoners, and others such as Dharmavyādha, attained the state of being worshipful to the great through the practice of the stage of equal vision. || 41 ||
For the sake of attaining success both in this world and the next, and for the pursuit of the goals of human life, those of noble intellect always conduct themselves with equanimity. (42)
One should desire neither death nor life;
conducting oneself according to what has been obtained, one should wander without causing harm. (43)
Having unified the state of both virtues and faults, equal toward pleasure and pain, high and low, and playful in his conduct,
he moves about with a sense of equanimity toward honor and dishonor, his form purified by the noble practice of his innate nature.

For whom virtues and non-virtues, as well as faults, are perceived through equanimity and have become, as it were, a single state or unified; or, according to the reading *paropatāpacintaḥ*, for whom the afflictions caused by others and the anxieties arising from them are likewise perceived through equanimity; likewise, for whom pleasure and pain are equal, and for whom those of superior birth and those of inferior birth are equal; and likewise, those who are equal...
He for whom there is neither contempt nor honor—such a one is liberated while living (jīvanmukta).

Because he lacks attachment even to worldly activities, his form is purified; therefore, being playful—that is, having a nature inclined toward sporting—he wanders through various lands for the sake of blessing the world; this is the meaning. || 44 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-eighth chapter, titled "Praise of the Equal Vision," in the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* of Valmīki, belonging to the *Deva*, *Mokṣa*, *Nirvāṇa*, and *Uttara* sections of the *Ārṣa*.
Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-eighth chapter, titled "Praise of Equanimous Vision," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The one hundred and ninety-ninth canto.
Śrī Rāma said:
"Because he is eternally established solely in knowledge and likewise delights in the Self,"
O Sage, why is the abandonment of karma not performed by those who are liberated?
For those who are liberated, there is no purpose served by actions performed, nor any harm caused by actions left undone;
nevertheless, it is described that they still continue to follow virtuous deeds.
By the liberated ones, those who are liberated while living. || 1 ||

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: For one whose two views of what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted have indeed perished, what purpose would there be in either abandoning action or resorting to action? (2)

With the intention that those who have well-practiced [the path] do not renounce their actions— because there is no fatigue in performing them, no purpose in abandoning them, and because they act out of a desire to benefit the world— he provides the answer with the verse beginning "heyā" (II.ii.2).
There is nothing here that should be abandoned by the knower which would cause him agitation;
nor is there anything to be acquired by him, for he has attained the state of supreme well-being.
Its nature as something most beneficial and as something that must necessarily be practiced. || 3 ||
For the wise man there is no purpose in the renunciation of actions, nor is there any purpose in the undertaking of actions;
therefore, whatever he remains doing, he does it exactly as it is.
Whatever is appropriate for one's caste and stage of life, he performs that very thing exactly as it stands. || 4 ||
O Rāma, as long as this body continues to vibrate, that is certain;
therefore, let it vibrate undisturbed according to its natural course—what need is there for anything else?

Since vibration is necessarily present in a living body, he states that only vibration in the form of well-practiced right conduct proceeds in that body: "As long as life lasts," [meaning] not by another abandonment of vibration, nor by a different kind of vibration. (5)

If an action were to be performed elsewhere in a manner different from its own sequence, what fault indeed would there be in the vibration of the action being the same, provided the sequence is correct? (6)

The meaning is: even though the sequence of scriptural and non-scriptural actions may be the same, what fault is there in following the scriptural sequence—that is, the conduct of the virtuous—such that one would abandon one's own [prescribed] sequence and act otherwise? The phrase "elsewhere" is for the sake of providing an illustration; just as there is no purpose in staying elsewhere when one’s own home is faultless, so it is here. || 6 ||
O Rāma, whatever is performed at all times with an even, pure, and constantly unchanging intellect is always free from fault.
With equanimity toward both success and failure.
O mighty-armed one, here on this earth there are many wise men of diverse views who dwell in various ways amidst manifold defects. (8)
Although for those engaged in ritual acts— such as the acquisition of materials, the selection of officiating priests, and the determination of matters to be performed—

there is the occurrence of many faults due to the necessity of labor, nevertheless, that equanimity and discernment can be easily avoided by them through sheer force; with this intention, he says "here" (iha), referring to those of broad vision.

They perceive the secrets of all scriptures and the world; they possess many perspectives that will be elaborated upon, and by the power of their equanimous vision, they are skilled even in the task of sustaining the world.
With an intellect free from attachment, they abide in their natural state; some householders engaged in worldly undertakings remain on earth as those liberated while living (jīvanmukta).
He elaborates on the statement "in many ways" with the words beginning "by one who has abandoned attachment," etc.; "as it stands" means following things as they have arisen. || 9 ||
Other royal sages who know that, like you, are free from passion, exercise sovereignty with unattached minds and devoid of all feverish distress.
"Those such as you"—this is an address to Rāma, relying on his future state. || 10 ||
Some follow the conventional practice of the meaning of the Vedas as it has come down;
they constantly eat what remains from sacrifices and remain steadfast in the Agnihotra fire-ritual.
Some remained among the four castes, performing their own duties such as meditation and the worship of deities, driven by various worldly desires.

One's own duty (*svakriyā*) is the action appropriate to one's respective caste and stage of life (*varṇāśramocita*); therein, meditation (*dhyāna*) is that which pertains to the fourth stage of life (*caturthāśramagocita*). By "endeavor" (*īhayā*) is meant purposeful activity (*ceṣṭayā*). || 12 ||
Some of noble disposition, having made the renunciation of everything their inner core, are constantly devoted to all actions; though they know that [reality], they remain like those who do not.
The renunciation of everything and the abandonment of attachment to the fruits [of action]. || 13 ||
In empty forest lands where even in dreams no other people are seen, and where the deer are utterly bewildered, some remain solely devoted to meditation.
"Even in a dream, worlds were not seen where people [like you] reside"—this is an exaggeration (atiśayokti). || 14 ||
Some remained in that sanctuary, which was always frequented by the meritorious, which causes the accumulation of merit, and where conduct characterized by tranquility prevailed.
In a sacred place, such as a holy ford or a hermitage of sages. || 15 ||
For the sake of abandoning passion and hatred, some, having renounced their country and being well-intentioned, took up residence by settling in another land. (16)
In the gathering of kinsmen, for the sake of abandoning [defilements] by avoiding thousands of distractions such as attachment and aversion; "pada" means a place. || 16 ||
Wandering from forest to forest, from city to village, from place to place, and from mountain to mountain,
some wise men have settled down for the sake of destroying the cycle of worldly existence.
For the sake of cutting off cyclic existence and for the purpose of avoiding the faults of attachment. || 17 ||
In the great city of Vārāṇasī, and at the purifying Prayāga, as well as at Śrīparvata, Siddhapura, and Badaryāśrama; || 18 ||

He elaborates upon the previously mentioned sacred sites (puṇyāyatana) with the words "In Vārāṇasī," and so forth. By the term "great city" (mahāpurī), it is indicated that it is the most excellent of all sacred sites. || 18 ||
In the highly meritorious Śālagrāma, in the hollow of Kalāpagrāma, in the auspicious Mathurā, and likewise on Mount Kālañjara; || 19 ||
In the groves of Mount Mahendra, on the ridges of Gandhamādana, on the slopes of Mount Dardura, and in the regions of the Sahya mountains; || 20 ||
On the slopes of the Vindhya mountains and in the interior of Malaya,
in the forest thickets of Kailāsa and in the caves of Ṛkṣavān.
In the marshes—regions abounding in water—and in the hollows of the Ṛkṣavat mountain, that is, in its caves. || 21 ||
In these and other forests and hermitages,
O Rāma, there are many ascetics who possess great insight.
They possess many views; that is, they have various perspectives conducive to the enjoyment of the fruits of their commenced karma (*prārabdha*). || 22 ||
Some have abandoned their own customary conduct, while others abide by the sequential stages;
some possess awakened minds, yet they always behave like madmen.

Having abandoned their own specific practices according to the rule of renunciation (saṃnyāsa), they are established in the successive stages of life (āśrama-dharma), beginning with celibacy (brahmacarya).
Some were deprived of their own countries, some had abandoned their native homes;
some delighted in staying in one place, while others wandered about or remained settled.
They are devoted to staying in one place, namely their own home; they are full of joy and, by being well-disposed toward all people, are free from distraction—so much is meant.
O high-minded one, among these great beings dwelling in the vault of the sky and those Daityas and others residing in the netherworld (pātāla), [he was preeminent].
With the intention that there are many who are liberated while living (jīvanmukta) even among the gods, daityas, and others in the worlds above and below, he says:
"Among these... The connection with what follows is as: "some among these possess awakened intellects," and so forth. || 25 ||
Having understood the various states of the world and purified by right vision,
some possess awakened intellects, having seen the higher and lower aspects of both the seer and the seen.
Some, whose intellects were not yet awakened and whose minds were swinging like a pendulum, desisted from sinful conduct and remained following virtuous people. (27)
Those of unawakened intellect and those of slightly awakened intellect; for this very reason, their minds are swayed like a swinging cradle. || 27 ||
Some, whose minds are only half-awakened, fall into a state of ruin by abandoning both [paths] due to the arrogance of their knowledge and the neglect of ritual conduct. (28)
"Anointed with knowledge, I am a knower of reality; what can the performance of forbidden acts do to me?"—thus [he thinks] out of pride. (28)
Thus, O Rāma, in this army of people, many who seek to cross over the cycle of birth have taken their stand in various ways with diverse perspectives. (29)
In the *janānīka*, which is a multitude of people. || 29 ||
In crossing over saṃsāra, dwelling in the forest is not the cause there, nor is dwelling in one's own country, nor are the practices of arduous asceticism. (30)
In that case, are even such things as dwelling in the forest caused by that [knowledge] means for crossing over saṃsāra? He says "no": "saṃsāra... (verse 30).
There is neither the abandonment of action nor the reliance upon action;
there is no undertaking of ritual practices that yield various diverse fruits. || 31 ||

They are called "undertakings" (samārambhāḥ) because they are commenced within the spheres of conduct and the performance of virtuous deeds; they are subsequent results consisting of a diverse collection of fruits, such as fame, gain, sovereignty, boons, curses, and powers. || 31 ||
One whose mind is unattached to what is called "intrinsic nature" as the cause for crossing over saṃsāra has crossed over the ocean of existence. (32)

Intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is the perfection of one's own true form, which consists of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*); its cause is the attainment of the complete removal of attachment by means of the mind. Thus he says: "unattached" (*asaṃsakta*). || 32 ||
Constantly performing auspicious and inauspicious deeds, and even while avoiding them, the sage whose mind is unattached does not return to saṃsāra. (33)

For this very reason, he says "śubha... [verse 33], explaining that even when those liberated while living (jīvanmukta) perform auspicious or inauspicious actions, they remain untainted by them precisely because of their lack of attachment.
Even though he constantly performs neither auspicious nor inauspicious deeds, the evil-minded and deceitful man, having abandoned his mind [to virtue], sinks indeed into saṃsāra. (34)
He by whom the mind has been abandoned and relinquished from sense objects—that person is a rogue, a deceiver of his own self. || 34 ||
Like a fly that knows the interior essence [of its victim], this mind bestows both suffering and non-suffering; it cannot be warded off, nor can it be killed. (35)
In that case, one might argue: "Let the mind itself be restrained from sense objects and let it be killed; what is the use of the knowledge of reality?
To this he replies: "Like a fly," and so forth. A mind that knows the inner essence—that is, one that has tasted the flavor of sense objects—is like a fly clinging to a jar of honey;
it cannot be restrained nor can it be killed. || 35 ||
Sometimes, by a chance occurrence like the "crow-and-palm" coincidence,
an inclination toward the realization of one's own self arises spontaneously for the sake of spiritual perfection.
Sometimes, by the power of fortune, when the fourfold means have been attained, an inclination toward the vision of the Self through the means of hearing and so forth arises spontaneously. || 36 ||
Having attained reality through contemplation, the mind becomes stainless, free from duality, unattached, and free from affliction. (37)

In that state, having attained purity through the contemplation of the mind and having realized reality, one becomes Brahman itself—free from dualities, and for that very reason unattached and free from affliction. || 37 ||
Having become mindless through a consciousness in the form of a sentient being, and having become equanimous, remain at ease, bearing the nature of a portion of the supreme space.
Abide as the bearer of that form which is the aspect of the substratum for all conceptual proliferation, such as the mind and so forth, and which is of the nature of supreme space. 38.
O Great-Souled One, you who have realized the ultimate truth, abandoned the defects of passion and the like, possess an equanimous mind, and awakened to the Self—
you, the son of Raghu, free from sorrow, remain alone and without fear in this purifying state that is liberated from birth and death.
You are that state. || 39 ||

O great-souled one, son of Raghu! You have attained the supreme goal; you are such that you have abandoned defects such as passion and the like, and you are such that the Self has arisen within you. Being thus even-minded, become the one, sorrowless, and great Self, and remain free from fear. For that state of Brahman is pure and liberated from birth and death.
The meaning is "you alone. || 39 ||
In this world, which is itself of a pure nature, there exists nowhere at all anything in the form of primordial matter, impurity, transformation, limiting adjuncts, or consciousness.
There clearly exists the uncreated Brahman, the abode of consciousness; realizing that "I myself am That," remain alone and free from doubt. (40)

Furthermore, in this world whose nature is pure Brahman, there exists nothing whatsoever—whether in the form of primordial matter (*prakṛti*), impurity, modification, or limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), nor in the form of its cognition, its will, effort, rejection, acquisition, enjoyment, and so forth; rather, there is only the uncreated abode of consciousness, Brahman. And that, having realized by its own direct experience "I am," is alone.
The meaning is: "Stay without fear. || 40 ||
O dear one, there is nothing else remaining for you to be instructed in for the sake of awakening through knowledge that is not already accessible through these extensive words.
O Rāghava, you indeed know all that is to be known; the entire essence of primordial knowledge has been fully set forth before you.
He was born. || 41 ||

"O dear one, O fortunate one, there is no other auspicious instruction to be taught that is distinct from this, nor anything further to be understood through words, for your primordial essence of knowledge has arisen in its entirety, unimpaired and complete;
indeed, the meaning is that you have now become one who has realized all that is to be known. || 41 ||
Śrī Vālmīki said:
Having spoken thus, while the leader of sages remained absorbed in one-pointed meditation, Rāghava was free from all desires, and the entire assembly stood in a state of reverent contemplation.
When the state of Brahman was attained through his pure intellect, the bee became silent, as if having finished its humming over the cluster of lotuses, and began to drink the nectar.

Having thus addressed Rāghava with the words "Vasiṣṭha is the leader of sages," when he had attained the state of Brahman through his pure intellect, and consequently had become one from whom all desires were entirely removed, and while the entire assembly remained as if absorbed in a single-pointed meditation, the Lord himself, intent upon tasting the elixir of Brahman, became silent in that assembly, just as follows:
Just as a six-legged bee, having made a humming sound over a cluster of lotuses, proceeds to drink the nectar—the *makaranda*—and then becomes silent, so too is the meaning [of this]. || 42 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-ninth canto, titled "The Description of the State of the Liberated Person," in the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa*, in the section concerning the Ultimate Reality (*Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa*), within the *Mumukṣu-vyavahāra* of the *Vālmīki-devarṣi*. 199.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the State of the Liberated Person," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The two-hundredth canto.
Śrī Vālmīki said:
When the composition of the discourse on liberation was concluded by the leader of sages,
When he brings about the cessation of subsequent speech, observed in its proper sequence. || 1 ||
Here, the Siddhas offer words of praise, a rain of flowers falls, and celestial drums resound;
thus is described by all the great festival of worshiping the Guru.

Having heard the instruction on the Self up to the section on Nirvāṇa, the perfected sages and humans who had achieved their purpose described the great festival of Vasiṣṭha’s worship in that assembly; thus the venerable Vālmīki said:
"Nirvāṇa... and so forth. The grammatical connection of all the words ending in the locative case is with the phrase "a tumult arose" in the sixth verse.

When the composition of the discourse on Nirvāṇa, consisting of this particular section, had reached its conclusion, and the leader of sages, Vasiṣṭha, was observing the final cessation of speech that followed the established sequence; || 1 ||
When all the assembly had attained equanimity through non-conceptual meditative absorption, and their mental activities had become peaceful and clear; (2)

When all the people gathered in the assembly, including the deities who partake of food, had attained equanimity— the state of being of one flavor with Brahman— through the hearing of the Sage’s words and by means of non-conceptual meditative absorption;
when they had ascended to the pinnacle of pure being and reached supreme sanctity.
Among all people who are learned in the principle of consciousness (saṃvittattva), [he is the foremost]. || 3 ||

By means of the process of non-conceptual meditative absorption (*nirvikalpa-samādhi*), when the principle of consciousness (*saṃvit-tattva*) has ascended to the pinnacle of existence—the state of pure being (*sanmātra-kāṣṭhā*) within the inner self (*pratīc*), and has thereby attained supreme purity—[then... || 3 ||
Instantly, it was carried away by the sky from the mouths of the Siddhas dwelling in the hollows of the firmament, who, with their minds previously liberated, uttered cries of "Well done! (sādhu).

"Ambarahṛt" means that which takes away or pervades the garments of Sanaka and others—who dwell in the hollow of the sky and whose intellects were previously liberated—by means of such "sādhuvāda," that is, by words of praise. || 4 ||
Likewise, there was a great accumulation of words of praise from the sages of purified souls seated in the assembly,
headed by the son of Gadhi (Vasiṣṭha).

Likewise, as Viśvāmitra, the son of Gādhi, stood in the assembly before those sages who were his masters, there suddenly arose a sweet clamor from the multitude of their voices of praise, which quickly filled the quarters of the sky; such is the connection with what follows. || 5 ||
A tumultuous clamor arose, filling the quarters of the sky,
like the sweet sound of hollow bamboos whistling in the wind.
It was like the sound of hollow bamboos—kīcakas—filled with wind, pervaded by it, and having their apertures full;
then, along with the shouts of "Well done! from the Siddhas, the celestial drums suddenly resounded, filling the mountains with their echoes.
The earth and the immovable mountains were filled with echoes, by which [sounds] they were made to resound. || 7 ||
Along with the celestial drums, a shower of flowers, beautiful like a downpour of snow, fell from all directions, veiling the entire horizon.
Like a shower of snow, the beautiful woman was white; by her, the circles of the quarters were completely covered and concealed.
The place was filled with a flood of flowers, its caves resounded with sound,
the sky was colored by pollen, and the wind was perfumed with fragrance.

The meaning of the two [verses] is: "That assembly, which was a collection or multitude of the three [groups] beginning with the *abdāḥ*, shone forth—being such that the four locations, beginning with the assembly hall (*sabhāsthāna*), were filled by the four [factors] beginning with the flood of flowers (*puṣpaugha*). || 9 ||
The convergence of the sound of "well-spoken" (sādhuvāda), the resonance of celestial musical instruments,
and the roar of the rain of flowers shone forth brilliantly.
The interior [of the hall] was darkened by the rays from the eyes of all the courtiers looking upward,
while deer, elephants, horses, birds, and cattle listened with pricked-up ears.
He describes that very same conjunction with two verses beginning with "unmukha" (verse 11).
He was gazed upon by children and women whose eyes were raised in wonder and fear, and he was looked at by the assembly of kings with faces smiling in amazement. || 12 ||
He was gazed upon by women and children, who, out of both wonder and fear, kept their eyes wide open.
With an intensity that was the very essence of a shower of flowers and surpassed all excellence of sound,
the cavity between heaven and earth quickly attained an unprecedented state.
The "rodorandhra" (earth-cavity) refers to the intermediate space between heaven and earth; "apūrvatā" refers to its extraordinary, world-transcending wonder. || 13 ||
Washed by a rain of flowers and nectar, and resounding with the "sughuṃghum" cries of shouting spirits,
the sky attained equality with the palace through the blowing of hundreds of conch shells.

The sky, washed and cleansed by a rain of flowers, nectar-like essences, and ambrosia; filled with a resonant and holy sound from the clamor of living beings and spirits; and wherein conchs were blown—such a sky attained equality with the palace, the residence of Daśaratha.
The world, resplendent with the abundant sound of "bhāṃkāra," surrounded by gods and celestial musicians,
and filled with intoxicated festivities, shone forth, adorned equally with flowers.
The world, having attained a festival of joy through me, shone forth as being equal in form to the house of Daśaratha. || 15 ||
Slowly, like a mass of flowers from the words of the multitude of Siddhas on the dundubhi drums,
it proceeded through the cavity between heaven and earth, as if toward the shore-mountain in the ocean.

By the word *dundubhi*, those sounds are indicated. The mass of those flowers—the words of the assembly of Siddhas—gradually proceeded through the opening between heaven and earth to the ends of the quarters at the same time, just as a wave in the ocean reaches the shore-mountain. || 16 ||
When that moment of agitation among the gods had passed in an instant, these words of the Siddhas became manifest: || 17 ||
During the agitation of the gods and the tumultuous clamor of the effort to shower flowers—these [verses] are about to be spoken. || 17 ||
The Siddhas said:
"Throughout the kalpas, thousands of means to liberation have been explained and heard among the assemblies of Siddhas; yet none such as these have ever existed."
We have explained such [teachings] similar to this book, and we have heard them from others as well. || 18 ||
By the playful charm of this sage’s words, animals, women, children, and even predatory beasts attain peace; of this there is no doubt. (19)
Regarding this, they speak of that excellence of quality as "the animals," having heard this through the playful discourse of the sage Vasiṣṭha in the form of this very text. 19.
Whether Arundhatī herself directly enlightens him, or not, just as Rāma has been awakened by means of examples, reasons, and logic; so [is he now]. (20)
They praise the Lord Vasiṣṭha’s extraordinary affection for Śrī Rāma, his primary disciple, by means of illustrative examples. || 20 ||
By this means of liberation, even animals have gone beyond disease;
they remain liberated—what human beings on earth, indeed, will not [attain it]? (21)
Even animals such as beasts and birds; what humans on earth indeed would not become liberated, provided they listen? This is the meaning. || 21 ||
Having drunk this nectar of knowledge with the cupped hands of our ears,
we have attained supreme glory, our perfections having become fully renewed.
Hearing this, the people in the assembly, their eyes wide with wonder,
beheld that hall as if it were filled with a shower of flowers and lotuses.
Hearing such words from the Siddhas as "The world! and "The people of Ayodhyā!", he beheld that assembly hall filled with showers of flowers, such as lotuses and other blossoms. || 23 ||
It had a mass of coverings formed by a profusion of great flowers such as the mandāra, and its courtyards and grounds were densely filled with clusters of pāribhadra creepers. (24)
The *pāribhadra* creeper is a variety of the *kalpalatā*. The *mandāra* and the others are the flowers of the five varieties of celestial trees. || 24 ||
It was adorned with the ground richly strewn with *pārijāta* blossoms,
and the hands of the assembly members were covered by a great cloud of *saṃtānaka* flowers.
With its tips adorned by crests of crest-jewels and resting upon yellow sandalwood,
it had canopies suspended like clouds hanging down from a mass of water.

Beholding that assembly hall—which, with its clusters of flowers hanging down, resembled clouds laden with heavy rain, and which was like a canopy formed by those very clouds—the people were moved to great shouts of "Well done!
and offered various appropriate words suited to the occasion. || 27 ||
The syntactical connection is as follows: being thus "udyata," meaning exerted, with various words of praise appropriate for that occasion, he honored Vasiṣṭha. || 27 ||
Then, bowing with all his senses, he honored Vasiṣṭha with a handful of flowers accompanied by prostrations.
Bowed down with all the groups of his sense organs, he became prostrate. || 28 ||
Then, when those garlands of royal prostrations had somewhat subsided, the king, with the vessel for offerings in his hand, spoke while honoring the sage: || 29 ||
King Daśaratha was one whose hand was accompanied by the *arghyapātra*—that is, holding the vessel for the *arghya* offering. || 29 ||
Daśaratha said: O Lord of Arundhatī, through awakening, the supreme state of fullness has arisen within you by means of the ultimate reality, which is free from decay and excess.
O Lord of Arundhatī, through the supreme awakening obtained by your instruction—a self-reality whose nature is unsurpassed bliss—the highest, most excellent fullness has arisen within him. || 30 ||
There is nothing on the surface of the earth, nor even among the gods in heaven, that is so great as to have not been attained by you, who are worthy of worship, through your acts of adoration. (31)

Thus, there exists no such object upon the surface of the earth, among men, in heaven among the gods, or even in the netherworld (pātāla), that would be fit for the worship of you, the bestower of such a supreme human goal. || 31 ||
Nevertheless, O Brahman, in order to make this sequence of mine not fruitless, I shall speak as it has come to me; you ought not to be angry. (32)

Nevertheless, I shall say something and offer a prayer in order to render fruitful—that is, to bring to fulfillment—this sequence of honoring my own teacher, which is my necessary duty, well-known in both scripture and the world, and obtained as it is. || 32 ||
With myself, with my wife, with the merit of both worlds, and with the entire kingdom and its servants, I worship you. (33)

By whatever auspicious merit and good deeds I have accumulated for the sake of enjoyment in both worlds—on earth and in heaven—with such a kingdom, including all vassals and servants (or alternatively, with all the multitude of servants), [I offer it] to you; "having been surrendered" is the ellipsis to be supplied. || 33 ||
All this, O Lord, is under your own control, like your own hermitage;
employ it as you direct, according to your own desired will.
I have given all this to you; it is now under your own control. Having become its master, employ it as you wish and issue your commands.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
O King, we Brahmins are satisfied with a mere salutation;
we are pleased by salutation alone, and that very one has been performed by you.
The syntactical connection is: "From where indeed does that salutation of yours arise? (35)
"You alone know how to protect it, and the kingdom shines for you alone;
let this remain yours here, for where are the Brahmins compared to sovereign rulers? (36)
To drink and to protect. || 36 ||
Daśaratha said:
"O Sage, we feel ashamed to ask how much of a kingdom there might be;
therefore, O Lord, act as you see fit regarding this matter with excellence. (37)

In this regard, as a return for the favor of granting liberation—the very nature of the supreme goal of human existence—how much could sovereignty possibly amount to? For the ultimate limit of human bliss is the undisputed lordship over the seven continents, filled with wealth and free from thorns; yet compared to that [liberation], [sovereignty is] a hundredfold less.

The bliss of human *gandharvas* is one hundred times greater than that; compared to that, the bliss of divine *gandharvas* is likewise a hundredfold—thus, as the bliss of sense objects increases in this sequence, the bliss of Hiraṇyagarbha is the ultimate limit.
Yet even that is merely like a spray of water in the ocean of the bliss of liberation; how insignificant is this [bliss of Hiraṇyagarbha] there, and where is it even worth counting?
The meaning is "it might be so. || 37 ||
Śrī Vālmīki said:
When the king had spoken thus, Rāma, offering a handful of flowers,
bowed down and spoke these words before his great preceptor.
Offering a handful of flowers at the feet of that great Guru. || 38 ||
O Great King, O Brahmā, who have rendered all others unsurpassed, I bow to you.
O Lord, I am Rāma, whose essence consists solely of prostration; here are my two feet [for your touch]. (39)
"From your words, 'We are satisfied by prostration alone,' it follows that for us, mere prostration is the essence—that which is essential because of its supreme excellence. (39)
Having spoken thus, she first bowed her head at his feet and then cast away the flowers from her joined palms, as a mass of snow leaves a mountain forest.
Just as the forest on the foothills of a mountain sheds the frost and dew clinging to its sprouts, so too [does he]. || 40 ||
With eyes filled with tears of joy, he who was skilled in policy bowed again and again to his guru with supreme devotion. || 41 ||
Śatrughna, Lakṣmaṇa, and others who were equal to them,
standing nearby, likewise quickly bowed down to the lord of sages.
They were his equals—companions of Rāma who resembled Śatrughna and Lakṣmaṇa. || 42 ||
Standing at a distance, kings, princes, and sages paid him homage with prostrations from afar and with handfuls of flowers accompanied by the movement of the wind.
With prostrations performed by those standing at a distance. || 43 ||
At that moment, amidst the showers of handfuls of flowers there,
the sage vanished like the Lord of the Snowy Mountains dissolving into snow.
Antardhi means concealment. || 44 ||
Then, when the agitation of the assembly had subsided and the multitude of prostrations had likewise ceased,
he reflected for a moment upon the teaching that [distinguishes] between the black and white intentions within truth.
In the presence of the venerable sages, as if doubting whether his own composed teaching— the scripture consisting of instruction—

regarding the subject of ultimate reality might be "black-intentioned," meaning flawed due to mental impurity, or "white-intentioned," meaning faultless due to pure intellect, he [demonstrated] discipline for the people through his own conduct.

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: remembering that something should be asked of the sages in the manner about to be described in order to receive instruction, he showed his face. || 45 ||
Shaking that heap of flowers aside with his two arms, the sage revealed his face, like the moon emerging from a white cloud.
Having cast aside white clouds from white clouds—this is a fifth case used with the elision of a word ending in *lyap* (the suffix of the gerund)—like the moon. 46.
When the multitude of the perfected ones' words had become silent, as did the sound of the drum, while there was a rain of celestial flowers and such a clamor from the assembly; (47)
Immediately after that salutation, when the people in his assembly— including Rāma and the others— had become as serene as a cloud when the wind has subsided, [he spoke].
When the people who honor and revere him have attained gentleness and composure, [he acts] toward those who honor him. || 48 ||
Hearing the cry of "Well done! from Viśvāmitra in a gentle voice, Vasiṣṭha, the leader of sages whose soul is beyond reproach, spoke these words.
O Sage, O Gādhi, O Lotus-clan, O Vāmadeva, O Nimi, O Kratu, O Bharadvāja, O Pulastya, O Atri, O Ghṛṣṭi, O Nārada, O Śāṇḍilya! (50)
O Viśvāmitra, O lotus of the Gādhi lineage, you who produce the fragrance of glory for the Gādhi family! 50.
"Bhāsa, Bhṛgu, Bhāraṇḍa, Vatsavatsa, Vātsyāyana, and others—these sages have indeed heard my words, which are but trivial. (51)

Whether it be Bhāsa, Vipaścit, or someone else—O sages, you who are worthy of honor, you might consider these words of mine to be trivial and contemptible due to their defects, and thus unworthy of acceptance; "nu" is used here in the sense of deliberation, meaning: "I think this may be so. || 51 ||
Whatever in this [work] may be inappropriate, whether it be difficult to understand or devoid of meaning, please tell me now out of your favor. (52)

"Therefore, whatever in this [work] may be considered improper, of evil meaning, devoid of sense, or meaningless—out of favor toward me and my disciples, please point it out now. This is the Lord’s humble speech for the purpose of instructing the world in discipline (*vinaya*), and by means of the Great Sage’s words, for the purpose of proclaiming the faultlessness of the treatise. || 52 ||
The members of the assembly said:
"O Brahmin, regarding the words of Vasiṣṭha, which are endowed with the single highest truth,
we have heard today for the first time indeed this very strange speech, that they can become meaningless."
The sages, headed by the son of Gādhi, having been addressed by the members of the assembly, said: "Because it is unknown anywhere in the world, only nine divine words have been heard. (53)
That impurity which had been accumulated by the endless defects of birth has today been wiped away by you here, just as gold is cleansed by fire.
O All-pervading Lord, we have been made to blossom by Your speech, which is expanded by the Brahman and is supremely cool with nectar, just as night-lotuses are by the radiance of the moon.
By that which has been expanded—that is, extended—within Brahman; or, in the case of the moon's radiance, by that which is extended within the sky, which resembles Brahman.
We here bow down to you, the leader of sages, the sole teacher, who bestows great awakening upon all sentient beings. (56)

"Exclusivity" means restriction; namely, [serving] the Guru alone and not anyone who is not a Guru. By this, the highest pinnacle of his superiority over the gurus of the lower sciences (aparavidyā) is indicated. || 56 ||
Śrī Vālmīki said:
Having spoken thus, they again addressed the Lord of Sages with the single word "Salutation to you! uttered in a loud, resonant voice as powerful as the roar of the ocean.

Furthermore, uttering the words "Salutations to you," they filled Vasiṣṭha once again with multitudes of flower-offerings cast down from the sky by themselves, just as the perfected ones (siddhas) had done; he was like the immovable Himavat mountain.
With showers of flower-offerings cast down from the sky by the Siddhas,
they filled Vasiṣṭha, just as clouds fill a mountain with snow.
Thus did those well-versed in the history of Rāghava praise King Daśaratha,
as well as Rāghava and Mādhava, who are the fourfold self.
Then, following the praise of Daśaratha, they praised Mādhava as the fourfold Rāghava;
the meaning is that they were well-versed in the account of how Rāghava was an incarnation of Viṣṇu. || 59 ||
The Siddhas said:
We bow to Rāma, the prince who is liberated while living, together with his brother, who is like another fourfold-natured Nārāyaṇa. 60.
[He saw] King Daśaratha, the protector of the circle of the earth bounded by the four oceans, who bore the insignia of a sovereign of the three times.

They further praised King Daśaratha, whose royal insignia—the marks of kingship that endure through the three periods of time and never perish—were present upon him, saying, "You are most blessed, for you are the father of Śrī Rāma. || 61 ||
To King Bhāskara, the lord of the sage-army and possessor of great splendor;
to Vasiṣṭha, rich in excellent speech; and to Viśvāmitra, a treasure-house of austerity.
They praised Vasiṣṭha, the lord and master of the sage-host, who possessed immense splendor and stood like the sun, as well as Viśvāmitra, who was seated near him. || 62 ||
By the power of these very [teachings], we have all heard this supreme method of knowledge which destroys delusion and agitation. (63)

They state the reason for the praise of these [qualities] as follows: "Of these very ones... The remainder of the sentence is: "[This is] the speech of Vasiṣṭha, which destroys delusion and agitation. (63)
Śrī Vālmīki said:
Having spoken thus, the Siddhas again scattered flowers from the sky;
then, with joyful hearts, they remained silent within the assembly hall.
In the same way, the Siddhas traveling through the sky again praised that person;
likewise, the members of the assembly there honored them with a profuse hymn of praise.
They honored those perfected ones with abundant praise, offering a profusion of hymns in such a manner as was fitting.
The sky-dwellers, the earth-dwellers, the lords of sages, the great seers, the hosts of gods, the twice-born,
and the kings thus honored Janma with vigor alone, along with heaps of hymns and the offering of flowers and water for the feet.

The sky-dwelling great seers, the hosts of gods, the earth-dwelling twice-born, the kings, and the lords of sages who move between both realms— having been described in this manner— they worshipped him with flowers and water-offerings, each according to their own power and capacity, using lofty words for every person. || 66 ||

Thus ends the two-hundredth canto, titled "The Description of the Homage and Acclamation of the Holy Ones," in the *Nirvāṇa-Uttara* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*, the Great Epic of Vasiṣṭha, belonging to the *Ārṣa* tradition. 200.
Thus ends the two-hundredth canto, titled "The Description of Acclamation and Worship," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The two hundred and first canto. Śrī Vālmīki said:
Then, as the cries of "Well done! gradually subsided...
Having received the instruction in knowledge, as if among kings who were shining with splendor. || 1 ||
In this regard, when questioned once again by Rāma,
the Guru respectfully revealed his own repose in the state of perfect bliss.
"Arvāk" means in the lower part of the assembly hall. || 1 ||
When the delusion of saṃsāra has been stilled, one truly laughs within one’s own mind at one’s own past conduct as it pursues the truth.
When the mind laughs at itself—its own conduct, its behavior in the state of ignorance—as it truly pursues and correctly perceives the reality of that very self; || 2 ||
While the minds of the assembly were subdued and intent on savoring the taste of knowledge, the hall was tranquil, as if established in meditative absorption. || 3 ||
When the world of people has gathered together, while the subtle faculty of the mind (*cittakalā*)—the movement of the mind—is turning back, revolving, and inclining inward;
and when one has become intent upon the perfect savoring of knowledge, which is of the singular essence of consciousness and bliss—[in that state]... || 3 ||
While Rāma, together with his brother, sat before the Guru in the bound lotus posture (baddhapadmāsana) with palms joined in reverence, his eyes were fixed upon the radiant face of the Guru.
His gaze was fixed upon the radiant and resplendent face of his guru.
The king savored, as it were, a certain state of meditative absorption—
an inner condition consisting of liberation while living, purifying the beginning, middle, and end.
While Daśaratha, the lord of the earth, remained as if absorbed in meditation, relishing a state of liberation while yet living. || 5 ||
The sage, who honors those who seek his favor, remained silent for a moment as if to accept the worship of his devotees, and then spoke with composed syllables.

The sage Vasiṣṭha, having remained silent for a moment as if in contemplation in order to accept the worship and honor of his devotees, the king and others, according to the manner previously described, spoke thereafter. || 6 ||
O Rāma, lotus-eyed one, you who are the cool-rayed moon in the sky of your own lineage—what else do you wish to hear? Speak according to your desire.
And what kind of state do you yourself experience now?
Tell me, what form does this worldly appearance take that you perceive? (8)
When this was said by that sage, the prince,
looking at the face of his teacher, spoke calmly, gently, and clearly.
Śrī Rāma said: "O Lord, by your grace I have attained supreme purity, like the vault of the sky from which every mark of blemish has been stilled. (10)
With all stains pacified, like the full moon whose mark is its spot, my delusions—which cause the destruction of existence—have all been stilled;
I remain like the clear sky, pure by its very nature. (11)
I stand with all knots dissolved and all specific attributes stilled; I am one whose intellect is as pure as crystal, situated within the abode of crystal.
In this world, which is as pure as the nature of Brahman—meaning, it is purified by the state of Brahman—he possesses such an intellect, like a crystal situated in the midst of a crystal palace. 12.
Furthermore, my tranquil mind has no desire to hear or acquire anything else;
it has attained supreme satisfaction and remains as if in deep sleep. (13)
The meaning is: "to fetch" and "to accomplish. || 13 ||
O Sage, my mind is peaceful, with all conceptualizations stilled, all curiosity departed, and all volitions completely abandoned. 14.

The distinction is as follows: *parāmarśa* is the recollection of the object; *tadbhoga* is the curiosity regarding its enjoyment; and *tadartha-saṃkalpāḥ* are the volitions directed toward that [enjoyment]. || 14 ||
While remaining awake for the sake of the world’s maintenance, I enter parinirvāṇa and attain peace;
I sleep, as it were, in a state free from affliction, without dreaming and without returning to further awakening. 15.

"I sleep," as it were—meaning free from dreams, which is the absence of mental perception of objects, and free from waking, which is the absence of sensory perception of objects. The word "as it were" (iva) is used to indicate that even the appearance of deep sleep is illusory, thereby revealing the state of the Fourth (turiya). || 15 ||
Laughing at my former state of being, which was centered on the body and distressed by desires, I remain established in myself, free from doubt, through the radiance of well-spoken truths. 16.

Having laughed at my former state of existence within this body—a state agitated by hopes and rendered distraught by the notion of "self"—I now remain composed through your radiant, well-spoken words of instruction. 16.
Neither by instruction, nor by wealth, nor by treatises, nor by kinsmen, nor even by the renunciation of these things, do I have any purpose for you now. (17)
Now, by my instruction, for the sake of wealth, or for some other purpose connected with that—by the abandonment of all these, there is no cause nor any purpose [for remaining]. || 17 ||
Or rather, I experience right here that very same state which exists in the imperial sovereignty of the sky— unperturbed and inseparable from my mind.
With her mind fixed solely upon the inner Self, she remains constant and eternal; this is the state of liberation while living.

Just as there is a state in the celestial realm (svarga) that is free from the disturbances caused by the Asuras and others, so too is this state experienced within the void (vyoman); such is the worldly perspective. || 18 ||
I see this world—which is nothing more than a mere portion of the space of consciousness—as exceedingly transparent, like food that has been swallowed;
today my vision has entered into a state where it perceives things according to their desire, their inception, their attainment, and their established condition. 19.

The meaning is: although I have attained the state of being a limb of the body through the perception of external vision and so forth, I see the world as nothing but pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), which is far more transparent than even space; I do not see it as insentient like an ignorant person. || 19 ||
"This entire world is nothing but space"—this is my singular certainty;
when this sky known as the "visible" has perished, I remain awake, imperishable. (20)
In this world, when destruction is afflicted by the sleep of delusion, I, the imperishable, am forever awake. || 20 ||
Whatever he says—according to his desire, as it has been obtained, and as if it were already established—I perform without obstacle, being free from all longing. (21)
I shall perform future tasks as desired, present tasks as they arise, and past tasks as they were situated;

whatever you have spoken, that I shall carry out according to the instructions of my teacher and the scriptures, free from longing and devoid of attachment to results. (In an alternative reading: *yathākāmam yathārambham yathāsthitam*)
In such a manner: regarding one's own affairs, according to one's desire and according to one's undertaking; regarding the affairs of others, as they have been obtained and as they stand. || 21 ||
I am neither pleased, nor elated, nor nourished, nor do I weep;
alone I perform what must be done, and my delusion has gone far away. (22)
I am not gratified within my inner mind, nor do I feel elated; I do not nourish pride in my outward body through the attainment of the desired.
Likewise, upon encountering the undesired, I do not weep. I perform whatever task must necessarily be done, whether it be worldly or Vedic. || 22 ||
Let this creation go to its end, or let the wind of dissolution blow;
let the region become pleasant, for I am established in my own self, remaining well.

With the intention that, while remaining thus established, there is no fear of encountering misfortune through the loss of kinsmen, wealth, kingdom, and so forth—things desired by my own commands—or through the shifts of planetary periods (*daśā*), he says: "Let it be otherwise. Let it be empty like the path of the moon, or let it be *saumya* (gentle). He remains self-abiding (*svastha*), free from distraction. || 23 ||
