I am at rest, I am beyond reproach, I am difficult to perceive, and I am free from affliction; O Sage, I am not bound by desires, just as the sky cannot be grasped by fists.
He is unperceivable by the external senses; he is imperceptible even by the mind; [he is untouched] by hopes, that is, by cravings. 24.
Just as fragrance from a flower on a tree reaches the realm of space and remains there,
so too do I remain, equanimous and transcending the body.

He provides an illustration for how that which is manifested in the body may exist transcending the body, beginning with the word "yathā" (just as). It is "samaḥ" (common/equal), because it is impossible to specify whether it belongs to this flower or to this body; thus, it is common to both. || 25 ||
Just as all kings dwell according to their pleasure—both those who are unawakened and those who are awakened—in their kingdoms with many duties. (26)
In that case, how and like what will you conduct yourself hereafter? To this he replies: "Just as... (yathaiva). || 26 ||
With joy, sorrow, and hope stilled, possessing steady and singular equanimity, I abide fearlessly within the Self; in that very state, I move about.
He states the distinction from those who are unawakened with the word "peaceful" (śānta). || 27 ||
"O Lord, though I am happy even above all, I do not desire happiness for myself;
I abide in equality with people—employ me as you wish. (28)

I am happy through the bliss of Brahman, which transcends all worldly objects, power, and pleasure; therefore, I do not desire nor seek sensual enjoyment within my body. Command me; give your orders regarding service and other such matters.
O holy one, as long as this body lasts, I shall maintain my existence in saṃsāra with a single, stainless vision, casting off all fear like a child at play. (29)
"As long as I possess this body, being a child, I shall maintain the condition of worldly existence just as it comes to me, like play or sport appropriate to my age. (29)
"I eat, I drink, I stand, and I perform my own duties;
O Lord of Sages, by your grace I have been born free from all fear. (30)
Śrī Rāma said: Oh, how wonderful! You have attained this state of great merit, wherein there is no sorrow, and which is without beginning, middle, or end.
The suffix *la* occurs after a verbal root (*bhāva*) when it denotes that state by remaining in which one does not grieve. (31)
In your own self, which is naturally cool and characterized by perfect equanimity and effortless application, you have yourself attained rest, as tranquil as the sky within the sky. (32)
By good fortune you have become free from sorrow; by good fortune you are firmly established;
by good fortune, your apprehension of misfortune in both worlds has come to rest.
In both worlds—this world and the next—there is apprehension regarding seen and unseen misfortunes and what has been heard.
By good fortune, O son of the Raghus, you have purified the lineage of your family—past, present, and future—through your awakening. (34)

"O daughter"—this is an address used out of excessive affection. You are "Saṃjñā," so called because you know perfectly; being a knower of the reality of the Self, you have purified the lineage of the Raghus—past, present, and future—through your enlightened understanding. || 34 ||
O Rāghava, having now fulfilled the request of Viśvāmitra, the lord of sages, and having enjoyed this earth together with your father, you may remain here. (The word "remain" is to be supplied. 35.

"Arthitām" means the state of desiring the removal of obstacles to the sacrifice. "Together with his father"—the intention is that while his father was still living, he did so by his command, having protected the earth through the slaying of the Rākṣasa. || 35 ||

Accompanied by you, along with their sons, servants, and kinsmen—whether on foot or in circles of chariots, elephants, and horses—may the Raghavas, O fortunate one, be free from illness, devoid of fear, possessed of stable prosperity, and ever successful;
[that is, may the servants and others related to the Raghu clan be so. 36.

O fortunate one, may you, accompanied by [your kin], united with your sons, together with your children and grandchildren, along with your servants and relatives, and including those with chariots, elephants, horses, and circles of foot-soldiers—indeed, both types of people alike—be free from ailment in body, devoid of fear in mind, and ever prosperous in their homes; such is my blessing and prayer. || 36 ||
Thus ends the two hundred and first chapter, titled "The Manifestation of Rest," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the glorious Vāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa, the scripture of the Sage. 201.
Thus ends the two hundred and first chapter, titled "The Manifestation of Rest," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The two hundred and second canto.
Śrī Vālmīki said:
Having heard these words of Vasiṣṭha in the assembly, the kings—
As if sprinkled by floods of nectar, they attained an inner coolness.
The kings and Rāma, delighted by his awakening, are described herein;
and by Rāma, his own state, purified by knowledge, was polished clear.
The mention of "the king" is intended as an illustration for all people. || 1 ||
Rāma, whose eyes were like lotus petals, shone with his moon-like face, like the full ocean filled with a beautiful flood of nectar. || 2 ||
It is called *sudhāpūra* because it is filled with nectar (*sudhā*); by its rising, [the world] was like the Ocean of Milk. || 2 ||
Vāmadeva and all the others, who were experts in the knowledge of reality, said with reverence: "Oh, the Blessed One has spoken of knowledge! (3)
Oh, what has been said is truly wonderful! || 3 ||
With his inner self pacified, King Daśaratha shone with joy;
his limbs thrilled with satisfaction, he attained a fresh radiance. || 4 ||
With his limbs thrilled by contentment and an excess of satisfaction, his body was covered in horripilation. || 4 ||
Then, when many discourses of praise had been uttered regarding those who have known what is to be known,
Rāma, his ignorance dissolved, spoke these words once more.
While many discourses of praise were being uttered. || 5 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
O Blessed One, Lord of the past and the future, our impurity has been thoroughly wiped away by you,
just as the blackness of gold is removed by fire.
Impurity is ignorance. || 6 ||
"O Lord, formerly we were ones who saw only our own bodies;
now we have become those who behold the entire universe in all directions. (7)
Those who perceive only the body hold the view of a self limited by the body; those who behold the universe perceive the universal self.
I stand complete in every respect; I am perfected and free from ailment.
I am born with all doubts dispelled; as a wise one, I now remain awake.
Being everything, he is complete. || 8 ||
I am gladdened so as not to grow weary, and I am happy for a long time;
the arising of the eternal goal stands for me so as never to set.
The ellipsis is: "the arising," that is, the manifestation, of my eternal goal, the supreme human aim (paramapuruṣārtha), has occurred. || 9 ||
"Aha! Oh, I have been sprinkled by you with the purifying, cool water of knowledge; I rejoice within my own heart like a lotus. (10)
Like a lotus, like the autumnal water-lily. || 10 ||
Today, by your grace, this state has been attained by me,
abiding in which the entire world has become nectar for me.
The path is the path to universal sovereignty. || 11 ||
With a mind serene within, all sorrow dispelled, I have attained splendor through tranquility, being indeed of pure intent;
having reached bliss in the Self by the Self alone, I have attained purity—homage be to me! 12.

His mind is serene within; for this very reason, all his sorrow has subsided. Since, through peace—the destruction of ignorance along with its effects and roots—I have attained bliss in the Self alone, whose inner disposition is now stainless;
and having thoroughly examined by means of the Self itself, I have accepted the self-evident purity perceived therein. Therefore, it is for me alone...
The meaning is "let there be salutation. || 12 ||

Thus ends the two hundred and second canto, titled "The Acceptance of Resting in the Self," in the latter half of the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the holy Vāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa of Valmīki, belonging to the Ṛṣi tradition.
Thus ends the two hundred and second chapter, titled "Accepting Rest in the Self," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa-tātparya-prakāśa*.
The two hundred and third canto.
Śrī Vālmīki said:
While the sage and Rāghava were thus absorbed in reflection, the two of them—
The sun ascended to the middle of the sky as if for the sake of hearing [the news]. || 1 ||
In this [chapter], the sounding of the midday trumpets, the daily activities, and the progression of the night are described;
furthermore, Rāma’s morning assembly and his state of being free from doubt are recounted.
"While the two were thus intent on reflection"—the locative dual is used here in the sense of a temporal or circumstantial characteristic (*bhāvalakṣaṇa*).
By implication, this suggests the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) that they were there specifically to hear the investigation of those two matters. || 1 ||
Then the heat quickly attained sharpness in every direction,
like the great intelligence of Rāma, for the purpose of expanding the multitude of objects.
"In all directions" means in every direction. "The expansion of the mass of objects" means their clear perception. (2)
Then, because their lotus-hearts were blossoming with such vastness,
those present there shone like kings in a playful lotus-pool.
The gardens and ponds have the form of playful lotuses; those situated there are like those present in that assembly. The mention of "the king" is an illustration for all people. || 3 ||
Immediately after the clusters of pearls, the net, having eclipsed the sun, seemed to dance as it traversed the sky,
as if out of a desire to hear the wisdom [of the Buddha].

The sky, as if dancing, seemed to float across— like a crystal lattice-windowpane characterized by a string of pearls strung together without any intervening gaps, which was pervaded by the sun that had entered it by way of reflection— due to the excellence of its own radiant splendor.
This is a poetic conceit (utprekṣā) that produces the wonder of direct experience: as if crossing the sky—the space of Brahman—by hearing the wisdom taught by Vasiṣṭha. || 4 ||
The rays of the young sun, having struck the rubies,
sparkled like flashes of intellect— the digits of knowledge— soaring from the surface of the sky.
Just as the splendors of the sun’s youthful radiance, reflected in rubies, appear as the beauty of their own shadows,
so too do the arts of knowledge arising from instruction flash forth within the intellect.
Thus, when Rāma—the white lotus of his own lineage—had attained liberation and remained as if in full bloom through the sight of the face of the Lord of Sages; (6)

From the conjunction with the light of the Lord of Munis' face, and because it causes the night-lotuses to bloom, his nature as the moon is understood even though it was not explicitly stated. || 6 ||
When the sky, resembling the submarine fire in its roar, attained the state of being the navel of the great ocean,
it became a mass of radiant energy with flickering flames that consumed all essences.
"Aurva-like" means resembling the submarine fire; that very similarity is established by the qualifying attributes. (7)
The blue sky-lotus shines,
its pollen falling away, lovely with the sun as its pericarp and shimmering rays as its filaments.
In this way, even the state of the sky being a blue lotus is established by means of qualifiers, beginning with the word "nabhaḥ" (sky).
It is beautiful because of its pericarp, which is characterized by the sun (dharmāṃśu). || 8 ||
They are the crest-ornaments of the Fortune of the World and the earrings for the ears of the three realms,
resplendent with rows of jewel-like stars shimmering within them.

The phrase ending with "as ear-ornaments" (*avataṃse*) constitutes a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) regarding the blue lotuses; "as earrings for the three worlds" (*trilokīkarṇakuṇḍale*) is another poetic fancy; and "hidden within" (*antarlīna*) is the justification for that [second fancy]. (9)
As the great waterless clouds, split by the heat, were held up like mirrors by the quarters of the sky acting as maidens with their massive peaks for hands; (10)

When the quarters of the sky, acting as brides, held up their hands in the form of great mountain peaks like mirrors within the vast clouds, those [clouds] were pierced, split, or divided by the heat of the sun's rays. || 10 ||
As if augmented by the fire arising from the excellent sun-stone (sūryakānta),
it blazes twice as intensely in the expanse of the sky when devoid of the sun.
Even in the sky which was devoid of the sun, when the fire arising from the finest sun-stones (sūryakānta) increased and blazed as if with double the intensity compared to the sun itself... || 11 ||
Filled with the fierce and violent breath from their mouths,
they roared like oceans at the end of an eon, swollen by the winds, when they are mistaken for midday.
Like the beauty of frost upon lotuses, or like the beauty of summer upon faces, she—resembling scattered pure pearls—set foot [there]. 13.
The beauty of the summer heat, manifesting as the splendor of beads of sweat, took its place upon the faces of the people.
Reverberating off the walls of the house and intensified by the agitation of living beings,
the splendor of that sound filled the ears like the ocean filling its own shore.

Reverberating back from the walls of the houses in the form of echoes, and intensified by the clamor of the sounds of living beings hurrying to their tasks, it filled the ears like the waters of a river or rain filling the ocean.
Uttered by the housewives to soothe the heat of the summer season, a fresh row of pale camphor clouds rose up. 15.
The row of clouds is characterized by the sprinkling of water mixed with camphor.
That king, together with his vassals, his subordinate monarchs, and his retinue,
rose up from the assembly along with Vasiṣṭha, Rāma, and his court.
The distinction between a vassal and a sovereign king arises from the difference in their authority over the territory of the mandala; [the same applies to] the assembly and the court. || 16 ||
The kings, princes, ministers, and likewise the sages,
having honored one another, departed joyfully for their own abodes.
At the front of the inner apartments, a fresh garland of clouds was created by camphor dust brought forth by the wind from palm-leaf fans.
At the front of the houses, at the entrances of the houses. || 18 ||
Then, as the sound of the midday drums resounded against the walls,
the leader of sages, skilled in speech, spoke these words.
It flashes forth with a crashing sound as it increases. || 19 ||

O Rāghava, everything that is worth hearing has been heard by you, and everything that is worth knowing has been known by you in its entirety; indeed, there remains nothing further of superior value to be known.
Just as you have been instructed by me, just as you perceive it through the scriptures,
and just as you experience this most excellent state, act accordingly with single-minded resolve.

He says "yathā" (as follows) to show that a state of syntactic unity—characterized by being fixed upon a single meaning—must be established so as not to contradict the teacher’s instruction, the Vedānta and other scriptures, and one's own experience. || 21 ||
Arise now for our task, O high-minded one;
it is midday for us, and this moment of the day is passing away.
Furthermore, O noble one, whatever you desire to ask for the sake of dispelling your doubts, that auspicious matter should be asked by you again tomorrow morning. (23)
The meaning is that if there is something worthy of being asked, something fit for inquiry, it must necessarily be asked in the morning; it should not be neglected.
Śrī Vālmīki said:
When the lord of sages had spoken thus, King Daśaratha himself honored all those virtuous members of the assembly with due reverence.
Together with Rāma, that righteous-souled one [honored] the sages, brahmins, and kings,
as well as those who travel through the sky, according to the sequence instructed by Vasiṣṭha and others.
With the value of heaps of jewels and pearls, with divine flowers, by the gift of precious gems, and by the offering of pearl necklaces. || 26 ||
Some he honored with wealth consisting of treasures such as clusters of jewels and pearls; others, however, by the direct gift of actual jewels and pearls. || 26 ||
Through affection, through prostration, through the gift of wealth,
through clothing, seats, food, and drink, as well as with gold and land.
By the giving away of a daughter and so forth. || 27 ||
The blameless lord of the earth honored all those who had come before him with incense, perfumes, and garlands, just as prescribed.
Then the giver of honor rose from the midst of the assembly along with the courtiers and the divine sages headed by Vasiṣṭha, like the evening moon rising from the sky.
Together with the assembly and the people present in the hall. || 29 ||
The time of the army's rising shone forth with great excitement,
as the ground became muddy from the flowers scattered by the gods, which reached up to their knees.
Or rather, "sa-saṃrambha" means [the time] accompanied by haste, along with the time of rising from the assembly, together with the time of rising from the assembly; that is "sa-saṃrambha. || 30 ||

The earth was reddened by the dust of jewels from his armlets, which were jingling as they struck one another; the night sky was adorned with stars consisting of the shimmering pearls from broken necklaces.

He describes that very [scene] with the words beginning "saṃghaṭṭa" and so forth: the ground is reddened by the gem-dust from armlets resulting from "saṃghaṭṭa"—which means rubbing—and "āghaṭṭa," which means mutual striking.
By this [ground], the sky—well-known for its stars during the time of night—is surpassed, as it possesses shimmering "star-moons" (pearls) fallen from broken necklaces. || 31 ||
It was crowded with the movement of celestial sages, hermits, eminent brahmins, and kings;
its fly-whisks were made restless by the hands of attendants and women who were busily waving them.
Vibrating with the act of making knowledge its object of measurement, he is not cruel;
he shines resplendent only upon the head, hands, three eyes, and tongues.

If one asks, "In that case, is it not cruel for all people to be driven by the haste for their own self-interest, resulting in the crushing of the weak? he says: No, because they move only for the purpose of making [the object] an object of cognition (*prameya*), and not out of haste for any other self-interest; therefore, it is not cruel. Furthermore, even when there is a slight jostling of limbs, the hands are placed upon the head for the sake of mutual forgiveness.

The meaning is this: among all those people—those with palms joined in reverence before him, on his sides, and behind him, whose eyes and tongues were engaged in gazing upon him and seeking his forgiveness—he shone resplendent; he was not faltering due to the negligence or cruelty of others, and thus there was not even the slightest possibility of any fault such as causing pain to others.
Then, having taken leave of one another, all the kings and sages, beginning with Daśaratha, were honored with gentle words.
Those whose utterances are refined, gentle, and sweet. || 34 ||
The virtuous ones returned to their own hermitages with hearts mutually content and affectionate,
like the gods residing in the seven worlds returning from the city of Śakra.

With hearts that were mutually satisfied by a longing for one another's virtues and filled with affection, they departed from Ayodhyā like the gods from the city of Śakra; they were inhabitants of all the seven worlds.
Having honored one another in turn out of mutual affection, they were dismissed by him; returning to their own homes, they performed their daily duties.
The daily ritual of the day. || 36 ||
Then all those beginning with Vasiṣṭha, as well as Daśaratha and the others—
both kings and sages— performed their daily duties.
Then, after they had performed their daily rites as they were wont to do,
the sun, a traveler of the sky, gradually reached its setting.
*Daivīsīṃ* means pertaining to the day. || 38 ||
Through that very conversation, by virtue of the awakening of those [sages] and of the high-minded Rāma,
that night quickly passed away.
Awakening is vigilance; it occurs through the power of that [practice]. || 39 ||
The sun arrived, transforming the world into a celestial palace, filled with flowers that were the dispelled darkness, dust, and stars.
Just as the dust of darkness is swept away by the morning sweeping of the house, he adorns the world—the abode of the universe—as if it were a dwelling filled with the flowers of stars. 40.
Then the young sun entered the ocean of the sky, reddening the quarters with his rays that shone like *karavīra* and safflower.
Kings, princes, ministers,
and sages such as Vasiṣṭha and others likewise assembled once again in the assembly hall of the son of Daśaratha.
In due order, according to their positions, their locations, and their seats,
she entered that assembly hall like the splendor of the celestial mansions in the sky.
The splendor of the sacrificial hearths, the beauty of the divine abodes and the lunar mansions. || 43 ||
Then, while Daśaratha and the others, including Sumantra and his companions, were praising the sage Vasiṣṭha as he sat upon his seat, [Kauśalyā spoke]. 44.
While they were praising and extolling Vasiṣṭha. || 44 ||
In the presence of his father Vasiṣṭha, the wise Rāghava, whose eyes were like lotus petals, spoke these words in gentle tones.
Śrī Rāma said: O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, great ocean of all knowledge, axe to all doubts, remover of grief and fear!
It removes the grief and fear of others, even of one's enemies.
What else remains for me to hear, or indeed what remains to be known? Whatever is yet to be heard, you should explain all of that to me. (47)
If it exists, then you ought to explain it. || 47 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
O Rāma, you have attained true awakening; there is nothing further for you to hear.
This intellect of yours has accomplished its purpose; having attained all that is to be attained, it is now established in the Self.
First, reflect within yourself with your own intellect and tell me:
what is your inner state today, and what remains for you to hear? (49)

"What kind of person are you today through your own experience? What remains for them to learn?"—the meaning is: "Tell me yourself what there is that must necessarily be heard as a remainder [of instruction]. || 49 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
O Brahman, I think thus: my mind has accomplished its purpose;
I am liberated, I am profoundly peaceful, and no desire remains within me.
"What was to be said has been spoken by you; everything that is to be known has been understood by me.
May your eloquence, having accomplished its purpose, now find rest. (51)
Viśrānti means cessation or rest; Sarasvatī means speech. || 51 ||

That which was to be attained has been attained; this entire object of knowledge has been reached by me. Duality has set and all oneness has vanished. Indeed, the appearance of the manifoldness of the visible world has completely dissolved.
Thoroughly casting off all attachment to the state of being a transmigrating being.

The entire world has attained a state of oneness with Brahman, reaching a specific uniformity where all distinction has vanished. Duality—the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman—has ceased, because that appearance of the distinction of the visible world, which serves as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), has dissolved.
To the question "Why is that so?", he says: "Indeed... (nanu), because the state of being a transmigrating being (*saṃsāritā*) has been skillfully investigated and cast aside by me.
The meaning is "abandoned. || 52 ||
Thus ends the two hundred and third canto, titled "The Description of Nirvāṇa," in the *Vāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa*, the *Mokṣopāya* section of the *Devala* recension of the *Ārṣa*.
Thus ends the two hundred and third chapter, titled "The Description of Nirvāṇa," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The two hundred and fourth chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
O mighty-armed one, listen once more to my supreme word.
The mirror, having been polished again and again, shines exceedingly. || 1 ||
Furthermore, by means of refined reasoning, the visible world is repeatedly cleansed within consciousness by Vasiṣṭha and Rāma for the sake of purifying the conscious self.
It is supreme because it is concise yet clear, and excellent because it teaches the means for cleansing away that which is perceived. || 1 ||
The object is a convention of sensation, and sound is like the noise of water;
this visible world is but the manifestation of consciousness—where did the universe come from, being like a dream? (2)
The visible object is indeed twofold, namely "form" (rūpa) and "name" (nāma). Regarding these, he states the means for cleansing the first [form] with the word "object" (artha).

For the objects of the four kinds of words are genus (jāti), quality (guṇa), action (kriyā), and configuration (saṃsthāna); as in the examples "cow," "blue," "fickle," and "named Bhadra. And these [words], though referring to a single object, take on the appearance of difference based on the distinctions among the things to be excluded (vyāvartyabheda).

The causes for the application of linguistic distinctions are merely imagined, based on erroneous cognition and convention; they are not real. This means that there is no fourfold reality therein, which is the purpose of the cleansing. He states the second method of cleansing with the word "sound" (*śabda*). Once the object has been cleansed, the sound becomes meaningless, like the sound of water, and thus attains the status of a mere name.

The meaning is that by abandoning the very state of being an object, one is purified simply through that purification; thus, it is established that both types of the visible world are merely the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa), like a dream. || 2 ||
The waking state, perceived as a dream, exists before one as a nature of memory;
it is pure consciousness, mere perception, which is real and pervaded by the forms of other things.

When even the waking state is false, then that very [waking state] becomes the object perceived in a dream by way of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*); and that, like a memory, is devoid of any objective reality of its own, appearing as if standing before one. Thus, it is merely the experience of consciousness itself, extended out in the form of something else; the meaning is that even there, nothing exists apart from consciousness. || 3 ||
Just as the space of consciousness within me, though appearing as a city in a dream,
is formless even while possessing form, so too are these three worlds.

And thus, because both are equal, he states that they consist of nothing but the space of consciousness (cidākāśa) with the words "yathā" (just as). [This occurs] in me, the inward-facing consciousness (pratyakcit). || 4 ||
Śrī Rāma said: How did this earth come into being? How did the mountains come into being? How did the waters come into being, and how did the stones come into being? (5)
The question is: how did insentience and the diversity of the earth and other elements arise therein? || 5 ||
And how is the fire endowed with power, and how is the ritual action perfected? How is time perfected, and how is the wind perfected?
And how is emptiness accomplished, and how is the sky accomplished?
This has been understood by me further; tell me for the sake of awakening, O Lord. (7)
All of this was already known to me even before your words; nevertheless, speak again for the sake of dispelling my lack of conviction and for the further increase of my understanding.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: "O Rāghava, tell me in truth: how did the earth come into being within that great city seen in the dream, and how did the sky come into being?"

With the intention that everything is to be understood as being just like a dream, Vasiṣṭha himself provides the answer by means of a counter-objection under the guise of a question, beginning with the words "Speak," etc. (verse 8).
How did the water come into being, and how did the stones come into being? How did fire come into being, and how did the quarters of space come into being? (9)
How is time perfected, and how is action perfected?
How is all this—beginning with the causal signs [or, according to another reading, "necessity" (niyati) and so forth]—said to be perfected?
By whom was this created, burnt, brought, fashioned, and accumulated?
What is its conduct, what is its nature, and how was it produced and manifested? || 11 ||
Śrī Rāma said: His self is solely the void; it is not the earth, mountains, and so forth of this world which is like a dream—formless and without support.

Just as in the case of the illustration, Rāma, imagining the perfection of the earth and other elements even in the subject of the illustration, himself elaborates upon the falsity of the world with the verse beginning "The Self of this... and so forth. The Self, the essential nature of this world, is merely the void (*vyoma*) alone. (12)
The Self alone is of the nature of space for this [universe], being supportless and formless;
or rather, since this space is itself formless, what need is there for a supporting cause? (13)
If it is asked, "Is it then merely of the nature of emptiness? he says, "It is the Self itself. "Cause" means the purpose. || 13 ||
This which has arisen is nothing at all, for it is not distinct from consciousness;
this so-called "shining forth of consciousness" is simply the mind itself abiding in such a state.
Having provisionally accepted the perfection of the forms of earth and so forth, this was said; however, in reality, even that perfection does not exist at all, as he says:
"Nothing whatsoever. This manifestation of consciousness in the form of the world is merely the mind itself existing in such a way like a dream, and nothing else.

Wherein space, time, and so forth are the manifestation of consciousness, and where the immobile earth and other elements are the manifestation of consciousness; likewise, water and so forth arise from consciousness, and the knower understands that air and the rest are the void of consciousness.
And because the mind is nothing but the vibration of consciousness (*citsphuraṇa*), he says "space, time," etc., that [mind] itself is everything.
For one who knows that—that is, for one who knows all principles (*sarvatattva*)—[it is so]. 15.
Consciousness alone, indeed, exists as the void, reaching the state of being space;
it remains as a stone due to its hardness, and like water due to its fluidity.
In reality, however, there is no such thing as earth or the like, nor is there any visibility;
that infinite space of consciousness is all, one, and its very essence. (17)
Just as water from the heart of the ocean becomes manifold through its various states of existence, so indeed does the non-dual consciousness become manifold within the Self, which is like the sky.

The meaning is that just as the water of this serene ocean, by its very nature of fluidity, can manifest as many various forms such as waves, foam, and whirlpools while remaining essentially non-different [from itself], so too is the space of consciousness (cidvyoma). || 18 ||
When consciousness attains the state of solidity, it perceives itself as a vast earth, as if it had become a mountain;
when it experiences emptiness, the conscious body perceives itself as void, like the sky. (19)
Through the perception of fluidity it knows water; through its vibration it knows wind;
and through the awareness of heat, it knows fire, without ever abandoning its own essential nature.

One perceives water through the perception of fluidity within the Self; likewise, one perceives air through the perception of its vibration. By stating that [these perceptions] do not abandon their own essential nature as the conscious substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna-cid-rūpa*), the doctrine of illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) is demonstrated. || 20 ||
This element of consciousness (ciddhātu), whose very nature is such, consists of the void;
that it thus manifests, displaying a sequence of qualities without cause, is its very essence.
Thus, the doctrine of "creation as perceived" (dṛṣṭasṛṣṭivāda) is revealed, wherein the sequence of qualities arises without an external cause. || 21 ||
And apart from these two, nothing else exists here whatsoever, other than emptiness and water, just as there is nothing other than the sky and the ocean. (22)

Just as there is no reality other than the water-nature of the ocean, and none other than the emptiness of space, so too, apart from this Self of Consciousness (cidātman), no reality whatsoever exists for the world. 22.
But nothing whatsoever exists apart from the sky of consciousness;
therefore, remain in a state of peace, free from notions such as "this," "you," or "I."
This world, consisting of "this," "you," "I," and so forth, is not other than the sky of consciousness; for nothing whatsoever can exist apart from it.
Just as you perceive fire, mountains, and so forth while acting within this house,
yet see them as having no physical form, so too is the sky of consciousness.
Acting, that is, fashioning [it] through dreams, mental desires, and so forth. || 24 ||
At the beginning of creation, it is the sky of consciousness that appears in the form of a body, but not a physical body;
since the latter is causeless and non-existent, one should contemplate that consciousness alone arises. 25.

When the body does not exist, then, due to the absence of a cause and because it is non-existent, consciousness arises in the form of a body through ignorance. This should be reflected upon and investigated by the wise; such is the meaning. || 25 ||
The mind, the intellect, the ego, the elements, the mountains, and the directions—
all remained as they were, silent like a stone-womb.
The meaning is that it consists of silence and is indeed inexpressible. || 26 ||
Thus, nothing has arisen and nothing has perished; nor is there anything at all.
The form of the world, as it truly exists, abides within the Self, which is Consciousness-Brahman. || 27 ||
That which is called manifestation within consciousness is the unfolding of its own nature;
this is what is called the "world," just as fluidity is the very nature of water. (28)
Bṛṃhaṇa is the full manifestation of one's own essential nature to its highest degree. || 28 ||
This appearance of the world is indeed non-appearance; the void of the sky of consciousness is the ultimate reality itself.
For one whose intellect perceives things as they truly are, it is the Buddha; for one whose intellect does not perceive them as such, let it be whatever it may be. (29)
Through the vision awakened by the perception of reality as it truly is, this world—though appearing as a phenomenal existence—is in fact non-existent;

the ultimate reality is only the sky of consciousness (cidvyoma). As for the ignorant person whose intellect is unawakened, let things be as they may; what is the use of investigating that? This is the meaning. || 29 ||
Thus ends the two hundred and fourth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Unity of the Consciousness-Ether," in the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa*, the *Vālmīki Devarṣi Mokṣopāya*.

Thus ends the two hundred and fourth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Unity of the Consciousness-Sky," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The two hundred and fifth canto (205).
Śrī Rāma said:
"O Blessed One, just as this supreme sky is seen in a dream in this manner..."
In the same way, if there were no web of doubt regarding the state of being awake, [then it would be established]. || 1 ||
This state of the world is merely an illusory manifestation, equal to a dream;
it has not arisen, does not abide, and does not cease—it is described as pure consciousness alone.

Having thus accepted the previously stated view that the world is a mere illusory transformation (*vivarta*) like a dream, Rāma asks—by means of two verses beginning with "evam"—that even such an illusory transformation is impossible within the immutable, non-dual pure consciousness, because of the absence of a cause. || 1 ||
O Blessed One, tell me this, my unsurpassed great question:
how does consciousness, though bodiless, appear like its own body during waking and dreaming?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Whether in the waking state or in a dream, the visible world has space as its support, consists of space, and is born from space;
and space itself is never anything else. There is no doubt about this, as it is established by reasoning.

For since there is an absence of a cause, you must concede that the transformation has no arising; and for that which has not arisen, there can be no persistence, so that it would be nothing but emptiness. Since this is precisely what he himself accepts, your reason for questioning and your doubt are devoid of justification.
To this, the Blessed One replies with the words beginning "The visible," etc., because [the world] has arisen from a causeless source like a sky-flower.

It must be established that the substratum of emptiness is itself of the nature of emptiness; for the void and emptiness are none other than the Supreme Brahman. Therefore, the meaning is that no inconsistency or doubt regarding the impossibility [of manifestation] arises in the case of a vivarta (illusory appearance), which is devoid of origination and so forth and is not in contradiction with the non-duality of Brahman. || 3 ||
In that whose form consists of the total disappearance of all causes and appearances,
no elements whatsoever come into being at the very beginning of creation.
He establishes non-arising itself by means of the verse beginning with "samasta" and so forth. || 4 ||
Therefore, this body is restricted to earth and the other elements; there is nothing else here.
Indeed, these are merely the primary elements (bhūtas); the body does not exist at all apart from them.
The question—“How can consciousness, which is bodiless, appear as if possessing a body in the waking and dreaming states?”—is also untenable;
for in the absence of earth and the other elements, there is likewise no existence of bodies consisting of the fourfold collection of beings. Thus he says:
"Earth and so forth... (verse 5).
Therefore, this sky of consciousness perceives appearances like a dream;
it is the mere shining forth of its own nature, appearing as if agitated by forms.
Therefore, he states that the theory of illusory manifestation (*vivartapakṣa*) is free from fault: "By that," etc. "Confused" means agitated by the qualities of *māyā*. || 6 ||
This form of the world, which is merely a manifestation and a mere appearance, is described by the conscious Self through the term "space" and the word "dream. (7)

That which is mere appearance is itself the manifestation of a dream; that very form of the world is described by such terms as "the world as a dream-transformation," using the word "world" (jagat) and so forth, in reference to the sky—that is, the very nature of the space of consciousness (cidākāśa). || 7 ||
This which is called "feeling" (vedanā) is the sky-like form of consciousness, stainless as the firmament; within this, the nature of consciousness exists as both dream and the world.
And thus, the meaning is that the form of the world appearing within sensation remains as sensation itself: as "dream" in its subtlety and as "the world" in its grossness. || 8 ||
Then, within this very expansive manifestation of its own nature, which is of the form of consciousness, these distinct designations such as "earth" and so forth were created by it. (9)

He says—"In this very [consciousness]"—because if such a proliferation (*prapañca*) as form consists of nothing but feeling (*vedana*), then even the proliferation of names results in being merely a differentiation of names for that same feeling. Thus: "by that," meaning by the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*) which is the self of consciousness (*cidātman*), and which fashions the differentiation of forms;
"then" means immediately thereafter. || 9 ||
That very manifestation of consciousness is designated by the terms "dream" and "world";
and this manifestation is its inherent nature, like space, which never ceases. (10)

For this very reason, he says that even when dreams and the like have subsided, that manifestation of reality never ceases—namely, "the manifestation of consciousness alone. Its inherent nature is reality. || 10 ||
The many diverse visions of creation are none other than Brahman within the ether of Brahman; like emptiness and the sky, they abide in and dissolve into the wind.
He states that "precisely because of its existence, many manifestations (vivarta) have proceeded therein" with the verse beginning "bāhya" (verse 11).
Śrī Rāma said:
O Blessed One, you have indeed spoken of millions of creations;
some are situated within the shell of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), while others are devoid of such an egg.
Desiring to hear this nature of the cosmic egg out of curiosity, Rāma constructs the framework for his inquiry with the words beginning "sargāṇām" (of the creations).

He restates those [creations] already mentioned in the Līlopākhyāna, the Bhuśuṇḍākhyāna, and elsewhere, using the words beginning "kāścit" (some...). These verses have been explained previously. || 12 ||
Some are situated within the treasury of the earth, some are established in the firmament;
some are contained within the treasury of fire, and some reside within the treasury of wind.
Some had the surface of the earth situated in the sky, with their determination of above and below reversed;
they had their hooves above the bottomless space, with forests and mountains hanging from them.

The terrestrial spheres have the shape of globes situated in space. Therein lie various certainties such as "we alone are above," "we alone are above," held by gods, asuras, and others who, like ants, are attached to the earth-globe and occupy positions above or below it. He states this clearly: "from the nether sky," because from the perspective of everyone's vision, living beings are located in the region beneath the earth.
From the space at the base—the foundational space of the earth—they have their hooves (feet) turned upward and their heads downward;
thus, because their roots are above and the branches and peaks are below, the forests and mountains therein appear as if they are hanging down.
Some were like floods consisting of the nature of wind; some were eternally bearing darkness;
some had the configuration of space; and some were teeming with swarms of worms.
In those [regions], the multitudes of beings—masses of living creatures whose nature is wind and whose bodies are air—reside in dense darkness that sustains the quality of *tamas*;
in them, the configuration of the bodies of living beings is like the void of space. 15.
Some were situated within the hollows of the sky, some within the hollows of rocks;
some were stationed within the hollows of shells, and some remained in the air like birds.
Those who, along with their wives and belongings, reside in houses, pavilions, and similar dwellings, just as those shown in the narrative of the Pavilion (maṇḍapa). || 16 ||
Among those [questions], O Blessed One, best of the knowers of reality, tell me how and in what manner this Brahmāṇḍa exists for us.
The question is: "Tell me how this universe, which is like our very foundation, exists. (17)
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
That which is unprecedented, unseen, unexperienced, or unheard is described through excellent illustrations; it is grasped and inferred thereby.

This question does not concern reality, nor is it conducive to the knowledge of reality; it possesses neither purpose nor utility for the subject at hand, nor is it novel, nor does it have a definitive meaning. This is because sages have described the configuration of the earth, the celestial spheres, and so forth in various ways across different astronomical systems (*jyotiṣasiddhānta*), as has already been demonstrated previously. Therefore...

Considering that there is neither any purpose nor any valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) in propounding a philosophical conclusion (*siddhānta*) with partiality toward one side or another regarding this world, which is illusory in nature and like a dream, Vasiṣṭha replies by stating: "That which... He implies that since this is the subject matter of other scriptures, it is already known to you and thus not worthy of inquiry. "Apūrva" means not being the object of any other means of knowledge.
The elaboration of that very [reality] is intended to show that it is not something seen, nor experienced, nor even heard;

its nature is established through perception, inference, and scripture. The meaning is that this alone is described by the teacher with excellent illustrations, grasped by the disciple through hearing, and understood through reflection, and nothing else. || 18 ||
But this cosmic egg, O Rāma, has been described in hundreds of ways by the scriptures, sages, and gods; and all of that has been known by you.
By the hundreds, in many ways, and in various manners. || 19 ||
Just as this has been known by you and described according to the scriptures, so does all this exist; what else remains to be described here? (20)
He says "yathā" (just as) to show that it is not correct to claim that a description of you, whose nature is already known, is not something unprecedented.
Śrī Rāma said:
O Brahmā, tell me how this great ether of consciousness came into being;
what is its extent, and for how long has it existed? (21)
Then Rāma asks: "How did Brahman become the form of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), and for how long will it remain thus?"—this is expressed by the word "katham" (how). || 21 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
This Brahman exists, eternal and imperishable, without beginning or end;
it possesses no beginning, middle, or end, nor does it have forms in the supreme ether.

Brahman has never become possessed of form, nor does it have any temporal limitation; rather, as long as there is non-awakening, it perceives its own self—as if asleep—in the form of the world. With this intention, he provides the answer beginning with the words "beginningless," etc. (verse 22).
This Brahman-space is without beginning or end, imperishable, and all-pervading;
this entire universe consists of it, being itself devoid of beginning or end in every respect.
That which is the self-manifestation of this supreme sky of consciousness within itself is called this "universe"; yet by that very fact, it is itself illusory.
Therefore, he himself stated that "the universe [is real]," and that too is false.
Just as a person has the perception of a city in a dream, so too does that [Self] appear like a city; this is what is called "this universe. (25)
Here there are no mountains that are solid, nor are there waters that are liquid;
this sky is not empty, nor is time of the nature of measurement.
He asks: how could natures such as the hardness of mountains—which are opposed to it—be real within Brahman, whose single nature is consciousness alone?
He answers with the verse beginning "They are hard. (26)

Just as a solid mass of self, or as that which is imperishable, is there perceived by consciousness through itself, so does it remain firmly established in that very essence of mind (cittattva), like a mountain and so forth. // 27 //
And thus, consciousness itself, though spread out by the conscious power of delusion as if it were situated in that way, does not exist in reality; so he says: "That which... (verse 27).
Just as non-stone becomes stone in a dream, or as the sky itself becomes a non-sky,
so too here the beginning of creation and the existence of the visible world occur within consciousness, like a dream.
The particle *eva* is displaced [in its position]; it means "just as non-space is indeed space. || 28 ||
Consciousness itself, being formless and tranquil, perceives this world as its own cognition, like a dream; and that [world] is said to be indeed formless in reality.
The meaning is that I have said this hundreds of times. || 29 ||
Just as the movement within the wind is nothing other than the wind itself in its continuity,
so too this Brahman within Brahman neither arises nor ceases.
Just as fluidity exists in water, just as emptiness exists in the sky,
and just as substantiality exists in a substance, so does this world exist in Brahman.
Neither has it departed nor has it arrived; without cause, it does not arise from a cause.
This world is neither non-existent nor existent when distinguished from the state of Brahman. (32)
"Departed" means concealed by dissolution; "come" means manifested. || 32 ||
Nor can the beginningless, appearance-less, and formless sky of consciousness possibly be the cause of any other perception anywhere. (33)
But Brahman is certainly not capable of being such a cause and so forth; thus he says, "And not," referring to any other vision of creation.
Therefore, just as the parts of a whole exist only as their own selves,
so too does the world-space reside within the partless space of Brahman.
They consist solely of their own self and do not exist as separate entities. || 34 ||
Everything is peaceful, without support, mere cognition, and free from affliction;
herein there is neither existence nor non-existence, nor is there any diversity whatsoever. (35)
The sense is that, regarding the denial of everything else, the scriptural text "not here, not manifold" (neha nānā) is the authoritative proof. || 35 ||
All this that is extended is like a mental construction, a dream, a city of the Gandharvas, or a dance;
it remains as even, peaceful, unborn, and imperishable as space.
He provides an illustration for such an appearance as well, stating: "In imagination," etc. (verse 36).

Having conceived the heart of the supreme ether of consciousness, that which shines forth as beautiful and stainless is this very world; it is perceived by that [consciousness] alone as its own form until the end of the aeon.

The stainless, clear, lovely, and throbbing heart of the supreme sky of consciousness—its very essence, its own nature—is the conscious self-nature itself. Whatever form it manifests through delusion, being fully capable of doing so, that very thing imagined by itself as its own form persists until the end of the aeon and the dissolution; by that alone is the world conceived and perceived.
The meaning is that it is nothing else. || 37 ||

Thus ends the two hundred and fifth chapter, titled "The Refutation of the Cause of Creation," in the *Ārṣa-Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*, in the section on the *Vairāgyaprakaraṇa*, within the *Mumukṣuvyavahāraprakaraṇa*. 205.
Thus ends the two hundred and fifth chapter, titled "The Refutation of the Cause of Creation," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The two hundred and sixth chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
That appearance which shines forth without a cause is nothing at all.
Thus, O sinless one, the ultimate reality stands as the ultimate reality by way of the ultimate truth.
The questions concerning the reasons for the conclusion that "only Brahman exists and the world does not," as spoken by the Lord of Kuśadvīpa, have been set forth here.

Brahman alone exists as the ultimate reality (paramārtha) from the perspective of the ultimate truth; that appearance of the world which shines forth without a cause does not exist at all. This is the summarized meaning of the preceding text, set forth as an introduction to the subsequent text. || 1 ||
In this regard, O Mahāmati, listen to this supreme great question asked by someone of me, for the sake of nourishing perfect awakening. (2)
In this regard, for the sake of nourishing right understanding, listen to this supreme and further great question that is about to be stated. || 2 ||
There is an island known as Kuśadvīpa, which is renowned throughout the three worlds and is situated on the earth like a ring, surrounded on both sides by two oceans.
It is surrounded on both sides like a ring by the two oceans, the Suroda and the Ghṛtoda. || 3 ||
There, in the northeast, is a golden city named Āstīlavatī,
whose ground and sky are fixed upon pillars composed of blazing flames.

In the intermediate direction between the east and the north; [this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound] according to the rule "names of directions in an intermediate space. It is there that the surface of the earth and the sky are interwoven by pillars consisting of rows of flames characterized by radiance. || 4 ||
In former times, there was a king in that city renowned as Prajñapti;
he was beloved by all living beings, like a second Śakra in heaven. (5)
In the eastern part of that city. || 5 ||
For some reason, on one occasion, I approached that king from the sky, like the sun at the time of universal dissolution fallen from the heavens.
Falling from the wheel of light at the time of dissolution, like the sun.
Having worshipped me with flowers, water for honor, and water for sipping, and having sat down, he asked this out of affection during the course of a certain conversation: ||| 7 ||
O Blessed One, when all things have been withdrawn, when one abides in emptiness,
in the ineffable supreme ether where all causes have ceased, (8)

In that which is extended and vast by way of emptiness, which is inexpressible because of the absence of the fourfold forms such as genus (*jāti*)—the cause for the occurrence of names—and when the destruction of all causes, such as seeds and the elements like earth, has occurred; || 8 ||
Tell me again: what is the root cause of the commencement of creation?
What are the auxiliary causes, from where do they arise, and how do they act?

The primary cause is the material cause (*upādāna*); the auxiliary causes are the instrumental causes (*nimittakāraṇa*). If these exist, then from where, how, and by what means did the material cause and the others arise? (9)
What is this world, and what is its creation and so forth? There are some eternal worlds devoid of darkness, some situated in the sky like oceans, and some teeming with swarms of worms.

What is this world that has arisen in reality? And what are its modifications, from creation to dissolution? Among those, some levels are eternally shrouded in darkness; others, such as the worlds of Brahmā and so forth, are oceans situated in space, according to the Śruti: "The two oceans are Ara and Aṇya. Still others are the levels of the hells and so forth, teeming with swarms of worms.
And what is the purpose of such variety as this? || 10 ||
Some reside within the hollow of space, and some dwell within the hollow of stones;
moreover, what indeed are the elements and the primordial matter, and from where do the intellect and the rest arise, and how?

The worlds beginning with the intermediate space (antarikṣa) reside within the treasury of space; the cities of the Daityas, Dānavas, and others go within the treasury of stones, being situated inside rocks. What, in reality, are the elements such as earth and the fourfold collection of living beings contained therein? And what, or how, are their internal counterparts such as the intellect (buddhi) and so forth? || 11 ||
Who is the agent, or who is the observer? What is the relationship between the substratum and the superstratum, and how does it exist?
It is certain that there is never any destruction of the worlds. (12)

Who is the creator and fashioner of all these? Or who is the witness? If, however, for the sake of avoiding contradiction with the entire meaning of the Vedic scriptures—consisting of both the *karma-kāṇḍa* and *brahma-kāṇḍa*—there is never at any time a great destruction or dissolution (*pralaya*) of the worlds, but rather worldly transactions always proceed in accordance with the respective karma of individual living beings; [then...]

If it is established that the world never functions in any way other than this [present manner], and thus the certainty is supported, then—given the well-known principle that experiences are exactly as they are perceived—would you say that perception itself is caused by the body and so forth, or something else? In the first case, is that perception indestructible and eternal, or is it composed of unreality and perishable? If it were indestructible...

In that case, it would be absolutely immutable (*kūṭastha*), and thus there could be no modification such as the body and so forth. If, on the other hand, it were perishable, then its cause at the time of origination must be stated;
yet that is difficult to state, because it cannot be established without consciousness. Thus, the connection with the following two verses is due to this contradiction. || 12 ||
It has been established so as not to contradict the meaning of the entire body of Vedic scriptures;
for just as there is such a thing as "consciousness," so too are there various experiences corresponding to names.
Since perception would arise from this or that [object], how could it be indestructible or composed of non-existence?
Furthermore, O Leader of Sages, today in a place such as Jambūdvīpa... (14)
Regarding the second [point] as well, he raises an objection with the words "And another," etc. (14).
For those who have died, whether cremated by fire here or whose bodies have perished,
the body serves as the instrument for the experience of hell or heaven in the absence of a physical form.

In this world, or in places such as Kuśadvīpa where bodies perish, and in Videha—a region devoid of mothers, fathers, and others who produce a body—what are the material causes (*upādāna-kāraṇa*), the auxiliary causes (*sahakāri*), or the efficient causes (*nimitta-kāraṇa*) with respect to the body? (15)
What then are its auxiliary causes, or what indeed are they? Dharma and adharma are both formless; how could there be form for that which is formless? (16)

[Objection: "But surely it is dharma and adharma themselves that transform into the form of the body and so forth. To this he replies: "From dharma and adharma... [The phrase] "the materiality of those two, which are immaterial, is inconsistent" is to be connected by supplying the missing words. || 16 ||
The argument that one makes something substanceless by means of substances is inconsistent;
for what cause could there be for the absence of parents and so forth in that case? (17)

Furthermore, the reasoning that both—that which is devoid of substance (*nirdravya*) and that which is non-substantial (*adravya*), being distinct from substance—constructs the body and so forth from substances such as the earthly elements, is also inconsistent.
He states that it is also inconsistent because of its lack of a seed (*nirbījatva*): "mother, father, etc. (verse 17).
What other causes could there possibly be, and how could there be the existence of substances and so forth?
For it is established that "there is no world beyond" according to one's own direct experience. (18)

"In that case, let it be the position of the nihilist"; to this he replies with the words "the next world. It is inconsistent to say that there is no next world for this agent of dharma, adharma, and so forth, because this very life is a "next world" in relation to a previous birth, and because this [life] exists according to its own experience. || 18 ||
Moreover, it is inconsistent because it contradicts all the world, the Vedas, and so forth;
for results [are obtained] by those who have gone to distant lands through actions performed without desire. (19)

Furthermore, because it would entail a contradiction with all the world, the Vedas, and so forth, he says "samasta... [etc. that the nihilist position is not to be accepted. Moreover, this world of living beings obtains results such as execution, imprisonment, and punishment from royal edicts and the like—even though these edicts do not fall within the scope of one's own volitional activity, have gone to another place, are for that very reason unrelated [to oneself], and are formless. And in that regard:
What is the sequence? What is the logical justification? || 19 ||
In this case, what sequence can there be for a progeny to obtain [results] from formless things that lack connection?
It is like a pillar becoming golden through a boon, without any coming or going of gold.
In that state, prosperity is achieved in an instant; how can it be described?
For injunctions and prohibitions flutter about there without any cause.

Furthermore, how and by what logic can that same prosperity be attributed even to a pillar made of stone and the like, where— without the coming and going of gods, sages, or other superior beings for the sake of acquiring gold— a golden pillar is produced in an instant? It would be without cause, since it is insentient and thus lacks a cause in the form of the accomplishment of a purpose.

What is the purpose of the scriptures of injunctions and prohibitions—which, though established through their prevalence in the world among those who act and proceed according to them, remain unestablished for others due to their non-performance? || 21 ||
Tell me, what is the purpose of [this discussion] regarding both those things that have taken root and those that have not?
Previously the world was non-existent (asat), and immediately thereafter it became existent (sat). (22)

Likewise, how can there be mutual consistency among such scriptural passages as: "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent; from that, the existent was born"; "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent"; "In the beginning, my dear, this was the existent alone, one only without a second"; and "Neither non-existence nor existence existed then"? 22.
"O Brahman, how is the consistency of this Vedic revelation to be explained?
And how, O great sage, could this [universe] become Brahmā? (23)
Furthermore, at the beginning of creation, how could this Brahmā Hiraṇyagarbha come into being from empty space?
If it were argued that space possesses such power, then why is it that no other Brahmā is produced everywhere from all things of such power that are distinct in every location? (23)
Why then are all medicinal herbs, or indeed all objects, not produced from such a sky, or why do they not abide within it? (24)

Furthermore, explain how medicinal plants possess their respective natures of producing seeds and so forth from their own predecessors, while others, such as fire, possess natures such as heat—how is that? (24)
O Lord of Sages, tell me according to your realization: what are the natures of life for a man and of death, [the former] being a friend and the latter an enemy? (25)

Furthermore, for a single person, life and death are simultaneously sought by a friend and an enemy respectively; when one dies at a field such as Prayāga that grants all desires, having made a request at the time of death, then—
due to the persistence of desire-vasanās both at the moment of death and thereafter— it is like the expression "he sleeps with his mouth open," referring to the subsequent states.
How can the use of the suffix *ktvā* [denoting priority] be justified by imagining that death occurs prior [to the other action]? How is that established? (25)

How can it be said that what is sought by dying in a sacred field such as Prayāga will be attained through the fruits of meditating with the thought, "May I become the imperishable full moon in the sky"? (26)

Furthermore, by the power of the inevitable manifestation [of the result] for many meditating worshippers who, with the desire "May I become the full moon in the sky," have practiced according to the injunctions for meditation that bring about the state of being the moon;
Why does the sky not simultaneously become possessed of a thousand moons—endowed with the fruits of the lunar state attained at the same time as the accumulated [karmas]? || 26 ||

Is the sky not filled with thousands of moons by those who have attained them simultaneously? Furthermore, how could a single woman be meditated upon in succession by hundreds of thousands of meditators? (27)
They obtained the fruit of meditation at the same time as their wifehood; whether virtuous or unvirtuous, she remained in her husband's house, supreme through her asceticism.
And how did they all come to have a single wife? And how was she situated as one woman in their separate houses in different lands?

Furthermore, how did she become a supreme ascetic through her own penance, yet through the individual penances of each of them, become both a virtuous wife and, due to being enjoyed by many, an unchaste woman? || 28 ||
And how was their wife so accomplished, O Great Sage? How did that king depart from his home for the seven continents until the end of the kalpa? (29)

It is also contradictory [to claim] that "I shall remain as a king within my home for the duration of an eon across the seven continents, without ever leaving the house even while not departing from it. Wherever something is accomplished through a boon or a curse, where does the status of being a "boon" reside if it is to be experienced only inside one's house? The meaning is: how can this be logically established? || 29 ||
Where does the end reside for the status of being a boon-granter through boons and curses, and for acts such as giving, righteousness, austerity, and rites for the deceased? (30)

Furthermore, if the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) of acts such as giving, dharma, and austerity, or funeral rites (*śrāddha*) for the deceased, were to arise at the very location where the action occurred, then how could those remaining here obtain the fruit in the next world, given that the place [of the original act] would be empty? Moreover, it must be said that the unseen merit produces a positive result by generating pleasure within the embodied body; yet, no such pleasure exists in the physical body located there [at the site of the act].
The meaning is that its existence is established. || 30 ||
For those who remain here and are formless, there exists the fruit of true merit through affection for the formed;
yet, no agent of worldly transaction exists here in either of the two worlds. (31)
If the disputant should say that the living self (*jīva*) is that which possesses that unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), and that where its experience occurs, there that [merit] exists—that is not so.

Because in both this world and the next, the embodied living self does not exist. Nor do the embodied bodies and so forth belonging to this place exist in another place or at another time; the meaning is that upon what basis could its fruit possibly arise?
O Sage, whether in another place or even after a long interval of time, the fruit of an action arises; yet that cannot occur without experience.
"How could this be so perfectly consistent?"—
cut through this multitude of doubts that has arisen within me with your cool and pure speech, just as the moon dispels the darkness of twilight with its radiance. (33)

"How can all these inconsistencies—such as these and others—be made consistent? O Lord, with your cool and pure speech, dispel this multitude of doubts at twilight, just as the moon dispels the gloom of the evening. 33.
By destroying doubt regarding the supreme reality, benefit for both worlds clearly arises;
therefore, grant me this here: for no one does association with the virtuous bear small fruit in this world. (34)

O Blessed One, because all doubts are destroyed through instruction regarding the supreme reality, the Supreme Self, that which is beneficial for both worlds—even the thousandfold fruit of contradictory [actions]—becomes clearly non-contradictory. Therefore, grant me the awakening to that supreme reality. But how can this great fruit be attained so suddenly?
I said there, "Excellent!"— the meaning being that for someone like me, even the meeting with a great soul such as you does not yield a small or insignificant result. || 34 ||
Thus ends the two hundred and sixth canto, titled "The Great Question," in the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa*, the *Vālmīki Dēvamanuṣyamokṣa Nirṇaya*.
Thus ends the two hundred and sixth chapter, titled "The Great Question," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The two hundred and seventh canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Listen, O King, as I shall explain this clearly to you.
By means of which all your doubts shall be completely rendered rootless. || 1 ||
Some questions here have been resolved in both sequential and reverse order;
furthermore, the noble-minded one will resolve others through three further chapters.

In this regard, he makes the following declaration—"Listen"—promising that by means of a single consciousness alone, because all consciousnesses [are subsumed therein] and all doubts are eliminated by cutting them off at the root, he will provide a general resolution to all questions:
"I shall explain this reality of the Self clearly and distinctly, like a myrobalan fruit in the palm of one's hand. (1)
Indeed, all entities in the world are always of the nature of non-existence;
yet they are also always of the nature of existence, because they persist exactly as they are perceived. (2)

In this regard, he states "all" [in verse 2], meaning that for those who follow self-validating self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) in establishing the reality of objects, no doubt whatsoever can arise concerning anything. The intended sense is that whether there is the cognition "this exists" or "this does not exist," in both cases, the Blessed Lady of Consciousness alone provides the support for both such forms. || 2 ||
O dear one, that consciousness wherein it is declared "this is thus" necessarily becomes that very thing—whether it be real or unreal. (3)

In whatever object there is a consciousness—whether determined that "this thing is blue," "yellow," "a jar," "a cloth," "it exists," "it does not exist," or "it is exactly thus"—O dear one, that object necessarily possesses that very form; whether that [form] be real or unreal, there is no doubt regarding it. This is the meaning. || 3 ||
Consciousness has such a nature that by it the body is manifested;
yet, in its own true essence, it remains one alone, and not as known by those who perceive it otherwise.
If one asks why that is so, he says "of this kind" (*īdṛk*), because consciousness has the nature of establishing an object exactly as it appears.
Thus, the question—"What could be the cause of the body for the experience of hell or heaven in the disembodied state?"—is resolved. He states:
by means of that body, the manifestation (*vidā*) and the unfolding (*vibhāvyate*) of that consciousness are perceived; the body is the self of consciousness.
And the phrase "and the nature of the body" means that contrariety is superimposed [upon it]. || 4 ||
The wise know this very body as such; from dreams and other states, a certain consciousness arises, yet there is no other nature of the body.

For this very reason, people know the body as "the knower" (*vit*) because it perceives in both dream and waking states; thus they experience the cognizer itself as being of such a nature. They understand that other consciousness, however, is a property of the cognizer and is not itself a cognizer. Therefore, the meaning is that only consciousness in the form of an error can constitute "bodiness," and there is no other kind of bodiness. || 5 ||
Just as this world appears as a manifestation of a dream experienced by one who has fallen asleep, so too does it shine here;
since there is an absence of all causes at the beginning of creation, what otherness could there be in this?
The first three questions should also be resolved in this same manner, with the intention that even the world is established solely through the power of consciousness;

thus he says: "relying," etc. At the beginning of creation, since all other causes are absent, the world must necessarily be relied upon as one who perceives a dream—hence it is called "the perception of a dream."
Thus, it is consciousness alone that shines forth. In this world, what otherness could there be, which would take the form of being contrary to a dream? None whatsoever.
Or rather, since the world is experienced solely through the nature of the inner self (pratyagātman) as "it exists" and "it shines," what otherness could there be? The meaning is: none whatsoever.
Thus, that very same stainless sensation which is designated as Brahman shines forth as this world; what, then, is the otherness of the world?
He says that very thing: "In this way" (evam) || 7 ||
Thus, the world’s existence is pure from beginning to end and immutable;
this has been experienced and declared by the worlds, the Vedas, and the great scriptures. (8)

The meaning is this: since it is the unchanging Brahman itself that exists in the form of the universe, we have experienced exactly this through the means of knowledge provided by the learned world, the Vedas, and the scriptures on the supreme self (adhyātma-śāstra); therefore, that alone has been cited, and nothing else. || 8 ||
Those fools who, like those in a single blind well, deny that which has been firmly established by the great-souled ones as the complete consciousness of all beings—[they are lost]. (9)

Those fools who, having rejected the fact that the world is eternally nothing but pure consciousness— as declared by the great-souled ones, established through firm experience, rooted in the consciousness of all beings and living creatures, and pervading everywhere as the very nature of existence— [deny this truth].

Those who take as their sole authority the mere experience of name-and-form (nāmarūpa) existing only in the present moment, and who have fallen into delusion—thinking that consciousness (saṃvit) does not exist eternally, but rather that the body alone is its cause, and thus it is an insentient quality of an insentient self—are merely madmen; this applies to the ignorant Naiyāyikas, Cārvākas, and others. This is the connection of the three [verses]. || 9 ||
Taking as their authority only the delusion that consists in the mere experience of the present, they have fallen into the error that consciousness is the cause of the body. (10)
Those ignorant ones are indeed like madmen; they are not fit for our discourse.
What conversation can there be between one who is sober and one who is intoxicated, both being of deluded intellect?
To the question "Why are they not suitable there?", he says: "akṣība... (verse 1).
That discourse by which all doubts are not destroyed, even for the wise—know that such a discourse to be nothing but the talk of fools throughout the three worlds. 12.
But that fool— the Cārvāka whose intellect is thus disposed—

who asserts that this phenomenal world has perception alone as its basis and authority, and that there is no means of knowledge other than perception, and therefore what is established by scripture and so forth should not be accepted; he, by that irrational and entirely contradictory statement, [is refuted].

Because his own speech is harsh to the ears of those possessing supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*) and its conduct is like that of a stone, all the wise have called this ignorant man "the frog in the well" (*kūpāndhadardura*). For, having abandoned the intellect that investigates what precedes and follows, he remains like a beast within the range of mere present perception through his own opinion; such is the connection between the two [statements]. || 12 ||
That fool says, "He is one who relies solely on direct perception"; therefore, by that statement devoid of logic, he acts like a stone.
He who speaks in contradiction to everything is called ignorant, like a frog in a well;
having abandoned the understanding of what precedes and follows, his mind is fixed only on the present. (14)
The Vedas, the worlds, and all these others, when questioned, declare this vision endowed with personal experience, so that all doubts may perish. (15)

Doubts are not destroyed by the arguments of the Cārvākas and others, because their assertions lack rational foundation due to their non-acceptance of means of valid cognition such as inference. However, the Vedas and other scriptures, when inquired about from the mouth of a Guru, are capable of accomplishing the goals of human life by cutting through all doubts; for they are endowed with one's own direct experience—this very vision which I have proclaimed.
He says "they say" and specifies "the Vedas"; "the worlds" refers to those people who know the truth. || 15 ||
"If consciousness itself were the body, why does a corpse not perceive?"—to one who holds such a view, this [following] is said here: "O fool! (16).
If the world, beginning with the body, is indeed the consciousness of the inner self (pratyagātman), then why does a corpse—a dead body—not perceive?
To that dull-witted person who harbors such a doubt and desires to hear, this is said: listen! (16)
This manifestation of the world is but an extended city of Brahmā’s creative imagination, just like the city seen in your dream. (17)
This world-form is the manifestation of Brahmā, who possesses the form of Brahman and the attire of Hiraṇyagarbha; it is a city of his volition, spread out and extensive. || 17 ||
All this is eternally nothing but the essence of pure consciousness, without interruption; you should have no delusion regarding this, just as one has none concerning a city in one's own dream.

In reality, that [city] is nothing but the continuous nature of pure consciousness; nevertheless, the meaning is that one should understand that the delusion of sentience found here in this city of dreams does not exist even in insentient things such as corpses. || 18 ||
In that state, you have the direct experience that the directions, the mountains, the earth and so forth, the cities and so forth—indeed everything—is the space consisting of consciousness. (19)
In that regard, when one investigates one's own experience within one's own dream, it is established by one's own experience. || 19 ||
The dense Brahman is the sky of consciousness; its city of volition is the Virāj.
Brahmā, consisting of pure consciousness, is said to be this very world.
Likewise, he states that the nature of consciousness (cinmayatva) should be recognized in the world as well, beginning with the word "saṃvit" (consciousness).
Brahmā is Hiraṇyagarbha; Virāṭ is the body of the cosmic egg. The meaning is that this very world is of such a nature, consisting solely of pure consciousness. || 20 ||
Just as whatever is conceived in the city of Brahmā’s mental construction is experienced exactly so, even so is it experienced in the city of your own mental construction.
Just as whatever is imagined in a city of one's imagination exists exactly in that way at that time, so too it is in the city of your own imagination.
