Therefore, just as these two— motion and non-motion— were fashioned by Brahmā through his consciousness for the governance of the body, so too did he experience them exactly in that way.

The meaning is this: since movement belongs to the body while it is alive and lack of movement belongs to it when dead, just as these two states—movement and non-movement—were ordained by Brahman in the form of Hiraṇyagarbha-consciousness, so too did he experience their existence; it was not otherwise. Therefore, there is no possibility of movement, which manifests consciousness, in a corpse. || 23 ||
At the conclusion of the great dissolution, creation proceeds once again;
however, due to the absence of all causes, no substance exists at that time. (24)

To resolve the objection that "the reasoning which renders a substance devoid of its constituent parts is inconsistent," he clarifies the underlying intention with the verse beginning "mahāpralaye" (half-verse 24).
Because the Lord of Creatures is liberated, memory does not arise;
therefore, this radiant Brahman alone shines as the world. (25)
[The opponent objects: "Surely the material substance fashioned by the previous Prajāpati will be employed here. To this he replies: "Because of his liberation" (*vimuktatvāt*).

The meaning is that since the former Lord of Creatures was liberated even before the previous dissolution, the world created by him underwent a dissolution without remainder; therefore, according to your own intention, even the instrumental causes such as the memory of that specific mode of creation do not exist.

[The opponent states his] position: "And this intention of yours is indeed favorable to the establishment of our own doctrine," he replies with the words "Brahmaiva" (It is Brahman alone). The meaning is that the world shines as Brahman itself, which is self-luminous light; there is no other world existing as a separate substance. || 25 ||
Therefore, the world, appearing as its own primordial self through Brahman by its own nature, is understood to be a city of mental construction— like space within space.

Clarifying this very point, he concludes with the words "therefore" (*tasmāt*). First, by Brahmā—that is, as the primordial Hiraṇyagarbha—the world appeared; the suffix *kta* is used here in the sense of a state (*bhāve*). Then, by him, the world was perceived as a city of his own volition (*saṃkalpa-nagara*). || 26 ||
Just as a city of imagination appears as pure consciousness alone,
so too does the world appear without a cause as the unfolding of pure consciousness alone.
Whether the body exists or not, wherever the sky of consciousness exists, there the self knows the world consisting of duality and non-duality. (28)
By this, he states that the question—"even in the absence of mother, father, and so forth"—is also resolved: "The body... (verse 28).
Therefore, just as one perceives a city in a dream or a city of one's own imagination, so does the sky of consciousness perceive the world after death. (29)
He states "therefore" (tasmāt) [in verse 29] to show that this same principle should be understood to apply even when perceiving the world after death.
The world appears as if composed of earth and other elements, though it is not so; just as this entire universe appeared so from the very beginning, so it remains even for one who has died.
From the beginning, from the first creation. || 30 ||
Just as for one who has awakened from sleep, space and time do not extend even an atom's breadth [in their perception],
so it is exactly the same for one who has departed to the other world.

Just as for one who has awakened—whether a knower of reality or one awakened from a dream—the space and time of the dream are not pervaded by the creation of the waking state even in the slightest degree, so too, for one who has reached the other world, the space and time of this world do not pervade that [other world].
This is the meaning. || 31 ||
Even though this world is clearly experienced by one who is awakened, it does not exist at all, just as there is no cause for anything in the sky. (32)
Thus, he says "this" [in verse 32] to show that even the world does not pervade the object of one who knows reality.
Just as this world appears radiant though it is non-existent to one who is unawakened,
so too does the void itself appear as a creation to one who has departed for the next world.
For one who is unawakened and sleeping, the sky is nothing but the sky of consciousness (cidvyoma). || 33 ||
To those who have departed for the next world, the sky itself— rich with the sun, the moon, the mountains, and the stars—
appears as if it were never before seen, yet it stretches out vast and wide as if it had existed before.
As in the case of what has occurred before, so in the case of what was previously established. || 34 ||
"Dead, I have been born again in the world of Yama; I am experiencing the results of my good and evil deeds"—thus the deceased person perceives an exceedingly dense delusion. (35)

"This very I, having died, has been reborn again as a denizen of hell; I have come to the world of Yama and there experience the results of my good and evil deeds"—such is the delusion [he experiences]. (35)
For those who disregard the means to liberation, this delusion does not subside;
through awakening and the absence of latent impressions, this delusion is pacified.
That delusion perishes entirely only through the practice of the means to liberation, and not otherwise; thus he says: "Liberation... (verse 36).
The consciousness of one who is unawakened is the latent impression of dharma and adharma;
that which appears as the void itself within the nature of the void is precisely what constitutes the existence of the world.

With the intention that this also favors the position of the believers (āstika-pakṣa), who maintain that dharma and adharma alone transform into the form of the world, he says: "Of the unawakened. [This] consciousness consists of the experience resulting from the performance of prescribed and prohibited actions. || 37 ||
The world, which is designated as Brahman, does not appear as having the nature of emptiness, nor does it appear as having a real nature of its own;
yet, through the power of non-recognition, it becomes a source of misfortune, while for one who has attained full recognition, it is of the nature of auspiciousness.

The nature of the world, though inherently empty in form, is neither of the nature of existence nor of non-existence; rather, it is consciousness alone, designated as Brahman, that shines as the nature of the world. And this [world], by virtue of ignorance, becomes a source of misfortune; however, for one who has fully realized it, it is of the nature of Śiva—the Self, the supreme auspiciousness, and unsurpassed bliss. This is the meaning. || 38 ||
Thus ends the two hundred and seventh chapter, titled "The Great Answer to the Question," in the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa*, the *Vālmīki Dēvamanuṣya Mānuṣa Nibandhana*.
Thus ends the two hundred and seventh chapter, titled "The Answer to the Great Question," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The two hundred and eighth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Just as good and evil arise for living beings in the context of domestic life, [so it is with the world].
Listen to this: though they are unconnected, non-obstructive, and situated at a distance. || 1 ||
Just as one obtains the fruit of progeny elsewhere through efforts made in a distant land,
such is described here as the will of the Creator.

He promises to state the answer to the question: "How can people obtain results here from things that are formless, unconnected, and located in distant lands, even though they do not intend them?"—with the words "The auspicious and the inauspicious," etc., referring to those things which are non-obstructive and formless. (1)
This world exists as a city of Brahmā’s mental construction;
that which is perceived through the perception of objects is Brahman alone, when seen through the realization of Brahman. (2)

Since Brahman alone, through the perception of the visible world arising from ignorance, becomes the visible world, and through the realization of Brahman becomes Brahman itself, it follows that this universe is a city of Brahma’s imagination; thus much has been established. || 2 ||
Whatever is conceived in the city of one's imagination, and however it is conceived,
that very thing is experienced at that time as being constructed in exactly that manner.
He states what follows from that: "Whatever... (verse 3).
Thus, when this house has come into being, this progeny is accomplished;
thus, when the world is endowed with such volitions, it becomes fully so.

To this he replies with "evam" (thus): just as this progeny of yours has come to be in accordance with your own volition within this house consisting of your will, so too in the world—which is brought forth by the volition of Brahman—this progeny likewise exists solely in accordance with the volition of Brahman; such is the meaning. || 4 ||
In this city of your own volition, whatever exists remains exactly as it is;
for indeed, you perceive whatever you conceive in whatever manner.
He states that very point clearly: "This," etc. (verse 5).
Just as pure consciousness is attained through both a boon and a curse,
so too does that consciousness come to be conceived as being nothing other than Brahman.

As for the fact that a difference from a city of our own imagination is experienced in this world, it should be understood as being like [the effects of] the fulfillment of a boon or a curse through volition; with this intention, he says: "Just as..."—meaning that the consciousness of sages, purified by the practice of restraints (yama), observances (niyama), and so forth, becomes capable of worldly transaction through boons and curses.

The meaning is that the consciousness of Brahmā is likewise of the same nature. Whatever occurs through boons or curses is also understood to belong to Brahmā alone; for it is by the ascetic Brahmā’s own power that boons and curses are made effective, according to the conception "let [these] be accomplished. Thus, the meaning is that this is indeed the truth-wielding volition (satya-saṃkalpa) of Brahmā. || 6 ||
Through the injunctions and prohibitions regarding progeny, by means of a single fixed rule, one obtains the very same fruit; such is the conception of the Brāhma [marriage]. (7)

The meaning is that this is a form of resolve (*saṃkalpa*) wherein one determines that, between the merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) made known by the scriptures of injunctions and prohibitions regarding worldly affairs, whatever fruit one obtains through a single, fixed state of commitment is indeed of the nature of Brahman alone. || 7 ||
Because embodied beings in this world are not perceived [in their ultimate reality], it is understood that the world was previously non-existent; yet it is perceived as being real. (8)
O dear one, this world exists solely by the power of the volition of Brahman, whose nature is consciousness;
the opening and closing of that consciousness are what constitute dissolution and emergence.

He states that even the appearance for a short time of this unreal world as something existent is solely due to the will of Brahman—beginning with the words "cidrūpa" (of the nature of consciousness). O dear one, this is the world. || 9 ||
The king said:
"What is not perceived first, and what is perceived later?
This world, with its moving form, shines with the undertaking of stable foundations. (10)
If the world exists by virtue of Brahman’s volition (*saṃkalpa*), then why was it not perceived previously during deep sleep or cosmic dissolution?

And for what purpose is it perceived afterwards at the time of waking and creation—this world, which has a moving body, is constantly undergoing transformation, yet appears as if it were established in a state of perfect stability and shines so brightly; what is the meaning of this, and how is it so? || 10 ||

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Within this city of volition situated in the space of consciousness, such is the nature of existence— that having come into being, it ceases to exist and then arises again in an instant.

He gives the answer that such is the very nature of this illusory [world] with the words "In this... (asmin). Since it exists in the states of creation and dream-waking, but does not exist at all during dissolution, deep sleep, and liberation, this state is indeed its inherent nature. || 11 ||

Indeed, these creations, appearing as both existent and non-existent, manifest within the conscious self like the imaginary cities of children or like the optical illusion of hair-tufts seen in the sky. (12)

Alternatively, its being such [i.e., unreal] is due to the determination of its nature as being either existent or non-existent, based on observing the rule that it persists only for the duration of the delusion of conceptualization within the city of a child's imagination and so forth; thus he says: "bāla... (verse 12).
Having constructed a city of conceptualization, you destroy it in that very instant;
for such is your own nature, according to the power of your own cognition as distinct from another.
He states that its nature is such because the Creator of the world also conceives of its dissolution, by saying "Thou.
Just as this is Thy own nature by virtue of another consciousness, by virtue of the conception of its dissolution, and by virtue of the conception of other forms,
so too is the stainless manifestation of the nature of that Brahman within the city of the conception of the space of consciousness (*cidvyoma*).
The subsequent [inference] is by means of positive concomitance (anvaya). || 13 ||
Know that the rising and sinking within the city of the imagination of the sky of consciousness is its own natural radiance, and likewise, it is pure.
But the sky of the three worlds is indeed the beginningless and endless void that is solid consciousness;
therefore, whatever it now performs or perceives, it is that very [consciousness] which does so.
Therefore, since the sky of the three worlds is merely the density of consciousness (saṃviddhanamātra), beginningless and endless, being the very space of Brahman; for that reason,
whatever this Supreme Lord perceives and whatever He creates—
all that occurs even across hundreds of leagues and through many ages by the power of His unobstructed and true resolve.

The meaning is that virtuous and sinful actions, though separated [by time], produce their effects—such as the enjoyment of heaven, hell, and sovereignty—in the next world and other realms, even when those states are present nearby. || 15 ||
Although this [consciousness] is unobstructed even across hundreds of yojanas and through eons,
it performs its functions like a dream, as if occurring in the present.
Indeed, that single Self which is eternally unobstructed both in another country and even in another world—what is there that it does not perceive? (17)

Even when separated by external space and time, that single Self which is the unobscured substratum for the superimposition of both the action and its fruit—since both are always in close proximity there—what indeed is that fruit of action which that living being does not perceive? The meaning is that it perceives everything. || 17 ||
Just as in a gem there occurs a transformation consisting of rising and sinking within its own radiance, so too does it occur for the worlds within the gem of consciousness.

Just as in a gem, its own radiance alone is experienced through the emergence and submergence of various specific beauties, so too in the gem of consciousness (cinmaṇi), the revolution of its own radiance—the cycle of the creation and dissolution of worlds, consisting of the manifold experiences of the fruits of various karmas—is what is meant by "revolution" (parāvarta). This is the meaning. || 18 ||
The purpose of injunctions and prohibitions is the maintenance of the world;
that very [purpose], being rooted in consciousness, remains the bestower of fruits even after death. (19)

He states that it is the very constitution of the world (*lokasaṃsthā*)—which renders the scriptures of injunctions and prohibitions effective—that, because it is firmly rooted in Brahman, postulates a fruit even for actions performed at a distance: "Of the injunctions...
[The word] "having died" (*pretya*) means having gone to the next world; the phrase "of one who remains" (*sthitasya*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. || 19 ||
Never does it set, nor does it ever rise;
Brahman, the manifestation of the consciousness of Brahman, is eternally established within the Self. (20)

In reality, however, birth and death do not exist for the Self at all; rather, their conceptualization occurs through delusion, just as one might falsely imagine them in relation to one's own self. Thus he says: "Never... (20).
Just as the city of conceptualization, due to the relationship between the seer and the seen, appears by itself like the world, so too is it said to have been "born. (21)
Likewise, that which is "born" is called birth; it is designated by speech, but not in reality—this is the meaning. || 21 ||
When, having withdrawn its manifestation from its own nature, it abides within itself as the single essence of the space of Brahman-consciousness, it is likewise called "peaceful."
Likewise, death too is merely the withdrawal of the delusory manifestation of the previous body and so forth, and nothing else; thus he says, "When...
The meaning is that the living being (jīva), when stilled, is said to be dead. || 22 ||
The nature of that which shines and does not shine is pure and imperishable;
just as these two—motion and stillness—are not other than the self of the wind.
And he says—“kacana” (shining)—that the shining and non-shining of the forms of the visible are indeed the very nature of consciousness as conditioned by ignorance. || 23 ||
"May these moments, which destroy old age and death, exist here individually, just as they exist in the city of your imagination. (24)

Even the extraordinary powers of gems, mantras, and medicinal herbs arise as such because they possess the very nature of Brahman’s true resolve (satya-saṃkalpa); thus he says with an illustration in two verses beginning with "jara... (24).
In this city of Brahmā’s volition, the inherent natures of all medicinal herbs, objects, and everything else throughout the three worlds have likewise arisen. (25)

O King, the self-conceiving agent himself does not conceive even a single blade of grass within the city of his own imagination; rather, like a child with toys, he fashions one straw after another as objects of play. (26)
In that case, is God imagined as one who forms volitions for the various distinctions of power, effects, and so forth, at every moment and for every object?

No; he says: "not as a volitional agent. God is not imagined as a volitional agent for every object at every moment; rather, like a child [creating] toys or specific mechanical devices, He does so all at once.
It conceives this: "Let it be of such a kind, let it perform such an action, and let that which is of such a kind arise in this manner.
By its very own power, it fashions each preceding blade of grass into each succeeding blade of grass through the sequence of seed, sprout, and so forth.
This is clearly its own inherent nature as this mass of consciousness.
Whatever he conceives of, his limbs [manifest] there instantly.

Instantly, in a mere moment, whatever he conceives, those various objects—possessing real constituent parts, including distinctions such as potentiality and actualized effect—as well as series of effects (indicated by the word "api"), are accomplished from that single act of volition alone; this is the inherent nature of the mass of consciousness. || 27 ||
They appear as having diverse natures through their own essence which is consciousness;
yet, though they abide in various forms and inherent characteristics, they remain possessed of a single core.

Those objects constructed by conceptualization, although existing as manifold in nature through their own individual essences, nevertheless shine forth as having the single essence of consciousness within the manifesting nature [of the Self]. Thus, although they possess various forms by their own nature, they remain as a single core of Being (sat). || 28 ||

It is said that within each [of these] there exists, in the self which is pure Brahman-consciousness, that [consciousness] which is the soul of all; in whatever manner it resides therein, in that very manner it shines forth.

In that regard, within each of those objects, there exists the state of Brahman as pure consciousness within its own self; for that very consciousness is the soul of all, meaning that it appears in whatever manner it exists, rather than otherwise. || 29 ||
Without beginning, middle, or end, possessing infinite vigor, it is neither something nor nothing, and though existent, it is unreal;
as it abides in whatever place, so is its nature there, being the source of all selves within the entire range of beings, from grass and such down to the elements.

Thus, Brahman—which is without beginning, middle, or end, possesses infinite vigor, and has unfathomable power—exists as both something and nothing; though unreal, it exists as real. According to the Śruti: "The real and the unreal became the Real.
Since it becomes the self of all, it is the "all-self" (*sarvātmabhū*); therefore, wherever among beings—that is, among living creatures and even among the species of grass and so forth—it resides.
The meaning is that whatever object is established as having a certain nature and a certain essence, it remains there having itself become that very essence. || 30 ||

Thus ends the two hundred and eighth chapter, titled "The Great Question and Liberation," in the *Deva-muni-nirvāṇa-upadeśa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, according to the tradition of the Ṛṣis.
Thus ends the two hundred and eighth chapter, titled "The Resolution of Great Questions," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The two hundred and ninth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
For a single man, life is [the gift] of a friend, and death is [the gift] of an enemy.
Listen now to this regarding that which is sought by dying at a sacred field such as Prayāga.
When actions with contradictory results are encountered simultaneously,
their compatibility and efficacy are established here through reasoning.
Having recited the very verse of the question for the purpose of restating it, he causes [the answer] to be heard by means of an exchange of its syllables: "Of one... (1).
For every field and for all objects, he ordained their respective fruits in his own city of creative will during the creation by Brahmā.

Regarding that qualified person who is about to be described, the fruit of all things— beginning with the field (kṣetra)— was ordained by Brahmā and established through his volition at the time of the original creation.
In whatever field and for whatever purpose merit is performed, if that field is treated accordingly by the one who employs it, then [the merit] rises from that expiation.

If there exists for that person who is eligible according to the scriptures the merit consisting of bathing, giving, austerity, sacrifice, and so forth, performed in that city of mental construction— namely, in sacred fields such as Prayāga which grant all desires for the sake of accomplishing the desired object of whichever authority it may be— and likewise the body refined by those two, then for him...

The meaning is that, having determined that "from this expiation (niṣkṛti) of the person, my desired fruit will certainly come to pass," the fruit wished for by him indeed rises up and manifests from such acts as dying at Prayāga.
Therefore, whether it be a portion or the entirety of that great sin,
that merit— which is of the nature of the power of consciousness— subsides after having circulated through the body.
Let it be so for one who has performed meritorious deeds; but what does the merit arising from death at Prayāga and other such places do for a sinner who possesses faith?

To this he says: "That" (tat). From that—namely, from death at Prayāga and so forth—there arises [merit] which neutralizes a single portion of all the sin, even the entire mass of great sins such as the killing of a Brāhmaṇa.
The meaning is that, by wandering according to the relative greatness of sacred fields (*kṣetra*) and thereby casting off [impurity], one becomes tranquil oneself;
for there is the scriptural statement: "By means of dharma, one dispels evil," and so forth. || 4 ||
If the evil of those to be converted is slight, yet the quality of the field is superior, then,
having destroyed that evil, the very name of that field resounds triumphantly.

If the sin of the person to be disciplined—the one to be instructed—is small, and the merit acquired from the field [of action] is greater, then, having destroyed that sin entirely, it leaps toward the fruit proclaimed by the Śrutis and other scriptures through that word. The meaning is that even a certain desirable fruit is indeed accomplished. However, where [the sin of] the person to be disciplined...

The person to be disciplined possesses sin equal in strength to the merit acquired through his field [of action]; because of this equality of strength, for the sake of experiencing both that merit and this sin—which cannot be removed by that merit alone—two bodies manifest, and within them two appearances of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*), consisting of illusory manifestations, shine forth. (5)
O Lord of the Earth, by virtue of that field-quality,
two bodies of this disciple shine forth perfectly within his own consciousness, consisting of the nature of creative intuition.
Thus, the great fruit of such evils and merits is exactly as it is fashioned by the volition of Brahmā; it is precisely so and not otherwise.
The meaning is that whatever is fashioned by the volition of Brahman, each thing remains established exactly in that manner. || 7 ||
This element of consciousness is called Brahman; it is the lotus-born Brahmā, the "I," and so forth.
In whatever manner it exists, that very thing is its conceptualization as the world.
Regarding the phrase "constructed by the volition of Brahman" (*brahmasaṃkalpakacitam*), what is that Brahman, or how is the world constructed by its volition? To this he says:
[The meaning is] that within the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the individual (*vyaṣṭi*) and the collective (*samaṣṭi*), there is His volition; the world also exists in that very manner. || 8 ||
The very intuition of the disciple arises in such a manner through the merit of the field, just as that [intuition] of the Buddha arises for one who is free from error. (9)

The element (*dhātu*) arises as a mere manifestation (*pratibhā*), like a dream, consisting of the experience of its fruit, in accordance with the intention of the one to be trained (*vineya*) and in accordance with the merit acquired in that field; just as a manifestation of hell and so forth arises for one who possesses sin, which is the opposite of merit. || 9 ||
Today I am alone; I am dead, while these are my kinsmen.
They weep, whereas I have reached the other world all by myself. (10)
He describes and demonstrates what kind of various reflections arise: "By my own self alone," and so forth. "Today I alone am dead by my own self;
these relatives of mine are all alive, and they weep for my sake. (10)
At that very place, at that very time, and in that very manner, his perception regarding his kinsmen was exactly like that [of the others],
as if he too were one whose elements were agitated.

It should be understood that even for his kinsmen, the death of this person— along with all its associated manifestations such as weeping, the removal of the corpse, the journey to the cremation ground, and the cremation— is merely a corresponding mental representation (*pratibhā*), just like the experience of those whose bodily constituents (*dhātu*) are disturbed, such as men whose wind, bile, and other elements are agitated by a derangement of the humors (*sannipāta*).
The form "tādṛśāḥ" is derived from the word ending in the suffix *kaj*, with the feminine suffix *āp* added according to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*). || 11 ||

Even the destinies of men, though they appear fixed, may become otherwise through the power of mental construction, whether by their own extremely intense merits or sins, or when observed by great souls. (12)

But when his merits or sins are extremely intense, then— whether he is being looked upon by those great beings who are themselves agitated by their own [karma] with a view toward restraint or favor, or whether he is observed by other agitated beings— the results, such as the body and so forth, exist or come to be through the power of the intellect's creative ideation (cit-kalanā), whether they are perceptible to others or otherwise imperceptible; this is the meaning.
They too behold him dead, unconscious and become a corpse;
they weep for him and cast him into the fire along with his kinsmen. (13)
Those people also sometimes see that disciple who has died due to extremely intense merits or demerits. || 13 ||
That person to be converted perceives himself as being free from old age and death, established in a state that is not suffering, by means of another form of consciousness. (14)

"The life of one man is [the result] of a friend's [merit], and his death [the result] of an enemy's; since he has died and attained [his goal] at a sacred field such as Prayāga, how can this be explained?"—this question is answered with the words beginning "vineya. The word *dehinā* (by the embodied one) should be split as *ajarāmaraṇam* (without old age or death). That single person, who is to be guided (*vineya*) by the actions of both the friend and the enemy, is [distinguished] from the other.
Just as requested by a friend who is an embodied being consisting of the nature of affection, he knows himself to be free from suffering, undecaying, and immortal. || 14 ||
With his body remaining as it was, he perceives the duration of his life;
however, death is perceived through another invisible form, impelled by the merit of the sacred field.

He asks: "Is it by another body? and answers: "No, as he stands [in this very body]. Then he asks: "In that case, how is the fulfillment of the desire of one who hates him? To this he replies: "Death. He perceives death through another body that is invisible to friends and kinsmen; he is impelled by an enemy who has performed meritorious deeds conducive to the death of the foe at a sacred site (kṣetra) such as Prayāga.
The meaning is: having been impelled toward death by force. || 15 ||
A turbid consciousness is perceived in an instant by a consciousness that is void [of objectivity];
for there is no effort for one whose limbs are already armored in piercing that which is unarmored. (16)

In that regard, one who knows how to discipline others and is devoid of counter-measures against the malevolent rites (*abhicāra*) performed by enemies experiences and undergoes death and so forth at that very moment, at that very instant. For suffering arises from the piercing of an enemy with armor and weapons when his body is armored, or with arrows, swords, and the like when his body is unarmored and trusting. || 16 ||
His kinsmen likewise behold him as one who has attained immortality;
thus he obtains both life and death as equal.
These three worlds are merely an illusion, initiated by that which is non-obstructive;
for what indeed can be a reversal of illusion within an illusion? (18)
With the intention that all contradictory questions are to be understood as resolved by this very same principle, he says: "This...
What indeed is a reversal of delusion? For what other delusion, even one contrary to a single delusion, is not possible?
The meaning is that even a thousand contradictions are seen to coexist in states such as dreams and derangements of the humors (*sannipāta*). || 18 ||

The delusion that is experienced in the cities of one’s imagination and dreams is greater than that which is experienced in the waking state; it is not less. (19) (Note: The reading *tato'dhiko 'yaṃ* is required here, though some manuscripts read *tato'dhikeyaṃ na nyūnā jāgrad iti*.)
He says that very thing: "saṃkalpa... (verse 19).
The King said:
O Brahman, how are dharma and adharma the cause of the consciousness of the body? And how does that which is formless alone attain the state of having two bodies? (20)

Having refined the very question—"Dharma and adharma are both formless"—in accordance with the requirements of the ongoing narrative, the king asks again: "Regarding dharma and adharma, in their state as formless—that is, in the absence of having a physical form—how do they attain a 'two-bodiedness,' that is, the state of possessing a second body? (20)
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
O high-minded one, in this world of Brahmā, which is like a city of imagination,
what indeed is not possible— whether it be real or even inconsistent?

With the intention that the Lord, whose resolve is truth, is capable of bringing even the formless into a state of form, he gives the reply: "In the city of his imagination" (saṃkalpanagare). || 21 ||
Just as that which cannot exist here in a city of one’s own imagination does not exist at all, so too, what could possibly exist within this conceptualization of Brahman? (22)
In both a dream and a city of one's imagination, a single thing attains the status of a multitude; likewise, in a dream, the one consciousness itself assumes the form of an army.
Thousands become one; thus, that very state is deep sleep (suṣuptaka).
Otherwise, there is the experience and recollection of the army of dreams and mental constructs.

That [dream army] becomes a single deep sleep through the dream-senya itself; the meaning is that it is established by universal experience that, when there is a memory of an army experienced through a dream-construct, it appears as a single form in its collective aspect, and by the conceptualization "that" in place of "this," there occurs an altered experience. || 24 ||
Who has not experienced this within this world, which consists of experience and is nothing but the space of consciousness, through the cities of one’s imagination and dreams? (25)
Therefore, within this world-soul, which is a mental construction of consciousness and space, what indeed is not possible, or what indeed is even possible? (26)
He concludes: "Therefore," [as stated in verse 26].
In this very way, this delusion appears as consisting of light and space;
herein there is nothing whatsoever—neither existent nor non-existent, nor even a mere "something" here.
Or rather, "na vā" means "not even slightly existent," that is to say, neither existent nor non-existent. || 27 ||

Whatever is experienced exactly as it is, that is so for the seer of reality; for one who is awakened in this regard, what else could there be? He alone is the limb [of realization]—enough of this! (28)
For one who is awakened, what indeed could be improper here? This is the implied sense. || 28 ||
If this dharma were ordained here [on earth], then mountains of nectar would exist in heaven;
yet, despite such a resolve, why did he not obtain those mountains here? (29)

He says "iha cet" (if here) to show that even people who practice dharma and adharma attain only those very heavens corresponding to the specific determinations established by the scriptures for each. Furthermore, the gods are immortal,
and there exist in heaven mountains filled with pools of cascading nectar, fruits, flowers, and so forth, which serve as their objects of enjoyment.
The meaning is: having understood this from the scriptures and formed a resolve accordingly, why does he not experience his own self upon reaching such mountains after going there? || 29 ||
"In this world, whatever action is performed is experienced in the next;
therefore, in this city of mental construction (saṃkalpapura), everything is entirely inconsistent."

But if your intellect holds that [the world] is inconsistent because it is false, then this world—in which there is the performance of dharma and so forth here, by means of which there is the next world and therein enjoyment—all this entire universe would indeed be inconsistent; thus he says: "In this [world]. That is, in this world. || 30 ||

If there were any entity whatsoever that was perfectly stable, it would become an object of perception; this is the universal rule. However, because they consist of consciousness, they remain established in their own respective natures.

If there were any entity in the world, such as the elements or the worlds, that were perfectly stable and real, then this contradiction would be visible; in that case, this entire principle—"this is consistent" and "this is inconsistent"—would remain unimpeded. However, because every observer is consciousness itself, what appears as the object of vision is nothing but one's own respective mental construction.
The meaning is "in reality. || 31 ||
Thus has this principle been stated; from that, experience is established in the perfected ones, because the worlds are the volition of consciousness by virtue of its nature as Brahman.

Thus, this very principle for avoiding inconsistency—namely, that experience conforms to all experience even within conceptual constructions established through dreams and volitions—should also be applied to the worlds themselves; for even the worlds are nothing but the volition of consciousness (cit) which abides as the very nature of Brahman. || 32 ||
Just as there is nothing impossible within the city of your own imagination,
so too there is nothing impossible within the creative resolve (saṃkalpa) of Brahmā regarding all things.
He says that very thing: "of you," etc. (33).
In whatever way something is conceptualized therein, it exists exactly as far as that conceptualization extends;
for it exists by its own nature in that very manner, because it possesses that particular configuration.
Whatever has been conceived therein within that Brahma-intention, exists by its very nature as possessing such a configuration. || 34 ||
Therefore, in this case, no confusion arises from mere observation;
the goal is not achieved otherwise than through another effort of consciousness.

Consequently, precisely because of the restrictive nature of such an arrangement, the perception of all objects by the organs of cognition proceeds with perfect non-contradiction; furthermore, no confusion arises in the functioning of the organs of action. An object whose specific arrangement has been established by the effort of one consciousness cannot be altered by the effort of another consciousness.
And it does not exist. The particle *tu* is used in the sense of *ca* (and). || 35 ||
Just as the world exists as it appears within the unceasing volition that lasts until the end of the kalpa,
so too shall another [world] arise through another form of volition.

Just as it appeared within the unborn creative resolve from the beginning of the kalpa until the dissolution, so too does it remain; furthermore, after the dissolution, there is yet another cosmic egg.
Consisting of volition itself, it shines forth by its own power as the world in every kalpa,
just as a city in a dream appears within the dream-consciousness of each individual living being.
There is nothing whatsoever that cannot arise from this body of the city of volition, for it is of the nature of consciousness;
since there is nothing other than the primordial and supreme essence of the Shaker, know, O dear one, that the entire universe is indeed Brahman.

The meaning is this: regarding this world, whose body is the city of mental construction (saṃkalpa), whatever you think cannot possibly exist—that does not exist; rather, everything is indeed possible, and that [world] is none other than us, the conscious self (cidātman) who imagines it. For that reason, know the world to be Brahman alone. || 38 ||

Thus ends the two hundred and ninth chapter, titled "The Vision of the Experience of the Existence of All," in the *Mokṣopāya* section of the *Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa*, within the *Vāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa*, a work of the Sage. 209.

Thus ends the two hundred and ninth chapter, titled "The Vision of the Experience of the Existence of All," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The two hundred and tenth canto. Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
When the fruit, appearing as the waning moon, was attained by hundreds of meditators in the sky, [the world] became like the void.
Listen to this narration, which is not like the hundred full moons.
Herein is set forth the resolution of Vasiṣṭha’s questions,
as well as the state of the body and the entire universe as being nothing but Brahman when viewed with right vision.

"In this sky, is there not a thousand moons, equal in time to the fruits attained by one who meditates on the inexhaustible full moon?"—this question is answered therein first with the verse beginning "phale" (the fruit), and so forth. // 1 //
Those who meditate upon the lunar orb have attained what is to be attained and are well-established;
they have not merely reached this expanse of the sky, nor have they simply resorted to this moon.

Those who meditate upon the orb of the true moon with the sense of "I" (ahaṃbhāva) become firmly established through long-term meditation by forgetting all other states; thus, by the logic of the moon (aindavanyāya), they have indeed attained the state of the moon.
Nevertheless, they have not reached this vault of the sky, nor have they resorted to this hare-marked moon—meaning, they have not actually entered it.
Tell me, how can another person ever reach the city of someone else’s imagination?
The attainment of the objects within that city of imagination belongs only to its creator, the living being himself, and not to anyone else.

To the question "Why is it not attained there?", he says: "kveva" (where indeed?). Where has this been seen—that one person attains the city imagined by another—such that it could be cited as an analogy for the present case? That [attainment] is observed only in the case of the living being who is the imaginer (*saṃkalpayitṛ*), namely in that very soul, and not in another, different soul. || 3 ||
Established within their own respective creations born of individual volition,
they shine like moons there, devoid of any waning of their digits.
To the question "Where, then, are they situated?", he says: "Separately" (pṛthak). || 4 ||
Having meditated, "I shall enter into this very moon," one who has abandoned the internal self, the intellect, and pleasure enters into this very moon.
"I shall enter the moon, endowed with the bliss of the lunar orb"—by meditating thus, one becomes a partaker of such bliss; this is the certain conclusion.

"Why did they all not enter this very moon with such ease? To this he replies: "I... The point is that they did not meditate in that manner; rather, in accordance with your question, they meditated with the desire, "May I become the imperishable full moon in the sky. || 6 ||
If one possesses firm conviction, then consciousness, which is imperishable by nature, connects with an object in such a way that it experiences that very object exactly as it is. || 7 ||
To the question, "Why does a different result not arise from meditating on something other than what it is? he says: "Just as" (yathā).

The meaning is that in whatever way this [person] contemplates his own nature—that is, meditates upon it with firm resolve—the immutable witness-consciousness experiences that very nature exactly so, and not otherwise. || 7 ||
Just as the state of being the moon appears individually to every meditator through their own mental construction,
even so the attainment of a woman is inherently conceptual.

Furthermore, he extends this [principle] by saying "as" (*yathā*), indicating that even the question—"How can one woman be meditated upon sequentially by hundreds of thousands of meditators as their wife at the same time?"—is to be resolved by this very logic. "Inherently" (*svataḥ*) means belonging to oneself, established through conceptualization (*kalpanāsiddha*). || 8 ||
That which appears as the meditator within meditation has become a virtuous wife;
the experience of that mental construction resides within their own being.

Whether she be virtuous or unvirtuous, as long as she remains in her husband’s house, she is supreme through her austerity; he states that this very same resolution applies even to the portion of the question, beginning with the word "ya" (she). [She is] in the Witness-self, which consists of pure being and is conditioned by the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa). || 9 ||
The living being, though not having stepped out from his home, remains as the master of the seven continents;
yet even for him, that kingdom is merely imaginary, existing within his own palace in the sky.
The king departed from his home with all his ornaments for the seven continents; thus he also resolved this question, saying:
"All this, from the birth of the first knower, is merely a mental construction (kalpanāmātra).
It is empty, unimpeded, and peaceful—otherwise, what else could exist even within those [seven continents]? (11)

The meaning is this: when even this entire world visible to us and others is merely a mental construction of Hiraṇyagarbha—the primordial being born of knowledge and possessed of innate omniscience—then what else could there be that is different or otherwise real within those worlds constructed by worshippers, such that there would be any inconsistency? || 11 ||
Listen as this is described: that which is the embodied fruit in the next world of formless acts such as charity, rites for the deceased, austerity, and recitation. 12.

Having restated the question—"Is there any embodied fruit after death for acts performed while residing here, such as charity, religious duties, austerity, and funeral rites (aurdhvadehika), which are themselves formless?"—he undertakes to state the resolution of that question with the verse beginning "dāna... (charity...).
Those whose intellects are marked by generosity and other virtues perceive the fruit in the next world as being like a dream;
through the conceptualization of the form of consciousness, they see that which is formless yet appears to have form, unborn.
For it is consciousness itself that is conceptualized as having the form of a physical body. || 13 ||
Furthermore, this [consciousness] consists of the nature of feeling and non-feeling, as well as vibration and non-vibration;
yet, upon the cessation of that delusion regarding this pure consciousness, it is the peaceful and stainless self.

Through the agreeable sense organs, there arises a delusion in the form of experiencing sensations; by means of that delusion, for the sake of attaining objects, that pure consciousness (cinmātra), together with the mind and the organs of action, becomes characterized by vibration and non-vibration. But upon the cessation of that delusion, it remains as the stainless, peaceful Self alone. || 14 ||
"By giving from this world, one obtains the highest [reward] there;
since it is of the nature of volition, O wise ones, why is that not perceived? (15)

The remainder of the sentence is: "The sages say that by means of this gift performed here in this world, that particular fruit—which consists of the appearance of consciousness and has the nature of a mere reflection of consciousness—is taken up and brought forth in the next world, the other world; and the living being (jīva), whose essence is volition, shall obtain it."
In this cycle of existence, which is of the nature of conceptual construction, volition is the uncreated fruit;
it may arise as previously described through either giving or not giving, since it is nothing other than pure consciousness.

The meaning is that this resolves all inconsistencies: whether from giving or not giving here, let the fruit of giving—such as enjoyments and sovereignty—or the fruit of not giving—such as poverty—be uncontrived in the next world; there is no contradiction whatsoever. || 16 ||
All this has been told to you, O lord of the earth, exactly as you asked:
this entire world, unimpeded and all-pervading, is a mere conceptual construction of consciousness alone.
Having resolved all questions both verbally and in their meaning, he concludes that Brahman alone is the reality of the world with the words "This" (etad). || 17 ||
The King said: O Blessed One, at the beginning of creation, how does this body—which is a mere conceptualization of consciousness—appear? And how can a lamp shine without a wall? || 18 ||

Observing that consciousness is manifested only within a body, and noting that delusion and the like are not seen where consciousness is unmanifested, the King—considering that there would be a circular dependency such that the establishment of delusion at the beginning of creation depends on the establishment of a body, and the establishment of a body depends on the establishment of delusion—asks: "At the beginning of creation? [The answer is: Pure consciousness is consciousness devoid of a body; it is produced by that [delusion].

How can the conception of a body appear? For, in the absence of a body, the manifestation of consciousness (cit) itself is not observed, because it would then be like the light of a lamp that has not yet reached a wall or other support; such is the meaning regarding consciousness at that time. || 18 ||

The venerable Vasiṣṭha said: O high-minded one, that meaning of the word "body" which has been understood by you does not exist at all for one who knows reality, like the dancing of a stone in the sky.
The position of those who know reality is that the body is not inert, but is the manifestor of consciousness; for in their view, even the inert is not established as such [independently].

However, with the intention that Brahman—being omniscient—is always consciousness manifest and projects everything such as the body and so forth, he provides the answer beginning with "by you" (tvayā). || 19 ||
That which is the meaning of the word "Brahman" is indeed the meaning of the word "body";
there exists no difference between these two meanings, just as there is none between water and its waves.

In the expression "ambvambhasoriva," because it is an imitation of two words, there is either an *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) according to the rule "even for dissimilar [words] that have the same meaning," or it is not a *dvandva* compound due to the prohibition against using [synonyms] together. || 20 ||
This very body of Brahmā, which is like a dream, is indeed a dream;
however, this logical reasoning is stated for the sake of your awakening, yet it is not itself a dream.

This body is like a dream; that which is Brahman is indeed that very thing. Now, since this same reasoning applies equally to dreams as well, how can there be the statement of an illustration by taking for granted the distinction that it is "like a dream" even if it is Brahman? To this he says: "For your awakening"—the dream is an object experienced by you; therefore, you are awakened by it.
But in the case of the manifestation of consciousness during creation, there is no similarity with the ashes of a dream.

To explain how this is useful for my awakening, he says: "In a dream. The meaning is that the conscious self (cidātman) possesses no similarity to the creation that appears [there], because it is accompanied by ash characterized as a dream—that is, by an object that has been sublated. || 22 ||

What indeed is this body there, and to whom do these belong? Or where is the dream-consciousness? By means of a dream, one who is ignorant is awakened from delusion by one who has already awakened. (23)
To whom do these dream-objects belong? || 23 ||
Therein, there is neither waking nor dreaming, nor deep sleep, nor anything else; this manifestation is something indescribable, mere space, silence, and stainless.
"Om": this is the instruction on the fourth state, which remains after the dissolution of the three preceding states beginning with Virāj. "Alam":
this indicates the perception that therein all means and human goals find their ultimate fulfillment. 24.
That which now appears as this very thing, though it was previously unmanifest, shines forth as if manifest;
for it is primordially luminous and utterly transparent, unlike the states of waking, dreaming, and so forth.

That which appears here today as if it were manifest was in fact unmanifest even before; and although it appeared thus, it is just like the states of waking and dreaming, which never exist at all. In that same way, there exists only the utterly transparent Brahman.
In the transition from one place to another, that which constitutes the form of consciousness in the interval—of that very nature is all this, both duality and non-duality. (26)
The word "deśāt" has been explained; the meaning is that it consists solely of consciousness devoid of objects. || 26 ||
Elsewhere, the dream-like state consisting of consciousness—whether dualistic or non-dualistic, auspicious or inauspicious—is compared to the sky of unconditioned pure consciousness alone. (27)
Apart from the perspective of the ignorant, from the perspective of the wise, everything—including dreams and so forth—is compared to the sky of pure consciousness alone. || 27 ||
Emptiness, the perception of objects, appearance and non-appearance, duality and unity, the unreal and the real—all this is the supreme sky of consciousness. (28)
From the Full, the Full flows forth; the world remains as nothing but the Full.
It has neither appeared nor not appeared, being like the interior of a solid stone.
Her waist, which was firm and bound by a crystal slab, was like that [waist]. || 29 ||
Since the manifestation of the world arises from consciousness, it is therefore of the nature of space and unimpeded;
wherever there is pure consciousness, there the world is appropriately present.
"It is proper to remain," is the ellipsis. || 30 ||
The sky of consciousness exists everywhere, and all this consists of the world;
everything is composed of Brahman, peaceful, though it is designated by the word "world. (31)
Brahman alone is that which consists of Brahman. || 31 ||
This universe, as it exists, is established in that very way, free from affliction;
it is Brahman alone, the faultless Self, whose form is created by the city of conscious volition.
Because no other logical connection is possible, this very reasoning alone is excellent;
however, an experience devoid of logic, as described here, does not shine for those who seek the truth.
"Before those who have a purpose"—that is, before the listeners who desire the goals of human life (puruṣārtha); this is the ellipsis to be supplied. || 33 ||
Whatever is established in the world, in the scriptures, or in the Vedas and so forth, that remains established;
for it is impossible anywhere to establish that which is existent as non-existent, or that which is non-existent as existent. (34)

That which is established by my own means of valid cognition, reasoning, and experience is indeed established and cannot be discarded. Thus, the meaning is that Brahman, established as "existent" (sat) by the Vedas and other authorities, must be accepted as such; likewise, duality, established as "non-existent" (asat), must be accepted as such. || 34 ||
When the entire universe, which exists as equal to that [Brahman], dissolves, then this very [universe], thus fully known, attains the state of Brahman. (35)
The universe, which was previously perceived as non-Brahman, thus comes to attain the state of Brahman when it is thoroughly known. When?
At that moment when, by means of that knowledge in the form of the final direct realization (*sākṣātkāra-vṛtti*), it dissolves while remaining in a state of identity with it. || 35 ||
By the reasoning stated here, everything—including worldly affairs, the Vedas, and so forth—is established. Therefore, he alone is fit for the state of liberation while living (jīvanmukti). || 36 ||

By the reasoning stated by me in the passage beginning with "The meaning of the word 'body' is [as follows]" and ending with these words, it is established that this entire world—including the living liberated state (jīvanmuktatva) along with those who are liberated while living, as well as the worlds, the Vedas, and so forth—is indeed Brahman alone. Therefore, the meaning is that this very reasoning of mine is fit to be adopted, because it is the means for attaining the supreme goal of human life (paramapuruṣārtha). || 36 ||
The sky of consciousness is fully known within the tree of ignorance;
"I am that," and "the three worlds"—this indeed is the definitive conclusion regarding bondage and liberation. (37)

In this *aśvattha* tree, which is characterized by the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) whose nature is merely the uncomprehended Self, that which is fully comprehended is the space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*) alone; there is not even an atom’s worth of anything other than that. The meaning of the conclusion is: "I alone am that space of consciousness, both uncomprehended and comprehended; I am the three worlds, and I am bondage and liberation in turn. || 37 ||
This visible world, as it truly exists, dissolves through thorough knowledge;
for one who knows that and has set [in liberation], only the silence of a stone remains.

To the question of how liberation consists in mere thorough knowledge, he says: "as it truly is" (*yathāsthitam*). The ellipsis to be supplied is "the essential nature of the knower of that. The meaning is that for one who has set [the world] as the object of the visible, only pure vision (*dṛṅmātra*) remains, which is inaccessible to speech and other faculties. || 38 ||
Whatever is established in the world, in the treatises, and in the Veda is indeed established;
that alone is experienced, and therefore it clearly bears fruit in this manner. (39)
That which is established in the world among those liberated while living through hundreds of investigations and firmly settled therein is experienced through one's own direct experience as well;
therefore, that very thing bears fruit as the state of the supreme human goal. || 39 ||
Whatever is intensely contemplated for a long time by means of the exclusion of all other objects, that alone is inevitably attained; this is true everywhere, as it is conditioned by nothing else.

He says "sakalārtha" (regarding all objects) to show that the means for attaining that [state] is exclusive devotion to it alone by abandoning all other objects; for by that means, it is necessarily attained. The meaning is that even in every worldly task, whatever else is contemplated occurs in that very same way. || 40 ||
Whatever is experienced exactly as it is, that very thing is experienced accordingly;
whether it be true or false, it remains so for as long as it is attained. (41)
In this regard, let there indeed be a distinction between worldly activity, which is unreal, and that called liberation, which is real;
however, with the intention that there is no difference in the exertion toward the means or in the experience of their results, he says: "Just as... (41).
Thus, O wise and noble-souled one, this investigation of the great questions has been spoken by me to you.
By means of this, proceed quickly upon the path so that you may become exalted, free from anxiety, free from disease, and free from calamity.

O wise one, O great-souled one, thus has this deliberation upon your great questions—consisting of a resolution in the form of a definitive conclusion of the fruits of inquiry—been declared by me. Proceed by this path; thereby, quickly becoming free from anxiety in the mind, free from disease in the body, and free from vice in the senses, you shall become "uccaiḥ," meaning supremely exalted.

Thus ends the two hundred and tenth canto, titled "The Conclusion of the Discourse on the Answer to the Great Question by Refuting the Perception of Duality and Unity," in the Holy Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa, the Forest Book (Araṇyakāṇḍa), in the Uttarakāṇḍa. 210.

Thus ends the two hundred and tenth chapter, titled "The Conclusion of the Words Answering the Great Questions," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The two hundred and eleventh chapter (211).
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Having sat down there, I was thus honored by that king.
Having accomplished his own purpose, he leaped into the sky to go to heaven.
Furthermore, it is clearly described here that Brahman alone is the entire universe, joined with the means for perceiving the multitude of worlds such as the Siddhas and the Sādhyas.
There, in the city named Ilāvati on the continent of Kuśadvīpa, by that king named Prajñapti, his own purpose—characterized by favoring him—was [fulfilled]. (1)
"O best among the wise, what has been spoken by you today—by means of this right vision—you shall become peaceful in mind and one whose self is the void. (2)
And furthermore, while you were present here in this Ayodhyā, so was I.
All this is indeed Brahman alone—the stainless sky, devoid of names; something indefinable, unborn, profoundly peaceful, and free from beginning, middle, and end.
Nameless and soundless, it is indeed like space. || 3 ||
It is said to be the mere manifestation of consciousness; it is designated by the name "Brahman";
it is proclaimed as that which is higher than the highest; yet that state is truly nameless.

The meaning is that even the name "Brahman" is assigned through conceptual construction and does not exist in reality; for in the immutable [Kūṭastha], there is no possibility of the increase (vṛddhi) and so forth denoted by the root *bṛh*. || 4 ||
Śrī Rāma said: O Brāhmaṇa, tell me how the worlds of the Siddhas, Sādhyas, Yamas, Brahmavidyādharas, and the celestial dwellers, as well as the world-supporting mountains, are seen.
How and by what means are those worlds, the people therein, and their supporting ground perceived? || 5 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
[He is the refuge] of the Siddhas, Sādhyas, Yamas, Brahmavidyādharas, and the celestial dwellers,
as well as of other beings, unprecedented and great-souled ones.
Night after night and day after day, you look before and behind, above and below; you behold the worlds, yet without seeing, you do not see.
Beholding—that is, seeing—by means of the specific forms of concentration (dhāraṇā) described in the narrative of Cūḍālā, you see; that is, you will see. || 7 ||
These worlds, it is said, are not far from their [the yogis'] abodes due to lack of practice;
these are called "worlds of volition," for by them everything is indeed pervaded.

For there are two kinds of perfected beings (*siddha-loka*): those known as Mahar, Janas, Tapas, and Satya, who are far removed by their station; and those perfected ones who move everywhere, established by such scriptural passages as, "If he becomes desirous of the world of the fathers, by his mere volition the fathers arise for him, and endowed with that world of the fathers, he is glorified."

The worlds known as Saṃkalpa and Loka pervade the entire universe everywhere; however, the meaning is that in the view of both [of these], the practice of concentration (dhāraṇā) is the cause [of their existence], and you do not possess that. || 8 ||
Just as these lights of conceptual construction are, so too is this world for us;
just as the wind is conceptual, so too are the worlds and the lights.

In that case, should I practice concentration (*dhāraṇā*) in order to see them? He shows that it should not be done because they lack substantiality, with the words beginning "Just as... Just as those worlds of theirs consist of mere conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), so too is this world of ours established through mere conceptual construction alone. For example, even a conceptual wind blows everywhere.
The meaning is that they wander in such a manner, whereas this one does not; this alone is the distinction. || 9 ||
Those worlds of your own volition and dreams which shine for you day and night—
those very same ones, and others like them, are made stable by that very volition.

Those worlds that appear to you in your creative resolve and dreams are indeed those well-known worlds of the Siddhas; other such worlds as well have been fashioned by them through resolve alone and rendered stable by that very same resolve. || 10 ||
If you, with a very steady mind, bring even those things that have been dissolved by meditation to a state of stability,
then they will quickly attain stability without obstacle.

And so, if you too bring these worlds—attained through your own resolve—to stability by means of meditation made firm through the practice of yoga-concentration, then they too shall attain stability. || 11 ||
A person enveloped by the power of the state of mental resolve perceives things according to their desired extent and desired excellence, just like a perfected being (siddha).

In the same way, if another person is also enveloped by the state of a very firm internal resolve as a meditator, he too perceives those [objects] as stable, just like one who has attained perfection. || 12 ||
However, they were brought to stability by the Siddhas through the excellence of their celestial vehicles;
yet by those unstable sufferings, they were made to rest in meditation. (13)
However, this much is the distinction: those perfected ones (siddhas) go to their respective celestial realms, the worlds of the siddhas;
because those worlds have been rendered stable by such prior perfection of merit (dharmasaṃpad), they are attained by them without effort.
But for others who strive for repose in meditation through present-day practices of concentration (dhāraṇā)—which are impermanent—[those realms are] attained with difficulty.
"By these labors, may these worlds be made stable. || 13 ||
The entire world is always an unobstructed, peaceful sky of consciousness;
just as it is firmly realized, so does it appear, and not otherwise.
"Saṃviditam" means ascertained. || 14 ||
It does not shine at all when it is unknown; it neither exists nor does it not exist, and there is no effort toward it.
For this is empty, non-obstructive, like the supreme space, and unimpeding. || 15 ||
Because, in that which is not perceived, there is no scope for the application of reasoning regarding whether it exists or does not exist. || 15 ||
Manifesting by virtue of its nature as consciousness, it appears like light;
yet, within this, there is no conceit of "I" (the ego), for that does not exist by its own nature. (16)

From where [does it arise] that it is empty and non-obstructive? To this he says: "by virtue of having consciousness as its own nature" (*citsvabhāvatayā*). That which appears through firm perception is seen as appearing like light by virtue of having consciousness as its own nature. However, when this is not consciously known, there is no self-conception of consciousness, nor is there any pervasion by the manifestation of the existence of consciousness; such is the meaning. (16)
If it is argued that [the world] exists due to the relation of cause and effect, no such discourse is possible here;
for how indeed could anything be produced, and in what manner, from the infinite and established ether? (17)
However, one should not even suspect that its existence will be something other than the power of the existence of its cause, for such a doubt has already been refuted; thus he says:
"The effect... [and so on]. Because at the beginning of creation, space (ākāśa) is in a state of dissolution (pralaya). || 17 ||
And that which appears as if born in the sky is in fact just the sky itself;
therein, how could there be any formless conception of oneness or duality? (18)
And that which appears as if born, such as the elements and the worlds, is merely space appearing as if born within space;
therefore, even the conceptualization of oneness or duality is difficult to find there, let alone the relationship of cause and effect—this is the meaning. || 18 ||
For that [Self] remains exactly as it was, changeless, like the sky which remains motionless even during a dream. (19)

In that case, let Brahman alone be the cause; to this he replies: "For that [is]... The meaning is that it is merely the substratum of the illusory manifestation (vivarta-adhiṣṭhāna) and not a transformer (vikārī), and thus it is not the [material] cause. || 19 ||
Just as a mountain appears as a form in the mind through the play of imagination,
yet that mountain is not real nor is that space, so too is the existence of the world within Brahman.
The phrase "having conceptualized a form" is to be understood as the ellipsis. || 20 ||
Maintaining silence like a piece of wood, even while they speak, these great-minded wise men here conduct themselves like wooden men.
For this very reason, he says "like wood" (kāṣṭhavat) [in verse 21]: from their own perspective, those liberated while living appear as if they were engaged in activity, but not in reality.
Just as the movements of waves and whirlpools exist within water and revolve as nothing other than it, so do all creations revolve within Brahman.
Just as vibrations exist in the wind and emptiness in the sky,
so too do the creations exist in Brahman— non-different from it and yet formless.
Just as a city of imagination exists as a void even while appearing as a city,
so too does this world exist within Brahman, appearing with form though it is without form.
Even though this triple world has been experienced for a long time, its purposeful activity is empty and formless, like a city of one's own imagination.
It is "beneficial" (arthakāri), meaning it is capable of accomplishing both worldly and Vedic tasks. || 25 ||
Just as a city is nothing other than a mental construction,
so too this pure Brahman is called the world in that very same way.
At that time, during the period of activity within the city of conceptual construction, so too is this perceived cycle of existence (saṃsāra). || 26 ||
Though experienced as eternal for a long time, the purpose of the world is nothing at all to the Puruṣa, just as one's own death in a dream [is nothing to oneself]. (27)
Just as a man may see his own cremation even when he is dead in a dream,
so too is this world seen by the Supreme as a mere appearance of existence though it is non-existent.
Both the state of being the world and the state of not being the world are the pure body of the Supreme alone;
and that which is called "the other" is the Supreme, yet it does not exist as something real from the perspective of ultimate truth. (29)
That which is other than the rope and so forth— that which is designated as "other" and becomes the object of designations such as "snake"— does not exist in ultimate reality.

"Let it be thus, or let it be otherwise; let it not be, or let it be—what cause for agitation is there in this? O you who are as fickle as the fruit of the *phalguna* tree, abandon your grasping for results; you have now understood, so enough with your labors! (30)

O Rāma, let the fruit of enjoying the world of the Siddhas and so forth be merely a mental construction (*kalpanāmātra*) in the manner described by me; or else, let it be otherwise, or even of a different kind as described by other sages. Even so, what concern or attachment can there be for you, who are liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*), regarding such insignificant fruits like the attainment of supernatural powers? To grasp at such a trivial fruit is a delusion.

Abandon the notion that there is a personal goal to be achieved; since you have realized the reality of Brahman, enough with these labors of seeking to know the splendors of the worlds of the Siddhas, which are merely of the nature of illusion. The meaning is that there is nothing further to be accomplished. || 30 ||

Thus ends the two hundred and eleventh chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Supreme Reality," in the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, within the *Dehastha Mokṣa Nirṇaya Upaniṣad*. 211.
Thus ends the two hundred and eleventh chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Supreme Reality," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*. 211.
The two hundred and twelfth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Because of its nature as consciousness, it is as if the void of Brahman itself knows by itself, "I am."
That very state of being the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin) is his; this entire world is his belly.
The conceptualization of the "I-ness" of Brahmā is Parameṣṭhin; the three worlds consist of his volition, and therefore it is described here that they are indeed Brahman alone.

In Brahman, first, there is the conceptualization of Hiraṇyagarbha as the collective ego-sense (*samaṣṭy-ahaṃkāra*); and within his belly, there is the conceptualization of the world of individual souls (*vyaṣṭi-jīva*). Thus, everything is merely an illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) of Brahman, established for superficial observation.
From the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha-dṛṣṭi*), however, neither Hiraṇyagarbha, nor the individual soul, nor the world exists at all; there is only Brahman alone.

He begins to describe at the end the distilled meaning of all the Vedāntas—that [the Self] abides as the fullness of the single essence of eternally pure Being-Consciousness-Bliss—with the words "Because of its nature as consciousness" (*cittvāt*). Brahman-itself, the Space of Consciousness, first perceives itself through the aggregate of the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) as "I," as it were; that very perception is its [nature].
The state of being Parameṣṭhin and the nature of Hiraṇyagarbha. || 1 ||
This being the case, there is neither Brahmā nor a world that has arisen and persists;
rather, it remains exactly as it is—the unborn, supreme Brahman itself, just as it was before.

And it is not the case that Brahman becomes non-Brahman through such a mere illusory offense; rather, he says "this being so" (evam sthite) to show that nothing else whatsoever, such as Hiraṇyagarbha and the like, had ever existed. || 2 ||
In consciousness, however, the form of the world appears in exactly this same way;
like a mirage, it is entirely false, for even while being perceived, it is non-existent.
If it did not exist at all, then how could it appear in consciousness? To this he says: "In consciousness" (*saṃvittau*).
It is thus merely phenomenal (*prātibhāsika*), not ultimately real (*paramārthasat*). || 3 ||
From this point forward, this new delusion has arisen as empty.
For where is this delusion, and what is it? Indeed, it is Brahman alone, which is free from all affliction.
Therefore, from the time of creation onwards, delusion has arisen; or rather, it has not arisen at all.
The world is but a whirlpool in the waters of Brahman; what indeed are duality and unity here?
Where is the duality between the whirlpool and the water, and where is their unity, given the absence of duality?
Granted that the world is an indefinable attribute of Brahman, even so there is no harm; thus he says: "The world... (verse 5).
That Brahman, dense and profoundly tranquil, by virtue of its consciousness perceives itself as "I," knowing its own inherent emptiness which resides within it like the sky with its vast interior.
Because it is conscious and its nature is the manifestation of the other, it perceives itself as the collective essence of the "I-maker" (ahaṃkāra), [thinking] "I am."
Just as the wind possesses motion, fire possesses heat,
and the full moon possesses its own coolness, so does existence possess the essence of the self.
Brahman alone perceives its own existence as the Self, as if it were an object. || 7 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
O Brahman, O Sage, when indeed did You not perceive that [reality] which is unobstructed and without beginning or end? Why is it that You perceive it now? (8)

Rāma asks: "If it is intended that the very consciousness of one's own nature (*svarūpacaitanya*) perceives objects just as it does itself, then since that [consciousness] exists always, why is it said that 'it perceives now'? He asks this with the words: "This... This [world] consisting of the "I" and so forth—when has it ever been perceived? For it is always unobscured, free from covering, beginningless and endless, and eternal; therefore, how can it be said that "now..."?
The meaning is: what is meant by saying that [he] "acts" (pracetati) starting from the time of creation? || 8 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
It is exactly so; this [consciousness] always perceives even "I" and so forth.
For this beginningless and unborn [Self], there is no dependence whatsoever upon its own self-awareness.

It is true that from the perspective of logical reasoning, one always perceives the true nature of the "I" and so forth as being both in the form of creation and non-creation; thus, it culminates in the validity of two perspectives on Brahman. Nevertheless, there exists a distinction between these two perspectives based on the existence or non-existence of their respective objects, according to their respective degrees of validity.
With the intention that [the two cases] are equal, he provides the answer as if accepting it, beginning with "This is so" (*evam etat*).

The meaning is that there is no dependence on anything else either for the manifestation of one's own nature through self-awareness (*svasaṃvit*)—that is, through the consciousness of one's own essence (*svarūpacaitanya*)—or for the manifestation of the ego and so forth through ignorance (*avidyā*). || 9 ||
Brahman, whose nature is like the sky—neither creation nor non-creation—is everywhere and at all times;
it is never "this," nor "not this," nor known as "this," nor as "nothing at all."
For this has never been known in the vision of ignorance, nor is there anything at all in the vision of knowledge.
The movement of the wind, the coolness of the moon, the emptiness of the sky,
and my own identity as Brahman— which is non-different from the Self— he never fails to perceive.
If that is so, what does one perceive in the state of mixed vision? To this he says: "pavana... (verse 11).
Such is the nature of all things at all times; it has never been otherwise.
Since the world is without beginning or end, it is indeed the stainless Self that is Brahman. 12.

"At all times" means that, according to the reasoning stated in the *Vipaścit* narrative, there is no established time for the cessation of the saṃsāra of all living beings; this is the intended sense. || 12 ||
But solely because you have not awakened, being pierced by the hearing of sounds, you perceive duality in this non-dual realization of Brahman. (13)

If you accept even this mixed view merely until the point of attaining awakening for the sake of establishing conventional activities such as hearing sounds, then accept it; however, [the author] says "only" (*kevalam*) to indicate that this is not from the perspective of ultimate reality. This is because, even when non-dual Brahman-knowledge has arisen, you continue to accept ignorance due to your state of being unawakened.
