The fifth case ending [is used] in the sense of "towards" (lyablope). The meaning is: upon hearing my instruction, being pierced—that is, having a mind attached—you accept a duality consisting of both the conceptualized (*saprapañca*) and the non-conceptualized (*niṣprapañca*), which is obtained through a mixed view; it is not so from the perspective of the vision of reality (*tattvadṛś*). || 13 ||
No one here ever perceives anything at all;
nor does anyone who is not that [Self] ever perceive it. || 14 ||

For in the view of the mixture (*miśradṛṣṭi*), Brahman consists of all things; and since a certain individual soul (*jīva*) included therein perceives something, it is Brahman itself that perceives through that [individual] self. Thus, through that self, everyone perceives everything.
And through the self of the undifferentiated Brahman, no one ever perceives anything at all. (14)
This appearance of the three worlds shines thus at all times;
yet it is the peaceful, equal Brahman—here there is nothing whatsoever that is manifold. (15)

And thus, from the perspective of one who is bound, Brahman always appears as the manifestation of the three worlds; however, from the perspective of one who is liberated, the meaning is that nothing at all appears, according to the realization: "There is no diversity here whatsoever. || 15 ||
Trees and mountains are never born from the sky, nor are the worlds born from Brahman; realizing this, attain supreme peace. 16.
In this regard, he says, "Never," [meaning] that because the view of one who is bound has its object sublated, you must indeed adopt the view of one who is liberated. || 16 ||
O one of limited intellect, as long as you have not awakened to the truth regarding the purpose of the teacher and the teaching during moments of doubt, so long do you maintain the notion of duality.
He says "by instruction" (upadeśya) to show that the view mixed with the activity of instruction was permitted by me:
"you accept; do accept. 17.

But for the awakened one who has been purified, there is no scripture and so forth, no cognition of words, no perception of difference, and no duality; he is something entirely unique, O Lord of Creatures.

The meaning is that thereafter, you will certainly no longer possess the notion of duality nor the notion of the reality of Prajāpati, who is the self of the world born from egoism and its volitions. || 18 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
"O Brahmin, this which you have uttered for the sake of my understanding has been understood by me; now explain that which was introduced."

"O Brahman, that which was asked by me, beginning with 'When indeed...', has been understood by me through what you have said. Explain—that is, set forth—the relevant discourse which was introduced for the purpose of my awakening, namely, to define the superimposition (adhyāsa) of the collective ego-sense (samaṣṭi-ahaṃkāra) and so forth. || 19 ||
When that conceived state of "I-ness" has been realized, does one attain the supreme state?
You have understood this; though I am eager to hear more, I truly do not reach satiety. (20)
Recalling that very point, he asks: "What?"—meaning, when that supreme state (*para-pada*) is realized as the "I-ness" (*ahantva*), what happens thereafter?
You, being omniscient, have understood everything; and I, desiring to hear your words, do not reach satiety; therefore, please speak. This is the meaning. || 20 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
When this state of egoity exists, the existence of space proceeds;
the existence of the directions, the existence of time, and the existence of differentiation arise as well.
The existence of space is the superimposition of space; the existence of difference is the superimposition of the threefold limitation. || 21 ||
When it is thought "I am here," then even "I am not here" does not appear;
thus, within the void, one's own Self alone arises as non-sequential duality.
He establishes that the superimposition of the ego (ahaṃkārādhyāsa) is the cause for the superimposition of spatial limitation (paricchedādhyāsa), beginning with the words "yadā" (when).

When this [ego] appears as "I" here in the body and so forth, then, in a place devoid of the body, the thought "I am not here" necessarily also appears; this is the limitation produced by space. In this manner, there is likewise a manifold limitation produced by time.
And having made a distinction regarding the objective entity, one's own self alone arises as non-sequential duality. || 22 ||
The cognition that designates these entities as being of the nature of space will occur at a later time; therefore, they are indeed just space.

He says—“of those whose nature is space”—because there will arise a superimposition of distinct names, which is occasioned by the conceptualization of differences in the grounds for the application [of words], such as genus, quality, and action, which serve to differentiate one from another.

“The cognition of these aforementioned existences as distinct categories” (etāsām uktānām padārthabheda-sattānām abhidhāna-dhīḥ) refers to the superimposition of expressive words (*vācaka-śabda-adhyāsa*). || 23 ||
When this formless sense of "I," which consists of the perception of space and time, has been fully perfected, it becomes like the sky, cognizing only that subtle essence.

In that regard, since there is no obscuration regarding the distinctions between the individual soul (jīva) and the witness-consciousness (sākṣin) due to the delimitation by the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), Brahman itself— though not non-Brahman— is manifested in its natural consciousness and appears in the form of the world superimposed upon it; thus he says with two verses beginning with "etasmin" [verse 24].
This luminous form called "the visible," which is sensation, shines forth;
having become Brahman itself, it is unassailable, yet it appears as if it were not Brahman.

Brahman alone is peaceful, unborn, one, and without beginning or middle; having conceived of it as space itself appearing as the notion of the individual soul (*jīva*), one perceives within that very unobstructed space the pervasive visible world and even one's own nature as if it were something else, due to the lack of self-knowledge. This is clearly stated: "Brahman alone... Space, which is devoid of the states of the individual soul and the world, is indeed Brahman.

Having meditated upon [the world] as if it were the life-force (jīvaka) and having superimposed it upon the unobstructed space that is the witness of the individual soul (jīvasākṣyākāśa), he perceives the visible world—which has spread out and become even more extensive—as if it were something other than his own nature, which is Brahman; this continues until the dawn of the knowledge of reality, meaning up to the limit of self-realization. || 26 ||
Thus ends the two hundred and twelfth canto, titled "The Exposition of the Ultimate Reality," in the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa*, the *Vālmīki Devarṣi Mokṣopāya*.
Thus ends the two hundred and twelfth chapter, titled "The Exposition of Ultimate Reality," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The two hundred and thirteenth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
O destroyer of enemies, regarding that which you have asked me today:
Previously, while you were indeed a disciple, you questioned me, your guru.
Herein is described the prior conversation between Rāma and Vasiṣṭha;
through this narrative of teacher and disciple, it is concluded that everything is Brahman.

Although the reality of the Self had been made directly manifest to Rāma— like a myrobalan fruit in the palm of his hand— through detailed instruction, the venerable Vasiṣṭha, desiring to make it firm by the maxim of "driving in a pillar" through the reminder that this was indeed the very same matter he had taught him in a previous birth, [composed] for the benefit of the entire world a work consisting of a compendium of the meaning of all scriptures.
At the conclusion of the treatise, he begins to impart the narrative of the teacher and the disciple, which is of the nature of the supreme auspiciousness, starting with the words "Just as...

and so forth: "O Rāma, just as you have today questioned me regarding the reality of the world and the reality of the Self, so too in a previous birth as another Rāma, when you were my disciple, I was your teacher."
He was questioned. || 1 ||
Indeed, in a certain ancient age, there existed in a forest such a manifestation of consciousness, consisting of the reality of the self and so forth, in the form of teacher and disciple. (2)

Having stated it briefly, he explains it in detail with the word "purā" (formerly). That world existed there; you were Rāma, I was the Self, Vasiṣṭha; and by the inclusion of the word "etcetera," this manifestation of consciousness—including your world-weariness, your coming to me, and your questions—existed in a certain forest in the form of teacher and disciple, just as now. This is the meaning. || 2 ||
I was the guru there and you were the disciple at that time;
standing before me, you, possessed of a bold and steady intellect, questioned me thus.
You have asked this which is about to be stated. || 3 ||
The disciple said:
O Blessed One, sever this great doubt of mine regarding everything:
what perishes during the Great Kalpa, and what entity does not perish?
Regarding the entire world as my object, this excessive doubt that is being expressed is a most profound uncertainty. || 4 ||
The Guru said:
"O son, the entire visible world perishes instantly and completely;
just so does the dream-city vanish for one who has attained the state of deep sleep."

Just as the city of a dream, for the Self that has entered the state of deep sleep, perishes entirely leaving nothing behind, so too the visible world perishes at the time of dissolution; this is the meaning. || 5 ||
Without distinction, the mountains of the earth, the ten directions, ritual action, time, and sequence—all these perish; nothing whatsoever remains.
All beings perish and even space itself dissolves,
because the perceiver of the appearance of the entire world is non-existent.

Even the ether, together with the manifestations of the entire world, perishes through dissolution into the unmanifest; for that which is perceived and experienced exists dependent upon the perceiver and experiencer, and at the time of dissolution, such a perceiver and experiencer is no longer possible. || 7 ||
For even those such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, and Rudra, who are indeed the cause of all causes—
of them too, at the end of the great kalpa, not even a name remains here.
To dispel the doubt that Brahmā and others alone will remain as the enjoyers of that [state] at that time, he says: "Brahman.
This refers to the dissolution at the end of a kalpa, which is both primordial (prākṛta) and intellectual (vaijñānika). || 8 ||
For the imperishable space of consciousness remains, which is inferred by this fact—
that there is a remainder of time caused by the experience of creation.

He establishes what was stated—that only the Self remains while everything else perishes—with the words "for that which remains. It is inferred that when the transformation (*vivarta*) of the imperishable conscious reality (*cidvastu*) has ceased, the space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*) remains; for this very reason, by means of this conscious Self alone, which is the cause for experiencing the creation superimposed upon itself.

The state of being a residue at that time, wherein all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) is empty, is established. The meaning is that if even that were destroyed, there would be no witness, and thus dissolution itself could not be established. || 9 ||
The disciple said:
"There is no being for the non-existent, nor is there non-being for the existent.
How is it that this expansive world, which is so manifest, goes nowhere? (10)
The student raises an objection, stating that for an existent world, destruction characterized by non-existence cannot be established at all: "Not of the non-existent" (nāsataḥ). || 10 ||
The Guru said:
"This [Self] indeed does not perish; therefore, O son, it does not cease to exist.
There is no coming into being for the non-existent, nor is there cessation of being for the existent. (11)

The Master provides the following resolution with the underlying intention that the destruction of the world—established through scripture, perception, inference, tradition, and so forth—cannot be denied; therefore, by the force of that evidence, the very reality [of the world] which appears to be such upon superficial observation is negated, and thus there is no fault.

The meaning is: "Since the destruction [of the world] is well-known, it does not exist at all; therefore, what you have stated—that there is no existence of this non-existent—is consistent [with our position]."
O Rāma, how indeed can that which does not exist as a reality at any time whatsoever— which is of the nature of non-existence— ever perish?
Whatever exists in reality cannot be non-existent by nature; for how could its existence—its very being—perish or fall into non-existence? (12)
Where does the water of a mirage abide? Where is the delusion of two moons stable?
Where do hairs seen in the sky remain fixed? And where is the experience of error ever stable? (13)

The existence of the world cannot be determined by mere superficial observation, because many things seen in that manner are not found to exist; thus he says, "Where? [referring to the verse]. "Firm" means established in reality. || 13 ||
"O son, all this that is visible is mere delusion, consisting of unreality;
it appears like a city in a dream—how is it that this does not subside? (14)
This [delusion] subsides entirely, in every respect and at all times, just as a dream ceases upon waking, or as waking ceases within a dream. (15)
He states that the mutual relationship of being examples for one another between waking and dreaming is well-known in establishing the state of being sublated, saying:
"It subsides. (15)
Just as a dream-city is peaceful and I do not know where it quickly goes, so too this visible world is peaceful, and I do not know where it quickly goes. (16)
But as for its being refuted, since it is not seen even by yogis as to where it goes or where it stays, its non-existence alone is the refuge; with this intention, he says: "Just as... (verse 16).
The disciple said:
"O Blessed One, what is this that shines, and what again does not shine?
Of what substance is this the form, belonging to the sky of consciousness whose shape is all-pervasive? (7)
If the visible object does not exist at all, then what entity, appearing in the guise of the visible for some time, shines forth from the perspective of ultimate reality?
And why is it that after awakening, it no longer shines forth in that same way? This is the meaning. || 17 ||
The Guru said:
"O son, this sky of consciousness shines forth clearly;
that which is called the world appears, yet no world other than this exists. (18)
It glistens like mother-of-pearl and flashes like silver through its own shimmering brilliance. || 18 ||
This is the form of this very reality, the expansive expanse of consciousness;
though it has not abandoned its own translucent nature, it appears in this manner. (19)
The meaning is that this is based on such scriptural passages as: "Of this [Brahman], there are these two forms: the formed and the formless," and so forth. || 19 ||
Its own body consists of creation and dissolution, shimmering and not shimmering;
it is of the nature of space, being both white and black, just like the body of a whole object.
Just as the body of a whole (avayavin), which is its own essential nature, appears as if divided by the distinctions of its parts—such is the meaning. || 20 ||
Just as you alone were here at the beginning within the white waters by means of your hair,
so too is Brahman— the pure Self— thus [present] during creation and imperishable even at the dissolution of creation.

Just as you, being well-known, have entered into this lake of white water with clear water and are one alone due to the cessation of the distinction between the original object (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*); and just as even before entering the lake, you were likewise one with an inexhaustible manifestation despite verbal descriptions of distinctions such as the state of the original object and its reflection— so too is Brahman in the act of creation.
The meaning is that at the end of creation, there is only one [reality] which arises as imperishable. || 21 ||
Just as in dream and deep sleep there is only one imperishable sleep throughout the day and night,
so too in this creation and in dissolution, Brahman alone is the immutable consciousness.
Consciousness is the immutable and changeless nature of consciousness. || 22 ||
Just as for the observer of the world in a dream, the world subsides entirely into peace, so too does this world of ours subside entirely into peace. (23)
Just as the world well-known in a dream becomes utterly tranquil in the states of waking and deep sleep, so too does it subside. || 23 ||
Therefore, my dear, we do not know how that which is called "space" could exist elsewhere in space;
for this is impossible in the space of another, whereas it is possible within the space of our own consciousness.

For this very reason, that which is called "space" (kha)—namely, the void (śūnya), that dream-world—is sublated; we do not know it to exist in the same way elsewhere, in another place, from the perspective of awakened vision. Furthermore, the notion that it will abide in the space of other persons—that is, in the living-space (jīvākāśa) of other individuals—is an unworthy doubt, one that should not even be entertained. Why? Because [the dream] consists of our own latent impressions (vāsanā) within the very sky of our own consciousness.
The meaning is that even in the state where [the world] has arisen and is not yet sublated, there is no possibility [of its existence] within the space of the supreme consciousness. || 24 ||
Just as the manifestation of our own consciousness-space occurs here at the dissolution of creation, so too does another consciousness-space exist; what proof is there that it is not thus? (25)

If the creation established by our own experience were sublated by awakening and were to enter the space of another's consciousness, then one would have to assume that there is no manifestation of the pure space of consciousness for that other person due to their awakening; yet, in that case, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to conceive such a thing—thus he says: "Just as... (verse 25).
The disciple said:
Just as in a dream the mind exists as the perception of the object distinct from the seer, so too I believe that elsewhere there exists the perception of the world and so forth. (26)

If, according to the manner stated above, the object of our own consciousness does not appear within the supreme consciousness, then just as there exists a waking person other than the dreamer who possesses the cognition of the visible world,
so too I believe— that is, I conceive— it possible that at the time of dissolution, the cognition of the world and so forth exists elsewhere, in another person. || 26 ||
The Guru said: "It is so, O one of great wisdom; however, that world is not the true nature [of reality].
That which is the true nature shines within consciousness, yet it does not shine in that same way as the world."

Accepting this, the Guru replies with "It is so. The implication is that for this very reason, the existence of the world even during dissolution was previously described by the Creator as being like that of Aindava. If the world were the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of consciousness, it would be common to all; however, it is not so, but rather appears as superimposed upon consciousness (*cityadhyasta*).
If it does not appear in the same way to other perceivers of that [object], then its nature is established according to each respective case; this is the meaning. || 27 ||
It does not shine, nor is it anything at all, yet it is not non-existent;
it is the manifestation of the space of consciousness—what room is there therein for the views of existence and non-existence?
Precisely because it does not appear as something common, it is not "nothing" in the sense of being void;

rather, while it is thus, it is merely the manifestation of the space of consciousness within each individual living being. In that state, who could perceive it as either existent or non-existent? || 28 ||
For that indeed exists everywhere, as everything, by everything, at all times;
and yet nothing whatsoever exists anywhere, at any time. (29)

If, however, it is said that [the world] exists in the form of the space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*), then that entire world exists in every way, everywhere, and at all times; yet in its own nature, nothing whatsoever exists anywhere at any time—this is the meaning. || 29 ||
Whatever exists at any time and in any way, all that is either real or unreal;
yet it is entirely composed of that space of consciousness (cidākāśa), which is neither subject to destruction nor is it destroyed.

Since that Brahman itself is both being and non-being, therefore the world also appears as both being and non-being; since the space of consciousness is indestructible, therefore the world, which consists of it, is also indestructible.

That which is indeed the space of Being-Consciousness (saccidākāśa), whose nature consists of creation and dissolution—that, when not fully known, leads to suffering; when fully known, it is supreme peace.

Since that very space of consciousness (cidākāśa) takes the form of creation and dissolution, when it is not fully known, it leads to suffering; but when it is fully known, it is supreme peace—the meaning being the destruction of all suffering. || 31 ||
This entire universe exists in every way, everywhere, and at all times;
yet this entire universe does not exist in any way, anywhere, or at any time. (32)
And that thorough knowledge exists or does not exist for the wise and the ignorant everywhere and at all times, respectively. || 32 ||
This deity is the jar, the mountain, the cloth, the thunderbolt, the bank, and the banyan tree; it is the grass, the fire, the stationary, the moving, and indeed everything.
He elaborates upon the fact that this very [Self] exists everywhere in every form, beginning with the words "This is the God," and so forth. || 33 ||
Existence and non-existence, emptiness, action, time, space, and earth;
being and non-being, birth, prosperity, destructions, bonds, and the auspicious and inauspicious—[all these are but forms of Māyā]. || 34 ||
Existence is birth. || 34 ||
That which is not eternal, nor singular, nor external, as well as beginning, middle, and end—that is, the three divisions of time—does not exist at all. (35)
Everything exists here by means of everything, everywhere, and at all times;
yet nothing exists here by means of anything, anywhere, or at any time. || 36 ||

O Rāma, at that very moment, when everything exists as the self of all at all times, it is indeed so by virtue of being Brahman, according to the analogy of the dream-consciousness and the city [of the Gandharvas]. || 37 ||

In the vision through the state of Brahman, he further elaborates that all entities, such as thirst and the rest, are individually the doers of all, the enjoyers of all, and the lords of all—beginning with the words "because of being the Self of Brahman.
(37) Grass is the doer, grass is the enjoyer; because it is the Self of Brahman, grass is all-pervasive.
The jar is the agent, the jar is the enjoyer, the jar is the Lord of all lords. || 38 ||
He is the Lord of all lords, beginning with Indra. || 38 ||
The cloth is the agent, the cloth is the enjoyer, the cloth is the Lord of all lords;
the Seer is the agent, the Seer is the enjoyer, the Seer is the Lord of all lords. || 39 ||
Giri is the creator, Giri is the enjoyer, Giri is the Lord of all lords;
Nara is the creator, Nara is the enjoyer, Nara is the Lord of all lords. || 40 ||
He is the creator and enjoyer of every single object, higher than the highest;
he is the sustainer without beginning or end, since everything has Brahman as its self. 41.
Among all things, each individual thing has a single agent and enjoyer who is higher than the highest and superior even to the most excellent.

But these things, such as grass, jars, and so forth, are established in this form by the omnipresent Lord through His own omnipotence—a form in which there is the manifestation of both decay and arising. (42)

By your own nature, which is the form of the inner self—if rise and fall appear within this form, then every such form is nothing but the omnipresent reality itself, abiding in this very manner. || 42 ||
The external object exists; it alone is here the agent and the enjoyer of such a kind.
For those who know thus, there exists only consciousness as the agent and the enjoyer. (43)
He corroborates the stated point with the experience of the disputants: "The external object.

For those who hold that there is an external object distinct from consciousness—such as the Vaiśeṣikas, Sautrāntikas, and others—it is that very object which is both the agent and the enjoyer. However, for those disputants for whom there is only consciousness, for such people, that [consciousness] alone is the agent and the enjoyer.
For those who know the truth, there is no agent here at all, nor likewise any enjoyer;
for those who know the truth, the Lord alone is the agent and the enjoyer here.

But for the proponents of emptiness (śūnyavādins), that very [non-existence] is the case; thus he says: "no one at all. For the Pāśupatas and others, however, it is a certain Lord (īśvara), well-known through their own system, who is both the agent and the enjoyer. || 44 ||
In that supreme of all states, everything indeed is possible;
what injunctions and prohibitions are there, and which ones do not exist? (45)
Thus, despite these differences of opinion, not one among the disputants can be said to propound an impossibility;
for within that supreme, supreme state—which is omnipotent, omnipresent, and the essence of all—everything is possible.
Within that state, all those distinct and mutually divergent positions favored by the various disputants [are contained].

The injunctions regarding the nature of categories, their means of accomplishment, their performance, and their fruits, as well as all their respective prohibitions, are possible without contradiction and remain unmixed; for within the consciousness delimited by each respective cognition, transformations occur according to one's own volition, following the analogy of a boon and a curse. (45)
In the pure space of consciousness, like a seer, one who contemplates as if there were an object of sight perceives his own self as the world; thus he should remain free from affliction.

In each instance, while manifesting within its own pure self—the sky of consciousness—as if there were objects of perception following various latent impressions (*vāsanā*), it remains, as it were, the seer itself; seeing its own Self as such a world, it actually abides in a state free from all affliction wherever it may be, meaning it is capable of remaining so. || 46 ||
All perceptions, as well as all perceptions of injunctions and prohibitions,
are preceded by specific volitions and cognitions;
they are eternally real in nature, yet not real in themselves, because their true essence here consists in the form [of the object] exactly as it is experienced.

O Rāma, because all perceptions of objects and so forth established by the individual experience of every living being, as well as all perceptions of injunctions and prohibitions that are mutually distinct,

arise from their respective volitions (*saṃkalpa*), specific cognitions (*vedana*), specific experiences (*anubhava*), and residual impressions (*vāsanā*) accompanied by their respective desires (*kāma*).

Because they are capable of their respective purposeful actions (*arthakriyā*), they are of the nature of reality from the perspective of others; however, since there is an absence of even such cognition [for the ignorant], they are not real in that sense, being like the horns of a hare. For the remainder [of the meaning]: the inner self (*pratyagātman*) assumes the form of the world exactly according to its experience. || 47 ||
Thus, in the past, you heard this from my presence as my disciple, yet because of that you did not understand it.
Consequently, having experienced existence in another world, you have now been born here and are asking about that very same thing.

O Rāma, in a former age, you previously remained as a disciple in my presence and heard instruction of this very nature; yet by means of that instruction, you did not then attain awakening. Thereafter, solely due to the fault of that lack of awakening, you experienced rebirth after rebirth and other worlds.
Today, in this Tretā age, you have been born here in the house of Daśaratha; that which you previously asked of me, you ask of me even now. (48)
This entire, supreme Śruti is indeed knowledge—the moon’s orb for the long night of worldly existence.
You have been born possessed of that stainless, singular awakening; having dispelled delusion, act according to what you have received.

In this matter as well, you have heard in its entirety—that is, completely—all that supreme, true knowledge taught by me, which has the ultimate reality as its object; for that very reason, it stands like the orb of the full moon, the white-rayed one, which dispels the darkness of suffering from the long night characterized by saṃsāra. By means of that, you must cast away delusion, which is ignorance.

Having attained the supreme human goal which is the form of unsurpassed bliss, you have become one whose nature is stainless, singular consciousness; thus, having accomplished all that was to be done, from now on perform your duties as they have come to you through the succession of worldly convention, such as the protection of your own kingdom and so forth. || 49 ||
Abiding thus within yourself, the supreme and stainless-natured Self that pervades all, shining forth and free from all objective phenomena,
with a mind supremely tranquil in Nirvana and as beautiful as the expanse of the sky, protect the kingdom through Dharma, having crossed over craving.

O Rāma, you, remaining as one liberated from all objects of perception within the Self— which is pure by nature, blazing, manifesting everywhere, and the essence of all— being thus extinguished and immersed in unsurpassed bliss, with a mind that has become peaceful in this very state, you are lovely and charming like the expanse of the sky; having crossed over craving, you abide in righteousness.
At the end, the benediction "Protect the kingdom" is for the sake of auspiciousness. || 50 ||
Thus ends the two hundred and thirteenth canto, titled "The Narrative of Being a Former Disciple of Rāma," in the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*, the *Vālmīkīya-Devarāja-Mokṣopadeśa*. 213.

Thus ends the two hundred and thirteenth canto, titled "The Narrative of Being a Former Disciple of Rāma," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The two hundred and fourteenth canto (214).
Śrī Vālmīki said:
When the sage had thus spoken, a celestial drum suddenly resounded from the sky, like a rain-cloud at the end of the monsoon.
A rain of flowers fell upon the earth, resembling a shower of snow, making the faces of all the quarters white.
In this [chapter], there is praise for the instruction, the fulfillment of the listeners' purpose,
and finally, a description of a most magnificent festival, both celestial and human.

At the conclusion of the great scripture, Vālmīki— desiring to describe the auspicious rites characterized by great festivals for the worship of gurus, the twice-born, gods, ancestors, and virtuous men, performed by both deities and humans— said "Thus," and so forth. When the sage Vasiṣṭha had spoken these words, then the celestial [beings], belonging to the immortals...

The drum resounded like a cloud filled with nectar for the sake of rain; by which all the faces of the quarters were instantly and suddenly made white, and therefore a shower of flowers fell upon the earth, resembling a fall of snow. || 1 ||

And that rain of flowers arrived as if from the city of the gods itself— the very personification of merit— possessing a thick body-unguent like the mass of filaments at the end of the day, wearing a white necklace as bright as the filaments shaken by the wind, and with limbs cooled by the soft spray rising from the bellies of the blossoms. She was one whose body-unguent was red, resembling the dense mass of filaments at the close of day.

Likewise, she whose limbs were cool with soft sprays of water rising from the interior of the flowers, and whose bright necklaces were the white filaments caught by the wind—she stood there like the very Fortune of Merit (Puṇyalakṣmī) who had descended from the city of the gods to behold the festival in person; such is the poetic fancy (utprekṣā). || 2 ||

Stationed in the sky, she mocks the host of stars with her widespread laughter, her terrifying radiance extending toward the faces of the quarters; she resembles a fruit fallen swiftly from the celestial tree—its withered branches shaken by the ape of the world’s end—at the time of the kalpa’s destruction.

Furthermore, what was that rain of flowers like? It fell swiftly from a celestial tree— whose branches, consisting of the various worlds of the guardians of the quarters, were dry and shaken by the monkey who bears the characteristics of the time of the world’s end— and it spread forth to fall instantly upon the faces of the directions.

Bhairava is Saṃhāra-Rudra; she mocks him—who possesses such a renowned luster—along with the multitude of stars situated in the sky, laughing not a little. Or rather, it is a poetic fancy (utprekṣā): she mocks both the multitude of stars and Bhairava, who possesses a laugh renowned among the multitude of stars. || 3 ||
Then that rain of flowers, thundering with the sound of drums and possessing clouds of pollen-masses, came to rest;
it filled the entire assembly with a flood of snow-white blossoms, causing the eyes of all to open wide in wonder.

Then there was that shower of flowers, which— thundering with the sounds of drums and characterized by heaps of filaments— filled the entire assembly like a rain-cloud; it was filled with a captivating flood of blossoms from the Himavat mountain, and thus, by its very sight, it acted as a cause for the expansion of joy through the blossoming of wonder.

It came to rest; or rather, it should be construed as "coming to rest in an instant," meaning either that it brought about the expansion of curiosity along with the eyes of the beholders, or that it subsided in a mere moment. || 4 ||
Having paid homage to Vasiṣṭha, those members of the assembly, standing below according to their respective positions, cast off their sorrow upon seeing those divine flowers. || 5 ||
Regarding "according to their respective positions": Vasiṣṭha was at the highest place; near him were the sages;

near them were Daśaratha, Rāma, and others; near them were the ministers and feudal lords; and below them, in descending order, were the merchants and the subjects. Thus situated, the members of the assembly took those divine flowers and placed them at the feet of Vasiṣṭha.
Having offered a handful of flowers and paid homage to Vasiṣṭha,
[he beheld her] who was afflicted by the impurity of perspiration and foul odor resulting from contact with the fragrance and coolness of the flowers,
who possessed the sorrow caused by disease, hunger, thirst, fatigue, and the like, and who was subject to all sorrows such as birth and death.
They abandoned it; they cast it off. || 5 ||
Daśaratha said:
"Aha! We, whose souls were deeply agitated by the vast expanse of saṃsāra, have finally found rest after long weariness, like pure clouds upon a mountain."

We, who were long exhausted by the vast and exceedingly long wilderness characterized by the nature of saṃsāra, have now found rest for a long time in that very Self—having become such as we are, those for whom the Self is easily accessible through the instruction of your grace. "Aho! expresses wonder; just as [the Self is] pure...
Just as autumn clouds, freed from dullness and darkness, come to rest upon immovable mountains such as the Himavat, so too [do these beings]. || 6 ||
The limit of karmas has been reached; the boundary of calamities has been seen. All that is to be known has been known in its entirety; we have come to rest in the supreme state.

Furthermore, the limit for our duties—which must necessarily be performed for the attainment of the goals of human life—is complete; that is to say, we have achieved the state of having fulfilled our obligations. And the ultimate boundary, the final limit, of calamities has been seen.
To the question "How so?", he says: "It is known" (verse 7).
Through the delusions of long-lasting experiences in the supreme void attained through meditation,
and through the gradual process of abandoning the body by resting in the support of *dhāraṇā*.

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: in the sixth verse, the perception of the visible world is wiped away by all the words ending in the third case, such as these and other examples. This occurs through the delusions of experiencing long-term dwelling and so forth in that other supreme space (*parama-vyoman*)—the imagined space attained through meditation—as illustrated in the *Līlopākhyāna* and other passages.

Even the process of abandoning the body is described as a mere play (*līlā*) through resting in Brahman, the support of all, by means of *dhāraṇā*. (8) [This is achieved] through the creation of new mental constructs, through the fevers of worlds seen in dreams, through the experiences of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, and through the perception of one's own death within a dream. (9)
By means of seeing one's own death in dreams, as is well known in the case of Hariścandra and others. || 9 ||
[They were] no different from the movements of the wind, no different from the flow of water,
like the filling of cities created by magic, or the clusters of cities of the Gandharvas.

[Through the enjoyments of cities filled with illusion, through the currents of rivers in a mirage, through the touch of the wind in the future, and through the arising of the experience of two moons. (11)
By means of illusions displaying the full expanse of rivers filled with water, and by the touch of fierce winds described as occurring in the future— at the time of universal dissolution— (11).
[One is deluded] by the throbbing of the temples, by the shaking of the earth, by the experiences of children such as yakṣas, and by the sight of hair-tufts in the sky. (12)
Through the tremors of the earth perceived due to the loss of discrimination caused by intoxication—
perceived through delusion despite being devoid of any indication of good or evil such as portents— and through the perception of tufts of hair in the sky [as seen by those with ophthalmia]. || 12 ||
"By such delusions and these illustrative examples that grant self-realization, oh! the vision of the visible world has been wiped away from me by the Blessed One. (13)
Śrī Rāma said:
"O Lord of Sages, through your grace, my delusion has vanished and the goal has been attained;
I have become truly perfected, with an intellect that is exceedingly pure. (14)
He has become the very Brahman that is Truth. || 14 ||
Standing firm, my doubts dispelled, in the essential nature that is the form of Brahman,
with unobstructed consciousness, I shall carry out your word.
Remembering again and again your words, which grant the bliss of a sprinkling of nectar,
I rejoice over and over, as if thrilled, even though I am already worthy and at peace.

"Honored" means worshipped. Furthermore, by the word "api ca" (even), it is implied that even when insulted, because joy and dejection do not arise through my vision of equality, though I am tranquil, I seem as if I were rejoicing. || 16 ||
Today I have no purpose whatsoever in what is done, nor any in what is left undone;
I remain just as I am, free from all feverish distress.
Just as I previously remained established in worldly activity, so do I remain now; free from fever, devoid of the distress inherent in attachment to worldly affairs. (17)
But what kind of means or vision does he have here?
Alas! How vast is this earth; how painful is such a state! (18)

By those words of yours, such a means of rest as this has been obtained; what other means could there be, or what other vision could there be? Oh, how vast and boundless a ground of the bliss of rest has been attained by me—just like this!
The meaning is: "Alas, how painful is the state of saṃsāra for living beings, crowded with the misfortunes of birth, death, and so forth! (18)
I have no enemy and no friend; neither field nor wicked person exists for me.
This world, agitated by ignorance, is in truth peaceful and beautiful in all its aspects.

But he says that for him there are no longer any causes of suffering at all—“There is no enemy,” etc. The “field” refers to the body and the external world; “people” refers to good people. This very consciousness of one’s own self (svātmacit) was the world, agitated and a source of suffering, as long as it was difficult to understand; but now, through the cessation of affliction, it has become peaceful and beautiful in every respect—this is the meaning. || 19 ||
How can people know this without your grace?
How could a child cross the ocean without a bridge or a boat? (20)
O Blessed One, how can a person understand this view without your grace? (20)
Lakṣmaṇa said:

Through the destruction of doubts accumulated over many lifetimes, and through the awakening by the words of the sage arising from hundreds of merits accumulated over many lifetimes, a light has been born today in my mind, like the moon. (21)

In me, who had thus exerted an effort toward inquiry through such an awakening brought about by the words of the Sage— an awakening which, by destroying the doubts induced by the accumulated evil tendencies of infinite past lives, likewise caused the emergence of hundreds of merits accumulated in other births and directed them toward the fruit of enlightenment.
The meaning is that today, within the mind, the light of the Supreme Self has arisen, producing supreme delight like the moon. || 21 ||
While such a vision is being perceived, the world is consumed like wood by its own misfortune, through hundreds of states of defect in that very vision. 22.
Although this vision of the Self— which consists of the manifestation of unsurpassed bliss—

is being perceived as eternally immediate through the instruction of a high-souled personage such as yourself, these people of the world remain devoid of service and attendance upon the great, due to the power of their own well-known misfortune and ill-fortune.
The meaning is that it is truly a marvel how [the fool] is burned day and night like wood by hundreds of states of defects such as passion, hatred, egoism, birth, and death. || 22 ||
Viśvāmitra said: "Aha! Oh, what great merit and knowledge have been heard from the mouth of the sage, by which we stand as if bathed in a thousand Gaṅgās! (23)
The word *batā* expresses joy, as in the phrase *sāma no batā*. 23.
Śrī Rāma said: "The supreme limit has been seen of all prosperities, of visions, of scriptures, of calamities, of words, and of the regions that have been beheld. (24)

The ultimate limit of all prosperity is the Self, because it is of the nature of unsurpassed bliss. The ultimate limit of all views is the view of the Self, because through the knowledge of one, there is the knowledge of all. The ultimate limit of all scriptures is the scripture of the inner self (*adhyātma-śāstra*), because it is the final authority. And the ultimate limit of all calamities—characterized by the loss of cattle, children, wealth, and so forth—is the destruction of the entire cycle of transmigration (*saṃsāra*).

The "limit" (*sīmānta*) is that beyond which there is no further destruction. Among all the rivers of speech—such as poetry, aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), and literary figures (*alaṅkāra*)—the teaching of Vasiṣṭha is the ultimate limit. Among all perceived objects that serve as causes for the repose of happiness—such as palaces, gardens, mountains, rivers, and riverbanks—the region of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is the ultimate limit.
The meaning is that it is seen as the ultimate limit because it is the cause of supreme rest; or rather, the meaning is that the Supreme Self alone is the ultimate limit everywhere. || 24 ||
Nārada said: That knowledge which has not been heard even in the world of Brahmā, nor in heaven, nor likewise upon the surface of the earth—
having heard it today with my ears, they have attained purity.
Lakṣmaṇa said: O Sage,
by you who have wiped away both internal and external darkness,
the state of the supreme sun has surely been revealed to us.
The state of being the supreme sun means a pre-eminence superior to that of the well-known sun. || 26 ||
Śatrughna said:
I am liberated; I am at peace; I have attained the supreme state.
For a long time I have been fulfilled, and I abide in absolute bliss. (27)
Daśaratha said: "O Lord of Sages, through merit acquired over many births, this steadfast one has told us that by which we have attained purification. (28)
He has spoken that supremely purifying thing or scripture to us, by which we have attained purity; this is the ellipsis. || 28 ||
Śrī Vālmīki said:
While those members of the assembly were speaking thus along with the king,
Vasiṣṭha spoke these words with a voice purified by knowledge.
"O King, sole moon of the Raghu dynasty, do as I say;
for at the conclusion of a historical narrative, the twice-born are worthy of honor. (30)

Now, the venerable Vasiṣṭha— following the sacred scripture cited by the revered Patañjali in the *Mahābhāṣya*, which states that "scriptures that begin with auspiciousness, have auspiciousness in their middle, and end with auspiciousness, become possessed of heroic men and long-lived men, and their students likewise become endowed with auspiciousness"— proceeds so that there may be freedom from obstacles.
At the conclusion of this great work, for the sake of accomplishing the fruits declared by the scriptures,
he issues a command by way of making known the propriety of auspicious rites such as the worship of Brahmins, gods, ancestors, and virtuous people:
"Therefore, today, you must satisfy the multitudes of Brahmins with all their desires."
You shall obtain the eternal fruit of the proper performance of the Vedic teachings. || 31 ||
The meaning of the Veda in this context is the purpose of the injunction for hearing; its "proper performance" is its accomplishment through the inclusion of all auxiliary parts.

The sense is that, since the injunction for hearing is a mandatory injunction (kāmyavidhi), the attainment of the result occurs only through the performance of it together with its auxiliaries. || 31 ||

Upon the completion of the discourse on the means to liberation, the honoring of the twice-born should be performed according to one's ability even by a mere insect; how much more so, then, by a sovereign?
The meaning is that even by a poor person, who is like a small insect unworthy of respect, this must be performed. || 32 ||
Having heard these words spoken in silence, the king summoned ten thousand brahmins who were exponents of the Vedas by means of messengers.

The word *maunam* spoken by the Sage means silence; or it means having heard [the teaching] in such a way that it becomes "unsurpassed silence" (*niruttara-mauna*), because the command of the Guru must be borne upon the head. || 33 ||
Having honored and summoned those twice-born men who reside in Mathurā, Surāṣṭra, and Gauḍa, he brought them from those families.
From families, from the most excellent of families, and from those gathered together individually. || 34 ||
At that time, the king fed ten thousand twice-born men who were by nature possessed of exceedingly superior knowledge. (35)
By him, the feeding of the twice-born was undertaken by commencing with those for whom knowledge is already very great, even greater than that which is the subject at hand.
Having thus honored those brahmins, as well as the ancestors, the gods, and the kings, with that gift of desired food and sacrificial fees; || 36 ||
[He gratifies] the ancestors with śrāddha and other rites; the gods with garlands, sweetmeats, offerings, and sacrifices such as the iṣṭi; and other kings with gifts of jewels and the like. || 36 ||
On that day, King Daśaratha, together with his friends, [dismissed] the citizens, ministers, servants, and those who were poor, blind, and miserable.
The connection with what follows is that he celebrated a festival together with his friends. || 37 ||
Having reached the end of his worldly existence, he celebrated a supreme festival in that royal palace, which was adorned with silk, jewels, and gold.
He by whom the limit of cyclic existence has been attained; here too, it should be understood that this is "together with his circle of friends. || 38 ||
And in that adorned city, as beautiful as the mountain of the gods,
intoxicated and amorous women, full of grace, danced in every house.
Likewise, on that beautiful mountain, there was Meru, the abode of the gods, and the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpadruma).
With cymbals, bamboo flutes, bronze lutes, and muraja and mardala drums,
they raised a tumultuous roar through their Tandava dance, placing one another upon each other's crests.
The *vaṃśalatā* here refers to the flute (*muralī*). There are two adverbs [in the following]. He describes those dancing girls with the verse beginning "anyonya... and so forth:
their crest-ornaments (*śekhara*) were fashioned in such a way as to be mutually distinct from one another, through differences in the arrangement of their hair, ornaments, and so on. (40)
The sky was overspread by the flickering illusions of hands moving through the agitated marketplace,
while masses of moonbeam-like rays were scattered from the teeth of their charming, loud laughter.

Whose garments and the sky were, as it were, overspread on all sides by the whirling of their hands— which, like marketplaces, were agitated and moved here and there and possessed various dramatic gestures—
while the clusters of moon-like rays from their teeth were scattered and cast about in every direction during their charming displays of the comic sentiment (*hāsyarasa*).
By which [verses]. || 41 ||

Their "hum" sounds were agitated by intoxication, their voices tremulous in their playful movements, and they struck the surface of the earth with ease by a mere blow from the sole of a single foot. || 42 ||

In the enactment of the heroic sentiment (*vīrarasa*), they utter *huṃkāra* sounds characterized by intoxication; in the playful enactments of sentiments such as compassion (*karuṇa*) and the marvelous (*adbhuta*), their voices are tremulous.

In the enactment of love (*śṛṅgāra*), pride (*māna*), and so forth, they are those by whom the surface of the earth was struck—meaning it was easily struck—with a single blow of the sole of the foot. || 42 ||
They were white with the showers of flowers falling from the garlands on their heads; their steps faltered as they stumbled over the pearls of broken necklaces dropped by the force of the downpour.

In the performance of passion, anger, and other emotions, their steps falter by chance upon the placement of feet where the broken strands of necklaces— dropped like showers of flowers falling from the stars as they were shaken by the tossing of garlands— have fallen like streaks of white water.
The women danced with passion, their ornaments swaying;
the Brahmins, the bards, and those very women recited with clear articulation.
With their shimmering ornaments, they seemed as if displaying the form of Kāma; or rather, they danced at will according to their desire, assuming artificial forms (*sākāram*).
They recited, in due order, the Vedic hymns of praise and songs. || 44 ||
The drinkers, radiant with intoxication, drank wine until they were thoroughly intoxicated;
adorned and seeking food, they partook of various kinds of delicacies. (45)

Among them, the non-Brahmins (pānapā aviprāḥ) drank the intoxicating liquor (madhvāsava); however, the Brahmins and others, desiring food, consumed various kinds of fit food—fourfold in its nature and endowed with a variety of diverse edibles. || 45 ||
The walls of the house, colored by a coating of lime and other substances,
shone with the light of the moon-like Rāma, adorned with flowers, incense, and unguents.
They shone with the moonlight of the bodily luster of Rāma-lakṣaṇa, who was like the moon, and with flowers, incense, and ointments. || 46 ||
Wearing variegated garments and adorned with excellent garlands and ornaments, the attendants and female servants, fragrant with lovely scents, moved about at the king’s sacrifice.
At the king's festival-sacrifice during the ritual. || 47 ||
Having applied yakṣakardama paste to their slender bodies, those women,
like dancers in the tāṇḍava dance, entered the courtyard which was the very essence of the erotic sentiment.
Camphor, aguru, musk, and kaṅkola were ground together with sandalwood to create *yakṣakardama*;

having applied this paste to their slender bodies, the women who were dancers of the *tāṇḍava*— their very selves the embodiment of erotic passion— proceeded to the middle of the royal assembly courtyard, which had been fully adorned.

Out of joy at the end of the long night of worldly existence, King Daśaratha, together with his assembly, celebrated a magnificent festival for seven nights, establishing an inexhaustible glory of constant giving and enjoyment.

King Daśaratha, having attained the imperishable state of Brahman, experienced for seven nights a splendor consisting of constant giving and enjoyment— accompanied by the glory of charity and pleasure— born of the joy resulting from the destruction of that "long night" characterized by worldly existence (*bhava*), which occurred at its conclusion through the rising of the sun of awakening.
He made the festival itself dense and accumulated. || 49 ||

Thus ends the two hundred and fourteenth canto, titled "The Description of the Great Festival," in the *Ārṣa Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, within the section concerning the departure of Daśaratha.
Thus ends the two hundred and fourteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Great Festival," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The two hundred and fifteenth canto (215).
Śrī Vālmīki said:
O Bharadvāja of great intelligence, leader of my disciples!
Thus Rāma and the others, having known that which is to be known, attained freedom from sorrow. || 1 ||
"Like Rāma and others, you are awakened; dwell happily as one liberated while living"—thus is the disciple Bharadvāja instructed here by Vālmīki.
Thus, in the manner described by this [verse], Rāma and the others attained and reached the state of being free from sorrow. || 1 ||
Holding fast to this very beautiful vision, remain at ease, free from passion, without fear, liberated while living, and with a tranquil intellect. (2)
You too, having firmly grasped and firmly relied upon this very vision of the Self as the full Brahman, remain established in it. || 2 ||
For one who has not practiced attachment, O sinless one, like Rāma and others,
does not become deluded even when immersed in dense ignorance or even when bewildered.
And with the intention that this knowledge taught by me should not be destroyed by bad association or by the habitual attachment to enjoyments, he says: "Fortitude," etc. (3).
Thus these great beings have attained the state of liberation while living—such as the princes Rāghava and others, and King Daśaratha and others. (4)
The kings beginning with Daśaratha; the substitution of *ḍā* for the case-ending *jas* is Vedic, according to the rule *supāṃ suluk*. || 4 ||
And you, my son Bharadvāja, were already liberated in intellect;
yet today you have become even more liberated by hearing this compendium on liberation. (5)

By means of your own inquiry alone, you were previously liberated in intellect like Rāma; but today, having heard this *Mokṣasaṃhitā*, you are even more liberated, because of the washing away of the mud of all doubts that had been entertained—this is the intended meaning. || 5 ||
Even a child, upon hearing these meritorious means to liberation which grant the fruit of direct experience, attains the state of a knower of reality; what then need be said of one such as you?

Because this scripture has the fruit of the supreme human goal as its object, it demonstrates that it is the most venerable of all scriptures and that it is capable of producing results even through practice by those of dull faculties—this is shown by the words "the means to liberation.
What need is there to mention the production of results for a primary qualified candidate such as yourself? || 6 ||
Just as the high-souled Raghava, free from sorrow, followed the path of merit, so too,
by the unfolding of Vasistha’s words, must the virtuous proceed toward that very first state.

O holy one, just as the noble Raghus, Rāma and the others, through the flow of Vasiṣṭha’s words into their hearts, attained the state of being liberated while living— having destroyed ignorance along with all doubts— and became free from sorrow, even so should you today likewise [attain it].

The meaning is that the state of liberation while living (jīvanmukta), characterized by the eternally established nature of Brahman, is the goal to be reached, and one should remain free from sorrow. || 7 ||
Through the conduct of the virtuous, service to the supreme, and inquiry into noble discourse,
the wise and heedful attain what is to be known, just as Rāghava and others did through association with Vasiṣṭha.

He states that for the attainment of that [state], even for others, the means is indeed service to the company of the virtuous, inquiry, and so forth—beginning with the words "of the virtuous" (satām).
This refers to training through right method (*naya*), and through supreme service characterized by love and uninterrupted devotion accompanied by the abandonment of greed, laziness, and sleep;
and through association with noble discourses (*kathā*) and narratives (*ākhyāyikā*) which serve as means to awakening, along with the instruction therein.

The wise, who are qualified and remain vigilant—meaning those who are single-mindedly devoted to that—attain or find the reality of the Self (ātmatattva), just as Rāghava and others did through the grace of Vasiṣṭha; such is the meaning. || 8 ||
Those knots rooted in the heart of the ignorant, bound by the firm fetters of the reins of craving—
all of them indeed attain dissolution through the investigation of the discourse on liberation, just as fools become non-fools.

Bound by firm knots of the leather thong characterized by craving— which have taken root in the heart of the ignorant in the form of the false superimposition (adhyāsa) of identity with the body, senses, and so forth,
as well as those characterized by the obsessive attachment of "mineness" toward home, children, wife, and the like— [the mind remains bound].

Because the state of uniformity consisting in the experience of the oneness of self in all beings is absent, all those knots which are the causes of passion, hatred, and so forth— indeed, all of them [are severed] by this investigation into the discourse on liberation; just as young women, though previously filled with distaste for their husbands due to childhood, attachment to play, and lack of knowledge regarding the aesthetic essence (*rasa*), [become devoted] in the course of time.
Just as mature and virtuous women attain non-difference and oneness with their husbands, so too do they attain non-difference and oneness among all beings; this is the meaning. || 9 ||

Those who are the best among the knowers of reality will understand the most powerful means to liberation; they shall not enter the cycle of worldly existence again. O son, what is the use of further prolixity? 10.

Having heard this, O Bharadvāja, out of compassion for his son, [the sage said]: "Because these means to liberation— though they are of great majesty— are capable of destroying ignorance even through the repeated hearing by those of dull faculties,
those who come to know them by hearing them from a guru shall become the most excellent among the knowers of reality and shall not enter into worldly existence again."
They shall come together. This is my concise statement of the supreme secret; what is the point, what is the purpose, of speaking much more? Such is the meaning. || 10 ||

Those who are deeply learned, having investigated and correctly awakened to the meaning, will speak to people; being virtuous, they will not fall back into the state of childishness—so what need is there for other words? (11)

Now, indicating the rule that even among speakers, the attainment of the fruit of awakening occurs only for those who have investigated through the mouth of a guru, correctly understood the meaning according to the tradition, and then taught it to others—and not for anyone else—he says:
"Those who are well-versed in the scriptures... Those virtuous ones who [study] this treatise from those who are well-versed in the scriptures...

Having personally and correctly investigated [the matter] before their gurus, and once the meaning has been correctly awakened in the text through a discourse that corroborates it, they will subsequently speak to those who desire to hear according to the tradition; they shall not fall back into childhood,
foolishness, or rebirth, and will certainly attain the fruit of the knowledge of reality.
The meaning is that they will attain [the goal]. What is the use of other sentences—whether heard or recited—which have not been mastered through the traditional lineage?
The meaning is: what purpose do they serve? || 11 ||

Those who will recite it regardless of its meaning, those who will have it written down as a book, or those who will cause a reader to be appointed along with an expounder in the auspicious noble land; (12)

Now, with two verses beginning with "ye vācayiṣyanti," he states the fruit of reciting the text, writing it down, or teaching its exposition— even without understanding the meaning— by imagining a livelihood for the reader.
"Anapekṣitārthāḥ" means those who, due to a lack of proficiency, are devoid of any expectation regarding the meaning.

Those who, without regard for the materials of the *pārāyaṇa* fee and free from greed, shall cause a manuscript to be written; or those who, for the sake of a livelihood, shall cause it to be recited by a person acting as an expounder or simply as a reader— if they are possessed of desire, being endowed with the fruit of the *rājasūya* sacrifice, they shall repeatedly go to heaven.

They shall depart. However, those of noble being who are free from desire, having obtained a superior birth and access to the hearing of true scriptures and the like from a genuine guru, shall attain liberation through the attainment of a third birth. "Like Lakṣmī" serves as the illustration for both cases. || 12 ||
Endowed with the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice, those noble-minded ones will repeatedly go to heaven and,
by attaining their third birth, will reach liberation, just as the meritorious attain prosperity.

Having previously reflected upon this well-compiled work consisting of liberation, Viriñca—whose form is inconceivable—uttered it from his true speech; and the words of him who speaks the truth never become false. (14)

To the question, "From where does this work derive such great fruitfulness? he says: "This... and so forth. In former times, Viriñca, whose form is inconceivable, having personally deliberated from beginning to end upon this well-compiled collection consisting of liberation composed by me, addressed these words to all the sages, who are the assembly of the virtuous. What [did he say]? "Those of truthful speech... and so on.
The word "ca" (and) is used for the purpose of indicating the granting of boons to Vālmīki, Vasiṣṭha, and himself, signifying that "no word of yours shall ever be untrue in this poem. || 14 ||

When this literary composition titled *Mokṣābhyupāya* has reached its conclusion through the diligent effort of the wise, the Brahmins should be fully honored by providing them with fine dwellings and the gift of desired food and drink. (15)
At the conclusion of this treatise, he states that the giving of houses, land, wealth, and so forth to Brahmins and others must certainly be performed:

"Indeed, sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) and other gifts desired by their hearts should be given to them according to one's own capacity and wealth. Considering it as merit acquired through association, that [merit] reaches him exactly as prescribed by the scriptures. (16)

In the midst of their own wealth, a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) desired by them should be given according to one's capacity. Having reflected and considered that "this performer will surely be attached to what he himself has done"—that is, he will certainly attain merit (puṇya) in the form of its fruit according to the scriptures—this is the meaning. || 16 ||

This great, stainless scripture, which expands upon the reality of Brahman and is adorned with illustrations and logical reasoning, has been told to you by the Buddhas through hundreds of sequences of discourse for the sake of awakening.
Having heard this, attain lasting peace; with your mind liberated while living, enjoy prosperity.
Having enjoyed that which is imperishable, he himself becomes imperishable, endowed with the sequence of knowledge, austerity, and ritual action.

O Bharadvāja, for the awakening of your intellect, I have narrated this scripture, which is adorned with examples and reasoning and expanded by hundreds of sequences of discourse, concerning the reality of Brahman. Having heard this, while still living, you shall become one whose latent impressions are liberated; and for the sake of favoring the world, [you shall attain] that which is endowed with the fruits of knowledge, austerity, and ritual action.

Having enjoyed the imperishable and long-enduring glory of the perfection of yoga-knowledge and sovereignty—which is the fruit of those karmas that must be experienced as part of *prārabdha*—may you, both while embodied and after becoming disembodied, intensely attain liberation, which is eternal, unsurpassed bliss and supreme peace; this is the benediction at the end for the sake of auspiciousness. (17)

Thus ends the two hundred and fifteenth canto, titled "The Praise of the Book and the Rules for Its Recitation," in the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*, a work of the Sage, belonging to the Vālmīki, Devala, Maudgalya, and Nārada recensions.

Thus ends the two hundred and fifteenth chapter, titled "The Praise of the Work and the Rules for its Recitation," in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*.
The two hundred and sixteenth canto. || 216 ||
Śrī Vālmīki said:
O King, this eloquent discourse of the jar-born sage has been told to you;
by means of this path of reality, you will certainly attain that supreme state.
In this [work], the fulfillment of purpose through Ariṣṭanemi, Suruci, Kāruṇya, and others is described, as well as the offering of oneself by disciples to their gurus.
The wise sayings of Kumbhayoni, Vasiṣṭha, Agastya, and others concerning Rāma and others, as well as regarding Sutīkṣṇa—these have been presented by him in the form of this book. || 1 ||
The king said:
"O Blessed One, your vision destroys the bondage of worldly existence; having been beheld by it, I have crossed over the ocean of saṃsāra. (2)
King Ariṣṭanemi said to Vālmīki: "Gaze" means a compassionate sidelong look. || 2 ||
The divine messenger said:
Having spoken thus, the king, his eyes wide with wonder,
addressed me with sweet words in a gentle voice.
The King said:
"O messenger of the gods, salutations to you; may it be well with you, O Lord.
It is said that friendship among the virtuous is formed by walking seven steps together, and that has been done by you."

"Maitra" means the state of friendship; it is called "sāptapada" because it is obtained through seven steps. This is a derivative form using the suffix *aṇ*. Thus, the meaning is that you have made true what has been declared by the virtuous. || 4 ||
Now go, may it be well with you, to the abode of the King of the Gods;
by this hearing, I am both relieved and gladdened.
He is extinguished by the cessation of all suffering and gladdened by the attainment of unsurpassed bliss. || 5 ||
"Reflecting on the meaning of what I have heard, I shall remain here, free from feverish distress.
When this was said, O blessed lady, I was then filled with great wonder.
Thus addressed by the king, I was filled with supreme wonder at his perfection of virtues such as discipline.
Never before had I heard this essence of knowledge; having now heard it, I am inwardly gladdened as if I have just drunk nectar.

He says that even for himself, through the power of association with the virtuous, his purpose has been fulfilled by attaining the opportunity to hear [this teaching]: "It was not heard before. This essence of knowledge, which had never been heard at any time previously, has now been heard by me through the company of the virtuous. || 7 ||
Then, having taken leave of Vālmīki, I have come into your presence.
O sinless one, I have related all this that was asked of me by you;
henceforth, I shall go toward the abode of Śakra.

"In your presence" means "in order to instruct you. By the address "O sinless one," it is indicated that having perceived your fulfillment of the requisite qualifications due to your freedom from sin, all of this has been told to you. Thus spoke the Apsaras.
Homage be to you, O illustrious messenger of the gods; through what you have made me hear, and through my understanding of its meaning, I have attained supreme peace.
"I have attained supreme bliss and peaceful rest"—this is the ellipsis. || 9 ||
I have achieved my purpose and am free from sorrow; I shall remain here, rid of all feverish distress.
Now go, may prosperity be yours, wherever you desire in the presence of Śakra.
Agniveśya said:
Then that excellent Suruci reflected upon that very matter;
she remained on the slopes of the Himavat, near Gandhamādana.
That very meaning, characterized by the identity of Brahman and the Self, was thus taught. || 11 ||
"O son, have you heard this instruction of Vasiṣṭha?
Having fully grasped all of that, do as you wish. (12)

"All that" means: the sense is that since your doubt—whether action is the cause of liberation or knowledge is the means to liberation—is resolved by the ascertainment of that [truth], its very root having been removed, its destruction is established. || 12 ||
Kāruṇya said:

Just as memory, speech, vision, and existence [are perceived] regarding the son of a barren woman or water in a mirage within a dream, so too is the worldly condition [perceived] through cognition. || 13 ||

For this very reason, because all doubts regarding his own self have been sublated along with their roots, nothing remains for the one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*) but to continue following things exactly as they appear, merely through the persistence of what has already been sublated. Thus Kāruṇya said, beginning with "Memory" (*smṛti*), etc.; memory [occurs] regarding objects that are past, future, or not in close proximity.

Cognition of the imperceptible, verbal usage, and conduct regarding the present, as well as the perception of existence, have now become objectless for me through the knowledge of reality—just as they were objectless regarding the son of a barren woman perceived in a dream. Furthermore, the entire condition of worldly existence is like a mirage in a waterless desert; thus has it been realized.
The meaning is that in no matter whatsoever does any doubt remain. || 13 ||
I have no purpose here with what is done, nor any with what is not done; I abide in whatever comes to me, for what insistence can there be on inaction? (14)
Just like Rāma and others, I shall abide and continue to abide by the conduct appropriate to my caste and stage of life as it has come to me;
[I shall not engage] in *akarmaṇi*, that is, in the forceful abandonment of action. 14.
Agastya said:
Having spoken thus, the virtuous Agniveśya’s son, out of compassion,
performed his duties as they arose and offered them at the proper times according to the prescribed rule.

Having attained his duties through marriage, and thus possessing the authority to perform those duties, he—at the proper times, that is, at the appropriate moments—performed the rites such as bathing, giving gifts, the agnihotra fire-sacrifice, and honoring guests; the meaning is that he carried them out. The particle *nāma* is used here in the sense of *kila* (indeed).
O Sutīkṣṇa, no doubt should be entertained here regarding knowledge and action;
for one who is full of doubt falls away from his own goal, and the doubting soul perishes.
O Sutīkṣṇa, regarding the performance of action following knowledge—that is, in the matter of the practice of action—no doubt should be entertained that such action will lead to bondage. || 16 ||
Having heard these words of the sage, which reveal the unity of many meanings,
he bowed to his teacher and, full of humility, spoke in his presence.

Having heard these words of the sage Agastya— which demonstrate the unity of the various worldly objects, consisting of many contradictory alternatives that are objects of doubt, by means of their essential nature as the ultimate reality of Brahman, thereby abandoning all contradictions— [he stood] nearby, in his presence. || 17 ||
Sutīkṣṇa said:
Ignorance and its effects have perished, and unsurpassed knowledge has been attained;
[all] actions now reside in the Witness, who is of manifest luster and eternal, like [the light of] a lamp.

In that Supreme Self, the witness of all, who is eternal, motionless, and firmly established—shining with a constant radiance precisely because He is self-luminous—all activities of the mind, which are rooted in vibration, proceed; these include both worldly and Vedic actions, just as the movements of actors, dancers, and others proceed by depending on the light of a lamp situated in a theater. And because of this:
Just as gold appears in various forms such as bracelets and the like, or as a series of waves upon the water, so does the world of appearances manifest;

having realized that this entire universe is that very [Reality] and not even an atom's worth of it can be established as separate from its actions, agents, fruits, and so forth, I shall follow the conduct of whichever stage of life (āśrama) I have entered.
This transposition of words is Vedic (chāndasa). || 18 ||
When that exists, the desires of the mind proceed preceded by movement, just as gold [appears] through bracelets, armlets, earrings, and anklets. (19)
Since the world of appearances vibrates like a series of waves upon milk,
this entire universe is established as full within the Full.
I follow what has been attained; who would transgress the word of the virtuous?
O Blessed One, by your grace I am established as one who has known that which is to be known.
My purpose is fulfilled; salutations to you! Prostrating like a staff upon the ground, I ask:
by what deed can disciples attain the state of having crossed over from their teacher? (22)

Now, seeing no means in this world to repay the favor of the gift of knowledge bestowed by the venerable Guru— which secures the supreme human goal— he bows at his feet and offers himself as a servant for as long as he lives,
beginning with the words "I am one who has attained his purpose" (kṛtārtho 'ham). || 22 ||
Therefore, the surrender of oneself by disciples through body, speech, and mind—that alone is the state of having crossed over to the teacher; it is not achieved by any other action whatsoever. (23)
There is no deliverance from the teacher's debt through any other action whatsoever. || 23 ||
O Lord, by your grace I have crossed the ocean of worldly existence;
with all doubts dispelled, I stand here, having filled the entire network of the universe.

"O Master, by your grace I have crossed the ocean of worldly existence; I remain such that the entire web of the universe is filled with the state of perfect bliss—of this there is no doubt. This is the meaning. || 24 ||
Salutation to that Self which is Brahman, for it is clearly proclaimed in the Sāman chant upon hearing the text: "All this, indeed, is Brahman; from it, by it, and into it [all things arise]. (25)

Indicating that this work is most worthy of reverence by those seeking liberation because it elaborates upon the essential meaning of all the Upaniṣads, [the author begins] from that Saccidānanda which is the Self of all, attained through knowledge accompanied by the most manifest means as shown in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad: "All this is indeed Brahman; it originates from Him, dissolves into Him, and breathes in Him; therefore, one should meditate with a tranquil mind."

Having contemplated the reality of the Veda-Brahman, he offers salutation at the end for the sake of auspiciousness: "To that which is all... He salutes that Brahman which, in the Sāmaveda, is proclaimed as the supreme purport so that it may become as clearly perceptible to qualified seekers—as if an amalaka fruit were in the palm of one's hand—according to the Śruti: "All this is indeed Brahman, for from it, by it, and into it [all things arise]. To that [Brahman].
The meaning is: "Salutation to the Self who remains as that [reality], who is inwardly conscious and a mass of bliss. || 25 ||
The bliss of Brahman, the bestower of supreme happiness, the embodiment of absolute knowledge, beyond duality, resembling the sky, the target of such mahāvākyas as "That thou art";
the one, eternal, pure, immovable, the witness of all intellects, transcending all objective existence, and devoid of the three qualities.
We bow to the venerable Vasiṣṭha. || 26 ||

I always worship within my heart the elephant-faced one, who possesses auspicious tusks, who supports the virtuous, who is the abode of all virtues, who is the dense essence of existence, consciousness, and bliss, and who is compassionate. (1)
Having immersed myself within the ocean of the nectar-like words of Vasiṣṭha through internal devotion, a few good points have been extracted here by the grace of my guru’s glance.
For who indeed, even with the greatest effort, could fathom the extent of the jewels within the belly of the ocean while searching for them?
The one who has accomplished his task. || 2 ||

I worship my own supreme Self, which is incomparable, self-expanded, free from saṃsāra, exceedingly profound, filled with the nectar of eternal bliss, and transcending both the near and the far shores.

It was completed on the seventh day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna in the auspicious Śaka year Vikārin (1766), during the winter season, under the constellation Rohiṇī and with the ascendant of Taurus presided over by Venus. || 4 ||
This handful of flowers of words has been offered by me with devotion at the lotus feet of the venerable Śiva and Śivā, who are the inspirers of my intellect. (5)

Thus ends the two hundred and sixteenth canto, titled "The Second Half of the Bālakāṇḍa," in the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Mokṣopāya* section spoken by the Divine Messenger within the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, in the collection consisting of one hundred and thirty-two thousand verses. 216.
Thus ends the two hundred and sixteenth chapter in the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparya-prakāśa*. (216)

Thus ends the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*, composed by the mendicant named Śrīmad Ānandabodhendrasarasvatī, disciple of the disciple of the venerable Śrīmat Sarvajñasarasvatī, the most eminent teacher among the wandering ascetics of the Paramahaṃsa order.
This chapter on Nirvāṇa is completed.
This treatise is finished.
